title: Theorem 1.7.3 (Lebesgue differentiation)
text: Theorem 1.7.3 (Lebesgue differentiation) . Let $f$ be a locally integrable function on $\Omega $. Then almost every $x\in \Omega $ is a Lebesgue point of $f$, that is, $f(x)$ is finite and \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac1{|Q(x,r)|} \int _{Q(x,r)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy=0, \qquad Q(x,r)=x+(-r,r)^ d.  \] At every Lebesgue point $x$ of $f$, the mollifications satisfy $f_\varepsilon (x)\to f(x)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Proof. We prove a maximal inequality on $\mathbb R^ d$, deduce the theorem for integrable functions by approximation with continuous ones, and then localize. The set $N$ where $f$ is infinite is a null set. Changing $f$ to $0$ on $N$ changes neither the averages in the statement nor the values $f(x)$ for $x\notin N$, so the modified function has the same Lebesgue points outside $N$ and the same mollifications. We may therefore assume that $f$ is finite everywhere. Consider first $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, and define its maximal function $Mf(x)$ as the supremum over $r>0$ of the averages of $|f|$ over $Q(x,r)$. For fixed $r$, the average of $|f|$ over $Q(x,r)$ depends continuously on $x$, because $\int _{Q(x,r)}|f|$ and $\int _{Q(x',r)}|f|$ differ by at most $\| f(\cdot +x-x')-f\| _1$, which tends to zero as $x'\to x$ by the continuity of translation in $L^1$ (lemma 1.4.1 (2)). As a supremum of continuous functions, $Mf$ is lower semicontinuous, so $\{ Mf>t\} $ is open. We claim the maximal inequality \[  |\{ Mf>t\} |\le \frac{3^ d}{t}\| f\| _1,\qquad t>0.  \] By inner regularity of Lebesgue measure, it suffices to bound $|L|$ for compact $L\subset \{ Mf>t\} $. Each point of $L$ is the center of an open cube over which the average of $|f|$ exceeds $t$, and finitely many of these cubes cover $L$. Select one of largest side length, discard all cubes meeting it, and repeat with the remaining ones. The selected cubes are disjoint, and each discarded cube meets a selected cube of at least the same side length, so it lies in the concentric cube with three times that side length. These enlarged cubes cover $L$, and therefore $|L|$ is at most $3^ d$ times the total volume of the selected cubes, which is less than $t^{-1}\| f\| _1$. Now let $g\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$. For every $x$ and $r$, \[  \begin{split}  \frac1{|Q(x,r)|}\int _{Q(x,r)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy\leq {}& M(f-g)(x)+|g(x)-f(x)|\\ & +\frac1{|Q(x,r)|}\int _{Q(x,r)}|g(y)-g(x)|\, \mathrm dy, \end{split}  \] and the last term tends to zero as $r\downarrow 0$ because $g$ is continuous at $x$. Hence the upper limit $\Lambda f(x)$ of the left side satisfies $\Lambda f\leq M(f-g)+|f-g|$, and for $t>0$ the set $\{ \Lambda f>2t\} $ is contained in $\{ M(f-g)>t\} \cup \{ |f-g|>t\} $, whose measure is at most $(3^ d+1)t^{-1}\| f-g\| _1$ by the maximal inequality and Chebyshev's inequality. By proposition 1.2.3 , $\| f-g\| _1$ can be made arbitrarily small, so $\{ \Lambda f>2t\} $ is contained in measurable sets of arbitrarily small measure and is therefore a null set. Letting $t$ run through the positive rationals shows that $\Lambda f=0$ almost everywhere. Next, let $f$ be locally integrable on $\Omega $, and let $(K_ j)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $. The function equal to $f$ on $\operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$ and to $0$ elsewhere belongs to $L^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, and for $x\in \operatorname{Int}K_ j$ and small $r$ the averages in the statement are the same for $f$ and for this function. Hence almost every point of each $\operatorname{Int}K_ j$, and therefore of $\Omega $, is a Lebesgue point of $f$. Finally, let $x$ be a Lebesgue point of $f$ and let $\varepsilon >0$ be so small that $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $. The function $\rho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )$ is bounded by $\varepsilon ^{-d}\sup \rho =2^ d\sup \rho /|Q(x,\varepsilon )|$ and vanishes outside $B(x,\varepsilon )\subset Q(x,\varepsilon )$. Since $\int \rho _\varepsilon =1$, \[  \begin{split}  |f_\varepsilon (x)-f(x)|& =\left|\int (f(y)-f(x))\rho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, \mathrm dy\right|\\ & \leq \frac{2^ d\sup \rho }{|Q(x,\varepsilon )|}\int _{Q(x,\varepsilon )}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy, \end{split}  \] which tends to zero as $\varepsilon \to 0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.7.4
text: Lemma 1.7.4 . Let $Q\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a closed cube of side length $l$, and let $F$ be a locally integrable function on an open neighborhood $V$ of $Q$ whose distributional first derivatives $\partial _ kF$ on $V$ are locally integrable. Put $F_ Q=|Q|^{-1}\int _ QF\, \mathrm dx$. Then \[  \int _ Q|F-F_ Q|\, \mathrm dx\le l\sum _{k=1}^ d\int _ Q|\partial _ kF|\, \mathrm dx.  \] The same assertion holds componentwise for vector-valued $F$. Proof. Suppose first that $F$ is continuously differentiable near $Q$. For $x,y\in Q$, the points $z^{(k)}=(y_1,\ldots ,y_ k,x_{k+1},\ldots ,x_ d)$, $0\leq k\leq d$, lead from $x$ to $y$ by changing one coordinate at a time. If $I_ k$ is the $k$th side interval of $Q$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  |F(y)-F(x)|\leq \sum _{k=1}^ d\int _{I_ k}|\partial _ kF(y_1,\ldots ,y_{k-1},t,x_{k+1},\ldots ,x_ d)|\, \mathrm dt.  \] Integrate over $(x,y)\in Q\times Q$. The $k$th term does not depend on the $d+1$ coordinates $x_1,\ldots ,x_ k,y_ k,\ldots ,y_ d$, which contribute a factor $l^{d+1}$, and integration over the remaining coordinates and $t$ gives $\int _ Q|\partial _ kF|\, \mathrm dx$. Since $|F(x)-F_ Q|\leq |Q|^{-1}\int _ Q|F(x)-F(y)|\, \mathrm dy$ and $|Q|=l^ d$, the inequality follows. In general, the mollifications $F_\varepsilon $ are smooth on $V_\varepsilon =\{ x\in V:\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus V)>\varepsilon \} $, which is a neighborhood of $Q$ for small $\varepsilon $. By lemma 1.4.1 (2) and proposition 1.4.3 (1), $F_\varepsilon \to F$ and $\partial _ kF_\varepsilon =(\partial _ kF)_\varepsilon \to \partial _ kF$ in $L^1(Q)$. Since $|(F_\varepsilon )_ Q-F_ Q|\leq |Q|^{-1}\| F_\varepsilon -F\| _{L^1(Q)}$, the left sides of the inequality for $F_\varepsilon $ and for $F$ differ by at most $2\| F_\varepsilon -F\| _{L^1(Q)}$, and the inequality for $F_\varepsilon $ passes to the limit. $\square$

Proposition 1.7.5 . Let $f\colon \Omega 	o \mathbb R$ be continuous, and suppose that its real distributional Hessian has locally bounded measurable coefficients, that is, $\partial _ a\partial _ bf=A_{ab}$ for measurable functions $A_{ab}$ on $\Omega $ that are bounded on compact sets, $1\leq a,b\leq d$. Then $f\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$: its first derivatives exist and are locally Lipschitz. More precisely, if $V\subset \Omega $ is a convex open set and $|A_{ab}|\leq C$ almost everywhere on $V$ for all $a$ and $b$, then $

More precisely, it suffices that every ball $B\Subset \Omega $ carry smooth functions $f_ j$ which converge to $f$ in the sense of distributions on $B$ and whose second derivatives are bounded on $B$ uniformly in $j$. Step 1: $f\in C^1(\Omega )$. Let $B=B(x_0,R)$ and $B'=B(x_0,R+s)$, where $R,s>0$ are such that $\overline{B(x_0,R+2s)}\subset \Omega $, and let $C$ bound the functions $|A_{ab}|$ on $B(x_0,R+2s)$. Thus the gradients $

Applying proposition 1.6.4 successively to the components of the maps $

Covering $\Omega $ by such balls $B$, we conclude that $f\in C^1(\Omega )$ and that its distributional first derivatives coincide with the continuous functions $\partial _ af$ on each such ball, hence on $\Omega $ by the last assertion of lemma 1.4.2 . Consequently, $\partial _ af_\varepsilon =(\partial _ af)_\varepsilon 	o \partial _ af$ uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega $, by lemma 1.4.1 (1). Step 2: the Lipschitz bound. Let $V\subset \Omega $ be convex and open with $|A_{ab}|\leq C$ almost everywhere on $V$, and let $x,y\in V$. The segment $[x,y]$ is a compact subset of $V$; choose $\delta >0$ smaller than its distance to $\mathbb R^ d\setminus V$. For $\varepsilon <\delta $ and $z\in [x,y]$, the closed ball $\overline{B(z,\varepsilon )}$ lies in $V$, so $z\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ and $|\partial _ a\partial _ bf_\varepsilon (z)|=|(A_{ab}*ho _\varepsilon )(z)|\leq C$. As in Step 1, $|

By theorem 1.7.3 , almost every point of $\Omega $ is a common Lebesgue point of the functions $A_{ab}$. Let $x$ be such a point, let $Q=(-1,1)^ d$, and choose $r_0>0$ with $x+3r_0\overline Q\subset \Omega $. The functions $|A_{ab}|$ are bounded on the compact set $x+3r_0\overline Q$ by some constant $C$, so by Step 2, $

The function $z\mapsto \psi ((z-x)/r)$ is a test function on $\Omega $, and the distributional derivative $\partial _ b$ of the continuous function $\partial _ af$ is $\partial _ b\partial _ af=\partial _ a\partial _ bf=A_{ab}$, since partial derivatives of distributions commute. title: 2 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
search_title: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: 2 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem Harmonic functions are the solutions of the Laplace equation $\Delta h=0$. In potential theory they play the role that affine functions play for convex functions: the subharmonic functions of chapter 3 are studied by comparison with them, and the fundamental solution of the Laplacian, together with the Green functions obtained from it by harmonic corrections, defines the potentials and energies of chapter 4 , chapter 5 . Unless stated otherwise, $\Omega $ denotes an open subset of $\mathbb R^ d$, where $d\geq 1$. We begin with mean values. After introducing surface measure, polar coordinates and the divergence theorem on balls, we show that a continuous function is harmonic exactly when its value at the center of every closed ball in its domain equals its mean over the boundary sphere (theorem 2.1.2 ). Averaging against a mollifier then shows that harmonic functions are smooth, with interior estimates for all their derivatives. A distribution in the sense of chapter 1 need not have pointwise values; nevertheless, Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) shows that a distribution with vanishing Laplacian is a smooth harmonic function. The fundamental solution of the Laplacian (proposition 2.2.1 ) fixes the sign conventions for all later potentials. The Dirichlet problem asks for a harmonic function with prescribed continuous boundary values. On a ball it is solved explicitly by the Poisson integral (theorem 2.3.1 ), whose kernel also yields the Harnack inequalities and the compactness of families of nonnegative harmonic functions. On a general bounded open set there is no such formula, and we use Perron's method instead. The candidate solution is the pointwise supremum of all continuous subsolutions whose boundary values do not exceed the data; replacing a subsolution on a small ball by the Poisson integral of its values shows that this envelope is harmonic (theorem 2.4.2 ). The envelope also depends linearly on the data (theorem 2.4.4 ). A boundary point is regular if the envelope attains the prescribed value there for all data. Regularity is decided by the existence of a barrier, which need only be constructed near the point (theorem 2.4.6 , proposition 2.4.7 ); for $d\geq 2$, regularity fails at the center of a punctured ball. When every boundary point is regular, the solution operator is integration against harmonic measure, and correcting the fundamental solution by the harmonic function with the same boundary values gives the Green function (theorem 2.5.2 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.2 .

title: 2.1 The Laplacian and mean values
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
2.1 The Laplacian and mean values Recall from section 1.4 that $B(x,r)$ is the open ball with center $x$ and radius $r>0$; its closure $\overline{B(x,r)}$ is the closed ball. We write $S^{d-1}=\{ y\in \mathbb R^ d:|y|=1\} $ for the unit sphere. The Laplacian is $\Delta =\sum _{j=1}^ d\partial _{x_ j}^2$. A real function $h\in C^2(\Omega )$ is harmonic if $\Delta h=0$, and a complex function is harmonic if its real and imaginary parts are harmonic. In dimension one the harmonic functions are the functions that are affine on each component interval of $\Omega $, because $h''=0$ on an interval forces $h'$ to be constant there. We define surface measure on the unit sphere through the Lebesgue measure of cones: for a Borel set $A\subset S^{d-1}$ put \[  S(A)=d\,  igl |\{ t\omega :0<t<1,\  \omega \in A\}  igr |.  \] The cone over $A$ is the inverse image of $A$ under the continuous map $y\mapsto y/|y|$ on $B(0,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $, so it is a Borel set; moreover, the cone over a countable union is the union of the cones, and cones over disjoint sets are disjoint. Hence $S$ is a finite Borel measure on $S^{d-1}$, the surface measure . It is invariant under every orthogonal transformation $Q$ of $\mathbb R^ d$: the cone over $QA$ is the image under $Q$ of the cone over $A$, and Lebesgue measure is invariant under orthogonal transformations. By linearity and monotone convergence (proposition 1.1.3 ), it follows that $\int _{S^{d-1}}g\circ Q\, \mathrm dS=\int _{S^{d-1}}g\, \mathrm dS$ for every nonnegative or integrable Borel function $g$. We write $s_{d-1}=S(S^{d-1})$ for the area of the unit sphere, so that the unit ball has volume $s_{d-1}/d$. For instance, $s_0=2$, because $S$ is counting measure on $S^0=\{ \pm 1\} $, and $s_1=2\pi $, because the unit disc has area $\pi $. On a sphere $\partial B(x,r)$ we use the measure obtained by translation and dilation, again denoted $\mathrm dS$: \[  \int _{\partial B(x,r)}g\, \mathrm dS=r^{d-1}\int _{S^{d-1}}g(x+r\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega ).  \] Next we express Lebesgue measure in polar coordinates. Let $0\leq a<b$ and let $A\subset S^{d-1}$ be a Borel set. By dilation, the cone $\{ t\omega :0<t<b,\  \omega \in A\} $ has Lebesgue measure $b^ dS(A)/d$. The set $\{ t\omega :0<t\leq a,\  \omega \in A\} $ is the intersection of the decreasing cones $\{ t\omega :0<t<a+1/n,\  \omega \in A\} $, so its measure is $\lim _ n(a+1/n)^ dS(A)/d=a^ dS(A)/d$. Subtracting and translating, we find that for every $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ the annular sector $\{ x+t\omega :a<t<b,\  \omega \in A\} $ has Lebesgue measure \[   rac{(b^ d-a^ d)S(A)}{d}=S(A)\int _ a^ bt^{d-1}\, \mathrm dt.  \] Now fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ and $R>0$, let $\lambda $ be the measure $t^{d-1}\, \mathrm dt$ on the Borel sets of $(0,R)$, and let $\Phi (t,\omega )=x+t\omega $. If $D$ is bounded and $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }h(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial D$, then $h\leq 0$ on $D$. Consequently, a harmonic function on a bounded open set which is continuous on its closure is determined by its boundary values. Proof. For the first assertion, suppose that $h$ attains its maximum $m$ at a point of $D$, and let $E=\{ x\in D:h(x)=m\} $. This set is nonempty and closed in $D$. If $x\in E$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset D$, the ball mean-value property gives $\int _{B(x,r)}(m-h)\, \mathrm dy=0$. The integrand is continuous and nonnegative, so it vanishes on $B(x,r)$. Thus $E$ is open, and $E=D$ by connectedness. For the minimum, apply this to $-h$. For the second assertion, let $\varepsilon >0$, and suppose that $h>\varepsilon $ somewhere in $D$; we derive a contradiction. Each $\zeta \in \partial D$ has a ball $B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$ such that $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\cap B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$. Since $D$ is bounded, $\partial D$ is compact, and finitely many of these balls cover it; let $W$ be their union. Then $K=\overline D\setminus W=D\setminus W$ is compact. Since $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\setminus K=D\cap W$, the set $K$ is nonempty. The maximum of $h$ over $K$ is attained at some point $x_0$, and $h(x_0)>\varepsilon $; hence $h(x_0)$ is also the maximum of $h$ over $D$. Since $\mathbb R^ d$ is connected and $D_0$ is a nonempty, bounded, open subset, $D_0$ is not closed, so it has a boundary point $\zeta $. i x	o \zeta }h(x)\geq h(x_0)>0$, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $h\leq \varepsilon $ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $h\leq 0$. section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Theorem 2.1.2 . A continuous function on $\Omega $ is harmonic if and only if it has the sphere mean-value property. Every harmonic function is smooth. If $h$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, then for every multi-index $\alpha $, 2.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:harmonic-interior-derivatives} |\partial ^\alpha h(x)|\leq C_{d,\alpha }r^{-d-|\alpha |}\int _{B(x,r)}|h(y)|\, \mathrm d y, \end{equation} where the constant $C_{d,\alpha }$ depends only on $d$ and $\alpha $. Moreover, every harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $ satisfies $h*\rho _\varepsilon =h$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ for every $\varepsilon >0$, where $\rho _\varepsilon $ and $\Omega _\varepsilon $ are as in section 1.4 . Proof. As in section 1.4 , we write $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $. Let $u$ be continuous with the sphere mean-value property, and let $\overline{B(x,\varepsilon )}\subset \Omega $. The compact set $\overline{B(x,\varepsilon )}$ has positive distance from $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega $, so $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $, and $M_ u(x,r)=u(x)$ for $0<r\leq \varepsilon $. Since $\rho $ is radial, we may write $\rho _\varepsilon (y)=\phi _\varepsilon (|y|)$; as $\rho _\varepsilon $ is even and vanishes outside $B(0,\varepsilon )$, ( 2.1 ) gives 2.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mean-value-mollifier} \begin{split}  u_\varepsilon (x)& =\int _{B(0,\varepsilon )}u(x+y)\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy=s_{d-1}\int _0^\varepsilon r^{d-1}\phi _\varepsilon (r)M_ u(x,r)\, \mathrm dr\\ & =u(x)\, s_{d-1}\int _0^\varepsilon r^{d-1}\phi _\varepsilon (r)\, \mathrm dr=u(x)\int _{\mathbb R^ d}\rho _\varepsilon \, \mathrm dy=u(x). \end{split} \end{equation} Every point of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ is the center of such a closed ball, so $u=u_\varepsilon $ on the open set $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $u_\varepsilon $ is smooth there (section 1.4 ). As $\Omega $ is the union of the sets $\Omega _\varepsilon $, the function $u$ is smooth. Next we show that $\Delta u=0$. Fix $x\in \Omega $. Taylor's formula gives \[  u(x+r\omega )=u(x)+r\sum _ j\partial _ ju(x)\, \omega _ j+\frac{r^2}{2}\sum _{j,k}\partial _ j\partial _ ku(x)\, \omega _ j\omega _ k+o(r^2),  \] uniformly in $\omega \in S^{d-1}$. We average over the sphere. The reflections $\omega \mapsto -\omega $ and $\omega _ j\mapsto -\omega _ j$ preserve $S$, so $\int \omega _ j\, \mathrm dS=0$ and $\int \omega _ j\omega _ k\, \mathrm dS=0$ for $j\neq k$. Permutations of the coordinates also preserve $S$, so the integrals $\int \omega _ j^2\, \mathrm dS$ are all equal, and their sum is $s_{d-1}$ because $\sum _ j\omega _ j^2=1$. Hence \[  M_ u(x,r)=u(x)+\frac{r^2}{2d}\Delta u(x)+o(r^2).  \] Since $M_ u(x,r)=u(x)$ for all small $r$, it follows that $\Delta u(x)=0$. Thus $u$ is harmonic. Conversely, harmonic functions have the sphere mean-value property by proposition 2.1.1 ; in particular they are smooth, and they satisfy $h=h_\varepsilon =h*\rho _\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ by the first part of the proof. Now let $h$ be harmonic and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. Then $x$ lies in the open set $\Omega _ r$, and $h=h_ r$ on $\Omega _ r$ by the first part of the proof. By the differentiation formula $\partial ^\alpha h_ r=h*\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r$ of section 1.4 , and since $\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r$ vanishes outside $B(0,r)$, we get \[  \partial ^\alpha h(x)=\int _{B(x,r)} h(y)\, (\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r)(x-y)\, \mathrm d y.  \] Since $\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r(z)=r^{-d-|\alpha |}(\partial ^\alpha \rho )(z/r)$, this proves ( 2.5 ) with $C_{d,\alpha }=\sup |\partial ^\alpha \rho |$, where $\rho $ is the mollifier on $\mathbb R^ d$ fixed in section 1.4 . $\square$

title: Proposition 2.1.3
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Proposition 2.1.3 . Let $h$ be a real harmonic function on an open set $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$. If $D$ is connected and $h$ attains its maximum or its minimum over $D$ at a point of $D$, then $h$ is constant. If $D$ is bounded and $\varlimsup _{D\ni x\to \zeta }h(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial D$, then $h\leq 0$ on $D$. Consequently, a harmonic function on a bounded open set which is continuous on its closure is determined by its boundary values. Proof. For the first assertion, suppose that $h$ attains its maximum $m$ at a point of $D$, and let $E=\{ x\in D:h(x)=m\} $. This set is nonempty and closed in $D$. If $x\in E$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset D$, the ball mean-value property gives $\int _{B(x,r)}(m-h)\, \mathrm dy=0$. The integrand is continuous and nonnegative, so it vanishes on $B(x,r)$. Thus $E$ is open, and $E=D$ by connectedness. For the minimum, apply this to $-h$. For the second assertion, let $\varepsilon >0$, and suppose that $h>\varepsilon $ somewhere in $D$; we derive a contradiction. Each $\zeta \in \partial D$ has a ball $B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$ such that $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\cap B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$. Since $D$ is bounded, $\partial D$ is compact, and finitely many of these balls cover it; let $W$ be their union. Then $K=\overline D\setminus W=D\setminus W$ is compact. Since $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\setminus K=D\cap W$, the set $K$ is nonempty. The maximum of $h$ over $K$ is attained at some point $x_0$, and $h(x_0)>\varepsilon $; hence $h(x_0)$ is also the maximum of $h$ over $D$. Let $D_0$ be the component of $D$ containing $x_0$; it is open, because every point of $D$ lies in a ball contained in $D$, and balls are connected. By the first assertion, $h=h(x_0)$ on $D_0$. Since $\mathbb R^ d$ is connected and $D_0$ is a nonempty, bounded, open subset, $D_0$ is not closed, so it has a boundary point $\zeta $. This point does not lie in $D$: otherwise the component of $D$ containing $\zeta $ would be an open neighborhood of $\zeta $, so it would meet $D_0$ and hence equal $D_0$, which does not contain its boundary point $\zeta $. Thus $\zeta \in \partial D$ and $\varlimsup _{D\ni x\to \zeta }h(x)\geq h(x_0)>0$, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $h\leq \varepsilon $ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $h\leq 0$. Finally, if two harmonic functions on a bounded open set are continuous on its closure and agree on its boundary, apply the second assertion to the real and imaginary parts of their difference and of its negative. $\square$

title: Theorem 2.1.4 (Weyl's lemma)
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Theorem 2.1.4 (Weyl's lemma) . Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ satisfy $\Delta T=0$. Then there is a unique smooth harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $ such that $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\int _\Omega h\chi \, \mathrm dx$ for every $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$. In particular, a locally integrable function whose distributional Laplacian vanishes agrees almost everywhere with a harmonic function. Proof. Recall from section 1.4 that $(T*\phi )(y)=\langle T,\phi (y-\cdot )\rangle $ for a test function $\phi $ on $\mathbb R^ d$ supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$ and $y\in \Omega _ s$, and that $T_\varepsilon =T*\rho _\varepsilon $. By part (1) of proposition 1.4.3 , $T*\phi $ is smooth on $\Omega _ s$ and $\partial ^\alpha (T*\phi )=T*\partial ^\alpha \phi $; moreover $\Delta T_\varepsilon =(\Delta T)_\varepsilon =0$, so $T_\varepsilon $ is a smooth harmonic function on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. We show that $T_\varepsilon $ converges to the required $h$, locally uniformly with all derivatives, by writing $T_\varepsilon =T*(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)$ near each point for a fixed $r>0$. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,3r)}\subset \Omega $, and let $0<\varepsilon <r$. Since $\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega )>3r$, every point of $B(x,2r)$ has distance greater than $r$ from $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega $, and every point of $B(x,r)$ has distance greater than $2r$; thus $B(x,2r)\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ and $B(x,r)\subset \Omega _{2r}$. Let $y\in B(x,r)$. The closed ball $\overline{B(y,r)}$ lies in $B(x,2r)$, where $T_\varepsilon $ is harmonic, so the last assertion of theorem 2.1.2 , applied to $T_\varepsilon $ on $B(x,2r)$, gives $T_\varepsilon (y)=\int T_\varepsilon (z)\rho _ r(y-z)\, \mathrm dz$. The test function $\chi =\rho _ r(y-\cdot )$ is supported in $\overline{B(y,r)}\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, so ( 1.7 ) gives $T_\varepsilon (y)=\langle T,\chi *\rho _\varepsilon \rangle $. Substituting $z=w+v$ and using that $\rho _\varepsilon $ is even, we find \begin{align*}  (\chi *\rho _\varepsilon )(w)& =\int \rho _ r(y-z)\rho _\varepsilon (w-z)\, \mathrm dz\\ & =\int \rho _\varepsilon (v)\rho _ r(y-w-v)\, \mathrm dv=(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)(y-w). \end{align*} The function $\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r$ is a test function supported in $\overline{B(0,\varepsilon +r)}\subset \overline{B(0,2r)}$, so we have shown that \[  T_\varepsilon =T*(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)\qquad \text{on }B(x,r).  \] Since $\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r=\rho _ r*\rho _\varepsilon $, part (3) of lemma 1.4.1 , applied on $\mathbb R^ d$ to $\rho _ r$, shows that $\partial ^\alpha (\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)\to \partial ^\alpha \rho _ r$ uniformly for every multi-index $\alpha $ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Let $C$ and $m$ be the constants of definition 1.3.1 for $T$ and the compact set $\overline{B(x,3r)}$, which contains the supports of $(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)(y-\cdot )$ and $\rho _ r(y-\cdot )$ for $y\in B(x,r)$. For $y\in B(x,r)$ and a multi-index $\alpha $, the difference $\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon (y)-\partial ^\alpha (T*\rho _ r)(y)$ is the pairing of $T$ with $w\mapsto \psi (y-w)$, where $\psi =\partial ^\alpha (\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r-\rho _ r)$, and the derivatives of order $\beta $ of this test function are $\pm (\partial ^\beta \psi )(y-w)$. Hence \[  \sup _{y\in B(x,r)}\bigl |\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon (y)-\partial ^\alpha (T*\rho _ r)(y)\bigr | \leq C\max _{|\beta |\leq m}\sup \bigl |\partial ^{\alpha +\beta }(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r-\rho _ r)\bigr |,  \] which tends to zero. Thus $T_\varepsilon \to T*\rho _ r$ on $B(x,r)$, uniformly with all derivatives. Every point of $\Omega $ is the center of such a ball. Therefore $h(y)=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}T_\varepsilon (y)$ exists for every $y\in \Omega $, and on each ball $B(x,r)$ as above it equals $T*\rho _ r$ and is the limit of $T_\varepsilon $ uniformly with all derivatives. Thus $h$ is smooth and $\Delta h=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\Delta T_\varepsilon =0$. Every compact subset of $\Omega $ is covered by finitely many of these balls, so $T_\varepsilon \to h$ uniformly on compact sets, and part (2) of proposition 1.4.3 gives $\int h\chi \, \mathrm dx=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm dx=\langle T,\chi \rangle $ for every test function $\chi $. If two continuous functions define the same distribution, they agree almost everywhere by part (4) of proposition 1.4.3 , and hence everywhere, since nonempty open sets have positive measure. This proves uniqueness. Finally, if $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $u$, then $u$ and $h$ define the same distribution, so $u=h$ almost everywhere by the same proposition. $\square$

section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
2.3 Poisson kernels and Harnack inequalities Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a bounded open set. The Dirichlet problem on $D$ asks, for a given $f\in C(\partial D)$, for a function $h$ which is harmonic on $D$ and continuous on $\overline D$ with $h=f$ on $\partial D$. By proposition 2.1.3 it has at most one solution. On a ball $B=B(c,R)$ the solution is given by an explicit integral formula: for $x\in B$ and $\zeta \in \partial B$ put 2.14  egin{equation} \label{eq:ball-poisson-kernel} P_ B(x,\zeta )= rac{R^2-|x-c|^2}{s_{d-1}R|x-\zeta |^ d}. \end{equation} This is the Poisson kernel of $B$. In dimension one, $B=(a,b)$, the boundary $\partial B=\{ a,b\} $ carries counting measure and $s_0=2$, so that $P_ B(x,a)=(b-x)/(b-a)$ and $P_ B(x,b)=(x-a)/(b-a)$; the Poisson integral below is then the affine interpolation of the two endpoint values. Theorem 2.3.1 . Let $B$ be a ball and $f\in C(\partial B)$. The Poisson integral \[  H_ Bf(x)=\int _{\partial B}P_ B(x,\zeta )f(\zeta )\, \mathrm d S(\zeta ),\qquad x\in B,  \] is the unique harmonic function on $B$ which extends continuously to $\overline B$ with boundary values $f$. The kernel is positive, and $\int _{\partial B}P_ B(x,\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )=1$ for every $x\in B$. The operator $H_ B$ is linear, preserves order, and satisfies $\sup _ B|H_ Bf|\leq \max _{\partial B}|f|$. Every function harmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ is the Poisson integral of its restriction to $\partial B$. Proof. If $d=1$ and $B=(a,b)$, then $H_ Bf$ is the affine function with the values $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ at the endpoints, as noted above. It is harmonic on $B$ and extends continuously to $\overline B$ with boundary values $f$, and the kernel is positive with $P_ B(x,a)+P_ B(x,b)=1$. The remaining assertions are proved below in all dimensions. Now let $d\geq 2$; after a translation we may assume that $c=0$. Fix $\zeta \in \partial B$ and put $A(x)=R^2-|x|^2$ and $t(x)=|x-\zeta |$ for $x
eq \zeta $. We have $
abla A=-2x$, $\Delta A=-2d$ and $
abla t^{-d}=-dt^{-d-2}(x-\zeta )$, and ( 2.13 ), applied to $F(t)=t^{-d}$ after translating $\zeta $ to the origin, gives $\Delta t^{-d}= igl (d(d+1)-d(d-1) igr )t^{-d-2}=2dt^{-d-2}$. By the product rule $\Delta (At^{-d})=(\Delta A)t^{-d}+2
abla A\cdot 
abla t^{-d}+A\Delta t^{-d}$, and since $t^2=|x|^2-2x\cdot \zeta +|\zeta |^2$, \[  \Delta (At^{-d})=2dt^{-d-2} igl (-t^2+2x\cdot (x-\zeta )+R^2-|x|^2 igr )=2dt^{-d-2}(R^2-|\zeta |^2)=0.  \] Thus $P_ B(\cdot ,\zeta )$ is harmonic on $B$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. Every partial derivative $\partial _ x^\alpha P_ B(x,\zeta )$ is continuous on $B	imes \partial B$, hence bounded on $K	imes \partial B$ for each compact set $K\subset B$, where $|x-\zeta |\geq \operatorname {dist}(K,\partial B)>0$. By the mean value theorem and dominated convergence on the finite measure space $(\partial B,S)$, we may therefore differentiate under the integral sign any number of times, so $H_ Bf$ is smooth on $B$ and $\Delta H_ Bf(x)=\int _{\partial B}\Delta _ xP_ B(x,\zeta )f(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )=0$. Next we show that the kernel has integral one. Taking $f=1$, we see that $I(x)=\int _{\partial B}P_ B(x,\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ is harmonic on $B$. It is also radial. Indeed, $P_ B(Qx,Q\zeta )=P_ B(x,\zeta )$ for every orthogonal transformation $Q$, and surface measure on $\partial B$ is invariant under $Q$, so $I(Qx)=I(x)$. Moreover, if $|x|=|x'|$ and $x
eq x'$, the orthogonal reflection $y\mapsto y-2(y\cdot e)e$ with $e=(x-x')/|x-x'|$ maps $x$ to $x'$. Hence $I(x)=F(|x|)$, where $F(r)=I(re_1)$ is smooth on $(-R,R)$ and $e_1$ is the first coordinate vector. By ( 2.13 ), $(r^{d-1}F'(r))'=0$ on $(0,R)$, so $r^{d-1}F'(r)$ is constant there. Since $F'$ is bounded near $0$ and $d\geq 2$, this constant is $\lim _{r	o 0}r^{d-1}F'(r)=0$. Hence $F$ is constant on $(0,R)$, and since $I$ is continuous at the origin, $I$ is constant on $B$, with value $I(0)=R^2\cdot s_{d-1}R^{d-1}/(s_{d-1}R\cdot R^ d)=1$. For the boundary behavior, fix $\zeta _0\in \partial B$ and $\varepsilon >0$, and choose $\delta >0$ such that $|f(\zeta )-f(\zeta _0)|<\varepsilon $ for $\zeta \in \partial B$ with $|\zeta -\zeta _0|<\delta $. Since the kernel is positive with integral one,  egin{align*}  |H_ Bf(x)-f(\zeta _0)|& \leq \int _{\partial B}P_ B(x,\zeta )|f(\zeta )-f(\zeta _0)|\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )\ & \leq \varepsilon +2\max _{\partial B}|f|\int _{\{ \zeta \in \partial B:|\zeta -\zeta _0|\geq \delta \} }P_ B(x,\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta ). \end{align*} If $|x-\zeta _0|<\delta /2$, then $|x-\zeta |\geq \delta /2$ in the last integral, so $P_ B(x,\zeta )\leq (R^2-|x-c|^2)/(s_{d-1}R(\delta /2)^ d)$ there, and the integral is at most $R^{d-2}(2/\delta )^ d(R^2-|x-c|^2)$. This tends to zero as $x	o \zeta _0$, because $|\zeta _0-c|=R$. Hence $\varlimsup _{x	o \zeta _0}|H_ Bf(x)-f(\zeta _0)|\leq \varepsilon $ for every $\varepsilon >0$. Since $f$ is continuous on $\partial B$, it follows that the function equal to $H_ Bf$ on $B$ and to $f$ on $\partial B$ is continuous on $\overline B$. Uniqueness follows from the last assertion of proposition 2.1.3 . The operator $H_ B$ is linear by definition, and since the kernel is positive with integral one, $H_ B$ preserves order and $|H_ Bf(x)|\leq \int _{\partial B}P_ B(x,\zeta )|f(\zeta )|\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )\leq \max _{\partial B}|f|$. Proposition 2.3.2 . Let $h\geq 0$ be harmonic on $B(0,R)$, let $x\in B(0,R)$ and put $r=|x|$. Then 2.15  egin{equation} \label{eq:harnack-ball}  rac{R^{d-2}(R-r)}{(R+r)^{d-1}}h(0) \leq h(x)\leq  rac{R^{d-2}(R+r)}{(R-r)^{d-1}}h(0). \end{equation} A nonnegative harmonic function on a domain is either positive everywhere or identically zero. Let $\Omega $ be a domain, $K\subset \Omega $ compact and $x_0\in \Omega $. Then there is a constant $C=C(K,x_0,\Omega )>0$ such that \[  \sup _ K h\leq C h(x_0)  \] for every nonnegative harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $. Proof. (1) Let $r<R'<R$. By theorem 2.3.1 on $B(0,R')$, both $h(x)$ and $h(0)$ are integrals of the nonnegative boundary values of $h$ against the Poisson kernel. For $|\zeta |=R'$ we have $R'-r\leq |x-\zeta |\leq R'+r$, so the ratio \[   rac{P_{B(0,R')}(x,\zeta )}{P_{B(0,R')}(0,\zeta )}= rac{R'^{d-2}(R'^2-r^2)}{|x-\zeta |^ d}  \] lies between the two coefficients in ( 2.15 ) with $R'$ in place of $R$. Integrating and letting $R'\uparrow R$ gives ( 2.15 ). (2) If a nonnegative harmonic function on a domain vanishes at a point, it attains its minimum there and is identically zero by proposition 2.1.3 . (3) We first apply (1), after a translation, to a ball $B(a,2t)\subset \Omega $: for $y\in B(a,t)$ we have $r=|y-a|<t$, and the right inequality in ( 2.15 ) on $B(a,2t)$ gives \[  h(y)\leq  rac{(2t)^{d-2}(2t+r)}{(2t-r)^{d-1}}h(a)\leq  rac{(2t)^{d-2}\cdot 3t}{t^{d-1}}h(a)=C_0h(a),\qquad C_0=3\cdot 2^{d-2}.  \] Now let $y\in \Omega $. Since $\Omega $ is connected, $y$ can be joined to $x_0$ by a polygonal path in $\Omega $: the set of points that can be so joined is open, and so is its complement in $\Omega $, because balls are convex. The path is compact, so there is $t>0$ with $B(z,2t)\subset \Omega $ for every point $z$ of the path. Choose points $x_0=p_0,p_1,\ldots ,p_ N=y$ along the path with $|p_{i+1}-p_ i|<t$. Applying the ball estimate on $B(p_ i,2t)$ for $i=0,\ldots ,N-1$ gives $h(y)\leq C_0^ Nh(x_0)$, and once more on $B(y,2t)$ gives $h\leq C_0^{N+1}h(x_0)$ on $B(y,t)$. Here $t$ and $N$ depend on $y$, $x_0$ and $\Omega $, but not on $h$. Finitely many of the balls $B(y,t)$, $y\in K$, cover $K$, and the largest of the corresponding constants $C_0^{N+1}$ is the required $C$. $\square$ A sequence of smooth functions on an open set $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ converges to $g$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets if, for every multi-index $\alpha $, the derivatives $\partial ^\alpha $ of its terms converge to $\partial ^\alpha g$ uniformly on compact subsets of $D$. Corollary 2.3.3 . Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a domain. Every sequence of nonnegative harmonic functions on $D$ which is bounded at one point of $D$ has a subsequence converging in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets; the limit is harmonic. An increasing sequence of harmonic functions on $D$ either converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to a finite harmonic function, or tends to $+\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets. A decreasing sequence of harmonic functions on $D$ either converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to a finite harmonic function, or tends to $-\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets. Proof. Let $h_ j\geq 0$ be harmonic on $D$ with $h_ j(x_0)\leq M$ for some $x_0\in D$. Let $K\subset D$ be compact and choose $\delta >0$ such that $K_\delta =\{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,K)\leq \delta \} $ is contained in $D$. By proposition 2.3.2 (3), $h_ j\leq C(K_\delta ,x_0,D)M$ on $K_\delta $ for all $j$, and ( 2.5 ) with radius $\delta $ then bounds each derivative $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$ on $K$ uniformly in $j$. Taking for $K$ a closed ball in $D$ and applying this bound to the first derivatives of $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$, we see that the functions $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$ are uniformly Lipschitz on every closed ball in $D$, and hence equicontinuous on compact subsets of $D$. Let $K_ m$ be the sets of the compact exhaustion of $D$ constructed in section 1.1 ; every compact subset of $D$ lies in some $K_ m$. Applying proposition 1.6.4 on each $K_ m$ and making a diagonal extraction over all $m$ and all multi-indices $\alpha $, we obtain a subsequence along which every $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$ converges uniformly on compact subsets of $D$, say to $g_\alpha $. To identify the limits, let $e_ k$ be the $k$th standard basis vector. Passing to the uniform limit in \[  \partial ^\alpha h_ j(y+te_ k)-\partial ^\alpha h_ j(y)=\int _0^ t\partial ^{\alpha +e_ k}h_ j(y+se_ k)\, \mathrm ds,  \] which holds whenever the segment from $y$ to $y+te_ k$ lies in $D$, we find that $\partial _ kg_\alpha =g_{\alpha +e_ k}$. By induction, $g=g_0$ is smooth with $\partial ^\alpha g=g_\alpha $, so the subsequence converges to $g$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets, and $\Delta g=\lim _ j\Delta h_ j=0$. This proves the first assertion. We also need a lower Harnack bound: for compact $K\subset D$ and $x_0\in D$ there is $c>0$ such that $h\geq c\, h(x_0)$ on $K$ for every nonnegative harmonic $h$ on $D$. Indeed, if $B(a,2t)\subset D$ and $y\in B(a,t)$, then $r=|y-a|<t$, and the left inequality in ( 2.15 ) on $B(a,2t)$ gives $h(y)\geq (2t)^{d-2}(2t-r)(2t+r)^{1-d}h(a)\geq c_0h(a)$ with $c_0=2^{d-2}3^{1-d}$. Cover $K$ by finitely many balls $B(a_ k,t_ k)$ with $B(a_ k,2t_ k)\subset D$. Proposition 2.3.2 (3), applied to the compact set $\{ x_0\} $ and the base point $a_ k$, gives $h(x_0)\leq C_ kh(a_ k)$. Hence $h\geq (c_0/\max _ kC_ k)h(x_0)$ on $K$. Now let $(h_ j)$ be increasing and fix $x_0\in D$. The functions $h_ j-h_1$ are nonnegative and harmonic. If $h_ j(x_0)$ is bounded, the first assertion applies to every subsequence of $(h_ j-h_1)$. Since the sequence increases and, by proposition 2.3.2 (3), is bounded on compact sets, it has a finite pointwise limit, and every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to this limit. Hence the whole sequence converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets, and the limit is a finite harmonic function. If $h_ j(x_0)	o +\infty $, the lower Harnack bound gives $h_ j-h_1\geq c(h_ j(x_0)-h_1(x_0))$ on each compact $K$, and since $h_1$ is bounded on $K$, $h_ j	o +\infty $ uniformly on $K$. For a decreasing sequence, apply this to $(-h_ j)$. $\square$ Corollary 2.3.4 . A real harmonic function on $\mathbb R^ d$ which is bounded above or bounded below is constant. Proof. After changing the sign and adding a constant, we may assume that the function $h$ is nonnegative. Fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ and put $r=|x|$. For $R>r$, ( 2.15 ) on $B(0,R)$ gives $c_ Rh(0)\leq h(x)\leq C_ Rh(0)$, where the coefficients $c_ R$ and $C_ R$ of ( 2.15 ) tend to one as $R	o \infty $. Letting $R	o \infty $ gives $h(x)=h(0)$. Hence $h$ is constant. $\square$
