title: Lemma 3.3.1
text: Lemma 3.3.1 . Let $\Omega $ be a domain and let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ that is uniformly bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Suppose that there are a compact set $K\subset \Omega $, points $x_ j\in K$ and a constant $C_0$ such that $u_ j(x_ j)\geq -C_0$ for all $j$. Then there is a subsequence $(u_{j_ k})$ such that $\sup _ k\int _ L|u_{j_ k}|\, \mathrm d x<\infty $ for every compact set $L\subset \Omega $. Proof. We first record a local estimate. Let $a\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(a,4r)}\subset \Omega $, and let $M\geq 0$ be a common upper bound of the functions $u_ j$ on $B(a,4r)$. Suppose that $u_ j(z)\geq -C$ for some index $j$, some point $z\in B(a,r)$ and some constant $C$. Then $B(a,r)\subset B(z,2r)$ and $\overline{B(z,2r)}\subset B(a,4r)$. Since $M-u_ j\geq 0$ on $B(z,2r)$, the ball submean inequality of theorem 3.1.3 gives \[  \int _{B(a,r)}(M-u_ j)\, \mathrm d x \leq \int _{B(z,2r)}(M-u_ j)\, \mathrm d x \leq |B(0,2r)|\, (M+C),  \] and since $|u_ j|\leq (M-u_ j)+M$, we obtain 3.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:subharmonic-local-l1-bound} \int _{B(a,r)}|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x\leq |B(0,2r)|\, (M+C)+|B(0,r)|\, M. \end{equation} Passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $x_ j\to x_0\in K$. Choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x_0,4r)}\subset \Omega $. Discarding finitely many terms, we may assume that $|x_ j-x_0|<r$ for all $j$. Then ( 3.4 ), with $a=x_0$, $z=x_ j$ and $C=C_0$, bounds $\int _{B(x_0,r)}|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x$ uniformly in $j$. Let $Y$ be the set of points $y\in \Omega $ that have a neighborhood $U$ with $\sup _ j\int _ U|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x<\infty $. Then $Y$ is open and contains $x_0$. Let $y\in \Omega $ lie in the closure of $Y$. Choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(y,4r)}\subset \Omega $ and an open ball $A$ with $\overline A\subset Y\cap B(y,r)$. Covering the compact set $\overline A$ by finitely many of the neighborhoods in the definition of $Y$, we find $C_ A=\sup _ j\int _ A|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x<\infty $. Put $C=C_ A/|A|$. For each $j$ there is a point $z_ j\in A$ with $u_ j(z_ j)\geq -C$, since otherwise $\int _ A|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x\geq \int _ A(-u_ j)\, \mathrm d x>C|A|=C_ A$. By ( 3.4 ), with $a=y$ and $z=z_ j$, the integrals $\int _{B(y,r)}|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x$ are bounded uniformly in $j$, so $y\in Y$. Thus $Y$ is closed in $\Omega $, and $Y=\Omega $ because $\Omega $ is connected. Finally, every compact subset of $\Omega $ is covered by finitely many of the neighborhoods in the definition of $Y$. $\square$
3.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:subharmonic-local-l1-bound} \int _{B(a,r)}|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x\leq |B(0,2r)|\, (M+C)+|B(0,r)|\, M. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 3.3.2
text: Theorem 3.3.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, and let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ that is uniformly bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $. If $\Omega $ is connected, then either $u_ j\to -\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega $, or a subsequence of $(u_ j)$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a locally integrable subharmonic function. If every $u_ j$ is locally integrable and $(u_ j)$ converges in the sense of distributions to some $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$, then $T$ is real, $\Delta T\geq 0$, and $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, where $u$ is the canonical representative of $T$. Proof. We prove (2) first, because (1) reduces to it. As observed after theorem 3.2.2 , $T$ is real, $\Delta T\geq 0$, and $T$ has a canonical representative $u$. We begin by showing that $(u_ j)$ is bounded in $L^1(L)$ for every compact set $L\subset \Omega $. Fix such a set $L$, let $\chi $ be a nonnegative test function equal to one near $L$, and let $M\geq 0$ bound all $u_ j$ from above on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. Then $|u_ j|\leq 2M-u_ j$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, so \[  \int _ L|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x\leq 2M\int \chi \, \mathrm d x-\int u_ j\chi \, \mathrm d x,  \] which is bounded because $\int u_ j\chi \, \mathrm d x$ converges. Next we show that the mollifications $u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon $ converge locally uniformly. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. For $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $, the function $\rho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )$ is a test function, so $u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x)\to \langle T,\rho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )\rangle =u*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$. Let $L\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ be compact; then $L'=\{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,L)\leq \varepsilon \} $ is a compact subset of $\Omega $, and the mean value theorem, applied to $\rho _\varepsilon $, gives \[  |u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x)-u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x')|\leq \sup |\nabla \rho _\varepsilon |\cdot |x-x'|\int _{L'}|u_ j|\, \mathrm d y,\qquad x,x'\in L.  \] Thus the functions $u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon $ are $A$-Lipschitz on $L$, where $A=\sup |\nabla \rho _\varepsilon |\cdot \sup _ j\int _{L'}|u_ j|\, \mathrm dy$, and so is their pointwise limit $u*\rho _\varepsilon $. Given $\tau >0$, cover $L$ by finitely many balls $B(x_ i,\tau /(3A+1))$ with $x_ i\in L$, and choose $j_0$ such that $|u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x_ i)-u*\rho _\varepsilon (x_ i)|<\tau /3$ for all $i$ and all $j\geq j_0$. Then $|u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon -u*\rho _\varepsilon |<\tau $ on $L$ for $j\geq j_0$, so the convergence is uniform on $L$. Now let $\chi $ be a nonnegative test function, choose $\varepsilon $ so small that $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, let $\delta >0$, and put $g=u*\rho _\varepsilon +\delta $. By ( 3.3 ), $u_ j\leq u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon $ and $u\leq u*\rho _\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. By the uniform convergence just proved, $u_ j\leq g$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ for all large $j$; also $u\leq g$. Hence $|u_ j-u|\leq (g-u_ j)+(g-u)$ almost everywhere on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and since $\int u_ j\chi \, \mathrm d x\to \int u\chi \, \mathrm d x$, \[  \begin{aligned}  \varlimsup _ j\int |u_ j-u|\chi \, \mathrm d x & \leq \lim _ j\int (g-u_ j)\chi \, \mathrm d x+\int (g-u)\chi \, \mathrm d x\\ & =2\int (u*\rho _\varepsilon +\delta -u)\chi \, \mathrm d x. \end{aligned}  \] Let $\delta \downarrow 0$, and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; since $u*\rho _\varepsilon \to u$ in $L^1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 1.4.1 ), the right-hand side tends to zero. Choosing $\chi $ equal to one on a prescribed compact set proves $L^1$ convergence on that set. This proves (2). (1) Suppose that $u_ j$ does not tend to $-\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets. Then there are a compact set $K\subset \Omega $, a constant $C_0$ and infinitely many indices $j$ with $\sup _ Ku_ j>-C_0$, and for these $j$ we can choose $x_ j\in K$ with $u_ j(x_ j)>-C_0$. By lemma 3.3.1 , a subsequence, which we again denote by $(u_ j)$, is bounded in $L^1(L)$ for every compact set $L\subset \Omega $; in particular, every $u_ j$ is locally integrable. By (2), it suffices to show that a further subsequence converges in the sense of distributions. Choose open sets $U_ m\Subset \Omega $ increasing to $\Omega $, for instance the interiors of the sets of a compact exhaustion (section 1.1 ), and constants $M_ m\geq 0$ with $u_ j\leq M_ m$ on $\overline{U_ m}$ for all $j$. On $U_ m$, the Borel measures $(M_ m-u_ j)\, \mathrm d x$ are positive, and their masses on a compact set $L\subset U_ m$ are at most $M_ m|L|+\sup _ j\int _ L|u_ j|\, \mathrm dx$, uniformly in $j$; in particular, they are Radon measures by proposition 1.1.2 . By theorem 1.5.5 and a diagonal extraction over $m$, we may assume that for each $m$ these measures converge vaguely on $U_ m$. Every $\chi \in C_ c(\Omega )$ has its support in some $U_ m$, so \[  \int u_ j\chi \, \mathrm d x=M_ m\int \chi \, \mathrm d x-\int (M_ m-u_ j)\chi \, \mathrm d x  \] converges. Let $T(\chi )$ denote the limit when $\chi $ is a test function. If $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset L$ with $L$ compact, then $|T(\chi )|\leq \sup _ j\int _ L|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x\cdot \sup |\chi |$. Hence $T$ is a distribution of order zero, and $u_ j\to T$ in the sense of distributions. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.3.3 (Hartogs' lemma)
text: Theorem 3.3.3 (Hartogs' lemma) . Let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence of locally integrable subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a function $v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Then $\Delta v\geq 0$ in the sense of distributions. Let $u$ be the canonical representative of $v$, that is, the locally integrable subharmonic function equal to $v$ almost everywhere. Then, for every $x\in \Omega $ and every sequence $x_ j\to x$ in $\Omega $, \[  \varlimsup _ j u_ j(x_ j)\leq u(x).  \] For every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ and every lower semicontinuous function $f\colon K\to \mathbb R$, for instance every real continuous function on $K$, \[  \varlimsup _ j\sup _ K(u_ j-f)\leq \sup _ K(u-f).  \] In particular, if $f\colon K\to \mathbb R$ is lower semicontinuous and $u<f$ on $K$, then $u_ j<f$ on $K$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Proof. Convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ implies convergence in the sense of distributions, because $|\int (u_ j-v)\chi \, \mathrm dx|\leq \sup |\chi |\int _{\operatorname{Supp}\chi }|u_ j-v|\, \mathrm dx$. Hence, as observed after theorem 3.2.2 , the distribution defined by $v$ is real, has positive Laplacian and has a canonical representative $u$. Let $x_ j\to x$, and choose $\varepsilon >0$ with $\overline{B(x,2\varepsilon )}\subset \Omega $. For $y\in B(x,\varepsilon )$ we have \[  |u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (y)-u*\rho _\varepsilon (y)|\leq \sup \rho _\varepsilon \int _{B(x,2\varepsilon )}|u_ j-v|\, \mathrm d z,  \] so $u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon \to u*\rho _\varepsilon $ uniformly on $B(x,\varepsilon )$. For large $j$ we have $x_ j\in B(x,\varepsilon )$. Since $u_ j\leq u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon $ by ( 3.3 ) and $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ is continuous, we obtain \[  \varlimsup _ j u_ j(x_ j)\leq \varlimsup _ ju_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x_ j)=u*\rho _\varepsilon (x).  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and using ( 3.3 ) again proves the first assertion. For the second assertion we may assume $K\neq \varnothing $. Since $u$ and $-f$ are upper semicontinuous on the compact set $K$, they are bounded above there, so $s=\sup _ K(u-f)$ lies in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. Suppose that $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ K(u_ j-f)>c>s$ for some real $c$. Then $\sup _ K(u_ j-f)>c$ for infinitely many $j$, so along a subsequence there are points $x_ j\in K$ with $u_ j(x_ j)-f(x_ j)>c$, and after passing to a further subsequence we may assume $x_ j\to x\in K$. Since $\varliminf _ jf(x_ j)\geq f(x)$ by lower semicontinuity, the first assertion, applied to this subsequence, gives \[  c\leq \varlimsup _ j\bigl (u_ j(x_ j)-f(x_ j)\bigr )\leq \varlimsup _ ju_ j(x_ j)-\varliminf _ jf(x_ j)\leq u(x)-f(x)\leq s<c,  \] a contradiction. Finally, if $u<f$ on $K$, then the upper semicontinuous function $u-f$ attains a negative maximum on $K$, so $\sup _ K(u-f)<0$, and the second assertion gives $\sup _ K(u_ j-f)<0$ for all large $j$. $\square$

title: 3.4 Upper envelopes and countable selection
text:
3.4 Upper envelopes and countable selection The pointwise supremum of a family of subharmonic functions need not be upper semicontinuous (example 3.4.3 ), so we regularize it. Let $F\colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be locally bounded above, that is, bounded above on a neighborhood of each point. Its upper semicontinuous regularization is \[  F^*(x)=\inf _{r>0}\sup _{B(x,r)\cap \Omega }F.  \] Since $x\in B(x,r)$, we have $F^*\geq F$. The function $F^*$ is upper semicontinuous: if $F^*(x)<c$, then $\sup _{B(x,r)\cap \Omega }F<c$ for some $r>0$, and hence $F^*<c$ on $B(x,r)\cap \Omega $. It is the smallest upper semicontinuous function that dominates $F$: if $G$ is such a function and $c>G(x)$, then $G<c$ on some ball $B(x,r)$, so $\sup _{B(x,r)}F\leq c$ and $F^*(x)\leq c$. We take the supremum of an empty family of functions to be the constant $-\infty $. A family of functions on $\Omega $ is locally uniformly bounded above if every point of $\Omega $ has a neighborhood on which all members of the family are bounded above by one constant. The following lemma reduces such families to countable subfamilies. Lemma 3.4.1 (Choquet's lemma) . Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty family of functions $\Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ that is locally uniformly bounded above, and let $F=\sup _{w\in \mathcal F}w$. Then there is a countable subfamily $\{ v_ j\} _{j\geq 1}\subset \mathcal F$ such that $v=\sup _ jv_ j$ satisfies $v^*=F^*$. Proof. Call $B(q,s)$ a rational ball if $q\in \mathbb Q^ d$ and $s$ is a positive rational number. Enumerate the rational balls $B$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ as $B_1,B_2,\ldots $, in such a way that each of them occurs infinitely often. Since $F$ is bounded above on the compact set $\overline{B_ j}$, we have $\sup _{B_ j}F<\infty $. If $\sup _{B_ j}F>-\infty $, choose $v_ j\in \mathcal F$ with $\sup _{B_ j}v_ j>\sup _{B_ j}F-1/j$; otherwise let $v_ j$ be any member of $\mathcal F$. Put $v=\sup _ jv_ j\leq F$. If $B$ is a rational ball with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, then $B=B_ j$ for infinitely many $j$, so $\sup _ Bv=\sup _ BF$. Every ball $B(x,r)$ contains a rational ball that contains $x$: choose $q\in \mathbb Q^ d$ with $|q-x|<r/3$ and a rational number $s\in (r/3,2r/3)$; then $x\in B(q,s)\subset B(x,r)$. Conversely, a rational ball $B(q,s)$ containing $x$ contains $B(x,s-|q-x|)$. Hence $F^*(x)$ is the infimum of $\sup _ BF$ over the rational balls $B
i x$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, and similarly for $v^*(x)$. Therefore $v^*=F^*$. $\square$ Theorem 3.4.2 . Let $\{ u_ t\} _{t\in I}$ be a family in $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ that is uniformly bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $, and let $F=\sup _ tu_ t$. Then $F^*$ is subharmonic. Moreover, $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and $F=F^*$ almost everywhere. The functions $F$ and $F^*$ need not coincide everywhere (example 3.4.3 ). Proof. If the family is empty, then $F=F^*=-\infty $. Otherwise, we replace the family by an increasing sequence, using Choquet's lemma, and identify the regularized limit of this sequence with a canonical representative. The connected components of $\Omega $ are open, because balls are connected; hence they are pairwise disjoint sets of positive Lebesgue measure, and there are at most countably many of them by lemma 1.1.5 . As a countable union of null sets is null, it suffices to prove the assertions on each component $\Omega '$. On $\Omega '$ the regularization $F^*$ coincides with the regularization of $F|_{\Omega '}$ in $\Omega '$, because small balls about a point of $\Omega '$ lie in $\Omega '$. If every $u_ t$ is identically $-\infty $ on $\Omega '$, then $F=F^*=-\infty $ there. Otherwise fix $t_0$ such that $u_{t_0}$ is nontrivial, hence locally integrable, on $\Omega '$. By lemma 3.4.1 , applied on $\Omega '$, there are indices $t_1,t_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k})^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$. Put $v_ j=\max \{ u_{t_0},u_{t_1},\ldots ,u_{t_ j}\} $ and $v=\sup _ jv_ j$. Since $\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k}\leq v\leq F$, we still have $v^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$. The functions $v_ j$ are subharmonic, increase with $j$, are uniformly bounded above on compact sets and satisfy $v_ j\geq u_{t_0}$; in particular, they are locally integrable on $\Omega '$. If $K\subset \Omega '$ is compact and $M$ bounds all $v_ j$ from above on $K$, then $0\leq M-v_ j\leq M-u_{t_0}$ on $K$ with $M-u_{t_0}$ integrable, and $M-v_ j$ decreases to $M-v$. Dominated convergence shows that $v$ is locally integrable and $v_ j	o v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega ')$, hence in the sense of distributions. As observed after theorem 3.2.2 , $v$ therefore has a canonical representative $w$: a subharmonic function on $\Omega '$ with $w=v$ almost everywhere. We claim that $w=v^*$. For each $j$ we have $v_ j\leq v$, so $v_ j*ho _\varepsilon \leq v*ho _\varepsilon =w*ho _\varepsilon $, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ in ( 3.3 ) gives $v_ j\leq w$ everywhere. Hence $v\leq w$, and $v^*\leq w$ because $w$ is upper semicontinuous. Conversely, by ( 3.3 ), $w(x)$ is the limit of the averages of $w$ over $B(x,r)$; these coincide with the averages of $v$, which are at most $\sup _{B(x,r)}v$. Letting $r\downarrow 0$ gives $w(x)\leq v^*(x)$. Thus $F^*=v^*=w$ is subharmonic on $\Omega '$. Finally, $v\leq F\leq F^*=w$ on $\Omega '$, and $v=w$ almost everywhere. The functions $v$ and $w$ are Borel measurable, so the set where $F
eq F^*$ is contained in the Borel null set $\{ v
eq w\} $. Since Lebesgue measure is complete, $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and $F=F^*$ almost everywhere. $\square$ Example 3.4.3 . Let $d\geq 2$. The fundamental solution $E_ d$ is negative on $B(0,1)$ and equals $-\infty $ at the origin. The functions $u_ j=\max \{ -1,E_ d/j\} $, $j\geq 1$, are subharmonic on $B(0,1)$, take values in $[-1,0)$ and increase with $j$. Their limit is $0$ on $B(0,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $ and $-1$ at the origin, whereas its upper semicontinuous regularization is identically zero. Thus even an increasing sequence of bounded subharmonic functions can have a limit that is not upper semicontinuous.

title: Lemma 3.4.1 (Choquet's lemma)
text: Lemma 3.4.1 (Choquet's lemma) . Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty family of functions $\Omega \to [-\infty ,\infty )$ that is locally uniformly bounded above, and let $F=\sup _{w\in \mathcal F}w$. Then there is a countable subfamily $\{ v_ j\} _{j\geq 1}\subset \mathcal F$ such that $v=\sup _ jv_ j$ satisfies $v^*=F^*$. Proof. Call $B(q,s)$ a rational ball if $q\in \mathbb Q^ d$ and $s$ is a positive rational number. Enumerate the rational balls $B$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ as $B_1,B_2,\ldots $, in such a way that each of them occurs infinitely often. Since $F$ is bounded above on the compact set $\overline{B_ j}$, we have $\sup _{B_ j}F<\infty $. If $\sup _{B_ j}F>-\infty $, choose $v_ j\in \mathcal F$ with $\sup _{B_ j}v_ j>\sup _{B_ j}F-1/j$; otherwise let $v_ j$ be any member of $\mathcal F$. Put $v=\sup _ jv_ j\leq F$. If $B$ is a rational ball with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, then $B=B_ j$ for infinitely many $j$, so $\sup _ Bv=\sup _ BF$. Every ball $B(x,r)$ contains a rational ball that contains $x$: choose $q\in \mathbb Q^ d$ with $|q-x|<r/3$ and a rational number $s\in (r/3,2r/3)$; then $x\in B(q,s)\subset B(x,r)$. Conversely, a rational ball $B(q,s)$ containing $x$ contains $B(x,s-|q-x|)$. Hence $F^*(x)$ is the infimum of $\sup _ BF$ over the rational balls $B\ni x$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, and similarly for $v^*(x)$. Therefore $v^*=F^*$. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.4.2
text: Theorem 3.4.2 . Let $\{ u_ t\} _{t\in I}$ be a family in $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ that is uniformly bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $, and let $F=\sup _ tu_ t$. Then $F^*$ is subharmonic. Moreover, $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and $F=F^*$ almost everywhere. The functions $F$ and $F^*$ need not coincide everywhere (example 3.4.3 ). Proof. If the family is empty, then $F=F^*=-\infty $. Otherwise, we replace the family by an increasing sequence, using Choquet's lemma, and identify the regularized limit of this sequence with a canonical representative. The connected components of $\Omega $ are open, because balls are connected; hence they are pairwise disjoint sets of positive Lebesgue measure, and there are at most countably many of them by lemma 1.1.5 . If every $u_ t$ is identically $-\infty $ on $\Omega '$, then $F=F^*=-\infty $ there. Otherwise fix $t_0$ such that $u_{t_0}$ is nontrivial, hence locally integrable, on $\Omega '$. By lemma 3.4.1 , applied on $\Omega '$, there are indices $t_1,t_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k})^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$. Put $v_ j=\max \{ u_{t_0},u_{t_1},\ldots ,u_{t_ j}\} $ and $v=\sup _ jv_ j$. Since $\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k}\leq v\leq F$, we still have $v^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$. The functions $v_ j$ are subharmonic, increase with $j$, are uniformly bounded above on compact sets and satisfy $v_ j\geq u_{t_0}$; in particular, they are locally integrable on $\Omega '$. If $K\subset \Omega '$ is compact and $M$ bounds all $v_ j$ from above on $K$, then $0\leq M-v_ j\leq M-u_{t_0}$ on $K$ with $M-u_{t_0}$ integrable, and $M-v_ j$ decreases to $M-v$. Dominated convergence shows that $v$ is locally integrable and $v_ j\to v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega ')$, hence in the sense of distributions. As observed after theorem 3.2.2 , $v$ therefore has a canonical representative $w$: a subharmonic function on $\Omega '$ with $w=v$ almost everywhere. We claim that $w=v^*$. For each $j$ we have $v_ j\leq v$, so $v_ j*\rho _\varepsilon \leq v*\rho _\varepsilon =w*\rho _\varepsilon $, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ in ( 3.3 ) gives $v_ j\leq w$ everywhere. Hence $v\leq w$, and $v^*\leq w$ because $w$ is upper semicontinuous. Conversely, by ( 3.3 ), $w(x)$ is the limit of the averages of $w$ over $B(x,r)$; these coincide with the averages of $v$, which are at most $\sup _{B(x,r)}v$. Letting $r\downarrow 0$ gives $w(x)\leq v^*(x)$. Thus $F^*=v^*=w$ is subharmonic on $\Omega '$. Finally, $v\leq F\leq F^*=w$ on $\Omega '$, and $v=w$ almost everywhere. The functions $v$ and $w$ are Borel measurable, so the set where $F\neq F^*$ is contained in the Borel null set $\{ v\neq w\} $. title: Example 3.4.3
text: Example 3.4.3 . Let $d\geq 2$. The fundamental solution $E_ d$ is negative on $B(0,1)$ and equals $-\infty $ at the origin. The functions $u_ j=\max \{ -1,E_ d/j\} $, $j\geq 1$, are subharmonic on $B(0,1)$, take values in $[-1,0)$ and increase with $j$. title: 3.5 Polar sets and removable singularities
text:
3.5 Polar sets and removable singularities The exceptional sets of potential theory are the sets that lie locally in the pole set of a nontrivial subharmonic function. They are Lebesgue null, and relatively closed ones are removable for subharmonic functions that are bounded above near them. Definition 3.5.1 . A set $A\subset \Omega $ is polar if every point of $A$ has a connected open neighborhood $V\subset \Omega $ on which there is a nontrivial $\psi \in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ with $A\cap V\subset \{ \psi =-\infty \} $. Every polar set $A$ has Lebesgue measure zero. Indeed, since $\mathbb R^ d$ has a countable base, $A$ is covered by countably many of the neighborhoods $V$ in the definition, and each $A\cap V$ lies in a pole set $\{ \psi =-\infty \} $, which is null by proposition 3.1.5 . Subsets of polar sets are polar. If $d\geq 2$, every one-point set $\{ a\} \subset \Omega $ is polar, since $E_ d(\cdot -a)$ is a nontrivial subharmonic function with a pole at $a$. If $d=1$, the only polar set is the empty set, because nontrivial subharmonic functions on intervals are finite (example 3.2.4 ). In particular, a Lebesgue null set need not be polar. Polar sets are the natural exceptional sets of the limit theorems above: for $d\geq 2$, theorem 4.4.4 in the next chapter shows that the set where $F
eq F^*$ in theorem 3.4.2 is not only Lebesgue null but polar. Theorem 3.5.2 . Let $A\subset \Omega $ be a relatively closed polar set, and let $u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega \setminus A)$ be bounded above on $K\setminus A$ for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $u$ has a unique subharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $; it is given on $A$ by \[  \widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{\Omega \setminus A
i y	o x}u(y).  \] If $\Omega $ is a domain, then $\Omega \setminus A$ is connected. Proof. Put $\widetilde u=u$ on $\Omega \setminus A$, and define $\widetilde u$ on $A$ by the displayed formula. Since $A$ has Lebesgue measure zero, it has no interior points, so every point of $A$ is a limit of points of $\Omega \setminus A$; together with the local upper bound for $u$, this shows that $\widetilde u(x)\in [-\infty ,\infty )$ is well defined for $x\in A$. We first show that $\widetilde u$ is upper semicontinuous and locally bounded above. On the open set $\Omega \setminus A$ both properties hold because $\widetilde u=u$ there. Let $x\in A$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. For $y\in A\cap B(x,r)$, the definition gives $\widetilde u(y)\leq \sup _{B(x,r)\setminus A}u$, hence \[  \sup _{B(x,r)}\widetilde u=\sup _{B(x,r)\setminus A}u.  \] The right-hand side is bounded above by hypothesis and tends to $\widetilde u(x)$ as $r\downarrow 0$, which proves both claims at $x$. Next we show that $\widetilde u$ is subharmonic near each point $x\in A$; near points of $\Omega \setminus A$ this holds because $\widetilde u=u$. The idea is to approximate $u$ from below by functions $u+\varepsilon \psi $ that tend to $-\infty $ at $A$. Let $V$ and $\psi $ be as in definition 3.5.1 . By proposition 3.1.5 , $\psi $ is locally integrable on the connected set $V$, so it is not identically $-\infty $ on any ball in $V$, and its pole set $\{ \psi =-\infty \} $ is a null set. Replacing $V$ by a ball centered at $x$ whose closure lies in $V$, and $\psi $ by $\psi $ minus an upper bound on that ball, we may therefore assume that $V$ is a ball, that $\psi \leq 0$ on $V$, and that $\psi $ is nontrivial on $V$. For $\varepsilon >0$ define $v_\varepsilon =u+\varepsilon \psi $ on $V\setminus A$ and $v_\varepsilon =-\infty $ on $A\cap V$. On the open set $V\setminus A$, $v_\varepsilon $ is subharmonic. At a point $y\in A\cap V$, $u$ is bounded above near $y$, and $\psi (z)	o -\infty $ as $z	o y$ because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous with $\psi (y)=-\infty $; hence $v_\varepsilon (z)	o -\infty $ as $z	o y$. So $v_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous at $y$, and the submean inequality at $y$ holds because $v_\varepsilon (y)=-\infty $. Thus $v_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{SH}(V)$. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the functions $v_\varepsilon $ increase because $\psi \leq 0$, and they are bounded above by $u$ on $V\setminus A$, hence uniformly bounded above on compact subsets of $V$. By theorem 3.4.2 , the regularized supremum $w=(\sup _{\varepsilon >0}v_\varepsilon )^*$ is subharmonic on $V$ and equals $\sup _{\varepsilon >0}v_\varepsilon $ almost everywhere. This supremum equals $u$ on $V\setminus (A\cup \{ \psi =-\infty \} )$, so $w=u$ almost everywhere on $V\setminus A$. Since $w$ and $u$ are subharmonic on the open set $V\setminus A$, they agree everywhere there by theorem 3.2.2 (2). It remains to show that $w=\widetilde u$ on $A\cap V$. Let $y\in A\cap V$. Since $w$ is upper semicontinuous and $w=u$ on $V\setminus A$, we have $w(y)\geq \varlimsup _{V\setminus A
i z	o y}u(z)=\widetilde u(y)$. Conversely, by ( 3.3 ), $w(y)$ is the limit of the averages of $w$ over $B(y,r)$. Since $A$ is null and $w=u$ off $A$, these averages are at most $\sup _{B(y,r)\setminus A}u$, which tends to $\widetilde u(y)$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Hence $\widetilde u=w$ on $V$, and $\widetilde u$ is subharmonic on $V$. This proves that $\widetilde u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. For uniqueness, let $u'\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ agree with $u$ on $\Omega \setminus A$. Since $A$ is null, $u'=\widetilde u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega $, and hence everywhere by theorem 3.2.2 (2). Finally, let $\Omega $ be a domain, and suppose that $\Omega \setminus A$ is the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets $W_0$ and $W_1$. The function $g$ equal to $0$ on $W_0$ and to $1$ on $W_1$ is harmonic, hence subharmonic, and bounded on $\Omega \setminus A$. Its subharmonic extension $\widetilde g$ to $\Omega $ takes values in $[0,1]$ and equals $1$ on $W_1$, so it attains the finite maximum $1$. By proposition 3.1.4 , $\widetilde g$ is identically $1$ on $\Omega $, contradicting $\widetilde g=0$ on $W_0$. $\square$

title: Definition 3.5.1
text: Definition 3.5.1 . A set $A\subset \Omega $ is polar if every point of $A$ has a connected open neighborhood $V\subset \Omega $ on which there is a nontrivial $\psi \in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ with $A\cap V\subset \{ \psi =-\infty \} $.

title: Theorem 3.5.2
text: Theorem 3.5.2 . Let $A\subset \Omega $ be a relatively closed polar set, and let $u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega \setminus A)$ be bounded above on $K\setminus A$ for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $u$ has a unique subharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $; it is given on $A$ by \[  \widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{\Omega \setminus A\ni y\to x}u(y).  \] If $\Omega $ is a domain, then $\Omega \setminus A$ is connected. Proof. Put $\widetilde u=u$ on $\Omega \setminus A$, and define $\widetilde u$ on $A$ by the displayed formula. Since $A$ has Lebesgue measure zero, it has no interior points, so every point of $A$ is a limit of points of $\Omega \setminus A$; together with the local upper bound for $u$, this shows that $\widetilde u(x)\in [-\infty ,\infty )$ is well defined for $x\in A$. We first show that $\widetilde u$ is upper semicontinuous and locally bounded above. On the open set $\Omega \setminus A$ both properties hold because $\widetilde u=u$ there. Let $x\in A$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. For $y\in A\cap B(x,r)$, the definition gives $\widetilde u(y)\leq \sup _{B(x,r)\setminus A}u$, hence \[  \sup _{B(x,r)}\widetilde u=\sup _{B(x,r)\setminus A}u.  \] The right-hand side is bounded above by hypothesis and tends to $\widetilde u(x)$ as $r\downarrow 0$, which proves both claims at $x$. Next we show that $\widetilde u$ is subharmonic near each point $x\in A$; near points of $\Omega \setminus A$ this holds because $\widetilde u=u$. The idea is to approximate $u$ from below by functions $u+\varepsilon \psi $ that tend to $-\infty $ at $A$. Let $V$ and $\psi $ be as in definition 3.5.1 . By proposition 3.1.5 , $\psi $ is locally integrable on the connected set $V$, so it is not identically $-\infty $ on any ball in $V$, and its pole set $\{ \psi =-\infty \} $ is a null set. Replacing $V$ by a ball centered at $x$ whose closure lies in $V$, and $\psi $ by $\psi $ minus an upper bound on that ball, we may therefore assume that $V$ is a ball, that $\psi \leq 0$ on $V$, and that $\psi $ is nontrivial on $V$. For $\varepsilon >0$ define $v_\varepsilon =u+\varepsilon \psi $ on $V\setminus A$ and $v_\varepsilon =-\infty $ on $A\cap V$. On the open set $V\setminus A$, $v_\varepsilon $ is subharmonic. At a point $y\in A\cap V$, $u$ is bounded above near $y$, and $\psi (z)\to -\infty $ as $z\to y$ because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous with $\psi (y)=-\infty $; hence $v_\varepsilon (z)\to -\infty $ as $z\to y$. So $v_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous at $y$, and the submean inequality at $y$ holds because $v_\varepsilon (y)=-\infty $. Thus $v_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{SH}(V)$. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the functions $v_\varepsilon $ increase because $\psi \leq 0$, and they are bounded above by $u$ on $V\setminus A$, hence uniformly bounded above on compact subsets of $V$. By theorem 3.4.2 , the regularized supremum $w=(\sup _{\varepsilon >0}v_\varepsilon )^*$ is subharmonic on $V$ and equals $\sup _{\varepsilon >0}v_\varepsilon $ almost everywhere. This supremum equals $u$ on $V\setminus (A\cup \{ \psi =-\infty \} )$, so $w=u$ almost everywhere on $V\setminus A$. Since $w$ and $u$ are subharmonic on the open set $V\setminus A$, they agree everywhere there by theorem 3.2.2 (2). It remains to show that $w=\widetilde u$ on $A\cap V$. Let $y\in A\cap V$. Since $w$ is upper semicontinuous and $w=u$ on $V\setminus A$, we have $w(y)\geq \varlimsup _{V\setminus A\ni z\to y}u(z)=\widetilde u(y)$. Conversely, by ( 3.3 ), $w(y)$ is the limit of the averages of $w$ over $B(y,r)$. Since $A$ is null and $w=u$ off $A$, these averages are at most $\sup _{B(y,r)\setminus A}u$, which tends to $\widetilde u(y)$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Hence $\widetilde u=w$ on $V$, and $\widetilde u$ is subharmonic on $V$. This proves that $\widetilde u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. For uniqueness, let $u'\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ agree with $u$ on $\Omega \setminus A$. Since $A$ is null, $u'=\widetilde u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega $, and hence everywhere by theorem 3.2.2 (2). Finally, let $\Omega $ be a domain, and suppose that $\Omega \setminus A$ is the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets $W_0$ and $W_1$. The function $g$ equal to $0$ on $W_0$ and to $1$ on $W_1$ is harmonic, hence subharmonic, and bounded on $\Omega \setminus A$. Its subharmonic extension $\widetilde g$ to $\Omega $ takes values in $[0,1]$ and equals $1$ on $W_1$, so it attains the finite maximum $1$. By proposition 3.1.4 , $\widetilde g$ is identically $1$ on $\Omega $, contradicting $\widetilde g=0$ on $W_0$. $\square$

title: 4 Potentials, energy and capacity
text: 4 Potentials, energy and capacity Polar sets were introduced in section 3.5 as the sets that lie locally in the pole set of a nontrivial subharmonic function. Every polar set has Lebesgue measure zero, but the converse fails: a sphere is a Lebesgue null set, yet its normalized surface measure has a bounded potential (example 4.3.6 ), and we shall see that this prevents the sphere from being polar. In this chapter we introduce two quantities adapted to the Laplacian, the energy of a measure and the capacity of a set. They characterize the polar sets, and they show that the exceptional sets of the limit theorems of chapter 3 are polar. The energy of a positive measure is the integral of its potential against the measure itself. The Newtonian kernel, and the logarithmic kernel on measures of total mass zero, define positive definite energies, and minimizing the energy over the probability measures on a compact set gives its equilibrium measure. Measures with finite continuous potentials give no mass to polar sets, and by the continuity principle (theorem 4.2.2 ) every compactly supported measure whose potential is finite almost everywhere with respect to the measure itself is a countable sum of such measures. We also construct a polar Cantor set carrying an atom-free probability measure (proposition 4.2.4 ); this measure reappears in example 15.3.8 . Capacity is defined by an extremal problem for subharmonic functions. For a compact set $K$ in a ball $B$, let $u_ K$ be the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of all nonpositive subharmonic functions on $B$ that are at most $-1$ on $K$. The relative capacity $C_ B(K)$ is the total mass of the Riesz measure of $u_ K$. A compact set is nonpolar if and only if it carries a nonzero measure of finite energy, if and only if its relative capacity is positive (theorem 4.3.3 ). With Choquet's capacitability theorem this extends to arbitrary sets with compact closure in $B$: such a set is polar if and only if its outer capacity vanishes (corollary 4.4.2 ). The main application, theorem 4.4.4 , has two parts. If subharmonic functions $v_ j$ converge to $v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then the inequality $\varlimsup _ jv_ j\leq v$ of Hartogs' lemma (theorem 3.3.3 ) is an equality outside a polar set. Moreover, the upper envelope of a family of subharmonic functions that is locally uniformly bounded above agrees with its upper semicontinuous regularization outside a polar set, which sharpens theorem 3.4.2 . The chapter closes with the Dirichlet energy of Green potentials and the quasi-continuity of subharmonic functions. Throughout this chapter $d\geq 2$; in dimension one the empty set is the only polar set (section 3.5 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.4 .

title: 4.1 Kernel energies and equilibrium measures
text:
4.1 Kernel energies and equilibrium measures Recall the fundamental solution $E_ d$ of ( 2.9 ), the kernel $\Gamma _ d=-E_ d$ of $-\Delta $, and the area $s_{d-1}$ of the unit sphere. For energy estimates we need kernels that are nonnegative on the sets under consideration, so we fix a compact set $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$. For $d\geq 3$ we put \[  k(x,y)=\Gamma _ d(x-y)= rac{|x-y|^{2-d}}{(d-2)s_{d-1}}.  \] In dimension two we fix a scale $D>\operatorname {diam}K$ and put \[  k_ D(x,y)= rac{1}{2\pi }\log  rac{D}{|x-y|}=\Gamma _2(x-y)+ rac{\log D}{2\pi }.  \] Both kernels equal $+\infty $ on the diagonal and are nonnegative on $K	imes K$. By a measure on $K$ we mean a finite positive Borel measure on $\mathbb R^ d$ supported on $K$; it is a Radon measure by proposition 1.1.2 . The potential and the energy of such a measure $\mu $ are \[  U^\mu (x)=\int k(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y),\qquad I(\mu )=\iint k(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (x)\, \mathrm d\mu (y),  \] with $k_ D$ in place of $k$ when $d=2$; when the scale must be specified, we write $I_ D$. We call $U^\mu $ and $I(\mu )$ the Newtonian potential and the Newtonian energy of $\mu $ if $d\geq 3$, and its logarithmic potential and logarithmic energy if $d=2$. For two measures $\mu $ and $
u $ on $K$, their mutual energy is $I(\mu ,
u )=\iint k(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (x)\, \mathrm d
u (y)$. The same integrals define the energy and the mutual energy of finite signed measures on $K$ whenever the kernel is integrable for the product of the total variations. The potential $U^\mu $ is lower semicontinuous on $\mathbb R^ d$: the kernel is a lower semicontinuous function of $x$ with values in $(-\infty ,\infty ]$, and it is bounded below for $x$ in a compact set and $y\in K$, so Fatou's lemma applies after adding a constant. Moreover, $U^\mu $ is related to the fundamental potential $E_ d*\mu $ of proposition 3.2.1 by $U^\mu =-E_ d*\mu $ if $d\geq 3$ and $U^\mu =-E_2*\mu +(2\pi )^{-1}\mu (K)\log D$ if $d=2$. Replacing $D$ by another scale $D'>\operatorname {diam}K$ adds $(2\pi )^{-1}\mu (K)^2\log (D'/D)$ to the energy; in particular, whether $\mu $ has finite energy does not depend on the scale. Fundamental potentials satisfy a reciprocity law. Let $\mu $ and $
u $ be finite positive measures with compact supports, and let $M$ be an upper bound of $E_ d$ on the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\mu -\operatorname{Supp}
u $. Applying Tonelli's theorem to the function $(x,y)\mapsto M-E_ d(x-y)$, which is nonnegative on $\operatorname{Supp}\mu 	imes \operatorname{Supp}
u $, using $E_ d(-z)=E_ d(z)$ and subtracting the finite number $M\mu (\mathbb R^ d)
u (\mathbb R^ d)$, we obtain 4.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:potential-reciprocity} \int (E_ d*
u )\, \mathrm d\mu =\int (E_ d*\mu )\, \mathrm d
u , \end{equation} where both sides lie in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. The positivity of the energy rests on the Gaussian kernels $\mathrm e^{-t|x-y|^2}$, $t>0$: each of them is an $L^2$ inner product of two Gaussians, and both $k$ and $k_ D$ are obtained from them by integration in $t$. Hence, for $\sigma ,	au \in \mathcal E$, the quadratic polynomial $s\mapsto I(\sigma +s	au )=I(\sigma )+2sI(\sigma ,	au )+s^2I(	au )$ is nonnegative on $\mathbb R$. Its discriminant is therefore nonpositive, which is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $I(\sigma ,	au )^2\leq I(\sigma )I(	au )$. $\square$

Theorem 4.1.3 . Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a compact set that carries a probability measure of finite energy; when $d=2$, the scale $D>\operatorname {diam}K$ is fixed. Then there is a unique probability measure $\mu _ K$ on $K$ of minimal energy, the equilibrium measure of $K$. Put $V(K)=I(\mu _ K)$, and $V_ D(K)=I_ D(\mu _ K)$ when $d=2$. Every probability measure $

u )\geq V(K)  \] (with $I_ D$ and $V_ D(K)$ when $d=2$). If $d\geq 3$, then $V(K)>0$, and the Newtonian capacity of $K$ is defined to be $1/V(K)$. If $d=2$, the logarithmic capacity of $K$ is defined to be $D\mathrm e^{-2\pi V_ D(K)}$; neither $\mu _ K$ nor this number depends on $D$. If $K$ carries no probability measure of finite energy, in particular if $K=\varnothing $, its Newtonian or logarithmic capacity is defined to be zero. Proof. Existence. Let $\mu _ j$ be probability measures on $K$ whose energies converge to the infimum $m$, which is finite by hypothesis. By theorem 1.5.5 , after passing to a subsequence, $\mu _ j$ converges vaguely to a Radon measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb R^ d$. By proposition 1.5.2 , applied to the open set $\mathbb R^ d\setminus K$, we have $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus K)\leq \varliminf _ j\mu _ j(\mathbb R^ d\setminus K)=0$, so $\mu $ is carried by $K$; testing against a function in $C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$ equal to one on $K$ then shows that $\mu (K)=1$. To prove that $I(\mu )\leq m$, we first show that \[  \iint F\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\longrightarrow \iint F\, \mathrm d\mu \, \mathrm d\mu  \] for every continuous function $F$ on $\mathbb R^ d	imes \mathbb R^ d$. Given $\delta >0$, cover $K$ by finitely many balls $B(x_ i,\delta )$ with $x_ i\in K$. By lemma 1.4.2 , there are functions $0\leq \varphi _ i\in C_ c^\infty (B(x_ i,\delta ))$ with $\sum _ i\varphi _ i=1$ on $K$. For $x,y\in K$, a term $\varphi _ i(x)\varphi _ l(y)$ is nonzero only if $|x-x_ i|<\delta $ and $|y-x_ l|<\delta $, so \[  \Bigl |F(x,y)-\sum _{i,l}F(x_ i,x_ l)\varphi _ i(x)\varphi _ l(y)\Bigr |\leq \omega (2\delta ),  \] where $\omega $ is the modulus of continuity of $F$ on $K	imes K$. The double integrals of the finite sums converge, since $\int \varphi _ i\, \mathrm d\mu _ j	o \int \varphi _ i\, \mathrm d\mu $. As all the measures are probability measures carried by $K$ and $\omega (2\delta )	o 0$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$, this proves the asserted convergence. For $n>0$, the truncated kernel $\min \{ k,n\} $ is continuous on $\mathbb R^ d	imes \mathbb R^ d$, including the diagonal, and it increases to $k$ as $n	o \infty $. Hence $\mu $ is a minimizer. Uniqueness. Let $\mu $ and $\mu '$ be minimizers. The signed measure $\sigma =\mu -\mu '$ has total mass zero. Since $|\sigma |\leq \mu +\mu '$, its positive and negative parts satisfy $\sigma ^+= rac12(|\sigma |+\sigma )\leq \mu $ and $\sigma ^-\leq \mu '$, so they have finite energy, the kernel being nonnegative on $K	imes K$. All mutual energies are finite by proposition 4.1.2 , so we may expand and obtain \[  I igl (	frac 12(\mu +\mu ') igr )=	frac 12I(\mu )+	frac 12I(\mu ')-	frac 14I(\sigma )=m-	frac 14I(\sigma ).  \] Since $ rac12(\mu +\mu ')$ is a probability measure on $K$, this energy is at least $m$, so $I(\sigma )\leq 0$. By proposition 4.1.2 , $\sigma =0$. The inequality. Let $

The kernel is at least $((d-2)s_{d-1})^{-1}(\operatorname {diam}K)^{2-d}>0$ on $K	imes K$, hence $V(K)>0$. Let $d=2$. title: 4.2 Continuous potentials and polar sets
text:
4.2 Continuous potentials and polar sets To relate energy to polarity we need measures whose fundamental potentials $E_ d*\mu $, or equivalently whose potentials $U^\mu $, are finite and continuous. We show that such measures are plentiful: every compactly supported measure whose potential is finite almost everywhere with respect to the measure itself is a countable sum of them. We begin with a version of Lusin's theorem. Lemma 4.2.1 . Let $\mu $ be a finite Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ d$, and let $f$ be a Borel function with values in $[-\infty ,\infty ]$ that is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. Then for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a compact set $L$ with $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus L)<\varepsilon $ such that $f$ is finite on $L$ and the restriction $f|_ L$ is continuous. Proof. The sets $\{ |f|>N\} $ decrease to the $\mu $-null set $\{ |f|=\infty \} $ as $N	o \infty $, and $\mu $ is finite, so we can choose $N$ with $\mu (\{ |f|>N\} )<\varepsilon /3$. The truncation $f_ N=\max \{ -N,\min \{ f,N\} \} $ is bounded, hence belongs to $L^1(\mu )$. By proposition 1.2.3 there are continuous functions $g_ j$, $j\geq 1$, with $\int |g_ j-f_ N|\, \mathrm d\mu <\varepsilon 2^{-2j}/3$. By Chebyshev's inequality, the set $E_ j=\{ |g_ j-f_ N|>2^{-j}\} $ satisfies $\mu (E_ j)<\varepsilon 2^{-j}/3$, so $\mu ( igcup _ jE_ j)<\varepsilon /3$. On the Borel set $F=\mathbb R^ d\setminus (\{ |f|>N\} \cup  igcup _ jE_ j)$ we have $f=f_ N$ and $|g_ j-f|\leq 2^{-j}$ for every $j$, so $g_ j	o f$ uniformly on $F$. Since $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus F)<2\varepsilon /3$, inner regularity gives a compact set $L\subset F$ with $\mu (F\setminus L)<\varepsilon /3$. Then $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus L)<\varepsilon $, and $f|_ L$ is finite and continuous as a uniform limit of continuous functions. $\square$ Theorem 4.2.2 . Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be compact, let $\mu $ be a finite positive measure on $\mathbb R^ d$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\mu \subset K$, and put $p=E_ d*\mu $. If $x\in K$ and the restriction $p|_ K$ is continuous at $x$, then $p$ is continuous at $x$ as a function on $\mathbb R^ d$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. If $p$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, then $\mu =\sum _ j\mu _ j$, where the $\mu _ j$ are the restrictions of $\mu $ to pairwise disjoint compact sets and every $E_ d*\mu _ j$ is finite and continuous on $\mathbb R^ d$. Proof. (1) Since $p$ is upper semicontinuous (proposition 3.2.1 ), $\varlimsup _{z	o x}p(z)\leq p(x)$; in particular $p$ is continuous at $x$ if $p(x)=-\infty $. Assume that $p(x)$ is finite; we must show that $\varliminf _{z	o x}p(z)\geq p(x)$. For $z\in \mathbb R^ d$ choose a point $z'\in K$ closest to $z$. Then $|z'-x|\leq |z'-z|+|z-x|\leq 2|z-x|$, so $z'	o x$ as $z	o x$, and $|z'-y|\leq |z'-z|+|z-y|\leq 2|z-y|$ for every $y\in K$. Consequently, for $y\in K$, \[  E_ d(z-y)\geq 2^{d-2}E_ d(z'-y)\quad (d\geq 3),\qquad E_2(z-y)\geq E_2(z'-y)- rac{\log 2}{2\pi }\quad (d=2).  \] Fix $\delta >0$ and split $p=p'_\delta +p''_\delta $, where $p'_\delta (w)=\int _{B(x,\delta )}E_ d(w-y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)$ is the near part and $p''_\delta $ the far part. The far part is continuous at $x$, since $E_ d(w-y)	o E_ d(x-y)$ uniformly for $y\in K$ with $|y-x|\geq \delta $ as $w	o x$, by the uniform continuity of $E_ d$ on compact subsets of $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $. The near part, restricted to $K$, is continuous at $x$, being the difference of $p|_ K$ and $p''_\delta |_ K$. Since $\mu $ is carried by $K$, we may integrate the inequalities above with respect to $\mu $ over $B(x,\delta )$; letting $z	o x$, we obtain for $d\geq 3$ \[  \varliminf _{z	o x}p(z)\geq p''_\delta (x)+2^{d-2}\lim _{z	o x}p'_\delta (z')=p(x)+(2^{d-2}-1)p'_\delta (x),  \] and for $d=2$ the bound $\varliminf _{z	o x}p(z)\geq p(x)-(2\pi )^{-1}\mu (B(x,\delta ))\log 2$. Since $p(x)$ is finite, the function $E_ d(x-\cdot )$ is $\mu $-integrable and $\mu (\{ x\} )=0$. By dominated convergence and continuity of $\mu $ from above, $p'_\delta (x)	o 0$ and $\mu (B(x,\delta ))	o 0$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$, which proves $\varliminf _{z	o x}p(z)\geq p(x)$. u _ j$ has mass less than $2^{-j}$, so $\mu =\sum _ j\mu _ j$. $\square$ Since the definition of polarity is local, a subset of an open set $\Omega $ is polar in $\Omega $ if and only if it is polar in $\mathbb R^ d$. Indeed, if $\psi $ is a nontrivial subharmonic function on a connected open set $V$, as in definition 3.5.1 , then its restriction to every ball contained in $V$ is nontrivial, because $\psi $ is locally integrable on $V$ (proposition 3.1.5 ). Hence the neighborhoods in definition 3.5.1 may be shrunk to balls contained in $\Omega $. We therefore speak simply of polar sets. The next result shows that a bounded polar set lies in the pole set of a single potential. Proposition 4.2.3 . If $A\subset \mathbb R^ d$ is polar and has compact closure, there is a finite positive measure $

By definition 3.5.1 , after shrinking the neighborhood as explained above, there are an open ball $V\subset W$ centered at $a$ and a nontrivial function $\psi \in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ with $A\cap V\subset \{ \psi =-\infty \} $; by proposition 3.1.5 , $\psi $ is locally integrable. Choose an open ball $B_ a$ centered at $a$ with $\overline{B_ a}\subset V$, and a cutoff $\eta \in C_ c^\infty (V)$ with $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ and $\eta =1$ near $\overline{B_ a}$. By the Riesz decomposition (theorem 3.2.3 ), $\psi =E_ d*(\eta \mu _\psi )+h$ on $B_ a$, where $\mu _\psi $ is the Riesz measure of $\psi $ and $h$ is harmonic, hence finite; therefore $E_ d*(\eta \mu _\psi )=-\infty $ on $A\cap B_ a$. The measure $\eta \mu _\psi $ is finite, positive and supported in $\overline W$. Since $\mathbb R^ d$ has a countable base, countably many of the balls $B_ a$ cover $A$. Let $

Now let $A= igcup _ kA_ k$ with polar sets $A_ k$, let $x\in \mathbb R^ d$, and let $B'$ be an open ball centered at $x$. Apply the construction above to the bounded polar sets $A_ k\cap B'$, with one and the same bounded open set $W\supset \overline{B'}$. It gives measures $

The next proposition constructs a polar Cantor set carrying an atom-free probability measure whose fundamental potential equals $-\infty $ at every point of the set. Proposition 4.2.4 . There are a compact Cantor set $K\subset [0,1/10]\subset \mathbb C$ and an atom-free probability measure $\mu $ supported on $K$ such that \[  p(z)=\int _ K\log |z-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)  \] is locally integrable and subharmonic on $\mathbb C$, finite and harmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus K$, and equal to $-\infty $ at every point of $K$. In particular, $K$ is polar and $\mu $ has infinite logarithmic energy. Proof. The set. Put $a_ j=\mathrm e^{-4^ j}$ for $j\geq 1$, and let $K$ be the set of all sums $\sum _{j\geq 1}\varepsilon _ ja_ j$ with $\varepsilon _ j\in \{ 0,1\} $. Since $a_{j+1}/a_ j=\mathrm e^{-3\cdot 4^ j}\leq \mathrm e^{-12}<1/2$, the tails $R_ k=\sum _{j>k}a_ j$ satisfy \[  R_ k\leq a_{k+1}\sum _{i\geq 0}2^{-i}=2a_{k+1}\quad (k\geq 0),\qquad 2a_{k+1}<a_ k\quad (k\geq 1).  \] In particular $K\subset [0,R_0]\subset [0,2\mathrm e^{-4}]\subset [0,1/10]$. Let $\mathcal S=\prod _{j\geq 1}\{ 0,1\} $ carry the product topology, and let $c\colon \mathcal S	o \mathbb R$ be the coding map $c(\varepsilon )=\sum _ j\varepsilon _ ja_ j$. If $\varepsilon $ and $\varepsilon '$ agree in their first $k$ digits, then $|c(\varepsilon )-c(\varepsilon ')|\leq R_ k$; hence $c$ is continuous, and $K=c(\mathcal S)$ is compact by lemma 1.6.2 . If $\varepsilon $ and $\varepsilon '$ first differ at the $k$-th digit, say $\varepsilon _ k=1$ and $\varepsilon '_ k=0$, then $c(\varepsilon )-c(\varepsilon ')\geq a_ k-R_ k>0$; hence $c$ is injective. For a word $\sigma \in \{ 0,1\} ^ k$, let $K_\sigma $ be the image of the sequences beginning with $\sigma $. The $2^ k$ sets $K_\sigma $ are compact, pairwise disjoint by injectivity, cover $K$, and have diameter at most $R_ k$. Consequently each $K_\sigma $ is open and closed in $K$, and two distinct points of $K$ lie in different sets $K_\sigma $ once $k$ is large; thus $K$ is totally disconnected. Changing the $k$-th digit of $\varepsilon $ produces a point of $K$ different from $c(\varepsilon )$ at distance $a_ k$, so $K$ has no isolated points. Hence $K$ is a Cantor set: a nonempty compact metric space that is totally disconnected and has no isolated points. The measure. For $t\in [0,1)$ let $\varepsilon _ j(t)$ be its binary digits, using the terminating expansion at dyadic rationals, and put $\Phi (t)=\sum _ j\varepsilon _ j(t)a_ j$. Each $\varepsilon _ j$ is a Borel step function, so $\Phi $ is Borel as a uniform limit of Borel functions. Let $\mu $ be the image of Lebesgue measure on $[0,1)$ under $\Phi $. It is a probability measure carried by the compact set $K$, and it is a Radon measure by proposition 1.1.2 . For $\sigma \in \{ 0,1\} ^ k$, injectivity of $c$ shows that $\Phi (t)\in K_\sigma $ if and only if the first $k$ binary digits of $t$ form the word $\sigma $, and this happens exactly on a dyadic interval of length $2^{-k}$. Hence $\mu (K_\sigma )=2^{-k}$. Every $x\in K$ lies in one of the sets $K_\sigma $ with $\sigma $ of length $k$, so $\mu (\{ x\} )\leq 2^{-k}$ for every $k$; thus $\mu $ has no atoms. The potential. Since $\log |z-a|^2=4\pi E_2(z-a)$, we have $p=4\pi E_2*\mu $, which is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\mathbb C$ by proposition 3.2.1 . Let $z_0
otin K$ and $\delta = rac12\operatorname {dist}(z_0,K)$. For $|z-z_0|<\delta $ and $a\in K$, the kernel and all its derivatives in $z$ are bounded uniformly, so differentiation under the integral sign shows that $p$ is smooth on $B(z_0,\delta )$ with $\Delta p(z)=\int \Delta _ z\log |z-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)=0$. Thus $p$ is finite and harmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus K$. Polarity. Let $x\in K$ and $k\geq 1$, and let $K_\sigma $, with $\sigma $ of length $k$, be the piece containing $x$. Since $\operatorname {diam}K\leq R_0<1$, every term $\log |x-a|^2$ with $a\in K$ is nonpositive, and for $a\in K_\sigma $ we have $|x-a|\leq R_ k\leq 2a_{k+1}$. Consequently \[  p(x)\leq \int _{K_\sigma }\log |x-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)\leq \mu (K_\sigma )\log  igl (4a_{k+1}^2 igr ) =2^{-k} igl (\log 4-2\cdot 4^{k+1} igr ).  \] The right side tends to $-\infty $ as $k	o \infty $, so $p(x)=-\infty $. Since $p$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb C$ and not identically $-\infty $, the set $K$ is polar. For $D>\operatorname {diam}K$, the logarithmic potential of the probability measure $\mu $ is $U^\mu =(2\pi )^{-1}\log D-p/(4\pi )$, which equals $+\infty $ on $K$. Since $\mu $ is carried by $K$, Tonelli's theorem gives $I_ D(\mu )=\int U^\mu \, \mathrm d\mu =+\infty $. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.2.1
text: Lemma 4.2.1 . Let $\mu $ be a finite Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ d$, and let $f$ be a Borel function with values in $[-\infty ,\infty ]$ that is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. Then for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a compact set $L$ with $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus L)<\varepsilon $ such that $f$ is finite on $L$ and the restriction $f|_ L$ is continuous. Proof. The sets $\{ |f|>N\} $ decrease to the $\mu $-null set $\{ |f|=\infty \} $ as $N\to \infty $, and $\mu $ is finite, so we can choose $N$ with $\mu (\{ |f|>N\} )<\varepsilon /3$. The truncation $f_ N=\max \{ -N,\min \{ f,N\} \} $ is bounded, hence belongs to $L^1(\mu )$. By proposition 1.2.3 there are continuous functions $g_ j$, $j\geq 1$, with $\int |g_ j-f_ N|\, \mathrm d\mu <\varepsilon 2^{-2j}/3$. By Chebyshev's inequality, the set $E_ j=\{ |g_ j-f_ N|>2^{-j}\} $ satisfies $\mu (E_ j)<\varepsilon 2^{-j}/3$, so $\mu (\bigcup _ jE_ j)<\varepsilon /3$. On the Borel set $F=\mathbb R^ d\setminus (\{ |f|>N\} \cup \bigcup _ jE_ j)$ we have $f=f_ N$ and $|g_ j-f|\leq 2^{-j}$ for every $j$, so $g_ j\to f$ uniformly on $F$. Since $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus F)<2\varepsilon /3$, inner regularity gives a compact set $L\subset F$ with $\mu (F\setminus L)<\varepsilon /3$. Then $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus L)<\varepsilon $, and $f|_ L$ is finite and continuous as a uniform limit of continuous functions. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.2.2
text:
Theorem 4.2.2 . Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be compact, let $\mu $ be a finite positive measure on $\mathbb R^ d$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\mu \subset K$, and put $p=E_ d*\mu $. If $x\in K$ and the restriction $p|_ K$ is continuous at $x$, then $p$ is continuous at $x$ as a function on $\mathbb R^ d$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. If $p$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, then $\mu =\sum _ j\mu _ j$, where the $\mu _ j$ are the restrictions of $\mu $ to pairwise disjoint compact sets and every $E_ d*\mu _ j$ is finite and continuous on $\mathbb R^ d$. Proof. (1) Since $p$ is upper semicontinuous (proposition 3.2.1 ), $\varlimsup _{z	o x}p(z)\leq p(x)$; in particular $p$ is continuous at $x$ if $p(x)=-\infty $. Assume that $p(x)$ is finite; we must show that $\varliminf _{z	o x}p(z)\geq p(x)$. For $z\in \mathbb R^ d$ choose a point $z'\in K$ closest to $z$. Then $|z'-x|\leq |z'-z|+|z-x|\leq 2|z-x|$, so $z'	o x$ as $z	o x$, and $|z'-y|\leq |z'-z|+|z-y|\leq 2|z-y|$ for every $y\in K$. Consequently, for $y\in K$, \[  E_ d(z-y)\geq 2^{d-2}E_ d(z'-y)\quad (d\geq 3),\qquad E_2(z-y)\geq E_2(z'-y)- rac{\log 2}{2\pi }\quad (d=2).  \] Fix $\delta >0$ and split $p=p'_\delta +p''_\delta $, where $p'_\delta (w)=\int _{B(x,\delta )}E_ d(w-y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)$ is the near part and $p''_\delta $ the far part. The far part is continuous at $x$, since $E_ d(w-y)	o E_ d(x-y)$ uniformly for $y\in K$ with $|y-x|\geq \delta $ as $w	o x$, by the uniform continuity of $E_ d$ on compact subsets of $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $. The near part, restricted to $K$, is continuous at $x$, being the difference of $p|_ K$ and $p''_\delta |_ K$. Since $\mu $ is carried by $K$, we may integrate the inequalities above with respect to $\mu $ over $B(x,\delta )$; letting $z	o x$, we obtain for $d\geq 3$ \[  \varliminf _{z	o x}p(z)\geq p''_\delta (x)+2^{d-2}\lim _{z	o x}p'_\delta (z')=p(x)+(2^{d-2}-1)p'_\delta (x),  \] and for $d=2$ the bound $\varliminf _{z	o x}p(z)\geq p(x)-(2\pi )^{-1}\mu (B(x,\delta ))\log 2$. Since $p(x)$ is finite, the function $E_ d(x-\cdot )$ is $\mu $-integrable and $\mu (\{ x\} )=0$. By dominated convergence and continuity of $\mu $ from above, $p'_\delta (x)	o 0$ and $\mu (B(x,\delta ))	o 0$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$, which proves $\varliminf _{z	o x}p(z)\geq p(x)$. title: Proposition 4.2.3
text:
Proposition 4.2.3 . If $A\subset \mathbb R^ d$ is polar and has compact closure, there is a finite positive measure $
