u _ j$ converge vaguely with supports in $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. All these integrals are finite, since $E_ d*\sigma $ is bounded on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. Adding the integrals of $h_ j$, which converge to $\int h\, \mathrm d\sigma $, proves that $\int v_ j\, \mathrm d\sigma 	o \int v\, \mathrm d\sigma >-\infty $. By Hartogs' lemma (theorem 3.3.3 ), $\varlimsup _ jv_ j\leq v$ everywhere, and the $v_ j$ are bounded above on $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $ by a common constant for large $j$. Reverse Fatou's lemma therefore gives \[  \int \varlimsup _ jv_ j\, \mathrm d\sigma \geq \lim _ j\int v_ j\, \mathrm d\sigma =\int v\, \mathrm d\sigma .  \] Since $v-\varlimsup _ jv_ j\geq 0$ and $\int v\, \mathrm d\sigma $ is finite, it follows that $\varlimsup _ jv_ j=v$ $\sigma $-almost everywhere. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open. If $v_ j$ and $v$ are locally integrable subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with $v_ j	o v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then the set $\{ \varlimsup _ jv_ j<v\} $ is polar. Let $\{ u_ t\} $ be a family of subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with a common upper bound on every compact subset, and let $F=\sup _ tu_ t$. Then the set $\{ F<F^*\} $, where the supremum differs from its upper semicontinuous regularization, is polar. Proof. (1) Let $N\subset \Omega $ be compact, and take $R$ so large that $N\subset B$. The set $E=\{ x\in N:\varlimsup _ jv_ j(x)<v(x)\} $ is the union, over rational numbers $a<b$ and integers $J\geq 1$, of the Borel sets \[  N\cap \{ v\geq b\} \cap  igcap _{j\geq J}\{ v_ j\leq a\} ,  \] so it is Borel. Suppose some compact subset $S$ of $E$ were not polar. By theorem 4.3.3 , $S$ would carry a nonzero positive measure $\sigma $ with $E_ d*\sigma $ finite and continuous, and lemma 4.4.3 would give $\varlimsup _ jv_ j=v$ $\sigma $-almost everywhere on $S$, which is impossible. Hence every compact subset of $E$ is polar and has capacity zero. By theorem 4.4.1 and corollary 4.4.2 , $E$ is polar. Since countably many compact sets $N$ cover $\Omega $, proposition 4.2.3 completes the proof. (2) If the family is empty, or if all its members are identically $-\infty $ on a component of $\Omega $, then $F=F^*=-\infty $ there. Let $\Omega '$ be a component on which some member $u_{t_0}$ is not identically $-\infty $; by proposition 3.1.5 , $u_{t_0}$ is locally integrable on $\Omega '$. By lemma 3.4.1 , applied on $\Omega '$, there are members $u_{t_1},u_{t_2},\ldots $ of the family with $(\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k})^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$. Put $w_ j=\max \{ u_{t_0},\ldots ,u_{t_ j}\} $ and $w=\sup _ jw_ j$. Since $\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k}\leq w\leq F$, we have $w^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$, and theorem 3.4.2 , applied to the family $(w_ j)$, shows that $F^*$ is subharmonic on $\Omega '$ and that $w=F^*$ almost everywhere on $\Omega '$. We show next that $w_ j	o F^*$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega ')$. As $u_{t_0}\leq w_ j\leq F^*$, the functions $w_ j$ and $F^*$ are locally integrable on $\Omega '$. If $Q\subset \Omega '$ is compact and $M$ is a common upper bound of the $w_ j$ on $Q$, then $0\leq M-w_ j\leq M-u_{t_0}$ on $Q$ and $M-w_ j$ decreases to $M-w$, so dominated convergence gives $w_ j	o w=F^*$ in $L^1(Q)$. Since $\varlimsup _ jw_ j=w$, part (1) shows that $\{ w<F^*\} \cap \Omega '$ is polar, and $\{ F<F^*\} \cap \Omega '$ is contained in it because $w\leq F$. The components of $\Omega $ are pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets, hence of positive Lebesgue measure, so there are at most countably many of them (lemma 1.1.5 ), and the union over them is polar by proposition 4.2.3 . $\square$ Capacitability also gives Frostman's description of the potential of the equilibrium measure. Proposition 4.4.5 . Let $K$ be a compact set carrying a probability measure of finite energy, and let $\mu _ K$ be its equilibrium measure (theorem 4.1.3 ). When $d=2$, $U^{\mu _ K}$ and $V(K)$ stand for the potential and the minimal energy with respect to a fixed scale $D>\operatorname {diam}K$. Then $U^{\mu _ K}\geq V(K)$ on $K$ outside a polar set, $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$ almost everywhere with respect to $\mu _ K$, and $U^{\mu _ K}\leq V(K)$ on all of $\mathbb R^ d$. Proof. Take $R$ so large that $K\subset B$. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and consider the set $E_\varepsilon =\{ x\in K:U^{\mu _ K}(x)<V(K)-\varepsilon \} $, which is Borel since $U^{\mu _ K}$ is lower semicontinuous. If $C_ B^*(E_\varepsilon )>0$, then by theorem 4.4.1 $E_\varepsilon $ contains a compact set of positive capacity, which is not polar by theorem 4.3.3 ; that theorem provides a probability measure $
u $ on this compact set with finite continuous potential, hence with finite energy. Then $I(\mu _ K,
u )=\int U^{\mu _ K}\, \mathrm d
u \leq V(K)-\varepsilon $, contradicting theorem 4.1.3 . Thus $C_ B^*(E_\varepsilon )=0$ for every $\varepsilon >0$, and countable subadditivity (theorem 4.3.5 ) and corollary 4.4.2 show that $\{ x\in K:U^{\mu _ K}(x)<V(K)\} $ is polar. The finite-energy measure $\mu _ K$ gives zero mass to this set (theorem 4.3.3 ), so $U^{\mu _ K}\geq V(K)$ $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere. Since $\int U^{\mu _ K}\, \mathrm d\mu _ K=V(K)$, it follows that $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$ $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere. Let $x\in \operatorname{Supp}\mu _ K$. Every neighborhood of $x$ has positive $\mu _ K$-measure and therefore contains points where $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$; by lower semicontinuity, $U^{\mu _ K}(x)\leq V(K)$. To extend this bound to $\mathbb R^ d$, decompose $\mu _ K=\sum _ j\mu _ j$ by theorem 4.2.2 , which applies because $E_ d*\mu _ K$ is finite $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere, and let $\pi _ N=\sum _{j\leq N}\mu _ j$. The potential $U^{\pi _ N}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^ d$ and, by differentiation under the integral sign, harmonic off the compact set $S_ N=\operatorname{Supp}\pi _ N\subset \operatorname{Supp}\mu _ K$. Since the kernel is nonnegative on $K	imes K$, we have $U^{\pi _ N}\leq U^{\mu _ K}\leq V(K)$ on $S_ N$. We claim that $U^{\pi _ N}\leq V(K)$ on $\mathbb R^ d$. If $\pi _ N=0$, this holds because $V(K)\geq 0$, so let $\pi _ N
eq 0$. As $|x|	o \infty $, the Newtonian potential $U^{\pi _ N}(x)$ tends to $0<V(K)$, and the logarithmic potential tends to $-\infty $. Applying the maximum principle (proposition 2.1.3 ) to $U^{\pi _ N}$ on the bounded open sets $B(0,ho )\setminus S_ N$ with $ho $ large, we obtain the claim. Finally, fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$. The kernel $k(x,\cdot )$ is bounded below on $K$ by a constant $-c_ x$ (with $c_ x=0$ in the Newtonian case), and monotone convergence applied to $k(x,\cdot )+c_ x$ gives $U^{\pi _ N}(x)	o U^{\mu _ K}(x)$. Hence $U^{\mu _ K}(x)\leq V(K)$. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.4.1
text: Theorem 4.4.1 . Let $L\subset B$ be compact. Every Borel set $A\subset L$ is capacitable. More generally, let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space, $f\colon X\to L$ a continuous map, and $\widetilde A=\bigcap _{i\geq 1}\bigcup _{k\geq 1}K_{ik}$ with compact sets $K_{ik}\subset X$; then $f(\widetilde A)$ is capacitable. In particular, every Borel set $A\subset L$ contains an increasing sequence of compact sets whose capacities increase to $C_ B^*(A)$. Proof. Capacitability of $f(\widetilde A)$. Replacing $K_{ik}$ by $K_{i1}\cup \cdots \cup K_{ik}$, we may assume that $K_{ik}$ increases with $k$. Put $A=f(\widetilde A)$ and fix $\varepsilon >0$. We choose integers $h_1,h_2,\ldots $ inductively. Put $\widetilde A_0=\widetilde A$, and suppose $\widetilde A_{p-1}$ has been defined. Since $\widetilde A_{p-1}\subset \bigcup _ kK_{pk}$, the sets $\widetilde A_{p-1}\cap K_{ph}$ increase with $h$ and have union $\widetilde A_{p-1}$, so their images under $f$ increase to $f(\widetilde A_{p-1})\subset L$. By part (3) of theorem 4.3.5 , we can choose $h_ p$ such that $\widetilde A_ p=\widetilde A_{p-1}\cap K_{p,h_ p}$ satisfies \[  C_ B^*\bigl (f(\widetilde A_ p)\bigr )>C_ B^*\bigl (f(\widetilde A_{p-1})\bigr )-\varepsilon 2^{-p}.  \] Hence $C_ B^*(f(\widetilde A_ p))>C_ B^*(A)-\varepsilon $ for every $p$. The sets $L_ p=K_{1,h_1}\cap \cdots \cap K_{p,h_ p}$ are compact, because compact subsets of the Hausdorff space $X$ are closed; they decrease and contain $\widetilde A_ p$, so the compact sets $f(L_ p)\subset L$ decrease and, by part (1) of theorem 4.3.5 and the monotonicity of $C_ B^*$, satisfy $C_ B(f(L_ p))=C_ B^*(f(L_ p))\geq C_ B^*(f(\widetilde A_ p))>C_ B^*(A)-\varepsilon $. Moreover $\bigcap _ pf(L_ p)=f(\bigcap _ pL_ p)$: if $y\in f(L_ p)$ for every $p$, the sets $f^{-1}(y)\cap L_ p$ form a decreasing sequence of nonempty compact sets, since $f^{-1}(y)$ is closed, and hence have a common point. Since $\bigcap _ pL_ p=\bigcap _ iK_{i,h_ i}\subset \widetilde A$, the compact set $\bigcap _ pf(L_ p)$ is contained in $A$, and by proposition 4.3.4 its capacity is $\lim _ pC_ B(f(L_ p))\geq C_ B^*(A)-\varepsilon $. As $\varepsilon $ is arbitrary, $A$ is capacitable. Borel sets. If $L=\varnothing $ there is nothing to prove, so let $L\neq \varnothing $. Call a subset of $L$ analytic if it has the form $f(\widetilde A)$ considered above; this is the notion of descriptive set theory and is unrelated to complex analytic sets. In such a representation we may assume that $X$ is nonempty, since the empty set is the image of the empty subset of a one-point space under a constant map. We may also assume that $X=Y\times L$ for a nonempty compact Hausdorff space $Y$ and that $f$ is the projection onto $L$. Indeed, put $Y=X$. The map $g\colon X\to Y\times L$, $g(x)=(x,f(x))$, is continuous and injective, so $g(\widetilde A)=\bigcap _ i\bigcup _ kg(K_{ik})$ with compact sets $g(K_{ik})$, and the projection of $g(\widetilde A)$ onto $L$ is $f(\widetilde A)$. Analytic sets are closed under countable intersections and countable unions. To see this, let $A_ j=\pi (\widetilde A_ j)$, $j\geq 1$, be analytic, with $\widetilde A_ j\subset Y_ j\times L$ as above and $\pi $ denoting projections onto $L$. The space $X=(\prod _ jY_ j)\times L$ is compact by lemma 1.6.2 and Hausdorff, as a product of Hausdorff spaces. Let $\widehat A_ j\subset X$ be the inverse image of $\widetilde A_ j$ under the continuous map $\pi _ j\colon (y,z)\mapsto (y_ j,z)$. If $\widetilde A_ j=\bigcap _ i\bigcup _ kK^{(j)}_{ik}$ with compact sets $K^{(j)}_{ik}\subset Y_ j\times L$, then $\widehat A_ j=\bigcap _ i\bigcup _ k\pi _ j^{-1}(K^{(j)}_{ik})$. Each $K^{(j)}_{ik}$ is closed, being a compact subset of a Hausdorff space, so $\pi _ j^{-1}(K^{(j)}_{ik})$ is a closed and hence compact subset of $X$. Thus each $\widehat A_ j$, and therefore also $\bigcap _ j\widehat A_ j$, is a countable intersection of countable unions of compact subsets of $X$. A point $z\in L$ lies in $\bigcap _ jA_ j$ if and only if for every $j$ there is $y_ j\in Y_ j$ with $(y_ j,z)\in \widetilde A_ j$, that is, if and only if $(y,z)\in \bigcap _ j\widehat A_ j$ for some $y=(y_ j)_ j\in \prod _ jY_ j$. Hence the projection of $\bigcap _ j\widehat A_ j$ onto $L$ is $\bigcap _ jA_ j$, and countable intersections of analytic sets are analytic. Since every $Y_ i$ is nonempty, the same reasoning shows that the projection of each $\widehat A_ j$ onto $L$ is $A_ j$. For unions, write $\widehat A_ j=\bigcap _ n\bigcup _ kH_{jnk}$ with compact $H_{jnk}\subset X$, and consider, in the product of $X$ with the one-point compactification $\{ 1,2,\ldots \} \cup \{ \infty \} $ of the positive integers (a compact Hausdorff space, homeomorphic to $\{ 1/j:j\geq 1\} \cup \{ 0\} \subset \mathbb R$), the set \[  \bigcap _ n\bigcup _{j,k}\bigl (H_{jnk}\times \{ j\} \bigr ).  \] A point $(x,j)$ belongs to it if and only if $j\neq \infty $ and $x\in \widehat A_ j$, so its projection onto $L$ is $\bigcup _ jA_ j$. Each $H_{jnk}\times \{ j\} $ is compact, so countable unions of analytic sets are analytic. Closed subsets of the compact metric space $L$ are compact, hence analytic, and an open set $U\subset L$ is the union of the compact sets $\{ z\in L:\operatorname {dist}(z,L\setminus U)\geq 1/n\} $, hence analytic. The family of sets $E\subset L$ such that both $E$ and $L\setminus E$ are analytic is closed under complements, and under countable unions, because the complement of a countable union is the countable intersection of the complements. It is therefore a $\sigma $-algebra containing all open subsets of $L$, so every Borel subset of $L$ is analytic and hence capacitable. Increasing compact sets. Let $A\subset L$ be Borel. Since $A$ is capacitable, there are compact sets $K_ j\subset A$ with $C_ B(K_ j)\to C_ B^*(A)$. The compact sets $K_1\cup \cdots \cup K_ j\subset A$ increase, and by monotonicity their capacities increase to $C_ B^*(A)$. $\square$

title: Corollary 4.4.2
text:
Corollary 4.4.2 . Let $A\Subset B$. Then $A$ is polar if and only if $C_ B^*(A)=0$. A compact set has Newtonian or logarithmic capacity zero if and only if it is polar. Proof. By theorem 4.3.5 , it remains to show that a polar set has outer capacity zero. By proposition 4.2.3 , $A$ is contained in the pole set of a function $E_ d*
u $ with $
u $ finite, positive and compactly supported. Let $N$ be a compact neighborhood of $\overline A$ in $B$. The set $P=N\cap \{ E_ d*
u =-\infty \} $ is Borel, being the intersection of $N$ with the open sets $\{ E_ d*
u <-n\} $, $n\geq 1$. Every compact subset of $P$ is polar and therefore has capacity zero by theorem 4.3.3 . By theorem 4.4.1 , $C_ B^*(P)=0$, and monotonicity gives $C_ B^*(A)=0$. For the kernel capacities, a compact set has capacity zero if and only if it carries no probability measure of finite energy (theorem 4.1.3 ), that is, no nonzero positive measure of finite energy; by theorem 4.3.3 this happens if and only if it is polar. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.4.4
text: Theorem 4.4.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open. If $v_ j$ and $v$ are locally integrable subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with $v_ j\to v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then the set $\{ \varlimsup _ jv_ j<v\} $ is polar. Let $\{ u_ t\} $ be a family of subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with a common upper bound on every compact subset, and let $F=\sup _ tu_ t$. Then the set $\{ F<F^*\} $, where the supremum differs from its upper semicontinuous regularization, is polar. Proof. (1) Let $N\subset \Omega $ be compact, and take $R$ so large that $N\subset B$. The set $E=\{ x\in N:\varlimsup _ jv_ j(x)<v(x)\} $ is the union, over rational numbers $a<b$ and integers $J\geq 1$, of the Borel sets \[  N\cap \{ v\geq b\} \cap \bigcap _{j\geq J}\{ v_ j\leq a\} ,  \] so it is Borel. Suppose some compact subset $S$ of $E$ were not polar. By theorem 4.3.3 , $S$ would carry a nonzero positive measure $\sigma $ with $E_ d*\sigma $ finite and continuous, and lemma 4.4.3 would give $\varlimsup _ jv_ j=v$ $\sigma $-almost everywhere on $S$, which is impossible. Hence every compact subset of $E$ is polar and has capacity zero. By theorem 4.4.1 and corollary 4.4.2 , $E$ is polar. Since countably many compact sets $N$ cover $\Omega $, proposition 4.2.3 completes the proof. (2) If the family is empty, or if all its members are identically $-\infty $ on a component of $\Omega $, then $F=F^*=-\infty $ there. Let $\Omega '$ be a component on which some member $u_{t_0}$ is not identically $-\infty $; by proposition 3.1.5 , $u_{t_0}$ is locally integrable on $\Omega '$. By lemma 3.4.1 , applied on $\Omega '$, there are members $u_{t_1},u_{t_2},\ldots $ of the family with $(\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k})^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$. Put $w_ j=\max \{ u_{t_0},\ldots ,u_{t_ j}\} $ and $w=\sup _ jw_ j$. Since $\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k}\leq w\leq F$, we have $w^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$, and theorem 3.4.2 , applied to the family $(w_ j)$, shows that $F^*$ is subharmonic on $\Omega '$ and that $w=F^*$ almost everywhere on $\Omega '$. We show next that $w_ j\to F^*$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega ')$. As $u_{t_0}\leq w_ j\leq F^*$, the functions $w_ j$ and $F^*$ are locally integrable on $\Omega '$. If $Q\subset \Omega '$ is compact and $M$ is a common upper bound of the $w_ j$ on $Q$, then $0\leq M-w_ j\leq M-u_{t_0}$ on $Q$ and $M-w_ j$ decreases to $M-w$, so dominated convergence gives $w_ j\to w=F^*$ in $L^1(Q)$. Since $\varlimsup _ jw_ j=w$, part (1) shows that $\{ w<F^*\} \cap \Omega '$ is polar, and $\{ F<F^*\} \cap \Omega '$ is contained in it because $w\leq F$. The components of $\Omega $ are pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets, hence of positive Lebesgue measure, so there are at most countably many of them (lemma 1.1.5 ), and the union over them is polar by proposition 4.2.3 . $\square$

title: Proposition 4.4.5
text:
Proposition 4.4.5 . Let $K$ be a compact set carrying a probability measure of finite energy, and let $\mu _ K$ be its equilibrium measure (theorem 4.1.3 ). When $d=2$, $U^{\mu _ K}$ and $V(K)$ stand for the potential and the minimal energy with respect to a fixed scale $D>\operatorname {diam}K$. Then $U^{\mu _ K}\geq V(K)$ on $K$ outside a polar set, $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$ almost everywhere with respect to $\mu _ K$, and $U^{\mu _ K}\leq V(K)$ on all of $\mathbb R^ d$. Proof. Take $R$ so large that $K\subset B$. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and consider the set $E_\varepsilon =\{ x\in K:U^{\mu _ K}(x)<V(K)-\varepsilon \} $, which is Borel since $U^{\mu _ K}$ is lower semicontinuous. If $C_ B^*(E_\varepsilon )>0$, then by theorem 4.4.1 $E_\varepsilon $ contains a compact set of positive capacity, which is not polar by theorem 4.3.3 ; that theorem provides a probability measure $
u $ on this compact set with finite continuous potential, hence with finite energy. Then $I(\mu _ K,
u )=\int U^{\mu _ K}\, \mathrm d
u \leq V(K)-\varepsilon $, contradicting theorem 4.1.3 . Thus $C_ B^*(E_\varepsilon )=0$ for every $\varepsilon >0$, and countable subadditivity (theorem 4.3.5 ) and corollary 4.4.2 show that $\{ x\in K:U^{\mu _ K}(x)<V(K)\} $ is polar. The finite-energy measure $\mu _ K$ gives zero mass to this set (theorem 4.3.3 ), so $U^{\mu _ K}\geq V(K)$ $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere. Since $\int U^{\mu _ K}\, \mathrm d\mu _ K=V(K)$, it follows that $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$ $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere. Let $x\in \operatorname{Supp}\mu _ K$. Every neighborhood of $x$ has positive $\mu _ K$-measure and therefore contains points where $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$; by lower semicontinuity, $U^{\mu _ K}(x)\leq V(K)$. To extend this bound to $\mathbb R^ d$, decompose $\mu _ K=\sum _ j\mu _ j$ by theorem 4.2.2 , which applies because $E_ d*\mu _ K$ is finite $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere, and let $\pi _ N=\sum _{j\leq N}\mu _ j$. The potential $U^{\pi _ N}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^ d$ and, by differentiation under the integral sign, harmonic off the compact set $S_ N=\operatorname{Supp}\pi _ N\subset \operatorname{Supp}\mu _ K$. Since the kernel is nonnegative on $K	imes K$, we have $U^{\pi _ N}\leq U^{\mu _ K}\leq V(K)$ on $S_ N$. We claim that $U^{\pi _ N}\leq V(K)$ on $\mathbb R^ d$. If $\pi _ N=0$, this holds because $V(K)\geq 0$, so let $\pi _ N
eq 0$. As $|x|	o \infty $, the Newtonian potential $U^{\pi _ N}(x)$ tends to $0<V(K)$, and the logarithmic potential tends to $-\infty $. Applying the maximum principle (proposition 2.1.3 ) to $U^{\pi _ N}$ on the bounded open sets $B(0,ho )\setminus S_ N$ with $ho $ large, we obtain the claim. Finally, fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$. The kernel $k(x,\cdot )$ is bounded below on $K$ by a constant $-c_ x$ (with $c_ x=0$ in the Newtonian case), and monotone convergence applied to $k(x,\cdot )+c_ x$ gives $U^{\pi _ N}(x)	o U^{\mu _ K}(x)$. Hence $U^{\mu _ K}(x)\leq V(K)$. $\square$

title: 4.5 Dirichlet energy and quasi-continuity
text:
4.5 Dirichlet energy and quasi-continuity The Green energy of a finite positive measure $\mu $ with compact support in $B$ is the integral $\int G_ B\mu \, \mathrm d\mu $ of its Green potential against the measure itself. The mutual Green energy of two such measures $\mu $ and $
u $ is $\iint G_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (x)\, \mathrm d
u (y)$. Both lie in $[0,\infty ]$ because $G_ B>0$. When the Green potentials are bounded, these energies are Dirichlet integrals of the potentials. This identity allows us to bound capacities by $L^2$ norms of gradients, and it leads to the quasi-continuity of subharmonic functions. Proposition 4.5.1 . Let $u$ and $v$ be bounded subharmonic functions on $B$ that tend to zero at $\partial B$ and whose Riesz measures $\mu $ and $
u $ are supported in compact subsets of $B$. Then their distributional gradients belong to $L^2(B)$, and \[   egin{aligned}  \int _ B|
abla u|^2\, \mathrm d x& =-\int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu ,\  \int _ B

u (y). \end{aligned}  \] In particular, the mutual Green energy on the right satisfies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and $\| 
abla u_ K\| _2^2\leq C_ B(K)$ for every compact set $K\subset B$. Moreover, $u$ admits smooth regularizations with the same boundary behavior: there are a compact set $Q\subset B$ and functions $u_\varepsilon $ on $B$, defined for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, with the following properties. Each $u_\varepsilon $ is the restriction of a smooth function on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, satisfies the hypotheses imposed on $u$ with Riesz measure supported in $Q$, and equals $u$ on $B\setminus Q$. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the functions $u_\varepsilon $ decrease to $u$ pointwise on $B$, and $

Since $u$ is bounded, hence locally integrable, the converse in part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 shows that $u=-G_ B\mu $; likewise $v=-G_ B
u $. Choose $0<r<R$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\mu \subset B(0,r)$, and put $R'=R^2/r$. By part (2) of that proposition, $u$ extends to a function $\widetilde u$ on $B(0,R')$ that is harmonic on the annulus $r<|x|<R'$ and vanishes on $\partial B$. This extension is subharmonic on $B(0,R')$, because subharmonicity is a local property and the open sets $B$ and $\{ r<|x|<R'\} $ cover $B(0,R')$. On $\operatorname{Supp}\mu $, the functions $\varphi _{\varepsilon ,\delta }=\widetilde u*ho _\varepsilon *ho _\delta $ are bounded by $\sup |\widetilde u|$ near $\overline B$, which is finite. Letting $\eta \downarrow 0$ and then $\eta '\downarrow 0$, we see that $\varphi _{\varepsilon ,\delta }	o u$ pointwise on $\operatorname{Supp}\mu $ as $\max \{ \varepsilon ,\delta \} 	o 0$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $L^2(B)$ now gives the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the Green energy. Finally, $u_ K$ satisfies the hypotheses by proposition 4.3.2 , and since $u_ K\geq -1$ and $\lambda _ K$ has total mass $C_ B(K)$, we get $\| 
abla u_ K\| _2^2=-\int u_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K\leq C_ B(K)$. $\square$ Theorem 4.5.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be an open set with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, and let $u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ be not identically $-\infty $ on $B$. Then $u$ is quasi-continuous: for every compact set $L\subset B$ and every $\eta >0$ there is an open set $O\Subset B$ with $C_ B(O)<\eta $ such that the restriction of $u$ to $L\setminus O$ is finite and continuous. Proof. The case of a bounded Green potential. Suppose first that $u$ is a bounded subharmonic function on $B$ that tends to zero at $\partial B$ and whose Riesz measure $\mu $ has compact support in $B$. Let $Q\subset B$ and $u_\varepsilon $ be the compact set and the regularizations given by the last assertion of proposition 4.5.1 . These regularizations are continuous on $\overline B$, decrease to $u$, equal $u$ on $B\setminus Q$, and $
abla u_\varepsilon 	o 
abla u$ in $L^2(B)$. For $\delta >0$, the set $O_{\delta ,\varepsilon }=\{ u_\varepsilon -u>\delta \} $ is open, because $u_\varepsilon -u$ is lower semicontinuous, and it is contained in $Q$, so it has compact closure in $B$. Let $K\subset O_{\delta ,\varepsilon }$ be compact. The function $u_\varepsilon -u$ is a difference of two functions satisfying the hypotheses of proposition 4.5.1 , and $\lambda _ K$ is supported on $K$, where $u_\varepsilon -u>\delta $. By the bilinear identity of that proposition, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the bound $\| 
abla u_ K\| _2^2\leq C_ B(K)$, \[  \delta C_ B(K)\leq \int (u_\varepsilon -u)\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K =-\int 
abla (u_\varepsilon -u)\mathbin {\cdot }
abla u_ K\, \mathrm d x \leq \| 
abla (u_\varepsilon -u)\| _2\, C_ B(K)^{1/2}.  \] Hence $C_ B(K)\leq \delta ^{-2}\| 
abla (u_\varepsilon -u)\| _2^2$, and taking the supremum over $K$ gives $C_ B(O_{\delta ,\varepsilon })\leq \delta ^{-2}\|

title: 5 Fine topology and balayage
text:
5 Fine topology and balayage Throughout this chapter $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ is open and $d\geq 2$. Subharmonic functions are upper semicontinuous but in general not continuous. For instance, let $e_1$ be the first coordinate unit vector, and let $u=E_ d*
u $ be the fundamental potential of the probability measure $
u =\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}\delta _{e_1/j}$, which is supported on the compact set $\{ 0\} \cup \{ e_1/j:j\geq 1\} $. By proposition 3.2.1 , $u$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$. At each atom we have $u(e_1/j)=-\infty $, because the integrand $E_ d(e_1/j-\cdot )$ is bounded above on the support of $
u $ and equals $-\infty $ at $e_1/j$. On the other hand, $u(0)=\sum _ j2^{-j}E_ d(e_1/j)$ is finite, since $|E_ d(e_1/j)|$ equals $(2\pi )^{-1}\log j$ if $d=2$ and a constant multiple of $j^{d-2}$ if $d\geq 3$. Hence $u$ is not continuous at $0$. By theorem 4.5.2 , the discontinuities of subharmonic functions are nevertheless controlled by capacity: on a compact subset of a ball, a nontrivial subharmonic function becomes continuous once an open set of arbitrarily small capacity has been removed. In this chapter we study two further constructions, the fine topology and balayage, in which the polar sets of chapter 3 , chapter 4 appear as exceptional sets. Both have counterparts in the pluripotential theory of 2 . The fine topology is the coarsest topology that contains the Euclidean topology and makes every subharmonic function continuous. In this topology, thinness of a set at a point becomes an ordinary neighborhood condition (proposition 5.1.3 ). Polar sets are finely closed, and the fine topology induces the discrete topology on them (proposition 5.1.5 ). Since there are uncountable compact polar sets, the fine topology is neither Lindelöf nor second countable (example 5.1.7 ). Up to polar sets, however, it has the Lindelöf property: by Choquet's lemma and theorem 4.4.4 , every union of finely open sets agrees with a countable subunion outside a polar set (theorem 5.4.1 ). Consequently finely open sets are measurable, and together with quasi-continuity this shows that they are open up to sets of small capacity (proposition 5.4.2 ). Balayage is based on reduction. For a nonnegative superharmonic function $s$ and a set $A$, the reduction $R_ s^ A$ of $s$ on $A$ is the infimum of all nonnegative superharmonic functions that majorize $s$ on $A$: it keeps the values of $s$ on $A$ and removes as much of $s$ elsewhere as superharmonicity permits. Its lower semicontinuous regularization $\widehat R_ s^ A$ is superharmonic and agrees with $R_ s^ A$ outside a polar set. On a ball, when $A$ is compact and $s$ is the Green potential of a measure $\mu $ whose potential is bounded on $A$ or whose Green energy is finite, $\widehat R_ s^ A$ is the Green potential of a measure $\mu ^ A$ carried by $A$, the balayage of $\mu $ onto $A$. We characterize $\mu ^ A$ by an orthogonality relation for the Green energy, which is a positive definite quadratic form on signed measures of finite energy (proposition 5.2.2 , theorem 5.3.1 , theorem 5.3.2 ), and express the balayage of a Dirac mass through harmonic measure (example 5.3.3 ). Finally, we compare the fine topology of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ with the topology generated by the functions that are subharmonic on complex lines, which becomes the plurifine topology of chapter 10 ; for $n\geq 2$ the two topologies differ (proposition 5.5.1 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.5 .

title: 5.1 Fine neighborhoods and thinness
text:
5.1 Fine neighborhoods and thinness A subharmonic function $u$ is upper semicontinuous, so its sublevel sets $\{ u<a\} $ are open. It is continuous exactly when its superlevel sets $\{ u>a\} $ are open as well. The fine topology is obtained by declaring all these superlevel sets open. Definition 5.1.1 . The classical fine topology on $\Omega $ is the coarsest topology on $\Omega $ that contains the Euclidean topology and makes every subharmonic function $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$, on every Euclidean open set $V\subset \Omega $, continuous as a map from $V$ with the induced topology to $[-\infty ,\infty )$. A set is finely open if it is open in this topology, and a fine neighborhood of a point is a neighborhood of it in this topology. Since the sublevel sets of upper semicontinuous functions are Euclidean open, a subbasis of the fine topology consists of the Euclidean open sets and the sets $\{ x\in V:u(x)>a\} $, where $V\subset \Omega $ is Euclidean open, $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ and $a\in \mathbb R$. Restricting finitely many such functions to the intersection of their domains, we see that the sets \[  V\cap \{ u_1>a_1\} \cap \dots \cap \{ u_ m>a_ m\} ,\qquad m\geq 0,\quad u_ i\in \mathrm{SH}(V),\quad a_ i\in \mathbb R,  \] with $V\subset \Omega $ Euclidean open, form a basis of the fine topology. Superharmonic functions, being negatives of subharmonic functions, are finely continuous as well. The fine topology depends on the pointwise values of subharmonic functions. These values are determined by the almost-everywhere class: by theorem 3.2.2 , a locally integrable subharmonic function is the canonical representative ( 3.3 ) of its distribution class. A function that merely agrees almost everywhere with a subharmonic function need not be finely continuous. For instance, the indicator function $\mathbf1_{\{ x_0\} }$ of a point $x_0\in \Omega $ agrees almost everywhere with the zero function, but $\{ \mathbf1_{\{ x_0\} }>1/2\} =\{ x_0\} $ is not finely open by proposition 5.1.4 below. In dimension one every subharmonic function is continuous, since on each component interval of its domain it is either identically $-\infty $ or finite, continuous and convex (example 3.2.4 ). The fine topology is then the Euclidean topology, and this is why we assume $d\geq 2$. Definition 5.1.2 . A set $A\subset \Omega $ is thin at a point $x\in \Omega $ if either $x$ does not belong to the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $, or there is a subharmonic function $u$ on a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$ such that \[  u(x)>\varlimsup _{\substack {y	o x\ y\in A\setminus \{ x\} }}u(y).  \] Proposition 5.1.3 . Let $A\subset \Omega $ and $x\in \Omega $. Then $A$ is thin at $x$ if and only if some fine neighborhood of $x$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Moreover, every fine neighborhood of $x$ contains a set $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $, where $V$ is a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$, $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$, $a\in \mathbb R$ and $u(x)>a$. Proof. Suppose first that $A$ is thin at $x$. If $x$ does not belong to the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $, some Euclidean neighborhood of $x$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Otherwise let $u$ be a subharmonic function on a Euclidean open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ as in definition 5.1.2 , and choose $a\in \mathbb R$ strictly between the upper limit in that definition and $u(x)$. By the definition of the upper limit, after shrinking $V$ we have $u<a$ on $(A\setminus \{ x\} )\cap V$. Hence $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $ is a fine neighborhood of $x$ that does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Conversely, let $N$ be a fine neighborhood of $x$. By the description of the basis above, $N$ contains a set \[  N_0=V\cap  igcap _{i=1}^ m\{ u_ i>a_ i\} ,\qquad u_ i\in \mathrm{SH}(V),\quad u_ i(x)>a_ i,  \] where $V$ is a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$; adding the function $0$ with the constant $-1$ if necessary, we may assume that $m\geq 1$. Each $u_ i(x)$ is finite, since $u_ i(x)>a_ i$. Put $b_ i=u_ i(x)-a_ i>0$ and \[  v=\sum _{i=1}^ m rac{u_ i-u_ i(x)}{b_ i}\in \mathrm{SH}(V).  \] Then $v(x)=0$. We claim that \[  \varlimsup _{\substack {y	o x\ y\in V\setminus N_0}}v(y)\leq -1.  \] There is nothing to prove if $x$ is not an accumulation point of $V\setminus N_0$. Otherwise let $y_ k	o x$ be a sequence in $V\setminus N_0$ along which $v(y_ k)$ converges to the upper limit. For each $k$ some index $i$ satisfies $u_ i(y_ k)\leq a_ i$, that is, $(u_ i(y_ k)-u_ i(x))/b_ i\leq -1$; passing to a subsequence, we may assume that this index $i$ is the same for all $k$. For every other index $j$, upper semicontinuity of $u_ j$ at $x$ gives $\varlimsup _ k(u_ j(y_ k)-u_ j(x))/b_ j\leq 0$. Hence $\lim _ kv(y_ k)\leq -1$, which proves the claim. If $N$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $, then $(A\setminus \{ x\} )\cap V\subset V\setminus N_0$, and the claim shows that either $x$ is not in the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $ or the upper limit of $v$ along $A\setminus \{ x\} $ is at most $-1<v(x)$. In both cases $A$ is thin at $x$. For the last assertion, the claim provides a Euclidean open neighborhood $V'\subset V$ of $x$ such that $v<-1/2$ on $V'\setminus N_0$. Thus $\{ y\in V':v(y)>-1/2\} \subset N_0\subset N$, and $v(x)=0>-1/2$. $\square$ Proposition 5.1.4 . Let $N$ be a fine neighborhood of a point $x\in \Omega $. Then every Euclidean ball centered at $x$ contains a Borel subset of $N$ of positive Lebesgue measure. In particular, the fine topology has no isolated points. Proof. By proposition 5.1.3 , $N$ contains a set $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $ with $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ and $u(x)>a$. It suffices to consider balls $B(x,r)$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset V$. The set $E=\{ y\in B(x,r):u(y)>a\} $ is a Borel subset of $N$, because $u$ is Borel measurable. Let $M$ be a finite upper bound for $u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$; then $M\geq u(x)>a$. Since $u\leq M$ on $E$ and $u\leq a$ on $B(x,r)\setminus E$, the ball submean inequality of theorem 3.1.3 gives \[  u(x)\leq  rac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int _{B(x,r)}u(y)\, \mathrm d y\leq a+(M-a) rac{|E|}{|B(x,r)|}.  \] Hence $|E|\geq |B(x,r)|\, (u(x)-a)/(M-a)>0$. As a singleton has Lebesgue measure zero, it is not a fine neighborhood of its point. $\square$ Proposition 5.1.5 . Let $A\subset \Omega $ be polar. For every $x\in \Omega $ there is a fine neighborhood $N$ of $x$ such that $N\cap A\subset \{ x\} $. Consequently, $A$ is finely closed, and the topology induced on $A$ by the fine topology is discrete. Proof. We construct a subharmonic function on $\mathbb R^ d$ that is finite at $x$ and equals $-\infty $ on $A\setminus \{ x\} $ near $x$. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $ho >0$ with $\overline{B(x,ho )}\subset \Omega $. For $k\geq 0$ put $r_ k=2^{-k}ho $, let $S_ k=\{ y:r_{k+1}\leq |y-x|\leq r_ k\} $ be the closed annulus, and let $A_ k=A\cap S_ k$; these sets cover $A\cap \overline{B(x,ho )}\setminus \{ x\} $. Each $A_ k$ is polar and has compact closure, so proposition 4.2.3 provides a finite positive measure $

u (\mathbb R^ d)=\sum _ kc_ k igl (p_ k(y)-C
u _ k(\mathbb R^ d) igr ),  \] where every term on the right is nonpositive. Hence $p(x)$ is finite, and $p=-\infty $ on $A\cap \overline{B(x,ho )}\setminus \{ x\} $, because there one term equals $-\infty $. Since $p$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$ (proposition 3.2.1 ), the set \[  N=\{ y\in B(x,ho ):p(y)>p(x)-1\}   \] is a fine neighborhood of $x$, and $N\cap A\subset \{ x\} $. If $x
otin A$, this shows that $\Omega \setminus A$ is a fine neighborhood of each of its points, so $A$ is finely closed. If $x\in A$, it shows that $\{ x\} $ is relatively open in $A$ for the fine topology. $\square$ Singletons are polar since $d\geq 2$, and countable unions of polar sets are polar by proposition 4.2.3 ; hence every countable set is polar. In particular, if $\Omega 
eq \varnothing $, the set $\Omega \cap \mathbb Q^ d$ is finely closed but Euclidean dense in $\Omega $, so the fine topology is strictly finer than the Euclidean topology. As we show in example 5.1.7 below, the fine topology is not even Lindelöf; this is why the countability theorem of section 5.4 must allow a polar exceptional set. To produce uncountable compact polar sets in every dimension, we use the following observation: a subharmonic function of some of the variables is subharmonic in all of them. Lemma 5.1.6 . Let $1\leq k<d$, write $x=(z,y)\in \mathbb R^ k	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$, let $V\subset \mathbb R^ k$ be open, and let $g\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$. Then the function $G(z,y)=g(z)$ is subharmonic on $V	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$. Proof. The function $G$ is upper semicontinuous, because $\{ G<a\} =\{ g<a\} 	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$ for every real $a$. Since subharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to show that $G$ is subharmonic on $D	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$ for every open ball $D=B(z_0,s)\subset \mathbb R^ k$ with $\overline{B(z_0,2s)}\subset V$. If $g$ is identically $-\infty $ on $B(z_0,2s)$, then so is $G$ on $B(z_0,2s)	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$, and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $g$ is locally integrable on the ball $B(z_0,2s)$ by proposition 3.1.5 . For $0<\varepsilon <s$, the $k$-dimensional mollification $g_\varepsilon =g*ho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $D$ and satisfies $\Delta _ zg_\varepsilon =(\Delta g)*ho _\varepsilon \geq 0$ there, by part (1) of theorem 3.2.2 and parts (1) and (3) of proposition 1.4.3 ; moreover, $g_\varepsilon $ decreases to $g$ on $D$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by ( 3.3 ). The function $G_\varepsilon (z,y)=g_\varepsilon (z)$ is smooth on $D	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$, with $\Delta _ xG_\varepsilon (z,y)=\Delta _ zg_\varepsilon (z)\geq 0$. By ( 2.4 ), its sphere means in $\mathbb R^ d$ increase with the radius, and they tend to its value at the center as the radius tends to zero, because $G_\varepsilon $ is continuous. Hence $G_\varepsilon $ satisfies the submean inequality and is subharmonic on $D	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$. Along the sequence $\varepsilon _ j=s/(j+1)$, the functions $G_{\varepsilon _ j}$ decrease to $G$, which is therefore subharmonic on $D	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$ by theorem 3.1.6 . $\square$ Example 5.1.7 . Every Euclidean ball in $\mathbb R^ d$ contains an uncountable compact polar set. Consequently, if $\Omega $ is nonempty, the fine topology on $\Omega $ is neither Lindelöf nor second countable. Proof. A similarity $x\mapsto a+tx$ with $t>0$ preserves upper semicontinuity and sphere means, and hence maps polar sets to polar sets. It therefore suffices to find one uncountable compact polar subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. For $d=2$ we take the Cantor set $K$ of proposition 4.2.4 . It is compact and polar, and it is uncountable because it carries an atom-free probability measure. For $d>2$, write $x=(z,y)\in \mathbb R^2	imes \mathbb R^{d-2}$. By lemma 5.1.6 , applied with $k=2$ to the subharmonic function $p$ of proposition 4.2.4 , the function $P(x)=p(z)$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$. It is finite when $z
otin K$ and equals $-\infty $ on $K	imes \mathbb R^{d-2}$. Hence $K	imes \{ 0\} $ is an uncountable compact polar subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. Now let $\Omega 
eq \varnothing $, and let $K'\subset \Omega $ be an uncountable compact polar set. By proposition 5.1.5 , $K'$ is finely closed, and its induced fine topology is discrete. A closed subspace $F$ of a Lindelöf space $X$ is Lindelöf: extend the members of an open cover of $F$ to open subsets of $X$, add $X\setminus F$, and pass to a countable subcover. On the other hand, the cover of an uncountable discrete space by its singletons has no countable subcover. Hence the fine topology on $\Omega $ is not Lindelöf. Nor is it second countable, because a second countable space is Lindelöf: given an open cover and a countable basis, choose, for each basis element contained in some member of the cover, one such member; these countably many members cover the space. $\square$

title: Definition 5.1.1
text: Definition 5.1.1 . The classical fine topology on $\Omega $ is the coarsest topology on $\Omega $ that contains the Euclidean topology and makes every subharmonic function $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$, on every Euclidean open set $V\subset \Omega $, continuous as a map from $V$ with the induced topology to $[-\infty ,\infty )$. A set is finely open if it is open in this topology, and a fine neighborhood of a point is a neighborhood of it in this topology.

title: Definition 5.1.2
text: Definition 5.1.2 . A set $A\subset \Omega $ is thin at a point $x\in \Omega $ if either $x$ does not belong to the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $, or there is a subharmonic function $u$ on a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$ such that \[  u(x)>\varlimsup _{\substack {y\to x\\ y\in A\setminus \{ x\} }}u(y).  \]

title: Proposition 5.1.3
text: Proposition 5.1.3 . Let $A\subset \Omega $ and $x\in \Omega $. Then $A$ is thin at $x$ if and only if some fine neighborhood of $x$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Moreover, every fine neighborhood of $x$ contains a set $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $, where $V$ is a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$, $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$, $a\in \mathbb R$ and $u(x)>a$. Proof. Suppose first that $A$ is thin at $x$. If $x$ does not belong to the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $, some Euclidean neighborhood of $x$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Otherwise let $u$ be a subharmonic function on a Euclidean open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ as in definition 5.1.2 , and choose $a\in \mathbb R$ strictly between the upper limit in that definition and $u(x)$. By the definition of the upper limit, after shrinking $V$ we have $u<a$ on $(A\setminus \{ x\} )\cap V$. Hence $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $ is a fine neighborhood of $x$ that does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Conversely, let $N$ be a fine neighborhood of $x$. By the description of the basis above, $N$ contains a set \[  N_0=V\cap \bigcap _{i=1}^ m\{ u_ i>a_ i\} ,\qquad u_ i\in \mathrm{SH}(V),\quad u_ i(x)>a_ i,  \] where $V$ is a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$; adding the function $0$ with the constant $-1$ if necessary, we may assume that $m\geq 1$. Each $u_ i(x)$ is finite, since $u_ i(x)>a_ i$. Put $b_ i=u_ i(x)-a_ i>0$ and \[  v=\sum _{i=1}^ m\frac{u_ i-u_ i(x)}{b_ i}\in \mathrm{SH}(V).  \] Then $v(x)=0$. We claim that \[  \varlimsup _{\substack {y\to x\\ y\in V\setminus N_0}}v(y)\leq -1.  \] There is nothing to prove if $x$ is not an accumulation point of $V\setminus N_0$. Otherwise let $y_ k\to x$ be a sequence in $V\setminus N_0$ along which $v(y_ k)$ converges to the upper limit. For each $k$ some index $i$ satisfies $u_ i(y_ k)\leq a_ i$, that is, $(u_ i(y_ k)-u_ i(x))/b_ i\leq -1$; passing to a subsequence, we may assume that this index $i$ is the same for all $k$. For every other index $j$, upper semicontinuity of $u_ j$ at $x$ gives $\varlimsup _ k(u_ j(y_ k)-u_ j(x))/b_ j\leq 0$. Hence $\lim _ kv(y_ k)\leq -1$, which proves the claim. If $N$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $, then $(A\setminus \{ x\} )\cap V\subset V\setminus N_0$, and the claim shows that either $x$ is not in the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $ or the upper limit of $v$ along $A\setminus \{ x\} $ is at most $-1<v(x)$. In both cases $A$ is thin at $x$. For the last assertion, the claim provides a Euclidean open neighborhood $V'\subset V$ of $x$ such that $v<-1/2$ on $V'\setminus N_0$. Thus $\{ y\in V':v(y)>-1/2\} \subset N_0\subset N$, and $v(x)=0>-1/2$. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.1.4
text: Proposition 5.1.4 . Let $N$ be a fine neighborhood of a point $x\in \Omega $. Then every Euclidean ball centered at $x$ contains a Borel subset of $N$ of positive Lebesgue measure. In particular, the fine topology has no isolated points. Proof. By proposition 5.1.3 , $N$ contains a set $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $ with $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ and $u(x)>a$. It suffices to consider balls $B(x,r)$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset V$. The set $E=\{ y\in B(x,r):u(y)>a\} $ is a Borel subset of $N$, because $u$ is Borel measurable. Let $M$ be a finite upper bound for $u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$; then $M\geq u(x)>a$. Since $u\leq M$ on $E$ and $u\leq a$ on $B(x,r)\setminus E$, the ball submean inequality of theorem 3.1.3 gives \[  u(x)\leq \frac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int _{B(x,r)}u(y)\, \mathrm d y\leq a+(M-a)\frac{|E|}{|B(x,r)|}.  \] Hence $|E|\geq |B(x,r)|\, (u(x)-a)/(M-a)>0$. As a singleton has Lebesgue measure zero, it is not a fine neighborhood of its point. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.1.5
text:
Proposition 5.1.5 . Let $A\subset \Omega $ be polar. For every $x\in \Omega $ there is a fine neighborhood $N$ of $x$ such that $N\cap A\subset \{ x\} $. Consequently, $A$ is finely closed, and the topology induced on $A$ by the fine topology is discrete. Proof. We construct a subharmonic function on $\mathbb R^ d$ that is finite at $x$ and equals $-\infty $ on $A\setminus \{ x\} $ near $x$. Since $p$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$ (proposition 3.2.1 ), the set \[  N=\{ y\in B(x,ho ):p(y)>p(x)-1\}   \] is a fine neighborhood of $x$, and $N\cap A\subset \{ x\} $. If $x

title: Lemma 5.1.6
text: Lemma 5.1.6 . Let $1\leq k<d$, write $x=(z,y)\in \mathbb R^ k\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$, let $V\subset \mathbb R^ k$ be open, and let $g\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$. Then the function $G(z,y)=g(z)$ is subharmonic on $V\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$. Proof. The function $G$ is upper semicontinuous, because $\{ G<a\} =\{ g<a\} \times \mathbb R^{d-k}$ for every real $a$. Since subharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to show that $G$ is subharmonic on $D\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$ for every open ball $D=B(z_0,s)\subset \mathbb R^ k$ with $\overline{B(z_0,2s)}\subset V$. If $g$ is identically $-\infty $ on $B(z_0,2s)$, then so is $G$ on $B(z_0,2s)\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$, and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $g$ is locally integrable on the ball $B(z_0,2s)$ by proposition 3.1.5 . For $0<\varepsilon <s$, the $k$-dimensional mollification $g_\varepsilon =g*\rho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $D$ and satisfies $\Delta _ zg_\varepsilon =(\Delta g)*\rho _\varepsilon \geq 0$ there, by part (1) of theorem 3.2.2 and parts (1) and (3) of proposition 1.4.3 ; moreover, $g_\varepsilon $ decreases to $g$ on $D$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by ( 3.3 ). The function $G_\varepsilon (z,y)=g_\varepsilon (z)$ is smooth on $D\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$, with $\Delta _ xG_\varepsilon (z,y)=\Delta _ zg_\varepsilon (z)\geq 0$. By ( 2.4 ), its sphere means in $\mathbb R^ d$ increase with the radius, and they tend to its value at the center as the radius tends to zero, because $G_\varepsilon $ is continuous. Hence $G_\varepsilon $ satisfies the submean inequality and is subharmonic on $D\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$. Along the sequence $\varepsilon _ j=s/(j+1)$, the functions $G_{\varepsilon _ j}$ decrease to $G$, which is therefore subharmonic on $D\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$ by theorem 3.1.6 . $\square$

title: Example 5.1.7
text: Example 5.1.7 . Every Euclidean ball in $\mathbb R^ d$ contains an uncountable compact polar set. Consequently, if $\Omega $ is nonempty, the fine topology on $\Omega $ is neither Lindelöf nor second countable. Proof. A similarity $x\mapsto a+tx$ with $t>0$ preserves upper semicontinuity and sphere means, and hence maps polar sets to polar sets. It therefore suffices to find one uncountable compact polar subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. For $d=2$ we take the Cantor set $K$ of proposition 4.2.4 . It is compact and polar, and it is uncountable because it carries an atom-free probability measure. For $d>2$, write $x=(z,y)\in \mathbb R^2\times \mathbb R^{d-2}$. By lemma 5.1.6 , applied with $k=2$ to the subharmonic function $p$ of proposition 4.2.4 , the function $P(x)=p(z)$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$. It is finite when $z\notin K$ and equals $-\infty $ on $K\times \mathbb R^{d-2}$. Hence $K\times \{ 0\} $ is an uncountable compact polar subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. Now let $\Omega \neq \varnothing $, and let $K'\subset \Omega $ be an uncountable compact polar set. By proposition 5.1.5 , $K'$ is finely closed, and its induced fine topology is discrete. A closed subspace $F$ of a Lindelöf space $X$ is Lindelöf: extend the members of an open cover of $F$ to open subsets of $X$, add $X\setminus F$, and pass to a countable subcover. On the other hand, the cover of an uncountable discrete space by its singletons has no countable subcover. Hence the fine topology on $\Omega $ is not Lindelöf. Nor is it second countable, because a second countable space is Lindelöf: given an open cover and a countable basis, choose, for each basis element contained in some member of the cover, one such member; these countably many members cover the space. $\square$

title: 5.2 Green energy and compact reduction
text:
5.2 Green energy and compact reduction This section prepares balayage: the Green energy is a positive definite quadratic form on signed measures of finite energy (proposition 5.2.2 ), and a regularized reduction on a compact set is the Green potential of a measure carried by that set (theorem 5.2.5 ). Fix an open ball $B\subset \mathbb R^ d$ and let $G_ B$ be its Green function (theorem 2.5.2 ); it is nonnegative and symmetric (lemma 4.3.1 ). The results of chapter 4 about balls are stated for balls centered at the origin; we apply them to $B$ after a translation. In this section and the next, unless signed measures are explicitly mentioned, a measure means a finite positive Borel measure with compact support in $B$. Recall from section 4.3 that the Green potential of a measure $\mu $ is $G_ B\mu (x)=\int G_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)$. We denote the mutual Green energy of measures $\mu $ and $
u $ and the Green energy of $\mu $ (section 4.5 ) by \[  I_ B(\mu ,
u )=\iint G_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (x)\, \mathrm d
u (y),\qquad I_ B(\mu )=I_ B(\mu ,\mu ).  \] By lemma 4.3.1 , $G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ is continuous on $B	imes B$, so $G_ B$ is a continuous function on $B	imes B$ with values in $[0,\infty ]$, and these integrals are defined in $[0,\infty ]$ by Tonelli's theorem. For finite signed measures we use the same formulas whenever $G_ B$ is integrable for the product of the total variations. Let $\mu $ be supported in a compact set $K\subset B$. By the definition of $G_ B$ in theorem 2.5.2 and by theorem 2.3.1 , the harmonic correction $G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)=-H_ B(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial B})(y)$ has absolute value at most $\max _{\zeta \in \partial B}|\Gamma _ d(\zeta -x)|$, which is bounded for $x\in K$ because $K$ has positive distance from $\partial B$. Hence, on $K	imes K$, the Green function differs by a bounded function from the kernel $k$ of section 4.1 if $d\geq 3$, and from the kernel $k_ D$ with $D>\operatorname {diam}K$ if $d=2$, because $k(x,y)=\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ and $k_ D(x,y)-\Gamma _2(x-y)$ is constant. Consequently $\mu $ has finite Green energy if and only if it has finite energy in the sense of section 4.1 . In particular, by theorem 4.3.3 , a measure $\mu $ of finite Green energy does not charge polar sets: every polar set is contained in a Borel set of $\mu $-measure zero. Definition 5.2.1 . A property holds quasi-everywhere on a set $E\subset \mathbb R^ d$ if it holds at every point of $E$ outside a polar set. Thus a property that holds quasi-everywhere on a compact set $K\subset B$ holds $\mu $-almost everywhere for every measure $\mu $ on $K$ with finite Green energy. In 2 the exceptional sets are pluripolar, and quasi-everywhere will mean outside a pluripolar set (definition 10.1.1 ). Proposition 5.2.2 . Let $\mu $ and $
u $ be measures with finite Green energy. Then the distributional gradients $
abla G_ B\mu $ and $
abla G_ B
u $ belong to $L^2(B)$, the mutual energy $I_ B(\mu ,
u )$ is finite, and \[  I_ B(\mu ,
u )=\int _ B
abla G_ B\mu \mathbin {\cdot }
abla G_ B
u \, \mathrm d x.  \] The same identity holds for finite signed measures whose positive and negative parts have finite Green energy. On such signed measures, $I_ B$ is a positive definite quadratic form, that is, $I_ B(\sigma )\geq 0$ with equality only for $\sigma =0$, and it satisfies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $I_ B(\sigma ,	au )^2\leq I_ B(\sigma )I_ B(	au )$. Moreover, every measure $\mu $ with finite Green energy is the sum of its restrictions $\mu ^{(1)},\mu ^{(2)},\ldots $ to countably many pairwise disjoint compact sets, and for every $n$ the Green potential of $\mu ^{(1)}+\cdots +\mu ^{(n)}$ is finite, continuous and bounded on $B$. Proof. We first prove the gradient identity for the partial sums of a decomposition of $\mu $ and $
u $ into pieces with bounded Green potentials, to which proposition 4.5.1 applies, and then pass to the limit. Translating, we may assume that $B=B(0,R)$ for some $R>0$, and we choose $r<R$ such that the supports of $\mu $ and $
u $ lie in $B(0,r)$. By lemma 4.3.1 , the function $\kappa (x,y)=G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ extends to a continuous function on the compact set $\overline B	imes \overline{B(0,r)}$; let $C$ be a bound for $|\kappa |$ there. Since $\Gamma _ d=-E_ d$, every finite positive measure $\lambda $ supported in $B(0,r)$ satisfies \[  G_ B\lambda (x)=-E_ d*\lambda (x)+\int \kappa (x,y)\, \mathrm d\lambda (y),\qquad x\in B,  \] and the last integral is a continuous function of $x\in \overline B$ bounded by $C\lambda (B)$. Step 1: decomposition. Since $\int G_ B\mu \, \mathrm d\mu =I_ B(\mu )<\infty $, the Green potential $G_ B\mu $ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, and by the display so is $E_ d*\mu $. By part (2) of theorem 4.2.2 , $\mu $ is therefore the sum of its restrictions to countably many disjoint compact sets, each of which has a finite and continuous fundamental potential. Let $\mu _ n$ be the sum of the first $n$ of these restrictions. Since $E_ d*\mu _ n$ is finite and continuous, the display shows that $G_ B\mu _ n$ is finite, continuous and bounded on $B$; this proves the last assertion of the proposition. By part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 , $-G_ B\mu _ n$ is a subharmonic function on $B$ with Riesz measure $\mu _ n$, which extends harmonically across $\partial B$ and vanishes on $\partial B$; in particular, it tends to zero at $\partial B$. Thus proposition 4.5.1 applies to the functions $-G_ B\mu _ n$, $n\geq 1$. Hence $
abla G_ B\mu _ n\in L^2(B)$ and \[  \int _ B
abla G_ B\mu _ n\mathbin {\cdot }
abla G_ B\mu _ m\, \mathrm d x=I_ B(\mu _ n,\mu _ m).  \] Step 2: the gradient of $G_ B\mu $. For $m>n$, expanding the square with the last display gives \[  \| 
abla G_ B\mu _ m-
abla G_ B\mu _ n\| _{L^2(B)}^2=I_ B(\mu _ m-\mu _ n)\leq I_ B(\mu -\mu _ n),  \] where the inequality holds because $0\leq \mu _ m-\mu _ n\leq \mu -\mu _ n$ and $G_ B\geq 0$. The measure $\mu -\mu _ n$ is the restriction of $\mu $ to a decreasing sequence of sets whose intersection is $\mu $-null. Since $G_ B$ is nonnegative and integrable for $\mu \otimes \mu $, dominated convergence gives $I_ B(\mu -\mu _ n)	o 0$. Thus $(
abla G_ B\mu _ n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^2(B)$; let $g$ be its limit. On the other hand, $G_ B\mu _ n\uparrow G_ B\mu $ pointwise by monotone convergence, and $G_ B\mu \in L^1(B)$. Indeed, for $y\in \operatorname{Supp}\mu $, the bound $|\kappa |\leq C$ and the local integrability of $\Gamma _ d$ (proposition 2.2.1 ) give \[  \int _ BG_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d x\leq \int _ B igl (|\Gamma _ d(x-y)|+C igr )\, \mathrm d x\leq \int _{B(0,2R)}|\Gamma _ d(z)|\, \mathrm d z+C|B|<\infty ,  \] and integrating against $\mu $, by Tonelli's theorem, shows that $\int _ BG_ B\mu \, \mathrm d x$ is at most $\mu (B)$ times the right side. Hence $G_ B\mu _ n	o G_ B\mu $ in $L^1(B)$ by monotone convergence. For a smooth compactly supported vector field $\varphi $ on $B$ we obtain \[  \int _ Bg\mathbin {\cdot }\varphi \, \mathrm d x=\lim _ n\int _ B
abla G_ B\mu _ n\mathbin {\cdot }\varphi \, \mathrm d x=-\lim _ n\int _ BG_ B\mu _ n\operatorname {div}\varphi \, \mathrm d x=-\int _ BG_ B\mu \operatorname {div}\varphi \, \mathrm d x,  \] so $g=
abla G_ B\mu $. Since $\| 
abla G_ B\mu _ n\| _2^2=I_ B(\mu _ n)\uparrow I_ B(\mu )$ by monotone convergence, we get $\| 
abla G_ B\mu \| _2^2=I_ B(\mu )$. Step 3: the mutual energy. Construct the partial sums $
u _ n$ of $
u $ in the same way. By proposition 4.5.1 and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $L^2(B)$, \[  I_ B(\mu _ n,
u _ n)=\int _ B
abla G_ B\mu _ n\mathbin {\cdot }
abla G_ B
u _ n\, \mathrm d x\leq I_ B(\mu _ n)^{1/2}I_ B(
u _ n)^{1/2}\leq I_ B(\mu )^{1/2}I_ B(
u )^{1/2}.  \] As $n	o \infty $, the left side increases to $I_ B(\mu ,
u )$ by monotone convergence, so the mutual energy is finite, while the integral converges to $\int _ B
abla G_ B\mu \mathbin {\cdot }
abla G_ B
u \, \mathrm d x$ by convergence in $L^2(B)$. This proves the identity for positive measures. For signed measures, we expand both sides bilinearly in the positive and negative parts. Step 4: positive definiteness. Let $\sigma $ be a signed measure as in the statement, and put $G_ B\sigma =G_ B\sigma ^+-G_ B\sigma ^-$, a function in $L^1(B)$ by Step 2. Then $I_ B(\sigma )=\| 
abla G_ B\sigma \| _2^2\geq 0$. Suppose that $I_ B(\sigma )=0$, so that $
abla G_ B\sigma =0$ as a distribution on $B$. Since $B$ is connected, corollary 1.4.4 shows that the distribution defined by $G_ B\sigma $ is a constant. On the other hand, $-\Delta G_ B\sigma =\sigma $ in the sense of distributions, by part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 . Hence $\sigma ^+$ and $\sigma ^-$, which are Radon measures by proposition 1.1.2 , define the same distribution, so $\sigma ^+=\sigma ^-$ by part (4) of proposition 1.4.3 , that is, $\sigma =0$. Finally, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for $I_ B$ follows from the gradient identity and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $L^2(B)$. $\square$ Recall from section 4.3 the relative extremal function $u_ K$ of a compact set $K\subset B$, its Riesz measure $\lambda _ K=\Delta u_ K$, the relative capacity $C_ B(K)=\lambda _ K(K)$, and the outer capacity $C_ B^*$. Proposition 5.2.3 . Let $K\subset B$ be compact. Then \[  C_ B(K)=\left(\inf _{\substack {	au \geq 0,\  \operatorname{Supp}	au \subset K\ 	au (K)=1}} I_ B(	au )ight)^{-1},  \] with the conventions that the infimum of an empty family is $+\infty $ and that $1/(+\infty )=0$. If $C_ B(K)>0$, then $\lambda _ K/C_ B(K)$ is the unique probability measure on $K$ minimizing $I_ B$. Moreover, if $D\subset B$ are open balls and $A\Subset D$, then $C_ B^*(A)\leq C_ D^*(A)$. Proof. By part (3) of proposition 4.3.2 , the function $w_ K=-u_ K$ is the Green potential $G_ B\lambda _ K$, and $0\leq w_ K\leq 1$ because $-1\leq u_ K\leq 0$. Since $u_ K$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the envelope $f_ K$, which equals $-1$ on $K$, part (2) of theorem 4.4.4 shows that $w_ K=1$ quasi-everywhere on $K$. In particular $I_ B(\lambda _ K)=\int w_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K\leq \lambda _ K(K)$, so $\lambda _ K$ has finite Green energy. As measures of finite Green energy do not charge polar sets, we obtain, with $m=C_ B(K)$, \[  I_ B(\lambda _ K)=\int _ Kw_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K=m,\qquad I_ B(\lambda _ K,	au )=\int _ Kw_ K\, \mathrm d	au =1  \] for every probability measure $	au $ on $K$ with finite Green energy; in the second identity we used the symmetry of $G_ B$. Suppose that $m>0$, and let $	au $ be a probability measure on $K$. If $I_ B(	au )<\infty $, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality of proposition 5.2.2 gives $1=I_ B(\lambda _ K,	au )^2\leq mI_ B(	au )$; thus $I_ B(	au )\geq 1/m$ in all cases. Equality holds for $	au =\lambda _ K/m$, whose energy is $m/m^2=1/m$. Hence the infimum equals $1/m$, which proves the formula. If $	au _1
eq 	au _2$ were two minimizers, their midpoint would again be a probability measure on $K$, and by positive definiteness \[  I_ B\Bigl ( rac{	au _1+	au _2}{2}\Bigr )= rac{I_ B(	au _1)+I_ B(	au _2)}{2}- rac{I_ B(	au _1-	au _2)}{4}< rac1m,  \] a contradiction. Suppose next that $m=0$. Then $K$ is polar by theorem 4.3.3 , so it carries no probability measure of finite energy, and the infimum is $+\infty $ (if $K=\varnothing $, the family is empty). For the last assertion, recall that balls are regular domains (theorem 2.4.6 ). The monotonicity of Green functions in the domain (theorem 2.5.2 ) gives $G_ D\leq G_ B$ on $D	imes D$. Hence $I_ B(	au )\geq I_ D(	au )$ for every measure $	au $ supported on a compact set $K\subset D$, and the variational formula, applied in $B$ and in $D$, gives $C_ B(K)\leq C_ D(K)$. Taking suprema over compact subsets, we obtain $C_ B(O)\leq C_ D(O)$ for every open $O\Subset D$. Every such $O$ containing $A$ is also allowed in the infimum defining $C_ B^*(A)$, so $C_ B^*(A)\leq C_ D^*(A)$. $\square$ We now turn to reduction. Let $U$ be an open set, $s$ a nonnegative superharmonic function on $U$, and $A\subset U$ an arbitrary subset. The reduction of $s$ on $A$, also called the réduite, and the regularized reduction are \[  R_ s^ A=\inf \{ h:h\geq 0	ext{ is superharmonic on }U,\  h\geq s	ext{ on }A\} , \qquad \widehat R_ s^ A=(R_ s^ A)_*.  \] Here $F_*=-(-F)^*$, with $(-F)^*$ the upper semicontinuous regularization of section 3.4 , is the lower semicontinuous regularization of a function $F$ that is locally bounded below; explicitly, $F_*(x)=\sup _{r>0}\inf _{B(x,r)\cap U}F$. We call the functions $h$ in this infimum admissible for $R_ s^ A$; the inequality $h\geq s$ is required at every point of $A$. If $U=B$, $s=1$ and $A\Subset B$, the admissible functions are exactly the negatives of the functions admissible for $A$ in the sense of section 4.3 , so that $R_1^ A=-f_ A$ and $\widehat R_1^ A=-u_ A$. Since $s$ itself is admissible, $0\leq R_ s^ A\leq s$, and $R_ s^ A=s$ on all of $A$. The negatives of the admissible functions form a family of subharmonic functions bounded above by zero, whose supremum is $-R_ s^ A$. Since $(-R_ s^ A)^*=-\widehat R_ s^ A$, theorem 3.4.2 shows that $\widehat R_ s^ A$ is superharmonic, and part (2) of theorem 4.4.4 shows that $R_ s^ A=\widehat R_ s^ A$ outside a polar set. Thus $\widehat R_ s^ A=s$ quasi-everywhere on $A$, though in general not everywhere on $A$: if $U$ is bounded, $s=1$ and $A\subset U$ is a nonempty polar set, then $\widehat R_ s^ A=0$ by proposition 5.2.4 below. The ball-average formula ( 3.3 ) holds for every subharmonic function, integrable or not. Applied to $-w$, it shows that every superharmonic function $w$ on an open set satisfies \[  w(x)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int _{B(x,r)}w(y)\, \mathrm d y  \] at every point $x$ of that set. Consequently, two superharmonic functions satisfying an inequality almost everywhere satisfy it everywhere. Proposition 5.2.4 . Let $s$ and $t$ be nonnegative superharmonic functions on an open set $U$, let $A\subset A'\subset U$, and let $c\geq 0$. Then \[  R_ s^ A\leq R_ s^{A'},\qquad R_{cs}^ A=cR_ s^ A,\qquad R_{s+t}^ A\leq R_ s^ A+R_ t^ A,  \] and $R_ s^ A\leq R_ t^ A$ if $s\leq t$. The same relations hold for the regularized reductions; in particular, \[  \widehat R_{s+t}^ A\leq \widehat R_ s^ A+\widehat R_ t^ A.  \] If $U$ is bounded and $A$ is polar, then there is a locally integrable nonnegative superharmonic function $p$ on $U$ with $p=+\infty $ on $A$, and $\widehat R_ s^ A=0$. Proof. Enlarging $A$ or $s$ shrinks the class of admissible functions, which proves the two monotonicity assertions. For $c>0$, multiplication by $c$ is a bijection between the admissible functions for $s$ and those for $cs$; for $c=0$, both sides vanish (with $0\cdot \infty =0$), since the zero function is admissible. If $h_1$ and $h_2$ are admissible for $s$ and $t$ respectively, then $h_1+h_2$ is admissible for $s+t$, so $R_{s+t}^ A\leq R_ s^ A+R_ t^ A$. Monotonicity and homogeneity are preserved by lower semicontinuous regularization. For subadditivity, recall that each reduction agrees with its regularization outside a polar set, hence almost everywhere. Therefore $\widehat R_{s+t}^ A\leq \widehat R_ s^ A+\widehat R_ t^ A$ almost everywhere. Both sides are superharmonic, so the inequality holds everywhere by the ball-average formula above. Now let $U$ be bounded and $A$ polar. Then $A$ has compact closure, so proposition 4.2.3 provides a finite positive measure $
u $ of compact support with $E_ d*
u =-\infty $ on $A$. The kernel $E_ d$ is bounded above on the bounded set of differences $x-y$ with $x\in U$ and $y\in \operatorname{Supp}

Hence $R_ s^ A\leq \varepsilon p$ for every $\varepsilon >0$, and so $R_ s^ A=0$ on the set $\{ p<\infty \} $. This set has full Lebesgue measure, because $p$ is locally integrable, and is therefore dense in $U$. Consequently $\widehat R_ s^ A=0$. $\square$ Theorem 5.2.5 . Let $A\subset B$ be compact, and let $s$ be a nonnegative superharmonic function on $B$ which is bounded on $A$. u \quad 	ext{on }B,\qquad r=s\quad 	ext{quasi-everywhere on }A.  \] Proof. The relative extremal function $u_ L$ takes values in $[-1,0]$ and tends to zero at $\partial B$ by part (1) of proposition 4.3.2 ; it equals $-1$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$, because it is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the envelope $f_ L$, which equals $-1$ on $L$. Hence $h_0=-Mu_ L$ is a nonnegative superharmonic function on $B$, bounded by $M$, which majorizes $s$ on $A$ and tends to zero at $\partial B$. If $h$ is admissible, so is $\min \{ h,h_0\} $. Therefore $R_ s^ A$ is also the infimum of the admissible functions $h$ with $h\leq h_0$; we call these capped . In particular $0\leq r\leq R_ s^ A\leq h_0\leq M$, so $r$ is bounded and tends to zero at $\partial B$. Step 2: Poisson modification. u $ on $B$. The reduction $R_ s^ A$ equals $s$ on $A$, and $r=R_ s^ A$ outside a polar set, so $r=s$ quasi-everywhere on $A$. Finally $I_ B(

title: Definition 5.2.1
text: Definition 5.2.1 . A property holds quasi-everywhere on a set $E\subset \mathbb R^ d$ if it holds at every point of $E$ outside a polar set.

title: Proposition 5.2.3
text: Proposition 5.2.3 . Let $K\subset B$ be compact. Then \[  C_ B(K)=\left(\inf _{\substack {\tau \geq 0,\  \operatorname{Supp}\tau \subset K\\ \tau (K)=1}} I_ B(\tau )\right)^{-1},  \] with the conventions that the infimum of an empty family is $+\infty $ and that $1/(+\infty )=0$. If $C_ B(K)>0$, then $\lambda _ K/C_ B(K)$ is the unique probability measure on $K$ minimizing $I_ B$. Moreover, if $D\subset B$ are open balls and $A\Subset D$, then $C_ B^*(A)\leq C_ D^*(A)$. Proof. By part (3) of proposition 4.3.2 , the function $w_ K=-u_ K$ is the Green potential $G_ B\lambda _ K$, and $0\leq w_ K\leq 1$ because $-1\leq u_ K\leq 0$. Since $u_ K$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the envelope $f_ K$, which equals $-1$ on $K$, part (2) of theorem 4.4.4 shows that $w_ K=1$ quasi-everywhere on $K$. In particular $I_ B(\lambda _ K)=\int w_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K\leq \lambda _ K(K)$, so $\lambda _ K$ has finite Green energy. As measures of finite Green energy do not charge polar sets, we obtain, with $m=C_ B(K)$, \[  I_ B(\lambda _ K)=\int _ Kw_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K=m,\qquad I_ B(\lambda _ K,\tau )=\int _ Kw_ K\, \mathrm d\tau =1  \] for every probability measure $\tau $ on $K$ with finite Green energy; in the second identity we used the symmetry of $G_ B$. Suppose that $m>0$, and let $\tau $ be a probability measure on $K$. If $I_ B(\tau )<\infty $, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality of proposition 5.2.2 gives $1=I_ B(\lambda _ K,\tau )^2\leq mI_ B(\tau )$; thus $I_ B(\tau )\geq 1/m$ in all cases. Equality holds for $\tau =\lambda _ K/m$, whose energy is $m/m^2=1/m$. Hence the infimum equals $1/m$, which proves the formula. If $\tau _1\neq \tau _2$ were two minimizers, their midpoint would again be a probability measure on $K$, and by positive definiteness \[  I_ B\Bigl (\frac{\tau _1+\tau _2}{2}\Bigr )=\frac{I_ B(\tau _1)+I_ B(\tau _2)}{2}-\frac{I_ B(\tau _1-\tau _2)}{4}<\frac1m,  \] a contradiction. Suppose next that $m=0$. Then $K$ is polar by theorem 4.3.3 , so it carries no probability measure of finite energy, and the infimum is $+\infty $ (if $K=\varnothing $, the family is empty). For the last assertion, recall that balls are regular domains (theorem 2.4.6 ). The monotonicity of Green functions in the domain (theorem 2.5.2 ) gives $G_ D\leq G_ B$ on $D\times D$. Hence $I_ B(\tau )\geq I_ D(\tau )$ for every measure $\tau $ supported on a compact set $K\subset D$, and the variational formula, applied in $B$ and in $D$, gives $C_ B(K)\leq C_ D(K)$. Taking suprema over compact subsets, we obtain $C_ B(O)\leq C_ D(O)$ for every open $O\Subset D$. Every such $O$ containing $A$ is also allowed in the infimum defining $C_ B^*(A)$, so $C_ B^*(A)\leq C_ D^*(A)$. $\square$

u $, so adding a constant to $-E_ d*
u $ gives a nonnegative superharmonic function $p$ on $U$ with $p=+\infty $ on $A$; by proposition 3.2.1 , $p$ is locally integrable. For every $\varepsilon >0$, the function $\varepsilon p$ is admissible, even at points of $A$ where $s=+\infty $. Hence $R_ s^ A\leq \varepsilon p$ for every $\varepsilon >0$, and so $R_ s^ A=0$ on the set $\{ p<\infty \} $. This set has full Lebesgue measure, because $p$ is locally integrable, and is therefore dense in $U$. Consequently $\widehat R_ s^ A=0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.2.5
text:
Theorem 5.2.5 . Let $A\subset B$ be compact, and let $s$ be a nonnegative superharmonic function on $B$ which is bounded on $A$. Then $r=\widehat R_ s^ A$ is bounded, harmonic on $B\setminus A$, and tends to zero at $\partial B$. Moreover, there is a finite positive measure $
u $ supported on $A$, with finite Green energy, such that \[  r=G_ B
u \quad 	ext{on }B,\qquad r=s\quad 	ext{quasi-everywhere on }A.  \] Proof. We show that $r$ is harmonic off $A$ by replacing admissible functions with their Poisson integrals on balls in $B\setminus A$ (Steps 1–3), and then identify $r$ with the Green potential of its Riesz measure (Step 4). Step 1: capped admissible functions. Choose a closed ball $L\subset B$ whose interior contains $A$, and a constant $M\geq 0$ with $s\leq M$ on $A$. The relative extremal function $u_ L$ takes values in $[-1,0]$ and tends to zero at $\partial B$ by part (1) of proposition 4.3.2 ; it equals $-1$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$, because it is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the envelope $f_ L$, which equals $-1$ on $L$. Hence $h_0=-Mu_ L$ is a nonnegative superharmonic function on $B$, bounded by $M$, which majorizes $s$ on $A$ and tends to zero at $\partial B$. If $h$ is admissible, so is $\min \{ h,h_0\} $. Therefore $R_ s^ A$ is also the infimum of the admissible functions $h$ with $h\leq h_0$; we call these capped . In particular $0\leq r\leq R_ s^ A\leq h_0\leq M$, so $r$ is bounded and tends to zero at $\partial B$. Step 2: Poisson modification. Let $D$ be an open ball with $\overline D\subset B\setminus A$, and let $h$ be a capped admissible function. Its restriction to $\partial D$ is bounded and lower semicontinuous, so by lemma 3.1.2 , applied to $-h$, it is the increasing limit of continuous functions $g_ k$ on $\partial D$. By monotone convergence, the Poisson integrals $H_ Dg_ k$ of theorem 2.3.1 increase to \[  H(y)=\int _{\partial D}P_ D(y,\zeta )h(\zeta )\, \mathrm d S(\zeta ),\qquad y\in D.  \] Since $0\leq h\leq M$ and the Poisson kernel has integral one, $0\leq H\leq M$, and $H$ is harmonic by part (2) of corollary 2.3.3 . For $\zeta \in \partial D$, lower semicontinuity gives $\varliminf _{y	o \zeta }h(y)\geq h(\zeta )\geq g_ k(\zeta )$, so the comparison principle for the superharmonic function $h$ (theorem 3.1.3 ) gives $H_ Dg_ k\leq h$ on $D$; hence $H\leq h$ on $D$. On the other hand, $H\geq H_ Dg_ k$, and $H_ Dg_ k$ extends continuously to $\overline D$ with boundary values $g_ k$; letting $k	o \infty $, we get \[  \varliminf _{D
i y	o \zeta }H(y)\geq h(\zeta ),\qquad \zeta \in \partial D.  \] Define $h^ D=H$ on $D$ and $h^ D=h$ on $B\setminus D$. The last inequality and the lower semicontinuity of $h$ show that $h^ D$ is lower semicontinuous, and $0\leq h^ D\leq h$. We check that $h^ D$ is superharmonic, using the converse part of theorem 3.1.3 . Let $E$ be a ball with $\overline E\subset B$, and let $q$ be harmonic on $E$ and continuous on $\overline E$ with $\varliminf _{E
i y	o \zeta }h^ D(y)\geq q(\zeta )$ for $\zeta \in \partial E$. Since $h\geq h^ D$, the function $h$ satisfies the same boundary inequality, so $h\geq q$ on $E$. In particular $h^ D=h\geq q$ on $E\setminus D$. On the open set $E\cap D$ consider the harmonic function $H-q$. At boundary points of $E\cap D$ lying on $\partial E$, its lower limits are nonnegative by the hypothesis on $q$. At boundary points $\zeta \in E\cap \partial D$, they are at least $h(\zeta )-q(\zeta )\geq 0$ by the inequality displayed above. The minimum principle (proposition 2.1.3 ) gives $H\geq q$ on $E\cap D$. Hence $h^ D\geq q$ on $E$, and $h^ D$ is superharmonic. Since $D\cap A=\varnothing $, the function $h^ D$ is again a capped admissible function. Finally, $h^ D$ depends monotonically on $h$, by the integral formula for $H$. Step 3: harmonicity off $A$. By Choquet's lemma (lemma 3.4.1 ), applied to the negatives of the capped admissible functions, there is a sequence of capped admissible functions whose infimum has the same lower semicontinuous regularization $r$ as $R_ s^ A$. By theorem 3.4.2 , applied to the negatives of this sequence, the infimum equals $r$ almost everywhere. Replacing the functions of the sequence by their successive minima, we obtain a decreasing sequence $(h_ j)$ of capped admissible functions whose limit equals $r$ almost everywhere. Now fix a ball $D$ as in Step 2. On $D$, the modified functions $h_ j^ D$ are harmonic, decrease, and lie between $0$ and $M$; by part (3) of corollary 2.3.3 , they converge on $D$ to a harmonic function $\Phi $. Each $h_ j^ D$ is admissible, so $h_ j^ D\geq R_ s^ A\geq r$; moreover $h_ j^ D\leq h_ j$. Thus $r\leq \Phi \leq \lim _ jh_ j=r$ almost everywhere on $D$. The bounded superharmonic functions $r$ and $\Phi $ therefore agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere on $D$ by theorem 3.2.2 . Since such balls cover $B\setminus A$, the function $r$ is harmonic on $B\setminus A$. Step 4: Green representation. The function $-r$ is bounded and subharmonic on $B$, so $
u =-\Delta r$ is a positive measure by part (1) of theorem 3.2.2 . As $r$ is harmonic on $B\setminus A$, the measure $
u $ is supported on the compact set $A$ and is therefore finite. The function $-r$ is bounded, hence locally integrable, its Riesz measure $
u $ has compact support in $B$, and it tends to zero at $\partial B$; so the converse in part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 gives $-r=-G_ B
u $, that is, $r=G_ B
u $ on $B$. The reduction $R_ s^ A$ equals $s$ on $A$, and $r=R_ s^ A$ outside a polar set, so $r=s$ quasi-everywhere on $A$. Finally $I_ B(
u )=\int r\, \mathrm d
u \leq M
u (A)<\infty $. $\square$

title: 5.3 Sweeping measures and harmonic measure

Applied to the Green potential of a measure, theorem 5.2.5 sweeps the measure onto a compact set without changing its potential there, apart from a polar set. The measure obtained in this way is characterized by an energy identity, and the uniqueness part of this characterization rests on the following consequence of proposition 5.2.2 . Let $

Then there is a unique positive measure $\mu ^ A$ supported on $A$ whose Green potential is $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A$. It has finite Green energy and satisfies \[  G_ B\mu ^ A\leq G_ B\mu ,\qquad G_ B\mu ^ A=G_ B\mu 	ext{ quasi-everywhere on }A, \qquad \mu ^ A(A)\leq \mu (B).  \] For every positive measure $	au $ supported on $A$ with finite Green energy, 5.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:balayage-orthogonality} I_ B(\mu ,	au )=I_ B(\mu ^ A,	au ). \end{equation} This identity characterizes $\mu ^ A$ among the positive measures on $A$ with finite Green energy. Consequently, sweeping is additive and positively homogeneous: if $\mu _1$ and $\mu _2$ satisfy the boundedness hypothesis, then $(\mu _1+\mu _2)^ A=\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$ and $(c\mu _1)^ A=c\mu _1^ A$ for $c\geq 0$. Proof. The function $G_ B\mu $ is nonnegative, superharmonic by part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 , and bounded on $A$. Applying theorem 5.2.5 to $s=G_ B\mu $, we see that $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A$ is the Green potential of a positive measure $\mu ^ A$ on $A$ with finite Green energy, and that $G_ B\mu ^ A=G_ B\mu $ quasi-everywhere on $A$. Since $G_ B\mu $ is itself admissible, $G_ B\mu ^ A=\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A\leq G_ B\mu $. The measure $\mu ^ A$ is unique because $-\Delta G_ B
u =
u $ for every measure $
u $, by part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 , so that a measure is determined by its Green potential. Since $-G_ B\mu \leq -G_ B\mu ^ A$ on $B$, the comparison of boundary fluxes in part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 , applied with $\lambda =\mu $ and $\lambda '=\mu ^ A$, gives the mass bound $\mu ^ A(A)\leq \mu (B)$. Let $	au $ be a positive measure on $A$ with finite Green energy. It does not charge polar sets, so we may integrate the equality $G_ B\mu =G_ B\mu ^ A$, valid quasi-everywhere on $A$, against $	au $. Both integrals are finite, since $0\leq G_ B\mu ^ A\leq G_ B\mu $ and $G_ B\mu $ is bounded on $A$. By Tonelli's theorem and the symmetry of $G_ B$, the two integrals are $I_ B(\mu ,	au )$ and $I_ B(\mu ^ A,	au )$, which proves ( 5.1 ). Suppose that $
u _1$ and $
u _2$ are positive measures on $A$ with finite Green energy which both satisfy ( 5.1 ) in place of $\mu ^ A$. Then $I_ B(
u _1,	au )=I_ B(\mu ,	au )=I_ B(
u _2,	au )$ for $	au =
u _1$ and $	au =
u _2$, so $

If $\mu _1$ and $\mu _2$ satisfy the boundedness hypothesis, so does $\mu _1+\mu _2$, and $\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$ is a positive measure on $A$ with finite Green energy satisfying ( 5.1 ) for the source $\mu _1+\mu _2$. By the characterization, $(\mu _1+\mu _2)^ A=\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$. The same argument gives $(c\mu _1)^ A=c\mu _1^ A$. $\square$ The measure $\mu ^ A$ is called the balayage , or swept measure , of $\mu $ onto $A$, relative to $B$. We now replace the boundedness of $G_ B\mu $ on $A$ by the assumption that $\mu $ has finite Green energy. Theorem 5.3.2 . Let $A\subset B$ be compact, and let $\mu $ be a measure with finite Green energy. Then the regularized reduction $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A$ is the Green potential of a unique positive measure $\mu ^ A$ supported on $A$, and $\mu ^ A$ has finite Green energy. All the conclusions of theorem 5.3.1 remain valid, additivity and homogeneity now holding for sources of finite Green energy. Moreover, \[  I_ B(\mu ,\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu ^ A),\qquad I_ B(\mu -\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu )-I_ B(\mu ^ A)\geq 0.  \] If $\mu $ is supported on $A$, then $\mu ^ A=\mu $. Proof. We sweep the partial sums of a decomposition of $\mu $ into pieces with bounded Green potentials, show that the swept measures increase to a measure $
u $ satisfying ( 5.1 ), and then identify $G_ B
u $ with the regularized reduction. By the last assertion of proposition 5.2.2 , $\mu $ is the sum of its restrictions to countably many pairwise disjoint compact sets, and the partial sums $\mu _ n$ of this series, which satisfy $\mu _ n\uparrow \mu $, have bounded Green potentials. Hence theorem 5.3.1 applies to the measures $\mu _ n$ and to the differences $\mu _ m-\mu _ n$ with $m>n$, whose Green potentials are bounded by $G_ B\mu _ m$. By additivity, $\mu _ m^ A=\mu _ n^ A+(\mu _ m-\mu _ n)^ A\geq \mu _ n^ A$. Hence the measures $\mu _ n^ A$ increase setwise, and $
u (E)=\lim _ n\mu _ n^ A(E)$ defines a measure $
u $ on $A$: if a Borel set $E$ is the disjoint union of Borel sets $E_ k$, the monotone convergence theorem for series gives $
u (E)=\lim _ n\sum _ k\mu _ n^ A(E_ k)=\sum _ k
u (E_ k)$. Moreover $
