u \qquad (n	o \infty ). \end{equation} This is clear for simple functions, and in general it follows by approximating $f$ from below by an increasing sequence of simple functions $f_ k$ and interchanging the suprema over $k$ and $n$ of $\int f_ k\, \mathrm d\mu _ n^ A$. Testing ( 5.1 ) for $\mu _ n$ against $	au =\mu _ n^ A$ and using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we get \[  I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)=I_ B(\mu _ n,\mu _ n^ A)\leq I_ B(\mu _ n)^{1/2}I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)^{1/2},  \] so that $I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)\leq I_ B(\mu _ n)\leq I_ B(\mu )$. We claim that $I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)\uparrow I_ B(
u )$. The sequence increases and is bounded by $I_ B(
u )$, because $\mu _ n^ A\leq \mu _{n+1}^ A\leq 
u $ and $G_ B\geq 0$. Conversely, applying ( 5.2 ) to $f=G_ B(x,\cdot )$, we get $G_ B\mu _ m^ A\uparrow G_ B
u $ pointwise as $m	o \infty $. For $m\leq n$ we have $I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)\geq \int G_ B\mu _ m^ A\, \mathrm d\mu _ n^ A$, and by ( 5.2 ) the right side tends to $\int G_ B\mu _ m^ A\, \mathrm d
u $ as $n	o \infty $; letting $m	o \infty $ and using monotone convergence for the fixed measure $

u \, \mathrm d
u =I_ B(
u )$. This proves the claim, and hence $I_ B(
u )\leq I_ B(\mu )<\infty $. Now let $	au $ be a positive measure on $A$ with finite Green energy. We have $I_ B(\mu _ n,	au )=I_ B(\mu _ n^ A,	au )$ for every $n$. As $n	o \infty $, the left side $\int G_ B	au \, \mathrm d\mu _ n$ increases to $\int G_ B	au \, \mathrm d\mu =I_ B(\mu ,	au )$ by monotone convergence, since $\mu _ n$ is the restriction of $\mu $ to an increasing sequence of sets whose union carries $\mu $, and the right side $\int G_ B	au \, \mathrm d\mu _ n^ A$ increases to $I_ B(
u ,	au )$ by ( 5.2 ). Hence $I_ B(\mu ,	au )=I_ B(
u ,	au )$, which is ( 5.1 ) for $
u $. By monotone convergence, $G_ B\mu _ n\uparrow G_ B\mu $ pointwise on $B$, and we have seen that $G_ B\mu _ n^ A\uparrow G_ B
u $. Since $G_ B\mu _ n^ A\leq G_ B\mu _ n$, it follows that $G_ B
u \leq G_ B\mu $ everywhere. Moreover, $G_ B\mu _ n^ A=G_ B\mu _ n$ on $A$ outside a polar set $E_ n$, so $G_ B
u =G_ B\mu $ on $A\setminus E$, where $E= igcup _ nE_ n$ is polar by proposition 4.2.3 . We now identify $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A$ with $G_ B
u $. Since $B$ is bounded and $E$ is polar, proposition 5.2.4 , applied with $U=B$ and with $E$ in place of $A$, provides a nonnegative superharmonic function $p$ on $B$, locally integrable and hence finite almost everywhere, with $p=+\infty $ on $E$. For every $\varepsilon >0$, the function $G_ B
u +\varepsilon p$ is nonnegative and superharmonic, and it is at least $G_ B\mu $ at every point of $A$: on $A\setminus E$ because $G_ B
u =G_ B\mu $ there, and on $E$ because $p=+\infty $. Hence $R_{G_ B\mu }^ A\leq G_ B

u $ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by the ball-average formula preceding proposition 5.2.4 , since both functions are superharmonic. Conversely, $G_ B\mu _ n\leq G_ B\mu $, so proposition 5.2.4 gives $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A\geq \widehat R_{G_ B\mu _ n}^ A=G_ B\mu _ n^ A$ for every $n$, and therefore $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A\geq G_ B
u $. Consequently $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A=G_ B
u $, and we put $\mu ^ A=
u $; this measure is unique because a measure is determined by its Green potential. It remains to collect the other conclusions. The inequality $G_ B\mu ^ A\leq G_ B\mu $, the equality quasi-everywhere on $A$, the mass bound and the orthogonality relation have been proved above. If $
u _1$ and $
u _2$ are positive measures on $A$ with finite Green energy satisfying ( 5.1 ) in place of $\mu ^ A$, then $I_ B(
u _1,	au )=I_ B(\mu ,	au )=I_ B(
u _2,	au )$ for $	au =
u _1$ and $	au =
u _2$, so $
u _1=
u _2$ by the uniqueness criterion at the beginning of this section; thus ( 5.1 ) characterizes $\mu ^ A$. If $\mu _1$ and $\mu _2$ have finite Green energy, so has $\mu _1+\mu _2$, because the mutual energy $I_ B(\mu _1,\mu _2)$ is finite; and $\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$ is a positive measure on $A$ with finite Green energy which satisfies ( 5.1 ) for the source $\mu _1+\mu _2$. By the characterization, $(\mu _1+\mu _2)^ A=\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$, and in the same way $(c\mu _1)^ A=c\mu _1^ A$ for $c\geq 0$. Taking $	au =\mu ^ A$ in ( 5.1 ) gives $I_ B(\mu ,\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu ^ A)$, and then \[  I_ B(\mu -\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu )-2I_ B(\mu ,\mu ^ A)+I_ B(\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu )-I_ B(\mu ^ A),  \] which is nonnegative by proposition 5.2.2 . Finally, if $\mu $ is supported on $A$, then $\mu $ itself satisfies ( 5.1 ), so $\mu ^ A=\mu $ by the characterization. $\square$ Example 5.3.3 . Let $A\subset B$ be a compact set such that $W=B\setminus A$ is a regular domain, and let $x\in W$. The Dirac measure $\delta _ x$ satisfies the hypothesis of theorem 5.3.1 , since $G_ B\delta _ x=G_ B(x,\cdot )$ is continuous on $B\setminus \{ x\} $ and therefore bounded on the compact set $A$. Its swept potential $r_ x=G_ B\delta _ x^ A$ is \[  r_ x(y)=  egin{cases}  G_ B(x,y),& y\in A,\  G_ B(x,y)-G_ W(x,y),& y\in W, \end{cases}  \] where at $y=x$ the difference $G_ B(x,y)-G_ W(x,y)$ is understood as the value of its harmonic extension across the common pole. Equivalently, let $f_ x$ be the function on $\partial W=\partial A\cup \partial B$ equal to $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $\partial A$ and to zero on $\partial B$. In terms of the harmonic measure $\omega _ y^ W$ of $W$ (proposition 2.5.1 ), \[  r_ x(y)=\int _{\partial W}f_ x(\zeta )\, \mathrm d\omega _ y^ W(\zeta ),\qquad y\in W.  \] The swept measure $\delta _ x^ A$ is supported on $\partial A$ and has mass at most one. For example, if $A$ is a closed ball concentric with $B$, then $W$ is a regular domain. Proof. We first check that $\partial W$ is the disjoint union of $\partial A$ and $\partial B$. Since $W=B\cap (\mathbb R^ d\setminus A)$ is the intersection of two open sets, $\partial W\subset \partial B\cup \partial A$, and $\partial A\subset A\subset B$ does not meet $\partial B$. Conversely, no point of $\partial B\cup \partial A$ lies in $W$. A point of $\partial B$ is a limit of points of $B\setminus A=W$, because the compact set $A\subset B$ has positive distance from $\partial B$. Every small ball around a point of $\partial A$ lies in $B$ and contains points outside $A$, that is, points of $W$. Consequently $\partial A$ and $\partial B$ are disjoint compact sets whose union is $\partial W$, and $f_ x$ is continuous on $\partial W$, because $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ is continuous on $B\setminus \{ x\} \supset A$. Let $H=H_ Wf_ x$ be the solution of the Dirichlet problem on $W$ with boundary values $f_ x$; it is continuous on $\overline W$ since $W$ is regular, and $H\geq 0$ because $f_ x\geq 0$ and $H_ W$ preserves order. The function $G_ B(x,\cdot )=G_ B\delta _ x$ is superharmonic on $B$ by part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 , it is continuous on $B\setminus \{ x\} $, and it tends to zero at $\partial B$ (theorem 2.5.2 ); hence its boundary limits on $\partial W$ are the values of $f_ x$. Therefore the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied to the subharmonic function $H-G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on the bounded open set $W$, gives $H\leq G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $W$. Define $r=H$ on $W$ and $r=G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $A$. Then $r$ is continuous on $B$, because $H$ and $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ have the same values on $\partial A$, and $0\leq r\leq G_ B(x,\cdot )$. To see that $r$ is superharmonic, we argue as in Step 2 of the proof of theorem 5.2.5 . Let $E$ be a ball with $\overline E\subset B$, and let $q$ be harmonic on $E$ and continuous on $\overline E$ with $q\leq r$ on $\partial E$. Then $q\leq G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $\partial E$, hence on $E$ by superharmonicity of $G_ B(x,\cdot )$; in particular $r\geq q$ on $E\cap A$. On $E\cap W$ the harmonic function $H-q$ has nonnegative boundary limits: at points of $\partial E$ because $H$ extends continuously to $r\geq q$ there, and at points of $E\cap \partial A$ because $H$ tends to $G_ B(x,\cdot )\geq q$ there. The minimum principle gives $H\geq q$ on $E\cap W$. Hence $r\geq q$ on $E$, and $r$ is superharmonic by theorem 3.1.3 . The function $r$ is admissible for $R_{G_ B(x,\cdot )}^ A$: it is nonnegative and superharmonic on $B$ and equals $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $A$. Let $h$ be any admissible function. Then $h\geq r$ on $A$. On $W$, the superharmonic function $h$ satisfies $\varliminf _{y	o \zeta }h(y)\geq h(\zeta )\geq f_ x(\zeta )$ at points $\zeta \in \partial A$, by lower semicontinuity, and $\varliminf _{y	o \zeta }h(y)\geq 0=f_ x(\zeta )$ at points $\zeta \in \partial B$, since $h\geq 0$. Applying proposition 3.1.4 to the subharmonic function $H-h$ on $W$, we get $h\geq H$ there. Hence $h\geq r$ on $B$, and $R_{G_ B(x,\cdot )}^ A=r$ pointwise. Since $r$ is continuous, $\widehat R_{G_ B(x,\cdot )}^ A=r$, that is, $r_ x=r$. On $W$, both $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ and $G_ W(x,\cdot )$ are locally integrable and satisfy $-\Delta =\delta _ x$ there (theorem 2.5.2 ). Their difference is therefore distributionally harmonic on $W$; by Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) it has a harmonic representative, which coincides with the difference off $x$. This harmonic function tends to $f_ x$ at $\partial W$, because $G_ W(x,\cdot )$ tends to zero there. By uniqueness of the solution of the Dirichlet problem (proposition 2.1.3 ), it equals $H$. The harmonic-measure formula is proposition 2.5.1 applied to $H=H_ Wf_ x$. Finally, the measure $\delta _ x^ A=-\Delta r_ x$ vanishes on $W$, where $r_ x=H$ is harmonic, and on $\operatorname{Int}A$, where $r_ x=G_ B(x,\cdot )$ is harmonic because $x
otin A$. It is therefore supported on $\partial A$, and its mass is at most $\delta _ x(B)=1$ by theorem 5.3.1 . For the last assertion, write $B=B(c,R)$ and let $A=\overline{B(c,ho )}$ with $0<ho <R$, so that $W=\{ y:ho <|y-c|<R\} $ is a bounded open annulus. It is connected: every point of $W$ is joined by a radial segment in $W$ to the sphere $\partial B(c,(ho +R)/2)$, which is path-connected because $d\geq 2$. By theorem 2.4.6 , it suffices to find, for every $\zeta \in \partial W$, a closed ball that meets $\overline W$ only at $\zeta $. If $|\zeta -c|=R$, the closed ball $\overline{B(2\zeta -c,R)}$ meets $\overline{B(c,R)}\supset \overline W$ only at $\zeta $, as noted at the beginning of section 2.5 . If $|\zeta -c|=ho $, let $m=(c+\zeta )/2$. Every $y\in \overline{B(m,ho /2)}$ satisfies $|y-c|\leq |y-m|+|m-c|\leq ho $, with equality only if $y-m=(\zeta -c)/2$, that is, $y=\zeta $. Since $|y-c|\geq ho $ on $\overline W$, the closed ball $\overline{B(m,ho /2)}$ meets $\overline W$ only at $\zeta $. Hence every boundary point of $W$ is regular, and $W$ is a regular domain. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.3.1
text:
Theorem 5.3.1 . Let $A\subset B$ be compact, and let $\mu $ be a measure such that $G_ B\mu $ is bounded on $A$. Then there is a unique positive measure $\mu ^ A$ supported on $A$ whose Green potential is $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A$. It has finite Green energy and satisfies \[  G_ B\mu ^ A\leq G_ B\mu ,\qquad G_ B\mu ^ A=G_ B\mu 	ext{ quasi-everywhere on }A, \qquad \mu ^ A(A)\leq \mu (B).  \] For every positive measure $	au $ supported on $A$ with finite Green energy, 5.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:balayage-orthogonality} I_ B(\mu ,	au )=I_ B(\mu ^ A,	au ). \end{equation} This identity characterizes $\mu ^ A$ among the positive measures on $A$ with finite Green energy. Consequently, sweeping is additive and positively homogeneous: if $\mu _1$ and $\mu _2$ satisfy the boundedness hypothesis, then $(\mu _1+\mu _2)^ A=\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$ and $(c\mu _1)^ A=c\mu _1^ A$ for $c\geq 0$. Proof. The function $G_ B\mu $ is nonnegative, superharmonic by part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 , and bounded on $A$. Applying theorem 5.2.5 to $s=G_ B\mu $, we see that $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A$ is the Green potential of a positive measure $\mu ^ A$ on $A$ with finite Green energy, and that $G_ B\mu ^ A=G_ B\mu $ quasi-everywhere on $A$. Since $G_ B\mu $ is itself admissible, $G_ B\mu ^ A=\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A\leq G_ B\mu $. The measure $\mu ^ A$ is unique because $-\Delta G_ B
u =

u $, by part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 , so that a measure is determined by its Green potential. Since $-G_ B\mu \leq -G_ B\mu ^ A$ on $B$, the comparison of boundary fluxes in part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 , applied with $\lambda =\mu $ and $\lambda '=\mu ^ A$, gives the mass bound $\mu ^ A(A)\leq \mu (B)$. Let $	au $ be a positive measure on $A$ with finite Green energy. It does not charge polar sets, so we may integrate the equality $G_ B\mu =G_ B\mu ^ A$, valid quasi-everywhere on $A$, against $	au $. Both integrals are finite, since $0\leq G_ B\mu ^ A\leq G_ B\mu $ and $G_ B\mu $ is bounded on $A$. By Tonelli's theorem and the symmetry of $G_ B$, the two integrals are $I_ B(\mu ,	au )$ and $I_ B(\mu ^ A,	au )$, which proves ( 5.1 ). Suppose that $
u _1$ and $
u _2$ are positive measures on $A$ with finite Green energy which both satisfy ( 5.1 ) in place of $\mu ^ A$. Then $I_ B(

If $\mu _1$ and $\mu _2$ satisfy the boundedness hypothesis, so does $\mu _1+\mu _2$, and $\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$ is a positive measure on $A$ with finite Green energy satisfying ( 5.1 ) for the source $\mu _1+\mu _2$. By the characterization, $(\mu _1+\mu _2)^ A=\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$. The same argument gives $(c\mu _1)^ A=c\mu _1^ A$. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.3.2
text:
Theorem 5.3.2 . Let $A\subset B$ be compact, and let $\mu $ be a measure with finite Green energy. Then the regularized reduction $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A$ is the Green potential of a unique positive measure $\mu ^ A$ supported on $A$, and $\mu ^ A$ has finite Green energy. All the conclusions of theorem 5.3.1 remain valid, additivity and homogeneity now holding for sources of finite Green energy. Moreover, \[  I_ B(\mu ,\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu ^ A),\qquad I_ B(\mu -\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu )-I_ B(\mu ^ A)\geq 0.  \] If $\mu $ is supported on $A$, then $\mu ^ A=\mu $. Proof. We sweep the partial sums of a decomposition of $\mu $ into pieces with bounded Green potentials, show that the swept measures increase to a measure $
u $ satisfying ( 5.1 ), and then identify $G_ B
u $ with the regularized reduction. By the last assertion of proposition 5.2.2 , $\mu $ is the sum of its restrictions to countably many pairwise disjoint compact sets, and the partial sums $\mu _ n$ of this series, which satisfy $\mu _ n\uparrow \mu $, have bounded Green potentials. Hence theorem 5.3.1 applies to the measures $\mu _ n$ and to the differences $\mu _ m-\mu _ n$ with $m>n$, whose Green potentials are bounded by $G_ B\mu _ m$. By additivity, $\mu _ m^ A=\mu _ n^ A+(\mu _ m-\mu _ n)^ A\geq \mu _ n^ A$. Hence the measures $\mu _ n^ A$ increase setwise, and $
u (E)=\lim _ n\mu _ n^ A(E)$ defines a measure $
u $ on $A$: if a Borel set $E$ is the disjoint union of Borel sets $E_ k$, the monotone convergence theorem for series gives $
u (E)=\lim _ n\sum _ k\mu _ n^ A(E_ k)=\sum _ k
u (E_ k)$. Moreover $
u (A)=\lim _ n\mu _ n^ A(A)\leq \mu (B)$. For every nonnegative Borel function $f$ we have 5.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:setwise-increasing-integrals} \int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ n^ A\uparrow \int f\, \mathrm d
u \qquad (n	o \infty ). \end{equation} This is clear for simple functions, and in general it follows by approximating $f$ from below by an increasing sequence of simple functions $f_ k$ and interchanging the suprema over $k$ and $n$ of $\int f_ k\, \mathrm d\mu _ n^ A$. Testing ( 5.1 ) for $\mu _ n$ against $	au =\mu _ n^ A$ and using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we get \[  I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)=I_ B(\mu _ n,\mu _ n^ A)\leq I_ B(\mu _ n)^{1/2}I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)^{1/2},  \] so that $I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)\leq I_ B(\mu _ n)\leq I_ B(\mu )$. We claim that $I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)\uparrow I_ B(
u )$. The sequence increases and is bounded by $I_ B(
u )$, because $\mu _ n^ A\leq \mu _{n+1}^ A\leq 
u $ and $G_ B\geq 0$. Conversely, applying ( 5.2 ) to $f=G_ B(x,\cdot )$, we get $G_ B\mu _ m^ A\uparrow G_ B
u $ pointwise as $m	o \infty $. For $m\leq n$ we have $I_ B(\mu _ n^ A)\geq \int G_ B\mu _ m^ A\, \mathrm d\mu _ n^ A$, and by ( 5.2 ) the right side tends to $\int G_ B\mu _ m^ A\, \mathrm d
u $ as $n	o \infty $; letting $m	o \infty $ and using monotone convergence for the fixed measure $
u $, we obtain $\lim _ nI_ B(\mu _ n^ A)\geq \int G_ B
u \, \mathrm d
u =I_ B(
u )$. This proves the claim, and hence $I_ B(
u )\leq I_ B(\mu )<\infty $. Now let $	au $ be a positive measure on $A$ with finite Green energy. We have $I_ B(\mu _ n,	au )=I_ B(\mu _ n^ A,	au )$ for every $n$. As $n	o \infty $, the left side $\int G_ B	au \, \mathrm d\mu _ n$ increases to $\int G_ B	au \, \mathrm d\mu =I_ B(\mu ,	au )$ by monotone convergence, since $\mu _ n$ is the restriction of $\mu $ to an increasing sequence of sets whose union carries $\mu $, and the right side $\int G_ B	au \, \mathrm d\mu _ n^ A$ increases to $I_ B(
u ,	au )$ by ( 5.2 ). Hence $I_ B(\mu ,	au )=I_ B(
u ,	au )$, which is ( 5.1 ) for $
u $. By monotone convergence, $G_ B\mu _ n\uparrow G_ B\mu $ pointwise on $B$, and we have seen that $G_ B\mu _ n^ A\uparrow G_ B
u $. Since $G_ B\mu _ n^ A\leq G_ B\mu _ n$, it follows that $G_ B
u \leq G_ B\mu $ everywhere. Moreover, $G_ B\mu _ n^ A=G_ B\mu _ n$ on $A$ outside a polar set $E_ n$, so $G_ B

Conversely, $G_ B\mu _ n\leq G_ B\mu $, so proposition 5.2.4 gives $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A\geq \widehat R_{G_ B\mu _ n}^ A=G_ B\mu _ n^ A$ for every $n$, and therefore $\widehat R_{G_ B\mu }^ A\geq G_ B

u _1$ and $

If $\mu _1$ and $\mu _2$ have finite Green energy, so has $\mu _1+\mu _2$, because the mutual energy $I_ B(\mu _1,\mu _2)$ is finite; and $\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$ is a positive measure on $A$ with finite Green energy which satisfies ( 5.1 ) for the source $\mu _1+\mu _2$. By the characterization, $(\mu _1+\mu _2)^ A=\mu _1^ A+\mu _2^ A$, and in the same way $(c\mu _1)^ A=c\mu _1^ A$ for $c\geq 0$. Taking $	au =\mu ^ A$ in ( 5.1 ) gives $I_ B(\mu ,\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu ^ A)$, and then \[  I_ B(\mu -\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu )-2I_ B(\mu ,\mu ^ A)+I_ B(\mu ^ A)=I_ B(\mu )-I_ B(\mu ^ A),  \] which is nonnegative by proposition 5.2.2 . Finally, if $\mu $ is supported on $A$, then $\mu $ itself satisfies ( 5.1 ), so $\mu ^ A=\mu $ by the characterization. $\square$

title: Example 5.3.3
text: Example 5.3.3 . Let $A\subset B$ be a compact set such that $W=B\setminus A$ is a regular domain, and let $x\in W$. The Dirac measure $\delta _ x$ satisfies the hypothesis of theorem 5.3.1 , since $G_ B\delta _ x=G_ B(x,\cdot )$ is continuous on $B\setminus \{ x\} $ and therefore bounded on the compact set $A$. Its swept potential $r_ x=G_ B\delta _ x^ A$ is \[  r_ x(y)= \begin{cases}  G_ B(x,y),& y\in A,\\  G_ B(x,y)-G_ W(x,y),& y\in W, \end{cases}  \] where at $y=x$ the difference $G_ B(x,y)-G_ W(x,y)$ is understood as the value of its harmonic extension across the common pole. Equivalently, let $f_ x$ be the function on $\partial W=\partial A\cup \partial B$ equal to $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $\partial A$ and to zero on $\partial B$. In terms of the harmonic measure $\omega _ y^ W$ of $W$ (proposition 2.5.1 ), \[  r_ x(y)=\int _{\partial W}f_ x(\zeta )\, \mathrm d\omega _ y^ W(\zeta ),\qquad y\in W.  \] The swept measure $\delta _ x^ A$ is supported on $\partial A$ and has mass at most one. For example, if $A$ is a closed ball concentric with $B$, then $W$ is a regular domain. Proof. We first check that $\partial W$ is the disjoint union of $\partial A$ and $\partial B$. Since $W=B\cap (\mathbb R^ d\setminus A)$ is the intersection of two open sets, $\partial W\subset \partial B\cup \partial A$, and $\partial A\subset A\subset B$ does not meet $\partial B$. Conversely, no point of $\partial B\cup \partial A$ lies in $W$. A point of $\partial B$ is a limit of points of $B\setminus A=W$, because the compact set $A\subset B$ has positive distance from $\partial B$. Every small ball around a point of $\partial A$ lies in $B$ and contains points outside $A$, that is, points of $W$. Consequently $\partial A$ and $\partial B$ are disjoint compact sets whose union is $\partial W$, and $f_ x$ is continuous on $\partial W$, because $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ is continuous on $B\setminus \{ x\} \supset A$. Let $H=H_ Wf_ x$ be the solution of the Dirichlet problem on $W$ with boundary values $f_ x$; it is continuous on $\overline W$ since $W$ is regular, and $H\geq 0$ because $f_ x\geq 0$ and $H_ W$ preserves order. The function $G_ B(x,\cdot )=G_ B\delta _ x$ is superharmonic on $B$ by part (2) of proposition 4.3.2 , it is continuous on $B\setminus \{ x\} $, and it tends to zero at $\partial B$ (theorem 2.5.2 ); hence its boundary limits on $\partial W$ are the values of $f_ x$. Therefore the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied to the subharmonic function $H-G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on the bounded open set $W$, gives $H\leq G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $W$. Define $r=H$ on $W$ and $r=G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $A$. Then $r$ is continuous on $B$, because $H$ and $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ have the same values on $\partial A$, and $0\leq r\leq G_ B(x,\cdot )$. To see that $r$ is superharmonic, we argue as in Step 2 of the proof of theorem 5.2.5 . Let $E$ be a ball with $\overline E\subset B$, and let $q$ be harmonic on $E$ and continuous on $\overline E$ with $q\leq r$ on $\partial E$. Then $q\leq G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $\partial E$, hence on $E$ by superharmonicity of $G_ B(x,\cdot )$; in particular $r\geq q$ on $E\cap A$. On $E\cap W$ the harmonic function $H-q$ has nonnegative boundary limits: at points of $\partial E$ because $H$ extends continuously to $r\geq q$ there, and at points of $E\cap \partial A$ because $H$ tends to $G_ B(x,\cdot )\geq q$ there. The minimum principle gives $H\geq q$ on $E\cap W$. Hence $r\geq q$ on $E$, and $r$ is superharmonic by theorem 3.1.3 . The function $r$ is admissible for $R_{G_ B(x,\cdot )}^ A$: it is nonnegative and superharmonic on $B$ and equals $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ on $A$. Let $h$ be any admissible function. Then $h\geq r$ on $A$. On $W$, the superharmonic function $h$ satisfies $\varliminf _{y\to \zeta }h(y)\geq h(\zeta )\geq f_ x(\zeta )$ at points $\zeta \in \partial A$, by lower semicontinuity, and $\varliminf _{y\to \zeta }h(y)\geq 0=f_ x(\zeta )$ at points $\zeta \in \partial B$, since $h\geq 0$. Applying proposition 3.1.4 to the subharmonic function $H-h$ on $W$, we get $h\geq H$ there. Hence $h\geq r$ on $B$, and $R_{G_ B(x,\cdot )}^ A=r$ pointwise. Since $r$ is continuous, $\widehat R_{G_ B(x,\cdot )}^ A=r$, that is, $r_ x=r$. On $W$, both $G_ B(x,\cdot )$ and $G_ W(x,\cdot )$ are locally integrable and satisfy $-\Delta =\delta _ x$ there (theorem 2.5.2 ). Their difference is therefore distributionally harmonic on $W$; by Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) it has a harmonic representative, which coincides with the difference off $x$. This harmonic function tends to $f_ x$ at $\partial W$, because $G_ W(x,\cdot )$ tends to zero there. By uniqueness of the solution of the Dirichlet problem (proposition 2.1.3 ), it equals $H$. The harmonic-measure formula is proposition 2.5.1 applied to $H=H_ Wf_ x$. Finally, the measure $\delta _ x^ A=-\Delta r_ x$ vanishes on $W$, where $r_ x=H$ is harmonic, and on $\operatorname{Int}A$, where $r_ x=G_ B(x,\cdot )$ is harmonic because $x\notin A$. It is therefore supported on $\partial A$, and its mass is at most $\delta _ x(B)=1$ by theorem 5.3.1 . For the last assertion, write $B=B(c,R)$ and let $A=\overline{B(c,\rho )}$ with $0<\rho <R$, so that $W=\{ y:\rho <|y-c|<R\} $ is a bounded open annulus. It is connected: every point of $W$ is joined by a radial segment in $W$ to the sphere $\partial B(c,(\rho +R)/2)$, which is path-connected because $d\geq 2$. By theorem 2.4.6 , it suffices to find, for every $\zeta \in \partial W$, a closed ball that meets $\overline W$ only at $\zeta $. If $|\zeta -c|=R$, the closed ball $\overline{B(2\zeta -c,R)}$ meets $\overline{B(c,R)}\supset \overline W$ only at $\zeta $, as noted at the beginning of section 2.5 . If $|\zeta -c|=\rho $, let $m=(c+\zeta )/2$. Every $y\in \overline{B(m,\rho /2)}$ satisfies $|y-c|\leq |y-m|+|m-c|\leq \rho $, with equality only if $y-m=(\zeta -c)/2$, that is, $y=\zeta $. Since $|y-c|\geq \rho $ on $\overline W$, the closed ball $\overline{B(m,\rho /2)}$ meets $\overline W$ only at $\zeta $. Hence every boundary point of $W$ is regular, and $W$ is a regular domain. $\square$

title: 5.4 Countable covers and quasi-open sets
text:
5.4 Countable covers and quasi-open sets The failure of countability in example 5.1.7 takes place on a polar set. We now show that, outside polar sets, Choquet's lemma recovers the countable operations needed for measures and capacity. Theorem 5.4.1 . Let $(U_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of finely open subsets of $\Omega $. Then there is an at most countable subset $J\subset I$ such that \[  \left( igcup _{i\in I}U_ iight)\setminus \left( igcup _{j\in J}U_ jight)  \] is polar. Moreover, every finely open set $U$ contains a set $V$ such that $U\setminus V$ is polar and $V$ is the union of countably many sets $Q_ k\cap \{ u_ k>a_ k\} $, where $Q_ k$ is an open ball with $\overline{Q_ k}\subset \Omega $, $u_ k$ is subharmonic on an open neighborhood of $\overline{Q_ k}$ in $\Omega $, and $a_ k\in \mathbb R$; in particular, $V$ is a Borel set. Consequently, $U$ is measurable for the completion of Lebesgue measure, and for the completion of every finite positive measure of compact support with finite energy. Proof. We first reduce to sets of a special form attached to balls with rational centers and radii; for each such ball, Choquet's lemma then selects countably many of these sets. Let $U= igcup _{i\in I}U_ i$. Call a set basic if it has the form $Q\cap \{ u>a\} $, where $Q$ is a ball with rational center and rational radius such that $\overline Q\subset \Omega $, $u$ is subharmonic on an open neighborhood of $\overline Q$ in $\Omega $, and $a\in \mathbb R$. Basic sets are finely open. Every point $x\in U$ lies in a basic set contained in some $U_ i$. Indeed, if $x\in U_ i$, then proposition 5.1.3 provides a Euclidean open set $V$, a function $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ and $a<u(x)$ with $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} \subset U_ i$, and we choose a rational ball $Q$ with $x\in Q$ and $\overline Q\subset V$. Let $\mathcal B$ be the family of basic sets contained in some $U_ i$; thus $U= igcup \mathcal B$. Fix a rational ball $Q$, and let $\mathcal B_ Q$ consist of the members of $\mathcal B$ of the form $Q\cap \{ u>a\} $; we may assume that $\mathcal B_ Q$ is nonempty. For every pair $(u,a)$ as in the definition of basic sets with $Q\cap \{ u>a\} \in \mathcal B_ Q$, put \[  v= rac{u-a}{1+\max \{ 0,\sup _ Q(u-a)\} }\quad 	ext{on }Q.  \] The supremum is less than $+\infty $, because $u$ is upper semicontinuous on a neighborhood of the compact set $\overline Q$ and hence bounded above on $\overline Q$. Thus $v$ is subharmonic on $Q$, $v\leq 1$, and $\{ v>0\} =Q\cap \{ u>a\} $. Let $F$ be the supremum of all the functions $v$ so obtained. By Choquet's lemma (lemma 3.4.1 ), there is a sequence $(v_ k)$ among them such that $F'=\sup _ kv_ k$ satisfies $(F')^*=F^*$. By part (2) of theorem 4.4.4 , the sets $\{ F
eq F^*\} $ and $\{ F'
eq (F')^*\} $ are polar; let $P_ Q$ be their union. If $y\in Q\setminus P_ Q$ and $v(y)>0$ for some $v$, then $F'(y)=(F')^*(y)=F^*(y)=F(y)>0$, so $v_ k(y)>0$ for some $k$. Hence the union of $\mathcal B_ Q$ is contained in the union of $P_ Q$ and the countably many basic sets $\{ v_ k>0\} $. Doing this for each of the countably many rational balls $Q$, we obtain countably many members of $\mathcal B$ whose union covers $U$ outside the set $P= igcup _ QP_ Q$, which is polar by proposition 4.2.3 . For each selected member choose one index $i$ such that the member is contained in $U_ i$. The set $J$ of chosen indices is at most countable, and $U\setminus  igcup _{j\in J}U_ j\subset P$. This proves the first assertion. For the second, let $U$ be finely open, and apply the first assertion to the family of all basic sets contained in $U$, whose union is $U$ by proposition 5.1.3 . We obtain countably many basic sets whose union $V\subset U$ is such that $U\setminus V$ is polar. Each basic set is Borel, since subharmonic functions are Borel measurable, so $V$ is Borel. For the measurability assertions, it suffices to show that the polar set $U\setminus V$ is contained in a Borel set $N$ that is null for Lebesgue measure and for every finite positive measure of compact support with finite energy. Since $\mathbb R^ d$ has a countable base, $U\setminus V$ is covered by countably many connected open sets $V_ k$ carrying nontrivial subharmonic functions $\psi _ k$ with $(U\setminus V)\cap V_ k\subset \{ \psi _ k=-\infty \} $. The Borel set $N= igcup _ k\{ \psi _ k=-\infty \} $ is polar by proposition 4.2.3 ; it is Lebesgue null by proposition 3.1.5 , and null for measures of finite energy by theorem 4.3.3 . $\square$ Proposition 5.4.2 . Let $U\subset \Omega $ be finely open, let $B\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be an open ball, let $L\subset B$ be compact, and let $\eta >0$. Then there is a Euclidean open set $O\Subset B$ with $C_ B(O)<\eta $ such that $(U\cup O)\cap L$ is relatively open in $L$. Equivalently, $U\cap (L\setminus O)$ is relatively open in $L\setminus O$. In this sense, every finely open set is locally quasi-open. Proof. We construct $O$ as the union of an open set covering the polar part of $U$ near $L$ and of open sets outside which the functions defining the rest of $U$ are continuous on $L$. By the second assertion of theorem 5.4.1 , there are at most countably many sets $V_ k=Q_ k\cap \{ u_ k>a_ k\} \subset U$, with $Q_ k$, $u_ k$ and $a_ k$ as there, whose union $V$ is such that $U\setminus V$ is contained in a polar set $P$. Discarding the empty ones, we may assume that every $V_ k$ is nonempty and that $k$ ranges over a set $\mathcal K\subset \{ 1,2,\ldots \} $. Since $V_ k
eq \varnothing $, we may assume that $u_ k$ is defined on an open ball $Q_ k'\supset \overline{Q_ k}$ and is nontrivial there; by proposition 3.1.5 , it is then locally integrable, hence not identically $-\infty $ on any ball in $Q_ k'$. Fix an open set $W_0$ with $L\subset W_0\Subset B$. First we cover the polar part. The set $P\cap W_0$ is polar and its closure is a compact subset of $B$, so $C_ B^*(P\cap W_0)=0$ by corollary 4.4.2 . Hence there is an open set $O_0$ with $P\cap W_0\subset O_0\subset W_0$ and $C_ B(O_0)<\eta /2$. Next we deal with the discontinuities of the functions $u_ k$. For each $k\in \mathcal K$, the compact set $\overline{Q_ k}\cap L$ lies in the open set $Q_ k'\cap B$. Each of its points therefore lies in a ball $D'$ such that $D'\Subset D\Subset Q_ k'\cap B$ for another ball $D$, and finitely many such balls $D'$ cover $\overline{Q_ k}\cap L$. Enumerate all the pairs of balls obtained in this way, for all $k\in \mathcal K$, as $(D'_ j,D_ j)$ with $j$ in a set $\mathcal J$ of positive integers, and let $k(j)$ be the index $k$ for which the pair $(D'_ j,D_ j)$ was chosen. For each $j\in \mathcal J$, the quasi-continuity theorem (theorem 4.5.2 ), applied to $u_{k(j)}$ on $Q_{k(j)}'$ with the ball $D_ j\Subset Q_{k(j)}'$ and the compact set $\overline{D'_ j}\cap L\subset D_ j$, provides an open set $O_ j\Subset D_ j$ with $C_{D_ j}(O_ j)<\eta 2^{-j-1}$ such that $u_{k(j)}$ is finite and continuous on $(\overline{D'_ j}\cap L)\setminus O_ j$. By proposition 5.2.3 , $C_ B(O_ j)=C_ B^*(O_ j)\leq C_{D_ j}^*(O_ j)=C_{D_ j}(O_ j)<\eta 2^{-j-1}$. Put $O=O_0\cup  igcup _{j\in \mathcal J}(O_ j\cap W_0)$. This is an open subset of $W_0$, so $O\Subset B$, and countable subadditivity and monotonicity of the outer capacity (theorem 4.3.5 ) give \[  C_ B(O)\leq C_ B(O_0)+\sum _{j\in \mathcal J}C_ B(O_ j)< rac\eta 2+\sum _{j\geq 1}\eta 2^{-j-1}=\eta .  \] It remains to show that $U\cap F$ is relatively open in $F=L\setminus O$. Since $L\subset W_0$, the set $(U\setminus V)\cap F$ is contained in $(P\cap W_0)\setminus O_0=\varnothing $, so $U\cap F=V\cap F$. Let $y\in V\cap F$. Then $y\in V_ k$ for some $k\in \mathcal K$; since $y\in \overline{Q_ k}\cap L$, we have $y\in D'_ j$ for some $j$ with $k(j)=k$. Since $L\subset W_0$, we have $O_ j\cap L\subset O$, so $D'_ j\cap F\subset (\overline{D'_ j}\cap L)\setminus O_ j$, and the function $u_ k$ is finite and continuous on $D'_ j\cap F$. Hence \[  \{ z\in D'_ j\cap Q_ k\cap F:u_ k(z)>a_ k\}   \] is relatively open in $F$, contains $y$, and is contained in $V_ k\cap F$. Therefore $U\cap F=V\cap F$ is relatively open in $F$. Write $U\cap F=T\cap F$ with $T$ open in $\mathbb R^ d$. Then $(U\cup O)\cap L=(U\cap F)\cup (O\cap L)=(T\cup O)\cap L$ is relatively open in $L$. Conversely, if $(U\cup O)\cap L$ is relatively open in $L$, then its intersection with $F$, which is $U\cap F$, is relatively open in $F$. This proves the equivalence of the two formulations. $\square$ Fine continuity should not be confused with quasi-continuity: a subharmonic function is continuous on all of $\Omega $ for the fine topology, whereas theorem 4.5.2 gives Euclidean continuity only after an open set of small capacity has been removed.

title: Theorem 5.4.1
text: Theorem 5.4.1 . Let $(U_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of finely open subsets of $\Omega $. Then there is an at most countable subset $J\subset I$ such that \[  \left(\bigcup _{i\in I}U_ i\right)\setminus \left(\bigcup _{j\in J}U_ j\right)  \] is polar. Moreover, every finely open set $U$ contains a set $V$ such that $U\setminus V$ is polar and $V$ is the union of countably many sets $Q_ k\cap \{ u_ k>a_ k\} $, where $Q_ k$ is an open ball with $\overline{Q_ k}\subset \Omega $, $u_ k$ is subharmonic on an open neighborhood of $\overline{Q_ k}$ in $\Omega $, and $a_ k\in \mathbb R$; in particular, $V$ is a Borel set. Consequently, $U$ is measurable for the completion of Lebesgue measure, and for the completion of every finite positive measure of compact support with finite energy. Proof. We first reduce to sets of a special form attached to balls with rational centers and radii; for each such ball, Choquet's lemma then selects countably many of these sets. Let $U=\bigcup _{i\in I}U_ i$. Call a set basic if it has the form $Q\cap \{ u>a\} $, where $Q$ is a ball with rational center and rational radius such that $\overline Q\subset \Omega $, $u$ is subharmonic on an open neighborhood of $\overline Q$ in $\Omega $, and $a\in \mathbb R$. Basic sets are finely open. Every point $x\in U$ lies in a basic set contained in some $U_ i$. Indeed, if $x\in U_ i$, then proposition 5.1.3 provides a Euclidean open set $V$, a function $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ and $a<u(x)$ with $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} \subset U_ i$, and we choose a rational ball $Q$ with $x\in Q$ and $\overline Q\subset V$. Let $\mathcal B$ be the family of basic sets contained in some $U_ i$; thus $U=\bigcup \mathcal B$. Fix a rational ball $Q$, and let $\mathcal B_ Q$ consist of the members of $\mathcal B$ of the form $Q\cap \{ u>a\} $; we may assume that $\mathcal B_ Q$ is nonempty. For every pair $(u,a)$ as in the definition of basic sets with $Q\cap \{ u>a\} \in \mathcal B_ Q$, put \[  v=\frac{u-a}{1+\max \{ 0,\sup _ Q(u-a)\} }\quad \text{on }Q.  \] The supremum is less than $+\infty $, because $u$ is upper semicontinuous on a neighborhood of the compact set $\overline Q$ and hence bounded above on $\overline Q$. Thus $v$ is subharmonic on $Q$, $v\leq 1$, and $\{ v>0\} =Q\cap \{ u>a\} $. Let $F$ be the supremum of all the functions $v$ so obtained. By Choquet's lemma (lemma 3.4.1 ), there is a sequence $(v_ k)$ among them such that $F'=\sup _ kv_ k$ satisfies $(F')^*=F^*$. By part (2) of theorem 4.4.4 , the sets $\{ F\neq F^*\} $ and $\{ F'\neq (F')^*\} $ are polar; let $P_ Q$ be their union. If $y\in Q\setminus P_ Q$ and $v(y)>0$ for some $v$, then $F'(y)=(F')^*(y)=F^*(y)=F(y)>0$, so $v_ k(y)>0$ for some $k$. Hence the union of $\mathcal B_ Q$ is contained in the union of $P_ Q$ and the countably many basic sets $\{ v_ k>0\} $. Doing this for each of the countably many rational balls $Q$, we obtain countably many members of $\mathcal B$ whose union covers $U$ outside the set $P=\bigcup _ QP_ Q$, which is polar by proposition 4.2.3 . For each selected member choose one index $i$ such that the member is contained in $U_ i$. The set $J$ of chosen indices is at most countable, and $U\setminus \bigcup _{j\in J}U_ j\subset P$. This proves the first assertion. For the second, let $U$ be finely open, and apply the first assertion to the family of all basic sets contained in $U$, whose union is $U$ by proposition 5.1.3 . We obtain countably many basic sets whose union $V\subset U$ is such that $U\setminus V$ is polar. Each basic set is Borel, since subharmonic functions are Borel measurable, so $V$ is Borel. For the measurability assertions, it suffices to show that the polar set $U\setminus V$ is contained in a Borel set $N$ that is null for Lebesgue measure and for every finite positive measure of compact support with finite energy. Since $\mathbb R^ d$ has a countable base, $U\setminus V$ is covered by countably many connected open sets $V_ k$ carrying nontrivial subharmonic functions $\psi _ k$ with $(U\setminus V)\cap V_ k\subset \{ \psi _ k=-\infty \} $. The Borel set $N=\bigcup _ k\{ \psi _ k=-\infty \} $ is polar by proposition 4.2.3 ; it is Lebesgue null by proposition 3.1.5 , and null for measures of finite energy by theorem 4.3.3 . $\square$

title: Proposition 5.4.2
text: Proposition 5.4.2 . Let $U\subset \Omega $ be finely open, let $B\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be an open ball, let $L\subset B$ be compact, and let $\eta >0$. Then there is a Euclidean open set $O\Subset B$ with $C_ B(O)<\eta $ such that $(U\cup O)\cap L$ is relatively open in $L$. Equivalently, $U\cap (L\setminus O)$ is relatively open in $L\setminus O$. In this sense, every finely open set is locally quasi-open. Proof. We construct $O$ as the union of an open set covering the polar part of $U$ near $L$ and of open sets outside which the functions defining the rest of $U$ are continuous on $L$. By the second assertion of theorem 5.4.1 , there are at most countably many sets $V_ k=Q_ k\cap \{ u_ k>a_ k\} \subset U$, with $Q_ k$, $u_ k$ and $a_ k$ as there, whose union $V$ is such that $U\setminus V$ is contained in a polar set $P$. Discarding the empty ones, we may assume that every $V_ k$ is nonempty and that $k$ ranges over a set $\mathcal K\subset \{ 1,2,\ldots \} $. Since $V_ k\neq \varnothing $, we may assume that $u_ k$ is defined on an open ball $Q_ k'\supset \overline{Q_ k}$ and is nontrivial there; by proposition 3.1.5 , it is then locally integrable, hence not identically $-\infty $ on any ball in $Q_ k'$. Fix an open set $W_0$ with $L\subset W_0\Subset B$. First we cover the polar part. The set $P\cap W_0$ is polar and its closure is a compact subset of $B$, so $C_ B^*(P\cap W_0)=0$ by corollary 4.4.2 . Hence there is an open set $O_0$ with $P\cap W_0\subset O_0\subset W_0$ and $C_ B(O_0)<\eta /2$. Next we deal with the discontinuities of the functions $u_ k$. For each $k\in \mathcal K$, the compact set $\overline{Q_ k}\cap L$ lies in the open set $Q_ k'\cap B$. Each of its points therefore lies in a ball $D'$ such that $D'\Subset D\Subset Q_ k'\cap B$ for another ball $D$, and finitely many such balls $D'$ cover $\overline{Q_ k}\cap L$. Enumerate all the pairs of balls obtained in this way, for all $k\in \mathcal K$, as $(D'_ j,D_ j)$ with $j$ in a set $\mathcal J$ of positive integers, and let $k(j)$ be the index $k$ for which the pair $(D'_ j,D_ j)$ was chosen. For each $j\in \mathcal J$, the quasi-continuity theorem (theorem 4.5.2 ), applied to $u_{k(j)}$ on $Q_{k(j)}'$ with the ball $D_ j\Subset Q_{k(j)}'$ and the compact set $\overline{D'_ j}\cap L\subset D_ j$, provides an open set $O_ j\Subset D_ j$ with $C_{D_ j}(O_ j)<\eta 2^{-j-1}$ such that $u_{k(j)}$ is finite and continuous on $(\overline{D'_ j}\cap L)\setminus O_ j$. By proposition 5.2.3 , $C_ B(O_ j)=C_ B^*(O_ j)\leq C_{D_ j}^*(O_ j)=C_{D_ j}(O_ j)<\eta 2^{-j-1}$. Put $O=O_0\cup \bigcup _{j\in \mathcal J}(O_ j\cap W_0)$. This is an open subset of $W_0$, so $O\Subset B$, and countable subadditivity and monotonicity of the outer capacity (theorem 4.3.5 ) give \[  C_ B(O)\leq C_ B(O_0)+\sum _{j\in \mathcal J}C_ B(O_ j)<\frac\eta 2+\sum _{j\geq 1}\eta 2^{-j-1}=\eta .  \] It remains to show that $U\cap F$ is relatively open in $F=L\setminus O$. Since $L\subset W_0$, the set $(U\setminus V)\cap F$ is contained in $(P\cap W_0)\setminus O_0=\varnothing $, so $U\cap F=V\cap F$. Let $y\in V\cap F$. Then $y\in V_ k$ for some $k\in \mathcal K$; since $y\in \overline{Q_ k}\cap L$, we have $y\in D'_ j$ for some $j$ with $k(j)=k$. Since $L\subset W_0$, we have $O_ j\cap L\subset O$, so $D'_ j\cap F\subset (\overline{D'_ j}\cap L)\setminus O_ j$, and the function $u_ k$ is finite and continuous on $D'_ j\cap F$. Hence \[  \{ z\in D'_ j\cap Q_ k\cap F:u_ k(z)>a_ k\}   \] is relatively open in $F$, contains $y$, and is contained in $V_ k\cap F$. Therefore $U\cap F=V\cap F$ is relatively open in $F$. Write $U\cap F=T\cap F$ with $T$ open in $\mathbb R^ d$. Then $(U\cup O)\cap L=(U\cap F)\cup (O\cap L)=(T\cup O)\cap L$ is relatively open in $L$. Conversely, if $(U\cup O)\cap L$ is relatively open in $L$, then its intersection with $F$, which is $U\cap F$, is relatively open in $F$. This proves the equivalence of the two formulations. $\square$

title: 5.5 Complex lines and the choice of topology
search_title: Complex lines and the choice of topology
text: 5.5 Complex lines and the choice of topology On $\mathbb C^ n$, identified with $\mathbb R^{2n}$, the classical fine topology is generated by all subharmonic functions of $2n$ real variables. In 2 we shall instead use the upper semicontinuous functions whose restriction to each connected component of the intersection of their domain with an affine complex line is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. On domains these are, apart from the constant $-\infty $, the plurisubharmonic functions of definition 8.1.1 , and we shall see in example 10.3.4 that they generate the plurifine topology of definition 10.3.1 in the same way. In complex dimension one the line condition is planar subharmonicity, so the two topologies coincide; in higher dimensions they differ. Proposition 5.5.1 . Let $n\geq 2$ and $H=\{ z\in \mathbb C^ n:z_1=0\} $. Then the classical fine topology of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ induces the discrete topology on $H$. On the other hand, let $\tau $ be the coarsest topology on $\mathbb C^ n$ that contains the Euclidean topology and makes continuous every upper semicontinuous function $u\colon V\to [-\infty ,\infty )$, where $V\subset \mathbb C^ n$ is open, such that for every affine complex line $L$ the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of $L\cap V$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Then no point of $H$ is isolated in the topology induced on $H$ by $\tau $. Proof. By example 3.2.4 , the function $w\mapsto \log |w|$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb C$. Hence $z\mapsto \log |z_1|$, a function of the first two real coordinates, is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^{2n}$ by lemma 5.1.6 ; it is finite off $H$ and equals $-\infty $ on $H$. Thus $H$ is polar, and proposition 5.1.5 shows that the classical fine topology induces the discrete topology on $H$. Now let $x\in H$, and let $N'$ be a neighborhood of $x$ for $\tau $. As in section 5.1 , upper semicontinuity turns every condition of the form $u<b$ into a Euclidean open condition, and restrictions to smaller open sets preserve the complex-line condition; hence $N'$ contains a set \[  N=V\cap \{ u_1>a_1\} \cap \dots \cap \{ u_ m>a_ m\} ,  \] where $V$ is a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$, the $u_ i$ are upper semicontinuous functions on $V$ satisfying the complex-line condition in the statement, and $u_ i(x)>a_ i$. Choose an affine complex line $\ell \subset H$ through $x$, which is possible since $n\geq 2$, and identify $\ell $ with $\mathbb C$. On the connected component of $\ell \cap V$ containing $x$, each restriction $u_ i|_\ell $ is subharmonic and is not identically $-\infty $, because $u_ i(x)$ is finite. Hence $\{ u_ i|_\ell >a_ i\} $ is open in the planar fine topology, and the intersection of these sets with that component is a planar fine neighborhood of $x$ contained in $N\cap \ell $. By proposition 5.1.4 , applied in the plane, it contains points other than $x$. These points lie in $H\cap N'$, so $x$ is not isolated in $H$. $\square$

title: 6 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
search_title: Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
section: 2.2 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: 6 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines This chapter develops the Fourier analysis on Euclidean space that the complex theory of 2 requires, and applies it to functions of several complex variables. Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, with $n\geq 2$, and let $u$ be a function on $D$ whose restriction to every complex line is subharmonic. On each line $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and hence bounded above on compact subsets of that line, but the hypothesis gives no control of these bounds as the line varies. We prove that a Borel function with this property is nevertheless locally bounded above on $D$ (corollary 6.5.4 ). In chapter 8 this is the step that makes upper semicontinuity automatic for functions that are subharmonic on complex lines (theorem 8.1.3 ). The proof is by contradiction. Suppose that $u(x_ j)\to \infty $ along a sequence $x_ j\to p$. By the submean inequality, $u\geq u(x_ j)$ on a subset of positive length of every sufficiently small circle centered at $x_ j$ in a complex line through $x_ j$. Choosing one such point on each circle, we obtain a probability measure on an annulus about $x_ j$, carried by the set where $u\geq u(x_ j)$, whose Riesz energy of order $2n-2$ is bounded independently of $j$ (theorem 6.4.2 ). By Plancherel's theorem, energy of this order is a constant multiple of the average, over all complex hyperplanes $H$ through the origin, of the squared $L^2$ norms of the densities of the measures projected onto $H$ (theorem 6.5.2 ). By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, a projected measure with a density of controlled $L^2$ norm cannot be concentrated on a set of small measure. An incidence argument then produces a single complex line that meets infinitely many of the sets $\{ u\geq u(x_ j)\} $ near $p$ (theorem 6.5.3 ), which contradicts the upper bound of $u$ on that line. The Fourier analysis is developed in section 6.1 , and the invariant measures used to average over directions and over hyperplanes are constructed in section 6.3 . The same Fourier methods give $L^ p$ estimates for second derivatives. In section 6.2 we show that, for $1<p<\infty $, the $L^ p$ norm of the Laplacian of a test function bounds the $L^ p$ norm of its full real Hessian. Together with Morrey's inequality, these estimates supply the real regularity of functions with bounded Laplacian that is used in chapter 16 to compute Monge–Ampère measures of envelopes below nonsmooth obstacles. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.6 .

title: 6.1 Fourier transform and energy
section: 2.2 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: 6.1 Fourier transform and energy Let $d\geq 1$. We develop the Fourier transform on $\mathbb R^ d$ as far as Plancherel's theorem, and use it to express the Riesz energy of a measure as a weighted $L^2$ norm of its Fourier transform (theorem 6.1.4 ). For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^ d)$ and a finite positive Borel measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb R^ d$ we use the Fourier transforms \[  \widehat f(\xi )=\int _{\mathbb R^ d}f(x)\mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d x, \qquad \widehat\mu (\xi )=\int \mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d\mu (x).  \] Both functions are bounded, by $\| f\| _1$ and by $\mu (\mathbb R^ d)$, respectively, and they are continuous by dominated convergence. The Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ consists of the smooth complex functions $f$ on $\mathbb R^ d$ such that $x^\alpha \partial ^\beta f$ is bounded for all multi-indices $\alpha ,\beta $. By the Leibniz rule, $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ is stable under differentiation and under multiplication by polynomials, and $C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)\subset \mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$. Every derivative $\partial ^\beta f$ of a Schwartz function is integrable: $(1+|x|^2)^ d\partial ^\beta f$ is a linear combination of the bounded functions $x^\alpha \partial ^\beta f$, so $|\partial ^\beta f|\leq C(1+|x|^2)^{-d}$, and $(1+|x|^2)^{-d}$ is integrable by polar coordinates ( 2.1 ), because $r^{d-1}(1+r^2)^{-d}\leq \min \{ r^{d-1},r^{-d-1}\} $. Lemma 6.1.1 . The Fourier transform maps $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ into itself, and for $f\in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ and $1\leq j\leq d$, 6.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:fourier-derivative-rules} \widehat{\partial _ jf}(\xi )=2\pi \mathrm i\xi _ j\widehat f(\xi ),\qquad \partial _{\xi _ j}\widehat f=\widehat{(-2\pi \mathrm i x_ jf)}. \end{equation} Moreover, for $t>0$, \[  \widehat{\mathrm e^{-\pi t|x|^2}}(\xi )=t^{-d/2}\mathrm e^{-\pi |\xi |^2/t}.  \] Proof. Let $f\in \mathcal S$. We first prove the second rule in ( 6.1 ). By the mean value theorem, the difference quotients of $\xi \mapsto \mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }$ in the direction of $\xi _ j$ are bounded by $2\pi |x_ j|$, and $x_ jf$ is integrable. Hence dominated convergence allows us to differentiate under the integral sign: $\partial _{\xi _ j}\widehat f$ exists and is the transform of $-2\pi \mathrm i x_ jf$, which is continuous. Since $x_ jf\in \mathcal S$, induction shows that $\widehat f$ is smooth and that $\partial ^\beta \widehat f$ is the transform of $(-2\pi \mathrm i x)^\beta f$. For the first rule, Fubini's theorem allows us to integrate in $x_ j$ before the other coordinates. For almost every value of the other coordinates, $f$ and $\partial _ jf$ are integrable on the corresponding line, and an integration by parts over $[-a,a]$ followed by $a\to \infty $ gives \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\partial _ jf(x)\, \mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d x_ j=2\pi \mathrm i\xi _ j\int _{\mathbb R}f(x)\, \mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d x_ j,  \] because the boundary terms are bounded by $|f(x)|$ at $x_ j=\pm a$, and $f(x)\to 0$ as $|x|\to \infty $. Integrating over the other coordinates proves the first rule. Combining the two rules, we find that $\xi ^\alpha \partial ^\beta \widehat f$ is a constant multiple of the transform of $\partial ^\alpha (x^\beta f)$. This function belongs to $\mathcal S$ and is therefore integrable, so $\xi ^\alpha \partial ^\beta \widehat f$ is bounded by a multiple of its $L^1$ norm. Hence $\widehat f\in \mathcal S$. For the Gaussian, consider first $d=1$, put $g(x)=\mathrm e^{-\pi x^2}$, which belongs to $\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$, and set $F=\widehat g$. Since $-2\pi \mathrm i xg=\mathrm i g'$, the two rules give $F'=\mathrm i\, \widehat{g'}=\mathrm i(2\pi \mathrm i\xi )F=-2\pi \xi F$, so $F(\xi )\mathrm e^{\pi \xi ^2}$ is constant. Moreover $F(0)=1$: squaring the positive integral $F(0)$ and using polar coordinates in the plane, where $s_1=2\pi $, gives $F(0)^2=2\pi \int _0^\infty r\mathrm e^{-\pi r^2}\, \mathrm d r=1$. Hence $F(\xi )=\mathrm e^{-\pi \xi ^2}$. In dimension $d$, Fubini's theorem writes the transform of $\mathrm e^{-\pi |x|^2}$ as a product of one-dimensional transforms, which proves the formula for $t=1$. For general $t$, the linear substitution $x=y/\sqrt t$ gives \[  \int \mathrm e^{-\pi t|x|^2}\mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d x=t^{-d/2}\int \mathrm e^{-\pi |y|^2}\mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i y\cdot \xi /\sqrt t}\, \mathrm d y=t^{-d/2}\mathrm e^{-\pi |\xi |^2/t}.  \] $\square$ Theorem 6.1.2 (Plancherel) . Every $f\in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ satisfies the inversion formula \[  f(x)=\int \widehat f(\xi )\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d\xi ,\qquad x\in \mathbb R^ d.  \] The Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator on $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$. This extension is unitary, its inverse is given on Schwartz functions by the integral with the exponential $\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }$, and on $L^1\cap L^2$ it agrees almost everywhere with the integral transform. Proof. Let $f\in \mathcal S$ and $\varepsilon >0$. Insert the factor $\mathrm e^{-\pi \varepsilon ^2|\xi |^2}$ into the inversion integral. By Fubini's theorem and lemma 6.1.1 with $t=\varepsilon ^2$, \[  \int \widehat f(\xi )\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\mathrm e^{-\pi \varepsilon ^2|\xi |^2}\, \mathrm d\xi =f*g_\varepsilon (x), \qquad g_\varepsilon (y)=\varepsilon ^{-d}\mathrm e^{-\pi |y|^2/\varepsilon ^2}.  \] The functions $g_\varepsilon $ are positive with integral one, and the substitution $y=\varepsilon y'$ shows that their mass outside a fixed ball $B(0,\delta )$ tends to zero as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Since $f$ is bounded, and uniformly continuous because its gradient is bounded, splitting the convolution integral into the regions $|y|<\delta $ and $|y|\geq \delta $ shows that $f*g_\varepsilon \to f$ uniformly. On the left-hand side, $\widehat f\in \mathcal S\subset L^1$ by lemma 6.1.1 , so dominated convergence lets $\varepsilon \to 0$ under the frequency integral. This proves the inversion formula. Write $\mathcal F$ for the Fourier transform on $\mathcal S$, $\mathcal F^*$ for the inverse integral transform $\mathcal F^*g(x)=\int g(\xi )\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d\xi $, and $Rf(x)=f(-x)$. The substitution $x\mapsto -x$ shows that $\mathcal F^*=R\mathcal F=\mathcal FR$ on $\mathcal S$. In particular $\mathcal F^*$ maps $\mathcal S$ into itself, and both compositions $\mathcal F^*\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F\mathcal F^*$ equal $R\mathcal F\mathcal F$, which is the identity on $\mathcal S$ by the inversion formula. For $f,g\in \mathcal S$, applying inversion to $g$ and Fubini's theorem, we obtain Parseval's identity \[  \int f\overline g\, \mathrm d x=\int \widehat f\, \overline{\widehat g}\, \mathrm d\xi ;  \] the interchange of integrals is justified because the double integral of the absolute value is at most $\| f\| _1\| \widehat g\| _1$. By lemma 1.4.1 (5), applied to Lebesgue measure, $C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$, and hence $\mathcal S$, is dense in $L^2$. By Parseval's identity, $\mathcal F$ maps sequences in $\mathcal S$ that are Cauchy in $L^2$ to Cauchy sequences, and $L^2$ is complete; therefore $\mathcal F$ extends uniquely from $\mathcal S$ to a bounded operator on $L^2$, and this extension is an isometry. Since $\mathcal F^*=R\mathcal F$, the inverse integral transform extends in the same way. Both compositions of the two extensions are continuous and equal to the identity on the dense subspace $\mathcal S$, hence everywhere. Thus the extension is unitary, with the stated inverse. Finally let $f\in L^1\cap L^2$. We choose $f_ j\in C_ c^\infty $ converging to $f$ both in $L^1$ and in $L^2$: first replace $f$ by $f\mathbf1_{B(0,R)}$ with $R$ large, and then mollify; by lemma 1.4.1 (2) the mollifications converge in both norms, since their supports lie in a fixed compact set. The integral transforms of the $f_ j$ converge uniformly to that of $f$, because the difference is bounded by $\| f_ j-f\| _1$, while by isometry they converge in $L^2$ to the $L^2$ transform of $f$. A subsequence of an $L^2$ convergent sequence converges almost everywhere: choose it so that the squared $L^2$ errors are summable, and apply Tonelli's theorem to the sum of the squared errors. Hence the two transforms of $f$ agree almost everywhere. $\square$ We continue to write $\widehat f$ for the $L^2$ transform of $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$, and we call its inverse the inverse $L^2$ transform. Proposition 6.1.3 . Let $\mu $ be a finite positive Borel measure on $\mathbb R^ d$ such that $\widehat\mu \in L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$. Then $\mu =g\, \mathrm d x$ for a nonnegative function $g\in L^1\cap L^2$, and $\| g\| _2=\| \widehat\mu \| _2$. Proof. Let $g\in L^2$ be the inverse $L^2$ transform of $\widehat\mu $, so that $\widehat g=\widehat\mu $. For $\phi \in \mathcal S$ we have \[  \int \phi \, \mathrm d\mu =\int \widehat\phi (\xi )\widehat\mu (-\xi )\, \mathrm d\xi =\int \phi g\, \mathrm d x.  \] The first equality follows from the inversion formula for $\phi $ and Fubini's theorem. For the second, we apply Parseval's identity to $\phi $ and $\overline g$; it extends from $\mathcal S$ to $L^2$ because the $L^2$ transform is unitary. We also use that the transform of $\overline g$ at $\xi $ is $\overline{\widehat g(-\xi )}$; this holds for Schwartz functions by definition, and it extends to $L^2$ because the maps $g\mapsto \widehat{\overline g}$ and $g\mapsto \overline{\widehat g(-\, \cdot \, )}$ are continuous from $L^2$ to $L^2$. Consequently, for every test function $\phi $ the number $\int \phi g\, \mathrm d x=\int \phi \, \mathrm d\mu $ is real when $\phi $ is real and nonnegative when $\phi \geq 0$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on compact sets, $g$ is locally integrable, so it defines a positive distribution. By proposition 1.4.3 (3) its mollifications $g*\rho _\varepsilon $ are nonnegative, and they converge to $g$ in $L^1$ on compact sets by lemma 1.4.1 (2). Hence $g$ is real and nonnegative almost everywhere. The measures $\mu $ and $g\, \mathrm d x$ are Radon by proposition 1.1.2 , and they define the same distribution; by proposition 1.4.3 (4), $\mu =g\, \mathrm d x$. In particular $\int g\, \mathrm d x=\mu (\mathbb R^ d)<\infty $, and $\| g\| _2=\| \widehat\mu \| _2$ because the $L^2$ transform is unitary. $\square$ For $0<s<d$, the Riesz $s$-energy of a finite positive Borel measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb R^ d$ is \[  I_ s(\mu )=\iint |x-y|^{-s}\, \mathrm d\mu (x)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)\in [0,\infty ].  \] The kernel $|x-y|^{-s}$ carries no normalizing constant. For comparison, if $d\geq 3$ and $\mu $ has compact support, the energy $I(\mu )$ of section 4.1 , defined with the normalized kernel $\Gamma _ d$, satisfies $(d-2)s_{d-1}I(\mu )=I_{d-2}(\mu )$, where $s_{d-1}$ is the area of the unit sphere $S^{d-1}$ (section 2.1 ). Theorem 6.1.4 . Let $\mu $ be a finite positive Borel measure on $\mathbb R^ d$, and let $0<s<d$. Then \[  I_ s(\mu )=b_{d,s}\int _{\mathbb R^ d}|\widehat\mu (\xi )|^2|\xi |^{s-d}\, \mathrm d\xi , \qquad b_{d,s}=\pi ^{s-d/2}\frac{\Gamma ((d-s)/2)}{\Gamma (s/2)},  \] where $\Gamma (a)=\int _0^\infty v^{a-1}\mathrm e^{-v}\, \mathrm d v$, $a>0$, is Euler's Gamma function. Both sides may be infinite. Proof. For $z\in \mathbb R^ d$, the substitution $v=\pi t|z|^2$ gives \[  |z|^{-s}=\frac{\pi ^{s/2}}{\Gamma (s/2)}\int _0^\infty t^{s/2-1}\mathrm e^{-\pi t|z|^2}\, \mathrm d t,  \] and both sides are $+\infty $ when $z=0$. By lemma 6.1.1 with $t$ replaced by $1/t$, we have $\mathrm e^{-\pi t|z|^2}=t^{-d/2}\int \mathrm e^{-\pi |\xi |^2/t}\mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i z\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d\xi $. Taking $z=x-y$ and integrating with respect to $\mu \times \mu $, we obtain \[  \iint \mathrm e^{-\pi t|x-y|^2}\, \mathrm d\mu (x)\, \mathrm d\mu (y) =t^{-d/2}\int \mathrm e^{-\pi |\xi |^2/t}|\widehat\mu (\xi )|^2\, \mathrm d\xi ;  \] Fubini's theorem applies here because the Gaussian in $\xi $ is integrable and $\mu \times \mu $ is finite. Now insert the integral formula for $|x-y|^{-s}$ into $I_ s(\mu )$. All integrands are nonnegative, so Tonelli's theorem allows us to integrate first in $(x,y)$, then use the last identity, and finally integrate in $t$ before $\xi $, even when the integrals are infinite: \[  I_ s(\mu )=\frac{\pi ^{s/2}}{\Gamma (s/2)}\int |\widehat\mu (\xi )|^2\int _0^\infty t^{(s-d)/2-1}\mathrm e^{-\pi |\xi |^2/t}\, \mathrm d t\, \mathrm d\xi .  \] For $\xi \neq 0$, the substitution $v=\pi |\xi |^2/t$ evaluates the inner integral as \[  \int _0^\infty t^{(s-d)/2-1}\mathrm e^{-\pi |\xi |^2/t}\, \mathrm d t =\pi ^{(s-d)/2}|\xi |^{s-d}\Gamma ((d-s)/2),  \] and the point $\xi =0$ is a Lebesgue null set. Multiplying the constants gives the formula. $\square$ Example 6.1.5 . The area of the unit sphere $S^{d-1}\subset \mathbb R^ d$ is 6.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:sphere-area} s_{d-1}=\frac{2\pi ^{d/2}}{\Gamma (d/2)}. \end{equation} For $0<s<d$, the probability measure $\mathrm d\mu =\mathrm e^{-\pi |x|^2}\, \mathrm d x$ on $\mathbb R^ d$ satisfies \[  I_ s(\mu )=\left(\frac\pi 2\right)^{s/2}\frac{\Gamma ((d-s)/2)}{\Gamma (d/2)}.  \] Proof. By lemma 6.1.1 with $\xi =0$ and $t=1$, the Gaussian $\mathrm e^{-\pi |x|^2}$ has integral one. Integrating in polar coordinates and substituting $v=\pi r^2$, we obtain \[  1=\int \mathrm e^{-\pi |x|^2}\, \mathrm d x=s_{d-1}\int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-\pi r^2}r^{d-1}\, \mathrm d r=\frac{s_{d-1}\Gamma (d/2)}{2\pi ^{d/2}},  \] which proves ( 6.2 ). By lemma 6.1.1 , $\widehat\mu (\xi )=\mathrm e^{-\pi |\xi |^2}$. Hence theorem 6.1.4 and polar coordinates give \[  I_ s(\mu )=b_{d,s}\int \mathrm e^{-2\pi |\xi |^2}|\xi |^{s-d}\, \mathrm d\xi =b_{d,s}s_{d-1}\int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-2\pi r^2}r^{s-1}\, \mathrm d r.  \] The substitution $v=2\pi r^2$ evaluates the radial integral as $\Gamma (s/2)/(2(2\pi )^{s/2})$. Inserting the values of $b_{d,s}$ and $s_{d-1}$ proves the formula. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.1.1
section: 2.2 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: Lemma 6.1.1 . The Fourier transform maps $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ into itself, and for $f\in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ and $1\leq j\leq d$, 6.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:fourier-derivative-rules} \widehat{\partial _ jf}(\xi )=2\pi \mathrm i\xi _ j\widehat f(\xi ),\qquad \partial _{\xi _ j}\widehat f=\widehat{(-2\pi \mathrm i x_ jf)}. \end{equation} Moreover, for $t>0$, \[  \widehat{\mathrm e^{-\pi t|x|^2}}(\xi )=t^{-d/2}\mathrm e^{-\pi |\xi |^2/t}.  \] Proof. Let $f\in \mathcal S$. We first prove the second rule in ( 6.1 ). By the mean value theorem, the difference quotients of $\xi \mapsto \mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }$ in the direction of $\xi _ j$ are bounded by $2\pi |x_ j|$, and $x_ jf$ is integrable. Hence dominated convergence allows us to differentiate under the integral sign: $\partial _{\xi _ j}\widehat f$ exists and is the transform of $-2\pi \mathrm i x_ jf$, which is continuous. Since $x_ jf\in \mathcal S$, induction shows that $\widehat f$ is smooth and that $\partial ^\beta \widehat f$ is the transform of $(-2\pi \mathrm i x)^\beta f$. For the first rule, Fubini's theorem allows us to integrate in $x_ j$ before the other coordinates. For almost every value of the other coordinates, $f$ and $\partial _ jf$ are integrable on the corresponding line, and an integration by parts over $[-a,a]$ followed by $a\to \infty $ gives \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\partial _ jf(x)\, \mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d x_ j=2\pi \mathrm i\xi _ j\int _{\mathbb R}f(x)\, \mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d x_ j,  \] because the boundary terms are bounded by $|f(x)|$ at $x_ j=\pm a$, and $f(x)\to 0$ as $|x|\to \infty $. Integrating over the other coordinates proves the first rule. Combining the two rules, we find that $\xi ^\alpha \partial ^\beta \widehat f$ is a constant multiple of the transform of $\partial ^\alpha (x^\beta f)$. This function belongs to $\mathcal S$ and is therefore integrable, so $\xi ^\alpha \partial ^\beta \widehat f$ is bounded by a multiple of its $L^1$ norm. Hence $\widehat f\in \mathcal S$. For the Gaussian, consider first $d=1$, put $g(x)=\mathrm e^{-\pi x^2}$, which belongs to $\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$, and set $F=\widehat g$. Since $-2\pi \mathrm i xg=\mathrm i g'$, the two rules give $F'=\mathrm i\, \widehat{g'}=\mathrm i(2\pi \mathrm i\xi )F=-2\pi \xi F$, so $F(\xi )\mathrm e^{\pi \xi ^2}$ is constant. Moreover $F(0)=1$: squaring the positive integral $F(0)$ and using polar coordinates in the plane, where $s_1=2\pi $, gives $F(0)^2=2\pi \int _0^\infty r\mathrm e^{-\pi r^2}\, \mathrm d r=1$. Hence $F(\xi )=\mathrm e^{-\pi \xi ^2}$. In dimension $d$, Fubini's theorem writes the transform of $\mathrm e^{-\pi |x|^2}$ as a product of one-dimensional transforms, which proves the formula for $t=1$. For general $t$, the linear substitution $x=y/\sqrt t$ gives \[  \int \mathrm e^{-\pi t|x|^2}\mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d x=t^{-d/2}\int \mathrm e^{-\pi |y|^2}\mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i y\cdot \xi /\sqrt t}\, \mathrm d y=t^{-d/2}\mathrm e^{-\pi |\xi |^2/t}.  \] $\square$

title: Theorem 6.1.2 (Plancherel)
section: 2.2 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: Theorem 6.1.2 (Plancherel) . Every $f\in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ satisfies the inversion formula \[  f(x)=\int \widehat f(\xi )\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d\xi ,\qquad x\in \mathbb R^ d.  \] The Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^ d)$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator on $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$. This extension is unitary, its inverse is given on Schwartz functions by the integral with the exponential $\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }$, and on $L^1\cap L^2$ it agrees almost everywhere with the integral transform. Proof. Let $f\in \mathcal S$ and $\varepsilon >0$. Insert the factor $\mathrm e^{-\pi \varepsilon ^2|\xi |^2}$ into the inversion integral. By Fubini's theorem and lemma 6.1.1 with $t=\varepsilon ^2$, \[  \int \widehat f(\xi )\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\mathrm e^{-\pi \varepsilon ^2|\xi |^2}\, \mathrm d\xi =f*g_\varepsilon (x), \qquad g_\varepsilon (y)=\varepsilon ^{-d}\mathrm e^{-\pi |y|^2/\varepsilon ^2}.  \] The functions $g_\varepsilon $ are positive with integral one, and the substitution $y=\varepsilon y'$ shows that their mass outside a fixed ball $B(0,\delta )$ tends to zero as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Since $f$ is bounded, and uniformly continuous because its gradient is bounded, splitting the convolution integral into the regions $|y|<\delta $ and $|y|\geq \delta $ shows that $f*g_\varepsilon \to f$ uniformly. On the left-hand side, $\widehat f\in \mathcal S\subset L^1$ by lemma 6.1.1 , so dominated convergence lets $\varepsilon \to 0$ under the frequency integral. This proves the inversion formula. Write $\mathcal F$ for the Fourier transform on $\mathcal S$, $\mathcal F^*$ for the inverse integral transform $\mathcal F^*g(x)=\int g(\xi )\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }\, \mathrm d\xi $, and $Rf(x)=f(-x)$. The substitution $x\mapsto -x$ shows that $\mathcal F^*=R\mathcal F=\mathcal FR$ on $\mathcal S$. In particular $\mathcal F^*$ maps $\mathcal S$ into itself, and both compositions $\mathcal F^*\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F\mathcal F^*$ equal $R\mathcal F\mathcal F$, which is the identity on $\mathcal S$ by the inversion formula. For $f,g\in \mathcal S$, applying inversion to $g$ and Fubini's theorem, we obtain Parseval's identity \[  \int f\overline g\, \mathrm d x=\int \widehat f\, \overline{\widehat g}\, \mathrm d\xi ;  \] the interchange of integrals is justified because the double integral of the absolute value is at most $\| f\| _1\| \widehat g\| _1$. By lemma 1.4.1 (5), applied to Lebesgue measure, $C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$, and hence $\mathcal S$, is dense in $L^2$. By Parseval's identity, $\mathcal F$ maps sequences in $\mathcal S$ that are Cauchy in $L^2$ to Cauchy sequences, and $L^2$ is complete; therefore $\mathcal F$ extends uniquely from $\mathcal S$ to a bounded operator on $L^2$, and this extension is an isometry. Since $\mathcal F^*=R\mathcal F$, the inverse integral transform extends in the same way. Both compositions of the two extensions are continuous and equal to the identity on the dense subspace $\mathcal S$, hence everywhere. Thus the extension is unitary, with the stated inverse. Finally let $f\in L^1\cap L^2$. We choose $f_ j\in C_ c^\infty $ converging to $f$ both in $L^1$ and in $L^2$: first replace $f$ by $f\mathbf1_{B(0,R)}$ with $R$ large, and then mollify; by lemma 1.4.1 (2) the mollifications converge in both norms, since their supports lie in a fixed compact set. The integral transforms of the $f_ j$ converge uniformly to that of $f$, because the difference is bounded by $\| f_ j-f\| _1$, while by isometry they converge in $L^2$ to the $L^2$ transform of $f$. A subsequence of an $L^2$ convergent sequence converges almost everywhere: choose it so that the squared $L^2$ errors are summable, and apply Tonelli's theorem to the sum of the squared errors. Hence the two transforms of $f$ agree almost everywhere. $\square$

title: 6.2 Second derivatives and singular integrals
section: 2.2 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
6.2 Second derivatives and singular integrals Let $d\geq 1$. For a function $v$ on $\mathbb R^ d$ we write $D^2v=(\partial _ a\partial _ bv)_{a,b=1}^ d$ for its real Hessian. In $L^ p$ norms of vector-valued and matrix-valued functions, vectors carry the Euclidean norm and matrices the Hilbert–Schmidt norm $|M|=(\sum _{a,b}|M_{ab}|^2)^{1/2}$. Constants denoted by $C_ d$ and $C_{d,p}$ depend only on the indicated parameters and may change from line to line. The Laplacian $\Delta v$ is the trace of $D^2v$. If $d\geq 2$, a bound for $\Delta v$ does not bound $D^2v$ pointwise: a test function equal to $x_1^2-x_2^2$ near the origin has vanishing Laplacian and nonzero Hessian there. We show that $\Delta v$ does bound $D^2v$ in $L^ p$ for $1<p<\infty $ (theorem 6.2.3 ). On the Fourier side, $\partial _ a\partial _ bv$ is obtained from $-\Delta v$ by multiplication with the bounded function $-\xi _ a\xi _ b/|\xi |^2$, so the case $p=2$ follows from Plancherel's theorem. For the other exponents we represent the corresponding operator, away from the support of a function, by a kernel that is smooth off the diagonal. We then use the Calderón–Zygmund decomposition: on each of its cubes the function minus its average has mean zero, and this cancellation makes the image of that part integrable far from the cube. The section ends with Sobolev spaces, on open subsets of $\mathbb R^ d$ and on compact manifolds, and with Morrey's inequality, which turns $L^ p$ bounds for second derivatives into Hölder continuity of first derivatives. Lemma 6.2.1 . Let $1\leq a,b\leq d$, and define an operator $T_{ab}$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ by \[  \widehat{T_{ab}f}(\xi )=- rac{\xi _ a\xi _ b}{|\xi |^2}\widehat f(\xi ), \qquad \xi 
eq 0,  \] the multiplier being zero at the origin. Then $T_{ab}$ is self-adjoint and has norm at most one. Moreover: There is a smooth real function $K_{ab}$ on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $ such that \[  |K_{ab}(z)|\leq C_ d|z|^{-d},\qquad |
abla K_{ab}(z)|\leq C_ d|z|^{-d-1}.  \] If $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact set $F$, then $f$ is integrable, and for almost every $x\in \mathbb R^ d\setminus F$, \[  T_{ab}f(x)=\int K_{ab}(x-y)f(y)\, \mathrm d y.  \] For $v\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ we have $\partial _ a\partial _ bv=T_{ab}(-\Delta v)$. Proof. The multiplier is real and bounded by one in absolute value, so Plancherel's theorem shows that $T_{ab}$ is self-adjoint with norm at most one. For $v\in C_ c^\infty $, the first rule in ( 6.1 ) (lemma 6.1.1 ), applied twice, gives $\widehat{-\Delta v}(\xi )=4\pi ^2|\xi |^2\widehat v(\xi )$ and $\widehat{\partial _ a\partial _ bv}(\xi )=-4\pi ^2\xi _ a\xi _ b\widehat v(\xi )$. Multiplying the first identity by the multiplier of $T_{ab}$ gives the second, which proves (3). To construct the kernel we use the heat kernel $H_ t(z)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\mathrm e^{-|z|^2/(4t)}$, $t>0$. By lemma 6.1.1 , $\widehat H_ t(\xi )=\mathrm e^{-4\pi ^2t|\xi |^2}$, and hence $\widehat{\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t}(\xi )=-4\pi ^2\xi _ a\xi _ b\mathrm e^{-4\pi ^2t|\xi |^2}$. For $0<\varepsilon <R<\infty $ put \[  k_{\varepsilon ,R}=\int _\varepsilon ^ R\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t\, \mathrm d t.  \] Since $\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)= igl (z_ az_ b/(4t^2)-\delta _{ab}/(2t) igr )H_ t(z)$, where $\delta _{ab}$ is the Kronecker symbol, we have \[  |\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|\leq C_ dt^{-d/2-1}(1+|z|^2/t)\mathrm e^{-|z|^2/(4t)}.  \] Hence $\sup _ z|\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|\leq C_ dt^{-d/2-1}$, and the substitution $z=\sqrt t\, w$ gives $\int |\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|\, \mathrm d z\leq C_ dt^{-1}$. Therefore the kernel $k_{\varepsilon ,R}$ is bounded and integrable, and Fubini's theorem, applied with the integrable majorant $|\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|$ on $\mathbb R^ d	imes [\varepsilon ,R]$, gives its Fourier transform: \[  \widehat{k_{\varepsilon ,R}}(\xi )=- rac{\xi _ a\xi _ b}{|\xi |^2}  igl (\mathrm e^{-4\pi ^2\varepsilon |\xi |^2} -\mathrm e^{-4\pi ^2R|\xi |^2} igr ),\qquad \xi 
eq 0.  \] Let $f\in L^1\cap L^2$. Then $k_{\varepsilon ,R}*f$ is bounded and integrable, hence in $L^2$, and by Fubini's theorem and the last assertion of theorem 6.1.2 its Fourier transform is $\widehat{k_{\varepsilon ,R}}\widehat f$. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and $R\uparrow \infty $, these multipliers are bounded by one and converge to $-\xi _ a\xi _ b/|\xi |^2$ for $\xi 
eq 0$. By dominated convergence on the Fourier side and Plancherel's theorem, $k_{\varepsilon ,R}*f	o T_{ab}f$ in $L^2$. For $z

Lemma 6.2.5 . Let $1\leq p<\infty $ and $\varepsilon >0$. There is a constant $C_{d,\varepsilon }$, depending only on $d$ and $\varepsilon $, such that \[  \| 
abla v\| _ p\leq \varepsilon \| D^2v\| _ p+C_{d,\varepsilon }\| v\| _ p, \qquad v\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d).  \] Proof. Let $e_ a$ be the $a$th coordinate vector and $h>0$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives \[  h\partial _ av(x)=v(x+he_ a)-v(x) -\int _0^ h(h-t)\partial _ a^2v(x+te_ a)\, \mathrm d t.  \] The $L^ p$ norm is invariant under translation. Moreover, $\omega (t)\, \mathrm d t=2h^{-2}(h-t)\, \mathrm d t$ is a probability measure on $[0,h]$, so Hölder's inequality gives $|\int _0^ hg\, \omega \, \mathrm d t|^ p\leq \int _0^ h|g|^ p\omega \, \mathrm d t$ for every measurable function $g$ on $[0,h]$. Applying this to $g(t)=\partial _ a^2v(x+te_ a)$, integrating in $x$ and using Tonelli's theorem, we obtain \[  \Bigl \| \int _0^ h(h-t)\partial _ a^2v(\cdot +te_ a)\, \mathrm d t\Bigr \| _ p\leq  rac{h^2}2\Bigl (\int _0^ h\| \partial _ a^2v(\cdot +te_ a)\| _ p^ p\, \omega (t)\, \mathrm d t\Bigr )^{1/p}= rac{h^2}2\| \partial _ a^2v\| _ p.  \] Hence $h\| \partial _ av\| _ p\leq 2\| v\| _ p+(h^2/2)\| \partial _ a^2v\| _ p$. Since $|
abla v|\leq \sum _ a|\partial _ av|$ and $|\partial _ a^2v|\leq |D^2v|$, summing over $a$ yields $\| 
abla v\| _ p\leq 2dh^{-1}\| v\| _ p+(dh/2)\| D^2v\| _ p$. The choice $h=2\varepsilon /d$ proves the lemma with $C_{d,\varepsilon }=d^2/\varepsilon $. $\square$ For a compact set $F\subset \mathbb R^ d$ and $0<\alpha \leq 1$, the Hölder norm of a function $v$ on $F$ is \[  \| v\| _{C^{0,\alpha }(F)}=\sup _ F|v|+\sup _{x,y\in F,\  x
eq y} rac{|v(x)-v(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha }.  \] A continuously differentiable function on an open set $U$ is of class $C^{1,\alpha }$ on a compact set $F\subset U$ if its first derivatives have finite $C^{0,\alpha }(F)$ norm, and it belongs to $C^{1,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ if it is of class $C^{1,\alpha }$ on every compact subset of $U$. Lemma 6.2.6 (Morrey's inequality) . Let $d<p<\infty $, put $\alpha =1-d/p$, and let $B'\Subset B$ be Euclidean balls in $\mathbb R^ d$. Every $v\in W^{1,p}(B)$ has a representative that is continuous on $B$ and satisfies \[  \| v\| _{C^{0,\alpha }(\overline{B'})}\leq C\| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B)},  \] where $C$ depends only on $d,p,B',B$. Consequently, for an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ d$, every function in $W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ has a representative in $C^{1,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Proof. We prove the estimate for smooth $v$, pass to general $v$ by mollification, and then apply the result to first derivatives. Assume first that $v$ is smooth on $B$. Let $Q\subset B$ be a ball of radius $r$, let $v_ Q=|Q|^{-1}\int _ Qv$ be the average of $v$ over $Q$, and let $x\in Q$. We claim that \[  |v(x)-v_ Q|\leq C_ d\int _ Q|
abla v(z)|\, |x-z|^{1-d}\, \mathrm d z.  \] For $z\in Q$, write $z=x+s	heta $ with $s=|z-x|$ and $	heta \in S^{d-1}$; then $|v(z)-v(x)|\leq \int _0^ s|
abla v(x+t	heta )|\, \mathrm d t$, and $|v(x)-v_ Q|$ is at most the average over $z\in Q$ of these segment integrals. Since $Q$ is convex and open and contains $x$, for each $	heta $ the radii $s>0$ with $x+s	heta \in Q$ form an interval $0<s<R(	heta )$, and $R(	heta )\leq 2r$. In polar coordinates about $x$ (( 2.1 ) on $B(x,2r)\supset Q$), the average of the segment integrals is \[   rac1{|Q|}\int _{S^{d-1}}\int _0^{R(	heta )}s^{d-1}\int _0^ s|
abla v(x+t	heta )|\, \mathrm d t\, \mathrm d s\, \mathrm d S(	heta ).  \] Interchanging the integrals in $s$ and $t$ produces the factor $|Q|^{-1}\int _ t^{R(	heta )}s^{d-1}\, \mathrm d s$, which is at most $(2r)^ d/(d|Q|)$ and hence bounded by a constant depending only on $d$. The remaining integral $\int _{S^{d-1}}\int _0^{R(	heta )}|
abla v(x+t	heta )|\, \mathrm d t\, \mathrm d S(	heta )$ is the integral on the right side of the claim, written in polar coordinates. This proves the claim. By Hölder's inequality with $p'=p/(p-1)$, the right side of the claim is at most $C_{d,p}r^{1-d/p}\| 
abla v\| _{L^ p(Q)}$, because \[  \int _ Q|x-z|^{(1-d)p'}\, \mathrm d z\leq \int _{B(x,2r)}|x-z|^{(1-d)p'}\, \mathrm d z=C_{d,p}r^{(1-d)p'+d},  \] and this integral is finite exactly when $(1-d)p'>-d$, that is, when $p>d$. (For $d=1$ the exponent $(1-d)p'$ is zero.) Let $\delta >0$ be the distance from $B'$ to $\mathbb R^ d\setminus B$. If $x,y\in B'$ and $0<|x-y|<\delta /2$, the ball $Q=B(x,2|x-y|)$ lies in $B$ and contains $x$ and $y$. Applying the preceding bound at both points gives \[  |v(x)-v(y)|\leq C_{d,p}|x-y|^{1-d/p}\| 
abla v\| _{L^ p(B)}.  \] For $x\in B'$, the same bound on the ball $Q=B(x,\delta /2)\subset B$, together with the estimate $|v_ Q|\leq |Q|^{-1/p}\| v\| _{L^ p(B)}$ from Hölder's inequality, gives $\sup _{B'}|v|\leq C\| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B)}$ with $C$ depending on $d,p,\delta $. If $|x-y|\geq \delta /2$, then $|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha \leq 2(\delta /2)^{-\alpha }\sup _{B'}|v|$. These bounds prove the estimate for smooth $v$ on $B'$, and hence on $\overline{B'}$, since $v$ is continuous on $B\supset \overline{B'}$. For general $v\in W^{1,p}(B)$, choose a ball $B''$, depending only on $B'$ and $B$, with $B'\Subset B''\Subset B$, and let $v_\varepsilon =v*ho _\varepsilon $, which is smooth on $B''$ for small $\varepsilon $. By the remark preceding lemma 6.2.4 , $\partial _ av_\varepsilon =(\partial _ av)_\varepsilon $, and $v_\varepsilon 	o v$ and $\partial _ av_\varepsilon 	o \partial _ av$ in $L^ p(B'')$. The estimate for smooth functions, applied on $B'\Subset B''$ to the differences of the $v_\varepsilon $, shows that they form a Cauchy family in the norm of $C^{0,\alpha }(\overline{B'})$. Their uniform limit is continuous on $\overline{B'}$, agrees almost everywhere with $v$, and satisfies the asserted estimate, because $\| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B'')}\leq \| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B)}$. Two continuous functions that agree almost everywhere on an open set agree everywhere on it. Hence the continuous representatives obtained from different balls $B'\Subset B$ agree on their overlaps and define a single continuous representative on $B$. Finally, let $v\in W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. On every ball $B\Subset U$, both $v$ and its first derivatives $\partial _ av$ belong to $W^{1,p}(B)$. By the preceding paragraph, on each smaller ball $B'\Subset B$ the mollifications $v_\varepsilon $ and $\partial _ av_\varepsilon =(\partial _ av)_\varepsilon $ converge uniformly to the continuous representatives $	ilde v$ of $v$ and $	ilde w_ a$ of $\partial _ av$. Passing to the limit in \[  v_\varepsilon (x+he_ a)-v_\varepsilon (x)=\int _0^ h\partial _ av_\varepsilon (x+te_ a)\, \mathrm d t  \] shows that $	ilde v$ has the continuous partial derivatives $\partial _ a	ilde v=	ilde w_ a$. Hence $	ilde v$ is continuously differentiable, and by the first part its first derivatives are Hölder continuous with exponent $\alpha $ on each $\overline{B'}$.
