title: Example 7.4.6
section: 5.1 Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Example 7.4.6 . Let $1\leq r\leq n$ and $f(z)=z_1^{a_1}\cdots z_ r^{a_ r}$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, with positive integers $a_ j$. Then $\log |f|^2=\sum _ ja_ j\log |z_ j|^2$ everywhere, both sides being $-\infty $ on the zero set, and theorem 7.4.5 applied to each $z_ j$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2=\sum _{j=1}^ r a_ j[\{ z_ j=0\} ]$ on all of $\mathbb C^ n$, including the intersections of the coordinate hyperplanes. More generally, let $g$ and $h$ be holomorphic and not identically zero on a connected coordinate neighborhood. The function $\log |g|^2-\log |h|^2$, defined outside the null set where $g$ or $h$ vanishes, is locally integrable, and its complex Hessian is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\log |g|^2-\log |h|^2)=[\operatorname{div}(g)]-[\operatorname{div}(h)]$. This current depends only on the quotient $g/h$: if $g',h'$ is another such pair with $gh'=g'h$, the two logarithmic differences agree almost everywhere, hence as distributions. We regard the difference only as an element of $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; in particular, it is assigned no values at the common zeros of $g$ and $h$.

title: 7.5 Maps of currents and local mass
search_title: Maps of currents and local mass
section: 5.1 Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: 7.5 Maps of currents and local mass Let $F\colon X\to Y$ be a holomorphic map between complex manifolds, with $\dim _{\mathbb C}X=m$ and $\dim _{\mathbb C}Y=n$. Smooth forms on $Y$ can be pulled back to $X$ by means of the derivative of $F$; the pullback commutes with $\mathrm d$, by ( 7.3 ), and also with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, because pullback by a holomorphic map preserves types. By duality, currents on $X$ can be pushed forward to $Y$ when $F$ is proper on their support, and currents on $Y$ can be pulled back when $F$ is a submersion. Closed positive $(1,1)$-currents can also be pulled back through their local potentials, as long as these do not become identically $-\infty $. Proposition 7.5.1 . Let $T$ be a current of bidegree $(p,q)$ on $X$, and assume that the restriction of $F$ to $\operatorname{Supp}T$ is proper, that is, $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(L)$ is compact for every compact set $L\subset Y$. Then the pushforward $F_*T$ defined below is a current of bidegree $(p+n-m,q+n-m)$ on $Y$; it is the zero current if this bidegree lies outside the range $0,\ldots ,n$. The pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{d}$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, and if $p=q$ and $T$ is positive, then $F_*T$ is positive. Proof. Let $\varphi $ be a test form on $Y$. By properness, the set $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$ is compact. Choose a smooth function $\chi \geq 0$ with compact support on $X$ that equals one on a neighborhood of this set (proposition 7.1.3 ), and define \[  (F_*T)(\varphi )=T(\chi F^*\varphi ).  \] The value does not depend on $\chi $: if $\chi '$ is another choice, then $(\chi -\chi ')F^*\varphi $ is a test form whose support is disjoint from $\operatorname{Supp}T$, since $\chi =\chi '$ near $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$ and $F^*\varphi =0$ outside $F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$; so $T$ vanishes on this form. For all test forms supported in a fixed compact set $L\subset Y$ a single cutoff serves, namely one equal to one near the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(L)$; in particular, $F_*T$ is linear. Now let $L$ lie in a chart of $Y$, fix such a cutoff $\chi $, cover $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ by finitely many charts of $X$ and choose a partition of unity subordinate to this cover near $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. By the chain rule, the coefficients of the pieces of $\chi F^*\varphi $ in these charts, together with their derivatives of order at most $m'$, are bounded by a constant times $\sum _ Jp_{L,m'}(\varphi _ J)$, where the $\varphi _ J$ are the coefficients of $\varphi $ (at points mapped outside $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $ they vanish). The estimates for $T$ in these charts therefore give the estimate in the definition of a current for $F_*T$. Pullback preserves bidegrees, and $T$ acts on test forms of bidegree $(m-p,m-q)$, so $F_*T$ has bidegree $(n-(m-p),n-(m-q))$. For differentiation, note that $\mathrm d(\chi F^*\varphi )=\chi F^*\mathrm d\varphi +\mathrm d\chi \wedge F^*\varphi $, and $T$ vanishes on the last term because its support is disjoint from $\operatorname{Supp}T$. Since the degrees of $T$ and $F_*T$ differ by the even integer $2(m-n)$, the signs in the definitions of $\mathrm dT$ and $\mathrm dF_*T$ agree, and $\mathrm d(F_*T)=F_*(\mathrm dT)$; the same argument applies to $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. If $\varphi $ is strongly positive, so is $\chi F^*\varphi $ by proposition 7.2.1 , which proves the last assertion. $\square$ For example, the current $[Z]$ of example 7.2.7 is the pushforward of the constant function $1$, regarded as a current of degree zero on $Z$, under the inclusion $Z\hookrightarrow X$, which is proper. A current with compact support can be pushed forward by every holomorphic map. Proposition 7.5.2 . Assume that $F$ is a submersion, that is, its complex derivative has rank $n$ at every point of $X$. Then every current $T$ on $Y$ has a pullback $F^*T$, a current on $X$ of the same bidegree, which agrees with the pullback of forms when $T$ is smooth, and with the locally integrable function $a\circ F$ when $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $a$ on $Y$. The map $T\mapsto F^*T$ is continuous for weak convergence, commutes with $\mathrm d$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, and maps positive currents to positive currents. Proof. Local construction. Let $x\in X$, and choose holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ near $F(x)$. Since $F$ is a submersion, the complex Jacobian matrix at $x$ of the $n$ components of $z\circ F$ has rank $n$ in every chart around $x$. By proposition 7.1.2 (3), these components are the first $n$ coordinates of holomorphic coordinates $(z,w)\in \mathbb C^ n\times \mathbb C^{m-n}$ near $x$, in which $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$; shrinking, we may assume that the coordinate domain is a product $U\times W$. For a distribution $a$ on $U$, define the distribution $F^*a$ on $U\times W$ by \[  \langle F^*a,\psi \rangle =\left\langle a,\int _{W}\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm{d}V_{2m-2n}(w)\right\rangle .  \] Integration in $w$ maps test functions on $U\times W$ continuously to test functions on $U$: the $z$-derivatives of $\int _ W\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ are the integrals of the $z$-derivatives of $\psi $, by differentiation under the integral sign, and its support lies in the projection of $\operatorname{Supp}\psi $. Hence $F^*a$ is a distribution, and if $a$ is locally integrable, then $F^*a$ is the function $(z,w)\mapsto a(z)$, by Fubini's theorem. For $T=\sum T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ on $U$ put $F^*T=\sum F^*T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. This is a linear map from currents on $U$ to currents on $U\times W$ preserving bidegrees, continuous for weak convergence, and equal to the pullback of forms for smooth $T$. It commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, since these act on the coefficients by differentiation, $\partial _{z_ l}F^*a=F^*\partial _{z_ l}a$, and $\partial _{w_ l}F^*a=0$ because $\int _ W\partial _{w_ l}\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)=0$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus; similarly for the conjugate derivatives. Continuity for weak convergence holds because the coefficients of a current depend continuously on it, by their explicit description in section 7.2 . Independence and gluing. Two such local constructions near $x$ agree. Indeed, mollifying the coefficients of $T$ in a chart near $F(x)$, we obtain smooth forms $T_\varepsilon \to T$ weakly on a neighborhood of $F(x)$, as in the discussion following theorem 7.2.5 . Both constructions are weakly continuous and agree with the pullback of forms on each $T_\varepsilon $, so they agree on $T$ near $x$. Consequently the local pullbacks agree on the overlaps of their domains, and by lemma 7.2.6 they glue to a unique current $F^*T$ on $X$ that agrees with each local pullback on its domain. Explicitly, if $(\chi _ c)$ is a partition of unity with compact supports subordinate to the cover of $X$ by the domains of the local pullbacks, and $(F^*T)_ c$ denotes a local pullback whose domain contains $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ c$, then $(F^*T)(\varphi )=\sum _ c(F^*T)_ c(\chi _ c\varphi )$. The local pullbacks are linear, preserve bidegrees and commute with $\mathrm d$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $; they give the pullback of forms if $T$ is smooth, and the function $a\circ F$ if $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $a$. By the uniqueness in lemma 7.2.6 , $F^*T$ has the same properties. Continuity for weak convergence follows from the explicit formula, since each of the finitely many nonzero terms $(F^*T)_ c(\chi _ c\varphi )$ depends continuously on $T$. Positivity. If $T$ is positive, the forms $T_\varepsilon $ are positive near $F(x)$, hence weakly positive at every point. By proposition 7.2.1 their pullbacks are weakly positive at every point, hence positive currents, and positivity passes to the weak limit, the local pullback of $T$ near $x$. Hence $F^*T$ is positive, by lemma 7.2.6 . $\square$ On currents of order zero, the submersion pullback is described by product measures. Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $W\subset \mathbb C^ k$ be open, and let $\lambda _ W$ be Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV_{2k}$ on $W$, which is the unit mass on the point $W=\mathbb C^0$ if $k=0$ and $W\neq \varnothing $. Every open subset of $U\times W$ is a countable union of products of open boxes, so the Borel sets of $U\times W$ form the $\sigma $-algebra generated by the products of Borel subsets of $U$ and of $W$. For a positive Radon measure $\sigma $ on $U$, which is $\sigma $-finite by proposition 1.1.2 , Tonelli's theorem therefore defines the product measure $\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W$ on the Borel sets of $U\times W$, and 7.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:product-measure-fubini} \int _{U\times W}h\, \mathrm d(\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W)=\int _ U\Bigl (\int _ Wh(z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2k}(w)\Bigr )\mathrm d\sigma (z) \end{equation} for every nonnegative Borel function $h$ on $U\times W$, the inner integral being a Borel function of $z$. A compact subset of $U\times W$ lies in the product of its two projections, which are compact, so $\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W$ is finite on compact sets and hence a positive Radon measure, by proposition 1.1.2 . For a complex Radon measure $\sigma =\sigma _1-\sigma _2+\mathrm i(\sigma _3-\sigma _4)$ on $U$ we put $\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W=\sigma _1\otimes \lambda _ W-\sigma _2\otimes \lambda _ W+\mathrm i(\sigma _3\otimes \lambda _ W-\sigma _4\otimes \lambda _ W)$. By linearity, ( 7.12 ) holds for every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support. Its right-hand side is the integral against $\sigma $ of the bounded Borel function $\widehat h(z)=\int _ Wh(z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2k}(w)$, which has compact support, so it does not depend on the decomposition of $\sigma $; neither does $\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W$, which is determined by its integrals of continuous functions with compact support. Corollary 7.5.3 . Let $F\colon X\to Y$ be a submersion, and let $T$ be a current of order zero on $Y$. Suppose that $X=U\times W$ and $Y=U$, where $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $W\subset \mathbb C^{m-n}$ are open, and that $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. Write $T=\sum _{I,J}T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. Then, with the product measures $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$ defined above, \[  F^*T=\sum _{I,J}(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J;  \] that is, in the coordinates $(z,w)$ the coefficient measure of $F^*T$ at $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ is $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$, and the coefficients at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish. In general, $F^*T$ has order zero, and \[  F^*(fT)=(f\circ F)\, F^*T  \] for every locally bounded Borel function $f$ on $Y$. In particular, $F^*(\mathbf1_ ET)=\mathbf1_{F^{-1}(E)}F^*T$ for every Borel set $E\subset Y$. Proof. (1) The local construction in the proof of proposition 7.5.2 can be carried out with the coordinates $z$ on $U$ and $(z,w)$ on $U\times W$, and it is then defined on all of $U\times W$. By the independence of the local constructions shown in that proof, $F^*T$ agrees with it near every point, hence on $U\times W$. Thus the coefficients of $F^*T$ at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish, and the coefficient at $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ is the distribution $\psi \mapsto \langle T_{IJ},\widehat\psi \rangle $, where $\widehat\psi (z)=\int _ W\psi (z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ is a test function on $U$. Since $T_{IJ}$ is a complex Radon measure, ( 7.12 ) gives $\langle T_{IJ},\widehat\psi \rangle =\int _ U\widehat\psi \, \mathrm dT_{IJ}=\int \psi \, \mathrm d(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)$ for every test function $\psi $ on $U\times W$. Hence this coefficient is the complex Radon measure $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$. (2) Let $x\in X$. As in the proof of proposition 7.5.2 , there are holomorphic coordinates $z$ on a chart of $Y$ around $F(x)$ and holomorphic coordinates $(z,w)$ on a neighborhood $N$ of $x$, with coordinate domain a product $U\times W$, in which $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. On $N$, the current $F^*T$ is the pullback of the restriction of $T$ to the open set $U$ by this projection. By (1), the coefficients of $F^*T$ in the chart $N$ are complex Radon measures. The charts $N$ obtained in this way form an atlas of $X$, so $F^*T$ has order zero, by the discussion following ( 7.8 ). Now let $f$ be a locally bounded Borel function on $Y$; then $f\circ F$ is a locally bounded Borel function on $X$, since $F$ is continuous. In the coordinates above, the coefficient measures of $fT$ are the measures $fT_{IJ}$, where $f$ is written in the coordinates $z$, so by (1) the coefficient measures of $F^*(fT)$ on $N$ are the measures $(fT_{IJ})\otimes \lambda _ W$, while those of $(f\circ F)F^*T$ are the measures $(f\circ F)(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)$; the coefficients at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish for both currents. Let $g$ be a continuous function with compact support in $U\times W$. The function $g\cdot (f\circ F)$ is bounded, Borel and compactly supported, and $\widehat g(z)=\int _ Wg(z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ is a bounded Borel function on $U$ with compact support. Applying ( 7.12 ) twice, we obtain \[  \int g\, (f\circ F)\, \mathrm d(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)=\int _ U\widehat g\, f\, \mathrm dT_{IJ}=\int _ U\widehat g\, \mathrm d(fT_{IJ})=\int g\, \mathrm d\bigl ((fT_{IJ})\otimes \lambda _ W\bigr ).  \] Hence the two currents have the same coefficient measures on $N$, and therefore agree on $N$. Since the sets $N$ cover $X$, the currents $F^*(fT)$ and $(f\circ F)F^*T$ coincide. The last assertion is the case $f=\mathbf1_ E$, since $\mathbf1_ E\circ F=\mathbf1_{F^{-1}(E)}$. $\square$ Proposition 7.5.4 . Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $Y$, and let $F\colon X\to Y$ be holomorphic. Suppose that every point of $X$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $F(W)$ lies in the domain of a canonical local potential $u$ of $T$ and $u\circ F$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $W$. Then the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$ on these neighborhoods glue to a closed positive current \[  F^*T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)  \] on $X$, which does not depend on the chosen potentials. It agrees with the pullback of forms if $T$ is smooth, and with the pullback of proposition 7.5.2 if $F$ is a submersion. Proof. Canonical local potentials are defined on manifolds of positive dimension (theorem 7.3.2 ), so $Y$ has positive dimension. If $X$ has dimension zero, every $(1,1)$-current on $X$ vanishes, and $F^*T=0$. Assume that $X$ has positive dimension, let $W$ and $u$ be as in the hypothesis, and let $W_0$ be a connected component of $W$. Each point of $W_0$ has a connected neighborhood $W'\subset W_0$ in a chart of $X$ such that $F(W')$ lies in a chart of $Y$ contained in the domain of $u$. In that chart, $u$ is the canonical subharmonic representative of its class, by the remark following proposition 7.3.3 , so by that proposition $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $ on $W'$, or locally integrable on $W'$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$. No point has neighborhoods $W'$ of both kinds, because a locally integrable function is finite almost everywhere. Hence the points of $W_0$ having a neighborhood of the first kind and those having one of the second kind form two disjoint open sets covering $W_0$. Since $W_0$ is connected and $u\circ F$ is not identically $-\infty $ on $W_0$, the first set is empty. Thus $u\circ F$ is locally integrable on $W$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$ there. Let $(\widetilde W,\widetilde u)$ be another pair as in the hypothesis. Near each point of the intersection of the domains of $u$ and $\widetilde u$ we have $\widetilde u=u+h$ with $h$ smooth and pluriharmonic, by theorem 7.3.2 and the remark following proposition 7.3.3 . Locally $h=\operatorname{Re}g$ with $g$ holomorphic, so $h\circ F=\operatorname{Re}(g\circ F)$ is smooth and pluriharmonic, and $\widetilde u\circ F=u\circ F+h\circ F$ near each point of $W\cap \widetilde W$. Consequently $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\widetilde u\circ F)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$ near each point of $W\cap \widetilde W$, hence on $W\cap \widetilde W$, since a current that vanishes near each point vanishes. By lemma 7.2.6 , the local currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$, which are positive and closed because $\mathrm d\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=0$, glue to a unique closed positive current $F^*T$ on $X$. It is independent of the choices: the currents obtained from two systems of choices agree near each point, by what we have just shown, and hence coincide by the uniqueness in lemma 7.2.6 . If $T$ is smooth, lemma 7.3.1 gives smooth real local potentials $v$ with $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$; they are subharmonic, by the matrix criterion and proposition 2.1.1 , hence their own canonical representatives, so we may use them as the potentials $u$. For a smooth potential $u$ the chain rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)=F^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=F^*T$. Now let $F$ be a submersion, and let $V$ be the domain of $u$. The restriction of $F$ to $F^{-1}(V)$ is a submersion to $V$, and its submersion pullback agrees on $F^{-1}(V)$ with that of $F$, since both are glued from the same local constructions. By proposition 7.5.2 , the locally integrable function $u\circ F$ represents the submersion pullback $F^*u$, and since this pullback commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, we obtain $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*u=F^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=F^*T$ on $F^{-1}(V)$, in particular on $W$. $\square$ Example 7.5.5 . On $\mathbb {C}^2$, the current $T=[\{ z_1=0\} ]$ has the canonical local potential $\log |z_1|^2$, by theorem 7.4.5 and proposition 7.4.3 . For $F(w)=(0,w)$, the composition $\log |z_1|^2\circ F$ is identically $-\infty $, and so is the composition of every canonical local potential, since these differ from $\log |z_1|^2$ by smooth functions; thus proposition 7.5.4 does not define $F^*T$. For $G(w)=(w,0)$, the composition is $\log |w|^2$, and $G^*T=[0]$ is the Dirac mass at the origin. Thus the current of integration over a line can be restricted to a transverse line, but not to the line itself. We finally compare trace measures in different charts by means of a Hermitian metric. A Hermitian metric on $X$ is a smooth field of positive definite Hermitian quadratic forms on its tangent spaces. In coordinates we write it as $h=\sum h_{j\bar k}\mathrm{d}z_ j\otimes \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$, with $(h_{j\bar k})$ a positive definite Hermitian matrix at each point, and we associate with it the real $(1,1)$-form $\omega =(\mathrm{i}/2)\sum h_{j\bar k}\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$; for the Euclidean metric $\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\otimes \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ we obtain $\omega =\beta $. Every complex manifold carries Hermitian metrics: a partition of unity combines the Euclidean metrics of charts into a locally finite convex combination, which is positive definite. By the matrix description of strict positivity in section 7.2 , the forms $\omega $ obtained in this way are exactly the smooth real $(1,1)$-forms that are strictly positive at every point; we call them Hermitian forms . A Hermitian form is a Kähler form if it is closed, and a complex manifold carrying a Kähler form is a Kähler manifold . For instance, $\beta $ is a Kähler form on $\mathbb C^ n$, but in general $\mathrm d\omega \neq 0$: on $\mathbb C^2$, the Hermitian form $\omega =\beta +\frac{\mathrm i}2|z_1|^2\mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_2$ has $\mathrm d\omega =\frac{\mathrm i}2(\bar z_1\mathrm dz_1+z_1\mathrm d\bar z_1)\wedge \mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_2\neq 0$. We usually denote Hermitian and Kähler forms by $\omega $; in 1 the same letter denoted other objects, such as points of the unit sphere and harmonic measures. For a positive current $T$ of bidegree $(p,p)$ on $X$, its trace measure with respect to $\omega $ is \[  \sigma _{T,\omega }=T\wedge \frac{\omega ^{n-p}}{(n-p)!}.  \] Since $\omega $ is positive, $\omega ^{n-p}$ is a smooth strongly positive form (proposition 7.2.1 ), so $T\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$ is a positive current of degree $2n$; hence $\sigma _{T,\omega }$ is a positive Radon measure on $X$, by the discussion following definition 7.2.4 , and unlike $\mu _ T$ it does not depend on a chart. It is comparable with the trace measures in charts. Let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart, choose a compact neighborhood $K'$ of $K$ in the chart, and let $0<c\leq C$ be lower and upper bounds for the eigenvalues of $(h_{j\bar k})$ on $K'$. At a point of $K'$, a unitary change of coordinates $w$ puts $\omega $ in the form $(\mathrm i/2)\sum _ j\lambda _ j\, \mathrm dw_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ j$ with $c\leq \lambda _ j\leq C$, while $\beta $ keeps its form. Expanding, \[  \frac{\omega ^{n-p}}{(n-p)!}=\sum _{|L|=n-p}\Big(\prod _{l\in L}\lambda _ l\Big)\bigwedge _{l\in L}\Big(\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dw_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ l\Big),  \] \[  \frac{\beta ^{n-p}}{(n-p)!}=\sum _{|L|=n-p}\bigwedge _{l\in L}\Big(\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dw_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ l\Big).  \] Hence $\omega ^{n-p}-c^{n-p}\beta ^{n-p}$ and $C^{n-p}\beta ^{n-p}-\omega ^{n-p}$ are strongly positive at every point of $K'$, and positivity of $T$ gives \[  c^{n-p}\mu _ T\leq (n-p)!\, \sigma _{T,\omega }\leq C^{n-p}\mu _ T\qquad \text{on }\operatorname{Int}K'\supset K.  \] Consequently, for a family of positive currents, locally uniform bounds for the trace measures in charts, as in theorem 7.2.5 , are equivalent to uniform bounds for $\sigma _{T,\omega }(K)$ on every compact set $K\subset X$, for any Hermitian metric. For a complex submanifold $Z$ of $X$ of dimension $r$, the restriction of $\omega ^ r/r!$ to $Z$ is the volume form of the Riemannian metric $\operatorname{Re}h$ restricted to $Z$, that is, the $2r$-form on $Z$ that takes the value $1$ on positively oriented bases of the tangent spaces which are orthonormal for $\operatorname{Re}h$. Indeed, at a point of $Z$ choose a basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ r$ of the complex tangent space of $Z$ that is orthonormal for $h$. Then $e_1,\mathrm ie_1,\ldots ,e_ r,\mathrm ie_ r$ is a positively oriented orthonormal basis for $\operatorname{Re}h$, and in the dual real coordinates the restriction of $\omega $ is $\sum _{j=1}^ r\mathrm{d}x_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}y_ j$, whose $r$th power divided by $r!$ is $\mathrm dx_1\wedge \mathrm dy_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dx_ r\wedge \mathrm dy_ r$. Consequently the trace measure $\sigma _{[Z],\omega }$, given by $\sigma _{[Z],\omega }(\chi )=\int _ Z\chi \, \omega ^ r/r!$, is the Riemannian volume measure of $Z$. Finally, in dimension zero all forms of positive degree and all $(1,1)$-currents vanish, and integration currents and currents of degree zero are sums over the discrete points of the manifold.

title: Proposition 7.5.1
section: 5.1 Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Proposition 7.5.1 . Let $T$ be a current of bidegree $(p,q)$ on $X$, and assume that the restriction of $F$ to $\operatorname{Supp}T$ is proper, that is, $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(L)$ is compact for every compact set $L\subset Y$. Then the pushforward $F_*T$ defined below is a current of bidegree $(p+n-m,q+n-m)$ on $Y$; it is the zero current if this bidegree lies outside the range $0,\ldots ,n$. The pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{d}$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, and if $p=q$ and $T$ is positive, then $F_*T$ is positive. Proof. Let $\varphi $ be a test form on $Y$. By properness, the set $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$ is compact. Choose a smooth function $\chi \geq 0$ with compact support on $X$ that equals one on a neighborhood of this set (proposition 7.1.3 ), and define \[  (F_*T)(\varphi )=T(\chi F^*\varphi ).  \] The value does not depend on $\chi $: if $\chi '$ is another choice, then $(\chi -\chi ')F^*\varphi $ is a test form whose support is disjoint from $\operatorname{Supp}T$, since $\chi =\chi '$ near $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$ and $F^*\varphi =0$ outside $F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$; so $T$ vanishes on this form. For all test forms supported in a fixed compact set $L\subset Y$ a single cutoff serves, namely one equal to one near the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(L)$; in particular, $F_*T$ is linear. Now let $L$ lie in a chart of $Y$, fix such a cutoff $\chi $, cover $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ by finitely many charts of $X$ and choose a partition of unity subordinate to this cover near $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. By the chain rule, the coefficients of the pieces of $\chi F^*\varphi $ in these charts, together with their derivatives of order at most $m'$, are bounded by a constant times $\sum _ Jp_{L,m'}(\varphi _ J)$, where the $\varphi _ J$ are the coefficients of $\varphi $ (at points mapped outside $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $ they vanish). The estimates for $T$ in these charts therefore give the estimate in the definition of a current for $F_*T$. Pullback preserves bidegrees, and $T$ acts on test forms of bidegree $(m-p,m-q)$, so $F_*T$ has bidegree $(n-(m-p),n-(m-q))$. For differentiation, note that $\mathrm d(\chi F^*\varphi )=\chi F^*\mathrm d\varphi +\mathrm d\chi \wedge F^*\varphi $, and $T$ vanishes on the last term because its support is disjoint from $\operatorname{Supp}T$. Since the degrees of $T$ and $F_*T$ differ by the even integer $2(m-n)$, the signs in the definitions of $\mathrm dT$ and $\mathrm dF_*T$ agree, and $\mathrm d(F_*T)=F_*(\mathrm dT)$; the same argument applies to $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. If $\varphi $ is strongly positive, so is $\chi F^*\varphi $ by proposition 7.2.1 , which proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 7.5.2
section: 5.1 Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Proposition 7.5.2 . Assume that $F$ is a submersion, that is, its complex derivative has rank $n$ at every point of $X$. Then every current $T$ on $Y$ has a pullback $F^*T$, a current on $X$ of the same bidegree, which agrees with the pullback of forms when $T$ is smooth, and with the locally integrable function $a\circ F$ when $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $a$ on $Y$. The map $T\mapsto F^*T$ is continuous for weak convergence, commutes with $\mathrm d$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, and maps positive currents to positive currents. Proof. Local construction. Let $x\in X$, and choose holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ near $F(x)$. Since $F$ is a submersion, the complex Jacobian matrix at $x$ of the $n$ components of $z\circ F$ has rank $n$ in every chart around $x$. By proposition 7.1.2 (3), these components are the first $n$ coordinates of holomorphic coordinates $(z,w)\in \mathbb C^ n\times \mathbb C^{m-n}$ near $x$, in which $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$; shrinking, we may assume that the coordinate domain is a product $U\times W$. For a distribution $a$ on $U$, define the distribution $F^*a$ on $U\times W$ by \[  \langle F^*a,\psi \rangle =\left\langle a,\int _{W}\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm{d}V_{2m-2n}(w)\right\rangle .  \] Integration in $w$ maps test functions on $U\times W$ continuously to test functions on $U$: the $z$-derivatives of $\int _ W\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ are the integrals of the $z$-derivatives of $\psi $, by differentiation under the integral sign, and its support lies in the projection of $\operatorname{Supp}\psi $. Hence $F^*a$ is a distribution, and if $a$ is locally integrable, then $F^*a$ is the function $(z,w)\mapsto a(z)$, by Fubini's theorem. For $T=\sum T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ on $U$ put $F^*T=\sum F^*T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. This is a linear map from currents on $U$ to currents on $U\times W$ preserving bidegrees, continuous for weak convergence, and equal to the pullback of forms for smooth $T$. It commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, since these act on the coefficients by differentiation, $\partial _{z_ l}F^*a=F^*\partial _{z_ l}a$, and $\partial _{w_ l}F^*a=0$ because $\int _ W\partial _{w_ l}\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)=0$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus; similarly for the conjugate derivatives. Continuity for weak convergence holds because the coefficients of a current depend continuously on it, by their explicit description in section 7.2 . Independence and gluing. Two such local constructions near $x$ agree. Indeed, mollifying the coefficients of $T$ in a chart near $F(x)$, we obtain smooth forms $T_\varepsilon \to T$ weakly on a neighborhood of $F(x)$, as in the discussion following theorem 7.2.5 . Both constructions are weakly continuous and agree with the pullback of forms on each $T_\varepsilon $, so they agree on $T$ near $x$. Consequently the local pullbacks agree on the overlaps of their domains, and by lemma 7.2.6 they glue to a unique current $F^*T$ on $X$ that agrees with each local pullback on its domain. Explicitly, if $(\chi _ c)$ is a partition of unity with compact supports subordinate to the cover of $X$ by the domains of the local pullbacks, and $(F^*T)_ c$ denotes a local pullback whose domain contains $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ c$, then $(F^*T)(\varphi )=\sum _ c(F^*T)_ c(\chi _ c\varphi )$. The local pullbacks are linear, preserve bidegrees and commute with $\mathrm d$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $; they give the pullback of forms if $T$ is smooth, and the function $a\circ F$ if $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $a$. By the uniqueness in lemma 7.2.6 , $F^*T$ has the same properties. Continuity for weak convergence follows from the explicit formula, since each of the finitely many nonzero terms $(F^*T)_ c(\chi _ c\varphi )$ depends continuously on $T$. Positivity. If $T$ is positive, the forms $T_\varepsilon $ are positive near $F(x)$, hence weakly positive at every point. By proposition 7.2.1 their pullbacks are weakly positive at every point, hence positive currents, and positivity passes to the weak limit, the local pullback of $T$ near $x$. Hence $F^*T$ is positive, by lemma 7.2.6 . $\square$

title: Corollary 7.5.3
section: 5.1 Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Corollary 7.5.3 . Let $F\colon X\to Y$ be a submersion, and let $T$ be a current of order zero on $Y$. Suppose that $X=U\times W$ and $Y=U$, where $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $W\subset \mathbb C^{m-n}$ are open, and that $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. Write $T=\sum _{I,J}T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. Then, with the product measures $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$ defined above, \[  F^*T=\sum _{I,J}(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J;  \] that is, in the coordinates $(z,w)$ the coefficient measure of $F^*T$ at $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ is $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$, and the coefficients at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish. In general, $F^*T$ has order zero, and \[  F^*(fT)=(f\circ F)\, F^*T  \] for every locally bounded Borel function $f$ on $Y$. In particular, $F^*(\mathbf1_ ET)=\mathbf1_{F^{-1}(E)}F^*T$ for every Borel set $E\subset Y$. Proof. (1) The local construction in the proof of proposition 7.5.2 can be carried out with the coordinates $z$ on $U$ and $(z,w)$ on $U\times W$, and it is then defined on all of $U\times W$. By the independence of the local constructions shown in that proof, $F^*T$ agrees with it near every point, hence on $U\times W$. Thus the coefficients of $F^*T$ at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish, and the coefficient at $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ is the distribution $\psi \mapsto \langle T_{IJ},\widehat\psi \rangle $, where $\widehat\psi (z)=\int _ W\psi (z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ is a test function on $U$. Since $T_{IJ}$ is a complex Radon measure, ( 7.12 ) gives $\langle T_{IJ},\widehat\psi \rangle =\int _ U\widehat\psi \, \mathrm dT_{IJ}=\int \psi \, \mathrm d(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)$ for every test function $\psi $ on $U\times W$. Hence this coefficient is the complex Radon measure $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$. (2) Let $x\in X$. As in the proof of proposition 7.5.2 , there are holomorphic coordinates $z$ on a chart of $Y$ around $F(x)$ and holomorphic coordinates $(z,w)$ on a neighborhood $N$ of $x$, with coordinate domain a product $U\times W$, in which $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. On $N$, the current $F^*T$ is the pullback of the restriction of $T$ to the open set $U$ by this projection. By (1), the coefficients of $F^*T$ in the chart $N$ are complex Radon measures. The charts $N$ obtained in this way form an atlas of $X$, so $F^*T$ has order zero, by the discussion following ( 7.8 ). Now let $f$ be a locally bounded Borel function on $Y$; then $f\circ F$ is a locally bounded Borel function on $X$, since $F$ is continuous. In the coordinates above, the coefficient measures of $fT$ are the measures $fT_{IJ}$, where $f$ is written in the coordinates $z$, so by (1) the coefficient measures of $F^*(fT)$ on $N$ are the measures $(fT_{IJ})\otimes \lambda _ W$, while those of $(f\circ F)F^*T$ are the measures $(f\circ F)(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)$; the coefficients at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish for both currents. Let $g$ be a continuous function with compact support in $U\times W$. The function $g\cdot (f\circ F)$ is bounded, Borel and compactly supported, and $\widehat g(z)=\int _ Wg(z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ is a bounded Borel function on $U$ with compact support. Applying ( 7.12 ) twice, we obtain \[  \int g\, (f\circ F)\, \mathrm d(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)=\int _ U\widehat g\, f\, \mathrm dT_{IJ}=\int _ U\widehat g\, \mathrm d(fT_{IJ})=\int g\, \mathrm d\bigl ((fT_{IJ})\otimes \lambda _ W\bigr ).  \] Hence the two currents have the same coefficient measures on $N$, and therefore agree on $N$. Since the sets $N$ cover $X$, the currents $F^*(fT)$ and $(f\circ F)F^*T$ coincide. The last assertion is the case $f=\mathbf1_ E$, since $\mathbf1_ E\circ F=\mathbf1_{F^{-1}(E)}$. $\square$

title: Proposition 7.5.4
section: 5.1 Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Proposition 7.5.4 . Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $Y$, and let $F\colon X\to Y$ be holomorphic. Suppose that every point of $X$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $F(W)$ lies in the domain of a canonical local potential $u$ of $T$ and $u\circ F$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $W$. Then the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$ on these neighborhoods glue to a closed positive current \[  F^*T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)  \] on $X$, which does not depend on the chosen potentials. It agrees with the pullback of forms if $T$ is smooth, and with the pullback of proposition 7.5.2 if $F$ is a submersion. Proof. Canonical local potentials are defined on manifolds of positive dimension (theorem 7.3.2 ), so $Y$ has positive dimension. If $X$ has dimension zero, every $(1,1)$-current on $X$ vanishes, and $F^*T=0$. Assume that $X$ has positive dimension, let $W$ and $u$ be as in the hypothesis, and let $W_0$ be a connected component of $W$. Each point of $W_0$ has a connected neighborhood $W'\subset W_0$ in a chart of $X$ such that $F(W')$ lies in a chart of $Y$ contained in the domain of $u$. In that chart, $u$ is the canonical subharmonic representative of its class, by the remark following proposition 7.3.3 , so by that proposition $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $ on $W'$, or locally integrable on $W'$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$. No point has neighborhoods $W'$ of both kinds, because a locally integrable function is finite almost everywhere. Hence the points of $W_0$ having a neighborhood of the first kind and those having one of the second kind form two disjoint open sets covering $W_0$. Since $W_0$ is connected and $u\circ F$ is not identically $-\infty $ on $W_0$, the first set is empty. Thus $u\circ F$ is locally integrable on $W$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$ there. Let $(\widetilde W,\widetilde u)$ be another pair as in the hypothesis. Near each point of the intersection of the domains of $u$ and $\widetilde u$ we have $\widetilde u=u+h$ with $h$ smooth and pluriharmonic, by theorem 7.3.2 and the remark following proposition 7.3.3 . Locally $h=\operatorname{Re}g$ with $g$ holomorphic, so $h\circ F=\operatorname{Re}(g\circ F)$ is smooth and pluriharmonic, and $\widetilde u\circ F=u\circ F+h\circ F$ near each point of $W\cap \widetilde W$. Consequently $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\widetilde u\circ F)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$ near each point of $W\cap \widetilde W$, hence on $W\cap \widetilde W$, since a current that vanishes near each point vanishes. By lemma 7.2.6 , the local currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$, which are positive and closed because $\mathrm d\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=0$, glue to a unique closed positive current $F^*T$ on $X$. It is independent of the choices: the currents obtained from two systems of choices agree near each point, by what we have just shown, and hence coincide by the uniqueness in lemma 7.2.6 . If $T$ is smooth, lemma 7.3.1 gives smooth real local potentials $v$ with $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$; they are subharmonic, by the matrix criterion and proposition 2.1.1 , hence their own canonical representatives, so we may use them as the potentials $u$. For a smooth potential $u$ the chain rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)=F^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=F^*T$. Now let $F$ be a submersion, and let $V$ be the domain of $u$. The restriction of $F$ to $F^{-1}(V)$ is a submersion to $V$, and its submersion pullback agrees on $F^{-1}(V)$ with that of $F$, since both are glued from the same local constructions. By proposition 7.5.2 , the locally integrable function $u\circ F$ represents the submersion pullback $F^*u$, and since this pullback commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, we obtain $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*u=F^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=F^*T$ on $F^{-1}(V)$, in particular on $W$. $\square$

section: 5.1 Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Example 7.5.5 . On $\mathbb {C}^2$, the current $T=[\{ z_1=0\} ]$ has the canonical local potential $\log |z_1|^2$, by theorem 7.4.5 and proposition 7.4.3 . For $F(w)=(0,w)$, the composition $\log |z_1|^2\circ F$ is identically $-\infty $, and so is the composition of every canonical local potential, since these differ from $\log |z_1|^2$ by smooth functions; thus proposition 7.5.4 does not define $F^*T$. For $G(w)=(w,0)$, the composition is $\log |w|^2$, and $G^*T=[0]$ is the Dirac mass at the origin. Thus the current of integration over a line can be restricted to a transverse line, but not to the line itself.

title: 8 Plurisubharmonic functions
text: 8 Plurisubharmonic functions Plurisubharmonic functions are the basic objects of pluripotential theory. On a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$, a plurisubharmonic function is an upper semicontinuous function whose restriction to every complex line is subharmonic. By ( 7.5 ), the Laplacian of a function on $\Omega $, viewed as an open subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$, is four times the trace of its complex Hessian, so subharmonicity controls only this trace. Subharmonicity on all complex lines is the pointwise counterpart of the positivity of the whole complex Hessian, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ determines $u$ only almost everywhere, the pointwise definition and the distributional condition must be kept apart. We first show that the upper semicontinuity required in the definition follows from the condition on complex lines (theorem 8.1.3 ); the proof combines the incidence estimate of chapter 6 with the distributional theory of chapter 3 . We then identify the plurisubharmonic functions with the canonical representatives, in the sense of theorem 3.2.2 , of the distributions with positive complex Hessian (theorem 8.2.1 ). This makes the potential theory of Part I available. A smooth function is plurisubharmonic exactly when its complex Hessian is positive semidefinite, and mollification approximates every plurisubharmonic function from above by smooth ones. Plurisubharmonicity is invariant under holomorphic maps, hence makes sense on complex manifolds, and it is preserved by decreasing limits, regularized upper envelopes and $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ limits. Moreover, plurisubharmonic functions belong to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $p$, and near each point $\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}$ is integrable for small $\alpha >0$. In the last two sections we extend plurisubharmonic functions across closed sets that are locally contained in zero sets of holomorphic functions or are small in the sense of Hausdorff measure, and we prove Kiselman's minimum principle: although an infimum of plurisubharmonic functions is in general not plurisubharmonic, a partial infimum over real variables is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ under convexity assumptions, provided that the function does not depend on the corresponding imaginary parts. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.8 .

title: 8.1 The line definition and upper semicontinuity

text:
8.1 The line definition and upper semicontinuity We identify $\mathbb {C}^ n$ with $\mathbb R^{2n}$ through $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm{i}y_ j$, and we call a function on an open subset of $\mathbb {C}^ n$ subharmonic if it is subharmonic in the sense of definition 3.1.1 on the corresponding open subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Recall from section 6.4 that an affine complex line is a set $L=\{ a+\zeta b:\zeta \in \mathbb {C}\} $ with $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ and $b\in \mathbb {C}^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $. For an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$, the section $L\cap \Omega $ is identified with the open set $\{ \zeta \in \mathbb {C}:a+\zeta b\in \Omega \} $, and a function on a connected component of $L\cap \Omega $ is called subharmonic if its composite with $\zeta \mapsto a+\zeta b$ is subharmonic; this does not depend on the parametrization of $L$. Accordingly, the restriction of a function $u$ on $\Omega $ to $L\cap \Omega $ is the function $\zeta \mapsto u(a+\zeta b)$. Definition 8.1.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain. If $n\ge 1$, a function $u\colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ is plurisubharmonic if $u

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$, let $u\colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a locally integrable function, let $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a unit vector, and let $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$ be nonnegative. Theorem 8.1.3 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$, and let $u\colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function that is not identically $-\infty $. Then $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and hence $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Proof. We first treat finite nonnegative functions, in Steps 1–3, and then reduce the general case to this one by truncation in Step 4. For the first part we prove by induction on $n\geq 1$ the following assertion: if $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain and $u\colon \Omega 	o [0,\infty )$ is a finite function whose restriction to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic, then $u$ is upper semicontinuous. Let $n\geq 2$, assume the assertion in dimension $n-1$, and let $u$ be as in the assertion. Write $z=(z',w)$ with $z'\in \mathbb {C}^{n-1}$ and $w\in \mathbb {C}$. Indeed, affine complex lines in $\mathbb {C}^{n-1}	imes \{ w\} $ are affine complex lines in $\mathbb {C}^ n$, a connected component of a line section of the slice lies in a connected component of the corresponding line section of $\Omega $, and subharmonicity is inherited by open subsets. Step 2: the canonical representative. By corollary 6.5.4 , the finite Borel function $u$ is locally bounded above. Since $u\geq 0$, it follows that $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. The set $Z=\{ u
e \widetilde u\} $ is Borel, by Step 1, and Lebesgue null, so the left-hand side of ( 8.1 ) vanishes for $F=\mathbf1_ Z$. Since the weight $|t|^{2n-2}$ is positive for $t
eq 0$, for $	au $-almost every $a$ the set $\{ t:|t|<r,\  x+ta\in Z\} $ has planar measure zero. Fix such an $a$. title: Definition 8.1.1
text: Definition 8.1.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain. If $n\ge 1$, a function $u\colon \Omega \to [-\infty ,\infty )$ is plurisubharmonic if $u\not\equiv -\infty $, $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and for every affine complex line $L$ the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of $L\cap \Omega $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. In dimension zero a domain is a single point, and the plurisubharmonic functions on it are the real-valued functions. Definition 1.1.3 . When $n\geq 1$, a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $ is a function $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ satisfying the following three conditions: $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $; $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous; for any complex line $L\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ and any connected component $U$ of $L\cap \Omega $, the restriction $\varphi |_ U$ is either subharmonic or constantly $-\infty $. Note. An extremely common mistake in the literature is to replace 3 by the condition that $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ in the sense of currents. For a concrete counterexample, consider a function $\varphi $ that takes a constant value $0$ at all but one single point, at which the value of $\varphi $ is $1$. When $n=0$, the only domain $\Omega $ is the singleton. In this case, a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $ is a real-valued function on $\Omega $. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$.

title: Lemma 8.1.2
text: Lemma 8.1.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$, let $u\colon \Omega \to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a locally integrable function, let $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a unit vector, and let $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$ be nonnegative. Assume that for almost every $v\in (\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ there is an open set $G_ v\subset \{ t\in \mathbb {C}:v+ta\in \Omega \} $ containing $K_ v$ such that the restriction of $t\mapsto u(v+ta)$ to each connected component of $G_ v$ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $. This is the case, in particular, if the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic. Proof. The map $(v,t)\mapsto v+ta$ is a unitary isomorphism of $(\mathbb {C}a)^\perp \times \mathbb {C}$ onto $\mathbb {C}^ n$, so it preserves Lebesgue measure, and by the chain rule $\partial _ t\partial _{\bar t}[\chi (v+ta)]=\sum _{j,k}a_ j\bar a_ k\chi _{j\bar k}(v+ta)$. We extend $u$ and $\chi $ by zero outside $\Omega $. Since $u$ is locally integrable and the derivatives of $\chi $ are bounded and supported in $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, Fubini's theorem gives \[  \Bigl \langle \sum _{j,k}a_ j\bar a_ ku_{j\bar k},\chi \Bigr \rangle =\int _{(\mathbb {C}a)^\perp }I(v)\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n-2}(v),  \] where \[  I(v)=\int _{\mathbb {C}}u(v+ta)\, \partial _ t\partial _{\bar t}[\chi (v+ta)]\, \mathrm{d}V_2(t).  \] Applied to $|u|\mathbf1_{\operatorname{Supp}\chi }$, Fubini's theorem also shows that for almost every $v$ the function $t\mapsto u(v+ta)$ is integrable on $K_ v$. It therefore suffices to show that $I(v)\geq 0$ for every $v$ for which this integrability holds and an open set $G_ v$ as in the hypothesis exists. Fix such a $v$. The compact set $K_ v$ is covered by the disjoint open connected components of $G_ v$, so it meets only finitely many of them, say $U_1,\ldots ,U_ N$, and each set $K_ v\cap U_ i$ is compact, being the complement in $K_ v$ of the open set $K_ v\cap \bigcup _{l\neq i}U_ l$. Hence the function $\chi _ i(t)=\chi (v+ta)$, $t\in U_ i$, is a nonnegative test function on $U_ i$, and \[  I(v)=\sum _{i=1}^ N\int _{U_ i}u(v+ta)\, \partial _ t\partial _{\bar t}\chi _ i(t)\, \mathrm{d}V_2(t).  \] If $\chi _ i\equiv 0$, the $i$-th term vanishes. Otherwise $\chi _ i>0$ on a nonempty open subset of $U_ i$, contained in $K_ v$, on which $t\mapsto u(v+ta)$ is integrable and hence finite almost everywhere. Thus the subharmonic function $w_ i(t)=u(v+ta)$ on the domain $U_ i$ is not identically $-\infty $, and it is locally integrable by proposition 3.1.5 . Since $\partial _ t\partial _{\bar t}=\frac14\Delta $, the $i$-th term equals $\frac14\langle \Delta w_ i,\chi _ i\rangle $, which is nonnegative by theorem 3.2.2 (1). Hence $I(v)\geq 0$. If the hypothesis holds for every unit vector $a$ and every $\chi $, then $\sum _{j,k}a_ j\bar a_ ku_{j\bar k}$ is a positive distribution for every unit vector $a$, and by homogeneity for every $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$. title: Theorem 8.1.3
text: Theorem 8.1.3 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$, and let $u\colon \Omega \to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function that is not identically $-\infty $. Assume that for every affine complex line $L$ the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of $L\cap \Omega $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Then $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and hence $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Proof. We first treat finite nonnegative functions, in Steps 1–3, and then reduce the general case to this one by truncation in Step 4. For the first part we prove by induction on $n\geq 1$ the following assertion: if $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain and $u\colon \Omega \to [0,\infty )$ is a finite function whose restriction to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic, then $u$ is upper semicontinuous. For $n=1$ the only affine complex line is $\mathbb {C}$, so $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega $ and in particular upper semicontinuous. Let $n\geq 2$, assume the assertion in dimension $n-1$, and let $u$ be as in the assertion. Write $z=(z',w)$ with $z'\in \mathbb {C}^{n-1}$ and $w\in \mathbb {C}$. By the induction hypothesis, $u(\, \cdot \, ,w)$ is therefore upper semicontinuous on this open set. For fixed $z'$, the function $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is subharmonic on each connected component of $\{ w:(z',w)\in \Omega \} $. Step 1: $u$ is Borel measurable. We need joint measurability of $u$ before we can integrate it. Fix a ball $B'\subset \mathbb {C}^{n-1}$, a point $w_0\in \mathbb {C}$ and $\rho >0$ with $B'\times B(w_0,2\rho )\subset \Omega $. For fixed $w$, the function $F_ r^ N(\, \cdot \, ,w)$ is upper semicontinuous: if $z'_ l\to z'$ in $B'$, the reverse Fatou lemma, applicable because $0\le u_ N\le N$, gives \[  \varlimsup _{l\to \infty }F_ r^ N(z'_ l,w) \le \frac{1}{\pi r^2}\int _{B(w,r)}\varlimsup _{l\to \infty }u_ N(z'_ l,\eta )\, \mathrm{d}V_2(\eta ) \le F_ r^ N(z',w),  \] where the last inequality holds because each $u_ N(\, \cdot \, ,\eta )$ is upper semicontinuous on $B'$. For fixed $z'$, the function $F_ r^ N(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is continuous: for $|w-v|\leq r$ the symmetric difference $B(w,r)\mathbin \triangle B(v,r)$ lies in the annulus $\{ r-|w-v|\leq |\eta -w|<r+|w-v|\} $, whose area is $4\pi r|w-v|$, so that $|F_ r^ N(z',w)-F_ r^ N(z',v)|\le 4N|w-v|/r$. A function on $B'\times B(w_0,\rho )$ that is Borel in $z'$ and continuous in $w$ is Borel; we check this for $F_ r^ N$. For $k\geq 1$ partition $B(w_0,\rho )$ into countably many Borel sets $E_{k,i}$ of diameter less than $1/k$, choose a point $w_{k,i}$ in each nonempty $E_{k,i}$, and put $F_ k(z',w)=F_ r^ N(z',w_{k,i})$ for $w\in E_{k,i}$. Each $F_ k$ is Borel, because each $F_ r^ N(\, \cdot \, ,w_{k,i})$ is upper semicontinuous, hence Borel, and $F_ k(z',w)\to F_ r^ N(z',w)$ for every $(z',w)$, because $F_ r^ N(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is continuous and the chosen points $w_{k,i}$ with $w\in E_{k,i}$ tend to $w$. Thus $F_ r^ N$ is Borel, and so is $G_ N=\varlimsup _{k\to \infty }F^ N_{\rho /(k+1)}$. Now fix $(z',w)\in B'\times B(w_0,\rho )$. The upper semicontinuous function $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is bounded above on the closed disc $\overline{B(w,\rho /2)}$ by some $M$. For $N\geq M$ the truncation does not change $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ on this disc, so $F^ N_{\rho /(k+1)}(z',w)$ is the mean of $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ over $B(w,\rho /(k+1))$. The function $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is subharmonic and finite on $B(w_0,2\rho )$, hence locally integrable there by proposition 3.1.5 , and by ( 3.3 ) its means over the discs $B(w,\rho /(k+1))$ converge to $u(z',w)$ as $k\to \infty $. Hence $G_ N(z',w)=u(z',w)$ for all $N\geq M$, and $u=\lim _ NG_ N$ is Borel on $B'\times B(w_0,\rho )$. Countably many such product sets cover $\Omega $, so $u$ is Borel on $\Omega $. Step 2: the canonical representative. By corollary 6.5.4 , the finite Borel function $u$ is locally bounded above. Since $u\geq 0$, it follows that $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Since the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic, lemma 8.1.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. In particular $\Delta u=4\sum _ ju_{j\bar j}\geq 0$, so by theorem 3.2.2 $u$ has a canonical subharmonic representative $\widetilde u$, a locally integrable subharmonic function on $\Omega $ equal to $u$ almost everywhere. Its complex Hessian is the same positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Applying proposition 7.3.3 to the parametrizations of affine complex lines, we see that the restriction of $\widetilde u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Since $\widetilde u$ is upper semicontinuous and agrees almost everywhere with the finite function $u$, we conclude that $\widetilde u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Step 3: $u=\widetilde u$ everywhere. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. The set $Z=\{ u\ne \widetilde u\} $ is Borel, by Step 1, and Lebesgue null, so the left-hand side of ( 8.1 ) vanishes for $F=\mathbf1_ Z$. Since the weight $|t|^{2n-2}$ is positive for $t\neq 0$, for $\tau $-almost every $a$ the set $\{ t:|t|<r,\  x+ta\in Z\} $ has planar measure zero. Fix such an $a$. On the disc $\{ |t|<r\} $, the function $t\mapsto u(x+ta)$ is finite and subharmonic, while $t\mapsto \widetilde u(x+ta)$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $; the latter is impossible, because the two functions agree almost everywhere on the disc. By proposition 3.1.5 both are locally integrable subharmonic functions on the disc that agree almost everywhere, so they agree everywhere by theorem 3.2.2 . At $t=0$ this gives $u(x)=\widetilde u(x)$. As $x$ was arbitrary, $u=\widetilde u$ is upper semicontinuous. This completes the induction. Step 4: truncation. Let $u$ be as in the theorem, and for integers $m\geq 1$ put $u_ m=\max \{ u,-m\} +m$. This is a finite nonnegative function. Its restriction to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic: if the restriction of $u$ is subharmonic, so is its maximum with the constant $-m$, and if the restriction of $u$ is identically $-\infty $, the restriction of $u_ m$ is the constant $0$. By the case already proved, each $u_ m$, and hence each $\max \{ u,-m\} $, is upper semicontinuous. For every real $c$ we have $\{ u<c\} =\bigcup _ m\{ \max \{ u,-m\} <c\} $, which is open. Thus $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and together with the hypotheses this gives $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. $\square$

title: 8.2 Positive Hessians and holomorphic maps
text:
8.2 Positive Hessians and holomorphic maps We now compare plurisubharmonicity with the distributional condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$, where $(u_{j ar k})$ is the complex Hessian of ( 7.5 ). The next theorem shows that every almost-everywhere class satisfying this condition contains exactly one plurisubharmonic function, namely its canonical representative. We then treat smooth functions, regularization and holomorphic maps, and define plurisubharmonic functions on complex manifolds. Theorem 8.2.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$. Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\Omega $, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Conversely, a real distribution $T$ on $\Omega $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$ has a unique plurisubharmonic representative, that is, there is exactly one $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ with $\langle T,\chi angle =\int _\Omega u\chi \, \mathrm dV_{2n}$ for every test function $\chi $. This representative is the canonical subharmonic representative of $T$ given by theorem 3.2.2 , and it satisfies ( 3.3 ). Proof. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Being upper semicontinuous, $u$ is bounded above on compact sets. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, and let $M$ be an upper bound for $u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$. For every unit vector $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the closed disc $\{ x+ta:|t|\leq r\} $ lies in $\Omega $, and the restriction $t\mapsto u(x+ta)$ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $, on a neighborhood of this disc. The monotonicity of circle means in theorem 3.1.3 therefore gives \[  u(x)\leq  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }u(x+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }a)\, \mathrm d	heta .  \] With $	au $ as in ( 8.1 ), we integrate this inequality over $a\in S^{2n-1}$ with respect to $	au $; by Tonelli's theorem, applied to the nonnegative function $M-u$, and by the invariance of $	au $ under $a\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }a$, the right-hand side becomes the sphere mean $\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(x+ra)\, \mathrm{d}	au (a)$. Thus $u$ satisfies the submean inequality of definition 3.1.1 at every point, so $u$ is subharmonic. Since $\Omega $ is connected and $u
ot\equiv -\infty $, proposition 3.1.5 shows that $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Since, moreover, the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $, lemma 8.1.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\ge 0$. Conversely, let $T$ be a real distribution with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$. Then $\Delta T=4\sum _ jT_{j ar j}\geq 0$, so by theorem 3.2.2 $T$ has a canonical subharmonic representative $v$, which is locally integrable and satisfies ( 3.3 ). Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$, proposition 7.3.3 shows that the restriction of $v$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. As $v$ is upper semicontinuous and locally integrable, hence not identically $-\infty $, it is plurisubharmonic. If $w$ is another plurisubharmonic representative of $T$, then $w$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function by the first part, and $w=v$ almost everywhere; by the uniqueness in theorem 3.2.2 , $w=v$ everywhere. $\square$ The condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $u$, whereas plurisubharmonicity is a pointwise property, and theorem 8.2.1 singles out one function in each class. For example, the function equal to $1$ at one point $x_0$ and to $0$ elsewhere is upper semicontinuous and has zero distributional complex Hessian, but it violates the submean inequality on complex lines at $x_0$; the plurisubharmonic representative of its class is the zero function. For smooth functions, plurisubharmonicity is a pointwise condition on the complex Hessian, and every plurisubharmonic function is, locally, the decreasing limit of smooth plurisubharmonic functions. In the next proposition, $ho _\varepsilon $ is the radial mollifier of section 1.4 and, as there, $\Omega _\varepsilon =\{ x\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon \} $ for an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $\varepsilon >0$. Proposition 8.2.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$. A real function $u$ of class $C^2$ on $\Omega $ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $ if and only if the Hermitian matrix $(u_{j ar k}(z))$ is positive semidefinite at every point $z\in \Omega $. Let $u$ be a function on $\Omega $ which is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $, and let $\varepsilon >0$. Then $u*ho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ and plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $u*ho _\varepsilon (x)$ decreases to $u(x)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, for every $x\in \Omega $. Proof. (1) Let $\Omega _0$ be a connected component of $\Omega $. We show that both conditions are equivalent to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$. Since $u$ is of class $C^2$, integration by parts shows that its distributional derivatives $u_{j ar k}$ are the continuous functions $\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}u$, so for $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the distribution $\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$ is the continuous real function $z\mapsto \sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}(z)\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$. A continuous real function is a positive distribution exactly when it is nonnegative: if it were negative at a point, it would be negative on a ball around that point, and its integral against a nonnegative test function supported in this ball and positive at its center would be negative. Hence, by the matrix criterion of section 7.3 , $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$ if and only if $(u_{j ar k}(z))$ is positive semidefinite at every $z\in \Omega _0$. If $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _0$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ there by theorem 8.2.1 . Conversely, if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$, then by theorem 8.2.1 the class of $u$ has a plurisubharmonic representative $v$ on $\Omega _0$ satisfying the ball-average formula in ( 3.3 ). Since $v=u$ almost everywhere and $u$ is continuous, $v(x)$ is the limit of the averages of $u$ over the balls $B(x,r)$ as $r	o 0$, that is, $v(x)=u(x)$. Hence $u=v$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _0$. (2) By theorem 8.2.1 , applied on each connected component of $\Omega $, the function $u$ is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\Omega $, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. By proposition 1.4.3 (1), $u*ho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and its derivatives are the mollifications of the distributional derivatives of $u$. Thus, for $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ n$, the function $\sum _{j,k}(u*ho _\varepsilon )_{j ar k}\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$ is the mollification of the distribution $\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$, which is positive by the matrix criterion; so it is nonnegative by proposition 1.4.3 (3). By (1), $u*ho _\varepsilon $ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $. Finally, since $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega $, theorem 3.2.2 (2) shows that $u*ho _\varepsilon (x)\downarrow u(x)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, for every $x\in \Omega $. $\square$ Let $u$ be a smooth real function on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$. We call $u$ strictly plurisubharmonic if its complex Hessian matrix $(u_{j ar k})$ is positive definite everywhere. For a general $u$, strict plurisubharmonicity means that every point has a neighborhood on which $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic for some $\varepsilon >0$; on a complex manifold we require this in local holomorphic coordinates around each point, and $\varepsilon $ may depend on the point and the coordinates. For smooth $u$ the two definitions agree. Since $(|z|^2)_{j ar k}=\delta _{jk}$, the complex Hessian of $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ is $(u_{j ar k})-\varepsilon I$. The smallest eigenvalue $\lambda (z)=\min _{|\xi |=1}\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}(z)\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$ of the matrix $(u_{j ar k}(z))$ is a continuous function of $z$, as the minimum over the compact unit sphere of a jointly continuous function of $(z,\xi )$. If the matrix is positive definite everywhere, then $\lambda $ is positive, hence bounded below by some $\varepsilon >0$ on a closed ball around each point, and on the open ball the smooth function $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ has a positive semidefinite complex Hessian, so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1). Conversely, the plurisubharmonicity of $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ on a ball around a point gives $(u_{j ar k})\geq \varepsilon I$ there, by the same criterion. Proposition 8.2.3 . Let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ and $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be domains, let $F\colon D	o \Omega $ be a holomorphic map, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $ or plurisubharmonic on $D$. More generally, if $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ is only assumed to be open, this alternative holds on each connected component of $D$. Proof. The statement for open $D$ follows by applying the statement for domains to each connected component of $D$. If $n=0$, then $\Omega $ is a point, $u$ is a real constant, and so is $u\circ F$. If $m=0$, then $D$ is a point and $u\circ F$ is a single value in $[-\infty ,\infty )$; it is either $-\infty $ or a real number, that is, a plurisubharmonic function on the point. Now let $m,n\geq 1$. By theorem 8.2.1 , $u$ is the canonical subharmonic representative of a locally integrable function with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$, so proposition 7.3.3 applies: $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $, or locally integrable and subharmonic, in particular upper semicontinuous. In the second case, the restriction of $u\circ F$ to a connected component of an affine complex-line section of $D$ is the composition of $u$ with a holomorphic map from an open subset of $\mathbb {C}$, so it is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ by the same proposition. Hence $u\circ F$ is plurisubharmonic. $\square$ Let $X$ be a complex manifold. A function $u\colon X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ is plurisubharmonic if its expression in every holomorphic chart with connected domain is plurisubharmonic in the sense of definition 8.1.1 ; we write $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ for the set of such functions. On a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, plurisubharmonicity is a local property: if every point of $\Omega $ has an open neighborhood on which $u$ is plurisubharmonic, then $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Indeed, upper semicontinuity is a local condition. Let $\Lambda $ be a connected component of an affine complex-line section of $\Omega $. Near each point of $\Lambda $, the restriction of $u$ to $\Lambda $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $, hence subharmonic; since subharmonicity is a local property, the restriction of $u$ to $\Lambda $ is subharmonic. Finally, $u$ is locally integrable by theorem 8.2.1 , hence not identically $-\infty $. It follows that it suffices to check the condition on $X$ for the charts of one atlas with connected chart domains. Indeed, the transition maps are biholomorphic, so by proposition 8.2.3 the expression of $u$ in another chart with connected domain is, on a connected neighborhood of each point, plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. The second alternative would make the expression of $u$ in a chart of the atlas identically $-\infty $ on a nonempty open set, which is impossible because plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable. Hence the expression of $u$ in the other chart is plurisubharmonic near each point, and therefore on its connected domain. Consequently plurisubharmonicity is also a local property on $X$: if every point of $X$ has a neighborhood on which $u$ is plurisubharmonic, then $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, because the expression of $u$ in a chart with connected domain is then plurisubharmonic near each point. Since a plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is locally integrable in charts, it is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $X$. On an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, regarded as a complex manifold, a function is plurisubharmonic exactly when it is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $: each component is a connected chart domain, and conversely the locality just proved applies. Limits of plurisubharmonic functions may degenerate to the constant $-\infty $. On a connected manifold, whether this happens can be decided locally. Lemma 8.2.4 . Let $X$ be a connected complex manifold, and let $v\colon X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function such that every point of $X$ has an open neighborhood on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Then $v$ is plurisubharmonic on $X$ or identically $-\infty $ on $X$. Proof. Let $A$ be the set of points of $X$ having an open neighborhood on which $v\equiv -\infty $, and $B$ the set of points having an open neighborhood on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic. Both sets are open, and they cover $X$ by hypothesis. They are disjoint: if $x\in A\cap B$, with open neighborhoods $W_1$ on which $v\equiv -\infty $ and $W_2$ on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic, then the restriction of $v$ to the nonempty open set $W_1\cap W_2$ is plurisubharmonic and identically $-\infty $, which is impossible because plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable. Since $X$ is connected, either $X=A$, and then $v\equiv -\infty $, or $X=B$, and then $v$ is plurisubharmonic near every point, hence on $X$, because plurisubharmonicity is a local property. $\square$ Every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on a complex manifold of positive dimension has local plurisubharmonic potentials: every point has a neighborhood on which $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ for a plurisubharmonic function $u$. Indeed, on a coordinate ball inside the neighborhood given by theorem 7.3.2 , the canonical local potential is the canonical subharmonic representative of a class with positive complex Hessian, hence plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . Proposition 8.2.5 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Nonnegative multiples, finite sums and maxima of nonempty finite families of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ are plurisubharmonic; here the zero multiple of a function is the zero function. Moreover, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, let $D\subset X$ be open, and let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(D)$. If \[  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\le u(x)\qquad 	ext{for every }x\in \partial D,  \] where $\partial D$ is the boundary of $D$ in $X$, then the function equal to $\max \{ u,v\} $ on $D$ and to $u$ on $X\setminus D$ is plurisubharmonic on $X$. This boundary inequality holds in particular if \[  \varliminf _{\substack {D
i y	o x\ v(y)>-\infty }}(u(y)-v(y))\ge 0 \qquad 	ext{for every }x\in \partial D.  \] Proof. In local coordinates, upper semicontinuity and the submean inequality on complex lines are preserved by nonnegative multiples, sums and maxima; for sums we use that circle means are additive on functions with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. It remains to check that the resulting functions are not identically $-\infty $ on any component. For $cu$ with $c>0$ this holds because $cu=-\infty $ exactly where $u=-\infty $; a sum of plurisubharmonic functions is locally integrable by theorem 8.2.1 , and a maximum dominates each of its members. This proves the first assertion. Let $w$ denote the glued function. On $D$ it equals $\max \{ u,v\} $, which is plurisubharmonic by the first part, and on the open set $X\setminus \overline D$ it equals $u$. At $x\in \partial D$ we have $w(x)=u(x)$, and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ together with the boundary inequality gives \[  \varlimsup _{y	o x}w(y)\leq \max \Bigl \{ \varlimsup _{y	o x}u(y),\  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\Bigr \} \leq u(x)=w(x).  \] Hence $w$ is upper semicontinuous. To verify the line condition, work in a chart and restrict $w$ to a connected component of an affine complex-line section. At points of $D$ and of $X\setminus \overline D$, the restriction satisfies the submean inequality on small circles, because $w$ is plurisubharmonic near such points. At a point $x\in \partial D$ we have $w\geq u$ everywhere and $w(x)=u(x)$, so each small circle mean of $w$ is at least the corresponding circle mean of $u$, which is at least $u(x)=w(x)$; if the restriction of $u$ is identically $-\infty $, then $w(x)=u(x)=-\infty $ and there is nothing to prove. Thus the restriction of $w$ is upper semicontinuous and satisfies the submean inequality on small circles at every point; that is, it is subharmonic. Finally $w\geq u$, so $w$ is not identically $-\infty $ in any chart, and $w$ is plurisubharmonic. For the sufficient condition, fix $x\in \partial D$ and $\varepsilon >0$. By hypothesis, $x$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $v(y)<u(y)+\varepsilon $ for all $y\in W\cap D$ with $v(y)>-\infty $. Hence $v\leq u+\varepsilon $ on $W\cap D$, the inequality being trivial where $v=-\infty $, and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ gives \[  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\leq \varlimsup _{y	o x}u(y)+\varepsilon \leq u(x)+\varepsilon .  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives the boundary inequality. $\square$

title: Theorem 8.2.1
text: Theorem 8.2.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$. Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\Omega $, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Conversely, a real distribution $T$ on $\Omega $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$ has a unique plurisubharmonic representative, that is, there is exactly one $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ with $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\int _\Omega u\chi \, \mathrm dV_{2n}$ for every test function $\chi $. This representative is the canonical subharmonic representative of $T$ given by theorem 3.2.2 , and it satisfies ( 3.3 ). Proof. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Being upper semicontinuous, $u$ is bounded above on compact sets. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, and let $M$ be an upper bound for $u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$. For every unit vector $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the closed disc $\{ x+ta:|t|\leq r\} $ lies in $\Omega $, and the restriction $t\mapsto u(x+ta)$ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $, on a neighborhood of this disc. The monotonicity of circle means in theorem 3.1.3 therefore gives \[  u(x)\leq \frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }u(x+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }a)\, \mathrm d\theta .  \] With $\tau $ as in ( 8.1 ), we integrate this inequality over $a\in S^{2n-1}$ with respect to $\tau $; by Tonelli's theorem, applied to the nonnegative function $M-u$, and by the invariance of $\tau $ under $a\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }a$, the right-hand side becomes the sphere mean $\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(x+ra)\, \mathrm{d}\tau (a)$. Thus $u$ satisfies the submean inequality of definition 3.1.1 at every point, so $u$ is subharmonic. Since $\Omega $ is connected and $u\not\equiv -\infty $, proposition 3.1.5 shows that $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Since, moreover, the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $, lemma 8.1.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\ge 0$. Conversely, let $T$ be a real distribution with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$. Then $\Delta T=4\sum _ jT_{j\bar j}\geq 0$, so by theorem 3.2.2 $T$ has a canonical subharmonic representative $v$, which is locally integrable and satisfies ( 3.3 ). Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$, proposition 7.3.3 shows that the restriction of $v$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. As $v$ is upper semicontinuous and locally integrable, hence not identically $-\infty $, it is plurisubharmonic. If $w$ is another plurisubharmonic representative of $T$, then $w$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function by the first part, and $w=v$ almost everywhere; by the uniqueness in theorem 3.2.2 , $w=v$ everywhere. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.2.2
text: Proposition 8.2.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$. A real function $u$ of class $C^2$ on $\Omega $ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $ if and only if the Hermitian matrix $(u_{j\bar k}(z))$ is positive semidefinite at every point $z\in \Omega $. Let $u$ be a function on $\Omega $ which is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $, and let $\varepsilon >0$. Then $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ and plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $u*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ decreases to $u(x)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, for every $x\in \Omega $. Proof. (1) Let $\Omega _0$ be a connected component of $\Omega $. We show that both conditions are equivalent to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$. Since $u$ is of class $C^2$, integration by parts shows that its distributional derivatives $u_{j\bar k}$ are the continuous functions $\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ k}u$, so for $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the distribution $\sum _{j,k}u_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ is the continuous real function $z\mapsto \sum _{j,k}u_{j\bar k}(z)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$. A continuous real function is a positive distribution exactly when it is nonnegative: if it were negative at a point, it would be negative on a ball around that point, and its integral against a nonnegative test function supported in this ball and positive at its center would be negative. Hence, by the matrix criterion of section 7.3 , $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$ if and only if $(u_{j\bar k}(z))$ is positive semidefinite at every $z\in \Omega _0$. If $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _0$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ there by theorem 8.2.1 . Conversely, if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$, then by theorem 8.2.1 the class of $u$ has a plurisubharmonic representative $v$ on $\Omega _0$ satisfying the ball-average formula in ( 3.3 ). Since $v=u$ almost everywhere and $u$ is continuous, $v(x)$ is the limit of the averages of $u$ over the balls $B(x,r)$ as $r\to 0$, that is, $v(x)=u(x)$. Hence $u=v$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _0$.
