(2) By theorem 8.2.1 , applied on each connected component of $\Omega $, the function $u$ is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\Omega $, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. By proposition 1.4.3 (1), $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and its derivatives are the mollifications of the distributional derivatives of $u$. Thus, for $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ n$, the function $\sum _{j,k}(u*\rho _\varepsilon )_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ is the mollification of the distribution $\sum _{j,k}u_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$, which is positive by the matrix criterion; so it is nonnegative by proposition 1.4.3 (3). By (1), $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $. Finally, since $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega $, theorem 3.2.2 (2) shows that $u*\rho _\varepsilon (x)\downarrow u(x)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, for every $x\in \Omega $. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.2.3
text: Proposition 8.2.3 . Let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ and $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be domains, let $F\colon D\to \Omega $ be a holomorphic map, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $ or plurisubharmonic on $D$. More generally, if $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ is only assumed to be open, this alternative holds on each connected component of $D$. Proof. The statement for open $D$ follows by applying the statement for domains to each connected component of $D$. If $n=0$, then $\Omega $ is a point, $u$ is a real constant, and so is $u\circ F$. If $m=0$, then $D$ is a point and $u\circ F$ is a single value in $[-\infty ,\infty )$; it is either $-\infty $ or a real number, that is, a plurisubharmonic function on the point. Now let $m,n\geq 1$. By theorem 8.2.1 , $u$ is the canonical subharmonic representative of a locally integrable function with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$, so proposition 7.3.3 applies: $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $, or locally integrable and subharmonic, in particular upper semicontinuous. In the second case, the restriction of $u\circ F$ to a connected component of an affine complex-line section of $D$ is the composition of $u$ with a holomorphic map from an open subset of $\mathbb {C}$, so it is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ by the same proposition. Hence $u\circ F$ is plurisubharmonic. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.2.4
text: Lemma 8.2.4 . Let $X$ be a connected complex manifold, and let $v\colon X\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function such that every point of $X$ has an open neighborhood on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Then $v$ is plurisubharmonic on $X$ or identically $-\infty $ on $X$. Proof. Let $A$ be the set of points of $X$ having an open neighborhood on which $v\equiv -\infty $, and $B$ the set of points having an open neighborhood on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic. Both sets are open, and they cover $X$ by hypothesis. They are disjoint: if $x\in A\cap B$, with open neighborhoods $W_1$ on which $v\equiv -\infty $ and $W_2$ on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic, then the restriction of $v$ to the nonempty open set $W_1\cap W_2$ is plurisubharmonic and identically $-\infty $, which is impossible because plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable. Since $X$ is connected, either $X=A$, and then $v\equiv -\infty $, or $X=B$, and then $v$ is plurisubharmonic near every point, hence on $X$, because plurisubharmonicity is a local property. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.2.5
text:
Proposition 8.2.5 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Nonnegative multiples, finite sums and maxima of nonempty finite families of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ are plurisubharmonic; here the zero multiple of a function is the zero function. Moreover, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, let $D\subset X$ be open, and let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(D)$. If \[  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\le u(x)\qquad 	ext{for every }x\in \partial D,  \] where $\partial D$ is the boundary of $D$ in $X$, then the function equal to $\max \{ u,v\} $ on $D$ and to $u$ on $X\setminus D$ is plurisubharmonic on $X$. This boundary inequality holds in particular if \[  \varliminf _{\substack {D
i y	o x\ v(y)>-\infty }}(u(y)-v(y))\ge 0 \qquad 	ext{for every }x\in \partial D.  \] Proof. In local coordinates, upper semicontinuity and the submean inequality on complex lines are preserved by nonnegative multiples, sums and maxima; for sums we use that circle means are additive on functions with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. It remains to check that the resulting functions are not identically $-\infty $ on any component. For $cu$ with $c>0$ this holds because $cu=-\infty $ exactly where $u=-\infty $; a sum of plurisubharmonic functions is locally integrable by theorem 8.2.1 , and a maximum dominates each of its members. This proves the first assertion. Let $w$ denote the glued function. On $D$ it equals $\max \{ u,v\} $, which is plurisubharmonic by the first part, and on the open set $X\setminus \overline D$ it equals $u$. At $x\in \partial D$ we have $w(x)=u(x)$, and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ together with the boundary inequality gives \[  \varlimsup _{y	o x}w(y)\leq \max \Bigl \{ \varlimsup _{y	o x}u(y),\  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\Bigr \} \leq u(x)=w(x).  \] Hence $w$ is upper semicontinuous. To verify the line condition, work in a chart and restrict $w$ to a connected component of an affine complex-line section. At points of $D$ and of $X\setminus \overline D$, the restriction satisfies the submean inequality on small circles, because $w$ is plurisubharmonic near such points. At a point $x\in \partial D$ we have $w\geq u$ everywhere and $w(x)=u(x)$, so each small circle mean of $w$ is at least the corresponding circle mean of $u$, which is at least $u(x)=w(x)$; if the restriction of $u$ is identically $-\infty $, then $w(x)=u(x)=-\infty $ and there is nothing to prove. Thus the restriction of $w$ is upper semicontinuous and satisfies the submean inequality on small circles at every point; that is, it is subharmonic. Finally $w\geq u$, so $w$ is not identically $-\infty $ in any chart, and $w$ is plurisubharmonic. For the sufficient condition, fix $x\in \partial D$ and $\varepsilon >0$. By hypothesis, $x$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $v(y)<u(y)+\varepsilon $ for all $y\in W\cap D$ with $v(y)>-\infty $. Hence $v\leq u+\varepsilon $ on $W\cap D$, the inequality being trivial where $v=-\infty $, and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ gives \[  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\leq \varlimsup _{y	o x}u(y)+\varepsilon \leq u(x)+\varepsilon .  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives the boundary inequality. $\square$

title: 8.3 Limits, envelopes and local integrability
text:
8.3 Limits, envelopes and local integrability This section treats limits and envelopes of plurisubharmonic functions and their local integrability. Throughout, $X$ is a complex manifold of positive dimension, except in theorem 8.3.7 , which also allows dimension zero. By theorem 8.2.1 , plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable, and we regard each of them as the distinguished representative of its class. Local $L^ p$ norms on $X$ are computed with Euclidean volume in local coordinates, and “almost everywhere” refers to Lebesgue measure in charts. Any smooth positive volume form gives the same local $L^ p$ spaces and the same $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence, since in coordinates its density is bounded above and below by positive constants on compact sets. By the discussion following definition 7.1.1 , each connected component of $X$ has a countable basis; $X$ itself need not have one, and we assume this explicitly when a global countable selection is needed. We call a subset of an open set in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ real polar if it is polar in the sense of definition 3.5.1 when $\mathbb {C}^ n$ is identified with $\mathbb R^{2n}$. The adjective distinguishes these sets from the pluripolar sets of chapter 10 . Real polar sets are Lebesgue null, by the remark following definition 3.5.1 . Theorem 8.3.1 . Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$, that is, $u_ j\leq u_ i$ whenever $i\leq j$, and let $u=\lim _ iu_ i=\inf _ iu_ i$ be its pointwise limit. Then on each connected component $X_0$ of $X$, exactly one of the following holds: either $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$ and $u_ i	o u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_0)$, or $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$ and $u_ i	o -\infty $ locally uniformly on $X_0$. Proof. The limit $u$ is upper semicontinuous, since $\{ u<c\} = igcup _ i\{ u_ i<c\} $ is open for every real $c$. Fix a connected component $X_0$ of $X$; it has a countable basis. Step 1: a decreasing sequence with the same limit. Let $i_0\in I$. We show that there are indices $i_0\leq i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ such that $u_{i_ l}\downarrow u$ pointwise on $X_0$. Replacing $I$ by the cofinal directed set $\{ i\in I:i\geq i_0\} $, which does not change the limit, we only have to find indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $. For each rational $c$, the open sets $\{ u_ i<c\} \cap X_0$ cover $\{ u<c\} \cap X_0$, and countably many of them suffice: for each basis element of $X_0$ contained in some set $\{ u_ i<c\} $, choose one such index $i$; every point of $\{ u<c\} \cap X_0$ lies in such a basis element. Let $k_1,k_2,\ldots $ be an enumeration, with repetitions allowed, of the indices chosen for all rational $c$. Since $I$ is directed, we can choose inductively $i_1\geq k_1$ and $i_{l+1}\geq i_ l,k_{l+1}$. The sequence $(u_{i_ l})$ is decreasing and bounded below by $u$. If $u(x)<c$ with $c$ rational and $x\in X_0$, then $u_{k_ l}(x)<c$ for some $l$, hence $u_{i_ l}(x)\leq u_{k_ l}(x)<c$. Therefore $u_{i_ l}\downarrow u$ on $X_0$. Step 2: the limit. Let $V\subset X_0$ be a connected coordinate neighborhood, identified with a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. On each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $V$, the restrictions of the $u_{i_ l}$ form a decreasing sequence of subharmonic functions, whose limit is subharmonic by theorem 3.1.6 . Since $u$ is upper semicontinuous, it is either plurisubharmonic on $V$ or identically $-\infty $ on $V$, by definition 8.1.1 . As $X_0$ is connected, lemma 8.2.4 shows that either $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$ or $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$. Step 3: convergence. Suppose first that $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$. Fix $i_0\in I$, take the sequence of Step 1, and let $K$ be a compact subset of a coordinate neighborhood in $X_0$. Then $0\leq u_{i_ l}-u\leq u_{i_0}-u$ almost everywhere, namely wherever $u$ is finite, and $u_{i_0}-u$ is integrable on $K$. By dominated convergence, $\| u_{i_ l}-u\| _{L^1(K)}	o 0$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose $l$ with $\| u_{i_ l}-u\| _{L^1(K)}<\varepsilon $; for every $i\geq i_ l$ we have $0\leq u_ i-u\leq u_{i_ l}-u$ almost everywhere, hence $\| u_ i-u\| _{L^1(K)}<\varepsilon $. Thus the net converges to $u$ in $L^1(K)$, and covering an arbitrary compact subset of $X_0$ by finitely many such sets $K$ gives convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_0)$. Suppose now that $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$, and let $K\subset X_0$ be compact and $A>0$. The open sets $\{ u_ i<-A\} $ cover $K$, so finitely many of them, say those with indices $j_1,\ldots ,j_ p$, already cover $K$. If $i\geq j_1,\ldots ,j_ p$, then $u_ i\leq u_{j_ q}$ for each $q$, and hence $u_ i<-A$ on $K$. This is locally uniform convergence to $-\infty $. $\square$ Recall that a function $F$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$ that is locally bounded above has an upper semicontinuous regularization $F^*$, the smallest upper semicontinuous function that dominates $F$. On $X$ it is given by $F^*(x)=\inf _ W\sup _ WF$, where $W$ ranges over the neighborhoods of $x$, and in a chart it is the regularization of section 3.4 . Theorem 8.3.2 . Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a nonempty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded above, and let $F=\sup _ iu_ i$ be its upper envelope. Then the upper semicontinuous regularization $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic, and $F=F^*$ almost everywhere; more precisely, in every coordinate chart the set $\{ F<F^*\} $ is real polar. If $X$ has a countable basis, there is a countable subset $J\subset I$ such that $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=F^*$. Proof. Since $F^*$ is defined by a local formula and plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to prove that $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic on every connected coordinate neighborhood $V$, which we identify with a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. By theorem 3.4.2 , $F^*$ is subharmonic on $V$, and $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and equal to $F^*$ almost everywhere on $V$. By Choquet's lemma, lemma 3.4.1 , there is a countable set $J_ V\subset I$ with $(\sup _{i\in J_ V}u_ i)^*=F^*$ on $V$. We next show that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*\geq 0$ on $V$. Fix $i_0\in I$, enumerate $J_ V\cup \{ i_0\} $ as $i_0,i_1,i_2,\ldots $, with repetitions if this set is finite, and put $v_ j=\max \{ u_{i_0},\ldots ,u_{i_ j}\} $. The functions $v_ j$ are plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 , increase with $j$, are locally uniformly bounded above, and dominate the locally integrable function $u_{i_0}$. Their limit $G=\sup _ jv_ j$ lies between $\sup _{i\in J_ V}u_ i$ and $F$, so $G^*=F^*$, and hence $G=F^*$ almost everywhere by theorem 3.4.2 applied to the countable family. On a compact set $K\subset V$ on which every $u_ i$ is bounded above by $M$, we have $0\leq v_ j-u_{i_0}\leq M-u_{i_0}$, so dominated convergence gives $v_ j	o F^*$ in $L^1(K)$. Therefore $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*\geq 0$, as a limit of positive currents. Since $F^*$ is subharmonic and dominates the locally integrable function $u_{i_0}$, it is locally integrable and hence the canonical representative of its class, and theorem 8.2.1 shows that $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic on $V$. If $X$ has a countable basis, cover $X$ by countably many connected coordinate neighborhoods $V_1,V_2,\ldots $ and put $J= igcup _ mJ_{V_ m}$. On each $V_ m$ we have $F^*=(\sup _{i\in J_{V_ m}}u_ i)^*\leq (\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*\leq F^*$, and since the regularization is local, $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=F^*$ on $X$. Finally, in each chart the functions $u_ i$ are subharmonic, so the second assertion of theorem 4.4.4 shows that $\{ F<F^*\} $ is polar in the corresponding open subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$, that is, real polar. $\square$ Proposition 8.3.3 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\geq 1$, and let $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$, $r\geq 1$, be a tuple of holomorphic functions on $\Omega $, not all identically zero. Then the function $\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2$, with the value $-\infty $ at the common zeros of the $g_ j$, is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. In particular, for every $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the function $\log |z-a|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Proof. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, with equality for $\lambda $ proportional to $(\overline{g_1(z)},\ldots ,\overline{g_ r(z)})$, we have \[  \log \sum _ j|g_ j(z)|^2 =\sup _{\sum _ j|\lambda _ j|^2=1}\log \left|\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j(z)ight|^2  \] for every $z\in \Omega $, both sides being $-\infty $ at a common zero. The supremum does not change if we omit the $\lambda $ for which $\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j$ vanishes identically: at a point $z$ that is not a common zero, the maximizing $\lambda $ gives $\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j(z)
eq 0$, and at a common zero all terms equal $-\infty $. Some $g_ j$ is not identically zero, so the remaining family is nonempty. Its members are plurisubharmonic by proposition 7.4.3 , theorem 8.2.1 , and they are locally uniformly bounded above by the left-hand side. Their supremum $\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2$ is already upper semicontinuous: it is continuous as a map to $[-\infty ,\infty )$, because $\sum _ j|g_ j|^2$ is continuous and its logarithm tends to $-\infty $ at a common zero. Hence it equals its regularization, which is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.2 . The particular case is the tuple $(z_1-a_1,\ldots ,z_ n-a_ n)$. $\square$ Theorem 8.3.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a domain, $n\geq 1$. Every sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ that is locally uniformly bounded above has a subsequence that either converges locally uniformly to $-\infty $ or converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a plurisubharmonic function. If a sequence $(u_ j)$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then its limit has a plurisubharmonic representative $u$, and the following holds: for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ and every lower semicontinuous function $f\colon K	o \mathbb R$ with $u<f$ on $K$, for instance every real continuous function on $K$, one has $u_ j<f$ on $K$ for all sufficiently large $j$. In particular $\varlimsup _ j u_ j(x)\le u(x)$ for every $x\in \Omega $. Proof. Plurisubharmonic functions are subharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . Hence, by the compactness theorem (theorem 3.3.2 ), a sequence as in the first assertion either tends to $-\infty $ locally uniformly, or has a subsequence converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a locally integrable subharmonic function $v$. In the second case $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0$, as a distributional limit of positive currents, and $v$ is the canonical representative of its class; so $v$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . Now let $(u_ j)$ converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to $T$. As above, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$, so $T$ has a plurisubharmonic representative $u$, namely its canonical subharmonic representative. The $u_ j$ are locally integrable subharmonic functions converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, and $u$ is the canonical representative of their limit, so the remaining assertions are Hartogs' lemma for subharmonic functions, theorem 3.3.3 , which requires no upper bound on the sequence; the last one is its first assertion with the constant sequence $x_ j=x$. $\square$ We next show that plurisubharmonic functions belong to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $p$, and that $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence of plurisubharmonic functions implies $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence. We first treat a subharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on the unit disc. By the Riesz decomposition (theorem 3.2.3 ), $v$ is locally the sum of a harmonic function and the fundamental potential $E_2*\mu $ of a measure, and the kernel $E_2(z)=(2\pi )^{-1}\log |z|$ belongs locally to every $L^ p$ with $p<\infty $; this gives an $L^ p$ bound in terms of the value of $v$ at the center. Applying this bound in one complex variable at a time then gives the estimate for plurisubharmonic functions on polydiscs. We write $D(a,r)=\{ z\in \mathbb C:|z-a|<r\} $ and $D=D(0,1)$, and for $t>0$ we write $tD=D(0,t)$; thus $D^ n$ is the unit polydisc in $\mathbb C^ n$ and $(tD)^ n$ the polydisc of radius $t$ centered at $0$. Integrals over discs and polydiscs are taken with respect to Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV$. Lemma 8.3.5 . There is a constant $C_0\geq 1$ with the following property. Let $v\leq 0$ be a subharmonic function on $D$ with $v(0)>-\infty $. Then there are a finite positive Borel measure $
u $ with support in $D(0,9/10)$ and a harmonic function $h$ on $D(0,4/5)$ such that 8.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:negative-subharmonic-disc-riesz-bounds}  egin{gathered} v(z)=P(z)+h(z)\quad (z\in D(0,4/5)),\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta ),\ 
u (D)\leq C_0|v(0)|,\qquad \sup _{\overline{D(0,1/2)}}|h|\leq C_0|v(0)|. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Moreover, for every $1\leq p<\infty $ there is a constant $C_ p>0$ such that every such $v$ satisfies \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(D(0,1/2))}\leq C_ p|v(0)|.  \] Proof. In this proof $C$ denotes constants that depend only on two cutoff functions $\chi $ and $\eta $ fixed below, and $C'$ constants that depend in addition on $p$. Since $v(0)>-\infty $, the function $v$ is not identically $-\infty $, and hence it is locally integrable by proposition 3.1.5 . For $0<r<1$, the ball submean inequality (theorem 3.1.3 ) and $v\leq 0$ give 8.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:negative-subharmonic-disc-lone} \| v\| _{L^1(D(0,r))}=-\int _{D(0,r)}v\, \mathrm dV\leq \pi r^2|v(0)|. \end{equation} Let $\mu =\Delta v$ be the Riesz measure of $v$, and choose a smooth cutoff $\chi \geq 0$ supported in $D(0,19/20)$ and equal to one on $D(0,9/10)$. By the definition of the distributional Laplacian and ( 8.5 ), \[  \mu (D(0,9/10))\leq \int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu =\int v\Delta \chi \, \mathrm dV\leq \sup |\Delta \chi |\, \| v\| _{L^1(D(0,19/20))}\leq C|v(0)|.  \] Next choose a smooth cutoff $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ supported in $D(0,9/10)$ and equal to one on a neighborhood of $\overline{D(0,4/5)}$. The fundamental solution in the plane is $(2\pi )^{-1}\log |z|$, so theorem 3.2.3 , applied with the measure $
u =\eta \mu $, which is finite and supported in $\operatorname{Supp}\eta \subset D(0,9/10)$, gives \[  v(z)=P(z)+h(z),\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta ),  \] for every $z\in D(0,4/5)$, with $h$ harmonic on $D(0,4/5)$. We estimate $P$. For $|\zeta |\leq 9/10$, the translated disc $D(0,4/5)-\zeta $ lies in $D(0,2)$, so \[  \int _{D(0,4/5)}|\log |z-\zeta ||^ p\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq L_ p=\int _{D(0,2)}|\log |z||^ p\, \mathrm dV(z)<\infty ;  \] the integral $L_ p$ is finite because its part over $D$ equals $2\pi \int _0^1r|\log r|^ p\, \mathrm dr$, whose integrand is bounded on $(0,1]$, while $|\log |z||\leq \log 2$ on the rest of $D(0,2)$. Let $m=
u (D)=\int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu $, so that $m\leq \mu (D(0,9/10))\leq C|v(0)|$. If $m=0$, then $P=0$. Otherwise, $|P(z)|\leq  rac m{2\pi }\int |\log |z-\zeta ||\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )/m$, and Hölder's inequality for the probability measure $
u /m$ gives \[  |P(z)|^ p\leq \Bigl ( rac m{2\pi }\Bigr )^ p\int |\log |z-\zeta ||^ p\,  rac{\mathrm d
u (\zeta )}m,  \] and integrating over $z\in D(0,4/5)$ with Tonelli's theorem yields $\| P\| _{L^ p(D(0,4/5))}\leq L_ p^{1/p}m/(2\pi )\leq C'|v(0)|$. We now estimate $h$. The case $p=1$ of the bound for $P$, in which $L_1$ is an absolute constant, and ( 8.5 ) give $\| h\| _{L^1(D(0,4/5))}\leq C|v(0)|$. For $|z|\leq 1/2$, the closed disc $\overline{D(z,1/4)}$ lies in $D(0,4/5)$, and the ball mean-value property of the harmonic function $h$ (proposition 2.1.1 ) gives $|h(z)|\leq (16/\pi )\| h\| _{L^1(D(0,4/5))}$. We have thus found a constant $C_0\geq 1$, depending only on the cutoff functions $\chi $ and $\eta $, such that $
u (D)=m\leq C_0|v(0)|$ and $\sup _{\overline{D(0,1/2)}}|h|\leq C_0|v(0)|$; this proves ( 8.4 ). Adding the estimates for $P$ and $h$ on $D(0,1/2)$, we obtain \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(D(0,1/2))}\leq \| P\| _{L^ p(D(0,4/5))}+(\pi /4)^{1/p}C_0|v(0)|\leq C'|v(0)|,  \] which proves the last assertion. $\square$ Proposition 8.3.6 . Let $n\geq 1$ and $1\leq p<\infty $. There are constants $C_{n,p},A_{n,p}>0$ such that every plurisubharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on the unit polydisc $D^ n$ satisfies \[  \| v\| _{L^ p((	frac 12D)^ n)}\leq C_{n,p}|v(0)| \quad 	ext{if }v(0)>-\infty ,  \] and 8.6  egin{equation} \label{eq:negative-psh-lp-lone-bound} \| v\| _{L^ p((	frac 14D)^ n)}\leq A_{n,p}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}. \end{equation} Here $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}$ may be infinite, in which case there is nothing to prove. Proof. We prove the first estimate by induction on $n$. For $n=1$ it is lemma 8.3.5 . Let $n\geq 2$, write $z=(z_1,z')$ with $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and let $v$ be as in the statement with $v(0)>-\infty $. The function $w(z')=v(0,z')$ is the composition of $v$ with the holomorphic map $z'\mapsto (0,z')$, so by proposition 8.2.3 it is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $D^{n-1}$. Since $w(0)=v(0)>-\infty $, it is plurisubharmonic, hence locally integrable and finite outside a Lebesgue null set $E\subset D^{n-1}$. For $z'\in D^{n-1}\setminus E$, the function $z_1\mapsto v(z_1,z')$ is subharmonic and nonpositive on $D$, with the finite value $w(z')$ at the center, so lemma 8.3.5 gives \[  \int _{ rac12D}|v(z_1,z')|^ p\, \mathrm dV(z_1) \leq C_ p^ p|w(z')|^ p.  \] We integrate over $z'\in (	frac 12D)^{n-1}$ using Tonelli's theorem; the null set $E$, on which the inner integral may be infinite, does not contribute. The induction hypothesis applied to $w$ then gives \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(( rac12D)^ n)}^ p\leq C_ p^ p\| w\| _{L^ p(( rac12D)^{n-1})}^ p\leq C_ p^ pC_{n-1,p}^ p|v(0)|^ p,  \] which is the first estimate with $C_{n,p}=C_ pC_{n-1,p}$. For the second estimate, let $Q=(	frac 1{10}D)^ n$ and $|Q|$ its volume. If $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}=0$, then $v=0$ almost everywhere, hence $v\equiv 0$ by theorem 8.2.1 , and there is nothing to prove; we may also assume that $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}<\infty $. Put $\lambda =2|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}>0$. By Chebyshev's inequality, the set of points of $Q$ with $|v|>\lambda $ has measure at most $\lambda ^{-1}\int _ Q|v|\, \mathrm dV\leq |Q|/2$, so its complement in $Q$ has positive measure. Since $v$ is finite almost everywhere, there is a point $a\in Q$ with $v(a)>-\infty $ and \[  |v(a)|\leq 2|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}.  \] The polydisc of radius $4/5$ centered at $a$ lies in $D^ n$, and the polydisc of radius $2/5$ centered at $a$ contains $(	frac 14D)^ n$, since $	frac 14+	frac 1{10}<	frac 25$. We apply the first estimate to the plurisubharmonic function $\zeta \mapsto v(a+	frac 45\zeta )\leq 0$ on $D^ n$ and change variables: \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(( rac14D)^ n)}\leq  igl (	frac 45 igr )^{2n/p}C_{n,p}|v(a)|\leq 2 igl (	frac 45 igr )^{2n/p}C_{n,p}|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}.  \] This is ( 8.6 ). $\square$ Theorem 8.3.7 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold and $1\leq p<\infty $. Every plurisubharmonic function on $X$ belongs to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. If a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$, then it converges in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ to the same limit. Proof. If $X$ has dimension zero, every compact subset of $X$ is finite, plurisubharmonic functions are real-valued, and convergence in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is pointwise convergence; so both assertions hold. Let $X$ have dimension $n\geq 1$. Every compact subset of $X$ is covered by finitely many coordinate polydiscs, so it suffices to work near a point $x\in X$ in a chart in which $x=0$ and the closed polydisc $\overline{(RD)^ n}$ lies in the chart, for some $R>0$. Let $v$ be plurisubharmonic. Being upper semicontinuous, $v$ is bounded above on $\overline{(RD)^ n}$ by some constant $A$. The function $\zeta \mapsto v(R\zeta )-A$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on $D^ n$, and its $L^1$ norm on $D^ n$ is finite because $v$ is locally integrable. By ( 8.6 ), $v$ belongs to $L^ p$ on the polydisc $(	frac R4D)^ n$. This proves the first assertion. Now let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. For $p=1$ there is nothing to prove, so let $p>1$. By theorem 8.3.4 applied in charts, together with the uniqueness in theorem 8.2.1 , the limit is represented by a plurisubharmonic function $u$. The norms $\| u_ j\| _{L^1((RD)^ n)}$ are bounded because the sequence converges. If $y\in (	frac R2D)^ n$, the ball $B(y,R/2)$ lies in $(RD)^ n$, so the ball submean inequality gives $u_ j(y)\leq |B(y,R/2)|^{-1}\| u_ j\| _{L^1((RD)^ n)}$. Hence there is a constant $M$, independent of $j$, with $u_ j\leq M$ and $u\leq M$ on $(	frac R2D)^ n$. Applying ( 8.6 ) to $\zeta \mapsto u_ j(	frac R2\zeta )-M$ and to $\zeta \mapsto u(	frac R2\zeta )-M$, whose $L^1$ norms on $D^ n$ are bounded independently of $j$, we obtain a bound for the $L^{2p}$ norms of $u_ j$ and $u$ on $(	frac R8D)^ n$ that is uniform in $j$. By a finite covering, for every compact set $K\subset X$ the norms $\| u_ j\| _{L^{2p}(K)}$ and $\| u\| _{L^{2p}(K)}$ are bounded independently of $j$. We interpolate between $L^1$ and $L^{2p}$. For a function $f$ on $K$, write $|f|^ p=|f|^{p/(2p-1)}\cdot |f|^{p(2p-2)/(2p-1)}$ and apply Hölder's inequality with the conjugate exponents $(2p-1)/p$ and $(2p-1)/(p-1)$; since $ rac{p(2p-2)}{2p-1}\cdot  rac{2p-1}{p-1}=2p$, this gives \[  \int _ K|f|^ p\, \mathrm dV\leq \Bigl (\int _ K|f|\, \mathrm dV\Bigr )^{p/(2p-1)}\Bigl (\int _ K|f|^{2p}\, \mathrm dV\Bigr )^{(p-1)/(2p-1)},  \] that is, $\| f\| _{L^ p(K)}\leq \| f\| _{L^1(K)}^{1/(2p-1)}\| f\| _{L^{2p}(K)}^{(2p-2)/(2p-1)}$. With $f=u_ j-u$, whose $L^{2p}(K)$ norms are bounded independently of $j$, we obtain \[  \| u_ j-u\| _{L^ p(K)} \leq \| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(K)}^{1/(2p-1)} \| u_ j-u\| _{L^{2p}(K)}^{(2p-2)/(2p-1)}\longrightarrow 0.  \] $\square$ The same Riesz decomposition gives exponential integrability: if $v\leq 0$ is plurisubharmonic on a ball, then $\mathrm e^{-\alpha v}$ is integrable on a smaller concentric ball for every sufficiently small $\alpha >0$, and the admissible $\alpha $ and the bound for the integral depend only on a bound for the $L^1$ norm of $v$. In one variable this follows from Jensen's inequality applied to the fundamental potential in the Riesz decomposition. In several variables we integrate the one-variable estimates over all complex lines through a suitable point. For $t>0$ we write $tB$ for the ball of radius $t$ centered at $0$ in $\mathbb C^ n$; thus $B$ is the unit ball. Lemma 8.3.8 . There are constants $ eta ,C>0$ such that every subharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on $D$ with $v(0)\geq -1$ satisfies \[  \int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C.  \] Proof. Since $v(0)\geq -1>-\infty $, lemma 8.3.5 gives a finite positive measure $
u $ with support in $D(0,9/10)$ and a harmonic function $h$ on $D(0,4/5)$ such that \[  v=P+h,\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )  \] at every point of $D(0,4/5)$. Since $|v(0)|\leq 1$, the bounds ( 8.4 ) give $M=
u (D)\leq C_0$ and $\sup _{D(0,1/2)}|h|\leq C_0$, where $C_0\geq 1$ is the universal constant of that lemma. Fix $ eta \in (0,1]$ with $ eta C_0\leq 2\pi $. We show that $\int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta P}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8\pi $. If $M=0$, then $P=0$, and this integral is $\pi /4$. Assume $M>0$ and put $b= eta M/(2\pi )\in (0,1]$. Fix $z\in D(0,1/2)$. For $N\geq 1$ the Borel function $f_ N(\zeta )=-b\max \{ \log |z-\zeta |,-N\} $ is bounded on $D(0,9/10)$, so Jensen's inequality (lemma 1.1.4 ), applied to the convex function $\exp $ on $\mathbb R$ and the probability measure $
u /M$, gives \[  \exp \Bigl (\int f_ N\,  rac{\mathrm d
u }M\Bigr )\leq \int \mathrm e^{f_ N}\,  rac{\mathrm d
u }M\leq  rac1M\int |z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta ).  \] As $N	o \infty $, the functions $f_ N$ increase to $-b\log |z-\zeta |$, which may take the value $+\infty $, and they are bounded below by the bounded function $f_1$. By monotone convergence, $\int f_ N\, \mathrm d
u /M$ increases to $\int -b\log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )/M=- eta P(z)$, and therefore \[  \mathrm e^{- eta P(z)}\leq  rac1M\int |z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )  \] for every $z\in D(0,1/2)$, with the convention $\mathrm e^{\infty }=\infty $. For every $\zeta \in D(0,9/10)$ the translated disc $D(0,1/2)-\zeta $ lies in $D(0,2)$, and $r^{-b}\leq 1+r^{-1}$ for $r>0$ because $0<b\leq 1$; hence \[  \int _{D(0,1/2)}|z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq \int _{D(0,2)}(1+|z|^{-1})\, \mathrm dV(z)=8\pi .  \] Integrating the bound for $\mathrm e^{- eta P(z)}$ over $z\in D(0,1/2)$ with Tonelli's theorem, we obtain $\int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta P}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8\pi $. Finally, since $\mathrm e^{- eta v}=\mathrm e^{- eta P}\mathrm e^{- eta h}\leq \mathrm e^{ eta C_0}\mathrm e^{- eta P}$ on $D(0,1/2)$, the lemma follows with $C=8\pi \mathrm e^{C_0}$. $\square$ Proposition 8.3.9 . Let $n\geq 1$, and let $B$ be the unit ball of $\mathbb C^ n$. There are constants $\alpha _ n,C_ n>0$ such that every plurisubharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on $B$ with $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq 1$ satisfies 8.7  egin{equation} \label{eq:negative-psh-exponential-lone-bound} \int _{ rac14B}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C_ n. \end{equation} More generally, if $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq M$ for some $M>0$, the same bound holds with the exponent $\alpha _ n/M$ in place of $\alpha _ n$. Proof. Put $A_ n=\max \{ 1,2/| rac18B|\} $. The mean of $|v|$ over $ rac18B$ is at most $1/| rac18B|<A_ n$. Hence the set of points of $ rac18B$ with $|v|\leq A_ n$ has positive measure, since otherwise $|v|>A_ n$ almost everywhere on $ rac18B$ and the mean would be at least $A_ n$; so there is a point $a\in  rac18B$ with $|v(a)|\leq A_ n$. For each unit vector $e\in \mathbb C^ n$, the disc $\{ a+	frac 34\zeta e:|\zeta |<1\} $ lies in $B$, so the function \[  \zeta \longmapsto A_ n^{-1}v(a+	frac 34\zeta e)  \] is subharmonic and nonpositive on $D$, with value at least $-1$ at $0$. Set $\alpha _ n= eta /A_ n$, with $ eta $ as in lemma 8.3.8 . That lemma and the change of variables $\zeta \mapsto  rac34\zeta $ give a bound, independent of $e$ and $v$, for \[  \int _{|\zeta |<3/8}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v(a+\zeta e)}\, \mathrm dV(\zeta ).  \] It remains to pass from these integrals over discs in complex lines to an integral over a ball. Let $	au $ and $s_{2n-1}$ be as in ( 8.1 ). By that identity, applied with center $a$, and since $|\zeta |^{2n-2}\leq r^{2n-2}$ for $|\zeta |<r$, every Borel function $F\geq 0$, possibly taking the value $+\infty $, satisfies \[  \int _{|z-a|<r}F(z)\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq  rac{s_{2n-1}r^{2n-2}}{2\pi } \int _{S^{2n-1}}\int _{|\zeta |<r}F(a+\zeta e)\, \mathrm dV(\zeta )\, \mathrm d	au (e)  \] for every $r>0$. We apply this with $F=\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}$ and $r=3/8$. Since $ rac14B\subset B(a,3/8)$, the uniform bound for the line integrals proves ( 8.7 ). Finally, if $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq M$ with $M>0$, then $v/M$ is a nonpositive plurisubharmonic function with $\| v/M\| _{L^1(B)}\leq 1$, and ( 8.7 ) for $v/M$ is the last assertion. $\square$ Consequently, every plurisubharmonic function $u$ on a complex manifold $X$ is locally exponentially integrable: every point $x\in X$ has a neighborhood $W$ for which there is $\alpha _0>0$ such that $\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}$ is integrable on $W$ for $0<\alpha \leq \alpha _0$, the integrals being computed in local coordinates. In dimension zero we may take $W=\{ x\} $. In dimension $n\geq 1$, choose a chart in which $x=0$ and the closed ball $\overline{B(0,R)}$ lies in the chart domain, for some $R>0$, and let $c$ be an upper bound for $u$ on this ball. The function $v(\zeta )=u(R\zeta )-c$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on the unit ball $B$, and since $u$ is locally integrable there is $A>0$ with $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq A$. Put $\alpha _0=\alpha _ n/A$ and $W=B(0,R/4)$. For $0<\alpha \leq \alpha _0$ we have $\mathrm e^{-\alpha v}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _0v}$, because $v\leq 0$, so the change of variables $z=R\zeta $ and the last assertion of proposition 8.3.9 give \[  \int _ W\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\, \mathrm dV=R^{2n}\mathrm e^{-\alpha c}\int _{ rac14B}\mathrm e^{-\alpha v}\, \mathrm dV\leq R^{2n}\mathrm e^{-\alpha c}C_ n<\infty .  \]

title: Theorem 8.3.1
text: Theorem 8.3.1 . Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$, that is, $u_ j\leq u_ i$ whenever $i\leq j$, and let $u=\lim _ iu_ i=\inf _ iu_ i$ be its pointwise limit. Then on each connected component $X_0$ of $X$, exactly one of the following holds: either $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$ and $u_ i\to u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_0)$, or $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$ and $u_ i\to -\infty $ locally uniformly on $X_0$. Proof. The limit $u$ is upper semicontinuous, since $\{ u<c\} =\bigcup _ i\{ u_ i<c\} $ is open for every real $c$. Fix a connected component $X_0$ of $X$; it has a countable basis. Step 1: a decreasing sequence with the same limit. Let $i_0\in I$. We show that there are indices $i_0\leq i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ such that $u_{i_ l}\downarrow u$ pointwise on $X_0$. Replacing $I$ by the cofinal directed set $\{ i\in I:i\geq i_0\} $, which does not change the limit, we only have to find indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $. For each rational $c$, the open sets $\{ u_ i<c\} \cap X_0$ cover $\{ u<c\} \cap X_0$, and countably many of them suffice: for each basis element of $X_0$ contained in some set $\{ u_ i<c\} $, choose one such index $i$; every point of $\{ u<c\} \cap X_0$ lies in such a basis element. Let $k_1,k_2,\ldots $ be an enumeration, with repetitions allowed, of the indices chosen for all rational $c$. Since $I$ is directed, we can choose inductively $i_1\geq k_1$ and $i_{l+1}\geq i_ l,k_{l+1}$. The sequence $(u_{i_ l})$ is decreasing and bounded below by $u$. If $u(x)<c$ with $c$ rational and $x\in X_0$, then $u_{k_ l}(x)<c$ for some $l$, hence $u_{i_ l}(x)\leq u_{k_ l}(x)<c$. Therefore $u_{i_ l}\downarrow u$ on $X_0$. Step 2: the limit. Let $V\subset X_0$ be a connected coordinate neighborhood, identified with a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. On each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $V$, the restrictions of the $u_{i_ l}$ form a decreasing sequence of subharmonic functions, whose limit is subharmonic by theorem 3.1.6 . Since $u$ is upper semicontinuous, it is either plurisubharmonic on $V$ or identically $-\infty $ on $V$, by definition 8.1.1 . As $X_0$ is connected, lemma 8.2.4 shows that either $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$ or $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$. Step 3: convergence. Suppose first that $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$. Fix $i_0\in I$, take the sequence of Step 1, and let $K$ be a compact subset of a coordinate neighborhood in $X_0$. Then $0\leq u_{i_ l}-u\leq u_{i_0}-u$ almost everywhere, namely wherever $u$ is finite, and $u_{i_0}-u$ is integrable on $K$. By dominated convergence, $\| u_{i_ l}-u\| _{L^1(K)}\to 0$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose $l$ with $\| u_{i_ l}-u\| _{L^1(K)}<\varepsilon $; for every $i\geq i_ l$ we have $0\leq u_ i-u\leq u_{i_ l}-u$ almost everywhere, hence $\| u_ i-u\| _{L^1(K)}<\varepsilon $. Thus the net converges to $u$ in $L^1(K)$, and covering an arbitrary compact subset of $X_0$ by finitely many such sets $K$ gives convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_0)$. Suppose now that $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$, and let $K\subset X_0$ be compact and $A>0$. The open sets $\{ u_ i<-A\} $ cover $K$, so finitely many of them, say those with indices $j_1,\ldots ,j_ p$, already cover $K$. If $i\geq j_1,\ldots ,j_ p$, then $u_ i\leq u_{j_ q}$ for each $q$, and hence $u_ i<-A$ on $K$. This is locally uniform convergence to $-\infty $. $\square$

title: Theorem 8.3.2
text: Theorem 8.3.2 . Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a nonempty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded above, and let $F=\sup _ iu_ i$ be its upper envelope. Then the upper semicontinuous regularization $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic, and $F=F^*$ almost everywhere; more precisely, in every coordinate chart the set $\{ F<F^*\} $ is real polar. If $X$ has a countable basis, there is a countable subset $J\subset I$ such that $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=F^*$. Proof. Since $F^*$ is defined by a local formula and plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to prove that $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic on every connected coordinate neighborhood $V$, which we identify with a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. By theorem 3.4.2 , $F^*$ is subharmonic on $V$, and $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and equal to $F^*$ almost everywhere on $V$. By Choquet's lemma, lemma 3.4.1 , there is a countable set $J_ V\subset I$ with $(\sup _{i\in J_ V}u_ i)^*=F^*$ on $V$. We next show that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*\geq 0$ on $V$. Fix $i_0\in I$, enumerate $J_ V\cup \{ i_0\} $ as $i_0,i_1,i_2,\ldots $, with repetitions if this set is finite, and put $v_ j=\max \{ u_{i_0},\ldots ,u_{i_ j}\} $. The functions $v_ j$ are plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 , increase with $j$, are locally uniformly bounded above, and dominate the locally integrable function $u_{i_0}$. Their limit $G=\sup _ jv_ j$ lies between $\sup _{i\in J_ V}u_ i$ and $F$, so $G^*=F^*$, and hence $G=F^*$ almost everywhere by theorem 3.4.2 applied to the countable family. On a compact set $K\subset V$ on which every $u_ i$ is bounded above by $M$, we have $0\leq v_ j-u_{i_0}\leq M-u_{i_0}$, so dominated convergence gives $v_ j\to F^*$ in $L^1(K)$. Therefore $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*\geq 0$, as a limit of positive currents. Since $F^*$ is subharmonic and dominates the locally integrable function $u_{i_0}$, it is locally integrable and hence the canonical representative of its class, and theorem 8.2.1 shows that $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic on $V$. If $X$ has a countable basis, cover $X$ by countably many connected coordinate neighborhoods $V_1,V_2,\ldots $ and put $J=\bigcup _ mJ_{V_ m}$. On each $V_ m$ we have $F^*=(\sup _{i\in J_{V_ m}}u_ i)^*\leq (\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*\leq F^*$, and since the regularization is local, $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=F^*$ on $X$. Finally, in each chart the functions $u_ i$ are subharmonic, so the second assertion of theorem 4.4.4 shows that $\{ F<F^*\} $ is polar in the corresponding open subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$, that is, real polar. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.3.3
text: Proposition 8.3.3 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\geq 1$, and let $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$, $r\geq 1$, be a tuple of holomorphic functions on $\Omega $, not all identically zero. Then the function $\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2$, with the value $-\infty $ at the common zeros of the $g_ j$, is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. In particular, for every $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the function $\log |z-a|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Proof. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, with equality for $\lambda $ proportional to $(\overline{g_1(z)},\ldots ,\overline{g_ r(z)})$, we have \[  \log \sum _ j|g_ j(z)|^2 =\sup _{\sum _ j|\lambda _ j|^2=1}\log \left|\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j(z)\right|^2  \] for every $z\in \Omega $, both sides being $-\infty $ at a common zero. The supremum does not change if we omit the $\lambda $ for which $\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j$ vanishes identically: at a point $z$ that is not a common zero, the maximizing $\lambda $ gives $\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j(z)\neq 0$, and at a common zero all terms equal $-\infty $. Some $g_ j$ is not identically zero, so the remaining family is nonempty. Its members are plurisubharmonic by proposition 7.4.3 , theorem 8.2.1 , and they are locally uniformly bounded above by the left-hand side. Their supremum $\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2$ is already upper semicontinuous: it is continuous as a map to $[-\infty ,\infty )$, because $\sum _ j|g_ j|^2$ is continuous and its logarithm tends to $-\infty $ at a common zero. Hence it equals its regularization, which is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.2 . The particular case is the tuple $(z_1-a_1,\ldots ,z_ n-a_ n)$. $\square$

title: Theorem 8.3.4
text: Theorem 8.3.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a domain, $n\geq 1$. Every sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ that is locally uniformly bounded above has a subsequence that either converges locally uniformly to $-\infty $ or converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a plurisubharmonic function. If a sequence $(u_ j)$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then its limit has a plurisubharmonic representative $u$, and the following holds: for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ and every lower semicontinuous function $f\colon K\to \mathbb R$ with $u<f$ on $K$, for instance every real continuous function on $K$, one has $u_ j<f$ on $K$ for all sufficiently large $j$. In particular $\varlimsup _ j u_ j(x)\le u(x)$ for every $x\in \Omega $. Proof. Plurisubharmonic functions are subharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . Hence, by the compactness theorem (theorem 3.3.2 ), a sequence as in the first assertion either tends to $-\infty $ locally uniformly, or has a subsequence converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a locally integrable subharmonic function $v$. In the second case $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0$, as a distributional limit of positive currents, and $v$ is the canonical representative of its class; so $v$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . Now let $(u_ j)$ converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to $T$. As above, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$, so $T$ has a plurisubharmonic representative $u$, namely its canonical subharmonic representative. The $u_ j$ are locally integrable subharmonic functions converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, and $u$ is the canonical representative of their limit, so the remaining assertions are Hartogs' lemma for subharmonic functions, theorem 3.3.3 , which requires no upper bound on the sequence; the last one is its first assertion with the constant sequence $x_ j=x$. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.3.5
text:
Lemma 8.3.5 . There is a constant $C_0\geq 1$ with the following property. Let $v\leq 0$ be a subharmonic function on $D$ with $v(0)>-\infty $. Then there are a finite positive Borel measure $
u $ with support in $D(0,9/10)$ and a harmonic function $h$ on $D(0,4/5)$ such that 8.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:negative-subharmonic-disc-riesz-bounds}  egin{gathered} v(z)=P(z)+h(z)\quad (z\in D(0,4/5)),\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta ),\ 
u (D)\leq C_0|v(0)|,\qquad \sup _{\overline{D(0,1/2)}}|h|\leq C_0|v(0)|. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Moreover, for every $1\leq p<\infty $ there is a constant $C_ p>0$ such that every such $v$ satisfies \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(D(0,1/2))}\leq C_ p|v(0)|.  \] Proof. In this proof $C$ denotes constants that depend only on two cutoff functions $\chi $ and $\eta $ fixed below, and $C'$ constants that depend in addition on $p$. Since $v(0)>-\infty $, the function $v$ is not identically $-\infty $, and hence it is locally integrable by proposition 3.1.5 . For $0<r<1$, the ball submean inequality (theorem 3.1.3 ) and $v\leq 0$ give 8.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:negative-subharmonic-disc-lone} \| v\| _{L^1(D(0,r))}=-\int _{D(0,r)}v\, \mathrm dV\leq \pi r^2|v(0)|. \end{equation} Let $\mu =\Delta v$ be the Riesz measure of $v$, and choose a smooth cutoff $\chi \geq 0$ supported in $D(0,19/20)$ and equal to one on $D(0,9/10)$. By the definition of the distributional Laplacian and ( 8.5 ), \[  \mu (D(0,9/10))\leq \int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu =\int v\Delta \chi \, \mathrm dV\leq \sup |\Delta \chi |\, \| v\| _{L^1(D(0,19/20))}\leq C|v(0)|.  \] Next choose a smooth cutoff $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ supported in $D(0,9/10)$ and equal to one on a neighborhood of $\overline{D(0,4/5)}$. The fundamental solution in the plane is $(2\pi )^{-1}\log |z|$, so theorem 3.2.3 , applied with the measure $
u =\eta \mu $, which is finite and supported in $\operatorname{Supp}\eta \subset D(0,9/10)$, gives \[  v(z)=P(z)+h(z),\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta ),  \] for every $z\in D(0,4/5)$, with $h$ harmonic on $D(0,4/5)$. We estimate $P$. For $|\zeta |\leq 9/10$, the translated disc $D(0,4/5)-\zeta $ lies in $D(0,2)$, so \[  \int _{D(0,4/5)}|\log |z-\zeta ||^ p\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq L_ p=\int _{D(0,2)}|\log |z||^ p\, \mathrm dV(z)<\infty ;  \] the integral $L_ p$ is finite because its part over $D$ equals $2\pi \int _0^1r|\log r|^ p\, \mathrm dr$, whose integrand is bounded on $(0,1]$, while $|\log |z||\leq \log 2$ on the rest of $D(0,2)$. Let $m=
u (D)=\int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu $, so that $m\leq \mu (D(0,9/10))\leq C|v(0)|$. If $m=0$, then $P=0$. Otherwise, $|P(z)|\leq  rac m{2\pi }\int |\log |z-\zeta ||\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )/m$, and Hölder's inequality for the probability measure $
u /m$ gives \[  |P(z)|^ p\leq \Bigl ( rac m{2\pi }\Bigr )^ p\int |\log |z-\zeta ||^ p\,  rac{\mathrm d
u (\zeta )}m,  \] and integrating over $z\in D(0,4/5)$ with Tonelli's theorem yields $\| P\| _{L^ p(D(0,4/5))}\leq L_ p^{1/p}m/(2\pi )\leq C'|v(0)|$. We now estimate $h$. The case $p=1$ of the bound for $P$, in which $L_1$ is an absolute constant, and ( 8.5 ) give $\| h\| _{L^1(D(0,4/5))}\leq C|v(0)|$. For $|z|\leq 1/2$, the closed disc $\overline{D(z,1/4)}$ lies in $D(0,4/5)$, and the ball mean-value property of the harmonic function $h$ (proposition 2.1.1 ) gives $|h(z)|\leq (16/\pi )\| h\| _{L^1(D(0,4/5))}$. We have thus found a constant $C_0\geq 1$, depending only on the cutoff functions $\chi $ and $\eta $, such that $
u (D)=m\leq C_0|v(0)|$ and $\sup _{\overline{D(0,1/2)}}|h|\leq C_0|v(0)|$; this proves ( 8.4 ). Adding the estimates for $P$ and $h$ on $D(0,1/2)$, we obtain \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(D(0,1/2))}\leq \| P\| _{L^ p(D(0,4/5))}+(\pi /4)^{1/p}C_0|v(0)|\leq C'|v(0)|,  \] which proves the last assertion. $\square$

8.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:negative-subharmonic-disc-riesz-bounds} \begin{gathered} v(z)=P(z)+h(z)\quad (z\in D(0,4/5)),\qquad P(z)=\frac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d\nu (\zeta ),\\ \nu (D)\leq C_0|v(0)|,\qquad \sup _{\overline{D(0,1/2)}}|h|\leq C_0|v(0)|. \end{gathered} \end{equation}
8.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:negative-subharmonic-disc-lone} \| v\| _{L^1(D(0,r))}=-\int _{D(0,r)}v\, \mathrm dV\leq \pi r^2|v(0)|. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 8.3.6
text: Proposition 8.3.6 . Let $n\geq 1$ and $1\leq p<\infty $. There are constants $C_{n,p},A_{n,p}>0$ such that every plurisubharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on the unit polydisc $D^ n$ satisfies \[  \| v\| _{L^ p((\tfrac 12D)^ n)}\leq C_{n,p}|v(0)| \quad \text{if }v(0)>-\infty ,  \] and 8.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:negative-psh-lp-lone-bound} \| v\| _{L^ p((\tfrac 14D)^ n)}\leq A_{n,p}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}. \end{equation} Here $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}$ may be infinite, in which case there is nothing to prove. Proof. We prove the first estimate by induction on $n$. For $n=1$ it is lemma 8.3.5 . Let $n\geq 2$, write $z=(z_1,z')$ with $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and let $v$ be as in the statement with $v(0)>-\infty $. The function $w(z')=v(0,z')$ is the composition of $v$ with the holomorphic map $z'\mapsto (0,z')$, so by proposition 8.2.3 it is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $D^{n-1}$. Since $w(0)=v(0)>-\infty $, it is plurisubharmonic, hence locally integrable and finite outside a Lebesgue null set $E\subset D^{n-1}$. For $z'\in D^{n-1}\setminus E$, the function $z_1\mapsto v(z_1,z')$ is subharmonic and nonpositive on $D$, with the finite value $w(z')$ at the center, so lemma 8.3.5 gives \[  \int _{\frac12D}|v(z_1,z')|^ p\, \mathrm dV(z_1) \leq C_ p^ p|w(z')|^ p.  \] We integrate over $z'\in (\tfrac 12D)^{n-1}$ using Tonelli's theorem; the null set $E$, on which the inner integral may be infinite, does not contribute. The induction hypothesis applied to $w$ then gives \[  \| v\| _{L^ p((\frac12D)^ n)}^ p\leq C_ p^ p\| w\| _{L^ p((\frac12D)^{n-1})}^ p\leq C_ p^ pC_{n-1,p}^ p|v(0)|^ p,  \] which is the first estimate with $C_{n,p}=C_ pC_{n-1,p}$. For the second estimate, let $Q=(\tfrac 1{10}D)^ n$ and $|Q|$ its volume. If $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}=0$, then $v=0$ almost everywhere, hence $v\equiv 0$ by theorem 8.2.1 , and there is nothing to prove; we may also assume that $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}<\infty $. Put $\lambda =2|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}>0$. By Chebyshev's inequality, the set of points of $Q$ with $|v|>\lambda $ has measure at most $\lambda ^{-1}\int _ Q|v|\, \mathrm dV\leq |Q|/2$, so its complement in $Q$ has positive measure. Since $v$ is finite almost everywhere, there is a point $a\in Q$ with $v(a)>-\infty $ and \[  |v(a)|\leq 2|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}.  \] The polydisc of radius $4/5$ centered at $a$ lies in $D^ n$, and the polydisc of radius $2/5$ centered at $a$ contains $(\tfrac 14D)^ n$, since $\tfrac 14+\tfrac 1{10}<\tfrac 25$. We apply the first estimate to the plurisubharmonic function $\zeta \mapsto v(a+\tfrac 45\zeta )\leq 0$ on $D^ n$ and change variables: \[  \| v\| _{L^ p((\frac14D)^ n)}\leq \bigl (\tfrac 45\bigr )^{2n/p}C_{n,p}|v(a)|\leq 2\bigl (\tfrac 45\bigr )^{2n/p}C_{n,p}|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}.  \] This is ( 8.6 ). $\square$
8.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:negative-psh-lp-lone-bound} \| v\| _{L^ p((\tfrac 14D)^ n)}\leq A_{n,p}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 8.3.7
text: Theorem 8.3.7 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold and $1\leq p<\infty $. Every plurisubharmonic function on $X$ belongs to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. If a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$, then it converges in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ to the same limit. Proof. If $X$ has dimension zero, every compact subset of $X$ is finite, plurisubharmonic functions are real-valued, and convergence in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is pointwise convergence; so both assertions hold. Let $X$ have dimension $n\geq 1$. Every compact subset of $X$ is covered by finitely many coordinate polydiscs, so it suffices to work near a point $x\in X$ in a chart in which $x=0$ and the closed polydisc $\overline{(RD)^ n}$ lies in the chart, for some $R>0$. Let $v$ be plurisubharmonic. Being upper semicontinuous, $v$ is bounded above on $\overline{(RD)^ n}$ by some constant $A$. The function $\zeta \mapsto v(R\zeta )-A$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on $D^ n$, and its $L^1$ norm on $D^ n$ is finite because $v$ is locally integrable. By ( 8.6 ), $v$ belongs to $L^ p$ on the polydisc $(\tfrac R4D)^ n$. This proves the first assertion. Now let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. For $p=1$ there is nothing to prove, so let $p>1$. By theorem 8.3.4 applied in charts, together with the uniqueness in theorem 8.2.1 , the limit is represented by a plurisubharmonic function $u$. The norms $\| u_ j\| _{L^1((RD)^ n)}$ are bounded because the sequence converges. If $y\in (\tfrac R2D)^ n$, the ball $B(y,R/2)$ lies in $(RD)^ n$, so the ball submean inequality gives $u_ j(y)\leq |B(y,R/2)|^{-1}\| u_ j\| _{L^1((RD)^ n)}$. Hence there is a constant $M$, independent of $j$, with $u_ j\leq M$ and $u\leq M$ on $(\tfrac R2D)^ n$. Applying ( 8.6 ) to $\zeta \mapsto u_ j(\tfrac R2\zeta )-M$ and to $\zeta \mapsto u(\tfrac R2\zeta )-M$, whose $L^1$ norms on $D^ n$ are bounded independently of $j$, we obtain a bound for the $L^{2p}$ norms of $u_ j$ and $u$ on $(\tfrac R8D)^ n$ that is uniform in $j$. By a finite covering, for every compact set $K\subset X$ the norms $\| u_ j\| _{L^{2p}(K)}$ and $\| u\| _{L^{2p}(K)}$ are bounded independently of $j$. We interpolate between $L^1$ and $L^{2p}$. For a function $f$ on $K$, write $|f|^ p=|f|^{p/(2p-1)}\cdot |f|^{p(2p-2)/(2p-1)}$ and apply Hölder's inequality with the conjugate exponents $(2p-1)/p$ and $(2p-1)/(p-1)$; since $\frac{p(2p-2)}{2p-1}\cdot \frac{2p-1}{p-1}=2p$, this gives \[  \int _ K|f|^ p\, \mathrm dV\leq \Bigl (\int _ K|f|\, \mathrm dV\Bigr )^{p/(2p-1)}\Bigl (\int _ K|f|^{2p}\, \mathrm dV\Bigr )^{(p-1)/(2p-1)},  \] that is, $\| f\| _{L^ p(K)}\leq \| f\| _{L^1(K)}^{1/(2p-1)}\| f\| _{L^{2p}(K)}^{(2p-2)/(2p-1)}$. With $f=u_ j-u$, whose $L^{2p}(K)$ norms are bounded independently of $j$, we obtain \[  \| u_ j-u\| _{L^ p(K)} \leq \| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(K)}^{1/(2p-1)} \| u_ j-u\| _{L^{2p}(K)}^{(2p-2)/(2p-1)}\longrightarrow 0.  \] $\square$

title: Lemma 8.3.8
text:
Lemma 8.3.8 . There are constants $ eta ,C>0$ such that every subharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on $D$ with $v(0)\geq -1$ satisfies \[  \int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C.  \] Proof. Since $v(0)\geq -1>-\infty $, lemma 8.3.5 gives a finite positive measure $
u $ with support in $D(0,9/10)$ and a harmonic function $h$ on $D(0,4/5)$ such that \[  v=P+h,\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )  \] at every point of $D(0,4/5)$. Since $|v(0)|\leq 1$, the bounds ( 8.4 ) give $M=
u (D)\leq C_0$ and $\sup _{D(0,1/2)}|h|\leq C_0$, where $C_0\geq 1$ is the universal constant of that lemma. Fix $ eta \in (0,1]$ with $ eta C_0\leq 2\pi $. We show that $\int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta P}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8\pi $. If $M=0$, then $P=0$, and this integral is $\pi /4$. Assume $M>0$ and put $b= eta M/(2\pi )\in (0,1]$. Fix $z\in D(0,1/2)$. For $N\geq 1$ the Borel function $f_ N(\zeta )=-b\max \{ \log |z-\zeta |,-N\} $ is bounded on $D(0,9/10)$, so Jensen's inequality (lemma 1.1.4 ), applied to the convex function $\exp $ on $\mathbb R$ and the probability measure $
u /M$, gives \[  \exp \Bigl (\int f_ N\,  rac{\mathrm d
u }M\Bigr )\leq \int \mathrm e^{f_ N}\,  rac{\mathrm d
u }M\leq  rac1M\int |z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta ).  \] As $N	o \infty $, the functions $f_ N$ increase to $-b\log |z-\zeta |$, which may take the value $+\infty $, and they are bounded below by the bounded function $f_1$. By monotone convergence, $\int f_ N\, \mathrm d
u /M$ increases to $\int -b\log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )/M=- eta P(z)$, and therefore \[  \mathrm e^{- eta P(z)}\leq  rac1M\int |z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )  \] for every $z\in D(0,1/2)$, with the convention $\mathrm e^{\infty }=\infty $. For every $\zeta \in D(0,9/10)$ the translated disc $D(0,1/2)-\zeta $ lies in $D(0,2)$, and $r^{-b}\leq 1+r^{-1}$ for $r>0$ because $0<b\leq 1$; hence \[  \int _{D(0,1/2)}|z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq \int _{D(0,2)}(1+|z|^{-1})\, \mathrm dV(z)=8\pi .  \] Integrating the bound for $\mathrm e^{- eta P(z)}$ over $z\in D(0,1/2)$ with Tonelli's theorem, we obtain $\int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta P}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8\pi $. Finally, since $\mathrm e^{- eta v}=\mathrm e^{- eta P}\mathrm e^{- eta h}\leq \mathrm e^{ eta C_0}\mathrm e^{- eta P}$ on $D(0,1/2)$, the lemma follows with $C=8\pi \mathrm e^{C_0}$. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.3.9
text: Proposition 8.3.9 . Let $n\geq 1$, and let $B$ be the unit ball of $\mathbb C^ n$. There are constants $\alpha _ n,C_ n>0$ such that every plurisubharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on $B$ with $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq 1$ satisfies 8.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:negative-psh-exponential-lone-bound} \int _{\frac14B}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C_ n. \end{equation} More generally, if $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq M$ for some $M>0$, the same bound holds with the exponent $\alpha _ n/M$ in place of $\alpha _ n$. Proof. Put $A_ n=\max \{ 1,2/|\frac18B|\} $. The mean of $|v|$ over $\frac18B$ is at most $1/|\frac18B|<A_ n$. Hence the set of points of $\frac18B$ with $|v|\leq A_ n$ has positive measure, since otherwise $|v|>A_ n$ almost everywhere on $\frac18B$ and the mean would be at least $A_ n$; so there is a point $a\in \frac18B$ with $|v(a)|\leq A_ n$. For each unit vector $e\in \mathbb C^ n$, the disc $\{ a+\tfrac 34\zeta e:|\zeta |<1\} $ lies in $B$, so the function \[  \zeta \longmapsto A_ n^{-1}v(a+\tfrac 34\zeta e)  \] is subharmonic and nonpositive on $D$, with value at least $-1$ at $0$. Set $\alpha _ n=\beta /A_ n$, with $\beta $ as in lemma 8.3.8 . That lemma and the change of variables $\zeta \mapsto \frac34\zeta $ give a bound, independent of $e$ and $v$, for \[  \int _{|\zeta |<3/8}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v(a+\zeta e)}\, \mathrm dV(\zeta ).  \] It remains to pass from these integrals over discs in complex lines to an integral over a ball. Let $\tau $ and $s_{2n-1}$ be as in ( 8.1 ). By that identity, applied with center $a$, and since $|\zeta |^{2n-2}\leq r^{2n-2}$ for $|\zeta |<r$, every Borel function $F\geq 0$, possibly taking the value $+\infty $, satisfies \[  \int _{|z-a|<r}F(z)\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq \frac{s_{2n-1}r^{2n-2}}{2\pi } \int _{S^{2n-1}}\int _{|\zeta |<r}F(a+\zeta e)\, \mathrm dV(\zeta )\, \mathrm d\tau (e)  \] for every $r>0$. We apply this with $F=\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}$ and $r=3/8$. Since $\frac14B\subset B(a,3/8)$, the uniform bound for the line integrals proves ( 8.7 ). Finally, if $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq M$ with $M>0$, then $v/M$ is a nonpositive plurisubharmonic function with $\| v/M\| _{L^1(B)}\leq 1$, and ( 8.7 ) for $v/M$ is the last assertion. $\square$
8.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:negative-psh-exponential-lone-bound} \int _{\frac14B}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C_ n. \end{equation}

title: 8.4 Extension across closed exceptional sets
text:
8.4 Extension across closed exceptional sets Let $S$ be a relatively closed subset of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$. We give two conditions under which plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega \setminus S$ extend across $S$. In the first, $S$ is locally contained in the zero set of a holomorphic function, and the function is assumed to be locally bounded above near $S$; a logarithmic barrier built from the holomorphic function then gives the extension. In the second, $S$ is small in the sense of Hausdorff measure, and the local upper bound is not assumed but follows from the smallness of $S$ by an argument with complex lines. Theorem 8.4.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$, and let $S\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed. Assume that every point of $S$ has a connected neighborhood $W\subset \Omega $ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W$ such that $S\cap W\subset \{ f=0\} $. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$ that is locally bounded above near $S$, that is, every point of $S$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Then $u$ has a unique plurisubharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, and its value at $x\in S$ is \[  \widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{\Omega \setminus S
i y	o x}u(y).  \] Proof. Define $\widetilde u$ by $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$ and by the displayed formula on $S$. Since plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to show that every point $x_0\in S$ has a neighborhood on which $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic; uniqueness is proved at the end. By hypothesis there are a connected neighborhood $W_0$ of $x_0$ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W_0$ such that $S\cap W_0\subset \{ f=0\} $, and a neighborhood $W_1$ of $x_0$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W_1\setminus S$. Choose a ball $W$ about $x_0$ with $\overline W\subset W_0\cap W_1$. By the identity theorem, $f$ does not vanish identically on $W$, and $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Multiplying $f$ by a nonzero constant, we may assume that $|f|\leq 1$, that is, $\log |f|^2\le 0$, on $W$. For $\varepsilon >0$ define $u_\varepsilon $ on $W$ by \[  u_\varepsilon =u+\varepsilon \log |f|^2\quad 	ext{on }W\setminus S,\qquad u_\varepsilon =-\infty \quad 	ext{on }S\cap W.  \] Step 1: $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$. At a point $x\in S\cap W$ we have $f(x)=0$, so $\log |f(y)|^2	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, while $u$ is bounded above near $x$; hence $u_\varepsilon (y)	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, and $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous at $x$. On $W\setminus S$, $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous as a sum of upper semicontinuous functions. Now let $\Lambda $ be a connected component of $L\cap W$ for an affine complex line $L$. If $f$ vanishes identically on $\Lambda $, then $u_\varepsilon \equiv -\infty $ on $\Lambda $. Otherwise the zeros of $f$ on the connected set $\Lambda $ are isolated, by the identity theorem in one variable. Since $S$ is relatively closed, $A=S\cap \Lambda $ is therefore a closed discrete subset of $\Lambda $, hence countable, because each of the countably many compact sets exhausting $\Lambda $ contains only finitely many of its points. It is polar, because points are polar in the plane and countable unions of polar sets are polar by proposition 4.2.3 . Each connected component of $\Lambda \setminus A$ is a connected subset of $L\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ and therefore lies in a connected component of this line section, on which the restriction of $u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Hence the restriction of $u$ to $\Lambda \setminus A$ is subharmonic, the constant $-\infty $ being subharmonic. The function $\log |f|^2$ is subharmonic on $\Lambda $ by example 3.2.4 . Thus $u_\varepsilon $ is subharmonic on $\Lambda \setminus A$, and it is bounded above there by $\sup _{W\setminus S}u$, because $\log |f|^2\leq 0$. By theorem 3.5.2 , it has a subharmonic extension to $\Lambda $ whose value at $x\in A$ is $\varlimsup _{\Lambda \setminus A
i y	o x}u_\varepsilon (y)=-\infty $, which is the value of $u_\varepsilon $ at $x$. Hence the restriction of $u_\varepsilon $ to $\Lambda $ is subharmonic. Finally, $u_\varepsilon $ is not identically $-\infty $, because $u$ is finite almost everywhere on $W\setminus S$ and $\{ f=0\} $ is Lebesgue null by lemma 7.4.1 . Thus $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$. Step 2: the extension. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ the functions $u_\varepsilon $ increase, because $\log |f|^2\leq 0$, and they are bounded above on $W$ by $\sup _{W\setminus S}u$. Let $F=\sup _{\varepsilon >0}u_\varepsilon $. By theorem 8.3.2 , $F^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$ and $F^*=F$ almost everywhere. Since $F=u$ outside the null set $\{ f=0\} $, we get $F^*=u$ almost everywhere on $W\setminus S$; both functions are locally integrable and subharmonic there, so $F^*=u$ everywhere on $W\setminus S$ by theorem 3.2.2 . It remains to show that $F^*=\widetilde u$ on $S\cap W$, which is Lebesgue null as a subset of $\{ f=0\} $. Let $x\in S\cap W$. Since $F^*=u$ on $W\setminus S$, the upper semicontinuity of $F^*$ gives $\widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{W\setminus S
i y	o x}u(y)\leq F^*(x)$. Conversely, for small $r>0$ the ball submean inequality for $F^*$ gives $F^*(x)\leq |B(x,r)|^{-1}\int _{B(x,r)\setminus S}F^*\, \mathrm dV\leq \sup _{B(x,r)\setminus S}u$, because removing the null set $S$ does not change the integral, and letting $r	o 0$ gives $F^*(x)\leq \widetilde u(x)$. Hence $\widetilde u=F^*$ on $W$, and $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic on $W$. Uniqueness. The set $S$ is Lebesgue null, since it is covered by countably many neighborhoods $W$ as in the hypothesis and $S\cap W\subset \{ f=0\} $ is null. Two plurisubharmonic extensions of $u$ therefore agree almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by theorem 8.2.1 . $\square$ For the second criterion we measure the size of $S$ by Hausdorff measure. Let $q>0$. A subset $E$ of a metric space is $\mathcal H^ q$-null if for all $\delta ,\eta >0$ it can be covered by countably many balls of radii $r_ l<\delta $ with $\sum _ l r_ l^ q<\eta $. This means that the $q$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of $E$, which is defined by coverings with sets of small diameter, vanishes, whatever its normalization: a set of diameter $\ell $ lies in the ball of radius $\ell '$ about any of its points for every $\ell '>\ell $, and a ball of radius $r$ has diameter at most $2r$. Every subset of an $\mathcal H^ q$-null set is $\mathcal H^ q$-null, and so is every countable union of $\mathcal H^ q$-null sets $E_1,E_2,\ldots $: cover $E_ l$ by balls of radii less than $\delta $ with sum of the $q$-th powers of the radii less than $2^{-l}\eta $. We use two further elementary properties. First, if $E$ is $\mathcal H^ q$-null and $\Phi $ is a Lipschitz map with constant $L>0$ from $E$ to a metric space, then $\Phi (E)$ is $\mathcal H^ q$-null. To see this, discard the covering balls that do not meet $E$, and replace each remaining ball $B(c,r)$ by $B(c',2r)$ with $c'\in E\cap B(c,r)$; then $\Phi (E\cap B(c',2r))\subset B(\Phi (c'),2Lr)$, so $\Phi (E)$ is covered by balls of radii $2Lr_ l<2L\delta $ with $\sum _ l(2Lr_ l)^ q<(2L)^ q\eta $. Second, if $q\leq b$, every $\mathcal H^ q$-null subset of $\mathbb R^ b$ is Lebesgue null, because the total volume of the covering balls is at most a constant times $\sum _ lr_ l^ b\leq \delta ^{b-q}\sum _ l r_ l^ q$. For $n\geq 2$, let $\sigma $ be the unitarily invariant probability measure on $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ and $d$ the metric on $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ introduced in section 6.3 . For $v\in \mathbb {C}^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ we write $[v]\in \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ for the complex line spanned by $v$; thus the restriction of $v\mapsto [v]$ to the unit sphere is the Hopf map of section 6.3 . For $y
eq x$ in $\mathbb {C}^ n$, the point $[y-x]$ is the direction of $y$ from $x$. Lemma 8.4.2 . Let $n\ge 2$ and let $K\subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a compact $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null set. Then: $K$ is real polar; for every $x\in \mathbb {C}^ n$, the set of directions from $x$ of the points of $K\setminus \{ x\} $ has $\sigma $-measure zero; the orthogonal projection of $K$ onto any complex hyperplane is Lebesgue null. Proof. (1) Suppose that $K$ is not polar. By theorem 4.3.3 , $K$ carries a nonzero positive measure of finite energy; dividing it by its mass, we obtain a probability measure $\mu $ on $K$ of finite energy $I(\mu )$ for the Newtonian kernel $k(x,y)=|x-y|^{2-2n}/((2n-2)s_{2n-1})$ of section 4.1 in $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Its potential $U^\mu $ is lower semicontinuous, and it is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere because $\int U^\mu \, \mathrm d\mu =I(\mu )<\infty $. The sets $E_ M=K\cap \{ U^\mu \le M\} $, $M\in \mathbb N$, are compact, because $U^\mu $ is lower semicontinuous, and they increase to a set of full $\mu $-measure; hence $\mu (E_ M)>0$ for $M$ large enough. Let $
u $ be the restriction of $\mu $ to $E_ M$. For $a\in E_ M$ and $r>0$, \[   rac{r^{2-2n}\, 
u (B(a,r))}{(2n-2)s_{2n-1}}\leq \int _{B(a,r)}k(a,y)\, \mathrm d
u (y)\leq U^\mu (a)\leq M,  \] so $
u (B(a,r))\le C_ nMr^{2n-2}$ with $C_ n=(2n-2)s_{2n-1}$. Now cover $E_ M$ by balls $B(c_ l,r_ l)$ with $r_ l<1$ and $\sum _ lr_ l^{2n-3}<\eta $, and discard those not meeting $E_ M$. Each remaining ball lies in $B(a_ l,2r_ l)$ for some $a_ l\in E_ M$, so \[  
u (E_ M)\leq \sum _ l
u (B(a_ l,2r_ l))\leq 2^{2n-2}C_ nM\sum _ lr_ l^{2n-2}\leq 2^{2n-2}C_ nM\eta ,  \] where we used $r_ l<1$. Since $\eta >0$ is arbitrary, $
u (E_ M)=0$, a contradiction. Hence $K$ is polar. (2) Fix $x$. For $m\geq 1$ the set $K_ m=K\cap \{ |y-x|\geq 1/m\} $ is compact and $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, and $K\setminus \{ x\} = igcup _ mK_ m$. The direction map $\Phi (y)=[y-x]$ is Lipschitz on $K_ m$. Indeed, $\Phi (y)=[(y-x)/|y-x|]$. The normalization $y\mapsto (y-x)/|y-x|$ has Lipschitz constant at most $2m$ on $\{ |y-x|\geq 1/m\} $: for nonzero vectors $a,b$, \[  \Bigl | rac a{|a|}- rac b{|b|}\Bigr |\leq  rac{|a-b|}{|a|}+|b|\, \Bigl | rac1{|a|}- rac1{|b|}\Bigr |= rac{|a-b|+ igl ||b|-|a| igr |}{|a|}\leq  rac{2|a-b|}{|a|},  \] and we apply this with $a=y-x$, $b=y'-x$ and $|a|\geq 1/m$. The Hopf map is Lipschitz with constant $\pi /2$ for the metric $d$. Indeed, let $e,e'$ be unit vectors and $\delta =\arccos \operatorname{Re}\langle e,e'angle \in [0,\pi ]$ their spherical distance. Since $d$ is the minimum of the spherical distance over the unit representatives (section 6.3 ), we have $d([e],[e'])\leq \delta $. Moreover $|e-e'|^2=2-2\cos \delta =4\sin ^2(\delta /2)$, and $\sin s\geq 2s/\pi $ for $0\leq s\leq \pi /2$, so $|e-e'|\geq 2\delta /\pi $. Hence \[  d([e],[e'])\leq \delta \leq 	frac \pi 2|e-e'|.  \] Since Lipschitz images of $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null sets are $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, the compact set $\Phi (K_ m)$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null in $(\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C),d)$. Cover it by balls of radii $r_ l<1$ with $\sum _ lr_ l^{2n-3}<\eta $. By lemma 6.3.2 , and since $r_ l<1$, we have $\sigma (\Phi (K_ m))\leq \sum _ lr_ l^{2n-2}<\eta $, so $\sigma (\Phi (K_ m))=0$. Hence the set of directions $\Phi (K\setminus \{ x\} )= igcup _ m\Phi (K_ m)$ is a Borel set of $\sigma $-measure zero. (3) An orthogonal projection onto a complex hyperplane $H\cong \mathbb R^{2n-2}$ is $1$-Lipschitz. Hence the projection of $K$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null in $H$, and therefore Lebesgue null because $2n-3<2n-2$. $\square$ Theorem 8.4.3 . Let $n\ge 2$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, and let $S\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed and locally $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, that is, every point of $S$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $S\cap W$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null. Then every plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$ extends uniquely to a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $, given on $S$ by the same upper-limit formula as in theorem 8.4.1 . Proof. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$. For every closed ball $\overline B\subset \Omega $, the compact set $S\cap \overline B$ is covered by finitely many neighborhoods $W$ as in the hypothesis, and is therefore $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null. Step 1: $u$ is locally bounded above near $S$. Fix $p\in S$ and $r>0$ with $\overline B=\overline{B(p,r)}\subset \Omega $, and write $B=B(p,r)$. By lemma 8.4.2 (2) applied with $x=p$, almost every complex line through $p$ meets $S\cap \overline B$ only at $p$; fix such a line $L=\{ p+te:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $, with $|e|=1$. The circle $\Gamma =L\cap \partial B$ is a compact subset of $\Omega \setminus S$, so the upper semicontinuous function $u$ is bounded above on $\Gamma $ by a finite constant $C$, and the open set $O=\{ y\in \Omega \setminus S:u(y)<C+1\} $ contains $\Gamma $. Suppose that $u$ is not bounded above near $p$. Then there are points $x_ j\in B\setminus S$ with $x_ j	o p$ and $u(x_ j)	o +\infty $. For each $j$, lemma 8.4.2 (2) applied with $x=x_ j$ shows that the directions of the lines through $x_ j$ meeting $S\cap \overline B$ form a $\sigma $-null set. Every nonempty open ball in $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ has positive $\sigma $-measure by lemma 6.3.2 , so the complement of this null set is dense. We can therefore choose directions $\xi _ j$ outside this null set with $d(\xi _ j,[e])<1/j$. Since $d$ is the minimum of the spherical distance over the unit representatives, $\xi _ j$ has a unit representative $e_ j$ whose spherical distance to $e$ is less than $1/j$, and then $|e_ j-e|<1/j$, because a chord is shorter than the arc. Thus $e_ j	o e$, and the lines $L_ j=\{ x_ j+te_ j:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $ do not meet $S\cap \overline B$. We claim that $L_ j\cap \partial B\subset O$ for all large $j$. Let $c_ j$ be the point of $L_ j$ closest to $p$, that is, the orthogonal projection of $p$ to $L_ j$; then $|c_ j-p|\leq |x_ j-p|	o 0$. Since $L_ j$ is a complex line, $c_ j=x_ j+\langle p-x_ j,e_ jangle e_ j$ and $\langle c_ j-p,e_ jangle =0$ for the Hermitian inner product, so $\operatorname{Re}\langle c_ j-p,se_ jangle =0$ and $|c_ j+se_ j-p|^2=|c_ j-p|^2+|s|^2$ for $s\in \mathbb {C}$. Hence $L_ j\cap \partial B$ is the circle $\{ c_ j+ho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e_ j\} $ with $ho _ j=(r^2-|c_ j-p|^2)^{1/2}	o r$. Since $|c_ j+ho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e_ j-p-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e|\leq |c_ j-p|+|ho _ j-r|+r|e_ j-e|$, these circles converge uniformly in $	heta $ to $\Gamma =\{ p+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e\} $. The distance from the compact set $\Gamma $ to the closed complement of the open set $O$ is positive, so the circles lie in $O$ for large $j$. For such $j$, the closed disc $\Delta _ j=L_ j\cap \overline B$ lies in $\Omega \setminus S$, and the restriction of $u$ to the connected component of $L_ j\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ containing $\Delta _ j$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Its values on the boundary circle of $\Delta _ j$ are less than $C+1$, so the maximum principle, that is, theorem 3.1.3 with the constant harmonic function $C+1$, gives $u\leq C+1$ on $\Delta _ j$. Since $x_ j\in B\cap L_ j\subset \Delta _ j$, this gives $u(x_ j)\leq C+1$, contradicting $u(x_ j)	o +\infty $. Hence $u$ is bounded above near every point of $S$. Step 2: the subharmonic extension. By lemma 8.4.2 (1), every compact set $S\cap \overline B$ as above is real polar. Countably many such sets cover $S$, so $S$ is real polar by proposition 4.2.3 . By Step 1 and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $u$ is bounded above on $K\setminus S$ for every compact $K\subset \Omega $. Moreover $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega \setminus S$ by theorem 8.2.1 . By theorem 3.5.2 , $u$ has a subharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, given on $S$ by the upper-limit formula. Since $S$ is Lebesgue null and $u$ is finite almost everywhere on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $\widetilde u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on the domain $\Omega $, so it is locally integrable. Step 3: $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic. We verify the hypothesis of lemma 8.1.2 for the locally integrable function $\widetilde u$. Fix a unit vector $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ and a nonnegative $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, and write $z=v+ta$ with $v\in (\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ and $t\in \mathbb {C}$, as in that lemma. The compact set $S\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, since it is covered by finitely many of the sets $S\cap \overline B$ of the first paragraph, so by lemma 8.4.2 (3) its orthogonal projection onto $(\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ is Lebesgue null. For $v$ outside this projection, the line $\{ v+ta:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $ meets $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ only in $\Omega \setminus S$. Thus the open set $G_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \Omega \setminus S\} $ contains $K_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi \} $, and its connected components are the connected components of an affine complex-line section of $\Omega \setminus S$, on each of which the restriction of $\widetilde u=u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. As $a$ and $\chi $ are arbitrary, lemma 8.1.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u\geq 0$. Since $\widetilde u$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function, it is the canonical representative of its class, and it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . Uniqueness follows from the same theorem, since two plurisubharmonic extensions agree outside the Lebesgue null set $S$. $\square$

title: Theorem 8.4.1
text:
Theorem 8.4.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$, and let $S\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed. Assume that every point of $S$ has a connected neighborhood $W\subset \Omega $ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W$ such that $S\cap W\subset \{ f=0\} $. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$ that is locally bounded above near $S$, that is, every point of $S$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Then $u$ has a unique plurisubharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, and its value at $x\in S$ is \[  \widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{\Omega \setminus S
i y	o x}u(y).  \] Proof. Define $\widetilde u$ by $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$ and by the displayed formula on $S$. Since plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to show that every point $x_0\in S$ has a neighborhood on which $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic; uniqueness is proved at the end. By hypothesis there are a connected neighborhood $W_0$ of $x_0$ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W_0$ such that $S\cap W_0\subset \{ f=0\} $, and a neighborhood $W_1$ of $x_0$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W_1\setminus S$. Choose a ball $W$ about $x_0$ with $\overline W\subset W_0\cap W_1$. By the identity theorem, $f$ does not vanish identically on $W$, and $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Multiplying $f$ by a nonzero constant, we may assume that $|f|\leq 1$, that is, $\log |f|^2\le 0$, on $W$. For $\varepsilon >0$ define $u_\varepsilon $ on $W$ by \[  u_\varepsilon =u+\varepsilon \log |f|^2\quad 	ext{on }W\setminus S,\qquad u_\varepsilon =-\infty \quad 	ext{on }S\cap W.  \] Step 1: $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$. At a point $x\in S\cap W$ we have $f(x)=0$, so $\log |f(y)|^2	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, while $u$ is bounded above near $x$; hence $u_\varepsilon (y)	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, and $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous at $x$. On $W\setminus S$, $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous as a sum of upper semicontinuous functions. Now let $\Lambda $ be a connected component of $L\cap W$ for an affine complex line $L$. If $f$ vanishes identically on $\Lambda $, then $u_\varepsilon \equiv -\infty $ on $\Lambda $. Otherwise the zeros of $f$ on the connected set $\Lambda $ are isolated, by the identity theorem in one variable. Since $S$ is relatively closed, $A=S\cap \Lambda $ is therefore a closed discrete subset of $\Lambda $, hence countable, because each of the countably many compact sets exhausting $\Lambda $ contains only finitely many of its points. It is polar, because points are polar in the plane and countable unions of polar sets are polar by proposition 4.2.3 . Each connected component of $\Lambda \setminus A$ is a connected subset of $L\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ and therefore lies in a connected component of this line section, on which the restriction of $u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $.
