9.6 The homogeneous Dirichlet problem and balayage A plurisubharmonic function is maximal if it cannot be increased on a compact set without losing plurisubharmonicity (definition 9.6.5 ). We show in theorem 9.6.6 that, for locally bounded functions, maximality is equivalent to $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$. The proof replaces $u$ on a ball by a solution $H$ of the homogeneous equation $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0$ with the same boundary values (corollary 9.6.4 ); in chapter 10 the same replacement shows that relative extremal functions have vanishing Monge–Ampère measure away from the sets on which they are constrained. We construct $H$ as an upper envelope. To show that it solves the equation, we bound its second differences by composing with automorphisms of the ball (lemma 9.6.1 ), which makes it twice differentiable almost everywhere (lemma 9.6.2 ). Lemma 9.6.1 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be the unit ball. For $a\in B$ and $h\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $|h|$ small, depending on $a$, there are biholomorphic automorphisms $S_{a,h}$ of $B$ such that $S_{a,0}$ is the identity and $S_{a,h}(a)=a+h$. Each $S_{a,h}$ extends to a holomorphic map on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ which maps $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$. For every compact set $K\subset B$ there is $h_0>0$ such that the map $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is defined and smooth on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n	imes \mathbb C^ n	imes \mathbb C^ n$ containing $K	imes \overline{B(0,h_0)}	imes \overline B$, and holomorphic in $z$ there. In particular, there is a constant $C$ such that, for $a\in K$, $|h|\le h_0$ and $z\in \overline B$, the first and second derivatives of $S_{a,h}(z)$ with respect to the real variable $h\in \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ are bounded by $C$. Proof. Use the Hermitian product $\langle z,aangle =\sum z_ j ar a_ j$, put $s_ a=\sqrt{1-|a|^2}$, and define \[  T_ a(z)= rac{s_ a z+\langle z,aangle a/(1+s_ a)-a}{1-\langle z,aangle }.  \] This expression depends smoothly on $(a,z)$ in the open set $\{ (a,z):|a|<1,\  |a||z|<1\} $, where the denominator does not vanish, and it is holomorphic in $z$; moreover $T_0$ is the identity. If $U$ is a unitary matrix, then $\langle Uz,Uaangle =\langle z,aangle $ and $s_{Ua}=s_ a$, so $T_{Ua}(Uz)=UT_ a(z)$. Given $a
e 0$, choose $U$ with $Ua=(t,0,\ldots ,0)$, $t=|a|$; it therefore suffices to verify the following identities for $a=(t,0,\ldots ,0)$ with $0\le t<1$, and also for $-a=(-t,0,\ldots ,0)$. Put $s=s_ a=\sqrt{1-t^2}$. Then $\langle z,aangle =tz_1$, and the first component of the numerator of $T_ a(z)$ is $sz_1+t^2z_1/(1+s)-t=z_1-t$, because $s(1+s)+t^2=s+s^2+t^2=1+s$. Hence \[   egin{aligned}  T_ a(z)& =\left( rac{z_1-t}{1-tz_1},  rac{s\, z_2}{1-tz_1},\ldots ,  rac{s\, z_ n}{1-tz_1}ight),\  T_{-a}(w)& =\left( rac{w_1+t}{1+tw_1},  rac{s\, w_2}{1+tw_1},\ldots ,  rac{s\, w_ n}{1+tw_1}ight), \end{aligned}  \] the second formula by the same computation with $t$ replaced by $-t$. In particular $T_ a(a)=0$ and $T_{-a}(0)=a$. If $w=T_ a(z)$, then \[  w_1+t= rac{(1-t^2)z_1}{1-tz_1},\qquad 1+tw_1= rac{1-t^2}{1-tz_1},  \] so the first component of $T_{-a}(w)$ is $z_1$ and the others are $s\cdot sz_ k/(1-tz_1)\cdot (1-tz_1)/(1-t^2)=z_ k$; thus $T_{-a}\circ T_ a=\mathrm{id}$, and by symmetry $T_ a\circ T_{-a}=\mathrm{id}$. Finally, \[  |1-tz_1|^2-|z_1-t|^2-(1-t^2)\sum _{k\ge 2}|z_ k|^2=(1-t^2)(1-|z_1|^2)-(1-t^2)\sum _{k\ge 2}|z_ k|^2,  \] because the terms $\mp 2t\operatorname{Re}z_1$ cancel; dividing by $|1-tz_1|^2$ gives \[  1-|T_ a(z)|^2= rac{(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)}{|1-\langle z,aangle |^2}.  \] Hence $T_ a$ maps $B$ into $B$ and the sphere $\partial B$ into itself, and the same holds for $T_{-a}$; since $T_{-a}$ is inverse to $T_ a$, the map $T_ a$ is a biholomorphic automorphism of $B$ which maps $\partial B$ onto itself. Set $S_{a,h}=T_{-(a+h)}\circ T_ a$ for $|a+h|<1$. It maps $a$ to $T_{-(a+h)}(0)=a+h$ and is the identity for $h=0$. The map $T_ a$ is holomorphic on the neighborhood $\{ z:|a||z|<1\} $ of $\overline B$, and, as we have just seen, it maps $\overline B$ into $\overline B$ and $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$; the same holds for $T_{-(a+h)}$. Hence $S_{a,h}$ is holomorphic on the neighborhood $\{ z:|a||z|<1,\  |a+h||T_ a(z)|<1\} $ of $\overline B$, and it maps $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$. Let $K\subset B$ be compact (we may assume $K
eq \varnothing $), put $t_ K=\max _ K|a|<1$, and choose $h_0>0$ with $t_ K+3h_0<1$. On the open set $O$ of all $(a,h,z)$ with $|a|<t_ K+h_0$, $|h|<2h_0$, $|a||z|<1$ and $(t_ K+3h_0)|T_ a(z)|<1$, we have $|a+h|<1$ and $|a+h||T_ a(z)|<1$, so $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is defined and smooth on $O$, and holomorphic in $z$. Since $|T_ a(z)|\le 1$ for $|z|\le 1$, the set $O$ contains the compact set $K	imes \overline{B(0,h_0)}	imes \overline B$, on which the continuous first and second derivatives of $S_{a,h}(z)$ with respect to $h$ are therefore bounded by a constant $C$. $\square$ A plurisubharmonic function whose second differences are bounded above is locally of class $C^{1,1}$, and its Monge–Ampère measure is then given by the determinant of its complex Hessian. Lemma 9.6.2 . Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$, and let $H$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $U$. Suppose that for every compact set $K\subset U$ there are constants $C_ K\ge 0$ and $h_ K>0$ such that, for all $a\in K$ and all $h\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $|h|\le h_ K$, the points $a\pm h$ lie in $U$ and 9.29  egin{equation} \label{eq:second-difference-bound} H(a+h)+H(a-h)-2H(a)\le 2C_ K|h|^2\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_ K). \end{equation} Then $H$ is continuous, $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and the distributional real Hessian of $H$ is a matrix $A=(A_{ab})$ of measurable functions which are bounded on compact subsets of $U$. Almost every $x\in U$ satisfies \[  H(x+h)=H(x)+
abla H(x)\cdot h+	frac 12h^ tA(x)h+o(|h|^2)\qquad (h	o 0).  \] Moreover, let $H_{j ar k}$ be the coefficients of the distributional complex Hessian of $H$, which are fixed complex linear combinations of the $A_{ab}$. Then the matrix $(H_{j ar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n= rac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det (H_{j ar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] Proof. Let $H_\varepsilon =H*ho _\varepsilon $. Fix $a_0\in U$ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(a_0,4r)}\subset U$, put $K=\overline{B(a_0,3r)}$, and let $M_0=\sup _ K|H|$, which is finite because $H$ is locally bounded. For $0<\varepsilon <r$, the regularization $H_\varepsilon $ is smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a_0,2r)}$ (proposition 8.2.2 ), and $|H_\varepsilon |\le M_0$ on $\overline{B(a_0,2r)}$, since its values there are averages of values of $H$ on $K$. For $x\in \overline{B(a_0,2r)}$ and $|h|\le h_ K$, \[   egin{aligned} & H_\varepsilon (x+h)+H_\varepsilon (x-h)-2H_\varepsilon (x)\ & \qquad =\int  igl (H(x-y+h)+H(x-y-h)-2H(x-y) igr )ho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy\le 2C_ K|h|^2, \end{aligned}  \] by ( 9.29 ), because $x-y\in K$ for $|y|\le \varepsilon $. Replacing $h$ by $th$ with $0<t\le 1$, dividing by $t^2$ and letting $t	o 0$, we get $D^2H_\varepsilon (x)[h,h]\le 2C_ K|h|^2$ for $|h|\le h_ K$, and hence, by homogeneity, for all $h\in \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$. On the other hand, the complex Hessian of the smooth plurisubharmonic function $H_\varepsilon $ is positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 ), and $D^2H_\varepsilon [h,h]+D^2H_\varepsilon [\mathrm ih,\mathrm ih]=4\sum _{j,k}(H_\varepsilon )_{j ar k}h_ j ar h_ k\ge 0$; hence $D^2H_\varepsilon (x)[h,h]\ge -2C_ K|h|^2$ as well. Thus the second derivatives of the $H_\varepsilon $ are bounded on $\overline{B(a_0,2r)}$ by a constant $\Lambda _0$ independent of $\varepsilon $. For $x\in \overline{B(a_0,r)}$ and a unit vector $e$, Taylor's formula \[  H_\varepsilon (x+re)=H_\varepsilon (x)+r\, \partial _ eH_\varepsilon (x)+\int _0^ r(r-t)D^2H_\varepsilon (x+te)[e,e]\, \mathrm dt  \] gives $|\partial _ eH_\varepsilon (x)|\le 2M_0/r+\Lambda _0r=\Lambda $. By the mean value theorem on the convex set $B(a_0,r)$, $|H_\varepsilon (x)-H_\varepsilon (y)|\le \Lambda |x-y|$ for $x,y\in B(a_0,r)$. Since $H_\varepsilon 	o H$ pointwise as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by ( 3.3 ), the same inequality holds for $H$. Hence $H$ is continuous on $B(a_0,r)$, and, as $a_0$ was arbitrary, on $U$. Moreover, $H_\varepsilon 	o H$ in $L^1$ on compact subsets of $U$, by dominated convergence, and hence in the sense of distributions; and every ball $B_0\Subset U$ is covered by finitely many balls $B(a_0,2r)$ as above, so the second derivatives of the $H_\varepsilon $ are bounded on $B_0$ uniformly in small $\varepsilon $. By the converse part of proposition 1.7.5 , the distributional real Hessian of $H$ has locally bounded measurable coefficients $A_{ab}$; hence $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and almost every $x\in U$ satisfies the second-order expansion of the statement. The functions $H_{j ar k}$ are bounded measurable functions on compact subsets of $U$. By proposition 1.4.3 , the complex Hessian of $H_\varepsilon $ has the coefficients $(H_{j ar k})_\varepsilon $; these are bounded on compact sets uniformly in small $\varepsilon $, and they converge to $H_{j ar k}$ at every Lebesgue point of $H_{j ar k}$, hence almost everywhere (theorem 1.7.3 ). In particular, the matrix $(H_{j ar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, as an almost everywhere limit of the positive semidefinite complex Hessians of the smooth plurisubharmonic functions $H_\varepsilon $. Since $H$ is continuous, $H_\varepsilon 	o H$ locally uniformly (lemma 1.4.1 (1)), so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_\varepsilon )^ n	o (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n$ weakly on every ball $B_0\Subset U$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ along a sequence, by proposition 9.1.4 applied on $B_0$. By ( 9.2 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_\varepsilon )^ n=n!\pi ^{-n}\det ((H_{j ar k})_\varepsilon )\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, and the determinants converge almost everywhere and are bounded on compact sets uniformly in small $\varepsilon $. Hence, for every test function $\chi $ supported in such a ball $B_0$, dominated convergence gives \[  \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n= rac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\int \chi \det (H_{j ar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] By lemma 1.4.2 , every test function on $U$ is a finite sum of test functions supported in balls $B_0\Subset U$, so this identity holds for all test functions on $U$, and the two Radon measures coincide by proposition 1.4.3 (4). $\square$ Theorem 9.6.3 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a ball and $\varphi $ a real continuous function on $\partial B$. There is a unique $H\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B)$ such that \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0\quad 	ext{on }B,\qquad H|_{\partial B}=\varphi .  \] It is the upper envelope of the class of all $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ with $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}v(z)\le \varphi (x)$ for every $x\in \partial B$. If $\varphi $ is the restriction of a $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\partial B$, then $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$. Proof. After an affine change of coordinates $z\mapsto z_0+Rz$ with $R>0$, we may assume that $B$ is the unit ball; plurisubharmonicity, the boundary conditions, $C^2$ data and the vanishing of the Monge–Ampère measure are preserved by such a change, by proposition 8.2.3 and proposition 9.1.2 (5). We call the functions $v$ in the statement the subsolutions for $\varphi $ of the homogeneous equation. If $v$ is a subsolution for $\varphi $ and $\varphi \le \varphi '+c$ on $\partial B$ with a constant $c$, then $v-c$ is a subsolution for $\varphi '$. Every subsolution is subharmonic on $B$ (theorem 8.2.1 ), so the comparison principle (theorem 3.1.3 and the remark following it), applied with the harmonic function $P\varphi $, the Poisson integral of $\varphi $ given by theorem 2.3.1 , gives $v\le P\varphi $, and $P\varphi \le \max _{\partial B}\varphi $ because the Poisson kernel is positive with integral $1$. Hence, as soon as the class of subsolutions is nonempty, its upper envelope $H$ is defined, and $H\le P\varphi $. Step 1: the envelope for $C^2$ data. Suppose that $\varphi $ is the restriction of a $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\partial B$. Multiplying this function by a cutoff equal to $1$ near $\partial B$, we obtain a $C^2$ function $	ilde\varphi $ with compact support in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ and $	ilde\varphi =\varphi $ on $\partial B$. Its complex Hessian is continuous with compact support, so there is $\lambda >0$ with $\sum _{j,k}	ilde\varphi _{j ar k}\xi _ j ar\xi _ k\ge -\lambda |\xi |^2$ everywhere. The function $s=	ilde\varphi +\lambda (|z|^2-1)$ is then of class $C^2$ with positive semidefinite complex Hessian, so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 . As $s=\varphi $ on $\partial B$, it is a subsolution. Hence $s\le H\le P\varphi $. By theorem 8.3.2 , the upper semicontinuous regularization $H^*$ is plurisubharmonic, and $s\le H^*\le P\varphi $ since $P\varphi $ is continuous. As $s$ and $P\varphi $ are continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $\varphi $, we have $H^*(z)	o \varphi (x)$ as $z	o x\in \partial B$; so $H^*$ is a subsolution, $H^*\le H$, and $H=H^*$ is plurisubharmonic. Moreover $H(z)	o \varphi (x)$ as $z	o x\in \partial B$, and $H$ is bounded. Step 2: second differences. Let $K\subset B$ be compact, and let $S_{a,h}$, $h_0$ and $C$ be as in lemma 9.6.1 . For $x\in \partial B$ and $a\in K$, the function $g(h)=	ilde\varphi (S_{a,h}(x))$, $|h|\le h_0$, is of class $C^2$, and by the chain rule its second derivatives are bounded by a constant $2C_ K$ independent of $a$ and $x$, since the first and second derivatives of $	ilde\varphi $ are bounded and those of $S_{a,h}(x)$ with respect to $h$ are bounded by $C$. Since $g(0)=\varphi (x)$, Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives $g(h)+g(-h)-2g(0)=\int _0^1(1-t) igl (D^2g(th)[h,h]+D^2g(-th)[h,h] igr )\, \mathrm dt\le 2C_ K|h|^2$. As $S_{a,\pm h}$ maps $\partial B$ to $\partial B$, where $	ilde\varphi =\varphi $, this reads \[  	frac 12 igl (\varphi \circ S_{a,h}+\varphi \circ S_{a,-h} igr ) \le \varphi +C_ K|h|^2\quad 	ext{on }\partial B\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_0).  \] The function $w= rac12(H\circ S_{a,h}+H\circ S_{a,-h})-C_ K|h|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$, by proposition 8.2.3 , proposition 8.2.5 , since $S_{a,\pm h}$ are automorphisms of $B$ and $H$ is bounded. If $y\in \partial B$ and $z	o y$ in $B$, then $S_{a,\pm h}(z)	o S_{a,\pm h}(y)\in \partial B$, so $H(S_{a,\pm h}(z))	o \varphi (S_{a,\pm h}(y))$ by Step 1, and the preceding inequality gives $\varlimsup _{z	o y}w(z)\le \varphi (y)$. Thus $w$ is a subsolution, so $w\le H$. Evaluating at $z=a$, where $S_{a,\pm h}(a)=a\pm h$, we obtain \[  H(a+h)+H(a-h)-2H(a)\le 2C_ K|h|^2\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_0).  \] Since $K$ was arbitrary and the points $a\pm h=S_{a,\pm h}(a)$ lie in $B$, lemma 9.6.2 applies on $U=B$. Thus $H$ is continuous on $B$ and belongs to $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, and its distributional real Hessian $A$ and complex Hessian $(H_{j ar k})$ have the properties stated there: the second-order expansion holds almost everywhere, $(H_{j ar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=n!\, \pi ^{-n}\det (H_{j ar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. Step 3: the equation. Suppose that $\det (H_{j ar k})>0$ on a set of positive measure, and choose a point $a$ of this set at which $(H_{j ar k}(a))$ is positive semidefinite and the second-order expansion holds. The Taylor polynomial $Q(z)=H(a)+
abla H(a)\cdot (z-a)+ rac12(z-a)^ tA(a)(z-a)$ is a real quadratic polynomial with real Hessian $A(a)$, so its complex Hessian is the constant matrix $(H_{j ar k}(a))$; this matrix is positive semidefinite with positive determinant, hence positive definite. Let $\eta >0$ be smaller than its smallest eigenvalue; then $Q-\eta |z-a|^2$ has positive semidefinite complex Hessian and is plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.2 ). For sufficiently small $r>0$ we have $\overline{B(a,r)}\subset B$ and, by the expansion, $|H-Q|<\eta r^2/2$ on the sphere $|z-a|=r$. The polynomial $	ilde Q=Q-\eta |z-a|^2+\eta r^2/4$ is then strictly smaller than $H$ on that sphere, since there $	ilde Q<H+\eta r^2/2-3\eta r^2/4$, and $	ilde Q(a)=H(a)+\eta r^2/4>H(a)$. By proposition 8.2.5 , applied with $D=B(a,r)$ and $v=	ilde Q$, whose boundary inequality holds because $	ilde Q$ and $H$ are continuous, the function equal to $\max \{ H,	ilde Q\} $ on $B(a,r)$ and to $H$ elsewhere is plurisubharmonic on $B$. It coincides with $H$ near $\partial B$, so it is a subsolution, and it exceeds $H$ at $a$, a contradiction. Hence $\det (H_{j ar k})=0$ almost everywhere, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0$. This proves the theorem for $C^2$ data, including the $C^{1,1}$ regularity, except for uniqueness. Step 4: continuous data and uniqueness. For continuous $\varphi $, the function $z\mapsto \varphi (z/|z|)$ is continuous on the annulus $\{ 1/2<|z|<2\} $, and its mollifications $\varphi _ j$, $j\ge 4$, are smooth on the neighborhood $\{ 3/4<|z|<3/2\} $ of $\partial B$ and converge to $\varphi $ uniformly on $\partial B$ (lemma 1.4.1 (1)). Let $H_ j$ be the envelope for $\varphi _ j|_{\partial B}$; by Steps 1–3 it is continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $\varphi _ j$, plurisubharmonic, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n=0$. Put $c_ j=\max _{\partial B}|\varphi _ j-\varphi |$. Since $H_ j-c_ j$ is a subsolution for $\varphi $, the class of subsolutions for $\varphi $ is nonempty, and its envelope $H$ satisfies $H_ j-c_ j\le H$; symmetrically, $H-c_ j\le H_ j$. Therefore $\sup _ B|H_ j-H|\le c_ j	o 0$, so $H$ is a uniform limit of continuous functions on $B$; it is continuous, extends continuously to $\overline B$ with the boundary values $\varphi $, and is plurisubharmonic, being equal to its regularization $H^*$, which is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.2 . By proposition 9.1.4 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\lim _ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n=0$. Finally, if $H'$ and $H''$ are two solutions, then $H'-H''	o 0$ at $\partial B$, and the last assertion of theorem 9.2.8 , applied in both directions, gives $H'=H''$. $\square$ Corollary 9.6.4 . Let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, and let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a ball. There is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\widehat u$ on $\Omega $ which equals $u$ outside $B$, satisfies $\widehat u\ge u$ on $B$, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat u)^ n=0$ on $B$. The function $\widehat u$ is increasing in $u$, and its restriction to $B$ is the largest plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $B$ with $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}v(z)\le u(x)$ for every $x\in \partial B$. Proof. Let $u_ j=u*ho _{\varepsilon _ j}$, with $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ smaller than the distance from $\overline B$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, be radial regularizations of $u$; they are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ decreasing to $u$ (proposition 8.2.2 ). Let $H_ j$ be the solution of theorem 9.6.3 with boundary values $u_ j|_{\partial B}$, that is, the upper envelope of the subsolutions for $u_ j|_{\partial B}$. Since $u_ j$ is such a subsolution, $u\le u_ j\le H_ j$ on $B$. Since $u_{j+1}\le u_ j$ on $\partial B$, every subsolution for $u_{j+1}|_{\partial B}$ is one for $u_ j|_{\partial B}$, so the envelopes decrease: $H_{j+1}\le H_ j$. Let $H=\lim _ jH_ j$. The function $H_1$ is subharmonic on $B$ and continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $u_1$, so $H_1\le \max _{\partial B}u_1$ by the comparison principle (theorem 3.1.3 ). Hence $\inf _{\overline B}u\le H\le \max _{\partial B}u_1$, so $H$ is bounded; it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.1 , and theorem 9.2.5 gives $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\lim _ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n=0$. For $x\in \partial B$, since $H\le H_ j$ and $H_ j$ is continuous on $\overline B$ with $H_ j=u_ j$ on $\partial B$, \[  \varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}H(z)\le u_ j(x)\quad 	ext{for every }j, \qquad 	ext{hence}\quad \varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}H(z)\le u(x).  \] By proposition 8.2.5 , the function $\widehat u$ equal to $\max \{ u,H\} =H$ on $B$ and to $u$ outside $B$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. It is locally bounded, since $H$ is bounded and $u$ is locally bounded; it equals $u$ outside $B$, satisfies $\widehat u\ge u$ on $B$, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat u)^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0$ on $B$ by locality. Let $v$ be plurisubharmonic on $B$ with $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}v(z)\le u(x)$ for $x\in \partial B$. Since $u\le u_ j$, the function $v$ is a subsolution for the boundary values $u_ j|_{\partial B}$, so $v\le H_ j$ by theorem 9.6.3 . Letting $j	o \infty $ gives $v\le H$. Conversely, $H$ belongs to this class by the displayed estimate, so $H$ is its largest member. If $u\le u'$, the class for $u$ is contained in the class for $u'$, which proves that $\widehat u\le \widehat{u'}$. $\square$ Definition 9.6.5 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. A plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $\Omega $ is maximal if every plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $\Omega $ with $v\le u$ outside a compact subset of $\Omega $ satisfies $v\le u$ everywhere. Theorem 9.6.6 . A locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $u$ on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is maximal if and only if $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$. In particular, maximality is a local property for locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions. Proof. Suppose that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$, and let $v$ be plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $ with $v\le u$ outside a compact set $K$. Choose a bounded open set $D$ with $K\subset D\Subset \Omega $. By upper semicontinuity, $v$ is bounded above on $\overline D$; since $u$ is bounded on $\overline D$, we may choose $M$ with $-M<\inf _ Du$. The function $\max \{ v,-M\} $ is bounded and plurisubharmonic on $D$, and it is at most $u$ on $D\setminus K$; since every point of $D$ near $\partial D$ lies in $D\setminus K$, we get $\varliminf _{D
i z	o x}(u(z)-\max \{ v(z),-M\} )\ge 0$ for $x\in \partial D$. The last assertion of theorem 9.2.8 therefore gives $\max \{ v,-M\} \le u$ on $D$. Hence $v\le u$ everywhere, and $u$ is maximal. Conversely, suppose that $u$ is maximal, and let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a ball. The function $\widehat u$ of corollary 9.6.4 is plurisubharmonic, satisfies $\widehat u\ge u$, and equals $u$ outside the compact set $\overline B$. Maximality gives $\widehat u\le u$, so $\widehat u=u$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat u)^ n=0$ on $B$. Since the balls $B\Subset \Omega $ cover $\Omega $, and a distribution vanishing on each member of a family of open sets vanishes on their union (lemma 1.4.2 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$ on $\Omega $. For the last assertion, let every point of $\Omega $ have an open neighborhood $U$ such that $u|_ U$ is maximal on $U$. By the first part applied on $U$, and by locality of the products (proposition 9.1.2 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ vanishes on each such $U$, hence on $\Omega $, and $u$ is maximal on $\Omega $. Conversely, if $u$ is maximal on $\Omega $, then $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$ on every open set $U\subset \Omega $, so $u|_ U$ is maximal on $U$. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.6.1
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 9.6.1 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be the unit ball. For $a\in B$ and $h\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $|h|$ small, depending on $a$, there are biholomorphic automorphisms $S_{a,h}$ of $B$ such that $S_{a,0}$ is the identity and $S_{a,h}(a)=a+h$. Each $S_{a,h}$ extends to a holomorphic map on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ which maps $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$. For every compact set $K\subset B$ there is $h_0>0$ such that the map $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is defined and smooth on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n\times \mathbb C^ n\times \mathbb C^ n$ containing $K\times \overline{B(0,h_0)}\times \overline B$, and holomorphic in $z$ there. In particular, there is a constant $C$ such that, for $a\in K$, $|h|\le h_0$ and $z\in \overline B$, the first and second derivatives of $S_{a,h}(z)$ with respect to the real variable $h\in \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ are bounded by $C$. Proof. Use the Hermitian product $\langle z,a\rangle =\sum z_ j\bar a_ j$, put $s_ a=\sqrt{1-|a|^2}$, and define \[  T_ a(z)=\frac{s_ a z+\langle z,a\rangle a/(1+s_ a)-a}{1-\langle z,a\rangle }.  \] This expression depends smoothly on $(a,z)$ in the open set $\{ (a,z):|a|<1,\  |a||z|<1\} $, where the denominator does not vanish, and it is holomorphic in $z$; moreover $T_0$ is the identity. If $U$ is a unitary matrix, then $\langle Uz,Ua\rangle =\langle z,a\rangle $ and $s_{Ua}=s_ a$, so $T_{Ua}(Uz)=UT_ a(z)$. Given $a\ne 0$, choose $U$ with $Ua=(t,0,\ldots ,0)$, $t=|a|$; it therefore suffices to verify the following identities for $a=(t,0,\ldots ,0)$ with $0\le t<1$, and also for $-a=(-t,0,\ldots ,0)$. Put $s=s_ a=\sqrt{1-t^2}$. Then $\langle z,a\rangle =tz_1$, and the first component of the numerator of $T_ a(z)$ is $sz_1+t^2z_1/(1+s)-t=z_1-t$, because $s(1+s)+t^2=s+s^2+t^2=1+s$. Hence \[  \begin{aligned}  T_ a(z)& =\left(\frac{z_1-t}{1-tz_1}, \frac{s\, z_2}{1-tz_1},\ldots , \frac{s\, z_ n}{1-tz_1}\right),\\  T_{-a}(w)& =\left(\frac{w_1+t}{1+tw_1}, \frac{s\, w_2}{1+tw_1},\ldots , \frac{s\, w_ n}{1+tw_1}\right), \end{aligned}  \] the second formula by the same computation with $t$ replaced by $-t$. In particular $T_ a(a)=0$ and $T_{-a}(0)=a$. If $w=T_ a(z)$, then \[  w_1+t=\frac{(1-t^2)z_1}{1-tz_1},\qquad 1+tw_1=\frac{1-t^2}{1-tz_1},  \] so the first component of $T_{-a}(w)$ is $z_1$ and the others are $s\cdot sz_ k/(1-tz_1)\cdot (1-tz_1)/(1-t^2)=z_ k$; thus $T_{-a}\circ T_ a=\mathrm{id}$, and by symmetry $T_ a\circ T_{-a}=\mathrm{id}$. Finally, \[  |1-tz_1|^2-|z_1-t|^2-(1-t^2)\sum _{k\ge 2}|z_ k|^2=(1-t^2)(1-|z_1|^2)-(1-t^2)\sum _{k\ge 2}|z_ k|^2,  \] because the terms $\mp 2t\operatorname{Re}z_1$ cancel; dividing by $|1-tz_1|^2$ gives \[  1-|T_ a(z)|^2=\frac{(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)}{|1-\langle z,a\rangle |^2}.  \] Hence $T_ a$ maps $B$ into $B$ and the sphere $\partial B$ into itself, and the same holds for $T_{-a}$; since $T_{-a}$ is inverse to $T_ a$, the map $T_ a$ is a biholomorphic automorphism of $B$ which maps $\partial B$ onto itself. Set $S_{a,h}=T_{-(a+h)}\circ T_ a$ for $|a+h|<1$. It maps $a$ to $T_{-(a+h)}(0)=a+h$ and is the identity for $h=0$. The map $T_ a$ is holomorphic on the neighborhood $\{ z:|a||z|<1\} $ of $\overline B$, and, as we have just seen, it maps $\overline B$ into $\overline B$ and $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$; the same holds for $T_{-(a+h)}$. Hence $S_{a,h}$ is holomorphic on the neighborhood $\{ z:|a||z|<1,\  |a+h||T_ a(z)|<1\} $ of $\overline B$, and it maps $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$. Let $K\subset B$ be compact (we may assume $K\neq \varnothing $), put $t_ K=\max _ K|a|<1$, and choose $h_0>0$ with $t_ K+3h_0<1$. On the open set $O$ of all $(a,h,z)$ with $|a|<t_ K+h_0$, $|h|<2h_0$, $|a||z|<1$ and $(t_ K+3h_0)|T_ a(z)|<1$, we have $|a+h|<1$ and $|a+h||T_ a(z)|<1$, so $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is defined and smooth on $O$, and holomorphic in $z$. Since $|T_ a(z)|\le 1$ for $|z|\le 1$, the set $O$ contains the compact set $K\times \overline{B(0,h_0)}\times \overline B$, on which the continuous first and second derivatives of $S_{a,h}(z)$ with respect to $h$ are therefore bounded by a constant $C$. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.6.2
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 9.6.2 . Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$, and let $H$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $U$. Suppose that for every compact set $K\subset U$ there are constants $C_ K\ge 0$ and $h_ K>0$ such that, for all $a\in K$ and all $h\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $|h|\le h_ K$, the points $a\pm h$ lie in $U$ and 9.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:second-difference-bound} H(a+h)+H(a-h)-2H(a)\le 2C_ K|h|^2\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_ K). \end{equation} Then $H$ is continuous, $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and the distributional real Hessian of $H$ is a matrix $A=(A_{ab})$ of measurable functions which are bounded on compact subsets of $U$. Almost every $x\in U$ satisfies \[  H(x+h)=H(x)+\nabla H(x)\cdot h+\tfrac 12h^ tA(x)h+o(|h|^2)\qquad (h\to 0).  \] Moreover, let $H_{j\bar k}$ be the coefficients of the distributional complex Hessian of $H$, which are fixed complex linear combinations of the $A_{ab}$. Then the matrix $(H_{j\bar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det (H_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] Proof. Let $H_\varepsilon =H*\rho _\varepsilon $. Fix $a_0\in U$ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(a_0,4r)}\subset U$, put $K=\overline{B(a_0,3r)}$, and let $M_0=\sup _ K|H|$, which is finite because $H$ is locally bounded. For $0<\varepsilon <r$, the regularization $H_\varepsilon $ is smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a_0,2r)}$ (proposition 8.2.2 ), and $|H_\varepsilon |\le M_0$ on $\overline{B(a_0,2r)}$, since its values there are averages of values of $H$ on $K$. For $x\in \overline{B(a_0,2r)}$ and $|h|\le h_ K$, \[  \begin{aligned} & H_\varepsilon (x+h)+H_\varepsilon (x-h)-2H_\varepsilon (x)\\ & \qquad =\int \bigl (H(x-y+h)+H(x-y-h)-2H(x-y)\bigr )\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy\le 2C_ K|h|^2, \end{aligned}  \] by ( 9.29 ), because $x-y\in K$ for $|y|\le \varepsilon $. Replacing $h$ by $th$ with $0<t\le 1$, dividing by $t^2$ and letting $t\to 0$, we get $D^2H_\varepsilon (x)[h,h]\le 2C_ K|h|^2$ for $|h|\le h_ K$, and hence, by homogeneity, for all $h\in \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$. On the other hand, the complex Hessian of the smooth plurisubharmonic function $H_\varepsilon $ is positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 ), and $D^2H_\varepsilon [h,h]+D^2H_\varepsilon [\mathrm ih,\mathrm ih]=4\sum _{j,k}(H_\varepsilon )_{j\bar k}h_ j\bar h_ k\ge 0$; hence $D^2H_\varepsilon (x)[h,h]\ge -2C_ K|h|^2$ as well. Thus the second derivatives of the $H_\varepsilon $ are bounded on $\overline{B(a_0,2r)}$ by a constant $\Lambda _0$ independent of $\varepsilon $. For $x\in \overline{B(a_0,r)}$ and a unit vector $e$, Taylor's formula \[  H_\varepsilon (x+re)=H_\varepsilon (x)+r\, \partial _ eH_\varepsilon (x)+\int _0^ r(r-t)D^2H_\varepsilon (x+te)[e,e]\, \mathrm dt  \] gives $|\partial _ eH_\varepsilon (x)|\le 2M_0/r+\Lambda _0r=\Lambda $. By the mean value theorem on the convex set $B(a_0,r)$, $|H_\varepsilon (x)-H_\varepsilon (y)|\le \Lambda |x-y|$ for $x,y\in B(a_0,r)$. Since $H_\varepsilon \to H$ pointwise as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by ( 3.3 ), the same inequality holds for $H$. Hence $H$ is continuous on $B(a_0,r)$, and, as $a_0$ was arbitrary, on $U$. Moreover, $H_\varepsilon \to H$ in $L^1$ on compact subsets of $U$, by dominated convergence, and hence in the sense of distributions; and every ball $B_0\Subset U$ is covered by finitely many balls $B(a_0,2r)$ as above, so the second derivatives of the $H_\varepsilon $ are bounded on $B_0$ uniformly in small $\varepsilon $. By the converse part of proposition 1.7.5 , the distributional real Hessian of $H$ has locally bounded measurable coefficients $A_{ab}$; hence $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and almost every $x\in U$ satisfies the second-order expansion of the statement. The functions $H_{j\bar k}$ are bounded measurable functions on compact subsets of $U$. By proposition 1.4.3 , the complex Hessian of $H_\varepsilon $ has the coefficients $(H_{j\bar k})_\varepsilon $; these are bounded on compact sets uniformly in small $\varepsilon $, and they converge to $H_{j\bar k}$ at every Lebesgue point of $H_{j\bar k}$, hence almost everywhere (theorem 1.7.3 ). In particular, the matrix $(H_{j\bar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, as an almost everywhere limit of the positive semidefinite complex Hessians of the smooth plurisubharmonic functions $H_\varepsilon $. Since $H$ is continuous, $H_\varepsilon \to H$ locally uniformly (lemma 1.4.1 (1)), so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_\varepsilon )^ n\to (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n$ weakly on every ball $B_0\Subset U$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ along a sequence, by proposition 9.1.4 applied on $B_0$. By ( 9.2 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_\varepsilon )^ n=n!\pi ^{-n}\det ((H_{j\bar k})_\varepsilon )\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, and the determinants converge almost everywhere and are bounded on compact sets uniformly in small $\varepsilon $. Hence, for every test function $\chi $ supported in such a ball $B_0$, dominated convergence gives \[  \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\int \chi \det (H_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] By lemma 1.4.2 , every test function on $U$ is a finite sum of test functions supported in balls $B_0\Subset U$, so this identity holds for all test functions on $U$, and the two Radon measures coincide by proposition 1.4.3 (4). $\square$

title: Theorem 9.6.3
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Theorem 9.6.3 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a ball and $\varphi $ a real continuous function on $\partial B$. There is a unique $H\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B)$ such that \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0\quad \text{on }B,\qquad H|_{\partial B}=\varphi .  \] It is the upper envelope of the class of all $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ with $\varlimsup _{B\ni z\to x}v(z)\le \varphi (x)$ for every $x\in \partial B$. If $\varphi $ is the restriction of a $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\partial B$, then $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$. Proof. After an affine change of coordinates $z\mapsto z_0+Rz$ with $R>0$, we may assume that $B$ is the unit ball; plurisubharmonicity, the boundary conditions, $C^2$ data and the vanishing of the Monge–Ampère measure are preserved by such a change, by proposition 8.2.3 and proposition 9.1.2 (5). We call the functions $v$ in the statement the subsolutions for $\varphi $ of the homogeneous equation. If $v$ is a subsolution for $\varphi $ and $\varphi \le \varphi '+c$ on $\partial B$ with a constant $c$, then $v-c$ is a subsolution for $\varphi '$. Every subsolution is subharmonic on $B$ (theorem 8.2.1 ), so the comparison principle (theorem 3.1.3 and the remark following it), applied with the harmonic function $P\varphi $, the Poisson integral of $\varphi $ given by theorem 2.3.1 , gives $v\le P\varphi $, and $P\varphi \le \max _{\partial B}\varphi $ because the Poisson kernel is positive with integral $1$. Hence, as soon as the class of subsolutions is nonempty, its upper envelope $H$ is defined, and $H\le P\varphi $. Step 1: the envelope for $C^2$ data. Suppose that $\varphi $ is the restriction of a $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\partial B$. Multiplying this function by a cutoff equal to $1$ near $\partial B$, we obtain a $C^2$ function $\tilde\varphi $ with compact support in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ and $\tilde\varphi =\varphi $ on $\partial B$. Its complex Hessian is continuous with compact support, so there is $\lambda >0$ with $\sum _{j,k}\tilde\varphi _{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k\ge -\lambda |\xi |^2$ everywhere. The function $s=\tilde\varphi +\lambda (|z|^2-1)$ is then of class $C^2$ with positive semidefinite complex Hessian, so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 . As $s=\varphi $ on $\partial B$, it is a subsolution. Hence $s\le H\le P\varphi $. By theorem 8.3.2 , the upper semicontinuous regularization $H^*$ is plurisubharmonic, and $s\le H^*\le P\varphi $ since $P\varphi $ is continuous. As $s$ and $P\varphi $ are continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $\varphi $, we have $H^*(z)\to \varphi (x)$ as $z\to x\in \partial B$; so $H^*$ is a subsolution, $H^*\le H$, and $H=H^*$ is plurisubharmonic. Moreover $H(z)\to \varphi (x)$ as $z\to x\in \partial B$, and $H$ is bounded. Step 2: second differences. Let $K\subset B$ be compact, and let $S_{a,h}$, $h_0$ and $C$ be as in lemma 9.6.1 . For $x\in \partial B$ and $a\in K$, the function $g(h)=\tilde\varphi (S_{a,h}(x))$, $|h|\le h_0$, is of class $C^2$, and by the chain rule its second derivatives are bounded by a constant $2C_ K$ independent of $a$ and $x$, since the first and second derivatives of $\tilde\varphi $ are bounded and those of $S_{a,h}(x)$ with respect to $h$ are bounded by $C$. Since $g(0)=\varphi (x)$, Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives $g(h)+g(-h)-2g(0)=\int _0^1(1-t)\bigl (D^2g(th)[h,h]+D^2g(-th)[h,h]\bigr )\, \mathrm dt\le 2C_ K|h|^2$. As $S_{a,\pm h}$ maps $\partial B$ to $\partial B$, where $\tilde\varphi =\varphi $, this reads \[  \tfrac 12\bigl (\varphi \circ S_{a,h}+\varphi \circ S_{a,-h}\bigr ) \le \varphi +C_ K|h|^2\quad \text{on }\partial B\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_0).  \] The function $w=\frac12(H\circ S_{a,h}+H\circ S_{a,-h})-C_ K|h|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$, by proposition 8.2.3 , proposition 8.2.5 , since $S_{a,\pm h}$ are automorphisms of $B$ and $H$ is bounded. If $y\in \partial B$ and $z\to y$ in $B$, then $S_{a,\pm h}(z)\to S_{a,\pm h}(y)\in \partial B$, so $H(S_{a,\pm h}(z))\to \varphi (S_{a,\pm h}(y))$ by Step 1, and the preceding inequality gives $\varlimsup _{z\to y}w(z)\le \varphi (y)$. Thus $w$ is a subsolution, so $w\le H$. Evaluating at $z=a$, where $S_{a,\pm h}(a)=a\pm h$, we obtain \[  H(a+h)+H(a-h)-2H(a)\le 2C_ K|h|^2\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_0).  \] Since $K$ was arbitrary and the points $a\pm h=S_{a,\pm h}(a)$ lie in $B$, lemma 9.6.2 applies on $U=B$. Thus $H$ is continuous on $B$ and belongs to $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, and its distributional real Hessian $A$ and complex Hessian $(H_{j\bar k})$ have the properties stated there: the second-order expansion holds almost everywhere, $(H_{j\bar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=n!\, \pi ^{-n}\det (H_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. Step 3: the equation. Suppose that $\det (H_{j\bar k})>0$ on a set of positive measure, and choose a point $a$ of this set at which $(H_{j\bar k}(a))$ is positive semidefinite and the second-order expansion holds. The Taylor polynomial $Q(z)=H(a)+\nabla H(a)\cdot (z-a)+\frac12(z-a)^ tA(a)(z-a)$ is a real quadratic polynomial with real Hessian $A(a)$, so its complex Hessian is the constant matrix $(H_{j\bar k}(a))$; this matrix is positive semidefinite with positive determinant, hence positive definite. Let $\eta >0$ be smaller than its smallest eigenvalue; then $Q-\eta |z-a|^2$ has positive semidefinite complex Hessian and is plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.2 ). For sufficiently small $r>0$ we have $\overline{B(a,r)}\subset B$ and, by the expansion, $|H-Q|<\eta r^2/2$ on the sphere $|z-a|=r$. The polynomial $\tilde Q=Q-\eta |z-a|^2+\eta r^2/4$ is then strictly smaller than $H$ on that sphere, since there $\tilde Q<H+\eta r^2/2-3\eta r^2/4$, and $\tilde Q(a)=H(a)+\eta r^2/4>H(a)$. By proposition 8.2.5 , applied with $D=B(a,r)$ and $v=\tilde Q$, whose boundary inequality holds because $\tilde Q$ and $H$ are continuous, the function equal to $\max \{ H,\tilde Q\} $ on $B(a,r)$ and to $H$ elsewhere is plurisubharmonic on $B$. It coincides with $H$ near $\partial B$, so it is a subsolution, and it exceeds $H$ at $a$, a contradiction. Hence $\det (H_{j\bar k})=0$ almost everywhere, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0$. This proves the theorem for $C^2$ data, including the $C^{1,1}$ regularity, except for uniqueness. Step 4: continuous data and uniqueness. For continuous $\varphi $, the function $z\mapsto \varphi (z/|z|)$ is continuous on the annulus $\{ 1/2<|z|<2\} $, and its mollifications $\varphi _ j$, $j\ge 4$, are smooth on the neighborhood $\{ 3/4<|z|<3/2\} $ of $\partial B$ and converge to $\varphi $ uniformly on $\partial B$ (lemma 1.4.1 (1)). Let $H_ j$ be the envelope for $\varphi _ j|_{\partial B}$; by Steps 1–3 it is continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $\varphi _ j$, plurisubharmonic, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n=0$. Put $c_ j=\max _{\partial B}|\varphi _ j-\varphi |$. Since $H_ j-c_ j$ is a subsolution for $\varphi $, the class of subsolutions for $\varphi $ is nonempty, and its envelope $H$ satisfies $H_ j-c_ j\le H$; symmetrically, $H-c_ j\le H_ j$. Therefore $\sup _ B|H_ j-H|\le c_ j\to 0$, so $H$ is a uniform limit of continuous functions on $B$; it is continuous, extends continuously to $\overline B$ with the boundary values $\varphi $, and is plurisubharmonic, being equal to its regularization $H^*$, which is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.2 . By proposition 9.1.4 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\lim _ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n=0$. Finally, if $H'$ and $H''$ are two solutions, then $H'-H''\to 0$ at $\partial B$, and the last assertion of theorem 9.2.8 , applied in both directions, gives $H'=H''$. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.6.4
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text:
Corollary 9.6.4 . Let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, and let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a ball. There is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\widehat u$ on $\Omega $ which equals $u$ outside $B$, satisfies $\widehat u\ge u$ on $B$, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat u)^ n=0$ on $B$. The function $\widehat u$ is increasing in $u$, and its restriction to $B$ is the largest plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $B$ with $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}v(z)\le u(x)$ for every $x\in \partial B$. Proof. Let $u_ j=u*ho _{\varepsilon _ j}$, with $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ smaller than the distance from $\overline B$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, be radial regularizations of $u$; they are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ decreasing to $u$ (proposition 8.2.2 ). Let $H_ j$ be the solution of theorem 9.6.3 with boundary values $u_ j|_{\partial B}$, that is, the upper envelope of the subsolutions for $u_ j|_{\partial B}$. Since $u_ j$ is such a subsolution, $u\le u_ j\le H_ j$ on $B$. Since $u_{j+1}\le u_ j$ on $\partial B$, every subsolution for $u_{j+1}|_{\partial B}$ is one for $u_ j|_{\partial B}$, so the envelopes decrease: $H_{j+1}\le H_ j$. Let $H=\lim _ jH_ j$. The function $H_1$ is subharmonic on $B$ and continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $u_1$, so $H_1\le \max _{\partial B}u_1$ by the comparison principle (theorem 3.1.3 ). Hence $\inf _{\overline B}u\le H\le \max _{\partial B}u_1$, so $H$ is bounded; it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.1 , and theorem 9.2.5 gives $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\lim _ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n=0$. For $x\in \partial B$, since $H\le H_ j$ and $H_ j$ is continuous on $\overline B$ with $H_ j=u_ j$ on $\partial B$, \[  \varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}H(z)\le u_ j(x)\quad 	ext{for every }j, \qquad 	ext{hence}\quad \varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}H(z)\le u(x).  \] By proposition 8.2.5 , the function $\widehat u$ equal to $\max \{ u,H\} =H$ on $B$ and to $u$ outside $B$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. It is locally bounded, since $H$ is bounded and $u$ is locally bounded; it equals $u$ outside $B$, satisfies $\widehat u\ge u$ on $B$, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat u)^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0$ on $B$ by locality. Let $v$ be plurisubharmonic on $B$ with $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}v(z)\le u(x)$ for $x\in \partial B$. Since $u\le u_ j$, the function $v$ is a subsolution for the boundary values $u_ j|_{\partial B}$, so $v\le H_ j$ by theorem 9.6.3 . Letting $j	o \infty $ gives $v\le H$. Conversely, $H$ belongs to this class by the displayed estimate, so $H$ is its largest member. If $u\le u'$, the class for $u$ is contained in the class for $u'$, which proves that $\widehat u\le \widehat{u'}$. $\square$

title: Definition 9.6.5
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Definition 9.6.5 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. A plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $\Omega $ is maximal if every plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $\Omega $ with $v\le u$ outside a compact subset of $\Omega $ satisfies $v\le u$ everywhere.

title: Theorem 9.6.6
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Theorem 9.6.6 . A locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $u$ on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is maximal if and only if $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$. In particular, maximality is a local property for locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions. Proof. Suppose that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$, and let $v$ be plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $ with $v\le u$ outside a compact set $K$. Choose a bounded open set $D$ with $K\subset D\Subset \Omega $. By upper semicontinuity, $v$ is bounded above on $\overline D$; since $u$ is bounded on $\overline D$, we may choose $M$ with $-M<\inf _ Du$. The function $\max \{ v,-M\} $ is bounded and plurisubharmonic on $D$, and it is at most $u$ on $D\setminus K$; since every point of $D$ near $\partial D$ lies in $D\setminus K$, we get $\varliminf _{D\ni z\to x}(u(z)-\max \{ v(z),-M\} )\ge 0$ for $x\in \partial D$. The last assertion of theorem 9.2.8 therefore gives $\max \{ v,-M\} \le u$ on $D$. Hence $v\le u$ everywhere, and $u$ is maximal. Conversely, suppose that $u$ is maximal, and let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a ball. The function $\widehat u$ of corollary 9.6.4 is plurisubharmonic, satisfies $\widehat u\ge u$, and equals $u$ outside the compact set $\overline B$. Maximality gives $\widehat u\le u$, so $\widehat u=u$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat u)^ n=0$ on $B$. Since the balls $B\Subset \Omega $ cover $\Omega $, and a distribution vanishing on each member of a family of open sets vanishes on their union (lemma 1.4.2 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$ on $\Omega $. For the last assertion, let every point of $\Omega $ have an open neighborhood $U$ such that $u|_ U$ is maximal on $U$. By the first part applied on $U$, and by locality of the products (proposition 9.1.2 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ vanishes on each such $U$, hence on $\Omega $, and $u$ is maximal on $\Omega $. Conversely, if $u$ is maximal on $\Omega $, then $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$ on every open set $U\subset \Omega $, so $u|_ U$ is maximal on $U$. $\square$

title: 9.7 Density lower bounds and mixed products
search_title: Density lower bounds and mixed products
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: 9.7 Density lower bounds and mixed products We now turn to the equation $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu $ with a prescribed measure $\mu $ on a ball, and to the lower bounds that mixed products inherit from lower bounds of the pure Monge–Ampère measures. From here to the end of section 9.11 , $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is open, $n\ge 1$, and \[  \eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2=\beta /\pi ,\qquad \text{so that}\qquad \eta ^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}  \] by ( 9.2 ). Densities of Monge–Ampère measures are taken with respect to $\eta ^ n$; thus, by ( 9.2 ) and the remark following proposition 9.1.4 , a plurisubharmonic function $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ satisfies $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\det (u_{j\bar k})\, \eta ^ n$. A lower bound $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ is a nonlinear condition on $u$, and it is not evident that it is preserved by convolution. We show that, for a continuous density $f$, it can be tested pointwise with $C^2$ functions touching $u$ from above, and that it is equivalent to a family of linear elliptic inequalities, one for each positive definite Hermitian matrix of determinant one (proposition 9.7.3 ). Two lemmas prepare it: an expression of $(\det A)^{1/n}$ as an infimum of traces, and a passage from test functions to distributions. Since linear inequalities are preserved by convolution, the determinant inequalities for mixed products of smooth functions then pass to locally bounded potentials (corollary 9.7.4 , corollary 9.7.6 ). The same characterization will make subsolutions of the Dirichlet problem stable under the operations used in section 9.8 . Let $u$ be a real function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. A real $C^2$ function $q$ defined near a point $x$ touches $u$ from above at $x$ if $q(x)=u(x)$ and $q\ge u$ on a neighborhood of $x$; we then call $q$ an upper test function for $u$ at $x$. Lemma 9.7.1 . Let $A$ be a positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix. Then \[  (\det A)^{1/n}=\inf \left\{ \frac{\operatorname {tr}(BA)}n:\  B\text{ positive definite Hermitian},\  \det B=1\right\} .  \] If $C$ is another positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix, define the numbers $M_ k(A,C)$, $0\le k\le n$, by \[  \det (tA+sC)=\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk M_ k(A,C)\, t^ ks^{n-k}\qquad (t,s\in \mathbb R).  \] Then $M_ n(A,C)=\det A$, $M_0(A,C)=\det C$, and for each integer $1\le k\le n-1$, \[  M_ k(A,C)\ge (\det A)^{k/n}(\det C)^{(n-k)/n}.  \] Proof. Let $B$ be positive definite with $\det B=1$. The positive semidefinite matrix $B^{1/2}AB^{1/2}$ has trace $\operatorname {tr}(BA)$ and determinant $\det A$, so the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for its eigenvalues gives $\operatorname {tr}(BA)/n\ge (\det A)^{1/n}$. If $A$ is positive definite, equality holds for $B=(\det A)^{1/n}A^{-1}$. If $A$ is singular, the matrices $B_\varepsilon =\det (A+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}(A+\varepsilon I)^{-1}$, $\varepsilon >0$, are admissible and \[  0\le \operatorname {tr}(B_\varepsilon A)\le \operatorname {tr}\bigl (B_\varepsilon (A+\varepsilon I)\bigr )=n\det (A+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}\longrightarrow 0  \] as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. The formulas for $M_ n$ and $M_0$ follow from $\det (tA)=t^ n\det A$ and $\det (sC)=s^ n\det C$. Suppose first that $A$ and $C$ are positive definite, and let $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n>0$ be the eigenvalues of $A^{-1/2}CA^{-1/2}$. Since $\det (tA+sC)=\det A\prod _{i=1}^ n(t+s\lambda _ i)$, comparison of coefficients gives \[  M_ k(A,C)=\frac{\det A}{\binom nk}\sum _{|J|=n-k}\prod _{j\in J}\lambda _ j,  \] the sum being over the subsets $J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $ with $n-k$ elements. Each eigenvalue occurs in exactly $\binom {n-1}{n-k-1}$ of these $\binom n{n-k}$ products, so the geometric mean of the products is $(\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ n)^{(n-k)/n}$. Since $\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ n=\det C/\det A$, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  M_ k(A,C)\ge \det A\left(\frac{\det C}{\det A}\right)^{(n-k)/n}=(\det A)^{k/n}(\det C)^{(n-k)/n}.  \] For semidefinite $A$ and $C$, apply this to $A+\varepsilon I$ and $C+\varepsilon I$ and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; both sides depend continuously on the matrices. $\square$ Lemma 9.7.2 . Let $d\ge 1$, let $(c_{kl})$ be a real symmetric positive definite $d\times d$ matrix, and put $L=\sum _{k,l=1}^ dc_{kl}\partial _ k\partial _ l$. Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, let $w\colon U\to \mathbb R$ be upper semicontinuous, and let $F\colon U\to \mathbb R$ be continuous. Suppose that, for every $x\in U$, every upper test function $q$ for $w$ at $x$ satisfies $Lq(x)\ge F(x)$. Then $w$ is locally integrable, and $Lw\ge F$ in the sense of distributions on $U$. Proof. We reduce to the Laplacian, treat the case $F=0$ by a maximum principle argument, and reduce the general case to it. Step 1. Reduction to $L=\Delta $. Let $C=(c_{kl})$, let $P$ be the positive definite square root of $C^{-1}$, so that $PCP=I$, and put $\tilde U=P(U)$, $\tilde w=w\circ P^{-1}$ and $\tilde F=F\circ P^{-1}$. If $q$ is a $C^2$ function near $x\in U$ and $\tilde q=q\circ P^{-1}$, then $\partial _ k\partial _ lq(x)=\sum _{a,b}P_{ak}P_{bl}(\partial _ a\partial _ b\tilde q)(Px)$ by the chain rule, and hence \[  (Lq)(x)=\sum _{a,b}(PCP)_{ab}(\partial _ a\partial _ b\tilde q)(Px)=(\Delta \tilde q)(Px).  \] The map $q\mapsto \tilde q$ is a bijection from the upper test functions for $w$ at $x$ onto those for $\tilde w$ at $Px$, so $\tilde w$, $\Delta $ and $\tilde F$ satisfy the hypothesis of the lemma on $\tilde U$. Suppose that the lemma holds for them. Then $w=\tilde w\circ P$ is locally integrable, and for every nonnegative test function $\chi $ on $U$ the change of variables $y=Px$, with $\tilde\chi =\chi \circ P^{-1}$ and $L\chi =(\Delta \tilde\chi )\circ P$, gives \[  \langle Lw,\chi \rangle =\int _ Uw\, L\chi \, \mathrm dx =\frac1{|\det P|}\int _{\tilde U}\tilde w\, \Delta \tilde\chi \, \mathrm dy \ge \frac1{|\det P|}\int _{\tilde U}\tilde F\tilde\chi \, \mathrm dy=\int _ UF\chi \, \mathrm dx;  \] the first equality is the definition of distributional derivatives. We may therefore assume that $L=\Delta $. Step 2. The case $F=0$. We show that $w$ satisfies assertion (1) of theorem 3.1.3 for every ball $D=B(y,r)$ with $\overline{B(y,r)}\subset U$; by the converse part of that theorem, $w$ is then subharmonic on $U$. Let $h$ be a real function which is harmonic on $B(y,r)$ and continuous on $\overline{B(y,r)}$, with $\varlimsup _{B(y,r)\ni x\to \zeta }w(x)\le h(\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B(y,r)$, and suppose that $w(x_1)>h(x_1)$ for some $x_1\in B(y,r)$. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that the upper semicontinuous function $g(x)=w(x)-h(x)-\varepsilon (r^2-|x-y|^2)$ on $B(y,r)$ satisfies $g(x_1)>0$. Since $h$ is continuous on the closed ball, $\varlimsup _{B(y,r)\ni x\to \zeta }g(x)\le 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B(y,r)$. Hence every $\zeta \in \partial B(y,r)$ has an open neighborhood $N_\zeta $ with $g<g(x_1)/2$ on $N_\zeta \cap B(y,r)$; finitely many of these neighborhoods cover the sphere, and the complement $K$ of their union in $\overline{B(y,r)}$ is a compact subset of $B(y,r)$ containing $x_1$. The upper semicontinuous function $g$ attains its maximum over $K$ at a point $x_0$, and $c=g(x_0)\ge g(x_1)>0$; since $g<g(x_1)/2$ outside $K$, we have $g\le c$ on $B(y,r)$. The function $q=h+\varepsilon (r^2-|x-y|^2)+c$ is smooth on $B(y,r)$, satisfies $q-w=c-g\ge 0$ there and $q(x_0)=w(x_0)$, so it is an upper test function for $w$ at $x_0$. But $\Delta q=-2d\varepsilon <0$, which contradicts the hypothesis. Hence $w\le h$ on $B(y,r)$, and $w$ is subharmonic on $U$. Being real-valued, it is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $U$, so theorem 3.2.2 (1) shows that $w$ is locally integrable and $\Delta w\ge 0$. Step 3. The general case. Let $V\Subset U$ be open. Every compact subset of $U$ lies in such a set $V$, so it suffices to show that $w$ is locally integrable on $V$ and that $\Delta w\ge F$ on $V$. Choose an open set $V'$ with $\overline V\subset V'\Subset U$. By lemma 1.4.1 (1), the mollifications of $F$ converge to $F$ uniformly on $\overline{V'}$; subtracting from each of them its maximal deviation from $F$ on $\overline{V'}$, we obtain smooth functions $F_ j$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{V'}$ such that $F_ j\le F$ on $\overline{V'}$ and $F_ j\to F$ uniformly there. Let $\vartheta \in C^\infty _ c(V')$ be equal to one on an open set $W\supset \overline V$ (lemma 1.4.1 (4)). By proposition 2.2.1 , the convolution $h_ j=E_ d*(\vartheta F_ j)$, where $\vartheta F_ j$ is extended by zero, is a smooth function on $\mathbb R^ d$ with $\Delta h_ j=\vartheta F_ j$; in particular $\Delta h_ j=F_ j$ on $W$. If $q$ is an upper test function for $w-h_ j$ at $x\in V$, then $q+h_ j$ is an upper test function for $w$ at $x$, so that $\Delta q(x)+F_ j(x)\ge F(x)$, that is, $\Delta q(x)\ge F(x)-F_ j(x)\ge 0$. Step 2, applied to the real upper semicontinuous function $w-h_ j$ on $V$, shows that $w-h_ j$ is locally integrable on $V$ and $\Delta (w-h_ j)\ge 0$ there. Hence $w$ is locally integrable on $V$ and $\Delta w\ge F_ j$ on $V$. Testing against a nonnegative test function on $V$ and letting $j\to \infty $, we obtain $\Delta w\ge F$ on $V$. $\square$ For a real $C^2$ function $q$ on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$, we write $\mathcal H(q)=(q_{j\bar k})$ for its complex Hessian matrix, normalized as in ( 7.5 ). For a positive definite Hermitian matrix $B$ with $\det B=1$, put \[  L_ Bq=\operatorname {tr}\bigl (B\mathcal H(q)\bigr ).  \] This is a real operator with constant coefficients, since $B$ and $\mathcal H(q)$ are Hermitian, and it is elliptic. Indeed, write $B=V\operatorname {diag}(b_1,\ldots ,b_ n)V^*$ with $V$ unitary and $b_1,\ldots ,b_ n>0$, and introduce coordinates $\zeta $ by $z=\bar V\zeta $. By the chain rule, the complex Hessian of $\tilde q(\zeta )=q(\bar V\zeta )$ is $V^*\mathcal H(q)V$, so that \[  L_ Bq=\operatorname {tr}\bigl (\operatorname {diag}(b_1,\ldots ,b_ n)\, V^*\mathcal H(q)V\bigr )=\sum _{j=1}^ nb_ j\tilde q_{j\bar j}=\frac14\sum _{j=1}^ nb_ j\Delta _ j\tilde q  \] by ( 7.5 ), where $\Delta _ j$ is the Laplacian in the variable $\zeta _ j$. The real-linear map $z\mapsto \zeta $ is orthogonal on $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$; let $O$ be its matrix. By the chain rule, in the real coordinates of $\mathbb C^ n$ the operator $L_ B$ takes the form $\sum _{k,l}c_{kl}\partial _ k\partial _ l$ with $(c_{kl})=O^ t\Lambda O$, where $\Lambda $ is the diagonal matrix with entries $b_1/4,b_1/4,\ldots ,b_ n/4,b_ n/4$. This matrix is symmetric and positive definite, so lemma 9.7.2 applies to $L_ B$. Proposition 9.7.3 . Let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $, and let $f\ge 0$ be a continuous function on $\Omega $. The following conditions are equivalent: $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ as measures on $\Omega $; $\det \mathcal H(q)(x)\ge f(x)$ for every $x\in \Omega $ and every upper test function $q$ for $u$ at $x$; $L_ Bu\ge nf^{1/n}$ in the sense of distributions on $\Omega $, for every positive definite Hermitian matrix $B$ with $\det B=1$. If these conditions hold, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ the mollification $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ satisfies $\det \mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. Proof. We first observe that the complex Hessian $\mathcal H(q)(x)$ of an upper test function $q$ for $u$ at $x$ is positive semidefinite. Indeed, let $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, and let $r>0$ be so small that the closed disc $\{ x+\zeta \xi :|\zeta |\le r\} $ lies in the neighborhood of $x$ on which $q\ge u$. The function $\zeta \mapsto u(x+\zeta \xi )$ is subharmonic near this disc and finite at $\zeta =0$, so theorem 3.1.3 (2) gives \[  q(x)=u(x)\le \frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }u(x+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\xi )\, \mathrm d\theta \le \frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }q(x+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\xi )\, \mathrm d\theta .  \] Write $q_ j=\partial _{z_ j}q$ and $q_{jk}=\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{z_ k}q$. Since $q$ is real and of class $C^2$, Taylor's formula gives \[  q(x+h)=q(x)+2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ jq_ j(x)h_ j+\operatorname{Re}\sum _{j,k}q_{jk}(x)h_ jh_ k+\sum _{j,k}q_{j\bar k}(x)h_ j\bar h_ k+o(|h|^2).  \] For $h=r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\xi $ the terms containing $\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }$ and $\mathrm e^{2\mathrm i\theta }$ have mean zero over $\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$, so the right-hand side of the preceding display equals $q(x)+r^2\sum _{j,k}q_{j\bar k}(x)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k+o(r^2)$. Dividing by $r^2$ and letting $r\downarrow 0$, we obtain $\sum _{j,k}q_{j\bar k}(x)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k\ge 0$. (1) implies (2). Assume (1), let $q$ be an upper test function for $u$ at $x$, and suppose that $\det \mathcal H(q)(x)<f(x)$. Since $\mathcal H(q)(x)$ is positive semidefinite, we can choose $\delta >0$ so small that $q_\delta =q+\delta |z-x|^2$ satisfies $\mathcal H(q_\delta )(x)=\mathcal H(q)(x)+\delta I>0$ and still $\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )(x)<f(x)$. Since $q$ is of class $C^2$ and $f$ is continuous, there is $r>0$ such that $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, $q\ge u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$, the complex Hessian $\mathcal H(q_\delta )$ is positive definite on $\overline{B(x,r)}$, and $\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )<f$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$; in particular, $q_\delta $ is plurisubharmonic on $B(x,r)$ by proposition 8.2.2 . Put $b=q_\delta -\delta r^2/2$. Then $b=q+\delta r^2/2>u$ on the sphere $\partial B(x,r)$, while $b(x)=u(x)-\delta r^2/2<u(x)$. The Borel set $S=\{ z\in B(x,r):b(z)<u(z)\} $ has positive Lebesgue measure. Otherwise $\max \{ u,b\} =b$ almost everywhere on $B(x,r)$; since both functions are plurisubharmonic, the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 gives $\max \{ u,b\} =b$ everywhere, contradicting $b(x)<u(x)$. The function $b-u$ is lower semicontinuous and positive on $\partial B(x,r)$, so $\varliminf _{z\to \zeta }(b(z)-u(z))>0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B(x,r)$. The comparison principle theorem 9.2.8 , applied on $B(x,r)$ with the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $b$ and $u$ in place of $u$ and $v$, therefore gives \[  \int _ S f\eta ^ n\le \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\le \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b)^ n=\int _ S\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )\, \eta ^ n.  \] Here $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b)^ n=\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )\, \eta ^ n$ on $B(x,r)$ because $b$ is a plurisubharmonic $C^2$ function there (see the beginning of this section), and the integrals are finite because $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is a Radon measure on $\Omega $ and $\overline{B(x,r)}$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $. Since $\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )<f$ on $S$ and $S$ has positive measure, the right side is strictly smaller than the left side, a contradiction. Thus (2) holds. (2) implies (3). Let $q$ be an upper test function for $u$ at $x$, and let $B$ be positive definite with $\det B=1$. Since $\mathcal H(q)(x)$ is positive semidefinite, the infimum formula of lemma 9.7.1 and (2) give \[  L_ Bq(x)=\operatorname {tr}\bigl (B\mathcal H(q)(x)\bigr )\ge n\bigl (\det \mathcal H(q)(x)\bigr )^{1/n}\ge nf(x)^{1/n}.  \] Since $u$ is real-valued and upper semicontinuous, lemma 9.7.2 , applied to $L_ B$ and the continuous function $nf^{1/n}$, gives (3). (3) implies (1). The mollifications $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ of section 1.4 are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ which decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ (proposition 8.2.2 ). Fix $B$ as in (3). The distribution $L_ Bu-nf^{1/n}$ is positive, so its mollification is a nonnegative function on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ (proposition 1.4.3 (3)). Since $L_ B$ has constant coefficients, proposition 1.4.3 (1) identifies the mollification of $L_ Bu$ with $L_ Bu_\varepsilon $, and we obtain the pointwise inequality \[  \operatorname {tr}\bigl (B\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )\bigr )\ge n\, (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )\quad \text{on }\Omega _\varepsilon \qquad (B>0,\  \det B=1).  \] Since $\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )$ is positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 ), taking the infimum over $B$ and using lemma 9.7.1 , we obtain $\det \mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n$, which is the last assertion of the proposition. By the formula recalled at the beginning of this section, it reads \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon )^ n\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n\eta ^ n\quad \text{on }\Omega _\varepsilon .  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the density on the right converges locally uniformly to $f$ by lemma 1.4.1 (1), and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon )^ n\to (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ weakly by theorem 9.2.5 , applied along any sequence $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. Testing against nonnegative functions in $C_ c(\Omega )$ gives (1). $\square$ Corollary 9.7.4 . Let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $, and let $f,g\ge 0$ be continuous functions on $\Omega $ such that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\ge g\eta ^ n$. Then, for each integer $1\le k\le n-1$, \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}\ge f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\eta ^ n.  \] For $k=0$ and $k=n$ the same inequality is the hypothesis. Proof. Let $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ and $v_\varepsilon =v*\rho _\varepsilon $, with the same mollifiers for both functions. By the last assertion of proposition 9.7.3 , applied to $u$ with the density $f$ and to $v$ with the density $g$, \[  \det \mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n, \qquad \det \mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\ge (g^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n.  \] For real $t$ and $s$, ( 9.2 ), applied to the smooth function $tu_\varepsilon +sv_\varepsilon $, gives $(t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon +s\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n=\det \bigl (t\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )+s\mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\bigr )\eta ^ n$ for the exterior powers of smooth forms. Since $2$-forms commute, the left side can be expanded by the binomial formula. Comparing the coefficients of $\binom nkt^ ks^{n-k}$, and recalling that Bedford–Taylor products of smooth functions are exterior products of smooth forms (proposition 9.1.2 (1)), we find \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^{n-k}=M_ k\bigl (\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon ),\mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\bigr )\eta ^ n\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ k(g^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^{n-k}\eta ^ n,  \] where the inequality is the second assertion of lemma 9.7.1 , applied to the matrices $\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )$ and $\mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )$, which are positive semidefinite by proposition 8.2.2 . As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the density on the right converges locally uniformly to $f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}$, while the left side converges weakly to $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}$ by theorem 9.2.5 , since $u_\varepsilon $ and $v_\varepsilon $ are smooth plurisubharmonic functions decreasing to $u$ and $v$ (proposition 8.2.2 ). $\square$

title: Lemma 9.7.1
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 9.7.1 . Let $A$ be a positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix. Then \[  (\det A)^{1/n}=\inf \left\{ \frac{\operatorname {tr}(BA)}n:\  B\text{ positive definite Hermitian},\  \det B=1\right\} .  \] If $C$ is another positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix, define the numbers $M_ k(A,C)$, $0\le k\le n$, by \[  \det (tA+sC)=\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk M_ k(A,C)\, t^ ks^{n-k}\qquad (t,s\in \mathbb R).  \] Then $M_ n(A,C)=\det A$, $M_0(A,C)=\det C$, and for each integer $1\le k\le n-1$, \[  M_ k(A,C)\ge (\det A)^{k/n}(\det C)^{(n-k)/n}.  \] Proof. Let $B$ be positive definite with $\det B=1$. The positive semidefinite matrix $B^{1/2}AB^{1/2}$ has trace $\operatorname {tr}(BA)$ and determinant $\det A$, so the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for its eigenvalues gives $\operatorname {tr}(BA)/n\ge (\det A)^{1/n}$. If $A$ is positive definite, equality holds for $B=(\det A)^{1/n}A^{-1}$. If $A$ is singular, the matrices $B_\varepsilon =\det (A+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}(A+\varepsilon I)^{-1}$, $\varepsilon >0$, are admissible and \[  0\le \operatorname {tr}(B_\varepsilon A)\le \operatorname {tr}\bigl (B_\varepsilon (A+\varepsilon I)\bigr )=n\det (A+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}\longrightarrow 0  \] as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. The formulas for $M_ n$ and $M_0$ follow from $\det (tA)=t^ n\det A$ and $\det (sC)=s^ n\det C$. Suppose first that $A$ and $C$ are positive definite, and let $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n>0$ be the eigenvalues of $A^{-1/2}CA^{-1/2}$. Since $\det (tA+sC)=\det A\prod _{i=1}^ n(t+s\lambda _ i)$, comparison of coefficients gives \[  M_ k(A,C)=\frac{\det A}{\binom nk}\sum _{|J|=n-k}\prod _{j\in J}\lambda _ j,  \] the sum being over the subsets $J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $ with $n-k$ elements. Each eigenvalue occurs in exactly $\binom {n-1}{n-k-1}$ of these $\binom n{n-k}$ products, so the geometric mean of the products is $(\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ n)^{(n-k)/n}$. Since $\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ n=\det C/\det A$, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  M_ k(A,C)\ge \det A\left(\frac{\det C}{\det A}\right)^{(n-k)/n}=(\det A)^{k/n}(\det C)^{(n-k)/n}.  \] For semidefinite $A$ and $C$, apply this to $A+\varepsilon I$ and $C+\varepsilon I$ and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; both sides depend continuously on the matrices. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.7.2
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 9.7.2 . Let $d\ge 1$, let $(c_{kl})$ be a real symmetric positive definite $d\times d$ matrix, and put $L=\sum _{k,l=1}^ dc_{kl}\partial _ k\partial _ l$. Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, let $w\colon U\to \mathbb R$ be upper semicontinuous, and let $F\colon U\to \mathbb R$ be continuous. Suppose that, for every $x\in U$, every upper test function $q$ for $w$ at $x$ satisfies $Lq(x)\ge F(x)$. Then $w$ is locally integrable, and $Lw\ge F$ in the sense of distributions on $U$. Proof. We reduce to the Laplacian, treat the case $F=0$ by a maximum principle argument, and reduce the general case to it. Step 1. Reduction to $L=\Delta $. Let $C=(c_{kl})$, let $P$ be the positive definite square root of $C^{-1}$, so that $PCP=I$, and put $\tilde U=P(U)$, $\tilde w=w\circ P^{-1}$ and $\tilde F=F\circ P^{-1}$. If $q$ is a $C^2$ function near $x\in U$ and $\tilde q=q\circ P^{-1}$, then $\partial _ k\partial _ lq(x)=\sum _{a,b}P_{ak}P_{bl}(\partial _ a\partial _ b\tilde q)(Px)$ by the chain rule, and hence \[  (Lq)(x)=\sum _{a,b}(PCP)_{ab}(\partial _ a\partial _ b\tilde q)(Px)=(\Delta \tilde q)(Px).  \] The map $q\mapsto \tilde q$ is a bijection from the upper test functions for $w$ at $x$ onto those for $\tilde w$ at $Px$, so $\tilde w$, $\Delta $ and $\tilde F$ satisfy the hypothesis of the lemma on $\tilde U$. Suppose that the lemma holds for them. Then $w=\tilde w\circ P$ is locally integrable, and for every nonnegative test function $\chi $ on $U$ the change of variables $y=Px$, with $\tilde\chi =\chi \circ P^{-1}$ and $L\chi =(\Delta \tilde\chi )\circ P$, gives \[  \langle Lw,\chi \rangle =\int _ Uw\, L\chi \, \mathrm dx =\frac1{|\det P|}\int _{\tilde U}\tilde w\, \Delta \tilde\chi \, \mathrm dy \ge \frac1{|\det P|}\int _{\tilde U}\tilde F\tilde\chi \, \mathrm dy=\int _ UF\chi \, \mathrm dx;  \] the first equality is the definition of distributional derivatives. We may therefore assume that $L=\Delta $. Step 2. The case $F=0$. We show that $w$ satisfies assertion (1) of theorem 3.1.3 for every ball $D=B(y,r)$ with $\overline{B(y,r)}\subset U$; by the converse part of that theorem, $w$ is then subharmonic on $U$. Let $h$ be a real function which is harmonic on $B(y,r)$ and continuous on $\overline{B(y,r)}$, with $\varlimsup _{B(y,r)\ni x\to \zeta }w(x)\le h(\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B(y,r)$, and suppose that $w(x_1)>h(x_1)$ for some $x_1\in B(y,r)$. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that the upper semicontinuous function $g(x)=w(x)-h(x)-\varepsilon (r^2-|x-y|^2)$ on $B(y,r)$ satisfies $g(x_1)>0$. Since $h$ is continuous on the closed ball, $\varlimsup _{B(y,r)\ni x\to \zeta }g(x)\le 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B(y,r)$. Hence every $\zeta \in \partial B(y,r)$ has an open neighborhood $N_\zeta $ with $g<g(x_1)/2$ on $N_\zeta \cap B(y,r)$; finitely many of these neighborhoods cover the sphere, and the complement $K$ of their union in $\overline{B(y,r)}$ is a compact subset of $B(y,r)$ containing $x_1$. The upper semicontinuous function $g$ attains its maximum over $K$ at a point $x_0$, and $c=g(x_0)\ge g(x_1)>0$; since $g<g(x_1)/2$ outside $K$, we have $g\le c$ on $B(y,r)$. The function $q=h+\varepsilon (r^2-|x-y|^2)+c$ is smooth on $B(y,r)$, satisfies $q-w=c-g\ge 0$ there and $q(x_0)=w(x_0)$, so it is an upper test function for $w$ at $x_0$. But $\Delta q=-2d\varepsilon <0$, which contradicts the hypothesis. Hence $w\le h$ on $B(y,r)$, and $w$ is subharmonic on $U$. Being real-valued, it is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $U$, so theorem 3.2.2 (1) shows that $w$ is locally integrable and $\Delta w\ge 0$. Step 3. The general case. Let $V\Subset U$ be open. Every compact subset of $U$ lies in such a set $V$, so it suffices to show that $w$ is locally integrable on $V$ and that $\Delta w\ge F$ on $V$. Choose an open set $V'$ with $\overline V\subset V'\Subset U$. By lemma 1.4.1 (1), the mollifications of $F$ converge to $F$ uniformly on $\overline{V'}$; subtracting from each of them its maximal deviation from $F$ on $\overline{V'}$, we obtain smooth functions $F_ j$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{V'}$ such that $F_ j\le F$ on $\overline{V'}$ and $F_ j\to F$ uniformly there. Let $\vartheta \in C^\infty _ c(V')$ be equal to one on an open set $W\supset \overline V$ (lemma 1.4.1 (4)). By proposition 2.2.1 , the convolution $h_ j=E_ d*(\vartheta F_ j)$, where $\vartheta F_ j$ is extended by zero, is a smooth function on $\mathbb R^ d$ with $\Delta h_ j=\vartheta F_ j$; in particular $\Delta h_ j=F_ j$ on $W$. If $q$ is an upper test function for $w-h_ j$ at $x\in V$, then $q+h_ j$ is an upper test function for $w$ at $x$, so that $\Delta q(x)+F_ j(x)\ge F(x)$, that is, $\Delta q(x)\ge F(x)-F_ j(x)\ge 0$. Step 2, applied to the real upper semicontinuous function $w-h_ j$ on $V$, shows that $w-h_ j$ is locally integrable on $V$ and $\Delta (w-h_ j)\ge 0$ there. Hence $w$ is locally integrable on $V$ and $\Delta w\ge F_ j$ on $V$. Testing against a nonnegative test function on $V$ and letting $j\to \infty $, we obtain $\Delta w\ge F$ on $V$. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.7.3
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Proposition 9.7.3 . Let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $, and let $f\ge 0$ be a continuous function on $\Omega $. The following conditions are equivalent: $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ as measures on $\Omega $; $\det \mathcal H(q)(x)\ge f(x)$ for every $x\in \Omega $ and every upper test function $q$ for $u$ at $x$; $L_ Bu\ge nf^{1/n}$ in the sense of distributions on $\Omega $, for every positive definite Hermitian matrix $B$ with $\det B=1$. If these conditions hold, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ the mollification $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ satisfies $\det \mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. Proof. We first observe that the complex Hessian $\mathcal H(q)(x)$ of an upper test function $q$ for $u$ at $x$ is positive semidefinite. Indeed, let $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, and let $r>0$ be so small that the closed disc $\{ x+\zeta \xi :|\zeta |\le r\} $ lies in the neighborhood of $x$ on which $q\ge u$. Since $q$ is real and of class $C^2$, Taylor's formula gives \[  q(x+h)=q(x)+2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ jq_ j(x)h_ j+\operatorname{Re}\sum _{j,k}q_{jk}(x)h_ jh_ k+\sum _{j,k}q_{j\bar k}(x)h_ j\bar h_ k+o(|h|^2).  \] For $h=r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\xi $ the terms containing $\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }$ and $\mathrm e^{2\mathrm i\theta }$ have mean zero over $\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$, so the right-hand side of the preceding display equals $q(x)+r^2\sum _{j,k}q_{j\bar k}(x)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k+o(r^2)$. Dividing by $r^2$ and letting $r\downarrow 0$, we obtain $\sum _{j,k}q_{j\bar k}(x)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k\ge 0$. (1) implies (2). Assume (1), let $q$ be an upper test function for $u$ at $x$, and suppose that $\det \mathcal H(q)(x)<f(x)$. Since $\mathcal H(q)(x)$ is positive semidefinite, we can choose $\delta >0$ so small that $q_\delta =q+\delta |z-x|^2$ satisfies $\mathcal H(q_\delta )(x)=\mathcal H(q)(x)+\delta I>0$ and still $\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )(x)<f(x)$. Since $q$ is of class $C^2$ and $f$ is continuous, there is $r>0$ such that $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, $q\ge u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$, the complex Hessian $\mathcal H(q_\delta )$ is positive definite on $\overline{B(x,r)}$, and $\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )<f$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$; in particular, $q_\delta $ is plurisubharmonic on $B(x,r)$ by proposition 8.2.2 . Put $b=q_\delta -\delta r^2/2$. Then $b=q+\delta r^2/2>u$ on the sphere $\partial B(x,r)$, while $b(x)=u(x)-\delta r^2/2<u(x)$. The Borel set $S=\{ z\in B(x,r):b(z)<u(z)\} $ has positive Lebesgue measure.
