By Step 1, $\varlimsup _ jv_ j\le v$ everywhere, so $(v_ j-v)_+	o 0$ pointwise. These functions are bounded by $2L$, so $\int (v_ j-v)_+\, \mathrm d
u 	o 0$ by dominated convergence. Since \[  |v_ j-v|=2(v_ j-v)_+-(v_ j-v),  \] Step 2 proves the assertion. Finally, suppose that $
u \le (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ with $w$ bounded and plurisubharmonic on $D$, and put $M=\sup _ Dw-\inf _ Dw$. If $M=0$, then $w$ is constant and $
u =0$. Otherwise $(w-\inf _ Dw)/M$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ (definition 9.3.2 ), whose Monge–Ampère measure is $M^{-n}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$. Hence $
u (A)\leq M^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ D(A)$ for every Borel set $A\subset D$, and $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(A)\le \operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(A)$ because $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ is increasing. If $E$ is as in the hypothesis, then $
u (E\cap K)=0$ for every compact $K\subset D$, and exhausting $D$ by countably many compact sets gives $
u (E)=0$. $\square$ Theorem 9.10.5 . Let $\mu $, $\mu _ j$ and $U_ j$ be as in proposition 9.10.3 . Suppose that a subsequence of $(U_ j)$, relabeled $(U_ j)$ together with the corresponding measures $\mu _ j$, converges in $L^1(B)$, and let $u$ be the plurisubharmonic representative of its limit, which is nonpositive by proposition 9.10.3 . Then $u\in L^2(\mu )$ and 9.49  egin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-self-integral-convergence} \int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu \longrightarrow 0, \qquad \int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} In particular, \[  \int _ B U_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n\longrightarrow \int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Proof. If $m=0$, then $\mu =\mu _ j=0$ and there is nothing to prove. We assume that $m>0$, and use the cubes $Q\in \mathcal Q_ j$, the polydiscs $P(z,r)$ and the estimate ( 9.46 ) of proposition 9.10.3 ; recall that $K$ denotes the support of $\mu $. Step 1. Convergence against the fixed measure $\mu $. By theorem 9.10.2 with $p=2$ and the uniform bound for $e_2(U_ j)$ in proposition 9.10.3 , we have $S=\sup _ j\int _ BU_ j^2\, \mathrm d\mu <\infty $. Fix $T>0$. The truncations $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ are plurisubharmonic with values in $[-T,0]$, and they converge to $\max \{ u,-T\} $ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, since $s\mapsto \max \{ s,-T\} $ is $1$-Lipschitz. The measure $\mu $ satisfies the hypothesis of lemma 9.10.4 , because $\mu \le (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$, so the truncations converge in $L^1(\mu )$. Since $|a^2-b^2|\le 2T|a-b|$ for $a,b\in [-T,0]$, it follows that $\int \max \{ u,-T\} ^2\, \mathrm d\mu \le S$. Letting $T	o \infty $, monotone convergence gives $\int u^2\, \mathrm d\mu \le S$; in particular $u\in L^2(\mu )$, and $u$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. For every measurable $v\le 0$ we have $\int _ B|v-\max \{ v,-T\} |\, \mathrm d\mu \le T^{-1}\int _ Bv^2\, \mathrm d\mu $, because $0\le \max \{ v,-T\} -v\le v^2/T$. Applying this to $v=U_ j$ and $v=u$, and using the convergence of the truncations in $L^1(\mu )$, we get $\varlimsup _ j\int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu \le 2S/T$, and letting $T	o \infty $ proves the first convergence in ( 9.49 ). Step 2. Cube averages. For $z\in K$ let $Q_ j(z)$ be the cube of $\mathcal Q_ j$ containing $z$, and write \[  \mathcal A_ jv(z)= rac1{|Q_ j(z)|}\int _{Q_ j(z)}v\, \mathrm dV  \] for the average over this cube of a function $v$ integrable on it. If $v$ is $\mu _ j$-integrable, then $v$ is integrable on every cube $Q$ with $\mu (Q)>0$; on a cube with $\mu (Q)=0$ on which $v$ is not integrable we set $\mathcal A_ jv=0$, which does not affect integrals against $\mu $. Since $\mu $ is carried by $K$, the definition of $\mu _ j$ gives 9.50  egin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-cell-pairing} \int _ Bv\, \mathrm d\mu _ j=\int _ K\mathcal A_ jv\, \mathrm d\mu . \end{equation} For a plurisubharmonic function $v\le 0$ on $B$ and $z\in K$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the probability measure $\mathrm dV/|Q_ j(z)|$ on $Q_ j(z)$ and ( 9.46 ) with $p=2$ give 9.51  egin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-cell-square} |\mathcal A_ jv(z)|^2 \leq \mathcal A_ j(v^2)(z)\leq D_{n,2}|v(z)|^2; \end{equation} if $v(z)=-\infty $, the right side is infinite. This applies in particular to the possibly unbounded function $u$. Fix $z\in K$ with $u(z)>-\infty $ and $\varepsilon >0$, and put $c=u(z)+2\varepsilon $. By upper semicontinuity of $u$ and Hartogs' lemma (theorem 8.3.4 ), there is a neighborhood of $z$ on which $u\le c$ and $U_ j\le c$ for all large $j$. Since the polydiscs $P(z,4\sqrt2\, h_ j)$ shrink to $z$, for $v=u$ or $v=U_ j$ and all large $j$ the function $v-c$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on $P(z,4\sqrt2\, h_ j)$. Then ( 9.46 ) with $p=1$, applied to $v-c$, gives $\mathcal A_ j(c-v)(z)\le D_{n,1}(c-v(z))$, while $\mathcal A_ jv(z)\le c$ because $v\le c$ on $Q_ j(z)$. Thus, for all large $j$, \[  c-D_{n,1}(c-v(z))\leq \mathcal A_ jv(z)\leq c, \qquad v=u\  	ext{or}\  v=U_ j.  \] Consequently $\mathcal A_ ju(z)	o u(z)$, and $\mathcal A_ jU_ j(z)	o u(z)$ whenever $U_ j(z)	o u(z)$. Indeed, in both cases the lower bound tends to $u(z)+2\varepsilon (1-D_{n,1})$ as $j	o \infty $, the upper bound is $u(z)+2\varepsilon $, and $\varepsilon >0$ is arbitrary. We use the following elementary fact: if Borel functions $F_ j$ on $K$ converge to zero $\mu $-almost everywhere and are bounded in $L^2(\mu )$, then $\int _ K|F_ j|\, \mathrm d\mu 	o 0$. Indeed, for $\varepsilon >0$ the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[  \int _ K|F_ j|\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \varepsilon m+\| F_ j\| _{L^2(\mu )} \mu (\{ |F_ j|>\varepsilon \} )^{1/2},  \] and $\mu (\{ |F_ j|>\varepsilon \} )=\int _ K\mathbf1_{\{ |F_ j|>\varepsilon \} }\, \mathrm d\mu 	o 0$ by dominated convergence; we let first $j	o \infty $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Since $u$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, we have shown that $\mathcal A_ ju	o u$ $\mu $-almost everywhere, so $\mathcal A_ ju	o u$ in $L^1(\mu )$ by the elementary fact. By the monotone convergence theorem, $\sum _ k|U_{j_ k}-u|$ is $\mu $-integrable, hence finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, so $U_{j_ k}	o u$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. The absolute difference. Put $g_ j=\mathcal A_ j((U_ j-u)_+)$ on $K$. Let $z\in K$ with $u(z)>-\infty $, and let $c$ be as in Step 2. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and ( 9.51 ) give \[  g_ j(z)^2\leq 2\mathcal A_ j(U_ j^2)(z) +2\mathcal A_ j(u^2)(z) \leq 2D_{n,2} igl (U_ j(z)^2+u(z)^2 igr ),  \] so the $g_ j$ are bounded in $L^2(\mu )$ by Step 1. text: Theorem 9.10.5 . Let $\mu $, $\mu _ j$ and $U_ j$ be as in proposition 9.10.3 . Suppose that a subsequence of $(U_ j)$, relabeled $(U_ j)$ together with the corresponding measures $\mu _ j$, converges in $L^1(B)$, and let $u$ be the plurisubharmonic representative of its limit, which is nonpositive by proposition 9.10.3 . Then $u\in L^2(\mu )$ and 9.49 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-self-integral-convergence} \int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu \longrightarrow 0, \qquad \int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} In particular, \[  \int _ B U_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n\longrightarrow \int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Proof. If $m=0$, then $\mu =\mu _ j=0$ and there is nothing to prove. We assume that $m>0$, and use the cubes $Q\in \mathcal Q_ j$, the polydiscs $P(z,r)$ and the estimate ( 9.46 ) of proposition 9.10.3 ; recall that $K$ denotes the support of $\mu $. Step 1. Convergence against the fixed measure $\mu $. By theorem 9.10.2 with $p=2$ and the uniform bound for $e_2(U_ j)$ in proposition 9.10.3 , we have $S=\sup _ j\int _ BU_ j^2\, \mathrm d\mu <\infty $. Fix $T>0$. The truncations $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ are plurisubharmonic with values in $[-T,0]$, and they converge to $\max \{ u,-T\} $ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, since $s\mapsto \max \{ s,-T\} $ is $1$-Lipschitz. The measure $\mu $ satisfies the hypothesis of lemma 9.10.4 , because $\mu \le (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$, so the truncations converge in $L^1(\mu )$. Since $|a^2-b^2|\le 2T|a-b|$ for $a,b\in [-T,0]$, it follows that $\int \max \{ u,-T\} ^2\, \mathrm d\mu \le S$. Letting $T\to \infty $, monotone convergence gives $\int u^2\, \mathrm d\mu \le S$; in particular $u\in L^2(\mu )$, and $u$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. For every measurable $v\le 0$ we have $\int _ B|v-\max \{ v,-T\} |\, \mathrm d\mu \le T^{-1}\int _ Bv^2\, \mathrm d\mu $, because $0\le \max \{ v,-T\} -v\le v^2/T$. Applying this to $v=U_ j$ and $v=u$, and using the convergence of the truncations in $L^1(\mu )$, we get $\varlimsup _ j\int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu \le 2S/T$, and letting $T\to \infty $ proves the first convergence in ( 9.49 ). Step 2. Cube averages. For $z\in K$ let $Q_ j(z)$ be the cube of $\mathcal Q_ j$ containing $z$, and write \[  \mathcal A_ jv(z)=\frac1{|Q_ j(z)|}\int _{Q_ j(z)}v\, \mathrm dV  \] for the average over this cube of a function $v$ integrable on it. If $v$ is $\mu _ j$-integrable, then $v$ is integrable on every cube $Q$ with $\mu (Q)>0$; on a cube with $\mu (Q)=0$ on which $v$ is not integrable we set $\mathcal A_ jv=0$, which does not affect integrals against $\mu $. Since $\mu $ is carried by $K$, the definition of $\mu _ j$ gives 9.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-cell-pairing} \int _ Bv\, \mathrm d\mu _ j=\int _ K\mathcal A_ jv\, \mathrm d\mu . \end{equation} For a plurisubharmonic function $v\le 0$ on $B$ and $z\in K$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the probability measure $\mathrm dV/|Q_ j(z)|$ on $Q_ j(z)$ and ( 9.46 ) with $p=2$ give 9.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-cell-square} |\mathcal A_ jv(z)|^2 \leq \mathcal A_ j(v^2)(z)\leq D_{n,2}|v(z)|^2; \end{equation} if $v(z)=-\infty $, the right side is infinite. This applies in particular to the possibly unbounded function $u$. Fix $z\in K$ with $u(z)>-\infty $ and $\varepsilon >0$, and put $c=u(z)+2\varepsilon $. By upper semicontinuity of $u$ and Hartogs' lemma (theorem 8.3.4 ), there is a neighborhood of $z$ on which $u\le c$ and $U_ j\le c$ for all large $j$. Since the polydiscs $P(z,4\sqrt2\, h_ j)$ shrink to $z$, for $v=u$ or $v=U_ j$ and all large $j$ the function $v-c$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on $P(z,4\sqrt2\, h_ j)$. Then ( 9.46 ) with $p=1$, applied to $v-c$, gives $\mathcal A_ j(c-v)(z)\le D_{n,1}(c-v(z))$, while $\mathcal A_ jv(z)\le c$ because $v\le c$ on $Q_ j(z)$. Thus, for all large $j$, \[  c-D_{n,1}(c-v(z))\leq \mathcal A_ jv(z)\leq c, \qquad v=u\  \text{or}\  v=U_ j.  \] Consequently $\mathcal A_ ju(z)\to u(z)$, and $\mathcal A_ jU_ j(z)\to u(z)$ whenever $U_ j(z)\to u(z)$. Indeed, in both cases the lower bound tends to $u(z)+2\varepsilon (1-D_{n,1})$ as $j\to \infty $, the upper bound is $u(z)+2\varepsilon $, and $\varepsilon >0$ is arbitrary. We use the following elementary fact: if Borel functions $F_ j$ on $K$ converge to zero $\mu $-almost everywhere and are bounded in $L^2(\mu )$, then $\int _ K|F_ j|\, \mathrm d\mu \to 0$. Indeed, for $\varepsilon >0$ the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[  \int _ K|F_ j|\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \varepsilon m+\| F_ j\| _{L^2(\mu )} \mu (\{ |F_ j|>\varepsilon \} )^{1/2},  \] and $\mu (\{ |F_ j|>\varepsilon \} )=\int _ K\mathbf1_{\{ |F_ j|>\varepsilon \} }\, \mathrm d\mu \to 0$ by dominated convergence; we let first $j\to \infty $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. By ( 9.51 ) and Step 1, the sequences $(\mathcal A_ jU_ j-u)$ and $(\mathcal A_ ju-u)$ are bounded in $L^2(\mu )$. Since $u$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, we have shown that $\mathcal A_ ju\to u$ $\mu $-almost everywhere, so $\mathcal A_ ju\to u$ in $L^1(\mu )$ by the elementary fact. By the first convergence in ( 9.49 ), every subsequence of $(U_ j)$ has a further subsequence $(U_{j_ k})$ with $\sum _ k\int _ B|U_{j_ k}-u|\, \mathrm d\mu <\infty $. By the monotone convergence theorem, $\sum _ k|U_{j_ k}-u|$ is $\mu $-integrable, hence finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, so $U_{j_ k}\to u$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. By the pointwise convergence proved above, applied along this subsequence, $\mathcal A_{j_ k}U_{j_ k}\to u$ $\mu $-almost everywhere, and hence in $L^1(\mu )$. Consequently the whole sequence $\mathcal A_ jU_ j$ converges to $u$ in $L^1(\mu )$. The function $U_ j-u$ is $\mu _ j$-integrable, since $u$ is locally integrable and $\mu _ j$ has a bounded density with compact support. Therefore ( 9.50 ) gives 9.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-signed-integral} \int _ B(U_ j-u)\, \mathrm d\mu _ j=\int _ K(\mathcal A_ jU_ j-\mathcal A_ ju)\, \mathrm d\mu \longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Step 3. The absolute difference. Put $g_ j=\mathcal A_ j((U_ j-u)_+)$ on $K$. Let $z\in K$ with $u(z)>-\infty $, and let $c$ be as in Step 2. For all large $j$ we have $U_ j\le c$ and $u\le c$ on $Q_ j(z)$, so $(U_ j-u)_+\le c-u$ there, and hence $0\le g_ j(z)\le c-\mathcal A_ ju(z)$. Since $\mathcal A_ ju(z)\to u(z)$, letting $j\to \infty $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $g_ j\to 0$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and ( 9.51 ) give \[  g_ j(z)^2\leq 2\mathcal A_ j(U_ j^2)(z) +2\mathcal A_ j(u^2)(z) \leq 2D_{n,2}\bigl (U_ j(z)^2+u(z)^2\bigr ),  \] so the $g_ j$ are bounded in $L^2(\mu )$ by Step 1. The elementary fact of Step 2 gives $\int _ Kg_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \to 0$, and by ( 9.50 ) this integral equals $\int _ B(U_ j-u)_+\, \mathrm d\mu _ j$. Combining this with ( 9.52 ) and the identity $|U_ j-u|=2(U_ j-u)_+-(U_ j-u)$, we obtain the second convergence in ( 9.49 ). Finally, since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n=\mu _ j$, we have $\int _ BU_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n=\int _ B(U_ j-u)\, \mathrm d\mu _ j+\int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu _ j$. The first term tends to zero by the second convergence in ( 9.49 ), and by ( 9.50 ) and Step 2 the second term equals $\int _ K\mathcal A_ ju\, \mathrm d\mu $, which tends to $\int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu $. This proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: 9.10.2 Capacity convergence and truncated measures
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text:
9.10.2 Capacity convergence and truncated measures In theorem 9.9.2 , a common bound for the densities forced the solutions to converge in capacity, and theorem 9.4.8 then identified the limiting equation. The canonical approximants $U_ j$ of proposition 9.10.3 have no such bound unless $\mu $ itself has a bounded density, since a bound $\mu _ j\leq M\, \mathrm dV$ for all $j$ would pass to the weak limit $\mu $; nor are the functions $U_ j$ uniformly bounded. We show that the convergence of the energy integrals in theorem 9.10.5 takes the place of the density bound once we pass to the uniformly bounded truncations $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $, whose Monge–Ampère measures differ from $\mu _ j$ by an error controlled by the energy (lemma 9.10.7 ). Thus a subsequence of canonical approximants that converges in $L^1(B)$ also converges locally in capacity, and the Monge–Ampère measures of the truncations of its limit approximate $\mu $ in total variation (theorem 9.10.9 ). As throughout this section, $B$ is a ball in $\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$. For finite positive Borel measures $
u _1,
u _2$ on $B$ we use the total variation distance \[  \| 
u _1-
u _2\| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\sup \left\{ \left|\int _ Bf\, \mathrm d(
u _1-
u _2)ight|: f	ext{ real Borel},\  |f|\leq 1ight\} .  \] The supremum does not change if $f$ ranges only over the real functions in $C_ c(B)$ with $|f|\leq 1$. Indeed, given a real Borel function $f$ with $|f|\leq 1$, proposition 1.2.3 provides functions in $C_ c(B)$ converging to $f$ in $L^1(
u _1+
u _2)$, which we may take real by passing to real parts; clamping them to $[-1,1]$ keeps them in $C_ c(B)$ and does not increase their distance from $f$. Let $T>0$ and $\delta >0$, and let $f,g$ be functions on $B$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. Then 9.53  egin{equation} \label{eq:truncation-level-inclusions}  egin{aligned}   igl \{ \max \{ f,-T\} >\max \{ g,-T\} +\delta  igr \} & \subset \{ f>g+\delta \} ,\   igl \{ \max \{ f,-T\} <\max \{ g,-T\} -\delta  igr \} & \subset \{ f<g-\delta \} . \end{aligned} \end{equation} Indeed, at a point of the first set we have $\max \{ f,-T\} >-T$, so $f=\max \{ f,-T\} >\max \{ g,-T\} +\delta \geq g+\delta $; the second inclusion is the first with $f$ and $g$ interchanged. Consequently, truncation at a fixed level preserves convergence locally in capacity (definition 9.4.5 ): if $f_ j	o f$, then $\max \{ f_ j,-T\} 	o \max \{ f,-T\} $. Modifying a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on a compact set does not change its total Monge–Ampère mass. Lemma 9.10.6 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, and let $\varphi ,\psi $ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ which coincide outside a compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$ agree on $\Omega \setminus K$ and assign the same finite mass to $K$. We pass this bound to the limit $u$. Since the $\varphi _ j$ are nonpositive, $u\leq 0$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by the submean inequality. Fix $S>0$. The truncations $\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} $ take values in $[-S,0]$ and converge to the plurisubharmonic function $\max \{ u,-S\} $ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, since $t\mapsto \max \{ t,-S\} $ is $1$-Lipschitz. Since $\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$, lemma 9.10.4 shows that they also converge in $L^1(\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n)$. As $t\mapsto t^ p$ is Lipschitz on $[0,S]$ and $(-\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} )^ p\leq (-\varphi _ j)^ p$, it follows that \[   egin{aligned}  \int _ L(-\max \{ u,-S\} )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n & =\lim _{j	o \infty }\int _ L(-\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\ & \leq C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}. \end{aligned}  \] Letting $S	o \infty $, monotone convergence gives the same bound for $\int _ L(-u)^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$. The set $U\cap \{ u<-T\} $ is open, because $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and it contains $K\cap \{ u<-T\} $. By Chebyshev's inequality its $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$-measure is at most $C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}T^{-p}$. Taking the supremum over $h$ bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(U\cap \{ u<-T\} )$, and hence the outer capacity in ( 9.58 ). Finally, $K\cap \{ u=-\infty \} $ is contained in $K\cap \{ u<-T\} $ for every $T$, so letting $T	o \infty $ shows that it has zero outer capacity. $\square$

text: Theorem 9.10.9 . Under the hypotheses of theorem 9.10.5 , the relabeled subsequence $U_ j$ converges to $u$ locally in capacity. Moreover, let $E_2=\sup _ je_2(U_ j)$, which is finite by proposition 9.10.3 . For every $T>0$, the Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ T=\max \{ u,-T\} $ has total mass at most $m$, and 9.61 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-truncated-measure-limit} \| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}. \end{equation} Proof. We estimate the capacities of the sets where the truncation $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ lies far below or far above $u_ T$ (Steps 1 and 2) and deduce convergence in capacity (Step 3). The estimate for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ then follows from the convergence of the truncated measures (Step 4). Fix $T>0$ and write $a_ j=\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ and $b=u_ T$. These plurisubharmonic functions take values in $[-T,0]$, and $a_ j\to b$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$ because truncation is $1$-Lipschitz. By theorem 9.10.5 , $\varepsilon _ j=\int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\to 0$. Step 1. The sets where $a_ j<b-\delta $. Let $\delta >0$. The set $\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} $ is relatively compact in $B$, because $b\leq 0$ while $a_ j$ tends to zero at $\partial B$. Applying lemma 9.9.1 with $s=t=\delta /2$ and then Chebyshev's inequality, we obtain \[  \begin{aligned}  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} ) & \leq \left(\frac2\delta \right)^ n\int _{\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n\\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}\int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n. \end{aligned}  \] The weight $(b-a_ j)_+$ takes values in $[0,T]$, and it is at most $|U_ j-u|$, since truncation does not increase distances. By ( 9.56 ) with $p=2$, $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n-\mu _ j\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}$, where $\mu _ j=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n$. Hence \[  \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n \leq \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+\, \mathrm d\mu _ j+T\cdot 2E_2T^{-2} \leq \varepsilon _ j+\frac{2E_2}T,  \] and therefore $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} )\leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}(\varepsilon _ j+2E_2/T)$. Step 2. The sets where $a_ j>b+\delta $. Let $L\subset B$ be compact. By theorem 9.4.2 , for every $\sigma >0$ there is an open set $G\subset B$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)<\sigma $ such that $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$. We claim that $L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} \subset G$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Let $z\in L\setminus G$. Since $b$ is upper semicontinuous, $b<b(z)+\delta /3$ on a closed ball $\overline{B(z,r)}\subset B$. Hartogs' lemma (theorem 8.3.4 ), applied to the sequence $a_ j$ with the constant majorant $b(z)+\delta /3$, gives $a_ j<b(z)+\delta /3$ on $\overline{B(z,r)}$ for all large $j$. Since $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$, after shrinking $r$ we also have $b>b(z)-\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$. Hence $a_ j-b<2\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$ for all large $j$. As $L\setminus G$ is compact, finitely many such balls cover it, which proves the claim. Consequently $\varlimsup _ j\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )\leq \sigma $ for every $\sigma >0$, that is, $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )\to 0$. Step 3. Convergence in capacity. Let $K\subset B$ be compact, and apply Step 2 to a compact set $L\subset B$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$. The bounded functions $a_ j-b$ are quasi-continuous by theorem 9.4.2 and the remark following definition 9.4.1 . Therefore lemma 9.4.4 , together with Steps 1 and 2 applied with $\delta /2$ in place of $\delta $, gives \[  \begin{aligned} & \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ |a_ j-b|>\delta \} )\\ & \qquad \leq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\bigl (\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta /2\} ) +\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} )\bigr )\\ & \qquad \leq 2^{2n+3}\delta ^{-(n+1)}\frac{E_2}T. \end{aligned}  \] It remains to remove the truncation. Outside $\{ U_ j<-T\} \cup \{ u<-T\} $ we have $a_ j=U_ j$ and $b=u$. Hence both sets $K\cap \{ U_ j>u+\delta \} $ and $K\cap \{ U_ j<u-\delta \} $ in definition 9.4.5 are contained in \[  \bigl (K\cap \{ |a_ j-b|>\delta \} \bigr )\cup \{ U_ j<-T\} \cup \bigl (K\cap \{ u<-T\} \bigr ).  \] By proposition 9.10.8 with $p=2$, applied in part (1) to $U_ j$, whose energy is at most $E_2$, and in part (2) to the sequence $(U_ j)$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ U_ j<-T\} )\leq \frac{2^{n+2}(n+1)!\, E_2}{T^{n+2}},\qquad \operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ u<-T\} )\leq \frac{C_{K,2}E_2^{2/(n+2)}}{T^2},  \] and the capacity of the open set $\{ U_ j<-T\} $ equals its outer capacity. By subadditivity of the outer capacity, the upper limits as $j\to \infty $ of the outer capacities of the two sets in definition 9.4.5 are bounded by the sum of three terms, each of which tends to zero as $T\to \infty $. Since these upper limits do not depend on $T$, they vanish. Thus $U_ j\to u$ locally in capacity. Step 4. The truncated limit measure. Fix $T>0$ again. By Step 3 and ( 9.53 ), the uniformly bounded functions $a_ j$ converge to $b$ locally in capacity, so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n\to (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ weakly on $B$ by theorem 9.4.8 . By lemma 9.10.7 , each $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n$ has total mass $\mu _ j(B)=m$. Testing with functions $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, and letting $\chi $ increase to one, we see that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ has total mass at most $m$. Moreover, ( 9.56 ) gives \[  \left|\int _ B\chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n-\int _ B\chi \, \mathrm d\mu _ j\right|\leq 2E_2T^{-2}  \] for every real $\chi \in C_ c(B)$ with $|\chi |\leq 1$. Since $\mu _ j\to \mu $ weakly by proposition 9.10.3 , letting $j\to \infty $ yields the same bound with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ and $\mu $ in place of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n$ and $\mu _ j$. Both limit measures are finite, so by the remark following the definition of the total variation distance, the supremum over such $\chi $ equals $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}$. This proves ( 9.61 ). $\square$

u _\varepsilon (\{ U_ j<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} ) \leq \mu _ j(\{ U_ j<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} ).  \] Let $j	o \infty $ and put $S=\{ u<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} $. By ( 9.68 ), \[  \mu (S)+\varepsilon ^ n\int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n\leq 
u _\varepsilon (S)\leq \mu (S).  \] Since $\mu (S)$ is finite, $S$ has Lebesgue measure zero. Thus $u\geq W_\varepsilon -\delta $ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere, by the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 applied to $\max \{ u,W_\varepsilon -\delta \} $ and $u$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ through admissible values and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain $W\leq u\leq 0$. As $W$ has zero boundary values, $u$ is bounded and has zero boundary values. For $T>\| u\| _\infty $ the truncation $\max \{ u,-T\} $ is $u$ itself, so ( 9.61 ) gives $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}$ for all large $T$. Hence $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu $. In particular $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ has finite mass $m$, and $u\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Step 4. Uniqueness and convergence of the whole sequence. Let $v$ be a bounded plurisubharmonic function on $B$ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq \mu $ and upper boundary limits at most zero, and put $v_\varepsilon =v+\varepsilon ho $ for $\varepsilon >0$. As in Step 1, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n\geq \mu +\varepsilon ^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n$. If one of the asserted convergences failed for the whole sequence, some subsequence would stay away from the stated limit, and no further subsequence could converge as just described. This contradiction proves all the assertions. $\square$

title: 9.10.4 Mixed energy and truncation
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: 9.10.4 Mixed energy and truncation In the next section we approximate several potentials at once by canonical approximants and pass to the limit in their mixed Monge–Ampère products. The approximants converge in capacity and have bounded energies, but we have no uniform bound for them, so theorem 9.4.8 does not apply to them directly. We therefore compare the mixed products with those of the truncated potentials, and for this we need to know that the sets where one of the potentials is very negative carry little mass of a mixed product. This follows from the mixed energy inequality of theorem 9.10.13 , which bounds a mixed energy by a constant multiple of the geometric mean of the energies $e_1$ of definition 9.10.1 . Theorem 9.10.13 . Let $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Then 9.69 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-mixed-local-energy} \int _ B(-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n \leq C_ n\prod _{l=0}^ n e_1(u_ l)^{1/(n+1)}, \qquad C_ n=2^{n+2}. \end{equation} In particular the integral is finite, and it vanishes if one of the energies $e_1(u_ l)$ vanishes. Proof. Write $B=B(a,R)$ and $\rho (z)=|z-a|^2-R^2$. We say that $v\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ has a quadratic collar if $v=c\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ in $B$ for some constant $c>0$. We first prove the inequality with constant one for potentials with quadratic collars (Steps 1 and 2), and then approximate arbitrary elements of $\mathcal E_0(B)$ by such potentials while keeping their energies under control (Steps 3 and 4). For functions $b_0,\ldots ,b_ n$ which either all have quadratic collars, or are smooth real functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ with $b_2,\ldots ,b_ n$ plurisubharmonic, put \[  I(b_0,\ldots ,b_ n) =\int _ B(-b_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ n.  \] The integral is finite: in the first case every mixed product of the $b_ l$ is smooth near $\partial B$ and locally finite on the rest of $B$, and in the second the integrand is a smooth form on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Step 1. Smooth functions. Let $b_0,\ldots ,b_ n$ be smooth real functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, with $b_2,\ldots ,b_ n$ plurisubharmonic and $b_0=0$ on $\partial B$, and put $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ n$, with $S=1$ if $n=1$. With $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ as in ( 7.6 ), we claim that 9.70 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-local-energy-gradient-form} I(b_0,b_1,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n) =\int _ B\mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S. \end{equation} Fix a smooth function $\theta \colon \mathbb R\to [0,1]$ with $\theta =1$ on $(-\infty ,-2]$ and $\theta =0$ on $[-1,\infty )$, and put $\chi _ k=\theta (k\rho )$ for $k\geq 1$; then $\chi _ k\in C^\infty _ c(B)$. The $(2n-1)$-form $\chi _ kb_0\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ is smooth with compact support in $B$, and $S$ is closed, so proposition 7.1.3 and the Leibniz rule give \[  0=\int _ B\chi _ k\, \mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S +\int _ Bb_0\, \mathrm d\chi _ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S +\int _ B\chi _ kb_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge S.  \] As $k\to \infty $, $\chi _ k\to 1$ pointwise on $B$, and the forms $\mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ and $b_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge S$ have bounded coefficients on $B$; by dominated convergence, the first and the last integral tend to $\int _ B\mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ and $-I(b_0,\ldots ,b_ n)$. In the middle integral, $\mathrm d\chi _ k=k\theta '(k\rho )\, \mathrm d\rho $ vanishes outside the set where $-2\leq k\rho \leq -1$. Let $\Lambda $ be the maximum of $|\nabla b_0|$ on $\overline B$. If $z\in B$ and $\zeta \in \partial B$ is a nearest boundary point, then $b_0(\zeta )=0$ and $|z-\zeta |=R-|z-a|$, so the mean value theorem on the segment from $z$ to $\zeta $ gives \[  |b_0(z)|\leq \Lambda (R-|z-a|)\leq \frac{\Lambda }{R}(R^2-|z-a|^2)=\frac{\Lambda }{R}|\rho (z)|.  \] Hence $|b_0\, k\theta '(k\rho )|\leq (\Lambda /R)|k\rho |\, |\theta '(k\rho )|\leq 2\Lambda \sup |\theta '|/R$ on $B$, uniformly in $k$, and $b_0\, k\theta '(k\rho )\to 0$ pointwise on $B$. Since $\mathrm d\rho \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ has bounded coefficients on $B$, dominated convergence shows that the middle integral tends to zero. This proves ( 9.70 ). As observed at the beginning of section 9.2 , $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}c\wedge S=\mathrm dc\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge S$ for smooth real $b,c$. Moreover, $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b=(\mathrm i/2\pi )\partial b\wedge \bar\partial b$ is a positive $(1,1)$-form, and so are the forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ l$, $l\geq 2$, since the complex Hessian of a smooth plurisubharmonic function is positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 ). Positive $(1,1)$-forms are strongly positive (section 7.2 ), so by proposition 7.2.1 the $(n,n)$-form $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge S$ is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form. Consequently the real bilinear form \[  Q(b,c)=\int _ B\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}c\wedge S,  \] defined for smooth real functions $b,c$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ vanishing on $\partial B$, is symmetric and positive semidefinite, and by ( 9.70 ) we have $Q(b,c)=I(b,c,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n)$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for $Q$, which follows from the nonnegativity of the quadratic polynomial $t\mapsto Q(b+tc,b+tc)$, therefore gives 9.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-local-energy-two-slot} I(b,c,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n)^2 \leq I(b,b,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n)I(c,c,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n). \end{equation} The symmetry of $Q$ allows us to interchange the first two arguments of $I$, and the symmetry of the products allows us to permute the last $n$ arguments. Hence $I$ is symmetric in all $n+1$ arguments when they are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ vanishing on $\partial B$. Step 2. Quadratic collars. Let $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n$ have quadratic collars, say $u_ l=c_ l\rho $ near $\partial B$. We first show that the assertions of Step 1 persist for them. Extend each $u_ l$ by $c_ l\rho $ to a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\vartheta _\varepsilon $ be the radial mollifiers of section 1.4 , denoted $\rho _\varepsilon $ there; we change the letter because $\rho $ is now the quadratic function above. Because $\rho $ is a quadratic polynomial and $\vartheta _\varepsilon $ is radial, $\rho *\vartheta _\varepsilon =\rho +\gamma \varepsilon ^2$ with the constant $\gamma =\int |y|^2\vartheta _1(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)$. Hence \[  u_{l,\varepsilon }=u_ l*\vartheta _\varepsilon -c_ l\gamma \varepsilon ^2  \] equals $c_ l\rho $ on a fixed neighborhood of $\partial B$ for all small $\varepsilon $. By proposition 8.2.2 , the convolutions $u_ l*\vartheta _\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ for small $\varepsilon $, and they decrease to $u_ l$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Hence each $u_{l,\varepsilon }$, which differs from $u_ l*\vartheta _\varepsilon $ by a constant, is smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ and vanishes on $\partial B$, although the $u_{l,\varepsilon }$ need not decrease. By theorem 9.2.5 , \[  (-u_0*\vartheta _\varepsilon )\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,\varepsilon }\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,\varepsilon } \longrightarrow (-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n  \] weakly, and the constant $c_0\gamma \varepsilon ^2$ changes the integral against a fixed test function only by an amount tending to zero, by the local mass bounds of theorem 9.1.3 . Near $\partial B$, all the $u_{l,\varepsilon }$ and $u_ l$ coincide with $c_ l\rho $. Splitting the integrals over $B$ by a cutoff in $C_ c(B)$ which equals one outside this neighborhood of $\partial B$, we conclude that $I(u_{0,\varepsilon },\ldots ,u_{n,\varepsilon })\to I(u_0,\ldots ,u_ n)$, and likewise for every rearrangement of the potentials. Passing to the limit in the smooth case proves that $I$ is symmetric and satisfies ( 9.71 ) for potentials with quadratic collars. We now prove the inequality with constant one for these potentials. Since $u_ l=c_ l\rho $ near $\partial B$ with $c_ l>0$, the energy $e_1(u_ l)$ is positive: already its integral over a neighborhood of $\partial B$ is positive. Since $I$ is positively homogeneous of degree one in each argument and $e_1(tv)=t^{n+1}e_1(v)$ for $t>0$, both sides of the inequality are multiplied by the same factor when each $u_ l$ is replaced by $e_1(u_ l)^{-1/(n+1)}u_ l$. We may therefore assume that $e_1(u_ l)=1$ for every $l$. Consider the finitely many ordered $(n+1)$-tuples whose entries are taken from the functions $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n$, and let $F$ be the largest value of $I$ on these tuples. Since $I(u_ l,\ldots ,u_ l)=e_1(u_ l)=1$, we have $F\geq 1$. Among the tuples on which $I$ equals $F$, choose one for which the sum of the squares of the multiplicities of its distinct entries is largest. Suppose that this tuple contains two distinct functions $b$ and $c$, with multiplicities $r$ and $s$. By symmetry we may place them in the first two slots. In ( 9.71 ), the left side is $F^2$, while the two factors on the right are nonnegative values of $I$ on tuples of our family, hence at most $F$. Therefore both factors equal $F$. Replacing one entry $c$ by $b$ changes the sum of the squares of the multiplicities by $(r+1)^2+(s-1)^2-r^2-s^2=2(r-s)+2$, and replacing one entry $b$ by $c$ changes it by $2(s-r)+2$. One of these numbers is positive, which contradicts the choice of the tuple. Hence the chosen tuple consists of a single function repeated $n+1$ times, and $F=1$. In particular $I(u_0,\ldots ,u_ n)\leq 1$, which is the inequality with constant one. Step 3. Approximation with controlled energy. Let $u\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, put $m_\rho =\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n$, and for $j\geq 1$ let \[  \delta _ j=j^{-n-1},\qquad v_ j=\max \{ u-\delta _ j,j\rho \} .  \] Since $u-\delta _ j\leq -\delta _ j$ while $j\rho >-\delta _ j$ near $\partial B$, the function $v_ j$ equals $j\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ in $B$. Since $v_ j$ and $j\rho $ coincide outside a compact subset of $B$, lemma 9.10.6 gives $\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n=j^ nm_\rho $, and hence $v_ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Moreover, $v_ j\to u$ uniformly on $B$. Indeed, let $s>0$, and choose a neighborhood $V$ of $\partial B$ with $u>-s$ on $V\cap B$. Since $u-\delta _ j\leq v_ j\leq 0$, we have $|v_ j-u|\leq s+\delta _ j$ on $V\cap B$. On the set $B\setminus V$, whose closure is a compact subset of $B$, the function $\rho $ is bounded away from zero and $u$ is bounded, so $j\rho <u-\delta _ j$, and hence $v_ j=u-\delta _ j$, there for all large $j$. Next we estimate $e_1(v_ j)$. Let $t>4\delta _ j$. Since $u\leq v_ j+\delta _ j$ and $v_ j\leq 0$, \[  \{ v_ j<-t\} \subset \{ u<v_ j/2-t/4\}  \subset \{ u<-t/4\} ;  \] for the first inclusion note that on $\{ v_ j<-t\} $ we have $v_ j/2<-t/2<-t/4-\delta _ j$, hence $u\leq v_ j+\delta _ j<v_ j/2-t/4$. As $u$ tends to $0$ and $v_ j/2-t/4$ tends to $-t/4$ at $\partial B$, the comparison theorem (theorem 9.2.8 ) applies to $u$ and $v_ j/2-t/4$ and gives \[  \int _{\{ v_ j<-t\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n \leq 2^ n\int _{\{ u<v_ j/2-t/4\} }\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ j/2)\bigr )^ n \leq 2^ n\int _{\{ u<-t/4\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n.  \] For $0<t\leq 4\delta _ j$ we use the total mass $j^ nm_\rho $ instead. The general case. Apply the construction of Step 3 to each $u_ l$, obtaining functions $v_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ which equal $j\rho $ near $\partial B$. They are uniformly bounded, since $u_ l-1\leq v_{l,j}\leq 0$, and they converge uniformly, hence locally in capacity, to $u_ l$. Let $\chi \in C_ c(B)$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. The weight $-u_0$ is bounded and quasi-continuous (theorem 9.4.2 ), so the weighted form of theorem 9.4.8 and Step 2 give \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ B\chi (-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n & =\lim _{j\to \infty }\int _ B\chi (-v_{0,j})\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{n,j}\\ & \leq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(v_{l,j})^{1/(n+1)}. \end{aligned}  \] By ( 9.72 ), the right side is at most \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ n\left(\frac{4m_\rho }j+C_ ne_1(u_ l)\right)^{1/(n+1)} =C_ n\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(u_ l)^{1/(n+1)}.  \] Letting $\chi $ increase to one proves ( 9.69 ). Vanishing energies need no separate treatment, since the energies of the $v_{l,j}$ are positive. $\square$ Corollary 9.10.14 . Let $E\geq 0$, and for $1\leq l\leq n$ and $j\geq 1$ let $u_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ with $e_1(u_{l,j})\leq E$. Suppose that, for each $l$, $u_{l,j}\to u_ l$ locally in capacity as $j\to \infty $, where $u_ l$ is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $B$. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j} \longrightarrow \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n  \] weakly on $B$. Proof. We compare the products with those of the truncations at a level $-T$: the latter converge by theorem 9.4.8 , and by theorem 9.10.13 the two differ by a term of order $1/T$. For $T>0$ put $a_{l,j}=\max \{ u_{l,j},-T\} $, and write \[  R_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j},\qquad R_{j,T}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{n,j}.  \] By lemma 9.10.7 , $a_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and $e_1(a_{l,j})\leq E$. For each $l$, theorem 9.10.13 with $u_0=u_{l,j}$, respectively $u_0=a_{l,j}$, gives \[  \int _ B(-u_{l,j})\, R_ j\leq C_ nE,\qquad \int _ B(-a_{l,j})\, R_{j,T}\leq C_ nE.  \] Let $D_{j,T}=\bigcup _{l=1}^ n\{ u_{l,j}\leq -T\} $. On $\{ u_{l,j}\leq -T\} $ both $-u_{l,j}$ and $-a_{l,j}$ are at least $T$, so Chebyshev's inequality gives \[  R_ j(D_{j,T})\leq nC_ nE/T,\qquad R_{j,T}(D_{j,T})\leq nC_ nE/T.  \] On the complement of $D_{j,T}$, every $u_{l,j}$ is greater than $-T$. For $0\leq k\leq n$ put \[  P_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{k,j}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k+1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j},  \] so that $P_0=R_ j$ and $P_ n=R_{j,T}$. By the symmetry of the products, $P_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{k,j}\wedge \Theta _ k$ and $P_{k-1}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k,j}\wedge \Theta _ k$ with the same closed positive current $\Theta _ k$ formed by the other $n-1$ factors, and maximum locality (proposition 9.2.7 with $p=1$, $u=u_{k,j}$, $v=-T$ and base current $\Theta _ k$) gives $P_ k=P_{k-1}$ on $\{ u_{k,j}>-T\} $. Hence $R_ j=R_{j,T}$ on the complement of $D_{j,T}$, and for every $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, \[  \left|\int _ B\chi \, (R_ j-R_{j,T})\right| \leq 2nC_ nE\| \chi \| _\infty /T.  \] Now fix $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, choose an open set $B'\Subset B$ containing $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and let $T>\max _ l\sup _{B'}|u_ l|$. By ( 9.53 ), the uniformly bounded functions $a_{l,j}$ converge to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\max \{ u_ l,-T\} $ locally in capacity, and theorem 9.4.8 shows that $R_{j,T}\to \bigwedge _ l\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u_ l,-T\} $ weakly on $B$. On $B'$ we have $\max \{ u_ l,-T\} =u_ l$, so by locality (proposition 9.1.2 ) this limit equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n$ there. Consequently \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\left|\int _ B\chi \, R_ j-\int _ B\chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n\right|\leq 2nC_ nE\| \chi \| _\infty /T  \] for all large $T$, and letting $T\to \infty $ completes the proof. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.10.13
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations

Integrating over $t$ by the layer-cake formula $e_1(v)=\int _0^\infty (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n(\{ v<-t\} )\, \mathrm dt$, we obtain 9.72 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-collar-energy-approximation} e_1(v_ j)\leq 4\delta _ j j^ n m_\rho +2^{n+2}e_1(u) =\frac{4m_\rho }j+C_ ne_1(u). \end{equation} Step 4. The general case. Apply the construction of Step 3 to each $u_ l$, obtaining functions $v_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ which equal $j\rho $ near $\partial B$. They are uniformly bounded, since $u_ l-1\leq v_{l,j}\leq 0$, and they converge uniformly, hence locally in capacity, to $u_ l$. Let $\chi \in C_ c(B)$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. The weight $-u_0$ is bounded and quasi-continuous (theorem 9.4.2 ), so the weighted form of theorem 9.4.8 and Step 2 give \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ B\chi (-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n & =\lim _{j\to \infty }\int _ B\chi (-v_{0,j})\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{n,j}\\ & \leq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(v_{l,j})^{1/(n+1)}. \end{aligned}  \] By ( 9.72 ), the right side is at most \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ n\left(\frac{4m_\rho }j+C_ ne_1(u_ l)\right)^{1/(n+1)} =C_ n\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(u_ l)^{1/(n+1)}.  \] Letting $\chi $ increase to one proves ( 9.69 ). Vanishing energies need no separate treatment, since the energies of the $v_{l,j}$ are positive. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.10.14
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Corollary 9.10.14 . Let $E\geq 0$, and for $1\leq l\leq n$ and $j\geq 1$ let $u_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ with $e_1(u_{l,j})\leq E$. Suppose that, for each $l$, $u_{l,j}\to u_ l$ locally in capacity as $j\to \infty $, where $u_ l$ is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $B$. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j} \longrightarrow \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n  \] weakly on $B$. Proof. We compare the products with those of the truncations at a level $-T$: the latter converge by theorem 9.4.8 , and by theorem 9.10.13 the two differ by a term of order $1/T$. For $T>0$ put $a_{l,j}=\max \{ u_{l,j},-T\} $, and write \[  R_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j},\qquad R_{j,T}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{n,j}.  \] By lemma 9.10.7 , $a_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and $e_1(a_{l,j})\leq E$. For each $l$, theorem 9.10.13 with $u_0=u_{l,j}$, respectively $u_0=a_{l,j}$, gives \[  \int _ B(-u_{l,j})\, R_ j\leq C_ nE,\qquad \int _ B(-a_{l,j})\, R_{j,T}\leq C_ nE.  \] Let $D_{j,T}=\bigcup _{l=1}^ n\{ u_{l,j}\leq -T\} $. On $\{ u_{l,j}\leq -T\} $ both $-u_{l,j}$ and $-a_{l,j}$ are at least $T$, so Chebyshev's inequality gives \[  R_ j(D_{j,T})\leq nC_ nE/T,\qquad R_{j,T}(D_{j,T})\leq nC_ nE/T.  \] On the complement of $D_{j,T}$, every $u_{l,j}$ is greater than $-T$. For $0\leq k\leq n$ put \[  P_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{k,j}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k+1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j},  \] so that $P_0=R_ j$ and $P_ n=R_{j,T}$. By the symmetry of the products, $P_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{k,j}\wedge \Theta _ k$ and $P_{k-1}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k,j}\wedge \Theta _ k$ with the same closed positive current $\Theta _ k$ formed by the other $n-1$ factors, and maximum locality (proposition 9.2.7 with $p=1$, $u=u_{k,j}$, $v=-T$ and base current $\Theta _ k$) gives $P_ k=P_{k-1}$ on $\{ u_{k,j}>-T\} $. Hence $R_ j=R_{j,T}$ on the complement of $D_{j,T}$, and for every $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, \[  \left|\int _ B\chi \, (R_ j-R_{j,T})\right| \leq 2nC_ nE\| \chi \| _\infty /T.  \] Now fix $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, choose an open set $B'\Subset B$ containing $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and let $T>\max _ l\sup _{B'}|u_ l|$. By ( 9.53 ), the uniformly bounded functions $a_{l,j}$ converge to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\max \{ u_ l,-T\} $ locally in capacity, and theorem 9.4.8 shows that $R_{j,T}\to \bigwedge _ l\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u_ l,-T\} $ weakly on $B$. On $B'$ we have $\max \{ u_ l,-T\} =u_ l$, so by locality (proposition 9.1.2 ) this limit equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n$ there. Consequently \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\left|\int _ B\chi \, R_ j-\int _ B\chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n\right|\leq 2nC_ nE\| \chi \| _\infty /T  \] for all large $T$, and letting $T\to \infty $ completes the proof. $\square$

title: 9.11 Mixed products for a common measure

9.11 Mixed products for a common measure Corollary 9.7.6 bounds a mixed Monge–Ampère product from below when the pure Monge–Ampère measures of the factors have continuous lower densities with respect to Lebesgue measure. For non-pluripolar products in chapter 15 we need the same inequality relative to an arbitrary positive Radon measure $\mu $, which may be singular with respect to Lebesgue measure. Instead of regularizing the potentials by convolution, as in the proof of that corollary, we restrict each pure Monge–Ampère measure to a compact set and replace it by its cube averages, as in proposition 9.10.3 . The averaged measures have piecewise constant densities, so the case of Lebesgue measure applies on each cube, and Hölder's inequality compares the resulting bound with the cube averages of the expected lower bound. The convergence results of section 9.10 then allow us to pass to the limit. Theorem 9.11.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$, and let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $. Let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $\Omega $, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ n$ be nonnegative Borel functions on $\Omega $. If \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n\geq f_ i\mu \qquad (1\leq i\leq n),  \] then 9.75  egin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-multifactor-common-measure} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n \geq \left(\prod _{i=1}^ nf_ i^{1/n}ight)\mu . \end{equation} For $n=1$ the assertion is the hypothesis. Proof. Let $n\geq 2$, and put $\lambda =(\prod _ if_ i^{1/n})\mu $. We first prove the theorem when $\Omega $ is a ball $B=B(a_0,R)$ and all $u_ i$ belong to $\mathcal E_0(B)$ (Steps 1 and 2), and then reduce the general case to this one by modifying the potentials near the boundary of a ball (Step 3). For a ball $B=B(a_0,R)$ we write $ho (z)=|z-a_0|^2-R^2$. We use the generalized Hölder inequality 9.76  egin{equation} \label{eq:generalized-holder-geometric-mean} \int _ A\prod _{i=1}^ ng_ i^{1/n}\, \mathrm d
u \leq \prod _{i=1}^ n\Bigl (\int _ Ag_ i\, \mathrm d
u \Bigr )^{1/n} \end{equation} for a positive measure $
u $, a measurable set $A$ and nonnegative measurable functions $g_ i$. If one of the integrals $c_ i=\int _ Ag_ i\, \mathrm d
u $ vanishes, then $g_ i=0$ $
u $-almost everywhere on $A$ and both sides vanish, with the convention $0\cdot \infty =0$; if none vanishes and one is infinite, the right side is infinite. Otherwise, integrating the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality $\prod _ i(g_ i/c_ i)^{1/n}\leq  rac1n\sum _ ig_ i/c_ i$ over $A$ gives $\int _ A\prod _ i(g_ i/c_ i)^{1/n}\, \mathrm d
u \leq 1$, which is ( 9.76 ). For every compact $K\subset \Omega $ we have $\int _ Kf_ i\, \mathrm d\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n(K)<\infty $ by hypothesis, so ( 9.76 ) shows that $\lambda $ is a positive Radon measure. Step 1. Exhaustion by compactly supported measures. Choose closed balls $K_ l\subset B$ concentric with $B$, increasing with $l$ and exhausting $B$, and set \[  \alpha _{i,l}=\mathbf1_{K_ l}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n.  \] These measures are finite since $u_ i\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, they have compact support in $B$, and they are dominated by the Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ i$. By theorem 9.10.12 , the equation $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A)^ n=\alpha _{i,l}$ has a bounded solution $A_{i,l}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ with zero boundary values, and $A_{i,l}$ is the largest bounded plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $B$ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq \alpha _{i,l}$ and upper boundary limits at most zero. The function $u_ i$ has these properties for every $l$, and so has $A_{i,l+1}$, because $\alpha _{i,l+1}\geq \alpha _{i,l}$. Therefore \[  u_ i\leq A_{i,l+1}\leq A_{i,l}\leq 0.  \] We claim that $A_{i,l}\downarrow u_ i$ as $l	o \infty $. The decreasing limit $A_{i,\infty }$ satisfies $u_ i\leq A_{i,\infty }\leq 0$, so it is a bounded plurisubharmonic function (theorem 8.3.1 ) with zero boundary values. By theorem 9.2.5 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,\infty })^ n$ is the weak limit of $\alpha _{i,l}$, that is, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,\infty })^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n$, and this measure has finite total mass. Let $\varepsilon >0$ and $S=\{ u_ i<A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho \} $. Since $u_ i-(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho )$ tends to zero at $\partial B$, the comparison theorem (theorem 9.2.8 ) applies. Expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho ))^ n$ and dropping the mixed terms, which are positive, we obtain \[  \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n+\varepsilon ^ n\int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n \leq \int _ S igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho ) igr )^ n \leq \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n.  \] The integrals of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n$ are finite, so $S$ is Lebesgue null. Hence $u_ i\geq A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho $ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere on $B$, by the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 applied to $\max \{ u_ i,A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho \} $ and $u_ i$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $A_{i,\infty }=u_ i$, as claimed. Step 2. A common grid. Fix $l$. Choose a sequence of partitions of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ into half-open cubes whose side lengths decrease to zero, the same for all $i$. Let $\alpha _{i,l,j}$ be the corresponding cube averages of $\alpha _{i,l}$, as in proposition 9.10.3 , and let $A_{i,l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ be the corresponding canonical approximants of $\alpha _{i,l}$, that is, the zero-boundary solutions of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j})^ n=\alpha _{i,l,j}$; they are defined for all large $j$. Discarding finitely many indices $j$, we may assume that they are defined for all $j$ and all $i$, and that every cube meeting $K_ l$ has its closure in $B$. By theorem 9.10.12 , $A_{i,l,j}	o A_{i,l}$ locally in capacity as $j	o \infty $. By proposition 9.10.3 , applied with the bounded subsolution $u_ i$, the energies $e_1(A_{i,l,j})$ are bounded uniformly in $j$; since there are only finitely many indices $i$, they have a common bound. (If $\alpha _{i,l}=0$, all these solutions vanish.) Therefore corollary 9.10.14 gives 9.77  egin{equation} \label{eq:common-measure-grid-mixed-limit}  igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j} \longrightarrow  igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l} \end{equation} weakly on $B$. Let $\lambda _ l=\mathbf1_{K_ l}\lambda $, a finite measure, and let $\lambda _{l,j}$ be its cube averages. For every cube $Q$, the hypothesis gives $\alpha _{i,l}(Q)\geq \int _{Q\cap K_ l}f_ i\, \mathrm d\mu $, and ( 9.76 ) then gives 9.78  egin{equation} \label{eq:common-measure-grid-holder} \prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{|Q|}ight)^{1/n} \geq  rac1{|Q|}\int _{Q\cap K_ l}\prod _{i=1}^ nf_ i^{1/n}\, \mathrm d\mu = rac{\lambda _ l(Q)}{|Q|}. \end{equation} Let $Q$ be a cube with $\lambda _ l(Q)>0$; it meets $K_ l$, so its interior lies in $B$. There the measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j})^ n=\alpha _{i,l,j}$ have the constant densities $\alpha _{i,l}(Q)/|Q|$ with respect to Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV$. Recall that $\eta ^ n=c_ n\, \mathrm dV$ with $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and $c_ n=n!\pi ^{-n}$, by ( 9.2 ). Applying corollary 9.7.6 on the open set $\operatorname{Int}Q$ to the constant densities $c_ n^{-1}\alpha _{i,l}(Q)/|Q|$ with respect to $\eta ^ n$, and using ( 9.78 ), we obtain on $\operatorname{Int}Q$ \[   igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j} \geq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{c_ n|Q|}ight)^{1/n}\eta ^ n =\prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{|Q|}ight)^{1/n}\mathrm dV \geq \lambda _{l,j}.  \] The factor $c_ n$ cancels because the $n$ exponents $1/n$ sum to one. The measure $\lambda _{l,j}$ vanishes on the cubes with $\lambda _ l(Q)=0$ and does not charge the cube boundaries, which are Lebesgue null. Since the mixed product is positive, we conclude that $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j}\geq \lambda _{l,j}$ on $B$. As $j	o \infty $, $\lambda _{l,j}	o \lambda _ l$ weakly. Indeed, for $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, replacing the values of $\chi $ by its cube averages changes $\int \chi \, \mathrm d\lambda _ l$ by at most $\lambda _ l(B)$ times the modulus of continuity of $\chi $ at the cube diameter. Letting $j	o \infty $ and using ( 9.77 ), we obtain $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l}\geq \lambda _ l$. Finally let $l	o \infty $. By Step 1, $A_{i,l}\downarrow u_ i$ with $u_ i\leq A_{i,l}\leq 0$, so theorem 9.2.5 gives $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l}	o  igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ weakly, while $\lambda _ l$ increases to $\lambda $. Testing with nonnegative functions in $C_ c(B)$ and using monotone convergence on the right, we obtain ( 9.75 ) for potentials in $\mathcal E_0(B)$. Step 3. Localization. Now let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded on $\Omega $. Choose a ball $B=B(a_0,R)$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ and a compact set $K\subset B$. Since adding constants does not change the products, we may assume that $u_ i\leq -1$ on $B$. With constants $C_ i>0$ so large that $C_ iho <\inf _ Bu_ i$ on a neighborhood of $K$, put \[  \widetilde u_ i=\max \{ u_ i,C_ iho \} .  \] Then $\widetilde u_ i=u_ i$ on a neighborhood of $K$, and $\widetilde u_ i=C_ iho $ near $\partial B$, because $C_ iho 	o 0$ at $\partial B$ while $u_ i\leq -1$. Thus $\widetilde u_ i\in \mathcal E_0(B)$: its Monge–Ampère measure is smooth near $\partial B$ and locally finite on the rest of $B$. By locality of the products on the open neighborhood of $K$ where $\widetilde u_ i=u_ i$, we have $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_ i)^ n\geq f_ i\mathbf1_ K\mu $ on $B$. The case already proved, applied to the measure $\mathbf1_ K\mu $, gives $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_ i\geq \mathbf1_ K\lambda $, and on a neighborhood of $K$ the left side equals $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ by locality. Thus $P= igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ satisfies $P(E)\geq \lambda (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset K$. The interiors of such compact sets $K$ cover $\Omega $, and since $\Omega $ has a countable basis, countably many of them, say $\operatorname{Int}L_1,\operatorname{Int}L_2,\ldots $, already cover $\Omega $. A Borel set $E\subset \Omega $ is the disjoint union of the Borel sets $E_ m=(E\cap L_ m)\setminus  igcup _{m'<m}L_{m'}$, and therefore $P(E)=\sum _ mP(E_ m)\geq \sum _ m\lambda (E_ m)=\lambda (E)$. $\square$ Corollary 9.11.2 . Let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, and let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $\Omega $. If $f,g$ are nonnegative Borel functions on $\Omega $ and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\geq f\mu ,\qquad (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq g\mu ,  \] then, for each integer $1\leq k\leq n-1$, 9.79  egin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-common-measure-mixed} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k} \geq f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\mu . \end{equation} For $k=0$ and $k=n$ the corresponding inequalities are the hypotheses; for $n=1$ only these occur. Proof. Apply theorem 9.11.1 to $k$ copies of $u$ with density $f$ and $n-k$ copies of $v$ with density $g$. $\square$ Corollary 9.11.3 . Under the hypotheses of corollary 9.11.2 , \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+v))^ n\geq (f^{1/n}+g^{1/n})^ n\mu .  \] Proof. By additivity and symmetry of the products, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+v))^ n=\sum _{k=0}^ n inom nk(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}$. Bound the terms with $1\leq k\leq n-1$ by corollary 9.11.2 and the terms with $k=0,n$ by the hypotheses; the binomial formula then gives the assertion. The density on the right is locally $\mu $-integrable, since $f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\leq f+g$ by the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, and $f$ and $g$ are locally $\mu $-integrable because $f\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ and $g\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$. $\square$

Expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho ))^ n$ and dropping the mixed terms, which are positive, we obtain \[  \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n+\varepsilon ^ n\int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n \leq \int _ S igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho ) igr )^ n \leq \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n.  \] The integrals of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n$ are finite, so $S$ is Lebesgue null. Hence $u_ i\geq A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho $ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere on $B$, by the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 applied to $\max \{ u_ i,A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho \} $ and $u_ i$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $A_{i,\infty }=u_ i$, as claimed. Step 2. A common grid. Fix $l$. Choose a sequence of partitions of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ into half-open cubes whose side lengths decrease to zero, the same for all $i$. Let $\alpha _{i,l,j}$ be the corresponding cube averages of $\alpha _{i,l}$, as in proposition 9.10.3 , and let $A_{i,l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ be the corresponding canonical approximants of $\alpha _{i,l}$, that is, the zero-boundary solutions of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j})^ n=\alpha _{i,l,j}$; they are defined for all large $j$. Discarding finitely many indices $j$, we may assume that they are defined for all $j$ and all $i$, and that every cube meeting $K_ l$ has its closure in $B$. By theorem 9.10.12 , $A_{i,l,j}	o A_{i,l}$ locally in capacity as $j	o \infty $. By proposition 9.10.3 , applied with the bounded subsolution $u_ i$, the energies $e_1(A_{i,l,j})$ are bounded uniformly in $j$; since there are only finitely many indices $i$, they have a common bound. (If $\alpha _{i,l}=0$, all these solutions vanish.) Therefore corollary 9.10.14 gives 9.77  egin{equation} \label{eq:common-measure-grid-mixed-limit}  igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j} \longrightarrow  igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l} \end{equation} weakly on $B$. Let $\lambda _ l=\mathbf1_{K_ l}\lambda $, a finite measure, and let $\lambda _{l,j}$ be its cube averages. For every cube $Q$, the hypothesis gives $\alpha _{i,l}(Q)\geq \int _{Q\cap K_ l}f_ i\, \mathrm d\mu $, and ( 9.76 ) then gives 9.78  egin{equation} \label{eq:common-measure-grid-holder} \prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{|Q|}ight)^{1/n} \geq  rac1{|Q|}\int _{Q\cap K_ l}\prod _{i=1}^ nf_ i^{1/n}\, \mathrm d\mu = rac{\lambda _ l(Q)}{|Q|}. \end{equation} Let $Q$ be a cube with $\lambda _ l(Q)>0$; it meets $K_ l$, so its interior lies in $B$. There the measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j})^ n=\alpha _{i,l,j}$ have the constant densities $\alpha _{i,l}(Q)/|Q|$ with respect to Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV$. Recall that $\eta ^ n=c_ n\, \mathrm dV$ with $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and $c_ n=n!\pi ^{-n}$, by ( 9.2 ). Applying corollary 9.7.6 on the open set $\operatorname{Int}Q$ to the constant densities $c_ n^{-1}\alpha _{i,l}(Q)/|Q|$ with respect to $\eta ^ n$, and using ( 9.78 ), we obtain on $\operatorname{Int}Q$ \[   igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j} \geq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{c_ n|Q|}ight)^{1/n}\eta ^ n =\prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{|Q|}ight)^{1/n}\mathrm dV \geq \lambda _{l,j}.  \] The factor $c_ n$ cancels because the $n$ exponents $1/n$ sum to one. The measure $\lambda _{l,j}$ vanishes on the cubes with $\lambda _ l(Q)=0$ and does not charge the cube boundaries, which are Lebesgue null. Since the mixed product is positive, we conclude that $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j}\geq \lambda _{l,j}$ on $B$. As $j	o \infty $, $\lambda _{l,j}	o \lambda _ l$ weakly. Indeed, for $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, replacing the values of $\chi $ by its cube averages changes $\int \chi \, \mathrm d\lambda _ l$ by at most $\lambda _ l(B)$ times the modulus of continuity of $\chi $ at the cube diameter. Letting $j	o \infty $ and using ( 9.77 ), we obtain $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l}\geq \lambda _ l$. Finally let $l	o \infty $. By Step 1, $A_{i,l}\downarrow u_ i$ with $u_ i\leq A_{i,l}\leq 0$, so theorem 9.2.5 gives $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l}	o  igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ weakly, while $\lambda _ l$ increases to $\lambda $. Testing with nonnegative functions in $C_ c(B)$ and using monotone convergence on the right, we obtain ( 9.75 ) for potentials in $\mathcal E_0(B)$. Step 3. Localization. Now let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded on $\Omega $. Choose a ball $B=B(a_0,R)$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ and a compact set $K\subset B$. Since adding constants does not change the products, we may assume that $u_ i\leq -1$ on $B$. With constants $C_ i>0$ so large that $C_ iho <\inf _ Bu_ i$ on a neighborhood of $K$, put \[  \widetilde u_ i=\max \{ u_ i,C_ iho \} .  \] Then $\widetilde u_ i=u_ i$ on a neighborhood of $K$, and $\widetilde u_ i=C_ iho $ near $\partial B$, because $C_ iho 	o 0$ at $\partial B$ while $u_ i\leq -1$. Thus $\widetilde u_ i\in \mathcal E_0(B)$: its Monge–Ampère measure is smooth near $\partial B$ and locally finite on the rest of $B$. By locality of the products on the open neighborhood of $K$ where $\widetilde u_ i=u_ i$, we have $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_ i)^ n\geq f_ i\mathbf1_ K\mu $ on $B$. The case already proved, applied to the measure $\mathbf1_ K\mu $, gives $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_ i\geq \mathbf1_ K\lambda $, and on a neighborhood of $K$ the left side equals $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ by locality. Thus $P= igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ satisfies $P(E)\geq \lambda (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset K$. The interiors of such compact sets $K$ cover $\Omega $, and since $\Omega $ has a countable basis, countably many of them, say $\operatorname{Int}L_1,\operatorname{Int}L_2,\ldots $, already cover $\Omega $. A Borel set $E\subset \Omega $ is the disjoint union of the Borel sets $E_ m=(E\cap L_ m)\setminus  igcup _{m'<m}L_{m'}$, and therefore $P(E)=\sum _ mP(E_ m)\geq \sum _ m\lambda (E_ m)=\lambda (E)$. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.11.2
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Corollary 9.11.2 . Let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, and let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $\Omega $. If $f,g$ are nonnegative Borel functions on $\Omega $ and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\geq f\mu ,\qquad (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq g\mu ,  \] then, for each integer $1\leq k\leq n-1$, 9.79 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-common-measure-mixed} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k} \geq f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\mu . \end{equation} For $k=0$ and $k=n$ the corresponding inequalities are the hypotheses; for $n=1$ only these occur. Proof. Apply theorem 9.11.1 to $k$ copies of $u$ with density $f$ and $n-k$ copies of $v$ with density $g$. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.11.3
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Corollary 9.11.3 . Under the hypotheses of corollary 9.11.2 , \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+v))^ n\geq (f^{1/n}+g^{1/n})^ n\mu .  \] Proof. By additivity and symmetry of the products, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+v))^ n=\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}$. Bound the terms with $1\leq k\leq n-1$ by corollary 9.11.2 and the terms with $k=0,n$ by the hypotheses; the binomial formula then gives the assertion. The density on the right is locally $\mu $-integrable, since $f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\leq f+g$ by the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, and $f$ and $g$ are locally $\mu $-integrable because $f\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ and $g\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$. $\square$
