text:
9.12 Bounded complex Hessians and contact sets Monge–Ampère measures of envelopes are computed on contact sets: if a potential $u$ lies below an obstacle $f$ and $u=f$ on a set $E$, one expects the Monge–Ampère measure of $u$ on $E$ to be determined by the Hessian of $f$. A contact set may have empty interior, and then the locality of the products on open sets (proposition 9.1.2 ) says nothing about it. We show that weak derivatives are local on arbitrary measurable sets: two functions whose weak derivatives up to order two are locally integrable have the same such derivatives almost everywhere on the set where they agree. For potentials with bounded complex Hessians this yields a formula for the Bedford–Taylor product restricted to a contact set (proposition 9.12.4 ), which is used for envelopes in chapter 16 . We use the Sobolev spaces $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ of section 6.2 , for open sets $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$, integers $k\ge 0$ and $p\in \{ 1,2\} $; thus a function belongs to $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ if it and its distributional derivatives of order at most $k$ belong to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Since $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\subset L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, we have $W^{k,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\subset W^{k,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Lemma 9.12.1 . Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open and let $g\in W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ be real. Then $
abla g=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. If moreover $g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then all first and second weak derivatives of $g$ vanish almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. Here $\{ g=0\} $ may be formed with any measurable representative of $g$, since changing $g$ on a null set changes this set only by a null set. Proof. We first prove the chain rule \[  \partial _ a\Phi (g)=\Phi '(g)\, \partial _ a g\qquad (1\le a\le d)  \] for a $C^1$ function $\Phi \colon \mathbb R	o \mathbb R$ with bounded derivative; note that $\Phi (g)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, since $|\Phi (g)|\leq |\Phi (0)|+\| \Phi '\| _\infty |g|$. Let $V\Subset D$ be open. The mollifications $g_\varepsilon =g*ho _\varepsilon $ converge to $g$ in $L^1(V)$, together with their first derivatives $\partial _ ag_\varepsilon =(\partial _ ag)*ho _\varepsilon $, by the remark preceding lemma 6.2.4 ; passing to a sequence $\varepsilon _ k	o 0$, we may also assume that $g_{\varepsilon _ k}	o g$ almost everywhere on $V$. Since $\Phi $ is Lipschitz, $\Phi (g_{\varepsilon _ k})	o \Phi (g)$ in $L^1(V)$. Moreover, \[  \Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\Phi '(g)\partial _ ag =\Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})(\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\partial _ ag) + igl (\Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})-\Phi '(g) igr )\partial _ ag  \] tends to zero in $L^1(V)$: the first term is bounded by $\| \Phi '\| _\infty |\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\partial _ ag|$, and the second tends to zero by dominated convergence, since it tends to zero almost everywhere, $\Phi '$ being continuous, and is bounded by $2\| \Phi '\| _\infty |\partial _ ag|$. For $\psi \in C^\infty _ c(V)$ the classical chain rule gives $\int \Phi (g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ a\psi =-\int \Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}\, \psi $, and letting $k	o \infty $ we obtain $\int \Phi (g)\partial _ a\psi =-\int \Phi '(g)\partial _ ag\, \psi $. As $V$ was arbitrary, this proves the chain rule. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ on $\mathbb R$ supported in $(-2,2)$, with $0\le \chi \le 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $[-1,1]$, and put $\Phi _\varepsilon (t)=\int _0^ t\chi (s/\varepsilon )\, \mathrm ds$ for $\varepsilon >0$. Then $\Phi _\varepsilon $ is smooth with $0\leq \Phi _\varepsilon '\leq 1$, $|\Phi _\varepsilon |\le 2\varepsilon $, and by the chain rule \[  
abla \Phi _\varepsilon (g)=\chi (g/\varepsilon )
abla g \longrightarrow \mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }
abla g \quad 	ext{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)  \] as $\varepsilon 	o 0$, by dominated convergence, since $\chi (g/\varepsilon )	o \mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }$ pointwise and $|\chi (g/\varepsilon )
abla g|\leq |
abla g|$. On the other hand, $\Phi _\varepsilon (g)	o 0$ uniformly, so $
abla \Phi _\varepsilon (g)	o 0$ in the sense of distributions. Since convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ implies convergence in the sense of distributions, the locally integrable function $\mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }
abla g$ defines the zero distribution, and hence vanishes almost everywhere (proposition 1.4.3 ). This is the first assertion. If $g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then each $\partial _ ag$ belongs to $W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ and, by the first assertion, vanishes almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. Applying the first assertion to $\partial _ ag$, formed with any measurable representative, shows that $
abla \partial _ ag=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ \partial _ ag=0\} $, a set which contains $\{ g=0\} $ up to a null set. Since there are finitely many derivatives, the union of the exceptional null sets is null. $\square$ Lemma 9.12.2 . Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, and let $f\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. If the distributional Laplacian $\Delta f$ belongs to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then $f\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. In particular, this holds if $f$ is continuous and $\Delta f$ is a locally bounded measurable function. Proof. Considering real and imaginary parts separately, we may assume that $f$ is real. Let $f_\varepsilon =f*ho _\varepsilon $ be the mollifications of $f$. For every compact set $L\subset D$ they are smooth on a neighborhood of $L$ for small $\varepsilon $, and by proposition 1.4.3 and lemma 1.4.1 , $f_\varepsilon 	o f$ and $\Delta f_\varepsilon =(\Delta f)*ho _\varepsilon 	o \Delta f$ in $L^2(L)$ as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. We first show that the gradients converge. Let $\chi $ be a real test function, and let $h$ be a real smooth function on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. Since $\int \partial _ a(\chi ^2h\, \partial _ ah)=0$ for each $a$, by Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have \[   egin{aligned}  \int \chi ^2|
abla h|^2& =-\int \chi ^2h\Delta h-2\int \chi h
abla \chi \cdot 
abla h\ & \le 	frac 12\int \chi ^2|
abla h|^2 +\int \chi ^2|h\Delta h|+2\int h^2|
abla \chi |^2, \end{aligned}  \] where we used $2xy\le x^2/2+2y^2$. Hence \[  \int \chi ^2|
abla h|^2\leq 2\| \chi \| _\infty ^2\| h\| _{L^2(S)}\| \Delta h\| _{L^2(S)}+4\| 
abla \chi \| _\infty ^2\| h\| _{L^2(S)}^2, \qquad S=\operatorname{Supp}\chi .  \] Let $L\subset D$ be compact, and choose $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(D)$ equal to one on $L$ (lemma 1.4.1 ). Apply the last inequality to $h=f_\varepsilon -f_\delta $. As $\varepsilon ,\delta 	o 0$, the norms $\| f_\varepsilon -f_\delta \| _{L^2(\operatorname{Supp}\chi )}$ tend to zero, while the norms $\| \Delta f_\varepsilon -\Delta f_\delta \| _{L^2(\operatorname{Supp}\chi )}$ stay bounded. Hence the gradients $
abla f_\varepsilon $ form a Cauchy family in $L^2(L)$. For $\psi \in C^\infty _ c(\operatorname{Int}L)$ we have $\int \partial _ af_\varepsilon \, \psi =-\int f_\varepsilon \, \partial _ a\psi 	o -\int f\, \partial _ a\psi $, so the $L^2$ limits are the distributional first derivatives of $f$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$. Since $L$ was arbitrary, the first derivatives of $f$ belong to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, and $
abla f_\varepsilon 	o 
abla f$ in $L^2(L)$ for every compact $L\subset D$. For the second derivatives, let $L\subset D$ be compact, choose $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(D)$ equal to one on a neighborhood $N$ of $L$, and for small $\varepsilon $ put $v_\varepsilon =\chi f_\varepsilon $, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$. These are smooth functions with compact support, and \[  \Delta v_\varepsilon =\chi \Delta f_\varepsilon +2
abla \chi \cdot 
abla f_\varepsilon +f_\varepsilon \Delta \chi  \] is a Cauchy family in $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$, by the first part applied on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. For every real $v\in C^\infty _ c(\mathbb R^ d)$, integrating by parts twice gives \[  \sum _{a,b=1}^ d\| \partial _ a\partial _ b v\| _2^2 =\sum _{a,b=1}^ d\int (\partial _ a^2v)(\partial _ b^2v) =\| \Delta v\| _2^2.  \] Applying this identity to $v_\varepsilon -v_\delta $, we see that all second derivatives of $v_\varepsilon $ form Cauchy families in $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions identifies their limits with the distributional second derivatives of $\chi f$, which agree with those of $f$ on $N$, where $\chi f=f$. Thus the second derivatives of $f$ are square-integrable on $L$. Since $L$ was arbitrary, $f\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. The last assertion holds because continuous functions and locally bounded measurable functions are locally square-integrable. $\square$ Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. We say that a continuous function $f$ on $\Omega $ has a bounded complex Hessian if its distributional derivatives $f_{j ar k}=\partial ^2 f/\partial z_ j\partial  ar z_ k$ are locally bounded measurable functions. Since the Laplacian of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ is $4\sum _ j\partial ^2/\partial z_ j\partial  ar z_ j$ by ( 7.5 ), such a function belongs to $W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ by lemma 9.12.2 . Proposition 9.12.3 . Let $f,g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ be real, and put $E=\{ f=g\} $, formed with any measurable representatives of $f$ and $g$. Then the real weak first and second derivatives of $f$ and $g$ agree almost everywhere on $E$. In particular, \[  \mathbf1_ E f_{j ar k}=\mathbf1_ E g_{j ar k} \quad 	ext{almost everywhere, for all }j,k.  \] Proof. Apply lemma 9.12.1 to $f-g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, whose zero set, formed with the chosen representatives, is $E$. The complex derivatives $f_{j ar k}$ and $g_{j ar k}$ are fixed linear combinations of the real second derivatives, which gives the second assertion. $\square$ As in section 9.7.1 , $D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)$ denotes the mixed discriminant of Hermitian $n	imes n$ matrices (section 7.2 ); in dimension zero we put $D()=1$. Proposition 9.12.4 . Let $u_1,\dots ,u_ n$ be continuous plurisubharmonic functions with bounded complex Hessians on $\Omega $, and let $A_ j=((u_ j)_{a ar b})$ be their complex Hessian matrices. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n = rac{n!}{\pi ^ n}D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] If $v_1,\dots ,v_ n\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ are real, with weak complex Hessian matrices $B_ j=((v_ j)_{a ar b})$, and $E= igcap _ j\{ u_ j=v_ j\} $, formed with any Borel representatives of the $v_ j$, then \[  \mathbf1_ E\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n = rac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\mathbf1_ E D(B_1,\dots ,B_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] In particular, the density $\mathbf1_ ED(B_1,\dots ,B_ n)$ is locally bounded. (In dimension zero, where $\mathbb C^0$ is a point and $\mathrm dV_0$ is the unit point mass, both sides of each identity equal $\mathrm dV_0$.) Proof. For smooth $u_ j$ we polarize ( 9.2 ), as in the proof of corollary 9.7.6 . Applied to the smooth function $\sum _ jt_ ju_ j$ with $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n\in \mathbb R$, it gives the identity \[  \Bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sum _ jt_ ju_ j\Bigr )^ n= rac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det \Bigl (\sum _ jt_ jA_ j\Bigr )\, \mathrm dV_{2n}  \] between exterior powers of smooth forms, and both sides are polynomials in $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n$. We compare the coefficients of $t_1\cdots t_ n$. Since $2$-forms commute, on the left this coefficient is $n!$ times the exterior product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n$, which is the Bedford–Taylor product by proposition 9.1.2 (1); on the right it is $(n!)^2\pi ^{-n}D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, by the definition of the mixed discriminant. This proves the first formula for smooth $u_ j$. For continuous $u_ j$, let $u_{j,\varepsilon }=u_ j*ho _\varepsilon $ be their radial mollifications, which are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ (proposition 8.2.2 ). They converge to $u_ j$ uniformly on compact sets (lemma 1.4.1 ), so their products converge weakly by proposition 9.1.4 . By proposition 1.4.3 , the complex Hessian matrix of $u_{j,\varepsilon }$ is the mollification $A_{j,\varepsilon }$ of the matrix $A_ j$ of locally bounded functions. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact. For small $\varepsilon $, the entries of $A_{j,\varepsilon }$ are bounded on $K$ by the bounds of the entries of $A_ j$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, and by lemma 1.4.1 they converge to those of $A_ j$ in $L^1(K)$. Products of functions which are bounded on $K$ uniformly in $\varepsilon $ and converge in $L^1(K)$ converge in $L^1(K)$, because $|ab-a'b'|\leq |a||b-b'|+|b'||a-a'|$. Since $D$ is a polynomial in the matrix entries, it follows that $D(A_{1,\varepsilon },\dots ,A_{n,\varepsilon })	o D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)$ in $L^1(K)$. By the first part, $(n!/\pi ^ n)D(A_{1,\varepsilon },\dots ,A_{n,\varepsilon })\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$ is the product of the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{j,\varepsilon }$, so the weak limit of these products is $(n!/\pi ^ n)D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. This proves the first formula in general. By lemma 9.12.2 , each $u_ j$ belongs to $W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )\subset W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so proposition 9.12.3 , applied to $u_ j$ and the chosen representative of $v_ j$, gives $A_ j=B_ j$ almost everywhere on $\{ u_ j=v_ j\} $, hence on $E$. Substituting into the first formula proves the second, and also shows that $\mathbf1_ ED(B_1,\dots ,B_ n)=\mathbf1_ ED(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)$ is locally bounded. $\square$ On a complex manifold, the second identity is applied in holomorphic charts to functions $u_ j$ which become plurisubharmonic after the addition of a smooth local potential $g_ j$ of a closed real $(1,1)$-form. If $g_ j+u_ j$ is plurisubharmonic with bounded complex Hessian, we apply proposition 9.12.4 to $g_ j+u_ j$ and $g_ j+v_ j$: adding the same smooth function to $u_ j$ and $v_ j$ does not change the contact set, and $g_ j+v_ j\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ whenever $v_ j\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

Lemma 9.12.1 . Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open and let $g\in W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ be real. Then $
abla g=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. If moreover $g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then all first and second weak derivatives of $g$ vanish almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. Here $\{ g=0\} $ may be formed with any measurable representative of $g$, since changing $g$ on a null set changes this set only by a null set. Proof. We first prove the chain rule \[  \partial _ a\Phi (g)=\Phi '(g)\, \partial _ a g\qquad (1\le a\le d)  \] for a $C^1$ function $\Phi \colon \mathbb R	o \mathbb R$ with bounded derivative; note that $\Phi (g)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, since $|\Phi (g)|\leq |\Phi (0)|+\| \Phi '\| _\infty |g|$. Let $V\Subset D$ be open. The mollifications $g_\varepsilon =g*ho _\varepsilon $ converge to $g$ in $L^1(V)$, together with their first derivatives $\partial _ ag_\varepsilon =(\partial _ ag)*ho _\varepsilon $, by the remark preceding lemma 6.2.4 ; passing to a sequence $\varepsilon _ k	o 0$, we may also assume that $g_{\varepsilon _ k}	o g$ almost everywhere on $V$. Since $\Phi $ is Lipschitz, $\Phi (g_{\varepsilon _ k})	o \Phi (g)$ in $L^1(V)$. Moreover, \[  \Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\Phi '(g)\partial _ ag =\Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})(\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\partial _ ag) + igl (\Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})-\Phi '(g) igr )\partial _ ag  \] tends to zero in $L^1(V)$: the first term is bounded by $\| \Phi '\| _\infty |\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\partial _ ag|$, and the second tends to zero by dominated convergence, since it tends to zero almost everywhere, $\Phi '$ being continuous, and is bounded by $2\| \Phi '\| _\infty |\partial _ ag|$. For $\psi \in C^\infty _ c(V)$ the classical chain rule gives $\int \Phi (g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ a\psi =-\int \Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}\, \psi $, and letting $k	o \infty $ we obtain $\int \Phi (g)\partial _ a\psi =-\int \Phi '(g)\partial _ ag\, \psi $. As $V$ was arbitrary, this proves the chain rule. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ on $\mathbb R$ supported in $(-2,2)$, with $0\le \chi \le 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $[-1,1]$, and put $\Phi _\varepsilon (t)=\int _0^ t\chi (s/\varepsilon )\, \mathrm ds$ for $\varepsilon >0$. Then $\Phi _\varepsilon $ is smooth with $0\leq \Phi _\varepsilon '\leq 1$, $|\Phi _\varepsilon |\le 2\varepsilon $, and by the chain rule \[  
abla \Phi _\varepsilon (g)=\chi (g/\varepsilon )
abla g \longrightarrow \mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }
abla g \quad 	ext{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)  \] as $\varepsilon 	o 0$, by dominated convergence, since $\chi (g/\varepsilon )	o \mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }$ pointwise and $|\chi (g/\varepsilon )
abla g|\leq |
abla g|$. On the other hand, $\Phi _\varepsilon (g)	o 0$ uniformly, so $
abla \Phi _\varepsilon (g)	o 0$ in the sense of distributions. Since convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ implies convergence in the sense of distributions, the locally integrable function $\mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }
abla g$ defines the zero distribution, and hence vanishes almost everywhere (proposition 1.4.3 ). This is the first assertion. If $g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then each $\partial _ ag$ belongs to $W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ and, by the first assertion, vanishes almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. Applying the first assertion to $\partial _ ag$, formed with any measurable representative, shows that $
abla \partial _ ag=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ \partial _ ag=0\} $, a set which contains $\{ g=0\} $ up to a null set. Since there are finitely many derivatives, the union of the exceptional null sets is null. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.12.2
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text:
Lemma 9.12.2 . Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, and let $f\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. If the distributional Laplacian $\Delta f$ belongs to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then $f\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. In particular, this holds if $f$ is continuous and $\Delta f$ is a locally bounded measurable function. Proof. Considering real and imaginary parts separately, we may assume that $f$ is real. Let $f_\varepsilon =f*ho _\varepsilon $ be the mollifications of $f$. For every compact set $L\subset D$ they are smooth on a neighborhood of $L$ for small $\varepsilon $, and by proposition 1.4.3 and lemma 1.4.1 , $f_\varepsilon 	o f$ and $\Delta f_\varepsilon =(\Delta f)*ho _\varepsilon 	o \Delta f$ in $L^2(L)$ as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. We first show that the gradients converge. Let $\chi $ be a real test function, and let $h$ be a real smooth function on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. Since $\int \partial _ a(\chi ^2h\, \partial _ ah)=0$ for each $a$, by Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have \[   egin{aligned}  \int \chi ^2|
abla h|^2& =-\int \chi ^2h\Delta h-2\int \chi h
abla \chi \cdot 
abla h\ & \le 	frac 12\int \chi ^2|
abla h|^2 +\int \chi ^2|h\Delta h|+2\int h^2|
abla \chi |^2, \end{aligned}  \] where we used $2xy\le x^2/2+2y^2$. Hence \[  \int \chi ^2|
abla h|^2\leq 2\| \chi \| _\infty ^2\| h\| _{L^2(S)}\| \Delta h\| _{L^2(S)}+4\| 
abla \chi \| _\infty ^2\| h\| _{L^2(S)}^2, \qquad S=\operatorname{Supp}\chi .  \] Let $L\subset D$ be compact, and choose $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(D)$ equal to one on $L$ (lemma 1.4.1 ). Apply the last inequality to $h=f_\varepsilon -f_\delta $. As $\varepsilon ,\delta 	o 0$, the norms $\| f_\varepsilon -f_\delta \| _{L^2(\operatorname{Supp}\chi )}$ tend to zero, while the norms $\| \Delta f_\varepsilon -\Delta f_\delta \| _{L^2(\operatorname{Supp}\chi )}$ stay bounded. Hence the gradients $
abla f_\varepsilon $ form a Cauchy family in $L^2(L)$. For $\psi \in C^\infty _ c(\operatorname{Int}L)$ we have $\int \partial _ af_\varepsilon \, \psi =-\int f_\varepsilon \, \partial _ a\psi 	o -\int f\, \partial _ a\psi $, so the $L^2$ limits are the distributional first derivatives of $f$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$. Since $L$ was arbitrary, the first derivatives of $f$ belong to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, and $
abla f_\varepsilon 	o 
abla f$ in $L^2(L)$ for every compact $L\subset D$. For the second derivatives, let $L\subset D$ be compact, choose $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(D)$ equal to one on a neighborhood $N$ of $L$, and for small $\varepsilon $ put $v_\varepsilon =\chi f_\varepsilon $, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$. These are smooth functions with compact support, and \[  \Delta v_\varepsilon =\chi \Delta f_\varepsilon +2
abla \chi \cdot 
abla f_\varepsilon +f_\varepsilon \Delta \chi  \] is a Cauchy family in $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$, by the first part applied on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. For every real $v\in C^\infty _ c(\mathbb R^ d)$, integrating by parts twice gives \[  \sum _{a,b=1}^ d\| \partial _ a\partial _ b v\| _2^2 =\sum _{a,b=1}^ d\int (\partial _ a^2v)(\partial _ b^2v) =\| \Delta v\| _2^2.  \] Applying this identity to $v_\varepsilon -v_\delta $, we see that all second derivatives of $v_\varepsilon $ form Cauchy families in $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions identifies their limits with the distributional second derivatives of $\chi f$, which agree with those of $f$ on $N$, where $\chi f=f$. Thus the second derivatives of $f$ are square-integrable on $L$. Since $L$ was arbitrary, $f\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. The last assertion holds because continuous functions and locally bounded measurable functions are locally square-integrable. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.12.3
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Proposition 9.12.3 . Let $f,g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ be real, and put $E=\{ f=g\} $, formed with any measurable representatives of $f$ and $g$. Then the real weak first and second derivatives of $f$ and $g$ agree almost everywhere on $E$. In particular, \[  \mathbf1_ E f_{j\bar k}=\mathbf1_ E g_{j\bar k} \quad \text{almost everywhere, for all }j,k.  \] Proof. Apply lemma 9.12.1 to $f-g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, whose zero set, formed with the chosen representatives, is $E$. The complex derivatives $f_{j\bar k}$ and $g_{j\bar k}$ are fixed linear combinations of the real second derivatives, which gives the second assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.12.4
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Proposition 9.12.4 . Let $u_1,\dots ,u_ n$ be continuous plurisubharmonic functions with bounded complex Hessians on $\Omega $, and let $A_ j=((u_ j)_{a\bar b})$ be their complex Hessian matrices. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n =\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] If $v_1,\dots ,v_ n\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ are real, with weak complex Hessian matrices $B_ j=((v_ j)_{a\bar b})$, and $E=\bigcap _ j\{ u_ j=v_ j\} $, formed with any Borel representatives of the $v_ j$, then \[  \mathbf1_ E\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n =\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\mathbf1_ E D(B_1,\dots ,B_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] In particular, the density $\mathbf1_ ED(B_1,\dots ,B_ n)$ is locally bounded. (In dimension zero, where $\mathbb C^0$ is a point and $\mathrm dV_0$ is the unit point mass, both sides of each identity equal $\mathrm dV_0$.) Proof. For smooth $u_ j$ we polarize ( 9.2 ), as in the proof of corollary 9.7.6 . Applied to the smooth function $\sum _ jt_ ju_ j$ with $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n\in \mathbb R$, it gives the identity \[  \Bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sum _ jt_ ju_ j\Bigr )^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det \Bigl (\sum _ jt_ jA_ j\Bigr )\, \mathrm dV_{2n}  \] between exterior powers of smooth forms, and both sides are polynomials in $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n$. We compare the coefficients of $t_1\cdots t_ n$. Since $2$-forms commute, on the left this coefficient is $n!$ times the exterior product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n$, which is the Bedford–Taylor product by proposition 9.1.2 (1); on the right it is $(n!)^2\pi ^{-n}D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, by the definition of the mixed discriminant. This proves the first formula for smooth $u_ j$. For continuous $u_ j$, let $u_{j,\varepsilon }=u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon $ be their radial mollifications, which are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ (proposition 8.2.2 ). They converge to $u_ j$ uniformly on compact sets (lemma 1.4.1 ), so their products converge weakly by proposition 9.1.4 . By proposition 1.4.3 , the complex Hessian matrix of $u_{j,\varepsilon }$ is the mollification $A_{j,\varepsilon }$ of the matrix $A_ j$ of locally bounded functions. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact. For small $\varepsilon $, the entries of $A_{j,\varepsilon }$ are bounded on $K$ by the bounds of the entries of $A_ j$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, and by lemma 1.4.1 they converge to those of $A_ j$ in $L^1(K)$. Products of functions which are bounded on $K$ uniformly in $\varepsilon $ and converge in $L^1(K)$ converge in $L^1(K)$, because $|ab-a'b'|\leq |a||b-b'|+|b'||a-a'|$. Since $D$ is a polynomial in the matrix entries, it follows that $D(A_{1,\varepsilon },\dots ,A_{n,\varepsilon })\to D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)$ in $L^1(K)$. By the first part, $(n!/\pi ^ n)D(A_{1,\varepsilon },\dots ,A_{n,\varepsilon })\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$ is the product of the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{j,\varepsilon }$, so the weak limit of these products is $(n!/\pi ^ n)D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. This proves the first formula in general. By lemma 9.12.2 , each $u_ j$ belongs to $W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )\subset W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so proposition 9.12.3 , applied to $u_ j$ and the chosen representative of $v_ j$, gives $A_ j=B_ j$ almost everywhere on $\{ u_ j=v_ j\} $, hence on $E$. Substituting into the first formula proves the second, and also shows that $\mathbf1_ ED(B_1,\dots ,B_ n)=\mathbf1_ ED(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)$ is locally bounded. $\square$

title: 9.13 Gradients against positive currents
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text:
9.13 Gradients against positive currents Several later arguments differentiate the product $v\Theta $ of a bounded plurisubharmonic function $v$ and a closed positive current $\Theta $; examples are the proof that non-pluripolar products are closed (theorem 15.2.1 ) and cutoff arguments on compact manifolds. For smooth $v$ the derivative is $\mathrm dv\wedge \Theta $, and its size is controlled by the gradient measure $\mathrm dv\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge \Theta $, with $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ as in ( 7.6 ). We extend both objects, together with the chain rule, to locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions by decreasing approximation. In this section $\eta $ denotes a real one-form, not the form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ of the preceding sections. Throughout, $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ is open and $\Theta $ is a closed positive current of bidimension $(1,1)$ on $U$, with trace measure $\mu =\Theta \wedge  eta $. We first describe $\Theta $ by a matrix of densities with respect to $\mu $. For $1\leq j,k\leq n$ let $
u _{jk}$ be the complex Radon measure $ rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\, \mathrm dz_ k\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j\wedge \Theta $. Up to a constant factor, $
u _{jk}$ is a coefficient measure of $\Theta $, so by theorem 7.2.5 there is a constant $C$, depending only on $n$, with $|
u _{jk}|\leq C\mu $. Hence $C\mu +\operatorname{Re}
u _{jk}$ and $C\mu +\operatorname{Im}
u _{jk}$ are positive measures bounded by $2C\mu $, and lemma 1.7.1 , applied to them, gives bounded Borel functions $h_{jk}$ with \[   rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\, \mathrm dz_ k\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j\wedge \Theta =h_{jk}\, \mu \qquad (1\leq j,k\leq n).  \] Since $\Theta $ is real (theorem 7.2.5 ), the complex conjugate of $
u _{jk}$ is $ rac{-\mathrm i}{2\pi }\, \mathrm d ar z_ k\wedge \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \Theta =
u _{kj}$; by the uniqueness of densities in lemma 1.7.1 , $h_{kj}= ar h_{jk}$ $\mu $-almost everywhere, so the matrix $H=(h_{jk})$ is Hermitian $\mu $-almost everywhere. Since $\sum _ j rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j= eta /\pi $, summing the identities with $j=k$ gives $\operatorname {tr}H=1/\pi $ $\mu $-almost everywhere. We identify a $(1,0)$-form $\xi =\sum _ k\xi _ k\, \mathrm dz_ k$ with its coefficient vector $(\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ n)\in \mathbb C^ n$, and write $\langle a,bangle =\sum _ ja_ j ar b_ j$ on $\mathbb C^ n$. For a constant $(1,0)$-form $\xi $, the measure $(\mathrm i/2\pi )\, \xi \wedge  ar\xi \wedge \Theta =\langle H\xi ,\xi angle \mu $ is positive, because $\mathrm i\xi \wedge  ar\xi $ is a strongly positive form and $\Theta $ is positive; so $\langle H\xi ,\xi angle \geq 0$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. Applying this to the countably many $\xi $ with rational real and imaginary parts, and using that $\xi \mapsto \langle H\xi ,\xi angle $ is continuous, we see that $H$ is positive semidefinite $\mu $-almost everywhere. Changing $H$ on a $\mu $-null set, we may assume that it is Hermitian and positive semidefinite with trace $1/\pi $ everywhere. Its eigenvalues then lie in $[0,1/\pi ]$, so that $\langle H\xi ,\xi angle \leq |\xi |^2/\pi $. Let $H^{1/2}$ be the positive semidefinite square root of $H$. It is a bounded Borel function on $U$. Indeed, by the Weierstrass approximation theorem there are real polynomials $p_ m$ with $p_ m(t)	o \sqrt t$ uniformly on $[0,1/\pi ]$. Diagonalizing $H(x)$ by a unitary matrix, we see that every entry of $p_ m(H(x))-H(x)^{1/2}$ is bounded by $\sup _{[0,1/\pi ]}|p_ m(t)-\sqrt t|$. The entries of $p_ m(H)$ are polynomials in the $h_{jk}$, hence Borel functions, and so are their pointwise limits, the entries of $H^{1/2}$. Moreover $|H^{1/2}\xi |^2=\langle H\xi ,\xi angle \leq |\xi |^2/\pi $. For a real $C^1$ function $w$, the coefficient vector of the form $\partial w$ is $(\partial w/\partial z_ k)_{k=1}^ n$, and we denote it also by $\partial w$. Since $\mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w=(\mathrm i/2\pi )\, \partial w\wedge  ar\partial w$ by ( 9.7 ), it follows that 9.82  egin{equation} \label{eq:current-gradient-density} \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \Theta = igl |H^{1/2}\partial w igr |^2\mu . \end{equation} Thus, for a compact set $K\subset U$, the square of the energy seminorm $\| H^{1/2}\partial w\| _{L^2(K,\mu )}$ is the mass that $\mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \Theta $ gives to $K$. Similarly, let $\eta $ be a real one-form with continuous coefficients and $(1,0)$-part $\sum _ ke_ k\, \mathrm dz_ k$, and put $e=(e_1,\ldots ,e_ n)$ and $w_ k=\partial w/\partial z_ k$. Only the $(1,1)$-part \[  \sum _{j,k}(e_ k ar w_ j- ar e_ jw_ k)\, \mathrm dz_ k\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j  \] of $\eta \wedge \mathrm dw$ contributes to $\eta \wedge \mathrm dw\wedge \Theta $, so that $\eta \wedge \mathrm dw\wedge \Theta =-2\pi \mathrm i igl (\langle He,\partial wangle -\langle H\partial w,eangle  igr )\mu $. Since $H$ is Hermitian, the second inner product is the complex conjugate of the first, and therefore 9.83  egin{equation} \label{eq:current-gradient-pairing} \eta \wedge \mathrm dw\wedge \Theta =4\pi \operatorname{Im} igl \langle H^{1/2}e,H^{1/2}\partial w igr angle \, \mu . \end{equation} Lemma 9.13.1 . Let $\Theta $ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(1,1)$ on an open set $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$, and let $v$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $U$. Then the current $\mathrm d(v\Theta )$ has measure coefficients; we denote it by $\mathrm dv\wedge \Theta $. The current 9.84  egin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-current-gradient-measure} E_\Theta (v)=\mathrm dv\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge \Theta =	frac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v^2\Theta )-v\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta \end{equation} is a positive measure, the gradient measure of $v$ with respect to $\Theta $. If smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ decrease to $v$ on a neighborhood of a compact set $K\subset U$, then their gradients $\partial v_ l$ converge in the energy seminorm on $K$, that is, $H^{1/2}\partial v_ l$ converges in $L^2(K,\mu )$. For every $f\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, 9.85  egin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-current-chain-rule} \mathrm d(f(v)\Theta )=f'(v)\, \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta . \end{equation} Finally, let $\eta $ be a compactly supported smooth real one-form on $U$, and let $	au \in C_ c(U)$, $	au \geq 0$, be equal to one on $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $. There is a constant $C_\eta $, depending only on $\eta $, such that for every bounded Borel function $a$, 9.86  egin{equation} \label{eq:current-gradient-cauchy-schwarz} \left|\int a\eta \wedge \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta ight|^2 \leq C_\eta \left(\int 	au E_\Theta (v)ight) \left(\int _{\operatorname{Supp}\eta }|a|^2\,  \Theta \wedge  eta ight). \end{equation} Proof. We approximate $v$ by smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ and pass to the limit, first in the gradients (Step 1) and then in each assertion of the lemma (Steps 2–5). All assertions are local, so we fix a compact set $K\subset U$ and an open neighborhood $W\subset U$ of $K$ on which smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ decrease to $v$. For the convergence assertion, $W$ and the $v_ l$ are given. Otherwise we take for $W$ a relatively compact open neighborhood of $K$ in $U$ and for $v_ l$ the radial mollifications $v*ho _{\varepsilon _ l}$, where $\varepsilon _ l\downarrow 0$ and $\varepsilon _1$ is less than the distance from $\overline W$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus U$; they are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $W$ and decrease to $v$ (proposition 8.2.2 ). Choose a compact set $K_1\subset W$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}K_1$, and a function $\sigma \in C^\infty _ c(W)$ with $\sigma \geq 0$ which equals one on a neighborhood of $K_1$. Since $v\leq v_ l\leq v_1$, the $v_ l$ are uniformly bounded on $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $. Step 1. Convergence of the gradients. For a smooth real function $w$, we have $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)=2\, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w+2w\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2\Theta )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)\wedge \Theta $ because $\Theta $ is closed. Hence \[  \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \Theta =	frac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2\Theta )-w\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge \Theta .  \] Apply this identity to $w=v_ l-v_ m$ and integrate against $\sigma $: \[  \int \sigma \, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \Theta =	frac 12\int (v_ l-v_ m)^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma \wedge \Theta -\int \sigma (v_ l-v_ m)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ l-v_ m)\wedge \Theta .  \] Both terms on the right tend to zero as $l,m	o \infty $. For the first, $|v_ l-v_ m|\leq v_ N-v$ for $l,m\geq N$, and $v_ N-v	o 0$ pointwise and boundedly on $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $; since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma \wedge \Theta $ is a signed measure with total variation bounded by a multiple of $\mu $ on $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $, dominated convergence applies. For the second, expand it into the four integrals $\int \sigma v_ p\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge \Theta $ with $p,q\in \{ l,m\} $, taken with the signs $+,-,-,+$. Given indices $l_ k,m_ k	o \infty $, pass to a subsequence along which both are strictly increasing; then $v_{l_ k}$ and $v_{m_ k}$ decrease to $v$, and the weighted form of theorem 9.2.5 on $W$, with the base current $\Theta $, shows that each of the four integrals tends to $\int \sigma v\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta $. Their signed sum therefore tends to zero, and since this holds for a subsequence of every such pair of index sequences, the second term tends to zero as $l,m	o \infty $. Since $\sigma \geq 0$, $\sigma =1$ on $K_1$ and $\mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \Theta $ is the positive measure $|H^{1/2}\partial w|^2\mu $, by ( 9.82 ), the left side bounds $\| H^{1/2}\partial v_ l-H^{1/2}\partial v_ m\| _{L^2(K_1,\mu )}^2$. Consequently $H^{1/2}\partial v_ l$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^2(K_1,\mu )$; let $\Gamma \in L^2(K_1,\mu )$ be its limit. In particular, $H^{1/2}\partial v_ l$ converges in $L^2(K,\mu )$, which is the convergence assertion. Step 2. The first derivative. Let $\eta $ be a smooth real one-form with compact support in $\operatorname{Int}K_1$, with $(1,0)$-part $\sum _ ke_ k\, \mathrm dz_ k$. By ( 9.83 ), \[  \int \eta \wedge \mathrm dv_ l\wedge \Theta =4\pi \int \operatorname{Im} igl \langle H^{1/2}e,H^{1/2}\partial v_ l igr angle \, \mathrm d\mu \longrightarrow 4\pi \int \operatorname{Im} igl \langle H^{1/2}e,\Gamma  igr angle \, \mathrm d\mu ,  \] since $H^{1/2}e$ is bounded and vanishes outside $K_1$, and $\mu (K_1)<\infty $. On the other hand, $\mathrm dv_ l\wedge \Theta =\mathrm d(v_ l\Theta )$ since $\Theta $ is closed, and $v_ l\Theta 	o v\Theta $ weakly on $W$ by dominated convergence on the coefficient measures; hence $\mathrm d(v_ l\Theta )	o \mathrm d(v\Theta )$ weakly. Therefore the pairing of $\mathrm d(v\Theta )$ with $\eta $, written $\int \eta \wedge \mathrm d(v\Theta )$, equals the last integral. Write $\langle H^{1/2}e,\Gamma angle =\sum _ ke_ kG_ k$, where $G_ k=\sum _ j(H^{1/2})_{jk} ar\Gamma _ j$ belongs to $L^2(K_1,\mu )\subset L^1(K_1,\mu )$, so that \[  4\pi \operatorname{Im} igl \langle H^{1/2}e,\Gamma  igr angle =\sum _ k igl (-2\pi \mathrm i\, G_ k\, e_ k+2\pi \mathrm i\,  ar G_ k\,  ar e_ k igr ).  \] Thus, on real test one-forms $\eta $ supported in $\operatorname{Int}K_1$, the current $\mathrm d(v\Theta )$ acts by integrating against $\mu $ the coefficients $e_ k$ and $ ar e_ k$ of $\eta $, multiplied by the functions $-2\pi \mathrm i\, G_ k$ and $2\pi \mathrm i\,  ar G_ k$, which are integrable on $K_1$. Every test one-form is a complex linear combination of two real ones, so on $\operatorname{Int}K_1$ the current $\mathrm d(v\Theta )$ has measure coefficients, which are absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu $ and finite on $K_1$. In particular, for a bounded Borel function $a$, \[  \int a\eta \wedge \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta =4\pi \int a\operatorname{Im} igl \langle H^{1/2}e,\Gamma  igr angle \, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Step 3. The gradient measure. Since $H^{1/2}\partial v_ l	o \Gamma $ in $L^2(K_1,\mu )$, the densities $|H^{1/2}\partial v_ l|^2$ converge to $|\Gamma |^2$ in $L^1(K_1,\mu )$, so the measures $\mathrm dv_ l\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v_ l\wedge \Theta =|H^{1/2}\partial v_ l|^2\mu $ converge weakly on $\operatorname{Int}K_1$ to the positive measure $|\Gamma |^2\mu $. text: Lemma 9.13.1 . Let $\Theta $ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(1,1)$ on an open set $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$, and let $v$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $U$. Then the current $\mathrm d(v\Theta )$ has measure coefficients; we denote it by $\mathrm dv\wedge \Theta $. The current 9.84 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-current-gradient-measure} E_\Theta (v)=\mathrm dv\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge \Theta =\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v^2\Theta )-v\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta \end{equation} is a positive measure, the gradient measure of $v$ with respect to $\Theta $. If smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ decrease to $v$ on a neighborhood of a compact set $K\subset U$, then their gradients $\partial v_ l$ converge in the energy seminorm on $K$, that is, $H^{1/2}\partial v_ l$ converges in $L^2(K,\mu )$. For every $f\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, 9.85 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-current-chain-rule} \mathrm d(f(v)\Theta )=f'(v)\, \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta . \end{equation} Finally, let $\eta $ be a compactly supported smooth real one-form on $U$, and let $\tau \in C_ c(U)$, $\tau \geq 0$, be equal to one on $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $. There is a constant $C_\eta $, depending only on $\eta $, such that for every bounded Borel function $a$, 9.86 \begin{equation} \label{eq:current-gradient-cauchy-schwarz} \left|\int a\eta \wedge \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta \right|^2 \leq C_\eta \left(\int \tau E_\Theta (v)\right) \left(\int _{\operatorname{Supp}\eta }|a|^2\,  \Theta \wedge \beta \right). \end{equation} Proof. We approximate $v$ by smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ and pass to the limit, first in the gradients (Step 1) and then in each assertion of the lemma (Steps 2–5). All assertions are local, so we fix a compact set $K\subset U$ and an open neighborhood $W\subset U$ of $K$ on which smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ decrease to $v$. For the convergence assertion, $W$ and the $v_ l$ are given. Otherwise we take for $W$ a relatively compact open neighborhood of $K$ in $U$ and for $v_ l$ the radial mollifications $v*\rho _{\varepsilon _ l}$, where $\varepsilon _ l\downarrow 0$ and $\varepsilon _1$ is less than the distance from $\overline W$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus U$; they are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $W$ and decrease to $v$ (proposition 8.2.2 ). Choose a compact set $K_1\subset W$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}K_1$, and a function $\sigma \in C^\infty _ c(W)$ with $\sigma \geq 0$ which equals one on a neighborhood of $K_1$. Since $v\leq v_ l\leq v_1$, the $v_ l$ are uniformly bounded on $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $. Step 1. Convergence of the gradients. For a smooth real function $w$, we have $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)=2\, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w+2w\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2\Theta )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)\wedge \Theta $ because $\Theta $ is closed. Hence \[  \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \Theta =\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2\Theta )-w\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge \Theta .  \] Apply this identity to $w=v_ l-v_ m$ and integrate against $\sigma $: \[  \int \sigma \, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \Theta =\tfrac 12\int (v_ l-v_ m)^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma \wedge \Theta -\int \sigma (v_ l-v_ m)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ l-v_ m)\wedge \Theta .  \] Both terms on the right tend to zero as $l,m\to \infty $. For the first, $|v_ l-v_ m|\leq v_ N-v$ for $l,m\geq N$, and $v_ N-v\to 0$ pointwise and boundedly on $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $; since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma \wedge \Theta $ is a signed measure with total variation bounded by a multiple of $\mu $ on $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $, dominated convergence applies. For the second, expand it into the four integrals $\int \sigma v_ p\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge \Theta $ with $p,q\in \{ l,m\} $, taken with the signs $+,-,-,+$. Given indices $l_ k,m_ k\to \infty $, pass to a subsequence along which both are strictly increasing; then $v_{l_ k}$ and $v_{m_ k}$ decrease to $v$, and the weighted form of theorem 9.2.5 on $W$, with the base current $\Theta $, shows that each of the four integrals tends to $\int \sigma v\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta $. Their signed sum therefore tends to zero, and since this holds for a subsequence of every such pair of index sequences, the second term tends to zero as $l,m\to \infty $. Since $\sigma \geq 0$, $\sigma =1$ on $K_1$ and $\mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \Theta $ is the positive measure $|H^{1/2}\partial w|^2\mu $, by ( 9.82 ), the left side bounds $\| H^{1/2}\partial v_ l-H^{1/2}\partial v_ m\| _{L^2(K_1,\mu )}^2$. Consequently $H^{1/2}\partial v_ l$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^2(K_1,\mu )$; let $\Gamma \in L^2(K_1,\mu )$ be its limit. In particular, $H^{1/2}\partial v_ l$ converges in $L^2(K,\mu )$, which is the convergence assertion. Step 2. The first derivative. Let $\eta $ be a smooth real one-form with compact support in $\operatorname{Int}K_1$, with $(1,0)$-part $\sum _ ke_ k\, \mathrm dz_ k$. By ( 9.83 ), \[  \int \eta \wedge \mathrm dv_ l\wedge \Theta =4\pi \int \operatorname{Im}\bigl \langle H^{1/2}e,H^{1/2}\partial v_ l\bigr \rangle \, \mathrm d\mu \longrightarrow 4\pi \int \operatorname{Im}\bigl \langle H^{1/2}e,\Gamma \bigr \rangle \, \mathrm d\mu ,  \] since $H^{1/2}e$ is bounded and vanishes outside $K_1$, and $\mu (K_1)<\infty $. On the other hand, $\mathrm dv_ l\wedge \Theta =\mathrm d(v_ l\Theta )$ since $\Theta $ is closed, and $v_ l\Theta \to v\Theta $ weakly on $W$ by dominated convergence on the coefficient measures; hence $\mathrm d(v_ l\Theta )\to \mathrm d(v\Theta )$ weakly. Therefore the pairing of $\mathrm d(v\Theta )$ with $\eta $, written $\int \eta \wedge \mathrm d(v\Theta )$, equals the last integral. Write $\langle H^{1/2}e,\Gamma \rangle =\sum _ ke_ kG_ k$, where $G_ k=\sum _ j(H^{1/2})_{jk}\bar\Gamma _ j$ belongs to $L^2(K_1,\mu )\subset L^1(K_1,\mu )$, so that \[  4\pi \operatorname{Im}\bigl \langle H^{1/2}e,\Gamma \bigr \rangle =\sum _ k\bigl (-2\pi \mathrm i\, G_ k\, e_ k+2\pi \mathrm i\, \bar G_ k\, \bar e_ k\bigr ).  \] Thus, on real test one-forms $\eta $ supported in $\operatorname{Int}K_1$, the current $\mathrm d(v\Theta )$ acts by integrating against $\mu $ the coefficients $e_ k$ and $\bar e_ k$ of $\eta $, multiplied by the functions $-2\pi \mathrm i\, G_ k$ and $2\pi \mathrm i\, \bar G_ k$, which are integrable on $K_1$. Every test one-form is a complex linear combination of two real ones, so on $\operatorname{Int}K_1$ the current $\mathrm d(v\Theta )$ has measure coefficients, which are absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu $ and finite on $K_1$. In particular, for a bounded Borel function $a$, \[  \int a\eta \wedge \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta =4\pi \int a\operatorname{Im}\bigl \langle H^{1/2}e,\Gamma \bigr \rangle \, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Step 3. The gradient measure. Since $H^{1/2}\partial v_ l\to \Gamma $ in $L^2(K_1,\mu )$, the densities $|H^{1/2}\partial v_ l|^2$ converge to $|\Gamma |^2$ in $L^1(K_1,\mu )$, so the measures $\mathrm dv_ l\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v_ l\wedge \Theta =|H^{1/2}\partial v_ l|^2\mu $ converge weakly on $\operatorname{Int}K_1$ to the positive measure $|\Gamma |^2\mu $. On the other hand, by the identity of Step 1, \[  \mathrm dv_ l\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v_ l\wedge \Theta =\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ l^2\Theta )-v_ l\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l\wedge \Theta \longrightarrow \tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v^2\Theta )-v\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta  \] weakly on $W$: the first term converges by dominated convergence on the coefficient measures of $v_ l^2\Theta $ and the weak continuity of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, and the second by theorem 9.2.5 . Hence the right side of ( 9.84 ) is the positive measure $|\Gamma |^2\mu $ on $\operatorname{Int}K_1$. Since $K$ was arbitrary and $K\subset \operatorname{Int}K_1$, the current $E_\Theta (v)$, which does not involve the approximations, is a positive measure on $U$. Step 4. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. Let $\eta $, $\tau $ and $a$ be as in the statement, and apply Steps 1–3 with $K=\operatorname{Supp}\tau $; then $\operatorname{Supp}\eta \subset K\subset \operatorname{Int}K_1$. For a smooth real function $w$ on $W$, ( 9.83 ) and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give \[  \left|\int a\eta \wedge \mathrm dw\wedge \Theta \right|^2 \leq 16\pi ^2\int _{\operatorname{Supp}\eta }|a|^2\bigl |H^{1/2}e\bigr |^2\, \mathrm d\mu \int _{\operatorname{Supp}\eta }\bigl |H^{1/2}\partial w\bigr |^2\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Since $|H^{1/2}e|^2\leq |e|^2/\pi $, we have $16\pi ^2|H^{1/2}e|^2\leq C_\eta $ with $C_\eta =16\pi \sup |e|^2$, which depends only on $\eta $. The second integral is at most $\int \tau \, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \Theta $, because $\tau \geq 0$ and $\tau =1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $. Apply this to $w=v_ l$ and let $l\to \infty $. The left side converges to $|\int a\eta \wedge \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta |^2$ by Step 2, since $a\, \operatorname{Im}\langle H^{1/2}e,H^{1/2}\partial v_ l\rangle \to a\, \operatorname{Im}\langle H^{1/2}e,\Gamma \rangle $ in $L^1(K_1,\mu )$, and $\int \tau \, \mathrm dv_ l\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v_ l\wedge \Theta \to \int \tau E_\Theta (v)$ by Step 3, since $\tau $ is continuous with compact support in $\operatorname{Int}K_1$. This proves ( 9.86 ). Step 5. The chain rule. Both sides of ( 9.85 ) are complex-linear in $f$, so we may assume that $f$ is real. Let first $f$ be smooth. The functions $v_ l$ and $v$ take values in a compact interval $J$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $. Since $f(v_ l)\to f(v)$ boundedly, $f(v_ l)\Theta \to f(v)\Theta $ weakly on $W$ by dominated convergence, and hence $\mathrm d(f(v_ l)\Theta )\to \mathrm d(f(v)\Theta )$. By the chain rule for smooth functions and the closedness of $\Theta $, $\mathrm d(f(v_ l)\Theta )=f'(v_ l)\, \mathrm dv_ l\wedge \Theta $. Moreover $f'(v_ l)H^{1/2}\partial v_ l\to f'(v)\Gamma $ in $L^2(K_1,\mu )$: the difference is \[  f'(v_ l)\bigl (H^{1/2}\partial v_ l-\Gamma \bigr )+\bigl (f'(v_ l)-f'(v)\bigr )\Gamma ,  \] where the first term tends to zero because $f'$ is bounded on $J$, and the second by dominated convergence. Now let $\eta $ be as in Step 2. Identity ( 9.83 ), multiplied by the continuous function $f'(v_ l)$, and Step 2 with $a=f'(v)$ give \[  \int \eta \wedge f'(v_ l)\, \mathrm dv_ l\wedge \Theta =4\pi \int \operatorname{Im}\bigl \langle H^{1/2}e,f'(v_ l)H^{1/2}\partial v_ l\bigr \rangle \, \mathrm d\mu \longrightarrow \int \eta \wedge f'(v)\, \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta .  \] Since the left side also tends to $\int \eta \wedge \mathrm d(f(v)\Theta )$, the currents $\mathrm d(f(v)\Theta )$ and $f'(v)\, \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta $ agree on $\operatorname{Int}K_1$. As $K$ was arbitrary, this proves ( 9.85 ) for smooth $f$. Now let $f\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, and let $f_ m=f*\rho _{1/m}$ be its mollifications on $\mathbb R$. By proposition 1.4.3 and lemma 1.4.1 , $f_ m\to f$ and $f_ m'=f'*\rho _{1/m}\to f'$ uniformly on compact subsets of $\mathbb R$. Since $v$ is locally bounded, $f_ m(v)\to f(v)$ and $f_ m'(v)\to f'(v)$ uniformly on compact subsets of $U$. As $\Theta $ and $\mathrm dv\wedge \Theta $ are currents of order zero, it follows that $f_ m(v)\Theta \to f(v)\Theta $ and $f_ m'(v)\, \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta \to f'(v)\, \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta $ weakly. Since $\mathrm d$ is weakly continuous, the identity $\mathrm d(f_ m(v)\Theta )=f_ m'(v)\, \mathrm dv\wedge \Theta $ passes to the limit. $\square$

section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: 10 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology The upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of a family of plurisubharmonic functions is plurisubharmonic, but it may differ from the supremum on an exceptional set (in dimension one, see example 3.4.3 with $d=2$). In chapter 9 we showed that, locally, this exceptional set has outer Monge–Ampère capacity zero (corollary 9.5.2 ), and that the same holds for the pole set of every plurisubharmonic function (proposition 9.3.4 ). The first aim of this chapter is the converse: every subset of a ball with outer capacity zero lies in the pole set of a single plurisubharmonic function on the ball. Sets that are locally contained in pole sets are called pluripolar; they play in pluripotential theory the role that polar sets play in the classical theory of chapter 3 , chapter 4 , chapter 5 . The link between capacity and pole sets is the relative extremal function $H_ E$ of a set $E$ in a ball $B$, the regularized upper envelope of the plurisubharmonic functions on $B$ that are nonpositive and at most $-1$ on $E$. For compact sets and for relatively compact open sets, the capacity of $E$ is the total Monge–Ampère mass of $H_ E$ (proposition 10.1.2 , proposition 10.1.3 ). If $E$ has outer capacity zero, the extremal functions of small open neighborhoods of $E$ therefore have small mass, and the comparison principle shows that $H_ E=0$; a convergent series of functions from the envelope then has poles on all of $E$ (theorem 10.1.4 ). It follows that countable unions of pluripolar sets are pluripolar and that the exceptional sets of upper envelopes are pluripolar (corollary 10.2.2 ). On $\mathbb C^ n$ the local functions can even be glued, with the help of small multiples of $\log ^+|z|$, into a single plurisubharmonic function on the whole space; this is Josefson's theorem (theorem 10.2.1 ). The second half of the chapter studies the plurifine topology, the analogue of the fine topology of chapter 5 defined by plurisubharmonic functions. Unbounded potentials force us to use it: the set $\{ u>-k\} $, on which a plurisubharmonic function $u$ coincides with its truncation $\max \{ u,-k\} $, is plurifine open but in general not open. We prove that Bedford–Taylor products of locally bounded potentials are local for the plurifine topology (theorem 10.4.3 ), by combining their locality on sets of the form $\{ u>v\} $ (proposition 9.2.7 ) with a quasi-Lindelöf theorem: every union of plurifine open sets coincides with a countable subunion outside a pluripolar set (theorem 10.4.1 ). Consequently, for plurisubharmonic functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$, the products of the truncations $\max \{ u_ l,-k\} $ do not depend on $k\ge m$ on the set $\bigcap _ l\{ u_ l>-m\} $ (proposition 10.4.4 ); this compatibility is the starting point of the non-pluripolar products of chapter 15 . Finally, the difference of two plurisubharmonic functions is plurifinely continuous off their common pole set. Its quasi-supremum and quasi-infimum on a plurifine open set, which disregard pluripolar sets, are therefore its ordinary supremum and infimum off any pluripolar set containing the common poles (corollary 10.5.3 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.10 .

text: 10.1 Pluripolar sets and relative extremal functions We define pluripolar sets on complex manifolds and then introduce, on a ball, the relative extremal functions that connect them with the Monge–Ampère capacity of section 9.3 . Definition 10.1.1 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold. A subset $E\subset X$ is pluripolar , or locally pluripolar , if every point of $X$ has a connected coordinate neighborhood $U$ carrying a function $V\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ with $E\cap U\subset \{ V=-\infty \} $. If $X$ is connected, a subset $E\subset X$ is globally pluripolar in $X$ if there is a single $V\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ with $E\subset \{ V=-\infty \} $. A property holds quasi-everywhere if it holds outside a pluripolar set. Pluripolar sets are not required to be Borel, and subsets of pluripolar sets are pluripolar. If $E\subset X$ is pluripolar and $W\subset X$ is open, then $E\cap W$ is pluripolar in $W$: restrict the functions of the definition to small coordinate balls in $W$. Every pluripolar set $E$ has Lebesgue measure zero in every chart. Indeed, a chart domain $C$ has a countable basis, so it is covered by countably many of the sets $U\cap C$, with $U$ as in the definition, and each set $E\cap U\cap C$ lies in the pole set of the corresponding function $V$. In the coordinates of the chart, $V$ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $U\cap C$, hence locally integrable there (theorem 8.2.1 ), so its pole set in $U\cap C$ is Lebesgue null. In dimension zero every plurisubharmonic function is finite, so the only pluripolar set is the empty set. From now on the complex dimension $n$ is positive. Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. By theorem 8.2.1 , the plurisubharmonic functions in definition 10.1.1 are nontrivial subharmonic functions when $\mathbb C^ n$ is identified with $\mathbb R^{2n}$, so every pluripolar subset of $\Omega $ is real polar in the sense of section 8.3 . For $n\ge 2$ the converse fails: example 10.2.3 exhibits a real polar subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ that is not pluripolar. For $n=1$ the converse holds, so that the pluripolar subsets of $\Omega $ are exactly its polar subsets in the sense of definition 3.5.1 . Indeed, let $A\subset \Omega $ be polar, and let $D$ be a disc with $\overline D\subset \Omega $. By proposition 4.2.3 , applied to $A\cap D$, there is a fundamental potential on $\mathbb C$ equal to $-\infty $ on $A\cap D$; it is a nontrivial subharmonic function by proposition 3.2.1 , hence plurisubharmonic on $D$. Since every point of $\Omega $, whether in $A$ or not, lies in such a disc, $A$ is pluripolar. This changes the meaning of quasi-everywhere . In definition 5.2.1 it meant outside a polar set of $\mathbb R^ d$; from now on, throughout 2 , it means outside a pluripolar set, as in definition 10.1.1 . Since pluripolar sets are real polar, a property that holds quasi-everywhere on $\Omega $ in the new sense also holds outside a real polar set; for $n=1$ the two notions agree, whereas for $n\ge 2$ the new notion is strictly stronger. For the rest of this section, $B$ denotes an open ball in $\mathbb C^ n$. Recall the capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ and the outer capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*$ of definition 9.3.2 ; the competitors for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ are the functions $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ with $0\le v\le 1$. For a set $E\subset B$ we define \[  h_ E(z)=\sup \{ v(z):v\in \mathrm{PSH}(B),\  v\le 0\  \text{on }B,\  v\le -1\  \text{on }E\} , \qquad H_ E=h_ E^*.  \] The functions $v$ in this supremum are called competitors for $E$ ; we always name the set, to distinguish them from the competitors for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$. The constant $-1$ is a competitor for $E$, and so is the maximum of a competitor for $E$ with $-1$; hence we may restrict the supremum to competitors with values in $[-1,0]$, and $-1\le h_ E\le H_ E\le 0$. Since every competitor for $E$ is at most $-1$ on $E$, we also have $h_ E=-1$ on $E$. If $v$ is a competitor for $E$ with values in $[-1,0]$, then $v+1$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$. By theorem 8.3.2 , $H_ E$ is plurisubharmonic; we call it the relative extremal function of $E$ with respect to $B$. It is the plurisubharmonic counterpart of the relative extremal function $u_ A$ of section 4.3 , which is defined by the same constraints on subharmonic functions. We shall use the following properties of these functions repeatedly. If $E\subset F\subset B$, then every competitor for $F$ is a competitor for $E$, so $h_ F\le h_ E$ and $H_ F\le H_ E$. If $B=B(a,R)$ and $\overline E$ is a compact subset of $B$, then for a sufficiently large constant $A>0$ the function $A(|z-a|^2-R^2)$ is at most $-1$ on $E$, hence it is a competitor for $E$, and 10.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-extremal-barrier} A(|z-a|^2-R^2)\le h_ E\le H_ E\le 0\quad \text{on }B; \end{equation} in particular $H_ E(z)\to 0$ as $z\to \partial B$. Next, Choquet's lemma (lemma 3.4.1 ) gives competitors $w_1,w_2,\ldots $ for $E$ with $(\sup _ kw_ k)^*=H_ E$. The finite maxima $v_ j=\max \{ -1,w_1,\ldots ,w_ j\} $ are competitors for $E$, and their limit $g=\lim _ jv_ j$ satisfies $\sup _ kw_ k\le g\le h_ E$; taking regularizations, we get $g^*=H_ E$. By theorem 8.3.2 , applied to the family $(v_ j)$, we have $g=g^*$ almost everywhere. Thus there are competitors $v_ j$ for $E$ with 10.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-extremal-choquet} -1\le v_1\le v_2\le \cdots \le 0,\qquad \lim _ jv_ j=H_ E\quad \text{almost everywhere on }B. \end{equation} Finally, by corollary 9.5.2 , for every compact set $L\subset B$ the set $L\cap \{ h_ E<H_ E\} $ has outer capacity zero in $B$. Exhausting $B$ by countably many compact sets and using the countable subadditivity of outer capacity (proposition 9.3.3 ), we obtain 10.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-extremal-discrepancy} \operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(\{ h_ E<H_ E\} )=0. \end{equation} A set $N\subset B$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(N)=0$ has outer measure zero for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ whenever $v$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$, since $\int _ G(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\le \operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)$ for every open set $G\supset N$. Proposition 10.1.2 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be an open ball, and let $K\subset B$ be compact. Then $H_ K(z)\to 0$ as $z\to \partial B$, the Monge–Ampère measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$ is carried by $K\cap \{ H_ K=-1\} $, and \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)=\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n.  \] If $(K_ j)$ is a decreasing sequence of compact subsets of $B$ with intersection $K$, then the functions $H_{K_ j}$ increase and converge to $H_ K$ almost everywhere, and $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K_ j)$ decreases to $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)$. In particular $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K)=\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)$. Proof. The boundary behavior of $H_ K$ follows from ( 10.1 ). Since $H_ K$ is bounded, its Monge–Ampère measure is defined (definition 9.1.1 ). We first show that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$ vanishes on $B\setminus K$. Choose competitors $v_ j$ for $K$ as in ( 10.2 ), and let $D$ be a ball with $\overline D\subset B\setminus K$. Let $\widehat v_ j$ be the function obtained from $v_ j$ by corollary 9.6.4 : it is plurisubharmonic on $B$, equals $v_ j$ outside $D$, and satisfies $\widehat v_ j\ge v_ j$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat v_ j)^ n=0$ on $D$. Each $\widehat v_ j$ is again a competitor for $K$. Indeed, $\widehat v_ j=v_ j\le -1$ on $K$. Moreover $\widehat v_ j\le 0$: outside $D$ because $\widehat v_ j=v_ j$, and on $D$ by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), since by upper semicontinuity the upper limit of $\widehat v_ j$ at each point $x\in \partial D$ is at most $\widehat v_ j(x)=v_ j(x)\le 0$. Since $\widehat v_ j$ is increasing in $v_ j$ by corollary 9.6.4 , the functions $\widehat v_ j$ increase with $j$, and $v_ j\le \widehat v_ j\le h_ K\le H_ K$ shows that $\widehat v_ j\to H_ K$ almost everywhere. They take values in $[-1,0]$, so theorem 9.5.1 gives $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat v_ j)^ n\to (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$ weakly, and therefore $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n=0$ on $D$. Covering the open set $B\setminus K$ by countably many such balls $D$, we conclude that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$ is carried by $K$. As $h_ K=-1$ on $K$, the Borel set $K\cap \{ H_ K>-1\} $ is contained in $\{ h_ K<H_ K\} $, which has outer capacity zero by ( 10.3 ). Because $H_ K+1$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$, this set is therefore null for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H_ K+1))^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$. Thus $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$ is carried by $K\cap \{ H_ K=-1\} $. We now prove the capacity formula. As $H_ K+1$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$ is carried by $K$, we have $\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n=\int _ K(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H_ K+1))^ n\le \operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)$. Conversely, let $v$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$, let $0<\varepsilon <1/2$, and put $w=(1-2\varepsilon )(v-1)-\varepsilon $. Then $-1+\varepsilon \le w\le -\varepsilon $. In particular $w>-1$, so $K\cap \{ H_ K\ge w\} \subset K\cap \{ H_ K>-1\} $; this set has outer capacity zero and is therefore null for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n=(1-2\varepsilon )^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$. Moreover $H_ K(z)\to 0$ as $z\to \partial B$ while $w\le -\varepsilon $, so $\varliminf _{z\to x}(H_ K(z)-w(z))\ge \varepsilon >0$ for every $x\in \partial B$, and the comparison principle (theorem 9.2.8 ) applies to $H_ K$ and $w$ on $B$. We obtain \[  \begin{aligned}  (1-2\varepsilon )^ n\int _ K(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n & =\int _{K\cap \{ H_ K<w\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n \le \int _{\{ H_ K<w\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n\\ & \le \int _{\{ H_ K<w\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n \le \int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n. \end{aligned}  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and taking the supremum over $v$, we get $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)\le \int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$. Now let $(K_ j)$ be compact subsets of $B$ decreasing to $K$. Since $K\subset K_{j+1}\subset K_ j$, the functions $H_{K_ j}$ increase and are bounded above by $H_ K$. Put $H=(\sup _ jH_{K_ j})^*$. By theorem 8.3.2 , $H$ is plurisubharmonic and equals $\sup _ jH_{K_ j}$ almost everywhere, and $H\le H_ K$ because $H_ K$ is upper semicontinuous. For the reverse inequality, let $v$ be a competitor for $K$ and let $0<\varepsilon <1$. The open set $G=\{ v<-1+\varepsilon \} $ contains $K$. The compact sets $K_ j\setminus G$ decrease and have empty intersection, so one of them is empty; hence $K_ j\subset G$ for all large $j$. For such $j$ the function $v/(1-\varepsilon )$ is a competitor for $K_ j$, and hence $v\le (1-\varepsilon )H_{K_ j}\le (1-\varepsilon )H$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\le H$, and taking the supremum over all competitors $v$ for $K$ gives $h_ K\le H$. As $H$ is upper semicontinuous, $H_ K\le H$. Therefore $H=H_ K$, and $H_{K_ j}\to H_ K$ almost everywhere. By theorem 9.5.1 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_{K_ j})^ n\to (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$ weakly. All these measures are carried by the fixed compact set $K_1$, so testing with a function in $C_ c(B)$ equal to one on $K_1$ shows that their total masses converge. By the capacity formula, $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K_ j)\to \operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)$, and this convergence is decreasing because capacity is increasing. Finally, $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)\le \operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K)$ because capacity is increasing. For the converse we may assume $K\neq \varnothing $, since both capacities of the empty set vanish. Choose $\delta >0$ such that the compact sets $K_ j=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le \delta /j\} $ lie in $B$. They decrease to $K$, and each contains $K$ in its interior. Hence $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K)\le \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\operatorname{Int}K_ j)\le \operatorname {Cap}_ B(K_ j)$, and the right-hand side tends to $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)$ by what we have just proved. $\square$ Proposition 10.1.3 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be an open ball, and let $G$ be an open set with $G\Subset B$. Then $h_ G=H_ G$, $H_ G=-1$ on $G$, $H_ G(z)\to 0$ as $z\to \partial B$, the measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ G)^ n$ is carried by $\overline G$, and \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)=\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ G)^ n.  \] Proof. Choose compact sets $K_ j$ with $K_ j\subset \operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$ and $\bigcup _ jK_ j=G$. Since the $K_ j$ increase, the functions $H_{K_ j}$ decrease. They take values in $[-1,0]$, so their limit $H$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.1 . Since $h_{K_ j}=-1$ on $K_ j$ and the upper regularization at a point only involves the values of $h_{K_ j}$ near that point, we have $H_{K_ j}=-1$ on $\operatorname{Int}K_ j$. Every point of $G$ lies in $\operatorname{Int}K_ j$ for all large $j$, so $H=-1$ on $G$. Thus $H$ is a competitor for $G$, and $H\le h_ G$. Conversely, every competitor for $G$ is a competitor for each $K_ j$, hence bounded above by every $H_{K_ j}$ and thus by $H$; so $h_ G\le H$. We have shown $h_ G=H$. As $H$ is upper semicontinuous, $H_ G=h_ G^*=H$; in particular $H_ G=-1$ on $G$. The boundary behavior follows from ( 10.1 ). By theorem 9.2.5 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_{K_ j})^ n\to (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ G)^ n$ weakly. By proposition 10.1.2 , these measures are carried by $K_ j\subset \overline G$. Hence the limit measure vanishes on the open set $B\setminus \overline G$, that is, it is carried by the compact set $\overline G$, and testing with a function in $C_ c(B)$ equal to one on $\overline G$ shows that the total masses converge. Since the Borel sets $K_ j$ increase to $G$, proposition 9.3.3 (2) gives $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K_ j)\to \operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)$. Together with the capacity formula of proposition 10.1.2 for the $K_ j$, this yields $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)=\lim _ j\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_{K_ j})^ n=\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ G)^ n$. $\square$ Theorem 10.1.4 . Let $E$ be a subset of an open ball $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$. The following conditions are equivalent: $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E)=0$; $E\subset \{ V=-\infty \} $ for some $V\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ with $V\le 0$; $H_ E=0$ on $B$. Every pluripolar subset of $B$ satisfies these conditions; in particular it is globally pluripolar in $B$. Consequently, on every complex manifold $X$, a countable union of pluripolar sets is pluripolar, and if $W\subset X$ is open, every subset of $W$ that is pluripolar in $W$ is pluripolar in $X$. Proof. We prove (2)$\Rightarrow $(1), then (1)$\Rightarrow $(3) for relatively compact sets $E$ and (3)$\Rightarrow $(2), deduce (1)$\Rightarrow $(2) in general by exhaustion, and finally prove (2)$\Rightarrow $(3). The remaining assertions then follow by localization. (2)$\Rightarrow $(1). We show more generally that every pluripolar set $E\subset B$ satisfies (1); a set as in (2) is pluripolar. By definition 10.1.1 , every point of $B$ has an open neighborhood $W\subset B$ carrying a plurisubharmonic function whose pole set contains $E\cap W$. The second assertion of proposition 9.3.4 , applied with $D=B$, therefore gives $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E\cap L)=0$ for every compact set $L\subset B$. Exhausting $B$ by countably many compact sets and using countable subadditivity, we obtain $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E)=0$. (1)$\Rightarrow $(3) when $E\Subset B$. Fix an open set $O$ with $\overline E\subset O\Subset B$. Since $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E)=0$, there are open sets $G_ j'\supset E$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G_ j')<1/j$. The open sets $G_ j=O\cap G_1'\cap \cdots \cap G_ j'$ decrease, contain $E$, lie in $O$, and satisfy $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G_ j)\to 0$. Since the $G_ j$ decrease, the functions $H_{G_ j}$ increase; put $H=(\sup _ jH_{G_ j})^*$. By theorem 8.3.2 , $H$ is plurisubharmonic, takes values in $[-1,0]$, and is the almost-everywhere limit of the $H_{G_ j}$. By proposition 10.1.3 , $\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_{G_ j})^ n=\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G_ j)\to 0$, and by theorem 9.5.1 these measures converge weakly to $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n$. Hence $\int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\lim _ j\int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_{G_ j})^ n\le \lim _ j\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G_ j)=0$ for every $\chi \in C_ c(B)$ with $0\le \chi \le 1$, and therefore $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0$. Since every $G_ j$ lies in $O$, the barrier ( 10.1 ), with a constant $A$ chosen for $O$, bounds every $H_{G_ j}$, and hence $H$, from below by one function tending to zero at $\partial B$; thus $H(z)\to 0$ as $z\to \partial B$. The last assertion of the comparison principle (theorem 9.2.8 ), applied to $u=H$ and $v=0$, gives $H\ge 0$, and therefore $H=0$. Finally, $E\subset G_ j$ gives $H_{G_ j}\le H_ E$ for all $j$; since $H_ E$ is upper semicontinuous, $0=H\le H_ E\le 0$. (3)$\Rightarrow $(2). Suppose $H_ E=0$, and choose competitors $v_ j$ for $E$ as in ( 10.2 ). Fix a point $a\in B$ with $v_ j(a)\to 0$, and choose indices $j_1<j_2<\cdots $ with $v_{j_ l}(a)>-2^{-l}$. Since every term is nonpositive, the partial sums of $V=\sum _ lv_{j_ l}$ form a decreasing sequence of nonpositive plurisubharmonic functions, and $V(a)\ge -1$. By theorem 8.3.1 , $V$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$; moreover $V\le 0$, and $V=-\infty $ on $E$ because every term is at most $-1$ there. (1)$\Rightarrow $(2) in general. Let $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E)=0$, and let $(L_ l)$ be an exhaustion of $B$ by compact sets. Each set $E\cap L_ l$ has outer capacity zero and is relatively compact in $B$, so the two preceding steps give $V_ l\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ with $V_ l\le 0$ and $E\cap L_ l\subset \{ V_ l=-\infty \} $. The pole sets of the $V_ l$ are Lebesgue null, so there is a point $a\in B$ at which all $V_ l$ are finite. Choose constants $c_ l>0$ with $c_ l|V_ l(a)|\le 2^{-l}$. The partial sums of $\sum _ lc_ lV_ l$ decrease and are at least $-1$ at $a$, so, as in the previous step, $V=\sum _ lc_ lV_ l$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.1 , and it is nonpositive. Every point of $E$ lies in some $L_ l$, where $c_ lV_ l=-\infty $ while all other terms are nonpositive; hence $V=-\infty $ on $E$. (2)$\Rightarrow $(3). If $V$ is as in (2), then $\varepsilon V$ is a competitor for $E$ for every $\varepsilon >0$, so $\varepsilon V\le h_ E\le 0$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we get $h_ E=0$ on the set $\{ V>-\infty \} $. This set has full measure and is therefore dense in $B$, so every neighborhood of a point contains points where $h_ E=0$. Hence $H_ E=h_ E^*\ge 0$, and $H_ E=0$. This completes the proof of the equivalences. By the proof of (2)$\Rightarrow $(1), every pluripolar subset of $B$ satisfies (1), and hence all three conditions; in particular, it is globally pluripolar in $B$. Now let $X$ be a complex manifold and $E=\bigcup _ mE_ m$, where each $E_ m\subset X$ is pluripolar. Let $x\in X$, and let $B$ be a coordinate ball around $x$, identified with an open ball in $\mathbb C^ n$. Each $E_ m\cap B$ is pluripolar in $B$, so $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E_ m\cap B)=0$ for every $m$, and $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E\cap B)=0$ by countable subadditivity. By (1)$\Rightarrow $(2), the set $E\cap B$ lies in the pole set of a plurisubharmonic function on the connected coordinate neighborhood $B$ of $x$. Hence $E$ is pluripolar. Finally, let $W\subset X$ be open and let $E\subset W$ be pluripolar in $W$. That $E$ is pluripolar in $X$ is not immediate from definition 10.1.1 at the boundary points of $W$, where a single plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood must have poles at all nearby points of $E$. Let $x\in X$, and let $U$ be a coordinate ball around $x$, identified with an open ball in $\mathbb C^ n$. The open set $W\cap U$ is a countable union of balls $D_ k$ with $\overline{D_ k}\subset W\cap U$. Each set $E\cap D_ k$ is pluripolar in $U$: at points of $\overline{D_ k}\subset W$ we may use, after restriction to small balls in $U$, the functions provided by the pluripolarity of $E$ in $W$, and every point of $U\setminus \overline{D_ k}$ has a neighborhood disjoint from $D_ k$. By the previous paragraph, applied in $U$, the countable union $E\cap U=\bigcup _ k(E\cap D_ k)$ is pluripolar in $U$, and hence, by the first part of the theorem, it lies in the pole set of a plurisubharmonic function on $U$. Thus $E$ is pluripolar in $X$. $\square$

title: Definition 10.1.1
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: Definition 10.1.1 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold. A subset $E\subset X$ is pluripolar , or locally pluripolar , if every point of $X$ has a connected coordinate neighborhood $U$ carrying a function $V\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ with $E\cap U\subset \{ V=-\infty \} $. If $X$ is connected, a subset $E\subset X$ is globally pluripolar in $X$ if there is a single $V\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ with $E\subset \{ V=-\infty \} $. A property holds quasi-everywhere if it holds outside a pluripolar set. Definition 1.1.15 . A subset $E\subseteq X$ is pluripolar if for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$ and a function $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ such that \[  \psi |_{E\cap U}\equiv -\infty .  \] A subset $E\subseteq X$ is non-pluripolar if $E$ is not pluripolar. A subset $F\subseteq X$ is co-pluripolar if $X\setminus F$ is pluripolar.

section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: Proposition 10.1.2 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be an open ball, and let $K\subset B$ be compact. Then $H_ K(z)\to 0$ as $z\to \partial B$, the Monge–Ampère measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$ is carried by $K\cap \{ H_ K=-1\} $, and \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)=\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n.  \] If $(K_ j)$ is a decreasing sequence of compact subsets of $B$ with intersection $K$, then the functions $H_{K_ j}$ increase and converge to $H_ K$ almost everywhere, and $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K_ j)$ decreases to $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)$. In particular $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K)=\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)$. Proof. The boundary behavior of $H_ K$ follows from ( 10.1 ). Since $H_ K$ is bounded, its Monge–Ampère measure is defined (definition 9.1.1 ). We first show that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ K)^ n$ vanishes on $B\setminus K$. Choose competitors $v_ j$ for $K$ as in ( 10.2 ), and let $D$ be a ball with $\overline D\subset B\setminus K$. Let $\widehat v_ j$ be the function obtained from $v_ j$ by corollary 9.6.4 : it is plurisubharmonic on $B$, equals $v_ j$ outside $D$, and satisfies $\widehat v_ j\ge v_ j$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat v_ j)^ n=0$ on $D$.
