Thus $Y'\cap \{ u\circ F>t\} $ is a plurifine open neighborhood of $y$ contained in $F^{-1}(\{ u>t\} )$. Hence preimages of subbasic sets are plurifine open. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.3.3
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: Proposition 10.3.3 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Every nonempty plurifine open subset of $X$ contains a Borel set of positive Lebesgue measure in some chart. The complement of every pluripolar set is dense for the plurifine topology. For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, the set $\{ u>-\infty \} $ is plurifine open. Proof. (1) Let $O$ be a nonempty plurifine open set and $a\in O$. By proposition 10.3.2 (2), $O$ contains a set $A=B\cap \{ \psi >0\} $ with $a\in A$, where $B$ is a coordinate ball and $\psi $ is a bounded plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. This set is Borel because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous. If $A$ had measure zero, then $\max \{ \psi ,0\} =0$ almost everywhere on $B$; since both functions are plurisubharmonic on $B$, they would coincide everywhere by the uniqueness in theorem 8.2.1 , contradicting $\psi (a)>0$. (2) A pluripolar set is Lebesgue null in every chart, so by (1) it contains no nonempty plurifine open set. Equivalently, its complement meets every nonempty plurifine open set. (3) The set $\{ u>-\infty \} =\bigcup _ m\{ u>-m\} $ is a union of subbasic plurifine open sets. $\square$

title: Example 10.3.4
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: Example 10.3.4 . Let $n\ge 2$ and $H=\{ z\in \mathbb C^ n:z_1=0\} $. Then $H$ is pluripolar, being the pole set of $\log |z_1|^2$ (proposition 8.3.3 ), but no point of $H$ is isolated in the topology induced on $H$ by the plurifine topology. This is the second assertion of proposition 5.5.1 , because the topology $\tau $ of that proposition is the plurifine topology. Indeed, every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(V)$, with $V\subset \mathbb C^ n$ open, satisfies the conditions in the definition of $\tau $, so every plurifine open set is open for $\tau $. Conversely, let $u\colon V\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be as in the definition of $\tau $. By definition 8.1.1 , $u$ is plurisubharmonic on the union $V'$ of the connected components of $V$ on which it is not identically $-\infty $. Hence its superlevel sets $\{ u>t\} =\{ z\in V':u(z)>t\} $, $t\in \mathbb R$, are plurifine open, while its sublevel sets are Euclidean open. Thus $u$ is continuous for the plurifine topology, and every $\tau $-open set is plurifine open. Consequently, neither conclusion of proposition 5.1.5 carries over to pluripolar sets: $H$ is not plurifinely discrete, and for $a\in H$ the pluripolar set $H\setminus \{ a\} $ is not plurifine closed, since every plurifine neighborhood of $a$ meets it.

title: Example 10.3.5
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: Example 10.3.5 . For every $n\ge 1$ there is a plurifine open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ that is not a Borel set. Let $K\subset [0,1/10]\subset \mathbb C$ be the compact polar set and $\mu $ the atom-free probability measure carried by $K$ of proposition 4.2.4 , and put $F(x)=\mu (K\cap (-\infty ,x])$ for $x\in \mathbb R$. The function $F$ is nondecreasing, $F=0$ on $(-\infty ,0)$ and $F=1$ on $[1/10,\infty )$. It is continuous: it is right continuous because $\mu $ is finite, and its jump at $x$ is $\mu (K\cap \{ x\} )=0$, because $\mu $ has no atoms. For $y\in (0,1)$ the set $\{ x\in \mathbb R:F(x)\ge y\} $ is closed, nonempty and bounded below, and we let $g(y)$ be its smallest element. Then $F(g(y))\ge y$, and $F(x)<y$ for $x<g(y)$, so $F(g(y))=y$ because $F$ is continuous at $g(y)$. Hence $g$ is injective; it is also nondecreasing, so $g$ is strictly increasing and in particular Borel measurable. Moreover $g(y)\in K$. Otherwise, since $K$ is closed, there is $\delta >0$ with $[g(y)-\delta ,g(y)]\cap K=\varnothing $; then $F(g(y)-\delta )=F(g(y))=y$, which contradicts the minimality of $g(y)$. Let $N\subset (0,1)$ be a set that is not Lebesgue measurable, and put $A=g(N)\subset K$. Since $g$ is injective, $N=g^{-1}(A)$; so if $A$ were a Borel subset of $\mathbb C$, then $A=A\cap \mathbb R$ would be a Borel subset of $\mathbb R$, and $N$ would be a Borel set. Hence $A$ is not a Borel subset of $\mathbb C$. As a subset of the polar set $K$, the set $A$ is polar, hence finely closed in $\mathbb C=\mathbb R^2$ by proposition 5.1.5 . Since the fine and the plurifine topologies of $\mathbb C$ coincide, as shown at the beginning of this section, $W_1=\mathbb C\setminus A$ is a plurifine open subset of $\mathbb C$ which is not Borel. For $n\ge 2$, the set $W=W_1\times \mathbb C^{n-1}$ is the preimage of $W_1$ under the holomorphic projection $z\mapsto z_1$, so it is plurifine open by proposition 10.3.2 (3). It is not Borel, because $W_1$ is its preimage under the continuous map $\zeta \mapsto (\zeta ,0,\ldots ,0)$.

title: 10.4 Countable selections and plurifine locality
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: 10.4 Countable selections and plurifine locality The plurifine topology is in general not Lindelöf: in dimension one it is the classical fine topology of $\mathbb C=\mathbb R^2$, which is not Lindelöf by example 5.1.7 . As in theorem 5.4.1 , countability is recovered outside an exceptional set, which is now pluripolar. Since Bedford–Taylor products of locally bounded potentials do not charge pluripolar sets (corollary 10.2.2 (3)), this allows us to pass from the local identity of lemma 10.4.2 to locality on arbitrary plurifine open sets. Applied to the truncations $\max \{ u,-k\} $ of unbounded potentials, plurifine locality shows that their products for different levels $k\ge m$ agree on the set where all the potentials exceed $-m$. Theorem 10.4.1 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold with a countable basis. For every family $(U_ i)_{i\in I}$ of plurifine open subsets of $X$, there is a countable set $J\subset I$ such that $\bigcup _{i\in I}U_ i\setminus \bigcup _{j\in J}U_ j$ is pluripolar. Every plurifine open set $U\subset X$ contains countably many sets $A_ k=Q_ k\cap \{ \psi _ k>0\} $, where each $Q_ k$ is a coordinate ball and $\psi _ k$ is a bounded plurisubharmonic function on $Q_ k$, such that $U\setminus \bigcup _ kA_ k$ is pluripolar. In particular, $U$ contains the Borel set $V=\bigcup _ kA_ k$, and $U\setminus V$ is pluripolar. Consequently, if $C\subset X$ is a chart domain and $\mu $ is a positive Borel measure on $C$ for which every pluripolar subset of $C$ has outer measure zero, then $U\cap C$ is measurable for the completion of $\mu $. Proof. Since $X$ has a countable basis, it is covered by countably many charts; in each chart, the coordinate balls with rational centers and radii and with closure in the chart domain form a countable basis. Let $\mathcal Q$ be the union of these countable families; it is a countable basis of $X$. (1) Let $U=\bigcup _ iU_ i$; if $I$ is empty, take $J$ empty. We call a set basic if it has the form $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $, where $Q\in \mathcal Q$ and $\psi $ is a bounded plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $\overline Q$. Every point $a\in U$ lies in a basic set contained in some $U_ i$: if $a\in U_ i$, then proposition 10.3.2 (2) gives a ball $B$ and a bounded plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ with $a\in B\cap \{ \psi >0\} \subset U_ i$, and it suffices to choose $Q\in \mathcal Q$ with $a\in Q\subset B$. Fix $Q\in \mathcal Q$, and let $\Psi _ Q$ be the set of bounded plurisubharmonic functions $\psi $ on neighborhoods of $\overline Q$ for which the basic set $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $ is contained in some $U_ i$. If $\Psi _ Q$ is empty, we put $P_ Q=\varnothing $ and select nothing for this $Q$. Otherwise, we may assume that all members of $\Psi _ Q$ take values in $[-1,1]$ on $Q$, since replacing $\psi $ by $\psi /c$, where $c>0$ bounds $|\psi |$ on $Q$, does not change $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $. Let $F_ Q$ be the pointwise supremum of the members of $\Psi _ Q$ on $Q$. By Choquet's lemma (lemma 3.4.1 ) there are $\psi _{Q,1},\psi _{Q,2},\ldots $ in $\Psi _ Q$ whose supremum $F_ Q'$ satisfies $(F_ Q')^*=F_ Q^*$. By corollary 10.2.2 (1) and the last assertion of theorem 10.1.4 , the set $P_ Q=\{ F_ Q<F_ Q^*\} \cup \{ F_ Q'<(F_ Q')^*\} $ is pluripolar in $Q$, and hence in $X$. If $z\in Q\setminus P_ Q$ and $\psi (z)>0$ for some $\psi \in \Psi _ Q$, then $F_ Q'(z)=F_ Q^*(z)=F_ Q(z)>0$, so $\psi _{Q,k}(z)>0$ for some $k$. Therefore \[  \bigcup _{\psi \in \Psi _ Q}\bigl (Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} \bigr )\subset P_ Q\cup \bigcup _ k\bigl (Q\cap \{ \psi _{Q,k}>0\} \bigr ).  \] For each $Q$ and $k$ choose an index $i(Q,k)\in I$ with $Q\cap \{ \psi _{Q,k}>0\} \subset U_{i(Q,k)}$, and let $J$ be the countable set of these indices. Every point of $U$ lies in some basic set $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $ with $\psi \in \Psi _ Q$, so $U\setminus \bigcup _{j\in J}U_ j$ is contained in $\bigcup _ QP_ Q$. This countable union of pluripolar sets is pluripolar by theorem 10.1.4 . (2) Apply the construction of (1) to the family consisting of the single set $U$. It selects countably many sets $Q\cap \{ \psi _{Q,k}>0\} $, where $Q\in \mathcal Q$ is a coordinate ball and $\psi _{Q,k}$ restricts to a bounded plurisubharmonic function on $Q$; these sets are contained in $U$, and their union $V$ satisfies $U\setminus V\subset \bigcup _ QP_ Q$, which is pluripolar. Each selected set is Borel, because $\psi _{Q,k}$ is upper semicontinuous, so the countable union $V$ is Borel. Finally, let $C$ and $\mu $ be as in the statement. The set $(U\setminus V)\cap C$ is pluripolar in $C$, so it has outer $\mu $-measure zero and is a null set for the completion of $\mu $. Since $U\cap C=(V\cap C)\cup \bigl ((U\setminus V)\cap C\bigr )$ and $V\cap C$ is Borel, $U\cap C$ is measurable for the completion of $\mu $. $\square$ We now turn to Bedford–Taylor products. The first step is their locality on a single superlevel set of a plurisubharmonic function, which we derive from their locality on the sets $\{ u>v\} $ (proposition 9.2.7 ). Lemma 10.4.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(r,r)$ on $\Omega $, let $u$ and $v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $, and let $t\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. If $u=v$ on $\{ t>0\} $, then, for every integer $0\le p\le r$, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ p\wedge T =\mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ p\wedge T.  \] Proof. Replacing $t$ by $\max \{ t,0\} $, which is plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.5 ) and has the same set $\{ t>0\} $, we may assume that $t\ge 0$. Then $t$ is locally bounded, because plurisubharmonic functions are bounded above on compact sets, and $u+\varepsilon t$ is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function for every $\varepsilon >0$. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $w_\varepsilon =\max \{ u+\varepsilon t,v\} $. On $\{ t>0\} $ we have $u+\varepsilon t>u=v$, so $\{ t>0\} \subset \{ u+\varepsilon t>v\} $, and proposition 9.2.7 , applied to $u+\varepsilon t$ and $v$, gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon )^ p\wedge T=\mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+\varepsilon t))^ p\wedge T.  \] Multiplying by $t$, which vanishes outside $\{ t>0\} $, we obtain $t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon )^ p\wedge T=t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+\varepsilon t))^ p\wedge T$. As $\varepsilon $ decreases to zero along a sequence, $w_\varepsilon $ decreases to $\max \{ u,v\} $ and $u+\varepsilon t$ decreases to $u$, because $t\ge 0$. The weighted form of theorem 9.2.5 , with the constant sequence of weights equal to $t$, therefore yields \[  t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u,v\} )^ p\wedge T=t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ p\wedge T.  \] Interchanging the roles of $u$ and $v$, we also get $t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u,v\} )^ p\wedge T=t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ p\wedge T$, and hence $t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ p\wedge T=t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ p\wedge T$. Finally, multiply the coefficient measures of both sides by $1/(t+\delta )$ and let $\delta \downarrow 0$. Since $t/(t+\delta )\to \mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }$ pointwise and boundedly, dominated convergence with respect to the total variations of the coefficient measures gives the assertion. $\square$ Bedford–Taylor products are local in the plurifine topology, in the following sense. Theorem 10.4.3 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n$, let $1\le q\le n$ be an integer, and let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ and $v_1,\ldots ,v_ q$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $X$. If $u_ l=v_ l$ on a plurifine open set $W\subset X$ for every $l$, then \[  \mathbf1_ W\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q =\mathbf1_ W\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q.  \] Here $W$ need not be Borel (example 10.3.5 ). It is measurable for the completions of the total variations of the coefficient measures of both products, and $\mathbf1_ W$ acts on these completed measures; up to null sets of these measures, $W$ coincides with a Borel set. Proof. The identity and the measurability of $W$ are local properties, so we may assume that $X$ is an open ball in $\mathbb C^ n$; by proposition 10.3.2 (3), the intersection of $W$ with this ball is plurifine open in the ball. Write $S_ u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q$ and $S_ v=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q$. We first prove the identity on sets of the form $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $, and then cover $W$ by countably many such sets up to a pluripolar set, which the products do not charge. Step 1: basic sets. We show that $\mathbf1_ AS_ u=\mathbf1_ AS_ v$ whenever $Q\subset X$ is open, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Q)$ and $A=Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} \subset W$. For every nonempty set $I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,q\} $, the functions $u_ I=\sum _{l\in I}u_ l$ and $v_ I=\sum _{l\in I}v_ l$ are locally bounded and plurisubharmonic on $Q$, and they coincide on $A$, because $u_ l=v_ l$ on $W$. By lemma 10.4.2 , applied on $Q$ with $t=\psi $, $T=1$ and $p=q$, we have $\mathbf1_ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q=\mathbf1_ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ I)^ q$. We now recover $S_ u$ from the products $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q$ by polarization. For a multi-index $\alpha \in \mathbb N^ q$ with $|\alpha |=q$, let $S_ u^\alpha $ be the product of $q$ factors in which $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l$ occurs $\alpha _ l$ times; it does not depend on the order of the factors, because products of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions are symmetric (theorem 9.2.5 ). Since these products are also additive in each factor (proposition 9.1.2 (3)), expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I=\sum _{l\in I}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l$ gives, exactly as in the multinomial expansion of $(\sum _{l\in I}x_ l)^ q$, \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q=\sum _\alpha \frac{q!}{\alpha !}\, S_ u^\alpha ,  \] where $\alpha $ ranges over the multi-indices with $|\alpha |=q$ and $\alpha _ l=0$ for $l\notin I$. Multiplying by $(-1)^{q-|I|}$ and summing over the nonempty sets $I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,q\} $, we obtain $\sum _\alpha c_\alpha S_ u^\alpha $, summed over all $\alpha $ with $|\alpha |=q$, where $c_\alpha $ is the coefficient of the monomial $x^\alpha $ on the right-hand side of the polarization identity ( 9.11 ) with $N=q$ (in which the term with $I=\varnothing $ vanishes). Both sides of that identity are polynomials in $x_1,\ldots ,x_ q$ that agree on $\mathbb R^ q$, so they have the same coefficients: $c_\alpha =q!$ if $\alpha =(1,\ldots ,1)$, and $c_\alpha =0$ otherwise. Since $S_ u^{(1,\ldots ,1)}=S_ u$, we obtain \[  q!\, S_ u=\sum _{\varnothing \ne I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,q\} }(-1)^{q-|I|}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q \quad \text{on }Q.  \] The same identity holds for the $v_ l$. Multiplying both identities by $\mathbf1_ A$ and using $\mathbf1_ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q=\mathbf1_ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ I)^ q$, we obtain $\mathbf1_ AS_ u=\mathbf1_ AS_ v$. Step 2: countable selection. By theorem 10.4.1 (2), applied to the ball $X$ and its plurifine open subset $W$, there are countably many sets $A_ k=Q_ k\cap \{ \psi _ k>0\} \subset W$, with $Q_ k\subset X$ open and $\psi _ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(Q_ k)$, whose union $V$ is Borel and such that $W\setminus V$ is pluripolar. By corollary 10.2.2 (3), every pluripolar subset of $X$ has outer measure zero for the total variations of the coefficient measures of $S_ u$ and $S_ v$. Hence, by the last assertion of theorem 10.4.1 (2), $W$ is measurable for their completions; moreover $W\setminus V$ is a null set for them, so $\mathbf1_ WS_ u=\mathbf1_ VS_ u$ and $\mathbf1_ WS_ v=\mathbf1_ VS_ v$. The Borel sets $A_ k'=A_ k\setminus (A_1\cup \cdots \cup A_{k-1})$ partition $V$, and Step 1 gives $\mathbf1_{A_ k'}S_ u=\mathbf1_{A_ k'}\mathbf1_{A_ k}S_ u=\mathbf1_{A_ k'}\mathbf1_{A_ k}S_ v=\mathbf1_{A_ k'}S_ v$. Summing over $k$, by countable additivity of the coefficient measures, we obtain $\mathbf1_ VS_ u=\mathbf1_ VS_ v$, which proves the theorem. $\square$ Step 1 of this proof works, with the same argument, for products $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ with an arbitrary closed positive current $T$, because lemma 10.4.2 does. Step 2 does not: such a current may charge pluripolar sets, and then the exceptional set $W\setminus V$ cannot be neglected. For instance, if $H=\{ z\in \mathbb C^ n:z_1=0\} $, the current of integration $[H]$ of example 7.2.7 has the trace measure $[H]\wedge \beta ^{n-1}$, which is $(n-1)!$ times the $(2n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure of $H$, because the restriction of $\beta ^{n-1}/(n-1)!$ to $H$ is the Euclidean volume form of $H$; so it gives positive mass to $H$, which is pluripolar as the pole set of $\log |z_1|^2$. Proposition 10.4.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $1\le q\le n$ be an integer, and let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. For every integer $m\ge 1$ put \[  u_ l^{(m)}=\max \{ u_ l,-m\} ,\qquad E_ m=\bigcap _{l=1}^ q\{ u_ l>-m\} ,\qquad S_ m=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1^{(m)}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q^{(m)}.  \] Then, for all integers $k\ge m\ge 1$, \[  \mathbf1_{E_ m}S_ k=\mathbf1_{E_ m}S_ m.  \] The restrictions $\mu _ m=\mathbf1_{E_ m}\mu _{S_ m}$ of the trace measures $\mu _{S_ m}$ (definition 7.2.4 ) increase with $m$, and every pluripolar subset of $\Omega $ has outer measure zero for each $\mu _ m$. Their increasing limit $\mu =\lim _ m\mu _ m$ is a Borel measure on $\Omega $, possibly of infinite mass on compact sets, for which every pluripolar subset of $\Omega $ also has outer measure zero. Proof. Each set $\{ u_ l>-m\} $ is a subbasic plurifine open set, so $E_ m$ is plurifine open; it is also Borel. On $E_ m$ we have $u_ l>-m$, and hence $u_ l^{(k)}=u_ l=u_ l^{(m)}$ for all $l$ and all $k\ge m$. The truncations are locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions, so theorem 10.4.3 gives $\mathbf1_{E_ m}S_ k=\mathbf1_{E_ m}S_ m$. Taking trace measures, and using $E_ m\subset E_ k$ and the positivity of $\mu _{S_ k}$, we obtain $\mu _ m=\mathbf1_{E_ m}\mu _{S_ k}\le \mathbf1_{E_ k}\mu _{S_ k}=\mu _ k$. By corollary 10.2.2 (3), every pluripolar subset of $\Omega $ has outer measure zero for $\mu _{S_ m}$, and hence for $\mu _ m$. For a Borel set $A\subset \Omega $ put $\mu (A)=\lim _ m\mu _ m(A)\in [0,\infty ]$. If $A$ is the disjoint union of Borel sets $A_ i$, then \[  \mu (A)=\lim _ m\sum _ i\mu _ m(A_ i)=\sum _ i\lim _ m\mu _ m(A_ i)=\sum _ i\mu (A_ i),  \] by monotone convergence for series of nonnegative terms that increase with $m$. Thus $\mu $ is a Borel measure. Finally, let $N\subset \Omega $ be pluripolar. Since $N$ has outer measure zero for each $\mu _ m$, there are Borel sets $G_{m,i}\supset N$ with $\mu _ m(G_{m,i})<1/i$ for all $m,i\ge 1$. The Borel set $G=\bigcap _{m,i}G_{m,i}$ contains $N$ and satisfies $\mu _ m(G)=0$ for every $m$, hence $\mu (G)=0$. Thus $N$ has outer measure zero for $\mu $. $\square$ In general $\mu $ is not locally finite (example 15.1.6 ), so a separate local mass estimate is needed before the restrictions $\mathbf1_{E_ m}S_ m$ can define a current of order zero in the limit; this is the subject of chapter 15 .

title: Theorem 10.4.1
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: Theorem 10.4.1 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold with a countable basis. For every family $(U_ i)_{i\in I}$ of plurifine open subsets of $X$, there is a countable set $J\subset I$ such that $\bigcup _{i\in I}U_ i\setminus \bigcup _{j\in J}U_ j$ is pluripolar. Every plurifine open set $U\subset X$ contains countably many sets $A_ k=Q_ k\cap \{ \psi _ k>0\} $, where each $Q_ k$ is a coordinate ball and $\psi _ k$ is a bounded plurisubharmonic function on $Q_ k$, such that $U\setminus \bigcup _ kA_ k$ is pluripolar. In particular, $U$ contains the Borel set $V=\bigcup _ kA_ k$, and $U\setminus V$ is pluripolar. Consequently, if $C\subset X$ is a chart domain and $\mu $ is a positive Borel measure on $C$ for which every pluripolar subset of $C$ has outer measure zero, then $U\cap C$ is measurable for the completion of $\mu $. Proof. Since $X$ has a countable basis, it is covered by countably many charts; in each chart, the coordinate balls with rational centers and radii and with closure in the chart domain form a countable basis. Let $\mathcal Q$ be the union of these countable families; it is a countable basis of $X$. (1) Let $U=\bigcup _ iU_ i$; if $I$ is empty, take $J$ empty. We call a set basic if it has the form $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $, where $Q\in \mathcal Q$ and $\psi $ is a bounded plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $\overline Q$. Every point $a\in U$ lies in a basic set contained in some $U_ i$: if $a\in U_ i$, then proposition 10.3.2 (2) gives a ball $B$ and a bounded plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ with $a\in B\cap \{ \psi >0\} \subset U_ i$, and it suffices to choose $Q\in \mathcal Q$ with $a\in Q\subset B$. Fix $Q\in \mathcal Q$, and let $\Psi _ Q$ be the set of bounded plurisubharmonic functions $\psi $ on neighborhoods of $\overline Q$ for which the basic set $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $ is contained in some $U_ i$. If $\Psi _ Q$ is empty, we put $P_ Q=\varnothing $ and select nothing for this $Q$. Otherwise, we may assume that all members of $\Psi _ Q$ take values in $[-1,1]$ on $Q$, since replacing $\psi $ by $\psi /c$, where $c>0$ bounds $|\psi |$ on $Q$, does not change $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $. Let $F_ Q$ be the pointwise supremum of the members of $\Psi _ Q$ on $Q$. By Choquet's lemma (lemma 3.4.1 ) there are $\psi _{Q,1},\psi _{Q,2},\ldots $ in $\Psi _ Q$ whose supremum $F_ Q'$ satisfies $(F_ Q')^*=F_ Q^*$. By corollary 10.2.2 (1) and the last assertion of theorem 10.1.4 , the set $P_ Q=\{ F_ Q<F_ Q^*\} \cup \{ F_ Q'<(F_ Q')^*\} $ is pluripolar in $Q$, and hence in $X$. If $z\in Q\setminus P_ Q$ and $\psi (z)>0$ for some $\psi \in \Psi _ Q$, then $F_ Q'(z)=F_ Q^*(z)=F_ Q(z)>0$, so $\psi _{Q,k}(z)>0$ for some $k$. Therefore \[  \bigcup _{\psi \in \Psi _ Q}\bigl (Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} \bigr )\subset P_ Q\cup \bigcup _ k\bigl (Q\cap \{ \psi _{Q,k}>0\} \bigr ).  \] For each $Q$ and $k$ choose an index $i(Q,k)\in I$ with $Q\cap \{ \psi _{Q,k}>0\} \subset U_{i(Q,k)}$, and let $J$ be the countable set of these indices. Every point of $U$ lies in some basic set $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $ with $\psi \in \Psi _ Q$, so $U\setminus \bigcup _{j\in J}U_ j$ is contained in $\bigcup _ QP_ Q$. This countable union of pluripolar sets is pluripolar by theorem 10.1.4 . (2) Apply the construction of (1) to the family consisting of the single set $U$. It selects countably many sets $Q\cap \{ \psi _{Q,k}>0\} $, where $Q\in \mathcal Q$ is a coordinate ball and $\psi _{Q,k}$ restricts to a bounded plurisubharmonic function on $Q$; these sets are contained in $U$, and their union $V$ satisfies $U\setminus V\subset \bigcup _ QP_ Q$, which is pluripolar. Each selected set is Borel, because $\psi _{Q,k}$ is upper semicontinuous, so the countable union $V$ is Borel. Finally, let $C$ and $\mu $ be as in the statement. The set $(U\setminus V)\cap C$ is pluripolar in $C$, so it has outer $\mu $-measure zero and is a null set for the completion of $\mu $. Since $U\cap C=(V\cap C)\cup \bigl ((U\setminus V)\cap C\bigr )$ and $V\cap C$ is Borel, $U\cap C$ is measurable for the completion of $\mu $. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.4.2
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: Lemma 10.4.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(r,r)$ on $\Omega $, let $u$ and $v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $, and let $t\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. If $u=v$ on $\{ t>0\} $, then, for every integer $0\le p\le r$, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ p\wedge T =\mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ p\wedge T.  \] Proof. Replacing $t$ by $\max \{ t,0\} $, which is plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.5 ) and has the same set $\{ t>0\} $, we may assume that $t\ge 0$. Then $t$ is locally bounded, because plurisubharmonic functions are bounded above on compact sets, and $u+\varepsilon t$ is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function for every $\varepsilon >0$. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $w_\varepsilon =\max \{ u+\varepsilon t,v\} $. On $\{ t>0\} $ we have $u+\varepsilon t>u=v$, so $\{ t>0\} \subset \{ u+\varepsilon t>v\} $, and proposition 9.2.7 , applied to $u+\varepsilon t$ and $v$, gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon )^ p\wedge T=\mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+\varepsilon t))^ p\wedge T.  \] Multiplying by $t$, which vanishes outside $\{ t>0\} $, we obtain $t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon )^ p\wedge T=t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+\varepsilon t))^ p\wedge T$. As $\varepsilon $ decreases to zero along a sequence, $w_\varepsilon $ decreases to $\max \{ u,v\} $ and $u+\varepsilon t$ decreases to $u$, because $t\ge 0$. The weighted form of theorem 9.2.5 , with the constant sequence of weights equal to $t$, therefore yields \[  t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u,v\} )^ p\wedge T=t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ p\wedge T.  \] Interchanging the roles of $u$ and $v$, we also get $t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u,v\} )^ p\wedge T=t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ p\wedge T$, and hence $t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ p\wedge T=t(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ p\wedge T$. Finally, multiply the coefficient measures of both sides by $1/(t+\delta )$ and let $\delta \downarrow 0$. Since $t/(t+\delta )\to \mathbf1_{\{ t>0\} }$ pointwise and boundedly, dominated convergence with respect to the total variations of the coefficient measures gives the assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.4.3
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: Theorem 10.4.3 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n$, let $1\le q\le n$ be an integer, and let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ and $v_1,\ldots ,v_ q$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $X$. If $u_ l=v_ l$ on a plurifine open set $W\subset X$ for every $l$, then \[  \mathbf1_ W\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q =\mathbf1_ W\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q.  \] Here $W$ need not be Borel (example 10.3.5 ). It is measurable for the completions of the total variations of the coefficient measures of both products, and $\mathbf1_ W$ acts on these completed measures; up to null sets of these measures, $W$ coincides with a Borel set. Proof. The identity and the measurability of $W$ are local properties, so we may assume that $X$ is an open ball in $\mathbb C^ n$; by proposition 10.3.2 (3), the intersection of $W$ with this ball is plurifine open in the ball. Write $S_ u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q$ and $S_ v=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q$. We first prove the identity on sets of the form $Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} $, and then cover $W$ by countably many such sets up to a pluripolar set, which the products do not charge. Step 1: basic sets. We show that $\mathbf1_ AS_ u=\mathbf1_ AS_ v$ whenever $Q\subset X$ is open, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Q)$ and $A=Q\cap \{ \psi >0\} \subset W$. For every nonempty set $I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,q\} $, the functions $u_ I=\sum _{l\in I}u_ l$ and $v_ I=\sum _{l\in I}v_ l$ are locally bounded and plurisubharmonic on $Q$, and they coincide on $A$, because $u_ l=v_ l$ on $W$. By lemma 10.4.2 , applied on $Q$ with $t=\psi $, $T=1$ and $p=q$, we have $\mathbf1_ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q=\mathbf1_ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ I)^ q$. We now recover $S_ u$ from the products $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q$ by polarization. For a multi-index $\alpha \in \mathbb N^ q$ with $|\alpha |=q$, let $S_ u^\alpha $ be the product of $q$ factors in which $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l$ occurs $\alpha _ l$ times; it does not depend on the order of the factors, because products of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions are symmetric (theorem 9.2.5 ). Since these products are also additive in each factor (proposition 9.1.2 (3)), expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I=\sum _{l\in I}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l$ gives, exactly as in the multinomial expansion of $(\sum _{l\in I}x_ l)^ q$, \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q=\sum _\alpha \frac{q!}{\alpha !}\, S_ u^\alpha ,  \] where $\alpha $ ranges over the multi-indices with $|\alpha |=q$ and $\alpha _ l=0$ for $l\notin I$. Multiplying by $(-1)^{q-|I|}$ and summing over the nonempty sets $I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,q\} $, we obtain $\sum _\alpha c_\alpha S_ u^\alpha $, summed over all $\alpha $ with $|\alpha |=q$, where $c_\alpha $ is the coefficient of the monomial $x^\alpha $ on the right-hand side of the polarization identity ( 9.11 ) with $N=q$ (in which the term with $I=\varnothing $ vanishes). Both sides of that identity are polynomials in $x_1,\ldots ,x_ q$ that agree on $\mathbb R^ q$, so they have the same coefficients: $c_\alpha =q!$ if $\alpha =(1,\ldots ,1)$, and $c_\alpha =0$ otherwise. Since $S_ u^{(1,\ldots ,1)}=S_ u$, we obtain \[  q!\, S_ u=\sum _{\varnothing \ne I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,q\} }(-1)^{q-|I|}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q \quad \text{on }Q.  \] The same identity holds for the $v_ l$. Multiplying both identities by $\mathbf1_ A$ and using $\mathbf1_ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ I)^ q=\mathbf1_ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ I)^ q$, we obtain $\mathbf1_ AS_ u=\mathbf1_ AS_ v$. Step 2: countable selection. By theorem 10.4.1 (2), applied to the ball $X$ and its plurifine open subset $W$, there are countably many sets $A_ k=Q_ k\cap \{ \psi _ k>0\} \subset W$, with $Q_ k\subset X$ open and $\psi _ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(Q_ k)$, whose union $V$ is Borel and such that $W\setminus V$ is pluripolar. By corollary 10.2.2 (3), every pluripolar subset of $X$ has outer measure zero for the total variations of the coefficient measures of $S_ u$ and $S_ v$. Hence, by the last assertion of theorem 10.4.1 (2), $W$ is measurable for their completions; moreover $W\setminus V$ is a null set for them, so $\mathbf1_ WS_ u=\mathbf1_ VS_ u$ and $\mathbf1_ WS_ v=\mathbf1_ VS_ v$. The Borel sets $A_ k'=A_ k\setminus (A_1\cup \cdots \cup A_{k-1})$ partition $V$, and Step 1 gives $\mathbf1_{A_ k'}S_ u=\mathbf1_{A_ k'}\mathbf1_{A_ k}S_ u=\mathbf1_{A_ k'}\mathbf1_{A_ k}S_ v=\mathbf1_{A_ k'}S_ v$. Summing over $k$, by countable additivity of the coefficient measures, we obtain $\mathbf1_ VS_ u=\mathbf1_ VS_ v$, which proves the theorem. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.4.4
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: Proposition 10.4.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $1\le q\le n$ be an integer, and let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. For every integer $m\ge 1$ put \[  u_ l^{(m)}=\max \{ u_ l,-m\} ,\qquad E_ m=\bigcap _{l=1}^ q\{ u_ l>-m\} ,\qquad S_ m=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1^{(m)}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q^{(m)}.  \] Then, for all integers $k\ge m\ge 1$, \[  \mathbf1_{E_ m}S_ k=\mathbf1_{E_ m}S_ m.  \] The restrictions $\mu _ m=\mathbf1_{E_ m}\mu _{S_ m}$ of the trace measures $\mu _{S_ m}$ (definition 7.2.4 ) increase with $m$, and every pluripolar subset of $\Omega $ has outer measure zero for each $\mu _ m$. Their increasing limit $\mu =\lim _ m\mu _ m$ is a Borel measure on $\Omega $, possibly of infinite mass on compact sets, for which every pluripolar subset of $\Omega $ also has outer measure zero. Proof. Each set $\{ u_ l>-m\} $ is a subbasic plurifine open set, so $E_ m$ is plurifine open; it is also Borel. On $E_ m$ we have $u_ l>-m$, and hence $u_ l^{(k)}=u_ l=u_ l^{(m)}$ for all $l$ and all $k\ge m$. The truncations are locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions, so theorem 10.4.3 gives $\mathbf1_{E_ m}S_ k=\mathbf1_{E_ m}S_ m$. Taking trace measures, and using $E_ m\subset E_ k$ and the positivity of $\mu _{S_ k}$, we obtain $\mu _ m=\mathbf1_{E_ m}\mu _{S_ k}\le \mathbf1_{E_ k}\mu _{S_ k}=\mu _ k$. By corollary 10.2.2 (3), every pluripolar subset of $\Omega $ has outer measure zero for $\mu _{S_ m}$, and hence for $\mu _ m$. For a Borel set $A\subset \Omega $ put $\mu (A)=\lim _ m\mu _ m(A)\in [0,\infty ]$. If $A$ is the disjoint union of Borel sets $A_ i$, then \[  \mu (A)=\lim _ m\sum _ i\mu _ m(A_ i)=\sum _ i\lim _ m\mu _ m(A_ i)=\sum _ i\mu (A_ i),  \] by monotone convergence for series of nonnegative terms that increase with $m$. Thus $\mu $ is a Borel measure. Finally, let $N\subset \Omega $ be pluripolar. Since $N$ has outer measure zero for each $\mu _ m$, there are Borel sets $G_{m,i}\supset N$ with $\mu _ m(G_{m,i})<1/i$ for all $m,i\ge 1$. The Borel set $G=\bigcap _{m,i}G_{m,i}$ contains $N$ and satisfies $\mu _ m(G)=0$ for every $m$, hence $\mu (G)=0$. Thus $N$ has outer measure zero for $\mu $. $\square$

title: 10.5 Common poles and quasi-extrema
section: 5.4 Pluripolar sets and the plurifine topology
text: 10.5 Common poles and quasi-extrema Let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be plurisubharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$. Their difference $\varphi -\psi $ is defined, with values in $[-\infty ,\infty ]$, outside the common pole set $\{ \varphi =\psi =-\infty \} $, on which it would be the meaningless expression $-\infty -(-\infty )$. We show that $\varphi -\psi $ is plurifinely continuous off the common pole set, and that its supremum and infimum over a plurifine open set do not change when an arbitrary pluripolar set containing the common poles is removed. Proposition 10.5.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and put $P=\{ \varphi =\psi =-\infty \} $. Then $P$ is plurifine closed and pluripolar, and the function $\varphi -\psi $ is continuous from the plurifine open set $\Omega \setminus P$, with the plurifine topology, to $[-\infty ,\infty ]$. The same holds for $\varphi -\psi +b$, for every continuous real function $b$ on $\Omega $. Proof. The function $\varphi $ is plurifinely continuous with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$, and $\{ -\infty \} $ is closed in $[-\infty ,\infty )$; hence the pole set $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $ is plurifine closed. The same holds for $\psi $, so $P$ is plurifine closed. It is pluripolar because it lies in the pole set of $\varphi $, which is pluripolar by definition 10.1.1 , applied with small balls in $\Omega $ as neighborhoods. The subtraction $(s,t)\mapsto s-t$ is continuous from $[-\infty ,\infty )^2\setminus \{ (-\infty ,-\infty )\} $ to $[-\infty ,\infty ]$. At points where $s$ and $t$ are finite, this is the continuity of subtraction on $\mathbb R^2$. If $s=-\infty $ and $t$ is finite, then for every $M>0$ we have $s'-t'<-M$ whenever $t'>t-1$ and $s'<t-1-M$; this is continuity with the value $-\infty $. Symmetrically, if $s$ is finite and $t=-\infty $, then $s'-t'>M$ whenever $s'>s-1$ and $t'<s-1-M$. Since $z\mapsto (\varphi (z),\psi (z))$ is plurifinely continuous on $\Omega \setminus P$ with values in this domain, $\varphi -\psi $ is plurifinely continuous on $\Omega \setminus P$. Finally, $b$ is continuous for the Euclidean topology, hence for the plurifine topology, and addition is continuous from $[-\infty ,\infty ]\times \mathbb R$ to $[-\infty ,\infty ]$. $\square$ Definition 10.5.2 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold, let $W\subset X$ be a nonempty plurifine open set, let $Z\subset X$ be pluripolar, and let $f\colon W\setminus Z\to [-\infty ,\infty ]$. The quasi-supremum and the quasi-infimum of $f$ on $W$ are \[  \operatorname *{q-sup}_ W f =\inf _{N}\, \sup _{W\setminus N}f, \qquad \operatorname *{q-inf}_ W f =\sup _{N}\, \inf _{W\setminus N}f,  \] where $N$ ranges over the pluripolar subsets of $X$ containing $Z$, and all suprema and infima are taken in $[-\infty ,\infty ]$. The sets $W\setminus N$ in this definition are nonempty: by proposition 10.3.3 (1), $W$ contains a Borel set of positive Lebesgue measure in some chart, whereas $N$ is Lebesgue null in every chart. Corollary 10.5.3 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, let $b$ be a continuous real function on $\Omega $, and let $f=\varphi -\psi +b$ on $\Omega \setminus P$, where $P=\{ \varphi =\psi =-\infty \} $. Let $Z\subset \Omega $ be a pluripolar set containing $P$, and let $W\subset \Omega $ be a nonempty plurifine open set. Then \[  \operatorname *{q-sup}_ W f=\sup _{W\setminus Z}f, \qquad \operatorname *{q-inf}_ W f=\inf _{W\setminus Z}f.  \] In particular, the right-hand sides do not depend on the choice of $Z$. Proof. The set $W'=W\setminus P$ is plurifine open, and $f$ is plurifinely continuous on $W'$, by proposition 10.5.1 . Let $N$ be a pluripolar set containing $P$. We claim that $\sup _{W'\setminus N}f=\sup _{W'}f$. The inequality $\le $ holds because $W'\setminus N\subset W'$. Conversely, if $s\in \mathbb R$ and $s<\sup _{W'}f$, then $\{ z\in W':f(z)>s\} $ is a nonempty plurifine open set. It meets $\Omega \setminus N$, which is plurifine dense by proposition 10.3.3 (2), and hence $\sup _{W'\setminus N}f>s$. This proves the claim, and the same argument with the sets $\{ f<s\} $ gives $\inf _{W'\setminus N}f=\inf _{W'}f$. Since $W\setminus N=W'\setminus N$ whenever $N\supset P$, every pluripolar set $N\supset Z$ gives $\sup _{W\setminus N}f=\sup _{W\setminus P}f$; taking $N=Z$, we also get $\sup _{W\setminus Z}f=\sup _{W\setminus P}f$. Hence $\operatorname *{q-sup}_ Wf=\sup _{W\setminus Z}f=\sup _{W\setminus P}f$, and similarly $\operatorname *{q-inf}_ Wf=\inf _{W\setminus Z}f=\inf _{W\setminus P}f$. The common values do not involve $Z$. $\square$

title: 11 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
search_title: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.1 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: 11 Weighted $L^2$ estimates and holomorphic extension Many constructions in the rest of the book need a holomorphic function $F$ on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ with a prescribed value at a point, or a prescribed restriction to a hyperplane section, together with a bound for the weighted $L^2$ norm $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$, where $\varphi $ is a plurisubharmonic weight. Gluing by a partition of unity does not preserve holomorphicity: if $f$ is holomorphic near the support of a smooth cutoff function $\chi $, then $\chi f$ is a global smooth function, but $\bar\partial (\chi f)=f\, \bar\partial \chi $ need not vanish. If we can solve $\bar\partial u=f\, \bar\partial \chi $ with an estimate in a weighted $L^2$ norm, then $F=\chi f-u$ is holomorphic. The weight has two tasks: it must make the equation solvable with a bound on $u$, and, where values are prescribed, it must be so singular that the finiteness of the weighted norm forces $u$ to vanish there. The basic existence theorem is Hörmander's estimate (theorem 11.3.3 , theorem 11.3.4 ). By the Hilbert space duality of section 11.1 , a solution of $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ with a norm bound exists as soon as an a priori inequality holds for the adjoint operator. For compactly supported forms this inequality follows from an integration-by-parts identity, the Bochner–Kodaira–Morrey–Kohn identity, in which the complex Hessian of the weight appears as a curvature term. To pass from compactly supported forms to the whole domain of the adjoint without any assumption on the boundary, we work on pseudoconvex open sets and modify the weight near the boundary by means of a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function, whose existence is proved in section 11.2 . In section 11.4 we apply these estimates. Adding the logarithmic pole ${n\log |z-a|^2}$ to the weight prescribes the value of a holomorphic function at the point $a$ (proposition 11.4.1 ). For extension from a hyperplane, a bounded twist of the weight and an explicit one-variable weight of $\log \log $ type yield the Ohsawa–Takegoshi extension theorem, with a constant that depends only on the width of the domain in the normal direction (theorem 11.4.4 ). Its consequences for point values and for integrable germs (corollary 11.4.5 , corollary 11.4.6 ) are the analytic input for the multiplier ideals of chapter 12 and the Bergman kernel approximation of chapter 13 . Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.11 .

section: 6.1 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
11.1 Hilbert spaces and closed operator complexes A complex Hilbert space is a complex vector space with an inner product $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle $ that is complete for the norm $\| x\| =\langle x,xangle ^{1/2}$; our inner products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second. A real Hilbert space is defined in the same way, with a real vector space and a real inner product, which is then symmetric and bilinear. All results of this section hold for real Hilbert spaces, with the same proofs: the completeness, proved below, of the spaces $L^2(\mu )$ of real-valued functions, and proposition 11.1.1 , proposition 11.1.2 , lemma 11.1.3 , theorem 11.1.4 . Indeed, these proofs use only the axioms of an inner product and completeness. For real spaces one omits all complex conjugations, reads “conjugate-linear” as “linear”, uses only real values of $t$ in the proof of proposition 11.1.1 , and replaces the coefficients in $\mathbb Q+\mathrm i\mathbb Q$ in the proof of proposition 11.1.2 by rational ones. The Hilbert spaces of this chapter are weighted $L^2$ spaces. For a positive measure $\mu $ on a measurable space, $L^2(\mu )$ carries the inner product $\langle f,gangle =\int f ar g\, \mathrm d\mu $, and it is complete. Indeed, let $(f_ j)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $L^2(\mu )$, and choose $j_1<j_2<\cdots $ with $\| f_{j_{k+1}}-f_{j_ k}\| \le 2^{-k}$. By the triangle inequality and the monotone convergence theorem, $g=\sum _ k|f_{j_{k+1}}-f_{j_ k}|$ satisfies $\| g\| \le 1$, so $g<\infty $ almost everywhere. Hence $(f_{j_ k})$ converges almost everywhere to a function $f$, and the bound $|f-f_{j_ k}|\le \sum _{l\ge k}|f_{j_{l+1}}-f_{j_ l}|$ gives $\| f-f_{j_ k}\| \le 2^{1-k}$. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. Every nonempty closed convex subset of $H$ contains a unique point of smallest distance to a given point of $H$. Since $(x_ j+x_ k)/2\in C$ by convexity, the parallelogram identity gives \[  \| x_ j-x_ k\| ^2=2\| x_ j\| ^2+2\| x_ k\| ^2 -4\| (x_ j+x_ k)/2\| ^2 \le 2\| x_ j\| ^2+2\| x_ k\| ^2-4d^2.  \] The right side tends to zero as $j,k	o \infty $, so $(x_ j)$ is a Cauchy sequence. Its limit lies in $C$, because $C$ is closed, and has norm $d$. If $x,x'\in C$ both have norm $d$, the same inequality with $x_ j=x$ and $x_ k=x'$ gives $\| x-x'\| ^2\le 0$, which proves uniqueness. Every bounded sequence in a Hilbert space $H$ has a weakly convergent subsequence, that is, a subsequence $(x_ j)$ for which there is $x\in H$ with $\langle x_ j,vangle 	o \langle x,vangle $ for every $v\in H$. The finite linear combinations of the $x_ j$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q+\mathrm i\mathbb Q$ form a countable dense subset of $V$. Applying the Gram–Schmidt process to it, and discarding the vectors that depend linearly on earlier ones, we obtain a finite or countable orthonormal family $(e_ k)$ whose linear span is dense in $V$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\| x\| ^2=\lim _ j\langle x_ j,xangle \le \varliminf _ j\| x_ j\| \, \| x\| $, and we divide by $\| x\| $. $\square$ Differential operators are defined only on subspaces of $L^2$ spaces, so we need the following notions. Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be Hilbert spaces. An operator $T$ from $H_0$ to $H_1$ is a linear map $T\colon \operatorname{Dom}T	o H_1$ defined on a linear subspace $\operatorname{Dom}T\subset H_0$, its domain . We write $\ker T$ for its kernel, $\operatorname {Ran}T=T(\operatorname{Dom}T)$ for its range, and $\operatorname {Gr}T=\{ (x,Tx):x\in \operatorname{Dom}T\} $ for its graph, a subspace of the Hilbert space $H_0\oplus H_1$ with the inner product $\langle (x,y),(x',y')angle =\langle x,x'angle +\langle y,y'angle $. The operator $T$ is densely defined if $\operatorname{Dom}T$ is dense in $H_0$, and closed if $\operatorname {Gr}T$ is closed; equivalently, $x_ j\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, $x_ j	o x$ and $Tx_ j	o y$ imply $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $Tx=y$. In particular, the kernel of a closed operator is a closed subspace. If $T$ is densely defined, its Hilbert adjoint $T^*$, an operator from $H_1$ to $H_0$, is defined as follows: $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ if the linear functional $x\mapsto \langle Tx,yangle $ on $\operatorname{Dom}T$ is bounded with respect to the norm of $H_0$, and then $T^*y$ is the vector determined by \[  \langle Tx,yangle =\langle x,T^*yangle \qquad (x\in \operatorname{Dom}T).  \] This vector is well defined: since $\operatorname{Dom}T$ is dense, the functional extends uniquely to a bounded linear functional on $H_0$, which proposition 11.1.1 represents by a unique vector. Lemma 11.1.3 . Let $T$ be a densely defined operator from $H_0$ to $H_1$. Then $T^*$ is closed and $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. If $T$ is also closed, then $T^*$ is densely defined and $T^{**}=T$. Proof. If $y_ j\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, $y_ j	o y$ and $T^*y_ j	o w$, then for every $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ \[  \langle Tx,yangle =\lim _ j\langle Tx,y_ jangle =\lim _ j\langle x,T^*y_ jangle =\langle x,wangle ;  \] hence $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=w$, so $T^*$ is closed. A vector $y\in H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Ran}T$ exactly when the functional $x\mapsto \langle Tx,yangle $ vanishes, that is, when $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=0$. This proves $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. In the same way, $(a,b)\in H_0\oplus H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Gr}T$ if and only if $\langle Tx,bangle =\langle x,-aangle $ for all $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, so \[  (\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =\{ (-T^*y,y):y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\} .  \] Now let $T$ be closed, and let $v\in H_1$ be orthogonal to $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Since $\operatorname {Gr}T$ is closed, proposition 11.1.1 and the description of $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp $ decompose $(0,v)$ as $(x,Tx)+(-T^*y,y)$ with $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus $x=T^*y$ and $v=Tx+y$. Since $v$ is orthogonal to $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, we obtain \[  0=\langle v,yangle =\langle Tx,yangle +\| y\| ^2=\langle x,T^*yangle +\| y\| ^2=\| x\| ^2+\| y\| ^2,  \] so $x=y=0$ and $v=0$. Hence $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$ is dense, and $T^{**}$ is defined. Let $J\colon H_1\oplus H_0	o H_0\oplus H_1$ and $J'\colon H_0\oplus H_1	o H_1\oplus H_0$ be the unitary maps $J(b,a)=(-a,b)$ and $J'(a,b)=(-b,a)$. The description of the orthogonal complement of a graph, applied to $T$ and to the densely defined operator $T^*$, reads $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =J(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)$ and $(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp =J'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})$. For a closed subspace $M$ we have $(M^\perp )^\perp =M$ by proposition 11.1.1 , and unitary maps carry orthogonal complements to orthogonal complements. Therefore \[  \operatorname {Gr}T= igl ((\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp  igr )^\perp =J igl ((\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp  igr ) =JJ'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})=\operatorname {Gr}T^{**},  \] because $JJ'=-\mathrm{id}$ and graphs are linear subspaces. Thus $T^{**}=T$. $\square$ The next theorem, the abstract form of Hörmander's method, produces a solution of $Tu=g$ from an inequality for the adjoint operator. The second operator $S$ allows us to require the inequality only on $\operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$; in the application in section 11.3 , smooth compactly supported forms are dense in this space, and for them the inequality follows from an integration by parts. Theorem 11.1.4 . Let $H_0,H_1,H_2$ be Hilbert spaces, let $T$ from $H_0$ to $H_1$ be a closed densely defined operator, and let $S$ from $H_1$ to $H_2$ be a closed operator with $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$. Let $g\in \ker S$ and $0\le M<\infty $, and assume that \[  |\langle g,fangle |^2\le M igl (\| T^*f\| ^2+\| Sf\| ^2 igr ) \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S).  \] Then the equation $Tu=g$ has a solution $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ with $\| u\| ^2\le M$. Among all solutions there is a unique one of smallest norm, and it is orthogonal to $\ker T$. Proof. Since $S$ is closed, $\ker S$ is a closed subspace, and $H_1=\ker S\oplus (\ker S)^\perp $ by proposition 11.1.1 . Since $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$, lemma 11.1.3 gives $(\ker S)^\perp \subset (\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp =\ker T^*$. Let $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, and write $f=f_0+f_1$ with $f_0\in \ker S$ and $f_1\in (\ker S)^\perp $. Then $f_1\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*f_1=0$, so $f_0\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$, $T^*f_0=T^*f$ and $Sf_0=0$. Moreover $\langle g,fangle =\langle g,f_0angle $, because $g\in \ker S$. The hypothesis applied to $f_0$ therefore gives \[  |\langle g,fangle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*f\| \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Consequently the map $\lambda \colon T^*f\mapsto \langle g,fangle $ is well defined on $\operatorname {Ran}T^*$: if $T^*f=T^*f'$, then $|\langle g,f-f'angle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*(f-f')\| =0$. It is conjugate-linear and bounded by $\sqrt M$, hence uniformly continuous, so it extends uniquely to a conjugate-linear functional $	ilde\lambda $ on the closed subspace $W=\overline{\operatorname {Ran}T^*}$, again bounded by $\sqrt M$. If $P_ W$ is the orthogonal projection onto $W$, then $x\mapsto 	ilde\lambda (P_ Wx)$ is a conjugate-linear functional on $H_0$ of norm at most $\sqrt M$, because $\| P_ Wx\| \le \| x\| $. By the representation of conjugate-linear functionals in proposition 11.1.1 , there is $u\in H_0$ with $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$ and \[  \langle u,T^*fangle =\langle g,fangle \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Taking complex conjugates, we get $\langle T^*f,uangle =\langle f,gangle $ for all $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus the functional $f\mapsto \langle T^*f,uangle $ is bounded on $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$, so $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T^{**}$ and $T^{**}u=g$. Since $T^{**}=T$ by lemma 11.1.3 , we conclude that $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $Tu=g$. The solutions of $Tu=g$ form the affine subspace $u+\ker T$, which is closed because $\ker T$ is closed. If $P$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto $\ker T$, then $\| u+k\| ^2=\| u-Pu\| ^2+\| Pu+k\| ^2$ for $k\in \ker T$. Hence $u-Pu$ is the unique solution of smallest norm; it is orthogonal to $\ker T$, and its norm is at most $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$. $\square$

text: Proposition 11.1.2 . Every bounded sequence in a Hilbert space $H$ has a weakly convergent subsequence, that is, a subsequence $(x_ j)$ for which there is $x\in H$ with $\langle x_ j,v\rangle \to \langle x,v\rangle $ for every $v\in H$. If $(x_ j)$ converges weakly to $x$, then $\| x\| \le \varliminf _ j\| x_ j\| $. Proof. Let $(x_ j)$ be a sequence with $\| x_ j\| \le C$, and let $V$ be the closed linear span of its terms. The finite linear combinations of the $x_ j$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q+\mathrm i\mathbb Q$ form a countable dense subset of $V$. Applying the Gram–Schmidt process to it, and discarding the vectors that depend linearly on earlier ones, we obtain a finite or countable orthonormal family $(e_ k)$ whose linear span is dense in $V$. For each $k$ the sequence $(\langle x_ j,e_ k\rangle )_ j$ is bounded by $C$, so by a diagonal argument we may pass to a subsequence, still denoted $(x_ j)$, such that $\langle x_ j,e_ k\rangle $ converges to a number $a_ k$ for every $k$. For every $N$, Bessel's inequality gives $\sum _{k\le N}|\langle x_ j,e_ k\rangle |^2\le C^2$; letting $j\to \infty $ and then $N\to \infty $, we get $\sum _ k|a_ k|^2\le C^2$. Since $\| \sum _{N<k\le N'}a_ ke_ k\| ^2=\sum _{N<k\le N'}|a_ k|^2$ by Pythagoras' theorem, the partial sums of the series $x=\sum _ ka_ ke_ k$ form a Cauchy sequence; the series therefore converges in the closed, hence complete, subspace $V$, and $\| x\| ^2=\sum _ k|a_ k|^2\le C^2$. By the continuity of the inner product and the orthonormality of the $e_ k$, we have $\langle x,e_ k\rangle =a_ k=\lim _ j\langle x_ j,e_ k\rangle $ for every $k$; hence $\langle x_ j,v\rangle \to \langle x,v\rangle $ for every $v$ in the linear span of the $e_ k$. If $v\in V$ and $v'$ lies in that span with $\| v-v'\| <\delta $, then $|\langle x_ j-x,v\rangle |\le |\langle x_ j-x,v'\rangle |+2C\delta $, so the convergence extends to all $v\in V$. For an arbitrary $v\in H$, write $v=v_1+v_2$ with $v_1\in V$ and $v_2\in V^\perp $ by proposition 11.1.1 ; since $x_ j$ and $x$ lie in $V$, we get $\langle x_ j-x,v\rangle =\langle x_ j-x,v_1\rangle \to 0$. For the last assertion we may assume that $x\ne 0$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\| x\| ^2=\lim _ j\langle x_ j,x\rangle \le \varliminf _ j\| x_ j\| \, \| x\| $, and we divide by $\| x\| $. $\square$

text: Lemma 11.1.3 . Let $T$ be a densely defined operator from $H_0$ to $H_1$. Then $T^*$ is closed and $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. If $T$ is also closed, then $T^*$ is densely defined and $T^{**}=T$. Proof. If $y_ j\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, $y_ j\to y$ and $T^*y_ j\to w$, then for every $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ \[  \langle Tx,y\rangle =\lim _ j\langle Tx,y_ j\rangle =\lim _ j\langle x,T^*y_ j\rangle =\langle x,w\rangle ;  \] hence $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=w$, so $T^*$ is closed. A vector $y\in H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Ran}T$ exactly when the functional $x\mapsto \langle Tx,y\rangle $ vanishes, that is, when $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=0$. This proves $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. In the same way, $(a,b)\in H_0\oplus H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Gr}T$ if and only if $\langle Tx,b\rangle =\langle x,-a\rangle $ for all $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, so \[  (\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =\{ (-T^*y,y):y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\} .  \] Now let $T$ be closed, and let $v\in H_1$ be orthogonal to $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Since $\operatorname {Gr}T$ is closed, proposition 11.1.1 and the description of $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp $ decompose $(0,v)$ as $(x,Tx)+(-T^*y,y)$ with $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus $x=T^*y$ and $v=Tx+y$. Since $v$ is orthogonal to $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, we obtain \[  0=\langle v,y\rangle =\langle Tx,y\rangle +\| y\| ^2=\langle x,T^*y\rangle +\| y\| ^2=\| x\| ^2+\| y\| ^2,  \] so $x=y=0$ and $v=0$. Hence $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$ is dense, and $T^{**}$ is defined. Let $J\colon H_1\oplus H_0\to H_0\oplus H_1$ and $J'\colon H_0\oplus H_1\to H_1\oplus H_0$ be the unitary maps $J(b,a)=(-a,b)$ and $J'(a,b)=(-b,a)$. The description of the orthogonal complement of a graph, applied to $T$ and to the densely defined operator $T^*$, reads $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =J(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)$ and $(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp =J'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})$. For a closed subspace $M$ we have $(M^\perp )^\perp =M$ by proposition 11.1.1 , and unitary maps carry orthogonal complements to orthogonal complements. Therefore \[  \operatorname {Gr}T=\bigl ((\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp \bigr )^\perp =J\bigl ((\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp \bigr ) =JJ'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})=\operatorname {Gr}T^{**},  \] because $JJ'=-\mathrm{id}$ and graphs are linear subspaces. Thus $T^{**}=T$. $\square$

section: 6.1 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Theorem 11.1.4 . Let $H_0,H_1,H_2$ be Hilbert spaces, let $T$ from $H_0$ to $H_1$ be a closed densely defined operator, and let $S$ from $H_1$ to $H_2$ be a closed operator with $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$. Let $g\in \ker S$ and $0\le M<\infty $, and assume that \[  |\langle g,f\rangle |^2\le M\bigl (\| T^*f\| ^2+\| Sf\| ^2\bigr ) \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S).  \] Then the equation $Tu=g$ has a solution $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ with $\| u\| ^2\le M$. Among all solutions there is a unique one of smallest norm, and it is orthogonal to $\ker T$. Proof. Since $S$ is closed, $\ker S$ is a closed subspace, and $H_1=\ker S\oplus (\ker S)^\perp $ by proposition 11.1.1 . Since $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$, lemma 11.1.3 gives $(\ker S)^\perp \subset (\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp =\ker T^*$. Let $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, and write $f=f_0+f_1$ with $f_0\in \ker S$ and $f_1\in (\ker S)^\perp $. Then $f_1\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*f_1=0$, so $f_0\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$, $T^*f_0=T^*f$ and $Sf_0=0$. Moreover $\langle g,f\rangle =\langle g,f_0\rangle $, because $g\in \ker S$. The hypothesis applied to $f_0$ therefore gives \[  |\langle g,f\rangle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*f\| \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Consequently the map $\lambda \colon T^*f\mapsto \langle g,f\rangle $ is well defined on $\operatorname {Ran}T^*$: if $T^*f=T^*f'$, then $|\langle g,f-f'\rangle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*(f-f')\| =0$. It is conjugate-linear and bounded by $\sqrt M$, hence uniformly continuous, so it extends uniquely to a conjugate-linear functional $\tilde\lambda $ on the closed subspace $W=\overline{\operatorname {Ran}T^*}$, again bounded by $\sqrt M$. If $P_ W$ is the orthogonal projection onto $W$, then $x\mapsto \tilde\lambda (P_ Wx)$ is a conjugate-linear functional on $H_0$ of norm at most $\sqrt M$, because $\| P_ Wx\| \le \| x\| $. By the representation of conjugate-linear functionals in proposition 11.1.1 , there is $u\in H_0$ with $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$ and \[  \langle u,T^*f\rangle =\langle g,f\rangle \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Taking complex conjugates, we get $\langle T^*f,u\rangle =\langle f,g\rangle $ for all $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus the functional $f\mapsto \langle T^*f,u\rangle $ is bounded on $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$, so $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T^{**}$ and $T^{**}u=g$. Since $T^{**}=T$ by lemma 11.1.3 , we conclude that $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $Tu=g$. The solutions of $Tu=g$ form the affine subspace $u+\ker T$, which is closed because $\ker T$ is closed. If $P$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto $\ker T$, then $\| u+k\| ^2=\| u-Pu\| ^2+\| Pu+k\| ^2$ for $k\in \ker T$. Hence $u-Pu$ is the unique solution of smallest norm; it is orthogonal to $\ker T$, and its norm is at most $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$. $\square$

title: 11.2 Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance
