title: Theorem 11.3.4
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.1 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Theorem 11.3.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a pseudoconvex open set, $n\ge 1$, let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and let $q$ be a smooth real function on $\Omega $ whose complex Hessian matrix $A=H_ q$ is positive semidefinite. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega $ with measurable coefficients such that \[  M=\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV<\infty  \] and $\bar\partial \alpha =0$. Then the equation $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution with $\int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M$. In particular, if $A\ge \lambda I$ for a positive continuous function $\lambda $ on $\Omega $, then $M$ may be replaced by $\int _\Omega \lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV$. Proof. We regularize $p$ on relatively compact pseudoconvex subsets of $\Omega $, apply theorem 11.3.3 there, and pass to a weak limit. Since the weight $p+q$ is bounded above on compact sets, the discussion preceding theorem 11.3.3 shows that $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$, so that $\bar\partial \alpha $ is defined. By corollary 11.2.5 there are pseudoconvex open sets $\Omega _1\subset \Omega _2\subset \cdots $ with $\Omega _ j\Subset \Omega $ and $\bigcup _ j\Omega _ j=\Omega $. Let $\rho _\varepsilon $ be the radial mollifier of section 1.4 , and choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ with $\varepsilon _ j<\operatorname {dist}(\overline\Omega _ j,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$. By proposition 8.2.2 (2), $p_ j=p*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}$ is defined, smooth and plurisubharmonic on the open neighborhood $\{ z\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon _ j\} $ of $\overline\Omega _ j$, so its complex Hessian is positive semidefinite there, and $p_ j\downarrow p$ pointwise as $j\to \infty $. Put $\varphi _ j=p_ j+q$. Then $\varphi _ j$ is smooth with complex Hessian matrix $H_{\varphi _ j}\ge A\ge 0$ near $\overline\Omega _ j$, so it is plurisubharmonic there by proposition 8.2.2 (1), and $\varphi _ j\ge p+q$. Since the dual energy decreases when the matrix increases, \[  \int _{\Omega _ j}|\alpha |_{H_{\varphi _ j}^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV \le \int _{\Omega _ j}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M.  \] By theorem 11.3.3 there is $u_ j$ on $\Omega _ j$ with $\bar\partial u_ j=\alpha $ and $\int _{\Omega _ j}|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV\le M$. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact. Then $K\subset \Omega _ k$ for some $k$, and for $j\ge k$ we have $\varphi _ j\le \varphi _ k$ on $K$, because $p_ j$ decreases. Hence $\int _ K|u_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{\max _ K\varphi _ k}M$ for $j\ge k$, so the sequence $(u_ j)$ is eventually bounded in $L^2(K)$ for every compact set $K$. Let $(K_ m)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ (section 1.1 ). By proposition 11.1.2 and a diagonal argument, we find a subsequence that converges weakly in $L^2(K_ m)$ for every $m$. The weak limits are compatible, because restriction from $K_{m+1}$ to $K_ m$ is a bounded linear map, and they define a function $u\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$; since every compact subset of $\Omega $ lies in some $K_ m$, the subsequence converges weakly to $u$ in $L^2(K)$ for every compact $K\subset \Omega $. Then $u_ j\to u$ in the sense of distributions, and $\bar\partial u=\alpha $. Now let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $k$ be so large that $K\subset \Omega _ k$. On $L^2(K)$ the norm with weight $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}$ is equivalent to the unweighted norm, so the subsequence also converges weakly for it, and the lower semicontinuity in proposition 11.1.2 gives \[  \int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _ K|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _ K|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV\le M.  \] This holds for all large $k$, and $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}$ increases to $\mathrm e^{-p-q}$ as $k\to \infty $; so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M$, and exhausting $\Omega $ by compact sets proves the estimate. The last assertion follows from the pointwise inequality $|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\le \lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |^2$. $\square$

title: Lemma 11.3.5

section: 6.1 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Lemma 11.3.5 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$. Every distribution $h$ on $\Omega $ with $\bar\partial h=0$ is a holomorphic function: there is $g\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $\langle h,\chi \rangle =\int _\Omega g\chi \, \mathrm dV$ for every test function $\chi $. Let $\varphi \colon \Omega \to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function that is bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Then the elements of $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ represented by holomorphic functions form a closed subspace $\mathcal K$. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form with distribution coefficients such that the equation $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. Then among these solutions there is exactly one of smallest norm, and a solution is of smallest norm if and only if it is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$. Proof. (1) The real and imaginary parts of $h$, given by $\operatorname{Re}\langle h,\chi \rangle $ and $\operatorname{Im}\langle h,\chi \rangle $ for real test functions $\chi $, are real distributions. Since derivatives of distributions commute, ( 7.5 ) shows that the Laplacian of $h$ is $4\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ j}h=0$. As the Laplacian has real coefficients, the real and imaginary parts of $h$ are harmonic distributions. By Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) they are given by smooth functions, and hence $h$ is given by a smooth function $g$. By integration by parts, the classical derivatives $\partial _{\bar z_ j}g$ represent the distributions $\partial _{\bar z_ j}h=0$, so they vanish almost everywhere by proposition 1.4.3 (4), and hence everywhere, being continuous functions. Thus $g$ is holomorphic. (2) Let $L\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $m_ L$ be a real upper bound for $\varphi $ on $L$. For $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ we have $\int _ L|u|^2\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{m_ L}\int _ L|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$. Hence $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })\subset L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so that $\bar\partial u$ is defined in the sense of distributions, and convergence in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ implies convergence in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, hence in the sense of distributions. The space $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ is a Hilbert space, by the completeness argument at the beginning of section 11.1 , applied to the positive measure $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$. The set $\mathcal K$ is a linear subspace. It is closed: if $g_ j\in \mathcal K$ converge to $g$ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$, then $g_ j\to g$ in the sense of distributions, so $\bar\partial g=\lim _ j\bar\partial g_ j=0$, and by (1) $g$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function, that is, $g\in \mathcal K$. Let $u_0$ be a solution of $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. By (1), an element $u$ of this space is a solution if and only if $\bar\partial (u-u_0)=0$, that is, $u-u_0\in \mathcal K$. Thus the solutions form the nonempty closed convex set $u_0+\mathcal K$, which by proposition 11.1.1 contains a unique element $u_{\min }$ of smallest norm. If a solution $u$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$, then $\| u+k\| ^2=\| u\| ^2+\| k\| ^2\geq \| u\| ^2$ for every $k\in \mathcal K$, so $u$ has smallest norm, that is, $u=u_{\min }$. Conversely, if $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal K$ (proposition 11.1.1 ), then $u_{\min }-Pu_{\min }$ is a solution orthogonal to $\mathcal K$, hence equal to $u_{\min }$; so $u_{\min }$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$. $\square$

text:
11.4 Interpolation and extension across a hyperplane We now construct holomorphic functions with a prescribed value at a point, or a prescribed restriction to a hyperplane, and with controlled weighted norms. In both cases, a smooth function with the right values is corrected by a solution of a $ ar\partial $-equation whose weight has a singular term forcing the correction to vanish where the values are prescribed. Proposition 11.4.1 . Let $r,L>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L$, let $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $B(a,2r)\subset \Omega $, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. If $h$ is holomorphic on $B(a,2r)$ and $\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $, then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=h(a),\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C(n,r,L) \int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV,  \] where the constant $C(n,r,L)$ depends only on $n$, $r$ and $L$, and not on $\Omega $, $p$, $h$ or $a$. Proof. Fix a smooth function $\kappa $ on $\mathbb R$ with $0\le \kappa \le 1$, $\kappa =1$ on $(-\infty ,1]$ and $\kappa =0$ on $[3/2,\infty )$, for instance $\kappa (x)=\kappa _0(2x-2)$ with the function $\kappa _0$ fixed at the beginning of section 11.3 , and put $\chi (z)=\kappa (|z-a|/r)$. Then $\chi $ is smooth, because $\kappa $ is constant near $0$; it has compact support in $B(a,2r)$, equals one on $B(a,r)$, and satisfies $| ar\partial \chi |\le c_0/r$ with $c_0=\sup |\kappa '|/2$, because $| ar\partial |z-a||=1/2$ for $z
e a$. Extend $\chi h$ by zero to $\Omega $. Then $\alpha = ar\partial (\chi h)=h\,  ar\partial \chi $ is a smooth $ ar\partial $-closed form supported in the shell $r\le |z-a|\le 2r$. The function $p+n\log |z-a|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $ by proposition 8.3.3 , proposition 8.2.5 . We apply theorem 11.3.4 with this function in place of $p$ and with $q=|z-a|^2$, for which $A=I$. Since $\mathrm e^{-|z-a|^2}\le 1$ and $|z-a|^{-2n}\le r^{-2n}$ on the support of $\alpha $, we obtain a solution of $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ with \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2|z-a|^{-2n}\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}\, \mathrm dV \le c_0^2r^{-2n-2}\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] On $B(a,r)$ we have $ ar\partial u=\alpha =0$, so $u$ is holomorphic there, by lemma 11.3.5 (1). Since $p$ is bounded above on $B(a,r)$, the factor $\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}$ is bounded below there by a positive constant. Moreover $F(z',0)=\lim _ jF_ j(z',0)=f(z')$ for $z'\in \Omega _0$. Finally, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $k$ be so large that $K\subset D_ k$. For $j\ge k$ we have $p_ j\le p_ k$ on $K$, so locally uniform convergence gives \[  \int _ K|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ k}\, \mathrm dV=\lim _ j\int _ K|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _{D_ j}|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ j}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I.  \] This holds for all large $k$, and $\mathrm e^{-p_ k}$ increases to $\mathrm e^{-p}$ as $k	o \infty $; so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _ K|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$, and exhausting $\Omega $ by compact sets gives $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$. $\square$ Applying the theorem once for each normal direction, we obtain extension from affine subspaces of any codimension, in particular from points. Corollary 11.4.5 . Let $C$ be the constant of theorem 11.4.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L>0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then for every $a\in \Omega $ with $p(a)>-\infty $ there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=1,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV \le C^ n L^{2n}\mathrm e^{-p(a)}.  \] More generally, let $V\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be an affine complex subspace of codimension $r$, $0\le r\le n$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on $\Omega \cap V$ with finite slice norm $\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$, computed with Lebesgue measure on $V$. Then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $F|_{\Omega \cap V}=f$ and $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C^ rL^{2r}\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$. Proof. We prove the second assertion; the first is the case $V=\{ a\} $, $r=n$ and $f=1$, whose slice norm with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$ is $\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$. If $r=0$ we take $F=f$, and if $\Omega \cap V=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. Assume now that $r\ge 1$ and $\Omega \cap V
e \varnothing $. Choose $b\in \Omega \cap V$ and unitary affine coordinates $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_ n)$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ centered at $b$ with $V=\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} $, and put $\Omega _ k=\Omega \cap \{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $ for $0\le k\le r$, an open subset of a space isomorphic to $\mathbb C^{n-k}$. Unitary coordinates preserve Lebesgue measure. Each $\Omega _ k$ with $k<n$ is pseudoconvex: the restriction of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $ to the closed subset $\Omega _ k$ of $\Omega $ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.3 , applied to the linear embedding of $\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $, and its sublevel sets are compact. By the discussion following definition 11.2.1 , every connected component of $\Omega _ k$ is pseudoconvex as well. Since $\Omega $ is open and has diameter at most $L$, we have $|z-b|<L$ for $z\in \Omega $ (a point $z\in \Omega $ with $|z-b|=L$ could be moved slightly away from $b$ inside $\Omega $), so the coordinate $w_ k$ takes its values in $\Delta _ L$ on $\Omega _{k-1}$. Put $f_ r=f$, let $1\le k\le r$, and assume that $f_ k\in \mathcal O(\Omega _ k)$ has finite norm $\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}$. Let $W$ be a connected component of $\Omega _{k-1}$; ordering the coordinates as $(w_{k+1},\ldots ,w_ n,w_ k)$, we regard $W$ as an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-k}	imes \Delta _ L$ whose slice by $\{ w_ k=0\} $ is the open subset $W\cap \Omega _ k$ of $\Omega _ k$. By proposition 8.2.3 , the restriction of $p$ to $W$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. In the second case $\mathrm e^{-p}=\infty $ on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, so the finiteness of the norm of $f_ k$ forces $f_ k=0$ almost everywhere on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, hence everywhere there, since $f_ k$ is continuous, and we put $f_{k-1}=0$ on $W$. In the first case, theorem 11.4.4 , applied to $W$ with normal coordinate $w_ k$, gives a holomorphic function $f_{k-1}$ on $W$ extending the restriction of $f_ k$ to $W\cap \Omega _ k$, with \[  \int _ W|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{W\cap \Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] The components $W$ are open, disjoint and cover $\Omega _{k-1}$, and the sets $W\cap \Omega _ k$ are disjoint and cover $\Omega _ k$. Hence these functions define $f_{k-1}\in \mathcal O(\Omega _{k-1})$ extending $f_ k$, and summing over $W$ gives \[  \int _{\Omega _{k-1}}|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] Proceeding in this way for $k=r,r-1,\ldots ,1$ and multiplying the $r$ estimates, we see that $F=f_0$ has the required properties. $\square$ Corollary 11.4.6 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold, let $Y\subset X$ be a complex submanifold, let $a\in Y$, and let $p$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Let $f$ be a holomorphic germ on $Y$ at $a$ such that $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p|_ Y}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $Y$. Then there is a holomorphic germ $F$ on $X$ at $a$ with $F|_ Y=f$ such that $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Here integrability refers to smooth positive volume forms on $Y$ and $X$; since any two such forms are locally comparable, the notion does not depend on their choice. Proof. Let $k=\dim Y$ and $n=\dim X$ near $a$. By the definition of a complex submanifold (definition 7.1.1 ), there are holomorphic coordinates $w=(w',w'')\in \mathbb C^ k	imes \mathbb C^{n-k}$ centered at $a$ in which $Y=\{ w''=0\} $; by proposition 8.2.3 , $p$ is plurisubharmonic near $0$ in these coordinates. On a compact neighborhood of $a$, the densities of smooth positive volume forms with respect to coordinate Lebesgue measure are bounded above and below by positive constants. Hence we may test integrability with Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV_{2k}$ on $Y=\mathbb C^ k	imes \{ 0\} $ and $\mathrm dV_{2n}$ in the coordinates $w$. Choose a ball $B$ around $0$ so small that $p$ is plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, that $f$ is defined on $B\cap Y$, and that $\int _{B\cap Y}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2k}<\infty $. The ball $B$ is a bounded pseudoconvex domain, by corollary 11.2.5 applied to the exhaustion function $|w|^2$ of $\mathbb C^ n$, and $B\cap Y$ is its intersection with the linear subspace $\{ w''=0\} $ of codimension $n-k$. By corollary 11.4.5 there is $F\in \mathcal O(B)$ with $F|_{B\cap Y}=f$ and $\int _ B|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}<\infty $. (If $k=0$, the integral over $Y$ is the weighted value $|f(a)|^2\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$; if $p|_ Y$ is identically $-\infty $ near $a$, then $f=0$ and $F=0$, in accordance with the conventions of theorem 11.4.4 .) $\square$

title: Proposition 11.4.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.1 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Proposition 11.4.1 . Let $r,L>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L$, let $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $B(a,2r)\subset \Omega $, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. If $h$ is holomorphic on $B(a,2r)$ and $\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $, then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=h(a),\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C(n,r,L) \int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV,  \] where the constant $C(n,r,L)$ depends only on $n$, $r$ and $L$, and not on $\Omega $, $p$, $h$ or $a$. Proof. Fix a smooth function $\kappa $ on $\mathbb R$ with $0\le \kappa \le 1$, $\kappa =1$ on $(-\infty ,1]$ and $\kappa =0$ on $[3/2,\infty )$, for instance $\kappa (x)=\kappa _0(2x-2)$ with the function $\kappa _0$ fixed at the beginning of section 11.3 , and put $\chi (z)=\kappa (|z-a|/r)$. Then $\chi $ is smooth, because $\kappa $ is constant near $0$; it has compact support in $B(a,2r)$, equals one on $B(a,r)$, and satisfies $|\bar\partial \chi |\le c_0/r$ with $c_0=\sup |\kappa '|/2$, because $|\bar\partial |z-a||=1/2$ for $z\ne a$. Extend $\chi h$ by zero to $\Omega $. Then $\alpha =\bar\partial (\chi h)=h\, \bar\partial \chi $ is a smooth $\bar\partial $-closed form supported in the shell $r\le |z-a|\le 2r$. The function $p+n\log |z-a|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $ by proposition 8.3.3 , proposition 8.2.5 . We apply theorem 11.3.4 with this function in place of $p$ and with $q=|z-a|^2$, for which $A=I$. Since $\mathrm e^{-|z-a|^2}\le 1$ and $|z-a|^{-2n}\le r^{-2n}$ on the support of $\alpha $, we obtain a solution of $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ with \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2|z-a|^{-2n}\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}\, \mathrm dV \le c_0^2r^{-2n-2}\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] On $B(a,r)$ we have $\bar\partial u=\alpha =0$, so $u$ is holomorphic there, by lemma 11.3.5 (1). Since $p$ is bounded above on $B(a,r)$, the factor $\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}$ is bounded below there by a positive constant. If $u(a)$ were nonzero, then $|u|$ would be bounded below by a positive constant near $a$, and the integral on the left would diverge, because $\int _{B(a,\rho )}|z-a|^{-2n}\, \mathrm dV$ is a positive multiple of $\int _0^\rho \tau ^{-2n}\tau ^{2n-1}\, \mathrm d\tau =\infty $ by integration in polar coordinates ( 2.1 ). Thus $u(a)=0$. The function $F=\chi h-u$ satisfies $\bar\partial F=0$, so it is holomorphic by the same lemma, and $F(a)=h(a)$. Since $|z-a|<L$ on $\Omega $, we have $|z-a|^{2n}\mathrm e^{|z-a|^2}\le L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}$, and therefore \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le c_0^2L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}r^{-2n-2}\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] Finally, $|F|^2\le 2|\chi h|^2+2|u|^2$ and $|\chi h|\le |h|\mathbf1_{B(a,2r)}$ give the assertion with $C(n,r,L)=2+2c_0^2L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}r^{-2n-2}$. $\square$

title: Lemma 11.4.2
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.1 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Lemma 11.4.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a pseudoconvex open set, $n\ge 1$, let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and let $\psi $ be a smooth bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Put $A=H_\psi $ and $h=| ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2$, where $ ar\partial \psi $ is identified with the vector $(\partial _{ ar z_ j}\psi )_ j$, and assume that $h<1$ almost everywhere. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega $ with measurable coefficients such that $E=\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $ and $ ar\partial \alpha =0$, let $0\le a<1$, and assume that $h\le a$ almost everywhere on $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $. Then $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution with \[  \int _\Omega (1-h)|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV \le  rac{1+\sqrt a}{1-\sqrt a}\, E.  \] Proof. The idea is that, if $u$ is the minimal solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$, then $u\mathrm e^\psi $ is the minimal solution of a twisted equation in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$, to which we apply Hörmander's estimate. Put $m=\sup _\Omega |\psi |<\infty $. Since $\mathrm e^{-m}\le \mathrm e^{\pm \psi }\le \mathrm e^ m$, the spaces $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$ and $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ consist of the same functions, with equivalent norms, and so contain the same holomorphic functions. By the discussion preceding theorem 11.3.3 , applied with the weight $p-\psi $, which is bounded above on compact sets, $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$; so $ ar\partial \alpha $ is defined. Since $\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\le \mathrm e^{2m}\mathrm e^{\psi -p}$, we have $\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{2m}E<\infty $. Hence theorem 11.3.4 , applied with the plurisubharmonic function $p$ and the smooth function $q=\psi $, whose complex Hessian matrix $A$ is positive semidefinite, shows that the equation $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })=L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$. Let $u$ be the minimal solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$, given by lemma 11.3.5 (2). The function $v=u\mathrm e^\psi $ belongs to $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ and solves \[   ar\partial v= eta =(\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi )\mathrm e^\psi .  \] For every holomorphic $g$ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ we have $\int v ar g\, \mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int u ar g\, \mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV=0$, so $v$ is the minimal solution of $ ar\partial v= eta $ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$, by lemma 11.3.5 (2). We now estimate $v$ by theorem 11.3.4 , applied again with $p$ and $q=\psi $. The form $ eta = ar\partial v$ is $ ar\partial $-closed, and it lies in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$ because $\alpha $ and $u$ are locally square integrable and $\psi $ is smooth. Since $E<\infty $ and $h<1$, the dual energies of $\alpha $ and $ ar\partial \psi $ are finite almost everywhere, and at such points both vectors lie in the subspace on which the dual energy is a Hermitian quadratic form. The triangle inequality $|\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}\le |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}+|u|h^{1/2}$ therefore gives \[  \int | eta |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV\le 2E+2\sup _\Omega \mathrm e^\psi \int |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty .  \] So theorem 11.3.4 yields a solution of $ ar\partial w= eta $ whose squared norm in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ is at most this integral, and the minimal solution $v$ has no larger norm. As $\int |v|^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int |u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV$, we obtain \[  \int |u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV \le \int |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] At almost every point, let $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _{A^{-1}}$ be the Hermitian inner product associated with the dual energy on the subspace where it is finite; by the polarization identity $\langle x,yangle _{A^{-1}}= rac14\sum _{k=0}^3\mathrm i^ k|x+\mathrm i^ ky|_{A^{-1}}^2$, the function $\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}}$ is measurable. We expand \[  |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2=|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2+2\operatorname{Re} igl ( ar u\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}} igr )+h|u|^2, \qquad |\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}}|\le |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2},  \] the second inequality being the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. The function $h|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}$ is integrable, since $h<1$ almost everywhere and $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$; moving its integral to the left, we find that $J=\int (1-h)|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV$, which is finite, satisfies \[  J\le E+2\int |u|\, |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2}\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] If $a=0$, then $h=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $, the last integral vanishes, and $J\le E$, as claimed. Let $a>0$. The last integrand vanishes outside $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $, where $h\le a$ and hence $h/(1-h)\le a/(1-a)$. For $t>1$, the inequality $2xy\le t^{-1}x^2+ty^2$ with $x=(1-h)^{1/2}|u|$ and $y=(h/(1-h))^{1/2}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}$ gives there \[  2|u|\, |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2}\le t^{-1}(1-h)|u|^2+ rac{ta}{1-a}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2.  \] Integrating, we obtain \[  J\le \left(1+ rac{ta}{1-a}ight)E+t^{-1}J.  \] Since $J$ is finite, this gives $J\le  rac t{t-1} igl (1+ rac{ta}{1-a} igr )E$. Choose $t=1+a^{-1/2}$. Then $1+ta/(1-a)=(1+\sqrt a)/(1-a)=1/(1-\sqrt a)$ and $t/(t-1)=1+\sqrt a$, so $J\le (1+\sqrt a)E/(1-\sqrt a)$. $\square$

title: Lemma 11.4.3
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.1 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Lemma 11.4.3 . Let $0<\varepsilon <1/4$. For $\zeta \in \mathbb C$ with $|\zeta |<1/4$ put \[  s=-\log (|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2),\qquad \eta =s+\log s,\qquad \psi _\varepsilon =-\log \eta .  \] Then $\psi _\varepsilon $ is a smooth, bounded, strictly subharmonic function on the disc $\Delta _{1/4}$. Let $h=|\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon |^2/(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }$. Then \[   egin{split}  (1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }& \ge (6s^2)^{-1},\  h& \le  rac{2}{-\log (2\varepsilon ^2)}\quad 	ext{for }|\zeta |\le \varepsilon ,\   rac{\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }}{|\zeta |^2(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }} & \le 25/4\quad 	ext{for }\varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon . \end{split}  \] In particular $h<1$ everywhere, and the bound for $h$ on the disc $|\zeta |\le \varepsilon $ tends to zero as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. Proof. Since $|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2<1/8$, we have $s>\log 8>2$, so $\eta >s>2$ and $\psi _\varepsilon <0$ is well defined. For fixed $\varepsilon $, $s$ ranges in a bounded interval, so $\psi _\varepsilon $ is bounded; and $\psi _\varepsilon =G(|\zeta |^2)$ for a function $G$ that is smooth near $[0,1/16)$, so $\psi _\varepsilon $ is smooth. For $\zeta 
e 0$ put $x=|\zeta |^2$, $t=\log x$ and $b=x/(x+\varepsilon ^2)\in (0,1)$, and denote derivatives with respect to $t$ by primes. Then $s'=-b$ and $b'=b(1-b)$, so $s''=-b(1-b)$. With $D=1+1/s$ we have $\eta '=s'+s'/s=-bD$ and $D'=-s'/s^2=b/s^2$. Hence $\psi _\varepsilon '=-\eta '/\eta =bD/\eta $ and $\psi _\varepsilon ''=(b'D+bD')/\eta -bD\eta '/\eta ^2$, that is, \[  \psi _\varepsilon '= rac{bD}{\eta },\qquad \psi _\varepsilon ''=A+B,\quad A= rac{b^2D^2}{\eta ^2},\quad B= rac{b(1-b)D}{\eta }+ rac{b^2}{\eta s^2}>0.  \] For a function $g$ of $t=\log |\zeta |^2$ we have $\partial _{ ar\zeta }g=g'/ ar\zeta $ and $\partial _\zeta \partial _{ ar\zeta }g=g''/|\zeta |^2$. Hence $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=\psi _\varepsilon ''/x>0$ and $h=(\psi _\varepsilon ')^2/\psi _\varepsilon ''=A/(A+B)<1$ for $\zeta 
e 0$. In general $\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon =G'(|\zeta |^2)\zeta $ and $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=G''(|\zeta |^2)|\zeta |^2+G'(|\zeta |^2)$, so at $\zeta =0$ we have $\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon =0$ and $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=G'(0)$, where $G'(x)=\psi _\varepsilon '/x=D/(\eta (x+\varepsilon ^2))>0$; so $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }>0$ and $h=0$ there. Thus $\psi _\varepsilon $ is strictly subharmonic, and $h<1$ everywhere. For the first estimate let $\zeta 
e 0$. Since $B\ge b^2/(\eta s^2)$, we have $A/B\le D^2s^2/\eta =(s+1)^2/\eta $, and therefore \[  (1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }= rac{B}{\eta (A+B)} \ge  rac1{\eta +(s+1)^2}\ge  rac1{6s^2},  \] because $\eta \le 2s\le 2s^2$ and $(s+1)^2\le 4s^2$ for $s\ge 1$. At $\zeta =0$ we have $(1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }=1/\eta \ge 1/(6s^2)$ as well. For the second estimate let $0<x\le \varepsilon ^2$. Then $b\le 1/2$, and $B\ge b(1-b)D/\eta $ gives \[  h\le  rac AB\le  rac{bD}{\eta (1-b)}\le  rac D\eta = rac{s+1}{s\eta }\le  rac2s,  \] since $s+1\le 2s\le 2\eta $; moreover $s\ge -\log (2\varepsilon ^2)$, because $x+\varepsilon ^2\le 2\varepsilon ^2$. Together with $h(0)=0$, this proves the second estimate. For the third, let $\varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon $. Then $1/5\le b\le 1/2$, so $\eta \psi _\varepsilon ''\ge \eta B\ge b(1-b)D\ge b(1-b)\ge 4/25$, and $\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }/(|\zeta |^2(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta })=1/(\eta \psi _\varepsilon '')\le 25/4$. $\square$

title: Theorem 11.4.4 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi)
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.1 Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Theorem 11.4.4 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi) . There is an absolute constant $C$ with the following property. Let $n\ge 1$ and $R>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _ R$ be a pseudoconvex open set, where $\Delta _ R\subset \mathbb C$ is the disc of radius $R$ centered at $0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Put $\Omega _0=\Omega \cap \{ z_ n=0\} $, which we identify with an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-1}$. Then every holomorphic function $f$ on $\Omega _0$ with \[  I=\int _{\Omega _0}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}<\infty  \] has an extension $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F|_{\Omega _0}=f,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}\le C R^2 I.  \] Here, for $n=1$, $\Omega _0$ is a point or empty, and $I$ is the weighted value of $|f|^2$ at that point, the integral with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$. If $\Omega _0=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. On a connected component of $\Omega _0$ on which the restriction of $p$ is identically $-\infty $, finiteness of $I$ forces $f=0$, and this component contributes zero to $I$. Proof. After a normalization, Step 1 treats smooth weights on relatively compact pseudoconvex subsets, by correcting a cutoff of $f$ with lemma 11.4.2 , lemma 11.4.3 , and Step 2 regularizes $p$ and passes to the limit. Normalization. The substitution $z_ n=4R\zeta $ maps $\mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _{1/4}$ onto $\mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _ R$, preserves the hyperplane and the integral $I$, and multiplies Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb C^ n$ by $16R^2$. Hence it suffices to show the following: if $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _{1/4}$, then $f$ has an extension $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$ for an absolute constant $C_0$; then $C=16C_0$ works. From now on we write the points of $\Omega $ as $(z',\zeta )$ with $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$ and $|\zeta |<1/4$; for $n=1$ the variable $z'$ is absent. We may assume $\Omega _0
e \varnothing $. Step 1: smooth weights on a relatively compact set. Let $D\Subset \Omega $ be a pseudoconvex open set, let $U\subset \Omega $ be an open neighborhood of $\overline D$, and let $\varphi $ be a smooth plurisubharmonic function on $U$. We show that there are an open set $P\Subset \Omega _0$ with $\overline P	imes \{ 0\} \subset U$ and a function $F\in \mathcal O(D)$ with $F(z',0)=f(z')$ whenever $(z',0)\in D$, such that 11.21  egin{equation} \label{eq:ot-smooth-step} \int _ D|F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le C_0\int _ P|f(z')|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (z',0)}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}(z'), \end{equation} where $C_0$ is an absolute constant; we write $I_ P$ for the integral over $P$ on the right. text: Corollary 11.4.5 . Let $C$ be the constant of theorem 11.4.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L>0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then for every $a\in \Omega $ with $p(a)>-\infty $ there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=1,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV \le C^ n L^{2n}\mathrm e^{-p(a)}.  \] More generally, let $V\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be an affine complex subspace of codimension $r$, $0\le r\le n$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on $\Omega \cap V$ with finite slice norm $\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$, computed with Lebesgue measure on $V$. Then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $F|_{\Omega \cap V}=f$ and $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C^ rL^{2r}\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$. Proof. We prove the second assertion; the first is the case $V=\{ a\} $, $r=n$ and $f=1$, whose slice norm with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$ is $\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$. If $r=0$ we take $F=f$, and if $\Omega \cap V=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. Assume now that $r\ge 1$ and $\Omega \cap V\ne \varnothing $. Choose $b\in \Omega \cap V$ and unitary affine coordinates $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_ n)$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ centered at $b$ with $V=\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} $, and put $\Omega _ k=\Omega \cap \{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $ for $0\le k\le r$, an open subset of a space isomorphic to $\mathbb C^{n-k}$. Unitary coordinates preserve Lebesgue measure. Each $\Omega _ k$ with $k<n$ is pseudoconvex: the restriction of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $ to the closed subset $\Omega _ k$ of $\Omega $ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.3 , applied to the linear embedding of $\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $, and its sublevel sets are compact. By the discussion following definition 11.2.1 , every connected component of $\Omega _ k$ is pseudoconvex as well. Since $\Omega $ is open and has diameter at most $L$, we have $|z-b|<L$ for $z\in \Omega $ (a point $z\in \Omega $ with $|z-b|=L$ could be moved slightly away from $b$ inside $\Omega $), so the coordinate $w_ k$ takes its values in $\Delta _ L$ on $\Omega _{k-1}$. Put $f_ r=f$, let $1\le k\le r$, and assume that $f_ k\in \mathcal O(\Omega _ k)$ has finite norm $\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}$. Let $W$ be a connected component of $\Omega _{k-1}$; ordering the coordinates as $(w_{k+1},\ldots ,w_ n,w_ k)$, we regard $W$ as an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-k}\times \Delta _ L$ whose slice by $\{ w_ k=0\} $ is the open subset $W\cap \Omega _ k$ of $\Omega _ k$. By proposition 8.2.3 , the restriction of $p$ to $W$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. In the second case $\mathrm e^{-p}=\infty $ on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, so the finiteness of the norm of $f_ k$ forces $f_ k=0$ almost everywhere on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, hence everywhere there, since $f_ k$ is continuous, and we put $f_{k-1}=0$ on $W$. In the first case, theorem 11.4.4 , applied to $W$ with normal coordinate $w_ k$, gives a holomorphic function $f_{k-1}$ on $W$ extending the restriction of $f_ k$ to $W\cap \Omega _ k$, with \[  \int _ W|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{W\cap \Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] The components $W$ are open, disjoint and cover $\Omega _{k-1}$, and the sets $W\cap \Omega _ k$ are disjoint and cover $\Omega _ k$. Hence these functions define $f_{k-1}\in \mathcal O(\Omega _{k-1})$ extending $f_ k$, and summing over $W$ gives \[  \int _{\Omega _{k-1}}|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] Proceeding in this way for $k=r,r-1,\ldots ,1$ and multiplying the $r$ estimates, we see that $F=f_0$ has the required properties. $\square$

text: Corollary 11.4.6 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold, let $Y\subset X$ be a complex submanifold, let $a\in Y$, and let $p$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Let $f$ be a holomorphic germ on $Y$ at $a$ such that $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p|_ Y}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $Y$. Then there is a holomorphic germ $F$ on $X$ at $a$ with $F|_ Y=f$ such that $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Here integrability refers to smooth positive volume forms on $Y$ and $X$; since any two such forms are locally comparable, the notion does not depend on their choice. Proof. Let $k=\dim Y$ and $n=\dim X$ near $a$. By the definition of a complex submanifold (definition 7.1.1 ), there are holomorphic coordinates $w=(w',w'')\in \mathbb C^ k\times \mathbb C^{n-k}$ centered at $a$ in which $Y=\{ w''=0\} $; by proposition 8.2.3 , $p$ is plurisubharmonic near $0$ in these coordinates. On a compact neighborhood of $a$, the densities of smooth positive volume forms with respect to coordinate Lebesgue measure are bounded above and below by positive constants. Hence we may test integrability with Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV_{2k}$ on $Y=\mathbb C^ k\times \{ 0\} $ and $\mathrm dV_{2n}$ in the coordinates $w$. Choose a ball $B$ around $0$ so small that $p$ is plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, that $f$ is defined on $B\cap Y$, and that $\int _{B\cap Y}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2k}<\infty $. The ball $B$ is a bounded pseudoconvex domain, by corollary 11.2.5 applied to the exhaustion function $|w|^2$ of $\mathbb C^ n$, and $B\cap Y$ is its intersection with the linear subspace $\{ w''=0\} $ of codimension $n-k$. By corollary 11.4.5 there is $F\in \mathcal O(B)$ with $F|_{B\cap Y}=f$ and $\int _ B|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}<\infty $. (If $k=0$, the integral over $Y$ is the weighted value $|f(a)|^2\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$; if $p|_ Y$ is identically $-\infty $ near $a$, then $f=0$ and $F=0$, in accordance with the conventions of theorem 11.4.4 .) $\square$

title: 12 Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
12 Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals A plurisubharmonic function can have a complicated pole set, but near each point its growth is governed by a single logarithmic rate. The Lelong number $
u (u,a)$ of a plurisubharmonic function $u$ at a point $a$ is the largest $c\geq 0$ such that $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+O(1)$ near $a$; with this normalization $
u (\log |z|^2,0)=1$. By the Jensen–Lelong formula, $
u (u,a)$ is also the limiting density at $a$ of the positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, which links the pointwise growth of $u$ with the measures studied in the preceding chapters. Lelong numbers do not, however, determine the integrability properties of a singular weight $\varphi $ (example 12.3.3 ). These are recorded by the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, which consists of the holomorphic germs $f$ for which $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is locally integrable. The $L^2$ estimates and extension theorems of chapter 11 make multiplier ideals accessible. Solving a $ ar\partial $-equation with a weight that has a logarithmic pole at a point, we approximate every germ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, to arbitrarily high order, by holomorphic functions on a polydisc that are square integrable against $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$; with the Krull intersection theorem and the strong Noetherian property, this shows that $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ is a coherent sheaf (theorem 12.2.7 ). Comparing the vanishing orders of the generators of $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ with the growth of $\varphi $ (lemma 12.3.1 ), we prove Siu's theorem that the sets where the Lelong number is at least $c>0$ are analytic. The same comparison shows that $\mathrm e^{-t\varphi }$ is integrable near a point $x$ for every $t>0$ if $
u (\varphi ,x)=0$, a fact used in chapter 15 for an example on the projective line. The Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem gives the restriction and subadditivity properties of multiplier ideals. Since its constant does not depend on the weight, it can be applied along a moving family of hyperplanes; comparing the resulting extensions on one fixed holomorphic curve, we prove that multiplier ideals are stable under increasing limits of weights and deduce the strong openness theorem $\mathcal I(\varphi )= igcup _{\varepsilon >0}\mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )$ (corollary 12.5.4 ). The last section studies integrability on modifications. For a weight with analytic singularities, the change of variables formula on a log resolution reduces membership in the multiplier ideal to explicit one-variable integrals (theorem 12.6.5 ). For a general weight, the ideals $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ recover the generic Lelong numbers of $\varphi $ along all prime divisors over the ambient manifold, and strong openness gives a valuative criterion for membership in $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ in which one positive parameter serves for all divisors (theorem 12.6.9 ). These results are the local foundation for comparing singularities through their multiplier ideals in later chapters. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.12 .

12.1 Logarithmic growth and the Jensen formula Proposition 12.1.1 . Let $n\geq 1$ and let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a\in \mathbb C^ n$. For sufficiently negative $t$ put \[  N(t)=\sup _{|z-a|<\exp (t/2)}u(z).  \] Then $N$ is finite, nondecreasing and convex, $N(t)$ is also the supremum of $u$ over the sphere $|z-a|=\exp (t/2)$, and the limit 12.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-growth-definition} 
u (u,a)=\lim _{t	o -\infty } rac{N(t)}{t} \end{equation} exists in $[0,\infty )$; it is zero if $u(a)>-\infty $. For every $r_0>0$ such that $\overline{B(a,r_0)}$ lies in the domain of $u$, 12.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-attained-growth} u(z)\leq 
u (u,a)\log  rac{|z-a|^2}{r_0^2} +\sup _{B(a,r_0)}u,\qquad 0<|z-a|<r_0. \end{equation} Consequently $
u (u,a)$ is the largest $c\geq 0$ for which $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+O(1)$ near $a$; moreover, if $c\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+C$ for all $z$ outside a Lebesgue null set in some neighborhood of $a$, then $
u (u,a)\geq c$. The Lelong number does not change under a holomorphic change of coordinates, nor under the addition of a bounded function, provided the resulting function is plurisubharmonic. Proof. We may assume $a=0$. Let $R_*\in (0,\infty ]$ be the supremum of the radii $r$ for which $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$; since closed balls are compact, $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain exactly when $0<r<R_*$. For such $r$ put $S(r)=\sup _{|z|=r}u(z)$. This number is less than $+\infty $ because $u$ is upper semicontinuous and hence bounded above on the compact sphere. It is also greater than $-\infty $. Otherwise, for every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)$, which is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, would be $-\infty $ on the circle $|\zeta |=r$ and hence, by upper semicontinuity, have upper limits $-\infty $ there; the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)+k$ for every $k>0$, would give $u=-\infty $ on the disc. Thus $u$ would be identically $-\infty $ on $B(0,r)$, which is impossible because $u$ is locally integrable (theorem 8.2.1 ). Let $0<r_1<r_2<r_3<R_*$, and let $h(\zeta )=A+B\log |\zeta |^2$ be the harmonic function on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $ equal to $S(r_1)$ on $|\zeta |=r_1$ and to $S(r_3)$ on $|\zeta |=r_3$. For every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-h(\zeta )$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed annulus $r_1\leq |\zeta |\leq r_3$, and by upper semicontinuity its upper limits at the two boundary circles are at most $0$; by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) it is at most $0$ on the annulus. Taking the supremum over $e$ on the circle $|\zeta |=r_2$ gives $S(r_2)\leq h(r_2)$. Since $h(r_2)$ is the value at $\log r_2^2$ of the affine function of $\log r^2$ that equals $S(r_1)$ and $S(r_3)$ at $\log r_1^2$ and $\log r_3^2$, this says that $S$ is a convex function of $\log r^2$ on $(0,R_*)$. Applying the maximum principle in the same way to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-S(r)$ on the disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, we obtain $u(\zeta e)\leq S(r)$ for $|\zeta |\leq r$; hence $S$ is nondecreasing and $u(0)\leq S(r)$. A finite convex function on an open interval is continuous, since on a compact subinterval its difference quotients are bounded between two fixed difference quotients taken outside the subinterval. Hence $\sup _{B(0,r)}u=\sup _{ho <r}S(ho )=S(r)$, so that $N(t)=S(\mathrm e^{t/2})$ for $t<\log R_*^2$; this proves the assertions about $N$. Fix $r_0$ as in the statement and put $t_0=\log r_0^2$. Since $N$ is convex and nondecreasing on $(-\infty ,t_0]$, the difference quotients $(N(t_0)-N(t))/(t_0-t)$ are nonnegative and decrease as $t\downarrow -\infty $; let $c\in [0,\infty )$ be their limit. Proposition 12.1.1 . Let $n\geq 1$ and let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a\in \mathbb C^ n$. For sufficiently negative $t$ put \[  N(t)=\sup _{|z-a|<\exp (t/2)}u(z).  \] Then $N$ is finite, nondecreasing and convex, $N(t)$ is also the supremum of $u$ over the sphere $|z-a|=\exp (t/2)$, and the limit 12.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-growth-definition} 
u (u,a)=\lim _{t	o -\infty } rac{N(t)}{t} \end{equation} exists in $[0,\infty )$; it is zero if $u(a)>-\infty $. For every $r_0>0$ such that $\overline{B(a,r_0)}$ lies in the domain of $u$, 12.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-attained-growth} u(z)\leq 
u (u,a)\log  rac{|z-a|^2}{r_0^2} +\sup _{B(a,r_0)}u,\qquad 0<|z-a|<r_0. \end{equation} Consequently $
u (u,a)$ is the largest $c\geq 0$ for which $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+O(1)$ near $a$; moreover, if $c\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+C$ for all $z$ outside a Lebesgue null set in some neighborhood of $a$, then $
u (u,a)\geq c$. The Lelong number does not change under a holomorphic change of coordinates, nor under the addition of a bounded function, provided the resulting function is plurisubharmonic. Proof. We may assume $a=0$. Let $R_*\in (0,\infty ]$ be the supremum of the radii $r$ for which $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$; since closed balls are compact, $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain exactly when $0<r<R_*$. For such $r$ put $S(r)=\sup _{|z|=r}u(z)$. This number is less than $+\infty $ because $u$ is upper semicontinuous and hence bounded above on the compact sphere. It is also greater than $-\infty $. Otherwise, for every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)$, which is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, would be $-\infty $ on the circle $|\zeta |=r$ and hence, by upper semicontinuity, have upper limits $-\infty $ there; the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)+k$ for every $k>0$, would give $u=-\infty $ on the disc. Thus $u$ would be identically $-\infty $ on $B(0,r)$, which is impossible because $u$ is locally integrable (theorem 8.2.1 ). Let $0<r_1<r_2<r_3<R_*$, and let $h(\zeta )=A+B\log |\zeta |^2$ be the harmonic function on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $ equal to $S(r_1)$ on $|\zeta |=r_1$ and to $S(r_3)$ on $|\zeta |=r_3$. For every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-h(\zeta )$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed annulus $r_1\leq |\zeta |\leq r_3$, and by upper semicontinuity its upper limits at the two boundary circles are at most $0$; by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) it is at most $0$ on the annulus. Taking the supremum over $e$ on the circle $|\zeta |=r_2$ gives $S(r_2)\leq h(r_2)$. Since $h(r_2)$ is the value at $\log r_2^2$ of the affine function of $\log r^2$ that equals $S(r_1)$ and $S(r_3)$ at $\log r_1^2$ and $\log r_3^2$, this says that $S$ is a convex function of $\log r^2$ on $(0,R_*)$. Applying the maximum principle in the same way to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-S(r)$ on the disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, we obtain $u(\zeta e)\leq S(r)$ for $|\zeta |\leq r$; hence $S$ is nondecreasing and $u(0)\leq S(r)$. A finite convex function on an open interval is continuous, since on a compact subinterval its difference quotients are bounded between two fixed difference quotients taken outside the subinterval. Hence $\sup _{B(0,r)}u=\sup _{ho <r}S(ho )=S(r)$, so that $N(t)=S(\mathrm e^{t/2})$ for $t<\log R_*^2$; this proves the assertions about $N$. Fix $r_0$ as in the statement and put $t_0=\log r_0^2$. Since $N$ is convex and nondecreasing on $(-\infty ,t_0]$, the difference quotients $(N(t_0)-N(t))/(t_0-t)$ are nonnegative and decrease as $t\downarrow -\infty $; let $c\in [0,\infty )$ be their limit. Writing $N(t)=N(t_0)-(t_0-t)\cdot  rac{N(t_0)-N(t)}{t_0-t}$ and dividing by $t$, we obtain $N(t)/t	o c$ as $t	o -\infty $. In particular $c$ does not depend on $t_0$, so for every fixed $s\leq t_0$ the quotients $(N(s)-N(s'))/(s-s')$ also tend to $c$ as $s'	o -\infty $. If $s'<s<t\leq t_0$, convexity gives $(N(t)-N(s))/(t-s)\geq (N(s)-N(s'))/(s-s')$; letting $s'	o -\infty $, we see that every difference quotient of $N$ on $(-\infty ,t_0]$ is at least $c$. Hence $N(t)-ct$ is nondecreasing, and $N(t)\leq c(t-t_0)+N(t_0)$ for $t<t_0$. Since $u(z)\leq S(|z|)=N(\log |z|^2)$, this is ( 12.2 ). Since $u(0)\leq S(r)$ for all $r$, we have $N(t)\geq u(0)$, hence $N(t)/t\leq u(0)/t$ for $t<0$, and $c=0$ if $u(0)>-\infty $. Conversely, if $c'\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c'\log |z|^2+C$ for $0<|z|<r'$, then $N(t)=S(\mathrm e^{t/2})\leq c't+C$ for all sufficiently negative $t$, and division by $t<0$ gives $c\geq c'$. This proves the characterization of $
u (u,a)$ as the largest admissible coefficient. Now let $c\geq 0$, and suppose that $u(z)\leq c\log |z|^2+C$ for all $z\in B(0,r)\setminus A$, where $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$ and $A$ is a Lebesgue null set. Let $0<|z|<r/2$ and $0<\delta <|z|/2$. The function $u$ is subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ), so theorem 3.1.3 gives $u(z)\leq |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}\int _{B(z,\delta )}u\, \mathrm dV$. Every $y\in B(z,\delta )\setminus A$ satisfies $u(y)\leq c\log (|z|+\delta )^2+C$, because $c\geq 0$ and $|y|\leq |z|+\delta $; since $A$ is a null set, we obtain $u(z)\leq c\log (|z|+\delta )^2+C$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$, we get $u(z)\leq c\log |z|^2+C$ for $0<|z|<r/2$, and the converse part of the characterization gives $
u (u,0)\geq c$. Let $F$ be a biholomorphic map from a neighborhood of $a$ onto a neighborhood of $F(a)$; by proposition 8.2.3 , $u\circ F^{-1}$ is plurisubharmonic near $F(a)$. The maps $F$ and $F^{-1}$ are continuously differentiable, hence Lipschitz near $a$ and $F(a)$, so $\log |F(z)-F(a)|^2-\log |z-a|^2$ is bounded near $a$, $z
eq a$. Since adding a bounded function also changes $u$ by a bounded amount, in both cases the characterization just proved shows that the Lelong number is unchanged. $\square$

Definition 12.1.2 . The number $
u (u,a)$ in ( 12.1 ) is the Lelong number of $u$ at $a$. If $u$ is plurisubharmonic on a complex manifold $X$ that has positive dimension at $a$, we compute $

u (u,a)$, where $u$ is a plurisubharmonic potential of $T$ near $a$, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T$. Such potentials exist, and two of them differ near $a$ by a smooth pluriharmonic function: by theorem 8.2.1 , the plurisubharmonic potentials of $T$ on a coordinate ball are exactly its canonical local potentials, to which theorem 7.3.2 applies. Since a smooth function is bounded near $a$, $

title: Theorem 12.1.3 (Jensen–Lelong)
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Theorem 12.1.3 (Jensen–Lelong) . Let $n\geq 1$, $R>0$, and let $u$ be plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset \mathbb C^ n$. Then the spherical mean $M_ u(a,r)$ of $u$ over $\partial B(a,r)$ is finite for every $0<r<R$, the function $r\mapsto D_ u(a,r)$ is nondecreasing on $(0,R)$, and 12.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:euclidean-jensen-lelong} M_ u(a,r_2)-M_ u(a,r_1) =\int _{\log r_1^2}^{\log r_2^2}D_ u(a,\exp (t/2))\, \mathrm dt, \qquad 0<r_1<r_2<R. \end{equation} In particular, 12.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-density-limit} 
u (u,a)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0}D_ u(a,r) =\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{M_ u(a,r)}{\log r^2}. \end{equation} Proof. Step 1: smooth functions. Suppose first that $u$ is smooth. By proposition 2.1.1 in $\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the substitution $r=\mathrm e^{t/2}$, for which $\mathrm dr/\mathrm dt=r/2$, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2}) = rac r2\cdot  rac{\mu (B(a,r))}{s_{2n-1}r^{2n-1}} =D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2}),  \] and ( 12.4 ) follows by integration, since $\mu =\Delta u\, \mathrm dV$ has a continuous density, so that the right side is continuous in $t$. To see that $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing, we show that $t\mapsto M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is a convex function on $(-\infty ,\log R^2)$; the derivative of a differentiable convex function is nondecreasing. For a unit vector $\omega \in S^{2n-1}$, the function $v_\omega (\zeta )=u(a+\zeta \omega )$ is smooth on a neighborhood of the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq R$ in $\mathbb C$, and by ( 7.5 ) its Laplacian is \[  \Delta v_\omega (\zeta )=4\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}(a+\zeta \omega )\, \omega _ j ar\omega _ k\geq 0,  \] because the complex Hessian of the smooth plurisubharmonic function $u$ is positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 (1)). Let $m_\omega (r)=(2\pi )^{-1}\int _0^{2\pi }v_\omega (r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })\, \mathrm d	heta $ be the circle means of $v_\omega $ about $0$; they are the spherical means of $v_\omega $ in $\mathbb R^2$, because surface measure on the unit circle is arc length (section 6.4 ). By proposition 2.1.1 in $\mathbb R^2$, where $s_1=2\pi $, and the same substitution, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}m_\omega (\mathrm e^{t/2})= rac1{4\pi }\int _{|\zeta |<\mathrm e^{t/2}}\Delta v_\omega \, \mathrm dV_2,  \] which is nondecreasing in $t$ because $\Delta v_\omega \geq 0$. By the mean value theorem, a differentiable function with nondecreasing derivative is convex; so $t\mapsto m_\omega (\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is convex. Surface measure on $S^{2n-1}$ is invariant under the orthogonal transformations $\omega \mapsto \mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega $ of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ (section 2.1 ), so $\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(a+r\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega )=\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(a+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega )$ for every $	heta $. Averaging over $	heta \in [0,2\pi ]$ and using Fubini's theorem for the continuous integrand, we obtain \[  M_ u(a,r)= rac1{s_{2n-1}}\int _{S^{2n-1}}m_\omega (r)\, \mathrm dS(\omega ),\qquad 0<r<R.  \] An average of convex functions is convex, so $t\mapsto M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is convex, and $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing on $(0,R)$. Step 2: approximation. For general $u$, let $u_\varepsilon =u*ho _\varepsilon $ be the regularizations of ( 3.3 ). For small $\varepsilon $ they are defined on a neighborhood of the compact set $\overline{B(a,R)}$, and by proposition 8.2.2 (2) they are smooth and plurisubharmonic there and decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Subtracting a constant, which changes neither side of ( 12.4 ), nor $D_ u$, nor the Lelong number, we may assume $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ on $\overline{B(a,R)}$ for all small $\varepsilon $. For $0\leq \eta <1$ put $\kappa _\eta =(1-\eta )/(1+\eta )^{2n-1}$. If $0<r<R$ and $|x-a|\leq \eta r$, the explicit formula ( 2.14 ) shows that the Poisson kernel $P$ of $B(a,r)$ satisfies $P(x,\zeta )\geq \kappa _\eta P(a,\zeta )=\kappa _\eta /(s_{2n-1}r^{2n-1})$ for $\zeta \in \partial B(a,r)$. Fix $0<r<R$ and choose $b\in B(a,r)$ with $u(b)>-\infty $, which is possible since the pole set of $u$ has measure zero; let $\eta =|b-a|/r$. By the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied to $u_\varepsilon $ minus the Poisson integral of its boundary values (theorem 2.3.1 ), we have $u_\varepsilon (x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u_\varepsilon (\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ for $x\in B(a,r)$. At $x=b$, since $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$, this gives \[  u(b)\leq u_\varepsilon (b)\leq \kappa _\eta M_{u_\varepsilon }(a,r).  \] Thus the integrals of the nonnegative functions $-u_\varepsilon $ over the sphere are bounded independently of $\varepsilon $. As $-u_\varepsilon $ increases to $-u$, the monotone convergence theorem shows that $M_ u(a,r)$ is finite and $M_{u_\varepsilon }(a,r)	o M_ u(a,r)$. For fixed $x\in B(a,r)$ the kernel $P(x,\cdot )$ is positive and bounded on $\partial B(a,r)$, so the same argument, applied to the functions $-P(x,\cdot )u_\varepsilon $, lets us pass to the limit in the Poisson inequality, and we obtain $u(x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ for $x\in B(a,r)$. Since the functions $u_\varepsilon $ decrease to the locally integrable function $u$, the monotone convergence theorem, applied to $u_{\varepsilon _0}-u_\varepsilon $ for a fixed $\varepsilon _0$, shows that $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; hence the positive measures $\Delta u_\varepsilon $ converge to $\mu $ in the sense of distributions, hence vaguely (proposition 1.5.1 ). By proposition 1.5.2 , $\Delta u_\varepsilon (B(a,r))	o \mu (B(a,r))$ for every radius $r$ with $\mu (\partial B(a,r))=0$; since the spheres $\partial B(a,r)$, $0<r<R$, are disjoint and $\mu $ is finite on $B(a,R)$, only countably many radii are excluded (lemma 1.1.5 ). Moreover, if $r_2<R$ and $\chi \in C^\infty _ c$ is a cutoff function with values in $[0,1]$, equal to one on $B(a,r_2)$, with support in a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a,R)}$ on which all $u_\varepsilon $ with small $\varepsilon $ are defined, then $\Delta u_\varepsilon (B(a,r_2))\leq \int \chi \, \Delta u_\varepsilon 	o \int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu $, so these masses are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $. By Step 1 each $D_{u_\varepsilon }(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing; letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we see that $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing on the dense set of radii with $\mu (\partial B(a,r))=0$, and hence on $(0,R)$, because $r\mapsto \mu (B(a,r))$ is left continuous. Finally, ( 12.4 ) holds for each $u_\varepsilon $ by Step 1. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, its left side converges to $M_ u(a,r_2)-M_ u(a,r_1)$, while the integrands on the right converge for all but countably many $t$ and are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $; dominated convergence gives ( 12.4 ) for $u$. Step 3: the limits. The nondecreasing nonnegative function $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ has a limit $\ell =\lim _{r\downarrow 0}D_ u(a,r)\in [0,\infty )$. Put $g(t)=M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ and fix $t_0<\log R^2$. Given $\delta >0$, choose $s_\delta <\min \{ t_0,0\} $ with $D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{s/2})\leq \ell +\delta $ for $s\leq s_\delta $. For $t<s_\delta $, ( 12.4 ) and the monotonicity of $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ give \[  \ell (t_0-t)\leq g(t_0)-g(t)\leq (\ell +\delta )(s_\delta -t)+(t_0-s_\delta )D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t_0/2}).  \] Dividing by $-t>0$ and letting $t	o -\infty $, we see that all limit points of $g(t)/t$ lie in $[\ell ,\ell +\delta ]$. Hence $M_ u(a,r)/\log r^2	o \ell $ as $r\downarrow 0$. It remains to show that $\ell =
u (u,a)$. Let $0<\eta <1$. For $x\in B(a,\eta r)$, the Poisson inequality of Step 2 and the kernel bound give, since $u\leq 0$, \[  u(x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta ) \leq \kappa _\eta M_ u(a,r).  \] Together with $M_ u(a,r)\leq \sup _{\partial B(a,r)}u=N(\log r^2)$, where $N$ is as in proposition 12.1.1 , we obtain \[  N(\log (\eta ^2r^2))\leq \kappa _\eta M_ u(a,r), \qquad M_ u(a,r)\leq N(\log r^2).  \] We divide by $\log r^2<0$ and let $r\downarrow 0$. Since $\log (\eta ^2r^2)/\log r^2	o 1$, this gives $
u (u,a)\geq \kappa _\eta \ell $ and $\ell \geq 
u (u,a)$. Letting $\eta \downarrow 0$, so that $\kappa _\eta 	o 1$, we conclude that $\ell =
u (u,a)$, which proves ( 12.5 ). $\square$

title: 12.2 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
12.2 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability From now on $X$ denotes a complex manifold, and $n\geq 0$ its dimension at the point under consideration. We also narrow a term of chapter 11 : a weight on $X$ is now a plurisubharmonic function on $X$, a special case of the measurable weights of section 11.3 ; in particular, a weight is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $X$. Restrictions of weights to submanifolds may be identically $-\infty $ on some components, and definition 12.2.5 allows this case. Local integrability on $X$ refers to Lebesgue measure in holomorphic charts, or equivalently to any smooth positive volume form, since the densities of two such measures with respect to each other are bounded above and below by positive constants on compact subsets of a chart. To pass from a Hilbert space of holomorphic functions to a coherent ideal sheaf we need two facts from local algebra, the Krull intersection theorem and the strong Noetherian property of coherent sheaves. We prove them first, the second by induction on the dimension with the help of Weierstrass polynomials. Lemma 12.2.1 . Let $x\in X$, let $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and let $E$ be a submodule of a finitely generated $R$-module $F$. Then \[   igcap _{k\geq 1}(E+\mathfrak m^ kF)=E.  \] In particular, if a sequence of holomorphic functions on a neighborhood of $x$ converges locally uniformly and the germs at $x$ of all its members belong to an ideal $J\subset R$, then the germ of the limit belongs to $J$. Proof. We derive the intersection formula from the Artin–Rees lemma, after collecting the facts about Noetherian rings that we need. A commutative ring $A$ is Noetherian if all its ideals are finitely generated. Let $A$ be Noetherian. (i) Every submodule $N$ of $A^ r$, $r\geq 1$, is finitely generated. For $r=1$ this is the definition. Let $r\geq 2$. The last coordinates of the elements of $N$ form an ideal of $A$; choose $v_1,\ldots ,v_ q\in N$ whose last coordinates generate it, and, by induction on $r$, finitely many generators of the submodule $N\cap (A^{r-1}	imes \{ 0\} )$, which is a submodule of $A^{r-1}$. If $v\in N$, subtracting from $v$ a combination of the $v_ i$ with the same last coordinate leaves an element of $N\cap (A^{r-1}	imes \{ 0\} )$; hence these finitely many elements generate $N$. (ii) Every submodule $N$ of a finitely generated $A$-module $M$ is finitely generated. Indeed, let $\pi \colon A^ r	o M$ map the standard basis to generators of $M$. By (i), the submodule $\pi ^{-1}(N)$ of $A^ r$ is finitely generated, and the images of its generators generate $N=\pi (\pi ^{-1}(N))$. (iii) The polynomial ring $A[t]$ is Noetherian (Hilbert's basis theorem). Let $I\subset A[t]$ be a nonzero ideal. The leading coefficients of the nonzero elements of $I$, together with $0$, form an ideal of $A$: if $f,g\in I$ have degrees $d\leq e$ and leading coefficients $a,b$ with $a+b
eq 0$, then $t^{e-d}f+g\in I$ has leading coefficient $a+b$, and if $c\in A$ with $ca
eq 0$, then $cf\in I$ has leading coefficient $ca$. Choose $p_1,\ldots ,p_ k\in I$ whose leading coefficients generate this ideal, and let $d_0$ be the largest of their degrees. If $f\in I$ has degree $d\geq d_0$, its leading coefficient is $\sum _ ia_ ic_ i$ for some $a_ i\in A$, where $c_ i$ is the leading coefficient of $p_ i$, and $f-\sum _ ia_ it^{d-\deg p_ i}p_ i$ is an element of $I$ of smaller degree. Repeating this, we see that $f$ differs from an element of $I\cap (A+At+\cdots +At^{d_0-1})$ by an element of the ideal generated by $p_1,\ldots ,p_ k$. The set $I\cap (A+At+\cdots +At^{d_0-1})$ is a submodule of the $A$-module $A+At+\cdots +At^{d_0-1}\cong A^{d_0}$, finitely generated by (i). Hence $I$ is generated by $p_1,\ldots ,p_ k$ and finitely many further elements. (iv) If $I\subset A$ is an ideal, then $A/I$ is Noetherian, since the ideals of $A/I$ are the images of the ideals of $A$ containing $I$. Hence, by (iii) and induction on the number of variables, every quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over $A$ is Noetherian.
