In general, the graph $\Gamma =\{ (x,f(x))\} $ is a complex submanifold of $X\times Y$, since in local coordinates $(x,y)$ the functions $(x,y-f(x))$ are holomorphic coordinates in which $\Gamma =\{ y-f(x)=0\} $; and $\iota (x)=(x,f(x))$ is a biholomorphism of $X$ onto $\Gamma $. The projection $q\colon X\times Y\to Y$ is a submersion, so $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ q)=q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y}$ by the first case. Since $\varphi \circ q\circ \iota =\varphi \circ f$, ( 12.14 ) applied to $\Gamma $ gives $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)\subset (q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y})|_\Gamma ^{\mathrm{im}}$ after transport by $\iota $. The right side is generated by the functions $g\circ q\circ \iota =g\circ f$ with $g$ a local section of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, so it equals $f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X$. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.4.3
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Proposition 12.4.3 . Every multiplier ideal is integrally closed: if a germ $F\in \mathcal O_{X,x}$ satisfies an equation $F^ d+a_1F^{d-1}+\cdots +a_ d=0$ with $a_ j\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x^ j$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. More explicitly, if $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ and a holomorphic germ $F$ satisfies $|F|\leq C(\sum _ j|g_ j|^2)^{1/2}$ near $x$ for a constant $C$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. Proof. The second assertion is immediate, since $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\leq C^2\sum _ j|g_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ near $x$. For the first, choose generators $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ (theorem 12.2.7 ), representatives of the $g_ j$, of $F$ and of the $a_ j$ on a common neighborhood, and put $|g|=(\sum _ j|g_ j|^2)^{1/2}$. Each $a_ j$ is a finite sum of products of $j$ generators with holomorphic coefficients, which are bounded on a smaller neighborhood; hence $|a_ j|\leq C_ j|g|^ j$ there. At a point where $|g|>0$, put $\lambda =|F|/|g|$. Dividing the equation by $|g|^ d$ gives $\lambda ^ d\leq \sum _ jC_ j\lambda ^{d-j}$, which forces $\lambda \leq C$ with $C=\max \{ 1,\sum _ jC_ j\} $. At a point where $|g|=0$, all the $a_ j$ vanish, so $F^ d=0$ and $F=0$. Thus $|F|\leq C|g|$ near $x$, and the second assertion applies. $\square$

Let $(\psi _ j)_{j\geq 1}$ be an increasing sequence of weights on $X$ that converges almost everywhere to a weight $\varphi $. Then at every $x\in X$, 12.18  egin{equation} \label{eq:monotone-multiplier-stability}  igcup _ j\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x, \end{equation} and $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ for all sufficiently large $j$; the required index may depend on $x$ and on the sequence. Proof. Since the $\psi _ j$ increase to $\varphi $ almost everywhere, $\psi _ j\leq \varphi $ almost everywhere. The plurisubharmonic functions $\max \{ \psi _ j,\varphi \} $ and $\varphi $ therefore agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere by theorem 8.2.1 ; that is, $\psi _ j\leq \varphi $ everywhere. Consequently $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )$ for every $j$, and the left side of ( 12.18 ) is contained in the right side. We prove the reverse inclusion by induction on the dimension $n$ of $X$ at $x$. If $n=0$, all the weights are finite at $x$ and all the ideals equal $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. Let $n\geq 1$, assume the theorem in dimension $n-1$, and take $x=0$ in a coordinate chart. Now lemma 12.5.2 gives $c|a_ i|^{-2}\leq 8C_0R^2G(a_ i)$ for all large $i$, contradicting $|a_ i|^2G(a_ i)	o 0$. Hence $F\in J$, which proves ( 12.18 ). Finally, $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ is generated by finitely many germs, which by ( 12.18 ) all lie in $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x$ for one index $j$. Then $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x\subset \mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x$, and equality holds for this and every later index, since the ideals increase and are contained in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. $\square$ Corollary 12.5.4 (Strong openness) . Let $\varphi $ and $\chi $ be weights on $X$, and let $x\in X$. Then 12.19  egin{equation} \label{eq:strong-openness} \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x= igcup _{\varepsilon >0} \mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )_ x \end{equation} and, more generally, \[  \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x= igcup _{\varepsilon >0} \mathcal I(\varphi +\varepsilon \chi )_ x.  \] Moreover, there is a single $\varepsilon >0$ with $\mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$, and similarly a single $\varepsilon >0$ with $\mathcal I(\varphi +\varepsilon \chi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. Proof. The assertions are local. On a relatively compact neighborhood of $x$ the weights are bounded above, and subtracting constants we may assume $\varphi \leq 0$ and $\chi \leq 0$ there; this changes $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi $ and $\varphi +\varepsilon \chi $ only by bounded amounts and hence changes none of the ideals. Then $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi $ and $\varphi +\varepsilon \chi $ decrease as $\varepsilon $ increases, so the corresponding ideals decrease with $\varepsilon $ and are contained in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. The sequences $(1+1/j)\varphi $ and $\varphi +\chi /j$ increase with $j$ and converge to $\varphi $ wherever $\varphi $ and $\chi $ are finite, hence almost everywhere. By theorem 12.5.3 , $\mathcal I((1+1/j)\varphi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ and $\mathcal I(\varphi +\chi /j)_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ for all large $j$, which proves both assertions. $\square$ Example 12.5.5 . Let $c\geq 0$ and $\varphi =c\log |z|^2$ on a disc around $0\in \mathbb C$, where $\varphi =0$ if $c=0$. A germ of order $k$ at $0$ is $z^ k$ times a unit, so by polar coordinates it belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ if and only if $\int _0^ rt^{2k-2c+1}\, \mathrm dt<\infty $, that is, $k+1>c$. Hence $\mathcal I(\varphi )=(z^{\lfloor cfloor })$. When $c$ is a positive integer, the germ $z^{c-1}$ just fails, because the radial integral diverges logarithmically. This strict threshold shows why theorem 12.5.3 concerns increasing sequences: on the unit disc, the weights $\varphi _ j=(1-1/j)\log |z|^2$, $j\geq 2$, decrease to $\log |z|^2$, yet $\mathcal I(\varphi _ j)=\mathcal O$ for every $j$, whereas $\mathcal I(\log |z|^2)=(z)$.

Lemma 12.5.2 . Let $q\geq 1$, and let $\gamma (t)=(t^ q,\gamma _2(t),\ldots ,\gamma _ n(t))$ be a holomorphic map from a disc around $0\in \mathbb C$ to $\mathbb C^ n$ with $\gamma (0)=0$, for instance a map as in lemma 12.5.1 . Let $\Omega =\Delta _ R	imes P\subset \mathbb C	imes \mathbb C^{n-1}$, where $\Delta _ R=\{ |z_1|<R\} $, $R>0$, and $P$ is a polydisc centered at $0$, and let $F$ be holomorphic on $\Omega $ with $F(\gamma (t))
eq 0$ for small $t
eq 0$. Then there are $r,c>0$, depending only on $\gamma $, $F$ and $\Omega $, with the following property. If $0<|a|<r$ and $H\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ satisfies \[  H(a,\cdot )=F(a,\cdot )	ext{ on }P,\qquad (H/F)\circ \gamma 	ext{ is holomorphic at }0	ext{ with value }0,  \] then 12.17  egin{equation} \label{eq:curve-extension-norm-lower-bound} \int _\Omega |H|^2\, \mathrm dV\geq c|a|^{-2}. \end{equation} For $n=1$, the polydisc $P$ is a point and carries counting measure. Proof. We bound the norm of $H$ from below by a weighted norm of $H\circ \gamma $ on a disc, and then use that $H\circ \gamma =F\circ \gamma $ at the points $t$ with $t^ q=a$. Choose $ho >0$ with $ho ^ q<R$ such that $\gamma $ is defined on a neighborhood of the closed disc $|t|\leq ho $, $F\circ \gamma $ has no zeros for $0<|t|\leq ho $, and, since $\gamma $ is continuous with $\gamma (0)=0$, $(\gamma _2(t),\ldots ,\gamma _ n(t))$ lies in a fixed polydisc $P'\Subset P$ centered at $0$ for $|t|\leq ho $. Let $\delta >0$ be half the distance from $P'$ to the complement of $P$. For $0<|z_1|<ho ^ q$, each of the $q$ points $\gamma (t)$ with $t^ q=z_1$ has the form $(z_1,w)$ with $w\in P'$, and ( 12.9 ) for the holomorphic function $H(z_1,\cdot )$ on the ball $B(w,\delta )\subset P$ gives $|H(z_1,w)|^2\leq C_\delta \int _ P|H(z_1,w')|^2\, \mathrm dV(w')$, where $C_\delta ^{-1}$ is the volume of a ball of radius $\delta $ in $\mathbb C^{n-1}$. Summing over the $q$ points, we obtain $\sum _{t^ q=z_1}|H(\gamma (t))|^2\leq qC_\delta \int _ P|H(z_1,w')|^2\, \mathrm dV(w')$. Now we integrate over $|z_1|<ho ^ q$. The map $t\mapsto t^ q$ maps each of the $q$ half-open sectors $\{ 0<|t|<ho ,\  2\pi k/q\leq \arg t<2\pi (k+1)/q\} $ bijectively onto the punctured disc $0<|z_1|<ho ^ q$, and on the interior of the sector it is a diffeomorphism onto the complement of a ray, with real Jacobian $|qt^{q-1}|^2$. By the change of variables formula, applied on each sector, $\int _{|t|<ho }\Phi (t)q^2|t|^{2q-2}\, \mathrm dV_2(t)=\int _{|z_1|<ho ^ q}\sum _{t^ q=z_1}\Phi (t)\, \mathrm dV_2(z_1)$ for every nonnegative measurable $\Phi $. Since $\Delta _{ho ^ q}	imes P\subset \Omega $, it follows that \[  \int _\Omega |H|^2\, \mathrm dV \geq c_0\int _{|t|<ho }|H(\gamma (t))|^2 q^2|t|^{2q-2}\, \mathrm dV_2(t)  \] with $c_0=1/(qC_\delta )$. If $n=1$, the same inequality holds with $c_0=1/q$, without the submean step. Write $F\circ \gamma (t)=t^ mv(t)$ with an integer $m\geq 0$ and $v$ without zeros on $|t|\leq ho $, and put $h=(H/F)\circ \gamma $. This function is holomorphic for $0<|t|<ho $, because $F\circ \gamma $ has no zeros there, and by hypothesis it extends holomorphically across $0$ with $h(0)=0$; thus $h(t)=\sum _{\ell \geq 1}h_\ell t^\ell $ for $|t|<ho $. Then $H\circ \gamma =t^ mvh$, and $|v|$ is bounded below by a positive constant on the compact disc $|t|\leq ho $, being continuous and without zeros there. On each circle $|t|=s<ho $ the power series of $h$ converges uniformly, and the monomials $t^\ell $ are orthogonal there, so $\int _0^{2\pi }|h(s\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })|^2\, \mathrm d	heta =2\pi \sum _\ell |h_\ell |^2s^{2\ell }$. Integrating in polar coordinates and using the monotone convergence theorem, we obtain \[  \int _\Omega |H|^2\, \mathrm dV \geq c_1\sum _{\ell \geq 1}  rac{|h_\ell |^2ho ^{2(\ell +m+q)}}{\ell +m+q}  \] with $c_1=\pi q^2c_0\min _{|t|\leq ho }|v(t)|^2$. eq 0$; hence $h(b)=1$. The average $q^{-1}\sum _{b^ q=a}b^\ell $ equals $a^{\ell /q}$ if $q$ divides $\ell $ and $0$ otherwise, so averaging $h$ over these roots gives $\sum _{j\geq 1}h_{qj}a^ j=1$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, \[  1\leq c_1^{-1}\| H\| _{L^2(\Omega )}^2 \sum _{j\geq 1} rac{(qj+m+q)|a|^{2j}}{ho ^{2(qj+m+q)}}.  \] If $|a|\leq ho ^ q/2$, the last sum equals $ho ^{-2(m+q)}\sum _{j\geq 1}(qj+m+q)x^ j$ with $x=|a|^2ho ^{-2q}\leq 1/4$, and this series is at most a constant times $x$. title: Theorem 12.5.3

text:
Theorem 12.5.3 . Let $(\psi _ j)_{j\geq 1}$ be an increasing sequence of weights on $X$ that converges almost everywhere to a weight $\varphi $. Then at every $x\in X$, 12.18  egin{equation} \label{eq:monotone-multiplier-stability}  igcup _ j\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x, \end{equation} and $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ for all sufficiently large $j$; the required index may depend on $x$ and on the sequence. Proof. Since the $\psi _ j$ increase to $\varphi $ almost everywhere, $\psi _ j\leq \varphi $ almost everywhere. The plurisubharmonic functions $\max \{ \psi _ j,\varphi \} $ and $\varphi $ therefore agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere by theorem 8.2.1 ; that is, $\psi _ j\leq \varphi $ everywhere. Consequently $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )$ for every $j$, and the left side of ( 12.18 ) is contained in the right side. We prove the reverse inclusion by induction on the dimension $n$ of $X$ at $x$. If $n=0$, all the weights are finite at $x$ and all the ideals equal $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. Let $n\geq 1$, assume the theorem in dimension $n-1$, and take $x=0$ in a coordinate chart. We argue by contradiction, extending a germ that is missing from $ igcup _ j\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_0$ from slices $\{ z_1=a_ i\} $ with $a_ i	o 0$, as outlined at the beginning of this section. Step 1: reduction to a curve. The union $J= igcup _ j\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_0$ is an ideal, because the ideals increase with $j$. By proposition A.1.2 it is generated by finitely many germs $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$, $k\geq 0$, and these all belong to $\mathcal I(\psi _{j_0})_0$ for some $j_0$. Suppose, to reach a contradiction, that some $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ does not belong to $J$; in particular $F
eq 0$. Choose representatives of $F$ and of the $g_ l$ on a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ on which $|g_ l|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _{j_0}}$ and $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ are integrable. If $|F|\leq C|g|$, with $|g|=(\sum _ l|g_ l|^2)^{1/2}$, held on a neighborhood of $0$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\psi _{j_0})_0\subset J$ by proposition 12.4.3 ; so no such bound holds. Lemma 12.5.1 now provides linear coordinates and a curve $\gamma (t)=(t^ q,\gamma _2(t),\ldots ,\gamma _ n(t))$ such that $F\circ \gamma $ has no zeros for small $t
eq 0$ and each $(g_ l/F)\circ \gamma $ extends holomorphically with value $0$ at $t=0$. In these coordinates choose polydiscs $\Delta _{R_0}	imes P_0\Subset U$ and $\Omega =\Delta _ R	imes P\Subset \Delta _{R_0}	imes P_0$ centered at $0$, and let $r,c>0$ be the constants of lemma 12.5.2 for $\gamma $, $F$ and $\Omega $. Subtracting the same constant from $\varphi $ and all $\psi _ j$, we may assume that $\varphi \leq 0$ on $\Delta _{R_0}	imes P_0$; then also $\psi _ j\leq 0$ there. Step 2: choice of slices. By Fubini's theorem, the function \[  G(a)=\int _{P_0}|F(a,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (a,w)}\, \mathrm dV_ w  \] is integrable on $\Delta _{R_0}$. Hence, given any null set $N\subset \Delta _{R_0}$, there is a sequence of points $a_ i
otin N$, $a_ i
eq 0$, with $a_ i	o 0$ and $|a_ i|^2G(a_ i)	o 0$; otherwise $G(a)\geq c'|a|^{-2}$ for almost every $a$ in some punctured disc around $0$, and $G$ would not be integrable. We take for $N$ the union of three sets: the set where $G=\infty $; the set of $a$ for which one of the countably many functions $\varphi (a,\cdot )$, $\psi _ j(a,\cdot )$ is identically $-\infty $ on $P_0$; and the set of $a$ for which $\psi _ j(a,\cdot )	o \varphi (a,\cdot )$ fails on a subset of $P_0$ of positive measure. The first set is null because $G$ is integrable, and the other two are null by Fubini's theorem, because pole sets of weights have measure zero and $\psi _ j	o \varphi $ almost everywhere. Then the functions $\psi _ j(a_ i,\cdot )$ and $\varphi (a_ i,\cdot )$ are weights on $P_0$ (proposition 8.2.3 ), and the former increase to the latter almost everywhere on $P_0$. Moreover $G(a_ i)>0$ for all large $i$, because $F(a_ i,\cdot )$ does not vanish identically on $P_0$: for small $|a_ i|$, the slice $\{ a_ i\} 	imes P_0$ contains the points $\gamma (b)$ with $b^ q=a_ i$, at which $F
eq 0$. Discarding finitely many terms, we assume that this holds for all $i$. Step 3: integrability on a fixed inner slice. Fix $i$. Since $G(a_ i)<\infty $, the germ of $F(a_ i,\cdot )$ at every point of $P_0$ belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi (a_ i,\cdot ))$. By the induction hypothesis, applied on $P_0$, each point of the compact set $\overline P\subset P_0$ has a neighborhood on which $|F(a_ i,\cdot )|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _ j(a_ i,\cdot )}$ is integrable for some $j$. Covering $\overline P$ by finitely many such neighborhoods and using that the $\psi _ j$ increase, we find one index $j$ for which $\int _ P|F(a_ i,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _ j(a_ i,w)}\, \mathrm dV_ w<\infty $. For larger $j$ these integrands decrease and converge almost everywhere to $|F(a_ i,\cdot )|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (a_ i,\cdot )}$, so by dominated convergence their integrals over $P$ converge to a number at most $G(a_ i)$. Since $G(a_ i)>0$, we can choose an index $j_ i$ with \[  \int _ P|F(a_ i,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _{j_ i}(a_ i,w)}\, \mathrm dV_ w \leq 2G(a_ i).  \] The polydisc $P$ does not depend on $i$; this is what makes the estimates of the next step uniform. Step 4: extension and contradiction. For large $i$ we have $|a_ i|<\min \{ r,R\} $, so that the normal coordinate $z_1-a_ i$ takes values in a disc of radius $2R$ on $\Omega $. The polydisc $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex by corollary 11.2.5 , being a product of discs, each of which is a sublevel set of a function $|\zeta -\zeta _0|^2$ on $\mathbb C$. Applying theorem 11.4.4 , after reordering the coordinates, with the normal coordinate $z_1-a_ i$, the radius $2R$ and the weight $\psi _{j_ i}$, and using the last display of Step 3, we obtain $H_ i\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $H_ i(a_ i,\cdot )=F(a_ i,\cdot )$ on $P$ and \[  \int _\Omega |H_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _{j_ i}}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8C_0R^2G(a_ i),  \] where $C_0$ is the absolute constant of that theorem. In particular the germ of $H_ i$ at $0$ lies in $\mathcal I(\psi _{j_ i})_0\subset J$, so $H_ i=\sum _ lb_ lg_ l$ near $0$ with holomorphic $b_ l$, and $(H_ i/F)\circ \gamma =\sum _ l(b_ l\circ \gamma )\cdot (g_ l/F)\circ \gamma $ extends holomorphically across $t=0$ with value $0$. Since $\psi _{j_ i}\leq 0$, the last display also bounds $\int _\Omega |H_ i|^2\, \mathrm dV$. Now lemma 12.5.2 gives $c|a_ i|^{-2}\leq 8C_0R^2G(a_ i)$ for all large $i$, contradicting $|a_ i|^2G(a_ i)	o 0$. Hence $F\in J$, which proves ( 12.18 ). Finally, $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ is generated by finitely many germs, which by ( 12.18 ) all lie in $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x$ for one index $j$. Then $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x\subset \mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x$, and equality holds for this and every later index, since the ideals increase and are contained in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. $\square$

title: Corollary 12.5.4 (Strong openness)
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Corollary 12.5.4 (Strong openness) . Let $\varphi $ and $\chi $ be weights on $X$, and let $x\in X$. Then 12.19 \begin{equation} \label{eq:strong-openness} \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x=\bigcup _{\varepsilon >0} \mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )_ x \end{equation} and, more generally, \[  \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x=\bigcup _{\varepsilon >0} \mathcal I(\varphi +\varepsilon \chi )_ x.  \] Moreover, there is a single $\varepsilon >0$ with $\mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$, and similarly a single $\varepsilon >0$ with $\mathcal I(\varphi +\varepsilon \chi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. Proof. The assertions are local. On a relatively compact neighborhood of $x$ the weights are bounded above, and subtracting constants we may assume $\varphi \leq 0$ and $\chi \leq 0$ there; this changes $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi $ and $\varphi +\varepsilon \chi $ only by bounded amounts and hence changes none of the ideals. Then $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi $ and $\varphi +\varepsilon \chi $ decrease as $\varepsilon $ increases, so the corresponding ideals decrease with $\varepsilon $ and are contained in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. The sequences $(1+1/j)\varphi $ and $\varphi +\chi /j$ increase with $j$ and converge to $\varphi $ wherever $\varphi $ and $\chi $ are finite, hence almost everywhere. By theorem 12.5.3 , $\mathcal I((1+1/j)\varphi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ and $\mathcal I(\varphi +\chi /j)_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ for all large $j$, which proves both assertions. $\square$

title: Example 12.5.5
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Example 12.5.5 . Let $c\geq 0$ and $\varphi =c\log |z|^2$ on a disc around $0\in \mathbb C$, where $\varphi =0$ if $c=0$. A germ of order $k$ at $0$ is $z^ k$ times a unit, so by polar coordinates it belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ if and only if $\int _0^ rt^{2k-2c+1}\, \mathrm dt<\infty $, that is, $k+1>c$. Hence $\mathcal I(\varphi )=(z^{\lfloor c\rfloor })$. When $c$ is a positive integer, the germ $z^{c-1}$ just fails, because the radial integral diverges logarithmically. This strict threshold shows why theorem 12.5.3 concerns increasing sequences: on the unit disc, the weights $\varphi _ j=(1-1/j)\log |z|^2$, $j\geq 2$, decrease to $\log |z|^2$, yet $\mathcal I(\varphi _ j)=\mathcal O$ for every $j$, whereas $\mathcal I(\log |z|^2)=(z)$.

text:
12.6 Birational change of variables and logarithmic thresholds On a modification of $X$, the change of variables formula turns membership in a multiplier ideal into an integrability condition twisted by the Jacobian (proposition 12.6.4 ), which becomes explicit on a log resolution. Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map between complex manifolds of dimension $n$. Thus there is a nowhere dense analytic subset $A\subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense in $Y$ and $\pi $ maps $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$ biholomorphically onto $X\setminus A$ (section A.3 ). In local coordinates $w$ on $Y$ and $z$ on $X$, the complex Jacobian determinant $J_\pi =\det (\partial z_ i/\partial w_ j)$ is holomorphic, and it does not vanish identically on any nonempty open set, since it has no zeros on the dense open set $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$. By the chain rule, a change of coordinates on either side multiplies $J_\pi $ by a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function; equivalently, $\pi ^*(\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n)=J_\pi \, \mathrm dw_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dw_ n$. Hence the functions $J_\pi $ are the local equations of an effective Cartier divisor $K_{Y/X}$ on $Y$ (section A.5 ), the relative canonical divisor , and $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$ is generated locally by $J_\pi ^{-1}$. We measure the vanishing of holomorphic functions along hypersurfaces as follows. Let $E\subset Y$ be a prime divisor, that is, an irreducible hypersurface. By corollary A.2.13 , applied to the family consisting of $E$ alone, its regular locus $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a connected manifold, dense in $E$. Let $p\in E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, choose coordinates $w=(w_1,w')$ at $p$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ near $p$, and let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$. The order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ is the supremum, in $\{ 0,1,2,\ldots \} \cup \{ +\infty \} $, of the integers $k\geq 0$ such that $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$, that is, $h=w_1^ kh_1$ near $p$ with $h_1$ holomorphic. By the next lemma, it does not depend on the coordinates, and for a function defined near $E$ it does not depend on the point of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Lemma 12.6.1 . Let $E$ be a prime divisor on a complex manifold $Y$, let $p\in E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, let $w=(w_1,w')$ be holomorphic coordinates at $p$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ near $p$, and let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$. Let $\Delta =\Delta _1	imes \Delta '$ be a polydisc centered at $p$, where $\Delta _1$ is a disc in the $w_1$-plane, so small that $E\cap \Delta =\{ w_1=0\} \cap \Delta $ and that ( 7.1 ) gives the expansion \[  h=\sum _{l\geq 0}a_ l(w')w_1^ l\quad 	ext{on }\Delta ,\qquad a_ l(w')= rac1{l!}\partial _{w_1}^ lh(0,w'),  \] where the functions $a_ l$ are holomorphic on $\Delta '$. Let $k\geq 0$ be an integer. If $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near some point of $E\cap \Delta $, then $a_ l=0$ for all $l<k$; conversely, if $a_ l=0$ for all $l<k$, then $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$. In particular, a holomorphic function that vanishes on $E$ near $p$ is divisible by $w_1$ near $p$, and if $	ilde w=(	ilde w_1,	ilde w')$ are other coordinates at $p$ with $E=\{ 	ilde w_1=0\} $ near $p$, then $	ilde w_1$ is a unit times $w_1$ near $p$. The order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ does not depend on the coordinates. It is the smallest $l$ with $a_ l
eq 0$, and it is $+\infty $ if and only if $h$ vanishes near $p$. In particular, $h$ is not divisible by $w_1$ near $p$ if and only if $h(0,\cdot )$ does not vanish identically near $p$. Moreover, the order of $h$ along $E$ is the same at all points of $E\cap \Delta $. For $q\in E\cap N$ we have $|w_1|\leq |w-q|$, so $m\varphi \circ \pi (w)\leq k\log |w-q|^2+C''$ near $q$, and proposition 12.1.1 , proposition 12.1.4 give $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,q)\geq k/m$. Since the generic value $

u (\varphi ,E)\geq k$. Dividing ( 12.28 ) by $m$ and letting $m	o \infty $ gives the limit formula. $\square$ Theorem 12.6.9 . Necessity, even with strict inequality, is proposition 12.6.7 . eq 0$. We compare $\varphi $ with a weight $\varphi _ m$ with analytic singularities defined by generators of $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$, apply theorem 12.6.5 to a multiple of $\varphi _ m$, and then return to $\varphi $. Put $\lambda =1+\varepsilon /2$ and choose an integer $m\geq 2$ with $\lambda \geq m/(m-1)$, that is, $(m-1)\lambda \geq m$. On a bounded polydisc $\Omega \subset V$ around $x$ on which $\varphi $ is bounded above, choose $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal H_{m\varphi }(\Omega )$ generating $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ near $x$, and put \[  \varphi _ m= rac1m\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2.  \] This is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.3.3 , since $\mathcal I(m\varphi )_ x
eq 0$ by lemma 12.3.1 , so that the $g_ i$ do not all vanish identically. By ( 12.11 ), $\varphi \leq \varphi _ m+C_ m$ on a neighborhood $W\subset V$ of $x$. Pulling this back to a smooth model and using the characterization of Lelong numbers in proposition 12.1.1 at every point, we see that $

u (\varphi ,E)$ for every prime divisor $E$ over an open subset of $W$. Hence, for every prime divisor $E$ over an open neighborhood of $x$ contained in $W$ whose center contains $x$, \[  \operatorname {ord}_ E f+A_ X(E)\geq (1+\varepsilon )
u (\varphi ,E)\geq (1+\varepsilon )

u (\varphi _ m,E)>0$ because $1+\varepsilon >\lambda $, and when $
u (\varphi _ m,E)=0$ because the left side is at least $A_ X(E)\geq 1$. Now let $\pi \colon Y	o W'$ be a log resolution of the ideal $(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$ over an open neighborhood $W'\subset W$ of $x$, with $(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)\mathcal O_ Y=\mathcal O_ Y(-D)$ and $D=\sum _ id_ iE_ i$. Let $q\in E_ i$, and choose coordinates $w$ at $q$ as before ( 12.22 ), so that the components of $D$ through $q$ are coordinate hyperplanes and $E_ i=\{ w_ i=0\} $. By ( 12.22 ), $\log \sum _ l|g_ l\circ \pi |^2=\sum _ jd_ j\log |w_ j|^2+O(1)\leq d_ i\log |w_ i|^2+C$ near $q$, where $j$ runs over the components through $q$; since $|w_ i|\leq |w-q|$, the characterization in proposition 12.1.1 gives $
u (\varphi _ m\circ \pi ,q)\geq d_ i/m$. If $q$ lies on no other component of $D$, then $\varphi _ m\circ \pi =(d_ i/m)\log |w_ i|^2+O(1)$ near $q$, and $
u (\varphi _ m\circ \pi ,q)=d_ i/m$ by proposition 12.1.4 . Such points exist, because $E_ i$ is not contained in the union of the other components of the support of $D$ (corollary A.2.13 ). Hence $
u (\varphi _ m,E_ i)=d_ i/m$. Every component $E_ i$ meeting $\pi ^{-1}(x)$ has a center containing $x$, so the strict inequality above reads $\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}f+A_ X(E_ i)>(\lambda /m)d_ i$ for these components, and theorem 12.6.5 , applied on $W'$ to the weight $\lambda \varphi _ m$ with $c=\lambda /m$ and $b=0$, gives $f\in \mathcal I(\lambda \varphi _ m)_ x$. It remains to pass from $\lambda \varphi _ m$ to $\varphi $. By the definition of the generators, 12.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-generator-exponential-integrability} \mathrm e^{m(\varphi _ m-\varphi )} =\sum _ i|g_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-m\varphi }\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}} \end{equation} near $x$. Shrinking the neighborhood and subtracting a constant from $\varphi _ m$, we may assume $\varphi _ m\leq 0$; this multiplies the functions in question by constants and changes none of the integrability statements. We split a small neighborhood of $x$ into the set where $\varphi \geq \lambda \varphi _ m$ and its complement, ignoring the null set formed by the poles of $\varphi $ and the common zeros of the $g_ i$, so that all exponents below are finite. On the first set, $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\leq |f|^2\mathrm e^{-\lambda \varphi _ m}$, which is integrable because $f\in \mathcal I(\lambda \varphi _ m)_ x$. On the complement we have $(m-1)\varphi <(m-1)\lambda \varphi _ m$, since $m\geq 2$; as $(m-1)\lambda \geq m$ and $\varphi _ m\leq 0$, it follows that \[  (m-1)\varphi -m\varphi _ m \leq ((m-1)\lambda -m)\varphi _ m\leq 0,  \] and therefore \[  |f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi } =|f|^2\mathrm e^{m(\varphi _ m-\varphi )} \mathrm e^{(m-1)\varphi -m\varphi _ m} \leq C\mathrm e^{m(\varphi _ m-\varphi )},  \] where $C$ is a local bound for $|f|^2$. By ( 12.30 ) the right side is integrable near $x$. Hence $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is integrable near $x$, that is, $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. $\square$ Example 12.6.10 . Let $c>0$ and $\varphi =c\log |z_1|^2$ on a polydisc in $\mathbb C^ n$. The ideal $(z_1)$ is already principal with smooth zero set, so the identity map is a log resolution, with $D=E=\{ z_1=0\} $, $d=1$ and $A_ X(E)=1$. By theorem 12.6.5 , a germ $f$ lies in $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ if and only if $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef+1>c$. Here the log resolution has no exceptional divisors, and the only condition comes from the non-exceptional component $E$; this is why theorem 12.6.5 involves all components of $D$ meeting the fiber, exceptional or not. For the blowup $\pi $ of the origin in dimension $n\geq 2$, consider the chart $z_1=w_1$, $z_ j=w_1w_ j$ for $j>1$ of proposition A.5.3 . The Jacobian matrix $(\partial z_ i/\partial w_ j)$ is lower triangular with diagonal entries $1,w_1,\ldots ,w_1$, so $J_\pi =w_1^{n-1}$, and the exceptional divisor $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ has $A_ X(E)=n$. Let $f$ be holomorphic near $0$ with homogeneous expansion $f=\sum _{k\geq k_0}P_ k$ and $P_{k_0}
eq 0$. Then $f\circ \pi (w)=\sum _{k\geq k_0}w_1^ kP_ k(1,w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)=w_1^{k_0}g(w)$ for small $w_1$ and bounded $(w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)$, where $g(0,w')=P_{k_0}(1,w')$; this polynomial is not identically zero, since $P_{k_0}(z)=z_1^{k_0}P_{k_0}(1,z_2/z_1,\ldots ,z_ n/z_1)$ for $z_1
eq 0$. Hence $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef=\operatorname {ord}_0f$. For $\varphi =c\log |z|^2$, this blowup is a log resolution of the maximal ideal, with $D=E$ and $d=1$, by proposition A.5.3 , so theorem 12.6.5 gives $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ if and only if $\operatorname {ord}_0f+n>c$. This agrees with a direct computation in polar coordinates: since $|f(z)|\leq C|z|^{k_0}$ near $0$ by ( 7.2 ), and $\int _{S^{2n-1}}|f(t\omega )|^2\, \mathrm dS(\omega )\geq c't^{2k_0}$ for small $t>0$, with $c'>0$, by ( 12.10 ), the integral of $|f|^2|z|^{-2c}$ over a small ball $B(0,r)$ is finite if and only if $\int _0^ rt^{2k_0-2c+2n-1}\, \mathrm dt<\infty $, by ( 2.1 ), that is, if and only if $k_0+n>c$.

title: Lemma 12.6.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Lemma 12.6.1 . Let $E$ be a prime divisor on a complex manifold $Y$, let $p\in E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, let $w=(w_1,w')$ be holomorphic coordinates at $p$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ near $p$, and let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$. Let $\Delta =\Delta _1	imes \Delta '$ be a polydisc centered at $p$, where $\Delta _1$ is a disc in the $w_1$-plane, so small that $E\cap \Delta =\{ w_1=0\} \cap \Delta $ and that ( 7.1 ) gives the expansion \[  h=\sum _{l\geq 0}a_ l(w')w_1^ l\quad 	ext{on }\Delta ,\qquad a_ l(w')= rac1{l!}\partial _{w_1}^ lh(0,w'),  \] where the functions $a_ l$ are holomorphic on $\Delta '$. Let $k\geq 0$ be an integer. If $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near some point of $E\cap \Delta $, then $a_ l=0$ for all $l<k$; conversely, if $a_ l=0$ for all $l<k$, then $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$. In particular, a holomorphic function that vanishes on $E$ near $p$ is divisible by $w_1$ near $p$, and if $	ilde w=(	ilde w_1,	ilde w')$ are other coordinates at $p$ with $E=\{ 	ilde w_1=0\} $ near $p$, then $	ilde w_1$ is a unit times $w_1$ near $p$. The order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ does not depend on the coordinates. It is the smallest $l$ with $a_ l
eq 0$, and it is $+\infty $ if and only if $h$ vanishes near $p$. In particular, $h$ is not divisible by $w_1$ near $p$ if and only if $h(0,\cdot )$ does not vanish identically near $p$. Moreover, the order of $h$ along $E$ is the same at all points of $E\cap \Delta $. If $h$ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $E$, then its order along $E$ is the same at all points of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Orders add under products: if $g$ is also holomorphic near $p$, then the order of $hg$ along $E$ at $p$ is the sum of the orders of $h$ and $g$. Proof. (1) If $h=w_1^ kh_1$ near a point $(0,w'_0)$ of $E\cap \Delta $, with $h_1$ holomorphic, then the Leibniz rule gives $\partial _{w_1}^ lh(0,w')=0$ for $l<k$ and $w'$ near $w'_0$; so $a_ l=0$ near $w'_0$, and hence on the connected set $\Delta '$ by the identity theorem. Conversely, if $a_ l=0$ for $l<k$, then $h=w_1^ k\sum _{l\geq k}a_ lw_1^{l-k}$ near $p$; the last series is obtained from the Taylor series of $h$ at $p$ by lowering the exponent of $w_1$ in each term by $k$, so it converges on the same polydiscs and defines a holomorphic function (section A.1 ). If $h$ vanishes on $E$ near $p$, then $a_0=h(0,\cdot )$ vanishes near the center of $\Delta '$, hence on $\Delta '$, and the case $k=1$ shows that $h$ is divisible by $w_1$ near $p$. Applying this to $	ilde w_1$, and to $w_1$ with the roles of the two coordinate systems exchanged, we obtain $	ilde w_1=c\, w_1$ and $w_1=	ilde c\, 	ilde w_1$ near $p$ with holomorphic $c$ and $	ilde c$. Then $c	ilde c=1$ off $E$; since the continuous function $c	ilde c$ equals $1$ on the dense set $\{ w_1
eq 0\} $, it equals $1$ near $p$, and $c$ is a unit. (2) By (1), $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$ if and only if it is divisible by $	ilde w_1^ k$ near $p$, so the order does not depend on the coordinates. Let $k_0$ be the smallest $l$ with $a_ l
eq 0$, and $k_0=+\infty $ if all $a_ l$ vanish. By (1), $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$ if and only if $k\leq k_0$, so the order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ is $k_0$. If all $a_ l$ vanish, then $h=0$ on $\Delta $; conversely, if $h$ vanishes near $p$, then all $a_ l$ vanish near the center of $\Delta '$, hence on $\Delta '$. The case $k_0=0$ gives the assertion about $h(0,\cdot )=a_0$, because $a_0$ vanishes identically on $\Delta '$ if and only if it vanishes near the center of $\Delta '$. Finally, let $q=(0,w'_ q)\in E\cap \Delta $. The coordinates $w$ are also coordinates at $q$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ near $q$, and by their formula the coefficients of the expansion of $h$ on a small polydisc centered at $q$ are the restrictions of the same functions $a_ l$. Since $\Delta '$ is connected, $a_ l$ vanishes near $w'_ q$ if and only if it vanishes on $\Delta '$, by the identity theorem. Hence the orders of $h$ along $E$ at $q$ and at $p$ are equal. (3) By the last assertion of (2), the order of $h$ along $E$ is a locally constant function on $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, which is connected (corollary A.2.13 ). Hence it is constant. (4) Shrinking $\Delta $, we may assume that $g$ is defined on $\Delta $; let $b_ j$ and $e_ m$ be the coefficients of the expansions of $g$ and $hg$ on $\Delta $. By the Leibniz rule, $e_ m=\sum _{i+j=m}a_ ib_ j$. If $h$ or $g$ has infinite order, then $hg$ vanishes near $p$ and has infinite order by (2). Otherwise let $k$ and $l$ be the orders of $h$ and $g$. Then $e_ m=0$ for $m<k+l$, because each term $a_ ib_ j$ with $i+j<k+l$ has $i<k$ or $j<l$, and $e_{k+l}=a_ kb_ l$. Since $a_ k$ and $b_ l$ are not identically zero and the ring of holomorphic functions on the connected set $\Delta '$ is an integral domain, by the identity theorem, $e_{k+l}
eq 0$. By (2), the order of $hg$ is $k+l$. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.6.2
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Lemma 12.6.2 . Let $w$ be holomorphic coordinates centered at a point $p$ of a complex manifold, let $0\leq \ell \leq n$, and let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$, not identically zero near $p$, with zero set near $p$ contained in $\{ w_1\cdots w_\ell =0\} $. For $i\leq \ell $ let $k_ i$ be the largest integer such that $h$ is divisible by $w_ i^{k_ i}$ near $p$. Then $h=u\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{k_ i}$ near $p$, with $u$ holomorphic and $u(p)
eq 0$. Moreover, a holomorphic function near $p$ that is divisible by $w_ i^{a_ i}$ near $p$ for each $i\leq \ell $ is divisible by $\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{a_ i}$. Proof. Let $g=\sum _\alpha c_\alpha w^\alpha $ be the power series at $p$ of a holomorphic function, as in ( 7.1 ). If $g=w_ i^ ag'$ near $p$, then multiplying the series of $g'$ by $w_ i^ a$ shows that $c_\alpha =0$ whenever $\alpha _ i<a$. Conversely, if $c_\alpha =0$ whenever $\alpha _ i<a_ i$ for some $i\leq \ell $, then $g=\prod _ iw_ i^{a_ i}\cdot \sum _\alpha c_\alpha w^{\alpha -\sum _ ia_ ie_ i}$, where $e_ i$ is the $i$th unit vector, and the last series converges on the same polydiscs as that of $g$. This proves the last assertion, and it shows that $k_ i<\infty $, since otherwise all $c_\alpha $ of $h$ would vanish. Hence $h=u\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{k_ i}$ with $u$ holomorphic near $p$, and $u$ is not divisible by any $w_ i$, $i\leq \ell $, by the maximality of $k_ i$. It remains to show that $u(p)
eq 0$. Suppose, to the contrary, that $u(p)=0$. The zero set of $u$ near $p$ lies in that of $h$, hence in $\{ w_1\cdots w_\ell =0\} $; so $\ell \geq 1$. We work in the coordinates $w$, with $p=0$. Let $P$ be the first nonzero homogeneous term of $u$; it has positive degree $m$. Choose $v\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $P(v)
eq 0$ and $v_ i
eq 0$ for all $i$, which is possible since the polynomial $P(v)v_1\cdots v_ n$ is not identically zero. Then $t\mapsto u(tv)$ has a zero of order $m$ at $t=0$; choose $\varepsilon >0$ such that it has no other zeros in $|t|\leq \varepsilon $, and such that all points $y+tv$ considered below lie in the neighborhood of $0$ where the hypothesis on the zero set holds. Since $(y,t)\mapsto u(y+tv)$ is continuous and does not vanish on the compact set $\{ 0\} 	imes \{ |t|=\varepsilon \} $, there is a connected neighborhood $N$ of $0$ such that $u(y+tv)
eq 0$ for $y\in N$ and $|t|=\varepsilon $. By the argument principle, the number of zeros of $t\mapsto u(y+tv)$ in $|t|<\varepsilon $, counted with multiplicity, is \[   rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|t|=\varepsilon } rac{\partial _ t[u(y+tv)]}{u(y+tv)}\, \mathrm dt,  \] a continuous integer-valued function of $y\in N$; it equals $m\geq 1$ at $y=0$, hence everywhere on $N$. So for every $y\in N$ there is $t$ with $u(y+tv)=0$, and then $y_ i+tv_ i=0$ for some $i\leq \ell $, that is, $u(\sigma _ i(y))=0$ for the linear projection $\sigma _ i(y)=y-(y_ i/v_ i)v$ onto the hyperplane $H_ i=\{ y_ i=0\} $. Hence the product of the holomorphic functions $u\circ \sigma _ i$, $i\leq \ell $, vanishes on $N$. If none of them vanished identically on $N$, each would be nonzero on a dense open subset of $N$, by the identity theorem, and so would be their product. Thus some $u\circ \sigma _ i$ vanishes on $N$; since $\sigma _ i(y)=y$ for $y\in H_ i$, the function $u$ vanishes on $H_ i\cap N$, which is a neighborhood of $0$ in $H_ i$. By the first paragraph, applied with $a=1$, $u$ is then divisible by $w_ i$ near $0$: all coefficients $c_\alpha $ of $u$ with $\alpha _ i=0$ vanish, since they are the coefficients of the restriction of $u$ to $H_ i$. This contradiction shows that $u(p)
eq 0$. $\square$

title: Definition 12.6.3
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Definition 12.6.3 . Let $E\subset Y$ be a prime divisor. Its center on $X$ is $\pi (E)$, which is an analytic subset of $X$ by theorem A.6.2 ; it is connected, because $E$ is. Let $f$ be a holomorphic function on an open set $V\subset X$ containing the center, and let $V_0$ be the connected component of $V$ containing it. If $f$ vanishes identically on $V_0$, for instance if $f=0$, we set $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef=+\infty $. Otherwise $f\circ \pi $ does not vanish identically on any nonempty open subset of $\pi ^{-1}(V_0)$, because such a set contains a nonempty open set mapped biholomorphically onto an open subset of $V_0$, on which $f$ does not vanish identically by the identity theorem; since $E\subset \pi ^{-1}(V_0)$, the order of $f$ along $E$ is $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef=\operatorname {ord}_ E(f\circ \pi )<\infty $. This order along a divisor differs from the order at a point of proposition 12.1.4 , although the two agree for the exceptional divisor of the blowup of a point (example 12.6.10 ). For a holomorphic germ $f$ at a point $x$, this defines $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef$ for the prime divisors $E$ on smooth models of open neighborhoods of $x$ on which $f$ is defined; this is how orders of germs enter the results below. The log discrepancy of $E$ is \[  A_ X(E)=1+\operatorname {ord}_ E K_{Y/X},  \] where $\operatorname {ord}_ EK_{Y/X}=\operatorname {ord}_ EJ_\pi $ is the coefficient of $E$ in $K_{Y/X}$. Since $J_\pi $ is holomorphic, $A_ X(E)\geq 1$, and a prime divisor on $X$ itself, with $\pi $ the identity, has log discrepancy one. The center, the order and the log discrepancy depend only on the prime divisor over $X$ represented by $E$.

title: Proposition 12.6.4
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Proposition 12.6.4 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$, $x\in X$, and $f\in \mathcal O_{X,x}$. Then $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ if and only if, near every point of the compact fiber $\pi ^{-1}(x)$, the function 12.20 \begin{equation} \label{eq:birational-weighted-integrand} |f\circ \pi |^2|J_\pi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi \circ \pi } \end{equation} is integrable with respect to Lebesgue measure in local coordinates on $Y$. Moreover, $\pi _*\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})=\mathcal O_ X$: if $U\subset X$ is open, then every section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$, that is, every function that is locally of the form $g/J_\pi $ with $g$ holomorphic, equals $f\circ \pi $ for a unique $f\in \mathcal O(U)$. Under this identification 12.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-birational-transform} \mathcal I(\varphi ) =\pi _*\bigl (\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )\bigr ), \end{equation} where $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$ is the sheaf of functions that are locally of the form $g/J_\pi $ with $g$ a section of $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$. Proof. By proposition A.7.3 , $\pi $ is biholomorphic over $X\setminus S$ for an analytic subset $S\subset X$ of codimension at least two; in particular $S$ is nowhere dense. The analytic subset $\pi ^{-1}(S)$ of $Y$ is nowhere dense as well, because every nonempty open subset of $Y$ contains a nonempty open set that $\pi $ maps biholomorphically onto an open subset of $X$, and such a set is not contained in $S$. Near each of their points, nowhere dense analytic subsets lie in the zero set of a holomorphic function that does not vanish identically on a connected neighborhood (section A.1 ); so $S$ and $\pi ^{-1}(S)$ are Lebesgue null sets in charts, by lemma 7.4.1 . In holomorphic coordinates the real Jacobian determinant of $\pi $, that is, the factor by which $\pi ^*$ multiplies the volume form $\mathrm dx_1\wedge \mathrm dy_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dx_ n\wedge \mathrm dy_ n$, is $|J_\pi |^2$. Indeed, since $\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j=\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$, this form equals $c_ n\, \mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ n$ with $c_ n=(\mathrm i/2)^ n(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$, the sign coming from moving each $\mathrm dz_ j$ to the left past $\mathrm d\bar z_1,\ldots ,\mathrm d\bar z_{j-1}$, and similarly in the coordinates $w$. Since $\pi ^*(\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n)=J_\pi \, \mathrm dw_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dw_ n$ and the conjugate identity holds for the $\mathrm d\bar z_ j$, the claim follows. The change of variables formula for nonnegative measurable functions, applied to the biholomorphism $\pi $ from $W\setminus \pi ^{-1}(S)$ onto its image, therefore gives \[  \int _{\pi (W\setminus \pi ^{-1}(S))}g\, \mathrm dV_ z =\int _ W(g\circ \pi )|J_\pi |^2\, \mathrm dV_ w  \] for every nonnegative measurable $g$ and every open set $W$ in a coordinate chart of $Y$ that is mapped into a coordinate chart of $X$, with $J_\pi $ computed in these coordinates. Now suppose that $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is integrable on a coordinate neighborhood $V$ of $x$. Applying the formula with $g=|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ to small coordinate neighborhoods $W\subset \pi ^{-1}(V)$, we see that ( 12.20 ) is integrable near every point of $\pi ^{-1}(V)$. Conversely, suppose that ( 12.20 ) is integrable near every point of $\pi ^{-1}(x)$, where $f$ is defined on a coordinate neighborhood $V_0$ of $x$. Cover the compact fiber by finitely many coordinate neighborhoods $W_1,\ldots ,W_ k\subset \pi ^{-1}(V_0)$ on which it is integrable. Since $\pi $ is proper, $\pi (Y\setminus (W_1\cup \cdots \cup W_ k))$ is closed and does not contain $x$, so there is a neighborhood $V\subset V_0$ of $x$ with $\pi ^{-1}(V)\subset W_1\cup \cdots \cup W_ k$. The sets $\pi (W_ l\setminus \pi ^{-1}(S))$ cover $V\setminus S$, and $S$ is a null set, so the formula gives $\int _ V|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\leq \sum _ l\int _{W_ l}|f\circ \pi |^2|J_\pi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi \circ \pi }\, \mathrm dV_ w<\infty $. Next let $U\subset X$ be open and $h$ a section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$; we may assume that $U$ is connected. Over $U\setminus S$ the map $\pi $ is biholomorphic and $J_\pi $ has no zeros, so $h$ is holomorphic on $\pi ^{-1}(U\setminus S)$, and $h=f\circ \pi $ there for the holomorphic function $f=h\circ (\pi |_{\pi ^{-1}(U\setminus S)})^{-1}$ on $U\setminus S$, which is connected by lemma A.1.7 . If $f\not\equiv 0$, the function $\log |f|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $U\setminus S$ (proposition 8.3.3 ), so by corollary A.2.15 it is locally bounded above near $S$; hence $f$ is locally bounded near $S$, and lemma A.1.7 extends $f$ holomorphically to $U$. Locally $h=g/J_\pi $ with $g$ holomorphic, and $g=(f\circ \pi )J_\pi $ on the dense open set $\pi ^{-1}(U\setminus S)$, hence everywhere; so $h=f\circ \pi $. The function $f$ is unique, since it is determined on $U\setminus S$, which is dense in $U$. Finally, let $U\subset X$ be open and $f\in \mathcal O(U)$. Since $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$ is locally generated by $J_\pi ^{-1}$, the function $f\circ \pi $ is a section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ if and only if $(f\circ \pi )J_\pi $ is a section of $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$ there, that is, if and only if ( 12.20 ) is integrable near every point of $\pi ^{-1}(U)$. By the first part, applied at every point of $U$, this holds if and only if $f$ is a section of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ over $U$. Together with the second part, which shows that every section of the right side of ( 12.21 ) over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ has the form $f\circ \pi $, this proves ( 12.21 ). $\square$

title: Theorem 12.6.5
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Theorem 12.6.5 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$ such that near $x$ \[  \varphi =c\log \left(\sum _{j=1}^ r|g_ j|^2\right)+b, \qquad c>0,\quad b\text{ bounded},  \] where the holomorphic functions $g_ j$ generate a nonzero ideal $\mathfrak a$. Let $V$ be an open neighborhood of $x$ on which this holds, and let $\pi \colon Y\to V$ be a log resolution of $\mathfrak a$ (section A.5 ), as supplied by theorem A.5.4 , theorem A.5.5 , with $\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ Y=\mathcal O_ Y(-D)$, where $D=\sum _ id_ iE_ i$ is an effective divisor with simple normal crossings support, the $E_ i$ being prime divisors and the $d_ i$ positive integers. Then a holomorphic function $f$ on $V$ belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ if and only if 12.23 \begin{equation} \label{eq:analytic-strict-valuative-threshold} \operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}f+A_ X(E_ i)>c d_ i \end{equation} for every component $E_ i$ of $D$ that meets $\pi ^{-1}(x)$, exceptional or not. Since $\pi $ restricts to a log resolution of $\mathfrak a$ over every smaller open neighborhood $V'$ of $x$, the criterion applies to every germ at $x$, with the components of the restriction of $D$ to $\pi ^{-1}(V')$ in place of the $E_ i$. Equivalently, with $\lfloor cD\rfloor =\sum _ i\lfloor cd_ i\rfloor E_ i$, near $x$ 12.24 \begin{equation} \label{eq:analytic-multiplier-divisor-formula} \mathcal I(\varphi )=\pi _*\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X}-\lfloor cD\rfloor ). \end{equation} For rational $c$, this computes the multiplier ideals of weights with analytic singularities (chapter 13 ). Proof. Let $p\in \pi ^{-1}(V)$, and choose coordinates $w$ at $p$ as before ( 12.22 ), so that $E_1,\ldots ,E_\ell $ are the components of $D$ through $p$ and $E_ i=\{ w_ i=0\} $ near $p$. Since $b$ is bounded, ( 12.22 ), applied to $\pi \colon Y\to V$, gives \[  \varphi \circ \pi =c\sum _{i=1}^{\ell }d_ i\log |w_ i|^2+O(1)  \] near $p$. Let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$; we decide when $|h|^2\prod _{i\leq \ell }|w_ i|^{-2cd_ i}$, or equivalently $|h|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi \circ \pi }$, is integrable near $p$. Let $k_ i$ be the order of $h$ along $E_ i$ at $p$, which is finite if $h$ does not vanish identically near $p$; if it does, the integrability is trivial and $k_ i=+\infty $. We claim that the integrability holds if and only if $k_ i+1>cd_ i$ for $i=1,\ldots ,\ell $. If these inequalities hold, write $h=\prod _ iw_ i^{k_ i}\tilde h$ with $\tilde h$ holomorphic, by lemma 12.6.2 ; the integrand is at most a constant times $\prod _ i|w_ i|^{2k_ i-2cd_ i}$, which is integrable near $p$ by Fubini's theorem and polar coordinates in each $w_ i$, since $2k_ i-2cd_ i>-2$. Conversely, suppose that $k_1+1\leq cd_1$, say, and write $h=w_1^{k_1}\tilde h$ with $\tilde h$ not divisible by $w_1$. Then $\tilde h$ does not vanish identically on $\{ w_1=0\} $ near $p$, by lemma 12.6.1 (2), so arbitrarily close to $p$ there are an open set $W'$ of points $w'=(w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)$ and $\delta ,\rho >0$ with $|\tilde h(w_1,w')|\geq \delta $ for $|w_1|<\rho $ and $w'\in W'$. There the integrand is at least a positive constant times $|w_1|^{2k_1-2cd_1}$, since the other factors $|w_ i|^{-2cd_ i}$ are bounded below; as $2k_1-2cd_1\leq -2$, its integral in $w_1$ diverges, and by Fubini's theorem the integrand is not integrable near $p$. Now let $f$ be holomorphic on $V$, and apply this to $h=(f\circ \pi )J_\pi $, with $J_\pi $ computed in local coordinates near $p$. The function $f\circ \pi $ is holomorphic on $\pi ^{-1}(V)$, which contains $E_ i$, so its order along $E_ i$ at $p$ is $\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}f$, by lemma 12.6.1 (3) and definition 12.6.3 ; the order of $J_\pi $ along $E_ i$ at $p$ is $\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}J_\pi $. Since orders add under products (lemma 12.6.1 (4)), $k_ i=\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}f+\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}J_\pi =\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}f+A_ X(E_ i)-1$. Thus, for $p\in \pi ^{-1}(x)$, the condition at $p$ is ( 12.23 ) for the components through $p$. As $p$ ranges over $\pi ^{-1}(x)$, these are exactly the components meeting the fiber, and proposition 12.6.4 proves the first assertion. For ( 12.24 ), let $U\subset V$ be open and $f\in \mathcal O(U)$, and put $h=(f\circ \pi )J_\pi $ on $\pi ^{-1}(U)$. For an integer $k$, the strict inequality $k+1>cd_ i$ is equivalent to $k\geq \lfloor cd_ i\rfloor $. By proposition 12.6.4 and the claim, applied at every point $p\in \pi ^{-1}(U)$, we have $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )(U)$ if and only if at every such $p$ the order of $h$ at $p$ along each component $E_ i$ through $p$ is at least $\lfloor cd_ i\rfloor $. By lemma 12.6.2 , this means that $h$ is divisible near every point of $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ by the local equation $\prod _ iw_ i^{\lfloor cd_ i\rfloor }$ of $\lfloor cD\rfloor $, that is, that $f\circ \pi =h/J_\pi $ is a section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X}-\lfloor cD\rfloor )$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$. Since $\lfloor cD\rfloor $ is effective, every section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X}-\lfloor cD\rfloor )$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ is a section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$, and hence of the form $f\circ \pi $ with $f\in \mathcal O(U)$, by proposition 12.6.4 . This proves ( 12.24 ) on $V$. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.6.7
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text: Proposition 12.6.7 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$ and $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. Then there are $\varepsilon >0$ and a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ on which $f$ is defined such that 12.27 \begin{equation} \label{eq:general-necessary-valuative-bound} \operatorname {ord}_ E f+A_ X(E)>(1+\varepsilon )\nu (\varphi ,E) \end{equation} for every prime divisor $E$ over an open subset of $V$; in particular, this holds for every prime divisor over an open neighborhood of $x$ contained in $V$ whose center contains $x$. Proof. By corollary 12.5.4 there are $\varepsilon >0$ and a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ on which $f$ is defined such that $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-(1+\varepsilon )\varphi }$ is integrable on $V$. Let $E$ be a prime divisor over an open set $U\subset V$, represented on a smooth model $\pi \colon Y\to U$; we may assume that $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef<\infty $. Since $f\in \mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )_ y$ for every $y\in U$, proposition 12.6.4 , applied to the weight $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi $ on $U$, shows that $|h|^2\mathrm e^{-(1+\varepsilon )\varphi \circ \pi }$, with $h=(f\circ \pi )J_\pi $, is integrable near every point of $Y$. Let $p\in E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Since orders add under products, the order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ is $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef+\operatorname {ord}_ EJ_\pi =\operatorname {ord}_ Ef+A_ X(E)-1$. By lemma 12.6.6 , applied to the weight $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi \circ \pi $, whose generic Lelong number along $E$ is $(1+\varepsilon )\nu (\varphi ,E)$ by proposition 12.1.4 , we obtain ( 12.27 ). $\square$

text:
Corollary 12.6.8 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$, let $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$, and let $m>0$ be a real number. Then 12.28  egin{equation} \label{eq:divisorial-multiplier-order-bounds} m
u (\varphi ,E)-A_ X(E) <\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(m\varphi ) \leq m
u (\varphi ,E). \end{equation} Here, for a smooth model $\pi \colon Y	o X$ on which $E$ lies, $\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ is the order along $E$ of the pulled-back ideal $\mathcal I(m\varphi )\mathcal O_ Y$, defined as follows. Near a point $p\in E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, let $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ generate $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ near $\pi (p)$. The minimum of the orders of the functions $g_ i\circ \pi $ along $E$ at $p$ does not depend on the choice of generators, since the members of a second system of generators are combinations of the $g_ i$ with holomorphic coefficients near $\pi (p)$, and conversely. This minimum is locally constant along $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, because the orders of the $g_ i\circ \pi $ are, by lemma 12.6.1 (2); hence it is constant on the connected manifold $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and it is $\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(m\varphi )$. As for the order of a function in definition 12.6.3 , it depends only on the prime divisor over $X$ represented by $E$. In particular, \[  
u (\varphi ,E)=\lim _{m	o \infty } rac1m \operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(m\varphi ).  \] Proof. Let $k=\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(m\varphi )$, and choose a point $p\in E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Put $y=\pi (p)$, choose a bounded polydisc $\Omega $ around $y$ in a chart on which $\varphi $ is bounded above, and choose $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal H_{m\varphi }(\Omega )$ generating $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ near $y$ (theorem 12.2.7 (3)). Near $p$, in coordinates $w=(w_1,w')$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $, let $k_ i$ be the order of $g_ i\circ \pi $ along $E$ at $p$, so that $k=\min _ ik_ i$; since $\mathcal I(m\varphi )_ y
eq 0$, this minimum is finite. For the lower bound, choose $i$ with $k_ i=k$. Since $|g_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-m\varphi }$ is integrable on $\Omega $, proposition 12.6.4 , applied to the weight $m\varphi $, shows that $|h|^2\mathrm e^{-m\varphi \circ \pi }$, with $h=(g_ i\circ \pi )J_\pi $, is integrable near $p$. The order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ is $k+A_ X(E)-1$, because orders add under products. By lemma 12.6.6 , applied to the weight $m\varphi \circ \pi $, whose generic Lelong number along $E$ is $m
u (\varphi ,E)$ by proposition 12.1.4 , we obtain $k+A_ X(E)>m
u (\varphi ,E)$. This is the left inequality. For the upper bound, lemma 12.2.8 gives $m\varphi \leq \log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+mC_ m$ on a neighborhood of $y$. Near $p$ we have $g_ i\circ \pi =w_1^{k_ i}u_ i$ with $u_ i$ holomorphic, so $|g_ i\circ \pi |\leq C|w_1|^{k_ i}\leq C|w_1|^ k$ where $|w_1|\leq 1$; it follows that $m\varphi \circ \pi \leq k\log |w_1|^2+C''$ on a neighborhood $N$ of $p$. For $q\in E\cap N$ we have $|w_1|\leq |w-q|$, so $m\varphi \circ \pi (w)\leq k\log |w-q|^2+C''$ near $q$, and proposition 12.1.1 , proposition 12.1.4 give $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,q)\geq k/m$. Since the generic value $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)$ is attained at points of $E$ arbitrarily close to $p$ (proposition 12.3.5 ), we conclude that $m

title: Theorem 12.6.9
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
text:
Theorem 12.6.9 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$, $x\in X$, and $f\in \mathcal O_{X,x}$. Then $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ if and only if there are $\varepsilon >0$ and a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ on which $f$ is defined such that 12.29  egin{equation} \label{eq:uniform-valuative-multiplier-criterion} \operatorname {ord}_ E f+A_ X(E)\geq (1+\varepsilon )
u (\varphi ,E) \end{equation} for every prime divisor $E$ over an open neighborhood of $x$ contained in $V$ whose center contains $x$. The criterion remains valid if $\geq $ is replaced by $>$. For a weight with analytic singularities, theorem 12.6.5 needs instead only the finitely many strict inequalities ( 12.23 ) on one log resolution, without a parameter $\varepsilon $. Proof. Necessity, even with strict inequality, is proposition 12.6.7 . Since the strict condition implies the non-strict one, it suffices to show that the non-strict condition implies $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$; we may assume $f
eq 0$. We compare $\varphi $ with a weight $\varphi _ m$ with analytic singularities defined by generators of $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$, apply theorem 12.6.5 to a multiple of $\varphi _ m$, and then return to $\varphi $. Put $\lambda =1+\varepsilon /2$ and choose an integer $m\geq 2$ with $\lambda \geq m/(m-1)$, that is, $(m-1)\lambda \geq m$. On a bounded polydisc $\Omega \subset V$ around $x$ on which $\varphi $ is bounded above, choose $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal H_{m\varphi }(\Omega )$ generating $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ near $x$, and put \[  \varphi _ m= rac1m\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2.  \] This is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.3.3 , since $\mathcal I(m\varphi )_ x
