Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map from a complex manifold $Y$. Then $Y$ is compact and connected, and $\varphi \mapsto \varphi \circ \pi $ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$, which is continuous for convergence in $L^1(X)$ and $L^1(Y)$, the latter taken with respect to any smooth positive volume form. For every prime divisor $E$ on $Y$, the generic Lelong numbers $
u (\varphi ,E)=
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)$ are bounded above uniformly for $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Proof. The manifold $Y=\pi ^{-1}(X)$ is compact, because $\pi $ is proper. By the definition of bimeromorphic maps (section A.3 ), there is a nowhere dense analytic subset $E_0\subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(E_0)$ is nowhere dense and $\pi $ restricts to an isomorphism of $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(E_0)$ onto $X\setminus E_0$. The set $X\setminus E_0$ is connected by lemma A.1.7 , hence so is its dense preimage, and therefore $Y$ is connected. The image $\pi (Y)$ is closed, since proper maps are closed, and it contains the dense set $X\setminus E_0$; so $\pi $ is surjective. By proposition A.7.3 there is an analytic subset $A\subset X$ of codimension at least two such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$. Then $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is an analytic subset of $Y$ different from $Y$, because $\pi $ is surjective. Since $Y$ is connected, $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is locally contained in the zero set of a holomorphic function that does not vanish identically on a connected neighborhood (section A.1 ), so it is nowhere dense and a null set (lemma 7.4.1 ). The same holds for $A$ in $X$. If $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, let $B$ be a coordinate ball and $h$ a smooth function on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $ (lemma 13.1.2 ). On every connected coordinate neighborhood $W\subset \pi ^{-1}(B)$ the function $(\varphi +h)\circ \pi $ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, by proposition 8.2.3 , and the second case is excluded because $\varphi +h$ is finite almost everywhere on the image under the biholomorphism $\pi $ of the nonempty open set $W\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$. Hence $\varphi \circ \pi =(\varphi +h)\circ \pi -h\circ \pi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, with $\pi ^*	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi \circ \pi )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((\varphi +h)\circ \pi )\geq 0$ on $\pi ^{-1}(B)$. Thus $\varphi \circ \pi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. If $\varphi \circ \pi =\varphi '\circ \pi $, then $\varphi =\varphi '$ on $X\setminus A$, hence almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section; this proves injectivity. Conversely, let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. Over $X\setminus A$ it descends to the function $\psi \circ \pi ^{-1}$, which is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic there. It is bounded above, because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $Y$. On a coordinate ball $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $ on $B$, the plurisubharmonic function $\psi \circ \pi ^{-1}+h$ on $B\setminus A$ is therefore locally bounded above near $A$, and it extends to a plurisubharmonic function on $B$ by theorem 8.4.1 . The extensions on two balls agree outside the null set $A$, hence everywhere, so they define $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. The pullback $\varphi \circ \pi $ equals $\psi $ outside the null set $\pi ^{-1}(A)$, hence everywhere. This proves surjectivity. For continuity, we use proposition 14.2.1 on $X$ and on $Y$; by its last assertion, its assertions for a fixed background hold on $Y$. Let $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. By the continuity of the supremum, it suffices to treat normalized functions, $\sup _ X\varphi _ j=\sup _ X\varphi =0$, since subtracting the suprema preserves $L^1$ convergence. The pullbacks have the same suprema, because $\pi $ is surjective, so they are relatively compact in $L^1(Y)$, and every cluster value lies in $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. On compact subsets of $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$, a change of variables shows that every $L^1$ cluster value of $(\varphi _ j\circ \pi )$ coincides almost everywhere with $\varphi \circ \pi $; since $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is a null set, every cluster value is $\varphi \circ \pi $. A relatively compact sequence in a metric space with a single cluster value converges to it; hence $\varphi _ j\circ \pi 	o \varphi \circ \pi $ in $L^1(Y)$. Finally, $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)$ is the infimum over $y\in E$ of the point Lelong numbers $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y)$. Near $y$ choose a smooth $g$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\pi ^*	heta $, so that the functions $\varphi \circ \pi +g$ are plurisubharmonic. By ( 12.8 ), applied to them, each $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y)$ is upper semicontinuous for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi \circ \pi $, hence, by the continuity just proved, for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi $; and an infimum of upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous. Since Lelong numbers do not change when a constant is added, we may restrict to the normalized functions, which form a compact set by proposition 14.2.1 . An upper semicontinuous function with finite values attains its maximum on a compact set, which gives the uniform bound. $\square$ Corollary 14.2.9 . Let $B'$ be a coordinate ball in $X$ and $B\Subset B'$ a ball in the same coordinates, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be bounded near $\overline{B'}$. There is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\psi \geq \varphi $, $\psi =\varphi $ on $X\setminus B$, $\psi $ bounded near $\overline B$, and $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=0$ on $B$. It is the largest function in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with these properties, and any two functions with these properties that are continuous on $\overline B$ coincide. Proof. Choose a ball $B''$ in the same coordinates with $\overline B\subset B''$ and $\overline{B''}\subset B'$. Write $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $B''$, with $h$ smooth (lemma 13.1.2 ), and apply corollary 9.6.4 to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\varphi +h$ on $B''$. Subtracting $h$ from the result on $B''$ and keeping $\varphi $ outside $B''$ gives $\psi $, since the result equals $\varphi +h$ on $B''\setminus B$; here $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi +h))^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $\psi +h$. If $\psi '$ is another function with the stated properties, then by upper semicontinuity $\varlimsup _{z	o \zeta ,\, z\in B}\psi '(z)\leq \psi '(\zeta )=\varphi (\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. Hence $\psi '+h$ belongs to the family whose upper envelope is $\psi +h$ in corollary 9.6.4 , and $\psi '\leq \psi $ on $B$. If $\psi '$ is continuous on $\overline B$, then its boundary values $\varphi |_{\partial B}$ are continuous, and $\psi '+h$ is the solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem with the continuous boundary values $(\varphi +h)|_{\partial B}$; by the uniqueness in theorem 9.6.3 , any two such continuous functions coincide. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.2.1
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Proposition 14.2.1 . Let $a\leq b$ be real numbers. The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$ is compact in $L^1(X)$, and the map $\varphi \mapsto \sup _ X\varphi $ is continuous on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for the $L^1$ topology. In particular, the functions $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi =0$ are uniformly bounded in $L^1(X)$. The same statements hold for a sequence of backgrounds: if smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ j$ converge smoothly to $\theta $ and $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ satisfy $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$, then a subsequence converges in $L^1(X)$ to some $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ j\to \sup _ X\varphi $ whenever $\varphi _ j\to \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ in $L^1(X)$. The assertions for a fixed background hold more generally on every connected compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension, for every smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta '$ on $X'$, with $L^1(X')$ taken with respect to any smooth positive volume form. Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$ covering $X$, smaller concentric balls $B'_ k$ still covering $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{B_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=\theta $ (lemma 13.1.2 , applied on slightly larger concentric balls). For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ the functions $\varphi +h_ k$ are plurisubharmonic on $B_ k$. Let $(\varphi _ j)$ be a sequence with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$. The plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ are uniformly bounded above on each $B_ k$. Since $\varphi _ j$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$, it attains its supremum at a point $x_ j$, and after passing to a subsequence $x_ j\to x$, since $X$ is compact and metrizable. Choose $k$ with $x\in B'_ k$. On $B_ k$ the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ cannot converge locally uniformly to $-\infty $, because their values at $x_ j$ are bounded below by $a+\inf _{B'_ k}h_ k$ for large $j$. By theorem 8.3.4 , a further subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ k)$. If $B_ l$ meets $B_ k$, the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ l$ cannot tend to $-\infty $ locally uniformly on $B_ l$, since on the nonempty open set $B_ k\cap B_ l$ they differ by the smooth function $h_ l-h_ k$ from a sequence that converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; so again a subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ l)$. Since $X$ is connected, every ball is joined to $B_ k$ by a finite chain of overlapping balls, and after finitely many extractions the sequence converges in $L^1(B'_ l)$ for every $l$, hence in $L^1(X)$, to some $\varphi $. The limit satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ as a distributional limit of positive currents, and its canonical representative belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Now let $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, all in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; we show that $\sup _ X\varphi _ j\to \sup _ X\varphi $. The submean inequality for $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ on small balls shows that the $\varphi _ j$ are uniformly bounded above. Let $x_ j\to x$; we claim that $\varlimsup _ j\varphi _ j(x_ j)\leq \varphi (x)$. Indeed, choose $k$ with $x\in B_ k$, let $c>\varphi (x)$ be real, and use upper semicontinuity to choose a closed ball $K\subset B_ k$ around $x$ on which $\varphi <c$. The function $c+h_ k$ is continuous near $K$ and $\varphi +h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$, so the second part of theorem 8.3.4 gives $\varphi _ j+h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$ for large $j$; hence $\varphi _ j(x_ j)<c$ for large $j$. Choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and points $x_ j$ with $\varphi _ j(x_ j)=\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ converge to some $x$; the claim gives $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq \varphi (x)\leq \sup _ X\varphi $. Conversely, choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and $\sum _ j\| \varphi _ j-\varphi \| _{L^1}<\infty $; by monotone convergence $\sum _ j|\varphi _ j-\varphi |$ is integrable, hence finite almost everywhere, so $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ almost everywhere along it. We get $\varphi \leq \varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. The two inequalities prove that the supremum is continuous; in particular, the limit in the previous paragraph satisfies $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$. Thus the set in question is sequentially compact, hence compact, in the metric space $L^1(X)$. The continuous function $\| \cdot \| _{L^1}$ is bounded on the compact set of normalized functions. The arguments so far use only that $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of positive dimension and that the volume form defining $L^1(X)$ is smooth and positive; hence they also prove the last assertion of the proposition. For smoothly convergent backgrounds, choose $C\geq 0$ with $\theta _ j\leq C\omega $ for all $j$. Then $C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\geq 0$, so all $\varphi _ j$ lie in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$, and the first part, applied to the closed form $C\omega $, gives an $L^1$-convergent subsequence and the convergence of the suprema. Since $\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\to \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ as distributions, the limit belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.2.2
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.2 . For every $1\leq p<\infty $ there is a constant $M_ p$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $, $\omega $ and $p$, such that \[  \| u\| _{L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)}\leq M_ p \quad \text{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\text{ with }\sup _ Xu=0.  \] Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is empty, there is nothing to prove.) Choose finitely many coordinate polydiscs $D_ k$ such that the polydiscs $\frac14D_ k$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{D_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=\theta $. For $u$ as in the statement, $v_ k=u+h_ k-\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ is a nonpositive plurisubharmonic function on $D_ k$. By proposition 14.2.1 and the boundedness of the $h_ k$ and of the coordinate volume densities, the norms $\| v_ k\| _{L^1(D_ k)}$ are bounded independently of $u$. After rescaling $D_ k$ to the unit polydisc, ( 8.6 ) bounds $\| v_ k\| _{L^ p(\frac14D_ k)}$ independently of $u$. Since $u=v_ k-h_ k+\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ on $D_ k$, the bounded functions $h_ k$ and the bounded volume densities give the assertion. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.2.3
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.3 . There are $\alpha ,C>0$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $ and $\omega $, such that 14.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normalized-global-psh-exponential-bound} \int _ X\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\omega ^ n\leq C \quad \text{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\text{ with }\sup _ Xu=0. \end{equation} Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is empty, any $\alpha ,C>0$ will do.) Choose finitely many coordinate unit balls $B_ j$ such that the balls $\frac14B_ j$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $\rho _ j$ near $\overline{B_ j}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho _ j=\theta $. For $u$ as in the statement put $v_ j=u+\rho _ j-\sup _{B_ j}\rho _ j$ on $B_ j$; then $v_ j$ is plurisubharmonic and $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$. By proposition 14.2.1 and comparison of the coordinate volume densities, $\| v_ j\| _{L^1(B_ j)}\leq M_ j$ for a constant $M_ j\geq 1$ independent of $u$. Applying proposition 8.3.9 to $v_ j/M_ j$, we see that $\int _{\frac14B_ j}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ is bounded independently of $u$, where $\alpha _ j=\alpha _ n/M_ j$. Put $\alpha =\min _ j\alpha _ j>0$. Since $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$ and $\alpha \leq \alpha _ j$, we have $\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ ju}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ on $B_ j$. Summing over $j$ and comparing the coordinate volume densities with $\omega ^ n$ gives ( 14.17 ). $\square$

section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: 14.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normalized-global-psh-exponential-bound} \int _ X\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\omega ^ n\leq C \quad \text{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\text{ with }\sup _ Xu=0. \end{equation}

title: Corollary 14.2.4
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.4 . Let $K\subset X$ be a compact set that is not pluripolar. Then there is a constant $C$ such that \[  \sup _ X\varphi \leq \sup _ K\varphi +C\qquad \text{for all }\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ).  \] Consequently, every subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ on which $\sup _ K\varphi $ is bounded above and below is relatively compact in $L^1(X)$. Proof. Suppose that no such constant exists. Since $\sup _ X\varphi -\sup _ K\varphi $ does not change when a constant is added to $\varphi $, there are $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi _ j=0$ and $\sup _ K\varphi _ j\leq -2^ j$. Choose $C\geq 0$ with $\theta \leq C\omega $ (lemma 13.1.1 ) and put $\psi _ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}\varphi _ j$. Since $\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\leq 1$, we have \[  C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ N=\Bigl (1-\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\Bigr )C\omega +\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq \sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq 0.  \] The sequence $(\psi _ N)$ is decreasing because $\varphi _ j\leq 0$, and $\| \psi _ N\| _{L^1}\leq \sup _ j\| \varphi _ j\| _{L^1}<\infty $ by proposition 14.2.1 . By monotone convergence the limit $\psi $ is integrable, so it is not identically $-\infty $, and theorem 8.3.1 , applied on coordinate balls after adding local potentials of $C\omega $, shows that $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$. On $K$ every term $2^{-j}\varphi _ j$ is at most $-1$, so $\psi =-\infty $ on $K$. On every coordinate ball $U$ with a smooth function $h$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=C\omega $, the function $\psi +h$ is plurisubharmonic and equals $-\infty $ on $K\cap U$. Hence $K$ is pluripolar, a contradiction. The last assertion follows: bounds for $\sup _ K\varphi $ give bounds for $\sup _ X\varphi $, and proposition 14.2.1 applies. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.2.5
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.5 . Let $(\varphi _ i)$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ whose suprema $\sup _ X\varphi _ i$ are bounded below. Then its pointwise infimum $\varphi $ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\varphi _ i\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ i\to \sup _ X\varphi $. Proof. Fix an index $i_0$. For $i\geq i_0$ the suprema are bounded above by $\sup _ X\varphi _{i_0}$, so the tail of the net lies in a compact subset of $L^1(X)$ by proposition 14.2.1 , and a subnet converges in $L^1$ to some $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For each fixed $i$, the members of the subnet are eventually below $\varphi _ i$, so $\psi \leq \varphi _ i$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. Hence the pointwise infimum $\varphi $ is at least $\psi $ and is not identically $-\infty $. Applying theorem 8.3.1 on the coordinate balls of a finite cover, after adding local potentials of $\theta $, we find that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi _ i\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. The continuity of the supremum in proposition 14.2.1 gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Definition 14.2.6
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Definition 14.2.6 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Recall from section 13.5 that $\varphi $ is more singular than $\psi $, written $\varphi \preceq \psi $, if $\varphi \leq \psi +C$ on $X$ for some constant $C$; we then also say that $\psi $ is less singular than $\varphi $. A potential $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities if every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is more singular than $\psi $. If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing $, put \[  V_\theta =\bigl (\sup \{ \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\varphi \leq 0\} \bigr )^*,  \] where ${}^*$ denotes the upper semicontinuous regularization.

title: Lemma 14.2.7
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.2.7 . Suppose that $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\neq \varnothing $. Then $V_\theta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\sup _ XV_\theta =0$, and $\varphi \leq V_\theta +\sup _ X\varphi $ for every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; in particular, $V_\theta $ has minimal singularities. Any two potentials with minimal singularities differ by a bounded function on the set where both are finite, and the notion of minimal singularities depends only on the class $\{ \theta \} $. Proof. The family whose upper envelope defines $V_\theta $ in definition 14.2.6 is nonempty, because $\varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $ belongs to it for every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and it is bounded above by $0$. Theorem 8.3.2 , applied on coordinate balls after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, therefore gives $V_\theta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $V_\theta \leq 0$; and $\sup _ XV_\theta =0$, because $V_\theta \geq \varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $ for every $\varphi $. The same inequality reads $\varphi \leq V_\theta +\sup _ X\varphi $, so $V_\theta $ has minimal singularities. Any two potentials with minimal singularities are each more singular than the other, so their difference is bounded on the set where both are finite. Replacing $\theta $ by $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ with $h$ smooth replaces $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ by $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )-h$; since $h$ is bounded, the notion of minimal singularities depends only on the class $\{ \theta \} $. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.2.8
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text:
Proposition 14.2.8 . Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map from a complex manifold $Y$. Then $Y$ is compact and connected, and $\varphi \mapsto \varphi \circ \pi $ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$, which is continuous for convergence in $L^1(X)$ and $L^1(Y)$, the latter taken with respect to any smooth positive volume form. For every prime divisor $E$ on $Y$, the generic Lelong numbers $
u (\varphi ,E)=
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)$ are bounded above uniformly for $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Proof. The manifold $Y=\pi ^{-1}(X)$ is compact, because $\pi $ is proper. By the definition of bimeromorphic maps (section A.3 ), there is a nowhere dense analytic subset $E_0\subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(E_0)$ is nowhere dense and $\pi $ restricts to an isomorphism of $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(E_0)$ onto $X\setminus E_0$. The set $X\setminus E_0$ is connected by lemma A.1.7 , hence so is its dense preimage, and therefore $Y$ is connected. The image $\pi (Y)$ is closed, since proper maps are closed, and it contains the dense set $X\setminus E_0$; so $\pi $ is surjective. By proposition A.7.3 there is an analytic subset $A\subset X$ of codimension at least two such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$. Then $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is an analytic subset of $Y$ different from $Y$, because $\pi $ is surjective. Since $Y$ is connected, $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is locally contained in the zero set of a holomorphic function that does not vanish identically on a connected neighborhood (section A.1 ), so it is nowhere dense and a null set (lemma 7.4.1 ). The same holds for $A$ in $X$. If $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, let $B$ be a coordinate ball and $h$ a smooth function on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $ (lemma 13.1.2 ). On every connected coordinate neighborhood $W\subset \pi ^{-1}(B)$ the function $(\varphi +h)\circ \pi $ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, by proposition 8.2.3 , and the second case is excluded because $\varphi +h$ is finite almost everywhere on the image under the biholomorphism $\pi $ of the nonempty open set $W\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$. Hence $\varphi \circ \pi =(\varphi +h)\circ \pi -h\circ \pi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, with $\pi ^*	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi \circ \pi )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((\varphi +h)\circ \pi )\geq 0$ on $\pi ^{-1}(B)$. Thus $\varphi \circ \pi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. If $\varphi \circ \pi =\varphi '\circ \pi $, then $\varphi =\varphi '$ on $X\setminus A$, hence almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section; this proves injectivity. Conversely, let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. Over $X\setminus A$ it descends to the function $\psi \circ \pi ^{-1}$, which is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic there. It is bounded above, because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $Y$. On a coordinate ball $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $ on $B$, the plurisubharmonic function $\psi \circ \pi ^{-1}+h$ on $B\setminus A$ is therefore locally bounded above near $A$, and it extends to a plurisubharmonic function on $B$ by theorem 8.4.1 . The extensions on two balls agree outside the null set $A$, hence everywhere, so they define $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. The pullback $\varphi \circ \pi $ equals $\psi $ outside the null set $\pi ^{-1}(A)$, hence everywhere. This proves surjectivity. For continuity, we use proposition 14.2.1 on $X$ and on $Y$; by its last assertion, its assertions for a fixed background hold on $Y$. Let $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. By the continuity of the supremum, it suffices to treat normalized functions, $\sup _ X\varphi _ j=\sup _ X\varphi =0$, since subtracting the suprema preserves $L^1$ convergence. The pullbacks have the same suprema, because $\pi $ is surjective, so they are relatively compact in $L^1(Y)$, and every cluster value lies in $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. On compact subsets of $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$, a change of variables shows that every $L^1$ cluster value of $(\varphi _ j\circ \pi )$ coincides almost everywhere with $\varphi \circ \pi $; since $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is a null set, every cluster value is $\varphi \circ \pi $. A relatively compact sequence in a metric space with a single cluster value converges to it; hence $\varphi _ j\circ \pi 	o \varphi \circ \pi $ in $L^1(Y)$. Finally, $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)$ is the infimum over $y\in E$ of the point Lelong numbers $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y)$. Near $y$ choose a smooth $g$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\pi ^*	heta $, so that the functions $\varphi \circ \pi +g$ are plurisubharmonic. By ( 12.8 ), applied to them, each $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y)$ is upper semicontinuous for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi \circ \pi $, hence, by the continuity just proved, for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi $; and an infimum of upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous. Since Lelong numbers do not change when a constant is added, we may restrict to the normalized functions, which form a compact set by proposition 14.2.1 . An upper semicontinuous function with finite values attains its maximum on a compact set, which gives the uniform bound. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.2.9
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.9 . Let $B'$ be a coordinate ball in $X$ and $B\Subset B'$ a ball in the same coordinates, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be bounded near $\overline{B'}$. There is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\psi \geq \varphi $, $\psi =\varphi $ on $X\setminus B$, $\psi $ bounded near $\overline B$, and $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=0$ on $B$. It is the largest function in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with these properties, and any two functions with these properties that are continuous on $\overline B$ coincide. Proof. Choose a ball $B''$ in the same coordinates with $\overline B\subset B''$ and $\overline{B''}\subset B'$. Write $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $B''$, with $h$ smooth (lemma 13.1.2 ), and apply corollary 9.6.4 to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\varphi +h$ on $B''$. Subtracting $h$ from the result on $B''$ and keeping $\varphi $ outside $B''$ gives $\psi $, since the result equals $\varphi +h$ on $B''\setminus B$; here $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi +h))^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $\psi +h$. If $\psi '$ is another function with the stated properties, then by upper semicontinuity $\varlimsup _{z\to \zeta ,\, z\in B}\psi '(z)\leq \psi '(\zeta )=\varphi (\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. Hence $\psi '+h$ belongs to the family whose upper envelope is $\psi +h$ in corollary 9.6.4 , and $\psi '\leq \psi $ on $B$. If $\psi '$ is continuous on $\overline B$, then its boundary values $\varphi |_{\partial B}$ are continuous, and $\psi '+h$ is the solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem with the continuous boundary values $(\varphi +h)|_{\partial B}$; by the uniqueness in theorem 9.6.3 , any two such continuous functions coincide. $\square$

title: 14.3 Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text:
14.3 Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition Let $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ and fix a smooth representative $	heta \in \alpha $. By theorem 14.1.7 , the closed currents in $\alpha $ are exactly the currents $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ with $\varphi $ a real distribution, so positivity properties of $\alpha $ become inequalities for $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $. Besides the positivity cones and the mixed Hodge index theorem, we prove Siu's decomposition of a closed positive current (theorem 14.3.7 ), which leads to modified nef classes. Definition 14.3.1 . A class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is pseudo-effective if it contains a closed positive current; Kähler if it contains a Kähler form; nef if for every $\varepsilon >0$ it contains a smooth form $	heta _\varepsilon $ with $	heta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $; big if it contains a closed current $T$ with $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$. A closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ with $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$ is called a Kähler current . The cones of pseudo-effective, Kähler, nef and big classes are denoted $\mathcal E$, $\mathcal K$, $\mathcal N$ and $\mathcal B$. The zero class belongs to the pseudo-effective cone and to the nef cone. These notions do not depend on $\omega $, because any two Hermitian forms on the compact manifold $X$ are bounded by constant multiples of each other (lemma 13.1.1 ). By corollary 14.1.9 , $\alpha $ is pseudo-effective if and only if $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
e \varnothing $. Proposition 14.3.2 . The pseudo-effective cone $\mathcal E$ is closed and convex, and the Kähler cone $\mathcal K$ is open and convex. Moreover $\mathcal N=\overline{\mathcal K}\subset \mathcal E$, the Kähler cone $\mathcal K$ is the interior of $\mathcal N$, and the big cone $\mathcal B$ is the interior of $\mathcal E$. Proof. Sums and positive multiples of positive currents, Kähler forms or nef representatives are of the same kind, which proves convexity of all four cones. Let $\alpha _ j	o \alpha $ be pseudo-effective classes, with positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$. Since the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution pairs to zero with the closed form $\omega ^{n-1}$, the trace masses are \[  \int _ XT_ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1} =\int _ X	heta _{\alpha _ j}\wedge \omega ^{n-1},  \] where $	heta _{\alpha _ j}$ are the representatives of ( 14.16 ); they are bounded because the classes converge. Let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart, $\chi $ a test function on the chart with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $K$, and $c'>0$ such that $ eta \leq c'\omega $ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 13.1.1 ), where $ eta $ is the Euclidean form ( 7.4 ) of the chart. By ( 14.12 ), applied with $\gamma _ j=c'\omega $ and $\gamma '_ j= eta $, the form $(c'\omega )^{n-1}- eta ^{n-1}$ is a sum of products of semipositive $(1,1)$-forms on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, hence strongly positive (proposition 7.2.1 ). Therefore $c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}-\chi  eta ^{n-1}=(1-\chi )c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}+\chi  igl (c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}- eta ^{n-1} igr )$, with $\chi  eta ^{n-1}$ extended by zero outside the chart, is a smooth strongly positive form on $X$, so the trace measures satisfy $\mu _{T_ j}(K)\leq T_ j(\chi  eta ^{n-1})\leq c'^{n-1}\int _ XT_ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$, which is bounded independently of $j$. By the compactness assertion of theorem 7.2.5 , a subsequence of $(T_ j)$ converges weakly to a closed positive current $T$, and $\{ T\} =\alpha $ because the class map is weakly continuous. Hence $\mathcal E$ is closed. If $\omega _0\in \alpha $ is a Kähler form, then $\omega _0\geq c\omega $ for some $c>0$, and by ( 14.16 ) the form $\omega _0+	heta _{\alpha '-\alpha }\in \alpha '$ is Kähler whenever $C\| \alpha '-\alpha \| <c$; hence $\mathcal K$ is open. If $\alpha $ is nef and $\varepsilon >0$, a representative $	heta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ gives the Kähler form $	heta _\varepsilon +2\varepsilon \omega \in \alpha +2\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, so $\alpha \in \overline{\mathcal K}$. Conversely, let Kähler classes $\alpha _ j$ with Kähler forms $\omega _ j\in \alpha _ j$ converge to $\alpha $. Then $\omega _ j+	heta _{\alpha -\alpha _ j}\in \alpha $ is at least $-C\| \alpha -\alpha _ j\| \omega $, so $\alpha $ is nef; thus $\mathcal N=\overline{\mathcal K}$, and $\mathcal N\subset \mathcal E$ because $\mathcal K\subset \mathcal E$ and $\mathcal E$ is closed. Since $\mathcal K$ is open and contained in $\mathcal N$, it lies in the interior of $\mathcal N$. If $\alpha $ is nef and $t>0$, then $\alpha +t\{ \omega \} $ is Kähler: take a representative $	heta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ with $\varepsilon <t$. If $\alpha $ lies in the interior of $\mathcal N$, then $\alpha -t\{ \omega \} $ is nef for small $t>0$, and therefore $\alpha =(\alpha -t\{ \omega \} )+t\{ \omega \} $ is Kähler. Thus $\mathcal K$ is the interior of $\mathcal N$. If $T\in \alpha $ and $T\geq \delta \omega $, then $T+	heta _{\alpha '-\alpha }\in \alpha '$ is positive whenever $C\| \alpha '-\alpha \| \leq \delta $, so a neighborhood of $\alpha $ lies in $\mathcal E$. Conversely, if $\alpha $ lies in the interior of $\mathcal E$, then $\alpha -\delta \{ \omega \} \in \mathcal E$ for some $\delta >0$, and adding $\delta \omega $ to a positive current in $\alpha -\delta \{ \omega \} $ gives a Kähler current in $\alpha $. Hence $\mathcal B$ is the interior of $\mathcal E$. $\square$ If $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ are smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms, Stokes' formula shows that $\int _ X	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$ is unchanged when one $	heta _ i$ is replaced by $	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth. We therefore write $\int _ X\alpha _1\cdots \alpha _ n=\int _ X	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$ for the intersection number of classes $\alpha _ i=\{ 	heta _ i\} $, and use the usual notation for powers, such as $\int _ X\alpha ^ n$. The values of $\widetilde v$ on the support of $D$ are upper limits of values of $v+h$, so $\widetilde v$ is bounded, and $\widetilde v=v+h$ outside the null set $\operatorname{Supp}D$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_ i|^2=[D_ i]$ (lemma A.2.16 ), the current $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ satisfies $T-[D]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\geq 0$ near the point, where $[D]=\sum _ ia_ i[D_ i]$. Thus $T-[D]$ is a positive current in $\{ 	heta \} -\{ D\} $ with locally bounded potentials. If $T\geq \delta \omega $, apply the same argument to $T-\delta \omega $, whose potential has the same logarithmic singularities; then $T-[D]\geq \delta \omega $. In both cases proposition 14.3.5 gives the assertion. $\square$

title: Definition 14.3.1
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Definition 14.3.1 . A class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is pseudo-effective if it contains a closed positive current; Kähler if it contains a Kähler form; nef if for every $\varepsilon >0$ it contains a smooth form $\theta _\varepsilon $ with $\theta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $; big if it contains a closed current $T$ with $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$. A closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ with $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$ is called a Kähler current . The cones of pseudo-effective, Kähler, nef and big classes are denoted $\mathcal E$, $\mathcal K$, $\mathcal N$ and $\mathcal B$. The zero class belongs to the pseudo-effective cone and to the nef cone.

title: Proposition 14.3.2
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Proposition 14.3.2 . The pseudo-effective cone $\mathcal E$ is closed and convex, and the Kähler cone $\mathcal K$ is open and convex. Moreover $\mathcal N=\overline{\mathcal K}\subset \mathcal E$, the Kähler cone $\mathcal K$ is the interior of $\mathcal N$, and the big cone $\mathcal B$ is the interior of $\mathcal E$. Proof. Sums and positive multiples of positive currents, Kähler forms or nef representatives are of the same kind, which proves convexity of all four cones. Let $\alpha _ j\to \alpha $ be pseudo-effective classes, with positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$. Since the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution pairs to zero with the closed form $\omega ^{n-1}$, the trace masses are \[  \int _ XT_ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1} =\int _ X\theta _{\alpha _ j}\wedge \omega ^{n-1},  \] where $\theta _{\alpha _ j}$ are the representatives of ( 14.16 ); they are bounded because the classes converge. Let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart, $\chi $ a test function on the chart with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $K$, and $c'>0$ such that $\beta \leq c'\omega $ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 13.1.1 ), where $\beta $ is the Euclidean form ( 7.4 ) of the chart. By ( 14.12 ), applied with $\gamma _ j=c'\omega $ and $\gamma '_ j=\beta $, the form $(c'\omega )^{n-1}-\beta ^{n-1}$ is a sum of products of semipositive $(1,1)$-forms on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, hence strongly positive (proposition 7.2.1 ). Therefore $c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}-\chi \beta ^{n-1}=(1-\chi )c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}+\chi \bigl (c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}-\beta ^{n-1}\bigr )$, with $\chi \beta ^{n-1}$ extended by zero outside the chart, is a smooth strongly positive form on $X$, so the trace measures satisfy $\mu _{T_ j}(K)\leq T_ j(\chi \beta ^{n-1})\leq c'^{n-1}\int _ XT_ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$, which is bounded independently of $j$. By the compactness assertion of theorem 7.2.5 , a subsequence of $(T_ j)$ converges weakly to a closed positive current $T$, and $\{ T\} =\alpha $ because the class map is weakly continuous. Hence $\mathcal E$ is closed. If $\omega _0\in \alpha $ is a Kähler form, then $\omega _0\geq c\omega $ for some $c>0$, and by ( 14.16 ) the form $\omega _0+\theta _{\alpha '-\alpha }\in \alpha '$ is Kähler whenever $C\| \alpha '-\alpha \| <c$; hence $\mathcal K$ is open. If $\alpha $ is nef and $\varepsilon >0$, a representative $\theta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ gives the Kähler form $\theta _\varepsilon +2\varepsilon \omega \in \alpha +2\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, so $\alpha \in \overline{\mathcal K}$. Conversely, let Kähler classes $\alpha _ j$ with Kähler forms $\omega _ j\in \alpha _ j$ converge to $\alpha $. Then $\omega _ j+\theta _{\alpha -\alpha _ j}\in \alpha $ is at least $-C\| \alpha -\alpha _ j\| \omega $, so $\alpha $ is nef; thus $\mathcal N=\overline{\mathcal K}$, and $\mathcal N\subset \mathcal E$ because $\mathcal K\subset \mathcal E$ and $\mathcal E$ is closed. Since $\mathcal K$ is open and contained in $\mathcal N$, it lies in the interior of $\mathcal N$. If $\alpha $ is nef and $t>0$, then $\alpha +t\{ \omega \} $ is Kähler: take a representative $\theta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ with $\varepsilon <t$. If $\alpha $ lies in the interior of $\mathcal N$, then $\alpha -t\{ \omega \} $ is nef for small $t>0$, and therefore $\alpha =(\alpha -t\{ \omega \} )+t\{ \omega \} $ is Kähler. Thus $\mathcal K$ is the interior of $\mathcal N$. If $T\in \alpha $ and $T\geq \delta \omega $, then $T+\theta _{\alpha '-\alpha }\in \alpha '$ is positive whenever $C\| \alpha '-\alpha \| \leq \delta $, so a neighborhood of $\alpha $ lies in $\mathcal E$. Conversely, if $\alpha $ lies in the interior of $\mathcal E$, then $\alpha -\delta \{ \omega \} \in \mathcal E$ for some $\delta >0$, and adding $\delta \omega $ to a positive current in $\alpha -\delta \{ \omega \} $ gives a Kähler current in $\alpha $. Hence $\mathcal B$ is the interior of $\mathcal E$. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.3.3 (The mixed Hodge index theorem)
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Theorem 14.3.3 (The mixed Hodge index theorem) . Let $n\geq 2$, let $\omega _3,\ldots ,\omega _ n$ be Kähler forms on $X$, and put $\Omega =\omega _3\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _ n$, with $\Omega =1$ when $n=2$. The symmetric bilinear form \[  Q(\alpha ,\beta )=\int _ Xa\wedge b\wedge \Omega , \qquad a\in \alpha ,\quad b\in \beta ,  \] on $H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ has signature $(1,\dim H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)-1)$. For every Kähler class $\gamma $, it is negative definite on the hyperplane $\{ \alpha :Q(\alpha ,\gamma )=0\} $. For Kähler classes $\alpha ,\beta $, 14.18 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-intersection-cauchy} Q(\alpha ,\beta )^2\geq Q(\alpha ,\alpha )Q(\beta ,\beta ). \end{equation} Proof. Let $\gamma $ be a Kähler class with a Kähler form $h\in \gamma $, and let $\alpha $ satisfy $Q(\alpha ,\gamma )=0$. Choose a smooth closed real form $a\in \alpha $; then $\int _ Xa\wedge h\wedge \Omega =0$. Apply lemma 14.1.4 with $A=h\wedge \Omega $, a product of $n-1$ Kähler forms, and $\eta =-a\wedge h\wedge \Omega $. The resulting $f$ makes $a'=a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\in \alpha $ satisfy $a'\wedge h\wedge \Omega =0$ at every point. At a point, in holomorphic coordinates, the wedge products of real $(1,1)$-forms are expressed by mixed discriminants of their Hermitian matrices, so lemma 7.2.3 gives $a'\wedge a'\wedge \Omega \leq 0$, with equality only if $a'$ vanishes at that point. By Stokes' formula, \[  Q(\alpha ,\alpha )=\int _ Xa'\wedge a'\wedge \Omega \leq 0.  \] If this integral vanishes, the smooth nonpositive density $a'\wedge a'\wedge \Omega $ vanishes everywhere, so $a'=0$ and $\alpha =0$. Thus $Q$ is negative definite on the hyperplane $\{ Q(\cdot ,\gamma )=0\} $. Since $Q(\gamma ,\gamma )=\int _ Xh^2\wedge \Omega >0$, every class splits uniquely as a multiple of $\gamma $ plus a class in that hyperplane. The space $H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is finite dimensional by theorem 14.1.7 , and $Q$ is positive on the line spanned by $\gamma $ and negative definite on its $Q$-orthogonal complement; this gives the signature. Finally, let $\alpha ,\beta $ be Kähler classes and write $\beta =c\alpha +\delta $ with $Q(\delta ,\alpha )=0$. Negative definiteness gives $Q(\beta ,\beta )=c^2Q(\alpha ,\alpha )+Q(\delta ,\delta )\leq c^2Q(\alpha ,\alpha )$, while $Q(\alpha ,\beta )=cQ(\alpha ,\alpha )$. Since $Q(\alpha ,\alpha )>0$, we obtain $Q(\alpha ,\beta )^2=c^2Q(\alpha ,\alpha )^2\geq Q(\alpha ,\alpha )Q(\beta ,\beta )$. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.3.4
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text:
Corollary 14.3.4 . Let $r\geq 1$, let $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ r$ be nef classes, and let $k_1,\ldots ,k_ r\geq 0$ be integers with $\sum _ i k_ i=n$. Then \[  \int _ X\alpha _1^{k_1}\cdots \alpha _ r^{k_ r} \geq \prod _{i:k_ i>0}\left(\int _ X\alpha _ i^ night)^{k_ i/n}.  \] In particular, for nef classes $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ n$, \[  \int _ X\alpha _1\cdots \alpha _ n \geq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left(\int _ X\alpha _ i^ night)^{1/n}.  \] Proof. Assume first that all $\alpha _ i$ are Kähler. Then all the intersection numbers $\int _ X\prod _ i\alpha _ i^{k_ i}$ are positive, and we put $b(k)=\log \int _ X\prod _ i\alpha _ i^{k_ i}$ for $k=(k_1,\ldots ,k_ r)$ with $\sum _ ik_ i=n$. If $n=1$, only one $k_ i$ is positive and there is nothing to prove; let $n\geq 2$. Let $i
eq j$ with $k_ i,k_ j\geq 1$, let $\Omega $ be the wedge product of Kähler representatives of the remaining $n-2$ factors, counted with multiplicity, and let $e_ i$ be the $i$th coordinate vector. Then ( 14.18 ) for $\alpha _ i,\alpha _ j$ reads \[  2b(k)\geq b(k+e_ i-e_ j)+b(k-e_ i+e_ j).  \] Fix the coordinates other than $i,j$ and put $s=k_ i+k_ j$. The inequality says that the finite sequence $l\mapsto b(\ldots ,l,\ldots ,s-l,\ldots )$, with $l$ in the $i$th and $s-l$ in the $j$th place, $0\leq l\leq s$, is concave: its consecutive differences decrease. A concave sequence lies above the linear interpolation between its endpoints, since the average of its first $l$ differences is at least the average of all $s$ differences. Consequently \[  b(k)\geq  rac{k_ i}{s}b(k^{(i)})+ rac{k_ j}{s}b(k^{(j)}),  \] where $k^{(i)}$ is obtained from $k$ by putting all $s$ factors in the $i$th place and $k^{(j)}$ by putting them in the $j$th place. We now prove $b(k)\geq \sum _ i(k_ i/n)\log \int _ X\alpha _ i^ n$ by induction on the number of positive coordinates of $k$. If only one coordinate is positive, this is an equality. Otherwise choose $i
e j$ with $k_ i,k_ j\geq 1$. The vectors $k^{(i)}$ and $k^{(j)}$ have one positive coordinate fewer, and inserting the induction hypothesis for them into the last display gives the claim: for $m
e i,j$ the coefficient of $\log \int _ X\alpha _ m^ n$ is $(k_ i/s+k_ j/s)\, k_ m/n=k_ m/n$, and the coefficients of $\log \int _ X\alpha _ i^ n$ and $\log \int _ X\alpha _ j^ n$ are $(k_ i/s)(s/n)=k_ i/n$ and $k_ j/n$. Exponentiating proves the corollary for Kähler classes. For nef classes, $\alpha _ i+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is Kähler for every $\varepsilon >0$ by proposition 14.3.2 , so the inequality holds for these classes. Each intersection number involved is a polynomial in $\varepsilon $ and tends to the corresponding number for the $\alpha _ i$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; in particular the limits $\int _ X\alpha _ i^ n$ are nonnegative. Since $t\mapsto t^{k_ i/n}$ is continuous on $[0,\infty )$, the inequality passes to the limit. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.3.5
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Proposition 14.3.5 . A class that contains a closed positive current with locally bounded potentials is nef. A class that contains a Kähler current with locally bounded potentials is Kähler. Every big class contains a Kähler current with gentle analytic singularities. Proof. Write the given current as $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. If $\varphi $ is bounded, then every $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ is the unit ideal, so the approximations $G_ m$ are smooth and satisfy $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq -(c/m)\omega $; hence the class is nef. If moreover $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $, then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta -\delta \omega )$, and the approximations for the background $\theta -\delta \omega $ satisfy $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq (\delta -c/m)\omega $; for large $m$ the smooth form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m$ is a Kähler form in the class. For the last assertion, let $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $ be a Kähler current in a big class, with $\varphi $ not necessarily bounded. The same inequality shows that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m$ is a Kähler current for large $m$, and $G_ m$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $(m^{-1},\mathcal I(m\varphi ))$ by lemma 13.4.1 . $\square$

title: Corollary 14.3.6
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.3.6 . If a closed positive current with minimal singularities is a Kähler current, then its class is Kähler. Moreover, in a Kähler class every potential with minimal singularities is bounded. Proof. Write the current as $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $, where $\varphi $ has minimal singularities, and normalize $\varphi \leq 0$. Choose $C'\geq 0$ with $-\theta \leq C'\omega $ (lemma 13.1.1 ). For $0<t\leq \delta /(\delta +C')$ the current \[  (1-t)T+t\theta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((1-t)\varphi \bigr )\geq \bigl ((1-t)\delta -tC'\bigr )\omega \geq 0  \] is positive, so $(1-t)\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By minimality, $(1-t)\varphi \leq \varphi +C$ for a constant $C$, so $\varphi \geq -C/t$ at every point where $\varphi $ is finite, hence almost everywhere. Since $\varphi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, the lower bound holds everywhere, as noted at the beginning of section 14.2 . Thus $\varphi $ is bounded, and proposition 14.3.5 shows that the class is Kähler. For the second assertion, suppose that the class contains a Kähler form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Then $u$ is smooth and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, so a potential $\varphi $ with minimal singularities satisfies $u\leq \varphi +C$; hence $\varphi $ is bounded below, and it is bounded above as every quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.3.7 (Siu's divisorial decomposition)
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text:
Theorem 14.3.7 (Siu's divisorial decomposition) . Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$. Then $
u (T,D)>0$ for at most countably many prime divisors $D$, the series below converges weakly, and 14.19  egin{equation} \label{eq:siu-divisorial-decomposition} T=R+\sum _ D
u (T,D)[D], \end{equation} where $R$ is a closed positive current with $
u (R,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$. In particular $T-
u (T,D)[D]\geq 0$ for every $D$. The decomposition is unique: if $T=R'+\sum _ Db_ D[D]$ for a weakly convergent series with coefficients $b_ D\geq 0$, at most countably many of them nonzero, and a closed positive current $R'$ with $
u (R',D)=0$ for every $D$, then $b_ D=
u (T,D)$ for every $D$ and $R'=R$. Proof. We first subtract one divisor, then show that only countably many divisors occur and that the series converges, and finally identify the residual current and prove uniqueness. Step 1: one divisor. Let $D$ be a prime divisor and $c=
u (T,D)$; we show that $T-c[D]\geq 0$. Near a regular point of $D$ choose coordinates with $D=\{ z_1=0\} $ on a coordinate polydisc $W$ with $|z_1|<1$, and a plurisubharmonic potential $u$ of $T$ on $W$. Since the Lelong numbers of $u$ at the points of $D\cap W$ are at least $c$, proposition 12.3.6 gives $u\leq c\log |z_1|^2+C$ near the point. Off $D$ the function $u-c\log |z_1|^2$ is plurisubharmonic, and it is bounded above near $D$; by theorem 8.4.1 it extends to a plurisubharmonic function $v$. Since $v=u-c\log |z_1|^2$ almost everywhere and $[D]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z_1|^2$ near the point (theorem 7.4.5 ), we get $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=T-c[D]$ there. Hence $T-c[D]$ is positive on a neighborhood of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and it equals $T$ on $X\setminus D$; so it is positive on the open set $X\setminus D_{\mathrm{sing}}$. To extend the positivity across $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$, let $\phi $ be a strongly positive test form of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$. Since $T$ and $[D]$ have measure coefficients (theorem 7.2.5 ), there is a real measure $m_\phi $ on $X$, a combination of the coefficient measures with the coefficients of $\phi $ as densities, such that $(T-c[D])(\chi \phi )=\int \chi \, \mathrm dm_\phi $ for test functions $\chi $. The restriction of $m_\phi $ to the open set $X\setminus D_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is a positive measure, because $(T-c[D])(\chi \phi )\geq 0$ for test functions $\chi \geq 0$ supported there; and its restriction to $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is that of the positive measure $\chi \mapsto T(\chi \phi )$, because $[D]$ gives no mass to $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$. Hence $(T-c[D])(\phi )=m_\phi (X)\geq 0$, that is, $T-c[D]\geq 0$. Step 2: the series. By theorem 12.3.4 , each set $E_ j=\{ x:
u (T,x)\geq 1/j\} $ is an analytic subset of $X$ different from $X$. Being compact, $E_ j$ has finitely many irreducible components $Z$ by corollary A.2.13 . We first show: 14.20  egin{equation} \label{eq:prime-divisor-component}  egin{gathered} 	ext{a prime divisor $D$ contained in an analytic subset $E
eq X$}\ 	ext{is an irreducible component of $E$.} \end{gathered} \end{equation} An analytic subset of the connected manifold $X$ with an interior point is all of $X$, since the set of its interior points is open and, by the identity theorem applied to local defining functions, closed. Hence $E$ has no interior points, so its germs, and their branches, have dimension at most $n-1$, and $E_{\mathrm{sing}}$ has dimension at most $n-2$ at every point (proposition A.2.7 , corollary A.2.10 ). At a point $y\in D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ the germ of $D$ has dimension $n-1$, so by monotonicity of dimension (see proposition A.2.7 and the remarks following it) it is not contained in the germ of $E_{\mathrm{sing}}$; thus there are points $y'\in D_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Near such a point $E$ is a complex submanifold of dimension at most $n-1$ containing the $(n-1)$-dimensional submanifold $D$, so $D$ and $E$ coincide near $y'$. Let $F$ be the connected component of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ containing $y'$. The analytic subset $D\cap F$ of the connected manifold $F$ has an interior point, so it is all of $F$, and $D$ contains the closure $Z$ of $F$, an irreducible component of $E$ (corollary A.2.13 ). Since $D$ is compact and the components of $E$ form a locally finite family, $D$ meets only finitely many of them and is the union of its intersections with these. By induction on the number of sets, an irreducible set is not a finite union of analytic subsets different from itself; hence $D=D\cap Z'$ for a component $Z'$. Then $Z\subset D\subset Z'$, and since no component is contained in another, $D=Z$. This proves ( 14.20 ). In particular, two distinct prime divisors are not contained in one another, and every prime divisor $D$ with $
u (T,D)\geq 1/j$, being contained in $E_ j$, is one of its finitely many components. Therefore at most countably many prime divisors have $
u (T,D)>0$. Let $D_1,D_2,\ldots $ be an enumeration of them and put $S_ N=\sum _{k\leq N}
u (T,D_ k)[D_ k]$. We claim that $T-S_ N\geq 0$ for every $N$, and argue by induction; suppose that $T-S_{N-1}\geq 0$. Choose a point $x\in D_ N$ outside the proper analytic subsets $D_ N\cap D_ k$, $k<N$, and outside the exceptional sets of proposition 12.3.5 for $T$ and $T-S_{N-1}$ along $D_ N$. Such points exist, because by that proposition the complement in $D_ N$ of a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $D_ N$ is dense in $D_ N$. The currents $[D_ k]$, $k<N$, vanish near $x$, so $T-S_{N-1}=T$ near $x$, and therefore $
u (T-S_{N-1},D_ N)=
u (T-S_{N-1},x)=
u (T,x)=
u (T,D_ N)$. Step 1, applied to $T-S_{N-1}$, gives $T-S_ N\geq 0$. Consequently the trace measures of the $S_ N$ in every chart are bounded by that of $T$, and the masses $\int _ XS_ N\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ are bounded by $\int _ XT\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$. We now show that the sequence $(S_ N)$ converges weakly. Every test form is a finite linear combination of test forms $g\gamma $, where $g\geq 0$ is a test function supported in a chart and $\gamma $ is a strongly positive form with constant coefficients in that chart. To see this, use a partition of unity (proposition 7.1.3 ), the fact that strongly positive forms span the real forms (proposition 7.2.1 ), and write a real test function $g$ as $(g+M\psi )-M\psi $ with $\psi \geq 0$ a test function equal to one on $\operatorname{Supp}g$ and $M\geq \sup |g|$. For such $g\gamma $ the numbers $S_ N(g\gamma )$ increase with $N$, since $S_{N+1}-S_ N\geq 0$, and they are bounded by $T(g\gamma )$; hence they converge, and so does $S_ N(\phi )$ for every test form $\phi $. By the compactness assertion of theorem 7.2.5 , a subsequence converges weakly to a closed positive current $S$, so $S_ N(\phi )	o S(\phi )$ for every $\phi $. Finally $R=T-S$ is closed and positive, as a weak limit of the closed positive currents $T-S_ N$. Step 3: properties of $R$ and uniqueness. Fix a prime divisor $D$ and write $T=R+
u (T,D)[D]+S_ D$, where $S_ D$ is the sum of the terms of the series for the other divisors. Lelong numbers are additive and nonnegative (proposition 12.1.4 ), and $
u ([D],x)=
u (\log |f|^2,x)=1$ at regular points $x$ of $D$, where $f$ is a local coordinate defining $D$. Hence, at a point of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ outside the countable union of proper analytic subsets where one of the currents $T$, $R$, $S_ D$ has a nongeneric Lelong number (such points exist by proposition 12.3.5 , since $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is also a proper analytic subset of $D$), \[  
u (T,D)=
u (R,D)+
u (T,D)+
u (S_ D,D)\geq 
u (R,D)+
u (T,D).  \] Hence $
u (R,D)=0$. Now consider any decomposition $T=R'+\sum _ Db_ D[D]$ as in the statement, fix $D$, and let $S'_ D$ be the sum of the terms for the other divisors. We first show that the coefficient measures of $S'_ D$ give no mass to $D$. If $D'
eq D$ is another prime divisor, then $D\cap D'_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is an analytic subset of the connected manifold $D'_{\mathrm{reg}}$ (corollary A.2.13 ) which is not all of it, since otherwise $D'\subset D$, and then $D'=D$ by ( 14.20 ). Hence $D\cap D'_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a null set for the surface measure of $D'_{\mathrm{reg}}$ (lemma 7.4.1 , in local coordinates of $D'_{\mathrm{reg}}$), and $[D']$ gives no mass to $D$. Now let $K\subset D$ be a compact subset of a chart, and for large $m$ let $\chi _ m$ be test functions with $0\leq \chi _ m\leq 1$, equal to one on $K$ and supported in the $1/m$-neighborhood of $K$ (lemma 1.4.1 ), all supported in a fixed compact subset of the chart, on which a test function $\psi $ equals one. For the trace measures in the chart, the weak convergence of the series gives $\mu _{S'_ D}(\chi _ m)=\sum _{D'}b_{D'}\mu _{[D']}(\chi _ m)$. As $m	o \infty $, $\chi _ m	o \mathbf1_ K$ pointwise, and dominated convergence, applied to the measure $\mu _{S'_ D}$ and to the series, whose terms are bounded by $b_{D'}\mu _{[D']}(\psi )$ with $\sum _{D'}b_{D'}\mu _{[D']}(\psi )=\mu _{S'_ D}(\psi )<\infty $, gives $\mu _{S'_ D}(K)=\sum _{D'}b_{D'}\mu _{[D']}(K)=0$. Since $D$ is covered by countably many such compact sets, the trace measures of $S'_ D$, and hence its coefficient measures (theorem 7.2.5 ), vanish on $D$. By Step 1, $S'_ D-
u (S'_ D,D)[D]\geq 0$; comparing the trace measures of both sides on $D$, where $[D]$ has positive trace mass, forces $
u (S'_ D,D)=0$. Additivity of Lelong numbers at generic points of $D$, applied to $T=R'+b_ D[D]+S'_ D$, gives $
u (T,D)=0+b_ D+0$. Thus $b_ D=

title: Definition 14.3.8
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Definition 14.3.8 . A class $\alpha $ is modified nef if for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a closed current $T_\varepsilon \in \alpha $ with $T_\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ and $\nu (T_\varepsilon +\varepsilon \omega ,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$. We write $\mathcal{MN}$ for the cone of modified nef classes. A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ with $\nu (T,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$ is called non-divisorial .

title: Corollary 14.3.9
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.3.9 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, let $D_1,\ldots ,D_ N$ be distinct prime divisors and $a_1,\ldots ,a_ N>0$ real numbers, and put $D=\sum _ ia_ iD_ i$. Suppose that $\varphi $ has logarithmic singularities along $D$ with bounded remainder: near each point, $\varphi =\sum _ ia_ i\log |s_ i|^2+v$ with $v$ bounded, where $s_ i$ is a local equation of $D_ i$ (lemma A.2.16 ), and $s_ i=1$ if the point does not lie on $D_ i$. Then $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef, where $\{ D\} =\sum _ ia_ i\{ [D_ i]\} $. If $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a Kähler current, then $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. Proof. Near a point, let $h$ be smooth with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\theta $. Off the support of $D$ the function $v+h=(\varphi +h)-\sum _ ia_ i\log |s_ i|^2$ is plurisubharmonic, since $\log |s_ i|^2$ is pluriharmonic there, and it is bounded above. On a connected coordinate neighborhood of the point, the support of $D$ lies in the zero set of the holomorphic function $\prod _ is_ i\not\equiv 0$, so theorem 8.4.1 extends $v+h$ to a plurisubharmonic function $\widetilde v$. The values of $\widetilde v$ on the support of $D$ are upper limits of values of $v+h$, so $\widetilde v$ is bounded, and $\widetilde v=v+h$ outside the null set $\operatorname{Supp}D$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_ i|^2=[D_ i]$ (lemma A.2.16 ), the current $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ satisfies $T-[D]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\geq 0$ near the point, where $[D]=\sum _ ia_ i[D_ i]$. Thus $T-[D]$ is a positive current in $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ with locally bounded potentials. If $T\geq \delta \omega $, apply the same argument to $T-\delta \omega $, whose potential has the same logarithmic singularities; then $T-[D]\geq \delta \omega $. In both cases proposition 14.3.5 gives the assertion. $\square$

14.4 Minimal multiplicities and positivity loci Let $\alpha $ be a class in the pseudo-effective cone $\mathcal E$ and $	heta \in \alpha $ a smooth representative. For every $\varepsilon >0$ the class $\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is big, since it contains $T+\varepsilon \omega $ for every positive current $T\in \alpha $, and its potential $V_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega }$ with minimal singularities measures the positivity of $\alpha $ that remains after the curvature is allowed to drop by $\varepsilon \omega $. The loci where positivity fails are described in theorem 14.4.4 , and at the end of the section we compare positivity on $X$ and on a modification of $X$. Definition 14.4.1 . For $\alpha \in \mathcal E$, $x\in X$ and a prime divisor $D\subset X$ put \[

u (\alpha ,x)>0\} .  \] If $\alpha $ is big, its non-Kähler locus is \[  E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )= igcap _ T\{ \varphi _ T=-\infty \} ,  \] where $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T$ ranges over the Kähler currents in $\alpha $ for which $\varphi _ T$ has analytic singularities. For a class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ that is not big we put $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=X$, and for a class that is not pseudo-effective we put $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )=X$. Hence the minimal potentials decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, their Lelong numbers increase, and the suprema in the definition may be taken along $\varepsilon =1/j$. Replacing $	heta $ by another smooth representative $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ changes $V_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega }$ only by a bounded function, because $V_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega }-g$ and $V_{	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g+\varepsilon \omega }$ both have minimal singularities in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g+\varepsilon \omega )$; and replacing $\omega $ by another Kähler form $\omega '$ with $C^{-1}\omega \leq \omega '\leq C\omega $ places $V_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega '}$ between $V_{	heta +C^{-1}\varepsilon \omega }$ and $V_{	heta +C\varepsilon \omega }$. Thus the minimal multiplicities and the two loci depend only on $\alpha $. u (\alpha ,x)$, respectively $\alpha \mapsto 
u (\alpha ,D)$, is positively homogeneous, convex and lower semicontinuous on the pseudo-effective cone $\mathcal E$, and continuous on the big cone $\mathcal B$. Proof. We treat $

The proof for $D$ is the same, except that the additivity of Lelong numbers along $D$ is applied at a point of $D$ at which all the functions involved attain their generic Lelong numbers along $D$ (proposition 12.3.5 ). For $t>0$ we have $\mathrm{PSH}(X,t	heta +\varepsilon \omega )=t\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +(\varepsilon /t)\omega )$, hence $V_{t	heta +\varepsilon \omega }=tV_{	heta +(\varepsilon /t)\omega }$, and taking suprema over $\varepsilon $ gives $

If $\alpha _1,\alpha _2\in \mathcal E$ have representatives $	heta _1,	heta _2$, the sum of the minimal currents with allowance $\varepsilon $ in the two classes is a current $	heta _1+	heta _2+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(V_{	heta _1+\varepsilon \omega }+V_{	heta _2+\varepsilon \omega })\geq -2\varepsilon \omega $ in $\alpha _1+\alpha _2$. By minimality and additivity of Lelong numbers, \[  
u (V_{	heta _1+	heta _2+2\varepsilon \omega },x)\leq 
u (V_{	heta _1+\varepsilon \omega },x)+
u (V_{	heta _2+\varepsilon \omega },x)\leq

Let $\alpha _ j	o \alpha $ in $\mathcal E$, with representatives $	heta _ j$, and fix $\varepsilon >0$. For large $j$, by ( 14.16 ), the class $\alpha -\alpha _ j$ has a smooth representative $\eta _ j$ with $-\varepsilon \omega \leq \eta _ j\leq \varepsilon \omega $. The current $	heta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_{	heta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }+\eta _ j\in \alpha $ is at least $-2\varepsilon \omega $, and its potential relative to $	heta $ differs from $V_{	heta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }$ by a smooth function. By minimality, \[  
u (V_{	heta +2\varepsilon \omega },x)\leq 
u (V_{	heta _ j+\varepsilon \omega },x)\leq 
u (\alpha _ j,x)  \] for large $j$, so $
u (V_{	heta +2\varepsilon \omega },x)\leq \varliminf _ j
u (\alpha _ j,x)$. Taking the supremum over $\varepsilon $ proves lower semicontinuity. Finally, a convex function $f$ with finite values on an open convex subset $U$ of a finite-dimensional real vector space is continuous. Indeed, let $Q\subset U$ be a small closed cube; by convexity the function is bounded above on $Q$ by the maximum $M$ of its values at the vertices. If $c$ is the center of $Q$ and $c\pm v\in Q$, then $f(c+v)\geq 2f(c)-f(c-v)\geq 2f(c)-M$, so $f$ is also bounded below on $Q$. If $y,z$ lie in the concentric cube of half the size, extend the segment from $z$ to $y$ beyond $y$ to the point $w$ at distance $s$ from $y$, where $s$ is half the side length of the smaller cube, so that $w\in Q$. The slope inequality for convex functions gives $f(y)-f(z)\leq |y-z|(f(w)-f(y))/|w-y|\leq |y-z|(M-\inf _ Qf)/s$, and by symmetry $f$ is Lipschitz on the smaller cube. Applied to the open convex cone $\mathcal B$, this proves continuity there. $\square$ Theorem 14.4.4 . Let $\alpha \in \mathcal E$. Then the non-nef locus $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )$ is a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $X$, and it is empty if and only if $\alpha $ is nef. If $\alpha $ is big, then $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$ is the pole set of the potential of a single Kähler current in $\alpha $ with analytic singularities; it is a proper analytic subset of $X$, it contains $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )$, and it is empty if and only if $\alpha $ is Kähler. Finally, for every class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$, 14.21  egin{equation} \label{eq:non-kahler-non-nef-allowance} E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=  igcap _{\varepsilon >0}E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha -\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ). \end{equation} Proof. The non-nef locus. By the monotonicity in $\varepsilon $, $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )$ is the union over positive integers $j,k$ of the sets $\{ x:
u (V_{	heta +\omega /j},x)\geq 1/k\} $. Each of them is analytic by theorem 12.3.4 , and proper, because it is contained in the pole set of $V_{	heta +\omega /j}$. If $\alpha $ is nef, then $\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is Kähler for every $\varepsilon >0$, so $V_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega }$ is bounded by corollary 14.3.6 and all these Lelong numbers vanish. Conversely, suppose that $
u (V_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega },x)=0$ for all $x\in X$ and $\varepsilon >0$. By corollary 12.3.2 , $\mathcal I(mV_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega })$ is the unit ideal at every point, so the approximations $G_ m$ of lemma 13.4.1 for the background $	heta +\varepsilon \omega $ are smooth and satisfy $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq -(\varepsilon +c/m)\omega $. Hence $\alpha $ is nef. Realization of the non-Kähler locus. Let $\alpha $ be big. Kähler currents with analytic singularities exist in $\alpha $ by proposition 14.3.5 , and their pole sets are closed analytic subsets of $X$. Since $X$ has a countable basis, countably many of the open complements of these pole sets already have the same union as all of them: for every element of a countable basis that is contained in one of these complements, choose one such complement. The intersection of the corresponding countably many pole sets $Z_1,Z_2,\ldots $ is therefore $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. Let $\mathcal I_{Z_ k}$ be the ideal sheaf of $Z_ k$, which is coherent by theorem A.2.8 . The increasing sequence of coherent ideals $\mathcal I_{Z_1}+\cdots +\mathcal I_{Z_ k}$, whose zero sets are $Z_1\cap \cdots \cap Z_ k$, is stationary on the compact manifold $X$ by lemma 12.2.4 . Hence $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=Z_1\cap \cdots \cap Z_ N$ for some $N$. Let $T_ k=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ k$, $k\leq N$, be the corresponding Kähler currents, and choose $\delta >0$ with $T_ k\geq \delta \omega $ for all $k\leq N$. Then $\varphi =\max _ k\varphi _ k$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )$, it has analytic singularities by proposition 13.1.7 , and its pole set is exactly $Z_1\cap \cdots \cap Z_ N=E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. Thus $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a Kähler current realizing $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$, which is a proper analytic subset because $\varphi $ is finite almost everywhere. If $
u (\alpha ,x)>0$, then $
u (\varphi ,x)\geq 
u (V_	heta ,x)=
u (\alpha ,x)>0$ by minimality of $V_	heta $ and proposition 14.4.2 , so $\varphi (x)=-\infty $; hence $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. If $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=\varnothing $, the potential $\varphi $ just constructed has analytic singularities and no poles, so it is bounded, and proposition 14.3.5 shows that $\alpha $ is Kähler. Conversely, if $\alpha $ contains a Kähler form $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, then $u$ is smooth and has analytic singularities without poles, so $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=\varnothing $. Hence $\alpha $ is big and $x

This proves ( 14.21 ); the argument also shows that $\alpha $ is big as soon as the right-hand side of ( 14.21 ) is not all of $X$, so the formula is consistent with the convention $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=X$ for classes that are not big. $\square$ We now turn to modifications. Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map from a Kähler manifold $Y$, with Kähler form $\omega _ Y$. By proposition 14.2.8 , $Y$ is compact and connected, so the results above apply on $Y$. Pullback of smooth forms induces a linear map $\pi ^*\colon H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)	o H^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb R)$. Pushforward of currents, $(\pi _*S)(\chi )=S(\pi ^*\chi )$, maps closed real $(1,1)$-currents on $Y$ to closed real $(1,1)$-currents on $X$, preserves positivity, and satisfies $\pi _*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\pi _*f$ for distributions $f$ (proposition 7.5.1 ); hence it induces a linear map $\pi _*\colon H^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb R)	o H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ with $\pi _*\{ S\} =\{ \pi _*S\} $. If $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a closed positive current on $X$ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, the pullbacks $(\varphi +h)\circ \pi $ of its local potentials, where $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $, are not identically $-\infty $, because $\varphi \circ \pi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$ by proposition 14.2.8 . Hence the pullback $\pi ^*T$ of proposition 7.5.4 is defined, and \[  \pi ^*T=\pi ^*	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi \circ \pi ),\qquad \{ \pi ^*T\} =\pi ^*\{ T\} .  \] For a prime divisor $E\subset Y$, the image $\pi (E)$ is an analytic subset of $X$ by Remmert's theorem (theorem A.6.2 ), and it is irreducible: if $\pi (E)=A_1\cup A_2$ with analytic subsets $A_1,A_2$, then $E=(E\cap \pi ^{-1}(A_1))\cup (E\cap \pi ^{-1}(A_2))$, so $E\subset \pi ^{-1}(A_ i)$ for some $i$ and $\pi (E)=A_ i$. The divisor $E$ is exceptional for $\pi $ if $\pi (E)$ has codimension at least two in $X$. Fix an analytic subset $A\subset X$ of codimension at least two outside which $\pi $ is an isomorphism (proposition A.7.3 ). We show that a prime divisor $E$ of $Y$ is exceptional if and only if $E\subset \pi ^{-1}(A)$. If $E\subset \pi ^{-1}(A)$, then $\pi (E)\subset A$ and $E$ is exceptional. Otherwise $E\cap \pi ^{-1}(A)$ is an analytic subset of $E$ different from $E$; it contains no nonempty open subset of the connected manifold $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, by the identity theorem, so it is nowhere dense in $E$. Then $\pi $ maps the dense open subset $E\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$ of $E$, a complex hypersurface of $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$, isomorphically onto $\pi (E)\setminus A$, which is therefore a complex hypersurface of $X\setminus A$ and is dense in $\pi (E)$, because $\pi (E)$ is the image of the closure of $E\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$ under the closed map $\pi $. Hence $\pi (E)$ is an irreducible analytic subset of codimension one, that is, a prime divisor $D$, and $E$ is not exceptional; this proves the claim. Moreover, $E$ is the strict transform of $D$, since the closure of $\pi ^{-1}(D\setminus A)=E\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$ is $E$. By the claim and ( 14.20 ), applied on $Y$, every exceptional prime divisor is an irreducible component of $\pi ^{-1}(A)$, while every other prime divisor $E$ of $Y$ is the strict transform of the prime divisor $\pi (E)$ of $X$, and $\pi $ is an isomorphism near the points of $E$ outside $\pi ^{-1}(A)$. Proposition 14.4.5 . Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be as above. Then $\pi ^*$ maps nef classes to nef classes, and $\pi _*$ maps modified nef classes to modified nef classes. The pushforward of a non-divisorial closed positive current on $Y$ is non-divisorial. Proof. By lemma 13.1.1 on the compact manifold $Y$, $\pi ^*\omega \leq C\omega _ Y$ for a constant $C$. If $	heta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ are nef representatives of a class on $X$, then $\pi ^*	heta _\varepsilon \geq -C\varepsilon \omega _ Y$, so the pullback class is nef. Let $S$ be a non-divisorial closed positive current on $Y$ and $D\subset X$ a prime divisor, with strict transform $D'$. Over $X\setminus A$ the map $\pi $ is a biholomorphism, which identifies $\pi _*S$ with $S$ and $D\setminus A$ with $D'\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$, and Lelong numbers are invariant under biholomorphisms (proposition 12.1.1 ). The generic value of the Lelong numbers of $S$ along $D'$ is attained on a dense subset of $D'$ (proposition 12.3.5 ), hence at some point $y$ of the nonempty open subset $D'\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$. Therefore $
u (\pi _*S,D)\leq 
u (\pi _*S,\pi (y))=
u (S,y)=
u (S,D')=0$. Hence $\pi _*S$ is non-divisorial. Let $ eta $ be a modified nef class on $Y$ and $t>0$. The class $ eta +t\{ \omega _ Y\} $ is big, and it is modified nef because $\mathcal{MN}$ is a convex cone containing the Kähler classes. By proposition 14.4.2 , a positive current with minimal singularities in this class is non-divisorial. Its pushforward is a non-divisorial positive current in $\pi _* eta +t\pi _*\{ \omega _ Y\} $, so this class is modified nef: the definition is satisfied with $T_\varepsilon $ equal to this current for every $\varepsilon $. These classes tend to $\pi _* eta $ as $t\downarrow 0$, and $\mathcal{MN}$ is closed, so $\pi _* eta $ is modified nef. $\square$ Lemma 14.4.6 . Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be as above, and let $S$ be a non-divisorial closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $Y$. Then \[  \pi ^*\pi _*S=S+\sum _ E c_ E[E],\qquad c_ E\geq 0,  \] where $E$ ranges over the finitely many exceptional prime divisors of $\pi $. For every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, $\pi _*\pi ^*T=T$. For a prime divisor $E$ on $Y$, $\pi _*[E]=0$ if $E$ is exceptional, and $\pi _*[E]=[\pi (E)]$ otherwise. Proof. Let $A$ be as above. The positive current $\pi ^*\pi _*S$, defined through local potentials as above, agrees with $S$ on $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$. Their difference is a closed real current with measure coefficients supported on the proper analytic subset $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ of $Y$. By theorem A.2.17 , it is a finite real linear combination of the currents of integration along the irreducible components of codimension one of the compact analytic set $\pi ^{-1}(A)$, which are exactly the exceptional prime divisors, as shown above; there are finitely many of them by corollary A.2.13 . It remains to show that the coefficients $c_ E$ are nonnegative. Near a regular point of an exceptional prime divisor $E$ that lies on no other component, the difference is $c_ E[E]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(c_ E\log |s_ E|^2)$, where $s_ E$ is a local equation of $E$ (lemma A.2.16 ), so local potentials $u'$ of $\pi ^*\pi _*S$ and $u$ of $S$ satisfy $u'=u+c_ E\log |s_ E|^2+p$ with $p$ pluriharmonic. The additivity of Lelong numbers (proposition 12.1.4 ), applied to this identity if $c_ E\geq 0$ and to $u=u'+|c_ E|\log |s_ E|^2-p$ otherwise, together with $
u (\log |s_ E|^2,y)=1$, gives $
u (u',y)=
u (u,y)+c_ E$ at such points $y$. At points that are moreover generic for both currents, which exist because the points of $E$ excluded by these conditions form a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $E$ (proposition 12.3.5 ), this reads $
u (\pi ^*\pi _*S,E)=
u (S,E)+c_ E$; hence $c_ E=
u (\pi ^*\pi _*S,E)\geq 0$, since $S$ is non-divisorial. Since $\pi $ is a biholomorphism over $X\setminus A$, the positive current $\pi _*\pi ^*T$ agrees with $T$ on $X\setminus A$. Hence $\pi _*\pi ^*T-T$ is a closed real current with measure coefficients (theorem 7.2.5 ) supported on $A$, which has codimension at least two, so it vanishes by theorem A.2.17 . For a prime divisor $E$ on $Y$, the current $\pi _*[E]$ is positive, closed and supported on the analytic set $\pi (E)$. If $E$ is exceptional, $\pi (E)$ has codimension at least two and $\pi _*[E]=0$ by the same theorem. Otherwise $\pi $ maps $E\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$ isomorphically onto $\pi (E)\setminus A$, so $\pi _*[E]=[\pi (E)]$ on $X\setminus A$, and the closed current $\pi _*[E]-[\pi (E)]$ of order zero is supported on $\pi (E)\cap A$, of codimension at least two in $X$; it vanishes by the same theorem. $\square$ Proposition 14.4.7 . Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be as above. Then $\pi ^*$ and $\pi _*$ map big classes to big classes. Proof. Choose $C$ with $\pi ^*\omega \leq C\omega _ Y$. Since $\pi _*$ preserves positivity, lemma 14.4.6 gives $\pi _*\omega _ Y\geq C^{-1}\pi _*\pi ^*\omega =C^{-1}\omega $. Hence a current $S\geq \delta \omega _ Y$ on $Y$ has $\pi _*S\geq \delta C^{-1}\omega $, which proves the assertion for $\pi _*$. Let $\alpha $ be big on $X$ and $T\in \alpha $ with $T\geq \delta \omega $. Choose a smooth closed representative $\eta $ of the class $\{ \pi _*\omega _ Y\} $, a constant $B>0$ with $\eta \leq B\omega $ (lemma 13.1.1 ), and $t>0$ with $tB\leq \delta $, so that $T-t\eta \geq 0$. The positive current $T-t\eta +t\pi _*\omega _ Y$ lies in $\alpha $. u (\alpha ,x)\leq 
u (V_	heta ,x)$, since the proof of equality uses a Kähler current in $\alpha $.

Theorem 14.4.4 . Let $\alpha \in \mathcal E$. Proposition 14.4.5 . Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be as above. Then $\pi ^*$ maps nef classes to nef classes, and $\pi _*$ maps modified nef classes to modified nef classes.
