section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text:
Lemma 14.6.1 . Let $\sigma $, $F$ and $h$ be as above, let $\gamma $ be a real $(1,1)$-form on $M$, let $x\in M$, and let $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ be a $\sigma $-unitary coframe at $x$ in which $\gamma =\mathrm i\sum _ j\lambda _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$. Put $e=	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$. For an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector $v=\sum _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ at $x$ we have $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v=\sum _ j\lambda _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ and $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}=\sum _ j\lambda _ j|v_ j|_ h^2$. In particular, $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]$ is positive semidefinite on $(n,1)$-covectors at $x$ if $\gamma \geq 0$ at $x$, and positive definite if $\gamma $ is positive definite at $x$. If $\alpha $ is a $(1,0)$-covector and $u$ an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-covector at $x$, then $|\langle  ar\alpha \wedge u,vangle _{\sigma ,h}|^2\leq |u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \langle [\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}$ for every $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector $v$ at $x$. Let $\gamma $ be positive definite at $x$, and let $g$ be an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector at $x$. Then the $(n,n)$-covector $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\, \mathrm dV_\sigma $ does not depend on the Hermitian form $\sigma $, and neither does $|u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma $ for an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-covector $u$ at $x$. If $\gamma \geq a\sigma $ at $x$ for a constant $a>0$, then $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\leq a^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2$. If $\sigma '$ is a second Hermitian form with $\sigma '\geq c\sigma $ at $x$ for a constant $c>0$, then $|g|_{\sigma ',h}^2\, \mathrm dV_{\sigma '}\leq c^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma $. Proof. In linear coordinates at $x$ with $\mathrm dz_ j=\sqrt2\, 	heta _ j$ we have $\sigma = rac{\mathrm i}{2}\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j=\sum _ j\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$ at $x$, so the Riemannian metric of $\sigma $ at $x$ is Euclidean in the real coordinates, and $\langle \mathrm dx_ j+\mathrm i\, \mathrm dy_ j,\mathrm dx_ k\pm \mathrm i\, \mathrm dy_ kangle =(1\pm 1)\delta _{jk}$ shows that the covectors $	heta _ j, ar	heta _ k$ form an orthonormal basis of the complexified cotangent space at $x$. Hence the products $	heta _ I\wedge  ar	heta _ J$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex covectors at $x$. Let $\iota _ j$ and $ ar\iota _ j$ be the adjoints of the exterior products with $	heta _ j$ and $ ar	heta _ j$; thus $\iota _ j$ maps $	heta _ j\wedge 	heta _ K\wedge  ar	heta _ L$ to $	heta _ K\wedge  ar	heta _ L$ for $j
otin K$ and annihilates the basis covectors that do not contain $	heta _ j$, and similarly for $ ar\iota _ j$. Since $\sigma \wedge {}$ is $\mathrm i\sum _ j(	heta _ j\wedge )( ar	heta _ j\wedge )$, its adjoint is $\Lambda _\sigma =-\mathrm i\sum _ j ar\iota _ j\iota _ j$. (1) The covector $\gamma \wedge v$ has bidegree $(n+1,2)$ and vanishes, so $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v=\gamma \wedge \Lambda _\sigma v$. We have $\iota _ j(e\wedge  ar	heta _ k)=(-1)^{j-1}	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n\wedge  ar	heta _ k$, and $ ar\iota _ j$ maps this to $(-1)^{j+n}\delta _{jk}\, 	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$, the factor $ ar	heta _ k$ standing in the $n$th place. Hence $\Lambda _\sigma v=-\mathrm i\sum _ j(-1)^{j+n}v_ j\, 	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$. In the product of the $j$th term with $\gamma $ only $\mathrm i\lambda _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ contributes, and $	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j\wedge 	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n=(-1)^{n-j}e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$; so $\gamma \wedge \Lambda _\sigma v=\sum _ j\lambda _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$. Since the covectors $e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ are orthonormal, this gives the formula for $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}$, and the last assertion follows because the $\lambda _ j$ are nonnegative if $\gamma \geq 0$ and positive if $\gamma $ is positive definite. (2) We may assume that $\alpha 
eq 0$. Since the assertion does not involve $\gamma $, we may choose the $\sigma $-unitary coframe with $	heta _1=\alpha /|\alpha |_\sigma $, by completing this unit covector to an orthonormal basis of the $(1,0)$-covectors. Then $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha =\mathrm i|\alpha |_\sigma ^2	heta _1\wedge  ar	heta _1$, so (1) gives $\langle [\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}=|\alpha |_\sigma ^2|v_1|_ h^2$. Writing $u=fe$, we have $ ar\alpha \wedge u=(-1)^ n|\alpha |_\sigma f\, e\wedge  ar	heta _1$, hence $|\langle  ar\alpha \wedge u,vangle _{\sigma ,h}|\leq |\alpha |_\sigma |f|_ h|v_1|_ h$, and $|f|_ h=|u|_{\sigma ,h}$. (3) Write $g=e\wedge 	au =\sum _ j	au _ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ with an $F$-valued $(0,1)$-covector $	au =\sum _ j	au _ j ar	heta _ j$. By (1), $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}=\sum _ j|	au _ j|_ h^2/\lambda _ j=|	au |_\gamma ^2$, the squared norm of $	au $ in the metric induced by $\gamma $ on $(0,1)$-covectors, which does not involve $\sigma $. Moreover $\mathrm dV_\sigma =\sigma ^ n/n!=c_ n\, e\wedge  ar e$ with $c_ n=\mathrm i^ n(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$. Hence $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\, \mathrm dV_\sigma =c_ n|	au |_\gamma ^2\, e\wedge  ar e$. If $\kappa =\mu ^{-1}e$, $\mu 
eq 0$, is another nonzero $(n,0)$-covector, then $g=\kappa \wedge \mu 	au $ and $c_ n|\mu 	au |_\gamma ^2\, \kappa \wedge  ar\kappa =c_ n|	au |_\gamma ^2\, e\wedge  ar e$. Thus the density equals $c_ n|	au '|_\gamma ^2\, \kappa \wedge  ar\kappa $ whenever $g=\kappa \wedge 	au '$, an expression that does not involve $\sigma $. In the same way, $|u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma =c_ n|f|_ h^2\, \kappa \wedge  ar\kappa $ for $u=f\kappa $. If $\gamma \geq a\sigma $, all $\lambda _ j$ are at least $a$, and $\sum _ j|	au _ j|_ h^2/\lambda _ j\leq a^{-1}\sum _ j|	au _ j|_ h^2=a^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2$. Finally, the eigenvalues of $\sigma '$ with respect to $\sigma '$ itself are all equal to one, so $[\sigma ',\Lambda _{\sigma '}]$ is the identity on $(n,1)$-covectors by (1), and the independence just proved gives \[   egin{aligned}  |g|_{\sigma ',h}^2\, \mathrm dV_{\sigma '}& =\langle [\sigma ',\Lambda _{\sigma '}]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ',h}\, \mathrm dV_{\sigma '}\ & =\langle [\sigma ',\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\, \mathrm dV_\sigma \leq c^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma \end{aligned}  \] if $\sigma '\geq c\sigma $. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.6.2
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.6.2 . Let $M$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Kähler form $\sigma $, and let $F\to M$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h$. In a holomorphic frame of $F$ with squared norm $\mathrm e^{-p}$, let $D'=\partial -\partial p\wedge $ and $D''=\bar\partial $, acting on the coefficients of $F$-valued forms; these are the components of the Chern connection, and they do not depend on the frame. Let $D'{}^*,D''{}^*$ be their formal adjoints for $\sigma $ and $h$, and put $B_\sigma =[2\pi c_1(F,h),\Lambda _\sigma ]$. Then, for every compactly supported smooth $F$-valued $(n,1)$-form $v$, 14.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:kahler-bundle-bochner} \| D''{}^*v\| _\sigma ^2+\| D''v\| _\sigma ^2 =\| D'{}^*v\| _\sigma ^2+ \int _ M\langle B_\sigma v,v\rangle _\sigma \, \mathrm dV_\sigma . \end{equation} Proof. If $e'=ge$ is a second holomorphic frame, with $g$ holomorphic and nowhere zero, then its weight is $p'=p-\log |g|^2$, and for a form $u'$ we have $\partial (gu')-\partial p\wedge gu'=g(\partial u'-\partial p'\wedge u')$, since $\partial \log |g|^2=g^{-1}\partial g$; so $D'$ does not depend on the frame. In a frame we have $D'D''+D''D'=\partial \bar\partial p\wedge $, and $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial p=2\pi c_1(F,h)$. We prove the Kähler identities at a point, in coordinates and a frame adapted to $\sigma $ and $h$, and deduce the Bochner–Kodaira formula from them. Fix a point, choose holomorphic coordinates centered at it in which $\sigma =\mathrm i\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ at the point and the first derivatives of the coefficients of $\sigma $ vanish there (lemma 14.1.5 , after replacing the coordinates $z$ by $z/\sqrt2$), and a frame with $\partial p=0$ at the point: replacing a frame $e$ by $e\exp (\sum _ j\partial _ jp(0)z_ j)$ replaces $p$ by $p-2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ j\partial _ jp(0)z_ j$. Let $\epsilon _ k,\bar\epsilon _ k$ denote exterior multiplication by $\mathrm dz_ k,\mathrm d\bar z_ k$, and $\iota _ k,\bar\iota _ k$ their pointwise adjoints, the contractions. At the point they satisfy $\iota _ j\epsilon _ k+\epsilon _ k\iota _ j=\delta _{jk}$ and $\bar\iota _ j\bar\epsilon _ k+\bar\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ j=\delta _{jk}$, while operators of different types anticommute; moreover $\Lambda _\sigma =-\mathrm i\sum _ j\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j$, as the adjoint of $\mathrm i\sum _ j\epsilon _ j\bar\epsilon _ j$. The formal adjoints of $\sum _ k\epsilon _ k\partial _ k$ and $\sum _ k\bar\epsilon _ k\partial _{\bar k}$ are $-\sum _ k\iota _ k\partial _{\bar k}$ and $-\sum _ k\bar\iota _ k\partial _ k$, with $\iota _ k,\bar\iota _ k$ computed for the metric at each point, plus zero-order terms whose coefficients are linear in the first derivatives of the coefficients of $\sigma $ and of $\mathrm e^{-p}$. Indeed, in the frame $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ the operators $\epsilon _ k$ have constant matrices, and the pointwise inner product of $F$-valued forms times the density of $\mathrm dV_\sigma $ is $\overline w^{\mathsf T}Hu$ for a smooth positive definite Hermitian matrix $H$ whose entries are smooth functions of the coefficients of $\sigma $ times $\mathrm e^{-p}$. For a constant matrix $A$ and compactly supported smooth $u,w$, integration by parts and $\partial _ k\overline w=\overline{\partial _{\bar k}w}$ give $\int \overline w^{\mathsf T}HA\, \partial _ ku=-\int \overline{(\partial _{\bar k}w)}^{\mathsf T}HAu-\int \overline w^{\mathsf T}(\partial _ kH)Au$, so the formal adjoint of $A\partial _ k$ is $-A^\dagger \partial _{\bar k}-H^{-1}A^*(\partial _{\bar k}H)$, where $A^\dagger =H^{-1}A^*H$ is the pointwise adjoint of $A$ and $A^*$ the conjugate transpose; the same computation applies with $\partial _ k$ and $\partial _{\bar k}$ exchanged. Since these first derivatives, and $\partial p$, vanish at the point, there \[  D'=\sum _ k\epsilon _ k\partial _ k,\quad D''=\sum _ k\bar\epsilon _ k\partial _{\bar k},\quad D'{}^*=-\sum _ k\iota _ k\partial _{\bar k},\quad D''{}^*=-\sum _ k\bar\iota _ k\partial _ k,  \] where $\partial _ k,\partial _{\bar k}$ act on the coefficients. The anticommutation rules give $\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j\epsilon _ k-\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j=\delta _{jk}\bar\iota _ j$ and $\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j\bar\epsilon _ k-\bar\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j=-\delta _{jk}\iota _ j$, hence $[\Lambda _\sigma ,D']=-\mathrm i\sum _ k\bar\iota _ k\partial _ k$ and $[\Lambda _\sigma ,D'']=\mathrm i\sum _ k\iota _ k\partial _{\bar k}$ at the point, since the coefficients of $\Lambda _\sigma $ in the frame $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ have vanishing first derivatives there. These are the Kähler identities \[  D''{}^*=-\mathrm i[\Lambda _\sigma ,D'],\qquad D'{}^*=\mathrm i[\Lambda _\sigma ,D''],  \] which therefore hold everywhere, the point being arbitrary. Substituting them into $\Delta ''=D''D''{}^*+D''{}^*D''$ and $\Delta '=D'D'{}^*+D'{}^*D'$, the mixed compositions $D''\Lambda _\sigma D'$ and $D'\Lambda _\sigma D''$ cancel in the difference, and the curvature identity gives the Bochner–Kodaira formula \[  \Delta ''-\Delta '=\mathrm i\bigl [D'D''+D''D',\Lambda _\sigma \bigr ]=[2\pi c_1(F,h),\Lambda _\sigma ],  \] that is, $\Delta ''-\Delta '=B_\sigma $. For a compactly supported smooth $(n,1)$-form $v$, the form $D'v$ vanishes for degree reasons, and integrating $\langle (\Delta ''-\Delta ')v,v\rangle _\sigma $ over $M$, using the definition of the formal adjoints, gives ( 14.25 ). $\square$

section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: 14.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:kahler-bundle-bochner} \| D''{}^*v\| _\sigma ^2+\| D''v\| _\sigma ^2 =\| D'{}^*v\| _\sigma ^2+ \int _ M\langle B_\sigma v,v\rangle _\sigma \, \mathrm dV_\sigma . \end{equation}

title: Lemma 14.6.3
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.6.3 . Let $M$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Hermitian form $\sigma $, and suppose that there are functions $\chi _ R\in C^\infty _ c(M)$, $R\geq 1$, with $0\leq \chi _ R\leq 1$, $\chi _ R\to 1$ pointwise as $R\to \infty $, and $|\mathrm d\chi _ R|_\sigma \leq C/R$ for a constant $C$. Let $F\to M$ be a holomorphic line bundle with smooth quadratic metrics $h_0,h_1,h_2$ such that the positive functions $h_1/h_0$ and $h_2/h_1$ are bounded on $M$, and let \[  T\colon L^2_{(n,0)}(\sigma ,h_0)\to L^2_{(n,1)}(\sigma ,h_1),\qquad S\colon L^2_{(n,1)}(\sigma ,h_1)\to L^2_{(n,2)}(\sigma ,h_2)  \] be the operators $D''=\bar\partial $ with maximal distributional domains, where the spaces $L^2_{(n,q)}(\sigma ,h_ k)$ of $F$-valued $(n,q)$-forms are defined by the pointwise norms of $\sigma $ and $h_ k$ and the volume form $\mathrm dV_\sigma =\sigma ^ n/n!$. Then $T$ and $S$ are closed and densely defined, and $ST=0$. Every compactly supported smooth $F$-valued $(n,1)$-form $v$ lies in $\operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$, and $T^*v=\delta v$, where $\delta $ is the formal adjoint of $\bar\partial $ for the pointwise inner products of $(\sigma ,h_0)$ on $(n,0)$-forms and of $(\sigma ,h_1)$ on $(n,1)$-forms. Compactly supported smooth $F$-valued $(n,1)$-forms are dense in $\operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$ for the graph norm $\| v\| +\| T^*v\| +\| Sv\| $. Proof. On a compact subset of a coordinate chart over which $F$ has a holomorphic frame, the pointwise norms of $\sigma $ and $h_ k$ are comparable with the Euclidean norms of the coefficients, and $\mathrm dV_\sigma $ with Lebesgue measure. Hence convergence in $L^2_{(n,q)}(\sigma ,h_ k)$ implies $L^2$ convergence of the coefficients on such sets, and therefore convergence in the sense of distributions; since $\bar\partial $ is continuous for distributional convergence, $T$ and $S$ are closed. Compactly supported smooth forms belong to $\operatorname{Dom}T$ and $\operatorname{Dom}S$, and they are dense in $L^2_{(n,0)}(\sigma ,h_0)$ and in $L^2_{(n,1)}(\sigma ,h_1)$: if $(\psi _ a)$ is a partition of unity with compact supports in such charts (proposition 7.1.3 ), then an $L^2$ form $u$ is the $L^2$ limit of the finite partial sums of $\sum _ a\psi _ au$, by dominated convergence, and each $\psi _ au$ is the $L^2$ limit of the forms whose coefficients are the mollifications of those of $\psi _ au$, by lemma 1.4.1 . Thus $T$ and $S$ are densely defined, and $ST=0$ because $\bar\partial \bar\partial =0$ on distributions. If $v$ is a compactly supported smooth $(n,1)$-form and $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, then $\langle Tu,v\rangle $ is the value of the distribution $\bar\partial u$ on a smooth compactly supported form built from $v$, and the definition of the distributional derivative gives $\langle Tu,v\rangle =\langle u,\delta v\rangle $; hence $v\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*v=\delta v$. For an arbitrary $v\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, testing with compactly supported smooth $u$ shows in the same way that $T^*v=\delta v$ in the sense of distributions, and $Sv=\bar\partial v$ in the sense of distributions for $v\in \operatorname{Dom}S$ by definition. For the density, multiplication by the cutoffs $\chi _ R$ first reduces the problem to forms with compact support. Let $v\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$ and $\chi =\chi _ R$. For $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, the Leibniz rule for distributions gives $\chi u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $T(\chi u)=\chi Tu+\bar\partial \chi \wedge u$, so that $\langle Tu,\chi v\rangle =\langle T(\chi u),v\rangle -\langle \bar\partial \chi \wedge u,v\rangle =\langle u,\chi T^*v-(\bar\partial \chi \wedge )^*v\rangle $, where $(\bar\partial \chi \wedge )^*$ is the adjoint of the bounded operator $\bar\partial \chi \wedge $ from $L^2_{(n,0)}(\sigma ,h_0)$ to $L^2_{(n,1)}(\sigma ,h_1)$. Hence $\chi v\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*(\chi v)=\chi T^*v-(\bar\partial \chi \wedge )^*v$; and the Leibniz rule gives $\chi v\in \operatorname{Dom}S$ with $S(\chi v)=\chi Sv+\bar\partial \chi \wedge v$. Since $|\bar\partial \chi _ R|_\sigma \leq |\mathrm d\chi _ R|_\sigma \leq C/R$ and the ratios $h_1/h_0$ and $h_2/h_1$ are bounded, the error terms have norm at most $C'\| v\| /R$, and $\chi _ Rv\to v$, $\chi _ RT^*v\to T^*v$, $\chi _ RSv\to Sv$ by dominated convergence. Second, a compactly supported form is approximated by local convolutions, after a finite partition of unity (proposition 7.1.3 ). For a first-order operator $P=\sum _ la_ l(x)\partial _ l+b(x)$ with smooth matrix coefficients and a mollifier $\rho _ t$, the commutator $[P,\rho _ t*\, \cdot \, ]$ applied to $v$ equals \[  \begin{aligned} & \sum _ l\int (a_ l(x)-a_ l(y))\, \partial _ l\rho _ t(x-y)\, v(y)\, \mathrm dy\\ & \qquad +\sum _ l\int (\partial _ l a_ l)(y)\, \rho _ t(x-y)\, v(y)\, \mathrm dy +\bigl (b\, (\rho _ t*v)-\rho _ t*(bv)\bigr ). \end{aligned}  \] On a fixed compact set, the mean-value bound $|a_ l(x)-a_ l(y)|\leq C|x-y|$ and the scaling of $\rho _ t$ bound the kernels of these integral operators by $k_ t(x-y)$, where $\int k_ t$ is bounded independently of $t$. An integral operator with a kernel bounded by $k(x-y)$, $k\geq 0$ integrable, has norm at most $\int k$ on $L^2$, since by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\int k(x-y)v(y)\, \mathrm dy|^2\leq \int k\cdot \int k(x-y)|v(y)|^2\, \mathrm dy$; so these operators are bounded on $L^2$ uniformly in $t$. For smooth $v$ the commutator tends to zero in $L^2$, and by the uniform bound and the density of smooth functions in $L^2$ it tends to zero for every $v\in L^2$. Now let $v\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$ have compact support, and let $(\psi _ a)$ be a finite partition of unity near $\operatorname{Supp}v$ by functions with compact supports in charts over which $F$ has frames. By the product rules above, with $\psi _ a$ in place of $\chi $, each $w=\psi _ av$ lies in $\operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$. In the chart and frame, $\delta $ and $\bar\partial $ are first-order operators with smooth matrix coefficients, and $T^*w=\delta w$ and $Sw=\bar\partial w$ lie in $L^2$. The forms $w_ t$ whose coefficients are the mollifications of those of $w$ are smooth with compact support, so $T^*w_ t=\delta w_ t=\rho _ t*(\delta w)+[\delta ,\rho _ t*\, \cdot \, ]w$ and $Sw_ t=\rho _ t*(\bar\partial w)+[\bar\partial ,\rho _ t*\, \cdot \, ]w$. By lemma 1.4.1 and the commutator bound, $w_ t\to w$ in the graph norm as $t\to 0$, which proves the density. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.6.4
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.6.4 . Let $\psi $ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ that is smooth outside its pole set $A=\{ \psi =-\infty \} $. Then there are a Kähler form $\sigma \geq \omega /2$ on $X\setminus A$ and functions $\chi _ R\in C^\infty _ c(X\setminus A)$, $R\geq 1$, with $0\leq \chi _ R\leq 1$, $\chi _ R\to 1$ pointwise as $R\to \infty $, and $|\mathrm d\chi _ R|_\sigma \leq C/R$ for a constant $C$. This applies in particular when $\psi $ is a finite sum of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions with gentle analytic singularities and of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions that are smooth outside a point $x_ k$ and equal to $c_ k\log |z-z(x_ k)|^2$ plus a smooth function near $x_ k$, in local coordinates, with $c_ k>0$; then $A$ is the union of their pole sets. Proof. The set $A$ is a null set, since $\psi $ is locally integrable, and in particular $A\neq X$. Choose $b\geq 0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq -b\omega $, which is possible by lemma 13.1.4 (4), and subtract a constant so that $\psi <-2b-2$; this is possible because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$. Put $\rho =-\log (-\psi )$ on $X\setminus A$. The chain rule gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho =-\frac1\psi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi + \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi \psi ^2}\partial \psi \wedge \bar\partial \psi .  \] Since $0<-1/\psi <1/(2b+2)$, the first term is at least $-\omega /2$, and since $\partial \rho =-\partial \psi /\psi $, the form $\sigma =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ satisfies \[  \sigma \geq \frac\omega 2+\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \rho \wedge \bar\partial \rho .  \] It is a Kähler form on $X\setminus A$. The rank-one form $\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \rho \wedge \bar\partial \rho $ has, in a $\sigma $-unitary coframe, the single eigenvalue $|\partial \rho |_\sigma ^2/(2\pi )$, so the last inequality gives $|\partial \rho |_\sigma ^2\leq 2\pi $; hence $|\mathrm d\rho |_\sigma $ is bounded by a numerical constant. The function $-\rho =\log (-\psi )$ tends to $+\infty $ at $A$, because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous and equal to $-\infty $ on $A$, and its sublevel sets $\{ -\rho \leq t\} =\{ \psi \geq -\mathrm e^ t\} $ are closed in $X$, because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous, and disjoint from $A$; so they are compact subsets of $X\setminus A$. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ on $\mathbb R$ equal to one on $(-\infty ,1]$ and to zero on $[2,\infty )$, with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, and put $\chi _ R=\chi (-\rho /R)$. Then $\chi _ R$ has compact support in $X\setminus A$, equals one on $\{ -\rho \leq R\} $, and $|\mathrm d\chi _ R|_\sigma \leq \sup |\chi '|\, |\mathrm d\rho |_\sigma /R$. The same gradient bound shows that every path in $X\setminus A$ that eventually leaves every compact subset of $X\setminus A$ has infinite $\sigma $-length, since $-\rho $ tends to $+\infty $ along it, by the compactness of its sublevel sets. For the last assertion, recall that a function $\varphi $ with gentle analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathfrak a)$ is smooth outside its pole set, where it equals $c$ times the logarithm of the smooth positive function $\exp (\varphi /c)$ (definition 13.1.11 ). Hence a finite sum as in the statement is quasi-plurisubharmonic and smooth outside the union of the pole sets of its terms, and this union is its pole set, since all terms are bounded above. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.6.5
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.6.5 . Let $M$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Hermitian form $\omega $ and the volume form $\mathrm dV=\omega ^ n/n!$, and let $F\to M$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h$ such that $c_1(F,h)\geq a\omega $ for a constant $a>0$. Suppose that $M$ carries a Kähler form $\sigma \geq \omega /2$ and functions $\chi _ R$ with the properties stated in lemma 14.6.4 . Let $g$ be an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-form with $\bar\partial g=0$ in the sense of distributions and $\int _ M|g|_{\omega ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Then there is an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-form $u$ with $\bar\partial u=g$ and 14.28 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-bundle-l2-estimate} \int _ M|u|_{\omega ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV \leq \frac1{2\pi a}\int _ M|g|_{\omega ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} Proof. Let $B_\sigma =[2\pi c_1(F,h),\Lambda _\sigma ]$. Since $c_1(F,h)$ is positive definite, $B_\sigma $ is positive definite on $(n,1)$-forms by lemma 14.6.1 (1). Let $T=D''\colon L^2_{(n,0)}\to L^2_{(n,1)}$ and $S=D''\colon L^2_{(n,1)}\to L^2_{(n,2)}$ be the operators with maximal distributional domains, for the norms defined by $\sigma $ and $h$. By lemma 14.6.3 , applied with $h_0=h_1=h_2=h$, they are closed and densely defined, $ST=0$, and compactly supported smooth forms are dense in $\operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$ for the graph norm $\| v\| +\| T^*v\| +\| Sv\| $. Let $v$ be a compactly supported smooth $(n,1)$-form. We integrate the pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\langle g,v\rangle _\sigma |^2\leq \langle B_\sigma ^{-1}g,g\rangle _\sigma \langle B_\sigma v,v\rangle _\sigma $ for the positive operator $B_\sigma $ and use ( 14.25 ), in which $D''{}^*v=T^*v$ (lemma 14.6.3 ) and $D''v=Sv$. This gives \[  \Bigl |\int _ M\langle g,v\rangle _\sigma \, \mathrm dV_\sigma \Bigr |^2 \leq \int _ M\langle B_\sigma ^{-1}g,g\rangle _\sigma \, \mathrm dV_\sigma \cdot \bigl (\| T^*v\| _\sigma ^2+\| Sv\| _\sigma ^2\bigr ).  \] By lemma 14.6.1 (3), the density $\langle B_\sigma ^{-1}g,g\rangle _\sigma \, \mathrm dV_\sigma $ does not depend on $\sigma $. Computing it with $\omega $ in place of $\sigma $, and using that $2\pi c_1(F,h)\geq 2\pi a\omega $, so that $\langle [2\pi c_1(F,h),\Lambda _\omega ]^{-1}g,g\rangle _{\omega ,h}\leq (2\pi a)^{-1}|g|_{\omega ,h}^2$ by the same lemma, we find that the first integral is at most the right side of ( 14.28 ). The form $g$ lies in $\ker S$, and in $L^2_{(n,1)}$ for $\sigma $ and $h$, because $\sigma \geq \omega /2$ gives $|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma \leq 2|g|_{\omega ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV$, again by lemma 14.6.1 (3). Hence both sides of the displayed inequality converge along a graph-convergent sequence, and by the density of compactly supported smooth forms the inequality extends to all $v\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$. Theorem 11.1.4 therefore gives $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ with $Tu=g$ and $\| u\| _\sigma ^2$ at most the first integral. Finally, $|u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma =|u|_{\omega ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV$ by lemma 14.6.1 (3), which gives exactly ( 14.28 ). $\square$

section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: 14.28 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-bundle-l2-estimate} \int _ M|u|_{\omega ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV \leq \frac1{2\pi a}\int _ M|g|_{\omega ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 14.6.6
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.6.6 . Let $A$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset of a complex manifold $U$. A holomorphic function on $U\setminus A$ which, extended arbitrarily to $A$, belongs to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ extends holomorphically to $U$. The same holds for sections of a holomorphic line bundle. Proof. The question is local. We show that the given function $f$ satisfies $\bar\partial f=0$ in the sense of distributions near each point of $A$, by a one-variable argument on complex lines. Near a point of $A$, the set $A$ is the common zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions on a connected coordinate neighborhood, and one of them, $b$, does not vanish identically, since otherwise $A$ would contain a nonempty open set. The lowest-order nonzero homogeneous term $P$ of $b$ at the point is a nonzero polynomial, so its zero set is closed and nowhere dense; hence we may choose linearly independent vectors $v_1,\ldots ,v_ n$ with $P(v_ k)\neq 0$, choosing each $v_ k$ outside the union of this zero set and the span of $v_1,\ldots ,v_{k-1}$. We use linear coordinates centered at the point in which the $v_ k$ are the coordinate unit vectors. Then $t\mapsto b(tv_ k)$ has a zero of finite order at $t=0$, so by the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 7.4.2 ), on a sufficiently small polydisc, $b$ is a unit times a monic polynomial in the $k$th coordinate with holomorphic coefficients in the others, for each $k$. Hence every complex line parallel to a coordinate axis meets the zero set of $b$ in this polydisc in finitely many points. By Fubini's theorem, $f$ is square integrable on almost every such line. On such a line, near each of the finitely many punctures, the Laurent expansion of $f$ has no terms of negative order: by orthogonality of the powers on circles, a term of order $-j$ with $j\geq 1$ would make the integral of $|f|^2$ diverge like $\int _0^ rt^{1-2j}\, \mathrm dt$. Hence the restriction of $f$ to almost every line extends holomorphically, and its $\bar\partial $-derivative along the line vanishes as a distribution. Integrating against compactly supported test functions and using Fubini's theorem, we find that every derivative $\partial f/\partial \bar z_ k$ vanishes as a distribution on the polydisc. A distribution with $\bar\partial f=0$ satisfies $\Delta f=4\sum _ k\partial _{z_ k}\partial _{\bar z_ k}f=0$, so it is smooth by Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) and therefore holomorphic. This holomorphic function agrees with $f$ on the complement of $A$, and the local extensions agree on overlaps. For sections of a line bundle, apply the result in local holomorphic frames. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.6.7
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Theorem 14.6.7 . There are constants $N,C>0$, depending only on $(X,\omega )$, with the following property. Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h_0$ and a plurisubharmonic metric $h=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ such that $c_1(L,h)\geq N\omega $. Let $x\in X$ with $\varphi (x)>-\infty $ and $v\in L_ x$. Then there is $s\in H^0(X,L)$ such that 14.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-point-extension} s(x)=v,\qquad \int _ X|s|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV\leq C|v|_ h^2. \end{equation} Proof. If $v=0$, take $s=0$; assume $v\neq 0$. We cut off a local extension of $v$ and correct the error with lemma 14.6.5 outside $x$ and the poles of gentle approximations of $\varphi $; a logarithmic pole at $x$ in the weight makes the correction vanish at $x$. Step 1: data independent of $x$. Choose finitely many coordinate charts and, inside them, balls $B_ k$ of radii $\varrho _ k$, with closures in the charts, whose concentric balls of half the radius cover $X$. Put $r_0=\min _ k\varrho _ k/8$. Then for every $x\in X$ there is $k$ with $x\in \frac12B_ k$, and the coordinate ball $B$ of radius $4r_0$ centered at $x$ in the $k$th chart lies in $B_ k$. Let $\lambda $ be a smooth function on $\mathbb R^{2n}$ with values in $[0,1]$, equal to one on the ball of radius $2r_0$ and zero outside the ball of radius $3r_0$, and put \[  \psi _ x=\lambda (z-z(x))\, n\log \frac{|z-z(x)|^2}{16r_0^2}\  \text{ on }B,\qquad \psi _ x=0\  \text{ outside }B,  \] where $z$ are the chart coordinates. Then $\psi _ x\leq 0$, $\psi _ x$ is plurisubharmonic where $\lambda (z-z(x))=1$, and on the annulus where $\lambda (z-z(x))$ is not constant the logarithm and its first two derivatives are bounded independently of $x$. Hence there is $b_0\geq 0$, independent of $x$, with \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ x\geq -b_0\omega , \qquad \psi _ x=n\log |z-z(x)|^2+O(1)\text{ near }x.  \] Choose $b_1\geq 0$ with $c_1(K_ X^{-1},h_{K^{-1},\omega })\geq -b_1\omega $ (lemma 13.1.1 ), and put $N=b_0+b_1+2$. Step 2: a local extension and its cutoff. By lemma 14.5.1 , $L$ has a holomorphic frame $e$ over $B$. With $|e|_{h_0}^2=\mathrm e^{-p_0}$, the local weight $p_0+\varphi $ of $h$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p_0+\varphi )=c_1(L,h)\geq 0$. By corollary 11.4.5 , applied in this frame on the ball of radius $r_0$ around $x$, whose diameter $2r_0$ is fixed, there is a holomorphic section $f$ of $L$ over this ball with $f(x)=v$ and \[  \int _{|z-z(x)|<r_0}|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV\leq C_0|v|_ h^2;  \] here $C_0$ does not depend on $x$, because the volume densities are uniformly comparable on the finite cover. Let $\chi $ be a cutoff equal to one for $|z-z(x)|<r_0/2$ and zero for $|z-z(x)|>3r_0/4$, obtained by translating a fixed one. Put $G=\chi f$, extended by zero, and $g=\bar\partial G=f\, \bar\partial \chi $. The form $g$ is supported in the annulus $r_0/2\leq |z-z(x)|\leq 3r_0/4$, on which $\psi _ x$ and $\bar\partial \chi $ are bounded independently of $x$. Step 3: global sections for the approximations of $\varphi $. Apply theorem 13.4.5 to $\varphi $ with the background $c_1(L,h_0)-N\omega $. It gives functions $\varphi _ j\downarrow \varphi $ with gentle analytic singularities, analytic pole sets $A_ j$, and $c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\geq (N-\varepsilon _ j)\omega $ with $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$. Since $\varphi _ j(x)\geq \varphi (x)>-\infty $, no $A_ j$ contains $x$. Put \[  F=L\otimes K_ X^{-1},\qquad h_{F,j}=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\otimes h_{K^{-1},\omega }.  \] For $j$ so large that $\varepsilon _ j\leq 1$, this metric is smooth on $M_ j=X\setminus (A_ j\cup \{ x\} )$ and its curvature is at least $(N-\varepsilon _ j-b_0-b_1)\omega \geq \omega $. By lemma 14.6.4 , applied to $\varphi _ j+\psi _ x$, the manifold $M_ j$ carries a Kähler form $\sigma \geq \omega /2$ and cutoffs as required in lemma 14.6.5 . The canonical identification of $L$-valued $(0,q)$-forms with $F$-valued $(n,q)$-forms preserves the pointwise norms for $\omega $, because the $(n,0)$-covector and its dual cancel. Under this identification $g$ is $\bar\partial $-closed, and since $\varphi _ j\geq \varphi $, \[  \int _{M_ j}|g|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\, \mathrm dV \leq C_1\int _{|z-z(x)|<r_0}|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV \leq C_1C_0|v|_ h^2,  \] with $C_1$ depending only on the fixed cutoffs and the bounds for $\psi _ x$ on the annulus. Lemma 14.6.5 , with $a=1$, gives $u_ j$ on $M_ j$ with $\bar\partial u_ j=g$ and \[  \int _{M_ j}|u_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\, \mathrm dV\leq \frac{C_1C_0}{2\pi }|v|_ h^2.  \] The section $s_ j=G-u_ j$ is holomorphic on $M_ j$. The weights $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}$ are bounded below by a positive constant, since $\varphi _ j\leq \varphi _1$ is bounded above and $\psi _ x\leq 0$; hence $s_ j$ is square integrable for $h_0$ near $A_ j\cup \{ x\} $, and lemma 14.6.6 extends it to a global holomorphic section. Near $x$ we have $g=0$ and no point of $A_ j$, so $u_ j=G-s_ j$ is holomorphic near $x$. Moreover $|u_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\geq c\, |u_ j|_{h_0}^2|z-z(x)|^{-2n}$ near $x$ for a constant $c>0$, by the upper bound for $\varphi _ j$ and since $\psi _ x=n\log |z-z(x)|^2+O(1)$. Since $\int _{|z-z(x)|<r}|z-z(x)|^{-2n}\, \mathrm dV=\infty $ for every $r>0$, by polar coordinates in $\mathbb R^{2n}$, the finiteness of the weighted integral of the continuous function $u_ j$ forces $u_ j(x)=0$. Hence $s_ j(x)=G(x)=v$. Since $\psi _ x\leq 0$, dropping the factor $\mathrm e^{-\psi _ x}$ only decreases the integrals, and with $|G|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\leq |f|_ h^2$ on the ball we obtain \[  \int _ X|s_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV \leq C_2|v|_ h^2,  \] where $C_2$ depends only on the fixed geometric cutoffs and on the constant of the local point estimate. Step 4: the limit. Since $\varphi _ j\leq \varphi _1\leq \sup _ X\varphi _1$, the sections $s_ j$ are bounded in $L^2$ for $h_0$, and by lemma 14.5.2 (2) a subsequence converges uniformly to a holomorphic section $s$ of $L$, which satisfies $s(x)=v$. Since $\varphi _ j\downarrow \varphi $, Fatou's lemma gives ( 14.29 ) with $C=C_2$. $\square$

section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: 14.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-point-extension} s(x)=v,\qquad \int _ X|s|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV\leq C|v|_ h^2. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 14.6.8
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.6.8 . Let $L$ and $T$ be holomorphic line bundles on $X$ with smooth quadratic metrics $h_0$ and $h_ T$, and let $\mathrm dV$ be a smooth positive volume form on $X$. For an integer $k\geq 1$ and a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$, the space \[  \mathcal H_ k=\left\{ s\in H^0(X,L^ k\otimes T): \int _ X|s|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2\mathrm e^{-k\varphi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty \right\}   \] is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space for the displayed squared norm $\| s\| _ k^2$. If $\mathcal H_ k\ne \{ 0\} $ and $s_1,\ldots ,s_{d_ k}$ is an orthonormal basis, then 14.30 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-bergman-potential} \varphi _ k=\frac1k\log \sup _{\| s\| _ k\leq 1}|s|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2 =\frac1k\log \sum _{i=1}^{d_ k}|s_ i|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2. \end{equation} Writing $\theta =c_1(L,h_0)$ and $\theta _ T=c_1(T,h_ T)$, the function $\varphi _ k$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +k^{-1}\theta _ T)$ and has gentle analytic singularities with coefficient $1/k$. Except for the gentle analytic singularities, which are defined only on compact Kähler manifolds (definition 13.1.11 ), these assertions hold more generally on every compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension in place of $X$. Proof. By lemma 14.5.2 (3), $H^0(X,L^ k\otimes T)$ and its linear subspace $\mathcal H_ k$ are finite dimensional. The weighted integral defines an inner product on $\mathcal H_ k$: the function $\varphi $ is finite almost everywhere, so the weight is positive almost everywhere, and a section of norm zero vanishes almost everywhere and hence identically. A finite-dimensional inner product space is complete. At a point $y$, with the coefficients $c_ i$ of $s=\sum _ ic_ is_ i$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $|s(y)|^2\leq \sum _ i|c_ i|^2\sum _ i|s_ i(y)|^2$, with equality when the $c_ i$ are proportional to the complex conjugates of the values of the $s_ i$ at $y$ in a local frame. This proves the equality in ( 14.30 ). In local frames with $|e|_{h_0}^2=\mathrm e^{-p_0}$ and $|e_ T|_{h_ T}^2=\mathrm e^{-p_ T}$, write $s_ i=f_ ie^ k\otimes e_ T$. Then \[  \varphi _ k=\frac1k\log \sum _ i|f_ i|^2-p_0-\frac{p_ T}k,  \] and $\theta +k^{-1}\theta _ T+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ k=k^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _ i|f_ i|^2\geq 0$ by proposition 8.3.3 . Hence $\varphi _ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +k^{-1}\theta _ T)$, with analytic singularities of type $(1/k,\mathfrak b)$, where $\mathfrak b$ is the ideal sheaf generated locally by the $f_ i$. This ideal sheaf does not depend on the frames, because a change of frames multiplies all $f_ i$ by the same nowhere vanishing holomorphic function, and it is coherent by lemma 12.2.4 . Moreover $\mathrm e^{k\varphi _ k}=\sum _ i|s_ i|^2$ is smooth on $X$. The local expressions for $\varphi _ k$ above are presentations with the smooth remainders $-p_0-p_ T/k$, so proposition 13.1.7 shows that on every log resolution $\pi $ of $\mathfrak b$, with $\pi ^*\mathfrak b=\mathcal O(-D)$, locally $\varphi _ k\circ \pi $ is $k^{-1}\log |s_ D|^2$ plus a smooth function. These are the conditions of definition 13.1.11 . Apart from this appeal to definition 13.1.11 , the proof uses only that $X$ is a compact complex manifold of positive dimension, since the last assertion of lemma 14.5.2 gives its part (3) in this generality; hence it also proves the last assertion of the lemma. $\square$

section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: 14.30 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-bergman-potential} \varphi _ k=\frac1k\log \sup _{\| s\| _ k\leq 1}|s|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2 =\frac1k\log \sum _{i=1}^{d_ k}|s_ i|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2. \end{equation}

title: Example 14.6.9
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Example 14.6.9 . On $\mathbb P^1$ take $L=\mathcal O(1)$ with its Fubini–Study metric, $T$ trivial, $\varphi =0$ and $\mathrm dV=\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. A section of $L^ k$ is $f(z)X_0^ k$ on the chart $[1:z]$ with $f$ entire, and in the chart at infinity, with $\zeta =1/z$, it equals $\zeta ^ kf(1/\zeta )X_1^ k$; holomorphicity at $\zeta =0$ and Cauchy's estimates show that $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $k$. Integration over circles makes the monomials orthogonal, and with $t=|z|^2$, \[  \| z^ j\| _ k^2=\int _0^\infty \frac{t^ j}{(1+t)^{k+2}}\, \mathrm dt =\frac{j!(k-j)!}{(k+1)!},\qquad 0\leq j\leq k;  \] the last equality follows from the substitution $u=t/(1+t)$ and repeated integration by parts. Thus the sections $\sqrt{(k+1)\binom {k}{j}}X_0^{k-j}X_1^ j$, $0\leq j\leq k$, form an orthonormal basis, and the sum of their squared norms is \[  \frac{k+1}{(1+|z|^2)^ k}\sum _{j=0}^ k\binom {k}{j}|z|^{2j}=k+1.  \] Consequently $\varphi _ k=k^{-1}\log (k+1)$, which tends to zero uniformly.

title: 14.7 Extension from a compact submanifold
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: 14.7 Extension from a compact submanifold In theorem 14.6.7 the error $\bar\partial (\chi f)$ of the cutoff is supported away from the interpolation point. To extend a section from a submanifold $Y$ of positive dimension, we must glue local extensions, and the gluing error then meets $Y$ itself. We control it in two steps. First, local extensions with a logarithmic gain (lemma 14.7.3 ) make the gluing error integrable against the critical weight $R_ Y^{-q}$, where $q$ is the codimension of $Y$ and $R_ Y$ is a smooth function vanishing to second order exactly along $Y$. Second, for weights with gentle analytic singularities, a computation on a resolution identifies the limit of the cutoff error with the norm of the prescribed section on $Y$ (lemma 14.7.7 ). This yields an estimate whose constant depends only on the geometry, and decreasing approximation then gives the result for arbitrary singular metrics (theorem 14.7.8 ). In section 14.7.1 a related gluing construction, by maxima instead of sums, extends potentials of Kähler currents from $Y$ to $X$. We solve the $\bar\partial $-equations of this section with the following twisted form of lemma 14.6.5 . The auxiliary function $a$ contributes the term $-\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial a$ to the curvature, at the price of the weight $1/(a+b)$ in the estimate for the solution. Lemma 14.7.1 . Let $M$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Hermitian form $\omega $ and the volume form $\mathrm dV=\omega ^ n/n!$, carrying a Kähler form $\sigma \geq \omega /2$ and functions $\chi _ R$ with the properties stated in lemma 14.6.4 . Let $F\to M$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h$, and let $a,b$ be smooth functions on $M$ that are bounded above and below by positive constants. Suppose that the real $(1,1)$-form \[  H=a\, 2\pi c_1(F,h)-\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial a -\frac{\mathrm i}{b}\partial a\wedge \bar\partial a  \] is positive definite, and put $B_\omega =[H,\Lambda _\omega ]$ on $(n,1)$-forms. Let $g$ be an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-form with $\bar\partial g=0$ in the sense of distributions, $g\in L^2_{(n,1)}(\omega ,h)$, and \[  M_ g=\int _ M\langle B_\omega ^{-1}g,g\rangle _{\omega ,h}\, \mathrm dV<\infty .  \] Then there is an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-form $u$ with $\bar\partial u=g$ and 14.31 \begin{equation} \label{eq:twisted-kahler-correction} \int _ M\frac{|u|_{\omega ,h}^2}{a+b}\, \mathrm dV\leq M_ g. \end{equation} Proof. The Bochner–Kodaira identity ( 14.25 ) of lemma 14.6.2 holds for every smooth metric on $F$; we apply it to the metric $ah$. Let $\delta _ h=D''{}^*$ be the formal adjoint for the metric $h$ and the Kähler form $\sigma $, and $C_ a=(\bar\partial a\wedge )^*$ the contraction with the dual of $\bar\partial a$. In a frame, the weight of $ah$ is $p-\log a$, so \[  \delta _{ah}=\delta _ h-a^{-1}C_ a,\qquad a\, 2\pi c_1(F,ah)=a\, 2\pi c_1(F,h) -\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial a +\frac{\mathrm i}{a}\partial a\wedge \bar\partial a.  \] On $(n,1)$-forms, the commutator with the last term is $[\frac{\mathrm i}{a}\partial a\wedge \bar\partial a,\Lambda _\sigma ]=a^{-1}C_ a^*C_ a$. Indeed, where $\partial a\neq 0$, choose a $\sigma $-unitary coframe with $\partial a=|\partial a|\theta _1$, so that $\bar\partial a=|\partial a|\bar\theta _1$, and put $e=\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ n$. By lemma 14.6.1 (1), the left side multiplies the coefficient $v_1$ of $e\wedge \bar\theta _1$ by $|\partial a|^2/a$ and annihilates the other coefficients; so does the right side, because $\bar\partial a\wedge fe=(-1)^ n|\partial a|f\, e\wedge \bar\theta _1$, whence $C_ av=(-1)^ n|\partial a|v_1e$. Where $\partial a=0$, both sides vanish. The limit $F$ satisfies $F(z',0)=f(z')$, and Fatou's lemma gives ( 14.34 ). $\square$ Lemma 14.7.4 . Let $Y\subset X$ be a nonempty connected closed complex submanifold of codimension $q\geq 1$. Let $Z$ be a complex manifold and $E\subset Z$ a smooth divisor. We consider finite sequences of blowups $Z_ k\to Z_{k-1}\to \cdots \to Z_0=Z$ with smooth centers in which the boundary of $Z_0$ is $E$, the boundary of $Z_ i$ is the union of the inverse image of the boundary of $Z_{i-1}$ and the exceptional divisor of $Z_ i\to Z_{i-1}$, and each center has normal crossings with the boundary of the model on which it lies. For a prime divisor $D$ on the final model, put $b_ D=\operatorname {ord}_ D(E)$, the vanishing order along $D$ of the pullback of a local equation of $E$, and $A_ D=A_ Z(D)$. We call $A_ D-b_ D$ the margin of $D$. Lemma 14.7.5 . In this situation, $A_ D-b_ D=0$ if $D$ is the strict transform of $E$, and $A_ D-b_ D>0$ for every other prime divisor $D$ in the boundary. Proof. We argue by induction on the number of blowups. On $Z$ itself, $A_ E=b_ E=1$, and every other prime divisor $D$ of $Z$ has $A_ D=1$ and $b_ D=0$. Strict transforms keep their log discrepancies and orders, hence their margins. Since every exceptional divisor lies in the boundary, a prime divisor of a model outside the boundary is the strict transform of a prime divisor of $Z$ other than $E$, so it has $A_ D=1$ and $b_ D=0$. Suppose that the statement holds on a model. Blowing up a center of codimension one is an isomorphism and creates no new divisor; it only adds the center to the boundary, and the center then has margin one if it was not a boundary component. It therefore suffices to show that the exceptional divisor $E_{\mathrm{new}}$ of the blowup of a center $C$ of codimension $c\geq 2$ has a positive margin. Suppose that $C$ is contained in exactly $r$ boundary components, near its generic point. Since $C$ has normal crossings with the boundary, $r\leq c$. Near such a point choose coordinates $(z,w)$, $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_ c)$, in which $C=\{ w=0\} $ and the boundary components through the point are coordinate hyperplanes; those containing $C$ are then hyperplanes $\{ w_ j=0\} $. By proposition A.5.3 , in the coordinates $(z,t,v)$ of ( A.8 ) we have $E_{\mathrm{new}}=\{ t=0\} $, and the Jacobian determinant of the blowup is $\pm t^{c-1}$, so it vanishes to order $c-1$ along $E_{\mathrm{new}}$. A local equation of a component $\{ w_ j=0\} $ containing $C$ is a unit times $w_ j$ (lemma 12.6.1 (1)), and $w_ j$ pulls back to $t$ or to $tv_ j$, which vanishes to order one along $E_{\mathrm{new}}$, because $v_ j$ does not vanish identically on $\{ t=0\} $ (lemma 12.6.1 (2),(4)). Thus the pullback of a local equation of each component containing $C$ vanishes to order one along $E_{\mathrm{new}}$. Hence $A_{\mathrm{new}}=c+\sum _{D\supset C}(A_ D-1)$ and $b_{\mathrm{new}}=\sum _{D\supset C}b_ D$, the sums running over the boundary components containing $C$ (other divisors through $C$ have $A_ D=1$ and $b_ D=0$ and contribute nothing). Therefore \[  A_{\mathrm{new}}-b_{\mathrm{new}} =c-r+\sum _{D\supset C}(A_ D-b_ D).  \] All terms on the right are nonnegative by the induction hypothesis. If one of the components containing $C$ has a positive margin, so does $E_{\mathrm{new}}$. Otherwise only the strict transform of $E$ can contain $C$, so $r\leq 1$ and $c-r\geq 1$, and again the margin of $E_{\mathrm{new}}$ is positive. $\square$ Lemma 14.7.6 . Let $L\to X$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h_0$ and a plurisubharmonic metric $h=h_0\mathrm e^{-\Phi }$. Let $Y$ be a nonempty connected closed complex submanifold of codimension $q\geq 1$ such that the restriction of $h$ to $Y$ is defined, and let $R_ Y$ be as in lemma 14.7.4 , with $\max _ XR_ Y<\mathrm e^{-4}$. If $f$ is a holomorphic section of $L|_ Y$ with $\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y<\infty $, there are $\kappa >0$, finitely many open sets $U_ i\subset X$, holomorphic sections $F_ i$ of $L$ over $U_ i$ with $F_ i=f$ on $Y\cap U_ i$, and smooth functions $\eta _ i$ with compact support in $U_ i$ and $\sum _ i\eta _ i=1$ on a neighborhood of $Y$, such that 14.36 \begin{equation} \label{eq:critical-local-extension-gain} \int _{U_ i}\frac{|F_ i|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-(1+\kappa )\Phi }}{R_ Y^ q(-\log R_ Y)^2}\, \mathrm dV<\infty \quad \text{for every }i, \end{equation} and such that $G=\sum _ i\eta _ iF_ i$, each term extended by zero, is a smooth global section of $L$ with $G|_ Y=f$, $\bar\partial G|_ Y=0$, and 14.37 \begin{equation} \label{eq:strengthened-critical-initial-norm} \int _ X\frac{(|G|_{h_0}^2+|\bar\partial G|_{\omega ,h_0}^2) \mathrm e^{-(1+\kappa )\Phi }}{R_ Y^ q(-\log R_ Y)^2}\, \mathrm dV<\infty . \end{equation} In particular 14.38 \begin{equation} \label{eq:critical-gluing-error-decay} \int _{\{ R_ Y<\varepsilon \} }|\bar\partial G|_{\omega ,h}^2R_ Y^{-q}\, \mathrm dV \longrightarrow 0\qquad (\varepsilon \downarrow 0). \end{equation} Here $\mathrm dV_ Y=\omega |_ Y^{n-q}/(n-q)!$; if $Y$ is a point, $\mathrm dV_ Y$ is the unit mass at that point. Proof. In a holomorphic frame of $L$ the local weight $p$ of $h$ is plurisubharmonic, and its restriction to $Y$ is plurisubharmonic, because the restriction is defined and $Y$ is connected. If $Y$ is a point, the value of $p$ there is finite and we take any $\kappa >0$. Otherwise, by the strong openness theorem (corollary 12.5.4 ), every point of $Y$ has a neighborhood in $Y$ on which $f$ is square integrable with the weight $\mathrm e^{-(1+\kappa )p|_ Y}$ for some $\kappa >0$; since $Y$ is compact, finitely many coordinate products $B'_ i\times B''_ i$ of the form of lemma 14.7.3 , with tangential balls slightly larger than needed and each contained in a neighborhood on which ( 14.35 ) holds, cover $Y$, and one $\kappa >0$ works for all of them. Lemma 14.7.3 , applied in a frame with the plurisubharmonic weight $(1+\kappa )p$, gives holomorphic extensions $F_ i$ of $f$ on these products whose critical integrals with the logarithmic gain are finite. Let $U_ i$ be smaller concentric products that still cover $Y$. On $U_ i$, the smooth factors coming from the frames and the comparison $c|w|^2\leq R_ Y\leq C|w|^2$ of ( 14.35 ) preserve this finiteness, which gives ( 14.36 ); for the logarithmic factor we use that $-\log R_ Y\geq c'(-\log |w|^2)$ for a constant $c'>0$, since $R_ Y\leq C|w|^2$ and both $R_ Y$ and $|w|^2$ are less than $\mathrm e^{-4}$. We now glue the local extensions. Choose smooth functions $\eta _ i$ with compact support in $U_ i$ whose sum is one on a neighborhood of $Y$; they are obtained by grouping the members of a partition of unity with compact supports subordinate to the cover of $X$ by the sets $U_ i$ and $X\setminus Y$ (proposition 7.1.3 ). Put $G=\sum _ i\eta _ iF_ i$, each term extended by zero. Then $G|_ Y=f$. Since all $F_ i$ are holomorphic with the same restriction $f$, we have $\bar\partial G=\sum _ i(\bar\partial \eta _ i)F_ i$, and on $Y$ this equals $f\, \bar\partial \sum _ i\eta _ i=0$. The bounds on the cutoffs and their derivatives and ( 14.36 ) give ( 14.37 ). Put $\gamma =|\bar\partial G|_{\omega ,h_0}^2$. Since $\bar\partial G$ is smooth and vanishes on $Y$, we have $\gamma \leq C|w|^2$ in normal coordinates near each point of $Y$, hence $\gamma \leq CR_ Y$ near $Y$, by ( 14.35 ) and the compactness of $Y$. Let $A=\{ R_ Y<\varepsilon \} $; all integrals below are taken with $\mathrm dV$. Hölder's inequality with the exponents $1+\kappa $ and $(1+\kappa )/\kappa $ gives \[  \int _ A\gamma \, \mathrm e^{-\Phi }R_ Y^{-q} \leq \left(\int _ A\frac{\gamma \mathrm e^{-(1+\kappa )\Phi }}{R_ Y^ q(-\log R_ Y)^2}\right)^{1/(1+\kappa )} \left(\int _ A\gamma R_ Y^{-q}(-\log R_ Y)^{2/\kappa }\right)^{\kappa /(1+\kappa )}.  \] The first factor is bounded by ( 14.37 ). In normal polar coordinates, using ( 14.35 ) and $\gamma =O(R_ Y)$, the integrability of $\gamma R_ Y^{-q}(-\log R_ Y)^{2/\kappa }$ near $Y$ reduces to $\int _0^ r(-\log t)^{2/\kappa }\, \mathrm dt<\infty $. Hence the second factor tends to zero as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by the absolute continuity of the integral, which proves ( 14.38 ). $\square$ Lemma 14.7.7 . Let $L\to X$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h_0$ and a plurisubharmonic metric $h=h_0\mathrm e^{-\Phi }$, where $\Phi $ has gentle analytic singularities. Let $Y$ be a nonempty connected closed complex submanifold of codimension $q\geq 1$ to which $h$ restricts, let $f$ be a holomorphic section of $L|_ Y$ with $\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y<\infty $, and let $G$ be constructed from $f$ as in lemma 14.7.6 . Then 14.39 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gentle-weighted-normal-residue} \varlimsup _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int _{\{ \varepsilon /2\leq R_ Y\leq \varepsilon \} } |G|_ h^2R_ Y^{-q}\, \mathrm dV \leq C_ Y\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y, \qquad \mathrm dV_ Y=\omega |_ Y^{n-q}/(n-q)!, \end{equation} where $C_ Y$ depends only on $Y$, $R_ Y$ and $\omega $, and not on $\Phi $ or $f$. Proof. We compute on a log resolution adapted to $\Phi $ and $Y$; by lemma 14.7.5 , only the strict transform of the exceptional divisor of the blowup of $Y$ contributes to the limit. A resolution adapted to $\Phi $ and $Y$. Let $\operatorname {Bl}_ YX\to X$ be the blowup of $Y$, with exceptional divisor $E$; for $q=1$ this is the identity and $E=Y$. By proposition A.5.3 , its Jacobian determinant is $\pm t^{q-1}$ in the charts of ( A.8 ), where $E=\{ t=0\} $, so its relative canonical divisor is $(q-1)E$. Let $\mathfrak a$ be the ideal in the type of $\Phi $. We apply theorem A.5.5 on the compact manifold $\operatorname {Bl}_ YX$ to the pullback of $\mathfrak a$, which is nonzero, and to the divisor $E$. This gives a finite sequence of blowups with smooth centers, each having normal crossings with the accumulated divisor of theorem A.5.5 , which starts with $E$; this accumulated divisor is the boundary in the sense of lemma 14.7.5 . On the final model the boundary has simple normal crossings, and the pullback of $\mathfrak a$ is the ideal of an effective divisor supported in the boundary. Denote the composite map to $X$ by $\pi $. It is a composite of blowups along closed submanifolds that principalizes $\mathfrak a$, that is, a log resolution of $\mathfrak a$ in the sense of section 13.1 . Since definition 13.1.11 requires a smooth remainder on every log resolution, $\Phi \circ \pi $ has a smooth remainder. Divisor orders. In a normal-crossing chart on the final model write \[  \Phi \circ \pi =\sum _ D a_ D\log |s_ D|^2+v,\qquad R_ Y\circ \pi =\prod _ D|s_ D|^{2b_ D}r,  \] with $v$ smooth, $r$ smooth and strictly positive, and $a_ D,b_ D\geq 0$. The Jacobian factor of the pulled-back volume is $\prod _ D|s_ D|^{2(A_ D-1)}$ times a smooth positive function, where $A_ D=A_ X(D)$ is the log discrepancy. Let $F_ i$ be one of the holomorphic extensions used in $G$, and suppose that the chart lies over the open set $U_ i$ of lemma 14.7.6 . Then $F_ i\circ \pi $ vanishes to some integral order $e_{i,D}\geq 0$ along each coordinate divisor $D$ of the chart. By ( 14.36 ), the integral of $|F_ i|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-(1+\kappa )\Phi }R_ Y^{-q}(-\log R_ Y)^{-2}$ over $U_ i$ is finite, and this forces 14.40 \begin{equation} \label{eq:critical-gain-divisor-orders} e_{i,D}+A_ D\geq (1+\kappa )a_ D+qb_ D\quad (b_ D>0), \qquad e_{i,D}+A_ D>(1+\kappa )a_ D\quad (b_ D=0). \end{equation} Indeed, fix the other coordinates away from their divisors and integrate radially in $s_ D$: the integrand behaves like $|s_ D|^{2(e_{i,D}+A_ D-(1+\kappa )a_ D-qb_ D)-2}(-\log |s_ D|^2)^{-2}$ when $b_ D>0$, and the squared logarithm in the denominator makes the exponent $-1$ of the radial variable integrable but cannot compensate a smaller exponent. If $b_ D=0$, the logarithmic factor is bounded above and below near generic points of $D$, and the inequality must be strict. This is the computation of theorem 12.6.5 with one additional logarithmic factor. Shrinking the chart, we may assume that for each $i$ either the chart lies over $U_ i$ or $\eta _ i\circ \pi $ vanishes on it, because $\operatorname{Supp}\eta _ i$ is a compact subset of the open set $U_ i$. Then, on a smaller chart, the pullback of $G=\sum _ i\eta _ iF_ i$ is the monomial $\prod _ Ds_ D^{e_ D}$, with $e_ D=\min _ ie_{i,D}$ over the indices $i$ of the first kind, times a smooth bounded function. The density of $|G|_ h^2R_ Y^{-q}\, \mathrm dV$ is therefore bounded by a constant times $\prod _ D|s_ D|^{2(\gamma _ D-1)}$, where \[  \gamma _ D=e_ D-a_ D-qb_ D+A_ D.  \] If $a_ D>0$, ( 14.40 ) gives $\gamma _ D\geq \kappa a_ D>0$, and if $a_ D=b_ D=0$, it gives $\gamma _ D>0$. If $a_ D=0$ and $b_ D>0$, the formula for the relative canonical divisor of the first blowup gives $A_ D=A_{\operatorname {Bl}_ YX}(D)+(q-1)\operatorname {ord}_ D(E)$, and $b_ D=\operatorname {ord}_ D(E)$ because $\mathcal I_ Y$ pulls back to the ideal of $E$; hence \[  A_ D-qb_ D=A_{\operatorname {Bl}_ YX}(D)-\operatorname {ord}_ D(E).  \] By lemma 14.7.5 , applied with $Z=\operatorname {Bl}_ YX$, this is positive unless $D$ is the strict transform of $E$. For that divisor $b_ E=1$ and $A_ E=q$, and $a_ E=0$: since the restriction of $h$ to $Y$ is defined, generic points of $Y$ lie outside the pole set of $\Phi $. Hence $\gamma _ E=e_ E\geq 0$, and the strict transform of $E$ is the only divisor along which $\gamma _ D$ can vanish. The annular limit. By a finite partition of unity on the compact inverse image of $Y$, it suffices to consider the integral over a small chart. If no coordinate divisor of the chart is the strict transform of $E$ with $\gamma _ E=0$, the density is integrable, the shells $\{ \varepsilon /2\leq R_ Y\leq \varepsilon \} $ shrink to the null set $\pi ^{-1}(Y)$, and dominated convergence shows that the integral over the shell tends to zero. Otherwise let $t$ be the coordinate defining the strict transform of $E$. The density is $|t|^{-2}$ times a smooth bounded coefficient and the factors $|s_ D|^{2(\gamma _ D-1)}$, $D\ne E$, which are integrable since $\gamma _ D>0$. For fixed values of the remaining coordinates $s$, the shell is $\varepsilon /2\leq |t|^2m(s)r(t,s)\leq \varepsilon $, with $m(s)=\prod _{D\ne E}|s_ D|^{2b_ D}$. Since $r$ is bounded above and below, the shell lies in a range of $\log |t|$ of bounded length, so the integral of $|t|^{-2}$ over it is bounded independently of $\varepsilon $ and $s$; this gives an integrable dominating function. As $\varepsilon \to 0$, the shell shrinks to $t=0$, the smooth coefficient tends to its value at $t=0$, and the integral of $|t|^{-2}$ over the shell tends to $\pi \log 2$. By dominated convergence, only the restriction to $t=0$ of the coefficient of $|t|^{-2}$ in the density contributes to the limit. Identification of the limit. The argument just given, applied after multiplying the density by a continuous function with compact support, shows that the integrals over the shells converge to $\pi \log 2$ times the total mass of a measure $\mu $ on the strict transform of $E$; in a chart as above, $\mu $ has the density obtained by restricting to $t=0$ the smooth coefficient of $|t|^{-2}$, multiplied by the factors $|s_ D|^{2(\gamma _ D-1)}$, $D\ne E$. Since $\mu $ is determined by the limits of integrals over the shells $\{ \varepsilon /2\leq R_ Y\leq \varepsilon \} $, it does not depend on the coordinates in which it is computed, and since its density in every chart is integrable, it gives no mass to proper analytic subsets. We may therefore compute $\mu $ on the dense open subset of the strict transform of $E$ lying over the complement of the pole set of $\Phi $ in $Y$ and over which the further blowups are isomorphisms, using coordinates of the first blowup $\operatorname {Bl}_ YX$. Let $(z',w)$ be coordinates on $X$ in which $Y=\{ w=0\} $, and write $\mathrm dV=J(z',w)\, \mathrm dV(z')\, \mathrm dV(w)$ with $J$ smooth and positive. By lemma 14.7.4 , $R_ Y=Q_{z'}(w)+O(|w|^3)$ locally uniformly, where $Q_{z'}$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $\mathbb C^ q$ depending continuously on $z'$. Over this chart, $\operatorname {Bl}_ YX$ is covered by charts with coordinates $(z',t,\xi )$, $\xi \in \mathbb C^{q-1}$, in which, after renumbering the coordinates $w$, we have $w=t(1,\xi )$ and $E=\{ t=0\} $ (for $q=1$ there is no $\xi $, and $t=w$). There $\mathrm dV(w)=|t|^{2(q-1)}\, \mathrm dV(t)\, \mathrm dV(\xi )$ and $R_ Y=|t|^2\bigl (Q_{z'}(1,\xi )+O(|t|)\bigr )$, so away from the poles of $\Phi $ the density of $|G|_ h^2R_ Y^{-q}\, \mathrm dV$ is $|t|^{-2}$ times the smooth function \[  |G|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi }\bigl (Q_{z'}(1,\xi )+O(|t|)\bigr )^{-q}J,  \] whose restriction to $t=0$ equals $|f(z')|_ h^2Q_{z'}(1,\xi )^{-q}J(z',0)$, because $G|_ Y=f$. The points of the projective normal fibers not covered by such a chart form a hyperplane in each fiber and are negligible. Integrating over $\xi $, we find that the image of $\mu $ under the projection to $Y$ has the density $c(z')|f(z')|_ h^2$ with respect to $\mathrm dV(z')$, where \[  c(z')=J(z',0)\int _{\mathbb C^{q-1}}Q_{z'}(1,\xi )^{-q}\, \mathrm dV(\xi ).  \] Since $Q_{z'}(1,\xi )\geq c_0(1+|\xi |^2)$ with $c_0>0$ locally uniformly in $z'$, and $(1+|\xi |^2)^{-q}$ is integrable on $\mathbb C^{q-1}$, the function $c$ is locally bounded. It depends only on $\omega $, $R_ Y$ and the chart. Covering the compact manifold $Y$ by finitely many such charts and comparing $\mathrm dV(z')$ with $\mathrm dV_ Y$, we obtain ( 14.39 ). $\square$ Theorem 14.7.8 . Let $Y\subset X$ be a nonempty closed connected complex submanifold, and put $\mathrm dV_ Y=\omega |_ Y^{\dim Y}/(\dim Y)!$, the unit mass if $Y$ is a point. There are constants $N,C>0$, depending only on $X$, $\omega $ and $Y$, with the following property. Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h_0$ and a plurisubharmonic metric $h=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ such that $c_1(L,h)\geq N\omega $, and suppose that the restriction of $h$ to $Y$ is defined, that is, the local weights of $h$ are not identically $-\infty $ on $Y$. Then every $f\in H^0(Y,L|_ Y)$ with $\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y<\infty $ has an extension $s\in H^0(X,L)$ such that 14.41 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-submanifold-extension} s|_ Y=f,\qquad \int _ X|s|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV\leq C\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y. \end{equation} Proof. If $Y=X$, take $s=f$, any $N$ and $C=1$. Suppose that $Y$ has codimension $q\geq 1$; if $f=0$, take $s=0$. As in the proof of theorem 14.6.7 , we cut off a smooth extension of $f$ and correct the error, now with lemma 14.7.1 ; a pole of order $q$ along $Y$ in the weight makes the correction vanish on $Y$. Fix $R=R_ Y$ and the constant $b$ of lemma 14.7.4 , with $\max _ XR<\mathrm e^{-4}$, and choose $b_ K\geq 0$ with $c_1(K_ X^{-1},h_{K^{-1},\omega })\geq -b_ K\omega $ (lemma 13.1.1 ). In Steps 1–4 we prove the theorem for a weight $\Phi $ with gentle analytic singularities, as for the approximations of theorem 13.4.5 , under the curvature bound \[  c_1(L,h_0\mathrm e^{-\Phi })\geq N_0\omega , \qquad N_0=b_ K+(q+2)b+2.  \] In these steps $h$ denotes the metric $h_0\mathrm e^{-\Phi }$, and $A$ the pole set of $\Phi $. Step 5 treats arbitrary weights. Step 1: the twisted curvature form. For the given $f$ choose $G$ and $\kappa $ by lemma 14.7.6 . On $M=X\setminus (A\cup Y)$ consider $F=L\otimes K_ X^{-1}$ with the metric $h\otimes h_{K^{-1},\omega }\mathrm e^{-q\psi }$, where $\psi =\log R$; the canonical identification of $L$-valued functions with $F$-valued $(n,0)$-forms preserves the squared norms times the volume. The manifold $M$ carries a Kähler form and cutoffs as required in lemma 14.7.1 , by lemma 14.6.4 applied to $\Phi +\psi $, which is quasi-plurisubharmonic, has pole set $A\cup Y$ and is smooth on $M$. The resulting Kähler form depends on $\Phi $, but the estimate of lemma 14.7.1 does not involve it. Let $\psi _\varepsilon =\log (\varepsilon +R)$, $\mu $, $a_\varepsilon $ and $b_\varepsilon $ be the functions of lemma 14.7.2 , applied on $M$ to the smooth function $R$, which satisfies $0<R<\mathrm e^{-4}$ there, for $0<\varepsilon <\mathrm e^{-4}$. For fixed $\varepsilon $, $a_\varepsilon $ and $b_\varepsilon $ are bounded above and below by positive constants, $a_\varepsilon \geq 1$ and $1\leq -\mu '(\psi _\varepsilon )\leq 2$. By part (2) of that lemma, applied with $2\pi $ times the curvature form of the metric of $F$, \[  H_\varepsilon =a_\varepsilon \bigl (2\pi c_1(L,h) +2\pi c_1(K_ X^{-1},h_{K^{-1},\omega }) +q\, \mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \psi \bigr ) -\mu '(\psi _\varepsilon )\,  \mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \psi _\varepsilon .  \] Since $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \psi =2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq -2\pi b\omega $, $0\leq R/(\varepsilon +R)\leq 1$ and $-\mu '\leq 2$, the identity ( 14.33 ) gives 14.42 \begin{equation} \label{eq:global-normal-twisted-curvature} H_\varepsilon \geq 2\pi \bigl (a_\varepsilon (N_0-b_ K-qb)-2b\bigr )\omega +\frac{\varepsilon }{R}\,  \mathrm i\partial \psi _\varepsilon \wedge \bar\partial \psi _\varepsilon \geq 2\pi \omega +\frac{\varepsilon }{R}\,  \mathrm i\partial \psi _\varepsilon \wedge \bar\partial \psi _\varepsilon , \end{equation} where in the last step we used $a_\varepsilon \geq 1$ and $N_0-b_ K-qb=2b+2$. All constants in this display depend only on the geometry. Step 2: the correction. Let $\rho \in C^\infty (\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0\leq \rho \leq 1$, $\rho =1$ on $(-\infty ,1/2]$ and $\rho =0$ on $[1,\infty )$, and put $G_\varepsilon =\rho (R/\varepsilon )G$. Since $\bar\partial R/\varepsilon =(1+R/\varepsilon )\bar\partial \psi _\varepsilon $, the $\bar\partial $-closed form $g_\varepsilon =\bar\partial G_\varepsilon $ splits as \[  g_\varepsilon =g_\varepsilon ^{(1)}+g_\varepsilon ^{(2)},\qquad g_\varepsilon ^{(1)}=\rho '(R/\varepsilon )(1+R/\varepsilon ) \bar\partial \psi _\varepsilon \, G, \qquad g_\varepsilon ^{(2)}=\rho (R/\varepsilon )\bar\partial G,  \] regarded as $F$-valued $(n,1)$-forms. As in the proof of lemma 14.7.3 , the rank-one part of ( 14.42 ) and lemma 14.6.1 (1),(2) give \[  |\langle g_\varepsilon ^{(1)},v\rangle |^2\leq 4\sup |\rho '|^2\, |G|^2\langle [H_\varepsilon ,\Lambda _\omega ]v,v\rangle  \] pointwise on the shell $\{ \varepsilon /2\leq R\leq \varepsilon \} $, where $R/\varepsilon \leq 1$, the norms being those of the metric of $F$. Hence the integral $M_{g_\varepsilon ^{(1)}}$ of lemma 14.7.1 , formed with $H_\varepsilon $, is at most $C_1\int _{\{ \varepsilon /2\leq R\leq \varepsilon \} }|G|_ h^2R^{-q}\, \mathrm dV$, whose upper limit as $\varepsilon \to 0$ is at most $C_2\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y$ by lemma 14.7.7 . Since $H_\varepsilon \geq 2\pi \omega $, lemma 14.6.1 (3) bounds $M_{g_\varepsilon ^{(2)}}$ by \[  C_3\int _{\{ R<\varepsilon \} }|\bar\partial G|_{\omega ,h}^2R^{-q}\, \mathrm dV,  \] which tends to zero by ( 14.38 ). Both forms are square integrable for the metric of $F$. For $g_\varepsilon ^{(1)}$, the derivative of the cutoff is bounded for fixed $\varepsilon $, and ( 14.37 ) bounds the integral of $|G|_ h^2R^{-q}$ over the shell, where the logarithm is bounded and $\mathrm e^{-\Phi }\leq \mathrm e^{\kappa \sup _ X\Phi }\mathrm e^{-(1+\kappa )\Phi }$; for $g_\varepsilon ^{(2)}$ this follows from ( 14.38 ). Since $M_{g'+g''}\leq 2(M_{g'}+M_{g''})$, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the positive form $\langle [H_\varepsilon ,\Lambda _\omega ]^{-1}\cdot ,\cdot \rangle $, lemma 14.7.1 gives $u_\varepsilon $ on $M$ with 14.43 \begin{equation} \label{eq:global-normal-correction-bound} \bar\partial u_\varepsilon =g_\varepsilon ,\qquad \varlimsup _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int _ M\frac{|u_\varepsilon |_ h^2R^{-q}}{a_\varepsilon +b_\varepsilon }\, \mathrm dV \leq C_4\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y. \end{equation} The constants $C_1,\ldots ,C_4$ depend only on the geometry and the fixed cutoff $\rho $; neither the exponent $\kappa $ nor the derivatives of the local extensions $F_ i$ enter them. Step 3: holomorphic sections with the trace $f$. For fixed $\varepsilon $ the denominator $a_\varepsilon +b_\varepsilon $ is bounded, and $h\geq \mathrm e^{-\sup _ X\Phi }h_0$ because $\Phi $ is bounded above on the compact manifold $X$. Hence $s_\varepsilon =G_\varepsilon -u_\varepsilon $, which is holomorphic on $M$, is square integrable for $h_0$, and it extends to a global holomorphic section by lemma 14.6.6 . Then $u_\varepsilon =G_\varepsilon -s_\varepsilon $ is smooth on $X$. It remains to show that $s_\varepsilon |_ Y=f$. Let $y\in Y\setminus A$, and choose holomorphic coordinates $(z',w)$ near $y$ with $Y=\{ w=0\} $. Near $y$ the weight $\Phi $ is smooth and $a_\varepsilon +b_\varepsilon $ is bounded, so $\int |u_\varepsilon |_{h_0}^2R^{-q}\, \mathrm dV$ is finite over a neighborhood of $y$. Since $R\leq C|w|^2$ near $y$ by lemma 14.7.4 , and $\int _{|w|<r}|w|^{-2q}\, \mathrm dV(w)=\infty $ in $\mathbb C^ q$ for every $r>0$, by polar coordinates, the continuous function $u_\varepsilon $ vanishes at $y$. Hence $u_\varepsilon =0$ on $Y\setminus A$, and $s_\varepsilon =G=f$ there. Since the restriction of $h$ to $Y$ is defined, $A\cap Y$ is a proper analytic subset of the connected manifold $Y$, and the identity theorem gives $s_\varepsilon |_ Y=f$. Step 4: the norm bound. For all sufficiently small $\varepsilon $, \[  (a_\varepsilon +b_\varepsilon )R^ q \leq C_5 R^ q(-\log R)^2\leq C_6,  \] because $a_\varepsilon +b_\varepsilon \leq 5\psi ^2$ by lemma 14.7.2 (1), and because $R^ q(-\log R)^2$ is bounded on $X$. Consequently ( 14.43 ) bounds $\int _ X|u_\varepsilon |_ h^2\, \mathrm dV$ by $C_6$ times the integral there. The section $G$ has finite $h$-norm, since ( 14.37 ) controls it, $\Phi $ being bounded above and $R^ q(-\log R)^2$ bounded; therefore $\| G_\varepsilon \| _ h\to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, by absolute continuity of the integral on the shrinking supports. The triangle inequality gives \[  \varlimsup _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\| s_\varepsilon \| _ h^2 \leq C_7\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y,  \] with $C_7=C_6C_4$. The sections $s_\varepsilon $ are bounded in $L^2$ for $h_0$, so, by lemma 14.5.2 (2), a sequence $\varepsilon _ k\to 0$ gives sections converging uniformly to a holomorphic section $s$. Its restriction to $Y$ is $f$, and Fatou's lemma gives $\| s\| _ h^2\leq C_7\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y$. This proves the theorem for gentle weights with the constant $C_7$, which depends only on the geometry. Step 5: arbitrary weights. Put $N=N_0+1$. By theorem 13.4.5 , applied to $\varphi $ with the background $c_1(L,h_0)-N\omega $, there are $\Phi _ j\downarrow \varphi $ with gentle analytic singularities of the kind required in the gentle case and $c_1(L,h_0\mathrm e^{-\Phi _ j})\geq (N-\delta _ j)\omega $, where $\delta _ j\to 0$; for large $j$ the curvature is at least $N_0\omega $. Since $\Phi _ j\geq \varphi $, the restrictions of the metrics $h_0\mathrm e^{-\Phi _ j}$ to $Y$ are defined, and the norms of $f$ for them are at most its norm for $h$. The gentle case gives $s_ j\in H^0(X,L)$ with $s_ j|_ Y=f$ and $\int _ X|s_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi _ j}\, \mathrm dV\leq C_7\int _ Y|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV_ Y$. Since $\Phi _ j\leq \Phi _1$, the $s_ j$ are bounded in $L^2$ for $h_0$, and by lemma 14.5.2 (2) a subsequence converges uniformly to a holomorphic section $s$ with $s|_ Y=f$. The weights $\mathrm e^{-\Phi _ j}$ converge to $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ wherever $\varphi $ is finite, hence almost everywhere, and Fatou's lemma gives ( 14.41 ) with $C=C_7$. $\square$ Corollary 14.7.9 . Let $L$ and $T$ be holomorphic line bundles on $X$ with smooth quadratic metrics $h_0$ and $h_ T$, put $\theta =c_1(L,h_0)$, and choose $b_ T\geq 0$ with $c_1(T,h_ T)\geq -b_ T\omega $. Let $\varphi $ be quasi-plurisubharmonic with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$, and let $Y\subset X$ be a nonempty closed connected complex submanifold such that $\varphi |_ Y$ is not identically $-\infty $. Let $N$ and $C$ be the constants of theorem 14.7.8 . Then for every integer $k\geq 1$ with $k\delta -b_ T\geq N$, every holomorphic section $f$ of $(T\otimes L^ k)|_ Y$ with finite norm for $h_ T\otimes h_0^ k\mathrm e^{-k\varphi |_ Y}$ extends to a holomorphic section $s$ of $T\otimes L^ k$ on $X$ with \[  \int _ X|s|_{h_ T\otimes h_0^ k}^2\mathrm e^{-k\varphi }\, \mathrm dV \leq C\int _ Y|f|_{h_ T\otimes h_0^ k}^2 \mathrm e^{-k\varphi |_ Y}\, \mathrm dV_ Y.  \] Proof. The metric $h_ T\otimes h_0^ k\mathrm e^{-k\varphi }$ on $T\otimes L^ k$ is plurisubharmonic, its curvature current is $c_1(T,h_ T)+k(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\geq (k\delta -b_ T)\omega \geq N\omega $, and its restriction to $Y$ is defined. Hence theorem 14.7.8 applies. Note that the finiteness of the norm on $Y$ means that $f$ lies locally in the multiplier ideal of $k\varphi |_ Y$, and that the constant $C$ is multiplied by $n!/(\dim Y)!$ if the volumes $\omega ^ n$ and $\omega |_ Y^{\dim Y}$ are used instead of $\mathrm dV$ and $\mathrm dV_ Y$. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.7.1
section: 9.1 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.7.1 . Let $M$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Hermitian form $\omega $ and the volume form $\mathrm dV=\omega ^ n/n!$, carrying a Kähler form $\sigma \geq \omega /2$ and functions $\chi _ R$ with the properties stated in lemma 14.6.4 . Let $F\to M$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h$, and let $a,b$ be smooth functions on $M$ that are bounded above and below by positive constants. Suppose that the real $(1,1)$-form \[  H=a\, 2\pi c_1(F,h)-\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial a -\frac{\mathrm i}{b}\partial a\wedge \bar\partial a  \] is positive definite, and put $B_\omega =[H,\Lambda _\omega ]$ on $(n,1)$-forms. Let $g$ be an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-form with $\bar\partial g=0$ in the sense of distributions, $g\in L^2_{(n,1)}(\omega ,h)$, and \[  M_ g=\int _ M\langle B_\omega ^{-1}g,g\rangle _{\omega ,h}\, \mathrm dV<\infty .  \] Then there is an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-form $u$ with $\bar\partial u=g$ and 14.31 \begin{equation} \label{eq:twisted-kahler-correction} \int _ M\frac{|u|_{\omega ,h}^2}{a+b}\, \mathrm dV\leq M_ g. \end{equation} Proof. The Bochner–Kodaira identity ( 14.25 ) of lemma 14.6.2 holds for every smooth metric on $F$; we apply it to the metric $ah$. Let $\delta _ h=D''{}^*$ be the formal adjoint for the metric $h$ and the Kähler form $\sigma $, and $C_ a=(\bar\partial a\wedge )^*$ the contraction with the dual of $\bar\partial a$. In a frame, the weight of $ah$ is $p-\log a$, so \[  \delta _{ah}=\delta _ h-a^{-1}C_ a,\qquad a\, 2\pi c_1(F,ah)=a\, 2\pi c_1(F,h) -\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial a +\frac{\mathrm i}{a}\partial a\wedge \bar\partial a.  \] On $(n,1)$-forms, the commutator with the last term is $[\frac{\mathrm i}{a}\partial a\wedge \bar\partial a,\Lambda _\sigma ]=a^{-1}C_ a^*C_ a$. Indeed, where $\partial a\neq 0$, choose a $\sigma $-unitary coframe with $\partial a=|\partial a|\theta _1$, so that $\bar\partial a=|\partial a|\bar\theta _1$, and put $e=\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ n$. By lemma 14.6.1 (1), the left side multiplies the coefficient $v_1$ of $e\wedge \bar\theta _1$ by $|\partial a|^2/a$ and annihilates the other coefficients; so does the right side, because $\bar\partial a\wedge fe=(-1)^ n|\partial a|f\, e\wedge \bar\theta _1$, whence $C_ av=(-1)^ n|\partial a|v_1e$. Where $\partial a=0$, both sides vanish. Writing ( 14.25 ) for $ah$ in terms of $h$, expanding $a|\delta _ hv-a^{-1}C_ av|^2$, cancelling the term $a^{-1}|C_ av|^2$ that appears on both sides, and dropping the nonnegative term $\| D'{}^*v\| ^2$, we obtain for compactly supported smooth $v$, with all integrals taken with respect to $h$, $\sigma $ and $\mathrm dV_\sigma $, \[  \int _ M a\bigl (|\delta _ hv|^2+|D''v|^2\bigr ) \geq \int _ M\langle [a\, 2\pi c_1(F,h) -\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial a,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,v\rangle +2\operatorname{Re}\int _ M\langle \delta _ hv,C_ av\rangle .  \] The inequality $2\operatorname{Re}\langle A,B\rangle \geq -b|A|^2-b^{-1}|B|^2$ and the identity $b^{-1}|C_ av|^2=\langle [\frac{\mathrm i}{b}\partial a\wedge \bar\partial a,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,v\rangle $ consequently give 14.32 \begin{equation} \label{eq:twisted-kahler-bochner} \int _ M\langle [H,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,v\rangle \leq \int _ M(a+b)|\delta _ hv|^2+a|D''v|^2. \end{equation} Consider the Hilbert spaces of $(n,0)$-, $(n,1)$- and $(n,2)$-forms with the respective weights $h/(a+b)$, $h$ and $ah$, and the operators $T=D''$ and $S=D''$ with maximal domains between them. Testing against compactly supported forms shows that $T^*=(a+b)\delta _ h$, so $\| T^*v\| ^2$ is the first term on the right of ( 14.32 ), and $\| Sv\| ^2$ is the second. Compactly supported smooth forms are dense in $\operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$ for the graph norm, by lemma 14.6.3 , applied with the metrics $h/(a+b)$, $h$ and $ah$, whose ratios $a+b$ and $a$ are bounded. The form $g$ lies in $\ker S$, and in the second space by lemma 14.6.1 (3), because $\sigma \geq \omega /2$. The operator $[H,\Lambda _\sigma ]$ is positive definite on $(n,1)$-forms by lemma 14.6.1 (1). As in the proof of lemma 14.6.5 , the pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for this operator, ( 14.32 ) and the density of compactly supported smooth forms give the hypothesis of theorem 11.1.4 , which yields a solution of $\bar\partial u=g$ whose squared norm in the first space is at most $\int \langle [H,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,g\rangle \, \mathrm dV_\sigma $. This integral, and the squared norm of $(n,0)$-forms times the volume form, do not depend on the Hermitian form used, by lemma 14.6.1 (3); hence the bound is $M_ g$, and we obtain ( 14.31 ). $\square$
