Theorem 14.7.12 . Let $Y\subset X$ be a closed complex submanifold, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\omega |_ Y)$ satisfy \[  \omega |_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \, \omega |_ Y  \] for some $\delta >0$. Suppose that $\mathrm e^\varphi $, defined to be zero at the poles of $\varphi $, is Hölder continuous on $Y$. Then there are $\widetilde\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $\varepsilon >0$ such that \[  \widetilde\varphi |_ Y=\varphi ,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde\varphi \geq \varepsilon \omega .  \] Moreover $\widetilde\varphi $ is continuous on $X\setminus Y$, and $\mathrm e^{\widetilde\varphi }$ is Hölder continuous on $X$. If $\varphi $ has analytic singularities, then so does $\widetilde\varphi $. Proof. We construct local extensions near $Y$ (Steps 1 and 2), compare them on overlaps (Step 3), glue them (Step 4), extend the result from a neighborhood of $Y$ to $X$ (Step 5), and finally treat analytic singularities (Step 6). Step 0. Reductions. If $Y=\varnothing $, the function $\widetilde\varphi =0$ and $\varepsilon =1$ have all the stated properties; $0=\log |1|^2$ has analytic singularities. Let $Y
eq \varnothing $. The connected components of $Y$ are open in the compact set $Y$, so there are finitely many of them, say $Y_1,\ldots ,Y_ r$; each $Y_ k$ is closed in $X$, hence a compact connected complex submanifold, and different components may have different dimensions. If some $Y_ k$ has dimension $n$, then it is open in $X$, because near each of its points it is a coordinate plane of full dimension; being also closed, it equals $X$, as $X$ is connected. Then $Y=X$, and $\widetilde\varphi =\varphi $ with $\varepsilon =\delta $ has the stated properties. We may therefore assume that every component of $Y$ has positive codimension; components of dimension zero are allowed. Fix $\varepsilon $ with $0<\varepsilon <\min \{ \delta /4,1/4\} $. By lemma 14.7.10 (2), $\mathrm e^\varphi $ is Hölder continuous with one exponent $\alpha \in (0,1]$ on finitely many coordinate neighborhoods covering $Y$. By lemma 14.7.10 (1), every point $p\in Y$ then has, in every system of coordinates of $Y$ near $p$, a neighborhood on which $\mathrm e^\varphi $ is Hölder continuous with exponent $\alpha $. Step 1. A small normal pole. For each $k$ let $R_ k=R_{Y_ k}$ be the function of lemma 14.7.4 for the submanifold $Y_ k$, and let $\kappa _ k\geq 0$ be the constant called $b$ there, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log R_ k\geq -\kappa _ k\omega $. Put \[  R=R_1\cdots R_ r,\qquad \kappa =\kappa _1+\cdots +\kappa _ r.  \] Then $R\geq 0$ is smooth and vanishes exactly on $Y$. The function $\log R=\sum _ k\log R_ k$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log R\geq -\kappa \omega $, and has analytic singularities by proposition 13.1.7 , as a sum of functions with analytic singularities. Choose a rational number $c$ with $0<c<\alpha $ and $c\kappa /2\leq 1-4\varepsilon $; this is possible because $1-4\varepsilon >0$. Put $F=(c/2)\log R$. Then \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F\geq \Bigl (1- rac{c\kappa }2\Bigr )\omega \geq 4\varepsilon \omega .  \] The function $F$ is smooth on $X\setminus Y$, equals $-\infty $ on $Y$, and has analytic singularities, since $c/2$ is rational. Its exponential $\mathrm e^ F=R^{c/2}$ is Hölder continuous on $X$ by lemma 14.7.10 (3). We need a lower bound for $R$ near $Y$. Let $p\in Y_ k$, and let $(z',w)$ be holomorphic coordinates near $p$ in which $Y=\{ w=0\} $. The function $P=\prod _{l
eq k}R_ l$ is smooth and positive near $p$, since the closed sets $Y_ l$, $l
eq k$, do not contain $p$. On a neighborhood of $p$ that does not meet these sets we have $Y_ k=Y=\{ w=0\} $, so the second inequality in ( 14.35 ) of lemma 14.7.4 , applied to $Y_ k$, bounds $R_ k$ below by a positive multiple of $|w|^2$ near $p$. Since $R=R_ kP$ and $P$ is bounded away from zero near $p$, there are a closed ball $K$ centered at $p$ and a constant $c_0>0$ such that 14.44  egin{equation} \label{eq:normal-exponential-lower-bound} R\geq c_0|w|^2,\qquad \mathrm e^ F=R^{c/2}\geq c_0^{c/2}|w|^ c\qquad 	ext{on }K. \end{equation} Moreover, at the points $(z',0)$ of the interior of $K$, the real Hessian $D_ w^2R(z',0)$ of $w\mapsto R(z',w)$ at $w=0$ is positive definite. Indeed, $R\geq 0$ attains its minimum $0$ at such a point, so its first derivatives vanish there, and Taylor's formula gives $R(z',t\xi )= rac{t^2}2D_ w^2R(z',0)[\xi ,\xi ]+O(t^3)$ as $t	o 0$, for every $\xi $; comparing with $R(z',t\xi )\geq c_0t^2|\xi |^2$ for small $t$, we obtain $D_ w^2R(z',0)[\xi ,\xi ]\geq 2c_0|\xi |^2$. Step 2. Local extensions. Every point of $Y$ has holomorphic coordinates $(z',w)\in \mathbb C^ m	imes \mathbb C^{n-m}$, centered at that point, in which $Y=\{ w=0\} $ on the coordinate domain, where $m<n$ is the dimension of the component of $Y$ through the point. A product of two small balls centered at the origin is then a chart $\widehat W=\widehat B'	imes \widehat B''$ with $Y\cap \widehat W=\widehat B'	imes \{ 0\} $. The products $B'	imes B''$ of the concentric balls of half the radii cover $Y$, and since $Y$ is compact, finitely many of them suffice. We thus obtain finitely many charts $W_ j=B'_ j	imes B''_ j$, relatively compact in charts $\widehat W_ j=\widehat B'_ j	imes \widehat B''_ j$ of the same form, with $Y\cap W_ j=B'_ j	imes \{ 0\} $ and with dimensions $m_ j<n$. Let $\pi _ j\colon \widehat W_ j	o Y$, $\pi _ j(z',w)=(z',0)$, be the holomorphic projection. Below we shrink the normal factors $B''_ j$ several times, keeping them balls centered at the origin; this does not change $Y\cap W_ j$, so the charts keep covering $Y$. If a property holds on an open set $O\subset \widehat W_ j$ containing the compact set $\overline{B'_ j}	imes \{ 0\} $, then this compact set has positive distance from the complement of $O$ in the coordinates, so $O$ contains $W_ j$ after the normal factor has been shrunk. We claim that there is $A>0$ such that, after such a shrinking, \[  a_ j=\varphi \circ \pi _ j+AR,\qquad b_ j=F+AR  \] belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(W_ j,(1-2\varepsilon )\omega )$ for every $j$. Since $4\varepsilon \leq \delta $, the hypothesis gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -(1-\delta )\omega |_ Y\geq -(1-4\varepsilon )\omega |_ Y$. Choose a ball $\widetilde B'_ j$, concentric with $B'_ j$, with $\overline{B'_ j}\subset \widetilde B'_ j\Subset \widehat B'_ j$, and a smooth function $s$ on $\widetilde B'_ j	imes \{ 0\} $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s=(1-4\varepsilon )\omega |_ Y$ there (lemma 13.1.2 ; if $m_ j=0$, take $s=0$). Then $\varphi +s$ is plurisubharmonic on $\widetilde B'_ j	imes \{ 0\} $, by lemma 13.1.4 (2). By proposition 8.2.3 , $(\varphi +s)\circ \pi _ j$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on the connected set $\widetilde B'_ j	imes \widehat B''_ j$, and the second alternative is excluded because $\pi _ j$ maps this set onto $\widetilde B'_ j	imes \{ 0\} $, where $\varphi +s$ is not identically $-\infty $. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(s\circ \pi _ j)=\pi _ j^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ for the smooth function $s$, we obtain that $\varphi \circ \pi _ j$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $\widetilde B'_ j	imes \widehat B''_ j\supset \overline{W_ j}$ and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi \circ \pi _ j)\geq -(1-4\varepsilon )\pi _ j^*(\omega |_ Y).  \] For $a_ j$ it therefore suffices that the smooth form \[  Q_ j=(1-2\varepsilon )\omega -(1-4\varepsilon )\pi _ j^*(\omega |_ Y)+A\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R  \] be positive on $W_ j$. We first examine $Q_ j$ at the points of $Y$. Write a real $(1,1)$-form on $W_ j$ as $\mathrm i\sum _{\mu ,
u }g_{\mu 
u }\, \mathrm d\zeta _\mu \wedge \mathrm d ar\zeta _
u $, where $\zeta =(z',w)$, and split its Hermitian coefficient matrix $(g_{\mu 
u })$ into blocks with respect to the tangential coordinates $z'$ and the normal coordinates $w$; the form is positive definite at a point if and only if this matrix is. The form $\pi _ j^*(\omega |_ Y)$ involves only $\mathrm dz'$ and $\mathrm d ar z'$, and at a point $(z',0)$ its coefficients are those of $\omega |_ Y$ at that point. Hence its mixed and normal blocks vanish, and at points of $Y$ its tangential block is the tangential block $\Omega _ T$ of $\omega $. The function $R$ vanishes on $Y$ together with its first derivatives. Differentiating the identities $R(z',0)=0$ and $\partial R/\partial  ar w_
u (z',0)=0$ with respect to $z'$ and $ ar z'$ shows that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ has zero tangential and mixed blocks along $Y$. Its normal block is $(2\pi )^{-1}$ times the matrix $N_ R=(\partial ^2R/\partial w_\mu \partial  ar w_
u )$, which is positive definite at points of $Y$: for $\xi \in \mathbb C^{n-m_ j}\setminus \{ 0\} $, applying the identity $\Delta =4\partial _ t\partial _{ ar t}$ to $t\mapsto R(z',t\xi )$ at $t=0$ gives \[  \sum _{\mu ,
u } rac{\partial ^2R}{\partial w_\mu \partial  ar w_
u }(z',0)\xi _\mu  ar\xi _
u = rac14 igl (D_ w^2R(z',0)[\xi ,\xi ]+D_ w^2R(z',0)[\mathrm i\xi ,\mathrm i\xi ] igr )>0  \] by Step 1. Consequently, at a point of $Y$, the tangential block of $Q_ j$ is $2\varepsilon \Omega _ T$, which is positive definite, its mixed block is the mixed block $\Omega _ M$ of $(1-2\varepsilon )\omega $, and its normal block is $\Omega _ N+AN_ R/(2\pi )$, where $\Omega _ N$ is the normal block of $(1-2\varepsilon )\omega $. By the Schur complement criterion for Hermitian block matrices whose upper left block is positive definite, $Q_ j$ is positive definite at a point of $Y$ if and only if \[  \Omega _ N+ rac A{2\pi }N_ R-\Omega _ M^* igl (2\varepsilon \, \Omega _ T igr )^{-1}\Omega _ M  \] is positive definite there. (If $m_ j=0$, there is no tangential block, and the condition reads $\Omega _ N+AN_ R/(2\pi )>0$.) All blocks depend continuously on the point, $N_ R$ is positive definite, and the sets $\overline{B'_ j}	imes \{ 0\} $ are compact and finite in number. Hence the smallest eigenvalue of $N_ R$ on them has a positive lower bound and the other two terms are bounded, so one $A$ makes this matrix positive definite at every point of every $\overline{B'_ j}	imes \{ 0\} $. Fix such an $A$. Since the coefficients of $Q_ j$ are continuous on $\widehat W_ j$ and positive definiteness is an open condition, $Q_ j$ is positive definite on an open set containing $\overline{B'_ j}	imes \{ 0\} $, and we shrink the normal factor $B''_ j$ so that $W_ j$ lies in this set. This proves the claim for $a_ j$. Along $Y$ the form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ is positive semidefinite, so $A\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R+\varepsilon \omega $ is positive definite on an open set containing $\overline{B'_ j}	imes \{ 0\} $; after shrinking the normal factors once more we have $A\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R\geq -\varepsilon \omega $ on every $W_ j$. Together with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F\geq -(1-4\varepsilon )\omega $ this gives \[  (1-2\varepsilon )\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ j\geq (1-2\varepsilon )\omega -(1-4\varepsilon )\omega -\varepsilon \omega =\varepsilon \omega \geq 0,  \] which proves the claim for $b_ j$. By lemma 14.7.11 , applied with $	heta =(1-2\varepsilon )\omega $, the functions \[  \varphi _ j=\log (\mathrm e^{a_ j}+\mathrm e^{b_ j}) =\log (\mathrm e^{\varphi \circ \pi _ j}+\mathrm e^ F)+AR  \] belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(W_ j,(1-2\varepsilon )\omega )$. On $Y$ we have $F=-\infty $, $R=0$ and $\varphi \circ \pi _ j=\varphi $, so $\varphi _ j=\varphi $ on $Y\cap W_ j$, also at the poles of $\varphi $. Off $Y$ the function $\mathrm e^ F$ is positive and continuous and $\mathrm e^{\varphi \circ \pi _ j}$ is continuous, so $\varphi _ j$ is continuous on $W_ j\setminus Y$. Finally $\mathrm e^{\varphi _ j}=(\mathrm e^\varphi \circ \pi _ j+\mathrm e^ F)\, \mathrm e^{AR}$ is Hölder continuous on $W_ j$ by lemma 14.7.10 (3),(4). Step 3. Comparison on overlaps. We claim that for every $p\in Y\cap W_ i\cap W_ j$ and every $\eta >0$ there is a neighborhood of $p$ on which 14.45  egin{equation} \label{eq:holder-extension-overlap} \varphi _ i\leq \varphi _ j+\eta . \end{equation} Work in the coordinates $(z',w)$ of $W_ i$, and write $p=(z'_ p,0)$. The coordinate $z'$ restricts to coordinates of $Y$ on $Y\cap W_ i$, so by Step 0 there are a neighborhood $V_ p$ of $p$ in $Y\cap W_ i$ and a constant $C_ H$ with $|\mathrm e^{\varphi (y_1)}-\mathrm e^{\varphi (y_2)}|\leq C_ H|z'(y_1)-z'(y_2)|^\alpha $ for $y_1,y_2\in V_ p$. Since $\pi _ i$ and $\pi _ j$ are continuous and fix $p$, there is a closed ball $K\subset W_ i\cap W_ j$ centered at $p$ such that $\pi _ i(K)\cup \pi _ j(K)\subset V_ p$ and ( 14.44 ) holds on $K$ in these coordinates. The map $z'\circ \pi _ j$ is smooth on the convex compact set $K$, so it is Lipschitz there with some constant $L$. Let $x=(z',w)\in K$, and put $y=(z',0)=\pi _ i(x)$. Then $|y-p|\leq |x-p|$, so $y\in K\cap Y$, and $\pi _ j(y)=y$ because $\pi _ j$ is the identity on $Y\cap W_ j$. Hence \[  |z'(\pi _ i(x))-z'(\pi _ j(x))|=|z'(\pi _ j(y))-z'(\pi _ j(x))|\leq L|y-x|=L|w|,  \] and therefore \[   igl |\mathrm e^{\varphi \circ \pi _ i}(x)-\mathrm e^{\varphi \circ \pi _ j}(x) igr |\leq C_ HL^\alpha |w|^\alpha .  \] Since $c<\alpha $, we have $C_ HL^\alpha |w|^\alpha \leq (\mathrm e^\eta -1)c_0^{c/2}|w|^ c$ whenever $|w|$ is sufficiently small, and then ( 14.44 ) gives $C_ HL^\alpha |w|^\alpha \leq (\mathrm e^\eta -1)\mathrm e^{F(x)}$. At such points $x\in K$, including the points of $Y$, \[  \mathrm e^{\varphi \circ \pi _ i}+\mathrm e^ F \leq \mathrm e^{\varphi \circ \pi _ j}+\mathrm e^\eta \mathrm e^ F \leq \mathrm e^\eta  igl (\mathrm e^{\varphi \circ \pi _ j}+\mathrm e^ F igr ).  \] The logarithm is increasing on $[0,\infty )$, with $\log 0=-\infty $, so taking logarithms and adding $AR$ to both sides gives ( 14.45 ) on the neighborhood of $p$ formed by the interior points $x$ of $K$ with $|w(x)|$ sufficiently small. Step 4. Gluing near $Y$. Every point of $Y$ has an open neighborhood whose closure is contained in some $W_ j$, and finitely many of these neighborhoods cover $Y$; let $W'_ j$ be the union of those chosen inside $W_ j$. Then $W'_ j\Subset W_ j$ and the $W'_ j$ cover $Y$. Choose open sets $U_ j$ and $T_ j$ with $W'_ j\Subset U_ j\Subset T_ j\Subset W_ j$, for instance sets of points whose coordinate distance from $\overline{W'_ j}$ is less than suitable small constants. The compact set $\overline{T_ j}\setminus U_ j$ is contained in the open set $W_ j\setminus \overline{W'_ j}$, so by proposition 7.1.3 there is a smooth function $f_ j\colon X	o [0,1]$ with compact support in $W_ j\setminus \overline{W'_ j}$ which equals one on a neighborhood of $\overline{T_ j}\setminus U_ j$; in particular $f_ j=0$ on the neighborhood $X\setminus \operatorname{Supp}f_ j$ of $\overline{W'_ j}$. Fix $\eta >0$ so small that $\eta \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j\leq \varepsilon \omega $ for every $j$. Since $(1-\varepsilon )\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\geq \varepsilon \omega $, the functions \[  \widehat\varphi _ j=\varphi _ j-\eta f_ j  \] belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(W_ j,(1-\varepsilon )\omega )$. On $W= igcup _ jT_ j$ define \[  \psi (x)=\max \{ \widehat\varphi _ j(x):x\in T_ j\} .  \] The set of indices in this maximum changes with $x$. We show that near $Y$ the maximum is nevertheless taken over a fixed set of indices. Let $p\in Y$, and choose $j$ with $p\in W'_ j$; then $f_ j=0$ near $p$, and $j$ occurs in the maximum near $p$. Let $l$ be an index with $p\in \partial T_ l$. Then $p\in \overline{T_ l}\setminus U_ l$, so $f_ l=1$ near $p$. Since $p\in Y\cap W_ l\cap W_ j$, the inequality ( 14.45 ) with $\eta /2$ in place of $\eta $ gives, near $p$, \[  \widehat\varphi _ l=\varphi _ l-\eta \leq \varphi _ j-\eta /2\leq \widehat\varphi _ j.  \] These are inequalities between functions with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$, valid also at common poles. As there are finitely many indices, $p$ has a neighborhood $O_ p$ on which the indices $l$ with $p\in \partial T_ l$ never affect the maximum, the indices with $p
otin \overline{T_ l}$ do not occur, and the indices with $p\in T_ l$ occur at every point. Thus, on $O_ p$, the function $\psi $ is the maximum of the $\widehat\varphi _ l$ over the fixed finite set of indices $l$ with $p\in T_ l$. Let $W_0= igcup _{p\in Y}O_ p$. A finite maximum of functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(O_ p,(1-\varepsilon )\omega )$ belongs to this class, by lemma 13.1.4 (3). Hence $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(W_0,(1-\varepsilon )\omega )$; moreover $\psi $ is continuous on $W_0\setminus Y$, and $\mathrm e^\psi $, which is locally a finite maximum of the functions $\mathrm e^{\widehat\varphi _ l}=\mathrm e^{\varphi _ l}\mathrm e^{-\eta f_ l}$, is Hölder continuous on $W_0$ by lemma 14.7.10 (3). On $Y$ every $\widehat\varphi _ l$ restricts to $\varphi -\eta f_ l\leq \varphi $, while $\widehat\varphi _ j=\varphi $ near $p$ for the index $j$ chosen above. Consequently $\psi |_ Y=\varphi $. Step 5. The global extension. Choose an open neighborhood $G$ of $Y$ with $\overline G\subset W_0$, for instance a finite union of coordinate balls with closures in $W_0$ covering the compact set $Y$. Its boundary $\partial G$ is compact and disjoint from $Y$, and both $\psi $ and $F$ are finite and continuous near $\partial G$. Choose a constant $M$ with $M>\max _{\partial G}(\psi -F)$ (if $\partial G=\varnothing $, every $M$ will do); since $F+M-\psi $ is continuous on $W_0\setminus Y$ and positive on $\partial G$, it is positive on an open neighborhood $G_1\subset W_0\setminus Y$ of $\partial G$. Set \[  \widetilde\varphi =  egin{cases}  \max \{ \psi ,F+M\} & 	ext{on }G,\  F+M& 	ext{on }X\setminus G. \end{cases}  \] The two expressions agree on $G_1$, so $\widetilde\varphi =F+M$ on the open set $G_1\cup (X\setminus \overline G)$, which contains $X\setminus G$. The function $F+M$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,(1-4\varepsilon )\omega )\subset \mathrm{PSH}(X,(1-\varepsilon )\omega )$, and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(W_0,(1-\varepsilon )\omega )$. Let $B$ be a coordinate ball whose closure lies in a chart, and $h$ a smooth function on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=(1-\varepsilon )\omega $ (lemma 13.1.2 ). Then $F+M+h\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ and $\psi +h\in \mathrm{PSH}(G\cap B)$. Every point $x$ of the boundary of $G\cap B$ in $B$ lies in $\partial G$, and $\varlimsup _{G
i y	o x}(\psi +h)(y)\leq F(x)+M+h(x)$, because $\psi <F+M$ on $G_1$ and $F+M+h$ is continuous at $x$. By proposition 8.2.5 , $\widetilde\varphi +h$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$. Since such balls cover $X$, $\widetilde\varphi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic and $(1-\varepsilon )\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde\varphi \geq 0$, that is, $\widetilde\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde\varphi \geq \varepsilon \omega $. Since $F=-\infty $ on $Y$, we have $\widetilde\varphi |_ Y=\psi |_ Y=\varphi $. The function $\widetilde\varphi $ is continuous on $X\setminus Y$, because $\psi $ and $F$ are continuous on $W_0\setminus Y$ and $X\setminus Y$, respectively. Its exponential equals $\max \{ \mathrm e^\psi ,\mathrm e^ M\mathrm e^ F\} $ on $G$ and $\mathrm e^ M\mathrm e^ F$ on the open set $G_1\cup (X\setminus \overline G)$; these two open sets cover $X$, so $\mathrm e^{\widetilde\varphi }$ is Hölder continuous on $X$ by lemma 14.7.10 (3). Step 6. Analytic singularities. Finally suppose that $\varphi $ has analytic singularities (definition 13.1.5 ). By proposition 13.1.7 , so does the holomorphic pullback $\varphi \circ \pi _ j$, which is not identically $-\infty $, and the function $F$ has analytic singularities by Step 1. By the same proposition, $\max \{ \varphi \circ \pi _ j,F\} $ has analytic singularities; adding the smooth function $AR$ changes the bounded remainder in its local presentations ( 13.1 ) by a locally bounded function, so $\max \{ \varphi \circ \pi _ j,F\} +AR$ has analytic singularities. By lemma 14.7.11 , \[  \max \{ \varphi \circ \pi _ j,F\} +AR\leq \varphi _ j\leq \max \{ \varphi \circ \pi _ j,F\} +AR+\log 2.  \] Hence a local presentation ( 13.1 ) of $\max \{ \varphi \circ \pi _ j,F\} +AR$ yields one of $\varphi _ j$, with the same holomorphic functions and a bounded remainder changed by at most $\log 2$; so $\varphi _ j$ has analytic singularities. Subtracting the smooth function $\eta f_ j$ changes the remainders by bounded functions, and the locally fixed finite maxima of Step 4 preserve analytic singularities by proposition 13.1.7 ; so $\psi $ has analytic singularities on $W_0$. On $G$, the function $\widetilde\varphi $ is the maximum of $\psi $ and $F+M$, and on the open set $G_1\cup (X\setminus \overline G)$ it equals $F+M$; both functions have analytic singularities. Therefore $\widetilde\varphi $ has analytic singularities on $X$. $\square$

14.8 Global poles on compact complex manifolds We end the chapter by dropping the Kähler assumption. Recall that a subset of a complex manifold is pluripolar if it is locally contained in pole sets of plurisubharmonic functions (definition 10.1.1 ), and that by Josefson's theorem (theorem 10.2.1 ) a pluripolar subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ lies in the pole set of a single plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb C^ n$. On a compact connected complex manifold, however, every plurisubharmonic function is constant: the set where it attains its maximum is nonempty and closed, by upper semicontinuity, and open, by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) applied in coordinate balls, where plurisubharmonic functions are subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ). A global pole function must therefore be quasi-plurisubharmonic, and we prove that every pluripolar subset of a compact complex manifold, Kähler or not, lies in the pole set of one quasi-plurisubharmonic function (theorem 14.8.7 ). Throughout this section $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$ (section 7.5 ), which need not be closed. Then definition 13.1.3 does not apply to $\omega $, but its formula still makes sense: we write $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ for the set of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $u$ on $X$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ in the sense of currents, and call its elements $\omega $-plurisubharmonic ; for an open set $D\subset X$ the class $\mathrm{PSH}(D,\omega )$ is defined in the same way. When $\omega $ is Kähler, this is the class of definition 13.1.3 . We put $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. By lemma 13.1.4 (4), every quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\Phi $ on $X$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi \geq -C\omega $ for some constant $C$, which we may take positive. Consequently $t\Phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ for $0<t\leq 1/C$. In local coordinates $ eta $ denotes the Euclidean form ( 7.4 ), and for a point $a$ of a chart, $\omega (a)$ denotes the form with constant coefficients equal to those of $\omega $ at $a$. A real $(1,1)$-form with constant coefficients $\gamma = rac{\mathrm i}2\sum _{j,k}c_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ k$, where the matrix $(c_{jk})$ is Hermitian, is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of the real quadratic polynomial $\pi \sum _{j,k}c_{jk}z_ j ar z_ k$, because $\partial  ar\partial (z_ j ar z_ k)=\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ k$. Since every plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is constant, only the empty set is globally pluripolar in $X$ in the sense of definition 10.1.1 . In this section we therefore call a set $A\subset X$ globally pluripolar if $A\subset \{ \Phi =-\infty \} $ for some quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\Phi $ on $X$. Subsets of globally pluripolar sets are again globally pluripolar. The proof adapts the capacity argument of section 10.1 . For a set $A\subset X$, the regularization of the global extremal function $T_ A$, the upper envelope of the $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions that are nonpositive on $A$, is bounded unless $A$ is globally pluripolar (lemma 14.8.4 ). If a piece of a pluripolar set were not globally pluripolar, we would approximate it by compact sublevel sets of small capacity. The Monge–Ampère measure of the extremal function of a compact set is carried by that set, and its mass is controlled by the capacity (proposition 14.8.6 ), so in the limit we would obtain a bounded potential with zero Monge–Ampère mass. Since $\omega $ need not be closed, Stokes' formula does not compute the total mass $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$; its positivity follows from a comparison principle for small gaps (proposition 14.8.3 ), in which the error terms produced by $\mathrm d\omega $ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ are absorbed by the size of the gap. To show that the Monge–Ampère measure of an extremal function vanishes off its set, we freeze the coefficients of $\omega $ on small balls and use the homogeneous balayage of corollary 9.6.4 and a local estimate for nearby bounded potentials (lemma 14.8.5 ). We first define products of the currents $\omega _ u$ for bounded $u$. They are built from Bedford–Taylor products (definition 9.1.1 ), which do not depend on the chart in which they are computed (proposition 9.1.2 (2),(5)) and are symmetric in their factors (theorem 9.2.5 ). We use the following rule for adding smooth functions to the potentials. Let $v_1,\ldots ,v_ k$, $0\leq k\leq n$, be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, and let $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ be smooth real functions on $\Omega $ such that the functions $v_ l+g_ l$ are plurisubharmonic. We prove ( 14.48 ) by induction on $k$; for $k=0$ both sides equal $1$. Let $k\geq 1$ and assume ( 14.48 ) for $k-1$ factors, so that $R= igwedge _{l\geq 2}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ l+g_ l)=\sum _ IS_ I\wedge \Gamma _ I$, where $I$ runs over the subsets of $\{ 2,\ldots ,k\} $, $S_ I= igwedge _{l\in I}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l$, and $\Gamma _ I= igwedge _{l\in \{ 2,\ldots ,k\} \setminus I}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ l$ is a smooth closed form of pure bidegree. By definition, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_1+g_1)\wedge R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_1R)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g_1R)$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g_1R)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_1\wedge R$ by ( 9.1 ). Multiplication of the coefficient measures by $v_1$ commutes with the exterior product by $\Gamma _ I$. Moreover, $\partial \Gamma _ I$ and $ ar\partial \Gamma _ I$ vanish, being the components of two different bidegrees of $\mathrm d\Gamma _ I=0$, so the Leibniz rule for currents (section 7.2 ) gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(R'\wedge \Gamma _ I)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R'\wedge \Gamma _ I$ for every current $R'$. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_1R)=\sum _ I\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_1S_ I)\wedge \Gamma _ I=\sum _ I(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge S_ I)\wedge \Gamma _ I$. Adding the two expansions gives ( 14.48 ) for $k$ factors. Now let $D$ be an open subset of a coordinate chart, identified with an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$, and let $q$ be a smooth function on $D$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \omega $, for instance a large multiple of $|z|^2$ if $D$ is a ball whose closure lies in the chart. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ is bounded, then $u+q$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+q)=\omega _ u+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q-\omega )\geq 0$, so it is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $D$ (lemma 13.1.4 (2), with $	heta =0$), and $\omega _ u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+q)+\sigma $ with the smooth form $\sigma =\omega -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$. For bounded $u_1,\ldots ,u_ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, where $1\leq p\leq n$, we define on $D$ 14.49  egin{equation} \label{eq:hermitian-product-expansion} \omega _{u_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{u_ p} =\sum _{J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,p\} }\Bigl ( igwedge _{l\in J}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ l+q)\Bigr )\wedge \sigma ^{p-|J|}. \end{equation} This does not depend on $q$. Let $q'$ be another such function on an open set $D'$. On $D\cap D'$ put $g=q'-q$ and $\gamma =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$, so that $\sigma '=\omega -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q'=\sigma -\gamma $. By ( 14.48 ), applied to $v_ l=u_ l+q$ and $g_ l=g$, the right side of ( 14.49 ) for $q'$ equals  egin{align*} & \sum _ J\sum _{I\subset J}S_ I\wedge \gamma ^{|J|-|I|}\wedge (\sigma -\gamma )^{p-|J|}\ & \qquad =\sum _ IS_ I\wedge \sum _{K\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,p\} \setminus I}\gamma ^{|K|}\wedge (\sigma -\gamma )^{p-|I|-|K|} =\sum _ IS_ I\wedge \sigma ^{p-|I|}, \end{align*} where $S_ I= igwedge _{l\in I}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ l+q)$ and the last step is the binomial formula for the commuting forms $\gamma $ and $\sigma -\gamma $. Hence the local definitions agree on overlaps, and with a partition of unity subordinate to a cover of $X$ by such sets $D$ (proposition 7.1.3 ) they define a current of order zero on $X$. When the $u_ l$ are smooth, proposition 9.1.2 (1) shows that this current is the exterior product of the forms $\omega _{u_ l}$. For $u_ p=0$, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(0+q)\wedge S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\wedge S$ for every Bedford–Taylor product $S$ by ( 9.1 ), the expansion ( 14.49 ) becomes $(\omega _{u_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{u_{p-1}})\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q+\sigma )$; thus a factor $\omega $ in the product is the exterior product with the smooth form $\omega $. The product is symmetric in its factors, because the Bedford–Taylor products are. It is affine in each potential. Indeed, let $u_1,u'_1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be bounded and $0\leq t\leq 1$. Then $tu_1+(1-t)u'_1+q=t(u_1+q)+(1-t)(u'_1+q)$, and Bedford–Taylor products are additive and positively homogeneous in each factor (proposition 9.1.2 (3)). Hence each term of ( 14.49 ) with $1\in J$ is the corresponding combination of the terms for $u_1$ and $u'_1$, while the terms with $1
otin J$ do not involve the first potential, and \[  \omega _{tu_1+(1-t)u'_1}\wedge \omega _{u_2}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{u_ p} =t\, \omega _{u_1}\wedge \omega _{u_2}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{u_ p} +(1-t)\, \omega _{u'_1}\wedge \omega _{u_2}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{u_ p}.  \] For $u_1=\cdots =u_ p=u$ we write $\omega _ u^ p$, and similarly $\omega _ u^ j\wedge \omega _ v^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-j-k}$ for mixed products. By lemma 14.8.1 (2) below, $\omega _ u^ n$ is a positive measure; we call it the Monge–Ampère measure of $u$ with respect to $\omega $. It is the global counterpart of the measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ of definition 9.1.1 . Lemma 14.8.1 . The class $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and the products of the currents $\omega _ u$ have the following properties. A finite maximum of functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and so does the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of a nonempty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ that is uniformly bounded above. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $D\subset X$ is open, $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(D,\omega )$, and $\varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\leq u(x)$ for every $x\in \partial D$, then the function equal to $\max \{ u,v\} $ on $D$ and to $u$ on $X\setminus D$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be bounded, $1\leq p\leq n$. The current $\omega _{u_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{u_ p}$ is positive. The total mass of its trace measure with respect to $\omega $ (section 7.5 ) is bounded by a constant depending only on $(X,\omega )$ and $\max _ l\sup _ X|u_ l|$, and every pluripolar set has outer measure zero for this trace measure. Moreover, if $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ is bounded and $g$ is a smooth function on an open subset $D$ of a coordinate chart with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq \omega $, then $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+g))^ n\geq \omega _ u^ n$ on $D$. For $1\leq l\leq p$ let $(u_{l,j})_{j\geq 1}$ be sequences in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\sup _{l,j}\sup _ X|u_{l,j}|<\infty $. Suppose that either each sequence decreases pointwise to a function $u_ l$, or each sequence increases and $u_ l$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of its limit. Then the $u_ l$ are bounded functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and $\omega _{u_{1,j}}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{u_{p,j}}	o \omega _{u_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{u_ p}$ weakly. Let $L^1(X)$ be taken with respect to the volume form $\omega ^ n$. The set of $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ is compact in $L^1(X)$, hence bounded in $L^1(X)$, and $u\mapsto \sup _ Xu$ is continuous on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ for the $L^1$ topology. Proof. (1) We freeze the coefficients of $\omega $ on small balls. Fix $\varepsilon >0$, a coordinate chart and a compact subset $L$ of it. By uniform continuity of the coefficients of $\omega $ on a compact neighborhood of $L$ in the chart, there is $r>0$ such that, for every $a\in L$, the ball $B(a,r)$ lies in the chart and the form $\gamma _ a=\omega (a)+	frac \varepsilon 2 eta $ satisfies $\omega \leq \gamma _ a\leq \omega +\varepsilon  eta $ on $B(a,r)$. Let $g_ a$ be the real quadratic polynomial with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ a=\gamma _ a$ described at the beginning of this section. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, then $u+g_ a$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+g_ a)=\omega _ u+(\gamma _ a-\omega )\geq 0$, so it is plurisubharmonic on $B(a,r)$; in the same way $v+g_ a$ is plurisubharmonic on $D\cap B(a,r)$. Let $w$ be the function in question: a finite maximum $\max _ iu_ i$, a regularized supremum $(\sup _ iu_ i)^*$, or the pasted function. We show that $w+g_ a$ is plurisubharmonic on $B(a,r)$. In the first case $w+g_ a$ is the maximum of the plurisubharmonic functions $u_ i+g_ a$, which is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 . In the second case $w+g_ a=(\sup _ i(u_ i+g_ a))^*$, because $g_ a$ is continuous, and it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.2 , since the family $(u_ i+g_ a)$ is uniformly bounded above on $B(a,r)$. In the third case $w+g_ a$ equals $\max \{ u+g_ a,v+g_ a\} $ on $D\cap B(a,r)$ and $u+g_ a$ elsewhere; every boundary point $x$ of $D\cap B(a,r)$ in $B(a,r)$ lies in $\partial D$, and $\varlimsup _{y	o x}(v+g_ a)(y)\leq u(x)+g_ a(x)$ because $g_ a$ is continuous, so proposition 8.2.5 applies on $B(a,r)$. Hence $w$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $B(a,r)$ and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \omega -\gamma _ a\geq -\varepsilon  eta $ there. The balls $B(a,r)$, $a\in L$, cover a neighborhood of $L$, and positivity of currents is a local property, so $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq -\varepsilon  eta $ on a neighborhood of $L$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0$ on the interior of $L$, and since the chart and $L$ were arbitrary, $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. (2) We first prove positivity on a coordinate ball $B$ whose closure lies in a chart, choosing $q=C|z|^2$ in ( 14.49 ). By uniform continuity of the coefficients of $\omega $, there are $	au _ k	o 0$ with $\omega *ho _ k\leq \omega +	au _ k eta $ on $B'$. Hence the smooth $(1,1)$-forms $\omega _{u_{l,k}}+	au _ k eta =(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l)*ho _ k+(\omega +	au _ k eta -\omega *ho _ k)$ are positive, and so is their exterior product, by proposition 7.2.1 . Hence each term converges weakly to the corresponding term of ( 14.49 ), the product is a weak limit of positive forms on $B'$, and it is positive. Since such balls $B'$ cover $X$, the product is positive on $X$. Cover $X$ by finitely many such balls $B'$, with $q$ defined on the larger balls $B$. On compact subsets of $B$, theorem 9.1.3 bounds the trace masses of the Bedford–Taylor products in ( 14.49 ) by a constant times a product of the numbers $\sup _ B|u_ l+q|$, and theorem 7.2.5 bounds the total variations of their coefficient measures in the same way. Since $\sigma $ and $\omega $ are smooth, the measure $(\omega _{u_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{u_ p})\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$ is a sum of the coefficient measures of these Bedford–Taylor products, and of a smooth density for $J=\varnothing $, multiplied by bounded smooth functions. Summing over the finite cover gives the asserted bound for the total mass of the trace measure. By corollary 10.2.2 (3), every pluripolar set has outer measure zero for the total variations of the coefficient measures of Bedford–Taylor products of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions; it is also Lebesgue null (remarks following definition 10.1.1 ). The trace measure is a positive measure bounded on each $B'$ by a finite sum of such total variations and of a multiple of Lebesgue measure, so every pluripolar set has outer measure zero for it. Finally, let $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq \omega $ on $D$. We may take $q=g$ in ( 14.49 ) on $D$. Put $A=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+g)$ and $\gamma =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g-\omega \geq 0$, so that $\sigma =-\gamma $ and ( 14.49 ) reads $\omega _ u^ k=\sum _{i=0}^ k inom ki A^ i\wedge (-\gamma )^{k-i}$, where $A^ i$ is a Bedford–Taylor power. Using $ inom nk inom ki= inom ni inom {n-i}{k-i}$ and $\sum _{m=0}^{n-i} inom {n-i}m(-1)^ m=0$ for $i<n$, we obtain \[  \sum _{k=0}^ n inom nk\omega _ u^ k\wedge \gamma ^{n-k} =\sum _{i=0}^ n inom niA^ i\wedge \gamma ^{n-i}\sum _{k=i}^ n inom {n-i}{k-i}(-1)^{k-i} =A^ n.  \] The currents $\omega _ u^ k$ are positive and the forms $\gamma ^{n-k}$ are strongly positive, so every term on the left is a positive measure, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+g))^ n=A^ n\geq \omega _ u^ n$. (3) On a coordinate ball, add a function $q$ as in ( 14.49 ). In the decreasing case, $u_ l$ is bounded, the functions $u_{l,j}+q$ are plurisubharmonic and decrease to $u_ l+q$, which is bounded below, so $u_ l+q$ is plurisubharmonic and $u_{l,j}+q	o u_ l+q$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by theorem 8.3.1 . Hence $u_ l$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l$ is the weak limit of the positive currents $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{l,j}$, so $u_ l\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The Bedford–Taylor products of the functions $u_{l,j}+q$ converge weakly by theorem 9.2.5 . In the increasing case, $u_ l\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ by (1), and $u_ l$ is bounded. The plurisubharmonic functions $u_{l,j}+q$ increase, and $u_ l+q$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of their limit, because $q$ is continuous; so $u_{l,j}+q	o u_ l+q$ almost everywhere by theorem 8.3.2 , and theorem 9.5.1 , applied on the ball, gives the weak convergence of the Bedford–Taylor products. In both cases we multiply by the fixed smooth forms $\sigma ^{p-|J|}$ and sum; a partition of unity subordinate to finitely many balls gives weak convergence on $X$. (4) Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$, with closures in charts, that cover $X$, concentric balls $B'_ k\Subset B_ k$ that still cover $X$, and smooth functions $q_ k$ on neighborhoods of $\overline{B_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ k\geq \omega $. For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ the functions $u+q_ k$ are plurisubharmonic on $B_ k$. Two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere on an open set agree everywhere on it, by lemma 13.1.4 (1). We may therefore regard $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ as a subset of $L^1(X)$; on compact subsets of a chart, $\omega ^ n$ is bounded above and below by positive multiples of Lebesgue measure. Continuity of the supremum. Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1(X)$; then $u_ j+q_ k	o u+q_ k$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ k)$ for every $k$. Choose points $x_ j$ with $u_ j(x_ j)=\sup _ Xu_ j$, which exist because $u_ j$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$, and a subsequence along which $\sup _ Xu_ j	o \varlimsup _ j\sup _ Xu_ j$ and $x_ j	o x$. Choose $k$ with $x\in B_ k$ and a real number $c>u(x)$, and a closed ball $K\subset B_ k$ centered at $x$ on which $u<c$. Since $c+q_ k$ is continuous and $u+q_ k<c+q_ k$ on $K$, the second part of theorem 8.3.4 gives $u_ j+q_ k<c+q_ k$ on $K$ for large $j$; hence $u_ j(x_ j)<c$ for large $j$. Letting $c\downarrow u(x)$ we obtain $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ Xu_ j\leq u(x)\leq \sup _ Xu$. Conversely, choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ Xu_ j$ tends to $s=\varliminf _ j\sup _ Xu_ j$ and $u_ j	o u$ almost everywhere. Then $u\leq s$ almost everywhere, so $s>-\infty $ because $u$ is integrable, and $u\leq s$ everywhere by lemma 13.1.4 (1), applied to $u$ and the constant $s$. Thus $\sup _ Xu\leq \varliminf _ j\sup _ Xu_ j$, and the supremum is continuous. Compactness. Let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$. On each $B_ k$ the plurisubharmonic functions $u_ j+q_ k$ are bounded above by $\sup _{B_ k}q_ k$. Choose $x_ j$ with $u_ j(x_ j)=0$, pass to a subsequence with $x_ j	o x$, and choose $k_0$ with $x\in B'_{k_0}$. On $B_{k_0}$ the functions $u_ j+q_{k_0}$ do not converge locally uniformly to $-\infty $, since for large $j$ their values at the points $x_ j\in \overline{B'_{k_0}}$ are at least $\min _{\overline{B'_{k_0}}}q_{k_0}$. By theorem 8.3.4 , a subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_{k_0})$. If $B_ l$ meets a ball $B_ k$ on which $(u_ j+q_ k)$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ k)$, then on the nonempty open set $B_ k\cap B_ l$ the functions $u_ j+q_ l=(u_ j+q_ k)+(q_ l-q_ k)$ converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to a locally integrable function, so they do not tend to $-\infty $ locally uniformly on $B_ l$, and a further subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ l)$. Since $X$ is connected, every ball is joined to $B_{k_0}$ by a finite chain of balls, each meeting the next, so after finitely many extractions $(u_ j+q_ k)$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ k)$ to a plurisubharmonic function $v_ k$ for every $k$ (theorem 8.3.4 ). Then $(u_ j)$ converges in $L^1(B'_ k)$ for every $k$, hence in $L^1(X)$. It remains to identify the limit. The quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ k-q_ k$ and $v_ l-q_ l$ agree almost everywhere on $B_ k\cap B_ l$, hence everywhere, so they define a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $X$, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ as a distributional limit of the positive currents $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$. Thus $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1(X)$, and $\sup _ Xu=\lim _ j\sup _ Xu_ j=0$ by the continuity just proved. The set of normalized functions is therefore sequentially compact, hence compact, in the metric space $L^1(X)$, and the continuous function $u\mapsto \| u\| _{L^1(X)}$ is bounded on it. $\square$ The comparison principle for small gaps rests on the next lemma, which controls the error term $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ produced by integration by parts against a product $T$ of currents $\omega _ u$; such a product need not be closed, since $\omega $ need not be. Lemma 14.8.2 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be bounded, put $E=\{ u<v\} $, and let $T$ be a product of $n-1$ factors, each equal to $\omega $, $\omega _ u$ or $\omega _ v$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ is a real measure on $X$, that is, a real current of order zero and degree $2n$, and 14.50  egin{equation} \label{eq:hermitian-one-factor-comparison} \int _ E(\omega _ v-\omega _ u)\wedge T \leq \int _ E(v-u)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T, \end{equation} where $(\omega _ v-\omega _ u)\wedge T=\omega _ v\wedge T-\omega _ u\wedge T$. Lemma 14.8.5 . Let $U,V$ be bounded plurisubharmonic functions on a ball $B(a,r)\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, with $|V-U|\leq \kappa r^2$ for some $\kappa \geq 0$. Put $A=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ and $D=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V$. For every integer $0\leq k\leq n$, \[  \int _{B(a,r/2)}\sum _{j=0}^ k A^ j\wedge D^{k-j}\wedge  eta ^{n-k} \leq C_ n\sum _{l=0}^ k \kappa ^{k-l} \int _{B(a,r)}A^ l\wedge  eta ^{n-l},  \] where $C_ n$ depends only on $n$ and $\kappa ^0=1$, also when $\kappa =0$. Proof. Put $ho _ i=r/2+ir/(2n)$ and $B_ i=B(a,ho _ i)$ for $0\leq i\leq n$, so that $B_0=B(a,r/2)$ and $B_ n=B(a,r)$. For $0\leq i<n$ fix a smooth function $\eta _ i\colon \mathbb R	o [0,1]$ with $\eta _ i=1$ on $(-\infty ,(ho _ i/r)^2]$ and $\eta _ i=0$ on $[((ho _ i+ho _{i+1})/(2r))^2,\infty )$; the numbers $ho _ i/r$ depend only on $n$ and $i$, so $\eta _ i$ can be chosen depending only on $n$ and $i$. By ( 14.57 ), the functions $\chi _ i(z)=\eta _ i(|z-a|^2/r^2)$ satisfy $\chi _ i\in C^\infty _ c(B_{i+1})$, $0\leq \chi _ i\leq 1$, $\chi _ i=1$ on $B_ i$ and $-C'r^{-2} eta \leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ i\leq C'r^{-2} eta $, where $C'=\max _ iC_{\eta _ i}$ depends only on $n$. For integers $j,m\geq 0$ with $j+m\leq n$ and $0\leq i\leq n$, put \[  I_ i(j,m)=\int _{B_ i}A^ j\wedge D^ m\wedge  eta ^{n-j-m}.  \] Let $m\geq 1$, $i<n$, and let $R=A^ j\wedge D^{m-1}\wedge  eta ^{n-j-m}$, a closed positive current by proposition 9.1.2 . Using $\mathbf1_{B_ i}\leq \chi _ i\leq \mathbf1_{B_{i+1}}$ and the positivity of the currents involved, we obtain \[  I_ i(j,m)\leq I_{i+1}(j+1,m-1)+C'\kappa \, I_{i+1}(j,m-1).  \] Both terms on the right have one factor $D$ fewer. Applying this inequality $m$ times, starting from $i=0$, we find \[  I_0(j,m)\leq \sum _{t=0}^ m inom mt(C'\kappa )^{m-t}I_ m(j+t,0) \leq \sum _{t=0}^ m inom mt(C'\kappa )^{m-t}\int _{B(a,r)}A^{j+t}\wedge  eta ^{n-j-t}.  \] Take $m=k-j$ and sum over $0\leq j\leq k$. With $l=j+t$ we have $m-t=k-l$, so every term with $A^ l$ carries the factor $\kappa ^{k-l}$, and the coefficients depend only on $n$. This proves the lemma; for $l=k$ the factor is $\kappa ^0=1$. $\square$ Proposition 14.8.6 . Let $K\subset X$ be compact, and suppose that $u=T_ K^*$ is bounded. Then the measure $\omega _ u^ n$ is carried by $K$. Moreover, with $S=\max \{ 1,\sup _ Xu\} $, 14.58  egin{equation} \label{eq:hermitian-extremal-capacity-bound} 0<\int _ X\omega _ u^ n\leq S^ n c_\omega (K). \end{equation} Proof. Steps 1–4 show that $\omega _ u^ n$ vanishes on $X\setminus K$: on small balls outside $K$ we compare $u$ with a homogeneous balayage computed with the coefficients of $\omega $ frozen. Step 5 proves the mass bound. Step 1. Increasing competitors. The competitors for $T_ K$ are bounded above by $\sup _ Xu$, and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ by lemma 14.8.1 (1). Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts. Applying Choquet's lemma (lemma 3.4.1 ) in each chart, we obtain for each chart a countable family of competitors whose supremum has, on that chart, the same upper semicontinuous regularization as $T_ K$. Let $v_1,v_2,\ldots $ be an enumeration of the union of these families. On each chart, $\sup _ kv_ k$ lies between the supremum of the family chosen for that chart and $T_ K$; since the regularization is computed locally, $(\sup _ kv_ k)^*=u$. The functions $u_ j=\max \{ 0,v_1,\ldots ,v_ j\} $ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ by lemma 14.8.1 (1), increase with $j$, vanish on $K$, and are competitors; hence $0\leq u_ j\leq T_ K\leq u$, and $(\sup _ ju_ j)^*=u$, because $\sup _ kv_ k\leq \sup _ ju_ j\leq T_ K$. Step 2. Frozen balayage. Let $G\subset X\setminus K$ be the domain of a coordinate chart, identified with an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$, and let $L\subset G$ be compact. Since $X\setminus K$ is open in the compact manifold $X$, it is a countable union of such sets $L$, so it suffices to show that $\omega _ u^ n(L)=0$. Choose open sets $G_2\Subset G_1\Subset G_0\Subset G$ with $L\subset G_2$. For $a\in G_2$ let $h_ a$ be the real quadratic polynomial with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ a=\omega (a)$ described at the beginning of this section. Choose $r_0>0$ with $2r_0<\operatorname {dist}(G_2,\mathbb C^ n\setminus G_1)$. The coefficients of $\omega $ have bounded first derivatives on $G_1$, so by the mean value inequality on balls there is $C_1$ such that, for $a\in G_2$ and $0<r\leq r_0$, the ball $B(a,2r)$ lies in $G_1$ and \[  -\delta  eta \leq \omega -\omega (a)\leq \delta  eta \quad 	ext{on }B(a,2r),\qquad \delta =C_1r;  \] indeed a Hermitian matrix whose entries are bounded by $	au $ lies between $-n	au $ and $n	au $ times the identity. Fix such $a$ and $r$, put $q=\pi |z-a|^2$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q= eta $ by ( 7.5 ), and let $B=B(a,r)$. The functions \[  U_ j=u_ j+h_ a+\delta q  \] are bounded and plurisubharmonic on $B(a,2r)$, since they are quasi-plurisubharmonic and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j=\omega _{u_ j}+(\omega (a)-\omega +\delta  eta )\geq 0$. Let $V_ j$ be the homogeneous balayage of $U_ j$ in $B$ given by corollary 9.6.4 , applied on $B(a,2r)$: it equals $U_ j$ outside $B$, satisfies $V_ j\geq U_ j$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^ n=0$ in $B$, and its restriction to $B$, being a member of the family described there, has upper boundary limits at most $U_ j$ on $\partial B$. We compare $V_ j$ with $u$. Put $ho =q-\pi r^2$, which is nonpositive on $B$ and vanishes on $\partial B$, and let $Z_ j=V_ j-h_ a-\delta q+2\delta ho $ on $B$. Then $Z_ j$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic and \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Z_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j+(\omega -\omega (a)+\delta  eta )\geq 0,  \] so $Z_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\omega )$, and for $x\in \partial B$ we have $\varlimsup _{B
i y	o x}Z_ j(y)\leq U_ j(x)-h_ a(x)-\delta q(x)=u_ j(x)$. By lemma 14.8.1 (1), the function equal to $\max \{ u_ j,Z_ j\} $ on $B$ and to $u_ j$ on $X\setminus B$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. It vanishes on $K$, because $B\cap K=\varnothing $, so it is a competitor for $T_ K$; hence $\max \{ u_ j,Z_ j\} \leq T_ K\leq u$ on $B$. Therefore \[  U_ j\leq V_ j\leq u+h_ a+\delta q-2\delta ho \quad 	ext{on }B.  \] The balayage is increasing in the data, so $V_ j$ increases with $j$. Since $U_1\leq V_ j\leq u+h_ a+\delta q+2\pi \delta r^2$, the $V_ j$ are uniformly bounded, $V$ is bounded and plurisubharmonic, and $V_ j	o V$ almost everywhere by theorem 8.3.2 ; hence $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^ n=0$ on $B$ by theorem 9.5.1 . Put $U=u+h_ a+\delta q$. Since $\sup _ jU_ j=\sup _ ju_ j+h_ a+\delta q$, $h_ a+\delta q$ is continuous and $(\sup _ ju_ j)^*=u$, upper regularization gives $V\geq (\sup _ jU_ j)^*=U$. The upper bound for $V_ j$ is upper semicontinuous, so it also holds for $V$. As $-2\delta ho \leq 2\pi \delta r^2$ on $B$, we conclude 14.59  egin{equation} \label{eq:hermitian-frozen-balayage-error} 0\leq V-U\leq 2\pi \delta r^2\quad 	ext{on }B. \end{equation} Step 3. A local mass estimate. Put $A=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ and $D=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V$ on $B$. The function $g=h_ a+\delta q$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\omega (a)+\delta  eta \geq \omega $ on $B(a,2r)$, so lemma 14.8.1 (2) gives $A^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+g))^ n\geq \omega _ u^ n$ on $B$. By ( 14.57 ), with a fixed function $\eta $ equal to $1$ on $(-\infty ,1/16]$ and to $0$ on $[1/5,\infty )$, there is $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B(a,r/2))$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, $\chi =1$ on $B(a,r/4)$ and $-C_2r^{-2} eta \leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \leq C_2r^{-2} eta $, where $C_2$ does not depend on $a$ and $r$. By the definition and the symmetry of Bedford–Taylor products, $A^ n-D^ n=\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}(A-D)\wedge A^ j\wedge D^{n-1-j}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} igl ((U-V)\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}A^ j\wedge D^{n-1-j} igr )$. Using $D^ n=0$, integration by parts against $\chi $, the positivity of the currents $A^ j\wedge D^{n-1-j}$ and ( 14.59 ), we obtain \[   egin{aligned}  \int _{B(a,r/4)}\omega _ u^ n & \leq \int \chi A^ n =\int (U-V)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \sum _{j=0}^{n-1}A^ j\wedge D^{n-1-j}\ & \leq 2\pi C_2\delta \int _{B(a,r/2)} \sum _{j=0}^{n-1}A^ j\wedge D^{n-1-j}\wedge  eta . \end{aligned}  \] Apply lemma 14.8.5 with $k=n-1$ and $\kappa =2\pi \delta =2\pi C_1r$; for $r\leq 1/(2\pi C_1)$ we have $\kappa \leq 1$, and the last integral is at most $C_ n\sum _{l=0}^{n-1}\int _{B(a,r)}A^ l\wedge  eta ^{n-l}$. To sum these estimates we replace $A$ by a current that does not depend on $a$ and $r$. Choose $C_0$ such that $C_0 eta \geq \omega $ on $G_0$ and $C_0 eta \geq \omega (a)+\delta  eta $ for all $a\in G_2$ and $r\leq r_0$. Then $\Gamma =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+C_0 eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+C_0\pi |z|^2)$, where $u+C_0\pi |z|^2$ is bounded and plurisubharmonic on $G_0$ because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+C_0\pi |z|^2)=\omega _ u+(C_0 eta -\omega )\geq 0$. On $B$ the difference $\Gamma -A$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of the smooth function $C_0\pi |z|^2-h_ a-\delta q$, and it equals the form $\gamma =C_0 eta -\omega (a)-\delta  eta \geq 0$ with constant coefficients. By ( 14.48 ), $\Gamma ^ l=\sum _{i=0}^ l inom liA^ i\wedge \gamma ^{l-i}$, and all terms are positive currents, so $A^ l\wedge  eta ^{n-l}\leq \Gamma ^ l\wedge  eta ^{n-l}$. Step 4. Zero mass off $K$. Let $r$ be as above and also smaller than $4\operatorname {dist}(L,\mathbb C^ n\setminus G_2)$, and consider the cubical grid $h\mathbb Z^{2n}\subset \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ of mesh $h=r/(4\sqrt{2n})$. The grid points $a$ within distance $r/4$ of $L$ are finitely many and belong to $G_2$. Every point of $\mathbb C^ n$ lies within distance $\sqrt{2n}\, h/2=r/8$ of a grid point, so the balls $B(a,r/4)$ centered at these grid points cover $L$. The centers of the balls $B(a,r)$ containing a given point $x$ lie in the cube of side $2r$ centered at $x$, which contains at most $(2r/h+1)^{2n}=(8\sqrt{2n}+1)^{2n}=N_ n$ grid points; so each point lies in at most $N_ n$ of these balls. Summing the local estimate over these balls, which lie in $G_1$, gives \[  \omega _ u^ n(L)\leq C_3N_ n\, r\sum _{l=0}^{n-1}\int _{\overline{G_1}}\Gamma ^ l\wedge  eta ^{n-l}.  \] The integrals on the right are finite by theorem 9.1.3 , applied in $G_0$, and do not depend on $r$. Letting $r\downarrow 0$ gives $\omega _ u^ n(L)=0$. Hence $\omega _ u^ n$ is carried by $K$. Step 5. The mass bound. Since $T_ K\geq 0$, we have $0\leq u\leq S$. The function $v=u/S$ satisfies $0\leq v\leq 1$ and belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ because $S\geq 1$: indeed $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=S^{-1}\omega _ u+(1-S^{-1})\omega \geq 0$. Since $v=S^{-1}u+(1-S^{-1})\cdot 0$ and the products are affine in each potential, expanding $\omega _ v^ n$ factor by factor gives $\omega _ v^ n=\sum _{k=0}^ n inom nkS^{-k}(1-S^{-1})^{n-k}\omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k}$, and all terms are positive measures; hence $\omega _ v^ n\geq S^{-n}\omega _ u^ n$. As $\omega _ u^ n$ is carried by $K$, \[  \int _ X\omega _ u^ n=\int _ K\omega _ u^ n\leq S^ n\int _ K\omega _ v^ n\leq S^ nc_\omega (K).  \] Finally $\int _ X\omega _ u^ n>0$ by proposition 14.8.3 . $\square$ Theorem 14.8.7 . Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold, and let $A\subset X$ be pluripolar (definition 10.1.1 ). Then there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\Phi $ on $X$ with $A\subset \{ \Phi =-\infty \} $; that is, $A$ is globally pluripolar. Proof. The compact manifold $X$ has finitely many connected components, which are open, and it suffices to construct $\Phi $ on each of them, since the intersection of $A$ with a component is pluripolar in that component. On a component of dimension zero, which is a point, pluripolar sets are empty and $\Phi =0$ works. We may therefore assume that $X$ is connected of dimension $n\geq 1$, and we fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$ (one exists by section 7.5 ), so that the notation of this section applies. Every point of $X$ has a coordinate ball $U$ and a plurisubharmonic function on $U$ whose pole set contains $A\cap U$, by definition 10.1.1 ; choose a smaller ball $U_1\Subset U$ around the point. By compactness finitely many of the balls $U_1$ cover $X$. By the last assertion of lemma 14.8.4 it therefore suffices to prove the following: if $U$ is a coordinate ball, $\varphi $ is plurisubharmonic on $U$ and $U_1\Subset U$ is a smaller ball, then $E=\{ \varphi =-\infty \} \cap U_1$ is globally pluripolar. If $E$ is empty, there is nothing to prove, so let $E
eq \varnothing $. Choose balls $U_1\Subset U_2\Subset U_3\Subset U$ and subtract a constant from $\varphi $ so that $\varphi \leq 0$ on $U_3$. Suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $E$ is not globally pluripolar. By lemma 14.8.4 , there is a constant $C$ with $0\leq T_ E^*\leq C$. From the extremal functions of compact sublevel sets of regularizations of $\varphi $, which have small capacity, we shall obtain a bounded function in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with zero Monge–Ampère mass. Step 1. Sublevel sets and their extremal functions. Convolution with radial mollifiers of radii decreasing to zero and smaller than the distance from $U_2$ to $\partial U_3$ gives smooth plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi _ j$ on $U_2$ that decrease to $\varphi $ as $j	o \infty $, by proposition 8.2.2 (2). Since $\varphi \leq 0$ on $U_3$, we have $\varphi \leq \varphi _ j\leq 0$ on $U_2$, so $\| \varphi _ j\| _{L^1(U_2)}\leq \| \varphi \| _{L^1(U_2)}<\infty $. For integers $N,j\geq 1$ put \[  K_{j,N}=\{ \varphi _ j\leq -N\} \cap \overline{U_1},\qquad O_{j,N}=\{ \varphi _ j<-N\} \cap U_1.  \] Then $K_{j,N}$ is compact and contains the open set $O_{j,N}$. Fix $x_0\in E$. Since $\varphi _ j(x_0)\downarrow -\infty $, there is $j_0(N)$ such that $x_0\in O_{j,N}$ for $j\geq j_0(N)$; we choose $j_0(N)$ nondecreasing in $N$. For these $j$ the set $K_{j,N}$ has nonempty interior, so $u_{j,N}=T_{K_{j,N}}^*$ is a bounded nonnegative function in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ by lemma 14.8.4 . Every competitor for $T_{K_{j,N}}$ is nonpositive on the open set $O_{j,N}$; hence so is $T_{K_{j,N}}$, and its upper semicontinuous regularization satisfies $u_{j,N}=0$ on $O_{j,N}$. For fixed $N$, the sets $K_{j,N}$ increase with $j$, because $\varphi _ j$ decreases. A competitor for $T_{K_{j+1,N}}$ is a competitor for $T_{K_{j,N}}$, so $u_{j,N}$ decreases with $j\geq j_0(N)$; let $u_ N$ be its limit. By lemma 14.8.1 (3), $u_ N\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and $0\leq u_ N\leq u_{j_0(N),N}$ is bounded. If $x\in U_1$ and $\varphi (x)<-N$, then $x\in O_{j,N}$ for all large $j$, so $u_ N(x)=0$. In particular $u_ N=0$ on $E$, so $u_ N$ is a competitor for $T_ E$, and \[  0\leq u_ N\leq T_ E^*\leq C.  \] For fixed $j$, the sets $K_{j,N}$ decrease as $N$ increases, so $u_{j,N}\leq u_{j,N+1}$ for $j\geq j_0(N+1)$; letting $j	o \infty $ gives $u_ N\leq u_{N+1}$. Let $u_\infty $ be the upper semicontinuous regularization of $\lim _ Nu_ N$. By lemma 14.8.1 (1), $u_\infty \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $0\leq u_\infty \leq C$. Step 2. Convergence of the masses. By lemma 14.8.1 (3), applied to the uniformly bounded decreasing sequence $(u_{j,N})_{j\geq j_0(N)}$ and to the uniformly bounded increasing sequence $(u_ N)_{N\geq 1}$, and testing the weak convergence with the constant function $1$ on the compact manifold $X$, we obtain \[  \int _ X\omega _{u_{j,N}}^ n\longrightarrow \int _ X\omega _{u_ N}^ n\quad (j	o \infty ),\qquad \int _ X\omega _{u_ N}^ n\longrightarrow \int _ X\omega _{u_\infty }^ n\quad (N	o \infty ).  \] Moreover $\int _ X\omega _{u_\infty }^ n>0$ by proposition 14.8.3 , since $u_\infty $ is bounded. Step 3. The capacity of $K_{j,N}$. Choose a smooth function $h$ on $U_2$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\geq \omega $ and $\sup _{U_2}|h|<\infty $, for instance a large multiple of $|z|^2$. If $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $0\leq v\leq 1$, then $v+h$ is plurisubharmonic on $U_2$ with $|v+h|\leq 1+\sup _{U_2}|h|$, and $\omega _ v^ n\leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+h))^ n$ on $U_2$ by lemma 14.8.1 (2). Since $K_{j,N}\subset \overline{U_1}$ and $-\varphi _ j\geq N$ on $K_{j,N}$, while $-\varphi _ j\geq 0$ on $U_2$, the weighted Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality (theorem 9.3.1 ), applied in $U_2$ to $\varphi _ j$, the compact set $\overline{U_1}$ and a compact neighborhood $L\subset U_2$ of $\overline{U_1}$, gives \[  \int _{K_{j,N}}\omega _ v^ n \leq  rac1N\int _{\overline{U_1}}(-\varphi _ j)\, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+h))^ n \leq  rac{C'}N.  \] The constant $C'$ depends on $\| \varphi _ j\| _{L^1(L)}\leq \| \varphi \| _{L^1(U_2)}$ and on the bound for $|v+h|$, but not on $v$, $j$ or $N$. Taking the supremum over $v$, we obtain $c_\omega (K_{j,N})\leq C'/N$. Step 4. Conclusion. By proposition 14.8.6 , \[  \int _ X\omega _{u_{j,N}}^ n\leq \max \{ 1,\sup _ Xu_{j,N}\} ^ n\,  rac{C'}N\qquad (j\geq j_0(N)).  \] For fixed $N$, the uniformly bounded functions $u_{j,N}$ decrease to $u_ N$, so $u_{j,N}	o u_ N$ in $L^1(X)$ by dominated convergence, and $\sup _ Xu_{j,N}	o \sup _ Xu_ N$ by lemma 14.8.1 (4). Letting $j	o \infty $ and using $u_ N\leq C$, we obtain $\int _ X\omega _{u_ N}^ n\leq \max \{ 1,C\} ^ nC'/N$. Letting $N	o \infty $ gives $\int _ X\omega _{u_\infty }^ n=0$, which contradicts Step 2. Hence $E$ is globally pluripolar, and the theorem is proved. $\square$
