This applies in particular to the regularized supremum of an increasing sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ that is bounded above: it belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ by theorem 8.3.2 , and it differs from the pointwise supremum only on a pluripolar set, by corollary 10.2.2 , hence only on a Lebesgue null set, because plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable. $\square$

title: 15.8 Maximal mass and comparison
text: 15.8 Maximal mass and comparison By the monotonicity just proved, potentials with minimal singularities have the largest non-pluripolar masses in a big class, and these maximal masses are invariants of the classes. We extend them to pseudo-effective classes by perturbing with a Kähler class, and then derive the comparison and domination principles for non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measures. Recall that $V_\theta $ denotes the extremal potential of definition 14.2.6 . Definition 15.8.1 . For big classes $\alpha _ j=\{ \theta _ j\} $, $1\leq j\leq p\leq n$, the positive mixed intersection number relative to the Kähler class $\{ \omega \} $ is \[  I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p) =\int _ X\left\langle \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p (\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_{\theta _ j})\right\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}.  \] For pseudo-effective classes $\alpha _ j$ that are not all big, we define $I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)$ as the limit of the numbers $I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots ,\alpha _ p+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )$, which decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ (proposition 15.8.2 ); when all $\alpha _ j$ are big, the same limit equals the number defined by the display. In top degree we put $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )=I_\omega (\alpha ,\ldots ,\alpha )$, the volume of $\alpha $; the factor $\omega ^{n-p}$ is then absent. Proposition 15.8.2 . The numbers of definition 15.8.1 do not depend on the chosen smooth representatives or minimal potentials, nor on the Kähler form within its class. The limit in definition 15.8.1 exists for all pseudo-effective classes, does not depend on the Kähler class used for the perturbation, and equals the number defined by the display when all $\alpha _ j$ are big. For closed positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$, \[  \int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p} \leq I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p).  \] The numbers are positively homogeneous in each class and increase when a pseudo-effective class is added to any argument. For nef classes they equal the cohomological intersection numbers $\int _ X\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$. Big classes have positive volume. Proof. Big classes. Any two potentials with minimal singularities in a fixed big class differ by a bounded function, and a change of smooth representative changes each potential by a smooth function. Hence corollary 15.7.5 shows that $I_\omega $ does not depend on these choices. The same corollary and minimality give the upper bound for closed positive currents in big classes. If $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is another Kähler form in the class of $\omega $, with $f$ smooth, then $\omega '^{n-p}-\omega ^{n-p}=\mathrm d\bigl (\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \sum _{i=0}^{n-p-1}\omega '^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-p-1-i}\bigr )$ is a smooth exact form. Its integral against the closed current $\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle $ vanishes, because $S(\mathrm d\psi )=\pm (\mathrm dS)(\psi )=0$ for a closed current $S$ and a smooth form $\psi $ on the compact manifold $X$. Hence the numbers for big classes do not depend on $\omega $ within its class, and neither do their limits, since the perturbing classes $\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ are the same. Let $\alpha $ be big and $\gamma $ pseudo-effective, represented by a closed positive current $S$. Adding $S$ to a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $ gives a current in the big class $\alpha +\gamma $, which by the upper bound has mixed mass at most the number with $\alpha $ replaced by $\alpha +\gamma $. By multilinearity and positivity, its mixed mass is at least the number for $\alpha $. Hence, when all arguments are big, replacing an argument $\alpha $ by $\alpha +\gamma $ increases the number. Homogeneity for big classes follows by scaling a minimal potential together with its background: if $c>0$, then $cV_\theta $ has minimal singularities in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,c\theta )$, and the product is homogeneous in each factor by proposition 15.1.5 . Pseudo-effective classes. By this monotonicity for big classes, the perturbed numbers decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; they are nonnegative, so the limit exists. Every Kähler form $\kappa $ satisfies $c^{-1}\omega \leq \kappa \leq c\omega $ for some $c\geq 1$ (lemma 13.1.1 ), so monotonicity places the perturbation by $\varepsilon \kappa $ between the perturbations by $c^{-1}\varepsilon \omega $ and $c\varepsilon \omega $, with the same fixed test form $\omega ^{n-p}$; this proves independence of the perturbing class. The same comparison shows that perturbing the arguments by different fixed multiples of $\varepsilon \omega $ gives the same limit, which extends homogeneity to pseudo-effective classes. Monotonicity also extends: if $\gamma $ is pseudo-effective, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ the number with an argument $\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ replaced by $\alpha +\gamma +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is at least the original one, by the big case, and we let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. If all $\alpha _ j$ are big, choose $\delta >0$ such that each $\alpha _ j$ contains a Kähler current $R_ j\geq \delta \omega $. Then $(1+\varepsilon /\delta )\alpha _ j-(\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )=(\varepsilon /\delta )\{ R_ j-\delta \omega \} $ is pseudo-effective, so monotonicity and homogeneity give \[  I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)\leq I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots ,\alpha _ p+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )\leq (1+\varepsilon /\delta )^ pI_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p),  \] and the limit is $I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)$. For arbitrary closed positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$, the upper bound in the big classes $\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, applied to $T_ j+\varepsilon \omega $, and multilinearity give $\int _ X\langle \bigwedge _ jT_ j\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}\leq I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots )$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the upper bound. Nef and big classes. If the $\alpha _ j$ are nef, their perturbations are Kähler classes: $\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ contains $\theta _{j,\varepsilon /2}+\varepsilon \omega \geq \varepsilon \omega /2$, where $\theta _{j,\varepsilon /2}\geq -(\varepsilon /2)\omega $ is a smooth representative of $\alpha _ j$ given by definition 14.3.1 . If $\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is a Kähler form with $f$ smooth, then $f\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega )$, so $V_{\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }\geq f-\sup _ Xf$ by lemma 14.2.7 ; since also $V_{\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }\leq 0$ by the same lemma, the minimal potentials are bounded. By proposition 15.4.1 , the perturbed numbers are the integrals $\int _ X\bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega )\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$, and their limits are the cohomological intersection numbers. Finally, let $\alpha $ be big and $T_0\in \alpha $ a Kähler current with $T_0\geq \delta \omega $. Expanding $T_0=\delta \omega +(T_0-\delta \omega )$ by multilinearity gives $\langle T_0^ n\rangle \geq \delta ^ n\omega ^ n$, so $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )\geq \delta ^ n\int _ X\omega ^ n>0$ by the upper bound. $\square$ Conversely, a pseudo-effective class of positive volume is big. The proof requires the construction of a Kähler current in the class and is given in section 17.4.4 , after Monge–Ampère equations with prescribed measures have been solved. Definition 15.8.3 . A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ has full Monge–Ampère mass if $\int _ X\langle T^ n\rangle =\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$. We write $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$ for the set of $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has full Monge–Ampère mass. For $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the class $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ consists of the potentials $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\leq \phi +O(1)$ and \[  \int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi )^ n\rangle ;  \] these potentials have full mass relative to $\phi $. In a big class, $\mathcal E(X,\theta )=\mathcal E(X,\theta ,V_\theta )$, because every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $u\leq V_\theta +\sup _ Xu$ and $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$ is the mass of $V_\theta $. The class $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$ should not be confused with the local Cegrell class $\mathcal E_0(B)$ of definition 9.10.1 , nor with the pseudo-effective cone of definition 14.3.1 , a cone of cohomology classes. Corollary 15.8.4 . Let $u_ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u_ k\leq \phi +C_ k$ for constants $C_ k$, let $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and suppose that $u_ k\to u$ in extended capacity. Then \[  \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k)^ n\rangle \longrightarrow \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle  \] weakly, and the masses converge. The same holds, without the constants $C_ k$, if $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta )$; in particular it holds for every sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ that decreases to an element of $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$. Proof. By theorem 15.7.4 , the mass of each $u_ k$ is at most that of $\phi $, which equals the mass of $u$. Hence theorem 15.6.5 , with $p=n$, gives weak convergence, and its lower inequality together with this bound gives convergence of the masses. If $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta )$, then by proposition 15.8.2 the mass of each $u_ k$ is at most $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$, which is the mass of $u$, and the same argument applies. Finally, decreasing sequences converge in extended capacity by lemma 15.6.3 . $\square$ Proposition 15.8.5 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ write $\mu _ u=\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle $. Then for all $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ v \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ u+\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )-\mu _ u(X).  \] The last two terms may be omitted if $u$ has full mass or if $u\geq v-O(1)$. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$. The function $w=\max \{ u,v-\varepsilon \} $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ and $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ are disjoint and plurifine open. Indeed, near each point we have $u-v=(u+h)-(v+h)$ for a smooth local potential $h$ of $\theta $, and $u+h$, $v+h$ are plurisubharmonic, so by proposition 10.5.1 the function $u-v$ is plurifinely continuous off the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, which is disjoint from both sets. Moreover $w$ equals $v-\varepsilon $ on the first set and $u$ on the second. By plurifine locality (proposition 15.1.5 ), \[  \mu _ w(X)\geq \mu _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} )+\mu _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} ).  \] The left side is at most $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$ by proposition 15.8.2 . The complement of $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ consists of $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $, which is contained in $\{ u<v\} $ up to the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, and that pluripolar set carries no mass. Hence \[  \mu _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} )\leq \operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )-\mu _ u(X)+\mu _ u(\{ u<v\} ).  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ increase to $\{ u<v\} $, which proves the inequality. If $u$ has full mass, the last two terms cancel. If $u\geq v-O(1)$, then $w-u$ is bounded, so $\mu _ w(X)=\mu _ u(X)$ by corollary 15.7.5 , and the same computation with $\mu _ u(X)$ in place of the volume gives the inequality without these terms. $\square$ Corollary 15.8.6 . Let $u,v,\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\geq v-O(1)$ and $u\geq \rho -O(1)$. If $u\geq v$ almost everywhere for $\mu _ u$, then $u\geq v$ almost everywhere for $\mu _\rho $. If, in addition, the class $\{ \theta \} $ is big and $u$ has minimal singularities, then $u\geq v$ everywhere on $X$. Proof. After adding a constant to $\rho $ we may assume $\rho \leq u$. For $0<t<1$ put $q_ t=(1-t)v+t\rho $. Then $u\geq q_ t-O(1)$, and $\{ u<q_ t\} \subset \{ u<v\} $, because $u<(1-t)v+t\rho \leq (1-t)v+tu$ forces $u<v$. Multilinearity and proposition 15.8.5 therefore give \[  t^ n\mu _\rho (\{ u<q_ t\} ) \leq \mu _{q_ t}(\{ u<q_ t\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<q_ t\} )\leq \mu _ u(\{ u<v\} )=0.  \] As $t\downarrow 0$, every point where $u<v$ and $\rho >-\infty $ eventually lies in $\{ u<q_ t\} $, so Fatou's lemma, applied along a sequence $t\downarrow 0$, gives $\mu _\rho (\{ u<v\} \cap \{ \rho >-\infty \} )=0$. Since $\mu _\rho $ gives no mass to the pole set of $\rho $, this proves the first assertion. Now let the class be big and $u$ have minimal singularities. The class contains a Kähler current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$. Then $u\geq \rho -O(1)$ by minimality, and $\mu _\rho \geq \delta ^ n\omega ^ n$, because multilinearity expands $\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n\rangle =\langle (\delta \omega +(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho -\delta \omega ))^ n\rangle $ into positive terms, one of which is $\delta ^ n\omega ^ n$. The first assertion gives $u\geq v$ almost everywhere with respect to $\omega ^ n$, that is, almost everywhere for Lebesgue measure in charts. Near each point, $u$ and $v$ become plurisubharmonic after adding a common smooth local potential $h$ of $\theta $, and then $\max \{ u,v\} +h$ and $u+h$ are plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere; by theorem 8.2.1 , theorem 3.2.2 they agree everywhere, that is, $u\geq v$ everywhere. $\square$

title: Definition 15.8.1
text: Definition 15.8.1 . For big classes $\alpha _ j=\{ \theta _ j\} $, $1\leq j\leq p\leq n$, the positive mixed intersection number relative to the Kähler class $\{ \omega \} $ is \[  I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p) =\int _ X\left\langle \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p (\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_{\theta _ j})\right\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}.  \] For pseudo-effective classes $\alpha _ j$ that are not all big, we define $I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)$ as the limit of the numbers $I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots ,\alpha _ p+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )$, which decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ (proposition 15.8.2 ); when all $\alpha _ j$ are big, the same limit equals the number defined by the display. In top degree we put $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )=I_\omega (\alpha ,\ldots ,\alpha )$, the volume of $\alpha $; the factor $\omega ^{n-p}$ is then absent.

title: Proposition 15.8.2
text: Proposition 15.8.2 . The numbers of definition 15.8.1 do not depend on the chosen smooth representatives or minimal potentials, nor on the Kähler form within its class. The limit in definition 15.8.1 exists for all pseudo-effective classes, does not depend on the Kähler class used for the perturbation, and equals the number defined by the display when all $\alpha _ j$ are big. For closed positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$, \[  \int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p} \leq I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p).  \] The numbers are positively homogeneous in each class and increase when a pseudo-effective class is added to any argument. For nef classes they equal the cohomological intersection numbers $\int _ X\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$. Big classes have positive volume. Proof. Big classes. Any two potentials with minimal singularities in a fixed big class differ by a bounded function, and a change of smooth representative changes each potential by a smooth function. Hence corollary 15.7.5 shows that $I_\omega $ does not depend on these choices. The same corollary and minimality give the upper bound for closed positive currents in big classes. If $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is another Kähler form in the class of $\omega $, with $f$ smooth, then $\omega '^{n-p}-\omega ^{n-p}=\mathrm d\bigl (\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \sum _{i=0}^{n-p-1}\omega '^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-p-1-i}\bigr )$ is a smooth exact form. Its integral against the closed current $\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\rangle $ vanishes, because $S(\mathrm d\psi )=\pm (\mathrm dS)(\psi )=0$ for a closed current $S$ and a smooth form $\psi $ on the compact manifold $X$. Hence the numbers for big classes do not depend on $\omega $ within its class, and neither do their limits, since the perturbing classes $\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ are the same. Let $\alpha $ be big and $\gamma $ pseudo-effective, represented by a closed positive current $S$. Adding $S$ to a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $ gives a current in the big class $\alpha +\gamma $, which by the upper bound has mixed mass at most the number with $\alpha $ replaced by $\alpha +\gamma $. By multilinearity and positivity, its mixed mass is at least the number for $\alpha $. Hence, when all arguments are big, replacing an argument $\alpha $ by $\alpha +\gamma $ increases the number. Homogeneity for big classes follows by scaling a minimal potential together with its background: if $c>0$, then $cV_\theta $ has minimal singularities in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,c\theta )$, and the product is homogeneous in each factor by proposition 15.1.5 . Pseudo-effective classes. By this monotonicity for big classes, the perturbed numbers decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; they are nonnegative, so the limit exists. Every Kähler form $\kappa $ satisfies $c^{-1}\omega \leq \kappa \leq c\omega $ for some $c\geq 1$ (lemma 13.1.1 ), so monotonicity places the perturbation by $\varepsilon \kappa $ between the perturbations by $c^{-1}\varepsilon \omega $ and $c\varepsilon \omega $, with the same fixed test form $\omega ^{n-p}$; this proves independence of the perturbing class. The same comparison shows that perturbing the arguments by different fixed multiples of $\varepsilon \omega $ gives the same limit, which extends homogeneity to pseudo-effective classes. Monotonicity also extends: if $\gamma $ is pseudo-effective, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ the number with an argument $\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ replaced by $\alpha +\gamma +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is at least the original one, by the big case, and we let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. If all $\alpha _ j$ are big, choose $\delta >0$ such that each $\alpha _ j$ contains a Kähler current $R_ j\geq \delta \omega $. Then $(1+\varepsilon /\delta )\alpha _ j-(\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )=(\varepsilon /\delta )\{ R_ j-\delta \omega \} $ is pseudo-effective, so monotonicity and homogeneity give \[  I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)\leq I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots ,\alpha _ p+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )\leq (1+\varepsilon /\delta )^ pI_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p),  \] and the limit is $I_\omega (\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)$. For arbitrary closed positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$, the upper bound in the big classes $\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, applied to $T_ j+\varepsilon \omega $, and multilinearity give $\int _ X\langle \bigwedge _ jT_ j\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-p}\leq I_\omega (\alpha _1+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ,\ldots )$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the upper bound. Nef and big classes. If the $\alpha _ j$ are nef, their perturbations are Kähler classes: $\alpha _ j+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ contains $\theta _{j,\varepsilon /2}+\varepsilon \omega \geq \varepsilon \omega /2$, where $\theta _{j,\varepsilon /2}\geq -(\varepsilon /2)\omega $ is a smooth representative of $\alpha _ j$ given by definition 14.3.1 . If $\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is a Kähler form with $f$ smooth, then $f\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega )$, so $V_{\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }\geq f-\sup _ Xf$ by lemma 14.2.7 ; since also $V_{\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega }\leq 0$ by the same lemma, the minimal potentials are bounded. By proposition 15.4.1 , the perturbed numbers are the integrals $\int _ X\bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\varepsilon \omega )\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$, and their limits are the cohomological intersection numbers. Finally, let $\alpha $ be big and $T_0\in \alpha $ a Kähler current with $T_0\geq \delta \omega $. Expanding $T_0=\delta \omega +(T_0-\delta \omega )$ by multilinearity gives $\langle T_0^ n\rangle \geq \delta ^ n\omega ^ n$, so $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )\geq \delta ^ n\int _ X\omega ^ n>0$ by the upper bound. $\square$

title: Definition 15.8.3
text: Definition 15.8.3 . A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ has full Monge–Ampère mass if $\int _ X\langle T^ n\rangle =\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$. We write $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$ for the set of $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has full Monge–Ampère mass. For $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the class $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ consists of the potentials $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\leq \phi +O(1)$ and \[  \int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi )^ n\rangle ;  \] these potentials have full mass relative to $\phi $. In a big class, $\mathcal E(X,\theta )=\mathcal E(X,\theta ,V_\theta )$, because every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $u\leq V_\theta +\sup _ Xu$ and $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$ is the mass of $V_\theta $.

title: Corollary 15.8.4
text: Corollary 15.8.4 . Let $u_ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u_ k\leq \phi +C_ k$ for constants $C_ k$, let $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and suppose that $u_ k\to u$ in extended capacity. Then \[  \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k)^ n\rangle \longrightarrow \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle  \] weakly, and the masses converge. The same holds, without the constants $C_ k$, if $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta )$; in particular it holds for every sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ that decreases to an element of $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$. Proof. By theorem 15.7.4 , the mass of each $u_ k$ is at most that of $\phi $, which equals the mass of $u$. Hence theorem 15.6.5 , with $p=n$, gives weak convergence, and its lower inequality together with this bound gives convergence of the masses. If $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta )$, then by proposition 15.8.2 the mass of each $u_ k$ is at most $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$, which is the mass of $u$, and the same argument applies. Finally, decreasing sequences converge in extended capacity by lemma 15.6.3 . $\square$

title: Proposition 15.8.5
text: Proposition 15.8.5 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ write $\mu _ u=\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle $. Then for all $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ v \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ u+\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )-\mu _ u(X).  \] The last two terms may be omitted if $u$ has full mass or if $u\geq v-O(1)$. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$. The function $w=\max \{ u,v-\varepsilon \} $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ and $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ are disjoint and plurifine open. Indeed, near each point we have $u-v=(u+h)-(v+h)$ for a smooth local potential $h$ of $\theta $, and $u+h$, $v+h$ are plurisubharmonic, so by proposition 10.5.1 the function $u-v$ is plurifinely continuous off the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, which is disjoint from both sets. Moreover $w$ equals $v-\varepsilon $ on the first set and $u$ on the second. By plurifine locality (proposition 15.1.5 ), \[  \mu _ w(X)\geq \mu _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} )+\mu _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} ).  \] The left side is at most $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )$ by proposition 15.8.2 . The complement of $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ consists of $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $, which is contained in $\{ u<v\} $ up to the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, and that pluripolar set carries no mass. Hence \[  \mu _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} )\leq \operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )-\mu _ u(X)+\mu _ u(\{ u<v\} ).  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ increase to $\{ u<v\} $, which proves the inequality. If $u$ has full mass, the last two terms cancel. If $u\geq v-O(1)$, then $w-u$ is bounded, so $\mu _ w(X)=\mu _ u(X)$ by corollary 15.7.5 , and the same computation with $\mu _ u(X)$ in place of the volume gives the inequality without these terms. $\square$

title: Corollary 15.8.6
text: Corollary 15.8.6 . Let $u,v,\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\geq v-O(1)$ and $u\geq \rho -O(1)$. If $u\geq v$ almost everywhere for $\mu _ u$, then $u\geq v$ almost everywhere for $\mu _\rho $. If, in addition, the class $\{ \theta \} $ is big and $u$ has minimal singularities, then $u\geq v$ everywhere on $X$. Proof. After adding a constant to $\rho $ we may assume $\rho \leq u$. For $0<t<1$ put $q_ t=(1-t)v+t\rho $. Then $u\geq q_ t-O(1)$, and $\{ u<q_ t\} \subset \{ u<v\} $, because $u<(1-t)v+t\rho \leq (1-t)v+tu$ forces $u<v$. Multilinearity and proposition 15.8.5 therefore give \[  t^ n\mu _\rho (\{ u<q_ t\} ) \leq \mu _{q_ t}(\{ u<q_ t\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<q_ t\} )\leq \mu _ u(\{ u<v\} )=0.  \] As $t\downarrow 0$, every point where $u<v$ and $\rho >-\infty $ eventually lies in $\{ u<q_ t\} $, so Fatou's lemma, applied along a sequence $t\downarrow 0$, gives $\mu _\rho (\{ u<v\} \cap \{ \rho >-\infty \} )=0$. Since $\mu _\rho $ gives no mass to the pole set of $\rho $, this proves the first assertion. Now let the class be big and $u$ have minimal singularities. The class contains a Kähler current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$. Then $u\geq \rho -O(1)$ by minimality, and $\mu _\rho \geq \delta ^ n\omega ^ n$, because multilinearity expands $\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n\rangle =\langle (\delta \omega +(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho -\delta \omega ))^ n\rangle $ into positive terms, one of which is $\delta ^ n\omega ^ n$. The first assertion gives $u\geq v$ almost everywhere with respect to $\omega ^ n$, that is, almost everywhere for Lebesgue measure in charts. Near each point, $u$ and $v$ become plurisubharmonic after adding a common smooth local potential $h$ of $\theta $, and then $\max \{ u,v\} +h$ and $u+h$ are plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere; by theorem 8.2.1 , theorem 3.2.2 they agree everywhere, that is, $u\geq v$ everywhere. $\square$

title: 16 Envelopes and model potentials
text: 16 Envelopes and model potentials Throughout this chapter $X$ is a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a fixed Kähler form $\omega $, and $\theta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, as in the two preceding chapters. Many potentials are defined as envelopes: given an obstacle $f$, one takes the largest $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function that lies below $f$ outside a pluripolar set. For instance, the extremal potential $V_\theta $ of definition 14.2.6 is the envelope of the obstacle $0$. Two features of the global setting require care. The obstacle is often only a Borel function, so we must keep track of which inequalities hold everywhere and which only quasi-everywhere. And there may be no $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function below the obstacle at all: two $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions need not have a common $\theta $-plurisubharmonic minorant (example 16.1.7 ). The basic property of an envelope is that its non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure is carried by the contact set, where the envelope touches the obstacle; for quasi-continuous obstacles in a big class this is theorem 16.2.5 . Away from the contact set, the envelope of a lower semicontinuous obstacle can be replaced locally by a maximal plurisubharmonic function, so its measure vanishes there, and quasi-continuity lets us approximate a general obstacle by lower semicontinuous ones. Regularity of the obstacles also passes to the envelope. If finitely many obstacles have bounded Laplacian with respect to the Riemannian metric of $\omega $, then so does the envelope of their minimum. For a Kähler background we prove this with an exponentially penalized Monge–Ampère equation (theorem 16.2.24 ), which also shows that envelopes of finite minima of $C^{1,1}$ obstacles are $C^{1,1}$ (theorem 16.2.26 ); in a big class the bound holds locally on the ample locus, the complement of the non-Kähler locus (theorem 16.2.29 ). On the contact set of such an obstacle with an arbitrary potential lying below it, the non-pluripolar measure of the potential is then computed from the second derivatives of the obstacle (theorem 16.2.31 ). The second half of the chapter studies envelopes that prescribe singularities rather than values. The singularity envelope $P_\theta [u]$ of a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$ is the upper envelope of all nonpositive $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions $v$ with $v\leq u+C$ for some constant $C$, which may depend on $v$. It has the same non-pluripolar masses as $u$ but may be less singular, and its fixed points of positive mass are called model potentials. The main tool is extrapolation (theorem 16.4.4 ): if $u$ is more singular than $v$ and has almost the same mass, then for some $a>1$ the function $v+a(u-v)$, which continues the segment from $v$ to $u$ beyond $u$, still has a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic minorant of positive mass. From this we derive the domination principle for potentials of full mass relative to a reference potential (theorem 16.4.6 ) and the characterization of $P_\theta [u]$, for $u$ of positive mass, as the largest nonpositive potential that is less singular than $u$ and has the same mass (theorem 16.4.7 ). Rooftop envelopes satisfy a mass inequality (theorem 16.5.5 ), and upper envelopes preserve the comparison of singularities through multiplier ideals (section 16.6 ). Finally we introduce the Monge–Ampère capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ relative to a reference potential $\phi $, prove that it is comparable with the capacity of a Kähler form when $\phi $ has positive mass (theorem 16.9.8 ), and use it to measure the deep sublevel sets $\{ u<\phi -s\} $ of potentials of full mass relative to $\phi $. These estimates are what the next chapter needs in order to integrate by parts with singular potentials. Singularity envelopes of potentials of zero mass, and contact concentration in arbitrary pseudo-effective classes, depend on the Monge–Ampère equations solved there (section 17.5 , section 17.4.4 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.16 .

title: 16.1 Obstacles and rooftops
text:
16.1 Obstacles and rooftops The fixed Kähler form $\omega $ serves as a reference: volumes, norms and the Laplacians of obstacles are taken with respect to $\omega $, also when an envelope is formed with respect to a different background. We call the elements of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ (definition 13.1.3 ) potentials ; they are pointwise defined functions, not identically $-\infty $. Recall from definition 14.2.6 that $u$ is more singular than $v$, written $u\preceq v$, if $u\leq v+C$ for some constant $C$. We write $u\sim v$, and say that $u$ and $v$ have the same singularity type , if $u\preceq v$ and $v\preceq u$. Two facts are used constantly. First, pluripolar sets have Lebesgue measure zero (see the remarks after definition 10.1.1 ). Second, if two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions satisfy $u\leq v$ almost everywhere, then $u\leq v$ everywhere, by lemma 13.1.4 (1). Consequently, an inequality between quasi-plurisubharmonic functions that holds quasi-everywhere, that is, outside a pluripolar set (definition 10.1.1 ), holds everywhere. In particular, if $u\sim v$, then $u$ and $v$ have the same pole set and $u-v$ is bounded outside it. Quasi-continuity on $X$ is the notion of definition 9.4.1 , read in local charts as in section 15.6 : a Borel function $f\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is quasi-continuous if its restriction to every coordinate chart, identified with a bounded open set $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$, is quasi-continuous for the Monge–Ampère capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ of definition 9.3.2 . The following lemma shows that it suffices to check this on the charts of one atlas; in proposition 16.9.9 we show that quasi-continuous functions are also continuous outside open sets of small global capacity. Lemma 16.1.1 . Let $D$ and $D'$ be coordinate charts of $X$, identified with bounded open subsets of $\mathbb C^ n$. For every compact set $L\subset D\cap D'$ there is a constant $c$ such that $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(E)\leq c\operatorname {Cap}_{D'}(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset L$. If $E\subset X$ is pluripolar, then $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(E\cap D)=0$. If a Borel function $f\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is quasi-continuous on each chart of an atlas of $X$, then it is quasi-continuous on every coordinate chart. Proof. Assertions (1) and (3) are contained in lemma 15.6.1 : (1) is its inequality for Borel sets, applied with the roles of $D$ and $D'$ exchanged, and (3) is its final assertion. For (2) we first observe that if $W\subset D$ is open, then every competitor $v$ for $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ restricts to a plurisubharmonic function on $W$ with values in $[0,1]$, and the restriction of the Bedford–Taylor measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ to $W$ is the Bedford–Taylor measure of this restriction. Hence $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(E)\leq \operatorname {Cap}_ W(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset W$, and, taking infima over the open sets $G$ with $A\subset G\subset W$, also $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(A)\leq \operatorname {Cap}_ W^*(A)$ for every set $A\subset W$. Now cover $D$ by countably many open balls $B_ k$, in the coordinates of $D$, with $\overline{B_ k}\subset D$. Since the condition in definition 10.1.1 is local, $E\cap B_ k$ is pluripolar in $B_ k$, so $\operatorname {Cap}_{B_ k}^*(E\cap B_ k)=0$ by theorem 10.1.4 . By the observation above, $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(E\cap B_ k)=0$, and the countable subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*$ (proposition 9.3.3 ) gives $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(E\cap D)=0$. $\square$ Quasi-plurisubharmonic functions are quasi-continuous, and quasi-continuity is preserved by the following operations. Lemma 16.1.2 . Let $	heta '$ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ')$ is quasi-continuous. In particular, every potential $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is quasi-continuous. Finite maxima and minima of quasi-continuous functions on $X$ are quasi-continuous. If $f$ is quasi-continuous on $X$ and $g\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is a Borel function that agrees with $f$ outside a pluripolar set, then $g$ is quasi-continuous. Proof. (1) By lemma 7.3.1 every point of $X$ has a neighborhood on which $	heta '=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ for a smooth function $h$, so $X$ is covered by finitely many coordinate balls $D_ i$ on which $	heta '=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ i$ with $h_ i$ smooth near $\overline{D_ i}$. On $D_ i$ the function $u+h_ i$ is plurisubharmonic by lemma 13.1.4 (2), hence quasi-continuous by theorem 9.4.2 , and so is $u=(u+h_ i)-h_ i$, because $h_ i$ is continuous and real. By lemma 16.1.1 (3), $u$ is quasi-continuous on every chart. (2) Let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ k$ be quasi-continuous, let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart $D$, and let $\varepsilon >0$. Choose open sets $G_ i\subset D$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G_ i)<\varepsilon /k$ such that $f_ i$ is continuous on $K\setminus G_ i$. By subadditivity, $G=G_1\cup \cdots \cup G_ k$ has capacity less than $\varepsilon $, and all the $f_ i$, hence also their maximum and minimum, are continuous on $K\setminus G$. (3) Let $D$ be a chart, $K\subset D$ compact and $\varepsilon >0$. The set $\{ f
e g\} $ is pluripolar, so by lemma 16.1.1 (2) its intersection with $D$ is contained in an open set $G'\subset D$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G')<\varepsilon /2$. If $G\subset D$ is an open set with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G)<\varepsilon /2$ such that $f$ is continuous on $K\setminus G$, then $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G\cup G')<\varepsilon $, and $g=f$ is continuous on $K\setminus (G\cup G')$. $\square$ Definition 16.1.3 . Let $f\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ be a Borel function, called an obstacle , and put \[  \mathcal A_	heta (f)=\{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):v\leq f 	ext{ quasi-everywhere}\} .  \] The members of $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ are called the competitors for $f$. If $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, the obstacle envelope of $f$ is \[  P_	heta (f)= igl (\sup \mathcal A_	heta (f) igr )^*,  \] where ${}^*$ denotes the upper semicontinuous regularization. If $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is empty, we put $P_	heta (f)=-\infty $. If $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty but not uniformly bounded above, $P_	heta (f)$ is not defined, and whenever we use $P_	heta (f)$ for an obstacle that is not bounded above, we verify the upper bound first. If $f\leq b$ quasi-everywhere for a constant $b$, the upper bound is automatic: every competitor satisfies $v\leq b$ quasi-everywhere, hence almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere by lemma 13.1.4 (1). As for the capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ (definition 9.3.2 ) and the relative extremal functions of chapter 10 , a competitor is a member of the family whose supremum defines the object under consideration; we always say which obstacle, envelope or capacity is meant. Proposition 16.1.4 . Let $f$ be a Borel obstacle. If $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, then $P_	heta (f)\in \mathcal A_	heta (f)$; thus $P_	heta (f)$ is the largest competitor for $f$. If $f$ is upper semicontinuous, then every competitor $v$ for $f$ satisfies $v\leq f$ everywhere. The envelope does not change when $f$ is modified on a pluripolar set, and $P_	heta (f+c)=P_	heta (f)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. If $g$ is a Borel obstacle with $f\leq g$ quasi-everywhere and $\mathcal A_	heta (g)$ is uniformly bounded above, then $P_	heta (f)\leq P_	heta (g)$. Suppose that $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, and let $g$ be a Borel obstacle with $f-c\leq g\leq f+c$ quasi-everywhere for a constant $c\geq 0$. Then $\mathcal A_	heta (g)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, and \[  P_	heta (f)-c\leq P_	heta (g)\leq P_	heta (f)+c.  \] In particular the two envelopes have the same pole set and differ by at most $c$ outside it. Let Borel obstacles $f_ j$ decrease pointwise to $f$, and suppose that $\mathcal A_	heta (f_1)$ is uniformly bounded above. Then $P_	heta (f_ j)$ decreases pointwise to $P_	heta (f)$. Here the families may be empty; in particular, $P_	heta (f_ j)$ decreases to the constant $-\infty $ if and only if $\mathcal A_	heta (f)=\varnothing $. Proof. (1) Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate balls on which $	heta $ has smooth local potentials $h$ (lemma 7.3.1 ). Applying theorem 8.3.2 on each ball to the plurisubharmonic functions $v+h$, $v\in \mathcal A_	heta (f)$, and taking the union of the resulting countable subfamilies, we find competitors $v_1,v_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _ kv_ k)^*=P_	heta (f)$. The finite maxima $w_ k=\max \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_ k\} $ are again competitors, and they increase with $k$. Each $w_ k$ satisfies $w_ k\leq f$ outside a pluripolar set $N_ k$, and $N= igcup _ kN_ k$ is pluripolar by theorem 10.1.4 . By corollary 10.2.2 , $\sup _ kw_ k=P_	heta (f)$ outside a pluripolar set $N'$. Hence $P_	heta (f)\leq f$ outside $N\cup N'$. Since the family is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, $P_	heta (f)$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.2 . Thus $P_	heta (f)$ is a competitor, and by construction it dominates every competitor. (2) Let $v$ be a competitor, let $x\in X$, and choose a coordinate ball $B(x,r)$ and a smooth function $h$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $ near its closure. Since $v+h$ is plurisubharmonic and $v\leq f$ outside a Lebesgue null set, the sub-mean value inequality gives \[  v(x)+h(x)\leq  rac1{|B(x,r)|}\int _{B(x,r)}(v+h)\, \mathrm dV_{2n} \leq \sup _{B(x,r)}(f+h).  \] As $r	o 0$, the right side tends to at most $f(x)+h(x)$, because $f+h$ is upper semicontinuous. Hence $v(x)\leq f(x)$. (3) A modification of $f$ on a pluripolar set does not change $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$, since the union of two pluripolar sets is pluripolar. Moreover $\mathcal A_	heta (f+c)=\mathcal A_	heta (f)+c$, and $\mathcal A_	heta (f)\subset \mathcal A_	heta (g)$ if $f\leq g$ quasi-everywhere. These relations between the families of competitors give the three assertions. (4) By (3), $\mathcal A_	heta (f)-c\subset \mathcal A_	heta (g)\subset \mathcal A_	heta (f)+c$. Hence $\mathcal A_	heta (g)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, and the two inequalities follow from (3). (5) By (3) the envelopes $P_	heta (f_ j)$ decrease; if some family $\mathcal A_	heta (f_ j)$ is empty, then so are all later ones and $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$. Let $v$ be the pointwise limit of $P_	heta (f_ j)$. Suppose first that $v(x_0)>-\infty $ for some $x_0$. Then $\sup _ XP_	heta (f_ j)\geq v(x_0)$ for every $j$, so $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ by corollary 14.2.5 . By (1), $v\leq P_	heta (f_ j)\leq f_ j$ outside a pluripolar set $N_ j$, so $v\leq \inf _ jf_ j=f$ outside the pluripolar set $ igcup _ jN_ j$. Thus $v$ is a competitor for $f$ and $v\leq P_	heta (f)$; the reverse inequality follows from $P_	heta (f)\leq P_	heta (f_ j)$. Suppose next that $v\equiv -\infty $. A competitor $w$ for $f$ would be a competitor for every $f_ j$, so $w\leq P_	heta (f_ j)$ for all $j$ and $w\leq v$, which is impossible. Hence $\mathcal A_	heta (f)=\varnothing $ and $P_	heta (f)=-\infty =v$. $\square$ Definition 16.1.5 . For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, the rooftop envelope of $u$ and $v$ is \[  P_	heta (u,v)=P_	heta (\min \{ u,v\} ).  \] We also put $P_	heta (u,-\infty )=P_	heta (-\infty ,u)=-\infty $ for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $. The obstacle $\min \{ u,v\} $ is upper semicontinuous and bounded above. By proposition 16.1.4 , a potential is therefore a competitor for it exactly when it lies below both $u$ and $v$ everywhere. Thus $P_	heta (u,v)$ is the largest common minorant of $u$ and $v$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ if they have one, and $P_	heta (u,v)=-\infty $ if they have none. Proposition 16.1.6 . The rooftop envelope is commutative, associative, increasing in both arguments and idempotent, that is, $P_	heta (u,u)=u$. For a constant $c$, $P_	heta (u+c,v+c)=P_	heta (u,v)+c$. If $u_ j,v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ decrease pointwise to $u$ and $v$, where the limits may be identically $-\infty $, then $P_	heta (u_ j,v_ j)$ decreases pointwise to $P_	heta (u,v)$. Finally, for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and every constant $C\in \mathbb R$, the rooftop envelope $P_	heta (u+C,V_	heta )$ is a potential with $P_	heta (u+C,V_	heta )\sim u$. Proof. Commutativity, monotonicity and idempotence follow directly from the description of $P_	heta (u,v)$ as the largest common minorant. For associativity, let also $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $. A potential lies below $P_	heta (u,v)$ and $w$ if and only if it lies below $u$, $v$ and $w$: when $P_	heta (u,v)
e -\infty $ this is the maximality of $P_	heta (u,v)$, and otherwise neither condition can be satisfied. Hence $P_	heta (P_	heta (u,v),w)$ and $P_	heta (u,P_	heta (v,w))$ are both the largest common minorant of $u$, $v$ and $w$, or both equal $-\infty $ if there is none. The behavior under constant shifts and decreasing limits follows from proposition 16.1.4 , applied to the obstacles $\min \{ u_ j,v_ j\} $, which are bounded above by $\sup _ Xu_1$ and decrease to $\min \{ u,v\} $. If $u$ or $v$ is identically $-\infty $, this limit obstacle has no competitor, in accordance with our convention. For the last assertion put $B=\max \{ \sup _ Xu,-C\} $. Then $u-B\leq 0$, so $u-B\leq V_	heta $, and also $u-B\leq u+C$. Hence $u-B$ is a common minorant of $u+C$ and $V_	heta $, and \[  u-B\leq P_	heta (u+C,V_	heta )\leq u+C.  \] $\square$ Example 16.1.7 . On $\mathbb P^1$ let $	heta =\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$ be the Fubini–Study form of example 14.5.6 , in the affine coordinate $z$, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^1}	heta =1$. Put \[  u_0=\log  rac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2},\qquad u_\infty =-\log (1+|z|^2).  \] In the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$ near $\infty $ we have $\log (1+|z|^2)=\log (1+|\zeta |^2)-\log |\zeta |^2$, so $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$ there, while $u_0=-\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$ and $u_\infty =\log (|\zeta |^2/(1+|\zeta |^2))$. Thus the substitution $z\leftrightarrow \zeta $ exchanges the two functions. On $\mathbb C$ we have $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=[0]$ by the Poincaré–Lelong formula (theorem 7.4.5 ), and $u_0$ is smooth near $\infty $ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0=0$ there. Hence $u_0,u_\infty \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,	heta )$, with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0=[0]$ and $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\infty =[\infty ]$, the currents of integration at the two points. Suppose that $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,	heta )$ is a common minorant of $u_0$ and $u_\infty $. Near $0$ the function $u_0$ is $\log |z|^2$ plus a smooth function, so $
u (u_0,0)=1$ by proposition 12.1.4 , and $w\leq u_0$ gives $
u (w,0)\geq 1$ by the description of Lelong numbers through logarithmic growth in proposition 12.1.1 ; likewise $
u (w,\infty )\geq 1$. In dimension one, the Lelong number of a subharmonic function $s$ at a point is the mass that the measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ gives to that point (theorem 12.1.3 ). Hence the positive measure $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ has atoms of mass at least one at $0$ and at $\infty $, whereas its total mass is $\int _{\mathbb P^1}	heta =1$, because $\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w,1angle =\langle w,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}1angle =0$. This contradiction shows that $P_	heta (u_0,u_\infty )=-\infty $, although $u_0$ and $u_\infty $ are both $	heta $-plurisubharmonic.

title: Lemma 16.1.1
text: Lemma 16.1.1 . Let $D$ and $D'$ be coordinate charts of $X$, identified with bounded open subsets of $\mathbb C^ n$. For every compact set $L\subset D\cap D'$ there is a constant $c$ such that $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(E)\leq c\operatorname {Cap}_{D'}(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset L$. If $E\subset X$ is pluripolar, then $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(E\cap D)=0$. If a Borel function $f\colon X\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is quasi-continuous on each chart of an atlas of $X$, then it is quasi-continuous on every coordinate chart. Proof. Assertions (1) and (3) are contained in lemma 15.6.1 : (1) is its inequality for Borel sets, applied with the roles of $D$ and $D'$ exchanged, and (3) is its final assertion. For (2) we first observe that if $W\subset D$ is open, then every competitor $v$ for $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ restricts to a plurisubharmonic function on $W$ with values in $[0,1]$, and the restriction of the Bedford–Taylor measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ to $W$ is the Bedford–Taylor measure of this restriction. Hence $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(E)\leq \operatorname {Cap}_ W(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset W$, and, taking infima over the open sets $G$ with $A\subset G\subset W$, also $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(A)\leq \operatorname {Cap}_ W^*(A)$ for every set $A\subset W$. Now cover $D$ by countably many open balls $B_ k$, in the coordinates of $D$, with $\overline{B_ k}\subset D$. Since the condition in definition 10.1.1 is local, $E\cap B_ k$ is pluripolar in $B_ k$, so $\operatorname {Cap}_{B_ k}^*(E\cap B_ k)=0$ by theorem 10.1.4 . By the observation above, $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(E\cap B_ k)=0$, and the countable subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*$ (proposition 9.3.3 ) gives $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(E\cap D)=0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.1.2
text: Lemma 16.1.2 . Let $\theta '$ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ is quasi-continuous. In particular, every potential $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is quasi-continuous. Finite maxima and minima of quasi-continuous functions on $X$ are quasi-continuous. If $f$ is quasi-continuous on $X$ and $g\colon X\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is a Borel function that agrees with $f$ outside a pluripolar set, then $g$ is quasi-continuous. Proof. (1) By lemma 7.3.1 every point of $X$ has a neighborhood on which $\theta '=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ for a smooth function $h$, so $X$ is covered by finitely many coordinate balls $D_ i$ on which $\theta '=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ i$ with $h_ i$ smooth near $\overline{D_ i}$. On $D_ i$ the function $u+h_ i$ is plurisubharmonic by lemma 13.1.4 (2), hence quasi-continuous by theorem 9.4.2 , and so is $u=(u+h_ i)-h_ i$, because $h_ i$ is continuous and real. By lemma 16.1.1 (3), $u$ is quasi-continuous on every chart. (2) Let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ k$ be quasi-continuous, let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart $D$, and let $\varepsilon >0$. Choose open sets $G_ i\subset D$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G_ i)<\varepsilon /k$ such that $f_ i$ is continuous on $K\setminus G_ i$. By subadditivity, $G=G_1\cup \cdots \cup G_ k$ has capacity less than $\varepsilon $, and all the $f_ i$, hence also their maximum and minimum, are continuous on $K\setminus G$. (3) Let $D$ be a chart, $K\subset D$ compact and $\varepsilon >0$. The set $\{ f\ne g\} $ is pluripolar, so by lemma 16.1.1 (2) its intersection with $D$ is contained in an open set $G'\subset D$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G')<\varepsilon /2$. If $G\subset D$ is an open set with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G)<\varepsilon /2$ such that $f$ is continuous on $K\setminus G$, then $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G\cup G')<\varepsilon $, and $g=f$ is continuous on $K\setminus (G\cup G')$. $\square$

title: Definition 16.1.3
text: Definition 16.1.3 . Let $f\colon X\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ be a Borel function, called an obstacle , and put \[  \mathcal A_\theta (f)=\{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):v\leq f \text{ quasi-everywhere}\} .  \] The members of $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ are called the competitors for $f$. If $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, the obstacle envelope of $f$ is \[  P_\theta (f)=\bigl (\sup \mathcal A_\theta (f)\bigr )^*,  \] where ${}^*$ denotes the upper semicontinuous regularization. If $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ is empty, we put $P_\theta (f)=-\infty $. If $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ is nonempty but not uniformly bounded above, $P_\theta (f)$ is not defined, and whenever we use $P_\theta (f)$ for an obstacle that is not bounded above, we verify the upper bound first. If $f\leq b$ quasi-everywhere for a constant $b$, the upper bound is automatic: every competitor satisfies $v\leq b$ quasi-everywhere, hence almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere by lemma 13.1.4 (1).

title: Proposition 16.1.4
text: Proposition 16.1.4 . Let $f$ be a Borel obstacle. If $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, then $P_\theta (f)\in \mathcal A_\theta (f)$; thus $P_\theta (f)$ is the largest competitor for $f$. If $f$ is upper semicontinuous, then every competitor $v$ for $f$ satisfies $v\leq f$ everywhere. The envelope does not change when $f$ is modified on a pluripolar set, and $P_\theta (f+c)=P_\theta (f)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. If $g$ is a Borel obstacle with $f\leq g$ quasi-everywhere and $\mathcal A_\theta (g)$ is uniformly bounded above, then $P_\theta (f)\leq P_\theta (g)$. Suppose that $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, and let $g$ be a Borel obstacle with $f-c\leq g\leq f+c$ quasi-everywhere for a constant $c\geq 0$. Then $\mathcal A_\theta (g)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, and \[  P_\theta (f)-c\leq P_\theta (g)\leq P_\theta (f)+c.  \] In particular the two envelopes have the same pole set and differ by at most $c$ outside it. Let Borel obstacles $f_ j$ decrease pointwise to $f$, and suppose that $\mathcal A_\theta (f_1)$ is uniformly bounded above. Then $P_\theta (f_ j)$ decreases pointwise to $P_\theta (f)$. Here the families may be empty; in particular, $P_\theta (f_ j)$ decreases to the constant $-\infty $ if and only if $\mathcal A_\theta (f)=\varnothing $. Proof. (1) Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate balls on which $\theta $ has smooth local potentials $h$ (lemma 7.3.1 ). Applying theorem 8.3.2 on each ball to the plurisubharmonic functions $v+h$, $v\in \mathcal A_\theta (f)$, and taking the union of the resulting countable subfamilies, we find competitors $v_1,v_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _ kv_ k)^*=P_\theta (f)$. The finite maxima $w_ k=\max \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_ k\} $ are again competitors, and they increase with $k$. Each $w_ k$ satisfies $w_ k\leq f$ outside a pluripolar set $N_ k$, and $N=\bigcup _ kN_ k$ is pluripolar by theorem 10.1.4 . By corollary 10.2.2 , $\sup _ kw_ k=P_\theta (f)$ outside a pluripolar set $N'$. Hence $P_\theta (f)\leq f$ outside $N\cup N'$. Since the family is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, $P_\theta (f)$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.2 . Thus $P_\theta (f)$ is a competitor, and by construction it dominates every competitor. (2) Let $v$ be a competitor, let $x\in X$, and choose a coordinate ball $B(x,r)$ and a smooth function $h$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\theta $ near its closure. Since $v+h$ is plurisubharmonic and $v\leq f$ outside a Lebesgue null set, the sub-mean value inequality gives \[  v(x)+h(x)\leq \frac1{|B(x,r)|}\int _{B(x,r)}(v+h)\, \mathrm dV_{2n} \leq \sup _{B(x,r)}(f+h).  \] As $r\to 0$, the right side tends to at most $f(x)+h(x)$, because $f+h$ is upper semicontinuous. Hence $v(x)\leq f(x)$. (3) A modification of $f$ on a pluripolar set does not change $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$, since the union of two pluripolar sets is pluripolar. Moreover $\mathcal A_\theta (f+c)=\mathcal A_\theta (f)+c$, and $\mathcal A_\theta (f)\subset \mathcal A_\theta (g)$ if $f\leq g$ quasi-everywhere. These relations between the families of competitors give the three assertions. (4) By (3), $\mathcal A_\theta (f)-c\subset \mathcal A_\theta (g)\subset \mathcal A_\theta (f)+c$. Hence $\mathcal A_\theta (g)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, and the two inequalities follow from (3). (5) By (3) the envelopes $P_\theta (f_ j)$ decrease; if some family $\mathcal A_\theta (f_ j)$ is empty, then so are all later ones and $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$. Let $v$ be the pointwise limit of $P_\theta (f_ j)$. Suppose first that $v(x_0)>-\infty $ for some $x_0$. Then $\sup _ XP_\theta (f_ j)\geq v(x_0)$ for every $j$, so $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ by corollary 14.2.5 . By (1), $v\leq P_\theta (f_ j)\leq f_ j$ outside a pluripolar set $N_ j$, so $v\leq \inf _ jf_ j=f$ outside the pluripolar set $\bigcup _ jN_ j$. Thus $v$ is a competitor for $f$ and $v\leq P_\theta (f)$; the reverse inequality follows from $P_\theta (f)\leq P_\theta (f_ j)$. Suppose next that $v\equiv -\infty $. A competitor $w$ for $f$ would be a competitor for every $f_ j$, so $w\leq P_\theta (f_ j)$ for all $j$ and $w\leq v$, which is impossible. Hence $\mathcal A_\theta (f)=\varnothing $ and $P_\theta (f)=-\infty =v$. $\square$

title: Definition 16.1.5
text: Definition 16.1.5 . For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the rooftop envelope of $u$ and $v$ is \[  P_\theta (u,v)=P_\theta (\min \{ u,v\} ).  \] We also put $P_\theta (u,-\infty )=P_\theta (-\infty ,u)=-\infty $ for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $. Definition 3.1.1 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we define their rooftop operator as follows: 3.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rooftopdef1} \varphi \land \psi =\sup \left\{ \eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\eta \leq \varphi ,\eta \leq \psi \right\} . \end{equation} For simplicity of notation, we extend the definition to the case where $\varphi $ or $\psi $ is constantly $-\infty $, in which case we simply set \[  \varphi \land \psi =-\infty .  \]

title: Proposition 16.1.6
text: Proposition 16.1.6 . The rooftop envelope is commutative, associative, increasing in both arguments and idempotent, that is, $P_\theta (u,u)=u$. For a constant $c$, $P_\theta (u+c,v+c)=P_\theta (u,v)+c$. If $u_ j,v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ decrease pointwise to $u$ and $v$, where the limits may be identically $-\infty $, then $P_\theta (u_ j,v_ j)$ decreases pointwise to $P_\theta (u,v)$. Finally, for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and every constant $C\in \mathbb R$, the rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u+C,V_\theta )$ is a potential with $P_\theta (u+C,V_\theta )\sim u$. Proof. Commutativity, monotonicity and idempotence follow directly from the description of $P_\theta (u,v)$ as the largest common minorant. For associativity, let also $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $. A potential lies below $P_\theta (u,v)$ and $w$ if and only if it lies below $u$, $v$ and $w$: when $P_\theta (u,v)\ne -\infty $ this is the maximality of $P_\theta (u,v)$, and otherwise neither condition can be satisfied. Hence $P_\theta (P_\theta (u,v),w)$ and $P_\theta (u,P_\theta (v,w))$ are both the largest common minorant of $u$, $v$ and $w$, or both equal $-\infty $ if there is none. The behavior under constant shifts and decreasing limits follows from proposition 16.1.4 , applied to the obstacles $\min \{ u_ j,v_ j\} $, which are bounded above by $\sup _ Xu_1$ and decrease to $\min \{ u,v\} $. If $u$ or $v$ is identically $-\infty $, this limit obstacle has no competitor, in accordance with our convention. For the last assertion put $B=\max \{ \sup _ Xu,-C\} $. Then $u-B\leq 0$, so $u-B\leq V_\theta $, and also $u-B\leq u+C$. Hence $u-B$ is a common minorant of $u+C$ and $V_\theta $, and \[  u-B\leq P_\theta (u+C,V_\theta )\leq u+C.  \] $\square$

title: Example 16.1.7
text:
Example 16.1.7 . On $\mathbb P^1$ let $	heta =\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$ be the Fubini–Study form of example 14.5.6 , in the affine coordinate $z$, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^1}	heta =1$. Put \[  u_0=\log  rac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2},\qquad u_\infty =-\log (1+|z|^2).  \] In the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$ near $\infty $ we have $\log (1+|z|^2)=\log (1+|\zeta |^2)-\log |\zeta |^2$, so $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$ there, while $u_0=-\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$ and $u_\infty =\log (|\zeta |^2/(1+|\zeta |^2))$. Thus the substitution $z\leftrightarrow \zeta $ exchanges the two functions. On $\mathbb C$ we have $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=[0]$ by the Poincaré–Lelong formula (theorem 7.4.5 ), and $u_0$ is smooth near $\infty $ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0=0$ there. Hence $u_0,u_\infty \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,	heta )$, with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0=[0]$ and $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\infty =[\infty ]$, the currents of integration at the two points. Suppose that $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,	heta )$ is a common minorant of $u_0$ and $u_\infty $. Near $0$ the function $u_0$ is $\log |z|^2$ plus a smooth function, so $
u (u_0,0)=1$ by proposition 12.1.4 , and $w\leq u_0$ gives $
u (w,0)\geq 1$ by the description of Lelong numbers through logarithmic growth in proposition 12.1.1 ; likewise $
u (w,\infty )\geq 1$. In dimension one, the Lelong number of a subharmonic function $s$ at a point is the mass that the measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ gives to that point (theorem 12.1.3 ). Hence the positive measure $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ has atoms of mass at least one at $0$ and at $\infty $, whereas its total mass is $\int _{\mathbb P^1}	heta =1$, because $\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w,1angle =\langle w,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}1angle =0$. This contradiction shows that $P_	heta (u_0,u_\infty )=-\infty $, although $u_0$ and $u_\infty $ are both $	heta $-plurisubharmonic.

title: 16.2 Measures on contact sets
text: 16.2 Measures on contact sets For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ we write $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and denote by $\mu _ u=\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $ the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of $u$, as in proposition 15.8.5 ; its total mass $\mu _ u(X)=\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $ is called the mass of $u$. When a different background is used, we say so or indicate it by a subscript. A contact set is a set $\{ u=f\} $ on which two functions agree; for Borel functions it is a Borel set, but it need not be closed (for instance, if $U\subset X$ is open, the functions $0$ and $\mathbf1_{X\setminus U}$ agree exactly on $U$). Three properties of these measures are used throughout. They give no mass to pluripolar sets (lemma 15.1.2 ), in particular to pole sets, so points where a potential equals $-\infty $ can be ignored in measure-theoretic statements. They are local in the plurifine topology (proposition 15.1.5 ): if two potentials agree on a plurifine open set $O$, their measures agree on $O$; and for potentials $u,v$ and $c\in \mathbb R$ the set $\{ u>v+c\} $ is plurifine open by proposition 10.5.1 . Finally, multilinearity and positivity give \[  \mu _{(1-t)u+tv}\geq t^ n\mu _ v \qquad (u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),\  0\leq t\leq 1),  \] and the mass is monotone: $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \leq \int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle $ if $u\preceq v$, with equality if $u\sim v$, by corollary 15.7.5 . Inequalities between measures will usually be obtained from weak limits, that is, by testing against continuous functions. The following lemma justifies this step, and it records the inner regularity of finite measures on $X$. Lemma 16.2.1 . Let $\lambda $ and $\lambda '$ be finite positive Borel measures on $X$. For every Borel set $E\subset X$, $\lambda (E)=\sup \{ \lambda (K):K\subset E\text{ compact}\} $. Let $W\subset X$ be open, and suppose that $\int _ X\chi \, \mathrm d\lambda \leq \int _ X\chi \, \mathrm d\lambda '$ for every continuous function $\chi \geq 0$ with compact support in $W$. Then $\lambda (E)\leq \lambda '(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset W$. Proof. (1) Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts $U_1,\ldots ,U_ N$, with homeomorphisms $\kappa _ i$ of $U_ i$ onto open sets $\Omega _ i\subset \mathbb R^{2n}$, and let $E\subset X$ be Borel and $\varepsilon >0$. The Borel sets $E_ i=(E\cap U_ i)\setminus (U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_{i-1})$ partition $E$. The image of the restriction of $\lambda $ to $U_ i$ under $\kappa _ i$ is a finite Borel measure on $\Omega _ i$, hence a Radon measure by proposition 1.1.2 , so there is a compact set $L_ i\subset \kappa _ i(E_ i)$ whose complement in $\kappa _ i(E_ i)$ has measure less than $\varepsilon /N$. Then $K=\bigcup _ i\kappa _ i^{-1}(L_ i)$ is a compact subset of $E$ with $\lambda (E\setminus K)<\varepsilon $. (2) Fix a metric $d$ on $X$ that induces its topology (lemma 7.1.4 ). Let $K\subset W$ be compact and nonempty; by compactness there is $r>0$ such that every point at distance at most $r$ from $K$ lies in $W$. For $k>1/r$ the continuous functions $\chi _ k=\max \{ 0,1-k\, d(\cdot ,K)\} $ take values in $[0,1]$, equal $1$ on $K$, have compact support in $W$, and decrease pointwise to $\mathbf1_ K$ as $k\to \infty $. By dominated convergence for the finite measures $\lambda $ and $\lambda '$, \[  \lambda (K)=\lim _{k\to \infty }\int _ X\chi _ k\, \mathrm d\lambda \leq \lim _{k\to \infty }\int _ X\chi _ k\, \mathrm d\lambda '=\lambda '(K).  \] If $E\subset W$ is Borel, then by (1), $\lambda (E)=\sup _ K\lambda (K)\leq \sup _ K\lambda '(K)\leq \lambda '(E)$, the suprema being taken over the compact sets $K\subset E$. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.2.1
text: Lemma 16.2.1 . Let $\lambda $ and $\lambda '$ be finite positive Borel measures on $X$. For every Borel set $E\subset X$, $\lambda (E)=\sup \{ \lambda (K):K\subset E\text{ compact}\} $. Let $W\subset X$ be open, and suppose that $\int _ X\chi \, \mathrm d\lambda \leq \int _ X\chi \, \mathrm d\lambda '$ for every continuous function $\chi \geq 0$ with compact support in $W$. Then $\lambda (E)\leq \lambda '(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset W$. Proof. (1) Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts $U_1,\ldots ,U_ N$, with homeomorphisms $\kappa _ i$ of $U_ i$ onto open sets $\Omega _ i\subset \mathbb R^{2n}$, and let $E\subset X$ be Borel and $\varepsilon >0$. The Borel sets $E_ i=(E\cap U_ i)\setminus (U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_{i-1})$ partition $E$. The image of the restriction of $\lambda $ to $U_ i$ under $\kappa _ i$ is a finite Borel measure on $\Omega _ i$, hence a Radon measure by proposition 1.1.2 , so there is a compact set $L_ i\subset \kappa _ i(E_ i)$ whose complement in $\kappa _ i(E_ i)$ has measure less than $\varepsilon /N$. Then $K=\bigcup _ i\kappa _ i^{-1}(L_ i)$ is a compact subset of $E$ with $\lambda (E\setminus K)<\varepsilon $. (2) Fix a metric $d$ on $X$ that induces its topology (lemma 7.1.4 ). Let $K\subset W$ be compact and nonempty; by compactness there is $r>0$ such that every point at distance at most $r$ from $K$ lies in $W$. For $k>1/r$ the continuous functions $\chi _ k=\max \{ 0,1-k\, d(\cdot ,K)\} $ take values in $[0,1]$, equal $1$ on $K$, have compact support in $W$, and decrease pointwise to $\mathbf1_ K$ as $k\to \infty $. By dominated convergence for the finite measures $\lambda $ and $\lambda '$, \[  \lambda (K)=\lim _{k\to \infty }\int _ X\chi _ k\, \mathrm d\lambda \leq \lim _{k\to \infty }\int _ X\chi _ k\, \mathrm d\lambda '=\lambda '(K).  \] If $E\subset W$ is Borel, then by (1), $\lambda (E)=\sup _ K\lambda (K)\leq \sup _ K\lambda '(K)\leq \lambda '(E)$, the suprema being taken over the compact sets $K\subset E$. $\square$

title: 16.2.1 Concentration on the contact set
text:
16.2.1 Concentration on the contact set We first show that the measure of an envelope is carried by its contact set with the obstacle, beginning with a comparison of the measures of two ordered potentials on the set where they agree. Lemma 16.2.2 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $u\leq v$. Then \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }\mu _ u\leq \mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }\mu _ v.  \] Proof. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $w_\varepsilon =\max \{ u,v-\varepsilon \} $. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, $w_\varepsilon $ increases to $\max \{ u,v\} =v$, so $\mu _{w_\varepsilon }	o \mu _ v$ weakly along every sequence $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by corollary 15.7.6 . On the plurifine open set $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ we have $w_\varepsilon =u$, hence $\mathbf1_{\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} }\mu _{w_\varepsilon }=\mathbf1_{\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} }\mu _ u$. This set contains every point of $\{ u=v\} $ at which $u$ is finite, and $\mu _ u$ does not charge the pole set of $u$. Therefore \[  \mu _{w_\varepsilon }\geq \mathbf1_{\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} }\mu _ u \geq \mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }\mu _ u.  \] The right side is a fixed finite measure. Integrating a continuous function $\chi \geq 0$ against both sides and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _ v\geq \int _ X\chi \mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }\, \mu _ u$, so $\mu _ v\geq \mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }\mu _ u$ by lemma 16.2.1 . Restricting both sides to $\{ u=v\} $ proves the lemma. $\square$ Lemma 16.2.3 . Suppose that $\{ 	heta \} $ is big. There is a proper analytic subset $A\subset X$, the pole set of a $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function with analytic singularities, such that every potential with minimal singularities is locally bounded on $X\setminus A$. The set $A$ is closed and pluripolar; in particular $\mu _ u(A)=0$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Proof. By proposition 14.3.5 , the big class contains a Kähler current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ whose potential $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ has analytic singularities, and we put $A=\{ \psi =-\infty \} $. Every point of $X$ has a connected coordinate neighborhood $V$ on which $\psi =c\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+b$, with $c>0$, $b$ bounded and holomorphic functions $g_ i$ that do not all vanish identically (definition 13.1.5 ). Thus $A\cap V$ is the common zero set of the $g_ i$, so $A$ is an analytic subset of $X$, different from $X$, and it is closed and pluripolar, being locally the pole set of the plurisubharmonic function $\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2$. On $V\setminus A$ the continuous function $\sum _ i|g_ i|^2$ is positive, so $\psi $ is locally bounded on $X\setminus A$. If $\varphi $ has minimal singularities, then $\psi \leq \varphi +C'$ for a constant $C'$, so $\varphi $ is locally bounded below on $X\setminus A$; it is bounded above, being upper semicontinuous on the compact space $X$. The last assertion holds because non-pluripolar products give no mass to pluripolar sets. $\square$ Lemma 16.2.4 . Suppose that $\{ 	heta \} $ is big and that $f$ is bounded and lower semicontinuous. Then $u=P_	heta (f)$ has minimal singularities, and $\mu _ u$ is carried by $\{ u=f\} $. Proof. Adding a constant to $f$, we may assume that $-C\leq f\leq 0$. Then $V_	heta -C\leq f$, so $V_	heta -C$ is a competitor, while every competitor is nonpositive and hence at most $V_	heta $. Thus $V_	heta -C\leq u\leq V_	heta $, and $u$ has minimal singularities. Let $A$ be the proper analytic subset of lemma 16.2.3 . Since $u$ has minimal singularities, it is locally bounded on $X\setminus A$, and $\mu _ u(A)=0$. Let $x\in X\setminus A$ with $u(x)<f(x)$, and choose $\delta >0$ with $u(x)<f(x)-3\delta $. Since $u$ is upper semicontinuous and $f$ is lower semicontinuous, there is a coordinate ball $B
i x$ with $\overline B\subset X\setminus A$ such that $u<u(x)+\delta $ and $f>f(x)-\delta $ on $\overline B$; thus $\sup _{\overline B}u\leq \inf _{\overline B}f-\delta $. Shrinking $B$, we may assume that $B\Subset B'$ for a coordinate ball $B'$ with $\overline{B'}\subset X\setminus A$ and that $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ near $\overline{B'}$ for a smooth function $h$ (lemma 7.3.1 ), and then, shrinking $B$ further, that the oscillation $\operatorname {osc}_{\overline B}h=\sup _{\overline B}h-\inf _{\overline B}h$ is less than $\delta $. We show that $\mu _ u$ vanishes on $B$. Since $u$ is bounded near $\overline{B'}$, corollary 14.2.9 gives $\widetilde u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\widetilde u\geq u$, $\widetilde u=u$ on $X\setminus B$ and $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u)^ n=0$ on $B$. The function $\widetilde u+h$ is plurisubharmonic, hence subharmonic, on $B$, and at every point $\zeta \in \partial B$ its upper limit from $B$ is at most $(\widetilde u+h)(\zeta )=(u+h)(\zeta )\leq \sup _{\overline B}(u+h)$, by upper semicontinuity. The maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) therefore gives \[  \widetilde u\leq \sup _{\overline B}(u+h)-h \leq \sup _{\overline B}u+\operatorname {osc}_{\overline B}h <\inf _{\overline B}f \qquad 	ext{on }B.  \] Hence $\widetilde u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere on $X$, so $\widetilde u$ is a competitor and $\widetilde u\leq u$. Therefore $\widetilde u=u$, and $\mu _ u=(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u)^ n$ vanishes on $B$. The set $\{ u<f\} $ is open, because $f-u$ is lower semicontinuous. Covering $\{ u<f\} \setminus A$ by countably many balls as above, we obtain $\mu _ u(\{ u<f\} \setminus A)=0$. Moreover $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere by proposition 16.1.4 , so the set $\{ u>f\} $ is pluripolar. Since $\mu _ u$ gives no mass to $A$ or to $\{ u>f\} $, it is carried by $\{ u=f\} $. $\square$ Theorem 16.2.5 . Suppose that $\{ 	heta \} $ is big, and let $f$ be a quasi-continuous Borel obstacle such that $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded above. Then $\mu _{P_	heta (f)}$ is carried by the contact set $\{ P_	heta (f)=f\} $, that is, \[  \mu _{P_	heta (f)}(\{ P_	heta (f)
e f\} )=0.  \] Proof. Write $u=P_	heta (f)$, which is a potential by proposition 16.1.4 , and let $A$ be the proper analytic subset of lemma 16.2.3 : every potential with minimal singularities is locally bounded on $X\setminus A$, and $A$ is closed and pluripolar. After reducing to obstacles that are bounded above, we treat bounded obstacles by approximating them with lower semicontinuous ones (Step 1), and then obstacles that are only bounded above by truncating them from below (Step 2). Choose a constant $C_0>\sup _ Xu$ and put $\widetilde f=\min \{ f,C_0\} $, a quasi-continuous Borel function that is bounded above (lemma 16.1.2 (2)). By proposition 16.1.4 , $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere, and $u<C_0$ everywhere, so $u\in \mathcal A_	heta (\widetilde f)\subset \mathcal A_	heta (f)$. Since $u$ is the largest member of $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$, it follows that $P_	heta (\widetilde f)=u$; moreover $\{ u=\widetilde f\} =\{ u=f\} $, because $u<C_0$. Replacing $f$ by $\widetilde f$, we may therefore assume that $f$ is bounded above. Step 1: bounded obstacles. Suppose first that $|f|\leq C'$ quasi-everywhere for a constant $C'$. Then $\{ |f|>C'\} $ is a pluripolar Borel set, and replacing $f$ by $0$ on it changes neither $P_	heta (f)$ (proposition 16.1.4 ) nor the quasi-continuity of $f$ (lemma 16.1.2 (3)); it changes the contact set only on a pluripolar set, which $\mu _ u$ does not charge. After this modification and the addition of a constant, we may therefore assume that $-C\leq f\leq 0$ everywhere. We first construct open sets of small capacity outside which $f$ is continuous. Fix finitely many coordinate balls $D_1,\ldots ,D_ N$, compact sets $K_ i\subset D_ i$ with $ igcup _ iK_ i=X$, and open sets $D_ i'$ with $K_ i\subset D_ i'\Subset D_ i$. For all $i$ and $k\geq 1$, the quasi-continuity of $f$ on $D_ i$ gives an open set $G_{ik}\subset D_ i'$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_{D_ i}(G_{ik})<2^{-k}$ such that $f$ is continuous on $K_ i\setminus G_{ik}$; intersecting with $D_ i'$ the open set provided by definition 9.4.1 does not change $K_ i\setminus G_{ik}$. Put \[  G_ j= igcap _{k=1}^ j igcup _{i=1}^ NG_{ik}.  \] These open sets decrease, and $X\setminus G_ j$ is the union of the finitely many closed sets $K_ i\setminus  igcup _{i'}G_{i'k}$, $1\leq i\leq N$, $1\leq k\leq j$. Since $f$ is continuous on each of them, it is continuous on the closed set $X\setminus G_ j$. Moreover, if $D$ is a coordinate ball and $L\subset D$ is compact, then $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G_ j\cap L)	o 0$. Indeed, $L\cap \overline{D_ i'}$ is a compact subset of $D\cap D_ i$, so lemma 16.1.1 (1) gives a constant $c_ i$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(E)\leq c_ i\operatorname {Cap}_{D_ i}(E)$ for all Borel sets $E\subset L\cap \overline{D_ i'}$. Since $G_ j\cap L\subset  igcup _ i(G_{ij}\cap L)$ and $G_{ij}\subset D_ i'$, it follows that \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ D(G_ j\cap L)\leq \sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\operatorname {Cap}_{D_ i}(G_{ij})\leq 2^{-j}\sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i.  \] Next we approximate $f$ by lower semicontinuous obstacles that agree with $f$ outside $G_ j$. Fix a metric on $X$ that induces its topology (lemma 7.1.4 ). By the Tietze extension theorem in the form of lemma 9.4.3 , applied to the restriction of $f+C/2$ to the compact set $X\setminus G_ j$, which takes values in $[-C/2,C/2]$, the restriction of $f$ to $X\setminus G_ j$ extends to a continuous function $g_ j\colon X	o [-C,0]$. Put \[  h_ j=\sup _{k\geq j}g_ k.  \] These functions are lower semicontinuous, take values in $[-C,0]$, and decrease with $j$. Since $G_ k\subset G_ j$ for $k\geq j$, we have $h_ j=f$ on $X\setminus G_ j$. The intersection $ igcap _ jG_ j$ is pluripolar: if $D$ is a coordinate ball and $U\Subset D$ is open, then $U\cap  igcap _ jG_ j$ is contained in the open sets $U\cap G_ j$, whose capacities $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ tend to zero, so it has outer capacity zero and lies in the pole set of a plurisubharmonic function on $D$ by theorem 10.1.4 . Outside $ igcap _ jG_ j$ we have $h_ j=f$ for all large $j$. Hence the limit $h$ of the $h_ j$ equals $f$ quasi-everywhere. Finally we pass to the limit in the contact property of the envelopes $w_ j=P_	heta (h_ j)$. By proposition 16.1.4 , $w_ j$ decreases to $P_	heta (h)=P_	heta (f)=u$. Since the obstacles $h_ j$ and $f$ take values in $[-C,0]$, the potential $V_	heta -C$ is a competitor for each of them, and every competitor is nonpositive, hence at most $V_	heta $; thus $V_	heta -C\leq w_ j\leq V_	heta $ and $V_	heta -C\leq u\leq V_	heta $. Fix a coordinate ball $D\Subset X\setminus A$ with a smooth potential $ho $ of $	heta $ near $\overline D$ (such balls exist around every point of $X\setminus A$, by lemma 7.3.1 ), and a continuous function $\chi \geq 0$ with compact support in $D$. On $D$ the functions $w_ j$ and $u$ are bounded uniformly in $j$. By lemma 16.2.4 , $\mu _{w_ j}$ is carried by $\{ w_ j=h_ j\} $, so \[  \int _ X\chi  igl (1-\mathrm e^{w_ j-h_ j} igr )\, \mu _{w_ j}=0.  \] The integrands with $h_ j$ and with $f$ are bounded uniformly in $j$ on the support of $\chi $, and they coincide outside $G_ j$. By lemma 9.4.7 , applied to the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $ho +w_ j$, the measures $\mu _{w_ j}$ of $G_ j\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ are at most a fixed constant times $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G_ j\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi )$, which tends to zero, as shown above. Consequently \[  \lim _{j	o \infty }\int _ X\chi  igl (1-\mathrm e^{w_ j-f} igr )\, \mu _{w_ j}=0.  \] The weights $1-\mathrm e^{w_ j-f}$ are bounded and quasi-continuous on $D$, and they converge in capacity to $1-\mathrm e^{u-f}$. Indeed, the uniformly bounded potentials $w_ j$ decrease to $u$ and therefore converge in capacity (proposition 9.4.6 ), and $|\mathrm e^{w_ j-f}-\mathrm e^{u-f}|\leq \mathrm e^{C}|w_ j-u|$, because $w_ j-f$ and $u-f$ are at most $C$. The weighted form of theorem 9.4.8 , applied to the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $ho +w_ j$ on $D$, therefore gives \[  \int _ X\chi  igl (1-\mathrm e^{u-f} igr )\, \mu _ u=0.  \] The integrand is nonnegative outside the pluripolar set $\{ u>f\} $, which $\mu _ u$ does not charge, and it is positive exactly at the points of $D$ where $u<f$. Since $\chi $ is arbitrary, lemma 16.2.1 (2), applied on $W=D$ to the positive measure $\max \{ 1-\mathrm e^{u-f},0\} \mu _ u$ and the zero measure, shows that this measure vanishes on $D$; hence $\mu _ u(\{ u<f\} \cap D)=0$. Covering $X\setminus A$ by such balls, and recalling that $\mu _ u$ does not charge the pluripolar sets $A$ and $\{ u>f\} $, we conclude that $\mu _ u$ is carried by $\{ u=f\} $. Step 2: obstacles bounded above. Adding a constant, we may assume that $f\leq 0$. Put $f_ j=\max \{ f,-j\} $ and $u_ j=P_	heta (f_ j)$. The obstacles $f_ j$ are quasi-continuous by lemma 16.1.2 (2), satisfy $-j\leq f_ j\leq 0$, and decrease to $f$; their families of competitors contain $V_	heta -j$ and are bounded above by $0$. By proposition 16.1.4 , $u_ j$ decreases to the potential $u$, and by Step 1, $\mu _{u_ j}$ is carried by $\{ u_ j=f_ j\} $. Moreover $V_	heta -j\leq u_ j\leq V_	heta $. The potentials $u_ j$ are not uniformly bounded below, so we pass to the limit on a fixed ball with truncated potentials, and with weights that vanish where the truncation is active. Fix a coordinate ball $D\Subset X\setminus A$ as in Step 1 and constants $M,\varepsilon >0$, and put \[  v_ j^ M=\max \{ u_ j,V_	heta -M\} ,\qquad a_ j= rac{v_ j^ M-V_	heta +M}{v_ j^ M-V_	heta +M+\varepsilon },  \] and define $v^ M$ and $a$ in the same way with $u$ in place of $u_ j$. On $D$ these truncated potentials are bounded uniformly in $j$ and decrease to $v^ M$, so they converge in capacity (proposition 9.4.6 ). The weights satisfy $0\leq a_ j\leq 1$ and $a_ j=0$ on $\{ u_ j\leq V_	heta -M\} $. They are quasi-continuous, and they converge in capacity to $a$, since $s\mapsto (s+M)/(s+M+\varepsilon )$ is Lipschitz on $[-M,0]$.
