title: Lemma 16.6.2
text:
Lemma 16.6.2 . Let $(v_ j)_{j\in J}$ be a nonempty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ that is uniformly bounded above, and let $v=(\sup _ jv_ j)^*$. Then \[  
u (v,E)=\inf _ j
u (v_ j,E)  \] for every prime divisor $E$ over $X$. Consequently, maxima, sums and positive multiples preserve the relation $\sim _{\mathcal I}$; and if two such families are termwise equivalent for $\sim _{\mathcal I}$, their upper envelopes are equivalent as well. Proof. Let $\pi \colon Y	o U$ be a smooth model of an open subset $U\subset X$ (possibly $U=X$) on which $E$ is a divisor, and let $Z\subset Y$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset outside which $\pi $ is a biholomorphism onto an open subset of $U$; such a set exists by the definition of a smooth model, and it has Lebesgue measure zero. We first show that $v\circ \pi $ is the regularized supremum of the family $(v_ j\circ \pi )$. By theorem 8.3.2 , a countable subfamily has the same regularized supremum $v$, and its increasing finite maxima $w_ k$ satisfy $\sup _ kw_ k=v$ almost everywhere. The functions $w_ k\circ \pi $ are $\pi ^*	heta $-plurisubharmonic, increase with $k$, and are locally uniformly bounded above; let $W$ be their regularized supremum, so that $W=\sup _ kw_ k\circ \pi $ almost everywhere by theorem 8.3.2 . If $N\subset U$ is a Lebesgue null set outside which $\sup _ kw_ k=v$, then $\pi ^{-1}(N)\setminus Z$ is a null set, because $\pi $ restricts to a biholomorphism of $Y\setminus Z$ onto an open set; hence $\sup _ kw_ k\circ \pi =v\circ \pi $ outside the null set $(\pi ^{-1}(N)\setminus Z)\cup Z$. Thus the quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $W$ and $v\circ \pi $ agree almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere. Since every $v_ j$ is at most $v$, we get $W\leq (\sup _ jv_ j\circ \pi )^*\leq v\circ \pi =W$, so $v\circ \pi $ is the regularized supremum of the whole family $(v_ j\circ \pi )$. It remains to compare Lelong numbers. Near a point $y\in E$, adding to all these functions the pullback of a smooth local potential of $	heta $ near $\pi (y)$ makes them plurisubharmonic, so proposition 12.1.4 gives $
u (v\circ \pi ,y)=\inf _ j
u (v_ j\circ \pi ,y)$ at every point $y\in E$. Taking the infimum over $y\in E$, which defines the generic Lelong number (proposition 12.3.5 ) and commutes with the infimum over $j$, we obtain the formula. For the remaining assertions, let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$, and recall from proposition 12.1.4 that Lelong numbers at a point are additive and positively homogeneous, and that the Lelong number of a maximum is the minimum of the Lelong numbers. Taking infima over $y\in E$, we obtain $
u (c\varphi ,E)=c
u (\varphi ,E)$ for $c>0$ and $
u (\max \{ \varphi ,\psi \} ,E)=\min \{ 
u (\varphi ,E),
u (\psi ,E)\} $. For sums we use that, by proposition 12.3.5 , the infima defining $
u (\varphi ,E)$, $
u (\psi ,E)$ and $
u (\varphi +\psi ,E)$ are attained at every point of $E$ outside a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $E$. Such a point exists, since by the same proposition the complement in $E$ of such a union is dense in $E$, and in particular nonempty. At a point of $E$ where the three infima are attained, the additivity at a point gives $
u (\varphi +\psi ,E)=
u (\varphi ,E)+
u (\psi ,E)$. By these three rules and proposition 16.6.1 , maxima, sums and positive multiples preserve $\sim _{\mathcal I}$, and by the formula just proved, so do upper envelopes of termwise equivalent families. $\square$

title: 16.7 Singularity constraints and relative capacity
text: 16.7 Singularity constraints and relative capacity We now combine a singularity constraint with an obstacle. For a bounded obstacle the resulting envelope stays within a bounded distance of the singularity envelope $P_\theta [u]$, and it satisfies a contact bound. We then introduce the capacity relative to a reference potential $\phi $, defined through the potentials in the strip $\phi -1\leq v\leq \phi $, and use it to measure the deep sublevel sets of potentials of full mass relative to $\phi $. Throughout this section $\{ \theta \} $ is big. Definition 16.7.1 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a Borel obstacle $f$, define \[  P_\theta [u](f)=\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): v\preceq u,\  v\leq f\text{ quasi-everywhere}\} \right)^*  \] when this family is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, and put $P_\theta [u](f)=-\infty $ when it is empty. For Borel obstacles $g$ and $f$ we write $P_\theta (g,f)=P_\theta (\min \{ g,f\} )$, under the same conditions on the family of competitors. By the rooftop representation in proposition 16.7.2 below, this is consistent with definition 16.4.9 when $f$ is a potential $\phi $ with $u\preceq \phi $. Proposition 16.7.2 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $f$ be a Borel obstacle for which the family in definition 16.7.1 is nonempty and uniformly bounded above. $P_\theta [u](f)\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. The envelope increases with $f$ and with the singularity type of $u$, does not change when $f$ is modified on a pluripolar set, and satisfies $P_\theta [u](f+c)=P_\theta [u](f)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. For all sufficiently large $k$, the rooftop envelopes $P_\theta (u+k,f)$ are potentials, and \[  P_\theta [u](f)=\left(\lim _{k\to \infty }P_\theta (u+k,f)\right)^*.  \] If $|f|\leq C$ quasi-everywhere, then \[  P_\theta [u]-C\leq P_\theta [u](f)\leq P_\theta [u]+C,  \] and $P_\theta [u](f)$ has the same mass as $u$. In particular, $P_\theta [u](0)=P_\theta [u]$ and $P_\theta [V_\theta ](f)=P_\theta (f)$ whenever these envelopes are defined. Proof. We begin with the final identities. A competitor for $P_\theta [u](0)$ is a nonpositive potential more singular than $u$, exactly as in definition 16.3.1 ; and every potential is more singular than $V_\theta $, by minimality, so the families defining $P_\theta [V_\theta ](f)$ and $P_\theta (f)$ coincide. (1) The maximum of two members of the family in definition 16.7.1 is again a member. By theorem 8.3.2 , applied on finitely many coordinate balls on which $\theta $ has smooth local potentials, there are members $v_1,v_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _ kv_ k)^*=P_\theta [u](f)$, and the maxima $w_ k=\max \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_ k\} $ form an increasing sequence of members with the same regularized supremum. By corollary 10.2.2 , $\sup _ kw_ k=P_\theta [u](f)$ outside a pluripolar set, and each $w_ k$ lies below $f$ outside a pluripolar set; since countable unions of pluripolar sets are pluripolar (theorem 10.1.4 ), $P_\theta [u](f)\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. (The envelope itself need not be more singular than $u$; see example 16.4.8 .) The other assertions follow from the corresponding properties of the families of competitors. (2) A competitor $h$ for the obstacle $\min \{ u+k,f\} $ satisfies $h\leq u+k$ quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere, and $h\leq f$ quasi-everywhere; so it belongs to the family of definition 16.7.1 . In particular these competitors are uniformly bounded above, $P_\theta (u+k,f)$ is defined, and when it is a potential, it belongs to the family. Conversely, every member $v$ of the family satisfies $v\leq u+k$ for all sufficiently large integers $k$, hence $v\leq \min \{ u+k,f\} $ quasi-everywhere and $v\leq P_\theta (u+k,f)$. Thus a fixed member shows that the rooftop envelopes, which increase with $k$, are potentials for all large $k$, and the family and the rooftop envelopes have the same supremum. This proves the representation. (3) Normalize $u\leq 0$. If $|f|\leq C$ quasi-everywhere, then $u-C$ is a competitor, and for large $k$ each rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u+k,f)$ lies between $u-C$ and $u+k$, so it has the singularity type of $u$ and mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $. By (2) and corollary 15.7.6 , $P_\theta [u](f)$ also has this mass. Comparing $f$ with the constants $-C$ and $C$, and using (1) together with $P_\theta [u](0)=P_\theta [u]$, gives the two bounds. $\square$ Proposition 16.7.3 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $f$ be a bounded quasi-continuous obstacle. Then $w=P_\theta [u](f)$ is a potential, and \[  \mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=P_\theta (f)\} }\mu _{P_\theta (f)}, \qquad \mu _ w(X\setminus \{ w=f\} )=0.  \] In particular $\int _ X(f-w)\, \mu _ w=0$, where the integrand may be given any value at the poles of $w$. Proof. Write $p=P_\theta (f)$ and choose $C$ with $|f|\leq C$. Then $V_\theta -C$ is a competitor for $f$, and every competitor $v$ satisfies $v-C\leq 0$, hence $v\leq V_\theta +C$; thus $V_\theta -C\leq p\leq V_\theta +C$. Consequently $p$ has minimal singularities, and its mass is that of $V_\theta $, namely $\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )>0$, by definition 15.8.1 , proposition 15.8.2 . A potential lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere if and only if it lies below $p$: one direction is the maximality of $p$, the other holds because $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Hence the two constrained families coincide, and $w=P_\theta [u](p)$. Since $u\preceq p$, this is the relative envelope of definition 16.4.9 , by proposition 16.7.2 . The measure bound in proposition 16.4.10 , which applies because $p$ has positive mass, gives the first inequality. By theorem 16.2.5 , $\mu _ p$ is carried by $\{ p=f\} $, so $\mu _ w$ is carried by $\{ w=p\} \cap \{ p=f\} \subset \{ w=f\} $. Finally, $f-w$ is nonnegative quasi-everywhere and vanishes $\mu _ w$-almost everywhere, which gives the integral identity. $\square$ Proposition 16.7.4 . Let $u,v,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, let $p$ be an integer with $1\leq p\leq n$, and let $T_1,\ldots ,T_{n-p}$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. For $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ put \[  \lambda _ q=\left\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ p \wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-p}\right\rangle .  \] If $u,v\preceq \phi $, then \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v\} )\leq \lambda _ u(\{ u<v\} ) +\lambda _\phi (X)-\lambda _ u(X).  \] If moreover $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle >0$ and $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\lambda _ u(X)=\lambda _\phi (X)$, and the inequality also holds with $\{ u\leq v\} $ in place of $\{ u<v\} $. Proof. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $q=\max \{ u,v-\varepsilon \} $. Write $T_ i=\theta _ i'+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ with smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ i'$ and $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i')$ (theorem 14.1.7 ). Since $q\preceq \phi $, the monotonicity of mixed masses in corollary 15.7.5 , applied with $n$ factors to the potentials $q,\ldots ,q,\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _{n-p}$ and $\phi ,\ldots ,\phi ,\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _{n-p}$, gives $\lambda _ q(X)\leq \lambda _\phi (X)$. On the disjoint plurifine open sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ and $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $, $q$ equals $v-\varepsilon $ and $u$ respectively, so plurifine locality gives \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} ) \leq \lambda _\phi (X)-\lambda _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} ).  \] Writing $\lambda _ u(\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} )=\lambda _ u(X)-\lambda _ u(\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} )$, enlarging $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $ to $\{ u<v\} $ up to the common pole set of $u$ and $v$, which carries no mass, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain the first inequality. Now let $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle >0$ and $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. By proposition 16.4.10 , $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [v]=P_\theta [\phi ]$. With the potentials $\varphi _ i$ of the currents $T_ i$ chosen above, the preservation of mixed masses in proposition 16.3.2 , applied to the $n$ potentials $u,\ldots ,u,\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _{n-p}$ and to the corresponding tuples for $v$ and $\phi $, gives $\lambda _ u(X)=\lambda _ v(X)=\lambda _\phi (X)$. Thus the last two terms in the inequality cancel. Applying the inequality with $u$ and $v$ interchanged, we get $\lambda _ u(\{ v<u\} )\leq \lambda _ v(\{ v<u\} )$, and subtracting this from $\lambda _ v(X)=\lambda _ u(X)$ gives $\lambda _ v(\{ u\leq v\} )\leq \lambda _ u(\{ u\leq v\} )$. $\square$ Definition 16.7.5 . For a reference potential $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a Borel set $A\subset X$, the Monge–Ampère capacity relative to $\phi $ is \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A) =\sup \{ \mu _ v(A):v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),\  \phi -1\leq v\leq \phi \} .  \] The potentials $v$ in this supremum are called competitors for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$. For $\phi =V_\theta $ we obtain the $\theta $-capacity . Proposition 16.7.6 . Let $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The relative capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ is monotone, countably subadditive, zero on pluripolar Borel sets and continuous along increasing sequences of Borel sets. Its total value is $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(X)=\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $, and it is inner regular on Borel sets: \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A) =\sup _{K\subset A\text{ compact}}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K).  \] It does not change when a constant is added to $\phi $. If $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $|\phi -\psi |\leq C$ outside the pole sets of $\phi $ and $\psi $, for a constant $C\geq 0$, then \[  (2C+1)^{-n}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(A) \leq \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A) \leq (2C+1)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(A).  \] Replacing $(\theta ,\phi )$ by $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g,\phi -g)$ for a smooth real function $g$ leaves the capacity unchanged. Proof. Every competitor has the singularity type of $\phi $ and hence mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $; since $\phi $ itself is a competitor, the capacity is finite and $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(X)=\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $. Monotonicity, countable subadditivity and continuity along increasing sequences hold for each measure $\mu _ v$ and pass to the supremum; for the last property, interchange the supremum over the sequence with the supremum over competitors. Inner regularity follows in the same way from the inner regularity of each finite measure $\mu _ v$ (lemma 16.2.1 ): $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A)=\sup _ v\sup _ K\mu _ v(K)=\sup _ K\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K)$, the inner suprema being taken over the compact sets $K\subset A$. Each $\mu _ v$ gives no mass to pluripolar sets. Adding a constant $c$ to $\phi $ corresponds to the bijection $v\mapsto v+c$ of competitors, which does not change $\mu _ v$. For the comparison, note first that $\phi \leq \psi +C$ and $\psi \leq \phi +C$ hold almost everywhere, hence everywhere; in particular $\phi $ and $\psi $ have the same pole set. Put $t=(2C+1)^{-1}$. If $\phi -1\leq v\leq \phi $, the potential $q=(1-t)\psi +tv-tC$ satisfies \[  q\leq (1-t)\psi +t(\psi +C)-tC=\psi ,\qquad q\geq (1-t)\psi +t(\psi -C-1)-tC=\psi -1,  \] so it is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$, and $\mu _ q\geq t^ n\mu _ v$. This proves the upper comparison, and exchanging $\phi $ and $\psi $ proves the lower one. The last assertion follows from the bijection $v\mapsto v-g$ between the two families of competitors, which preserves the current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. $\square$ Proposition 16.7.7 . Let $u,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $, and let $s\in \mathbb R$ and $0<t\leq 1$. Then \[  t^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(\{ u<\phi -s-t\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<\phi -s\} )+\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle .  \] In particular, if $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(\{ u<\phi -s\} )\to 0$ as $s\to \infty $. Proof. Let $v$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$, and put $q=(1-t)\phi +tv-s$. Then $\phi -s-t\leq q\leq \phi -s$, so \[  \{ u<\phi -s-t\} \subset \{ u<q\} \subset \{ u<\phi -s\} .  \] Moreover $q\sim \phi $ and $\mu _ q\geq t^ n\mu _ v$. Proposition 16.7.4 , with $p=n$, applied to $u$ and $q$, gives \[  t^ n\mu _ v(\{ u<\phi -s-t\} )\leq \mu _ q(\{ u<q\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<\phi -s\} )+\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle ,  \] and taking the supremum over $v$ proves the inequality. If $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $. With $t=1$, the right side tends to zero as $s\to \infty $ by dominated convergence, because the sets $\{ u<\phi -s\} $ decrease to the pole set of $u$, which is $\mu _ u$-null. $\square$

title: Definition 16.7.1
text: Definition 16.7.1 . title: Proposition 16.7.4
text: Proposition 16.7.4 . Let $u,v,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, let $p$ be an integer with $1\leq p\leq n$, and let $T_1,\ldots ,T_{n-p}$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. Applying the inequality with $u$ and $v$ interchanged, we get $\lambda _ u(\{ v<u\} )\leq \lambda _ v(\{ v<u\} )$, and subtracting this from $\lambda _ v(X)=\lambda _ u(X)$ gives $\lambda _ v(\{ u\leq v\} )\leq \lambda _ u(\{ u\leq v\} )$. $\square$

title: Definition 16.7.5
text: Definition 16.7.5 . For a reference potential $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a Borel set $A\subset X$, the Monge–Ampère capacity relative to $\phi $ is \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A) =\sup \{ \mu _ v(A):v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),\  \phi -1\leq v\leq \phi \} .  \] The potentials $v$ in this supremum are called competitors for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$. For $\phi =V_\theta $ we obtain the $\theta $-capacity .

title: Proposition 16.7.6
text: Proposition 16.7.6 . Let $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The relative capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ is monotone, countably subadditive, zero on pluripolar Borel sets and continuous along increasing sequences of Borel sets. Its total value is $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(X)=\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $, and it is inner regular on Borel sets: \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A) =\sup _{K\subset A\text{ compact}}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K).  \] It does not change when a constant is added to $\phi $. If $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $|\phi -\psi |\leq C$ outside the pole sets of $\phi $ and $\psi $, for a constant $C\geq 0$, then \[  (2C+1)^{-n}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(A) \leq \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A) \leq (2C+1)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(A).  \] Replacing $(\theta ,\phi )$ by $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g,\phi -g)$ for a smooth real function $g$ leaves the capacity unchanged. Proof. Every competitor has the singularity type of $\phi $ and hence mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $; since $\phi $ itself is a competitor, the capacity is finite and $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(X)=\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $. Monotonicity, countable subadditivity and continuity along increasing sequences hold for each measure $\mu _ v$ and pass to the supremum; for the last property, interchange the supremum over the sequence with the supremum over competitors. Inner regularity follows in the same way from the inner regularity of each finite measure $\mu _ v$ (lemma 16.2.1 ): $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(A)=\sup _ v\sup _ K\mu _ v(K)=\sup _ K\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K)$, the inner suprema being taken over the compact sets $K\subset A$. Each $\mu _ v$ gives no mass to pluripolar sets. Adding a constant $c$ to $\phi $ corresponds to the bijection $v\mapsto v+c$ of competitors, which does not change $\mu _ v$. For the comparison, note first that $\phi \leq \psi +C$ and $\psi \leq \phi +C$ hold almost everywhere, hence everywhere; in particular $\phi $ and $\psi $ have the same pole set. Put $t=(2C+1)^{-1}$. If $\phi -1\leq v\leq \phi $, the potential $q=(1-t)\psi +tv-tC$ satisfies \[  q\leq (1-t)\psi +t(\psi +C)-tC=\psi ,\qquad q\geq (1-t)\psi +t(\psi -C-1)-tC=\psi -1,  \] so it is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$, and $\mu _ q\geq t^ n\mu _ v$. This proves the upper comparison, and exchanging $\phi $ and $\psi $ proves the lower one. The last assertion follows from the bijection $v\mapsto v-g$ between the two families of competitors, which preserves the current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.7.7
text: Proposition 16.7.7 . Let $u,\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $, and let $s\in \mathbb R$ and $0<t\leq 1$. Then \[  t^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(\{ u<\phi -s-t\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<\phi -s\} )+\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle .  \] In particular, if $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(\{ u<\phi -s\} )\to 0$ as $s\to \infty $. Proof. Let $v$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$, and put $q=(1-t)\phi +tv-s$. Then $\phi -s-t\leq q\leq \phi -s$, so \[  \{ u<\phi -s-t\} \subset \{ u<q\} \subset \{ u<\phi -s\} .  \] Moreover $q\sim \phi $ and $\mu _ q\geq t^ n\mu _ v$. Proposition 16.7.4 , with $p=n$, applied to $u$ and $q$, gives \[  t^ n\mu _ v(\{ u<\phi -s-t\} )\leq \mu _ q(\{ u<q\} ) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u<\phi -s\} )+\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle ,  \] and taking the supremum over $v$ proves the inequality. If $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle $. With $t=1$, the right side tends to zero as $s\to \infty $ by dominated convergence, because the sets $\{ u<\phi -s\} $ decrease to the pole set of $u$, which is $\mu _ u$-null. $\square$

title: 16.8 Quantitative rooftop extrapolation
text: 16.8 Quantitative rooftop extrapolation In theorem 16.4.4 the potentials are ordered by $u\preceq v$. We now show that it suffices to order their singularity envelopes, $P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [v]$. The obstacle $au+(1-a)v$ may then be unbounded above near the poles of $v$, so we must show separately that its competitors are uniformly bounded above. This follows from the uniform $L^1$ bound for normalized potentials, applied on a set of positive volume on which the obstacle is bounded. As before, $\{ \theta \} $ is big. Theorem 16.8.1 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$ and $P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [v]$, and let $a>1$ satisfy \[  a^ n\left(\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \right)<\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle .  \] Consider the obstacle $au+(1-a)v$, evaluated where $u$ and $v$ are both finite and given arbitrary Borel values on the remaining pluripolar set. Then $\eta =P_\theta (au+(1-a)v)$ is a potential of positive mass, and \[  a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u, \qquad P_\theta [\eta ]\leq P_\theta [u].  \] If $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [v]$, then every $a>1$ is allowed, $P_\theta [\eta ]=P_\theta [u]$, and $\eta $ has the same mass as $u$. Proof. Write $\phi =P_\theta [u]$ and $\psi =P_\theta [v]$. Then $u\preceq \phi \leq \psi $, and by proposition 16.3.2 and the monotonicity of mass, \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle \geq \int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0.  \] Hence theorem 16.4.4 , applied to $u$ and $\psi $, gives a potential $\eta '=P_\theta (au+(1-a)\psi )$ of positive mass. Choose $C$ with $v\leq \psi +C$. Since $1-a<0$, we have $\eta '-(a-1)C\leq au+(1-a)v$ quasi-everywhere, so $\eta '-(a-1)C$ is a competitor for the obstacle $au+(1-a)v$. We show that the competitors are uniformly bounded above. Since $u$ and $v$ are finite almost everywhere, there is a Borel set $K$ of positive $\omega ^ n$-volume on which both are bounded; the obstacle is then bounded above on $K$ by a constant $D$. Let $h$ be a competitor. By proposition 14.2.1 , there is a constant $B$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $ and $\omega $, such that \[  \int _ X|h-\sup _ Xh|\, \omega ^ n\leq B.  \] Since $h\leq D$ almost everywhere on $K$, integration over $K$ gives $\sup _ Xh\leq D+B/\int _ K\omega ^ n$. Hence the envelope $\eta $ is a potential. It dominates $\eta '-(a-1)C$, so it has positive mass. The inequality $\eta \leq au+(1-a)v$, which holds quasi-everywhere, is equivalent there to $a^{-1}\eta +(1-a^{-1})v\leq u$; this inequality between quasi-plurisubharmonic functions therefore holds everywhere. Next we compare singularity envelopes. Put $t=a^{-1}$. For all sufficiently large integers $k$, the potential $tP_\theta (\eta +k,0)+(1-t)P_\theta (v+k,0)$ is nonpositive and more singular than $t\eta +(1-t)v\leq u$; here $P_\theta (\eta +k,0)=P_\theta (\min \{ \eta +k,0\} )$, as in definition 16.7.1 , and similarly for $v$. It is therefore a competitor for $\phi $. By proposition 16.7.2 , $P_\theta (\eta +k,0)$ and $P_\theta (v+k,0)$ increase almost everywhere to $P_\theta [\eta ]$ and $\psi $ as $k\to \infty $. Hence \[  tP_\theta [\eta ]+(1-t)\psi \leq \phi  \] almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere. Since $\phi \leq \psi $, subtracting $(1-t)\psi $ where $\phi $ is finite gives $P_\theta [\eta ]\leq \phi $ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. Suppose finally that $\phi =\psi $. Then $u$ and $v$ have the same mass, so every $a>1$ is allowed, and theorem 16.4.4 shows that $\eta '$ also has this mass. Since $\eta \geq \eta '-(a-1)C$, the mass of $\eta $ is at least that of $u$, by monotonicity. Conversely, $P_\theta [\eta ]\leq \phi $ and the preservation of mass by singularity envelopes show that the mass of $\eta $ is at most that of $\phi $, which is the mass of $u$. Thus $\phi $ is nonpositive, has the same mass as $\eta $, and is less singular than $\eta $, because $\eta \preceq P_\theta [\eta ]\leq \phi $. The characterization of $P_\theta [\eta ]$ in theorem 16.4.7 therefore gives $\phi \leq P_\theta [\eta ]$, so $P_\theta [\eta ]=\phi $. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.8.1
text: Theorem 16.8.1 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle >0$ and $P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [v]$, and let $a>1$ satisfy \[  a^ n\left(\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \right)<\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle .  \] Consider the obstacle $au+(1-a)v$, evaluated where $u$ and $v$ are both finite and given arbitrary Borel values on the remaining pluripolar set. For all sufficiently large integers $k$, the potential $tP_\theta (\eta +k,0)+(1-t)P_\theta (v+k,0)$ is nonpositive and more singular than $t\eta +(1-t)v\leq u$; here $P_\theta (\eta +k,0)=P_\theta (\min \{ \eta +k,0\} )$, as in definition 16.7.1 , and similarly for $v$. It is therefore a competitor for $\phi $. By proposition 16.7.2 , $P_\theta (\eta +k,0)$ and $P_\theta (v+k,0)$ increase almost everywhere to $P_\theta [\eta ]$ and $\psi $ as $k\to \infty $. Hence \[  tP_\theta [\eta ]+(1-t)\psi \leq \phi  \] almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere. Then $u$ and $v$ have the same mass, so every $a>1$ is allowed, and theorem 16.4.4 shows that $\eta '$ also has this mass.
