18.1 Closed convex functions and supporting slopes The conjugate of a finite convex function is in general finite only on a convex subset of the dual space. We therefore allow convex functions to take the value $+\infty $, and we impose lower semicontinuity as the regularity condition that controls their behavior at the boundary of the set where they are finite. The definitions and results of this section and the next are stated on $N_{\mathbb R}$; they apply equally to functions on $M_{\mathbb R}$, with the roles of the two spaces interchanged. Definition 18.1.1 . A function $F\colon N_{\mathbb R}	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is convex if its epigraph \[  \operatorname {epi}F=\{ (x,r)\in N_{\mathbb R}	imes \mathbb R:r\geq F(x)\}   \] is convex. A convex function is proper if it does not take the value $-\infty $ and its effective domain $\operatorname {dom}F=\{ x:F(x)<+\infty \} $ is nonempty; a proper convex function is closed if it is lower semicontinuous. The relative interior $\operatorname {ri}C$ of a convex set $C$ is its interior in its affine span, and $\overline C\setminus \operatorname {ri}C$ is its relative boundary . For a proper convex function $F$ and $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$, the subgradient set of $F$ at $x$ is \[  \partial F(x)=\{ p\in M_{\mathbb R}:F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p,y-xangle 	ext{ for every }y\in N_{\mathbb R}\} .  \] Its elements are the subgradients , or supporting slopes , of $F$ at $x$: they are the slopes of the affine functions that lie below $F$ and agree with $F$ at $x$. We set $\partial F(x)=\varnothing $ for $x
otin \operatorname {dom}F$ and $\partial F(E)= igcup _{x\in E}\partial F(x)$ for $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$. For a function $F$ with values in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$, the epigraph is convex if and only if $F((1-\lambda )x+\lambda y)\leq (1-\lambda )F(x)+\lambda F(y)$ for all $x,y\in N_{\mathbb R}$ and $0<\lambda <1$. Indeed, suppose that the epigraph is convex. If $F(x)$ and $F(y)$ are finite, the inequality expresses that the corresponding combination of $(x,F(x))$ and $(y,F(y))$ lies in $\operatorname {epi}F$; otherwise its right side is $+\infty $. Conversely, for $(x,r),(y,s)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ the inequality gives $F((1-\lambda )x+\lambda y)\leq (1-\lambda )r+\lambda s$. Thus definition 18.1.1 extends the usual notion of a convex function, with the sign convention fixed in the Conventions, to functions with values in $[-\infty ,+\infty ]$. The effective domain of a convex function is convex, being the image of its epigraph under the projection to $N_{\mathbb R}$. A convex set contains every convex combination $\sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ ix_ i$ of its points, where $\lambda _ i\geq 0$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ i=1$: for $q\geq 2$ and $\lambda _ q<1$ this follows by induction on $q$ from $\sum _ i\lambda _ ix_ i=(1-\lambda _ q)\sum _{i<q} rac{\lambda _ i}{1-\lambda _ q}x_ i+\lambda _ qx_ q$. Consequently, the convex hull of a set $S$, that is, the smallest convex set containing $S$, is the set of all convex combinations of points of $S$, since this set is convex and contains $S$. Applied to the epigraph, the same fact gives the finite form of Jensen's inequality \[  F\Bigl (\sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ ix_ i\Bigr )\leq \sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ iF(x_ i)  \] for every convex function $F$ with values in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$ and every convex combination. A function with values in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is lower semicontinuous if and only if its epigraph is closed in $N_{\mathbb R}	imes \mathbb R$. Indeed, if $F$ is lower semicontinuous and $(x_ k,r_ k)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ converge to $(x,r)$, then $F(x)\leq \varliminf _ kF(x_ k)\leq r$. Conversely, if the epigraph is closed and $x_ k	o x$ with $\varliminf _ kF(x_ k)<r<F(x)$ for some real $r$, then $(x_ k,r)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ for infinitely many $k$, and in the limit $(x,r)\in \operatorname {epi}F$, which is impossible. A finite convex function is a real-valued one. A finite convex function $F$ on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$ is identified with the proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$ that equals $F$ on $\Omega $ and $+\infty $ elsewhere; this extension is convex, since its convexity inequality is trivial when $x$ or $y$ lies outside $\Omega $. In particular, $\partial F(x)$ is defined for $x\in \Omega $. The subgradient notation $\partial F$ is unrelated to the boundary $\partial E$ of a set. We shall need a Lipschitz bound on cubes. Let $Q'\subset Q$ be closed cubes with a common center and half-sides $\delta $ and $2\delta $ in affine coordinates on an affine subspace of $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $|\cdot |$ be the Euclidean norm of these coordinates. If a convex function $F$ is finite on $Q$, with oscillation $\omega =\sup _ QF-\inf _ QF<\infty $, then 18.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:convex-cube-lipschitz} |F(z)-F(y)|\leq  rac{\omega }{\delta }|z-y|\qquad (y,z\in Q'). \end{equation} Indeed, for $y
eq z$ in $Q'$ the point $w=z+\delta (z-y)/|z-y|$ lies in $Q$, and $z=(1-\lambda )y+\lambda w$ with $\lambda =|z-y|/(|z-y|+\delta )\leq |z-y|/\delta $. Convexity gives $F(z)-F(y)\leq \lambda (F(w)-F(y))\leq (\omega /\delta )|z-y|$, and we may exchange $y$ and $z$. Lemma 18.1.2 . Let $W$ be a real vector space of finite dimension $n$, and let $C\subset W$ be convex. If $C$ is closed and nonempty and $z\in W\setminus C$, there is a linear functional $\ell $ on $W$ with $\sup _ C\ell <\ell (z)$. If $C$ is closed and $z$ is a boundary point of $C$ in $W$, there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell $ on $W$ with $\sup _ C\ell =\ell (z)$; that is, $C$ has a supporting hyperplane at $z$. Every point of the convex hull of a set $S\subset W$ is a convex combination of affinely independent points of $S$, hence of at most $n+1$ points of $S$. If $C
eq \varnothing $, then $\operatorname {ri}C
eq \varnothing $, and $(1-t)x_0+ty\in \operatorname {ri}C$ whenever $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}C$, $y\in \overline C$ and $0\leq t<1$. Moreover, \[  \overline{\operatorname {ri}C}=\overline C,\qquad \operatorname {ri}C=\operatorname {ri}\overline C,  \] and the relative boundary of $C$ has Lebesgue measure zero in the affine span of $C$. Proof. Fix a Euclidean inner product $y\cdot w$ on $W$, with norm $|y|$. (1) Choose $y_ k\in C$ with $|z-y_ k|	o \inf _{w\in C}|z-w|$. The sequence $(y_ k)$ is bounded, so a subsequence converges to a point $y$, which lies in $C$ because $C$ is closed. Thus $y$ minimizes the distance to $z$ on $C$, and $y
eq z$. For $w\in C$ and $0\leq t\leq 1$ the point $y+t(w-y)$ lies in $C$, so the function $t\mapsto |z-y-t(w-y)|^2$ on $[0,1]$ is minimal at $t=0$, and its derivative there, $-2(z-y)\cdot (w-y)$, is nonnegative. Hence $\ell (w)=(z-y)\cdot w$ satisfies $\ell (w)\leq \ell (y)=\ell (z)-|z-y|^2<\ell (z)$ for every $w\in C$. (2) Since $z$ is a boundary point of $C$, there are points $z_ k
otin C$ with $z_ k	o z$. By (1) there are unit vectors $a_ k$ with $a_ k\cdot w<a_ k\cdot z_ k$ for all $w\in C$. A subsequence of $(a_ k)$ converges to a unit vector $a$, and in the limit $a\cdot w\leq a\cdot z$ for all $w\in C$. As $z\in C$, the functional $\ell (w)=a\cdot w$ has the required property. (3) Let $x=\sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ ix_ i$ with $x_ i\in S$, $\lambda _ i>0$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ i=1$. If the points $x_ i$ are affinely dependent, the vectors $(x_ i,1)\in W	imes \mathbb R$ are linearly dependent, say $\sum _ i\mu _ i(x_ i,1)=0$ with not all $\mu _ i$ zero. Since $\sum _ i\mu _ i=0$, some $\mu _ i$ is positive. Replacing each $\lambda _ i$ by $\lambda _ i-s\mu _ i$, where $s=\min \{ \lambda _ i/\mu _ i:\mu _ i>0\} $, preserves $\sum _ i\lambda _ i$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ ix_ i$, keeps all coefficients nonnegative and makes at least one of them zero. We discard the points with zero coefficient and repeat. Eventually the remaining points are affinely independent, and an affinely independent subset of $W$ has at most $n+1$ elements. (4) Let $A$ be the affine span of $C$, of dimension $k$, and write $B_ A(x,r)$ for the open ball of $A$ with center $x$ and radius $r$. If $k=0$, then $C$ is a point, equal to its relative interior and to its closure, and its relative boundary is empty; so assume $k\geq 1$. A maximal affinely independent subset of $C$ spans an affine subspace containing $C$, hence equal to $A$, so it consists of $k+1$ points $x_0',\ldots ,x_ k'$. Every point $y\in A$ has unique barycentric coordinates $\lambda _ i(y)$, which are affine functions of $y$ with $\sum _ i\lambda _ i(y)=1$ and $y=\sum _ i\lambda _ i(y)x_ i'$. At the barycenter $c$ of the simplex with vertices $x_ i'$ all of them equal $1/(k+1)$, so they are positive on a ball $B_ A(c,r)$; every point of this ball is then a convex combination of the $x_ i'$ and lies in $C$. Hence $c\in \operatorname {ri}C$. Now let $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}C$, choose $r>0$ with $B_ A(x_0,r)\subset C$, and let $y\in \overline C$ and $0\leq t<1$. If $y\in C$, convexity gives $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty,(1-t)r)=(1-t)B_ A(x_0,r)+ty\subset C$. In general choose $y_ k\in C$ with $y_ k	o y$; then $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty_ k,(1-t)r)\subset C$, and for large $k$ this ball contains $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty,(1-t)r/2)$. Thus $(1-t)x_0+ty\in \operatorname {ri}C$. Letting $t\uparrow 1$, we see that every point of $\overline C$ is a limit of points of $\operatorname {ri}C$, so $\overline{\operatorname {ri}C}=\overline C$. Next, $\operatorname {ri}C\subset \operatorname {ri}\overline C$, since both are interiors in the same affine space $A$. Conversely, if $x\in \operatorname {ri}\overline C$, then $y=x+\varepsilon (x-c)$ lies in $\overline C$ for small $\varepsilon >0$, and $x=(1-t)c+ty$ with $t=1/(1+\varepsilon )<1$; hence $x\in \operatorname {ri}C$. For the measure assertion, translate so that $c=0$ and identify $A$ with $\mathbb R^ k$ by a linear isomorphism, which changes Lebesgue measure on $A$ only by a constant factor. Let $Z=\overline C\setminus \operatorname {ri}C$ be the relative boundary; it is closed in $A$, because $\operatorname {ri}C$ is open in $A$, hence Borel, and $0
otin Z$. We claim that the dilates $sZ$, $s>0$, are pairwise disjoint. Indeed, suppose that $sz=s'z'$ with $z,z'\in Z$ and $0<s<s'$. Then $z'=(s/s')z$ is of the form $(1-t)\cdot 0+tz$ with $z\in \overline C$ and $0<t<1$, so $z'\in \operatorname {ri}C$ by what we have just shown, which is impossible. Now fix $R>0$ and put $Z_ R=Z\cap B(0,R)$. The sets $sZ_ R$ with $s$ rational in $[ rac12,1]$ are pairwise disjoint subsets of $B(0,R)$, and each has measure $s^ k|Z_ R|\geq 2^{-k}|Z_ R|$. Since infinitely many of them fit into a set of finite measure, $|Z_ R|=0$. Letting $R	o \infty $, we obtain $|Z|=0$. $\square$ Proposition 18.1.3 . Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Then $F$ is locally Lipschitz on $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and $\partial F(x)
eq \varnothing $ for every $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Now let $F$ be a finite convex function on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$. Then the following hold. The sets $\partial F(x)$, $x\in \Omega $, are compact and bounded uniformly for $x$ in each compact subset of $\Omega $, and the graph $\{ (x,p):x\in \Omega ,\  p\in \partial F(x)\} $ is closed in $\Omega 	imes M_{\mathbb R}$. For $x\in \Omega $ and $v\in N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  F'(x;v)=\lim _{t\downarrow 0} rac{F(x+tv)-F(x)}t =\max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle .  \] $F$ is differentiable at $x\in \Omega $ if and only if $\partial F(x)$ is a singleton; in that case $\partial F(x)=\{ 
abla F(x)\} $, where $
abla F(x)\in M_{\mathbb R}$ denotes the differential of $F$ at $x$. $F$ is differentiable almost everywhere on $\Omega $. More precisely, the set $\Omega _ F$ of points of $\Omega $ at which $F$ is differentiable is a Borel set whose complement in $\Omega $ is a null set, and $
abla F\colon \Omega _ F	o M_{\mathbb R}$ is a Borel map. Proof. We first show that $F$ is bounded, hence Lipschitz, near each point of $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and find a subgradient there by separation; then we prove (1)–(4). Let $A$ be the affine span of $\operatorname {dom}F$, of dimension $k$, and let $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Choose affine coordinates on $A$ centered at $x$, with the associated Euclidean norm $|\cdot |$; since all norms on $A$ are equivalent, local Lipschitz continuity does not depend on this choice. For small $\delta >0$ the cube $Q$ of points of $A$ whose coordinates are at most $2\delta $ in absolute value lies in $\operatorname {dom}F$. Every point of $Q$ is a convex combination of the $2^ k$ vertices of $Q$; this follows by induction on $k$, since writing the last coordinate of a point as a convex combination of $\pm 2\delta $ exhibits the point as a convex combination of two points of the opposite faces of $Q$, which are cubes of dimension $k-1$. By the finite form of Jensen's inequality, $F\leq C$ on $Q$, where $C$ is the largest value of $F$ at a vertex. If $y\in Q$, then also $2x-y\in Q$, and $F(x)\leq  rac12(F(y)+F(2x-y))$ gives $F(y)\geq 2F(x)-C$. Thus $F$ is bounded on $Q$, and by ( 18.1 ) it is Lipschitz on the cube of half-side $\delta $ centered at $x$. Next we construct a subgradient at $x$. Since $\operatorname {dom}F\subset A$, the epigraph of $F$ lies in $A	imes \mathbb R$; let $E$ be its closure, a closed convex subset of $A	imes \mathbb R$. Because $F$ is continuous at $x$ as a function on $A$, the points $(x,F(x)-\varepsilon )$, $\varepsilon >0$, do not belong to $E$, so $(x,F(x))$ is a boundary point of $E$ in $A	imes \mathbb R$. By lemma 18.1.2 (2), applied in $A	imes \mathbb R$ with origin $(x,F(x))$, there are a linear functional $a$ on the linear subspace $A_0=\{ y-y':y,y'\in A\} $ parallel to $A$ and a real number $c$, not both zero, such that \[  \langle a,y-xangle +c\, (s-F(x))\geq 0\qquad 	ext{for all }(y,s)\in E.  \] Letting $s	o +\infty $ shows that $c\geq 0$. If $c=0$, then $a
eq 0$ and $\langle a,y-xangle \geq 0$ for all $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$; but $\operatorname {dom}F$ contains a ball of $A$ about $x$, and this ball contains points $y$ with $\langle a,y-xangle <0$. Hence $c>0$, and taking $s=F(y)$ we obtain $F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p_ A,y-xangle $ for $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$, where $p_ A=-a/c$. Extend $p_ A$ to a linear functional $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$. The inequality $F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p,y-xangle $ holds for $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$, because then $y-x\in A_0$, and also for $y
otin \operatorname {dom}F$, where $F(y)=+\infty $. Thus $p\in \partial F(x)$. From now on let $F$ be a finite convex function on the open convex set $\Omega $, so that $A=N_{\mathbb R}$ and $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)=\Omega $. Fix a basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ of $N_{\mathbb R}$, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the set $K_ r=\{ y+\sum _ is_ ie_ i:y\in K,\  |s_ i|\leq r\} $ lies in $\Omega $. If $x\in K$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at the points $x\pm re_ i$, gives $\pm r\langle p,e_ iangle \leq F(x\pm re_ i)-F(x)$, hence $|\langle p,e_ iangle |\leq 2r^{-1}\max _{K_ r}|F|$, where $F$ is bounded on the compact set $K_ r$ because it is continuous. This is the uniform bound in (1). If $x_ k	o x$ in $\Omega $, $p_ k\in \partial F(x_ k)$ and $p_ k	o p$, then letting $k	o \infty $ in $F(y)\geq F(x_ k)+\langle p_ k,y-x_ kangle $ and using that $F$ is continuous at $x$, we get $p\in \partial F(x)$. Thus the graph is closed, and each $\partial F(x)$ is closed and bounded, hence compact. For (2) and (4) we use the following slope inequalities for a convex function $\phi $ on an interval: if $s_1<s_2<s_3$, then 18.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:convex-three-slopes}  rac{\phi (s_2)-\phi (s_1)}{s_2-s_1}\leq  rac{\phi (s_3)-\phi (s_1)}{s_3-s_1}\leq  rac{\phi (s_3)-\phi (s_2)}{s_3-s_2}. \end{equation} Indeed, $s_2=\lambda s_1+(1-\lambda )s_3$ with $\lambda =(s_3-s_2)/(s_3-s_1)\in (0,1)$, and the convexity inequality $\phi (s_2)\leq \lambda \phi (s_1)+(1-\lambda )\phi (s_3)$ is equivalent to each of the two inequalities. Now fix $x$ and $v$, and apply ( 18.2 ) to $\phi (t)=F(x+tv)$, which is convex on the open interval of those $t$ with $x+tv\in \Omega $: with $s_1=0$ it shows that the difference quotient in (2) is nondecreasing in $t>0$, so its limit as $t\downarrow 0$ exists in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$. Each $p\in \partial F(x)$ gives $F(x+tv)-F(x)\geq t\langle p,vangle $; hence $F'(x;v)\geq \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle $, the maximum being attained by compactness. Conversely, choose $p_ t\in \partial F(x+tv)$. The subgradient inequality at $x+tv$, evaluated at $x$, gives $F(x+tv)-F(x)\leq t\langle p_ t,vangle $. By (1) the vectors $p_ t$ stay bounded as $t\downarrow 0$, and each of their cluster points lies in $\partial F(x)$. Therefore $F'(x;v)\leq \varlimsup _{t\downarrow 0}\langle p_ t,vangle \leq \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle $. For (3), suppose that $\partial F(x)=\{ p\} $, and choose $p_ h\in \partial F(x+h)$. By (1), every cluster point of $p_ h$ as $h	o 0$ lies in $\partial F(x)$, so $p_ h	o p$. The subgradient inequalities at $x$ and at $x+h$ give \[  0\leq F(x+h)-F(x)-\langle p,hangle \leq \langle p_ h-p,hangle =o(|h|),  \] so $F$ is differentiable at $x$, with $
abla F(x)=p$. Conversely, if $F$ is differentiable at $x$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, dividing $F(x+tv)-F(x)\geq t\langle p,vangle $ by $t$ and letting $t\downarrow 0$ gives $\langle 
abla F(x),vangle \geq \langle p,vangle $ for every $v$, hence $p=
abla F(x)$. As $\partial F(x)
eq \varnothing $, it equals $\{ 
abla F(x)\} $. For (4), fix $i$, and write $D_ i^+F(x)=F'(x;e_ i)$ and $D_ i^-F(x)=-F'(x;-e_ i)$ for the one-sided partial derivatives; they are finite by (2). Let $\phi $ be the restriction of $F$ to the intersection of $\Omega $ with a line parallel to $e_ i$, parametrized as $\phi (s)=F(y+se_ i)$ on an open interval. By ( 18.2 ), $\phi $ has one-sided derivatives $\phi '_\pm $ at every point, $\phi '_-(s)\leq \phi '_+(s)$, and $\phi '_+(s)\leq \phi '_-(s')$ whenever $s<s'$, because both are bounded by the slope of the chord from $s$ to $s'$. Hence the open intervals $(\phi '_-(s),\phi '_+(s))$ are pairwise disjoint; each nonempty one contains a rational number, so only countably many of them are nonempty, and $\phi '_-=\phi '_+$ outside a countable set. Next, $D_ i^+F$ is the pointwise limit on $\Omega $ of the Borel functions equal to $k(F(x+e_ i/k)-F(x))$ where $x+e_ i/k\in \Omega $ and to $0$ elsewhere, so it is a Borel function, and similarly for $D_ i^-F$. Thus the set $Z_ i\subset \Omega $ where $D_ i^+F
eq D_ i^-F$ is a Borel set that meets each line parallel to $e_ i$ in a countable set, and Fubini's theorem, in the coordinates of the basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$, shows that $Z_ i$ is a null set. At a point $x
otin Z_1\cup \cdots \cup Z_ n$, (2) gives \[  \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,e_ iangle =D_ i^+F(x)=D_ i^-F(x)=\min _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,e_ iangle  \] for every $i$, so all subgradients at $x$ coincide, and $F$ is differentiable at $x$ by (3). Conversely, if $F$ is differentiable at $x$, then $D_ i^+F(x)=D_ i^-F(x)=\langle 
abla F(x),e_ iangle $ for every $i$. Therefore $\Omega _ F=\Omega \setminus (Z_1\cup \cdots \cup Z_ n)$ is a Borel set with null complement, and the coordinates $\langle 
abla F,e_ iangle =D_ i^+F$ of $
abla F$ are Borel functions on $\Omega _ F$. $\square$ Proposition 18.1.4 . Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\overline F$ be its lower semicontinuous regularization, that is, the largest lower semicontinuous function on $N_{\mathbb R}$ that is at most $F$. Then $\overline F$ is a closed proper convex function, and $\overline F=F$ on $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. A closed proper convex function is determined by its values on the relative interior of its effective domain. Finally, if a sequence of finite convex functions on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$ converges to a finite limit at each point of a dense subset of $\Omega $, then it converges locally uniformly on $\Omega $ to a finite convex function. Proof. By proposition 18.1.3 , $F$ has a subgradient $p$ at some point $x_1\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, so $F$ lies above the affine function $\ell (y)=F(x_1)+\langle p,y-x_1angle $. The closure $E$ of $\operatorname {epi}F$ is convex, and it lies above the graph of $\ell $ because $\ell $ is continuous. Hence, for each $x$, the set $\{ r:(x,r)\in E\} $ is closed and bounded below by $\ell (x)$, and with each of its points $r$ it contains $[r,+\infty )$, because $\operatorname {epi}F$ has this property. So this set is either empty or a closed half-line $[\widetilde F(x),+\infty )$ with $\widetilde F(x)\geq \ell (x)>-\infty $. Setting $\widetilde F(x)=+\infty $ in the first case, we see that $E$ is the epigraph of a convex function $\widetilde F$. It is lower semicontinuous because its epigraph is closed, and $\widetilde F\leq F$, so $\operatorname {dom}\widetilde F\supset \operatorname {dom}F
eq \varnothing $. If $G\leq F$ is lower semicontinuous, then $\operatorname {epi}G$ is closed and contains $\operatorname {epi}F$, hence also $E$, and so $G\leq \widetilde F$. Thus $\widetilde F=\overline F$, which is therefore closed, proper and convex. Let $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. If $(y_ k,r_ k)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ converge to $(x,r)$, then $y_ k$ lies in the affine span of $\operatorname {dom}F$, on which $F$ is continuous at $x$; hence $r\geq \lim _ kF(y_ k)=F(x)$. This shows $\overline F(x)\geq F(x)$, and so $\overline F(x)=F(x)$. Now let $F$ be closed, fix $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and let $x\in \overline{\operatorname {dom}F}$. By lemma 18.1.2 (4), the points $(1-t)x_0+tx$ with $0\leq t<1$ lie in $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, so the convex function $\phi (t)=F((1-t)x_0+tx)$ is finite on $[0,1)$. Convexity gives $\phi (t)\leq (1-t)\phi (0)+t\phi (1)$, hence $\varlimsup _{t\uparrow 1}\phi (t)\leq \phi (1)$, while lower semicontinuity gives $\varliminf _{t\uparrow 1}\phi (t)\geq \phi (1)$. Therefore \[  F(x)=\lim _{t\uparrow 1}F((1-t)x_0+tx) \qquad (x\in \overline{\operatorname {dom}F}),  \] also when $F(x)=+\infty $. Since $F=+\infty $ outside $\overline{\operatorname {dom}F}$, which is the closure of $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, the function $F$ is determined by its restriction to $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Finally, let $(F_ j)$ be a sequence of finite convex functions on $\Omega $ converging to a finite limit at every point of a dense set $S\subset \Omega $. We show that near each point of $\Omega $ the functions $F_ j$ are uniformly bounded, hence uniformly Lipschitz, so that convergence on $S$ propagates to uniform convergence. Fix a basis of $N_{\mathbb R}$, write $Q(y,ho )$ for the closed cube of half-side $ho $ centered at $y$ in the corresponding coordinates, and let $x\in \Omega $ and $ho >0$ with $Q(x,2ho )\subset \Omega $. For each vertex $y$ of $Q(x,ho )$ choose a point of $S$ whose coordinates differ from those of $y$ by less than $ho /2$, and let $S_0\subset S\cap Q(x,2ho )$ be the finite set of these points. Its convex hull $H$ is compact as the image of a simplex under a linear map, and it contains $Q(x,ho /2)$. Indeed, let $\ell $ be a nonzero linear functional, $\ell (z)=\sum _ ia_ iz_ i$ in the chosen coordinates, and put $\| a\| =\sum _ i|a_ i|$. At a vertex $y^*$ of $Q(x,ho )$ where $\ell $ is maximal, $\ell (y^*)=\ell (x)+ho \| a\| $, and the point $s\in S_0$ chosen for $y^*$ satisfies $\ell (s)>\ell (y^*)- racho 2\| a\| =\max _{Q(x,ho /2)}\ell $. Hence no point of $Q(x,ho /2)$ can be separated from $H$ as in lemma 18.1.2 (1). The sequences $(F_ j(s))_ j$, $s\in S_0$, converge, so they are bounded above by some $C$, and the finite form of Jensen's inequality gives $F_ j\leq C$ on $H$ for all $j$. Choose $s_0\in S\cap Q(x,ho /8)$. Then $Q(s_0,3ho /8)\subset Q(x,ho /2)$, and for $y\in Q(s_0,3ho /8)$ the reflected point $2s_0-y$ lies in the same cube, so that $F_ j(y)\geq 2F_ j(s_0)-C\geq 2\inf _ kF_ k(s_0)-C$. Hence $|F_ j|\leq B$ on $Q(x,ho /4)\subset Q(s_0,3ho /8)$ for all $j$, with a constant $B$. By ( 18.1 ), applied with $\delta =ho /8$ and $\omega \leq 2B$, the $F_ j$ are Lipschitz on $Q(x,ho /8)$ with the common constant $L=16B/ho $, for the Euclidean norm $|\cdot |$ of the chosen coordinates. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose a finite set $S_\varepsilon \subset S\cap Q(x,ho /8)$ such that every point of $Q(x,ho /8)$ lies within distance $\varepsilon /L$ of $S_\varepsilon $. To this end, cover the compact cube $Q(x,ho /8)$ by finitely many balls of radius $\varepsilon /(2L)$ centered in the cube, and pick a point of the dense set $S$ in the intersection of each ball with the interior of the cube, a nonempty open set. For all sufficiently large $j,k$ we have $|F_ j-F_ k|<\varepsilon $ on $S_\varepsilon $, hence $|F_ j-F_ k|<3\varepsilon $ on $Q(x,ho /8)$. Thus $(F_ j)$ is uniformly Cauchy on $Q(x,ho /8)$. Finitely many such cubes cover any given compact subset of $\Omega $, so $(F_ j)$ converges locally uniformly to a finite continuous function, which is convex because the convexity inequalities pass to pointwise limits. $\square$

title: Definition 18.1.1
text: Definition 18.1.1 . A function $F\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is convex if its epigraph \[  \operatorname {epi}F=\{ (x,r)\in N_{\mathbb R}\times \mathbb R:r\geq F(x)\}   \] is convex. A convex function is proper if it does not take the value $-\infty $ and its effective domain $\operatorname {dom}F=\{ x:F(x)<+\infty \} $ is nonempty; a proper convex function is closed if it is lower semicontinuous. The relative interior $\operatorname {ri}C$ of a convex set $C$ is its interior in its affine span, and $\overline C\setminus \operatorname {ri}C$ is its relative boundary . For a proper convex function $F$ and $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$, the subgradient set of $F$ at $x$ is \[  \partial F(x)=\{ p\in M_{\mathbb R}:F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle \text{ for every }y\in N_{\mathbb R}\} .  \] Its elements are the subgradients , or supporting slopes , of $F$ at $x$: they are the slopes of the affine functions that lie below $F$ and agree with $F$ at $x$. We set $\partial F(x)=\varnothing $ for $x\notin \operatorname {dom}F$ and $\partial F(E)=\bigcup _{x\in E}\partial F(x)$ for $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$.
18.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:convex-cube-lipschitz} |F(z)-F(y)|\leq \frac{\omega }{\delta }|z-y|\qquad (y,z\in Q'). \end{equation}

title: Lemma 18.1.2
text:
Lemma 18.1.2 . Let $W$ be a real vector space of finite dimension $n$, and let $C\subset W$ be convex. If $C$ is closed and nonempty and $z\in W\setminus C$, there is a linear functional $\ell $ on $W$ with $\sup _ C\ell <\ell (z)$. If $C$ is closed and $z$ is a boundary point of $C$ in $W$, there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell $ on $W$ with $\sup _ C\ell =\ell (z)$; that is, $C$ has a supporting hyperplane at $z$. Every point of the convex hull of a set $S\subset W$ is a convex combination of affinely independent points of $S$, hence of at most $n+1$ points of $S$. If $C
eq \varnothing $, then $\operatorname {ri}C
eq \varnothing $, and $(1-t)x_0+ty\in \operatorname {ri}C$ whenever $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}C$, $y\in \overline C$ and $0\leq t<1$. Moreover, \[  \overline{\operatorname {ri}C}=\overline C,\qquad \operatorname {ri}C=\operatorname {ri}\overline C,  \] and the relative boundary of $C$ has Lebesgue measure zero in the affine span of $C$. Proof. Fix a Euclidean inner product $y\cdot w$ on $W$, with norm $|y|$. (1) Choose $y_ k\in C$ with $|z-y_ k|	o \inf _{w\in C}|z-w|$. The sequence $(y_ k)$ is bounded, so a subsequence converges to a point $y$, which lies in $C$ because $C$ is closed. Thus $y$ minimizes the distance to $z$ on $C$, and $y
eq z$. For $w\in C$ and $0\leq t\leq 1$ the point $y+t(w-y)$ lies in $C$, so the function $t\mapsto |z-y-t(w-y)|^2$ on $[0,1]$ is minimal at $t=0$, and its derivative there, $-2(z-y)\cdot (w-y)$, is nonnegative. Hence $\ell (w)=(z-y)\cdot w$ satisfies $\ell (w)\leq \ell (y)=\ell (z)-|z-y|^2<\ell (z)$ for every $w\in C$. (2) Since $z$ is a boundary point of $C$, there are points $z_ k
otin C$ with $z_ k	o z$. By (1) there are unit vectors $a_ k$ with $a_ k\cdot w<a_ k\cdot z_ k$ for all $w\in C$. A subsequence of $(a_ k)$ converges to a unit vector $a$, and in the limit $a\cdot w\leq a\cdot z$ for all $w\in C$. As $z\in C$, the functional $\ell (w)=a\cdot w$ has the required property. (3) Let $x=\sum _{i=1}^ q\lambda _ ix_ i$ with $x_ i\in S$, $\lambda _ i>0$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ i=1$. If the points $x_ i$ are affinely dependent, the vectors $(x_ i,1)\in W	imes \mathbb R$ are linearly dependent, say $\sum _ i\mu _ i(x_ i,1)=0$ with not all $\mu _ i$ zero. Since $\sum _ i\mu _ i=0$, some $\mu _ i$ is positive. Replacing each $\lambda _ i$ by $\lambda _ i-s\mu _ i$, where $s=\min \{ \lambda _ i/\mu _ i:\mu _ i>0\} $, preserves $\sum _ i\lambda _ i$ and $\sum _ i\lambda _ ix_ i$, keeps all coefficients nonnegative and makes at least one of them zero. We discard the points with zero coefficient and repeat. Eventually the remaining points are affinely independent, and an affinely independent subset of $W$ has at most $n+1$ elements. (4) Let $A$ be the affine span of $C$, of dimension $k$, and write $B_ A(x,r)$ for the open ball of $A$ with center $x$ and radius $r$. If $k=0$, then $C$ is a point, equal to its relative interior and to its closure, and its relative boundary is empty; so assume $k\geq 1$. A maximal affinely independent subset of $C$ spans an affine subspace containing $C$, hence equal to $A$, so it consists of $k+1$ points $x_0',\ldots ,x_ k'$. Every point $y\in A$ has unique barycentric coordinates $\lambda _ i(y)$, which are affine functions of $y$ with $\sum _ i\lambda _ i(y)=1$ and $y=\sum _ i\lambda _ i(y)x_ i'$. At the barycenter $c$ of the simplex with vertices $x_ i'$ all of them equal $1/(k+1)$, so they are positive on a ball $B_ A(c,r)$; every point of this ball is then a convex combination of the $x_ i'$ and lies in $C$. Hence $c\in \operatorname {ri}C$. Now let $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}C$, choose $r>0$ with $B_ A(x_0,r)\subset C$, and let $y\in \overline C$ and $0\leq t<1$. If $y\in C$, convexity gives $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty,(1-t)r)=(1-t)B_ A(x_0,r)+ty\subset C$. In general choose $y_ k\in C$ with $y_ k	o y$; then $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty_ k,(1-t)r)\subset C$, and for large $k$ this ball contains $B_ A((1-t)x_0+ty,(1-t)r/2)$. Thus $(1-t)x_0+ty\in \operatorname {ri}C$. Letting $t\uparrow 1$, we see that every point of $\overline C$ is a limit of points of $\operatorname {ri}C$, so $\overline{\operatorname {ri}C}=\overline C$. Next, $\operatorname {ri}C\subset \operatorname {ri}\overline C$, since both are interiors in the same affine space $A$. Conversely, if $x\in \operatorname {ri}\overline C$, then $y=x+\varepsilon (x-c)$ lies in $\overline C$ for small $\varepsilon >0$, and $x=(1-t)c+ty$ with $t=1/(1+\varepsilon )<1$; hence $x\in \operatorname {ri}C$. For the measure assertion, translate so that $c=0$ and identify $A$ with $\mathbb R^ k$ by a linear isomorphism, which changes Lebesgue measure on $A$ only by a constant factor. Let $Z=\overline C\setminus \operatorname {ri}C$ be the relative boundary; it is closed in $A$, because $\operatorname {ri}C$ is open in $A$, hence Borel, and $0
otin Z$. We claim that the dilates $sZ$, $s>0$, are pairwise disjoint. Indeed, suppose that $sz=s'z'$ with $z,z'\in Z$ and $0<s<s'$. Then $z'=(s/s')z$ is of the form $(1-t)\cdot 0+tz$ with $z\in \overline C$ and $0<t<1$, so $z'\in \operatorname {ri}C$ by what we have just shown, which is impossible. Now fix $R>0$ and put $Z_ R=Z\cap B(0,R)$. The sets $sZ_ R$ with $s$ rational in $[ rac12,1]$ are pairwise disjoint subsets of $B(0,R)$, and each has measure $s^ k|Z_ R|\geq 2^{-k}|Z_ R|$. Since infinitely many of them fit into a set of finite measure, $|Z_ R|=0$. Letting $R	o \infty $, we obtain $|Z|=0$. $\square$

title: Proposition 18.1.3
text:
Proposition 18.1.3 . Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Then $F$ is locally Lipschitz on $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and $\partial F(x)
eq \varnothing $ for every $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Now let $F$ be a finite convex function on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$. Then the following hold. The sets $\partial F(x)$, $x\in \Omega $, are compact and bounded uniformly for $x$ in each compact subset of $\Omega $, and the graph $\{ (x,p):x\in \Omega ,\  p\in \partial F(x)\} $ is closed in $\Omega 	imes M_{\mathbb R}$. For $x\in \Omega $ and $v\in N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  F'(x;v)=\lim _{t\downarrow 0} rac{F(x+tv)-F(x)}t =\max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle .  \] $F$ is differentiable at $x\in \Omega $ if and only if $\partial F(x)$ is a singleton; in that case $\partial F(x)=\{ 
abla F(x)\} $, where $
abla F(x)\in M_{\mathbb R}$ denotes the differential of $F$ at $x$. $F$ is differentiable almost everywhere on $\Omega $. More precisely, the set $\Omega _ F$ of points of $\Omega $ at which $F$ is differentiable is a Borel set whose complement in $\Omega $ is a null set, and $
abla F\colon \Omega _ F	o M_{\mathbb R}$ is a Borel map. Proof. We first show that $F$ is bounded, hence Lipschitz, near each point of $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and find a subgradient there by separation; then we prove (1)–(4). Let $A$ be the affine span of $\operatorname {dom}F$, of dimension $k$, and let $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Choose affine coordinates on $A$ centered at $x$, with the associated Euclidean norm $|\cdot |$; since all norms on $A$ are equivalent, local Lipschitz continuity does not depend on this choice. For small $\delta >0$ the cube $Q$ of points of $A$ whose coordinates are at most $2\delta $ in absolute value lies in $\operatorname {dom}F$. Every point of $Q$ is a convex combination of the $2^ k$ vertices of $Q$; this follows by induction on $k$, since writing the last coordinate of a point as a convex combination of $\pm 2\delta $ exhibits the point as a convex combination of two points of the opposite faces of $Q$, which are cubes of dimension $k-1$. By the finite form of Jensen's inequality, $F\leq C$ on $Q$, where $C$ is the largest value of $F$ at a vertex. If $y\in Q$, then also $2x-y\in Q$, and $F(x)\leq  rac12(F(y)+F(2x-y))$ gives $F(y)\geq 2F(x)-C$. Thus $F$ is bounded on $Q$, and by ( 18.1 ) it is Lipschitz on the cube of half-side $\delta $ centered at $x$. Next we construct a subgradient at $x$. Since $\operatorname {dom}F\subset A$, the epigraph of $F$ lies in $A	imes \mathbb R$; let $E$ be its closure, a closed convex subset of $A	imes \mathbb R$. Because $F$ is continuous at $x$ as a function on $A$, the points $(x,F(x)-\varepsilon )$, $\varepsilon >0$, do not belong to $E$, so $(x,F(x))$ is a boundary point of $E$ in $A	imes \mathbb R$. By lemma 18.1.2 (2), applied in $A	imes \mathbb R$ with origin $(x,F(x))$, there are a linear functional $a$ on the linear subspace $A_0=\{ y-y':y,y'\in A\} $ parallel to $A$ and a real number $c$, not both zero, such that \[  \langle a,y-xangle +c\, (s-F(x))\geq 0\qquad 	ext{for all }(y,s)\in E.  \] Letting $s	o +\infty $ shows that $c\geq 0$. If $c=0$, then $a
eq 0$ and $\langle a,y-xangle \geq 0$ for all $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$; but $\operatorname {dom}F$ contains a ball of $A$ about $x$, and this ball contains points $y$ with $\langle a,y-xangle <0$. Hence $c>0$, and taking $s=F(y)$ we obtain $F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p_ A,y-xangle $ for $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$, where $p_ A=-a/c$. Extend $p_ A$ to a linear functional $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$. The inequality $F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle p,y-xangle $ holds for $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$, because then $y-x\in A_0$, and also for $y
otin \operatorname {dom}F$, where $F(y)=+\infty $. Thus $p\in \partial F(x)$. From now on let $F$ be a finite convex function on the open convex set $\Omega $, so that $A=N_{\mathbb R}$ and $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)=\Omega $. Fix a basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ of $N_{\mathbb R}$, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the set $K_ r=\{ y+\sum _ is_ ie_ i:y\in K,\  |s_ i|\leq r\} $ lies in $\Omega $. If $x\in K$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at the points $x\pm re_ i$, gives $\pm r\langle p,e_ iangle \leq F(x\pm re_ i)-F(x)$, hence $|\langle p,e_ iangle |\leq 2r^{-1}\max _{K_ r}|F|$, where $F$ is bounded on the compact set $K_ r$ because it is continuous. If $x_ k	o x$ in $\Omega $, $p_ k\in \partial F(x_ k)$ and $p_ k	o p$, then letting $k	o \infty $ in $F(y)\geq F(x_ k)+\langle p_ k,y-x_ kangle $ and using that $F$ is continuous at $x$, we get $p\in \partial F(x)$. Now fix $x$ and $v$, and apply ( 18.2 ) to $\phi (t)=F(x+tv)$, which is convex on the open interval of those $t$ with $x+tv\in \Omega $: with $s_1=0$ it shows that the difference quotient in (2) is nondecreasing in $t>0$, so its limit as $t\downarrow 0$ exists in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$. Each $p\in \partial F(x)$ gives $F(x+tv)-F(x)\geq t\langle p,vangle $; hence $F'(x;v)\geq \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle $, the maximum being attained by compactness. Conversely, choose $p_ t\in \partial F(x+tv)$. The subgradient inequality at $x+tv$, evaluated at $x$, gives $F(x+tv)-F(x)\leq t\langle p_ t,vangle $. By (1) the vectors $p_ t$ stay bounded as $t\downarrow 0$, and each of their cluster points lies in $\partial F(x)$. Therefore $F'(x;v)\leq \varlimsup _{t\downarrow 0}\langle p_ t,vangle \leq \max _{p\in \partial F(x)}\langle p,vangle $. For (3), suppose that $\partial F(x)=\{ p\} $, and choose $p_ h\in \partial F(x+h)$. By (1), every cluster point of $p_ h$ as $h	o 0$ lies in $\partial F(x)$, so $p_ h	o p$. The subgradient inequalities at $x$ and at $x+h$ give \[  0\leq F(x+h)-F(x)-\langle p,hangle \leq \langle p_ h-p,hangle =o(|h|),  \] so $F$ is differentiable at $x$, with $

title: Proposition 18.1.4
text: Proposition 18.1.4 . Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\overline F$ be its lower semicontinuous regularization, that is, the largest lower semicontinuous function on $N_{\mathbb R}$ that is at most $F$. Then $\overline F$ is a closed proper convex function, and $\overline F=F$ on $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. A closed proper convex function is determined by its values on the relative interior of its effective domain. Finally, if a sequence of finite convex functions on an open convex set $\Omega \subset N_{\mathbb R}$ converges to a finite limit at each point of a dense subset of $\Omega $, then it converges locally uniformly on $\Omega $ to a finite convex function. Proof. By proposition 18.1.3 , $F$ has a subgradient $p$ at some point $x_1\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, so $F$ lies above the affine function $\ell (y)=F(x_1)+\langle p,y-x_1\rangle $. The closure $E$ of $\operatorname {epi}F$ is convex, and it lies above the graph of $\ell $ because $\ell $ is continuous. Hence, for each $x$, the set $\{ r:(x,r)\in E\} $ is closed and bounded below by $\ell (x)$, and with each of its points $r$ it contains $[r,+\infty )$, because $\operatorname {epi}F$ has this property. So this set is either empty or a closed half-line $[\widetilde F(x),+\infty )$ with $\widetilde F(x)\geq \ell (x)>-\infty $. Setting $\widetilde F(x)=+\infty $ in the first case, we see that $E$ is the epigraph of a convex function $\widetilde F$. It is lower semicontinuous because its epigraph is closed, and $\widetilde F\leq F$, so $\operatorname {dom}\widetilde F\supset \operatorname {dom}F\neq \varnothing $. If $G\leq F$ is lower semicontinuous, then $\operatorname {epi}G$ is closed and contains $\operatorname {epi}F$, hence also $E$, and so $G\leq \widetilde F$. Thus $\widetilde F=\overline F$, which is therefore closed, proper and convex. Let $x\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. If $(y_ k,r_ k)\in \operatorname {epi}F$ converge to $(x,r)$, then $y_ k$ lies in the affine span of $\operatorname {dom}F$, on which $F$ is continuous at $x$; hence $r\geq \lim _ kF(y_ k)=F(x)$. This shows $\overline F(x)\geq F(x)$, and so $\overline F(x)=F(x)$. Now let $F$ be closed, fix $x_0\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and let $x\in \overline{\operatorname {dom}F}$. By lemma 18.1.2 (4), the points $(1-t)x_0+tx$ with $0\leq t<1$ lie in $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, so the convex function $\phi (t)=F((1-t)x_0+tx)$ is finite on $[0,1)$. Convexity gives $\phi (t)\leq (1-t)\phi (0)+t\phi (1)$, hence $\varlimsup _{t\uparrow 1}\phi (t)\leq \phi (1)$, while lower semicontinuity gives $\varliminf _{t\uparrow 1}\phi (t)\geq \phi (1)$. Therefore \[  F(x)=\lim _{t\uparrow 1}F((1-t)x_0+tx) \qquad (x\in \overline{\operatorname {dom}F}),  \] also when $F(x)=+\infty $. Since $F=+\infty $ outside $\overline{\operatorname {dom}F}$, which is the closure of $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, the function $F$ is determined by its restriction to $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$. Finally, let $(F_ j)$ be a sequence of finite convex functions on $\Omega $ converging to a finite limit at every point of a dense set $S\subset \Omega $. We show that near each point of $\Omega $ the functions $F_ j$ are uniformly bounded, hence uniformly Lipschitz, so that convergence on $S$ propagates to uniform convergence. Fix a basis of $N_{\mathbb R}$, write $Q(y,\rho )$ for the closed cube of half-side $\rho $ centered at $y$ in the corresponding coordinates, and let $x\in \Omega $ and $\rho >0$ with $Q(x,2\rho )\subset \Omega $. For each vertex $y$ of $Q(x,\rho )$ choose a point of $S$ whose coordinates differ from those of $y$ by less than $\rho /2$, and let $S_0\subset S\cap Q(x,2\rho )$ be the finite set of these points. Its convex hull $H$ is compact as the image of a simplex under a linear map, and it contains $Q(x,\rho /2)$. Indeed, let $\ell $ be a nonzero linear functional, $\ell (z)=\sum _ ia_ iz_ i$ in the chosen coordinates, and put $\| a\| =\sum _ i|a_ i|$. At a vertex $y^*$ of $Q(x,\rho )$ where $\ell $ is maximal, $\ell (y^*)=\ell (x)+\rho \| a\| $, and the point $s\in S_0$ chosen for $y^*$ satisfies $\ell (s)>\ell (y^*)-\frac\rho 2\| a\| =\max _{Q(x,\rho /2)}\ell $. Hence no point of $Q(x,\rho /2)$ can be separated from $H$ as in lemma 18.1.2 (1). The sequences $(F_ j(s))_ j$, $s\in S_0$, converge, so they are bounded above by some $C$, and the finite form of Jensen's inequality gives $F_ j\leq C$ on $H$ for all $j$. Choose $s_0\in S\cap Q(x,\rho /8)$. Then $Q(s_0,3\rho /8)\subset Q(x,\rho /2)$, and for $y\in Q(s_0,3\rho /8)$ the reflected point $2s_0-y$ lies in the same cube, so that $F_ j(y)\geq 2F_ j(s_0)-C\geq 2\inf _ kF_ k(s_0)-C$. Hence $|F_ j|\leq B$ on $Q(x,\rho /4)\subset Q(s_0,3\rho /8)$ for all $j$, with a constant $B$. By ( 18.1 ), applied with $\delta =\rho /8$ and $\omega \leq 2B$, the $F_ j$ are Lipschitz on $Q(x,\rho /8)$ with the common constant $L=16B/\rho $, for the Euclidean norm $|\cdot |$ of the chosen coordinates. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose a finite set $S_\varepsilon \subset S\cap Q(x,\rho /8)$ such that every point of $Q(x,\rho /8)$ lies within distance $\varepsilon /L$ of $S_\varepsilon $. To this end, cover the compact cube $Q(x,\rho /8)$ by finitely many balls of radius $\varepsilon /(2L)$ centered in the cube, and pick a point of the dense set $S$ in the intersection of each ball with the interior of the cube, a nonempty open set. For all sufficiently large $j,k$ we have $|F_ j-F_ k|<\varepsilon $ on $S_\varepsilon $, hence $|F_ j-F_ k|<3\varepsilon $ on $Q(x,\rho /8)$. Thus $(F_ j)$ is uniformly Cauchy on $Q(x,\rho /8)$. Finitely many such cubes cover any given compact subset of $\Omega $, so $(F_ j)$ converges locally uniformly to a finite continuous function, which is convex because the convexity inequalities pass to pointwise limits. $\square$

title: 18.1.1 Invariant functions on tubes and complex tori
search_title: Invariant functions on tubes and complex tori
text: 18.1.1 Invariant functions on tubes and complex tori We now prove the correspondence between invariant plurisubharmonic functions and convex functions described at the beginning of the chapter. For a nonempty open convex set $V\subset \mathbb R^ n$, $n\geq 1$, consider the tube \[  V+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n=\{ t+\mathrm is:t\in V,\  s\in \mathbb R^ n\} \subset \mathbb C^ n,  \] with coordinates $w=t+\mathrm is$. Recall from section 8.5 , here without the variables $z$, that a function $U$ on the tube is invariant under imaginary translations if $U(w+\mathrm is')=U(w)$ for all $s'\in \mathbb R^ n$, that is, if $U(t+\mathrm is)$ depends only on $t$. As observed there, the complex Hessian of a smooth function of this kind is a quarter of its real Hessian in $t$, so plurisubharmonicity becomes convexity; the general case follows by smoothing. In addition, local integrability of $U$ excludes the value $-\infty $. Proposition 18.1.5 . Let $n\geq 1$, let $V\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be a nonempty open convex set, and let $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(V+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n)$ be invariant under imaginary translations. Then there is a finite convex function $f\colon V\to \mathbb R$ such that $U(t+\mathrm is)=f(t)$ for all $t\in V$ and $s\in \mathbb R^ n$. Conversely, for every finite convex function $f$ on $V$, the function $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic on $V+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$ and invariant under imaginary translations. Proof. Define $f(t)=U(t)$, identifying $t\in V$ with $t+\mathrm i0$; by invariance, $U(t+\mathrm is)=f(t)$. By theorem 8.2.1 , $U$ is locally integrable, so the set $\{ U=-\infty \} =\{ f=-\infty \} +\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$ is a Lebesgue null set in $\mathbb C^ n$. Applying Fubini's theorem on products of compact boxes in $t$ and in $s$, we see that $\{ f=-\infty \} $ is a null set in $V$. For $\varepsilon >0$ let $V_\varepsilon =\{ t\in V:\operatorname {dist}(t,\mathbb R^ n\setminus V)>\varepsilon \} $. A point $t$ lies in $V_\varepsilon $ if and only if the closed ball $\overline{B(t,\varepsilon )}$ lies in $V$, so $V_\varepsilon $ is the intersection of the convex sets $V-y$, $|y|\leq \varepsilon $, and is convex. The points of the tube at distance more than $\varepsilon $ from its complement form the tube $V_\varepsilon +\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$. On this set let $U_\varepsilon =U*\rho _\varepsilon $, where $\rho _\varepsilon $ is the radial mollifier of section 1.4 on $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$. The function $U_\varepsilon $ is smooth, and its complex Hessian matrix $(\partial ^2U_\varepsilon /\partial w_ j\partial \bar w_ k)$ is positive semidefinite. Indeed, for $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$, the function $\sum _{j,k}(\partial ^2U_\varepsilon /\partial w_ j\partial \bar w_ k)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ is, by proposition 1.4.3 (1), the mollification of the distribution $\sum _{j,k}(\partial ^2U/\partial w_ j\partial \bar w_ k)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$, which is positive by theorem 8.2.1 and the matrix criterion of section 7.3 , so it is nonnegative by proposition 1.4.3 (3). Moreover, $U_\varepsilon \downarrow U$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ by ( 3.3 ), because $U$ is subharmonic and locally integrable (theorem 8.2.1 ). Since imaginary translations commute with convolution, $U_\varepsilon $ is invariant under them; write $U_\varepsilon (t+\mathrm is)=f_\varepsilon (t)$. For a function of $t=\operatorname{Re}w$ alone we have $\partial /\partial w_ j=\frac12\partial /\partial t_ j=\partial /\partial \bar w_ j$, hence \[  \frac{\partial ^2U_\varepsilon }{\partial w_ j\partial \bar w_ k} =\frac14\frac{\partial ^2f_\varepsilon }{\partial t_ j\partial t_ k}.  \] The left side is a positive semidefinite matrix, so $f_\varepsilon $ has positive semidefinite real Hessian. Hence the restriction of $f_\varepsilon $ to every segment in the convex set $V_\varepsilon $ has nonnegative second derivative, and $f_\varepsilon $ is convex on $V_\varepsilon $. Suppose that $f(t_0)=-\infty $ for some $t_0\in V$, and choose $r\in (0,1)$ with $\overline{B(t_0,3r)}\subset V$. The upper semicontinuous function $U$ is bounded above, say by $C$, on the compact set $\overline{B(t_0,3r)}+\mathrm i[-1,1]^ n$. Since $U_\varepsilon (w)$ is an average of $U$ over the ball $\overline{B(w,\varepsilon )}$, we get $U_\varepsilon \leq C$ on $B(t_0,2r)$ for $\varepsilon <r$; moreover $B(t_0,2r)\subset V_\varepsilon $ for such $\varepsilon $. For $t\in B(t_0,r)$, the point $2t-t_0$ lies in $B(t_0,2r)$, and $t$ is the midpoint of $t_0$ and $2t-t_0$. Convexity of $f_\varepsilon $ therefore gives \[  f_\varepsilon (t) \leq \tfrac 12f_\varepsilon (t_0) +\tfrac 12f_\varepsilon (2t-t_0) \leq \tfrac 12f_\varepsilon (t_0)+\tfrac 12C.  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, $f_\varepsilon (t_0)\downarrow f(t_0)=-\infty $ and $f_\varepsilon (t)\downarrow f(t)$, so $f=-\infty $ on $B(t_0,r)$. This contradicts the fact that $\{ f=-\infty \} $ is a null set. Hence $f$ is finite. Finally, every segment $[a,b]\subset V$ is compact and therefore lies in $V_\varepsilon $ for small $\varepsilon $; the convexity inequalities for $f_\varepsilon $ on $[a,b]$ pass to the pointwise limit, so $f$ is convex. Conversely, let $f$ be a finite convex function on $V$. By proposition 18.1.3 , $f$ is continuous and has a subgradient $p\in \mathbb R^ n$ at every point. Let $w_0=t_0+\mathrm is_0$ be a point of the tube, $a\in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, and $r>0$ such that the circle $\{ w_0+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a:\theta \in [0,2\pi ]\} $ lies in the tube. If $p$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $t_0$, then \[  f\bigl (\operatorname{Re}(w_0+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a)\bigr ) \geq f(t_0)+r\left\langle p, \operatorname{Re}(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a)\right\rangle =f(t_0)+r\operatorname{Re}\Bigl (\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\sum _ jp_ ja_ j\Bigr ).  \] The last term has mean zero over $\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$, so the mean of the left side over the circle is at least $f(t_0)=f(\operatorname{Re}w_0)$. Since $w_0$, $a$ and $r$ are arbitrary, the restriction of the continuous function $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ to every affine complex line satisfies the submean inequality of definition 3.1.1 at every point, and it is therefore subharmonic. As $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is finite and continuous and the tube is a domain, definition 8.1.1 shows that $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic. It is invariant under imaginary translations by construction. $\square$ Corollary 18.1.6 . Let $n\geq 1$, let $V\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be a nonempty open convex set, and put \[  \Omega _ V=\{ z\in (\mathbb C^*)^ n: (\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)\in V\} .  \] Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega _ V)$ be invariant under the action of the compact torus $(S^1)^ n$ by separate rotations of the coordinates, $(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)\mapsto (\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta _1}z_1,\ldots ,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta _ n}z_ n)$. Then there is a finite convex function $f$ on $V$ such that \[  \varphi (z)=f(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)\qquad (z\in \Omega _ V).  \] Conversely, for every finite convex function $f$ on $V$ this formula defines an $(S^1)^ n$-invariant plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega _ V$. In particular, an $(S^1)^ n$-invariant plurisubharmonic function on $(\Delta ^*)^ n$ or on $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ is finite everywhere, where $\Delta ^*=\{ \zeta \in \mathbb C:0<|\zeta |<1\} $. Proof. Consider the holomorphic map \[  E\colon \mathbb C^ n\to (\mathbb C^*)^ n,\qquad E(w)=(\exp (w_1/2),\ldots ,\exp (w_ n/2)).  \] Since $\log |E_ j(w)|^2=\operatorname{Re}w_ j$, it maps the tube $V+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$ onto $\Omega _ V$; in particular, $\Omega _ V$ is connected. By proposition 8.2.3 , $\varphi \circ E$ is either plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on the tube, and the second alternative is impossible because $E$ is surjective and $\varphi $ is nontrivial. Since $E(w+\mathrm is')=(\mathrm e^{\mathrm is_1'/2}E_1(w),\ldots ,\mathrm e^{\mathrm is_ n'/2}E_ n(w))$, the rotation invariance of $\varphi $ makes $\varphi \circ E$ invariant under imaginary translations. Proposition 18.1.5 now gives a finite convex function $f$ with $\varphi (E(w))=f(\operatorname{Re}w)$, which is the asserted formula. Conversely, let $f$ be finite and convex. Then $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic on the tube by proposition 18.1.5 . Near each point of $\Omega _ V$, the map $E$ has the holomorphic local inverse $z\mapsto (2\log z_1,\ldots ,2\log z_ n)$, defined with local branches of the logarithm, and $f(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)$ is the composition of $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ with this inverse. By proposition 8.2.3 it is plurisubharmonic near that point, since it is finite. Plurisubharmonicity is a local property, so the function is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _ V$, and it is $(S^1)^ n$-invariant because it depends only on $|z_1|,\ldots ,|z_ n|$. The domains $(\Delta ^*)^ n$ and $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ are $\Omega _ V$ for $V=(-\infty ,0)^ n$ and $V=\mathbb R^ n$. $\square$

Since $E(w+\mathrm is')=(\mathrm e^{\mathrm is_1'/2}E_1(w),\ldots ,\mathrm e^{\mathrm is_ n'/2}E_ n(w))$, the rotation invariance of $\varphi $ makes $\varphi \circ E$ invariant under imaginary translations. Proposition 18.1.5 now gives a finite convex function $f$ with $\varphi (E(w))=f(\operatorname{Re}w)$, which is the asserted formula. Conversely, let $f$ be finite and convex. Then $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic on the tube by proposition 18.1.5 . Near each point of $\Omega _ V$, the map $E$ has the holomorphic local inverse $z\mapsto (2\log z_1,\ldots ,2\log z_ n)$, defined with local branches of the logarithm, and $f(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)$ is the composition of $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ with this inverse. By proposition 8.2.3 it is plurisubharmonic near that point, since it is finite. Plurisubharmonicity is a local property, so the function is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _ V$, and it is $(S^1)^ n$-invariant because it depends only on $|z_1|,\ldots ,|z_ n|$. The domains $(\Delta ^*)^ n$ and $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ are $\Omega _ V$ for $V=(-\infty ,0)^ n$ and $V=\mathbb R^ n$. $\square$

title: 18.2 Legendre duality and convex envelopes
text: 18.2 Legendre duality and convex envelopes The Legendre transform exchanges convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and on $M_{\mathbb R}$, and points with slopes: up to closure, the slopes of $F$ are the points where $F^*$ is finite. We prove the duality theorem and compute the conjugates of envelopes and sums. Definition 18.2.1 . The Legendre transform , or convex conjugate , of a function $F\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ is the function on $M_{\mathbb R}$ given by \[  F^*(p)=\sup _{x\in N_{\mathbb R}}(\langle p,x\rangle -F(x)).  \] The conjugate of a function on $M_{\mathbb R}$ is defined in the same way and is a function on $N_{\mathbb R}$; we write $F^{**}=(F^*)^*$. The convex indicator function $\chi _ C$ of a nonempty set $C$, in either space, is $0$ on $C$ and $+\infty $ elsewhere. The support function of a nonempty set $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is \[  h_ P(x)=\sup _{p\in P}\langle p,x\rangle \qquad (x\in N_{\mathbb R});  \] it is convex with values in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$, and it is finite when $P$ is bounded. Theorem 18.2.2 . Let $F$ be a proper convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Then $F^*$ is a closed proper convex function on $M_{\mathbb R}$, and \[  F^{**}=\overline F,\qquad (\overline F)^*=F^*.  \] If $F$ is closed, then for $x\in N_{\mathbb R}$ and $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$ the following conditions are equivalent: \[  p\in \partial F(x),\qquad x\in \partial F^*(p),\qquad F(x)+F^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle ;  \] moreover, \[  \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F^*)\subset \partial F(N_{\mathbb R}) \subset \operatorname {dom}F^*,\qquad \overline{\partial F(N_{\mathbb R})} =\overline{\operatorname {dom}F^*}.  \] Finally, for every nonempty closed convex set $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$, the support function and the convex indicator function are conjugate: $h_ P=\chi _ P^*$ and $\chi _ P=h_ P^*$. Proof. The conjugate is the supremum of the continuous affine functions $p\mapsto \langle p,x\rangle -F(x)$, $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$, so it is convex and lower semicontinuous. Since $\operatorname {dom}F\neq \varnothing $, we have $F^*(p)\geq \langle p,x_0\rangle -F(x_0)>-\infty $ for any $x_0\in \operatorname {dom}F$. By proposition 18.1.3 , $F$ has a subgradient $p_0$ at some point $x_1\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F)$, and then $F^*(p_0)=\langle p_0,x_1\rangle -F(x_1)<+\infty $. Thus $F^*$ is closed and proper. The definition of $F^*$ gives $F(x)\geq \langle p,x\rangle -F^*(p)$ for all $p$, that is, $F^{**}\leq F$. We next show that $F^{**}=F$ when $F$ is closed. An affine function $\langle p,\cdot \rangle -c$ lies below $F$ if and only if $c\geq F^*(p)$. Hence $F^{**}$ is the supremum of all affine minorants of $F$, and it suffices to find, for every $x$ and every real $r<F(x)$, an affine minorant of $F$ whose value at $x$ exceeds $r$. The point $(x,r)$ does not belong to the closed convex set $\operatorname {epi}F$, so by lemma 18.1.2 (1), applied in $N_{\mathbb R}\times \mathbb R$, there are $a\in M_{\mathbb R}$, $c\in \mathbb R$ and $\delta >0$ with \[  \langle a,y\rangle +cs\geq \langle a,x\rangle +cr+\delta \qquad \text{for all }(y,s)\in \operatorname {epi}F.  \] Letting $s\to +\infty $ shows that $c\geq 0$. If $c>0$, taking $s=F(y)$ gives the affine minorant $y\mapsto r+(\delta -\langle a,y-x\rangle )/c$, whose value at $x$ is $r+\delta /c>r$. If $c=0$, then $\langle a,y\rangle \geq \langle a,x\rangle +\delta $ for all $y\in \operatorname {dom}F$. Let $L_0$ be an affine minorant of $F$, which exists by the first paragraph. For $k>0$ the affine functions \[  L_0(y)+k\bigl (\langle a,x\rangle +\delta /2-\langle a,y\rangle \bigr )  \] are again minorants of $F$, since the added term is at most $-k\delta /2$ on $\operatorname {dom}F$, and their values at $x$ tend to $+\infty $ as $k\to \infty $. In both cases the required minorant exists, so $F^{**}=F$. For a general proper convex $F$, a continuous affine function lies below $F$ if and only if it lies below the largest lower semicontinuous minorant $\overline F$. Therefore $F^*=(\overline F)^*$, and since $\overline F$ is closed and proper by proposition 18.1.4 , $F^{**}=(\overline F)^{**}=\overline F$. Let $F$ be closed. By definition, $p\in \partial F(x)$ means that $x\in \operatorname {dom}F$ and $\langle p,y\rangle -F(y)\leq \langle p,x\rangle -F(x)$ for all $y$, that is, the supremum defining $F^*(p)$ is attained at $x$; equivalently, $F(x)+F^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle $. (If $x\notin \operatorname {dom}F$, both conditions fail, since then $F(x)+F^*(p)=+\infty $.) Applying this to the closed proper function $F^*$ and using $F^{**}=F$, we find that $x\in \partial F^*(p)$ if and only if $F^*(p)+F(x)=\langle p,x\rangle $. This proves the equivalences. If $p\in \operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F^*)$, then $F^*$ has a subgradient $x$ at $p$ by proposition 18.1.3 , and $p\in \partial F(x)$ by the equivalences; this is the first inclusion. If $p\in \partial F(x)$, then $F^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle -F(x)<+\infty $, which gives the second. The closures coincide because $\operatorname {ri}(\operatorname {dom}F^*)$ is dense in $\operatorname {dom}F^*$ by lemma 18.1.2 (4). Finally, $\chi _ P^*=h_ P$ by the definitions, and $\chi _ P$ is a closed proper convex function, so $h_ P^*=\chi _ P^{**}=\chi _ P$. $\square$ Proposition 18.2.3 . The pointwise supremum of a family of convex functions is convex. The pointwise limit of a decreasing net of convex functions is convex; it may take the value $-\infty $. Let $(F_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a nonempty family of proper convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and put \[  H(x)=\inf \sum _{j=1}^ q\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j),  \] where the infimum is taken over the values $\sum _ j\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j)$ of all admissible combinations for $x$, that is, over all $q\geq 1$, $i_ j\in I$, $x_ j\in \operatorname {dom}F_{i_ j}$ and $\lambda _ j>0$ with $\sum _ j\lambda _ j=1$ and $\sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j=x$; we set $H(x)=+\infty $ if no such combination exists. Then $H$, the convex envelope of the family, is the largest convex function below $\inf _ iF_ i$, and $H^*=\sup _ iF_ i^*$. If $H$ has an affine minorant, then its lower semicontinuous regularization $\overline H$ is the largest lower semicontinuous convex function below $\inf _ iF_ i$, and $\overline H=(\sup _ iF_ i^*)^*$. For proper convex functions $F,G$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$, the infimal convolution \[  (F\mathbin \square G)(x)=\inf _{y+z=x}(F(y)+G(z))  \] is convex, and $(F\mathbin \square G)^*=F^*+G^*$. Let $F,G$ be finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and $p\in M_{\mathbb R}$. Then \[  (F+G)^*(p)=\min _{q+r=p}(F^*(q)+G^*(r))  \] whenever the right-hand side is finite, the minimum being attained; and $(F+G)^*(p)=+\infty $ if $F^*(q)+G^*(r)=+\infty $ for every decomposition $p=q+r$. Proof. (1) The epigraph of a supremum is the intersection of the epigraphs. Let $(F_ i)$ be a decreasing net of convex functions with limit $F=\inf _ iF_ i$, let $x,y\in N_{\mathbb R}$ and $0<\lambda <1$, and let $a>F(x)$ and $b>F(y)$ be real numbers. Choose indices $i_1,i_2$ with $F_{i_1}(x)<a$ and $F_{i_2}(y)<b$, and an index $i$ following both. Then $F_ i(x)<a$ and $F_ i(y)<b$, and convexity of $\operatorname {epi}F_ i$ gives \[  F((1-\lambda )x+\lambda y)\leq F_ i((1-\lambda )x+\lambda y)\leq (1-\lambda )a+\lambda b.  \] Since $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary, this shows that $\operatorname {epi}F$ is convex; this also covers the case where $F(x)$ or $F(y)$ equals $-\infty $. (2) If $H(x)<a$ and $H(x')<a'$, we can choose admissible combinations for $x$ and $x'$ with values below $a$ and $a'$; mixing them with weights $1-\lambda $ and $\lambda $ gives an admissible combination for $(1-\lambda )x+\lambda x'$ with value below $(1-\lambda )a+\lambda a'$. Hence $H$ is convex. Combinations with $q=1$ show $H\leq F_ i$ for each $i$. If $G$ is convex and $G\leq F_ i$ for all $i$, then for every admissible combination the points $(x_ j,F_{i_ j}(x_ j))$ lie in $\operatorname {epi}G$, and so does their convex combination with the weights $\lambda _ j$, since a convex set contains the convex combinations of its points; that is, \[  G\Bigl (\sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j\Bigr )\leq \sum _ j\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j).  \] Hence $G\leq H$. For the conjugate, the supremum defining $H^*(p)$ is the supremum over all admissible combinations of \[  \Bigl \langle p,\sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j\Bigr \rangle -\sum _ j\lambda _ jF_{i_ j}(x_ j)=\sum _ j\lambda _ j\bigl (\langle p,x_ j\rangle -F_{i_ j}(x_ j)\bigr )\leq \sup _ iF_ i^*(p),  \] and combinations with $q=1$ give equality. Since affine functions are convex, an affine function lies below $H$ if and only if it lies below $\inf _ iF_ i$. Suppose that $H$ has an affine minorant. Then $H$ is proper, so $\overline H$ is a closed proper convex function by proposition 18.1.4 , and $\overline H=H^{**}=(\sup _ iF_ i^*)^*$ by theorem 18.2.2 . A lower semicontinuous convex function below $\inf _ iF_ i$ lies below $H$, and therefore below $\overline H$. (3) Convexity of $F\mathbin \square G$ follows as in (2), by mixing decompositions $x=y+z$ and $x'=y'+z'$ whose values $F(y)+G(z)$ are close to the infima. The two suprema over $y$ and $z$ in \[  (F\mathbin \square G)^*(p)=\sup _{y,z}\bigl (\langle p,y\rangle -F(y)+\langle p,z\rangle -G(z)\bigr )=F^*(p)+G^*(p)  \] are independent, which gives the conjugate formula. (4) If $n=0$, then $F$ and $G$ are constants and both sides equal $-F(0)-G(0)$; so let $n\geq 1$. Let $J(p)=\inf _{q+r=p}(F^*(q)+G^*(r))$. Each conjugate is bounded below by minus its value at the origin: $F^*\geq -F(0)$ and $G^*\geq -G(0)$. Moreover, for every $R>0$, choosing $x$ with $|x|=R$ and $\langle q,x\rangle =R|q|$ gives \[  F^*(q)\geq R|q|-\max _{|x|\leq R}F(x),  \] and the analogous bound holds for $G^*$. Consequently, if $p$ stays bounded and $F^*(q)+G^*(r)$ stays bounded above, then $q$ and $r=p-q$ stay bounded: for instance $F^*(q)\leq F^*(q)+G^*(r)+G(0)$, and the last bound with $R=1$ controls $|q|$. Lower semicontinuity of $F^*$ and $G^*$ therefore implies that the infimum defining $J(p)$ is attained whenever it is finite: a minimizing sequence of decompositions has a convergent subsequence. The same argument, applied to $p_ k\to p$ and decompositions attaining $J(p_ k)$, shows that $J$ is lower semicontinuous. By (3), $J=F^*\mathbin \square G^*$ is convex; it is bounded below by $-F(0)-G(0)$, and it is proper, since $J(q_0+r_0)\leq F^*(q_0)+G^*(r_0)<+\infty $ for subgradients $q_0\in \partial F(0)$ and $r_0\in \partial G(0)$. Finite convex functions are continuous, so $F$ and $G$ are closed and $F^{**}=F$, $G^{**}=G$. By (3), $J^*=F^{**}+G^{**}=F+G$, and theorem 18.2.2 gives $J=J^{**}=(F+G)^*$. $\square$

text: Proposition 18.2.3 . The pointwise supremum of a family of convex functions is convex. The pointwise limit of a decreasing net of convex functions is convex; it may take the value $-\infty $. title: 18.3 Slope bodies and bounded growth
text: 18.3 Slope bodies and bounded growth We now study the finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ whose growth at infinity is controlled by the support function $h_ P$ of a convex body $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$. By duality, such control is a condition on the set where the conjugate is finite, that is, on the slopes of the function. Definition 18.3.1 . Let $F,G$ be finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$. As for functions on a compact manifold (section 13.5 ), we write $F\preceq G$ if $F\leq G+C$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ for some constant $C$, and $F\sim G$ if $F\preceq G$ and $G\preceq F$. The closed convex set \[  K_ F=\overline{\operatorname {dom}F^*}\subset M_{\mathbb R}  \] is nonempty, and by theorem 18.2.2 it is the closure of the set $\partial F(N_{\mathbb R})$ of all supporting slopes of $F$; when it is compact we call it the slope body of $F$. For a convex body $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$, let $\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ be the set of finite convex functions $F$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with $F\preceq h_ P$, and let the bounded class $\mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$ be the set of those with $F\sim h_ P$. If $P$ has nonempty interior, the full-mass class $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the set of $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ with $K_ F=P$; if $P$ has empty interior, we set $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)=\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$. Finally, the finite-energy class $\mathcal E^1(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the set of $F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ with $\int _ PF^*\, \mathrm dp<+\infty $. Since $F^*\geq -F(0)$ by the definition of $F^*$, this integral is well defined in $(-\infty ,+\infty ]$. The notation is chosen by analogy with the classes $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )\subset \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )\subset \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ of definition 15.8.3 , definition 17.2.1 , with the support function $h_ P$ in the role of the model potential $\phi $. Proposition 18.3.2 . Let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body and $F$ a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. The following conditions are equivalent: \[  F\preceq h_ P,\qquad \operatorname {dom}F^*\subset P, \qquad \partial F(N_{\mathbb R})\subset P.  \] If they hold, then $\max _ x(F(x)-h_ P(x))=F(0)$, and $F$ is Lipschitz on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with constant $\max _{p\in P}|p|$. Moreover, $F\sim h_ P$ if and only if $F^*$ is bounded on $P$ and equal to $+\infty $ outside $P$, and \[  \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)\subset \mathcal E^1(N_{\mathbb R},P)\subset \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)\subset \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P).  \] If $F,G$ are finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and $K_ F$ is compact, then \[  K_{F+G}=K_ F+K_ G.  \] In particular, if $P'\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is another convex body, $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$, then $F+G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$. Proof. If $F\leq h_ P+C$, conjugation reverses the inequality and gives $F^*\geq h_ P^*-C=\chi _ P-C$ by theorem 18.2.2 , so $\operatorname {dom}F^*\subset P$. Every subgradient of $F$ lies in $\operatorname {dom}F^*$ by the same theorem, so the second condition implies the third. If all slopes of $F$ lie in $P$ and $p\in \partial F(x)$, the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at $0$, gives \[  F(x)-F(0)\leq \langle p,x\rangle \leq h_ P(x).  \] Thus $F\leq h_ P+F(0)$, which proves the first condition and, since $h_ P(0)=0$, the identity $\max _ x(F(x)-h_ P(x))=F(0)$. If $p_ x\in \partial F(x)$ and $p_ y\in \partial F(y)$, the subgradient inequalities give $\langle p_ y,y-x\rangle \geq F(y)-F(x)\geq \langle p_ x,y-x\rangle $, so $|F(y)-F(x)|\leq \max _{p\in P}|p|\, |y-x|$. Conjugation reverses inequalities, and $F^{**}=F$ because the finite convex function $F$ is continuous. Hence $h_ P-C\leq F\leq h_ P+C$ holds if and only if $\chi _ P-C\leq F^*\leq \chi _ P+C$, that is, if and only if $F^*=+\infty $ outside $P$ and $|F^*|\leq C$ on $P$. In that case $K_ F=P$, so $F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ (by the convention if $P$ has empty interior), and $\int _ PF^*\, \mathrm dp\leq C\operatorname {vol}(P)<\infty $; thus $\mathcal E^\infty \subset \mathcal E^1$. The inclusions $\mathcal E^1\subset \mathcal E\subset \mathcal P$ hold by definition. If $P$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $P$ lies in a proper affine subspace, because its relative interior is nonempty and open in its affine span (lemma 18.1.2 (4)); hence $\operatorname {vol}(P)=0$, every integral over $P$ vanishes, and $\mathcal E^1=\mathcal E=\mathcal P$. Now let $F,G$ be finite convex functions with $K_ F$ compact. By proposition 18.2.3 (4), $(F+G)^*(p)$ is finite exactly when $p=q+r$ with $q\in \operatorname {dom}F^*$ and $r\in \operatorname {dom}G^*$, so \[  \operatorname {dom}(F+G)^*=\operatorname {dom}F^*+\operatorname {dom}G^*.  \] It remains to pass to closures. Since addition $M_{\mathbb R}\times M_{\mathbb R}\to M_{\mathbb R}$ is continuous, $K_ F+K_ G$ lies in the closure of $\operatorname {dom}F^*+\operatorname {dom}G^*$. Conversely, if $q_ k+r_ k\to s$ with $q_ k\in \operatorname {dom}F^*$ and $r_ k\in \operatorname {dom}G^*$, then a subsequence of $(q_ k)$ converges to some $q\in K_ F$, because $K_ F$ is compact, and along it $r_ k\to s-q\in K_ G$; hence $s\in K_ F+K_ G$. This proves $K_{F+G}=K_ F+K_ G$. Finally, if $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$, then $F\preceq h_ P$ and $G\preceq h_{P'}$ by the first part, and $h_ P+h_{P'}=h_{P+P'}$; hence $F+G\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$ and $K_{F+G}=P+P'$, so that $F+G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$. $\square$ For smooth approximation we use mollification, which preserves convexity and, on convex functions, is monotone in the radius. Lemma 18.3.3 . Let $A$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\rho _\varepsilon (y)=\varepsilon ^{-n}\rho (y/\varepsilon )$ be the mollifiers of section 1.4 , in the coordinates of a basis of $N$. Then the functions $A*\rho _\varepsilon $, $\varepsilon >0$, are smooth and convex, $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ is a nondecreasing function of $\varepsilon >0$ with $A*\rho _\varepsilon \geq A$ for every $x$, and $A*\rho _\varepsilon \to A$ locally uniformly as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Proof. If $n=0$, then $A*\rho _\varepsilon =A$ and there is nothing to prove; let $n\geq 1$. Recall that $\rho $ is smooth, nonnegative, even, supported in the unit ball, and has integral one. Since $A$ is continuous, being locally Lipschitz by proposition 18.1.3 , the functions $A*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth by section 1.4 , and they converge to $A$ locally uniformly by lemma 1.4.1 (1). They are convex, because $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)=\int A(x-y)\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy$ and the convexity inequalities of the functions $x\mapsto A(x-y)$ can be integrated against $\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy\geq 0$. For fixed $x$, consider the function \[  g(\varepsilon )=\int A(x-\varepsilon y)\rho (y)\, \mathrm dy\qquad (\varepsilon \in \mathbb R),  \] which is finite because $A$ is continuous and $\rho $ has compact support. The substitution $y\mapsto \varepsilon y$ shows that $g(\varepsilon )=A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ for $\varepsilon >0$, and $g(0)=A(x)$. For each $y$, the function $\varepsilon \mapsto A(x-\varepsilon y)$ is convex, so $g$ is convex; and $g$ is even, because $\rho $ is even. A convex even function on $\mathbb R$ is nondecreasing on $[0,+\infty )$: if $0\leq a<b$, then $a=\lambda b+(1-\lambda )(-b)$ with $\lambda =(a+b)/(2b)\in (0,1]$, so that $g(a)\leq \lambda g(b)+(1-\lambda )g(-b)=g(b)$. Hence $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ is nondecreasing in $\varepsilon >0$ and bounded below by $g(0)=A(x)$. $\square$ Proposition 18.3.4 . Let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body. Every $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the pointwise limit of a decreasing sequence of smooth functions $F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$, and the convergence is locally uniform. If functions $F_ j\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to (-\infty ,+\infty ]$ decrease pointwise to a function $F$, then the conjugates $F_ j^*$ increase pointwise to $F^*$. A sequence of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ converges pointwise to a finite function if and only if it converges locally uniformly. Proof. Let $A_ j=\max \{ F,h_ P-j\} $. These are convex functions, decreasing in $j$, with $A_ j\sim h_ P$, and $A_ j=F$ on every compact set on which $h_ P-F\leq j$; hence $A_ j\to F$ locally uniformly. With the mollifiers $\rho _\varepsilon $ of lemma 18.3.3 , choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ and set $F_ j=A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}$. By that lemma, these functions are smooth and convex, and the monotonicity in $\varepsilon $ together with $A_{j+1}\leq A_ j$ gives $F_{j+1}=A_{j+1}*\rho _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}=F_ j$, and $F_ j\geq A_ j\geq F$. By proposition 18.3.2 , $F$ and $h_ P$ are Lipschitz with constant $\max _{p\in P}|p|$, hence so is $A_ j$, and therefore $|F_ j-A_ j|\leq C\varepsilon _ j$ with $C=\max _{p\in P}|p|\int |y|\rho (y)\, \mathrm dy$. Consequently $F_ j\sim A_ j\sim h_ P$, so $F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$, and $F_ j\to F$ locally uniformly. If $F_ j\downarrow F$ pointwise, then \[  \sup _ jF_ j^*(p)=\sup _ j\sup _ x\bigl (\langle p,x\rangle -F_ j(x)\bigr )=\sup _ x\sup _ j\bigl (\langle p,x\rangle -F_ j(x)\bigr )=F^*(p),  \] and the conjugates $F_ j^*$ increase, because conjugation reverses inequalities. Finally, if a sequence of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ converges pointwise to a finite function, it converges locally uniformly by proposition 18.1.4 , applied with $\Omega $ and the dense subset both equal to $N_{\mathbb R}$, and conversely local uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence. $\square$ Example 18.3.5 . The hypotheses $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$ in the last assertion of proposition 18.3.2 cannot be replaced by $F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and $G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P')$: when $P$ has empty interior, membership in $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ does not force a function to use every slope in $P$. Let $N_{\mathbb R}=M_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^2$ with the standard pairing, $P=[0,1]\times \{ 0\} $ and $P'=\{ 0\} \times [0,1]$. Both bodies have empty interior, and the zero function belongs to $\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)=\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and to $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P')$, since $0\leq h_ P$ and $0\leq h_{P'}$. The sum of the zero function with itself is zero, whose slope body is $\{ 0\} $, whereas $P+P'=[0,1]^2$ has nonempty interior. Hence the zero function does not belong to $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$. Finally, we compare logarithms of sums of exponentials with linear functions. Lemma 18.3.6 . Let $m\geq 1$ and $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m,\alpha \in M_{\mathbb R}$. The function \[  x\longmapsto \log \sum _{i=1}^ m\mathrm e^{\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle } -\langle \alpha ,x\rangle  \] is bounded below on $N_{\mathbb R}$ if and only if $\alpha $ belongs to the convex hull of $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m$. Suppose that all $\beta _ i$ and $\alpha $ lie in $M$, identify $M$ with $\mathbb Z^ n$ by a basis and $N_{\mathbb R}$ with $\mathbb R^ n$ by the dual basis, and write $z^\alpha =z_1^{\alpha _1}\cdots z_ n^{\alpha _ n}$. Then this condition is also equivalent to the boundedness on $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ of \[  \frac{|z^\alpha |^2}{\sum _ i|z^{\beta _ i}|^2}.  \] Proof. If $\alpha =\sum _ i\lambda _ i\beta _ i$ is a convex combination, then $\langle \alpha ,x\rangle \leq \max _ i\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle \leq \log \sum _ i\mathrm e^{\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle }$, so the function is nonnegative. Conversely, suppose that $\alpha $ is not in the convex hull. The hull is compact, being the image of the standard simplex under the linear map $(\lambda _ i)\mapsto \sum _ i\lambda _ i\beta _ i$, and convex, so lemma 18.1.2 (1), applied in $M_{\mathbb R}$, gives $v\in N_{\mathbb R}$ with $\langle \alpha ,v\rangle >\max _ i\langle \beta _ i,v\rangle $. Since the logarithmic sum differs from $\max _ i\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle $ by a number in $[0,\log m]$, the value of the function at $x=tv$ is at most $t(\max _ i\langle \beta _ i,v\rangle -\langle \alpha ,v\rangle )+\log m$, which tends to $-\infty $ as $t\to +\infty $. For the last assertion, put $x_ j=\log |z_ j|^2$. Then $|z^\gamma |^2=\mathrm e^{\langle \gamma ,x\rangle }$ for every $\gamma \in \mathbb Z^ n$, including exponents with negative entries, so the displayed quotient equals the exponential of minus the function above; and $z\mapsto x$ maps $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ onto $\mathbb R^ n$. $\square$

title: Definition 18.3.1
text: Definition 18.3.1 . Let $F,G$ be finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$. As for functions on a compact manifold (section 13.5 ), we write $F\preceq G$ if $F\leq G+C$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ for some constant $C$, and $F\sim G$ if $F\preceq G$ and $G\preceq F$. The closed convex set \[  K_ F=\overline{\operatorname {dom}F^*}\subset M_{\mathbb R}  \] is nonempty, and by theorem 18.2.2 it is the closure of the set $\partial F(N_{\mathbb R})$ of all supporting slopes of $F$; when it is compact we call it the slope body of $F$. title: Lemma 18.3.3
text: Lemma 18.3.3 . Let $A$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\rho _\varepsilon (y)=\varepsilon ^{-n}\rho (y/\varepsilon )$ be the mollifiers of section 1.4 , in the coordinates of a basis of $N$. title: Proposition 18.3.4
text: Proposition 18.3.4 . Let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body. Every $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the pointwise limit of a decreasing sequence of smooth functions $F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$, and the convergence is locally uniform. If functions $F_ j\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to (-\infty ,+\infty ]$ decrease pointwise to a function $F$, then the conjugates $F_ j^*$ increase pointwise to $F^*$. title: 18.4 The real Monge–Ampère measure
text:
18.4 The real Monge–Ampère measure Let $F$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Following Alexandrov, we measure a set $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$ by the volume of the set $\partial F(E)$ of supporting slopes of $F$ at points of $E$. For a smooth $F$ with positive definite Hessian, $\partial F(E)=
abla F(E)$, and the change of variables formula gives $\operatorname {vol}(
