title: Proposition A.1.2
text: Proposition A.1.2 . Every ideal of $\mathcal O_ n$ is finitely generated, and every submodule of $\mathcal O_ n^ r$, $r\geq 1$, is finitely generated. Consequently, every increasing sequence of ideals of $\mathcal O_ n$, or of submodules of a finitely generated $\mathcal O_ n$-module, is eventually constant. Proof. We first recall three algebraic facts about a commutative ring $\Lambda $ all of whose ideals are finitely generated. Every submodule $N$ of $\Lambda ^ r$ is finitely generated, by induction on $r$: the projection of $N$ to the last coordinate is an ideal; choose elements of $N$ whose last coordinates generate it, and add generators of $N\cap (\Lambda ^{r-1}\times \{ 0\} )$, which exist by the induction hypothesis. A finitely generated module is a quotient of some $\Lambda ^ r$, and the inverse image of a submodule is a submodule of $\Lambda ^ r$; hence submodules of finitely generated modules are finitely generated. Finally, the union of an increasing sequence of submodules is a submodule; its finitely many generators already lie in one member of the sequence, which is therefore stationary from then on. It remains to prove that the ideals of $\mathcal O_ n$ are finitely generated, which we do by induction on $n$. The ring $\mathcal O_0=\mathbb C$ is a field. Let $n\geq 1$ and let $I\subset \mathcal O_ n$ be an ideal. If $I=0$ or $I$ contains a unit, it is generated by one element. Otherwise choose a nonzero germ in $I$, and coordinates in which it is distinguished in $w$. By the preparation theorem it is a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial $P$ of some degree $m\geq 1$, and $P\in I$. Divide every $f\in I$ by $P$ using proposition A.1.1 ; the remainder $R_ f=f-Pq$ again belongs to $I$. The remainders of degree less than $m$ that lie in $I$ form an $\mathcal O_{n-1}$-submodule of $\mathcal O_{n-1}[w]$, which we identify, through their coefficients, with a submodule of $\mathcal O_{n-1}^ m$. By the induction hypothesis and the first paragraph, it is generated by finitely many remainders $R_1,\ldots ,R_ k$. Then $P,R_1,\ldots ,R_ k$ generate $I$. $\square$

title: Lemma A.1.3
text: Lemma A.1.3 . Let $n\geq 1$, let $P(z',w)=w^\mu +a_1(z')w^{\mu -1}+\cdots +a_\mu (z')$ be a monic polynomial in $w$ whose coefficients are holomorphic near a point $x'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and let $w_0$ be a root of multiplicity $\mu '\geq 1$ of $P(x',\cdot )$. Then, near $x=(x',w_0)$, \[  P=P_ xQ_ x,  \] where $P_ x$ is a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$ with respect to the coordinates $(z'-x',w-w_0)$, and $Q_ x$ is a monic polynomial of degree $\mu -\mu '$ in $w$ with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$ and $Q_ x(x)\neq 0$. Proof. In the coordinates $(z'-x',w-w_0)$ centered at $x$, the function $w\mapsto P(x',w)$ has a zero of order $\mu '$ at $w_0$. By the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 7.4.2 ), $P$ is, near $x$, a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function $U$ times a Weierstrass polynomial $P_ x$ of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$. Since $P_ x$ is monic in $w$, Euclidean division of the polynomial $P$ by $P_ x$, with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$, gives $P=P_ xQ+R$, where $Q$ is a monic polynomial of degree $\mu -\mu '$ in $w$ and $R$ is a polynomial in $w$, equivalently in $w-w_0$, of degree less than $\mu '$. The identities $P=P_ xQ+R$ and $P=P_ xU+0$ are two divisions of the germ of $P$ at $x$ by $P_ x$; by the uniqueness in proposition A.1.1 , applied in the coordinates centered at $x$, we get $Q=U$ near $x$ and $R=0$. Hence $Q_ x=Q$ has the required properties, with $Q_ x(x)=U(x)\neq 0$. $\square$

title: Lemma A.1.4
text: Lemma A.1.4 . Let $\mathcal A$ be a sheaf of rings. Kernels, images and cokernels of morphisms between coherent $\mathcal A$-modules are coherent. If two of the three sheaves in an exact sequence $0\to \mathcal F\to \mathcal S\to \mathcal G\to 0$ of $\mathcal A$-modules are coherent, so is the third. Finite direct sums of coherent sheaves are coherent. If $\mathcal A$ is coherent as a module over itself, every locally finitely generated $\mathcal A$-submodule of $\mathcal A^ r$ is coherent. Proof. A locally finitely generated submodule of a coherent sheaf is coherent, because its sections have the same relations when they are regarded as sections of the larger sheaf. The image of a morphism from a coherent sheaf is locally generated by the images of local generators of the source, so the image of a morphism between coherent sheaves is coherent. For the kernel of a morphism $\phi \colon \mathcal F\to \mathcal G$ between coherent sheaves, choose local generators $F_1,\ldots ,F_ p$ of $\mathcal F$ and local generators $R_ j=(R_{j1},\ldots ,R_{jp})$ of the relations of $\phi (F_1),\ldots ,\phi (F_ p)$. If $\sum _ ia_ iF_ i$ lies in the kernel, then $(a_ i)$ is a relation of the $\phi (F_ i)$, hence a combination of the $R_ j$; so the sections $\sum _ iR_{ji}F_ i$ generate the kernel, which is therefore coherent. Let $\mathcal F\subset \mathcal S$ be coherent sheaves and consider $\mathcal G=\mathcal S/\mathcal F$; this covers cokernels, because images are coherent. Local generators of $\mathcal S$ map to local generators of $\mathcal G$. Given sections $G_1,\ldots ,G_ p$ of $\mathcal G$, lift them locally to sections $S_1,\ldots ,S_ p$ of $\mathcal S$, and choose local generators $F_1,\ldots ,F_ k$ of $\mathcal F$. A tuple $(a_ i)$ is a relation of the $G_ i$ exactly when $\sum _ ia_ iS_ i\in \mathcal F$, that is, when $(a,b)$ is a relation of $(S_1,\ldots ,S_ p,F_1,\ldots ,F_ k)$ in $\mathcal S$ for some $b$. Hence the projections to the first $p$ coordinates of local generators of the latter relations generate the relations of the $G_ i$, and $\mathcal G$ is coherent. Now let $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal G$ be coherent. Local lifts of generators of $\mathcal G$, together with local generators of $\mathcal F$, generate $\mathcal S$. Given sections $S_1,\ldots ,S_ p$ of $\mathcal S$, let $R_1,\ldots ,R_ l$ generate the relations of their images in $\mathcal G$. The combinations $H_ j=\sum _ iR_{ji}S_ i$ lie in $\mathcal F$; let $Q_1,\ldots ,Q_ k$ generate their relations. Every relation $(a_ i)$ of the $S_ i$ is first a relation of their images, so $a=\sum _ jc_ jR_ j$, and then $\sum _ jc_ jH_ j=\sum _ ia_ iS_ i=0$, so $c$ is a combination of $Q_1,\ldots ,Q_ k$. Hence the tuples $\sum _ jQ_{\nu j}R_ j$, $1\leq \nu \leq k$, which are relations of the $S_ i$, generate all of them, and $\mathcal S$ is coherent. The remaining case of the exact sequence, with $\mathcal S$ and $\mathcal G$ coherent, is the kernel case. A finite direct sum is an extension $0\to \mathcal F\to \mathcal F\oplus \mathcal G\to \mathcal G\to 0$. Finally, if $\mathcal A$ is coherent, so is $\mathcal A^ r$, and the last assertion follows from the first sentence of the proof. $\square$

title: Theorem A.1.5 (Oka's coherence theorem)
text: Theorem A.1.5 (Oka's coherence theorem) . The sheaf $\mathcal O_ M$ of holomorphic functions on a complex manifold $M$ is coherent. In particular, the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal O_ U^ q\to \mathcal O_ U^ p$ defined by a $p\times q$ matrix of holomorphic functions on an open set $U\subset M$ is locally finitely generated. Proof. The sheaf $\mathcal O_ M$ is generated by the constant $1$, and the statement is local, so we must show that the relations of finitely many holomorphic functions $F_1,\ldots ,F_ q$ near a point of $\mathbb C^ n$, which we take to be the origin, are locally finitely generated. We argue by induction on $n$: we reduce to relations that are polynomials in one variable of bounded degree, and apply the induction hypothesis to their coefficients. For $n=0$ the assertion is finite-dimensional linear algebra. Let $n\geq 1$. If the germ of some $F_ j$ at $0$ is zero, then $F_ j$ vanishes on a connected neighborhood, and the relations of the $F_ i$ are those of the remaining functions, with an arbitrary $j$th coordinate; so we may assume that no germ $F_ j$ is zero (if all are zero, every tuple is a relation). Choose coordinates $(z',w)$ in which all $F_ j$ are distinguished in $w$. By the preparation theorem, on a small polydisc each $F_ j$ is a holomorphic unit $u_ j$ times a Weierstrass polynomial; since $(g_ j)$ is a relation of the $F_ j$ exactly when $(u_ jg_ j)$ is a relation of the Weierstrass polynomials, we may assume that each $F_ j$ is a Weierstrass polynomial in $w$ whose coefficients are holomorphic on a polydisc $\Delta '\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$. Renumbering, let $F_ q$ have the maximal degree $\mu $. We claim that at every point $x=(x',w_0)$ of the polydisc, the stalk of relations is generated by relations whose coordinates are polynomials in $w$ of degree at most $\mu $ with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$. If $F_ q(x)\neq 0$, then for a relation $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ q)$ we have $g_ q=-\sum _{j<q}g_ jF_ j/F_ q$, so $g=\sum _{j<q}(g_ j/F_ q)(F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q)$ is a combination of the elementary relations $F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q$, which are polynomial of degree at most $\mu $. Suppose that $F_ q(x)=0$, and let $\mu '\geq 1$ be the order of the root $w_0$ of $F_ q(x',\cdot )$. By lemma A.1.3 , near $x$ the monic polynomial $F_ q$ is the product of a Weierstrass polynomial $P_ x$ of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$ and a monic polynomial $Q_ x$ in $w$ of degree $\mu -\mu '$: \[  F_ q=P_ xQ_ x,\qquad Q_ x(x)\neq 0.  \] Let $g$ be a relation at $x$. Dividing each $g_ j$, $j<q$, by $P_ x$ (proposition A.1.1 ) and writing $P_ x=F_ qQ_ x^{-1}$, we obtain $g_ j=F_ qt_ j+r_ j$ with $\deg _ wr_ j<\mu '$. Subtracting $\sum _{j<q}t_ j(F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q)$ from $g$, we obtain a relation whose first $q-1$ coordinates are $r_1,\ldots ,r_{q-1}$; we call its last coordinate $r_ q$. Then \[  P_ xQ_ xr_ q=-\sum _{j<q}F_ jr_ j.  \] The right-hand side is a polynomial in $w$; dividing it by $P_ x$ as a polynomial and comparing with the uniqueness of division at $x$, we find that $Q_ xr_ q$ is a polynomial of degree less than $\mu $. Each $Q_ xr_ j$, $j<q$, is also a polynomial of degree at most $(\mu -\mu ')+(\mu '-1)<\mu $. Thus $(Q_ xr_1,\ldots ,Q_ xr_ q)$ is a polynomial relation of degree less than $\mu $, and $(r_ j)$ is its product with the unit $Q_ x^{-1}$. This proves the claim. A tuple of polynomials $g_ j=\sum _{k=0}^{\mu }c_{jk}(z')w^ k$ is a relation exactly when the $2\mu +1$ coefficients of the polynomial $\sum _ jF_ jg_ j$ vanish. These coefficients are given by a holomorphic matrix acting on the coefficient vectors $(c_{jk})$, with entries formed from the coefficients of the $F_ j$. By the induction hypothesis and lemma A.1.4 , the kernel of this matrix is coherent, so it has finitely many generators on a smaller polydisc $\Delta '_1$, generating its stalk at every point of $\Delta '_1$. The corresponding polynomial tuples are relations of the $F_ j$, and they generate, over the rings of germs on the base, all polynomial relations of degree at most $\mu $ at every point over $\Delta '_1$. By the claim, they generate all relations at every point of the polydisc over $\Delta '_1$. This proves that $\mathcal O_ M$ is coherent. The last assertion follows from lemma A.1.4 , since the kernel of a morphism between the coherent sheaves $\mathcal O_ U^ q$ and $\mathcal O_ U^ p$ is coherent. $\square$

title: Lemma A.1.6
text: Lemma A.1.6 . Let $A$ be a proper analytic subset of a connected complex manifold $M$. Then $A$ is nowhere dense in $M$. Moreover, if $U\subset M$ is a nonempty connected open set and $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ are holomorphic functions on $U$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $, then some $g_ i$ is not identically zero on $U$. In particular, every point of $A$ has a connected open neighborhood $U$ with a holomorphic function $g\not\equiv 0$ on $U$ such that $A\cap U\subset \{ g=0\} $. Proof. The interior of $A$ is open, and we show that it is closed in $M$. Let $a\in M$ be a limit of interior points of $A$, and choose a connected coordinate neighborhood $U$ of $a$ and functions $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $. Each $g_ i$ vanishes on a nonempty open subset of $U$, hence on $U$ by the identity theorem; so $U\subset A$, and $a$ is an interior point. Since $M$ is connected and $A\neq M$, the interior of $A$ is empty. In the second assertion, if all $g_ i$ vanished identically on $U$, the nonempty open set $U$ would lie in $A$, contradicting the first. For the third, take for $U$ a connected coordinate ball on which $A$ is the common zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions, and for $g$ one of them that is not identically zero, which exists by the second assertion. $\square$

title: Lemma A.1.7
text:
Lemma A.1.7 . Let $A$ be a proper analytic subset of a connected complex manifold $M$. Every holomorphic function on $M\setminus A$ which is locally bounded near $A$ extends uniquely to a holomorphic function on $M$, and $M\setminus A$ is connected. Moreover, let $b,c\in \mathcal O_ n$ with $c
eq 0$, and suppose that representatives satisfy $|b|\leq C|c|$ on a neighborhood of $0$ for a constant $C$. Then $b\in c\, \mathcal O_ n$. In particular, the ring $\mathcal O_ n$ is integrally closed. Proof. Let $f$ be holomorphic on $M\setminus A$ and locally bounded near $A$. If $\dim M=0$, then $A=\varnothing $ and there is nothing to prove. Fix $a\in A$. By lemma A.1.6 there is a holomorphic function $g
ot\equiv 0$ on a connected neighborhood of $a$ vanishing on $A$; choose linear coordinates $(z',w)$ centered at $a$ in which $g$ is distinguished in $w$. By the Weierstrass preparation theorem and ( A.1 ), there is a polydisc $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ centered at $a$, with $\Delta =\{ |w|<r\} $, on which $g$ is a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial $W$ and $f$ is bounded off $A$, such that all roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in \Delta '$, have modulus at most some $ho <r$. For fixed $z'\in \Delta '$, the function $f(z',\cdot )$ is holomorphic on $\Delta $ outside the finitely many points of $A$ in the fiber, which are roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, and it is bounded near them; by the removable singularity theorem in one variable it extends holomorphically to $\Delta $. For $ho <s<r$ the function \[  F(z',w)= rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s} rac{f(z',\zeta )}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\qquad z'\in \Delta ',\  |w|<s,  \] is holomorphic, by differentiation under the integral sign, since $f$ is holomorphic near $\Delta '	imes \{ |\zeta |=s\} $, a set disjoint from $A$. By Cauchy's formula for the extended functions $f(z',\cdot )$, it agrees with $f$ outside $A$. Letting $s\uparrow r$, we obtain a holomorphic extension of $f$ to $\Delta '	imes \Delta $. Since $A$ is nowhere dense, two holomorphic extensions on overlapping open sets agree, being continuous functions that coincide on a dense subset; so the local extensions glue to a holomorphic function on $M$, and this extension is unique. If $M\setminus A$ were disconnected, the function equal to $0$ on one nonempty union of its connected components and to $1$ on the others would be bounded and holomorphic on $M\setminus A$. Its holomorphic extension is continuous and takes values in $\{ 0,1\} $ on the dense set $M\setminus A$, hence everywhere; since $M$ is connected, it is constant, a contradiction. Now let $b,c\in \mathcal O_ n$, $c
eq 0$, with $|b|\leq C|c|$ on a connected neighborhood $U$ of the origin on which both are defined. The set $\{ c=0\} $ is a proper analytic subset of $U$, and the holomorphic function $b/c$ on $U\setminus \{ c=0\} $ is bounded by $C$. By the first part it extends to a holomorphic function $h$ on $U$, and $ch=b$ on the dense set $U\setminus \{ c=0\} $, hence on $U$; so $b\in c\, \mathcal O_ n$. Finally, let $b/c\in \operatorname {Frac}(\mathcal O_ n)$, with $c
eq 0$, satisfy a monic equation $(b/c)^ m+a_1(b/c)^{m-1}+\cdots +a_ m=0$ with $a_ j\in \mathcal O_ n$. Multiplying by $c^ m$, we obtain the identity $b^ m+a_1b^{m-1}c+\cdots +a_ mc^ m=0$ between germs, which holds on a connected neighborhood of $0$ on which the $a_ j$ are bounded. At the points of this neighborhood where $c
eq 0$, the number $b/c$ is a root of a monic polynomial with bounded coefficients, so $|b/c|$ is bounded there by ( A.1 ); at the points where $c=0$ the identity gives $b^ m=0$. Hence $|b|\leq C|c|$ on this neighborhood for some constant $C$, and by what we have just proved, $b/c\in \mathcal O_ n$, which proves that $\mathcal O_ n$ is integrally closed. $\square$

title: A.2 Analytic sets and their local branches
search_title: Analytic sets and their local branches
text:
A.2 Analytic sets and their local branches The local study of an analytic set rests on the parametrization of an irreducible germ as a branched covering of a polydisc (theorem A.2.3 ). From it we derive the Nullstellensatz, the dimension theory, Cartan's coherence theorem, the structure of the singular locus and the irreducible components. The section ends with hypersurfaces and the currents supported on analytic sets. Let $M$ be a complex manifold and $x\in M$. Two subsets of $M$ define the same germ at $x$ if they agree on a neighborhood of $x$; an analytic germ at $x$ is the germ $(A,x)$ of an analytic subset $A$ of a neighborhood of $x$. Holomorphic coordinates identify the ring $\mathcal O_{M,x}$ of germs of holomorphic functions at $x$ with $\mathcal O_ n$. For an analytic germ $(A,x)$ let $I_{A,x}\subset \mathcal O_{M,x}$ be the ideal of germs vanishing on $(A,x)$. Conversely, for an ideal $I\subset \mathcal O_{M,x}$ let $V(I)$ be the germ at $x$ of the common zero set of finitely many generators of $I$, which exist by proposition A.1.2 ; it does not depend on the choice of generators. Both operations reverse inclusions, and $V(I_{A,x})=(A,x)$, because local defining functions of $A$ belong to $I_{A,x}$. Finite unions and finite intersections of analytic subsets are analytic: they are defined locally by the products of the defining functions and by the union of the families of defining functions, respectively. A nonempty analytic germ is irreducible if it is not the union of two analytic subgerms different from it. A point $a$ of an analytic subset $A\subset M$ is regular if $A$ is a complex submanifold of $M$ near $a$; the dimension of this submanifold is the dimension of $A$ at the regular point $a$. The regular points form an open subset $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of $A$, the regular locus , and $A_{\mathrm{sing}}=A\setminus A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is the singular locus . Proposition A.2.1 . Every analytic germ is the union of finitely many irreducible analytic germs, and this decomposition is unique up to order if none of its members is contained in another. A nonempty analytic germ is irreducible if and only if its ideal is prime. The members of the decomposition are called the irreducible branches , or local branches , of the germ. Proof. A decreasing sequence of analytic germs is eventually constant, because the corresponding ideals increase and are eventually constant by proposition A.1.2 , and $V(I_{A,x})=(A,x)$. Split a reducible germ into two analytic subgerms different from it, split each reducible piece again, and so on. If this process did not terminate, the resulting tree, in which every vertex has at most two children, would be infinite, and choosing at each level a child with infinitely many descendants would produce a strictly decreasing infinite sequence of analytic germs, which is impossible. Hence a finite decomposition into irreducible germs exists; removing members contained in others, we may assume that no member is contained in another. An irreducible germ contained in a finite union of analytic germs is contained in one of them, since it is the union of its intersections with them. Now let $ igcup _ iA_ i= igcup _ jB_ j$ be two such decompositions. Each $A_ i$ is contained in some $B_ j$, which in turn is contained in some $A_ k$; then $A_ i\subset A_ k$ forces $k=i$ and $A_ i=B_ j$. By symmetry the two decompositions agree. Let $(A,x)$ be irreducible. Its ideal is proper, since $x\in A$. If $fg$ vanishes on $(A,x)$, then $(A,x)$ is the union of its intersections with $\{ f=0\} $ and $\{ g=0\} $, so one of them is all of $(A,x)$, and $f$ or $g$ belongs to $I_{A,x}$; thus $I_{A,x}$ is prime. Conversely, suppose that $(A,x)$ is the union of two analytic subgerms $(B,x)$ and $(C,x)$ different from it. Since $V(I_{B,x})=(B,x)
eq (A,x)$, there is a germ $f\in I_{B,x}\setminus I_{A,x}$, and similarly $g\in I_{C,x}\setminus I_{A,x}$. Then $fg$ vanishes on $(A,x)$ while neither factor does, so $I_{A,x}$ is not prime. $\square$ Multiple roots of polynomials are detected by the discriminant, which we define by a polynomial formula in the coefficients. For a monic polynomial $P(T)=T^ q+a_1T^{q-1}+\cdots +a_ q$, $q\geq 1$, with coefficients in a commutative ring, let $C_ P$ be its companion matrix , the $q	imes q$ matrix with entries $1$ just below the diagonal, last column $(-a_ q,\ldots ,-a_1)^{\mathsf T}$ and zeros elsewhere. Put $S_ k=\operatorname {tr}(C_ P^ k)$ for $k\geq 0$, and define the discriminant $\operatorname {Disc}(P)=\det (S_{j+l})_{0\leq j,l\leq q-1}$, a polynomial with integer coefficients in $a_1,\ldots ,a_ q$. If the $a_ j$ are complex numbers and $	au _1,\ldots ,	au _ q$ are the roots of $P$, counted with multiplicity, then A.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:discriminant-roots} \operatorname {Disc}(P)=\prod _{i<k}(	au _ i-	au _ k)^2; \end{equation} in particular $\operatorname {Disc}(P)
eq 0$ if and only if the roots of $P$ are distinct. Indeed, the characteristic polynomial of $C_ P$ is $P$, as one sees by expanding $\det (TI-C_ P)$ along its last column, so after triangularizing $C_ P$ over $\mathbb C$ we find $S_ k=\sum _ i	au _ i^ k$. Hence $(S_{j+l})=\Lambda ^{\mathsf T}\Lambda $ for the Vandermonde matrix $\Lambda =(	au _ i^ j)_{1\leq i\leq q,\, 0\leq j<q}$, whose determinant is $\prod _{i<k}(	au _ k-	au _ i)$. Lemma A.2.2 . Let $d\geq 0$, let $K=\operatorname {Frac}(\mathcal O_ d)$, and let $B$ be an integral domain containing $\mathcal O_ d$ that is finitely generated as an $\mathcal O_ d$-module and is generated as an $\mathcal O_ d$-algebra by elements $b_1,\ldots ,b_ r$. Then the field of fractions $L$ of $B$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over $K$; let $q$ be its dimension. Moreover: Let $x\in L$ be integral over $\mathcal O_ d$. Then the minimal polynomial of $x$ over $K$, that is, the monic polynomial of least degree in $K[T]$ vanishing at $x$, has degree at most $q$ and coefficients in $\mathcal O_ d$. For all $c\in \mathbb C^ r$ outside finitely many proper linear subspaces, the powers $1,u,\ldots ,u^{q-1}$ of $u=\sum _ jc_ jb_ j$ form a basis of $L$ over $K$. In particular, the minimal polynomial $W(T)=T^ q+w_1T^{q-1}+\cdots +w_ q$ of $u$ has degree $q$, and $w_1,\ldots ,w_ q\in \mathcal O_ d$. For such $u$, the discriminant $\delta =\operatorname {Disc}(W)\in \mathcal O_ d$ is not zero, and every $g\in L$ that is integral over $\mathcal O_ d$ satisfies \[  \delta g=\sum _{j=0}^{q-1}d_ ju^ j,\qquad d_ j\in \mathcal O_ d.  \] Proof. We represent elements of $L$ by multiplication matrices over $K$ and evaluate these at points of $\mathbb C^ d$; integrality bounds their eigenvalues, and lemma A.1.7 turns bounded elements of $K$ into elements of $\mathcal O_ d$. We first recall the determinant criterion for integrality. Let $R$ be a subring of an integral domain $D$, let $b\in D$, and suppose that multiplication by $b$ maps an $R$-submodule of $D$ generated by elements $v_1,\ldots ,v_ N$, not all zero, into itself: $bv_ i=\sum _ ja_{ij}v_ j$ with $a_{ij}\in R$. Multiplying the matrix $bI-(a_{ij})$ by its adjugate shows that the monic polynomial $\det (bI-(a_{ij}))$ in $b$ annihilates every $v_ i$; since $D$ is a domain, this determinant is zero, and $b$ is integral over $R$. In particular, every element of $B$ is integral over $\mathcal O_ d$; take for the $v_ i$ generators of the $\mathcal O_ d$-module $B$. Conversely, if $x_1,\ldots ,x_ k\in D$ are integral over $R$, then $R[x_1,\ldots ,x_ k]$ is a finitely generated $R$-module, since powers of each $x_ i$ can be reduced with its monic equation; by the criterion, sums and products of integral elements are integral. The ring $KB=\{ b/a:b\in B,\  a\in \mathcal O_ d\setminus \{ 0\} \} $ is a domain, and it is spanned over $K$ by finitely many module generators of $B$, so it is a finite-dimensional vector space over $K$. Multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective linear map of $KB$, hence surjective; so $KB$ is a field, and it equals $L$. Choose a basis $e_1=1,e_2,\ldots ,e_ q$ of $L$ over $K$ consisting of elements of $B$; it can be extracted from $1$ and the module generators of $B$. For $x\in L$ let $[x]\in K^{q	imes q}$ be the matrix of the $K$-linear map $y\mapsto xy$ in this basis. The map $x\mapsto [x]$ is an injective homomorphism of $K$-algebras, because the first column of $[x]$ is the coordinate vector of $xe_1=x$. Let $\operatorname {Tr}(x)=\operatorname {tr}[x]$, which does not depend on the basis, and let $\chi _ x(T)=\det (TI-[x])\in K[T]$, a monic polynomial of degree $q$; by the Cayley–Hamilton theorem $[\chi _ x(x)]=\chi _ x([x])=0$, so $\chi _ x(x)=0$. The minimal polynomial $\mu _ x$ of $x$ exists, because $1,x,\ldots ,x^ q$ are linearly dependent over $K$, and $\deg \mu _ x\leq q$. By Euclidean division in $K[T]$, $\mu _ x$ divides every polynomial in $K[T]$ that vanishes at $x$. Values of elements of $K$. Let $U$ be a connected neighborhood of $0$ in $\mathbb C^ d$. An element of $K$ is defined at $z'\in U$ if it can be written as $a/h$ with $a,h$ holomorphic on $U$ and $h(z')
eq 0$; its value at $z'$ is then $a(z')/h(z')$. This value does not depend on the representation, since two representations $a/h=a'/h'$ satisfy $ah'=a'h$ near $0$, hence on $U$ by the identity theorem. If finitely many elements of $K$ are defined at $z'$, so are their sums and products, and their quotients by those with nonzero value at $z'$, with the corresponding values. Finitely many elements of $K$ can be written with a common denominator $h
eq 0$ and numerators holomorphic on some connected neighborhood $U$ of $0$; they are then all defined at the points of $U\setminus \{ h=0\} $, a dense open subset of $U$. We shall use the following boundedness criterion : if the values of an element $a/h$ of $K$ at the points of $V\setminus \{ h=0\} $ are bounded, for some neighborhood $V\subset U$ of $0$, then $a/h\in \mathcal O_ d$. Indeed, $|a|\leq C|h|$ on $V\setminus \{ h=0\} $, hence on $V$, since both sides are continuous functions on $V$ and $V\setminus \{ h=0\} $ is dense in $V$; so $a/h\in \mathcal O_ d$ by lemma A.1.7 . (For $d=0$, the space $\mathbb C^0$ is a point and $K=\mathcal O_0=\mathbb C$.) Proof of (1). Let $x\in L$ be integral over $\mathcal O_ d$, say $f(x)=0$ with $f(T)=T^ m+f_1T^{m-1}+\cdots +f_ m$ and $f_ j\in \mathcal O_ d$. Then $f([x])=[f(x)]=0$. Since $\chi _ x(x)=0$, we can write $\chi _ x=\mu _ xho $ with $ho \in K[T]$. Write the entries of $[x]$ and the coefficients of $\mu _ x$ and $ho $ with a common denominator $h$, so that they are all defined at the points of $U\setminus \{ h=0\} $ for a connected neighborhood $U$ of $0$; the coefficients of $\chi _ x$, polynomials in the entries of $[x]$, can then be written with the denominator $h^ q$. At the points $z'\in U\setminus \{ h=0\} $ near $0$ the complex matrix $[x](z')$ satisfies $f(z',[x](z'))=0$.
