Multiplying the matrix $(a/h)I-(c_{ij})$ by its adjugate, we see that its determinant, a monic polynomial in $a/h$ with coefficients in $\mathcal O_{X,y}$, annihilates every $g_ i$, hence $\mathcal I_ y$ and in particular $h$; since $h$ is invertible in the total ring of fractions, this polynomial vanishes, and $a/h$ is integral over $\mathcal O_{X,y}$. Hence, by proposition A.3.3 , \[  \mathcal O_ U\subset \mathcal F\subset \widetilde{\mathcal O}_ U.  \] We claim that the support of the coherent sheaf $\mathcal F/\mathcal O_ U$ is the set of nonnormal points of $U$; this proves the first assertion. At a normal point $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,y}=\mathcal O_{X,y}$, so $\mathcal F_ y=\mathcal O_{X,y}$. Let $y$ be a nonnormal point, so that $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,y}
eq \mathcal O_{X,y}$. By the analytic Nullstellensatz (corollary A.2.6 ), applied in a local model, every element of $\mathcal I_ y$ has a power in $h\mathcal O_{X,y}$. Let $g_1,\ldots ,g_ N$ generate $\mathcal I_ y$, and choose $e$ with $g_ i^ e\in h\mathcal O_{X,y}$ for all $i$. Every monomial of degree $\ell =N(e-1)+1$ in the $g_ i$ contains some $g_ i$ at least $e$ times, so $\mathcal I_ y^\ell \subset h\mathcal O_{X,y}$, and therefore $\mathcal I_ y^\ell \widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,y}\subset h\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,y}\subset \mathcal O_{X,y}$. Let $k$ be the least integer with $\mathcal I_ y^ k\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,y}\subset \mathcal O_{X,y}$; then $k\geq 1$, and we may choose $w\in \mathcal I_ y^{k-1}\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,y}$ with $w
otin \mathcal O_{X,y}$. Then $w\mathcal I_ y\subset \mathcal O_{X,y}$, and every product $wg$, $g\in \mathcal I_ y$, vanishes on $\{ h=0\} $: at regular points because $g$ vanishes there and $w$ is holomorphic, and at singular points because $w$ is locally bounded, $g$ tends to zero, and $wg$ is continuous. Thus $w\mathcal I_ y\subset \mathcal I_ y$, so multiplication by $w$ belongs to $\mathcal F_ y$; it is not multiplication by an element of $\mathcal O_{X,y}$, since $w
otin \mathcal O_{X,y}$ and $h$ is a nonzerodivisor. This proves the claim. For the last assertion, let $f$ be a holomorphic function on $X\setminus E$ that is locally bounded near $E$. Since $E$ is nowhere dense, an extension is unique. The set $E\cap X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ meets every connected open subset of the manifold $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ in a nowhere dense analytic subset, so $f$ extends holomorphically to $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ by lemma A.1.7 . The extension is locally bounded near $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$, because on a neighborhood of each point it is bounded by a bound of $f$ on the dense subset $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus E$; hence it is weakly holomorphic, and therefore holomorphic, because $X$ is normal. It agrees with $f$ on $X\setminus E$, since both functions are continuous there and agree on the dense subset $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus E$. $\square$

title: Lemma A.3.5
text:
Lemma A.3.5 . Let $X$ be an analytic subset of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ N$, with coordinates $z$, let $x\in X$, and let $X_1,\ldots ,X_ p$ be sufficiently small representatives of the branches of $(X,x)$. There is an open neighborhood $W\subset \Omega $ of $x$ with the following properties. For each $i$ there are functions $f_{i1},\ldots ,f_{im_ i}$, weakly holomorphic on $X_ i\cap W$, and monic polynomials $P_{ij}(z,T)$ in $T$ with coefficients holomorphic on $W$, such that $P_{ij}(z,f_{ij})=0$ on $(X_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap W$. The closure $Y_ i$ in $W	imes \mathbb C^{m_ i}$ of the graph of $(f_{i1},\ldots ,f_{im_ i})$ over $(X_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap W$ is a normal analytic subset of $W	imes \mathbb C^{m_ i}$, on which $P_{ij}(z,w_ j)=0$ for all $j$, and the projection $
u _ i\colon Y_ i	o X_ i\cap W$, $(z,w)\mapsto z$, is finite and bimeromorphic, is an isomorphism over $(X_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap W$, and has a single point over $x$. The map from the disjoint union of $Y_1,\ldots ,Y_ p$ to $X\cap W$ given by the $
u _ i$ is finite and bimeromorphic, is an isomorphism over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap W$, and has $p$ points over $x$. All these properties persist when $W$ is replaced by a smaller open neighborhood of $x$ and each $Y_ i$ by its part over it. Proof. Step 1: the construction for an irreducible germ. Suppose first that $p=1$, so that $(X,x)$ is irreducible. Choose generators $f_1,\ldots ,f_ m$ of the $\mathcal O_{X,x}$-module $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,x}$ and a denominator $h$ as in proposition A.3.3 , so that $hf_ j=g_ j$ with $g_ j$ holomorphic. Choose a neighborhood $W\subset \Omega $ of $x$ on which $h$ and the $g_ j$ are holomorphic, the $f_ j$ are weakly holomorphic, and each $f_ j$ satisfies a monic equation $P_ j(z,f_ j)=0$ whose coefficients are holomorphic on $W$. On $(X\cap W)\setminus \{ h=0\} $ the functions $g_ j/h$ are holomorphic and agree with $f_ j$ on $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Let $Y$ be the closure in $W	imes \mathbb C^ m$ of the graph of $(g_1/h,\ldots ,g_ m/h)$ over $(X\cap W)\setminus \{ h=0\} $. This graph is the part outside $\{ h=0\} $ of the analytic set \[  Z=\{ (z,w)\in W	imes \mathbb C^ m:\  z\in X,\  h(z)w_ j=g_ j(z)\  	ext{for all }j\} .  \] By lemma A.2.5 , applied in $W	imes \mathbb C^ m$ to $Z$ and the analytic set $\{ h=0\} $, the closure $Y$ of $Z\setminus \{ h=0\} $ is analytic; near each point it is the union of the branches of $Z$ on which $h$ does not vanish identically. The monic equations $P_ j(z,g_ j/h)=0$ hold on $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus \{ h=0\} $, which is dense in $X\setminus \{ h=0\} $, and their left-hand sides are continuous there; so they hold on the graph, hence on its closure $Y$: $P_ j(z,w_ j)=0$. By ( A.1 ) they bound $w$ over compact subsets of $X\cap W$ and leave finitely many possible values of $w$ over each point. Hence the projection $
u \colon Y	o X\cap W$ is proper with finite fibers. Over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the set $Y$ is the graph of $f=(f_1,\ldots ,f_ m)$: a point of $Y$ over $z_0\in X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a limit of graph points over points $z_ k	o z_0$, and since the $f_ j$ are continuous at $z_0$, it equals $(z_0,f(z_0))$. Conversely, $(z_0,f(z_0))$ lies in $Y$, because $z_0$ is a limit of points of $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus \{ h=0\} $: the germ of $h$ at $z_0$ is not identically zero on the manifold germ $(X,z_0)$, so $\{ h=0\} $ is nowhere dense in $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ near $z_0$, by lemma A.1.6 . Hence $
u $ is an isomorphism over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap W$, with inverse $z\mapsto (z,f(z))$. This graph is dense in $Y$, because $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus \{ h=0\} $ is dense in $X\setminus \{ h=0\} $ and $(g_1/h,\ldots ,g_ m/h)$ is continuous there; so $Y$ is the closure of the graph of $f$ over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap W$, the set $
u ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is nowhere dense, and $
u $ is bimeromorphic. Every point of $Y$ over $x$ is a limit of points $(z_ k,f(z_ k))$ with $z_ k\in X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $z_ k	o x$; by the last assertion of proposition A.3.3 , the fiber over $x$ is the single point $y=(x,\lim _{z	o x}f(z))$. Step 2: normality of $Y$ at $y$. Let $a$ be a weakly holomorphic function on $Y$ near $y$. Since $
u ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{reg}})$ is a manifold, it is contained in $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and $b=a\circ (
u |_{
u ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{reg}})})^{-1}$ is holomorphic on $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ near $x$. It is bounded near $x$: by properness and since the fiber over $x$ is $\{ y\} $, the inverse image of a small neighborhood of $x$ lies in a neighborhood of $y$ on which $a$ is bounded. Thus $b\in \widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,x}$, and $b=\sum _ ja_ jf_ j$ with $a_ j\in \mathcal O_{X,x}$. Lift the $a_ j$ to holomorphic functions $\widetilde a_ j$ near $x$ in $\Omega $. The function $\sum _ j\widetilde a_ j(z)w_ j$ is holomorphic near $y$, and it equals $a$ on $
u ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{reg}})$ near $y$, which is dense in $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$; since both functions are continuous on $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$, they agree on $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ near $y$. Hence $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{Y,y}=\mathcal O_{Y,y}$, and $y$ is a normal point. By lemma A.3.4 , all points of $Y$ near $y$ are normal, and by properness the inverse image of a small neighborhood $U$ of $x$ lies in this set of normal points. Replacing $W$ by $U$ and $Y$ by $
u ^{-1}(U)$, we obtain the assertions of the lemma for $p=1$. They persist when $W$ is replaced by a smaller open neighborhood of $x$, because the closure of the graph over the smaller set is the part of $Y$ over it, and normality, finiteness, bimeromorphy and being an isomorphism over the regular locus are preserved under restriction over open subsets of $X$. Step 3: several branches. In general, apply Steps 1 and 2 to each irreducible germ $(X_ i,x)$, with $X_ i$ regarded as an analytic subset of a ball around $x$ in $\Omega $, and let $W$ be the intersection of the resulting neighborhoods; by the persistence just noted, the assertions about the individual $Y_ i$ hold over $W$. The disjoint union of the $Y_ i$ is normal, and its map to $X\cap W$ is finite, with $p$ points over $x$. It is an isomorphism over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap W$, because, by corollary A.2.10 (1), $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap W$ is the disjoint union of the open sets $X_ i\cap X_{\mathrm{reg}}=(X_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus  igcup _{j
eq i}X_ j$, over which $
u _ i$ is an isomorphism. It is bimeromorphic, with the nowhere dense analytic subset $X_{\mathrm{sing}}\cap W$ of $X\cap W$. Indeed, by corollary A.2.10 (1), $X_{\mathrm{sing}}\cap X_ i=(X_ i)_{\mathrm{sing}}\cup (X_ i\cap  igcup _{j
eq i}X_ j)$, which is a nowhere dense analytic subset of $X_ i\cap W$ by corollary A.2.4 ; so its inverse image under the bimeromorphic map $
u _ i$ is nowhere dense in $Y_ i$, by lemma A.3.1 . These properties again persist for smaller neighborhoods of $x$. $\square$

title: Theorem A.3.6 (Normalization)
text:
Theorem A.3.6 (Normalization) . Every complex space $X$ has a normalization : a normal complex space $\widetilde X$ with a finite bimeromorphic holomorphic map $
u \colon \widetilde X	o X$ that is an isomorphism over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$. It is unique up to a unique isomorphism over $X$. The fiber $
u ^{-1}(x)$ has one point for each irreducible branch of $(X,x)$, and \[  
u _*\mathcal O_{\widetilde X}=\widetilde{\mathcal O}_ X.  \] Proof. Step 1: local normalizations. Let $x\in X$, and choose a local model of a neighborhood of $x$. By lemma A.3.5 , applied to sufficiently small representatives of the branches of $(X,x)$, there is a neighborhood $W$ of $x$ such that $X\cap W$ has a normalization, namely the disjoint union of the normal spaces $Y_ i$ with the maps $
u _ i$, whose fiber over $x$ has one point for each branch of $(X,x)$. Step 2: uniqueness. Let $
u _1\colon Y_1	o X$ and $
u _2\colon Y_2	o X$ be finite bimeromorphic maps from normal complex spaces that are isomorphisms over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ there is a unique isomorphism $\phi _0=
u _2^{-1}\circ 
u _1$ commuting with the maps to $X$; we show that it extends holomorphically. Let $p\in Y_1$ and $x=
u _1(p)$. Choose disjoint open neighborhoods $W_ l$ of the finitely many points $q_ l$ of $
u _2^{-1}(x)$, each relatively compact in the domain $W'_ l$ of a local model of $Y_2$, so that the coordinate functions of these models are bounded on $W_ l$. By properness of $
u _2$, there is a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ with $
u _2^{-1}(U)\subset  igcup _ lW_ l$. The analytic subset $E=
u _1^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ of $Y_1$ is nowhere dense, because $
u _1$ is bimeromorphic and $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is nowhere dense in $X$ (lemma A.3.1 ). Since $Y_1$ is normal, the germ $(Y_1,p)$ is irreducible, and a sufficiently small parametrization neighborhood $V$ of $p$ with $
u _1(V)\subset U$ has the property that $V\setminus E$ is connected: its connected covering locus remains connected after removing the analytic subset $E$, which is nowhere dense in it, by lemma A.1.7 , and the result is dense in $V\setminus E$. Hence $\phi _0(V\setminus E)$ lies in a single $W_ l$. The coordinate functions of $W'_ l$ composed with $\phi _0$ are bounded holomorphic functions on $V\setminus E$, and they extend holomorphically to $V$ by lemma A.3.4 . The extended map takes values in $\overline{W_ l}\subset W'_ l$, and it satisfies the equations of the local model, which hold on the dense set $V\setminus E$; so it is a holomorphic map $V	o Y_2$ extending $\phi _0$. These local extensions are unique, by density of $V\setminus E$, and therefore glue to a holomorphic map $\phi \colon Y_1	o Y_2$ with $
u _2\circ \phi =
u _1$. Extending $\phi _0^{-1}$ in the same way, we obtain the inverse map, since the compositions are the identity on dense open sets. Any isomorphism over $X$ agrees with $\phi _0$ over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$, so it equals $\phi $. This proves uniqueness. Step 3: gluing. By the uniqueness just proved, applied over the overlaps of their domains, the local normalizations of Step 1 are canonically isomorphic there, and these isomorphisms are compatible on triple overlaps, because an isomorphism over $X$ between two normalizations is unique; so they glue to a space $\widetilde X$ with a map $
u \colon \widetilde X	o X$. The space $\widetilde X$ is Hausdorff, since points with different images are separated by inverse images of disjoint neighborhoods and points with the same image lie in one local normalization. Since $X$ has a countable basis, countably many of the open sets over which local normalizations were constructed cover $X$, and each of these local normalizations, a finite disjoint union of analytic subsets of open subsets of the spaces $\mathbb C^{N+m_ i}$, has a countable basis; hence so has $\widetilde X$. Being locally compact and Hausdorff with a countable basis, $\widetilde X$ is paracompact. Being finite, normal and bimeromorphic are local properties over $X$, so $
u $ is a normalization. The description of the fibers follows from Step 1. Step 4: the direct image. Let $U\subset X$ be open. If $g$ is holomorphic on $
u ^{-1}(U)$, then $g\circ 
u ^{-1}$ is holomorphic on $U\cap X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and locally bounded near $U\cap X_{\mathrm{sing}}$, because $
u $ is proper; so it is weakly holomorphic. Conversely, if $f$ is weakly holomorphic on $U$, then $f\circ 
u $ is holomorphic on $
u ^{-1}(U\cap X_{\mathrm{reg}})$ and locally bounded near the nowhere dense analytic subset $
u ^{-1}(U\cap X_{\mathrm{sing}})$; by lemma A.3.4 , applied on the normal space $
u ^{-1}(U)$, it extends holomorphically to $
u ^{-1}(U)$. These two maps are inverse to each other, which proves $
u _*\mathcal O_{\widetilde X}=\widetilde{\mathcal O}_ X$. $\square$

title: Corollary A.3.7
text:
Corollary A.3.7 . Let $X$ be an analytic subset of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ N$, with coordinates $z$, let $
u \colon \widetilde X	o X$ be its normalization, and let $x\in X$. Let $W$ and $
u _ i\colon Y_ i	o X_ i\cap W$, $1\leq i\leq p$, be as in lemma A.3.5 , for sufficiently small representatives $X_1,\ldots ,X_ p$ of the branches of $(X,x)$. Then each $
u _ i$ is a normalization of $X_ i\cap W$ whose fiber over $x$ is a single point, and there is an isomorphism of $
u ^{-1}(W)$ onto the disjoint union of $Y_1,\ldots ,Y_ p$ under which $
u $ corresponds to the maps $
u _ i$. In particular, every holomorphic function on $\widetilde X$ near a point of $
u ^{-1}(x)$ corresponds, near that point, to the restriction to some $Y_ i$ of a holomorphic function of $(z,w)$. Proof. By lemma A.3.5 , each $Y_ i$ is normal, and $
u _ i$ is finite, bimeromorphic and an isomorphism over $(X_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap W$, with a single point over $x$; so $
u _ i$ is a normalization of $X_ i\cap W$. Likewise, the disjoint union of the $Y_ i$ is a normalization of $X\cap W$. So is $
u ^{-1}(W)	o X\cap W$, because being finite, normal, bimeromorphic and an isomorphism over the regular locus are local properties over $X$. By the uniqueness in theorem A.3.6 , there is an isomorphism over $X\cap W$ between them. The last assertion holds because the holomorphic functions on the analytic set $Y_ i$ are, locally, restrictions of holomorphic functions of the ambient coordinates $(z,w)$. $\square$

title: Definition A.3.8
text: Definition A.3.8 . A complex space is unibranch if all its germs $(X,x)$ are irreducible. Equivalently, each local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a domain whose integral closure in its field of fractions is a local ring. Indeed, in a local model $\mathcal O_{X,x}=\mathcal O_ N/I_{X,x}$, so by proposition A.2.1 the germ $(X,x)$ is irreducible if and only if $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a domain. In this case, by proposition A.3.3 , the integral closure is $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,x}$, and taking the limit at $x$, which exists by the same proposition, is a ring homomorphism $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,x}\to \mathbb C$. An element with nonzero limit is a unit, because its reciprocal is holomorphic and bounded on $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ near $x$, hence weakly holomorphic; an element with limit zero is not a unit. So the non-units form the ideal of elements with limit zero, and $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_{X,x}$ is a local ring. Thus this definition agrees with the definition of unibranch local rings in commutative algebra.

title: Corollary A.3.9
text: Corollary A.3.9 . The normalization of a unibranch complex space is a homeomorphism. Every point $x$ of a complex space with $(X,x)$ irreducible, in particular every point of a unibranch space, has arbitrarily small neighborhoods $U$ such that $U\setminus A$ is connected for every nowhere dense analytic subset $A$ of $U$. Proof. On a unibranch space the normalization has one-point fibers, so it is a continuous bijection; being proper, it is closed, hence a homeomorphism. For the second assertion, let $U$ be the intersection of $X$ with a parametrization polydisc of $(X,x)$. Its covering locus is a connected manifold, dense in $U$; it remains connected after deleting $A$, by lemma A.1.7 , because $A$ is nowhere dense, and the result is dense in $U\setminus A$. Hence $U\setminus A$ is connected. $\square$

title: Example A.3.10
text: Example A.3.10 . The curve $\{ zw=0\} \subset \mathbb C^2$ has two branches at the origin, the coordinate axes, whose germs are irreducible, being germs of submanifolds (lemma A.2.9 ). The disjoint union of the two axes, mapped to the curve by the inclusions, is a manifold, hence normal, and the map is finite, bimeromorphic and an isomorphism over the regular locus $\{ zw=0\} \setminus \{ 0\} $; by the uniqueness in theorem A.3.6 it is the normalization. Its fiber over the origin has two points, and the curve is not unibranch. The cusp $C=\{ w^2=z^3\} $ is normalized by $\gamma (t)=(t^2,t^3)$. Indeed, $\gamma $ is a holomorphic bijection of $\mathbb C$ onto $C$: for $(z,w)\in C$ with $z\neq 0$, the equations $t^2=z$, $t^3=w$ force $t=w/z$, and $t=w/z$ satisfies them, since $(w/z)^2=z$ and $(w/z)^3=(w/z)z=w$; and $\gamma (t)=0$ only for $t=0$. The points of $C\setminus \{ 0\} $ are regular: at such a point $z\neq 0$, so the map $(z,w)\mapsto (w^2-z^3,w)$ has the nonzero Jacobian determinant $-3z^2$ there, and by proposition 7.1.2 (1) the functions $w^2-z^3$ and $w$ form holomorphic coordinates near such a point, in which $C$ is a coordinate line; so $C$ is a submanifold there. On $C\setminus \{ 0\} $ the inverse of $\gamma $ is the holomorphic function $t=w/z$. This function satisfies $t^2=z$, so it tends to $0$ at the origin; hence $\gamma $ is a homeomorphism. The function $t$ is not the restriction of a holomorphic function $F(z,w)$ near the origin, because $F(t^2,t^3)$ has no term of degree one in $t$. Hence the origin is a singular point of $C$. Otherwise $t$, which is bounded near the origin, would extend holomorphically across it on the manifold $C$, by lemma A.1.7 , and would therefore be the restriction of a holomorphic function of $(z,w)$: in coordinates in which a submanifold is a coordinate plane, a holomorphic function on it extends independently of the other coordinates. So $t$ is weakly holomorphic on $C$, and integral, since $t^2=z$, but it is not holomorphic at the origin, so $C$ is not normal there. Thus $\gamma $ is a finite bimeromorphic map from a manifold that is an isomorphism over $C_{\mathrm{reg}}=C\setminus \{ 0\} $, and by the uniqueness in theorem A.3.6 it is the normalization. The cusp is therefore unibranch but not normal, and it distinguishes unibranch spaces from normal spaces.

title: A.4 Analytic curves and finite maps
text:
A.4 Analytic curves and finite maps Holomorphic curves through a point of a complex space reduce questions about functions near singular points to one complex variable: for instance, a holomorphic function whose modulus has a local maximum at a point is constant along every curve through that point. We parametrize irreducible germs of dimension one, construct curves through a given point that avoid a given analytic subgerm, and study finite maps onto balls, which control the dimension of zero sets of holomorphic functions. Proposition A.4.1 . Let $(C,x)$ be an irreducible analytic germ of dimension one. There are a disc $\Delta \subset \mathbb C$ centered at $0$, a representative $C$ of the germ and a holomorphic bijection $\gamma \colon \Delta 	o C$ with $\gamma (0)=x$ that restricts to a biholomorphism of $\Delta \setminus \{ 0\} $ onto $C\setminus \{ x\} $. In the coordinates of a local parametrization of $(C,x)$, the projection of $\gamma $ is $t\mapsto t^ q$ for some integer $q\geq 1$. A normal complex space of dimension one is a complex manifold. Proof. Embed $C$ in a local model and apply theorem A.2.3 . The base is a disc $\Delta '=\{ |z|<r\} $, and since the zeros of $\delta $ are isolated, we may take the parametrization polydisc so small that $\delta $ has no zero in $\Delta '\setminus \{ 0\} $. Let $C$ be the representative in this polydisc and $C^*=C\setminus \{ x\} =\pi ^{-1}(\Delta '\setminus \{ 0\} )$. Then $C^*$ is a covering of the punctured disc $\Delta '\setminus \{ 0\} $ with $q$ sheets, and it is connected: if $\delta (0)=0$, it is the covering locus, and if $\delta (0)
eq 0$, then $q=1$, because the fiber over $0$ is $\{ x\} $. We shall show that lifting a circle around the puncture permutes the $q$ points of a fiber cyclically, and then obtain $\gamma $ by lifting the exponential map to $C^*$. We first recall two facts about coverings. A path in $\Delta '\setminus \{ 0\} $ lifts uniquely to $C^*$ once its initial point is prescribed: subdivide the path into finitely many pieces lying in discs over which the covering is trivial, and lift piece by piece. If two paths with the same endpoints are homotopic with fixed endpoints, their lifts with the same initial point have the same endpoint. Indeed, let $h\colon [0,1]^2	o \Delta '\setminus \{ 0\} $ be the homotopy, with $h(0,s)$ and $h(1,s)$ independent of $s$, and let $e(s)$ be the endpoint of the lift of $h(\cdot ,s)$ with the prescribed initial point. By uniform continuity there is an integer $m\geq 1$ such that $h$ maps each square $Q_{jl}=[(j-1)/m,j/m]	imes [(l-1)/m,l/m]$ into a disc $D_{jl}$ over which the covering is trivial. A lift of a path in $D_{jl}$ stays in the sheet over $D_{jl}$ that contains its initial point, because these sheets are open and disjoint. Fix $l$ and $s,s'\in [(l-1)/m,l/m]$. We show by induction on $j$ that the lifts of $h(\cdot ,s)$ and $h(\cdot ,s')$ over $[(j-1)/m,j/m]$ lie in one sheet over $D_{jl}$. For $j=1$ they start at the same point. If this holds for some $j<m$, the points of the two lifts at the parameter $j/m$ are joined by the lift, inside this sheet, of the path $h(j/m,\cdot )$ between $s$ and $s'$; this lift is a connected set lying over $D_{jl}\cap D_{j+1,l}$, so it lies in one sheet over $D_{j+1,l}$, which then contains both lifts over $[j/m,(j+1)/m]$. For $j=m$ we obtain two points in one sheet over $D_{ml}$ lying over the same point $h(1,s)=h(1,s')$, so $e(s)=e(s')$. Hence $e$ is constant on each interval $[(l-1)/m,l/m]$, and therefore on $[0,1]$. Next, every loop based at a point $b\in \Delta '\setminus \{ 0\} $ is homotopic with fixed endpoints to the $k$th power of the circle around $0$ through $b$, for some integer $k$. Indeed, lifting the argument continuously along the loop, we write the loop as $\exp $ of a path in the half-plane $H=\{ \zeta :\operatorname{Re}\zeta <\log r\} $ from some $\zeta _0$ to $\zeta _0+2\pi \mathrm ik$; the straight-line homotopy to the segment from $\zeta _0$ to $\zeta _0+2\pi \mathrm ik$ stays in the convex set $H$. Let $\sigma $ be the permutation of the fiber over $b$ obtained by lifting the circle. Lifting any loop at $b$ therefore induces a power of $\sigma $. Since $C^*$ is connected, any two points of the fiber over $b$ are joined by a path in $C^*$, whose image is a loop at $b$; hence the powers of $\sigma $ act transitively on the $q$ points of the fiber, and $\sigma $ is a cycle of length $q$. The map $\exp \colon H	o \Delta '\setminus \{ 0\} $ lifts to a map $\Phi \colon H	o C^*$ with $\pi \circ \Phi =\exp $: lift along paths from a base point $\zeta _0$, starting at a chosen point of the fiber; since $H$ is convex, the endpoint does not depend on the path. The map $\Phi $ is holomorphic, because locally it is $\exp $ followed by the inverse of $\pi $ on a sheet. The vertical segment from $\zeta $ to $\zeta +2\pi \mathrm i$ is mapped by $\exp $ onto the circle through $\mathrm e^\zeta $; so $\Phi (\zeta +2\pi \mathrm i)=\sigma _\zeta (\Phi (\zeta ))$, where $\sigma _\zeta $ is the permutation of the fiber over $\mathrm e^\zeta $ obtained by lifting this circle. By the preceding paragraph, applied with $b=\mathrm e^\zeta $, it is a cycle of length $q$; hence $\Phi (\zeta +2\pi \mathrm iq)=\Phi (\zeta )$. Therefore \[  \gamma (t)=\Phi (q\log t),\qquad 0<|t|<r^{1/q},  \] does not depend on the branch of the logarithm; it is holomorphic, and $\pi (\gamma (t))=t^ q$. The coordinates of $\gamma $ are bounded, because $C$ lies in the bounded parametrization polydisc, so by the removable singularity theorem they extend holomorphically to $t=0$. Since $\pi $ is proper, $\gamma (t)$ stays in a compact subset of $C$ as $t	o 0$; hence $\gamma (0)\in C$, and $\gamma (0)=x$ because $\gamma (0)$ lies over $0$. Let $\Delta =\{ |t|<r^{1/q}\} $. The map $\gamma \colon \Delta 	o C$ is surjective: the points of $C$ over $z_0=\mathrm e^{\zeta }
eq 0$ are $\Phi (\zeta +2\pi \mathrm ik)=\gamma (\mathrm e^{(\zeta +2\pi \mathrm ik)/q})$, $0\leq k<q$, because $\sigma _\zeta $ is a $q$-cycle. It is injective: if $\gamma (t_1)=\gamma (t_2)$ with $t_1,t_2
eq 0$, then $t_1^ q=t_2^ q$, so $t_2=t_1\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm ik/q}$; writing $q\log t_1=\zeta $, we get $\gamma (t_2)=\Phi (\zeta +2\pi \mathrm ik)=\sigma _\zeta ^ k(\gamma (t_1))$, which forces $k\equiv 0$ modulo $q$. On $\Delta \setminus \{ 0\} $ the map $\gamma $ is a local biholomorphism into the manifold $C^*$, since $\pi \circ \gamma (t)=t^ q$ has nonzero derivative; being bijective, it is a biholomorphism of $\Delta \setminus \{ 0\} $ onto $C\setminus \{ x\} $. Finally, let $X$ be a normal complex space of dimension one, and let $x\in X$; if $x$ is an isolated point, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise the germ $(X,x)$ has dimension one, and it is irreducible by the definition of normal points; let $\gamma \colon \Delta 	o C$ be the map just constructed for a representative $C$ of this germ. Its inverse is holomorphic on the manifold $C\setminus \{ x\} $, which is contained in the regular locus, and it is bounded; so it is weakly holomorphic and, by normality, extends to a holomorphic function $	au $ near $x$. Then $	au \circ \gamma =\mathrm{id}$ on $\Delta \setminus \{ 0\} $, hence on $\Delta $, and $\gamma \circ 	au =\mathrm{id}$ on $C\setminus \{ x\} $, hence on $C$, because these maps are continuous and the punctured sets are dense. Thus $\gamma $ is an isomorphism of $\Delta $ onto a neighborhood of $x$, and $x$ is a regular point. $\square$ Proposition A.4.2 . Let $(X,x)$ be an irreducible analytic germ of positive dimension, and let $(B,x)$ be an analytic subgerm different from $(X,x)$. There is a nonconstant holomorphic map $\gamma $ from a disc $\Delta $ centered at $0$ into $X$ with $\gamma (0)=x$ and $\gamma (t)\in X_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus B$ for $t
eq 0$. Proof. The germ of $B\cup X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is again different from $(X,x)$, since $(X,x)$ is irreducible and $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ has smaller dimension by corollary A.2.10 (1). Since every analytic germ $(A,x)$ satisfies $V(I_{A,x})=(A,x)$, the ideals of these two germs differ, and we can choose a holomorphic germ $f$ that vanishes on $B\cup X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ but not identically on $X$. Take a local parametrization of $(X,x)$ over a polydisc $\Delta '\subset \mathbb C^ d$, $d\geq 1$, with covering locus $X_\delta $, and for $z'\in \Delta '\setminus \{ \delta =0\} $ let $N(z')$ be the product of the values of $f$ at the $q$ points of $X$ over $z'$. This function is holomorphic and bounded, so it extends holomorphically to $\Delta '$ by lemma A.1.7 . It is not identically zero. Otherwise, choose a small ball in $\Delta '\setminus \{ \delta =0\} $ over which the $q$ points are given by holomorphic sections $s_1,\ldots ,s_ q$; the product of the functions $f\circ s_ i$ would vanish identically there, so one of these functions would vanish on an open set. Then $f$ would vanish on a nonempty open subset of the connected manifold $X_\delta $, hence on $X_\delta $ by the identity theorem, and on $X$ by density, which is not the case. The function $g=N\delta $ is holomorphic and not identically zero on $\Delta '$. Choose a vector $v\in \mathbb C^ d$ at which the first nonzero homogeneous term of $g$ does not vanish, and $ho >0$ such that $g(tv)
eq 0$ for $0<|t|<ho $ and the ball $U=\{ |z'|<ho |v|\} $ lies in $\Delta '$. Then $Y=X\cap \pi ^{-1}(\{ tv:|t|<ho \} )$ is an analytic subset of $X\cap \pi ^{-1}(U)$. Over the punctured disc, $Y$ consists of points of $X_\delta $ at which $f
eq 0$, and it is a covering of the punctured disc; over $0$ it consists of the single point $x$. Thus $Y\setminus \{ x\} $ is a complex manifold of dimension one, and by properness of $\pi $ its points accumulate at $x$, so $x$ is not an isolated point of $Y$. Let $(C,x)$ be a branch of $(Y,x)$ of positive dimension. Its regular points near $x$ lie in the one-dimensional manifold $Y\setminus \{ x\} $, so $(C,x)$ has dimension one. Let $\gamma \colon \Delta 	o C$ be the parametrization of proposition A.4.1 . For $t
eq 0$, the point $\gamma (t)$ lies in $C\setminus \{ x\} \subset Y\setminus \{ x\} $, hence in $X_\delta \subset X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and outside $\{ f=0\} \supset B$. $\square$ Corollary A.4.3 . Let $f$ be a holomorphic function near a point $x$ of a complex space $X$ such that $|f|$ has a local maximum at $x$. Then $f$ is constant on each irreducible branch of $(X,x)$. Moreover, every compact analytic subset of an open subset of $\mathbb C^ N$ is finite. Proof. Let $X_1$ be a branch of $(X,x)$. If $X_1$ has dimension zero, it is the point $x$. Otherwise, suppose that $f-f(x)$ does not vanish identically on $X_1$, and apply proposition A.4.2 to $X_1$ and its subgerm $X_1\cap \{ f=f(x)\} $. The holomorphic function $f\circ \gamma $ on the disc has a local maximum of its modulus at $0$, so it is constant by the maximum principle in one variable, and $f(\gamma (t))=f(x)$ for all $t$, contradicting the choice of $\gamma $. For the second assertion, let $K$ be a compact analytic subset of an open set in $\mathbb C^ N$, and let $K_+$ be the set of its non-isolated points. The isolated points form an open subset of $K$, so $K_+$ is compact. Suppose that $K_+
eq \varnothing $, and let $y$ be a point of $K_+$ where $|z|^2$ attains its maximum on $K_+$. Since $y$ is not isolated, some branch of $(K,y)$ has positive dimension, and its small representatives, being pure-dimensional, consist of non-isolated points of $K$. So proposition A.4.2 , applied to this branch and the subgerm $\{ y\} $, gives a nonconstant holomorphic curve $\gamma $ in $K_+$ with $\gamma (0)=y$. The function $|\gamma (t)|^2$ is subharmonic, with Laplacian $4\sum _ j|\gamma _ j'(t)|^2$, and it has a local maximum at $0$; by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) it is constant near $0$, so its Laplacian vanishes, all $\gamma _ j'$ vanish, and $\gamma $ is constant, a contradiction. Hence $K_+=\varnothing $, and $K$ is compact and discrete, hence finite. $\square$ The surjectivity of finite maps onto balls (lemma A.4.5 ) rests on the following elementary fact. Lemma A.4.4 . Let $B\subset \mathbb R^ N$, $N\geq 2$, be an open ball, and let $E\subset B$ be relatively closed and $\mathcal H^{N-1}$-null. Then $B\setminus E$ is path connected. Proof. Fix $a,b\in B\setminus E$. If $c\in B$ and the segment $[a,c]$ meets $E$ at a point $e=a+s(c-a)$, then $0<s\leq 1$, since $a
otin E$, so $c=a+t(e-a)$ with $t=1/s\geq 1$. We show that the set of such $c$ has $N$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Exhaust $E$ by the compact sets $E_ k=E\cap \overline{B_ k}$, where $B_ k$ are concentric balls increasing to $B$. Since $a
otin E_ k$, the parameter $t$ is bounded on $\{ (e,t):e\in E_ k,\  a+t(e-a)\in B\} $, say by $T_ k$, and the map $(e,t)\mapsto a+t(e-a)$ is Lipschitz on $E_ k	imes [1,T_ k]$. Cover $E_ k$ by balls of radii $r_ l$ with $\sum _ lr_ l^{N-1}$ arbitrarily small. The image of each product of such a ball with $[1,T_ k]$ is covered by at most $C_ k/r_ l$ balls of radius $C_ kr_ l$, whose total volume is at most $C'_ kr_ l^{N-1}$. Hence the image of $E_ k	imes [1,T_ k]$ is Lebesgue null, and so is the union over $k$. The same holds with $b$ in place of $a$. Choose $c\in B$ outside both null sets. Then the path $[a,c]\cup [c,b]$ lies in the convex set $B$ and does not meet $E$. $\square$ Lemma A.4.5 . Let $(X,x)$ be a pure $d$-dimensional analytic germ, and let $F\colon (X,x)	o (\mathbb C^ d,0)$ be a holomorphic map germ such that $x$ is an isolated point of $F^{-1}(0)$. Then $F$ has arbitrarily small representatives that map properly, with finite fibers, onto balls centered at $0$: for every neighborhood $V$ of $x$ there are an open neighborhood $X'\subset V$ of $x$ in a representative of $(X,x)$ and a ball $B_\varepsilon \subset \mathbb C^ d$ centered at $0$ such that $F\colon X'	o B_\varepsilon $ is proper, has finite fibers and is surjective. In particular, the image under $F$ of every neighborhood of $x$ in $X$ contains a neighborhood of $0$. Proof. For $d=0$ the germ is the point $x$, and there is nothing to prove. Let $d\geq 1$, embed a representative $X$ in a local model $X\subset \Omega \subset \mathbb C^ N$ such that $X$ is pure $d$-dimensional and $F$ is the restriction of a holomorphic map on $\Omega $, also denoted $F$, and choose a closed ball $\overline{B(x,ho )}\subset \Omega $, with $X\cap B(x,ho )\subset V$, whose intersection with $X\cap F^{-1}(0)$ is $\{ x\} $. The compact set $X\cap \partial B(x,ho )$ does not meet $F^{-1}(0)$, so $|F|$ has a positive minimum $\eta $ on it (if it is empty, put $\eta =\infty $). Let $B_\varepsilon $ be the ball of radius $\varepsilon <\eta $ about $0\in \mathbb C^ d$, and let $X'=X\cap B(x,ho )\cap F^{-1}(B_\varepsilon )$. Then $F\colon X'	o B_\varepsilon $ is proper: the inverse image of a compact set $K\subset B_\varepsilon $ is $X\cap \overline{B(x,ho )}\cap F^{-1}(K)$, which is compact and contains no point of the boundary sphere. Its fibers are compact analytic subsets of the open ball $B(x,ho )$, hence finite by corollary A.4.3 . It remains to prove surjectivity. On each connected component of the manifold $X'_{\mathrm{reg}}$, which has dimension $d$, the differential of $F$ has rank $d$ at some point. Otherwise its maximal rank $r$ on some component would be smaller; near a point where the rank is $r$, the rank would be constantly $r$, and by lemma A.2.11 , applied in a chart of $X'_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the fibers near this point would be submanifolds of positive dimension $d-r$, contradicting their finiteness. Let $C$ be the union of $X'_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the set of regular points where the rank of $F$ is less than $d$. In the local model, $C$ is the union of $X'_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the common zero set in $X'$ of the minors of size $N$ of the matrix formed by the differentials of local generators of the ideal of $X$ and the rows of $\mathrm dF$; so $C$ is analytic. It contains no branch of $X'$ at any point. Indeed, each branch contains a nonempty open subset of $X'_{\mathrm{reg}}$, consisting of regular points of the branch outside the other branches (corollary A.2.4 ), and on each component of $X'_{\mathrm{reg}}$ the points of rank less than $d$ form a proper analytic subset, which is nowhere dense by lemma A.1.6 . Hence $C$ has dimension at most $d-1$ by proposition A.2.7 . Its image $E=F(C)$ is closed in $B_\varepsilon $ by properness, and it is $\mathcal H^{2d-1}$-null. Indeed, by corollary A.2.10 (2), $C$ is a finite union of complex submanifolds of open subsets of $\Omega $ of dimensions at most $d-1$, on each of which $F$ has rank at most $d-1$, so lemma A.2.12 (1) applies. Over $B_\varepsilon \setminus E$, the map $F$ is a local biholomorphism at every point of its source, by proposition 7.1.2 (1) applied in charts of $X'_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and it is proper; so its image is open and closed in $B_\varepsilon \setminus E$. This image is nonempty: at a regular point of rank $d$, the image of a neighborhood is open, and it is not contained in $E$, which is Lebesgue null because it is $\mathcal H^{2d-1}$-null. Since $B_\varepsilon \setminus E$ is connected by lemma A.4.4 , the image contains $B_\varepsilon \setminus E$, which is dense in $B_\varepsilon $; being closed in $B_\varepsilon $, it equals $B_\varepsilon $. $\square$ Proposition A.4.6 . Let $X$ be a pure $d$-dimensional complex space, and let $f$ be a holomorphic function on $X$ that is not identically zero on any branch of $(X,y)$, for every $y\in X$. Then the zero set of $f$ is either empty or pure of dimension $d-1$. Proof. If $d=0$, then $f$ has no zeros. Let $d\geq 1$ and let $x$ be a zero of $f$. We first show that $\dim (\{ f=0\} ,x)=d-1$. For each branch $X_0$ of $(X,x)$, the germ $\{ f=0\} \cap X_0$ is a subgerm of $X_0$ different from it, so $\dim (\{ f=0\} ,x)\leq d-1$ by proposition A.2.7 . Fix a branch $X_0$, and choose linear forms $\ell _1,\ldots ,\ell _{d-1}$ on the ambient space of a local model, vanishing at $x$, inductively such that $\ell _ j$ does not vanish identically on any positive-dimensional branch of the germ at $x$ of $\{ f=0\} \cap X_0\cap \{ \ell _1=\cdots =\ell _{j-1}=0\} $. At each step this excludes finitely many proper linear subspaces, and, by proposition A.2.7 , it lowers the dimension of this germ by at least one as long as it is positive. Since the initial dimension is at most $d-1$, the point $x$ is isolated in the common zero set of $\Phi =(f,\ell _1,\ldots ,\ell _{d-1})$ on $X_0$. Suppose that $\dim (\{ f=0\} ,x)<d-1$; then $d\geq 2$, and by upper semicontinuity $\dim (\{ f=0\} ,y)\leq d-2$ for all zeros $y$ of $f$ near $x$. By lemma A.4.5 , applied to the germ $(X_0,x)$, which is pure-dimensional, there is a neighborhood $X'_0$ of $x$ in a small representative of $X_0$, on which this bound holds, such that $\Phi $ maps $X'_0$ onto a ball $B\subset \mathbb C^ d$ centered at $0$. Hence $\Phi $ maps $\{ f=0\} \cap X'_0$ onto the set $B\cap \{ w_1=0\} $, which has positive $(2d-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure; here $w_1$ is the first coordinate of $\mathbb C^ d$. On the other hand, by corollary A.2.10 (2), $\{ f=0\} \cap X'_0$ is a finite union of complex submanifolds of dimensions at most $d-2$ of open subsets of the ambient space, on each of which $\Phi $ has rank at most $d-2$; by lemma A.2.12 (1), its image under $\Phi $ is $\mathcal H^{2d-2}$-null, hence Lebesgue null in $\{ w_1=0\} \cong \mathbb R^{2d-2}$. This contradiction shows that $\dim (\{ f=0\} ,x)=d-1$. Now let $V_1$ be a branch of $(\{ f=0\} ,x)$. By corollary A.2.4 , there are regular points $y$ of $V_1$ arbitrarily close to $x$ that do not lie on the other branches. Near such a point, $\{ f=0\} $ coincides with $V_1$, which is a manifold of dimension $\dim V_1$ by purity. The hypotheses hold at $y$, so the first part gives $\dim (\{ f=0\} ,y)=d-1$, and therefore $\dim V_1=d-1$. $\square$

title: Proposition A.4.1
text:
