title: A.6 Proper images and relative principalization
text: A.6 Proper images and relative principalization We now show that the image of a proper holomorphic map is analytic (Remmert's theorem). It is proved together with the Remmert–Stein theorem, which says that an analytic set whose branches all have large dimension remains analytic after adding its limit points on an analytic set of smaller dimension. In this book the mapping theorem is applied mainly to images of exceptional sets of compositions of blowups. We then prove a relative principalization theorem: one sequence of blowups principalizes an ideal on a compact manifold and, at the same time, its restriction to a given submanifold, and the ideal of the submanifold transforms in a controlled way. Theorem A.6.1 (Remmert–Stein) . Let $X$ be a complex space, let $p\geq 0$ be an integer, and let $A\subset X$ be an analytic subset of dimension at most $p$. Let $Z$ be an analytic subset of $X\setminus A$ all of whose local branches have dimension greater than $p$. Then the closure of $Z$ in $X$ is analytic. Theorem A.6.2 (Remmert) . The image of a proper holomorphic map between complex spaces is analytic. Proof. We prove the two theorems together by induction on dimension. Let $R_ m$ denote the assertion of theorem A.6.1 for sets $Z$ of dimension at most $m$, and $P_ m$ the assertion of theorem A.6.2 for maps whose source has dimension at most $m$. Both assertions are local on $X$. A proper map has compact inverse image over a compact neighborhood of a point of the target, and near this compact set its source has finite dimension; so, locally on the target, every proper map falls under some $P_ m$. The assertion $P_0$ holds because a source of dimension zero is discrete, so the image of a proper map from it is closed and locally finite, hence analytic. The assertion $R_0$ holds trivially: a set $Z$ of dimension zero has no branches of dimension greater than $p\geq 0$, so $Z=\varnothing $. We show that $P_{m-1}$ implies $R_ m$, and that $R_ m$ and $P_{m-1}$ imply $P_ m$. Step 1: $P_{m-1}$ implies $R_ m$; reductions. Since the assertion is local, we may assume that $X$ is an analytic subset of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ N$; then $Z$ is an analytic subset of $\Omega \setminus A$, and its closure in $X$ is its closure in $\Omega $. We first reduce to the case where $A$ is a submanifold of dimension $p$, by induction on $p$. Let $A''$ be the union of $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the irreducible components of $A$ of dimension less than $p$; it is analytic of dimension at most $p-1$ (empty if $p=0$), and $A\setminus A''$ is a closed submanifold of $\Omega \setminus A''$ of dimension $p$. Suppose that the closure $Z_1$ of $Z$ in $\Omega \setminus A''$ is analytic. No branch $B$ of a germ of $Z_1$ is contained in $A$: since $Z$ is dense in $Z_1$, the branches not contained in $A$ already have union $Z_1$ near the base point, and the decomposition into branches is irredundant. Hence $B\setminus A$ is dense in $B$, and at its regular points outside the other branches $B$ coincides with $Z$, whose branches have dimension greater than $p$. Hence all branches of $Z_1$ have dimension greater than $p>p-1$, and by the induction hypothesis on $p$ the closure of $Z_1$ in $\Omega $, which is the closure of $Z$, is analytic. Thus we may assume that $A$ is a $p$-dimensional submanifold. Fix a point of $A$ in the closure of $Z$; after a holomorphic change of coordinates it is the origin, and near it $A$ is a linear subspace $L$ of dimension $p$. Finally, the irreducible components of $Z$ are pure-dimensional by corollary A.2.14 (1), and their dimensions exceed $p$, because each component contains regular points of $Z$ near which $Z$ coincides with it. The union of the components of a given dimension $s$ is analytic in $\Omega \setminus A$, by corollary A.2.13 , and only the finitely many values $p<s\leq m$ occur; so we may assume that $Z$ is pure of dimension $s$, with $p<s\leq m$. We shall present $Z$ near the origin as a branched covering over an open subset of $\mathbb C^ s$ and write down equations for its closure. Choice of a projection. We choose linear forms $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ s$ on $\mathbb C^ N$ with the following properties: (i) for each $j<s$, the form $\xi _{j+1}$ does not vanish identically on any irreducible component of $Z\cap \{ \xi _1=\cdots =\xi _ j=0\} $; (ii) the restrictions of $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ p$ to $L$ are linearly independent; (iii) at a point $z_\alpha $ chosen in each connected component $Z^\circ _\alpha $ of the manifold $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the restrictions of $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ s$ to the tangent space of $Z$ are linearly independent. We choose the forms one at a time. Suppose that $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ j$, $j<s$, have been chosen and that $Z_ j=Z\cap \{ \xi _1=\cdots =\xi _ j=0\} $ is pure of dimension $s-j$, which holds for $j=0$. Since $\Omega $ has a countable basis, $Z_ j$ has countably many irreducible components and $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has countably many connected components $Z^\circ _\alpha $, by corollary A.2.13 . The three properties exclude, for $\xi _{j+1}$, countably many proper linear subspaces of the dual space of $\mathbb C^ N$: by (i), the forms vanishing on a given component of $Z_ j$, which has positive dimension $s-j$; by (ii), if $j<p$, the forms whose restriction to $L$ is a combination of those of $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ j$; and by (iii), the forms whose restriction to the $s$-dimensional tangent space of $Z$ at $z_\alpha $ is a combination of those of $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ j$. A countable union of proper linear subspaces has Lebesgue measure zero, so $\xi _{j+1}$ can be chosen. Then $Z_{j+1}$ is empty or pure of dimension $s-j-1$, by proposition A.4.6 ; here we use that a holomorphic function vanishing identically on a local branch of $Z_ j$ vanishes on the irreducible component of $Z_ j$ containing this branch. Indeed, the branch contains regular points of $Z_ j$ outside the other branches, by corollary A.2.4 , and hence a nonempty open subset of the regular locus of this component, so corollary A.2.13 applies. Replacing $\xi _ j$, $j>p$, by $\xi _ j-\sum _{i\leq p}a_{ji}\xi _ i$ with suitable constants, we may assume that $\xi _{p+1},\ldots ,\xi _ s$ vanish on $L$; this triangular change does not affect the zero sets $\{ \xi _1=\cdots =\xi _ j=0\} $ or the independence at the points $z_\alpha $. Complete $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ s$ by linear forms vanishing on $L$ to linear coordinates $z=(z',z'')$ with $z'=(\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ s)\in \mathbb C^ s$. Then $L=\mathbb C^ p\times \{ 0\} $, and we let $\pi (z)=z'$. A proper projection. By (i), the set $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(0)$ is discrete in $\Omega \setminus A$, and by (ii), $A\cap \pi ^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $ near $0$. Choose a ball $B''$ centered at $0$ in the $z''$-space whose boundary sphere does not meet $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(0)$; this excludes countably many radii. The set $Z\cup A$ is closed near $0$ and does not meet the compact set $\{ 0\} \times \partial B''$, so there is a ball $B'\subset \mathbb C^ s$ centered at $0$ with $(Z\cup A)\cap (\overline{B'}\times \partial B'')=\varnothing $. Let $L'=B'\cap (\mathbb C^ p\times \{ 0\} )$, so that $A\cap (B'\times B'')$ lies over $L'$. The projection of $Z\cap (B'\times B'')$ over $B'\setminus L'$ is proper, because over a compact set $K\subset B'\setminus L'$ it is the compact set $(Z\cup A)\cap (K\times \overline{B''})$, and its fibers are compact analytic subsets of $B''$, hence finite by corollary A.4.3 . The exceptional sets in the base. Let $S_1$ be the set of singular points of $Z$ over $B'\setminus L'$. It is analytic of dimension at most $s-1\leq m-1$, and its projection is proper, so $S_1'=\pi (S_1)$ is analytic in $B'\setminus L'$ by $P_{m-1}$. Over $B'\setminus (L'\cup S_1')$ the set $Z$ is a manifold of dimension $s$; let $S_2$ be the set of its points where $\pi |_ Z$ has rank less than $s$. It is analytic, given locally by a Jacobian determinant. Each connected component of this manifold is an open subset of some $Z^\circ _\alpha $, and on the connected manifold $Z^\circ _\alpha $ the set where the rank of $\pi $ is less than $s$ is a proper analytic subset, since the rank is $s$ at $z_\alpha $ by (iii); so it is nowhere dense, and $S_2$ has dimension at most $s-1$. By $P_{m-1}$, $S_2'=\pi (S_2)$ is analytic in $B'\setminus (L'\cup S_1')$. By lemma A.2.12 (3), the sets $S_1'$ and $S_2'$ have dimension at most $s-1$, so they are nowhere dense in the open subsets of $\mathbb C^ s$ in which they are analytic. Applying lemma A.1.7 first to $L'$, then to $S_1'$ and then to $S_2'$, we see that \[  G=B'\setminus (L'\cup S_1'\cup S_2')  \] is connected; applying it in the opposite order, we see that every bounded holomorphic function on $G$ extends holomorphically to $B'$. The set $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(G)$ is dense in $Z\cap (B'\times B'')$. Indeed, on each irreducible component $Z_\alpha =\overline{Z^\circ _\alpha }$, the functions $\xi _{p+1},\ldots ,\xi _ s$ do not all vanish identically, because $\pi |_ Z$ is open near $z_\alpha $ and $s>p$; so $Z_\alpha \cap \pi ^{-1}(L')$ is a proper analytic subset of $Z_\alpha $, and it is nowhere dense by corollary A.2.14 (2). Moreover, the points at which $\pi |_ Z$ has rank $s$ are dense in $Z$, by the previous paragraph, and near such points $\pi $ is open; hence $\pi ^{-1}(S_1')$ and $\pi ^{-1}(S_2')$, inverse images of nowhere dense sets, are nowhere dense in $Z$ over $B'\setminus L'$ and over $B'\setminus (L'\cup S_1')$, respectively. Over $G$, the projection $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(G)\to G$ is proper and, by proposition 7.1.2 (1) applied in charts of the $s$-dimensional manifold $Z$ over $G$, a local biholomorphism, so its image is open and closed in the connected set $G$; it is nonempty, because $Z\cap (B'\times B'')$ is nonempty and $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(G)$ is dense in it. Hence it is a covering of $G$ with a fixed number $q\geq 1$ of sheets. Indeed, let $z'\in G$ and let $y_1,\ldots ,y_ l$ be the points of the finite fiber over $z'$; choose disjoint neighborhoods $V_ i$ of the $y_ i$ mapped biholomorphically onto neighborhoods of $z'$, and, by properness, a connected neighborhood $N$ of $z'$ in $G$, contained in all these images, such that every point of $Z$ over $N$ lies in $\bigcup _ iV_ i$. Then the part of $Z$ over $N$ is the disjoint union of $l$ graphs over $N$, so the number of points in the fibers is locally constant, hence constant on $G$. Equations for the closure. For a linear form $\lambda $ on the $z''$-space and $z'\in G$ put \[  P_\lambda (z',T)=\prod _{z\in Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(z')} (T-\lambda (z'')).  \] The coefficient of $T^{q-k}$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $k$ in the coefficients of $\lambda $, whose coefficients are symmetric polynomials in the coordinates of the $q$ points of the fiber; these are bounded holomorphic functions on $G$, and they extend holomorphically to $B'$. Thus $P_\lambda (z',\lambda (z''))=\sum _\beta g_\beta (z)\lambda ^\beta $, where $\lambda ^\beta $ runs over the monomials in the coefficients of $\lambda $ and the $g_\beta $ are holomorphic on $B'\times B''$. Let $W=\{ g_\beta =0\text{ for all }\beta \} $, the set of points where $P_\lambda (z',\lambda (z''))=0$ for every $\lambda $; it is analytic. Over $G$, the set $W$ is $Z$: a point outside a finite fiber can be separated from all its points by a linear form. Every fiber of $W$ over $B'$ has at most $q$ points, because a linear form taking distinct values at $q+1$ points of one fiber would give $q+1$ distinct roots of a polynomial of degree $q$. The closure. Choose a smaller ball $B''_1\subset B''$ whose boundary does not meet the finite set $W\cap \pi ^{-1}(0)$, and then a ball $B'_1\subset B'$ centered at $0$ with $W\cap (\overline{B'_1}\times \partial B''_1)=\varnothing $. Then $W_1=W\cap (B'_1\times B''_1)$ is proper with finite fibers over $B'_1$. Every branch of $W_1$ has dimension at most $s$: at a regular point of a branch of dimension $e$, the projection restricted to the branch has finite fibers, so by lemma A.2.11 , applied near a point where its rank is maximal, its maximal rank is $e$, and $e\leq s$. Let $W_ s$ be the union of the irreducible components of $W_1$ of dimension $s$, and $W_{<s}$ the union of the others. We claim that the closure of $Z$ in $B'_1\times B''_1$ is $W_ s$, which is analytic; this proves $R_ m$. Each component of $W_ s$ is pure of dimension $s$, by corollary A.2.14 (1), and the image under $\pi $ of every neighborhood of each of its points in it contains a neighborhood of the image point, by lemma A.4.5 ; so its points over the dense set $G$ are dense in it, and they belong to $Z$. Conversely, let $y\in Z\cap (B'_1\times B''_1)$ lie over $G$. The germ $(W,y)=(Z,y)$ is a manifold germ of dimension $s$, hence irreducible by lemma A.2.9 , so it equals $(W_ s,y)$ or $(W_{<s},y)$, and the latter has smaller dimension. Hence $y\in W_ s$, and since $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(G)$ is dense in $Z$ and $W_ s$ is closed, the closure of $Z$ in $B'_1\times B''_1$ is contained in $W_ s$. Step 2: $R_ m$ and $P_{m-1}$ imply $P_ m$. Let $F\colon Y\to X$ be proper, with $\dim Y\leq m$. Let $\rho \colon M\to Y$ be a resolution given by theorem A.5.4 . It is proper, and it is surjective, because its image is closed and contains the dense set $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$; so replacing $F$ by $F\circ \rho $ does not change the image. Moreover $\dim M\leq m$: the set $\rho ^{-1}(Y_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is nowhere dense, because $\rho $ is bimeromorphic (lemma A.3.1 ), so every connected component of $M$ contains a nonempty open set mapped isomorphically onto an open subset of $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Fix a point of $X$, a relatively compact open neighborhood $U'$ of it and an open neighborhood $U''\Subset X$ of $\overline{U'}$ embedded in a domain of some $\mathbb C^ N$. The compact set $(F\circ \rho )^{-1}(\overline{U'})$ meets only finitely many connected components $M_1,\ldots ,M_ k$ of the manifold $(F\circ \rho )^{-1}(U'')$, and the restriction $F_ j\colon M_ j\to U''$ of $F\circ \rho $ is proper. It suffices to show that each $F_ j(M_ j)$ is analytic in $U''$. Let $r$ be the maximal rank of the differential of $F_ j$ on the connected manifold $M_ j$. If $r=0$, the components of $F_ j$ have zero differential and are constant, so the image is a point. Let $r\geq 1$. The critical set $C=\{ \operatorname {rank}\mathrm dF_ j<r\} $ is an analytic subset of $M_ j$, defined by minors, and it is not all of $M_ j$; so it has dimension at most $m-1$, and $F_ j(C)$ is analytic by $P_{m-1}$. It has dimension at most $r-1$. Indeed, by corollary A.2.10 (2), $C$ is a finite union of complex submanifolds of open subsets of $M_ j$, and the restriction of $F_ j$ to each of them has rank at most $r-1$; so $F_ j(C)$ is $\mathcal H^{2r}$-null by lemma A.2.12 (1), and $\dim F_ j(C)\leq r-1$ by lemma A.2.12 (2). If $F_ j(C)=F_ j(M_ j)$, we are done. Otherwise $F_ j^{-1}(F_ j(C))$ is an analytic subset of the connected manifold $M_ j$ different from $M_ j$, and on its complement $M'_ j$ the rank of $F_ j$ is constantly $r$. The restriction $M'_ j\to U''\setminus F_ j(C)$ is proper, and a proper map of constant rank has analytic image. Indeed, at a point $w$ of the image, cover the compact fiber by finitely many open sets $V_ l$ such that, by lemma A.2.11 applied in charts of $M'_ j$, each $F_ j(V_ l)$ is a closed submanifold of dimension $r$ of a neighborhood of $w$. By properness, the inverse image of a small neighborhood $O$ of $w$ lies in $\bigcup _ lV_ l$, so the image meets $O$ in a finite union of closed submanifolds of dimension $r$. Thus $F_ j(M_ j)\setminus F_ j(C)=F_ j(M'_ j)$ is an analytic subset of $U''\setminus F_ j(C)$, pure of dimension $r\leq m$. Since $\dim F_ j(C)<r$, the assertion $R_ m$ shows that its closure in $U''$ is analytic. This closure is $F_ j(M_ j)$, because $M'_ j$ is dense in $M_ j$ and $F_ j(M_ j)$ is closed by properness. This proves $P_ m$ and completes the induction. $\square$ Corollary A.6.3 . The composite of two proper bimeromorphic holomorphic maps $g\colon Z\to Y$ and $f\colon Y\to X$ between complex spaces is proper and bimeromorphic. Proof. The composite is proper. Let $E_ X\subset X$ and $E_ Y\subset Y$ be nowhere dense analytic subsets as in the definition of bimeromorphic maps for $f$ and $g$. The image $f(E_ Y)$ is analytic by theorem A.6.2 , and it is nowhere dense: an open set $G\subset f(E_ Y)$ satisfies $G\setminus E_ X\subset f(E_ Y\setminus f^{-1}(E_ X))$, which corresponds under the isomorphism $f\colon Y\setminus f^{-1}(E_ X)\to X\setminus E_ X$ to the nowhere dense set $E_ Y\setminus f^{-1}(E_ X)$; so $G\subset E_ X$, and $G=\varnothing $. Hence $B=E_ X\cup f(E_ Y)$ is a nowhere dense analytic subset of $X$. The map $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus B$, and $f^{-1}(X\setminus B)$ does not meet $E_ Y$, so $f\circ g$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus B$. Finally, $f^{-1}(B)$ is a nowhere dense analytic subset of $Y$, and $(f\circ g)^{-1}(B)=g^{-1}(f^{-1}(B))$ is nowhere dense in $Z$, by two applications of lemma A.3.1 . $\square$ Definition A.6.4 . A composition of blowups with smooth centers on a complex manifold is adapted to a closed submanifold $W$ if at each step the center is either contained in the current strict transform of $W$ and of positive codimension in it at each of its points, or disjoint from it. The identity, the composition of no blowups, is allowed. Theorem A.6.5 . Let $M$ be a compact connected complex manifold, $W\subsetneq M$ a closed connected smooth submanifold, and $\mathfrak a\subset \mathcal O_ M$ a coherent ideal whose restriction $\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ W$ is nonzero. There is an adapted composition $f\colon M'\to M$, with strict transform $W'$, and effective divisors $H,H'$ on $M'$ such that $H$ is exceptional for $f$, $H'$ is disjoint from $W'$, and A.11 \begin{align}  \mathcal I_ W\mathcal O_{M'}& =\mathcal O_{M'}(-H)\mathcal I_{W'}, \label{eq:relative-center-ideal}\\  \mathfrak a\mathcal O_{M'}& =\mathcal O_{M'}(-H-H'), \label{eq:relative-ideal-principalization}\\  (\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ W)\mathcal O_{W'} & =\mathcal O_{W'}(-H|_{W'}). \label{eq:relative-restricted-ideal} \end{align} The restriction $f|_{W'}\colon W'\to W$ is a composition of smooth-center blowups and an isomorphism outside a proper analytic subset of $W$. Proof. Let $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ W$. We first principalize $\mathfrak b$ by blowups of $W$, perform the same blowups on $M$, and then principalize the remaining ideal away from the strict transform of $W$. If $\dim W=0$, then $W$ is a point, $\mathfrak b$ is the unit ideal, the first sequence below is empty, and the argument applies with $H=0$. Step 1: principalizing the restriction. Apply theorem A.5.5 to the ideal $\mathfrak b$ on the compact manifold $W$, with empty divisor. We obtain a finite sequence of blowups $W_ i\to W_{i-1}$ with smooth centers $C_ i\subset W_{i-1}$, $1\leq i\leq t$, and ideals $\mathfrak b_ i$ with $\mathfrak b_0=\mathfrak b$, $\mathfrak b_ i=\mathcal O_{W_ i}(E^ W_ i)\mathfrak b_{i-1}\mathcal O_{W_ i}$, where $E^ W_ i$ is the inverse image of $C_ i$, and $\mathfrak b_ t=\mathcal O_{W_ t}$. By induction on $i$, each $W_{i-1}$ is connected, $\mathfrak b_{i-1}$ is nonzero, and $C_ i$ has positive codimension in $W_{i-1}$ at each of its points; for $i=1$, the first two assertions are hypotheses of the theorem. Assume them for some $i\leq t$. A nonzero coherent ideal on a connected manifold has nonzero stalks at all points, since the points at which its stalk vanishes form an open set, and so, by the identity theorem, do the points at which it does not vanish; hence its zero set is nowhere dense. So $C_ i\subset V(\mathfrak b_{i-1})$ is nowhere dense in $W_{i-1}$, that is, of positive codimension at each of its points. Then $W_ i\setminus E^ W_ i\cong W_{i-1}\setminus C_ i$ is connected by lemma A.1.7 and dense in $W_ i$, so $W_ i$ is connected; and $\mathfrak b_ i$ is nonzero, because it agrees with $\mathfrak b_{i-1}$ on this set. We perform the same blowups on the ambient manifolds: let $M_0=M$ and let $\sigma _ i\colon M_ i\to M_{i-1}$ be the blowup along $C_ i$, where $W_{i-1}\subset M_{i-1}$ is the strict transform of $W$. The center $C_ i$ is closed in $M_{i-1}$, because $W_{i-1}$ is closed, and it has codimension at least two in $M_{i-1}$. By proposition A.5.3 , the strict transform of $W_{i-1}$ in $M_ i$ is $\operatorname {Bl}_{C_ i}W_{i-1}=W_ i$, and $E_ i\cap W_ i=E^ W_ i$, where $E_ i=\sigma _ i^{-1}(C_ i)$. More precisely, in the charts of that proposition whose pivot is one of the coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ k$ along $W_{i-1}$, which are the only ones meeting $W_ i$, a local equation $e_ i$ of $E_ i$ restricts to a local equation of $E^ W_ i$. This sequence is adapted to $W$. Step 2: the transformed ideals. Put $H_0=0$ and $\mathfrak a_0=\mathfrak a$, and define inductively \[  H_ i=\sigma _ i^*H_{i-1}+E_ i,\qquad \mathfrak a_ i=\mathcal O_{M_ i}(E_ i) \mathfrak a_{i-1}\mathcal O_{M_ i}.  \] We show by induction that $\mathfrak a_ i$ is a holomorphic ideal and that $\mathfrak a_ i\mathcal O_{W_ i}=\mathfrak b_ i$. Every local section $h$ of $\mathfrak a_{i-1}$ vanishes on $C_ i$, because its restriction to $W_{i-1}$ belongs to $\mathfrak b_{i-1}$ and $C_ i\subset V(\mathfrak b_{i-1})$. Hence $h\in \mathcal I_{C_ i}$, and $h\circ \sigma _ i$ belongs to $\mathcal I_{C_ i}\mathcal O_{M_ i}=\mathcal O_{M_ i}(-E_ i)$; that is, it is divisible by the local equation $e_ i$ of $E_ i$, and $\mathfrak a_ i$ is holomorphic. Restricting $(h\circ \sigma _ i)/e_ i$ to $W_ i$ divides $h|_{W_{i-1}}\circ \sigma _ i|_{W_ i}$ by the local equation $e_ i|_{W_ i}$ of $E^ W_ i$, which gives $\mathfrak a_ i\mathcal O_{W_ i}=\mathfrak b_ i$; this holds also when $C_ i$ is a hypersurface in $W_{i-1}$. Iterating ( A.9 ) and the definition of $\mathfrak a_ i$, we obtain \[  \mathcal I_ W\mathcal O_{M_ t}=\mathcal O_{M_ t}(-H_ t)\mathcal I_{W_ t}, \qquad \mathfrak a\mathcal O_{M_ t}=\mathcal O_{M_ t}(-H_ t)\mathfrak a_ t.  \] Since $\mathfrak b_ t=\mathcal O_{W_ t}$, the ideal $\mathfrak a_ t$ is the unit ideal at each point of $W_ t$: a local section whose restriction to $W_ t$ does not vanish at a point is a unit of the local ring of $M_ t$ there. Hence $V(\mathfrak a_ t)$ is disjoint from $W_ t$. Step 3: principalizing away from $W_ t$. The manifold $M_ t$ is compact, and it is connected by the argument given for the $W_ i$ in Step 1; the ideal $\mathfrak a_ t$ is not zero, being the unit ideal near $W_ t$. Apply theorem A.5.5 to $\mathfrak a_ t$ on $M_ t$, with empty divisor. Each center lies in the zero set of the current transformed ideal; since the blowups are isomorphisms near the successive copies of $W_ t$, which do not meet the centers, these transformed ideals remain the unit ideal near these copies, and all centers are disjoint from them. Let $g\colon M'\to M_ t$ be the composite, and let $H'$ be the effective divisor with $\mathfrak a_ t\mathcal O_{M'}=\mathcal O_{M'}(-H')$ obtained by iterating ( A.10 ); put $H=g^*H_ t$ and $f=\sigma _1\circ \cdots \circ \sigma _ t\circ g$. The composition $f$ is adapted to $W$, and the strict transform $W'=g^{-1}(W_ t)$ is mapped isomorphically onto $W_ t$. By proposition A.5.3 , $\mathcal I_{W_ t}\mathcal O_{M'}=\mathcal I_{W'}$, and pulling back the two identities of Step 2 gives ( A.11 ) and ( A.12 ). The divisor $H'$ is supported on the exceptional divisors of $g$, which are disjoint from $W'$. Step 4: exceptional divisors and restriction. Every component of the support of $H$ maps into the union of the images in $M$ of the centers $C_ i$; each such image lies in $W$, is analytic by theorem A.6.2 , and has dimension at most $\dim C_ i<\dim W\leq \dim M-1$ by lemma A.2.12 (3), so it has codimension at least two in $M$. Hence $H$ is exceptional for $f$, which is proper and bimeromorphic by proposition A.5.2 , corollary A.6.3 . No component of $H$ contains $W'$: by Step 1, the restriction to $W_ i$ of a local equation of $E_ i$ is a local equation of the hypersurface $E^ W_ i$ of $W_ i$, so by induction the restriction to $W_ t$ of a local equation of $H_ t$ is not identically zero, and $g$ is an isomorphism near $W'$. Hence $H|_{W'}$ is defined, and restricting ( A.12 ) to $W'$, where $H'$ vanishes, gives ( A.13 ). Finally, $f|_{W'}$ is the composition of the blowups $W_ i\to W_{i-1}$ followed by the isomorphism $W'\to W_ t$. It is an isomorphism outside the union of the images in $W$ of the centers $C_ i$ that have codimension at least two in $W_{i-1}$; this union is a finite union of analytic subsets of dimension smaller than $\dim W$, hence a proper analytic subset of $W$. $\square$

title: Theorem A.6.1 (Remmert–Stein)
text: Theorem A.6.1 (Remmert–Stein) . Let $X$ be a complex space, let $p\geq 0$ be an integer, and let $A\subset X$ be an analytic subset of dimension at most $p$. Let $Z$ be an analytic subset of $X\setminus A$ all of whose local branches have dimension greater than $p$. Then the closure of $Z$ in $X$ is analytic.

title: Theorem A.6.2 (Remmert)
text: Theorem A.6.2 (Remmert) . The image of a proper holomorphic map between complex spaces is analytic. Proof. We prove the two theorems together by induction on dimension. Let $R_ m$ denote the assertion of theorem A.6.1 for sets $Z$ of dimension at most $m$, and $P_ m$ the assertion of theorem A.6.2 for maps whose source has dimension at most $m$. Both assertions are local on $X$. A proper map has compact inverse image over a compact neighborhood of a point of the target, and near this compact set its source has finite dimension; so, locally on the target, every proper map falls under some $P_ m$. The assertion $P_0$ holds because a source of dimension zero is discrete, so the image of a proper map from it is closed and locally finite, hence analytic. The assertion $R_0$ holds trivially: a set $Z$ of dimension zero has no branches of dimension greater than $p\geq 0$, so $Z=\varnothing $. We show that $P_{m-1}$ implies $R_ m$, and that $R_ m$ and $P_{m-1}$ imply $P_ m$. Step 1: $P_{m-1}$ implies $R_ m$; reductions. Since the assertion is local, we may assume that $X$ is an analytic subset of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ N$; then $Z$ is an analytic subset of $\Omega \setminus A$, and its closure in $X$ is its closure in $\Omega $. We first reduce to the case where $A$ is a submanifold of dimension $p$, by induction on $p$. Let $A''$ be the union of $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the irreducible components of $A$ of dimension less than $p$; it is analytic of dimension at most $p-1$ (empty if $p=0$), and $A\setminus A''$ is a closed submanifold of $\Omega \setminus A''$ of dimension $p$. Suppose that the closure $Z_1$ of $Z$ in $\Omega \setminus A''$ is analytic. No branch $B$ of a germ of $Z_1$ is contained in $A$: since $Z$ is dense in $Z_1$, the branches not contained in $A$ already have union $Z_1$ near the base point, and the decomposition into branches is irredundant. Hence $B\setminus A$ is dense in $B$, and at its regular points outside the other branches $B$ coincides with $Z$, whose branches have dimension greater than $p$. Hence all branches of $Z_1$ have dimension greater than $p>p-1$, and by the induction hypothesis on $p$ the closure of $Z_1$ in $\Omega $, which is the closure of $Z$, is analytic. Thus we may assume that $A$ is a $p$-dimensional submanifold. Fix a point of $A$ in the closure of $Z$; after a holomorphic change of coordinates it is the origin, and near it $A$ is a linear subspace $L$ of dimension $p$. Finally, the irreducible components of $Z$ are pure-dimensional by corollary A.2.14 (1), and their dimensions exceed $p$, because each component contains regular points of $Z$ near which $Z$ coincides with it. The union of the components of a given dimension $s$ is analytic in $\Omega \setminus A$, by corollary A.2.13 , and only the finitely many values $p<s\leq m$ occur; so we may assume that $Z$ is pure of dimension $s$, with $p<s\leq m$. We shall present $Z$ near the origin as a branched covering over an open subset of $\mathbb C^ s$ and write down equations for its closure. Choice of a projection. We choose linear forms $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ s$ on $\mathbb C^ N$ with the following properties: (i) for each $j<s$, the form $\xi _{j+1}$ does not vanish identically on any irreducible component of $Z\cap \{ \xi _1=\cdots =\xi _ j=0\} $; (ii) the restrictions of $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ p$ to $L$ are linearly independent; (iii) at a point $z_\alpha $ chosen in each connected component $Z^\circ _\alpha $ of the manifold $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the restrictions of $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ s$ to the tangent space of $Z$ are linearly independent. We choose the forms one at a time. Suppose that $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ j$, $j<s$, have been chosen and that $Z_ j=Z\cap \{ \xi _1=\cdots =\xi _ j=0\} $ is pure of dimension $s-j$, which holds for $j=0$. Since $\Omega $ has a countable basis, $Z_ j$ has countably many irreducible components and $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has countably many connected components $Z^\circ _\alpha $, by corollary A.2.13 . The three properties exclude, for $\xi _{j+1}$, countably many proper linear subspaces of the dual space of $\mathbb C^ N$: by (i), the forms vanishing on a given component of $Z_ j$, which has positive dimension $s-j$; by (ii), if $j<p$, the forms whose restriction to $L$ is a combination of those of $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ j$; and by (iii), the forms whose restriction to the $s$-dimensional tangent space of $Z$ at $z_\alpha $ is a combination of those of $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ j$. A countable union of proper linear subspaces has Lebesgue measure zero, so $\xi _{j+1}$ can be chosen. Then $Z_{j+1}$ is empty or pure of dimension $s-j-1$, by proposition A.4.6 ; here we use that a holomorphic function vanishing identically on a local branch of $Z_ j$ vanishes on the irreducible component of $Z_ j$ containing this branch. Indeed, the branch contains regular points of $Z_ j$ outside the other branches, by corollary A.2.4 , and hence a nonempty open subset of the regular locus of this component, so corollary A.2.13 applies. Replacing $\xi _ j$, $j>p$, by $\xi _ j-\sum _{i\leq p}a_{ji}\xi _ i$ with suitable constants, we may assume that $\xi _{p+1},\ldots ,\xi _ s$ vanish on $L$; this triangular change does not affect the zero sets $\{ \xi _1=\cdots =\xi _ j=0\} $ or the independence at the points $z_\alpha $. Complete $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ s$ by linear forms vanishing on $L$ to linear coordinates $z=(z',z'')$ with $z'=(\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ s)\in \mathbb C^ s$. Then $L=\mathbb C^ p\times \{ 0\} $, and we let $\pi (z)=z'$. A proper projection. By (i), the set $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(0)$ is discrete in $\Omega \setminus A$, and by (ii), $A\cap \pi ^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} $ near $0$. Choose a ball $B''$ centered at $0$ in the $z''$-space whose boundary sphere does not meet $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(0)$; this excludes countably many radii. The set $Z\cup A$ is closed near $0$ and does not meet the compact set $\{ 0\} \times \partial B''$, so there is a ball $B'\subset \mathbb C^ s$ centered at $0$ with $(Z\cup A)\cap (\overline{B'}\times \partial B'')=\varnothing $. Let $L'=B'\cap (\mathbb C^ p\times \{ 0\} )$, so that $A\cap (B'\times B'')$ lies over $L'$. The projection of $Z\cap (B'\times B'')$ over $B'\setminus L'$ is proper, because over a compact set $K\subset B'\setminus L'$ it is the compact set $(Z\cup A)\cap (K\times \overline{B''})$, and its fibers are compact analytic subsets of $B''$, hence finite by corollary A.4.3 . The exceptional sets in the base. Let $S_1$ be the set of singular points of $Z$ over $B'\setminus L'$. It is analytic of dimension at most $s-1\leq m-1$, and its projection is proper, so $S_1'=\pi (S_1)$ is analytic in $B'\setminus L'$ by $P_{m-1}$. Over $B'\setminus (L'\cup S_1')$ the set $Z$ is a manifold of dimension $s$; let $S_2$ be the set of its points where $\pi |_ Z$ has rank less than $s$. It is analytic, given locally by a Jacobian determinant. Each connected component of this manifold is an open subset of some $Z^\circ _\alpha $, and on the connected manifold $Z^\circ _\alpha $ the set where the rank of $\pi $ is less than $s$ is a proper analytic subset, since the rank is $s$ at $z_\alpha $ by (iii); so it is nowhere dense, and $S_2$ has dimension at most $s-1$. By $P_{m-1}$, $S_2'=\pi (S_2)$ is analytic in $B'\setminus (L'\cup S_1')$. By lemma A.2.12 (3), the sets $S_1'$ and $S_2'$ have dimension at most $s-1$, so they are nowhere dense in the open subsets of $\mathbb C^ s$ in which they are analytic. Applying lemma A.1.7 first to $L'$, then to $S_1'$ and then to $S_2'$, we see that \[  G=B'\setminus (L'\cup S_1'\cup S_2')  \] is connected; applying it in the opposite order, we see that every bounded holomorphic function on $G$ extends holomorphically to $B'$. The set $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(G)$ is dense in $Z\cap (B'\times B'')$. Indeed, on each irreducible component $Z_\alpha =\overline{Z^\circ _\alpha }$, the functions $\xi _{p+1},\ldots ,\xi _ s$ do not all vanish identically, because $\pi |_ Z$ is open near $z_\alpha $ and $s>p$; so $Z_\alpha \cap \pi ^{-1}(L')$ is a proper analytic subset of $Z_\alpha $, and it is nowhere dense by corollary A.2.14 (2). Moreover, the points at which $\pi |_ Z$ has rank $s$ are dense in $Z$, by the previous paragraph, and near such points $\pi $ is open; hence $\pi ^{-1}(S_1')$ and $\pi ^{-1}(S_2')$, inverse images of nowhere dense sets, are nowhere dense in $Z$ over $B'\setminus L'$ and over $B'\setminus (L'\cup S_1')$, respectively. Over $G$, the projection $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(G)\to G$ is proper and, by proposition 7.1.2 (1) applied in charts of the $s$-dimensional manifold $Z$ over $G$, a local biholomorphism, so its image is open and closed in the connected set $G$; it is nonempty, because $Z\cap (B'\times B'')$ is nonempty and $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(G)$ is dense in it. Hence it is a covering of $G$ with a fixed number $q\geq 1$ of sheets. Indeed, let $z'\in G$ and let $y_1,\ldots ,y_ l$ be the points of the finite fiber over $z'$; choose disjoint neighborhoods $V_ i$ of the $y_ i$ mapped biholomorphically onto neighborhoods of $z'$, and, by properness, a connected neighborhood $N$ of $z'$ in $G$, contained in all these images, such that every point of $Z$ over $N$ lies in $\bigcup _ iV_ i$. Then the part of $Z$ over $N$ is the disjoint union of $l$ graphs over $N$, so the number of points in the fibers is locally constant, hence constant on $G$. Equations for the closure. For a linear form $\lambda $ on the $z''$-space and $z'\in G$ put \[  P_\lambda (z',T)=\prod _{z\in Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(z')} (T-\lambda (z'')).  \] The coefficient of $T^{q-k}$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $k$ in the coefficients of $\lambda $, whose coefficients are symmetric polynomials in the coordinates of the $q$ points of the fiber; these are bounded holomorphic functions on $G$, and they extend holomorphically to $B'$. Thus $P_\lambda (z',\lambda (z''))=\sum _\beta g_\beta (z)\lambda ^\beta $, where $\lambda ^\beta $ runs over the monomials in the coefficients of $\lambda $ and the $g_\beta $ are holomorphic on $B'\times B''$. Let $W=\{ g_\beta =0\text{ for all }\beta \} $, the set of points where $P_\lambda (z',\lambda (z''))=0$ for every $\lambda $; it is analytic. Over $G$, the set $W$ is $Z$: a point outside a finite fiber can be separated from all its points by a linear form. Every fiber of $W$ over $B'$ has at most $q$ points, because a linear form taking distinct values at $q+1$ points of one fiber would give $q+1$ distinct roots of a polynomial of degree $q$. The closure. Choose a smaller ball $B''_1\subset B''$ whose boundary does not meet the finite set $W\cap \pi ^{-1}(0)$, and then a ball $B'_1\subset B'$ centered at $0$ with $W\cap (\overline{B'_1}\times \partial B''_1)=\varnothing $. Then $W_1=W\cap (B'_1\times B''_1)$ is proper with finite fibers over $B'_1$. Every branch of $W_1$ has dimension at most $s$: at a regular point of a branch of dimension $e$, the projection restricted to the branch has finite fibers, so by lemma A.2.11 , applied near a point where its rank is maximal, its maximal rank is $e$, and $e\leq s$. Let $W_ s$ be the union of the irreducible components of $W_1$ of dimension $s$, and $W_{<s}$ the union of the others. We claim that the closure of $Z$ in $B'_1\times B''_1$ is $W_ s$, which is analytic; this proves $R_ m$. Each component of $W_ s$ is pure of dimension $s$, by corollary A.2.14 (1), and the image under $\pi $ of every neighborhood of each of its points in it contains a neighborhood of the image point, by lemma A.4.5 ; so its points over the dense set $G$ are dense in it, and they belong to $Z$. Conversely, let $y\in Z\cap (B'_1\times B''_1)$ lie over $G$. The germ $(W,y)=(Z,y)$ is a manifold germ of dimension $s$, hence irreducible by lemma A.2.9 , so it equals $(W_ s,y)$ or $(W_{<s},y)$, and the latter has smaller dimension. Hence $y\in W_ s$, and since $Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(G)$ is dense in $Z$ and $W_ s$ is closed, the closure of $Z$ in $B'_1\times B''_1$ is contained in $W_ s$. Step 2: $R_ m$ and $P_{m-1}$ imply $P_ m$. Let $F\colon Y\to X$ be proper, with $\dim Y\leq m$. Let $\rho \colon M\to Y$ be a resolution given by theorem A.5.4 . It is proper, and it is surjective, because its image is closed and contains the dense set $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$; so replacing $F$ by $F\circ \rho $ does not change the image. Moreover $\dim M\leq m$: the set $\rho ^{-1}(Y_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is nowhere dense, because $\rho $ is bimeromorphic (lemma A.3.1 ), so every connected component of $M$ contains a nonempty open set mapped isomorphically onto an open subset of $Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Fix a point of $X$, a relatively compact open neighborhood $U'$ of it and an open neighborhood $U''\Subset X$ of $\overline{U'}$ embedded in a domain of some $\mathbb C^ N$. The compact set $(F\circ \rho )^{-1}(\overline{U'})$ meets only finitely many connected components $M_1,\ldots ,M_ k$ of the manifold $(F\circ \rho )^{-1}(U'')$, and the restriction $F_ j\colon M_ j\to U''$ of $F\circ \rho $ is proper. It suffices to show that each $F_ j(M_ j)$ is analytic in $U''$. Let $r$ be the maximal rank of the differential of $F_ j$ on the connected manifold $M_ j$. If $r=0$, the components of $F_ j$ have zero differential and are constant, so the image is a point. Let $r\geq 1$. The critical set $C=\{ \operatorname {rank}\mathrm dF_ j<r\} $ is an analytic subset of $M_ j$, defined by minors, and it is not all of $M_ j$; so it has dimension at most $m-1$, and $F_ j(C)$ is analytic by $P_{m-1}$. It has dimension at most $r-1$. Indeed, by corollary A.2.10 (2), $C$ is a finite union of complex submanifolds of open subsets of $M_ j$, and the restriction of $F_ j$ to each of them has rank at most $r-1$; so $F_ j(C)$ is $\mathcal H^{2r}$-null by lemma A.2.12 (1), and $\dim F_ j(C)\leq r-1$ by lemma A.2.12 (2). If $F_ j(C)=F_ j(M_ j)$, we are done. Otherwise $F_ j^{-1}(F_ j(C))$ is an analytic subset of the connected manifold $M_ j$ different from $M_ j$, and on its complement $M'_ j$ the rank of $F_ j$ is constantly $r$. The restriction $M'_ j\to U''\setminus F_ j(C)$ is proper, and a proper map of constant rank has analytic image. Indeed, at a point $w$ of the image, cover the compact fiber by finitely many open sets $V_ l$ such that, by lemma A.2.11 applied in charts of $M'_ j$, each $F_ j(V_ l)$ is a closed submanifold of dimension $r$ of a neighborhood of $w$. By properness, the inverse image of a small neighborhood $O$ of $w$ lies in $\bigcup _ lV_ l$, so the image meets $O$ in a finite union of closed submanifolds of dimension $r$. Thus $F_ j(M_ j)\setminus F_ j(C)=F_ j(M'_ j)$ is an analytic subset of $U''\setminus F_ j(C)$, pure of dimension $r\leq m$. Since $\dim F_ j(C)<r$, the assertion $R_ m$ shows that its closure in $U''$ is analytic. This closure is $F_ j(M_ j)$, because $M'_ j$ is dense in $M_ j$ and $F_ j(M_ j)$ is closed by properness. This proves $P_ m$ and completes the induction. $\square$

title: Corollary A.6.3
text: Corollary A.6.3 . The composite of two proper bimeromorphic holomorphic maps $g\colon Z\to Y$ and $f\colon Y\to X$ between complex spaces is proper and bimeromorphic. Proof. The composite is proper. Let $E_ X\subset X$ and $E_ Y\subset Y$ be nowhere dense analytic subsets as in the definition of bimeromorphic maps for $f$ and $g$. The image $f(E_ Y)$ is analytic by theorem A.6.2 , and it is nowhere dense: an open set $G\subset f(E_ Y)$ satisfies $G\setminus E_ X\subset f(E_ Y\setminus f^{-1}(E_ X))$, which corresponds under the isomorphism $f\colon Y\setminus f^{-1}(E_ X)\to X\setminus E_ X$ to the nowhere dense set $E_ Y\setminus f^{-1}(E_ X)$; so $G\subset E_ X$, and $G=\varnothing $. Hence $B=E_ X\cup f(E_ Y)$ is a nowhere dense analytic subset of $X$. The map $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus B$, and $f^{-1}(X\setminus B)$ does not meet $E_ Y$, so $f\circ g$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus B$. Finally, $f^{-1}(B)$ is a nowhere dense analytic subset of $Y$, and $(f\circ g)^{-1}(B)=g^{-1}(f^{-1}(B))$ is nowhere dense in $Z$, by two applications of lemma A.3.1 . $\square$

title: Definition A.6.4
text: Definition A.6.4 . A composition of blowups with smooth centers on a complex manifold is adapted to a closed submanifold $W$ if at each step the center is either contained in the current strict transform of $W$ and of positive codimension in it at each of its points, or disjoint from it. The identity, the composition of no blowups, is allowed.

title: Theorem A.6.5
text: Theorem A.6.5 . Let $M$ be a compact connected complex manifold, $W\subsetneq M$ a closed connected smooth submanifold, and $\mathfrak a\subset \mathcal O_ M$ a coherent ideal whose restriction $\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ W$ is nonzero. There is an adapted composition $f\colon M'\to M$, with strict transform $W'$, and effective divisors $H,H'$ on $M'$ such that $H$ is exceptional for $f$, $H'$ is disjoint from $W'$, and A.11 \begin{align}  \mathcal I_ W\mathcal O_{M'}& =\mathcal O_{M'}(-H)\mathcal I_{W'}, \label{eq:relative-center-ideal}\\  \mathfrak a\mathcal O_{M'}& =\mathcal O_{M'}(-H-H'), \label{eq:relative-ideal-principalization}\\  (\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ W)\mathcal O_{W'} & =\mathcal O_{W'}(-H|_{W'}). \label{eq:relative-restricted-ideal} \end{align} The restriction $f|_{W'}\colon W'\to W$ is a composition of smooth-center blowups and an isomorphism outside a proper analytic subset of $W$. Proof. Let $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ W$. We first principalize $\mathfrak b$ by blowups of $W$, perform the same blowups on $M$, and then principalize the remaining ideal away from the strict transform of $W$. If $\dim W=0$, then $W$ is a point, $\mathfrak b$ is the unit ideal, the first sequence below is empty, and the argument applies with $H=0$. Step 1: principalizing the restriction. Apply theorem A.5.5 to the ideal $\mathfrak b$ on the compact manifold $W$, with empty divisor. We obtain a finite sequence of blowups $W_ i\to W_{i-1}$ with smooth centers $C_ i\subset W_{i-1}$, $1\leq i\leq t$, and ideals $\mathfrak b_ i$ with $\mathfrak b_0=\mathfrak b$, $\mathfrak b_ i=\mathcal O_{W_ i}(E^ W_ i)\mathfrak b_{i-1}\mathcal O_{W_ i}$, where $E^ W_ i$ is the inverse image of $C_ i$, and $\mathfrak b_ t=\mathcal O_{W_ t}$. By induction on $i$, each $W_{i-1}$ is connected, $\mathfrak b_{i-1}$ is nonzero, and $C_ i$ has positive codimension in $W_{i-1}$ at each of its points; for $i=1$, the first two assertions are hypotheses of the theorem. Assume them for some $i\leq t$. A nonzero coherent ideal on a connected manifold has nonzero stalks at all points, since the points at which its stalk vanishes form an open set, and so, by the identity theorem, do the points at which it does not vanish; hence its zero set is nowhere dense. So $C_ i\subset V(\mathfrak b_{i-1})$ is nowhere dense in $W_{i-1}$, that is, of positive codimension at each of its points. Then $W_ i\setminus E^ W_ i\cong W_{i-1}\setminus C_ i$ is connected by lemma A.1.7 and dense in $W_ i$, so $W_ i$ is connected; and $\mathfrak b_ i$ is nonzero, because it agrees with $\mathfrak b_{i-1}$ on this set. We perform the same blowups on the ambient manifolds: let $M_0=M$ and let $\sigma _ i\colon M_ i\to M_{i-1}$ be the blowup along $C_ i$, where $W_{i-1}\subset M_{i-1}$ is the strict transform of $W$. The center $C_ i$ is closed in $M_{i-1}$, because $W_{i-1}$ is closed, and it has codimension at least two in $M_{i-1}$. By proposition A.5.3 , the strict transform of $W_{i-1}$ in $M_ i$ is $\operatorname {Bl}_{C_ i}W_{i-1}=W_ i$, and $E_ i\cap W_ i=E^ W_ i$, where $E_ i=\sigma _ i^{-1}(C_ i)$. More precisely, in the charts of that proposition whose pivot is one of the coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ k$ along $W_{i-1}$, which are the only ones meeting $W_ i$, a local equation $e_ i$ of $E_ i$ restricts to a local equation of $E^ W_ i$. This sequence is adapted to $W$. Step 2: the transformed ideals. Put $H_0=0$ and $\mathfrak a_0=\mathfrak a$, and define inductively \[  H_ i=\sigma _ i^*H_{i-1}+E_ i,\qquad \mathfrak a_ i=\mathcal O_{M_ i}(E_ i) \mathfrak a_{i-1}\mathcal O_{M_ i}.  \] We show by induction that $\mathfrak a_ i$ is a holomorphic ideal and that $\mathfrak a_ i\mathcal O_{W_ i}=\mathfrak b_ i$. Every local section $h$ of $\mathfrak a_{i-1}$ vanishes on $C_ i$, because its restriction to $W_{i-1}$ belongs to $\mathfrak b_{i-1}$ and $C_ i\subset V(\mathfrak b_{i-1})$. Hence $h\in \mathcal I_{C_ i}$, and $h\circ \sigma _ i$ belongs to $\mathcal I_{C_ i}\mathcal O_{M_ i}=\mathcal O_{M_ i}(-E_ i)$; that is, it is divisible by the local equation $e_ i$ of $E_ i$, and $\mathfrak a_ i$ is holomorphic. Restricting $(h\circ \sigma _ i)/e_ i$ to $W_ i$ divides $h|_{W_{i-1}}\circ \sigma _ i|_{W_ i}$ by the local equation $e_ i|_{W_ i}$ of $E^ W_ i$, which gives $\mathfrak a_ i\mathcal O_{W_ i}=\mathfrak b_ i$; this holds also when $C_ i$ is a hypersurface in $W_{i-1}$. Iterating ( A.9 ) and the definition of $\mathfrak a_ i$, we obtain \[  \mathcal I_ W\mathcal O_{M_ t}=\mathcal O_{M_ t}(-H_ t)\mathcal I_{W_ t}, \qquad \mathfrak a\mathcal O_{M_ t}=\mathcal O_{M_ t}(-H_ t)\mathfrak a_ t.  \] Since $\mathfrak b_ t=\mathcal O_{W_ t}$, the ideal $\mathfrak a_ t$ is the unit ideal at each point of $W_ t$: a local section whose restriction to $W_ t$ does not vanish at a point is a unit of the local ring of $M_ t$ there. Hence $V(\mathfrak a_ t)$ is disjoint from $W_ t$. Step 3: principalizing away from $W_ t$. The manifold $M_ t$ is compact, and it is connected by the argument given for the $W_ i$ in Step 1; the ideal $\mathfrak a_ t$ is not zero, being the unit ideal near $W_ t$. Apply theorem A.5.5 to $\mathfrak a_ t$ on $M_ t$, with empty divisor. Each center lies in the zero set of the current transformed ideal; since the blowups are isomorphisms near the successive copies of $W_ t$, which do not meet the centers, these transformed ideals remain the unit ideal near these copies, and all centers are disjoint from them. Let $g\colon M'\to M_ t$ be the composite, and let $H'$ be the effective divisor with $\mathfrak a_ t\mathcal O_{M'}=\mathcal O_{M'}(-H')$ obtained by iterating ( A.10 ); put $H=g^*H_ t$ and $f=\sigma _1\circ \cdots \circ \sigma _ t\circ g$. The composition $f$ is adapted to $W$, and the strict transform $W'=g^{-1}(W_ t)$ is mapped isomorphically onto $W_ t$. By proposition A.5.3 , $\mathcal I_{W_ t}\mathcal O_{M'}=\mathcal I_{W'}$, and pulling back the two identities of Step 2 gives ( A.11 ) and ( A.12 ). The divisor $H'$ is supported on the exceptional divisors of $g$, which are disjoint from $W'$. Step 4: exceptional divisors and restriction. Every component of the support of $H$ maps into the union of the images in $M$ of the centers $C_ i$; each such image lies in $W$, is analytic by theorem A.6.2 , and has dimension at most $\dim C_ i<\dim W\leq \dim M-1$ by lemma A.2.12 (3), so it has codimension at least two in $M$. Hence $H$ is exceptional for $f$, which is proper and bimeromorphic by proposition A.5.2 , corollary A.6.3 . No component of $H$ contains $W'$: by Step 1, the restriction to $W_ i$ of a local equation of $E_ i$ is a local equation of the hypersurface $E^ W_ i$ of $W_ i$, so by induction the restriction to $W_ t$ of a local equation of $H_ t$ is not identically zero, and $g$ is an isomorphism near $W'$. Hence $H|_{W'}$ is defined, and restricting ( A.12 ) to $W'$, where $H'$ vanishes, gives ( A.13 ). Finally, $f|_{W'}$ is the composition of the blowups $W_ i\to W_{i-1}$ followed by the isomorphism $W'\to W_ t$. It is an isomorphism outside the union of the images in $W$ of the centers $C_ i$ that have codimension at least two in $W_{i-1}$; this union is a finite union of analytic subsets of dimension smaller than $\dim W$, hence a proper analytic subset of $W$. $\square$

title: A.7 Connected fibers and resolution models
text:
A.7 Connected fibers and resolution models A proper bimeromorphic map can contract analytic sets, so its fibers may have positive dimension. Over a unibranch space they are nevertheless connected (theorem A.7.1 ). Consequently a finite bimeromorphic map onto a normal space is an isomorphism, and a proper bimeromorphic map between manifolds is an isomorphism outside a set of codimension at least two. We then introduce smooth models and prime divisors over a complex space, and show that every prime divisor over a compact space is realized after finitely many blowups with smooth centers. Theorem A.7.1 . Let $f\colon Y	o X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map between complex spaces, and let $x\in X$ be a point at which the germ $(X,x)$ is irreducible. Then the fiber $f^{-1}(x)$ is connected. In particular, if $X$ is unibranch, every fiber of $f$ is connected. Proof. Choose a nowhere dense analytic subset $A\subset X$ such that $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense and $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$. Suppose that the compact fiber over $x$ is disconnected, and write it as the union of two disjoint nonempty compact sets. Since $Y$ is Hausdorff, they have disjoint open neighborhoods $V_1$ and $V_2$. Since $f$ is proper, hence closed, $U=X\setminus f(Y\setminus (V_1\cup V_2))$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ with $f^{-1}(U)\subset V_1\cup V_2$. As $(X,x)$ is irreducible, corollary A.3.9 allows us to shrink $U$ so that $U\setminus A$ is connected. Each set $V_ i\cap f^{-1}(U)$ is open and nonempty, so it meets the dense set $Y\setminus f^{-1}(A)$. Therefore $V_1$ and $V_2$ split $f^{-1}(U\setminus A)$ into two disjoint nonempty open sets. This contradicts the connectedness of $U\setminus A$, which is isomorphic to $f^{-1}(U\setminus A)$. $\square$ Corollary A.7.2 . A finite bimeromorphic holomorphic map to a normal complex space is an isomorphism. Let $\phi \colon S	o X$ be a holomorphic map from a normal complex space to a complex space such that $\phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is nowhere dense in $S$. Then $\phi $ factors uniquely through the normalization $
u \colon \widetilde X	o X$: there is a unique holomorphic map $\psi \colon S	o \widetilde X$ with $
u \circ \psi =\phi $. Proof. Let $f\colon Y	o X$ be finite and bimeromorphic, with $X$ normal, and let $A\subset X$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset such that $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$ and $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense. Normal spaces are unibranch, so the finite fibers of $f$ are connected by theorem A.7.1 , hence consist of at most one point. The image of $f$ is closed, because $f$ is proper, and contains the dense set $X\setminus A$; so $f$ is a continuous closed bijection, that is, a homeomorphism. Let $x\in X$ and $y=f^{-1}(x)$. Choose a neighborhood $V$ of $y$, relatively compact in the domain of a local model of $Y$, so that the coordinate functions of the model are bounded on $V$. Composed with $f^{-1}$, they are bounded holomorphic functions on $f(V)\setminus A$, where $f^{-1}$ is holomorphic, and $f(V)$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. By lemma A.3.4 they extend holomorphically to $f(V)$, and the extensions are the continuous functions $(	ext{coordinates})\circ f^{-1}$. Hence $f^{-1}$ is holomorphic. For the second assertion, over the dense open set $S\setminus \phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ there is a unique lift $\psi _0=
u ^{-1}\circ \phi $, because $
u $ is an isomorphism over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$. We extend it by the argument used for the uniqueness in the proof of theorem A.3.6 . Let $s\in S$ and $x=\phi (s)$, choose disjoint neighborhoods $W_ l$ of the finitely many points of $
u ^{-1}(x)$, relatively compact in domains $W'_ l$ of local models of $\widetilde X$, and a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ with $
u ^{-1}(U)\subset  igcup _ lW_ l$, which exists by properness. On $	au _{i-1}^{-1}(N_{i-1})$ we have $Z_{i-1}\subset C_ i\subset V(\mathfrak a_{i-1})=	au _{i-1}^{-1}(Z^\circ _{i-1})\subset Z_{i-1}$, so $C_ i$ coincides there with a copy of the open subset $Z^\circ _{i-1}$ of $Z$, which is pure of codimension $r$. The set $Z_{i-1}$ is connected, being the closure of the connected manifold $(Z_{i-1})_{\mathrm{reg}}$, so it lies in one connected component of the manifold $C_ i$, and this component has codimension $r$. By ( A.8 ) and proposition A.5.3 , near points over this component the Jacobian determinant of $\sigma _ i$ is, in any local coordinates, a unit times the $(r-1)$st power of a local equation of the exceptional divisor $E_ i=\sigma _ i^{-1}(C_ i)$. Since $Z_ i=ho _ i(E')$ lies over $Z_{i-1}\subset C_ i$, the function $J_{\sigma _ i}\circ ho _ i$ vanishes on $E'$; it does not vanish identically near any point, because $J_{\sigma _ i}$ vanishes only on $E_ i$, and $ho _ i^{-1}(E_ i)$ is nowhere dense, $ho _ i$ being proper and bimeromorphic as the composite of $f'$ with $\sigma _{i+1}\circ \cdots \circ \sigma _ t$ (corollary A.6.3 ). Hence it has positive order along $E'$. The Jacobians of the other blowups composed with the corresponding maps $ho _ j$ are holomorphic, so they have nonnegative order, and by the chain rule $J_\sigma \circ f'=\prod _ j(J_{\sigma _ j}\circ ho _ j)$. Thus \[  \operatorname {ord}_{E'}(J_\sigma \circ f')\geq 1.  \] Applying ( A.14 ) to $f\circ h=\sigma \circ f'$ and using Step 2, we obtain \[  0\leq \operatorname {ord}_{E'}J_{f'} =k-\operatorname {ord}_{E'}(J_\sigma \circ f')\leq k-1.  \] Step 4: conclusion. The pair $(M',E')$ represents the given prime divisor, as we see on the common smooth model $M'$, and $X'$ is a compact manifold. We repeat Step 3 with $X'$, $f'$ and $E'$ in place of $X$, $f$ and $E$. Each repetition in which the center has codimension at least two lowers the nonnegative integer $k$ by at least one, so after at most $k$ repetitions the center is a hypersurface on the current model, which is obtained from $X$ by a finite sequence of blowups with smooth centers, and it represents the given prime divisor. Finally, by lemma A.7.5 (2), principalizing the ideal of this hypersurface by theorem A.5.5 gives a further sequence of blowups with smooth centers, finite because the model is compact, on which the strict transform of the hypersurface is smooth and represents the same prime divisor. $\square$

title: Theorem A.7.1
text: Theorem A.7.1 . Let $f\colon Y\to X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map between complex spaces, and let $x\in X$ be a point at which the germ $(X,x)$ is irreducible. Then the fiber $f^{-1}(x)$ is connected. In particular, if $X$ is unibranch, every fiber of $f$ is connected. Proof. Choose a nowhere dense analytic subset $A\subset X$ such that $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense and $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$. Suppose that the compact fiber over $x$ is disconnected, and write it as the union of two disjoint nonempty compact sets. Since $Y$ is Hausdorff, they have disjoint open neighborhoods $V_1$ and $V_2$. Since $f$ is proper, hence closed, $U=X\setminus f(Y\setminus (V_1\cup V_2))$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ with $f^{-1}(U)\subset V_1\cup V_2$. As $(X,x)$ is irreducible, corollary A.3.9 allows us to shrink $U$ so that $U\setminus A$ is connected. Each set $V_ i\cap f^{-1}(U)$ is open and nonempty, so it meets the dense set $Y\setminus f^{-1}(A)$. Therefore $V_1$ and $V_2$ split $f^{-1}(U\setminus A)$ into two disjoint nonempty open sets. This contradicts the connectedness of $U\setminus A$, which is isomorphic to $f^{-1}(U\setminus A)$. $\square$

title: Corollary A.7.2
text:
Corollary A.7.2 . A finite bimeromorphic holomorphic map to a normal complex space is an isomorphism. Let $\phi \colon S	o X$ be a holomorphic map from a normal complex space to a complex space such that $\phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is nowhere dense in $S$. Then $\phi $ factors uniquely through the normalization $
u \colon \widetilde X	o X$: there is a unique holomorphic map $\psi \colon S	o \widetilde X$ with $
u \circ \psi =\phi $. Proof. Let $f\colon Y	o X$ be finite and bimeromorphic, with $X$ normal, and let $A\subset X$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset such that $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$ and $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense. Normal spaces are unibranch, so the finite fibers of $f$ are connected by theorem A.7.1 , hence consist of at most one point. The image of $f$ is closed, because $f$ is proper, and contains the dense set $X\setminus A$; so $f$ is a continuous closed bijection, that is, a homeomorphism. Let $x\in X$ and $y=f^{-1}(x)$. Choose a neighborhood $V$ of $y$, relatively compact in the domain of a local model of $Y$, so that the coordinate functions of the model are bounded on $V$. Composed with $f^{-1}$, they are bounded holomorphic functions on $f(V)\setminus A$, where $f^{-1}$ is holomorphic, and $f(V)$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. By lemma A.3.4 they extend holomorphically to $f(V)$, and the extensions are the continuous functions $(	ext{coordinates})\circ f^{-1}$. Hence $f^{-1}$ is holomorphic. For the second assertion, over the dense open set $S\setminus \phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ there is a unique lift $\psi _0=
u ^{-1}\circ \phi $, because $
u $ is an isomorphism over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$. We extend it by the argument used for the uniqueness in the proof of theorem A.3.6 . Let $s\in S$ and $x=\phi (s)$, choose disjoint neighborhoods $W_ l$ of the finitely many points of $
u ^{-1}(x)$, relatively compact in domains $W'_ l$ of local models of $\widetilde X$, and a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ with $
u ^{-1}(U)\subset  igcup _ lW_ l$, which exists by properness. Since $S$ is normal, hence unibranch, corollary A.3.9 gives a neighborhood $V$ of $s$ with $\phi (V)\subset U$ such that $V\setminus \phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is connected. Then $\psi _0$ maps this set into a single $W_ l$. The coordinate functions of $W'_ l$ composed with $\psi _0$ are bounded and extend holomorphically to $V$, by lemma A.3.4 ; the extended map takes values in $\overline{W_ l}\subset W'_ l$, and it satisfies the equations of the local model, which hold on a dense subset of $V$. This gives a holomorphic lift on $V$, with $
u \circ \psi =\phi $ by density. Lifts agree on the dense set where $\psi _0$ is defined, so these local lifts glue, and the lift is unique. $\square$

title: Proposition A.7.3
text: Proposition A.7.3 . A proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map $f\colon M'\to M$ between complex manifolds is an isomorphism outside an analytic subset $S$ of $M$ of codimension at least two. In particular, every irreducible hypersurface $D$ in $M$ has a well-defined strict transform in $M'$, namely the closure $D'$ of $f^{-1}(D\setminus S)$, which does not depend on the choice of $S$; it is an irreducible hypersurface, $f(D')=D$, and $f$ maps $D'$ isomorphically onto $D$ over the dense open subset $D\setminus S$ of $D$. Proof. We take for $S$ the image of the critical set of $f$; the main point is that a component of $S$ of codimension one would contain a point over which $f$ is finite, hence an isomorphism by corollary A.7.2 . Step 1: the set $S$. We may work over each connected component of $M$, of dimension $n$ say; every connected component of its inverse image has dimension $n$ as well, because it contains a nonempty open set mapped isomorphically onto an open subset of $M$, by lemma A.3.1 . The map $f$ is surjective, since its image is closed and dense. The critical set of $f$, where the Jacobian determinant vanishes in local coordinates, is analytic, and its image $S$ is analytic by theorem A.6.2 . Over $M\setminus S$ the map $f$ is proper and, by proposition 7.1.2 (1), a local biholomorphism, so its fibers are discrete and finite. They are connected by theorem A.7.1 , and nonempty; so they are single points, and $f$ is a bijective local biholomorphism, hence an isomorphism, over $M\setminus S$. Since $f$ is an isomorphism over a dense open subset of $M$, it has no critical points over this set, so $S$ does not meet it and is nowhere dense. Step 2: $S$ has codimension at least two. Suppose that $S$ has an irreducible component $D_0$ of codimension one. Choose a point of $(D_0)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ outside the other components of $S$, and a coordinate polydisc $U$ centered at it in which $D_0\cap U=S\cap U=\{ h=0\} $ for one of the coordinate functions $h$; then $D_0\cap U$ is a connected manifold. Let $A\subset M$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset such that $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense and $f$ is an isomorphism over $M\setminus A$. The function $h\circ f$ does not vanish identically on any connected component $V$ of $f^{-1}(U)$: otherwise $f$ would map the nonempty open set $V\setminus f^{-1}(A)$ isomorphically onto an open subset of $M$ contained in the hypersurface $D_0$, which is impossible. By proposition A.4.6 , $E=f^{-1}(D_0\cap U)$ is pure of dimension $n-1$. Let $K\subset D_0\cap U$ be a compact neighborhood of the chosen point in $D_0$. Only finitely many irreducible components $E_1,\ldots ,E_ k$ of $E$ meet the compact set $f^{-1}(K)$, and by theorem A.6.2 each image $f(E_ j)$ is an analytic subset of $D_0\cap U$. If its dimension is $n-1$, then $f(E_ j)$ contains an open subset of the connected manifold $D_0\cap U$ and therefore equals it, since proper analytic subsets of connected manifolds are nowhere dense (lemma A.1.6 ); we then call $E_ j$ dominating. Otherwise $f(E_ j)$ has dimension at most $n-2$. For a dominating $E_ j$, the maximal rank of $f$ restricted to the connected manifold $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$, as a map into the coordinate hyperplane $D_0\cap U$, is $n-1$. Otherwise $f((E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}})$ would be $\mathcal H^{2n-2}$-null by lemma A.2.12 (1); so would $f((E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}})$, by the same lemma, since $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ has dimension at most $n-2$ by corollary A.2.10 (1) and is therefore, by (2) of the same corollary, a finite union of complex submanifolds of dimension at most $n-2$; and $f(E_ j)$ would have dimension at most $n-2$ by lemma A.2.12 (2). Let $R_ j$ be the union of $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the regular points where this rank is less than $n-1$. It is analytic. Indeed, near a point of $E_ j$, let $e$ be a local equation of the irreducible hypersurface $E_ j$ as in lemma A.2.16 , and let $f'$ be the map formed by the $n-1$ coordinates of $f$ in the coordinate hyperplane $D_0\cap U$. At a regular point $p$ of $E_ j$ we have $\mathrm de(p)\neq 0$ and $T_ pE_ j=\ker \mathrm de(p)$, so the rank of $f'|_{E_ j}$ at $p$ is $n-1$ exactly when the Jacobian determinant of $(e,f')$ does not vanish at $p$. Hence $R_ j$ is, near this point, the union of the analytic set $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the zero set in $E_ j$ of this Jacobian determinant. It is different from $E_ j$, because the rank $n-1$ is attained on $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$; so it is nowhere dense in the irreducible set $E_ j$ and has dimension at most $n-2$, by corollary A.2.14 (2), and $f(R_ j)$ is analytic of dimension at most $n-2$, by theorem A.6.2 and lemma A.2.12 (3). Choose a point $a$ in the interior of $K$ outside the finitely many sets $f(E_ j)$, $E_ j$ not dominating, and $f(R_ j)$, $E_ j$ dominating. Let $p\in f^{-1}(a)$. Since $f^{-1}(a)\subset E\cap f^{-1}(K)$, the point $p$ lies on some of the components $E_1,\ldots ,E_ k$. Each of them that contains $p$ is dominating, and $p\notin R_ j$, so $f|_{E_ j}$ is a local biholomorphism at $p$ onto an open subset of $D_0$, by proposition 7.1.2 (1) in charts, and $p$ is isolated in $f^{-1}(a)\cap E_ j$. The components of $E$ not containing $p$ form a locally finite family of closed sets, so near $p$ the set $f^{-1}(a)$ lies in the union of the components containing $p$, and $p$ is isolated in $f^{-1}(a)$. Thus $f^{-1}(a)$ is discrete, and being compact, it is finite. Let $p_1,\ldots ,p_ l$ be the points of $f^{-1}(a)$, and choose disjoint coordinate balls $B_1,\ldots ,B_ l$ around them. By properness there is a neighborhood $U_0$ of $a$ with $f^{-1}(U_0)\subset \bigcup _ iB_ i$. The fibers of $f$ over $U_0$ are compact analytic subsets of these balls, hence finite by corollary A.4.3 . Thus $f$ is finite and bimeromorphic over the manifold $U_0$, which is normal, and it is an isomorphism over $U_0$ by corollary A.7.2 . In particular $f$ has no critical points over $U_0$, which contradicts $a\in S$. Therefore $S$ has codimension at least two. Step 3: strict transforms. Let $D$ be an irreducible hypersurface. Then $S\cap D$ has dimension at most $n-2$, so $D\setminus S$ is dense in $D$ by corollary A.2.14 (2). The closure $D'$ of $f^{-1}(D\setminus S)=f^{-1}(D)\setminus f^{-1}(S)$ is analytic by lemma A.2.5 , and $f$ is an isomorphism from $D'\setminus f^{-1}(S)=f^{-1}(D\setminus S)$ onto $D\setminus S$. The set $f(D')$ is closed, because $f$ is proper, it contains the dense subset $D\setminus S$ of $D$, and it is contained in the closed set $D$; so $f(D')=D$. The set $Q=f^{-1}(D_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus S)$ is a connected manifold of dimension $n-1$, because $D_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus S$ is connected by lemma A.1.7 ; it is open in $D'$ and dense in $D'$, since $D_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus S$ is open and dense in $D\setminus S$. Hence $Q$ consists of regular points of $D'$ and lies in a single connected component of $(D')_{\mathrm{reg}}$, whose closure, an irreducible component of $D'$ by corollary A.2.13 , contains $\overline Q=D'$; so $D'$ is irreducible, of dimension $n-1$. Finally, if $S_1$ is another analytic subset of codimension at least two off which $f$ is an isomorphism, then $D\setminus (S\cup S_1)$ is dense in $D\setminus S$ and in $D\setminus S_1$, by corollary A.2.14 (2), so $f^{-1}(D\setminus (S\cup S_1))$ is dense in both $f^{-1}(D\setminus S)$ and $f^{-1}(D\setminus S_1)$, and the two closures agree. $\square$

title: Definition A.7.4
text: Definition A.7.4 . Let $X$ be a complex space. A prime divisor over $X$ is represented by a pair consisting of a smooth model $M\to X$ and an irreducible hypersurface $F\subset M$; two pairs are identified if the strict transforms of their hypersurfaces, in the sense of proposition A.7.3 , agree on a common smooth model. The prime divisor is exceptional if the image of $F$ in $X$ has codimension at least two.

title: Lemma A.7.5
text: Lemma A.7.5 . Let $X$ be a complex space. The identification of pairs in definition A.7.4 is an equivalence relation, and the image in $X$ of the hypersurface $F$ of a representative $(M,F)$ depends only on the prime divisor. Let $(M,F)$ represent a prime divisor over $X$, and let $g\colon M'\to M$ be the composite of the principalization of $\mathcal I_ F$ given by theorem A.5.5 with the empty divisor. Then $g$ is proper and bimeromorphic, the strict transform $F'$ of $F$ is a smooth irreducible hypersurface of $M'$, and $(M',F')$ represents the same prime divisor. In particular, every prime divisor over $X$ has a representative $(M,F)$ with $F$ smooth. Proof. We begin with two remarks used in the proof of (1). First, two maps from a smooth model $M_3$ to a smooth model $M_1$ that commute with the maps to $X$ agree. Indeed, let $U\subset X$ be the complement of a nowhere dense analytic subset over which both models are isomorphisms; the two maps agree over $U$, and the part of $M_3$ over $U$ is dense, by lemma A.3.1 . Second, strict transforms are compatible with composition. Let $g\colon P\to N$ and $h\colon N\to M$ be proper bimeromorphic maps between complex manifolds, so that $h\circ g$ is proper and bimeromorphic by corollary A.6.3 , and let $D\subset M$ be an irreducible hypersurface, with strict transform $D^ N$ in $N$. We claim that the strict transform of $D^ N$ under $g$ is the strict transform $D^ P$ of $D$ under $h\circ g$. Let $S_ h,S_{hg}\subset M$ and $S_ g\subset N$ be analytic subsets of codimension at least two as in proposition A.7.3 for $h$, $h\circ g$ and $g$, and let $T=S_ h\cup S_{hg}\cup h(S_ g)$, which is analytic of codimension at least two by theorem A.6.2 and lemma A.2.12 (3). The set $O=D^ N\cap h^{-1}(M\setminus T)=h^{-1}(D\setminus T)$ is open in $D^ N$, nonempty, and does not meet $S_ g$; its complement $D^ N\cap h^{-1}(T)$ is an analytic subset of the irreducible set $D^ N$ different from $D^ N$, hence nowhere dense by corollary A.2.14 (2). So $O$ is dense in $D^ N\setminus S_ g$, and since $g$ is an isomorphism over $N\setminus S_ g$, the strict transform of $D^ N$ under $g$ is the closure of $g^{-1}(O)=(h\circ g)^{-1}(D\setminus T)$. By the independence of the choice of $S_{hg}$ in proposition A.7.3 , applied with $T$, this closure is also $D^ P$. Now let $(M_ i,F_ i)$, $i=1,2,3$, be pairs such that $(M_1,F_1)$ and $(M_2,F_2)$ are identified on a common smooth model $N_{12}$, and $(M_2,F_2)$ and $(M_3,F_3)$ on $N_{23}$. Let $P$ be a common smooth model of $N_{12}$ and $N_{23}$, and let $p_ i\colon P\to M_ i$ be the composite maps; by the first remark, the two composite maps $P\to M_2$, through $N_{12}$ and through $N_{23}$, coincide. By the second remark, the strict transforms of $F_1$ and $F_2$ under $p_1$ and $p_2$ are the strict transforms in $P$ of their strict transforms in $N_{12}$, which agree; similarly for $F_2$ and $F_3$. Hence $F_1$ and $F_3$ have the same strict transform in $P$, and the identification is transitive; it is reflexive, with $M_1$ itself as common smooth model, and symmetric by definition. Since $p_ i$ maps the strict transform of $F_ i$ onto $F_ i$ (proposition A.7.3 ), the images of $F_1$ and $F_3$ in $X$ both equal the image of their common strict transform in $P$; so the image of $F$ in $X$ depends only on the prime divisor. We now prove (2). Let $(M,F)$ represent a prime divisor. The ideal $\mathcal I_ F$ is coherent by theorem A.2.8 , and it is not identically zero on any component of $M$, because $F$ is nowhere dense. Let $g\colon M'\to M$ be as in (2), so that $\mathcal I_ F\mathcal O_{M'}=\mathcal O_{M'}(-H)$ with $H$ an effective divisor whose support has simple normal crossings; $g$ is proper, it is an isomorphism off $g^{-1}(F)$, and $g^{-1}(F)$, the support of $H$, is nowhere dense, so $g$ is bimeromorphic. The strict transform $F'$ of $F$ is an irreducible hypersurface contained in the support of $H$, so by corollary A.2.14 (4) and (3) it is one of its irreducible components, which are smooth. The pair $(M',F')$ represents the same prime divisor, as we see on the common smooth model $M'$, which is a smooth model of $X$ by corollary A.6.3 . $\square$

title: Theorem A.7.6
A.14
text: A.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:divisor-jacobian-order-chain} \operatorname {ord}_ E J_{g\circ h} =\operatorname {ord}_ E J_ h+ \operatorname {ord}_ E(J_ g\circ h), \end{equation}

title: A.8 Plurisubharmonic functions on reduced spaces
text:
A.8 Plurisubharmonic functions on reduced spaces At a singular point of a complex space there is no intrinsic complex Hessian, so we define plurisubharmonic functions on a complex space as local restrictions of plurisubharmonic functions on ambient domains. Their compositions with holomorphic discs are then subharmonic, and together with the curves of section A.4 this gives a maximum principle on compact spaces and local upper bounds near analytic subsets of codimension at least two. Definition A.8.1 . Let $X$ be a complex space. A function $u\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty )$ is locally plurisubharmonic if every point of $X$ has a local model, which identifies a neighborhood of the point with an analytic subset of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ N$, and a ball $V\subset \Omega $ around the point such that $u$ is the restriction to $X\cap V$ of a function on $V$ that is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. We write $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ if, in addition, $u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any irreducible component of $X$, the components being defined as in corollary A.2.13 . Locally plurisubharmonic functions are allowed to be identically $-\infty $ on some components; we use them in this generality when only local properties are needed. The following lemma shows that this definition does not depend on the local models, and that it agrees with the definition of section 8.2 on complex manifolds. Lemma A.8.2 . Let $X$ be a complex space. Let $u$ be locally plurisubharmonic on $X$. For every local model of a neighborhood of a point of $X$, there is a ball $V$ around the point in the ambient domain such that $u$ is the restriction to $X\cap V$ of a function on $V$ that is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. If $u$ is locally plurisubharmonic on $X$ and $F\colon Y	o X$ is a holomorphic map of complex spaces, then $u\circ F$ is locally plurisubharmonic on $Y$. In particular, if $Y$ is a one-dimensional complex manifold, such as a disc, then $u\circ F$ is subharmonic, in the sense of definition 3.1.1 , in every local coordinate of $Y$, and on the whole disc if $Y$ is a disc. If $X$ is a complex manifold, then a function on $X$ is locally plurisubharmonic if and only if, on each connected component of $X$, it is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Moreover, $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ agrees with the set defined in section 8.2 . Proof. We prove (1) and the first assertion of (2) together. Let $u$ be locally plurisubharmonic on $X$, let $F\colon Y	o X$ be holomorphic, and let $y\in Y$. Choose a local model of a neighborhood of $F(y)$, with ambient coordinates $w$ and a ball $V$ around $F(y)$ on which $u$ is the restriction of a function $v$ that is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, and an arbitrary local model of a neighborhood of $y$, with ambient coordinates $z$. By the definition of holomorphic maps and of $\mathcal O_ Y$, the components of $F$ in the $w$-model extend holomorphically to a neighborhood of $y$ in the $z$-ambient space, and their joint extension $G$, being continuous with $G(y)=F(y)$, maps a smaller ball $V'$ around $y$ into $V$. By proposition 8.2.3 , $v\circ G$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $V'$, and its restriction to $Y\cap V'$ is $u\circ F$. Hence $u\circ F$ is locally plurisubharmonic, with respect to every local model of $Y$. For $Y=X$ and $F$ the identity, with two local models at the same point, this is (1). If $Y$ is a one-dimensional complex manifold, its holomorphic charts are local models. By what we have just proved, $u\circ F$ is therefore, in local coordinates near each point of $Y$, plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, that is, subharmonic in the sense of definition 3.1.1 . Subharmonicity is a local property, so $u\circ F$ is subharmonic in every local coordinate, and on the whole disc if $Y$ is a disc. (3) Holomorphic charts are local models. So by (1), every point of $X$ has a coordinate ball on which a locally plurisubharmonic function $u$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, and by lemma 8.2.4 , $u$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each connected component of $X$. Conversely, a function with this property is locally plurisubharmonic, with the charts as local models, since its expressions in charts with connected domains are plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. The irreducible components of the manifold $X$ are its connected components, by corollary A.2.13 . Hence $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$, in the sense of definition A.8.1 , consists of the functions that are plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $X$, which are the plurisubharmonic functions in the sense of section 8.2 , since plurisubharmonicity is a local property there. $\square$ Proposition A.8.3 . A locally plurisubharmonic function on a compact connected complex space is constant, possibly equal to $-\infty $. Proof. Let $u$ be locally plurisubharmonic on the compact connected space $X$. It is upper semicontinuous, so it attains its maximum $M\in [-\infty ,\infty )$. If $M=-\infty $, then $u\equiv -\infty $. Suppose that $M$ is finite, and let $x$ be a point with $u(x)=M$. We show that $u=M$ near $x$. If $x$ is an isolated point, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, let $X_1$ be a branch of $(X,x)$ of positive dimension, and take a parametrization of $(X_1,x)$, with its connected covering locus $X_{1,\delta }$, dense in the representative $X_1$. By proposition A.4.2 , applied to the subgerm consisting of the singular locus of $X$ and the points of $X_1$ outside $X_{1,\delta }$, there is a nonconstant holomorphic curve $\gamma $ with $\gamma (0)=x$ and $\gamma (t)\in X_{1,\delta }\cap X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ for $t
eq 0$. The function $u\circ \gamma $ is subharmonic by lemma A.8.2 (2), and it attains its finite maximum $M$ at $0$; by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) it equals $M$ near $0$. Thus $u$ attains the value $M$ at points of $X_{1,\delta }$. By lemma A.8.2 (2) and (3), applied to the inclusion of the connected manifold $X_{1,\delta }$, the restriction of $u$ to $X_{1,\delta }$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, hence plurisubharmonic, since it takes the value $M$. On a coordinate ball around a point where $u=M$, it is subharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 , and it attains its maximum $M$ at the center, so it equals $M$ on this ball by proposition 3.1.4 . Thus the set where $u=M$ is open in $X_{1,\delta }$; it is closed by upper semicontinuity and nonempty, so $u=M$ on $X_{1,\delta }$. Since $X_{1,\delta }$ is dense in $X_1$, upper semicontinuity gives $u\geq M$, hence $u=M$, on all of $X_1$. Doing this for each branch, we find that $u=M$ on a neighborhood of $x$. Hence the set $\{ u=M\} $ is open. It is also closed, because $\{ u<M\} $ is open for an upper semicontinuous function bounded above by $M$. Since $X$ is connected, $u\equiv M$. $\square$ Proposition A.8.4 . Let $A$ be an analytic subset of a complex space $X$ such that, at every point of $A$, the intersection of $A$ with each irreducible branch of $X$ has codimension at least two in that branch. Then every locally plurisubharmonic function on $X\setminus A$ is locally bounded above near $A$. Proof. Let $u$ be locally plurisubharmonic on $X\setminus A$, and let $x\in A$. We bound $u$ over a circle that avoids the image of $A$ under a finite projection, and carry the bound inward along one-dimensional slices by the maximum principle. It suffices to bound $u$ from above near $x$ on each branch of $(X,x)$, and the restriction of $u$ to a branch is locally plurisubharmonic by lemma A.8.2 (2); so we may work on the representative $X_1$ of a branch on a parametrization polydisc. Let $X_2,\ldots ,X_ p$ be representatives of the other branches. The hypothesis is inherited by $X_1$ near $x$. Indeed, let $y\in X_1$ be close to $x$, and let $Y$ be a branch of $(X_1,y)$.
