For the constraints by multiplier ideals used in the chapter on envelopes of that book, proposition 16.6.1 combines the uniform valuative criterion theorem 12.6.9 with lemma 16.6.2 , the formula $\nu (v,E)=\inf _ j\nu (v_ j,E)$ for the Lelong numbers along divisors of an upper envelope $v=(\sup _ jv_ j)^*$. In the proof of this formula, a local pullback argument shows that these Lelong numbers are preserved under the countable selection of Choquet's lemma. The proposition thus provides the closure property used in [ Propositions 3.2.6 and 3.2.9 , XiaSampleBook ] ; the construction itself and its algebraic consequences are not treated here. The comparison of capacities in section 16.9 follows Lu [ arXiv version, Lemmas 3.1–3.4 and Theorem 3.5, pp. 8–13 , Lu21 ] . Integration by parts for bounded potentials on a compact manifold, lemma 15.4.2 , is derived from the calculus of gradients in section 9.13 , and, together with approximation by smooth bounded potentials, it gives the weighted estimate lemma 16.9.2 . The envelopes with increasing penalties of lemma 16.9.3 provide the concentration on compact sets and the two growth bounds, which replace the properties of relative extremal functions quoted in the preprint. The comparison then proceeds in three steps: powers of model potentials in Kähler classes (proposition 16.9.6 ), comparison downwards for potentials of full mass (lemma 16.9.7 ), and comparison in both directions (theorem 16.9.8 ). Finally, proposition 16.9.9 compares, by a local extension construction, these capacities with the local capacities of chapter 9 ; in particular, local convergence in capacity implies convergence in each relative capacity.

title: B.17 Relative energy and integration by parts
search_title: Relative energy and integration by parts
text: B.17 Relative energy and integration by parts The identity for differences of bounded type, lemma 17.1.2 , follows [ arXiv version, Lemma 4.1, pp. 13–15 , Lu21 ] . Its proof reduces to bounded potentials by truncation, first for a strictly positive background; an expansion in polynomials then removes this restriction. The general integration by parts formula, theorem 17.1.3 , follows the argument by differentiation and polarization in [ arXiv version, proof of Theorem 1.2, pp. 15–16 , Lu21 ] . In his introduction, pp. 1–3, Lu credits the earlier integration by parts formula to Mingchen Xia. The general formula is stated in the introduction of [ Theorem 1.1 and discussion, pp. 1–2 , Xia2019v1 ] (first arXiv version), which also describes a proof by a projective construction; the proof followed here is Lu's later argument with capacities. Relative energy classes and the relative energy are defined in [ Definitions 3.1.5–3.1.6 , XiaSampleBook ] , and the cocycle formula for potentials of bounded type, the bounds by tangents, concavity and continuity along decreasing sequences are [ Lemmas 3.1.3–3.1.5 and Proposition 3.1.16 , XiaSampleBook ] . In proposition 17.2.3 the first variation of the energy along a segment is computed directly from the integral formula for the energy and the integration by parts theorem, and the cocycle formula follows by integrating it. In proposition 17.2.6 , proposition 17.2.7 the energy is extended by means of the canonical truncations $\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $, and continuity is proved for decreasing nets, not only for sequences, the limit being the pointwise limit. For theorem 17.2.8 , lemma 17.2.11 , proposition 17.2.12 compare [ Proposition 3.1.17, Lemma 3.1.6, Corollary 3.1.6 and Proposition 3.1.18 , XiaSampleBook ] . In our proof, a uniform bound at finite levels for the integral of a potential against its own Monge–Ampère measure shows that finite energy by itself implies full mass. Continuity of the energy along increasing nets, proposition 17.3.1 , follows [ Proposition 3.1.20 , XiaSampleBook ] ; the uniform bound for the tails is ( 17.25 ). The proof of [ Proposition 3.1.21 , XiaSampleBook ] uses an exponential Monge–Ampère equation; in proposition 17.3.6 we instead integrate the bound for the measures of rooftop envelopes on contact sets, corollary 16.2.6 . This closure of finite energy under rooftop envelopes guarantees that the slices of Perron segments have finite energy. The closure under upper envelopes of families and the envelopes of mutual singularities follow [ Propositions 3.1.23–3.1.24 , XiaSampleBook ] . The derivative of the energy along affine segments, proposition 17.3.8 , also appears in [ Lemma 3.1.11 , XiaSampleBook ] . Here it follows from the cocycle formula, which is polynomial in the parameter. The family of smooth potentials on $\mathbb P^1$ in example 17.3.10 shows that convergence in $L^1$ does not imply convergence of the energy. The characterization of solutions as maximizers of a functional and the derivative of the energy of projections (theorem 17.4.4 , proposition 17.4.3 ) follow the variational approach of [ Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.2, pp. 207–209 , BBGZ13 ] , whose normalization of the operator agrees with ours. We prove the derivative of the energy of projections directly, with a model potential as reference, from the theorem on contact sets and the bounds of the energy by tangents. For Monge–Ampère equations relative to a model potential, with prescribed measure and with an exponential factor, compare [ arXiv version, Theorem 4.3, p. 20; Theorem 5.3 and Lemma 5.4, pp. 24–25 , DDNL19log ] . That source uses $\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial $; its potential corresponding to our $u$ is $u/(2\pi )$, and its exponential parameter is $2\pi \lambda $. We solve the prescribed-measure equation with bounded densities (theorem 17.4.5 ) and the exponential equation for every finite non-pluripolar measure (theorem 17.4.11 ) by compactness in the variational approach. The relative comparison and domination principles give proposition 17.4.6 for every finite non-pluripolar measure, when the reference has positive mass. For the continuity of integrals against a fixed non-pluripolar measure compare [ Theorem 3.10, pp. 203–205 , BBGZ13 ] . Lemma 17.4.9 proves the case of uniformly bounded functions. The upper limit is controlled outside a pluripolar set; for the lower limit we use convex combinations of the tails with almost minimal $L^2$ norm for the given measure, which form a Cauchy sequence by the parallelogram identity. Applied to exponentials, the lemma allows the same variational construction for arbitrary finite non-pluripolar measures. The lower bound for limits in lemma 17.4.12 follows [ arXiv version, Lemma 2.8, pp. 12–13 , DDNL19log ] ; a fixed lower measure is restricted before weak limits are taken. The existence of solutions with prescribed measure, theorem 17.4.13 , is obtained instead by letting the exponential parameter tend to zero; for the existence statement compare Theorem 4.7, p. 23, of that preprint. Uniqueness for the relative equations is proved in [ Theorem 4.29 and its proof, pp. 2079–2080 , DDNL18mono ] by adapting the argument of Kołodziej and Dinew based on the concentration of mass; in that section the model reference has positive mass and small unbounded locus. Our theorem 17.4.14 allows an arbitrary model reference of positive mass. It follows the same strategy, using the existence theorem, the comparison and domination principles for full mass and the lower bound for products with respect to a common measure (corollary 15.4.7 ); the domination principle turns inequalities almost everywhere for the common measure into pointwise inequalities. The iteration with capacities in theorem 17.4.15 , corollary 17.4.17 follows [ arXiv version, Theorem 3.3 and its proof, pp. 14–15 , DDNL19log ] . Here the measure is assumed to be dominated by the power $1+\delta $ of the capacity, and an iteration with geometrically decreasing steps shows directly that the capacities of the relevant sublevel sets vanish beyond a finite level. The uniform bound for moments is corollary 14.2.2 . The estimates of volume and of measures with $L^ p$ densities by capacity (proposition 16.9.4 , corollary 16.9.5 ) follow [ Proposition 4.30, pp. 2081–2082 , DDNL18mono ] , which assumes a small unbounded locus and uses uniform Skoda integrability; the formulation for arbitrary model potentials is [ arXiv version, Lemma 3.9 and Proposition 3.10, p. 18 , DDNL19log ] . Here the prerequisites are the uniform exponential bound corollary 14.2.3 and the penalized envelopes of lemma 16.9.3 . At fixed potentials, the background $2\pi \theta $ of the source gives measures and capacities that are $(2\pi )^ n$ times ours, while their ratios to the mass of the reference are unchanged. The criterion that a class containing a current of positive non-pluripolar mass is big, which is used in [ Proposition 2.4.1 , XiaSampleBook ] , is [ Proposition 1.22, p. 222 , BEGZ10 ] . There the criterion is attributed to Boucksom; in the published article [ Section 4.3, Theorem 4.7, pp. 1057–1061 , Bou02b ] the numbering differs from that citation, and the volume is defined through the determinant of the absolutely continuous part. Our proof of theorem 17.4.20 uses instead the Monge–Ampère equations of section 17.4 , solved in the big classes obtained by adding $\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ to the given class, the mixed trace estimate lemma 17.4.19 and Lamari's criterion. The proof also shows that a pseudo-effective class is big if and only if its volume is positive, without using an identity between the determinant volume and the non-pluripolar volume. Lamari's duality criterion, lemma 17.4.18 , is [ Lemma 3.3 and its proof, pp. 275–276 , Lamari1999 ] ; the cohomological statement on annihilators is on p. 267. We prove the Kähler case by extending a positive linear functional with the Hahn–Banach argument, together with the scalar Poisson equation and the identity for the trace and the Hodge star proved earlier. The pointwise trace estimate for smooth forms and the integrated Cauchy–Schwarz argument are [ Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and their proofs, pp. 4–6 , Popovici2014v1 ] (first arXiv version). Lemma 17.4.19 states the estimate for an arbitrary strictly positive form $\tau $ of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, and extends it, by local decreasing convolution and linearization of the determinant, to currents whose local potentials are locally bounded outside a closed set of Lebesgue measure zero; the first factor on its left-hand side is the full mass of $S\wedge \tau $, including any mass on the poles. The preprint writes $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $ for potentials, whereas our proof uses the normalization of this book throughout. The inequality between mixed masses and the geometric mean of the masses, with its consequences for the concavity of roots and logarithms of masses, is [ arXiv version, Theorem 6.1 and its proof, p. 26 , DDNL19log ] ; it is the result referred to in [ Theorem 2.4.1 , XiaSampleBook ] . Theorem 17.4.23 follows the proof in the source by relative Monge–Ampère equations. Because this proof uses the criterion for bigness, the theorem comes after that criterion; the case of vanishing masses is treated separately. At fixed potentials, the operator $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $ of the source multiplies all measures of top degree by $(2\pi )^ n$; by homogeneity this factor cancels in the inequality. The identities for envelopes of arbitrary mass in theorem 17.5.3 are [ Theorem 1.2, p. 4 , PSWZ26 ] , an arXiv preprint; they include potentials of zero mass, to which theorem 16.4.7 does not apply. Their proof there (Section 5, Theorem 5.1, pp. 37–42) uses a uniform bound for normalized tails and the recovery of volume for perturbations of positive mass; proposition 17.5.1 follows this approach. Monotonicity gives the limit directly, and the solutions with constant density that are needed are provided by theorem 17.4.5 . Applying the limit to each member of the family $\mathcal F_ u$ that defines the ceiling proves the identity $(\sup _{v\in \mathcal F_ u}v)^*=P_\theta [u]$, without a separate formula for the regularization of the ceiling and without a second family of perturbations. The source uses the operator $\mathrm{dd^ c}=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /\pi $ (p. 7). At fixed potentials, its backgrounds $2\theta $ and $2\omega $ give measures of top degree that are $2^ n$ times ours, while the normalized tail ratios and the constant densities of the auxiliary equations are unchanged.

title: B.18 Weak geodesics
text: B.18 Weak geodesics The definition of subgeodesics on a strip and their convexity and boundary behavior (definition 17.6.1 , proposition 17.6.4 ) follow [ Definition 4.1.1 and Proposition 4.1.2 , XiaSampleBook ] , and lemma 17.6.6 , lemma 17.6.5 , theorem 17.6.8 follow the arguments of [ Proposition 4.1.3, Lemma 4.1.1 and Proposition 4.2.1 , XiaSampleBook ] . Rooftop envelopes and the identity for envelopes of mutual singularities show that the Perron segment is not identically $-\infty $ and has the prescribed endpoints. The formula of proposition 17.6.10 , which expresses the Perron segment through rooftop envelopes and a Legendre transform, follows by taking supporting affine functions of the convex function of time on each fiber where it is finite; the regularization in the space variable is retained. That the relative energy is affine along weak geodesics, theorem 17.7.3 , follows the argument of [ Proposition 4.3.3 , XiaSampleBook ] on a compact extension of the strip. The proof uses the fiber integration formula corollary 15.5.1 and integration by parts for bounded differences, theorem 17.1.3 . The vanishing of the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of a maximal plurisubharmonic function, bounded or not, is lemma 17.7.1 ; it is proved with the homogeneous balayages of the bounded truncations. The maximality of the complexified Perron segment, lemma 17.7.2 , is proved with its envelope under rotations of the annulus, or under imaginary translations of the strip. Approximating the endpoints by their decreasing truncations then extends the identity from potentials of bounded type to potentials of finite energy.

title: B.19 Extremal slopes and singularity cutoffs
text: B.19 Extremal slopes and singularity cutoffs The identity for the supremum of the difference along a weak geodesic is [ Proposition 4.2.2 , XiaSampleBook ] , in the chapter on rays; for the infimum, [ Proposition 4.2.3 , XiaSampleBook ] refers to an analogous argument. Proposition 17.8.1 gives this argument by reversing the segment and using canonical representatives; it also identifies the essential extrema with the extrema over the set where the potentials are finite. The assertion on bounded shifts that follows [ Example 4.3.1 , XiaSampleBook ] is justified there by comparing long segments with truncated endpoints. Proposition 17.8.2 makes this comparison quantitative: a bound $C$ at the terminal endpoint contributes at most $Cs/T$ at time $s$ on a segment of length $T$. Passing to the regularized limits as $T\to \infty $ gives invariance under bounded perturbations and monotonicity with respect to the preorder $\preceq $ of singularities. The construction of the associated rays and the formula for their energy in terms of mixed masses are not treated here.

title: B.20 Convex duality and real Monge–Ampère measures
search_title: Convex duality and real Monge–Ampère measures
text: B.20 Convex duality and real Monge–Ampère measures For the separation of convex sets and for the local regularity and subgradients of convex functions (lemma 18.1.2 , proposition 18.1.3 ) compare [ Theorem 2.1.10 and Corollaries 2.1.11–2.1.13, pp. 44–45; Theorem 2.1.22, pp. 55–56 , Hor07 ] . Closed convex functions and Legendre conjugation are treated in [ Propositions 2.2.1–2.2.2 and Theorem 2.2.4, pp. 66–68; Theorem 2.2.5, pp. 68–69; Theorem 2.2.8, p. 70 , Hor07 ] . The corresponding duality statements in this book are theorem 18.2.2 , proposition 18.2.3 ; in the formula for a sum in which the infimum is attained, both functions are assumed to be finite on the whole space. The classes of convex functions, the formulas involving slope bodies and the real Monge–Ampère measures follow the appendix on convex analysis of [ XiaSampleBook ] ; as there, the factor $n!$ is kept, with Lebesgue measure normalized by the lattice. In theorem 18.4.1 , measurability with respect to the completed Lebesgue measure and countable additivity are proved using the fact that the inverse of the subgradient map is single-valued almost everywhere. Theorem 18.4.2 concerns vague convergence, and example 18.4.3 shows that narrow convergence requires an additional condition that prevents mass from escaping to infinity. The mixed measures of proposition 18.4.4 are obtained from the positivity of matrices, convolution and polarization. We keep the convention of the source for full mass when a slope body has empty interior, and example 18.3.5 shows that the hypotheses on slope bodies in the formula for sums cannot be omitted. The lemma on the finiteness of rotation-invariant plurisubharmonic functions, [ Lemma 1.2.1 , XiaSampleBook ] , is proved there by the logarithmic convexity of circle means, and it provides the finiteness step in [ Lemma 5.2.1 , XiaSampleBook ] . Proposition 18.1.5 , Corollary 18.1.6 give a direct proof, by smoothing and the fact that the complex Hessian of a function invariant under imaginary translations is one quarter of its real Hessian; this proof does not use Kiselman's minimum principle. For the conjugate of the maximum of finitely many convex functions, the convex appendix of [ XiaSampleBook ] uses [ Theorem 16.5 , Roc70 ] . Lemma 18.5.1 proves the case of functions whose domains lie in a compact set, which is the case of the finite suprema in the chapter on ample toric varieties, [ Proposition 5.2.4 , XiaSampleBook ] ; compactness takes care of points whose weights tend to zero. The computation of the energy in [ Proposition 5.2.9, Step 1 , XiaSampleBook ] passes to the limit in integrals of a bounded function on a noncompact space against real Monge–Ampère measures; lemma 18.5.2 justifies this passage to the limit by a cutoff and the convergence of total masses. The asymptotic count of lattice points used in [ Section 5.2 , XiaSampleBook ] follows from the case of saturated cones in [ Theorem 1.15, p. 939 , KK12 ] , where Kaveh and Khovanskii reduce the assertion to Riemann sums; their introduction states the more general theorem on the growth of semigroups on p. 929. Theorem 18.6.3 gives a complete proof for convex bodies by means of fundamental cells, allowing arbitrary translations, bodies of smaller dimension and sublinear errors at the boundary. The continuity of volume needed in its proof is proposition 18.6.2 , and corollary 18.6.4 isolates the two-sided bound used in the toric computation of dimensions. The chapter on ample toric varieties in [ XiaSampleBook ] relies on the theory of toric varieties developed in [ CLS11 ] . Here the smooth projective toric variety of a Delzant lattice polytope is constructed directly from its characters in theorem 18.7.3 ; its fan and its boundary divisors are identified in proposition 18.8.1 , proposition 18.8.2 , and the basis of global sections given by characters, theorem 18.8.5 , is obtained from Laurent expansions in the charts at the vertices. No general classification of toric varieties is needed. The potential of theorem 18.9.1 , built from the function $G_0=\sum _\rho \ell _\rho \log \ell _\rho $, is Guillemin's reference potential. For the Legendre computation compare [ Proposition 2, pp. 7–8; Theorem 1, pp. 9–10 , CDG03v1 ] (first arXiv version). That source uses $G=\frac12\sum _\rho \ell _\rho \log \ell _\rho $ and holomorphic logarithmic coordinates $y+\mathrm i\theta $; with $x=2y=\log |w|^2$ we have $G_0=2G$ and $F_0(x)=2F(x/2)$, up to an additive constant. Its convention $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f=-\mathrm df\circ J$ gives $\mathrm d\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=2\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $; with the curvature convention of this book the form is divided by $2\pi $. Smooth extension and strict positivity in the monomial charts are proved by the inverse function theorem at every face, including the vertices.

title: B.21 Analytic spaces and modifications
text: B.21 Analytic spaces and modifications The Weierstrass division theorem and the Noetherian property of the ring of germs of holomorphic functions (proposition A.1.1 , proposition A.1.2 ) follow [ Chapter II, (2.3)–(2.7), pp. 80–81 , DemBook ] . For coherent sheaves and Oka's coherence theorem (lemma A.1.4 , theorem A.1.5 ) compare [ Chapter II, (3.8)–(3.22), pp. 87–90 , DemBook ] . Local irreducible components, local parametrization, the Nullstellensatz, dimension and Cartan's theorem on the coherence of the ideal sheaf of an analytic set are treated in [ Chapter II, (4.1)–(4.31), pp. 91–100 , DemBook ] . The algebraic facts on finite field extensions and discriminants used in these constructions are proved in lemma A.2.2 by linear algebra over the field of fractions, with matrices of multiplication and the trace form, and they are applied in theorem A.2.3 . In our proof of Cartan's theorem, theorem A.2.8 , a single denominator works at all nearby stalks, which is more than finite generation of each stalk. The Nullstellensatz and the strict decrease of dimension for proper analytic subgerms of an irreducible germ (corollary A.2.6 , proposition A.2.7 ) are deduced from the same local parametrization: division by the discriminant identifies each prime ideal with the ideal of its zero set, and the connectedness of the generic sheets gives the decrease of dimension. The proof of the Nullstellensatz includes the description of the radical as an intersection of prime ideals. The support theorem for closed currents of order zero, theorem A.2.17 , is the case of bidegree $(1,1)$ of [ Chapter III, (2.10)–(2.14), pp. 141–143 , DemBook ] . Our proof uses smooth normal coordinates, convolution in tangential directions and induction over the singular loci of the analytic set; the theorem is applied in lemma 14.4.6 . In the proof of proposition 14.4.7 , the pullback is corrected with the pushforward of a Kähler form, which gives the required strict positivity directly. For universal denominators of weakly holomorphic functions and for normalization (proposition A.3.3 , theorem A.3.6 ) compare [ Chapter II, (7.1)–(7.15), pp. 110–116 , DemBook ] . The cusp and the pair of crossing lines in example A.3.10 illustrate the difference between being normal and being unibranch. The Remmert–Stein extension theorem and Remmert's proper mapping theorem are proved together in [ Chapter II, (8.7)–(8.8), pp. 118–121 , DemBook ] . Our proof of theorem A.6.1 , theorem A.6.2 also treats them together, but it uses the resolution of singularities, theorem A.5.4 , to reduce to proper maps defined on manifolds, and it proves the statements on finite maps and on the dimension of hypersurfaces separately. The resolution and principalization theorems (theorem A.5.4 , theorem A.5.5 ) are the analytic versions of [ Theorems 1.1 and 1.3, pp. 611 and 614; Definitions 2.1–2.2, pp. 618–619 , BM08 ] ; that the results apply to complex analytic spaces is stated on p. 611 there. The relative principalization theorem, theorem A.6.5 , follows the lemma on relative principalization in the unpublished manuscript [ Lemma relative-principalization , VuXiaNakamaye ] . At each step of this construction, the centers in the ambient manifold divide the ideal by exactly one exceptional factor, as required for the controlled transform of the restricted ideal. In our statement the submanifold is closed and the ambient manifold is connected, so that the global blowups and the identities between ideals hold as stated. Theorem A.7.1 states that a proper bimeromorphic map has connected fibers over the points at which the germ of the target is irreducible, in particular over unibranch spaces. Its proof follows the argument with complements of branches in [ Appendix on unibranch spaces , XiaSampleBook ] ; properness is used to place the inverse image of a small neighborhood inside neighborhoods of the pieces of the fiber. The local upper bound near analytic subsets of codimension at least two in a reduced space, proposition A.8.4 , is proved by slicing with curves over a finite projection and the maximum principle for subharmonic functions. It complements the extension theorem on manifolds, corollary A.2.15 , which follows from the criterion in terms of Hausdorff measure. The corollary on the realization of divisors, in the appendix of [ XiaSampleBook ] on unibranch spaces, underlies the comparison of multiplier ideals with Lelong numbers along divisors in Part I of that book. Theorem A.7.6 proves this corollary by principalizing the successive centers and decreasing the order of the Jacobian along a fixed divisor. The definition of plurisubharmonic functions on reduced spaces by local ambient extension, definition A.8.1 , suffices for pullback by holomorphic maps, for the maximum principle on compact fibers and for the upper bound obtained by slicing with curves. On the manifolds used in Part I of that book, the descent of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions under modifications, proposition 14.2.8 , is proved directly by extension across an analytic set of codimension at least two.

title: Preface
text: Preface This book is an expanded version of my lecture notes at the Institute for Advanced Study in Mathematics (IASM) at Zhejiang University. My initial goal was modest: to write a self-contained reference for the participants in the lectures. But I soon realized that many results circulating in the area had never been rigorously proved anywhere in the literature. Each attempt to resolve these loose ends produced new ones, and the notes grew steadily until they became the present book.

title: Three pluripotential theories.
text: Three pluripotential theories. The aim of this book is to present, from a unified point of view, three different but interrelated theories that all deserve to be called a global pluripotential theory : the pluripotential theory on compact Kähler manifolds; the pluripotential theory on the Berkovich analytification of a projective variety; the toric pluripotential theory on a projective toric variety. The three theories are bound together by a common circle of ideas. Many results were originally proved in one setting and have analogues, sometimes evident and sometimes far from evident, in the others.

title: The central question: classifying singularities.
text: The central question: classifying singularities. Let us begin with the analytic side. Fix a compact Kähler manifold $X$. The central objects are the quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ — functions which are locally the sum of a smooth function and a plurisubharmonic function. We are mostly interested in their singularities : the locus where $\varphi =-\infty $ and the rate at which $\varphi $ tends to $-\infty $ near this locus. Singularities are not pathological exceptions; they are forced upon us by geometry. In typical applications, $X$ is the compactification of the moduli space of some class of geometric objects, with a Zariski-open locus $U\subseteq X$ parameterizing smooth objects. The natural metric on the associated polarizing line bundle is then smooth only on $U$, and the Grauert–Remmert extension theorem (theorem B.2.3 ) extends it to all of $X$ at the cost of introducing singularities along $X\setminus U$. Understanding such singularities is therefore not an aesthetic refinement but a prerequisite for any moduli-theoretic application. The local theory of these singularities is intricate, and a complete classification is essentially out of reach: locally, (quasi-)plurisubharmonic functions exhibit extremely complicated behavior, and the natural local invariants (Lelong numbers and multiplier ideal sheaves) capture only their rough features. For example, a function with log-log singularities has the same local invariants as a bounded one. The picture changes drastically when one passes to the global setting. On a compact manifold, there are three natural equivalence relations on $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, of decreasing fineness: the singularity-type relation $\sim $, identifying $\varphi ,\psi $ whose difference $\varphi -\psi $ is bounded; the $P$-equivalence $\sim _ P$, two potentials with $\varphi \leq \psi $ are identified if the mixed non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère masses \[  \int _ X \omega _\varphi ^ j\wedge \omega _\phi ^{n-j} = \int _ X \omega _\psi ^ j\wedge \omega _\phi ^{n-j},\qquad j=0,\ldots ,n,  \] agree against every reference potential $\phi $. Here $\omega $ is a sufficiently large Kähler form. In other words, $\varphi $ and $\psi $ behave similarly with respect to the global non-pluripolar mass (definition 6.1.1 ); the $\mathcal{I}$-equivalence $\sim _\mathcal {I}$, identifying $\varphi ,\psi $ for which the multiplier ideal sheaves agree, $\mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(k\psi )$ for every $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$ — equivalently, $\varphi $ and $\psi $ have the same generic Lelong numbers along every prime divisor over every modification of $X$ (definition 6.1.6 ). The first relation records the finest information one can hope to capture by global invariants; $\sim _ P$ retains the global mass side, while $\sim _\mathcal {I}$ retains the algebraic-geometric side. They are studied systematically in chapter 6 . A natural plan to classify singularities is the three-step decomposition: classify the $\mathcal{I}$-equivalence classes; classify the $P$-equivalence classes inside a given $\mathcal{I}$-class; classify the singularity types inside a given $P$-class. Step 3 has been the subject of much activity in the past decade under the name of pluripotential theory with prescribed singularities , and is by now reasonably well understood. The first goal of this book is to give a complete answer to Step 1, and a satisfactory answer to Step 2 in the cases that arise in geometry.

title: I-good singularities.
text: $\mathcal{I}$-good singularities. Step 1 is the subject of chapter 7 . We characterize $\mathcal{I}$-equivalence classes very explicitly through approximations by an explicit class of singularities, known as analytic singularities ; the analogous problem of approximating a plurisubharmonic function by ones with analytic singularities was studied in detail by Demailly. The class of $\mathcal{I}$-good potentials is the central protagonist of this book. In a single equivalence theorem (theorem 7.1.1 ), $\mathcal{I}$-goodness admits three intuitive descriptions, each capturing a different facet of what it means for a singularity to be “well-behaved.” In the non-degenerate case, a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ with $\theta _{\varphi }=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ for some closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good if and only if any of the following hold: $\varphi $ is the limit, with respect to the $d_ S$-pseudometric introduced in chapter 6 , of a sequence of potentials with analytic singularities. ( Topological description : $\mathcal{I}$-good potentials are precisely those reachable as limits of the explicit, well-understood class of analytic singularities.) The non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère mass of $\varphi $ equals the algebraic volume introduced in definition 3.2.9 : \[  \int _ X \theta _\varphi ^ n = \operatorname{vol}\theta _\varphi .  \] ( Mass–volume identity : no mass is lost to pluripolar sets, so the analytic mass and the algebraic volume coincide.) The $P$-envelope and the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope of $\varphi $ introduced in chapter 3 agree: \[  P_\theta [\varphi ] = P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] ( Analytic–algebraic envelope agreement : the two natural least-singular representatives, one constructed from the $P$-equivalence relation and one from multiplier ideals, coincide.) The reader is invited to keep these three pictures in mind throughout the book; we will use whichever is most convenient at any given moment. Step 2 is the more delicate one, and its difficulty turns out to be a feature, not a bug. A given $\mathcal{I}$-equivalence class can consist of an enormous number of $P$-equivalence classes; constructing such examples is easy. By contrast, in the toric and non-Archimedean settings, Step 2 is essentially trivial: every $\mathcal{I}$-equivalence class consists of a single $P$-equivalence class. In the toric case, an $\mathcal{I}$- (or $P$-) equivalence class is a sub-convex body of the Newton body. In the non-Archimedean case, it is a homogeneous plurisubharmonic metric. The discrepancy between the analytic and the toric/non-Archimedean theories suggests that, in the pluripotential theory on compact Kähler manifolds, a great many $\mathcal{I}$-classes are pathological, and that what one really wants is to single out within each $\mathcal{I}$-class a canonical $P$-class. The functions in this canonical class will be called $\mathcal{I}$-good . The development of the theory of $\mathcal{I}$-good singularities, in chapter 7 , is the technical core of this book. As the reader will see, almost every singularity that arises naturally in geometric applications is $\mathcal{I}$-good. A useful guiding analogy is with measure theory. There exist many non-measurable functions, but unless one constructs one by hand using the axiom of choice, one only encounters measurable functions in practice. Similarly, although the space of non-$\mathcal{I}$-good singularities is non-empty, it is essentially invisible to geometric applications. Once one accepts the framework of $\mathcal{I}$-good singularities, Step 2 becomes essentially solved.

title: Tools, applications, conventions.
text: Tools, applications, conventions. The classification of singularities, in the form just described, is somewhat abstract. To put it to use, we develop two general techniques that allow induction on $\dim X$. For a prime divisor $Y$ in general position, the analytic Bertini theorem relates quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ and on $Y$. For non-generic $Y$, the trace operator associates with $\varphi $ a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on the normalization of $Y$, well-defined modulo $\mathcal{I}$-equivalence. These tools occupy chapter 8 . The toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles is mostly classical and is recalled, with full proofs, in chapter 5 . The corresponding theory for big toric line bundles, which has never been written down in the literature, requires the partial Okounkov body machinery developed in chapter 10 and is the content of chapter 12 . The applications to non-Archimedean pluripotential theory occupy chapter 13 , building on the test-curve theory of chapter 9 . The convergence of partial Bergman kernels with arbitrary singular weight, extending the Berman–Boucksom–Witt Nyström theorem, is proved in chapter 14 .

title: Reading guide.
text:
Reading guide. This book is not an elementary introduction to pluripotential theory. It should not be the reader's first textbook in this field. The reader is expected to be comfortable with the basic pluripotential theory at the level of [ GZ17 ] , which is essentially the only prerequisite for the main body of the book. This book is not “a compilation of all the author's works”. Rather, it presents a new point of view on this theory, with new results and new insights. A reader who has gone through all my related papers is still encouraged to read at least part of this book. This book is not an encyclopedia of pluripotential theory. For example, the reader would not find the definition of a pseudoconvex domain, nor the full details from the long research papers or books I depend on in the application part. These points irritated the referee, but I hope that these omissions are understandable, taking into account that this book is already over 500 pages long. Although I tried my best to make the book as self-contained as possible, certain proofs based on techniques far beyond the scope of this book are still omitted. Results in this book are presented in the greatest possible generality. An expert reader may use this book as a convenient reference for the most general statements, and skip the proofs of the more general results if they are already familiar with them in a special case. The reader is expected to read Part II linearly, and consult the necessary preliminaries in Part I when necessary. A reader interested only in one application chapter may skip directly to it once the relevant Part II prerequisites are in place. chapter 5 is needed only for chapter 12 ; it can otherwise be skipped without loss. Some chapters in this book draw on more specialised background, recorded in the appendices: chapter A for convex analysis, chapter B for pluripotential theory on unibranch Kähler spaces, and chapter C for the almost-semigroup machinery underlying the partial Okounkov body construction. In order to develop the theory of b-divisors as in chapter 11 , we need to take limits with respect to the net of all modifications of $X$. In general, this net does not admit a cofinal sequence. As a consequence, nets are widely used in this book, and the reader is expected to be familiar with their basic properties. The books [ Wil70 , Kel75 ] are good references for the basic theory. It is essential to remember that the dominated convergence theorem and Fatou's lemma both fail for nets. A version of the monotone convergence theorem does hold, as in [ Proposition 7.12 , Fol99 ] . I made a great effort to make sure that every single expression involving $(-\infty )-(-\infty )$ or $0\cdot \infty $ is explained. This point is often overlooked in the literature. In most cases, the fix is simple, but in some cases, it requires a non-trivial amount of work. Therefore a number of our proofs seem more complicated than in the original papers. Similarly, in the literature, many constants are only correct up to a constant involving $2$ or $\pi $. I tried to make sure that every constant in this book is correct, and hence there is an extensive discussion of the normalizations of various objects in chapter 1 , which again irritated the same referee. I hope that the reader will appreciate the effort and find the book more readable as a result. Comments and questions are always welcome, and I will maintain an errata page on my homepage as long as I am still alive, no matter whether I remain in academia or not. Mingchen Xia in Hangzhou, March 2024 Contact information: Mingchen Xia , Institute of Geometry and Physics , USTC Email address : xiamingchen2008@gmail.com Homepage : https://mingchenxia.github.io/ . title: Conventions
text: Conventions In the whole book, we adopt the following conventions: A complex space is always assumed to be reduced , paracompact and Hausdorff . A modification of a complex space $X$ is a proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ that is locally obtained from a finite composition of blow-ups with smooth centers. A subnet of a net refers to a Willard subnet. More precisely, if $f\colon I\rightarrow X$ and $f'\colon I'\rightarrow X$ are nets, namely, maps from directed sets $I$ and $I'$ to the same set $X$, we say $f'$ is a subnet of $f$ if there is an increasing final function $h\colon I'\rightarrow I$ such that $f\circ h=f'$. A domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ refers to a connected open subset. A complex manifold is assumed to be paracompact. A submanifold of a complex manifold means a closed complex submanifold. A neighborhood is not necessarily open. The set $\mathbb {N}$ of natural numbers includes $0$. Increasing functions and decreasing functions are not necessarily strictly monotone. Positive forms are not necessarily strictly positive. The function $\mathbb {R}\ni x \mapsto x^2$ is convex instead of concave. This is different from the convention in [ CLS11 ] . We say a positive measure $\mu $ on a measurable space $X$ is carried by a measurable subset $Y$ if $\mu (X\setminus Y)=0$. $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ means $(2\pi )^{-1}\mathrm{i}\partial \overline{\partial }$.

title: 1 Preliminaries
text:
1 Preliminaries This part sets up the analytic and geometric language used throughout the book. It recalls the basic theory of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, non-pluripolar products, envelope operators, geodesics of singular potentials and the toric-convex dictionary in the ample case. A reader already familiar with pluripotential theory on compact Kähler manifolds may skim parts of chapter 1 , chapter 2 , but the later chapters use the precise conventions fixed here. chapter 1 recalls plurisubharmonic and quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, pluripolar sets, the plurifine topology, Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, analytic singularities, positivity of currents and singular Hermitian metrics. The presentation is concise, but we include proofs of several points whose conventions are important later, especially those involving Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals and quasi-equisingular approximation. chapter 2 introduces the non-pluripolar product and the basic tools for manipulating Monge–Ampère masses of singular currents. chapter 3 develops the two envelope operators that organize the singularity theory of the book. The $P$-envelope records the singularity type relevant to non-pluripolar mass, while the $\mathcal I$-envelope records the singularity type detected by multiplier ideals. Their interaction is one of the main themes of the book. chapter 4 studies subgeodesics, geodesics and geodesic rays in spaces of singular potentials. It also introduces the finite-energy space $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and the metric structures that will later be used to define convergence of singularity types. Finally, chapter 5 treats the ample toric case. There the pluripotential theory of toric metrics is translated into convex analysis on the associated polytope. This chapter is logically independent of much of the rest of the book, but it provides a model for the big toric theory developed later in chapter 12 . Once Frigyes Riesz Note. Frigyes Riesz (1880–1956), known as Frédéric Riesz in French and Frederic Riesz in English, was the first mathematician to define the general notion of subharmonic functions, and he also gave these functions a Frenglish name from the very beginning — fonctions subharmoniques . gave a brilliant explanation of why scientific work is easy. “Everyone has ideas, both right ideas and wrong ideas,” he said. “Scientific work consists merely of separating them.” 
— Istvan Vincze

title: 1 Plurisubharmonic functions
text: 1 Plurisubharmonic functions The aim of this chapter is to recall the basic theory of plurisubharmonic functions and to fix the conventions used throughout the rest of the book. We assume only standard background in several complex variables and complex geometry, but we record a number of details whose normalization will matter later. General references for the material include [ GZ17 ] , [ Dem12 ] and [ DemBook ] . The chapter begins with plurisubharmonic functions on domains in $\mathbb C^ n$ and on complex manifolds. We also include the $0$-dimensional case, which is occasionally convenient in inductive arguments. The basic permanence properties of plurisubharmonic functions are recalled: stability under upper envelopes and decreasing limits, Choquet's lemma, local integrability, gluing, extension across analytic subsets, and Kiselman's principle. We then discuss the plurifine topology. This topology is the natural one for many local arguments in pluripotential theory, especially those involving contact sets and non-pluripolar products. We include the Bedford–Taylor base theorem in a form suited to later applications, following the approach of [ BT87 ] and [ EMW06 ] . The next part of the chapter fixes our conventions for Lelong numbers and multiplier ideal sheaves. These conventions differ by harmless but important factors from some common references; the conversions are explained in 1.4.2 , 1.4.10 . We also recall Siu's semicontinuity theorem, the strong openness theorem of Guan–Zhou, the Ohsawa–Takegoshi extension theorem, and the valuative characterization of multiplier ideals. The remaining sections develop the global language used throughout the book. We introduce $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions, quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, the preorder $\preceq $ of singularity types, and compactness properties in $L^1$. We then recall analytic singularities, log resolutions and quasi-equisingular approximation. Finally, we discuss closed positive $(1,1)$-currents, pseudo-effective and big classes, Kähler currents, Siu decomposition, non-Kähler and non-nef loci, modified nef classes, and singular Hermitian metrics on line bundles. A reader familiar with this material may skim the chapter on a first pass, but the normalizations in section 1.4 and the approximation results in section 1.6 will be used repeatedly later. In this book, unlike in many references, we use the language of nets a lot. We remind the readers that subnets in the whole book mean Willard subnets . In particular, a subnet of a monotone net is still monotone. The readers can find more details about nets or Moore–Smith convergence in Willard's textbook [ Wil70 ] or Kelley's [ Kel75 ] . But one has to be careful that Willard's notion of subnets is stricter than Kelley's.

title: 1.1 The definition of plurisubharmonic functions
text: 1.1 The definition of plurisubharmonic functions In this section, we recall the notion of plurisubharmonic functions. We will also take care of the $0$-dimensional case, which makes a number of induction arguments easier to carry out. None of our references treats the $0$-dimensional case, but the reader can easily verify that the results in this section hold in this exceptional case.

title: 1.1.1 The -dimensional case
text: 1.1.1 The $1$-dimensional case Let $\Omega $ be a domain (a connected open subset) in $\mathbb {C}$. Definition 1.1.1 . A subharmonic function on $\Omega $ is a function $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ satisfying the following three conditions: $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $; $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous; $\varphi $ satisfies the sub-mean value inequality : For any $a\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ such that $\overline{B_1(a,r)}\subseteq \Omega $, we have \[  \varphi (a)\leq \frac{1}{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi } \varphi (a+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })\, \mathrm{d}\theta .\footnotemark  \] Note. Condition 2 guarantees that $\varphi $ is measurable and locally bounded from above, and hence the integral in Condition 3 makes sense. We will denote the set of subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ by $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. Here, $B_1(a,r)\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:|z-a|<r\} $ denotes the open ball with center $a$ and radius $r$. In fact, for each $a\in \Omega $, in 3 , it suffices to require the sub-mean value inequality for all small enough $r>0$. Intuitively, at a specific point $a\in \Omega $, Condition 2 says $\varphi (a)$ is no smaller than the upper limit of nearby values, while Condition 3 says $\varphi (a)$ is no larger than the mean. This intuition leads to the following rigidity theorem: Theorem 1.1.2 . Let $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\Delta \varphi \geq 0$. $\varphi $ coincides almost everywhere with a subharmonic function $\psi $ on $\Omega $. Moreover, the subharmonic function $\psi $ in 2 is unique. Here in Condition 1 , $\Delta \varphi =2\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial \varphi $ is the Laplacian in the sense of currents. This is a special case of theorem 1.1.6 below. This theorem gives a very useful way of constructing subharmonic functions.

title: Definition 1.1.1
text: Definition 1.1.1 . A subharmonic function on $\Omega $ is a function $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ satisfying the following three conditions: $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $; $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous; $\varphi $ satisfies the sub-mean value inequality : For any $a\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ such that $\overline{B_1(a,r)}\subseteq \Omega $, we have \[  \varphi (a)\leq \frac{1}{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi } \varphi (a+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })\, \mathrm{d}\theta .\footnotemark  \] Note. Condition 2 guarantees that $\varphi $ is measurable and locally bounded from above, and hence the integral in Condition 3 makes sense. We will denote the set of subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ by $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$.

title: Theorem 1.1.2
text: Theorem 1.1.2 . Let $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\Delta \varphi \geq 0$. $\varphi $ coincides almost everywhere with a subharmonic function $\psi $ on $\Omega $. Moreover, the subharmonic function $\psi $ in 2 is unique.

title: 1.1.2 The higher dimensional case
text: 1.1.2 The higher dimensional case We will fix $n\in \mathbb {N}$ and a domain $\Omega $ (a connected open subset) in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Definition 1.1.3 . When $n\geq 1$, a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $ is a function $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ satisfying the following three conditions: $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $; $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous; for any complex line $L\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ and any connected component $U$ of $L\cap \Omega $, the restriction $\varphi |_ U$ is either subharmonic or constantly $-\infty $. Note. An extremely common mistake in the literature is to replace 3 by the condition that $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ in the sense of currents. For a concrete counterexample, consider a function $\varphi $ that takes a constant value $0$ at all but one single point, at which the value of $\varphi $ is $1$. When $n=0$, the only domain $\Omega $ is the singleton. In this case, a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $ is a real-valued function on $\Omega $. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. A plurisubharmonic function is also called a psh function for short. The relevant notations are indicated in 1.1 . Note. Recall that most figures in this book are somewhat misleading: We usually draw a complex dimension as a real dimension. The figures should not be read literally! 1.1 A domain $\Omega $ cut by a complex line $L$. Example 1.1.4 . When $n=0$, we have a canonical bijection $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )\cong \mathbb {R}$. Example 1.1.5 . When $n=1$, we have $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )=\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. Similar to theorem 1.1.2 , we have a rigidity theorem for plurisubharmonic functions as well. Theorem 1.1.6 . Let $\varphi \colon \Omega \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$; $\varphi $ coincides almost everywhere with a plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on $\Omega $. Moreover, the plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ is unique. Here, the operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is normalized so that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial }.  \] For the proof, we refer to [ Proposition 1.43 , GZ17 ] . Plurisubharmonic functions have nice functorialities: Proposition 1.1.7 . Let $n'\in \mathbb {N}$ and $\Omega '\subseteq \mathbb {C}^{n'}$ be a domain. Given any holomorphic map $f\colon \Omega \rightarrow \Omega '$ and any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$, exactly one of the following cases occurs: $f^*\varphi \equiv -\infty $; $f^*\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. We refer to [ Proposition 1.44 , GZ17 ] for the proof Note. Recall that the statement of [ Proposition 1.44 , GZ17 ] is flawed. One has to reduce to the case where Case 1 does not occur before following their proof. . For each $n\in \mathbb {N}$, $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ and $r>0$, we write 1.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Bnar} B_ n(a,r)=\left\{  z\in \mathbb {C}^ n: |z-a|<r \right\} . \end{equation} Proposition 1.1.8 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B_ n(a,r_0))$ for some $r_0>0$. Then the function \[  (-\infty ,\log r_0)\rightarrow \mathbb {R},\quad \log r\mapsto \sup _{B_ n(a,r)}\varphi  \] is convex and increasing. See [ Theorem 4.1.13 , Hor07 ] for the case $n>1$ and [ Corollary 2.4 , Bou17 ] for the general case. Proposition 1.1.9 . Let $a<b$ be two real numbers. Let $f\colon (a,b)\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function. Define \[  g\colon \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:a<\operatorname{Re}z<b\} \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad z\mapsto f(\operatorname{Re}z).  \] Suppose that $g$ is subharmonic. Then $f$ is convex. In particular, $f$ takes real values only. See [ Theorem 2.12 , HK76 ] for a more general result.

1.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Bnar} B_ n(a,r)=\left\{  z\in \mathbb {C}^ n: |z-a|<r \right\} . \end{equation}

Define \[  g\colon \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:a<\operatorname{Re}z<b\} \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad z\mapsto f(\operatorname{Re}z).  \] Suppose that $g$ is subharmonic. Then $f$ is convex.
