title: 1.1.3 The manifold case
text: 1.1.3 The manifold case Let $X$ be a complex manifold. In the whole book, complex manifolds are assumed to be paracompact, namely, all connected components have countable bases. Definition 1.1.10 . A plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is a function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that for any $x\in X$, there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$, an integer $n\in \mathbb {N}$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ and a biholomorphic map $F\colon \Omega \rightarrow U$ such that $F^*(\varphi |_ U)\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Example 1.1.11 . When $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$, the notions of plurisubharmonic functions in definition 1.1.10 and in definition 1.1.3 coincide. Example 1.1.12 . Write $\{ X_ i\} _{i\in I}$ for the set of connected components of $X$. Then we have a natural bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}(X) \cong \prod _{i\in I} \mathrm{PSH}(X_ i).  \] Here the product is in the category of sets. In particular, if $X=\varnothing $, then $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ is a singleton. This example allows us to reduce to the case of connected manifolds when studying general plurisubharmonic functions. Proposition 1.1.13 . Let $Y$ be a complex manifold and $f\colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a holomorphic map. Then for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, exactly one of the following cases occurs: $f^*\varphi $ is identically $-\infty $ on some connected component of $Y$; $f^*\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y)$. This proposition follows from proposition 1.1.7 applied separately on each connected component of $Y$. theorem 1.1.6 implies immediately the general form of the rigidity theorem: Theorem 1.1.14 . Let $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$; $\varphi $ coincides almost everywhere with a plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on $X$. Moreover, the plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ in 2 is unique. Definition 1.1.15 . A subset $E\subseteq X$ is pluripolar if for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$ and a function $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ such that \[  \psi |_{E\cap U}\equiv -\infty .  \] A subset $E\subseteq X$ is non-pluripolar if $E$ is not pluripolar. A subset $F\subseteq X$ is co-pluripolar if $X\setminus F$ is pluripolar. When $X$ has dimension $1$, a pluripolar set is called a polar set . We say some property about objects on $X$ holds quasi-everywhere if it holds outside a pluripolar set. Theorem 1.1.16 (Josefson's theorem) . Let $E\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a pluripolar set. Then there is $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C}^ n)$ such that $\varphi |_ E\equiv -\infty $. See [ Corollary 4.41 , GZ17 ] for the proof of a more general result. There is also a global version of Josefson's theorem: Theorem 1.1.17 . Assume that $X$ is a compact complex manifold and $E\subseteq X$ is a pluripolar set. Then there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$ with $\varphi |_ E\equiv -\infty $. For a proof, see [ Vu19 ] . The notion of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions will be recalled in definition 1.5.1 below.

title: Definition 1.1.10
text: Definition 1.1.10 . A plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is a function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that for any $x\in X$, there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$, an integer $n\in \mathbb {N}$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ and a biholomorphic map $F\colon \Omega \rightarrow U$ such that $F^*(\varphi |_ U)\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$.

title: Example 1.1.11
text: Example 1.1.11 . When $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$, the notions of plurisubharmonic functions in definition 1.1.10 and in definition 1.1.3 coincide.

title: Example 1.1.12
text: Example 1.1.12 . Write $\{ X_ i\} _{i\in I}$ for the set of connected components of $X$. Then we have a natural bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}(X) \cong \prod _{i\in I} \mathrm{PSH}(X_ i).  \] Here the product is in the category of sets. In particular, if $X=\varnothing $, then $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ is a singleton.

title: Proposition 1.1.13
text: Proposition 1.1.13 . Let $Y$ be a complex manifold and $f\colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a holomorphic map. Then for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, exactly one of the following cases occurs: $f^*\varphi $ is identically $-\infty $ on some connected component of $Y$; $f^*\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y)$.

title: Theorem 1.1.14
text: Theorem 1.1.14 . Let $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi $ is locally integrable and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$; $\varphi $ coincides almost everywhere with a plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on $X$. Moreover, the plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ in 2 is unique.

title: Theorem 1.1.16 (Josefson's theorem)
text: Theorem 1.1.16 (Josefson's theorem) . Let $E\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a pluripolar set. Then there is $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C}^ n)$ such that $\varphi |_ E\equiv -\infty $.

title: Theorem 1.1.17
text: Theorem 1.1.17 . Assume that $X$ is a compact complex manifold and $E\subseteq X$ is a pluripolar set. Then there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$ with $\varphi |_ E\equiv -\infty $.

title: 1.2 Properties of plurisubharmonic functions
text:
1.2 Properties of plurisubharmonic functions In this section, we explore the basic properties of plurisubharmonic functions. Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Proposition 1.2.1 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then for any $p\geq 1$, $\varphi \in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. See [ Theorem 1.46, Theorem 1.48 , GZ17 ] . Note. We remind the readers that the third displayed formula in the proof of [ Theorem 1.48 , GZ17 ] Step 2 is wrong. But this is irrelevant for our purpose. Proposition 1.2.2 . Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ such that $\varphi \coloneqq \inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $X$. Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Furthermore, $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}} \varphi $. Here $\operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}$ denotes the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum. When $I$ is a finite family, observe that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i= \sup _{i\in I}\varphi _ i.  \] When $I=\{ 1,\ldots ,m\} $, we write \[  \varphi _1\lor \cdots \lor \varphi _ m\coloneqq \sup _{i\in I}\varphi _ i.  \] We refer to [ Proposition 1.28, Proposition 1.40 , GZ17 ] Note. In [ Proposition 1.28 , GZ17 ] , the second part is only stated for sequences, the net version is obvious using the sub-mean value inequality and the monotone convergence theorem for nets as in [ Proposition 7.12 , Fol99 ] . Note. The proof of [ Proposition 1.40 , GZ17 ] contains a gap: The measurability of $u$ is not established during the proof, so the claim $u \ast \chi _{\epsilon }$ converges to $u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is not valid. One needs to choose the sequence $(v_ j)_ j$ carefully so that $v\leq u$, and use the fact that $v \ast \chi _{\epsilon }$ converges to $v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ instead. . Proposition 1.2.3 (Choquet's lemma) . Assume that $X$ has countably many connected components. Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. There exists a countable subset $J\subseteq I$ such that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{j\in J}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ j.  \] In the sequel, we say a subset $B\subseteq X$ is a holomorphic ball if $B$ has smooth boundary in $X$, and $B$ is biholomorphic to an open ball in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. Since by our convention, the complex manifold $X$ is paracompact, it can be covered by countably many holomorphic balls, so we can easily reduce to the case where $X$ is an open ball in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. In this case, the result is proved in [ Lemma 4.31 , GZ17 ] . $\square$ Proposition 1.2.4 . A pluripolar set $E\subseteq X$ is a Lebesgue null set. Proof. This is a trivial consequence of proposition 1.2.1 . $\square$ Proposition 1.2.5 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then the set \[  \left\{ x\in X: \sup _{i\in I}\varphi _ i<\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i ight\}   \] is pluripolar and hence Lebesgue null. See [ Corollary 4.28 , GZ17 ] . Proposition 1.2.6 . Suppose that $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. If $\varphi \leq \psi $ almost everywhere, then $\varphi \leq \psi $ everywhere. In particular, if $\varphi =\psi $ almost everywhere, then $\varphi =\psi $ everywhere. Proof. Replace $\varphi $ by $\varphi \lor \psi $. Then $\varphi ,\psi $ are two plurisubharmonic functions that coincide almost everywhere. The uniqueness statement in theorem 1.1.14 gives $\varphi =\psi $. $\square$ Proposition 1.2.7 . Let $(E_ i)_{i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be a sequence of pluripolar sets in $X$. Then \[  E\coloneqq  igcup _{i=1}^{\infty }E_ i  \] is also pluripolar. Proof. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a bounded domain. In this case, by theorem 1.1.16 for each $i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$ we can choose $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C}^ n)$ such that \[  \psi _ i|_{E_ i}\equiv -\infty ,\quad \psi _ i|_ X\leq 0  \] for all $i>0$. By proposition 1.2.1 , we have $\psi _ i|_ X\in L^1(X)$ for all $i>0$. After rescaling, we may also assume that $\| \psi _ i\| _{L^1(X)}\leq 1$ for all $i>0$. We then define \[  \psi =\sum _{i=1}^{\infty }2^{-i} \psi _ i|_ X.  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ according to proposition 1.2.2 and $\psi |_{E}=-\infty $. $\square$ Corollary 1.2.8 . Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}}\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then 1.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:L1limsup1} \varphi =\mathop{\vphantom {\operatorname {sup}^{*}}\inf }\limits _{j>0} \operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ k, \end{equation} and the set \[  \left\{ x\in X: \varphi (x)
eq \varlimsup _{j	o \infty }\varphi _ j(x)ight\}   \] is pluripolar. Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. We first observe that $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. This follows from [ Exercise 1.20 , GZ17 ] . For each $j\geq 1$, let \[  \psi _ j=\operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ k.  \] Then $\psi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 1.2.2 . Moreover, $(\psi _ j)_ j$ is a decreasing sequence and $\psi _ j\geq \varphi _ j$ for all $j$. After considering a subsequence of $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ which converges to $\varphi $ almost everywhere, we get $\varphi \leq \psi \coloneqq \inf _ j \psi _ j$ almost everywhere. In particular, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 1.2.2 . On the other hand, by proposition 1.2.5 , there exist pluripolar sets $Z_ j\subseteq X$ such that \[  \psi _ j=\sup _{k\geq j}\varphi _ k  \] on $X\setminus Z_ j$. Let \[  Z= igcup _{j=1}^{\infty } Z_ j.  \] Then $Z$ is a pluripolar set by proposition 1.2.7 , and for any $x\in X\setminus Z$, we have $\psi (x)=\varlimsup _ j \varphi _ j(x)$. Moreover, $\psi =\varphi $ almost everywhere by [ Theorem 1.46 , GZ17 ] , and hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . Hence we conclude ( 1.2 ). Moreover, for all $x\in X\setminus Z$, \[  \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{j	o \infty } \varphi _ j(x).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Theorem 1.2.9 (Brelot, Grauert–Remmert) . Let $Z$ be an analytic subset in $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X\setminus Z)$. Then the function $\varphi $ admits an extension to $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ in the following two cases: The set $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ everywhere. The set $Z$ has codimension at least $1$ everywhere and $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above near each point of $Z$. In both cases, the extension is unique and is given by 1.3  egin{equation} \label{eq:GRextvarphiexp} \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{X\setminus Z
i y	o x}\varphi (y),\quad x\in Z. \end{equation} 1.2 Notation in the proof of theorem 1.2.9 1 . Proof. The extension is unique thanks to proposition 1.2.6 . We shall prove the existence. 2 Thanks to the uniqueness of the extension, the problem is local, so we may assume that $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ with $n>0$ and there is a non-zero holomorphic function $f$ on $X$ vanishing on $Z$. For each $\epsilon >0$, we claim that the function $\varphi _{\epsilon }$ defined by \[  \varphi _{\epsilon }(x)\coloneqq \left\{   egin{aligned}  \varphi (x)+\epsilon \log |f(x)|^2,& \quad x\in X\setminus Z;\  -\infty ,& \quad x\in Z \end{aligned} ight.  \] is plurisubharmonic on $X$. By definition 1.1.3 , it suffices to verify the case $n=1$. In this case, we may assume that $Z=\{ 0\} $. It is clear that $ \varphi _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{SH}(X\setminus Z)$. It suffices to verify the sub-mean value inequality at $0$, which is immediate. Next observe that the net $\varphi _{\epsilon }$ is increasing as $\epsilon \searrow 0$ and $\varphi _{\epsilon }$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. It follows from proposition 1.2.2 that $	ilde{\varphi }\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{\epsilon >0}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Moreover, $	ilde{\varphi }$ clearly extends $\varphi $. Note that ( 1.3 ) follows from the construction. 1 We invite the reader to consult 1.2 for the notations used in the proof. Thanks to 2 , it suffices to verify that $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above near each point of $Z$. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ with $n\geq 2$. Suppose the assertion fails. Then there exist $z\in Z$ and a sequence $(x_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ in $X\setminus Z$ converging to $z$ such that 1.6  egin{equation} \label{eq:limphiinfty_temp1} \lim _{j	o \infty } \varphi (x_ j)=\infty . \end{equation} Since $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ Note. In fact, codimension at least $1$ suffices for this step. , we may choose a complex line $L$ through $z$ which meets $Z$ in a discrete set; after shrinking $X$ we may further assume that \[  L\cap Z=\{ z\} .  \] Pick an open ball $B_ n(z,r)\Subset X$. After adding a constant to $\varphi $, we may arrange $\varphi <0$ on $L\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)$. Since $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous, there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq X\setminus Z$ of $L\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)$ such that \[  \varphi |_ U<0.  \] For each $j\geq 1$ we now choose a complex line $L_ j$ through $x_ j$, disjoint from $Z\cap B_ n(z,r)$, with $L_ j	o L$ as $j	o \infty $ (the convergence being in the Grassmannian of affine complex lines in $\mathbb {C}^ n$). The existence of such $L_ j$ is precisely where the assumption $\operatorname {codim} Z\geq 2$ enters: after replacing $B_ n(z,r)$ by a slightly smaller ball if necessary, the closure of $Z\cap B_ n(z,r)$ is analytic in a neighborhood of the closed ball. The projection to the space of directions is proper on this compact analytic set, so by Remmert's theorem its image is contained in a proper analytic subset of $\mathbb {P}^{n-1}$. Hence its complement contains directions arbitrarily close to that of $L$. For $j$ large enough we now have \[  L_ j\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)\subseteq U,  \] so applying the maximum principle to $\varphi |_{L_ j\cap X}$ at $x_ j$ yields $\varphi (x_ j)<0$, contradicting ( 1.6 ). $\square$ Lemma 1.2.10 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}((\Delta ^*)^ n)$ be an $(S^1)^ n$-invariant plurisubharmonic function. Then $\varphi $ is finite everywhere. Here \[  \Delta ^*\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: 0<|z|<1\}   \] denotes the punctured unit disk. Proof. It clearly suffices to handle the case $n=1$. In this case, by [ Theorem 2.12 , HK76 ] , the map \[  \log r\mapsto \int _{0}^{1} \varphi \left(r\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm{i}	heta }ight)\, \mathrm{d}	heta =\varphi (r)  \] is a convex function of $\log r$. So, the set $\{ r\in (0,1): \varphi (r)=-\infty \} $ is convex. But $\varphi $ is almost everywhere finite by proposition 1.2.1 . Since $\varphi $ is $S^1$-invariant, $\varphi |_{(0,1)}$ is almost everywhere finite. It follows from the convexity that it is everywhere finite. $\square$ Proposition 1.2.11 (Kiselman's principle) . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ m	imes \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a pseudoconvex domain. Assume that for each $z\in \mathbb {C}^ m$, the set \[  \Omega _ z\coloneqq  igl \{ w\in \mathbb {C}^ n: (z,w)\in \Omega  igr \}   \] has the form $E+\mathrm{i}\mathbb {R}^ n$, where $E\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ is a subset. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, assume that $\varphi $ is independent of the imaginary part of the variable in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Let $\Omega '$ be the projection of $\Omega $ to $\mathbb {C}^ m$. Define $\psi \colon \Omega 'ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ as follows: \[  \psi (z)=\inf _{w\in \Omega _ z}\varphi (z,w).  \] Then either $\psi \equiv -\infty $ or $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. See [ Theorem 7.5 , DemBook ] for the proof as well as the notion of pseudoconvex domains. Lemma 1.2.12 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain and $\Omega '\subseteq \Omega $ be a subdomain. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. Assume that 1.7  egin{equation} \label{eq:gluecond} \varliminf _{\substack {\Omega '
i y	o x,\ \psi (y)
eq -\infty }} igl (\varphi (y)-\psi (y) igr )\geq 0 \end{equation} for any $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Define \[  \eta (z)=\left\{   egin{aligned}  \varphi (z)\lor \psi (z),& \quad 	ext{if }z\in \Omega ',\  \varphi (z),& \quad 	ext{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{aligned} ight.  \] Then $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. This is essentially [ Proposition 1.30 , GZ17 ] . Since the statement in the reference is slightly misleading for our purposes, we include the proof for clarification. 1.3 Gluing procedure Proof. See 1.3 for the notations used in the proof. Take $\epsilon >0$. We first define \[  \eta _{\epsilon }(z)= egin{cases}  \varphi (z)\lor (\psi (z)-2\epsilon ),&  	extup{if }z\in \Omega ';\  \varphi (z),&  	extup{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{cases}  \] We claim that \[  \eta _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ).  \] By our assumption, for each $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, we can find an open neighborhood $U_ x\subseteq \Omega $ such that for any $y\in U_ x\cap \Omega '$, we have $\varphi (y)\geq \psi (y)-\epsilon $. Therefore, by taking a union of the $U_ x$'s for various $x$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ such that \[  \varphi (y)\geq \psi (y)-\epsilon ,\quad  orall y\in U\cap \Omega '.  \] Since $U$ contains $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, the set $(\Omega \setminus \Omega ')\cup U$ is open in $\Omega $. On this open set we have $\eta _{\epsilon }=\varphi $, hence $\eta _{\epsilon }$ is plurisubharmonic there. It is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega '$ by proposition 1.2.2 . These two descriptions agree on the overlap $U\cap \Omega '$, so our claim follows from the local nature of plurisubharmonicity. Next we observe that as $\epsilon $ decreases to $0$, the functions $\eta _{\epsilon }$ increase to $\eta $. The family $(\eta _\epsilon )_{0<\epsilon \leq 1}$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. This is clear away from $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Near $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, applying the previous estimate with $\epsilon =1$ gives an open neighborhood $U_1$ of $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ such that $\psi \leq \varphi +1$ on $U_1\cap \Omega '$, hence $\eta _\epsilon \leq \varphi +1$ on $U_1$ for all $0<\epsilon \leq 1$. Therefore, $\eta ^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ by proposition 1.2.2 . It remains to observe that $\eta $ is upper semicontinuous. This is only non-trivial on the boundary of $\Omega '$. Take $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ and let $(y_ i)_{i>0}$ be a sequence in $\Omega '$ with limit $x$. We first show that 1.12  egin{equation} \label{eq:limsuppsiphitemp1} \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)\leq \varphi (x). \end{equation} We may assume that $\psi (y_ i)
eq -\infty $ for all $i>0$ and the left-hand side of ( 1.12 ) is not $-\infty $. Then we can compute \[  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)\leq \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)+\varliminf _{i	o \infty }  igl (\varphi (y_ i)-\psi (y_ i) igr )\leq \varlimsup _{i	o \infty }\varphi (y_ i)\leq \varphi (x).  \] Combining this with the upper semicontinuity of $\varphi $, we get \[  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } igl (\varphi (y_ i)\lor \psi (y_ i) igr )\leq \varphi (x)=\eta (x).  \] This proves upper semicontinuity across $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Therefore, $\eta =\eta ^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. $\square$ Note that the boundary condition ( 1.7 ) enters the proof only through ( 1.12 ), therefore, we can formulate a variant of 1.2.12 : Corollary 1.2.13 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain and $\Omega '\subseteq \Omega $ be a subdomain Note. In [ Proposition 1.30 , GZ17 ] , Guedj–Zeriahi assumed in addition that $\Omega '$ is relatively compact in $\Omega $. This assumption is not necessary for the proof, and the applications of this proposition in [ GZ17 ] usually do not satisfy this condition. . Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. Assume that \[  \varlimsup _{\Omega '
i y	o x}\psi (y)\leq \varphi (x)  \] for any $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Define \[  \eta (z)= egin{cases}  \varphi (z)\lor \psi (z),& \quad 	extup{if }z\in \Omega ';\  \varphi (z),& \quad 	extup{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{cases}  \] Then $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Using the ideas of 1.2.12 and the solution of the homogeneous Monge–Ampère equations on a strong pseudoconvex domain, one can prove the following: Proposition 1.2.14 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, let $D \Subset \Omega $ be a strongly pseudoconvex domain, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ be locally bounded. Then there exists a unique locally bounded $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ such that \[   egin{cases}  \left(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi ight)^ n = 0&  	extup{on } D,\  \psi = \varphi &  	extup{on } \Omega \setminus D. \end{cases}  \] Moreover, $\psi \geq \varphi $. See [ Proposition 9.1 , BT82 ] for the proof. We sometimes say $\psi $ is the balayage of $\varphi $ on $D$. Let us also recall the following domination principle: Proposition 1.2.15 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a bounded domain. Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ be locally bounded. Assume that for each $z\in \partial \Omega $, we have \[  \varliminf _{\Omega 
i w	o z} \Bigl (\psi (w)-\varphi (w)\Bigr )\geq 0;  \] $\varphi \leq \psi $ a.e. with respect to $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$, Then $\varphi \leq \psi $. This is [ Corollary 3.31 , GZ17 ] . Note. The statement in the reference is flawed, but the proof is correct.

title: Proposition 1.2.1
text: Proposition 1.2.1 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then for any $p\geq 1$, $\varphi \in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$.

title: Proposition 1.2.2
text: Proposition 1.2.2 . Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ such that $\varphi \coloneqq \inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $X$. Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Furthermore, $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}} \varphi $.

title: Proposition 1.2.3 (Choquet's lemma)
text: Proposition 1.2.3 (Choquet's lemma) . Assume that $X$ has countably many connected components. Assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. There exists a countable subset $J\subseteq I$ such that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{j\in J}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ j.  \] Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. Since by our convention, the complex manifold $X$ is paracompact, it can be covered by countably many holomorphic balls, so we can easily reduce to the case where $X$ is an open ball in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. In this case, the result is proved in [ Lemma 4.31 , GZ17 ] . $\square$

title: Proposition 1.2.4
text: Proposition 1.2.4 . A pluripolar set $E\subseteq X$ is a Lebesgue null set. Proof. This is a trivial consequence of proposition 1.2.1 . $\square$

title: Proposition 1.2.5
text: Proposition 1.2.5 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then the set \[  \left\{ x\in X: \sup _{i\in I}\varphi _ i<\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i \right\}   \] is pluripolar and hence Lebesgue null.

title: Proposition 1.2.6
text: Proposition 1.2.6 . Suppose that $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. If $\varphi \leq \psi $ almost everywhere, then $\varphi \leq \psi $ everywhere. In particular, if $\varphi =\psi $ almost everywhere, then $\varphi =\psi $ everywhere. Proof. Replace $\varphi $ by $\varphi \lor \psi $. Then $\varphi ,\psi $ are two plurisubharmonic functions that coincide almost everywhere. The uniqueness statement in theorem 1.1.14 gives $\varphi =\psi $. $\square$

title: Proposition 1.2.7
text: Proposition 1.2.7 . Let $(E_ i)_{i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be a sequence of pluripolar sets in $X$. Then \[  E\coloneqq \bigcup _{i=1}^{\infty }E_ i  \] is also pluripolar. Proof. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a bounded domain. In this case, by theorem 1.1.16 for each $i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$ we can choose $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C}^ n)$ such that \[  \psi _ i|_{E_ i}\equiv -\infty ,\quad \psi _ i|_ X\leq 0  \] for all $i>0$. By proposition 1.2.1 , we have $\psi _ i|_ X\in L^1(X)$ for all $i>0$. After rescaling, we may also assume that $\| \psi _ i\| _{L^1(X)}\leq 1$ for all $i>0$. We then define \[  \psi =\sum _{i=1}^{\infty }2^{-i} \psi _ i|_ X.  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ according to proposition 1.2.2 and $\psi |_{E}=-\infty $. $\square$

title: Corollary 1.2.8
text: Corollary 1.2.8 . Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}}\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then 1.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:L1limsup1} \varphi =\mathop{\vphantom {\operatorname {sup}^{*}}\inf }\limits _{j>0} \operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ k, \end{equation} and the set \[  \left\{ x\in X: \varphi (x)\neq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\varphi _ j(x)\right\}   \] is pluripolar. Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. We first observe that $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. This follows from [ Exercise 1.20 , GZ17 ] . For each $j\geq 1$, let \[  \psi _ j=\operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ k.  \] Then $\psi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 1.2.2 . Moreover, $(\psi _ j)_ j$ is a decreasing sequence and $\psi _ j\geq \varphi _ j$ for all $j$. After considering a subsequence of $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ which converges to $\varphi $ almost everywhere, we get $\varphi \leq \psi \coloneqq \inf _ j \psi _ j$ almost everywhere. In particular, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 1.2.2 . On the other hand, by proposition 1.2.5 , there exist pluripolar sets $Z_ j\subseteq X$ such that \[  \psi _ j=\sup _{k\geq j}\varphi _ k  \] on $X\setminus Z_ j$. Let \[  Z=\bigcup _{j=1}^{\infty } Z_ j.  \] Then $Z$ is a pluripolar set by proposition 1.2.7 , and for any $x\in X\setminus Z$, we have $\psi (x)=\varlimsup _ j \varphi _ j(x)$. Moreover, $\psi =\varphi $ almost everywhere by [ Theorem 1.46 , GZ17 ] , and hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . Hence we conclude ( 1.2 ). Moreover, for all $x\in X\setminus Z$, \[  \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{j\to \infty } \varphi _ j(x).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$
1.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:L1limsup1} \varphi =\mathop{\vphantom {\operatorname {sup}^{*}}\inf }\limits _{j>0} \operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ k, \end{equation}

title: Theorem 1.2.9 (Brelot, Grauert–Remmert)
text: Theorem 1.2.9 (Brelot, Grauert–Remmert) . Let $Z$ be an analytic subset in $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X\setminus Z)$. Then the function $\varphi $ admits an extension to $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ in the following two cases: The set $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ everywhere. The set $Z$ has codimension at least $1$ everywhere and $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above near each point of $Z$. In both cases, the extension is unique and is given by 1.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:GRextvarphiexp} \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{X\setminus Z\ni y\to x}\varphi (y),\quad x\in Z. \end{equation} Proof. The extension is unique thanks to proposition 1.2.6 . We shall prove the existence. 2 Thanks to the uniqueness of the extension, the problem is local, so we may assume that $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ with $n>0$ and there is a non-zero holomorphic function $f$ on $X$ vanishing on $Z$. For each $\epsilon >0$, we claim that the function $\varphi _{\epsilon }$ defined by \[  \varphi _{\epsilon }(x)\coloneqq \left\{  \begin{aligned}  \varphi (x)+\epsilon \log |f(x)|^2,& \quad x\in X\setminus Z;\\  -\infty ,& \quad x\in Z \end{aligned} \right.  \] is plurisubharmonic on $X$. By definition 1.1.3 , it suffices to verify the case $n=1$. In this case, we may assume that $Z=\{ 0\} $. It is clear that $ \varphi _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{SH}(X\setminus Z)$. It suffices to verify the sub-mean value inequality at $0$, which is immediate. Next observe that the net $\varphi _{\epsilon }$ is increasing as $\epsilon \searrow 0$ and $\varphi _{\epsilon }$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. It follows from proposition 1.2.2 that $\tilde{\varphi }\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{\epsilon >0}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Moreover, $\tilde{\varphi }$ clearly extends $\varphi $. Note that ( 1.3 ) follows from the construction. 1 We invite the reader to consult 1.2 for the notations used in the proof. Thanks to 2 , it suffices to verify that $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above near each point of $Z$. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ with $n\geq 2$. Suppose the assertion fails. Then there exist $z\in Z$ and a sequence $(x_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ in $X\setminus Z$ converging to $z$ such that 1.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:limphiinfty_temp1} \lim _{j\to \infty } \varphi (x_ j)=\infty . \end{equation} Since $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ Note. In fact, codimension at least $1$ suffices for this step. , we may choose a complex line $L$ through $z$ which meets $Z$ in a discrete set; after shrinking $X$ we may further assume that \[  L\cap Z=\{ z\} .  \] Pick an open ball $B_ n(z,r)\Subset X$. After adding a constant to $\varphi $, we may arrange $\varphi <0$ on $L\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)$. Since $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous, there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq X\setminus Z$ of $L\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)$ such that \[  \varphi |_ U<0.  \] For each $j\geq 1$ we now choose a complex line $L_ j$ through $x_ j$, disjoint from $Z\cap B_ n(z,r)$, with $L_ j\to L$ as $j\to \infty $ (the convergence being in the Grassmannian of affine complex lines in $\mathbb {C}^ n$). The existence of such $L_ j$ is precisely where the assumption $\operatorname {codim} Z\geq 2$ enters: after replacing $B_ n(z,r)$ by a slightly smaller ball if necessary, the closure of $Z\cap B_ n(z,r)$ is analytic in a neighborhood of the closed ball. The projection to the space of directions is proper on this compact analytic set, so by Remmert's theorem its image is contained in a proper analytic subset of $\mathbb {P}^{n-1}$. Hence its complement contains directions arbitrarily close to that of $L$. For $j$ large enough we now have \[  L_ j\cap \partial B_ n(z,r)\subseteq U,  \] so applying the maximum principle to $\varphi |_{L_ j\cap X}$ at $x_ j$ yields $\varphi (x_ j)<0$, contradicting ( 1.6 ). $\square$
1.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:GRextvarphiexp} \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{X\setminus Z\ni y\to x}\varphi (y),\quad x\in Z. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 1.2.10
text: Lemma 1.2.10 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}((\Delta ^*)^ n)$ be an $(S^1)^ n$-invariant plurisubharmonic function. Then $\varphi $ is finite everywhere. Proof. It clearly suffices to handle the case $n=1$. In this case, by [ Theorem 2.12 , HK76 ] , the map \[  \log r\mapsto \int _{0}^{1} \varphi \left(r\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm{i}\theta }\right)\, \mathrm{d}\theta =\varphi (r)  \] is a convex function of $\log r$. So, the set $\{ r\in (0,1): \varphi (r)=-\infty \} $ is convex. But $\varphi $ is almost everywhere finite by proposition 1.2.1 . Since $\varphi $ is $S^1$-invariant, $\varphi |_{(0,1)}$ is almost everywhere finite. It follows from the convexity that it is everywhere finite. $\square$

title: Proposition 1.2.11 (Kiselman's principle)
text: Proposition 1.2.11 (Kiselman's principle) . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a pseudoconvex domain. Assume that for each $z\in \mathbb {C}^ m$, the set \[  \Omega _ z\coloneqq \bigl \{ w\in \mathbb {C}^ n: (z,w)\in \Omega \bigr \}   \] has the form $E+\mathrm{i}\mathbb {R}^ n$, where $E\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ is a subset. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, assume that $\varphi $ is independent of the imaginary part of the variable in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Let $\Omega '$ be the projection of $\Omega $ to $\mathbb {C}^ m$. Define $\psi \colon \Omega '\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ as follows: \[  \psi (z)=\inf _{w\in \Omega _ z}\varphi (z,w).  \] Then either $\psi \equiv -\infty $ or $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$.

title: Lemma 1.2.12
text:
Lemma 1.2.12 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain and $\Omega '\subseteq \Omega $ be a subdomain. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. Assume that 1.7  egin{equation} \label{eq:gluecond} \varliminf _{\substack {\Omega '
i y	o x,\ \psi (y)
eq -\infty }} igl (\varphi (y)-\psi (y) igr )\geq 0 \end{equation} for any $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Define \[  \eta (z)=\left\{   egin{aligned}  \varphi (z)\lor \psi (z),& \quad 	ext{if }z\in \Omega ',\  \varphi (z),& \quad 	ext{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{aligned} ight.  \] Then $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Proof. See 1.3 for the notations used in the proof. Take $\epsilon >0$. We first define \[  \eta _{\epsilon }(z)= egin{cases}  \varphi (z)\lor (\psi (z)-2\epsilon ),&  	extup{if }z\in \Omega ';\  \varphi (z),&  	extup{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{cases}  \] We claim that \[  \eta _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ).  \] By our assumption, for each $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, we can find an open neighborhood $U_ x\subseteq \Omega $ such that for any $y\in U_ x\cap \Omega '$, we have $\varphi (y)\geq \psi (y)-\epsilon $. Therefore, by taking a union of the $U_ x$'s for various $x$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ such that \[  \varphi (y)\geq \psi (y)-\epsilon ,\quad  orall y\in U\cap \Omega '.  \] Since $U$ contains $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, the set $(\Omega \setminus \Omega ')\cup U$ is open in $\Omega $. On this open set we have $\eta _{\epsilon }=\varphi $, hence $\eta _{\epsilon }$ is plurisubharmonic there. It is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega '$ by proposition 1.2.2 . These two descriptions agree on the overlap $U\cap \Omega '$, so our claim follows from the local nature of plurisubharmonicity. Next we observe that as $\epsilon $ decreases to $0$, the functions $\eta _{\epsilon }$ increase to $\eta $. The family $(\eta _\epsilon )_{0<\epsilon \leq 1}$ is locally uniformly bounded from above. This is clear away from $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Near $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$, applying the previous estimate with $\epsilon =1$ gives an open neighborhood $U_1$ of $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ such that $\psi \leq \varphi +1$ on $U_1\cap \Omega '$, hence $\eta _\epsilon \leq \varphi +1$ on $U_1$ for all $0<\epsilon \leq 1$. Therefore, $\eta ^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ by proposition 1.2.2 . It remains to observe that $\eta $ is upper semicontinuous. This is only non-trivial on the boundary of $\Omega '$. Take $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$ and let $(y_ i)_{i>0}$ be a sequence in $\Omega '$ with limit $x$. We first show that 1.12  egin{equation} \label{eq:limsuppsiphitemp1} \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)\leq \varphi (x). \end{equation} We may assume that $\psi (y_ i)
eq -\infty $ for all $i>0$ and the left-hand side of ( 1.12 ) is not $-\infty $. Then we can compute \[  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)\leq \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } \psi (y_ i)+\varliminf _{i	o \infty }  igl (\varphi (y_ i)-\psi (y_ i) igr )\leq \varlimsup _{i	o \infty }\varphi (y_ i)\leq \varphi (x).  \] Combining this with the upper semicontinuity of $\varphi $, we get \[  \varlimsup _{i	o \infty } igl (\varphi (y_ i)\lor \psi (y_ i) igr )\leq \varphi (x)=\eta (x).  \] This proves upper semicontinuity across $\Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Therefore, $\eta =\eta ^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. $\square$
1.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gluecond} \varliminf _{\substack {\Omega '\ni y\to x,\\ \psi (y)\neq -\infty }}\bigl (\varphi (y)-\psi (y)\bigr )\geq 0 \end{equation}

title: Corollary 1.2.13
text: Corollary 1.2.13 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain and $\Omega '\subseteq \Omega $ be a subdomain Note. In [ Proposition 1.30 , GZ17 ] , Guedj–Zeriahi assumed in addition that $\Omega '$ is relatively compact in $\Omega $. This assumption is not necessary for the proof, and the applications of this proposition in [ GZ17 ] usually do not satisfy this condition. . Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$. Assume that \[  \varlimsup _{\Omega '\ni y\to x}\psi (y)\leq \varphi (x)  \] for any $x\in \Omega \cap \partial \Omega '$. Define \[  \eta (z)=\begin{cases}  \varphi (z)\lor \psi (z),& \quad \textup{if }z\in \Omega ';\\  \varphi (z),& \quad \textup{if }z\in \Omega \setminus \Omega '. \end{cases}  \] Then $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$.

title: Proposition 1.2.14
text: Proposition 1.2.14 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, let $D \Subset \Omega $ be a strongly pseudoconvex domain, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ be locally bounded. Then there exists a unique locally bounded $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ such that \[  \begin{cases}  \left(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \right)^ n = 0&  \textup{on } D,\\  \psi = \varphi &  \textup{on } \Omega \setminus D. \end{cases}  \] Moreover, $\psi \geq \varphi $.

title: Proposition 1.2.15
text: Proposition 1.2.15 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a bounded domain. Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ be locally bounded. Assume that for each $z\in \partial \Omega $, we have \[  \varliminf _{\Omega \ni w\to z} \Bigl (\psi (w)-\varphi (w)\Bigr )\geq 0;  \] $\varphi \leq \psi $ a.e. with respect to $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$, Then $\varphi \leq \psi $.

title: 1.3 Plurifine topology
text: 1.3 Plurifine topology In this section, we introduce the notion of plurifine topology. Unlike other sections in this chapter, this section contains full details. This is mainly due to the unfortunate omissions and numerous minor problems in the foundational paper [ BT87 ] . In particular, the key theorem theorem 1.3.9 was claimed by Bedford–Taylor without proof. Our presentation largely follows [ EMW06 ] . We also include enough details so that this section is readable for those who are not familiar with the classical potential theory. Very recently, El Kadiri–Fuglede published a book [ EKF ] about classical fine potential theory, containing essentially all results in this section. The interested reader may consult their book for further details.

title: 1.3.1 Plurifine topology on domains
Proposition 1.3.2
text: Proposition 1.3.2 . The plurifine topology on $\Omega $ is finer than the Euclidean topology. Proof. It suffices to show that the unit ball $\{ z\in \mathbb {C}^ n:|z|<1\} $ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. This follows from the observation that this set can be written as \[  \{ \psi <0\}  \quad \textup{with}\quad \psi (z)\coloneqq (\log |z|) \lor (-1).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$

title: Example 1.3.3
text: Example 1.3.3 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and $C\in \mathbb {R}$. Then the sets $\{ \varphi >C\} $ and $\{ \varphi <C\} $ are both $\mathcal{F}$-open. In fact, the latter case follows from proposition 1.3.2 , while the former follows from the observation \[  \{ \varphi >C\} =\{ \varphi \lor (C-1)>C\} .  \]

title: Definition 1.3.4
text: Definition 1.3.4 . A subset $E\subseteq \Omega $ is thin Note. A more proper name would be plurithin . But since we will never need the classical notion of thin sets à la Cartan in this book, we prefer omitting the prefix pluri- . at $x\in \Omega $ if one of the following conditions holds: $x\not\in \overline{E}$; $x\in \overline{E}$ and there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq \Omega $ of $x$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ such that \[  \varlimsup _{(U\cap E)\setminus \{ x\}  \ni y\to x} \varphi (y)<\varphi (x).  \] We say $E$ is thin if it is thin at all $x\in \Omega $.

title: Remark 1.3.5
text: Remark 1.3.5 . In the second case, we can always arrange that \[  \varphi |_{(E\setminus \{ x\} )\cap U}=0.  \] In fact, we may assume that $\varphi \leq 0$ and $C<0$ is such that \[  \varlimsup _{(U\cap E)\setminus \{ x\}  \ni y\to x} \varphi (y)<C<\varphi (x).  \] We let \[  \psi =(-C)^{-1}(\varphi \lor C)+1.  \] Then $\psi $ satisfies our requirements for a smaller $U$.

title: Proposition 1.3.6 (Bedford–Taylor)

text: 1.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:BTthin_choosedelta} \psi (y)<2^{-j-2}\quad \textup{whenever } |y|<\delta _ j. \end{equation}
1.18 \begin{equation} \label{eq:BTthin_summable} \sum _{j=1}^\infty \frac{2^{-j-1}}{|\log \delta _ j|} \leq \sum _{j=1}^\infty 2^{-j-1}=\frac{1}{2} \end{equation}

title: Lemma 1.3.7
text: Lemma 1.3.7 . Let $E_1,E_2\subseteq \Omega $. Assume that $E_1$, $E_2$ are both thin at $x\in \Omega $. Then so is $E_1\cup E_2$. Proof. We may assume that $x\in \overline{E_1}\cap \overline{E_2}$. Take an open neighborhood $U\subseteq \Omega $ of $x$ and $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ such that \[  \varlimsup _{y\to x,y\in E_ i\setminus \{ x\} } \varphi _ i(y)<\varphi _ i(x),\quad i=1,2.  \] Then $\varphi _1+\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ and \[  \varlimsup _{y\to x,y\in (E_1\cup E_2)\setminus \{ x\} } (\varphi _1+\varphi _2)(y)<\varphi _1(x)+\varphi _2(x).  \] In particular, $E_1\cup E_2$ is thin at $x$. $\square$

title: Theorem 1.3.8 (H.Cartan)
text: Theorem 1.3.8 (H. Cartan) . Consider a set $E\subseteq \Omega $ and $x\in E$. Then the following are equivalent: $E$ is an $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood of $x$; $\Omega \setminus E$ is thin at $x$. Proof. 2 $\implies $ 1 . Assume 2 . We may assume that $x\in \overline{\Omega \setminus E}$. Otherwise, our assertion follows from proposition 1.3.2 . By proposition 1.3.6 , there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $\Omega $ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C}^ n)$ such that \[  \varphi (x)>\sup _{y\in U\cap (\Omega \setminus E)} \varphi (y)\eqqcolon \lambda .  \] Let $F=\{ y\in \Omega : \varphi (y)>\lambda \} $. Then $x\in F$ and $F$ is $\mathcal{F}$-open by example 1.3.3 . Moreover, $U\cap F\subseteq E$. By proposition 1.3.2 , we conclude 1 . 1 $\implies $ 2 . Assume 1 . We may always replace $E$ by smaller $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhoods of $x$. In particular, we may assume that $E$ has the following form \[  \{ y\in U:\varphi _1(y)>\lambda _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ m(y)>\lambda _ m\} ,  \] where $U\subseteq \Omega $ is an open neighborhood of $x$, and $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ m$ are $\mathbb {R}$-valued psh functions on $\Omega $, and $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ m\in \mathbb {R}$. Since $x\in U$, the set $\Omega \setminus U$ is thin at $x$. Moreover, \[  \Omega \setminus E=(\Omega \setminus U)\cup \bigcup _{i=1}^ m\{ y\in U:\varphi _ i(y)\leq \lambda _ i\} .  \] By 1.3.7 , it is enough to prove that each set $\{ y\in U:\varphi _ i(y)\leq \lambda _ i\} $ is thin at $x$. Thus we may assume $m=1$. In this case, $\Omega \setminus E$ is clearly thin at $x$. $\square$

title: Theorem 1.3.9
text: Theorem 1.3.9 . A base of the plurifine topology on $\Omega $ is given by sets of the following form: 1.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:basis_fine} \left\{ x\in U: \varphi (x)>0\right\} , \end{equation} where $U\subseteq \Omega $ is an open subset and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$. Proof. Observe that sets of the form ( 1.21 ) are $\mathcal{F}$-open. Note. This is not entirely obvious by definition, as $\varphi $ is not defined on the whole $\Omega $. By theorem 1.3.8 , it suffices to show its complement in $\Omega $ is thin at each point of ( 1.21 ), which is obvious. Now consider $x\in \Omega $ and an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood $V\subseteq \Omega $ of $x$. We want to find a set of the form ( 1.21 ) contained in $V$ and containing $x$. Write $E=\Omega \setminus V$. In case $x\in \operatorname{Int}V$, there is nothing to prove. So we may assume that $x\in \overline{E}$. By theorem 1.3.8 , $E$ is thin at $x$. By definition, there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq \Omega $ of $x$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ such that \[  \varlimsup _{y\to x,y\in U\cap (E\setminus \{ x\} )}\varphi (y)<\varphi (x).  \] We may assume that $\varphi |_{E\cap U}\leq 0<\varphi (x)$. Then the set $\{ y\in U:\varphi (y)>0\} $ suffices for our purpose. $\square$
1.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:basis_fine} \left\{ x\in U: \varphi (x)>0\right\} , \end{equation}

title: Remark 1.3.10
text: Remark 1.3.10 . Recall that in general, an $\mathcal{F}$-open set is not a countable union of sets of the form ( 1.21 ). In fact, an $\mathcal{F}$-open set is not a Borel set in general. See [ EK23 ] for a concrete example.

title: Corollary 1.3.11
text: Corollary 1.3.11 . Let $\Omega _1\subseteq \Omega _2\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be two non-empty open subsets. Then the plurifine topology on $\Omega _1$ is the same as the subspace topology induced from the plurifine topology on $\Omega _2$.

title: Corollary 1.3.12
text: Corollary 1.3.12 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ be an $\mathcal{F}$-open subset and $x\in \Omega $. Then $x$ has a compact $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood contained in $\Omega $. Proof. By theorem 1.3.9 , it suffices to prove the assertion after replacing $\Omega $ by a smaller $\mathcal F$-open neighborhood of $x$. Thus we may assume that \[  \Omega =\{ y\in U:\varphi (y)>0\}   \] for some open set $U\subseteq \mathbb C^ n$ and some $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$. Take a compact neighborhood $K$ of $x$ in $U$. Now $\{ y\in K: \varphi (y)\geq \varphi (x)/2\} $ is a compact $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood of $x$ contained in $\Omega $. $\square$

title: Corollary 1.3.13
text: Corollary 1.3.13 . Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$, $\Omega '\subseteq \mathbb {C}^{n'}$ be two domains and $F\colon \Omega '\rightarrow \Omega $ be a holomorphic map. Then $F$ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous. Proof. It suffices to show that the inverse image $F^{-1}(U)$ of each $\mathcal{F}$-open subset $U\subseteq \Omega $ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. By theorem 1.3.9 , after possibly shrinking $\Omega $ and $\Omega '$, we may assume that $U$ has the form $\{ x\in \Omega :\psi (x)>0\} $, where $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Clearly, we may assume that $F^{-1}(U)$ is non-empty. Then $F^*\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ')$ by proposition 1.1.13 , we find that \[  F^{-1}(U)=\{ y\in \Omega ': F^*\psi (y)>0\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. $\square$

title: 1.3.2 Plurifine topology on manifolds
text:
1.3.2 Plurifine topology on manifolds Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Definition 1.3.14 . The plurifine topology on $X$ is the topology with a base consisting of sets of the form $F^{-1}(V)$, where $U\subseteq X$ is an open subset, $F\colon Uightarrow \Omega $ is a biholomorphic map, $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain for some $n\in \mathbb {N}$, and $V\subseteq \Omega $ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Note that these sets form a topological base thanks to corollary 1.3.13 . Moreover, it also follows from corollary 1.3.13 that the plurifine topologies on domains defined in definition 1.3.14 and in definition 1.3.1 coincide. We refer to definition 1.5.1 for the notion of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. Proposition 1.3.15 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous. Proof. It suffices to show that $\varphi |_{\{ \varphi 
eq -\infty \} }$ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous, since $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $ is $\mathcal{F}$-closed. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain and $\varphi =\psi +g$, where $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ and $g\in C^{\infty }(X)$ and $|g|\leq C$ for some $C>0$. For an open interval $(a,b)\subseteq \mathbb {R}$, it suffices to show that \[  U\coloneqq \left\{  x\in X:a<\varphi (x)<bight\} =\left\{  x\in X:a-g(x)<\psi (x)<b-g(x)ight\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Take $x\in U$. We can find an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $U$ such that \[  \sup _{y\in V} \left( a-g(y)ight)<\psi (x)< \inf _{y\in V} \left( b-g(y) ight).  \] Therefore, \[  \left\{ z\in V:\sup _{y\in V} \left(a-g(y)ight)<\psi (z)<\inf _{y\in V} \left(b-g(y)ight)ight\}   \] is an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ in $U$. We conclude that $U$ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. $\square$ Corollary 1.3.16 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Then the set \[  \{ x\in X: \varphi (x)>\psi (x)\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Proof. It suffices to show that for any $x\in X$ such that $\varphi (x)>\psi (x)$, the same holds on an $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood $U$ of $x$. Observe that $\varphi (x)
eq -\infty $. If $\psi (x)
eq -\infty $, then it suffices to apply proposition 1.3.15 . Otherwise, take \[  U\coloneqq \{ y\in X: \varphi (y)>\varphi (x)-1\} \cap \{ y\in X: \psi (y)<\varphi (x)-1\} .  \] This is an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ contained in $\{ \varphi >\psi \} $. $\square$ Lemma 1.3.17 . Let $Z\subseteq X$ be a pluripolar subset. Then \[  \overline{X\setminus Z}^{\mathcal{F}}=X.  \] Proof. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X$ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ and that there is $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ with $Z\subseteq \{ \varphi =-\infty \} $. It suffices to show that $\{ \varphi >-\infty \} $ is $\mathcal{F}$-dense. Let $x\in X$ be a point with $\varphi (x)=-\infty $ and $U\subseteq X$ be an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ in $X$. We need to show that $U\cap \{ \varphi >-\infty \} 
eq \varnothing $. Thanks to theorem 1.3.9 , after shrinking $U$, we may assume that there is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ such that $U=\{ \psi >0\} $. Observe that $U$ is not a pluripolar set: Otherwise, $\psi \leq 0$ almost everywhere by proposition 1.2.4 , and hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . So $\varphi |_ U
ot\equiv -\infty $. We conclude that $U\cap \{ \varphi >-\infty \} 
eq \varnothing $, as desired. $\square$ Corollary 1.3.18 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Set \[  W=\left\{ x\in X:\varphi (x)=-\infty ight\} 	extup{ or }W=\left\{ x\in X:\psi (x)=-\infty ight\} .  \] Then for any pluripolar set $Z\subseteq X$, we have \[  \sup _{X\setminus W}(\varphi -\psi ) =\sup _{X\setminus (W\cup Z)}(\varphi -\psi ),\quad \inf _{X\setminus W}(\varphi -\psi ) =\inf _{X\setminus (W\cup Z)}(\varphi -\psi ).  \] In particular, taking $\psi =0$, we find that \[  \sup _{X\setminus Z}\varphi =\sup _ X \varphi .  \] Proof. This is an immediate consequence of 1.3.17 and proposition 1.3.15 . $\square$ In the literature about pluripotential theory, one often finds the careless expressions like $\sup _ X (\varphi -\psi )$. The issue is that $\varphi -\psi $ is not defined everywhere, and hence this expression does not make sense if you read it literally. corollary 1.3.18 tells you that you do not have to worry too much about the details on a pluripolar set. In other words, $\sup $ and $\inf $ could always be understood as a kind of essential supremum and essential infimum modulo pluripolar sets. There is a convenient way to fix this issue in the literature — just replace the suprema by quasi-suprema: Definition 1.3.19 . Let $Z\subseteq X$ be a pluripolar set, and $f\colon X\setminus Zightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a function. We define the quasi-supremum and the quasi-infimum of $f$ as follows: \[   egin{split}  \operatorname *{q-sup}_ X f\coloneqq & \inf \left\{ \sup _{X\setminus W} f:W\supseteq Z, W 	extup{ is pluripolar}ight\} ,\  \operatorname *{q-inf}_ X f\coloneqq & \sup \left\{ \inf _{X\setminus W} f:W\supseteq Z, W 	extup{ is pluripolar}ight\} . \end{split}  \] For two functions $f$ and $g$ equal quasi-everywhere, the quasi-suprema and quasi-infima of them are equal, as is clear from the definition. For a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $, we have \[  \operatorname *{q-sup}_ X \varphi =\sup _ X \varphi ,  \] as a consequence of corollary 1.3.18 .

title: Proposition 1.3.15
text: Proposition 1.3.15 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous. Proof. It suffices to show that $\varphi |_{\{ \varphi \neq -\infty \} }$ is $\mathcal{F}$-continuous, since $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $ is $\mathcal{F}$-closed. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain and $\varphi =\psi +g$, where $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ and $g\in C^{\infty }(X)$ and $|g|\leq C$ for some $C>0$. For an open interval $(a,b)\subseteq \mathbb {R}$, it suffices to show that \[  U\coloneqq \left\{  x\in X:a<\varphi (x)<b\right\} =\left\{  x\in X:a-g(x)<\psi (x)<b-g(x)\right\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Take $x\in U$. We can find an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $U$ such that \[  \sup _{y\in V} \left( a-g(y)\right)<\psi (x)< \inf _{y\in V} \left( b-g(y) \right).  \] Therefore, \[  \left\{ z\in V:\sup _{y\in V} \left(a-g(y)\right)<\psi (z)<\inf _{y\in V} \left(b-g(y)\right)\right\}   \] is an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ in $U$. We conclude that $U$ is $\mathcal{F}$-open. $\square$

title: Corollary 1.3.16
text: Corollary 1.3.16 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Then the set \[  \{ x\in X: \varphi (x)>\psi (x)\}   \] is $\mathcal{F}$-open. Proof. It suffices to show that for any $x\in X$ such that $\varphi (x)>\psi (x)$, the same holds on an $\mathcal{F}$-neighborhood $U$ of $x$. Observe that $\varphi (x)\neq -\infty $. If $\psi (x)\neq -\infty $, then it suffices to apply proposition 1.3.15 . Otherwise, take \[  U\coloneqq \{ y\in X: \varphi (y)>\varphi (x)-1\} \cap \{ y\in X: \psi (y)<\varphi (x)-1\} .  \] This is an $\mathcal{F}$-open neighborhood of $x$ contained in $\{ \varphi >\psi \} $. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.3.17
Corollary 1.3.18
text: Corollary 1.3.18 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Set \[  W=\left\{ x\in X:\varphi (x)=-\infty \right\} \textup{ or }W=\left\{ x\in X:\psi (x)=-\infty \right\} .  \] Then for any pluripolar set $Z\subseteq X$, we have \[  \sup _{X\setminus W}(\varphi -\psi ) =\sup _{X\setminus (W\cup Z)}(\varphi -\psi ),\quad \inf _{X\setminus W}(\varphi -\psi ) =\inf _{X\setminus (W\cup Z)}(\varphi -\psi ).  \] In particular, taking $\psi =0$, we find that \[  \sup _{X\setminus Z}\varphi =\sup _ X \varphi .  \] Proof. This is an immediate consequence of 1.3.17 and proposition 1.3.15 . $\square$

title: Definition 1.3.19
text: Definition 1.3.19 . Let $Z\subseteq X$ be a pluripolar set, and $f\colon X\setminus Z\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a function. We define the quasi-supremum and the quasi-infimum of $f$ as follows: \[  \begin{split}  \operatorname *{q-sup}_ X f\coloneqq & \inf \left\{ \sup _{X\setminus W} f:W\supseteq Z, W \textup{ is pluripolar}\right\} ,\\  \operatorname *{q-inf}_ X f\coloneqq & \sup \left\{ \inf _{X\setminus W} f:W\supseteq Z, W \textup{ is pluripolar}\right\} . \end{split}  \]

1.4 Lelong numbers and multiplier ideal sheaves In this section, we briefly recall the notions of Lelong numbers and multiplier ideal sheaves. Our presentation is by no means intended to be complete. Readers are encouraged to read the textbooks [ Section 2.3 , GZ17 ] and [ Dem12 ] . Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Definition 1.4.1 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ and $x\in X$. The Lelong number $
u (\varphi ,x)$ of $\varphi $ at $x$ is defined as follows: If $x$ is a point on a $0$-dimensional connected component of $X$, we set \[  
u (\varphi ,x)=0.  \] Otherwise, take an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$ and a biholomorphic map $F\colon Uightarrow \Omega $, where $\Omega $ is a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Then we define 1.24  egin{equation} \label{eq:nuvarphix} 
u (\varphi ,x)\coloneqq \sup \left\{  \gamma \in \mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}: \varphi (F^{-1}(y))\leq \gamma \log |y-F(x)|^2+\mathcal{O}(1)	extup{ as }y	o F(x) ight\} . \end{equation} Observe that $
u (\varphi ,x)$ does not depend on the choices of $U$ and $F$, see [ Page 167, Corollary 7.2 , DemBook ] . Furthermore, it follows from proposition 1.4.3 below that the supremum in ( 1.24 ) is a maximum. Remark 1.4.2 . Our definition of the Lelong number is not standard. It differs from the standard definition by a factor of $2$. As a mnemonic, just remember \[  
u \left(\log |z|^2,0ight)=1 \quad (	ext{instead of } 2).  \] Our convention of the Lelong numbers together with the convention of the multiplier ideal sheaves below make sure that ( 1.30 ) has no extra factors. Proposition 1.4.3 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B_ n(0,1))$. Then 1.25  egin{equation} \label{eq:Lelongnewdef} 
u (\varphi ,0)=\lim _{r 	o 0+}  rac{\sup _{B_ n(0,r)}\varphi }{\log r^2}\in [0,\infty ). \end{equation} Proof. Note that ( 1.25 ) is trivial when $n=0$, so we may assume that $n>0$ in the proof. It follows from proposition 1.1.8 that the limit in ( 1.25 ) exists and is finite. We shall denote the limit by $
u '(\varphi ,0)$ for the time being. We first observe that by proposition 1.1.8 , for any fixed $r_1\in (0,1)$ there is a constant $C_{r_1}$ such that 1.26  egin{equation} \label{eq:varphixlocalupperbd} \varphi (x)\leq 
u '(\varphi ,0)\log |x|^2+C_{r_1} \end{equation} when $x\in B_ n(0,r_1)\setminus \{ 0\} $. In particular, $

u '(\varphi ,0)$. In order to argue the reverse inequality, we may assume that $
u (\varphi ,0)>0$. Next observe that by ( 1.24 ), for each small enough $\epsilon >0$, we can find $r_0\in (0,1)$ and $C>0$ so that for all $x\in B_ n(0,r_0)\setminus \{ 0\} $, we have \[  \varphi (x)\leq (
u (\varphi ,0)-\epsilon )\log |x|^2+C.  \] It follows that $
u '(\varphi ,0)\geq 
u (\varphi ,0)-\epsilon $. Letting $\epsilon 	o 0+$, we conclude that $
u '(\varphi ,0)\geq 
u (\varphi ,0)$, which combined with the previous inequality gives ( 1.25 ). $\square$ We recall Siu's semicontinuity theorem. Theorem 1.4.4 (Siu) . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then the map $X

u (\varphi ,x)$ is upper semicontinuous with respect to the Zariski topology. For an elegant proof we refer to [ Theorem 2.10 , Dem12 ] . Proposition 1.4.5 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, $\lambda \in \mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}$ and $x\in X$. Then \[   egin{aligned}

u (\varphi ,x),

All properties follow directly from proposition 1.4.3 . $\square$ Corollary 1.4.6 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ locally uniformly bounded from above and $x\in X$. Then \[  
u \left(\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i,xight)=\inf _{i\in I}
u (\varphi _ i,x).  \] Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. Write $\varphi =\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i$. Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ by proposition 1.2.2 . We observe that the $\leq $ inequality is trivial. It remains to argue the reverse inequality. It follows from proposition 1.2.3 that we may assume that $I$ is countable. When $I$ is finite, this is already proved in proposition 1.4.5 . Otherwise, we may further assume that $I=\mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. Thanks to proposition 1.4.5 , we may further assume that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ is an increasing sequence. Furthermore, since the problem is local, we may assume that $x=0$, that $X=B_ n(0,1)$ for some $n\in \mathbb {N}$, and that $(\varphi _ i)_ i$ is uniformly bounded from above on some ball $B_ n(0,r_1)$ with $0<r_1<1$. Since the sequence $(\varphi _ i)_ i$ is increasing, the sequence $
u (\varphi _ i,0)$ is decreasing. Thus the constants in ( 1.26 ) can be chosen independently of $i$, and we have \[  \varphi _ i(x)\leq 
u (\varphi _ i,0)\log |x|^2+C  \] for all $x\in B_ n(0,r_1)\setminus \{ 0\} $ and all $i\geq 1$, where $C$ is a constant independent of $i$. In particular, thanks to proposition 1.2.5 , for almost all $x\in B_ n(0,r_1)$, we have \[  \varphi (x)\leq \lim _{i	o \infty }

u (\varphi ,F)\coloneqq \min _{x\in F}
u (\varphi ,x).  \] Note that the minimum is attained by Siu's semicontinuity theorem theorem 1.4.4 . Definition 1.4.8 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Let $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$ (see definition B.1.1 ). Take a proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ from a complex manifold $Y$ such that $E$ is a prime divisor on $Y$, then we define the generic Lelong number of $\varphi $ along $E$ as \[  
u (\varphi ,E)\coloneqq 
u (\pi ^*\varphi ,E).  \] It follows from theorem 1.4.4 that $
u (\varphi ,E)$ does not depend on the choice of $\pi $. Definition 1.4.9 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, the multiplier ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}(\varphi )$  of $\varphi $ is by definition the ideal sheaf given by \[  \Gamma \left(U,\mathcal{I}(\varphi )ight)=\left\{  f\in \mathcal{O}_ X(U) : |f|^2\exp (-\varphi )\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U) ight\}   \] for any open subset $U\subseteq X$. The conventions adopted in the current book are the most convenient ones as far as I know. They simplify a number of formulae. As a mnemonic, for any real $\lambda >0$, we have \[  \mathcal{I}(\lambda \log |z|^2)=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {C}}\left(-\lfloor \lambda floor \{ 0\} ight)\quad \Bigl (	extup{instead of }\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {C}}\left(-\lfloor 2\lambda floor \{ 0\} ight)\Bigr ),  \] where $z$ is a variable in $\mathbb {C}$ and $\{ 0\} $ is the divisor defined by $0\in \mathbb {C}$. Proposition 1.4.11 (Nadel) . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then $\mathcal{I}(\varphi )$ is coherent. See [ Proposition 5.7 , Dem12 ] . Theorem 1.4.12 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then \[  \mathcal{I}(\varphi +\psi )\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal{I}(\psi ).  \] See [ DEL00 ] , [ Theorem 14.2 , Dem12 ] . The two invariants are related by the following simple result: Proposition 1.4.13 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ and $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$. Then 1.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:LelongMIS} 
u (\varphi ,E)=\lim _{k	o \infty } rac{1}{k}\operatorname{ord}_ E\mathcal{I}(k\varphi ). \end{equation} See [ Proposition 2.14 , DX21 ] . Recall that this particular form of the formula is compatible with our conventions of $
u $ and $\mathcal{I}$. As a consistency check, consider $\varphi =\log |z|^2$ with $z\in \mathbb {C}$ and let $E$ be the divisor $\{ 0\} $. Then both sides of ( 1.30 ) are equal to $1$. See 1.4.2 and 1.4.10 . Also observe the following simple lemma: Lemma 1.4.14 . Let $x \in X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be the blow-up of $X$ at $x$ with exceptional divisor $E$. Then \[  
u (\varphi ,x)=
u (\varphi ,E),  \] See [ Corollaire 1.1.8 , Bou02 ] . Conversely, the information of the generic Lelong numbers determines the multiplier ideal sheaves: Theorem 1.4.15 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Let $x\in X$ and $f\in \mathcal{O}_{X,x}$, $f
eq 0$. Then the following are equivalent: $f\in \mathcal{I}(\varphi )_ x$; there exists $\epsilon >0$ such that for any prime divisor $E$ over $X$ such that $x$ is contained in the center of $E$ on $X$, we have 1.31  egin{equation} \label{eq:ordfLelonglogdis} \operatorname{ord}_ E(f)\geq (1+\epsilon ) 
u (\varphi ,E)-A_ X(E). \end{equation} In case $\varphi $ has analytic singularities and $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ is a log resolution of $\varphi $ (see definition 1.6.6 for the definition) with finitely many exceptional divisors $\{ E_ i\} $ whose centers on $X$ contain $x$, one may replace ( 1.31 ) by 1.32  egin{equation} \label{eq:ordfLelonglogdis2} \operatorname{ord}_{E_ i}(f)> 
u (\varphi ,E_ i)-A_ X(E_ i)\quad  orall i. \end{equation} Here $A_ X( ullet )$ denotes the log discrepancy of prime divisors. Note that in (2), it suffices to consider the prime divisors contained in $\{ \pi ^*\varphi =-\infty \} $. We refer to [ Corollary 10.18, Proposition 10.12 , Bou17 ] for the proof and the precise definition of $A_ X$. The notion of analytic singularities is recalled in section 1.6 . Recall the strong openness theorem: Theorem 1.4.16 (Guan–Zhou) . Let $\varphi ,\psi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ ($j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$) such that $\psi _ j$ is an increasing sequence converging to $\varphi $ almost everywhere. Then for any $x\in X$, the germs satisfy \[  \mathcal{I}\left(\psi _ jight)_ x=\mathcal{I}(\varphi )_ x  \] when $j$ is large enough. See [ GZ15 , Hiep14 ] for the proof. Proposition 1.4.17 . Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a smooth morphism between complex manifolds. Assume that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Then \[  \mathcal{I}(\pi ^*\varphi )=\pi ^*\mathcal{I}(\varphi ).  \] Proof. It follows from [ Théorème 3.10 , SHC6 ] that locally $\pi $ can be written as the composition of an étale morphism and a projection. It suffices to handle the two cases separately. Recall that in the complex analytic setting, an étale morphism is locally biholomorphic, so there is nothing to prove in this case. Next, assume that $Y=X	imes U$, where $U\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain and $\pi $ is the natural projection. It follows from Fubini's theorem that \[  \mathcal{I}(\pi ^*\varphi )\supseteq \pi ^*\mathcal{I}(\varphi ).  \] The reverse inequality is proved in [ Proposition 14.3 , Dem12 ] Note. In [ Proposition 14.3 , Dem12 ] , Demailly used the highly non-standard notation $f^*\mathcal{I}(\varphi )$ to denote the image of $f^*\mathcal{I}(\varphi )ightarrow \mathcal{O}_ X$, even when $f$ is not flat. . $\square$ Definition 1.4.18 . Given a coherent ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}$ on $X$ and a closed complex subspace $Y\subseteq X$, the restriction $\operatorname{Res}_ Y\mathcal{I}$  is the coherent ideal sheaf given by 1.33  egin{equation} \label{eq:RestI} \operatorname{Res}_ Y\mathcal{I}\coloneqq \mathcal{I}/(\mathcal{I}\cap \mathcal{I}_ Y), \end{equation} where $\mathcal{I}_ Y$ is the ideal sheaf defining $Y$.
