Recall that in the complex analytic setting, an étale morphism is locally biholomorphic, so there is nothing to prove in this case. Next, assume that $Y=X\times U$, where $U\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ is a domain and $\pi $ is the natural projection. It follows from Fubini's theorem that \[  \mathcal{I}(\pi ^*\varphi )\supseteq \pi ^*\mathcal{I}(\varphi ).  \] The reverse inequality is proved in [ Proposition 14.3 , Dem12 ] Note. In [ Proposition 14.3 , Dem12 ] , Demailly used the highly non-standard notation $f^*\mathcal{I}(\varphi )$ to denote the image of $f^*\mathcal{I}(\varphi )\rightarrow \mathcal{O}_ X$, even when $f$ is not flat. . $\square$

title: Definition 1.4.18
text: Definition 1.4.18 . Given a coherent ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}$ on $X$ and a closed complex subspace $Y\subseteq X$, the restriction $\operatorname{Res}_ Y\mathcal{I}$  is the coherent ideal sheaf given by 1.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:RestI} \operatorname{Res}_ Y\mathcal{I}\coloneqq \mathcal{I}/(\mathcal{I}\cap \mathcal{I}_ Y), \end{equation} where $\mathcal{I}_ Y$ is the ideal sheaf defining $Y$.
1.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:RestI} \operatorname{Res}_ Y\mathcal{I}\coloneqq \mathcal{I}/(\mathcal{I}\cap \mathcal{I}_ Y), \end{equation}
1.34 \begin{equation} \label{eq:pullbacktoinverimage} i_ Y^*\mathcal{I}= \mathcal{I}/(\mathcal{I}\cdot \mathcal{I}_ Y)\rightarrow \operatorname{Res}_ Y \mathcal{I}, \end{equation}

title: Theorem 1.4.19 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi)
text: Theorem 1.4.19 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi) . Let $Y$ be a connected submanifold of $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Assume that $\varphi |_ Y\not\equiv -\infty $. Then \[  \mathcal{I}\left(\varphi |_ Y\right)\subseteq \operatorname{Res}_ Y\mathcal{I}(\varphi ).  \]

title: 1.5 Quasi-plurisubharmonic functions
text:
1.5 Quasi-plurisubharmonic functions In practice, it is important to consider a variant of plurisubharmonic functions. We will fix a complex manifold $X$. Definition 1.5.1 . Let $	heta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. A $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function or $	heta $-psh function for short on $X$ is a function $\varphi \colon Xightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that for each $x\in X$ and each open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$ satisfying the condition that $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some smooth function $g$ on $U$, we have $g+\varphi |_ U\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$. The set of $	heta $-psh functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. A quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is a function $\varphi \colon Xightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that there exists a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta '$ on $X$ such that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ')$. The set of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. There is a natural preorder on $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ defined as follows: Definition 1.5.2 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, we say that $\varphi $ is more singular than $\psi $ and write $\varphi \preceq \psi $ Note. Some people write $\psi \preceq \varphi $. if there is $C\in \mathbb {R}$ such that $\varphi \leq \psi +C$. We also say $\psi $ is less singular than $\varphi $ and write $\psi \succeq \varphi $. In case $\varphi \preceq \psi $ and $\psi \preceq \varphi $, we say $\varphi $ and $\psi $ have the same singularity type . We write $\varphi \sim \psi $  in this case. It is sometimes convenient to include the constant function $-\infty $ as well. Then we always write $-\infty \preceq \varphi $ for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Formally, we write $-\infty \sim -\infty $ as well. When $X$ is not compact, one can still define similar notions, but the generalization is not unique, and we shall not consider them in this book. Remark 1.5.3 . The preceding results concerning plurisubharmonic functions can be extended mutatis mutandis to quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. We will apply these extensions without further explanations. Proposition 1.5.4 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $	heta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then for any $a,b\in \mathbb {R}$, $a\leq b$, the set \[  \left\{  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ): \sup _ X \varphi \in [a,b]ight\}   \] is compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology. Moreover, $\varphi \mapsto \sup _ X \varphi $ is $L^1$-continuous for $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. This is an immediate consequence of [ Proposition 8.5, Exercise 1.20 , GZ17 ] Note. In the proof of [ Proposition 8.5 , GZ17 ] , there is a misleading sentence: This is a dcreasing sequence of $\omega $-psh functions , which should be removed. . Remark 1.5.5 . More generally, if $K\subseteq X$ is a closed non-pluripolar subset, then \[  \left\{  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ): \sup _ K \varphi \in [a,b]ight\}   \] is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology. See [ Corollary 4.3 , GZ05 ] . As a consequence, if $\sup _ K \varphi \leq C_0$ for some $C_0\in \mathbb {R}$, then $\sup _ X \varphi \leq C_1$ for some $C_1\in \mathbb {R}$ as well. To see this, we may assume that $C_0>0$. When $\sup _ K \varphi \in [0,C_0]$, our assertion follows from the above. If $\sup _ K \varphi <0$, it suffices to observe that \[  \varphi \leq \varphi -\sup _ K \varphi .  \] Corollary 1.5.6 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $	heta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ such that $\sup _ X \varphi _ i$ is uniformly bounded from below. Then $\varphi =\inf _{i\in I} \varphi _ i$ is a $	heta $-psh function and 1.35  egin{equation} \label{eq:decreasingnetL1conv} \adjustlimits \lim _{i\in I}\sup _ X \varphi _ i=\sup _ X \varphi ,\quad \varphi _ i\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi . \end{equation} Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. It suffices to show that $\varphi 
ot\equiv -\infty $. From this, it follows that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $\varphi _ i	o \varphi $ in $L^1$ by proposition 1.2.2 . The $L^1$-continuity of $\eta \mapsto \sup _ X\eta $ on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ from proposition 1.5.4 then gives the first equality in ( 1.35 ). Fix $i_0\in I$ and replace $I$ by the cofinal tail $I_{\geq i_0}$. This does not change the infimum. On this tail we have \[  \sup _ X\varphi _ i\leq \sup _ X\varphi _{i_0},  \] while the suprema are bounded from below by assumption. Hence proposition 1.5.4 shows that the net $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology. We may therefore take a subnet $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in J}$ converging in $L^1$ to some $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Since $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in J}$ is a Willard subnet of $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$, we know that it is also decreasing. Therefore, $\psi =\inf _{j\in J} \varphi _ j$ due to proposition 1.2.2 and proposition 1.2.6 . Fix $i_0\in I$. For all sufficiently large $j\in J$, the corresponding index of the subnet dominates $i_0$, hence \[  \varphi _ j\leq \varphi _{i_0}.  \] Therefore, $\psi \leq \varphi _{i_0}$. As $i_0$ was arbitrary, $\psi \leq \varphi $ everywhere. In particular, $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $. $\square$ Proposition 1.5.7 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $	heta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ and $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$. Then \[  \sup \Bigl \{  
u (\varphi ,E): \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ) \Bigr \} <\infty .  \] Proof. It follows from the proof of [ Exercise 2.7 , GZ17 ] that $
u ( ullet ,E)$ is upper semicontinuous with respect to the $L^1$-topology on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Since adding a constant does not change Lelong numbers, we may restrict to the compact set $\{ \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):\sup _ X\varphi =0\} $ from proposition 1.5.4 . The desired upper bound follows. $\square$ Proposition 1.5.8 . Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $	heta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then the pull-back gives a bijection \[  \pi ^*\colon \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\xlongrightarrow {\sim }\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta ).  \] This follows from a more general result theorem B.1.4 . Since we shall constantly need the balayage argument of proposition 1.2.14 , we explain explicitly the global version of it. Proposition 1.5.9 . Fix a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ on $X$. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and $B\Subset B' \subseteq X$ be two holomorphic balls. Assume that $\varphi $ is locally bounded on $B'$. Then there is a unique $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ so that $\psi $ is bounded on an open neighborhood of $\overline{B}$, and \[   egin{cases}  \left( 	heta |_ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi |_ B ight)^ n = 0,\  \psi = \varphi \quad 	extup{on } X\setminus B. \end{cases}  \] Moreover, $\psi \geq \varphi $. We shall call $\psi $ the balayage of $\varphi $ on $B$. Proof. By the Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma, after possibly shrinking $B'$, we may write $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some bounded function $g\in C^{\infty }(B')$. We can then use $g$ to translate $	heta $-psh functions to psh functions, and our assertion follows immediately from proposition 1.2.14 . $\square$

title: Definition 1.5.1
text: Definition 1.5.1 . Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. A $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function or $\theta $-psh function for short on $X$ is a function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that for each $x\in X$ and each open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $X$ satisfying the condition that $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some smooth function $g$ on $U$, we have $g+\varphi |_ U\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$. The set of $\theta $-psh functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. A quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is a function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that there exists a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta '$ on $X$ such that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$. The set of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)$.

title: Definition 1.5.2
text: Definition 1.5.2 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, we say that $\varphi $ is more singular than $\psi $ and write $\varphi \preceq \psi $ Note. Some people write $\psi \preceq \varphi $. if there is $C\in \mathbb {R}$ such that $\varphi \leq \psi +C$. We also say $\psi $ is less singular than $\varphi $ and write $\psi \succeq \varphi $. In case $\varphi \preceq \psi $ and $\psi \preceq \varphi $, we say $\varphi $ and $\psi $ have the same singularity type . We write $\varphi \sim \psi $  in this case. Definition 1.12.1 . Let $u,v$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$. We write $u\preceq v$ if there is a constant $C\in \mathbb R$ such that $u\leq v+C$ on $X$, and $u\sim v$ if both $u\preceq v$ and $v\preceq u$; in the latter case $u$ and $v$ have the same singularity type . When this has to be distinguished from the multiplier-ideal type introduced below, we speak of the ordinary singularity type , or simply the ordinary type .

title: Remark 1.5.3
text: Remark 1.5.3 . The preceding results concerning plurisubharmonic functions can be extended mutatis mutandis to quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. We will apply these extensions without further explanations.

title: Proposition 1.5.4
text: Proposition 1.5.4 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then for any $a,b\in \mathbb {R}$, $a\leq b$, the set \[  \left\{  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): \sup _ X \varphi \in [a,b]\right\}   \] is compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology. Moreover, $\varphi \mapsto \sup _ X \varphi $ is $L^1$-continuous for $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$.

title: Remark 1.5.5
text: Remark 1.5.5 . More generally, if $K\subseteq X$ is a closed non-pluripolar subset, then \[  \left\{  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): \sup _ K \varphi \in [a,b]\right\}   \] is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology. See [ Corollary 4.3 , GZ05 ] . As a consequence, if $\sup _ K \varphi \leq C_0$ for some $C_0\in \mathbb {R}$, then $\sup _ X \varphi \leq C_1$ for some $C_1\in \mathbb {R}$ as well. To see this, we may assume that $C_0>0$. When $\sup _ K \varphi \in [0,C_0]$, our assertion follows from the above. If $\sup _ K \varphi <0$, it suffices to observe that \[  \varphi \leq \varphi -\sup _ K \varphi .  \]

title: Corollary 1.5.6
text: Corollary 1.5.6 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\sup _ X \varphi _ i$ is uniformly bounded from below. Then $\varphi =\inf _{i\in I} \varphi _ i$ is a $\theta $-psh function and 1.35 \begin{equation} \label{eq:decreasingnetL1conv} \adjustlimits \lim _{i\in I}\sup _ X \varphi _ i=\sup _ X \varphi ,\quad \varphi _ i\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi . \end{equation} Proof. We may assume that $X$ is connected. It suffices to show that $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $. From this, it follows that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi _ i\to \varphi $ in $L^1$ by proposition 1.2.2 . The $L^1$-continuity of $\eta \mapsto \sup _ X\eta $ on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ from proposition 1.5.4 then gives the first equality in ( 1.35 ). Fix $i_0\in I$ and replace $I$ by the cofinal tail $I_{\geq i_0}$. This does not change the infimum. On this tail we have \[  \sup _ X\varphi _ i\leq \sup _ X\varphi _{i_0},  \] while the suprema are bounded from below by assumption. Hence proposition 1.5.4 shows that the net $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology. We may therefore take a subnet $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in J}$ converging in $L^1$ to some $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Since $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in J}$ is a Willard subnet of $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$, we know that it is also decreasing. Therefore, $\psi =\inf _{j\in J} \varphi _ j$ due to proposition 1.2.2 and proposition 1.2.6 . Fix $i_0\in I$. For all sufficiently large $j\in J$, the corresponding index of the subnet dominates $i_0$, hence \[  \varphi _ j\leq \varphi _{i_0}.  \] Therefore, $\psi \leq \varphi _{i_0}$. As $i_0$ was arbitrary, $\psi \leq \varphi $ everywhere. In particular, $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $. $\square$
1.35 \begin{equation} \label{eq:decreasingnetL1conv} \adjustlimits \lim _{i\in I}\sup _ X \varphi _ i=\sup _ X \varphi ,\quad \varphi _ i\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi . \end{equation}

title: Proposition 1.5.7
text: Proposition 1.5.7 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ and $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$. Then \[  \sup \Bigl \{  \nu (\varphi ,E): \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ) \Bigr \} <\infty .  \] Proof. It follows from the proof of [ Exercise 2.7 , GZ17 ] that $\nu (\bullet ,E)$ is upper semicontinuous with respect to the $L^1$-topology on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Since adding a constant does not change Lelong numbers, we may restrict to the compact set $\{ \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\sup _ X\varphi =0\} $ from proposition 1.5.4 . The desired upper bound follows. $\square$

title: Proposition 1.5.8
text: Proposition 1.5.8 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then the pull-back gives a bijection \[  \pi ^*\colon \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\xlongrightarrow {\sim }\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta ).  \]

title: Proposition 1.5.9
text: Proposition 1.5.9 . Fix a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $B\Subset B' \subseteq X$ be two holomorphic balls. Assume that $\varphi $ is locally bounded on $B'$. Then there is a unique $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ so that $\psi $ is bounded on an open neighborhood of $\overline{B}$, and \[  \begin{cases}  \left( \theta |_ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi |_ B \right)^ n = 0,\\  \psi = \varphi \quad \textup{on } X\setminus B. \end{cases}  \] Moreover, $\psi \geq \varphi $. Proof. By the Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma, after possibly shrinking $B'$, we may write $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some bounded function $g\in C^{\infty }(B')$. We can then use $g$ to translate $\theta $-psh functions to psh functions, and our assertion follows immediately from proposition 1.2.14 . $\square$

title: 1.6 Analytic singularities
text: 1.6 Analytic singularities The simplest type of plurisubharmonic singularities is given by the so-called analytic singularities . The notion is fairly subtle and there are several mutually incompatible definitions in the literature, as we shall explain below. Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Definition 1.6.1 . We say $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities if for each $x\in X$, we can find a connected open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $\varphi |_ U$ has the form: 1.38 \begin{equation} \label{eq:anasinglocal} c\log (|f_1|^2+\cdots +|f_ N|^2)+R, \end{equation} where $f_1,\ldots ,f_ N$ are holomorphic functions on $U$, $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ and $R$ is a bounded function on $U$. Note. Note that since $\varphi |_ U\not\equiv -\infty $ by assumption, it is implicit in the definition that $\{ f_1=\cdots =f_ N=0\} \subseteq U$ is a proper subset. When $R$ can be taken to be smooth Note. The decomposition ( 1.38 ) is highly non-unique. Here we mean for any $x$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ and a decomposition of the form ( 1.38 ) with $R$ smooth. In the non-trivial cases, $R$ cannot be smooth for all decompositions ( 1.38 ). , we say $\varphi $ has neat analytic singularities . Suppose that there is a coherent ideal $\mathcal{I}\subseteq \mathcal{O}_ X$ on $X$ such that we can choose $U$ so that the $f_1,\ldots ,f_ N$ can be chosen as the generators of $\Gamma (U,\mathcal{I})$ and $c$ is independent of the choice of $U$. Then we say $\varphi $ has analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathcal{I})$. If $X$ is compact, each potential with analytic singularities has a type. The type is not uniquely determined. We refer to [ Bou02 ] and [ Bou02b ] for the details. Some authors allow $c\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}$ in ( 1.38 ). We keep $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ because the following closure property, which is essential in constructing Demailly approximations, would otherwise fail. Proposition 1.6.2 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be potentials with analytic singularities. Then so are $\lambda \varphi $ ($\lambda \in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$), $\varphi +\psi $ and $\varphi \lor \psi $. Proof. The assertion for $\lambda \varphi $ follows by multiplying the rational coefficient in ( 1.38 ). The assertion for $\lor $ is proved in [ Proposition 4.1.8 , Dem15 ] . For the addition assertion, take local presentations as in ( 1.38 ) and multiply the corresponding finite systems of holomorphic generators. $\square$ Definition 1.6.3 . Let $D$ be an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor Note. Divisors and $\mathbb {Q}$-divisors are implicitly assumed to have locally finite coefficients as usual. on $X$. We say $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has log singularities (along $D$) on $X$ if for each $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $D|_ U$ has finitely many irreducible components and can be written as \[  D|_ U=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ i D_ i  \] with $D_ i$ prime divisors on $U$, $a_ i\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ and $s_ i$ holomorphic functions on $U$ defining $D_ i$, and we have 1.39 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logsingreminder} \varphi |_ U=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ i\log |s_ i|^2+R, \end{equation} where $R$ is a bounded function on $U$. By proposition 1.6.2 , $\varphi $ has analytic singularities. Lemma 1.6.4 . Suppose that $X$ is a compact Kähler manifold, $\theta $ is a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Suppose that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$ on $X$. Then the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef. Moreover, if in addition $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current Note. That is, there is a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ such that $\theta _{\varphi }\geq \omega $ in the sense of currents. , then the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. Here and in the sequel, we write $\theta _{\varphi }$ for $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $. Proof. The current $\theta _{\varphi }-[D]$ has bounded local potentials. Therefore, the class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef. If $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, say $\theta _{\varphi }\geq \omega $ for a Kähler form $\omega $, then $\theta _{\varphi }-[D]-\omega $ is positive and has bounded local potentials, and therefore represents a nef class. We conclude that $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. $\square$ The following proposition follows immediately from the definitions: Proposition 1.6.5 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a complex manifold $Y$. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities (resp. has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$). Then $\pi ^*\varphi $ has analytic singularities (resp. has log singularities along $\pi ^*D$). Definition 1.6.6 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. A log resolution of $\varphi $ is a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $\pi ^*\varphi $ has log singularities along a simple normal crossing effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor. See definition B.1.5 for the notion of modifications. Theorem 1.6.7 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities. Then there is a log resolution of $\varphi $. For a proof, we refer to the arguments on [ Page 104 , MM07 ] . A general quasi-plurisubharmonic function can be nicely approximated by those with analytic singularities. We need a few preliminary definitions. Definition 1.6.8 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. A sequence $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ in $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ is quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ if $\varphi _ j$ has analytic singularities for each $j$; $\varphi _ j$ is decreasing with limit $\varphi $; there is a decreasing sequence $\epsilon _ j\geq 0$ with limit $0$ and a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ such that $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\epsilon _ j\omega )$; for each $\lambda '>\lambda >0$, there is $j>0$ such that 1.40 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quasi_eq_prop} \mathcal{I}(\lambda ' \varphi _ j)\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi ). \end{equation} We also say $(\theta _{\varphi _ j})_ j$ is a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\theta _{\varphi }$. Definition 1.6.9 . Let $\mathcal{I}\subseteq \mathcal O_ X$ be a coherent ideal sheaf and $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$. A function $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ is said to have gentle analytic singularities (of type $(c,\mathcal{I})$) if $\varphi $ has analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathcal{I})$; $\mathrm{e}^{{\varphi }/{c}}\colon X\to \mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}$ is a smooth function; there is a proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon \widetilde{X}\to X$ from a Kähler manifold $\widetilde{X}$ and an effective $\mathbb {Z}$-divisor $D$ on $\widetilde{X}$ such that one can write $\pi ^*\varphi $ locally as \[  \pi ^*\varphi =c\log |g|^2+h,  \] where $g$ is a local equation of the divisor $D$ and $h$ is smooth. Theorem 1.6.10 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ admits a quasi-equisingular approximation $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$. Moreover, we can guarantee that for all $j>0$, $\varphi _ j$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $\left(2^{-j},\mathcal{I}(2^ j\varphi )\right)$. We refer to [ Dem92reg , DPS01 ] for the proof. Quasi-equisingular approximations are essentially unique in the following sense: Proposition 1.6.11 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Let $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ and $(\psi _ j)_ j$ be two quasi-equisingular approximations of $\varphi $. Then for any $\epsilon \in (0,1)$ and any $j>0$, we can find $k_0>0$ such that for any $k\geq k_0$, we have \[  \psi _ k\preceq (1-\epsilon )\varphi _ j.  \] See [ Corollary 4.1.7 , Dem15 ] . Definition 1.6.12 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. Then we define $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )$  as the ideal sheaf consisting of germs $f$ of holomorphic functions such that $\log |f|^2\leq \varphi +C$ for some $C\in \mathbb {R}$. By definition, $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\varphi )$. Lemma 1.6.13 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. The sheaf $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )$ is coherent. Proof. By theorem 1.6.7 , we may find a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $\pi ^*\varphi $ has log singularities. Observe that \[  \mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )=\pi _*\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\pi ^*\varphi ),  \] so we may replace $X$ and $\varphi $ by $Y$ and $\pi ^*\varphi $ and assume that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$. We decompose $D$ into its irreducible components: \[  D=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ iD_ i.  \] In this case, observe that \[  \mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )=\mathcal{O}_ X\left(-\sum _{i=1}^ N\left(\lceil a_ i \rceil D_ i\right)\right)  \] is clearly coherent. $\square$ The multiplier ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}$ and the sheaf $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }$ are not very different in the asymptotic sense, as shown by the following lemma: Lemma 1.6.14 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. Then for any $\epsilon >0$, we can find $k_0>0$ such that for each $k\geq k_0$, we have 1.41 \begin{equation} \label{eq:IandIinf} \mathcal{I}\left(k(1+\epsilon )\varphi \right)\subseteq \mathcal{I}_{\infty }(k\varphi ). \end{equation} Proof. We shall prove a more precise local result. Take $x\in X$, take an open neighborhood $U\subseteq X$ of $x$, on which \[  \varphi =c\log \left( |g_1|^2 +\cdots +|g_ N|^2\right)+\mathcal{O}(1),  \] where $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ and $g_1,\ldots ,g_ N$ are holomorphic functions on $U$. Then we claim that for any $\lambda >0$, we have 1.42 \begin{equation} \label{eq:IIinf_temp1} \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi )_ x\subseteq \mathcal{I}_{\infty }\left( \left( \lambda -c^{-1}n \right)_+\varphi \right)_ x, \end{equation} where for any $a\in \mathbb {R}$, $a_+$ means $a\lor 0$. Note that ( 1.41 ) is a straightforward consequence of ( 1.42 ). The global result follows easily from the local result by the compactness of $X$. Fix a smooth volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$. Take $f\in \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi )$. By strong openness theorem 1.4.16 , we can find $\epsilon >0$ so that $f\in \mathcal{I}((\lambda +\epsilon /c)\varphi )$. Therefore, we can find an open neighborhood $W\subseteq U$ of $x$ so that \[  \int _ W |f|^2\left( |g_1|^2 +\cdots +|g_ N|^2\right)^{-c\lambda -\epsilon }\, \mathrm{d}V<\infty .  \] But it follows from the Briançon–Skoda division theorem ( [ Sko72 ] , [ SB74 ] , [ Theorem 11.17 , Dem12 ] ) that \[  f_ x\in \left(g_{1,x},\ldots ,g_{N,x} \right)^\alpha ,  \] where $\alpha =\left(\lfloor c \lambda \rfloor -n+1\right)_+$. Here $\left(g_{1,x},\ldots ,g_{N,x} \right)$ denotes the ideal in $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ generated by the germs of $g_1,\ldots ,g_ N$ at $x$. Note that $\alpha \geq (c\lambda -n)_+$. It follows that on a neighborhood of $x$, we have \[  \log |f|^2\leq \alpha \log \left( |g_1|^2 +\cdots +|g_ N|^2\right)+\mathcal{O}(1)\leq c^{-1}\alpha \varphi +\mathcal{O}(1).  \] Hence ( 1.42 ) follows. $\square$ Theorem 1.6.15 . Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold and $Y\subseteq X$ be a connected closed submanifold. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\omega |_ Y)$ such that $\omega |_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a Kähler current and $\mathrm{e}^{\varphi }$ is a Hölder continuous function on $Y$. Then there exists $\tilde{\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfying $\tilde{\varphi }|_ Y=\varphi $; $\omega _{\tilde{\varphi }}$ is a Kähler current. In addition, if $\varphi $ has analytic singularities, then so does $\tilde{\varphi }$. See [ Theorem 6.1 , DRWNXZ ] .
1.38 \begin{equation} \label{eq:anasinglocal} c\log (|f_1|^2+\cdots +|f_ N|^2)+R, \end{equation}

title: Proposition 1.6.2
text: Proposition 1.6.2 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be potentials with analytic singularities. Then so are $\lambda \varphi $ ($\lambda \in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$), $\varphi +\psi $ and $\varphi \lor \psi $. Proof. The assertion for $\lambda \varphi $ follows by multiplying the rational coefficient in ( 1.38 ). The assertion for $\lor $ is proved in [ Proposition 4.1.8 , Dem15 ] . For the addition assertion, take local presentations as in ( 1.38 ) and multiply the corresponding finite systems of holomorphic generators. $\square$

title: Definition 1.6.3
text: Definition 1.6.3 . Let $D$ be an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor Note. Divisors and $\mathbb {Q}$-divisors are implicitly assumed to have locally finite coefficients as usual. on $X$. We say $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has log singularities (along $D$) on $X$ if for each $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $D|_ U$ has finitely many irreducible components and can be written as \[  D|_ U=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ i D_ i  \] with $D_ i$ prime divisors on $U$, $a_ i\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ and $s_ i$ holomorphic functions on $U$ defining $D_ i$, and we have 1.39 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logsingreminder} \varphi |_ U=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ i\log |s_ i|^2+R, \end{equation} where $R$ is a bounded function on $U$.
1.39 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logsingreminder} \varphi |_ U=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ i\log |s_ i|^2+R, \end{equation}

title: Lemma 1.6.4
text: Lemma 1.6.4 . Suppose that $X$ is a compact Kähler manifold, $\theta $ is a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Suppose that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$ on $X$. Then the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef. Moreover, if in addition $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current Note. That is, there is a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ such that $\theta _{\varphi }\geq \omega $ in the sense of currents. , then the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. Proof. The current $\theta _{\varphi }-[D]$ has bounded local potentials. Therefore, the class $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef. If $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, say $\theta _{\varphi }\geq \omega $ for a Kähler form $\omega $, then $\theta _{\varphi }-[D]-\omega $ is positive and has bounded local potentials, and therefore represents a nef class. We conclude that $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. $\square$

title: Proposition 1.6.5
text: Proposition 1.6.5 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a complex manifold $Y$. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities (resp. has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$). Then $\pi ^*\varphi $ has analytic singularities (resp. has log singularities along $\pi ^*D$).

title: Definition 1.6.6
text: Definition 1.6.6 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. A log resolution of $\varphi $ is a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $\pi ^*\varphi $ has log singularities along a simple normal crossing effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor.

title: Theorem 1.6.7
text: Theorem 1.6.7 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities. Then there is a log resolution of $\varphi $.
1.40 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quasi_eq_prop} \mathcal{I}(\lambda ' \varphi _ j)\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi ). \end{equation}

title: Definition 1.6.9
text: Definition 1.6.9 . Let $\mathcal{I}\subseteq \mathcal O_ X$ be a coherent ideal sheaf and $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$. A function $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ is said to have gentle analytic singularities (of type $(c,\mathcal{I})$) if $\varphi $ has analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathcal{I})$; $\mathrm{e}^{{\varphi }/{c}}\colon X\to \mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}$ is a smooth function; there is a proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon \widetilde{X}\to X$ from a Kähler manifold $\widetilde{X}$ and an effective $\mathbb {Z}$-divisor $D$ on $\widetilde{X}$ such that one can write $\pi ^*\varphi $ locally as \[  \pi ^*\varphi =c\log |g|^2+h,  \] where $g$ is a local equation of the divisor $D$ and $h$ is smooth.

title: Theorem 1.6.10
text: Theorem 1.6.10 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ admits a quasi-equisingular approximation $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$. Moreover, we can guarantee that for all $j>0$, $\varphi _ j$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $\left(2^{-j},\mathcal{I}(2^ j\varphi )\right)$.

title: Proposition 1.6.11
text: Proposition 1.6.11 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Consider $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Let $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ and $(\psi _ j)_ j$ be two quasi-equisingular approximations of $\varphi $. Then for any $\epsilon \in (0,1)$ and any $j>0$, we can find $k_0>0$ such that for any $k\geq k_0$, we have \[  \psi _ k\preceq (1-\epsilon )\varphi _ j.  \]

title: Definition 1.6.12
text: Definition 1.6.12 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. Then we define $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )$  as the ideal sheaf consisting of germs $f$ of holomorphic functions such that $\log |f|^2\leq \varphi +C$ for some $C\in \mathbb {R}$.

title: Lemma 1.6.13
text: Lemma 1.6.13 . Assume that $X$ is compact. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be a potential with analytic singularities. The sheaf $\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )$ is coherent. Proof. By theorem 1.6.7 , we may find a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $\pi ^*\varphi $ has log singularities. Observe that \[  \mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )=\pi _*\mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\pi ^*\varphi ),  \] so we may replace $X$ and $\varphi $ by $Y$ and $\pi ^*\varphi $ and assume that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor $D$. We decompose $D$ into its irreducible components: \[  D=\sum _{i=1}^ N a_ iD_ i.  \] In this case, observe that \[  \mathcal{I}_{\infty }(\varphi )=\mathcal{O}_ X\left(-\sum _{i=1}^ N\left(\lceil a_ i \rceil D_ i\right)\right)  \] is clearly coherent. $\square$

title: Theorem 1.6.15
text: Theorem 1.6.15 . Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold and $Y\subseteq X$ be a connected closed submanifold. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\omega |_ Y)$ such that $\omega |_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a Kähler current and $\mathrm{e}^{\varphi }$ is a Hölder continuous function on $Y$. Then there exists $\tilde{\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfying $\tilde{\varphi }|_ Y=\varphi $; $\omega _{\tilde{\varphi }}$ is a Kähler current. In addition, if $\varphi $ has analytic singularities, then so does $\tilde{\varphi }$.

title: 1.7 The space of currents
text:
1.7 The space of currents Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$ and $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$. Definition 1.7.1 . Let $Y$ be a complex manifold of dimension $N$ and $m\in \mathbb {N}$. We say an $(m,m)$-current $T$ on $Y$ is positive Note. This notion is sometimes known as weak positivity . if either $m>N$ or for any smooth $(1,0)$-forms $ eta _1,\ldots , eta _{N-m}$ on $Y$, the measure \[  T\wedge \mathrm{i} eta _1\wedge \overline{ eta _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{i} eta _{N-m}\wedge \overline{ eta _{N-m}}  \] is positive. The basic properties of positive currents can be found in [ Section III.1 , DemBook ] . Recall that a positive current is necessarily real. Definition 1.7.2 . We say $\alpha $ is pseudo-effective if there is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current in $\alpha $. We say $\alpha $ is big if there is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ in $\alpha $ dominating a Kähler form. Such currents are called Kähler currents . Given classes $\alpha , eta \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$, we say $\alpha \leq  eta $ if $ eta -\alpha $ is pseudo-effective. Definition 1.7.3 . We introduce the following notations: $\mathcal{Z}_+(X)$  denotes the space of closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$; given a pseudo-effective $(1,1)$-class $\alpha $ on $X$, we write $\mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$  for the set of $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$ such that $\{ T\} =\alpha $. Here $\{ T\} $ denotes the cohomology class represented by $T$. definition 1.5.2 has a natural analogue for currents. Definition 1.7.4 . Given $T,T'\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$, we write $T\preceq T'$ and say $T$ is more singular than $T'$ if when we write $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $, $T'=	heta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi '$, we have $\varphi \preceq \varphi '$. We write $T\sim T'$ if $T\preceq T'$ and $T'\preceq T$. In this case, we say $T$ and $T'$ have the same singularity type . Remark 1.7.5 . Observe that \[  \mathcal{Z}_+(X)/\sim \cong \mathrm{QPSH}(X)/\sim  \] canonically. The correspondence sends the class of a closed positive current $	heta _{\varphi }=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ to the class of $\varphi $. We will adopt the following convention: Whenever we have a notion for quasi-plurisubharmonic functions which depends only on the singularity type, we use the same notation and the same definition for closed positive $(1,1)$-currents. Example 1.7.6 . As an important example of 1.7.5 , given $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$ and $x\in X$, we define 1.43  egin{equation} \label{eq:convnuTx} 
u (T,x)=
u (\varphi ,x). \end{equation} Again, as in 1.4.2 , this differs from the definitions in some literature by a factor of $2$. But given our normalization \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}= rac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial },  \] ( 1.43 ) seems to be the most natural choice. The key example to keep in mind is the following: \[  
u ([0],0)=1,  \] where $[0]$ is the current of integration at $0\in \mathbb {P}^1$. In fact, as a simple application of the Green's second identity, one can verify that \[   rac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial }\log |z|^2=\delta _0,  \] where the right-hand side is the Dirac delta distribution at $0\in \mathbb {C}$. Definition 1.7.7 . Given $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$, represent $T$ as $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ for some closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ on $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. The polar locus of $T$ is defined as the set $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $. It is clear that the polar locus of $T$ is independent of the choices of $	heta $ and $\varphi $. We also call the set $\{ -\infty \} $ the polar locus of $\varphi $. Definition 1.7.8 . Assume that $\alpha $ is big. The non-Kähler locus $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$ of $\alpha $ is the intersection of the polar loci of all Kähler currents with analytic singularities in $\alpha $. Theorem 1.7.9 (Boucksom) . Assume that $\alpha $ is big. There is a Kähler current $T\in \alpha $ with analytic singularities, such that the polar locus of $T$ is exactly $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$. In particular, $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$ is a proper Zariski closed subset of $X$. See [ Théorème 2.1.20 , Bou02 ] . Definition 1.7.10 . Assume that $\alpha $ is big. The non-nef locus $\operatorname{nn}(\alpha )$ of $\alpha $ is the following set: \[  \operatorname{nn}(\alpha )\coloneqq \{ x\in X :
u (T_{\min },x)>0\} ,  \] where $T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $. Note that $\operatorname{nn}(\alpha )\subseteq \operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$. Thanks to theorem 1.4.4 , $\operatorname{nn}(\alpha )$ is a countable union of proper Zariski closed subsets of $X$. The non-Kähler locus and non-nef locus are studied in detail in [ Bou02 ] . Lemma 1.7.11 (Siu's decomposition) . Let $E$ be a prime divisor on $X$. Then for any closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, the difference $T-
u (T,E)[E]$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current. Here $[E]$ is the current of integration associated with $E$, while $\{ E\} $ denotes the cohomology class of $E$. See [ Page 386, Example 1 , GH14 ] for the precise definition. See [ Lemma 2.17 , Dem12 ] for the proof. As a consequence, for each closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, we can write 1.44  egin{equation} \label{eq:Siudec} T=\operatorname{Reg}T+\sum _{i} c_ i [E_ i], \end{equation} where $\{ E_ i\} $ is a countable collection of prime divisors on $X$, $c_ i>0$. Definition 1.7.12 . A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ is non-divisorial (resp. divisorial ) if $T=\operatorname{Reg}T$ (resp. $\operatorname{Reg}T=0$). It is helpful to check that our conventions are always consistent: There is no extra factor of $2$ or $1/2$ anywhere. One can verify this using our favorite example as in example 1.7.6 . Next we recall the notion of modified nef classes. Definition 1.7.13 . A class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ is modified nef if the following condition holds: after fixing a reference Kähler metric $\omega $ on $X$, for any $\epsilon >0$, we can find a closed $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ such that $T+\epsilon \omega \geq 0$; $
u (T+\epsilon \omega ,D)=0$ for any prime divisor $D$ on $X$. This definition is independent of the choice of $\omega $. These classes are called nef en codimension $1$ in Boucksom's thesis [ Bou02 ] , where they were introduced for the first time. They are also known as movable classes in other references. Modified nef classes form a closed convex cone in $\mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$. Note that a modified nef class is necessarily pseudo-effective. A nef class is obviously modified nef. Recall the multiplicity of a cohomology class as defined in [ Section 2.1.3 , Bou02 ] : Definition 1.7.14 . Let $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ be a pseudo-effective class and $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. We define the Lelong number $
u (\alpha ,D)$ as follows: When $\alpha $ is big, define $
u (\alpha ,D)=
u (T,D)$ for any closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ with minimal singularities. In general, define \[  
u (\alpha ,D)\coloneqq \lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+}
u (\alpha +\epsilon \{ \omega \} ,D).  \] When $\alpha $ is big, 2 is compatible with 1 and the definition is independent of the choice of $\omega $. By definition, a pseudo-effective class $\alpha $ is modified nef if and only if $
u (\alpha ,D)=0$ for all prime divisors $D$ on $X$. Let us recall the behavior of several cones under modifications. Proposition 1.7.15 . Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. For any nef class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi ^*\alpha $ is nef. For any modified nef class $ eta \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi _* eta $ is modified nef. Proof. Only 2 requires a proof. Fix a Kähler class $\gamma $ on $Y$. Since the modified nef cone is closed, replacing $ eta $ by $ eta +\epsilon \gamma $ and then letting $\epsilon 	o 0+$ reduces the proof to the case where $ eta $ is big as well. Let $T$ (resp. $S$) be a current with minimal singularities in $\pi _* eta $ (resp. in $ eta $), and let $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. It suffices to show that \[  
u (T,D)=0.  \] Since $ eta $ is modified nef, $S$ is non-divisorial. Hence by 1.7.16 below, $
u (\pi _*S,D)=0$. Since $T$ has minimal singularities in $\pi _* eta $, we have $T\succeq \pi _*S$, and the desired equality follows. $\square$ Recall that non-divisorial currents are introduced in definition 1.7.12 . Lemma 1.7.16 . Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $T$ be a non-divisorial current on $Y$. Then $\pi _*T$ is non-divisorial. Conversely, if $S$ is a non-divisorial current on $X$, $\pi ^*S$ could have divisorial part. As a simple example, consider $S$ on $\mathbb {P}^2$, whose local potential near $0\in \mathbb {C}^2_{z,w}$ looks like $\log (|z|^2+|w|^2)$. Proof. Let $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. It follows from Zariski's main theorem theorem B.1.4 that $D$ is not contained in the exceptional locus of $\pi $. Let $D'$ be the strict transform of $D$. Thanks to Siu's semicontinuity theorem theorem 1.4.4 , we have \[  
u (\pi _*T,D)=
u (T,D')=0.  \] Hence $\pi _*T$ is non-divisorial. $\square$

text: Definition 1.7.1 . Let $Y$ be a complex manifold of dimension $N$ and $m\in \mathbb {N}$. We say an $(m,m)$-current $T$ on $Y$ is positive Note. text:

But given our normalization \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}= rac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial },  \] ( 1.43 ) seems to be the most natural choice. u ([0],0)=1,  \] where $[0]$ is the current of integration at $0\in \mathbb {P}^1$. In fact, as a simple application of the Green's second identity, one can verify that \[   rac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \overline{\partial }\log |z|^2=\delta _0,  \] where the right-hand side is the Dirac delta distribution at $0\in \mathbb {C}$.
1.43 \begin{equation} \label{eq:convnuTx} \nu (T,x)=\nu (\varphi ,x). \end{equation}

title: Definition 1.7.7
text: Definition 1.7.7 . Given $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X)$, represent $T$ as $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ for some closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The polar locus of $T$ is defined as the set $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $.

title: Definition 1.7.8
text: Definition 1.7.8 . Assume that $\alpha $ is big. The non-Kähler locus $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$ of $\alpha $ is the intersection of the polar loci of all Kähler currents with analytic singularities in $\alpha $.

title: Theorem 1.7.9 (Boucksom)
text: Theorem 1.7.9 (Boucksom) . Assume that $\alpha $ is big. There is a Kähler current $T\in \alpha $ with analytic singularities, such that the polar locus of $T$ is exactly $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$. In particular, $\operatorname{nK}(\alpha )$ is a proper Zariski closed subset of $X$.

title: Definition 1.7.10
text: Definition 1.7.10 . Assume that $\alpha $ is big. The non-nef locus $\operatorname{nn}(\alpha )$ of $\alpha $ is the following set: \[  \operatorname{nn}(\alpha )\coloneqq \{ x\in X :\nu (T_{\min },x)>0\} ,  \] where $T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $.

title: Lemma 1.7.11 (Siu's decomposition)
text: Lemma 1.7.11 (Siu's decomposition) . Let $E$ be a prime divisor on $X$. Then for any closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, the difference $T-\nu (T,E)[E]$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current.
1.44 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Siudec} T=\operatorname{Reg}T+\sum _{i} c_ i [E_ i], \end{equation}

title: Definition 1.7.12
text: Definition 1.7.12 . A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ is non-divisorial (resp. divisorial ) if $T=\operatorname{Reg}T$ (resp. $\operatorname{Reg}T=0$).

title: Definition 1.7.13
text: Definition 1.7.13 . A class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ is modified nef if the following condition holds: after fixing a reference Kähler metric $\omega $ on $X$, for any $\epsilon >0$, we can find a closed $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ such that $T+\epsilon \omega \geq 0$; $\nu (T+\epsilon \omega ,D)=0$ for any prime divisor $D$ on $X$. This definition is independent of the choice of $\omega $.

title: Definition 1.7.14
text:
Definition 1.7.14 . Let $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ be a pseudo-effective class and $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. We define the Lelong number $
u (\alpha ,D)$ as follows: When $\alpha $ is big, define $
u (\alpha ,D)=
u (T,D)$ for any closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T\in \alpha $ with minimal singularities. In general, define \[  
u (\alpha ,D)\coloneqq \lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+}
u (\alpha +\epsilon \{ \omega \} ,D).  \]

title: Proposition 1.7.15
text: Proposition 1.7.15 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. For any nef class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi ^*\alpha $ is nef. For any modified nef class $\beta \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi _*\beta $ is modified nef. Proof. Only 2 requires a proof. Fix a Kähler class $\gamma $ on $Y$. Since the modified nef cone is closed, replacing $\beta $ by $\beta +\epsilon \gamma $ and then letting $\epsilon \to 0+$ reduces the proof to the case where $\beta $ is big as well. Let $T$ (resp. $S$) be a current with minimal singularities in $\pi _*\beta $ (resp. in $\beta $), and let $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. It suffices to show that \[  \nu (T,D)=0.  \] Since $\beta $ is modified nef, $S$ is non-divisorial. Hence by 1.7.16 below, $\nu (\pi _*S,D)=0$. Since $T$ has minimal singularities in $\pi _*\beta $, we have $T\succeq \pi _*S$, and the desired equality follows. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.7.16
text: Lemma 1.7.16 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $T$ be a non-divisorial current on $Y$. Then $\pi _*T$ is non-divisorial. Proof. Let $D$ be a prime divisor on $X$. It follows from Zariski's main theorem theorem B.1.4 that $D$ is not contained in the exceptional locus of $\pi $. Let $D'$ be the strict transform of $D$. Thanks to Siu's semicontinuity theorem theorem 1.4.4 , we have \[  \nu (\pi _*T,D)=\nu (T,D')=0.  \] Hence $\pi _*T$ is non-divisorial. $\square$

title: 1.8 Plurisubharmonic metrics on line bundles
text:
1.8 Plurisubharmonic metrics on line bundles A natural source of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions is the metrics on line bundles. Let $X$ be a connected Kähler manifold and $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$. Usually, we do not distinguish $L$ from the associated invertible sheaf $\mathcal{O}_ X(L)$. Definition 1.8.1 . Let $V$ be a $1$-dimensional complex linear space. A Hermitian form $h$ on $V$ is a map $h\colon V\times V\rightarrow \mathbb {C}$ such that $h$ is $\mathbb {C}$-linear in the second variable and conjugate linear in the first, and \[  |v|_ h^2\coloneqq h(v,v)\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}  \] for each $v\in V\setminus \{ 0\} $. We usually identify $h$ with the quadratic form $V\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ sending $v$ to $|v|_ h^2$. We write $|v|_ h=\sqrt{|v|_ h^2}$ for any $v\in V$. The singular Hermitian form on $V$ is the map $V\rightarrow \{ 0,\infty \} $ sending $0$ to $0$ and other elements to $\infty $. Definition 1.8.2 . Let $V_1$ and $V_2$ be $1$-dimensional complex linear spaces. Given two maps $h_ i\colon V_ i\rightarrow [0,\infty ]$ ($i=1,2$), each of which is either a Hermitian form or a singular Hermitian form, we define the tensor product $h_1\otimes h_2\colon V_1\otimes V_2\rightarrow [0,\infty ]$ as follows: If either $h_1$ or $h_2$ is singular, we define $h_1\otimes h_2$ as the singular Hermitian form; otherwise, define $h_1\otimes h_2$ as the usual tensor product: For any $v_1\in V_1$, $v_2\in V_2$, set \[  h_1\otimes h_2(v_1\otimes v_2)=h_1(v_1)h_2(v_2).  \] Definition 1.8.3 . A Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ is a family of Hermitian forms $(h_ x)_{x\in X}$, such that for each $x\in X$, $h_ x$ is a Hermitian form on $L_ x$, and for each local holomorphic section $s$ of $\mathcal{O}_ X(L)$, the map $x\mapsto |s(x)|^2_{h_ x}$ is smooth. The pair $(L,h)$ is called a Hermitian line bundle . We shall write $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)$ Note. The unusual notation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ is sometimes referred to as the Göteborg notation because it is widely used by complex geometers in Göteborg (usually spelled as Gothenburg in English, the second largest (yet very poorly known) city in Sweden). As I identify myself as Göteborgare , I do not feel guilty about this notation. for the first Chern form of $h$ Note. In the literature, people sometimes define the curvature form of $(L,h)$ as $\Theta _{h}=-2\pi \mathrm{i}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. , normalized so that \[  [c_1(L,h)]=c_1(L).  \] The map $x\mapsto |s(x)|_{h_ x}$ will be denoted by $|s|_ h$. To be more precise, if $U\subseteq X$ is an open subset on which $L$ admits a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section $s$, then we define \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)|_ U=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left(-\log |s|_ h^2\right).  \] Proposition 1.8.4 (Lelong–Poincaré) . Let $s\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L)$ be non-zero and $h$ be a Hermitian metric on $L$. Then 1.45 \begin{equation} \label{eq:LP} c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_ h^2=[Z(s)], \end{equation} where $Z(s)$ is the zero divisor defined by $s$ and $[\bullet ]$ denote the associated current of integration. See [ (3.11) , Dem12 ] . Again, we want to check that our conventions are compatible by investigating the following simple example. Example 1.8.5 . Let $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $L=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^1}(1)$. The homogeneous coordinates on $\mathbb {P}^1$ will be denoted by $[X_0:X_1]$. At a point $x=[X_0:X_1]\in \mathbb {P}^1$, the fiber $L_ x$ is identified with the dual of $[x]$, where $[x]\subseteq \mathbb {C}^2$ is the line represented by $x$. In order to introduce the Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$, we fix the standard Hermitian norm $\| \bullet \| $ on $\mathbb {C}^2$. Then given $\lambda \in L_ x=[x]^{\vee }$, we introduce \[  |\lambda |_{h_ x}=\frac{|\lambda (\tilde{x})|}{\| \tilde{x}\| },  \] where $\tilde{x}$ is an arbitrary non-zero element in $[x]$. The reader can easily verify that $h$ is indeed a Hermitian metric on $L$. The Hermitian metric $h$ is known as the Fubini–Study metric . A holomorphic section $s\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L)$ can be formally identified with a linear form $a_0X_0+a_1X_1$: At $x\in X$, the corresponding linear form on $[x]$ is given by sending $(X_0,X_1)$ to $a_0X_0+a_1X_1$. Next we compute $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)$. For this purpose, we cover $\mathbb {P}^1$ by $\mathbb {C}=\mathbb {P}^1\setminus \{ \infty \} $ and $\mathbb {P}^1\setminus \{ 0\} $. Both are holomorphic coordinate charts with coordinate function $z=X_0/X_1$ and $z^{-1}=X_1/X_0$ respectively. We claim that on $\mathbb {C}$, 1.46 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curvFS} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2). \end{equation} In fact, let $t$ be the nowhere vanishing section of $L$ on $\mathbb {C}$ corresponding to $X_1$. Then for $z\in \mathbb {C}$, we have an obvious lift $(z,1)\in [z]$, so \[  |t|_ h^2(z)=\frac{1}{|z|^2+1}.  \] So ( 1.46 ) follows. In order to obtain a non-trivial case of the Lelong–Poincaré formula, we need to consider a section which vanishes at some points in $\mathbb {C}$. Let $s$ be the holomorphic section of $L$ corresponding to $X_0$. Then \[  \log |s|_ h^2(z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{|z|^2+1}  \] for any $z\in \mathbb {C}$ using the same argument as above. Therefore, we find that restricted to $\mathbb {C}$, we have \[  c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_ h^2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=[0],  \] where $f(z)=\log |z|^2$. So the Lelong–Poincaré formula ( 1.45 ) is verified in this case. The Kähler form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $\mathbb {P}^1$ is also known as the Fubini–Study metric . Definition 1.8.6 . A (singular) plurisubharmonic metric (or psh metric for short) Note. In the literature, people usually refer to such metrics as positively curved singular Hermitian metrics . I dislike this terminology, as having positive curvature only determines a plurisubharmonic metric almost everywhere, not everywhere. $h$ on $L$ is a family $(h_ x)_{x\in X}$ such that for each $x\in X$, $h_ x$ is either a Hermitian form on $L_ x$ or the singular Hermitian form on $L_ x$, and there is a Hermitian metric $h_0$ on $L$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$ such that for each $x\in X$ and each $v\in L_ x$, we have 1.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:htwist} |v|^2_{h_ x}= \left\{  \begin{aligned}  0,& \quad \textup{if }v=0;\\  |v|^2_{h_{0,x}}\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi (x)},& \quad \textup{if }v\neq 0. \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation} The (first) Chern current of $h$ is by definition \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)\coloneqq c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] The set of psh metrics on $L$ will be denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(L)$. We shall write the plurisubharmonic metric defined by ( 1.47 ) as $h_0\exp (-\varphi )$ Note. Be careful, this is not $h_0^2\exp (-\varphi )$, as I prefer to think of $h_0$ as a quadratic form. . With these conventions, $c_1(L,h)$ does not depend on the choice of $h_0$. Given a local holomorphic section $s$ of $L$, we shall use the following notations interchangeably to denote the map $x\mapsto h_ x(s)$: \[  |s|^2_ h=h(s)=h(s,s).  \] Remark 1.8.7 . In the literature, some people prefer the convention that in ( 1.47 ), neither side has the square. Our choice seems to be the most natural one given our normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. Observe that once a Hermitian metric $h_0$ on $L$ is given, the construction in 2 gives a bijection between $\mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$ and the set of plurisubharmonic metrics on $L$. Based on this correspondence, plurisubharmonic metrics have the same functoriality property as quasi-plurisubharmonic functions in proposition 1.1.13 . In particular, given a connected closed submanifold $Y$ of $X$, $h|_ Y$ is a plurisubharmonic metric as long as it is not singular everywhere. Definition 1.8.8 . Given two holomorphic line bundles $L_1$, $L_2$ on $X$ and plurisubharmonic metrics $h_1$ on $L_1$ and $h_2$ on $L_2$, we define the tensor product plurisubharmonic metric $h_1\otimes h_2$ on $L_1\otimes L_2$ as follows: for each $x\in X$, define \[  (h_1\otimes h_2)_ x=h_{1,x}\otimes h_{2,x}  \] in the sense of definition 1.8.2 . We can easily verify that $h_1\otimes h_2$ is indeed a plurisubharmonic metric on $L_1\otimes L_2$. Example 1.8.9 . We continue with our example example 1.8.5 . Let $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $L=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^1}(1)$. Let $h^0$ denote the Fubini–Study metric on $L$ as defined in example 1.8.5 . Note that we have changed the notation from $h$ to $h^0$. Let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h^0$. We construct $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ as follows: On $\mathbb {C}$, define 1.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logsingP1ex} \varphi (z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}. \end{equation} Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C},\omega |_{\mathbb {C}})$ by ( 1.46 ). Setting $\varphi (\infty )=0$, we can easily verify that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {P}^1,\omega )$. Note. This can also be verified using the Grauert–Remmert extension theorem theorem 1.2.9 . We then get a plurisubharmonic metric $h=h^0\exp (-\varphi )$. To be more explicit, the fiber metric $h$ at $0$ is singular, $h_{\infty }=h^0_{\infty }$, while for $z\in \mathbb {C}\setminus \{ 0\} $ and $\lambda \in [z]^{\vee }$, we have \[  |\lambda |_{h_ z}=\frac{|\lambda (z,1)|}{|z|}.  \] In the remainder of this section, we assume that $X$ is compact. Definition 1.8.10 . Assume that $L$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. A Fubini–Study metric on $L$ is a psh metric $h$ on $L$ of the following form: There exists $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, finitely many sections $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ m)$ and $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ N\in \mathbb {Q}$ such that for any local nowhere vanishing holomorphic section $s$ of $L$, we have \[  |s|_ h^2=\min _{i=1,\ldots ,N}\left| \frac{s^{\otimes m}}{\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ i/2}s_ i}\right|^{2m^{-1}}.  \] We write $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ for the set of Fubini–Study metrics on $L$. If we fix a reference smooth Hermitian metric $h_0$ on $L$ with $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_0$, we can write $h=h_0\exp (-\varphi )$ with \[  \varphi =\frac{1}{m}\max _{i=1,\ldots ,N}\left(\log |s_ i|^2_{h_0^{m}}+\lambda _ i\right).  \] Similarly, we write $\mathrm{FS}(X,\theta )$ for the set of such functions. Definition 1.8.11 . Assume that $L$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. The set $\widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$ of generalized Fubini–Study metrics is the smallest subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(L)$ containing $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ which is closed under the following two operations: $\mathbb {Q}$-convex combinations: if $h_1,h_2\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$ and $t\in (0,1)$, then \[  h_1^ t \otimes h_2^{1-t}\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L);  \] minima: if $h_1,h_2\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$, then \[  \min \{ h_1,h_2\} \in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L).  \] We shall need the following Ohsawa–Takegoshi type extension theorem. Theorem 1.8.12 . Assume that $L$ is big and $T$ is a holomorphic line bundle on $X$. Fix a Hermitian metric $h_ T$ on $T$. Fix a Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ and let $\theta =c_1(L,h)$. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Let $Y\subseteq X$ be a connected closed submanifold of dimension $m$. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta - \delta \omega )$ for some $\delta >0$ and $\varphi |_ Y\not\equiv -\infty $. Then there exists $k_0(\delta ,h_ T)>0$ such that for all $k \geq k_0$ and $s \in \mathrm{H}^0(Y, T\otimes L|_ Y^ k \otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi |_ Y))$ Note. Here and in the sequel, we usually abbreviate $\otimes k$ in the superscript as $k$ to save space. , there exists an extension $\tilde s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X, T\otimes L^ k \otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$ such that \[  \int _ X |\tilde{s}|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\, \omega ^ n \leq C \int _ Y |s|^2_{(h^ k\otimes h_ T)|_ Y} \mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi |_ Y}\, \omega |_ Y^ m,  \] where $C>0$ is an absolute constant, independent of the data $(\varphi ,s,k)$. This is a special case of [ Theorem 1.4 , His12 ] . Let us also recall a simple result about the Bergman kernel approximations: Proposition 1.8.13 . Let $(L,h)$ be a Hermitian line bundle on $X$ and set $\theta =c_1(L,h)$. Let $(T,h_ T)$ be a Hermitian line bundle on $X$. Assume that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is a potential with analytic singularities such that $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. For each $k\geq 1$, we let 1.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Bergman_seq_def} \varphi _ k \coloneqq \frac{1}{k} \log \sup _{\substack {s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k \otimes T)\\ \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi } \omega ^ n \leq 1}} |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}. \end{equation} Then for all sufficiently large $k$, \[  \varphi \preceq \varphi _ k\preceq \alpha _ k \varphi ,  \] where $\alpha _ k\in (0,1)$ is an increasing sequence with limit $1$. Proof. First we prove $\varphi \preceq \varphi _ k$. Since $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, there is $\delta >0$ such that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta -\delta \omega )$. Let $x\in X$ with $\varphi (x)>-\infty $. Applying theorem 1.8.12 to the point $Y=\{ x\} $, for all sufficiently large $k$ and every unit vector $e_ x\in (L^ k\otimes T)_ x$, there is a section $\tilde{s}\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$ with $\tilde{s}(x)=e_ x$ and \[  \int _ X |\tilde{s}|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\omega ^ n\leq C\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi (x)}.  \] After rescaling $\tilde{s}$, the definition of $\varphi _ k$ gives \[  \varphi _ k(x)\geq \varphi (x)-\frac{\log C}{k}.  \] This proves $\varphi \preceq \varphi _ k$. The other part of the inequality follows from 1.6.14 and ( 1.42 ). More precisely, if $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$, with respect to the $L^2$-norm: \[  s\mapsto \left( \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\, \omega ^ n \right)^{1/2},  \] then by ( 1.42 ), \[  s_ i\in \mathrm{H}^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}_{\infty }\left((k-c^{-1}n)_+\varphi \right)\right),  \] where $c>0$ depends only on $\varphi $. So there is $C_ k>0$ so that \[  \sum _{i=1}^ N |s_ i|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-(k-c^{-1}n)_+\varphi }\leq C_ k\quad \textup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] In other words, \[  \varphi _ k\preceq \frac{1}{k}\left( k-c^{-1}n \right)_+ \varphi .  \] It suffices to take $\alpha _ k=(1-k^{-1}c^{-1}n)_+$. $\square$ Pour exprimer d'une manière frappante que le monument que j'élève sera placé sous l'invocation de la Science, j'ai décidé d'inscrire en lettres d'or sur la grande frise du premier étage et à la place d'honneur, les noms des plus grands savants Note. Gaspard Monge, Comte de Péluse (1746–1818), known oddly by his family name instead of de Péluse , is one of the 72 names scribed on the Eiffel tower. Apart from being a mathematician, he was also a politician, active mainly after the French Revolution. qui ont honoré la France depuis 1789 jusqu'à nos jours. 
— Gustave Eiffel, 1889

title: Example 1.8.5
text: Example 1.8.5 . Let $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $L=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^1}(1)$. The homogeneous coordinates on $\mathbb {P}^1$ will be denoted by $[X_0:X_1]$.
