Then given $\lambda \in L_ x=[x]^{\vee }$, we introduce \[  |\lambda |_{h_ x}=\frac{|\lambda (\tilde{x})|}{\| \tilde{x}\| },  \] where $\tilde{x}$ is an arbitrary non-zero element in $[x]$. The reader can easily verify that $h$ is indeed a Hermitian metric on $L$. The Hermitian metric $h$ is known as the Fubini–Study metric . A holomorphic section $s\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L)$ can be formally identified with a linear form $a_0X_0+a_1X_1$: At $x\in X$, the corresponding linear form on $[x]$ is given by sending $(X_0,X_1)$ to $a_0X_0+a_1X_1$. Next we compute $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)$. For this purpose, we cover $\mathbb {P}^1$ by $\mathbb {C}=\mathbb {P}^1\setminus \{ \infty \} $ and $\mathbb {P}^1\setminus \{ 0\} $. Both are holomorphic coordinate charts with coordinate function $z=X_0/X_1$ and $z^{-1}=X_1/X_0$ respectively. We claim that on $\mathbb {C}$, 1.46 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curvFS} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2). \end{equation} In fact, let $t$ be the nowhere vanishing section of $L$ on $\mathbb {C}$ corresponding to $X_1$. Then for $z\in \mathbb {C}$, we have an obvious lift $(z,1)\in [z]$, so \[  |t|_ h^2(z)=\frac{1}{|z|^2+1}.  \] So ( 1.46 ) follows. In order to obtain a non-trivial case of the Lelong–Poincaré formula, we need to consider a section which vanishes at some points in $\mathbb {C}$. Let $s$ be the holomorphic section of $L$ corresponding to $X_0$. Then \[  \log |s|_ h^2(z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{|z|^2+1}  \] for any $z\in \mathbb {C}$ using the same argument as above. Therefore, we find that restricted to $\mathbb {C}$, we have \[  c_1(L,h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_ h^2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=[0],  \] where $f(z)=\log |z|^2$. So the Lelong–Poincaré formula ( 1.45 ) is verified in this case. The Kähler form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $\mathbb {P}^1$ is also known as the Fubini–Study metric .
1.46 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curvFS} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2). \end{equation}

title: Definition 1.8.6
text: Definition 1.8.6 . A (singular) plurisubharmonic metric (or psh metric for short) Note. In the literature, people usually refer to such metrics as positively curved singular Hermitian metrics . I dislike this terminology, as having positive curvature only determines a plurisubharmonic metric almost everywhere, not everywhere. $h$ on $L$ is a family $(h_ x)_{x\in X}$ such that for each $x\in X$, $h_ x$ is either a Hermitian form on $L_ x$ or the singular Hermitian form on $L_ x$, and there is a Hermitian metric $h_0$ on $L$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$ such that for each $x\in X$ and each $v\in L_ x$, we have 1.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:htwist} |v|^2_{h_ x}= \left\{  \begin{aligned}  0,& \quad \textup{if }v=0;\\  |v|^2_{h_{0,x}}\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi (x)},& \quad \textup{if }v\neq 0. \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation} The (first) Chern current of $h$ is by definition \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=c_1(L,h)\coloneqq c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] The set of psh metrics on $L$ will be denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(L)$.

1.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:htwist} |v|^2_{h_ x}= \left\{  \begin{aligned}  0,& \quad \textup{if }v=0;\\  |v|^2_{h_{0,x}}\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi (x)},& \quad \textup{if }v\neq 0. \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation}

title: Remark 1.8.7
text: Remark 1.8.7 . In the literature, some people prefer the convention that in ( 1.47 ), neither side has the square. Our choice seems to be the most natural one given our normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$.

title: Definition 1.8.8
text: Definition 1.8.8 . Given two holomorphic line bundles $L_1$, $L_2$ on $X$ and plurisubharmonic metrics $h_1$ on $L_1$ and $h_2$ on $L_2$, we define the tensor product plurisubharmonic metric $h_1\otimes h_2$ on $L_1\otimes L_2$ as follows: for each $x\in X$, define \[  (h_1\otimes h_2)_ x=h_{1,x}\otimes h_{2,x}  \] in the sense of definition 1.8.2 .

title: Example 1.8.9
text: Example 1.8.9 . We continue with our example example 1.8.5 . Let $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $L=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^1}(1)$. Let $h^0$ denote the Fubini–Study metric on $L$ as defined in example 1.8.5 . Note that we have changed the notation from $h$ to $h^0$. Let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h^0$. We construct $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ as follows: On $\mathbb {C}$, define 1.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logsingP1ex} \varphi (z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}. \end{equation} Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {C},\omega |_{\mathbb {C}})$ by ( 1.46 ). Setting $\varphi (\infty )=0$, we can easily verify that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb {P}^1,\omega )$. Note. This can also be verified using the Grauert–Remmert extension theorem theorem 1.2.9 . We then get a plurisubharmonic metric $h=h^0\exp (-\varphi )$. To be more explicit, the fiber metric $h$ at $0$ is singular, $h_{\infty }=h^0_{\infty }$, while for $z\in \mathbb {C}\setminus \{ 0\} $ and $\lambda \in [z]^{\vee }$, we have \[  |\lambda |_{h_ z}=\frac{|\lambda (z,1)|}{|z|}.  \]
1.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logsingP1ex} \varphi (z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}. \end{equation}

title: Definition 1.8.10
text: Definition 1.8.10 . Assume that $L$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. A Fubini–Study metric on $L$ is a psh metric $h$ on $L$ of the following form: There exists $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, finitely many sections $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ m)$ and $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ N\in \mathbb {Q}$ such that for any local nowhere vanishing holomorphic section $s$ of $L$, we have \[  |s|_ h^2=\min _{i=1,\ldots ,N}\left| \frac{s^{\otimes m}}{\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ i/2}s_ i}\right|^{2m^{-1}}.  \] We write $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ for the set of Fubini–Study metrics on $L$.

title: Definition 1.8.11
text: Definition 1.8.11 . Assume that $L$ is a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. The set $\widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$ of generalized Fubini–Study metrics is the smallest subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(L)$ containing $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ which is closed under the following two operations: $\mathbb {Q}$-convex combinations: if $h_1,h_2\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$ and $t\in (0,1)$, then \[  h_1^ t \otimes h_2^{1-t}\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L);  \] minima: if $h_1,h_2\in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L)$, then \[  \min \{ h_1,h_2\} \in \widetilde{\mathrm{FS}}(L).  \]

title: Theorem 1.8.12
text: Theorem 1.8.12 . Assume that $L$ is big and $T$ is a holomorphic line bundle on $X$. Fix a Hermitian metric $h_ T$ on $T$. Fix a Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ and let $\theta =c_1(L,h)$. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Let $Y\subseteq X$ be a connected closed submanifold of dimension $m$. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta - \delta \omega )$ for some $\delta >0$ and $\varphi |_ Y\not\equiv -\infty $. Then there exists $k_0(\delta ,h_ T)>0$ such that for all $k \geq k_0$ and $s \in \mathrm{H}^0(Y, T\otimes L|_ Y^ k \otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi |_ Y))$ Note. Here and in the sequel, we usually abbreviate $\otimes k$ in the superscript as $k$ to save space. , there exists an extension $\tilde s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X, T\otimes L^ k \otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$ such that \[  \int _ X |\tilde{s}|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\, \omega ^ n \leq C \int _ Y |s|^2_{(h^ k\otimes h_ T)|_ Y} \mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi |_ Y}\, \omega |_ Y^ m,  \] where $C>0$ is an absolute constant, independent of the data $(\varphi ,s,k)$.

title: Proposition 1.8.13
text: Proposition 1.8.13 . Let $(L,h)$ be a Hermitian line bundle on $X$ and set $\theta =c_1(L,h)$. Let $(T,h_ T)$ be a Hermitian line bundle on $X$. Assume that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is a potential with analytic singularities such that $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. For each $k\geq 1$, we let 1.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Bergman_seq_def} \varphi _ k \coloneqq \frac{1}{k} \log \sup _{\substack {s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k \otimes T)\\ \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi } \omega ^ n \leq 1}} |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}. \end{equation} Then for all sufficiently large $k$, \[  \varphi \preceq \varphi _ k\preceq \alpha _ k \varphi ,  \] where $\alpha _ k\in (0,1)$ is an increasing sequence with limit $1$. Proof. First we prove $\varphi \preceq \varphi _ k$. Since $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, there is $\delta >0$ such that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta -\delta \omega )$. Let $x\in X$ with $\varphi (x)>-\infty $. Applying theorem 1.8.12 to the point $Y=\{ x\} $, for all sufficiently large $k$ and every unit vector $e_ x\in (L^ k\otimes T)_ x$, there is a section $\tilde{s}\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$ with $\tilde{s}(x)=e_ x$ and \[  \int _ X |\tilde{s}|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\omega ^ n\leq C\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi (x)}.  \] After rescaling $\tilde{s}$, the definition of $\varphi _ k$ gives \[  \varphi _ k(x)\geq \varphi (x)-\frac{\log C}{k}.  \] This proves $\varphi \preceq \varphi _ k$. The other part of the inequality follows from 1.6.14 and ( 1.42 ). More precisely, if $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))$, with respect to the $L^2$-norm: \[  s\mapsto \left( \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi }\, \omega ^ n \right)^{1/2},  \] then by ( 1.42 ), \[  s_ i\in \mathrm{H}^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes T\otimes \mathcal{I}_{\infty }\left((k-c^{-1}n)_+\varphi \right)\right),  \] where $c>0$ depends only on $\varphi $. So there is $C_ k>0$ so that \[  \sum _{i=1}^ N |s_ i|^2_{h^ k\otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-(k-c^{-1}n)_+\varphi }\leq C_ k\quad \textup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] In other words, \[  \varphi _ k\preceq \frac{1}{k}\left( k-c^{-1}n \right)_+ \varphi .  \] It suffices to take $\alpha _ k=(1-k^{-1}c^{-1}n)_+$. $\square$

1.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Bergman_seq_def} \varphi _ k \coloneqq \frac{1}{k} \log \sup _{\substack {s \in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k \otimes T)\\ \int _ X |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}\mathrm{e}^{-k\varphi } \omega ^ n \leq 1}} |s|^2_{h^ k \otimes h_ T}. \end{equation}

title: 2 Non-pluripolar products
text: 2 Non-pluripolar products Let $X$ be a complex manifold and let $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. When the functions $\varphi _ i$ are smooth, the differential form 2.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixedMAtype} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \end{equation} is defined by the usual calculus. A central problem in pluripotential theory is to extend this product to singular plurisubharmonic functions in a reasonable way. In this book we use the non-pluripolar product. This construction, originating in the work of Bedford–Taylor and developed in the global setting by Guedj–Zeriahi and Boucksom–Eyssidieux–Guedj–Zeriahi, has two features that are essential for us: it is defined for arbitrary quasi-plurisubharmonic singularities, and it satisfies the monotonicity theorem for non-pluripolar masses. These two properties make it possible to compare singularity types through Monge–Ampère mass. The chapter is organized as follows. We first recall the Bedford–Taylor product for locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions. We then introduce the non-pluripolar product and record its basic functorial and locality properties. After a short discussion of quasi-continuous functions and capacity, we prove the convergence and concentration results used later in the theory of envelopes. The key tools extracted from this chapter are the monotonicity theorem, semicontinuity theorem, the concentration theorem for envelopes and the domination principle. The reader may consult [ BEGZ10 ] and [ DDNLsurv ] for broader background. Our presentation is adapted to the later use of envelopes and singularity types, so some estimates are stated in a form slightly more specific than in the standard references.
2.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixedMAtype} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \end{equation}

title: 2.1 Bedford–Taylor theory
text: 2.1 Bedford–Taylor theory Let $X$ be a complex manifold and $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$ ($p\in \mathbb {N}$) be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ Note. In the literature, some people use $\mathrm{PSH}(X)\cap L^{\infty }_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ to denote the set of such functions, which is an abuse of notation. However, this is legitimate thanks to the rigidity theorem 1.1.14 . . In this case, there is a canonical definition of the Monge–Ampère type product ( 2.1 ). Definition 2.1.1 . We define the closed positive $(p,p)$-current ( 2.1 ) on $X$ as follows: We proceed by induction on $p\geq 0$. When $p=0$, we define ( 2.1 ) as the $(0,0)$-current $[X]$. When $p>0$, we let \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left( \varphi _1\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _2 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \right).  \] We call this product the Bedford–Taylor product . Remark 2.1.2 . There is also a slightly more general version of this construction. Given a closed positive current $T$, one can also define the product \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \wedge T  \] in a very similar way. Proposition 2.1.3 . The product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is a closed positive $(p,p)$-current on $X$. Moreover, the product is symmetric in the $\varphi _ i$'s. See [ Proposition 3.3, Corollary 3.12 , GZ17 ] . Note. In [ Proposition 3.3 , GZ17 ] , the authors claim that $\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T$ is closed, which is wrong already in the smooth case. The proof relies crucially on an important estimate, known as the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality . See [ CLN69 ] or [ Theorem 3.9 , GZ17 ] . The Bedford–Taylor theory has many satisfactory properties. Theorem 2.1.4 . Let $(\varphi _ i^ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be decreasing sequences (resp. increasing sequences) of locally bounded psh functions on $X$ converging (resp. converging a.e.) to locally bounded psh functions $\varphi _ i$'s, where $i=0,\ldots ,p$. Then \[  \varphi _0^ j\,  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ j\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ j\rightharpoonup \varphi _0\,  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p  \] as $j\to \infty $. In particular, if $(\varphi _0^ j)_ j$ is the constant sequence $1$, we have \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ j\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ j\rightharpoonup \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p.  \] Here the notation $\rightharpoonup $ denotes the weak-* convergence of currents. We refer to [ Theorem 3.18, Theorem 3.23 , GZ17 ] for the proofs. By contrast, we emphasize that the Bedford–Taylor product is not continuous with respect to the $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$-convergence in general. A simple example can be found in [ Example 3.25 , GZ17 ] . Lemma 2.1.5 . Let $Q\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ and $D\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ m$ be domains, let $p_2\colon Q\times D\to D$ be the second projection, and let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(m,m)$-form on $D$. Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded psh functions on $Q\times D$, and put \[  M=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n,\qquad M_ z=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_1)_ z\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_ n)_ z.  \] Here $(u_ r)_ z(x)=u_ r(x,z)$. For every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support in $Q\times D$, 2.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:boundedfibrefubini} \int _{Q\times D}h\, p_2^*\eta \wedge M =\int _ D\left(\int _ Q h_ z\, M_ z\right)\eta (z), \qquad h_ z(x)=h(x,z). \end{equation} Proof. By linearity, it suffices to consider $\eta \geq 0$. We first prove ( 2.2 ) when $h$ is continuous. On a product neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}h$, choose smooth psh functions $u_ r^{(l)}\searrow u_ r$, $1\leq r\leq n$. For the smooth approximants, decompose each $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ r^{(l)}$ according to the $x$- and $z$-directions. After wedging with $p_2^*\eta $, every term containing a factor $\mathrm{d}z_\alpha $ or $\mathrm{d}\bar z_\beta $ vanishes; hence only the factors $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_ r^{(l)})_ z$ remain, and ( 2.2 ) follows from the usual Fubini theorem. As $l\to \infty $, the Bedford–Taylor monotone continuity theorem theorem 2.1.4 gives convergence on $Q\times D$ and on every fibre. Fix $K\Subset Q$ and $L\Subset D$ containing the projections of $\operatorname{Supp}h$. The Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate [ Theorem 3.9 , GZ17 ] , together with the local uniform bounds for $u_ r^{(l)}$, bounds the masses of the fibre products on $K$ uniformly for $z\in L$ and $l$. Since $h_ z=0$ for $z\notin L$, dominated convergence proves ( 2.2 ). It remains to pass from continuous to bounded Borel functions. Fix relatively compact open sets $U\Subset Q$ and $V\Subset D$. If $\chi \in C_ c(U)$, then \[  F_\chi (z)\coloneqq \int _ U\chi \, M_ z, \qquad z\in V,  \] is Borel measurable. Indeed, choose the smooth decreasing approximations on a neighborhood of $\overline U\times \overline V$ and set \[  M_ z^{(l)}\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_1^{(l)})_ z\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_ n^{(l)})_ z.  \] The functions $z\mapsto \int _ U\chi \, M_ z^{(l)}$ are continuous on $V$ and converge pointwise to $F_\chi $ by theorem 2.1.4 . Let $\mathcal{A}_{U,V}$ be the vector space of bounded Borel functions $\chi $ on $U$ for which $F_\chi $ is Borel measurable on $V$. It is closed under bounded increasing pointwise limits of non-negative functions by the monotone convergence theorem. Taking compactly supported continuous cut-off functions increasing to $1$ on $U$ shows that $1\in \mathcal{A}_{U,V}$. Thus $\mathcal{A}_{U,V}$ contains the algebra $\mathbb {R}+C_ c(U)$, which generates the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $U$. The functional monotone class theorem therefore shows that $\mathcal{A}_{U,V}$ contains every bounded Borel function on $U$. Next, let $\mathcal{B}_{U,V}$ be the vector space of bounded Borel functions $g$ on $U\times V$ such that \[  z\longmapsto \int _ U g_ z\, M_ z, \qquad g_ z(x)=g(x,z),  \] is Borel measurable on $V$. This space is again closed under bounded increasing pointwise limits of non-negative functions. It contains every product $g(x,z)=\chi (x)\psi (z)$ of bounded Borel functions, by the preceding paragraph. Finite sums of such products form an algebra containing the indicators of all Borel rectangles $A\times B\subseteq U\times V$; hence this algebra generates the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $U\times V$. A second application of the functional monotone class theorem shows that $\mathcal{B}_{U,V}$ contains every bounded Borel function on $U\times V$. To pass from $U\times V$ to $Q\times D$, choose exhaustions $U_ j\Subset Q$ and $V_ j\Subset D$ by relatively compact open sets. For a Borel set $E\subseteq Q\times D$, the preceding paragraph, applied to the restriction of $\mathds {1}_ E$ to $U_ j\times V_ j$, shows that \[  G_ j(z)\coloneqq \mathds {1}_{V_ j}(z)\int _{U_ j}\mathds {1}_ E(x,z)\, M_ z  \] is Borel measurable on $D$. We may take both exhaustions increasing, so $G_ j\nearrow M_ z(E_ z)$ pointwise, where \[  E_ z\coloneqq \{ x\in Q:(x,z)\in E\} .  \] Thus $z\mapsto M_ z(E_ z)$ is Borel measurable on $D$. We may therefore define \[  \lambda (E)\coloneqq \int _ D M_ z(E_ z)\, \eta (z).  \] The monotone convergence theorem, first on each fibre and then on $D$, shows that $\lambda $ is a Borel measure on $Q\times D$. The local uniform mass bound above shows that $\lambda $ is locally finite and hence Radon. Approximation by non-negative simple functions gives \[  \int _{Q\times D}h\, \mathrm{d}\lambda =\int _ D\left(\int _ Qh_ z\, M_ z\right)\eta (z)  \] for every non-negative Borel function $h$. For continuous compactly supported $h$, the first part of the proof shows that $\lambda $ agrees with $p_2^*\eta \wedge M$. The uniqueness of Radon measures then gives the same equality for every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support. $\square$

title: Definition 2.1.1
text: Definition 2.1.1 . We define the closed positive $(p,p)$-current ( 2.1 ) on $X$ as follows: We proceed by induction on $p\geq 0$. When $p=0$, we define ( 2.1 ) as the $(0,0)$-current $[X]$. When $p>0$, we let \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left( \varphi _1\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _2 \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \right).  \] We call this product the Bedford–Taylor product .

title: Remark 2.1.2
text: Remark 2.1.2 . There is also a slightly more general version of this construction. Given a closed positive current $T$, one can also define the product \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p \wedge T  \] in a very similar way.

title: Proposition 2.1.3
text: Proposition 2.1.3 . The product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is a closed positive $(p,p)$-current on $X$. Moreover, the product is symmetric in the $\varphi _ i$'s.

title: Theorem 2.1.4
text: Theorem 2.1.4 . Let $(\varphi _ i^ j)_{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be decreasing sequences (resp. increasing sequences) of locally bounded psh functions on $X$ converging (resp. converging a.e.) to locally bounded psh functions $\varphi _ i$'s, where $i=0,\ldots ,p$. Then \[  \varphi _0^ j\,  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ j\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ j\rightharpoonup \varphi _0\,  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p  \] as $j\to \infty $. In particular, if $(\varphi _0^ j)_ j$ is the constant sequence $1$, we have \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ j\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ j\rightharpoonup \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p.  \]

title: Lemma 2.1.5
text: Lemma 2.1.5 . Let $Q\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ n$ and $D\subseteq \mathbb {C}^ m$ be domains, let $p_2\colon Q\times D\to D$ be the second projection, and let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(m,m)$-form on $D$. Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded psh functions on $Q\times D$, and put \[  M=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n,\qquad M_ z=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_1)_ z\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_ n)_ z.  \] Here $(u_ r)_ z(x)=u_ r(x,z)$. For every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support in $Q\times D$, 2.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:boundedfibrefubini} \int _{Q\times D}h\, p_2^*\eta \wedge M =\int _ D\left(\int _ Q h_ z\, M_ z\right)\eta (z), \qquad h_ z(x)=h(x,z). \end{equation} Proof. By linearity, it suffices to consider $\eta \geq 0$. We first prove ( 2.2 ) when $h$ is continuous. On a product neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}h$, choose smooth psh functions $u_ r^{(l)}\searrow u_ r$, $1\leq r\leq n$. For the smooth approximants, decompose each $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ r^{(l)}$ according to the $x$- and $z$-directions. After wedging with $p_2^*\eta $, every term containing a factor $\mathrm{d}z_\alpha $ or $\mathrm{d}\bar z_\beta $ vanishes; hence only the factors $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_ r^{(l)})_ z$ remain, and ( 2.2 ) follows from the usual Fubini theorem. As $l\to \infty $, the Bedford–Taylor monotone continuity theorem theorem 2.1.4 gives convergence on $Q\times D$ and on every fibre. Fix $K\Subset Q$ and $L\Subset D$ containing the projections of $\operatorname{Supp}h$. The Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate [ Theorem 3.9 , GZ17 ] , together with the local uniform bounds for $u_ r^{(l)}$, bounds the masses of the fibre products on $K$ uniformly for $z\in L$ and $l$. Since $h_ z=0$ for $z\notin L$, dominated convergence proves ( 2.2 ). It remains to pass from continuous to bounded Borel functions. Fix relatively compact open sets $U\Subset Q$ and $V\Subset D$. If $\chi \in C_ c(U)$, then \[  F_\chi (z)\coloneqq \int _ U\chi \, M_ z, \qquad z\in V,  \] is Borel measurable. Indeed, choose the smooth decreasing approximations on a neighborhood of $\overline U\times \overline V$ and set \[  M_ z^{(l)}\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_1^{(l)})_ z\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(u_ n^{(l)})_ z.  \] The functions $z\mapsto \int _ U\chi \, M_ z^{(l)}$ are continuous on $V$ and converge pointwise to $F_\chi $ by theorem 2.1.4 . Let $\mathcal{A}_{U,V}$ be the vector space of bounded Borel functions $\chi $ on $U$ for which $F_\chi $ is Borel measurable on $V$. It is closed under bounded increasing pointwise limits of non-negative functions by the monotone convergence theorem. Taking compactly supported continuous cut-off functions increasing to $1$ on $U$ shows that $1\in \mathcal{A}_{U,V}$. Thus $\mathcal{A}_{U,V}$ contains the algebra $\mathbb {R}+C_ c(U)$, which generates the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $U$. The functional monotone class theorem therefore shows that $\mathcal{A}_{U,V}$ contains every bounded Borel function on $U$. Next, let $\mathcal{B}_{U,V}$ be the vector space of bounded Borel functions $g$ on $U\times V$ such that \[  z\longmapsto \int _ U g_ z\, M_ z, \qquad g_ z(x)=g(x,z),  \] is Borel measurable on $V$. This space is again closed under bounded increasing pointwise limits of non-negative functions. It contains every product $g(x,z)=\chi (x)\psi (z)$ of bounded Borel functions, by the preceding paragraph. Finite sums of such products form an algebra containing the indicators of all Borel rectangles $A\times B\subseteq U\times V$; hence this algebra generates the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $U\times V$. A second application of the functional monotone class theorem shows that $\mathcal{B}_{U,V}$ contains every bounded Borel function on $U\times V$. To pass from $U\times V$ to $Q\times D$, choose exhaustions $U_ j\Subset Q$ and $V_ j\Subset D$ by relatively compact open sets. For a Borel set $E\subseteq Q\times D$, the preceding paragraph, applied to the restriction of $\mathds {1}_ E$ to $U_ j\times V_ j$, shows that \[  G_ j(z)\coloneqq \mathds {1}_{V_ j}(z)\int _{U_ j}\mathds {1}_ E(x,z)\, M_ z  \] is Borel measurable on $D$. We may take both exhaustions increasing, so $G_ j\nearrow M_ z(E_ z)$ pointwise, where \[  E_ z\coloneqq \{ x\in Q:(x,z)\in E\} .  \] Thus $z\mapsto M_ z(E_ z)$ is Borel measurable on $D$. We may therefore define \[  \lambda (E)\coloneqq \int _ D M_ z(E_ z)\, \eta (z).  \] The monotone convergence theorem, first on each fibre and then on $D$, shows that $\lambda $ is a Borel measure on $Q\times D$. The local uniform mass bound above shows that $\lambda $ is locally finite and hence Radon. Approximation by non-negative simple functions gives \[  \int _{Q\times D}h\, \mathrm{d}\lambda =\int _ D\left(\int _ Qh_ z\, M_ z\right)\eta (z)  \] for every non-negative Borel function $h$. For continuous compactly supported $h$, the first part of the proof shows that $\lambda $ agrees with $p_2^*\eta \wedge M$. The uniqueness of Radon measures then gives the same equality for every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support. $\square$
2.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:boundedfibrefubini} \int _{Q\times D}h\, p_2^*\eta \wedge M =\int _ D\left(\int _ Q h_ z\, M_ z\right)\eta (z), \qquad h_ z(x)=h(x,z). \end{equation}

title: 2.2 The non-pluripolar products
text: 2.2 The non-pluripolar products The proofs of the standard results recalled in this section can be found in [ BEGZ10 ] . Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Definition 2.2.1 . Let $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. We set \[  O_ k \coloneqq \bigcap _{j=1}^ p \{ \varphi _ j>-k\} ,\quad k\in \mathbb {N}.  \] We say that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined if for each connected open subset $U\subseteq X$, any smooth positive $(1,1)$-form $\omega $ on $U$, and each compact subset $K\subseteq U$, we have 2.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:welldefinepluri} \sup _{k\geq 0} \int _{K\cap O_ k}\left.\left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi _ j\lor (-k))\right)\right|_ U\wedge \omega ^{\dim U-p}<\infty . \end{equation} In this case, we define the non-pluripolar product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ by 2.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:npp} \mathds {1}_{O_ k}\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p=\mathds {1}_{O_ k}\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left( \varphi _ j\lor (-k)\right) \end{equation} on $\bigcup _{k\geq 0} O_ k$ and extend it by zero to $X$. As recalled in section 1.3 , an $\mathcal{F}$-open subset means an open subset with respect to the plurifine topology. Proposition 2.2.2 . Let $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. The product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is local with respect to the plurifine topology in the following sense: Let $O\subseteq X$ be an $\mathcal{F}$-open subset and $\psi _1,\ldots ,\psi _ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Assume that \[  \varphi _ j|_{O}=\psi _ j|_{O},\quad j=1,\ldots ,p,  \] and that \[  \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\textup{ and } \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j  \] are both well-defined, then 2.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp1} \left.\left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\right)\right|_{O}=\left.\left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j\right)\right|_{O}. \end{equation} If furthermore $O$ is open in the usual topology, then the product \[  \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j|_{O}  \] on $O$ is well-defined and 2.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp2} \left. \left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\right)\right|_{O}=\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j|_{O}. \end{equation} Let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open covering of $X$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined if and only if each product \[  \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j|_{U},\quad U\in \mathcal{U}.  \] The current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ and the fact that it is well-defined depend only on the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$, not on the choice of the $\varphi _ j$'s nor on the ordering of the $\varphi _ j$'s. When $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ p\in L^{\infty }_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$, the non-pluripolar product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined and is equal to the Bedford–Taylor product. More generally, if $q\leq p$, and we only assume that $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ q\in L^{\infty }_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$, and that the non-pluripolar product $T\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _{q+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined, then the non-pluripolar product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is also well-defined, and is equal to the Bedford–Taylor product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ q\wedge T$ as in 2.1.2 . Assume that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ puts no mass on pluripolar sets. Assume that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined. Then $\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$ is a closed positive $(p,p)$-current on $X$. Note. This current is in fact strongly positive, as shown in [ Xiabdiv2 ] . The product is multilinear: Let $\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, $a,b>0$ then 2.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp6} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\varphi _1+b\psi _1)\wedge \bigwedge _{j=2}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j =a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \bigwedge _{j=2}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j + b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _1\wedge \bigwedge _{j=2}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j \end{equation} in the sense that the left-hand side is well-defined if and only if both terms on the right-hand side are well-defined, and the equality holds in that case. In view of 3 , we do not need to specify whether our product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is the Bedford–Taylor product or the non-pluripolar product when the $\varphi _ i$'s are all locally bounded. Example 2.2.3 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, then 2.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:1dimnpp} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^1=\mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-\infty \} }\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi . \end{equation} Here $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^1$ on the left-hand side denotes the non-pluripolar product, while $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ on the right-hand side denotes the usual derivative in the sense of current. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X=\Delta ^ n$, the unit polydisk in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Take $f\in C^{\infty }_ c(\Delta ^ n)$ with $f\geq 0$. We need to show that \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } \int _{\Delta ^ n} \mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-k\} }f\,  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (\varphi \lor (-k)\bigr )\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=\int _{\Delta ^ n} \mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-\infty \} }f\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \omega ^{n-1},  \] where $\omega $ is the standard Kähler form on $\mathbb {C}^ n$. By the dominated convergence theorem, this reduces immediately to the $1$-dimensional case: \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } \int _{\Delta ^1} \mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-k\} }f\,  \Delta \bigl (\varphi \lor (-k)\bigr )=\int _{\Delta ^1} \mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-\infty \} }f\, \Delta \varphi ,  \] for any subharmonic function $\varphi $ on the unit disk $\Delta ^1$, which is a special case of [ Proposition 3.3 , EK24 ] . Definition 2.2.4 . Let $T_1,\ldots ,T_ p$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. We say that $T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p$ is well-defined if there exists an open covering $\mathcal{U}$ of $X$ such that on each $U\in \mathcal{U}$, we can find $\varphi _ j^ U\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ ($j=1,\ldots ,p$) such that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j^ U=T_ j,\quad j=1,\ldots ,p  \] and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ U\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ U$ is well-defined. In this case, we define the non-pluripolar product $T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p$ as the closed positive $(p,p)$-current on $X$ defined by 2.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp5} \left(T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\right)|_ U=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ U\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ U,\quad U\in \mathcal{U}. \end{equation} The product $T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p$ is independent of the choices we made thanks to proposition 2.2.2 1 and 2 . proposition 2.2.2 can be formulated in terms of currents without any difficulty. Remark 2.2.5 . Similar to 2.1.2 , there is also an extension of the non-pluripolar theory allowing us to define \[  T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\cap T  \] for any closed positive current $T$. This is the relative non-pluripolar product introduced by Vu [ Vu20 ] . Unlike the relative Bedford–Taylor products, the relative non-pluripolar products present some pathological behaviors. For example, they are not linear in general. Remark 2.2.6 . Another possible generalization of the non-pluripolar products is motivated by proposition 2.2.2 1 . One could begin by defining a generalized notion of plurisubharmonic functions on $\mathcal{F}$-open sets, called $\mathcal{F}$-plurisubharmonic functions and define their non-pluripolar products. See [ EKFW11 , EKW14 ] . Proposition 2.2.7 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and let $T_1,\ldots ,T_ p$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. Then $T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p$ is well-defined. This proposition explains why we usually work in the setting of compact Kähler manifolds. Corollary 2.2.8 . Let $X$ and $Z$ be connected compact Kähler manifolds of dimensions $n$ and $m$, respectively, and let $p_1\colon X\times Z\to X$ and $p_2\colon X\times Z\to Z$ be the projections. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $\gamma $ be a closed smooth positive $(1,1)$-form on $Z$. Put \[  Y=X\times Z,\qquad \Theta =p_1^*\theta +p_2^*\gamma ,\qquad \Phi =p_1^*\phi .  \] Suppose that $W\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\Theta )$ and $\Phi -C\leq W\leq \Phi +C$ for some $C>0$. Set \[  T=\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W,\qquad S=\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi ,  \] and write $W_ z(x)=W(x,z)$. Then $W_ z\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for every $z\in Z$. For $0\leq j\leq n$ and every smooth real $(m,m)$-form $\eta $ on $Z$, 2.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compactrelativeenergyslicing} \begin{aligned} & \int _ Y(W-\Phi )p_2^*\eta \wedge T^ j\wedge S^{n-j}\\ & \qquad =\int _ Z\left(\int _ X(W_ z-\phi )\,  \theta _{W_ z}^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}\right)\eta (z), \end{aligned} \end{equation} and 2.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compactfibreslicingconstant} \int _ Y p_2^*\eta \wedge T^ n =\int _ Z\left(\int _ X\theta _{W_ z}^ n\right)\eta (z). \end{equation} Proof. By linearity, it suffices to consider $\eta \geq 0$. All the non-pluripolar products that occur below are well-defined by proposition 2.2.7 . We work on a relatively compact product chart $Q\times D\subseteq X\times Z$ and let $a$ and $b$ be smooth local potentials of $p_1^*\theta $ and $p_2^*\gamma $. After subtracting constants, put $w=W+a+b\leq 0$ and $f=\Phi +a+b\leq 0$. For $k\geq 1$, set \[  \begin{aligned}  w_ k& =w\lor (-k),&  f_ k& =f\lor (-k),\\  O_ k& =\{ w>-k\} \cap \{ f>-k\} ,&  \mu _{j,k}& =\mathds {1}_{O_ k}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ k)^ j\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ k)^{n-j}. \end{aligned}  \] For $z\in D$, write $w_ z(x)=w(x,z)$ and $f_ z(x)=f(x,z)$, and set \[  \mu _{j,k,z} =\mathds {1}_{\{ w_ z>-k\} \cap \{ f_ z>-k\} } \bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(w_ z\lor (-k))\bigr )^ j\wedge \bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(f_ z\lor (-k))\bigr )^{n-j}.  \] Apply 2.1.5 with $u_1=\cdots =u_ j=w_ k$, $u_{j+1}=\cdots =u_ n=f_ k$, and \[  h=\rho G\mathds {1}_{O_ k},\qquad \rho \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty }_ c(Q\times D),\quad \rho \geq 0,  \] where $G$ is any bounded non-negative Borel function. This gives 2.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finitelevelfubini} \int _{Q\times D}\rho G\, p_2^*\eta \wedge \mu _{j,k} =\int _ D\left(\int _ Q\rho _ zG_ z\, \mu _{j,k,z}\right)\eta (z). \end{equation} By plurifine locality, $\mu _{j,k}$ increases to the local expression of $T^ j\wedge S^{n-j}$, while, for every $z\in D$, $\mu _{j,k,z}$ increases to the local expression of $\theta _{W_ z}^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}$. Taking $G=\delta +C\geq 0$ in ( 2.16 ), applying monotone convergence, subtracting the corresponding constant-weight identity, and summing over a non-negative partition of unity proves ( 2.10 ). The same argument with constant weight and degree $n$ proves ( 2.13 ). $\square$

title: Definition 2.2.1
text: Definition 2.2.1 . Let $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. We set \[  O_ k \coloneqq \bigcap _{j=1}^ p \{ \varphi _ j>-k\} ,\quad k\in \mathbb {N}.  \] We say that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined if for each connected open subset $U\subseteq X$, any smooth positive $(1,1)$-form $\omega $ on $U$, and each compact subset $K\subseteq U$, we have 2.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:welldefinepluri} \sup _{k\geq 0} \int _{K\cap O_ k}\left.\left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi _ j\lor (-k))\right)\right|_ U\wedge \omega ^{\dim U-p}<\infty . \end{equation} In this case, we define the non-pluripolar product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ by 2.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:npp} \mathds {1}_{O_ k}\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p=\mathds {1}_{O_ k}\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left( \varphi _ j\lor (-k)\right) \end{equation} on $\bigcup _{k\geq 0} O_ k$ and extend it by zero to $X$.

2.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:welldefinepluri} \sup _{k\geq 0} \int _{K\cap O_ k}\left.\left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi _ j\lor (-k))\right)\right|_ U\wedge \omega ^{\dim U-p}<\infty . \end{equation}

2.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:npp} \mathds {1}_{O_ k}\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p=\mathds {1}_{O_ k}\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left( \varphi _ j\lor (-k)\right) \end{equation}

title: Proposition 2.2.2
text: Proposition 2.2.2 . Let $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. The product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is local with respect to the plurifine topology in the following sense: Let $O\subseteq X$ be an $\mathcal{F}$-open subset and $\psi _1,\ldots ,\psi _ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Assume that \[  \varphi _ j|_{O}=\psi _ j|_{O},\quad j=1,\ldots ,p,  \] and that \[  \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\textup{ and } \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j  \] are both well-defined, then 2.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp1} \left.\left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\right)\right|_{O}=\left.\left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j\right)\right|_{O}. \end{equation} If furthermore $O$ is open in the usual topology, then the product \[  \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j|_{O}  \] on $O$ is well-defined and 2.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp2} \left. \left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\right)\right|_{O}=\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j|_{O}. \end{equation} Let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open covering of $X$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined if and only if each product \[  \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j|_{U},\quad U\in \mathcal{U}.  \] The current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ and the fact that it is well-defined depend only on the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$, not on the choice of the $\varphi _ j$'s nor on the ordering of the $\varphi _ j$'s. When $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ p\in L^{\infty }_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$, the non-pluripolar product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined and is equal to the Bedford–Taylor product. More generally, if $q\leq p$, and we only assume that $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ q\in L^{\infty }_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$, and that the non-pluripolar product $T\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _{q+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined, then the non-pluripolar product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is also well-defined, and is equal to the Bedford–Taylor product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ q\wedge T$ as in 2.1.2 . Assume that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ puts no mass on pluripolar sets. Assume that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p$ is well-defined. Then $\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$ is a closed positive $(p,p)$-current on $X$. Note. This current is in fact strongly positive, as shown in [ Xiabdiv2 ] . The product is multilinear: Let $\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, $a,b>0$ then 2.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp6} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\varphi _1+b\psi _1)\wedge \bigwedge _{j=2}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j =a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \bigwedge _{j=2}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j + b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _1\wedge \bigwedge _{j=2}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j \end{equation} in the sense that the left-hand side is well-defined if and only if both terms on the right-hand side are well-defined, and the equality holds in that case.

2.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp1} \left.\left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\right)\right|_{O}=\left.\left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j\right)\right|_{O}. \end{equation}

2.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp2} \left. \left(\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\right)\right|_{O}=\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j|_{O}. \end{equation}

2.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp6} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\varphi _1+b\psi _1)\wedge \bigwedge _{j=2}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j =a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1\wedge \bigwedge _{j=2}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j + b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _1\wedge \bigwedge _{j=2}^ p \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j \end{equation}

title: Example 2.2.3
text: Example 2.2.3 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, then 2.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:1dimnpp} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^1=\mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-\infty \} }\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi . \end{equation} Here $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^1$ on the left-hand side denotes the non-pluripolar product, while $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ on the right-hand side denotes the usual derivative in the sense of current. The problem is local, so we may assume that $X=\Delta ^ n$, the unit polydisk in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Take $f\in C^{\infty }_ c(\Delta ^ n)$ with $f\geq 0$. We need to show that \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } \int _{\Delta ^ n} \mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-k\} }f\,  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (\varphi \lor (-k)\bigr )\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=\int _{\Delta ^ n} \mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-\infty \} }f\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \omega ^{n-1},  \] where $\omega $ is the standard Kähler form on $\mathbb {C}^ n$. By the dominated convergence theorem, this reduces immediately to the $1$-dimensional case: \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } \int _{\Delta ^1} \mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-k\} }f\,  \Delta \bigl (\varphi \lor (-k)\bigr )=\int _{\Delta ^1} \mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-\infty \} }f\, \Delta \varphi ,  \] for any subharmonic function $\varphi $ on the unit disk $\Delta ^1$, which is a special case of [ Proposition 3.3 , EK24 ] .
2.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:1dimnpp} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^1=\mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >-\infty \} }\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi . \end{equation}

title: Definition 2.2.4
text: Definition 2.2.4 . Let $T_1,\ldots ,T_ p$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. We say that $T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p$ is well-defined if there exists an open covering $\mathcal{U}$ of $X$ such that on each $U\in \mathcal{U}$, we can find $\varphi _ j^ U\in \mathrm{PSH}(U)$ ($j=1,\ldots ,p$) such that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j^ U=T_ j,\quad j=1,\ldots ,p  \] and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ U\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ U$ is well-defined. In this case, we define the non-pluripolar product $T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p$ as the closed positive $(p,p)$-current on $X$ defined by 2.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp5} \left(T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\right)|_ U=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ U\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ U,\quad U\in \mathcal{U}. \end{equation}

2.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppp5} \left(T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\right)|_ U=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1^ U\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ p^ U,\quad U\in \mathcal{U}. \end{equation}

title: Remark 2.2.5
text: Remark 2.2.5 . Similar to 2.1.2 , there is also an extension of the non-pluripolar theory allowing us to define \[  T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p\cap T  \] for any closed positive current $T$. This is the relative non-pluripolar product introduced by Vu [ Vu20 ] . Unlike the relative Bedford–Taylor products, the relative non-pluripolar products present some pathological behaviors. For example, they are not linear in general.

title: Remark 2.2.6
text: Remark 2.2.6 . Another possible generalization of the non-pluripolar products is motivated by proposition 2.2.2 1 . One could begin by defining a generalized notion of plurisubharmonic functions on $\mathcal{F}$-open sets, called $\mathcal{F}$-plurisubharmonic functions and define their non-pluripolar products. See [ EKFW11 , EKW14 ] .

title: Proposition 2.2.7
text: Proposition 2.2.7 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold and let $T_1,\ldots ,T_ p$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. Then $T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ p$ is well-defined.

title: Corollary 2.2.8
text: Corollary 2.2.8 . Let $X$ and $Z$ be connected compact Kähler manifolds of dimensions $n$ and $m$, respectively, and let $p_1\colon X\times Z\to X$ and $p_2\colon X\times Z\to Z$ be the projections. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $\gamma $ be a closed smooth positive $(1,1)$-form on $Z$. Put \[  Y=X\times Z,\qquad \Theta =p_1^*\theta +p_2^*\gamma ,\qquad \Phi =p_1^*\phi .  \] Suppose that $W\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\Theta )$ and $\Phi -C\leq W\leq \Phi +C$ for some $C>0$. Set \[  T=\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W,\qquad S=\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi ,  \] and write $W_ z(x)=W(x,z)$. Then $W_ z\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for every $z\in Z$. For $0\leq j\leq n$ and every smooth real $(m,m)$-form $\eta $ on $Z$, 2.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compactrelativeenergyslicing} \begin{aligned} & \int _ Y(W-\Phi )p_2^*\eta \wedge T^ j\wedge S^{n-j}\\ & \qquad =\int _ Z\left(\int _ X(W_ z-\phi )\,  \theta _{W_ z}^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}\right)\eta (z), \end{aligned} \end{equation} and 2.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compactfibreslicingconstant} \int _ Y p_2^*\eta \wedge T^ n =\int _ Z\left(\int _ X\theta _{W_ z}^ n\right)\eta (z). \end{equation} Proof. By linearity, it suffices to consider $\eta \geq 0$. All the non-pluripolar products that occur below are well-defined by proposition 2.2.7 . We work on a relatively compact product chart $Q\times D\subseteq X\times Z$ and let $a$ and $b$ be smooth local potentials of $p_1^*\theta $ and $p_2^*\gamma $. After subtracting constants, put $w=W+a+b\leq 0$ and $f=\Phi +a+b\leq 0$. For $k\geq 1$, set \[  \begin{aligned}  w_ k& =w\lor (-k),&  f_ k& =f\lor (-k),\\  O_ k& =\{ w>-k\} \cap \{ f>-k\} ,&  \mu _{j,k}& =\mathds {1}_{O_ k}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ k)^ j\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ k)^{n-j}. \end{aligned}  \] For $z\in D$, write $w_ z(x)=w(x,z)$ and $f_ z(x)=f(x,z)$, and set \[  \mu _{j,k,z} =\mathds {1}_{\{ w_ z>-k\} \cap \{ f_ z>-k\} } \bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(w_ z\lor (-k))\bigr )^ j\wedge \bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x(f_ z\lor (-k))\bigr )^{n-j}.  \] Apply 2.1.5 with $u_1=\cdots =u_ j=w_ k$, $u_{j+1}=\cdots =u_ n=f_ k$, and \[  h=\rho G\mathds {1}_{O_ k},\qquad \rho \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty }_ c(Q\times D),\quad \rho \geq 0,  \] where $G$ is any bounded non-negative Borel function. This gives 2.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finitelevelfubini} \int _{Q\times D}\rho G\, p_2^*\eta \wedge \mu _{j,k} =\int _ D\left(\int _ Q\rho _ zG_ z\, \mu _{j,k,z}\right)\eta (z). \end{equation} By plurifine locality, $\mu _{j,k}$ increases to the local expression of $T^ j\wedge S^{n-j}$, while, for every $z\in D$, $\mu _{j,k,z}$ increases to the local expression of $\theta _{W_ z}^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}$. Taking $G=\delta +C\geq 0$ in ( 2.16 ), applying monotone convergence, subtracting the corresponding constant-weight identity, and summing over a non-negative partition of unity proves ( 2.10 ). The same argument with constant weight and degree $n$ proves ( 2.13 ). $\square$

2.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compactrelativeenergyslicing} \begin{aligned} & \int _ Y(W-\Phi )p_2^*\eta \wedge T^ j\wedge S^{n-j}\\ & \qquad =\int _ Z\left(\int _ X(W_ z-\phi )\,  \theta _{W_ z}^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}\right)\eta (z), \end{aligned} \end{equation}
2.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compactfibreslicingconstant} \int _ Y p_2^*\eta \wedge T^ n =\int _ Z\left(\int _ X\theta _{W_ z}^ n\right)\eta (z). \end{equation}
2.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finitelevelfubini} \int _{Q\times D}\rho G\, p_2^*\eta \wedge \mu _{j,k} =\int _ D\left(\int _ Q\rho _ zG_ z\, \mu _{j,k,z}\right)\eta (z). \end{equation}

title: 2.3 Quasi-continuous functions
text: 2.3 Quasi-continuous functions Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$ and $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class. Definition 2.3.1 . Let $A\subseteq X$ be a Borel subset. The $\theta $-capacity $\operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(A)$ of $A$ is defined as \[  \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(A)\coloneqq \sup \left\{  \int _ A\theta _{\varphi }^ n : \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),V_{\theta }-1\leq \varphi \leq V_{\theta } \right\} .  \] Here $V_{\theta }$ is defined in ( 2.20 ) below. As we will recall below, the non-pluripolar product $\theta _{\varphi }^ n$ is well-defined. The capacity is not very sensitive to the choice of $\theta $: Theorem 2.3.2 . Let $\theta '$ be another closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class. Then there are continuous functions $f,g\colon [0,\infty )\rightarrow [0,\infty )$, with $f(0)=g(0)=0$, such that for any Borel subset $E\subseteq X$, we have \[  \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(E)\leq f\left( \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta '}(E)\right),\quad \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta '}(E)\leq g\left( \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(E)\right).  \] A more general result is proved in [ Lu21 ] . Similar comparison results hold between $\theta $-capacity and the classical Bedford–Taylor capacity, see [ Section 9.2 , GZ17 ] for the proof. As a consequence, we can freely apply the results in [ Section 4.2 , GZ17 ] , even though capacity has a different meaning there. Definition 2.3.3 . Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$. A function $f\colon U\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ is quasi-continuous if it is Borel measurable and for any $\epsilon >0$, there is an open subset $G\subseteq U$ such that $\operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(G)\leq \epsilon $; $f|_{U\setminus G}$ is real-valued and continuous. Thanks to theorem 2.3.2 , the notion of quasi-continuous functions is independent of the choice of $\theta $. Note that if $f,g\colon U\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ are two Borel measurable functions equal quasi-everywhere (see definition 1.1.15 ), then $f$ is quasi-continuous if and only if $g$ is. Theorem 2.3.4 . Let $A\subseteq X$ be a Borel set. Then the following are equivalent: $A$ is pluripolar; $\operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(A)=0$. See [ Theorem 4.40 , GZ17 ] for the proof. Example 2.3.5 . A quasi-plurisubharmonic function on an open subset $U\subseteq X$ is always quasi-continuous. See [ Theorem 4.20 , GZ17 ] for the proof. More generally, if $\varphi ,\psi $ are two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $U$, then the following function \[  f(x)\coloneqq \begin{cases}  \varphi (x)-\psi (x),& \textup{if }(\varphi \lor \psi )(x)\neq -\infty ;\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise} \end{cases}  \] is quasi-continuous. Note. In the literature, people usually say carelessly that $\varphi -\psi $ is quasi-continuous. Definition 2.3.6 . Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$. Let $(f_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net of Borel measurable functions $f_ i\colon U\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$, and $f\colon U\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a Borel measurable function. We say $(f_ i)_{i\in I}$ converges to $f$ in capacity if for any $\delta >0$, we have \[  \lim _{i\in I} \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }\Bigl ( \{ f_ i>f+\delta \}  \Bigr )=0,\quad \lim _{i\in I} \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }\Bigl ( \{ f_ i<f-\delta \}  \Bigr )=0\footnotemark .  \] Note. It is very tempting to write $\lim _{i\in I} \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }\left( \{ |f_ i-f|>\delta \}  \right)=0$, as in [ Definition 4.23 , GZ17 ] for example. But the set where $f_ i-f$ is not defined is not a pluripolar set in general. Hence this abuse of notation is not acceptable. We sometimes write $f_ i\xrightarrow {\mathrm{C}} f$. Note that $f$ is not uniquely determined by the net $(f_ i)_{i\in I}$. Thanks to theorem 2.3.2 , the notion of convergence in capacity is independent of the choice of $\theta $. Proposition 2.3.7 . Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$. Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(U,\theta )$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U,\theta )$. Assume one of the following conditions holds: $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is decreasing and $\varphi $ is the limit of the net; $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is increasing and converges almost everywhere to $\varphi $. Then $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ converges to $\varphi $ in capacity. See [ Proposition 4.25 , GZ17 ] for the proof. The reference concerns only the sequence case, but the proof works for nets as well. Theorem 2.3.8 . Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$. Let $(\chi _ i\colon U\rightarrow [0,\infty ))_ i$ be a sequence of quasi-continuous functions. Assume that the sequence is uniformly bounded and converges in capacity to $\chi \colon U\rightarrow [0,\infty )$. For each $j=1,\ldots ,p$, let $(\varphi _ j^ i)_ i$ be uniformly bounded sequences in $\mathrm{PSH}(U,\theta _ j)$ converging in capacity to bounded $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(U,\theta _ j)$. Then \[  \chi _ i\, \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \theta _{j,\varphi _ j^ i}\rightharpoonup \chi \, \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \theta _{j,\varphi _ j}  \] weakly as currents on $U$. See [ Theorem 4.26 , GZ17 ] Note. In the displayed formula in the statement of [ Theorem 4.26 , GZ17 ] , $1\leq j\leq p$ should be $1\leq i\leq p$ on both sides. .

title: Definition 2.3.1
text: Definition 2.3.1 . Let $A\subseteq X$ be a Borel subset. The $\theta $-capacity $\operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(A)$ of $A$ is defined as \[  \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(A)\coloneqq \sup \left\{  \int _ A\theta _{\varphi }^ n : \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),V_{\theta }-1\leq \varphi \leq V_{\theta } \right\} .  \]

title: Theorem 2.3.2
text: Theorem 2.3.2 . Let $\theta '$ be another closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class. Then there are continuous functions $f,g\colon [0,\infty )\rightarrow [0,\infty )$, with $f(0)=g(0)=0$, such that for any Borel subset $E\subseteq X$, we have \[  \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(E)\leq f\left( \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta '}(E)\right),\quad \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta '}(E)\leq g\left( \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(E)\right).  \]

title: Definition 2.3.3
text: Definition 2.3.3 . Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$. A function $f\colon U\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ is quasi-continuous if it is Borel measurable and for any $\epsilon >0$, there is an open subset $G\subseteq U$ such that $\operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(G)\leq \epsilon $; $f|_{U\setminus G}$ is real-valued and continuous.

title: Theorem 2.3.4
text: Theorem 2.3.4 . Let $A\subseteq X$ be a Borel set. Then the following are equivalent: $A$ is pluripolar; $\operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }(A)=0$.

title: Example 2.3.5
text: Example 2.3.5 . A quasi-plurisubharmonic function on an open subset $U\subseteq X$ is always quasi-continuous. See [ Theorem 4.20 , GZ17 ] for the proof. More generally, if $\varphi ,\psi $ are two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $U$, then the following function \[  f(x)\coloneqq \begin{cases}  \varphi (x)-\psi (x),& \textup{if }(\varphi \lor \psi )(x)\neq -\infty ;\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise} \end{cases}  \] is quasi-continuous. Note. In the literature, people usually say carelessly that $\varphi -\psi $ is quasi-continuous.

title: Definition 2.3.6
text: Definition 2.3.6 . Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$. Let $(f_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net of Borel measurable functions $f_ i\colon U\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$, and $f\colon U\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a Borel measurable function. We say $(f_ i)_{i\in I}$ converges to $f$ in capacity if for any $\delta >0$, we have \[  \lim _{i\in I} \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }\Bigl ( \{ f_ i>f+\delta \}  \Bigr )=0,\quad \lim _{i\in I} \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }\Bigl ( \{ f_ i<f-\delta \}  \Bigr )=0\footnotemark .  \] Note. It is very tempting to write $\lim _{i\in I} \operatorname{Cap}_{\theta }\left( \{ |f_ i-f|>\delta \}  \right)=0$, as in [ Definition 4.23 , GZ17 ] for example. But the set where $f_ i-f$ is not defined is not a pluripolar set in general. Hence this abuse of notation is not acceptable. We sometimes write $f_ i\xrightarrow {\mathrm{C}} f$.

title: Proposition 2.3.7
text: Proposition 2.3.7 . Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$. Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(U,\theta )$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(U,\theta )$. Assume one of the following conditions holds: $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is decreasing and $\varphi $ is the limit of the net; $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is increasing and converges almost everywhere to $\varphi $. Then $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ converges to $\varphi $ in capacity.

title: Theorem 2.3.8
text: Theorem 2.3.8 . Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$. Let $(\chi _ i\colon U\rightarrow [0,\infty ))_ i$ be a sequence of quasi-continuous functions. Assume that the sequence is uniformly bounded and converges in capacity to $\chi \colon U\rightarrow [0,\infty )$. For each $j=1,\ldots ,p$, let $(\varphi _ j^ i)_ i$ be uniformly bounded sequences in $\mathrm{PSH}(U,\theta _ j)$ converging in capacity to bounded $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(U,\theta _ j)$. Then \[  \chi _ i\, \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \theta _{j,\varphi _ j^ i}\rightharpoonup \chi \, \bigwedge _{j=1}^ p \theta _{j,\varphi _ j}  \] weakly as currents on $U$.

title: 2.4 Properties of non-pluripolar products
text:
2.4 Properties of non-pluripolar products Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$ and $	heta ,	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ be closed real smooth $(1,1)$-forms on $X$. We write 2.19  egin{equation} \label{eq:PSHpos} \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )_{>0}=\left\{  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ): \int _ X	heta _{\varphi }^ n>0 ight\} . \end{equation} The non-pluripolar product $	heta _{\varphi }^ n$ is well-defined thanks to proposition 2.2.7 . Remark 2.4.1 . Suppose that $X$ is a connected complex manifold of dimension $0$, namely, $X$ is a single point. In this case, by definition, the non-pluripolar product $	heta _{\varphi }^ n$ is given by the current of integration at the unique point. So $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )_{>0}=\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cong \mathbb {R}$ in this case and $\int _ X 	heta _{\varphi }^ n=1$ for all $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Recall the following basic result: Proposition 2.4.2 . Assume that $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )_{>0}$ is non-empty. Then the cohomology class $\{ 	heta \} $ is big. See [ Proposition 1.22 , BEGZ10 ] . We recall a few basic facts about the non-pluripolar masses. Proposition 2.4.3 . Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$ and $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. Then \[  \int _ Y (\pi ^*T_1)\wedge \cdots \wedge (\pi ^*T_ n)=\int _ X T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ n.  \] Similarly, if $S_1,\ldots ,S_ n$ are closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $Y$, then \[  \int _ Y S_1\wedge \cdots \wedge S_ n=\int _ X \left(\pi _*S_1ight)\wedge \cdots \wedge \left(\pi _*S_ night).  \] Here $\pi ^*T_ i$ is defined as follows: Write $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ for some closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $	heta _ i$ on $X$ and $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ i)$, then $\pi ^*T_ i=\pi ^*	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\pi ^*\varphi _ i$. The pull-back $\pi ^*T_ i$ is clearly independent of the choices of $	heta _ i$ and $\varphi _ i$. Proof. The assertions follow from proposition 2.2.2 1 on the Zariski open set where $\pi $ is an isomorphism. The exceptional locus is pluripolar, and the relevant non-pluripolar products put no mass on pluripolar sets by proposition 2.2.2 4 . $\square$ Theorem 2.4.4 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Then the map \[  [0,1] 
i t\mapsto \log \int _ X 	heta _{t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0}^ n  \] is concave. More generally, given closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n$ on $X$, we have \[  \int _ X T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ n\geq \prod _{i=1}^ n \left( \int _ X T_ i^ n ight)^{1/n}.  \] See [ DDNL19log ] for the proof. Remark 2.4.5 . Here and in the sequel, when we write expressions like $t\varphi +(1-t)\psi $ for $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, we will follow the convention that when $t=0$, the value is $\psi $ and when $t=1$, the value is $\varphi $. We shall write 2.20  egin{equation} \label{eq:Vtheta} V_{	heta }=\sup \left\{  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):\varphi \leq 0 ight\} . \end{equation} Note that the upper semicontinuous regularization $V_{	heta }^*$ of $V_{	heta }$ is itself a candidate of ( 2.20 ) if $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
eq \varnothing $ as follows from proposition 1.2.2 , therefore, $V_{	heta }=V_{	heta }^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ if $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
eq \varnothing $. The function $V_{	heta }$ should be regarded as a canonical representative of the least singular potentials in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. We recall the following result: Lemma 2.4.6 . Suppose that $\{ 	heta \} $ is big. The potential $V_{	heta }$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus \operatorname{nK}(\{ 	heta \} )$. Recall that $\operatorname{nK}(\{ 	heta \} )$ is the non-Kähler locus introduced in definition 1.7.8 . Proof. By definition of $\operatorname{nK}(\{ 	heta \} )$, it suffices to show that if $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ has analytic singularities and $	heta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, then $V_{	heta }$ is locally bounded outside $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $. After replacing $\varphi $ by $\varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $, the function $\varphi $ is a candidate in ( 2.20 ); hence $V_{	heta }\geq \varphi $ and $V_{	heta }\leq 0$. Since $\varphi $ is locally bounded outside its pole set, so is $V_{	heta }$. $\square$ The non-pluripolar product has a lower semicontinuity property. Theorem 2.4.7 (Semicontinuity theorem) . Let $\varphi _ j, \varphi _ j^ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$ ($k\in \mathbb {N}$, $j=1,\ldots ,n$). Let $\chi _ k,\chi $ ($k\in \mathbb {N}$) be non-negative uniformly bounded quasi-continuous functions on $X$ such that $(\chi _ k)_ k$ converges to $\chi $ in capacity. Assume that for any $j=1,\ldots ,n$, as $k	o \infty $, either $\varphi _ j^ k$ decreases to $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$ or increases to $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$ almost everywhere. Then 2.21  egin{equation} \label{eq:semicon1} \varliminf _{k	o \infty }\int _ X\chi _ k \, 	heta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k} \geq \int _ X \chi \, 	heta _{1,\varphi _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n}. \end{equation} If in addition, \[  \lim _{k	o \infty }\int _ X	heta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k} =\int _ X 	heta _{1,\varphi _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n},  \] then \[  \chi _ k \, 	heta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}ightharpoonup \chi \, 	heta _{1,\varphi _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n}  \] weakly as measures Note. Recall that the weak convergence of Radon measures is stronger than the weak convergence as currents in general. When the Radon measures have uniformly bounded total variation, they are equivalent. . In particular, the limit in ( 2.21 ) exists and equality holds in ( 2.21 ). See [ Theorem 2.6 , DDNLsurv ] for the proof. The non-pluripolar mass is a monotone quantity with respect to the singularity type. Theorem 2.4.8 (Monotonicity theorem) . Let $\varphi _ j,\psi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$ for $j=1,\ldots ,n$. Assume that $\varphi _ j \succeq \psi _ j$ Note. See definition 1.5.2 for the notation. for every $j$, then \[  \int _{X} 	heta _{1,\varphi _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n} \geq \int _{X} 	heta _{1,\psi _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\psi _ n}.  \] In particular, if $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\varphi \succeq \psi $, then \[  \int _ X 	heta _{\varphi }^ n\geq \int _ X 	heta _{\psi }^ n.  \] In other words, the non-pluripolar mass increases as the potentials become less singular. See [ Theorem 1.1 , DDNL18mono ] . We will prove a vast extension of this theorem in proposition 6.1.16 . By this theorem, the non-pluripolar mass $\int _ X 	heta _{\varphi }^ n$ can be used as a rough measure of the singularities of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. In section 3.1 , we shall refine this measure by defining the notion of $P$-envelope. As a corollary, we obtain that Corollary 2.4.9 . Fix a directed set $I$. For each $j=1,\ldots ,n$, take an increasing net $(\varphi _ j^ i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$, uniformly bounded from above. Set \[  \varphi _ j\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ j^ i,\quad j=1,\ldots ,n.  \] Then 2.22  egin{equation} \label{eq:increseqnppcont} \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X 	heta _{1,\varphi _1^ i}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n^ i} = \int _ X 	heta _{1,\varphi _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n}. \end{equation} In particular, if the nets are indeed sequences, we have \[  	heta _{1,\varphi _1^ i}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n^ i} ightharpoonup 	heta _{1,\varphi _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{n,\varphi _ n}.  \] Proof. The final assertion follows from ( 2.22 ) together with theorem 2.4.7 . It remains to establish ( 2.22 ). We may assume that $I$ is infinite as there is nothing to prove otherwise. Thanks to theorem 2.4.8 , we already know the $\leq $ inequality in ( 2.22 ). We prove the reverse inequality. When $I\cong \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$ as directed sets, the reverse inequality follows from theorem 2.4.7 . In general, by Choquet's lemma proposition 1.2.3 , we can find a countable infinite subset $R\subseteq I$ such that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{r\in R}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi ^ r_ j=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi ^ i_ j  \] for all $j=1,\ldots ,n$. We fix a bijection $R\cong \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. For any $j=1,\ldots ,n$, we will then denote elements $\varphi _ j^ r$ ($r\in R$) by $\varphi _ j^1,\varphi _ j^2,\dots $. We shall write \[  \psi _ j^ a=\varphi _ j^1\lor \cdots \lor \varphi _ j^ a  \] for each $a\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. For every $a$ we may choose $i_ a\in I$ dominating the finitely many indices corresponding to $\varphi _ j^1,\ldots ,\varphi _ j^ a$ for all $j$.
