For each $C>0$ and $j\geq 1$, we let \[  \varphi _ C\coloneqq \varphi \lor (\phi -C),\quad \varphi _{j,C}\coloneqq \varphi _ j\lor (\phi -C).  \] By Step 1, for each $C>0$, we have \[  \lim _{j\to \infty } E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{j,C})= E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{C})\geq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ).  \] It suffices therefore to show that 3.136 \begin{equation} \label{eq:limCCEphi_temp1} \lim _{C\to \infty } E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{j,C})-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{j})=0\quad \textup{uniformly for $j$ in a tail}. \end{equation} Fix $i\geq 1$. For $j\geq i$, we compute \[  \begin{aligned} &  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{j,C})-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{j})\\  \leq &  \int _ X \left( \varphi _{j,C}-\varphi _{j}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi _{j}}^ n & \textup{by proposition \gerbyref{EFA21885}{3.1.46}}\\  \leq &  \int _{\{ \varphi _ j\leq \phi -C\} } (\phi -C-\varphi _ j)\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n\\  =&  \int _ C^{\infty }\int _{\{ \varphi _ j\leq \phi -t\} } \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n\, \mathrm{d}t\\  \leq &  \int _ C^{\infty }\int _{\{ \varphi _ i\leq (\varphi _ j+\phi -t)/2\} } \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n\, \mathrm{d}t\\  \leq &  2^ n\int _ C^{\infty }\int _{\{ \varphi _ i\leq (\varphi _ j+\phi -t)/2\} } \theta _{(\varphi _ j+\phi -t)/2}^ n\, \mathrm{d}t\\  \leq &  2^ n\int _ C^{\infty }\int _{\{ \varphi _ i\leq (\varphi _ j+\phi -t)/2\} } \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n\, \mathrm{d}t &  \textup{by proposition \gerbyref{EEAA4F47}{3.1.32}}\\  \leq & 2^ n\int _ C^{\infty }\int _{\{ \varphi _ i\leq \phi -t/2\} } \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n\, \mathrm{d}t\\  = &  2^{n+1}\int _{\{ \varphi _ i< \phi -C/2\} } (\phi -\varphi _ i-C/2)\, \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n\\  = &  2^{n+1}\int _{\{ \varphi _ i< \phi -C/2\} } (\phi -\varphi _ i)\, \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n-C 2^ n\int _{\{ \varphi _ i< \phi -C/2\} }\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n. \end{aligned}  \] As $C\to \infty $, the first term converges to $0$ since $\varphi _ i\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. As for the second term, \[  \lim _{C\to \infty }C\int _{\{ \varphi _ i< \phi -C/2 \} } \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n\leq 2 \lim _{C\to \infty }\int _{\{ \varphi _ i< \phi -C/2 \} }(\phi -\varphi _ i)\,  \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n = 0.  \] We conclude ( 3.136 ). We now pass from sequences to nets. By 3.1.36 , the net $(E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i))_{i\in I}$ is increasing and bounded above by $E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )$. Let \[  L\coloneqq \lim _{i\in I}E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i).  \] Then $L\leq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )$. By proposition 1.2.6 , we have \[  \varphi =\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i.  \] Moreover, $\varphi _ i\leq \varphi $ for all $i\in I$, so the family is locally uniformly bounded above. Applying Choquet's lemma proposition 1.2.3 , we can find a countable subset $J\subseteq I$ such that \[  \varphi =\operatorname *{sup}_{j\in J}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ j.  \] Enumerate $J=\{ j_1,j_2,\ldots \} $, repeating elements if necessary. Since $I$ is directed, we can choose an increasing sequence $(i_ k)_{k\geq 1}$ in $I$ such that $i_ k$ dominates $j_1,\ldots ,j_ k$. It follows that $(\varphi _{i_ k})_ k$ increases almost everywhere to $\varphi $. Applying the sequence case to this sequence gives \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{i_ k})=E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ).  \] Since $E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{i_ k})\leq L$ for every $k$, we conclude $E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )\leq L$. $\square$
3.133 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Iconv_mono} \lim _{i\in I} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i)=E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ). \end{equation}

3.136 \begin{equation} \label{eq:limCCEphi_temp1} \lim _{C\to \infty } E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{j,C})-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{j})=0\quad \textup{uniformly for $j$ in a tail}. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 3.1.48
text: Lemma 3.1.48 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then there is $\gamma \in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ such that 3.147 \begin{equation} \label{eq:solution_thetavarphiephiu} \theta _{\gamma }^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma -\varphi }\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n+\mathrm{e}^{\gamma -\psi }\, \theta _{\psi }^ n. \end{equation} Proof. For each $j\geq 1$, let $\varphi _ j\coloneqq \varphi \lor (-j)$, $\psi _ j\coloneqq \psi \lor (-j)$. These functions are not necessarily $\theta $-psh. Let \[  \mu _ j=\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi _ j}\theta _{\varphi }^ n+\mathrm{e}^{-\psi _ j}\theta _{\psi }^ n.  \] By theorem 3.1.34 , we can find $\gamma _ j\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ such that 3.148 \begin{equation} \label{eq:thetagammaj_temp1} \theta _{\gamma _ j}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j}\mu _ j=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\theta _{\varphi }^ n+\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\psi _ j}\theta _{\psi }^ n. \end{equation} Take a constant $C>0$ so that $\psi -2C\leq \varphi \leq \psi +2C$. Let \[  \eta \coloneqq \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-C-n\log 2.  \] Then $\eta \in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and we have the following inequalities: \[  \begin{aligned}  \theta _{\eta }^ n =&  \theta _{(\varphi +\psi )/2}^ n\\  \geq &  2^{-n}\theta _{\varphi }^ n+2^{-n}\theta _{\psi }^ n\\  \geq &  2^{-n}\mathrm{e}^{(\varphi +\psi )/2}\mathrm{e}^{-C}\left( \mathrm{e}^{-\varphi }\theta _{\varphi }^ n+\mathrm{e}^{-\psi }\theta _{\psi }^ n \right)\\  \geq &  2^{-n}\mathrm{e}^{(\varphi +\psi )/2}\mathrm{e}^{-C}\left( \mathrm{e}^{-\varphi _ j}\theta _{\varphi }^ n+\mathrm{e}^{-\psi _ j}\theta _{\psi }^ n \right)\\  = &  \mathrm{e}^{\eta }\mu _ j. \end{aligned}  \] Hence, $\gamma _ j\geq \eta $ by theorem 3.1.34 . By theorem 3.1.34 again, $\gamma _ j$ is decreasing in $j$; let $\gamma =\inf _{j>0}\gamma _ j$. Then $\gamma \geq \eta $, hence $\gamma \in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Now observe that \[  \theta _{\gamma _ j}^ n\rightharpoonup \theta _{\gamma }^ n  \] as $j\to \infty $, by theorem 2.4.7 . Finally observe that there is a constant $C'>0$ so that \[  \gamma _1\leq \varphi +C',\quad \gamma _1\leq \psi +C',  \] since $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Therefore, for each $j>0$, \[  \gamma _ j\leq \varphi _ j+C',\quad \gamma _ j\leq \psi _ j+C'.  \] Hence, ( 3.147 ) follows from ( 3.148 ) and the dominated convergence theorem by letting $j\to \infty $. $\square$
3.147 \begin{equation} \label{eq:solution_thetavarphiephiu} \theta _{\gamma }^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma -\varphi }\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n+\mathrm{e}^{\gamma -\psi }\, \theta _{\psi }^ n. \end{equation}

3.148 \begin{equation} \label{eq:thetagammaj_temp1} \theta _{\gamma _ j}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j}\mu _ j=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\theta _{\varphi }^ n+\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\psi _ j}\theta _{\psi }^ n. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 3.1.49
text: Lemma 3.1.49 . Let $\varphi ,\psi ,\gamma \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Assume that $\varphi \leq \psi \leq \gamma $. Then \[  \int _ X (\gamma -\psi )\, \theta _{\psi }^ n\leq 2^{n+1}\int _ X (\gamma -\varphi )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] Proof. Observe that for any $t\geq 0$, 3.154 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppgcomp} \begin{split}  \{ \gamma >\psi +2t\} \setminus \{ \psi =-\infty \} \subseteq \left\{ (\gamma +\psi )/2>\psi +t\right\} \\  \subseteq \left\{ (\gamma +\psi )/2>\varphi +t\right\} \subseteq \{ \gamma >\varphi +t\} . \end{split} \end{equation} So \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ X (\gamma -\psi )\, \theta _{\psi }^ n =&  2\int _0^{\infty } \int _{\{ \gamma -\psi >2t\} }\, \theta _{\psi }^ n\, \mathrm{d}t & \\  \leq &  2\int _0^{\infty } \int _{\left\{ (\gamma +\psi )/2>\psi +t\right\} }\, \theta _{\psi }^ n\, \mathrm{d}t &  \textup{by (\gerbyref{E29AC9D9}{3.154})}\\  \leq &  2^{n+1}\int _0^{\infty } \int _{\left\{ (\gamma +\psi )/2>\varphi +t\right\} }\, \theta _{(\gamma +\psi )/2}^ n\, \mathrm{d}t & \\  \leq &  2^{n+1}\int _0^{\infty } \int _{\left\{ (\gamma +\psi )/2>\varphi +t\right\} }\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\, \mathrm{d}t &  \textup{by proposition \gerbyref{EEAA4F47}{3.1.32}}\\  \leq & 2^{n+1}\int _0^{\infty } \int _{\left\{ \gamma >\varphi +t\right\} }\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\, \mathrm{d}t & \textup{by (\gerbyref{E29AC9D9}{3.154})}\\  =&  2^{n+1} \int _ X (\gamma -\varphi )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n & . \end{aligned}  \] This completes the proof. $\square$

3.154 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ppgcomp} \begin{split}  \{ \gamma >\psi +2t\} \setminus \{ \psi =-\infty \} \subseteq \left\{ (\gamma +\psi )/2>\psi +t\right\} \\  \subseteq \left\{ (\gamma +\psi )/2>\varphi +t\right\} \subseteq \{ \gamma >\varphi +t\} . \end{split} \end{equation}

title: Lemma 3.1.50
text: Lemma 3.1.50 . Let $\varphi _ j\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ ($j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$) and $\gamma \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Assume that $\varphi _ j\leq \gamma $ for each $j$ and that $\varphi _ j$ converges to $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with respect to the $L^1$-topology. Assume that there is a constant $A>0$ such that for any $j>0$, \[  \int _ X (\varphi _ j-\gamma )\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n\geq -A.  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and 3.163 \begin{equation} \label{eq:intvarphigammageqm2np3A} \int _ X (\varphi -\gamma )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\geq - 2^{n+3}A. \end{equation} Proof. Replacing simultaneously $\gamma ,\varphi _ j,\varphi $ by $\gamma -B,\varphi _ j-B,\varphi -B$ for $B\gg 1$, we may assume that $\gamma \leq 0$. The assumptions and the conclusion are invariant under this translation. Since $\gamma \in \mathcal E(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $, we then have $\gamma \leq \phi $. Step 1 . Assume that $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is decreasing. In this case, we prove 3.164 \begin{equation} \label{eq:intvarphigammageqm4A_temp1} \int _ X (\varphi -\gamma )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\geq -4A. \end{equation} By 3.1.43 , for any $j, k>0$, \[  \int _ X (\varphi _ j-\gamma )\, \theta _{\varphi _ k}^ n\geq -4A.  \] For any $C>0$, \[  \int _ X \Bigl (\varphi _ j \lor (\gamma -C)-\gamma \Bigr )\, \theta _{\varphi _ k}^ n\geq \int _ X (\varphi _ j-\gamma ) \, \theta _{\varphi _ k}^ n\geq -4A.  \] Letting $k\to \infty $, by theorem 2.4.7 , we find \[  \int _ X \Bigl (\varphi _ j \lor (\gamma -C)-\gamma \Bigr )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\geq -4A.  \] Letting $j\to \infty $, by the monotone convergence theorem, we get \[  \int _ X \Bigl (\varphi \lor (\gamma -C)-\gamma \Bigr )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\geq -4A.  \] Then we let $C\to \infty $, again by the monotone convergence theorem, we conclude ( 3.164 ). Step 2 . In general, let \[  \psi _ j=\operatorname *{sup}_{k\geq j}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ k.  \] Then $\varphi =\inf _{j>0}\psi _ j$ due to corollary 1.2.8 . For each $C>0$, let \[  \psi _{j,C}=\psi _ j \lor (\gamma -C),\quad \varphi _ C=\varphi \lor (\gamma -C).  \] Then $\psi _{j,C},\varphi _ C\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ since $\gamma -C\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ thanks to the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 . Observe that $\psi _{j,C}$ decreases to $\varphi _ C$ as $j\to \infty $. Moreover, \[  \gamma \geq \psi _{j,C} \geq \psi _ j\geq \varphi _ j.  \] By 3.1.49 , \[  \int _ X (\psi _{j,C}-\gamma )\, \theta _{\psi _{j,C}}^ n\geq -2^{n+1}A.  \] By Step 1, 3.165 \begin{equation} \label{eq:inproof1} \int _ X(\varphi _ C-\gamma )\, \theta _{\varphi _ C}^ n\geq -2^{n+3}A. \end{equation} In particular, by the plurifine locality of the non-pluripolar product proposition 2.2.2 1 , \[  \int _{\{ \varphi >\gamma -C\} }(\varphi -\gamma )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\geq -2^{n+3}A.  \] Letting $C\to \infty $, we conclude ( 3.163 ). As a consequence, \[  \int _ X (\gamma -\varphi )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n<\infty .  \] We still have to prove that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. In fact, by ( 3.165 ), for any $C>0$, \[  \int _{\{ \varphi \leq \gamma -C\} }\, \theta _{\varphi _ C}^ n\leq \frac{1}{C}\int _ X (\gamma -\varphi _ C)\, \theta _{\varphi _ C}^ n\leq 2^{n+3}C^{-1}A.  \] Using the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 and the plurifine locality of the non-pluripolar product proposition 2.2.2 1 , we find \[  \int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ C}^ n=\int _{\{ \varphi \leq \gamma -C\} }\, \theta _{\varphi _ C}^ n+\int _{\{ \varphi >\gamma -C\} }\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] Letting $C\to \infty $, we conclude that \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n=\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n.  \] This completes the proof. $\square$
3.163 \begin{equation} \label{eq:intvarphigammageqm2np3A} \int _ X (\varphi -\gamma )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\geq - 2^{n+3}A. \end{equation}
3.164 \begin{equation} \label{eq:intvarphigammageqm4A_temp1} \int _ X (\varphi -\gamma )\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\geq -4A. \end{equation}
3.165 \begin{equation} \label{eq:inproof1} \int _ X(\varphi _ C-\gamma )\, \theta _{\varphi _ C}^ n\geq -2^{n+3}A. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 3.1.51
text: Proposition 3.1.51 . Assume that $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$, $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$), then so is $\varphi \land \psi $. Proof. The case of $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ is trivial. We consider the case $\mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. It follows from proposition 3.1.15 that $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By theorem 3.1.18 , we have \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n\geq \int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n.  \] By the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 , equality holds. By theorem 3.1.9 , we conclude that \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi \land \psi ]=\phi .  \] Finally, assume that $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We may assume that $\varphi ,\psi \leq \phi $. For each $j\geq 1$, consider the approximations: \[  \varphi _ j\coloneqq \varphi \lor (\phi -j)\, ,\quad \psi _ j\coloneqq \psi \lor (\phi -j).  \] By 3.1.48 , we can take $\gamma _ j\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ solving the following equation: \[  \theta _{\gamma _ j}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n+\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\psi _ j}\, \theta _{\psi _ j}^ n.  \] In particular, \[  \theta _{\gamma _ j}^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n.  \] We claim that this implies $\gamma _ j\leq \varphi _ j$. Indeed, by proposition 3.1.32 , \[  \int _{\{ \varphi _ j<\gamma _ j\} }\theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n \geq \int _{\{ \varphi _ j<\gamma _ j\} }\theta _{\gamma _ j}^ n \geq \int _{\{ \varphi _ j<\gamma _ j\} }\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n.  \] Hence \[  \int _{\{ \varphi _ j<\gamma _ j\} }\left(\mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}-1\right)\theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n=0.  \] It follows that $\int _{\{ \varphi _ j<\gamma _ j\} }\theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n=0$, and the domination principle theorem 2.4.17 gives $\gamma _ j\leq \varphi _ j$. Similarly, $\gamma _ j\leq \psi _ j$. In particular, $\gamma _ j\leq \varphi _ j\land \psi _ j$. We claim that 3.166 \begin{equation} \label{eq:intgammajphi_unif_lower} \int _ X (\gamma _ j-\phi )\, \theta _{\gamma _ j}^ n >-C \end{equation} for some $C$ independent of $j$. Assume the claim is true for now. We get immediately that \[  \sup _{X}\gamma _ j=\sup _{X\setminus \{ \phi =-\infty \} }(\gamma _ j-\phi )\geq -\frac{C}{\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n},  \] where the first equality follows from proposition 3.1.13 . By proposition 1.5.4 , after possibly extracting a subsequence, we may assume that $\gamma _ j\to \gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ in $L^1$-topology. Then $\gamma \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ by 3.1.50 and proposition 3.1.40 . Since $\gamma \leq \varphi \land \psi \leq \phi $, the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 gives \[  \int _ X\theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n=\int _ X\theta _\phi ^ n.  \] Moreover, by the monotonicity of $E^\phi _\theta $, \[  E^\phi _\theta (\varphi \land \psi )\geq E^\phi _\theta (\gamma )>-\infty .  \] Thus $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ by proposition 3.1.40 . Now we prove the claim ( 3.166 ). By symmetry, it suffices to prove \[  \int _ X (\phi -\gamma _ j) \mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n\leq C.  \] But note that \[  \int _ X (\phi -\gamma _ j) \mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n=\int _ X (\phi -\varphi _ j) \mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n+\int _ X (\varphi _ j-\gamma _ j) \mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n.  \] But $x \mathrm{e}^{-x}\leq \mathrm{e}^{-1}$ for $x\geq 0$ (with maximum at $x=1$), so the second term is bounded; it remains to prove \[  \int _ X (\phi -\varphi _ j) \mathrm{e}^{\gamma _ j-\varphi _ j}\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n\leq C.  \] As $\gamma _ j\leq \varphi _ j$, it suffices to prove 3.167 \begin{equation} \label{eq:inproof2} \int _ X (\phi -\varphi _ j)\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n\leq C. \end{equation} We compute, using ( 3.69 ) and the fact that the $k<n$ terms $\int _ X(\varphi _ j-\phi )\theta _{\varphi _ j}^ k\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-k}$ are all non-positive (since $\varphi _ j\leq \phi $), \[  \int _ X (\varphi _ j-\phi )\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n\geq (n+1)E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ j).  \] Since $\varphi _ j\searrow \varphi $ and $E_\theta ^{\phi }$ is continuous along decreasing sequences (proposition 3.1.39 ), $E_\theta ^{\phi }(\varphi _ j)$ is bounded below uniformly in $j$. Thus, ( 3.167 ) follows. $\square$
3.166 \begin{equation} \label{eq:intgammajphi_unif_lower} \int _ X (\gamma _ j-\phi )\, \theta _{\gamma _ j}^ n >-C \end{equation}
3.167 \begin{equation} \label{eq:inproof2} \int _ X (\phi -\varphi _ j)\, \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n\leq C. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 3.1.52
text: Proposition 3.1.52 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be potentials such that $\varphi \preceq \psi \preceq \phi $. Assume that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$, $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$), then so is $\psi $. Proof. We may assume that $\varphi \leq \psi $. The case $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ is trivial. The case $\mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ follows from theorem 2.4.8 . The case $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ follows from the characterization of $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ in proposition 3.1.40 and the monotonicity of $E_{\theta }^{\phi }$ proved in 3.1.36 . $\square$

title: Proposition 3.1.53
text: Proposition 3.1.53 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a uniformly bounded from above non-empty family in $\mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$, $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$), then so is $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i$. Proof. Thanks to proposition 3.1.52 , it suffices to show that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i\preceq \phi .  \] Since $\phi $ is model and $\varphi _ i\preceq \phi $, we know that \[  \varphi _ i-\sup _ X \varphi _ i \leq \phi  \] for any $i\in I$. Since $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is uniformly bounded from above by assumption, our assertion follows. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.1.54
text: Proposition 3.1.54 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ](\psi )=\operatorname *{sup}_{C > 0}{}\! {}^{*} (\varphi +C)\land \psi =\psi .  \] Proof. The first equality follows from the definition of $P_{\theta }[\varphi ](\psi )$. We focus on the second equality. Since for each $C\geq 0$, \[  (\varphi \land \psi +C)\land \psi \leq (\varphi +C)\land \psi \leq \psi ,  \] we may replace $\varphi $ by $\varphi \land \psi $ (cf. proposition 3.1.51 ) and assume that $\varphi \leq \psi $. Let \[  \gamma \coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{C > 0}{}\! {}^{*} (\varphi +C)\land \psi .  \] Observe that $\gamma \leq \psi $, and $\gamma \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ due to proposition 3.1.51 and proposition 3.1.53 . Then corollary 3.1.8 guarantees that \[  \int _{\{ \gamma <\psi \}  } \theta _{\gamma }^ n=0.  \] Therefore, we can apply the domination principle theorem 2.4.17 to conclude that $\gamma =\psi $. $\square$

title: Lemma 3.1.55
text: Lemma 3.1.55 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Define \[  \eta _ t\coloneqq \Bigl ( (1-t)\varphi +t\psi \Bigr )\land \psi ,\quad t\in [0,1].  \] Then $E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ t)$ is differentiable for $t\in [0,1]$ and 3.168 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Iphit_diff} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ t)=\int _{X} \Bigl ( \psi -\min \{ \varphi ,\psi \}  \Bigr )\, \theta _{\eta _ t}^ n. \end{equation} Proof. Let us prove ( 3.168 ) with right-derivative instead of derivative, and $t\in [0,1)$. The left-derivative case is completely parallel. For each $t\in [0,1]$, we let \[  f_ t=\min \{  (1-t)\varphi +t\psi , \psi \} .  \] Fix $t\in [0,1)$ and $s>0$ small enough so that $t+s<1$. Thanks to proposition 3.1.46 , we have \[  \begin{aligned}  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _{t+s})-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _{t})\leq &  \int _ X \left(\eta _{t+s}-\eta _ t\right)\, \theta _{\eta _ t}^ n \\  =&  \int _ X \left(\eta _{t+s}-f_ t\right)\, \theta _{\eta _ t}^ n & \textup{by \gerbyref{FEE0E763}{3.1.3}}\\  \leq &  \int _ X \left(f_{t+s}-f_ t \right)\, \theta _{\eta _ t}^ n\\  =&  s\int _ X \Bigl (\psi -\min \{ \varphi ,\psi \} \Bigr )\, \theta _{\eta _ t}^ n. \end{aligned}  \] Similarly, we get \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _{t+s})-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _{t})\geq s\int _ X \Bigl (\psi -\min \{ \varphi ,\psi \} \Bigr )\, \theta _{\eta _{t+s}}^ n.  \] Observe that $\eta _{t+s}$ converges in capacity (in fact, even uniformly) to $\eta _ t$ as $s\to 0+$. The desired result ( 3.168 ) is then just a consequence of theorem 2.3.8 . $\square$

3.168 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Iphit_diff} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ t)=\int _{X} \Bigl ( \psi -\min \{ \varphi ,\psi \}  \Bigr )\, \theta _{\eta _ t}^ n. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 3.1.56
text: Lemma 3.1.56 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^{1}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, and set \[  \varphi _ t\coloneqq (1-t)\varphi +t\psi ,\qquad t\in [0,1].  \] Then the function \[  t\mapsto E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ t)  \] is differentiable on $[0,1]$, where the derivative at the endpoints is understood as the one-sided derivative. Moreover, 3.173 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Eaffinediff} \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ t) = \int _ X(\psi -\varphi )\, \theta _{\varphi _ t}^ n. \end{equation} Proof. By corollary 3.1.42 , $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for all $t\in [0,1]$. For $a=0,\ldots ,n$, put \[  M_ a=\int _ X(\psi -\varphi )\, \theta _{\psi }^ a\wedge \theta _{\varphi }^{n-a}.  \] Note that each $M_ a$ is finite by corollary 3.1.44 . By the multi-linearity of the non-pluripolar product proposition 2.2.2 6 , the quantity \[  \int _ X(\psi -\varphi )\, \theta _{\varphi _ t}^ n  \] is therefore a polynomial in $t$ with coefficients given by the $M_ a$'s. In particular, the right-hand side of ( 3.173 ) is finite and continuous in $t$. We prove the formula for the right derivative at a point $t\in [0,1)$. Let $s>0$ be small enough so that $t+s\leq 1$. By the cocycle formula proposition 3.1.45 , we have \[  \begin{aligned}  \frac{E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{t+s})-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ t)}{s} =& \frac{1}{(n+1)s}\sum _{j=0}^ n \int _ X(\varphi _{t+s}-\varphi _ t)\,  \theta _{\varphi _{t+s}}^ j\wedge \theta _{\varphi _ t}^{n-j} \\  =& \frac{1}{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n \int _ X(\psi -\varphi )\,  \theta _{\varphi _{t+s}}^ j\wedge \theta _{\varphi _ t}^{n-j}. \end{aligned}  \] Again by proposition 2.2.2 6 , for each fixed $j$ the last integral is a polynomial in $s$, expressed as a linear combination of the $M_ a$'s with coefficients depending on $t$. Letting $s\to 0+$, it converges to \[  \int _ X(\psi -\varphi )\, \theta _{\varphi _ t}^ n.  \] Therefore, \[  \lim _{s\to 0+} \frac{E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _{t+s})-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ t)}{s} = \int _ X(\psi -\varphi )\, \theta _{\varphi _ t}^ n.  \] The proof for the left derivative is identical, using $s<0$ with $t+s\in [0,1]$. Thus the left and right derivatives agree for $t\in (0,1)$, and the endpoint derivatives are given by the same formula. $\square$
3.173 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Eaffinediff} \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ t) = \int _ X(\psi -\varphi )\, \theta _{\varphi _ t}^ n. \end{equation}

title: Corollary 3.1.57
text: Corollary 3.1.57 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then 3.176 \begin{equation} \label{eq:diam_E} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \lor \psi )+E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi )\geq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )+E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ). \end{equation} Proof. Step 1 . We first reduce to the case where $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Assume that ( 3.176 ) is known in that case. For each $C>0$, we let \[  \varphi _ C=\varphi \lor (\phi -C),\quad \psi _ C=\psi \lor (\phi -C).  \] Then \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ C\lor \psi _ C)+E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ C\land \psi _ C)\geq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi _ C)+E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ C).  \] As $C\to \infty $, we have \[  \varphi _ C\searrow \varphi ,\quad \psi _ C\searrow \psi ,\quad \varphi _ C\lor \psi _ C\searrow \varphi \lor \psi ,  \] and, by the monotonicity and maximality of the rooftop, \[  \varphi _ C\land \psi _ C\searrow \varphi \land \psi .  \] Applying proposition 3.1.39 to these four decreasing sequences gives ( 3.176 ). Step 2 . We assume that $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Thanks to 3.1.56 and the plurifine locality of the non-pluripolar product proposition 2.2.2 1 , we have \[  \begin{aligned}  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \lor \psi )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )=& \int _0^1\int _ X (\varphi \lor \psi -\varphi )\, \theta _{(1-t)\varphi +t(\varphi \lor \psi )}^ n\, \mathrm{d}t\\  =&  \int _0^1 \int _{\{ \psi >\varphi \} } (\psi -\varphi )\, \theta _{(1-t)\varphi +t\psi }^ n\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{aligned}  \] On the other hand, \[  \begin{aligned} & E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi )\\  =&  \int _0^1 \int _ X (\psi -\min \{ \varphi ,\psi \} )\, \theta _{((1-t)\varphi +t\psi )\land \psi }^ n\, \mathrm{d}t\\  \leq &  \int _0^1 \int _{\{ \varphi <\psi \} } (\psi -\varphi )\, \theta _{(1-t)\varphi +t\psi }^ n\, \mathrm{d}t&  \textup{by \gerbyref{FEE0E763}{3.1.3}}. \end{aligned}  \] Adding these equations together, we conclude ( 3.176 ). $\square$
3.176 \begin{equation} \label{eq:diam_E} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \lor \psi )+E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi )\geq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )+E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ). \end{equation}

title: 3.2 The -envelope
text: 3.2 The $\mathcal{I}$-envelope From the algebraic point of view, a more natural envelope operator is given by the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope. In this section, $X$ will denote a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$.

title: 3.2.1 -equivalence
text:
3.2.1 $\mathcal{I}$-equivalence Proposition 3.2.1 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, the following are equivalent: For any $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have \[  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(k\psi );  \] for any $\lambda \in \mathbb {R}_{>0}$, we have \[  \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi )=\mathcal{I}(\lambda \psi );  \] for any modification $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ and any $y\in Y$, we have \[  
u (\pi ^*\varphi ,y)=
u (\pi ^*\psi ,y);  \] for any proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ from a Kähler manifold and any $y\in Y$, we have \[  
u (\pi ^*\varphi ,y)=
u (\pi ^*\psi ,y);  \] for any prime divisor $E$ over $X$, we have \[  
u (\varphi ,E)=
u (\psi ,E).  \] See definition B.1.1 for the definition of prime divisors over $X$. Recall that in the whole book, a modification of a compact complex space means a finite composition of blow-ups with smooth centers. This terminology is highly non-standard. For simplicity, we usually write \[  
u (\varphi ,y)=
u (\pi ^*\varphi ,y)  \] when $\pi $ is obvious from the context. Proof. 4 $\iff $ 5 . This follows from 1.4.14 . 3 $\iff $ 5 . This follows from corollary B.1.8 . 1 $\implies $ 5 . This follows from proposition 1.4.13 . 5 $\implies $ 2 . This follows from theorem 1.4.15 . 2 $\implies $ 1 . This is the restriction to positive integral values of $\lambda $. $\square$ Definition 3.2.2 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, we say they are $\mathcal{I}$-equivalent and write $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi $ if the equivalent conditions in proposition 3.2.1 are satisfied. Clearly, $\sim _{\mathcal{I}}$ is an equivalence relation on $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Proposition 3.2.3 . Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$ to $X$. For $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, the following are equivalent: $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi $; $\pi ^*\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\pi ^*\psi $. Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . This follows from proposition 3.2.1 4 . 2 $\implies $ 1 . This follows from the simple fact that \[  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\pi _* \left( \omega _{Y/X}\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\pi ^*\varphi ) ight),\quad \mathcal{I}(k\psi )=\pi _* \left( \omega _{Y/X}\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\pi ^*\psi ) ight)  \] for any $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, where $\omega _{Y/X}$ is the relative dualizing sheaf. See [ Proposition 5.8 , Dem12 ] . $\square$ Proposition 3.2.4 . Let $\varphi ,\varphi ',\psi ,\psi '\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ and $\lambda >0$. Assume that $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi $ and $\varphi '\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi '$. Then \[  \varphi \lor \varphi '\sim _{\mathcal{I}} \psi \lor \psi ',\quad \varphi +\varphi '\sim _{\mathcal{I}} \psi +\psi ',\quad \lambda \varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\lambda \psi .  \] Similarly, if $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$, $(\psi _ i)_{i\in I}$ are two non-empty uniformly bounded from above families in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ for some closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ on $X$ such that $\varphi _ i\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi _ i$ for all $i\in I$, then \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \psi _ i.  \] Proof. This follows from proposition 1.4.5 and corollary 1.4.6 . $\square$

title: Proposition 3.2.1
text:
Proposition 3.2.1 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, the following are equivalent: For any $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have \[  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(k\psi );  \] for any $\lambda \in \mathbb {R}_{>0}$, we have \[  \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi )=\mathcal{I}(\lambda \psi );  \] for any modification $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ and any $y\in Y$, we have \[  
u (\pi ^*\varphi ,y)=
u (\pi ^*\psi ,y);  \] for any proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ from a Kähler manifold and any $y\in Y$, we have \[  
u (\pi ^*\varphi ,y)=
u (\pi ^*\psi ,y);  \] for any prime divisor $E$ over $X$, we have \[  
u (\varphi ,E)=
u (\psi ,E).  \] Proof. 4 $\iff $ 5 . This follows from 1.4.14 . 3 $\iff $ 5 . This follows from corollary B.1.8 . 1 $\implies $ 5 . This follows from proposition 1.4.13 . 5 $\implies $ 2 . This follows from theorem 1.4.15 . 2 $\implies $ 1 . This is the restriction to positive integral values of $\lambda $. $\square$

title: Definition 3.2.2
text: Definition 3.2.2 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, we say they are $\mathcal{I}$-equivalent and write $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi $ if the equivalent conditions in proposition 3.2.1 are satisfied.

title: Proposition 3.2.3
text: Proposition 3.2.3 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$ to $X$. For $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, the following are equivalent: $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi $; $\pi ^*\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\pi ^*\psi $. Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . This follows from proposition 3.2.1 4 . 2 $\implies $ 1 . This follows from the simple fact that \[  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\pi _* \left( \omega _{Y/X}\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\pi ^*\varphi ) \right),\quad \mathcal{I}(k\psi )=\pi _* \left( \omega _{Y/X}\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\pi ^*\psi ) \right)  \] for any $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, where $\omega _{Y/X}$ is the relative dualizing sheaf. See [ Proposition 5.8 , Dem12 ] . $\square$

title: Proposition 3.2.4
text: Proposition 3.2.4 . Let $\varphi ,\varphi ',\psi ,\psi '\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ and $\lambda >0$. Assume that $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi $ and $\varphi '\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi '$. Then \[  \varphi \lor \varphi '\sim _{\mathcal{I}} \psi \lor \psi ',\quad \varphi +\varphi '\sim _{\mathcal{I}} \psi +\psi ',\quad \lambda \varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\lambda \psi .  \] Similarly, if $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$, $(\psi _ i)_{i\in I}$ are two non-empty uniformly bounded from above families in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for some closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ such that $\varphi _ i\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\psi _ i$ for all $i\in I$, then \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \psi _ i.  \] Proof. This follows from proposition 1.4.5 and corollary 1.4.6 . $\square$

title: 3.2.2 The definition of the -envelope
text: 3.2.2 The definition of the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope Fix a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. Definition 3.2.5 . Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we define its $\mathcal{I}$-envelope as follows: 3.182 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Ienvelopedef} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}\{ \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): \psi \leq 0,\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi \} . \end{equation} If $\varphi =P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$, we say $\varphi $ is an $\mathcal{I}$-model potential (in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$). Note that by proposition 1.2.2 , $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proposition 3.2.6 . Let $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some $g\in C^{\infty }(X)$. Then for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we have $\varphi '\coloneqq \varphi -g\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ and \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. By symmetry, it suffices to show that \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\preceq P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] After replacing $g$ by $g+C$ for a suitable constant $C$, which only changes $\varphi '$ by an additive constant, we may assume that $g\geq 0$. Let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be such that $\psi \leq 0$ and $\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi $. Then $\psi '\coloneqq \psi -g$ lies in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$, satisfies $\psi '\leq 0$, and is $\mathcal{I}$-equivalent to $\varphi '$ since adding a smooth function does not change multiplier ideals. Hence \[  \psi -g=\psi '\leq P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] It follows that \[  \psi -\sup _ X g\leq P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Taking the upper envelope over all such $\psi $ gives \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}-\sup _ X g\leq P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal{I}},  \] which proves the desired comparison. $\square$ Proposition 3.2.7 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$ to $X$. Then for $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we have \[  P_{\pi ^*\theta }[\pi ^*\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=\pi ^* P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. Let \[  \eta =P_{\pi ^*\theta }[\pi ^*\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] First take a candidate $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ in ( 3.182 ), so that $\psi \leq 0$ and $\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi $. Then $\pi ^*\psi \leq 0$ and $\pi ^*\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\pi ^*\varphi $ by proposition 3.2.3 ; hence $\pi ^*\psi \leq \eta $. Taking the upper envelope over all such $\psi $ gives \[  \pi ^* P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq \eta .  \] Conversely, let $\chi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta )$ be a candidate in the definition of $\eta $, so that $\chi \leq 0$ and $\chi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\pi ^*\varphi $. By proposition 1.5.8 , there is a unique $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\chi =\pi ^*\psi $. Since $\pi $ is surjective, $\psi \leq 0$. By proposition 3.2.3 , the relation $\chi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\pi ^*\varphi $ implies $\psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi $. Thus $\psi \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$, and hence \[  \chi \leq \pi ^* P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Taking the upper envelope over all such $\chi $ gives the reverse inequality. $\square$ Proposition 3.2.8 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  \varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] In particular, \[  P_{\theta }\Bigl [ P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}} \Bigr ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}  \] and the upper semicontinuous regularization in ( 3.182 ) is not necessary. Proof. In view of proposition 3.2.1 , it suffices to show that for $k \in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have 3.183 \begin{equation} \label{eq:IenvelopepreservLelong} \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}). \end{equation} By proposition 1.2.3 , we can find $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ ($i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$) such that $\psi _ i\leq 0$, $\psi _ i\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi $ for all $i\geq 1$ and \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i>0}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _ i=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] By proposition 3.2.4 , we may replace $\psi _ i$ by $\psi _1\lor \cdots \lor \psi _ i$ and assume that the sequence $\psi _ i$ is increasing. In this case, it follows from the strong openness theorem theorem 1.4.16 that for each $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have \[  \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}(k\psi _ j)=\mathcal{I} (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}})  \] for $j$ large enough. $\square$ Definition 3.2.9 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we define the volume Note. We choose to call this quantity the volume instead of the $\mathcal{I}$-volume so that the terminology is consistent with the line bundle case. $\operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )$ as \[  \operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )=\int _ X \Bigl (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}} \Bigr )^ n.  \] Proposition 3.2.10 . Let $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ for some $g\in C^{\infty }(X)$. Then for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we have $\varphi '=\varphi -g\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ and \[  \operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )= \operatorname{vol}\left(\theta ',\varphi '\right).  \] Proof. By proposition 3.2.6 , the currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$ and $\theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta '}[\varphi ']_{\mathcal I}$ have the same singularity type in the same cohomology class. Applying the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 gives equality of their non-pluripolar masses. $\square$ In view of proposition 3.2.10 , the volume $\operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi )$ depends only on the current $\theta _{\varphi }$, and we may write 3.184 \begin{equation} \label{eq:volcurrdef} \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }=\operatorname{vol}(\theta ,\varphi ). \end{equation} Definition 3.2.11 . Let $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$ be a pseudo-effective class. The volume $\operatorname{vol}\alpha $ of $\alpha $ is defined as \[  \operatorname{vol}\alpha =\operatorname{vol}T_{\min },  \] where $T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $. Note that $\operatorname{vol}\alpha $ is independent of the choice of $T_{\min }$, thanks to theorem 2.4.8 . Let us recall the following elementary result for later use. Proposition 3.2.12 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a Kähler manifold $Y$. For any big class $\alpha \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi ^*\alpha $ is big. Moreover, $\operatorname{vol}\pi ^*\alpha =\operatorname{vol}\alpha $. For any big class $\beta \in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})$, $\pi _*\beta $ is big. Moreover, $\operatorname{vol}\pi _*\beta \geq \operatorname{vol}\beta $. Proof. 1 Take a current $T_{\min }$ with minimal singularities in $\alpha $. Then $\pi ^*T_{\min }$ is a current with minimal singularities in $\pi ^*\alpha $. Our assertion follows from proposition 2.4.3 . 2 Let $S_{\min }$ be a current with minimal singularities in $\beta $. Then $\pi _*S_{\min }$ is a positive current in the cohomology class $\pi _*\beta $. A current with minimal singularities in $\pi _*\beta $ is less singular than $\pi _*S_{\min }$, hence by the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 \[  \operatorname{vol}(\pi _*\beta )\geq \int _ X\left(\pi _*S_{\min }\right)^ n.  \] By proposition 2.4.3 , \[  \int _ X \left(\pi _*S_{\min }\right)^ n\geq \int _ Y S_{\min }^ n=\operatorname{vol}\beta .  \] We conclude $\operatorname{vol}\pi _*\beta \geq \operatorname{vol}\beta $. $\square$ The $\mathcal{I}$-envelope and the $P$-envelope are related in a simple manner. Proposition 3.2.13 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}},\quad \varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ].  \] As a consequence, 3.185 \begin{equation} \label{eq:PthetaIP_comp} P_{\theta }\Bigl [P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation} Proof. It suffices to show that $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$. Namely, for each $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we have 3.186 \begin{equation} \label{eq:IkvarphiIkP} \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )=\mathcal{I}\Bigl (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr ). \end{equation} Fix $k$ for now. It follows from ( 3.4 ) and the strong openness theorem theorem 1.4.16 that \[  \mathcal{I}\Bigl (kP_{\theta }[\varphi ]\Bigr )=\mathcal{I}\Bigl ((k\varphi +C)\land kV_{\theta }\Bigr ),  \] when $C$ is large enough. Since $(k\varphi +C)\land kV_{\theta }\sim k\varphi $, we have \[  \mathcal{I}\Bigl ((k\varphi +C)\land kV_{\theta }\Bigr )=\mathcal{I}(k\varphi )  \] and ( 3.186 ) follows. $\square$ In particular, we obtain an interesting relation between the non-pluripolar mass and the volume. Corollary 3.2.14 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n\leq \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }.  \] The reverse inequality fails in general, see example 6.1.14 . Proof. This follows from proposition 3.2.13 , theorem 2.4.8 and proposition 3.1.6 . $\square$ We note the following special case: Proposition 3.2.15 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Assume that $\varphi $ has analytic singularities. Then 3.187 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ana_sing_phi_PI_eq} \varphi \sim P_{\theta }[\varphi ] \sim P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation} Hence, $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$ and $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ both have analytic singularities. In particular, 3.188 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ana_sing_mass_vol} \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n= \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }. \end{equation} Proof. First observe that ( 3.188 ) follows from ( 3.187 ) and theorem 2.4.8 . It remains to establish ( 3.187 ). In view of proposition 3.2.13 , it suffices to show that 3.189 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Pprecvarphitemp1} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\preceq \varphi . \end{equation} By proposition 3.2.7 , proposition 3.1.23 and theorem 1.6.7 , after passing to a log resolution we may assume that $\varphi $ has log singularities along an effective $\mathbb Q$-divisor $D$. This reduction does not change the assertion, since both the $P$- and the $\mathcal I$-envelope are compatible with bimeromorphic pull-back. After multiplying $\theta $ and $\varphi $ by a sufficiently divisible positive integer, and then dividing the final comparison by the same integer, we may assume that $D$ is integral. In this case the Bergman-type quasi-equisingular approximants of $\varphi $ associated to the ideals $\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi )$ have the same singularity type as $\varphi $. Since \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\sim _{\mathcal I}\varphi  \] by proposition 3.2.8 , we have \[  \mathcal I(2^ jP_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I})=\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi ).  \] Thus the quasi-equisingular approximants $\eta _ j$ of $P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$ and $\varphi _ j$ of $\varphi $ may be chosen with the same singularity type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi ))$. Consequently $\eta _ j\sim \varphi _ j\sim \varphi $ for $j\gg 1$. Since $\eta _ j\searrow P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$, choosing one such large $j$ gives \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\leq \eta _ j\leq \varphi +C_ j,  \] and hence ( 3.189 ) holds. $\square$

title: 3.2.3 Properties of the -envelope
text: 3.2.3 Properties of the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope Let $\theta ,\theta _1,\theta _2$ be smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$. We have the following properties of the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope. Proposition 3.2.16 . Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb {R}_{>0}$. Then \[  P_{\lambda \theta }[\lambda \varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=\lambda P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Suppose that $\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ and $\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$. Then \[  P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[\varphi _1+\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}\geq P_{\theta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}+P_{\theta _2}[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Suppose that $\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ and $\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$. Then \[  P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[\varphi _1+\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}+P_{\theta _2}[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Suppose that $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi _1\lor \varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim _{\mathcal{I}} P_{\theta }[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}\lor P_{\theta }[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. 1 This follows by rescaling the candidates in the definition of the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope. 2 Suppose that $\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ and $\psi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$ satisfy \[  \psi _ i\leq 0,\quad \psi _ i \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi _ i  \] for $i=1,2$. Then thanks to proposition 3.2.4 , \[  \psi _1+\psi _2\leq 0,\quad \psi _1+\psi _2 \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi _1+\varphi _2.  \] It follows that \[  \psi _1+\psi _2\leq P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[\varphi _1+\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Since $\psi _1$ and $\psi _2$ are arbitrary, we conclude. 3 and 4 : These follow easily from proposition 3.2.8 and proposition 3.2.4 . $\square$ Lemma 3.2.17 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Assume that $\varphi \preceq \psi $. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq P_{\theta }[\psi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. We may assume that $\psi \leq 0$. Observe that $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\lor \psi \sim _{\mathcal{I}} \psi $ as a consequence of proposition 1.4.5 and proposition 3.2.8 . So \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\lor \psi \leq P_{\theta }[\psi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] The desired inequality follows. $\square$ Proposition 3.2.18 . Consider a decreasing net $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ of model potentials, with $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for all $i\in I$. Set \[  \varphi \coloneqq \inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i.  \] Suppose that $\varphi \not\equiv -\infty $ and $\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n>0$. Then \[  \inf _{i\in I} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] In particular, if the $\varphi _ i$'s are all $\mathcal{I}$-model, then so is $\varphi $. Proof. Let $\eta =\inf _{i\in I} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}$. We have $\eta \geq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ as a consequence of 3.2.17 . In particular, $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By proposition 3.1.26 , we have \[  \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n=\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n>0.  \] We may assume that for each $i\in I$, $\int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n>\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n$, since otherwise $\varphi _ i=\varphi $ by theorem 3.1.9 , and hence $P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ due to ( 3.185 ); the same holds for all $j\geq i$, and there is nothing to prove. So by 2.4.15 , we can find a decreasing net $\epsilon _ i\searrow 0$ ($i\in I$) with $\epsilon _ i\in (0,1)$ and $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that for all $i\in I$, \[  (1-\epsilon _ i) \varphi _ i+\epsilon _ i\psi _ i\leq \varphi .  \] We can, for example, take \[  \epsilon _ i^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}\left( 1+\left(\frac{\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n}{\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n-\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n}\right)^{1/n} \right).  \] By proposition 3.2.16 and 3.2.17 , we have \[  \eta +\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq (1-\epsilon _ i) \eta +\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq (1-\epsilon _ i) P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}+\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Each $P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}$ has supremum $0$, so proposition 1.5.4 shows that the family is bounded in $L^1$. Hence $\epsilon _ iP_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\to 0$ in $L^1$, and the preceding inequality gives $\eta \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ almost everywhere. By proposition 1.2.6 , the inequality holds everywhere. $\square$ Proposition 3.2.19 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be an increasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ uniformly bounded from above. Let $\varphi \coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i$. Then \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] In particular, if the $\varphi _ i$'s are all $\mathcal{I}$-model, then so is $\varphi $. Proof. Let $\eta =\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}$. Then $\eta \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ as a consequence of 3.2.17 . By corollary 2.4.9 , we have \[  \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n=\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n>0.  \] We may assume that for each $i\in I$, $\int _ X\theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n<\int _ X\theta _{\varphi }^ n$, since otherwise $P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$ by theorem 3.1.9 , and hence $P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ due to ( 3.185 ); the same holds for all $j\geq i$, and there is nothing to prove. So by 2.4.15 , we can find a decreasing net $\epsilon _ i\searrow 0$ ($i\in I$) as in ( 3.50 ) with $\epsilon _ i\in (0,1)$ and $\psi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that for all $i\in I$, \[  (1-\epsilon _ i) \varphi +\epsilon _ i\psi _ i\leq \varphi _ i.  \] By proposition 3.2.16 and 3.2.17 , we have \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}+\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq (1-\epsilon _ i) P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}+\epsilon _ i P_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq \eta .  \] As above, $\epsilon _ iP_{\theta }[\psi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\to 0$ in $L^1$. It follows that $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq \eta $ almost everywhere, hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . $\square$ Remark 3.2.20 . One could also define the following interpolation between the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope and the $P$-envelope: Suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$, $j\in \{ 0,\ldots ,n\} $. Then we let \[  \begin{split}  P_{\theta ,j}[\varphi ]\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}\left\{  \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): \psi \leq 0,\varphi \preceq \psi , \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}}^{n-j}\right.\\  \left.=\int _ X \theta _{\psi }^ j\wedge \theta _{P_{\theta }[\psi ]_{\mathcal{I}}}^{n-j} \right\} . \end{split}  \] Based on the techniques developed in chapter 6 , one could show that $P_{\theta ,j}[\bullet ]$ is a projection operator. The cases $j=0$ and $j=n$ recover the $\mathcal{I}$- and $P$-envelopes respectively; the intermediate operators $P_{\theta ,j}$ have not, to our knowledge, been systematically studied in the literature. section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: 4 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials When $\omega $ is a Kähler form, the space of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials carries the Mabuchi $L^2$-metric. Its geodesic equation is the homogeneous complex Monge–Ampère equation on $X\times \{ 0<\operatorname{Re}z<1\} $. Subsolutions of this equation are subgeodesics, and the geodesic between two boundary potentials is obtained as a Perron envelope. This construction continues to make sense for singular potentials, even when no smooth geodesic exists. The goal of this chapter is to further develop the corresponding theory for $\theta $-plurisubharmonic potentials, where $\theta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form representing a big class. We define subgeodesics by requiring the complexification $\Phi (x,z)=\varphi _{\operatorname{Re}z}(x)$ to be plurisubharmonic. Geodesics are then defined as Perron envelopes of subgeodesics with prescribed boundary values. This point of view is flexible enough to handle unbounded potentials and singularity constraints. The first section sets up the basic properties of subgeodesics. We then construct geodesics with prescribed singular endpoints and study geodesic rays. The results are formulated relative to a model potential $\phi $, so that the endpoints and rays live in a fixed relative singularity class. The final part of the chapter studies the finite-energy space $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and the Darvas $d_1$-metric. We prove the basic metric properties needed later, including completeness and monotone convergence criteria. The radial version of the metric on geodesic rays will be used in the study of test curves and singularity types. This chapter provides the analytic bridge between envelopes and the later non-Archimedean theory. The space $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and the $d_1$-geometry developed here feed into the pseudometric $d_ S$ of chapter 6 , while geodesic rays will later be related to test curves and non-Archimedean potentials.

text:
4.1 Subgeodesics Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$ and $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class. Definition 4.1.1 . Let us fix $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. A subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ is a family $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ such that if we define \[  \Phi \colon X	imes \Bigl \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z\in (0,1) \Bigr \} ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad (x,z)\mapsto \varphi _{\operatorname{Re}z}(x),  \] then $\Phi $ is $p_1^*	heta $-psh, where $p_1\colon X	imes \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z\in (0,1)\} ightarrow X$ is the natural projection; when $t	o 0+$ (resp. $t	o 1-$), $\varphi _ t$ converges to $\varphi _0$ (resp. $\varphi _1$) with respect to the $L^1$-topology. We also say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. We call $\Phi $ the complexification of the subgeodesic $(\varphi _ t)_ t$. When we do not want to specify $\varphi _0$ and $\varphi _1$, we shall say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a subgeodesic Note. Note that it is implicit in the definition that $\varphi _ t$ as $t	o 0+$ or $t	o 1-$ admits an $L^1$-limit. . More generally, a family $(\psi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ (resp. $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$) in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ for some $a\leq b$ is called a subgeodesic if $(\psi _{tb+(1-t)a})_{t\in [0,1]}$ (resp. $(\psi _{tb+(1-t)a})_{t\in (0,1)}$) is a subgeodesic. Remark 4.1.2 . Note that given a subgeodesic $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$, the endpoints $\psi _ a$ and $\psi _ b$ are uniquely determined, in view of proposition 1.2.6 . Remark 4.1.3 . In the literature, people sometimes regard $\Phi $ as a function defined on $X	imes \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \mathrm{e}^{-1}<|z|<1\} $, with $\Phi (x,z)=\varphi _{-\log |z|}(x)$. We sometimes also use this convention; the ambient strip or annulus will make the convention clear. In general, there are no subgeodesics from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. In fact, by proposition 4.1.6 below, the existence of a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ forces $\varphi _0\land \varphi _1
ot\equiv -\infty $, a condition that may fail (see example 5.2.8 ). We first note that the subgeodesics are well-behaved under the change of $	heta $: Proposition 4.1.4 . Let $g$ be a smooth real function on $X$. Let $	heta '=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$. Suppose that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Then $(\varphi _ t-g)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ')$. Proof. This follows directly from the definition of the complexification. $\square$ Example 4.1.5 . Let $\varphi _0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, $C\in \mathbb {R}$. Let \[  \varphi _ t=\varphi _0+tC,\quad t\in [0,1].  \] Then $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. Indeed, since $\operatorname{Re}z$ is harmonic in $z$, the complexification $\Phi (x,z)=\varphi _0(x)+C\, \operatorname{Re}z$ is $p_1^*	heta $-psh. As a consequence, the constant $(\varphi _0)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic, called the constant subgeodesic at $\varphi _0$. A more general version is as follows: Suppose that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, $C_1,C_2\in \mathbb {R}$. Then $(\varphi _ t+C_1t+C_2)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is also a subgeodesic. Proposition 4.1.6 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then for each $x\in X$, $[0,1] 
i t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is a convex function. Furthermore, \[  \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ),\quad \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0\land \varphi _1.  \] Proof. Let $\Phi $ be the complexification of $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$. For each $x\in X$, the map \[  \Bigl \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \operatorname{Re}z\in (0,1) \Bigr \} ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad z\mapsto \Phi (x,z)  \] is either subharmonic or constantly $-\infty $, as follows from definition 4.1.1 1 and proposition 1.1.13 . In the latter case, the convexity of $[0,1] 
i t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is trivial. In the former case, the convexity on the interval $(0,1)$ follows from proposition 1.1.9 . In order to verify the convexity at the boundary, let us fix $s\in (0,1)$. We need to show that 4.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:varphisconvextemp1} \varphi _ s(x)\leq s\varphi _1(x)+(1-s)\varphi _0(x) \end{equation} for all $x\in X$. Thanks to proposition 1.2.6 , it suffices to prove this for almost all $x$. Choose sequences $a_ j\searrow 0$ and $b_ j
earrow 1$ such that $\varphi _{a_ j}	o \varphi _0$ and $\varphi _{b_ j}	o \varphi _1$ almost everywhere. Outside a set $Z\subseteq X$ of zero Lebesgue measure, all these convergences hold and all the values involved are finite. For $x\in X\setminus Z$ and $j$ large enough that $a_ j<s<b_ j$, the convexity on $(0,1)$ gives \[  \varphi _ s(x)\leq  rac{b_ j-s}{b_ j-a_ j}\varphi _{a_ j}(x)+ rac{s-a_ j}{b_ j-a_ j}\varphi _{b_ j}(x).  \] Letting $j	o \infty $ gives ( 4.1 ) almost everywhere. Let us prove the last assertion. Let \[  \varphi \coloneqq \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t.  \] By Kiselman's principle proposition 1.2.11 , we know that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $. Since the complexification $\Phi $ is not identically $-\infty $, Fubini's theorem shows that for almost every $x\in X$, the function $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is finite for almost every $t\in (0,1)$. For such an $x$, the convexity just proved implies that $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is a finite convex function on $(0,1)$, hence it is bounded from below on $(0,1)$. Thus $\varphi 
ot\equiv -\infty $, and so $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. For any $t\in (0,1)$, using the convexity established above, we have \[  \varphi \leq (1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi _1.  \] It follows that $\varphi \leq \varphi _0$ and $\varphi \leq \varphi _1$ almost everywhere and hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . Our assertion follows. $\square$ Corollary 4.1.7 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then 4.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:varphitconvexbdry} \lim _{t	o 0+}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0,\quad \lim _{t	o 1-}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _1. \end{equation} Moreover, \[  \lim _{t	o 0+}\varphi _ t=\varphi _0,\quad \lim _{t	o 1-}\varphi _ t=\varphi _1\quad 	extup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] The inequalities in ( 4.2 ) are not equalities everywhere in general. For example, consider an arbitrary subgeodesic from an unbounded $\varphi _0\in \mathcal{E}(X,\omega )$ to a bounded $\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ for some Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Proof. The inequalities in ( 4.2 ) and the existence of the limits follow from the convexity in proposition 4.1.6 . Let us prove the quasi-everywhere equality at $t=0$. Take a decreasing sequence $t_ j\searrow 0$ with $t_ j>0$. Then $\varphi _{t_ j}	o \varphi _0$ in $L^1(X)$ as $j	o \infty $. So by corollary 1.2.8 , we have \[  \varlimsup _{j	o \infty }\varphi _{t_ j}= \varphi _0\quad 	extup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] Therefore, we have \[  \varphi _0=\varlimsup _{j	o \infty }\varphi _{t_ j}=\lim _{t	o 0+}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0\quad 	extup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] The assertion at $t=1$ is similar. $\square$ Corollary 4.1.8 . Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Then 4.3  egin{equation} \label{eq:supconvexsubgeod} \adjustlimits \sup _ X \inf _{s\in (0,1)}\varphi _ s \leq \sup _ X \varphi _ t\leq \sup _ X \varphi _0\lor \sup _ X \varphi _1 \end{equation} for all $t\in (0,1)$. Furthermore, $[0,1] 
i t\mapsto \varphi _ t$ is continuous with respect to the $L^1$-topology. In particular, in view of proposition 1.5.4 , the family $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in [0,1]}$ is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Proof. ( 4.3 ) follows immediately from proposition 4.1.6 . Let us verify the continuity of $t\mapsto \varphi _ t$. The continuity at $t=0$ or $t=1$ follows from the definition of subgeodesic. While the continuity on $(0,1)$ follows from the convexity of $t\mapsto \varphi _ t$, and the fact that $\varphi _ t\in L^1(X)$ for each $t\in (0,1)$. $\square$ Proposition 4.1.9 . Let $(\varphi ^ i_0)_{i\in I}$, $(\varphi ^ i_1)_{i\in I}$ be two non-empty uniformly bounded from above families in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Let $(\varphi ^ i_ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be subgeodesics from $\varphi _0^ i$ to $\varphi _1^ i$ for each $i\in I$. Then \[  \left(\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi ^ i_ tight)_{t\in (0,1)}  \] is a subgeodesic from $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_0$ to $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_1$. Proof. We may assume that $\varphi _0^ i,\varphi _1^ i\leq 0$ for all $i\in I$. Then it follows that $\varphi _ t^ i\leq 0$ for all $t\in (0,1)$ and all $i\in I$ by proposition 4.1.6 . We define \[  \varphi _ t\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )  \] for all $t\in [0,1]$. Observe that $[0,1] 
i t\mapsto \varphi _ t$ is convex by the same argument leading to ( 4.1 ). Let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the subgeodesic whose complexification $\Phi _{\psi }$ corresponds to $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \Phi _{\varphi ^ i}$, where $\Phi _{\varphi ^ i}$ is the complexification of $(\varphi ^ i_ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$. Then clearly, $\varphi _ t\leq \psi _ t$ for each $t\in (0,1)$. On the other hand, by proposition 1.2.5 , \[  \psi _ t=\sup _{i\in I}\varphi ^ i_ t=\varphi _ t\quad 	extup{almost everywhere}  \] for almost all $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, using proposition 1.2.6 , we find $\psi _ t=\varphi _ t$ for almost all $t\in (0,1)$. Since both functions are convex in $t$, we conclude that $\psi _ t=\varphi _ t$ for all $t\in (0,1)$. It remains to argue that $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$ as $t	o 0+$ and $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _1$ as $t	o 1-$. By symmetry, it suffices to argue the former. By Choquet's lemma proposition 1.2.3 , applied to the uniformly bounded above family of complexifications $(\Phi _{\varphi ^ i})_{i\in I}$ on the strip, there is a countable subset $I'\subset I$ such that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\Phi _{\varphi ^ i}=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I'}{}\! {}^{*}\Phi _{\varphi ^ i}.  \] Applying Choquet's lemma proposition 1.2.3 once more to the endpoint families if necessary, and enlarging $I'$, we may also assume \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _0^ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I'}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _0^ i,\quad \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _1^ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I'}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _1^ i.  \] Thus, after replacing $I$ by $I'$, we may assume that $I$ is countable. We know that for any $t\in (0,1)$ and any $j\in I$, \[  \varphi ^ j_ t\leq \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0.  \] Letting $t	o 0+$, we find that \[  \varphi _0^ j\leq \varlimsup _{t	o 0+}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0  \] almost everywhere. Since $I$ is countable, we conclude that 4.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:varphi0limsuptemp1} \varphi _0=\varlimsup _{t	o 0+}\varphi _ t \end{equation} almost everywhere. Fix $i_0\in I$. Recall that by proposition 4.1.6 , for each $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \adjustlimits \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\sup _ X \varphi _ t\geq \adjustlimits \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\sup _ X \varphi ^{i_0}_ t\geq \adjustlimits \sup _ X \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi ^{i_0}_ t>-\infty ,  \] so the set $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in (0,1)}$ is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology by proposition 1.5.4 . Let $\psi $ be a cluster point as $t	o 0+$. It suffices to show that $\psi =\varphi _0$. By corollary 1.2.8 and ( 4.4 ), this holds almost everywhere. Therefore, it holds everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . $\square$ Proposition 4.1.10 . Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Then for any $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$, the segment $(\varphi _{t})_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic. Proof. It suffices to show that \[  \varphi _{tb+(1-t)a}\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _ a,\quad \varphi _{tb+(1-t)a}\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _ b  \] as $t	o 0+$ and $t	o 1-$ respectively. In other words, we need to show that for any $c\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _ c  \] as $t	o c$. For this purpose, observe that by proposition 4.1.6 , \[  \adjustlimits \sup _ X \inf _{s\in (0,1)}\varphi _ s\leq \sup _{X}\varphi _ t\leq \left( \sup _ X \varphi _0 ight) \lor \left( \sup _ X\varphi _1 ight)  \] for any $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in (0,1)}$ is a relatively compact family with respect to the $L^1$-topology on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ by proposition 1.5.4 . It suffices to show that any cluster point $\psi $ of $\varphi _ t$ as $t	o c$ is equal to $\varphi _ c$. By corollary 1.2.8 and the convexity proposition 4.1.6 , we have $\varphi _ c=\psi $ almost everywhere and hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . $\square$ For the purpose of this chapter, it is useful to reformulate the gluing lemma corollary 1.2.13 in the following way, which allows us to glue subgeodesics directly: Lemma 4.1.11 . Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Let $0\leq a<b\leq 1$ and let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ be a subgeodesic such that $\psi _ a=\varphi _ a$, $\psi _ b=\varphi _ b$, and \[  \psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t,\quad t\in (a,b).  \] Define \[  \gamma _ t=  egin{cases}  \psi _ t,& 	extup{if }t\in (a,b),\  \varphi _ t,& 	extup{if }t\in [0,1]\setminus (a,b). \end{cases}  \] Then $(\gamma _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. Proof. The $L^1$-convergence of $\gamma _ t$ to $\varphi _0$ at $0$ and $\varphi _1$ at $1$ follows immediately from the corresponding property for $(\varphi _ t)_ t$ and $(\psi _ t)_ t$. It remains to prove that the complexification of $(\gamma _ t)_ t$ is $p_1^*	heta $-psh. Let \[  S=\{ z\in \mathbb {C}:0<\operatorname{Re}z<1\} ,\quad S'=\{ z\in \mathbb {C}:a<\operatorname{Re}z<b\} .  \] Let $\Phi $ and $\Psi $ be the complexifications of $(\varphi _ t)_ t$ and $(\psi _ t)_ t$ on the corresponding strips. Since $\Psi \geq \Phi $ on $X	imes S'$, the complexification of $(\gamma _ t)_ t$ is equal to $\Phi \lor \Psi $ on $X	imes S'$ and to $\Phi $ on $X	imes (S\setminus S')$. By the gluing lemma corollary 1.2.13 , it is enough to verify that \[  \varlimsup _{\substack {S'
i z'	o z\ x'	o x}}\Psi (x',z')\leq \Phi (x,z)  \] at every point $(x,z)\in X	imes S$ with $\operatorname{Re}z=a$ or $\operatorname{Re}z=b$. Suppose for instance that $a>0$, and let $(x_ j,z_ j)$ tend to $(x,z)$ with $\operatorname{Re}z=a$ and $a<\operatorname{Re}z_ j<b$. Set $t_ j=\operatorname{Re}z_ j$. Since $(\psi _ t)_ t$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$, the sequence $\psi _{t_ j}$ converges to $\varphi _ a$ in $L^1$. Applying corollary 1.2.8 to this sequence gives \[  \varphi _ a=\inf _{m>0}\left(\operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq m}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _{t_ j}ight).  \] For fixed $m$, the upper semicontinuity of $\operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq m}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _{t_ j}$ gives \[  \varlimsup _{j	o \infty }\psi _{t_ j}(x_ j)\leq \left(\operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq m}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _{t_ j}ight)(x).  \] Letting $m	o \infty $, we get \[  \varlimsup _{j	o \infty }\psi _{t_ j}(x_ j)\leq \varphi _ a(x).  \] Since $\Phi (x,z)=\varphi _ a(x)$ when $\operatorname{Re}z=a$, this is the desired boundary inequality along $\{ \operatorname{Re}z=a\} $. The same argument applies along $\{ \operatorname{Re}z=b\} $ when $b<1$. Hence corollary 1.2.13 shows that the pasted complexification is $p_1^*	heta $-psh. $\square$ Definition 4.1.12 . A ray $\ell =(\ell _ t)_{t\geq 0}$ is a subgeodesic ray in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ if for any $0\leq a\leq b$, the segment $(\ell _{t})_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. We say $\ell $ emanates from $\ell _0$. The complexification of a subgeodesic ray $\ell $ is defined as the potential \[  \Phi \colon X	imes \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z>0\} ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad (x,z)\mapsto \ell _{\operatorname{Re}z}(x).  \] Note that $\Phi $ is $p_1^*	heta $-psh, where $p_1\colon X	imes \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z>0\} ightarrow X$ is the natural projection. Remark 4.1.13 . As in 4.1.3 , one may also define the complexification as a function $X	imes \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: 0<|z|<1\} ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$.

text: Definition 4.1.1 . Let us fix $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. A subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ is a family $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that if we define \[  \Phi \colon X\times \Bigl \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z\in (0,1) \Bigr \} \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad (x,z)\mapsto \varphi _{\operatorname{Re}z}(x),  \] then $\Phi $ is $p_1^*\theta $-psh, where $p_1\colon X\times \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z\in (0,1)\} \rightarrow X$ is the natural projection; when $t\to 0+$ (resp. $t\to 1-$), $\varphi _ t$ converges to $\varphi _0$ (resp. $\varphi _1$) with respect to the $L^1$-topology. We also say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. We call $\Phi $ the complexification of the subgeodesic $(\varphi _ t)_ t$.

text: Proposition 4.1.4 . Let $g$ be a smooth real function on $X$. Let $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$. Suppose that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then $(\varphi _ t-g)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$. Proof. This follows directly from the definition of the complexification. $\square$

title: Example 4.1.5
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Example 4.1.5 . Let $\varphi _0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $C\in \mathbb {R}$. Let \[  \varphi _ t=\varphi _0+tC,\quad t\in [0,1].  \] Then $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. Indeed, since $\operatorname{Re}z$ is harmonic in $z$, the complexification $\Phi (x,z)=\varphi _0(x)+C\, \operatorname{Re}z$ is $p_1^*\theta $-psh. As a consequence, the constant $(\varphi _0)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic, called the constant subgeodesic at $\varphi _0$. A more general version is as follows: Suppose that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $C_1,C_2\in \mathbb {R}$. Then $(\varphi _ t+C_1t+C_2)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is also a subgeodesic.

Proposition 4.1.6 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then for each $x\in X$, $[0,1] 
i t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is a convex function. Furthermore, \[  \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ),\quad \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0\land \varphi _1.  \] Proof. Let $\Phi $ be the complexification of $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$. For each $x\in X$, the map \[  \Bigl \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \operatorname{Re}z\in (0,1) \Bigr \} ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad z\mapsto \Phi (x,z)  \] is either subharmonic or constantly $-\infty $, as follows from definition 4.1.1 1 and proposition 1.1.13 . In the latter case, the convexity of $[0,1] 
i t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is trivial. In the former case, the convexity on the interval $(0,1)$ follows from proposition 1.1.9 . In order to verify the convexity at the boundary, let us fix $s\in (0,1)$. We need to show that 4.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:varphisconvextemp1} \varphi _ s(x)\leq s\varphi _1(x)+(1-s)\varphi _0(x) \end{equation} for all $x\in X$. Thanks to proposition 1.2.6 , it suffices to prove this for almost all $x$. Choose sequences $a_ j\searrow 0$ and $b_ j
earrow 1$ such that $\varphi _{a_ j}	o \varphi _0$ and $\varphi _{b_ j}	o \varphi _1$ almost everywhere. Outside a set $Z\subseteq X$ of zero Lebesgue measure, all these convergences hold and all the values involved are finite. For $x\in X\setminus Z$ and $j$ large enough that $a_ j<s<b_ j$, the convexity on $(0,1)$ gives \[  \varphi _ s(x)\leq  rac{b_ j-s}{b_ j-a_ j}\varphi _{a_ j}(x)+ rac{s-a_ j}{b_ j-a_ j}\varphi _{b_ j}(x).  \] Letting $j	o \infty $ gives ( 4.1 ) almost everywhere. Let us prove the last assertion. Let \[  \varphi \coloneqq \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t.  \] By Kiselman's principle proposition 1.2.11 , we know that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $. Since the complexification $\Phi $ is not identically $-\infty $, Fubini's theorem shows that for almost every $x\in X$, the function $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is finite for almost every $t\in (0,1)$. For such an $x$, the convexity just proved implies that $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is a finite convex function on $(0,1)$, hence it is bounded from below on $(0,1)$. Thus $\varphi 
ot\equiv -\infty $, and so $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. For any $t\in (0,1)$, using the convexity established above, we have \[  \varphi \leq (1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi _1.  \] It follows that $\varphi \leq \varphi _0$ and $\varphi \leq \varphi _1$ almost everywhere and hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . Our assertion follows. $\square$

text: Corollary 4.1.7 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then 4.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:varphitconvexbdry} \lim _{t\to 0+}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0,\quad \lim _{t\to 1-}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _1. \end{equation} Moreover, \[  \lim _{t\to 0+}\varphi _ t=\varphi _0,\quad \lim _{t\to 1-}\varphi _ t=\varphi _1\quad \textup{quasi-everywhere}.  \] Proof. text: Proposition 4.1.9 . Let $(\varphi ^ i_0)_{i\in I}$, $(\varphi ^ i_1)_{i\in I}$ be two non-empty uniformly bounded from above families in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Let $(\varphi ^ i_ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be subgeodesics from $\varphi _0^ i$ to $\varphi _1^ i$ for each $i\in I$. Then \[  \left(\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi ^ i_ t\right)_{t\in (0,1)}  \] is a subgeodesic from $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_0$ to $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_1$. Proof. We may assume that $\varphi _0^ i,\varphi _1^ i\leq 0$ for all $i\in I$. Then it follows that $\varphi _ t^ i\leq 0$ for all $t\in (0,1)$ and all $i\in I$ by proposition 4.1.6 . We define \[  \varphi _ t\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )  \] for all $t\in [0,1]$. Observe that $[0,1] \ni t\mapsto \varphi _ t$ is convex by the same argument leading to ( 4.1 ). Let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the subgeodesic whose complexification $\Phi _{\psi }$ corresponds to $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \Phi _{\varphi ^ i}$, where $\Phi _{\varphi ^ i}$ is the complexification of $(\varphi ^ i_ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$. Then clearly, $\varphi _ t\leq \psi _ t$ for each $t\in (0,1)$. On the other hand, by proposition 1.2.5 , \[  \psi _ t=\sup _{i\in I}\varphi ^ i_ t=\varphi _ t\quad \textup{almost everywhere}  \] for almost all $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, using proposition 1.2.6 , we find $\psi _ t=\varphi _ t$ for almost all $t\in (0,1)$. Since both functions are convex in $t$, we conclude that $\psi _ t=\varphi _ t$ for all $t\in (0,1)$. It remains to argue that $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$ as $t\to 0+$ and $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _1$ as $t\to 1-$. By symmetry, it suffices to argue the former. By Choquet's lemma proposition 1.2.3 , applied to the uniformly bounded above family of complexifications $(\Phi _{\varphi ^ i})_{i\in I}$ on the strip, there is a countable subset $I'\subset I$ such that \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\Phi _{\varphi ^ i}=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I'}{}\! {}^{*}\Phi _{\varphi ^ i}.  \] Applying Choquet's lemma proposition 1.2.3 once more to the endpoint families if necessary, and enlarging $I'$, we may also assume \[  \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _0^ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I'}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _0^ i,\quad \operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _1^ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I'}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _1^ i.  \] Thus, after replacing $I$ by $I'$, we may assume that $I$ is countable. We know that for any $t\in (0,1)$ and any $j\in I$, \[  \varphi ^ j_ t\leq \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0.  \] Letting $t\to 0+$, we find that \[  \varphi _0^ j\leq \varlimsup _{t\to 0+}\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0  \] almost everywhere. Since $I$ is countable, we conclude that 4.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:varphi0limsuptemp1} \varphi _0=\varlimsup _{t\to 0+}\varphi _ t \end{equation} almost everywhere. Fix $i_0\in I$. Recall that by proposition 4.1.6 , for each $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \adjustlimits \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\sup _ X \varphi _ t\geq \adjustlimits \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\sup _ X \varphi ^{i_0}_ t\geq \adjustlimits \sup _ X \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi ^{i_0}_ t>-\infty ,  \] so the set $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in (0,1)}$ is relatively compact with respect to the $L^1$-topology by proposition 1.5.4 . Let $\psi $ be a cluster point as $t\to 0+$. It suffices to show that $\psi =\varphi _0$. By corollary 1.2.8 and ( 4.4 ), this holds almost everywhere. Therefore, it holds everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . $\square$
