text: Proposition 4.1.10 . Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then for any $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$, the segment $(\varphi _{t})_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic. Proof. It suffices to show that \[  \varphi _{tb+(1-t)a}\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _ a,\quad \varphi _{tb+(1-t)a}\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _ b  \] as $t\to 0+$ and $t\to 1-$ respectively. In other words, we need to show that for any $c\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _ c  \] as $t\to c$. For this purpose, observe that by proposition 4.1.6 , \[  \adjustlimits \sup _ X \inf _{s\in (0,1)}\varphi _ s\leq \sup _{X}\varphi _ t\leq \left( \sup _ X \varphi _0 \right) \lor \left( \sup _ X\varphi _1 \right)  \] for any $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in (0,1)}$ is a relatively compact family with respect to the $L^1$-topology on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ by proposition 1.5.4 . It suffices to show that any cluster point $\psi $ of $\varphi _ t$ as $t\to c$ is equal to $\varphi _ c$. By corollary 1.2.8 and the convexity proposition 4.1.6 , we have $\varphi _ c=\psi $ almost everywhere and hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . $\square$

text: Lemma 4.1.11 . Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Let $0\leq a<b\leq 1$ and let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ be a subgeodesic such that $\psi _ a=\varphi _ a$, $\psi _ b=\varphi _ b$, and \[  \psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t,\quad t\in (a,b).  \] Define \[  \gamma _ t= \begin{cases}  \psi _ t,& \textup{if }t\in (a,b),\\  \varphi _ t,& \textup{if }t\in [0,1]\setminus (a,b). \end{cases}  \] Then $(\gamma _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. Proof. The $L^1$-convergence of $\gamma _ t$ to $\varphi _0$ at $0$ and $\varphi _1$ at $1$ follows immediately from the corresponding property for $(\varphi _ t)_ t$ and $(\psi _ t)_ t$. It remains to prove that the complexification of $(\gamma _ t)_ t$ is $p_1^*\theta $-psh. Let \[  S=\{ z\in \mathbb {C}:0<\operatorname{Re}z<1\} ,\quad S'=\{ z\in \mathbb {C}:a<\operatorname{Re}z<b\} .  \] Let $\Phi $ and $\Psi $ be the complexifications of $(\varphi _ t)_ t$ and $(\psi _ t)_ t$ on the corresponding strips. Since $\Psi \geq \Phi $ on $X\times S'$, the complexification of $(\gamma _ t)_ t$ is equal to $\Phi \lor \Psi $ on $X\times S'$ and to $\Phi $ on $X\times (S\setminus S')$. By the gluing lemma corollary 1.2.13 , it is enough to verify that \[  \varlimsup _{\substack {S'\ni z'\to z\\ x'\to x}}\Psi (x',z')\leq \Phi (x,z)  \] at every point $(x,z)\in X\times S$ with $\operatorname{Re}z=a$ or $\operatorname{Re}z=b$. Suppose for instance that $a>0$, and let $(x_ j,z_ j)$ tend to $(x,z)$ with $\operatorname{Re}z=a$ and $a<\operatorname{Re}z_ j<b$. Set $t_ j=\operatorname{Re}z_ j$. Since $(\psi _ t)_ t$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$, the sequence $\psi _{t_ j}$ converges to $\varphi _ a$ in $L^1$. Applying corollary 1.2.8 to this sequence gives \[  \varphi _ a=\inf _{m>0}\left(\operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq m}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _{t_ j}\right).  \] For fixed $m$, the upper semicontinuity of $\operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq m}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _{t_ j}$ gives \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\psi _{t_ j}(x_ j)\leq \left(\operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq m}{}\! {}^{*}\psi _{t_ j}\right)(x).  \] Letting $m\to \infty $, we get \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\psi _{t_ j}(x_ j)\leq \varphi _ a(x).  \] Since $\Phi (x,z)=\varphi _ a(x)$ when $\operatorname{Re}z=a$, this is the desired boundary inequality along $\{ \operatorname{Re}z=a\} $. The same argument applies along $\{ \operatorname{Re}z=b\} $ when $b<1$. Hence corollary 1.2.13 shows that the pasted complexification is $p_1^*\theta $-psh. $\square$

section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Definition 4.1.12 . A ray $\ell =(\ell _ t)_{t\geq 0}$ is a subgeodesic ray in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ if for any $0\leq a\leq b$, the segment $(\ell _{t})_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. We say $\ell $ emanates from $\ell _0$. The complexification of a subgeodesic ray $\ell $ is defined as the potential \[  \Phi \colon X\times \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z>0\} \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad (x,z)\mapsto \ell _{\operatorname{Re}z}(x).  \] Note that $\Phi $ is $p_1^*\theta $-psh, where $p_1\colon X\times \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\operatorname{Re}z>0\} \rightarrow X$ is the natural projection.

text:
4.2 Geodesics in the space of potentials Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$ and $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class. Fix a model potential $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )_{>0}$. See definition 3.1.10 for the definition. Definition 4.2.1 . Let $\varphi _0, \varphi _1 \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. The geodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ is the family of potentials $\varphi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )\cup \{ -\infty \} $ such that 4.7  egin{equation} \label{eq:Perron2}  egin{split}  \varphi _ t=\operatorname *{sup}_{}{}\! {}^{*}&  \left\{  \psi _ t: (\psi _{s})_ s 	extup{ is a subgeodesic from }\psi _0	extup{ to }\psi _1,ight.\ & \psi _0,\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ),\left.\psi _0\leq \varphi _0,\psi _1\leq \varphi _1ight\} . \end{split} \end{equation} More generally, let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ ($a,b\in \mathbb {R}$, $a\leq b$) be a curve in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. We say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic if the curve $(\varphi _{tb+(1-t)a})_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. We also say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ is a geodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. The envelopes of the form ( 4.7 ) are usually referred to as the Perron envelopes . In general, the geodesic defined by ( 4.7 ) fails to have the correct limit when $t	o 0+$ or $t	o 1-$. Therefore, a priori it is not a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. In the sequel, we use the word geodesic only in situations where the endpoint behavior has been verified. Lemma 4.2.2 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Assume that there is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then the geodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Proof. This is an immediate consequence of proposition 4.1.9 . $\square$ Example 4.2.3 . Let $\varphi _0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $C\in \mathbb {R}$. Then the subgeodesic $(\varphi _0+tC)_{t\in [0,1]}$ studied in example 4.1.5 is a geodesic. This follows easily from proposition 4.1.6 . In particular, when $C=0$, we find that the constant subgeodesic at $\varphi _0$ is indeed a geodesic, which we call the constant geodesic at $\varphi _0$. More generally, suppose that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a geodesic and $C_1,C_2\in \mathbb {R}$, then $(\varphi _ t+C_1t+C_2)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is also a geodesic. This follows immediately from example 4.1.5 . Next we want to show that under mild assumptions, there exist subgeodesics between two potentials. The assumption below turns out to be necessary as well, as we shall prove in theorem 6.1.23 later. Proposition 4.2.4 . Given $\varphi _0, \varphi _1 \in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$, the geodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ defined by ( 4.7 ) is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ for each $t\in (0,1)$. Moreover, for any $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$, the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic. If furthermore $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$), then $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$) for all $t\in (0,1)$. We refer to 3.1.3 for the definition of $\mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$. Our assumption means that $P_{	heta }[\varphi _0]=P_{	heta }[\varphi _1]=\phi $. As a consequence of this proposition, the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is also a subgeodesic since $\varphi _ a,\varphi _ b\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ as well. Proof. After subtracting suitable constants from $\varphi _0$ and $\varphi _1$ and adding back the corresponding affine function of $t$, we may assume that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\leq \phi $. It follows from proposition 4.1.6 that $\varphi _ t\leq \phi $ for all $t\in (0,1)$. In fact, we have the stronger estimate 4.10  egin{equation} \label{eq:geodesicconvextemp1} \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0,\quad t\in (0,1). \end{equation} We first observe that when $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$, so is $\varphi _0\land \varphi _1$, see proposition 3.1.51 . In particular, the constant subgeodesic $t\mapsto \varphi _0\land \varphi _1$ is a candidate in the Perron envelope ( 4.7 ). So 4.11  egin{equation} \label{eq:varphitgeqlandtemp1} \varphi _ t\geq \varphi _0\land \varphi _1,\quad t\in (0,1). \end{equation} By proposition 4.1.9 , $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a subgeodesic. Note. Be careful, here $t\in (0,1)$ instead of $[0,1]$. It follows from proposition 3.1.52 that $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ for all $t\in (0,1)$. Next, we show that as $t	o 0+$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$. The corresponding result at $t=1$ is similar. We first argue the special case where $\varphi _0\preceq \varphi _1$. Take a constant $C>0$ such that \[  \varphi _0-C\leq \varphi _1.  \] Then $(\varphi _0-Ct)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is clearly a candidate in ( 4.7 ), see example 4.1.5 . Therefore, for all $t\in (0,1)$, 4.12  egin{equation} \label{eq:varphi0andvarphit} \varphi _0-Ct\leq \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0. \end{equation} It follows that $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$ as $t	o 0+$. Let us come back to the general case. By corollary 4.1.8 , $\{ \varphi _ t:t\in (0,1)\} $ is a relatively compact subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with respect to the $L^1$-topology. Let $\psi $ be an $L^1$-cluster point of $\varphi _ t$ as $t\searrow 0$, and it suffices to show that $\psi =\varphi _0$. For each $M\in \mathbb {N}$, we write \[  \varphi _0^ M=\varphi _0\land (\varphi _1+M).  \] Observe that $\varphi _0^ M\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ by proposition 3.1.51 . Let $(\varphi _ t^ M)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0^ M$ to $\varphi _1$. Since $\varphi _0^ M\preceq \varphi _1$, the special case proved above applies to the geodesic $(\varphi _ t^ M)_ t$, and \[  \varphi _ t^ M\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0^ M \quad 	extup{as }t	o 0+.  \] Moreover, every candidate for the geodesic from $\varphi _0^ M$ to $\varphi _1$ is also a candidate for the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$, so \[  \varphi _ t^ M\leq \varphi _ t,\quad t\in (0,1).  \] Letting $t	o 0+$ along a sequence for which $\varphi _ t	o \psi $ in $L^1$, and using corollary 1.2.8 , we obtain \[  \psi \geq \varphi _0^ M  \] almost everywhere, hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . On the other hand, by ( 4.10 ), $\psi \leq \varphi _0$. So it suffices to show that \[  \varphi _0\land (\varphi _1+M)\xrightarrow {L^1} \varphi _0  \] as $M	o \infty $, which is shown in proposition 3.1.54 . Now we have shown that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. Next, take $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$. We want to show that the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. We may assume that $a<b$. The argument is the standard balayage argument. Let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. Since $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic by proposition 4.1.10 , we have $\psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t$ for all $t\in (a,b)$. We define \[  \eta _ t= \left\{   egin{aligned}  \psi _ t,& \quad 	ext{if }t\in (a,b),\  \varphi _ t,& \quad 	ext{if }t\in (0,1)\setminus (a,b). \end{aligned} ight.  \] Extending it by setting $\psi _ a=\varphi _ a$ and $\psi _ b=\varphi _ b$, the first part of the proof applied to the endpoints $\varphi _ a,\varphi _ b$ shows that $(\psi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. Since $\psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t$ for $t\in (a,b)$, the gluing lemma 4.1.11 shows that $(\eta _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Therefore, for all $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\geq \eta _ t.  \] In particular, for $t\in (a,b)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\geq \eta _ t=\psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t.  \] In other words, $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}=(\psi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ is the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. Finally, assume furthermore that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$). Thanks to ( 4.11 ), proposition 3.1.51 and proposition 3.1.52 , we find $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$) for all $t\in (0,1)$. $\square$ Lemma 4.2.5 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\varphi _1\leq \varphi _0$. Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Assume that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is also a subgeodesic. Then $\varphi _ t$ is decreasing in $t\in [0,1]$. Proof. Fix $0< r<s\leq 1$ and put $\delta =(s-r)/(1-r)$. Then $(\varphi _{\delta +(1-\delta )t})_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _\delta $ to $\varphi _1$. Since \[  \varphi _\delta \leq (1-\delta )\varphi _0+\delta \varphi _1\leq \varphi _0,  \] we have $\varphi _{\delta +(1-\delta )t}\leq \varphi _ t$ for all $t\in (0,1)$ by the definition of geodesic. In particular, $\varphi _ s=\varphi _{\delta +(1-\delta )r}\leq \varphi _ r$. It remains to prove that for any $t\in (0,1)$, we have $\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0$, but this is an immediate consequence of proposition 4.1.6 : \[  \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0\leq \varphi _0.  \] $\square$ Proposition 4.2.6 . Let $\varphi _1,\varphi _0\in \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ with $\varphi _1\preceq \varphi _0$. Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then 4.15  egin{equation} \label{eq:tsupsuptemp1} s\sup _{\{ \varphi _0
eq -\infty \} }(\varphi _1-\varphi _0)=\sup _{\{ \varphi _0
eq -\infty \} }(\varphi _ s-\varphi _0) \end{equation} for all $s\in [0,1]$. 4.1 Typical behaviour of $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ Proof. The notations in the proof are indicated in 4.1 . Note. When dealing with convex functions, drawing a picture is the easiest way to keep track of the directions of inequalities. We may assume that $s\in (0,1)$ since there is nothing to prove when $s=0$ or $s=1$. After replacing $\varphi _ t$ by $\varphi _ t-C't$ for some large enough $C'>0$, we may assume that $\varphi _1\leq \varphi _0$. This procedure preserves the geodesic property by example 4.2.3 . Then $\varphi _ t$ is decreasing in $t$ by 4.2.5 . Let 4.16  egin{equation} \label{eq:Cdefsupvarphi1m0temp1} C=\sup _{\{ \varphi _1
eq -\infty \} } \left(\varphi _1-\varphi _0ight)=\sup _{\{ \varphi _0
eq -\infty \} } \left(\varphi _1-\varphi _0ight)\leq 0, \end{equation} where the equality is due to corollary 1.3.18 . Then by proposition 1.2.6 , we have \[  \varphi _1\leq \varphi _0+C.  \] So $(\varphi _1-C(1-t))_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a candidate in ( 4.7 ) and hence 4.17  egin{equation} \label{eq:varphi1leqvarphittemp} \varphi _1-C(1-t)\leq \varphi _ t,\quad t\in (0,1). \end{equation} By proposition 4.2.4 , we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _1$ as $t	o 1-$. Since $\varphi _ t$ is decreasing in $t\in (0,1)$, it follows that $\varphi _1=\inf _{t\in (0,1)}\varphi _ t$. Therefore, we can find a pluripolar set $Z\subseteq X$ such that $\varphi _ t(x)ightarrow \varphi _1(x)>-\infty $ as $t	o 1-$ for all $x\in X\setminus Z$. Similarly, since $\varphi _0=\operatorname *{sup}_{t\in (0,1)}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ t$, after enlarging $Z$, we may also guarantee that $\varphi _ t(x)ightarrow \varphi _0(x)>-\infty $ as $t	o 0+$ for all $x\in X\setminus Z$ by proposition 1.2.5 . For any such $x\in X\setminus Z$, the function $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is a real-valued continuous convex function on $[0,1]$. In particular, $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)$ is absolutely continuous on $[0,1]$. Hence, for any $s\in [0,1)$, we have 4.18  egin{equation} \label{eq:varphi1minusvarphi0temp1} \varphi _1(x)-\varphi _ s(x)=\int _ s^1  rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varphi _ t(x)\, \mathrm{d}t\leq (1-s)\lim _{t	o 1-} rac{\varphi _1(x)-\varphi _ t(x)}{1-t}\leq (1-s)C, \end{equation} where the second inequality follows from ( 4.17 ). Taking supremum in ( 4.18 ), we find that 4.19  egin{equation} \label{eq:supvarphi1sleqleqtemp1} \sup _{X\setminus Z} (\varphi _1-\varphi _ s)\leq (1-s)\adjustlimits \sup _{x\in X\setminus Z}\lim _{t	o 1-} rac{\varphi _1(x)-\varphi _ t(x)}{1-t}\leq (1-s)C. \end{equation} When $s=0$, we deduce from corollary 1.3.18 and ( 4.16 ) that \[  C=\sup _{\{ \varphi _1

In other words, 4.20  egin{equation} \label{eq:supvarphi1mivarphi0temp1} \sup _{\{ \varphi _1

Let $\varphi _1,\varphi _0\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$. Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then \[  t\inf _{\{ \phi

eq -\infty \} }(\varphi _ t-\varphi _0)  \] for all $t\in (0,1]$. Definition 4.2.8 . Let $\ell =(\ell _ t)_{t\geq 0}$ be a family in $\mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$. We say $\ell $ is a geodesic ray in $\mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ emanating from $\ell _0$ if for each $0\leq a\leq b$, the restriction $(\ell _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic. The set of geodesic rays in $\mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ emanating from $\phi $ is denoted by $\mathcal{R}(X,	heta ;\phi )$. We say a geodesic ray $\ell \in \mathcal{R}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ has finite energy if $\ell _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$ for all $t>0$. The set of geodesic rays with finite energy is denoted by $\mathcal{R}^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$. We say a geodesic ray $\ell \in \mathcal{R}(X,	heta ;\phi )$ is bounded if $\ell _ t\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$ for all $t\geq 0$. The set of bounded geodesic rays is denoted by $\mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$. Given $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}(X,	heta ;\phi )$, we write $\ell \leq \ell '$ if $\ell _ t\leq \ell '_ t$ for each $t\geq 0$. When $\phi =V_{	heta }$, we usually omit it from the notations and write $\mathcal{R}(X,	heta )$, $\mathcal{R}^1(X,	heta )$ and $\mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,	heta )$ respectively. Proposition 4.2.9 . Let $\ell \in \mathcal{R}(X,	heta ;\phi )$. Then there is a constant $C\in \mathbb {R}$ such that \[  \sup _{X}\ell _ t=Ct,\quad t\geq 0.  \] Proof. It follows from proposition 4.2.6 that \[  \sup _{\{ \phi 
eq -\infty \} }(\ell _ t-\phi )=t\sup _{\{ \phi 
eq -\infty \} }(\ell _1-\phi )  \] for all $t\geq 0$. It suffices to show that for any $t\geq 0$, \[  \sup _{\{ \phi 
eq -\infty \} }(\ell _ t-\phi )=\sup _ X \ell _ t.  \] This was already proved in proposition 3.1.13 . $\square$

We say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic if the curve $(\varphi _{tb+(1-t)a})_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. We also say $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ is a geodesic in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$.

title: Proposition 4.2.4

section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Proposition 4.2.4 . Given $\varphi _0, \varphi _1 \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, the geodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ defined by ( 4.7 ) is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for each $t\in (0,1)$. Moreover, for any $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$, the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic. If furthermore $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$), then $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$) for all $t\in (0,1)$. Proof. After subtracting suitable constants from $\varphi _0$ and $\varphi _1$ and adding back the corresponding affine function of $t$, we may assume that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\leq \phi $. It follows from proposition 4.1.6 that $\varphi _ t\leq \phi $ for all $t\in (0,1)$. In fact, we have the stronger estimate 4.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:geodesicconvextemp1} \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0,\quad t\in (0,1). \end{equation} We first observe that when $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, so is $\varphi _0\land \varphi _1$, see proposition 3.1.51 . In particular, the constant subgeodesic $t\mapsto \varphi _0\land \varphi _1$ is a candidate in the Perron envelope ( 4.7 ). So 4.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:varphitgeqlandtemp1} \varphi _ t\geq \varphi _0\land \varphi _1,\quad t\in (0,1). \end{equation} By proposition 4.1.9 , $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a subgeodesic. Note. Be careful, here $t\in (0,1)$ instead of $[0,1]$. It follows from proposition 3.1.52 that $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for all $t\in (0,1)$. Next, we show that as $t\to 0+$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$. The corresponding result at $t=1$ is similar. We first argue the special case where $\varphi _0\preceq \varphi _1$. Take a constant $C>0$ such that \[  \varphi _0-C\leq \varphi _1.  \] Then $(\varphi _0-Ct)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is clearly a candidate in ( 4.7 ), see example 4.1.5 . Therefore, for all $t\in (0,1)$, 4.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:varphi0andvarphit} \varphi _0-Ct\leq \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0. \end{equation} It follows that $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$ as $t\to 0+$. Let us come back to the general case. By corollary 4.1.8 , $\{ \varphi _ t:t\in (0,1)\} $ is a relatively compact subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with respect to the $L^1$-topology. Let $\psi $ be an $L^1$-cluster point of $\varphi _ t$ as $t\searrow 0$, and it suffices to show that $\psi =\varphi _0$. For each $M\in \mathbb {N}$, we write \[  \varphi _0^ M=\varphi _0\land (\varphi _1+M).  \] Observe that $\varphi _0^ M\in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ by proposition 3.1.51 . Let $(\varphi _ t^ M)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0^ M$ to $\varphi _1$. Since $\varphi _0^ M\preceq \varphi _1$, the special case proved above applies to the geodesic $(\varphi _ t^ M)_ t$, and \[  \varphi _ t^ M\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0^ M \quad \textup{as }t\to 0+.  \] Moreover, every candidate for the geodesic from $\varphi _0^ M$ to $\varphi _1$ is also a candidate for the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$, so \[  \varphi _ t^ M\leq \varphi _ t,\quad t\in (0,1).  \] Letting $t\to 0+$ along a sequence for which $\varphi _ t\to \psi $ in $L^1$, and using corollary 1.2.8 , we obtain \[  \psi \geq \varphi _0^ M  \] almost everywhere, hence everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . On the other hand, by ( 4.10 ), $\psi \leq \varphi _0$. So it suffices to show that \[  \varphi _0\land (\varphi _1+M)\xrightarrow {L^1} \varphi _0  \] as $M\to \infty $, which is shown in proposition 3.1.54 . Now we have shown that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic. Next, take $0\leq a\leq b\leq 1$. We want to show that the restriction $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. We may assume that $a<b$. The argument is the standard balayage argument. Let $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. Since $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic by proposition 4.1.10 , we have $\psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t$ for all $t\in (a,b)$. We define \[  \eta _ t= \left\{  \begin{aligned}  \psi _ t,& \quad \text{if }t\in (a,b),\\  \varphi _ t,& \quad \text{if }t\in (0,1)\setminus (a,b). \end{aligned} \right.  \] Extending it by setting $\psi _ a=\varphi _ a$ and $\psi _ b=\varphi _ b$, the first part of the proof applied to the endpoints $\varphi _ a,\varphi _ b$ shows that $(\psi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. Since $\psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t$ for $t\in (a,b)$, the gluing lemma 4.1.11 shows that $(\eta _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Therefore, for all $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\geq \eta _ t.  \] In particular, for $t\in (a,b)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\geq \eta _ t=\psi _ t\geq \varphi _ t.  \] In other words, $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}=(\psi _ t)_{t\in (a,b)}$ is the geodesic from $\varphi _ a$ to $\varphi _ b$. Finally, assume furthermore that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$). Thanks to ( 4.11 ), proposition 3.1.51 and proposition 3.1.52 , we find $\varphi _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$) for all $t\in (0,1)$. $\square$

text: Lemma 4.2.5 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\varphi _1\leq \varphi _0$. Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Assume that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is also a subgeodesic. Then $\varphi _ t$ is decreasing in $t\in [0,1]$. Proof. Fix $0< r<s\leq 1$ and put $\delta =(s-r)/(1-r)$. Then $(\varphi _{\delta +(1-\delta )t})_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _\delta $ to $\varphi _1$. Since \[  \varphi _\delta \leq (1-\delta )\varphi _0+\delta \varphi _1\leq \varphi _0,  \] we have $\varphi _{\delta +(1-\delta )t}\leq \varphi _ t$ for all $t\in (0,1)$ by the definition of geodesic. In particular, $\varphi _ s=\varphi _{\delta +(1-\delta )r}\leq \varphi _ r$. It remains to prove that for any $t\in (0,1)$, we have $\varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0$, but this is an immediate consequence of proposition 4.1.6 : \[  \varphi _ t\leq t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0\leq \varphi _0.  \] $\square$

text: Definition 4.2.8 . Let $\ell =(\ell _ t)_{t\geq 0}$ be a family in $\mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We say $\ell $ is a geodesic ray in $\mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ emanating from $\ell _0$ if for each $0\leq a\leq b$, the restriction $(\ell _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ is a geodesic. The set of geodesic rays in $\mathcal{E}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ emanating from $\phi $ is denoted by $\mathcal{R}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We say a geodesic ray $\ell \in \mathcal{R}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ has finite energy if $\ell _ t\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for all $t>0$. The set of geodesic rays with finite energy is denoted by $\mathcal{R}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We say a geodesic ray $\ell \in \mathcal{R}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ is bounded if $\ell _ t\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for all $t\geq 0$. The set of bounded geodesic rays is denoted by $\mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Given $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, we write $\ell \leq \ell '$ if $\ell _ t\leq \ell '_ t$ for each $t\geq 0$. When $\phi =V_{\theta }$, we usually omit it from the notations and write $\mathcal{R}(X,\theta )$, $\mathcal{R}^1(X,\theta )$ and $\mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta )$ respectively.

text:
4.3 The metrics on the spaces of potentials and rays Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$ and $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class. Fix a model potential $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. We first study a natural metric on $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Definition 4.3.1 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$, we define the Darvas metric $d_1$ as follows: \[  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )+E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )-2E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi ).  \] Note that by proposition 3.1.51 , $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Recall that $E_{\theta }^{\phi }$ is defined in definition 3.1.35 . In particular, if $\varphi \leq \psi $, we have 4.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d1asEdiff} d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ). \end{equation} We wish to show that $d_1$ is a complete metric. We first prove a contraction property: Proposition 4.3.2 . Let $\varphi ,\psi ,\gamma \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then 4.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d1contract} d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\geq d_1(\varphi \land \gamma ,\psi \land \gamma ). \end{equation} Proof. Step 1 . We first assume that $\varphi \geq \psi $. Then \[  \begin{aligned}  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=&  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )\\  \geq &  E_{\theta }^{\phi }\Bigl ((\varphi \land \gamma )\lor \psi \Bigr )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi ) &  \textup{by \gerbyref{BACDFA8A}{3.1.36}}\\  \geq &  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi \land \gamma )& \textup{by corollary \gerbyref{A2918C6C}{3.1.57}}. \end{aligned}  \] Step 2 . We prove the general case. By Step 1, we have \[  d_1(\varphi ,\varphi \land \psi )\geq d_1(\varphi \land \gamma ,\varphi \land \psi \land \gamma ),\quad d_1(\psi ,\varphi \land \psi )\geq d_1(\psi \land \gamma ,\varphi \land \psi \land \gamma ).  \] Adding the two inequalities together, we conclude ( 4.22 ). $\square$ Lemma 4.3.3 . The function $d_1$ is a metric on $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Proof. There are two facts to prove, as in the two steps below. Step 1 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Assume that $d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=0$. Then we will show that $\varphi =\psi $. We first treat the case $\psi \leq \varphi $. Then $d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=E_\theta ^\phi (\varphi )-E_\theta ^\phi (\psi )=0$, and proposition 3.1.45 gives \[  \int _ X (\varphi -\psi )\, \theta _{\psi }^ n=0.  \] We conclude that $\psi =\varphi $ using the domination principle theorem 2.4.17 . In general, put $\gamma =\varphi \land \psi $. Since \[  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=d_1(\varphi ,\gamma )+d_1(\psi ,\gamma ),  \] both terms on the right vanish. Applying the comparable case to the pairs $(\varphi ,\gamma )$ and $(\psi ,\gamma )$ gives $\varphi =\gamma =\psi $. Step 2 . Let $\varphi ,\psi ,\gamma \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We prove the triangle inequality: \[  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\leq d_1(\varphi ,\gamma )+d_1(\psi ,\gamma ).  \] This can be translated to \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi )\leq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi \land \gamma ).  \] We just have to compute using proposition 4.3.2 : \[  \begin{aligned}  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi \land \gamma )\geq &  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi \land \gamma )\\  \geq & E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi ), \end{aligned}  \] where the second line follows from 3.1.36 . $\square$ We introduce an auxiliary functional. Definition 4.3.4 . Define $I_{\theta }\colon \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )\times \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )\rightarrow \mathbb {R}\cup \{ \infty \} $ as follows: 4.28 \begin{equation}  I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi )\coloneqq \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\left( \theta _{\varphi }^ n+\theta _{\psi }^ n \right). \end{equation} We will soon see that $I_{\theta }$ is always finite, see theorem 4.3.6 . We observe the following elementary equality. Lemma 4.3.5 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then \[  I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi )=I_{\theta }(\varphi \lor \psi ,\varphi )+I_{\theta }(\varphi \lor \psi ,\psi ).  \] Proof. By the plurifine locality of non-pluripolar products proposition 2.2.2 1 , we can write \[  \begin{aligned}  I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi )=& \int _{ \{ \varphi <\psi \} } (\psi -\varphi ) \left( \theta _{\varphi }^ n+\theta _{\psi }^ n \right)+\int _{ \{ \varphi >\psi \} } (\varphi -\psi ) \left( \theta _{\varphi }^ n+\theta _{\psi }^ n \right),\\  I_{\theta }(\varphi \lor \psi ,\varphi )=&  \int _{\{ \psi >\varphi \} } (\psi -\varphi )\left(\theta _{\psi }^ n+\theta _{\varphi }^ n \right),\\  I_{\theta }(\varphi \lor \psi ,\psi )=&  \int _{\{ \psi <\varphi \} } (\varphi -\psi )\left(\theta _{\psi }^ n+\theta _{\varphi }^ n \right). \end{aligned}  \] The desired equality follows by comparing these terms. $\square$ We have an interesting relation between $d_1$ and $I_{\theta }$ defined in definition 4.3.4 . Theorem 4.3.6 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then 4.32 \begin{equation} \label{eq:I_d1_comp} \frac{1}{C_ n} I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi )\leq d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\leq I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi ), \end{equation} where $C_ n=3\cdot 2^{n+2}(n+1)$. Proof. Step 1 . We first prove the right-hand part of ( 4.32 ). Thanks to proposition 3.1.46 and 3.1.3 , we have \[  \begin{aligned}  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi )\leq &  \int _ X (\varphi -\varphi \land \psi )\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n \\  \leq &  \int _{\{ \psi =\varphi \land \psi \} } (\varphi -\psi )\, \theta _{\psi }^ n\\  \leq &  \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\, \theta _{\psi }^ n. \end{aligned}  \] Similarly, \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi )\leq \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] Adding these inequalities up, we find \[  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\leq I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi ).  \] Step 2 . We prove the left-hand part of ( 4.32 ). We claim that 4.36 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d_1varphivarphipsimean_temp1} d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\leq \frac{3(n+1)}{2} d_1(\varphi ,\psi ). \end{equation} For this purpose, we compute directly \[  \begin{aligned} & d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\\  =& d_1\left(\varphi ,\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)+d_1\left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2},\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\\  \leq &  d_1\left(\varphi ,\varphi \land \psi \right)+d_1\left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2},\varphi \land \psi \right)& \textup{by \gerbyref{BACDFA8A}{3.1.36}}\\  \leq &  \int _ X \left( \varphi -\varphi \land \psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n+ \int _ X \left( \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \land \psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n & \textup{by proposition \gerbyref{EFA21885}{3.1.46}}\\  =&  \frac{3}{2}\int _ X \left( \varphi -\varphi \land \psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n+\frac{1}{2}\int _ X \left( \psi -\varphi \land \psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n \\  \leq &  \frac{3(n+1)}{2}d_1\left(\varphi ,\varphi \land \psi \right) + \frac{n+1}{2}d_1(\psi ,\varphi \land \psi )&  \textup{by (\gerbyref{8FC62B3F}{3.110})}\\  \leq &  \frac{3(n+1)}{2}d_1(\varphi ,\psi ), \end{aligned}  \] and ( 4.36 ) follows. We now estimate the left-hand side of ( 4.36 ): \[  \begin{aligned}  d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\geq &  d_1\left(\varphi ,\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\\  \geq &  \int _ X \left(\varphi -\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  \geq &  \int _{\{ \varphi >\psi \} }\left(\varphi -\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n \\  \geq &  \int _{\{ \varphi >\psi \} }\left(\varphi -\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  =&  \frac{1}{2}\int _{\{ \varphi >\psi \} }\left(\varphi -\psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n, \end{aligned}  \] where the second inequality follows from proposition 3.1.46 . Similarly, \[  \begin{aligned}  d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\geq &  d_1\left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2},\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\\  \geq &  \int _ X \left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{(\varphi +\psi )/2}^ n\\  \geq &  2^{-n} \int _ X \left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  \geq &  2^{-n} \int _{\{ \varphi <\psi \} } \left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  \geq &  2^{-n} \int _{\{ \varphi <\psi \} } \left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  =&  2^{-n-1} \int _{\{ \varphi <\psi \} } \left(\psi -\varphi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n, \end{aligned}  \] where the third inequality follows from the multi-linearity of the non-pluripolar product proposition 2.2.2 6 . Adding these estimates up, we find \[  2^{n+2} d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\geq \left(2^{n+1}+2\right) d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\geq \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] Therefore, combined with ( 4.36 ) we conclude \[  3\cdot 2^{n+1}(n+1)d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\geq \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] By symmetry, we also get a similar expression after exchanging $\varphi $ and $\psi $. Adding these inequalities together, we find \[  3\cdot 2^{n+2}(n+1)d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\geq I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi ).  \] The left-hand part of ( 4.32 ) then follows. $\square$ Corollary 4.3.7 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then 4.55 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d1maxonearg} d_1(\varphi \lor \psi ,\varphi )\leq C_ n d_1(\varphi ,\psi ), \end{equation} where $C_ n$ is the constant in theorem 4.3.6 . Proof. By theorem 4.3.6 and 4.3.5 , we have \[  d_1(\varphi \lor \psi ,\varphi )\leq I_{\theta }(\varphi \lor \psi ,\varphi )\leq I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi )\leq C_ n d_1(\varphi ,\psi ).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Lemma 4.3.8 . There is $A,B>0$ so that for any $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$, we have 4.56 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d1bdsupX} d_1(\varphi ,\phi )\geq -\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n\cdot \sup _ X \varphi \geq -Ad_1(\varphi ,\phi )-B. \end{equation} Proof. When $\sup _ X \varphi \leq 0$, the right-hand part of ( 4.56 ) is trivial. Since $\varphi \leq \phi $, we find \[  d_1(\phi ,\varphi )=-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )\geq -\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n\cdot \sup _{\{ \phi \neq -\infty \} } (\varphi -\phi )=-\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n\cdot \sup _ X \varphi ,  \] where the last equality follows from proposition 3.1.13 . We can therefore assume that $\sup _ X \varphi > 0$. In this case, the left-hand part of ( 4.56 ) is trivial. Take a Kähler form $\omega \geq \theta $ on $X$. Then thanks to theorem 3.1.7 , we can find a constant $C>0$ so that \[  \theta _{\phi }^ n\leq C\omega ^ n.  \] Thanks to proposition 1.5.4 , there is a constant $C'>0$, independent of the choice of $\varphi $, so that \[  \int _ X \left( \phi -\varphi +\sup _ X \varphi \right)\, \theta _{\phi }^ n\leq C'.  \] We estimate \[  \begin{aligned}  I_{\theta }(\phi ,\varphi )\geq &  \int _ X |\varphi -\phi |\, \theta _{\phi }^ n\\  \geq &  \left(\sup _ X \varphi \right)\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n-\int _ X \left( \phi -\varphi +\sup _ X \varphi \right)\, \theta _{\phi }^ n \\  \geq &  \left(\sup _ X \varphi \right)\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n-C'. \end{aligned}  \] The right-hand part of ( 4.56 ) then follows from theorem 4.3.6 . $\square$ Next we handle the completeness of $d_1$. The completeness can be proved in a more general framework. Definition 4.3.9 . Let $E$ be a set. A pre-rooftop structure on $E$ is a binary operator $\land :E\times E\rightarrow E$, satisfying the following axioms: For $x,y,z\in E$, $x\land y=y\land x$. $(x\land y)\land z=x\land (y\land z)$. $x\land x=x$. We call $(E,\land )$ a pre-rooftop space . A pre-rooftop structure $\land $ defines a partial order $\leq $ on $E$ as follows: \[  x\leq y\quad \text{if and only if } \quad x\land y=x.  \] Here by abuse of notation, we use $\leq $ to denote the partial order. In particular, it makes sense to talk about increasing and decreasing sequences in $E$. Definition 4.3.10 . Let $(E,d)$ be a metric space. A pre-rooftop structure on $(E,d)$ is a pre-rooftop structure $\land $ on $E$. We say $(E,d,\land )$ is a pre-rooftop metric space . A rooftop structure on $(E,d)$ is a pre-rooftop structure $\land $ on $E$ such that 4.60 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rtdef} d(x\land z,y\land z)\leq d(x,y),\quad \forall x,y,z\in E. \end{equation} We call $(E,d,\land )$ a rooftop metric space . Lemma 4.3.11 . Let $(E,d,\land )$ be a rooftop metric space. Let $x,y,x',y'\in E$. Then 4.61 \begin{equation}  d(x\land y,x'\land y')\leq d(x,x')+d(y,y'). \end{equation} In particular, $\land \colon E\times E\rightarrow E$ is continuous. Proof. We compute \[  d(x\land y,x'\land y')\leq d(x\land y,x\land y')+d(x\land y',x'\land y')\leq d(x,x')+d(y,y').  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Proposition 4.3.12 . Let $(E,d,\land )$ be a rooftop metric space. Then $(E,d)$ is complete if and only if both of the following hold: Each increasing Cauchy sequence converges. Each decreasing Cauchy sequence converges. Proof. The direct implication is trivial. Conversely, assume that both conditions are true. Let $(x_ j)_{j>0}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $E$. We want to prove that $(x_ j)_ j$ converges. By passing to a subsequence, we may assume that \[  d\left(x_ j,x_{j+1}\right)\leq 2^{-j}.  \] For $k,j\geq 1$, let \[  y_ j^ k\coloneqq x_ k\land \cdots \land x_{k+j}.  \] Then $(y_ j^ k)_ j$ is decreasing, and \[  d\left(y_ j^ k,y_{j+1}^ k\right)\leq d\left(x_{k+j},x_{k+j+1}\right)\leq 2^{-k-j}.  \] So $(y_ j^ k)_ j$ is a decreasing Cauchy sequence. Define \[  y^ k\coloneqq \lim _{j\to \infty }y_ j^ k.  \] Then \[  d\left(y^ k,y^{k+1}\right)=\lim _{j\to \infty }d\left(y_{j+1}^ k,y_ j^{k+1}\right)\leq d\left(x_ k,x_{k+1}\right)\leq 2^{-k}.  \] We also need to check that the sequence $(y^ k)_ k$ is increasing. For each $j\geq 1$, we have \[  y_ j^ k=x_ k\land y_{j-1}^{k+1}\leq y_{j-1}^{k+1}.  \] Equivalently, \[  y_ j^ k\land y_{j-1}^{k+1}=y_ j^ k.  \] Letting $j\to \infty $ and using the continuity of $\land $ from 4.3.11 , we obtain \[  y^ k\land y^{k+1}=y^ k.  \] Thus $y^ k\leq y^{k+1}$. So $(y^ k)_ k$ is an increasing Cauchy sequence. Let \[  y\coloneqq \lim _{k\to \infty }y^ k.  \] For every $j\geq 0$, we have \[  d\left(y_ j^ k,x_ k\right)\leq \sum _{r=k}^{k+j-1}d\left(x_ r,x_{r+1}\right),  \] with the empty sum understood as $0$. Indeed, this is trivial for $j=0$, and the induction step follows from \[  y_ j^ k=x_ k\land y_{j-1}^{k+1}  \] and \[  d\left(y_ j^ k,x_ k\right)\leq d\left(y_{j-1}^{k+1},x_ k\right)\leq d\left(y_{j-1}^{k+1},x_{k+1}\right)+d\left(x_{k+1},x_ k\right).  \] Letting $j\to \infty $, we get \[  d\left(y^ k,x_ k\right)\leq \sum _{r=k}^{\infty }d\left(x_ r,x_{r+1}\right)\leq 2^{1-k}.  \] So $(x_ k)_ k$ converges to $y$. $\square$ Theorem 4.3.13 . The metric space $(\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi ),d_1)$ is complete. It follows from the proof below that if $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$ is a monotone sequence in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ with $d_1$-limit $\varphi $, then $\varphi $ is the almost everywhere limit of $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$. We will use this result without further explanation in the sequel. Proof. As we have seen in 4.3.3 and proposition 4.3.2 , the triple \[  \left(\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi ),d_1,\land \right)  \] is a rooftop metric space. Hence thanks to proposition 4.3.12 , it remains to show that each increasing or decreasing Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ converges. We first consider an increasing sequence $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. The Cauchy property simply means that \[  \sup _{i>0} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i)<\infty .  \] We claim that \[  \varphi \coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{i>0}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i  \] is the $d_1$-limit of the sequence. We first observe that $(\sup _ X \varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ is bounded, as a consequence of 4.3.8 . Therefore, proposition 3.1.53 guarantees that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$, and hence our assertion follows from proposition 3.1.47 . Next we consider a decreasing sequence $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. The Cauchy property simply means that \[  \inf _{i>0} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i)>-\infty .  \] We claim that \[  \varphi \coloneqq \inf _{i>0}\varphi _ i  \] is the $d_1$-limit of the sequence. Equivalently, we need to show that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and 4.62 \begin{equation} \label{eq:E_cont_decnet_temp1} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )=\lim _{i\to \infty } E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i). \end{equation} We first observe that $(\sup _ X \varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ is bounded, as a consequence of 4.3.8 . Therefore, $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and $\varphi _ i\xlongrightarrow {L^1} \varphi $, see corollary 1.5.6 . We claim that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. For this purpose, we may assume that $\varphi _1\leq 0$. Since $(\varphi _ i)_ i$ is decreasing, $\varphi _ i\leq \varphi _1\leq 0$ for all $i>0$. As $\varphi _ i\preceq \phi $ and $\phi $ is model, each $\varphi _ i$ is a candidate for $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $, so $\varphi _ i\leq \phi $. Thus, using the energy formula ( 3.69 ) and the fact that all mixed terms are non-positive, we get for each $i>0$, \[  \frac{1}{n+1}\int _ X \left(\varphi _ i-\phi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n\geq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i)\geq \inf _{j>0} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ j)>-\infty .  \] We can then apply 3.1.50 , with $\gamma =\phi $, to conclude that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Our assertion ( 4.62 ) then follows from proposition 3.1.39 . We conclude the proof. $\square$ Lemma 4.3.14 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ be a sequence in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ with $d_1$-limit $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then after replacing $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ by a subsequence, we can find two sequences $(\psi _ i)_{i>0}$ and $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$ in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ such that $(\psi _ i)_{i>0}$ is decreasing with $d_1$ and pointwise limit $\varphi $; $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$ is increasing with $d_1$ and almost everywhere limit $\varphi $. $\eta _ i\leq \varphi _ i\leq \psi _ i$ for all $i>0$. Proof. We first note that as a consequence of 4.3.8 , $(\sup _ X \varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ is bounded. Let $C_ n$ be the constant in theorem 4.3.6 . After replacing $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ by a subsequence, we may assume that \[  d_1(\varphi _ i,\varphi _{i+1})\leq \min \{ C_ n^{-2i},2^{-i}\} .  \] We first construct $(\psi _ i)_{i>0}$. For this purpose, it suffices to define \[  \psi _ i\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ j  \] for each $i>0$. It follows from proposition 3.1.53 that $\psi _ i\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for each $i>0$. For $k\geq 0$, set \[  \psi _ i^ k\coloneqq \varphi _ i\lor \varphi _{i+1}\lor \cdots \lor \varphi _{i+k}.  \] Iterating corollary 4.3.7 gives \[  d_1(\varphi _ i,\psi _ i^ k)\leq \sum _{a=i}^{i+k-1}C_ n^{a+1-i}d_1(\varphi _ a,\varphi _{a+1})\leq \sum _{a=i}^{i+k-1}C_ n^{a+1-i}C_ n^{-2a}.  \] Since $\psi _ i^ k$ increases almost everywhere to $\psi _ i$, letting $k\to \infty $ and using proposition 3.1.47 , we get \[  d_1(\varphi _ i,\psi _ i)\leq \frac{C_ n^{1-2i}}{1-C_ n^{-1}}.  \] Thus $\psi _ i\to \varphi $ in $d_1$. Since $(\psi _ i)_ i$ is decreasing, the monotone case in the proof of theorem 4.3.13 shows that $\psi _ i$ converges almost everywhere to $\varphi $, hence pointwise by proposition 1.2.6 . Next we construct $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$. For each $i>0$ and $k\geq 0$, we let \[  \eta _ i^ k\coloneqq \varphi _ i\land \varphi _{i+1}\land \cdots \land \varphi _{i+k}.  \] Then \[  \begin{aligned}  d_1(\varphi _ i,\eta _ i^ k)\leq &  \sum _{j=0}^{k-1} d_1\left(\eta _ i^ j,\eta _ i^{j+1}\right)\\  \leq & \sum _{j=0}^{k-1} d_1\left(\varphi _{i+j},\varphi _{i+j+1}\right) & \textup{by proposition \gerbyref{BB01FE5E}{4.3.2}}\\  \leq &  \sum _{j=0}^{k-1} 2^{-i-j}\\  \leq &  2^{1-i}. \end{aligned}  \] Since $\eta _ i^ k\leq \varphi _ i$, the preceding estimate gives \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ i^ k)\geq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i)-2^{1-i},\quad k\geq 0.  \] The sequence $(\eta _ i^ k)_{k\geq 0}$ is decreasing, and the monotonicity of $E_{\theta }^{\phi }$ shows that the sequence $\left(E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ i^ k)\right)_{k\geq 0}$ is decreasing and bounded from below, hence convergent. Thus, for $k\leq l$, \[  d_1(\eta _ i^ k,\eta _ i^ l)=E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ i^ k)-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ i^ l),  \] and $(\eta _ i^ k)_{k\geq 0}$ is a decreasing Cauchy sequence. Therefore, the monotone case in the proof of theorem 4.3.13 shows that \[  \eta _ i\coloneqq \lim _{k\to \infty }\eta _ i^ k=\inf _{k\geq 0} \eta _ i^ k  \] is the $d_1$-limit of $(\eta _ i^ k)_{k\geq 0}$ and proposition 3.1.47 shows that \[  d_1(\varphi _ i,\eta _ i)\leq 2^{1-i}.  \] By construction, $\eta _ i\leq \varphi _ i$ and $(\eta _ i)_ i$ is increasing. Therefore, $\varphi $ is the $d_1$-limit of the increasing sequence $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$. As we have seen in the proof of theorem 4.3.13 , this implies that $\varphi $ is also the almost everywhere limit of $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$. $\square$ Theorem 4.3.15 . The functional $E_{\theta }^{\phi }\colon \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi ) \rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ is continuous. Proof. Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$ be a sequence in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ with $d_1$-limit $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We wish to show that 4.67 \begin{equation} \label{eq:limjE_temp1} \lim _{j\to \infty } E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ j)=E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ). \end{equation} It suffices to prove that every subsequence has a further subsequence along which ( 4.67 ) holds. Thus, after replacing $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$ by a subsequence, let $(\eta _ j)_ j$ and $(\psi _ j)_ j$ be the monotone sequences supplied by 4.3.14 . From the construction, $\eta _ j\leq \varphi _ j\leq \psi _ j$. By proposition 3.1.47 , \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ j)\to E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ),\quad E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi _ j)\to E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ).  \] The monotonicity of $E_{\theta }^{\phi }$ then squeezes $E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ j)$, proving ( 4.67 ). $\square$ Proposition 4.3.16 . Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ be a geodesic in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then $t\mapsto E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ t)$ is a linear function on $[a,b]$. We recall the terminology used in the proof. Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ be Euclidean open. A function $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is maximal if, for every open $G\Subset \Omega $ and every upper semicontinuous function $v$ on $\overline G$ such that $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(G)$ and $v\leq u$ on $\partial G$, one has $v\leq u$ on $G$. Let $\mathcal F$ denote the plurifine topology. If $U$ is $\mathcal F$-open and $u$ is $\mathcal F$-psh on $U$, then $u$ is $\mathcal F$-maximal if, for every bounded $\mathcal F$-open set $G$ with $G\subset \overline G^{\mathcal F}\subset U$ and every bounded-above $\mathcal F$-upper semicontinuous function $v$ on $\overline G^{\mathcal F}$ that is $\mathcal F$-psh on $G$, one has \[  v\leq u\textup{ on }\partial _{\mathcal F}G \quad \Longrightarrow \quad v\leq u\textup{ on }G.  \] See [ Definition 5.9.1 , EKF ] . Proof. By an affine change of parameter, we may assume that $[a,b]=[0,1]$. Step 1 . Assume first that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Let $Y=X\times \mathbb {P}^1$, and let $p_1,p_2$ be the two projections. On \[  A\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\mathrm{e}^{-1}<|z|<1\} , \qquad U(x,z)\coloneqq \varphi _{-\log |z|}(x),  \] the function $U$ is $p_1^*\theta $-psh. Choose $C>0$ such that \[  \phi -C\leq \varphi _0,\varphi _1\leq \phi +C.  \] The constant subgeodesic at $\phi -C$ and proposition 4.1.6 give 4.68 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relgeoduniformbound} \phi -C\leq \varphi _ t\leq (1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi _1\leq \phi +C, \qquad 0<t<1. \end{equation} Fix concentric annuli $A_0\Subset A_1\Subset A$ and a unit-mass Fubini–Study form $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ on $\mathbb {P}^1$. Put \[  \beta =p_2^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}},\qquad \Theta _ B=p_1^*\theta +B\beta ,\qquad \Phi =p_1^*\phi .  \] The class represented by $\Theta _ B$ is big. Since $\phi =P_\theta [\phi ]$, we have $\phi \leq 0$. For every $B>0$, $\Phi =P_{\Theta _ B}[\Phi ]$. Indeed, if $\Psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\Theta _ B)$ satisfies $\Psi \leq 0$ and $\Psi \preceq \Phi $, then on each fibre $X\times \{ z\} $, either $\Psi _ z\equiv -\infty $, or $\Psi _ z\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is a candidate in the definition of $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $. Thus $\Psi _ z\leq \phi $ in both cases. Conversely, $\Phi $ itself is a candidate. From proposition 4.1.6 , we know that for any $C>t>0$, we have \[  \ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t\leq \frac{t}{C}\Bigl ((V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi \Bigr )+\frac{C-t}{C}\cdot V_{\theta }\leq 0,  \] while the linear subgeodesic $V_\theta -t$ is a candidate in the same Perron envelope, so $V_\theta -t\leq \ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t$. Therefore, by proposition 1.2.2 , 4.105 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ellphitexp} \ell _ t^{\varphi }\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{C>t}{}\! {}^{*}\ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ) \end{equation} for all $t\geq 0$. Thanks to proposition 3.1.47 , we have \[  \ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t\xrightarrow {d_1} \ell _ t^{\varphi }  \] as $C\to \infty $ for all $t\geq 0$. Applying proposition 4.3.17 on each interval $[0,T]$ to the increasing family $(\ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t)_{t\in [0,T]}$, $C\geq T$, shows that $\ell ^{\varphi }\in \mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta )$. It remains to compute the energy of $\ell ^{\varphi }$. We first fix $C\geq t>0$ and compute using proposition 4.3.16 : \[  E_{\theta }\left(\ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t\right)=\frac{t}{C}E_{\theta }\Bigl ((V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi \Bigr ).  \] Letting $C\to \infty $ and applying proposition 3.1.47 , we find that \[  E_{\theta }(\ell ^{\varphi }_ t)=\lim _{C\to \infty }\frac{t}{C}E_{\theta }\Bigl ((V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi \Bigr )  \] for any $t\geq 0$. It follows that \[  \mathbf{E}(\ell ^{\varphi })=\lim _{C\to \infty }\frac{1}{C}E_{\theta }\Bigl ((V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi \Bigr ).  \] Using the definition of $E_{\theta }$, in order to obtain ( 4.103 ), it suffices to show that for each $j=0,\ldots ,n$, we have 4.106 \begin{equation} \label{eq:limCintXtemp1} \lim _{C\to \infty }\int _ X \frac{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi -V_{\theta }}{C} \, \theta _{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^{j}\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}-\int _ X \theta _{V_{\theta }}^ n. \end{equation} For this purpose, for each $C>0$, we decompose $X$ as $\{ \varphi > V_{\theta }-C\} $ and $\{ \varphi \leq V_{\theta }-C\} $. We have \[  \begin{aligned} & \int _{\{ \varphi > V_{\theta }-C\} } \frac{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi -V_{\theta }}{C} \, \theta _{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}\\  =&  \int _{\{ \varphi > V_{\theta }-C\} } \frac{\varphi -V_{\theta }}{C} \, \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}. \end{aligned}  \] On the other hand, \[  \begin{aligned} & \int _{\{ \varphi \leq V_{\theta }-C\} } \frac{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi -V_{\theta }}{C} \, \theta _{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}\\  =&  -\int _{\{ \varphi \leq V_{\theta }-C\} } \theta _{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}\\  =&  -\int _ X \theta _{V_{\theta }}^ n+\int _{\{ \varphi > V_{\theta }-C\} } \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}. \end{aligned}  \] Observe that for $C>0$, the function $\mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >V_{\theta }-C\} }C^{-1}(\varphi -V_{\theta })$ is defined quasi-everywhere. Since $\varphi \leq V_\theta $, it takes values in $[-1,0]$ outside a pluripolar set. When $C\to \infty $, these functions converge to $0$ quasi-everywhere, so the first integral above converges to $0$ by dominated convergence. Similarly, the indicators $\mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >V_\theta -C\} }$ increase to $1$ outside a pluripolar set, hence \[  \lim _{C\to \infty }\int _{\{ \varphi >V_{\theta }-C\} } \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j} = \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}.  \] Therefore, ( 4.106 ) follows. $\square$ There are two principal ways to formulate mathematical assertions (problems, conjectures, theorems, …): Russian and French. The Russian way is to choose the most simple and specific case (so that nobody could simplify the formulation preserving the main point). The French way is to generalize the statement as far as nobody could generalize it further. 
— Vladimir Arnold Note. Vladimir Igorevich Arnold (1937–2010), who became a professor at l'Université Paris IX after the dissolution of USSR, was always sick of France (so am I!). In the public lecture entitled “Sur l'éducation mathématique” in 1997, he invented the famous joke “Combien font $2+3$?” to question the French education system.

Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$, we define the Darvas metric $d_1$ as follows: \[  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )+E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )-2E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi ).  \] Note that by proposition 3.1.51 , $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$.

title: Proposition 4.3.2
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Proposition 4.3.2 . Let $\varphi ,\psi ,\gamma \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then 4.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d1contract} d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\geq d_1(\varphi \land \gamma ,\psi \land \gamma ). \end{equation} Proof. Step 1 . We first assume that $\varphi \geq \psi $. Then \[  \begin{aligned}  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=&  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )\\  \geq &  E_{\theta }^{\phi }\Bigl ((\varphi \land \gamma )\lor \psi \Bigr )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi ) &  \textup{by \gerbyref{BACDFA8A}{3.1.36}}\\  \geq &  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi \land \gamma )& \textup{by corollary \gerbyref{A2918C6C}{3.1.57}}. \end{aligned}  \] Step 2 . We prove the general case. By Step 1, we have \[  d_1(\varphi ,\varphi \land \psi )\geq d_1(\varphi \land \gamma ,\varphi \land \psi \land \gamma ),\quad d_1(\psi ,\varphi \land \psi )\geq d_1(\psi \land \gamma ,\varphi \land \psi \land \gamma ).  \] Adding the two inequalities together, we conclude ( 4.22 ). $\square$

title: Lemma 4.3.3
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Lemma 4.3.3 . The function $d_1$ is a metric on $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Proof. There are two facts to prove, as in the two steps below. Step 1 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Assume that $d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=0$. Then we will show that $\varphi =\psi $. We first treat the case $\psi \leq \varphi $. Then $d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=E_\theta ^\phi (\varphi )-E_\theta ^\phi (\psi )=0$, and proposition 3.1.45 gives \[  \int _ X (\varphi -\psi )\, \theta _{\psi }^ n=0.  \] We conclude that $\psi =\varphi $ using the domination principle theorem 2.4.17 . In general, put $\gamma =\varphi \land \psi $. Since \[  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )=d_1(\varphi ,\gamma )+d_1(\psi ,\gamma ),  \] both terms on the right vanish. Applying the comparable case to the pairs $(\varphi ,\gamma )$ and $(\psi ,\gamma )$ gives $\varphi =\gamma =\psi $. Step 2 . Let $\varphi ,\psi ,\gamma \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We prove the triangle inequality: \[  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\leq d_1(\varphi ,\gamma )+d_1(\psi ,\gamma ).  \] This can be translated to \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi )\leq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi \land \gamma ).  \] We just have to compute using proposition 4.3.2 : \[  \begin{aligned}  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi \land \gamma )\geq &  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi \land \gamma )\\  \geq & E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \gamma )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi ), \end{aligned}  \] where the second line follows from 3.1.36 . $\square$

title: Definition 4.3.4
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Definition 4.3.4 . Define $I_{\theta }\colon \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )\times \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )\rightarrow \mathbb {R}\cup \{ \infty \} $ as follows: 4.28 \begin{equation}  I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi )\coloneqq \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\left( \theta _{\varphi }^ n+\theta _{\psi }^ n \right). \end{equation}

title: Lemma 4.3.5
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Lemma 4.3.5 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then \[  I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi )=I_{\theta }(\varphi \lor \psi ,\varphi )+I_{\theta }(\varphi \lor \psi ,\psi ).  \] Proof. By the plurifine locality of non-pluripolar products proposition 2.2.2 1 , we can write \[  \begin{aligned}  I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi )=& \int _{ \{ \varphi <\psi \} } (\psi -\varphi ) \left( \theta _{\varphi }^ n+\theta _{\psi }^ n \right)+\int _{ \{ \varphi >\psi \} } (\varphi -\psi ) \left( \theta _{\varphi }^ n+\theta _{\psi }^ n \right),\\  I_{\theta }(\varphi \lor \psi ,\varphi )=&  \int _{\{ \psi >\varphi \} } (\psi -\varphi )\left(\theta _{\psi }^ n+\theta _{\varphi }^ n \right),\\  I_{\theta }(\varphi \lor \psi ,\psi )=&  \int _{\{ \psi <\varphi \} } (\varphi -\psi )\left(\theta _{\psi }^ n+\theta _{\varphi }^ n \right). \end{aligned}  \] The desired equality follows by comparing these terms. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.3.6
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Theorem 4.3.6 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then 4.32 \begin{equation} \label{eq:I_d1_comp} \frac{1}{C_ n} I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi )\leq d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\leq I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi ), \end{equation} where $C_ n=3\cdot 2^{n+2}(n+1)$. Proof. Step 1 . We first prove the right-hand part of ( 4.32 ). Thanks to proposition 3.1.46 and 3.1.3 , we have \[  \begin{aligned}  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi )\leq &  \int _ X (\varphi -\varphi \land \psi )\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n \\  \leq &  \int _{\{ \psi =\varphi \land \psi \} } (\varphi -\psi )\, \theta _{\psi }^ n\\  \leq &  \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\, \theta _{\psi }^ n. \end{aligned}  \] Similarly, \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi )-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi \land \psi )\leq \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] Adding these inequalities up, we find \[  d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\leq I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi ).  \] Step 2 . We prove the left-hand part of ( 4.32 ). We claim that 4.36 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d_1varphivarphipsimean_temp1} d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\leq \frac{3(n+1)}{2} d_1(\varphi ,\psi ). \end{equation} For this purpose, we compute directly \[  \begin{aligned} & d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\\  =& d_1\left(\varphi ,\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)+d_1\left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2},\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\\  \leq &  d_1\left(\varphi ,\varphi \land \psi \right)+d_1\left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2},\varphi \land \psi \right)& \textup{by \gerbyref{BACDFA8A}{3.1.36}}\\  \leq &  \int _ X \left( \varphi -\varphi \land \psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n+ \int _ X \left( \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \land \psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n & \textup{by proposition \gerbyref{EFA21885}{3.1.46}}\\  =&  \frac{3}{2}\int _ X \left( \varphi -\varphi \land \psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n+\frac{1}{2}\int _ X \left( \psi -\varphi \land \psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi \land \psi }^ n \\  \leq &  \frac{3(n+1)}{2}d_1\left(\varphi ,\varphi \land \psi \right) + \frac{n+1}{2}d_1(\psi ,\varphi \land \psi )&  \textup{by (\gerbyref{8FC62B3F}{3.110})}\\  \leq &  \frac{3(n+1)}{2}d_1(\varphi ,\psi ), \end{aligned}  \] and ( 4.36 ) follows. We now estimate the left-hand side of ( 4.36 ): \[  \begin{aligned}  d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\geq &  d_1\left(\varphi ,\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\\  \geq &  \int _ X \left(\varphi -\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  \geq &  \int _{\{ \varphi >\psi \} }\left(\varphi -\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n \\  \geq &  \int _{\{ \varphi >\psi \} }\left(\varphi -\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  =&  \frac{1}{2}\int _{\{ \varphi >\psi \} }\left(\varphi -\psi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n, \end{aligned}  \] where the second inequality follows from proposition 3.1.46 . Similarly, \[  \begin{aligned}  d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\geq &  d_1\left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2},\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\\  \geq &  \int _ X \left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{(\varphi +\psi )/2}^ n\\  \geq &  2^{-n} \int _ X \left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  \geq &  2^{-n} \int _{\{ \varphi <\psi \} } \left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \land \frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  \geq &  2^{-n} \int _{\{ \varphi <\psi \} } \left(\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}-\varphi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n\\  =&  2^{-n-1} \int _{\{ \varphi <\psi \} } \left(\psi -\varphi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n, \end{aligned}  \] where the third inequality follows from the multi-linearity of the non-pluripolar product proposition 2.2.2 6 . Adding these estimates up, we find \[  2^{n+2} d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\geq \left(2^{n+1}+2\right) d_1\left(\varphi ,\frac{\varphi +\psi }{2}\right)\geq \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] Therefore, combined with ( 4.36 ) we conclude \[  3\cdot 2^{n+1}(n+1)d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\geq \int _ X |\varphi -\psi |\, \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] By symmetry, we also get a similar expression after exchanging $\varphi $ and $\psi $. Adding these inequalities together, we find \[  3\cdot 2^{n+2}(n+1)d_1(\varphi ,\psi )\geq I_{\theta }(\varphi ,\psi ).  \] The left-hand part of ( 4.32 ) then follows. $\square$

text: Corollary 4.3.7 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. title: Lemma 4.3.8
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Lemma 4.3.8 . There is $A,B>0$ so that for any $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$, we have 4.56 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d1bdsupX} d_1(\varphi ,\phi )\geq -\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n\cdot \sup _ X \varphi \geq -Ad_1(\varphi ,\phi )-B. \end{equation} Proof. When $\sup _ X \varphi \leq 0$, the right-hand part of ( 4.56 ) is trivial. Since $\varphi \leq \phi $, we find \[  d_1(\phi ,\varphi )=-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )\geq -\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n\cdot \sup _{\{ \phi \neq -\infty \} } (\varphi -\phi )=-\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n\cdot \sup _ X \varphi ,  \] where the last equality follows from proposition 3.1.13 . We can therefore assume that $\sup _ X \varphi > 0$. In this case, the left-hand part of ( 4.56 ) is trivial. Take a Kähler form $\omega \geq \theta $ on $X$. Then thanks to theorem 3.1.7 , we can find a constant $C>0$ so that \[  \theta _{\phi }^ n\leq C\omega ^ n.  \] Thanks to proposition 1.5.4 , there is a constant $C'>0$, independent of the choice of $\varphi $, so that \[  \int _ X \left( \phi -\varphi +\sup _ X \varphi \right)\, \theta _{\phi }^ n\leq C'.  \] We estimate \[  \begin{aligned}  I_{\theta }(\phi ,\varphi )\geq &  \int _ X |\varphi -\phi |\, \theta _{\phi }^ n\\  \geq &  \left(\sup _ X \varphi \right)\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n-\int _ X \left( \phi -\varphi +\sup _ X \varphi \right)\, \theta _{\phi }^ n \\  \geq &  \left(\sup _ X \varphi \right)\int _ X \theta _{\phi }^ n-C'. \end{aligned}  \] The right-hand part of ( 4.56 ) then follows from theorem 4.3.6 . $\square$

title: Definition 4.3.9

text: Definition 4.3.9 . Let $E$ be a set. A pre-rooftop structure on $E$ is a binary operator $\land :E\times E\rightarrow E$, satisfying the following axioms: For $x,y,z\in E$, $x\land y=y\land x$. $(x\land y)\land z=x\land (y\land z)$. $x\land x=x$. We call $(E,\land )$ a pre-rooftop space .

title: Definition 4.3.10

text: Definition 4.3.10 . Let $(E,d)$ be a metric space. A pre-rooftop structure on $(E,d)$ is a pre-rooftop structure $\land $ on $E$. We say $(E,d,\land )$ is a pre-rooftop metric space . A rooftop structure on $(E,d)$ is a pre-rooftop structure $\land $ on $E$ such that 4.60 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rtdef} d(x\land z,y\land z)\leq d(x,y),\quad \forall x,y,z\in E. \end{equation} We call $(E,d,\land )$ a rooftop metric space .

title: Lemma 4.3.11
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Lemma 4.3.11 . Let $(E,d,\land )$ be a rooftop metric space. Let $x,y,x',y'\in E$. Then 4.61 \begin{equation}  d(x\land y,x'\land y')\leq d(x,x')+d(y,y'). \end{equation} Proof. We compute \[  d(x\land y,x'\land y')\leq d(x\land y,x\land y')+d(x\land y',x'\land y')\leq d(x,x')+d(y,y').  \] This completes the proof. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.3.12
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Proposition 4.3.12 . Let $(E,d,\land )$ be a rooftop metric space. Then $(E,d)$ is complete if and only if both of the following hold: Each increasing Cauchy sequence converges. Each decreasing Cauchy sequence converges. Proof. The direct implication is trivial. Conversely, assume that both conditions are true. Let $(x_ j)_{j>0}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $E$. We want to prove that $(x_ j)_ j$ converges. By passing to a subsequence, we may assume that \[  d\left(x_ j,x_{j+1}\right)\leq 2^{-j}.  \] For $k,j\geq 1$, let \[  y_ j^ k\coloneqq x_ k\land \cdots \land x_{k+j}.  \] Then $(y_ j^ k)_ j$ is decreasing, and \[  d\left(y_ j^ k,y_{j+1}^ k\right)\leq d\left(x_{k+j},x_{k+j+1}\right)\leq 2^{-k-j}.  \] So $(y_ j^ k)_ j$ is a decreasing Cauchy sequence. Define \[  y^ k\coloneqq \lim _{j\to \infty }y_ j^ k.  \] Then \[  d\left(y^ k,y^{k+1}\right)=\lim _{j\to \infty }d\left(y_{j+1}^ k,y_ j^{k+1}\right)\leq d\left(x_ k,x_{k+1}\right)\leq 2^{-k}.  \] We also need to check that the sequence $(y^ k)_ k$ is increasing. For each $j\geq 1$, we have \[  y_ j^ k=x_ k\land y_{j-1}^{k+1}\leq y_{j-1}^{k+1}.  \] Equivalently, \[  y_ j^ k\land y_{j-1}^{k+1}=y_ j^ k.  \] Letting $j\to \infty $ and using the continuity of $\land $ from 4.3.11 , we obtain \[  y^ k\land y^{k+1}=y^ k.  \] Thus $y^ k\leq y^{k+1}$. So $(y^ k)_ k$ is an increasing Cauchy sequence. Let \[  y\coloneqq \lim _{k\to \infty }y^ k.  \] For every $j\geq 0$, we have \[  d\left(y_ j^ k,x_ k\right)\leq \sum _{r=k}^{k+j-1}d\left(x_ r,x_{r+1}\right),  \] with the empty sum understood as $0$. Indeed, this is trivial for $j=0$, and the induction step follows from \[  y_ j^ k=x_ k\land y_{j-1}^{k+1}  \] and \[  d\left(y_ j^ k,x_ k\right)\leq d\left(y_{j-1}^{k+1},x_ k\right)\leq d\left(y_{j-1}^{k+1},x_{k+1}\right)+d\left(x_{k+1},x_ k\right).  \] Letting $j\to \infty $, we get \[  d\left(y^ k,x_ k\right)\leq \sum _{r=k}^{\infty }d\left(x_ r,x_{r+1}\right)\leq 2^{1-k}.  \] So $(x_ k)_ k$ converges to $y$. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.3.13
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Theorem 4.3.13 . The metric space $(\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi ),d_1)$ is complete. Proof. As we have seen in 4.3.3 and proposition 4.3.2 , the triple \[  \left(\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi ),d_1,\land \right)  \] is a rooftop metric space. Hence thanks to proposition 4.3.12 , it remains to show that each increasing or decreasing Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ converges. We first consider an increasing sequence $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. The Cauchy property simply means that \[  \sup _{i>0} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i)<\infty .  \] We claim that \[  \varphi \coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{i>0}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i  \] is the $d_1$-limit of the sequence. We first observe that $(\sup _ X \varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ is bounded, as a consequence of 4.3.8 . Therefore, proposition 3.1.53 guarantees that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$, and hence our assertion follows from proposition 3.1.47 . Next we consider a decreasing sequence $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. The Cauchy property simply means that \[  \inf _{i>0} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i)>-\infty .  \] We claim that \[  \varphi \coloneqq \inf _{i>0}\varphi _ i  \] is the $d_1$-limit of the sequence. Equivalently, we need to show that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and 4.62 \begin{equation} \label{eq:E_cont_decnet_temp1} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi )=\lim _{i\to \infty } E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i). \end{equation} We first observe that $(\sup _ X \varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ is bounded, as a consequence of 4.3.8 . Therefore, $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and $\varphi _ i\xlongrightarrow {L^1} \varphi $, see corollary 1.5.6 . We claim that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. For this purpose, we may assume that $\varphi _1\leq 0$. Since $(\varphi _ i)_ i$ is decreasing, $\varphi _ i\leq \varphi _1\leq 0$ for all $i>0$. As $\varphi _ i\preceq \phi $ and $\phi $ is model, each $\varphi _ i$ is a candidate for $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $, so $\varphi _ i\leq \phi $. Thus, using the energy formula ( 3.69 ) and the fact that all mixed terms are non-positive, we get for each $i>0$, \[  \frac{1}{n+1}\int _ X \left(\varphi _ i-\phi \right)\, \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n\geq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i)\geq \inf _{j>0} E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ j)>-\infty .  \] We can then apply 3.1.50 , with $\gamma =\phi $, to conclude that $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Our assertion ( 4.62 ) then follows from proposition 3.1.39 . We conclude the proof. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.3.14
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Lemma 4.3.14 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ be a sequence in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ with $d_1$-limit $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then after replacing $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ by a subsequence, we can find two sequences $(\psi _ i)_{i>0}$ and $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$ in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ such that $(\psi _ i)_{i>0}$ is decreasing with $d_1$ and pointwise limit $\varphi $; $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$ is increasing with $d_1$ and almost everywhere limit $\varphi $. $\eta _ i\leq \varphi _ i\leq \psi _ i$ for all $i>0$. Proof. We first note that as a consequence of 4.3.8 , $(\sup _ X \varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ is bounded. Let $C_ n$ be the constant in theorem 4.3.6 . After replacing $(\varphi _ i)_{i>0}$ by a subsequence, we may assume that \[  d_1(\varphi _ i,\varphi _{i+1})\leq \min \{ C_ n^{-2i},2^{-i}\} .  \] We first construct $(\psi _ i)_{i>0}$. For this purpose, it suffices to define \[  \psi _ i\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{j\geq i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ j  \] for each $i>0$. It follows from proposition 3.1.53 that $\psi _ i\in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ for each $i>0$. For $k\geq 0$, set \[  \psi _ i^ k\coloneqq \varphi _ i\lor \varphi _{i+1}\lor \cdots \lor \varphi _{i+k}.  \] Iterating corollary 4.3.7 gives \[  d_1(\varphi _ i,\psi _ i^ k)\leq \sum _{a=i}^{i+k-1}C_ n^{a+1-i}d_1(\varphi _ a,\varphi _{a+1})\leq \sum _{a=i}^{i+k-1}C_ n^{a+1-i}C_ n^{-2a}.  \] Since $\psi _ i^ k$ increases almost everywhere to $\psi _ i$, letting $k\to \infty $ and using proposition 3.1.47 , we get \[  d_1(\varphi _ i,\psi _ i)\leq \frac{C_ n^{1-2i}}{1-C_ n^{-1}}.  \] Thus $\psi _ i\to \varphi $ in $d_1$. Since $(\psi _ i)_ i$ is decreasing, the monotone case in the proof of theorem 4.3.13 shows that $\psi _ i$ converges almost everywhere to $\varphi $, hence pointwise by proposition 1.2.6 . Next we construct $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$. For each $i>0$ and $k\geq 0$, we let \[  \eta _ i^ k\coloneqq \varphi _ i\land \varphi _{i+1}\land \cdots \land \varphi _{i+k}.  \] Then \[  \begin{aligned}  d_1(\varphi _ i,\eta _ i^ k)\leq &  \sum _{j=0}^{k-1} d_1\left(\eta _ i^ j,\eta _ i^{j+1}\right)\\  \leq & \sum _{j=0}^{k-1} d_1\left(\varphi _{i+j},\varphi _{i+j+1}\right) & \textup{by proposition \gerbyref{BB01FE5E}{4.3.2}}\\  \leq &  \sum _{j=0}^{k-1} 2^{-i-j}\\  \leq &  2^{1-i}. \end{aligned}  \] Since $\eta _ i^ k\leq \varphi _ i$, the preceding estimate gives \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ i^ k)\geq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ i)-2^{1-i},\quad k\geq 0.  \] The sequence $(\eta _ i^ k)_{k\geq 0}$ is decreasing, and the monotonicity of $E_{\theta }^{\phi }$ shows that the sequence $\left(E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ i^ k)\right)_{k\geq 0}$ is decreasing and bounded from below, hence convergent. Thus, for $k\leq l$, \[  d_1(\eta _ i^ k,\eta _ i^ l)=E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ i^ k)-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ i^ l),  \] and $(\eta _ i^ k)_{k\geq 0}$ is a decreasing Cauchy sequence. Therefore, the monotone case in the proof of theorem 4.3.13 shows that \[  \eta _ i\coloneqq \lim _{k\to \infty }\eta _ i^ k=\inf _{k\geq 0} \eta _ i^ k  \] is the $d_1$-limit of $(\eta _ i^ k)_{k\geq 0}$ and proposition 3.1.47 shows that \[  d_1(\varphi _ i,\eta _ i)\leq 2^{1-i}.  \] By construction, $\eta _ i\leq \varphi _ i$ and $(\eta _ i)_ i$ is increasing. Therefore, $\varphi $ is the $d_1$-limit of the increasing sequence $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$. As we have seen in the proof of theorem 4.3.13 , this implies that $\varphi $ is also the almost everywhere limit of $(\eta _ i)_{i>0}$. $\square$

text: Theorem 4.3.15 . The functional $E_{\theta }^{\phi }\colon \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi ) \rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ is continuous. Proof. Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$ be a sequence in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ with $d_1$-limit $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We wish to show that 4.67 \begin{equation} \label{eq:limjE_temp1} \lim _{j\to \infty } E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ j)=E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ). \end{equation} It suffices to prove that every subsequence has a further subsequence along which ( 4.67 ) holds. Thus, after replacing $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$ by a subsequence, let $(\eta _ j)_ j$ and $(\psi _ j)_ j$ be the monotone sequences supplied by 4.3.14 . From the construction, $\eta _ j\leq \varphi _ j\leq \psi _ j$. By proposition 3.1.47 , \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ j)\to E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ),\quad E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\psi _ j)\to E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi ).  \] The monotonicity of $E_{\theta }^{\phi }$ then squeezes $E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ j)$, proving ( 4.67 ). $\square$
