text:
Proposition 4.3.16 . Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [a,b]}$ be a geodesic in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$. Then $t\mapsto E_{	heta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ t)$ is a linear function on $[a,b]$. Proof. By an affine change of parameter, we may assume that $[a,b]=[0,1]$. Step 1 . Assume first that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\phi )$. Let $Y=X	imes \mathbb {P}^1$, and let $p_1,p_2$ be the two projections. On \[  A\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}:\mathrm{e}^{-1}<|z|<1\} , \qquad U(x,z)\coloneqq \varphi _{-\log |z|}(x),  \] the function $U$ is $p_1^*	heta $-psh. Choose $C>0$ such that \[  \phi -C\leq \varphi _0,\varphi _1\leq \phi +C.  \] The constant subgeodesic at $\phi -C$ and proposition 4.1.6 give 4.68  egin{equation} \label{eq:relgeoduniformbound} \phi -C\leq \varphi _ t\leq (1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi _1\leq \phi +C, \qquad 0<t<1. \end{equation} Fix concentric annuli $A_0\Subset A_1\Subset A$ and a unit-mass Fubini–Study form $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ on $\mathbb {P}^1$. Put \[   eta =p_2^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}},\qquad \Theta _ B=p_1^*	heta +B eta ,\qquad \Phi =p_1^*\phi .  \] The class represented by $\Theta _ B$ is big. Since $\phi =P_	heta [\phi ]$, we have $\phi \leq 0$. For every $B>0$, $\Phi =P_{\Theta _ B}[\Phi ]$. Indeed, if $\Psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\Theta _ B)$ satisfies $\Psi \leq 0$ and $\Psi \preceq \Phi $, then on each fibre $X	imes \{ z\} $, either $\Psi _ z\equiv -\infty $, or $\Psi _ z\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is a candidate in the definition of $P_	heta [\phi ]=\phi $. Thus $\Psi _ z\leq \phi $ in both cases. Conversely, $\Phi $ itself is a candidate. Moreover, proposition 2.2.2 6 gives 4.69  egin{equation} \label{eq:productmodelmass} \int _ Y(\Theta _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )^{n+1} =(n+1)B\int _ X	heta _\phi ^ n>0. \end{equation} Choose an $S^1$-invariant smooth function $q$ on $\mathbb {P}^1$ such that \[  q<-C-1\  	extup{ on }A_0, \qquad q>C+1\  	extup{ near }\partial A_1.  \] After increasing $B$, we may assume that $B\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq 0$. Identifying $q$ with $p_2^*q$, define \[  W=  egin{cases}  U\lor (\Phi +q),& 	extup{on }X	imes A_1,\  \Phi +q,& 	extup{on }Y\setminus (X	imes A_1). \end{cases}  \] The gluing lemma corollary 1.2.13 shows that $W\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\Theta _ B)$. By construction, 4.72  egin{equation} \label{eq:compactgluedpotential} W=U\  	extup{ on }X	imes A_0, \qquad \Phi -C'\leq W\leq \Phi +C' \end{equation} for some $C'>0$. Hence $W\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(Y,\Theta _ B;\Phi )$ by ( 4.69 ). Set \[  T=\Theta _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W,\qquad S=\Theta _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi .  \] Define the order-zero current on $\mathbb {P}^1$ 4.73  egin{equation} \label{eq:compactrelativeenergycurrent} \mathcal{H}_ W\coloneqq  rac{1}{n+1}(p_2)_*\left((W-\Phi )\sum _{j=0}^ n T^ j\wedge S^{n-j}ight). \end{equation} The integration-by-parts formula [ Xia19b ] , applied against a smooth test function on $\mathbb {P}^1$, gives 4.74  egin{equation} \label{eq:compactrelativeenergyddc} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\mathcal{H}_ W = rac{1}{n+1}(p_2)_*\left(T^{n+1}-S^{n+1}ight). \end{equation} By ( 3.69 ), ( 4.72 ), and corollary 2.2.8 , on $A_0$ the current $\mathcal{H}_ W$ is represented almost everywhere by \[  z\longmapsto E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _{-\log |z|}).  \] This representative is continuous. Indeed, on every smaller annulus, the convex functions $t\mapsto \varphi _ t(x)-\phi (x)$, considered on the common locus where both values are finite, are uniformly bounded by ( 4.68 ), hence uniformly Lipschitz. The resulting inequalities between the potentials hold almost everywhere and therefore everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 . The monotonicity in 3.1.36 and ( 3.71 ) then give the local Lipschitz continuity of $t\mapsto E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _ t)$. On $X	imes A_0$, define the signed Radon measure 4.75  egin{equation} \label{eq:horizontaldefectrelative} \mu _ U\coloneqq \left(T^{n+1}-(n+1)B eta \wedge T^ night)|_{X	imes A_0}. \end{equation} This measure is positive. To see this, take a relatively compact product coordinate ball $Q\subset X	imes A_0$. Let $a$ be a smooth local potential of $p_1^*	heta $, put $h=U+a\leq 0$ and $h_ k=h\lor (-k)$, and choose a smooth local potential $b$ of $B eta $ with $|b|\leq C_ Q$. For $p=n,n+1$, set \[   egin{aligned}  
u _ k^{b,p}& =\mathds {1}_{\{ h+b>-k\} }  igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((h+b)\lor (-k)) igr )^ p,\  
u _ k^{h,p}& =\mathds {1}_{\{ h>-k\} }  igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k+B eta  igr )^ p. \end{aligned}  \] Plurifine locality and $|b|\leq C_ Q$ give, for $k>C_ Q$, \[  
u _{k-C_ Q}^{h,p}\leq 
u _ k^{b,p}\leq 
u _{k+C_ Q}^{h,p}.  \] Thus the two cofinal truncation families have the same limit. By proposition 2.2.2 6 and $ eta ^2=0$, 4.78  egin{equation} \label{eq:horizontalfinitelevelrelative}  egin{aligned} & \mathds {1}_{\{ h>-k\} }\left[ (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k+B eta )^{n+1} -(n+1)B eta \wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k+B eta )^ night]\ & \qquad =\mathds {1}_{\{ h>-k\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k)^{n+1}\geq 0. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Passing to the increasing truncation limit yields 4.81  egin{equation} \label{eq:horizontaltruncationrelative} \mu _ U|_ Q=\lim _{k	o \infty } \mathds {1}_{\{ h>-k\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k)^{n+1}\geq 0. \end{equation} By ( 2.13 ), \[  (p_2)_*( eta \wedge T^ n) =\left(\int _ X	heta _\phi ^ night)\omega _{\mathrm{FS}},  \] since $W_ z\sim \phi $ on every fibre and proposition 3.1.6 applies. On the other hand, \[  (p_2)_*S^{n+1} =(n+1)B\left(\int _ X	heta _\phi ^ night)\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}  \] by proposition 2.2.2 6 . Together with ( 4.74 ) and ( 4.75 ), these identities give on $A_0$ 4.82  egin{equation} \label{eq:relativeenergycurvature} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ z E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _{-\log |z|}) = rac{1}{n+1}(p_2)_*\mu _ U. \end{equation} Step 2 . We prove that $\mu _ U=0$. Let $D\Subset X	imes A$ be a coordinate domain, let $a$ be a smooth local potential of $p_1^*	heta $ near $\overline D$, and set $h=U+a$. If $v$ is a psh function on $D$ with the boundary inequality required in the definition of maximality, max-pasting gives \[  \widetilde U=U\lor (v-a)\  	extup{ on }D, \qquad \widetilde U=U\  	extup{ outside }D.  \] The function $\widetilde U$ need not be radial. Its $S^1$-symmetrization \[  V(x,z)=\operatorname *{sup}_{|\lambda |=1}{}\! {}^{*}\widetilde U(x,\lambda z)  \] is radial and $p_1^*	heta $-psh. The $S^1$-saturation of $D$ is relatively compact in $X	imes A$, so $V=U$ near $X	imes \partial A$. Hence the family $V_ t(x)=V(x,\mathrm{e}^{-t})$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$ by definition 4.1.1 . The definition ( 4.7 ) therefore gives \[  \widetilde U\leq V\leq U.  \] It follows that $v\leq h$ on $D$, so $h$ is a maximal psh function. On a product coordinate ball $Q\Subset X	imes A_0$, put $O_ k=Q\cap \{ h>-k\} $. By [ Proposition 5.9.3 , EKF ] , $h$ is $\mathcal F$-maximal. The function $h_ k=h\lor (-k)$ is locally bounded and agrees with $h$ on the $\mathcal F$-open set $O_ k$, hence is $\mathcal F$-maximal there. Therefore [ Theorem 5.10.1 , EKF ] gives \[  \mathds {1}_{O_ k}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k)^{n+1}=0.  \] By ( 4.81 ), $\mu _ U=0$. Since $A_0\Subset A$ was arbitrary, ( 4.82 ) shows that $z\mapsto E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _{-\log |z|})$ is radial and harmonic on $A$. Thus $t\mapsto E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _ t)$ is affine on $(0,1)$. Choose $C_0>0$ such that $|\varphi _1-\varphi _0|\leq C_0$ on their common finite locus; equivalently, the two resulting inequalities between the potentials hold everywhere. Affine barriers and proposition 4.1.6 give \[   egin{aligned}  \varphi _0-C_0t& \leq \varphi _ t\leq \varphi _0+C_0t,\  \varphi _1-C_0(1-t)& \leq \varphi _ t\leq \varphi _1+C_0(1-t). \end{aligned}  \] By 3.1.36 and ( 3.71 ), the energy converges to the corresponding endpoint energy as $t	o 0+$ and $t	o 1-$. Hence 4.85  egin{equation} \label{eq:relativeenergylinearbounded} E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _ t) =(1-t)E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _0)+tE_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _1) \end{equation} when the endpoints belong to $\mathcal E^\infty (X,	heta ;\phi )$. Step 3 . Let now $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ;\phi )$. By example 4.2.3 and ( 3.71 ), we may add different constants to the endpoints and assume that $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\leq \phi $. Put \[  \varphi _ j^{(k)}=\varphi _ j\lor (\phi -k),\qquad j=0,1,  \] and let $(\varphi _ t^{(k)})_{t\in [0,1]}$ be the corresponding geodesic. The endpoint truncations decrease to $\varphi _ j$, and Perron monotonicity gives \[  \varphi _ t\leq \varphi _ t^{(k+1)}\leq \varphi _ t^{(k)}.  \] Let $h_ t=\lim _{k	o \infty }\varphi _ t^{(k)}$. The decreasing limit of the complexifications is $p_1^*	heta $-psh and is not identically $-\infty $. Taking the limit in the convex upper bound gives, first almost everywhere and then everywhere by proposition 1.2.6 , 4.86  egin{equation} \label{eq:finiteenergygeodesicsandwich} \varphi _ t\leq h_ t\leq (1-t)\varphi _0+t\varphi _1. \end{equation} Note that \[  |h_ t-\varphi _0| \leq |\varphi _ t-\varphi _0|+t|\varphi _1-\varphi _0|\quad 	extup{a.e.}.  \] Since $\varphi _ t	o \varphi _0$ in $L^1$ as $t	o 0+$ and $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in L^1(X)$, it follows that $h_ t	o \varphi _0$ in $L^1$. The same argument at $t=1$ gives $h_ t	o \varphi _1$ in $L^1$. Together with the $p_1^*	heta $-psh complexification constructed above, these endpoint limits show by definition 4.1.1 that $(h_ t)$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Hence ( 4.7 ) gives $h_ t\leq \varphi _ t$. Together with ( 4.86 ), this proves \[  \varphi _ t^{(k)}\searrow \varphi _ t,\qquad 0<t<1.  \] Applying proposition 3.1.47 at the endpoints and at each interior slice, and then using ( 4.85 ), gives \[   egin{aligned}  E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _ t) & =\lim _{k	o \infty }E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _ t^{(k)})\ & =\lim _{k	o \infty }\left((1-t)E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _0^{(k)}) +tE_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _1^{(k)})ight)\ & =(1-t)E_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _0)+tE_	heta ^\phi (\varphi _1). \end{aligned}  \] This concludes the proof. $\square$

text: Proposition 4.3.17 . Let $(\varphi ^ i_0)_{i\in I}$, $(\varphi ^ i_1)_{i\in I}$ be two uniformly bounded from above increasing nets in $\mathcal{E}^{1}(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Let $(\varphi ^ i_ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0^ i$ to $\varphi _1^ i$ for each $i\in I$. Then \[  \left(\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi ^ i_ t\right)_{t\in (0,1)}  \] is the geodesic from $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_0$ to $\operatorname *{sup}_{i}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi ^ i_1$. Proof. Put \[  \varphi _ j=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ j^ i\quad (j=0,1), \qquad h_ t=\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ t^ i,  \] and let $(g_ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. By proposition 3.1.53 , $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. The slice families are uniformly bounded from above by proposition 4.1.6 ; hence $h_ t\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ by proposition 3.1.53 . Moreover, proposition 4.1.9 shows that $(h_ t)$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Thus 4.90 \begin{equation} \label{eq:suprelativegeodesicorder} h_ t\leq g_ t. \end{equation} For each $t$, the net $(\varphi _ t^ i)_{i\in I}$ is increasing. By proposition 1.2.5 , its pointwise supremum agrees with $h_ t$ almost everywhere, and the analogous assertion holds at the endpoints. Therefore proposition 3.1.47 , proposition 4.3.16 gives \[  \begin{aligned}  E_\theta ^\phi (h_ t) & =\lim _{i\in I}E_\theta ^\phi (\varphi _ t^ i)\\ & =\lim _{i\in I}\left((1-t)E_\theta ^\phi (\varphi _0^ i) +tE_\theta ^\phi (\varphi _1^ i)\right)\\ & =(1-t)E_\theta ^\phi (\varphi _0)+tE_\theta ^\phi (\varphi _1) =E_\theta ^\phi (g_ t). \end{aligned}  \] By ( 4.21 ), ( 4.90 ), and 4.3.3 , \[  d_1(h_ t,g_ t)=E_\theta ^\phi (g_ t)-E_\theta ^\phi (h_ t)=0,  \] so $h_ t=g_ t$ for all $t\in (0,1)$. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.3.18
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Proposition 4.3.18 . Let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$, $(\psi _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be geodesics in $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then the distance $d_1(\varphi _ t,\psi _ t)$ is a convex function of $t\in [0,1]$. Proof. By definition of $d_1$ and proposition 4.3.16 , it suffices to show the concavity of \[  [0,1]\ni t\mapsto E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _ t\land \psi _ t).  \] Let $(\eta _ t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0\land \psi _0$ to $\varphi _1\land \psi _1$. Then for each $t\in [0,1]$, we have $\eta _ t\leq \varphi _ t\land \psi _ t$. Hence, by the monotonicity of $E_\theta ^\phi $ and proposition 4.3.16 , \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }( \varphi _ t\land \psi _ t)\geq E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\eta _ t)=(1-t)E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _0\land \psi _0)+tE_{\theta }^{\phi }(\varphi _1\land \psi _1)  \] for each $t\in [0,1]$. Applying the same argument to the restrictions of $(\varphi _ t)_ t$ and $(\psi _ t)_ t$ to any subinterval of $[0,1]$, which are again geodesics by proposition 4.2.4 , gives a similar inequality on every subinterval. Hence $t\mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (\varphi _ t\land \psi _ t)$ is concave, and our assertion follows. $\square$

title: Definition 4.3.19
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Definition 4.3.19 . Let $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We define \[  d_1(\ell ,\ell ')\coloneqq \lim _{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{t}d_1(\ell _ t,\ell '_ t).  \] The limit exists in $[0,\infty ]$ by proposition 4.3.18 .

title: Theorem 4.3.20
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Theorem 4.3.20 . The function $d_1$ defined in definition 4.3.19 is a metric on $\mathcal{R}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Proof. Symmetry and the triangle inequality follow from the corresponding pointwise properties of $d_1$ on $\mathcal{E}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We next show that $d_1(\ell ,\ell ')<\infty $ for any $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Let $C_\ell $ be the constant in proposition 4.2.9 , and set $\tilde{\ell }_ t=\ell _ t-C_\ell t$. Then $\tilde{\ell }$ is again a geodesic ray, $\sup _ X\tilde{\ell }_ t=0$, and hence $\tilde{\ell }_ t\leq \phi $ by proposition 3.1.13 . Thus, by proposition 4.3.16 , \[  d_1(\tilde{\ell }_ t,\phi )=-E_\theta ^\phi (\tilde{\ell }_ t)=-tE_\theta ^\phi (\tilde{\ell }_1).  \] Moreover, by ( 3.71 ), $d_1(\ell _ t,\tilde{\ell }_ t)=|C_\ell |t\int _ X\theta _{\phi }^ n$. Hence $d_1(\ell _ t,\phi )$ grows at most linearly in $t$. The same argument applies to $\ell '$, and the triangle inequality gives $d_1(\ell ,\ell ')<\infty $. It remains to prove separation: suppose that $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and $d_1(\ell ,\ell ')=0$. Fix $s>0$. Then it follows from proposition 4.3.18 that \[  \frac{d_1(\ell _ s,\ell '_ s)}{s}\leq \lim _{t\to \infty }\frac{d_1(\ell _ t,\ell '_ t)}{t}=d_1(\ell ,\ell ')=0.  \] Therefore, $\ell _ s=\ell '_ s$ and hence $\ell =\ell '$. $\square$

title: Definition 4.3.21

text: Definition 4.3.21 . We define the radial Monge–Ampère energy $\mathbf{E}^{\phi }\colon \mathcal{R}(X,\theta ;\phi )\rightarrow \mathbb {R}\cup \{ \pm \infty \} $ as follows: \[  \mathbf{E}^{\phi }(\ell )\coloneqq \varlimsup _{t\to \infty }\frac{E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\ell _ t)}{t}.  \] When $\phi =V_{\theta }$, we write $\mathbf{E}$ instead of $\mathbf{E}^{V_{\theta }}$.

title: Proposition 4.3.22
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Proposition 4.3.22 . Let $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}^1(X,\theta ;\phi )$ and $\ell \leq \ell '$. Then 4.94 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d1rayscompa} d_1(\ell ,\ell ')=\mathbf{E}^{\phi }(\ell ')-\mathbf{E}^{\phi }(\ell ). \end{equation} Proof. By proposition 4.3.16 , the energy is linear along finite energy rays. Hence \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\ell _ t)=tE_{\theta }^{\phi }(\ell _1),\quad E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\ell '_ t)=tE_{\theta }^{\phi }(\ell '_1).  \] Since $\ell _ t\leq \ell '_ t$ for all $t\geq 0$, ( 4.21 ) gives \[  \frac{1}{t}d_1(\ell _ t,\ell '_ t)=\frac{1}{t}\left(E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\ell '_ t)-E_{\theta }^{\phi }(\ell _ t)\right).  \] Letting $t\to \infty $ proves the assertion. $\square$

text: Definition 4.3.23 . Let $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. We define $\ell \lor \ell '$ as the minimal ray in $\mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ lying above both $\ell $ and $\ell '$.

title: Proposition 4.3.24
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Proposition 4.3.24 . Given $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Then $\ell \lor \ell '\in \mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ exists, and 4.95 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Elor} \mathbf{E}^{\phi }(\ell \lor \ell ')=\lim _{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{t}E_{\theta }^{\phi }\left(\ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t\right). \end{equation} Proof. For each $t>0$, let $(\ell ''^ t_{s})_{s\in [0,t]}$ be the geodesic from $\phi $ to $\ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t$. Step 1 . We first show that for each fixed $s\geq 0$, $\ell ''^ t_{s}$ is increasing in $t\in [s,\infty )$. To see this, fix $s\geq 0$ and choose $t'>t\geq s$. We need to show that 4.96 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ellppdombyellpptemp1} \ell ''^{t'}_ s\geq \ell ''^{t}_ s. \end{equation} Since $(\ell ''^{t'}_ a)_{a\in [0,t]}$ is a geodesic, it suffices to show that $(\ell ''^ t_ a)_{a\in [0,t]}$ is a candidate in the Perron envelope defining the former geodesic. In other words, in verifying ( 4.96 ), we may assume that either $s=0$ or $s=t$. The case $s=0$ is of course trivial. So it remains to prove the following: \[  \ell ''^{t'}_ t\geq \ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t.  \] By symmetry, it suffices to prove \[  \ell ''^{t'}_ t\geq \ell _ t.  \] But since $(\ell _ a)_{a\in [0,t']}$ is a candidate in the Perron envelope defining $\ell ''^{t'}$, this inequality follows. Step 2 . Next, observe that for a fixed $s\geq 0$, we have \[  \sup _ X \ell ''^ t_ s\leq \frac{s}{t}\sup _ X\ell ''^ t_ t+ \frac{t-s}{t}\sup _ X \ell ''^ t_0=\frac{s}{t}\left( \sup _ X\ell _ t \right)\lor \left( \sup _ X\ell '_ t \right)  \] for all $t>s$. The right-hand side is bounded from above by a constant independent of $t\geq s$ by proposition 4.2.9 . Let 4.97 \begin{equation} \label{eq:llorlp} (\ell \lor \ell ')_ s\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{t>s}{}\! {}^{*} \ell ''^ t_{s}. \end{equation} Then proposition 4.3.17 guarantees that $\ell \lor \ell '\in \mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$. Step 3 . We need to show that $\ell \lor \ell '$ defined in this way is indeed the minimal ray lying above $\ell $ and $\ell '$. First, by Step 1, we have \[  \ell ''^ t_ s\geq \ell ''^ s_ s\geq \ell _ s  \] for any $t\geq s\geq 0$. Therefore, \[  (\ell \lor \ell ')_ s\geq \ell _ s  \] for all $s\geq 0$. In other words, $\ell \lor \ell '\geq \ell $. Similarly, $\ell \lor \ell '\geq \ell '$. Next, let $L\in \mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$ be a ray lying above both $\ell $ and $\ell '$. Then we have \[  L_ t\geq \ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t  \] for all $t\geq 0$. In particular, \[  L_ s\geq \ell ''^ t_ s  \] for all $t\geq s\geq 0$. It follows that \[  L_ s\geq (\ell \lor \ell ')_ s  \] for all $s\geq 0$. Step 4 . It remains to argue ( 4.95 ). Since the energy is linear along bounded rays, \[  \mathbf{E}^{\phi }(\ell \lor \ell ')=E_{\theta }^{\phi }\left((\ell \lor \ell ')_1\right).  \] Moreover, $\ell ''^ t_1$ increases to $(\ell \lor \ell ')_1$ as $t\to \infty $. By proposition 3.1.47 , \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }\left((\ell \lor \ell ')_1\right)=\lim _{t\to \infty } E_{\theta }^{\phi }\left(\ell ''^ t_1\right).  \] Finally, by proposition 4.3.16 applied to $(\ell ''^ t_ s)_{s\in [0,t]}$, \[  E_{\theta }^{\phi }\left(\ell ''^ t_1\right)=\frac{1}{t}E_{\theta }^{\phi }\left(\ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t\right).  \] Combining these identities gives ( 4.95 ). $\square$

title: Lemma 4.3.25
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Lemma 4.3.25 . For any $\ell ,\ell '\in \mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\phi )$, we have 4.98 \begin{equation} \label{eq:d1maxineq} d_1(\ell ,\ell ')\leq d_1(\ell ,\ell \lor \ell ')+d_1(\ell ',\ell \lor \ell ')\leq C_ nd_1(\ell ,\ell '), \end{equation} where $C_ n=3(n+1)2^{n+2}$. Proof. The first inequality is trivial. As for the second, we estimate \[  \begin{aligned}  d_1(\ell ,\ell \lor \ell ')=&  \mathbf{E}^{\phi }(\ell \lor \ell ')-\mathbf{E}^{\phi }(\ell )& \textup{by proposition \gerbyref{BEF0ABBC}{4.3.22}}\\  =& \lim _{t\to \infty } \frac{1}{t}E_{\theta }^{\phi }\left(\ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t\right)-\mathbf{E}^{\phi }(\ell )& \textup{by (\gerbyref{2BE4A6D4}{4.95})}\\  =&  \lim _{t\to \infty } \frac{1}{t} d_1\left(\ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t,\ell _ t\right)& \textup{by (\gerbyref{BF10DF27}{4.21})}. \end{aligned}  \] By symmetry, we find \[  d_1(\ell ,\ell \lor \ell ')+d_1(\ell ',\ell \lor \ell ')\leq \lim _{t\to \infty } \frac{1}{t} \Bigl (d_1\left(\ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t,\ell _ t\right)+d_1\left(\ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t,\ell '_ t\right)\Bigr ).  \] By theorem 4.3.6 and 4.3.5 , for each $t>0$, \[  d_1\left(\ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t,\ell _ t\right)+d_1\left(\ell _ t\lor \ell '_ t,\ell '_ t\right)\leq 3(n+1)2^{n+2} d_1(\ell _ t,\ell '_ t).  \] Now ( 4.98 ) follows. $\square$

title: Example 4.3.26
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 14.2 Geodesic rays in the space of potentials
text: Example 4.3.26 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Assume that $\varphi \leq 0$. For each $C>0$, let $(\ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t)_{t\in [0,C]}$ be the geodesic from $V_{\theta }$ to $(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi $. For each $t\geq 0$, there is $\ell ^{\varphi }_ t\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta )$ such that 4.102 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ellvarphiraydef} \ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t\xrightarrow {d_1}\ell ^{\varphi }_ t \end{equation} as $C\to \infty $. Then $\ell ^{\varphi }\in \mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta )$ and 4.103 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Elphi} \mathbf{E}(\ell ^{\varphi })=\frac{1}{n+1} \sum _{j=0}^ n \left(\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}-\int _ X \theta _{V_{\theta }}^ n\right). \end{equation} Proof. We first show that for each fixed $t\geq 0$, $\ell _ t^{\varphi ,C}$ is increasing in $C\geq t$. To see this, choose $t\leq C_1<C_2$. We need to show that \[  \ell ^{\varphi ,C_1}_ t\leq \ell ^{\varphi ,C_2}_ t.  \] Since both sides are geodesics for $t\in [0,C_1]$, it suffices to show that 4.104 \begin{equation} \label{eq:VthetaminusC1temp1} (V_{\theta }-C_1)\lor \varphi \leq \ell _{C_1}^{\varphi ,C_2}. \end{equation} Now $((V_{\theta }-t)\lor \varphi )_{t\in [0,C_2]}$ is a subgeodesic from $V_{\theta }$ to $(V_{\theta }-C_2)\lor \varphi $ by proposition 4.1.9 . Note. Here we need $\varphi \leq 0$. It is therefore a candidate in the Perron envelope defining $\ell ^{\varphi ,C_2}$, and evaluating at $t=C_1$ gives exactly ( 4.104 ). From proposition 4.1.6 , we know that for any $C>t>0$, we have \[  \ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t\leq \frac{t}{C}\Bigl ((V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi \Bigr )+\frac{C-t}{C}\cdot V_{\theta }\leq 0,  \] while the linear subgeodesic $V_\theta -t$ is a candidate in the same Perron envelope, so $V_\theta -t\leq \ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t$. Therefore, by proposition 1.2.2 , 4.105 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ellphitexp} \ell _ t^{\varphi }\coloneqq \operatorname *{sup}_{C>t}{}\! {}^{*}\ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(X,\theta ) \end{equation} for all $t\geq 0$. Thanks to proposition 3.1.47 , we have \[  \ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t\xrightarrow {d_1} \ell _ t^{\varphi }  \] as $C\to \infty $ for all $t\geq 0$. Applying proposition 4.3.17 on each interval $[0,T]$ to the increasing family $(\ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t)_{t\in [0,T]}$, $C\geq T$, shows that $\ell ^{\varphi }\in \mathcal{R}^{\infty }(X,\theta )$. It remains to compute the energy of $\ell ^{\varphi }$. We first fix $C\geq t>0$ and compute using proposition 4.3.16 : \[  E_{\theta }\left(\ell ^{\varphi ,C}_ t\right)=\frac{t}{C}E_{\theta }\Bigl ((V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi \Bigr ).  \] Letting $C\to \infty $ and applying proposition 3.1.47 , we find that \[  E_{\theta }(\ell ^{\varphi }_ t)=\lim _{C\to \infty }\frac{t}{C}E_{\theta }\Bigl ((V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi \Bigr )  \] for any $t\geq 0$. It follows that \[  \mathbf{E}(\ell ^{\varphi })=\lim _{C\to \infty }\frac{1}{C}E_{\theta }\Bigl ((V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi \Bigr ).  \] Using the definition of $E_{\theta }$, in order to obtain ( 4.103 ), it suffices to show that for each $j=0,\ldots ,n$, we have 4.106 \begin{equation} \label{eq:limCintXtemp1} \lim _{C\to \infty }\int _ X \frac{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi -V_{\theta }}{C} \, \theta _{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^{j}\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}-\int _ X \theta _{V_{\theta }}^ n. \end{equation} For this purpose, for each $C>0$, we decompose $X$ as $\{ \varphi > V_{\theta }-C\} $ and $\{ \varphi \leq V_{\theta }-C\} $. We have \[  \begin{aligned} & \int _{\{ \varphi > V_{\theta }-C\} } \frac{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi -V_{\theta }}{C} \, \theta _{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}\\  =&  \int _{\{ \varphi > V_{\theta }-C\} } \frac{\varphi -V_{\theta }}{C} \, \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}. \end{aligned}  \] On the other hand, \[  \begin{aligned} & \int _{\{ \varphi \leq V_{\theta }-C\} } \frac{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi -V_{\theta }}{C} \, \theta _{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}\\  =&  -\int _{\{ \varphi \leq V_{\theta }-C\} } \theta _{(V_{\theta }-C)\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}\\  =&  -\int _ X \theta _{V_{\theta }}^ n+\int _{\{ \varphi > V_{\theta }-C\} } \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}. \end{aligned}  \] Observe that for $C>0$, the function $\mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >V_{\theta }-C\} }C^{-1}(\varphi -V_{\theta })$ is defined quasi-everywhere. Since $\varphi \leq V_\theta $, it takes values in $[-1,0]$ outside a pluripolar set. When $C\to \infty $, these functions converge to $0$ quasi-everywhere, so the first integral above converges to $0$ by dominated convergence. Similarly, the indicators $\mathds {1}_{\{ \varphi >V_\theta -C\} }$ increase to $1$ outside a pluripolar set, hence \[  \lim _{C\to \infty }\int _{\{ \varphi >V_{\theta }-C\} } \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j} = \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}.  \] Therefore, ( 4.106 ) follows. $\square$

title: 5 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
search_title: Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: 5 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles This chapter develops the toric form of pluripotential theory in the case of an ample line bundle. Throughout the chapter, $P\subseteq M_{\mathbb R}$ is a full-dimensional smooth lattice polytope, $\Sigma $ is the corresponding fan, $X=X_\Sigma $ is the associated smooth projective toric variety, and $L=\mathcal O_ X(D_ P)$ is the ample toric line bundle defined by $P$. The basic principle is that toric plurisubharmonic metrics on $L$ can be described by convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Under this dictionary, singularity type, rooftop envelopes, Monge–Ampère mass and energy all admit convex-analytic interpretations. The Newton body of a toric potential is the main invariant in this chapter: it records the effective convex domain seen by multiplier ideals and non-pluripolar mass. The central result is Yao's theorem, stated as theorem 5.2.14 . It characterizes the torus characters belonging to multiplier-ideal spaces in terms of the Newton body. As a consequence, the asymptotic dimension of \[  \mathrm{H}^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal I(k\varphi )\right)  \] is governed by the Euclidean volume of the Newton body. This gives a toric model for the general volume theorem proved later in chapter 7 and shows, in the ample toric setting, why multiplier ideals and non-pluripolar mass should be related. The chapter also proves the real Monge–Ampère formula for toric metrics, the toric energy formula, and the expression of the $d_1$-distance in convex terms. These results will be used again in chapter 12 , where the ample assumption is removed and the Newton body is compared with partial Okounkov bodies. We assume familiarity with basic toric geometry at the level of [ CLS11 ] . Some convex-analytic facts used below are recalled in chapter A . The chapter can be skipped on a first reading if the reader is only interested in the non-toric theory, but it provides useful examples and a guiding model for several later constructions. Finally, throughout the book convex functions are understood in the usual sense: the function $\mathbb R\ni x\mapsto x^2$ is convex. This convention is opposite to the convention often used in toric geometry, including parts of [ CLS11 ] ; care is therefore needed when comparing formulas.

title: 5.1 Toric setup
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: 5.1 Toric setup Let $T$ be a complex torus of dimension $n$ Note. Namely, an algebraic group defined over $\mathbb {C}$, which is isomorphic to $\mathbb {G}_{\mathrm{m}}^ n$. and let $T_ c\subseteq T(\mathbb {C})$ denote the corresponding compact torus. Write $M$ for the character lattice of $T$, which is a free Abelian group of rank $n$. Similarly, let $N$ be the cocharacter lattice of $T$, which is the dual lattice of $M$. Given $m\in M$, the corresponding character of $T$ is denoted by $\chi ^ m$. Write $M_{\mathbb {R}}=M\otimes _{\mathbb {Z}} \mathbb {R}$ and $N_{\mathbb {R}}=N\otimes _{\mathbb {Z}}\mathbb {R}$. The pairing between $M_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $N_{\mathbb {R}}$ is denoted by $\langle \bullet ,\bullet \rangle $. Let $P\subseteq M_{\mathbb {R}}$ be a full-dimensional smooth Note. Recall that smooth means that for every vertex $v\in P$, if $w_ E$ denotes the first lattice point after $v$ as one traverses each edge $E$ of $P$ containing $v$, then $\{ w_ E-v\} _ E$ forms a basis of $M$. See [ Definition 2.4.2 , CLS11 ] . We also say $P$ is a Delzant polytope in this case. lattice polytope Note. A lattice polytope in $M_{\mathbb {R}}$ is the convex hull of finitely many points in $M$. . Given any (closed) facet $F$ of $P$, let $u_ F\in N$ denote the unique ray generator (the first non-zero integral element) of the inward normal ray of $F$. Then $P$ can be represented as 5.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Pfacetrep} P=\left\{ m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}: \langle m,u_ F \rangle \geq -a_ F\textup{ for all facets }F\textup{ of } P\right\}  \end{equation} for some uniquely determined integers $a_ F$. The presentation is called the facet presentation of $P$. Given any (closed) face $Q$ of $P$, we let $\sigma _ Q\subseteq N_{\mathbb {R}}$ be the closed convex cone generated by the $u_ F$'s, where $F$ runs over all facets of $P$ containing $Q$. When $Q=P$, $\sigma _ P$ is understood as $\{ 0\} $. Let $\Sigma $ be the (inner) normal fan of $P$. Namely, \[  \Sigma =\left\{ \sigma _ Q:Q\textup{ is a face of }P\right\} .  \] The notation $\Sigma (1)$ denotes the set of rays in $\Sigma $. Note that $\Sigma (1)$ is in bijective correspondence with the set of facets of $P$. In fact, given any facet $F$ of $P$, the cone $\sigma _ F$ is just the ray generated by $u_ F$, namely, the inward normal ray of $F$. For any $\rho \in \Sigma (1)$, let $u_{\rho }\in N$ denote the ray generator of $\rho $, namely the first non-zero element in $N\cap \rho $. If $\rho =\sigma _ F$ for some facet $F$ of $P$, then $u_{\rho }=u_ F$. Now the facet presentation ( 5.1 ) can be equivalently rewritten as \[  P=\left\{ m\in M_{\mathbb {R}} : \langle m,u_{\rho } \rangle \geq -a_{\rho }\textup{ for all }\rho \in \Sigma (1) \right\} .  \] Let $\operatorname{Supp}_ P\colon N_{\mathbb {R}} \rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ denote the support function of $P$. Recall that the support function (example A.1.5 ) of $P$ is defined as \[  \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)=\max \left\{  \langle m,n \rangle : m\in P \right\} .  \] Note that our support function differs from [ Proposition 4.2.14 , CLS11 ] , where instead of a maximum, they took the minimum. Recall that the characteristic function $\chi _ P\colon M_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow \{ 0,\infty \} $ of $P$ is defined as in example A.1.4 : \[  \chi _ P(m)\coloneqq \begin{cases}  0,& \quad m\in P;\\  \infty ,& \quad m\not\in P. \end{cases}  \] Let $X=X_{\Sigma }$ be the smooth projective toric variety corresponding to $\Sigma $. See [ Theorem 3.1.5 , CLS11 ] for the construction of $X$ and [ Theorem 3.1.19 , CLS11 ] for the smoothness of $X$. There is a canonical embedding $T\subseteq X$ as a dense Zariski open subset. Let $D$ be the Cartier divisor on $X$ defined by $P$: \[  D=\sum _{\rho \in \Sigma (1)} a_{\rho }D_{\rho },  \] where $D_{\rho }$ is the toric prime divisor defined by $\rho $ under the orbit-cone correspondence [ Theorem 3.2.6 , CLS11 ] . Let $L$ be the toric line bundle induced by $P$, namely $L=\mathcal{O}_ X(D)$. Since $P$ is a smooth (Delzant) lattice polytope, $L$ is very ample by [ Proposition 2.4.4, Proposition 6.1.10 , CLS11 ] ; in particular, $L$ is ample. We will choose the base $\mathrm{e}$ for the logarithm map 5.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:log} \mathbb {C}^*\rightarrow \mathbb {R},\quad z\mapsto \log |z|^2.\footnotemark \end{equation} Note. Be careful when you compare with other references, some people prefer $\log |z|$, $-\log |z|$ or $-\log |z|^2$ instead. This choice is fixed throughout the book. We have a canonical identification \[  T(\mathbb {C})=\mathrm{Hom}(M,\mathbb {C}^*)\xlongrightarrow {\sim } N\otimes _{\mathbb {Z}}\mathbb {C}^*.  \] The logarithm map then induces a tropicalization map after tensoring with $N$: 5.5 \begin{equation}  \operatorname{Trop}\colon T(\mathbb {C})\rightarrow N_{\mathbb {R}},\quad p\mapsto \left( M \ni m\mapsto \log \left|\chi ^ m(p)\right|^2 \right). \end{equation} Before proceeding, it is always helpful to understand everything in our favorite example. Example 5.1.1 . We take $n=1$ and $P=[0,1]\subseteq M_{\mathbb {R}}=\mathbb {R}$. In this case, the facet representation ( 5.1 ) becomes \[  P=\bigl \{ m\in \mathbb {R}: \langle m,1 \rangle \geq 0, \langle m,-1 \rangle \geq -1\bigr \} ,  \] with $u_{\{ 0\} }=1$, $u_{\{ 1\} }=-1$, $a_{\{ 0\} }=0$ and $a_{\{ 1\} }=1$. The normal fan $\Sigma $ is \[  \Sigma =\bigl \{ (-\infty ,0], \{ 0\} , [0,\infty ) \bigr \} .  \] See 5.1 . 5.1 The fan $\Sigma $ of $\mathbb {P}^1$ in $N_{\mathbb {R}}=\mathbb {R}$, consisting of the two rays $(-\infty ,0]$, $[0,\infty )$ and the cone $\{ 0\} $. The corresponding toric variety is just $X=\mathbb {P}^1$. Under the orbit-cone correspondence, we have \[  D_{[0,\infty )}=[0],\quad D_{(-\infty ,0]}=[\infty ].  \] The associated divisor $D=[\infty ]$ and therefore, \[  L=\mathcal{O}_ X(D)=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^1}(1).  \]

5.2 Toric plurisubharmonic functions We continue to use the notations of section 5.1 . Lemma 5.2.1 . Let $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a function. Then the following are equivalent: $F$ is convex and takes values in $\mathbb {R}$, and $\operatorname{Trop}^*F$ is plurisubharmonic on $T(\mathbb {C})$. Proof. We may choose an identification $N\cong \mathbb {Z}^ n$ so that we have an identification $T(\mathbb {C})\cong \mathbb {C}^{*n}$. Then $\operatorname{Trop}$ is identified with the map \[  \operatorname{Trop}\colon \mathbb {C}^{*n}ightarrow \mathbb {R}^ n,\quad (z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)\mapsto \left(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2ight).  \] 1 $\implies $ 2 . By the standard convolution regularization of finite convex functions, let $F_ k\in C^{\infty }(\mathbb {R}^ n)\cap \mathrm{Conv}(\mathbb {R}^ n)$ be a decreasing sequence with limit $F$. It follows from a straightforward computation that 5.6  egin{equation} \label{eq:ddctrop}  egin{split}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Trop}^*F_ k(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n) =&  rac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi } \sum _{i,j=1}^ n \partial _{ij}F_ k\left(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2ight)\ & 	imes z_ i^{-1}\overline{z_ j}^{-1}\mathrm{d}z_ i\wedge \mathrm{d}\overline{z_ j}. \end{split} \end{equation} So $\operatorname{Trop}^* F_ k$ is plurisubharmonic. It follows from proposition 1.2.2 that $\operatorname{Trop}^* F$ is plurisubharmonic. 2 $\implies $ 1 . It follows from 1.2.10 that $F$ is finite. Moreover, by radial regularization, we may find a decreasing sequence $\varphi _ k$ of $(S^1)^ n$-invariant smooth psh functions on $\mathbb {C}^{*n}$ with limit $\operatorname{Trop}^*F$. Write $\varphi _ k=\operatorname{Trop}^* F_ k$ for some function $F_ k\colon \mathbb {R}^ nightarrow \mathbb {R}$; it follows from ( 5.6 ) that $F_ k$ is convex for all $k$. Therefore, $F$ is convex by A.1.12 . $\square$ Next we define a canonical Kähler form in $c_1(L)$. Let $G_0\colon M_{\mathbb {R}}ightarrow (-\infty ,\infty ]$ be defined as 5.9  egin{equation} \label{eq:G0def} G_0(m)\coloneqq  egin{cases}  \sum \limits _{ho \in \Sigma (1)} \left(\langle m, u_{ho }angle +a_{ho }ight)\log \left(\langle m, u_{ho }angle +a_{ho }ight) ootnotemark ,& 	extup{if }m\in P,\  \infty ,&  	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Note. We understand that $0\log 0=0$ in this expression. This is a closed proper convex function and $G_0\sim \chi _ P$, where $\sim $ is the relation defined in definition A.1.17 . Let 5.12  egin{equation} \label{eq:F0def} F_0=G_0^* \in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N_{\mathbb {R}},P). \end{equation} Here $G_0^*$ is the Legendre transform of $G_0$, as recalled in definition A.2.1 . The set $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N_{\mathbb {R}},P)$ is defined in definition A.3.1 . By Guillemin's theorem [ Gui94 , CDG03 ] , $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Trop}^* F_0$ can be extended to a unique Kähler form $\omega $ in $c_1(L)$. The Kähler form $\omega $ is clearly $T_ c$-invariant. For each $ho \in \Sigma (1)$, we write \[  r_{ho }(m)=\log \left(\langle m,u_{ho }angle +a_{ho }ight)+1,\quad m\in P.  \] It follows from ( 5.9 ) that 5.13  egin{equation} \label{eq:nablaG0} 
abla G_0(m)=\sum _{ho \in \Sigma (1)} r_{ho }(m)u_{ho },\quad m\in \operatorname{Int}P. \end{equation} Example 5.2.2 . Let us move on with our favorite example example 5.1.1 . We continue to use the same notations. In this case, \[  G_0(m)=  egin{cases}  m\log m+(1-m)\log (1-m),&  	extup{if } m\in [0,1],\  \infty ,& 	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] The Legendre transform is given Note. While reading an advanced mathematical textbook/paper, I usually tend to trust the authors for their elementary computations. A few years ago, I was asked to present the result of a landmark paper written by two respected mathematicians on a conference. After spending a few days on the elementary integrals, I found out that all non-trivial constants in that paper were wrong. So I ask the readers to really verify this expression, if it is not obvious to you. by \[  F_0(n)=\log \left(1+\mathrm{e}^ night).  \] Composing with the tropicalization map, we find that \[  \omega |_{\mathbb {C}^*}(z)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \left(1+|z|^2ight).  \] This is exactly the Fubini–Study metric as we have seen in example 1.8.5 . We can now explain one subtlety: in our expression ( 5.9 ), there is no factor $1/2$ before the sum; the absence of the factor $1/2$ matches the choice $\operatorname{Trop}(z)=\log |z|^2$ rather than $\log |z|$ in our tropicalization map ( 5.4 ). Let $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ denote the set of $T_ c$-invariant $\omega $-psh functions. Theorem 5.2.3 . There are canonical bijections between the following three sets: The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$, the set $\mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P)$ in definition A.3.1 , namely, the set of convex functions $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}ightarrow \mathbb {R}$ satisfying $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$, and the set of closed proper convex functions $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying \[  G|_{M_{\mathbb {R}}\setminus P}\equiv \infty .  \] For the notions of closedness and properness, we refer to definition A.1.2 and definition A.1.13 . Proof. The bijection between 2 and 3 is the classical Legendre duality. Given $F$ as in 2 , we construct $G=F^*$ and vice versa , see proposition A.2.12 . The map from 1 to 2 is given as follows: Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$, since $\varphi $ is $T_ c$-invariant, we can find $f\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that 5.16  egin{equation} \label{ex:varphitropf} \varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})}=\operatorname{Trop}^*f. \end{equation} We then define $F=f+F_0$. Then $\operatorname{Trop}^* F\in \mathrm{PSH}(T(\mathbb {C}))$. By 5.2.1 , $F(n)$ is finite for any $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $F$ is convex. Moreover, $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ since $\varphi $ is bounded from above on the compact space $X$ and $F_0\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$. Conversely, given a map $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P)$, then \[  \operatorname{Trop}^*(F-F_0)\in \mathrm{PSH}\left(T(\mathbb {C}),\omega |_{T(\mathbb {C})}ight).  \] Since $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ and $F_0\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P$, the difference $F-F_0$ is bounded from above. Hence the corresponding local psh potentials are locally bounded from above near $X\setminus T(\mathbb {C})$. It follows from theorem 1.2.9 that this function can be extended uniquely to an $\omega $-psh function on $X$. The uniqueness of the extension guarantees its $T_ c$-invariance. The two maps are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$ Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$, we will write $F_{\varphi }$ and $G_{\varphi }$ for the convex functions given by theorem 5.2.3 . From the proof, we have the following relations: 5.17  egin{equation} \label{eq:FvarphidefGdef} \varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})}=\operatorname{Trop}^*\left(F_{\varphi }-F_0ight),\quad G_{\varphi }=F_{\varphi }^*. \end{equation} In particular, $\varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})}$ is locally bounded. We will frequently use this result without further explanation. Example 5.2.4 . Let us take our favorite example example 5.2.2 again. We will continue to use the same notations. Recall that in example 1.8.9 and example 3.1.14 , we constructed two $S^1$-invariant functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. We begin with the function $\varphi $ in example 1.8.9 . Recall that \[  \varphi (z)=\log  rac{|z|^2}{|z|^2+1}  \] for $z\in \mathbb {C}$. The function $f\colon \mathbb {R}ightarrow \mathbb {R}$ in ( 5.16 ) is therefore \[  f(n)=\log  rac{\mathrm{e}^{n}}{1+\mathrm{e}^{n}}.  \] Therefore, $F_{\varphi }\colon \mathbb {R}ightarrow \mathbb {R}$ is \[  F_{\varphi }(n)=n.  \] Correspondingly, $G_{\varphi }\colon \mathbb {R}ightarrow \mathbb {R}$ is \[  G_{\varphi }(m)=  egin{cases}  0,& 	extup{if } m=1;\  \infty ,& 	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Similarly, if $\psi $ denotes the function in example 3.1.14 , then the function $f$ in ( 5.16 ) is \[  f(n)=  egin{cases}  -\log \left(\mathrm{e}^ n+1 ight)+(-\log (-n))\lor (n+2),& 	extup{if } n<-\log 2;\  2+\log  rac{\mathrm{e}^{n}}{1+\mathrm{e}^{n}},& 	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Therefore, \[  F_{\psi }(n)=  egin{cases}  (-\log (-n))\lor (n+2),& 	extup{if } n<-\log 2;\  2+n,& 	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] The Legendre transform is tricky to compute. Let $\lambda $ be the large solution of $\log x=x-2$. So $\lambda \approx 3.146$. The smaller solution is around $0.159<\log 2\approx 0.693$. It might be helpful to have a look at the poorly drawn picture 5.2 . 5.2 The graphs of $\log x$ and $x-2$. It is immediate that $G_{\psi }(m)=\infty $ unless $m\in [0,1]$. Let us assume that $m\in [0,1]$. Then \[   egin{aligned}  G_{\psi }(m)=& \sup _{n\in \mathbb {R}} \left( mn-F_{\psi }(n)ight)\  =&  \sup _{n<-\log 2} \left( mn-(-\log (-n))\lor (n+2)ight) \lor \sup _{n\geq -\log 2} (mn-n-2)\  =&  \sup _{n>\log 2} \left( -mn+(\log n)\land (n-2)ight) \lor \left((1-m)\log 2-2ight). \end{aligned}  \] Let us focus on the first part, which can be decomposed further into \[   egin{aligned} &  \sup _{n>\log 2} \left( -mn+(\log n)\land (n-2)ight)\  =&  \sup _{n\in \left(\log 2,\lambda ight]} (n-2-mn) \lor \sup _{n>\lambda } (\log n-mn)\  =&  \left( (1-m)\lambda -2 ight) \lor \sup _{n>\lambda } \left(\log n-mnight). \end{aligned}  \] The latter part can be computed easily: \[  \sup _{n>\lambda } \left(\log n-mnight)=  egin{cases}  -\log m-1,& 	extup{if } m\in \left(0,\lambda ^{-1}ight];\  \log \lambda -m\lambda ,&  	extup{if }m\in \left(\lambda ^{-1},1ight]. \end{cases}  \] Putting everything together, we find \[  G_{\psi }(m)=  egin{cases}  (-\log m-1)\lor \left( (1-m)\lambda -2 ight) ,& 	extup{if } m\in \left(0,\lambda ^{-1}ight];\  (\log \lambda -m\lambda )\lor \left( (1-m)\lambda -2 ight),&  	extup{if }m\in \left(\lambda ^{-1},1ight]. \end{cases}  \] This can be further simplified, the final result is \[  G_{\psi }(m)=  egin{cases}  -\log m-1 ,& 	extup{if } m\in \left(0,\lambda ^{-1}ight];\  (1-m)\lambda -2 ,&  	extup{if }m\in \left(\lambda ^{-1},1ight];\  \infty ,& 	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] The graph of $G_{\psi }$ on $(0,1]$ is sketched in 5.3 . 5.3 The graph of $G_{\psi }$ on $(0,1]$. We observe a few elementary facts. Proposition 5.2.5 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$. The following are equivalent: $\varphi \preceq \psi $, $F_{\varphi }\preceq F_{\psi }$, and $G_{\psi }\preceq G_{\varphi }$. The same holds if we replace all $\preceq $'s by $\leq $. Proof. The equivalence between 1 and 2 follows from the definition ( 5.17 ). The equivalence between 2 and 3 follows from the definition of the Legendre transform. $\square$ Similarly, we have Proposition 5.2.6 . Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ and $C\in \mathbb {R}$. We have \[  F_{\varphi +C}=F_{\varphi }+C,\quad G_{\varphi +C}=G_{\varphi }-C.  \] Proof. The first equality follows from ( 5.17 ). The second is obtained by taking the Legendre transform. $\square$ Proposition 5.2.7 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ with $\varphi \land \psi 
ot\equiv -\infty $, then $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ and \[  F_{\varphi \land \psi }=F_{\varphi }\land F_{\psi },\quad G_{\varphi \land \psi }=G_{\varphi }\lor G_{\psi }.  \] The operators $\land $ and $\lor $ are defined in definition A.1.9 and definition A.1.10 . Proof. By proposition 3.1.2 , we have $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Since $\varphi $ and $\psi $ are $T_ c$-invariant, the set of candidates in the definition of $\varphi \land \psi $ is preserved by the action of $T_ c$. Hence $\varphi \land \psi $ is $T_ c$-invariant as well. So $\varphi \land \psi $ is the biggest element in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ which is dominated by both $\varphi $ and $\psi $. In view of theorem 5.2.3 and proposition 5.2.5 , $G_{\varphi \land \psi }$ is the smallest closed proper convex function $G$ on $M_{\mathbb {R}}$ dominating both $G_{\varphi }$ and $G_{\psi }$, which is just $G_{\varphi }\lor G_{\psi }$. For the statement about $F$, we use proposition A.2.10 : \[  F_{\varphi \land \psi }=(G_\varphi \lor G_\psi )^*=\operatorname{cl}(F_\varphi \land F_\psi ).  \] Since $\varphi \land \psi 
ot\equiv -\infty $, $F_{\varphi \land \psi }=(G_\varphi \lor G_\psi )^*$ is finite on all of $N_{\mathbb R}$. It follows that $F_\varphi \land F_\psi >-\infty $, and hence is finite on all of $N_{\mathbb R}$ as well. Being finite and convex on $N_{\mathbb R}$, it is continuous, hence closed. Therefore \[  F_{\varphi \land \psi }=F_\varphi \land F_\psi .  \] $\square$ Example 5.2.8 . Now we can give an example of $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ with $\varphi \land \psi \equiv -\infty $. We take $P=[0,1]$ so that $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $\omega $ is the Fubini–Study metric. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be such that \[  \varphi (z)=\log  rac{|z|^2}{|z|^2+1}  \] for $z\in \mathbb {C}$. We have computed that $G_{\varphi }$ in example 5.2.4 : \[  G_{\varphi }(m)=  egin{cases}  0,& 	extup{if } m=1,\  \infty ,& 	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Now we define $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ as the unique function such that \[  \psi (z)=\log  rac{1}{|z|^2+1}  \] for $z\in \mathbb {C}$. Then a similar computation shows that \[  G_{\psi }(m)=  egin{cases}  0,& 	extup{if } m=0,\  \infty ,& 	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Now we claim that $\varphi \land \psi \equiv -\infty $. Otherwise, we would have \[  G_{\varphi \land \psi }=G_{\varphi }\lor G_{\psi }\equiv \infty ,  \] which is not proper. Proposition 5.2.9 . Let $\{ \varphi _ i\} _{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ and \[  F_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}= igvee _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}=\operatorname{cl} igwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Moreover, if $I$ is finite, then \[  G_{\max _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}= igwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Similarly, if $\{ \varphi _ i\} _{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ such that $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i
ot\equiv -\infty $, then $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ and \[  F_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\inf _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}= igvee _{i\in I}G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Recall that the closure $\operatorname{cl}$ is defined in definition A.1.13 . Proof. Thanks to A.1.12 and proposition A.1.7 , in both cases, the statement for $F$ is clear. The corresponding statement for $G$ is obtained via proposition A.2.10 . When $I$ is finite, the convex function $ igvee _ i F_{\varphi _ i}$ is finite on all $N_{\mathbb R}$, hence closed. Therefore no additional closure is needed. $\square$ The complex Monge–Ampère operator is closely related to the real one: Proposition 5.2.10 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$. Then 5.41  egin{equation} \label{eq:tropMAmea} \operatorname{Trop}_* \left(\omega |_{T(\mathbb {C})}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})} ight)^ n=\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}(F_{\varphi }). \end{equation} In particular, \[  \int _ X \omega _{\varphi }^ n =\int _{N_{\mathbb {R}}}\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}(F_{\varphi })=n! \operatorname{vol}\overline{\{ G_{\varphi }<\infty \} }  \] and \[  \int _ X \omega ^ n=n!\operatorname{vol}P.  \] Here the real Monge–Ampère operator is defined in definition A.4.1 . The normalization of the Lebesgue measure $\operatorname{vol}$ on $M_{\mathbb {R}}$ is such that the fundamental lattice cube has measure $1$. Note. In some references like [ GKZ08 ] , the normalization is so that the fundamental lattice cube has measure $n!$. Be careful when making comparisons with these references. Proof. We only need to prove ( 5.41 ). By proposition A.3.5 , we can find a decreasing sequence \[  F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)\cap C^\infty (N_{\mathbb R})  \] with limit $F_\varphi $. By theorem 5.2.3 , each $F_ j$ corresponds to a bounded toric potential $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$. By theorem 2.1.4 and theorem A.4.4 , it suffices to establish ( 5.41 ) for the $\varphi _ j$'s. We may therefore reduce to the case where $F_{\varphi }$ is smooth. We write $F=F_{\varphi }$ to simplify the notations. The notations $a_ i=\log |z_ i|^2$ will be used, where $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Next we fix an identification $N=\mathbb {Z}^ n$. text: Lemma 5.2.1 . Let $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a function. Then the following are equivalent: $F$ is convex and takes values in $\mathbb {R}$, and $\operatorname{Trop}^*F$ is plurisubharmonic on $T(\mathbb {C})$. Proof. We may choose an identification $N\cong \mathbb {Z}^ n$ so that we have an identification $T(\mathbb {C})\cong \mathbb {C}^{*n}$. Then $\operatorname{Trop}$ is identified with the map \[  \operatorname{Trop}\colon \mathbb {C}^{*n}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}^ n,\quad (z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)\mapsto \left(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2\right).  \] 1 $\implies $ 2 . By the standard convolution regularization of finite convex functions, let $F_ k\in C^{\infty }(\mathbb {R}^ n)\cap \mathrm{Conv}(\mathbb {R}^ n)$ be a decreasing sequence with limit $F$. It follows from a straightforward computation that 5.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ddctrop} \begin{split}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Trop}^*F_ k(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n) =& \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi } \sum _{i,j=1}^ n \partial _{ij}F_ k\left(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2\right)\\ & \times z_ i^{-1}\overline{z_ j}^{-1}\mathrm{d}z_ i\wedge \mathrm{d}\overline{z_ j}. \end{split} \end{equation} So $\operatorname{Trop}^* F_ k$ is plurisubharmonic. It follows from proposition 1.2.2 that $\operatorname{Trop}^* F$ is plurisubharmonic. 2 $\implies $ 1 . It follows from 1.2.10 that $F$ is finite. Moreover, by radial regularization, we may find a decreasing sequence $\varphi _ k$ of $(S^1)^ n$-invariant smooth psh functions on $\mathbb {C}^{*n}$ with limit $\operatorname{Trop}^*F$. Write $\varphi _ k=\operatorname{Trop}^* F_ k$ for some function $F_ k\colon \mathbb {R}^ n\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$; it follows from ( 5.6 ) that $F_ k$ is convex for all $k$. Therefore, $F$ is convex by A.1.12 . $\square$

title: Example 5.2.2
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Example 5.2.2 . Let us move on with our favorite example example 5.1.1 . We continue to use the same notations. In this case, \[  G_0(m)= \begin{cases}  m\log m+(1-m)\log (1-m),&  \textup{if } m\in [0,1],\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] The Legendre transform is given Note. While reading an advanced mathematical textbook/paper, I usually tend to trust the authors for their elementary computations. A few years ago, I was asked to present the result of a landmark paper written by two respected mathematicians on a conference. After spending a few days on the elementary integrals, I found out that all non-trivial constants in that paper were wrong. So I ask the readers to really verify this expression, if it is not obvious to you. by \[  F_0(n)=\log \left(1+\mathrm{e}^ n\right).  \] Composing with the tropicalization map, we find that \[  \omega |_{\mathbb {C}^*}(z)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \left(1+|z|^2\right).  \] This is exactly the Fubini–Study metric as we have seen in example 1.8.5 . We can now explain one subtlety: in our expression ( 5.9 ), there is no factor $1/2$ before the sum; the absence of the factor $1/2$ matches the choice $\operatorname{Trop}(z)=\log |z|^2$ rather than $\log |z|$ in our tropicalization map ( 5.4 ).

title: Theorem 5.2.3
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Theorem 5.2.3 . There are canonical bijections between the following three sets: The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$, the set $\mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P)$ in definition A.3.1 , namely, the set of convex functions $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ satisfying $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$, and the set of closed proper convex functions $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying \[  G|_{M_{\mathbb {R}}\setminus P}\equiv \infty .  \] Proof. The bijection between 2 and 3 is the classical Legendre duality. Given $F$ as in 2 , we construct $G=F^*$ and vice versa , see proposition A.2.12 . The map from 1 to 2 is given as follows: Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$, since $\varphi $ is $T_ c$-invariant, we can find $f\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that 5.16 \begin{equation} \label{ex:varphitropf} \varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})}=\operatorname{Trop}^*f. \end{equation} We then define $F=f+F_0$. Then $\operatorname{Trop}^* F\in \mathrm{PSH}(T(\mathbb {C}))$. By 5.2.1 , $F(n)$ is finite for any $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $F$ is convex. Moreover, $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ since $\varphi $ is bounded from above on the compact space $X$ and $F_0\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$. Conversely, given a map $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P)$, then \[  \operatorname{Trop}^*(F-F_0)\in \mathrm{PSH}\left(T(\mathbb {C}),\omega |_{T(\mathbb {C})}\right).  \] Since $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ and $F_0\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P$, the difference $F-F_0$ is bounded from above. Hence the corresponding local psh potentials are locally bounded from above near $X\setminus T(\mathbb {C})$. It follows from theorem 1.2.9 that this function can be extended uniquely to an $\omega $-psh function on $X$. The uniqueness of the extension guarantees its $T_ c$-invariance. The two maps are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$

title: Example 5.2.4
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Example 5.2.4 . Let us take our favorite example example 5.2.2 again. We will continue to use the same notations. Recall that in example 1.8.9 and example 3.1.14 , we constructed two $S^1$-invariant functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. We begin with the function $\varphi $ in example 1.8.9 . Recall that \[  \varphi (z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{|z|^2+1}  \] for $z\in \mathbb {C}$. The function $f\colon \mathbb {R}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ in ( 5.16 ) is therefore \[  f(n)=\log \frac{\mathrm{e}^{n}}{1+\mathrm{e}^{n}}.  \] Therefore, $F_{\varphi }\colon \mathbb {R}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ is \[  F_{\varphi }(n)=n.  \] Correspondingly, $G_{\varphi }\colon \mathbb {R}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ is \[  G_{\varphi }(m)= \begin{cases}  0,& \textup{if } m=1;\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Similarly, if $\psi $ denotes the function in example 3.1.14 , then the function $f$ in ( 5.16 ) is \[  f(n)= \begin{cases}  -\log \left(\mathrm{e}^ n+1 \right)+(-\log (-n))\lor (n+2),& \textup{if } n<-\log 2;\\  2+\log \frac{\mathrm{e}^{n}}{1+\mathrm{e}^{n}},& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Therefore, \[  F_{\psi }(n)= \begin{cases}  (-\log (-n))\lor (n+2),& \textup{if } n<-\log 2;\\  2+n,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] The Legendre transform is tricky to compute. Let $\lambda $ be the large solution of $\log x=x-2$. So $\lambda \approx 3.146$. The smaller solution is around $0.159<\log 2\approx 0.693$. It might be helpful to have a look at the poorly drawn picture 5.2 . 5.2 The graphs of $\log x$ and $x-2$. It is immediate that $G_{\psi }(m)=\infty $ unless $m\in [0,1]$. Let us assume that $m\in [0,1]$. Then \[  \begin{aligned}  G_{\psi }(m)=& \sup _{n\in \mathbb {R}} \left( mn-F_{\psi }(n)\right)\\  =&  \sup _{n<-\log 2} \left( mn-(-\log (-n))\lor (n+2)\right) \lor \sup _{n\geq -\log 2} (mn-n-2)\\  =&  \sup _{n>\log 2} \left( -mn+(\log n)\land (n-2)\right) \lor \left((1-m)\log 2-2\right). \end{aligned}  \] Let us focus on the first part, which can be decomposed further into \[  \begin{aligned} &  \sup _{n>\log 2} \left( -mn+(\log n)\land (n-2)\right)\\  =&  \sup _{n\in \left(\log 2,\lambda \right]} (n-2-mn) \lor \sup _{n>\lambda } (\log n-mn)\\  =&  \left( (1-m)\lambda -2 \right) \lor \sup _{n>\lambda } \left(\log n-mn\right). \end{aligned}  \] The latter part can be computed easily: \[  \sup _{n>\lambda } \left(\log n-mn\right)= \begin{cases}  -\log m-1,& \textup{if } m\in \left(0,\lambda ^{-1}\right];\\  \log \lambda -m\lambda ,&  \textup{if }m\in \left(\lambda ^{-1},1\right]. \end{cases}  \] Putting everything together, we find \[  G_{\psi }(m)= \begin{cases}  (-\log m-1)\lor \left( (1-m)\lambda -2 \right) ,& \textup{if } m\in \left(0,\lambda ^{-1}\right];\\  (\log \lambda -m\lambda )\lor \left( (1-m)\lambda -2 \right),&  \textup{if }m\in \left(\lambda ^{-1},1\right]. \end{cases}  \] This can be further simplified, the final result is \[  G_{\psi }(m)= \begin{cases}  -\log m-1 ,& \textup{if } m\in \left(0,\lambda ^{-1}\right];\\  (1-m)\lambda -2 ,&  \textup{if }m\in \left(\lambda ^{-1},1\right];\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] The graph of $G_{\psi }$ on $(0,1]$ is sketched in 5.3 . 5.3 The graph of $G_{\psi }$ on $(0,1]$.

title: Proposition 5.2.5
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Proposition 5.2.5 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$. The following are equivalent: $\varphi \preceq \psi $, $F_{\varphi }\preceq F_{\psi }$, and $G_{\psi }\preceq G_{\varphi }$. The same holds if we replace all $\preceq $'s by $\leq $. Proof. The equivalence between 1 and 2 follows from the definition ( 5.17 ). The equivalence between 2 and 3 follows from the definition of the Legendre transform. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.2.6
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Proposition 5.2.6 . Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ and $C\in \mathbb {R}$. We have \[  F_{\varphi +C}=F_{\varphi }+C,\quad G_{\varphi +C}=G_{\varphi }-C.  \] Proof. The first equality follows from ( 5.17 ). The second is obtained by taking the Legendre transform. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.2.7
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Proposition 5.2.7 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ with $\varphi \land \psi \not\equiv -\infty $, then $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ and \[  F_{\varphi \land \psi }=F_{\varphi }\land F_{\psi },\quad G_{\varphi \land \psi }=G_{\varphi }\lor G_{\psi }.  \] Proof. By proposition 3.1.2 , we have $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Since $\varphi $ and $\psi $ are $T_ c$-invariant, the set of candidates in the definition of $\varphi \land \psi $ is preserved by the action of $T_ c$. Hence $\varphi \land \psi $ is $T_ c$-invariant as well. So $\varphi \land \psi $ is the biggest element in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ which is dominated by both $\varphi $ and $\psi $. In view of theorem 5.2.3 and proposition 5.2.5 , $G_{\varphi \land \psi }$ is the smallest closed proper convex function $G$ on $M_{\mathbb {R}}$ dominating both $G_{\varphi }$ and $G_{\psi }$, which is just $G_{\varphi }\lor G_{\psi }$. For the statement about $F$, we use proposition A.2.10 : \[  F_{\varphi \land \psi }=(G_\varphi \lor G_\psi )^*=\operatorname{cl}(F_\varphi \land F_\psi ).  \] Since $\varphi \land \psi \not\equiv -\infty $, $F_{\varphi \land \psi }=(G_\varphi \lor G_\psi )^*$ is finite on all of $N_{\mathbb R}$. It follows that $F_\varphi \land F_\psi >-\infty $, and hence is finite on all of $N_{\mathbb R}$ as well. Being finite and convex on $N_{\mathbb R}$, it is continuous, hence closed. Therefore \[  F_{\varphi \land \psi }=F_\varphi \land F_\psi .  \] $\square$

title: Example 5.2.8
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Example 5.2.8 . Now we can give an example of $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ with $\varphi \land \psi \equiv -\infty $. We take $P=[0,1]$ so that $X=\mathbb {P}^1$ and $\omega $ is the Fubini–Study metric. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be such that \[  \varphi (z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{|z|^2+1}  \] for $z\in \mathbb {C}$. We have computed that $G_{\varphi }$ in example 5.2.4 : \[  G_{\varphi }(m)= \begin{cases}  0,& \textup{if } m=1,\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Now we define $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ as the unique function such that \[  \psi (z)=\log \frac{1}{|z|^2+1}  \] for $z\in \mathbb {C}$. Then a similar computation shows that \[  G_{\psi }(m)= \begin{cases}  0,& \textup{if } m=0,\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Now we claim that $\varphi \land \psi \equiv -\infty $. Otherwise, we would have \[  G_{\varphi \land \psi }=G_{\varphi }\lor G_{\psi }\equiv \infty ,  \] which is not proper.

title: Proposition 5.2.9
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Proposition 5.2.9 . Let $\{ \varphi _ i\} _{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ and \[  F_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}=\bigvee _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}=\operatorname{cl}\bigwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Moreover, if $I$ is finite, then \[  G_{\max _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\bigwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Similarly, if $\{ \varphi _ i\} _{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ such that $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i\not\equiv -\infty $, then $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ and \[  F_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\inf _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\bigvee _{i\in I}G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Proof. Thanks to A.1.12 and proposition A.1.7 , in both cases, the statement for $F$ is clear. The corresponding statement for $G$ is obtained via proposition A.2.10 . When $I$ is finite, the convex function $\bigvee _ i F_{\varphi _ i}$ is finite on all $N_{\mathbb R}$, hence closed. Therefore no additional closure is needed. $\square$

title: Definition 5.2.11
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Definition 5.2.11 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$. We define its Newton body as \[  \Delta (\omega ,\varphi )\coloneqq \overline{\{ G_{\varphi }<\infty \} }\subseteq P.  \] Note that $\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )$ is a convex body.

title: Example 5.2.12
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Example 5.2.12 . By ( 5.9 ), we have \[  \Delta (\omega ,0)=P.  \] In the case of example 5.2.4 , we have \[  \Delta (\omega ,\varphi )=\{ 1\} ,\quad \Delta (\omega ,\psi )=[0,1].  \] Observe that in the latter case, \[  \{ G_{\psi }<\infty \} \subsetneq P.  \]

title: Proposition 5.2.13
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Proposition 5.2.13 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$. Then $P_{\omega }[\varphi ]\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$ and 5.53 \begin{equation} \label{eq:toricPenv} G_{P_{\omega }[\varphi ]}(x)= \begin{cases}  G_0(x),& \textup{if } x\in \Delta (\omega ,\varphi );\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Proof. By ( 3.4 ), we have \[  P_{\omega }[\varphi ]=\operatorname *{sup}_{C\in \mathbb {R}}{}\! {}^{*}\bigl ((\varphi +C)\land 0\bigr ).  \] It follows from proposition 5.2.6 , proposition 5.2.7 and proposition 5.2.9 that $P_{\omega }[\varphi ]\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$. Moreover, by the same propositions, we have \[  G_{P_{\omega }[\varphi ]}=\operatorname{cl}\inf _{C\in \mathbb {R}} \left( G_{0}\lor (G_{\varphi }-C) \right).  \] We spell out the last closure. Set \[  K=\inf _{C\in \mathbb {R}} \left( G_{0}\lor (G_{\varphi }-C) \right).  \] If $x\in \operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }$, then $G_{\varphi }(x)-C\leq G_0(x)$ for $C$ large enough, hence $K(x)=G_0(x)$. If $x\notin \operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }$, then $K(x)=\infty $. Since $\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }}$ and $G_0$ is continuous on $P$, the lower semicontinuous regularization $\operatorname{cl}K$ is equal to $G_0$ on $\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )$ and equal to $\infty $ outside $\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )$. This is exactly ( 5.53 ). $\square$

title: Corollary 5.2.15
section: 18.3 Toric pluripotential theory on ample line bundles
text: Corollary 5.2.15 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\omega )$. Then \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }\frac{n!}{k^ n}h^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )\right)= n!\operatorname{vol}\Delta (\omega ,\varphi ).  \] Proof. Take $k>0$. Let $F_{0,k}$ denote the Guillemin potential associated with the polytope $kP$. On $T(\mathbb C)$, set \[  \widetilde\varphi _ k=\operatorname{Trop}^*(kF_\varphi -F_{0,k}).  \] Then $\widetilde\varphi _ k$ is the toric potential, with respect to the reference metric associated with $kP$, corresponding to the singular metric $h^ k\exp (-k\varphi )$ on $L^ k$. It differs from $k\varphi $ by the smooth toric function $\operatorname{Trop}^*(kF_0-F_{0,k})$. Hence \[  \mathcal I(\widetilde\varphi _ k)=\mathcal I(k\varphi ).  \] Moreover, the convex function associated with $\widetilde\varphi _ k$ is $kF_\varphi $, so its Legendre transform is \[  (kF_\varphi )^*(m)=kG_\varphi (m/k).  \] Thus the Newton body of $\widetilde\varphi _ k$ is $k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )$. Applying theorem 5.2.14 1 to the line bundle $L^ k$ and the potential $k\varphi $, whose Newton body is $k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )$, we have \[  \#  \left( k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )\cap M\right)\leq h^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )\right).  \] Here $\# $ denotes the number of elements. Therefore, \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }k^{-n}\# \left( k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )\cap M\right)\leq \varliminf _{k\to \infty } k^{-n} h^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )\right).  \] The left-hand side is just $\operatorname{vol}\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )$, as follows from theorem C.2.3 . So we conclude that \[  \varliminf _{k\to \infty }\frac{n!}{k^ n}h^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )\right)\geq n!\operatorname{vol}\Delta (\omega ,\varphi ).  \] It remains to prove the reverse inequality. We choose an identification $M\cong \mathbb {Z}^ n$. In particular, there is a natural distance $\mathrm{d}$ on $M_{\mathbb {R}}\cong \mathbb {R}^ n$. Given a convex body $K$ and $\epsilon >0$, we let \[  K^{\epsilon }\coloneqq \left\{ x\in \mathbb {R}^ n: \mathrm{d}(x,K)\leq \epsilon \right\} .  \] This is again a convex body, since it can be realized as the Minkowski sum of $K$ with a closed ball of radius $\epsilon $. Applying theorem 5.2.14 2 to the polytope $kP$ and the potential $\widetilde\varphi _ k$, we can find $C>0$ uniform in $k$ such that for each $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, \[  \bigl \{  m\in M:\chi ^ m\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi ))\bigr \}  \subseteq \left(k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )\right)^ C.  \] Indeed, if a point $m\in kP\cap M$ is at distance at least $C$ from $k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )$, the separating hyperplane theorem gives a unit vector $v\in N_{\mathbb R}$ such that \[  \langle m,v\rangle -\operatorname{Supp}_{k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )}(v)\geq C.  \] Since the fan $\Sigma $ is finite and covers $N_{\mathbb R}$, there is a constant $\Lambda >0$ with the following property: every unit vector $v\in N_{\mathbb R}$ can be written in the form \[  v=-\lambda \sum _ i c_ i u_{\rho _ i},\quad 0<\lambda \leq \Lambda ,\quad c_ i>0,\quad \sum _ i c_ i=1,  \] where the rays $\rho _ i$ are contained in a single cone of $\Sigma $. Put \[  u\coloneqq \sum _ i c_ i u_{\rho _ i}.  \] Since the support function is positively homogeneous, we have \[  \begin{aligned}  \langle m,-u\rangle -\operatorname{Supp}_{k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )}(-u)& =\lambda ^{-1}\left(\langle m,v\rangle -\operatorname{Supp}_{k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )}(v)\right)\\ & \geq C/\Lambda . \end{aligned}  \] Choosing $C>\Lambda $ makes ( 5.56 ) applicable, uniformly in $k$. Fix $\epsilon >0$. Then for large enough $k$, we have \[  \left(k\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )\right)^{C}\subseteq k\left(\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )^{\epsilon }\right).  \] It follows that \[  h^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )\right)\leq \#  \left( k\left(\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )^{\epsilon }\right) \cap M\right).  \] Applying theorem C.2.3 again, we conclude that \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } \frac{n!}{k^ n} h^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )\right)\leq n! \operatorname{vol}\left(\Delta (\omega ,\varphi )^{\epsilon }\right).  \] Letting $\epsilon \to 0+$ and applying theorem C.1.4 , we find \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } \frac{n!}{k^ n} h^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal{I}(k\varphi )\right)\leq n! \operatorname{vol}\Delta (\omega ,\varphi ).  \] Our assertion follows. $\square$
