Choose $n+1$ distinct numbers $t_0,\ldots ,t_ n\in (0,1)$. Lagrange interpolation expresses $Q_ k(0)-Q(0)$ as a fixed linear combination of the numbers $Q_ k(t_ a)-Q(t_ a)$, which tend to $0$. Hence the same formula holds at $t=0$. From this, ( 6.56 ) follows. Step 2 . We now assume that the assumptions mentioned at the beginning of Step 1 are met. Note that we may assume that $\varphi _ j^ k$, $\varphi _ j$ are model potentials for all $j=1,\ldots ,n$, $k>0$ by proposition 6.2.4 and corollary 3.1.12 . We first handle the following monotone situation. Assume that, for each fixed $i$, the sequence $(\varphi _ i^ k)_ k$ is either increasing or decreasing. Let $\tilde{\varphi }_ i$ denote its pointwise limit, namely \[  \tilde{\varphi }_ i=\inf _{k>0}\varphi _ i^ k  \] in the decreasing case and \[  \tilde{\varphi }_ i=\operatorname *{sup}_{k>0}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i^ k  \] in the increasing case. We assume moreover that $\tilde{\varphi }_ i\sim _ P\varphi _ i$ for every $i$. Since mixed non-pluripolar masses are invariant under replacing each entry by a $P$-equivalent potential, it suffices in this monotone situation to prove convergence to the mixed mass of the $\tilde{\varphi }_ i$'s. After reordering the indices, we may assume that there is $i_0\in \{ 0,\ldots ,n\} $ such that $(\varphi _ i^ k)_ k$ is decreasing for $i\leq i_0$ and increasing for $i>i_0$. Therefore, for each $k>0$, using theorem 2.4.8 , we have \[  \int _ X \theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}\geq \int _ X \theta _{1,\tilde{\varphi }_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{i_0,\tilde{\varphi }_{i_0}}\wedge \theta _{i_0+1,\varphi ^ k_{i_0+1}}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}.  \] Using corollary 2.4.9 , we therefore conclude that \[  \varliminf _{k\to \infty }\int _ X \theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}\geq \int _ X \theta _{1,\tilde{\varphi }_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\tilde{\varphi }_ n}.  \] It remains to prove 6.59 \begin{equation} \label{eq:limsup} \varlimsup _{k\to \infty }\int _ X \theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}\leq \int _ X \theta _{1,\tilde{\varphi }_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\tilde{\varphi }_ n}. \end{equation} By theorem 2.4.8 , for each $k>0$, we have \[  \int _ X \theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}\leq \int _ X \theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{i_0,\varphi _{i_0}^ k}\wedge \theta _{i_0+1,\tilde{\varphi }_{i_0+1}}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\tilde{\varphi }_{n}}.  \] When proving ( 6.59 ), we may replace $\varphi _ j^ k$ by $\tilde{\varphi }_ j$ whenever $j>i_0$, $k>0$. Thus, we are reduced to the case where for all $i$, $(\varphi _ i^ k)_ k$ is decreasing. By proposition 3.1.26 , the masses $\int _ X\theta _{i,\varphi _ i^ k}^ n$ decrease to $\int _ X\theta _{i,\tilde{\varphi }_ i}^ n$. Hence, thanks to 2.4.15 , for each $i=1,\ldots ,n$, we may take an increasing sequence $(b^ k_ i)_ k$ tending to $\infty $ satisfying \[  b_ i^ k\in \left(1, \left( \frac{\int _ X \theta _{i,\varphi _ i^ k}^ n}{\int _ X \theta _{i,\varphi _ i^ k}^ n-\int _ X \theta _{i,\tilde{\varphi }_ i}^ n} \right)^{1/n} \right)  \] where the upper endpoint is understood as $\infty $ if the denominator is $0$. For each such $b_ i^ k$, 2.4.15 gives $\rho _ i^ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$ with \[  (b^ k_ i)^{-1}\rho _ i^ k+\left(1-(b^ k_ i)^{-1}\right)\varphi _ i^ k\leq \tilde{\varphi }_ i.  \] Then by theorem 2.4.8 again, \[  \prod _{i=1}^ n\left(1-(b^ k_ i)^{-1}\right)\int _ X \theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}\leq \int _ X \theta _{1,\tilde{\varphi }_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\tilde{\varphi }_ n}.  \] Letting $k\to \infty $, we conclude ( 6.59 ). This proves the monotone situation. We now return to the general case. It suffices to prove that any subsequence of \[  \int _ X \theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}  \] has a further subsequence converging to the desired limit. Starting with an arbitrary subsequence, we pass to a further subsequence, still indexed by $k$, so that the construction in proposition 6.2.12 applies simultaneously to the finitely many sequences $(\varphi _ i^ k)_ k$, $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Thus, after discarding finitely many terms and relabeling, for each $i$ there are model potentials $\eta _ i^ k,\psi _ i^ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$ such that $(\eta _ i^ k)_ k$ is increasing, $(\psi _ i^ k)_ k$ is decreasing, and \[  \eta _ i^ k\leq \varphi _ i^ k\leq \psi _ i^ k,\quad \eta _ i^ k\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi _ i,\quad \psi _ i^ k\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi _ i.  \] For the upper sequence, we take $\psi _ i^ k=P_{\theta _ i}[\operatorname *{sup}_{\ell \geq k}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i^\ell ]$; as in ( 6.40 ), this gives $\inf _ k\psi _ i^ k=\varphi _ i$. For the lower sequence, the construction in proposition 6.2.12 together with proposition 3.1.25 shows that the $\eta _ i^ k$'s are model after discarding finitely many terms, and the proof of proposition 6.2.12 shows that their increasing limit is $P$-equivalent to $\varphi _ i$. By theorem 2.4.8 , for every $k$, \[  \int _ X\theta _{1,\eta _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\eta _ n^ k} \leq \int _ X\theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k} \leq \int _ X\theta _{1,\psi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\psi _ n^ k}.  \] The monotone situation just proved applies to both the lower and upper sequences, and both limiting mixed masses are equal to \[  \int _ X\theta _{1,\varphi _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n}.  \] The squeeze theorem therefore gives the desired convergence along this further subsequence. This concludes the proof. $\square$

6.56 \begin{equation} \label{eq:convmixedmassds} \lim _{k\in I}\int _ X\theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}=\int _ X\theta _{1,\varphi _1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n}. \end{equation}

6.59 \begin{equation} \label{eq:limsup} \varlimsup _{k\to \infty }\int _ X \theta _{1,\varphi _1^ k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\varphi _ n^ k}\leq \int _ X \theta _{1,\tilde{\varphi }_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{n,\tilde{\varphi }_ n}. \end{equation}

title: Corollary 6.2.18
text: Corollary 6.2.18 . Suppose that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $; $\varphi _ i\lor \varphi \xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $ and 6.60 \begin{equation} \label{eq:massconv_varphii} \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j} \end{equation} for each $j=0,\ldots ,n$; for each $j=0,\ldots ,n$, ( 6.60 ) holds and 6.61 \begin{equation} \label{eq:massconv_varphii2} \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}. \end{equation} Proof. The equivalence between 2 and 3 follows directly from 6.2.5 . 1 $\implies $ 2 . That $\varphi _ i\lor \varphi \xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $ follows from corollary 6.2.7 . While ( 6.60 ) follows from theorem 6.2.17 . 2 $\implies $ 1 . By ( 6.24 ), we need to show that for each $j=0,\ldots ,n$, we have \[  2\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}-\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}-\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}\to 0.  \] This follows from theorem 6.2.17 and ( 6.60 ). $\square$

6.60 \begin{equation} \label{eq:massconv_varphii} \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j} \end{equation}

6.61 \begin{equation} \label{eq:massconv_varphii2} \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}. \end{equation}

title: Corollary 6.2.19
text: Corollary 6.2.19 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Let $\omega $ be a closed smooth positive $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta }}\varphi $; $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta +\omega }}\varphi $. Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . It suffices to show that for each $j=0,\ldots ,n$, we have \[  \begin{split}  2\int _ X (\theta +\omega )_{\varphi _ i\lor \varphi }^ j\wedge (\theta +\omega )_{V_{\theta +\omega }}^{n-j}-\int _ X (\theta +\omega )_{\varphi _ i}^ j\wedge (\theta +\omega )_{V_{\theta +\omega }}^{n-j}\\  -\int _ X (\theta +\omega )_{\varphi }^ j\wedge (\theta +\omega )_{V_{\theta +\omega }}^{n-j}\to 0. \end{split}  \] Note that this quantity is a linear combination of terms of the following form: \[  \begin{split}  2\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i\lor \varphi }^ r\wedge \omega ^{j-r}\wedge (\theta +\omega )_{V_{\theta +\omega }}^{n-j}-\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ r\wedge \omega ^{j-r}\wedge (\theta +\omega )_{V_{\theta +\omega }}^{n-j}\\  -\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ r\wedge \omega ^{j-r}\wedge (\theta +\omega )_{V_{\theta +\omega }}^{n-j}, \end{split}  \] where $r=0,\ldots ,j$. By theorem 6.2.17 , it suffices to show that $\varphi \lor \varphi _ i \xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $. But this follows from corollary 6.2.18 . 2 $\implies $ 1 . From the direction we already proved, for each $C\geq 1$, we have \[  \varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta +C\omega }}\varphi .  \] By theorem 6.2.17 , it follows that \[  \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X (\theta +C\omega )_{\varphi _ i}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X (\theta +C\omega )_{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}  \] for all $j=0,\ldots ,n$. It follows that 6.66 \begin{equation} \label{eq:varphijmass_limit} \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}. \end{equation} By corollary 6.2.18 , it remains to show that $\varphi _ i\lor \varphi \xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta }}\varphi $. By corollary 6.2.18 again, we know that $\varphi _ i\lor \varphi \xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta +\omega }}\varphi $. So it suffices to apply ( 6.66 ) to $\varphi _ i\lor \varphi $ instead of $\varphi _ i$, and we conclude by 6.2.5 . $\square$

6.66 \begin{equation} \label{eq:varphijmass_limit} \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}. \end{equation}

title: Corollary 6.2.20
text: Corollary 6.2.20 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Define $\varphi _ t=t\varphi _1+(1-t)\varphi _0$ for $t\in (0,1)$. Then \[  \varphi _ t\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi _0  \] as $t\to 0+$. Proof. First note that for each $j=0,\ldots ,n$, \[  \lim _{t\to 0+}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ t}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _0}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}.  \] So thanks to corollary 6.2.18 , it remains to argue that for all $j=0,\ldots ,n$, \[  \lim _{t\to 0+}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ t\lor \varphi _0}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _0}^ j\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-j}.  \] Observe that for $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \varphi _ t\lor \varphi _0=t(\varphi _1\lor \varphi _0)+(1-t)\varphi _0,  \] so the desired limit follows by the same binomial expansion. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.2.21
text: Corollary 6.2.21 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}, (\psi _ i)_{i\in I}, (\eta _ i)_{i\in I}$ be three nets in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Assume that $\psi _ i\preceq _ P \varphi _ i\preceq _ P \eta _ i$ for each $i\in I$; $\eta _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S} \varphi $, $\psi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S} \varphi $. Then $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $. Proof. By corollary 6.2.19 , we may replace $\theta $ by $\theta +\omega $, where $\omega $ is a Kähler form on $X$. In particular, we may assume that $\varphi _ i,\psi _ i,\eta _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for all $i\in I$. By proposition 6.2.4 , we may assume that $\varphi _ i,\psi _ i,\eta _ i$ are model potentials for all $i\in I$ and hence $\psi _ i \leq \varphi _ i\leq \eta _ i$ for all $i\in I$. It follows from theorem 2.4.8 that for each $k=0,\ldots ,n$, we have \[  \int _ X \theta _{\psi _ i}^ k\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-k}\leq \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ k\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-k}\leq \int _ X \theta _{\eta _ i}^ k\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-k}  \] for all $i\in I$. By theorem 6.2.17 , the limits, with respect to $i\in I$, of the two outer terms are $\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ k\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-k}$. It follows that 6.67 \begin{equation} \label{eq:thetak_conv} \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ k\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-k}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ k\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-k}. \end{equation} By corollary 6.2.18 , it remains to prove that $\varphi _ i \lor \varphi \xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $. By corollary 6.2.18 and proposition 6.1.20 , up to replacing $\psi _ i$ (resp. $\varphi _ i$, $\eta _ i$) by $\psi _ i\lor \varphi $ (resp. $\varphi _ i\lor \varphi $, $\eta _ i\lor \varphi $), we may assume from the beginning that $\psi _ i,\varphi _ i,\eta _ i\geq \varphi $. Now $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $ by ( 6.67 ) and 6.2.5 . $\square$

6.67 \begin{equation} \label{eq:thetak_conv} \lim _{i\in I}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ k\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-k}=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ k\wedge \theta _{V_{\theta }}^{n-k}. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 6.2.22
text: Lemma 6.2.22 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Fix $\lambda >0$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta }}\varphi $; $\lambda \varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_{S,\lambda \theta }}\lambda \varphi $. Proof. We have $V_{\lambda \theta }=\lambda V_{\theta }$. The middle expression in ( 6.24 ) for the pair $(\lambda \varphi _ i,\lambda \varphi )$ in the class $\lambda \theta $ is therefore $\lambda ^ n$ times the corresponding expression for $(\varphi _ i,\varphi )$ in the class $\theta $. The equivalence follows from corollary 6.2.7 . $\square$

title: Proposition 6.2.23
text: Proposition 6.2.23 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ (resp. $(\psi _ i)_{i\in I}$) be a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\varphi _ i \xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ (resp. $\psi _ i \xrightarrow {d_ S}\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$). Then \[  \varphi _ i\lor \psi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi \lor \psi .  \] Proof. Since $d_ S$ is a pseudometric, we may assume that both nets are actually sequences and $I=\mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. By corollary 6.2.19 , we may assume that the masses $\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n>0$, $\int _ X \theta _{\psi }^ n>0$. By proposition 6.2.4 and proposition 6.1.20 , replacing all potentials by their $P$-envelopes changes neither the hypotheses nor the conclusion. Thus we may assume that the $\varphi _ j$'s, the $\psi _ j$'s, $\varphi $ and $\psi $ are all model. After discarding finitely many terms, the masses of the two sequences are bounded below by a positive constant. Applying proposition 6.2.12 to both sequences and using the sandwich criterion corollary 6.2.21 , it is enough to treat the case where each of $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ and $(\psi _ j)_ j$ is monotone. In this reduced situation, $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ (resp. $(\psi _ j)_ j$) converges to $\varphi $ (resp. $\psi $) almost everywhere due to proposition 6.2.26 , corollary 6.2.9 and proposition 3.1.28 . We handle three cases separately. Step 1 . Assume that both sequences are increasing. In this case, we have $\varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j\nearrow \varphi \lor \psi $ almost everywhere. Therefore, $\varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S} \varphi \lor \psi $ by corollary 6.2.9 . Step 2 . Assume that one sequence, say $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is increasing while the other is decreasing. Then we have \[  \varphi _ j \lor \psi \leq \varphi _ j \lor \psi _ j \leq \varphi \lor \psi _ j.  \] Thanks to corollary 6.2.21 , it suffices to show that both sides converge to $\varphi \lor \psi $ with respect to $d_ S$. So we reduce to the case where both sequences are decreasing. Step 3 . Assume that both sequences are decreasing. In this case, due to corollary 6.2.11 , it suffices to show that 6.68 \begin{equation} \label{eq:masslortemp1} \lim _{j\to \infty } \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j}^ n=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi \lor \psi }^ n. \end{equation} The $\geq $ direction follows from theorem 2.4.8 ; it remains to argue the $\leq $ direction. Thanks to 2.4.15 , we may find a sequence $(\epsilon _ j)_ j$ in $(0,1)$ with limit $0$ and a sequence $(\eta _ j)_ j$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ such that \[  (1-\epsilon _ j)\varphi _ j+\epsilon _ j \eta _ j \leq \varphi ,\quad \eta _ j \leq \varphi _ j.  \] It follows that for each $j\geq 1$, we have \[  (1-\epsilon _ j)(\varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j)+\epsilon _ j \eta _ j \leq \varphi \lor \psi _ j.  \] Therefore by theorem 2.4.8 , \[  (1-\epsilon _ j)^ n \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j}^ n\leq \int _ X \theta _{\varphi \lor \psi _ j}^ n.  \] Letting $j\to \infty $, we find that \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j}^ n\leq \lim _{j\to \infty }\int _ X \theta _{\varphi \lor \psi _ j}^ n.  \] Therefore, in order to prove ( 6.68 ), we may assume that one of the sequences is constant; let us say $\psi _ j=\psi $ for all $j$. Repeating the same argument as before and constructing $(\epsilon _ j)_ j$, $(\eta _ j)_ j$ as above, we get \[  (1-\epsilon _ j)^ n \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j\lor \psi }^ n\leq \int _ X \theta _{\varphi \lor \psi }^ n.  \] Letting $j\to \infty $, we conclude ( 6.68 ). $\square$
6.68 \begin{equation} \label{eq:masslortemp1} \lim _{j\to \infty } \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j}^ n=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi \lor \psi }^ n. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 6.2.24
text: Proposition 6.2.24 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$, $(\psi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be nets in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S} \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\psi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Assume that $\varphi _ i\preceq _ P \psi _ i$ for all $i\in I$. Then $\varphi \preceq _ P \psi $. Proof. It follows from proposition 6.2.23 that \[  \varphi _ i\lor \psi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi \lor \psi .  \] By 6.1.8 , we have $\varphi _ i\lor \psi _ i\sim _ P \psi _ i$ for all $i\in I$. In particular, by proposition 6.2.4 , \[  \varphi _ i\lor \psi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\psi .  \] By proposition 6.2.4 again, $\varphi \lor \psi \sim _ P\psi $ and hence $\varphi \preceq _ P \psi $ by 6.1.8 . $\square$

title: Theorem 6.2.25
text: Theorem 6.2.25 . Let $\theta _1$, $\theta _2$ be smooth real closed $(1,1)$-forms on $X$ representing big cohomology classes. Suppose that $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ (resp. $(\psi _ i)_{i\in I}$) be a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ (resp. $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$) and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ (resp. $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$). Consider the following three conditions: $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_{S}}\varphi $; $\psi _ i\xrightarrow {d_{S}}\psi $; $\varphi _ i+\psi _ i\xrightarrow {d_{S}}\varphi +\psi $. Then any two of these conditions imply the third. Proof. By corollary 6.2.19 , we may assume that $\theta _1,\theta _2$ are both Kähler forms. We denote them by $\omega _1,\omega _2$ instead. Let $\omega =\omega _1+\omega _2$. 1 + 2 $\implies $ 3 . It suffices to show that for each $r=0,\ldots ,n$, \[  2\int _ X \omega _{(\varphi _ i+\psi _ i)\lor (\varphi +\psi )}^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}-\int _ X \omega _{\varphi _ i+\psi _ i}^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}-\int _ X \omega _{\varphi +\psi }^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}\to 0.  \] Observe that for each $i\in I$, \[  (\varphi _ i+\psi _ i)\lor (\varphi +\psi )\leq (\varphi _ i\lor \varphi )+(\psi _ i \lor \psi ).  \] The expression with the actual rooftop is non-negative and is bounded above by the same expression with this larger potential in place of $(\varphi _ i+\psi _ i)\lor (\varphi +\psi )$. Thus, it suffices to show that \[  2\int _ X \omega _{(\varphi _ i\lor \varphi )+(\psi _ i\lor \psi )}^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}-\int _ X \omega _{\varphi _ i+\psi _ i}^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}-\int _ X \omega _{\varphi +\psi }^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}\to 0.  \] The left-hand side is a linear combination of \[  2\int _ X \omega _{1,\varphi _ i\lor \varphi }^ a\wedge \omega _{2,\psi _ i\lor \psi }^{r-a}\wedge \omega ^{n-r}-\int _ X \omega _{1,\varphi _ i}^ a\wedge \omega _{2,\psi _ i}^{r-a} \wedge \omega ^{n-r}-\int _ X \omega _{1,\varphi }^ a\wedge \omega _{2,\psi }^{r-a} \wedge \omega ^{n-r}  \] with $a=0,\ldots ,r$. Observe that $\varphi _ i\lor \varphi \xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $ and $\psi _ i\lor \psi \xrightarrow {d_ S}\psi $ by corollary 6.2.7 , each term tends to $0$ by theorem 6.2.17 . 1 + 3 $\implies $ 2 . For each $C\geq 1$, from the direction we already proved together with 6.2.22 , \[  C\varphi _ i+\psi _ i\xrightarrow {d_{S}} C\varphi +\psi .  \] By theorem 6.2.17 , for each $j=0,\ldots ,n$, \[  \begin{split} & \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X \Bigl (C\omega _1+\omega _2+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(C\varphi _ i+\psi _ i)\Bigr )^ j\wedge \omega _2^{n-j}\\  = & \int _ X \Bigl (C\omega _1+\omega _2+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(C\varphi +\psi )\Bigr )^ j\wedge \omega _2^{n-j}. \end{split}  \] Both sides are polynomials in $C$. Comparing the constant terms gives 6.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:psii_quant_conv} \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X \omega _{2,\psi _ i}^ j\wedge \omega _2^{n-j}=\int _ X \omega _{2,\psi }^ j\wedge \omega _2^{n-j}. \end{equation} Therefore, 2 follows if $\psi _ i\geq \psi $ for each $i$ by 6.2.5 . Next we prove the general case. By the direction that we already proved, we know that $\varphi _ i+\psi \xrightarrow {d_{S}} \varphi +\psi $. By proposition 6.2.23 , we have \[  \varphi _ i+(\psi _ i\lor \psi )\xrightarrow {d_{S}} \varphi +\psi .  \] It follows from the special case above that $\psi _ i\lor \psi \xrightarrow {d_{S}}\psi $. It follows from ( 6.71 ) and corollary 6.2.18 that 2 holds. 2 + 3 $\implies $ 1 . This is similar. $\square$
6.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:psii_quant_conv} \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X \omega _{2,\psi _ i}^ j\wedge \omega _2^{n-j}=\int _ X \omega _{2,\psi }^ j\wedge \omega _2^{n-j}. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 6.2.26
text: Proposition 6.2.26 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, decreasing with respect to the $P$-partial order. Assume that there is $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ with $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $, then 6.72 \begin{equation} \label{eq:decPorderPenvconve} \inf _{i\in I} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]. \end{equation} Proof. First observe that by our assumption, $(P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i])_{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net. By the continuity of non-pluripolar masses corollary 6.2.10 , we have \[  \lim _{i\in I} \int _ X \theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]}^ n=\lim _{i\in I} \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n= \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] Replacing $I$ by a tail, we may therefore assume that $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for each $i\in I$. Since $\varphi _ i\sim _ P P_\theta [\varphi _ i]$, replacing $\varphi _ i$ by $P_\theta [\varphi _ i]$ does not change its $d_ S$-class by proposition 6.2.4 . We may assume that each $\varphi _ i$ is model and $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ is decreasing. In this case, by proposition 3.1.26 , the potential \[  \psi \coloneqq \inf _{i\in I} \varphi _ i  \] is model in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ with \[  \int _ X \theta _{\psi }^ n=\lim _{i\in I} \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ i}^ n= \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] Therefore, by corollary 6.2.11 , we find $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\psi $. In particular, $\varphi \sim _ P \psi $ by proposition 6.2.4 . Therefore, \[  \psi =P_{\theta }[\psi ]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ].  \] Therefore, ( 6.72 ) follows. $\square$
6.72 \begin{equation} \label{eq:decPorderPenvconve} \inf _{i\in I} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 6.2.27
text: Theorem 6.2.27 . The map \[  P_{\theta }[\bullet ]_{\mathcal{I}}\colon \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}\rightarrow \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}  \] is continuous with respect to $d_ S$. Proof. Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ such that $\varphi _ i\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. We want to show that 6.73 \begin{equation}  P_{\theta }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation} We may assume that the $\varphi _ i$'s and $\varphi $ are all model potentials by proposition 6.2.4 . By proposition 6.2.12 and corollary 6.2.21 , we may assume that $(\varphi _ i)_ i$ is either increasing or decreasing. In the increasing case, we apply proposition 3.2.19 and corollary 6.2.9 , while in the decreasing case, we apply proposition 3.2.18 , proposition 3.1.26 and corollary 6.2.11 . $\square$

title: Lemma 6.2.28
text: Lemma 6.2.28 . Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. As $\epsilon \to 0$ (from both sides), we have 6.74 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Vthetaeps_dS} V_{\theta +\epsilon \omega }\xlongrightarrow {d_ S}V_{\theta }. \end{equation} Proof. There are two assertions to prove, as detailed in the two steps. Step 1 . We first handle the case where $\epsilon \to 0+$. In this case ( 6.74 ) means \[  V_{\theta +\epsilon \omega }\xlongrightarrow {d_{S,\theta +\omega }}V_{\theta }  \] as $\epsilon \to 0+$. So thanks to corollary 6.2.11 and proposition 3.1.26 , it suffices to prove the following: 6.75 \begin{equation} \label{eq:epsil_P_temp1} \inf _{\epsilon >0} P_{\theta +\omega }\left[ V_{\theta +\epsilon \omega } \right]=P_{\theta +\omega }\left[ V_{\theta } \right]. \end{equation} First observe that \[  V_{\theta }=\inf _{\epsilon >0} V_{\theta +\epsilon \omega }.  \] In fact, the $\leq $ direction is trivial. As for the reverse inequality, it suffices to observe that the right-hand side lies in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Therefore, due to proposition 3.1.26 , \[  \lim _{\epsilon \to 0+} \int _ X \left( \theta +\epsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_{\theta +\epsilon \omega } \right)^ n=\int _ X \theta _{V_{\theta }}^ n.  \] Therefore, for all $\epsilon >0$ small enough, we can find $\eta _{\epsilon }\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\epsilon \omega )$ and $a_{\epsilon }>0$ decreasing to $0$ so that \[  (1-a_\epsilon )V_{\theta +\epsilon \omega } + a_\epsilon \eta _\epsilon \leq V_{\theta }.  \] Therefore, thanks to proposition 3.1.24 , \[  (1-a_\epsilon )P_{\theta +\omega }\left[ V_{\theta +\epsilon \omega } \right] + a_\epsilon P_{\theta +\omega }\left[\eta _\epsilon \right] \leq P_{\theta +\omega }\left[V_{\theta }\right].  \] Since the envelopes $P_{\theta +\omega }[\eta _\epsilon ]$ have supremum $0$, they are uniformly bounded in $L^1$ by proposition 1.5.4 ; hence $a_\epsilon P_{\theta +\omega }[\eta _\epsilon ]\to 0$ in $L^1$. Letting $\epsilon \to 0$ and using proposition 1.2.6 , we conclude ( 6.75 ). Step 2 . We then handle the case where $\epsilon \to 0-$. In this case, ( 6.74 ) simply means \[  V_{\theta -\epsilon \omega }\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta }}V_{\theta }  \] as $\epsilon \to 0+$. But this follows from corollary 6.2.9 if we can prove 6.76 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Vthetamepsomega_temp1} \operatorname *{sup}_{\epsilon >0}{}\! {}^{*} V_{\theta -\epsilon \omega }=V_{\theta }, \end{equation} where we understand that $\epsilon $ is small enough so that $\theta -\epsilon \omega $ represents a big cohomology class. Since $\{ \theta \} $ is big, we can find $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ so that \[  \varphi \leq 0,\quad \theta _{\varphi }\geq \delta \omega  \] for some $\delta >0$. For a small $\epsilon >0$, we then have \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left( \left(1-\frac{\epsilon }{\delta }\right)V_{\theta }+ \frac{\epsilon }{\delta }\varphi \right)\geq \epsilon \omega .  \] Therefore, \[  \left(1-\frac{\epsilon }{\delta }\right)V_{\theta }+ \frac{\epsilon }{\delta }\varphi \leq V_{\theta -\epsilon \omega }.  \] Letting $\epsilon \to 0+$, we then find \[  V_{\theta }\leq \operatorname *{sup}_{\epsilon >0}{}\! {}^{*} V_{\theta -\epsilon \omega }.  \] The reverse inequality is trivial, hence ( 6.76 ) is established. $\square$
6.74 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Vthetaeps_dS} V_{\theta +\epsilon \omega }\xlongrightarrow {d_ S}V_{\theta }. \end{equation}
6.75 \begin{equation} \label{eq:epsil_P_temp1} \inf _{\epsilon >0} P_{\theta +\omega }\left[ V_{\theta +\epsilon \omega } \right]=P_{\theta +\omega }\left[ V_{\theta } \right]. \end{equation}
6.76 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Vthetamepsomega_temp1} \operatorname *{sup}_{\epsilon >0}{}\! {}^{*} V_{\theta -\epsilon \omega }=V_{\theta }, \end{equation}

title: 6.2.3 Continuity of invariants
text:
6.2.3 Continuity of invariants In this section, we prove the continuity of a few invariants of the singularities with respect to $d_ S$. Theorem 6.2.29 . Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in I}$ be a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Then for any prime divisor $E$ over $X$, we have 6.77  egin{equation} \label{eq:convnu} \lim _{j\in I}
u (\varphi _ j,E)=
u (\varphi ,E). \end{equation} Proof. First observe that since $d_ S$ is a pseudometric, it suffices to prove ( 6.77 ) when $I=\mathbb {Z}_{>0}$ as partially ordered sets. By corollary 6.2.19 , after adding a Kähler form to $	heta $, we may assume that the masses of $\varphi _ j$ and of $\varphi $ are bounded from below by a positive constant. By theorem 6.2.27 , we may assume that $\varphi _ j$ and $\varphi $ are both $\mathcal{I}$-model and hence model. When proving ( 6.77 ), we are free to pass to subsequences. By proposition 6.2.12 and a sandwich argument, we may assume that the sequence $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is either increasing or decreasing. In the increasing case, the Lelong numbers $
u (\varphi _ j,E)$ decrease to a limit at least $
u (\varphi ,E)$, while $L^1$-convergence gives the opposite inequality by upper semicontinuity of Lelong numbers. In the decreasing case, ( 6.77 ) follows from proposition 3.1.26 . $\square$ Theorem 6.2.30 . Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in I}$ be a net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )_{>0}$. Assume that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $. Then 6.78  egin{equation} \label{eq:Ivolcont} \operatorname{vol}	heta _{\varphi _ j}	o \operatorname{vol}	heta _{\varphi },\quad \int _ X 	heta _{\varphi _ j}^ n	o \int _ X 	heta _{\varphi }^ n. \end{equation} Recall the volume is defined in definition 3.2.9 . In fact, we do not have to assume the positivity of the mass of $\varphi $. The proof of the general statement is slightly more involved. See corollary 7.3.7 below. Proof. The latter part of ( 6.78 ) is just a special case of theorem 6.2.17 . It remains to prove the former part. We may therefore assume that $\int _ X 	heta _{\varphi _ j}^ n>0$ for all $j\in I$ after passing to a tail. Then by theorem 6.2.27 , we have \[  P_{	heta }[\varphi _ j]_{\mathcal{I}}\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{	heta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Therefore, the first part of ( 6.78 ) follows again from theorem 6.2.17 . $\square$ Next we show that $d_ S$-convergent sequences have a sort of quasi-equisingular property (cf. ( 1.40 )). Theorem 6.2.31 . Let $\varphi _ j,\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ ($j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$). Assume that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $. Adrien Douady (1935–2006) was a French mathematician known for his pioneering work in complex dynamics and fractal geometry. Along with John H. Hubbard, he proved important results about the Mandelbrot set and developed renormalization theory for polynomial mappings. He discovered the Douady Rabbit , a famous fractal Julia set. 
Douady studied at École Normale Supérieure (the place where I began to hate France, thanks to Claude Viterbo) and taught at several French universities. He was also a member of the Bourbaki group.

title: 7 -good singularities
text: 7 $\mathcal{I}$-good singularities The class of $\mathcal I$-good singularities is the central object of this part of the book. These are the singularities for which the pluripotential-theoretic and multiplier-ideal notions of singularity type agree. Equivalently, they are the positive-mass potentials for which the ordinary model envelope and the $\mathcal I$-model envelope coincide, or for which the non-pluripolar mass equals the volume defined through multiplier ideals. The starting point is the characterization theorem theorem 7.1.1 . For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$, it shows that the following three conditions are equivalent: $\varphi $ lies in the $d_ S$-closure of potentials with analytic singularities; the mass-volume identity \[  \int _ X\theta _\varphi ^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _\varphi  \] holds; and \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]=P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] After establishing this characterization, the chapter develops the basic calculus of $\mathcal I$-good singularities. We prove stability under natural operations, including linear combinations and suprema, and record the main examples: analytic singularities, $\mathcal I$-model potentials, elementary metrics, and toric potentials. These closure properties are used repeatedly in later chapters, especially for traces, test curves and non-Archimedean potentials. The next part of the chapter introduces mixed volumes for singular currents. The definition is first made in positive-volume classes by replacing each current with its $\mathcal I$-model envelope, and is then extended by Kähler perturbation. We prove symmetry, multilinearity, monotonicity, birational invariance, log-concavity and continuity with respect to $d_ S$-convergence. The final section proves the asymptotic Riemann–Roch formula theorem 7.4.2 . For a Hermitian pseudo-effective line bundle $(L,h)$ on a connected compact Kähler manifold $X$ of dimension $n$, the theorem identifies \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }\frac{n!}{k^ n} h^0\left(X,L^ k\otimes \mathcal I(h^ k)\right)  \] with the volume of the Chern current of $h$. This result is the main algebraic manifestation of $\mathcal I$-goodness. It will be used later in the construction of partial Okounkov bodies and in the study of partial Bergman kernels.

title: 7.1 The notion of -good singularities
text: 7.1 The notion of $\mathcal{I}$-good singularities Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$. Theorem 7.1.1 . Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class, and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. Then the following are equivalent: There exists a sequence $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $; we have 7.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nppmassequalvolume} \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }; \end{equation} we have 7.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:PequpI} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation} In 1 , we can in addition require that each $\theta _{\varphi _ j}$ is a Kähler current. Moreover, if $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, one may take the sequence in 1 to be any quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Since $(\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),d_ S)$ is a pseudometric space, in 1 we can also replace the word sequence by net . Recall that according to corollary 3.2.14 and proposition 3.2.13 , one direction of ( 7.1 ) and ( 7.2 ) always holds: \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n\leq \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi },\quad P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . By theorem 6.2.17 , we have \[  \lim _{j\to \infty } \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n>0.  \] We may therefore assume that $\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n>0$ for all $j \geq 1$. It follows from proposition 3.2.15 that \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi _ j}  \] for any $j\geq 1$. Using theorem 6.2.30 , we conclude ( 7.1 ). 2 $\iff $ 3 . By definition, \[  \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }= \int _ X\theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}}^ n.  \] Moreover, $\varphi -\sup _ X\varphi \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$. Thus, if 2 holds, theorem 3.1.9 gives $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$; the reverse inequality follows from proposition 3.2.13 . Conversely, if 3 holds, then 2 follows from proposition 3.1.6 . 3 $\implies $ 1 . Note that the condition in 1 characterizes the closure of analytic singularities in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Step 1 . We first assume that $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. We will prove the following more general result in this case: Without assuming 3 , $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ always lies in the closure of analytic singularities. Let $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ be a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. We will show that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$. Let \[  \psi =\inf _{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ j].  \] Since $\varphi \leq \varphi _ j$ for all $j>0$, we have \[  \varphi -\sup _ X\varphi \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi _ j]  \] for all $j$, and hence \[  \varphi -\sup _ X\varphi \leq \psi .  \] In particular, $\int _ X\theta _\psi ^ n>0$. Now proposition 6.2.4 , proposition 3.1.26 and corollary 6.2.11 give \[  \varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\psi .  \] Moreover, observe that $\psi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-model by proposition 3.2.18 and proposition 3.2.15 . Hence, if $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal I}\psi $, then \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}=P_\theta [\psi ]_{\mathcal I}=\psi .  \] So it suffices to show that $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal I}\psi $. It only remains to argue that $\psi \preceq _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi $. For this purpose, take $\lambda >0$. We need to show that \[  \mathcal{I}(\lambda \psi )\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi ).  \] By the strong openness theorem 1.4.16 , we may take $\lambda '>\lambda $ such that $\mathcal{I}(\lambda \psi )=\mathcal{I}(\lambda ' \psi )$. It follows from the definition of the quasi-equisingular approximation that \[  \mathcal{I}(\lambda '\psi )\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\lambda '\varphi _ j)\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi )  \] for large enough $j$, where the first inclusion uses $\psi \leq P_\theta [\varphi _ j]$ and $P_\theta [\varphi _ j]\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi _ j$. Our assertion follows. It follows from the proof that we may take $\varphi _ j$ so that $\theta _{\varphi _ j}$ is a Kähler current for all $j\geq 1$. Step 2 . We handle the general case. Assume 3 holds. By 2.4.19 , we can find $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ so that $\theta _{\psi }$ is a Kähler current and $\psi \leq \varphi $. We let \[  \psi _ j=(1-j^{-1})\varphi +j^{-1}\psi  \] for each $j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>1}$. Then $(\psi _ j)_ j$ is an increasing sequence converging almost everywhere to $\varphi $. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\psi _ j]_{\mathcal{I}}\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]  \] by proposition 3.2.19 , corollary 6.2.9 . From Step 1, we know that each $P_{\theta }[\psi _ j]_{\mathcal{I}}$ lies in the closure of analytic singularities, hence so is $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\sim _ P \varphi $. Therefore, 1 follows. $\square$ Definition 7.1.2 . We say a potential $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good if for some smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ such that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$, we have 7.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:envelopeeq} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation} Remark 7.1.3 . In view of theorem 7.1.1 and corollary 3.2.14 , the failure of $\mathcal{I}$-goodness of a given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ can be characterized using the difference between the volume and the mass. We therefore introduce \[  \mathrm{Defect}(\theta _{\varphi })\coloneqq \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }-\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \] An immediate question is to verify that definition 7.1.2 is independent of the choice of $\theta $. Lemma 7.1.4 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for some smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Then the following are equivalent: $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$; $P_{\theta +\omega }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta +\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$. Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . By theorem 7.1.1 , we can find a sequence $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta }}\varphi $. By corollary 6.2.19 , we have $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta +\omega }}\varphi $. Therefore, by theorem 7.1.1 again, 2 holds. 2 $\implies $ 1 . Suppose that 1 fails, so that \[  \int _ X (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n< \int _ X (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}})^ n.  \] Since $\varphi \preceq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$, the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 gives \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-i}\leq \int _ X \theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}}^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-i}  \] for all $i=0,\ldots ,n$, and the inequality is strict for $i=n$. It follows that \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ X (\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n =&  \sum _{i=0}^ n\binom {n}{i}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-i}\\  <&  \sum _{i=0}^ n\binom {n}{i}\int _ X \theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}}^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-i}\\  =&  \int _ X (\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}})^ n \\  \leq & \int _ X (\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta +\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}})^ n. \end{aligned}  \] So 2 fails as well. $\square$ Corollary 7.1.5 . Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class. Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in I}$ be a net of $\mathcal{I}$-good potentials in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. Note that we do not need to assume that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. Proof. By adding a Kähler form to $\theta $, and using 7.1.4 , corollary 6.2.19 , we may assume that $\varphi _ j,\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for all $j\in I$. It follows from theorem 7.1.1 that \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi _ j}  \] for all $j\in I$. Taking limit with respect to $j$ with the help of theorem 6.2.30 , we conclude that \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }.  \] Therefore, by theorem 7.1.1 again, we find that $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. $\square$ Example 7.1.6 . Assume that $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. This is proved in proposition 3.2.15 . In particular, the potential in example 1.8.9 is $\mathcal{I}$-good. Example 7.1.7 . Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ Note. It is not known to us whether the same holds when $\varphi $ has vanishing mass. be an $\mathcal{I}$-model potential. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. In particular, $V_{\theta }$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. Example 7.1.8 . Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class, and let $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta )$. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. In fact, since $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=V_{\theta }$, we deduce that $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=V_{\theta }$ as well. In particular, the potential in example 3.1.14 is $\mathcal{I}$-good. A further class of examples of $\mathcal{I}$-good singularities will be given in example 7.4.5 below. There do exist, however, non-$\mathcal{I}$-good potentials. Example 7.1.9 . The potential in example 6.1.14 is not $\mathcal{I}$-good. In fact, since all Lelong numbers of $\varphi $ vanish, we know that $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}0$, hence \[  P_{2\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=0.  \] On the other hand, \[  \int _ X (2\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^1=\int _ X \omega <\int _ X (2\omega ),  \] where $(2\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^1$ is understood in the non-pluripolar sense. Quasi-equisingular approximations and $d_ S$-convergent sequences are related in the following manner: Corollary 7.1.10 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ and $(\epsilon _ j)_ j$ be a decreasing sequence in $\mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}$ with limit $0$. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Consider a decreasing sequence $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$, where each $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\epsilon _ j\omega )$ is a potential with analytic singularities. Assume that $\varphi =\inf _ j \varphi _ j$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ Note. Just to be sure, this means $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta +\epsilon \omega }}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ for any $\epsilon >0$. The choice of $\epsilon $ is irrelevant due to corollary 6.2.19 . , and $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $. Proof. By corollary 6.2.19 and example 7.1.7 , we may replace $\theta $ by $\theta +C\omega $ for some large constant $C>0$ and assume that $\varphi ,\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta -\omega )$ for all $j\geq 1$. Here the limit in 1 is unchanged by this replacement. Indeed, $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$ is $\mathcal I$-model, hence $\mathcal I$-good by example 7.1.7 . This implies \[  P_{\theta +C\omega }\bigl [P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\bigr ]=P_{\theta +C\omega }\bigl [P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\bigr ]_{\mathcal I}=P_{\theta +C\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Thus the old and new targets are $P$-equivalent in the enlarged class, and proposition 6.2.4 , corollary 6.2.19 shows that condition 1 is unchanged. 2 $\implies $ 1 . This is already proved in the proof of theorem 7.1.1 . 1 $\implies $ 2 . This follows from theorem 6.2.31 . $\square$ Corollary 7.1.11 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and let $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ be a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $. Then $(\pi ^*\varphi _ j)_ j$ is a quasi-equisingular approximation of the $\pi ^*\theta $-psh function $\pi ^*\varphi $. This result is by no means obvious from the definition of quasi-equisingular approximations. Proof. Let $(\epsilon _ j)_ j$ and $\omega $ be as in definition 1.6.8 , so that $\epsilon _ j\searrow 0$ and $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\epsilon _ j\omega )$ for all $j$. Choose a Kähler form $\tilde\omega $ on $Y$ and a constant $C>0$ such that $\pi ^*\omega \leq C\tilde\omega $. Then \[  \pi ^*\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta +C\epsilon _ j\tilde\omega ).  \] Moreover, the sequence $(\pi ^*\varphi _ j)_ j$ is decreasing, has analytic singularities, and decreases to $\pi ^*\varphi $. It remains to verify the quasi-equisingular condition definition 1.6.8 4 . Fix a constant $A>0$. Then $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is also a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ with respect to $\theta +A\omega $. Since $\theta _{\varphi }+A\omega $ is a Kähler current, corollary 7.1.10 gives \[  \varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{\theta +A\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Viewing the convergence in a fixed enlarged background class, pulling back and using corollary 6.2.8 , proposition 3.2.7 , we get \[  \pi ^*\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\pi ^*P_{\theta +A\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I} =P_{\pi ^*(\theta +A\omega )}[\pi ^*\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The domination $\pi ^*\omega \leq C\tilde\omega $ also gives \[  \pi ^*\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}\bigl (Y,\pi ^*(\theta +A\omega )+C\epsilon _ j\tilde\omega \bigr ),  \] so the preceding convergence is in the setting of corollary 7.1.10 on $Y$. The potential $\pi ^*\varphi $ has positive mass with respect to $\pi ^*(\theta +A\omega )$ by the bimeromorphic invariance of non-pluripolar products proposition 2.4.3 . Applying corollary 7.1.10 again on $Y$ shows that $(\pi ^*\varphi _ j)_ j$ satisfies the quasi-equisingular condition definition 1.6.8 4 for $\pi ^*\varphi $. Combining this with the first paragraph proves the assertion with respect to $\pi ^*\theta $. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.1.1
text: Theorem 7.1.1 . Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class, and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. Then the following are equivalent: There exists a sequence $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $; we have 7.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nppmassequalvolume} \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }; \end{equation} we have 7.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:PequpI} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation} In 1 , we can in addition require that each $\theta _{\varphi _ j}$ is a Kähler current. Moreover, if $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, one may take the sequence in 1 to be any quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . By theorem 6.2.17 , we have \[  \lim _{j\to \infty } \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n=\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n>0.  \] We may therefore assume that $\int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n>0$ for all $j \geq 1$. It follows from proposition 3.2.15 that \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi _ j}  \] for any $j\geq 1$. Using theorem 6.2.30 , we conclude ( 7.1 ). 2 $\iff $ 3 . By definition, \[  \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }= \int _ X\theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}}^ n.  \] Moreover, $\varphi -\sup _ X\varphi \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$. Thus, if 2 holds, theorem 3.1.9 gives $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\leq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]$; the reverse inequality follows from proposition 3.2.13 . Conversely, if 3 holds, then 2 follows from proposition 3.1.6 . 3 $\implies $ 1 . Note that the condition in 1 characterizes the closure of analytic singularities in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Step 1 . We first assume that $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. We will prove the following more general result in this case: Without assuming 3 , $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ always lies in the closure of analytic singularities. Let $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ be a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. We will show that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$. Let \[  \psi =\inf _{j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}} P_{\theta }[\varphi _ j].  \] Since $\varphi \leq \varphi _ j$ for all $j>0$, we have \[  \varphi -\sup _ X\varphi \leq P_{\theta }[\varphi _ j]  \] for all $j$, and hence \[  \varphi -\sup _ X\varphi \leq \psi .  \] In particular, $\int _ X\theta _\psi ^ n>0$. Now proposition 6.2.4 , proposition 3.1.26 and corollary 6.2.11 give \[  \varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\psi .  \] Moreover, observe that $\psi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-model by proposition 3.2.18 and proposition 3.2.15 . Hence, if $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal I}\psi $, then \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}=P_\theta [\psi ]_{\mathcal I}=\psi .  \] So it suffices to show that $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal I}\psi $. It only remains to argue that $\psi \preceq _{\mathcal{I}} \varphi $. For this purpose, take $\lambda >0$. We need to show that \[  \mathcal{I}(\lambda \psi )\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi ).  \] By the strong openness theorem 1.4.16 , we may take $\lambda '>\lambda $ such that $\mathcal{I}(\lambda \psi )=\mathcal{I}(\lambda ' \psi )$. It follows from the definition of the quasi-equisingular approximation that \[  \mathcal{I}(\lambda '\psi )\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\lambda '\varphi _ j)\subseteq \mathcal{I}(\lambda \varphi )  \] for large enough $j$, where the first inclusion uses $\psi \leq P_\theta [\varphi _ j]$ and $P_\theta [\varphi _ j]\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\varphi _ j$. Our assertion follows. It follows from the proof that we may take $\varphi _ j$ so that $\theta _{\varphi _ j}$ is a Kähler current for all $j\geq 1$. Step 2 . We handle the general case. Assume 3 holds. By 2.4.19 , we can find $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ so that $\theta _{\psi }$ is a Kähler current and $\psi \leq \varphi $. We let \[  \psi _ j=(1-j^{-1})\varphi +j^{-1}\psi  \] for each $j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>1}$. Then $(\psi _ j)_ j$ is an increasing sequence converging almost everywhere to $\varphi $. Then \[  P_{\theta }[\psi _ j]_{\mathcal{I}}\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]  \] by proposition 3.2.19 , corollary 6.2.9 . From Step 1, we know that each $P_{\theta }[\psi _ j]_{\mathcal{I}}$ lies in the closure of analytic singularities, hence so is $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\sim _ P \varphi $. Therefore, 1 follows. $\square$
7.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nppmassequalvolume} \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }; \end{equation}
7.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:PequpI} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation}

title: Definition 7.1.2
text: Definition 7.1.2 . We say a potential $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good if for some smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ such that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$, we have 7.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:envelopeeq} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation}
7.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:envelopeeq} P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}. \end{equation}

title: Remark 7.1.3
text: Remark 7.1.3 . In view of theorem 7.1.1 and corollary 3.2.14 , the failure of $\mathcal{I}$-goodness of a given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ can be characterized using the difference between the volume and the mass. We therefore introduce \[  \mathrm{Defect}(\theta _{\varphi })\coloneqq \operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }-\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n.  \]

title: Lemma 7.1.4
text: Lemma 7.1.4 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for some smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Then the following are equivalent: $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$; $P_{\theta +\omega }[\varphi ]=P_{\theta +\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$. Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . By theorem 7.1.1 , we can find a sequence $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta }}\varphi $. By corollary 6.2.19 , we have $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta +\omega }}\varphi $. Therefore, by theorem 7.1.1 again, 2 holds. 2 $\implies $ 1 . Suppose that 1 fails, so that \[  \int _ X (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n< \int _ X (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}})^ n.  \] Since $\varphi \preceq P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$, the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 gives \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-i}\leq \int _ X \theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}}^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-i}  \] for all $i=0,\ldots ,n$, and the inequality is strict for $i=n$. It follows that \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ X (\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n =&  \sum _{i=0}^ n\binom {n}{i}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-i}\\  <&  \sum _{i=0}^ n\binom {n}{i}\int _ X \theta _{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}}^ i\wedge \omega ^{n-i}\\  =&  \int _ X (\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}})^ n \\  \leq & \int _ X (\theta +\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\theta +\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}})^ n. \end{aligned}  \] So 2 fails as well. $\square$

title: Corollary 7.1.5
text: Corollary 7.1.5 . Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class. Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in I}$ be a net of $\mathcal{I}$-good potentials in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. Proof. By adding a Kähler form to $\theta $, and using 7.1.4 , corollary 6.2.19 , we may assume that $\varphi _ j,\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for all $j\in I$. It follows from theorem 7.1.1 that \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi _ j}^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi _ j}  \] for all $j\in I$. Taking limit with respect to $j$ with the help of theorem 6.2.30 , we conclude that \[  \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n=\operatorname{vol}\theta _{\varphi }.  \] Therefore, by theorem 7.1.1 again, we find that $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. $\square$

title: Example 7.1.6
text: Example 7.1.6 . Assume that $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ has analytic singularities. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. This is proved in proposition 3.2.15 . In particular, the potential in example 1.8.9 is $\mathcal{I}$-good.

title: Example 7.1.7
text: Example 7.1.7 . Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ Note. It is not known to us whether the same holds when $\varphi $ has vanishing mass. be an $\mathcal{I}$-model potential. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. In particular, $V_{\theta }$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good.

title: Example 7.1.8
text: Example 7.1.8 . Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class, and let $\varphi \in \mathcal{E}(X,\theta )$. Then $\varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. In fact, since $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=V_{\theta }$, we deduce that $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=V_{\theta }$ as well. In particular, the potential in example 3.1.14 is $\mathcal{I}$-good.

title: Example 7.1.9
text: Example 7.1.9 . The potential in example 6.1.14 is not $\mathcal{I}$-good. In fact, since all Lelong numbers of $\varphi $ vanish, we know that $\varphi \sim _{\mathcal{I}}0$, hence \[  P_{2\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=0.  \] On the other hand, \[  \int _ X (2\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^1=\int _ X \omega <\int _ X (2\omega ),  \] where $(2\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^1$ is understood in the non-pluripolar sense.

title: Corollary 7.1.10
text: Corollary 7.1.10 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ and $(\epsilon _ j)_ j$ be a decreasing sequence in $\mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}$ with limit $0$. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. Consider a decreasing sequence $(\varphi _ j)_{j>0}$, where each $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\epsilon _ j\omega )$ is a potential with analytic singularities. Assume that $\varphi =\inf _ j \varphi _ j$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ Note. Just to be sure, this means $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_{S,\theta +\epsilon \omega }}P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ for any $\epsilon >0$. The choice of $\epsilon $ is irrelevant due to corollary 6.2.19 . , and $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $. Proof. By corollary 6.2.19 and example 7.1.7 , we may replace $\theta $ by $\theta +C\omega $ for some large constant $C>0$ and assume that $\varphi ,\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta -\omega )$ for all $j\geq 1$. Here the limit in 1 is unchanged by this replacement. Indeed, $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$ is $\mathcal I$-model, hence $\mathcal I$-good by example 7.1.7 . This implies \[  P_{\theta +C\omega }\bigl [P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\bigr ]=P_{\theta +C\omega }\bigl [P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}\bigr ]_{\mathcal I}=P_{\theta +C\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Thus the old and new targets are $P$-equivalent in the enlarged class, and proposition 6.2.4 , corollary 6.2.19 shows that condition 1 is unchanged. 2 $\implies $ 1 . This is already proved in the proof of theorem 7.1.1 . 1 $\implies $ 2 . This follows from theorem 6.2.31 . $\square$

title: Corollary 7.1.11
text: Corollary 7.1.11 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and let $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ be a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $. Then $(\pi ^*\varphi _ j)_ j$ is a quasi-equisingular approximation of the $\pi ^*\theta $-psh function $\pi ^*\varphi $. Proof. Let $(\epsilon _ j)_ j$ and $\omega $ be as in definition 1.6.8 , so that $\epsilon _ j\searrow 0$ and $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\epsilon _ j\omega )$ for all $j$. Choose a Kähler form $\tilde\omega $ on $Y$ and a constant $C>0$ such that $\pi ^*\omega \leq C\tilde\omega $. Then \[  \pi ^*\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta +C\epsilon _ j\tilde\omega ).  \] Moreover, the sequence $(\pi ^*\varphi _ j)_ j$ is decreasing, has analytic singularities, and decreases to $\pi ^*\varphi $. It remains to verify the quasi-equisingular condition definition 1.6.8 4 . Fix a constant $A>0$. Then $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is also a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ with respect to $\theta +A\omega $. Since $\theta _{\varphi }+A\omega $ is a Kähler current, corollary 7.1.10 gives \[  \varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}P_{\theta +A\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Viewing the convergence in a fixed enlarged background class, pulling back and using corollary 6.2.8 , proposition 3.2.7 , we get \[  \pi ^*\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\pi ^*P_{\theta +A\omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I} =P_{\pi ^*(\theta +A\omega )}[\pi ^*\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The domination $\pi ^*\omega \leq C\tilde\omega $ also gives \[  \pi ^*\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}\bigl (Y,\pi ^*(\theta +A\omega )+C\epsilon _ j\tilde\omega \bigr ),  \] so the preceding convergence is in the setting of corollary 7.1.10 on $Y$. The potential $\pi ^*\varphi $ has positive mass with respect to $\pi ^*(\theta +A\omega )$ by the bimeromorphic invariance of non-pluripolar products proposition 2.4.3 . Applying corollary 7.1.10 again on $Y$ shows that $(\pi ^*\varphi _ j)_ j$ satisfies the quasi-equisingular condition definition 1.6.8 4 for $\pi ^*\varphi $. Combining this with the first paragraph proves the assertion with respect to $\pi ^*\theta $. $\square$

title: 7.2 Properties of -good singularities
text: 7.2 Properties of $\mathcal{I}$-good singularities Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$. We show that $\mathcal{I}$-goodness is preserved by a number of natural operations. Proposition 7.2.1 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be $\mathcal{I}$-good and $\lambda >0$. Then the following potentials are all $\mathcal{I}$-good: $\varphi +\psi $; $\varphi \lor \psi $; $\lambda \varphi $. Proof. Take a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ such that $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. It follows from theorem 7.1.1 that there are sequences $(\varphi _ j)_ j,(\psi _ j)_ j$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $ and $\psi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\psi $. By theorem 6.2.25 , proposition 6.2.23 , we have \[  \varphi _ j+\psi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi +\psi ,\quad \varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi \lor \psi .  \] By proposition 1.6.2 , the potentials $\varphi _ j+\psi _ j$ and $\varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j$ have analytic singularities. So $\varphi +\psi $ and $\varphi \lor \psi $ are $\mathcal{I}$-good by theorem 7.1.1 . On the other hand, 6.2.22 gives \[  \lambda \varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\lambda \varphi .  \] Here the convergence is understood in the scaled class. So by theorem 7.1.1 , in order to show that $\lambda \varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good, it suffices to show that $\lambda \varphi _ j$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. In other words, we may assume that $\varphi $ has analytic singularities. We may further assume that $\varphi \leq 0$. In this case, take a decreasing sequence of rational numbers $\lambda _ j\searrow \lambda $. Take a sufficiently large Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ so that $\lambda _ j\varphi ,\lambda \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )_{>0}$ for any $j$. Then observe that \[  \lambda \varphi =\operatorname *{sup}_{j>0}{}\! {}^{*} \lambda _ j \varphi .  \] Therefore, $\lambda _ j\varphi \xrightarrow {d_ S} \lambda \varphi $ by corollary 6.2.9 . Each $\lambda _ j \varphi $ has analytic singularities, and hence is $\mathcal{I}$-good by example 7.1.6 . Therefore, $\lambda \varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good by theorem 7.1.1 . $\square$ Example 7.2.2 . Let $L$ be a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. Elementary metrics on $L$ are defined in definition 6.1.15 . Let $h$ be an elementary metric on $L$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. This is a direct consequence of proposition 7.2.1 and example 7.1.6 , and the fact that $\mathcal{I}$-goodness depends only on the $P$-singularity type. Proposition 7.2.3 . Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in I}$ be a non-empty family of $\mathcal{I}$-good potentials in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for some closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. Assume that this family is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{j\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ j$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. Proof. After adding a Kähler form to $\theta $, we may assume that $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for all $j\in I$. When $I$ is finite, this result follows from proposition 7.2.1 . When $I$ is infinite, by Choquet's lemma proposition 1.2.3 , we may assume that $I=\mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. Replacing $\varphi _ j$ by $\varphi _1\lor \cdots \lor \varphi _ j$ and using proposition 7.2.1 , we may assume that the sequence $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is increasing. In this case, as shown in corollary 6.2.9 , \[  \varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\operatorname *{sup}_{ i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i.  \] Therefore, $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good by corollary 7.1.5 . $\square$

title: Proposition 7.2.1
text: Proposition 7.2.1 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ be $\mathcal{I}$-good and $\lambda >0$. Then the following potentials are all $\mathcal{I}$-good: $\varphi +\psi $; $\varphi \lor \psi $; $\lambda \varphi $. Proof. Take a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ such that $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. It follows from theorem 7.1.1 that there are sequences $(\varphi _ j)_ j,(\psi _ j)_ j$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities such that $\varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi $ and $\psi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\psi $. By theorem 6.2.25 , proposition 6.2.23 , we have \[  \varphi _ j+\psi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi +\psi ,\quad \varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\varphi \lor \psi .  \] By proposition 1.6.2 , the potentials $\varphi _ j+\psi _ j$ and $\varphi _ j\lor \psi _ j$ have analytic singularities. So $\varphi +\psi $ and $\varphi \lor \psi $ are $\mathcal{I}$-good by theorem 7.1.1 . On the other hand, 6.2.22 gives \[  \lambda \varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\lambda \varphi .  \] Here the convergence is understood in the scaled class. So by theorem 7.1.1 , in order to show that $\lambda \varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good, it suffices to show that $\lambda \varphi _ j$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. In other words, we may assume that $\varphi $ has analytic singularities. We may further assume that $\varphi \leq 0$. In this case, take a decreasing sequence of rational numbers $\lambda _ j\searrow \lambda $. Take a sufficiently large Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$ so that $\lambda _ j\varphi ,\lambda \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )_{>0}$ for any $j$. Then observe that \[  \lambda \varphi =\operatorname *{sup}_{j>0}{}\! {}^{*} \lambda _ j \varphi .  \] Therefore, $\lambda _ j\varphi \xrightarrow {d_ S} \lambda \varphi $ by corollary 6.2.9 . Each $\lambda _ j \varphi $ has analytic singularities, and hence is $\mathcal{I}$-good by example 7.1.6 . Therefore, $\lambda \varphi $ is $\mathcal{I}$-good by theorem 7.1.1 . $\square$

title: Example 7.2.2
text: Example 7.2.2 . Let $L$ be a pseudo-effective line bundle on $X$. Elementary metrics on $L$ are defined in definition 6.1.15 . Let $h$ be an elementary metric on $L$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. This is a direct consequence of proposition 7.2.1 and example 7.1.6 , and the fact that $\mathcal{I}$-goodness depends only on the $P$-singularity type.

title: Proposition 7.2.3
text: Proposition 7.2.3 . Let $(\varphi _ j)_{j\in I}$ be a non-empty family of $\mathcal{I}$-good potentials in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for some closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. Assume that this family is locally uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{j\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ j$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. Proof. After adding a Kähler form to $\theta $, we may assume that $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )_{>0}$ for all $j\in I$. When $I$ is finite, this result follows from proposition 7.2.1 . When $I$ is infinite, by Choquet's lemma proposition 1.2.3 , we may assume that $I=\mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. Replacing $\varphi _ j$ by $\varphi _1\lor \cdots \lor \varphi _ j$ and using proposition 7.2.1 , we may assume that the sequence $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ is increasing. In this case, as shown in corollary 6.2.9 , \[  \varphi _ j\xrightarrow {d_ S}\operatorname *{sup}_{ i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i.  \] Therefore, $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good by corollary 7.1.5 . $\square$

title: 7.3 Mixed volumes
text:
7.3 Mixed volumes We first extend the notion of volume in definition 3.2.9 to the mixed case. Let $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ be smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$ representing pseudo-effective classes. Definition 7.3.1 . Let $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ i)$ for $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Write $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ for each $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Assume that $\operatorname{vol}T_ i>0$ for all $i=1,\ldots ,n$. We define the mixed volume $\operatorname{vol}(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n)$ as follows: 7.8  egin{equation} \label{eq:volmixed} \operatorname{vol}(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n)=\int _ X \left(	heta _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\wedge \dots \wedge \left(	heta _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _ n}[\varphi _ n]_{\mathcal{I}}ight). \end{equation} When $\operatorname{vol}T_ i>0$ for each $i=1,\ldots ,n$, the definition ( 7.8 ) does not depend on how we represent $T_ i$ as $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$, this is a consequence of theorem 2.4.8 and proposition 3.2.6 . Lemma 7.3.2 . The mixed volume is symmetric in its $n$-variables. For any Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$, we have 7.9  egin{equation} \label{eq:mix_vol_comp1} \operatorname{vol}\left(T_1,\ldots ,T_ night)=\lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+} \operatorname{vol}\left(T_1+\epsilon \omega ,\ldots ,T_ n+\epsilon \omega ight). \end{equation} Consider closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n,T_1'$ on $X$ with positive volumes, then 7.10  egin{equation}  \operatorname{vol}(T_1+T_1',T_2,\ldots ,T_ n)=\operatorname{vol}(T_1,T_2,\ldots ,T_ n)+\operatorname{vol}(T_1',T_2,\ldots ,T_ n). \end{equation} Consider closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n$ on $X$ with positive volumes and $\lambda > 0$, then \[  \operatorname{vol}(\lambda T_1,T_2,\ldots ,T_ n)=\lambda \operatorname{vol}(T_1,T_2,\ldots ,T_ n).  \] Suppose that $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n,S_1,\ldots ,S_ n$ are closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$ with positive volumes such that $T_ i\preceq _{\mathcal{I}} S_ i$ and $\{ T_ i\} =\{ S_ i\} $ for each $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Then 7.11  egin{equation}  \operatorname{vol}(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n)\leq \operatorname{vol}(S_1,\ldots ,S_ n). \end{equation} The notation $\operatorname{Reg}$ is defined in ( 1.44 ). Proof. 1 This follows from the symmetry of the mixed non-pluripolar product in ( 7.8 ), cf. proposition 2.2.2 2 . 2 For each $i$ and each $\epsilon >0$, we have \[  P_{	heta _ i}[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim _ P P_{	heta _ i+\epsilon \omega }\left[P_{	heta _ i}[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}ight]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{	heta _ i+\epsilon \omega }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}  \] as a consequence of example 7.1.7 . Hence using proposition 6.1.16 and the multi-linearity of the non-pluripolar product proposition 2.2.2 6 , \[   egin{aligned} & \lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+}\operatorname{vol}(T_1+\epsilon \omega ,\ldots ,T_ n+\epsilon \omega )\  =& \lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+}\int _ X \left(	heta _1+\epsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\wedge \cdots \wedge \left(	heta _ n+\epsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _ n}[\varphi _ n]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\  =&  \operatorname{vol}(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n). \end{aligned}  \] 3 We write $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ as before for each $i$ and $T_1'=	heta _1'+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1'$. The potentials $P_{	heta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal I}$ and $P_{	heta _1'}[\varphi _1']_{\mathcal I}$ are $\mathcal I$-model with positive masses, hence $\mathcal I$-good. By proposition 7.2.1 , their sum is $\mathcal I$-good. Moreover, it is $\mathcal I$-equivalent to $\varphi _1+\varphi _1'$. Then thanks to proposition 7.2.1 , \[  P_{	heta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}+P_{	heta _1'}[\varphi _1']_{\mathcal{I}}\sim _ P P_{	heta _1+	heta _1'}\left[P_{	heta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}+P_{	heta _1'}[\varphi _1']_{\mathcal{I}} ight]_{\mathcal{I}} = P_{	heta _1+	heta _1'}\left[\varphi _1+\varphi _1'ight]_{\mathcal{I}}  \] Thus by proposition 6.1.16 , we have \[   egin{aligned} & \operatorname{vol}(T_1+T_1',T_2,\ldots ,T_ n)\  =& \int _ X \left( 	heta _1+	heta _1'+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _1+	heta _1'}[\varphi _1+\varphi _1']_{\mathcal{I}} ight)\wedge \left( 	heta _2+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _2}[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\wedge \cdots \ & \wedge \left( 	heta _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _ n}[\varphi _ n]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\  =& \int _ X \left( 	heta _1+	heta _1'+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _1}[\varphi _1]_{\mathcal{I}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _1'}[\varphi _1']_{\mathcal{I}} ight)\wedge \left( 	heta _2+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _2}[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\wedge \cdots \ & \wedge \left( 	heta _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _ n}[\varphi _ n]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\  =&  \operatorname{vol}(T_1,T_2,\ldots ,T_ n)+\operatorname{vol}(T_1',T_2,\ldots ,T_ n). \end{aligned}  \] 4 This follows from ( 7.8 ), proposition 3.2.16 1 and proposition 2.2.2 6 . 5 Our assertion follows from the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 . $\square$ In view of 7.3.2 2 , we may extend the definition of mixed volumes to the more general setting as follows: Definition 7.3.3 . Let $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ i)$ for $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Write $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ for each $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. We define the mixed volume $\operatorname{vol}(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n)$ as 7.21  egin{equation} \label{eq:volmixedgeneral} \operatorname{vol}\left(T_1,\ldots ,T_ night)=\lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+}\operatorname{vol}\left(T_1+\epsilon \omega ,\ldots ,T_ n+\epsilon \omega ight). \end{equation} Note that $\operatorname{vol}(T_1+\epsilon \omega ,\ldots ,T_ n+\epsilon \omega )$ is decreasing as $\epsilon 	o 0+$ due to 7.3.2 3 , so the limit exists. Furthermore, $\operatorname{vol}(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n)$ does not depend on the choice of $\omega $, as a consequence of 7.3.2 3 . Proposition 7.3.4 . The mixed volume is symmetric in its $n$-variables. Consider closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n,T_1'$ on $X$, then 7.22  egin{equation}  \operatorname{vol}(T_1+T_1',T_2,\ldots ,T_ n)=\operatorname{vol}(T_1,T_2,\ldots ,T_ n)+\operatorname{vol}(T_1',T_2,\ldots ,T_ n). \end{equation} Consider closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n$ on $X$ and $\lambda \geq 0$, then \[  \operatorname{vol}(\lambda T_1,T_2,\ldots ,T_ n)=\lambda \operatorname{vol}(T_1,T_2,\ldots ,T_ n).  \] Suppose that $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n,S_1,\ldots ,S_ n$ are closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$ such that $T_ i\preceq _{\mathcal{I}} S_ i$ and $\{ T_ i\} =\{ S_ i\} $ for each $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Then 7.23  egin{equation}  \operatorname{vol}(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n)\leq \operatorname{vol}(S_1,\ldots ,S_ n). \end{equation} Suppose that $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n$ are closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. Then 7.24  egin{equation}  \operatorname{vol}\left(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n ight)=\operatorname{vol}\left(\operatorname{Reg}T_1,\ldots ,\operatorname{Reg}T_ n ight). \end{equation} For any closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, we have 7.25  egin{equation} \label{eq:mix_vol_ext_pure} \operatorname{vol}(T,\ldots ,T)=\operatorname{vol}T. \end{equation} Proof. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 are immediate consequences of the corresponding properties proved in 7.3.2 . 5 Using 3 and 4 , it suffices to establish the following: Suppose that 7.26  egin{equation} \label{eq:T_count_sum_temp1} T=\sum _ i c_ i[E_ i] \end{equation} is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$, where $\{ E_ i\} $ is a countable collection of prime divisors on $X$ and $c_ i>0$. Then 7.27  egin{equation} \label{eq:volTT2Tn_temp1} \operatorname{vol}\left(T,T_2,\ldots ,T_ n ight)=0 \end{equation} for any closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_2,\ldots ,T_ n$ on $X$. Step 1 . We first assume that ( 7.26 ) is a finite sum. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. In this case, thanks to 3 and 4 again, we may assume that $T=[E]$ for some prime divisor $E$ on $X$. Write $[E]=	heta _{\varphi }$. Then $\varphi $ has analytic singularities thanks to proposition 1.8.4 . Therefore, $P_{	heta +\epsilon \omega }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\sim \varphi $ for any $\epsilon >0$ due to proposition 3.2.15 . Write $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ for $i=2,\ldots ,n$, and choose $C>0$ so that $C\omega +	heta _ i$ are Kähler forms for each $i=2,\ldots ,n$. Then \[   egin{aligned} & \operatorname{vol}(T,T_2,\ldots ,T_ n)\  =&  \lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+} \int _ X \left([E]+\epsilon \omega ight)\wedge \left( 	heta _2+\epsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _2+\epsilon \omega }[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\wedge \cdots \ & \wedge \left( 	heta _ n+\epsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _ n+\epsilon \omega }[\varphi _ n]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\  =& \lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+} \epsilon \int _ X \omega \wedge \left( 	heta _2+\epsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _2+\epsilon \omega }[\varphi _2]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\wedge \cdots \ & \wedge \left( 	heta _ n+\epsilon \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{	heta _ n+\epsilon \omega }[\varphi _ n]_{\mathcal{I}}ight)\  \leq & \lim _{\epsilon 	o 0+} \epsilon \int _ X \omega \wedge \left( 	heta _2+C\omega ight)\wedge \cdots \wedge \left( 	heta _ n+C\omega ight)\  =& 0, \end{aligned}  \] where the inequality step follows from the monotonicity theorem theorem 2.4.8 and the fact that $P_{	heta _ i+\epsilon \omega }[\varphi _ i]_{\mathcal{I}}\leq 0$ for all $i=2,\ldots ,n$. Step 2 . We prove the case where $\{ E_ i\} $ is infinite. We may assume that $i$ runs over $\mathbb {Z}_{>0}$.
