None The general case Definition 10.4.12 . Let $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$. Take a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. We define 10.90  egin{equation} \label{eq:DeltaTgeneral} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)= igcap _{j=1}^{\infty }\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T+j^{-1}\omega ). \end{equation} The same definition makes sense when $\alpha $ is only pseudo-effective. This definition is clearly independent of the choice of $\omega $ by 10.4.11 . Moreover, it extends definition 10.4.7 and definition 10.4.3 as a result of 10.4.11 . The main properties of $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$ are summarized as follows: Theorem 10.4.13 . The convex bodies $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$ satisfy the following properties: Suppose that $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}$. We have 10.91  egin{equation} \label{eq:volpobgeneral} \operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)= rac{1}{n!}\operatorname{vol}T. \end{equation} For $T,S \in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$ satisfying $T\preceq _{\mathcal{I}}S$, we have \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(S)\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\alpha ).  \] For any current $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$ with minimal singularities, we have \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\alpha ).  \] The map $\mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}ightarrow \mathcal{K}_ n$ given by $T\mapsto \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$ is continuous, where we endow the $d_ S$-pseudometric on $\mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}$ and the Hausdorff topology on $\mathcal{K}_ n$. Let $\pi \colon Yightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism, where $Y$ is a Kähler manifold. Assume that the lifting $(W_{ ullet },g)$ of $Y_{ ullet }$ to $Y$ exists. Then for any $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}$, we have \[  \Delta _{W_{ ullet }}(\pi ^*T)=\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)g.  \] For $T,S\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$, we have 10.92  egin{equation} \label{eq:pobadditiv} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)+\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(S)\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T+S). \end{equation} Proof. 1 By ( 10.90 ) and ( 10.87 ), for any Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$, \[  \operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=\lim _{j	o \infty }\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T+j^{-1}\omega )= rac{1}{n!}\lim _{j	o \infty }\operatorname{vol}(T+j^{-1}\omega ).  \] The right-hand side is computed in proposition 7.3.4 . Hence, ( 10.91 ) follows. 2 Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. By corollary 10.4.9 , for each $j\geq 1$, \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T+j^{-1}\omega )\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(S+j^{-1}\omega )\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\alpha +j^{-1}\{ \omega \} ).  \] It remains to show that \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\alpha )= igcap _{j=1}^{\infty }\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\alpha +j^{-1}\{ \omega \} ).  \] The $\subseteq $ direction is clear. Comparing the volumes using theorem 10.4.2 , we conclude that equality holds. 3 This follows from 1 and 2 . 4 Let $(T_ j)_ j$ be a sequence in $\mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}$ converging to $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}$ with respect to $d_ S$. We want to show that $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T_ j)\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$. By 2 , replacing the potential of each current by its $\mathcal I$-model representative does not change its partial Okounkov body. Thus we may represent the singularity types by model potentials of uniformly positive mass. Applying proposition 6.2.12 , after passing to a subsequence we may sandwich the sequence between an increasing and a decreasing sequence converging to $T$ in $d_ S$. Hence it suffices to treat the monotone cases. In either monotone case, 2 gives monotonicity of the convex bodies, while 1 and corollary 6.2.10 give convergence of their volumes to $\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$. Every Hausdorff cluster point is therefore a monotone limit with the same volume as $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$, hence is equal to $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$. 5 We may assume that $T$ is $\mathcal{I}$-good. It follows from 4 and theorem 7.1.1 that we may reduce to the case where $T$ has analytic singularities. Our assertion follows from 10.4.5 . 6 By ( 10.90 ), in order to prove ( 10.92 ), we may assume that $T$ and $S$ are both Kähler currents. Take quasi-equisingular approximations $(T_ j)_ j$ and $(S_ j)_ j$ of $T$ and $S$ respectively. By theorem 6.2.25 , $T_ j+S_ j\xrightarrow {d_ S} T+S$. By 4 , we may therefore assume that $T$ and $S$ have analytic singularities. Replacing $X$ by a suitable modification, we may assume that $T$ and $S$ both have log singularities, say \[  T=[D]+R,\quad S=[D']+R',  \] where $D$ and $D'$ are $\mathbb {Q}$-divisors on $X$ and $R$ and $R'$ are closed positive $(1,1)$-currents with bounded potentials. We need to show that \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R\} )+\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R'\} )+
u _{Y_{ ullet }}([D])+
u _{Y_{ ullet }}([D'])\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R+R'\} )+
u _{Y_{ ullet }}([D+D']).  \] By proposition 10.2.7 , this is equivalent to \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R\} )+\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R'\} )\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R+R'\} ),  \] which is already proved in theorem 10.4.2 . $\square$ Corollary 10.4.14 . Assume that $L$ is a big line bundle on $X$ and $h$ is a plurisubharmonic metric on $L$ with positive volume. Then 10.93  egin{equation} \label{eq:tranOkounandalgOkoun} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)=\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(L,h). \end{equation} Similarly, the definition ( 10.60 ) is compatible with the definition in definition 10.4.12 . Proof. We may assume that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ has positive mass and is $\mathcal{I}$-good. By the $d_ S$-continuity of both sides of ( 10.93 ) as proved in theorem 10.4.13 and theorem 10.3.18 , together with theorem 7.1.1 , we may assume that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ has analytic singularities. In this case, using the birational invariance of both sides of ( 10.93 ) as proved in proposition 10.3.19 and theorem 10.4.13 , we may assume that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ has log singularities. Finally, after all these reductions, the equality ( 10.93 ) holds by construction. $\square$

text:
10.4.3 The valuative characterization In this section, we will characterize the partial Okounkov bodies using valuations of currents. Lemma 10.4.15 . Let $ eta $ be a big and nef class on $X$. Then 10.94  egin{equation} \label{eq:Deltaresttox10} \left\{  y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}( eta )ight\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}( eta |_{Y_1}). \end{equation} Here the right-hand side is understood in the sense of definition 10.4.12 when $ eta |_{Y_1}$ is not big. Proof. Step 1 . We first reduce to the case where $ eta $ is a Kähler class. Take a Kähler class $\alpha $ on $X$. It follows from the volume formula in theorem 10.4.2 that \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}( eta )= igcap _{\epsilon >0}\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}( eta +\epsilon \alpha ).  \] Since $ eta |_{Y_1}$ is nef, hence pseudo-effective, definition 10.4.12 similarly gives \[  \Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}( eta |_{Y_1})=  igcap _{\epsilon >0}\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}( eta |_{Y_1}+\epsilon \alpha |_{Y_1}).  \] So it suffices to prove ( 10.94 ) with $ eta +\epsilon \alpha $ in place of $ eta $. Step 2 . Assume that $ eta $ is a Kähler class. The $\supseteq $ direction in ( 10.94 ) follows from the extension theorem theorem 1.6.15 . To prove the other direction, recall that by theorem 10.4.2 , for $t>0$ small enough, we have \[  \left\{  y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (t,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}( eta ) ight\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}\left(( eta -t\{ Y_1\} )|_{Y_1}ight).  \] As $t	o 0+$, the right-hand side converges to $\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}( eta |_{Y_1})$ with respect to the Hausdorff metric as a consequence of theorem 10.4.2 , while the left-hand side converges to \[  \left\{  y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}( eta ) ight\}   \] by C.1.7 . We conclude our assertion. $\square$ Lemma 10.4.16 . Let $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$ be a Kähler current. Assume that $
u (T,Y_1)=0$. Then 10.95  egin{equation} \label{eq:Deltaslice} \left\{  y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)ight\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}\left(\operatorname{Tr}^{\alpha |_{Y_1}}_{Y_1}(T)ight). \end{equation} More generally, if $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$ and $
u (T,Y_1)=0$, suppose in addition that $\operatorname{Tr}^{\alpha |_{Y_1}}_{Y_1}(T)$ is defined, then ( 10.95 ) still holds. See 8.1.8 for the definition of $\operatorname{Tr}^{\alpha |_{Y_1}}_{Y_1}(T)$. Note that $\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}\left(\operatorname{Tr}^{\alpha |_{Y_1}}_{Y_1}(T)ight)$ is independent of the choice of the representative $\operatorname{Tr}^{\alpha |_{Y_1}}_{Y_1}(T)$. Proof. Let $\omega $ be a Kähler form on $X$. The last assertion follows from the first by perturbing $	heta $ to $	heta +\epsilon \omega $. Step 1 . We first handle the case where $T$ has analytic singularities. Let $\pi \colon Zightarrow X$ be a modification such that $Y_{ ullet }$ admits a lifting $(W_{ ullet },g)$, and $\pi ^*T=[D]+R$, where $D$ is an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor on $Z$ and $R$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current with bounded potential. This is possible by theorem 1.6.7 and theorem 10.2.11 . By 8.2.4 , \[  \Pi ^*\operatorname{Tr}_{Y_1}(T)\sim _ P \operatorname{Tr}_{W_1}(\pi ^*T),  \] where $\Pi \colon W_1ightarrow Y_1$ is the restriction of $\pi $. It follows from theorem 10.4.13 that \[   egin{split}  \Delta _{W_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq W_ n}(\operatorname{Tr}_{W_1}(\pi ^*T))=&  \Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\operatorname{Tr}_{Y_1}(T))\operatorname{cor}(Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n,\Pi ),\  \Delta _{W_{ ullet }}(\pi ^*T)=& \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)g. \end{split}  \] Taking ( 10.13 ) into account, we find that it suffices to show that \[  \left\{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}:(0,y)\in \Delta _{W_{ ullet }}(\pi ^*T) ight\} =\Delta _{W_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq W_ n}(\operatorname{Tr}_{W_1}(\pi ^*T)).  \] We may assume that $\pi $ is the identity map. Since $
u (T,Y_1)=0$, the divisor $D$ does not contain $Y_1$. Hence we have \[  T=[D]+R,\quad T|_{Y_1}=[D]|_{Y_1}+R|_{Y_1}.  \] Note that $[D]|_{Y_1}$ is the current of integration along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor on $Y_1$. In particular, \[   egin{split}  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=&  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R\} )+
u _{Y_{ ullet }}([D]),\  \Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(T|_{Y_1})=&  \Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\{ R\} |_{Y_1})+
u _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}([D]|_{Y_1}). \end{split}  \] The first coordinate of $
u _{Y_{ ullet }}([D])$ is $0$, and the remaining coordinates are exactly $
u _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}([D]|_{Y_1})$. Thus it suffices to show that \[  \left\{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R\} )ight\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\{ R\} |_{Y_1}).  \] Since $R$ has bounded potential, its cohomology class is nef; it is big because $T$ is a Kähler current. Thus the last identity is exactly 10.4.15 . Step 2 . Next we consider the case where $T$ is a Kähler current. Take a quasi-equisingular approximation $(T_ j)_ j$ of $T$ in $\mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$. From Step 1, we know that for large $j\geq 1$, \[  \left\{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T_ j)ight\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\operatorname{Tr}_{Y_1}(T_ j)).  \] Letting $j	o \infty $ and applying theorem 10.4.13 and proposition 8.2.2 , we conclude ( 10.95 ). $\square$ Remark 10.4.17 . More generally, the same argument shows the following result: Let $k=0,\ldots ,n$ and $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$ such that $
u (T,Y_ k)=0$. Assume that $\operatorname{Tr}^{\alpha |_{Y_ k}}_{Y_ k}(T)$ is defined. Then 10.100  egin{equation}  \left\{  y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-k}: (0,\ldots ,0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)ight\} =\Delta _{Y_ k\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}\left(\operatorname{Tr}^{\alpha |_{Y_ k}}_{Y_ k}(T)ight). \end{equation} Also note that this result extends [ Theorem 3.4 , Jow10 ] and hence gives simpler proofs of [ Theorem A, Theorem B , Jow10 ] . Theorem 10.4.18 . Assume that $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}$ is a Kähler current. We have 10.101  egin{equation} \label{eq:minOkounkov} \min _{\mathrm{lex}} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T). \end{equation} Here the minimum is with respect to the lexicographic order. Proof. We argue by induction on $n\geq 0$. The case $n=0$ is of course trivial. Let us assume that $n>0$ and the case $n-1$ has been proved. We first observe that by theorem 10.4.13 , \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T-
u (T,Y_1)[Y_1])+(
u (T,Y_1),0,\ldots ,0)\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T).  \] By proposition 7.3.4 5 , removing the divisorial part does not change the volume. Comparing the volumes of both sides using theorem 10.4.13 and proposition 7.3.4 , we find that equality holds: \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T-
u (T,Y_1)[Y_1])+(
u (T,Y_1),0,\ldots ,0)=\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T).  \] Replacing $T$ by $T-
u (T,Y_1)[Y_1]$, we may therefore assume that $
u (T,Y_1)=0$. It suffices to apply 10.4.16 and the inductive hypothesis. $\square$ Corollary 10.4.19 . For any $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$, \[  
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\alpha ).  \] Proof. When $T$ is a Kähler current, this follows from theorem 10.4.18 . In general, by definition, $
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T+\omega )$ for any Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. It follows that \[  
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T+\omega )  \] for any Kähler form $\omega $. It follows that $
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$. $\square$ Theorem 10.4.20 . For any $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}$, 10.102  egin{equation} \label{eq:DeltaTequalallval} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=\overline{\left\{ 
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(S):S\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha ),S\preceq _{\mathcal{I}}Tight\} }. \end{equation} In particular, Note. According to Ya Deng, the definition ( 10.103 ) of $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\alpha )$ was what Demailly originally proposed for Deng's thesis. Due to the lack of the techniques of the trace operators, Deng had to work with analytic singularities instead. As a consequence, the transcendental analogue of proposition 10.3.19 is not obvious. This is one of the two main technical difficulties of theorem 10.4.2 . This problem also led me to finally develop the theory of trace operators, a notion that had been on the author's mind for several years. 10.103  egin{equation} \label{eq:TPOB_val} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\alpha )=\overline{\left\{ 
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(S):S\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )ight\} }. \end{equation} Remark 10.4.21 . We expect that the closure operation in ( 10.102 ) is not necessary. This problem is closely related to the Dirichlet problem of the trace operator, see Page  for more details. Proof. The $\supseteq $ direction in ( 10.102 ) follows from corollary 10.4.19 together with theorem 10.4.13 2 . Let us write \[  D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=\left\{ 
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(S):S\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha ),S\preceq _{\mathcal{I}}Tight\}   \] for the time being. Step 1 . Assume that $T$ has analytic singularities. We have \[   egin{split}  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\supseteq &  \overline{D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T)}\  \supseteq &  \overline{\left\{ 
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(S):\mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )
i S 	extup{ has gentle analytic singularities}, S\preceq Tight\} }. \end{split}  \] It follows easily from theorem 10.4.2 that the volume of the right-hand side is equal to the volume of $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$, so ( 10.102 ) holds. Step 2 . Assume that $T$ is a Kähler current. Take a quasi-equisingular approximation $T_ j\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$ of $T$. Next we use the language of psh functions. Let $\varphi _ j,\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be the potentials corresponding to $T_ j,T$ for each $j\geq 1$. Fix an integer $N>0$. For large enough $j\geq 1$, we can find $\psi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )_{>0}$ such that \[  P_{	heta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\geq (1-N^{-1})\varphi _ j+N^{-1} \psi _ j.  \] The existence of $\psi _ j$ follows from 2.4.15 . It follows that \[   egin{aligned}  D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\supseteq &  D_{Y_{ ullet }}\left(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left((1-N^{-1})\varphi _ j+N^{-1} \psi _ jight)ight)\  \supseteq &  (1-N^{-1})D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T_ j)+N^{-1} D_{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j). \end{aligned}  \] We claim that \[  \overline{D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T)}\supseteq  igcap _{j=1}^{\infty }\overline{D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T_ j)}.  \] Let $x$ be a point in the right-hand side. Fix $N>0$. For all large $j$, choose \[  y_ j\in D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T_ j),\quad z_ j\in D_{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j)  \] with $y_ j	o x$. By the preceding inclusion, \[  (1-N^{-1})y_ j+N^{-1}z_ j\in D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T).  \] The points $x,y_ j,z_ j$ all lie in the compact set $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\alpha )$ after taking closures, by corollary 10.4.19 . Hence, letting $j	o \infty $ and then $N	o \infty $, we get $x\in \overline{D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T)}$, proving the claim. Therefore, by Step 1, we conclude that \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)= igcap _{j=1}^{\infty }\overline{\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T_ j)}= igcap _{j=1}^{\infty }\overline{D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T_ j)}\subseteq \overline{D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T)}.  \] The reverse direction is already known. Step 3 . Finally, consider the general case. Take a Kähler current $T'\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$ more singular than $T$ (the existence of which is given by 2.4.19 ). For each $\epsilon \in (0,1)$, we know that \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}((1-\epsilon )T+\epsilon T')=\overline{D_{Y_{ ullet }}((1-\epsilon )T+\epsilon T')} \subseteq \overline{D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T)}.  \] Letting $\epsilon 	o 0+$ and using the $d_ S$-continuity in theorem 10.4.13 4 , we find that \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\subseteq \overline{D_{Y_{ ullet }}(T)}.  \] As the other inclusion is already known, we conclude. $\square$ Corollary 10.4.22 . Assume that $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}$. We have 10.108  egin{equation} \label{eq:minOkounkov3} \min _{\mathrm{lex}} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T). \end{equation} Proof. By theorem 10.4.20 , it is clear that \[  \min _{\mathrm{lex}} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\leq _{\mathrm{lex}}
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T).  \] On the other hand, we clearly have \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\subseteq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T+\omega )  \] for any Kähler form $\omega $ on $X$. It follows that \[  \min _{\mathrm{lex}} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)\geq _{\mathrm{lex}} \min _{\mathrm{lex}} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T+\omega ).  \] By theorem 10.4.18 , the right-hand side is just $
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T+\omega )=
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)$. We conclude the proof. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.4.15
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma 10.4.15 . Let $\beta $ be a big and nef class on $X$. Then 10.94 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Deltaresttox10} \left\{  y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\beta )\right\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\beta |_{Y_1}). \end{equation} Proof. Step 1 . We first reduce to the case where $\beta $ is a Kähler class. Take a Kähler class $\alpha $ on $X$. It follows from the volume formula in theorem 10.4.2 that \[  \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\beta )=\bigcap _{\epsilon >0}\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\beta +\epsilon \alpha ).  \] Since $\beta |_{Y_1}$ is nef, hence pseudo-effective, definition 10.4.12 similarly gives \[  \Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\beta |_{Y_1})= \bigcap _{\epsilon >0}\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\beta |_{Y_1}+\epsilon \alpha |_{Y_1}).  \] So it suffices to prove ( 10.94 ) with $\beta +\epsilon \alpha $ in place of $\beta $. Step 2 . Assume that $\beta $ is a Kähler class. The $\supseteq $ direction in ( 10.94 ) follows from the extension theorem theorem 1.6.15 . To prove the other direction, recall that by theorem 10.4.2 , for $t>0$ small enough, we have \[  \left\{  y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (t,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\beta ) \right\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}\left((\beta -t\{ Y_1\} )|_{Y_1}\right).  \] As $t\to 0+$, the right-hand side converges to $\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\beta |_{Y_1})$ with respect to the Hausdorff metric as a consequence of theorem 10.4.2 , while the left-hand side converges to \[  \left\{  y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\beta ) \right\}   \] by C.1.7 . We conclude our assertion. $\square$

Lemma 10.4.16 . Let $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$ be a Kähler current. Assume that $
u (T,Y_1)=0$. Then 10.95  egin{equation} \label{eq:Deltaslice} \left\{  y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)ight\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}\left(\operatorname{Tr}^{\alpha |_{Y_1}}_{Y_1}(T)ight). \end{equation} More generally, if $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$ and $
u (T,Y_1)=0$, suppose in addition that $\operatorname{Tr}^{\alpha |_{Y_1}}_{Y_1}(T)$ is defined, then ( 10.95 ) still holds. Proof. Let $\omega $ be a Kähler form on $X$. The last assertion follows from the first by perturbing $	heta $ to $	heta +\epsilon \omega $. Step 1 . We first handle the case where $T$ has analytic singularities. Let $\pi \colon Zightarrow X$ be a modification such that $Y_{ ullet }$ admits a lifting $(W_{ ullet },g)$, and $\pi ^*T=[D]+R$, where $D$ is an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor on $Z$ and $R$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current with bounded potential. This is possible by theorem 1.6.7 and theorem 10.2.11 . By 8.2.4 , \[  \Pi ^*\operatorname{Tr}_{Y_1}(T)\sim _ P \operatorname{Tr}_{W_1}(\pi ^*T),  \] where $\Pi \colon W_1ightarrow Y_1$ is the restriction of $\pi $. It follows from theorem 10.4.13 that \[   egin{split}  \Delta _{W_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq W_ n}(\operatorname{Tr}_{W_1}(\pi ^*T))=&  \Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\operatorname{Tr}_{Y_1}(T))\operatorname{cor}(Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n,\Pi ),\  \Delta _{W_{ ullet }}(\pi ^*T)=& \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)g. \end{split}  \] Taking ( 10.13 ) into account, we find that it suffices to show that \[  \left\{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}:(0,y)\in \Delta _{W_{ ullet }}(\pi ^*T) ight\} =\Delta _{W_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq W_ n}(\operatorname{Tr}_{W_1}(\pi ^*T)).  \] We may assume that $\pi $ is the identity map. Since $
u (T,Y_1)=0$, the divisor $D$ does not contain $Y_1$. Hence we have \[  T=[D]+R,\quad T|_{Y_1}=[D]|_{Y_1}+R|_{Y_1}.  \] Note that $[D]|_{Y_1}$ is the current of integration along an effective $\mathbb {Q}$-divisor on $Y_1$. In particular, \[   egin{split}  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=&  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R\} )+
u _{Y_{ ullet }}([D]),\  \Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(T|_{Y_1})=&  \Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\{ R\} |_{Y_1})+
u _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}([D]|_{Y_1}). \end{split}  \] The first coordinate of $
u _{Y_{ ullet }}([D])$ is $0$, and the remaining coordinates are exactly $
u _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}([D]|_{Y_1})$. Thus it suffices to show that \[  \left\{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\{ R\} )ight\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\{ R\} |_{Y_1}).  \] Since $R$ has bounded potential, its cohomology class is nef; it is big because $T$ is a Kähler current. Thus the last identity is exactly 10.4.15 . Step 2 . Next we consider the case where $T$ is a Kähler current. Take a quasi-equisingular approximation $(T_ j)_ j$ of $T$ in $\mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )$. From Step 1, we know that for large $j\geq 1$, \[  \left\{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}: (0,y)\in \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T_ j)ight\} =\Delta _{Y_1\supseteq \cdots \supseteq Y_ n}(\operatorname{Tr}_{Y_1}(T_ j)).  \] Letting $j	o \infty $ and applying theorem 10.4.13 and proposition 8.2.2 , we conclude ( 10.95 ). $\square$

Theorem 10.4.18 . Assume that $T\in \mathcal{Z}_+(X,\alpha )_{>0}$ is a Kähler current. We have 10.101  egin{equation} \label{eq:minOkounkov} \min _{\mathrm{lex}} \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(T)=

u (T,Y_1)[Y_1])+(

title: 10.5 Okounkov test curves
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text:
10.5 Okounkov test curves Fix $n\in \mathbb {N}$. Let $\Delta ,\Delta '\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ be convex bodies with positive volumes. The standard Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb {R}^ n$ is denoted by $\operatorname{vol}$. Recall that $\mathcal{K}_ n$ denotes the set of convex bodies in $\mathbb {R}^ n$ and $d_{\mathrm{Haus}}$ denotes the Hausdorff metric. We refer to chapter C for the basic properties of these objects. We study the notion of Okounkov test curves in this section; this leads to the definition of the Duistermaat–Heckman measure of a non-Archimedean metric in section 13.3 below. This section can be skipped on a first reading. Definition 10.5.1 . An Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta $ consists of a number $\Delta _{\max }\in \mathbb {R}$ and an assignment $(-\infty ,\Delta _{\max })
i 	au \mapsto \Delta _{	au }\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ satisfying the assignment $	au \mapsto \Delta _{	au }$ is decreasing and concave Note. Here concavity refers to the concavity with respect to the Minkowski sum. ; we have $\Delta _{	au }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta $ as $	au 	o -\infty $. The set of Okounkov test curves relative to $\Delta $ is denoted by $\mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. An Okounkov test curve $\Delta _{ ullet }$ relative to $\Delta $ is bounded if $\Delta _{	au }=\Delta $ when $	au $ is small enough. The subset of bounded Okounkov test curves is denoted by $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta )$. An Okounkov test curve $\Delta _{ ullet }$ relative to $\Delta $ is said to have finite energy if 10.109  egin{equation} \label{eq:Otestcurvenergy} \mathbf{E}(\Delta _{ ullet })\coloneqq n!\Delta _{\max } \operatorname{vol}\Delta +n!\int _{-\infty }^{\Delta _{\max }} \left(\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au }-\operatorname{vol}\Delta ight)\, \mathrm{d}	au >-\infty . \end{equation} The subset of Okounkov test curves with finite energy is denoted by $\mathrm{TC}^{1}(\Delta )$. Given $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ and $\Delta '_{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ')$, we say $\Delta _{ ullet }\leq \Delta '_{ ullet }$ if $\Delta _{\max }\leq \Delta '_{\max }$ and for any $	au <\Delta _{\max }$, we have $\Delta _{	au }\subseteq \Delta '_{	au }$. Sometimes it is convenient to introduce 10.110  egin{equation} \label{eq:DeltaDeltamax} \Delta _{\Delta _{\max }}= igcap _{	au <\Delta _{\max }}\Delta _{	au }\in \mathcal{K}_ n. \end{equation} We shall always make this extension in the sequel when we talk about $\Delta _{\Delta _{\max }}$. Observe that $(-\infty ,\Delta _{\max }]
i 	au \mapsto \Delta _{	au }$ is still concave. Proposition 10.5.2 . Any Okounkov test curve $(\Delta _{	au })_{	au < \Delta _{\max }}$ relative to $\Delta $ is continuous in $	au $. Moreover, $\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au }>0$ for all $	au <\Delta _{\max }$. Proof. We first claim that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au '}>0$ for all $	au '<\Delta _{\max }$. By Condition (2b) in definition 10.5.1 and theorem C.1.4 , we know that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au ''}>0$ when $	au ''$ is small enough. Fix one such $	au ''$. We may assume that $	au ''\leq 	au '$ since otherwise there is nothing to prove. Next take $	au '''\in (	au ',\Delta _{\max })$. Take $t\in (0,1)$ such that $	au '=t	au '''+(1-t)	au ''$. It follows that \[  \operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au '}\geq \operatorname{vol}\left( t\Delta _{	au '''}+(1-t)\Delta _{	au ''}ight)\geq (1-t)^ n\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au ''}>0.  \] Next we claim that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au }$ is continuous for $	au < \Delta _{\max }$. In fact, it follows from theorem C.1.12 that $(-\infty ,\Delta _{\max }) 
i 	au \mapsto \log \operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au }$ is concave, but we already know that it is finite, hence the continuity follows. Next we show that \[  \Delta _{	au }= igcap _{	au '<	au }\Delta _{	au '}.  \] The $\subseteq $ direction is obvious. By the continuity of the volume, both sides have the same volume and the volume is positive, we therefore obtain the equality. Similarly, we have \[  \Delta _{	au }=\overline{ igcup _{	au '>	au }\Delta _{	au '}}.  \] The continuity of $\Delta _{	au }$ at $	au <\Delta _{\max }$ is proved. $\square$ Definition 10.5.3 . A test function on $\Delta $ is a function $G\colon \Delta ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that $G$ is concave, $G$ is finite on $\operatorname{Int}\Delta $, and $G$ is upper semicontinuous. A test function $G$ is bounded if $G$ is bounded from below. A test function $G$ has finite energy if 10.111  egin{equation} \label{eq:EF} \mathbf{E}(G)\coloneqq n!\int _{\Delta } G\, \mathrm{d}\lambda >-\infty . \end{equation} Definition 10.5.4 . Let $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. We define its Legendre transform as \[  G[\Delta _{ ullet }] \colon \Delta ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad a\mapsto \sup \left\{ 	au <\Delta _{\max }:a\in \Delta _{	au }ight\} .  \] Given a test function $G\colon \Delta ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$, we define its inverse Legendre transform $\Delta [G]_{ ullet }$ as the Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta $ defined as follows: $\Delta [G]_{\max }=\sup _{\Delta } G$, and for each $	au <\sup _{\Delta } G$, we set \[  \Delta [G]_{	au }=\{ x\in \Delta :G\geq 	au \} .  \] We observe that 10.112  egin{equation} \label{eq:GDeltamax} G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)=\max \left\{ 	au \leq \Delta _{\max }: a\in \Delta _{	au }ight\} ,	extup{ if } G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)>-\infty . \end{equation} Lemma 10.5.5 . Let $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. Then $G[\Delta _{ ullet }]$ defined in definition 10.5.4 is a test function. Similarly, if $G\colon \Delta ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is a test function, then $\Delta [G]_{ ullet }$ is an Okounkov test curve. Proof. First suppose that $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. We want to verify that $G[\Delta _{ ullet }]$ satisfies the conditions in definition 10.5.3 . We first verify the concavity. Take $a,b\in \Delta $. We want to prove that for any $t\in (0,1)$, 10.113  egin{equation} \label{eq:GDeltaconc} G[\Delta _{ ullet }](ta+(1-t)b)\geq tG[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)+(1-t)G[\Delta _{ ullet }](b). \end{equation} There is nothing to prove if $G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)$ or $G[\Delta _{ ullet }](b)$ is $-\infty $. So we assume that both are finite. In this case, by ( 10.112 ), \[  a\in \Delta _{G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)},\quad b\in \Delta _{G[\Delta _{ ullet }](b)}.  \] Thus, \[  ta+(1-t)b\in t \Delta _{G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)}+(1-t)\Delta _{G[\Delta _{ ullet }](b)}\subseteq \Delta _{tG[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)+(1-t)G[\Delta _{ ullet }](b)}.  \] We deduce that \[  G[\Delta _{ ullet }](ta+(1-t)b)\geq tG[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)+(1-t)G[\Delta _{ ullet }](b).  \] Therefore, ( 10.113 ) follows. It is clear that $G[\Delta _{ ullet }]$ is finite on the interior of $\Delta $. It remains to argue that $G[\Delta _{ ullet }]$ is upper semicontinuous. Let $(a_ i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a sequence in $\Delta $ with limit $a\in \Delta $. Define $	au _ i=G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a_ i)$. Let $	au =\varlimsup _ i 	au _ i$. We need to show that 10.114  egin{equation} \label{eq:ainDelta1} G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)\geq 	au . \end{equation} There is nothing to prove if $	au =-\infty $. We assume that this is not the case. Passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $	au _ i	o 	au $. In particular, we can assume that $	au _ i
eq -\infty $ for all $i\geq 1$. It follows from ( 10.112 ) that $a_ i\in \Delta _{	au _ i}$ for all $i\geq 1$. If $	au <\Delta _{\max }$, then $\Delta _{	au _ i}\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{	au }$, so theorem C.1.5 implies that $a\in \Delta _{	au }$. If $	au =\Delta _{\max }$, then the same conclusion follows from the definition $\Delta _{\Delta _{\max }}= igcap _{	au '<\Delta _{\max }}\Delta _{	au '}$. Thus, ( 10.114 ) follows. Conversely, suppose that $G\colon \Delta ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is a test function. We argue that $\Delta [G]_{ ullet }$ is an Okounkov test curve. We verify the conditions in definition 10.5.1 . Firstly, for each $	au < \sup _{\Delta }G$, the set $\Delta [G]_{	au }$ is a convex body as $G$ is concave and usc. Moreover, $\Delta [G]_{	au }$ is clearly decreasing in $	au $. Secondly, for each $a\in \Delta $, we can write $a=\lim _{i}a_ i$ with $a_ i\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta $. By assumption, $G$ is finite at $a_ i$. Thus, \[  a\in \overline{\{ G>-\infty \} }=\overline{ igcup _{	au <\sup _{\Delta }G}\Delta [G]_{	au }}.  \] By theorem C.1.5 , $\Delta [G]_{	au }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta $ as $	au 	o -\infty $. Thirdly, $\Delta [G]$ is concave. To see this, take $	au ,	au '< \Delta _{\max }$. We need to prove that for any $t\in (0,1)$, 10.115  egin{equation} \label{eq:Deconc} \Delta [G]_{t	au +(1-t)	au '}\supseteq t\Delta [G]_{	au }+(1-t)\Delta [G]_{	au '}. \end{equation} Let $a\in \Delta [G]_{	au }$ and $b\in \Delta [G]_{	au '}$. We have $G(a)\geq 	au $ and $G(b)\geq 	au '$. As $G$ is concave, we have $G(ta+(1-t)b)\geq t	au +(1-t)	au '$. Thus, \[  ta+(1-t)b\in \Delta [G]_{t	au +(1-t)	au '}  \] and ( 10.115 ) follows. $\square$ Theorem 10.5.6 . The Legendre transform and inverse Legendre transform are inverse to each other, defining a bijection between $\mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ and the set of test functions on $\Delta $. Under this bijection, $\mathrm{TC}^1(\Delta )$ corresponds to test functions on $\Delta $ with finite energy and $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta )$ corresponds to bounded test functions on $\Delta $. Proof. Thanks to 10.5.5 , in order to prove the first assertion, it only remains to see that the Legendre transform and the inverse Legendre transform are inverse to each other, which is immediate by definition. It is obvious that $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta )$ corresponds to bounded test functions. Moreover, a direct computation shows that if $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$, then \[  \mathbf{E}(\Delta _{ ullet })=\mathbf{E}(G[\Delta _{ ullet }]),  \] concluding the $\mathrm{TC}^{1}(\Delta )$ case. $\square$ Proposition 10.5.7 . Let $(\Delta ^ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathcal{K}_ n$ such that $\Delta \subseteq  igcap _{i\in I}\Delta ^ i$. Consider a decreasing net $(\Delta ^ i_{ ullet })_{i\in I}$ with $\Delta ^ i_{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ^ i)$ for all $i\in I$ such that there is $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ satisfying the following properties: $\Delta _{\max }= \lim _{i\in I}\Delta ^ i_{\max }$; for any $	au <\Delta _{\max }$, we have $\Delta ^ i_{	au }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{	au }$. Then for any $a\in \Delta $, we have 10.116  egin{equation} \label{eq:pwconvLegendre} \lim _{i\in I} G[\Delta ^ i_{ ullet }](a)=G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a). \end{equation} Note that in general, \[  \Delta \subsetneq  igcap _{i\in I}\Delta ^ i.  \] Proof. Fix $a\in \Delta $. It follows immediately from the definition of $G$ that the net $(G[\Delta ^ i_{ ullet }](a))_{i\in I}$ is decreasing and the $\geq $ direction in ( 10.116 ) holds. Let us prove the reverse inequality. Let $	au $ denote the left-hand side of ( 10.116 ) for the moment. By definition, for any $\epsilon >0$ and any $i\in I$, we have $a\in \Delta ^ i_{	au -\epsilon }$. It follows that \[  a\in \Delta _{	au -\epsilon }.  \] Therefore, \[  	au \leq G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Similarly, for increasing nets, we have: Proposition 10.5.8 . Let $(\Delta ^ i)_{i\in I}$ be an increasing net in $\mathcal{K}_ n$ with Hausdorff limit $\Delta $ such that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta ^ i>0$ for all $i\in I$. Consider an increasing net $(\Delta ^ i_{ ullet })_{i\in I}$ with $\Delta ^ i_{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ^ i)$ for all $i\in I$. Let $\Delta _{\max }=\lim _{i\in I}\Delta ^ i_{\max }$. For any $	au <\Delta _{\max }$, let $\Delta _{	au }$ be the Hausdorff limit of $\Delta ^ i_{	au }$. Then $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ and 10.117  egin{equation} \label{eq:apwconvLegendre} \lim _{i\in I}G[\Delta ^ i_{ ullet }](a)=G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a) \end{equation} for any $a\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta $. Proof. It is obvious that $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. Fix $a\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta $. Since $\Delta ^ i\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta $, we have $a\in \Delta ^ i$ for all large enough $i$. By definition, the net $(G[\Delta ^ i_{ ullet }](a))_{i\in I}$ is increasing and the $\leq $ direction in ( 10.117 ) holds. Let us write $	au =G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)$ for the time being. By definition of $G$, for any $\epsilon >0$, we have \[  a\in \Delta _{	au -\epsilon /2}.  \] The concavity of $\Delta _{ ullet }$ guarantees that \[  a\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta _{	au -\epsilon }.  \] Indeed, choose $\sigma \ll 0$ so that a small ball around $a$ is contained in $\Delta _\sigma $. Since $a\in \Delta _{	au -\epsilon /2}$ and \[  	au -\epsilon =t\sigma +(1-t)(	au -\epsilon /2)  \] for a suitable $t\in (0,1)$, concavity gives a small ball around $a$ contained in $\Delta _{	au -\epsilon }$. Since $\Delta ^ i_{	au -\epsilon }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{	au -\epsilon }$ and $a\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta _{	au -\epsilon }$, it follows that for all large enough $i\in I$, \[  a\in \Delta ^ i_{	au -\epsilon }.  \] Therefore, \[  	au -\epsilon \leq G[\Delta ^ i_{ ullet }](a)  \] for all large enough $i$. Taking the limit with respect to $i$ and then with respect to $\epsilon $, we conclude the desired inequality. $\square$ Definition 10.5.9 . Let $\Delta _{ ullet }$ be an Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta $. We define the Duistermaat–Heckman measure $\operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet })$ as \[  \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet })\coloneqq G[\Delta _{ ullet }]_*(\operatorname{vol}).  \] It is a Radon measure on $\mathbb {R}$, since $G[\Delta _{ ullet }]$ is finite on $\operatorname{Int}\Delta $. In other words, $\operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet })$ is the distribution of the random variable $G[\Delta _{ ullet }]$. Proposition 10.5.10 . Let $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. Let $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. Then the following extended moment identity holds: 10.118  egin{equation} \label{eq:momentcalc} \int _{\mathbb {R}}x^ m \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet })(x)=\Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta +m\int _{-\infty }^{\Delta _{\max }} 	au ^{m-1}(\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au }-\operatorname{vol}\Delta )\, \mathrm{d}	au \end{equation} and 10.119  egin{equation} \label{eq:massDHm1} \int _{\mathbb {R}}\operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet })=\operatorname{vol}\Delta . \end{equation} Proof. In fact, ( 10.119 ) follows immediately from the definition. Let $G=G[\Delta _{ ullet }]$. We first assume that $G$ is bounded from below. Then ( 10.118 ) follows from a straightforward computation: \[   egin{aligned} & \int _{\mathbb {R}}x^ m \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet })(x)\  =&  \int _{\Delta } G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)^ m\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(a)\  =&  \int _{\Delta } \left( \Delta _{\max }^ m-\int _{G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a)}^{\Delta _{\max }} m	au ^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}	au ight)\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(a)\  =&  \Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta -m\int _{\mathbb {R}}\int _{\Delta } \mathds {1}_{[G[\Delta _{ ullet }](a),\Delta _{\max }]}(	au )	au ^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(a)\, \mathrm{d}	au \  =&  \Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta -m\int _{-\infty }^{\Delta _{\max }}\int _{\Delta \setminus \Delta _{	au }} 	au ^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(a)\, \mathrm{d}	au \  =&  \Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta -m\int _{-\infty }^{\Delta _{\max }} 	au ^{m-1}\left(\operatorname{vol}\Delta -\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au }ight)\, \mathrm{d}	au . \end{aligned}  \] In general, set $G_ A=G\lor (-A)$. The same pointwise identity applied to $G_ A$ gives \[  \int _{\Delta }G_ A^ m\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}=\Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta +m\int _{-A}^{\Delta _{\max }}	au ^{m-1}(\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{	au }-\operatorname{vol}\Delta )\, \mathrm{d}	au .  \] Letting $A	o \infty $ gives ( 10.118 ): if $m$ is even, this follows from monotone convergence applied to $G_ A^ m
earrow G^ m$; if $m$ is odd, apply monotone convergence to $\Delta _{\max }^ m-G_ A^ m
earrow \Delta _{\max }^ m-G^ m$. Thus both sides of ( 10.118 ) are interpreted in the corresponding extended sense. $\square$ Lemma 10.5.11 . Let $(\Delta ^ i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a decreasing sequence in $\mathcal{K}_ n$ with limit $\Delta $. Suppose that $(\Delta _{ ullet }^ i)_{i\geq 1}$ is a decreasing sequence with $\Delta _{ ullet }^ i\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ^ i)$. Suppose that there is $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ such that $\Delta _{\max }=\lim _{i	o \infty }\Delta ^ i_{\max }$; for any $	au <\Delta _{\max }$, we have $\Delta ^ i_{	au }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{	au }$. Then $\operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet }^ i)ightharpoonup \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet })$. Proof. Let $f\in C_ c(\mathbb {R})$. It follows from proposition 10.5.7 that \[  G[\Delta _{ ullet }^ i]	o G[\Delta _{ ullet }]  \] pointwise on $\Delta $. Hence the dominated convergence theorem gives \[  \int _{\Delta } f(G[\Delta _{ ullet }^ i])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda 	o \int _{\Delta } f(G[\Delta _{ ullet }])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda .  \] Since $\Delta ^ i\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta $, theorem C.1.4 gives $\operatorname{vol}(\Delta ^ i\setminus \Delta )	o 0$. The contribution of $\Delta ^ i\setminus \Delta $ is bounded by $\| f\| _{\infty }\operatorname{vol}(\Delta ^ i\setminus \Delta )$, so \[  \int _{\Delta ^ i} f(G[\Delta _{ ullet }^ i])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda 	o \int _{\Delta } f(G[\Delta _{ ullet }])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda .  \] This is the weak convergence. $\square$ Similarly, we have Lemma 10.5.12 . Let $(\Delta ^ i)_{i\geq 1}$ be an increasing sequence in $\mathcal{K}_ n$ with Hausdorff limit $\Delta $ such that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta ^ i>0$ for all $i\geq 1$. Consider an increasing sequence $(\Delta ^ i_{ ullet })_{i\geq 1}$ with $\Delta ^ i_{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ^ i)$ for all $i\geq 1$. Let $\Delta _{ ullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ be defined as $\Delta _{\max }=\lim _{i	o \infty }\Delta ^ i_{\max }$; for any $	au <\Delta _{\max }$, $\Delta _{	au }$ is the Hausdorff limit of $\Delta ^ i_{	au }$. Then we have \[  \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet }^ i)ightharpoonup \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{ ullet }).  \] Proof. Let $f\in C_ c(\mathbb {R})$. It follows from proposition 10.5.8 that \[  G[\Delta _{ ullet }^ i]	o G[\Delta _{ ullet }]  \] almost everywhere on $\Delta $. Extending $f(G[\Delta _{ ullet }^ i])$ by $0$ outside $\Delta ^ i$, we also have $\mathds {1}_{\Delta ^ i}	o \mathds {1}_{\Delta }$ almost everywhere on $\Delta $, since the boundary of the convex body $\Delta $ has Lebesgue measure zero. The dominated convergence theorem gives \[  \int _{\Delta ^ i} f(G[\Delta _{ ullet }^ i])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda 	o \int _{\Delta } f(G[\Delta _{ ullet }])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda .  \] This is the weak convergence. $\square$ The main source of Okounkov test curves is the following: Theorem 10.5.13 . Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold and $	heta $ be a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class $\alpha $. Let $Y_{ ullet }$ be a smooth flag on $X$ and $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}(X,	heta )_{>0}$. Then the map \[  (-\infty ,\Gamma _{\max })
i 	au \mapsto \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma )_{	au }\coloneqq \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{	au })  \] defines an Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{-\infty })$. If furthermore $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}^1(X,	heta ;\Gamma _{-\infty })$ (resp. $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\Gamma _{-\infty })$), then we have $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma )\in \mathrm{TC}^1(\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }))$ (resp. $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }))$). See definition 9.1.1 and definition 9.1.5 for the relevant definitions. Proof. Consider $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}(X,	heta )_{>0}$. We need to verify that $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma )$ is an Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{-\infty })$. First observe that $	au \mapsto \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{	au })$ is concave and decreasing for $	au <\Gamma _{\max }$. The decreasing property follows from theorem 10.4.13 2 . For concavity, use the valuative characterization theorem 10.4.20 together with the additivity of valuations in proposition 10.2.7 : if $x\in \Delta _{Y_ ullet }(	heta ,\Gamma _	au )$ and $y\in \Delta _{Y_ ullet }(	heta ,\Gamma _{	au '})$, then $tx+(1-t)y$ is obtained from the current $tS+(1-t)S'$, which is more singular than $\Gamma _{t	au +(1-t)	au '}$. Hence \[  t\Delta _{Y_ ullet }\left(	heta ,\Gamma _	au ight)+(1-t)\Delta _{Y_ ullet }\left(	heta ,\Gamma _{	au '}ight)\subseteq \Delta _{Y_ ullet }\left(	heta ,\Gamma _{t	au +(1-t)	au '}ight).  \] Next we show that as $	au 	o -\infty $, we have \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{	au })\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }).  \] By theorem 10.4.13 2 , the bodies $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{	au })$ are contained in $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{-\infty })$ and increase as $	au 	o -\infty $. Thus it suffices to compute their volumes: \[   egin{split}  \lim _{	au 	o -\infty }\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{	au })= rac{1}{n!}\lim _{	au 	o -\infty }\operatorname{vol}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma _{	au })= rac{1}{n!}\operatorname{vol}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma _{-\infty }) \  =\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }), \end{split}  \] where we applied theorem 10.4.13 and theorem 6.2.30 . When $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(X,	heta ;\Gamma _{-\infty })$, it is clear that $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma )\in \mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }))$. When $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}^{1}(X,	heta ;\Gamma _{-\infty })$, by theorem 10.4.13 1 , ( 9.5 ) and ( 10.109 ), we have \[  \mathbf{E}^{\Gamma _{-\infty }}(\Gamma )=\mathbf{E}(\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma )).  \] Indeed, by theorem 10.4.13 1 , \[  n!\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _	au )=\int _ X	heta _{\Gamma _	au }^ n  \] for every $	au <\Gamma _{\max }$, and the same identity holds at $	au =-\infty $. Comparing ( 9.5 ) with ( 10.109 ) gives the asserted equality of energies. So $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma )\in \mathrm{TC}^1(\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }))$. $\square$ Remark 10.5.14 . As a special case of this construction, suppose that $\Gamma $ is the test curve induced by a test configuration as in example 9.3.9 and 9.3.10 , then for any $	au <\Gamma _{\max }$, $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\Gamma _{	au })$ is the Okounkov body of a graded linear series \[   igoplus _{k=0}^{\infty }\mathcal{F}^{k	au }_ k,  \] where $\mathcal{F}$ is the filtration induced by the test configuration. See [ Theorem 5.28 , Xia21 ] for the details. In particular, in this case, our theory of partial Okounkov bodies recovers the Okounkov bodies of the filtered linear series in the sense of [ BC11 ] . Beauty is the first test: There is no permanent place in this world for ugly mathematics. 
— Godfrey Harold Hardy Note. Godfrey Harold Hardy (1877–1947) was a British mathematician famous for his work in number theory and mathematical analysis. Apart from his research, Hardy was a strong advocate for pure mathematics and believed that mathematics should be pursued for its own beauty, not just for practical use. 
He remained lifelong unmarried and dedicated much of his life entirely to mathematics, fitting into the common stereotype of a mathematician.

title: Definition 10.5.1
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Definition 10.5.1 . An Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta $ consists of a number $\Delta _{\max }\in \mathbb {R}$ and an assignment $(-\infty ,\Delta _{\max })\ni \tau \mapsto \Delta _{\tau }\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ satisfying the assignment $\tau \mapsto \Delta _{\tau }$ is decreasing and concave Note. Here concavity refers to the concavity with respect to the Minkowski sum. ; we have $\Delta _{\tau }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta $ as $\tau \to -\infty $. The set of Okounkov test curves relative to $\Delta $ is denoted by $\mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. An Okounkov test curve $\Delta _{\bullet }$ relative to $\Delta $ is bounded if $\Delta _{\tau }=\Delta $ when $\tau $ is small enough. The subset of bounded Okounkov test curves is denoted by $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta )$. An Okounkov test curve $\Delta _{\bullet }$ relative to $\Delta $ is said to have finite energy if 10.109 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Otestcurvenergy} \mathbf{E}(\Delta _{\bullet })\coloneqq n!\Delta _{\max } \operatorname{vol}\Delta +n!\int _{-\infty }^{\Delta _{\max }} \left(\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau }-\operatorname{vol}\Delta \right)\, \mathrm{d}\tau >-\infty . \end{equation} The subset of Okounkov test curves with finite energy is denoted by $\mathrm{TC}^{1}(\Delta )$. Given $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ and $\Delta '_{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ')$, we say $\Delta _{\bullet }\leq \Delta '_{\bullet }$ if $\Delta _{\max }\leq \Delta '_{\max }$ and for any $\tau <\Delta _{\max }$, we have $\Delta _{\tau }\subseteq \Delta '_{\tau }$.

text: 10.110 \begin{equation} \label{eq:DeltaDeltamax} \Delta _{\Delta _{\max }}=\bigcap _{\tau <\Delta _{\max }}\Delta _{\tau }\in \mathcal{K}_ n. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 10.5.2
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Proposition 10.5.2 . Any Okounkov test curve $(\Delta _{\tau })_{\tau < \Delta _{\max }}$ relative to $\Delta $ is continuous in $\tau $. Moreover, $\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau }>0$ for all $\tau <\Delta _{\max }$. Proof. We first claim that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau '}>0$ for all $\tau '<\Delta _{\max }$. By Condition (2b) in definition 10.5.1 and theorem C.1.4 , we know that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau ''}>0$ when $\tau ''$ is small enough. Fix one such $\tau ''$. We may assume that $\tau ''\leq \tau '$ since otherwise there is nothing to prove. Next take $\tau '''\in (\tau ',\Delta _{\max })$. Take $t\in (0,1)$ such that $\tau '=t\tau '''+(1-t)\tau ''$. It follows that \[  \operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau '}\geq \operatorname{vol}\left( t\Delta _{\tau '''}+(1-t)\Delta _{\tau ''}\right)\geq (1-t)^ n\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau ''}>0.  \] Next we claim that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau }$ is continuous for $\tau < \Delta _{\max }$. In fact, it follows from theorem C.1.12 that $(-\infty ,\Delta _{\max }) \ni \tau \mapsto \log \operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau }$ is concave, but we already know that it is finite, hence the continuity follows. Next we show that \[  \Delta _{\tau }=\bigcap _{\tau '<\tau }\Delta _{\tau '}.  \] The $\subseteq $ direction is obvious. By the continuity of the volume, both sides have the same volume and the volume is positive, we therefore obtain the equality. Similarly, we have \[  \Delta _{\tau }=\overline{\bigcup _{\tau '>\tau }\Delta _{\tau '}}.  \] The continuity of $\Delta _{\tau }$ at $\tau <\Delta _{\max }$ is proved. $\square$

title: Definition 10.5.3
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Definition 10.5.3 . A test function on $\Delta $ is a function $G\colon \Delta \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ such that $G$ is concave, $G$ is finite on $\operatorname{Int}\Delta $, and $G$ is upper semicontinuous. A test function $G$ is bounded if $G$ is bounded from below. A test function $G$ has finite energy if 10.111 \begin{equation} \label{eq:EF} \mathbf{E}(G)\coloneqq n!\int _{\Delta } G\, \mathrm{d}\lambda >-\infty . \end{equation}

topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: 10.111 \begin{equation} \label{eq:EF} \mathbf{E}(G)\coloneqq n!\int _{\Delta } G\, \mathrm{d}\lambda >-\infty . \end{equation}

title: Definition 10.5.4
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Definition 10.5.4 . Let $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. We define its Legendre transform as \[  G[\Delta _{\bullet }] \colon \Delta \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ),\quad a\mapsto \sup \left\{ \tau <\Delta _{\max }:a\in \Delta _{\tau }\right\} .  \] Given a test function $G\colon \Delta \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$, we define its inverse Legendre transform $\Delta [G]_{\bullet }$ as the Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta $ defined as follows: $\Delta [G]_{\max }=\sup _{\Delta } G$, and for each $\tau <\sup _{\Delta } G$, we set \[  \Delta [G]_{\tau }=\{ x\in \Delta :G\geq \tau \} .  \]

topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: 10.112 \begin{equation} \label{eq:GDeltamax} G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)=\max \left\{ \tau \leq \Delta _{\max }: a\in \Delta _{\tau }\right\} ,\textup{ if } G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)>-\infty . \end{equation}

title: Lemma 10.5.5
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma 10.5.5 . Let $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. Then $G[\Delta _{\bullet }]$ defined in definition 10.5.4 is a test function. Similarly, if $G\colon \Delta \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is a test function, then $\Delta [G]_{\bullet }$ is an Okounkov test curve. Proof. First suppose that $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. We want to verify that $G[\Delta _{\bullet }]$ satisfies the conditions in definition 10.5.3 . We first verify the concavity. Take $a,b\in \Delta $. We want to prove that for any $t\in (0,1)$, 10.113 \begin{equation} \label{eq:GDeltaconc} G[\Delta _{\bullet }](ta+(1-t)b)\geq tG[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)+(1-t)G[\Delta _{\bullet }](b). \end{equation} There is nothing to prove if $G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)$ or $G[\Delta _{\bullet }](b)$ is $-\infty $. So we assume that both are finite. In this case, by ( 10.112 ), \[  a\in \Delta _{G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)},\quad b\in \Delta _{G[\Delta _{\bullet }](b)}.  \] Thus, \[  ta+(1-t)b\in t \Delta _{G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)}+(1-t)\Delta _{G[\Delta _{\bullet }](b)}\subseteq \Delta _{tG[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)+(1-t)G[\Delta _{\bullet }](b)}.  \] We deduce that \[  G[\Delta _{\bullet }](ta+(1-t)b)\geq tG[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)+(1-t)G[\Delta _{\bullet }](b).  \] Therefore, ( 10.113 ) follows. It is clear that $G[\Delta _{\bullet }]$ is finite on the interior of $\Delta $. It remains to argue that $G[\Delta _{\bullet }]$ is upper semicontinuous. Let $(a_ i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a sequence in $\Delta $ with limit $a\in \Delta $. Define $\tau _ i=G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a_ i)$. Let $\tau =\varlimsup _ i \tau _ i$. We need to show that 10.114 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ainDelta1} G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)\geq \tau . \end{equation} There is nothing to prove if $\tau =-\infty $. We assume that this is not the case. Passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $\tau _ i\to \tau $. In particular, we can assume that $\tau _ i\neq -\infty $ for all $i\geq 1$. It follows from ( 10.112 ) that $a_ i\in \Delta _{\tau _ i}$ for all $i\geq 1$. If $\tau <\Delta _{\max }$, then $\Delta _{\tau _ i}\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{\tau }$, so theorem C.1.5 implies that $a\in \Delta _{\tau }$. If $\tau =\Delta _{\max }$, then the same conclusion follows from the definition $\Delta _{\Delta _{\max }}=\bigcap _{\tau '<\Delta _{\max }}\Delta _{\tau '}$. Thus, ( 10.114 ) follows. Conversely, suppose that $G\colon \Delta \rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is a test function. We argue that $\Delta [G]_{\bullet }$ is an Okounkov test curve. We verify the conditions in definition 10.5.1 . Firstly, for each $\tau < \sup _{\Delta }G$, the set $\Delta [G]_{\tau }$ is a convex body as $G$ is concave and usc. Moreover, $\Delta [G]_{\tau }$ is clearly decreasing in $\tau $. Secondly, for each $a\in \Delta $, we can write $a=\lim _{i}a_ i$ with $a_ i\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta $. By assumption, $G$ is finite at $a_ i$. Thus, \[  a\in \overline{\{ G>-\infty \} }=\overline{\bigcup _{\tau <\sup _{\Delta }G}\Delta [G]_{\tau }}.  \] By theorem C.1.5 , $\Delta [G]_{\tau }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta $ as $\tau \to -\infty $. Thirdly, $\Delta [G]$ is concave. To see this, take $\tau ,\tau '< \Delta _{\max }$. We need to prove that for any $t\in (0,1)$, 10.115 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Deconc} \Delta [G]_{t\tau +(1-t)\tau '}\supseteq t\Delta [G]_{\tau }+(1-t)\Delta [G]_{\tau '}. \end{equation} Let $a\in \Delta [G]_{\tau }$ and $b\in \Delta [G]_{\tau '}$. We have $G(a)\geq \tau $ and $G(b)\geq \tau '$. As $G$ is concave, we have $G(ta+(1-t)b)\geq t\tau +(1-t)\tau '$. Thus, \[  ta+(1-t)b\in \Delta [G]_{t\tau +(1-t)\tau '}  \] and ( 10.115 ) follows. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.5.6
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Theorem 10.5.6 . The Legendre transform and inverse Legendre transform are inverse to each other, defining a bijection between $\mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ and the set of test functions on $\Delta $. Under this bijection, $\mathrm{TC}^1(\Delta )$ corresponds to test functions on $\Delta $ with finite energy and $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta )$ corresponds to bounded test functions on $\Delta $. Proof. Thanks to 10.5.5 , in order to prove the first assertion, it only remains to see that the Legendre transform and the inverse Legendre transform are inverse to each other, which is immediate by definition. It is obvious that $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta )$ corresponds to bounded test functions. Moreover, a direct computation shows that if $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$, then \[  \mathbf{E}(\Delta _{\bullet })=\mathbf{E}(G[\Delta _{\bullet }]),  \] concluding the $\mathrm{TC}^{1}(\Delta )$ case. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.5.7
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Proposition 10.5.7 . Let $(\Delta ^ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathcal{K}_ n$ such that $\Delta \subseteq \bigcap _{i\in I}\Delta ^ i$. Consider a decreasing net $(\Delta ^ i_{\bullet })_{i\in I}$ with $\Delta ^ i_{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ^ i)$ for all $i\in I$ such that there is $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ satisfying the following properties: $\Delta _{\max }= \lim _{i\in I}\Delta ^ i_{\max }$; for any $\tau <\Delta _{\max }$, we have $\Delta ^ i_{\tau }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{\tau }$. Then for any $a\in \Delta $, we have 10.116 \begin{equation} \label{eq:pwconvLegendre} \lim _{i\in I} G[\Delta ^ i_{\bullet }](a)=G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a). \end{equation} Proof. Fix $a\in \Delta $. It follows immediately from the definition of $G$ that the net $(G[\Delta ^ i_{\bullet }](a))_{i\in I}$ is decreasing and the $\geq $ direction in ( 10.116 ) holds. Let us prove the reverse inequality. Let $\tau $ denote the left-hand side of ( 10.116 ) for the moment. By definition, for any $\epsilon >0$ and any $i\in I$, we have $a\in \Delta ^ i_{\tau -\epsilon }$. It follows that \[  a\in \Delta _{\tau -\epsilon }.  \] Therefore, \[  \tau \leq G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a).  \] This completes the proof. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.5.8
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Proposition 10.5.8 . Let $(\Delta ^ i)_{i\in I}$ be an increasing net in $\mathcal{K}_ n$ with Hausdorff limit $\Delta $ such that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta ^ i>0$ for all $i\in I$. Consider an increasing net $(\Delta ^ i_{\bullet })_{i\in I}$ with $\Delta ^ i_{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ^ i)$ for all $i\in I$. Let $\Delta _{\max }=\lim _{i\in I}\Delta ^ i_{\max }$. For any $\tau <\Delta _{\max }$, let $\Delta _{\tau }$ be the Hausdorff limit of $\Delta ^ i_{\tau }$. Then $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ and 10.117 \begin{equation} \label{eq:apwconvLegendre} \lim _{i\in I}G[\Delta ^ i_{\bullet }](a)=G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a) \end{equation} for any $a\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta $. Proof. It is obvious that $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. Fix $a\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta $. Since $\Delta ^ i\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta $, we have $a\in \Delta ^ i$ for all large enough $i$. By definition, the net $(G[\Delta ^ i_{\bullet }](a))_{i\in I}$ is increasing and the $\leq $ direction in ( 10.117 ) holds. Let us write $\tau =G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)$ for the time being. By definition of $G$, for any $\epsilon >0$, we have \[  a\in \Delta _{\tau -\epsilon /2}.  \] The concavity of $\Delta _{\bullet }$ guarantees that \[  a\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta _{\tau -\epsilon }.  \] Indeed, choose $\sigma \ll 0$ so that a small ball around $a$ is contained in $\Delta _\sigma $. Since $a\in \Delta _{\tau -\epsilon /2}$ and \[  \tau -\epsilon =t\sigma +(1-t)(\tau -\epsilon /2)  \] for a suitable $t\in (0,1)$, concavity gives a small ball around $a$ contained in $\Delta _{\tau -\epsilon }$. Since $\Delta ^ i_{\tau -\epsilon }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{\tau -\epsilon }$ and $a\in \operatorname{Int}\Delta _{\tau -\epsilon }$, it follows that for all large enough $i\in I$, \[  a\in \Delta ^ i_{\tau -\epsilon }.  \] Therefore, \[  \tau -\epsilon \leq G[\Delta ^ i_{\bullet }](a)  \] for all large enough $i$. Taking the limit with respect to $i$ and then with respect to $\epsilon $, we conclude the desired inequality. $\square$

title: Definition 10.5.9
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Definition 10.5.9 . Let $\Delta _{\bullet }$ be an Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta $. We define the Duistermaat–Heckman measure $\operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{\bullet })$ as \[  \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{\bullet })\coloneqq G[\Delta _{\bullet }]_*(\operatorname{vol}).  \] It is a Radon measure on $\mathbb {R}$, since $G[\Delta _{\bullet }]$ is finite on $\operatorname{Int}\Delta $.

title: Proposition 10.5.10
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Proposition 10.5.10 . Let $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$. Let $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. Then the following extended moment identity holds: 10.118 \begin{equation} \label{eq:momentcalc} \int _{\mathbb {R}}x^ m \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{\bullet })(x)=\Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta +m\int _{-\infty }^{\Delta _{\max }} \tau ^{m-1}(\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau }-\operatorname{vol}\Delta )\, \mathrm{d}\tau \end{equation} and 10.119 \begin{equation} \label{eq:massDHm1} \int _{\mathbb {R}}\operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{\bullet })=\operatorname{vol}\Delta . \end{equation} Proof. In fact, ( 10.119 ) follows immediately from the definition. Let $G=G[\Delta _{\bullet }]$. We first assume that $G$ is bounded from below. Then ( 10.118 ) follows from a straightforward computation: \[  \begin{aligned} & \int _{\mathbb {R}}x^ m \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{\bullet })(x)\\  =&  \int _{\Delta } G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)^ m\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(a)\\  =&  \int _{\Delta } \left( \Delta _{\max }^ m-\int _{G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a)}^{\Delta _{\max }} m\tau ^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}\tau \right)\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(a)\\  =&  \Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta -m\int _{\mathbb {R}}\int _{\Delta } \mathds {1}_{[G[\Delta _{\bullet }](a),\Delta _{\max }]}(\tau )\tau ^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(a)\, \mathrm{d}\tau \\  =&  \Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta -m\int _{-\infty }^{\Delta _{\max }}\int _{\Delta \setminus \Delta _{\tau }} \tau ^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(a)\, \mathrm{d}\tau \\  =&  \Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta -m\int _{-\infty }^{\Delta _{\max }} \tau ^{m-1}\left(\operatorname{vol}\Delta -\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau }\right)\, \mathrm{d}\tau . \end{aligned}  \] In general, set $G_ A=G\lor (-A)$. The same pointwise identity applied to $G_ A$ gives \[  \int _{\Delta }G_ A^ m\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}=\Delta _{\max }^ m\operatorname{vol}\Delta +m\int _{-A}^{\Delta _{\max }}\tau ^{m-1}(\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{\tau }-\operatorname{vol}\Delta )\, \mathrm{d}\tau .  \] Letting $A\to \infty $ gives ( 10.118 ): if $m$ is even, this follows from monotone convergence applied to $G_ A^ m\nearrow G^ m$; if $m$ is odd, apply monotone convergence to $\Delta _{\max }^ m-G_ A^ m\nearrow \Delta _{\max }^ m-G^ m$. Thus both sides of ( 10.118 ) are interpreted in the corresponding extended sense. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.5.11
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma 10.5.11 . Let $(\Delta ^ i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a decreasing sequence in $\mathcal{K}_ n$ with limit $\Delta $. Suppose that $(\Delta _{\bullet }^ i)_{i\geq 1}$ is a decreasing sequence with $\Delta _{\bullet }^ i\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ^ i)$. Suppose that there is $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ such that $\Delta _{\max }=\lim _{i\to \infty }\Delta ^ i_{\max }$; for any $\tau <\Delta _{\max }$, we have $\Delta ^ i_{\tau }\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{\tau }$. Then $\operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{\bullet }^ i)\rightharpoonup \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{\bullet })$. Proof. Let $f\in C_ c(\mathbb {R})$. It follows from proposition 10.5.7 that \[  G[\Delta _{\bullet }^ i]\to G[\Delta _{\bullet }]  \] pointwise on $\Delta $. Hence the dominated convergence theorem gives \[  \int _{\Delta } f(G[\Delta _{\bullet }^ i])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda \to \int _{\Delta } f(G[\Delta _{\bullet }])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda .  \] Since $\Delta ^ i\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta $, theorem C.1.4 gives $\operatorname{vol}(\Delta ^ i\setminus \Delta )\to 0$. The contribution of $\Delta ^ i\setminus \Delta $ is bounded by $\| f\| _{\infty }\operatorname{vol}(\Delta ^ i\setminus \Delta )$, so \[  \int _{\Delta ^ i} f(G[\Delta _{\bullet }^ i])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda \to \int _{\Delta } f(G[\Delta _{\bullet }])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda .  \] This is the weak convergence. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.5.12
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma 10.5.12 . Let $(\Delta ^ i)_{i\geq 1}$ be an increasing sequence in $\mathcal{K}_ n$ with Hausdorff limit $\Delta $ such that $\operatorname{vol}\Delta ^ i>0$ for all $i\geq 1$. Consider an increasing sequence $(\Delta ^ i_{\bullet })_{i\geq 1}$ with $\Delta ^ i_{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta ^ i)$ for all $i\geq 1$. Let $\Delta _{\bullet }\in \mathrm{TC}(\Delta )$ be defined as $\Delta _{\max }=\lim _{i\to \infty }\Delta ^ i_{\max }$; for any $\tau <\Delta _{\max }$, $\Delta _{\tau }$ is the Hausdorff limit of $\Delta ^ i_{\tau }$. Then we have \[  \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{\bullet }^ i)\rightharpoonup \operatorname{DH}(\Delta _{\bullet }).  \] Proof. Let $f\in C_ c(\mathbb {R})$. It follows from proposition 10.5.8 that \[  G[\Delta _{\bullet }^ i]\to G[\Delta _{\bullet }]  \] almost everywhere on $\Delta $. Extending $f(G[\Delta _{\bullet }^ i])$ by $0$ outside $\Delta ^ i$, we also have $\mathds {1}_{\Delta ^ i}\to \mathds {1}_{\Delta }$ almost everywhere on $\Delta $, since the boundary of the convex body $\Delta $ has Lebesgue measure zero. The dominated convergence theorem gives \[  \int _{\Delta ^ i} f(G[\Delta _{\bullet }^ i])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda \to \int _{\Delta } f(G[\Delta _{\bullet }])\, \mathrm{d}\lambda .  \] This is the weak convergence. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.5.13
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Theorem 10.5.13 . Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ be a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ representing a big cohomology class $\alpha $. Let $Y_{\bullet }$ be a smooth flag on $X$ and $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. Then the map \[  (-\infty ,\Gamma _{\max })\ni \tau \mapsto \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma )_{\tau }\coloneqq \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{\tau })  \] defines an Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{-\infty })$. If furthermore $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}^1(X,\theta ;\Gamma _{-\infty })$ (resp. $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\Gamma _{-\infty })$), then we have $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma )\in \mathrm{TC}^1(\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }))$ (resp. $\mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }))$). Proof. Consider $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}(X,\theta )_{>0}$. We need to verify that $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma )$ is an Okounkov test curve relative to $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{-\infty })$. First observe that $\tau \mapsto \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{\tau })$ is concave and decreasing for $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$. The decreasing property follows from theorem 10.4.13 2 . For concavity, use the valuative characterization theorem 10.4.20 together with the additivity of valuations in proposition 10.2.7 : if $x\in \Delta _{Y_\bullet }(\theta ,\Gamma _\tau )$ and $y\in \Delta _{Y_\bullet }(\theta ,\Gamma _{\tau '})$, then $tx+(1-t)y$ is obtained from the current $tS+(1-t)S'$, which is more singular than $\Gamma _{t\tau +(1-t)\tau '}$. Hence \[  t\Delta _{Y_\bullet }\left(\theta ,\Gamma _\tau \right)+(1-t)\Delta _{Y_\bullet }\left(\theta ,\Gamma _{\tau '}\right)\subseteq \Delta _{Y_\bullet }\left(\theta ,\Gamma _{t\tau +(1-t)\tau '}\right).  \] Next we show that as $\tau \to -\infty $, we have \[  \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{\tau })\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }).  \] By theorem 10.4.13 2 , the bodies $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{\tau })$ are contained in $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{-\infty })$ and increase as $\tau \to -\infty $. Thus it suffices to compute their volumes: \[  \begin{split}  \lim _{\tau \to -\infty }\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{\tau })=\frac{1}{n!}\lim _{\tau \to -\infty }\operatorname{vol}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma _{\tau })=\frac{1}{n!}\operatorname{vol}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma _{-\infty }) \\  =\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }), \end{split}  \] where we applied theorem 10.4.13 and theorem 6.2.30 . When $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(X,\theta ;\Gamma _{-\infty })$, it is clear that $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma )\in \mathrm{TC}^{\infty }(\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }))$. When $\Gamma \in \mathrm{TC}^{1}(X,\theta ;\Gamma _{-\infty })$, by theorem 10.4.13 1 , ( 9.5 ) and ( 10.109 ), we have \[  \mathbf{E}^{\Gamma _{-\infty }}(\Gamma )=\mathbf{E}(\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma )).  \] Indeed, by theorem 10.4.13 1 , \[  n!\operatorname{vol}\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _\tau )=\int _ X\theta _{\Gamma _\tau }^ n  \] for every $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$, and the same identity holds at $\tau =-\infty $. Comparing ( 9.5 ) with ( 10.109 ) gives the asserted equality of energies. So $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma )\in \mathrm{TC}^1(\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{-\infty }))$. $\square$

title: Remark 10.5.14
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Remark 10.5.14 . As a special case of this construction, suppose that $\Gamma $ is the test curve induced by a test configuration as in example 9.3.9 and 9.3.10 , then for any $\tau <\Gamma _{\max }$, $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta ,\Gamma _{\tau })$ is the Okounkov body of a graded linear series \[  \bigoplus _{k=0}^{\infty }\mathcal{F}^{k\tau }_ k,  \] where $\mathcal{F}$ is the filtration induced by the test configuration. See [ Theorem 5.28 , Xia21 ] for the details. In particular, in this case, our theory of partial Okounkov bodies recovers the Okounkov bodies of the filtered linear series in the sense of [ BC11 ] .

title: 11 The theory of b-divisors
text: 11 The theory of b-divisors The purpose of this chapter is to translate the singularity theory developed in the preceding chapters into the language of b-divisors. A b-divisor records, on all proper bimeromorphic models of $X$, the cohomological data attached to a singular object. Given a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, we associate to it a b-divisor $\mathbb D(T)$ by taking, on each modification $\pi \colon Y\to X$, the cohomology class of the regular part of $\pi ^*T$ with respect to Siu's decomposition. This construction removes divisorial components and keeps track of the moving positivity of $T$ on every model. The resulting b-divisor is nef in a suitable sense, and its volume agrees with the volume of $T$. The first part of the chapter develops this construction and studies its basic properties. We prove that $d_ S$-convergence of currents implies convergence of the associated b-divisors, and we compare the $P$- and $\mathcal I$-orders through their b-divisorial data. This gives a birational way to read some of the singularity information encoded by envelopes and multiplier ideals. The second part relates b-divisors to $\mathcal I$-good currents. In the big case, $\mathcal I$-good non-divisorial currents give rise to big and nef b-divisors, and conversely big and nef b-divisors can be represented by such currents. The final part defines mixed intersection numbers of nef b-divisors. For big and nef b-divisors this is done through the corresponding $\mathcal I$-good currents and the mixed volume formalism of chapter 7 ; the general nef case is obtained by Kähler perturbation. We prove symmetry, multilinearity, monotonicity, continuity under decreasing nets, and upper semicontinuity. These results provide the b-divisorial counterpart of the mixed volume theory.

title: 11.1 The notion of b-divisors
text: 11.1 The notion of b-divisors The b-divisors defined in this section are sometimes called b-divisor classes. We always omit the word classes to save space. Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$. Let us recall the following elementary result regarding how cohomology behaves under blow-up. Proposition 11.1.1 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a blow-up with connected smooth center of codimension at least $2$ with exceptional divisor $E$. Then there is a natural identification 11.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:H11blowup} \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})=\mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})\oplus \mathbb {R}\{ E\} . \end{equation} See [ RYY19 ] for a much more general result.

title: Proposition 11.1.1
text: Proposition 11.1.1 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a blow-up with connected smooth center of codimension at least $2$ with exceptional divisor $E$. Then there is a natural identification 11.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:H11blowup} \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})=\mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})\oplus \mathbb {R}\{ E\} . \end{equation}
11.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:H11blowup} \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})=\mathrm{H}^{1,1}(X,\mathbb {R})\oplus \mathbb {R}\{ E\} . \end{equation}

title: 11.1.1 Nef b-divisors
text: 11.1.1 Nef b-divisors Definition 11.1.2 . A (Weil) b-divisor $\mathbb {D}$ over $X$ is an assignment $(\mathbb {D}_{\pi })_{\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X}$, where $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ runs over all modifications of $X$ such that $\mathbb {D}_{\pi }\in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})$; The classes are compatible under push-forwards: If $\pi '\colon Z\rightarrow X$ and $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ are both modifications of $X$ and $\pi '$ dominates $\pi $ through $g\colon Z\rightarrow Y$, then $g_*\mathbb {D}_{\pi '}=\mathbb {D}_{\pi }$. We also write $\mathbb {D}_ Y=\mathbb {D}_{\pi }$ if there is no risk of confusion. Given two Weil b-divisors $\mathbb {D}$ and $\mathbb {D}'$ over $X$, we say $\mathbb {D}\leq \mathbb {D}'$ if for each modification $\pi $ of $X$, we have $\mathbb {D}_{\pi }\leq \mathbb {D}'_{\pi }$. Recall that by definition, this means the class $\mathbb {D}'_{\pi }-\mathbb {D}_{\pi }$ is pseudo-effective. A Weil b-divisor with $\mathbb {D}\geq 0$ is called pseudo-effective . The class $\mathbb {D}_ X$ is called the root of $\mathbb {D}$. The set of Weil b-divisors over $X$ has the natural structure of a real vector space. Definition 11.1.3 . The volume of a pseudo-effective Weil b-divisor $\mathbb {D}$ over $X$ is \[  \operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}\coloneqq \lim _{\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X} \operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}_ Y.  \] The right-hand side is a decreasing net due to proposition 3.2.12 , hence the limit always exists. The volume of a non-pseudo-effective Weil b-divisor is defined to be $0$. We say $\mathbb {D}$ is big if $\operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}>0$. Lemma 11.1.4 . Let $(\mathbb {D}_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net of pseudo-effective b-divisors converging to a Weil b-divisor $\mathbb {D}$. Then 11.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:vollimsup} \varlimsup _{i\in I}\operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}_ i\leq \operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}. \end{equation} If the net is decreasing, then \[  \lim _{i\in I}\operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}_ i=\operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}.  \] Here we say $(\mathbb {D}_ i)_{i\in I}$ converges to $\mathbb {D}$ if for any modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$, we have $\mathbb {D}_{i,Y}\to \mathbb {D}_ Y$ with respect to the Euclidean topology. Proof. First observe that $\mathbb {D}$ is pseudo-effective, since $\mathbb {D}_ i\geq 0$ for all $i$. Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a modification. Then \[  \operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}_ Y=\lim _{i\in I} \operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}_{i,Y}\geq \varlimsup _{i\in I} \operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}_ i.  \] The inequality ( 11.2 ) follows. As for the decreasing case, it suffices to observe that both sides of ( 11.2 ) can be written as \[  \inf _ i \inf _{\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X} \operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}_{i,Y}.  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Example 11.1.5 . In general, equality need not hold in ( 11.2 ). Let $X=\mathbb {P}^2$, and let $H=c_1(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^2}(1))$. Choose a sequence of points $p_ i\in X$ converging to the generic point in the following sense: for every algebraic curve $C\subseteq X$, the set of indices $i$ with $p_ i\in C$ is finite. Let \[  \pi _ i\colon X_ i\rightarrow X  \] be the blow-up of $X$ at $p_ i$, with exceptional divisor $E_ i$. Let $\mathbb {D}_ i$ be the Cartier b-divisor realized on $X_ i$ by the nef class \[  \pi _ i^*H-\{ E_ i\} ,  \] and let $\mathbb {D}$ be the Cartier b-divisor realized on $X$ by $H$. Then $\mathbb {D}_ i\to \mathbb {D}$. Indeed, for any fixed modification $\rho \colon Y\rightarrow X$, the morphism $\rho $ is an isomorphism over $p_ i$ for all large enough $i$, hence the trace of $\mathbb {D}_ i$ on $Y$ is $\rho ^*H$ for all large enough $i$. On the other hand, \[  \operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}_ i=\left(\pi _ i^*H-\{ E_ i\} \right)^2=0  \] for all $i$, whereas \[  \operatorname{vol}\mathbb {D}=H^2=1.  \] Thus the inequality in ( 11.2 ) is strict for this sequence. Definition 11.1.6 . A Cartier b-divisor $\mathbb {D}$ over $X$ is a Weil b-divisor $\mathbb {D}$ over $X$ such that there exists a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ and a class $\alpha _ Y\in \mathrm{H}^{1,1}(Y,\mathbb {R})$ so that for each $\pi '\colon Z\rightarrow X$ dominating $\pi $, the class $\mathbb {D}_ Z$ is the pull-back of $\alpha _ Y$. Any such $(\pi ,\alpha _ Y)$ is called a realization of $\mathbb {D}$. By abuse of language, we also say $(Y,\alpha _ Y)$ is a realization of $\mathbb {D}$. The realization is not unique in general. Definition 11.1.7 . A Cartier b-divisor $\mathbb {D}$ over $X$ is nef if there exists a realization $(\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X, \alpha _ Y)$ of $\mathbb {D}$ such that $\alpha _ Y$ is nef. Definition 11.1.8 . A Weil b-divisor $\mathbb {D}$ over $X$ is nef if it is the limit of a net of nef Cartier b-divisors $(\mathbb {D}_ i)_ i$ over $X$. In other words, for each modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$, we have $\mathbb {D}_{i,Y}\to \mathbb {D}_ Y$. Note that thanks to proposition 1.7.15 , each $\mathbb {D}_ Y$ is necessarily modified nef, but it is not nef in general. The notion of modified nef classes is defined in definition 1.7.13 . A priori , for a Cartier b-divisor, nefness could mean either the notion defined by definition 11.1.7 or the one defined by definition 11.1.8 .
