eq (0,0)\} ,\quad D_{\sigma _0}=\mathbb {P}^2. \end{aligned}  \] In particular, $\Sigma (1)=\{ \sigma _4,\sigma _5,\sigma _6\} $. We shall take \[  D=D_{\sigma _4}.  \] In other words, \[  a_{\sigma _5}=a_{\sigma _6}=0,\quad a_{\sigma _4}=1.  \] Note that the ray generators are given by \[  u_{\sigma _4}=(-1,-1),\quad u_{\sigma _5}=(1,0),\quad u_{\sigma _6}=(0,1).  \] It follows that \[  P_ D=\{ m=(m_1,m_2)\in \mathbb {R}^2: m_1+m_2\leq 1, m_1\geq 0, m_2\geq 0\} .  \] Therefore, $P_ D$ is just the polytope in 12.2 . 12.2 The polytope $P_ D$. In this case, the Cartier data for $2$-dimensional cones are given as follows: \[  m_{\sigma _1}=(0,0),\quad m_{\sigma _2}=(1,0),\quad m_{\sigma _3}=(0,1);  \] while the remaining Cartier data are determined by ( 12.3 ). In this case, $L=\mathcal{O}_ X(D)=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^2}(1)$. Hence the line bundle $L$ is ample. We also observe that \[   egin{aligned}  Q_{\sigma _1}=& \{ (0,0)\} ,\quad Q_{\sigma _2}=\{ (1,0)\} ,\quad Q_{\sigma _3}=\{ (0,1)\} ,\  Q_{\sigma _4}=&  \{ (m_1,m_2):m_1\geq 0,m_2\geq 0,m_1+m_2=1\} ,\  Q_{\sigma _5}=&  \{ 0\} 	imes [0,1],\quad Q_{\sigma _6}= [0,1]	imes \{ 0\} ,\  Q_{\sigma _0}=&  P_ D. \end{aligned}  \] Next we give three non-ample examples. Example 12.1.4 . Let $\Sigma $ be the fan shown in 12.3 . 12.3 The fan of $\mathrm{Bl}_0\mathbb {P}^2$. Adding the ray $\sigma _7$ generated by $(1,1)$ subdivides the cone $\sigma _1$ into two full-dimensional cones $\sigma _1',\sigma _1''$. Comparing with our previous example 12.1 , we have divided $\sigma _1$ from the middle, giving rise to two additional $2$-dimensional cones $\sigma _1'$ and $\sigma _1''$, and one additional $1$-dimensional cone $\sigma _7$. The corresponding $X=\mathrm{Bl}_0 \mathbb {P}^2$ is just the blow-up of $\mathbb {P}^2$ at the origin $0=[1:0:0]$ and hence $L=\pi ^*\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^2}(1)$. Let $\pi \colon Xightarrow \mathbb {P}^2$ denote the blow-up morphism. Let \[  D=D_{\sigma _4}.  \] Then $D$ is the pull-back of the divisor $D$ in example 12.1.3 . Note that $D$ is not ample, since it has degree $0$ on the exceptional divisor. In this case, we have \[  \Sigma (1)=\{ \sigma _4,\sigma _5,\sigma _6,\sigma _7\} ,  \] and $D_{\sigma _7}$ is just the exceptional divisor. The corresponding ray generators are \[  u_{\sigma _4}=(-1,-1),\quad u_{\sigma _5}=(1,0),\quad u_{\sigma _6}=(0,1),\quad u_{\sigma _7}=(1,1),  \] while \[  m_{\sigma _1'}=m_{\sigma _1''}=(0,0),\quad m_{\sigma _2}=(1,0),\quad m_{\sigma _3}=(0,1).  \] Therefore, $P_ D$ is the same as in 12.2 . We also observe that \[   egin{aligned}  Q_{\sigma _1'}=& \{ (0,0)\} ,\quad Q_{\sigma _1''}=\{ (0,0)\} ,\quad Q_{\sigma _7}=\{ (0,0)\} ,\  Q_{\sigma _2}=& \{ (1,0)\} ,\quad Q_{\sigma _3}=\{ (0,1)\} ,\  Q_{\sigma _4}=&  \{ (m_1,m_2):m_1\geq 0,m_2\geq 0,m_1+m_2=1\} ,\  Q_{\sigma _5}=&  \{ 0\} 	imes [0,1],\quad Q_{\sigma _6}= [0,1]	imes \{ 0\} ,\  Q_{\sigma _0}=&  P_ D. \end{aligned}  \] Example 12.1.5 . We continue with the surface in example 12.1.4 with $X=\mathrm{Bl}_0\mathbb {P}^2$. Let $\pi \colon Xightarrow \mathbb {P}^2$ be the blow-up morphism, and write \[  H=D_{\sigma _4},\quad E=D_{\sigma _7}.  \] Consider the toric Cartier divisor \[  D=2D_{\sigma _4}+D_{\sigma _7}=2H+E.  \] This gives a simple example of a big toric divisor which is not nef. Indeed, the intersection numbers on $X$ are \[  H^2=1,\quad H\cdot E=0,\quad E^2=-1.  \] Hence \[  D\cdot E=(2H+E)\cdot E=-1<0,  \] so $D$ is not nef. The inequalities defining $P_ D$ are \[  m_1\geq 0,\quad m_2\geq 0,\quad m_1+m_2\leq 2,\quad m_1+m_2\geq -1.  \] The last inequality, corresponding to the exceptional ray $\sigma _7$, is redundant. Thus \[  P_ D=\{ m=(m_1,m_2)\in M_{\mathbb {R}}:m_1\geq 0,\  m_2\geq 0,\  m_1+m_2\leq 2\} ,  \] as illustrated in 12.4 . 12.4 The polytope $P_ D$ for $D=2D_{\sigma _4}+D_{\sigma _7}$. The blue lines are the four affine hyperplanes $a_{ho }+\langle m,u_{ho }angle =0$ for $ho \in \Sigma (1)$. Example 12.1.6 . We give a surface example in which $P_ D$ is not a lattice polytope. Let $\Sigma $ be the fan in $N_{\mathbb {R}}\simeq \mathbb {R}^2$ whose rays are generated, in cyclic order, by \[  u_{ho _1}=(1,0),\quad u_{ho _2}=(0,1),\quad u_{ho _3}=(-1,2),\quad u_{ho _4}=(0,-1).  \] The corresponding smooth projective toric surface is the Hirzebruch surface $\mathbb {F}_2$. title: Proposition 12.1.1
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Proposition 12.1.1 . The base locus $\operatorname{Bs}(D)$ (with the reduced complex structure) of $D$ is a toric-invariant (possibly reducible) subvariety given by the union of $V(\tau )$, where $\tau $ runs over elements in $\Sigma $ satisfying the following condition: 12.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:arhononcrit} a_{\rho }+\langle m, u_{\rho }\rangle >0\quad \textup{for some }\rho \in \tau (1) \end{equation} for each $m\in M\cap P_ D$. Proof. Recall that \[  \mathrm{H}^0(X,L)\cong \bigoplus _{m\in M\cap P_ D} \mathbb {C}\chi ^ m.  \] See [ Proposition 4.3.3 , CLS11 ] for example. So we only need to understand the common zeros of $D+\operatorname{div}\chi ^ m$ for all $m\in M\cap P_ D$. But we know that \[  D+\operatorname{div}\chi ^ m=\sum _{\rho \in \Sigma (1)} \left( a_{\rho }+\langle m, u_{\rho }\rangle \right) D_{\rho }.  \] Our assertion follows. $\square$

title: Corollary 12.1.2

text: Corollary 12.1.2 . The stable base locus (with the reduced complex structure) of $D$ is a toric-invariant (possibly reducible) subvariety given by the union of the $V(\tau )$'s, where $\tau $ runs over elements in $\Sigma $ satisfying ( 12.7 ) for each $m\in P_ D$. Proof. It follows from proposition 12.1.1 that the stable base locus of $D$ is given by the union of the $V(\tau )$'s, where $\tau $ runs over elements of $\Sigma $ satisfying ( 12.7 ) for all $m\in M_{\mathbb {Q}}\cap P_ D$. That is, \[  M_{\mathbb {Q}}\cap \left\{  m\in P_ D : a_{\rho }+\langle m, u_{\rho }\rangle =0\quad \forall \rho \in \tau (1) \right\} =\varnothing .  \] Since the latter part is a rational polytope, this statement is equivalent to 12.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:PDcapvarnot} \left\{  m\in P_ D : a_{\rho }+\langle m, u_{\rho }\rangle =0\quad \forall \rho \in \tau (1) \right\} =\varnothing . \end{equation} Our first assertion follows. $\square$

title: Example 12.1.3
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles

Example 12.1.3 . In this case, $\Sigma $ is the fan in 12.1 consisting of three $2$-dimensional cones $\sigma _1$, $\sigma _2$ and $\sigma _3$; three $1$-dimensional cones $\sigma _4$, $\sigma _5$ and $\sigma _6$; one $0$-dimensional cone $\sigma _0$. 12.1 The fan $\Sigma $ of $\mathbb {P}^2$. eq (0,0)\} ,\  D_{\sigma _5}=&  \{ [X_0:0:X_2]:(X_0,X_2)

text: Example 12.1.4 . Let $\Sigma $ be the fan shown in 12.3 . 12.3 The fan of $\mathrm{Bl}_0\mathbb {P}^2$. Adding the ray $\sigma _7$ generated by $(1,1)$ subdivides the cone $\sigma _1$ into two full-dimensional cones $\sigma _1',\sigma _1''$. Comparing with our previous example 12.1 , we have divided $\sigma _1$ from the middle, giving rise to two additional $2$-dimensional cones $\sigma _1'$ and $\sigma _1''$, and one additional $1$-dimensional cone $\sigma _7$. The corresponding $X=\mathrm{Bl}_0 \mathbb {P}^2$ is just the blow-up of $\mathbb {P}^2$ at the origin $0=[1:0:0]$ and hence $L=\pi ^*\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^2}(1)$. Let $\pi \colon X\rightarrow \mathbb {P}^2$ denote the blow-up morphism. Let \[  D=D_{\sigma _4}.  \] Then $D$ is the pull-back of the divisor $D$ in example 12.1.3 . Note that $D$ is not ample, since it has degree $0$ on the exceptional divisor. In this case, we have \[  \Sigma (1)=\{ \sigma _4,\sigma _5,\sigma _6,\sigma _7\} ,  \] and $D_{\sigma _7}$ is just the exceptional divisor. The corresponding ray generators are \[  u_{\sigma _4}=(-1,-1),\quad u_{\sigma _5}=(1,0),\quad u_{\sigma _6}=(0,1),\quad u_{\sigma _7}=(1,1),  \] while \[  m_{\sigma _1'}=m_{\sigma _1''}=(0,0),\quad m_{\sigma _2}=(1,0),\quad m_{\sigma _3}=(0,1).  \] Therefore, $P_ D$ is the same as in 12.2 . We also observe that \[  \begin{aligned}  Q_{\sigma _1'}=& \{ (0,0)\} ,\quad Q_{\sigma _1''}=\{ (0,0)\} ,\quad Q_{\sigma _7}=\{ (0,0)\} ,\\  Q_{\sigma _2}=& \{ (1,0)\} ,\quad Q_{\sigma _3}=\{ (0,1)\} ,\\  Q_{\sigma _4}=&  \{ (m_1,m_2):m_1\geq 0,m_2\geq 0,m_1+m_2=1\} ,\\  Q_{\sigma _5}=&  \{ 0\} \times [0,1],\quad Q_{\sigma _6}= [0,1]\times \{ 0\} ,\\  Q_{\sigma _0}=&  P_ D. \end{aligned}  \]

title: Example 12.1.5
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Example 12.1.5 . We continue with the surface in example 12.1.4 with $X=\mathrm{Bl}_0\mathbb {P}^2$. Let $\pi \colon X\rightarrow \mathbb {P}^2$ be the blow-up morphism, and write \[  H=D_{\sigma _4},\quad E=D_{\sigma _7}.  \] Consider the toric Cartier divisor \[  D=2D_{\sigma _4}+D_{\sigma _7}=2H+E.  \] This gives a simple example of a big toric divisor which is not nef. Indeed, the intersection numbers on $X$ are \[  H^2=1,\quad H\cdot E=0,\quad E^2=-1.  \] Hence \[  D\cdot E=(2H+E)\cdot E=-1<0,  \] so $D$ is not nef. The inequalities defining $P_ D$ are \[  m_1\geq 0,\quad m_2\geq 0,\quad m_1+m_2\leq 2,\quad m_1+m_2\geq -1.  \] The last inequality, corresponding to the exceptional ray $\sigma _7$, is redundant. This is a typical phenomenon in the non-ample situation. Thus \[  P_ D=\{ m=(m_1,m_2)\in M_{\mathbb {R}}:m_1\geq 0,\  m_2\geq 0,\  m_1+m_2\leq 2\} ,  \] as illustrated in 12.4 . 12.4 The polytope $P_ D$ for $D=2D_{\sigma _4}+D_{\sigma _7}$. The blue lines are the four affine hyperplanes $a_{\rho }+\langle m,u_{\rho }\rangle =0$ for $\rho \in \Sigma (1)$.

text: Example 12.1.6 . We give a surface example in which $P_ D$ is not a lattice polytope. Let $\Sigma $ be the fan in $N_{\mathbb {R}}\simeq \mathbb {R}^2$ whose rays are generated, in cyclic order, by \[  u_{\rho _1}=(1,0),\quad u_{\rho _2}=(0,1),\quad u_{\rho _3}=(-1,2),\quad u_{\rho _4}=(0,-1).  \] The corresponding smooth projective toric surface is the Hirzebruch surface $\mathbb {F}_2$. Consider the toric Cartier divisor \[  D=-D_{\rho _3}+2D_{\rho _4}.  \] Thus \[  a_{\rho _1}=a_{\rho _2}=0,\quad a_{\rho _3}=-1,\quad a_{\rho _4}=2.  \] Hence \[  P_ D=\left\{ m=(m_1,m_2)\in M_{\mathbb {R}}: m_1\geq 0,\  \frac{m_1+1}{2}\leq m_2\leq 2 \right\} .  \] See 12.5 . 12.5 A surface example where $P_ D$ is not a lattice polytope.

title: 12.2 Toric partial Okounkov bodies
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: 12.2 Toric partial Okounkov bodies We continue to use the notations in section 12.1 . In order to study the toric-invariant singular plurisubharmonic metrics on $L$, we need to fix a reference toric-invariant smooth Hermitian metric, so that the psh metrics can be identified with quasi-psh functions. Unlike the ample case studied in chapter 5 , in the case of big line bundles, there does not seem to be a natural choice of a smooth Hermitian metric on $L$ similar to Guillemin's metric. We shall fix a $T_ c$-invariant Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ so that $\theta =c_1(L,h)$. The first observation is the following: Lemma 12.2.1 . There is a smooth function $F_{\theta }\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ such that \[  \theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{\theta }\quad \textup{on }T(\mathbb {C}).  \] Proof. Step 1 . We first prove the existence of $F_{\theta }$ for a specific choice of $h$. Write $D$ as the difference of two toric-invariant ample divisors, say $D_1-D_2$. Let $h_1$ and $h_2$ be the associated Guillemin's metrics on $D_1$ and $D_2$ respectively. We define $h=h_1\otimes h_2^{-1}$. In this case, our assertion follows since it holds in the case of Guillemin's metrics. Step 2 . In general, fix $h_0$ as in Step 1. Then the general $h$ can be written as $h_0\exp (-g)$ for some smooth function $g$ on $X$. Since both metrics are $T_ c$-invariant, so is $g$, and on the open torus we may write $g=\operatorname{Trop}^* r$ for some smooth function $r$ on $N_{\mathbb {R}}$. Hence it suffices to modify $F_{\theta }$ in Step 1 by $r$ to conclude. $\square$ Note that $F_{\theta }$ is well-defined up to a linear term. Next, we make an additional requirement on $F_{\theta }$ to fix the linear term. Let $s_ D$ be a rational section of $L$ corresponding to $D$. Then $s_ D$ is well-defined up to a non-zero multiple. By Lelong–Poincaré formula proposition 1.8.4 , we have \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left( \operatorname{Trop}^*F_{\theta }+\log |s_ D|_ h^2 \right)=0  \] on $T(\mathbb {C})$. Therefore, $\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{\theta }+\log |s_ D|_ h^2$ is the tropicalization of a linear function. Hence, after adding a linear function to $F_{\theta }$, we can guarantee that 12.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normF0} \operatorname{Trop}^*F_{\theta }+\log |s_ D|_ h^2=0 \end{equation} from now on. Note that a different choice of $s_ D$ means adding a constant to $F_{\theta }$. Summarizing the situation, we have chosen the following data in addition to the fan $\Sigma $ so far: A divisor $D$, a Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ and a rational section $s_ D$ of $L$ subject to various conditions.

title: 12.2.1 Newton bodies
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: 12.2.1 Newton bodies Let $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ be the set of $T_ c$-invariant functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Definition 12.2.2 . A function $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ can be written as \[  \varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})}=\operatorname{Trop}^*f  \] for some unique function $f\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$. Then we define $F_{\varphi }\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ as follows: 12.23 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Fvarphibig1} F_{\varphi }=F_{\theta }+f. \end{equation} Observe that $F_{\varphi }$ is a convex function and takes finite values by 5.2.1 . In particular, $f$ is also real-valued. Once $D$ and $h$ are fixed, $F_{\varphi }$ is well-defined up to a constant since $F_{\theta }$ is. Definition 12.2.3 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$, we define its Newton body as \[  \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\coloneqq \overline{\nabla F_{\varphi }(N_{\mathbb {R}})}\subseteq M_{\mathbb {R}}.  \] Here the gradient is understood in the sense of Alexandrov, see definition A.2.6 for the details. Note that $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$ is independent of the choice of $s_ D$. The Newton body $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$ depends on the choice of $D$, not only on the associated line bundle $L$: A different choice of $D$ inducing the same line bundle corresponds to a translation of $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$. We will see in a while (theorem 12.2.9 ) that once $D$ is fixed $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$ depends only on the current $\theta _{\varphi }$. Hence, the choice of $h$ is irrelevant. For the moment, it is not clear if $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\subseteq P_ D$ or not. We shall prove this result using the theory of partial Okounkov bodies in the next section. Proposition 12.2.4 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. Then 12.24 \begin{equation} \label{eq:tropMAmea2} \operatorname{Trop}_* \left(\theta |_{T(\mathbb {C})}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})} \right)^ n=\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}\left(F_{\varphi }\right). \end{equation} In particular, 12.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:toricmass2} \int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n =n! \operatorname{vol}\Delta (\theta ,\varphi ) \end{equation} Proof. Let $F_0$ be a smooth convex function on $N_{\mathbb {R}}$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Trop}^* F_0$ can be extended to a Kähler form on $X$. For example, Guillemin's construction ( 5.9 ) with respect to a suitable Delzant polytope gives such an example. Write $\omega $ for a Kähler form on $X$ extending $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Trop}^*F_0$. Then for any large enough $C>0$, $\theta +C\omega $ is a Kähler form. So we conclude from proposition 5.2.10 that \[  \operatorname{Trop}_* \left((\theta +C\omega )|_{T(\mathbb {C})}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi |_{T(\mathbb {C})} \right)^ n=\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}(F_{\varphi }+CF_0).  \] By the multi-linearity of the non-pluripolar product proposition 2.2.2 6 , the left-hand side is a polynomial in $C$. By the expansion formula for the mixed real Monge–Ampère measure theorem A.4.7 1 , the right-hand side is also a polynomial in $C$. We conclude that the same holds for $C=0$. Therefore, ( 12.24 ) follows. ( 12.25 ) is a direct consequence of ( 12.24 ). $\square$

12.2.2 Partial Okounkov bodies There are some canonical choices of smooth flags in the toric setting. Since $X$ is smooth and projective, we can choose a full-dimensional cone $\sigma $ in $\Sigma $ with rays $ho _1,\ldots ,ho _ n\in \sigma (1)$ such that $u_{ho _1},\ldots ,u_{ho _ n}$ form a basis of $N$. Define \[  Y_ i=D_{ho _1}\cap \cdots \cap D_{ho _ i},\quad i=1,\ldots ,n.  \] Then $Y_{ ullet }$ is a smooth flag on $X$. Let 12.26  egin{equation} \label{eq:isoMZncanonical} \Phi \colon Mightarrow \mathbb {Z}^ n,\quad m\mapsto \left(\langle m-m_{\sigma },u_{ho _1} angle ,\dots ,\langle m-m_{\sigma },u_{ho _ n} angle ight). \end{equation} Then $\Phi $ is an isomorphism of lattices. It induces an $\mathbb {Z}$-affine isomorphism \[  \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}\colon M_{\mathbb {R}}ightarrow \mathbb {R}^ n.  \] Proposition 12.2.5 . We have 12.27  egin{equation} \label{eq:DeltakLtoric} k^{-1}
u _{Y_{ ullet }}\left(\mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k)^{	imes } ight)=\Phi _{\mathbb {R}} \left(P_{D}\cap k^{-1}Might) \end{equation} for any $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. In particular, 12.28  egin{equation}  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(L)=\Phi _{\mathbb {R}}(P_ D). \end{equation} Recall that $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(L)\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ is the Okounkov body defined in definition 10.3.5 . Proof. We first reduce to the case where $D|_{U_{\sigma }}=0$. In fact, replacing $D$ by $D+\operatorname{div}\chi ^{m_{\sigma }}$ would result in changing $P_ D$ to $P_ D-m_{\sigma }$. So in view of ( 12.5 ), we may assume that $D|_{U_{\sigma }}=0$ and hence $m_{\sigma }=0$. Fix $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. Let $s\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k)$ be a non-zero toric eigen-section, say $\chi ^ m$ for some $m\in kP_ D\cap M$. The zero-divisor of $s$ on $U_{\sigma }$ is given by \[  \sum _{i=1}^ n \langle m, u_{ho _ i} angle D_{ho _ i},  \] see [ Proposition 4.1.2 , CLS11 ] . Therefore, \[  
u _{Y_{ ullet }}(s)=\Bigl (\langle m, u_{ho _1} angle ,\dots ,\langle m, u_{ho _ n} angle \Bigr )=\Phi (m).  \] Conversely, every section of $L^ k$ is a finite linear combination of such characters. In the coordinates on $U_{\sigma }$ determined by $u_{ho _1},\ldots ,u_{ho _ n}$, the Okounkov valuation of a non-zero linear combination is the lexicographically first exponent among the characters with non-zero coefficient. Hence arbitrary sections give no valuations beyond the right-hand side of ( 12.27 ), and ( 12.27 ) follows. $\square$ Example 12.2.6 . Let us continue the example of $\mathbb {P}^2$ in example 12.1.3 . We use the same notations. Take $\sigma _1$ as our reference cone, and $ho _1=\sigma _5$, $ho _2=\sigma _6$. Then \[  Y_1=\Bigl \{ [X_0:0:X_2]:(X_0,X_2)
eq (0,0) \Bigr \} ,\quad Y_2=\Bigl \{ [X_0:0:0]:X_0
eq 0\Bigr \} .  \] The map $\Phi $ is given by \[  \Phi (m_1,m_2)=(m_1,m_2).  \] In this case, we see easily \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}\left(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^2}(1)ight)=P_ D  \] is the polytope in 12.2 . Example 12.2.7 . Let us continue the example of $\mathrm{Bl}_{0}\mathbb {P}^2$ in example 12.1.4 . This time, let us take $\sigma _1'$ as our reference cone and $ho _1=\sigma _5$, $ho _2=\sigma _7$. Then $Y_1$ is just the strict transform of the line $\{ [X_0:0:X_2]:X_0X_2
eq 0\} $ in $\mathbb {P}^2$, while $Y_2$ is the point $Y_1\cap E$, where $E$ is the exceptional divisor. In this case, the map $\Phi $ is given by \[  \Phi (m_1,m_2)=(m_1,m_1+m_2).  \] We find that \[  \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}\left(\mathrm{Bl}_{0}\mathbb {P}^2,\pi ^*\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^2}(1)ight)  \] is the polytope in 12.6 . 12.6 The Okounkov body $\Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(\mathrm{Bl}_{0}\mathbb {P}^2,\pi ^*\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^2}(1))$. Note that it differs from the polytope in example 12.2.6 . Note. Although these examples are almost trivial, they did confuse me a lot at the beginning of 2023, when Kewei Zhang, Tamás Darvas and I were collaborating on [ DRWNXZ ] . At that time, Kewei himself already proved the main theorem for a generic flag. I realized that some simple birational geometry would suffice to prove the same result for general flags. I persuaded myself and Kewei that the Okounkov bodies are always birationally invariant, and deduced some apparently wrong conclusions. I got no clue for a couple of weeks, then one day, on the noisy metro line 7 of Paris, I got nothing to do, so I said to myself: Why not compute the simplest toric examples? Then after a few minutes, all of a sudden, the whole picture became completely clear. Lemma 12.2.8 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ and assume that $	heta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. Then $\varphi $ admits a quasi-equisingular approximation $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ with the following additional properties: $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ and $	heta _{\varphi _ j}$ is a Kähler current for all $j\geq 1$; for each $j\geq 1$, there are $q_ j\in \mathbb Z_{>0}$ and toric eigen-sections \[  s_{j,1},\ldots ,s_{j,a_ j}\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^{q_ j})  \] such that \[  \varphi _ j= rac{1}{q_ j}\log \sum _{\ell =1}^{a_ j}|s_{j,\ell }|_{h^{q_ j}}^2+\mathcal O(1).  \] Proof. Apply Demailly's Bergman-kernel approximation theorem [ Theorem 13.21 , Dem12 ] to the singular Hermitian metric $h\exp (-\varphi )$ on $L$. Since $	heta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, the theorem applies to the Hilbert spaces \[  \mathrm{H}^0 igl (X,L^ q\otimes \mathcal I(q\varphi ) igr )  \] for $q\gg 1$, endowed with the $L^2$-norm induced by $h^ q\exp (-q\varphi )$ and a fixed Kähler volume form. The usual decreasing extraction in Demailly's construction gives a quasi-equisingular approximation; taking $q$ sufficiently large at each step ensures that the approximants still have Kähler Chern currents. It remains to note that this construction is compatible with the torus action. Indeed, both $h$ and $\varphi $ are $T_ c$-invariant, hence the above Hilbert spaces and their $L^2$-inner products are $T_ c$-invariant. Since $T_ c$ is compact and abelian, each of these finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces admits an orthonormal basis consisting of toric eigen-sections. title: Proposition 12.2.5
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Proposition 12.2.5 . We have 12.27 \begin{equation} \label{eq:DeltakLtoric} k^{-1}\nu _{Y_{\bullet }}\left(\mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k)^{\times } \right)=\Phi _{\mathbb {R}} \left(P_{D}\cap k^{-1}M\right) \end{equation} for any $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. In particular, 12.28 \begin{equation}  \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(L)=\Phi _{\mathbb {R}}(P_ D). \end{equation} Proof. We first reduce to the case where $D|_{U_{\sigma }}=0$. In fact, replacing $D$ by $D+\operatorname{div}\chi ^{m_{\sigma }}$ would result in changing $P_ D$ to $P_ D-m_{\sigma }$. So in view of ( 12.5 ), we may assume that $D|_{U_{\sigma }}=0$ and hence $m_{\sigma }=0$. Fix $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. Let $s\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^ k)$ be a non-zero toric eigen-section, say $\chi ^ m$ for some $m\in kP_ D\cap M$. The zero-divisor of $s$ on $U_{\sigma }$ is given by \[  \sum _{i=1}^ n \langle m, u_{\rho _ i} \rangle D_{\rho _ i},  \] see [ Proposition 4.1.2 , CLS11 ] . Therefore, \[  \nu _{Y_{\bullet }}(s)=\Bigl (\langle m, u_{\rho _1} \rangle ,\dots ,\langle m, u_{\rho _ n} \rangle \Bigr )=\Phi (m).  \] Conversely, every section of $L^ k$ is a finite linear combination of such characters. In the coordinates on $U_{\sigma }$ determined by $u_{\rho _1},\ldots ,u_{\rho _ n}$, the Okounkov valuation of a non-zero linear combination is the lexicographically first exponent among the characters with non-zero coefficient. Hence arbitrary sections give no valuations beyond the right-hand side of ( 12.27 ), and ( 12.27 ) follows. $\square$

title: Example 12.2.7

text: Example 12.2.7 . Let us continue the example of $\mathrm{Bl}_{0}\mathbb {P}^2$ in example 12.1.4 . This time, let us take $\sigma _1'$ as our reference cone and $\rho _1=\sigma _5$, $\rho _2=\sigma _7$. Then $Y_1$ is just the strict transform of the line $\{ [X_0:0:X_2]:X_0X_2\neq 0\} $ in $\mathbb {P}^2$, while $Y_2$ is the point $Y_1\cap E$, where $E$ is the exceptional divisor. In this case, the map $\Phi $ is given by \[  \Phi (m_1,m_2)=(m_1,m_1+m_2).  \] We find that \[  \Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}\left(\mathrm{Bl}_{0}\mathbb {P}^2,\pi ^*\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^2}(1)\right)  \] is the polytope in 12.6 . 12.6 The Okounkov body $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\mathrm{Bl}_{0}\mathbb {P}^2,\pi ^*\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb {P}^2}(1))$. Note that it differs from the polytope in example 12.2.6 . Note. Although these examples are almost trivial, they did confuse me a lot at the beginning of 2023, when Kewei Zhang, Tamás Darvas and I were collaborating on [ DRWNXZ ] . At that time, Kewei himself already proved the main theorem for a generic flag. I realized that some simple birational geometry would suffice to prove the same result for general flags. I persuaded myself and Kewei that the Okounkov bodies are always birationally invariant, and deduced some apparently wrong conclusions. I got no clue for a couple of weeks, then one day, on the noisy metro line 7 of Paris, I got nothing to do, so I said to myself: Why not compute the simplest toric examples? Then after a few minutes, all of a sudden, the whole picture became completely clear.

title: Lemma 12.2.8
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Lemma 12.2.8 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and assume that $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current. Then $\varphi $ admits a quasi-equisingular approximation $(\varphi _ j)_ j$ with the following additional properties: $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and $\theta _{\varphi _ j}$ is a Kähler current for all $j\geq 1$; for each $j\geq 1$, there are $q_ j\in \mathbb Z_{>0}$ and toric eigen-sections \[  s_{j,1},\ldots ,s_{j,a_ j}\in \mathrm{H}^0(X,L^{q_ j})  \] such that \[  \varphi _ j=\frac{1}{q_ j}\log \sum _{\ell =1}^{a_ j}|s_{j,\ell }|_{h^{q_ j}}^2+\mathcal O(1).  \] Proof. Apply Demailly's Bergman-kernel approximation theorem [ Theorem 13.21 , Dem12 ] to the singular Hermitian metric $h\exp (-\varphi )$ on $L$. Since $\theta _{\varphi }$ is a Kähler current, the theorem applies to the Hilbert spaces \[  \mathrm{H}^0\bigl (X,L^ q\otimes \mathcal I(q\varphi )\bigr )  \] for $q\gg 1$, endowed with the $L^2$-norm induced by $h^ q\exp (-q\varphi )$ and a fixed Kähler volume form. The usual decreasing extraction in Demailly's construction gives a quasi-equisingular approximation; taking $q$ sufficiently large at each step ensures that the approximants still have Kähler Chern currents. It remains to note that this construction is compatible with the torus action. Indeed, both $h$ and $\varphi $ are $T_ c$-invariant, hence the above Hilbert spaces and their $L^2$-inner products are $T_ c$-invariant. Since $T_ c$ is compact and abelian, each of these finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces admits an orthonormal basis consisting of toric eigen-sections. With such a basis, the corresponding Bergman potential has the displayed form and is $T_ c$-invariant. This proves the lemma. $\square$

12.3 The pluripotential theory We continue to use the notations in section 12.1 . Theorem 12.3.1 . There are canonical bijections Note. In the earlier version of this book, I required additional conditions in 2 and 3 , namely $F\preceq F_{V_{	heta }}$ and $G\succeq G_{V_{	heta }}$ respectively. These conditions can be removed, since $G_{V_{	heta }}$ is always bounded, as suggested by Robert Berman. See theorem 12.2.12 . between the following sets: The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$; the set of $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$, and the set of closed proper convex functions $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying \[  G|_{M_{\mathbb {R}}\setminus P_ D}\equiv \infty .  \] The set $\mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$ is defined in definition A.3.1 . As before, we write $F_{\varphi }$, $G_{\varphi }$ for the functions determined by this construction. Proof. The proof is similar to that of theorem 5.2.3 , but due to its importance, we give the details. Again, the correspondence between 2 and 3 follows easily from proposition A.2.12 . Given $\varphi $, we can construct $F_{\varphi }$ in 2 as explained earlier in ( 12.23 ). Conversely, suppose that $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$, then $F\preceq F_{V_{	heta }}$ by theorem 12.2.12 . Then \[  \operatorname{Trop}^*\left(F-F_{	heta }ight)\in \mathrm{PSH}\left(T(\mathbb {C}),	heta |_{T(\mathbb {C})}ight)  \] by 5.2.1 . Since $F\preceq F_{V_{	heta }}$, we see that $\operatorname{Trop}^*(F-F_{	heta })$ is bounded from above. It follows that Grauert–Remmert's extension theorem theorem 1.2.9 is applicable, and this function extends to a unique $	heta $-psh function $\varphi $. The uniqueness of the extension guarantees that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$. The two maps are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$ We fix a model potential $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )_{>0}$ with Newton body $\Delta (	heta ,\phi )$. A similar argument guarantees the following: Corollary 12.3.2 . There is a canonical bijection between the following sets: The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta ;\phi )$, the set of $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},\Delta (	heta ,\phi ))$, and the set of closed proper convex functions $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying \[  G|_{M_{\mathbb {R}}\setminus \Delta (	heta ,\phi )}=\infty .  \] Moreover, under these correspondences, we have the following bijections: The set $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta ;\phi )$, the set of $F\in \mathcal{E}(N_{\mathbb {R}},\Delta (	heta ,\phi ))$, and the set of closed proper convex functions $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying \[  \overline{\operatorname{Int}\{ G<\infty \} }=\Delta (	heta ,\phi ).  \] Here the notations are defined as follows: \[   egin{aligned}  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta ;\phi )\coloneqq &  \{  \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta ):\varphi \preceq \phi \} ,\  \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta ;\phi )\coloneqq &  \mathcal{E}(X,	heta ;\phi )\cap \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta ). \end{aligned}  \] The proofs of the following results are similar to the ample case studied in chapter 5 . We omit the details. Proposition 12.3.3 . Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ and $C\in \mathbb {R}$. We have \[  F_{\varphi +C}=F_{\varphi }+C,\quad G_{\varphi +C}=G_{\varphi }-C.  \] Proposition 12.3.4 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$, assume that $\varphi \land \psi 
ot\equiv -\infty $, then $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ and \[  F_{\varphi \land \psi }=F_{\varphi }\land F_{\psi },\quad G_{\varphi \land \psi }=G_{\varphi }\lor G_{\psi }.  \] Proposition 12.3.5 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ and \[  F_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}= igvee _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}=\operatorname{cl} igwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Moreover, if $I$ is finite, then \[  G_{ igvee _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}= igwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Similarly, if $\{ \varphi _ i\} _{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ such that $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i
ot\equiv -\infty $, then $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ and \[  F_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}= igwedge _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}= igvee _{i\in I}G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Proposition 12.3.6 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$. Then $P_{	heta }[\varphi ]\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ and 12.44  egin{equation} \label{eq:toricPenvbig} G_{P_{	heta }[\varphi ]}(x)=  egin{cases}  G_{V_{	heta }}(x),& 	extup{if } x\in \Delta (	heta ,\varphi );\  \infty ,& 	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Proof. By ( 3.4 ), \[  P_{	heta }[\varphi ]=\operatorname *{sup}_{C\in \mathbb {R}}{}\! {}^{*} igl ((\varphi +C)\land V_{	heta } igr ).  \] Hence $P_{	heta }[\varphi ]\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ by proposition 12.3.3 , proposition 12.3.4 , proposition 12.3.5 . The same results give \[  G_{P_{	heta }[\varphi ]}=\operatorname{cl}\inf _{C\in \mathbb {R}}\left(G_{V_{	heta }}\lor (G_{\varphi }-C)ight).  \] Put \[  K=\inf _{C\in \mathbb {R}}\left(G_{V_{	heta }}\lor (G_{\varphi }-C)ight).  \] If $x\in \operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }$, then $G_{\varphi }(x)-C\leq G_{V_{	heta }}(x)$ for all large enough $C$, so $K(x)=G_{V_{	heta }}(x)$. If $x
otin \operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }$, then $K(x)=\infty $. By proposition A.2.9 , we have $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }}$. Moreover, theorem 12.2.12 gives $F_{V_{	heta }}\sim \operatorname{Supp}_{P_ D}$, hence $G_{V_{	heta }}\sim \chi _{P_ D}$ by Legendre duality. In particular, $G_{V_{	heta }}$ is finite and continuous on $P_ D$. Thus the lower semicontinuous regularization of $K$ is equal to $G_{V_{	heta }}$ on $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )$ and equal to $\infty $ outside $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )$. $\square$ As a consequence, we have Corollary 12.3.7 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi \preceq _ P \psi $; $\varphi \preceq _{\mathcal{I}} \psi $; $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\subseteq \Delta (	heta ,\psi )$. Proof. 1 $\iff $ 2 . This follows from the $\mathcal{I}$-goodness of $\varphi $ and $\psi $, see example 7.4.5 . 1 $\iff $ 3 . When $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )_{>0}$, this follows from proposition 12.3.6 . In general, fix an ample toric-invariant divisor $H$ on $X$ and a toric-invariant Hermitian metric $h_ H$ on $\mathcal{O}_ X(H)$ such that $\omega _ H\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ H$ is a Kähler form. We perturb $L$ to $L+m^{-1}H$ for $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, then thanks to A.3.7 , we find that \[  \Delta (	heta +m^{-1}\omega _ H,\varphi )\coloneqq m^{-1}\Delta (m	heta +\omega _ H,m\varphi )=\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )+m^{-1}\Delta \left(\mathcal{O}_ X(H)ight).  \] Then since $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta +m^{-1}\omega _ H)_{>0}$, we know that $\varphi \preceq _ P \psi $ if and only if \[  \Delta (	heta ,\varphi )+m^{-1}\Delta \left(\mathcal{O}_ X(H)ight)\subseteq \Delta (	heta ,\psi )+m^{-1}\Delta \left(\mathcal{O}_ X(H)ight)  \] for any $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. The latter condition is equivalent to $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\subseteq \Delta (	heta ,\psi )$. $\square$ Corollary 12.3.8 . There is a canonical bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )/\sim _{P}=\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )/\sim _{\mathcal{I}}ightarrow \left\{ K\in \mathcal{K}_ n: K \subseteq P_ D ight\} .  \] Here $\mathcal{K}_ n$ denotes the set of convex bodies in $\mathbb {R}^ n$, as in section C.1 . More precisely, given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$, the corresponding convex body is $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )$. Proof. Thanks to corollary 12.3.7 , we have the equality \[  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )/\sim _{P}=\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )/\sim _{\mathcal{I}},  \] and the map \[  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )/\sim _{\mathcal{I}}ightarrow \left\{ K\in \mathcal{K}_ n: K \subseteq P_ D ight\}   \] is well-defined and injective. In order to see the surjectivity, take $K\in \mathcal{K}_ n$, $K\subseteq P_ D$. Let $\chi _ K$ be the characteristic function of $K$ as defined in example A.1.4 . Since $\chi _ K$ satisfies Condition 3 of theorem 12.3.1 , we can find $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ so that $\chi _ K=G_{\varphi }$. Then $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )=K$ due to proposition A.2.9 . $\square$ Next we handle subgeodesics. Proposition 12.3.9 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$. There is a canonical bijection between the following sets: The set of $T_ c$-invariant subgeodesics from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$; the set of convex functions $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}	imes (0,1)ightarrow \mathbb {R}$ such that for each $r\in (0,1)$, the function 12.47  egin{equation} \label{eq:Ftdefsubgeo} F_ r\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}ightarrow \mathbb {R},\quad n\mapsto F(n,r) \end{equation} satisfies $F_ r	o F_{\varphi _1}$ (resp. $F_ r	o F_{\varphi _0}$) everywhere as $r	o 1-$ (resp. $r	o 0+$). Proof. We begin with a subgeodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then we define $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}	imes (0,1)ightarrow \mathbb {R}$ as follows: \[  F(n,t)=F_{\varphi _ t}(n).  \] Define $F_ t$ as in ( 12.47 ), we have \[  \operatorname{Trop}^* F_ t-\operatorname{Trop}^* F_{	heta }=\varphi _ t,\quad t\in (0,1).  \] Let $t_ j	o 0+$. Since $\varphi _{t_ j}	o \varphi _0$ in $L^1$, after passing to a subsequence we have almost-everywhere convergence on $X$. Restricted to the open torus and using the tropical coordinates, this gives $F_{t_ j}	o F_{\varphi _0}$ almost everywhere on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Since the $F_{t_ j}$'s are convex and locally uniformly bounded above, theorem A.1.18 upgrades this to pointwise convergence everywhere. As the limit is independent of the subsequence, $F_ t	o F_{\varphi _0}$ everywhere as $t	o 0+$. Similarly, $F_ t	o F_{\varphi _1}$ everywhere as $t	o 1-$. Next we show that $F$ is convex. Let $p_1\colon X	imes Sightarrow X$ be the projection, where \[  S\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \mathrm{e}^{-1}<|z|^2<1\} .  \] Since $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a subgeodesic, its complexification $\Phi $ is $p_1^*	heta $-psh. Recall that $\Phi $ is defined as 12.48  egin{equation} \label{eq:Phixz} \Phi (x,z)=\operatorname{Trop}^*\left( F_{-\log |z|^2}-F_{	heta } ight)(x). \end{equation} In particular, $\Psi \colon T(\mathbb {C})	imes Sightarrow \mathbb {R}$ defined by \[  \Psi (x,z)\coloneqq \Phi (x,z)+\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{	heta }(x)=\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{-\log |z|^2}(x)  \] is plurisubharmonic and $T_ c	imes S^1$-invariant. Fix a small enough $\epsilon >0$. We can find a decreasing sequence of $T_ c	imes S^1$-invariant plurisubharmonic functions $\Psi _ i$ on $T(\mathbb {C})	imes S_{\epsilon }$ converging to $\Psi $ everywhere, where \[  S_{\epsilon }\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \mathrm{e}^{-1+\epsilon }<|z|^2<\mathrm{e}^{-\epsilon }\} .  \] Let us write \[  \Psi _ i(x,z)=\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{i,-\log |z|^2}(x)  \] for some $F_ i\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}	imes (\epsilon ,1-\epsilon )ightarrow \mathbb {R}$. The same computation as in 5.2.1 shows that $F_ i$ is convex. It follows that $F$, as the decreasing limit of $F_ i$, is also convex on $N_{\mathbb {R}}	imes (\epsilon ,1-\epsilon )$. Since $\epsilon >0$ is arbitrary, we conclude that $F$ is convex on $N_{\mathbb {R}}	imes (0,1)$. Conversely, suppose that we are given $F$ in 2 . We define $\Phi \colon T(\mathbb {C})	imes Sightarrow \mathbb {R}$ using ( 12.48 ). The arguments in the previous part can be reversed to show that $\Phi $ is $p_1^*	heta |_{T(\mathbb {C})	imes S}$-psh. By our assumption, for each $t\in (0,1)$, we have 12.49  egin{equation} \label{eq:Ftupptemp1} F_ t\leq tF_{\varphi _1}+(1-t)F_{\varphi _0}\leq F_{V_{	heta }}+C \end{equation} for some constant $C\in \mathbb {R}$ independent of the choice of $t$. Therefore, $\Phi $ is bounded from above and hence, by theorem 1.2.9 , admits a unique $p_1^*	heta $-psh extension to $X	imes S$, which we still denote by $\Phi $. We let \[  \varphi _ t(x)=\Phi (x,\mathrm{e}^{-t/2})  \] for all $t\in (0,1)$ and $x\in X$. We claim that $(\varphi _ t)$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. For this purpose, we only need to show that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ has the correct boundary value. But from our assumption in 2 , we know that as $t	o 0+$ (resp. $t	o 1-$), $\varphi _ t	o \varphi _0$ (resp. $\varphi _ t	o \varphi _1$) almost everywhere. In particular, $\sup _ X \varphi _ t\geq -C'$ for some large constant $C'>0$ independent of $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, together with ( 12.49 ), we deduce from proposition 1.5.4 that $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in (0,1)}$ is a relatively compact family with respect to the $L^1$-topology. We need to show that each cluster point $\psi $ as $t	o 0+$ is equal to $\varphi _0$. But we already know that $\psi =\varphi _0$ almost everywhere. Hence we deduce $\psi =\varphi _0$ from proposition 1.2.6 . As $t	o 0+$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$. Similarly, as $t	o 1-$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _1$. The two constructions are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$ Corollary 12.3.10 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$. Then there is a canonical bijection between the following sets: The set of $T_ c$-invariant subgeodesics from $\psi _0$ to $\psi _1$, where $\psi _0,\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ and $\psi _0\leq \varphi _0$, $\psi _1\leq \varphi _1$; the set of closed proper convex functions $\Psi $ on $M_{\mathbb {R}}	imes \mathbb {R}$ such that there is a closed proper convex function $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying 12.50  egin{equation} \label{eq:Psilower} G(m)+(s\lor 0)\geq \Psi (m,s)\geq G_{\varphi _0}(m)\lor \left( G_{\varphi _1}(m)+s ight) \end{equation} for all $m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $s\in \mathbb {R}$. Proof. Let us begin with a subgeodesic $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ as in 1 . Let $F$ be the convex function as in proposition 12.3.9 . We extend $F$ to a function $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}	imes \mathbb {R}ightarrow \mathbb {R}$ as follows: For any $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$, we define \[  F(n,t)= egin{cases}  F_{\psi _ t}(n),& 	extup{if }0<t<1,\  F_{\psi _0}(n),&  	extup{if }t=0,\  F_{\psi _1}(n),& 	extup{if }t=1,\  \infty ,& 	extup{if } t>1 	extup{ or }t<0. \end{cases}  \] Then $F$ is a proper closed convex function on $N_{\mathbb {R}}	imes \mathbb {R}$. Let $\Psi $ be the Legendre transform of $F$. Then $\Psi $ is a proper closed convex function on $M_{\mathbb {R}}	imes \mathbb {R}$ by theorem A.2.2 . By ( A.6 ), for any $m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $s\in \mathbb {R}$, we have \[   egin{aligned}  \Psi (m,s)=& \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}},t\in [0,1]} \left( \langle m,nangle + ts-F(n,t)ight)\  =&  \sup _{t\in [0,1]} \left( ts+F_ t^*(m) ight). \end{aligned}  \] Therefore, the latter half of ( 12.50 ) follows. Next recall that \[  \eta \coloneqq \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\psi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta ),  \] as follows from proposition 4.1.6 . Therefore, \[   egin{aligned}  \Psi (m,s)=& \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}},t\in [0,1]} \left( \langle m,nangle + ts-F(n,t)ight)\  \leq &  \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}},t\in [0,1]} \left( \langle m,nangle + ts-F_{\eta }(n)ight)\  =&  \sup _{t\in [0,1]}ts+G_{\eta }(m)\  =&  (s\lor 0)+G_{\eta }(m). \end{aligned}  \] Conversely, let us begin with a function $\Psi $ as in 2 . Let $F$ be the Legendre transform of $\Psi $. We first observe that $F(n,t)=\infty $ for all $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $t
ot\in [0,1]$. Indeed, the upper bound $\Psi \leq G+(s\lor 0)$ gives \[  F(n,t)\geq G^*(n)+\sup _{s\in \mathbb {R}}\left(ts-(s\lor 0)ight),  \] and the last supremum is infinite exactly when $t
otin [0,1]$. For $t\in [0,1]$, the lower bound $\Psi \geq G_{\varphi _0}\lor (G_{\varphi _1}+s)$ implies \[  \Psi (m,s)\geq (1-t)G_{\varphi _0}(m)+tG_{\varphi _1}(m)+ts.  \] Consequently, \[  F(n,t)\leq \left((1-t)G_{\varphi _0}+tG_{\varphi _1}ight)^*(n) \leq (1-t)F_{\varphi _0}(n)+tF_{\varphi _1}(n)  \] for all $t\in [0,1]$ and $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$. On the other hand, the upper bound $\Psi \leq G+(s\lor 0)$ gives \[   egin{aligned}  F(n,t)=& \sup _{m\in M_{\mathbb {R}},s\in \mathbb {R}} \left(\langle m,nangle +ts-\Psi (m,s)ight)\  \geq &  \sup _{m\in M_{\mathbb {R}},s\in \mathbb {R}} \left(\langle m,nangle +ts-G(m)-(s\lor 0)ight)\  =&  G^*(n)+\sup _{s\in \mathbb {R}} \left( ts-(s\lor 0)ight)\  =&  egin{cases}  G^*(n),& 	ext{if }t\in [0,1],\  \infty ,& 	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}\end{aligned}  \] The convexity of $F$ gives one-sided boundary limits \[  F_0(n)\coloneqq \lim _{t	o 0+}F(n,t),\quad F_1(n)\coloneqq \lim _{t	o 1-}F(n,t).  \] The estimates above give $F_0\leq F_{\varphi _0}$ and $F_1\leq F_{\varphi _1}$, and also show that $F_0,F_1\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$. Let $\psi _0,\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$ be the corresponding potentials given by theorem 12.3.1 . Then $\psi _0\leq \varphi _0$ and $\psi _1\leq \varphi _1$. Applying proposition 12.3.9 to the restriction of $F$ to $N_{\mathbb {R}}	imes (0,1)$, we get a subgeodesic $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\psi _0$ to $\psi _1$. Thus $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ satisfies 1 . The two operations are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$ As an immediate corollary, Corollary 12.3.11 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )\cap \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )_{>0}$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi _0\sim _ P \varphi _1$; there is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. If these conditions are satisfied, let $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ be the geodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Conversely, given $\ell \in \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta ;\phi )$, it follows from corollary 12.3.11 that $G_{\ell _ t}$ is linear in $t\geq 0$ after restriction to $\operatorname{Int}\{ G_{\phi }<\infty \} $. Let \[  g'(m)=  egin{cases}  G_{\ell _1}(m)-G_{\phi }(m),&  m\in \operatorname{Int}\{ G_{\phi }<\infty \} ;\  \infty ,&  m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}\setminus \operatorname{Int}\{ G_{\phi }<\infty \} . \end{cases}  \] Note that for $m\in \operatorname{Int}\{ G_{\phi }<\infty \} $, we actually have \[  g'(m)=\lim _{t	o \infty }t^{-1}G_{\ell _ t}(m).  \] Hence, $g'$ is a proper convex function on $M_{\mathbb {R}}$. Then \[  \ell ^*_{	au }=\inf _{t>0} \left(\ell _ t-t	au ight)  \] is clearly toric-invariant. Therefore, \[  F_{\ell ^*_{	au }}=\inf _{t>0} \left(F_{\ell _ t}-t	au ight).  \] Fix $m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}$. We compute \[   egin{aligned}  G_{\ell ^*_{	au }}(m)=&  \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}}\left( \langle m, nangle -F_{\ell ^*_{	au }}(n) ight)\  =&  \sup _{t>0}\sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}}\left( \langle m, nangle - F_{\ell _ t}(n) +t	au ight)\  =& \sup _{t>0} \left(G_{\ell _ t}(m)+t	au ight)\  =&  G_{\phi }(m)+\sup _{t>0} t\left(g(m)+	au ight)\  =&  egin{cases}  G_{\phi }(m),& 	extup{if }g(m)+	au \leq 0;\  \infty ,& 	extup{otherwise}. \end{cases}\end{aligned}  \] Our assertions follow. $\square$ Next we consider the trace operator studied in chapter 8 . We wish to understand the trace operator in the toric situation. For this purpose, we will need to fix a $T$-invariant subvariety $Y\subseteq X$. With this choice, $Q_{\sigma }-m_{\sigma }$ is naturally contained in $P_{D_ Y}$. Theorem 12.3.14 . With the above choice of representative $m_{\sigma }$, let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )_{>0}$ satisfy $
u (\varphi ,Y)=0$. If $\operatorname{Tr}_ Y^{	heta }(\varphi )$ is defined and $\operatorname{vol}(	heta |_ Y,\operatorname{Tr}_ Y^{	heta }(\varphi ))>0$ Note. eq \varnothing $ by corollary 12.2.11 . Since $Y$ itself is a smooth toric variety, the preceding constructions of $X$ all apply to $Y$. We briefly summarize the situation in 12.1 . The idea of the proof is that since 10.4.16 , 10.4.17 describe how partial Okounkov bodies behave under restriction, and theorem 12.2.9 compares partial Okounkov bodies with Newton bodies, we can deduce the behavior of Newton bodies under restriction as well. First we note that by our assumption, $L|_ Y$ is a big line bundle. In particular, if we set $r=\dim \sigma $, then $\dim Y=n-r$. We also note that $\operatorname{Tr}_ Y^	heta (\varphi )$ is $T_{Y,c}$-invariant. Indeed, for any $g\in T_ c$, let $g_ Y$ be the induced automorphism of $Y$. Then $g_ Y^*\operatorname{Tr}_ Y(\varphi )$ is again a trace of $g^*\varphi =\varphi $ along $Y$. Hence $g_ Y^*\operatorname{Tr}_ Y(\varphi )\sim _ P\operatorname{Tr}_ Y(\varphi )$ by proposition 8.1.5 . Since $	heta |_ Y$ is $T_{Y,c}$-invariant and the $P$-envelope depends only on the $P$-equivalence class, we get $g_ Y^*\operatorname{Tr}_ Y^	heta (\varphi )=\operatorname{Tr}_ Y^	heta (\varphi )$. As the image of $T_ c$ in $\operatorname{Aut}(Y)$ is $T_{Y,c}$, the assertion follows. For this purpose, let $\sigma ^0$ be an $n$-dimensional cone of $\Sigma $ containing $\sigma $. The image $\overline{\sigma ^0}$ in $N(\sigma )$ is then an $(n-r)$-dimensional cone of $\mathrm{Star}(\sigma )$. We shall use these cones as the reference cones while defining the partial Okounkov bodies. We list the rays in $\sigma ^0(1)$ as follows: 12.82  egin{equation} \label{eq:rayssigma0} ho _1,\ldots ,ho _ n, \end{equation} where $ho _1,\ldots ,ho _ r\in \sigma (1)$ and hence $ho _{r+1},\ldots ,ho _ n
ot\in \sigma (1)$. In particular, the images 12.83  egin{equation} \label{eq:rayssigma0bar} \overline{ho _{r+1}},\ldots ,\overline{ho _{n}} \end{equation} of the latter give a list of $\overline{\sigma ^0}(1)$. We construct the flag $Y_{ ullet }$ on $X$ using the rays ( 12.82 ) and the flag $Z_{ ullet }$ on $Y$ using the rays ( 12.83 ). Note that \[  Z_ i=Y_{r+i},  \] where $i=1,\ldots ,n-r$. Next we compute the Cartier data associated with $\overline{\sigma ^0}$ for the divisor $D_ Y$. By definition, $m_{\overline{\sigma ^0}}\in M(\sigma )$ is the unique element satisfying \[  \langle m_{\overline{\sigma ^0}},u_{\overline{ho _ j}}angle =-a_{ho _ j}-\langle m_{\sigma },u_{ho _ j}angle  \] for all $j=r+1,\ldots ,n$. Since $m_{\sigma ^0}-m_{\sigma }$ vanishes on $\sigma $, it lies in $M(\sigma )$, and the preceding formula gives \[  m_{\overline{\sigma ^0}}=m_{\sigma ^0}-m_{\sigma }.  \] Let $\Phi \colon Mightarrow \mathbb {Z}^ n$ and $\Psi \colon M(\sigma )ightarrow \mathbb {Z}^{n-r}$ be defined as \[   egin{aligned}  \Phi (m)=& \left( \langle m-m_{\sigma ^0},u_{ho _1} angle ,\dots ,\langle m-m_{\sigma ^0},u_{ho _ n} angle ight)\  =&  \left( \langle m,u_{ho _1}angle ,\dots ,\langle m,u_{ho _ n}angle ight) + (a_{ho _1},\ldots ,a_{ho _ n}),\  \Psi (m)=& \left( \langle m-m_{\overline{\sigma ^0}},u_{\overline{ho _{r+1}}} angle ,\dots ,\langle m-m_{\overline{\sigma ^0}},u_{\overline{ho _ n}} angle ight) \end{aligned}  \] Observe that for $i=r+1,\ldots ,n$, we have \[  u_{\overline{ho _ i}}=u_{ho _ i}\mod N\cap \langle \sigma angle ,  \] so \[   egin{aligned}  \Psi (m)=& \left( \langle m,u_{ho _{r+1}} angle ,\ldots , \langle m,u_{ho _{n}} angle ight)\ & +\left(a_{ho _{r+1}}+\langle m_{\sigma },u_{ho _{r+1}}angle ,\ldots ,a_{ho _ n}+\langle m_{\sigma },u_{ho _ n}angle ight) \end{aligned}  \] for $m\in M(\sigma )$. eq \varnothing .  \] In particular, the first $r$ valuation coordinates of $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ along the flag $Y_ ullet $ vanish. By 10.4.16 and 10.4.17 , \[   egin{aligned}  \Delta _{Z_{ ullet }}\Bigl (	heta |_ Y,\operatorname{Tr}_{Y}^{	heta }(\varphi )\Bigr )=&  L \Bigl ( \Delta _{Y_{ ullet }}(	heta ,\varphi ) \cap (\{ 0\} ^ r 	imes \mathbb {R}^{n-r})\Bigr )\  =&  L\Bigl ( \Phi _{\mathbb {R}}(\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )) \cap (\{ 0\} ^ r 	imes \mathbb {R}^{n-r}) \Bigr )\  =&  L\circ \Phi _{\mathbb {R}} \Bigl (\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\cap Q_{\sigma } \Bigr )\  =&  \Psi _{\mathbb {R}}\Bigl ((\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\cap Q_{\sigma })-m_{\sigma }\Bigr ). \end{aligned}  \] In the third line, we used $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\subseteq P_ D$ from theorem 12.2.12 , the identity ( 12.6 ), and the fact that $m_{\sigma ^0}-m_\sigma $ vanishes on $\sigma $. Since $\Psi _{\mathbb {R}}$ is an affine isomorphism, our assertion follows. $\square$ Corollary 12.3.15 . For any $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta )$, we have 12.93  egin{equation} \label{eq:volTr_tor} \operatorname{vol}\left(	heta |_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Tr}_ Y^{	heta }(\varphi )ight)=(\dim Y)!\operatorname{vol}_{\dim Y} \Bigl (\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\cap Q_{\sigma }\Bigr ). \end{equation} The left-hand side of ( 12.93 ) is understood as $0$ if $\operatorname{Tr}_ Y^{	heta }(\varphi )$ is not defined. On the right-hand side, we translate $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\cap Q_{\sigma }$ by $-m_{\sigma }$ and compute the $\dim Y$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on $M(\sigma )_{\mathbb {R}}$, normalized so that a fundamental parallelepiped for $M(\sigma )$ has volume $1$. Proof. If $
u (\varphi ,Y)>0$, then by corollary 12.2.11 , $\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\cap Q_\sigma =\varnothing $. By convention the right-hand side of ( 12.93 ) is $0$, and the trace is not defined, so the left-hand side is $0$. Assume now that $
u (\varphi ,Y)=0$. Take a toric-invariant ample line bundle $H$ on $X$ and a toric-invariant Kähler metric $\omega \in c_1(H)$. For $\epsilon \in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$, write $Q_{\sigma ,\epsilon }$ for the face corresponding to $\sigma $ for the divisor $D+\epsilon H$, with the same convention on the Cartier datum along $\sigma $. Since $	heta _{\varphi }+\epsilon \omega $ is a toric Kähler current and $

Hence theorem 12.3.14 gives \[  \operatorname{vol}\left(	heta |_ Y+\epsilon \omega |_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Tr}_ Y^{	heta +\epsilon \omega }(\varphi )ight)= (\dim Y)!\operatorname{vol}_{\dim Y} \Bigl (\Delta (	heta +\epsilon \omega ,\varphi )\cap Q_{\sigma ,\epsilon }\Bigr ).  \] By A.3.7 , \[  \Delta (	heta +\epsilon \omega ,\varphi )=\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )+\epsilon P_ H.  \] We choose the Cartier datum of $D+\epsilon H$ along $\sigma $ to be the sum of the chosen datum of $D$ and $\epsilon $ times the chosen datum of $H$. With this convention, the face of $P_ D+\epsilon P_ H$ corresponding to $\sigma $ is $Q_\sigma +\epsilon Q_\sigma ^ H$. In particular, \[  \Delta (	heta +\epsilon \omega ,\varphi )\cap Q_{\sigma ,\epsilon }=(\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\cap Q_{\sigma })+\epsilon Q^ H_{\sigma },  \] where $Q^ H_{\sigma }$ denotes the corresponding face of the polytope of $H$. Indeed, the defining inequalities along the rays of $\sigma $ are non-negative on both summands, so equality for their sum forces equality on each summand. By example 8.1.12 , the left-hand side converges to \[  \operatorname{vol}\left(	heta |_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\operatorname{Tr}_ Y^	heta (\varphi )ight),  \] with the convention that this limit is $0$ when the trace in the limiting class is not defined. The right-hand side converges to \[  (\dim Y)!\operatorname{vol}_{\dim Y}\Bigl (\Delta (	heta ,\varphi )\cap Q_\sigma \Bigr ).  \] Hence ( 12.93 ) follows. $\square$ As a corollary, we obtain an elegant characterization of the augmented base locus in the toric setting. Corollary 12.3.16 . The augmented base locus (with the reduced complex structure) of $D$ is a toric-invariant (possibly reducible) subvariety given by the union of the $V(	au )$'s, where $	au $ runs over the elements in $\Sigma $ such that \[  \dim Q_{	au }<n-\dim 	au  ootnotemark .  \] Note. Here we understand that $\dim \varnothing =-\infty $. Intuitively, we should think of $n-\dim 	au $ as the expected dimension of $Q_{	au }$. This corollary says that $Q_{	au }$ fails to attain the expected dimension if and only if it corresponds to a subvariety in the augmented base locus. With the help of some knowledge of convex geometry, we can also deduce this corollary from corollary 12.1.2 . Proof. Apply corollary 12.3.15 to $\varphi =V_{	heta }$. Together with Nakamaye's theorem [ Theorem 5.7 , ELMNP09 ] and theorem 8.3.2 , this says that $V(	au )$ lies in the augmented base locus exactly when the $\dim V(	au )$-dimensional volume of $Q_{	au }$ is zero, which is equivalent to $\dim Q_{	au }<n-\dim 	au $. $\square$ Example 12.3.17 . Let us consider the example example 12.1.4 again, we consider the subvariety corresponding to $\sigma _7$. We have \[  Q_{\sigma _7}=\Bigl \{ m\in P_ D: \langle m,(1,1) angle =0 \Bigr \} .  \] The situation is explained in 12.7 . 12.7 The face $Q_{\sigma _7}=\{ m\in P_ D:\langle m,(1,1)angle =0\} $ is the single point $\{ (0,0)\} $, of dimension $0$ rather than the expected $1$. We find that $\dim Q_{\sigma _7}=0$, but the expected dimension is $2-1=1$. So the corresponding divisor, namely the exceptional divisor on $\mathrm{Bl}_0\mathbb {P}^2$ is in the non-Kähler locus. Similarly, we can verify that the non-Kähler locus consists only of this divisor. Finally, we compute the mixed volumes of Newton bodies. Theorem 12.3.18 . Take $T$-invariant big divisors $D_1,\ldots ,D_ n$ on $X$. Consider $T_ c$-invariant closed positive $(1,1)$-currents $T_ i$ in $c_1(\mathcal{O}_ X(D_ i))$ for $i=1,\ldots ,n$. Then 12.94  egin{equation} \label{eq:mixvol_pob} n! \operatorname{vol}\Bigl ( \Delta (T_1),\ldots ,\Delta (T_ n) \Bigr )=\operatorname{vol}\left(T_1,\ldots ,T_ n ight). \end{equation} The mixed volume of currents is studied in section 7.3 . Proof. It suffices to prove the following assertion: 12.95  egin{equation} \label{eq:Delta_add} \Delta (T_1+T_2)=\Delta (T_1)+\Delta (T_2). ootnotemark \end{equation} Note. This is slightly problematic when $n=1$, since $T_2$ is not defined stricto sensu . We take $D_2,T_2$ satisfying the same assumptions as $D_1,T_1$ in this case. In fact, assuming this, by induction, for each tuple of non-negative integers $C_1,\ldots ,C_ n$, we have \[  \Delta \left( \sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i T_ i ight)=\sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i \Delta (T_ i).  \] Comparing the volumes, we have \[  \operatorname{vol}\Delta \left( \sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i T_ i ight)=\sum _{i_1,\ldots ,i_ n=1}^ n C_{i_1}\cdots C_{i_ n} \operatorname{vol}\left(\Delta \left(T_{i_1}ight),\ldots ,\Delta \left(T_{i_ n}ight)ight).  \] On the other hand, by proposition 12.2.4 , the $\mathcal{I}$-goodness of toric singularities example 7.4.5 , and proposition 7.3.4 , we have \[  n! \operatorname{vol}\Delta \left( \sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i T_ i ight)=\operatorname{vol}\left( \sum _{i=1}^ n C_ i T_ i ight)=\sum _{i_1,\ldots ,i_ n=1}^ n C_{i_1}\cdots C_{i_ n} \operatorname{vol}\left(T_{i_1},\ldots ,T_{i_ n}ight).  \] Comparing the coefficients of the above two expressions, we conclude ( 12.94 ). It only remains to establish ( 12.95 ). For this purpose, we fix smooth $T_ c$-invariant Hermitian metrics $h_1$ and $h_2$ on $\mathcal{O}_ X(D_1)$ and $\mathcal{O}_ X(D_2)$ respectively. Correspondingly, take $h_1\otimes h_2$ as the reference Hermitian metric on $\mathcal{O}_ X(D_1+D_2)$. Write \[  	heta _1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_1,\quad 	heta _2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_2.  \] We choose the rational section of $\mathcal O_ X(D_1+D_2)$ to be $s_{D_1}\otimes s_{D_2}$. With this choice and with the reference metric $h_1\otimes h_2$, the normalization ( 12.22 ) gives \[  F_{	heta _1+	heta _2}=F_{	heta _1}+F_{	heta _2}.  \] Thus \[  F_{\varphi _1+\varphi _2}=F_{\varphi _1}+F_{\varphi _2}.  \] Take $\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,	heta _ i)$ with $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ i$ for $i=1,2$. Then $F_{\varphi _1}+F_{\varphi _2}$ is a candidate for $F_{\varphi _1+\varphi _2}$; see ( 12.23 ). Therefore, ( 12.95 ) follows from the equality of closed gradient images proved in A.3.7 . $\square$ A good theorem lasts forever. Once proved, it will always stay proved, and other mathematicians are free to use it and build on it as they please, sometimes to great effect.

However, his aversion to publishing papers arguably impeded the progress of the development of mathematics to some extent. text: Theorem 12.3.1 . There are canonical bijections Note. In the earlier version of this book, I required additional conditions in 2 and 3 , namely $F\preceq F_{V_{\theta }}$ and $G\succeq G_{V_{\theta }}$ respectively. These conditions can be removed, since $G_{V_{\theta }}$ is always bounded, as suggested by Robert Berman. See theorem 12.2.12 . between the following sets: The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$; the set of $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$, and the set of closed proper convex functions $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying \[  G|_{M_{\mathbb {R}}\setminus P_ D}\equiv \infty .  \] Proof. The proof is similar to that of theorem 5.2.3 , but due to its importance, we give the details. Again, the correspondence between 2 and 3 follows easily from proposition A.2.12 . Given $\varphi $, we can construct $F_{\varphi }$ in 2 as explained earlier in ( 12.23 ). Conversely, suppose that $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$, then $F\preceq F_{V_{\theta }}$ by theorem 12.2.12 . Then \[  \operatorname{Trop}^*\left(F-F_{\theta }\right)\in \mathrm{PSH}\left(T(\mathbb {C}),\theta |_{T(\mathbb {C})}\right)  \] by 5.2.1 . Since $F\preceq F_{V_{\theta }}$, we see that $\operatorname{Trop}^*(F-F_{\theta })$ is bounded from above. It follows that Grauert–Remmert's extension theorem theorem 1.2.9 is applicable, and this function extends to a unique $\theta $-psh function $\varphi $. The uniqueness of the extension guarantees that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. The two maps are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$

section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Corollary 12.3.2 . There is a canonical bijection between the following sets: The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, the set of $F\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},\Delta (\theta ,\phi ))$, and the set of closed proper convex functions $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying \[  G|_{M_{\mathbb {R}}\setminus \Delta (\theta ,\phi )}=\infty .  \] Moreover, under these correspondences, we have the following bijections: The set $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta ;\phi )$, the set of $F\in \mathcal{E}(N_{\mathbb {R}},\Delta (\theta ,\phi ))$, and the set of closed proper convex functions $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying \[  \overline{\operatorname{Int}\{ G<\infty \} }=\Delta (\theta ,\phi ).  \]

title: Proposition 12.3.3
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Proposition 12.3.3 . Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and $C\in \mathbb {R}$. We have \[  F_{\varphi +C}=F_{\varphi }+C,\quad G_{\varphi +C}=G_{\varphi }-C.  \]

title: Proposition 12.3.4
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Proposition 12.3.4 . Given $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$, assume that $\varphi \land \psi \not\equiv -\infty $, then $\varphi \land \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and \[  F_{\varphi \land \psi }=F_{\varphi }\land F_{\psi },\quad G_{\varphi \land \psi }=G_{\varphi }\lor G_{\psi }.  \]

title: Proposition 12.3.5
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Proposition 12.3.5 . Let $(\varphi _ i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ uniformly bounded from above. Then $\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*} \varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and \[  F_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}=\bigvee _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\operatorname *{sup}_{i\in I}{}\! {}^{*}\varphi _ i}=\operatorname{cl}\bigwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Moreover, if $I$ is finite, then \[  G_{\bigvee _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\bigwedge _{i\in I} G_{\varphi _ i}.  \] Similarly, if $\{ \varphi _ i\} _{i\in I}$ is a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ such that $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i\not\equiv -\infty $, then $\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and \[  F_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\bigwedge _{i\in I}F_{\varphi _ i},\quad G_{\inf _{i\in I}\varphi _ i}=\bigvee _{i\in I}G_{\varphi _ i}.  \]

title: Proposition 12.3.6
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Proposition 12.3.6 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. Then $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and 12.44 \begin{equation} \label{eq:toricPenvbig} G_{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]}(x)= \begin{cases}  G_{V_{\theta }}(x),& \textup{if } x\in \Delta (\theta ,\varphi );\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{equation} Proof. By ( 3.4 ), \[  P_{\theta }[\varphi ]=\operatorname *{sup}_{C\in \mathbb {R}}{}\! {}^{*}\bigl ((\varphi +C)\land V_{\theta }\bigr ).  \] Hence $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ by proposition 12.3.3 , proposition 12.3.4 , proposition 12.3.5 . The same results give \[  G_{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]}=\operatorname{cl}\inf _{C\in \mathbb {R}}\left(G_{V_{\theta }}\lor (G_{\varphi }-C)\right).  \] Put \[  K=\inf _{C\in \mathbb {R}}\left(G_{V_{\theta }}\lor (G_{\varphi }-C)\right).  \] If $x\in \operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }$, then $G_{\varphi }(x)-C\leq G_{V_{\theta }}(x)$ for all large enough $C$, so $K(x)=G_{V_{\theta }}(x)$. If $x\notin \operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }$, then $K(x)=\infty $. By proposition A.2.9 , we have $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}G_{\varphi }}$. Moreover, theorem 12.2.12 gives $F_{V_{\theta }}\sim \operatorname{Supp}_{P_ D}$, hence $G_{V_{\theta }}\sim \chi _{P_ D}$ by Legendre duality. In particular, $G_{V_{\theta }}$ is finite and continuous on $P_ D$. Thus the lower semicontinuous regularization of $K$ is equal to $G_{V_{\theta }}$ on $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$ and equal to $\infty $ outside $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )$. $\square$

section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: 12.44 \begin{equation} \label{eq:toricPenvbig} G_{P_{\theta }[\varphi ]}(x)= \begin{cases}  G_{V_{\theta }}(x),& \textup{if } x\in \Delta (\theta ,\varphi );\\  \infty ,& \textup{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{equation}

title: Corollary 12.3.7
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Corollary 12.3.7 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi \preceq _ P \psi $; $\varphi \preceq _{\mathcal{I}} \psi $; $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\subseteq \Delta (\theta ,\psi )$. Proof. 1 $\iff $ 2 . This follows from the $\mathcal{I}$-goodness of $\varphi $ and $\psi $, see example 7.4.5 . 1 $\iff $ 3 . When $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )_{>0}$, this follows from proposition 12.3.6 . In general, fix an ample toric-invariant divisor $H$ on $X$ and a toric-invariant Hermitian metric $h_ H$ on $\mathcal{O}_ X(H)$ such that $\omega _ H\coloneqq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ H$ is a Kähler form. We perturb $L$ to $L+m^{-1}H$ for $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, then thanks to A.3.7 , we find that \[  \Delta (\theta +m^{-1}\omega _ H,\varphi )\coloneqq m^{-1}\Delta (m\theta +\omega _ H,m\varphi )=\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )+m^{-1}\Delta \left(\mathcal{O}_ X(H)\right).  \] Then since $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta +m^{-1}\omega _ H)_{>0}$, we know that $\varphi \preceq _ P \psi $ if and only if \[  \Delta (\theta ,\varphi )+m^{-1}\Delta \left(\mathcal{O}_ X(H)\right)\subseteq \Delta (\theta ,\psi )+m^{-1}\Delta \left(\mathcal{O}_ X(H)\right)  \] for any $m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. The latter condition is equivalent to $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )\subseteq \Delta (\theta ,\psi )$. $\square$

title: Corollary 12.3.8
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Corollary 12.3.8 . There is a canonical bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{P}=\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\rightarrow \left\{ K\in \mathcal{K}_ n: K \subseteq P_ D \right\} .  \] Here $\mathcal{K}_ n$ denotes the set of convex bodies in $\mathbb {R}^ n$, as in section C.1 . Proof. Thanks to corollary 12.3.7 , we have the equality \[  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{P}=\mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{\mathcal{I}},  \] and the map \[  \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )/\sim _{\mathcal{I}}\rightarrow \left\{ K\in \mathcal{K}_ n: K \subseteq P_ D \right\}   \] is well-defined and injective. In order to see the surjectivity, take $K\in \mathcal{K}_ n$, $K\subseteq P_ D$. Let $\chi _ K$ be the characteristic function of $K$ as defined in example A.1.4 . Since $\chi _ K$ satisfies Condition 3 of theorem 12.3.1 , we can find $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ so that $\chi _ K=G_{\varphi }$. Then $\Delta (\theta ,\varphi )=K$ due to proposition A.2.9 . $\square$

title: Proposition 12.3.9
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Proposition 12.3.9 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. There is a canonical bijection between the following sets: The set of $T_ c$-invariant subgeodesics from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$; the set of convex functions $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (0,1)\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ such that for each $r\in (0,1)$, the function 12.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Ftdefsubgeo} F_ r\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\rightarrow \mathbb {R},\quad n\mapsto F(n,r) \end{equation} satisfies $F_ r\to F_{\varphi _1}$ (resp. $F_ r\to F_{\varphi _0}$) everywhere as $r\to 1-$ (resp. $r\to 0+$). Proof. We begin with a subgeodesic $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. Then we define $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (0,1)\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ as follows: \[  F(n,t)=F_{\varphi _ t}(n).  \] Define $F_ t$ as in ( 12.47 ), we have \[  \operatorname{Trop}^* F_ t-\operatorname{Trop}^* F_{\theta }=\varphi _ t,\quad t\in (0,1).  \] Let $t_ j\to 0+$. Since $\varphi _{t_ j}\to \varphi _0$ in $L^1$, after passing to a subsequence we have almost-everywhere convergence on $X$. Restricted to the open torus and using the tropical coordinates, this gives $F_{t_ j}\to F_{\varphi _0}$ almost everywhere on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Since the $F_{t_ j}$'s are convex and locally uniformly bounded above, theorem A.1.18 upgrades this to pointwise convergence everywhere. As the limit is independent of the subsequence, $F_ t\to F_{\varphi _0}$ everywhere as $t\to 0+$. Similarly, $F_ t\to F_{\varphi _1}$ everywhere as $t\to 1-$. Next we show that $F$ is convex. Let $p_1\colon X\times S\rightarrow X$ be the projection, where \[  S\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \mathrm{e}^{-1}<|z|^2<1\} .  \] Since $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ is a subgeodesic, its complexification $\Phi $ is $p_1^*\theta $-psh. Recall that $\Phi $ is defined as 12.48 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Phixz} \Phi (x,z)=\operatorname{Trop}^*\left( F_{-\log |z|^2}-F_{\theta } \right)(x). \end{equation} In particular, $\Psi \colon T(\mathbb {C})\times S\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ defined by \[  \Psi (x,z)\coloneqq \Phi (x,z)+\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{\theta }(x)=\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{-\log |z|^2}(x)  \] is plurisubharmonic and $T_ c\times S^1$-invariant. Fix a small enough $\epsilon >0$. We can find a decreasing sequence of $T_ c\times S^1$-invariant plurisubharmonic functions $\Psi _ i$ on $T(\mathbb {C})\times S_{\epsilon }$ converging to $\Psi $ everywhere, where \[  S_{\epsilon }\coloneqq \{ z\in \mathbb {C}: \mathrm{e}^{-1+\epsilon }<|z|^2<\mathrm{e}^{-\epsilon }\} .  \] Let us write \[  \Psi _ i(x,z)=\operatorname{Trop}^*F_{i,-\log |z|^2}(x)  \] for some $F_ i\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (\epsilon ,1-\epsilon )\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$. The same computation as in 5.2.1 shows that $F_ i$ is convex. It follows that $F$, as the decreasing limit of $F_ i$, is also convex on $N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (\epsilon ,1-\epsilon )$. Since $\epsilon >0$ is arbitrary, we conclude that $F$ is convex on $N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (0,1)$. Conversely, suppose that we are given $F$ in 2 . We define $\Phi \colon T(\mathbb {C})\times S\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ using ( 12.48 ). The arguments in the previous part can be reversed to show that $\Phi $ is $p_1^*\theta |_{T(\mathbb {C})\times S}$-psh. By our assumption, for each $t\in (0,1)$, we have 12.49 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Ftupptemp1} F_ t\leq tF_{\varphi _1}+(1-t)F_{\varphi _0}\leq F_{V_{\theta }}+C \end{equation} for some constant $C\in \mathbb {R}$ independent of the choice of $t$. Therefore, $\Phi $ is bounded from above and hence, by theorem 1.2.9 , admits a unique $p_1^*\theta $-psh extension to $X\times S$, which we still denote by $\Phi $. We let \[  \varphi _ t(x)=\Phi (x,\mathrm{e}^{-t/2})  \] for all $t\in (0,1)$ and $x\in X$. We claim that $(\varphi _ t)$ is a subgeodesic from $\varphi _0$ to $\varphi _1$. For this purpose, we only need to show that $(\varphi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ has the correct boundary value. But from our assumption in 2 , we know that as $t\to 0+$ (resp. $t\to 1-$), $\varphi _ t\to \varphi _0$ (resp. $\varphi _ t\to \varphi _1$) almost everywhere. In particular, $\sup _ X \varphi _ t\geq -C'$ for some large constant $C'>0$ independent of $t\in (0,1)$. Therefore, together with ( 12.49 ), we deduce from proposition 1.5.4 that $\{ \varphi _ t\} _{t\in (0,1)}$ is a relatively compact family with respect to the $L^1$-topology. We need to show that each cluster point $\psi $ as $t\to 0+$ is equal to $\varphi _0$. But we already know that $\psi =\varphi _0$ almost everywhere. Hence we deduce $\psi =\varphi _0$ from proposition 1.2.6 . As $t\to 0+$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _0$. Similarly, as $t\to 1-$, we have $\varphi _ t\xrightarrow {L^1}\varphi _1$. The two constructions are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$

title: Corollary 12.3.10
section: 18.4 Toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles
text: Corollary 12.3.10 . Let $\varphi _0,\varphi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$. Then there is a canonical bijection between the following sets: The set of $T_ c$-invariant subgeodesics from $\psi _0$ to $\psi _1$, where $\psi _0,\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ and $\psi _0\leq \varphi _0$, $\psi _1\leq \varphi _1$; the set of closed proper convex functions $\Psi $ on $M_{\mathbb {R}}\times \mathbb {R}$ such that there is a closed proper convex function $G\in \mathrm{Conv}(M_{\mathbb {R}})$ satisfying 12.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Psilower} G(m)+(s\lor 0)\geq \Psi (m,s)\geq G_{\varphi _0}(m)\lor \left( G_{\varphi _1}(m)+s \right) \end{equation} for all $m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $s\in \mathbb {R}$. Proof. Let us begin with a subgeodesic $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ as in 1 . Let $F$ be the convex function as in proposition 12.3.9 . We extend $F$ to a function $F\colon N_{\mathbb {R}}\times \mathbb {R}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ as follows: For any $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$, we define \[  F(n,t)=\begin{cases}  F_{\psi _ t}(n),& \textup{if }0<t<1,\\  F_{\psi _0}(n),&  \textup{if }t=0,\\  F_{\psi _1}(n),& \textup{if }t=1,\\  \infty ,& \textup{if } t>1 \textup{ or }t<0. \end{cases}  \] Then $F$ is a proper closed convex function on $N_{\mathbb {R}}\times \mathbb {R}$. Let $\Psi $ be the Legendre transform of $F$. Then $\Psi $ is a proper closed convex function on $M_{\mathbb {R}}\times \mathbb {R}$ by theorem A.2.2 . By ( A.6 ), for any $m\in M_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $s\in \mathbb {R}$, we have \[  \begin{aligned}  \Psi (m,s)=& \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}},t\in [0,1]} \left( \langle m,n\rangle + ts-F(n,t)\right)\\  =&  \sup _{t\in [0,1]} \left( ts+F_ t^*(m) \right). \end{aligned}  \] Therefore, the latter half of ( 12.50 ) follows. Next recall that \[  \eta \coloneqq \inf _{t\in (0,1)}\psi _ t\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta ),  \] as follows from proposition 4.1.6 . Therefore, \[  \begin{aligned}  \Psi (m,s)=& \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}},t\in [0,1]} \left( \langle m,n\rangle + ts-F(n,t)\right)\\  \leq &  \sup _{n\in N_{\mathbb {R}},t\in [0,1]} \left( \langle m,n\rangle + ts-F_{\eta }(n)\right)\\  =&  \sup _{t\in [0,1]}ts+G_{\eta }(m)\\  =&  (s\lor 0)+G_{\eta }(m). \end{aligned}  \] Conversely, let us begin with a function $\Psi $ as in 2 . Let $F$ be the Legendre transform of $\Psi $. We first observe that $F(n,t)=\infty $ for all $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$ and $t\not\in [0,1]$. Indeed, the upper bound $\Psi \leq G+(s\lor 0)$ gives \[  F(n,t)\geq G^*(n)+\sup _{s\in \mathbb {R}}\left(ts-(s\lor 0)\right),  \] and the last supremum is infinite exactly when $t\notin [0,1]$. For $t\in [0,1]$, the lower bound $\Psi \geq G_{\varphi _0}\lor (G_{\varphi _1}+s)$ implies \[  \Psi (m,s)\geq (1-t)G_{\varphi _0}(m)+tG_{\varphi _1}(m)+ts.  \] Consequently, \[  F(n,t)\leq \left((1-t)G_{\varphi _0}+tG_{\varphi _1}\right)^*(n) \leq (1-t)F_{\varphi _0}(n)+tF_{\varphi _1}(n)  \] for all $t\in [0,1]$ and $n\in N_{\mathbb {R}}$. On the other hand, the upper bound $\Psi \leq G+(s\lor 0)$ gives \[  \begin{aligned}  F(n,t)=& \sup _{m\in M_{\mathbb {R}},s\in \mathbb {R}} \left(\langle m,n\rangle +ts-\Psi (m,s)\right)\\  \geq &  \sup _{m\in M_{\mathbb {R}},s\in \mathbb {R}} \left(\langle m,n\rangle +ts-G(m)-(s\lor 0)\right)\\  =&  G^*(n)+\sup _{s\in \mathbb {R}} \left( ts-(s\lor 0)\right)\\  =& \begin{cases}  G^*(n),& \text{if }t\in [0,1],\\  \infty ,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}\end{aligned}  \] The convexity of $F$ gives one-sided boundary limits \[  F_0(n)\coloneqq \lim _{t\to 0+}F(n,t),\quad F_1(n)\coloneqq \lim _{t\to 1-}F(n,t).  \] The estimates above give $F_0\leq F_{\varphi _0}$ and $F_1\leq F_{\varphi _1}$, and also show that $F_0,F_1\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P_ D)$. Let $\psi _0,\psi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}_{\mathrm{tor}}(X,\theta )$ be the corresponding potentials given by theorem 12.3.1 . Then $\psi _0\leq \varphi _0$ and $\psi _1\leq \varphi _1$. Applying proposition 12.3.9 to the restriction of $F$ to $N_{\mathbb {R}}\times (0,1)$, we get a subgeodesic $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ from $\psi _0$ to $\psi _1$. Thus $(\psi _ t)_{t\in (0,1)}$ satisfies 1 . The two operations are inverse to each other by construction. $\square$
