title: A brief history
text: A brief history Here we recall the origin of various results. chapter 1 . The notion of plurisubharmonic functions was introduced by Lelong [ Lel45 ] and Oka [ Oka42 ] , based on F. Riesz's theory of subharmonic functions [ Rie26 ] . See [ Bre72 ] for an excellent introduction to the early history of the subject. We refer to [ Bre65 ] for the foundations of potential theory and [ GZ17 ] for the pluripotential theory. The study of Josefson-type theorems was initiated by Josefson [ Jos78 ] , who proved theorem 1.1.16 . The global Josefson theorem theorem 1.1.17 was due to Vu [ Vu19 ] . In the projective setting, it was due to Dinh–Sibony [ DS06 ] and in the Kähler setting, it was established by Guedj–Zeriahi [ GZ05 ] . The extension theorem theorem 1.2.9 was proved in [ GR56 ] . In fact, they proved a more general version for complex spaces, see theorem B.2.3 . For some related important extension theorems, see [ Shi72 , Wan22 , CGZ13 ] . proposition 1.2.11 was due to Kiselman [ Kis78 ] . The idea of fine topology was due to H. Cartan [ Car41 ] . The plurifine topology was introduced by Fuglede during the Séminaire d'analyse de Lelong–Dolbeault–Skoda of the year 1983/1984 [ Lel86 ] , but often wrongly attributed to Bedford–Taylor. The key result theorem 1.3.9 was claimed in Bedford–Taylor's work [ Theorem 2.3 , BT87 ] without proof. The first rigorous proof was given by El Marzguioui–Wiegerinck [ EMW06 ] . A weaker result was proved earlier in [ Theorem 4.8.7 , Kl91 ] . Results in 1.3.2 are certainly well-known and are already implicitly used in the literature. I could not find the proofs in the literature, so all details are presented. The semicontinuity theorem theorem 1.4.4 was due to Siu [ Siu74 ] . Multiplier ideal sheaves were introduced by Nadel [ Nad90 ] . The idea of theorem 1.4.15 first appeared in the ground-breaking work of Boucksom–Favre–Jonsson [ BFJ08 ] . The openness conjecture was formulated and studied by Demailly–Kollár [ DK01 ] and later proved by Berndtsson [ Bern13b ] . The strong openness theorem 1.4.16 was first established by Guan–Zhou [ GZ15 ] . 1.6.14 was due to [ Proposition 4.1.6 , Dem15 ] . The notions of positivity of currents definition 1.7.1 are due to Lelong [ Lel68 ] and Harvey–Knapp [ HK74 ] , although it is often mistakenly attributed to Demailly. The $L^2$ extension theorems such as theorem 1.4.19 were first studied by Ohsawa–Takegoshi [ OT87 ] . Since then, it has become a very active area. It is almost impossible to give a complete list of the various generalizations and improvements. chapter 2 The Monge–Ampère operators for bounded plurisubharmonic functions were introduced by Bedford–Taylor [ BT76 , BT82 ] . The non-pluripolar product was due to Bedford–Taylor [ BT87 ] , Guedj–Zeriahi [ GZ07 ] and Boucksom–Eyssidieux–Guedj–Zeriahi [ BEGZ10 ] . example 2.2.3 was claimed in [ BEGZ10 ] right after Definition 1.1 without proof. The first proof was essentially due to El Kadiri in [ EK24 ] . The semicontinuity theorem theorem 2.4.7 and the domination principle theorem 2.4.17 were due to [ DDNL18fullmass ] . The monotonicity theorem was due to [ WN19 , DDNL18mono ] . The key lemma 2.4.15 was proved in [ DDNLmetric ] . theorem 2.4.14 was due to [ DDNLsurv ] . chapter 3 3.1.3 was proved in [ Lemma 3.7 , DDNL18mono ] . The notion of the $P$-envelope is due to Ross–Witt Nyström [ RWN14 ] based on the ideas of Rashkovskii–Sigurdsson [ RS05 ] . theorem 3.1.7 is due to [ Theorem 3.8 , DDNL18mono ] . The diamond inequality theorem 3.1.18 and proposition 3.1.15 are due to [ Theorem 5.4 , DDNLmetric ] . Most results in 3.1.3 are simple generalizations of the corresponding results in [ DDNL18big , DDNL18fullmass ] . The study of finite energy potentials was initiated by Cegrell [ Ceg98 ] in the local setup; see also his general definition of the complex Monge–Ampère operator [ Ceg04 ] . The global setup was first studied by Guedj–Zeriahi [ GZ07 ] . The variational approach to degenerate complex Monge–Ampère equations in big cohomology classes was developed by Boucksom–Eyssidieux–Guedj–Zeriahi [ BEGZ10 ] and Berman–Boucksom–Guedj–Zeriahi [ BBGZ13 ] . For the complex Monge–Ampère equation and pluripotential methods for weak solutions, see Kołodziej [ Kol98 , Kol05 ] and the references therein. The $\mathcal{I}$-envelope was introduced by Darvas–Xia [ DX22 ] , inspired by the works of Dano Kim [ Kim15 ] and Boucksom–Favre–Jonsson [ BFJ08 ] . The notion of $\mathcal{I}$-model singularities was first formulated in the explicit way in [ DX22 ] in 2020, although it was already essentially known in Boucksom–Jonsson's work. In fact, they correspond exactly to the homogeneous non-Archimedean potentials assuming that the relevant masses do not vanish. A less explicit equivalent formulation of $\mathcal{I}$-model potentials also appeared in [ Dem15 ] . A few months later, the same notion was rediscovered by Trusiani [ Tru22 ] . theorem 2.4.24 is due to [ DNT21 ] . chapter 4 The study of geodesics in the space of Kähler metrics was initiated by Mabuchi [ Mab87 ] , Semmes [ Sem92 ] and Donaldson [ Don99 ] . The existence of geodesics with smooth boundary data was established by Chen [ Chen00 ] . The metric geometry and Mabuchi completion of finite-energy classes in the Kähler case were developed by Darvas [ Dar15 , Dar17 ] . The notion of weak geodesics was studied in detail by Darvas [ Da17 ] in the Kähler case. The case of general big classes was partly handled in [ DDNL18fullmass ] , [ DDNL18big ] . However, the key fact that the geodesics between two full mass potentials have the correct limit at the end points does not seem to have been proved in any references. We give a proof in proposition 4.2.4 . We also extend the relevant results to the relative setting. In the special case $\phi =V_\theta $, proposition 4.3.16 was proved in [ Theorem 3.12 , DDNL18fullmass ] , while the sequential case of proposition 4.3.17 was proved in [ Proposition 3.3 , DDNL18fullmass ] . Previously, proposition 4.2.6 and proposition 4.2.9 were only known in the Kähler case. Most results in section 4.3 are simple extensions of [ DDNL18big ] . chapter 5 Classical toric Kähler geometry is rooted in the works of Atiyah [ Ati82 ] , Delzant [ Del88 ] , Guillemin [ Gui94 ] , Abreu [ Abr98 ] and Donaldson [ Don02 ] . The pluripotential-theoretic toric framework used here was first written down by Berman–Berndtsson [ BB13 ] and Coman–Guedj–Sahin–Zeriahi [ CGSZ19 ] . The beautiful theorem theorem 5.2.14 was first proved by Yi Yao, who did not publish the result. Later on, a new proof was found by Botero–Burgos Gil–Holmes–de Jong [ BBGHdJ21 ] . We chose to present the approach of Yao, which integrates naturally with our framework. Proposition 5.2.19 is an extension of [ Proposition 2.9 , BB13 ] . chapter 6 The notion of $P$-preorder is new, as well as most results in section 6.1 . The $d_ S$-pseudometric was introduced in [ DDNLmetric ] . The basic properties are proved in [ DDNLmetric ] and [ Xia21 ] . example 6.1.14 was due to Berman–Boucksom–Jonsson [ BBJ21 ] . theorem 6.2.25 can be viewed as a vast generalization of [ Cao15 ] , where a question raised by Demailly was confirmed. theorem 6.2.29 is proved in [ Xia22 ] . theorem 6.2.31 and theorem 6.2.30 appear to be new. These results appeared previously in the form of lecture notes. chapter 7 The notion of $\mathcal{I}$-good singularities was due to [ DX21 ] . The name $\mathcal{I}$-good was chosen in [ Xia22 ] . The key results theorem 7.1.1 and theorem 7.4.2 are due to [ DX21 , DX22 ] . Previously, Rashkovskii [ Ra13 ] also studied the local approximation problem with a different motivation. There are some further examples of $\mathcal{I}$-good singularities provided by [ BBGHdJ21 ] with applications in the theory of modular forms in [ BBGHdJ22 ] . chapter 8 The trace operator was introduced in [ DX24 ] . Here we present a different point of view. theorem 8.4.1 was proved in [ DX24 ] . The analytic Bertini theorem theorem 8.5.1 was proved in [ XiaBer ] , based on the works of Matsumura–Fujino [ FM21 ] and Fujino [ Fuj23 ] . A weaker result was established by Meng–Zhou [ MZ23 ] . chapter 9 The technique of test curves originates from [ RWN14 ] . It was generalized by Darvas–Di Nezza–Lu [ DDNL18big ] , [ DX21 ] , [ DZ22 ] and [ DXZ23 ] . We give the full details of the proofs. Test curves in definition 9.1.1 are called maximal test curves in the literature, a terminology which I do not like. I prefer to call the usual notion of test curves in the literature sub-test curves . proposition 9.2.13 was first proved by He–Testorf–Wang in [ HTW23 ] . proposition 9.2.14 was due to Hisamoto [ His16 ] . 9.3.11 was a folklore result. I am unaware of any written proof in the literature before our paper [ DX22 ] . Finski [ Fin22b ] also gave a different proof with different techniques later on. definition 9.3.7 was not the original definition of maximal geodesic rays of Berman–Boucksom–Jonsson in [ BBJ21 ] . One of the first major applications of our theory was this pluripotential-theoretical characterization of maximal geodesic rays, as proved in our very first paper [ DX22 ] . example 9.3.9 is essentially due to Ross–Witt Nyström [ RWN14 ] . The Phong–Sturm geodesics were first constructed in [ PS07 ] . For the related link between test configurations, filtrations and Okounkov bodies, see Boucksom–Chen [ BC11 ] and Witt Nyström [ WN12 ] . For filtrations and generalized test configurations in K-stability, see Székelyhidi [ Sze15 ] . Results in section 9.4 are easy generalizations of the results proved in [ Xia23Operations ] . chapter 10 The algebraic theory of partial Okounkov bodies was developed in [ Xia21 ] . The transcendental Okounkov body was first defined by Deng [ Deng17 ] as suggested by Demailly. The volume identity was proved in [ DRWNXZ ] . The transcendental theory of partial Okounkov bodies is new. chapter 11 The notion of b-divisors was introduced by Shokurov [ Sho93 ] in the context of minimal model programs. The applications of b-divisors in pluripotential theory began with [ BFJ09 ] . The intersection theory of nef b-divisors was introduced by Dang–Favre [ DF20 ] . The technique of singularity b-divisors was introduced in [ XiaPPT ] in 2020. The general form first appeared in [ Xia22 ] . One year later, a special case was rediscovered in [ BBGHdJ21 ] . The current chapter reproduces a large part of [ Xiabdiv ] . For further developments, we refer to [ Xiabdiv2 ] . example 11.1.5 is reproduced from [ Example 3.3 , DF20 ] . chapter 12 The whole chapter appears to be new. The study of toric pluripotential theory on big line bundles was made possible by the development of partial Okounkov bodies. The key result is theorem 12.2.12 . Most results in this chapter resulted from discussions with Yi Yao. chapter 13 Most results in this chapter come from [ Xia23Operations ] . Results from section 13.3 are new, although the main idea was already contained in [ Xia21 ] . The terminology of Duistermaat–Heckman measures goes back to the classical theorem of Duistermaat–Heckman [ DH82 ] ; see also their addendum [ DH83 ] . In the setting of Kähler geometry, the Duistermaat–Heckman measures were studied in detail by Boucksom–Hisamoto–Jonsson [ BHJ17 ] . Foundational non-Archimedean global pluripotential theory was developed by Boucksom–Favre–Jonsson [ BFJ16b ] and, over a trivially valued field, by Boucksom–Jonsson [ BJ22 ] . theorem 13.4.24 is due to [ DXZ23 ] . An alternative approach to the transcendental theory is due to Mesquita-Piccione [ MP24 ] . For further progress in this direction, we refer to [ MPWN25 , WN25 ] . Special cases of the results in this section have been applied to study K-stability, see [ XiaPPT ] , [ DZ22 ] , [ DXZ23 ] and [ DR22 ] . In [ DX22 ] , we established the bijective correspondence between a class of $\mathcal{I}$-model test curves and the maximal geodesic rays in the sense of [ BBJ21 ] . chapter 14 The study of asymptotic expansions of Bergman kernels in Kähler geometry was initiated by Tian [ Ti90 ] with later improvements due to Bouché [ Bou90 ] , Ruan [ Rua98 ] , Catlin [ Cat99 ] , Zelditch [ Zel98 ] , Lu [ Lu00 ] among many others. The special case of theorem 14.3.7 without the prescribed singularity $\varphi $ was due to Berman–Boucksom–Witt Nyström, see [ BB10 ] , [ BBWN11 ] . The general case is due to [ DX21 ] .

title: Open problems
text: Open problems We give a list of important open problems in this theory. We do not repeat the conjectures mentioned in the main text. Conjecture 14.3.19 . Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold and $Y$ be a submanifold. Fix a Kähler class $\alpha $ on $X$. For each Kähler current $S\in \alpha |_ Y$, we can find a Kähler current $T\in \alpha $ such that \[  \operatorname{Tr}_ Y(T)\sim _{\mathcal{I}}S.  \] If we formally view $\operatorname{Tr}_ Y$ as an analogue of the trace operator in the theory of Sobolev spaces, then this conjecture corresponds exactly to the Dirichlet problem. Problem 14.3.20 . Is it possible to extend the definition of the trace operator $\operatorname{Tr}_ Y$ to the case where the ambient variety is only unibranch? The difficulty lies in the lack of Demailly type regularization theorems. Problem 14.3.21 . Is there a natural definition of the transcendental Okounkov body of a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ with $0$-mass so that its dimension is equal to the numerical dimension of $T$? See [ Cao14 ] for the definition of the numerical dimension of a current. The following two problems are proposed by Witt Nyström. Problem 14.3.22 . Consider a compact Kähler manifold $X$ and a connected submanifold $Y$. We have defined the trace operator $\operatorname{Tr}_ Y$ from a subset of $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)/\sim _\mathcal {I}$ to $\mathrm{QPSH}(Y)/\sim _\mathcal {I}$. Is it possible to refine this operator to one from a subset of $\mathrm{QPSH}(X)/\sim _ P$ to $\mathrm{QPSH}(Y)/\sim _ P$? Problem 14.3.23 . Consider a connected compact Kähler manifold $X$ of dimension $n$ and a smooth flag $Y_{\bullet }$ on $X$. Consider a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ representing a big cohomology class and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n>0$. Can one define a refined notion of partial Okounkov bodies $\Delta '_{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ contained in $\Delta _{Y_{\bullet }}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ with volume given by $\frac{1}{n!}\int _ X \theta _{\varphi }^ n$? Note that a satisfactory solution to the latter problem is not very likely, as can be easily seen from examples on $\mathbb {P}^1$. We also look for generalizations of our theory to more general settings. Problem 14.3.24 . To what extent can the results in the current book be generalized to the non-Kähler setting? The non-pluripolar products in the non-Kähler setting were recently studied by Boucksom–Guedj–Lu in [ BGL24 ] . See also the references therein. Problem 14.3.25 . To what extent can the results in the current book about closed positive $(1,1)$-currents be generalized to closed positive currents of higher bidegree? A fundamental issue is the lack of a strong enough Demailly type approximation for general currents. The regularization theorem of Dinh–Sibony [ DS04 ] seems too weak for our purposes.

title: A Convex functions and convex bodies
text: A Convex functions and convex bodies This appendix collects the basic facts about convex functions and convex bodies that are used throughout the book. Our standard reference is [ Roc70 ] . All results stated for convex functions apply equally to concave functions, after replacing the function by its negative.

title: A.1 The notion of convex functions
text:
A.1 The notion of convex functions Let $N$ be a real vector space of finite dimension. Definition A.1.1 . Let $F\colon Nightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a function. The epigraph of $F$ is defined as the following set \[  \operatorname{epi}F\coloneqq \left\{  (n,r)\in N	imes \mathbb {R}: r\geq F(n) ight\} .  \] Definition A.1.2 . A convex function on $N$ is a function $F\colon Nightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ such that the epigraph $\operatorname{epi}F$ is a convex subset of $N	imes \mathbb {R}$. The effective domain of $F$ is the set \[  \operatorname{Dom}F\coloneqq \left\{  n\in N : F(n)<\infty ight\} .  \] A convex function $F$ on $N$ such that $\operatorname{Dom}F
eq \varnothing $ and $F(n)
eq -\infty $ for all $n\in N$ is said to be proper . The set of convex functions on $N$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Conv}(N)$. The subset of proper convex functions is denoted by $\mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. The following characterization of convex functions is well-known. Lemma A.1.3 . Let $F\colon Nightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$. Then $F$ is convex if and only if the following condition holds: suppose that $n,r\in N$ and $a,b\in \mathbb {R}$ such that $a>F(n)$, $b>F(r)$, then for any $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  F(tn+(1-t)r)<ta+(1-t)b.  \] See [ Theorem 4.2 , Roc70 ] for the proof. Example A.1.4 . Let $A\subseteq N$ be a convex subset. Then the characteristic function $\chi _ A\colon Nightarrow \{ 0,\infty \} $ of $A$ is defined by \[  \chi _ A(n)\coloneqq \left\{   egin{aligned}  0,& \quad n\in A;\  \infty ,& \quad n
ot\in A. \end{aligned} ight.  \] The function $\chi _ A$ lies in $\mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Example A.1.5 . Let $M$ be the dual vector space of $N$ and $P\subseteq M$ be a convex subset. The support function $\operatorname{Supp}_ P\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ of $P$ is defined as follows: \[  \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)\coloneqq \sup \{  \langle m,n angle : m\in P \} .  \] It is well-known that convexity is preserved by a number of natural operations. We recall a few to fix the notation. Definition A.1.6 . Let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ m\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$ ($m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$). We define their infimal convolution $F_1 \square \cdots \square F_ m\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ as follows: \[  F_1 \square \cdots \square F_ m(n)\coloneqq \inf \left\{  \sum _{i=1}^ m F_ i(n_ i):n_ i\in N, \sum _{i=1}^ m n_ i=n ight\} .  \] The fact $F_1 \square \cdots \square F_ m\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ is proved in [ Theorem 5.4 , Roc70 ] . One should note that $F_1 \square \cdots \square F_ m$ is not always proper. Proposition A.1.7 . Let $\{ F_ i\} _{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Then $\sup _{i\in I} F_ i\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. This follows from [ Theorem 5.5 , Roc70 ] . In particular, this allows us to introduce Definition A.1.8 . Let $f\colon Nightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$. The lower convex envelope of $f$ is defined as \[  \operatorname{CE}f\coloneqq \sup \{ F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N): F\leq f \} .  \] It follows from proposition A.1.7 that $\operatorname{CE}f\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Definition A.1.9 . Given a non-empty family $\{ F_ i\} _{i\in I}$ in $\mathrm{Conv}(N)$, we define \[   igwedge _{i\in I}F_ i\coloneqq \operatorname{CE}\left(\inf _{i\in I} F_ iight).  \] When the family $I$ is finite, say $I=\{ 1,\ldots ,m\} $, we also write \[  F_1\land \cdots \land F_ m= igwedge _{i\in I}F_ i.  \] Definition A.1.10 . Given a non-empty family $\{ F_ i\} _{i\in I}$ in $\mathrm{Conv}(N)$, we define \[   igvee _{i\in I}F_ i\coloneqq \sup _{i\in I} F_ i.  \] When the family $I$ is finite, say $I=\{ 1,\ldots ,m\} $, we also write \[  F_1\lor \cdots \lor F_ m= igvee _{i\in I}F_ i.  \] Recall that $ igvee _{i\in I}F_ i\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ by proposition A.1.7 . Proposition A.1.11 . Let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ m\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then \[   egin{split}  F_1\land \cdots \land F_ m(x)=\inf \left\{ \sum _{i=1}^ m \lambda _ i F_ i(x_ i):x_ i\in \operatorname{Dom}(F_ i),ight.\  \left.\lambda _ i\in [0,1],\sum _{i=1}^ m\lambda _ i=1, \sum _{i=1}^ m\lambda _ i x_ i=x ight\} . \end{split}  \] See [ Theorem 5.6 , Roc70 ] for the more general result. Lemma A.1.12 . Let $\{ F_ i\} _{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Then $\inf _{i\in I} F_ i\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Proof. Write $F=\inf _{i\in I} F_ i$. We shall apply the characterization in A.1.3 . Take $n,r\in N$, $a,b\in \mathbb {R}$ such that $a>F(n)$, $b>F(r)$ and $t\in (0,1)$. We need to show that A.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:convtemp1} F(tn+(1-t)r)<ta+(1-t)b. \end{equation} By definition, there are $j_ n,j_ r\in I$ such that $a>F_ i(n)$ for $i\geq j_ n$ and $b>F_ i(r)$ for $i\geq j_ r$. Since $I$ is directed, we can find $j\in I$ dominating both $j_ n$ and $j_ r$, and then for any $i\geq j$, we have \[  a>F_ i(n),\quad b>F_ i(r).  \] It follows from A.1.3 that \[  F_ i(tn+(1-t)r)<ta+(1-t)b  \] for any $i\geq j$. Since $F_ i$ is decreasing in $i$, we conclude ( A.5 ). $\square$ Definition A.1.13 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. The closure $\operatorname{cl}F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ of $F$ is defined as follows: If $F(n)=-\infty $ for some $n\in N$, then $\operatorname{cl}F\coloneqq -\infty $. Otherwise, we define $\operatorname{cl}F$ as the lower semicontinuity regularization of $F$. A convex function $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ is closed if $F=\operatorname{cl}F$. In other words, $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ is closed if one of the following conditions holds: $F\equiv -\infty $; $F\equiv \infty $; $F$ is proper and lower semicontinuous. Proposition A.1.14 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ be a closed convex function. Then $F$ is the supremum of all affine functions lying below $F$. See [ Theorem 12.1 , Roc70 ] . Theorem A.1.15 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then $\operatorname{cl}F$ is a closed proper convex function. Moreover, $\operatorname{cl}F$ agrees with $F$ except possibly on the relative boundary of $\operatorname{Dom}F$. See [ Theorem 7.4 , Roc70 ] . Proposition A.1.16 . Let $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ be closed convex functions. Assume that $\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F=\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F'$, and $F=F'$ on $\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F$. Then $F=F'$. This is a special case of [ Corollary 7.3.4 , Roc70 ] . Definition A.1.17 . Given $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$, we write $F\preceq F'$ if there is $C\in \mathbb {R}$ such that \[  F\leq F'+C.  \] We say $F\sim F'$ if $F\preceq F'$ and $F'\preceq F$ both hold. Theorem A.1.18 . Let $C\subseteq N$ be an open subset. Let $(f_ i)_{i>0}$ be a sequence of real-valued convex functions on $C$. Suppose that the sequence converges on a dense subset of $C$ and the limit is finite. Then the limit \[  f(x)\coloneqq \lim _{i	o \infty } f_ i(x)  \] exists for all $x\in C$ and is convex on $C$. Moreover, the sequence $(f_ i)_ i$ converges uniformly to $f$ on each compact subset of $C$. This is a special case of [ Theorem 10.8 , Roc70 ] .

title: Definition A.1.1

title: Definition A.1.2
text: Definition A.1.2 . A convex function on $N$ is a function $F\colon N\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ such that the epigraph $\operatorname{epi}F$ is a convex subset of $N\times \mathbb {R}$. text: Lemma A.1.12 . Let $\{ F_ i\} _{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Then $\inf _{i\in I} F_ i\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Proof. Write $F=\inf _{i\in I} F_ i$. Since $I$ is directed, we can find $j\in I$ dominating both $j_ n$ and $j_ r$, and then for any $i\geq j$, we have \[  a>F_ i(n),\quad b>F_ i(r).  \] It follows from A.1.3 that \[  F_ i(tn+(1-t)r)<ta+(1-t)b  \] for any $i\geq j$. title: Definition A.1.13
text: Definition A.1.13 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. The closure $\operatorname{cl}F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ of $F$ is defined as follows: If $F(n)=-\infty $ for some $n\in N$, then $\operatorname{cl}F\coloneqq -\infty $. Otherwise, we define $\operatorname{cl}F$ as the lower semicontinuity regularization of $F$. A convex function $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ is closed if $F=\operatorname{cl}F$. In other words, $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ is closed if one of the following conditions holds: $F\equiv -\infty $; $F\equiv \infty $; $F$ is proper and lower semicontinuous.

title: Proposition A.1.14
text: Proposition A.1.14 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ be a closed convex function. Then $F$ is the supremum of all affine functions lying below $F$.

title: Theorem A.1.15
text: Theorem A.1.15 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then $\operatorname{cl}F$ is a closed proper convex function. Moreover, $\operatorname{cl}F$ agrees with $F$ except possibly on the relative boundary of $\operatorname{Dom}F$.

title: Proposition A.1.16
text: Proposition A.1.16 . Let $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ be closed convex functions. Assume that $\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F=\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F'$, and $F=F'$ on $\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F$. Then $F=F'$.

title: Definition A.1.17
text: Definition A.1.17 . Given $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$, we write $F\preceq F'$ if there is $C\in \mathbb {R}$ such that \[  F\leq F'+C.  \] We say $F\sim F'$ if $F\preceq F'$ and $F'\preceq F$ both hold.

title: Theorem A.1.18
text: Theorem A.1.18 . Let $C\subseteq N$ be an open subset. Let $(f_ i)_{i>0}$ be a sequence of real-valued convex functions on $C$. Suppose that the sequence converges on a dense subset of $C$ and the limit is finite. Then the limit \[  f(x)\coloneqq \lim _{i\to \infty } f_ i(x)  \] exists for all $x\in C$ and is convex on $C$. Moreover, the sequence $(f_ i)_ i$ converges uniformly to $f$ on each compact subset of $C$.

title: A.2 Legendre transform
text:
A.2 Legendre transform Let $N$ be a real vector space of finite dimension and $M$ be the dual vector space. The pairing $M	imes Nightarrow \mathbb {R}$ will be denoted by $\langle  ullet ,  ullet angle $. Definition A.2.1 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ be a convex function. We define the Legendre transform of $F$ as the function $F^*\in \mathrm{Conv}(M)$: A.6  egin{equation} \label{eq:Legtrandef} F^*(m)\coloneqq \sup _{n\in N} \left( \langle m,n angle -F(n) ight)=\sup _{n\in \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F} \left( \langle m,n angle -F(n) ight). \end{equation} The latter equality follows from [ Corollary 12.2.2 , Roc70 ] . Recall the well-known Legendre–Fenchel duality [ Theorem 12.2 , Roc70 ] . Theorem A.2.2 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Then $F^*$ is a closed convex function. The function $F^*$ is proper if and only if $F$ is. Moreover, we have $(\operatorname{cl}F)^*=F^*$ and \[  F^{**}=\operatorname{cl}F.  \] Example A.2.3 . Let $P\subseteq M$ be a closed convex subset. Then \[  \operatorname{Supp}_ P^*=\chi _ P,\quad \chi _ P^*=\operatorname{Supp}_ P.  \] See [ Theorem 13.2 , Roc70 ] . The following special case will be useful to us in the sequel. Corollary A.2.4 . Let $F\colon (0,\infty )ightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a convex function. If we define $G\colon \mathbb {R}ightarrow (-\infty ,\infty ]$ by \[  G(	au )=\sup _{t>0} \Bigl ( t	au -F(t) \Bigr ),  \] then $G$ is a convex function and A.7  egin{equation} \label{eq:Leginvpartdef} F(t)=G^*(t),\quad  orall t>0. \end{equation} Moreover, A.8  egin{equation} \label{eq:LegratQ} G(	au )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t	au -F(t) \Bigr )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t	au -F(t) \Bigr ). \end{equation} Proof. We distinguish two cases. First suppose that $F(t)=-\infty $ for some $t>0$. Then $F(t)=-\infty $ for all $t>0$ by the convexity of $F$. Our assertions are clear in this case. Next assume that $F(t)
eq -\infty $ for all $t>0$. In this case, theorem A.1.15 guarantees that $F$ admits a closed proper extension $	ilde{F}\in \mathrm{Conv}(\mathbb {R})$ with \[  	ilde{F}(t)=\infty ,\quad  orall t<0.  \] It follows from ( A.6 ) that \[  G(	au )=	ilde{F}^*(	au ),\quad  orall 	au \in \mathbb {R}.  \] Now theorem A.2.2 implies ( A.7 ). Finally ( A.8 ) follows from the continuity of $F$. $\square$ Proposition A.2.5 . Let $F\colon Nightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$. Define $F^*\colon Mightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ by \[  F^*(m)\coloneqq \sup _{n\in N} \left( \langle m,n angle -F(n) ight).  \] Then \[  F^*=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{CE}F)^*.  \] See [ Corollary 12.1.1 , Roc70 ] . Definition A.2.6 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ and $n\in N$. An element $m\in M$ is a subgradient (in the sense of Alexandrov) of $F$ at $n$ if A.9  egin{equation} \label{eq:subgrad} F(n')\geq F(n)+\langle n'-n,m angle ,\quad  orall n'\in N. \end{equation} The set of subgradients of $F$ at $n$ is denoted by $
abla F(n)$. More generally, for any subset $E\subseteq N$, we write \[  
abla F(E)= igcup _{n\in E}
abla F(n).  \] Definition A.2.7 . Given $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$, we write $F\preceq _ P F'$ if \[  \overline{
abla F(N)}\subseteq \overline{
abla F'(N)}.  \] We write $F\sim _ P F'$ if $F\preceq _ P F'$ and $F'\preceq _ P F$. Theorem A.2.8 . Suppose that $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then the following hold: For any $n
ot\in \operatorname{Dom}F$, $
abla F(n)=\varnothing $; for any $n\in \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F$, $
abla F(n)
eq \varnothing $; moreover, for any $n'\in N$, we have \[  \partial _{n'} F(n)=\sup \left\{ \langle n', m angle : m\in 
abla F(n)ight\} ;  \] for $n\in N$, the set $
abla F(n)$ is non-empty and bounded if and only if $n\in \operatorname{Int}\operatorname{Dom}F$. For the proof, we refer to [ Theorem 23.4 , Roc70 ] . Proposition A.2.9 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then \[  
abla F(N)\subseteq \operatorname{Dom}F^*.  \] If moreover $F$ is closed, we have A.10  egin{equation} \label{eq:relintdomFstar} \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F^*\subseteq 
abla F(N). \end{equation} In particular, if $F$ is a proper closed convex function on $N$, then \[  \overline{
abla F(N)}=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F^*}.  \] Proof. Suppose that $m\in 
abla F(n)$ for some $n\in N$. Then ( A.9 ) holds. In particular, \[  \langle m,n'angle -F(n')\leq \langle m,nangle -F(n).  \] It follows that \[  F^*(m)\leq \langle m,nangle -F(n)<\infty .  \] ( A.10 ) is proved in [ Corollary 23.5.1 , Roc70 ] . For the last assertion, it suffices to observe that $\overline{\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F^*}=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F^*}$. $\square$ Proposition A.2.10 . Let $\{ F_ i\} _{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then \[  \left( igwedge _{i\in I} F_ iight)^*= igvee _{i\in I} F_ i^*,\quad \left( igvee _{i\in I} \operatorname{cl}F_ iight)^*=\operatorname{cl} igwedge _{i\in I} F_ i^*.  \] If $I$ is finite and $\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F_ i}$ is independent of the choice of $i\in I$, then \[  \left( igvee _{i\in I} F_ iight)^*= igwedge _{i\in I} F_ i^*.  \] Recall that $\wedge $ is defined in definition A.1.9 and $\lor $ in definition A.1.10 . See [ Theorem 16.5 , Roc70 ] for the proof. Proposition A.2.11 . Let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ r\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$ ($r\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$). Assume that \[   igcap _{i=1}^ r\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}(F_ i)
eq \varnothing ,  \] then for any $m\in M$, \[  \left( \sum _{i=1}^ r F_ i ight)^*(m)=\inf \left\{ \sum _{i=1}^ r F_ i^*(m_ i):m_1,\ldots ,m_ r\in M, \sum _{i=1}^ r m_ i=m ight\} .  \] See [ Theorem 16.4 , Roc70 ] for the proof. Proposition A.2.12 . Let $P\subseteq M$ be a convex body Note. Here a convex body refers to a non-empty compact convex subset, not necessarily having non-empty interior. and $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. The following are equivalent: $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$; $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ and $F^*|_{M\setminus P}\equiv \infty $; $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ and $
abla F(N)\subseteq P$. Moreover, under these conditions, A.11  egin{equation} \label{eq:Fsupequal} F(n)-\operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)\leq F(0),\quad  orall n\in N. \end{equation} Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . It is clear that $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ since $\operatorname{Dom}\operatorname{Supp}_ P=N$. From $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ and example A.2.3 , we know that \[  \chi _ P=\operatorname{Supp}_ P^*\preceq F^*.  \] So 2 follows. 2 $\implies $ 3 . This follows from proposition A.2.9 . 3 $\implies $ 1 . The function $t\mapsto F(tn)$ is convex on $[0,1]$, hence absolutely continuous and differentiable almost everywhere. For almost every $t\in (0,1)$, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}F(tn)=\partial _ n F(tn) \leq \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)  \] by theorem A.2.8 and the assumption $
abla F(N)\subseteq P$. Integrating in $t$ gives \[  F(n)-F(0)\leq \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n).  \] In particular, ( A.11 ) also follows. $\square$

title: Definition A.2.1
text: Definition A.2.1 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ be a convex function. We define the Legendre transform of $F$ as the function $F^*\in \mathrm{Conv}(M)$: A.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Legtrandef} F^*(m)\coloneqq \sup _{n\in N} \left( \langle m,n \rangle -F(n) \right)=\sup _{n\in \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F} \left( \langle m,n \rangle -F(n) \right). \end{equation}

title: A.6
text: A.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Legtrandef} F^*(m)\coloneqq \sup _{n\in N} \left( \langle m,n \rangle -F(n) \right)=\sup _{n\in \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F} \left( \langle m,n \rangle -F(n) \right). \end{equation}

title: Theorem A.2.2
text: Theorem A.2.2 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$. Then $F^*$ is a closed convex function. The function $F^*$ is proper if and only if $F$ is. Moreover, we have $(\operatorname{cl}F)^*=F^*$ and \[  F^{**}=\operatorname{cl}F.  \]

title: Example A.2.3
text: Example A.2.3 . Let $P\subseteq M$ be a closed convex subset. Then \[  \operatorname{Supp}_ P^*=\chi _ P,\quad \chi _ P^*=\operatorname{Supp}_ P.  \] See [ Theorem 13.2 , Roc70 ] .

title: Corollary A.2.4
text: Corollary A.2.4 . Let $F\colon (0,\infty )\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a convex function. If we define $G\colon \mathbb {R}\rightarrow (-\infty ,\infty ]$ by \[  G(\tau )=\sup _{t>0} \Bigl ( t\tau -F(t) \Bigr ),  \] then $G$ is a convex function and A.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Leginvpartdef} F(t)=G^*(t),\quad \forall t>0. \end{equation} Moreover, A.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:LegratQ} G(\tau )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t\tau -F(t) \Bigr )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t\tau -F(t) \Bigr ). \end{equation} Proof. We distinguish two cases. First suppose that $F(t)=-\infty $ for some $t>0$. Then $F(t)=-\infty $ for all $t>0$ by the convexity of $F$. Our assertions are clear in this case. Next assume that $F(t)\neq -\infty $ for all $t>0$. In this case, theorem A.1.15 guarantees that $F$ admits a closed proper extension $\tilde{F}\in \mathrm{Conv}(\mathbb {R})$ with \[  \tilde{F}(t)=\infty ,\quad \forall t<0.  \] It follows from ( A.6 ) that \[  G(\tau )=\tilde{F}^*(\tau ),\quad \forall \tau \in \mathbb {R}.  \] Now theorem A.2.2 implies ( A.7 ). Finally ( A.8 ) follows from the continuity of $F$. $\square$

title: A.7
text: A.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Leginvpartdef} F(t)=G^*(t),\quad \forall t>0. \end{equation}

title: A.8
text: A.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:LegratQ} G(\tau )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {R}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t\tau -F(t) \Bigr )=\sup _{t\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}} \Bigl ( t\tau -F(t) \Bigr ). \end{equation}

title: Proposition A.2.5
text: Proposition A.2.5 . Let $F\colon N\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$. Define $F^*\colon M\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty ]$ by \[  F^*(m)\coloneqq \sup _{n\in N} \left( \langle m,n \rangle -F(n) \right).  \] Then \[  F^*=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{CE}F)^*.  \]

title: Definition A.2.6
text:
Definition A.2.6 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ and $n\in N$. An element $m\in M$ is a subgradient (in the sense of Alexandrov) of $F$ at $n$ if A.9  egin{equation} \label{eq:subgrad} F(n')\geq F(n)+\langle n'-n,m angle ,\quad  orall n'\in N. \end{equation} The set of subgradients of $F$ at $n$ is denoted by $
abla F(n)$. More generally, for any subset $E\subseteq N$, we write \[  
abla F(E)= igcup _{n\in E}
abla F(n).  \]

title: A.9
text: A.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:subgrad} F(n')\geq F(n)+\langle n'-n,m \rangle ,\quad \forall n'\in N. \end{equation}

title: Definition A.2.7
text: Definition A.2.7 . Given $F,F'\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$, we write $F\preceq _ P F'$ if \[  \overline{\nabla F(N)}\subseteq \overline{\nabla F'(N)}.  \] We write $F\sim _ P F'$ if $F\preceq _ P F'$ and $F'\preceq _ P F$.

title: Theorem A.2.8
text:
Theorem A.2.8 . Suppose that $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then the following hold: For any $n
ot\in \operatorname{Dom}F$, $
abla F(n)=\varnothing $; for any $n\in \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F$, $
abla F(n)
eq \varnothing $; moreover, for any $n'\in N$, we have \[  \partial _{n'} F(n)=\sup \left\{ \langle n', m angle : m\in 
abla F(n)ight\} ;  \] for $n\in N$, the set $
abla F(n)$ is non-empty and bounded if and only if $n\in \operatorname{Int}\operatorname{Dom}F$.

title: Proposition A.2.9
text:
Proposition A.2.9 . Let $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then \[  
abla F(N)\subseteq \operatorname{Dom}F^*.  \] If moreover $F$ is closed, we have A.10  egin{equation} \label{eq:relintdomFstar} \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F^*\subseteq 
abla F(N). \end{equation} In particular, if $F$ is a proper closed convex function on $N$, then \[  \overline{
abla F(N)}=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F^*}.  \] Proof. Suppose that $m\in 
abla F(n)$ for some $n\in N$. Then ( A.9 ) holds. In particular, \[  \langle m,n'angle -F(n')\leq \langle m,nangle -F(n).  \] It follows that \[  F^*(m)\leq \langle m,nangle -F(n)<\infty .  \] ( A.10 ) is proved in [ Corollary 23.5.1 , Roc70 ] . For the last assertion, it suffices to observe that $\overline{\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F^*}=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F^*}$. $\square$

title: A.10
text: A.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relintdomFstar} \operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}F^*\subseteq \nabla F(N). \end{equation}

title: Proposition A.2.10
text: Proposition A.2.10 . Let $\{ F_ i\} _{i\in I}$ be a non-empty family in $\mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. Then \[  \left(\bigwedge _{i\in I} F_ i\right)^*=\bigvee _{i\in I} F_ i^*,\quad \left(\bigvee _{i\in I} \operatorname{cl}F_ i\right)^*=\operatorname{cl}\bigwedge _{i\in I} F_ i^*.  \] If $I$ is finite and $\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F_ i}$ is independent of the choice of $i\in I$, then \[  \left(\bigvee _{i\in I} F_ i\right)^*=\bigwedge _{i\in I} F_ i^*.  \]

title: Proposition A.2.11
text: Proposition A.2.11 . Let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ r\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$ ($r\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$). Assume that \[  \bigcap _{i=1}^ r\operatorname{RelInt}\operatorname{Dom}(F_ i)\neq \varnothing ,  \] then for any $m\in M$, \[  \left( \sum _{i=1}^ r F_ i \right)^*(m)=\inf \left\{ \sum _{i=1}^ r F_ i^*(m_ i):m_1,\ldots ,m_ r\in M, \sum _{i=1}^ r m_ i=m \right\} .  \]

title: Proposition A.2.12
text: Proposition A.2.12 . Let $P\subseteq M$ be a convex body Note. Here a convex body refers to a non-empty compact convex subset, not necessarily having non-empty interior. and $F\in \mathrm{Conv}^{\mathrm{prop}}(N)$. The following are equivalent: $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$; $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ and $F^*|_{M\setminus P}\equiv \infty $; $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ and $\nabla F(N)\subseteq P$. Moreover, under these conditions, A.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Fsupequal} F(n)-\operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)\leq F(0),\quad \forall n\in N. \end{equation} Proof. 1 $\implies $ 2 . It is clear that $\operatorname{Dom}F=N$ since $\operatorname{Dom}\operatorname{Supp}_ P=N$. From $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ and example A.2.3 , we know that \[  \chi _ P=\operatorname{Supp}_ P^*\preceq F^*.  \] So 2 follows. 2 $\implies $ 3 . This follows from proposition A.2.9 . 3 $\implies $ 1 . The function $t\mapsto F(tn)$ is convex on $[0,1]$, hence absolutely continuous and differentiable almost everywhere. For almost every $t\in (0,1)$, \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}F(tn)=\partial _ n F(tn) \leq \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)  \] by theorem A.2.8 and the assumption $\nabla F(N)\subseteq P$. Integrating in $t$ gives \[  F(n)-F(0)\leq \operatorname{Supp}_ P(n).  \] In particular, ( A.11 ) also follows. $\square$

title: A.11
text: A.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Fsupequal} F(n)-\operatorname{Supp}_ P(n)\leq F(0),\quad \forall n\in N. \end{equation}

title: A.3 Classes of convex functions
Definition A.3.1
text: Definition A.3.1 . We define the set $\mathcal{P}(N,P)$ as the set of proper convex functions $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ such that $F\preceq \operatorname{Supp}_ P$. We define the set $\mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)$ as the set of closed convex functions $F\in \mathrm{Conv}(N)$ such that $F\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P$. We define the set $\mathcal{E}(N,P)$ as follows: Suppose that $\operatorname{Int}P=\varnothing $. Then $\mathcal{E}(N,P)\coloneqq \mathcal{P}(N,P)$; otherwise, let \[  \mathcal{E}(N,P)=\left\{ F\in \mathcal{P}(N,P) : P=\overline{\nabla F(N)} \right\} .  \] We define the set $\mathcal{E}^1(N,P)$ as the subset of $\mathcal{E}(N,P)$ consisting of $F\in \mathcal{E}(N,P)$ with \[  \int _ P F^*\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}<\infty ,  \] where $\mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}$ is any Lebesgue measure on $M$.

title: Proposition A.3.2
text:
Proposition A.3.2 . We have \[  \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)\subseteq \mathcal{E}^{1}(N,P)\subseteq \mathcal{E}(N,P) \subseteq \mathcal{P}(N,P).  \] Proof. When $\operatorname{Int}P=\varnothing $, the assertion is clear. We assume that $\operatorname{Int}P
eq \varnothing $. The second inclusion follows from the definition. We only handle the first inequality. Take $F\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)$. By definition, $F\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P$ and hence $F^*\sim \chi _ P$. It follows that $P=\operatorname{Dom}F^*$. By proposition A.2.12 , we already know that \[  
abla F(N)\subseteq P=\operatorname{Dom}F^*.  \] On the other hand, by proposition A.2.9 , we have \[  \operatorname{Int}P\subseteq 
abla F(N).  \] So it follows that \[  P=\overline{
abla F(N)}.  \] It is clear that $F^*\sim \chi _ P$ is integrable. $\square$

title: Proposition A.3.3
text: Proposition A.3.3 . For any $F\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)$, we have $F^*|_{M\setminus P}\equiv \infty $ and $F^*$ is bounded on $P$. Proof. From $F\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P$, we take the Legendre transform to get $F^*\sim \operatorname{Supp}_ P^*=\chi _ P$, where we applied example A.2.3 . $\square$

title: Definition A.3.4
text: Definition A.3.4 . We endow the topology of pointwise convergence on $\mathcal{P}(N,P)$.

title: Proposition A.3.5
text: Proposition A.3.5 . Let $F\in \mathcal{P}(N,P)$. Then there is a decreasing sequence $F_ j\in \mathcal{E}^{\infty }(N,P)\cap C^{\infty }(N)$ converging to $F$.

title: Proposition A.3.6
text: Proposition A.3.6 . For any $F\in \mathcal{P}(N,P)$, we have \[  \max _{N}(F-\operatorname{Supp}_ P)=F(0).  \] Proof. It follows from ( A.11 ) that \[  \sup _{N}(F-\operatorname{Supp}_ P)\leq F(0).  \] The equality is clearly obtained at $0\in N$. $\square$

title: Lemma A.3.7
A.12
text: A.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:overlineDom_temp1} \overline{\operatorname{Dom}(F+F')^*}=\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F^*}+\overline{\operatorname{Dom}F'{}^*}. \end{equation}

title: A.4 Monge–Ampère measures
Definition A.4.1
text: Definition A.4.1 . Let $F$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb {R}}$. We define the real Monge–Ampère measure $\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F$ as the Alexandrov measure on $N_{\mathbb {R}}$ given as follows: for each Borel measurable set $E\subseteq N_{\mathbb {R}}$, define A.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:MARFE} \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F(E)\coloneqq n!\int _{\nabla F(E)} \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}. \end{equation} The measurability and countable additivity in this definition are standard properties of the subgradient map; see for example [ Section 2.1 , Fig17 ] .

title: A.13
text: A.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:MARFE} \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F(E)\coloneqq n!\int _{\nabla F(E)} \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}. \end{equation}

title: Proposition A.4.2
text: Proposition A.4.2 . Suppose that $F\in C^{1,1}(N_{\mathbb {R}})\cap \mathrm{Conv}(N_{\mathbb {R}})$. Fix an identification $N=\mathbb {Z}^ n$. Then \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F=n!\cdot \det \nabla ^2 F \, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}.  \]

title: Proposition A.4.3
A.14
text: A.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cvxfullmass} \int _{N_{\mathbb {R}}}\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}F=n! \operatorname{vol}P. \end{equation}

title: Theorem A.4.4
text: Theorem A.4.4 . Let $F,F_ j\in \mathcal{P}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P)$ ($j\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$). Assume that $F_ j\to F$. Then \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}(F_ j)\rightharpoonup \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb {R}}(F)  \] weakly.

title: Theorem A.4.5
Lemma A.4.6
text:
Lemma A.4.6 . Let $F\in \mathcal{E}(N_{\mathbb {R}},P)$ and set $G=F^*$. Then the map $
abla G$ pushes forward $n!\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}|_{P}$ to $\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$. Equivalently, for every bounded Borel function $h$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  \int _{N_{\mathbb R}} h\, \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)= n!\int _ P h(
abla G(m))\, \mathrm{d}\operatorname{vol}(m).  \] Proof. If $\operatorname{vol}P=0$, the assertion is clear from proposition A.2.12 and the definition of $\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}$. We may therefore assume that $P$ has non-empty interior. Since $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$, we have $\operatorname{Dom}G\subseteq P$ by proposition A.2.12 . On the other hand, by the definition of $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and proposition A.2.9 , \[  P=\overline{
abla F(N_{\mathbb R})}\subseteq \overline{\operatorname{Dom}G}.  \] Hence $\overline{\operatorname{Dom}G}=P$. Since $\operatorname{Dom}G$ is convex, $G$ is finite on $\operatorname{Int}P$ and is equal to $\infty $ outside $P$. Let $D$ be the set of points in $\operatorname{Int}P$ at which $G$ is differentiable. By [ Theorem 25.5 , Roc70 ] , $P\setminus D$ has measure zero. By [ Theorem 23.5 , Roc70 ] , $m\in 
abla F(n)$ if and only if $n\in 
abla G(m)$. Hence for any Borel set $E\subseteq N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  \{ m\in D:
abla G(m)\in E\} =D\cap 
abla F(E).  \] It follows from definition A.4.1 that \[  n!\operatorname{vol}\{ m\in P:
abla G(m)\in E\} =n!\operatorname{vol}

title: Theorem A.4.7
text: Theorem A.4.7 . There is a symmetric map assigning to every $n$-tuple of finite convex functions $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ a positive Radon measure \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)  \] on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with the following properties: For every $q\in \mathbb Z_{>0}$, finite convex functions $F_1,\ldots ,F_ q$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ q\geq 0$, \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(\lambda _1F_1+\cdots +\lambda _ qF_ q) =\sum _{i_1,\ldots ,i_ n=1}^ q \lambda _{i_1}\cdots \lambda _{i_ n} \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_{i_1},\ldots ,F_{i_ n}).  \] For every finite convex function $F$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F,\ldots ,F)=\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F).  \] The map $\operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}$ is additive and positively homogeneous of degree $1$ in each entry. In other words, for finite convex functions $F,G,F_2,\ldots ,F_ n$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ and $\lambda ,\mu \geq 0$, \[  \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(\lambda F+\mu G,F_2,\ldots ,F_ n) =\lambda \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(F,F_2,\ldots ,F_ n) +\mu \operatorname{MA}_{\mathbb R}(G,F_2,\ldots ,F_ n).  \]

title: A.5 Several lemmata
text: A.5 Several lemmata Lemma A.5.1 . Let $\alpha ,\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m\in \mathbb {Z}^ n$. Let $\Delta $ be the polytope generated by $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m$. Then the following are equivalent: A.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:zalpha} |z^{\alpha }|^2\left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1} \end{equation} is a bounded function on $\mathbb {C}^{*n}$. $\alpha \in \Delta $. Proof. 2 $\implies $ 1 . Write $\alpha =\sum _ i t_ i\beta _ i$, where $t_ i\in [0,1]$, $\sum _ i t_ i=1$. Then \[  \begin{aligned}  |z^{\alpha }|^2\left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1} & =\prod _ i |z^{\beta _ i}|^{2t_ i}\left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1}\\ & \leq \prod _ i\left(\sum _{j=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ j}|^2\right)^{t_ i} \left(\sum _{i=1}^ m |z^{\beta _ i}|^2 \right)^{-1}=1. \end{aligned}  \] 1 $\implies $ 2 . Assume that $\alpha \not\in \Delta $. By the strict separation theorem, there is $a=(a_1,\ldots ,a_ n)\in \mathbb {R}^ n$ such that \[  a\cdot \alpha >\max _ i a\cdot \beta _ i.  \] Set \[  z(t)\coloneqq (t^{a_1},\ldots ,t^{a_ n}).  \] Then ( A.15 ) evaluated at $z(t)$ grows like \[  \frac{t^{2a\cdot \alpha }}{\sum _ i t^{2a\cdot \beta _ i}}  \] as $t\to \infty $, and hence is not bounded. $\square$ Lemma A.5.2 . Let $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m\in \mathbb {N}^ n$ and $\beta \in \mathbb {R}^ n$. Then the following are equivalent: $\log \sum _{i=1}^ m \mathrm{e}^{x\cdot \beta _ i}-x\cdot \beta $ is bounded from below. $\beta $ is in the convex hull of the $\beta _ i$'s. Proof. If $\beta =\sum _ i t_ i\beta _ i$ with $t_ i\in [0,1]$ and $\sum _ i t_ i=1$, then by the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, \[  x\cdot \beta =\sum _ i t_ i\, x\cdot \beta _ i \leq \log \sum _ i t_ i\mathrm{e}^{x\cdot \beta _ i} \leq \log \sum _ i \mathrm{e}^{x\cdot \beta _ i}.  \] This proves that the function in 1 is bounded from below. Conversely, if $\beta $ does not lie in the convex hull of the $\beta _ i$'s, choose $a\in \mathbb {R}^ n$ such that \[  a\cdot \beta >\max _ i a\cdot \beta _ i.  \] Evaluating at $x=ta$ and letting $t\to \infty $, we find \[  \log \sum _ i \mathrm{e}^{t a\cdot \beta _ i}-t\, a\cdot \beta \to -\infty ,  \] contradicting 1 . $\square$ Lemma A.5.3 . Let $I\subseteq \mathbb {R}$ be an open interval containing $0$. Let $(f_ k\colon I\rightarrow \mathbb {R})_{k\geq 1}$ be a sequence of convex functions, and let $g\colon I\to \mathbb {R}$ be a function. Assume that \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } f_ k(t)\leq g(t)\quad \text{for every } t\in I,  \] and that \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } f_ k(0)=g(0).  \] If each $f_ k$ and $g$ is differentiable at $0$, then \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)=g'(0).  \] Proof. Since $f_ k$ is convex and differentiable at $0$, for every $t\in I$, \[  f_ k(t)\geq f_ k(0)+t f_ k'(0).  \] Taking the upper limit as $k\to \infty $ and using the assumptions gives \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } t f_ k'(0) \leq g(t)-g(0).  \] For $t>0$, this yields \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0) \leq \frac{g(t)-g(0)}{t}.  \] Letting $t\to 0+$ and using the differentiability of $g$ at $0$, we get \[  \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)\leq g'(0).  \] For $t<0$, the same inequality gives \[  \varliminf _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0) \geq \frac{g(t)-g(0)}{t}.  \] Letting $t\to 0-$ and again using the differentiability of $g$ at $0$, we obtain \[  \varliminf _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)\geq g'(0).  \] Therefore \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } f_ k'(0)=g'(0),  \] as claimed. $\square$

title: B Pluripotential theory on unibranch spaces
text: B Pluripotential theory on unibranch spaces This appendix explains how much of the pluripotential theory developed in the body of the book extends from compact Kähler manifolds to compact unibranch Kähler spaces. The unibranch hypothesis is the natural generality in which plurisubharmonic functions descend through resolutions and the basic envelope formalism remains meaningful. Some constructions, especially the trace operator of chapter 8 , require extra care in the singular setting; we record here the precise statements needed in the main text.

title: B.1 Complex spaces
text: B.1 Complex spaces A complex space is assumed to be reduced, Hausdorff and paracompact in the whole book. Definition B.1.1 . A prime divisor over an irreducible complex space $Z$ is a connected smooth hypersurface $E\subseteq X'$, where $X'\rightarrow Z$ is a proper bimeromorphic morphism with $X'$ smooth. Such a morphism $X'\rightarrow Z$ is also called a resolution of $Z$. The center of the prime divisor is defined as the image of $E$ in $Z$. Two prime divisors $E_1\subseteq X'_1$ and $E_2\subseteq X'_2$ over $Z$ are equivalent if there is a common resolution $X''\rightarrow Z$ dominating both $X_1'$ and $X_2'$ such that the strict transforms of $E_1$ and $E_2$ coincide. The set $Z^{\operatorname{div}}$ is the set of pairs $(c,E)$, where $c\in \mathbb {Q}_{>0}$ and $E$ is an equivalence class of a prime divisor over $Z$. For simplicity, we will denote the pair $(c,E)$ by $c\operatorname{ord}_ E$, although one should not really think of this object as a valuation unless $Z$ is projective and irreducible. Note that a prime divisor on $Z$ does not always define a prime divisor over $Z$ if $Z$ is singular. Definition B.1.2 . A complex space $X$ is unibranch if for all $x\in X$, the local ring $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ is unibranch. See [ Tag 0BPZ , stacks-project ] for the notion of unibranch local rings. In [ CAS ] , the same notion is known as local irreducibility . We prefer the name unibranchness , because the corresponding terminology in algebraic geometry is standard and goes back to Grothendieck [ (0.23.2.1) , EGAIV1 ] . The notion of unibranchness coincides with the usual one when $\mathcal{X}$ is an algebraic variety: Proposition B.1.3 . Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a reduced scheme of finite type over $\mathbb {C}$, and let $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}$ be the associated complex space. Then $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}$ is unibranch in the sense above if and only if $\mathcal{X}$ is unibranch in the algebraic sense (see [ Tag 0BQ2 , stacks-project ] ). This is [ Remark 2.7 , Xia23Mabuchi ] in the arXiv version. Proof. Let $x\in \mathcal{X}(\mathbb {C})$. Then we claim that $\mathcal{X}$ is unibranch at $x$ if and only if $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}$ is unibranch at $x$. By GAGA, there is a natural morphism of ringed spaces $(\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}},\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}}})\rightarrow (\mathcal{X},\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}})$. Then since $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X},x}$ is excellent, $\mathcal{X}$ is unibranch at $x$ if and only if $\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X},x}}=\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}},x}}$ is integral ( [ Théorème 18.9.1 , EGAIV4 ] ). The latter implies that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}},x}$ is unibranch by [ Chapitre 5, Exercise 2.8 , AC ] . Running the same argument the other way round, we conclude that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X},x}$ is unibranch if and only if $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{An}},x}$ is. $\square$ Theorem B.1.4 (Zariski's main theorem) . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism between complex spaces. Assume that $X$ is unibranch. Then $\pi $ has connected fibers. We follow [ Proof of Théorème 1.7 , Dem85 ] . Proof. Let $Z\subseteq X$ be the smallest nowhere dense analytic subset such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus Z$. Assume that the fiber $F=\pi ^{-1}(x)$ over some $x\in X$ is disconnected. Since $\pi $ is proper, $F$ is compact. Choose a decomposition $F=F_1\sqcup F_2$ into two non-empty disjoint compact open subsets of $F$, and choose disjoint open neighborhoods $W_1,W_2$ of $F_1,F_2$ in $Y$. Since proper maps are closed, after shrinking an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, we may assume that \[  \pi ^{-1}(U)\subseteq W_1\cup W_2.  \] Thus $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ is disconnected. Since $X$ is unibranch, we may shrink $U$ further so that $U$ is irreducible. Then $U\setminus Z$ is connected (cf. [ Chapter 9, §1.2 , CAS ] ). Since $\pi $ is bimeromorphic, every irreducible component of $Y$ maps onto an irreducible component of $X$. Hence $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$ contains no irreducible component of $Y$ and is nowhere dense. On the other hand, write \[  \pi ^{-1}(U)=V_1\sqcup V_2  \] as a union of two non-empty disjoint open subsets. Each $V_ i$ meets $\pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)$: otherwise $V_ i$ would be a non-empty open subset of $Y$ contained in the nowhere dense analytic subset $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$, which is impossible. Hence \[  \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z) = \bigl (V_1\cap \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)\bigr ) \sqcup \bigl (V_2\cap \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)\bigr )  \] is disconnected. This contradicts the fact that $\pi \colon \pi ^{-1}(U\setminus Z)\rightarrow U\setminus Z$ is an isomorphism and $U\setminus Z$ is connected. $\square$ Definition B.1.5 . A modification of a compact complex space $X$ is a finite composition of blow-ups with smooth centers. We say a modification $\pi '\colon Z\rightarrow X$ dominates another $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ if there is a morphism $g\colon Z\rightarrow Y$ of complex spaces making the following diagram commutative: B.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:domi} \gerbyimage{sgpt/e990208a4c04572f2ffe.svg}{Mathematical diagram from the source} \end{equation} The modifications of $X$ together with the domination relation form a directed set. Theorem B.1.6 (Hironaka's Chow lemma) . Suppose that $X$ is a compact complex space. Then every proper bimeromorphic morphism to $X$ can be dominated by a modification. This follows from the proof of [ Corollary 2 , Hir75 ] . Theorem B.1.7 . Let $X$ be a compact complex space. Then there is a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $Y$ is smooth. See [ BM97 , Wlo09 ] . Corollary B.1.8 . Let $X$ be an irreducible compact complex space and $E$ be a prime divisor over $X$. Then there is a modification $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ such that $Y$ is smooth and $E$ can be realized as a prime divisor on $Y$. Proof. Choose a smooth model $X'\rightarrow X$ on which $E$ is realized. By theorem B.1.6 , this proper bimeromorphic morphism is dominated by a modification $Y\rightarrow X$. After further resolving the pair if necessary, we may assume that $Y$ is smooth and that the strict transform of $E$ on $Y$ is smooth. This strict transform realizes the same prime divisor over $X$. $\square$

title: B.2 Plurisubharmonic functions
text:
B.2 Plurisubharmonic functions Let $X$ be a complex space. Definition B.2.1 . A function $\varphi \colon Xightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is plurisubharmonic if $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $ on any irreducible component of $X$, and for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $X$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ N$, a closed immersion $V\hookrightarrow \Omega $ and a plurisubharmonic function $	ilde{\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ such that $\varphi |_ V=	ilde{\varphi }|_ V$ under this immersion. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Similarly, if $	heta $ is a smooth closed Note. Here closed means that locally $	heta $ is defined by a closed form under a local embedding. real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, then a function $\varphi \colon Xightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic if for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $X$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ N$, a closed immersion $V\hookrightarrow \Omega $ and a smooth function $g$ on $\Omega $ such that $	heta =(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)|_ V$ and $g|_ V+\varphi |_ V\in \mathrm{PSH}(V)$. Theorem B.2.2 (Fornaess–Narasimhan) . Let $\varphi \colon Xightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function. Assume that $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $ on any irreducible component of $X$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi $ is psh; $\varphi $ is usc and for any morphism $f\colon \Delta ightarrow X$ from the open unit disk $\Delta $ in $\mathbb {C}$ to $X$ such that $f^*\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $, the pull-back $f^*\varphi $ is subharmonic. See [ FN80 ] . Theorem B.2.3 (Grauert–Remmert) . Let $X$ be a unibranch Note. Unibranchness is very important here. Otherwise, consider the case where $X$ is the union of two copies of $\mathbb {C}$ intersecting only at their origins, $Z$ is the common origin. If we set $\varphi \equiv 0$ on one punctured plane and $\varphi \equiv 1$ on the other, then it is clear that $\varphi $ cannot be extended to $X$. This leads to a few misleading statements in the modern literature. The problem is that in the early German literature, komplexer Raum is assumed to be either normal or unibranch! complex space, let $Z$ be an analytic subset in $X$, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X\setminus Z)$. Then the function $\varphi $ admits an extension to $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ in the following two cases: The set $Z$ has codimension at least $2$ everywhere. The set $Z$ has codimension at least $1$ everywhere and $\varphi $ is locally bounded from above on an open neighborhood of $Z$. In both cases, the extension is unique and is given by B.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:GRextvarphi} \varphi (x)=\varlimsup _{X\setminus Z
i y	o x}\varphi (y),\quad x\in X. \end{equation} The proof given below combines [ Théorème 1.7 , Dem85 ] and [ GR56 ] . Note. This theorem has a quite entangled history. The corresponding results for subharmonic functions are generally attributed to Brelot. In [ GR56 ] , they cited a paper of Brelot written in 1934, which I cannot find. But in 1949, on the very first issue of Annales de l'Institut Fourier , Brelot published a paper [ Bre49 ] with a very similar title, studying the behavior of a subharmonic function on the punctured neighborhood of a point. The general theorem was due to Grauert and Remmert, see [ GR56 ] . Their original proof was quite complicated, due to the fact that resolution of singularities was not available at that time. title: Definition B.2.1
text: Definition B.2.1 . A function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is plurisubharmonic if $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $ on any irreducible component of $X$, and for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $X$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ N$, a closed immersion $V\hookrightarrow \Omega $ and a plurisubharmonic function $\tilde{\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ such that $\varphi |_ V=\tilde{\varphi }|_ V$ under this immersion. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$. Similarly, if $\theta $ is a smooth closed Note. Here closed means that locally $\theta $ is defined by a closed form under a local embedding. real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, then a function $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic if for any $x\in X$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $X$, a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {C}^ N$, a closed immersion $V\hookrightarrow \Omega $ and a smooth function $g$ on $\Omega $ such that $\theta =(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)|_ V$ and $g|_ V+\varphi |_ V\in \mathrm{PSH}(V)$.

title: Theorem B.2.2 (Fornaess–Narasimhan)
text: Theorem B.2.2 (Fornaess–Narasimhan) . Let $\varphi \colon X\rightarrow [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function. Assume that $\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $ on any irreducible component of $X$. Then the following are equivalent: $\varphi $ is psh; $\varphi $ is usc and for any morphism $f\colon \Delta \rightarrow X$ from the open unit disk $\Delta $ in $\mathbb {C}$ to $X$ such that $f^*\varphi $ is not identically $-\infty $, the pull-back $f^*\varphi $ is subharmonic.

title: Corollary B.2.4
text: Corollary B.2.4 . Let $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ be a proper bimeromorphic morphism between compact Kähler spaces. Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Assume that $X$ is unibranch. Then the pull-back induces a bijection \[  \pi ^*\colon \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\xlongrightarrow {\sim }\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta ).  \] Proof. Injectivity follows from the surjectivity of $\pi $. For surjectivity, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta )$. The assertion is local on $X$, so after subtracting a local potential of $\theta $ we may assume that $\theta =0$. By theorem B.1.4 , the fibers of $\pi $ are connected. The restriction of $u$ to any compact fiber is psh, hence is constant by the maximum principle. Thus $u$ descends to a function $v$ on $X$. Since $\pi $ is proper, $v$ is upper semicontinuous. It remains to check that $v$ is psh. By theorem B.2.2 , it suffices to test on holomorphic disks. Let $f\colon \Delta \rightarrow X$ be a holomorphic disk such that $f^*v\not\equiv -\infty $. As in the proof of theorem B.2.3 , after a finite ramified cover $\rho \colon \Delta \rightarrow \Delta $, the germ of $f\circ \rho $ lifts to $Y$. The pull-back $(f^*v)\circ \rho $ is therefore subharmonic, so $f^*v$ is subharmonic. Hence $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, and the general $\theta $-psh case follows by adding back the local potentials. $\square$

title: B.3 Extensions of the results in the smooth setting
search_title: Extensions of the results in the smooth setting
text: B.3 Extensions of the results in the smooth setting Let $X$ be an irreducible unibranch compact Kähler space of dimension $n$. Let $\theta $ be a closed real smooth $(1,1)$-form on $X$. We say the cohomology class $\{ \theta \} $ is big if for any proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$, $\{ \pi ^*\theta \} $ is big. This definition is independent of the choice of $\pi $. The non-pluripolar products can be defined exactly as in chapter 2 and the results in that chapter hold mutatis mutandis . The results in chapter 3 can also be easily extended. The definition of the $P$-envelope remains unchanged. As for the $\mathcal{I}$-envelope, we define Definition B.3.1 . Given $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, we define $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ as the unique element with the following property: If $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ is a proper bimeromorphic morphism from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$, then \[  \pi ^*P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}=P_{\pi ^*\theta }[\pi ^*\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}.  \] It follows from corollary B.2.4 and proposition 3.2.7 that $P_{\theta }[\varphi ]_{\mathcal{I}}$ is independent of the choice of $\pi $ and is well-defined. The other results can be easily extended. chapter 4 and chapter 6 can be extended without big changes. The only exception is theorem 6.2.31 , where we do not have the notion of multiplier ideal sheaves. So we do not know how to extend this theorem. chapter 7 can be extended except for section 7.4 for the same reason as above. If $Y\subseteq X$ is an irreducible analytic subspace not contained in $X^{\operatorname{Sing}}$, then the trace operator of chapter 8 can be extended to this setting by using an embedded resolution. In general, due to the lack of Demailly regularization on singular spaces, we do not know how to define the trace operator. chapter 9 can be easily extended. chapter 10 is easy to extend since the partial Okounkov bodies are bimeromorphically invariant in the sense of theorem 10.4.13 . chapter 11 is unchanged, since we always take projective limits with respect to all models in that section. chapter 12 can be extended using the toric resolution [ Theorem 11.1.9 , CLS11 ] . chapter 13 can be extended except for the parts involving the trace operator. chapter 14 can be easily extended by considering a resolution.

title: C Almost semigroups
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: C Almost semigroups This appendix develops the theory of almost semigroups in $\mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$ that underpins the partial Okounkov body construction of chapter 10 . Almost semigroups generalize the integral semigroups arising in the classical Lazarsfeld–Mustaţă and Kaveh–Khovanskii constructions to the setting where the underlying graded family is no longer multiplicative. The main result is the construction of a convex body $\Delta (S)\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ out of an almost semigroup $S$. The corresponding statements were stated without proof in chapter 10 ; the proofs are given here.

title: C.1 Convex bodies
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: C.1 Convex bodies Fix $n\in \mathbb {N}$. Definition C.1.1 . A convex body in $\mathbb {R}^ n$ is a non-empty compact convex set. We allow a convex body to have empty interior. We write $\mathcal{K}_ n$ for the set of convex bodies in $\mathbb {R}^ n$. Definition C.1.2 . The Hausdorff metric between $K_1,K_2\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ is given by \[  d_{\mathrm{Haus}}(K_1,K_2)\coloneqq \max \left\{ \adjustlimits \sup _{x_1\in K_1}\inf _{x_2\in K_2}|x_1-x_2|, \adjustlimits \sup _{x_2\in K_2}\inf _{x_1\in K_1}|x_1-x_2|\right\} .  \] It is well-known that the metric space $(\mathcal{K}_ n,d_{\mathrm{Haus}})$ is complete. We will need the following fundamental theorem: Theorem C.1.3 (Blaschke selection theorem) . The metric space $(\mathcal{K}_ n,d_{\mathrm{Haus}})$ is locally compact. We refer to [ Theorem 1.8.7 , Sch14 ] for details. Theorem C.1.4 . The Lebesgue volume $\operatorname{vol}\colon \mathcal{K}_ n\rightarrow \mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}$ is continuous. See [ Theorem 1.8.20 , Sch14 ] . Theorem C.1.5 . Let $K_ i, K\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ ($i\in \mathbb {N}$). Then $K_ i\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}K$ if and only if the following conditions hold: each point $x\in K$ is the limit of a sequence $x_ i\in K_ i$, and the limit of any convergent sequence $(x_{i_ j})_{j\in \mathbb {N}}$ with $x_{i_ j}\in K_{i_ j}$ lies in $K$, where $i_ j$ is a strictly increasing sequence in $\mathbb {Z}_{>0}$. See [ Theorem 1.8.8 , Sch14 ] . For a convex body $K\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ and $\epsilon >0$, we write $K_\epsilon \coloneqq \{ x\in K: B(x,\epsilon )\subseteq K\} $ for the inner $\epsilon $-shrinking of $K$. (Compare with the outer thickening $K^\epsilon $ used in corollary 5.2.15 ; the two are different operations.) Lemma C.1.6 . Let $K\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ be a convex body with positive volume and $K'\in \mathcal{K}_ n$. Assume that, for some $k\in \mathbb Z_{>0}$, $K'$ contains $K\cap (k^{-1}\mathbb Z)^ n$. Then \[  K'\supseteq K_{n^{1/2}/k}.  \] Proof. Let $x\in K_{n^{1/2}k^{-1}}$. By assumption, the closed ball $B$ with center $x$ and radius $n^{1/2}k^{-1}$ is contained in $K$. Observe that $x$ can be written as a convex combination of points in $B\cap (k^{-1}\mathbb {Z})^ n$, which are contained in $K'$ by assumption. It follows that $x\in K'$. $\square$ Given a sequence of convex bodies $K_ i$ ($i\in \mathbb {N}$), we set \[  \varliminf _{i\to \infty }K_ i= \overline{\bigcup _{i=0}^{\infty }\bigcap _{j\geq i}K_ j}.  \] Suppose $K$ is the limit of a subsequence of $K_ i$, we have C.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:liminflimsup} \varliminf _{i\to \infty }K_ i\subseteq K. \end{equation} This is a simple consequence of theorem C.1.5 . Lemma C.1.7 . Assume that $n>0$. Let $K\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ be a convex body. Let \[  t_{\min }\coloneqq \min \{ t\in \mathbb {R}:\{ x_1=t\} \cap K\neq \varnothing \} ,\quad t_{\max }\coloneqq \max \{ t\in \mathbb {R}:\{ x_1=t\} \cap K\neq \varnothing \} .  \] Then for $t\in [t_{\min },t_{\max }]$, the map \[  t\mapsto \{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}:(t,y)\in K\}   \] is continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric. Here $x_1$ denotes the first coordinate in $\mathbb {R}^ n$. Proof. We may assume that $t_{\min }<t_{\max }$ as otherwise there is nothing to prove. For each $t\in [t_{\min },t_{\max }]$, we write $K_ t=\{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}:(t,y)\in K\} $. Let $t_ j\to t$ be a convergent sequence in $[t_{\min },t_{\max }]$, we want to show that $K_{t_ j}$ converges to $K_ t$ with respect to the Hausdorff metric. Recall that this amounts to the following two assertions: For each convergent sequence $y_ j\in K_{t_ j}$ with limit $y$, we have $y\in K_ t$; Given any $y\in K_ t$, up to replacing $t_ j$ by a subsequence, we can find $y_ j\in K_{t_ j}$ converging to $y$. The first assertion is obvious. Let us prove the second. Take $y\in K_ t$. Up to replacing $t_ j$ by a subsequence and taking the symmetry into account, we may assume that $t_ j> t$ for all $j$. In particular, $t<t_{\max }$. We can find a point $z=(z^1,z')\in K$ such that $z^1>t$ (for example, there is always such a point with $z^1=t_{\max }$). Replacing $t_ j$ by a subsequence, we may assume that $t_ j\in (t,z^1)$ for all $j$. Then it suffices to take \[  y_ j=\frac{z^1-t_ j}{z^1-t}y+\frac{t_ j-t}{z^1-t}z'.  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Lemma C.1.8 . Assume that $n>0$. The maps $\mathcal{K}_ n\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ given by \[  K\mapsto \min _{x\in K}x_1,\qquad K\mapsto \max _{x\in K}x_1  \] are continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric. Proof. We prove the assertion for the maximum; the proof for the minimum is the same. Let $K,L\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ and set $\epsilon =d_{\mathrm{Haus}}(K,L)$. For every $x\in K$, there exists $y\in L$ with $|x-y|\leq \epsilon $, hence \[  x_1\leq y_1+\epsilon \leq \max _{z\in L}z_1+\epsilon .  \] Taking the maximum over $x\in K$ gives \[  \max _{x\in K}x_1\leq \max _{z\in L}z_1+\epsilon .  \] Interchanging $K$ and $L$, we get \[  \left|\max _{x\in K}x_1-\max _{z\in L}z_1\right|\leq d_{\mathrm{Haus}}(K,L).  \] This proves the continuity. $\square$ Lemma C.1.9 . Let $D_ j\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ $(j\geq 1)$ be a decreasing sequence of bounded convex sets. Assume that $\operatorname{vol}\bigcap _ j D_ j>0$. Then \[  \overline{\bigcap _{j=1}^{\infty }D_ j}=\bigcap _{j=1}^{\infty }\overline{D_ j}.  \] Proof. The $\subseteq $ direction is clear. By convexity, it suffices to show that both sides have the same positive volume: indeed, a proper inclusion of closed convex sets with positive volume would cut off a non-empty relatively open convex piece by a separating hyperplane, hence would strictly decrease the volume. As the boundary of convex sets has zero Lebesgue measure, it follows that the volumes of both sides are equal to $\lim _{j\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}D_ j$. $\square$ Definition C.1.10 . Let $K,K'\in \mathcal{K}_ n$, their Minkowski sum is given by \[  K+K'\coloneqq \{ x+x': x\in K,x'\in K'\} .  \] Proposition C.1.11 . The Minkowski sum $\mathcal{K}_ n\times \mathcal{K}_ n\rightarrow \mathcal{K}_ n$ is continuous. See [ Page 139 , Sch14 ] . Theorem C.1.12 (Brunn–Minkowski) . Let $K,K'\in \mathcal{K}_ n$. Then for any $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \operatorname{vol}\bigl ((1-t)K'+tK\bigr )\geq \bigl (\operatorname{vol}K'\bigr )^{1-t}\bigl (\operatorname{vol}K\bigr )^ t.  \] In other words, the volume is log concave. See [ Page 372 , Sch14 ] .

title: Definition C.1.1
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Definition C.1.1 . A convex body in $\mathbb {R}^ n$ is a non-empty compact convex set.

title: Definition C.1.2
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Definition C.1.2 . The Hausdorff metric between $K_1,K_2\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ is given by \[  d_{\mathrm{Haus}}(K_1,K_2)\coloneqq \max \left\{ \adjustlimits \sup _{x_1\in K_1}\inf _{x_2\in K_2}|x_1-x_2|, \adjustlimits \sup _{x_2\in K_2}\inf _{x_1\in K_1}|x_1-x_2|\right\} .  \]

title: Theorem C.1.3 (Blaschke selection theorem)
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Theorem C.1.3 (Blaschke selection theorem) . The metric space $(\mathcal{K}_ n,d_{\mathrm{Haus}})$ is locally compact.

title: Theorem C.1.4
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Theorem C.1.4 . The Lebesgue volume $\operatorname{vol}\colon \mathcal{K}_ n\rightarrow \mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}$ is continuous.

title: Theorem C.1.5
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Theorem C.1.5 . Let $K_ i, K\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ ($i\in \mathbb {N}$). Then $K_ i\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}K$ if and only if the following conditions hold: each point $x\in K$ is the limit of a sequence $x_ i\in K_ i$, and the limit of any convergent sequence $(x_{i_ j})_{j\in \mathbb {N}}$ with $x_{i_ j}\in K_{i_ j}$ lies in $K$, where $i_ j$ is a strictly increasing sequence in $\mathbb {Z}_{>0}$.

title: Lemma C.1.6
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.1.6 . Let $K\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ be a convex body with positive volume and $K'\in \mathcal{K}_ n$. Assume that, for some $k\in \mathbb Z_{>0}$, $K'$ contains $K\cap (k^{-1}\mathbb Z)^ n$. Then \[  K'\supseteq K_{n^{1/2}/k}.  \] Proof. Let $x\in K_{n^{1/2}k^{-1}}$. By assumption, the closed ball $B$ with center $x$ and radius $n^{1/2}k^{-1}$ is contained in $K$. Observe that $x$ can be written as a convex combination of points in $B\cap (k^{-1}\mathbb {Z})^ n$, which are contained in $K'$ by assumption. It follows that $x\in K'$. $\square$

title: C.1
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: C.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:liminflimsup} \varliminf _{i\to \infty }K_ i\subseteq K. \end{equation}

title: Lemma C.1.7
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.1.7 . Assume that $n>0$. Let $K\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ be a convex body. Let \[  t_{\min }\coloneqq \min \{ t\in \mathbb {R}:\{ x_1=t\} \cap K\neq \varnothing \} ,\quad t_{\max }\coloneqq \max \{ t\in \mathbb {R}:\{ x_1=t\} \cap K\neq \varnothing \} .  \] Then for $t\in [t_{\min },t_{\max }]$, the map \[  t\mapsto \{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}:(t,y)\in K\}   \] is continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric. Proof. We may assume that $t_{\min }<t_{\max }$ as otherwise there is nothing to prove. For each $t\in [t_{\min },t_{\max }]$, we write $K_ t=\{ y\in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}:(t,y)\in K\} $. Let $t_ j\to t$ be a convergent sequence in $[t_{\min },t_{\max }]$, we want to show that $K_{t_ j}$ converges to $K_ t$ with respect to the Hausdorff metric. Recall that this amounts to the following two assertions: For each convergent sequence $y_ j\in K_{t_ j}$ with limit $y$, we have $y\in K_ t$; Given any $y\in K_ t$, up to replacing $t_ j$ by a subsequence, we can find $y_ j\in K_{t_ j}$ converging to $y$. The first assertion is obvious. Let us prove the second. Take $y\in K_ t$. Up to replacing $t_ j$ by a subsequence and taking the symmetry into account, we may assume that $t_ j> t$ for all $j$. In particular, $t<t_{\max }$. We can find a point $z=(z^1,z')\in K$ such that $z^1>t$ (for example, there is always such a point with $z^1=t_{\max }$). Replacing $t_ j$ by a subsequence, we may assume that $t_ j\in (t,z^1)$ for all $j$. Then it suffices to take \[  y_ j=\frac{z^1-t_ j}{z^1-t}y+\frac{t_ j-t}{z^1-t}z'.  \] This completes the proof. $\square$

title: Lemma C.1.8
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.1.8 . Assume that $n>0$. The maps $\mathcal{K}_ n\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ given by \[  K\mapsto \min _{x\in K}x_1,\qquad K\mapsto \max _{x\in K}x_1  \] are continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric. Proof. We prove the assertion for the maximum; the proof for the minimum is the same. Let $K,L\in \mathcal{K}_ n$ and set $\epsilon =d_{\mathrm{Haus}}(K,L)$. For every $x\in K$, there exists $y\in L$ with $|x-y|\leq \epsilon $, hence \[  x_1\leq y_1+\epsilon \leq \max _{z\in L}z_1+\epsilon .  \] Taking the maximum over $x\in K$ gives \[  \max _{x\in K}x_1\leq \max _{z\in L}z_1+\epsilon .  \] Interchanging $K$ and $L$, we get \[  \left|\max _{x\in K}x_1-\max _{z\in L}z_1\right|\leq d_{\mathrm{Haus}}(K,L).  \] This proves the continuity. $\square$

title: Lemma C.1.9
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.1.9 . Let $D_ j\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$ $(j\geq 1)$ be a decreasing sequence of bounded convex sets. Assume that $\operatorname{vol}\bigcap _ j D_ j>0$. Then \[  \overline{\bigcap _{j=1}^{\infty }D_ j}=\bigcap _{j=1}^{\infty }\overline{D_ j}.  \] Proof. The $\subseteq $ direction is clear. By convexity, it suffices to show that both sides have the same positive volume: indeed, a proper inclusion of closed convex sets with positive volume would cut off a non-empty relatively open convex piece by a separating hyperplane, hence would strictly decrease the volume. As the boundary of convex sets has zero Lebesgue measure, it follows that the volumes of both sides are equal to $\lim _{j\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}D_ j$. $\square$

title: Definition C.1.10
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Definition C.1.10 . Let $K,K'\in \mathcal{K}_ n$, their Minkowski sum is given by \[  K+K'\coloneqq \{ x+x': x\in K,x'\in K'\} .  \]

title: Proposition C.1.11
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Proposition C.1.11 . The Minkowski sum $\mathcal{K}_ n\times \mathcal{K}_ n\rightarrow \mathcal{K}_ n$ is continuous.
