text: Theorem C.1.12 (Brunn–Minkowski) . Let $K,K'\in \mathcal{K}_ n$. Then for any $t\in (0,1)$, we have \[  \operatorname{vol}\bigl ((1-t)K'+tK\bigr )\geq \bigl (\operatorname{vol}K'\bigr )^{1-t}\bigl (\operatorname{vol}K\bigr )^ t.  \]

title: C.2 The Okounkov bodies of almost semigroups
search_title: The Okounkov bodies of almost semigroups
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: C.2 The Okounkov bodies of almost semigroups Fix an integer $n\geq 0$. Fix a closed convex cone $C\subseteq \mathbb {R}^{n}\times \mathbb {R}_{\geq 0}$ such that $C\cap \{ x_{n+1}=0\} =\{ 0\} $. Here $x_{n+1}$ is the last coordinate of $\mathbb {R}^{n+1}$.

title: C.2.1 Generalities on semigroups
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: C.2.1 Generalities on semigroups Write $\hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$ for the set of subsets of $C\cap \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$ and $\mathcal{S}(C)$ for the set of subsemigroups $S\subseteq C\cap \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$. For each $k\in \mathbb {N}$ and $S\in \hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$, we write \[  S_ k\coloneqq \left\{ x\in \mathbb {Z}^ n: (x,k)\in S \right\} .  \] Note that $S_ k$ is a finite set by our assumption on $C$. We introduce a pseudometric on $\hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$ as follows: C.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:dsgdefapp} d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')\coloneqq \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } k^{-n} \left(|S_ k|+|S'_ k|-2|(S\cap S')_ k|\right). \end{equation} Here $|\bullet |$ denotes the cardinality of a finite set. Lemma C.2.1 . The above defined $d_{\mathrm{sg}}$ is a pseudometric on $\hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$. Proof. Only the triangle inequality needs to be argued. Take $S,S',S''\in \hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$. We claim that for any $k\in \mathbb {N}$, \[  |S_ k|+|S'_ k|-2|S_ k\cap S'_ k|+|S''_ k|+|S'_ k|-2|S''_ k\cap S'_ k|\geq |S_ k|+|S''_ k|-2|S_ k\cap S''_ k|.  \] From this the triangle inequality follows. To argue the claim, we rearrange it to the following form: \[  |S'_ k|-|S_ k\cap S'_ k| \geq |S'_ k\cap S''_ k|-|S_ k\cap S''_ k|,  \] which is obvious. $\square$ Given $S,S'\in \hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$, we say $S$ is equivalent to $S'$ and write $S\sim S'$ if $d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')=0$. This is an equivalence relation by C.2.1 . Lemma C.2.2 . Given $S,S',S''\in \hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$, we have \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S\cap S'',S'\cap S'')\leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S').  \] In particular, if $S^ i,S'^ i\in \hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$ ($i\in \mathbb {N}$) and $S^ i\to S$, $S'^ i\to S'$, then \[  S^ i\cap S'^ i\to S\cap S'.  \] Proof. Observe that for any $k\in \mathbb {N}$, \[  |S_ k\cap S_ k''|-|S_ k\cap S_ k'\cap S_ k''|\leq |S_ k|-|S_ k\cap S_ k'|.  \] The same holds if we interchange $S$ with $S'$. It follows that \[  |S_ k\cap S_ k''|+|S_ k'\cap S_ k''|-2|S_ k\cap S_ k'\cap S_ k''|\leq |S_ k|+|S'_ k|-2|S_ k\cap S_ k'|.  \] The first assertion follows. Next we compute \[  \begin{split}  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i\cap S'^ i,S\cap S')\leq &  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i\cap S'^ i,S^ i\cap S')+d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i\cap S',S\cap S')\\  \leq &  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S'^ i,S')+d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i,S) \end{split}  \] and the second assertion follows. $\square$ The volume of $S\in \mathcal{S}(C)$ is defined as \[  \operatorname{vol}S\coloneqq \lim _{k\to \infty } (ka)^{-n}|S_{ka}|=\varlimsup _{k\to \infty } k^{-n}|S_ k|,  \] where $a$ is a sufficiently divisible positive integer. The existence of the limit and its independence from $a$ both follow from the more precise result [ Theorem 2 , KK12 ] , a special case of which can be stated as follows: Theorem C.2.3 (Kaveh–Khovanskii) . Let $S\in \mathcal{S}(C)$. Then, for every sufficiently divisible positive integer $a$, the limit \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }(ka)^{-n}|S_{ka}|  \] exists, is independent of $a$, and is equal to $\varlimsup _{k\to \infty } k^{-n}|S_ k|$. If moreover $S$ generates $\mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$ as an Abelian group, and if $C(S)$ denotes the closed convex cone generated by $S\cup \{ 0\} $, then \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } k^{-n}|S_ k| = \operatorname{vol}\{ x\in \mathbb {R}^ n:(x,1)\in C(S)\} .  \] In particular, for every convex body $K\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$, \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } k^{-n}\# \left(kK\cap \mathbb {Z}^ n\right)=\operatorname{vol}K.  \] The same assertion holds with $\mathbb {Z}^ n$ replaced by any lattice, provided the Lebesgue measure is normalized by that lattice. This is the part of [ Theorem 2 , KK12 ] used in this book. Lemma C.2.4 . Let $S,S'\in \mathcal{S}(C)$. Then \[  |\operatorname{vol}S-\operatorname{vol}S'|\leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S').  \] Proof. Choose a sufficiently divisible positive integer $a$. Taking the limsup in the definition of $d_{\mathrm{sg}}$ along $k=ma$ gives \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')\geq \operatorname{vol}S+\operatorname{vol}S'-2\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S').  \] It follows that $\operatorname{vol}S-\operatorname{vol}S'\leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')$ and $\operatorname{vol}S'-\operatorname{vol}S\leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')$. $\square$ We define $\overline{\mathcal{S}}(C)$ as the closure of $\mathcal{S}(C)$ in $\hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$ with respect to the topology defined by the pseudometric $d_{\mathrm{sg}}$. By C.2.4 , $\operatorname{vol}\colon \mathcal{S}(C)\rightarrow \mathbb {R}$ admits a unique $1$-Lipschitz extension to C.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:volexapp} \operatorname{vol}\colon \overline{\mathcal{S}}(C)\rightarrow \mathbb {R}. \end{equation} Lemma C.2.5 . Suppose that $S,S'\in \overline{\mathcal{S}}(C)$ and $S\subseteq S'$. Then \[  \operatorname{vol}S\leq \operatorname{vol}S'.  \] Proof. Take sequences $S^ j,S'^ j$ in $\mathcal{S}(C)$ such that $S^ j\to S$, $S'^ j\to S'$. By C.2.2 , after replacing $S^ j$ by $S^ j\cap S'^ j$, we may assume that $S^ j\subseteq S'^ j$ for each $j$. Then our assertion follows easily. $\square$

title: C.2

text: C.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:dsgdefapp} d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')\coloneqq \varlimsup _{k\to \infty } k^{-n} \left(|S_ k|+|S'_ k|-2|(S\cap S')_ k|\right). \end{equation}

title: Lemma C.2.1
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.2.1 . The above defined $d_{\mathrm{sg}}$ is a pseudometric on $\hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$. Proof. Only the triangle inequality needs to be argued. Take $S,S',S''\in \hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$. We claim that for any $k\in \mathbb {N}$, \[  |S_ k|+|S'_ k|-2|S_ k\cap S'_ k|+|S''_ k|+|S'_ k|-2|S''_ k\cap S'_ k|\geq |S_ k|+|S''_ k|-2|S_ k\cap S''_ k|.  \] From this the triangle inequality follows. To argue the claim, we rearrange it to the following form: \[  |S'_ k|-|S_ k\cap S'_ k| \geq |S'_ k\cap S''_ k|-|S_ k\cap S''_ k|,  \] which is obvious. $\square$

title: Lemma C.2.2
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.2.2 . Given $S,S',S''\in \hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$, we have \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S\cap S'',S'\cap S'')\leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S').  \] In particular, if $S^ i,S'^ i\in \hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$ ($i\in \mathbb {N}$) and $S^ i\to S$, $S'^ i\to S'$, then \[  S^ i\cap S'^ i\to S\cap S'.  \] Proof. Observe that for any $k\in \mathbb {N}$, \[  |S_ k\cap S_ k''|-|S_ k\cap S_ k'\cap S_ k''|\leq |S_ k|-|S_ k\cap S_ k'|.  \] The same holds if we interchange $S$ with $S'$. It follows that \[  |S_ k\cap S_ k''|+|S_ k'\cap S_ k''|-2|S_ k\cap S_ k'\cap S_ k''|\leq |S_ k|+|S'_ k|-2|S_ k\cap S_ k'|.  \] The first assertion follows. Next we compute \[  \begin{split}  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i\cap S'^ i,S\cap S')\leq &  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i\cap S'^ i,S^ i\cap S')+d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i\cap S',S\cap S')\\  \leq &  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S'^ i,S')+d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i,S) \end{split}  \] and the second assertion follows. $\square$

title: Theorem C.2.3 (Kaveh–Khovanskii)
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Theorem C.2.3 (Kaveh–Khovanskii) . Let $S\in \mathcal{S}(C)$. Then, for every sufficiently divisible positive integer $a$, the limit \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }(ka)^{-n}|S_{ka}|  \] exists, is independent of $a$, and is equal to $\varlimsup _{k\to \infty } k^{-n}|S_ k|$. If moreover $S$ generates $\mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$ as an Abelian group, and if $C(S)$ denotes the closed convex cone generated by $S\cup \{ 0\} $, then \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } k^{-n}|S_ k| = \operatorname{vol}\{ x\in \mathbb {R}^ n:(x,1)\in C(S)\} .  \] In particular, for every convex body $K\subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n$, \[  \lim _{k\to \infty } k^{-n}\# \left(kK\cap \mathbb {Z}^ n\right)=\operatorname{vol}K.  \] The same assertion holds with $\mathbb {Z}^ n$ replaced by any lattice, provided the Lebesgue measure is normalized by that lattice.

title: Lemma C.2.4
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.2.4 . Let $S,S'\in \mathcal{S}(C)$. Then \[  |\operatorname{vol}S-\operatorname{vol}S'|\leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S').  \] Proof. Choose a sufficiently divisible positive integer $a$. Taking the limsup in the definition of $d_{\mathrm{sg}}$ along $k=ma$ gives \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')\geq \operatorname{vol}S+\operatorname{vol}S'-2\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S').  \] It follows that $\operatorname{vol}S-\operatorname{vol}S'\leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')$ and $\operatorname{vol}S'-\operatorname{vol}S\leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')$. $\square$

title: C.5
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: C.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:volexapp} \operatorname{vol}\colon \overline{\mathcal{S}}(C)\rightarrow \mathbb {R}. \end{equation}

title: Lemma C.2.5
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.2.5 . Suppose that $S,S'\in \overline{\mathcal{S}}(C)$ and $S\subseteq S'$. Then \[  \operatorname{vol}S\leq \operatorname{vol}S'.  \] Proof. Take sequences $S^ j,S'^ j$ in $\mathcal{S}(C)$ such that $S^ j\to S$, $S'^ j\to S'$. By C.2.2 , after replacing $S^ j$ by $S^ j\cap S'^ j$, we may assume that $S^ j\subseteq S'^ j$ for each $j$. Then our assertion follows easily. $\square$

title: C.2.2 Okounkov bodies of semigroups
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: C.2.2 Okounkov bodies of semigroups Given $S\in \hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$, we will write $C(S)\subseteq C$ for the closed convex cone generated by $S\cup \{ 0\} $. Moreover, for each $k\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}$, we define \[  \Delta _ k(S)\coloneqq \mathrm{Conv}\left\{ k^{-1}x\in \mathbb {R}^ n:x\in S_ k \right\} \subseteq \mathbb {R}^ n.  \] Here $\mathrm{Conv}$ denotes the convex hull. Definition C.2.6 . Let $\mathcal{S}'(C)$ be the subset of $\mathcal{S}(C)$ consisting of semigroups $S$ such that $S$ generates $\mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$ (as an Abelian group). Note that for any $S\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$, the cone $C(S)$ has full dimension (i.e., the topological interior is non-empty). Given a full-dimensional subcone $C'\subseteq C$, the semigroup $C'\cap \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$ lies in $\mathcal{S}'(C)$. This class behaves well under intersections: Lemma C.2.7 . Let $S,S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. Assume that $\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S')>0$. Then $S\cap S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$, and \[  C(S\cap S')=C(S)\cap C(S').  \] The lemma obviously fails if $\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S')=0$. Proof. We first observe that the cone $C(S)\cap C(S')$ has full dimension since otherwise $\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S')=0$. Take a full-dimensional subcone $C'$ in $C(S)\cap C(S')$ such that $C'$ intersects the boundary of $C(S)\cap C(S')$ only at $0$. It follows from [ Theorem 1 , KK12 ] that there is an integer $N>0$ such that any $x\in \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}\cap C'$ with Euclidean norm at least $N$ lies in $S\cap S'$. Therefore, $S\cap S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. Since $C'$ can be chosen around any ray in the interior of $C(S)\cap C(S')$, the same argument also shows that \[  C(S\cap S')=C(S)\cap C(S').  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ We recall the following definition from [ KK12 ] . Definition C.2.8 . Given $S\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$, its Okounkov body is defined as follows \[  \Delta (S)\coloneqq \left\{ x\in \mathbb {R}^ n:(x,1)\in C(S) \right\} .  \] Theorem C.2.9 . For each $S\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$, we have C.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:volWvolDeltaapp} \operatorname{vol}S=\lim _{k\to \infty } k^{-n}|S_ k|=\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S)>0. \end{equation} Moreover, as $k\to \infty $, C.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:HausconvDeltaGLSapp} \Delta _{k}(S)\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta (S). \end{equation} This is essentially proved in [ Lemma 4.8 , WN14 ] , which itself follows from a theorem of Khovanskii [ Kho92 ] . Proof. The equalities ( C.6 ) follow from theorem C.2.3 . It remains to prove ( C.7 ). By the argument of [ Lemma 4.8 , WN14 ] , for any compact set $K\subseteq \operatorname{Int}\Delta (S)$, there is $k_0>0$ such that for any $k\geq k_0$, $\alpha \in K\cap (k^{-1}\mathbb {Z})^ n$ implies that $\alpha \in \Delta _ k(S)$. To conclude, fix $\epsilon >0$. Choose $\delta >0$ such that $K\coloneqq \Delta (S)_{\delta }$ has positive volume and $d_{\mathrm{Haus}}(K,\Delta (S))<\epsilon /2$. Applying C.1.6 to $K$, we find that $\Delta _ k(S)$ contains $K_{n^{1/2}k^{-1}}$ for all large $k$. After increasing $k$, we may also assume that $d_{\mathrm{Haus}}(K,K_{n^{1/2}k^{-1}})<\epsilon /2$. Since $\Delta _ k(S)\subseteq \Delta (S)$, this implies ( C.7 ). $\square$ Corollary C.2.10 . Let $S,S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. Assume that $\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S')>0$. Then we have \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')=\operatorname{vol}(S)+\operatorname{vol}(S')-2\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S').  \] Proof. This is a direct consequence of C.2.7 and ( C.6 ). $\square$ Lemma C.2.11 . Given $S\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$, we have $S\sim \operatorname{Reg}(S)$. Recall that the regularization $\operatorname{Reg}(S)$ of $S$ is defined as $C(S)\cap \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$. Proof. Since $S$ and $\operatorname{Reg}(S)$ have the same Okounkov body, we have $\operatorname{vol}S=\operatorname{vol}\operatorname{Reg}(S)$ by theorem C.2.9 . By corollary C.2.10 again, \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(\operatorname{Reg}(S),S)=\operatorname{vol}\operatorname{Reg}(S)-\operatorname{vol}S=0.  \] This completes the proof. $\square$ Lemma C.2.12 . Let $S,S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. Assume that $d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')=0$. Then $\Delta (S)=\Delta (S')$. Proof. Observe that $\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S')>0$, as otherwise \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')\geq \operatorname{vol}S+\operatorname{vol}S'>0,  \] which is a contradiction. It follows from C.2.7 that $S\cap S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. It suffices to show that $\Delta (S)=\Delta (S\cap S')$. In fact, suppose that this holds, since $\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S')=\operatorname{vol}S'=\operatorname{vol}S=\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S)$, the inclusion $\Delta (S')\supseteq \Delta (S\cap S')=\Delta (S)$ is an equality. After replacing $S'$ by $S\cap S'$, we still have $d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')=0$ by C.2.2 , and now $S'\subseteq S$. Hence corollary C.2.10 gives \[  0=d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')=\operatorname{vol}S-\operatorname{vol}S',  \] so $\operatorname{vol}S=\operatorname{vol}S'$. Therefore \[  \operatorname{vol}\Delta (S)=\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S')>0  \] by ( C.6 ). Therefore, they are equal. $\square$ Lemma C.2.13 . Suppose that $S^ i\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ is a decreasing sequence such that \[  \lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}S^ i>0.  \] Then there is $S\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ such that $S^ i\to S$. In general, one cannot simply take $S=\bigcap _ i S^ i$. For example, consider the sequence $S^ i=S^1\cap \{ x_{n+1}\geq i\} $. Proof. By C.2.11 , we may replace $S^ i$ by its regularization and assume that $S^ i=C(S^ i)\cap \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$. We define \[  S=\left( \bigcap _{i=1}^{\infty }C(S^ i) \right) \cap \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}.  \] The convex bodies $\Delta (S^ i)$ form a decreasing sequence and satisfy \[  \lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S^ i)=\lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}S^ i>0.  \] By continuity from above for Lebesgue measure, \[  \operatorname{vol}\bigcap _ i\Delta (S^ i)=\lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S^ i)>0.  \] Set \[  K\coloneqq \bigcap _{i=1}^{\infty }C(S^ i).  \] The cone $K$ is full-dimensional. As noted above, $K\cap \mathbb Z^{n+1}$ generates $\mathbb Z^{n+1}$ as an Abelian group; hence $S=K\cap \mathbb Z^{n+1}$ lies in $\mathcal S'(C)$. Moreover, the closed convex cone generated by $S$ is exactly $K$. Therefore \[  \Delta (S)=\{ x:(x,1)\in K\} =\bigcap _{i=1}^{\infty }\{ x:(x,1)\in C(S^ i)\} =\bigcap _{i=1}^{\infty }\Delta (S^ i).  \] By corollary C.2.10 and theorem C.2.9 , we can compute the distance \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S^ i)=\operatorname{vol}S^ i-\operatorname{vol}S=\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S^ i)-\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S),  \] which tends to $0$ by construction. $\square$

title: Lemma C.2.7
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.2.7 . Let $S,S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. Assume that $\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S')>0$. Then $S\cap S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$, and \[  C(S\cap S')=C(S)\cap C(S').  \] Proof. We first observe that the cone $C(S)\cap C(S')$ has full dimension since otherwise $\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S')=0$. Take a full-dimensional subcone $C'$ in $C(S)\cap C(S')$ such that $C'$ intersects the boundary of $C(S)\cap C(S')$ only at $0$. It follows from [ Theorem 1 , KK12 ] that there is an integer $N>0$ such that any $x\in \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}\cap C'$ with Euclidean norm at least $N$ lies in $S\cap S'$. Therefore, $S\cap S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. Since $C'$ can be chosen around any ray in the interior of $C(S)\cap C(S')$, the same argument also shows that \[  C(S\cap S')=C(S)\cap C(S').  \] This completes the proof. $\square$

title: Definition C.2.8
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Definition C.2.8 . Given $S\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$, its Okounkov body is defined as follows \[  \Delta (S)\coloneqq \left\{ x\in \mathbb {R}^ n:(x,1)\in C(S) \right\} .  \]

title: Lemma C.2.11
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.2.11 . Given $S\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$, we have $S\sim \operatorname{Reg}(S)$. Proof. Since $S$ and $\operatorname{Reg}(S)$ have the same Okounkov body, we have $\operatorname{vol}S=\operatorname{vol}\operatorname{Reg}(S)$ by theorem C.2.9 . By corollary C.2.10 again, \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(\operatorname{Reg}(S),S)=\operatorname{vol}\operatorname{Reg}(S)-\operatorname{vol}S=0.  \] This completes the proof. $\square$

title: Lemma C.2.12
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.2.12 . Let $S,S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. Assume that $d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')=0$. Then $\Delta (S)=\Delta (S')$. Proof. Observe that $\operatorname{vol}(S\cap S')>0$, as otherwise \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')\geq \operatorname{vol}S+\operatorname{vol}S'>0,  \] which is a contradiction. It follows from C.2.7 that $S\cap S'\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. It suffices to show that $\Delta (S)=\Delta (S\cap S')$. In fact, suppose that this holds, since $\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S')=\operatorname{vol}S'=\operatorname{vol}S=\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S)$, the inclusion $\Delta (S')\supseteq \Delta (S\cap S')=\Delta (S)$ is an equality. After replacing $S'$ by $S\cap S'$, we still have $d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')=0$ by C.2.2 , and now $S'\subseteq S$. Hence corollary C.2.10 gives \[  0=d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S')=\operatorname{vol}S-\operatorname{vol}S',  \] so $\operatorname{vol}S=\operatorname{vol}S'$. Therefore \[  \operatorname{vol}\Delta (S)=\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S')>0  \] by ( C.6 ). Therefore, they are equal. $\square$

title: Lemma C.2.13
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Lemma C.2.13 . Suppose that $S^ i\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ is a decreasing sequence such that \[  \lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}S^ i>0.  \] Then there is $S\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ such that $S^ i\to S$. Proof. By C.2.11 , we may replace $S^ i$ by its regularization and assume that $S^ i=C(S^ i)\cap \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}$. We define \[  S=\left( \bigcap _{i=1}^{\infty }C(S^ i) \right) \cap \mathbb {Z}^{n+1}.  \] The convex bodies $\Delta (S^ i)$ form a decreasing sequence and satisfy \[  \lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S^ i)=\lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}S^ i>0.  \] By continuity from above for Lebesgue measure, \[  \operatorname{vol}\bigcap _ i\Delta (S^ i)=\lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S^ i)>0.  \] Set \[  K\coloneqq \bigcap _{i=1}^{\infty }C(S^ i).  \] The cone $K$ is full-dimensional. As noted above, $K\cap \mathbb Z^{n+1}$ generates $\mathbb Z^{n+1}$ as an Abelian group; hence $S=K\cap \mathbb Z^{n+1}$ lies in $\mathcal S'(C)$. Therefore \[  \Delta (S)=\{ x:(x,1)\in K\} =\bigcap _{i=1}^{\infty }\{ x:(x,1)\in C(S^ i)\} =\bigcap _{i=1}^{\infty }\Delta (S^ i).  \] By corollary C.2.10 and theorem C.2.9 , we can compute the distance \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S,S^ i)=\operatorname{vol}S^ i-\operatorname{vol}S=\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S^ i)-\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S),  \] which tends to $0$ by construction. $\square$

title: C.2.3 Okounkov bodies of almost semigroups
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: C.2.3 Okounkov bodies of almost semigroups Definition C.2.14 . We define $\overline{\mathcal{S}'(C)}_{>0}$ to be the set of elements in the closure of $\mathcal{S}'(C)$ in $\hat{\mathcal{S}}(C)$ with positive volume. An element in $\overline{\mathcal{S}'(C)}_{>0}$ is called an almost semigroup in $C$. Recall that the volume here is defined in ( C.5 ). Our goal is to prove the following theorem: Theorem C.2.15 . The Okounkov body map $\Delta \colon \mathcal{S}'(C) \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_ n$ as defined in definition C.2.8 admits a unique continuous extension C.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Deltagensgapp} \Delta \colon \overline{\mathcal{S}'(C)}_{>0}\rightarrow \mathcal{K}_ n. \end{equation} Moreover, for any $S\in \overline{\mathcal{S}'(C)}_{>0}$, we have C.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:volWfinalapp} \operatorname{vol}S=\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S). \end{equation} Proof. The uniqueness of the extension is clear once existence is known. Moreover, ( C.9 ) follows easily from theorem C.2.9 and theorem C.1.4 by continuity. It remains to argue the existence of the continuous extension. We first construct an extension and prove its continuity. Step 1 . We construct the desired map ( C.8 ). Let $S\in \overline{\mathcal{S}'(C)}_{>0}$. We wish to construct a convex body $\Delta (S)\in \mathcal{K}_ n$. Let $S^ i\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ be a sequence that converges to $S$ such that \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i,S^{i+1})\leq 2^{-i}.  \] For each $i,j\geq 0$, we introduce \[  S^{i,j}=S^ i\cap S^{i+1}\cap \cdots \cap S^{i+j}.  \] Then by C.2.2 , \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^{i,j},S^{i,j+1})\leq 2^{-i-j}.  \] Take $i_0>0$ large enough so that, for $i\geq i_0$, we have $\operatorname{vol}S^ i>2^{-1}\operatorname{vol}S$ and $2^{2-i}< \operatorname{vol}S$. Then \[  \operatorname{vol}S^ i-\operatorname{vol}S^{i,j}\leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^{i,0},S^{i,1})+d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^{i,1},S^{i,2})+\cdots +d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^{i,j-1},S^{i,j})\leq 2^{1-i}.  \] It follows that $\operatorname{vol}S^{i,j}> 2^{-1}\operatorname{vol}S-2^{1-i}>0$ whenever $i\geq i_0$. In particular, by C.2.7 , $S^{i,j}\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ for $i\geq i_0$. By C.2.13 , for $i\geq i_0$, there exists $T^ i\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ such that $S^{i,j}\to T^ i$ as $j\to \infty $. Moreover, \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(T^ i,S)=\lim _{j\to \infty } d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^{i,j},S)\leq \lim _{j\to \infty } d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^{i,j},S^ i)+d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i,S)\leq 2^{1-i}+d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i,S).  \] Therefore, $T^ i\to S$. We then define \[  \Delta (S)\coloneqq \overline{\bigcup _{i=i_0}^{\infty } \Delta (T^ i)}.  \] In other words, we have defined \[  \Delta (S)\coloneqq \varliminf _{i\to \infty }\Delta (S^ i).  \] Indeed, by the construction in the proof of C.2.13 and the cone equality in C.2.7 , \[  \Delta (T^ i)=\bigcap _{j\geq 0}\Delta (S^{i,j}) =\bigcap _{j\geq i}\Delta (S^ j).  \] Thus the bodies $\Delta (T^ i)$ are increasing in $i$ and are all contained in the compact slice $\{ x\in \mathbb {R}^ n:(x,1)\in C\} $. In particular, $\Delta (S)$ is a convex body and \[  \operatorname{vol}\Delta (S)=\lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}\Delta (T^ i)=\lim _{i\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}T^ i=\operatorname{vol}S.  \] This is an honest limit: if $\Delta $ is the limit of a subsequence of $\Delta (S^ i)$, then $\Delta (S)\subseteq \Delta $ by ( C.1 ). Moreover, \[  \operatorname{vol}\Delta =\lim _{m\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}\Delta (S^{i_ m})=\lim _{m\to \infty }\operatorname{vol}S^{i_ m}=\operatorname{vol}S.  \] Comparing the volumes, we find that equality holds. So by theorem C.1.3 , C.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:deltawtempapp} \Delta (S)=\lim _{i\to \infty }\Delta (S^ i). \end{equation} Next we claim that $\Delta (S)$ as defined above does not depend on the choice of the sequence $S^ i$. In fact, suppose that $S'^ i\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ is another sequence satisfying the same conditions as $S^ i$. By C.2.2 , we have \[  R^ i=S^{i+1}\cap S'^{i+1}\longrightarrow S\cap S=S.  \] Since $\operatorname{vol}S>0$ and the volume is continuous on $\overline{\mathcal S}(C)$, we have $\operatorname{vol}R^ i>0$ for all large $i$. Thus $R^ i\in \mathcal S'(C)$ by C.2.7 . Moreover, \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(R^ i,R^{i+1}) \leq d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^{i+1},S^{i+2}) + d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S'^{i+1},S'^{i+2}).  \] Passing simultaneously to subsequences of $S^ i$ and $S'^ i$, we may assume \[  d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^{i+1},S^{i+2})+d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S'^{i+1},S'^{i+2})\leq 2^{-i}.  \] Then the construction above applies to $R^ i=S^{i+1}\cap S'^{i+1}$. Since $R^ i\subseteq S^{i+1}$ and $R^ i\subseteq S'^{i+1}$, every Hausdorff limit of $\Delta (R^ i)$ is contained in the corresponding limits of $\Delta (S^ i)$ and $\Delta (S'^ i)$. The volumes of all three limits are $\operatorname{vol}S$, hence the inclusions are equalities. The same is true with $S'^ i$ in place of $S^ i$. So we conclude that $\Delta (S)$ as in ( C.10 ) does not depend on the choices we made. Step 2 . It remains to prove the continuity of $\Delta $ defined in Step 1. Suppose that $S^ i\in \overline{\mathcal{S}'(C)}_{>0}$ is a sequence with limit $S\in \overline{\mathcal{S}'(C)}_{>0}$. We want to show that C.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:temp5app} \Delta (S^ i)\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta (S). \end{equation} We first reduce to the case where $S^ i\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$. By ( C.10 ), for each $i$, we can choose $T^ i\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ such that $d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i,T^ i)<2^{-i}$ and $d_{\mathrm{Haus}}(\Delta (S^ i),\Delta (T^ i))<2^{-i}$. If we have shown $\Delta (T^ i)\xrightarrow {d_{\mathrm{Haus}}}\Delta (S)$, then ( C.11 ) follows immediately. Next we reduce to the case where $d_{\mathrm{sg}}(S^ i,S^{i+1})\leq 2^{-i}$. Thanks to theorem C.1.3 , in order to prove ( C.11 ), it suffices to show that each subsequence of $\Delta (S^ i)$ admits a subsequence that converges to $\Delta (S)$. Hence, we may pass to a sufficiently fast subsequence and reduce to the required case. After these reductions, ( C.11 ) is nothing but ( C.10 ). $\square$ Corollary C.2.16 . Suppose that $S,S'\in \overline{\mathcal{S}'(C)}_{>0}$ with $S\subseteq S'$. Then C.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:Deltacontainapp} \Delta (S)\subseteq \Delta (S'). \end{equation} Proof. Let $S^ j,S'^ j\in \mathcal{S}'(C)$ be elements such that $S^ j\to S$, $S'^ j\to S'$. Then it follows from C.2.2 that $S^ j\cap S'^ j \to S$. Since $\operatorname{vol}$ is continuous, for large $j$, $S^ j\cap S'^ j$ has positive volume and hence lies in $\mathcal{S}'(C)$ by C.2.7 . We may therefore replace $S^ j$ by $S^ j\cap S'^ j$ and assume that $S^ j\subseteq S'^ j$. Hence, ( C.12 ) follows from the continuity of $\Delta $ proved in theorem C.2.15 . $\square$ Remark C.2.17 . The construction of $\Delta $ is independent of the choice of $C$ in the following sense. If $C'$ is another cone satisfying the same assumptions as $C$ and $C'\supseteq C$, then the Okounkov body map $\Delta \colon \overline{\mathcal{S}'(C')}_{>0}\rightarrow \mathcal{K}_ n$ extends the corresponding map ( C.8 ). We will use this fact without further comment.

title: Introduction
text: Introduction A singular potential can be studied through its growth near its poles, through the holomorphic functions that remain integrable there, or through its Monge–Ampère measure. These descriptions lead to ordinary singularity types, multiplier ideals and curvature measures. Global pluripotential theory relates them and asks which singularities can be approximated by analytic ones. This book develops that theory for Hermitian backgrounds, starting from Singularities in global pluripotential theory [ SGPT ] . In a fixed Kähler class, all bounded potentials have the same Monge–Ampère mass. The non-pluripolar mass of a singular potential can therefore be compared with a fixed total mass, and this comparison connects analytic approximation, envelopes and energy. A nonclosed Hermitian background changes this relation at its first step: the mass can vary even among smooth potentials. Ordinary singularity type, which identifies potentials with bounded difference, no longer determines a single mass. Envelopes and multiplier ideals remain available, but their connection to mass requires different arguments. This loss of closedness is distinct from the geometry of the manifold. A non-Kähler manifold can carry closed positive currents, and a Kähler manifold can be equipped with a nonclosed Hermitian form. Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. A function $u$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic if it is locally the sum of a plurisubharmonic function and a smooth function and the current $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is positive. If $\theta $ is closed, this current is locally a complex Hessian. For a general background, a smooth local correction still makes $u$ plurisubharmonic, but leaves a smooth remainder in the current. Compactness, regularization and multiplier ideals thus survive locally; the new difficulties arise when these constructions are related globally.

title: Closedness, mass and energy
text: Closedness, mass and energy Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$, that is, a smooth strictly positive $(1,1)$-form. If $\omega $ is Kähler, every smooth real potential $u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ satisfies \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\int _ X\omega ^ n.  \] The identity extends to bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials. For singular potentials, the non-pluripolar product can have smaller total mass, and the difference measures the mass excluded at the poles. For a general Hermitian form, integration by parts gives instead \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n-\int _ X\omega ^ n =\sum _{k=1}^{n-1}\binom nk \int _ X u(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{k-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-k})  \] for every smooth $u$. The derivatives of the background already affect the mass before singularities appear. Chapter 2 proves that mass invariance is equivalent to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)=0$ for $1\leq j\leq n-1$. The usual global comparison inequality would force this invariance, so a comparison argument in an arbitrary Hermitian background must account for these derivatives. Once mass varies, its upper and lower bounds become separate questions. The scalar Hopf manifolds of dimension at least three have unbounded masses of smooth potentials with positive perturbed form, while the standard Hopf threefold has a positive infimum of those masses. A different compact threefold carries a balanced metric with bounded masses whose infimum is zero (chapter 8 , section 26.18 ). Neither bound follows from the other. The envelope and measure constructions below accommodate this variation; 9 develops volume comparison and equation theory under explicit mass bounds. Mass conservation does not by itself restore the Kähler energy. At a smooth potential $u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, consider the one-form \[  \alpha _ u(v)=\int _ X v(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n  \] on the space of such potentials, where $v$ is a smooth real tangent direction. For a Kähler form, it is the differential of the Monge–Ampère energy. In dimension at least two, a primitive even near the zero potential forces $\mathrm d\omega =0$ (theorem 3.1.3 ). On a non-Kähler surface, a Gauduchon metric conserves mass but has no such primitive. Perron interpolation and Legendre duality can still be constructed by envelopes; an interpretation through a metric energy needs a separate justification. A Gauduchon metric supplies a conserved linear trace in place of the varying nonlinear mass. Its form $\gamma $ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$, and hence, for every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic potential, \[  \int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] This trace measure determines $u$ up to an additive constant. In a fixed background, for a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm dV$ and the normalization $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm dV=0$, weak convergence of trace measures is equivalent to $L^1$ convergence of potentials (chapter 5 ). The trace stays finite even when the nonlinear Monge–Ampère mass is infinite. Extended non-pluripolar products and finite damped measures make it possible to study such potentials, while passage from damped to undamped measures requires control near the poles.

title: Singularity types and envelopes
text: Singularity types and envelopes Multiplier ideals record the holomorphic functions locally square integrable against $\mathrm e^{-ku}$, for every $k>0$. This gives a second equivalence relation on potentials, coarser than ordinary singularity type. To compare the two, fix $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and take envelopes in the same background. The ordinary envelope $P_\theta [u]$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of the $\theta $-plurisubharmonic $h\leq 0$ with $h\leq u+C$ for some constant $C$. The multiplier-ideal envelope $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ uses instead the $h\leq 0$ with the same multiplier ideals as $u$ at every positive weight. In a closed big class on a compact Kähler manifold, for potentials of positive mass, the equality of these two envelopes characterizes $\mathcal I$-good singularities and is equivalent to a mass identity and approximation by analytic singularities. In the Hermitian setting, analytic approximation still relates the envelopes even when a mass identity is unavailable. Correcting the curvature errors keeps the dyadic approximants in a positive Hermitian background, and their envelopes decrease to the multiplier-ideal envelope. In such a positive background, comparing the two envelopes defines a uniform topology on ordinary classes in which their equality characterizes the closure of the analytic classes, including classes with infinite-mass representatives (theorem 16.6.3 ). This topology can identify distinct ordinary classes. The obstacle in an envelope is part of this construction. A smooth change $\theta \mapsto \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ transforms potentials by $u\mapsto u-\chi $ and transforms their obstacles as well. Keeping only the obstacle zero need not give an invariant topology; allowing all smooth obstacles does. Whether equality of the envelopes at zero implies equality at every smooth obstacle is therefore a substantive question. It holds in a smooth big background with bounded mass when the multiplier-ideal envelope has positive lower volume, as well as on curves and on certain product loci without those volume conditions (proposition 30.8.2 , corollary 30.13.2 , corollary 16.6.44 ). The general case at zero volume remains open. Envelopes and mass give complementary ways to compare singularities. An ordinary model is a fixed point $P_\theta [u]=u$, and the infimum and supremum of mass over an ordinary type define its lower and upper singularity volumes. These volumes need not agree. In a smooth big background with bounded mass, volume comparison gives a completely metrizable topology on the models of positive lower volume. At zero volume, the comparison can fail to distinguish models, so an extension must retain information that mass has lost. On curves, the polar curvature—the part of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ carried by the pole set—determines a model. Total variation of this measure gives a complete metric that includes zero-volume models, with the ideal models as the closure of the analytic models. The construction extends to certain higher-dimensional product loci without an ambient mass bound (proposition 16.6.43 ). A general higher-dimensional model contains more information: residual top-degree mass may lie on a diffuse pole set although every polar curvature current on every modification vanishes. Distinct models can even have the same residual measure and both volumes, while their comparison distance is positive (proposition 16.6.78 ). Thus a classification by measures already has limitations in closed Kähler backgrounds. Restriction raises a related question. A potential may be identically $-\infty $ on a submanifold even though its generic Lelong number there is zero. In this case, the restrictions of its ambient multiplier ideals define finite divisorial data on every modification. Trace envelopes turn this data into constraints on potentials of the submanifold. Exact realization is possible on curves and in sufficiently large backgrounds on Kähler targets, and projective pullback data also admit exact realizations on Hopf manifolds of unbounded mass (theorem 19.8.2 ). Thus failure of a mass bound does not itself prevent realization. Exact divisorial data nevertheless need not determine the Monge–Ampère mass, or a single ordinary type.

title: Equations with prescribed data
text: Equations with prescribed data The varying mass also changes the normalization of an equation. Given a smooth real function $F$ on $X$, one seeks a smooth pair $(u,c)$ satisfying \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c\, \mathrm e^ F\, \mathrm dV, \qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu=0.  \] In a Kähler background, integration determines $c>0$ before solving for $u$. In a Hermitian background the left-hand mass depends on the unknown potential, so the constant must be found together with it. Such a smooth pair exists and is unique. The linearization gives an adjoint Gauduchon probability measure describing the variation of $\log c$ with the density, and leads to a variational volume defined by Gauduchon test forms. This volume remains finite even on manifolds with unbounded upper Monge–Ampère mass. Positive variational volume, however, need not imply that a background is big, meaning that it admits a potential $\rho $ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$. A nef nonclosed background on a projective manifold has positive variational volume and fails this condition (theorem 26.13.2 ). Up to a smooth change of representative, the same example occurs at a finite maximal Chern–Ricci time (theorem 26.20.5 ). An argument for geometric convergence that needs bigness therefore cannot substitute positive variational volume for it. For a nonnegative, nonzero $L^ p$ density, $p>1$, continuous solutions still exist and the positive constant is still unique, but uniqueness of the potential is a separate matter. A smooth density with zeros may have distinct normalized smooth solutions. For a continuous density whose positive set is connected and dense, bounded solutions are unique up to constants (theorem 11.4.1 ). Selection by approximation must also be distinguished from uniqueness. Moreover, when singularities are prescribed, distinct divisorial types can have the same normalization functional and supporting Gauduchon probabilities (chapter 15 ); the scalar response does not recover the full type. Replacing the determinant by an intermediate elementary symmetric polynomial leads to the Hessian measure $H_ m(u)=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}$, for $2\leq m<n$. Its admissible cone permits negative eigenvalues of the perturbed form, so bounded products require capacity estimates beyond the plurisubharmonic calculus. Derivatives of the background again obstruct the usual comparison inequality. Rescaling one potential and working on a sufficiently small sublevel set, however, allows the torsion error to be absorbed. The resulting modified comparison gives strict domination on an arbitrary Hermitian background. For example, for every $a>0$ and smooth real $F$, the equation $H_ m(u)=\mathrm e^{au+F}\omega ^ n$ has exactly one bounded admissible solution, and it is smooth ( 12.12.10 ). Thus the increasing dependence on the potential can recover uniqueness and regularity even when mass is not conserved. To prescribe singularities as well as the measure, one fixes a reference potential and uses relative envelopes to control the solution. For general finite non-pluripolar measures, 9 proves existence in two regimes: semipositive big backgrounds of positive lower mass, with a model reference admitting a competitor in a smaller background, and arbitrary smooth big backgrounds of bounded mass, with a model reference of positive lower volume. These solutions belong to a relative envelope class. Membership in the prescribed ordinary type requires the stronger conclusion that their difference from the reference is bounded; additional estimates give this conclusion for suitable data.

title: Geometric constructions
text: Geometric constructions Logarithmic poles give concrete tests of the theory. On a resolution, removing a prescribed divisorial pole can leave a strictly positive residual form, where a bounded equation determines the remaining potential. A divisor forced by the background behaves differently: it belongs to the type of minimal singularities, and removing it can force the current to descend. The constructions in section 14.21 , section 14.22 distinguish a freely prescribed pole from such a compulsory one. The regularity of a potential also affects the geometry of its current. When that current is smooth and strictly positive off an analytic set, a Hölder potential places the analytic set at finite distance, making the regular metric incomplete if the set is nonempty (theorem 1.18.1 ). Boundedness alone is insufficient: radial examples in closed Kähler classes have continuous minimal residuals and complete regular ends. The integral controlling the potential differs from the one controlling path length. This distinction comes from regularity, even before closedness is lost. Holomorphic sections link singularities to geometry through a closed line-bundle curvature, so counting sections cannot measure an arbitrary Hermitian Monge–Ampère mass. Gauduchon degrees control section growth and flag valuations, while fibrations can concentrate equilibrium measures on a lower-dimensional base. Partial Bergman kernels connect these section spaces to envelopes of singular weights. Closed Bott–Chern classes and locally conformally Kähler structures give further settings where the differential constraints can be used more precisely.

title: Reading the book
text: Reading the book We assume familiarity with complex manifolds, differential forms and currents. Chapter 1 develops the plurisubharmonic tools used throughout. On a first reading, the maximum principle, normalized compactness and exponential integrability are the starting points; the longer approximation and descent arguments can be consulted when needed. The mass and energy calculations explain the obstructions above, and Gauduchon traces, non-pluripolar products and the Hopf construction complete the foundations. The equation chapters develop smooth and weak estimates and comparison principles; the Hessian chapter examines how these arguments change when positivity is weakened. Envelopes and analytic approximation then develop the comparison of ordinary and ideal types; interpolation, restriction and holomorphic sections connect it to geometry. 9 gives the volume and equation theory under mass hypotheses. The appendix explains descent to compact unibranch spaces and solves equations on cones, normalized curves and cuspidal products. Open questions are collected in chapter 33 , and the sources and precise dependencies in chapter 34 ; monograph references also appear where they are used.

title: Conventions
text: Conventions Unless otherwise stated, $X$ denotes a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$. A Hermitian form is a smooth real strictly positive $(1,1)$-form. The letter $\omega $ is reserved for such a form, while $\theta $ denotes an arbitrary smooth real $(1,1)$-form. Whenever $\theta $ or $\omega $ is assumed to be closed, this is stated explicitly. We follow the normalizations of [ SGPT ] : \[  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }(\bar\partial -\partial ), \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial .  \] Thus, on a disk in $\mathbb C$ with coordinate $z$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2$ is the unit Dirac measure at the origin. Multiplier ideals of a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ are defined with the weight $\exp (-u)$, and Monge–Ampère masses carry no factor $1/n!$.

title: 1 The Hermitian foundations
text: 1 The Hermitian foundations

title: 1 Plurisubharmonic functions and singularities
text: 1 Plurisubharmonic functions and singularities A function whose complex Hessian is bounded below by a smooth form becomes plurisubharmonic after a local smooth correction. This brings the local theory of plurisubharmonic functions to a compact complex manifold, provided the smooth remainder left by the correction is kept when potentials are glued, when their Hessians are multiplied and when one integrates by parts. Normalization by the supremum then controls the resulting families globally, giving compactness, uniform exponential integrability and capacity estimates on the whole manifold. Products of Hessians require more care than the potentials themselves: without a common bound, convergence of potentials in $L^1$, or even in capacity, does not prevent their Monge–Ampère measures from concentrating. To keep track of singularities under these operations, we compare potentials in two ways: by domination up to an additive constant, which leads to ordinary singularity types and their envelopes, and by the local integrability of holomorphic functions against exponential weights, which leads to multiplier ideals. Lelong numbers, analytic approximation and modifications are the main tools for computing the latter.

title: 1.1 Plurisubharmonic potentials
text: 1.1 Plurisubharmonic potentials Throughout the chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$, unless a statement specifies another setting. There are two distinct extensions of the Kähler setting: one can study a closed background on a non-Kähler manifold, or allow the background itself to be nonclosed. In both cases positivity is expressed through quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. On an open set $U$ in a complex manifold, a plurisubharmonic function is a locally integrable upper semicontinuous function satisfying the submean inequality on every complex line in local coordinates. We write $\mathrm{PSH}(U)$ for the set of these functions. A function is quasi-plurisubharmonic if it is locally the sum of a plurisubharmonic function and a smooth real function; the set of such functions is denoted by $\mathrm{QPSH}(U)$. The following relative positivity condition makes sense on any such open set as well. Definition 1.1.1 . A quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $X$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic if \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0  \] as a current. We denote the set of these functions by $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Since $\omega >0$, every constant function belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Proposition 1.1.2 . Every real distribution $u$ on $X$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ has a unique $\theta $-plurisubharmonic representative. On each relatively compact coordinate ball with coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$, there is a constant $A>0$ such that $u+A|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic. Conversely, every quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $X$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$ for some constant $C>0$. Proof. On a coordinate ball with compact closure in a larger chart, smoothness of $\theta $ gives \[  \theta \leq A\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2  \] for a sufficiently large $A$. Consequently, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+A|z|^2)\geq A\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2-\theta \geq 0.  \] The local distributional characterization of plurisubharmonic functions, [ Chapter I, Theorem 5.8 , DemCADG ] , gives a unique plurisubharmonic representative of $u+A|z|^2$. Subtracting the smooth correction gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative of $u$ on the ball. These representatives agree on overlaps: after a common local smooth correction, two of them become plurisubharmonic functions that are equal almost everywhere, hence everywhere. They therefore glue to a unique $\theta $-plurisubharmonic representative. For the converse, cover $X$ by finitely many open sets $V_ j\Subset U_ j$, where each $U_ j$ is a chart on which $u=p_ j+f_ j$, with $p_ j$ plurisubharmonic and $f_ j$ smooth. On the compact set $\overline V_ j$, the smooth form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j$ is bounded below by $-C_ j\omega $ for some constant $C_ j$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j\geq -C_ j\omega $ on $V_ j$. Any constant $C>0$ larger than all the $C_ j$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq -C\omega $ on $X$. $\square$ For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, choose coordinates $z$ and a constant $A>0$ as in proposition 1.1.2 , and put $p=u+A|z|^2$. Then \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p+(\theta -A\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2).  \] Thus local plurisubharmonic theory applies to $p$, while the smooth remainder $\theta -A\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ records the original background; this remainder must be kept when forming products or integrating by parts. Proposition 1.1.3 . If $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ on an open set for a smooth function $\rho $, then $\mathrm{d}\theta =0$ on that set. In particular, at a point where $\mathrm{d}\theta \neq 0$, no neighborhood admits such a representation. Proof. Apply $\mathrm{d}$ and use $\mathrm{d}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=0$. $\square$ Conversely, a closed real $(1,1)$-form has smooth local $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-potentials on sufficiently small coordinate balls, by the local $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma; this local fact does not require $X$ to admit a Kähler metric. The exterior derivative also constrains the regularity of a potential whose current is pointwise proportional to a Hermitian form. In dimension at least two, differentiating such an identity expresses the derivative of the proportionality factor through smooth coefficients. Lemma 1.1.4 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and let $\gamma $ be a Hermitian form on $X$. Suppose that real-valued $u,a\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ satisfy \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=a\gamma  \] as currents. Then $a$ and $u$ are smooth. Proof. Taking the exterior derivative and multiplying by $\gamma ^{n-2}$ gives \[  \mathrm{d}a\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\mathrm{d}\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-2} -a\, \mathrm{d}\gamma \wedge \gamma ^{n-2}.  \] At each point, $\xi \mapsto \xi \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is an isomorphism from real one-forms to real $(2n-1)$-forms, as one sees in a unitary frame. Its inverse depends smoothly on the point. Let $B$ and $C$ be the images of $\mathrm{d}\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-2}$ and $\mathrm{d}\gamma \wedge \gamma ^{n-2}$ under this inverse. They are smooth real one-forms, and \[  \mathrm{d}a=B-aC  \] in the sense of distributions. Since $a\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, the right-hand side is locally integrable, so $a\in W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Differentiating the equation and using the smoothness of its coefficients, we obtain inductively $a\in W^{k,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every integer $k$, and the local Sobolev embedding shows that $a$ is smooth. Consequently $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=a\gamma -\theta $ is smooth; taking its trace in local coordinates and applying elliptic regularity shows that $u$ is smooth as well. $\square$

text: Lemma 1.1.4 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and let $\gamma $ be a Hermitian form on $X$. Suppose that real-valued $u,a\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ satisfy \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=a\gamma  \] as currents. Then $a$ and $u$ are smooth. Proof. Taking the exterior derivative and multiplying by $\gamma ^{n-2}$ gives \[  \mathrm{d}a\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\mathrm{d}\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-2} -a\, \mathrm{d}\gamma \wedge \gamma ^{n-2}.  \] At each point, $\xi \mapsto \xi \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is an isomorphism from real one-forms to real $(2n-1)$-forms, as one sees in a unitary frame. title: 1.2 Changes of background
text: 1.2 Changes of background A positive current can be written as a smooth form plus a complex Hessian in more than one way. Changing the decomposition by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact form changes the potential by a bounded function, and positive linear combinations allow us to compare potentials belonging to different backgrounds. In this section, $\eta $ denotes a second smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Proposition 1.2.1 . Let $f$ be a smooth real function on $X$, and set $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. Then \[  \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\longrightarrow \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta '), \qquad u\longmapsto u-f  \] is a bijection. It preserves the positive current and changes each potential by a bounded function. Moreover, $\mathrm{d}\theta '=\mathrm{d}\theta $. Proof. For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  \theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-f)=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u.  \] The inverse map is $v\mapsto v+f$, and $f$ is bounded because $X$ is compact. The last assertion follows from $\mathrm{d}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=0$. $\square$ Thus the natural object is the class of $\theta $ modulo smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact forms. This quotient of all smooth real $(1,1)$-forms contains nonclosed classes; the usual Bott–Chern cohomology group is the corresponding quotient of closed forms. Proposition 1.2.2 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$, then, for $a,b\geq 0$ with $a+b>0$, \[  au+bv\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,a\theta +b\eta ).  \] In particular, $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is convex. If $\eta \geq \theta $, then $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\subseteq \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$. Proof. Omitting a term whose coefficient is zero, we see that $au+bv$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic. Moreover, \[  a\theta +b\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(au+bv) =a(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+b(\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)\geq 0.  \] For the inclusion, add the semipositive smooth form $\eta -\theta $ to $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. $\square$ By proposition 1.1.2 , any two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$ for a common sufficiently large constant $C$. This allows us to compare their singularities within one positive background.

title: Proposition 1.2.1
text: Proposition 1.2.1 . Let $f$ be a smooth real function on $X$, and set $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. Then \[  \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\longrightarrow \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta '), \qquad u\longmapsto u-f  \] is a bijection. It preserves the positive current and changes each potential by a bounded function. Moreover, $\mathrm{d}\theta '=\mathrm{d}\theta $. Proof. For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  \theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-f)=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u.  \] The inverse map is $v\mapsto v+f$, and $f$ is bounded because $X$ is compact. The last assertion follows from $\mathrm{d}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=0$. $\square$

title: Proposition 1.2.2
text: Proposition 1.2.2 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$, then, for $a,b\geq 0$ with $a+b>0$, \[  au+bv\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,a\theta +b\eta ).  \] In particular, $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is convex.
