title: Lemma 1.17.3
text: Lemma 1.17.3 . Let $Z$ be a complex manifold and $T$ a closed real $(1,1)$-current on $Z$. There are a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\beta $ and a real distribution $v$ such that \[  T=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v.  \] If $T\geq 0$, then $v$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic. Any two distributional potentials in such decompositions differ by a smooth function. Proof. The local $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-Poincaré lemma gives real distributional potentials $v_ i$ on the sets of a cover of $Z$ by coordinate neighborhoods, with $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ i$; for positive $T$ these potentials are plurisubharmonic. See [ Chapter III, Section 1.18 and Proposition 1.19 , DemCADG ] . On overlaps $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ i-v_ j)=0$. Taking the Euclidean trace shows that $v_ i-v_ j$ is a harmonic distribution, so it is smooth by elliptic regularity. Choose a smooth locally finite partition of unity $(\chi _ i)$ subordinate to the cover and put $v=\sum _ i\chi _ i v_ i$, each term being extended by zero as a distribution. On the $j$th neighborhood, \[  v-v_ j=\sum _ i\chi _ i(v_ i-v_ j)  \] is smooth. Thus $\beta =T-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v-v_ j)$ is smooth on each neighborhood, hence on $Z$, and it is real and closed. For positive $T$, the same identity expresses $v$ locally as a plurisubharmonic function plus a smooth function. Finally, if $T=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=\beta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v'$ are two such decompositions, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v-v')=\beta '-\beta $ is smooth; taking a smooth Hermitian trace and applying elliptic regularity shows that $v-v'$ is smooth. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.17.4
text:
Lemma 1.17.4 . Let $Y$ be a connected compact complex manifold. Let $(D_ j)$ be a finite or countable family of distinct prime divisors on $Y$ and $c_ j>0$ real coefficients such that $S=\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]$ is a positive current of finite mass, and let $ eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $Y$. Let $v\in \mathrm{QPSH}(Y)$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=S- eta .  \] Then, for $a\in \mathrm{QPSH}(Y)$, the following conditions are equivalent: \[  a\preceq v,\qquad a\preceq _{\mathcal I}v,\qquad 
u (a,D_ j)\geq c_ j\quad \hbox{for every }j.  \] Proof. We first note that $
u (v,D_ j)=c_ j$. Indeed, the restriction of $S$ to $D_ j$ is $c_ j[D_ j]$: distinct divisors intersect in codimension at least two, and such sets carry no mass of any divisor current, also after countable summation. Smooth forms give every divisor zero mass. The local form of Siu's decomposition, applied after a smooth correction, therefore gives $
u (v,D_ j)=c_ j$. Ordinary domination implies ideal domination by proposition 1.12.4 , and ideal domination implies the asserted inequalities for generic Lelong numbers by theorem 1.16.3 . It remains to prove that these inequalities imply ordinary domination. Choose a Hermitian form $\Lambda $ with $a\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\Lambda )$. By lemma 1.17.1 and the inequalities $
u (a,D_ j)\geq c_ j$, each finite partial sum of $S$ can be subtracted from $\Lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ without losing positivity. Letting the partial sums increase to $S$ gives \[  \Lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a-S\geq 0.  \] Consequently $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a-v)\geq  eta -\Lambda $. Hence the integrable function $a-v$ has a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative, which is bounded above on the compact manifold $Y$. This yields $a\leq v+C$ almost everywhere, and lemma 1.3.3 extends this inequality everywhere. Thus $a\preceq v$. $\square$

title: Corollary 1.17.5
text: Corollary 1.17.5 . Let $Z$ be a connected compact complex manifold, let $(D_ j)$ be a finite or countable family of distinct prime divisors on $Z$, and let $c_ j>0$. Suppose that $S=\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]$ is a closed positive current of finite mass. Then there are quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $v$ on $Z$ satisfying \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=S-\beta  \] for a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\beta $, and any two such functions differ by a smooth function. In particular, they determine a canonical ordinary singularity type, which depends only on $S$. Proof. Lemma 1.17.3 , applied to $T=S$, gives the decomposition, with $v$ quasi-plurisubharmonic since $S\geq 0$, and shows that any two such potentials differ by a smooth function. By proposition 1.12.2 , they have the same ordinary singularity type. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.17.6
text:
Lemma 1.17.6 . Let $u_ j,u$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on a complex manifold with a common smooth lower curvature bound, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\geq - eta $ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq - eta $ for one smooth real $(1,1)$-form $ eta $. If $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then at every point $x$, \[  
u (u,x)\geq \limsup _ j
u (u_ j,x).  \] Proof. On a coordinate ball about $x$, add one smooth function to all the potentials to make them plurisubharmonic, and write $p_ j,p$ for the resulting functions. Let $n$ be the dimension and $\kappa $ the Euclidean form of the chart. Distributional convergence gives weak convergence of the positive trace measures $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_ j\wedge \kappa ^{n-1}$ to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p\wedge \kappa ^{n-1}$. For every sufficiently small radius $r$ such that the sphere of radius $r$ about $x$ has zero mass for the limit measure, the masses of the balls converge. The Lelong monotonicity formula bounds each $
u (p_ j,x)$ by the normalized trace mass of $p_ j$ on such a ball. Taking the upper limit in $j$, and then letting these radii decrease to zero, gives $\limsup _ j
u (p_ j,x)\leq 
u (p,x)$. Since smooth additions do not change Lelong numbers, this proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.17.7
text: Lemma 1.17.7 . Let $Z$ be a connected compact complex manifold and let $\beta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form. There is a finite constant $C_\beta $ such that \[  \nu (v,z)\leq C_\beta \qquad \text{for every }v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Z,\beta )\text{ and every }z\in Z.  \] In particular, the generic Lelong numbers of all $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Z,\beta )$ along all prime divisors are bounded by $C_\beta $. No normalization of the potentials is needed. Proof. Since adding a constant does not change Lelong numbers, we may assume that $\sup _ Zv=0$. By theorem 1.4.2 , these normalized potentials have a common $L^1$ bound. Cover $Z$ by finitely many triples of concentric coordinate balls, a smaller, an intermediate and a larger one, such that the smaller balls cover $Z$. On each larger ball choose a fixed smooth quadratic function $r$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r\geq \beta $, so that $p=v+r$ is plurisubharmonic there. The functions $p$ obtained in this way have uniformly bounded local $L^1$ norms. Write $d=\dim Z$ and let $\kappa $ be the Euclidean form in the chart. Choose a nonnegative smooth cutoff $\chi $ supported in the larger ball and equal to one on an intermediate ball. Positivity and distributional integration by parts give \[  \int _{\text{intermediate ball}}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p\wedge \kappa ^{d-1} \leq \int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p\wedge \kappa ^{d-1} =\int p\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \kappa ^{d-1} \leq C\| p\| _{L^1}.  \] Every point of the smaller ball is the center of a Euclidean ball of a fixed radius contained in the intermediate ball. The local Lelong monotonicity formula, recalled in [ SGPT ] , bounds the Lelong number at this center by a fixed multiple of the trace mass of the intermediate ball. The finite cover gives one bound on $Z$. Since smooth additions and additive constants do not change Lelong numbers, this proves the assertion for the original potentials. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.17.8
text:
Lemma 1.17.8 . For a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $X$, every local divisor $E$ over $X$, and every real $m>0$, one has \[  \max \! \left\{ 
u _ E(u)- rac{A_ U(E)}m,0ight\}  \leq  rac1m\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(mu) \leq 
u _ E(u).  \] Here $\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(mu)$ is the order along $E$ of the pulled-back ideal. Consequently, if locally $a_ m=m^{-1}\log \sum _ k|f_{m,k}|^2+O(1)$, where the $f_{m,k}$ generate $\mathcal I(mu)$, then $
u _ E(a_ m)	o 
u _ E(u)$ as $m	o \infty $. Proof. The upper estimate follows from the local Bergman lower bound in proposition 1.14.1 : the logarithm of the sum of squared moduli of local generators of $\mathcal I(mu)$, divided by $m$, is at least $u$ up to a locally bounded term. Pulling back and taking generic Lelong numbers along $E$ reverses this inequality. For the lower estimate, take a local generator $f$ of the ideal and set $k=\operatorname {ord}_ E(f\circ \pi )$. Near a generic point of $E$, choose a local coordinate $z_1$ defining $E$. Divisorial removal (lemma 1.17.1 ), after a smooth correction, gives \[  u\circ \pi \leq 
u _ E(u)\log |z_1|^2+C.  \] Shrink around a point where the factors of $f\circ \pi $ and of the Jacobian complementary to the powers of $z_1$ do not vanish. The change-of-variables formula and local integrability of $|f|^2\mathrm{e}^{-mu}$ then require integrability in $z_1$ of \[  |z_1|^{2(k+A_ U(E)-1-m
u _ E(u))}.  \] This implies $k+A_ U(E)>m
u _ E(u)$, and in particular the weaker non-strict lower bound in the statement. Taking the minimum over a finite set of local generators and using that orders are nonnegative proves the lower estimate. Since $
u _ E(a_ m)=m^{-1}\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(mu)$, the last assertion follows by letting $m	o \infty $. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.17.9
text:
Lemma 1.17.9 . Let $U$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n$, let $u$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic on $U$, and let $\pi :Y	o U$ be a modification with smooth source. Fix $y\in Y$ and an integer $m\geq 1$. Write $J_\pi $ for the holomorphic Jacobian in local coordinates near $y$. If a nonzero holomorphic germ $g$ at $\pi (y)$ belongs to $\mathcal I(mu)$, then \[  \operatorname {ord}_ y(g\circ \pi ) \geq m
u (u\circ \pi ,y)-n-\operatorname {ord}_ yJ_\pi .  \] Proof. If $n\geq 2$, let $ho :\widetilde Y	o Y$ be the blowup of $y$ and let $E$ be its exceptional divisor. For $n=1$, take $ho $ to be the identity and $E=\{ y\} $. Set $F=\pi \circ ho $ and write $J_ F$ for its local holomorphic Jacobian determinant. Generic orders along $E$ give \[  
u (u\circ F,E)=
u (u\circ \pi ,y),\qquad \operatorname {ord}_ E(g\circ F)=\operatorname {ord}_ y(g\circ \pi ).  \] On a standard blowup chart the Jacobian of $ho $ has order $n-1$ along $E$. The chain rule therefore gives the log discrepancy over $U$ as \[  A_ U(E)=1+\operatorname {ord}_ E J_ F =n+\operatorname {ord}_ yJ_\pi .  \] Since $g\in \mathcal I(mu)$, the order of $g\circ F$ along $E$ is at least the order of this ideal. The lower estimate in lemma 1.17.8 , applied to $F$, therefore proves the inequality. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.17.10
text:
Lemma 1.17.10 . Let $v$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic on $X$, and let $a$ have analytic singularities on $X$. If $v\preceq _{\mathcal I}a$, then $v\preceq a$. More precisely, it suffices to assume the finitely many inequalities \[  
u (v\circ \pi ,E)\geq 
u (a\circ \pi ,E)  \] for the prime components $E$ of the divisor obtained by principalizing, on one log resolution $\pi $, the ideal of an analytic presentation of $a$. Proof. Principalize the coherent ideal of an analytic presentation of $a$ by a log resolution $\pi :Y	o X$ with smooth $Y$. In suitable local coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ n$ on $Y$, \[  a\circ \pi =\sum _{i=1}^ r b_ i\log |z_ i|^2+B, \qquad b_ i\geq 0,\qquad B\in L^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}},  \] where $r\leq n$. The finitely many inequalities in the statement give $
u (v\circ \pi ,\{ z_ i=0\} )\geq b_ i$; if $v\preceq _{\mathcal I}a$, these inequalities follow from theorem 1.16.3 . Add a smooth local function to $v\circ \pi $ to make it plurisubharmonic. Divisorial removal for this closed positive complex Hessian shows that \[  v\circ \pi -\sum _ i b_ i\log |z_ i|^2  \] has a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative; here the difference is first interpreted off the divisor, or as a locally integrable distribution. Such a representative is locally bounded above. Since $B$ is locally bounded, $v\circ \pi \leq a\circ \pi +C$ on each relatively compact chart of $Y$, away from the divisor. Since $\pi $ is proper, finitely many such charts cover the inverse image of a smaller coordinate neighborhood in $X$, which makes $C$ uniform there. Push the inequality down off the analytic exceptional set; as quasi-plurisubharmonic functions are determined by their values almost everywhere, it then holds everywhere. Finitely many neighborhoods cover the compact manifold, so $v\leq a+C$ globally. The only input from resolution of singularities is the principalization of a coherent ideal. Divisorial removal is applied to the closed positive complex Hessian obtained after a local smooth correction, so no closed background on $X$ is needed. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.17.11
text:
Lemma 1.17.11 . Let $u,v$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic on $X$, and let $s$ have analytic singularities on $X$. Suppose that $u+v\leq s+O(1)$, and let $U_ m,V_ m$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions of analytic types $(1/m,\mathcal I(mu))$ and $(1/m,\mathcal I(mv))$. Then there are numbers $\delta _ m\downarrow 0$ such that \[  U_ m+V_ m\leq (1-\delta _ m)s+O(1) \quad \hbox{for all sufficiently large integers }m.  \] The bounded error may depend on $m$. Proof. If $s$ is bounded, upper bounds for $U_ m$ and $V_ m$ give the assertion with $\delta _ m=1/m$ for $m>1$. Otherwise principalize the ideal of $s$ by a log resolution $\pi :\widetilde X	o X$ with smooth $\widetilde X$. Let $E_ i$ be the components of the resulting divisor, with positive coefficients $c_ i$ in $s\circ \pi $; in local coordinates $z_ i$ defining these components, the singular part of $s\circ \pi $ is $\sum _ i c_ i\log |z_ i|^2$. Set $A_ i=1+\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}(\operatorname {Jac}\pi )$. The hypothesis and lemma 1.17.8 give \[  
u (U_ m\circ \pi ,E_ i)+
u (V_ m\circ \pi ,E_ i) \geq 
u (u\circ \pi ,E_ i)+
u (v\circ \pi ,E_ i)- rac{2A_ i}{m} \geq c_ i- rac{2A_ i}{m}.  \] Choose a positive integer $N\geq \max _ i2A_ i/c_ i$ and put $\delta _ m=N/m$, which is less than one for large $m$. Then the right-hand side above is at least $(1-\delta _ m)c_ i$. After a smooth local correction, divisorial removal from the positive Hessian of $(U_ m+V_ m)\circ \pi $ shows that \[  (U_ m+V_ m)\circ \pi -(1-\delta _ m)\sum _ i c_ i\log |z_ i|^2  \] has a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative, which is locally bounded above. A finite cover of $\widetilde X$ by charts and descent along the proper map $\pi $, as in the proof of lemma 1.17.10 , therefore give $U_ m+V_ m\leq (1-\delta _ m)s+O(1)$. The bounded constant may depend on $m$. $\square$

title: 1.18 Potential regularity and metric distance
text: 1.18 Potential regularity and metric distance A Hölder modulus of continuity of the potential controls the trace mass of a positive current on small balls. Averaging the lengths of segments against this trace measure then bounds the distance of the metric defined by the current on its regular locus. This turns regularity of the potential into a metric estimate without any pointwise bound on the Hessian. Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a coordinate domain with Euclidean form $\omega _{\mathrm E}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and Euclidean volume $\mathrm{d}\lambda $. Let $0<\alpha \leq 1$, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $U$, and let $v\in C^{0,\alpha }(U)$ satisfy $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0$. Write $\mu =T\wedge \omega _{\mathrm E}^{n-1}$ for the trace measure of $T$. Theorem 1.18.1 . For every open set $V\Subset U$ there are constants $C,r_0>0$ such that 1.59 \begin{equation} \label{eq:trace-ball} \mu (B(x,r))\leq C r^{2n-2+\alpha },\qquad x\in V,\quad 0<r<r_0. \end{equation} The total variation of every coefficient measure of $T$ is bounded by a constant multiple of $\mu $. Hence the coefficient measures of $T$ vanish on sets of zero Hausdorff $(2n-2+\alpha )$-measure, and all Lelong numbers of $v$ vanish. The estimate implies neither absolute continuity of $\mu $ nor a pointwise bound for the Hessian of $v$. Suppose in addition that $T$ is a smooth Hermitian form $\eta $ on $U\setminus A$ for a proper analytic subset $A\subset U$. For $x,y\in U\setminus A$, let $d_\eta ^ U(x,y)$ be the infimum of the $\eta $-lengths of piecewise smooth paths in $U\setminus A$ joining $x$ and $y$. Then every point of $U$ has a neighborhood $V\Subset U$ such that, for a constant $C$, 1.60 \begin{equation} \label{eq:holder-distance} d_\eta ^ U(x,y)\leq C|x-y|^{\alpha /2},\qquad x,y\in V\setminus A. \end{equation} In particular, all sequences in $V\setminus A$ converging to a given point of $A\cap V$ are Cauchy for $d_\eta ^ U$ and have a common limit in the metric completion. If these local hypotheses hold in charts covering $X$, with a proper analytic subset $A\subset X$ and a Hermitian form $\eta $ on $X\setminus A$, then the metric completion of $X\setminus A$ for its intrinsic $\eta $-distance is compact, and the identity of $X\setminus A$ extends to a continuous surjection of $X$ onto it. The metric $\eta $ is incomplete when $A\ne \varnothing $. Both exponents in ( 1.59 ) and ( 1.60 ) are sharp. Proof. Choose a nonnegative cutoff function $\chi $ equal to one on $B(x,r)$ and supported in $B(x,2r)$, with second derivatives bounded by $Cr^{-2}$. Positivity and integration by parts, after subtracting the constant $v(x)$ from $v$, give \[  \mu (B(x,r))\leq C_1r^{2n}+C_2r^{2n-2} \operatorname {osc}_{B(x,2r)}v \leq Cr^{2n-2+\alpha }.  \] Here we used that the constant $v(x)$ integrates to zero against $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \omega _{\mathrm E}^{n-1}$. The matrix $(a_{ij})$ of Radon–Nikodym derivatives of the coefficient measures with respect to $\mu $ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, so $|a_{ij}|\leq (a_{ii}+a_{jj})/2$. A ball cover proves the assertion about Hausdorff null sets. After a smooth local correction making $v$ plurisubharmonic, dividing ( 1.59 ) by $r^{2n-2}$ shows that all Lelong numbers vanish. For the distance estimate, let $m=2n$ and let $\tau $ be the Euclidean trace of $\eta $. Then $\tau \, \mathrm{d}\lambda \leq C\mu $ on the regular locus and $|\xi |_\eta \leq C\sqrt\tau |\xi |_{\mathrm E}$ for tangent vectors $\xi $. Polar integration bounds the average $\eta $-length of the segments from $x$ to the points of $B(x,R)$ by a constant times $\int _{B(x,R)}\sqrt\tau (\zeta )|\zeta -x|^{1-m}\, \mathrm{d}\lambda (\zeta )$. On a dyadic annulus of radius $s$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and ( 1.59 ) bound the contribution to this integral by $Cs^{1-m}s^{m/2}s^{(m-2+\alpha )/2}=Cs^{\alpha /2}$. Summing over the annuli gives the bound $CR^{\alpha /2}$. Now let $x,y\in V\setminus A$, and average the lengths of the broken segments $[x,z]\cup [z,y]$ over $z$ in the ball of radius $|x-y|/2$ about the midpoint of $x$ and $y$. By the preceding bound, some such path has length at most $C|x-y|^{\alpha /2}$. For almost every $z$, both segments avoid $A$: proper analytic sets are locally countable unions of smooth strata of real codimension at least two, and the cones from a fixed regular point over these strata have zero volume. If $V$ is small enough, all these paths stay inside $U$. By this estimate, all regular sequences converging to a point of $A$ have a common limit in the completion, and the identity of the regular locus extends continuously across $A$. By compactness, the image of this extension is the entire completion; different points of $A$ may be identified. A sequence converging to a point of $A$ cannot converge in the metric to a regular point, since $\eta $ is bounded below by a positive multiple of the Euclidean metric on a small closed neighborhood of that point. Hence the metric $\eta $ is incomplete when $A$ is nonempty. Finally, the local model $v=|z|^\alpha +|w|^2$, in coordinates $(z,w)\in \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^{n-1}$, has trace mass of exact order $r^{2n-2+\alpha }$ on balls centered on $\{ z=0\} $, and the distance to $\{ z=0\} $ is of exact order $|z|^{\alpha /2}$; this proves both sharpness claims. In later applications to potentials with logarithmic poles, the theorem is applied to the positive residual current that remains after the divisorial part has been removed. $\square$

title: 1.18.1 Dini moduli and limits of distances
search_title: Dini moduli and limits of distances
text: 1.18.1 Dini moduli and limits of distances The annular argument of theorem 1.18.1 also applies to a continuous potential whose modulus of continuity is not a power; what matters is a Dini condition on the square root of the modulus. This gives uniform distance estimates for families whose Hölder constants are not controlled. Keep the coordinate domain $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ with its Euclidean form $\omega _{\mathrm E}$ and volume $\mathrm{d}\lambda $, but now let $v\in C^0(U)$ and let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0$. On the relatively compact charts under consideration, choose a nondecreasing function $m:(0,r_0)\to [0,+\infty )$ with $m(r)\to 0$ as $r\to 0$ such that \[  |v(x)-v(y)|\leq m(|x-y|),\qquad |x-y|<r_0.  \] Put 1.61 \begin{equation} \label{eq:dini-distance-modulus} D(r)=r+\int _0^ r\frac{\sqrt{m(t)}}{t}\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{equation} Theorem 1.18.2 . Assume that $D(r_0/2)<+\infty $ and that $T$ is a smooth Hermitian form $\eta $ on $U\setminus A$ for a proper analytic subset $A\subset U$. Then every point of $U$ has a neighborhood $V\Subset U$ with constants $C,r_1>0$ such that, for $x,y\in V$, \[  d_\eta ^ U(x,y)\leq C D(8|x-y|), \qquad x,y\notin A,\quad |x-y|<r_1.  \] The constants depend only on the charts and an upper bound for $|\theta |$; the dependence on $v$ enters only through $D$. All sequences in $V\setminus A$ converging to a given point of $A\cap V$ have a common limit in the metric completion. If these hypotheses hold on a finite cover of a compact connected manifold by charts, the metric completion of the regular locus is compact, and the identity of the regular locus extends to a continuous surjection of the manifold onto it. If $A$ is nonempty, the metric $\eta $ on the regular locus is incomplete. Proof. Write $d=2n$ and $\mu =T\wedge \omega _{\mathrm E}^{n-1}$. The same cutoff calculation as in theorem 1.18.1 , with a constant subtracted from $v$, gives \[  \mu (B(x,s))\leq C\bigl (s^ d+s^{d-2}m(2s)\bigr ).  \] This uses only the bound for $\theta $; closedness of $\theta $ is not needed. If $\tau $ is the Euclidean trace of $\eta $, then $\tau \, \mathrm{d}\lambda \leq C\mu $ on the regular locus. Polar integration bounds the average length of the segments from a regular point $x$ to the points of $B(x,R)$ by \[  C\int _{B(x,R)}\sqrt{\tau (\zeta )} |\zeta -x|^{1-d}\, \mathrm{d}\lambda (\zeta ).  \] On an annulus of outer radius $s$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the trace bound make the contribution to this integral at most \[  Cs^{1-d}s^{d/2} \bigl (s^ d+s^{d-2}m(2s)\bigr )^{1/2} \leq C\bigl (s+\sqrt{m(2s)}\bigr ).  \] For $s_ j=2^{-j}R$, monotonicity gives \[  \sum _{j\geq 0}\sqrt{m(2s_ j)} \leq \frac1{\log 2}\int _0^{4R}\frac{\sqrt{m(t)}}t\, \mathrm{d}t.  \] Indeed, $\sqrt{m(2s_ j)}\log 2$ is at most the integral of $\sqrt{m(t)}/t$ over $[2s_ j,4s_ j]$, and these intervals have disjoint interiors; no doubling condition on $m$ is needed. The average length is therefore at most $CD(4R)$. For $x,y\in V\setminus A$, average the lengths of the broken segments $[x,z]\cup [z,y]$ over $z$ in the ball of radius $|x-y|/2$ about the midpoint of $x$ and $y$, applying the preceding bound with $R=2|x-y|$ at each endpoint. Since the volume of this ball is comparable to $R^ d$, some broken path has length at most $CD(8|x-y|)$. As in the proof of theorem 1.18.1 , almost every such path avoids $A$, and for small $V$ it stays inside $U$. Since $D(r_0/2)<+\infty $, we have $D(r)\to 0$ as $r\to 0$. Hence any two regular sequences converging to the same point are Cauchy and have the same limit in the completion. The argument for the completion in the proof of theorem 1.18.1 applies with this modulus. A positive lower bound for $\eta $ near a regular point prevents a sequence converging to a point of $A$ from converging in the metric to the regular point. This also proves incompleteness when $A$ is nonempty. $\square$ Corollary 1.18.3 . In the setting of theorem 1.18.2 , let $V$ be as in the theorem. For $0<\beta \leq 1$, a modulus $m(r)\leq Cr^\beta $ gives $d_\eta ^ U(x,y)\leq C'|x-y|^{\beta /2}$ for sufficiently close $x,y\in V\setminus A$. If instead \[  m(r)\leq C(-\log r)^{-a},\qquad a>2,  \] then for sufficiently close $x,y\in V\setminus A$, \[  d_\eta ^ U(x,y)\leq C'(-\log |x-y|)^{1-a/2}.  \] These are only sufficient conditions; we do not claim that the Dini condition is necessary. Proof. Integrating the square root of the power modulus gives a multiple of $r^{\beta /2}$. For the logarithmic modulus, the substitution $s=-\log t$ gives \[  \int _0^ r\frac{(-\log t)^{-a/2}}t\, \mathrm{d}t =\frac{(-\log r)^{1-a/2}}{a/2-1}.  \] In either case the term $r$ in $D(r)$ is bounded by the asserted rate for small $r$. The theorem now gives both estimates; the fixed dilation of the argument of $D$ changes only the constants. $\square$ Corollary 1.18.4 . Let $\omega _0$ be a Hermitian form on $X$ and $d_{\omega _0}$ the distance of the associated Riemannian metric. For each $j$, let $T_ j=\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq 0$, where $\theta _ j$ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, $v_ j$ is continuous, and $T_ j$ is a smooth Hermitian form off a proper analytic subset $A_ j$. Assume \[  |\theta _ j|_{\omega _0}\leq \Lambda ,\qquad |v_ j(x)-v_ j(y)|\leq m(d_{\omega _0}(x,y)),  \] with one fixed $\Lambda $ and one nondecreasing modulus $m$ tending to zero such that the function in ( 1.61 ) satisfies $D(r_0/2)<+\infty $. By theorem 1.18.2 , the identity of $X\setminus A_ j$ extends to a continuous surjection of $X$ onto the metric completion of $X\setminus A_ j$; let $d_ j$ be the pseudometric on $X$ obtained by pulling back the completed distance. Then the diameters of the $d_ j$ are uniformly bounded, and a subsequence converges uniformly on $X\times X$ to a continuous pseudometric. If $T_ j\geq c\omega _0$ on the regular loci for one $c>0$, the limit is a metric and dominates $\sqrt c\, d_{\omega _0}$. Proof. A finite fixed chart cover and the theorem give common constants $C,r_1>0$ such that \[  d_ j(x,y)\leq CD(Cd_{\omega _0}(x,y)), \qquad d_{\omega _0}(x,y)<r_1.  \] For a pair meeting $A_ j$, approximate it by regular pairs in the manifold topology. The completed distance and $D$ are continuous, so the same estimate holds for all such pairs in $X\times X$. No uniform bound on the geometry of the analytic sets enters the constants. Dividing a minimizing geodesic of $d_{\omega _0}$ into a uniformly bounded number of short pieces and using the triangle inequality gives a uniform diameter bound. The triangle inequality also gives \[  |d_ j(x,y)-d_ j(x',y')| \leq d_ j(x,x')+d_ j(y,y'),  \] so the distance functions are equicontinuous. The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem gives a subsequence $d_{j_ k}$ converging uniformly on $X\times X$ to a function $d_\infty $. Nonnegativity, symmetry, vanishing on the diagonal and the triangle inequality pass to the limit. The lower bound $T_ j\geq c\omega _0$ gives $d_ j\geq \sqrt c\, d_{\omega _0}$, first for regular pairs and then for all pairs, which proves the last assertion. Without this lower bound the limit may degenerate. For $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, take $\theta _ j=\varepsilon _ j\omega _0$ and $v_ j=0$, with $A_ j=\varnothing $. These data satisfy the hypotheses with $m(r)=r^2$, and $d_ j=\sqrt{\varepsilon _ j}\, d_{\omega _0}$ converges uniformly to zero. $\square$
1.61 \begin{equation} \label{eq:dini-distance-modulus} D(r)=r+\int _0^ r\frac{\sqrt{m(t)}}{t}\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 1.18.2
text: Theorem 1.18.2 . Assume that $D(r_0/2)<+\infty $ and that $T$ is a smooth Hermitian form $\eta $ on $U\setminus A$ for a proper analytic subset $A\subset U$. Then every point of $U$ has a neighborhood $V\Subset U$ with constants $C,r_1>0$ such that, for $x,y\in V$, \[  d_\eta ^ U(x,y)\leq C D(8|x-y|), \qquad x,y\notin A,\quad |x-y|<r_1.  \] The constants depend only on the charts and an upper bound for $|\theta |$; the dependence on $v$ enters only through $D$. All sequences in $V\setminus A$ converging to a given point of $A\cap V$ have a common limit in the metric completion. If these hypotheses hold on a finite cover of a compact connected manifold by charts, the metric completion of the regular locus is compact, and the identity of the regular locus extends to a continuous surjection of the manifold onto it. If $A$ is nonempty, the metric $\eta $ on the regular locus is incomplete. Proof. Write $d=2n$ and $\mu =T\wedge \omega _{\mathrm E}^{n-1}$. The same cutoff calculation as in theorem 1.18.1 , with a constant subtracted from $v$, gives \[  \mu (B(x,s))\leq C\bigl (s^ d+s^{d-2}m(2s)\bigr ).  \] This uses only the bound for $\theta $; closedness of $\theta $ is not needed. Since the volume of this ball is comparable to $R^ d$, some broken path has length at most $CD(8|x-y|)$. As in the proof of theorem 1.18.1 , almost every such path avoids $A$, and for small $V$ it stays inside $U$. Since $D(r_0/2)<+\infty $, we have $D(r)\to 0$ as $r\to 0$. Hence any two regular sequences converging to the same point are Cauchy and have the same limit in the completion. The argument for the completion in the proof of theorem 1.18.1 applies with this modulus. A positive lower bound for $\eta $ near a regular point prevents a sequence converging to a point of $A$ from converging in the metric to the regular point. This also proves incompleteness when $A$ is nonempty. $\square$

title: 1.19 Obstacle envelopes
text: 1.19 Obstacle envelopes Given an obstacle function, one looks for the largest $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function lying below it. The local upper-envelope theorem constructs this envelope as soon as the competitors have a common upper bound, and normalized compactness provides such a bound for an obstacle that is finite almost everywhere or prescribed on a non-pluripolar compact set. Letting the obstacles $\min (u+C,0)$ increase with $C$ produces the envelope $P_\theta [u]$ of the ordinary singularity type of $u$. A smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ is called big if there are $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\delta >0$ such that \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \omega .  \] Here $\omega $ is any Hermitian form; changing it changes $\delta $ but not the condition. The definition does not require $\theta $ to be closed. Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form. For an extended-real function $f$ on $X$, defined at least outside a pluripolar set (the obstacle ), write \[  P_\theta (f)=\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):v\leq f \  \hbox{q.e.}\} \right)^*.  \] As in section 1.6 , q.e. (quasi-everywhere) means outside a pluripolar set. The functions $v$ in the supremum are called competitors ; the empty supremum is $-\infty $. For obstacles $f_1,\ldots ,f_ N$, we write $P_\theta (f_1,\ldots ,f_ N)=P_\theta (\min _ if_ i)$; when the $f_ i$ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, this is their rooftop envelope . For an upper semicontinuous obstacle, the pointwise constraint $v\leq f$ gives the same competitors: by the local submean inequality and upper semicontinuity of $f$, a quasi-plurisubharmonic function lying below $f$ almost everywhere lies below it everywhere. If the family of competitors is nonempty and uniformly bounded above, then $P_\theta (f)\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. To apply the local upper-envelope theorem while keeping the exact lower bound $-\theta $, fix a constant positive form $\kappa $ in local coordinates. For each $\epsilon >0$, shrink the coordinate neighborhood and choose a constant form $\theta '$ with $-\epsilon \kappa \leq \theta -\theta '\leq \epsilon \kappa $. A smooth function $r$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=\theta '+\epsilon \kappa $ makes every competitor plus $r$ plurisubharmonic, so the local envelope theorem gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_\theta (f)\geq -2\epsilon \kappa $ there. Letting $\epsilon $ tend to zero proves the exact bound. The same local theorem shows that the regularization changes the supremum only on a pluripolar set. The following observation gives the upper bound for an unbounded obstacle. Suppose that $f\leq A$, for a real constant $A$, on a Borel set $E$ with $\operatorname {Vol}(E)=\int _ E\mathrm{d}V>0$, where $\mathrm{d}V$ is the volume form fixed in theorem 1.4.2 . If $h$ is a competitor, put $\widetilde h=h-\sup _ Xh$. By theorem 1.4.2 , \[  (\sup _ Xh-A)\operatorname {Vol}(E) \leq \int _ E|\widetilde h|\, \mathrm{d}V\leq C_\theta \quad \hbox{whenever }\sup _ Xh>A.  \] Thus $\sup _ Xh\leq A+C_\theta /\operatorname {Vol}(E)$ for every competitor. In particular, the competitors for a measurable obstacle that is finite almost everywhere have a common upper bound: apply this to a sublevel set $\{ f\leq A\} $ of positive volume. An obstacle bound on a non-pluripolar compact set also bounds every competitor globally, even when that set has zero smooth volume. Lemma 1.19.1 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact and non-pluripolar, and let $w\in C(K,\mathbb R)$. There is a constant $C=C(\theta ,K,w)$ such that every $a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfying $a\leq w$ quasi-everywhere on $K$ has $\sup _ X a\leq C$. Proof. Otherwise there are such functions $a_ j$ with \[  M_ j:=\sup _ Xa_ j\geq 2^ j+\max _ Kw.  \] The normalized functions $v_ j=a_ j-M_ j\leq 0$ have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms by theorem 1.4.2 . Choose $A>0$ with $\theta \leq A\omega $. The partial sums \[  s_ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}v_ j  \] decrease, have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms, and satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s_ N\geq -A\omega $. By corollary 1.4.3 , their limit $s$ is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function; in particular, $s$ is not identically $-\infty $. Let $N_ j\subseteq K$ be a pluripolar set outside which $a_ j\leq w$ on $K$. On $K\setminus \bigcup _ jN_ j$ one has $v_ j\leq -2^ j$ for every $j$, hence $s=-\infty $. The pole set $\{ s=-\infty \} $ of the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $s$ is pluripolar, and so is the countable union of the $N_ j$. Their union would contain all of $K$, contradicting the hypothesis on $K$. $\square$ Suppose that $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is nonempty. Then the envelope of the zero obstacle, \[  V_\theta =P_\theta (0),  \] belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$: the competitors are bounded above by zero, and they include $u-\sup _ Xu$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. In particular, \[  u-\sup _ Xu\leq V_\theta \qquad (u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )).  \] A potential $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities if $u\preceq v$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By the last inequality, $V_\theta $ has minimal singularities, and every potential $v$ with minimal singularities satisfies $v\sim V_\theta $. If $\theta \geq 0$, then $0$ is a competitor, and hence $V_\theta =0$. Lemma 1.19.2 . Let $\eta $ be a smooth semipositive real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. If an obstacle $f$ is finite almost everywhere and bounded below quasi-everywhere by a constant, then $P_\eta (f)$ is a bounded $\eta $-plurisubharmonic function. Proof. Since $\eta \geq 0$, constants are $\eta $-plurisubharmonic, so the constant lower bound of $f$ is a competitor. The finite-sublevel argument above gives a common upper bound for all competitors. Hence $P_\eta (f)$ is an $\eta $-plurisubharmonic function lying between these two constants. $\square$ Proposition 1.19.3 . If $f\in C^0(X)$, then $P_\omega (f)$ is continuous. Moreover, \[  \| P_\omega (f)-P_\omega (g)\| _\infty \leq \| f-g\| _\infty \quad (f,g\in C^0(X)).  \] Proof. The constant $\min _ Xf$ is a competitor, so $p=P_\omega (f)$ is bounded. The local envelope theorem gives $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere, and continuity of $f$ makes this inequality hold everywhere. By theorem 1.11.1 , there are smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ j\downarrow p$. Fix $\epsilon >0$. The continuous functions $v_ j-f$ decrease to a function that is at most zero, so $v_ j\leq f+\epsilon $ everywhere for all large $j$; otherwise the decreasing compact sets $\{ v_ j-f\geq \epsilon \} $ would have nonempty intersection. Hence $v_ j-\epsilon $ is a competitor, and \[  p\leq v_ j\leq p+\epsilon .  \] Thus $v_ j\to p$ uniformly, which proves continuity. The last inequality follows from the monotonicity of $P_\omega $ in the obstacle and the identity $P_\omega (g+c)=P_\omega (g)+c$ for constants $c$, applied with $c=\| f-g\| _\infty $. $\square$ Definition 1.19.4 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, set \[  P_\theta [u] =\left(\lim _{C\to +\infty }P_\theta (u+C,0)\right)^* =\left(\sup \{ h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):h\preceq u,\  h\leq 0\} \right)^*.  \] We call $u$ an envelope fixed point , or an ordinary model , if $P_\theta [u]=u$; in the Kähler literature such potentials are called model potentials . For $F\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, replacing the constraint $h\leq 0$ by $h\leq F$ defines $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$. The two expressions agree, because the family in the second one is the increasing union over $C$ of the families defining $P_\theta (u+C,0)$. They do not change if zero is replaced by $V_\theta $, since every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function below zero lies below $V_\theta $. The competitors include $u-\sup _ Xu$ and are bounded above by zero, so $P_\theta [u]\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $u-\sup _ Xu\leq P_\theta [u]\leq 0$. In particular, $u\preceq P_\theta [u]$; this does not assert that $P_\theta [u]-u$ is bounded. Directly from the definition, $P_\theta [u]$ depends only on the ordinary singularity type of $u$, and \[  u\preceq v\quad \Longrightarrow \quad P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [v].  \] Replacing the condition $h\preceq u$ by $h\sim _{\mathcal I}u$ gives the multiplier-ideal envelope $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ of definition 16.2.1 . This is a different operator; its relation to $P_\theta [u]$ is studied in chapter 16 . For a bounded obstacle in a big background, exceptional sets in the competitor inequality can be removed by a small singular perturbation. Lemma 1.19.5 . Let $\theta $ be big, let $f$ be a bounded function on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Then there are $u_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $t>0$, such that $u_ t\leq f$ everywhere and $u_ t\to u$ almost everywhere as $t\downarrow 0$. Proof. Choose $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa \omega $ for some $\kappa >0$. The exceptional set $E=\{ u>f\} $ is pluripolar. The global form of Josefson's theorem on compact complex manifolds gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\chi $ with $\chi =-\infty $ on $E$; see [ Theorem 1.1.5 , SGPT ] . After rescaling and adding a constant, we may assume that $\chi \leq 0$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \geq -\omega $. Subtract a constant from $\rho $ so that $\rho \leq \inf _ X f$. With $s=t/\kappa $, put \[  u_ t=\frac{u+t\chi +s\rho }{1+s}.  \] All three functions in the numerator are finite almost everywhere, so $u_ t$ is not identically $-\infty $. Moreover, \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t =\frac{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi +s(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )}{1+s} \geq 0.  \] Outside $E$, both $u$ and $\rho $ are at most $f$, while $\chi \leq 0$, so $u_ t\leq f$. On $E$ the numerator is $-\infty $. Finally, $u_ t\to u$ wherever all three functions are finite, which is a set of full measure. $\square$ For an obstacle prescribed only on a compact set, the same perturbation shows that pluripolar exceptions in the constraint do not change the regularized envelope. Proposition 1.19.6 . Let $\theta $ be big, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact and non-pluripolar, and let $\psi $ be a bounded real function on $K$. Set \[  \begin{aligned}  R& =\sup \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\leq \psi \text{ on }K\} ,\\  Q& =\sup \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\leq \psi \text{ q.e. on }K\} . \end{aligned}  \] Then $R^*=Q^*$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and has minimal singularities; it is bounded if $\theta \geq 0$. Moreover, this regularized envelope does not change if the pointwise constraint is imposed only on $K\setminus E$, for any pluripolar subset $E\subseteq K$. Proof. Put $m=\inf _ K\psi $ and $M=\sup _ K\psi $. Since $\theta $ is big, $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is nonempty, and $V_\theta \leq 0$; hence $V_\theta +m$ belongs to the family defining $R$. Applying lemma 1.19.1 with the constant obstacle $M$ gives a common upper bound $C$ for the larger family defining $Q$. The upper-envelope argument at the beginning of section 1.19 therefore shows that $R^*$ and $Q^*$ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Now fix a competitor $u$ for $Q$ and define a bounded function on $X$ by \[  f(x)= \begin{cases}  \psi (x),& x\in K,\\  \max \{ \sup _ Xu,M\} ,& x\notin K. \end{cases}  \] Then $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. By lemma 1.19.5 , there are $u_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfying $u_ t\leq f$ everywhere and $u_ t\to u$ almost everywhere. Each $u_ t$ is a competitor for $R$, so $R^*\geq u$ almost everywhere, and lemma 1.3.3 gives this inequality everywhere. Taking the supremum over $u$ and regularizing yields $R^*\geq Q^*$; the inclusion of the competitor families gives the reverse inequality. Write $F=R^*=Q^*$. Since $F\leq C$, the potential $F-C$ is a competitor for $V_\theta $. Thus \[  V_\theta +m\leq F\leq V_\theta +C,  \] which proves minimal singularities and, when $\theta \geq 0$, boundedness. Finally, if $E\subseteq K$ is pluripolar, the family constrained on $K\setminus E$ lies between the families defining $R$ and $Q$, so its regularized supremum also equals $F$. Note that this argument uses the upper bound obtained from the compact set $K$, even when $K\setminus E$ is not compact. $\square$ A potential with minimal singularities stays away from the poles of a strictly positive potential with analytic singularities, in the following sense. Lemma 1.19.7 . Let $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have analytic singularities with smooth remainder and satisfy $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Set $\Omega =\{ \rho >-\infty \} $. If $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities and is continuous on $\Omega $, then $\varphi -\rho $ is continuous, bounded below, and proper on $\Omega $: all its sublevel sets are compact in $\Omega $. Proof. Adding constants to $\rho $ and $\varphi $ does not affect the assertions, so we may assume that $\rho \leq 0$ and $\sup _ X\varphi =0$. Since $\varphi $ has minimal singularities, there is a constant $C$ with $\varphi \geq V_\theta -C$. Choose $M\geq 0$ with $\theta \geq -M\omega $. If $a\in (0,1)$ is sufficiently close to one, then \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\rho ) =a(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )+(1-a)\theta \geq \bigl (a\varepsilon -(1-a)M\bigr )\omega >0.  \] Thus $a\rho $ is a competitor for $V_\theta $, and therefore \[  0\geq \varphi \geq V_\theta -C\geq a\rho -C,  \] and hence 1.66 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-gap-proper} \varphi -\rho \geq (1-a)(-\rho )-C. \end{equation} By hypothesis $\varphi $ is continuous on $\Omega $, and $\rho $ is smooth there because it has analytic singularities with smooth remainder. Hence $\varphi -\rho $ is continuous on $\Omega $, and by ( 1.66 ) it is bounded below. Since $\rho \to -\infty $ at $X\setminus \Omega $, the sets $\{ \rho \geq -c\} $ are compact subsets of $\Omega $, and ( 1.66 ) places every sublevel set of $\varphi -\rho $ in one of them. Being closed in $\Omega $, each sublevel set is therefore compact. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.19.1
text: Lemma 1.19.1 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact and non-pluripolar, and let $w\in C(K,\mathbb R)$. There is a constant $C=C(\theta ,K,w)$ such that every $a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfying $a\leq w$ quasi-everywhere on $K$ has $\sup _ X a\leq C$. Proof. Otherwise there are such functions $a_ j$ with \[  M_ j:=\sup _ Xa_ j\geq 2^ j+\max _ Kw.  \] The normalized functions $v_ j=a_ j-M_ j\leq 0$ have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms by theorem 1.4.2 . Choose $A>0$ with $\theta \leq A\omega $. The partial sums \[  s_ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}v_ j  \] decrease, have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms, and satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s_ N\geq -A\omega $. By corollary 1.4.3 , their limit $s$ is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function; in particular, $s$ is not identically $-\infty $. Let $N_ j\subseteq K$ be a pluripolar set outside which $a_ j\leq w$ on $K$. On $K\setminus \bigcup _ jN_ j$ one has $v_ j\leq -2^ j$ for every $j$, hence $s=-\infty $. The pole set $\{ s=-\infty \} $ of the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $s$ is pluripolar, and so is the countable union of the $N_ j$. Their union would contain all of $K$, contradicting the hypothesis on $K$. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.19.2
text: Lemma 1.19.2 . Let $\eta $ be a smooth semipositive real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. If an obstacle $f$ is finite almost everywhere and bounded below quasi-everywhere by a constant, then $P_\eta (f)$ is a bounded $\eta $-plurisubharmonic function. Proof. Since $\eta \geq 0$, constants are $\eta $-plurisubharmonic, so the constant lower bound of $f$ is a competitor. The finite-sublevel argument above gives a common upper bound for all competitors. Hence $P_\eta (f)$ is an $\eta $-plurisubharmonic function lying between these two constants. $\square$

title: Proposition 1.19.3
text: Proposition 1.19.3 . If $f\in C^0(X)$, then $P_\omega (f)$ is continuous. Moreover, \[  \| P_\omega (f)-P_\omega (g)\| _\infty \leq \| f-g\| _\infty \quad (f,g\in C^0(X)).  \] Proof. The constant $\min _ Xf$ is a competitor, so $p=P_\omega (f)$ is bounded. The local envelope theorem gives $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere, and continuity of $f$ makes this inequality hold everywhere. By theorem 1.11.1 , there are smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ j\downarrow p$. Fix $\epsilon >0$. The continuous functions $v_ j-f$ decrease to a function that is at most zero, so $v_ j\leq f+\epsilon $ everywhere for all large $j$; otherwise the decreasing compact sets $\{ v_ j-f\geq \epsilon \} $ would have nonempty intersection. Hence $v_ j-\epsilon $ is a competitor, and \[  p\leq v_ j\leq p+\epsilon .  \] Thus $v_ j\to p$ uniformly, which proves continuity. The last inequality follows from the monotonicity of $P_\omega $ in the obstacle and the identity $P_\omega (g+c)=P_\omega (g)+c$ for constants $c$, applied with $c=\| f-g\| _\infty $. $\square$

title: Definition 1.19.4
text: Definition 1.19.4 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, set \[  P_\theta [u] =\left(\lim _{C\to +\infty }P_\theta (u+C,0)\right)^* =\left(\sup \{ h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):h\preceq u,\  h\leq 0\} \right)^*.  \] We call $u$ an envelope fixed point , or an ordinary model , if $P_\theta [u]=u$; in the Kähler literature such potentials are called model potentials . For $F\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, replacing the constraint $h\leq 0$ by $h\leq F$ defines $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$.

title: Lemma 1.19.5
text: Lemma 1.19.5 . Let $\theta $ be big, let $f$ be a bounded function on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Then there are $u_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $t>0$, such that $u_ t\leq f$ everywhere and $u_ t\to u$ almost everywhere as $t\downarrow 0$. Proof. Choose $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa \omega $ for some $\kappa >0$. The exceptional set $E=\{ u>f\} $ is pluripolar. The global form of Josefson's theorem on compact complex manifolds gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\chi $ with $\chi =-\infty $ on $E$; see [ Theorem 1.1.5 , SGPT ] . After rescaling and adding a constant, we may assume that $\chi \leq 0$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \geq -\omega $. Subtract a constant from $\rho $ so that $\rho \leq \inf _ X f$. With $s=t/\kappa $, put \[  u_ t=\frac{u+t\chi +s\rho }{1+s}.  \] All three functions in the numerator are finite almost everywhere, so $u_ t$ is not identically $-\infty $. Moreover, \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t =\frac{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi +s(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )}{1+s} \geq 0.  \] Outside $E$, both $u$ and $\rho $ are at most $f$, while $\chi \leq 0$, so $u_ t\leq f$. On $E$ the numerator is $-\infty $. Finally, $u_ t\to u$ wherever all three functions are finite, which is a set of full measure. $\square$

title: Proposition 1.19.6
text: Proposition 1.19.6 . Let $\theta $ be big, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact and non-pluripolar, and let $\psi $ be a bounded real function on $K$. Set \[  \begin{aligned}  R& =\sup \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\leq \psi \text{ on }K\} ,\\  Q& =\sup \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\leq \psi \text{ q.e. on }K\} . \end{aligned}  \] Then $R^*=Q^*$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and has minimal singularities; it is bounded if $\theta \geq 0$. Moreover, this regularized envelope does not change if the pointwise constraint is imposed only on $K\setminus E$, for any pluripolar subset $E\subseteq K$. Proof. Put $m=\inf _ K\psi $ and $M=\sup _ K\psi $. Since $\theta $ is big, $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is nonempty, and $V_\theta \leq 0$; hence $V_\theta +m$ belongs to the family defining $R$. Applying lemma 1.19.1 with the constant obstacle $M$ gives a common upper bound $C$ for the larger family defining $Q$. The upper-envelope argument at the beginning of section 1.19 therefore shows that $R^*$ and $Q^*$ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Now fix a competitor $u$ for $Q$ and define a bounded function on $X$ by \[  f(x)= \begin{cases}  \psi (x),& x\in K,\\  \max \{ \sup _ Xu,M\} ,& x\notin K. \end{cases}  \] Then $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. By lemma 1.19.5 , there are $u_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfying $u_ t\leq f$ everywhere and $u_ t\to u$ almost everywhere. Each $u_ t$ is a competitor for $R$, so $R^*\geq u$ almost everywhere, and lemma 1.3.3 gives this inequality everywhere. Taking the supremum over $u$ and regularizing yields $R^*\geq Q^*$; the inclusion of the competitor families gives the reverse inequality. Write $F=R^*=Q^*$. Since $F\leq C$, the potential $F-C$ is a competitor for $V_\theta $. Thus \[  V_\theta +m\leq F\leq V_\theta +C,  \] which proves minimal singularities and, when $\theta \geq 0$, boundedness. Finally, if $E\subseteq K$ is pluripolar, the family constrained on $K\setminus E$ lies between the families defining $R$ and $Q$, so its regularized supremum also equals $F$. Note that this argument uses the upper bound obtained from the compact set $K$, even when $K\setminus E$ is not compact. $\square$

title: Lemma 1.19.7
text: Lemma 1.19.7 . Let $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have analytic singularities with smooth remainder and satisfy $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Set $\Omega =\{ \rho >-\infty \} $. If $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities and is continuous on $\Omega $, then $\varphi -\rho $ is continuous, bounded below, and proper on $\Omega $: all its sublevel sets are compact in $\Omega $. Proof. Adding constants to $\rho $ and $\varphi $ does not affect the assertions, so we may assume that $\rho \leq 0$ and $\sup _ X\varphi =0$. Since $\varphi $ has minimal singularities, there is a constant $C$ with $\varphi \geq V_\theta -C$. Choose $M\geq 0$ with $\theta \geq -M\omega $. If $a\in (0,1)$ is sufficiently close to one, then \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\rho ) =a(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )+(1-a)\theta \geq \bigl (a\varepsilon -(1-a)M\bigr )\omega >0.  \] Thus $a\rho $ is a competitor for $V_\theta $, and therefore \[  0\geq \varphi \geq V_\theta -C\geq a\rho -C,  \] and hence 1.66 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-gap-proper} \varphi -\rho \geq (1-a)(-\rho )-C. \end{equation} By hypothesis $\varphi $ is continuous on $\Omega $, and $\rho $ is smooth there because it has analytic singularities with smooth remainder. Hence $\varphi -\rho $ is continuous on $\Omega $, and by ( 1.66 ) it is bounded below. Since $\rho \to -\infty $ at $X\setminus \Omega $, the sets $\{ \rho \geq -c\} $ are compact subsets of $\Omega $, and ( 1.66 ) places every sublevel set of $\varphi -\rho $ in one of them. Being closed in $\Omega $, each sublevel set is therefore compact. $\square$

title: 1.19.1 A hyperplane Green envelope on the ball
search_title: A hyperplane Green envelope on the ball
text: 1.19.1 A hyperplane Green envelope on the ball For a logarithmic pole along a hyperplane section of the unit ball, the envelope can be computed explicitly by restricting to the complex lines normal to the hyperplane. The example also shows how envelopes of bounded obstacles recover the finite part of a logarithmic pole, and that continuity inside the domain does not imply continuity up to the boundary. In this subsection let $n\geq 2$, let $m\geq 1$ be an integer, and write \[  B=\{ (\zeta ,w)\in \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^{n-1}:|\zeta |^2+|w|^2<1\} , \qquad D=B\cap \{ \zeta =0\} .  \] Define $G_ m$ as the pointwise supremum of the functions $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ such that $u\leq 0$ and, near every point of $D$, $u\leq m\log |\zeta |^2+C$ for some local constant $C$. In particular, $u=-\infty $ on $D$. The constants need not stay bounded as the point of $D$ approaches $\partial B$. Proposition 1.19.8 . The envelope $G_ m$ is given by 1.67 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ball-divisor-green} G_ m(\zeta ,w)=m\log \frac{|\zeta |^2}{1-|w|^2}. \end{equation} It is plurisubharmonic and continuous on $B$ with values in $[-\infty ,0)$. The finite part $G_ m-m\log |\zeta |^2$, first defined off $D$, extends smoothly across $D$ as the plurisubharmonic function \[  H_ m(w)=-m\log (1-|w|^2).  \] Proof. The function $-\log (1-|w|^2)$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic on $|w|<1$: its complex Hessian is \[  \left(\frac{\delta _{jk}}{1-|w|^2} +\frac{\overline w_ jw_ k}{(1-|w|^2)^2}\right)_{j,k}.  \] Thus the right-hand side of ( 1.67 ) is plurisubharmonic; it is negative on $B$ and satisfies the pole condition, so it is a competitor. For the reverse inequality, fix a competitor $u$ and a point $w$ with $|w|<1$. The restriction $u(\cdot ,w)$ is either identically $-\infty $ or subharmonic on the disk of radius $R=(1-|w|^2)^{1/2}$. In the latter case, $u(\zeta ,w)-m\log |\zeta |^2$ is subharmonic on the punctured disk and, by the pole condition, bounded above near zero, so it extends as a subharmonic function across zero. Since $u\leq 0$, this extension is at most $-m\log r^2$ on every circle $|\zeta |=r<R$. The maximum principle and then $r\uparrow R$ give \[  u(\zeta ,w)\leq m\log \frac{|\zeta |^2}{R^2}.  \] On $D$ both sides are $-\infty $. Taking the supremum over $u$ proves the formula. Near a point of $D$, the function $H_ m$ is bounded and the logarithmic term tends to $-\infty $, which proves continuity there as an extended-real function. $\square$ For a finite continuous obstacle $\Phi $ on $B$, put \[  P_ B\Phi =\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(B):v\leq \Phi \} \right)^*.  \] The local upper-envelope theorem used in section 1.19 applies whenever this family is nonempty and locally uniformly bounded above. Continuity of $\Phi $ ensures that the regularized envelope still satisfies $P_ B\Phi \leq \Phi $. Proposition 1.19.9 . For $t>0$, define \[  \Phi _ t(\zeta ,w)=\min \{ -m\log |\zeta |^2,t\} , \qquad V_ t=P_ B\Phi _ t,  \] with $\Phi _ t=t$ on $D$. Then $0\leq V_ t\leq t$, and 1.68 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ball-green-truncation-squeeze} -m\log \bigl (1-(1-\mathrm e^{-t/m})|w|^2\bigr ) \leq V_ t(\zeta ,w)\leq H_ m(w). \end{equation} In particular, $V_ t\uparrow H_ m$ pointwise on all of $B$, including $D$. The convergence is uniform on every compact subset, with 1.69 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ball-green-truncation-rate} 0\leq H_ m-V_ t \leq \frac{m\mathrm e^{-t/m}R^2}{1-R^2} \qquad \text{where }|w|\leq R<1. \end{equation} Proof. The obstacle is continuous, nonnegative and at most $t$. Zero is a competitor, so the upper-envelope theorem gives $V_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ with $0\leq V_ t\leq \Phi _ t\leq t$. Consequently $m\log |\zeta |^2+V_ t$ is a competitor for $G_ m$, and proposition 1.19.8 gives $V_ t\leq H_ m$ off $D$. At a point $(0,w)$, the submean inequality on any sufficiently small circle in the normal line gives the same bound, since $H_ m$ does not depend on $\zeta $. For the lower bound, set $a_ t=1-\mathrm e^{-t/m}$ and $F_ t(w)=-m\log (1-a_ t|w|^2)$. The Hessian calculation above, with $|w|^2$ replaced by $a_ t|w|^2$, shows that $F_ t$ is plurisubharmonic. Moreover, $0\leq F_ t\leq t$, and $F_ t\leq H_ m\leq -m\log |\zeta |^2$ on $B\setminus D$ because $|\zeta |^2<1-|w|^2$. Thus $F_ t\leq \Phi _ t$ everywhere, and hence $F_ t\leq V_ t$. Finally, \[  H_ m-F_ t =m\log \left(1+\frac{\mathrm e^{-t/m}|w|^2}{1-|w|^2}\right) \leq \frac{m\mathrm e^{-t/m}|w|^2}{1-|w|^2}.  \] This proves ( 1.69 ) and the convergence; the monotonicity of $V_ t$ in $t$ follows from that of $\Phi _ t$. $\square$ Example 1.19.10 . At every point $p=(0,w_0)\in \partial B$ with $|w_0|=1$, the cluster set of $G_ m$ at $p$, that is, the set of limits of $G_ m$ along sequences in $B$ converging to $p$, is all of $[-\infty ,0]$. Indeed, set $w_ s=(1-s^2)^{1/2}w_0$ for $0<s<1$. For every fixed $0<a<1$, the points $(as,w_ s)$ belong to $B$, tend to $p$ as $s\to 0$, and satisfy $G_ m=m\log a^2$. Choosing $a=a_ s<1$ with $a_ s\to 1$ gives the limit zero, whereas the points $(s^2,w_ s)$ give $G_ m=m\log s^2\to -\infty $. These realize every value in $[-\infty ,0]$, and negativity excludes all others. Thus $G_ m$, although continuous on $B$, has no continuous extension to any point of $\partial B$ in the closure of $D$.

title: 1.20 The minimum principle
text: 1.20 The minimum principle An infimum of plurisubharmonic functions need not be plurisubharmonic. Kiselman's minimum principle describes an important exception: the infimum over a real parameter $t$ of a family $u_ t$ whose complexification $u_{\operatorname{Re}z}$ is plurisubharmonic in the joint variables. Freezing the coefficients of the background form, we show that the principle preserves the exact lower curvature bound $-\theta $. Lemma 1.20.1 . Let $I\subset \mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, set $S_ I=\{ z\in \mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z\in I\} $, and let $\pi :X\times S_ I\to X$ be the projection. Let $(u_ t)_{t\in I}$ be a family of functions on $X$ such that $U(x,z)=u_{\operatorname{Re}z}(x)$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $X\times S_ I$ and $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U\geq 0$. For each $x$, the function $t\mapsto u_ t(x)$ is finite and convex or identically $-\infty $. The finite alternative holds for almost every $x$. Proof. A local smooth correction making $U$ plurisubharmonic can be chosen to depend only on $x$. Hence the restriction of $U$ to $\{ x\} \times S_ I$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. In the first case its distributional Laplacian is the second derivative of $t\mapsto u_ t(x)$, which is therefore nonnegative. The resulting convex representative is finite on $I$, and by the submean inequality it agrees everywhere with the subharmonic function. Finally, $U$ is locally integrable on the product, and Fubini's theorem, applied on products of coordinate balls with a fixed rectangle in $S_ I$, excludes the identically $-\infty $ alternative for almost every $x$. $\square$ Corollary 1.20.2 . Let $I\subset \mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval. A radial function $z\mapsto q(\log |z|^2)$ is subharmonic on the annulus $\{ z:\log |z|^2\in I\} $ if and only if $q$ is finite and convex on $I$. If the function identically equal to $-\infty $ is also regarded as subharmonic, the alternative $q\equiv -\infty $ has to be added. Proof. The holomorphic covering map $z=\mathrm{e}^{w/2}$ pulls the function back to $q(\operatorname{Re}w)$, and the argument of lemma 1.20.1 proves necessity. Conversely, a finite convex function $q$ has nonnegative distributional second derivative. Thus $q(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is subharmonic, and subharmonicity descends through the local biholomorphisms of the covering. $\square$ Proposition 1.20.3 . Under the hypotheses of lemma 1.20.1 , the function \[  q(x)=\inf _{t\in I}u_ t(x)  \] is either $\theta $-plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $; in particular, the infimum need not be regularized. If $I$ is bounded, then $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proof. The classical local Kiselman principle states that if a plurisubharmonic function on the product of a domain with a strip does not depend on the imaginary part of the strip variable, then its infimum over the real part is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $; the interval of the real part may be unbounded. We use this local result from [ SGPT ] . Fix $x_0\in X$, choose local holomorphic coordinates centered at $x_0$, and let $\kappa $ be their Euclidean form. Fix $\eta >0$. On a sufficiently small coordinate ball the constant form $\beta =\theta (x_0)$ satisfies \[  \beta -\eta \kappa \leq \theta \leq \beta +\eta \kappa .  \] Choose a quadratic function $r$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=\beta +\eta \kappa $. Then $U+r\circ \pi $ is plurisubharmonic on the product of the ball with $S_ I$. Its infimum over the parameter is $q+r$, so the local principle shows that $q+r$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on the ball; in the first case \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq -\beta -\eta \kappa \geq -\theta -2\eta \kappa .  \] In a fixed atlas, the Euclidean forms are bounded by a fixed multiple of $\omega $, so letting $\eta \downarrow 0$ proves the exact lower bound $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq -\theta $. Since a plurisubharmonic function cannot be identically $-\infty $ on a nonempty open set, the local alternative propagates across overlapping balls on the connected manifold $X$. Thus either $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ or $q\equiv -\infty $. No regularization is needed, because an infimum of upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous. Now suppose that $I$ is bounded. By lemma 1.20.1 , the function $t\mapsto u_ t(x)$ is finite and convex for almost every $x$, and a supporting affine function at any point of $I$ bounds it from below on the bounded interval $I$. Hence $q(x)>-\infty $ almost everywhere, which excludes the alternative $q\equiv -\infty $. $\square$ For example, the proposition applies to $u_ t-t\tau $ for a fixed real number $\tau $. On an unbounded interval the infimum may be identically $-\infty $; this alternative will encode the cutoff of a test curve (definition 18.1.1 ).

title: Lemma 1.20.1
text: Lemma 1.20.1 . Let $I\subset \mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, set $S_ I=\{ z\in \mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z\in I\} $, and let $\pi :X\times S_ I\to X$ be the projection. Let $(u_ t)_{t\in I}$ be a family of functions on $X$ such that $U(x,z)=u_{\operatorname{Re}z}(x)$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $X\times S_ I$ and $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U\geq 0$. For each $x$, the function $t\mapsto u_ t(x)$ is finite and convex or identically $-\infty $. The finite alternative holds for almost every $x$. Proof. A local smooth correction making $U$ plurisubharmonic can be chosen to depend only on $x$. Hence the restriction of $U$ to $\{ x\} \times S_ I$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. In the first case its distributional Laplacian is the second derivative of $t\mapsto u_ t(x)$, which is therefore nonnegative. The resulting convex representative is finite on $I$, and by the submean inequality it agrees everywhere with the subharmonic function. Finally, $U$ is locally integrable on the product, and Fubini's theorem, applied on products of coordinate balls with a fixed rectangle in $S_ I$, excludes the identically $-\infty $ alternative for almost every $x$. $\square$

title: Corollary 1.20.2
text: Corollary 1.20.2 . Let $I\subset \mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval. A radial function $z\mapsto q(\log |z|^2)$ is subharmonic on the annulus $\{ z:\log |z|^2\in I\} $ if and only if $q$ is finite and convex on $I$. If the function identically equal to $-\infty $ is also regarded as subharmonic, the alternative $q\equiv -\infty $ has to be added. Proof. The holomorphic covering map $z=\mathrm{e}^{w/2}$ pulls the function back to $q(\operatorname{Re}w)$, and the argument of lemma 1.20.1 proves necessity. Conversely, a finite convex function $q$ has nonnegative distributional second derivative. Thus $q(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is subharmonic, and subharmonicity descends through the local biholomorphisms of the covering. $\square$

title: Proposition 1.20.3
text: Proposition 1.20.3 . Under the hypotheses of lemma 1.20.1 , the function \[  q(x)=\inf _{t\in I}u_ t(x)  \] is either $\theta $-plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $; in particular, the infimum need not be regularized. If $I$ is bounded, then $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proof. The classical local Kiselman principle states that if a plurisubharmonic function on the product of a domain with a strip does not depend on the imaginary part of the strip variable, then its infimum over the real part is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $; the interval of the real part may be unbounded. We use this local result from [ SGPT ] . Fix $x_0\in X$, choose local holomorphic coordinates centered at $x_0$, and let $\kappa $ be their Euclidean form. Fix $\eta >0$. On a sufficiently small coordinate ball the constant form $\beta =\theta (x_0)$ satisfies \[  \beta -\eta \kappa \leq \theta \leq \beta +\eta \kappa .  \] Choose a quadratic function $r$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=\beta +\eta \kappa $. Then $U+r\circ \pi $ is plurisubharmonic on the product of the ball with $S_ I$. Its infimum over the parameter is $q+r$, so the local principle shows that $q+r$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on the ball; in the first case \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq -\beta -\eta \kappa \geq -\theta -2\eta \kappa .  \] In a fixed atlas, the Euclidean forms are bounded by a fixed multiple of $\omega $, so letting $\eta \downarrow 0$ proves the exact lower bound $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq -\theta $. Since a plurisubharmonic function cannot be identically $-\infty $ on a nonempty open set, the local alternative propagates across overlapping balls on the connected manifold $X$. Thus either $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ or $q\equiv -\infty $. No regularization is needed, because an infimum of upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous. Now suppose that $I$ is bounded. By lemma 1.20.1 , the function $t\mapsto u_ t(x)$ is finite and convex for almost every $x$, and a supporting affine function at any point of $I$ bounds it from below on the bounded interval $I$. Hence $q(x)>-\infty $ almost everywhere, which excludes the alternative $q\equiv -\infty $. $\square$

title: 1.20.1 Pointwise Legendre transforms
text: 1.20.1 Pointwise Legendre transforms The minimum principle can also show that a supremum is already upper semicontinuous. For a concave family of potentials, the regularized Legendre transform is a potential on a product. The minimum principle identifies its inverse transforms with the original family everywhere, and applying the one-variable duality once more identifies the regularization with the pointwise supremum. We first state this duality precisely, including its behavior at the endpoints; the general Legendre–Fenchel theorem is recalled in [ appendix on convex analysis , SGPT ] . Lemma 1.20.4 . Let $c\in \mathbb R$. Suppose $g:\mathbb R\to [-\infty ,0]$ is upper semicontinuous, concave and decreasing, finite somewhere, and equal to $-\infty $ on $(c,\infty )$. Then \[  f(t)=\sup _{\tau <c}\bigl (g(\tau )+t\tau \bigr ),\qquad t>0,  \] is finite and convex, satisfies $f(t)\leq ct$, and obeys \[  g(\tau )=\inf _{t>0}\bigl (f(t)-t\tau \bigr ),\qquad \lim _{t\downarrow 0}f(t)=\sup _{\tau <c}g(\tau ).  \] Conversely, every finite convex $f$ on $(0,\infty )$ with $f(t)\leq ct$ is recovered by the first formula from $g(\tau )=\inf _{t>0}(f(t)-t\tau )$, and satisfies the same endpoint identity. The formulas also hold for $g\equiv -\infty $, with $f\equiv -\infty $. Proof. Since $g$ is decreasing and finite somewhere, it is finite on a half-line $(-\infty ,\tau _1)$. Hence the defining supremum is finite for $t>0$: it is bounded above by $ct$ and below by any one of its finite terms. Concavity and upper semicontinuity give $g(c)=\lim _{\tau \uparrow c}g(\tau )$, so including $\tau =c$ does not change the supremum. The Legendre transform $t\mapsto \sup _\tau (g(\tau )+t\tau )$ of $-g$ is infinite for $t<0$. At $t=0$ it equals $m=\sup _{\tau <c}g(\tau )$, and the bounds \[  g(\tau )+t\tau \leq f(t)\leq m+ct  \] show that $f(t)\to m$ as $t\downarrow 0$. The biconjugacy theorem for the closed convex function $-g$ therefore gives the inverse formula; the value at $t=0$ may be omitted without changing the infimum. Conversely, start with $f$. At each $t>0$, choose the slope $p$ of a supporting line of $f$. The upper bound $f(s)\leq cs$ as $s\to \infty $ forces $p\leq c$. If $p<c$, the supporting line gives $g(p)=f(t)-tp$, so the first formula recovers $f(t)$. If $p=c$, then $f(s)-cs$ is constant for $s\geq t$, because this function is convex and bounded above, hence decreasing, while its supporting line at $t$ is horizontal. Consequently, for every $\tau <c$, \[  f(t)-ct\leq g(\tau )\leq f(t)-t\tau .  \] and letting $\tau \uparrow c$ again recovers $f(t)$. In particular, $g$ is finite somewhere. As an infimum of affine functions with slopes $-s<0$, it is upper semicontinuous, concave and decreasing. Letting $s\downarrow 0$ in the bound $f(s)-s\tau \leq s(c-\tau )$ gives $g\leq 0$, and letting $s\to \infty $ gives $g=-\infty $ for $\tau >c$. The endpoint identity now follows from the first part. The case of functions identically equal to $-\infty $ follows directly from the formulas. $\square$ Fix $c\in \mathbb R$, and let $\Gamma _\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for $\tau <c$ be functions with $\Gamma _\tau \leq 0$ such that $\tau \mapsto \Gamma _\tau (x)$ is concave and decreasing for every $x$. Extend the family to $\tau =c$ by the decreasing limit $\Gamma _ c=\lim _{\tau \uparrow c}\Gamma _\tau $, and by $\Gamma _\tau \equiv -\infty $ for $\tau >c$. Define the forward transform of the family by 1.70 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hermitian-legendre-forward} U_ t(x)=\sup _{\tau <c}\bigl (\Gamma _\tau (x)+t\tau \bigr ), \qquad t>0. \end{equation} For a family $(u_ t)_{t>0}$, the inverse transform is 1.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hermitian-legendre-backward} \widehat u_\tau (x)=\inf _{t>0}\bigl (u_ t(x)-t\tau \bigr ). \end{equation} Lemma 1.20.5 . At each $x$, the extended function $\tau \mapsto \Gamma _\tau (x)$ is upper semicontinuous and concave, or identically $-\infty $. Its forward transform satisfies \[  \Gamma _\tau (x)=\inf _{t>0}\bigl (U_ t(x)-t\tau \bigr ) \qquad (\tau \in \mathbb R).  \] Proof. Fix $\tau <c$ and let $\tau _ j\uparrow \tau $. The decreasing limit of the functions $\Gamma _{\tau _ j}$ dominates $\Gamma _\tau $, so it belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Choose $r\in (\tau ,c)$. Outside the pole set of $\Gamma _ r$, the concave function $s\mapsto \Gamma _ s(x)$ is finite near $\tau $ and hence continuous there. Thus the decreasing limit equals $\Gamma _\tau $ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . This proves left continuity at every $\tau <c$; at $c$ it holds by definition. Since the function is decreasing, left continuity gives upper semicontinuity, also where the value is $-\infty $, and concavity survives the extension. The inverse formula is lemma 1.20.4 at each $x$. $\square$ Theorem 1.20.6 . For the preceding family $(\Gamma _\tau )_{\tau <c}$, the pointwise supremum in ( 1.70 ) is already upper semicontinuous on $X\times (0,\infty )$. Its complexification $U(x,z)=U_{\operatorname{Re}z}(x)$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $X\times \{ \operatorname{Re}z>0\} $ and satisfies $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U\geq 0$, where $\pi :X\times \{ \operatorname{Re}z>0\} \to X$ is the projection. Each slice belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proof. Each term $(x,z)\mapsto \Gamma _\tau (x)+\tau \operatorname{Re}z$ of the supremum satisfies the current inequality on the product, since $\operatorname{Re}z$ is pluriharmonic. The bound $\Gamma _\tau \leq 0$ gives $U_ t\leq ct$, while any fixed $\tau _0<c$ gives the minorant $\Gamma _{\tau _0}+t\tau _0$. By the local upper-envelope theorem, as in section 1.19 , the upper semicontinuous regularization $V$ of $U$ on the product is quasi-plurisubharmonic, satisfies $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\geq 0$, and agrees with $U$ almost everywhere. It does not depend on $\operatorname {Im}z$ and satisfies $V_ t\leq ct$. The pointwise supremum $U$ is measurable, since by the left continuity in lemma 1.20.5 the parameters may be restricted to rational numbers. By Fubini's theorem, there is a set $Z\subset X$ of zero smooth volume, containing the pole set of $\Gamma _{\tau _0}$, such that $U_ t(x)=V_ t(x)$ for almost every $t>0$ whenever $x\notin Z$. For such $x$, both sides are finite convex functions of $t$, by lemma 1.20.4 , lemma 1.20.1 , so by continuity the equality holds for every $t>0$. For each $\tau <c$, proposition 1.20.3 gives \[  \chi _\tau =\inf _{t>0}(V_ t-t\tau ) \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cup \{ -\infty \} .  \] Off $Z$ it equals $\Gamma _\tau $ by lemma 1.20.5 . In particular, $\chi _\tau $ is not identically $-\infty $, and lemma 1.3.3 gives $\chi _\tau =\Gamma _\tau $ everywhere. At each $x$, the convex function $t\mapsto V_ t(x)$ can be recovered from these inverse transforms by lemma 1.20.4 , also when it is identically $-\infty $. We obtain \[  V_ t(x)=\sup _{\tau <c}\bigl (\chi _\tau (x)+t\tau \bigr )=U_ t(x).  \] Finally, the minorant $\Gamma _{\tau _0}+t\tau _0$ shows that no slice $U_ t$ is identically $-\infty $, so every slice belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\square$

title: 1.21 Chern-connection regularization
text:
1.21 Chern-connection regularization Convolution in local coordinates does not directly produce global approximants with a controlled lower curvature bound. Demailly's regularization instead averages over the fibers of the tangent bundle, using the Chern connection of $\omega $, and a Kiselman-type minimum of these averages controls the loss of positivity. The classical curvature estimate for this minimum holds in a Hermitian background, while the $L^1$ and gradient bounds for the averages are elementary. Fix $C_0>0$ and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $-C_0\leq u\leq 0$. Distances, gradients and norms of tensors are taken with respect to the Riemannian metric associated with $\omega $. For small $t>0$, let $R_ tu$ be Demailly's regularization of $u$ formed with the Chern connection of $\omega $. It averages $u$ over the image of the ball of radius $t$ in each tangent space, with a fixed smooth nonnegative radial kernel of integral one. The map used for this purpose is a smooth realization of the holomorphic part of the formal fiberwise expansion of the exponential map; it need not be holomorphic in the fiber. The following classical estimate controls the Kiselman-type transform of these averages, including its mixed base–fiber terms; see section 34.1 for the sources. Lemma 1.21.1 . There are constants $A,K>0$ and $t_*>0$, depending only on $(X,\omega )$ and $C_0$, such that $R_ tu$ is smooth for $0<t<t_*$, \[  -C_0\leq R_ tu\leq 0,\qquad R_ tu+Kt^2\downarrow u\quad 	ext{as }t\downarrow 0.  \] For $0<\delta <t_*$ and $c>0$, the bounded function \[  \Phi _{c,\delta } =\inf _{0<t\leq \delta } \left\{ R_ tu+K(t^2-\delta ^2)+K(t-\delta ) -c\log (t/\delta )ight\}   \] is quasi-plurisubharmonic and satisfies \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _{c,\delta }\geq -(Ac+2K\delta )\omega .  \] At every point, the infimum is attained at some $t>0$. We use only this curvature estimate from the classical theory. The linear term $K(t-\delta )$ is needed in the Hermitian case, where it absorbs the mixed base–fiber terms in the complex Hessian of the regularization. Since $-c\log (t/\delta )$ tends to $+\infty $ as $t\downarrow 0$ while $u$ is bounded, the infimum is attained away from zero. We need neither smoothness of the minimizing radius nor smoothness of the transform across the region where this radius equals $\delta $. Next we prove two elementary estimates for the averaging operators. They do not rely on any volume identity from Kähler geometry. Lemma 1.21.2 . For all sufficiently small $t>0$, \[  \| R_ tu-u\| _{L^1(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq Ct^2, \qquad \| 
abla R_ tu\| _\infty \leq C/t.  \] The constants are uniform for $-C_0\leq u\leq 0$. Proof. Let $z$ be local coordinates on $X$ and $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$ the fiber variable with respect to a smooth orthonormal frame of the tangent bundle. Write $ho (|\xi |^2)$ for the fixed radial averaging kernel, normalized with respect to Lebesgue measure $\mathrm{d}\xi $ and supported in $|\xi |\leq 1$. In these coordinates the averaging map $F$ gives \[  R_ tu(z)=\int u(F(z,t\xi ))ho (|\xi |^2)\, \mathrm{d}\xi , \qquad F(z,0)=z.  \] The map $F$ is smooth in these variables, and its fiber differential at zero is an isomorphism. Let $R_ t^*$ be the formal adjoint of $R_ t$ with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$, so that $\int _ X(R_ ta)b\, \mathrm{d}V=\int _ Xa\, R_ t^*b\, \mathrm{d}V$. We first claim that \[  R_ t^*1=1+O(t^2)  \] uniformly. To see this, insert a smooth partition of unity in the variable $z$, each term being compactly supported in a chart on which the frame is defined. For fixed $\xi $, change variables $x=F(z,t\xi )$ on a neighborhood of the support of a term. The inverse map and its Jacobian have uniform Taylor expansions in $t$. The term of order zero in the transformed density is the chosen partition function at $x$, and the term of order one is linear in $\xi $, so it integrates to zero against the even radial kernel. The remaining density is bounded by $Ct^2\mathrm{d}V(x)$, since the second derivatives of all maps, partition functions and volume coefficients are bounded on these finitely many compact charts. Summing over the partition functions proves the claim. Consequently, \[  \left|\int _ X(R_ tu-u)\, \mathrm{d}Vight| =\left|\int _ Xu(R_ t^*1-1)\, \mathrm{d}Vight|\leq Ct^2.  \] By lemma 1.21.1 , $R_ tu-u\geq -Kt^2$. A real function $a\geq -Kt^2$ satisfies $|a|\leq a+2Kt^2$; applying this to $a=R_ tu-u$ and integrating gives the first estimate. For the derivative bound, change variables in the fiber to write $R_ tu(z)=\int _ Xu(x)k_ t(z,x)\, \mathrm{d}V(x)$. In local coordinates the smooth kernel $k_ t$ is supported where $|x-z|\leq Ct$ and satisfies \[  |
abla _ z k_ t(z,x)|\leq Ct^{-2n-1}.  \] Indeed, the inverse fiber map and its Jacobian have uniformly bounded derivatives, and differentiating the rescaled radial argument introduces at most one factor $t^{-1}$ in addition to $t^{-2n}$. Since the kernel is smooth with compact support, there are no boundary terms. Integration over a ball of volume at most $Ct^{2n}$ gives $\int |
abla _ zk_ t|\, \mathrm{d}V\leq C/t$, and multiplication by the uniform bound for $u$ proves the assertion. $\square$ The first estimate relies on the cancellation of the odd first-order term against the even kernel, and not on conservation of Monge–Ampère mass.
