1.23.2 Vanishing exponents
text: 1.23.2 Vanishing exponents Proposition 1.23.2 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be unbounded below, and for each $\lambda >0$ let $u_\lambda $ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with $u_\lambda \sim \varphi $. Then, for each $\lambda >0$, the function $\lambda u_\lambda $ has infinite distance in $L^\infty (\mathrm{d}V)$ from every constant. In particular, $\lambda u_\lambda $ cannot converge uniformly on $X$ to a finite constant as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Proof. Since $u_\lambda \leq \varphi +C$ for a constant $C$, the function $u_\lambda $ is unbounded below. Every nonempty strict sublevel set $\{ u_\lambda <t\} $ of the upper semicontinuous function $u_\lambda $ is open, hence of positive smooth volume. Thus $u_\lambda $, and with it $\lambda u_\lambda $, is essentially unbounded below, and both conclusions follow. $\square$ A vanishing exponent gives convergence of the exponentials to one, even when the normalized potentials vary. Lemma 1.23.3 . Let $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $\sup _ Xv_ j=0$, and let $\lambda _ j>0$ decrease to zero. For every finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $, \[  \int _ X\left|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_ j}-1\right|\, \mathrm{d}\mu \longrightarrow 0.  \] If $f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for some $p>1$, then more precisely \[  \int _ X\left|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_ j}-1\right|\, |f|\, \mathrm{d}V \leq C_ p\lambda _ j\| f\| _{L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)}.  \] The constant depends on the fixed background, $p$ and $\mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta $, so that $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Omega )$. By lemma 1.8.1 , for every $T>1$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (\{ v_ j<-T\} )\leq C/T  \] uniformly in $j$. Since $v_ j\leq 0$ and $1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}\leq x$ for $x\geq 0$, splitting the integral at this sublevel set gives \[  \int _ X(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_ j})\, \mathrm{d}\mu \leq \lambda _ jT\mu (X)+\mu (\{ v_ j<-T\} ).  \] By lemma 1.8.11 , the second term is uniformly small when $T$ is large, and for this fixed $T$ the first term tends to zero as $j\to \infty $. This proves the general assertion; here the exponential is given the value zero at a pole, and pole sets have zero $\mu $-measure. For the quantitative assertion, lemma 1.5.1 , applied in the background $\Omega $, gives a uniform $L^ q$ bound for $-v_ j$, where $q=p/(p-1)$. Hölder's inequality and the bound \[  0\leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_ j}\leq \lambda _ j|v_ j|  \] give the claimed estimate for every $j$. $\square$

title: 1.23.3 Measures with bounded potentials
text: 1.23.3 Measures with bounded potentials The fixed measure can be replaced by moving mixed Monge–Ampère measures of uniformly bounded potentials, provided these potentials converge in capacity. Since $\omega $ need not be closed, the proof has to control the torsion terms that appear in integration by parts. Lemma 1.23.4 . Let $a_ j,a,w_ j,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be uniformly bounded, and write $\omega _ v=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. If $a_ j\to a$ in $L^1(X)$ and $w_ j\to w$ in capacity, then, for $0\leq k\leq n$, \[  \int _ X|a_ j-a|\, \omega _{w_ j}^{k}\wedge \omega ^{n-k} \longrightarrow 0.  \] The same conclusion holds if, instead of $a_ j,a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, the uniformly bounded functions $a_ j,a$ have any fixed smooth lower curvature bound. Proof. By lemma 1.4.1 , the tail envelopes $A_ j=(\sup _{\ell \geq j}a_\ell )^*$ decrease to $a$. Since $a\leq \max (a_ j,a)\leq A_ j$, monotone convergence in capacity of bounded potentials (lemma 1.8.12 ) implies \[  \alpha _ j:=\max (a_ j,a)\longrightarrow a\quad \text{in capacity}.  \] We split $|a_ j-a|=(\alpha _ j-a)+(\alpha _ j-a_ j)$. The integral of the first part against the moving products tends to zero by lemma 1.8.9 . For the second part, put $h_ j=\alpha _ j-a_ j\geq 0$. We compare its integrals against the measures with indices $j$ and $\ell $. The case $k=0$ follows from the assumed $L^1$ convergence. For $k\geq 1$, put $z=w_ j-w_\ell $ and \[  T=\sum _{s=0}^{k-1}\omega _{w_ j}^{s}\wedge \omega _{w_\ell }^{k-1-s}\wedge \omega ^{n-k}.  \] Factorization and Stokes' theorem on the compact manifold $X$ give \begin{align*} & \int _ Xh_ j\bigl (\omega _{w_ j}^{k}-\omega _{w_\ell }^{k}\bigr ) \wedge \omega ^{n-k}\\ & \hspace{20mm}=\int _ Xh_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}z\wedge T =\int _ Xz\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_ jT). \end{align*} Since $\omega $ is not assumed to be closed, $T$ need not be closed, and the product rule reads 1.75 \begin{equation} \label{eq:moving-measure-torsion} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_ jT)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ j\wedge T+\mathrm{d}h_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}T -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}T+h_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T. \end{equation} None of the terms involving derivatives of $T$ need vanish. We estimate the four terms. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ j=\omega _{\alpha _ j}-\omega _{a_ j}$, the absolute contribution of the first is at most \[  \int _ X|z|(\omega _{\alpha _ j}+\omega _{a_ j})\wedge T.  \] It tends to zero as $j,\ell \to \infty $ by lemma 1.8.9 , since $w_ j-w_\ell \to 0$ in capacity. Differentiating each factor shows that $\mathrm{d}T=\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge R$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}T=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge R$, where $R$ is a positive linear combination of mixed products of bidegree $(n-2,n-2)$. Moreover, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ is a sum of terms consisting of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ times mixed products of degree $n-2$, or of $\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $ times mixed products of degree $n-3$; terms of negative degree are absent. These smooth torsion factors are bounded in absolute value by fixed multiples of $\omega ^2$ and $\omega ^3$, respectively. As $h_ j$ is uniformly bounded, the contribution of $h_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ also tends to zero, by the same capacity estimate. For the two gradient terms, the pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for a positive mixed product gives, for example, \[  \left|\int _ Xz\, \mathrm{d}h_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge R\right|^2 \leq C\left(\int _ X|z|\, \mathrm{d}h_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j\wedge \omega \wedge R\right) \left(\int _ X|z|\, \omega ^2\wedge R\right).  \] The second factor tends to zero, and the first is uniformly bounded. Indeed, if $p$ is any of the uniformly bounded potentials and $S$ any positive mixed product of degree $n-1$ occurring here, then \[  \int _ X\mathrm{d}p\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}p\wedge S =\frac12\int _ Xp^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S-\int _ Xp\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p\wedge S.  \] Expand $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S$ with all its torsion terms as above, and write $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=\omega _ p-\omega $. Boundedness of $p$ and lemma 1.8.9 bound both integrals uniformly. Finally, $\mathrm{d}h_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j\leq 2\mathrm{d}\alpha _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\alpha _ j+2\mathrm{d}a_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}a_ j$ as positive quadratic forms, which proves the asserted bound. The other gradient term is estimated in the same way. In dimension one, $T=1$ and all torsion terms in ( 1.75 ) vanish. These integration-by-parts and energy identities hold for smooth potentials. They extend to bounded potentials through smooth decreasing approximations in the Hermitian background, using the local Bedford–Taylor chain rule, its gradient products and quasi-continuity; equivalently, they follow from the bounded current calculus of section 1.7 . Only the common bound on the potentials enters the estimates. We have shown that the difference between the integrals of $h_ j$ against the measures with indices $j$ and $\ell $ tends to zero as $j,\ell \to \infty $. For a fixed index $\ell $, the measure $\omega _{w_\ell }^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k}$ is a fixed finite non-pluripolar measure, and lemma 1.23.1 , applied separately to $\alpha _ j\to a$ and $a_ j\to a$ in $L^1(X)$, gives \[  \int _ Xh_ j\, \omega _{w_\ell }^{k}\wedge \omega ^{n-k}\longrightarrow 0 \qquad \text{as }j\to \infty .  \] Choosing first $\ell $ large and then letting $j\to \infty $, we conclude that the integrals of $h_ j$ against $\omega _{w_ j}^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k}$ tend to zero. Together with the estimate for $\alpha _ j-a$, this proves the result. If the $a_ j$ only have some other fixed lower curvature bound, choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \omega $ such that they are $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic. By section 1.8 , convergence in capacity is unchanged by this replacement. Apply the result just proved with $\Omega $ in place of $\omega $; by positivity, the original mixed measures are bounded by their counterparts for $\Omega $. $\square$

title: 1.24 Curvature of line bundles
text: 1.24 Curvature of line bundles Let $M$ be a complex manifold and let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $M$. To relate potentials to holomorphic sections, we ask when a current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, with $u$ locally integrable, can be the curvature current of a metric on a line bundle. The transition law for the local weights of such a metric forces a closedness condition on the background. Proposition 1.24.1 . The curvature current of a singular Hermitian metric with locally integrable weights on a holomorphic line bundle is closed. In particular, a nonclosed form $\theta $ cannot itself be the curvature current of such a metric, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is not closed on any neighborhood of a point where $\mathrm{d}\theta \neq 0$. Proof. Let $h$ be a singular Hermitian metric on a holomorphic line bundle $L\to M$. Choose a local holomorphic frame $e$ of $L$ and write its squared norm as $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi }$; the curvature current is then locally $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $. If $e'=ge$ is another frame, with $g$ holomorphic and nowhere zero, the new weight is $\varphi -\log |g|^2$. Since $\log |g|^2$ is pluriharmonic, these local currents agree on overlaps and glue to a global current, which is closed because $\mathrm{d}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=0$. The final assertion follows from the identity \[  \mathrm{d}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)=\mathrm{d}\theta  \] of currents. $\square$ Accordingly, when we study sections subject to multiplier-ideal conditions, we specify both the line bundle, whose curvature is closed, and any auxiliary Hermitian form on $M$. An algebraic interpretation then requires relating the invariants of the line bundle to this analytic background.

title: 1.25 Polar curvature
text:
1.25 Polar curvature For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, the restriction of the current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ to the pole set $\{ u=-\infty \} $ is called the polar curvature of $u$. A bounded change of the potential preserves more than its Lelong numbers: it preserves the whole polar curvature. Indeed, a local energy estimate puts the bounded difference of two potentials in a Sobolev space, while pole sets admit smooth test functions of arbitrarily small energy, and these test functions show that no coefficient measure of the Hessian of the difference charges the pole set. Polar curvature is closed even when the pole set is not closed, so a local elliptic equation recovers it from its scalar Hermitian trace. Lemma 1.25.1 . Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open and let $w\in L^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. If $\Delta w$ is a locally finite signed Radon measure, then $w\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Proof. Fix a smooth function $0\leq \psi \leq 1$ with compact support in $U$, and a relatively compact open neighborhood $V$ of its support. Mollify $w$ inside $V$ with a standard mollifier $ho _\varepsilon $, writing $w_\varepsilon =w*ho _\varepsilon $ and $
u _\varepsilon =(\Delta w)*ho _\varepsilon $. For small $\varepsilon $, integration by parts and Young's inequality give \[   egin{split}  \int \psi ^2|

abla w_\varepsilon |^2$ that is independent of $\varepsilon $. Taking $\psi =1$ on a prescribed smaller compact set, weak compactness in $W^{1,2}$ and convergence of the mollifications in $L^2$ identify the weak limit with $w$. This proves the assertion. $\square$ Lemma 1.25.2 . Let $v$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic on a complex manifold, let $U$ be a coordinate ball with compact closure in a larger chart, and let $K\subset U\cap \{ v=-\infty \} $ be compact. For every open $O\subset U$ containing $K$, there are real $\varphi _ j\in C^\infty _ c(O)$ with $0\leq \varphi _ j\leq 1$, equal to one near $K$, such that $\| \varphi _ j\| _{W^{1,2}(U)}	o 0$. The norm uses the Euclidean coordinates. Proof. Adding a smooth quadratic function and subtracting a constant, we obtain a negative plurisubharmonic function $h$ on $U$ with the same pole set as $v$. Put $h_ M=\max (h,-M)$ for $M\geq 1$, and choose $\psi \in C^\infty _ c(O)$ with $0\leq \psi \leq 1$ and $\psi =1$ near $K$. On a fixed compact neighborhood of $\operatorname {supp}\psi $, the positive measures $\Delta h_ M$ have uniformly bounded mass: choose a nonnegative smooth function $\chi $ with compact support in $U$, equal to one on this neighborhood, and use \[  \int \chi \, \Delta h_ M=\int h_ M\Delta \chi , \qquad |h_ M|\leq |h|\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U).  \] Apply the integration-by-parts estimate of the preceding proof to mollifications of $h_ M$. Their absolute values are at most $M$, and their squares are at most $M$ times their absolute values. The uniform bounds for the mass of the Laplacians and for the local $L^1$ norms therefore give, after passing to the weak limit in $W^{1,2}$, \[  \int \psi ^2|
abla h_ M|^2\leq CM, \qquad \left\|  rac{-\psi h_ M}{M}ight\| _{W^{1,2}(U)}^2\leq  rac{C}{M}.  \] Here $C$ depends on the fixed cutoffs and the local $L^1$ norm of $h$, but not on $M$. The second inequality also uses $h_ M^2\leq M|h|$ in the terms containing $\psi $ and $
abla \psi $. The Sobolev function $-\psi h_ M/M$ takes values between zero and one. It equals one on a neighborhood of $K$, since $h$ is upper semicontinuous and therefore $\{ h<-M\} $ is an open neighborhood of $K$. Extend it by zero and mollify with a sufficiently small radius: the support stays in $O$, the function remains equal to one on a smaller neighborhood of $K$, and its Sobolev norm does not increase. title: Lemma 1.25.2
text: Lemma 1.25.2 . Let $v$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic on a complex manifold, let $U$ be a coordinate ball with compact closure in a larger chart, and let $K\subset U\cap \{ v=-\infty \} $ be compact. For every open $O\subset U$ containing $K$, there are real $\varphi _ j\in C^\infty _ c(O)$ with $0\leq \varphi _ j\leq 1$, equal to one near $K$, such that $\| \varphi _ j\| _{W^{1,2}(U)}\to 0$. The norm uses the Euclidean coordinates. Proof. Adding a smooth quadratic function and subtracting a constant, we obtain a negative plurisubharmonic function $h$ on $U$ with the same pole set as $v$. Put $h_ M=\max (h,-M)$ for $M\geq 1$, and choose $\psi \in C^\infty _ c(O)$ with $0\leq \psi \leq 1$ and $\psi =1$ near $K$. On a fixed compact neighborhood of $\operatorname {supp}\psi $, the positive measures $\Delta h_ M$ have uniformly bounded mass: choose a nonnegative smooth function $\chi $ with compact support in $U$, equal to one on this neighborhood, and use \[  \int \chi \, \Delta h_ M=\int h_ M\Delta \chi , \qquad |h_ M|\leq |h|\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U).  \] Apply the integration-by-parts estimate of the preceding proof to mollifications of $h_ M$. Their absolute values are at most $M$, and their squares are at most $M$ times their absolute values. The uniform bounds for the mass of the Laplacians and for the local $L^1$ norms therefore give, after passing to the weak limit in $W^{1,2}$, \[  \int \psi ^2|\nabla h_ M|^2\leq CM, \qquad \left\| \frac{-\psi h_ M}{M}\right\| _{W^{1,2}(U)}^2\leq \frac{C}{M}.  \] Here $C$ depends on the fixed cutoffs and the local $L^1$ norm of $h$, but not on $M$. The second inequality also uses $h_ M^2\leq M|h|$ in the terms containing $\psi $ and $\nabla \psi $. The Sobolev function $-\psi h_ M/M$ takes values between zero and one. It equals one on a neighborhood of $K$, since $h$ is upper semicontinuous and therefore $\{ h<-M\} $ is an open neighborhood of $K$. Extend it by zero and mollify with a sufficiently small radius: the support stays in $O$, the function remains equal to one on a smaller neighborhood of $K$, and its Sobolev norm does not increase. Letting $M\to \infty $ gives the required smooth functions. $\square$

text: 2 Torsion and the variation of mass Throughout this chapter, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$. If $\omega $ were closed, Stokes' theorem would make the total Monge–Ampère mass $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ independent of the potential $u$. For a nonclosed Hermitian form this invariance can fail. Integration by parts expresses the mass of a smooth potential as a polynomial whose coefficients pair the potential with the complex Hessians of the powers of $\omega $, and polarization shows that the vanishing of these Hessians is also necessary for invariance. When they do not vanish, even smooth potentials of the same singularity type can have different masses, and the usual global comparison principle fails. The masses may nevertheless remain bounded, and whether they do depends only on the manifold, not on the chosen Hermitian form.

text: 2.1 Integration by parts with a nonclosed form Integration by parts moves the complex Hessian of a function onto the form against which it is integrated. When that form is a power of a nonclosed $(1,1)$-form, its complex Hessian contains, besides the complex Hessian of the form itself, a quadratic term in its exterior derivative. Lemma 2.1.1 . For a smooth real function $f$ and a smooth form $T$ of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T=\int _ X f\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T.  \] Proof. Since $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f$ is a one-form, $\mathrm{d}(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge T)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T-\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{d}T$, and Stokes' theorem gives the first equality in \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T =\int _ X\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{d}T =\int _ X f\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T.  \] For the second, recall that the integral of $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\sigma $ vanishes for every form $\sigma $ of total degree $2n-1$, by Stokes' theorem for $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. We apply this to $\sigma =f\, \mathrm{d}T$ and use $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{d}=-\mathrm{d}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$. $\square$ Lemma 2.1.2 . For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ and an integer $q\geq 1$, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\theta ^ q) =q\, \theta ^{q-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\theta +q(q-1)\, \theta ^{q-2}\wedge \mathrm{d}\theta \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\theta ,  \] where the second term is omitted when $q=1$. Proof. For $q=1$ there is nothing to prove. For $q\geq 2$, since $\theta $ has even degree, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\theta ^ q)=q\, \theta ^{q-1}\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\theta $. Applying $\mathrm{d}$ and using again that $\theta ^{q-1}$ has even degree, we obtain \[  \mathrm{d}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\theta ^ q) =q(q-1)\, \theta ^{q-2}\wedge \mathrm{d}\theta \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\theta +q\, \theta ^{q-1}\wedge \mathrm{d}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\theta .  \] $\square$ Thus the quadratic torsion term $\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $ can make the higher powers of $\omega $ fail to be $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed even when $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. The mass expansion below involves the complex Hessians of all these powers separately.

text: 2.2 The mass polynomial For a smooth real function $u$ on $X$, write $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and set \[  \mathcal H_\omega =\{ u\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R):\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0\} , \qquad \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n.  \] The set $\mathcal H_\omega $ of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions is convex and open in the $C^2$ topology, while the mass $\mathrm M_\omega (u)$ is defined for every smooth real $u$. Expanding it along a smooth direction gives a polynomial whose nonconstant coefficients detect the complex Hessians of the powers of the background. Theorem 2.2.1 . For every smooth real function $u$, 2.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mass-expansion} \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^ n+ \sum _{k=1}^{n-1}\binom nk \int _ X u(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{k-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-k}). \end{equation} Proof. Expand $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ by the binomial theorem. The term with $k=n$ integrates to zero, since it is exact: \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mathrm{d}\bigl (\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-1}\bigr ).  \] For $1\leq k\leq n-1$, apply lemma 2.1.1 with $f=u$ and $T=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{k-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-k}$. Since both $\mathrm{d}$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ annihilate $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{k-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-k}),  \] which gives the $k$th term of ( 2.1 ). When $n=1$, the sum is empty and the mass is constant. $\square$ If every $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)$ with $1\leq j\leq n-1$ vanishes, ( 2.1 ) shows that the mass is constant. Conversely, varying the potential in several independent directions recovers each of these forms by polarization. Theorem 2.2.2 (Chiose) . Assume $n\geq 2$. The following conditions are equivalent: $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is independent of $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $; $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)=0$ for $1\leq j\leq n-1$; $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega =0$. They are also equivalent to the condition that $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ be the same for all bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u$, where $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of section 1.7 . Under these conditions the common mass is $\int _ X\omega ^ n$. Proof. Step 1: the first condition implies the second. Let $u$ be a smooth real function. For $|t|$ small, $tu$ belongs to $\mathcal H_\omega $ for both signs of $t$, so the polynomial $t\mapsto \int _ X(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is constant on an interval and its nonconstant coefficients vanish. For $1\leq j\leq n-1$ this gives \[  \int _ X\omega ^ j\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-j}=0.  \] Replace $u$ by a linear combination of $n-j$ smooth real functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_{n-j}$ and compare the coefficients of the monomial in which every parameter appears once. We obtain \[  \int _ X\omega ^ j\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n-j}=0.  \] Integrating by parts in the first factor and using that $u_1$ is arbitrary, we obtain the pointwise identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n-j}=0  \] for every choice of the remaining functions. At a given point, the complex Hessians of these functions can be prescribed arbitrarily: multiply a quadratic polynomial in a coordinate chart by a cutoff function equal to one near that point. Since the identity is multilinear, we may complexify it and use the quadratic monomials $z_ a\bar z_ b$. Wedge products of their complex Hessians give all coordinate forms of the complementary bidegree, and pairing with these forms shows that every coefficient of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)$ vanishes. When $j=n-1$ there are no remaining factors, and the same conclusion follows directly from the arbitrariness of $u_1$. This proves the second condition. Step 2: the remaining equivalences for smooth potentials. The second condition implies the first by theorem 2.2.1 . For $n\geq 3$, the identities for $j=1,2$ and lemma 2.1.2 give $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ and \[  0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=2\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega +2\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega ,  \] so the second condition implies the third. For $n=2$, the second condition is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$, while $\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $ vanishes for degree reasons; the implication is again immediate. Conversely, lemma 2.1.2 derives all the identities of the second condition from the third. Step 3: bounded potentials. Assume the first condition and let $u$ be a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. By theorem 1.11.1 , there are uniformly bounded functions $u_ j\in \mathcal H_\omega $ decreasing to $u$. Their masses all equal $\int _ X\omega ^ n$, and the continuity of the bounded products of section 1.7 along such sequences passes this common value to the limit. Conversely, every element of $\mathcal H_\omega $ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, so constancy for bounded potentials implies the first condition. The zero potential shows that the common mass is $\int _ X\omega ^ n$. $\square$ In particular, a closed background has invariant mass. Under the equivalent conditions above, ( 2.1 ) even gives $\mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^ n$ for every smooth real $u$, not only for $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. In dimension one the mass is always $\int _ X\omega $. Mass invariance can also hold in a nonclosed background. In theorem 26.17.6 , a pluriclosed metric with nonzero exterior derivative satisfies all the lower-power identities above. Those identities fix its bounded-potential mass, even though a family of scalar perturbations can have its least relative eigenvalue tend to zero. The first variation of the mass involves only the complex Hessian of the power $\omega _ u^{n-1}$ of the perturbed form. Proposition 2.2.3 . For smooth real functions $u,v$ on $X$, 2.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mass-first-variation} \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_{t=0}\mathrm M_\omega (u+tv) =n\int _ X v\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _ u^{n-1}). \end{equation} If $\mathrm M_\omega $ is constant on $\mathcal H_\omega $, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _ u^{n-1})=0$ for every $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. Proof. Since $\mathrm M_\omega (u+tv)$ is a polynomial in $t$, its derivative at $t=0$ is \[  n\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \omega _ u^{n-1},  \] and lemma 2.1.1 turns this into the right-hand side of ( 2.2 ). For the second assertion, fix $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. For every smooth real direction $v$, the segment $u+tv$ lies in $\mathcal H_\omega $ when $|t|$ is sufficiently small, so the right-hand side of ( 2.2 ) vanishes for all smooth real $v$. Hence the smooth top-degree form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _ u^{n-1})$ vanishes. $\square$ Corollary 2.2.4 . If $n=2$, then for every smooth real function $u$ on $X$, \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^2+2\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega .  \] Consequently, $\mathrm M_\omega $ is constant on $\mathcal H_\omega $ if and only if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. Proof. The formula is the case $n=2$ of ( 2.1 ), and it shows that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ implies constancy. Conversely, if the mass is constant, proposition 2.2.3 at $u=0$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. $\square$ The identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-1})=0$ makes the first variation vanish at $u=0$; Hermitian forms satisfying it are the Gauduchon metrics of chapter 4 . On a surface this identity already gives mass invariance. In dimension three, however, ( 2.1 ) reads \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^3 +3\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2) +3\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega .  \] Vanishing of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)$ removes the linear term, while $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ still governs the quadratic term. Thus stationarity of the mass at one potential must be distinguished from its invariance on $\mathcal H_\omega $; an explicit example is given in example 4.8.3 .

text: 2.3 Mass variation on a complex torus By corollary 2.2.4 , the mass on a surface varies precisely through the pairing $2\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ of the potential with the complex Hessian of the background. A product of elliptic curves gives an explicit background and a family of smooth potentials for which this pairing is nonzero. Example 2.3.1 . Let $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z))^2$. For $j=1,2$, let $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$ be the standard coordinates on the universal cover $\mathbb C^2$, with $x_ j,y_ j$ real, and put \[  \beta _ j=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j.  \] The forms $\beta _ j$ descend to $X$. For a real parameter $t$, define \[  b(x_1)=2+\cos (2\pi x_1),\qquad \omega =\beta _1+b(x_1)\beta _2,\qquad u_ t=t\cos (2\pi x_1).  \] Since $1\leq b\leq 3$, the form $\omega $ is Hermitian. It is not closed, because $\mathrm{d}\omega =\mathrm{d}b\wedge \beta _2$ is not identically zero. For a function $f$ of $x_1$ alone, one has $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=(f''/4)\beta _1$, where the prime denotes differentiation in $x_1$. Hence \[  \omega _{u_ t} =\bigl (1-\pi ^2t\cos (2\pi x_1)\bigr )\beta _1+b\beta _2>0 \quad \text{if}\quad |t|<\pi ^{-2}.  \] Writing $B=\int _ X\beta _1\wedge \beta _2>0$, we have 2.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:torus-mass} \mathrm M_\omega (u_ t)=(4-\pi ^2t)B. \end{equation} Indeed, \[  \omega _{u_ t}^2 =2\bigl (1-\pi ^2t\cos (2\pi x_1)\bigr ) \bigl (2+\cos (2\pi x_1)\bigr )\beta _1\wedge \beta _2,  \] and over a period the average of $\cos (2\pi x_1)$ is zero while that of its square is $1/2$. Although the complex torus is Kähler, the background $\omega $ chosen above is not closed, and this already allows the mass to vary. On non-Kähler manifolds even an upper bound for the mass can fail; the Hopf manifolds of chapter 8 give examples. Corollary 2.3.2 . In general, the total Monge–Ampère mass is not determined by the ordinary singularity type or by the multiplier ideals, even among smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials. Proof. The potentials $u_ t$ of example 2.3.1 are smooth on the compact manifold $X$, so any two of them differ by a bounded function and have the same singularity type in the sense of section 1.12 . For the same reason, their multiplier ideals are the structure sheaf for every positive multiple of the weight. By ( 2.3 ), their masses differ. $\square$

title: 2.4 Comparison and mass invariance

text: 2.4 Comparison and mass invariance The global comparison principle of Kähler geometry compares the Monge–Ampère measures of two potentials on the set where one lies below the other. Adding a constant to a potential leaves its Monge–Ampère measure unchanged, and after a large constant shift this set becomes the whole manifold. Such an inequality would therefore compare total masses, and the varying mass of example 2.3.1 rules it out. Proposition 2.4.1 . Suppose that every pair $u,v\in \mathcal H_\omega $ satisfies 2.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:naive-comparison} \int _{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ v^ n \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ u^ n. \end{equation} Then $\mathrm M_\omega $ is constant on $\mathcal H_\omega $. Proof. Fix $u,v\in \mathcal H_\omega $. By compactness there is a constant $C$ such that $u<v+C$ everywhere. Since $\omega _{v+C}=\omega _ v$, applying ( 2.4 ) to $u$ and $v+C$ gives $\mathrm M_\omega (v)\leq \mathrm M_\omega (u)$. Exchanging the roles of $u$ and $v$ gives the opposite inequality. $\square$ Corollary 2.4.2 . The inequality ( 2.4 ) does not hold for every Hermitian form on a compact complex manifold. Proof. Let $X$, $\omega $, $u_ t$ and $B=\int _ X\beta _1\wedge \beta _2$ be as in example 2.3.1 . For $-\pi ^{-2}<t<0$, set $u=0$ and $v=u_ t+C$ with $C>|t|$. Then $\{ u<v\} =X$, but \[  \int _ X\omega _ v^2=(4-\pi ^2t)B>4B=\int _ X\omega _ u^2.  \] Thus this pair violates ( 2.4 ). $\square$ The modified comparison principle of theorem 10.2.1 compensates for the derivatives of the background. Conversely, under the equivalent conditions of theorem 2.2.2 , the ordinary comparison principle holds for bounded potentials, by 11.5.2 .

title: 2.5 Uniform mass bounds

text: 2.5 Uniform mass bounds Although the mass varies, it may remain bounded. Set \[  \overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\omega )=\sup _{u\in \mathcal H_\omega }\mathrm M_\omega (u)\in (0,+\infty ],  \] the supremum of the masses of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials. Comparing two Hermitian forms and rescaling the potentials shows that the finiteness of this supremum depends only on $X$. Proposition 2.5.1 . If $\eta $ is another Hermitian form and $\omega \leq C\eta $ for a constant $C>0$, then \[  \overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\omega )\leq C^ n\overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\eta ).  \] In particular, finiteness of $\overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}$ is independent of the Hermitian form. Proof. Let $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. Since $C\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, the function $u/C$ belongs to $\mathcal H_\eta $. The top exterior power is monotone on positive $(1,1)$-forms: for positive Hermitian matrices $A\leq B$, all eigenvalues of $A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}$ are at least one, so $\det A\leq \det B$. Applying this pointwise gives \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n \leq C^ n\int _ X\bigl (\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u/C)\bigr )^ n \leq C^ n\overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\eta ).  \] Taking the supremum over $u$ proves the inequality. Since any two Hermitian forms on the compact manifold $X$ are comparable in both directions, the last assertion follows. $\square$ The smooth supremum considered here is also the upper mass over all bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials: proposition 6.5.2 proves this using approximation by smooth strict potentials and continuity of bounded products. In chapter 6 , we then pass to unbounded truncations. By corollary 6.6.2 , finiteness of this common supremum is equivalent to finiteness of the extended non-pluripolar mass of every $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potential.

text: Proposition 2.5.1 . If $\eta $ is another Hermitian form and $\omega \leq C\eta $ for a constant $C>0$, then \[  \overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\omega )\leq C^ n\overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\eta ).  \] In particular, finiteness of $\overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}$ is independent of the Hermitian form. Proof. Let $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. Since $C\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, the function $u/C$ belongs to $\mathcal H_\eta $. The top exterior power is monotone on positive $(1,1)$-forms: for positive Hermitian matrices $A\leq B$, all eigenvalues of $A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}$ are at least one, so $\det A\leq \det B$. Applying this pointwise gives \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n \leq C^ n\int _ X\bigl (\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u/C)\bigr )^ n \leq C^ n\overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\eta ).  \] Taking the supremum over $u$ proves the inequality. Since any two Hermitian forms on the compact manifold $X$ are comparable in both directions, the last assertion follows. $\square$

title: 3 Monge–Ampère energy and torsion
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 3 Monge–Ampère energy and torsion Throughout this chapter, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$, and $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and the space $\mathcal H_\omega $ of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions are as in chapter 2 . For a Kähler form, the Monge–Ampère operator is the gradient of an energy: there is a functional on $\mathcal H_\omega $ whose derivative at $u$ in every smooth real direction $v$ is $\int _ Xv\, \omega _ u^ n$. For a Hermitian form, such a primitive exists exactly when $\omega $ is closed. Symmetry of its mixed second derivatives first forces $\mathrm d(\omega _ u^{n-1})=0$, and varying the potential then forces $\mathrm d\omega =0$; this is stronger than the mass invariance of chapter 2 . For a nonclosed background, integrating the Monge–Ampère one-form along radial segments still defines a functional, and its first variation shows which torsion terms enter the corresponding Euler equation. A different energy is available for Hermitian symplectic forms on fourfolds: along potential variations, this completion energy changes by minus the change of the volume. It is therefore constant along potential variations exactly when the mass is invariant, although even then the Monge–Ampère one-form has no primitive unless $\omega $ is closed.

title: 3.1 Primitives of the Monge–Ampère one-form
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 3.1 Primitives of the Monge–Ampère one-form On $\mathcal H_\omega $ consider the Monge–Ampère one-form \[  \alpha _ u(v)=\int _ Xv\, \omega _ u^ n,\qquad v\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R).  \] Let $U\subseteq \mathcal H_\omega $ be open in the $C^2$ topology on smooth functions. A primitive of $\alpha $ on $U$ is a functional $E$ on $U$ such that, for every $u\in U$ and every smooth real direction $v$, the directional derivative \[  DE_ u(v)=\left.\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\right|_{t=0}E(u+tv)  \] exists and equals $\alpha _ u(v)$. Restrict $E$ to the intersection of $U$ with a finite-dimensional affine plane. Its first derivatives are values of $\alpha $, which depend smoothly on the parameters, so its mixed second derivatives agree. The following integration-by-parts criterion identifies the differential condition imposed by this symmetry. Lemma 3.1.1 . For a smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Omega $, the pairing $B(v,w)=\int _ Xw\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Omega $ is symmetric on smooth real functions if and only if $\mathrm{d}\Omega =0$. Proof. By lemma 2.1.1 , $B(v,w)=\int _ Xv\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w\Omega )$. Since $v$ is arbitrary, symmetry is therefore equivalent to the pointwise identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w\Omega )-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge \Omega =w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega +\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Omega -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \mathrm{d}\Omega =0  \] for every smooth real $w$. Taking $w=1$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega =0$. The remaining expression is linear in the first jet of $w$, so we may complexify the test functions. At a chosen point, take a holomorphic linear function multiplied by a cutoff function, so that $\partial w=\lambda $ is an arbitrary $(1,0)$-covector and $\bar\partial w=0$ at that point. There the first-order expression equals \[  \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\bigl (\partial w\wedge \bar\partial \Omega -\bar\partial w\wedge \partial \Omega \bigr ).  \] It follows that $\lambda \wedge \bar\partial \Omega =0$ for every $(1,0)$-covector $\lambda $. Since the wedge pairing between $(1,0)$-covectors and forms of bidegree $(n-1,n)$ is nondegenerate, $\bar\partial \Omega =0$, and $\partial \Omega =0$ because $\Omega $ is real. Conversely, if $\mathrm{d}\Omega =0$, then $\partial \Omega =\bar\partial \Omega =0$ by type, so $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Omega =0$, and the same product formula proves symmetry. $\square$ Lemma 3.1.2 . Let $T$ be a form of type $(2,1)+(1,2)$ on a complex vector space of dimension $n\geq 2$. If $T\wedge A^{n-2}=0$ for every real $(1,1)$-form $A$ in an open neighborhood of a positive form, then $T=0$. Proof. For $n=2$ the assertion is immediate. Otherwise the expression $T\wedge A^{n-2}$ is polynomial in the real coefficients of $A$, so it vanishes for every real $(1,1)$-form $A$. Polarization and then complexification give $T\wedge A_1\wedge \cdots \wedge A_{n-2}=0$ for arbitrary complex $(1,1)$-forms $A_ j$, and such products span all forms of bidegree $(n-2,n-2)$. Since these wedges preserve type, the identity holds separately for the two type components of $T$. Wedging the identity for $T^{2,1}$ with arbitrary $(0,1)$-covectors, we obtain test forms spanning bidegree $(n-2,n-1)$, which pairs perfectly with bidegree $(2,1)$ into top degree. Thus $T^{2,1}=0$. The component $T^{1,2}$ is treated in the same way with $(1,0)$-covectors. $\square$ Theorem 3.1.3 . For $n\geq 2$, the one-form $\alpha $ has a primitive on $\mathcal H_\omega $ if and only if $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$. In fact, a primitive on a $C^2$-open neighborhood of $0$ already forces $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$. Proof. Suppose that a primitive $E$ exists on such a neighborhood $U$. For $u\in U$ and smooth real directions $v,w$, the mixed second derivatives of $(s,t)\mapsto E(u+sv+tw)$ at the origin agree. After division by $n$, this equality reads 3.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:energy-symmetry} \int _ Xw\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \omega _ u^{n-1} =\int _ Xv\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge \omega _ u^{n-1}. \end{equation} By lemma 3.1.1 , \[  0=\mathrm{d}(\omega _ u^{n-1}) =(n-1)\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-2}.  \] Fix a point $x$. A real quadratic polynomial in local coordinates, multiplied by a cutoff function equal to one near $x$, realizes any prescribed real $(1,1)$-form $H$ as $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u(x)$. These functions can be chosen to depend linearly on $H$, with global $C^2$ norms bounded by a fixed constant times the coefficient norm of $H$. Thus every sufficiently small $H$ is realized by a potential in $U$, and the preceding identity holds at $x$ with $\omega (x)+H$ ranging over an open neighborhood of the positive form $\omega (x)$. Applying lemma 3.1.2 with $T=\mathrm{d}\omega (x)$, we conclude that $\mathrm{d}\omega (x)=0$. Since $x$ was arbitrary, $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$. Conversely, proposition 3.2.1 below constructs a primitive for a closed background. $\square$ In dimension one every real $(1,1)$-form is closed, and proposition 3.2.1 always gives a primitive. For $n\geq 2$, the symmetry condition at a single potential $u$ is $\mathrm d(\omega _ u^{n-1})=0$; the theorem uses it on an open set of potentials. Mass invariance alone does not suffice. Indeed, let $X$ be a compact complex surface admitting no Kähler metric, and let $\omega $ be a Gauduchon form on $X$, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ (definition 4.1.1 ); such forms exist by theorem 4.1.2 . The mass of $\omega $ is constant by corollary 2.2.4 , but $\omega $ is not closed, so its Monge–Ampère one-form has no primitive.

title: 3.2 Radial energy and closed backgrounds
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 3.2 Radial energy and closed backgrounds Integrating the Monge–Ampère one-form along the segment from $0$ to $u$ defines a functional for an arbitrary background. Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. For $u\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, put $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and define the radial energy 3.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:closed-energy} \begin{aligned}  E_\theta (u) & =\int _0^1\int _ Xu(\theta +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\, \mathrm{d}t\\ & =\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n \int _ Xu\, \theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta ^{n-j}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} To obtain the second expression, write $\theta +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(1-t)\theta +t\theta _ u$, expand, and use \[  \binom nj\int _0^1t^ j(1-t)^{n-j}\, \mathrm dt=\frac1{n+1}.  \] We write $DE_{\theta ,u}(v)$ for the derivative of $E_\theta $ at $u$ in the direction $v$. When $\theta $ is closed, integration by parts makes the derivatives of the mixed terms telescope. Proposition 3.2.1 . If $\mathrm d\theta =0$, then $DE_{\theta ,u}(v)=\int _ Xv\theta _ u^ n$ for every pair of smooth real functions $u,v$. Proof. Differentiate the finite sum in ( 3.2 ). The term indexed by $j$ contributes \[  \int _ Xv\theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta ^{n-j} +j\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \theta _ u^{j-1}\wedge \theta ^{n-j},  \] the second summand being absent for $j=0$. For $j\geq 1$, the form $\theta _ u^{j-1}\wedge \theta ^{n-j}$ is closed, so by lemma 3.1.1 we may interchange $u$ and $v$ in the second summand. Using $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\theta _ u-\theta $, we can then write the contribution of the term with $j\geq 1$ as \[  (j+1)\int _ Xv\theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta ^{n-j} -j\int _ Xv\theta _ u^{j-1}\wedge \theta ^{n-j+1}.  \] Together with the contribution $\int _ Xv\theta ^ n$ of the term $j=0$, these expressions telescope to $(n+1)\int _ Xv\theta _ u^ n$. Dividing by $n+1$ completes the proof. $\square$ Thus, when $\mathrm d\omega =0$, the restriction of $E_\omega $ to $\mathcal H_\omega $ is the primitive required in theorem 3.1.3 .

title: 3.3 First variation in a nonclosed background
search_title: First variation in a nonclosed background
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 3.3 First variation in a nonclosed background For the Hermitian background $\theta =\omega $, the functional ( 3.2 ) integrates $\alpha $ along the segment from $0$ to $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. When $\omega $ is not closed, the derivative of $E_\omega $ differs from $\alpha $ by the terms produced when integration by parts differentiates the background powers. Computing this difference gives the Euler equation of $E_\omega $ even when no primitive exists. Proposition 3.3.1 . For $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ and $v\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, put $\Omega _ t=(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-1}$ for $0\leq t\leq 1$. Then 3.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-torsion-defect} \begin{split}  DE_{\omega ,u}(v)-\int _ Xv\omega _ u^ n =n\int _0^1t\int _ Xv\bigl (& u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega _ t +\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Omega _ t\\ & -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}\Omega _ t\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{split} \end{equation} Proof. Differentiating the radial integral in ( 3.2 ) in the direction $v$ gives \[  DE_{\omega ,u}(v) =\int _0^1\left(\int _ Xv(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n +nt\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Omega _ t\right)\mathrm dt.  \] On the other hand, \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ Xv\omega _ u^ n & =\int _0^1\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} \left(t\int _ Xv(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\right)\mathrm dt\\ & =\int _0^1\left(\int _ Xv(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n +nt\int _ Xv\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \Omega _ t\right)\mathrm dt. \end{aligned}  \] The terms without a factor $nt$ cancel in the difference, leaving \[  \begin{aligned}  DE_{\omega ,u}(v)-\int _ Xv\omega _ u^ n & =n\int _0^1t\int _ X (u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v-v\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \Omega _ t\, \mathrm dt\\ & =n\int _0^1t\int _ Xv \bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\Omega _ t)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \Omega _ t\bigr )\, \mathrm dt. \end{aligned}  \] The second equality is lemma 2.1.1 . Expanding the last parenthesis by the product rule in the proof of lemma 3.1.1 gives ( 3.5 ). When $n=1$, one has $\Omega _ t=1$ and the right-hand side vanishes. $\square$ Proposition 3.3.2 . If $n=2$, then every $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ satisfies \[  E_\omega (u)=\int _ Xu\omega ^2 +\int _ Xu\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u +\frac13\int _ Xu(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2.  \] For every smooth real direction $v$, its differential satisfies 3.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-defect} DE_{\omega ,u}(v)-\int _ Xv\omega _ u^2 =\int _ Xv\bigl (u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega +\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}\omega \bigr ). \end{equation} Proof. Expanding the radial integral gives the first identity. For $n=2$, one has $\Omega _ t=\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and since $\mathrm d$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ annihilate $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, the derivatives $\mathrm d\Omega _ t$, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Omega _ t$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega _ t$ are those of $\omega $. Formula ( 3.5 ) and $2\int _0^1t\, \mathrm dt=1$ give the second identity. $\square$ Consequently, if $n=2$ and $\mu $ is a fixed smooth real $(2,2)$-form on $X$, a critical point $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ of the functional $E_\omega (u)-\int _ Xu\, \mu $ satisfies \[  \omega _ u^2+u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega +\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}\omega =\mu  \] rather than the Monge–Ampère equation $\omega _ u^2=\mu $. On a Gauduchon surface the term $u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ vanishes, but the first-order torsion terms can persist. The radial Euler equation can therefore differ from the Monge–Ampère equation even when the total mass is invariant.

title: 3.4 Symplectic completions and potential variations
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
3.4 Symplectic completions and potential variations The radial energy is built from the Monge–Ampère one-form, and its first variation exhibits the torsion of the background. When a Hermitian form is the $(1,1)$-part of a closed real two-form, there is another natural energy: the squared $L^2$ norm of the smallest $(2,0)$-part needed to close it. In complex dimension four, adding a complex Hessian to the form changes this energy by minus the change of the volume. Its potential variations are therefore governed by the volume, and not by a primitive of the Monge–Ampère one-form. Throughout this section we assume $n=4$. A Hermitian form $\omega $ is Hermitian symplectic if there is a smooth $(2,0)$-form $ho $, called a completion of $\omega $, such that \[  \partial ho =0,\qquad  ar\partial ho =-\partial \omega .  \] Equivalently, the real two-form $\omega +ho + arho $ is closed. Applying $ ar\partial $ to the second equation shows that $\omega $ is pluriclosed, meaning $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. Two completions differ by a closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-form, so the completions of $\omega $ form an affine space over the finite-dimensional space of closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-forms. The quadratic norm \[  \| ho \| _{L^2(\omega )}^2 = rac12\int _ Xho \wedge  arho \wedge \omega ^2  \] is positive definite on $(2,0)$-forms, and minimizing it over this affine space gives a unique canonical completion $ho _\omega $. It is characterized by being orthogonal to every closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-form. Define the completion energy and the volume of $\omega $ by \[  F(\omega )=\| ho _\omega \| _{L^2(\omega )}^2, \qquad V(\omega )= rac1{4!}\int _ X\omega ^4.  \] The completion energy is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when $\omega $ is Kähler: a zero canonical completion forces $\partial \omega =0$, while a closed $\omega $ has the zero completion. Since $\omega $ is pluriclosed, it defines an Aeppli cohomology class, whose real $(1,1)$-representatives are the forms $\omega +\partial  ar	au + ar\partial 	au $, with $	au $ a smooth $(1,0)$-form. We call a real form $\psi =\partial  ar	au + ar\partial 	au $ an Aeppli variation . If $ho $ completes $\omega $ and $\omega +t\psi $ is positive for a real $t$, then $\omega +t\psi $ has the completion $ho +t\partial 	au $. In particular, the positive representatives $\omega +\partial  ar	au + ar\partial 	au >0$ of the Aeppli class of $\omega $ are again Hermitian symplectic. Every positive potential variation $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ belongs to this class and has the same exterior derivative as $\omega $. We write $DF_\omega (\psi )$ for the derivative of $t\mapsto F(\omega +t\psi )$ at $t=0$. Lemma 3.4.1 . Let $\omega $ be Hermitian symplectic, with canonical completion $ho =ho _\omega $. Every Aeppli variation $\psi =\partial  ar	au + ar\partial 	au $ satisfies 3.13  egin{equation} \label{eq:completion-first-variation} DF_\omega (\psi )=\int _ X\left( \operatorname {Re}(\partial 	au \wedge  arho \wedge \omega ^2) +ho \wedge  arho \wedge \psi \wedge \omega ight). \end{equation} Proof. The canonical completion of $\omega +t\psi $ is $ho +t\partial 	au -h(t)$, where $h(t)$ is a closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-form and $h(0)=0$. In a fixed basis of these holomorphic forms, the orthogonal projection defining $h(t)$ solves a positive definite Gram system whose coefficients are smooth in $t$. Since $ho $ is orthogonal to closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-forms, the contribution of $h'(0)$ to the first derivative of the squared norm vanishes. We may therefore differentiate using the completion $ho +t\partial 	au $. Differentiating its two factors and the factor $(\omega +t\psi )^2/2$ gives the formula. $\square$ Proposition 3.4.2 . Let $\omega $ be Hermitian symplectic. For every smooth real function $\varphi $ with $\omega _\varphi =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$, one has $ho _{\omega _\varphi }=ho _\omega $ and 3.14  egin{equation} \label{eq:completion-energy-volume} F(\omega _\varphi )+V(\omega _\varphi )=F(\omega )+V(\omega ). \end{equation} Moreover, $DF_\omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )=0$ for every smooth real $\varphi $ if and only if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^3)=0$. Thus a critical point of $F$ in its Aeppli class is Gauduchon. Proof. Fix any completion $\zeta $ of $\omega $ and put $\Theta _\zeta =\omega +\zeta + ar\zeta $. Expansion by type gives \[   rac1{4!}\int _ X\Theta _\zeta ^4 =V(\omega )+ rac12\int _ X\zeta \wedge  ar\zeta \wedge \omega ^2 + rac14\int _ X\zeta ^2\wedge  ar\zeta ^2.  \] Since $\partial \omega _\varphi =\partial \omega $, the forms $\omega _\varphi $ and $\omega $ have the same completions. With $\zeta $ fixed, replacing $\omega $ by $\omega _\varphi $ changes the closed form $\Theta _\zeta $ by an exact form, so the integral on the left is unchanged; so is the last integral on the right, which does not involve $\omega $. Hence \[  \| \zeta \| _{L^2(\omega _\varphi )}^2 -\| \zeta \| _{L^2(\omega )}^2=V(\omega )-V(\omega _\varphi ).  \] This difference is independent of $\zeta $, so the two norms have the same minimizer, which gives $ho _{\omega _\varphi }=ho _\omega $ and ( 3.14 ). Differentiating at $t=0$ along $\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ and using lemma 2.1.1 , we obtain \[  DF_\omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )=- rac16\int _ X\varphi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^3).  \] Since $\varphi $ is arbitrary, this proves the remaining assertions. $\square$ The positive index of a real quadratic form on a real vector space is the supremum of the dimensions of the finite-dimensional subspaces on which it is positive definite; the negative index is defined in the same way. Thus the positive index is infinite when the form is positive definite on subspaces of arbitrarily large finite dimension. Theorem 3.4.3 . Let $\omega $ be Hermitian symplectic, and let $H_\omega $ be the Hessian of $F$ at $\omega $ along the affine space of real representatives of the Aeppli class of $\omega $, so that $H_\omega (\psi ,\psi )$ is the second derivative of $t\mapsto F(\omega +t\psi )$ at $t=0$. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)
e 0$, the restriction of $H_\omega $ to potential directions $\psi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ has infinite positive and negative index. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$, then $F(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )=F(\omega )$ whenever $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$. Consequently, every local minimum of $F$ in an Aeppli class satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$. Proof. Step 1: the Hessian formula. Pluriclosedness and Stokes' theorem give $\int _ X\omega \wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^3=\int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^4=0$. Thus the volume and, by ( 3.14 ), the energy along a potential line $t\mapsto \omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ are polynomials of degree at most two in $t$. Differentiating twice and integrating by parts, we obtain 3.15  egin{equation} \label{eq:completion-potential-hessian}  egin{aligned}  H_\omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi ,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi ) & =- rac12\int _ X\omega ^2\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^2\ & = rac12\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)\wedge \mathrm d\varphi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\varphi . \end{aligned} \end{equation} For the second equality, apply lemma 2.1.1 once and then use the identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi ^2/2)=\varphi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi +\mathrm d\varphi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\varphi $ against the closed form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)$. Step 2: both indices are infinite if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)
e 0$. Put $\Psi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)$. At each point, $\xi \mapsto \Psi \wedge \mathrm i\xi \wedge  ar\xi $, divided by a positive volume form, is a Hermitian quadratic form in the $(1,0)$-covector $\xi $, and these quadratic forms determine $\Psi $. Their traces with respect to $\omega $ are positive multiples of the density $\Psi \wedge \omega $, whose integral vanishes by Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. If the quadratic forms took no strictly positive value, they would be negative semidefinite everywhere, with nonpositive traces of integral zero; the traces, and hence $\Psi $, would vanish identically. The same argument applies with the signs reversed. Therefore, if $\Psi 
e 0$, the quadratic forms take a strictly positive value somewhere and a strictly negative value somewhere. Fix one of the two signs. Choose holomorphic coordinates on a ball such that, with $x=\operatorname {Re}z_1$, the density $\Psi \wedge \mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x$ has that sign on the ball; this is possible because $\mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x$ is a positive multiple of $\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm d ar z_1$. For a nonzero real cutoff function $a$ supported in the ball, set $\varphi _ N=a\cos (Nx)$. Formula ( 3.15 ) gives \[  H_\omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ N,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ N) = rac{N^2}{2}\int _ Xa^2\sin ^2(Nx)\Psi \wedge \mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x+O(N),  \] where the constant in $O(N)$ depends on $\Psi $, the chart and the cutoff, but not on $N$. By integration by parts in $x$, the integral tends to half the same integral without the factor $\sin ^2(Nx)$. Hence the Hessian has the chosen sign for large $N$. For a positive integer $k$, apply this construction on $k$ disjoint smaller balls in that region. By the local integral formula, the resulting nonzero directions are linearly independent and pairwise orthogonal for the Hessian, so their span is a $k$-dimensional subspace on which $H_\omega $ is definite of the chosen sign. Repeating the argument with the opposite sign proves that both indices are infinite. Each finite-dimensional span admits sufficiently small variations preserving positivity. Step 3: flatness if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$. If $\Psi =0$, lemma 2.1.2 and pluriclosedness give $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^3)=3\omega \wedge \Psi =0$. Both derivatives at $t=0$ of the quadratic polynomial $t\mapsto F(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ vanish, so it is constant on the interval of $t$ for which $\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$. This interval contains $0$ and $1$ whenever $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$. Finally, a local minimum cannot have a potential direction along which the Hessian is negative, so it satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$ by Step 2. $\square$ Corollary 3.4.4 . For a Hermitian symplectic form $\omega $ on $X$, the following conditions are equivalent: $F(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ is independent of the smooth real function $\varphi $ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$; $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$; $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^4$ is independent of the bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $u$. The common mass in the third condition is $24V(\omega )$. Every local minimum of $F$ in an Aeppli class has these properties. Proof. By ( 3.14 ), the energy is constant along smooth positive potential variations if and only if their volume is. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$, lemma 2.1.2 , theorem 2.2.2 show that this smooth mass invariance is equivalent to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$ and to mass invariance for bounded potentials. The zero potential gives the common mass. The last assertion follows from theorem 3.4.3 . $\square$

title: 3.4.1 Completion energy on products of complex tori

text:
3.4.1 Completion energy on products of complex tori Products of two complex two-tori give explicit Hermitian symplectic forms in both regimes of theorem 3.4.3 . Each factor carries a nonclosed form with an explicit completion. If both factors carry such a form, the product is critical for $F$ under every Aeppli variation although its potential Hessian is indefinite. If only one factor does, the energy is constant along potential variations but varies in the Aeppli class. Consider the square complex two-torus $S=\mathbb C^2/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)^2$. Let $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$ be the coordinates on its cover and put $\eta =\mathrm i\sum _{j=1}^2\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$. For $0<s<1$, the periodic forms \[  v_ s= rac{s}{\pi }\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x_1}\mathrm dz_2, \qquad \alpha _ s=\eta +\partial  ar v_ s+ ar\partial v_ s  \] are well defined on $S$. The Hermitian matrix of $\alpha _ s$ with respect to the forms $\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ k$ is \[   egin{pmatrix} 1

& -s\mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x_1}

\  -s\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x_1}

& 1

\end{pmatrix},  \] with eigenvalues $1-s$ and $1+s$, so $\alpha _ s$ is a Hermitian form. It has the completion $ho _ s=\partial v_ s=\mathrm i s\mathrm e^{2\pi \mathrm i x_1}\mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm dz_2$, and with $\mu _0=\eta ^2/2$, \[   rac{\alpha _ s^2}{2}=(1-s^2)\mu _0, \qquad ho _ s\wedge  arho _ s=s^2\mu _0.  \] Example 3.4.5 . On $X=S	imes S$, let $\omega $ be the sum of the pullbacks of $\alpha _{1/\sqrt2}$ from the two factors. This form is Hermitian symplectic but not Kähler, and it is critical for $F$ under every Aeppli variation, including those with mixed factor components. If $V_0=\int _ S\mu _0$, then $F(\omega )=V_0^2/2>0$. The potential Hessian of $F$ at $\omega $ has infinite positive and negative index, even though potential variations preserve $\mathrm d\omega $. Proof. Denote the two factor forms by $\alpha _ i,ho _ i$, and put $\mu _ i=\alpha _ i^2/2$ and $
u _ i=ho _ i\wedge  arho _ i$; we suppress pullbacks from the notation. Every holomorphic form on a complex torus has constant coefficients. On each factor, the $L^2$ pairing of $ho _ i=\partial v_ i$ with a holomorphic two-form is a multiple of their wedge pairing, which vanishes by Stokes' theorem. On the product, pure and mixed two-forms are pointwise orthogonal, and the pairing with a pure-factor form is the vanishing pairing on that factor times the volume of the other factor. Thus $ho =ho _1+ho _2$ is the canonical completion of $\omega $. Since $\mu _ i=
u _ i$ is half the pullback of $\mu _0$, expansion gives $F(\omega )=\int _ X(
u _1\wedge \mu _2+\mu _1\wedge 
u _2)=V_0^2/2$. Put $\Theta _ i=\alpha _ i+ho _ i+ arho _ i$ and let $\Theta =\Theta _1+\Theta _2$, which is closed. For an arbitrary real $(1,1)$-form $\psi $ and $(2,0)$-form $\sigma $ on $X$, expansion on the two factors gives \[  \operatorname {Re}(\sigma \wedge  arho \wedge \omega ^2) +ho \wedge  arho \wedge \psi \wedge \omega = rac1{12}(\psi +\sigma + ar\sigma )\wedge \Theta ^3.  \] Indeed, the mixed components of $\psi $ and $\sigma $ have odd degree on both factors and contribute zero. The pure components on the left give $(\psi +\sigma + ar\sigma )\wedge (\Theta _1\wedge \mu _2+\Theta _2\wedge \mu _1)$, and since $\Theta _ i^2=4\mu _ i$, the cube on the right is twelve times the same complementary form. Apply lemma 3.4.1 with $\psi =\partial  ar	au + ar\partial 	au $ and $\sigma =\partial 	au $. The derivative is $ rac1{12}\int _ X\mathrm d(	au + ar	au )\wedge \Theta ^3=0$, since $\Theta $ is closed. This proves criticality under every Aeppli variation. Each $\partial \alpha _ i=- ar\partial ho _ i$ is nonzero, so $\omega $ is not Kähler. In $\partial \omega \wedge  ar\partial \omega $, the terms coming from a single factor vanish for dimension reasons, while the two cross terms are nonzero and have different bidegrees on the factors, so they cannot cancel. Hence $\mathrm d\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega 
e 0$, and since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$, lemma 2.1.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)
e 0$. It remains to apply theorem 3.4.3 . $\square$ If only one factor carries a nonclosed form, the energy becomes constant along potential variations, while the same explicit family shows that it still varies in the Aeppli class. Example 3.4.6 . For $0<s<1$, let $\widehat\omega _ s$ on $X=S	imes S$ be the sum of the pullbacks of $\alpha _ s$ from the first factor and of $\eta $ from the second, and set $V_0=\int _ S\mu _0$. Then $\mathrm d\widehat\omega _ s
e 0$ and \[  F(\widehat\omega _ s)=s^2V_0^2,\qquad V(\widehat\omega _ s)=(1-s^2)V_0^2.  \] The energy is constant on all positive smooth potential variations of $\widehat\omega _ s$, and every bounded $\widehat\omega _ s$-plurisubharmonic function has mass $24(1-s^2)V_0^2$. The form $\widehat\omega _ s$ is not a critical point of $F$ in its Aeppli class, and its Monge–Ampère one-form has no primitive on any $C^2$-open neighborhood of zero. Proof. The pullback of $ho _ s$ from the first factor is a completion of $\widehat\omega _ s$. title: 4 Gauduchon metrics and linear mass
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4 Gauduchon metrics and linear mass Throughout this chapter, $\omega $ is a fixed Hermitian form on $X$, and $n\geq 2$ unless a section specifies another setting. The mass variation in chapter 2 leaves a linear conservation law. If $\gamma $ is a Gauduchon metric, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$, integration against $\gamma ^{n-1}$ annihilates every complex Hessian. Thus the trace mass $\int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ of a positive current depends only on its smooth background $\theta $, even when $u$ is unbounded. Gauduchon's theorem produces such a metric in every conformal class, providing conserved pairings when the background is not closed. These pairings determine positivity as well as mass. A smooth form $\theta $ admits a positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ exactly when all its Gauduchon degrees are nonnegative. Normalizing the degrees gives the largest lower curvature bound obtainable by adding a complex Hessian. This bound is always attained by a potential; a minimizing test exists in the weak closure of the normalized smooth Gauduchon forms, although a smooth minimizing metric generally does not exist. Applied to $\omega _ u$, the conformal construction also gives the adjoint probability of the linearized Monge–Ampère operator. It identifies the compatibility condition for that operator and explains the extra term in entropy dissipation for a nonclosed background. For a holomorphic line bundle, the conserved pairing is the degree of its curvature, and a positive degree excludes a metric with nonpositive curvature. Fiber averaging extends this obstruction to plurisubharmonic norms near a direct sum of line bundles. Polar duality and homogeneous regularization then turn it into an obstruction to semipositive Finsler curvature. The stable ample bundles constructed on Hirzebruch surfaces show that ampleness alone does not remove the obstruction; their projective complements give a geometric way to measure it. The same scalar equation can improve curvature when the mean curvature is nonnegative: a conformal change spreads directional positivity from a nonempty open set to the whole manifold. Ricci-flat Kähler surfaces illustrate the distinction between this directional condition and positivity on every tangent and fiber pair. On a projective manifold, positivity on every such pair admits another duality criterion, expressed by positive measures over the dual bundle.

title: 4.1 Conformal Gauduchon metrics
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.1 Conformal Gauduchon metrics By proposition 2.2.3 , the first variation of the mass at $u=0$ vanishes exactly when $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-1})=0$. This condition can be achieved in every conformal class: finding a conformal factor amounts to finding a positive generator of the kernel of the adjoint of a scalar elliptic operator. Definition 4.1.1 . A Hermitian form $\gamma $ is Gauduchon , or a Gauduchon metric , if \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0.  \] It is balanced if $\mathrm d(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$, and pluriclosed if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma =0$. Theorem 4.1.2 (Gauduchon's theorem) . Every Hermitian form $\eta $ has a conformal Gauduchon representative. More precisely, there is a smooth strictly positive function $\rho $, unique up to multiplication by a positive constant, such that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \eta ^{n-1})=0.  \] The associated Gauduchon form is $\gamma =\rho ^{1/(n-1)}\eta $. Proof. For a smooth real function $v$ on $X$, define \[  Lv=n\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \eta ^{n-1}}{\eta ^ n}.  \] This real second-order operator has positive definite principal symbol and no zeroth-order term. By the maximum principle, its kernel consists of the constants. Its index is zero, since the linear path joining it to a Laplace operator consists of elliptic operators. Fredholm theory and elliptic regularity therefore show that the formal adjoint $L^*$ of $L$ with respect to $\eta ^ n$ has a one-dimensional kernel, generated by a nonzero smooth real function $\rho $. We first prove that $\int _ X\rho \eta ^ n\ne 0$. Otherwise the constant function $1$ would be orthogonal to the kernel of $L^*$, and the Fredholm alternative would solve $Lv=1$, which is impossible at a maximum point of $v$. We may therefore rescale so that $\int _ X\rho \eta ^ n=1$. Next we show that $\rho \geq 0$. Suppose instead that $\rho $ is negative somewhere. Choose a nonzero smooth function $h\geq 0$ supported where $\rho <0$, and put $c=\int _ Xh\rho \eta ^ n<0$. The function $h-c$ is strictly positive and orthogonal to the kernel of $L^*$, so the Fredholm alternative would solve $Lv=h-c>0$, which is again impossible at a maximum point of $v$. In real local coordinates $(x_1,\ldots ,x_{2n})$, write $L^*=A^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j+B^ i\partial _ i+C$, where $\partial _ i=\partial /\partial x_ i$, the coefficients are smooth, and repeated indices are summed from $1$ to $2n$. The leading symbol $(A^{ij})$ is positive definite. Since $\rho \geq 0$, \[  (L^*-\max (C,0))\rho =-\max (C,0)\rho \leq 0,  \] and the operator $L^*-\max (C,0)$ has nonpositive zeroth-order term. By the strong minimum principle, a zero of $\rho $ would force $\rho $ to vanish identically on the connected manifold $X$. Hence $\rho >0$. Finally, integration by parts gives \[  \int _ X\rho Lv\, \eta ^ n =n\int _ Xv\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \eta ^{n-1}).  \] Thus the equation $L^*\rho =0$ is precisely $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \eta ^{n-1})=0$, and the one-dimensional adjoint kernel gives uniqueness up to positive scaling. Since $\gamma ^{n-1}=\rho \eta ^{n-1}$, the form $\gamma $ is Gauduchon. $\square$ A Kähler form, that is, a closed Hermitian form, is both balanced and pluriclosed, and every balanced form is Gauduchon. On surfaces, balanced forms are Kähler, and the Gauduchon and pluriclosed conditions coincide.

title: 4.2 Conservation of the trace mass
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.2 Conservation of the trace mass The power $\gamma ^{n-1}$ of a Gauduchon metric annihilates every complex Hessian under integration. It therefore assigns to a positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ a mass depending only on its smooth background $\theta $, also when the potential $u$ is unbounded. Proposition 4.2.1 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, let $u$ be a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function, and let $\gamma $ be a Gauduchon metric. Then 4.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gauduchon-trace} \int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}. \end{equation} Proof. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$, distributional integration by parts gives \[  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,\gamma ^{n-1}\rangle =\langle u,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})\rangle =0.  \] The product on the left of ( 4.1 ) is a positive measure, whose total mass is therefore the finite number on the right. $\square$ We call $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ the Gauduchon degree of $\theta $ with respect to $\gamma $. Here $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is the full distributional current, including any mass carried by the pole set of $u$. The non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of chapter 6 discards this mass; example 7.5.1 illustrates the difference on a curve. Corollary 4.2.2 . There are constants $0<a\leq b<+\infty $, depending only on $\omega $ and a chosen Gauduchon metric, such that every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfies \[  a\leq \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \omega ^{n-1}\leq b.  \] Proof. Fix a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ on $X$ and choose positive constants $c,C$ with $c\gamma ^{n-1}\leq \omega ^{n-1}\leq C\gamma ^{n-1}$. Wedging these inequalities with the positive current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and integrating, we obtain, by proposition 4.2.1 , the bounds $cA$ and $CA$, where $A=\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}>0$. $\square$ The trace bound controls the mass of positive currents and hence their weak compactness. By itself it gives no bound for the Monge–Ampère mass, since a bound on the integral of a trace does not bound the integral of its $n$th power. The pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality relates the conserved trace to the density in a smooth Monge–Ampère equation. Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$. Proposition 4.2.3 . For any two Hermitian forms $\eta ,\gamma $, 4.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gauduchon-amgm} \eta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq \left(\frac{\eta ^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \end{equation} pointwise. Consequently, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $f$ a smooth strictly positive function. If $u\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $c>0$ satisfy $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, then 4.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gauduchon-c-bound} c^{1/n} \int _ X\left(\frac{f\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \end{equation} for every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. Proof. In a frame where $\gamma $ is the identity, let $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n>0$ be the eigenvalues of $\eta $. The ratios of the two sides of ( 4.2 ) to $\gamma ^ n$ are $n^{-1}\sum _ j\lambda _ j$ and $(\prod _ j\lambda _ j)^{1/n}$, respectively, and their comparison is the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. For the second assertion, apply ( 4.2 ) with $\eta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, integrate, and use ( 4.1 ). $\square$ The corresponding density inequality for unbounded potentials in a Hermitian background is proved in lemma 6.4.2 .
