title: 4.3 The Gauduchon criterion for positivity
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.3 The Gauduchon criterion for positivity The trace identity gives a necessary condition for $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ to be nonempty: every Gauduchon degree of $\theta $ must be nonnegative. The condition is also sufficient. A Hahn–Banach separation produces a positive current with the prescribed pairings, and a scalar elliptic equation shows that its difference from $\theta $ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. Theorem 4.3.1 (The generalized Lamari criterion) . For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, the following conditions are equivalent: There exists $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq 0$ for every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. To apply separation, we express the test in terms of smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-forms $\Gamma $. Every strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Gamma $ has a unique strictly positive $(1,1)$-root $\gamma $, that is, $\Gamma =\gamma ^{n-1}$. Indeed, in a frame in which $\Gamma $ is diagonal, and with the same wedge normalization on both sides, the coefficients $g_ i$ of $\Gamma $ are the products $\prod _{j\neq i}\lambda _ j$ of the eigenvalues $\lambda _ j$ of $\gamma $. Hence \[  \lambda _ i=\frac{(\prod _ jg_ j)^{1/(n-1)}}{g_ i}.  \] This spectral formula uses only a positive determinant and a matrix inverse, so the root depends smoothly on the coefficients of $\Gamma $, also at repeated eigenvalues, and pointwise uniqueness makes the local roots agree on overlaps. Consequently, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0$ says exactly that the root $\gamma $ is Gauduchon. of theorem 4.3.1 . Necessity is proposition 4.2.1 . For sufficiency, let $F$ be the real vector space of smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, and let \[  E=\{ \Gamma \in F:\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0\} ,\qquad \ell (\Gamma )=\int _ X\theta \wedge \Gamma \quad (\Gamma \in E).  \] Fix a strictly positive $\Gamma _0\in E$, which exists by theorem 4.1.2 . By the root calculation above, the hypothesis says that $\ell $ is nonnegative on the strictly positive elements of $E$. Adding $\epsilon \Gamma _0$ and letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, we see that $\ell $ is also nonnegative on the semipositive elements of $E$. Step 1: a positive extension of $\ell $. For $\Phi \in F$ put \[  p(\Phi )=\inf \{ \ell (\Gamma ):\Gamma \in E,\  \Gamma \geq \Phi \} .  \] This is a finite sublinear function. To see finiteness, choose $C$ with $-C\Gamma _0\leq \Phi \leq C\Gamma _0$. The admissible element $C\Gamma _0$ gives an upper bound, while every admissible $\Gamma $ satisfies $\Gamma +C\Gamma _0\geq 0$ and hence $\ell (\Gamma )\geq -C\ell (\Gamma _0)$. Sublinearity follows by adding and rescaling competitors. For $\Phi \in E$, the nonnegativity of $\ell (\Gamma -\Phi )$ for admissible $\Gamma $ shows that $p(\Phi )=\ell (\Phi )$. The Hahn–Banach theorem gives a real linear extension $T$ of $\ell $ to $F$ with $T(\Phi )\leq p(\Phi )$ for all $\Phi \in F$. If $\Phi \geq 0$, the zero form is admissible for $p(-\Phi )$, so $T(-\Phi )\leq 0$, that is, $T(\Phi )\geq 0$. Moreover, the bounds by $C\Gamma _0$ show that $T$ is continuous for the uniform norm. It is therefore a positive $(1,1)$-current, and the current $S=T-\theta $ annihilates $E$. Step 2: $S$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. To recover a potential from $S$, consider the scalar operator \[  Dv=\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\Gamma _0)}{\mathrm{d}V},  \] where $\mathrm dV$ is the smooth positive volume form fixed above. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma _0=0$, this is an elliptic scalar operator with no zeroth-order term. Its kernel consists of the constants and its index is zero, while Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ XDv\, \mathrm{d}V=0$. Consequently its range is exactly the space of smooth functions of integral zero, and by elliptic estimates its inverse on functions normalized by $\int _ Xv\, \mathrm{d}V=0$ is continuous in the smooth topology. For a smooth top-degree form $\zeta $ with $\int _ X\zeta =0$, solve $Dv=\zeta /\mathrm{d}V$ with this normalization and set $R\zeta =v\Gamma _0$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R\zeta =\zeta $, and $R$ is continuous. Define a distribution $u$ on such top-degree forms by \[  \langle u,\zeta \rangle =S(R\zeta ),  \] and extend it to all top-degree forms by assigning an arbitrary value on one fixed volume form of integral one. For every $\Phi \in F$, the form $\Phi -R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )$ belongs to $E$, and $S$ annihilates it. It follows that \[  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,\Phi \rangle =S(R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi ))=S(\Phi ).  \] Thus $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T\geq 0$, and proposition 1.1.2 gives a representative of $u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\square$ Applying the criterion to $\theta -a\omega $, for $a\in \mathbb R$, determines the largest lower curvature bound attainable in the background $\theta $. Corollary 4.3.2 . For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, set \[  \kappa _\omega (\theta )= \inf _{\gamma \  \mathrm{Gauduchon}} \frac{\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}.  \] This is a finite real number, and it is the largest real $a$ for which there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ satisfying \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq a\omega .  \] In particular, this largest value is attained, and $\theta $ is big, in the sense of section 1.19 , precisely when $\kappa _\omega (\theta )>0$. Proof. Since $\theta $ is smooth, $-C\omega \leq \theta \leq C\omega $ for some $C$, so the infimum lies in $[-C,C]$. If $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq a\omega $, the trace identity applied to the background $\theta -a\omega $ shows that $a$ is at most each of the ratios in the definition, hence $a\leq \kappa _\omega (\theta )$. Conversely, for $a=\kappa _\omega (\theta )$, all Gauduchon degrees of $\theta -a\omega $ are nonnegative, and theorem 4.3.1 applied to this smooth form gives the required $u$. The last assertion follows, since bigness means the existence of a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic $u$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$. $\square$ Whether the infimum defining $\kappa _\omega (\theta )$ is attained by a smooth Gauduchon metric is decided by a rigidity property of the trace: a positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with vanishing Gauduchon degree is zero. Lemma 4.3.3 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing $. If \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=0  \] for one Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, then $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$. Conversely, a form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth has zero degree with respect to every Gauduchon metric. The same conclusions hold for $n=1$, with $\gamma ^{n-1}=1$. Proof. Choose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and put $S=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. By proposition 4.2.1 , $\int _ XS\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=0$. Since the trace measure $S\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ of the positive current $S$ controls all its coefficient measures, $S=0$. Taking the trace of the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=-\theta $ with respect to $\omega $ gives an elliptic equation with smooth right-hand side, so $u$ is smooth by elliptic regularity, and $f=-u$ has the required property. The converse is Stokes' theorem. For $n=1$, the trace measure is $S$ itself and the same argument applies. $\square$ For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, put $a=\kappa _\omega (\theta )$. By corollary 4.3.2 , the form $\theta -a\omega $ admits a positive current $\theta -a\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. A Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ attains the infimum defining $\kappa _\omega (\theta )$ precisely when the Gauduchon degree of $\theta -a\omega $ with respect to $\gamma $ vanishes. Hence lemma 4.3.3 shows that the infimum is attained by a smooth Gauduchon metric if and only if \[  \theta -a\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\quad \text{for some }f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R),  \] and in that case every Gauduchon metric attains it. Thus a positive current at the threshold always exists, whereas a smooth minimizing Gauduchon metric exists only in this exceptional situation.

title: Theorem 4.3.1 (The generalized Lamari criterion)
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 4.3.1 (The generalized Lamari criterion) . For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, the following conditions are equivalent: There exists $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq 0$ for every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. of theorem 4.3.1 . Necessity is proposition 4.2.1 . For sufficiency, let $F$ be the real vector space of smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, and let \[  E=\{ \Gamma \in F:\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0\} ,\qquad \ell (\Gamma )=\int _ X\theta \wedge \Gamma \quad (\Gamma \in E).  \] Fix a strictly positive $\Gamma _0\in E$, which exists by theorem 4.1.2 . By the root calculation above, the hypothesis says that $\ell $ is nonnegative on the strictly positive elements of $E$. Adding $\epsilon \Gamma _0$ and letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, we see that $\ell $ is also nonnegative on the semipositive elements of $E$. Step 1: a positive extension of $\ell $. For $\Phi \in F$ put \[  p(\Phi )=\inf \{ \ell (\Gamma ):\Gamma \in E,\  \Gamma \geq \Phi \} .  \] This is a finite sublinear function. To see finiteness, choose $C$ with $-C\Gamma _0\leq \Phi \leq C\Gamma _0$. The admissible element $C\Gamma _0$ gives an upper bound, while every admissible $\Gamma $ satisfies $\Gamma +C\Gamma _0\geq 0$ and hence $\ell (\Gamma )\geq -C\ell (\Gamma _0)$. Sublinearity follows by adding and rescaling competitors. For $\Phi \in E$, the nonnegativity of $\ell (\Gamma -\Phi )$ for admissible $\Gamma $ shows that $p(\Phi )=\ell (\Phi )$. The Hahn–Banach theorem gives a real linear extension $T$ of $\ell $ to $F$ with $T(\Phi )\leq p(\Phi )$ for all $\Phi \in F$. If $\Phi \geq 0$, the zero form is admissible for $p(-\Phi )$, so $T(-\Phi )\leq 0$, that is, $T(\Phi )\geq 0$. Moreover, the bounds by $C\Gamma _0$ show that $T$ is continuous for the uniform norm. It is therefore a positive $(1,1)$-current, and the current $S=T-\theta $ annihilates $E$. Step 2: $S$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. To recover a potential from $S$, consider the scalar operator \[  Dv=\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\Gamma _0)}{\mathrm{d}V},  \] where $\mathrm dV$ is the smooth positive volume form fixed above. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma _0=0$, this is an elliptic scalar operator with no zeroth-order term. Its kernel consists of the constants and its index is zero, while Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ XDv\, \mathrm{d}V=0$. Consequently its range is exactly the space of smooth functions of integral zero, and by elliptic estimates its inverse on functions normalized by $\int _ Xv\, \mathrm{d}V=0$ is continuous in the smooth topology. For a smooth top-degree form $\zeta $ with $\int _ X\zeta =0$, solve $Dv=\zeta /\mathrm{d}V$ with this normalization and set $R\zeta =v\Gamma _0$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R\zeta =\zeta $, and $R$ is continuous. Define a distribution $u$ on such top-degree forms by \[  \langle u,\zeta \rangle =S(R\zeta ),  \] and extend it to all top-degree forms by assigning an arbitrary value on one fixed volume form of integral one. For every $\Phi \in F$, the form $\Phi -R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )$ belongs to $E$, and $S$ annihilates it. It follows that \[  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,\Phi \rangle =S(R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi ))=S(\Phi ).  \] Thus $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T\geq 0$, and proposition 1.1.2 gives a representative of $u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\square$

title: 4.4 Compactness and duality of Gauduchon currents
search_title: Compactness and duality of Gauduchon currents
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.4 Compactness and duality of Gauduchon currents When no smooth Gauduchon metric attains the threshold, a minimizer can still be found among weak limits of normalized Gauduchon forms. The normalization bounds the coefficient measures and hence gives compactness. Let $\mathscr G_\omega $ be the set of positive $(n-1,n-1)$-currents $T$ on $X$ satisfying \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0,\qquad \int _ X\omega \wedge T=1.  \] We call them normalized Gauduchon currents . Let $\mathscr C_\omega $ be the weak closure of the set of smooth strictly positive members of $\mathscr G_\omega $. By the root calculation preceding the proof of theorem 4.3.1 , these smooth members are exactly the normalized powers $\gamma ^{n-1}/\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ of Gauduchon metrics $\gamma $. Proposition 4.4.1 . The sets $\mathscr G_\omega $ and $\mathscr C_\omega $ are nonempty, compact and convex. For every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, 4.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gauduchon-linear-minimum} \kappa _\omega (\theta ) =\min _{T\in \mathscr C_\omega }\int _ X\theta \wedge T. \end{equation} Moreover, a current $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ belongs to $\mathscr C_\omega $ if and only if 4.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gauduchon-linear-polar} \int _ X\theta \wedge T\geq 0 \quad \text{for every smooth real }\theta \text{ with }\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing . \end{equation} Proof. Gauduchon's theorem gives a smooth strictly positive member of $\mathscr G_\omega $ after normalization. The fixed trace mass bounds the total variation of all coefficient measures in finitely many local frames, so weak compactness of finite measures gives compactness of the family of positive currents with this trace. Positivity, the trace normalization and the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ pass to weak limits. On this bounded set, testing against smooth forms or against forms with continuous coefficients gives the same topology, by uniform approximation, and this topology is metrizable since the space of continuous test forms is separable. Thus the compactness can also be used sequentially. The defining conditions of $\mathscr G_\omega $ are convex. Its smooth strictly positive members form a convex set, so their closure $\mathscr C_\omega $ is compact and convex as well. Pairing with a fixed smooth $\theta $ is weakly continuous. Its minimum on the closure of the smooth members is therefore their infimum, which proves ( 4.4 ). The Lamari criterion shows that ( 4.5 ) holds for every smooth strictly positive member, and hence for every member of their weak closure. Conversely, suppose that $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ does not belong to $\mathscr C_\omega $, and separate this point from the compact convex set $\mathscr C_\omega $ in the space of currents with the weak topology. A continuous linear functional for that topology is evaluation against a smooth form. After changing its sign if necessary, we obtain a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\beta $ such that \[  \int _ X\beta \wedge T <\min _{R\in \mathscr C_\omega }\int _ X\beta \wedge R =\kappa _\omega (\beta ).  \] By corollary 4.3.2 , the smooth form $\beta -\kappa _\omega (\beta )\omega $ admits a positive current. Its pairing with $T$ is negative, because $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$. This contradicts ( 4.5 ) and proves the converse. $\square$ Corollary 4.4.2 . The function $\kappa _\omega $ is concave, positively homogeneous and invariant under the addition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. Let $\theta $ and $\eta $ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms and let $\varepsilon \geq 0$. If $-\varepsilon \omega \leq \theta -\eta \leq \varepsilon \omega $, then \[  |\kappa _\omega (\theta )-\kappa _\omega (\eta )|\leq \varepsilon .  \] If smooth real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ j$ converge uniformly to a smooth form $\theta $ and $T_ j\in \mathscr C_\omega $ minimize their pairings, every weak cluster point of $(T_ j)$ minimizes the pairing with $\theta $. Proof. By ( 4.4 ), $\kappa _\omega $ is an infimum of linear functionals, which proves concavity and positive homogeneity. Invariance under the addition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ follows from $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$. The normalization of the trace gives \[  \left|\int _ X(\theta -\eta )\wedge T\right|\leq \varepsilon \quad (T\in \mathscr C_\omega ),  \] and taking infima proves the estimate. For the last assertion, pass to a subsequence $T_ j\rightharpoonup T\in \mathscr C_\omega $. The estimate and the uniform convergence of the backgrounds give \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge T =\lim _ j\int _ X\theta _ j\wedge T_ j =\lim _ j\kappa _\omega (\theta _ j)=\kappa _\omega (\theta ).  \] Thus $T$ is a minimizer. $\square$ In general, the closure $\mathscr C_\omega $ cannot be replaced by all of $\mathscr G_\omega $: the exceptional-curve example in example 28.8.2 separates the two sets by a smooth closed form. Testing against all of $\mathscr G_\omega $ instead detects smooth positivity and nefness, as shown in theorem 26.20.1 .

title: 4.5 Transverse concentration of Gauduchon tests
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.5 Transverse concentration of Gauduchon tests Let $\mathcal T_\omega $ be the smooth strictly positive members of the normalized current cone $\mathscr G_\omega $ of section 4.4 . Thus every $\Theta \in \mathcal T_\omega $ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta =0$ and $\int _ X\omega \wedge \Theta =1$. These tests form a weakly relatively compact family, but their pairings with a form concentrating transversely to a hypersurface need not stay bounded. A uniform bound would, by duality, produce a potential whose curvature charges the local hypersurface. Analyticity of Lelong level sets then forces a global hypersurface. Choose a product coordinate chart $(z,\zeta )\in U\times \Delta _ r$, with $z\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and a smooth compactly supported $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ on $U$, equal to one on a nonempty connected smaller polydisk $U'$. Put $\sigma _\zeta =(\mathrm i/(2\pi ))\, \mathrm d\zeta \wedge \mathrm d\bar\zeta $. Fix $p\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb C)$, nonnegative and supported in the closed unit disk, with $\int p\, \sigma _\zeta =1$. For small $\delta >0$ extend \[  B_\delta =\chi (z)\delta ^{-2}p(\zeta /\delta )\sigma _\zeta  \] by zero to $X$, and set \[  C_\delta =\sup _{\Theta \in \mathcal T_\omega } \int _ XB_\delta \wedge \Theta .  \] The form $B_\delta $ is smooth and semipositive. For fixed $\delta $ it is bounded above by a finite multiple of $\omega $, so $C_\delta <\infty $. Theorem 4.5.1 . If $C_{\delta _ j}$ stays bounded along a sequence $\delta _ j\downarrow 0$, then some global analytic hypersurface contains $U'\times \{ 0\} $. In particular, on a manifold without analytic hypersurfaces, $C_\delta \to \infty $ as $\delta \downarrow 0$. Proof. Suppose $C_{\delta _ j}\leq M$ and put $\kappa =(M+1)^{-1}$. Normalizing any smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed complementary form gives \[  \int _ X(\omega -\kappa B_{\delta _ j})\wedge \Theta \geq 0.  \] The generalized Lamari criterion, theorem 4.3.1 , supplies $v_ j$ with \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq \kappa B_{\delta _ j},\qquad \sup _ Xv_ j=0.  \] Since $B_{\delta _ j}\geq 0$, the potentials belong to the fixed normalized $\omega $-plurisubharmonic family. By theorem 1.4.2 , a subsequence converges in $L^1$ to $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The transverse approximate identity converges to $\chi [\zeta =0]$, so passing in distributions gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \kappa \chi [\zeta =0].  \] On a smaller chart meeting the inner hypersurface, add a smooth $\rho $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \omega $. The closed positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+\rho )$ dominates $\kappa [\zeta =0]$ where $\chi =1$. Hence the Lelong number of $v$ is at least $\kappa $ at every point of $U'\times \{ 0\} $. By Siu's theorem in 1.13.1 , the set $Z=\{ \nu (v,\cdot )\geq \kappa \} $ is analytic and has dimension at most $n-1$. Smooth local corrections do not change its definition. The compact analytic set $Z$ has finitely many global irreducible components. Their intersections with the connected inner hypersurface are analytic subsets covering it. At least one intersection is the whole hypersurface, since finitely many proper analytic subsets cannot cover an open polydisk. That component has dimension $n-1$ and is the required global hypersurface. If no such hypersurface exists, there is no bounded sequence $C_{\delta _ j}$ with $\delta _ j\downarrow 0$, which proves the asserted divergence. $\square$ Proposition 4.5.2 . Suppose an effective Cartier divisor agrees, with multiplicity one, with $\{ \zeta =0\} $ throughout the chosen coordinate chart. Then $C_\delta $ is uniformly bounded for all sufficiently small $\delta $. Proof. Let $s$ be the canonical section of its divisor line bundle. In the chart write $s=\zeta e$ with $e$ a nonvanishing holomorphic frame. Choose a smooth Hermitian metric $h$ with $|e|_ h=1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname {supp}\chi \times \{ |\zeta |\leq \delta _0\} $ for a fixed small $\delta _0>0$. The smooth global functions $\psi _\delta =\log (|s|_ h^2+\delta ^2)$ satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta \geq -C\omega $ with one $C\geq 1$. Off the divisor their Hessians are a bounded scalar multiple of the negative curvature of $h$, plus a semipositive gradient term; continuity gives the same lower bound at the divisor. Fix $0<\epsilon \leq (2C)^{-1}$, so $\omega +\epsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta \geq \omega /2$. On the flat-frame region, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta =\frac{\delta ^2}{(|\zeta |^2+\delta ^2)^2}\sigma _\zeta \geq \frac1{4\delta ^2}\sigma _\zeta \quad (|\zeta |\leq \delta ).  \] If $P=\| p\| _\infty $, then $B_\delta \leq P\delta ^{-2}\sigma _\zeta $ on its support. Therefore \[  \omega +\epsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta \geq \frac{\epsilon }{4P}B_\delta  \] globally for $\delta \leq \delta _0$. Every $\Theta \in \mathcal T_\omega $ gives, by smooth Stokes, \[  1=\int _ X(\omega +\epsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta )\wedge \Theta \geq \frac{\epsilon }{4P}\int _ XB_\delta \wedge \Theta .  \] Taking the supremum proves $C_\delta \leq 4P/\epsilon $. $\square$ The uniform bound requires the divisor to agree on the entire cutoff chart. A global hypersurface supplied by the preceding theorem can have further branches there, so the theorem does not provide this converse at arbitrary intersections. Divergence of the transverse pairing alone also gives no lower bound for the volume of the positive root of a test.

text: Proposition 4.5.2 . Suppose an effective Cartier divisor agrees, with multiplicity one, with $\{ \zeta =0\} $ throughout the chosen coordinate chart. Then $C_\delta $ is uniformly bounded for all sufficiently small $\delta $. Proof. Let $s$ be the canonical section of its divisor line bundle. In the chart write $s=\zeta e$ with $e$ a nonvanishing holomorphic frame. Choose a smooth Hermitian metric $h$ with $|e|_ h=1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname {supp}\chi \times \{ |\zeta |\leq \delta _0\} $ for a fixed small $\delta _0>0$. The smooth global functions $\psi _\delta =\log (|s|_ h^2+\delta ^2)$ satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta \geq -C\omega $ with one $C\geq 1$. Off the divisor their Hessians are a bounded scalar multiple of the negative curvature of $h$, plus a semipositive gradient term; continuity gives the same lower bound at the divisor. Fix $0<\epsilon \leq (2C)^{-1}$, so $\omega +\epsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta \geq \omega /2$. On the flat-frame region, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta =\frac{\delta ^2}{(|\zeta |^2+\delta ^2)^2}\sigma _\zeta \geq \frac1{4\delta ^2}\sigma _\zeta \quad (|\zeta |\leq \delta ).  \] If $P=\| p\| _\infty $, then $B_\delta \leq P\delta ^{-2}\sigma _\zeta $ on its support. Therefore \[  \omega +\epsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta \geq \frac{\epsilon }{4P}B_\delta  \] globally for $\delta \leq \delta _0$. Every $\Theta \in \mathcal T_\omega $ gives, by smooth Stokes, \[  1=\int _ X(\omega +\epsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta )\wedge \Theta \geq \frac{\epsilon }{4P}\int _ XB_\delta \wedge \Theta .  \] Taking the supremum proves $C_\delta \leq 4P/\epsilon $. $\square$

title: 4.6 Convex norms and Gauduchon degrees
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
4.6 Convex norms and Gauduchon degrees For holomorphic line bundles, the trace identity of proposition 4.2.1 becomes a statement about curvature. Let $F$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$ and $k$ a smooth Hermitian metric on $F$. In a local holomorphic frame $e$ of $F$ we identify $k$ with the positive function $|e|_ k^2$, and the curvature form of $k$ is $R_ k=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log k$. Let $\Theta $ be a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta =0$; by the root calculation preceding the proof of theorem 4.3.1 , $\Theta =\gamma ^{n-1}$ for a unique Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. The degree of $F$ with respect to $\Theta $ is \[  \deg _\Theta F=\int _ XR_ k\wedge \Theta .  \] Two metrics on $F$ differ by a factor $\mathrm e^{-u}$ with $u$ smooth, which adds $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ to the curvature, so the degree is independent of $k$ by lemma 2.1.1 . It is the Gauduchon degree of the curvature form with respect to $\gamma $; the form $\Theta $ need not be $\mathrm d$-closed. The squared norm $v\mapsto |v|_ k^2$ is plurisubharmonic on the total space of $F$ off the zero section exactly when $\log k$ is plurisubharmonic, that is, when $R_ k\leq 0$; this follows from the Levi form computation in the proof of lemma 4.6.11 below. A line bundle of positive degree therefore admits no metric with plurisubharmonic squared norm. This section extends the obstruction to direct sums of line bundles of positive degree, to all holomorphic structures sufficiently close to such a direct sum, and to norms that need not be Hermitian. The mechanism is again integration against $\Theta $: averaging the horizontal complex Hessians of a norm near the line summands produces a negative multiple of the degrees, and this negativity is stable under small changes of the holomorphic structure. For a smooth complex vector bundle $F$, a smooth complex norm is a continuous function $p:F	o [0,+\infty )$, positive away from the zero section and smooth there, such that \[  p(\lambda v)=|\lambda |p(v),\qquad p(v+w)\leq p(v)+p(w)  \] for $\lambda \in \mathbb C$ and vectors $v,w$ in the same fiber. Its square $G=p^2$ satisfies $G(\lambda v)=|\lambda |^2G(v)$. Near each line summand of a direct sum, the triangle inequality controls the fiber derivatives of $G$, and these estimates control the averaged horizontal complex Hessians. Lemma 4.6.1 . Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mu $ on $X$. Every holomorphic line bundle $F$ has a Hermitian metric $k$ satisfying \[  R_ k\wedge \Theta =\lambda \mu , \qquad \lambda = rac{\deg _\Theta F}{\int _ X\mu }.  \] Proof. Start with any metric $k^0$, and put $\mathcal Lu=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \Theta )/\mu $. This scalar operator is uniformly elliptic, has no zeroth-order term, and its kernel consists of the constants by the maximum principle. On Hölder spaces, the homotopy to a Laplace operator used in the proof of theorem 4.1.2 shows that its index is zero, so its cokernel is one-dimensional. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta =0$, integration by parts gives $\int _ X\mathcal Lu\, \mu =0$, and therefore its image consists exactly of the smooth functions of zero $\mu $-mean. Hence we can solve \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \Theta =\lambda \mu -R_{k^0}\wedge \Theta ,  \] whose right-hand side has integral zero, and elliptic regularity makes $u$ smooth. Then $k=k^0\mathrm e^{-u}$ has the required curvature. $\square$ Let $F_0= igoplus _{s=1}^ rF_ s$ be a direct sum of holomorphic line bundles, with $r\geq 2$. Choose Hermitian metrics $k_ s$ on $F_ s$ and write $k= igoplus _ sk_ s$. Let $P_ s$ be the orthogonal projection onto $F_ s$, and let \[  \Sigma =\{ v\in F_0:|v|_ k=1\}   \] be the unit sphere bundle, with fibers $\Sigma _ x$. On each fiber sphere $\Sigma _ x$ we use the rotation-invariant probability measure $\mathrm d\sigma _ x$. Fix a nonnegative smooth function $\chi $ supported in $(-1,1)$ and positive near zero. For $0<\varepsilon <1/2$, define weights $ho _ s$ on $\Sigma $ by \[  ho _ s(v)=c_\varepsilon \chi \left( rac{|(I-P_ s)v|_ k^2}{\varepsilon ^2}ight), \qquad \int _{\Sigma _ x}ho _ s\, \mathrm d\sigma _ x=1.  \] In unitary frames respecting the splitting, these weights and the normalizing constant $c_\varepsilon $ are independent of the base point and of the index $s$. Independent phase rotations of the summands preserve them, so they are globally defined. The support of $ho _ s$ lies within distance $\varepsilon $ of the unit circle of $F_ s$. Lemma 4.6.2 . For a smooth complex norm on $F_0$ with square $G$, put \[  a_ s(x)=G(e_ s),\qquad N(x)=\sum _ sa_ s(x),\qquad D_ jG(v)=\mathrm d_ vG(P_ jv),  \] where $e_ s$ is any $k_ s$-unit vector in the fiber of $F_ s$ at $x$; complex homogeneity makes $a_ s$ well defined. Then \[  G(v)\leq N|v|_ k^2,\qquad |\mathrm d_ vG(w)|\leq 2N|v|_ k|w|_ k.  \] On the support of $ho _ s$, \[  |D_ jG|\leq 2\varepsilon N\quad (j
e s),\qquad |D_ sG-2a_ s|\leq 10\varepsilon N.  \] Proof. The triangle inequality and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give $p(v)\leq \sum _ s|v_ s|_ k\sqrt{a_ s}\leq \sqrt N|v|_ k$. Differentiating $|p(v+tw)-p(v)|\leq |t|p(w)$ in the real variable $t$ gives $|\mathrm d_ vp(w)|\leq p(w)$, and both global bounds follow. For $v$ in the support of $ho _ s$, set $w=(I-P_ s)v$ and $e_ s=P_ sv/|P_ sv|_ k$. Then $|w|_ k<\varepsilon $ and $|v-e_ s|_ k\leq |w|_ k+1-|P_ sv|_ k<2\varepsilon $. The segment from $e_ s$ to $v$ stays in the unit ball and avoids zero, so integrating the derivative bound along it gives $|G(v)-a_ s|\leq 4\varepsilon N$. For $j
e s$, we have $|P_ jv|_ k<\varepsilon $, which gives the first axis bound. Euler's identity $\mathrm d_ vG(v)=2G(v)$ yields \[  D_ sG-2a_ s=2(G(v)-a_ s)-\sum _{j
e s}D_ jG.  \] The sum on the right is $\mathrm d_ vG(w)$, whose absolute value is at most $2\varepsilon N$. This proves the second axis bound. $\square$ Write $\pi :F_0	o X$ for the bundle projection. For $v\in F_0$ with $\pi (v)=x$, let $H_{0,v}:T_ xX	o T_ vF_0$ be the horizontal lift for the Chern connection of $k$. For a smooth real function $G$ on $F_0\setminus \{ 0\} $, define a $(1,1)$-form $ eta _ s(G)$ and functions $U_ s$, $V_{sj}$ on $X$ by \[   egin{aligned}   eta _ s(G)& =\int _{\Sigma _ x}ho _ s H_{0,v}^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G)\, \mathrm d\sigma _ x,\  U_ s& =\int _{\Sigma _ x}Gho _ s\, \mathrm d\sigma _ x,\  V_{sj}& =\int _{\Sigma _ x}D_ jGho _ s\, \mathrm d\sigma _ x. \end{aligned}  \] Lemma 4.6.3 . At the base point, the first base derivatives of $\zeta _ j$ vanish, and its mixed second base derivatives are $- rac12(\varphi _ j)_{\alpha  ar eta }\zeta _ j$ and their conjugates. Both the spherical measure and $ho _ s$ are independent of $z$ in unitary coordinates, so averaging the identity gives the result, since $R_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$. $\square$ Theorem 4.6.4 . Suppose that for each $s$ there is a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Theta _ s$ satisfying \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta _ s=0,\qquad \deg _{\Theta _ s}F_ s>0.  \] Then there is a $C^4$ neighborhood of the split Dolbeault operator on the underlying smooth bundle of $F_0$ such that no integrable Dolbeault operator in this neighborhood admits a smooth complex norm whose square is plurisubharmonic off the zero section. Proof. Step 1: the split structure. Fix $\mu $ and use lemma 4.6.1 to choose $k_ s$ with $R_ s\wedge \Theta _ s=\lambda _ s\mu $, where $\lambda _ s>0$. Put \[  \lambda _* =\min _ s\lambda _ s,\qquad C=5\sum _ s\lambda _ s+ \sum _ s\sum _{j
e s}\sup _ X\left| rac{R_ j\wedge \Theta _ s}{\mu }ight|.  \] For a squared norm $G$, define $I_0(G)=\sum _ s\int _ X eta _ s(G)\wedge \Theta _ s$. By lemma 4.6.3 , the term $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ s$ integrates to zero against $\Theta _ s$, and the axis estimates of lemma 4.6.2 then give \[  I_0(G)=- rac12\sum _{s,j}\int _ XV_{sj}R_ j\wedge \Theta _ s \leq -(\lambda _* -\varepsilon C)\int _ XN\mu .  \] Choose $\varepsilon $ so that $\varepsilon C<\lambda _*/2$, and keep all weights fixed. Step 2: nearby holomorphic structures. Write a nearby operator as $ ar\partial _ A= ar\partial _0+A$, with $ ar\partial _ A^2=0$. Its Chern connection for $k$ is $D_ A=D_0+A-A^{*k}$, where the adjoint changes the type from $(0,1)$ to $(1,0)$. Let $J_ A$ be the corresponding complex structure on the total space and $H_{A,v}$ the horizontal lift of $D_ A$. These depend smoothly on $A$, and $H_{A,v}$ is complex linear and tangent to the fixed sphere bundle $\Sigma $. For $g\in C^\infty (\Sigma ,\mathbb R)$, define its homogeneous extension by \[  (\mathcal Eg)(v)=|v|_ k^2g(v/|v|_ k),  \] and define a real differential operator on $\Sigma $ by \[  (\mathcal P_ Ag)(v)=\sum _ sho _ s(v)  rac{H_{A,v}^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_{J_ A}\mathcal Eg)_ v\wedge \Theta _ s(x)}{\mu (x)}, \qquad x=\pi (v).  \] It has order at most two. By the identity $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}_ Jf=-(4\pi )^{-1}\mathrm df\circ J$, its coefficients depend on $A$ and its first derivatives, as well as on the fixed smooth data. Consequently they converge in $C^2$ as $A	o 0$ in $C^4$. Step 3: the adjoint operator. Take the formal adjoint $\mathcal P_ A^*$ for the fixed density $\mathrm d
u =\mathrm d\sigma _ x\, \mu (x)$ on the compact sphere bundle, and put $b_ A=\mathcal P_ A^*1$. Locally, if $\mathrm d
u =m(y)\, \mathrm dy$ and $\mathcal P_ A=\sum _{|\alpha |\leq 2}c_{\alpha ,A}\partial ^\alpha $, then \[  b_ A=m^{-1}\sum _{|\alpha |\leq 2}(-1)^{|\alpha |} \partial ^\alpha (mc_{\alpha ,A}).  \] Thus $\| b_ A-b_0\| _{C^0}	o 0$ as $A	o 0$ in $C^4$. For $g=G|_\Sigma $, homogeneity gives $\mathcal Eg=G$ and \[  I_ A(G):=\int _\Sigma \mathcal P_ Ag\, \mathrm d
u =\int _\Sigma gb_ A\, \mathrm d
u .  \] Since $0<g\leq N\circ \pi $ and the spherical measures have mass one, \[  |I_ A(G)-I_0(G)| \leq \| b_ A-b_0\| _{C^0}\int _ XN\mu .  \] Choose the neighborhood so that $\| b_ A-b_0\| _{C^0}<\lambda _*/4$ in it. Then $I_ A(G)\leq - rac14\lambda _*\int _ XN\mu <0$ for every smooth squared complex norm $G$. If $G$ were plurisubharmonic for $J_ A$, all horizontal pullbacks of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_{J_ A}G$ would be semipositive, and their pairings with $\Theta _ s$, weighted by $ho _ s\geq 0$, would give $I_ A(G)\geq 0$, a contradiction. $\square$ The neighborhood depends on the bundle and on the test forms $\Theta _ s$, and different line summands may require different tests. Its size is independent of all derivatives of the candidate norms: integration over the fixed sphere bundle transfers those derivatives to the coefficients of the adjoint operator. To apply theorem 4.6.4 to norms obtained by duality, we first need to regularize continuous norms while preserving a strict convexity margin. Polar duality then turns the obstruction into a failure of semipositive Kobayashi curvature on the dual bundle. Stable ample bundles on Hirzebruch surfaces provide concrete examples, and a fixed Stein hypersurface detects the failure for every Finsler metric on such a bundle. Dual support norms also connect this obstruction with the geometry of neighborhoods of the zero section. This leads to bounds for the convexity of a projective complement. Curvature supplies a second way to study these complements, through explicit exhaustions. A uniformly negative bundle over a Kähler base with a proper psh exhaustion instead gives logarithmic weights and a complete metric on its punctured total space ( 4.6.10 ). The distinction between these spaces matters: the final flat and Hopf examples use restrictions and topology to obtain further bounds for the projective complement.

title: 4.6.1 Homogeneous convex regularization
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.6.1 Homogeneous convex regularization Theorem 4.6.4 concerns smooth norms, whereas the norms produced by duality later in this section are in general only continuous. We show that a continuous homogeneous function with strict positivity margins can be approximated by smooth ones with the same margins, so the obstruction applies to it as well. The local step is Wu's convolution in projective coordinates, written as an average of holomorphic linear shears; the local approximations are glued by the argument of Greene and Wu. We give both steps in order to keep track of strict plurisubharmonicity and of strong convexity in the fibers; see section 34.3 for attribution. Let $\pi :F\to X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle, and write $F^\times $ for the complement of its zero section. A continuous real function $Q$ on $F$ is complex homogeneous of degree two if \[  Q(\lambda v)=|\lambda |^2Q(v)\qquad (\lambda \in \mathbb C).  \] We call $Q$ locally strongly convex in the fibers if, in a local bundle frame and near every point of $F^\times $, there is a constant $c>0$ such that $Q(z,v)-c|v|^2$ is convex on sufficiently small real fiber balls. For continuous functions, strict plurisubharmonicity means that subtracting a sufficiently small positive multiple of the Euclidean squared norm in local coordinates of the total space leaves a plurisubharmonic function. Both conditions are local, and on compact subsets of $F^\times $ they hold with uniform positive margins. The strong convexity required here holds with one constant on a neighborhood in the total space. Strong convexity of every fixed fiber is weaker, even for a plurisubharmonic squared complex norm. Example 4.6.5 . On the trivial bundle $D\times \mathbb C^2$, where $D=\{ z\in \mathbb C:|z|<1/2\} $, put \[  Q(z,v)=\max \left\{  |v_1|^2+|v_2|^2, \frac{|v_1|^2}{1-|z|^2}+|z|^2|v_2|^2 \right\} .  \] This is a continuous plurisubharmonic function, positive off the zero section and complex homogeneous of degree two. Its square root is a complex norm on every fiber, and for each fixed $z$, the real function $Q(z,\cdot )$ is strongly convex. Nevertheless, $Q$ is not locally strongly convex in the fibers near $(z,v)=(0,(1,0))$ in the sense defined above. Proof. Write $t=|z|^2$. Both branches are continuous, positive semidefinite Hermitian quadratic forms in $v$, and the first is positive definite. Their square roots satisfy the triangle inequality and complex homogeneity; their maximum therefore is a complex norm. In particular $Q$ is positive off zero and continuous, also on the zero section. The first branch is plurisubharmonic on the total space. For the second, the locally uniformly convergent expansion \[  \frac{|v_1|^2}{1-|z|^2}+|z|^2|v_2|^2 =\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }|z^ kv_1|^2+|zv_2|^2  \] expresses it as a limit of sums of squared moduli of holomorphic functions. Thus it too is plurisubharmonic, and so is their maximum. For $0<t<1/4$, subtracting $t|v|^2$ gives \[  Q(z,v)-t|v|^2 =\max \left\{ (1-t)|v|^2, \left(\frac1{1-t}-t\right)|v_1|^2\right\} ,  \] which is convex. At $z=0$, one has $Q(0,v)=|v|^2$. Hence each fixed fiber has a positive strong convexity margin. To test a margin on a neighborhood of $(0,(1,0))$, fix any $c>0$ and choose a nonzero $z$ arbitrarily close to zero with $t<c$. At $v=(1,0)$ the second branch is strictly larger than the first, so it remains the maximum on a small fiber ball. Along the real line $v=(1,s)$ in this ball, \[  Q(z,(1,s))-c|(1,s)|^2 =\frac1{1-t}-c+(t-c)s^2.  \] Its second derivative is negative. Thus no positive $c$ makes $Q-c|v|^2$ convex on the fiber balls in any such total-space neighborhood. A fiber-linear change of smooth frame and its inverse are uniformly bounded on a smaller base neighborhood, so a positive quadratic margin in another frame would give one in this frame. This proves the failure of the local margin. $\square$ Lemma 4.6.6 . Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold and let $\mathcal S$ be a sheaf of germs of continuous real functions on $M$, whose elements we call sections. Suppose that $\mathcal S$ is closed under maxima and has the following two properties. Stability: if $f$ is a section near a compact set $K$, then $f+u$ is a section near $K$ whenever $u$ is smooth and sufficiently small in the $C^\infty $ topology on a neighborhood of $K$. Local approximation: every point has a neighborhood $U$ such that, for every compact $K\Subset U$, a section near $K$ can be approximated uniformly on $K$ by smooth sections near $K$, with arbitrarily small errors in any prescribed finite collection of derivative norms on compact subsets where the section is already smooth. Then every global section can be approximated uniformly on $M$ by smooth global sections. Proof. We first describe a gluing step. Let $f$ be a global section that is smooth near a compact set $L_1$, and let $L_2$ be a compact subset of one of the neighborhoods $U$ in the statement. Choose relatively compact open sets $W_3,W_4$ with $L_1\subset W_3$, $f$ smooth near $\overline W_3$, and $L_2\subset W_4\Subset U$. Choose a smooth function $0\leq \rho \leq 1$ equal to one near $\overline W_3$, with compact support in the region where $f$ is smooth. Put $V=W_3\cup W_4$, and choose a smooth function $-1\leq \psi \leq 1$ equal to one near $L_1\cup L_2$ and equal to minus one near $M\setminus V$. By stability, for sufficiently small $\xi >0$ the function $f_\xi =f+\xi \psi $ is still a global section. Approximate $f_\xi $ on $\overline W_4$ by a smooth section $g$, with uniform error less than $\delta <\xi /2$, and with arbitrarily small derivative errors near the compact set $\overline W_4\cap \operatorname {supp}\rho $, where $f_\xi $ is smooth. On $V$ define \[  h=f_\xi \quad \hbox{on }W_3,\qquad h=\rho f_\xi +(1-\rho )g\quad \hbox{on }W_4.  \] These definitions agree on the overlap, and $h$ is smooth. Where $\rho $ vanishes, $h$ is the section $g$. Where $\rho $ can be nonzero, $h-f_\xi =(1-\rho )(g-f_\xi )$, and stability applied to the smooth section $f_\xi $ makes $h$ a section if the derivative errors of $g-f_\xi $ are sufficiently small. Moreover, $|h-f_\xi |<\delta $. Define $f_1=\max \{ f,h\} $ on $V$ and $f_1=f$ outside $V$. Near $L_1\cup L_2$ we have $h>f$, and near the boundary of $V$ we have $h<f$. Thus $f_1$ is continuous, it is a section because $\mathcal S$ is closed under maxima, and it is smooth near $L_1\cup L_2$. Also $\| f_1-f\| _{C^0}<\xi +\delta $. Near $L_1$ it equals $f+\xi $, so the previous smoothness is preserved. Now cover $M$ by finitely many compact sets $L_2$ of this kind and repeat the step, starting with $L_1$ empty and then taking for $L_1$ the union of the previously treated compact sets. At every step choose $\xi $ and $\delta $ so small that the sum of the finitely many uniform errors is below the prescribed tolerance. In a holomorphic bundle chart, write $v=(v',v_ r)$ and use the affine projective coordinate $w=v'/v_ r$ on the cone $v_ r\ne 0$. Suppose that a positive continuous complex homogeneous function $Q$ of degree two is strictly plurisubharmonic and locally strongly convex in the fibers on this cone, and put $q(z,w)=Q(z,(w,1))$. For a nonnegative smooth approximate identity $\eta _\delta (s,t)$ of integral one, define \[  q_\delta (z,w)=\int q(z-s,w-t)\eta _\delta (s,t)\, \mathrm ds\, \mathrm dt, \qquad Q_\delta (z,v)=|v_ r|^2q_\delta (z,v'/v_ r).  \] On every relatively compact projective subchart, for sufficiently small $\delta $, $Q_\delta $ is a smooth positive complex homogeneous function of degree two that is strictly plurisubharmonic and locally strongly convex in the fibers. As $\delta \to 0$, it converges to $Q$ uniformly on compact subsets of the cone consisting of vectors of norm one, and in every finite derivative norm wherever $Q$ is already smooth. Proof. Complex homogeneity gives the identity \[  Q_\delta (z,v) =\int Q(z-s,T_ tv)\eta _\delta (s,t)\, \mathrm ds\, \mathrm dt, \qquad T_ t(v',v_ r)=(v'-v_ rt,v_ r).  \] For fixed $(s,t)$, the map $(z,v)\mapsto (z-s,T_ tv)$ is holomorphic and invertible, and its restriction to each fiber is linear. The same argument with real quadratic barriers in the fibers preserves local strong convexity. Only fiber segments contained in the local cone neighborhood are used here. Ordinary convolution makes $q_\delta $ smooth, and the formula for $Q_\delta $ makes it smooth on the cone and complex homogeneous. Let $Q:F\to [0,+\infty )$ be continuous, positive on $F^\times $, complex homogeneous of degree two, strictly plurisubharmonic on $F^\times $, and locally strongly convex in the fibers. Then there are continuous complex homogeneous functions $Q_ j$ of degree two, smooth on $F^\times $, strictly plurisubharmonic there and locally strongly convex in the fibers, which converge to $Q$ uniformly on the unit sphere bundle of any fixed smooth Hermitian metric. The quotient $m=Q/G$ is a positive continuous function on the compact manifold $M$. Define a sheaf $\mathcal S$ on $M$ by requiring that the corresponding function $Gm$ on the cone be positive, strictly plurisubharmonic, and locally strongly convex in the fibers. This sheaf is closed under maxima. Indeed, multiplication by $G>0$ commutes with maxima. Near a point of the cone, subtract a common positive quadratic barrier from both functions; their maximum remains plurisubharmonic, and on sufficiently small fiber balls it remains convex. Positivity is also preserved. For stability on a compact subset $K$ of $M$, restrict to vectors of norm one lying over $K$, and to a fixed compact annulus around them. Finitely many bundle charts provide positive common lower bounds for both barriers. If $u$ is a smooth function on $M$ that is sufficiently small in $C^2$ near $K$, the Levi form and the real fiber Hessian of $Gu$ are smaller than half these bounds on that annulus. The perturbed function is therefore still positive and has both strict margins. Homogeneity transports the local conditions to the rest of the cone over $K$. This proves the stability required in lemma 4.6.6 . On a sufficiently small projective coordinate chart, lemma 4.6.7 gives local approximation, including derivative control on compact subsets where $m$ is smooth; dividing its regularizations by $G$ gives local smooth sections of $\mathcal S$. Local convexity in the fibers away from zero implies convexity on the whole fiber. Indeed, the restriction of $Q_ j$ to a real line avoiding zero is locally convex and hence convex, while on a real line through zero, homogeneity gives $Q_ j(tv)=t^2Q_ j(v)$ for real $t$, which is convex including at zero. Thus the set $B_ x=\{ v:Q_ j(v)\leq 1\} $ is convex, balanced and absorbing, and its gauge is $\sqrt{Q_ j}$. If $v,w$ are nonzero, convexity applied to $v/p_ j(v)$ and $w/p_ j(w)$, with weights proportional to $p_ j(v)$ and $p_ j(w)$, gives the triangle inequality; the cases with a zero vector follow directly. Suppose that $F$ admits a smooth positive complex homogeneous function $H$ of degree two that is strictly plurisubharmonic on $F^\times $. For every holomorphic structure in the neighborhood of theorem 4.6.4 , there is no positive continuous complex homogeneous function of degree two that is both strictly plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the fibers. If that structure admits a function $H$ as in proposition 4.6.9 , there is also no positive continuous complex homogeneous function of degree two that is plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the fibers. Proof. For the first assertion, theorem 4.6.8 would produce a smooth complex norm with plurisubharmonic square, contrary to theorem 4.6.4 . For the second, use proposition 4.6.9 and the same obstruction. $\square$ The second assertion requires the strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function $H$, which need not exist for an arbitrary holomorphic bundle; 4.6.2 shows that it exists when the dual bundle is ample. title: Example 4.6.5
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Example 4.6.5 . On the trivial bundle $D\times \mathbb C^2$, where $D=\{ z\in \mathbb C:|z|<1/2\} $, put \[  Q(z,v)=\max \left\{  |v_1|^2+|v_2|^2, \frac{|v_1|^2}{1-|z|^2}+|z|^2|v_2|^2 \right\} .  \] This is a continuous plurisubharmonic function, positive off the zero section and complex homogeneous of degree two. Its square root is a complex norm on every fiber, and for each fixed $z$, the real function $Q(z,\cdot )$ is strongly convex. Nevertheless, $Q$ is not locally strongly convex in the fibers near $(z,v)=(0,(1,0))$ in the sense defined above. Proof. Write $t=|z|^2$. Both branches are continuous, positive semidefinite Hermitian quadratic forms in $v$, and the first is positive definite. Their square roots satisfy the triangle inequality and complex homogeneity; their maximum therefore is a complex norm. In particular $Q$ is positive off zero and continuous, also on the zero section. The first branch is plurisubharmonic on the total space. For the second, the locally uniformly convergent expansion \[  \frac{|v_1|^2}{1-|z|^2}+|z|^2|v_2|^2 =\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }|z^ kv_1|^2+|zv_2|^2  \] expresses it as a limit of sums of squared moduli of holomorphic functions. Thus it too is plurisubharmonic, and so is their maximum. For $0<t<1/4$, subtracting $t|v|^2$ gives \[  Q(z,v)-t|v|^2 =\max \left\{ (1-t)|v|^2, \left(\frac1{1-t}-t\right)|v_1|^2\right\} ,  \] which is convex. At $z=0$, one has $Q(0,v)=|v|^2$. Hence each fixed fiber has a positive strong convexity margin. To test a margin on a neighborhood of $(0,(1,0))$, fix any $c>0$ and choose a nonzero $z$ arbitrarily close to zero with $t<c$. At $v=(1,0)$ the second branch is strictly larger than the first, so it remains the maximum on a small fiber ball. Along the real line $v=(1,s)$ in this ball, \[  Q(z,(1,s))-c|(1,s)|^2 =\frac1{1-t}-c+(t-c)s^2.  \] Its second derivative is negative. Thus no positive $c$ makes $Q-c|v|^2$ convex on the fiber balls in any such total-space neighborhood. A fiber-linear change of smooth frame and its inverse are uniformly bounded on a smaller base neighborhood, so a positive quadratic margin in another frame would give one in this frame. This proves the failure of the local margin. $\square$

4.6.2 Strict positivity from the tautological metric The second part of corollary 4.6.10 requires a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function on $F^	imes $ that is complex homogeneous of degree two. Such a function is the squared norm of a vector, viewed as a point of the tautological line it spans, for a suitable metric on the tautological line bundle. Its Levi form is strictly positive exactly when the dual tautological metric is positively curved, so the function exists when $F^*$ is ample. Let $F	o X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of positive rank. In this subsection, $\mathbb P(F)$ parametrizes complex lines in $F$, $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(-1)$ is the tautological line bundle whose fiber over a line is that line, and \[  L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(1) =\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(-1)^*.  \] The map $v\mapsto ([v],v)$ identifies $F^	imes $ holomorphically with the complement of the zero section in $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(-1)$. We use the curvature convention $R_ h=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h$ of section 4.6 . Lemma 4.6.11 . A smooth Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ determines a positive smooth complex homogeneous function $H$ of degree two on $F^	imes $: the squared norm of $v$ in the dual metric on the tautological line $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(-1)_{[v]}$. The function $H$ is strictly plurisubharmonic if and only if $R_ h$ is strictly positive on $\mathbb P(F)$. Proof. Take local holomorphic coordinates $y$ on $\mathbb P(F)$ and a holomorphic frame $e$ of the tautological line bundle, and write the metric of the dual frame as $h=\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$. The dual metric gives \[  H(y,\lambda e)=|\lambda |^2\mathrm e^{\varphi (y)},\qquad R_ h=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] Let $\mathcal L$ denote the complex Hessian, without the factor $\mathrm i/(2\pi )$ of the curvature normalization. Differentiating at a point with $\lambda 
e 0$ gives \[  \mathcal L H(u,t) =H\left(\mathcal L\varphi (u)+ \left| rac{t}{\lambda }+\partial \varphi (u)ight|^2ight), \qquad (u,t)\in T_ y^{1,0}\mathbb P(F)\oplus \mathbb C.  \] If $\mathcal L\varphi $ is positive definite, the right-hand side is positive for every nonzero $(u,t)$: the first term detects $u
e 0$, and the second detects $t
e 0$ when $u=0$. Conversely, for $u
e 0$, set $t=-\lambda \partial \varphi (u)$; strict positivity of $\mathcal L H$ then forces $\mathcal L\varphi (u)>0$. This is exactly positivity of $R_ h$. The squared tautological norm is independent of the chosen frame and is complex homogeneous, so the local functions define the asserted global function $H$. $\square$ A line bundle is very ample when its complete linear system defines a holomorphic embedding, and ample when some positive tensor power is very ample. With the convention above, a vector bundle $F^*$ is called ample when $L$ is ample. Proposition 4.6.12 . If $F^*$ is ample, there is a positive complex homogeneous function $H$ of degree two on $F^	imes $ that is smooth and strictly plurisubharmonic there and, after extension by zero, continuous on $F$. Proof. Choose $m\geq 1$ such that $L^ m$ is very ample. Its complete linear system gives an embedding $\iota :\mathbb P(F)	o \mathbb P^ N$ with $L^ m=\iota ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$. Pull back the Fubini–Study metric to a metric $k$ on $L^ m$, and take its positive $m$th root $h$ on $L$: in a local frame $h=k^{1/m}$, and the transformation law for $L^ m$ makes these local roots a metric on $L$. Its curvature is \[  R_ h= rac1m\iota ^*\omega _{m FS}>0,  \] because the differential of the embedding is injective. Apply lemma 4.6.11 . Since the base is compact, the resulting $H$ is bounded on the unit sphere bundle of a fixed Hermitian metric. Homogeneity then gives $0<H(v)\leq C|v|^2$ off zero, which proves continuity of the extension by zero. $\square$ Corollary 4.6.13 . Let $F$ carry a holomorphic structure in the neighborhood of theorem 4.6.4 . If $F^*$ is ample, there is no positive continuous complex homogeneous function of degree two on $F$ that is plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the fibers. Proof. By proposition 4.6.12 , ampleness of $F^*$ gives the function $H$ required in proposition 4.6.9 . A function $Q$ as in the statement would therefore give a smooth complex norm on $F$ with strictly plurisubharmonic square, contradicting theorem 4.6.4 . $\square$ The function $H$ is not the square of a Hermitian norm in general, since the metric on the tautological line may vary with the line. It provides the strict plurisubharmonicity on the total space needed for regularization, whereas local strong convexity in the fibers remains a separate hypothesis in the continuous obstruction.

e 0$ gives \[  \mathcal L H(u,t) =H\left(\mathcal L\varphi (u)+ \left| rac{t}{\lambda }+\partial \varphi (u)ight|^2ight), \qquad (u,t)\in T_ y^{1,0}\mathbb P(F)\oplus \mathbb C.  \] If $\mathcal L\varphi $ is positive definite, the right-hand side is positive for every nonzero $(u,t)$: the first term detects $u
e 0$, and the second detects $t
e 0$ when $u=0$. Conversely, for $u
e 0$, set $t=-\lambda \partial \varphi (u)$; strict positivity of $\mathcal L H$ then forces $\mathcal L\varphi (u)>0$. This is exactly positivity of $R_ h$. title: Proposition 4.6.12
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 4.6.12 . If $F^*$ is ample, there is a positive complex homogeneous function $H$ of degree two on $F^\times $ that is smooth and strictly plurisubharmonic there and, after extension by zero, continuous on $F$. Proof. Choose $m\geq 1$ such that $L^ m$ is very ample. Its complete linear system gives an embedding $\iota :\mathbb P(F)\to \mathbb P^ N$ with $L^ m=\iota ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$. Pull back the Fubini–Study metric to a metric $k$ on $L^ m$, and take its positive $m$th root $h$ on $L$: in a local frame $h=k^{1/m}$, and the transformation law for $L^ m$ makes these local roots a metric on $L$. Its curvature is \[  R_ h=\frac1m\iota ^*\omega _{\rm FS}>0,  \] because the differential of the embedding is injective. Apply lemma 4.6.11 . Since the base is compact, the resulting $H$ is bounded on the unit sphere bundle of a fixed Hermitian metric. Homogeneity then gives $0<H(v)\leq C|v|^2$ off zero, which proves continuity of the extension by zero. $\square$

title: Corollary 4.6.13
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Corollary 4.6.13 . Let $F$ carry a holomorphic structure in the neighborhood of theorem 4.6.4 . If $F^*$ is ample, there is no positive continuous complex homogeneous function of degree two on $F$ that is plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the fibers. Proof. By proposition 4.6.12 , ampleness of $F^*$ gives the function $H$ required in proposition 4.6.9 . A function $Q$ as in the statement would therefore give a smooth complex norm on $F$ with strictly plurisubharmonic square, contradicting theorem 4.6.4 . $\square$

title: 4.6.3 Polar norms of semipositive Finsler metrics
search_title: Polar norms of semipositive Finsler metrics
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.6.3 Polar norms of semipositive Finsler metrics For a holomorphic vector bundle that is not assumed to carry a positively curved Hermitian metric, positivity can be measured by Finsler metrics and their Kobayashi curvature. Polar duality converts a Finsler metric on $E$ with semipositive Kobayashi curvature into a continuous norm on $E^*$ whose square is plurisubharmonic and uniformly convex in the fibers. With the regularization of 4.6.1 , theorem 4.6.4 therefore excludes such Finsler metrics on an ample bundle whose dual is close to a split bundle with positive Gauduchon degrees. Let $E\to X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of positive rank; in this subsection $n\geq 1$. Write $E^\times $ for the complement of its zero section. A squared Finsler metric on $E$ is a positive smooth function $G$ on $E^\times $ with \[  G(x,tv)=|t|^2G(x,v),\qquad t\in \mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} ,  \] extended continuously by zero to the zero section. It is strongly pseudoconvex if its vertical complex Hessian $(G_{i\bar j})$ is positive definite; this does not require convexity in the real fiber variables. In local holomorphic base and fiber coordinates $(z,v)$, with Greek indices for base coordinates, Latin indices for fiber coordinates and summation over repeated indices, put \[  \begin{gathered} S_{\alpha \bar\beta } =G_{\alpha \bar\beta } -G_{\alpha \bar j}G^{\bar j i}G_{i\bar\beta },\\ \mathcal K_ G=-\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi G} S_{\alpha \bar\beta }\, \mathrm dz^\alpha \wedge \mathrm d\bar z^\beta , \end{gathered}  \] where $(G^{\bar j i})$ is the inverse of the vertical Hessian. We use this convention for the Kobayashi curvature $\mathcal K_ G$, a horizontal $(1,1)$-form at each point of $E^\times $. Thus $\mathcal K_ G\geq 0$ means $S\leq 0$, and $\mathcal K_ G>0$ means that $S$ is negative definite. Lemma 4.6.14 . Let $G$ be a strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric. If $\mathcal K_ G>0$, then for every $v_0\in E_{x_0}^\times $ there is a local holomorphic section $\sigma $ with $\sigma (x_0)=v_0$ and \[  G(z,\sigma (z))\leq G(x_0,v_0)  \] near $x_0$. Moreover, without any curvature assumption, on a coordinate ball, for $\varphi =|z|^2$ and $\varepsilon >0$, the metric $G_\varepsilon =\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon \varphi }G$ is strongly pseudoconvex and satisfies \[  \mathcal K_{G_\varepsilon }=\mathcal K_ G+\varepsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] Proof. Since the vertical Hessian is positive, the Levi-orthogonal complement $H_{G,v}$ of the vertical tangent space at $v$ projects isomorphically onto the base tangent space. The Levi form of $G$ on $H_{G,v}$ is the Schur complement $S$, which is negative definite when $\mathcal K_ G>0$. For the vertical radial vector $R=v_ i\partial _{v_ i}$, complex homogeneity gives \[  \partial G(R)=G,\qquad \mathcal L_ G(a,\bar R)=\partial G(a)  \] for every tangent vector $a$, where $\mathcal L_ G$ is the Levi form. Since $R$ is vertical, the second identity implies $\partial G|_{H_{G,v}}=0$. Choose a holomorphic section $\sigma _0$ through $v_0$ whose tangent space at $x_0$ is $H_{G,v_0}$. In coordinates centered at $x_0$, the function $G\circ \sigma _0$ has zero first derivative and Taylor expansion \[  G(x_0,v_0)+P(z)+\overline{P(z)} +S_{\alpha \bar\beta }z^\alpha \bar z^\beta +O(|z|^3),  \] where $P$ is a homogeneous holomorphic quadratic polynomial. The identity $\partial _ vG(v_0)(v_0)=G(v_0)>0$ gives a vertical vector $b$ with $\partial _ vG(v_0)(b)=1$. Set $\sigma =\sigma _0-bP$ in the local frame. This changes only the pure quadratic terms and cancels $P+\bar P$. The remaining quadratic form is negative definite, and therefore dominates the cubic remainder on a sufficiently small ball. The section stays nonzero there and satisfies the asserted inequality. For the last assertion, differentiate $\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon \varphi }G$ in the Schur complement. Euler's identities give $G_{\bar j}=v_ iG_{i\bar j}$ and $G_\alpha =G_{\alpha \bar j}\bar v_ j$. Hence the terms containing $\partial \varphi $, including its square, cancel between the base Hessian and the mixed block product, leaving \[  S(G_\varepsilon )=\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon \varphi } \bigl (S(G)-\varepsilon G(\varphi _{\alpha \bar\beta })\bigr ).  \] Dividing by $G_\varepsilon $ gives the curvature formula. The vertical Hessian of $G_\varepsilon $ is the positive multiple $\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon \varphi }(G_{i\bar j})$, so $G_\varepsilon $ is again strongly pseudoconvex. $\square$ Proposition 4.6.15 . Let $G$ be a strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with $\mathcal K_ G\geq 0$. Its polar square \[  Q(x,\xi )=\max _{[v]\in \mathbb P(E_ x)} \frac{|\xi (v)|^2}{G(x,v)},\qquad \xi \in E_ x^*,  \] is continuous and plurisubharmonic on the total space of $E^*$, positive off the zero section and complex homogeneous of degree two. The function $\log Q$ is plurisubharmonic off the zero section, and $\sqrt Q$ is a complex norm on each fiber. Proof. The ratio is invariant under complex rescaling of $v$, so the maximum can be taken over the compact unit sphere in a local frame, which proves continuity. Positive upper and lower bounds for $G$ on that sphere compare $Q$ with a Hermitian squared dual norm; this gives positivity off zero and continuity at zero, and complex homogeneity is clear. Moreover, \[  \sqrt{Q(x,\xi )}=\sup _{v\ne 0}\frac{|\xi (v)|}{\sqrt{G(x,v)}}.  \] Each term satisfies the triangle inequality in $\xi $, and so does their supremum. On a coordinate ball, set $G_\varepsilon =\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon |z|^2}G$. By lemma 4.6.14 , its Kobayashi curvature is strictly positive, and its polar square is $Q_\varepsilon =\mathrm e^{\varepsilon |z|^2}Q$. At a point $(x_0,\xi _0)$ with $\xi _0\ne 0$, choose a maximizing line and a vector $v_0$ on it. The lemma, applied to $G_\varepsilon $, gives a holomorphic section $\sigma $ such that \[  \log Q_\varepsilon (z,\xi ) \geq \log |\xi (\sigma (z))|^2-\log G_\varepsilon (x_0,v_0),  \] with equality at $(x_0,\xi _0)$. The pairing $\xi (\sigma (z))$ is nonzero near that point, so the right-hand side is pluriharmonic there. Restriction to sufficiently small holomorphic disks centered at the point therefore gives the submean inequality for $\log Q_\varepsilon $. This argument applies at every point off the zero section, and together with continuity it shows that $\log Q_\varepsilon $ is plurisubharmonic there. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the functions $\log Q_\varepsilon =\log Q+\varepsilon |z|^2$ converge locally uniformly off the zero section. Passing to the limit in the submean inequalities on disks proves that $\log Q$ is plurisubharmonic off the zero section. Since the exponential is increasing and convex, Jensen's inequality shows that $Q=\exp (\log Q)$ is plurisubharmonic there. At a point of the zero section, $Q=0$ and $Q\geq 0$, so every centered disk satisfies the submean inequality there. Together with continuity and the submean inequalities at nonzero points, this proves plurisubharmonicity on the whole total space of $E^*$. $\square$ Lemma 4.6.16 . Let $k$ be a smooth Hermitian metric on $E$, and let $G$ be a positive smooth complex homogeneous function of degree two on $E^\times $, extended by zero. Then its polar square $Q$, defined as in proposition 4.6.15 , has a constant $c>0$ such that \[  Q(x,\xi )-c|\xi |_{k^*}^2  \] is real convex on every dual fiber. Neither strong pseudoconvexity nor real convexity of $G$ is required here. Proof. The real fiber Hessian of $G$ is bounded above by $2L$ times $k$ on the compact unit sphere bundle of $k$, for some $L>0$, and homogeneity extends this bound to every nonzero vector. Also, $G$ is $C^1$ at zero with derivative zero, since its value is $O(|v|^2)$ and its first fiber derivative is $O(|v|)$, uniformly over the base. Integrating the Hessian estimate along a segment gives 4.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:polar-finsler-upper-quadratic} G(v+w)\leq G(v)+\mathrm d_ vG(w)+L|w|_ k^2; \end{equation} a segment passing through zero is handled by splitting it there and using the continuity of the first derivative. Complex homogeneity and completing the square on each complex line give the identity 4.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:polar-finsler-legendre} Q(x,\xi )=\max _{v\in E_ x} \{ 2\operatorname {Re}\xi (v)-G(x,v)\} . \end{equation} The maximum exists because $G(v)\geq a|v|_ k^2$ for a uniform constant $a>0$. Fix a maximizer $v_0$ for $\xi _0$. Differentiation, including the case $\xi _0=v_0=0$, gives $\mathrm dG(v_0)=2\operatorname {Re}\xi _0$. Evaluate the expression in ( 4.10 ) for $\xi _0+\zeta $ at $v_0+w$ and apply ( 4.9 ). The terms involving $\xi _0(w)$ cancel, and we obtain \[  Q(\xi _0+\zeta )\geq Q(\xi _0)+2\operatorname {Re}\zeta (v_0) +2\operatorname {Re}\zeta (w)-L|w|_ k^2.  \] Taking the supremum over $w$ yields \[  Q(\xi _0+\zeta )\geq Q(\xi _0)+2\operatorname {Re}\zeta (v_0) +L^{-1}|\zeta |_{k^*}^2.  \] Set $c=L^{-1}$ and $\Phi =Q-c|\cdot |_{k^*}^2$. After subtracting the square, this inequality gives a real affine function on the whole dual fiber that lies below $\Phi $ and equals $\Phi $ at $\xi _0$. Hence $\Phi $ is the supremum of such affine functions, and therefore convex. Neither uniqueness of the maximizer nor real convexity of $G$ has been used. $\square$ Corollary 4.6.17 . If $E$ is ample and has a strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with semipositive Kobayashi curvature, then $E^*$ admits a smooth complex norm whose square is strictly plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the real fibers. Proof. By proposition 4.6.15 , the polar square is a positive continuous plurisubharmonic complex homogeneous function of degree two, and by lemma 4.6.16 it has the strong convexity in the fibers required in proposition 4.6.9 . Applying proposition 4.6.12 to $F=E^*$, whose dual $F^*=E$ is ample, gives the positive smooth strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function $H$ on $E^*$. Hence proposition 4.6.9 applies. Its proof uses theorem 4.6.8 , which preserves strong convexity in the fibers, and the square root of the resulting function is the asserted smooth norm. $\square$ Corollary 4.6.18 . Let $F$ be the underlying smooth bundle of $F_0$ in theorem 4.6.4 , with a holomorphic structure in the neighborhood given there. If $F^*$ is ample, then $F^*$ admits no strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with semipositive Kobayashi curvature. Proof. Apply corollary 4.6.17 to $E=F^*$. Such a metric would produce a smooth complex norm on $F$ with plurisubharmonic square, contrary to theorem 4.6.4 . $\square$ The corollary applies only near a split bundle whose line summands have positive Gauduchon degrees, and it is not vacuous only if such a neighborhood contains holomorphic structures with ample dual. On Hirzebruch surfaces, theorem 4.6.30 gives stable ample bundles whose duals lie in this neighborhood. Since the polar square need not be smooth, the regularization of 4.6.1 is an essential step of the argument.
