text: 4.6.10 Negative bundle metrics and logarithmic weights For positive curvature, the reciprocal norm in lemma 4.6.41 is useful near a removed zero section. With negative curvature, the squared norm itself is plurisubharmonic. Adding its logarithm gives a weight whose Levi form controls both the base and the fiber directions. In this subsection the base $X$ need not be compact. Suppose that it has a Kähler form $\omega $ and a smooth nonnegative plurisubharmonic exhaustion $\rho $. Here an exhaustion has compact sublevel sets; a constant function qualifies on a compact base. Let $\pi :E\to X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r\geq 1$, with a smooth Hermitian metric $h$, and let $Z$ be its zero section. Use the unscaled curvature and coefficient forms $\alpha _{h,v}$ of 4.6.9 , and assume \[  \alpha _{h,v}\leq -|v|_ h^2\omega \qquad (x\in X,\  v\in E_ x).  \] This is a uniform negative curvature bound with respect to the chosen base form. Proposition 4.6.46 . Put $U(v)=|v|_ h^2$, $q=U\mathrm e^ U$ and $\Psi =\rho \circ \pi +U$. Then $\Psi $ is a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion of $E$ and \[  \Omega =\pi ^*\omega +2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U  \] is a Kähler form on $E$. The function $\log q$, extended by $-\infty $ on $Z$, is plurisubharmonic and satisfies \[  2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log q\geq \Omega \quad \hbox{on }E\setminus Z.  \] Both $U$ and $q$ are strictly plurisubharmonic off $Z$. For the real radial vector field $\mathcal R$, whose flow is $v\mapsto \mathrm e^ s v$, one has $\mathcal Rq=2(1+U)q$. In particular $q$ has no critical points off $Z$. Proof. At $x$, choose a Chern-normal unitary holomorphic frame as in lemma 4.6.41 . Write a tangent vector at $(x,v)$ as $(a,b)$, with $a$ horizontal and $b$ vertical. The first base derivatives and mixed base–fiber derivatives of $U$ vanish there. The same normal-frame calculation gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \mathcal L_ U(a,b) & =-h(R_ h(a,\bar a)v,v)+|b|_ h^2 \geq U\omega (a,\bar a)+|b|_ h^2,\\  \mathcal L_{\log U}(a,b) & =-\frac{h(R_ h(a,\bar a)v,v)}U +\frac{|b|_ h^2U-|h(b,v)|^2}{U^2} \geq \omega (a,\bar a)\quad (v\ne 0). \end{aligned}  \] The last vertical term is nonnegative by Cauchy–Schwarz. Here $\mathcal L$ is the unscaled complex Hessian, corresponding to $2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $. These formulas show that $U$ is plurisubharmonic, that $\Omega $ is positive definite even on $Z$, and that $2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\log U+U)\geq \Omega $ off $Z$. The form $\Omega $ is closed because $\omega $ is closed. The first formula gives strict positivity for $U$ off $Z$; exponentiating $\log q$ gives it for $q$. Locally, $U$ is comparable to the squared Euclidean fiber norm, so $\log q$ tends to $-\infty $ at $Z$ and is locally bounded above. By lemma 1.3.7 , the upper-limit extension is plurisubharmonic and has value $-\infty $ on $Z$. The function $\Psi $ is plurisubharmonic. Its sublevel set of height $M$ lies over the compact set $\{ \rho \leq M\} $ and in the disk bundle $\{ U\leq M\} $ over that set, which is compact. The sublevel is closed, so $\Psi $ is an exhaustion. Finally, $\mathcal RU=2U$ gives the radial identity and excludes critical points where $q>0$. $\square$ Corollary 4.6.47 . For every $m>0$, \[  \mathcal I(m\log q) =\mathcal I_ Z^{\max \{ \lfloor m\rfloor -r+1,0\} }.  \] In particular, if $k\geq 1$ is an integer and $m\geq r+k-1$, a holomorphic function that is locally square integrable against $q^{-m}$ times a smooth positive volume form vanishes to order at least $k$ along $Z$. If $m<r+k-1$, this conclusion fails for some local holomorphic functions. Proof. In a local bundle frame, $\log q=\log |v|^2+O(1)$ near $Z$. Apply lemma 1.16.1 in codimension $r$. Its radial integrability condition for a homogeneous fiber term of degree $a$ is $a+r>m$. For $m<r+k-1$, a monomial of degree $k-1$ satisfies this condition and has insufficient vanishing order. Smooth positive volume forms do not change local integrability. $\square$ Corollary 4.6.48 . The manifold $E\setminus Z$ admits a complete Kähler metric. Proof. Choose a smooth convex increasing function $\eta $ on $\mathbb R$ equal to $-\log (-t)$ for $t\leq -1$. On $E\setminus Z$ put \[  \widehat\Omega =\Omega +2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Psi ^2) +2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta (\log q).  \] The added forms are nonnegative, so this is Kähler. Since $\Psi \geq 0$ is plurisubharmonic, $2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Psi ^2)\geq 2\mathrm i\partial \Psi \wedge \bar\partial \Psi $. Thus $\Psi $ has bounded gradient for $\widehat\Omega $, and a curve of finite length stays in a compact sublevel of $\Psi $ in $E$. The only possible escape from that compact set within $E\setminus Z$ is approach to $Z$. Where $\log q\leq -1$, set $\tau =\log (-\log q)$. Convexity and the chain rule give \[  2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta (\log q) \geq \mathrm i\partial \tau \wedge \bar\partial \tau .  \] Hence $\tau $ also has bounded gradient there, while $\tau \to +\infty $ on approach to $Z$. A finite-length curve cannot escape in this way either. The criterion that every escaping curve has infinite length proves completeness. $\square$ For example, let $B\to X$ have a smooth Hermitian metric with positive unscaled curvature form $\omega $. The direct sum $E=(B^*)^{\oplus r}$ with its induced metric satisfies $\alpha _{h,v}=-|v|_ h^2\omega $. Thus the construction applies whenever this base also has the stated plurisubharmonic exhaustion, including a compact base. If the base is connected, compact and has positive dimension, one may take $\rho =0$. Then $U$ is an exhaustion that is strictly plurisubharmonic off $Z$, but the total space $E$ is not Stein: every holomorphic function on $E$ restricts to a constant on the compact connected zero section and therefore fails to separate its distinct points. Strict positivity away from a compact analytic set does not remove this obstruction.

text: 4.6.11 External tensor products and complement convexity On a product of $k$ manifolds, the external tensor product of bundles with positive mean curvature has, at every nonzero fiber vector, a positive curvature direction tangent to each factor. Indeed, the curvature of the tensor product metric has no components mixing different factors, so this count applies to every fiber vector, including vectors that are not decomposable tensors. Theorem 4.6.42 then improves the convexity bound by $k$. Let $k\geq 2$. For $1\leq i\leq k$, let $X_ i$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n_ i\geq 1$, let $E_ i\to X_ i$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r_ i\geq 1$, and choose a smooth Hermitian metric $h_ i$ on $E_ i$ and a Hermitian form $\omega _ i$ on $X_ i$. With $p_ i:X=\prod _ iX_ i\to X_ i$ the projections, put \[  E=\bigotimes _{i=1}^ kp_ i^*E_ i,\qquad h=\bigotimes _{i=1}^ kp_ i^*h_ i, \qquad n=\sum _ i n_ i,\quad r=\prod _ i r_ i.  \] For an endomorphism $A_ i$ of $E_ i$, write $\widehat A_ i$ for its action on the $i$th tensor factor, with the identity on every other factor. We use the Chern curvature, the forms $\alpha _{h,v}$ and the mean curvatures of 4.6.9 . Lemma 4.6.49 . The curvature of $h$ is \[  F_ h=\sum _ i\widehat{p_ i^*F_{h_ i}}.  \] For every $v\in E_ x$, the coefficient form of $\alpha _{h,v}$ is block diagonal with respect to the decomposition $T_ x^{1,0}X=\bigoplus _ iT_{x_ i}^{1,0}X_ i$, and \[  \operatorname {tr}_{\omega _ i}\bigl (\alpha _{h,v}|_{T_{x_ i}X_ i}\bigr ) =h\bigl (\widehat K_ i v,v\bigr ),\qquad K_ i=K_{\omega _ i,h_ i}.  \] Proof. In product holomorphic frames, the matrix of the metric is $M=\bigotimes _ iM_ i$, and its connection matrix is \[  M^{-1}\partial M=\sum _ i\widehat{M_ i^{-1}\partial M_ i}.  \] Each summand depends only on the coordinates of $X_ i$. Applying $\bar\partial $ gives the curvature formula and shows that all components mixing different factors vanish. Pairing with $v$ gives the block diagonal form. Contracting the $i$th block with $\omega _ i$ commutes with the identity actions on the other tensor factors, which gives the trace identity. $\square$ Theorem 4.6.50 . If every $K_ i$ is positive definite, then \[  \mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X\oplus E)\setminus \mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X)  \] is $(n+r-k)$-convex. Proof. At each point, choose an $h_ i$-orthonormal eigenbasis of $K_ i$. The resulting product basis is $h$-orthonormal, and $\widehat K_ i$ has the positive eigenvalues of $K_ i$, repeated according to the dimensions of the other tensor factors. Hence $h(\widehat K_ i v,v)>0$ for every nonzero $v$, whether or not $v$ is decomposable. By lemma 4.6.49 , each diagonal block of $\alpha _{h,v}$ has positive trace and therefore a positive eigenvalue, so the block diagonal form has at least $k$ positive eigenvalues. Since $k\leq n$, theorem 4.6.42 with $s=k$ gives the assertion. $\square$ Corollary 4.6.51 . Suppose that each $\omega _ i$ is Gauduchon, that $E_ i$ is $\omega _ i$-slope-stable as in definition 4.6.43 , and that $\deg _{\omega _ i}E_ i>0$. Then the complement $\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X\oplus E)\setminus \mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X)$ is $(n+r-k)$-convex. For $k$ stable ample Hirzebruch examples as in corollary 4.6.45 , with their polarizations, this gives $(2^ k+k)$-convexity. Proof. As in the proof of corollary 4.6.44 , choose a Hermitian–Einstein metric on each $E_ i$. Its mean curvature is $\lambda _ i\operatorname {Id}_{E_ i}$, with $\lambda _ i>0$ by the positivity of the degree and the integrated trace identity. Apply theorem 4.6.50 . For the Hirzebruch factors, $n_ i=r_ i=2$, so $n+r-k=2k+2^ k-k=2^ k+k$. $\square$

title: 4.6.12 Homogeneous plurisubharmonic functions and Hopf complements

text:
4.6.12 Homogeneous plurisubharmonic functions and Hopf complements Curvature gives upper bounds for the least convexity index of a projective complement. Lower bounds come from plurisubharmonic functions: a smooth positive plurisubharmonic function on the punctured bundle that is homogeneous of degree two excludes every improvement of the trivial bound, and closed submanifolds transfer such lower bounds by lemma 4.6.38 . On Hopf manifolds these tools determine the least index for line bundles whose de Rham first Chern class vanishes. The answer depends on the sign of their Gauduchon degree, which therefore detects information invisible to de Rham cohomology. Let $F	o B$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r\geq 1$ over a connected compact complex manifold $B$ of dimension $n\geq 1$. Write $F^	imes $ for the complement of its zero section, and put $N=n+r$ and \[  U_ F=\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ B\oplus F)\setminus \mathbb P(\mathcal O_ B).  \] The reciprocal-norm exhaustion in theorem 4.6.42 with $s=0$ shows that $U_ F$ is $N$-convex. Proposition 4.6.52 . Suppose that $F^	imes $ admits a smooth positive plurisubharmonic function $G$ satisfying $G(cv)=|c|^2G(v)$ for every $c\in \mathbb C^*$ and $v\in F^	imes $. Then the least smooth convexity index of $U_ F$ is $N$. Proof. Since every smaller convexity index would imply it, it suffices to exclude $(N-1)$-convexity. title: 4.7 Pluriharmonic currents
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.7 Pluriharmonic currents A current is pluriharmonic if its $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ vanishes. The normalized Gauduchon currents of section 4.4 are positive pluriharmonic currents of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$. This section proves four basic properties of positive pluriharmonic currents of arbitrary bidegree. Positivity and the second-order equation control their concentration on a smooth hypersurface. On compact Kähler manifolds, a closed test form bounds the mass of their pullbacks, and the heat equation smooths those with continuous coefficients. Finally, a positive pluriharmonic $(1,1)$-current with vanishing vertical trace descends along a fiber bundle whose fibers are entire lines or compact curves; this is used for elliptic fibrations in chapter 28 . Lemma 4.7.1 . Let $Z$ be a complex manifold of dimension $m\geq 2$, and let $j:D\hookrightarrow Z$ be a smooth closed hypersurface. If a positive $(q,q)$-current $R$, $1\leq q\leq m$, is supported on $D$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ has order zero, then there is a unique positive $(q-1,q-1)$-current $S$ on $D$ such that $R=j_*S$. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=0$. In particular, if $q=1$, $D$ is compact and connected, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$, then $R=c[D]$ for some $c\geq 0$. Proof. Use local coordinates $(z,w_1,\ldots ,w_{m-1})$ with $D=\{ z=0\} $. Both $R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ have measure coefficients supported on $D$. Suppose first that $q<m$. For every compactly supported smooth form $\eta $ of bidegree $(m-q-1,m-q-1)$, \[  0=\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R,|z|^2\eta \rangle =\langle R,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(|z|^2\eta )\rangle =\langle R,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2\wedge \eta \rangle ,  \] where the first equality holds because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ is a measure supported on $D$, on which $|z|^2$ vanishes, and the last one because the terms containing $|z|^2$ or its first derivatives vanish on $D$. Thus $R\wedge \mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z=0$, which removes the coefficients of $R$ containing neither normal differential. Fix a constant positive Hermitian form $\tau $ in the $w$ variables. The current $M_\tau =R\wedge \tau ^{m-q-1}$ is positive of bidegree $(m-1,m-1)$, and $M_\tau \wedge \mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z=0$. Its Hermitian matrix of measure densities therefore has zero diagonal entry in the normal direction, and positivity removes the corresponding row and column, so \[  M_\tau \wedge \mathrm{d}z=0, \qquad M_\tau \wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z=0.  \] Put $s=m-q-1$. The powers $\tau ^ s$, as $\tau $ varies over the positive Hermitian forms, span the real horizontal $(s,s)$-forms. Indeed, a linear functional vanishing on these powers vanishes on a polynomial over an open cone; polarization makes it vanish on products of arbitrary real $(1,1)$-forms, and these products span the forms of that bidegree. Their products with a horizontal one-form span the complementary test forms for the mixed coefficients of $R$. The identities above therefore remove every coefficient containing exactly one normal differential. For $q=m$, every top-degree coefficient already contains both normal differentials, and this reduction is unnecessary. The remaining coefficients are measures on $\{ z=0\} $ multiplying both normal differentials. They therefore define a unique current $S$ on $D$ with $R=j_*S$. Testing against extensions of strongly positive forms on $D$ proves positivity of $S$, and uniqueness makes these local currents agree on overlaps. Pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ and is injective for a closed embedding, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$ implies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=0$. When $q=1$, the current $S$ is a nonnegative distribution on $D$. The equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=0$ and Weyl's lemma make it a smooth nonnegative pluriharmonic function. If $D$ is compact and connected, the maximum principle makes it a constant $c\geq 0$, proving the last assertion. $\square$ For smooth pluriharmonic forms on compact Kähler manifolds, the mass of the pullback under a fixed holomorphic map is controlled by pairing with a fixed closed form. The test object is the pushforward of a power of the Kähler form on the source, which is closed; the form being pulled back need only be $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. Lemma 4.7.2 . Let $F:Y\to X$ be a holomorphic map between compact Kähler manifolds of dimensions $N\geq n$, with Kähler forms $\Omega $ and $\omega $. For $1\leq p\leq n$, there is a constant $C$ such that every smooth positive $(p,p)$-form $S$ on $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=0$ satisfies \[  \int _ Y F^*S\wedge \Omega ^{N-p} \leq C\int _ X S\wedge \omega ^{n-p}.  \] Proof. The positive closed current $\Gamma =F_*(\Omega ^{N-p})$ has bidegree $(n-p,n-p)$ on $X$. The classical $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-lemma for currents on compact Kähler manifolds gives a smooth real closed form $\gamma $ of this bidegree and a current $U$ with $\Gamma =\gamma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$. For $p=n$, a closed current of degree zero is already a smooth locally constant function, and one may take $U=0$. Since $S$ is smooth, pairing it with $U$ is legitimate, and \[  \int _ Y F^*S\wedge \Omega ^{N-p} =\langle \Gamma ,S\rangle =\int _ X\gamma \wedge S+\langle U,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S\rangle =\int _ X\gamma \wedge S.  \] The pairing with the fixed smooth form $\gamma $ is bounded in absolute value by a constant times the trace mass $\int _ XS\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$ of the positive form $S$. This proves the estimate. $\square$ For continuous coefficients on a compact Kähler manifold, the Hodge heat flow smooths a positive form while preserving the pluriharmonic equation, and a small multiple of a power of the Kähler form restores positivity. Lemma 4.7.3 . Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$, and let $1\leq p\leq n$. Every continuous positive real $(p,p)$-form $R$ satisfying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$ in the sense of currents is a uniform limit of smooth positive real $(p,p)$-forms $R_ j$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R_ j=0$. If $R$ is closed, the approximants can also be chosen closed. Proof. Let $\Delta $ be the real Hodge Laplacian of the Kähler metric. Its heat operators $H_ t=\mathrm e^{-t\Delta }$ are smoothing for $t>0$. The Kähler identities give $\Delta =2\Delta _\partial =2\Delta _{\bar\partial }$, so $H_ t$ preserves bidegree, reality and the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$. We recall why $H_ tR\to R$ uniformly for a continuous form $R$. The Weitzenböck formula writes $\Delta =\nabla ^*\nabla +A$, with a bounded curvature term $A$ of order zero. For smooth initial data $\beta $, the heat equation and the maximum principle give \[  \| H_ t\beta \| _{C^0}\leq \mathrm e^{Ct}\| \beta \| _{C^0} \qquad (0<t\leq 1),  \] where $C$ depends only on the fixed metric and the degree. Indeed, the scalar equation for $|H_ t\beta |^2$ has a nonpositive gradient term and a curvature term bounded above by $2C|H_ t\beta |^2$. The classical smooth heat solution converges uniformly to its smooth initial data. Approximating a continuous form by smooth forms and using this bound proves uniform convergence for continuous initial data. The resulting heat solution is smooth for $t>0$, and since the commutation with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ extends to currents, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ tR=0$. Set $\epsilon _ t=\| H_ tR-R\| _{C^0}$, which tends to zero. A fixed constant $c>0$ satisfies \[  E+c\| E\| _{C^0}\omega ^ p\geq 0  \] for every continuous real $(p,p)$-form $E$; to see this, evaluate on decomposable unit $p$-vectors, on which $\omega ^ p$ has a uniformly positive value. Consequently \[  R_ t=H_ tR+c\epsilon _ t\omega ^ p  \] is smooth and positive. Since $\omega $ is Kähler, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega ^ p=0$, and hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R_ t=0$. Moreover, $R_ t\to R$ uniformly. The Hodge heat flow also commutes with $\mathrm{d}$, and $\omega ^ p$ is closed, so $\mathrm{d}R=0$ implies $\mathrm{d}R_ t=0$. Choosing any sequence $t_ j\downarrow 0$ proves the assertion. $\square$ We next consider a positive $(1,1)$-current with vanishing vertical trace on the total space of a fiber bundle. Positivity removes its vertical and mixed coefficients. For a closed current the remaining coefficients are constant along the fibers. For a pluriharmonic current they are only harmonic along the fibers, but positivity gives the same conclusion when the fiber is the whole complex line or a compact connected curve. Lemma 4.7.4 . Let $Y$ be a complex manifold of dimension $\ell \geq 1$, let $\eta $ be a Hermitian form on $Y$, and let $\pi :Z\to Y$ be a holomorphic fiber bundle whose fiber is either $\mathbb C$ or a compact connected Riemann surface. If $S$ is a positive real $(1,1)$-current on $Z$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=0$ and $S\wedge \pi ^*\eta ^\ell =0$, then there is a unique positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(1,1)$-current $R$ on $Y$ such that $S=\pi ^*R$. If $S$ is closed, then $R$ is closed. Proof. Fix a local trivialization $\pi ^{-1}(U)=U\times F$ of the bundle, with base coordinates $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_\ell )$ and a local fiber coordinate $z$. The coefficient measures of $S$ have a positive Hermitian matrix of densities relative to their trace measure. The identity $S\wedge \pi ^*\eta ^\ell =0$ makes the vertical diagonal entry zero, and the inequality $|s_{\alpha \bar z}|^2\leq s_{\alpha \bar\alpha }s_{z\bar z}$ then removes all mixed entries. Thus \[  S=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\sum _{\alpha ,\beta =1}^\ell s_{\alpha \bar\beta }(w,z)\, \mathrm{d}w_\alpha \wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w_\beta ,  \] with distribution coefficients. In the equation $\partial \bar\partial S=0$, the coefficient containing both vertical differentials and the horizontal pair $(\alpha ,\beta )$ gives $\partial _ z\partial _{\bar z}s_{\alpha \bar\beta }=0$. Fix $v\in \mathbb C^\ell $ and a nonnegative smooth function $\xi $ with compact support in $U$. Pairing the positive coefficient distribution $\sum _{\alpha ,\beta }s_{\alpha \bar\beta }v_\alpha \bar v_\beta $, in the base variables, with $\xi $ times the Euclidean volume form defines a nonnegative harmonic distribution on the whole fiber $F$. Its definition does not depend on the fiber coordinate, since the remaining differentials are horizontal. Weyl's lemma makes it a nonnegative harmonic function. Such a function is constant on $\mathbb C$ by the Liouville theorem for harmonic functions, and on a compact connected curve by the maximum principle. Polarization in $v$ and linearity in the base test function show that every coefficient $s_{\alpha \bar\beta }$ is the pullback of a distribution $r_{\alpha \bar\beta }$ on $U$. To identify this distribution, pair against any nonnegative smooth fiber density of total integral one; this also proves positivity of the resulting current $R_ U$ on $U$ and injectivity of the pullback. Consequently $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=\pi ^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R_ U)=0$ implies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R_ U=0$. On overlaps, injectivity makes the currents $R_ U$ agree, so they glue to a current $R$, and injectivity also proves uniqueness. If $\mathrm{d}S=0$, the same argument gives $\mathrm{d}R=0$. $\square$ The assumption that the fibers are entire lines or compact curves is essential. On the bidisk $\Delta _ z\times \Delta _ w$, the current \[  S=(2+\operatorname {Re}z)\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\, \mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w  \] is positive and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, and its vertical trace vanishes. Its horizontal coefficient depends on $z$, so it does not descend under the projection to $\Delta _ w$.

title: Lemma 4.7.1
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Lemma 4.7.1 . Let $Z$ be a complex manifold of dimension $m\geq 2$, and let $j:D\hookrightarrow Z$ be a smooth closed hypersurface. If a positive $(q,q)$-current $R$, $1\leq q\leq m$, is supported on $D$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ has order zero, then there is a unique positive $(q-1,q-1)$-current $S$ on $D$ such that $R=j_*S$. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=0$. In particular, if $q=1$, $D$ is compact and connected, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$, then $R=c[D]$ for some $c\geq 0$. Proof. Use local coordinates $(z,w_1,\ldots ,w_{m-1})$ with $D=\{ z=0\} $. Both $R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ have measure coefficients supported on $D$. Suppose first that $q<m$. For every compactly supported smooth form $\eta $ of bidegree $(m-q-1,m-q-1)$, \[  0=\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R,|z|^2\eta \rangle =\langle R,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(|z|^2\eta )\rangle =\langle R,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2\wedge \eta \rangle ,  \] where the first equality holds because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ is a measure supported on $D$, on which $|z|^2$ vanishes, and the last one because the terms containing $|z|^2$ or its first derivatives vanish on $D$. Thus $R\wedge \mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z=0$, which removes the coefficients of $R$ containing neither normal differential. Fix a constant positive Hermitian form $\tau $ in the $w$ variables. The current $M_\tau =R\wedge \tau ^{m-q-1}$ is positive of bidegree $(m-1,m-1)$, and $M_\tau \wedge \mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z=0$. Its Hermitian matrix of measure densities therefore has zero diagonal entry in the normal direction, and positivity removes the corresponding row and column, so \[  M_\tau \wedge \mathrm{d}z=0, \qquad M_\tau \wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z=0.  \] Put $s=m-q-1$. The powers $\tau ^ s$, as $\tau $ varies over the positive Hermitian forms, span the real horizontal $(s,s)$-forms. Indeed, a linear functional vanishing on these powers vanishes on a polynomial over an open cone; polarization makes it vanish on products of arbitrary real $(1,1)$-forms, and these products span the forms of that bidegree. Their products with a horizontal one-form span the complementary test forms for the mixed coefficients of $R$. The identities above therefore remove every coefficient containing exactly one normal differential. For $q=m$, every top-degree coefficient already contains both normal differentials, and this reduction is unnecessary. The remaining coefficients are measures on $\{ z=0\} $ multiplying both normal differentials. They therefore define a unique current $S$ on $D$ with $R=j_*S$. Testing against extensions of strongly positive forms on $D$ proves positivity of $S$, and uniqueness makes these local currents agree on overlaps. Pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ and is injective for a closed embedding, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$ implies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=0$. When $q=1$, the current $S$ is a nonnegative distribution on $D$. The equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=0$ and Weyl's lemma make it a smooth nonnegative pluriharmonic function. If $D$ is compact and connected, the maximum principle makes it a constant $c\geq 0$, proving the last assertion. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.7.2
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Lemma 4.7.2 . Let $F:Y\to X$ be a holomorphic map between compact Kähler manifolds of dimensions $N\geq n$, with Kähler forms $\Omega $ and $\omega $. For $1\leq p\leq n$, there is a constant $C$ such that every smooth positive $(p,p)$-form $S$ on $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=0$ satisfies \[  \int _ Y F^*S\wedge \Omega ^{N-p} \leq C\int _ X S\wedge \omega ^{n-p}.  \] Proof. The positive closed current $\Gamma =F_*(\Omega ^{N-p})$ has bidegree $(n-p,n-p)$ on $X$. The classical $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-lemma for currents on compact Kähler manifolds gives a smooth real closed form $\gamma $ of this bidegree and a current $U$ with $\Gamma =\gamma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$. For $p=n$, a closed current of degree zero is already a smooth locally constant function, and one may take $U=0$. Since $S$ is smooth, pairing it with $U$ is legitimate, and \[  \int _ Y F^*S\wedge \Omega ^{N-p} =\langle \Gamma ,S\rangle =\int _ X\gamma \wedge S+\langle U,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S\rangle =\int _ X\gamma \wedge S.  \] The pairing with the fixed smooth form $\gamma $ is bounded in absolute value by a constant times the trace mass $\int _ XS\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$ of the positive form $S$. This proves the estimate. $\square$

title: 4.8 The adjoint measure of the linearization

topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.8 The adjoint measure of the linearization The derivative of the logarithmic Monge–Ampère operator $u\mapsto \log (\omega _ u^ n/\mathrm dV)$ annihilates the constants, so its linearized equation can be solved only under a compatibility condition. The Gauduchon multiplier of theorem 4.1.2 identifies this condition. Fix $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ and write $\eta =\omega _ u$. For a smooth real direction $v$, logarithmic differentiation gives the linearized operator 4.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:linearized-ma} L_ u v=n\, \frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \eta ^{n-1}}{\eta ^ n}. \end{equation} Choose the Gauduchon multiplier $\rho _ u$ of $\eta $ given by theorem 4.1.2 , normalized by \[  \int _ X\rho _ u\eta ^ n=1, \qquad \text{and put}\qquad \mathrm{d}\mu _ u:=\rho _ u\eta ^ n.  \] The adjoint measure $\mu _ u$ is a smooth positive probability measure. Proposition 4.8.1 . For every smooth real $v$, 4.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:adjoint-identity} \int _ X L_ uv\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u=0. \end{equation} Moreover, for smooth real $h$, the equation $L_ uv=h$ has a smooth solution if and only if $\int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u=0$. When it exists, the solution is unique modulo constants. Proof. The integral in ( 4.16 ) is \[  n\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \rho _ u\eta ^{n-1} =n\int _ Xv\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _ u\eta ^{n-1})=0.  \] This proves that the compatibility condition is necessary. By the Fredholm argument in the proof of theorem 4.1.2 , the range of $L_ u:C^{k+2,\alpha }(X)\to C^{k,\alpha }(X)$ has codimension one for every integer $k\geq 0$ and $0<\alpha <1$. The nonzero functional $h\mapsto \int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u$ annihilates that range, so its kernel is the range. Elliptic regularity gives a smooth solution, and since the kernel of $L_ u$ consists of the constants, the solution is unique modulo constants. $\square$ By its defining equation and the uniqueness in theorem 4.1.2 , the multiplier $\rho _ u$ is constant precisely when $\eta $ is Gauduchon. Thus \[  \mu _ u=\frac{\eta ^ n}{\int _ X\eta ^ n} \quad \text{if }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\eta ^{n-1})=0.  \] On a surface, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega _ u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $, so every positive potential perturbation of a Gauduchon form is still Gauduchon. In higher dimension this persistence requires more than the Gauduchon condition at $u=0$. Write $M=\int _ X\omega ^ n$. Proposition 4.8.2 . Every form $\omega _ u$ with $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ is Gauduchon if and only if \[  \int _ X\omega _ u^ n=M \quad \text{for every }u\in \mathcal H_\omega .  \] In that case the normalized multiplier is $\rho _ u=M^{-1}$ and $\mu _ u=M^{-1}\omega _ u^ n$ for every $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. Proof. If all the forms $\omega _ u$ are Gauduchon, the mass derivative ( 2.2 ) vanishes at every point of $\mathcal H_\omega $ and in every direction. Since $\mathcal H_\omega $ is convex, integration along the segment from $0$ to $u$ gives the mass identity. Conversely, proposition 2.2.3 shows that constant mass forces $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _ u^{n-1})=0$ for every $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. In that case the normalized multiplier is the constant $M^{-1}$, by theorem 4.1.2 . $\square$ By theorem 2.2.2 , this persistence is equivalent to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)=0$ for all integers $1\leq j\leq n-1$. The following example distinguishes it from the single Gauduchon identity in dimension three. Example 4.8.3 . Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$ and $X=E^3$. For $1\leq j\leq 3$, write $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$ for the coordinates on the covering space, and let $\eta _ j$ be the form on $X$ induced by $(\mathrm i/2)\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$. The periodic functions \[  b=\exp (\cos (2\pi x_1)),\qquad c=b^{-1}  \] define a Hermitian form \[  \omega =\eta _1+b\eta _2+c\eta _3.  \] Since $bc=1$, \[  \omega ^2=2b\eta _1\wedge \eta _2 +2c\eta _1\wedge \eta _3+2\eta _2\wedge \eta _3.  \] The functions $b$ and $c$ depend only on $x_1$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}c$ are multiples of $\eta _1$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$. Thus $\omega $ is Gauduchon. Put $v=\cos (2\pi x_2)$ and $h=-\pi \cos (2\pi x_2)$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=h\eta _2$. For a real $s$ with $0<|s|<1/(\pi \mathrm e)$, the form \[  \omega _{sv}=\eta _1+(b+sh)\eta _2+c\eta _3  \] is positive, since $b\geq \mathrm e^{-1}$ and $|h|\leq \pi $. However, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _{sv}^2) =2s\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v =2sh\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}c\wedge \eta _2\wedge \eta _3\ne 0.  \] Indeed, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}c=(c''/(4\pi ))\eta _1$, where the prime denotes differentiation in $x_1$, and $c''(0)=4\pi ^2\mathrm e^{-1}$, while $h=-\pi $ at $x_2=0$. Thus a Gauduchon form can have arbitrarily small positive potential perturbations that are not Gauduchon. When persistence holds, the one-form $v\mapsto \int _ Xv\, \mathrm d\mu _ u$ on $\mathcal H_\omega $ is the Monge–Ampère one-form of chapter 3 divided by $M$. By theorem 3.1.3 , it therefore has a primitive exactly when $\omega $ is closed.

text:
4.8.1 Convex entropies along a Monge–Ampère flow The logarithmic Monge–Ampère operator generates a parabolic flow whose linearization is the operator $L_ u$ of ( 4.15 ). Along this flow, the ratio of the Monge–Ampère measure to a fixed target measure satisfies a heat-type equation. Integrating a convex function of this ratio by parts produces, besides the usual nonpositive gradient term, a term involving $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _{u_ t}^{n-1})$. If the forms along the flow are Gauduchon, this additional term vanishes and all convex entropies decrease. 4.8.2 Total variation between two evolving probabilities The entropies of 4.8.1 compare one evolving probability with the fixed target. Two solutions of the flow with different initial potentials can nevertheless move apart. On a flat torus, even with a closed background, their total-variation distance can increase at the initial time, while no convex entropy relative to the target increases. We show this by computing the initial derivatives explicitly. By a logarithmic Monge–Ampère flow with target $
u $ we mean a smooth solution of the equation in ( 4.17 ), with an arbitrary smooth initial potential. For this example, let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$ and $X=E^2$, with covering coordinates $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$. Write \[  \eta _ j= rac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j, \qquad \kappa =\eta _1+\eta _2, \qquad \mu =\eta _1\wedge \eta _2= rac{\kappa ^2}2.  \] Thus $\mu $ is a probability volume form and $\int _ X\kappa ^2=2$. Put \[  c_ j=\cos (2\pi x_ j),\qquad S=c_1+c_2,\qquad P=c_1c_2.  \] Lemma 4.8.7 . The averages of $|S|$ and $P|S|$ are \[  \int _ X|S|\mu = rac8{\pi ^2}, \qquad \int _ XP|S|\mu = rac8{3\pi ^2}.  \] Proof. The integrands do not depend on $y_1,y_2$. The degree-two map of real tori $(a,b)\mapsto (a+b,a-b)$ preserves normalized Haar averages. With the angles $A=2\pi a$ and $B=2\pi b$, it gives \[  S=2\cos A\cos B,\qquad P= rac{\cos (2A)+\cos (2B)}2.  \] The one-variable averages of $|\cos A|$ and $|\cos A|^3$ are $2/\pi $ and $4/(3\pi )$, respectively, so the average of $\cos (2A)|\cos A|$ is $2/(3\pi )$. Multiplying the averages over the two independent angles gives both formulas. $\square$ For a fixed real number $K>3$, define the smooth target probability $
u _ K$ by \[  Z_ K=\int _ X\mathrm e^{KP}\mu , \qquad f_ K=Z_ K^{-1}\mathrm e^{KP}, \qquad 
u _ K=f_ K\mu .  \] For $0<\varepsilon <1/\pi $, the initial potentials $\varepsilon S$ and zero give positive forms. Set \[  A_\varepsilon =1-\pi \varepsilon c_1, \qquad B_\varepsilon =1-\pi \varepsilon c_2, \qquad r_\varepsilon =A_\varepsilon B_\varepsilon ,  \] so that $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varepsilon S)=A_\varepsilon \eta _1+B_\varepsilon \eta _2$ and its normalized Monge–Ampère probability is $r_\varepsilon \mu $. Consider the short smooth paths 4.24  egin{equation} \label{eq:torus-parabolic-initial-paths} U_\varepsilon (t)=\varepsilon S+t\log  rac{r_\varepsilon }{f_ K}, \qquad V(t)=-t\log f_ K. \end{equation} They remain positive for sufficiently small $|t|$, and at $t=0$ their velocities are exactly those prescribed by the logarithmic Monge–Ampère flow with target $
u _ K$. Their normalized probabilities are \[  \mu _\varepsilon (t)= rac{(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_\varepsilon (t))^2}2, \qquad \mu _0(t)= rac{(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V(t))^2}2,  \] which have mass one because the background $\kappa $ is closed. For the paths ( 4.24 ), \[  D'_\varepsilon (0) =4\varepsilon \left( rac K3-1ight)+o(\varepsilon ) \quad 	ext{as }\varepsilon \downarrow 0.  \] In particular, this derivative is positive for sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. u _ K$ and these initial potentials have the same positive initial derivative of their total-variation distance. Proof. Differentiating the determinant at the diagonal initial matrices gives \[   egin{split}  \left.\partial _ t(R_\varepsilon -R_0)ight|_{t=0} = rac1{4\pi } igl (& B_\varepsilon \partial _{x_1}^2\log A_\varepsilon +A_\varepsilon \partial _{x_2}^2\log B_\varepsilon \ & -K(B_\varepsilon -1)\partial _{x_1}^2P -K(A_\varepsilon -1)\partial _{x_2}^2P igr ). \end{split}  \] Since $\partial _{x_ j}^2P=-4\pi ^2P$, Taylor expansion in $\varepsilon $ yields the uniform estimate \[  \left.\partial _ t(R_\varepsilon -R_0)ight|_{t=0} =\pi ^2\varepsilon S(1-KP)+O(\varepsilon ^2).  \] At $t=0$, the difference of the densities is \[  q_\varepsilon =r_\varepsilon -1 =-\pi \varepsilon S+\pi ^2\varepsilon ^2P.  \] For each fixed $x_2$, its coefficient of $c_1$ is $-\pi \varepsilon (1-\pi \varepsilon c_2)
e 0$, so as a function of $x_1$ it has at most two zeros in a period, and its zero set has measure zero. text: 4.9 Fredholm theory for a continuous Hermitian form A continuous positive Hermitian form still defines a uniformly elliptic trace operator. Its range is most conveniently described in Sobolev spaces: continuity of the coefficients suffices for the local $W^{2,p}$ estimate, while the maximum principle identifies the kernel. Lemma 4.9.1 . Let $\sigma $ be a continuous positive real $(1,1)$-form on a connected compact complex $n$-fold, and let $\mathrm dV$ be a smooth positive volume. For $p>2n$, the real operator \[  L_\sigma v=\operatorname {tr}_\sigma \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v, \qquad L_\sigma :W^{2,p}(X)\longrightarrow L^ p(\mathrm dV),  \] is Fredholm of index zero. Its kernel consists of the constants, and its range has a one-dimensional annihilator in $L^{p'}(\mathrm dV)$, where $p'=p/(p-1)$. Proof. Fix a smooth positive Hermitian form $\eta $ and put $L_ s=(1-s)L_\eta +sL_\sigma $, $0\leq s\leq 1$. On a finite holomorphic cover these operators have uniformly positive real principal matrices and a common modulus of continuity. They have no lower-order terms in these coordinates. Write $d=2n$ for the real dimension. Local estimates. For a constant positive real matrix $a_0$, the symbols $\xi _ i\xi _ j/(1+a_0^{kl}\xi _ k\xi _ l)$ satisfy the order-zero multiplier estimates. Consequently \[  \| D^2z\| _ p\leq C\bigl (\| a_0^{ij}D_{ij}z\| _ p+\| z\| _ p\bigr ) \qquad (z\in C_ c^\infty ).  \] Freeze the principal matrix of $L_ s$ at a point and shrink the ball until the coefficient oscillation times this constant is less than $1/2$. The oscillation term can then be absorbed on the left. Differentiating a cutoff adds first derivatives; the interpolation inequality $\| Dz\| _ p\leq \varepsilon \| D^2z\| _ p+C_\varepsilon \| z\| _ p$ absorbs them. This inequality follows by comparing $Dz$ with its mollification at scale $\varepsilon $ and estimating the derivative of the mollified function by $C\varepsilon ^{-1}\| z\| _ p$. A partition of unity and smooth density give, uniformly in $s$, 4.27 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-hermitian-wtwo} \| v\| _{W^{2,p}}\leq C\bigl (\| L_ sv\| _ p+\| v\| _ p\bigr ). \end{equation} Maximum principles. We give the local estimate needed to pass comparison to $W^{2,p}$. Let $L=a^{ij}D_{ij}$ on a bounded smooth coordinate domain $D$, with $a\geq \vartheta I$, and let $z$ be smooth with nonnegative boundary values and minimum $-M<0$. Set $R=\operatorname {diam}D$. Every vector $\xi $ with $|\xi |<M/(2R)$ is the gradient at an interior lower supporting point of $z$: minimize $z(x)-\xi \cdot (x-x_0)$, where $z(x_0)=-M$. Its boundary values exceed $-M/2$, whereas its value at $x_0$ is $-M$. At a supporting point $D^2z\geq 0$, and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  \det D^2z\leq \left(\frac{\operatorname {tr}(aD^2z)}{d\vartheta }\right)^ d.  \] The area formula for the gradient, restricted to these supporting points, therefore bounds the volume of the slope ball by $(d\vartheta )^{-d}\int _ D((Lz)^+)^ d$. Thus 4.28 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-hermitian-local-minimum} -\min _ Dz\leq C_ d\vartheta ^{-1}R\| (Lz)^+\| _{L^ d(D)}. \end{equation} This calculation uses no derivative of $a$. Approximate a $W^{2,p}$ function smoothly on the closure of a smaller smooth domain. The approximation converges in $C^1$, and its $L$ errors converge in $L^ d$ because $p>d$. Correct the vanishing boundary error in ( 4.28 ). Passage to the limit shows that $Lv\leq 0$ and $v|_{\partial D}\geq 0$ imply $v\geq 0$. The same comparison proves the strong maximum principle. If $v\in W^{2,p}$, $Lv\geq 0$, and $v$ has an interior maximum $M$, put $w=M-v\geq 0$. If $w$ is positive somewhere and zero somewhere, a small ball contained in $\{ w>0\} $ and tangent to its zero set can be chosen inside a coordinate chart. On the outer half-annulus of this ball, \[  \zeta (x)=\exp (-k|x-c|^2)-\exp (-kr^2)  \] is positive and has $L\zeta >0$ for sufficiently large $k$, by uniform ellipticity. A small positive multiple of $\zeta $ is bounded above by $w$ on both boundary spheres, hence throughout the annulus by comparison. At the tangent point this forces a positive inward derivative of $w$, contradicting $Dw=0$. Connectedness proves that $v$ is constant. Applied to $L_ s$ on $X$, it gives $\ker L_ s=\mathbb R$. If $(L_ s-1)v=0$ and $v$ has a positive maximum, apply the strong maximum principle on its positive component, where $L_ sv=v>0$. Constancy contradicts that equation. Applying the argument to $-v$ rules out a negative minimum. Hence $\ker (L_ s-1)=0$. Index and range. Compactness of $W^{2,p}\hookrightarrow L^ p$ and ( 4.27 ) now give 4.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-hermitian-inverse} \| v\| _{W^{2,p}}\leq C\| (L_ s-1)v\| _ p \end{equation} uniformly in $s$. Otherwise normalize a contradicting sequence in $W^{2,p}$, pass to $s_ j\to s$ and a strongly $L^ p$ convergent subsequence, and apply ( 4.27 ) to differences. Operator norm continuity in $s$ gives strong $W^{2,p}$ convergence to a nonzero member of $\ker (L_ s-1)$, which is impossible. The smooth operator $L_\eta -1$ has index zero and trivial kernel, hence is an isomorphism, by smooth elliptic theory. The method of continuity and ( 4.29 ) show that every $L_ s-1$ is an isomorphism. Finally, $L_\sigma $ differs from $L_\sigma -1$ by the compact inclusion $W^{2,p}\hookrightarrow L^ p$, so it is Fredholm of index zero. Its one-dimensional kernel makes its range have codimension one. $L^ p$ duality gives the annihilator assertion. $\square$

title: 4.10 Limits of adjoint measures
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.10 Limits of adjoint measures When every positive potential perturbation of $\omega $ is Gauduchon, the adjoint probability is the normalized Monge–Ampère measure. Mass invariance and the continuity of bounded products then extend this description to bounded potentials. Proposition 4.10.1 . Assume that $\omega _ v$ is Gauduchon for every $v\in \mathcal H_\omega $. For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, the measure \[  \mu _ u:=M^{-1}(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n  \] is a probability measure, which agrees with the preceding definition when $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. If $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ are uniformly bounded and $u_ j\to u$ in capacity, then $\mu _{u_ j}\rightharpoonup \mu _ u$. Proof. By proposition 4.8.2 , theorem 2.2.2 , the positive bounded product $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ has mass $M$, and for $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ its normalization is the smooth adjoint measure by proposition 4.8.2 . The continuity of bounded products under convergence in capacity, in the sense of section 1.8 , gives weak convergence of the products, and division by $M$ preserves it. $\square$ The proposition applies in particular to Gauduchon surfaces. For a general Hermitian background, passing from smooth $u_ j\in \mathcal H_\omega $ to a limit $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ requires control of the multipliers $\rho _{u_ j}$ as well as of the potentials. The supporting probabilities of chapter 15 recover $\mu _ u$ in the smooth case. If a bounded solution has a continuous positive complex Hessian, theorem 15.2.6 gives a stationary supporting probability and approximation independence under uniform convergence of the logarithmic densities. We do not know whether, in general, the limit is independent of the approximating sequence, or whether a weak linearization satisfies an adjoint identity.

title: Definition 4.11.1
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Definition 4.11.1 . The metric $h$ is RC-positive at $x$ if, for every $0\ne v\in E_ x$, there is a tangent vector $u\in T_ x^{1,0}X$ such that \[  h(R_ h(u,\bar u)v,v)>0.  \] It is uniformly RC-positive at $x$ if one tangent vector $u$ works for every nonzero $v\in E_ x$. A metric has either property on a set if it has that property at every point of the set.

title: Theorem 4.11.3
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 4.11.3 . Suppose that $K_{\omega ,h}\geq 0$ on $X$ and that $h$ is RC-positive on a nonempty open set $U$. Then there is a smooth real function $f$ such that $h_ t=\mathrm e^{-tf}h$ is RC-positive on all of $X$ for every sufficiently small $t>0$. Proof. By theorem 4.1.2 , choose a conformal Gauduchon form $\gamma =\mathrm e^ a\omega $. Then $K_{\gamma ,h}=\mathrm e^{-a}K_{\omega ,h}\geq 0$. Choose a closed coordinate ball $Q\subset U$ and a smooth function $\chi \geq 0$ supported in its interior, with $\int _ X\chi \gamma ^ n>0$, and set \[  \rho =1-\frac{\int _ X\gamma ^ n}{\int _ X\chi \gamma ^ n}\chi .  \] Thus $\rho =1$ on $X\setminus Q$ and $\int _ X\rho \gamma ^ n=0$. Since $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, proposition 4.8.1 , applied with $\gamma $ in place of $\omega $ and $u=0$, gives a smooth real solution $f$ of 4.30 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rc-gauduchon-poisson} P_\gamma f:=\operatorname {tr}_\gamma (\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial f)=\rho . \end{equation} Indeed, with $L_\gamma f=n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}/\gamma ^ n$ as in ( 4.15 ), we have $P_\gamma =2\pi L_\gamma $, and the adjoint probability of $L_\gamma $ is $\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$. The curvature transforms by 4.31 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rc-conformal-curvature} F_{h_ t}=F_ h+t\partial \bar\partial f\, \operatorname {Id}_ E, \qquad \alpha _{h_ t,v}=\mathrm e^{-tf} \bigl (\alpha _{h,v}+t|v|_ h^2\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial f\bigr ). \end{equation} On $X\setminus Q$, the $\gamma $-trace of the expression in parentheses is at least $t|v|_ h^2\rho =t|v|_ h^2>0$ for $v\ne 0$, so it has a positive eigenvalue there. Over $Q$, the unit sphere bundle $\{ |v|_ h=1\} $ is compact. The largest $\gamma $-eigenvalue of $\alpha _{h,v}$ is continuous and strictly positive on it, so it has a positive minimum $\delta $. Let $C$ be the maximum on $X$ of the operator norm of $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial f$ relative to $\gamma $. For every unit vector over $Q$, the largest eigenvalue of the expression in parentheses in ( 4.31 ) is at least $\delta -tC$, which is positive for small $t>0$. Homogeneity in $v$ and the positive factor $\mathrm e^{-tf}$ prove the assertion on $Q$ as well. $\square$

title: Example 4.11.4
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Example 4.11.4 . On a sufficiently small ball in $\mathbb C^2$, equip the trivial bundle of rank two with the metric \[  H(z)=\operatorname {Id}-zz^*+\tfrac 12|z|^2\operatorname {Id}.  \] At the origin this metric has zero mean curvature for the Euclidean Hermitian form and is RC-positive, but it is not uniformly RC-positive. Proof. The two eigenvalues of $H(z)$ are $1-\tfrac 12|z|^2$ and $1+\tfrac 12|z|^2$, so the metric is positive on a small ball. Its first derivatives vanish at the origin, where \[  F_{i\bar j}=e_ ie_ j^*-\tfrac 12\delta _{ij}\operatorname {Id},\qquad h(R_ h(u,\bar u)v,v)=|v^*u|^2-\tfrac 12|u|^2|v|^2.  \] The sum $F_{1\bar1}+F_{2\bar2}$ is zero. For each nonzero $v$, taking $u=v$ gives a positive evaluation. For each nonzero $u$, taking $v\perp u$ gives a negative evaluation, so no single $u$ works for every $v$. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.11.5
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 4.11.5 . If $\det E$ admits a flat Hermitian metric, then no smooth Hermitian metric on $E$ is uniformly RC-positive on $X$ or has positive definite mean curvature relative to a Hermitian form. This applies in particular when $\det E$ is holomorphically trivial. Proof. If $h$ were uniformly RC-positive, then at each point some $u$ would make the $h$-Hermitian endomorphism $R_ h(u,\bar u)$ positive definite, and its trace would be strictly positive. Since the curvature of the induced metric on $\det E$ is $\operatorname {tr}F_ h$, the determinant metric would be RC-positive as a metric on a line bundle. If instead $K_{\omega ,h}>0$, the $\omega $-trace of the determinant curvature would be $\operatorname {tr}K_{\omega ,h}>0$, which again gives a positive tangent evaluation. Fix a flat Hermitian metric $h_0$ on $\det E$ and write $\det h=\mathrm e^ b h_0$ for a smooth real function $b$. The determinant curvature is then $-\partial \bar\partial b$. At a global minimum of $b$, this curvature has no positive tangent evaluation, contradicting the RC-positivity of the determinant metric. Finally, a holomorphic trivialization of $\det E$ gives a flat metric, by assigning constant norm to the trivializing frame. $\square$

e 0$ somewhere. Finally, the induced determinant metric of $h$ is flat because its Chern curvature is the Ricci form of $\omega $, which vanishes. title: 4.13 Holomorphic sectional curvature
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
4.13 Holomorphic sectional curvature The curvature conditions above test a tangent direction and a fiber vector separately. For a metric on the tangent bundle, holomorphic sectional curvature tests the same vector in both places. Averaging these diagonal evaluations controls a symmetrized curvature trace. A second trace occurs when one differentiates the trace of the metric itself; their difference contains torsion and an exact form. With a Kähler metric for the contraction, integration removes the exact form and the torsion terms cancel. This gives an obstruction even when the metric whose curvature is tested is not closed. In this section, $g$ is a Kähler metric on $X$, with form $\omega _ g$, and $h$ is any smooth Hermitian metric on $T^{1,0}X$, with form $\omega _ h$. We retain $n\geq 2$. The unscaled Chern curvature convention of 4.6.9 gives the coefficients \[  R^ h_{i ar j k ar l} =-\partial _ i\partial _{ ar j}h_{k ar l} +h^{p ar q}(\partial _ i h_{k ar q}) (\partial _{ ar j}h_{p ar l}).  \] The Chern holomorphic sectional curvature is 4.33  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-holomorphic-sectional-curvature}\index{Holomorphic sectional curvature!Chern connection} H_ h(x,[v])= rac{R^ h(v, ar v,v, ar v)}{|v|_ h^4}, \qquad 0
e v\in T_ x^{1,0}X. \end{equation} It is quasi-negative if it is nonpositive everywhere and strictly negative in every direction at some point. Put \[  u=\operatorname {tr}_ g h,\qquad q=\operatorname {tr} igl ((g^{-1}h)^2 igr ).  \] In a $g$-unitary frame, define the real contractions \[  Q_ g(h)=\sum _{i,k}R^ h_{i ar i k ar k},\qquad B_ g(h)=\sum _{i,k}R^ h_{i ar k k ar i},\qquad \mathcal R_ g(h)=	frac 12 igl (Q_ g(h)+B_ g(h) igr ).  \] These expressions are invariant under a change of unitary frame. For a general $h$, the two traces $Q_ g(h)$ and $B_ g(h)$ can differ. Lemma 4.13.1 . At a point where $H_ h\leq -\kappa $ for some $\kappa \geq 0$, one has \[  \mathcal R_ g(h)\leq - rac{\kappa }{2}(u^2+q).  \] In particular, nonpositive holomorphic sectional curvature gives $\mathcal R_ g(h)\leq 0$. Proof. In a $g$-unitary frame, let $Z_1,\ldots ,Z_ n$ be independent standard complex Gaussian variables, with density $\pi ^{-1}\mathrm e^{-|z|^2}$ on $\mathbb C$. Their second and fourth moments are $\mathbb E|Z_ i|^2=1$ and $\mathbb E|Z_ i|^4=2$. Independence and invariance under coordinate phases give \[  \mathbb E[Z_ i\overline{Z_ j}Z_ k\overline{Z_ l}] =\delta _{ij}\delta _{kl}+\delta _{il}\delta _{kj}.  \] Thus $\mathbb E R^ h(Z, ar Z,Z, ar Z)=Q_ g(h)+B_ g(h)$ and $\mathbb E|Z|_ h^4=u^2+q$. Taking expectations in the homogeneous inequality $R^ h(Z, ar Z,Z, ar Z)\leq -\kappa |Z|_ h^4$ proves the result. $\square$ Let $A=
abla ^ h-
abla ^ g$ be the difference of the Chern connections, viewed as a tensor with two holomorphic covariant indices and a tangent-bundle value. Write \[  S(v,w)=	frac 12 igl (A(v,w)+A(w,v) igr ),\qquad T(v,w)=A(v,w)-A(w,v).  \] Since $g$ is Kähler, $T$ is the Chern torsion of $h$. Norms such as $|S|_{g,h}^2=\sum _{i,k}|S(e_ i,e_ k)|_ h^2$ use $g$ in the covariant indices and $h$ in the value. Let $r_{i ar j}$ be the coefficients of the Ricci form $\operatorname {Ric}(g)=-\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial \log \det (g_{i ar j})$, and in a $g$-unitary frame set \[  I_ g(h)=\sum _{i,k}r_{i ar k}h_{k ar i},\qquad \mathrm dV_ g= rac{\omega _ g^ n}{n!},\qquad P_ g f=\operatorname {tr}_{\omega _ g}(\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial f).  \] Proposition 4.13.2 . The two metrics satisfy 4.34  egin{equation} \label{eq:integrated-hermitian-chern-lu} \int _ X igl (|S|_{g,h}^2+I_ g(h)-\mathcal R_ g(h) igr )\, \mathrm dV_ g=0. \end{equation} Proof. We first compute the exact term that distinguishes the two curvature traces. Define  egin{align*}  D_{i ar j k ar l} ={}& \partial _ i\partial _{ ar j}h_{k ar l} +\partial _ k\partial _{ ar l}h_{i ar j}\ & -\partial _ i\partial _{ ar l}h_{k ar j} -\partial _ k\partial _{ ar j}h_{i ar l}. \end{align*} This is a tensor: putting holomorphic differentials first gives \[  \mathrm i\partial  ar\partial \omega _ h =\sum _{i<k,\, j<l}D_{i ar j k ar l} \, \mathrm dz^ i\wedge \mathrm dz^ k \wedge \mathrm d ar z^ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z^ l.  \] For $D_ g=\sum _{i,k}D_{i ar i k ar k}$ in a $g$-unitary frame, expansion of the wedge product gives \[  D_ g\, \mathrm dV_ g =2\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial \omega _ h \wedge  rac{\omega _ g^{n-2}}{(n-2)!}.  \] Indeed, each pair $i<k$ contributes $D_{i ar i k ar k}\mathrm dV_ g$ to the wedge product and occurs twice in the contraction. Closedness of $\omega _ g$ and Stokes' theorem therefore give $\int _ XD_ g\, \mathrm dV_ g=0$. The four-term antisymmetrization of the curvature formula is  egin{align*} & R^ h_{i ar j k ar l}+R^ h_{k ar l i ar j} -R^ h_{i ar l k ar j}-R^ h_{k ar j i ar l}\ & \hspace{3em}=h_{p ar q}T^ p_{ik}\overline{T^ q_{jl}} -D_{i ar j k ar l}. \end{align*} The second derivatives give $-D$, and the quadratic terms give the squared connection difference in the two skew indices. Contracting gives $2(Q_ g(h)-B_ g(h))=|T|_{g,h}^2-D_ g$, hence \[  Q_ g(h)=\mathcal R_ g(h)+	frac 14|T|_{g,h}^2-	frac 14D_ g.  \] In $g$-normal holomorphic coordinates, the first derivatives of $g$ vanish. Differentiating $u=g^{k ar l}h_{k ar l}$ twice, the inverse-metric term is $I_ g(h)$ by the Kähler curvature symmetries of $g$, while the second derivatives of $h$ give $-Q_ g(h)+|A|_{g,h}^2$. Thus  egin{align*}  P_ g u& =|A|_{g,h}^2+I_ g(h)-Q_ g(h)\ & =|S|_{g,h}^2+I_ g(h)-\mathcal R_ g(h)+	frac 14D_ g, \end{align*} where symmetric and skew tensors are orthogonal and $|A|_{g,h}^2=|S|_{g,h}^2+|T|_{g,h}^2/4$. Integrating removes both $P_ g u$ and $D_ g$, proving ( 4.34 ). $\square$ Corollary 4.13.3 . Suppose that $\operatorname {Ric}(g)\geq 0$. Every Hermitian tangent metric $h$ with $H_ h\leq 0$ satisfies $\operatorname {Ric}(g)=0$ and $H_ h=0$ in every direction. In particular, $X$ admits no Hermitian tangent metric with quasi-negative Chern holomorphic sectional curvature. Proof. The Ricci assumption gives $I_ g(h)\geq 0$, and lemma 4.13.1 gives $-\mathcal R_ g(h)\geq 0$. All three continuous terms in ( 4.34 ) are nonnegative, so each vanishes everywhere. A positive definite $h$ pairs strictly positively with every nonzero semipositive Ricci matrix; hence $I_ g(h)=0$ forces $\operatorname {Ric}(g)=0$. At each point, the Gaussian expectation in the averaging proof is now zero. Its integrand $R^ h(Z, ar Z,Z, ar Z)$ is nonpositive. If it were negative in one direction, continuity and the strictly positive Gaussian density would make its expectation negative. It is therefore zero in every direction, which gives $H_ h=0$ and excludes quasi-negativity. $\square$ For the Ricci-flat surfaces of section 4.12 , this obstruction concerns all Hermitian tangent metrics, including nonclosed ones. It coexists with the RC-positive metric of theorem 4.12.3 : that condition allows the positive tangent direction to depend on the fiber vector, while holomorphic sectional curvature evaluates the same direction twice.

title: 4.13.1 Rigidity on complex tori
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.13.1 Rigidity on complex tori For a flat reference metric, the vanishing symmetric connection term has a stronger consequence. Periodic integration by parts forces the second metric to be translation invariant, and hence to have zero full Chern curvature. Proposition 4.13.4 . Let $Y=\mathbb C^ m/\Lambda $ be a complex torus, with $m\geq 1$. A smooth Hermitian tangent metric $h$ on $Y$ has nonpositive Chern holomorphic sectional curvature if and only if it is translation invariant. Such a metric is Kähler and has zero Chern curvature. Proof. Suppose first that $m\geq 2$, and take the flat Kähler metric $g$ induced by a constant Hermitian inner product on $\mathbb C^ m$. Choose linear coordinates in which this inner product is the identity. The coordinate vector fields descend to $Y$, even though the coordinates themselves need not. By corollary 4.13.3 , $H_ h=0$; ( 4.34 ) also gives $S=0$. Since $g$ has zero connection coefficients, multiplying $S=0$ by $h$ gives \[  \partial _ i h_{k\bar l}+\partial _ k h_{i\bar l}=0 \qquad \text{for all }i,k,l.  \] Fix $l$ and put $a_ k=h_{k\bar l}$. With respect to the flat volume, integration by parts and commutation of constant coordinate derivatives give \[  \sum _{i,k}\int _ Y\partial _ i a_ k\,  \overline{\partial _ k a_ i}\, \mathrm dV_ g =\int _ Y\left|\sum _ k\partial _{\bar k}a_ k\right|^2\mathrm dV_ g.  \] Consequently, \[  \begin{aligned}  0& =\sum _{i,k}\int _ Y|\partial _ i a_ k+\partial _ k a_ i|^2\, \mathrm dV_ g\\ & =2\sum _{i,k}\int _ Y|\partial _ i a_ k|^2\, \mathrm dV_ g +2\int _ Y\left|\sum _ k\partial _{\bar k}a_ k\right|^2\mathrm dV_ g. \end{aligned}  \] Thus every $\partial _ i h_{k\bar l}$ vanishes. Hermitian symmetry gives the vanishing of the conjugate derivatives as well, so all coefficients of $h$ are constant. For $m=1$, write the lifted metric as $h(z)|\mathrm dz|^2$, with $h$ positive and $\Lambda $-periodic. Its curvature coefficient is $-h\, \partial _ z\partial _{\bar z}\log h$. Nonpositive sectional curvature therefore gives $\partial _ z\partial _{\bar z}\log h\geq 0$. The complex Laplacian has zero integral over $Y$, so it vanishes. Integration by parts then shows that $\log h$ has zero gradient, and $h$ is constant. Conversely, a constant positive Hermitian matrix defines a closed form and has zero connection and curvature coefficients. This proves all the assertions. $\square$ Corollary 4.13.5 . Let $Y$ be a connected compact complex manifold admitting a finite unramified holomorphic covering $\pi :Z\to Y$ by a complex torus. Every smooth Hermitian tangent metric on $Y$ with nonpositive Chern holomorphic sectional curvature is Kähler and Chern flat. Proof. The covering is locally biholomorphic, so the pullback metric has the same sectional-curvature sign. By proposition 4.13.4 , its associated form is closed and its Chern curvature is zero. Both conclusions descend through the covering. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.13.4
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 4.13.4 . Let $Y=\mathbb C^ m/\Lambda $ be a complex torus, with $m\geq 1$. A smooth Hermitian tangent metric $h$ on $Y$ has nonpositive Chern holomorphic sectional curvature if and only if it is translation invariant. Such a metric is Kähler and has zero Chern curvature. Proof. Suppose first that $m\geq 2$, and take the flat Kähler metric $g$ induced by a constant Hermitian inner product on $\mathbb C^ m$. Choose linear coordinates in which this inner product is the identity. The coordinate vector fields descend to $Y$, even though the coordinates themselves need not. By corollary 4.13.3 , $H_ h=0$; ( 4.34 ) also gives $S=0$. Since $g$ has zero connection coefficients, multiplying $S=0$ by $h$ gives \[  \partial _ i h_{k\bar l}+\partial _ k h_{i\bar l}=0 \qquad \text{for all }i,k,l.  \] Fix $l$ and put $a_ k=h_{k\bar l}$. With respect to the flat volume, integration by parts and commutation of constant coordinate derivatives give \[  \sum _{i,k}\int _ Y\partial _ i a_ k\,  \overline{\partial _ k a_ i}\, \mathrm dV_ g =\int _ Y\left|\sum _ k\partial _{\bar k}a_ k\right|^2\mathrm dV_ g.  \] Consequently, \[  \begin{aligned}  0& =\sum _{i,k}\int _ Y|\partial _ i a_ k+\partial _ k a_ i|^2\, \mathrm dV_ g\\ & =2\sum _{i,k}\int _ Y|\partial _ i a_ k|^2\, \mathrm dV_ g +2\int _ Y\left|\sum _ k\partial _{\bar k}a_ k\right|^2\mathrm dV_ g. \end{aligned}  \] Thus every $\partial _ i h_{k\bar l}$ vanishes. Hermitian symmetry gives the vanishing of the conjugate derivatives as well, so all coefficients of $h$ are constant. For $m=1$, write the lifted metric as $h(z)|\mathrm dz|^2$, with $h$ positive and $\Lambda $-periodic. Its curvature coefficient is $-h\, \partial _ z\partial _{\bar z}\log h$. Nonpositive sectional curvature therefore gives $\partial _ z\partial _{\bar z}\log h\geq 0$. The complex Laplacian has zero integral over $Y$, so it vanishes. Integration by parts then shows that $\log h$ has zero gradient, and $h$ is constant. Conversely, a constant positive Hermitian matrix defines a closed form and has zero connection and curvature coefficients. This proves all the assertions. $\square$

title: 4.14 Projective first jets and positive bundle metrics
search_title: Projective first jets and positive bundle metrics
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.14 Projective first jets and positive bundle metrics RC-positivity asks for one positive tangent direction for each fiber vector, whereas Griffiths positivity asks for positivity on every pair of nonzero tangent and fiber vectors. The Lamari criterion of theorem 4.3.1 characterizes positivity of a $(1,1)$-form by a duality with Gauduchon tests, and Griffiths positivity on a projective manifold admits an analogous duality. A Griffiths-positive metric on $E$ is the same as a strictly plurisubharmonic squared norm on the dual bundle, which is a linear condition on the dual Hermitian form. Twisting by powers of a very ample line bundle gives finite-dimensional spaces of candidate forms. At each level, either some candidate is strictly plurisubharmonic or a finite atomic positive measure annihilates the Levi forms of all candidates, and if every level fails, a weak limit of these measures annihilates the Levi forms of all smooth Hermitian forms. This measure lives over the dual bundle, whereas the Gauduchon currents in theorem 4.3.1 live on the base. Throughout this section, $X$ is a projective manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$, $E\to X$ is a holomorphic vector bundle of positive rank, and $F=E^*$. Fix a very ample line bundle $A$, a basis $t_1,\ldots ,t_ d$ of $H^0(X,A)$, and the Fubini–Study metric $a$ on $A$ determined by this basis. Fix also an integer $m_0\geq 0$ for which $E\otimes A^{m_0}$ is globally generated; this integer is part of the data. In a local frame of $A$, put \[  \rho =\sum _{\alpha =1}^ d|t_\alpha |^2, \qquad a=\mathrm e^{-\phi },\qquad \phi =\log \rho .  \] We use the curvature conventions of 4.6.9 . A Hermitian metric $g$ on a holomorphic vector bundle over $X$ is strictly Griffiths-positive if $g(R_ g(u,\bar u)v,v)>0$ for every $x\in X$, every nonzero $u\in T_ x^{1,0}X$ and every nonzero vector $v$ in the fiber over $x$; it is strictly Griffiths-negative if the reverse strict inequality holds. For a smooth Hermitian form $h$ on $F$, not initially assumed positive, let $G_ h(v)=h(v,v)$ on its total space. Write $\mathcal L G_ h(\xi )$ for the complex Hessian evaluated on $\xi \in T^{1,0}F$; in local coordinates it is $\sum (G_ h)_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$, the coefficient form of $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial G_ h$, without the factor $1/(2\pi )$. Lemma 4.14.1 . The function $G_ h$ is strictly plurisubharmonic off the zero section if and only if $h$ is a smooth positive Hermitian metric with strictly Griffiths-negative curvature. Equivalently, its dual metric on $E$ is strictly Griffiths-positive. Proof. On vertical tangent vectors the Levi form is $h$ itself, so strict positivity forces $h>0$. At a fixed base point, choose a holomorphic frame in which the matrix $H$ of $h$ is the identity and has vanishing first derivatives. Then $R_ h(u,\bar u)=-H_{u\bar u}$ at this point. A tangent vector to $F$ has horizontal and vertical components $(u,w)$, and \[  \mathcal L G_ h(u,w)=|w|^2+v^*H_{u\bar u}v =|w|^2-h(R_ h(u,\bar u)v,v).  \] For $v\ne 0$, this is positive for every nonzero $(u,w)$ precisely when the curvature evaluation is negative for every nonzero $u$. The curvature of the dual metric is the negative transpose of the original curvature, with respect to the dual Hermitian pairing, which gives the last assertion. $\square$ The Levi forms will be tested on a compact set. Choose any smooth Hermitian metric $k$ on $F$, let $S=\{ v:k(v,v)=1\} $ be its unit sphere bundle, and choose a smooth positive Hermitian form $b$ on the complex vector bundle $W=T^{1,0}F|_ S$ over $S$. The set \[  K=\{ (v,\xi ):v\in S,\  \xi \in W_ v,\  b(\xi ,\xi )=1\}   \] is compact. Define the real-linear operator $D$ by $D h=\mathcal L G_ h|_ S$, viewed as a Hermitian form on $W$. It is continuous from the $C^2$ norm of Hermitian forms on $F$ to the uniform norm on $W$, since its coefficients involve at most two base derivatives of $h$ and the fiber vectors range over a compact set. Fiber dilation $v\mapsto cv$ gives \[  G_ h(cv)=|c|^2G_ h(v),\qquad \mathcal L G_ h|_{cv}(\mathrm d(v\mapsto cv)\xi ) =|c|^2\mathcal L G_ h|_ v(\xi ).  \] Thus strict positivity of $\mathcal LG_ h$ on $K$ is equivalent to strict positivity off the zero section.

title: 4.14.1 The finite-dimensional alternative
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.14.1 The finite-dimensional alternative For $m\geq m_0$, choose a basis of $V_ m=H^0(X,E\otimes A^ m)$ and write $N_ m=\dim V_ m$. Pairing these sections with $v\in F_ x$ and using a local frame of $A^ m$, we obtain a column $p_ m(v)$ of local holomorphic functions on the total space of $F$. For any Hermitian $N_ m\times N_ m$ matrix $B$, set \[  G_{m,B}(v)=\mathrm e^{-m\phi (x)}p_ m(v)^*B p_ m(v).  \] This function is globally defined and quadratic on each fiber, so $G_{m,B}=G_{h_{m,B}}$ for a smooth Hermitian form $h_{m,B}$ on $F$. The matrix $B$ is allowed to have negative eigenvalues. For $(v,\xi )\in K$, let $u$ be the projection of $\xi $ to $T_ x^{1,0}X$, write $\phi _ u=\partial \phi (u)$, and put \begin{align*}  r_ m& =\mathrm dp_ m(\xi )-m\phi _ u p_ m(v),\qquad \kappa =\phi _{u\bar u},\\  \Psi _ m(v,\xi )& =\mathrm e^{-m\phi } \bigl (r_ mr_ m^*-m\kappa p_ m p_ m^*\bigr ). \end{align*} Differentiating the weighted quadratic function gives 4.37 \begin{equation} \label{eq:first-jet-levi-matrix} (D h_{m,B})_ v(\xi ,\xi )=\operatorname {tr}(B\Psi _ m(v,\xi )). \end{equation} All entries involve only the first jets of the sections: if $t=(t_\alpha )$ is the column of the sections of $A$, then \[  \phi _ u=\frac{t^*\mathrm dt(u)}{\rho },\qquad \kappa =\frac{\rho |\mathrm dt(u)|^2-|t^*\mathrm dt(u)|^2}{\rho ^2}.  \] Changing the frame of $A$ by a nowhere-zero holomorphic factor $\lambda $ changes $p_ m$ to $\lambda ^{-m}p_ m$ and $\phi $ to $\phi -\log |\lambda |^2$. It changes $r_ m$ by the same factor and leaves $\kappa $ unchanged, so $\Psi _ m$ is frame independent. A change of the basis of $V_ m$ replaces $\Psi _ m$ by a congruent matrix, so whether the convex hull of the values of $\Psi _ m$ contains zero does not depend on that choice. Proposition 4.14.2 . At each fixed $m$, exactly one of the following holds: Some Hermitian matrix $B$ satisfies $\operatorname {tr}(B\Psi _ m)>0$ everywhere on $K$. There is a probability measure $\mu $ on $K$, supported on at most $N_ m^2+1$ points, such that $\int _ K\Psi _ m\, \mathrm d\mu =0$. The first alternative holds precisely when $0\notin \operatorname {conv}(\Psi _ m(K))$. Proof. The real vector space of Hermitian $N_ m\times N_ m$ matrices has dimension $N_ m^2$. Carathéodory's theorem expresses every point of the convex hull as a convex combination of at most $N_ m^2+1$ points of the compact image $\Psi _ m(K)$, so the hull is compact. If it contains zero, the coefficients of such an expression define the required atomic probability measure $\mu $, and then $\int _ K\operatorname {tr}(B\Psi _ m)\, \mathrm d\mu =0$ excludes the first alternative. If the hull misses zero, let $Z_0$ be its point of least Hilbert–Schmidt norm. Differentiating the squared norm along the segment from $Z_0$ to any $Z$ in the hull gives \[  \operatorname {tr}(Z_0Z)\geq \operatorname {tr}(Z_0^2)>0.  \] Taking $B=Z_0$ proves the first alternative. $\square$

title: 4.14.2 Approximation with two derivatives
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.14.2 Approximation with two derivatives Let $\mathcal H_ m=\{ h_{m,B}:B=B^*\} $. To pass from these finite-dimensional tests to all smooth metrics, we need approximation in $C^2$, since $D$ involves two derivatives. Lemma 4.14.3 . The matrix-valued map $Y=tt^*/\rho $ embeds $X$ as a compact smooth submanifold of the real vector space of Hermitian $d\times d$ matrices. Restrictions of real polynomials in its real coordinates are dense in $C^2(X,\mathbb R)$ for the $C^2$ norm. Proof. The normalized rank-one projector $Y$ determines the point $[t]$ of projective space, and its differential vanishes only in directions in which $\mathrm dt$ is proportional to $t$. Since $A$ is very ample, $Y$ is therefore injective with injective differential, and compactness makes it an embedding. A $C^2$ function on this image extends to a $C^2$ function on an ambient cube: use local coordinates in which the image is a graph, extend constantly in the normal coordinates, and combine these extensions with a finite smooth partition of unity and a cutoff. Rescale the cube to $[0,1]^ q$. For such an extension $f$, its multivariate Bernstein polynomial is \[  B_ Nf(y)=\sum _{0\leq j_1,\ldots ,j_ q\leq N} f(j/N)\prod _{\ell =1}^ q \binom N{j_\ell }y_\ell ^{j_\ell }(1-y_\ell )^{N-j_\ell },  \] where $j=(j_1,\ldots ,j_ q)$. For a multi-index $\alpha $ with $|\alpha |\leq 2$, differentiation expresses $\partial ^\alpha B_ Nf$ as an average of $\Delta _{1/N}^\alpha f(j/N)$, with prefactor $\prod _\ell (N)_{\alpha _\ell }$ and Bernstein degrees $N-\alpha _\ell $. Here $(N)_ r=N(N-1)\cdots (N-r+1)$, and $\Delta ^\alpha _{1/N}$ is the corresponding iterated forward difference with step $1/N$. Repeated use of the fundamental theorem of calculus expresses $N^{|\alpha |}\Delta _{1/N}^\alpha f(j/N)$ as an average of $\partial ^\alpha f$ at points within $2/N$ in each affected coordinate. The remaining Bernstein weights are the law of independent binomial variables of degrees $N-\alpha _\ell $, divided by $N$. Their means differ from $y_\ell $ by at most $2/N$ and their variances are at most $1/(4N)$. Uniform continuity of $\partial ^\alpha f$, splitting the average into a fixed small neighborhood of $y$ and its complement, and Chebyshev's inequality give uniform convergence to $\partial ^\alpha f$. The prefactor divided by $N^{|\alpha |}$ tends to one. This proves convergence for every derivative of order at most two, including the function itself. Restrict to the embedded image and use the chain rule in a finite collection of charts to obtain the asserted $C^2$ approximation. $\square$ Lemma 4.14.4 . The spaces $\mathcal H_ m$ are nested, and their union is $C^2$ dense in the space of $C^2$ Hermitian forms on $F$. Proof. For nesting, multiply the sections in $V_ m$ by each $t_\alpha $ and express the products in the basis of $V_{m+1}$. The identity $\sum _\alpha \mathrm e^{-\phi }|t_\alpha |^2=1$ writes $G_{m,B}$ as the sum of the corresponding weighted quadratic functions at level $m+1$, which combine into one Hermitian coefficient matrix at that level. Surjectivity of the multiplication map is not needed. For density, write $p_{m_0}(v)=P_0v$ in a local frame of $F$, and put $L=\mathrm e^{-m_0\phi /2}P_0$. Global generation of $E\otimes A^{m_0}$ means that $L$ is injective, so $M=L^*L$ is positive definite. If a $C^2$ Hermitian form has matrix $H$, define \[  C(x)=L M^{-1}H M^{-1}L^*.  \] Then $L^*CL=H$. A change of frame of $F$ cancels in this expression; a change of frame of $A$ multiplies $L$ by a scalar of modulus one, which also cancels. Thus $C$ is a globally defined $C^2$ Hermitian matrix function on $X$. Applying lemma 4.14.3 to its real coordinates in the vector space of Hermitian matrices, we obtain Hermitian matrix polynomials in the entries of $Y$ that converge to $C$ in $C^2$; their degrees may increase along the sequence. Let $C_ q(Y)$ be such a polynomial, of degree at most $q$. Every monomial of degree $k$ in $Y$ has the form $t^ I\bar t^ J/\rho ^ k$, with $|I|=|J|=k$. For a polynomial of degree at most $q$, multiply each numerator by $\rho ^{q-k}$ to use the common denominator $\rho ^ q$. Consequently \[  \mathrm e^{-m_0\phi }p_{m_0}^*C_ q(Y)p_{m_0}  \] is a quadratic expression in the product sections $\sigma _ i t^ I$ of $E\otimes A^{m_0+q}$, with weight $\mathrm e^{-(m_0+q)\phi }$. Express these products in the basis of $V_{m_0+q}$ and replace the coefficient matrix by its Hermitian part, which does not change the real function. The result is an element of $\mathcal H_{m_0+q}$. Since $L^*CL=H$ and multiplication by the fixed smooth matrix $L$ is continuous in $C^2$, these elements converge to $H$. $\square$
