title: 4.14.3 The metric and measure alternatives
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.14.3 The metric and measure alternatives A positive matrix-valued measure on $W\to S$ is a linear functional $T$ on the space of continuous Hermitian forms $\Phi $ on $W$ such that $\langle T,\Phi \rangle \geq 0$ whenever $\Phi \geq 0$. Its trace mass relative to $b$ is $\langle T,b\rangle $. We write $D^*T=0$ if $\langle T,Dh\rangle =0$ for every smooth Hermitian form $h$ on $F$. Theorem 4.14.5 . With the fixed projective data above, the following are equivalent: $E$ admits a smooth strictly Griffiths-positive Hermitian metric. For some $m\geq m_0$, a Hermitian matrix $B$ makes $G_{m,B}$ strictly plurisubharmonic off the zero section. For some $m\geq m_0$, $0\notin \operatorname {conv}(\Psi _ m(K))$. There is no nonzero positive matrix-valued measure $T$ on $W\to S$ satisfying $D^*T=0$. Proof. Given a metric as in the first assertion, its dual metric $h$ on $F$ satisfies $Dh\geq \delta b$ on $S$ for some $\delta >0$, by lemma 4.14.1 and compactness. The $C^2$ density in lemma 4.14.4 and the continuity of $D$ give a form $h_{m,B}$ with $D h_{m,B}\geq \delta b/2$, which proves the second assertion. Conversely, if $G_{m,B}$ is strictly plurisubharmonic, its vertical Levi form shows that $h_{m,B}$ is positive, and lemma 4.14.1 shows that its dual metric is strictly Griffiths-positive. The second and third assertions are equivalent by proposition 4.14.2 . If the first assertion holds, every nonzero positive matrix-valued measure $T$ has positive trace mass, and \[  \langle T,Dh\rangle \geq \delta \langle T,b\rangle >0,  \] so such a measure cannot satisfy $D^*T=0$. Conversely, suppose that the third assertion fails at every level. By proposition 4.14.2 , choose at each level $m$ an atomic probability measure $\mu _ m$ on $K$ with $\int _ K\Psi _ m\, \mathrm d\mu _ m=0$, so that $\mu _ m$ annihilates $Dh$ for every $h\in \mathcal H_ m$. A subsequence converges weakly to a probability measure $\mu $ on the compact set $K$. Since the spaces $\mathcal H_ m$ are nested, the limit annihilates $Dh$ for every $h$ in each fixed $\mathcal H_ j$, and the $C^2$ density and the continuity of $D$ extend this to every smooth Hermitian form. Define \[  \langle T,\Phi \rangle =\int _ K\Phi _ v(\xi ,\xi )\, \mathrm d\mu (v,\xi ).  \] This is a positive matrix-valued measure on $W\to S$ with $\langle T,b\rangle =1$ and $D^*T=0$. Its entries in local frames are represented by scalar measures: positivity bounds the functional on Hermitian forms of uniform norm at most one by the trace mass, so the Riesz representation theorem applies to the coordinate functionals, and a finite partition of unity combines these local representations. This contradicts the fourth assertion and completes the proof. $\square$ The equation $D^*T=0$ concerns a bundle over the sphere bundle $S\subset F=E^*$; it should not be confused with the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ for currents on $X$. The theorem gives no bound for the first successful level, and no finite procedure for deciding that all levels fail. Corollary 4.14.6 . If $E$ is globally generated and $m_0=0$, the level-zero test succeeds exactly when the complete evaluation map $\Phi :F\to H^0(X,E)^*$ is an immersion off the zero section. Proof. At $m=0$, one has $\Psi _0=\mathrm d\Phi (\xi )\mathrm d\Phi (\xi )^*$, where $\Phi $ is written in the coordinates given by the chosen basis. If $\mathrm d\Phi $ is injective off the zero section, $B=\operatorname {Id}$ gives a strictly positive Levi form. If $\mathrm d\Phi $ has a nonzero kernel vector there, fiber dilation and normalization of the tangent vector place such a vector in $K$, where $\Psi _0=0$, and no Hermitian matrix can separate the image from zero. $\square$ When this untwisted test fails, the higher twists remain available. The finite alternatives use all Hermitian coefficient matrices and the complete spaces of sections; testing only positive coefficient matrices or a smaller collection of sections gives a different criterion.

title: Theorem 4.14.5
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 4.14.5 . With the fixed projective data above, the following are equivalent: $E$ admits a smooth strictly Griffiths-positive Hermitian metric. For some $m\geq m_0$, a Hermitian matrix $B$ makes $G_{m,B}$ strictly plurisubharmonic off the zero section. For some $m\geq m_0$, $0\notin \operatorname {conv}(\Psi _ m(K))$. There is no nonzero positive matrix-valued measure $T$ on $W\to S$ satisfying $D^*T=0$. Proof. Given a metric as in the first assertion, its dual metric $h$ on $F$ satisfies $Dh\geq \delta b$ on $S$ for some $\delta >0$, by lemma 4.14.1 and compactness. The $C^2$ density in lemma 4.14.4 and the continuity of $D$ give a form $h_{m,B}$ with $D h_{m,B}\geq \delta b/2$, which proves the second assertion. Conversely, if $G_{m,B}$ is strictly plurisubharmonic, its vertical Levi form shows that $h_{m,B}$ is positive, and lemma 4.14.1 shows that its dual metric is strictly Griffiths-positive. The second and third assertions are equivalent by proposition 4.14.2 . If the first assertion holds, every nonzero positive matrix-valued measure $T$ has positive trace mass, and \[  \langle T,Dh\rangle \geq \delta \langle T,b\rangle >0,  \] so such a measure cannot satisfy $D^*T=0$. Conversely, suppose that the third assertion fails at every level. By proposition 4.14.2 , choose at each level $m$ an atomic probability measure $\mu _ m$ on $K$ with $\int _ K\Psi _ m\, \mathrm d\mu _ m=0$, so that $\mu _ m$ annihilates $Dh$ for every $h\in \mathcal H_ m$. A subsequence converges weakly to a probability measure $\mu $ on the compact set $K$. Since the spaces $\mathcal H_ m$ are nested, the limit annihilates $Dh$ for every $h$ in each fixed $\mathcal H_ j$, and the $C^2$ density and the continuity of $D$ extend this to every smooth Hermitian form. Define \[  \langle T,\Phi \rangle =\int _ K\Phi _ v(\xi ,\xi )\, \mathrm d\mu (v,\xi ).  \] This is a positive matrix-valued measure on $W\to S$ with $\langle T,b\rangle =1$ and $D^*T=0$. Its entries in local frames are represented by scalar measures: positivity bounds the functional on Hermitian forms of uniform norm at most one by the trace mass, so the Riesz representation theorem applies to the coordinate functionals, and a finite partition of unity combines these local representations. This contradicts the fourth assertion and completes the proof. $\square$

title: Corollary 4.14.6
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Corollary 4.14.6 . If $E$ is globally generated and $m_0=0$, the level-zero test succeeds exactly when the complete evaluation map $\Phi :F\to H^0(X,E)^*$ is an immersion off the zero section. Proof. At $m=0$, one has $\Psi _0=\mathrm d\Phi (\xi )\mathrm d\Phi (\xi )^*$, where $\Phi $ is written in the coordinates given by the chosen basis. If $\mathrm d\Phi $ is injective off the zero section, $B=\operatorname {Id}$ gives a strictly positive Levi form. If $\mathrm d\Phi $ has a nonzero kernel vector there, fiber dilation and normalization of the tangent vector place such a vector in $K$, where $\Psi _0=0$, and no Hermitian matrix can separate the image from zero. $\square$

title: 4.15 Ramified section tests and a positive root metric

topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.15 Ramified section tests and a positive root metric The untwisted test of corollary 4.14.6 can fail even for a line bundle with a positively curved metric, because the evaluation map of a globally generated bundle may fail to be an immersion where a holomorphic map ramifies. We give an explicit example on the product of a hyperelliptic curve with a projective space, where the complete spaces of sections can be computed. The same example gives a family of weighted tests, built from a root of the Fubini–Study weight of a very ample power instead of the twists of the preceding section, whose first successful level is explicit and can be made arbitrarily large. Fix integers $n\geq 2$ and $q\geq 2$. Choose a section $\beta \in H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(2q))$ with $2q$ distinct zeros. Let $\pi :C\to \mathbb P^1$ be the double cover defined in the total space of $\mathcal O(q)$ by the equation $w^2=\beta $, where $w$ is the tautological coordinate, and put \[  \begin{gathered} X=C\times \mathbb P^{n-1},\qquad L_ C=\pi ^*\mathcal O(1),\\ L=L_ C\boxtimes \mathcal O(1),\qquad A=L^ q,\qquad F=L^{-1}. \end{gathered}  \] Lemma 4.15.1 . The manifold $X$ is smooth compact projective. The line bundle $L$ is globally generated, $A$ is very ample, and for every integer $k\geq 0$, \[  \begin{aligned}  H^0(X,L^ k)& = \bigl (H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(k)) \oplus H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(k-q))\bigr ) \\ & \qquad \otimes H^0(\mathbb P^{n-1},\mathcal O(k)). \end{aligned}  \] In the second summand, the sections are multiplied by the coordinate $w$ of the cover. In particular, \[  h^0(X,L^ k)=\bigl (k+1+\max (k-q+1,0)\bigr ) \binom {n-1+k}{k}.  \] For a basis $\sigma _1,\ldots ,\sigma _ N$ of $H^0(X,A)$, the Fubini–Study weight and the corresponding root weight, in a local frame of $L$ and the induced frame of $A=L^ q$, are \[  \phi _ A=\log \sum _{i=1}^ N|\sigma _ i|^2, \qquad \phi =\phi _ A/q.  \] The metric $\mathrm e^{-\phi }$ on $L$ has strictly positive curvature. Thus it is strictly Griffiths-positive, and $G(v)=\mathrm e^{\phi }|v|^2$ is strictly plurisubharmonic on $F$ off its zero section. Proof. The direct image of the structure sheaf of $C$ is $\mathcal O\oplus \mathcal O(-q)\, w$, with multiplication of the second summand given by $w^2=\beta $. Tensoring by $\mathcal O(k)$, the local basis $1,w$ gives the stated decomposition of sections on $C$. Simple zeros of $\beta $ make the cover smooth: near a branch point the equation gives a coordinate $w$ with the base coordinate a nonzero multiple of $w^2$ to leading order. The cover is connected because the rational function representing $\beta $ has a simple zero and therefore is not a square. Finiteness over compact $\mathbb P^1$ makes $C$ compact. On $C$, the complete sections of $L_ C^ q$ are the degree-$q$ base monomials together with $w$. The map to projective space defined by these sections separates the base points by the Veronese coordinates, separates the two sheets by $w$, and has injective differential. At the ramification points the coordinate $w$ gives the missing derivative, and elsewhere the base coordinates do. Compactness makes this map an embedding. This shows that $C$ is projective and that $L_ C^ q$ is very ample. For the decomposition of sections on the product, expand a section on each $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ fiber in its complete degree-$k$ monomial basis. The coefficients depend holomorphically on $C$ and transform as sections of $L_ C^ k$. This proves the displayed tensor identity without a cohomological vanishing assumption. The dimensions follow from the monomial counts, since line bundles of negative degree on $\mathbb P^1$ have no nonzero sections. The degree-one base sections generate $L_ C$, hence $L$. The product of the curve embedding and the degree-$q$ Veronese embedding, followed by the Segre embedding, shows that $A$ is very ample. Its complete linear system therefore defines an immersion, so the Fubini–Study metric on $A$ has strictly positive curvature. Dividing its weight by $q$ defines a metric on $L$, since the transition functions of $A=L^ q$ are the $q$th powers of those of $L$, and its curvature is $1/q$ times that positive form. The final assertion follows from lemma 4.14.1 . $\square$

text: 4.15.1 The weighted family and its first successful level Keep the root metric $\mathrm e^{-\phi }$ on $L$, and choose the sphere bundle $S$ and the compact set $K$ for $F$ as in section 4.14 . For each integer $j\geq 0$, use the complete space \[  \widetilde V_ j=H^0(X,L^{j+1})  \] and pair its basis with $v\in F_ x$ to get a local column $p_ j(v)$, written in a local frame of $L^ j$. For every Hermitian coefficient matrix $B$, define \[  \widetilde G_{j,B}(v)=\mathrm e^{-j\phi (x)}p_ j(v)^*B p_ j(v).  \] These are globally defined functions, quadratic on each fiber. Their Levi matrices are \[  \begin{gathered} \widetilde\Psi _ j(v,\xi )=\mathrm e^{-j\phi } (r_ jr_ j^*-j\kappa p_ jp_ j^*),\\ r_ j=\mathrm dp_ j(\xi )-j\phi _ u p_ j,\qquad \kappa =\phi _{u\bar u}, \end{gathered}  \] where $u$ is the projection of $\xi $ to the base. As in ( 4.37 ), direct differentiation gives $\mathcal L\widetilde G_{j,B}(\xi )=\operatorname {tr}(B\widetilde\Psi _ j)$, and $\widetilde\Psi _ j$ transforms in the same way under changes of frames. Proposition 4.15.2 . The first integer $j\geq 0$ for which some $\widetilde G_{j,B}$, with $B$ an arbitrary Hermitian matrix, is strictly plurisubharmonic off the zero section is $j=q-1$. At every lower level, zero belongs to $\operatorname {conv}(\widetilde\Psi _ j(K))$; one atom witnesses this at $j=0$, and two atoms suffice at each $1\leq j<q-1$. Proof. At $j=q-1$, choose the basis $\sigma _ i$ that defines $\phi _ A$ and take $B=\operatorname {Id}$. Since $p_ j(v)=v(\sigma _ i(x))_ i$ in the chosen frames, \[  \widetilde G_{q-1,\operatorname {Id}}(v) =\mathrm e^{-(q-1)\phi }|v|^2\mathrm e^{q\phi } =\mathrm e^\phi |v|^2.  \] This function is strictly plurisubharmonic by lemma 4.15.1 . Now suppose that $0\leq j<q-1$. Then $j+1<q$, so by lemma 4.15.1 every section in $\widetilde V_ j$ comes from the first summand of the decomposition, which does not involve $w$. At a ramification point of $C$, choose a local coordinate $t$ on $C$, and use frames of the bundles pulled back from $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1}$. Writing $\zeta $ for the coordinates of the factor $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, the column has the form $p_ j(v)=vU_ j(\pi (t),\zeta )$. It is nonzero for $v\ne 0$, since $L^{j+1}$ is globally generated, and since $\pi $ ramifies at the point, its derivative in the $t$ direction vanishes there when $v$ is held fixed. Choose such a fiber vector $v$ on the sphere bundle $S$. Write tangent vectors to the total space of $F$ by their components in the $t$ direction, in the $\zeta $ directions and in the fiber direction. Let $\xi _ v=(0,0,v)$ be the vertical radial vector, let $u=\partial /\partial t$, and let $\xi _ h=(u,0,j\phi _ u v)$. At this point $\mathrm dp_ j(\xi _ v)=p_ j$ and $r_ j(\xi _ h)=0$. Thus \[  \begin{aligned}  \widetilde\Psi _ j(v,\xi _ v)& =\mathrm e^{-j\phi }p_ jp_ j^*,\\  \widetilde\Psi _ j(v,\xi _ h)& =-j\kappa \mathrm e^{-j\phi }p_ jp_ j^*, \qquad \kappa >0. \end{aligned}  \] Let $a_ v$ and $a_ h$ be the squared norms of $\xi _ v$ and $\xi _ h$ for the form $b$, and divide each tangent vector by its norm to obtain points of $K$. At $j=0$ the second matrix is zero, which gives the witness with one atom. For $j>0$, the matrix at the second normalized point is $-c$ times the matrix at the first, with $c=j\kappa a_ v/a_ h>0$. The probability measure giving these two points the weights $c/(1+c)$ and $1/(1+c)$ has zero matrix integral, which excludes strict positivity for every Hermitian $B$. This proves failure at all lower levels, so the first successful level is $j=q-1$. $\square$

title: 4.15.2 Relation to the fixed very ample criterion
search_title: Relation to the fixed very ample criterion
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 4.15.2 Relation to the fixed very ample criterion Corollary 4.15.3 . For the data $E=L$ and $A=L^ q$, with the Fubini–Study metric of a basis of $H^0(X,A)$, the criterion of theorem 4.14.5 applies with $m_0=0$. Its untwisted level fails, although $E$ carries a strictly Griffiths-positive metric, and a higher level succeeds. The atom witnessing the failure at level zero annihilates only the Levi forms of the level-zero test space, and does not give a measure with $D^*T=0$. Proof. By lemma 4.15.1 , $L$ is globally generated and $A$ is very ample, as the criterion requires. At a ramification point, the complete untwisted evaluation map has a nonzero tangent vector in its kernel, in the direction of the cover, as in the preceding proof; hence corollary 4.14.6 gives failure at level zero. The positive root metric and theorem 4.14.5 give success at some higher level. Moreover, the Levi form of the dual of this positive metric pairs strictly positively with every nonzero positive matrix-valued measure on $W\to S$, so the atom at level zero cannot annihilate the Levi forms of all smooth Hermitian forms. $\square$ The level $m$ of the criterion in theorem 4.14.5 corresponds to $j=qm$ in the root-weight family, since $E\otimes A^ m=L^{qm+1}$ and $m\phi _ A=qm\phi $. The first success at $j=q-1$ therefore gives no bound on the first successful level $m$ of that criterion. The root-weight family is nested in steps of $q$, because multiplication by the sections of $A$ uses $\sum _ i|\sigma _ i|^2=\mathrm e^{q\phi }$; we do not claim that it is nested in steps of one. As $q$ grows, the root-weight family has arbitrarily many failed initial levels, although the bundle carries a strictly positive metric.

section: 10.4 Gauduchon traces and the topology of potentials
text: 5 Gauduchon traces and the topology of potentials Throughout this chapter, $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, $\mathrm{d}V$ is a smooth positive probability volume form used for $L^1$ norms, and $\gamma $ is a Gauduchon metric, that is, a Hermitian form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$ (definition 4.1.1 ). In dimension one every Hermitian form is Gauduchon, since $\gamma ^{n-1}=1$. The current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has a conserved linear trace even when its non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure has infinite mass, as we shall see in chapter 6 . By proposition 4.2.1 , the positive measure $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ has the same total mass for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The ellipticity of $f\mapsto \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ makes the trace more informative than this mass alone: its kernel consists of the constants, so the trace measure determines the potential up to an additive constant. On mean-normalized potentials, this correspondence also identifies the topologies: weak convergence of trace measures is equivalent to $L^1$ convergence of potentials. Lipschitz tests give a complete metric for this topology, and the inverse elliptic operator compares it with the $L^1$ norm by sharp power bounds. Extending the conserved pairing to a positive pluriharmonic current requires more than this elliptic inversion. For continuous potentials, a gradient-energy estimate defines the derivative terms in the product and gives continuity under uniform approximation.

u -	heta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$, so uniqueness gives $w=u$ as distributions. Conversely, if $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0$, then proposition 1.1.2 gives a $	heta $-plurisubharmonic representative $u$ of $w$. It has mean zero by construction, and ( 5.1 ) gives $\mathcal T_\gamma (u)=
u $. $\square$ In dimension one the positivity condition is automatic, because $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=
u $; thus every positive measure of mass $M_{	heta ,\gamma }$ is the trace of a normalized potential. In higher dimensions, positivity of the trace measure $

title: Theorem 5.1.1
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 10.4 Gauduchon traces and the topology of potentials
text: Theorem 5.1.1 . The trace map $\mathcal T_\gamma $ is an affine homeomorphism from the compact convex set $\mathcal K^0_{\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}$, with its $L^1$ topology, onto a compact convex set of positive measures of mass $M_{\theta ,\gamma }$, with the weak topology. In other words, for $u_ j,u\in \mathcal K^0_{\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}$, \[  u_ j\longrightarrow u\text{ in }L^1 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \mathcal T_\gamma (u_ j)\rightharpoonup \mathcal T_\gamma (u).  \] If $M_{\theta ,\gamma }=0$ and $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing $, both sets consist of a single point. Proof. The set $\mathcal K^0_{\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}$ is convex. It is the image of the compact set $\mathcal K_\theta $ of theorem 1.4.2 under the continuous map $v\mapsto v-\int _ Xv\, \mathrm{d}V$, and is therefore compact. If $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ as currents, so the trace measures converge in the sense of distributions. Since they are positive measures of the same finite mass, and every continuous function is a uniform limit of smooth functions, they also converge weakly as measures. Thus $\mathcal T_\gamma $ is continuous. To prove injectivity, suppose that $\mathcal T_\gamma (u)=\mathcal T_\gamma (v)$. Then $A(u-v)=0$ in the sense of distributions. Elliptic regularity for $A$ shows that $u-v$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth function, and the maximum principle shows that this function is constant. Its mean is zero, so $u=v$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . A continuous injection from a compact space into a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image; here the target is the space of positive measures of mass $M_{\theta ,\gamma }$ with the weak topology. Since $\mathcal T_\gamma $ is affine, its image is convex. If $M_{\theta ,\gamma }=0$, every trace measure is zero, so injectivity shows that $\mathcal K^0_{\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}$ has at most one point; it has exactly one when $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is nonempty, since the mean of any $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function can be subtracted. In this case lemma 4.3.3 also gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=0$ for the unique normalized potential $u$, which is therefore smooth. $\square$

title: 5.2 A metric on normalized potentials
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 10.4 Gauduchon traces and the topology of potentials
text: 5.2 A metric on normalized potentials By theorem 5.1.1 , every metric for the weak topology on positive measures of mass $M_{\theta ,\gamma }$ pulls back to a metric for the $L^1$ topology on $\mathcal K^0_{\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}$. We use the bounded Lipschitz metric on measures, which can be compared quantitatively with the $L^1$ norm through the inverse of $A$. Fix a distance $d$ on $X$ induced by a smooth Riemannian metric. For a real Lipschitz function $f$ on $X$, write $\operatorname {Lip}_ d(f)=\sup _{x\ne y}|f(x)-f(y)|/d(x,y)$, and for $u,v\in \mathcal K^0_{\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}$ put \[  d_{\gamma ,d}(u,v) =\sup _{\substack {\| f\| _\infty \leq 1\\ \operatorname {Lip}_ d(f)\leq 1}} \left|\int _ X f\, \mathrm{d}\bigl (\mathcal T_\gamma (u)-\mathcal T_\gamma (v)\bigr )\right|.  \] We call $d_{\gamma ,d}$ the Gauduchon trace metric . Corollary 5.2.1 . The function $d_{\gamma ,d}$ is a bounded complete metric on $\mathcal K^0_{\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}$ inducing its $L^1$ topology. Changing $\gamma $ or $d$ gives the same topology and a uniformly equivalent metric on this compact space. Proof. Symmetry and the triangle inequality follow directly from the definition, and $d_{\gamma ,d}\leq 2M_{\theta ,\gamma }$ because both trace measures have mass $M_{\theta ,\gamma }$. Let $\mathcal F$ denote the family of test functions in the supremum. After rescaling, $\mathcal F$ contains a positive multiple of every Lipschitz function, and Lipschitz functions are uniformly dense in $C(X)$. Hence $\mathcal F$ separates finite measures, and together with the injectivity of $\mathcal T_\gamma $ this shows that $d_{\gamma ,d}$ is a metric. The same density, together with the common mass bound, shows that convergence in $d_{\gamma ,d}$ implies weak convergence of the trace measures. Conversely, $\mathcal F$ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous, so the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem gives a finite uniform $\epsilon $-net in $\mathcal F$ for every $\epsilon >0$. Weak convergence on the finitely many functions of the net, and the bound $2M_{\theta ,\gamma }\epsilon $ for the remaining error, give convergence in $d_{\gamma ,d}$. Thus $d_{\gamma ,d}$ is the pullback by the homeomorphism of theorem 5.1.1 of a metric for the weak topology. The resulting metric space is compact, hence complete. For two choices of the auxiliary data, both metrics induce the same compact $L^1$ topology, so the identity map is uniformly continuous in both directions. $\square$ Proposition 5.2.2 . There is a constant $C\geq 1$, depending only on $X,\theta ,\gamma ,\mathrm{d}V$ and $d$, such that \[  C^{-1}\| u-v\| _{L^1} \leq d_{\gamma ,d}(u,v) \leq C\| u-v\| _{L^1}^{1/2} \qquad (u,v\in \mathcal K^0_{\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}).  \] Proof. The lower bound follows by duality from the inverse of $A^*$, and the upper bound by smoothing the test functions. Put $w=u-v$, $\sigma =\mathcal T_\gamma (u)-\mathcal T_\gamma (v)$ and $M=M_{\theta ,\gamma }$, and write $\| \sigma \| _{\mathrm{TV}}$ for the total variation of $\sigma $. Then $\int _ Xw\, \mathrm{d}V=0$, $\sigma =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ and $\| \sigma \| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2M$. If $M=0$, theorem 5.1.1 gives $u=v$, and both estimates hold trivially. For the lower bound, let $g$ be a smooth real function. Since $\ker A=\ker A^*=\mathbb R$, the equation \[  A^*\phi =g-\int _ Xg\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \int _ X\phi \, \mathrm{d}V=0,  \] has a unique smooth solution. For $p>2n$, elliptic $W^{2,p}$ estimates on functions of mean zero and the Sobolev embedding theorem give $\| \phi \| _\infty +\operatorname {Lip}_ d(\phi )\leq C\| g\| _\infty $.  Pairing the distributional equation $Aw\, \mathrm{d}V=\sigma $ with $\phi $, and using $\int _ Xw\, \mathrm{d}V=0$, we obtain \[  \left|\int _ Xwg\, \mathrm{d}V\right| =\left|\int _ X\phi \, \mathrm{d}\sigma \right| \leq C\| g\| _\infty d_{\gamma ,d}(u,v).  \] Taking the supremum over smooth real $g$ with $\| g\| _\infty \leq 1$ gives $\| w\| _{L^1}\leq C d_{\gamma ,d}(u,v)$. For the upper bound, let $f$ be any test function in the definition of $d_{\gamma ,d}$. Using a fixed finite coordinate cover, a smooth partition of unity and convolution at scale $0<\epsilon <\epsilon _0$, we obtain smooth functions $f_\epsilon $ satisfying \[  \| f-f_\epsilon \| _\infty \leq C\epsilon , \qquad \| A^*f_\epsilon \| _\infty \leq C\epsilon ^{-1},  \] with constants uniform over this family of test functions. To see the second bound, localize $f$ by the fixed partition of unity. The localized functions have uniformly bounded values and first weak derivatives. In each second derivative of their convolutions, move one derivative onto the mollifier, whose derivative has $L^1$ norm $O(\epsilon ^{-1})$. The lower-order terms of $A^*$ have fixed smooth coefficients and satisfy the same bound. Since $\int _ Xf_\epsilon \, \mathrm{d}\sigma =\int _ XwA^*f_\epsilon \, \mathrm{d}V$, it follows that \[  \left|\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}\sigma \right| \leq C\bigl (M\epsilon +\epsilon ^{-1}\| w\| _{L^1}\bigr ).  \] If $0<\| w\| _{L^1}<\epsilon _0^2$, choose $\epsilon =\| w\| _{L^1}^{1/2}$. For larger norms use $d_{\gamma ,d}(u,v)\leq 2M$, and for $w=0$ use injectivity. Taking the supremum over $f$ proves the upper bound. $\square$ Both exponents in proposition 5.2.2 are optimal, already on an elliptic curve. Example 5.2.3 . Let $X=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z)$, with coordinate $z=x+\mathrm{i}y$. Take $\theta =\gamma =\eta $, where $\eta =(\mathrm{i}/2)\mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z$, together with $\mathrm{d}V=\eta $ and the flat distance $d$. For integers $k\geq 1$, set \[  u_ k=\frac{\cos (2\pi kx)}{2\pi k^2}.  \] These smooth potentials have mean zero and satisfy \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k=\left(1-\frac12\cos (2\pi kx)\right)\eta >0, \qquad \| u_ k\| _{L^1}=\frac1{\pi ^2k^2}.  \] The function $f_ k=\cos (2\pi kx)/(2\pi k)$ has supremum norm at most one and Lipschitz constant at most one. It follows that \[  d_{\gamma ,d}(u_ k,0) \geq \left|\int _ Xf_ k\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k\right| =\frac1{8\pi k}.  \] Consequently, the exponent $1/2$ in proposition 5.2.2 cannot be replaced by any larger exponent, even for smooth strictly positive potentials on a fixed curve. Nor can the power one in the lower bound be replaced by a smaller positive power: for $0<t\leq 1$, both $\| tu_1\| _{L^1}$ and $d_{\gamma ,d}(tu_1,0)$ equal $t$ times their positive values at $t=1$.

title: 5.3 Continuous potentials and pluriharmonic traces
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 10.4 Gauduchon traces and the topology of potentials
text: 5.3 Continuous potentials and pluriharmonic traces The Gauduchon trace pairs $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with the smooth form $\gamma ^{n-1}$, which is positive and pluriharmonic. In this section $n\geq 2$, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$, and $G$ is a positive pluriharmonic $(n-1,n-1)$-current, that is, a positive current with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$ (see section 4.7 ). Such currents include $\gamma ^{n-1}$, but in general their coefficients are only measures, and the product $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge G$ is not defined a priori. Its integration-by-parts formula contains gradient terms, since $G$ need not be $d$-closed. The equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$ converts uniform control of a potential difference into a bound for its gradient energy against $G$. This estimate defines the gradient currents for a continuous potential and makes the product stable under uniform approximation. Lemma 5.3.1 . Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$, and let $G$ be a positive $(n-1,n-1)$-current with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$. Put $\mu =\omega \wedge G$ and $M=\mu (X)$. If $a,b$ are smooth real functions and $C\geq 0$ is a constant with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\geq -C\omega $, then \[  0\leq \int _ X\mathrm{d}(a-b)\wedge \mathrm{d}^ c(a-b)\wedge G \leq 2C M\| a-b\| _\infty .  \] For every smooth real function $v$, the total variation norms of the order-zero currents $\mathrm{d}v\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G$ satisfy \[  \| \mathrm{d}v\wedge G\| _{\mathrm{TV}}+ \| \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq C_\omega M^{1/2} \left(\int _ X\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G\right)^{1/2}.  \] Here the total variation norms are computed with respect to $\omega $, and $C_\omega $ depends only on $(X,\omega )$. Proof. Set $v=a-b$. The identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v^2)=2\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv+2v\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$, integrated against $G$, and the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$ give \[  \int _ X\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G =-\int _ Xv\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge G.  \] The measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a+C\omega )\wedge G$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b+C\omega )\wedge G$ are positive, and each has mass $CM$, because the terms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge G$ integrate to zero. Their difference $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge G$ therefore has total variation at most $2CM$, which proves the upper bound. The lower bound holds because $\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )\partial v\wedge \bar\partial v$ is a positive $(1,1)$-form. For the second estimate, work in a local unitary frame for $\omega $. Positivity of $G$ means that its coefficients form a positive semidefinite matrix of measures. These entries are absolutely continuous with respect to the trace measure $\mu $: the diagonal entries are dominated by the trace, and the off-diagonal entries by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for positive semidefinite matrices. The resulting matrix of densities has trace bounded by a constant depending only on the normalization. Pairing $\mathrm{d}v\wedge G$ or $\mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G$ with a test one-form $\eta $, and applying the matrix Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and then the integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we obtain \[  |\langle \mathrm{d}v\wedge G,\eta \rangle | +|\langle \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G,\eta \rangle | \leq C_\omega \| \eta \| _\infty M^{1/2} \left(\int _ X\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G\right)^{1/2}.  \] A finite cover by such frames and a partition of unity give the global estimate. Taking the supremum over smooth test forms of norm at most one yields the total variation bound. When $M=0$, positivity gives $G=0$, and both estimates hold trivially. $\square$ Theorem 5.3.2 . Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$, let $\alpha $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\alpha )\cap C^0(X)$. For every positive $(n-1,n-1)$-current $G$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$, the product \[  (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge G  \] has a canonical definition as a positive measure of mass $\int _ X\alpha \wedge G$, which agrees with the usual product if $u$ or $G$ is smooth. If $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\alpha )\cap C^0(X)$ and $u_ j\to u$ uniformly, and if positive pluriharmonic currents $G_ j$ converge weakly to $G$, then \[  (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\wedge G_ j \rightharpoonup (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge G.  \] Proof. We first define the gradient currents $\mathrm{d}u\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ cu\wedge G$ as limits, then define the product by an integration-by-parts formula, and finally prove joint continuity. Step 1: gradient currents. Choose smooth approximants $a_ k\to u$ as in lemma 1.21.4 . There is a common constant $C>0$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k\geq -C\omega $. Write $M=\int _ X\omega \wedge G$. Since $a_ k$ converges uniformly, lemma 5.3.1 shows that $\mathrm{d}a_ k\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ ca_ k\wedge G$ are Cauchy sequences in total variation. Denote their limits, which are currents of order zero, by $\mathrm{d}u\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ cu\wedge G$. Applying the same lemma to two uniformly convergent smooth sequences with a common lower Hessian bound shows that the limits do not depend on the sequence. Uniform convergence also gives $a_ kG\to uG$ in total variation. Step 2: the product. Define 5.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-pluriharmonic-product} (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge G =\alpha \wedge G+\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{d}^ cu\wedge G) -\mathrm{d}^ c(\mathrm{d}u\wedge G)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uG) \end{equation} in the sense of distributions. For smooth $u$, the Leibniz rule and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$ show that this agrees with the usual product. Consequently $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k)\wedge G$ converges in distributions to the right-hand side of ( 5.2 ). With $\varepsilon _ k\to 0$ as in lemma 1.21.4 , the measures $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k+\varepsilon _ k\omega )\wedge G$ are positive, with masses $\int _ X\alpha \wedge G+\varepsilon _ kM$. Their distributional limit is therefore a positive measure, and testing against the constant function one gives its mass. The uniform mass bound upgrades distributional convergence to weak convergence of measures. If $G$ is smooth, the uniform convergence of $a_ k$ also identifies the limit with the product of the current $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and the smooth form $G$. Step 3: independence of the decomposition. Adding a smooth function $h$ to $u$ adds $\mathrm{d}h\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ ch\wedge G$ to the gradient currents, so replacing $(\alpha ,u)$ by $(\alpha -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h,u+h)$ leaves the product unchanged. If two continuous decompositions define the same $(1,1)$-current, the difference of their potentials has smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$; taking its trace in a coordinate chart and applying elliptic regularity shows that this difference is smooth. Thus the product depends only on the current $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and on $G$. Step 4: joint continuity. For $u$ and for each $u_ j$, keep only those smooth approximants from lemma 1.21.4 whose curvature errors are at most one. Choosing $C$ with $\alpha \leq (C-1)\omega $, all these approximants satisfy the same lower Hessian bound $-C\omega $. The numbers $M_ j=\int _ X\omega \wedge G_ j$ are bounded, by weak convergence. Fix a smooth approximant $a_ k$ of $u$, and put $\delta _{j,k}=\| u_ j-a_ k\| _\infty $. Applying lemma 5.3.1 to $a_ k$ and to smooth approximants of $u_ j$, and passing to the gradient limits, we find that the total variations of the differences $(\mathrm{d}u_ j-\mathrm{d}a_ k)\wedge G_ j$ and $(\mathrm{d}^ cu_ j-\mathrm{d}^ ca_ k)\wedge G_ j$ are at most $C'M_ j\sqrt{\delta _{j,k}}$, where $C'$ is independent of $j$ and $k$. For a smooth real test function $\phi $, formula ( 5.2 ) now gives \[  \left|\left\langle (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\wedge G_ j -(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k)\wedge G_ j,\phi \right\rangle \right| \leq C_\phi M_ j(\sqrt{\delta _{j,k}}+\delta _{j,k}),  \] where $C_\phi $ depends on the first two derivatives of $\phi $, on $\omega $ and on $C$. The same estimate holds with $u_ j,G_ j$ replaced by $u,G$. For fixed $k$, the products $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k)\wedge G_ j$ of a fixed smooth form with $G_ j$ converge weakly to $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k)\wedge G$. Let first $j\to \infty $ and then $k\to \infty $; since $u_ j\to u$ uniformly, the error tends to zero. This proves convergence in distributions, and positivity together with the bounded masses $\int _ X\alpha \wedge G_ j$ upgrades it to weak convergence of measures. $\square$ For $G=\gamma ^{n-1}$ and $\alpha =\theta $, the product in theorem 5.3.2 is the Gauduchon trace of a continuous potential. Its conserved mass controls a linear pairing of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$; the nonlinear powers of this current, constructed for unbounded potentials in chapter 6 , require a separate mass analysis.

title: Lemma 5.3.1
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 10.4 Gauduchon traces and the topology of potentials
text: Lemma 5.3.1 . Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$, and let $G$ be a positive $(n-1,n-1)$-current with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$. Put $\mu =\omega \wedge G$ and $M=\mu (X)$. If $a,b$ are smooth real functions and $C\geq 0$ is a constant with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\geq -C\omega $, then \[  0\leq \int _ X\mathrm{d}(a-b)\wedge \mathrm{d}^ c(a-b)\wedge G \leq 2C M\| a-b\| _\infty .  \] For every smooth real function $v$, the total variation norms of the order-zero currents $\mathrm{d}v\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G$ satisfy \[  \| \mathrm{d}v\wedge G\| _{\mathrm{TV}}+ \| \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq C_\omega M^{1/2} \left(\int _ X\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G\right)^{1/2}.  \] Here the total variation norms are computed with respect to $\omega $, and $C_\omega $ depends only on $(X,\omega )$. Proof. Set $v=a-b$. The identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v^2)=2\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv+2v\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$, integrated against $G$, and the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$ give \[  \int _ X\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G =-\int _ Xv\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge G.  \] The measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a+C\omega )\wedge G$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b+C\omega )\wedge G$ are positive, and each has mass $CM$, because the terms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge G$ integrate to zero. Their difference $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge G$ therefore has total variation at most $2CM$, which proves the upper bound. The lower bound holds because $\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )\partial v\wedge \bar\partial v$ is a positive $(1,1)$-form. For the second estimate, work in a local unitary frame for $\omega $. Positivity of $G$ means that its coefficients form a positive semidefinite matrix of measures. These entries are absolutely continuous with respect to the trace measure $\mu $: the diagonal entries are dominated by the trace, and the off-diagonal entries by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for positive semidefinite matrices. The resulting matrix of densities has trace bounded by a constant depending only on the normalization. Pairing $\mathrm{d}v\wedge G$ or $\mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G$ with a test one-form $\eta $, and applying the matrix Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and then the integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we obtain \[  |\langle \mathrm{d}v\wedge G,\eta \rangle | +|\langle \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G,\eta \rangle | \leq C_\omega \| \eta \| _\infty M^{1/2} \left(\int _ X\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm{d}^ cv\wedge G\right)^{1/2}.  \] A finite cover by such frames and a partition of unity give the global estimate. Taking the supremum over smooth test forms of norm at most one yields the total variation bound. When $M=0$, positivity gives $G=0$, and both estimates hold trivially. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.3.2
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 10.4 Gauduchon traces and the topology of potentials
text: Theorem 5.3.2 . Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$, let $\alpha $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\alpha )\cap C^0(X)$. For every positive $(n-1,n-1)$-current $G$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$, the product \[  (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge G  \] has a canonical definition as a positive measure of mass $\int _ X\alpha \wedge G$, which agrees with the usual product if $u$ or $G$ is smooth. If $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\alpha )\cap C^0(X)$ and $u_ j\to u$ uniformly, and if positive pluriharmonic currents $G_ j$ converge weakly to $G$, then \[  (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\wedge G_ j \rightharpoonup (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge G.  \] Proof. We first define the gradient currents $\mathrm{d}u\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ cu\wedge G$ as limits, then define the product by an integration-by-parts formula, and finally prove joint continuity. Step 1: gradient currents. Choose smooth approximants $a_ k\to u$ as in lemma 1.21.4 . There is a common constant $C>0$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k\geq -C\omega $. Write $M=\int _ X\omega \wedge G$. Since $a_ k$ converges uniformly, lemma 5.3.1 shows that $\mathrm{d}a_ k\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ ca_ k\wedge G$ are Cauchy sequences in total variation. Denote their limits, which are currents of order zero, by $\mathrm{d}u\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ cu\wedge G$. Applying the same lemma to two uniformly convergent smooth sequences with a common lower Hessian bound shows that the limits do not depend on the sequence. Uniform convergence also gives $a_ kG\to uG$ in total variation. Step 2: the product. Define 5.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-pluriharmonic-product} (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge G =\alpha \wedge G+\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{d}^ cu\wedge G) -\mathrm{d}^ c(\mathrm{d}u\wedge G)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uG) \end{equation} in the sense of distributions. For smooth $u$, the Leibniz rule and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=0$ show that this agrees with the usual product. Consequently $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k)\wedge G$ converges in distributions to the right-hand side of ( 5.2 ). With $\varepsilon _ k\to 0$ as in lemma 1.21.4 , the measures $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k+\varepsilon _ k\omega )\wedge G$ are positive, with masses $\int _ X\alpha \wedge G+\varepsilon _ kM$. Their distributional limit is therefore a positive measure, and testing against the constant function one gives its mass. The uniform mass bound upgrades distributional convergence to weak convergence of measures. If $G$ is smooth, the uniform convergence of $a_ k$ also identifies the limit with the product of the current $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and the smooth form $G$. Step 3: independence of the decomposition. Adding a smooth function $h$ to $u$ adds $\mathrm{d}h\wedge G$ and $\mathrm{d}^ ch\wedge G$ to the gradient currents, so replacing $(\alpha ,u)$ by $(\alpha -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h,u+h)$ leaves the product unchanged. If two continuous decompositions define the same $(1,1)$-current, the difference of their potentials has smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$; taking its trace in a coordinate chart and applying elliptic regularity shows that this difference is smooth. Thus the product depends only on the current $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and on $G$. Step 4: joint continuity. For $u$ and for each $u_ j$, keep only those smooth approximants from lemma 1.21.4 whose curvature errors are at most one. Choosing $C$ with $\alpha \leq (C-1)\omega $, all these approximants satisfy the same lower Hessian bound $-C\omega $. The numbers $M_ j=\int _ X\omega \wedge G_ j$ are bounded, by weak convergence. Fix a smooth approximant $a_ k$ of $u$, and put $\delta _{j,k}=\| u_ j-a_ k\| _\infty $. Applying lemma 5.3.1 to $a_ k$ and to smooth approximants of $u_ j$, and passing to the gradient limits, we find that the total variations of the differences $(\mathrm{d}u_ j-\mathrm{d}a_ k)\wedge G_ j$ and $(\mathrm{d}^ cu_ j-\mathrm{d}^ ca_ k)\wedge G_ j$ are at most $C'M_ j\sqrt{\delta _{j,k}}$, where $C'$ is independent of $j$ and $k$. For a smooth real test function $\phi $, formula ( 5.2 ) now gives \[  \left|\left\langle (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\wedge G_ j -(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k)\wedge G_ j,\phi \right\rangle \right| \leq C_\phi M_ j(\sqrt{\delta _{j,k}}+\delta _{j,k}),  \] where $C_\phi $ depends on the first two derivatives of $\phi $, on $\omega $ and on $C$. The same estimate holds with $u_ j,G_ j$ replaced by $u,G$. For fixed $k$, the products $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k)\wedge G_ j$ of a fixed smooth form with $G_ j$ converge weakly to $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k)\wedge G$. Let first $j\to \infty $ and then $k\to \infty $; since $u_ j\to u$ uniformly, the error tends to zero. This proves convergence in distributions, and positivity together with the bounded masses $\int _ X\alpha \wedge G_ j$ upgrades it to weak convergence of measures. $\square$

title: 6 Non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measures
text: 6 Non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measures Throughout this chapter, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$ and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a smooth positive probability volume form used for $L^1$ norms and integrals. As in section 1.7 , we write $\theta _ v=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$, and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ when $v$ is bounded; convergence in capacity refers to the capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ of section 1.8 . For an unbounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, the Bedford–Taylor products of proposition 1.7.1 are not defined. On the set $\{ u>-t\} $, however, $u$ coincides with its bounded truncation $\max (u,-t)$, and since bounded products are plurifinely local, the restricted measures are compatible as $t$ increases. Their limit is a measure on the complement of the pole set, the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of $u$. For a general smooth background $\theta $, the truncation need not be $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, so positivity of the restricted products requires a local argument. The total mass of the limit may also be infinite. For a Hermitian background, finiteness of this mass for every potential is equivalent to a uniform bound on the Monge–Ampère masses of bounded potentials, the bounded mass property. When the property fails, we construct a potential of infinite mass whose multiplier ideals are all trivial; its complex Hessian even has integrable coefficients, although its determinant is not integrable.

title: 6.1 Truncation and non-pluripolar measures
text: 6.1 Truncation and non-pluripolar measures Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For $t>0$, put \[  u_ t=\max (u,-t),\qquad D_ t=\{ u>-t\} .  \] Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta $. Then $u_ t$ is bounded and $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic, so proposition 1.7.1 defines the product $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n$ as a signed measure. It need not be positive on $X$, but its restriction to the plurifinely open set $D_ t$ is positive. The proof replaces $u_ t$ near each point by a local truncation that preserves positivity up to an arbitrarily small smooth error. Lemma 6.1.1 . With the notation above, \[  0\leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n \leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n.  \] More generally, let $\theta _1,\ldots ,\theta _ n$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms, let $u^ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$, and let $D$ be the set where $u^ i>-t$ for every $i$. Then the mixed product of the currents $\theta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (u^ i,-t)$ is positive on $D$. Proof. Work in a coordinate ball with a fixed positive constant form $\kappa $, and fix $\epsilon >0$. Every point has a smaller neighborhood carrying a constant real form $\theta '$ such that \[  -\epsilon \kappa \leq \theta -\theta '\leq \epsilon \kappa .  \] Take a smooth local potential $r$ for $\theta '+\epsilon \kappa $. Then $u+r$ is plurisubharmonic. On a relatively compact smaller neighborhood choose $k>t+\sup |r|$ and set \[  h_ k=\max (u+r,-k)-r.  \] This function is locally bounded and equals $u_ t=u$ on $D_ t$. Moreover, \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k+2\epsilon \kappa =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (u+r,-k)+(\theta -\theta '+\epsilon \kappa )  \] is the sum of a positive closed current with bounded potential and a smooth positive form, so its bounded products are positive. By plurifine locality, the restriction of $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t+2\epsilon \kappa )^ n$ to $D_ t$ is positive on this neighborhood. These neighborhoods cover the coordinate ball. Now let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. The product with the fixed bounded potential $u_ t$ is a polynomial in $\epsilon $ whose coefficients have locally finite variation, so it converges in local total variation, also after restriction to $D_ t$. This proves the first inequality. The same construction, applied to each factor, gives the positivity of mixed products. For the second inequality, expand the difference of the two powers by the telescoping identity, using the smooth positive form $\Omega -\theta $. Every summand is a mixed product of factors that are positive on $D_ t$, as just proved. The difference is therefore nonnegative there. $\square$ Theorem 6.1.2 (Extended non-pluripolar measure) . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The measures $\mathbf1_{D_ t}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n$ increase with $t$. Their limit 6.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:extended-ma} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) :=\lim _{t\to +\infty }\mathbf1_{\{ u>-t\} } (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (u,-t))^ n \end{equation} is a positive Borel measure that puts no mass on pluripolar sets; it is finite on each $D_ t$ and $\sigma $-finite on $X$. It depends only on the current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$; in particular, it is unchanged when a constant is added to $u$. If $\Omega $ is a Hermitian form with $\theta \leq \Omega $, then \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Omega (u).  \] The total mass of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ may be infinite. Proof. For $s>t$, plurifine locality on $D_ t\subset D_ s$ gives \[  \mathbf1_{D_ t}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ s)^ n =\mathbf1_{D_ t}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n.  \] Together with lemma 6.1.1 , this proves that the measures increase. Their increasing limit is countably additive by monotone convergence, and it vanishes on pluripolar sets because each bounded product does. The comparison with $\Omega $ passes to the limit. By the compatibility just proved, \[  \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) =\mathbf1_{D_ t}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n,  \] and the mass of this measure is bounded by that of the bounded product $(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n$. The sets $D_ t$ exhaust the complement of $\{ u=-\infty \} $, which has zero mass, so the limit is $\sigma $-finite. For a smooth real function $f$, consider $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ and $u'=u-f$. On a common superlevel set of $u$ and $u'$, sufficiently deep truncations of $u$ and $u'$ define the same current with bounded potentials, so their restricted products agree. These sets exhaust the complement of the common pole set, which proves invariance under this change of decomposition. By the elliptic-regularity argument in the proof of proposition 1.7.1 , any two smooth decompositions of the same current differ in this way, and adding a constant is a special case. $\square$ We call $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of $u$; the word extended indicates that its total mass may be infinite. On compact $X$ it defines a current of order zero exactly when its total mass is finite. In that case it is the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure in the usual sense, namely the extension by zero across $\{ u=-\infty \} $ of the plurifinely local bounded products. If $u$ is bounded, then $D_ t=X$ for large $t$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$. In accordance with the usual notation for non-pluripolar products, we also write $\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\rangle $ for $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$; lower powers $\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\rangle $ are defined by the same truncation where they are used.

title: 6.2 Contact sets
text: 6.2 Contact sets The bounded contact inequality of lemma 1.7.2 extends to unbounded potentials on common finite levels. As in the previous section, local positive corrections are needed, because the global truncations need not remain $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. Proposition 6.2.1 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u\leq v$. Then \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v).  \] Proof. Fix a coordinate ball with a constant positive form $\kappa $, a level $t>0$, and $\epsilon >0$. On smaller neighborhoods, freeze $\theta $ to a constant form $\theta '$ with $-\epsilon \kappa \leq \theta -\theta '\leq \epsilon \kappa $, and choose a quadratic function $r$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=\theta '+\epsilon \kappa $. Then $u+r$ and $v+r$ are plurisubharmonic. For a large integer $k$ put \[  a_ k=\max (u+r,-k)-r,\qquad b_ k=\max (v+r,-k)-r.  \] These functions are bounded on relatively compact neighborhoods, satisfy $a_ k\leq b_ k$, and \[  \theta +2\epsilon \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ k =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (u+r,-k)+(\theta -\theta '+\epsilon \kappa )\geq 0,  \] with the same inequality for $b_ k$. We may therefore apply the top-degree case of lemma 1.7.2 with background $\theta +2\epsilon \kappa $. On $D_ t=\{ u>-t\} $, both $u$ and $v$ are larger than $-t$. Taking $k>t+\sup |r|$ makes $a_ k=u$ and $b_ k=v$ on $D_ t$. Restricting the bounded inequality to $\{ u=v\} \cap D_ t$ and using locality, we obtain the contact inequality for the background $\theta +2\epsilon \kappa $ on that set. The smaller neighborhoods cover the original ball, so the restricted inequality holds throughout it. Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta $. The truncations $u_ t=\max (u,-t)$ and $v_ t=\max (v,-t)$ are bounded and $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic, so their signed products with background $\theta $ are defined. On $D_ t$, the products used above are the restrictions of $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t+2\epsilon \kappa )^ n$ and $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ t+2\epsilon \kappa )^ n$. These are polynomials in $\epsilon $ whose coefficients have locally finite variation, so they converge in local total variation as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, also after restriction to $\{ u=v\} \cap D_ t$. This proves the inequality for the background $\theta $ on each finite level. Finally let $t\to +\infty $: the common pole set has zero extended mass, and the sets $\{ u=v\} \cap D_ t$ exhaust its complement in the contact set. $\square$

title: Proposition 6.2.1

title: 6.3 Weighted lower semicontinuity
text: 6.3 Weighted lower semicontinuity Products of uniformly bounded potentials are continuous under convergence in capacity. Multiplying the extended measure by a cutoff in the potential that vanishes below a fixed level reduces it to such bounded products, and letting the level tend to $-\infty $ gives lower semicontinuity of the extended measures, even when their masses are infinite. The weights are allowed to vary with the potentials. Lemma 6.3.1 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form. Suppose $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have a common upper bound and $u_ j\to u$ in capacity. If $b_ j,b$ are nonnegative uniformly bounded quasi-continuous functions and $b_ j\to b$ in capacity, then \[  \int _ Xb\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq \liminf _ j\int _ Xb_ j\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j).  \] Both sides may be infinite. Proof. Subtracting a common constant, we may assume that all the potentials are nonpositive. Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta $. title: 6.4 Density and trace inequalities
text: 6.4 Density and trace inequalities The mixed density inequality of lemma 1.7.6 passes to unbounded potentials on common finite levels. It gives a lower bound for the extended measure of a convex combination of potentials and, by comparison with a smooth metric, a lower bound for the full trace measure. Lemma 6.4.1 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth semipositive $(1,1)$-form and let $f,g\geq 0$ be measurable functions on $X$. Suppose $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)\geq f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Then, for $0\leq t\leq 1$, 6.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:singular-convex-density} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (tu+(1-t)v) \geq \bigl (tf^{1/n}+(1-t)g^{1/n}\bigr )^ n\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} Proof. The cases $t=0$ and $t=1$ are the hypotheses. Let $0<t<1$, translate $u,v$ to be nonpositive, and put $u_ k=\max (u,-k)$ and $v_ k=\max (v,-k)$. Since $\theta $ is semipositive, these are bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions, and by locality \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_ k)\geq \mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_ k)\geq \mathbf1_{\{ v>-k\} }g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Apply lemma 1.7.6 to each mixed term in the positive expansion of $\theta _{tu_ k+(1-t)v_ k}^{n}$. On $E_ k=\{ u>-k\} \cap \{ v>-k\} $ this gives the density on the right of ( 6.4 ). On the same set, plurifine locality identifies the left-hand side with the extended measure of $tu+(1-t)v$. As $k\to \infty $, the sets $E_ k$ exhaust the complement of the two pole sets, which have zero smooth volume. Monotone convergence on Borel sets proves the inequality. $\square$ The same mixed inequality gives a lower bound for the full trace measure of an unbounded potential. Unlike the extended measure, the full current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ keeps its mass on the pole set; the bound below concerns only its absolutely continuous part. Lemma 6.4.2 . Let $\gamma $ be a Hermitian form. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $0\leq g\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ satisfy $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V$, then \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq (g\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Proof. For bounded $u$, lemma 1.7.6 , applied in local coordinates with $T_1=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, $T_2=\gamma $ and $k=1$, gives the asserted inequality. In general, subtract a constant so that $u\leq 0$, and put $u_ k=\max (u,-k)$. Positivity and locality give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_ k)\geq \mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }g\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] so the bounded case applies to $u_ k$ with the density $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-k\} }g$. Since $u_ k\to u$ in $L^1$, the positive measures $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ converge weakly to $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$. The densities on the right converge in $L^1$, because $g^{1/n}$ is integrable and the pole set has zero smooth volume. Passing to the limit proves the assertion. $\square$

title: 6.5 The bounded mass property
text: 6.5 The bounded mass property When $\omega $ is a Kähler form, all bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions have the same Monge–Ampère mass $\int _ X\omega ^ n$. For a general Hermitian form, the mass can depend on the potential, as in example 2.3.1 , and the following two numbers measure its range. Definition 6.5.1 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$. The lower mass and the upper mass of $\omega $ are \[  \begin{split}  v_-(\omega )& = \inf _{v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n,\\  v_+(\omega )& = \sup _{v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n. \end{split}  \] The manifold $X$ has the bounded mass property , abbreviated BMP, if $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $. The form $\omega $ has positive lower mass if $v_-(\omega )>0$. Testing with $v=0$ gives $v_-(\omega )\leq \int _ X\omega ^ n\leq v_+(\omega )$. By the next proposition, the bounded mass property does not depend on the choice of $\omega $. Since the extended measure ( 6.1 ) is built from products of bounded potentials, the upper mass also controls the extended measures of unbounded potentials (proposition 6.5.3 ). Proposition 6.5.2 . The bounded mass property is independent of the Hermitian form. Moreover, the supremum in definition 6.5.1 is unchanged if only smooth potentials are used. Proof. For another Hermitian form $\eta $, choose $C>0$ such that $\eta \leq C\omega $. If $v$ is a bounded $\eta $-plurisubharmonic function, then $v/C$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic and \[  0\leq \eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v \leq C\bigl (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v/C)\bigr ).  \] By positivity of mixed bounded products, $\int _ X(\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\leq C^ n v_+(\omega )$. Interchanging the two forms proves metric independence. For the last assertion, approximate a bounded potential by theorem 1.11.1 . The smooth approximants decrease and remain uniformly bounded, so the continuity of bounded products along decreasing sequences gives convergence of their total masses. The reverse inequality between the two suprema is immediate. $\square$ Proposition 6.5.3 . Assume $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $. If $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\theta \leq C\omega $ for some $C>0$, and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, then \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)(X)\leq C^ n v_+(\omega ).  \] Proof. The comparison in theorem 6.1.2 , applied with the Hermitian form $C\omega $, gives \[  \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}(C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n.  \] Since $u_ t/C$ is bounded and $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, the right-hand side has mass at most $C^ n v_+(\omega )$. Let $t\to \infty $. $\square$

title: 6.6 Infinite mass with trivial multiplier ideals
search_title: Infinite mass with trivial multiplier ideals
text: 6.6 Infinite mass with trivial multiplier ideals If the bounded mass property fails, there are smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u_ j$ whose masses $M_ j$ tend to infinity. In a convex combination $U=\sum _ ja_ ju_ j$, positivity of mixed products shows that each summand contributes at least $a_ j^ nM_ j$ to the extended measure of $U$. Choosing the masses $M_ j$ to outgrow $a_ j^{-n}$ therefore forces infinite mass. On the other hand, each tail $\sum _{j>N}a_ ju_ j$ is a small multiple of a convex combination of normalized potentials, and the uniform exponential integrability of lemma 1.5.1 applies to it at every exponent. Theorem 6.6.1 . If $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, there is $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $U\leq 0$, such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)(X)=+\infty , \qquad \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pU}\, \mathrm{d}V<+\infty \quad \hbox{for every }p>0.  \] In particular, $\mathcal I(pU)=\mathcal O_ X$ for every $p>0$. Proof. Set $a_ j=2^{-j}$ for $j\geq 1$. By proposition 6.5.2 , we can choose smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u_ j$ with $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$ and \[  M_ j:=\int _ X\omega _{u_ j}^ n\geq 2^{j(n+1)}.  \] The partial sums $U_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}a_ ju_ j$ decrease and satisfy \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N =\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j\omega _{u_ j} +\left(1-\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j\right)\omega \geq 0.  \] Their $L^1$ norms are bounded by ( 1.1 ), so their limit $U$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic and nonpositive. We first prove that the mass is infinite. Fix $j$ and write $v_ j=U-a_ ju_ j$. Passing to the limit in the remaining partial sums gives $(1-a_ j)\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq 0$. For $t>0$, put \[  v_{j,t}=\max (v_ j,-t),\qquad W_{j,t}=a_ ju_ j+v_{j,t}.  \] The function $v_{j,t}$ is a bounded potential for the positive background $(1-a_ j)\omega $, so $W_{j,t}$ is bounded and $\omega $-plurisubharmonic. On $D_ t=\{ U>-t\} $, the inequality $u_ j\leq 0$ gives $v_ j=U-a_ ju_ j\geq U>-t$, and hence $W_{j,t}=U=\max (U,-t)$ there. Plurifine locality and positivity of bounded mixed products yield \begin{align*}  \mathbf1_{D_ t}\omega _{\max (U,-t)}^ n & =\mathbf1_{D_ t} \bigl (a_ j\omega _{u_ j} +(1-a_ j)\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{j,t}\bigr )^ n\\ & \geq a_ j^ n\mathbf1_{D_ t}\omega _{u_ j}^ n. \end{align*} The sets $D_ t$ exhaust $X\setminus \{ U=-\infty \} $. This pole set is pluripolar, hence has zero smooth volume, so the smooth measure $\omega _{u_ j}^ n$ gives it no mass. Letting $t\to +\infty $, we obtain \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)(X) \geq a_ j^ nM_ j\geq 2^ j.  \] Since $j$ is arbitrary, the mass is infinite. For the integrability, fix $p>0$, let $\alpha $ be the exponent of lemma 1.5.1 , and take $N$ so large that $p\delta \leq \alpha $, where $\delta =\sum _{j>N}a_ j=2^{-N}$. Write $U=A_ N+V_ N$ with $A_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}a_ ju_ j$ smooth. For a finite tail ending at $m>N$, Jensen's inequality for the convex exponential function, with the unused weight assigned to the value zero, gives \begin{align*}  \exp \! \left(-p\sum _{N<j\leq m}a_ ju_ j\right) & \leq \sum _{N<j\leq m}\frac{a_ j}{\delta } \mathrm{e}^{-p\delta u_ j} +1-\sum _{N<j\leq m}\frac{a_ j}{\delta }. \end{align*} Because $u_ j\leq 0$ and $p\delta \leq \alpha $, the integrals of the exponentials on the right are uniformly bounded. Integrating and letting $m\to +\infty $ by monotone convergence, we obtain $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pV_ N}\mathrm{d}V<+\infty $. Multiplication by the bounded smooth function $\mathrm{e}^{-pA_ N}$ proves $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pU}\mathrm{d}V<+\infty $. Consequently, the constant germ $1$ is locally integrable against each weight $\mathrm{e}^{-pU}$, and every multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(pU)$ is the whole structure sheaf. $\square$ Corollary 6.6.2 . The bounded mass property holds if and only if $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)(X)<+\infty $ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. If the bounded mass property fails, there are potentials with infinite extended mass and trivial multiplier ideals $\mathcal I(pu)=\mathcal O_ X$, $p>0$, arbitrarily close to zero in $L^1$. Proof. The first assertion follows from proposition 6.5.3 , theorem 6.6.1 . For the second, take $\varepsilon U$, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, with $U$ as in theorem 6.6.1 . It is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic and has the required exponential integrability. On $D_ t=\{ U>-t\} $, its truncation at level $\varepsilon t$ is $\varepsilon \max (U,-t)$, and \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (\varepsilon \max (U,-t)\bigr ) =\varepsilon \omega _{\max (U,-t)}+(1-\varepsilon )\omega .  \] Positivity of mixed products bounds the restricted measure of $\varepsilon U$ below by $\varepsilon ^ n$ times that of $U$. Its limiting mass is therefore infinite. Finally, $\| \varepsilon U\| _{L^1}\to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. $\square$

title: 6.7 Integrable Hessians and infinite mass
text: 6.7 Integrable Hessians and infinite mass In the construction of theorem 6.6.1 , the Gauduchon identity of proposition 4.2.1 fixes the trace integral of every positive summand $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$. The series defining $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ therefore converges in the coefficient $L^1$ norm, although its determinant is not integrable. The trace measures converge in total variation, yet the Monge–Ampère mass is infinite. In chapter 7 , weights that decay on deep sublevel sets will control these masses. Fix a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ and set $M=\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$. For a real $(1,1)$-form $T$ with measurable coefficients, let $A_ T$ be its Hermitian matrix relative to $\gamma $, and let $|A_ T|=(A_ T^2)^{1/2}$ be its positive matrix absolute value. We use the norm \[  \| T\| _{L^1(\gamma )} =\frac1n\int _ X\operatorname {tr}|A_ T|\, \gamma ^ n.  \] For $T\geq 0$ this equals $\int _ XT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$. On compact $X$, any other smooth Hermitian form gives an equivalent norm and hence the same space of integrable coefficients. When the coefficients of $T$ are integrable, we write $\det _\gamma T=\det A_ T$; this function is defined almost everywhere, and $T^ n=(\det _\gamma T)\gamma ^ n$ when $T$ is smooth. Proposition 6.7.1 . Suppose $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. For the potential $U$ and its smooth decreasing approximants $U_ N$ constructed in the proof of theorem 6.6.1 , the current $T=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ has integrable coefficients and \[  \| \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N-T\| _{L^1(\gamma )} \leq 2^{1-N}M.  \] Its pointwise determinant satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U) \geq (\det _\gamma T)\gamma ^ n, \qquad \int _ X(\det _\gamma T)\gamma ^ n=+\infty .  \] Moreover, \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N)^ n\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Proof. Write $T_ j=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ for the smooth positive forms in that construction, and put \[  S_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}a_ jT_ j,\qquad \delta _ N=\sum _{j>N}a_ j=2^{-N}.  \] The smooth positive forms $S_ N$ increase pointwise, and the Gauduchon identity gives \[  \int _ XS_ N\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=(1-\delta _ N)M.  \] By monotone convergence of their traces, the series of matrices has a finite positive limit $S$ almost everywhere. The coefficients of $S$ are integrable, because in a $\gamma $-unitary frame the absolute value of every coefficient of a positive matrix is bounded by its trace. Positivity and the same trace identity give \[  \| S-S_ N\| _{L^1(\gamma )}=\delta _ N M.  \] In particular, $S_ N\to S$ in the sense of distributions. Since \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N=S_ N+\delta _ N\omega \longrightarrow \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U  \] in the sense of distributions, by $L^1$ convergence of the potentials, we obtain $T=S$. The triangle inequality now gives \[  \| \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N-T\| _{L^1(\gamma )} \leq \| S_ N-S\| _{L^1(\gamma )} +\delta _ N\| \omega \| _{L^1(\gamma )} =2\delta _ N M.  \] To compare $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)$ with the determinant, fix $N$ and set $V_ N=U-U_ N$. The remaining partial sums give $\delta _ N\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ N\geq 0$ and $V_ N\leq 0$. For $t>0$, the function $W_{N,t}=U_ N+\max (V_ N,-t)$ is bounded, and its current is the sum of two positive terms: \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W_{N,t} =S_ N+\bigl (\delta _ N\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (V_ N,-t)\bigr ).  \] On $D_ t=\{ U>-t\} $, the inequality $U_ N\leq 0$ gives $V_ N\geq U>-t$, and consequently $W_{N,t}=U=\max (U,-t)$ there. Locality and positivity of bounded products imply \[  \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U) \geq \mathbf1_{D_ t}S_ N^ n.  \] The smooth measure $S_ N^ n$ gives no mass to the pluripolar pole set of $U$, so letting $t\to \infty $ proves $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)\geq S_ N^ n$. The positive matrices $S_ N$ increase to $T$ almost everywhere, so their determinants increase to $\det _\gamma T$. Monotone convergence on every Borel set gives the asserted inequality between $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)$ and the determinant measure. Finally, for every $N\geq j$, positivity gives $S_ N\geq a_ jT_ j$. Hence both the measurable limit and the smooth approximating forms satisfy \[  \int _ X(\det _\gamma T)\gamma ^ n \geq a_ j^ n\int _ XT_ j^ n\geq 2^ j, \qquad \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N)^ n \geq a_ j^ n\int _ XT_ j^ n\geq 2^ j.  \] The first bound holds for every $j$, and the second for every $N\geq j$; together they prove the two assertions about infinite mass. $\square$ Corollary 6.7.2 . If the bounded mass property fails, there are nonpositive potentials $w_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $0<\varepsilon <1$, such that \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon \geq (1-\varepsilon )\omega , \qquad \mathcal I(pw_\varepsilon )=\mathcal O_ X\quad (p>0),  \] and such that both the integral of the pointwise determinant $\det _\gamma (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon )$ against $\gamma ^ n$ and the extended Monge–Ampère mass of $w_\varepsilon $ are infinite. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the potentials converge to zero in $L^1$, their currents converge to $\omega $ in the coefficient $L^1$ norm, and their full trace measures $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ converge to $\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ in total variation. Proof. Take $w_\varepsilon =\varepsilon U$, with $U$ and $T=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ as in proposition 6.7.1 . Its current is \[  T_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )\omega +\varepsilon T.  \] The lower bound and the two $L^1$ convergence assertions follow immediately. The full trace measures have integrable densities, and their distance from $\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ in total variation is at most \[  \varepsilon \| T-\omega \| _{L^1(\gamma )}.  \] Every multiplier ideal is trivial by the exponential integrability of $U$ proved in theorem 6.6.1 . Since $T_\varepsilon \geq \varepsilon T$ almost everywhere, the determinant integral of $T_\varepsilon $ is at least $\varepsilon ^ n$ times that of $T$, hence infinite. The extended mass of $w_\varepsilon $ is infinite by the proof of corollary 6.6.2 . $\square$ For smooth potentials, the total masses can be prescribed in advance while both the currents and the exponential weights converge. Corollary 6.7.3 . Suppose $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. Let $(\varepsilon _ j)_{j\geq 1}$ and $(b_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ be real sequences with $0<\varepsilon _ j<1$, $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$, and $b_ j>\int _ X\omega ^ n$. There are smooth potentials $w_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\sup _ Xw_ j=0$ such that \[  \begin{gathered} \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j\geq (1-\varepsilon _ j)\omega , \qquad \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ n=b_ j, \\ \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j\| _{L^1(\gamma )} \leq 2M\varepsilon _ j. \end{gathered}  \] Moreover, $w_ j\to 0$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-pw_ j}\to 1$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ for every fixed $p>0$. The full Gauduchon trace measures converge to $\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ in total variation. Proof. By proposition 6.5.2 , we can choose a smooth $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$ and \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n>\varepsilon _ j^{-n}b_ j.  \] Put $T_ j=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$. The polynomial \[  F_ j(s)=\int _ X\bigl ((1-s)\omega +sT_ j\bigr )^ n, \qquad 0\leq s\leq \varepsilon _ j,  \] satisfies $F_ j(0)<b_ j$, and also $F_ j(\varepsilon _ j)\geq \varepsilon _ j^ n\int _ XT_ j^ n>b_ j$ by positivity of the mixed terms. The intermediate value theorem gives $s_ j\in (0,\varepsilon _ j)$ with $F_ j(s_ j)=b_ j$. Set $w_ j=s_ ju_ j$. Then $\sup _ Xw_ j=0$, $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j=(1-s_ j)\omega +s_ jT_ j\geq (1-\varepsilon _ j)\omega $, and $w_ j$ has the prescribed mass $b_ j$. The Gauduchon identity gives $\| T_ j\| _{L^1(\gamma )}=\| \omega \| _{L^1(\gamma )}=M$. Hence \[  \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j\| _{L^1(\gamma )} =s_ j\| T_ j-\omega \| _{L^1(\gamma )} \leq 2M\varepsilon _ j.  \] Since the absolute value of the trace of a Hermitian matrix is bounded by the trace of its absolute value, the same bound holds for the total variation of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$. With $K_\omega $ as in ( 1.1 ), we also have $\| w_ j\| _{L^1(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq K_\omega \varepsilon _ j$. Finally, let $\alpha ,C$ be the constants of lemma 1.5.1 for $(X,\omega ,\mathrm{d}V)$, and fix $p>0$. For all sufficiently large $j$, one has $ps_ j\leq \alpha $. Convexity of the exponential function, applied with weight $ps_ j/\alpha $, gives \[  0\leq \mathrm{e}^{-pw_ j}-1 \leq \frac{ps_ j}{\alpha }\bigl (\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha u_ j}-1\bigr ).  \] Integrating, we bound the $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ norm of $\mathrm{e}^{-pw_ j}-1$ by $pC\varepsilon _ j/\alpha $, which proves the last convergence. $\square$
