title: 7 Weighted Monge–Ampère measures
text: 7 Weighted Monge–Ampère measures Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n$, and let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form. Capacity refers to the capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ of section 1.8 . For nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ we write \[  \mu _ u=\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)  \] for the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 6.1.2 , and we put \[  r_ n=\max (n-2,0).  \] By chapter 6 , the measure $\mu _ u$ can have infinite mass when the bounded mass property fails. Its mass above depth $t$, on the superlevel set $\{ u\geq -t\} $, is nevertheless bounded by a polynomial of degree $r_ n$ in $t$, because the masses of bounded potentials grow at most polynomially in their range. A weight that decreases sufficiently fast in the depth $-u$ compensates for this growth. If $w:[0,+\infty )\to [0,+\infty )$ is a nonincreasing function with $w(t)\to 0$ as $t\to +\infty $, we call \[  w(-u)\, \mu _ u  \] the damped Monge–Ampère measure of $u$ with weight $w$; the weight is set to zero on the pole set $\{ u=-\infty \} $, which $\mu _ u$ does not charge. The main examples are the exponential weights $\mathrm{e}^{-pt}$ and the polynomial weights $(1+t)^{-q}$. For suitable weights the damped measures are finite, uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to capacity, and continuous under convergence in capacity, a property that the extended measures themselves lack. Removing the weight requires uniform control of the mass on deep sublevel sets; we characterize this control and show by examples that such mass can persist although the potentials converge in capacity.

title: 7.1 Range and restricted mass
text: 7.1 Range and restricted mass We first bound the Monge–Ampère mass of a bounded potential polynomially in its range. The first mixed mass $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ is bounded independently of $v$ by the Gauduchon trace. Local Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimates turn this into a bound of degree $j-1$ in the range for the $j$th mixed mass, and Stokes' theorem expresses the top mass in terms of the lower ones. Proposition 7.1.1 . There is a constant $C_\omega $ such that, for every $A\geq 0$, \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\leq C_\omega (1+A)^{r_ n} \quad \text{if }v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega ),\  0\leq v\leq A.  \] Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls whose concentric smaller balls, with compact closure in the larger ones, cover $X$. On each larger ball choose a fixed quadratic function $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \omega $, shifted so that $p=v+q$ is plurisubharmonic with $0\leq p\leq A+C$. Let $\kappa $ be the Euclidean form. In the identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q-\omega ),  \] the integral of the first term against $\kappa ^{n-1}$ is bounded by a fixed multiple of the global trace mass, which is bounded by corollary 4.2.2 , and the second term is smooth and fixed. Thus $\int \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p\wedge \kappa ^{n-1}$ is bounded uniformly in $v$ and $A$; in dimension one, Stokes' theorem replaces the trace bound. By ( 1.4 ), on each smaller ball, \[  \int (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)^ j\wedge \kappa ^{n-j}\leq C_ j(1+A)^{j-1} \quad (1\leq j\leq n).  \] Expand $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ j=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p+\omega -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ j$ and sum over the finite cover. Since the smooth factors have bounded coefficients, the positive mixed masses satisfy \[  0\leq M_ j(v):=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ j\wedge \omega ^{n-j} \leq C_ j(1+A)^{\max (j-1,0)} \quad (0\leq j\leq n).  \] For smooth $v$, the exact form $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ integrates to zero, as in the proof of theorem 2.2.1 ; the regularization of theorem 1.11.1 and the continuity of bounded products give the same identity for bounded $v$. Thus \[  0=\int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n =\sum _{j=0}^ n(-1)^{n-j}\binom nj M_ j(v).  \] Since the mixed masses are nonnegative, it follows that \[  M_ n(v)\leq \sum _{j=0}^{n-1}\binom nj M_ j(v) \leq C_\omega (1+A)^{r_ n}.  \] The largest power is $n-2$ when $n\geq 2$; for $n=1$, only the constant term remains. $\square$ For $n\leq 2$ the bound is uniform, so every compact complex curve or surface has the bounded mass property. In higher dimensions the bound grows with the range, and truncation turns it into a bound for the mass of an unbounded potential above a finite depth. Lemma 7.1.2 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be nonpositive. For $t\geq 0$ and every Borel set $E\subset X$, 7.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:restricted-mass-growth} \mu _ u(\{ u\geq -t\} )\leq C_\omega (1+t)^{r_ n}, \qquad \mu _ u(E\cap \{ u\geq -t\} )\leq (1+t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E). \end{equation} Proof. Put $v_ t=\max (u,-t-1)+t+1$. It is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic and takes values in $[0,t+1]$, and by plurifine locality its Monge–Ampère measure equals $\mu _ u$ on $\{ u\geq -t\} \subset \{ u>-t-1\} $. The first estimate therefore follows from proposition 7.1.1 , after enlarging the constant. For the second, $v_ t/(1+t)$ is a test function for the capacity, and positivity gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ t)^ n \leq (1+t)^ n\bigl (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ t/(1+t))\bigr )^ n.  \] Restricting this inequality to $E\cap \{ u\geq -t\} $ proves the capacity bound. $\square$

title: Lemma 7.1.2
text: Lemma 7.1.2 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be nonpositive. For $t\geq 0$ and every Borel set $E\subset X$, 7.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:restricted-mass-growth} \mu _ u(\{ u\geq -t\} )\leq C_\omega (1+t)^{r_ n}, \qquad \mu _ u(E\cap \{ u\geq -t\} )\leq (1+t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E). \end{equation} Proof. Put $v_ t=\max (u,-t-1)+t+1$. It is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic and takes values in $[0,t+1]$, and by plurifine locality its Monge–Ampère measure equals $\mu _ u$ on $\{ u\geq -t\} \subset \{ u>-t-1\} $. The first estimate therefore follows from proposition 7.1.1 , after enlarging the constant. For the second, $v_ t/(1+t)$ is a test function for the capacity, and positivity gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ t)^ n \leq (1+t)^ n\bigl (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ t/(1+t))\bigr )^ n.  \] Restricting this inequality to $E\cap \{ u\geq -t\} $ proves the capacity bound. $\square$

title: 7.2 Exponential damping
text:
7.2 Exponential damping The exponential weight can be handled directly. A convex increasing function with bounded range transforms $u$ into a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, and the chain rule shows that the transformed current dominates an exponential multiple of $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. The Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded transform therefore controls the damped measure. For $a>0$ put $F_ a(t)=a^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{at}$ for $t\leq 0$, with $F_ a(-\infty )=0$. Then $0\leq F_ a\leq a^{-1}$, while $0<F_ a'\leq 1$ and $F_ a''\geq 0$ at finite arguments. Proposition 7.2.1 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $u\leq 0$, then $F_ a(u)$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, and \[  \mathrm{e}^{na u}\mu _ u\leq \mathrm{MA}_\omega (F_ a(u)).  \] Proof. First suppose that $u$ is bounded. The chain rule ( 1.10 ) gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F_ a(u) =\mathrm{e}^{au}(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+(1-\mathrm{e}^{au})\omega +a\mathrm{e}^{au}\, \mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u.  \] All three summands are positive, and positivity of their bounded mixed products yields the claimed inequality. For general $u$, use the truncations $u_ t=\max (u,-t)$. The bounded functions $F_ a(u_ t)$ decrease and take values between zero and $a^{-1}$, so their limit $F_ a(u)$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. On the plurifinely open set $D_ t=\{ u>-t\} $, it agrees with $F_ a(u_ t)$. Locality and the bounded case therefore give \[  \mathrm{e}^{na u}\mathbf1_{D_ t}\mu _ u \leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_\omega (F_ a(u)).  \] Let $t	o +\infty $. The pole set is not charged by $\mu _ u$, and it has zero mass for the bounded product on the right. $\square$ Theorem 7.2.2 . For $p>0$, the damped measures $
u _{p,u}=\mathrm{e}^{pu}\mu _ u$ satisfy \[  
u _{p,u}(X)\leq C_\omega (1+p^{-1})^{r_ n}, \qquad 
u _{p,u}(E)\leq \max (1,n/p)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)  \] for every Borel set $E\subset X$, uniformly over all nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Proof. Take $a=p/n$ in proposition 7.2.1 . Since $F_{p/n}(u)$ takes values in $[0,n/p]$, proposition 7.1.1 with $A=n/p$ gives the total mass bound, after enlarging $C_\omega $. For the capacity bound put $B=\max (1,n/p)$ and $v=F_{p/n}(u)$. Then $v/B$ is a test function for the capacity, and \[  B igl (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v/B) igr ) =(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(B-1)\omega \geq \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v.  \] Consequently $
u _{p,u}\leq \mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)\leq B^ n\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v/B)$, which gives the second bound. The measures $
u _{p,u}$ do not charge pluripolar sets, because $\mu _ u$ does not. $\square$ Since $\mu _ u$ does not charge the pole set, multiplication by $\mathrm{e}^{-pu}$ recovers $\mu _ u$ from $
u _{p,u}$, including when its mass is infinite. An additive shift $u\mapsto u+c$ multiplies the damped measure by $\mathrm{e}^{pc}$.

title: 7.3 Decreasing weights and capacity continuity
text:
7.3 Decreasing weights and capacity continuity For a general decreasing weight $w$, writing $w(s)=\int _ s^\infty (-w'(t))\, \mathrm{d}t$ and integrating the finite-depth estimate ( 7.1 ) in $t$ bounds both the total mass and the mass on deep sublevel sets. Above any fixed depth, the damped measure is a weighted product of bounded potentials, which is continuous under convergence in capacity; the tail bound then removes the restriction to a fixed depth. Theorem 7.3.1 . Let $w:[0,+\infty )	o (0,+\infty )$ be continuously differentiable and nonincreasing, with $w(t)	o 0$ as $t	o +\infty $. For $T\geq 0$ define \[  B_ w(T)=\int _ T^\infty (1+t)^{r_ n}(-w'(t))\, \mathrm{d}t.  \] Assume $B_ w(0)<+\infty $. For nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, the damped measures $
u _{w,u}=w(-u)\mu _ u$ satisfy \[  
u _{w,u}(X)\leq C_\omega B_ w(0),\qquad 
u _{w,u}(\{ u<-T\} )\leq C_\omega B_ w(T).  \] For every Borel set $E$ and $T\geq 0$, \[  
u _{w,u}(E)\leq w(0)(1+T)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)+C_\omega B_ w(T).  \] In particular, these measures are uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to capacity. If nonpositive $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfy $u_ j	o u$ in capacity, then $
u _{w,u_ j}ightharpoonup 
u _{w,u}$. Proof. Write $s=-u$. Since $w(s)=\int _ s^\infty (-w'(t))\, \mathrm{d}t$ for finite $s$, and since $\mu _ u$ does not charge the pole set $\{ s=+\infty \} $, Tonelli's theorem and lemma 7.1.2 give \[  \int _ X w(s)\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u =\int _0^\infty (-w'(t))\mu _ u(\{ s\leq t\} )\, \mathrm{d}t \leq C_\omega B_ w(0).  \] Restricting the integral to $\{ s>T\} $ gives the same bound with $B_ w(T)$ in place of $B_ w(0)$, since the inner set is then $\{ T<s\leq t\} $, which is empty unless $t>T$. For the capacity bound, the second estimate in ( 7.1 ) gives \[  \int _{E\cap \{ s\leq T\} }w(s)\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u \leq w(0)(1+T)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E).  \] Adding the tail estimate for $\{ s>T\} $ proves the asserted bound. Since $B_ w(T)	o 0$, choosing first $T$ large and then the capacity small gives uniform absolute continuity. To prove continuity, fix a continuous nonincreasing $\eta :[0,+\infty )	o [0,1]$, equal to one on $[0,1]$ and zero on $[2,+\infty )$, and put $\eta _ T(s)=\eta (s/T)$. For fixed $T>0$, set $v_{j,T}=\max (u_ j,-2T)$ and $g_ T(t)=\eta _ T(-t)w(-t)$ on $[-2T,0]$. Since $g_ T(-2T)=0$, locality gives 7.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:weighted-truncation-identity} \eta _ T(-u_ j)w(-u_ j)\mu _{u_ j} =g_ T(v_{j,T})\, \mathrm{MA}_\omega (v_{j,T}). \end{equation} Truncation preserves convergence in capacity. The functions $g_ T(v_{j,T})$ are uniformly bounded and quasi-continuous, and they converge in capacity to the corresponding function for $u$. The weighted continuity of bounded products in section 1.6 , section 1.8 therefore gives weak convergence of the measures in ( 7.2 ) for each fixed $T$. The measure $(1-\eta _ T(-u_ j))
u _{w,u_ j}$ is carried by $\{ u_ j<-T\} $, so by the tail bound its integral against a continuous test function $f$ is at most $C_\omega B_ w(T)\| f\| _\infty $, uniformly in $j$; the same holds for $u$. Letting $T	o \infty $ completes the proof. $\square$ For $w(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-pt}$, $p>0$, the integral $B_ w(0)$ is finite because the exponential dominates the polynomial factor. Thus the exponentially damped measures of theorem 7.2.2 are continuous under convergence in capacity. By that theorem, their tails also satisfy \[  
u _{p,u}(\{ u<-T\} ) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-pT/2}
u _{p/2,u}(X) \leq C_ p\mathrm{e}^{-pT/2}.  \] For polynomial weights, the general estimate takes the following explicit form. Theorem 7.3.2 . For every $q>r_ n$, the damped measures \[  \sigma _{q,u}:=(1-u)^{-q}\mu _ u  \] have uniformly bounded mass for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $u\leq 0$. More precisely, \[  \sigma _{q,u}(\{ u<-T\} ) \leq C rac{q}{q-r_ n}(1+T)^{r_ n-q}\quad (T\geq 0),  \] where $C$ depends only on $\omega $. There is also a constant $C_ q$ such that, for every Borel set $E\subset X$, \[  \sigma _{q,u}(E)\leq C_ q\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)^{(q-r_ n)/(q+n-r_ n)}.  \] Proof. For $w(t)=(1+t)^{-q}$, direct integration gives \[  B_ w(T)=q\int _ T^\infty (1+t)^{r_ n-q-1}\, \mathrm{d}t = rac{q}{q-r_ n}(1+T)^{r_ n-q}.  \] Thus proposition 7.3.1 gives the mass and tail estimates. For the capacity bound put $\delta =\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)$. If $0<\delta \leq 1$, choose $T=\delta ^{-1/(q+n-r_ n)}\geq 1$ in that theorem. Both $T^ n\delta $ and $T^{r_ n-q}$ equal $\delta ^{(q-r_ n)/(q+n-r_ n)}$, so its two terms have the required bound. If $\delta =0$, let $T	o \infty $; if $\delta >1$, use the total mass bound. $\square$ For $n\geq 2$, the capacity exponent is $1-n/(q+2)$. The threshold $q>n-2$ comes from the mixed-mass estimate in proposition 7.1.1 . Logarithmic factors give weights at the threshold. For $n\geq 3$ and $a>1$, put $r=n-2>0$ and \[  w(t)=(1+t)^{-r}[\log (\mathrm{e}+t)]^{-a}.  \] Differentiation gives \[  (1+t)^ r(-w'(t)) = rac{r}{(1+t)[\log (\mathrm{e}+t)]^ a} + rac{a}{(\mathrm{e}+t)[\log (\mathrm{e}+t)]^{a+1}}.  \] The ratios $(\mathrm{e}+t)/(1+t)$ are bounded. The substitution $y=\log (\mathrm{e}+t)$ therefore bounds the integrals of the two terms over $[T,+\infty )$ by fixed multiples of $[\log (\mathrm{e}+T)]^{1-a}$ and $[\log (\mathrm{e}+T)]^{-a}$, respectively. Since $a>1$ and $\log (\mathrm{e}+T)\geq 1$, we obtain $B_ w(T)\leq C_{n,a}[\log (\mathrm{e}+T)]^{1-a}$. Hence, by proposition 7.3.1 , the damped measures $(1-u)^{-(n-2)}[\log (\mathrm{e}-u)]^{-a}\mu _ u$ have uniformly bounded mass, their mass on $\{ u<-T\} $ is at most a constant times $[\log (\mathrm{e}+T)]^{1-a}$, and they are continuous under convergence in capacity. In dimensions one and two, $r_ n=0$ and $B_ w(T)=w(T)$, so every weight satisfying the monotonicity, differentiability and vanishing conditions of proposition 7.3.1 can be used. Damping can restore convergence when every undamped measure has infinite mass. When the bounded mass property fails, take the potential $U$ constructed in the proof of theorem 6.6.1 , whose current has integrable coefficients by proposition 6.7.1 , and normalize it by $\sup _ XU=0$. For $0<\varepsilon <1$, the potentials $\varepsilon U$ converge to zero in capacity as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$: by ( 1.26 ), the capacity of $\{ \varepsilon U<-\delta \} $ is at most $C\varepsilon /\delta $ for each fixed $\delta >0$ and small $\varepsilon $. Consequently, for $p>0$ and $q>r_ n$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{p\varepsilon U}\mu _{\varepsilon U}ightharpoonup \omega ^ n, \qquad (1-\varepsilon U)^{-q}\mu _{\varepsilon U}ightharpoonup \omega ^ n,  \] although $\mu _{\varepsilon U}(X)=+\infty $ for every $0<\varepsilon <1$. The full currents also converge to $\omega $ in the coefficient $L^1$ norm, and their Gauduchon traces converge in total variation.

text: Theorem 7.3.2 . For every $q>r_ n$, the damped measures \[  \sigma _{q,u}:=(1-u)^{-q}\mu _ u  \] have uniformly bounded mass for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $u\leq 0$. title: 7.4 Uniform tails and undamped convergence
text: 7.4 Uniform tails and undamped convergence On deep sublevel sets the damping weight tends to zero, so convergence of the weighted measures can leave their undamped mass uncontrolled. Uniformly vanishing deep tails supply the additional control: the following condition gives a finite limit measure and weak convergence of the undamped measures $\mu _{u_ j}$. It can equivalently be expressed by an increasing integrability weight. Theorem 7.4.1 . Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be nonpositive and suppose $u_ j\to u$ in capacity. Assume \[  \lim _{T\to \infty }\sup _ j\mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<-T\} )=0.  \] Then $\mu _ u$ is finite and $\mu _{u_ j}\rightharpoonup \mu _ u$. Proof. Choose $T_0$ such that every tail $\mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<-T\} )$ with $T\geq T_0$ is at most one. By lemma 7.1.2 , $\mu _{u_ j}(X)\leq C(1+T_0)^{r_ n}+1$, so the tail condition already gives a uniform bound for the total masses. With the cutoffs $\eta _ T$ of ( 7.2 ), the fixed-level argument in the proof of theorem 7.3.1 , applied with $w\equiv 1$, gives \[  \eta _ T(-u_ j)\mu _{u_ j}\rightharpoonup \eta _ T(-u)\mu _ u \quad \text{for every fixed }T>0.  \] The masses of the measures on the left are bounded by the uniform bound for the total masses. Since $\eta _ T(-u)$ increases to one off the pole set as $T\to \infty $, monotone convergence proves $\mu _ u(X)<+\infty $. For a continuous test function $f:X\to \mathbb R$, the error made by inserting $\eta _ T(-u_ j)$ is at most $\| f\| _\infty \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<-T\} )$, which is small for large $T$, uniformly in $j$. For the limit potential, the corresponding error tends to zero because $\mu _ u$ is finite and does not charge the pole set. Let first $j\to \infty $ with $T$ fixed, and then $T\to \infty $. $\square$ Let $\chi :[0,+\infty )\to [1,+\infty )$ be continuous, nondecreasing and unbounded. For a nonpositive potential $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ define \[  J_{\chi ,\omega }(u)=\int _ X\chi (-u)\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u,  \] with the value $+\infty $ allowed. Since $\chi (T)\to +\infty $, a uniform bound for this functional forces the sublevel tails to vanish uniformly. Corollary 7.4.2 . Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be nonpositive. If $u_ j\to u$ in capacity and $\sup _ jJ_{\chi ,\omega }(u_ j)\leq C$, then \[  J_{\chi ,\omega }(u)\leq C,\qquad \mu _{u_ j}\rightharpoonup \mu _ u.  \] Proof. Since $\chi \geq 1$, the total masses are at most $C$, and \[  \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<-T\} )\leq C/\chi (T).  \] Thus theorem 7.4.1 applies. For the bound on $J_{\chi ,\omega }(u)$, use ( 7.2 ) with the compactly supported continuous function $s\mapsto \chi (s)\eta _ T(s)$ in place of $w\eta _ T$. The corresponding weighted integrals converge for each fixed $T$, and they are at most $C$. Let $T\to \infty $ and use monotone convergence. $\square$ Proposition 7.4.3 . For a family of nonpositive potentials in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, the uniform tail condition of theorem 7.4.1 is equivalent to a uniform bound on $J_{\chi ,\omega }$ for some continuous nondecreasing unbounded function $\chi \geq 1$. Proof. One implication was proved in corollary 7.4.2 . Conversely, write the family as $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$. As in the proof of theorem 7.4.1 , the tail condition and lemma 7.1.2 give a uniform bound for the total masses. Choose numbers $T_ k\to +\infty $, with $T_{k+1}>T_ k+1$, such that $\mu _{u_ i}(\{ -u_ i>T_ k\} )\leq 2^{-k}$ for every $i\in I$. Let $\rho _ k$ be a continuous nondecreasing function, equal to zero on $[0,T_ k]$ and to one on $[T_ k+1,+\infty )$, and define \[  \chi (s)=1+\sum _{k\geq 1}\rho _ k(s).  \] The sum is locally finite, so $\chi $ is continuous, nondecreasing and unbounded. Tonelli's theorem gives \[  J_{\chi ,\omega }(u_ i) \leq \mu _{u_ i}(X)+\sum _{k\geq 1}\mu _{u_ i}(\{ -u_ i>T_ k\} ) \leq \sup _{i\in I}\mu _{u_ i}(X)+1,  \] so this weight gives a uniform integrability bound for the whole family. $\square$

title: Proposition 7.4.3
text: Proposition 7.4.3 . For a family of nonpositive potentials in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, the uniform tail condition of theorem 7.4.1 is equivalent to a uniform bound on $J_{\chi ,\omega }$ for some continuous nondecreasing unbounded function $\chi \geq 1$. Proof. One implication was proved in corollary 7.4.2 . Conversely, write the family as $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$. As in the proof of theorem 7.4.1 , the tail condition and lemma 7.1.2 give a uniform bound for the total masses. Choose numbers $T_ k\to +\infty $, with $T_{k+1}>T_ k+1$, such that $\mu _{u_ i}(\{ -u_ i>T_ k\} )\leq 2^{-k}$ for every $i\in I$. Let $\rho _ k$ be a continuous nondecreasing function, equal to zero on $[0,T_ k]$ and to one on $[T_ k+1,+\infty )$, and define \[  \chi (s)=1+\sum _{k\geq 1}\rho _ k(s).  \] The sum is locally finite, so $\chi $ is continuous, nondecreasing and unbounded. Tonelli's theorem gives \[  J_{\chi ,\omega }(u_ i) \leq \mu _{u_ i}(X)+\sum _{k\geq 1}\mu _{u_ i}(\{ -u_ i>T_ k\} ) \leq \sup _{i\in I}\mu _{u_ i}(X)+1,  \] so this weight gives a uniform integrability bound for the whole family. $\square$

title: 7.5 Mass concentration
text:
7.5 Mass concentration The tail condition excludes mass carried by sublevel sets that disappear in the capacity limit. On a curve this mass can concentrate at a pole of the limit. When the bounded mass property fails, it can also persist along smooth potentials converging to zero. Example 7.5.1 . On $X=\mathbb P^1$, let $z$ be the standard affine coordinate and let $\delta _0$ denote the unit Dirac measure at its origin. Take the Fubini–Study form \[  \omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2),\qquad \int _ X\omega =1,  \] and the global nonpositive potential \[  u(z)=\log  rac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2},\qquad u_ j=\max (u,-j).  \] At infinity, in the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$, the function $u$ equals $-\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$, so it is smooth there. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\delta _0, \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=0.  \] The second identity holds because the extended measure discards the pole set and the current vanishes on its complement. Each $u_ j$ is bounded and $\omega $-plurisubharmonic. Its measure $\mu _ j=\mu _{u_ j}=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ has mass one by Stokes' theorem, and $\mu _ j=0$ on the open set $\{ u>-j\} $ by locality. Hence \[  \operatorname {supp}\mu _ j\subset \{ u\leq -j\}  =\left\{ |z|^2\leq  rac{\mathrm{e}^{-j}}{1-\mathrm{e}^{-j}}ight\} .  \] These disks shrink to the origin, so $\mu _ jightharpoonup \delta _0$.  On their supports, $u_ j=-j$. Consequently, for $j>T$, \[  \mu _ j(\{ u_ j<-T\} )=1, \qquad \mathrm{e}^{pu_ j}\mu _ j=\mathrm{e}^{-pj}\mu _ jightharpoonup 0 \quad (p>0).  \] Nevertheless, $u_ j	o u$ in capacity. Indeed, outside any neighborhood of the origin the functions eventually agree with $u$, and the origin has arbitrarily small neighborhoods of arbitrarily small capacity. Thus bounded mass and capacity convergence do not prevent the undamped measures from acquiring mass at a pole of the limit. The damped limit is the extended measure of $u$, as predicted by theorem 7.3.1 . We return to a general compact Hermitian manifold $(X,\omega )$. Corollary 7.5.2 . Assume $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $ and put $V_\omega =\int _ X\omega ^ n$. Fix a real number $b>V_\omega $ and a sequence $0<\varepsilon _ j<1$ tending to zero. The smooth potentials $w_ j$ of corollary 6.7.3 , chosen with mass $b$, converge to zero in capacity. For every $T>0$, \[  \left\| \mathbf1_{\{ w_ j\geq -T\} }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ n-\omega ^ n ight\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow 0, \qquad \int _{\{ w_ j<-T\} }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ n\longrightarrow b-V_\omega .  \] After passage to a subsequence, there is a positive measure $\sigma $ of mass $b-V_\omega $ such that \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ nightharpoonup \omega ^ n+\sigma , \qquad \mathbf1_{\{ w_ j<-T\} }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ nightharpoonup \sigma \quad 	ext{for every }T>0.  \] Proof. The construction in corollary 6.7.3 gives $w_ j=s_ j u_ j$, where $u_ j$ is smooth and $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$ and $0<s_ j<\varepsilon _ j$. The sublevel estimate ( 1.26 ) gives, for every fixed $\delta >0$ and all sufficiently large $j$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ |w_ j|>\delta \} ) =\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ u_ j<-\delta /s_ j\} ) \leq Cs_ j/\delta \longrightarrow 0.  \] Put $\mu _ j=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ n$. Fix $T>0$ and write $E_{j,T}=\{ w_ j\geq -T\} $. The lower bound in corollary 6.7.3 gives \[  \mathbf1_{E_{j,T}}\mu _ j\geq \lambda _{j,T}:=(1-\varepsilon _ j)^ n\mathbf1_{E_{j,T}}\omega ^ n.  \] Since $w_ j	o 0$ in $L^1$, the smooth volume of $X\setminus E_{j,T}$ tends to zero, and hence $\lambda _{j,T}	o \omega ^ n$ in total variation. For every $p>0$, theorem 7.3.1 gives $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{pw_ j}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ j	o V_\omega $, and therefore \[  \limsup _ j\mu _ j(E_{j,T}) \leq \mathrm{e}^{pT}\lim _ j\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{pw_ j}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ j =\mathrm{e}^{pT}V_\omega .  \] Letting $p\downarrow 0$ and combining with the lower bound, we obtain $\mu _ j(E_{j,T})	o V_\omega $. Positivity now yields \[   egin{split}  \| \mathbf1_{E_{j,T}}\mu _ j-\omega ^ n\| _{\mathrm{TV}} & \leq \mu _ j(E_{j,T})-\lambda _{j,T}(X) +\| \lambda _{j,T}-\omega ^ n\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\ & \longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] Subtracting this shallow mass from $\mu _ j(X)=b$ proves the assertion about the mass on $\{ w_ j<-T\} $. The positive measures $\mu _ j$ have fixed mass on the compact manifold $X$, so a subsequence converges weakly to a measure $
u $ of mass $b$. The inequality $\mu _ j\geq (1-\varepsilon _ j)^ n\omega ^ n$ gives $
u \geq \omega ^ n$. Set $\sigma =
u -\omega ^ n$. For each $T>0$, subtracting the total-variation limit of the shallow restrictions from $\mu _ jightharpoonup 
u $ gives the last assertion along the same subsequence, for every $T$. $\square$ Thus the defect $\sigma $ in corollary 7.5.2 carries the whole excess mass $b-V_\omega $, although the currents $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j$ converge to $\omega $ in the coefficient $L^1$ norm and their Gauduchon traces converge in total variation. The location of $\sigma $ is constrained by the limits of the intermediate powers of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j$, as we now show.

title: 7.5.1 Intermediate currents of a shrinking sequence
search_title: Intermediate currents of a shrinking sequence
text: 7.5.1 Intermediate currents of a shrinking sequence We formulate the result for a connected compact complex manifold $Y$ of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Hermitian form $h$, since it will be applied with different metrics in chapter 8 . Consider smooth functions \[  v_ j=s_ ju_ j,\qquad u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,h),\qquad \sup _ Yu_ j=0,\qquad 0<s_ j\longrightarrow 0.  \] Suppose that their Monge–Ampère masses $\int _ Y(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n$ equal a fixed number $b$ and that \[  (h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n\rightharpoonup h^ n+\sigma .  \] The lower bound $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq (1-s_ j)h$ shows that $\sigma $ is positive. Although $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\to 0$ in the trace norm, its intermediate powers can have nonzero limits, and these limits determine $\sigma $. Proposition 7.5.3 . After passage to a common subsequence, the positive forms \[  H_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j+s_ jh=s_ j(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)  \] satisfy $H_ j^ k\rightharpoonup K_ k$ for $1\leq k\leq n$. The currents $K_ k$ are positive and closed, and $K_1=K_ n=0$. For every smooth real $(n-k,n-k)$-form $\eta $ with $\mathrm{d}\eta =0$ or $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0$, \[  \int _ Y K_ k\wedge \eta =0.  \] Moreover, 7.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:shrinking-defect-current-decomposition} \sigma =\sum _{k=2}^{n-1}\binom nk h^{n-k}\wedge K_ k. \end{equation} If $\vartheta $ is a smooth closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form on $Y$, then $\sigma $ is supported on $\{ \vartheta ^ n=0\} $. In dimension three the same conclusion holds for every smooth semipositive $(1,1)$-form $\vartheta $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\vartheta =0$. Proof. For $s_ j<1/2$, positivity in the expansion \[  (h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n =\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk(1-s_ j)^{n-k}h^{n-k}\wedge H_ j^ k  \] gives a uniform bound for each $\int _ Yh^{n-k}\wedge H_ j^ k$. In local unitary coordinates, the coefficient matrix of the smooth positive form $H_ j^ k$ on exterior powers is positive semidefinite, so its entries are bounded in absolute value by its trace, up to a dimensional constant. The trace bounds therefore bound every coefficient in total variation, and weak compactness of measures gives a common subsequence and positive limits $K_ k$. For $n\geq 2$, choose a Gauduchon form $\gamma $. By proposition 4.2.1 , \[  \int _ Y H_ j\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =s_ j\int _ Yh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Since $\gamma $ and $h$ are equivalent smooth metrics, it follows that $H_ j\to 0$ in coefficient total variation. For $n=1$ the same conclusion follows from $\int _ YH_ j=s_ j\int _ Yh$. Thus $K_1=0$ in all dimensions. Since $\mathrm{d}H_ j=s_ j\mathrm{d}h$, \[  \mathrm{d}(H_ j^ k)=ks_ j\mathrm{d}h\wedge H_ j^{k-1}\longrightarrow 0  \] as currents, because the preceding trace bounds control multiplication by the fixed smooth form $\mathrm{d}h$. Hence every $K_ k$ is closed. The smooth form $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ k$ is both $\mathrm{d}$-exact and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact: \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ k =\mathrm{d}\bigl (\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v_ j\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^{k-1}\bigr ) =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (v_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^{k-1}\bigr ).  \] Its integral against either kind of test form $\eta $ in the statement is therefore zero by Stokes' formula. Expanding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j=H_ j-s_ jh$ gives \[  \int _ Y\eta \wedge H_ j^ k =-\sum _{r=0}^{k-1}\binom kr(-s_ j)^{k-r} \int _ Y\eta \wedge h^{k-r}\wedge H_ j^ r =O(s_ j).  \] Each integral on the right is bounded by the trace bound for $H_ j^ r$. Taking $k=n$ and $\eta =1$ shows that the positive measures $H_ j^ n$ tend to zero in total variation, which proves $K_ n=0$; the other vanishing integrals follow by weak convergence. Finally, letting $j\to \infty $ in the positive expansion above, the terms with $k=0$ tend to $h^ n$ and those with $k=1$ and $k=n$ vanish in the limit, which proves ( 7.5 ). For closed semipositive $\vartheta $, apply the vanishing integrals to $\eta =\vartheta ^{n-k}$. The measure $K_ k\wedge \vartheta ^{n-k}$ is positive and has zero mass. On every relatively compact open set where $\vartheta >0$, it dominates a positive multiple of the trace measure of $K_ k$, so $K_ k$ vanishes there. The decomposition gives the asserted support. In dimension three only $K_2$ occurs, and the same argument applies to the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed test form $\vartheta $ itself. $\square$ In dimensions at most two the decomposition forces $\sigma =0$. A threefold carrying a pluriclosed Hermitian metric, that is, a Hermitian form $\vartheta $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\vartheta =0$, has no nonzero defect $\sigma $ of this form either. In higher dimensions, the vanishing integrals impose necessary conditions on each intermediate current; they do not by themselves produce a smooth sequence with prescribed intermediate limits.

title: 7.6 Damping for a smooth background
text: 7.6 Damping for a smooth background For a general smooth background $\theta $, truncation at a constant level may fail to preserve $\theta $-plurisubharmonicity. A larger Hermitian form makes the truncations plurisubharmonic and dominates the extended measure, and the local expansion of the $\theta $-product gives continuity at each fixed truncation level. Theorem 7.6.1 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, and for nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ put $\mu _{\theta ,u}=\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$. The mass bounds, capacity estimates and capacity-continuity statements for damped measures in this chapter, including proposition 7.3.1 , hold for the measures $\mu _{\theta ,u}$ in place of $\mu _ u$, with constants depending on $\theta $ and $\omega $. In particular, for $p>0$ and $q>r_ n$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{pu}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{\theta ,u} \leq C(1+p^{-1})^{r_ n},\qquad \int _ X(1-u)^{-q}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{\theta ,u}\leq C_ q.  \] The undamped tail criterion of theorem 7.4.1 and the integrability criterion of corollary 7.4.2 also hold with $\mu _{\theta ,u}$ in place of $\mu _ u$. Proof. Choose $C_0\geq 1$ such that $\theta \leq \Omega :=C_0\omega $. Then $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Omega )$, and theorem 6.1.2 gives \[  0\leq \mu _{\theta ,u}\leq \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Omega (u).  \] All the mass, tail and capacity bounds therefore follow from the estimates already proved for $\Omega $. The metric comparison in section 1.8 gives, for every Borel set $E\subset X$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E) \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (E) \leq C_0^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E).  \] For continuity, let nonpositive $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ converge in capacity, and use ( 7.2 ) with the $\theta $-product. The truncations are bounded and $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic. The weighted capacity continuity of section 1.6 , section 1.8 applies term by term to the local expansion of their signed $\theta $-products, with the same bounded quasi-continuous coefficients. Since the cutoff vanishes at the truncation level, the result is exactly the restricted positive measure. The uniform tails obtained from the domination by $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Omega $ remove the cutoff. Domination also gives the sublevel estimate, so the preceding proofs of the undamped tail and integrability criteria apply without change. $\square$

title: 8 Unbounded mass on Hopf manifolds
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 8 Unbounded mass on Hopf manifolds By proposition 7.1.1 , every compact complex curve or surface has the bounded mass property. The property can fail in dimension three even when the metric is Gauduchon. We prove this on a Hopf threefold, then extend the construction to every scalar Hopf manifold of dimension at least three. The threefold mass formula provides the starting point. Its linear term vanishes for a Gauduchon metric, and for the standard Hopf metric the quadratic term is a positive multiple of the Dirichlet energy along the elliptic fibers over $\mathbb P^2$. We therefore seek smooth potentials with large vertical energy whose perturbed forms stay positive. A fiber heat kernel supplies the concentration. Varying its time across the base controls the mixed derivatives; a function of the base then restores positivity without changing the vertical energy. The higher-dimensional extension follows by comparing the angular densities. We next use the fiber structure to study minimum mass, damping and weak limits. Fiber averaging identifies the bounded potentials of minimum mass. For normalized potentials invariant under unitary rotations of the last two coordinates, a positive fiber flux yields the sharp square-root damping threshold; concentration at the endpoint separates individual finiteness from uniform tails and capacity continuity. Finally, we classify the excess measures produced by shrinking smooth potentials. They are exactly the lifts of base measures by the normalized area measures on the elliptic fibers, for the standard metric and for every other Hermitian metric on this threefold. Theorem 8.0.1 (Xia–Zhang) . The compact threefold \[  X=(\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-1}z\rangle  \] admits a Gauduchon form $\omega $ and smooth real functions $V_ j$ such that \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j>0,\qquad \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^3\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] In particular, $X$ does not have the bounded mass property.

text: 8.1 The Hopf metric and its mass The projection to $\mathbb P^2$ separates the horizontal and vertical parts of the metric. We normalize the fiber measure to have mass one; this fixes the constants in the mass formula. On the covering space $\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} $, with coordinates $z=(z_0,z_1,z_2)$, put \[  s=\log |z|^2,\qquad \alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s,\qquad \beta =\mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s =\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial s\wedge \bar\partial s, \qquad \omega =\alpha +\beta .  \] The contraction $z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-1}z$ changes $s$ by the constant $-2$, so these forms descend to $X$. A closed spherical shell between two successive radii is a compact fundamental domain; this also proves that the quotient is compact. Let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^2$, given by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|\xi |^2)$ in affine coordinates $\xi =(\xi _1,\xi _2)$. Projectivization gives a holomorphic map \[  \pi :X\longrightarrow \mathbb P^2, \qquad \alpha =\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}},\qquad \int _{\mathbb P^2}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2=1.  \] The form $\alpha $ has rank two and is positive transversally to the fibers, while the rank-one form $\beta $ is positive on the vertical line. Their kernels intersect only in zero, and therefore $\omega >0$. We shall use the identities 8.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-torsion} \alpha ^3=0,\quad \beta ^2=0,\quad \mathrm{d}\alpha =0, \quad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =-\alpha ^2, \quad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0. \end{equation} The first three follow from the definitions and the dimension of the base. For the fourth, differentiating $\beta =\mathrm i\partial s\wedge \bar\partial s/(2\pi )$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =(\partial \bar\partial s)^2/(4\pi ^2)=-\alpha ^2$. Finally, $\omega ^2=\alpha ^2+2\alpha \wedge \beta $, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=-2\alpha ^3=0$. Thus $\omega $ is Gauduchon, although $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\alpha ^2\ne 0$. On the affine base chart $U_0=\{ [z_0:z_1:z_2]\in \mathbb P^2:z_0\ne 0\} \simeq \mathbb C^2$ write \[  \xi _ j=z_ j/z_0\quad (j=1,2),\qquad w=\log z_0.  \] The choice of logarithm and the contraction change $w$ by elements of $\Lambda =\mathbb Z+2\pi \mathrm i\mathbb Z$. Hence \[  \pi ^{-1}(U_0)\simeq U_0\times E,\qquad E=\mathbb C/\Lambda ,\qquad \mathrm{d}A_ E=\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w, \quad \int _ E\mathrm{d}A_ E=1.  \] On another base chart the fiber coordinate changes by a holomorphic function of the base. Consequently, the vertical derivative $\partial _ w$ and the fiber integral below are globally defined. For a smooth function $V$ on $X$, write $V_ w=\partial V/\partial w$. Proposition 8.1.1 . For every $V\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, 8.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-mass} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^3 =6+6\int _{\mathbb P^2} \left(\int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}|V_ w|^2\, \mathrm{d}A_ E\right) \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2(y). \end{equation} In particular, positivity of $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V$ is not required. Proof. Since $\beta $ restricts to $2\mathrm{d}A_ E$ on each fiber, \[  \int _ X\omega ^3=3\int _ X\alpha ^2\wedge \beta =6.  \] By ( 2.1 ) and ( 8.1 ), followed by an integration by parts against the closed form $\alpha ^2$, \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^3-\int _ X\omega ^3 & =3\int _ X V\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\\ & =-3\int _ X V\alpha ^2\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V =3\int _ X\mathrm{d}V\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}V\wedge \alpha ^2. \end{split}  \] Wedging with $\alpha ^2$ removes every component of $\mathrm{d}V\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}V$ except the vertical one, which is $\mathrm i|V_ w|^2\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w/(2\pi )=2|V_ w|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E$. Integration over the fibers proves the formula. $\square$

topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Lemma 8.3.3 . There is a constant $C$ depending only on $E$ with the following property. For $0<\kappa <1/(200C_0)$, $0<\eta <1/10$, $0<t\leq 1$ and $1/2\leq \mu \leq 1$, define $\sigma >0$ and the functions $h,\zeta $ of $w\in E$ by \[  \sigma ^2=\frac{2\kappa }{\eta }\log \frac1{\eta t},\qquad h=\eta k_ t,\qquad \zeta =\frac{\sigma }{\mu }\, t\partial _{\bar w}\log k_ t.  \] Then 8.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-square} \kappa tk_ t- \frac{\mu ^2(1-\eta )h}{1-\eta +h} \left|\zeta -\frac1{1-\eta }\right|^2 \leq C\kappa \exp \left(-\frac1{C\sigma ^2t}\right). \end{equation} Proof. If $\sigma ^2t\geq 1/100$, the bound $tk_ t\leq C_0$ gives ( 8.13 ) after enlarging $C$. Assume therefore that $\sigma ^2t<1/100$. If $|\zeta -(1-\eta )^{-1}|\geq 1/4$, the subtracted expression is at least $h/[100(1+h)]$. Since $\log (1/(\eta t))>2$, the definition of $\sigma $ gives \[  \kappa t(1+h)\leq \frac{\eta }{400}+C_0\kappa \eta <\frac{\eta }{100}.  \] Multiplication by $k_ t/(1+h)$ shows that the left side of ( 8.13 ) is nonpositive. title: 8.4 Variation of the heat time
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 8.4 Variation of the heat time The heat time will remain small on a fixed base ball and then increase with the radial variable until the fiber potential can be cut off. We choose its rate of increase so that the negative part of the Schur complement has small integral in the radial variable. Fix $\kappa $ as in lemma 8.3.3 . All estimates below concern the limit $\eta \downarrow 0$, with $\kappa $ fixed. Write \[  L=\log (1/\eta ),\quad \varepsilon =\eta ^{1/\eta ^2},\quad q_0=\sqrt{\log \frac1{\eta \varepsilon }},\quad a=\sqrt{\frac\kappa {2\eta }}.  \] Fix a smooth nondecreasing $\chi :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, independent of $\eta $, equal to zero on $(-\infty ,0]$ and one on $[1,+\infty )$, with $\int _0^1\chi =1/2$. Define 8.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-scale} q(x)=q_0-\int _0^{ax}\chi (s)\, \mathrm{d}s, \qquad t(x)=\eta ^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-q(x)^2}. \end{equation} Thus $t=\varepsilon $ on $x\leq 0$, and $q=q_0+1/2-ax$ on $x\geq a^{-1}$. Put \[  b=\frac{q_0-1/2}{a},\qquad x_* =\frac{q_0+1/2}{a}.  \] For small $\eta $, we have $0<a^{-1}<b<x_*$, with 8.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-scale-size} q(b)=1,\quad q(x_*)=0,\quad b,x_*=O\bigl (\sqrt{L/\eta }\bigr ),\quad \eta b=o(1). \end{equation} Fix also a smooth cutoff $\vartheta :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, independent of $\eta $, zero on $(-\infty ,0]$ and one on $[1,+\infty )$, and define \[  W(x,w)=\vartheta (q(x))F_\eta (t(x),w).  \] This function equals $F_\eta (\varepsilon ,w)$ for $x\leq 0$ and vanishes for $x\geq x_*$. Moreover, by ( 8.8 ), 8.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-vertical-positive} 1+W_{w\bar w}=1+\vartheta (q)\eta (k_ t-1)>1-\eta . \end{equation} Lemma 8.4.1 . For the functions just constructed, let \[  d_\eta (x)=\max _{w\in E}\max \{ -Q[W](x,w),0\} .  \] For all sufficiently small $\eta $, the function $d_\eta $ is continuous, supported in $[0,b]$, and 8.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-small-defect} \int _\mathbb Rd_\eta (x)\, \mathrm{d}x=o(1),\qquad \sup _{\mathbb R\times E}\max \{ -W_ x,0\} =o(1). \end{equation} On $[-2,-1]\times E$, one also has $Q[W]\geq 2/27$. Proof. We first derive an exact formula for $Q[W]$ on $[0,b]$, then bound its negative part separately on $[0,a^{-1}]$ and on $[a^{-1},b]$, integrate these bounds, and finally examine the ends of the radial line. Step 1: the Schur complement on $[0,b]$. Write $F=F_\eta $ for the heat potential. On $[0,b]$ we have $q\geq 1$, hence $\vartheta (q)=1$ and $W=F(t(x),w)$. Set \[  h=\eta k_ t,\qquad \sigma =(\log t)_ x,\qquad \zeta =\frac{\sigma t}{\mu }\partial _{\bar w}\log k_ t.  \] The heat equation gives $F_ t=h-\eta $, and the chain rule gives \[  W_ x=\sigma tF_ t,\quad W_{xx}=(\sigma _ x+\sigma ^2)tF_ t+\sigma ^2t^2F_{tt}, \quad W_{x\bar w}=\sigma tF_{t\bar w}.  \] Substituting these in $Q[W]$, using $h_ t=h((\log k_ t)_{w\bar w}+|\partial _{\bar w}\log k_ t|^2)$, and completing the square, we obtain the exact identity 8.18 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-Q-identity} \begin{split}  Q[W]={}& \sigma ^2t\{ h[1+t(\log k_ t)_{w\bar w}]-\eta \}  +\sigma _ xtF_ t+\mu (1-\mu )-\frac{\mu ^2\eta }{1-\eta }\\ & +\frac{\mu ^2(1-\eta )h}{1-\eta +h} \left|\zeta -\frac1{1-\eta }\right|^2. \end{split} \end{equation} By ( 8.9 ), the part $\sigma ^2th[1+t(\log k_ t)_{w\bar w}]$ is nonnegative. Step 2: the initial interval $[0,a^{-1}]$. Here \[  \sigma =2aq\chi (ax),\qquad \sigma _ x=-\frac\kappa \eta \chi (ax)^2 +\frac\kappa \eta q\chi '(ax).  \] Moreover $q_0-1/2\leq q\leq q_0$ and $t\leq \varepsilon \mathrm{e}^{q_0}$, and the latter tends to zero faster than any power of $\eta $. In particular, \[  \kappa q\chi '(ax)t\leq \eta ,\qquad \sigma ^2t\leq \eta ^2.  \] At each point where $\chi (ax)>0$, apply lemma 8.3.3 with $\kappa \chi (ax)^2$ in place of $\kappa $; its constant is uniform in $x$. The positive square in ( 8.18 ) then absorbs the negative term $-\kappa \chi ^2tk_ t$ coming from $\sigma _ xtF_ t$. The remaining part of $\sigma _ xtF_ t$, which involves $\chi '$, is at least $-\eta $, because $F_ t\geq -\eta $. The other negative terms in ( 8.18 ) are $O(\eta )$, and so is the exponential error of lemma 8.3.3 , since $\sigma ^2t\leq \eta ^2$. Thus $d_\eta \leq C\eta $ on this interval. At points where $\chi (ax)=0$, the smooth nonnegative function $\chi $ has a minimum, so $\chi '(ax)=0$ and directly \[  Q[W]=\mu -\frac{\mu ^2}{1-\eta +h}>0,  \] since $\mu \leq \mu (a^{-1})<1-\eta $ for small $\eta $. Step 3: the interval $[a^{-1},b]$. Here the formulas simplify to 8.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-time-change} \sigma =2aq,\qquad \sigma _ x=-\kappa /\eta ,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=-\frac{\mathrm{d}q}{a}=\sqrt{\frac\eta {2\kappa }}\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{tq}. \end{equation} For $t\leq 1$, lemma 8.3.3 and ( 8.18 ) give 8.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-defect-small-time} d_\eta (x)\leq 2\eta +2\kappa q^2t +C\kappa \exp \left(-\frac\eta {C\kappa q^2t}\right). \end{equation} Indeed, $-\eta \sigma ^2t=-2\kappa q^2t$ and $\sigma _ xtF_ t=-\kappa tk_ t+\kappa t$; these are the two terms for which the scale was chosen. When $t\geq 1$, we insert the exponential derivative estimates ( 8.11 ) directly in the definition of $Q$. The denominator stays above $1-\eta $, and the chain rule gives 8.23 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-defect-large-time} d_\eta (x)\leq C\kappa q^2t^2\mathrm{e}^{-t/4}. \end{equation} The perturbing derivatives are bounded by constants times $\eta \mathrm{e}^{-t/4}$, $\eta \sigma t \mathrm{e}^{-t/4}$ and $\eta [(|\sigma _ x|+\sigma ^2)t+\sigma ^2t^2]\mathrm{e}^{-t/4}$. Since $q,t\geq 1$ here, each is bounded by a constant times the right side of ( 8.23 ). Since $1+W_{w\bar w}\geq 1-\eta $, subtracting the two quotients gives \[  |Q[W]-Q[0]|\leq |W_{xx}|+ C\bigl (|W_{x\bar w}|+|W_{x\bar w}|^2+|W_{w\bar w}|\bigr ).  \] The square of the mixed derivative is at most $C\kappa \eta q^2t^2\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}$, so it satisfies the same bound. Since $Q[0]>0$, this proves ( 8.23 ). Step 4: integration of the negative part. The constant $2\eta $ and the initial interval contribute $O(\eta b)=o(1)$, by ( 8.15 ). In the small-time region, $q\geq \sqrt L$ and $t=\eta ^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-q^2}$. Therefore \[  \int 2\kappa q^2t\, \mathrm{d}x \leq \frac{2\kappa }{a\eta } \int _{\sqrt L}^{\infty }q^2\mathrm{e}^{-q^2}\, \mathrm{d}q \leq C\sqrt{\eta L}=o(1).  \] For the exponential term the integral is at most \[  \frac{C\kappa }{a} \int _{\sqrt L}^{q_0} \exp \left(-\frac{\eta ^2\mathrm{e}^{q^2}}{C\kappa q^2}\right)\, \mathrm{d}q.  \] The interval $[\sqrt L,2\sqrt L]$ has length $O(\sqrt L)$. For $q\geq 2\sqrt L$ and sufficiently small $\eta $, $\eta ^2\mathrm{e}^{q^2}/q^2\geq \mathrm{e}^{q^2/4}$. The integrand on this remaining interval is bounded by $\exp (-\mathrm{e}^{q^2/4}/(C\kappa ))$, which is integrable on $[1,+\infty )$. The prefactor is $O(\sqrt\eta )$, and the initial interval contributes $O(\sqrt{\eta L})$, so the full expression is $o(1)$. In the large-time region, ( 8.21 ) gives \[  \int d_\eta (x)\, \mathrm{d}x \leq C\sqrt\eta \int _1^{1/(\mathrm{e}\eta )}qt \mathrm{e}^{-t/4}\, \mathrm{d}t \leq C\sqrt{\eta L}\int _1^\infty t \mathrm{e}^{-t/4}\, \mathrm{d}t=o(1).  \] This proves the integral assertion on $[0,b]$. Step 5: the radial slope. The negative part of $W_ x$ is uniformly small as well. For $t\leq 1$, we have $F_ t\geq -\eta $ and $0\leq \sigma \leq 2aq$, so \[  \max \{ -W_ x,0\} \leq \sqrt{2\kappa \eta }\,  t\sqrt{\log \frac1{\eta t}}\leq C\sqrt{\eta L}.  \] The last inequality follows because $t\sqrt{L+\log (1/t)}$ is increasing on $(0,1]$ when $L>1$. For $t\geq 1$ and $q\geq 1$, use $|W_ x|\leq C\sqrt\eta \, qt \mathrm{e}^{-t/4}$ and $q\leq \sqrt L$. Step 6: the ends. It remains to consider the two ends, including the cutoff region. If $b\leq x\leq x_*$, then $0\leq q\leq 1$ and $1/(\mathrm{e}\eta )\leq t\leq 1/\eta $. The derivatives of the cutoffs and scale have at most polynomial growth in $\eta ^{-1}$. Thus ( 8.11 ) implies \[  \sup _ w\bigl (|W_ x|+|Q[W]-Q[0]|\bigr ) \leq C\mathrm{e}^{-1/(5\mathrm{e}\eta )}.  \] But $Q[0]=\mu (1-\mu )\geq \mathrm{e}^{-x_*}/4$ on this interval, and ( 8.15 ) shows that the error is $o(\mathrm{e}^{-x_*})$. Hence $Q[W]>0$ there. For $x\geq x_*$, $W=0$ and positivity is immediate. For $x\leq 0$, $W_ x=0$ and \[  Q[W]\geq \mu \left(1-\frac\mu {1-\eta }\right)>0,  \] since $\mu \leq 1/2$. On $[-2,-1]$, the bounds $1/9\leq \mu \leq 3/10$ and $1-\eta \geq 9/10$ give $Q[W]\geq 2/27$. Finally, $Q[W]$ is continuous, with positive denominator, so the maximum of its negative part over the compact fiber $E$ is continuous in $x$. This proves the assertions about support and continuity, and completes the proof. $\square$

text: 8.5 A base correction and unbounded mass Adding a function of $x$ alone changes $Q[W]$ by its second derivative and leaves the vertical energy unchanged. The integral bound for $d_\eta $ lets us choose this second derivative larger than $d_\eta $ and compensate its integral on an interval where $Q[W]$ is uniformly positive. The correction has small first derivative, so the remaining horizontal coefficient stays positive as well. of theorem 8.0.1 . Choose a smooth function $r_\eta \geq 0$ supported in $(-1/2,b+1/2)$ with \[  r_\eta >d_\eta \  \hbox{on }[0,b],\qquad m_\eta :=\int _\mathbb Rr_\eta \, \mathrm{d}x\leq \int _\mathbb Rd_\eta \, \mathrm{d}x+\eta =o(1).  \] Such a majorant exists by uniform approximation of the compactly supported continuous function $d_\eta $, followed by adding a positive bump on $[0,b]$; for each fixed $\eta $ the approximation error can be chosen small enough for the integral bound. Fix a smooth $\psi \geq 0$ supported in $(-2,-1)$ with integral one and set \[  g_\eta (x)=\int _{-\infty }^ x(x-s) (r_\eta (s)-m_\eta \psi (s))\, \mathrm{d}s, \qquad V_\eta =W+g_\eta .  \] The negative part of $g_\eta ''$ lies to the left of its positive part, and their integrals agree. Consequently, \[  -m_\eta \leq g_\eta '\leq 0, \qquad g_\eta '=0\  \hbox{for }x\leq -2 \  \hbox{and for }x\geq b+1/2.  \] Thus $g_\eta $ vanishes for $x\leq -2$ and is constant for $x\geq b+1/2$, and $V_\eta $ has the properties at the two ends required for smooth extension to $X$. Since $g_\eta $ is independent of $w$, the Schur complement changes by exactly its second derivative: \[  Q[V_\eta ]=Q[W]+r_\eta -m_\eta \psi .  \] This is positive on $[0,b]$ because $r_\eta >d_\eta $ there. On $(-2,-1)$ it is at least $2/27-m_\eta \| \psi \| _\infty >0$ for small $\eta $. Elsewhere $Q[W]>0$, $\psi =0$ and $r_\eta \geq 0$. The vertical coefficient remains above $1-\eta $ by ( 8.16 ). For the remaining coefficient, if $x\leq -2$, both $W_ x$ and $g_\eta '$ vanish; if $-2\leq x\leq 0$, then $W_ x=0$ and $\mu \geq \mu (-2)>0$, while $|g_\eta '|\leq m_\eta =o(1)$; and if $x\geq 0$, then $\mu \geq 1/2$ and $W_ x\geq -o(1)$. In all cases $\mu +(V_\eta )_ x>0$ for sufficiently small $\eta $. Therefore lemma 8.2.1 gives $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta >0$ on $X$. On the fixed ball $B=\{ |\xi |^2<\mathrm{e}^{-3}\} \Subset U_0$, one has $V_\eta =F_\eta (\varepsilon ,w)$, including at $\xi =0$. Thus \[  \int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}|(V_\eta )_ w|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E =2\eta ^2\log (1/\varepsilon )+O(\eta ^2) =2\log (1/\eta )+O(\eta ^2)\longrightarrow +\infty  \] uniformly for $y\in B$. Since $\int _ B\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2>0$, the mass identity ( 8.2 ) shows that $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta )^3\to +\infty $, and the theorem follows by taking $V_ j=V_{\eta _ j}$ along any sequence $\eta _ j\downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.6.1
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 8.24 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-dimensional-density} J_ n(V;x,w)=\frac{n(n-1)}6 (\mu +V_ x)^{n-3}J_3(V;x,w). \end{equation}

title: Theorem 8.6.2
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Theorem 8.6.2 . For every $n\geq 3$, the Gauduchon metric $\omega _ n$ admits smooth potentials $V_\eta $ with $\omega _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta >0$ whose total Monge–Ampère masses tend to infinity as $\eta \downarrow 0$. Proof. Use exactly the functions $V_\eta =W+g_\eta $ constructed in the proof of theorem 8.0.1 , including the heat scale $\varepsilon =\eta ^{1/\eta ^2}$. Their endpoint properties give smooth potentials on every $H_ n$, and lemma 8.6.1 gives strict positivity. The slope bounds in lemma 8.4.1 and $-m_\eta \leq g_\eta '\leq 0$ imply \[  \mu +(V_\eta )_ x\geq \tfrac 14 \qquad (x\geq 0)  \] for all sufficiently small $\eta $. We must first localize the divergent threefold mass to this region. On $x<0$, the heat potential is $W=F_\eta (\varepsilon ,w)$ and has no $x$ derivatives. The determinant formula in the preceding proof and $\int _ E F_{w\bar w}\, \mathrm dA_ E=0$ give \[  \int _ E J_3(V_\eta ;x,w)\, \mathrm dA_ E =12(\mu +g_\eta ') \bigl (g_\eta ''+\mu (1-\mu )\bigr ).  \] Here $0<\mu +g_\eta '\leq \mu $, and $g_\eta ''=r_\eta -m_\eta \psi $ with $\int r_\eta =m_\eta $ and $\int \psi =1$. Hence \[  \int _{x<0}\! J_3(V_\eta )\, \mathrm dx\, \mathrm dA_ E \leq 12\int _{-\infty }^0\mu ^2(1-\mu )\, \mathrm dx +12\int _{\mathbb R}|g_\eta ''|\, \mathrm dx \leq \tfrac 32+24m_\eta .  \] No bound on the amplitude of the fiber Hessian is required; its mean has been integrated exactly. Since the total threefold mass tends to infinity, its mass on $x\geq 0$ tends to infinity. The dimensional comparison now gives \[  \int _{H_ n}(\omega _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta )^ n \geq \frac{n(n-1)}6\, 4^{-(n-3)} \int _{x\geq 0}J_3(V_\eta )\, \mathrm dx\, \mathrm dA_ E \longrightarrow +\infty .  \] $\square$

title: Corollary 8.6.3
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Corollary 8.6.3 . Every Hermitian metric on $H_ n$, $n\geq 3$, fails the bounded mass property. Proof. For a Hermitian form $h$, compactness gives $h\geq c\omega _ n$ for some $c>0$. The potentials $cV_\eta $ satisfy $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(cV_\eta )\geq c(\omega _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta )>0$, and positivity of determinants bounds their masses below by $c^ n$ times the divergent masses in theorem 8.6.2 . $\square$

title: 8.7 Minimum mass and fiber averaging
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text:
8.7 Minimum mass and fiber averaging We return to the threefold $X=H_3$ and its form $\omega $. Averaging along the elliptic fibers removes the variation measured by ( 8.2 ). The Poincaré inequality on the fibers bounds the distance from a potential to its average by the excess mass. Bounded regularization preserves this inequality, which therefore identifies all bounded potentials of minimal mass and shows that potentials of almost minimal mass are close to them. Let $E$ act on $X$ by scalar multiplication: $	au _ a[z]=[\mathrm{e}^ a z]$ for $a\in E$. The action preserves $\alpha $, $ eta $ and $\omega $, and $\mathrm{d}A_ E$ is the Haar probability measure of $E$. For a bounded Borel function $u:X	o \mathbb R$, set \[  \mathrm{d}
u = rac{\omega ^3}{6}= rac12\alpha ^2\wedge  eta , \qquad Au(p)=\int _ Eu(	au _ a(p))\, \mathrm{d}A_ E(a) \quad (p\in X).  \] Thus $Au$ is constant on each fiber, and $
u $ is the probability measure whose disintegration along $\pi $ has fiber measures $\mathrm{d}A_ E$ and base measure $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2$. Proposition 8.7.1 . For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, the average $Au$ is the pullback of a bounded $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^2$, and 8.25  egin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-average-mass} \| u-Au\| _{L^2(X,
u )}^2 \leq  rac23\left(\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3-6ight). \end{equation} The coefficient $2/3$ is optimal, even for smooth $u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Moreover, \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=6 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u=\pi ^*v\quad 	ext{for some } v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\omega _{\mathrm{FS}})\cap L^\infty (\mathbb P^2).  \] Proof. First suppose that $u$ is smooth and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Averaging the positive forms $	au _ a^*(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$ gives $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Au>0$. Since $Au$ is smooth and constant on the fibers, $Au=\pi ^*v$ for a smooth function $v$ on $\mathbb P^2$. At each point, the kernel of $\partial s$ maps isomorphically onto the tangent space of the base, and $ eta $ vanishes on it. Restricting $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Au=\pi ^*(\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+ eta $ to this kernel therefore shows that $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. For a smooth function $f:E	o \mathbb R$, the nonconstant Fourier characters in ( 8.7 ), indexed by $(p,q)\in \mathbb Z^2\setminus \{ (0,0)\} $, have eigenvalues $\pi ^2p^2+q^2/4\geq 1/4$ for $-\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}$. Parseval's identity therefore gives \[  \int _ E\left|f-\int _ Ef\, \mathrm{d}A_ Eight|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E \leq 4\int _ E|f_ w|^2\, \mathrm{d}A_ E.  \] Applying this inequality on every fiber, integrating against $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2$ and using the mass identity ( 8.2 ), we obtain ( 8.25 ). For bounded $u$, choose uniformly bounded smooth functions $u_ j\downarrow u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0$ by theorem 1.11.1 . Their averages decrease pointwise to $Au$ by dominated convergence. The corresponding smooth base potentials $v_ j$ decrease to a bounded $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function $v$, so $Au=\pi ^*v$. Dominated convergence gives $u_ j	o u$ and $Au_ j	o Au$ in $L^2(X,
u )$, while bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives convergence of the total masses. Thus ( 8.25 ) passes to $u$. If the mass is $6$, the inequality gives $u=Au$ almost everywhere. Since both functions are bounded and quasi-plurisubharmonic, lemma 1.3.4 gives equality everywhere. Conversely, if $u=\pi ^*v$ with bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\omega _{\mathrm{FS}})$, choose smooth $v_ j\downarrow v$ with $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j>0$ by theorem 1.11.1 . The pullbacks decrease to $u$ and are uniformly bounded. They are strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic because the base forms are positive and $ eta $ is positive on the vertical line. Their vertical derivatives vanish, so ( 8.2 ) gives mass $6$ for each of them. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives the same mass for $u$. It remains to prove that the constant $2/3$ is optimal. Choose a nonzero real $ho \in C_ c^\infty (U_0)$. For $\delta \in \mathbb R$, the function \[  u(\xi ,w)=\delta ho (\xi )\cos (\operatorname {Im}w)  \] extends by zero to a smooth function on $X$. For sufficiently small nonzero real $\delta $, it satisfies $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Its fiber average is zero, and its only fiber frequencies are $(p,q)=(0,\pm 1)$, with eigenvalue $1/4$. Hence equality holds in the fiber inequality, and therefore in ( 8.25 ), with nonzero left-hand side. No smaller coefficient can hold. $\square$ Corollary 8.7.2 . The Hopf metric satisfies \[  v_-(\omega )=6,\qquad v_+(\omega )=+\infty .  \] Proof. The lower bound $v_-(\omega )\geq 6$ follows from ( 8.25 ), and it is attained by constants. Theorem 8.0.1 gives $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. $\square$ In particular, for any sequence of bounded potentials whose masses tend to $6$, the differences from their fiber averages tend to zero in $L^2(X,
u )$. This controls only the variation along the fibers; the averaged potentials can still be arbitrary bounded potentials on the base. For nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ on this threefold, proposition 7.3.1 gives finite damped measures for the weight $(1-u)^{-1}[\log (\mathrm{e}-u)]^{-a}$, $a>1$, at the threshold $r_3=1$, with uniform tails and capacity continuity. The optimal damping rate for all normalized potentials on this threefold remains open. Under unitary rotations of the last two coordinates, theorem 8.8.9 gives the exact square-root threshold.

title: Proposition 8.7.1
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Proposition 8.7.1 . For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, the average $Au$ is the pullback of a bounded $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^2$, and 8.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-average-mass} \| u-Au\| _{L^2(X,\nu )}^2 \leq \frac23\left(\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3-6\right). \end{equation} The coefficient $2/3$ is optimal, even for smooth $u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Moreover, \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=6 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u=\pi ^*v\quad \text{for some } v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\omega _{\mathrm{FS}})\cap L^\infty (\mathbb P^2).  \] Proof. First suppose that $u$ is smooth and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Averaging the positive forms $\tau _ a^*(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$ gives $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Au>0$. Since $Au$ is smooth and constant on the fibers, $Au=\pi ^*v$ for a smooth function $v$ on $\mathbb P^2$. At each point, the kernel of $\partial s$ maps isomorphically onto the tangent space of the base, and $\beta $ vanishes on it. Restricting $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Au=\pi ^*(\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+\beta $ to this kernel therefore shows that $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. For a smooth function $f:E\to \mathbb R$, the nonconstant Fourier characters in ( 8.7 ), indexed by $(p,q)\in \mathbb Z^2\setminus \{ (0,0)\} $, have eigenvalues $\pi ^2p^2+q^2/4\geq 1/4$ for $-\partial _ w\partial _{\bar w}$. Parseval's identity therefore gives \[  \int _ E\left|f-\int _ Ef\, \mathrm{d}A_ E\right|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E \leq 4\int _ E|f_ w|^2\, \mathrm{d}A_ E.  \] Applying this inequality on every fiber, integrating against $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2$ and using the mass identity ( 8.2 ), we obtain ( 8.25 ). For bounded $u$, choose uniformly bounded smooth functions $u_ j\downarrow u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0$ by theorem 1.11.1 . Their averages decrease pointwise to $Au$ by dominated convergence. The corresponding smooth base potentials $v_ j$ decrease to a bounded $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function $v$, so $Au=\pi ^*v$. Dominated convergence gives $u_ j\to u$ and $Au_ j\to Au$ in $L^2(X,\nu )$, while bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives convergence of the total masses. Thus ( 8.25 ) passes to $u$. If the mass is $6$, the inequality gives $u=Au$ almost everywhere. Since both functions are bounded and quasi-plurisubharmonic, lemma 1.3.4 gives equality everywhere. Conversely, if $u=\pi ^*v$ with bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\omega _{\mathrm{FS}})$, choose smooth $v_ j\downarrow v$ with $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j>0$ by theorem 1.11.1 . The pullbacks decrease to $u$ and are uniformly bounded. They are strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic because the base forms are positive and $\beta $ is positive on the vertical line. Their vertical derivatives vanish, so ( 8.2 ) gives mass $6$ for each of them. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives the same mass for $u$. It remains to prove that the constant $2/3$ is optimal. Choose a nonzero real $\rho \in C_ c^\infty (U_0)$. For $\delta \in \mathbb R$, the function \[  u(\xi ,w)=\delta \rho (\xi )\cos (\operatorname {Im}w)  \] extends by zero to a smooth function on $X$. For sufficiently small nonzero real $\delta $, it satisfies $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Its fiber average is zero, and its only fiber frequencies are $(p,q)=(0,\pm 1)$, with eigenvalue $1/4$. Hence equality holds in the fiber inequality, and therefore in ( 8.25 ), with nonzero left-hand side. No smaller coefficient can hold. $\square$

title: 8.8 Sharp damping under unitary rotations
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 8.8 Sharp damping under unitary rotations The general damping estimate controls mass by the depth of a potential. On the standard Hopf threefold, unitary symmetry gives a stronger estimate: after integration along the elliptic fibers, a positive radial flux has total mass one. A semiconvexity estimate bounds the remaining radial coefficient by the square root of the depth. The resulting damping threshold is sharp, and at its endpoint finite measures can still concentrate on a pole divisor. We retain the standard threefold $X$, form $\omega $, projection $\pi :X\to \mathbb P^2$, fiber $E$ and probability area $\mathrm dA_ E$ of this chapter. Let $\mathcal R$ be the class of $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ invariant under \[  (z_0,z')\longmapsto (z_0,Az'),\qquad A\in U(2),\quad z'=(z_1,z_2).  \] This holomorphic action preserves $\omega $. The class includes bounded and unbounded potentials. For a positive $C^1$ nonincreasing function $W:[0,+\infty )\to (0,+\infty )$ tending to zero, write \begin{gather*}  \mu _ u=\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u),\qquad \nu _{W,u}=W(-u)\mu _ u,\\  Q_ T(W)=\sup _{t\geq T}(1+\sqrt{2t})W(t),\qquad Q(W)=Q_0(W). \end{gather*} The weighted measure gives zero mass to the pole set, as does the extended non-pluripolar measure. Capacity always means $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ of section 1.8 .

title: 8.8.1 Positive fiber flux
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 8.26 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rotational-positive-density} \mathrm{MA}_\omega (V)=12 A_ V\Delta _ V\,  \mathrm dx\, \mathrm d\Omega \, \mathrm dA_ E. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 8.8.1
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Lemma 8.8.1 . For every smooth invariant $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, \[  \int _{\mathbb R\times E}\Delta _ V\, \mathrm dx\, \mathrm dA_ E=1.  \] If in addition $V\leq 0$, then \[  |V_ x|^2\leq -2V,\qquad 0\leq A_ V\leq 1+\sqrt{-2V}.  \] Proof. Set $m(x)=\int _ EV\, \mathrm dA_ E$ and $e(x)=\int _ E|V_ w|^2\, \mathrm dA_ E$. Periodic integration by parts gives \[  \begin{split}  \int _ E V_{w\bar w}V_{xx}\, \mathrm dA_ E & =-\operatorname {Re}\int _ EV_{\bar w}V_{xxw}\, \mathrm dA_ E,\\  e''& =2\int _ E|V_{xw}|^2\, \mathrm dA_ E +2\operatorname {Re}\int _ EV_{\bar w}V_{xxw}\, \mathrm dA_ E. \end{split}  \] The mean of every fiber derivative vanishes. Expanding $\Delta _ V$ yields \[  \int _ E\Delta _ V\, \mathrm dA_ E =m''+\mu (1-\mu )-\tfrac 12e''.  \] Thus $f(x)=\log (1+\mathrm e^ x)+m(x)-e(x)/2$ is convex. Both $m$ and $e$ are smooth global functions on the projective base: local fiber coordinates change by holomorphic translations, preserving fiber Haar area, the vertical derivative and the Dirichlet integral. They are $U(2)$-invariant. Smoothness and radial invariance at $\xi =0$ give $m',e'\to 0$ at the negative end. At the positive end use a normal coordinate $z_0/z_1$ to the hyperplane $\{ z_0=0\} $ on the base. The invariant base functions are constant along this hyperplane and smooth across it; their $x$ derivatives tend to zero. This does not require that the pointwise potential be constant on its elliptic fibers at that end. Consequently $f'(-\infty )=0$ and $f'(+\infty )=1$. Integrating the nonnegative $f''$ proves the flux identity. For each fixed $w$, $R_ V\geq 0$ implies $V_{xx}\geq -1$ on all of $\mathbb R$. Hence for every real $h$, \[  V(x+h,w)\geq V(x,w)+hV_ x(x,w)-h^2/2.  \] Taking $h=V_ x(x,w)$ and using $V\leq 0$ proves the derivative bound. Finally $\mu \leq 1$ proves the bound for $A_ V$. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.8.2
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Lemma 8.8.2 . Every bounded invariant $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, with $-L\leq u\leq 0$, admits smooth invariant $\omega $-plurisubharmonic approximants with the same bounds converging to $u$ in capacity. Proof. The compact group $G=U(3)\times (\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)$ acts transitively and holomorphically on $X$ by unitary transformations and positive scalar multiplication. It preserves $\omega $. Choose a nonnegative smooth central approximate identity $\rho _\epsilon $ on $G$, supported near its identity, and put \[  u_\epsilon (p)=\int _ Gu(gp)\rho _\epsilon (g)\, \mathrm dg.  \] Convolution on a compact homogeneous space is smooth. Averaging preserves the current inequality and the bounds, and centrality makes convolution commute with the $U(2)$ action. Transporting the bounded tests defining capacity shows that $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ is $G$-invariant. Suppose $L>0$. By quasi-continuity, choose an open set $O$ of arbitrarily small capacity such that $u$ is continuous on $X\setminus O$. When $g$ is sufficiently close to the identity, $u(gp)$ and $u(p)$ are uniformly close whenever both points lie outside $O$. Thus, outside $O$ and for small kernel support, \[  \{ |u_\epsilon -u|>\delta \}  \subset \{ P_\epsilon \mathbf1_ O>\delta /(4L)\} ,\qquad P_\epsilon \mathbf1_ O(p)=\int _ G\mathbf1_ O(gp)\rho _\epsilon (g)\, \mathrm dg.  \] Markov's inequality, followed by capacity invariance, gives \[  \begin{split}  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega \{ P_\epsilon \mathbf1_ O>\delta /(4L)\}  & \leq \frac{4L}{\delta }\sup _{0\leq v\leq 1} \int _ XP_\epsilon \mathbf1_ O\, (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^3\\ & \leq \frac{4L}{\delta }\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (O), \end{split}  \] where the supremum runs over $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Letting the capacity of $O$ tend to zero proves the claim. If $L=0$, $u=0$ and no approximation is needed. $\square$

title: 8.8.2 Heat concentration at large depth
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 8.8.2 Heat concentration at large depth The flux estimate suggests the depth scale at which a counterexample must place its mass. A faster initial heat time than in the unbounded-mass construction gives mass of order $\eta ^{-1}$ at depth of order $\eta ^{-2}$. Its integrated radial defect remains small after a fixed parameter is chosen, but no longer tends to zero. We therefore need a correction with a small fixed total slope. We use the heat kernel $k_ t$ of ( 8.6 ) and its potential $F_\eta $ of lemma 8.3.1 . The following value estimates complement the derivative bounds already proved. Lemma 8.8.4 . Uniformly in $\eta $ and $w$, $F_\eta (t,w)\leq C\eta $ for $t>0$, and $F_\eta (t,w)\geq -2\eta \log (1/t)-C\eta $ for $0<t\leq 1$. Uniformly on $\sqrt t\leq |w|\leq 2\sqrt t$ near the origin of $E$, as $t\to 0$, \begin{align*}  F_\eta (t,w)& =2\eta \log t+O(\eta ),\\  t k_ t(w)& =2\mathrm e^{-|w|^2/t}+O(\mathrm e^{-1/(Ct)}),\\  t\partial _{\bar w}\log k_ t(w)& =-w+O(\mathrm e^{-1/(Ct)}). \end{align*} Proof. For the upper bound use $k_ r\geq 0$ on $(0,1]$ and ( 8.11 ). The nonnegative Fourier coefficients imply $k_ r(w)\leq k_ r(0)$, and Gaussian summation gives $k_ r(0)\leq 2/r+C r^{-1}\mathrm e^{-1/(2r)}$ for $r\leq 1$. Its integrable error proves the lower bound. On the indicated annulus the nonzero-lattice terms and their derivatives are exponentially small relative to the zero-lattice term, proving the last two identities. For the first, split the defining integral at a fixed small $r_0$. On $[t,r_0]$ the nonzero-lattice contributions have bounded integral, and the difference between $(2/r)\mathrm e^{-|w|^2/r}$ and $2/r$ has integral at most $2|w|^2/t\leq 8$. The remaining integral is uniformly bounded. $\square$ Theorem 8.8.5 . There are $A,B,D,\eta _0>0$ such that for every $0<\eta <\eta _0$ there exist $u_\eta \in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)\cap \mathcal R$ and a measurable $K_\eta \subset X$ satisfying \begin{gather*}  \sup _ Xu_\eta =0,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\eta >0, \qquad 0\leq -u_\eta \leq B\eta ^{-2}\quad \text{on }X,\\  A\eta ^{-2}\leq -u_\eta \leq B\eta ^{-2}\quad \text{on }K_\eta , \qquad \int _{K_\eta }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\eta )^3\geq D\eta ^{-1}. \end{gather*} Proof. Fix $\kappa $ as in lemma 8.3.3 , also with $\kappa <1/100$. Choose a small fixed $c>0$ later and set \begin{gather*}  \varepsilon =\mathrm e^{-c\eta ^{-3}},\qquad q_0=\sqrt{c\eta ^{-3}+\log (1/\eta )},\qquad a=\sqrt{\kappa /(2\eta )},\\  q(x)=q_0-\int _0^{ax}\chi (s)\, \mathrm ds,\qquad t(x)=\eta ^{-1}\mathrm e^{-q(x)^2},\\  b=(q_0-1/2)/a,\qquad x_*=(q_0+1/2)/a,\qquad Z_\eta (x,w)=\vartheta (q(x))F_\eta (t(x),w). \end{gather*} Use the cutoffs $\chi $ and $\vartheta $ from the earlier heat-time construction. Then $Z_\eta =F_\eta (\varepsilon ,\cdot )$ for $x\leq 0$, $Z_\eta =0$ for $x\geq x_*$, and \[  \eta b,\eta x_*\longrightarrow \ell :=\sqrt{2c/\kappa },\qquad 1+(Z_\eta )_{w\bar w}>1-\eta .  \] The larger value of $q_0$ changes the integrated positivity defect; we estimate it at this scale. Write $r_-=\max (-r,0)$ for the negative part of a real number $r$. On $[0,b]$ we have $\vartheta =1$. Write $F=F_\eta $ and put $\sigma =(\log t)_ x$, $h=\eta k_ t$ and $\zeta =\sigma t\partial _{\bar w}\log k_ t/\mu $. The identity ( 8.18 ) applies to $Z_\eta $ on this interval. The contribution involving $h[1+t(\log k_ t)_{w\bar w}]$ is nonnegative. On $[0,a^{-1}]$, \[  \sigma =2aq\chi (ax),\quad \sigma _ x=-\frac\kappa \eta \chi (ax)^2+\frac\kappa \eta q\chi '(ax), \quad t\leq \varepsilon \mathrm e^{q_0}.  \] This upper bound for $t$ is smaller than every power of $\eta $. Thus $\kappa q\chi 't\leq \eta $ and $\sigma ^2t\leq \eta ^2$. Use ( 8.13 ) with $\kappa \chi ^2$ where $\chi >0$, and $F_ t\geq -\eta $ for the $\chi '$ term. It follows that $[Q[Z_\eta ]]_-\leq C\eta $. Where $\chi =0$ also $\chi '=0$, and $Q[Z_\eta ]=\mu -\mu ^2/(1-\eta +h)>0$, since $x\leq a^{-1}=o(1)$. On $[a^{-1},b]$, $\sigma =2aq$, $\sigma _ x=-\kappa /\eta $, $\mathrm dx=-\mathrm dq/a$. For $t\leq 1$, ( 8.18 ) and ( 8.13 ) give \[  [Q[Z_\eta ]]_-\leq 2\eta +2\kappa q^2t+C\kappa \exp \left(-\frac\eta {C\kappa q^2t}\right).  \] For $t\geq 1$, ( 8.11 ) gives instead $[Q[Z_\eta ]]_-\leq C\kappa q^2t^2\mathrm e^{-t/4}$. Put $L=\log (1/\eta )$. Integrating the $q^2t$ term uses $\int _{\sqrt L}^\infty q^2\mathrm e^{-q^2}\, \mathrm dq\leq C\sqrt L\eta $. For the exponential term split at $2\sqrt L$: the initial interval has length $O(\sqrt L)$, and on the rest $\eta ^2\mathrm e^{q^2}/q^2\geq \mathrm e^{q^2/4}$ for small $\eta $. Its remaining integral is uniformly bounded even with upper endpoint infinity. For large time use $\mathrm dx=\sqrt{\eta /(2\kappa )}\, \mathrm dt/(tq)$, $q\leq \sqrt L$, and the integrability of $t\mathrm e^{-t/4}$. Including the constant term and initial interval yields 8.34 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rotational-integrated-defect} \int _0^ b\max _{w\in E}[Q[Z_\eta ](x,w)]_-\, \mathrm dx \leq C\eta b+C\sqrt{\eta L}\leq C\ell +o(1). \end{equation} All constants here are independent of $q_0,c,\eta $ with fixed $\kappa $. The bound is small after choosing $c$, although it need not tend to zero. Also $\sup [(Z_\eta )_ x]_-=O(\sqrt{\eta L})$: for $t\leq 1$ use $F_ t\geq -\eta $ and $t\sqrt{L+\log (1/t)}\leq \sqrt L$; for $t\geq 1$ use ( 8.11 ). On $[b,x_*]$, $0\leq q\leq 1$ and $(\mathrm e\eta )^{-1}\leq t\leq \eta ^{-1}$, so differentiated cutoffs and ( 8.11 ) give \[  \sup _ w\bigl (|(Z_\eta )_ x|+|Q[Z_\eta ]-Q[0]|\bigr ) \leq C\mathrm e^{-1/(5\mathrm e\eta )}.  \] Choose $c$ so that $\ell <1/(10\mathrm e)$. Since $Q[0]=\mu (1-\mu )\geq \mathrm e^{-x_*}/4$ here, this implies $Q[Z_\eta ]>0$ on the cutoff interval. For $x\leq 0$ use $Q[Z_\eta ]\geq \mu (1-\mu /(1-\eta ))>0$, and for $x\geq x_*$ use $Z_\eta =0$. On $[-2,-1]$ the same formula gives $Q[Z_\eta ]\geq 2/27$. The continuous defect $d_\eta (x)=\max _ w[Q[Z_\eta ]]_-$ is therefore supported in $[0,b]$. Choose a smooth nonnegative $r_\eta $, supported in $(-1/2,b+1/2)$, with $r_\eta >d_\eta $ on $[0,b]$ and $m_\eta :=\int r_\eta \leq \int d_\eta +\eta $. Uniform approximation and a positive bump give this choice for each fixed $\eta $; no uniform derivative bound is needed. Fix a smooth probability bump $\psi $ supported in $(-2,-1)$ and put \[  g_\eta (x)=\int _{-\infty }^ x(x-s)(r_\eta (s)-m_\eta \psi (s))\, \mathrm ds, \qquad V_\eta =Z_\eta +g_\eta .  \] The support order implies $-m_\eta \leq g_\eta '\leq 0$; $g_\eta =0$ at the negative end and is constant at the positive end. Furthermore $g_\eta \leq 0$ and $|g_\eta |\leq m_\eta (b+3)=O_ c(\eta ^{-1})$. Shrink the fixed $c$ so that ( 8.34 ) ensures \[  m_\eta <\min \{ \mu (-2)/2,\, 1/8,\, 1/(27\| \psi \| _\infty )\}   \] for all sufficiently small $\eta $. Now $Q[V_\eta ]=Q[Z_\eta ]+r_\eta -m_\eta \psi >0$ everywhere: use the majorant on $[0,b]$, the margin $2/27$ on $(-2,-1)$, and the established positivity elsewhere. The vertical coefficient is above $1-\eta $. For the horizontal coefficient, derivatives vanish for $x\leq -2$; on $[-2,0]$ use $\mu \geq \mu (-2)>m_\eta $; on $[0,\infty )$ use $\mu \geq 1/2$ and $(Z_\eta )_ x\geq -o(1)$. Thus ( 8.5 ) gives a smooth globally strictly positive potential. On $x<-3$, $V_\eta =F_\eta (\varepsilon ,\cdot )$ has fiber mean zero, so $0\leq \sup _ XV_\eta \leq C\eta $ by lemma 8.8.4 and $g_\eta \leq 0$. Set $u_\eta =V_\eta -\sup _ XV_\eta $. Where the cutoff is nonzero $t\geq \varepsilon $, giving 8.35 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rotational-global-depth} 0\leq -u_\eta \leq 2c\eta ^{-2}+O_ c(\eta ^{-1})+O(\eta ). \end{equation} Multiplication by a cutoff between zero and one preserves this lower bound for $Z_\eta $, including where $F_\eta $ is positive. Mass and depth on the concentration region. Let $K_\eta $ consist of all radial angular directions and \[  q_0/2\leq q(x)\leq 3q_0/4,\qquad \sqrt{t(x)}\leq |w|\leq 2\sqrt{t(x)},  \] using the small lift near zero in $E$. This lies in the linear transport region, with $\vartheta =1$, $x\asymp _ c\eta ^{-1}\to \infty $, $\sigma =2aq\asymp _ c\eta ^{-2}$, and superexponentially small $t$. Lemma 8.8.4 gives, uniformly, \[  0<c_1\leq tk_ t\leq 3,\quad h\to \infty ,\quad \zeta \to 0,\quad \eta \sigma ^2t\to 0,\quad \mu \to 1.  \] In ( 8.18 ) the first $h$ contribution is nonnegative, $\sigma _ xtF_ t=-\kappa t(k_ t-1)\geq -3\kappa $, and the completed square tends to one. Its other negative terms tend to zero. Thus $Q[Z_\eta ]\geq 1/4$ for small $\eta $. On the core $\psi =0$ and $g_\eta ''=r_\eta \geq 0$, so $Q[V_\eta ]\geq 1/4$. Also \[  \mu +(V_\eta )_ x\geq c_2\eta \sigma ,\qquad 1+(V_\eta )_{w\bar w}\geq c_1\eta /t.  \] Indeed $(Z_\eta )_ x=\eta \sigma (tk_ t-t)$ and $\mu +g_\eta '>0$ here; the vertical inequality follows from $1-\eta +\eta k_ t$. In ( 8.26 ), $\Delta _{V_\eta }=(1+(V_\eta )_{w\bar w})Q[V_\eta ]$. The fiber annulus has area $3t/2$.
