They lie in its smooth locus, so no mass is assigned to poles. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.8.4
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Lemma 8.8.4 . Uniformly in $\eta $ and $w$, $F_\eta (t,w)\leq C\eta $ for $t>0$, and $F_\eta (t,w)\geq -2\eta \log (1/t)-C\eta $ for $0<t\leq 1$. Uniformly on $\sqrt t\leq |w|\leq 2\sqrt t$ near the origin of $E$, as $t\to 0$, \begin{align*}  F_\eta (t,w)& =2\eta \log t+O(\eta ),\\  t k_ t(w)& =2\mathrm e^{-|w|^2/t}+O(\mathrm e^{-1/(Ct)}),\\  t\partial _{\bar w}\log k_ t(w)& =-w+O(\mathrm e^{-1/(Ct)}). \end{align*} Proof. For the upper bound use $k_ r\geq 0$ on $(0,1]$ and ( 8.11 ). The nonnegative Fourier coefficients imply $k_ r(w)\leq k_ r(0)$, and Gaussian summation gives $k_ r(0)\leq 2/r+C r^{-1}\mathrm e^{-1/(2r)}$ for $r\leq 1$. Its integrable error proves the lower bound. On the indicated annulus the nonzero-lattice terms and their derivatives are exponentially small relative to the zero-lattice term, proving the last two identities. For the first, split the defining integral at a fixed small $r_0$. On $[t,r_0]$ the nonzero-lattice contributions have bounded integral, and the difference between $(2/r)\mathrm e^{-|w|^2/r}$ and $2/r$ has integral at most $2|w|^2/t\leq 8$. The remaining integral is uniformly bounded. $\square$

Its other negative terms tend to zero. Thus $Q[Z_\eta ]\geq 1/4$ for small $\eta $. On the core $\psi =0$ and $g_\eta ''=r_\eta \geq 0$, so $Q[V_\eta ]\geq 1/4$. Also \[  \mu +(V_\eta )_ x\geq c_2\eta \sigma ,\qquad 1+(V_\eta )_{w\bar w}\geq c_1\eta /t.  \] Indeed $(Z_\eta )_ x=\eta \sigma (tk_ t-t)$ and $\mu +g_\eta '>0$ here; the vertical inequality follows from $1-\eta +\eta k_ t$. In ( 8.26 ), $\Delta _{V_\eta }=(1+(V_\eta )_{w\bar w})Q[V_\eta ]$. The fiber annulus has area $3t/2$. Integrating the preceding lower bounds and using $\sigma \, \mathrm dx=-2q\, \mathrm dq$ yields \[  \int _{K_\eta }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\eta )^3 \geq c_3\eta ^2\int _{q_0/2}^{3q_0/4}2q\, \mathrm dq =c_4\eta ^2q_0^2\geq c_5\eta ^{-1}.  \] The annular value estimate also gives \[  -u_\eta =2\eta q^2+O_ c(\eta ^{-1})+O(\eta \log (1/\eta )).  \] As $\eta q_0^2=c\eta ^{-2}+\eta \log (1/\eta )$, this is bounded above and below by fixed positive multiples of $\eta ^{-2}$ on the core. Together with ( 8.35 ), this proves the asserted mass and depth bounds. All these potentials are bounded: truncations beyond their individual depth equal them everywhere, so the defining extended product equals ( 8.26 ). $\square$

title: Corollary 8.8.6
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Corollary 8.8.6 . Let $W:[0,\infty )\to (0,\infty )$ be nonincreasing. A uniform bound for the weighted masses \[  \int _ X W(-u)\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)  \] over all normalized $\omega $-psh potentials requires \[  \sup _{T\gg 1}\sqrt T\, W(T)<\infty .  \] Uniform deep tails over that class require $\sqrt T\, W(T)\to 0$. Proof. On $K_\eta $, monotonicity of $W$ gives \[  \int _ XW(-u_\eta )\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u_\eta ) \geq D\eta ^{-1}W(B\eta ^{-2}).  \] Every sufficiently large $T$ equals $B\eta ^{-2}$ for some sufficiently small $\eta $, proving the necessary bound. Also $K_\eta \subset \{ -u_\eta >A\eta ^{-2}/2\} $, so uniform deep tails force this lower bound to tend to zero. $\square$

title: Theorem 8.8.7
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Theorem 8.8.7 . Suppose $W$ is positive and nonincreasing, finite on compact intervals, and \[  \sup _{T\gg 1}\sqrt T W(T)=\infty .  \] Then there is a single $U\in \mathcal R$ such that \[  \int _ XW(-U)\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)=\infty .  \] Proof. First select the correction with additional local control. Put \[  x_{\rm pre}=(q_0+1/2-2\sqrt L)/a.  \] Then $t(x_{\rm pre})=\eta ^3$, $x_{\rm pre}\to \infty $, and $b-x_{\rm pre}=O(\sqrt{\eta L})\to 0$. For a fixed large $K$ the preceding defect estimates give $d_\eta \leq (K/2)\eta $ on $[0,x_{\rm pre}]$: on the linear portion $q^2t\leq 4L\eta ^3$, and the exponential error is $O(\exp (-1/(C\kappa \eta ^2L)))=o(\eta )$. On the initial portion use the previously proved $C\eta $ bound. The integral of $d_\eta $ on $[x_{\rm pre},b]$ tends to zero by the same integrated estimates and this interval's length. Choose a fixed left cutoff, zero for $x\leq -1/2$ and one for $x\geq -1/4$, and a translated right cutoff, one for $x\leq x_{\rm pre}$ and zero for $x\geq x_{\rm pre}+1/4$. Let $r^0_\eta $ be $K\eta $ times their product. It strictly exceeds $d_\eta $ on $[0,x_{\rm pre}]$. The continuous function $e_\eta =\max (d_\eta -r^0_\eta ,0)$ is supported in $[x_{\rm pre},b]$. Add a smooth nonnegative majorant $s_\eta >e_\eta $ on that interval, supported in $(x_{\rm pre}-1/4,b+1/2)$, with $\int s_\eta \leq \int e_\eta +\eta $. Set $r_\eta =r^0_\eta +s_\eta $. Then \[  r_\eta >d_\eta \quad \text{on }[0,b],\qquad m_\eta =\int r_\eta \leq K\eta b+O(\sqrt{\eta L})+O(\eta ).  \] After shrinking the fixed $c$, this is bounded by a fixed $m_0$ within all the positivity tolerances above. The conclusions of theorem 8.8.5 therefore hold for this choice, with fixed $A,B,D$. On every fixed compact interval $I\Subset (0,\infty )$, for sufficiently small $\eta $ we have $r_\eta =K\eta $ and exactly 8.36 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rotational-controlled-correction} g_\eta (x)=-m_\eta (x-\mu _\psi ) +K\eta (x^2/2+b_0x+b_1),\qquad \mu _\psi =\int s\psi (s)\, \mathrm ds. \end{equation} Here $b_0,b_1$ depend only on the fixed left cutoff. Globally $0\leq -g_\eta (x)\leq m_0(x+2)$ for $x\geq 0$. Let $G(w)=-\int _0^\infty (k_ r(w)-1)\, \mathrm dr$ for $w\ne 0$ on $E$. Gaussian integration gives the uniform bound 8.37 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rotational-off-pole-value} -F_\eta (t,w)\leq C\eta \bigl (1+\log ^+(1/\operatorname {dist}_ E(w,0)^2)\bigr ),\quad t>0. \end{equation} Indeed the nearest Gaussian has integral bounded by $C+2\log ^+(1/\operatorname {dist}_ E(w,0)^2)$ on $(0,1]$; the other lattice terms have bounded integral and large times decay. The same bound applies after the cutoff. On a fixed $I\Subset (0,\infty )$, $\vartheta =1$ for small $\eta $ and $t_\eta (x)\leq \exp (-c/(2\eta ^3))$. Every fixed $x$ derivative of $t_\eta $ has this bound times a polynomial in $\eta ^{-1}$. On compact fiber sets away from zero, \[  F_\eta (t_\eta (x),w)/\eta \longrightarrow G(w) \quad \text{in }C^\ell \text{ for every fixed }\ell .  \] To verify derivatives, subtract $G$ from $G_ t=F_\eta (t,\cdot )/\eta $: $G_ t-G=\int _0^ t(k_ r-1)\, \mathrm dr=-t+O(\exp (-d^2/(Ct)))$ when $d$ stays positive. Differentiated Gaussian errors have only polynomial factors in $t^{-1}$, and repeated $x$ differentiation preserves their decay. Together with ( 8.36 ) and $0\leq \sup V_\eta \leq C\eta $, this gives uniform $C^\ell $ bounds for $u_\eta $ on each such fixed compact product set, for all sufficiently small $\eta $. The threshold may depend on the set and derivative order. Fix $a_ j=2^{-j-2}$, $j\geq 1$, so $\sum a_ j=1/4$. Choose scales $\eta _ j\downarrow 0$ recursively and write $u_ j=u_{\eta _ j}$, $K_ j=K_{\eta _ j}$. Require the minimum $x$ on $K_ j$ to exceed every earlier $x_{*,i}$ by two. Choose a relatively compact product neighborhood $O_ j$ of $K_ j$, with positive $x$ interval and fiber closure away from zero, on which the earlier $u_ i$ are constant. The $K_ j$ are pairwise disjoint. With $E_ j=\sum _{i<j}a_ i\| u_ i\| _\infty $, impose \begin{gather*}  E_ j\leq a_ j\eta _ j^{-2},\qquad \eta _ j\leq a_ j,\\  a_ j\eta _ j\leq 2^{-j}a_ i\eta _ i\quad (i<j). \end{gather*} For each earlier $O_ i$, require the preceding uniform derivative bounds to hold for $u_ j$ through order $j$. All are finite constraints at stage $j$, achievable by making $\eta _ j$ smaller. They ensure that the future series $\sum _{k>i}a_ ku_ k$ converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $O_ i$: for every fixed derivative order the sufficiently late terms have a uniform bound there, and $\sum a_ k<\infty $. These constraints also give $\sum _{k>j}a_ k\eta _ k\leq a_ j\eta _ j$. On $K_ j$ the coordinate and distance estimates are \[  x\leq C_ c\eta _ j^{-1},\qquad \log ^+(1/\operatorname {dist}_ E(w,0)^2)\leq C_ c\eta _ j^{-3}.  \] Using ( 8.37 ), the global slope bound on $g_ k$, and the supremum constants, the future depth is at most \[  C_ c\eta _ j^{-3}\sum _{k>j}a_ k\eta _ k +C_ c\eta _ j^{-1}\sum _{k>j}a_ k \leq C_ c a_ j\eta _ j^{-2}+C_ c\eta _ j^{-1}/4.  \] The last term is at most a fixed multiple of $a_ j\eta _ j^{-2}$ since $\eta _ j\leq a_ j$. Including the earlier and current terms, there is a fixed $C_*>0$, independent of the scales, such that 8.38 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rotational-series-depth} -\sum _ i a_ iu_ i\leq C_*a_ j\eta _ j^{-2}\quad \text{on }K_ j. \end{equation} Fix this constant before the scale choice. Since $\sqrt T W(T)$ is unbounded, at each stage choose arbitrarily large $T_ j$ such that \[  \frac D{\sqrt{C_*}}a_ j^{5/2}\sqrt{T_ j}W(T_ j)\geq 1, \qquad \eta _ j=\sqrt{C_*a_ j/T_ j},  \] and so small a scale that all finite preceding constraints hold. Such values occur arbitrarily far out because $W$ is finite on compact intervals. Thus the recursive choice is possible. The smooth nonpositive partial sums $v_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}a_ ju_ j$ decrease, and \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ N =(1-\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j)\omega +\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\geq \tfrac 34\omega .  \] By theorem 1.4.2 , $\int _ X(-v_ N)\, \mathrm dV\leq C\sum _ j a_ j<+\infty $. Thus corollary 1.4.3 gives a $\omega $-plurisubharmonic limit $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 3\omega /4$. Its supremum is finite and nonpositive. On $O_ j$ the earlier terms are constant and the future series converges smoothly. Thus $v$ is smooth there and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq a_ j(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)$ pointwise. The determinant inequality for positive Hermitian matrices gives on $K_ j$ \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (v)\geq a_ j^3(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^3.  \] On these sets the extended product is the smooth product: on a compact neighborhood of $K_ j$ all sufficiently deep canonical truncations equal $v$. Set $U=v-\sup _ Xv$. Since $\sup v\leq 0$, $-U\leq -v$, and its local currents are unchanged. Monotonicity of $W$ and ( 8.38 ) give \[  \int _{K_ j}W(-U)\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U) \geq D a_ j^3\eta _ j^{-1}W(C_*a_ j\eta _ j^{-2}) =\frac D{\sqrt{C_*}}a_ j^{5/2}\sqrt{T_ j}W(T_ j)\geq 1.  \] The disjoint $K_ j$ prove infinite total mass for this single potential. They lie in its smooth locus, so no mass is assigned to poles. $\square$

title: 8.8.3 Concentration at the critical weight
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text:
8.8.3 Concentration at the critical weight Lemma 8.8.8 . Suppose $\sqrt t\, W(t)$ is bounded but does not tend to zero. There are smooth $u_ j\in \mathcal R$ converging in capacity to $g\in \mathcal R$ such that a weak cluster measure of $
u _{W,u_ j}$ gives positive mass to the pole divisor \[  H=\pi ^{-1}\{ [z_0:z_1:z_2]:z_0=0\} ,  \] whereas $
u _{W,g}(H)=0$. Proof. Use the correction chosen in the proof of theorem 8.8.7 . Its plateau and its late supplement satisfy \[  \int r^0_\eta =K\eta x_{m pre}+O(\eta ),\qquad \int s_\eta =O(\sqrt{\eta L})+O(\eta ),\qquad \eta x_{m pre}	o \ell .  \] Therefore $m_\eta 	o m:=K\ell >0$. Shrink the fixed $c$ so that $m$ satisfies all the established positivity margins. On each fixed finite $x$ interval, $r_\eta $ and all its derivatives tend to zero; the late supplement escapes the interval. Thus $g_\eta $ converges smoothly there to \[  g(x)=-m\int _{-\infty }^ x(x-s)\psi (s)\, \mathrm ds.  \] It is zero for $x\leq -2$ and equals $-m(x-\mu _\psi )$ for $x\geq -1$. The same margins give $\mu +g'>0$ and $g''+\mu (1-\mu )\geq 0$ at finite $x$. Across $H$, its extension has logarithmic singularity of coefficient $m$: a local defining function $\zeta $ gives $g=m\log |\zeta |^2+O(1)$. Its upper semicontinuous extension is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, has supremum zero and belongs to $\mathcal R$. The bound ( 8.37 ) and $F_\eta \leq C\eta $ imply that, on compact base sets away from $H$, each fixed-depth exceptional set lies in an exponentially shrinking tube about the local holomorphic zero section $w=0$. These tubes have capacity tending to zero. Indeed, on a relatively compact coordinate chart, $\log |w|^2$ is locally integrable and plurisubharmonic; the weighted Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate of section 1.6 bounds the relative capacity of $\{ \log |w|^2<-T\} $ by $C/T$. A finite cover and the local capacity comparison transfer this estimate to $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $. The corrections converge uniformly on compact base sets away from $H$, including $\xi =0$, and the supremum normalization is $O(\eta )$. Since $g$ has its logarithmic pole on $H$, the estimate ( 1.26 ) gives neighborhoods of $H$ with arbitrarily small capacity. Removing one such neighborhood proves $u_\eta 	o g$ in capacity. Assume $\sqrt t\, W(t)$ is bounded but does not tend to zero. Choose the preceding sequence of cores with weighted mass bounded below by $c_0>0$. The proved upper bound makes their full weighted measures uniformly finite, so a subsequence has a weak cluster measure $
u $. For each fixed closed neighborhood $H_ r$ of $H$, all sufficiently late cores lie in $H_ r$. Portmanteau gives $
u (H_ r)\geq c_0$; decreasing continuity of the finite measure gives $
u (H)\geq c_0$. But $
u _{W,g}(H)=0$ by its defining non-pluripolar truncation. $\square$ Theorem 8.8.9 . Within $\mathcal R$ the following assertions hold. Every individual $
u _{W,u}$ is finite if and only if $\sup _{t\gg 1}\sqrt t\, W(t)<\infty $. This is also equivalent to a uniform total-mass bound. In this case \[  \sup _{u\in \mathcal R}
u _{W,u}(X)\leq 12Q(W).  \] If the condition fails there is one $u\in \mathcal R$ with infinite measure. Uniform deep tails hold if and only if $\sqrt t\, W(t)	o 0$. For all $u\in \mathcal R$ and $T\geq 0$, \[  
u _{W,u}(\{ -u>T\} )\leq 12Q_ T(W).  \] The inequality is understood in the extended sense. Uniform absolute continuity relative to $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ holds if and only if $\sqrt t\, W(t)	o 0$. The assignment $u\mapsto 
u _{W,u}$ is a map into finite measures and is continuous from capacity convergence in $\mathcal R$ to weak measure convergence if and only if $\sqrt t\, W(t)	o 0$. When $\sqrt t\, W(t)$ is bounded but does not tend to zero, there are smooth $u_ j\in \mathcal R$ converging in capacity to $g\in \mathcal R$, whose weighted measures have a weak cluster measure charging the pole divisor of $g$. Proof. The sufficient conditions are proposition 8.8.3 . The necessary uniform mass and tail conditions follow from corollary 8.8.6 , whose smooth potentials are invariant. If $\sqrt t\, W(t)$ is unbounded, theorem 8.8.7 disproves universal individual finiteness and prevents a map into finite measures. For uniform absolute continuity, the concentration regions of theorem 8.8.5 lie in $\{ x\geq c_1/\eta \} $ for a fixed $c_1>0$, hence in shrinking neighborhoods of $H$. The globally defined $h_ H=\log (|z_0|^2/|z|^2)$ has supremum zero and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ H= eta +[H]\geq 0$. Its sublevel estimate ( 1.26 ) shows that these neighborhoods have capacity tending to zero. If $\limsup _{t	o +\infty }\sqrt t\, W(t)>0$, choose the scales so that $D\eta ^{-1}W(B\eta ^{-2})$ stays bounded below. The weighted masses on these regions then violate uniform absolute continuity. Finally, lemma 8.8.8 disproves capacity-to-weak continuity whenever $\sqrt t\, W(t)$ is bounded but does not tend to zero. $\square$ Corollary 8.8.10 . For a weight $W$ satisfying the assumptions of this section and agreeing for large $t$ with \[  W_{p,a}(t)=(1+t)^{-p}[\log (\mathrm e+t)]^{-a},  \] universal individual finiteness and uniform total-mass bounds in $\mathcal R$ hold exactly when $p>1/2$, or $p=1/2$ and $a\geq 0$. Uniform deep tails, uniform capacity absolute continuity and capacity-to-weak continuity hold exactly when $p>1/2$, or $p=1/2$ and $a>0$. Proof. Apply theorem 8.8.9 to $\sqrt t\, W_{p,a}(t)\sim t^{1/2-p}(\log t)^{-a}$. A smooth decreasing modification on a compact interval changes none of these conditions. $\square$ The necessary conditions and the single infinite-measure example also apply to the class of all normalized potentials on $X$. The sufficient conditions proved here use the $U(2)$ symmetry. For the unrestricted class, proposition 7.3.1 still gives the sufficient condition $\int _0^{+\infty }(1+t)(-W'(t))\, \mathrm dt<+\infty $; its optimal damping rate remains open.

title: 8.9 Limits of shrinking smooth potentials
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 8.9 Limits of shrinking smooth potentials When the bounded mass property fails, corollary 7.5.2 produces smooth potentials converging to zero whose Monge–Ampère measures keep an excess mass in the limit. On the Hopf threefold we can determine exactly which excess measures occur: they are the lifts of arbitrary base measures by the fiber probability measures. The proof combines the intermediate currents of proposition 7.5.3 with averaging over the automorphism group. On a general Hermitian manifold, the restrictions on the intermediate currents in proposition 7.5.3 are still necessary; we do not know whether they are sufficient, or what the support and pluripolar behavior of shrinking defects can be in general. We keep the Hopf threefold $X$, its projection $\pi :X\to \mathbb P^2$, and the forms $\omega =\alpha +\beta $ of the previous sections. For $p\in \mathbb P^2$, let $h_ p$ be the Haar probability measure on the elliptic fiber $\pi ^{-1}(p)$, that is, the measure $\mathrm{d}A_ E$ transported by the action of $E$. For a finite positive measure $\mu $ on the base, define its fiberwise lift $\mathcal L\mu $ by \[  \int _ X\varphi \, \mathrm{d}\mathcal L\mu =\int _{\mathbb P^2}\left(\int _{\pi ^{-1}(p)}\varphi \, \mathrm{d}h_ p\right)\mathrm{d}\mu (p), \qquad \varphi \in C(X).  \] Since fiber integrals of continuous functions are continuous in $p$, the map $\mathcal L$ is weakly continuous. The normalization $\int _{\pi ^{-1}(p)}\beta =2$ gives 8.39 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-fiber-lift-normalization} \mathcal L\mu =\tfrac 12\beta \wedge \pi ^*\mu , \qquad \mathcal L(\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2)=\tfrac 16\omega ^3. \end{equation} Here $\pi ^*\mu $ denotes the pullback of a top-degree current by the submersion $\pi $; locally it is the base measure with constant coefficients in the fiber directions. For a Hermitian form $\Omega $ on $X$, put \[  M_\Omega (f)=\int _ X(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^3,\qquad V_\Omega =\int _ X\Omega ^3  \] for smooth real $f$, and let $b$ be a real number. To use this scalar identity in a weak limit, we also need a positive measure that represents the quadratic term. Lemma 8.9.1 . Let $f$ be smooth, $0<t<1$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\geq -t\omega $. Set $H=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f+t\omega $, $d=M_\omega (f)-6$, and $
u =3\omega \wedge H^2$. Then $d\geq 0$ and \[   egin{gathered} \int _ X\omega ^2\wedge H=6t,\qquad \int _ X\omega \wedge H^2=d/3+6t^2,\qquad \int _ XH^3=td+6t^3,\  igl \| (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^3-\omega ^3-
u  igr \| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 36t+2td+24t^3. \end{gathered}  \] Proof. title: 8.9.3 Fiber measures
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 8.9.3 Fiber measures The intermediate currents force every shrinking defect to be a lift of a base measure, and the automorphisms of $X$ realize all such lifts. Lemma 8.9.3 . Let $f_ j=t_ ju_ j$, where $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ are smooth, $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$ and $0<t_ j\to 0$. Suppose that $M_\omega (f_ j)=6+m$ and $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j)^3\rightharpoonup \omega ^3+\sigma $. Then there is a unique positive measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb P^2$, of mass $m$, such that \[  \sigma =\mathcal L\mu ,\qquad (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j+t_ j\omega )^2\rightharpoonup \tfrac 16\pi ^*\mu .  \] Proof. Put $H_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j+t_ j\omega $. By proposition 7.5.3 , applied with $h=\omega $ and $n=3$, every convergent subsequence of $H_ j^2$ has a positive closed limit $K$ with $\sigma =3\omega \wedge K$; moreover $\alpha \wedge K=0$, because $\alpha $ is closed and semipositive, so that $\alpha \wedge K$ is a positive measure with $\int _ X\alpha \wedge K=0$. In holomorphic coordinates $(\xi _1,\xi _2,w)$ on a local trivialization of the elliptic bundle, the coefficient matrix of $K$ on the three exterior pairs is positive semidefinite as a matrix of measures. To see this directly, note that positivity of the matrices of $H_ j^2$ passes to the limit when they are tested against constant vectors, and take Radon–Nikodym derivatives with respect to the diagonal trace. Since $\alpha $ is strictly positive in the horizontal directions, the identity $\alpha \wedge K=0$ makes both diagonal entries containing $\mathrm{d}w$ vanish. Positivity then makes their rows and columns vanish, so only the horizontal top-degree coefficient remains. Since $K$ is closed, both real fiber derivatives of that coefficient vanish in the sense of distributions. Testing against a compactly supported base function times a nonconstant Fourier mode on $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+2\pi \mathrm{i}\mathbb Z)$ shows that every such mode vanishes. By density of trigonometric polynomials in $C(E)$, the coefficient is a base measure times the constant fiber area. Changes of bundle coordinates translate $w$ by a holomorphic function of the base and preserve that area. Thus $K=\pi ^*\tau $ for a positive measure $\tau $ on $\mathbb P^2$. Since $\alpha \wedge K=0$, ( 8.39 ) gives $\sigma =3\beta \wedge \pi ^*\tau =\mathcal L(6\tau )$. Therefore $\mu =6\tau =\pi _*\sigma $ is uniquely determined by $\sigma $, and it has mass $m$. In particular, every subsequential limit of $H_ j^2$ is the same, which proves convergence of the entire sequence. $\square$ Lemma 8.9.4 . For every $p\in \mathbb P^2$, the measure $mh_ p$ is a shrinking defect for $(\omega ,6+m)$. Proof. Start with smooth $f_ j=t_ ju_ j$ realizing the shrinking defect $(m/6)\omega ^3=\mathcal L(m\, \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2)$, and put $H_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j+t_ j\omega $. By lemma 8.9.3 , $H_ j^2\rightharpoonup (m/6)\alpha ^2$, while $H_ j$ has trace mass $O(t_ j)$. Fix $A\in GL(3,\mathbb C)$, regarded as an automorphism of $X$, and let $a$ be the induced projective transformation of $\mathbb P^2$. Choose $C_ A\geq 1$ with $A^*\omega \leq C_ A\omega $, and put \[  R_ A=C_ A\omega -A^*\omega \geq 0,\qquad H_ j^ A=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f_ j\circ A)+C_ At_ j\omega =A^*H_ j+t_ jR_ A.  \] For this fixed $A$, the trace mass of $A^*H_ j$ is $O_ A(t_ j)$, and the positive difference $(H_ j^ A)^2-A^*(H_ j^2)$ has trace mass $O_ A(t_ j^2)$. Since $\alpha =\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, it follows that \[  (H_ j^ A)^2\rightharpoonup \frac m6\pi ^*(a^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2), \qquad 3\omega \wedge (H_ j^ A)^2\rightharpoonup \mathcal L(m a^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2).  \] The limiting measure has mass $m$, so the integral identity of lemma 8.9.1 , applied with the parameter $C_ At_ j$, gives $d_ j^ A=M_\omega (f_ j\circ A)-6\to m$. For large $j$, multiply $f_ j\circ A$ by $\sqrt{m/d_ j^ A}\to 1$. The mass is then exactly $6+m$, and the weak limit is unchanged. The underlying normalized potential is $u_ j\circ A/C_ A\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, with parameter $C_ At_ j\sqrt{m/d_ j^ A}\to 0$. The total-variation estimate of lemma 8.9.1 therefore shows that $\mathcal L(m\, a^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2)$ is a shrinking defect; any prescribed bounds $\varepsilon _ j$ are met by passing to a sufficiently late subsequence. Now take $A_ l=\operatorname {diag}(R_ l^{-1},1,1)$, $R_ l\to +\infty $. Since \[  a_ l^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2=(a_ l^{-1})_*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2,  \] and $a_ l^{-1}[q_0:q_1:q_2]=[R_ lq_0:q_1:q_2]\to [1:0:0]$ outside the hyperplane $\{ q_0=0\} $, which has zero volume, dominated convergence gives $a_ l^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2\rightharpoonup \delta _{[1:0:0]}$. By weak continuity of $\mathcal L$, the shrinking defects $\mathcal L(m\, a_ l^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2)$ converge to $mh_{[1:0:0]}$. For each $l$, choose one corrected potential for $A_ l$, sufficiently late in its sequence that its parameter is less than $\varepsilon _ l$ and its measure differs from the corresponding limit by less than $1/l$ on the first $l$ functions of a fixed dense sequence of test functions. This diagonal sequence has the exact mass $6+m$ and the limit $\omega ^3+mh_{[1:0:0]}$. Unitary automorphisms move this fiber to any prescribed fiber. $\square$ Theorem 8.9.5 . For $b>6$, the shrinking defects for $(\omega ,b)$ are exactly $\mathcal L\mu $, where $\mu $ ranges over all positive measures on $\mathbb P^2$ of mass $b-6$. Each such defect has support $\pi ^{-1}(\operatorname {supp}\mu )$ and has no point atoms. It charges no pluripolar sets if and only if $\mu $ charges no pluripolar sets on $\mathbb P^2$. Proof. Put $m=b-6$. Necessity follows from lemma 8.9.3 . Finite convex combinations of the measures $mh_ p$ are shrinking defects by lemma 8.9.4 , proposition 8.9.2 , the latter applied to an atomic measure $\rho $ supported on unitary maps that move a fixed fiber to the desired fibers. Approximate an arbitrary base measure of mass $m$ by finite atomic measures of the same mass, using finite partitions of diameter tending to zero. Weak continuity of $\mathcal L$ and the diagonal choice on dense test functions used in the preceding proof give a realizing sequence for every prescribed sequence $\varepsilon _ j$. Every nonempty open subset of a fiber has positive Haar measure. Local trivializations therefore show that $\mathcal L\mu $ has support $\pi ^{-1}(\operatorname {supp}\mu )$, and the fiber measures have no point atoms. If $B$ is a pluripolar subset of the base, local plurisubharmonic functions whose pole sets contain $B$ pull back by the submersion to such functions on $X$. Hence $\pi ^{-1}(B)$ is pluripolar, and $\mathcal L\mu (\pi ^{-1}(B))=\mu (B)$; thus $\mathcal L\mu $ charges a pluripolar set whenever $\mu $ does. Conversely, suppose that $\mu $ charges no pluripolar subset of the base. Cover a pluripolar set in $X$ by countably many local product charts, each carrying a plurisubharmonic function $q(\xi ,w)\not\equiv -\infty $ whose pole set contains the part of the set in that chart. For a relatively compact disk $D$ in the fiber direction, the function \[  F(\xi )=\frac1{|D|}\int _ Dq(\xi ,w)\, \mathrm{d}A(w)  \] is plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $ on a smaller base chart. Indeed, local integrability of $q$ and Fubini's theorem show that $F$ is locally integrable, and in particular finite almost everywhere; a common upper bound and the reverse Fatou lemma give upper semicontinuity; and integrating the submean inequalities in the base directions gives the submean property. The restriction of $q$ to a fiber is either subharmonic with a pole set of zero area or identically $-\infty $. The fibers of the second kind lie over the pluripolar set $\{ F=-\infty \} $, which has zero $\mu $-measure. Integrating the Haar measures of the fibers against $\mu $ therefore shows that each local pole set has zero $\mathcal L\mu $-measure, and the countable cover proves the assertion for this pluripolar set. For arbitrary pluripolar subsets, the same argument applies to Borel pole sets containing them, with outer measure. Similarly, for the first implication, a Borel $\mathcal L\mu $-null set containing $\pi ^{-1}(B)$ has a measurable fiber-mass function equal to one on $B$, which gives the corresponding outer-measure statement. $\square$ For every nonempty closed set $F\subseteq \mathbb P^2$, a measure $m\sum _{l\geq 1}2^{-l}\delta _{p_ l}$ carried by a countable dense subset $\{ p_ l\} $ of $F$ has support $F$. Thus every closed set of the form $\pi ^{-1}(F)$ is the support of a shrinking defect. The fibers themselves are pluripolar in a global sense: for the fiber over $[1:0:0]$, the function \[  \psi =\log \frac{|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2}{|z|^2},\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq -\alpha ,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq \beta \geq 0.  \] is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, and its pole set is exactly that fiber; unitary maps give the other fibers. In particular, for $0\leq \lambda \leq 1$ and $p\in \mathbb P^2$, the measure \[  m\lambda h_ p+\frac{m(1-\lambda )}6\omega ^3  \] is a shrinking defect. It gives mass $m\lambda $ to the pluripolar fiber $\pi ^{-1}(p)$, while every pluripolar set has mass at most $m\lambda $. For $0<\lambda <1$ its support is all of $X$, despite this positive mass on a pluripolar set.

title: 8.9.4 Changing the Hermitian metric
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 8.9.4 Changing the Hermitian metric For a general Hermitian form, the fiber Haar measures are replaced by the normalized area measures of the form. Let $\Omega $ be any Hermitian form on the Hopf threefold $X$. Its restriction to each elliptic fiber has positive area \[  A_\Omega (p)=\int _{\pi ^{-1}(p)}\Omega .  \] These areas depend smoothly on $p$ and are bounded above and below by positive constants. Define the probability measures $h_ p^\Omega =\Omega |_{\pi ^{-1}(p)}/A_\Omega (p)$ on the fibers, and define the lift $\mathcal L_\Omega \mu $ of a finite positive measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb P^2$ by the formula defining $\mathcal L\mu $, with $h_ p^\Omega $ in place of $h_ p$. Theorem 8.9.6 . For every Hermitian form $\Omega $ on $X$ and every $b>V_\Omega $, the shrinking defects for $(\Omega ,b)$ are exactly \[  \mathcal L_\Omega \mu ,\qquad \mu \geq 0,\qquad \mu (\mathbb P^2)=b-V_\Omega .  \] Their supports are $\pi ^{-1}(\operatorname {supp}\mu )$, they have no point atoms, and they charge no pluripolar sets exactly when $\mu $ charges no base pluripolar sets. Moreover, $v_+(\Omega )=+\infty $. Proof. Put $m=b-V_\Omega >0$. For necessity, let $\sigma $ be a shrinking defect for $(\Omega ,b)$. Proposition 7.5.3 , applied with $h=\Omega $, gives a positive closed limit $K$ of the squares of the intermediate forms with $\sigma =3\Omega \wedge K$, and $\alpha \wedge K=0$ as in the proof of lemma 8.9.3 . The local coefficient and Fourier argument of that proof gives $K=\pi ^*\tau $ for a positive measure $\tau $ on $\mathbb P^2$. Consequently \[  \sigma =\mathcal L_\Omega \mu ,\qquad \mu =3A_\Omega \tau =\pi _*\sigma ,  \] and $\mu $ has mass $m$. Conversely, fix such a $\mu $ and set $\tau =\mu /(3A_\Omega )$. By theorem 8.9.5 , choose a sequence $f_ j=t_ ju_ j$ realizing the shrinking defect $\mathcal L(6\tau )$ for $\omega $. The positive forms $H_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j+t_ j\omega $ have trace mass $O(t_ j)$, and $H_ j^2\rightharpoonup \pi ^*\tau $ by lemma 8.9.3 . Choose $C\geq 1$ with $\omega \leq C\Omega $, and put \[  R=C\Omega -\omega \geq 0,\qquad G_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j+Ct_ j\Omega =H_ j+t_ jR\geq 0.  \] The trace mass of $G_ j$ is $O(t_ j)$, and $G_ j^2-H_ j^2$ has trace mass $O(t_ j^2)$. Thus $G_ j^2\rightharpoonup \pi ^*\tau $ and $3\Omega \wedge G_ j^2\rightharpoonup \mathcal L_\Omega \mu $. Unlike $\omega $, the form $\Omega $ need not be Gauduchon, so the mass polynomial may have a linear term. Define \[  \ell _ j=3\int _ X\Omega ^2\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j=O(t_ j),\qquad q_ j=3\int _ X\Omega \wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j)^2\longrightarrow m.  \] These estimates follow by expanding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j=G_ j-Ct_ j\Omega $ and using the preceding trace bounds. Stokes' formula removes the cubic integral, so \[  M_\Omega (\lambda f_ j)=V_\Omega +\lambda \ell _ j+\lambda ^2q_ j.  \] For large $j$, $q_ j>0$. The positive root 8.41 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-hermitian-mass-correction} \lambda _ j=\frac{-\ell _ j+\sqrt{\ell _ j^2+4mq_ j}}{2q_ j} \longrightarrow 1 \end{equation} gives $M_\Omega (\lambda _ jf_ j)=b$. The normalized function $U_ j=u_ j/C$ is $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic, and $w_ j=\lambda _ j f_ j=r_ jU_ j$ with $r_ j=\lambda _ jCt_ j\to 0$. To identify the full weak limit, first note that expanding $G_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j+Ct_ j\Omega $ gives \[  \int _ XG_ j^3=Ct_ jq_ j+(Ct_ j)^2\ell _ j+(Ct_ j)^3V_\Omega =O(t_ j).  \] Hence $G_ j^3\to 0$ in total variation. text: Theorem 8.9.6 . For every Hermitian form $\Omega $ on $X$ and every $b>V_\Omega $, the shrinking defects for $(\Omega ,b)$ are exactly \[  \mathcal L_\Omega \mu ,\qquad \mu \geq 0,\qquad \mu (\mathbb P^2)=b-V_\Omega .  \] Their supports are $\pi ^{-1}(\operatorname {supp}\mu )$, they have no point atoms, and they charge no pluripolar sets exactly when $\mu $ charges no base pluripolar sets. The local coefficient and Fourier argument of that proof gives $K=\pi ^*\tau $ for a positive measure $\tau $ on $\mathbb P^2$. Consequently \[  \sigma =\mathcal L_\Omega \mu ,\qquad \mu =3A_\Omega \tau =\pi _*\sigma ,  \] and $\mu $ has mass $m$. Conversely, fix such a $\mu $ and set $\tau =\mu /(3A_\Omega )$. The positive expansion \[  (\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^3 =(1-r_ j)^3\Omega ^3 +3(1-r_ j)^2\lambda _ j\Omega ^2\wedge G_ j +3(1-r_ j)\lambda _ j^2\Omega \wedge G_ j^2 +\lambda _ j^3G_ j^3  \] converges weakly to $\Omega ^3+\mathcal L_\Omega \mu $, since the second and fourth terms tend to zero in total variation. title: 9 Smooth Monge–Ampère equations
text: 9 Smooth Monge–Ampère equations Throughout this chapter, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$ and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a smooth positive volume form. Given $F\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, we seek a smooth real potential $u$ and a scalar $b\in \mathbb R$ satisfying 9.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:smooth-ma} \omega _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{F+b}\mathrm{d}V,\qquad \omega _ u>0. \end{equation} Here $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and adding a constant to $u$ does not change the equation. For a closed background, integration determines $b$ from the prescribed density. For a Hermitian background, the total mass can depend on $u$, so the potential and the scalar must be found together. The existence proof combines weighted integration, which bounds the normalized potential, with a trace estimate for the complex Hessian, which gives uniform ellipticity. The adjoint probability measure of proposition 4.8.1 supplies the compatibility condition for the linearized equation. Including $b$ as an unknown removes this obstruction, and the estimates give the compactness needed for the continuity method. A positive exponential of the potential instead makes the equation strictly monotone and gives existence without an additional scalar. After proving existence, we differentiate the solution with respect to the prescribed logarithmic density. The same adjoint probability measure gives the first and second variations of $b$, proving concavity and a Lipschitz bound. On the Hopf threefold of chapter 8 , the fiber-energy formula measures exactly how its normalization differs from the closed-background formula. The last part of the chapter concerns a different variation of the metric. For $n\geq 2$, we deform its $(n-1)$st power through a scalar Aeppli ansatz. If the initial metric is Gauduchon, this deformation preserves both the Gauduchon condition and its Aeppli class. The first-order torsion terms have a specific matrix structure, which makes the second-derivative estimate possible; rescaling then reduces the gradient bound to a Liouville theorem on $\mathbb C^ n$. The resulting uniqueness concerns the scalar ansatz. We finish by studying the variation of its normalization constant.

title: 9.1 Scalar bounds and uniqueness
text: 9.1 Scalar bounds and uniqueness Evaluating the equation at the extrema of the potential bounds the normalization scalar in terms of the prescribed data. Applied to the difference of two solutions, the same argument shows that their scalars agree, and ellipticity then determines the potential up to a constant. The scalar bounds will also give uniform control along the continuity path. Theorem 9.1.1 (Tosatti–Weinkove) . For every smooth real $F$, ( 9.1 ) has a unique pair $(u,b)\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)\times \mathbb R$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$. In dimension one, integration determines $\mathrm{e}^ b=\int _ X\omega /\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F \mathrm{d}V$, and the remaining equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{e}^{F+b}\mathrm{d}V-\omega $ is a Poisson equation whose right-hand side has integral zero, so it has a smooth solution, unique up to a constant; positivity of $\omega _ u$ is automatic. Thus the theorem holds in that dimension, and we prove it for $n\geq 2$ at the end of section 9.5 . Proposition 9.1.2 . Every solution of ( 9.1 ) satisfies \[  \inf _ X\! \left(\log \frac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}-F\right) \leq b\leq \sup _ X\! \left(\log \frac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}-F\right).  \] Proof. At a maximum point $x_+$ of $u$, the real $(1,1)$-form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is nonpositive, so $0<\omega _ u\leq \omega $ there. Hence $\omega _ u^ n(x_+)\leq \omega ^ n(x_+)$, and $b\leq \log (\omega ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)(x_+)-F(x_+)$. At a minimum point the reverse argument gives the lower bound. $\square$ When $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$, integration gives the familiar explicit formula 9.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:closed-b} b=\log \frac{\int _ X\omega ^ n}{\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F \mathrm{d}V}. \end{equation} The same formula holds whenever the mass-invariance criterion of theorem 2.2.2 is satisfied. In general, integrating the equation gives only \[  \mathrm{e}^ b=\frac{\mathrm M_\omega (u)}{\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F \mathrm{d}V},  \] where $\mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega _ u^ n$ is the mass of theorem 2.2.1 ; the numerator depends on the unknown potential. Proposition 9.1.3 . Suppose $(u,b)$ and $(v,c)$ are smooth solutions of ( 9.1 ) with the same $F$ and $\mathrm{d}V$. Then $b=c$ and $u-v$ is constant. Proof. At a maximum of $u-v$, one has $\omega _ u\leq \omega _ v$, so the equations give $\mathrm{e}^ b\leq \mathrm{e}^ c$. At a minimum one obtains $\mathrm{e}^ b\geq \mathrm{e}^ c$. Therefore $b=c$. Put $h=u-v$ and $\eta _ t=\omega _ v+t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=(1-t)\omega _ v+t\omega _ u$ for $0\leq t\leq 1$. These forms are strictly positive. Subtracting the logarithms of the two equations and writing the difference as the integral of its derivative along the segment, we obtain \[  0=\int _0^1 n\, \frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \eta _ t^{n-1}}{\eta _ t^ n}\, \mathrm{d}t.  \] The right-hand side is a linear second-order operator applied to $h$. Its coefficients are smooth, its principal part is uniformly elliptic on the compact manifold, and it has no zeroth-order term. The strong maximum principle therefore implies that $h$ is constant. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.1.1 (Tosatti–Weinkove)
text: Theorem 9.1.1 (Tosatti–Weinkove) . For every smooth real $F$, ( 9.1 ) has a unique pair $(u,b)\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)\times \mathbb R$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$. of theorem 9.1.1 . The case $n=1$ was treated after the statement of the theorem. For $n\geq 2$ put $G=F+\log (\mathrm{d}V/\omega ^ n)$ and consider \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n=\mathrm{e}^{tG+b_ t}\omega ^ n, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ t=0,\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] At $t=0$, take $u_0=0$ and $b_0=0$. The local implicit-function argument in proposition 9.3.1 , with the additive constant temporarily fixed by a linear mean, shows that the set of solvable parameters is open. At every solvable parameter, proposition 9.1.2 gives \[  -\sup _ X(tG)\leq b_ t\leq -\inf _ X(tG), \qquad \mathrm{e}^{tG+b_ t}\leq \mathrm{e}^{\operatorname {osc}_ XG}.  \] The constants $b_ t$ are therefore uniformly bounded, and theorem 9.2.3 bounds $u_ t$ in $C^0$. By corollary 9.4.4 , the solutions are bounded in every $C^ k$ norm. Along any sequence of solvable parameters converging in $[0,1]$, a subsequence of $(u_ t,b_ t)$ therefore converges smoothly to a solution; uniform equivalence of the metrics preserves strict positivity, and the supremum normalization passes to the limit. Thus the solvable set is closed. Since it is nonempty, open and closed, connectedness of $[0,1]$ gives a solution at $t=1$, and proposition 9.1.3 gives uniqueness. $\square$

title: 9.2 The potential bound from weighted integration

text: 9.2 The potential bound from weighted integration We now show that an upper bound for the density controls the normalized potential, following the method of Cherrier. Integrating the equation against $\mathrm{e}^{-pu}$ produces a gradient term and mixed weighted masses; a finite recurrence absorbs the latter together with the torsion error. Moser iteration then gives a set of uniformly positive volume near the minimum, and normalized $L^1$ compactness bounds that minimum. Norms below are computed with respect to the fixed metric $\omega $. Lemma 9.2.1 . There is a constant $C$ depending on $\omega $ such that, for every positive $(1,1)$-form $\eta $, every smooth real $f$, every $\delta >0$, and $0\leq k\leq n-2$, \[  \begin{split}  |\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k-2}| \leq {}& \frac C\delta \, \mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k-1}\\ & +C\delta \, \eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k}. \end{split}  \] Here the absolute value of a top-degree form is the absolute value of its coefficient relative to the positive volume form $\omega ^ n$. Proof. At a given point, choose an $\omega $-unitary frame in which $\eta $ is diagonal, with positive eigenvalues $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n$. Expand $\eta ^ k$ as a sum over $k$-element subsets $I$ of $\{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $, with coefficients that are positive dimensional multiples of $\lambda _ I=\prod _{i\in I}\lambda _ i$. After wedging with $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \omega ^{n-k-2}$, each surviving term is a bounded coefficient of $\mathrm{d}\omega $ times $\lambda _ I$ times one first derivative $f_ a$ with $a\notin I$. Young's inequality bounds its absolute value by \[  C\lambda _ I|f_ a|\leq (C/\delta )\lambda _ I|f_ a|^2 +C\delta \lambda _ I.  \] The sum of the first terms is bounded by a fixed multiple of the first form on the right of the assertion, whose diagonal expansion consists of the terms $\lambda _ I|f_ a|^2$ with $a\notin I$. The second form on the right contains all the $\lambda _ I$. Since there are finitely many indices and $\mathrm{d}\omega $ is bounded, the constant $C$ is uniform. $\square$ Lemma 9.2.2 . Suppose $u$ is smooth, $\eta =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, and $\eta ^ n\leq \Lambda \omega ^ n$ for a fixed $\Lambda >0$. There are constants $p_0\geq 1$ and $C$ depending only on $\omega $ and $\Lambda $ such that \[  \int _ X\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2})\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2})\wedge \omega ^{n-1} \leq Cp\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\omega ^ n\quad (p\geq p_0).  \] Proof. For a fixed real $p\geq 1$, define $M_ k$ for $0\leq k\leq n$ and $J_ k$ for $0\leq k\leq n-1$ by \[  M_ k=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k},\qquad J_ k=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k-1}, \quad J=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}J_ k.  \] All these numbers are nonnegative. The proof first bounds $pJ$ in terms of the masses $M_ k$, and then bounds these masses by a recurrence. Let $T=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k-1}$, so that $\eta ^ n-\omega ^ n=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T$. Since $\mathrm{d}\eta =\mathrm{d}\omega $, differentiation gives \[  \mathrm{d}T=n\sum _{k=0}^{n-2}\eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k-2}\wedge \mathrm{d}\omega .  \] The sum is empty when $n=1$. Stokes' theorem gives the exact identity \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}(\eta ^ n-\omega ^ n) & =\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T\\ & =pJ+\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}T. \end{split}  \] The density assumption bounds the left-hand side above by $(\Lambda +1)M_0$. Apply lemma 9.2.1 to the last integral, with $\delta =K/p$ for a sufficiently large fixed $K$. The contribution proportional to $J/\delta $ is then at most $pJ/2$, and after absorbing it we obtain 9.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weighted-first-bound} pJ\leq CM_0+\frac Cp\sum _{k=0}^{n-2}M_ k. \end{equation} This estimate alone does not suffice, because the mixed weighted masses on the right have not yet been bounded. For $1\leq k\leq n-2$, a second integration by parts gives 9.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weighted-recurrence} M_ k-M_{k-1}=pJ_{k-1}+R_ k, \qquad R_ k=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}(\eta ^{k-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-k}). \end{equation} The derivative in $R_ k$ has two terms, with coefficients $k-1$ and $n-k$. Applying the pointwise estimate with $\delta =1/p$ to each of them, and omitting terms with negative indices, we obtain \[  |R_ k|\leq Cp(J_{k-2}+J_{k-1}) +\frac Cp(M_{k-2}+M_{k-1}), \qquad M_{-1}=J_{-1}=0.  \] Consequently, for $p\geq 1$, \[  M_ k\leq C(M_{k-1}+M_{k-2}+pJ).  \] Induction over the finitely many values of $k$ proves \[  \sum _{k=0}^{n-2}M_ k\leq C(M_0+pJ).  \] For $n=2$ this is immediate, and for $n=1$ the sum is empty. Inserting this bound in ( 9.7 ) gives $pJ\leq CM_0+C'J$. For $p\geq 2C'$ the last term can be absorbed, and $pJ\leq CM_0$. Finally, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2})\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2})\wedge \omega ^{n-1} =\frac{p^2}{4}J_0\leq \frac{p^2}{4}J\leq CpM_0.  \] This proves the claimed estimate for all $p\geq p_0$. $\square$ Theorem 9.2.3 . For each $\Lambda >0$ there is $C_\Lambda $ such that every smooth $u$ with \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu=0,\qquad (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\leq \Lambda \omega ^ n  \] satisfies $\| u\| _\infty \leq C_\Lambda $. Proof. Let $\mathrm{d}\mu =\omega ^ n/\int _ X\omega ^ n$. The Sobolev inequality for the Riemannian metric of $\omega $ gives, for some $\beta >1$ and every smooth real function $w$, \[  \left(\int _ X |w|^{2\beta }\, \mathrm{d}\mu \right)^{1/\beta } \leq C\left(\int _ X\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \omega ^{n-1} +\int _ X|w|^2\, \mathrm{d}\mu \right).  \] We may take $\beta =n/(n-1)$ if $n\geq 2$, and for example $\beta =2$ if $n=1$. Choose $p_0$ as in lemma 9.2.2 . Applying the Sobolev inequality to $w=\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2}$ and using that lemma, we obtain, with $Z=\mathrm{e}^{-u}$, \[  \| Z\| _{L^{p\beta }(\mu )}\leq (Cp)^{1/p}\| Z\| _{L^ p(\mu )} \quad (p\geq p_0).  \] Iterating with $p=p_0\beta ^ j$, $j=0,1,2,\ldots $, we obtain a bound for $\sup _ XZ$; the product of the constants is finite because $\sum _ j(1+\log (p_0\beta ^ j))/(p_0\beta ^ j)<\infty $. Hence, for a uniform $C_1\geq 1$ and $m=\inf _ Xu$, 9.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:near-minimum-integral} \mathrm{e}^{-p_0m}\leq C_1\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-p_0u}\, \mathrm{d}\mu . \end{equation} The right-hand side still involves the unknown potential. Divide by $\mathrm{e}^{-p_0m}$ and set $A=p_0^{-1}\log (2C_1)$. The integrand $\mathrm{e}^{-p_0(u-m)}$ is at most one everywhere and at most $(2C_1)^{-1}$ outside $S=\{ u\leq m+A\} $. Therefore ( 9.9 ) implies \[  \mu (S)\geq \frac1{2C_1}=:\delta >0.  \] Since $\sup _ Xu=0$, theorem 1.4.2 gives $\int _ X(-u)\, \mathrm{d}\mu \leq C_0$. On $S$ we have $-u\geq -m-A$, so \[  C_0\geq \int _ X(-u)\, \mathrm{d}\mu \geq \delta (-m-A)  \] when $-m\geq A$; otherwise the desired bound is immediate. Thus $-m\leq A+C_0/\delta $, proving the theorem. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.2.2
text: Lemma 9.2.2 . Suppose $u$ is smooth, $\eta =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, and $\eta ^ n\leq \Lambda \omega ^ n$ for a fixed $\Lambda >0$. There are constants $p_0\geq 1$ and $C$ depending only on $\omega $ and $\Lambda $ such that \[  \int _ X\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2})\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2})\wedge \omega ^{n-1} \leq Cp\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\omega ^ n\quad (p\geq p_0).  \] Proof. For a fixed real $p\geq 1$, define $M_ k$ for $0\leq k\leq n$ and $J_ k$ for $0\leq k\leq n-1$ by \[  M_ k=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k},\qquad J_ k=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k-1}, \quad J=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}J_ k.  \] All these numbers are nonnegative. The proof first bounds $pJ$ in terms of the masses $M_ k$, and then bounds these masses by a recurrence. Let $T=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k-1}$, so that $\eta ^ n-\omega ^ n=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T$. Since $\mathrm{d}\eta =\mathrm{d}\omega $, differentiation gives \[  \mathrm{d}T=n\sum _{k=0}^{n-2}\eta ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k-2}\wedge \mathrm{d}\omega .  \] The sum is empty when $n=1$. Stokes' theorem gives the exact identity \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}(\eta ^ n-\omega ^ n) & =\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T\\ & =pJ+\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}T. \end{split}  \] The density assumption bounds the left-hand side above by $(\Lambda +1)M_0$. Apply lemma 9.2.1 to the last integral, with $\delta =K/p$ for a sufficiently large fixed $K$. The contribution proportional to $J/\delta $ is then at most $pJ/2$, and after absorbing it we obtain 9.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weighted-first-bound} pJ\leq CM_0+\frac Cp\sum _{k=0}^{n-2}M_ k. \end{equation} This estimate alone does not suffice, because the mixed weighted masses on the right have not yet been bounded. For $1\leq k\leq n-2$, a second integration by parts gives 9.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weighted-recurrence} M_ k-M_{k-1}=pJ_{k-1}+R_ k, \qquad R_ k=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}(\eta ^{k-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-k}). \end{equation} The derivative in $R_ k$ has two terms, with coefficients $k-1$ and $n-k$. Applying the pointwise estimate with $\delta =1/p$ to each of them, and omitting terms with negative indices, we obtain \[  |R_ k|\leq Cp(J_{k-2}+J_{k-1}) +\frac Cp(M_{k-2}+M_{k-1}), \qquad M_{-1}=J_{-1}=0.  \] Consequently, for $p\geq 1$, \[  M_ k\leq C(M_{k-1}+M_{k-2}+pJ).  \] Induction over the finitely many values of $k$ proves \[  \sum _{k=0}^{n-2}M_ k\leq C(M_0+pJ).  \] For $n=2$ this is immediate, and for $n=1$ the sum is empty. Inserting this bound in ( 9.7 ) gives $pJ\leq CM_0+C'J$. For $p\geq 2C'$ the last term can be absorbed, and $pJ\leq CM_0$. Finally, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{d}(\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2})\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2})\wedge \omega ^{n-1} =\frac{p^2}{4}J_0\leq \frac{p^2}{4}J\leq CpM_0.  \] This proves the claimed estimate for all $p\geq p_0$. $\square$
9.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weighted-first-bound} pJ\leq CM_0+\frac Cp\sum _{k=0}^{n-2}M_ k. \end{equation}

9.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weighted-recurrence} M_ k-M_{k-1}=pJ_{k-1}+R_ k, \qquad R_ k=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-pu}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}(\eta ^{k-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-k}). \end{equation}

title: Theorem 9.2.3
text: Theorem 9.2.3 . For each $\Lambda >0$ there is $C_\Lambda $ such that every smooth $u$ with \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu=0,\qquad (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\leq \Lambda \omega ^ n  \] satisfies $\| u\| _\infty \leq C_\Lambda $. Proof. Let $\mathrm{d}\mu =\omega ^ n/\int _ X\omega ^ n$. The Sobolev inequality for the Riemannian metric of $\omega $ gives, for some $\beta >1$ and every smooth real function $w$, \[  \left(\int _ X |w|^{2\beta }\, \mathrm{d}\mu \right)^{1/\beta } \leq C\left(\int _ X\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \omega ^{n-1} +\int _ X|w|^2\, \mathrm{d}\mu \right).  \] We may take $\beta =n/(n-1)$ if $n\geq 2$, and for example $\beta =2$ if $n=1$. Choose $p_0$ as in lemma 9.2.2 . Applying the Sobolev inequality to $w=\mathrm{e}^{-pu/2}$ and using that lemma, we obtain, with $Z=\mathrm{e}^{-u}$, \[  \| Z\| _{L^{p\beta }(\mu )}\leq (Cp)^{1/p}\| Z\| _{L^ p(\mu )} \quad (p\geq p_0).  \] Iterating with $p=p_0\beta ^ j$, $j=0,1,2,\ldots $, we obtain a bound for $\sup _ XZ$; the product of the constants is finite because $\sum _ j(1+\log (p_0\beta ^ j))/(p_0\beta ^ j)<\infty $. Hence, for a uniform $C_1\geq 1$ and $m=\inf _ Xu$, 9.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:near-minimum-integral} \mathrm{e}^{-p_0m}\leq C_1\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-p_0u}\, \mathrm{d}\mu . \end{equation} The right-hand side still involves the unknown potential. Divide by $\mathrm{e}^{-p_0m}$ and set $A=p_0^{-1}\log (2C_1)$. The integrand $\mathrm{e}^{-p_0(u-m)}$ is at most one everywhere and at most $(2C_1)^{-1}$ outside $S=\{ u\leq m+A\} $. Therefore ( 9.9 ) implies \[  \mu (S)\geq \frac1{2C_1}=:\delta >0.  \] Since $\sup _ Xu=0$, theorem 1.4.2 gives $\int _ X(-u)\, \mathrm{d}\mu \leq C_0$. On $S$ we have $-u\geq -m-A$, so \[  C_0\geq \int _ X(-u)\, \mathrm{d}\mu \geq \delta (-m-A)  \] when $-m\geq A$; otherwise the desired bound is immediate. Thus $-m\leq A+C_0/\delta $, proving the theorem. $\square$
9.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:near-minimum-integral} \mathrm{e}^{-p_0m}\leq C_1\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{-p_0u}\, \mathrm{d}\mu . \end{equation}

title: 9.3 The linearized equation and smooth dependence
search_title: The linearized equation and smooth dependence
text: 9.3 The linearized equation and smooth dependence Recall from ( 4.15 ) that the linearization of $u\mapsto \log (\omega _ u^ n/\mathrm{d}V)$ at $u$ is $L_ uv=n\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \omega _ u^{n-1}/\omega _ u^ n$. This operator annihilates constants, and by proposition 4.8.1 its range consists of the functions with zero mean under the adjoint probability measure $\mu _ u$. Including the scalar $b$ as an unknown removes this obstruction. In dimension one, $\mu _ u=\omega _ u/\int _ X\omega _ u$, and the compatibility condition follows from Stokes' theorem. The normalization $\sup _ Xu=0$ is convenient for compactness, but it need not depend differentiably on the data. To differentiate solutions, we use instead the linear normalization \[  \int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}V=0.  \] Passing from one normalization to the other only adds a constant to $u$ and leaves $b$ unchanged. Proposition 9.3.1 . With this linear normalization, the solution $(u,b)$ of ( 9.1 ) depends smoothly on $F$ in Hölder spaces, and hence smoothly on the parameters of every smooth finite-dimensional family of smooth data. Proof. Fix an integer $k\geq 0$ and a real exponent $0<\alpha <1$. Consider the map \[  (u,b,F)\longmapsto \log \frac{(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}-F-b  \] on the open set of potentials in $C^{k+2,\alpha }$ with $\omega _ u>0$, restricted to $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}V=0$. Its derivative in $(u,b)$ is \[  (v,a)\longmapsto L_ uv-a.  \] Given $h\in C^{k,\alpha }$, integrating $L_ uv-a=h$ against $\mu _ u$ forces $a=-\int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u$. For this value, the equation for $v$ satisfies the compatibility condition of proposition 4.8.1 , and it has a unique solution with zero $\mathrm{d}V$-mean. Schauder estimates show that this inverse is bounded. The implicit function theorem in Banach spaces therefore gives a smooth local solution map around any given solution; this step does not use the global existence theorem. Uniqueness identifies the local maps wherever they overlap, and elliptic regularity allows arbitrary $k$ for smooth data. $\square$

text: 9.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hermitian-trace-inequality} \Delta _ h\log S\geq \frac2{S^2}\operatorname {Re}\bigl (h^{k\bar q}\tau _ k S_{\bar q}\bigr ) +\frac{\Delta _ gG}{S}-C_ gB. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 9.4.2
text: Theorem 9.4.2 . Fix $D,K>0$ and a smooth real function $G$ on $X$. Suppose $u$ is smooth, $\omega _ u>0$, and \[  \operatorname {osc}_ Xu\leq D,\qquad \omega _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^ G\omega ^ n,\qquad |G|\leq K,\qquad \Delta _ gG\geq -K.  \] There is a constant $C=C(\omega ,D,K)$ such that \[  C^{-1}\omega \leq \omega _ u\leq C\omega .  \] Proof. Use $h=g+(u_{i\bar j})$, $S=\operatorname {tr}_ g h$, and $B=\operatorname {tr}_ h g$ as in lemma 9.4.1 . Write $s=u-\inf _ Xu+1$, so that $1\leq s\leq D+1$, and consider the maximum of \[  Q=\log S-Au+s^{-1}  \] on $X$, where $A\geq 1$ will be fixed below. Let $x$ be a maximum point. If $S(x)<1$, an upper bound for $S$ on $X$ already follows from the oscillation bound and the definition of $Q$, as at the end of the proof. We may therefore assume $S(x)\geq 1$ and use lemma 9.4.1 . Since the eigenvalues of $h$ relative to $g$ are positive, $SB\geq n^2$, and hence $\Delta _ gG/S\geq -KB/n^2$. Moreover, $\partial Q=0$ at $x$ gives \[  \frac{S_ k}{S}=(A+s^{-2})u_ k.  \] Because $|\tau |_ h^2\leq C_ gB$, the absolute value of the torsion term is bounded by 9.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:trace-torsion-absorption} \begin{split}  \left|\frac2{S^2}\operatorname {Re}(h^{k\bar q}\tau _ kS_{\bar q})\right| & \leq \frac{C_ g(A+1)}S\sqrt B\, |\partial u|_ h\\ & \leq \frac{|\partial u|_ h^2}{s^3} +\frac{C_ g(A+1)^2s^3}{S^2}B. \end{split} \end{equation} If $S(x)^2\leq (A+1)^2(D+1)^3$, then $S(x)$ is bounded once $A$ is fixed, and again so is $S$ on $X$. In the remaining case the coefficient of $B$ in the last term is at most $C_ g$. On the other hand, direct computation gives \[  \Delta _ hQ=\Delta _ h\log S+(A+s^{-2})(B-n) +2s^{-3}|\partial u|_ h^2.  \] The trace inequality and ( 9.15 ) imply at $x$ \[  0\geq \Delta _ hQ\geq (A-C_ g-K/n^2)B-n(A+1),  \] after a fixed enlargement of $C_ g$. Choosing $A>C_ g+K/n^2+1$, we conclude that $B(x)$ is bounded. If $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n$ are the eigenvalues of $h$ relative to $g$, then $\prod _ i\lambda _ i=\mathrm{e}^ G$, and for $n\geq 2$ \[  S=\sum _ i\lambda _ i =\mathrm{e}^ G\sum _ i\prod _{j\ne i}\lambda _ j^{-1} \leq n \mathrm{e}^ K B^{n-1}.  \] For $n=1$, directly $S=\mathrm{e}^ G$. Thus $S(x)$ is bounded in all cases. For every $y\in X$, the maximality of $Q$ at $x$ gives \[  \log S(y)\leq \log S(x)+A(u(y)-u(x))+s(x)^{-1}-s(y)^{-1} \leq \log S(x)+AD+1.  \] This proves $S\leq C$ on $X$. The lower bound for the determinant then gives $\lambda _ i\geq \mathrm{e}^{-K}C^{-(n-1)}$, which proves the uniform equivalence. $\square$

9.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:trace-torsion-absorption} \begin{split}  \left|\frac2{S^2}\operatorname {Re}(h^{k\bar q}\tau _ kS_{\bar q})\right| & \leq \frac{C_ g(A+1)}S\sqrt B\, |\partial u|_ h\\ & \leq \frac{|\partial u|_ h^2}{s^3} +\frac{C_ g(A+1)^2s^3}{S^2}B. \end{split} \end{equation}

title: Lemma 9.4.3
text: Lemma 9.4.3 . Let $A,M\geq 0$. There is $C=C(g,A,M)$ such that every smooth real function $v$ on $X$ satisfying \[  \operatorname {osc}_ Xv\leq M,\qquad \| \Delta _ gv\| _{L^\infty } \leq A\bigl (1+\| \mathrm{d}v\| _{L^\infty (g)}\bigr )  \] also satisfies \[  \| \mathrm{d}v\| _{L^\infty (g)}+\| \Delta _ gv\| _{L^\infty }\leq C.  \] Here all volume and function-space norms use the fixed smooth metric $g$. Proof. Subtract $\inf _ Xv$, so that $0\leq v\leq M$, and put $K=\| \mathrm{d}v\| _{L^\infty (g)}$. Fix $p>2n$ and $0<\alpha <1-2n/p$. The fixed operator $\Delta _ g$ is uniformly elliptic on the underlying real manifold. The local $W^{2,p}$ estimates, patched by a finite atlas, and Morrey's inequality give \[  \| v\| _{C^{1,\alpha }} \leq C_ g\| v\| _{W^{2,p}} \leq C_ g\bigl (\| v\| _{L^ p}+\| \Delta _ gv\| _{L^ p}\bigr ) \leq C_ g\bigl (M+A(1+K)\bigr ).  \] These are the standard linear elliptic estimates of [ Chapter 9 , GT01 ] ; the constants depend on the fixed metric and on the chosen $p,\alpha $. For $0<t\leq t_0$, with $t_0$ fixed by the atlas, integration along a coordinate segment of length $t$ gives \[  K\leq C_ g t^{-1}M+C_ g t^\alpha \| v\| _{C^{1,\alpha }}.  \] Indeed, the difference quotient is bounded by $2M/t$, and its difference from the derivative at the initial point is bounded by $C_ gt^\alpha \| v\| _{C^{1,\alpha }}$. A finite atlas with smaller charts controls every point and coordinate direction; equivalence with the $g$-norm gives the displayed estimate. Consequently, \[  K\leq C_ gt^{-1}M+C_ g^2t^\alpha (M+A) +C_ g^2At^\alpha K.  \] Choose $t\leq t_0$ so small that $C_ g^2At^\alpha \leq 1/2$. This choice depends only on $g,A$, including when $A=0$. Absorbing the last term bounds $K$ in terms of $g,A,M$, and the assumed trace estimate then bounds $\| \Delta _ gv\| _\infty $. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.4.4
text: Corollary 9.4.4 . Fix $\omega $. For smooth solutions of \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mathrm{e}^ G\omega ^ n,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,  \] a uniform $C^0$ bound for $u$ and uniform bounds for the smooth real logarithmic density $G$ in every $C^ k$ norm imply uniform bounds for $u$ in every $C^ k$ norm. Proof. Theorem 9.4.2 gives uniform ellipticity and a bound for $\Delta _ gu=S-n$. The linear elliptic $W^{2,p}$ estimates for the fixed operator $\Delta _ g$ first bound $u$ in $C^{1,\alpha }$ for every $0<\alpha <1$. The local Evans–Krylov estimate for the concave logarithmic determinant then gives a uniform $C^{2,\beta }$ bound for some $0<\beta <1$. To apply it in its real form, project real symmetric Hessians to their complex Hermitian part and extend the logarithmic determinant concavely from the compact set of positive matrices given by the preceding theorem. The extension is uniformly elliptic on real symmetric matrices because the projection preserves positivity and the trace, so the usual Evans–Krylov theorem applies. Finally, differentiating the equation gives linear uniformly elliptic equations with Hölder coefficients, and Schauder estimates and induction give all higher bounds. No regularity results beyond these standard local elliptic estimates are needed. $\square$

title: 9.5 The continuity method
text: 9.5 The continuity method We join the background density to the prescribed one by a path of equations. The local inverse of proposition 9.3.1 shows that the set of solvable parameters is open. The extremum bound for the scalar, the potential estimate and the derivative estimates give compactness along the path, and uniform ellipticity preserves positivity at a limiting parameter. of theorem 9.1.1 . The case $n=1$ was treated after the statement of the theorem. For $n\geq 2$ put $G=F+\log (\mathrm{d}V/\omega ^ n)$ and consider \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^ n=\mathrm{e}^{tG+b_ t}\omega ^ n, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ t=0,\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] At $t=0$, take $u_0=0$ and $b_0=0$. The local implicit-function argument in proposition 9.3.1 , with the additive constant temporarily fixed by a linear mean, shows that the set of solvable parameters is open. At every solvable parameter, proposition 9.1.2 gives \[  -\sup _ X(tG)\leq b_ t\leq -\inf _ X(tG), \qquad \mathrm{e}^{tG+b_ t}\leq \mathrm{e}^{\operatorname {osc}_ XG}.  \] The constants $b_ t$ are therefore uniformly bounded, and theorem 9.2.3 bounds $u_ t$ in $C^0$. By corollary 9.4.4 , the solutions are bounded in every $C^ k$ norm. Along any sequence of solvable parameters converging in $[0,1]$, a subsequence of $(u_ t,b_ t)$ therefore converges smoothly to a solution; uniform equivalence of the metrics preserves strict positivity, and the supremum normalization passes to the limit. Thus the solvable set is closed. Since it is nonempty, open and closed, connectedness of $[0,1]$ gives a solution at $t=1$, and proposition 9.1.3 gives uniqueness. $\square$

title: 9.6 The smooth exponential equation
text: 9.6 The smooth exponential equation When the logarithmic density contains a positive multiple of the potential, the extrema of the potential are bounded directly, and the linearization acquires a negative zeroth-order term. The continuity method then needs neither an additive normalization nor an extra scalar unknown. Proposition 9.6.1 . Let $\lambda >0$, let $F$ be smooth, and let $v,w$ be smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions. If \[  \omega _ v^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v+F}\omega ^ n, \qquad \omega _ w^ n\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w+F}\omega ^ n,  \] then $v\leq w$. In particular, two smooth solutions coincide. Proof. Suppose that $v-w$ has a positive maximum at a point $x$. Then $\omega _ v(x)\leq \omega _ w(x)$, and taking determinants and applying the two assumptions gives $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v(x)+F(x)}\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w(x)+F(x)}$, which contradicts $v(x)>w(x)$. For two solutions, apply the comparison in both orders. $\square$ Theorem 9.6.2 . For every $\lambda >0$ and every smooth real $F$, there is a unique smooth $u$ with $\omega _ u>0$ such that \[  \omega _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u+F}\omega ^ n.  \] The solution satisfies \[  -\lambda ^{-1}\sup _ XF\leq u\leq -\lambda ^{-1}\inf _ XF.  \] Proof. At a minimum of $u$, the equation gives $\lambda u+F\geq 0$; at a maximum it gives $\lambda u+F\leq 0$. These inequalities prove the stated bounds. Consider the equations \[  \omega _{u_ t}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ t+tF}\omega ^ n,\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] At $t=0$, $u_0=0$ is a solution. The linearization in $u$ is $L_ u-\lambda $, whose kernel is zero by the maximum principle. Its Fredholm index is zero: deform its principal coefficients to those of a fixed Laplacian while keeping the negative zeroth-order term; the latter operator is invertible, and the index is constant along this deformation of elliptic operators. Thus $L_ u-\lambda $ is an isomorphism between the usual Hölder spaces, with bounded inverse by Schauder theory, and the implicit function theorem proves that the set of solvable parameters is open. The extremum bounds give $\| u_ t\| _\infty \leq \lambda ^{-1}\| F\| _\infty $. The semilinear version of theorem 9.4.2 and corollary 9.4.4 , stated in the remark following that corollary, then gives uniform ellipticity and bounds in every $C^ k$ norm. Along any convergent sequence of solvable parameters, a subsequence of the solutions therefore converges smoothly to a strictly positive solution at the limit parameter. This proves closedness, and hence existence at $t=1$. Uniqueness is proposition 9.6.1 . $\square$ For a fixed smooth real obstacle $f$ on $X$ and a parameter $\beta >0$, the choice $\lambda =\beta $ and $F=-\beta f$ gives \[  \omega _{u_\beta }^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\beta (u_\beta -f)}\omega ^ n.  \] These equations penalize values above the obstacle. In proposition 13.1.1 we use them to construct the envelope of $f$ and to show that its Monge–Ampère measure is supported on the contact set. The convergence argument there uses only bounded regularization and the comparison just proved.

title: 9.7 Variation of the normalization scalar
text: 9.7 Variation of the normalization scalar Integration against the adjoint probability measure eliminates the derivatives of the potential from the first variation of $b$. In the second variation, the second derivative of the logarithmic determinant contributes a nonnegative square with a minus sign. This gives concavity of $b$ and identifies the equality case. Write $b(F)$ for the scalar in ( 9.1 ), and use the linear normalization $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}V=0$. For a smooth family $F_ t$, with $t$ in an open interval $I\subset \mathbb R$, write $(u_ t,b_ t)$ for the corresponding solutions and put $\eta _ t=\omega _{u_ t}$. By proposition 9.3.1 these depend smoothly on $t$; a dot denotes differentiation in $t$. Theorem 9.7.1 . Let $A_ t=\eta _ t^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u_ t$ be the endomorphism of the tangent bundle that represents the real $(1,1)$-form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u_ t$ with respect to $\eta _ t$; it is Hermitian with respect to $\eta _ t$. The normalization constant satisfies 9.18 \begin{align}  \dot b_ t& =-\int _ X\dot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t},\label{eq:b-first}\\  \ddot b_ t& =-\int _ X\ddot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t} -\int _ X\operatorname {tr}(A_ t^2)\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}.\label{eq:b-second} \end{align} In particular, for smooth real functions $F_0,G$ on $X$ and the affine family $F_ t=F_0+tG$, the function $b_ t$ is concave. Its second derivative vanishes at a parameter value if and only if $G$ is constant on $X$. Proof. Differentiating the logarithm of ( 9.1 ) gives \[  L_{u_ t}\dot u_ t=\dot F_ t+\dot b_ t.  \] Integration against $\mu _{u_ t}$ proves ( 9.18 ). For a smooth family of positive Hermitian matrices $H_ t$, differentiation of the inverse matrix gives \[  \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\log \det H_ t =\operatorname {tr}(H_ t^{-1}\ddot H_ t) -\operatorname {tr}\bigl ((H_ t^{-1}\dot H_ t)^2\bigr ).  \] Apply this pointwise to the matrices of $\eta _ t$, using $\dot\eta _ t=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u_ t$ and $\ddot\eta _ t=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\ddot u_ t$. The second derivative of the logarithmic equation is \[  L_{u_ t}\ddot u_ t-\operatorname {tr}(A_ t^2) =\ddot F_ t+\ddot b_ t.  \] Integrating against $\mu _{u_ t}$ at this fixed parameter proves ( 9.19 ); there is no need to differentiate the measure. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u_ t=0$, and the maximum principle shows that $\dot u_ t$ is constant. The first differentiated equation then gives $G=-\dot b_ t$, a constant. Conversely, if $G$ is constant, the solution metric is independent of $t$ and $b_ t=b_0-tG$. $\square$ Corollary 9.7.2 . For two smooth functions $F,G$, the normalization constants satisfy \[  -\sup _ X(G-F)\leq b(G)-b(F)\leq -\inf _ X(G-F).  \] In particular, $|b(G)-b(F)|\leq \| G-F\| _\infty $. If $G-F$ is nonconstant, both inequalities in the first display are strict. Proof. Apply ( 9.18 ) along $F_ t=F+t(G-F)$ and integrate over $0\leq t\leq 1$. Each $\mu _{u_ t}$ is a probability measure with strictly positive smooth density, so the integral of a nonconstant continuous function against it lies strictly between the minimum and the maximum of that function. $\square$ Thus $b$ is a decreasing, concave, Lipschitz functional of the logarithmic density, with $b(F+a)=b(F)-a$ for every real constant $a$. By uniform approximation, it extends uniquely to a Lipschitz functional of continuous $F$. This extension concerns the scalar functional only; the existence and regularity of corresponding potentials require further estimates.

9.9 Prescribing a Gauduchon volume form
text: 9.9 Prescribing a Gauduchon volume form We now return to a general connected compact complex manifold $X$, of dimension $n\geq 2$. To stay in a fixed Aeppli class of Gauduchon metrics, we vary the $(n-1)$st power of the metric by a term of the form $\partial \xi +\bar\partial \bar\xi $. The resulting scalar ansatz contains first derivatives of the potential as well as its complex Hessian. Theorem 9.9.1 (Székelyhidi–Tosatti–Weinkove) . Fix a Hermitian form $\gamma _0$, a Gauduchon form $\gamma $, and a smooth real function $F$. There is a unique pair $(u,b)\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)\times \mathbb R$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ such that the $(n-1,n-1)$-form \[  \Gamma _ u=\gamma _0^{n-1}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \gamma ^{n-2} +\operatorname {Re}\left( \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial u\wedge \bar\partial (\gamma ^{n-2}) \right)  \] is strictly positive, and the Hermitian form $\eta _ u$ with $\eta _ u^{n-1}=\Gamma _ u$ satisfies \[  \eta _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{F+b}\gamma ^ n.  \] Here we use the linear-algebra fact that a real $(n-1,n-1)$-form is strictly positive if and only if it is the $(n-1)$st power of a Hermitian form, and that this Hermitian form is unique; the matrix form of this correspondence is described in section 9.12 . Keep $\gamma _0$ and $\gamma $ fixed for the remainder of the chapter, and write $\mathcal D_\gamma u=\Gamma _ u-\gamma _0^{n-1}$ for the part of the ansatz that is linear in $u$. To see which geometry is preserved, set $\xi _ u=\mathrm i\, \bar\partial u\wedge \gamma ^{n-2}/(4\pi )$. The Leibniz rule gives $\Gamma _ u-\gamma _0^{n-1}=\partial \xi _ u+\bar\partial \overline{\xi _ u}$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\partial \xi _ u+\bar\partial \overline{\xi _ u})=0$, if $\gamma _0$ is Gauduchon then so is $\eta _ u$, and the $(n-1)$st powers of $\gamma _0$ and $\eta _ u$ have the same Aeppli class. The uniqueness in theorem 9.9.1 concerns this scalar ansatz; it does not assert uniqueness among all Gauduchon metrics in the Aeppli class.

title: Theorem 9.9.1 (Székelyhidi–Tosatti–Weinkove)
text: Theorem 9.9.1 (Székelyhidi–Tosatti–Weinkove) . Fix a Hermitian form $\gamma _0$, a Gauduchon form $\gamma $, and a smooth real function $F$. There is a unique pair $(u,b)\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)\times \mathbb R$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ such that the $(n-1,n-1)$-form \[  \Gamma _ u=\gamma _0^{n-1}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \gamma ^{n-2} +\operatorname {Re}\left( \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial u\wedge \bar\partial (\gamma ^{n-2}) \right)  \] is strictly positive, and the Hermitian form $\eta _ u$ with $\eta _ u^{n-1}=\Gamma _ u$ satisfies \[  \eta _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{F+b}\gamma ^ n.  \] of theorem 9.9.1 . Let \[  F_0=\log \frac{\gamma _0^ n}{\gamma ^ n},\qquad F_ t=(1-t)F_0+tF,\quad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] We use the continuity method along the path $F_ t$. At $t=0$, the pair $u=0$, $b=0$ solves the equation, since $\eta _0=\gamma _0$. During the continuity argument we normalize potentials by $\int _ Xu\, \gamma ^ n=0$; adding a constant does not affect the equation, and at the end we impose $\sup _ Xu=0$ instead. For openness, the derivative of the equation with respect to the mean-zero potential and the scalar is $(w,a)\mapsto \mathcal L_ uw-a$. Given a right-hand side $q$, integration against the adjoint probability measure of proposition 9.11.1 forces $a=-\int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma $. The Fredholm alternative then gives a unique mean-zero solution $w$, and Schauder estimates bound this inverse between Hölder spaces. Since positivity of $\Gamma _ u$ is an open condition, the implicit function theorem gives solutions for all nearby parameters. For closedness, note that the functions $F_ t$ are uniformly bounded in every $C^ k$ norm. After supremum normalization, proposition 9.10.1 bounds $u$ and $b$, the second-order and rescaling estimates bound the gradient and the complex Hessian, and lemma 9.16.1 gives all higher bounds. Subtracting the mean preserves all derivative bounds and changes the potentials by uniformly bounded constants. A subsequence of mean-zero solutions along a convergent sequence of parameters therefore converges smoothly to a solution at the limiting parameter, and the bounds $aI\leq Q\leq b_0I$ preserve strict positivity in the limit. Thus the set of solvable parameters is nonempty, open and closed, hence equal to $[0,1]$. Finally, consider two solutions $(u,b)$ and $(w,c)$ for the same $F$. At a maximum of $u-w$ their gradients agree and their complex Hessians are ordered, so the first-order terms are equal there and, since $P_ n$ preserves the order, $Q_ u\leq Q_ w$. The equation then gives $b\leq c$, and at a minimum the reverse inequality gives $b\geq c$. Hence $b=c$. Along the segment between $u$ and $w$, the matrices $Q$ remain positive because the ansatz is affine in the potential. Integrating the derivative of the logarithmic determinant along that segment produces a uniformly elliptic scalar operator with first-order terms and no zeroth-order term that annihilates $u-w$. The maximum principle shows that $u-w$ is constant, and the supremum normalization makes the constant zero. $\square$
