text: 9.11 The adjoint equation for Gauduchon volume As for the Monge–Ampère equation, solving the linearized Gauduchon volume equation requires a compatibility condition, given by an adjoint probability measure. Taking the $(n-1)$st root multiplies the trace linearization by the factor $n/(n-1)$, and the first-order term of the ansatz introduces a drift term. We compute the linearized operator at any potential with $\Gamma _ u>0$, and then express its adjoint condition as an equation for a positive $(1,1)$-form. Throughout this section we put $K=\gamma ^{n-2}$. Proposition 9.11.1 . On the open set of smooth potentials $u$ with $\Gamma _ u>0$, the derivative of \[  \mathcal G(u)=\log \frac{\eta _ u^ n}{\gamma ^ n}  \] is the real elliptic operator 9.23 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-volume-linearization} \mathcal L_ uv= \frac{n}{n-1}\frac{\eta _ u\wedge \mathcal D_\gamma v}{\eta _ u^ n}. \end{equation} It has no zeroth-order term, and its kernel consists of the constants. There is a unique smooth positive function $\rho _ u$, normalized by $\int _ X\rho _ u\eta _ u^ n=1$, such that the probability measure \[  \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma =\rho _ u\eta _ u^ n  \] satisfies $\int _ X\mathcal L_ uv\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma =0$ for every smooth real $v$. Proof. For a smooth path of potentials $u(t)$, write $\eta =\eta _{u(t)}$ and $\Gamma =\Gamma _{u(t)}$. Differentiating $\eta ^{n-1}=\Gamma $ gives $(n-1)\dot\eta \wedge \eta ^{n-2}=\dot\Gamma $, where $\dot\Gamma =\mathcal D_\gamma \dot u$. Wedging with $\eta $ and dividing by $\eta ^ n$, we obtain \[  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\log \eta ^ n =\frac{n}{n-1}\frac{\eta \wedge \dot\Gamma }{\eta ^ n},  \] which proves ( 9.23 ). Only the second-order term $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \gamma ^{n-2}$ of $\mathcal D_\gamma v$ contributes to the principal symbol. For a nonzero complex covector $\zeta $ of type $(1,0)$, the form \[  \eta _ u\wedge \mathrm i\zeta \wedge \overline\zeta \wedge \gamma ^{n-2}  \] is a positive volume form. Hence the principal symbol is positive definite, and by compactness the operator is uniformly elliptic for each fixed $u$. The remaining term is of first order, and constants are annihilated, so the strong maximum principle gives $\ker \mathcal L_ u=\mathbb R$. The Fredholm and positivity arguments in the proof of theorem 4.1.2 apply to this real elliptic operator with first-order terms and no zeroth-order term. Its index is zero by deformation to a Laplacian, so its formal adjoint with respect to $\eta _ u^ n$ has a one-dimensional kernel spanned by a smooth strictly positive function. Normalizing its integral to one gives $\rho _ u$ and proves uniqueness. $\square$ The adjoint condition can be expressed as an equation for the positive $(1,1)$-form $\rho _ u\eta _ u$. For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $A$, set \[  \mathcal A_\gamma (A) =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A\wedge \gamma ^{n-2} +\operatorname {Re}\left(\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi } \partial A\wedge \bar\partial (\gamma ^{n-2})\right).  \] This is a real form of top degree, and $\mathcal A_\gamma $ is the formal adjoint of $\mathcal D_\gamma $ under the pairing of $(1,1)$-forms with $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, as the proof below shows. Proposition 9.11.2 . The function $\rho _ u$ of proposition 9.11.1 is characterized by 9.24 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-volume-form-adjoint} \mathcal A_\gamma (\rho _ u\eta _ u)=0, \qquad \int _ X\rho _ u\eta _ u^ n=1. \end{equation} When $n=2$, its first equation is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _ u\eta _ u)=0$. When $\eta _ u=\gamma $, the function $\rho _ u$ is constant and $\mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma =\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$. Proof. We first prove that, for every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $A$ and every smooth real function $v$ on $X$, 9.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-volume-integration} \int _ X A\wedge \mathcal D_\gamma v =\int _ X v\, \mathcal A_\gamma (A). \end{equation} Write $c=\mathrm i/(2\pi )$. Since $A,K,v$ are real, expanding the real part gives \[  \mathcal D_\gamma v =c\, \partial \bar\partial v\wedge K +\frac c2\bigl (\partial v\wedge \bar\partial K -\bar\partial v\wedge \partial K\bigr ).  \] Integrating the first term by parts twice gives $\int _ Xv\, c\partial \bar\partial (A\wedge K)$, and integrating each first-order term by parts once gives the correction \[  \int _ Xv\, \frac c2 \bigl (-\partial A\wedge \bar\partial K +\bar\partial A\wedge \partial K -2A\wedge \partial \bar\partial K\bigr ).  \] Finally, \[  \partial \bar\partial (A\wedge K) =\partial \bar\partial A\wedge K -\bar\partial A\wedge \partial K +\partial A\wedge \bar\partial K +A\wedge \partial \bar\partial K.  \] Adding these contributions cancels the terms containing $A\wedge \partial \bar\partial K$ and leaves $\mathcal A_\gamma (A)$. This proves ( 9.25 ). Applied to $A=\rho _ u\eta _ u$, it shows by ( 9.23 ) that $\int _ X\mathcal L_ uv\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma $ is a fixed positive multiple of $\int _ Xv\, \mathcal A_\gamma (\rho _ u\eta _ u)$, so the adjoint condition is equivalent to ( 9.24 ). For $n=2$, we have $K=1$, which gives the first special case. For the second, the product rule gives \[  \mathcal A_\gamma (\gamma ) =\frac1{n-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0.  \] By uniqueness, $\rho _ u$ is consequently the constant $(\int _ X\gamma ^ n)^{-1}$. $\square$ For $n>2$ the equation for $\rho _ u\eta _ u$ involves the first derivatives of $\gamma ^{n-2}$, so the fixed auxiliary metric $\gamma $ remains part of the adjoint equation; it is not simply the Gauduchon condition for $\eta _ u$.

title: 9.13 The largest-eigenvalue estimate

We apply the maximum principle to the largest eigenvalue of $g$, corrected by functions of the gradient and of the potential. The missing torsion indices allow the concavity square to absorb the third derivatives. If the smallest eigenvalue is not too negative, the positive background closes the estimate; otherwise that eigenvalue produces a large positive Hessian square. We keep the notation of section 9.12 . Plain subscripts on scalar functions and subscripts after a comma on matrix coefficients denote coordinate derivatives, and the coefficients of the Chern connection of $\gamma $ are written $\Gamma ^ q_{ik}$. If $\| v\| _{C^0}$ and $\| h\| _{C^2}$ are bounded, then \[  \sup _ X|\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial v|_\gamma \leq C igl (1+\sup _ X|\partial v|_\gamma ^2 igr ),  \] where $C$ depends only on these bounds and the fixed smooth data. title: 9.14 A Liouville theorem for the limiting cone

text:
9.14 A Liouville theorem for the limiting cone Rescaling at a point of large gradient removes the background and first-order terms of the Gauduchon equation and leaves a degenerate equation on $\mathbb C^ n$, whose solutions are maximal for a cone of matrices. We show that its bounded Lipschitz solutions are constant. The proof argues by induction on the dimension: if the energy of a solution in some complex direction becomes small on large balls, a limit is independent of one variable; if all directional energies stay positive, they give a strictly admissible comparison function. On $\mathbb C^ n$ we use Euclidean coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$, the identity matrix $I$, the Euclidean balls $B(x,r)$ and Euclidean volume $\mathrm{d}y$. In this section $
abla $ and $\Delta $ denote the Euclidean real gradient and Laplacian, and $\partial _\xi $ denotes differentiation in a complex direction $\xi $. For $n\geq 2$ and a Hermitian matrix $H$, set \[  P_ n(H)= rac{(\operatorname {tr}H)I-H}{n-1}.  \] This is the map $P_\gamma $ of section 9.12 for the Euclidean metric. It preserves nonnegativity and satisfies $P_ n(I)=I$ and $\operatorname {tr}P_ n(H)=\operatorname {tr}H$. For a real function $v$ write $H(v)=(v_{i ar j})$ in Euclidean coordinates. A continuous function $v$ on an open set of $\mathbb C^ n$ is admissible if $P_ n(H(v))\geq 0$ in the sense of matrix-valued distributions. It is maximal for this cone if it is admissible and every smooth function $h$ touching $v$ from below at a point satisfies \[  P_ n(H(h))
ot>0  \] at that point. Here touching means that $v-h$ has a local minimum with value zero, which need not be a strict minimum. Maximality is thus the viscosity supersolution condition for the degenerate equation $\det P_ n(H(v))=0$ on the boundary of the cone, together with distributional admissibility. Taking the trace shows that admissible functions are subharmonic. Since $P_ n$ is linear, convolution preserves admissibility, and so do nonnegative linear combinations and integrals of admissible smooth functions. Translations and unitary changes of coordinates preserve both conditions, as do multiplication by a positive constant and addition of a constant. Lemma 9.14.1 . Local uniform limits of admissible maximal functions are admissible and maximal. If $v$ is maximal on a bounded open set $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $h$ is smooth and admissible on $D$, both functions are continuous on $\overline D$, and $h\leq v$ on $\partial D$, then $h\leq v$ on $D$. Proof. Let $v_ j$ be admissible maximal functions converging locally uniformly to $v$. Distributional positivity is preserved under this convergence. For maximality, suppose that a smooth function $h$ touches $v$ from below at $z_0$ and $P_ n(H(h)(z_0))>0$. Choose a small ball on which $v-h\geq 0$. Replacing $h$ by $h-\delta |z-z_0|^2$, with $\delta >0$ sufficiently small, keeps its matrix strictly positive near $z_0$ and makes the minimum strict. Uniform convergence then produces interior minimum points of $v_ j-h+\delta |z-z_0|^2$ tending to $z_0$. Adding the minimum value to the test function gives a function touching $v_ j$ from below with strictly positive matrix, a contradiction. For comparison, choose $R$ with $\overline D\subset \{ |z|\leq R\} $. If $h>v$ somewhere, then for small $\delta >0$ the smooth function \[  h_\delta =h+\delta (|z|^2-R^2)  \] still exceeds $v$ at some interior point and is at most $v$ on the boundary. Hence the negative minimum of $v-h_\delta $ is attained in the interior. But $P_ n(H(h_\delta ))=P_ n(H(h))+\delta I>0$ there, which contradicts maximality after the minimum value is added to $h_\delta $. No boundary regularity of $D$ is needed for this argument. $\square$ Theorem 9.14.2 . A bounded globally Lipschitz function on $\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 2$, that is maximal for this cone is constant. Proof. Let $v$ be a bounded globally Lipschitz maximal function on $\mathbb C^ n$. We argue by induction on $n$. For $n=2$, $P_2(H)\geq 0$ is equivalent to $H\geq 0$, so $v$ is plurisubharmonic, and lemma 1.3.5 shows that it is constant. We first explain the reduction in dimension for $n\geq 3$. If a function is independent of $z_ n$, its complex Hessian has the block form $H\oplus 0$. The first block of $P_ n(H\oplus 0)$ is \[   rac{n-2}{n-1}P_{n-1}(H),  \] and the last entry is $\operatorname {tr}H/(n-1)$. Nonnegativity of $P_{n-1}(H)$ implies $\operatorname {tr}H\geq 0$, and positive definiteness implies $\operatorname {tr}H>0$. Thus $P_ n(H\oplus 0)$ is nonnegative, respectively positive definite, exactly when $P_{n-1}(H)$ is. The distributional version follows from the same linear identities. A test function in $n-1$ variables extends to $\mathbb C^ n$ independently of $z_ n$, so maximality also passes to $n-1$ variables. Consequently the induction hypothesis applies to bounded Lipschitz maximal functions that are independent of one complex variable. Suppose now that $v$ is nonconstant. Adding a constant and multiplying by a positive constant, we may assume that $\inf v=0$ and $\sup v=1$. Let $L$ be the Lipschitz constant of $v$. Choose a smooth radial nonnegative probability kernel $\eta $, supported in the closed unit ball and strictly positive in its interior. For a bounded measurable function $f$ and $r>0$, write \[  [f]_ r(x)=\int _{\mathbb C^ n}f(x+y)\eta _ r(y)\, \mathrm{d}y, \qquad \eta _ r(y)=r^{-2n}\eta (y/r),\qquad v_\epsilon =[v]_\epsilon .  \] Both $v$ and $v^2$ are subharmonic. For $v^2$, use $v_\epsilon \geq 0$ and $\Delta (v_\epsilon ^2)=2v_\epsilon \Delta v_\epsilon +2|
abla v_\epsilon |^2\geq 0$, and pass to the uniform limit as $\epsilon 	o 0$. For $f=v$ and for $f=v^2$, the averages $[f]_ r(x)$ increase with $r$, by the monotonicity of spherical means of subharmonic functions. Their limit as $r	o \infty $ is independent of $x$, since \[  |[f]_ r(x)-[f]_ r(y)| \leq \| f\| _\infty \| \eta _ r(\cdot -x)-\eta _ r(\cdot -y)\| _{L^1} \leq C rac{|x-y|}{r}.  \] By the submean inequality this limit is at least $f(x)$ for every $x$, while it is at most $\sup f=1$. Therefore 9.48  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-large-averages} [v]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1,\qquad [v^2]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1. \end{equation} We distinguish two cases. First suppose that there exist $ho >0$, sequences $\epsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ and $r_ k	o \infty $, points $x_ k$ and unit complex directions $\xi _ k$ such that 9.49  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-gap-case} [v^2]_{r_ k}(x_ k)+[v]_ho (x_ k)-2v(x_ k)\geq  rac43, \qquad \int _{B(x_ k,r_ k)}|\partial _{\xi _ k}v_{\epsilon _ k}|^2\, \mathrm{d}y \longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Translate $x_ k$ to the origin and make $\xi _ k$ the last complex direction by a unitary change of coordinates. The resulting functions have the same bounds and Lipschitz constant, so by the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem and lemma 9.14.1 a subsequence converges locally uniformly to a maximal function $a$. The corresponding mollifications at scale $\epsilon _ k$ have the same local uniform limit, and by the integral condition their derivatives in the last complex direction tend to zero in $L^2$ on every fixed ball. Hence $\partial a/\partial z_ n=0$ in the sense of distributions. Since $a$ is real and continuous, it is independent of $z_ n$. The dimension reduction and the induction hypothesis show that $a$ is a constant $c\in [0,1]$. In the first inequality of ( 9.49 ), the first term is at most one, while the average at the fixed radius $ho $ and the value at the origin both tend to $c$. It would follow that $4/3\leq 1-c\leq 1$, a contradiction. In the remaining case, for every fixed $ho >0$ there is $C_ho \geq 1$ such that, whenever $0<\epsilon <C_ho ^{-1}$, $r>C_ho $, and \[  [v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_ho (x)-2v(x)\geq  rac43,  \] one has 9.50  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-directional-energy} \int _{B(x,r)}|\partial _\xi v_\epsilon |^2\, \mathrm{d}y \geq C_ho ^{-1} \quad \hbox{for every unit complex direction }\xi . \end{equation} Indeed, if this failed for $C_ho =k$ for every integer $k$, a diagonal choice would give sequences as in ( 9.49 ). After a translation we may assume that $v(0)<1/12$. By ( 9.48 ), choose $ho $ with $[v]_ho (0)>3/4$, and then $r>C_ho $ with $[v^2]_ r(0)>3/4$. The open set \[  D=\{ x:2v(x)<[v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_ho (x)-4/3\}   \] contains the origin. We claim that, for some $c>0$, \[  [v^2]_ r-c|z|^2  \] is smooth and admissible on $D$. To prove the claim, differentiate the square of the smooth mollification: \[  H(v_\epsilon ^2) =2v_\epsilon H(v_\epsilon ) +2(\partial _ i v_\epsilon \, \overline{\partial _ jv_\epsilon })_{ij}.  \] Denote by $A_\epsilon $ and $B_\epsilon $ the convolutions at the fixed radius $r$ of these two terms. The first satisfies $P_ n(A_\epsilon )\geq 0$, because $v_\epsilon \geq 0$, $v_\epsilon $ is admissible, and $P_ n$ is linear. The second satisfies $B_\epsilon \geq c_0I$ on $D$ for small $\epsilon $, with a constant $c_0>0$. Here the passage from the unweighted integral in ( 9.50 ) to the convolution needs care. The bound $|
abla v_\epsilon |\leq L$ makes the energy of a sufficiently thin boundary annulus of $B(x,r)$ at most $C_ho ^{-1}/2$, uniformly in $x,\epsilon ,\xi $. On the remaining smaller closed ball, the fixed kernel $\eta _ r$ has a positive minimum. For points $x\in D$, ( 9.50 ) then gives a uniform positive lower bound for the weighted integral in every direction, which is the asserted matrix inequality for $B_\epsilon $. Choose $0<c\leq c_0$. Since $P_ n$ preserves nonnegative matrices, \[  P_ n igl (H([v_\epsilon ^2]_ r)-cI igr )\geq 0 \quad \hbox{on }D.  \] As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, $v_\epsilon ^2	o v^2$ uniformly, and convolution at the fixed positive radius $r$ gives convergence of all derivatives. This proves the claim. The smooth function \[  h=	frac 12 igl ([v^2]_ r-c|z|^2+[v]_ho -4/3 igr )  \] is therefore admissible on $D$. The set $D'=\{ v<h\} $ contains the origin, it is bounded because $v$ and its averages are bounded, and it lies in $D$. Moreover $v=h$ on $\partial D'$. Lemma 9.14.1 , applied on $D'$, gives $h\leq v$ there, which contradicts the definition of $D'$. This excludes the second case and proves the theorem. $\square$ The Lipschitz bound is used both for the compactness of translates and for the annulus estimate. For $n>1$, the conclusion would not follow from boundedness and subharmonicity alone, since $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ carries nonconstant bounded subharmonic functions.

If a function is independent of $z_ n$, its complex Hessian has the block form $H\oplus 0$. The first block of $P_ n(H\oplus 0)$ is \[  \frac{n-2}{n-1}P_{n-1}(H),  \] and the last entry is $\operatorname {tr}H/(n-1)$. Their limit as $r\to \infty $ is independent of $x$, since \[  |[f]_ r(x)-[f]_ r(y)| \leq \| f\| _\infty \| \eta _ r(\cdot -x)-\eta _ r(\cdot -y)\| _{L^1} \leq C\frac{|x-y|}{r}.  \] By the submean inequality this limit is at least $f(x)$ for every $x$, while it is at most $\sup f=1$. Therefore 9.48 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cone-large-averages} [v]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1,\qquad [v^2]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1. \end{equation} We distinguish two cases. First suppose that there exist $\rho >0$, sequences $\epsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ and $r_ k\to \infty $, points $x_ k$ and unit complex directions $\xi _ k$ such that 9.49 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cone-gap-case} [v^2]_{r_ k}(x_ k)+[v]_\rho (x_ k)-2v(x_ k)\geq \frac43, \qquad \int _{B(x_ k,r_ k)}|\partial _{\xi _ k}v_{\epsilon _ k}|^2\, \mathrm{d}y \longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Translate $x_ k$ to the origin and make $\xi _ k$ the last complex direction by a unitary change of coordinates. The resulting functions have the same bounds and Lipschitz constant, so by the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem and lemma 9.14.1 a subsequence converges locally uniformly to a maximal function $a$. The corresponding mollifications at scale $\epsilon _ k$ have the same local uniform limit, and by the integral condition their derivatives in the last complex direction tend to zero in $L^2$ on every fixed ball. Hence $\partial a/\partial z_ n=0$ in the sense of distributions. Since $a$ is real and continuous, it is independent of $z_ n$. The dimension reduction and the induction hypothesis show that $a$ is a constant $c\in [0,1]$. In the first inequality of ( 9.49 ), the first term is at most one, while the average at the fixed radius $\rho $ and the value at the origin both tend to $c$. It would follow that $4/3\leq 1-c\leq 1$, a contradiction. In the remaining case, for every fixed $\rho >0$ there is $C_\rho \geq 1$ such that, whenever $0<\epsilon <C_\rho ^{-1}$, $r>C_\rho $, and \[  [v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_\rho (x)-2v(x)\geq \frac43,  \] one has 9.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cone-directional-energy} \int _{B(x,r)}|\partial _\xi v_\epsilon |^2\, \mathrm{d}y \geq C_\rho ^{-1} \quad \hbox{for every unit complex direction }\xi . \end{equation} Indeed, if this failed for $C_\rho =k$ for every integer $k$, a diagonal choice would give sequences as in ( 9.49 ). After a translation we may assume that $v(0)<1/12$. By ( 9.48 ), choose $\rho $ with $[v]_\rho (0)>3/4$, and then $r>C_\rho $ with $[v^2]_ r(0)>3/4$. The open set \[  D=\{ x:2v(x)<[v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_\rho (x)-4/3\}   \] contains the origin. We claim that, for some $c>0$, \[  [v^2]_ r-c|z|^2  \] is smooth and admissible on $D$. To prove the claim, differentiate the square of the smooth mollification: \[  H(v_\epsilon ^2) =2v_\epsilon H(v_\epsilon ) +2(\partial _ i v_\epsilon \, \overline{\partial _ jv_\epsilon })_{ij}.  \] Denote by $A_\epsilon $ and $B_\epsilon $ the convolutions at the fixed radius $r$ of these two terms. The first satisfies $P_ n(A_\epsilon )\geq 0$, because $v_\epsilon \geq 0$, $v_\epsilon $ is admissible, and $P_ n$ is linear. The second satisfies $B_\epsilon \geq c_0I$ on $D$ for small $\epsilon $, with a constant $c_0>0$. Here the passage from the unweighted integral in ( 9.50 ) to the convolution needs care. The bound $|\nabla v_\epsilon |\leq L$ makes the energy of a sufficiently thin boundary annulus of $B(x,r)$ at most $C_\rho ^{-1}/2$, uniformly in $x,\epsilon ,\xi $. On the remaining smaller closed ball, the fixed kernel $\eta _ r$ has a positive minimum. For points $x\in D$, ( 9.50 ) then gives a uniform positive lower bound for the weighted integral in every direction, which is the asserted matrix inequality for $B_\epsilon $. Choose $0<c\leq c_0$. Since $P_ n$ preserves nonnegative matrices, \[  P_ n\bigl (H([v_\epsilon ^2]_ r)-cI\bigr )\geq 0 \quad \hbox{on }D.  \] As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, $v_\epsilon ^2\to v^2$ uniformly, and convolution at the fixed positive radius $r$ gives convergence of all derivatives. This proves the claim. The smooth function \[  h=\tfrac 12\bigl ([v^2]_ r-c|z|^2+[v]_\rho -4/3\bigr )  \] is therefore admissible on $D$. The set $D'=\{ v<h\} $ contains the origin, it is bounded because $v$ and its averages are bounded, and it lies in $D$. Moreover $v=h$ on $\partial D'$. Lemma 9.14.1 , applied on $D'$, gives $h\leq v$ there, which contradicts the definition of $D'$. This excludes the second case and proves the theorem. $\square$

title: 9.15 The gradient bound by rescaling
text: 9.15 The gradient bound by rescaling If the gradients of a family of solutions were unbounded, rescaling at points of maximal gradient would produce functions on growing Euclidean balls with gradient one at the origin. The Hessian estimate makes these functions compact in $C^1$ on every fixed ball, so a limit is a bounded Lipschitz function on $\mathbb C^ n$ with nonzero gradient at the origin. The rescaled determinant tends to zero, so the limit is maximal for the cone of section 9.14 , which contradicts theorem 9.14.2 . Consider a family of smooth solutions $(u,b)$ of the equation in theorem 9.9.1 , normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, with $\| F\| _{C^0}\leq M$ for a fixed $M>0$. By proposition 9.10.1 , $\| u\| _{C^0}$ and $|b|$ are uniformly bounded. The following proposition shows that a Hessian estimate in terms of the squared gradient implies bounds for both. Proposition 9.15.1 . Suppose there is a constant $K$ such that every solution in this family satisfies 9.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:stw-second-order-required} \sup _ X|\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u|_\gamma \leq K\bigl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_\gamma ^2\bigr ). \end{equation} Then $\sup _ X|\partial u|_\gamma $ and $\sup _ X|\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u|_\gamma $ are bounded by a constant depending only on $X,\gamma _0,\gamma ,M$ and $K$. Proof. We use the matrices $Q_ u$ of ( 9.26 ). Their background term $Q_0$ is fixed, and $Z$ is linear in the first derivatives of $u/(2\pi )$. Suppose that the gradient bound fails. Then there are solutions $(u_ j,b_ j)$ with prescribed functions $F_ j$ such that \[  A_ j=\sup _ X|\partial u_ j|_\gamma =|\partial u_ j(x_ j)|_\gamma \longrightarrow \infty .  \] After passing to a subsequence, the points $x_ j$ lie in one fixed coordinate neighborhood. Translate the coordinates so that $x_ j$ becomes the origin, and apply a uniformly controlled complex linear change of coordinates so that the matrix of $\gamma $ at $x_ j$ is the identity; a coordinate ball of fixed radius remains available around every $x_ j$. On balls whose radii tend to infinity define \[  v_ j(z)=u_ j(x_ j+z/A_ j),  \] in these coordinates. The coefficient matrices $g_ j(z)$ of $\gamma $ at the points $x_ j+z/A_ j$ converge smoothly to the identity on every fixed ball. In this notation \[  |v_ j|\leq C, \qquad |\partial v_ j|_{g_ j}\leq 1, \qquad |\partial v_ j(0)|=1.  \] The assumed estimate ( 9.51 ) gives a uniform bound for all complex Hessian entries of $v_ j$ on every fixed ball, since two derivatives contribute the factor $A_ j^{-2}$. Hence the Euclidean Laplacians of the $v_ j$ are uniformly bounded, and the interior estimates for the Laplacian give local $W^{2,p}$ bounds for every finite $p$. Choosing $p>2n$ and using Sobolev embedding and compactness, we extract a diagonal subsequence converging in $C^1$ on compact subsets to a function $v$ on $\mathbb C^ n$. This function is bounded and globally Lipschitz, and \[  |\partial v(0)|=1.  \] Now divide the matrix in ( 9.26 ) by $A_ j^2$ and evaluate it at the scaled points. The background term becomes $O(A_ j^{-2})$, and the first-order term becomes $O(A_ j^{-1})$, since one derivative of $u_ j$ is $A_ j$ times a derivative of $v_ j$. Since the complex Hessians of $v_ j$ are uniformly bounded and $g_ j\to I$, we obtain on any fixed ball 9.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:stw-rescaled-matrix} A_ j^{-2}Q_{u_ j} =P_ n\left(\frac{H(v_ j)}{2\pi }\right)+o(1), \qquad \det (A_ j^{-2}Q_{u_ j}) =A_ j^{-2n}\mathrm{e}^{(n-1)(F_ j+b_ j)}\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} To be precise, we compute in the unitary frames obtained from the positive square roots $S_ j=g_ j^{-1/2}$. In these frames the principal matrix is $P_ n(S_ jH(v_ j)S_ j/(2\pi ))$, which differs from $P_ n(H(v_ j)/(2\pi ))$ by an error tending to zero uniformly; no derivatives of the frames are taken, and the determinant identity is exact in unitary frames. Since the matrices on the left of ( 9.52 ) are positive and the positive factor $1/(2\pi )$ does not change the cone, passing to the limit in the sense of distributions gives $P_ n(H(v))\geq 0$. It remains to check maximality. Suppose that a smooth function $h$ touches $v$ from below at $z_0$ and $P_ n(H(h)(z_0))>0$. Subtract $\delta |z-z_0|^2$ with $\delta >0$ small; on a small ball this makes the contact strict and preserves strict positivity of the matrix. Local uniform convergence gives points $z_ j\to z_0$ at which $v_ j$ minus this perturbed test function has an interior local minimum. At such a minimum, \[  H(v_ j)(z_ j)\geq H(h)(z_ j)-\delta I.  \] Because $P_ n$ preserves nonnegative matrices, ( 9.52 ) now implies $A_ j^{-2}Q_{u_ j}(z_ j)\geq cI$ for a fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $j$. The determinant of this matrix is then at least $c^ n$, which contradicts the limit zero in ( 9.52 ). Thus $v$ is maximal for the cone of section 9.14 . By theorem 9.14.2 , $v$ is constant, which contradicts $|\partial v(0)|=1$. This proves the uniform gradient bound, and substitution in ( 9.51 ) gives the uniform complex Hessian bound. $\square$ For prescribed functions $F$ bounded in $C^2$, proposition 9.10.1 bounds $u$ and $b$, and theorem 9.13.1 , applied to $v=u/(2\pi )$ and $h=(n-1)(F+b)$, proves ( 9.51 ). Thus both the gradient and the complex Hessian are uniformly bounded.

title: 9.16 Existence for the Gauduchon ansatz
text: 9.16 Existence for the Gauduchon ansatz The potential, gradient and Hessian bounds put the matrices $Q_ u$ in a compact set of positive matrices. This yields uniform ellipticity after the real Hessian is projected to its complex part and transformed by $P_ n$, so local elliptic regularity gives the compactness needed for closedness in the continuity method; the adjoint probability measure gives openness. The maximum principle then proves uniqueness within the scalar ansatz. Lemma 9.16.1 . Let $\gamma _0,\gamma $ be as in theorem 9.9.1 . If the prescribed functions $F$ range over a set of smooth functions bounded in every $C^ k$ norm, then the smooth solutions $(u,b)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ are bounded in every $C^ k$ norm. Proof. Work with $v=u/(2\pi )$ and write $Q=Q_ u$ for the matrix in ( 9.26 ). By proposition 9.10.1 , theorem 9.13.1 , proposition 9.15.1 , the function $v$, its gradient and its complex Hessian are uniformly bounded, and so are the constants $b$. Hence the eigenvalues of $Q$ are uniformly bounded above, and by the equation its determinant is uniformly bounded below. Every eigenvalue is therefore also bounded below by a positive constant. Choose fixed numbers $0<a<b_0$ such that $aI\leq Q\leq b_0I$ in unitary frames for every solution. The function $\Delta _\gamma v=\operatorname {tr}_\gamma (\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v)$ is uniformly bounded, and $\Delta _\gamma $ is a fixed uniformly elliptic operator. Its interior $W^{2,p}$ estimates, applied on a finite cover, bound $v$ in $W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$. Choose $p>2n$ and $0<\alpha <1-2n/p$; Sobolev embedding gives a uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound. Thus the matrix $R(x)=Q_0(x)+Z_ x(\partial v(x))$ is uniformly bounded in $C^\alpha $. On a coordinate ball, let $\mathcal H_ x(A)$ denote the Hermitian matrix of $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v$ at $x$ in a fixed smooth unitary frame, expressed as a function of the real Hessian $A=D^2_{\mathbb R}v(x)$. It is a real linear function of $A$ depending smoothly on $x$. If a real symmetric matrix $N$ is nonnegative, then $\mathcal H_ x(N)\geq 0$, and its trace is comparable to $\operatorname {tr}_{\mathbb R}N$ with uniform positive constants on the ball. This follows by evaluating on a vector and its rotation by $\mathrm i$, or from the coordinate formula for $v_{i\bar j}$. Freeze the function $\partial v(x)$ already obtained in $R(x)$, and define for all real symmetric matrices $A$ \[  \widetilde\Phi (A,x)= \inf _{aI\leq B\leq b_0I} \left\{ \log \det B+ \operatorname {tr}\left[B^{-1} \bigl (R(x)+P_ n(\mathcal H_ x(A))-B\bigr )\right]\right\} .  \] The infimum is over a fixed compact set of positive Hermitian matrices, and each expression in braces is an affine function of $A$, so $\widetilde\Phi $ is concave in $A$. If $R(x)+P_ n(\mathcal H_ x(A))$ lies in that compact set, then $\widetilde\Phi (A,x)$ equals its logarithmic determinant: each expression in braces is a tangent affine function of the concave logarithmic determinant, and the tangent at that matrix itself attains equality. For $N\geq 0$, each of these affine functions increases by \[  \operatorname {tr}\bigl (B^{-1}P_ n(\mathcal H_ x(N))\bigr )  \] when $A$ is replaced by $A+N$. Since $P_ n$ preserves positivity and trace, this increment lies between fixed positive multiples of $\operatorname {tr}_{\mathbb R}N$, uniformly in $B$ and $x$. Taking infima preserves both inequalities, so $\widetilde\Phi $ is uniformly elliptic on all real symmetric matrices. Smoothness of $\mathcal H_ x$ and the uniform $C^\alpha $ bound for $R$ also give \[  |\widetilde\Phi (A,x)-\widetilde\Phi (A,y)| \leq C|x-y|^\alpha (1+\| A\| ).  \] These are the hypotheses of the local Evans–Krylov estimate for concave uniformly elliptic equations with Hölder dependence on $x$, in the formulation given in section 34.6 . The value $\widetilde\Phi (0,x)$ is uniformly bounded, by the compactness of the set of matrices $B$ and the bound for $R$. By the choice of $a$ and $b_0$, the given smooth function solves \[  \widetilde\Phi (D^2_{\mathbb R}v,x)=(n-1)(F+b)  \] on the ball. The Evans–Krylov estimate, applied on smaller balls of a finite cover, yields a uniform $C^{2,\beta }$ bound for some $\beta >0$. Differentiating the original matrix equation gives linear uniformly elliptic equations for the first derivatives of $v$, whose coefficients, including the first-order coefficients coming from $Z$, are now Hölder continuous. Local Schauder estimates give $C^{3,\beta }$ bounds, and differentiation and induction give all higher bounds. The finite coordinate cover makes the bounds global. The only regularity results used here are the standard $W^{2,p}$ estimates for the Laplacian, the Evans–Krylov estimate for concave equations, and the Schauder estimates. $\square$ of theorem 9.9.1 . Let \[  F_0=\log \frac{\gamma _0^ n}{\gamma ^ n},\qquad F_ t=(1-t)F_0+tF,\quad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] We use the continuity method along the path $F_ t$. At $t=0$, the pair $u=0$, $b=0$ solves the equation, since $\eta _0=\gamma _0$. During the continuity argument we normalize potentials by $\int _ Xu\, \gamma ^ n=0$; adding a constant does not affect the equation, and at the end we impose $\sup _ Xu=0$ instead. For openness, the derivative of the equation with respect to the mean-zero potential and the scalar is $(w,a)\mapsto \mathcal L_ uw-a$. Given a right-hand side $q$, integration against the adjoint probability measure of proposition 9.11.1 forces $a=-\int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma $. The Fredholm alternative then gives a unique mean-zero solution $w$, and Schauder estimates bound this inverse between Hölder spaces. Since positivity of $\Gamma _ u$ is an open condition, the implicit function theorem gives solutions for all nearby parameters. For closedness, note that the functions $F_ t$ are uniformly bounded in every $C^ k$ norm. After supremum normalization, proposition 9.10.1 bounds $u$ and $b$, the second-order and rescaling estimates bound the gradient and the complex Hessian, and lemma 9.16.1 gives all higher bounds. Subtracting the mean preserves all derivative bounds and changes the potentials by uniformly bounded constants. A subsequence of mean-zero solutions along a convergent sequence of parameters therefore converges smoothly to a solution at the limiting parameter, and the bounds $aI\leq Q\leq b_0I$ preserve strict positivity in the limit. Thus the set of solvable parameters is nonempty, open and closed, hence equal to $[0,1]$. Finally, consider two solutions $(u,b)$ and $(w,c)$ for the same $F$. At a maximum of $u-w$ their gradients agree and their complex Hessians are ordered, so the first-order terms are equal there and, since $P_ n$ preserves the order, $Q_ u\leq Q_ w$. The equation then gives $b\leq c$, and at a minimum the reverse inequality gives $b\geq c$. Hence $b=c$. Along the segment between $u$ and $w$, the matrices $Q$ remain positive because the ansatz is affine in the potential. Integrating the derivative of the logarithmic determinant along that segment produces a uniformly elliptic scalar operator with first-order terms and no zeroth-order term that annihilates $u-w$. The maximum principle shows that $u-w$ is constant, and the supremum normalization makes the constant zero. $\square$

title: 9.17 Normalization for the Gauduchon equation
text: 9.17 Normalization for the Gauduchon equation By theorem 9.9.1 , every smooth real function $F$ determines a scalar $b_\gamma (F)$, the constant $b$ of that theorem. As for the Monge–Ampère equation, its variation is governed by the adjoint probability measure $\mu _ u^\gamma $ of proposition 9.11.1 and by the concavity of the logarithmic determinant. To differentiate solutions, we fix a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_0$ and use the normalization $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}V_0=0$ in place of $\sup _ Xu=0$. Lemma 9.17.1 . The solution $(u,b_\gamma (F))$, normalized by $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}V_0=0$, depends smoothly on the parameters of every smooth finite-dimensional family of functions $F$. Proof. The map $\Gamma \mapsto \eta $ with $\eta ^{n-1}=\Gamma $ is smooth on positive forms, since in a frame it is the inverse of the smooth map $\eta \mapsto \eta ^{n-1}$, whose differential is invertible. The openness argument in the proof of theorem 9.9.1 , with the $\mathrm{d}V_0$-mean in place of the $\gamma ^ n$-mean, gives a bounded inverse for the derivative with respect to the potential and the scalar between the relevant Hölder spaces. The implicit function theorem gives local smooth solution maps, and uniqueness shows that they agree on overlaps. Applying this for every order of Hölder regularity gives the assertion for smooth data. $\square$ For a smooth family of prescribed functions $F_ t\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, with $t$ in an open interval of $\mathbb R$, let $u_ t$ be the corresponding solutions with $\int _ Xu_ t\, \mathrm{d}V_0=0$, and set $Q_ t=Q_{u_ t}$ as in ( 9.26 ). The expression \[  \operatorname {tr}\bigl ((Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t)^2\bigr )  \] is independent of the chosen frame and nonnegative, because $Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t$ is similar to the Hermitian matrix $Q_ t^{-1/2}\dot Q_ t Q_ t^{-1/2}$. Theorem 9.17.2 . For a smooth family $F_ t$ and its solutions, \begin{align*}  \dot b_\gamma (F_ t)& =-\int _ X\dot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma ,\\  \ddot b_\gamma (F_ t)& =-\int _ X\ddot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma -\frac1{n-1}\int _ X \operatorname {tr}\bigl ((Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t)^2\bigr ) \, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma . \end{align*} In particular, $b_\gamma $ is concave, and along $F_ t=F_0+tG$ its second derivative is strictly negative unless $G$ is constant. Moreover, for smooth real functions $F,G$ on $X$ and every real constant $a$, \[  b_\gamma (F+a)=b_\gamma (F)-a, \qquad |b_\gamma (G)-b_\gamma (F)|\leq \| G-F\| _\infty .  \] Proof. By ( 9.26 ), \[  \mathcal G(u)=\frac1{n-1}\log \det _\gamma Q_ u.  \] Differentiating $\mathcal G(u_ t)=F_ t+b_\gamma (F_ t)$ once gives $\mathcal L_{u_ t}\dot u_ t=\dot F_ t+\dot b_\gamma (F_ t)$, and integration against the adjoint probability measure gives the first formula. Because $\Gamma _ u$ is affine in $u$, its second derivative along the family is $\mathcal D_\gamma \ddot u_ t$. The formula for the second derivative of $\log \det $ used in the proof of theorem 9.7.1 therefore gives \[  \mathcal L_{u_ t}\ddot u_ t -\frac1{n-1}\operatorname {tr}\bigl ((Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t)^2\bigr ) =\ddot F_ t+\ddot b_\gamma (F_ t).  \] Integrating against $\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma $ at this fixed parameter gives the second formula; no derivative of the measure is needed. For affine $F_ t$, we have $\ddot F_ t=0$, and positivity of the density of $\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma $ proves concavity. If the second derivative vanishes, then $\dot Q_ t=0$, so $\dot\Gamma _{u_ t}=0$ and $\mathcal L_{u_ t}\dot u_ t=0$. By proposition 9.11.1 , $\dot u_ t$ is constant, and the first differentiated equation forces $G$ to be constant. Conversely, adding a constant to $F$ changes only $b$, by the opposite constant. Finally, integrate the first derivative along the segment from $F$ to $G$: since $\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma $ is a probability measure, the derivative lies between $-\sup _ X(G-F)$ and $-\inf _ X(G-F)$, which proves the Lipschitz bound. $\square$ The Lipschitz bound extends $b_\gamma $ uniquely to continuous functions $F$. Constructing corresponding weak solutions would require, in addition, a volume measure for the $(n-1)$st roots of singular forms in the Aeppli ansatz, compactness of their potentials, and stability of the adjoint equation. On a surface with Gauduchon background form $\gamma _0$, conservation of the total mass makes the scalar and the adjoint probability measure explicit. Example 9.17.3 . If $n=2$ and $\gamma _0$ is Gauduchon, then $\Gamma _ u=\gamma _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\eta _ u$, and $\eta _ u$ is also Gauduchon. The mass identity of theorem 2.2.2 gives $\int _ X\eta _ u^2=\int _ X\gamma _0^2$. Therefore \[  b_\gamma (F)=\log \int _ X\gamma _0^2- \log \int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F\gamma ^2, \qquad \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma =\frac{\mathrm{e}^ F\gamma ^2}{\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F\gamma ^2}.  \] The adjoint equation of proposition 9.11.2 gives the same measure, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ u=0$ and hence $\rho _ u$ is constant. Along $F+tG$, the second derivative of $b_\gamma $ is minus the variance of $G$ with respect to this probability measure. In chapter 10 we return to the potential equation for $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Smooth approximation will extend its solvability to nonnegative, nonzero $L^ p$ densities, $p>1$; control of the normalization constant and uniform convergence of the potentials will replace the derivative estimates used here.

title: 10 Continuous solutions and normalization
text: 10 Continuous solutions and normalization Throughout this chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a smooth positive volume form on $X$. As in chapter 9 , we write $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$; for a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, the power $\omega _ u^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of proposition 1.7.1 . We fix $p>1$ and a nonnegative $f\in L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V)$ with $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V>0$. Norms and almost-everywhere statements refer to $\mathrm{d}V$ unless another measure is specified. We seek continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solutions of $\omega _ u^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$, with an unknown constant $c>0$, and of $\omega _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, with $\lambda >0$. Smooth positive approximations of $f$ give solutions by chapter 9 . To pass to a limit, we need uniform control of both their constants and their potentials. Integration against a Gauduchon metric bounds the constants and hence the $L^ p$ norms of the resulting densities. Modified comparison then turns normalized $L^1$ compactness into uniform compactness, which identifies the limiting Monge–Ampère measure. For the exponential equation, a weighted Gauduchon mean also controls the additive constants. Letting $\lambda $ decrease to zero determines the normalization constant $c$ from $f$, even when the normalized potential is not unique. When a bounded solution has a smooth positive density depending on the point and the potential, proper exponential equations with a frozen smooth approximation of that potential give a trace estimate and prove that the solution is smooth. On the Hopf threefold, the constant has a sharp lower bound, with equality exactly for densities pulled back from the projective plane. For densities of unit integral with a common $L^ p$ bound, $1<p<\infty $, near equality forces normalized potentials to approach their fiber averages uniformly and gives weak convergence in $L^ p$ for the density differences. Smooth oscillating examples show why strong $L^1$ convergence of the densities need not follow. For $n\geq 2$, the final two sections fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\chi $ and study concave functions of the eigenvalues of $\omega ^{-1}(\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$. An admissible reference with a strict asymptotic gap controls an auxiliary Monge–Ampère comparison, giving stability as positive right-hand sides tend to zero. Equicontinuous data then give uniform compactness. Nearby smooth admissible functions yield a gradient bound if the first derivatives of the data are uniformly bounded.

title: 10.1 Continuous solvability
text: 10.1 Continuous solvability There are two natural ways to normalize the prescribed density: by an unknown positive constant, or by an exponential of the potential. Theorem 10.1.1 (Kołodziej–Nguyen) . There are $c>0$ and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ such that \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The potential can be normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. The constant $c$ is uniquely determined by $f$, by proposition 10.6.1 . The normalized potential, however, need not be unique, even for a smooth density; see theorem 11.6.1 . Theorem 10.1.2 (Nguyen) . For every $\lambda >0$, there is a unique continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $u_\lambda $ satisfying 10.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-exp} (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\lambda )^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 10.1.1 (Kołodziej–Nguyen)
text: Theorem 10.1.1 (Kołodziej–Nguyen) . There are $c>0$ and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ such that \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The potential can be normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. of theorem 10.1.1 . Choose smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V)$. By theorem 9.1.1 , there are smooth $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ and constants $c_ j$ such that \[  \omega _{u_ j}^ n=c_ jf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0,\qquad c_ j>0.  \] We first bound the constants. For $n\geq 2$, fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. By proposition 4.2.3 , \[  c_ j^{1/n}A_ j\leq \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}, \qquad A_ j=\int _ X(f_ j\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Since $|x^{1/n}-y^{1/n}|\leq |x-y|^{1/n}$ for $x,y\geq 0$, Hölder's inequality gives $A_ j\to A>0$, where $A=\int _ X(f\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. Thus $c_ j$ is bounded above. In dimension one, Stokes' theorem gives the same estimate, with $A_ j=\int _ Xf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. The lower bound for the density norm in theorem 10.3.3 gives $c_ j\| f_ j\| _ p\geq c_ p$, so the constants are bounded away from zero. The densities $c_ jf_ j$ are therefore uniformly bounded in $L^ p$, and the same theorem gives a common bound for the $u_ j$. By theorem 1.4.2 , we may pass to a subsequence with $c_ j\to c>0$ and $u_ j$ Cauchy in $L^1$. By theorem 10.3.4 , $u_ j\to u$ uniformly, with $u$ continuous and $\sup _ Xu=0$. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives $\omega _{u_ j}^ n\rightharpoonup \omega _ u^ n$, while $c_ jf_ j\to cf$ in $L^ p$. Hence $\omega _ u^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$, as required. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.1.2 (Nguyen)
text: Theorem 10.1.2 (Nguyen) . For every $\lambda >0$, there is a unique continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $u_\lambda $ satisfying 10.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-exp} (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\lambda )^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} of theorem 10.1.2 . Choose smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p$. By theorem 9.6.2 , there are smooth $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ and $\omega _{u_ j}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. The preceding lemma bounds $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$, and consequently bounds $F_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j$ in $L^ p$. The normalized potentials $\psi _ j=u_ j-M_ j$ are uniformly bounded by theorem 10.3.3 . We may pass to a subsequence with $M_ j\to M$ and $\psi _ j$ Cauchy in $L^1$. Theorem 10.3.4 gives uniform convergence $u_ j\to u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$. Uniform convergence and $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p$ give $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f$ in $L^ p$, and continuity of bounded products therefore gives $\omega _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Uniqueness, even among all bounded solutions, follows from bounded exponential comparison, corollary 10.2.4 . $\square$
10.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-exp} (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\lambda )^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation}

title: 10.2 The modified comparison principle
text: 10.2 The modified comparison principle For a Hermitian background, the total Monge–Ampère mass varies with the potential, and the ordinary comparison principle fails in general (see 11.5.2 ). A weaker form survives. Replacing the comparison potential $v$ by $(1-\varepsilon )v$ leaves the strictly positive form $\varepsilon \omega $ in reserve, and this reserve absorbs the torsion terms. On a sublevel set of height $s$, integration by parts makes the error proportional to $s$, and a finite induction controls the intermediate mixed products. The resulting multiplicative correction tends to one as $s$ tends to zero with $\varepsilon $ fixed. Since $X$ is compact and $\omega $ is positive, we can choose $B_0\geq 1$ such that \[  -B_0\omega ^2\leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq B_0\omega ^2, \qquad -B_0\omega ^3\leq \mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \leq B_0\omega ^3.  \] These inequalities are understood after wedging with positive forms of complementary degree; forms of degree larger than $2n$ vanish, and the corresponding terms below are omitted. Theorem 10.2.1 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $0<\varepsilon <1$. For $s>0$, put \[  m_\varepsilon =\inf _ X\bigl (u-(1-\varepsilon )v\bigr ),\qquad U_{\varepsilon ,s}=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )v+m_\varepsilon +s\} .  \] If $0<s<\varepsilon ^3/(32B_0n^2)$, then, with $a=B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3}$, 10.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:modified-comparison} (1-4a)^ n\int _{U_{\varepsilon ,s}}\omega _{(1-\varepsilon )v}^{\, n} \leq \int _{U_{\varepsilon ,s}}\omega _ u^ n. \end{equation} In particular, the reverse factor $(1-4a)^{-n}$ tends to one as $s\downarrow 0$ for fixed $\varepsilon $. Proof. Write $v_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )v$, $U=U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ and \[  \phi =\max (u,v_\varepsilon +m_\varepsilon +s),\qquad T_ k=\omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{n-k},\qquad I_ k=\int _ U T_ k\quad (0\leq k\leq n).  \] Set $I_{-1}=I_{-2}=0$. Then $0\leq \phi -u\leq s$, this difference vanishes outside $U$, and on $U$ plurifine locality gives $\omega _\phi =\omega _{v_\varepsilon }\geq \varepsilon \omega $ in all bounded products. By lemma 1.7.2 , for every fixed positive mixed product $W$ of $n-1$ bounded-potential factors, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=\phi \} }\omega _ u\wedge W \leq \mathbf1_{\{ u=\phi \} }\omega _\phi \wedge W.  \] For $0\leq k\leq n-1$, apply this with $W=\omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{n-k-1}$. Since $u=\phi $ on $X\setminus U$, the difference $T_ k-T_{k+1}=(\omega _\phi -\omega _ u)\wedge W$ is nonnegative there. Consequently 10.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:comparison-stokes} I_ k-I_{k+1} \leq \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi -u)\wedge W =\int _ X(\phi -u)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W. \end{equation} This integration by parts is valid for bounded potentials. To see this, approximate $u$ and $\phi $ by decreasing sequences of smooth, uniformly bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions, using theorem 1.11.1 . For smooth functions the identity is ordinary integration by parts. The form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W$ expands as below into bounded Hessian products and smooth forms, and bounded Bedford–Taylor convergence, also against bounded quasi-continuous coefficients converging in capacity, passes each term to the limit. Set $r=n-k-1$. Since $\mathrm{d}\omega _ u=\mathrm{d}\omega _\phi =\mathrm{d}\omega $, expansion gives \[  \begin{split}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W={}& k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^{k-1}\wedge \omega _\phi ^ r +r\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{r-1}\\ & +k(k-1)\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^{k-2}\wedge \omega _\phi ^ r\\ & +2kr\, \mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^{k-1}\wedge \omega _\phi ^{r-1}\\ & +r(r-1)\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{r-2}. \end{split}  \] Terms containing a negative power have coefficient zero and are omitted. On $U$ we may replace each $\omega ^ j$ in an upper bound by $\varepsilon ^{-j}\omega _\phi ^ j$, since $\omega _\phi \geq \varepsilon \omega $ there. Using $\phi -u\leq s$ and $\varepsilon ^{-2}\leq \varepsilon ^{-3}$ in ( 10.3 ), we obtain \[  I_ k-I_{k+1}\leq B_0s\varepsilon ^{-3} \bigl (k(k-1)I_{k-2}+k(1+2r)I_{k-1}+r^2I_ k\bigr ).  \] Each coefficient is at most $n^2$, and $a=B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3}$. Hence 10.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:comparison-recurrence} I_ k-I_{k+1}\leq a(I_{k-2}+I_{k-1}+I_ k). \end{equation} Put $q=1-4a$; the assumption on $s$ gives $a<1/32$, so $q>7/8$. Suppose inductively that $qI_ j\leq I_{j+1}$ for $j<k$. Then $I_{k-1}\leq q^{-1}I_ k$ and $I_{k-2}\leq q^{-2}I_ k$ whenever the indices exist. Since \[  1+q^{-1}+q^{-2}\leq 1+8/7+64/49<4,  \] ( 10.8 ) gives $qI_ k\leq I_{k+1}$. The case $k=0$ follows from the same formula with the two absent terms set to zero. By induction, $q^ n I_0\leq I_ n$. Since $T_0=\omega _{v_\varepsilon }^ n$ on $U$ and $T_ n=\omega _ u^ n$, this is the theorem. In dimension one all torsion terms vanish and the same argument applies. $\square$ A strict multiplicative inequality between the Monge–Ampère measures on $\{ u<v\} $ absorbs the error in modified comparison. One first chooses the positivity reserve $\varepsilon $, and then a sublevel set thin enough to preserve the strict inequality. Theorem 10.2.2 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, and let $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ u^ n \leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ v^ n,  \] then $u\geq v$. In particular, $\omega _ u^ n(\{ u<v\} )=0$ implies $u\geq v$. Proof. Suppose $m=\inf _ X(u-v)<0$. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that \[  (1-\varepsilon )^ n>c, \qquad 2\varepsilon \| v\| _\infty <-m/4,  \] omitting the second restriction if $v=0$. Let $m_\varepsilon $ and $U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ be defined as in theorem 10.2.1 for this pair $u,v$. Since $|m_\varepsilon -m|\leq \varepsilon \| v\| _\infty $, for all sufficiently small $s>0$ the set $U=U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ is contained in $\{ u<v\} $: there \[  u-v<m_\varepsilon +s-\varepsilon v \leq m+2\varepsilon \| v\| _\infty +s<0.  \] The set $U$ is nonempty by the definition of the infimum and has positive volume by lemma 1.3.4 . Decrease $s$ further so that theorem 10.2.1 applies and $(1-4B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3})^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n>c$. Write the first factor as $q^ n$. Positivity of every mixed term gives \[  \omega _{(1-\varepsilon )v}^ n \geq (1-\varepsilon )^ n\omega _ v^ n+\varepsilon ^ n\omega ^ n.  \] Modified comparison and the assumption would therefore imply \[  q^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n\int _ U\omega _ v^ n +q^ n\varepsilon ^ n\int _ U\omega ^ n \leq \int _ U\omega _ u^ n\leq c\int _ U\omega _ v^ n.  \] All integrals are finite, so the choice $q^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n>c$ and the positive volume of $U$ make this impossible. Hence $m\geq 0$. $\square$ Corollary 10.2.3 . Every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function has strictly positive Monge–Ampère mass. Proof. Let $u$ be a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. If $\omega _ u^ n=0$, then theorem 10.2.2 , applied with $c=0$ and the constant potential $v=\sup _ Xu+1$, would give $u\geq v$, a contradiction. $\square$ The positive lower bound in corollary 10.2.3 depends on the potential. A bound that is uniform over all bounded potentials is the condition $v_-(\omega )>0$ of definition 6.5.1 . Corollary 10.2.4 . If $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $\lambda >0$, then \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\omega _ v^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\omega _ u^ n \quad \Longrightarrow \quad v\leq u.  \] Proof. For every $t>0$, the assumption gives $\omega _ u^ n\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\omega _ v^ n$ on $\{ u<v-t\} $. Since $\omega _{v-t}=\omega _ v$, theorem 10.2.2 , applied to $u$ and $v-t$, gives $u\geq v-t$. Letting $t\downarrow 0$ proves $v\leq u$. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.2.1
text: Theorem 10.2.1 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $0<\varepsilon <1$. For $s>0$, put \[  m_\varepsilon =\inf _ X\bigl (u-(1-\varepsilon )v\bigr ),\qquad U_{\varepsilon ,s}=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )v+m_\varepsilon +s\} .  \] If $0<s<\varepsilon ^3/(32B_0n^2)$, then, with $a=B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3}$, 10.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:modified-comparison} (1-4a)^ n\int _{U_{\varepsilon ,s}}\omega _{(1-\varepsilon )v}^{\, n} \leq \int _{U_{\varepsilon ,s}}\omega _ u^ n. \end{equation} In particular, the reverse factor $(1-4a)^{-n}$ tends to one as $s\downarrow 0$ for fixed $\varepsilon $. Proof. Write $v_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )v$, $U=U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ and \[  \phi =\max (u,v_\varepsilon +m_\varepsilon +s),\qquad T_ k=\omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{n-k},\qquad I_ k=\int _ U T_ k\quad (0\leq k\leq n).  \] Set $I_{-1}=I_{-2}=0$. Then $0\leq \phi -u\leq s$, this difference vanishes outside $U$, and on $U$ plurifine locality gives $\omega _\phi =\omega _{v_\varepsilon }\geq \varepsilon \omega $ in all bounded products. By lemma 1.7.2 , for every fixed positive mixed product $W$ of $n-1$ bounded-potential factors, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=\phi \} }\omega _ u\wedge W \leq \mathbf1_{\{ u=\phi \} }\omega _\phi \wedge W.  \] For $0\leq k\leq n-1$, apply this with $W=\omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{n-k-1}$. Since $u=\phi $ on $X\setminus U$, the difference $T_ k-T_{k+1}=(\omega _\phi -\omega _ u)\wedge W$ is nonnegative there. Consequently 10.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:comparison-stokes} I_ k-I_{k+1} \leq \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi -u)\wedge W =\int _ X(\phi -u)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W. \end{equation} This integration by parts is valid for bounded potentials. To see this, approximate $u$ and $\phi $ by decreasing sequences of smooth, uniformly bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions, using theorem 1.11.1 . For smooth functions the identity is ordinary integration by parts. The form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W$ expands as below into bounded Hessian products and smooth forms, and bounded Bedford–Taylor convergence, also against bounded quasi-continuous coefficients converging in capacity, passes each term to the limit. Set $r=n-k-1$. Since $\mathrm{d}\omega _ u=\mathrm{d}\omega _\phi =\mathrm{d}\omega $, expansion gives \[  \begin{split}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W={}& k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^{k-1}\wedge \omega _\phi ^ r +r\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{r-1}\\ & +k(k-1)\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^{k-2}\wedge \omega _\phi ^ r\\ & +2kr\, \mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^{k-1}\wedge \omega _\phi ^{r-1}\\ & +r(r-1)\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{r-2}. \end{split}  \] Terms containing a negative power have coefficient zero and are omitted. On $U$ we may replace each $\omega ^ j$ in an upper bound by $\varepsilon ^{-j}\omega _\phi ^ j$, since $\omega _\phi \geq \varepsilon \omega $ there. Using $\phi -u\leq s$ and $\varepsilon ^{-2}\leq \varepsilon ^{-3}$ in ( 10.3 ), we obtain \[  I_ k-I_{k+1}\leq B_0s\varepsilon ^{-3} \bigl (k(k-1)I_{k-2}+k(1+2r)I_{k-1}+r^2I_ k\bigr ).  \] Each coefficient is at most $n^2$, and $a=B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3}$. Hence 10.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:comparison-recurrence} I_ k-I_{k+1}\leq a(I_{k-2}+I_{k-1}+I_ k). \end{equation} Put $q=1-4a$; the assumption on $s$ gives $a<1/32$, so $q>7/8$. Suppose inductively that $qI_ j\leq I_{j+1}$ for $j<k$. Then $I_{k-1}\leq q^{-1}I_ k$ and $I_{k-2}\leq q^{-2}I_ k$ whenever the indices exist. Since \[  1+q^{-1}+q^{-2}\leq 1+8/7+64/49<4,  \] ( 10.8 ) gives $qI_ k\leq I_{k+1}$. The case $k=0$ follows from the same formula with the two absent terms set to zero. By induction, $q^ n I_0\leq I_ n$. Since $T_0=\omega _{v_\varepsilon }^ n$ on $U$ and $T_ n=\omega _ u^ n$, this is the theorem. In dimension one all torsion terms vanish and the same argument applies. $\square$
10.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:modified-comparison} (1-4a)^ n\int _{U_{\varepsilon ,s}}\omega _{(1-\varepsilon )v}^{\, n} \leq \int _{U_{\varepsilon ,s}}\omega _ u^ n. \end{equation}
10.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:comparison-stokes} I_ k-I_{k+1} \leq \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi -u)\wedge W =\int _ X(\phi -u)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W. \end{equation}
10.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:comparison-recurrence} I_ k-I_{k+1}\leq a(I_{k-2}+I_{k-1}+I_ k). \end{equation}

title: Theorem 10.2.2
text: Theorem 10.2.2 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, and let $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ u^ n \leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ v^ n,  \] then $u\geq v$. In particular, $\omega _ u^ n(\{ u<v\} )=0$ implies $u\geq v$. Proof. Suppose $m=\inf _ X(u-v)<0$. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that \[  (1-\varepsilon )^ n>c, \qquad 2\varepsilon \| v\| _\infty <-m/4,  \] omitting the second restriction if $v=0$. Let $m_\varepsilon $ and $U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ be defined as in theorem 10.2.1 for this pair $u,v$. Since $|m_\varepsilon -m|\leq \varepsilon \| v\| _\infty $, for all sufficiently small $s>0$ the set $U=U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ is contained in $\{ u<v\} $: there \[  u-v<m_\varepsilon +s-\varepsilon v \leq m+2\varepsilon \| v\| _\infty +s<0.  \] The set $U$ is nonempty by the definition of the infimum and has positive volume by lemma 1.3.4 . Decrease $s$ further so that theorem 10.2.1 applies and $(1-4B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3})^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n>c$. Write the first factor as $q^ n$. Positivity of every mixed term gives \[  \omega _{(1-\varepsilon )v}^ n \geq (1-\varepsilon )^ n\omega _ v^ n+\varepsilon ^ n\omega ^ n.  \] Modified comparison and the assumption would therefore imply \[  q^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n\int _ U\omega _ v^ n +q^ n\varepsilon ^ n\int _ U\omega ^ n \leq \int _ U\omega _ u^ n\leq c\int _ U\omega _ v^ n.  \] All integrals are finite, so the choice $q^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n>c$ and the positive volume of $U$ make this impossible. Hence $m\geq 0$. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.2.3
text: Corollary 10.2.3 . Every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function has strictly positive Monge–Ampère mass. Proof. Let $u$ be a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. If $\omega _ u^ n=0$, then theorem 10.2.2 , applied with $c=0$ and the constant potential $v=\sup _ Xu+1$, would give $u\geq v$, a contradiction. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.2.4
text: Corollary 10.2.4 . If $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $\lambda >0$, then \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\omega _ v^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\omega _ u^ n \quad \Longrightarrow \quad v\leq u.  \] Proof. For every $t>0$, the assumption gives $\omega _ u^ n\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\omega _ v^ n$ on $\{ u<v-t\} $. Since $\omega _{v-t}=\omega _ v$, theorem 10.2.2 , applied to $u$ and $v-t$, gives $u\geq v-t$. Letting $t\downarrow 0$ proves $v\leq u$. $\square$

title: 10.3 Capacity estimates and uniform compactness
text: 10.3 Capacity estimates and uniform compactness Let $\operatorname {Cap}=\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ denote the capacity of section 1.8 . Modified comparison bounds the capacity of a thin sublevel set by the Monge–Ampère mass of a slightly larger one. A bound by a power $1+\alpha $ of capacity, $\alpha >0$, makes the resulting iteration converge. For an $L^ p$ density, corollary 1.8.2 supplies the case $\alpha =1$. Iterating the two inequalities gives a lower bound for the capacity of every sublevel set of fixed height above the minimum. Since the capacity of deep sublevel sets of normalized potentials is small by the tail estimate ( 1.26 ), this bounds the depth of a normalized solution. Lemma 10.3.1 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, with $-H\leq v\leq 0$ and $H\geq 1$. Fix $0<\varepsilon <1$, and put \[  m=\inf _ X(u-(1-\varepsilon )v),\qquad U_ s=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )v+m+s\} .  \] There are $\delta _\varepsilon >0$, depending only on $(X,\omega ,\varepsilon )$, and $C_ H>0$, depending only on $(n,H)$, such that 10.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:thin-capacity} t^ n\operatorname {Cap}(U_ s)\leq C_ H\int _{U_{s+t}}\omega _ u^ n \qquad (0<s,t,\  s+t<\delta _\varepsilon ). \end{equation} Every $U_ s$, $s>0$, has positive capacity. Proof. Let $B_0$ be the constant of theorem 10.2.1 , and set \[  \delta _\varepsilon =\min \{ 1-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon ^3/(128B_0n^2)\} .  \] For a capacity test $0\leq \rho \leq 1$, put \[  \tau =\frac{t}{2(1-\varepsilon )(H+1)},\quad w=(1-\tau )v+\tau \rho ,\quad m'=\inf _ X(u-(1-\varepsilon )w).  \] Then $0<\tau <1$ and $0\leq (1-\varepsilon )(w-v)\leq t/2$, so $m-t/2\leq m'\leq m$. Consequently \[  U_ s\subset V:=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )w+m'+s+t/2\}  \subset U_{s+t}.  \] We apply modified comparison to $u,w$ at height $s+t/2<\delta _\varepsilon $; by the choice of $\delta _\varepsilon $, its inverse factor is at most $(8/7)^ n$. Moreover, \[  \omega _{(1-\varepsilon )w} \geq (1-\varepsilon )\tau \omega _\rho =\frac{t}{2(H+1)}\omega _\rho .  \] Integrating over $U_ s\subset V$, applying modified comparison on $V$, and taking the supremum over $\rho $, we obtain ( 10.9 ) with $C_ H=[2(H+1)]^ n(8/7)^ n$. Finally, each $U_ s$ is nonempty by the definition of the infimum, so it has positive smooth volume by lemma 1.3.4 , and hence positive capacity, as the constant test function shows. $\square$ Lemma 10.3.2 . In the setting of lemma 10.3.1 , suppose that $A,\alpha >0$ and \[  \omega _ u^ n(E)\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)^{1+\alpha } \qquad (E\subset X\text{ Borel}).  \] For every $0<D<\delta _\varepsilon $, 10.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:power-sublevel-lower} D\leq C_\alpha (C_ HA)^{1/n} \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (U_ D)^{\alpha /n}, \qquad C_\alpha =\frac{2}{1-2^{-\alpha }}. \end{equation} In particular, when $\alpha =1$, 10.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:sublevel-capacity-lower} \operatorname {Cap}(U_ D)\geq \frac{D^ n}{4^ nC_ HA}. \end{equation} Proof. Put $a(s)=\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (U_ s)^{1/n}>0$ and $K=(C_ HA)^{1/n}$. The thin-sublevel estimate gives \[  t\, a(s)\leq K a(s+t)^{1+\alpha } \qquad (0<s,t,\  s+t<\delta _\varepsilon ).  \] Suppose $C_\alpha K a(D)^\alpha <D$. Starting with $s_0=D$, set \[  t_ j=2K a(s_ j)^\alpha ,\qquad s_{j+1}=s_ j-t_ j.  \] If $a(s_ i)\leq 2^{-i}a(D)$ for $0\leq i\leq j$, then \[  \sum _{i=0}^ jt_ i \leq 2K a(D)^\alpha \sum _{i=0}^ j2^{-i\alpha } <C_\alpha K a(D)^\alpha <D.  \] Thus $s_{j+1}>0$, and the sublevel estimate, applied with $s=s_{j+1}$ and $t=t_ j$, gives $a(s_{j+1})\leq a(s_ j)/2$. Induction justifies every step. The decreasing sequence $s_ j$ has a limit \[  s_\infty \geq D-C_\alpha K a(D)^\alpha >0.  \] Monotonicity now gives $0<a(s_\infty )\leq 2^{-j}a(D)$ for every $j$, a contradiction. This proves ( 10.10 ), including the case in which $U_ D=X$. $\square$ Theorem 10.3.3 . There are constants $C_ p,c_ p>0$, depending only on $(X,\omega ,\mathrm{d}V,p)$, such that, whenever $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, $\sup _ Xu=0$, and \[  \omega _ u^ n=F\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad F\in L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V),\quad F\geq 0,  \] we have 10.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lp-potential-bound} \| u\| _\infty \leq C_ p(1+\| F\| _ p), \qquad \| F\| _ p\geq c_ p. \end{equation} Proof. By corollary 10.2.3 , $F$ is not almost everywhere zero. Apply lemma 10.3.2 with $v=0$, $H=1$, $\varepsilon =1/2$, and $A=C\| F\| _ p>0$, where $C$ is the constant of corollary 1.8.2 . Fix $D=\delta _{1/2}/2$, and put $M=-\inf _ Xu$. Since $U_ D=\{ u<-M+D\} $, the resulting inequality reads \[  \operatorname {Cap}(\{ u<-M+D\} )\geq c/\| F\| _ p.  \] If $M>D+1$, ( 1.26 ) bounds this capacity above by $C/(M-D)$, and the first assertion follows; the case $M\leq D+1$ is immediate. Bounding the same capacity above by $\operatorname {Cap}(X)$ gives the second assertion. $\square$ Suppose that two uniformly bounded solutions are far apart at some point. The preceding estimates give a fixed positive lower bound for the capacity of a sublevel set of their difference. If their $L^1$ distance is small, this set has small volume, and the uniform $L^ p$ bound for the densities then makes its Monge–Ampère mass small. This contradicts the sublevel estimate ( 10.9 ), and so upgrades $L^1$ compactness to uniform compactness. Put $p'=p/(p-1)$. Theorem 10.3.4 . Suppose $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$, $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$, and \[  \omega _{u_ j}^ n=F_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad F_ j\geq 0,\qquad \sup _ j\| F_ j\| _ p<\infty  \] for the fixed $p>1$. If $(u_ j)$ is Cauchy in $L^1(X,\mathrm{d}V)$, then it is Cauchy uniformly. In particular, every such family has a subsequence converging uniformly to a continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. Proof. By theorem 10.3.3 , there is a common $H\geq 1$ with $-H\leq u_ j\leq 0$. Suppose that the sequence is not uniformly Cauchy. After exchanging indices if necessary, we find $a>0$ and arbitrarily large $j,k$ with \[  S:=\inf _ X(u_ k-u_ j)\leq -a.  \] Choose $0<\varepsilon <1$ such that $\varepsilon H<a/4$, and choose a fixed $D>0$ with $2D<\delta _\varepsilon $ and $2D<a/4$. Apply the preceding sublevel lemmas with $u=u_ k$ and $v=u_ j$. Since $v\leq 0$, $m=\inf (u-(1-\varepsilon )v)\leq S$. Thus \[  U_{2D}\subset \{ u-v<S+2D+\varepsilon H\}  \subset \{ |u-v|>a/2\} .  \] The capacity lower bound ( 10.11 ), with a constant $A$ independent of $j,k$ given by corollary 1.8.2 , yields $\operatorname {Cap}(U_ D)\geq c>0$. On the other hand, ( 10.9 ) and the inequalities of Hölder and Chebyshev give \[  \begin{split}  D^ n\operatorname {Cap}(U_ D) & \leq C_ H\int _{U_{2D}}F_ k\, \mathrm{d}V\\ & \leq C_ H\| F_ k\| _ p \left(\frac{2\| u_ k-u_ j\| _1}{a}\right)^{1/p'} \longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] This contradiction proves that the sequence is uniformly Cauchy. For the last assertion, the normalized compactness theorem, theorem 1.4.2 , gives an $L^1$-Cauchy subsequence of any such family. Its uniform limit is continuous, and distributional convergence preserves $\omega $-plurisubharmonicity. $\square$

10.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:thin-capacity} t^ n\operatorname {Cap}(U_ s)\leq C_ H\int _{U_{s+t}}\omega _ u^ n \qquad (0<s,t,\  s+t<\delta _\varepsilon ). \end{equation}

title: Lemma 10.3.2
text: Lemma 10.3.2 . In the setting of lemma 10.3.1 , suppose that $A,\alpha >0$ and \[  \omega _ u^ n(E)\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)^{1+\alpha } \qquad (E\subset X\text{ Borel}).  \] For every $0<D<\delta _\varepsilon $, 10.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:power-sublevel-lower} D\leq C_\alpha (C_ HA)^{1/n} \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (U_ D)^{\alpha /n}, \qquad C_\alpha =\frac{2}{1-2^{-\alpha }}. \end{equation} In particular, when $\alpha =1$, 10.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:sublevel-capacity-lower} \operatorname {Cap}(U_ D)\geq \frac{D^ n}{4^ nC_ HA}. \end{equation} Proof. This proves ( 10.10 ), including the case in which $U_ D=X$. $\square$
10.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:power-sublevel-lower} D\leq C_\alpha (C_ HA)^{1/n} \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (U_ D)^{\alpha /n}, \qquad C_\alpha =\frac{2}{1-2^{-\alpha }}. \end{equation}
10.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:sublevel-capacity-lower} \operatorname {Cap}(U_ D)\geq \frac{D^ n}{4^ nC_ HA}. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 10.3.3
text: Theorem 10.3.3 . There are constants $C_ p,c_ p>0$, depending only on $(X,\omega ,\mathrm{d}V,p)$, such that, whenever $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, $\sup _ Xu=0$, and \[  \omega _ u^ n=F\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad F\in L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V),\quad F\geq 0,  \] we have 10.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lp-potential-bound} \| u\| _\infty \leq C_ p(1+\| F\| _ p), \qquad \| F\| _ p\geq c_ p. \end{equation} Proof. Fix $D=\delta _{1/2}/2$, and put $M=-\inf _ Xu$. Since $U_ D=\{ u<-M+D\} $, the resulting inequality reads \[  \operatorname {Cap}(\{ u<-M+D\} )\geq c/\| F\| _ p.  \] If $M>D+1$, ( 1.26 ) bounds this capacity above by $C/(M-D)$, and the first assertion follows; the case $M\leq D+1$ is immediate. 10.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lp-potential-bound} \| u\| _\infty \leq C_ p(1+\| F\| _ p), \qquad \| F\| _ p\geq c_ p. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 10.3.4
text: Theorem 10.3.4 . Suppose $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$, $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$, and \[  \omega _{u_ j}^ n=F_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad F_ j\geq 0,\qquad \sup _ j\| F_ j\| _ p<\infty  \] for the fixed $p>1$. By theorem 10.3.3 , there is a common $H\geq 1$ with $-H\leq u_ j\leq 0$. Suppose that the sequence is not uniformly Cauchy. After exchanging indices if necessary, we find $a>0$ and arbitrarily large $j,k$ with \[  S:=\inf _ X(u_ k-u_ j)\leq -a.  \] Choose $0<\varepsilon <1$ such that $\varepsilon H<a/4$, and choose a fixed $D>0$ with $2D<\delta _\varepsilon $ and $2D<a/4$. Thus \[  U_{2D}\subset \{ u-v<S+2D+\varepsilon H\}  \subset \{ |u-v|>a/2\} .  \] The capacity lower bound ( 10.11 ), with a constant $A$ independent of $j,k$ given by corollary 1.8.2 , yields $\operatorname {Cap}(U_ D)\geq c>0$. title: 10.3.1 Stability under a power capacity bound
search_title: Stability under a power capacity bound
text: 10.3.1 Stability under a power capacity bound The capacity lower bound of lemma 10.3.2 turns an integral error against the solution measure into a uniform error. The argument uses only the power capacity bound on this measure and therefore applies to singular measures as well. Proposition 10.3.5 . Fix $A,\alpha >0$ and $H\geq 1$. Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ satisfy $\sup _ Xu=0$ and $-H\leq v\leq 0$, and suppose \[  \mu (E)\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)^{1+\alpha }, \qquad \mu =\omega _ u^ n, \qquad E\subset X\text{ Borel}.  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on $(X,\omega ),A,\alpha ,H$, such that 10.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:power-one-sided-stability} \sup _ X(v-u)_+ \leq C\left(\int _ X(v-u)_+\, \mathrm d\mu \right)^{\sigma _\alpha }, \qquad \sigma _\alpha =\frac{\alpha }{3n(1+\alpha )+\alpha }. \end{equation} For the square-capacity bound, $\alpha =1$, the exponent is $1/(6n+1)$. Proof. Write $L=\int _ X(v-u)_+\, \mathrm d\mu $ and $S=\sup _ X(v-u)_+$. Apply lemma 10.3.2 with competitor zero, $\varepsilon =1/2$ and one fixed $0<D<\delta _{1/2}$. It bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega \{ u<\inf _ Xu+D\} $ below by a positive constant. The tail estimate ( 1.26 ) therefore bounds $-\inf _ Xu$ in terms of $(X,\omega ),A,\alpha $. Consequently $S$ has a fixed upper bound. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/2$, choose a fixed small $c>0$ and put $D=c\varepsilon ^3$. The formula for $\delta _\varepsilon $ in lemma 10.3.1 allows $c$ to be chosen so that $2D<\delta _\varepsilon $ and $4D\leq \varepsilon $. With \[  m=\inf _ X(u-(1-\varepsilon )v),\qquad U_ s=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )v+m+s\} ,  \] we have $m\leq -S$ when $S>0$, since $v\leq 0$. On $U_{2D}$, \[  v-u>S-\varepsilon H-2D.  \] If $S>2\varepsilon H+4D$, this is greater than $S/2$. The backwards and thin-sublevel estimates give \[  c_0D^{n(1+1/\alpha )} \leq D^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (U_ D) \leq C_ H\mu (U_{2D})\leq \frac{2C_ HL}{S},  \] where $c_0>0$ depends only on the stated data. Hence $S\leq CL\varepsilon ^{-3n(1+1/\alpha )}$ in this case. In the other case, $S\leq (2H+1)\varepsilon $. For sufficiently small $L>0$, choose $\varepsilon =L^{\sigma _\alpha }$. The two alternatives give ( 10.15 ). The remaining positive values of $L$ are covered by the fixed upper bound for $S$. If $L=0$, the first alternative is impossible for every small $\varepsilon $, and the second gives $S=0$ on letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.3.5
text: Proposition 10.3.5 . Fix $A,\alpha >0$ and $H\geq 1$. Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ satisfy $\sup _ Xu=0$ and $-H\leq v\leq 0$, and suppose \[  \mu (E)\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)^{1+\alpha }, \qquad \mu =\omega _ u^ n, \qquad E\subset X\text{ Borel}.  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on $(X,\omega ),A,\alpha ,H$, such that 10.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:power-one-sided-stability} \sup _ X(v-u)_+ \leq C\left(\int _ X(v-u)_+\, \mathrm d\mu \right)^{\sigma _\alpha }, \qquad \sigma _\alpha =\frac{\alpha }{3n(1+\alpha )+\alpha }. \end{equation} For the square-capacity bound, $\alpha =1$, the exponent is $1/(6n+1)$. Proof. Write $L=\int _ X(v-u)_+\, \mathrm d\mu $ and $S=\sup _ X(v-u)_+$. Apply lemma 10.3.2 with competitor zero, $\varepsilon =1/2$ and one fixed $0<D<\delta _{1/2}$. It bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega \{ u<\inf _ Xu+D\} $ below by a positive constant. The tail estimate ( 1.26 ) therefore bounds $-\inf _ Xu$ in terms of $(X,\omega ),A,\alpha $. Consequently $S$ has a fixed upper bound. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/2$, choose a fixed small $c>0$ and put $D=c\varepsilon ^3$. The formula for $\delta _\varepsilon $ in lemma 10.3.1 allows $c$ to be chosen so that $2D<\delta _\varepsilon $ and $4D\leq \varepsilon $. With \[  m=\inf _ X(u-(1-\varepsilon )v),\qquad U_ s=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )v+m+s\} ,  \] we have $m\leq -S$ when $S>0$, since $v\leq 0$. On $U_{2D}$, \[  v-u>S-\varepsilon H-2D.  \] If $S>2\varepsilon H+4D$, this is greater than $S/2$. The backwards and thin-sublevel estimates give \[  c_0D^{n(1+1/\alpha )} \leq D^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (U_ D) \leq C_ H\mu (U_{2D})\leq \frac{2C_ HL}{S},  \] where $c_0>0$ depends only on the stated data. Hence $S\leq CL\varepsilon ^{-3n(1+1/\alpha )}$ in this case. In the other case, $S\leq (2H+1)\varepsilon $. For sufficiently small $L>0$, choose $\varepsilon =L^{\sigma _\alpha }$. The two alternatives give ( 10.15 ). The remaining positive values of $L$ are covered by the fixed upper bound for $S$. If $L=0$, the first alternative is impossible for every small $\varepsilon $, and the second gives $S=0$ on letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$
