title: 10.4 Construction of continuous solutions
text: 10.4 Construction of continuous solutions Smooth approximation gives solutions with unknown normalization constants. A Gauduchon trace bounds these constants above, and the lower bound for the density norm in theorem 10.3.3 bounds them away from zero. The resulting uniform $L^ p$ bound puts the potentials in the compact family of theorem 10.3.4 , so their limit solves the prescribed equation. of theorem 10.1.1 . Choose smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V)$. By theorem 9.1.1 , there are smooth $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ and constants $c_ j$ such that \[  \omega _{u_ j}^ n=c_ jf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0,\qquad c_ j>0.  \] We first bound the constants. For $n\geq 2$, fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. By proposition 4.2.3 , \[  c_ j^{1/n}A_ j\leq \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}, \qquad A_ j=\int _ X(f_ j\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Since $|x^{1/n}-y^{1/n}|\leq |x-y|^{1/n}$ for $x,y\geq 0$, Hölder's inequality gives $A_ j\to A>0$, where $A=\int _ X(f\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. Thus $c_ j$ is bounded above. In dimension one, Stokes' theorem gives the same estimate, with $A_ j=\int _ Xf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. The lower bound for the density norm in theorem 10.3.3 gives $c_ j\| f_ j\| _ p\geq c_ p$, so the constants are bounded away from zero. The densities $c_ jf_ j$ are therefore uniformly bounded in $L^ p$, and the same theorem gives a common bound for the $u_ j$. By theorem 1.4.2 , we may pass to a subsequence with $c_ j\to c>0$ and $u_ j$ Cauchy in $L^1$. By theorem 10.3.4 , $u_ j\to u$ uniformly, with $u$ continuous and $\sup _ Xu=0$. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives $\omega _{u_ j}^ n\rightharpoonup \omega _ u^ n$, while $c_ jf_ j\to cf$ in $L^ p$. Hence $\omega _ u^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$, as required. $\square$ For the exponential equation, the role of the normalization constant is played by $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \sup _ Xu}$. Its upper bound comes from Jensen's inequality: weighting the Gauduchon volume by the $n$th root of the density relates $\sup _ Xu$ to the Gauduchon trace of $\omega _ u$, which does not depend on $u$. The lower bound for the density norm again gives the reverse bound. Lemma 10.4.1 . Fix $\lambda >0$. Suppose that smooth functions $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ solve \[  \omega _{u_ j}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where the smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j$ converge in $L^ p$ to a nonnegative nonzero $f$. Then $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$ is bounded above and below, uniformly in $j$. Proof. Absorbing the fixed smooth positive ratio $\mathrm{d}V/\omega ^ n$ into $f_ j$ and $f$ preserves their $L^ p$ convergence, so we may assume $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n$. Choose $\rho >0$ smooth with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \omega ^{n-1})=0$, using theorem 4.1.2 ; for $n=1$, take $\rho =1$. Put \[  \alpha =\int _ X\rho \omega ^ n,\quad A_ j=\int _ X f_ j^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n,\quad \psi _ j=u_ j-M_ j\leq 0.  \] Set $A=\int _ X f^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n$. The inequality for $n$th roots used in the preceding existence proof gives $A_ j\to A>0$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \omega ^{n-1})=0$, the trace $\int _ X\omega _{u_ j}\wedge \rho \omega ^{n-1}$ equals $\alpha $; the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality therefore implies \[  \alpha =\int _ X\omega _{u_ j}\wedge \rho \omega ^{n-1} \geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda M_ j/n}\int _ X \mathrm{e}^{\lambda \psi _ j/n}f_ j^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n.  \] Applying Jensen's inequality to the probability measure $A_ j^{-1}f_ j^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n$ and taking logarithms, we obtain 10.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gauduchon-exponential-mean} \lambda M_ j\leq n\log (\alpha /A_ j) +\frac{\lambda }{A_ j}\int _ X(-\psi _ j)f_ j^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n. \end{equation} By lemma 1.5.1 , the normalized potentials $\psi _ j$ have uniform $L^ q$ bounds for every finite $q$. With $q=np/(np-1)$, Hölder's inequality gives a uniform bound for the last integral, since $\| f_ j^{1/n}\| _{np}=\| f_ j\| _ p^{1/n}$. This proves the upper bound for $M_ j$. Finally, the density $F_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j$ satisfies $\| F_ j\| _ p\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda M_ j}\| f_ j\| _ p$. The lower-density bound of theorem 10.3.3 , applied to $\psi _ j$, gives $c_ p\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda M_ j}\| f_ j\| _ p$, which bounds $M_ j$ below. $\square$ of theorem 10.1.2 . Choose smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p$. By theorem 9.6.2 , there are smooth $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ and $\omega _{u_ j}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. The preceding lemma bounds $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$, and consequently bounds $F_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j$ in $L^ p$. The normalized potentials $\psi _ j=u_ j-M_ j$ are uniformly bounded by theorem 10.3.3 . We may pass to a subsequence with $M_ j\to M$ and $\psi _ j$ Cauchy in $L^1$. Theorem 10.3.4 gives uniform convergence $u_ j\to u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$. Uniform convergence and $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p$ give $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f$ in $L^ p$, and continuity of bounded products therefore gives $\omega _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Uniqueness, even among all bounded solutions, follows from bounded exponential comparison, corollary 10.2.4 . $\square$ For the exponential equation, a larger density gives a smaller solution, since the factor $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ has to compensate for the increase. Bounded exponential comparison gives this monotonicity even where the densities vanish. Lemma 10.4.2 . Let $\lambda >0$, and let $f_ a,f_ b$ be nonnegative nonzero $L^ p$ densities. Suppose that $a,b\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ solve \[  \omega _ a^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda a}f_ a\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \omega _ b^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda b}f_ b\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] If $f_ a\leq f_ b$ almost everywhere, then $b\leq a$ on $X$. Proof. Since $f_ a\leq f_ b$, the two equations give $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda b}\omega _ b^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda a}\omega _ a^ n$. Hence $b\leq a$ by corollary 10.2.4 , applied with $u=a$ and $v=b$. $\square$ Corollary 10.4.3 . Every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solution of $\omega _ u^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is continuous. Proof. Since $u$ is bounded, the density $\mathrm{e}^{-u}f$ is nonnegative, nonzero and belongs to $L^ p$. By theorem 10.1.2 , applied with $\lambda =1$ to this density, there is a continuous solution $r$ of \[  \omega _ r^ n=\mathrm{e}^{r-u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The bounded potential $u$ solves the same exponential equation. Applying lemma 10.4.2 with $f_ a=f_ b=\mathrm{e}^{-u}f$ in both orders gives $u=r$, so $u$ is continuous. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.4.1

title: Lemma 10.4.2
text: Lemma 10.4.2 . Let $\lambda >0$, and let $f_ a,f_ b$ be nonnegative nonzero $L^ p$ densities. Suppose that $a,b\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ solve \[  \omega _ a^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda a}f_ a\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \omega _ b^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda b}f_ b\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] If $f_ a\leq f_ b$ almost everywhere, then $b\leq a$ on $X$. Proof. Since $f_ a\leq f_ b$, the two equations give $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda b}\omega _ b^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda a}\omega _ a^ n$. Hence $b\leq a$ by corollary 10.2.4 , applied with $u=a$ and $v=b$. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.4.3
text: Corollary 10.4.3 . Every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solution of $\omega _ u^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is continuous. Proof. Since $u$ is bounded, the density $\mathrm{e}^{-u}f$ is nonnegative, nonzero and belongs to $L^ p$. By theorem 10.1.2 , applied with $\lambda =1$ to this density, there is a continuous solution $r$ of \[  \omega _ r^ n=\mathrm{e}^{r-u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The bounded potential $u$ solves the same exponential equation. Applying lemma 10.4.2 with $f_ a=f_ b=\mathrm{e}^{-u}f$ in both orders gives $u=r$, so $u$ is continuous. $\square$

title: 10.5 Smoothness of bounded solutions
text: 10.5 Smoothness of bounded solutions The continuous solutions constructed above have low regularity when the density is merely integrable. If the density is a smooth positive function of the point and the potential, every bounded solution is smooth. Differentiating that density directly would require derivatives of the solution. We instead freeze its occurrence in a smooth approximation and solve a proper exponential equation. A square of the prescribed potential in the maximum-principle function gives a trace estimate independent of its derivatives. We first prove this estimate, retaining the matrix notation $g,h$, the traces $S,B$ and the torsion trace $\tau $ of lemma 9.4.1 . Lemma 10.5.1 . Fix $M\geq 0$ and a smooth real function $G$ on $X\times [-M,M]$. There is $C$, depending only on $\omega $, $M$ and $\| G\| _{C^2}$, with the following property. If $v,u$ are smooth, $\omega _ v,\omega _ u>0$, $|v|\leq M$, and \[  \omega _ u^ n=\mathrm e^{u+G(x,v)}\omega ^ n,  \] then \[  |u|\leq \| G\| _{C^0},\qquad C^{-1}\omega \leq \omega _ u\leq C\omega .  \] Proof. The extrema of $u$ give the first bound, as in theorem 9.6.2 . Put $k=g+(v_{i\bar j})$, $S_ v=\operatorname {tr}_ gk$, and $D=2\| G\| _{C^0}$. The chain rule and Cauchy–Schwarz give, for $H=u+G(x,v)$, \[  \Delta _ gH\geq -C_0\bigl (1+S_ v+|\partial v|_ g^2\bigr ).  \] Indeed $\Delta _ gu=S-n\geq -n$, $\Delta _ gv=S_ v-n$, and the mixed derivatives of $G(x,v)$ are bounded below by $-C_0(1+|\partial v|_ g^2)$. Here and below constants depend only on the declared data. Set $r=v+M+1$, $R=2M+1$ and $s=u-\inf _ Xu+1$, so $1\leq r\leq R$ and $1\leq s\leq D+1$. For constants $A,L>0$ to be chosen, maximize \[  Q=\log S+Ar^2-Lu+s^{-1}  \] on $X$. If $S<1$ at the maximum, the bounded ranges of $r,u,s$ already bound $S$ everywhere. Otherwise lemma 9.4.1 applies there. Positivity gives \[  SB\geq n^2,\qquad S_ v\leq S\operatorname {tr}_ hk, \qquad |\partial v|_ g^2\leq S|\partial v|_ h^2.  \] The middle inequality follows by diagonalizing $h$ relative to $g$: every eigenvalue of $h$ is at most $S$, and the diagonal entries of $k$ are positive. Consequently, \[  \frac{\Delta _ gH}{S} \geq -C_1 B-C_0\operatorname {tr}_ hk-C_0|\partial v|_ h^2.  \] At the maximum, \[  \frac{\partial S}{S}=(L+s^{-2})\partial u-2Ar\partial v.  \] Since $|\tau |_ h^2\leq C_ gB$, Young's inequality bounds the torsion term by \[  \left|\frac2{S^2}\operatorname {Re}(h^{i\bar j}\tau _ iS_{\bar j})\right| \leq s^{-3}|\partial u|_ h^2+A|\partial v|_ h^2 +\frac{C_ g\bigl ((L+1)^2(D+1)^3+AR^2\bigr )}{S^2}B.  \] Also \begin{align*}  \Delta _ h(Ar^2)& \geq 2A\operatorname {tr}_ hk-2AR B+2A|\partial v|_ h^2,\\  \Delta _ h(-Lu+s^{-1})& =(L+s^{-2})(B-n)+2s^{-3}|\partial u|_ h^2. \end{align*} Combining these inequalities with ( 9.10 ) yields \[  \begin{split}  0\geq \Delta _ hQ\geq {}&  \left(L-2AR-C_2- \frac{C_ g((L+1)^2(D+1)^3+AR^2)}{S^2}\right)B-n(L+1)\\ & +(2A-C_0)\operatorname {tr}_ hk+(A-C_0)|\partial v|_ h^2 +s^{-3}|\partial u|_ h^2. \end{split}  \] Choose $A>C_0+1$ and then $L>2AR+C_2+2$. If the fraction in the coefficient of $B$ is at least one, $S^2$ at the maximum is bounded by its numerator. Otherwise the displayed inequality gives $B\leq n(L+1)$ there. For $n\geq 2$, the bounded determinant gives \[  S\leq n\mathrm e^{2\| G\| _{C^0}}B^{n-1}.  \] For $n=1$, $S=\mathrm e^{u+G(x,v)}$ directly. Thus $S$ is bounded at the maximum in every case. Maximality of $Q$ and the bounded ranges of $r,u,s$ give the same bound globally. The positive lower determinant bound then bounds every eigenvalue of $h$ away from zero. $\square$ Theorem 10.5.2 . Let $F\in C^\infty (X\times \mathbb R,\mathbb R)$. Every bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfying \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mathrm e^{F(x,u)}\, \mathrm dV  \] is smooth on $X$, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Proof. The density $\mathrm e^{F(x,u)}$ is bounded and strictly positive, so corollary 10.4.3 makes $u$ continuous. Choose smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $v_ j\downarrow u$ by theorem 1.11.1 . They have a common bound $M$ and converge uniformly by Dini's theorem. Define \[  G(x,t)=F(x,t)-t+\log \frac{\mathrm dV}{\omega ^ n}.  \] By theorem 9.6.2 , there is a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $a_ j$ with \[  \omega _{a_ j}^ n=\mathrm e^{a_ j+G(x,v_ j)}\omega ^ n.  \] Put $\delta _ j=\| G(x,v_ j)-G(x,u)\| _{C^0}\to 0$. The given $u$ solves the proper equation with coefficient $G(x,u)$. The weighted measures of $a_ j-\delta _ j$ and $a_ j+\delta _ j$ bracket its coefficient, so corollary 10.2.4 gives \[  a_ j-\delta _ j\leq u\leq a_ j+\delta _ j.  \] Hence $a_ j\to u$ uniformly. By lemma 10.5.1 , $C^{-1}\omega \leq \omega _{a_ j}\leq C\omega $ uniformly. In particular $\Delta _ ga_ j$ is uniformly bounded. Fixed-operator elliptic estimates give uniform $W^{2,q}$ bounds for every finite $q$, so $u\in C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ for every $0<\alpha <1$. We explain the uniformly elliptic passage to higher regularity, using the concave extension from corollary 9.4.4 . On a relatively compact coordinate chart, let $P$ send a real Hessian to its complex Hermitian part, with the coordinate normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. All matrices $g(x)+P(D^2a_ j)$ lie in a fixed compact interval $\mathcal K=\{ \lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I\} $ of positive matrices. Define \[  \mathcal F(x,N)=\inf _{A\in \mathcal K} \left\{ \log \det A+\operatorname {tr}\bigl [A^{-1}(g(x)+P(N)-A)\bigr ]\right\}  -\log \det g(x).  \] The tangent inequality for the concave logarithmic determinant shows that this is the original operator whenever $g(x)+P(N)\in \mathcal K$. It is concave and uniformly elliptic on real symmetric matrices: for $N'\geq 0$, $P(N')\geq 0$ and its trace is a fixed positive multiple of $\operatorname {tr}N'$, while $A^{\pm 1}$ have uniform bounds. Its dependence on $x$ is uniformly Lipschitz on this chart. Thus the $a_ j$ are classical, and hence viscosity, solutions of \[  \mathcal F(x,D^2a_ j)=a_ j+G(x,v_ j).  \] Both sides converge uniformly except for the Hessian variable. Stability of viscosity solutions gives $\mathcal F(x,D^2u)=u+G(x,u)$ in the viscosity sense. The right-hand side is Hölder because $u\in C^{1,\alpha }$. The local Evans–Krylov estimate therefore gives $u\in C^{2,\beta }$ for some $\beta >0$. The metric bounds pass to the limit, so the original equation is now uniformly elliptic with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Differentiating it and applying Schauder estimates repeatedly proves $u\in C^\infty (X)$. $\square$

For $n\geq 2$, the bounded determinant gives \[  S\leq n\mathrm e^{2\| G\| _{C^0}}B^{n-1}.  \] For $n=1$, $S=\mathrm e^{u+G(x,v)}$ directly. Thus $S$ is bounded at the maximum in every case. Maximality of $Q$ and the bounded ranges of $r,u,s$ give the same bound globally. The positive lower determinant bound then bounds every eigenvalue of $h$ away from zero. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.5.2
text: Theorem 10.5.2 . Let $F\in C^\infty (X\times \mathbb R,\mathbb R)$. Every bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfying \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mathrm e^{F(x,u)}\, \mathrm dV  \] is smooth on $X$, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Proof. The density $\mathrm e^{F(x,u)}$ is bounded and strictly positive, so corollary 10.4.3 makes $u$ continuous. Choose smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $v_ j\downarrow u$ by theorem 1.11.1 . They have a common bound $M$ and converge uniformly by Dini's theorem. Define \[  G(x,t)=F(x,t)-t+\log \frac{\mathrm dV}{\omega ^ n}.  \] By theorem 9.6.2 , there is a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $a_ j$ with \[  \omega _{a_ j}^ n=\mathrm e^{a_ j+G(x,v_ j)}\omega ^ n.  \] Put $\delta _ j=\| G(x,v_ j)-G(x,u)\| _{C^0}\to 0$. The given $u$ solves the proper equation with coefficient $G(x,u)$. The weighted measures of $a_ j-\delta _ j$ and $a_ j+\delta _ j$ bracket its coefficient, so corollary 10.2.4 gives \[  a_ j-\delta _ j\leq u\leq a_ j+\delta _ j.  \] Hence $a_ j\to u$ uniformly. By lemma 10.5.1 , $C^{-1}\omega \leq \omega _{a_ j}\leq C\omega $ uniformly. In particular $\Delta _ ga_ j$ is uniformly bounded. Fixed-operator elliptic estimates give uniform $W^{2,q}$ bounds for every finite $q$, so $u\in C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ for every $0<\alpha <1$. We explain the uniformly elliptic passage to higher regularity, using the concave extension from corollary 9.4.4 . On a relatively compact coordinate chart, let $P$ send a real Hessian to its complex Hermitian part, with the coordinate normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. All matrices $g(x)+P(D^2a_ j)$ lie in a fixed compact interval $\mathcal K=\{ \lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I\} $ of positive matrices. Define \[  \mathcal F(x,N)=\inf _{A\in \mathcal K} \left\{ \log \det A+\operatorname {tr}\bigl [A^{-1}(g(x)+P(N)-A)\bigr ]\right\}  -\log \det g(x).  \] The tangent inequality for the concave logarithmic determinant shows that this is the original operator whenever $g(x)+P(N)\in \mathcal K$. It is concave and uniformly elliptic on real symmetric matrices: for $N'\geq 0$, $P(N')\geq 0$ and its trace is a fixed positive multiple of $\operatorname {tr}N'$, while $A^{\pm 1}$ have uniform bounds. Its dependence on $x$ is uniformly Lipschitz on this chart. Thus the $a_ j$ are classical, and hence viscosity, solutions of \[  \mathcal F(x,D^2a_ j)=a_ j+G(x,v_ j).  \] Both sides converge uniformly except for the Hessian variable. Stability of viscosity solutions gives $\mathcal F(x,D^2u)=u+G(x,u)$ in the viscosity sense. The right-hand side is Hölder because $u\in C^{1,\alpha }$. The local Evans–Krylov estimate therefore gives $u\in C^{2,\beta }$ for some $\beta >0$. The metric bounds pass to the limit, so the original equation is now uniformly elliptic with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Differentiating it and applying Schauder estimates repeatedly proves $u\in C^\infty (X)$. $\square$

title: 10.6 The vanishing exponent and scalar uniqueness
search_title: The vanishing exponent and scalar uniqueness
text: 10.6 The vanishing exponent and scalar uniqueness To show that the constant in theorem 10.1.1 is unique, we compare the solution $u_\lambda $ of ( 10.1 ) with constant translates of a solution $u$ of the normalized equation. Translating $u$ by its maximum and by its minimum gives two barriers for the exponential equation, whose separation is the oscillation of $u$. After multiplication by $\lambda $, both barriers converge to the logarithm of the constant as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Since $u_\lambda $ depends only on $f$ and $\lambda $, the constant is determined by $f$. Proposition 10.6.1 . Suppose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ and $c>0$ satisfy $\omega _ u^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Set $m=\inf _ Xu$ and $M=\sup _ Xu$. Then, for every $\lambda >0$, the solution of ( 10.1 ) satisfies 10.19 \begin{equation} \label{eq:exp-barriers} u+\frac{\log c}{\lambda }-M \leq u_\lambda \leq u+\frac{\log c}{\lambda }-m. \end{equation} In particular, \[  \| \lambda u_\lambda -\log c\| _\infty \leq \lambda (M-m), \qquad \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }\longrightarrow c \quad \hbox{uniformly on }X\hbox{ as }\lambda \downarrow 0.  \] Consequently, $c$ is the only constant for which the equation $\omega _ v^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a solution $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$. Proof. Set $a=u+\lambda ^{-1}\log c-M$ and $b=u+\lambda ^{-1}\log c-m$. These translates of $u$ have the same Monge–Ampère measure as $u$, and since $m\leq u\leq M$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{\lambda a}f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq cf\, \mathrm{d}V=\omega _ a^ n=\omega _ b^ n \leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda b}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Thus $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda a}\omega _ a^ n\geq f\, \mathrm{d}V=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u_\lambda }\omega _{u_\lambda }^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda b}\omega _ b^ n$. Applying corollary 10.2.4 first to the pair $(u_\lambda ,a)$ and then to the pair $(b,u_\lambda )$ gives $a\leq u_\lambda \leq b$, which is ( 10.19 ). Multiplying these inequalities by $\lambda $ and using $m\leq u\leq M$ gives the norm bound, and the uniform convergence follows. If $(v,c')$ is another such pair, the same argument applied to $v$ gives $\lambda u_\lambda \to \log c'$, because $u_\lambda $ depends only on $f$ and $\lambda $. Hence $c'=c$. $\square$ The barriers also give $\operatorname {osc}_ Xu_\lambda \leq 2(M-m)$, and the densities $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f$ converge to $cf$ in $L^ p$. By theorem 10.3.4 , the normalized potentials $u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $ are therefore precompact in $C^0(X)$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, and every cluster point solves the equation with constant $c$. Uniqueness of the constant does not, however, single out one cluster point; proposition 14.19.1 describes the symmetries that these limits inherit. For $C^2$ potentials, uniqueness of the constant also follows directly from the maximum principle: replacing one potential $v$ by $(1+\varepsilon )v$ leaves a strictly positive multiple of $\omega $ in reserve at an extremum. Proposition 10.6.2 . Let $u,v\in C^2(X,\mathbb R)$, and set $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $B=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. If $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=cB^ n$ for a constant $c>0$, then $c=1$. Proof. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. At a maximum point of $u-(1+\varepsilon )v$, the complex Hessian of this function is nonpositive, so that \[  A+\varepsilon \omega \leq (1+\varepsilon )B.  \] At this point $B>0$, because $A+\varepsilon \omega >0$. Monotonicity of the determinant and $A^ n=cB^ n$ give $c\leq (1+\varepsilon )^ n$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $c\leq 1$, and interchanging the two potentials gives $c^{-1}\leq 1$. $\square$

title: 10.7 Normalization on the Hopf threefold
Proposition 10.7.1

text: 10.20 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-lp-average} \| u-Au\| _{L^2(X,\nu )}^2\leq 4(c_ f I_ f-1). \end{equation}

title: Proposition 10.7.2
Example 10.7.3
text: Example 10.7.3 . Choose $0<a<1/2$, and use the function $s=\log |z|^2$ on the covering space $\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} $ from chapter 8 . Since $s$ changes by $-2$ under the defining contraction, every $2$-periodic function of $s$ descends to $X$. For an integer $m\geq 1$, define the smooth normalized potential \[  u_ m=\frac{a}{\pi ^2m^2}\bigl (\cos (\pi m s)-1\bigr ), \qquad \| u_ m-Au_ m\| _{C^0}=\frac{a}{\pi ^2m^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Primes below denote derivatives with respect to $s$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s=\alpha $ and $\mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s=\beta $, the chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ m=(1+u_ m')\alpha +(1+u_ m'')\beta , \quad u_ m'=-\frac{a}{\pi m}\sin (\pi m s),\quad u_ m''=-a\cos (\pi m s).  \] Both coefficients are bounded below by positive constants independent of $m$. The rank identities $\alpha ^3=\beta ^2=0$ imply \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ m)^3=H_ m\omega ^3,\qquad H_ m=\left(1-\frac{a}{\pi m}\sin (\pi m s)\right)^2 \bigl (1-a\cos (\pi m s)\bigr ).  \] On each fiber, $s$ is twice the real Haar coordinate plus a constant depending on the base point, so its distribution modulo $2$ is uniform. When the periodic expression $H_ m=(1+u_ m')^2(1+u_ m'')$ is averaged, the terms $u_ m'$, $u_ m''$, $u_ m'u_ m''$ and $(u_ m')^2u_ m''$ contribute zero, since they are derivatives of periodic functions. Hence \[  I_ m:=\int _ XH_ m\, \mathrm{d}\nu =AH_ m =1+\frac{a^2}{2\pi ^2m^2}.  \] Set $f_ m=H_ m/I_ m$. These smooth densities have unit integral and common strictly positive lower and finite upper bounds. Uniqueness of the constant gives $c_{f_ m}=I_ m\to 1$, and $Af_ m=1$. Nevertheless, \[  \| f_ m-1+a\cos (\pi m s)\| _{C^0(X)}=O(m^{-1}), \qquad \lim _{m\to \infty }\| f_ m-Af_ m\| _{L^1(X,\nu )}=\frac{2a}{\pi }>0.  \] Here the constant in $O(m^{-1})$ depends only on $a$, and the last identity uses the fact that the average of $|\cos |$ over a period is $2/\pi $. Thus near equality does not imply strong $L^1$ convergence to the fiber average, even for uniformly positive bounded smooth densities. For any pullback $g$ of a function on the base, the contraction property gives $\| f_ m-Af_ m\| _1\leq 2\| f_ m-g\| _1$, so approximation by such pullbacks also fails in $L^1$.

title: 10.8 Stability for concave equations
text: 10.8 Stability for concave equations We now consider fully nonlinear equations defined by a concave symmetric function of the eigenvalues of $\omega ^{-1}(\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$. For such equations, a fixed admissible reference with a strict asymptotic gap replaces the determinant bounds used above: it bounds the positive matrix perturbations of the reference along which the operator stays below a given level. An auxiliary Monge–Ampère equation, whose density is concentrated where the difference of two solutions is nearly maximal, then shows that this set cannot be small. The resulting stability estimate remains uniform when the positive right-hand sides tend to zero. Throughout this section and the next, $n\geq 2$, and $\chi $ is a fixed smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. In these two sections the letter $f$ denotes the function of eigenvalues introduced below, not the density fixed at the beginning of the chapter. For a smooth real function $w$ and an endomorphism $A$ of $T^{1,0}X$ that is Hermitian with respect to $\omega $, put \[  A_ w=\omega ^{-1}(\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w),\qquad F(A)=f(\lambda (A)),  \] where $\lambda (A)\in \mathbb R^ n$ is the vector of eigenvalues of $A$. Let $\Gamma $ be an open convex symmetric cone with $\Gamma _ n\subseteq \Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$, where $\Gamma _ n$ is the positive orthant and $\Gamma _1=\{ \sum _ i\lambda _ i>0\} $. Assume that $f\in C^\infty (\Gamma )\cap C^0(\overline\Gamma )$ is symmetric, concave, positive on $\Gamma $, zero on $\partial \Gamma $, and satisfies \[  f_ i>0,\qquad \lim _{t\to \infty }f(t\lambda )=+\infty \quad (\lambda \in \Gamma ),  \] where $f_ i=\partial f/\partial \lambda _ i$. We call $w$ admissible if $\lambda (A_ w)\in \Gamma $ everywhere. Write $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ for the standard basis of $\mathbb R^ n$ and $\mathbf1=(1,\ldots ,1)$. For $\mu \in \Gamma $, define \[  f_{\infty ,i}(\mu )=\lim _{t\to \infty }f(\mu +te_ i),\qquad f_\infty (\mu )=\min _ i f_{\infty ,i}(\mu ),  \] allowing the value $+\infty $. Fix a smooth admissible function $\underline u$ and positive constants $H_0,\delta _0$. We consider smooth admissible solutions $u$ of \[  F(A_ u)=h,\qquad 0<h\leq H_0,\qquad f_\infty (\lambda (A_{\underline u}(x)))\geq h(x)+\delta _0,  \] where the right-hand side $h$ is a positive function on $X$; the last condition is the strict asymptotic gap at the reference $\underline u$. The right-hand sides satisfying these two conditions form the family of right-hand sides, and the solutions are normalized by $\inf _ Xu=0$. We call $X,\omega ,\chi ,f,\Gamma ,\underline u,H_0,\delta _0$ the fixed data ; all constants in this section depend only on them. Norms are taken with respect to $\omega ^ n$, and $\langle a\rangle _\omega =(\int _ X\omega ^ n)^{-1}\int _ Xa\omega ^ n$ denotes the average of a function $a$. Lemma 10.8.1 . There are a positive continuous function $H$ on $X$ and constants $r,R,\delta >0$ with the following properties. Every right-hand side in the family satisfies $h\leq H$; on $X$, \[  \mu -2r\mathbf1\in \Gamma ,\qquad f_\infty (\mu -2r\mathbf1)\geq H+3\delta , \qquad \mu =\lambda (A_{\underline u});  \] and at every point of $X$, every positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphism $P$ satisfies \[  F(A_{\underline u}-r\operatorname {Id}+P)\leq H+2\delta \quad \Longrightarrow \quad P\leq R\operatorname {Id}.  \] Proof. Each $f_{\infty ,i}$ is an increasing limit of positive concave functions, hence concave with values in $(0,+\infty ]$. Suppose it is infinite at one point and finite at another point of $\Gamma $. Extend the segment joining them slightly beyond the second point, inside the open cone. The second point is then an interior point of the longer segment, so concavity forces the value there to be infinite, a contradiction. Thus $f_{\infty ,i}$ is either finite everywhere, and then continuous, or infinite everywhere. By symmetry, the same alternative holds for every $i$. Take $\delta =\frac18\min \{ \delta _0,\min _ Xf(\mu )\} >0$. In the finite case set $H=\min \{ H_0,f_\infty (\mu )-4\delta \} $; otherwise set $H=H_0$. Since $f_\infty (\mu )\geq f(\mu )\geq 8\delta $, this function is positive. The conditions on the family give $h\leq H$ and $f_\infty (\mu )\geq H+4\delta $. Since $\mu (X)$ is a compact subset of $\Gamma $ and the functions $f_{\infty ,i}$ are continuous (or identically infinite), a sufficiently small $r>0$ gives $\mu -2r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $ and $f_\infty (\mu -2r\mathbf1)\geq H+3\delta $ on $X$. If the matrix bound failed, there would be points $x_ j\to x_*$ and $P_ j\geq 0$ with unbounded norms and $F(A_{\underline u}(x_ j)-r\operatorname {Id}+P_ j)\leq H(x_ j)+2\delta $. By monotonicity of eigenvalues, the ordered eigenvalues $\lambda ^{(j)}$ of $A_{\underline u}(x_ j)-r\operatorname {Id}+P_ j$ satisfy $\lambda _ i^{(j)}\geq \mu _ i(x_ j)-r$. Their sum tends to infinity, so some component $k$ tends to infinity along a subsequence. For every fixed $t>0$, eventually \[  \lambda ^{(j)}\geq \mu (x_*)-2r\mathbf1+te_ k.  \] Since $f$ is increasing in each variable, letting $t\to \infty $ shows that the lower limit of $F(A_{\underline u}(x_ j)-r\operatorname {Id}+P_ j)$ is at least $f_\infty (\mu (x_*)-2r\mathbf1)\geq H(x_*)+3\delta $, which contradicts the upper bound $H(x_ j)+2\delta $. Adding positive semidefinite matrices preserves the cone, so all these comparisons take place in $\Gamma $. $\square$ Proposition 10.8.2 . Every solution satisfies $0\leq u\leq C$. Proof. Put $\theta =\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline u$ and $w=u-\underline u-\sup _ X(u-\underline u)\leq 0$. Since $\Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$, we have $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq -\operatorname {tr}_\omega \theta \geq -C$. The Green-kernel argument in the proof of proposition 9.10.1 , applied to the operator $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, therefore bounds $\| w\| _{L^1}$ uniformly. Center a holomorphic coordinate ball of fixed size at a minimum point of $w$, and rescale it to the real unit ball. For a fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, set $q=w+\varepsilon |x|^2$ and $m=\min _ Xw$. The real contact-set construction of ( 9.22 ) gives a compact set $E$ on which \[  D^2q\geq 0,\qquad q\leq m+\varepsilon /2, \qquad |B_{\varepsilon /2}|\leq \int _ E\det D^2q\, \mathrm dx.  \] On $E$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq -C\varepsilon \omega $. Choose $\varepsilon $ so that $C\varepsilon <r$. Then $P=\omega ^{-1}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+r\omega )\geq 0$ and \[  F(A_{\underline u}-r\operatorname {Id}+P)=F(A_ u)=h\leq H.  \] Lemma 10.8.1 bounds $P$, and hence the complex trace of the Hessian of $q$. The nonnegative real Hessian of $q$ on $E$ therefore has bounded trace, and hence bounded determinant, so the contact inequality implies $|E|\geq c>0$. Since $w\leq m+\varepsilon /2$ on $E$, the $L^1$ bound gives $c(-m-\varepsilon /2)\leq C$. This bounds the oscillation of $w$, hence that of $u$; with the normalization $\inf _ Xu=0$, this is the assertion. $\square$ Theorem 10.8.3 . There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data, such that any two normalized solutions $u_1,u_2$ with right-hand sides $h_1,h_2$ in the family satisfy \[  \| u_1-u_2\| _\infty \leq C\bigl (\| h_1-h_2\| _\infty +\| u_1-u_2\| _{L^1}\bigr ).  \] In particular, $C$ does not depend on a positive lower bound for the $h_ i$ or on bounds for their derivatives. Proof. Set $a=u_1-\underline u$, $b=u_2-\underline u$ and $\theta =\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline u$. By proposition 10.8.2 , $|a|,|b|\leq C_0$ for a fixed $C_0\geq 1$. It suffices to bound $s=\max _ X(b-a)$ when it is positive; the opposite difference is handled by interchanging the solutions. Fix $r,R,\delta $ from lemma 10.8.1 and put $\alpha =r\omega $. For every smooth positive $\rho $ with \[  \rho \geq \tfrac 12,\qquad \langle \rho \rangle _\alpha =1,\qquad \langle \rho ^2\rangle _\alpha \leq 4,  \] theorem 9.1.1 gives a smooth solution \[  (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=c\rho \alpha ^ n,\qquad \alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi >0,\qquad \sup _ X\psi =0.  \] At a maximum of $\psi $, $c\rho \leq 1$, so $c\leq 2$. Apply theorem 10.3.3 with $p=2$ and background $\alpha $. Its potential and lower-density bounds give fixed $c_0,C_\psi >0$ with \[  c\geq c_0,\qquad -C_\psi \leq \psi \leq 0.  \] These constants depend only on the three bounds for $\rho $, and not on the cutoff function chosen below. Choose $\kappa >0$ so that $2C_0\kappa \leq 1/4$, $\kappa C_0\leq 1/16$ and $\kappa C_\psi /2\leq 1/16$. Next choose $M\geq 1$ with $2^{-n}c_0Mr^ n>R^ n$, and then $\varepsilon _0>0$ with \[  \tfrac {16}{7}\varepsilon _0\leq \min \{ (2M)^{-1},M^{-2}\} .  \] If one of the inequalities \[  \| h_1-h_2\| _\infty \leq \kappa \delta s, \qquad \langle (b-a)_+\rangle _\omega \leq \varepsilon _0s.  \] fails, then $s\leq C(\| h_1-h_2\| _\infty +\| u_1-u_2\| _{L^1})$, with $C$ depending only on $\kappa ,\delta ,\varepsilon _0$ and the volume of $X$. We assume both and derive a contradiction. Put $t=\kappa s$; since $s\leq 2C_0$, we have $t\leq 1/4$. On $\Omega =\{ (1-t)b-a>s/2\} $, we have $b-a>7s/16$, so by Chebyshev's inequality the relative volume of $\Omega $ is at most $16\varepsilon _0/7$. Take a smooth $\zeta :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, zero on $(-\infty ,1/2]$ and one on $[3/4,\infty )$, and set \[  \rho =b_0+M\zeta \bigl (((1-t)b-a)/s\bigr ),\qquad b_0=1-M\bigl \langle \zeta \bigl (((1-t)b-a)/s\bigr )\bigr \rangle _\omega .  \] The second term is supported in $\Omega $, so $1/2\leq b_0\leq 1$ and $\langle \rho ^2\rangle _\alpha \leq 2+2M^2(16\varepsilon _0/7)\leq 4$; here we use that averages with respect to $\alpha =r\omega $ and $\omega $ agree. Thus the auxiliary solution for this $\rho $ satisfies the bounds with the same constants $c_0,C_\psi $. At a point where $b-a=s$, the function $\Phi =(1-t)b-a+t\psi /2$ is at least $7s/8$, by the choice of $\kappa $. At a maximum point $x_0$ of $\Phi $, therefore, $(1-t)b-a\geq 7s/8$ because $\psi \leq 0$, and so $\rho (x_0)\geq M$. The second derivative test gives, at $x_0$, \[  P=\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((a-(1-t)b)/t\bigr ) \geq \tfrac 12(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )+\tfrac 12\alpha >0.  \] The identity \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a =t\bigl ((\theta -\alpha )+P\bigr )+(1-t)(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b)  \] and concavity imply \[  F\bigl (\omega ^{-1}((\theta -\alpha )+P)\bigr ) \leq h_2+(h_1-h_2)/t\leq H+\delta .  \] Both forms in the convex combination are admissible, since $\mu -r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $ and $P>0$. By lemma 10.8.1 , $P\leq R\omega $. On the other hand, $P\geq \frac12(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )$, so the auxiliary equation gives \[  R^ n\geq P^ n/\omega ^ n \geq 2^{-n}c\rho r^ n\geq 2^{-n}c_0Mr^ n>R^ n,  \] a contradiction. Hence one of the two smallness inequalities fails, which gives the required bound for $s$. Interchanging the solutions proves the theorem. $\square$ Corollary 10.8.4 . Let $\mathcal H$ be a set of right-hand sides in the family that is equicontinuous. Then the normalized solutions with right-hand sides in $\mathcal H$ form a precompact subset of $C^0(X)$ and have a common modulus of continuity. Proof. Admissibility and $\Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$ give $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq -C$. By theorem 4.1.2 , there is a smooth function $\rho _0>0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _0\omega ^{n-1})=0$, so that $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \rho _0\omega ^{n-1}=0$ for every smooth $\varphi $. Integrating the product rule $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)=2u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+2\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u$ against $\rho _0\omega ^{n-1}$, and using $0\leq u\leq C$ from proposition 10.8.2 , we obtain a uniform bound for $\int _ X|\mathrm du|_\omega ^2\omega ^ n$, because $\rho _0$ is bounded above and below. Rellich's theorem therefore gives precompactness in $L^1$. Given a sequence of such solutions, the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem gives a subsequence whose right-hand sides converge uniformly, since they are equicontinuous and bounded by $H_0$. A further subsequence of the solutions is Cauchy in $L^1$, and theorem 10.8.3 makes it uniformly Cauchy. This proves precompactness in $C^0(X)$. A common modulus of continuity follows from a finite uniform $\varepsilon /3$-net, since each of its finitely many members is uniformly continuous. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.8.1
text: Lemma 10.8.1 . There are a positive continuous function $H$ on $X$ and constants $r,R,\delta >0$ with the following properties. Every right-hand side in the family satisfies $h\leq H$; on $X$, \[  \mu -2r\mathbf1\in \Gamma ,\qquad f_\infty (\mu -2r\mathbf1)\geq H+3\delta , \qquad \mu =\lambda (A_{\underline u});  \] and at every point of $X$, every positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphism $P$ satisfies \[  F(A_{\underline u}-r\operatorname {Id}+P)\leq H+2\delta \quad \Longrightarrow \quad P\leq R\operatorname {Id}.  \] Proof. Each $f_{\infty ,i}$ is an increasing limit of positive concave functions, hence concave with values in $(0,+\infty ]$. Suppose it is infinite at one point and finite at another point of $\Gamma $. Extend the segment joining them slightly beyond the second point, inside the open cone. The second point is then an interior point of the longer segment, so concavity forces the value there to be infinite, a contradiction. Thus $f_{\infty ,i}$ is either finite everywhere, and then continuous, or infinite everywhere. By symmetry, the same alternative holds for every $i$. Take $\delta =\frac18\min \{ \delta _0,\min _ Xf(\mu )\} >0$. In the finite case set $H=\min \{ H_0,f_\infty (\mu )-4\delta \} $; otherwise set $H=H_0$. Since $f_\infty (\mu )\geq f(\mu )\geq 8\delta $, this function is positive. The conditions on the family give $h\leq H$ and $f_\infty (\mu )\geq H+4\delta $. Since $\mu (X)$ is a compact subset of $\Gamma $ and the functions $f_{\infty ,i}$ are continuous (or identically infinite), a sufficiently small $r>0$ gives $\mu -2r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $ and $f_\infty (\mu -2r\mathbf1)\geq H+3\delta $ on $X$. If the matrix bound failed, there would be points $x_ j\to x_*$ and $P_ j\geq 0$ with unbounded norms and $F(A_{\underline u}(x_ j)-r\operatorname {Id}+P_ j)\leq H(x_ j)+2\delta $. By monotonicity of eigenvalues, the ordered eigenvalues $\lambda ^{(j)}$ of $A_{\underline u}(x_ j)-r\operatorname {Id}+P_ j$ satisfy $\lambda _ i^{(j)}\geq \mu _ i(x_ j)-r$. Their sum tends to infinity, so some component $k$ tends to infinity along a subsequence. For every fixed $t>0$, eventually \[  \lambda ^{(j)}\geq \mu (x_*)-2r\mathbf1+te_ k.  \] Since $f$ is increasing in each variable, letting $t\to \infty $ shows that the lower limit of $F(A_{\underline u}(x_ j)-r\operatorname {Id}+P_ j)$ is at least $f_\infty (\mu (x_*)-2r\mathbf1)\geq H(x_*)+3\delta $, which contradicts the upper bound $H(x_ j)+2\delta $. Adding positive semidefinite matrices preserves the cone, so all these comparisons take place in $\Gamma $. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.8.2
text: Proposition 10.8.2 . Every solution satisfies $0\leq u\leq C$. Proof. Put $\theta =\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline u$ and $w=u-\underline u-\sup _ X(u-\underline u)\leq 0$. Since $\Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$, we have $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq -\operatorname {tr}_\omega \theta \geq -C$. The Green-kernel argument in the proof of proposition 9.10.1 , applied to the operator $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, therefore bounds $\| w\| _{L^1}$ uniformly. Center a holomorphic coordinate ball of fixed size at a minimum point of $w$, and rescale it to the real unit ball. For a fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, set $q=w+\varepsilon |x|^2$ and $m=\min _ Xw$. The real contact-set construction of ( 9.22 ) gives a compact set $E$ on which \[  D^2q\geq 0,\qquad q\leq m+\varepsilon /2, \qquad |B_{\varepsilon /2}|\leq \int _ E\det D^2q\, \mathrm dx.  \] On $E$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq -C\varepsilon \omega $. Choose $\varepsilon $ so that $C\varepsilon <r$. Then $P=\omega ^{-1}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+r\omega )\geq 0$ and \[  F(A_{\underline u}-r\operatorname {Id}+P)=F(A_ u)=h\leq H.  \] Lemma 10.8.1 bounds $P$, and hence the complex trace of the Hessian of $q$. The nonnegative real Hessian of $q$ on $E$ therefore has bounded trace, and hence bounded determinant, so the contact inequality implies $|E|\geq c>0$. Since $w\leq m+\varepsilon /2$ on $E$, the $L^1$ bound gives $c(-m-\varepsilon /2)\leq C$. This bounds the oscillation of $w$, hence that of $u$; with the normalization $\inf _ Xu=0$, this is the assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.8.3
text: Theorem 10.8.3 . There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data, such that any two normalized solutions $u_1,u_2$ with right-hand sides $h_1,h_2$ in the family satisfy \[  \| u_1-u_2\| _\infty \leq C\bigl (\| h_1-h_2\| _\infty +\| u_1-u_2\| _{L^1}\bigr ).  \] In particular, $C$ does not depend on a positive lower bound for the $h_ i$ or on bounds for their derivatives. Proof. Set $a=u_1-\underline u$, $b=u_2-\underline u$ and $\theta =\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline u$. By proposition 10.8.2 , $|a|,|b|\leq C_0$ for a fixed $C_0\geq 1$. It suffices to bound $s=\max _ X(b-a)$ when it is positive; the opposite difference is handled by interchanging the solutions. Fix $r,R,\delta $ from lemma 10.8.1 and put $\alpha =r\omega $. For every smooth positive $\rho $ with \[  \rho \geq \tfrac 12,\qquad \langle \rho \rangle _\alpha =1,\qquad \langle \rho ^2\rangle _\alpha \leq 4,  \] theorem 9.1.1 gives a smooth solution \[  (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=c\rho \alpha ^ n,\qquad \alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi >0,\qquad \sup _ X\psi =0.  \] At a maximum of $\psi $, $c\rho \leq 1$, so $c\leq 2$. Apply theorem 10.3.3 with $p=2$ and background $\alpha $. Its potential and lower-density bounds give fixed $c_0,C_\psi >0$ with \[  c\geq c_0,\qquad -C_\psi \leq \psi \leq 0.  \] These constants depend only on the three bounds for $\rho $, and not on the cutoff function chosen below. Choose $\kappa >0$ so that $2C_0\kappa \leq 1/4$, $\kappa C_0\leq 1/16$ and $\kappa C_\psi /2\leq 1/16$. Next choose $M\geq 1$ with $2^{-n}c_0Mr^ n>R^ n$, and then $\varepsilon _0>0$ with \[  \tfrac {16}{7}\varepsilon _0\leq \min \{ (2M)^{-1},M^{-2}\} .  \] If one of the inequalities \[  \| h_1-h_2\| _\infty \leq \kappa \delta s, \qquad \langle (b-a)_+\rangle _\omega \leq \varepsilon _0s.  \] fails, then $s\leq C(\| h_1-h_2\| _\infty +\| u_1-u_2\| _{L^1})$, with $C$ depending only on $\kappa ,\delta ,\varepsilon _0$ and the volume of $X$. We assume both and derive a contradiction. Put $t=\kappa s$; since $s\leq 2C_0$, we have $t\leq 1/4$. On $\Omega =\{ (1-t)b-a>s/2\} $, we have $b-a>7s/16$, so by Chebyshev's inequality the relative volume of $\Omega $ is at most $16\varepsilon _0/7$. Take a smooth $\zeta :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, zero on $(-\infty ,1/2]$ and one on $[3/4,\infty )$, and set \[  \rho =b_0+M\zeta \bigl (((1-t)b-a)/s\bigr ),\qquad b_0=1-M\bigl \langle \zeta \bigl (((1-t)b-a)/s\bigr )\bigr \rangle _\omega .  \] The second term is supported in $\Omega $, so $1/2\leq b_0\leq 1$ and $\langle \rho ^2\rangle _\alpha \leq 2+2M^2(16\varepsilon _0/7)\leq 4$; here we use that averages with respect to $\alpha =r\omega $ and $\omega $ agree. Thus the auxiliary solution for this $\rho $ satisfies the bounds with the same constants $c_0,C_\psi $. At a point where $b-a=s$, the function $\Phi =(1-t)b-a+t\psi /2$ is at least $7s/8$, by the choice of $\kappa $. At a maximum point $x_0$ of $\Phi $, therefore, $(1-t)b-a\geq 7s/8$ because $\psi \leq 0$, and so $\rho (x_0)\geq M$. The second derivative test gives, at $x_0$, \[  P=\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((a-(1-t)b)/t\bigr ) \geq \tfrac 12(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )+\tfrac 12\alpha >0.  \] The identity \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a =t\bigl ((\theta -\alpha )+P\bigr )+(1-t)(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b)  \] and concavity imply \[  F\bigl (\omega ^{-1}((\theta -\alpha )+P)\bigr ) \leq h_2+(h_1-h_2)/t\leq H+\delta .  \] Both forms in the convex combination are admissible, since $\mu -r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $ and $P>0$. By lemma 10.8.1 , $P\leq R\omega $. On the other hand, $P\geq \frac12(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )$, so the auxiliary equation gives \[  R^ n\geq P^ n/\omega ^ n \geq 2^{-n}c\rho r^ n\geq 2^{-n}c_0Mr^ n>R^ n,  \] a contradiction. Hence one of the two smallness inequalities fails, which gives the required bound for $s$. Interchanging the solutions proves the theorem. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.8.4
text: Corollary 10.8.4 . Let $\mathcal H$ be a set of right-hand sides in the family that is equicontinuous. Then the normalized solutions with right-hand sides in $\mathcal H$ form a precompact subset of $C^0(X)$ and have a common modulus of continuity. Proof. Admissibility and $\Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$ give $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq -C$. By theorem 4.1.2 , there is a smooth function $\rho _0>0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _0\omega ^{n-1})=0$, so that $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \rho _0\omega ^{n-1}=0$ for every smooth $\varphi $. Integrating the product rule $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)=2u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+2\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u$ against $\rho _0\omega ^{n-1}$, and using $0\leq u\leq C$ from proposition 10.8.2 , we obtain a uniform bound for $\int _ X|\mathrm du|_\omega ^2\omega ^ n$, because $\rho _0$ is bounded above and below. Rellich's theorem therefore gives precompactness in $L^1$. Given a sequence of such solutions, the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem gives a subsequence whose right-hand sides converge uniformly, since they are equicontinuous and bounded by $H_0$. A further subsequence of the solutions is Cauchy in $L^1$, and theorem 10.8.3 makes it uniformly Cauchy. This proves precompactness in $C^0(X)$. A common modulus of continuity follows from a finite uniform $\varepsilon /3$-net, since each of its finitely many members is uniformly continuous. $\square$

title: 10.9 Gradient bounds for concave equations
text:
10.9 Gradient bounds for concave equations We keep the fixed data, the family of right-hand sides and the normalization of section 10.8 , and assume in addition that $\| \partial h\| _{L^\infty (\omega )}\leq H_1$; throughout the section, $u$ denotes a solution with such a right-hand side $h$. The gradient bound is obtained by comparison with a nearby smooth admissible function $V$. A maximum principle for a weighted gradient quantity bounds the gradient of $u$ in terms of that of $V$, provided $\| u-V\| _\infty $ is below a threshold that does not depend on the derivatives of $V$. The $C^0$ compactness of corollary 10.8.4 then shows that finitely many such comparison functions suffice for all solutions. For the derivative calculation, write $U=u/(2\pi )$ and $\underline U=\underline u/(2\pi )$. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial U$. For any smooth real $V$, put $\mathcal A_ V=\omega ^{-1}(\chi +\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial V)$ and call $V$ admissible if $\lambda (\mathcal A_ V)\in \Gamma $. We use the Chern connection of $\omega $, and define the endomorphism $B=DF(\mathcal A_ U)$ by $ rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}F(\mathcal A_ U+tM)|_{t=0}=\operatorname {tr}(BM)$. Write $\lambda =(\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n)=\lambda (\mathcal A_ U)$. At a point where $\mathcal A_ U$ is diagonal in a unitary frame, set \[  B_ i=f_ i(\lambda ),\qquad \mathcal Lq=\sum _ iB_ iq_{i ar i},\qquad T=\sum _ iB_ i, \qquad |\partial q|_ B^2=\sum _ iB_ i|q_ i|^2.  \] Here subscripts denote frame derivatives, $U_{ki}=
abla _ iU_ k$ and $U_{i ar j}=\partial _ i\partial _{ ar j}U$; the second derivatives $U_{ki}$ need not be symmetric. The trace expressions below do not depend on the unitary frame. Lemma 10.9.1 . There are fixed $	au ,\kappa >0$ such that  egin{gather*}  T\geq 	au ,\qquad 0\leq \operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)\leq h,\  \mathcal L(U-V)\leq h\quad (V	ext{ admissible}),\qquad \mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq -h. \end{gather*} Moreover, at every point at least one of the alternatives \[  \mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq \kappa T, \qquad B\geq \kappa T\operatorname {Id}  \] holds. The constants depend only on the fixed data; in particular they are uniform for all right-hand sides in the family. Proof. If $\lambda (P)\in \Gamma $, then $\mathcal A_ U+tP$ is admissible for $t\geq 0$. The function $t\mapsto F(\mathcal A_ U+tP)$ is positive and concave on $[0,\infty )$, so its derivative at $t=0$ cannot be negative; thus $\operatorname {tr}(BP)\geq 0$. Since $F$ is concave and $F(0)=0$, the tangent inequality at $\mathcal A_ U$, evaluated at the origin, gives $\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)\leq h$. Choose $a_*>0$ with $F(a_*\operatorname {Id})>H_0+1$. Concavity gives \[  H_0+1<F(a_*\operatorname {Id}) \leq h+a_*T-\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)\leq H_0+a_*T.  \] Thus $T\geq a_*^{-1}$. Since $\mathcal L(U-V)=\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)-\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ V)$ and $\mathcal L(\underline U-U)=\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_{\underline U})-\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)$, the remaining two bounds follow from the nonnegativity of $\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ V)$ and $\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_{\underline U})$. We derive the alternative from the strict gap. Fix $r,H,\delta $ from lemma 10.8.1 , and put $\mu =\lambda (\mathcal A_{\underline U})$. Compactness and the gap give one $S>r$ such that \[  f(\mu -2r\mathbf1+Se_ i)>H+2\delta \qquad (1\leq i\leq n)  \] everywhere. We first prove a scalar alternative. At a point of $X$, let $\lambda \in \Gamma $ satisfy $f(\lambda )=\sigma $, where $\sigma =h$ at that point, and consider the set \[  K=\{ v\geq \mu -r\mathbf1:f(v)\leq \sigma \} .  \] It is contained in $\Gamma $ because $\mu -r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $, it is closed, and the matrix bound of lemma 10.8.1 , applied to diagonal matrices, makes it bounded; thus $K$ is compact. When nonempty, it contains $\mu -r\mathbf1$ and is star-shaped about that point: moving along a segment toward it decreases each coordinate, hence decreases $f$. Thus $K$ is connected. Let $N=
abla f(\lambda )$, whose entries are positive, and let $\Pi $ be the tangent hyperplane $N\cdot (v-\lambda )=0$. If $f(\mu -r\mathbf1)>\sigma $, concavity gives $N\cdot (\mu -\lambda )>r\sum _ iN_ i$. Otherwise $\mu -r\mathbf1\in K$. The diagonal ray $\mu -r\mathbf1+t\mathbf1$, $t\geq 0$, meets $\{ f=\sigma \} $, since $f$ diverges along it; at the meeting point $v$, the tangent inequality gives $N\cdot (v-\lambda )\geq 0$. If $\Pi $ misses $K$, connectedness makes $N\cdot (v-\lambda )$ strictly positive throughout $K$, and in particular at $\mu -r\mathbf1$; this again gives $N\cdot (\mu -\lambda )>r\sum _ iN_ i$. If $v\in \Pi \cap K$, put $z_ i=v-r\mathbf1+Se_ i$. Then $z_ i\geq \mu -2r\mathbf1+Se_ i$, so $f(z_ i)>\sigma $. The tangent inequality at $\lambda $ gives \[  0<N\cdot (z_ i-v)=SN_ i-r\sum _ jN_ j.  \] Thus $N_ i>(r/S)\sum _ jN_ j$ for every $i$. We have proved that $N\cdot (\mu -\lambda )>r\sum _ iN_ i$ or $N_ i>(r/S)\sum _ jN_ j$ for all $i$, at every positive level $\sigma $, with constants independent of $\sigma $. To pass to matrices, take $\lambda =\lambda (\mathcal A_ U)$, and order $\lambda $ and $\mu $ decreasingly. By concavity and symmetry, the numbers $f_ i(\lambda )$ are then ordered increasingly. In the eigenframe of $\mathcal A_ U$, the diagonal of $\mathcal A_{\underline U}$ is a doubly stochastic average of permutations of $\mu $, so the rearrangement inequality gives \[  \operatorname {tr} igl (B(\mathcal A_{\underline U}-\mathcal A_ U) igr ) \geq \sum _ if_ i(\lambda )(\mu _ i-\lambda _ i).  \] Since $N=(f_ i(\lambda ))_ i=(B_ i)_ i$, taking $\kappa $ smaller than $\min \{ r,r/S\} $ proves the matrix alternative. $\square$ Lemma 10.9.2 . Put $Q=1+|\partial U|_\omega ^2$. For any smooth real $\xi $, one has  egin{align*}  \mathrm e^{-\xi }\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q) & \geq \sum _{i,k}B_ i|U_{ki}+U_ k\xi _ i|^2 + rac14\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2+Q\mathcal L\xi +|\partial \xi |_ B^2\ & \quad +2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ iU_ i\xi _{ ar i} -2\operatorname{Re}\sum _{i,k}B_ i\chi _{i ar k}U_ k\xi _{ ar i} -C_ gTQ-2H_1|\partial U|_\omega , \end{align*} where $C_ g$ depends only on $\omega $ and $\chi $. Proof. Write $\mathscr T^ p_{ik}$ and $R^ p_{i ar jk}$ for the torsion and curvature of the Chern connection. The commutation formula and the differentiated equation read  egin{gather*}  
abla _{ ar j}
abla _ iU_ k =
abla _ kU_{i ar j}+\sum _ p igl (R^ p_{i ar jk}U_ p-\mathscr T^ p_{ik}U_{p ar j} igr ),\  \sum _ iB_ i
abla _ kU_{i ar i}=h_ k-\sum _ iB_ i
abla _ k\chi _{i ar i}. \end{gather*} The product rule for $|\partial U|^2$ gives both squares $\sum B_ i|U_{ki}|^2$ and $\sum B_ i|U_{k ar i}|^2$, the term $2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ kh_ kU_{ ar k}$, a curvature error bounded by $CT|\partial U|^2$, and the errors from $
abla \chi $ and torsion. The latter are bounded by \[  CT|\partial U|+CT|\partial U|^2 +C|\partial U|T^{1/2}\Bigl (\sum _{i,k}B_ i|U_{k ar i}|^2\Bigr )^{1/2}.  \] Absorb the last term into half of the mixed square. Since $U_{i ar j}=\lambda _ i\delta _{ij}-\chi _{i ar j}$, the remaining half is at least $ rac14\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2-CT$. Hence \[  \mathcal L|\partial U|^2\geq \sum _{i,k}B_ i|U_{ki}|^2 + rac14\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2-C_ gTQ-2H_1|\partial U|.  \] Finally, \[  \partial _ i|\partial U|^2 =\sum _ kU_{ki}U_{ ar k}+\lambda _ iU_ i-\sum _ k\chi _{i ar k}U_ k.  \] In the product rule for $\mathrm e^\xi Q$, combine the cross term coming from the first sum with $|\partial U|^2|\partial \xi |_ B^2$ and with the square $\sum B_ i|U_{ki}|^2$. This gives $\sum B_ i|U_{ki}+U_ k\xi _ i|^2$, while the remaining weight term is $|\partial \xi |_ B^2$. $\square$ Proposition 10.9.3 . There are constants $\eta ,C>0$, depending only on the fixed data and $H_1$, such that every smooth admissible $V$ with $\| U-V\| _\infty \leq \eta $ satisfies \[  \| \partial U\| _\infty \leq C igl (1+\| \partial V\| _\infty ^2 igr ).  \] The comparison radius $\eta $ is independent of the derivatives of $V$. Proof. Let $a\geq 1$ and $ eta >1$ be constants, to be chosen below. Assuming $\| U-V\| _\infty \leq  eta ^{-1}$, put \[  w=U-V- eta ^{-1},\qquad \xi =a(\underline U-U)+ eta w^2,\qquad K_ V=1+\| \partial \underline U\| _\infty +\| \partial V\| _\infty .  \] Then $-2 eta ^{-1}\leq w\leq 0$ and \[  \xi _ i=a(\underline U_ i-V_ i)+(-a+2 eta w)(U_ i-V_ i), \qquad |-a+2 eta w|\leq a+4.  \] Writing $D=|\partial (U-V)|_ B^2$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives  egin{align*}  \left|2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ iU_ i\xi _{ ar i}ight| & \leq  rac18\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2+C_ aK_ V^4T+C_ a(Q+K_ V^2)D,\  \left|2\operatorname{Re}\sum _{i,k}B_ i\chi _{i ar k}U_ k\xi _{ ar i}ight| & \leq 	frac 12QD+C_ aT+C_ aK_ VQ^{1/2}T. \end{align*} For the first line, split $\xi _ i$ as above and use $\sum B_ i|U_ i|^2\leq 2D+2K_ V^2T$; then apply Young's inequality to the resulting three products, each absorbing at most $ rac1{24}\sum B_ i\lambda _ i^2$. For the second line, use $|\partial \xi |_ B\leq aK_ VT^{1/2}+(a+4)D^{1/2}$ and the bound for $\chi $. In both lines, $C_ a$ depends on $a$ but not on $ eta $ or on the derivatives of $V$. By lemma 10.9.1 and $w\leq 0$, \[  \mathcal L\xi \geq a\mathcal L(\underline U-U)-4H_0+2 eta D.  \] Choose $a$ so large that $(a\kappa -C_ g-2)	au >4H_0+2H_1+1$, and then $ eta \geq 2C_ a+2$. Combining the preceding bounds with lemma 10.9.2 , we obtain, at every point where $Q\geq C'(1+K_ V^4)$ for a suitable constant $C'$,  egin{align*}  \mathrm e^{-\xi }\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q) & \geq  rac18\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2\ & \quad +Q igl [a\mathcal L(\underline U-U)-(C_ g+2)T + eta D-(4H_0+2H_1) igr ]. \end{align*} Indeed, the coefficient of $D$ before absorption is $(2 eta -C_ a-1/2)Q-C_ aK_ V^2$, which is at least $ eta Q$ once $C'$ is large enough. The other errors satisfy $C_ aK_ V^4\leq Q$ and $C_ a+C_ aK_ VQ^{1/2}\leq Q$, and they account for the additional term $-2T$ in the bracket. Consider a maximum point of $\mathrm e^\xi Q$ at which $Q\geq C'(1+K_ V^4)$. In the first alternative of lemma 10.9.1 , the bracket is positive by the choice of $a$, since $T\geq 	au $. In the second, $D\geq \kappa T|\partial (U-V)|^2$. For $Q\geq 4(1+K_ V^2)$, the triangle inequality gives $|\partial (U-V)|^2\geq c_*Q$, where $c_*=(\sqrt3-1)^2/4$. Since $\mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq -H_0$, the bracket is then at least \[  ( eta \kappa c_*Q-C_ g-2)T-(a+4)H_0-2H_1.  \] This is positive once $C'$ is large enough, because $T\geq 	au $. In both cases $\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q)>0$ at a maximum point, which contradicts the second derivative test. Thus $Q\leq C(1+K_ V^4)$ at the maximum point. The weight has uniformly bounded oscillation: \[  \operatorname {osc}_ X\xi \leq a(\operatorname {osc}_ X\underline U+\operatorname {osc}_ XU)+4/ eta .  \] By the potential bound in proposition 10.8.2 , this oscillation is bounded independently of $V$, so the estimate at the maximum point gives $Q\leq C(1+K_ V^4)$ everywhere. Taking square roots and setting $\eta = eta ^{-1}$ proves the assertion. $\square$ Theorem 10.9.4 . There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data and $H_1$, such that $\| \mathrm du\| _{L^\infty (\omega )}\leq C$ for every normalized solution $u$ whose right-hand side $h$ lies in the family and satisfies $\| \partial h\| _\infty \leq H_1$. In particular, the bound is uniform as the positive right-hand sides tend to zero. Proof. The right-hand sides in the family with $\| \partial h\| _\infty \leq H_1$ form an equicontinuous set. By corollary 10.8.4 , the corresponding functions $U$ form a precompact subset of $C^0(X)$. Choose a finite $\eta $-net in this set, consisting of smooth admissible functions $V_1,\ldots ,V_ N$. Each solution is within $\eta $ of some $V_ j$, so proposition 10.9.3 bounds its gradient by $C(1+\max _ j\| \partial V_ j\| _\infty ^2)$. The set of solutions, and hence the chosen finite net, depends only on the fixed data and $H_1$. Finally, $u=2\pi U$, so the same conclusion holds for $\mathrm du$. $\square$ In chapter 11 we return to the Monge–Ampère equation for $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and ask when two potentials with the same density agree up to a constant. The uniqueness of the normalization scalar does not determine the potential: where the density vanishes, the polarized linear equation for the difference can be degenerate.

title: Lemma 10.9.1
text: Lemma 10.9.1 . There are fixed $\tau ,\kappa >0$ such that \begin{gather*}  T\geq \tau ,\qquad 0\leq \operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)\leq h,\\  \mathcal L(U-V)\leq h\quad (V\text{ admissible}),\qquad \mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq -h. \end{gather*} Moreover, at every point at least one of the alternatives \[  \mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq \kappa T, \qquad B\geq \kappa T\operatorname {Id}  \] holds. The constants depend only on the fixed data; in particular they are uniform for all right-hand sides in the family. Proof. If $\lambda (P)\in \Gamma $, then $\mathcal A_ U+tP$ is admissible for $t\geq 0$. The function $t\mapsto F(\mathcal A_ U+tP)$ is positive and concave on $[0,\infty )$, so its derivative at $t=0$ cannot be negative; thus $\operatorname {tr}(BP)\geq 0$. Since $F$ is concave and $F(0)=0$, the tangent inequality at $\mathcal A_ U$, evaluated at the origin, gives $\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)\leq h$. Choose $a_*>0$ with $F(a_*\operatorname {Id})>H_0+1$. Concavity gives \[  H_0+1<F(a_*\operatorname {Id}) \leq h+a_*T-\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)\leq H_0+a_*T.  \] Thus $T\geq a_*^{-1}$. Since $\mathcal L(U-V)=\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)-\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ V)$ and $\mathcal L(\underline U-U)=\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_{\underline U})-\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)$, the remaining two bounds follow from the nonnegativity of $\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ V)$ and $\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_{\underline U})$. We derive the alternative from the strict gap. Fix $r,H,\delta $ from lemma 10.8.1 , and put $\mu =\lambda (\mathcal A_{\underline U})$. Compactness and the gap give one $S>r$ such that \[  f(\mu -2r\mathbf1+Se_ i)>H+2\delta \qquad (1\leq i\leq n)  \] everywhere. We first prove a scalar alternative. At a point of $X$, let $\lambda \in \Gamma $ satisfy $f(\lambda )=\sigma $, where $\sigma =h$ at that point, and consider the set \[  K=\{ v\geq \mu -r\mathbf1:f(v)\leq \sigma \} .  \] It is contained in $\Gamma $ because $\mu -r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $, it is closed, and the matrix bound of lemma 10.8.1 , applied to diagonal matrices, makes it bounded; thus $K$ is compact. When nonempty, it contains $\mu -r\mathbf1$ and is star-shaped about that point: moving along a segment toward it decreases each coordinate, hence decreases $f$. Thus $K$ is connected. Let $N=\nabla f(\lambda )$, whose entries are positive, and let $\Pi $ be the tangent hyperplane $N\cdot (v-\lambda )=0$. If $f(\mu -r\mathbf1)>\sigma $, concavity gives $N\cdot (\mu -\lambda )>r\sum _ iN_ i$. Otherwise $\mu -r\mathbf1\in K$. The diagonal ray $\mu -r\mathbf1+t\mathbf1$, $t\geq 0$, meets $\{ f=\sigma \} $, since $f$ diverges along it; at the meeting point $v$, the tangent inequality gives $N\cdot (v-\lambda )\geq 0$. If $\Pi $ misses $K$, connectedness makes $N\cdot (v-\lambda )$ strictly positive throughout $K$, and in particular at $\mu -r\mathbf1$; this again gives $N\cdot (\mu -\lambda )>r\sum _ iN_ i$. If $v\in \Pi \cap K$, put $z_ i=v-r\mathbf1+Se_ i$. Then $z_ i\geq \mu -2r\mathbf1+Se_ i$, so $f(z_ i)>\sigma $. The tangent inequality at $\lambda $ gives \[  0<N\cdot (z_ i-v)=SN_ i-r\sum _ jN_ j.  \] Thus $N_ i>(r/S)\sum _ jN_ j$ for every $i$. We have proved that $N\cdot (\mu -\lambda )>r\sum _ iN_ i$ or $N_ i>(r/S)\sum _ jN_ j$ for all $i$, at every positive level $\sigma $, with constants independent of $\sigma $. To pass to matrices, take $\lambda =\lambda (\mathcal A_ U)$, and order $\lambda $ and $\mu $ decreasingly. By concavity and symmetry, the numbers $f_ i(\lambda )$ are then ordered increasingly. In the eigenframe of $\mathcal A_ U$, the diagonal of $\mathcal A_{\underline U}$ is a doubly stochastic average of permutations of $\mu $, so the rearrangement inequality gives \[  \operatorname {tr}\bigl (B(\mathcal A_{\underline U}-\mathcal A_ U)\bigr ) \geq \sum _ if_ i(\lambda )(\mu _ i-\lambda _ i).  \] Since $N=(f_ i(\lambda ))_ i=(B_ i)_ i$, taking $\kappa $ smaller than $\min \{ r,r/S\} $ proves the matrix alternative. $\square$

text:
Lemma 10.9.2 . Put $Q=1+|\partial U|_\omega ^2$. For any smooth real $\xi $, one has  egin{align*}  \mathrm e^{-\xi }\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q) & \geq \sum _{i,k}B_ i|U_{ki}+U_ k\xi _ i|^2 + rac14\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2+Q\mathcal L\xi +|\partial \xi |_ B^2\ & \quad +2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ iU_ i\xi _{ ar i} -2\operatorname{Re}\sum _{i,k}B_ i\chi _{i ar k}U_ k\xi _{ ar i} -C_ gTQ-2H_1|\partial U|_\omega , \end{align*} where $C_ g$ depends only on $\omega $ and $\chi $. Proof. Write $\mathscr T^ p_{ik}$ and $R^ p_{i ar jk}$ for the torsion and curvature of the Chern connection. The commutation formula and the differentiated equation read  egin{gather*}
