The latter are bounded by \[  CT|\partial U|+CT|\partial U|^2 +C|\partial U|T^{1/2}\Bigl (\sum _{i,k}B_ i|U_{k ar i}|^2\Bigr )^{1/2}.  \] Absorb the last term into half of the mixed square. Since $U_{i ar j}=\lambda _ i\delta _{ij}-\chi _{i ar j}$, the remaining half is at least $ rac14\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2-CT$. Hence \[  \mathcal L|\partial U|^2\geq \sum _{i,k}B_ i|U_{ki}|^2 + rac14\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2-C_ gTQ-2H_1|\partial U|.  \] Finally, \[  \partial _ i|\partial U|^2 =\sum _ kU_{ki}U_{ ar k}+\lambda _ iU_ i-\sum _ k\chi _{i ar k}U_ k.  \] In the product rule for $\mathrm e^\xi Q$, combine the cross term coming from the first sum with $|\partial U|^2|\partial \xi |_ B^2$ and with the square $\sum B_ i|U_{ki}|^2$. This gives $\sum B_ i|U_{ki}+U_ k\xi _ i|^2$, while the remaining weight term is $|\partial \xi |_ B^2$. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.9.3
text: Proposition 10.9.3 . There are constants $\eta ,C>0$, depending only on the fixed data and $H_1$, such that every smooth admissible $V$ with $\| U-V\| _\infty \leq \eta $ satisfies \[  \| \partial U\| _\infty \leq C\bigl (1+\| \partial V\| _\infty ^2\bigr ).  \] The comparison radius $\eta $ is independent of the derivatives of $V$. Proof. Let $a\geq 1$ and $\beta >1$ be constants, to be chosen below. Assuming $\| U-V\| _\infty \leq \beta ^{-1}$, put \[  w=U-V-\beta ^{-1},\qquad \xi =a(\underline U-U)+\beta w^2,\qquad K_ V=1+\| \partial \underline U\| _\infty +\| \partial V\| _\infty .  \] Then $-2\beta ^{-1}\leq w\leq 0$ and \[  \xi _ i=a(\underline U_ i-V_ i)+(-a+2\beta w)(U_ i-V_ i), \qquad |-a+2\beta w|\leq a+4.  \] Writing $D=|\partial (U-V)|_ B^2$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \begin{align*}  \left|2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ iU_ i\xi _{\bar i}\right| & \leq \frac18\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2+C_ aK_ V^4T+C_ a(Q+K_ V^2)D,\\  \left|2\operatorname{Re}\sum _{i,k}B_ i\chi _{i\bar k}U_ k\xi _{\bar i}\right| & \leq \tfrac 12QD+C_ aT+C_ aK_ VQ^{1/2}T. \end{align*} For the first line, split $\xi _ i$ as above and use $\sum B_ i|U_ i|^2\leq 2D+2K_ V^2T$; then apply Young's inequality to the resulting three products, each absorbing at most $\frac1{24}\sum B_ i\lambda _ i^2$. For the second line, use $|\partial \xi |_ B\leq aK_ VT^{1/2}+(a+4)D^{1/2}$ and the bound for $\chi $. In both lines, $C_ a$ depends on $a$ but not on $\beta $ or on the derivatives of $V$. By lemma 10.9.1 and $w\leq 0$, \[  \mathcal L\xi \geq a\mathcal L(\underline U-U)-4H_0+2\beta D.  \] Choose $a$ so large that $(a\kappa -C_ g-2)\tau >4H_0+2H_1+1$, and then $\beta \geq 2C_ a+2$. Combining the preceding bounds with lemma 10.9.2 , we obtain, at every point where $Q\geq C'(1+K_ V^4)$ for a suitable constant $C'$, \begin{align*}  \mathrm e^{-\xi }\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q) & \geq \frac18\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2\\ & \quad +Q\bigl [a\mathcal L(\underline U-U)-(C_ g+2)T +\beta D-(4H_0+2H_1)\bigr ]. \end{align*} Indeed, the coefficient of $D$ before absorption is $(2\beta -C_ a-1/2)Q-C_ aK_ V^2$, which is at least $\beta Q$ once $C'$ is large enough. The other errors satisfy $C_ aK_ V^4\leq Q$ and $C_ a+C_ aK_ VQ^{1/2}\leq Q$, and they account for the additional term $-2T$ in the bracket. Consider a maximum point of $\mathrm e^\xi Q$ at which $Q\geq C'(1+K_ V^4)$. In the first alternative of lemma 10.9.1 , the bracket is positive by the choice of $a$, since $T\geq \tau $. In the second, $D\geq \kappa T|\partial (U-V)|^2$. For $Q\geq 4(1+K_ V^2)$, the triangle inequality gives $|\partial (U-V)|^2\geq c_*Q$, where $c_*=(\sqrt3-1)^2/4$. Since $\mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq -H_0$, the bracket is then at least \[  (\beta \kappa c_*Q-C_ g-2)T-(a+4)H_0-2H_1.  \] This is positive once $C'$ is large enough, because $T\geq \tau $. In both cases $\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q)>0$ at a maximum point, which contradicts the second derivative test. Thus $Q\leq C(1+K_ V^4)$ at the maximum point. The weight has uniformly bounded oscillation: \[  \operatorname {osc}_ X\xi \leq a(\operatorname {osc}_ X\underline U+\operatorname {osc}_ XU)+4/\beta .  \] By the potential bound in proposition 10.8.2 , this oscillation is bounded independently of $V$, so the estimate at the maximum point gives $Q\leq C(1+K_ V^4)$ everywhere. Taking square roots and setting $\eta =\beta ^{-1}$ proves the assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.9.4
text: Theorem 10.9.4 . There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data and $H_1$, such that $\| \mathrm du\| _{L^\infty (\omega )}\leq C$ for every normalized solution $u$ whose right-hand side $h$ lies in the family and satisfies $\| \partial h\| _\infty \leq H_1$. In particular, the bound is uniform as the positive right-hand sides tend to zero. Proof. The right-hand sides in the family with $\| \partial h\| _\infty \leq H_1$ form an equicontinuous set. By corollary 10.8.4 , the corresponding functions $U$ form a precompact subset of $C^0(X)$. Choose a finite $\eta $-net in this set, consisting of smooth admissible functions $V_1,\ldots ,V_ N$. Each solution is within $\eta $ of some $V_ j$, so proposition 10.9.3 bounds its gradient by $C(1+\max _ j\| \partial V_ j\| _\infty ^2)$. The set of solutions, and hence the chosen finite net, depends only on the fixed data and $H_1$. Finally, $u=2\pi U$, so the same conclusion holds for $\mathrm du$. $\square$

title: 11 Uniqueness for degenerate equations
text: 11 Uniqueness for degenerate equations Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form, and let $\mathrm dV$ be a smooth positive volume form. For a nonzero nonnegative density $f\in L^ p(X,\mathrm dV)$, $p>1$, the preceding chapter determines the constant $c$ in $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=cf\, \mathrm dV$. We now ask whether the potential is determined up to a constant. For real potentials $u,v$, with the regularity stated in each result, set \[  A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,\qquad B=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v,\qquad w=u-v, \qquad T=\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}A^ j\wedge B^{n-1-j}.  \] Then 11.1 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:linearization} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=A^ n-B^ n. \end{equation} For $A,B\geq 0$ with equal Monge–Ampère measures, $w$ solves $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$, whose cofactor may be degenerate or nonclosed. Coefficient products for Sobolev potentials are interpreted almost everywhere. For $C^{1,1}$ solutions with a common continuous density, perturbing $w$ locates its extrema in elliptic regions; the maximum principle propagates their values along the corresponding components. For $C^2$ potentials, a continuous weight $h>0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ in distributions gives a global energy identity forcing $\mathrm dw$ to vanish in the positive directions of the cofactor. For bounded solutions, an energy measure replaces the pointwise gradient calculation. A continuous density whose positive set is connected and dense then gives uniqueness. When the background has invariant mass, ordinary comparison proves uniqueness for nonzero nonnegative $L^ p$ densities, $p>1$, even if the density vanishes on an open set. The examples on $\mathbb P^3$ have bounded mass and a smooth nonclosed Hermitian background, yet distinct smooth normalized solutions share one density. Its zero set separates the elliptic regions: it can be an open band or two hypersurfaces with quadratic vanishing, even for a real analytic density. Finite upper mass therefore does not ensure uniqueness.
11.1 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:linearization} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=A^ n-B^ n. \end{equation}

title: 11.1 Extrema and density sublevels
text:
11.1 Extrema and density sublevels To apply the strong maximum principle to $w=u-v$, we first locate a maximum point and a minimum point of $w$ in the region where the linear equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$ is uniformly elliptic. Maximizing a small perturbation of $w$ by a function $\chi $ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi >0$ does this, even when the Hessians are only measurable. The strong maximum principle then makes $w$ constant on the components of this region that contain these points, and $w$ is constant if the closures of the two components meet. In this section, $u,v\in C^{1,1}(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ almost everywhere and 11.2  egin{equation}  A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad f\in C^0(X),\qquad f\geq 0. \label{uni-eq:density} \end{equation} Fix a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form $ eta $, put $H=A+B$, and let $E_{m unif}$ be the set of points near which $H$ is uniformly positive: 11.3  egin{equation}  E_{m unif} =\left\{ x: egin{array}{l} 	ext{there are a neighborhood }V
i x	ext{ and }c>0\  	ext{with }H\geq c eta 	ext{ almost everywhere on }V \end{array}ight\} . \label{uni-eq:Eunif} \end{equation} This open set does not depend on $ eta $ or on the choice of representatives of the measurable coefficients. Theorem 11.1.1 . Assume ( 11.2 ). If $\chi \in C^2(X,\mathbb R)$ satisfies $C:=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi >0$, put \[  P_\chi =\{ x\in X:f(x)\mathrm{d}V_ x\geq C_ x^ n\} ,\qquad U=\{ f>0\} .  \] Then $P_\chi $ is a nonempty compact subset of $U$, and $U\subset E_{m unif}$. There are components $G_+,G_-$ of $E_{m unif}$, each meeting $P_\chi $, such that $w=u-v$ satisfies 11.4  egin{equation}  w\equiv \max _ Xw\quad \hbox{on }\overline{G_+},\qquad w\equiv \min _ Xw\quad \hbox{on }\overline{G_-}. \label{uni-eq:extrema-components} \end{equation} If $w$ is nonconstant, these closures are disjoint. Consequently $w$ is constant if any one of the following holds: every two components of $E_{m unif}$ meeting $P_\chi $ have intersecting closures; $E_{m unif}$ is connected; $E_{m unif}$ is dense and has at most two components. The assertions about components, including the three criteria, also hold with $U$ in place of $E_{m unif}$. In particular, $w$ is constant when $\{ f=0\} $ is a nonempty connected embedded $C^1$ real hypersurface; this hypersurface need not be orientable or coorientable. Since the Hessians of $C^{1,1}$ functions exist only almost everywhere, the contact argument must use points where they exist. The following lemma finds such points near a maximum; it also provides the strict comparison step in the measurable strong maximum principle. Lemma 11.1.2 . In Euclidean space $\mathbb R^ m$, let $B(p,r)$ be the ball of center $p$ and radius $r>0$, and let $I$ be the identity matrix. Let $g\in C^{1,1}$ near $\overline{B(p,r)}\subset \mathbb R^ m$, suppose $g\leq g(p)$ on the ball, and let $E$ be any subset of full measure in the ball at whose points $g$ has a second-order Taylor expansion. For every $\delta >0$ and $0<ho <r$, there is $x\in E\cap B(p,ho )$ such that \[  D^2g(x)\leq 2\delta I.  \] Proof. Put $g_\delta (x)=g(x)-\delta |x-p|^2$. The gradient map $F=
abla g_\delta $ is Lipschitz on the ball, so it maps the null set $N=\overline{B(p,r)}\setminus E$ to a null set. Choose $s\in B(0,\delta ho )\setminus F(N)$ and maximize $g_\delta (x)-s\cdot (x-p)$ on the closed ball. At any point with $|x-p|\geq ho $, its value is strictly smaller than its value at $p$, because \[  g(x)-g(p)-\delta |x-p|^2-s\cdot (x-p) \leq -\delta |x-p|^2+|s|\, |x-p|<0.  \] Thus a maximizer $x$ lies in $B(p,ho )$. The first-order condition at $x$ gives $F(x)=s$, so $x
otin N$. The second-order Taylor expansion at this upper contact point gives $D^2g(x)\leq 2\delta I$. Finally, sets $E$ as in the statement exist: by Rademacher's theorem, applied to the Lipschitz gradient of $g$, the function $g$ has a second-order Taylor expansion almost everywhere. $\square$ Lemma 11.1.3 . Let $a=(a^{ij})$ be a measurable symmetric matrix field on a connected domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ m$. For each compact $K\Subset \Omega $, suppose there are constants $0<\lambda _ K\leq \Lambda _ K<\infty $ such that \[  \lambda _ K I\leq a(x)\leq \Lambda _ KI  \] almost everywhere on $K$, where $I$ is the identity matrix. Repeated indices $i,j=1,\ldots ,m$ are summed, and $z_{ij}=\partial _ i\partial _ jz$. If $z\in W^{2,\infty }_{m loc}(\Omega )$, $a^{ij}z_{ij}\geq 0$ almost everywhere, and $z$ attains its supremum at a point of $\Omega $, then $z$ is constant. Proof. We first prove strict weak comparison on a relatively compact domain: if $b\in C^{1,1}$, $Lb:=a^{ij}b_{ij}\geq \kappa >0$ almost everywhere, and $b\leq M$ on the boundary, then $b\leq M$ inside. Otherwise an interior maximum point lies in a closed ball on which $a\leq \Lambda I$. Apply 11.1.2 to the set of full measure where both the differential inequality and the Taylor expansion hold. Choosing $2\delta m\Lambda <\kappa $ gives the contradiction $\kappa \leq Lb\leq 2\delta \operatorname {tr}a\leq 2\delta m\Lambda $. Take the $C^{1,1}$ representative of $z$, write $M=\sup _\Omega z$, and suppose that $K=\{ z=M\} $ is a nonempty proper subset of $\Omega $. Near a relative boundary point of $K$, choose $y
otin K$ so that the ball of radius $r=\operatorname {dist}(y,K)>0$ is compactly contained in $\Omega $ and touches $K$ at $x_0$. On the closed annulus $r/2\leq |x-y|\leq r$, use fixed bounds $\lambda I\leq a\leq \Lambda I$ and set \[  b(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha |x-y|^2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha r^2}.  \] For sufficiently large $\alpha $, \[  Lb=\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha |x-y|^2}  igl (4\alpha ^2 a^{ij}(x_ i-y_ i)(x_ j-y_ j) -2\alpha \operatorname {tr}a igr )\geq \kappa >0  \] almost everywhere on the annulus. On its inner sphere $z<M$ uniformly; on its outer sphere $b=0$. Choose $\eta >0$ small enough that $z+\eta b\leq M$ on both spheres. Strict weak comparison, applied to $z+\eta b$, gives this inequality throughout the annulus. At $x_0$, however, $z=M$, $b=0$, $
abla z=0$, and $b$ increases to first order in the inward radial direction, which contradicts that inequality. Thus $K$ has no relative boundary point in $\Omega $, and connectedness proves the assertion. The argument uses no derivatives of the measurable coefficients. $\square$ At a point where $A,B$ are semipositive, define the cofactor quadratic form on real cotangent vectors 11.5  egin{equation}  Q_ x(\xi )\mathrm{d}V_ x =\mathrm{i}\, \xi ^{1,0}\wedge \overline{\xi ^{1,0}}\wedge T_ x . \label{uni-eq:Q} \end{equation} Here $\xi ^{1,0}$ is the $(1,0)$-part of $\xi $, and forms of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$ are ordered by testing against $\mathrm i\xi ^{1,0}\wedge \overline{\xi ^{1,0}}$ in this way. Mixed products of semipositive $(1,1)$-forms are semipositive in this order. Expanding $H^{n-1}$, where $H=A+B$, gives 11.6  egin{equation}  2^{-(n-1)}H^{n-1}\leq T\leq H^{n-1}. \label{uni-eq:cofactor-comparison} \end{equation} At a point, choose a $ eta $-unitary coframe $\mathrm{d}z_1,\ldots ,\mathrm{d}z_ n$ that diagonalizes $H$, and write $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n$ for the eigenvalues of $H$. For a $(1,0)$-covector $\alpha =\sum _{k=1}^ n b_ k\, \mathrm{d}z_ k$ with complex coefficients $b_ k$, the coefficient of $\mathrm{i}\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha \wedge H^{n-1}$ in this coframe is a positive constant depending only on $n$, times 11.7  egin{equation}  \sum _{k=1}^ n |b_ k|^2\prod _{\ell 
e k}\lambda _\ell . \label{uni-eq:cofactor-eigen} \end{equation} For $n\geq 2$, ( 11.6 ) and ( 11.7 ) show that $Q$ is locally uniformly elliptic exactly on $E_{m unif}$, that is, where $H$ has a local essential positive lower bound. The implication from ellipticity of $Q$ to a lower bound for $H$ uses the local upper bound for $H$: testing each eigendirection bounds every product $\prod _{\ell 
e k}\lambda _\ell $ below, and choosing $k$ different from an index of a smallest eigenvalue then bounds that eigenvalue below. For $n=1$ one has $T=1$, so the linearized equation is elliptic everywhere. of 11.1.1 . We first locate the extrema. Fix $s>0$ and consider a maximum point of 11.8  egin{equation}  w-s(v-\chi ). \label{uni-eq:pertmax} \end{equation} For smooth data, the complex Hessian of this function is nonpositive at a maximum point, that is, 11.9  egin{equation}  (1+s)B\geq A+sC. \label{uni-eq:matrixcontact} \end{equation} Since $sC>0$, this gives $B>0$, and since $A^ n=B^ n$, also $A>0$. In a $B$-unitary frame put $J=B^{-1/2}AB^{-1/2}$, $K=B^{-1/2}CB^{-1/2}$. Since $\det J=1$, arithmetic–geometric mean and ( 11.9 ) give \[  n+s\operatorname {tr}K\leq \operatorname {tr}J+s\operatorname {tr}K \leq n(1+s).  \] Consequently $\operatorname {tr}K\leq n$, $B\geq C/n$, and $\det K\leq (\operatorname {tr}K/n)^ n\leq 1$. In particular $B^ n\geq C^ n$. For $C^{1,1}$ potentials, fix a maximum point $p$ of ( 11.8 ) and apply 11.1.2 on a coordinate ball, with radii tending to zero and errors $\delta _ j\downarrow 0$. For the set of full measure in that lemma, take the points where both Hessians are defined and semipositive and have the common determinant given by ( 11.2 ). With $ eta _0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$, the resulting points $x_ j	o p$ satisfy \[  A(x_ j)+s C_ j(x_ j)\leq (1+s)B(x_ j),\qquad C_ j=C-(\delta _ j/s) eta _0>0  \] for large $j$. The matrix argument just given yields $f(x_ j)\mathrm{d}V_{x_ j}\geq C_ j(x_ j)^ n$. Since $f$, $\mathrm{d}V$ and $C$ are continuous, letting $j	o \infty $ gives $p\in P_\chi $; no continuity of the Hessians is needed. Thus every maximum point of the perturbed function lies in $P_\chi $. The set $P_\chi $ is closed, by continuity of $f$, $\mathrm{d}V$ and $C$, hence compact, and it is contained in $U$ because $C^ n>0$. Letting $s\downarrow 0$, a limit point of these maximum points is a maximum point of $w$ lying in $P_\chi $. Applying the same argument to $-w$ gives a minimum point of $w$ in $P_\chi $ as well. In particular, $P_\chi $ is nonempty. On a relatively compact ball in $U$, the determinants of $A$ and $B$ have a positive lower bound, while their coefficients have an essential upper bound. Every eigenvalue is therefore bounded below by the determinant lower bound divided by a fixed power of the upper bound. Thus $U\subset E_{m unif}$. By ( 11.1 ), $w$ solves a linear equation in nondivergence form with measurable coefficients, whose principal quadratic form is a fixed positive multiple of $Q$. On each relatively compact coordinate ball in $E_{m unif}$, these coefficients are uniformly elliptic. 11.1.3 , applied to $w$ and to $-w$, makes $w$ constant on the component of $E_{m unif}$ containing the maximum point found above, and constant on the component containing the minimum point found above. Continuity extends the two constant values to the closures, proving ( 11.4 ). Distinct extrema force disjoint closures. The same argument applies on $U$ itself, since $U$ contains the extremal points found in $P_\chi $ and the cofactor is locally uniformly elliptic on $U\subset E_{m unif}$. This proves the assertions with $U$ in place of $E_{m unif}$. The component criteria are immediate except for the dense two-component case. If an open dense subset of connected $X$ has at most two components with disjoint closures, those closures are disjoint nonempty closed sets whose union is $X$, contradicting connectedness. Finally, when $Z=\{ f=0\} $ is a connected embedded real hypersurface, flattening charts assign to each point of $Z$ the unordered pair of components containing its two local sides. This pair is locally constant along $Z$, so connectedness makes it independent of the point; the two labels may coincide or be exchanged along a loop. Every component of $X\setminus Z$ has a nonempty boundary in $Z$, since otherwise it would be both open and closed in connected $X$. Near such a boundary point it contains a local side. Thus the pair accounts for every component, and $U$ has at most two components. It is dense because a hypersurface has empty interior. This proves the last assertion without choosing a global side. $\square$ In this argument, the $C^{1,1}$ bound controls the measurable coefficients, and continuity of the density places the limiting contact points in $\{ f>0\} $. The next criterion gives a quantitative condition for $\{ f>0\} $ to be connected.
11.2 \begin{equation}  A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad f\in C^0(X),\qquad f\geq 0. \label{uni-eq:density} \end{equation}

11.3 \begin{equation}  E_{\rm unif} =\left\{ x:\begin{array}{l} \text{there are a neighborhood }V\ni x\text{ and }c>0\\  \text{with }H\geq c\beta \text{ almost everywhere on }V \end{array}\right\} . \label{uni-eq:Eunif} \end{equation}

title: Theorem 11.1.1
text: Theorem 11.1.1 . Assume ( 11.2 ). If $\chi \in C^2(X,\mathbb R)$ satisfies $C:=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi >0$, put \[  P_\chi =\{ x\in X:f(x)\mathrm{d}V_ x\geq C_ x^ n\} ,\qquad U=\{ f>0\} .  \] Then $P_\chi $ is a nonempty compact subset of $U$, and $U\subset E_{\rm unif}$. There are components $G_+,G_-$ of $E_{\rm unif}$, each meeting $P_\chi $, such that $w=u-v$ satisfies 11.4 \begin{equation}  w\equiv \max _ Xw\quad \hbox{on }\overline{G_+},\qquad w\equiv \min _ Xw\quad \hbox{on }\overline{G_-}. \label{uni-eq:extrema-components} \end{equation} If $w$ is nonconstant, these closures are disjoint. Consequently $w$ is constant if any one of the following holds: every two components of $E_{\rm unif}$ meeting $P_\chi $ have intersecting closures; $E_{\rm unif}$ is connected; $E_{\rm unif}$ is dense and has at most two components. The assertions about components, including the three criteria, also hold with $U$ in place of $E_{\rm unif}$. In particular, $w$ is constant when $\{ f=0\} $ is a nonempty connected embedded $C^1$ real hypersurface; this hypersurface need not be orientable or coorientable. of 11.1.1 . We first locate the extrema. Fix $s>0$ and consider a maximum point of 11.8 \begin{equation}  w-s(v-\chi ). \label{uni-eq:pertmax} \end{equation} For smooth data, the complex Hessian of this function is nonpositive at a maximum point, that is, 11.9 \begin{equation}  (1+s)B\geq A+sC. \label{uni-eq:matrixcontact} \end{equation} Since $sC>0$, this gives $B>0$, and since $A^ n=B^ n$, also $A>0$. In a $B$-unitary frame put $J=B^{-1/2}AB^{-1/2}$, $K=B^{-1/2}CB^{-1/2}$. Since $\det J=1$, arithmetic–geometric mean and ( 11.9 ) give \[  n+s\operatorname {tr}K\leq \operatorname {tr}J+s\operatorname {tr}K \leq n(1+s).  \] Consequently $\operatorname {tr}K\leq n$, $B\geq C/n$, and $\det K\leq (\operatorname {tr}K/n)^ n\leq 1$. In particular $B^ n\geq C^ n$. For $C^{1,1}$ potentials, fix a maximum point $p$ of ( 11.8 ) and apply 11.1.2 on a coordinate ball, with radii tending to zero and errors $\delta _ j\downarrow 0$. For the set of full measure in that lemma, take the points where both Hessians are defined and semipositive and have the common determinant given by ( 11.2 ). With $\beta _0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$, the resulting points $x_ j\to p$ satisfy \[  A(x_ j)+s C_ j(x_ j)\leq (1+s)B(x_ j),\qquad C_ j=C-(\delta _ j/s)\beta _0>0  \] for large $j$. The matrix argument just given yields $f(x_ j)\mathrm{d}V_{x_ j}\geq C_ j(x_ j)^ n$. Since $f$, $\mathrm{d}V$ and $C$ are continuous, letting $j\to \infty $ gives $p\in P_\chi $; no continuity of the Hessians is needed. Thus every maximum point of the perturbed function lies in $P_\chi $. The set $P_\chi $ is closed, by continuity of $f$, $\mathrm{d}V$ and $C$, hence compact, and it is contained in $U$ because $C^ n>0$. Letting $s\downarrow 0$, a limit point of these maximum points is a maximum point of $w$ lying in $P_\chi $. Applying the same argument to $-w$ gives a minimum point of $w$ in $P_\chi $ as well. In particular, $P_\chi $ is nonempty. On a relatively compact ball in $U$, the determinants of $A$ and $B$ have a positive lower bound, while their coefficients have an essential upper bound. Every eigenvalue is therefore bounded below by the determinant lower bound divided by a fixed power of the upper bound. Thus $U\subset E_{\rm unif}$. By ( 11.1 ), $w$ solves a linear equation in nondivergence form with measurable coefficients, whose principal quadratic form is a fixed positive multiple of $Q$. On each relatively compact coordinate ball in $E_{\rm unif}$, these coefficients are uniformly elliptic. 11.1.3 , applied to $w$ and to $-w$, makes $w$ constant on the component of $E_{\rm unif}$ containing the maximum point found above, and constant on the component containing the minimum point found above. Continuity extends the two constant values to the closures, proving ( 11.4 ). Distinct extrema force disjoint closures. The same argument applies on $U$ itself, since $U$ contains the extremal points found in $P_\chi $ and the cofactor is locally uniformly elliptic on $U\subset E_{\rm unif}$. This proves the assertions with $U$ in place of $E_{\rm unif}$. The component criteria are immediate except for the dense two-component case. If an open dense subset of connected $X$ has at most two components with disjoint closures, those closures are disjoint nonempty closed sets whose union is $X$, contradicting connectedness. Finally, when $Z=\{ f=0\} $ is a connected embedded real hypersurface, flattening charts assign to each point of $Z$ the unordered pair of components containing its two local sides. This pair is locally constant along $Z$, so connectedness makes it independent of the point; the two labels may coincide or be exchanged along a loop. Every component of $X\setminus Z$ has a nonempty boundary in $Z$, since otherwise it would be both open and closed in connected $X$. Near such a boundary point it contains a local side. Thus the pair accounts for every component, and $U$ has at most two components. It is dense because a hypersurface has empty interior. This proves the last assertion without choosing a global side. $\square$

title: Lemma 11.1.2
text: Lemma 11.1.2 . In Euclidean space $\mathbb R^ m$, let $B(p,r)$ be the ball of center $p$ and radius $r>0$, and let $I$ be the identity matrix. Let $g\in C^{1,1}$ near $\overline{B(p,r)}\subset \mathbb R^ m$, suppose $g\leq g(p)$ on the ball, and let $E$ be any subset of full measure in the ball at whose points $g$ has a second-order Taylor expansion. For every $\delta >0$ and $0<\rho <r$, there is $x\in E\cap B(p,\rho )$ such that \[  D^2g(x)\leq 2\delta I.  \] Proof. Put $g_\delta (x)=g(x)-\delta |x-p|^2$. The gradient map $F=\nabla g_\delta $ is Lipschitz on the ball, so it maps the null set $N=\overline{B(p,r)}\setminus E$ to a null set. Choose $s\in B(0,\delta \rho )\setminus F(N)$ and maximize $g_\delta (x)-s\cdot (x-p)$ on the closed ball. At any point with $|x-p|\geq \rho $, its value is strictly smaller than its value at $p$, because \[  g(x)-g(p)-\delta |x-p|^2-s\cdot (x-p) \leq -\delta |x-p|^2+|s|\, |x-p|<0.  \] Thus a maximizer $x$ lies in $B(p,\rho )$. The first-order condition at $x$ gives $F(x)=s$, so $x\notin N$. The second-order Taylor expansion at this upper contact point gives $D^2g(x)\leq 2\delta I$. Finally, sets $E$ as in the statement exist: by Rademacher's theorem, applied to the Lipschitz gradient of $g$, the function $g$ has a second-order Taylor expansion almost everywhere. $\square$

title: Lemma 11.1.3
text: Lemma 11.1.3 . Let $a=(a^{ij})$ be a measurable symmetric matrix field on a connected domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ m$. For each compact $K\Subset \Omega $, suppose there are constants $0<\lambda _ K\leq \Lambda _ K<\infty $ such that \[  \lambda _ K I\leq a(x)\leq \Lambda _ KI  \] almost everywhere on $K$, where $I$ is the identity matrix. Repeated indices $i,j=1,\ldots ,m$ are summed, and $z_{ij}=\partial _ i\partial _ jz$. If $z\in W^{2,\infty }_{\rm loc}(\Omega )$, $a^{ij}z_{ij}\geq 0$ almost everywhere, and $z$ attains its supremum at a point of $\Omega $, then $z$ is constant. Proof. We first prove strict weak comparison on a relatively compact domain: if $b\in C^{1,1}$, $Lb:=a^{ij}b_{ij}\geq \kappa >0$ almost everywhere, and $b\leq M$ on the boundary, then $b\leq M$ inside. Otherwise an interior maximum point lies in a closed ball on which $a\leq \Lambda I$. Apply 11.1.2 to the set of full measure where both the differential inequality and the Taylor expansion hold. Choosing $2\delta m\Lambda <\kappa $ gives the contradiction $\kappa \leq Lb\leq 2\delta \operatorname {tr}a\leq 2\delta m\Lambda $. Take the $C^{1,1}$ representative of $z$, write $M=\sup _\Omega z$, and suppose that $K=\{ z=M\} $ is a nonempty proper subset of $\Omega $. Near a relative boundary point of $K$, choose $y\notin K$ so that the ball of radius $r=\operatorname {dist}(y,K)>0$ is compactly contained in $\Omega $ and touches $K$ at $x_0$. On the closed annulus $r/2\leq |x-y|\leq r$, use fixed bounds $\lambda I\leq a\leq \Lambda I$ and set \[  b(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha |x-y|^2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha r^2}.  \] For sufficiently large $\alpha $, \[  Lb=\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha |x-y|^2} \bigl (4\alpha ^2 a^{ij}(x_ i-y_ i)(x_ j-y_ j) -2\alpha \operatorname {tr}a\bigr )\geq \kappa >0  \] almost everywhere on the annulus. On its inner sphere $z<M$ uniformly; on its outer sphere $b=0$. Choose $\eta >0$ small enough that $z+\eta b\leq M$ on both spheres. Strict weak comparison, applied to $z+\eta b$, gives this inequality throughout the annulus. At $x_0$, however, $z=M$, $b=0$, $\nabla z=0$, and $b$ increases to first order in the inward radial direction, which contradicts that inequality. Thus $K$ has no relative boundary point in $\Omega $, and connectedness proves the assertion. The argument uses no derivatives of the measurable coefficients. $\square$

title: 11.1.1 A square-root threshold
text: 11.1.1 A square-root threshold A nonnegative $C^{1,1}$ density grows at most quadratically away from each of its zeros. If its zero set separates a small ball, a family of parallel segments crossing the zero set therefore contributes at least a constant times $\sqrt t$ to the volume of $\{ f\leq t\} $ for small $t>0$. Excluding this lower bound makes $\{ f>0\} $ connected, and 11.1.1 then gives uniqueness. Write $\operatorname {Vol}(E)=\int _ E\mathrm{d}V$ for Borel sets $E$. Theorem 11.1.4 . Let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f\geq 0$ is $C^{1,1}$. If 11.10 \begin{equation}  \liminf _{t\downarrow 0} \frac{\operatorname {Vol}\{ f\leq t\} }{\sqrt t}=0, \label{uni-eq:sqrtcriterion} \end{equation} then $\{ f>0\} $ is connected and $u-v$ is constant. In particular this holds when $f^{-1/2}\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, with $f^{-1/2}=+\infty $ on $\{ f=0\} $. The exponent $1/2$ is sharp in every dimension $n\geq 3$. Proof. Write $Z=\{ f=0\} $. Condition ( 11.10 ) first implies $\operatorname {Vol}(Z)=0$. We show that the complement of $Z$ in every sufficiently small coordinate ball is connected. Fix such a ball with convex Euclidean image. If the complement of $Z$ in it were disconnected, choose points $a,b$ in different components and small closed disks centered at $a$ and $b$, perpendicular to the segment $[a,b]$ and contained in those respective components. By making the disks small, all parallel segments between corresponding points stay in the ball. Each segment meets $Z$, since otherwise it would connect the two components. On a fixed coordinate region containing the closed ball, the gradient of $f$ is Lipschitz with some constant $K>0$. Since $f\geq 0$, we have $\nabla f(z)=0$ at every zero $z$, hence 11.11 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:quadratic-upper} f(x)\leq \frac K2|x-z|^2 \end{equation} whenever the segment from $z$ to $x$ stays in that region. The endpoint disks are compact and disjoint from $Z$, so the parts of the segments near them contain no zeros. Thus every parallel segment contains a zero at a fixed positive distance from its endpoints. For small $t>0$, ( 11.11 ) gives on that segment an interval of length $2\sqrt{2t/K}$ contained in $\{ f\leq t\} $. Integrating over the transverse disk, which has positive measure, and using that $\mathrm{d}V$ is comparable to coordinate volume, we obtain \[  \operatorname {Vol}\{ f\leq t\} \geq c\sqrt t  \] for all sufficiently small $t$, contradicting ( 11.10 ). This proves the local connectedness assertion. For each such ball, the complement of $Z$ in it is nonempty, since $Z$ has zero volume, and it lies in one component of $U=X\setminus Z$. Two overlapping balls give the same component, because their open overlap contains a point outside $Z$. Since $X$ is connected, all these balls give the same component. Hence $U$ is connected, and 11.1.1 shows that $u-v$ is constant. If $f^{-1/2}\in L^1$, then, outside the null zero set, \[  \frac{\operatorname {Vol}\{ f\leq t\} }{\sqrt t} \leq \int _{\{ f\leq t\} }f^{-1/2}\, \mathrm{d}V\longrightarrow 0  \] by dominated convergence. This proves the sufficient integrability condition. The sharpness assertion follows from the examples in 11.9 , as quantified at the end of that section. $\square$

title: 11.2 Polarized cofactors and propagation
text: 11.2 Polarized cofactors and propagation Uniform ellipticity is sufficient for the propagation of an extremum, but it is not necessary: the directions in which the cofactor is positive may already connect enough points to force constancy. For $C^2$ potentials, the quadratic form $Q$ in ( 11.5 ) is continuous, and its polarization defines $Q^\sharp :T^*X\to TX$ by $\eta (Q^\sharp \xi )=Q(\xi ,\eta )$. The reachable set of a point consists of the endpoints of absolutely continuous curves starting there whose velocity lies in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $ almost everywhere. The control orbit of a point consists of the endpoints of finite concatenations of flow lines, starting there, of locally Lipschitz vector fields with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $. A positive weight $h$ satisfying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ gives an energy identity that controls $\mathrm{d}w$ everywhere. Without such a weight, a degenerate maximum principle gives propagation only from the extremal sets. This distinction accounts for the different density assumptions on reachable sets and on orbits in the following theorem. Theorem 11.2.1 . Let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n$, and put $w=u-v$. If there is a continuous $h>0$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ in distributions, then 11.12 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{i}\, \partial w\wedge \bar\partial w\wedge T\equiv 0. \label{uni-eq:energyzero} \end{equation} It follows that $w$ is constant if the set where $T$ is strictly positive is dense, or if the reachable set of one point is dense. Without the weight hypothesis, the sets where $w$ attains its maximum and its minimum are invariant under the flow of every locally Lipschitz vector field with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $. If every control orbit is dense, then $w$ is constant. For smooth data it is enough that smooth vector fields with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $, for example the columns of the symbol $a$ in ( 11.18 ) below, together with their iterated Lie brackets, span $TX$ at every point.

title: Theorem 11.2.1
text: Theorem 11.2.1 . Let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n$, and put $w=u-v$. If there is a continuous $h>0$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ in distributions, then 11.12 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{i}\, \partial w\wedge \bar\partial w\wedge T\equiv 0. \label{uni-eq:energyzero} \end{equation} It follows that $w$ is constant if the set where $T$ is strictly positive is dense, or if the reachable set of one point is dense. Without the weight hypothesis, the sets where $w$ attains its maximum and its minimum are invariant under the flow of every locally Lipschitz vector field with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $. If every control orbit is dense, then $w$ is constant. For smooth data it is enough that smooth vector fields with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $, for example the columns of the symbol $a$ in ( 11.18 ) below, together with their iterated Lie brackets, span $TX$ at every point. of 11.2.1 (1). The product rule gives 11.14 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:w2} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)=2w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+2\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w =2w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\pi }\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w. \end{equation} Approximate $w^2$ in $C^2$ by smooth functions $\varphi $ in ( 11.13 ). Since $hT$ is continuous and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$ by ( 11.1 ), this gives 11.15 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:energy} 0=\frac1\pi \int _ X h\, \mathrm{i}\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w\wedge T. \end{equation} The continuous integrand is nonnegative, so it vanishes identically, which is ( 11.12 ). By ( 11.5 ), ( 11.12 ) says that $Q(\mathrm{d}w)=0$. For the nonnegative quadratic form $Q$, this implies $Q(\mathrm{d}w,\eta )=0$ for every $\eta $. Therefore 11.16 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:annihilate} \mathrm{d}w_ x\bigl (Q_ x^\sharp \eta \bigr )=0\qquad (x\in X,\  \eta \in T_ x^*X). \end{equation} By the chain rule and ( 11.16 ), $w$ is constant along every absolutely continuous curve whose velocity lies in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $ almost everywhere. Thus $w$ is constant on each reachable set, and by continuity one dense reachable set suffices. If instead $Q$ is positive definite on a dense set, ( 11.15 ) gives $\mathrm{d}w=0$ there, and hence everywhere. $\square$ of 11.2.1 (2). Apply the preceding argument to $W=w$ and to $W=-w$ in each chart; both satisfy $LW=0$ by ( 11.1 ). The maximum set of $w$ is nonempty, closed, and contains every control orbit starting in it. If every orbit is dense, this maximum set is all of $X$, proving constancy. The argument for the minimum set is identical. It remains to prove the bracket criterion. Suppose that a family of smooth vector fields with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $ is bracket generating. At $p$, let $\mathcal D_ p$ be the span of the values of all original fields pushed forward by finite compositions of their local flows and inverse flows. This distribution contains the original fields and is invariant under their flows. Differentiation of pushed-forward fields along a flow shows that it contains their nested Lie brackets; finite-dimensional subspaces are closed, so the derivative remains in $\mathcal D_ p$. Induction and the Jacobi identity give every iterated bracket. The assumed rank condition therefore gives $\mathcal D_ p=T_ pX$. Choose $2n$ such pushed-forward fields independent at $p$. The flow of each is a conjugate of an original flow and hence preserves its orbit. The map obtained by successively flowing for $2n$ small times has invertible derivative at zero. The inverse function theorem puts a neighborhood of $p$ in its orbit. All orbits are open, and their partition of connected $X$ has only one member. This proves the Hörmander-type sufficient condition; it requires neither a constant-rank hypothesis nor a smooth matrix square root of $a$. In particular, the columns of a smooth symbol $a$ may be used as the original vector fields. $\square$

title: 11.2.1 Weighted energy
text: 11.2.1 Weighted energy Testing the weighted cofactor against $w^2$ produces a nonnegative gradient integral. Only distributional $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closedness of $hT$ is needed: for a continuous $h>0$, the condition is 11.13 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:weightedclosed} \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge hT=0\qquad (\varphi \in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)). \end{equation} of 11.2.1 (1). The product rule gives 11.14 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:w2} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)=2w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+2\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w =2w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\pi }\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w. \end{equation} Approximate $w^2$ in $C^2$ by smooth functions $\varphi $ in ( 11.13 ). Since $hT$ is continuous and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$ by ( 11.1 ), this gives 11.15 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:energy} 0=\frac1\pi \int _ X h\, \mathrm{i}\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w\wedge T. \end{equation} The continuous integrand is nonnegative, so it vanishes identically, which is ( 11.12 ). By ( 11.5 ), ( 11.12 ) says that $Q(\mathrm{d}w)=0$. For the nonnegative quadratic form $Q$, this implies $Q(\mathrm{d}w,\eta )=0$ for every $\eta $. Thus $w$ is constant on each reachable set, and by continuity one dense reachable set suffices. If instead $Q$ is positive definite on a dense set, ( 11.15 ) gives $\mathrm{d}w=0$ there, and hence everywhere. $\square$ The argument uses only the test function $w^2$. For general test functions, integration by parts introduces derivatives of $hT$; the condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ alone does not make $L\varphi =(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge T)/\mathrm{d}V$ a symmetric operator in divergence form.

title: 11.2.3 The unweighted energy defect
text: 11.2.3 The unweighted energy defect Integration against $w^2$ also measures the obstruction to using the unweighted cofactor, that is, the case $h=1$. For smooth potentials, the error is exactly the pairing of $w^2$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$. On a surface, the Gauduchon condition makes this error vanish for every pair of potentials; in dimension three, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ contains an additional term depending on the potentials. Proposition 11.2.2 . Let $n\geq 2$, and let $u,v$ be smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions with $A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ for a smooth function $f\geq 0$. Then 11.20 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-uniqueness-defect} \int _ X \mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge T =\frac12\int _ X w^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T. \end{equation} If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ and $\{ f>0\} $ is dense in $X$, then $u-v$ is constant. Proof. By ( 11.1 ), $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$. Integrating ( 11.14 ) against $T$, and applying Stokes' theorem twice to the left-hand side, yields \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)\wedge T=\int _ Xw^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T.  \] Substitution proves ( 11.20 ). For the uniqueness assertion, apply 11.2.1 (1) with $h=1$. At every point where $f>0$, the form $B$ is positive definite, so the term $B^{n-1}$ makes the cofactor $T$ strictly positive. The set where $T$ is strictly positive is therefore dense, as required. $\square$ Corollary 11.2.3 . Assume $n=2$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. Let $f\geq 0$ be smooth, with a zero set of empty interior, and let $c>0$. Then any two smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solutions of \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2=cf\, \mathrm{d}V  \] normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$ coincide. Proof. Here $T=A+B$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. The set $\{ f>0\} $ is dense, so the proposition, applied to the density $cf$, makes the difference of the two solutions constant, and the normalization makes this constant zero. $\square$ In dimension three, direct expansion gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=3\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)+3\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+v).  \] The Gauduchon condition cancels the first term but need not cancel the second. title: 11.3 Integral rigidity in dimensions two and three
search_title: Integral rigidity in dimensions two and three
text: 11.3 Integral rigidity in dimensions two and three In dimensions two and three, if two positive forms $A,B$ have equal determinants, an algebraic expression quadratic in $A-B$ has a strict sign unless the two forms agree. On a surface its integral vanishes because it is exact. On a threefold the integral is a term involving $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $, so a sign condition on $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ leads to the same conclusion. Approximation in the Sobolev norm justifies the integral identities for $W^{2,n}$ potentials. In this section $n\in \{ 2,3\} $. Norms of coefficients of forms are taken with respect to a fixed smooth metric and $\mathrm{d}V$. Theorem 11.3.1 . Let $u,v\in W^{2,n}(X,\mathbb R)$, and assume that $A,B\geq 0$ almost everywhere and \[  A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad f>0\quad \hbox{almost everywhere}.  \] If $n=3$, assume in addition that 11.21 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm{i}\eta \wedge \bar\eta \leq 0 \label{uni-eq:threefold-sign} \end{equation} for every $(1,0)$-covector $\eta $; for $n=2$ no condition on $\omega $ is needed. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-v)=0$ in the sense of distributions, and $u-v$ is almost everywhere constant. For the $\omega $-plurisubharmonic representatives of $u$ and $v$, the difference is constant everywhere. Proof. Put \[  \begin{gathered} s=(u+v)/2,\qquad D=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=A-B,\\ C=(A+B)/2=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s. \end{gathered}  \] The coefficients of $C$ and $D$ lie in $L^ n$, so their products of top degree are integrable by Hölder's inequality. At almost every point the common determinant is positive, so $A$ and $B$ are positive definite there, and we may diagonalize them simultaneously by congruence: for a suitable coframe of $(1,0)$-covectors $\theta _1,\ldots ,\theta _ n$, write $A=\sum e_ j$, $B=\sum \lambda _ j e_ j$, where $e_ j=\mathrm{i}\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j$, $\lambda _ j>0$, and $\prod \lambda _ j=1$. In dimension two, 11.22 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:surface-sign} D^2=A^2+B^2-2A\wedge B =2(2-\lambda _1-\lambda _2)e_1\wedge e_2\leq 0, \end{equation} with equality if and only if $A=B$. In dimension three, 11.23 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:threefold-algebra} 2C\wedge D^2=A^3+B^3-A^2\wedge B-A\wedge B^2\leq 0. \end{equation} Indeed, with $E=e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3$, the four terms on the right are \[  6E,\qquad 6E,\qquad 2\Bigl (\sum _ j\lambda _ j\Bigr )E, \qquad 2\Bigl (\sum _{i<j}\lambda _ i\lambda _ j\Bigr )E.  \] By the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and $\prod _ j\lambda _ j=1$, each sum is at least three, and equality forces all $\lambda _ j=1$, that is, $A=B$. Choose smooth real functions $w_ k\to w$ in $W^{2,n}$ and set $D_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ k$; such approximations are obtained by a partition of unity and convolution, and they need not preserve semipositivity. For $n=2$, Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ XD_ k^2=0$, since $D_ k^2=\mathrm{d}(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k\wedge D_ k)$. For a fixed norm-comparison constant $C_0>0$, \[  \| D_ k^2-D^2\| _{L^1} \leq C_0\| D_ k-D\| _{L^2}(\| D_ k\| _{L^2}+\| D\| _{L^2})\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $\int _ XD^2=0$, and the nonpositive integrand in ( 11.22 ) vanishes almost everywhere. By the equality case, $D=0$ almost everywhere. For $n=3$, also choose smooth functions $s_ k\to s$ in $W^{2,3}$, and put $C_ k=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s_ k$. We need the identity 11.24 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:torsion-integral} \int _ X C_ k\wedge D_ k^2 =\int _ X\omega \wedge D_ k^2 =-\int _ X\mathrm{d}w_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega . \end{equation} The first equality holds because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s_ k\wedge D_ k^2=\mathrm{d}(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s_ k\wedge D_ k^2)$. For the second equality, including its sign, put $J_ k=\mathrm{d}w_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k$. Using $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{d}=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ and $(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c})^2=0$, \[  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k=-D_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}J_ k=-D_ k^2.  \] Stokes, first for $\mathrm{d}(\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k)$ and then for $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge J_ k)$, gives \begin{align*}  \int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}J_ k& =-\int _ X\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k,\\  0& =-\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge J_ k-\int _ X\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k. \end{align*} Combining them yields ( 11.24 ). With a fixed norm-comparison constant $C_0>0$, strong $L^3$ convergence implies convergence in $L^1$ of all products of three factors. For example, \[  \| (C_ k-C)\wedge D_ k^2\| _1 \leq C_0\| C_ k-C\| _3\| D_ k\| _3^2\longrightarrow 0,  \] and \[  \| C\wedge (D_ k^2-D^2)\| _1 \leq C_0\| C\| _3\| D_ k-D\| _3(\| D_ k\| _3+\| D\| _3)\longrightarrow 0.  \] Also $\mathrm{d}w_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k\to \mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w$ in $L^{3/2}$, so the right side of ( 11.24 ) converges. Consequently 11.25 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:torsion-limit} \int _ XC\wedge D^2=-\int _ X\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \geq 0. \end{equation} The sign follows from $\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w=(\mathrm{i}/(2\pi ))\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w$ and ( 11.21 ). The integrand on the left is nonpositive by ( 11.23 ), so it vanishes almost everywhere, and the equality case, which applies where the common determinant is positive, gives $D=0$ almost everywhere. In both dimensions, therefore, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=0$ in the sense of distributions. By proposition 1.1.2 with background zero, $w$ has a plurisubharmonic representative on $X$. It attains its maximum on the compact manifold $X$, so the maximum principle and connectedness make it constant. For the $\omega $-plurisubharmonic representatives, lemma 1.3.3 upgrades the almost-everywhere equality $u=v+\text{constant}$ to equality everywhere. In particular, normalizing the means gives equality in the Sobolev class, and normalizing the suprema gives equality of the plurisubharmonic representatives. $\square$ Corollary 11.3.2 . Let $n\in \{ 2,3\} $, and let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f\geq 0$ is continuous and positive on a dense set. If $n=3$, assume ( 11.21 ); for instance, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ suffices. Then $u-v$ is constant. Proof. Put $D=A-B$ and $C=(A+B)/2$. At a point where the common top power vanishes, the algebraic expressions in the proof of 11.3.1 are still nonpositive: in dimension two $D^2=-2A\wedge B$, and in dimension three $2C\wedge D^2=-A^2\wedge B-A\wedge B^2$. The same integral identities force these continuous expressions to vanish everywhere. The equality cases give $D=0$ on $\{ f>0\} $, and density and continuity then give $D=0$ on $X$. As in the proof of the theorem, $u-v$ is then constant. $\square$ For example, on the Hopf threefold $X$ of chapter 8 , with projection $\pi :X\to \mathbb P^2$ and the semipositive form $\alpha =\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, where $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the Fubini–Study form, the Hermitian metric $\omega $ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\alpha ^2$, and hence ( 11.21 ). 11.3.1 therefore applies to this metric, even though its upper mass $v_+(\omega )$ of definition 6.5.1 is infinite by theorem 8.0.1 . The following sections return to a general Hermitian background.

title: Corollary 11.3.2
text: Corollary 11.3.2 . Let $n\in \{ 2,3\} $, and let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f\geq 0$ is continuous and positive on a dense set. title: 11.4 Bounded uniqueness and connectedness
text: 11.4 Bounded uniqueness and connectedness For a continuous density whose positive set is connected and dense, bounded solutions are unique up to a constant. An energy measure of $w=u-v$ recovers the information supplied by differentiability. Its pushforward under $w$ has a Lipschitz density vanishing at the extreme values. If $w$ were nonconstant, these properties would force both extremal sets to have zero mass for the common Monge–Ampère measure. A smooth test potential with a larger density near one of these sets then contradicts modified comparison. Theorem 11.4.1 . Let $F\in C^0(X)$ satisfy $F\geq 0$, $F\not\equiv 0$, with $U=\{ F>0\} $ connected and dense. If bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u,v$ satisfy \[  \omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n,  \] then $u-v$ is constant. In particular, $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv$ implies $u=v$. Continuity of $F$ supplies the local positive lower bounds and the neighborhoods of the extremal set used below. The auxiliary test densities are chosen smooth independently of $F$. Bounded solutions are continuous by corollary 10.4.3 , so we may use pointwise extrema throughout the proof. We shall also use modified comparison in the following form. If $b$ is continuous and $\omega _ b\geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $0<\varepsilon <1$, then $b/(1-\varepsilon )$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, so theorem 10.2.1 applies with $(1-\varepsilon )v=b$. Thus its thin-sublevel estimate applies directly to such a strictly positive comparison potential $b$, and the correction factor tends to one as the height of the sublevel set tends to zero, with $\varepsilon $ fixed. Proposition 11.4.2 . Let $u,v$ be continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions with $\omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n$, where $F\geq 0$ is bounded and measurable. Let $q$ be a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, and write $\omega _ q^ n=G\omega ^ n$. Then for every $0<\kappa <1$ and $\eta >0$, 11.26 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-localization-min} F\omega ^ n\bigl (\{ u-v<\min _ X(u-v)+\eta \} \cap \{ F>\kappa G\} \bigr )>0. \end{equation} The analogous assertion holds for the set $\{ u-v>\max _ X(u-v)-\eta \} $. Proof. Choose $\delta \in (0,1]$ with $\omega _ q\geq \delta \omega $. For $0<t<1$, put $b_ t=(1-t)v+tq$, $m_ t=\min _ X(u-b_ t)$, and $E_ s=\{ u<b_ t+m_ t+s\} $. Then $\omega _{b_ t}\geq t\delta \omega $. Write $\mu =F\omega ^ n$, $d=\kappa ^{-1/n}-1$, and $\gamma =nd$. By ( 1.23 ), \[  \omega _{b_ t}^ n\geq \bigl ((1-t)F^{1/n}+tG^{1/n}\bigr )^ n \omega ^ n.  \] On $L=\{ F\leq \kappa G\} $ this is at least $(1+\gamma t)\mu $, since $G^{1/n}\geq (1+d)F^{1/n}$ there, and on $R=\{ F>\kappa G\} $ it is at least $(1-nt)\mu $. Choose $s>0$ so small that the reverse comparison factor in ( 10.2 ), with $\varepsilon =t\delta $, is at most $1+\gamma t/2$. Modified comparison on $E_ s$, with $x=\mu (E_ s\cap L)$ and $y=\mu (E_ s\cap R)$, gives \[  (1+\gamma t)x+(1-nt)y\leq (1+\gamma t/2)(x+y), \qquad \text{and hence}\qquad y\geq \frac{1-\kappa ^{1/n}}2\, \mu (E_ s).  \] The open set $E_ s$ is nonempty by the definition of $m_ t$. As $\omega _{b_ t}^ n\geq (t\delta )^ n\omega ^ n$, ( 10.2 ) forces $\mu (E_ s)>0$, hence $y>0$. Let $a=\min _ X(u-v)$ and $\Lambda =\| v-q\| _\infty $. Since $u-b_ t=u-v+t(v-q)$, we have $|m_ t-a|\leq t\Lambda $ and $E_ s\subset \{ u-v<a+2t\Lambda +s\} $. Given $\eta $, choose $t$ and then $s$ with $2t\Lambda +s<\eta $. Since $y=\mu (E_ s\cap R)>0$, this proves ( 11.26 ). Interchanging $u$ and $v$ gives the assertion for the near-maximum set. $\square$

title: Theorem 11.4.1
text: Theorem 11.4.1 . Let $F\in C^0(X)$ satisfy $F\geq 0$, $F\not\equiv 0$, with $U=\{ F>0\} $ connected and dense. If bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u,v$ satisfy \[  \omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n,  \] then $u-v$ is constant. In particular, $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv$ implies $u=v$. of theorem 11.4.1 . By corollary 10.4.3 , $u,v$ are continuous. In dimension one, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=0$, so the maximum principle makes $w$ constant. Assume $n\geq 2$. Suppose that $w=u-v$ is nonconstant. Let $a=\min _ Xw$, $K=\{ w=a\} $, and $\mu =F\omega ^ n$. By lemma 11.4.4 , $\mu (K)=0$. Choose $B_0>\| 1\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}$ and let $\varepsilon >0$ be the constant from proposition 11.4.5 . Since $\mu (K)=0$, the compact set $K_0=K\cap \{ F\geq \varepsilon /2\} $ has zero $\omega ^ n$-volume. Fix $A>1$ with $\varepsilon A>\max _ XF$. By outer regularity of the smooth volume measure, choose an open neighborhood $O$ of $K_0$ so small that \[  \int _ X\omega ^ n+(A^2-1)\int _ O\omega ^ n<B_0^2.  \] Take a smooth $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ equal to one near $K_0$ and supported in $O$, and set $g=1+(A-1)\chi $. If $K_0=\varnothing $, take $\chi =0$. Then $g\geq 1$, $g=A$ on $K_0$, and $\| g\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}<B_0$. By proposition 11.4.5 , there is a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $q$ with $\omega _ q^ n=G\omega ^ n\geq \varepsilon g\omega ^ n$. On $K_0$ we have $G\geq \varepsilon A>F$; on $K\setminus K_0$ we have $F<\varepsilon /2<\varepsilon \leq G$. Thus $G>F$ throughout the compact set $K$. By compactness and continuity, we can choose $0<\kappa <1$ such that $F<\kappa G$ on $K$; put $W=\{ F<\kappa G\} $. The complement of this open neighborhood of $K$ is compact, and $w-a$ has a strictly positive minimum there if it is nonempty. Hence some $\eta >0$ satisfies $\{ w<a+\eta \} \subset W$. Proposition 11.4.2 asserts that $\mu (\{ w<a+\eta \} \cap \{ F>\kappa G\} )>0$. By the preceding inclusion, however, this set is empty. This contradiction shows that $w$ is constant. If $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv$, the constant is zero. $\square$

title: Proposition 11.4.2
text: Proposition 11.4.2 . Let $u,v$ be continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions with $\omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n$, where $F\geq 0$ is bounded and measurable. Let $q$ be a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, and write $\omega _ q^ n=G\omega ^ n$. Then for every $0<\kappa <1$ and $\eta >0$, 11.26 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-localization-min} F\omega ^ n\bigl (\{ u-v<\min _ X(u-v)+\eta \} \cap \{ F>\kappa G\} \bigr )>0. \end{equation} The analogous assertion holds for the set $\{ u-v>\max _ X(u-v)-\eta \} $. Proof. Choose $\delta \in (0,1]$ with $\omega _ q\geq \delta \omega $. For $0<t<1$, put $b_ t=(1-t)v+tq$, $m_ t=\min _ X(u-b_ t)$, and $E_ s=\{ u<b_ t+m_ t+s\} $. Then $\omega _{b_ t}\geq t\delta \omega $. Write $\mu =F\omega ^ n$, $d=\kappa ^{-1/n}-1$, and $\gamma =nd$. By ( 1.23 ), \[  \omega _{b_ t}^ n\geq \bigl ((1-t)F^{1/n}+tG^{1/n}\bigr )^ n \omega ^ n.  \] On $L=\{ F\leq \kappa G\} $ this is at least $(1+\gamma t)\mu $, since $G^{1/n}\geq (1+d)F^{1/n}$ there, and on $R=\{ F>\kappa G\} $ it is at least $(1-nt)\mu $. Choose $s>0$ so small that the reverse comparison factor in ( 10.2 ), with $\varepsilon =t\delta $, is at most $1+\gamma t/2$. Modified comparison on $E_ s$, with $x=\mu (E_ s\cap L)$ and $y=\mu (E_ s\cap R)$, gives \[  (1+\gamma t)x+(1-nt)y\leq (1+\gamma t/2)(x+y), \qquad \text{and hence}\qquad y\geq \frac{1-\kappa ^{1/n}}2\, \mu (E_ s).  \] The open set $E_ s$ is nonempty by the definition of $m_ t$. As $\omega _{b_ t}^ n\geq (t\delta )^ n\omega ^ n$, ( 10.2 ) forces $\mu (E_ s)>0$, hence $y>0$. Let $a=\min _ X(u-v)$ and $\Lambda =\| v-q\| _\infty $. Since $u-b_ t=u-v+t(v-q)$, we have $|m_ t-a|\leq t\Lambda $ and $E_ s\subset \{ u-v<a+2t\Lambda +s\} $. Given $\eta $, choose $t$ and then $s$ with $2t\Lambda +s<\eta $. Since $y=\mu (E_ s\cap R)>0$, this proves ( 11.26 ). Interchanging $u$ and $v$ gives the assertion for the near-maximum set. $\square$
11.26 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-localization-min} F\omega ^ n\bigl (\{ u-v<\min _ X(u-v)+\eta \} \cap \{ F>\kappa G\} \bigr )>0. \end{equation}

title: 11.4.1 The energy of the difference
text:
11.4.1 The energy of the difference In this subsection, $u,v$ are continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions with $A^ n=B^ n=F\omega ^ n$ for a bounded measurable function $F\geq 0$, and $w=u-v$. Although the cofactor $T$ is now only a current, its product with $\mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w$ still defines a positive measure. The identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$ determines how this energy is distributed over the level sets of $w$. Proposition 11.4.3 . There is a finite positive measure $E=\mathrm{d} w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge T$, defined below as a limit of regularizations, with the following properties. For every smooth real function $\chi $ on $\mathbb R$, 11.27  egin{equation} \label{eq:weak-energy-chain} \int _ X\chi ''(w)\, \mathrm{d} E=\int _ X\chi (w)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T. \end{equation} The signed current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ is a finite measure. If $a=\min _ Xw$, $b=\max _ Xw$, and \[  k(t)=\int _ X(w-t)_+\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T,  \] then $k$ is nonnegative, globally Lipschitz, supported on $[a,b]$, and 11.28  egin{equation} \label{eq:weak-energy-pushforward} w_*E=k(t)\, \mathrm{d} t. \end{equation} In particular, $E$ charges no level set of $w$. Let $V$ be a relatively compact coordinate domain such that $F$ has a positive essential lower bound on a neighborhood of $\overline V$. Then there is $C_ V<\infty $ such that every piecewise $C^1$ Lipschitz function $p$ on $[a,b]$ satisfies 11.29  egin{equation} \label{eq:weak-local-coercivity} \int _ V|\mathrm{d}(p(w))|\, \mathrm{d}\lambda \leq C_ V\left(\int _ V|p'(w)|^2\, \mathrm{d} Eight)^{1/2}, \end{equation} where $\mathrm{d}\lambda $ is Euclidean coordinate volume. Proof. Locally, expand $T$ into powers of the smooth form $\omega $ multiplied by closed Bedford–Taylor products of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. The operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ then acts only on the powers of $\omega $, and the local mass bounds in section 1.6 show that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ is a finite signed measure. We first construct $E$ and prove ( 11.27 ). On a coordinate ball, convolve $u$, $v$ and the coefficients of $\omega $ with a common nonnegative radial mollifier. Write the resulting smooth positive forms as $A_ho =\omega _ho +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ho $ and $B_ho =\omega _ho +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ho $, and let $T_ho $ be their mixed sum. On a slightly larger ball, add the same fixed multiple of $|z|^2$ to each potential to obtain plurisubharmonic functions. Their radial regularizations decrease to the originals, so Bedford–Taylor continuity applies to all closed Hessian products. Since $u,v$ are continuous, $u_ho ,v_ho ,w_ho $ converge uniformly on compact subsets. For a closed smooth product $S_ho $ appearing in $T_ho $, the identity 11.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:weak-energy-regularization} \mathrm{d} w_ho \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ho \wedge S_ho =	frac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w_ho ^2S_ho )-w_ho \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ho \wedge S_ho \end{equation} has a distributional limit: both Hessian products on the right converge weakly with uniformly bounded local variation, and their weights converge uniformly. The same holds after multiplication by the convergent smooth factors coming from $\omega _ho $. Thus the positive measures $E_ho =\mathrm{d} w_ho \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ho \wedge T_ho $ converge to a finite positive measure $E$. By ( 11.30 ), this limit does not depend on the regularization, so the local limits agree on overlapping charts. For smooth regularizations, the chain rule gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi (w_ho )\wedge T_ho =\chi ''(w_ho )E_ho +\chi '(w_ho )\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ho \wedge T_ho .  \] The last current tends to zero, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ho \wedge T_ho =A_ho ^ n-B_ho ^ n$ tends weakly to $A^ n-B^ n=0$ with uniformly bounded variation, and $\chi '(w_ho )$ converges uniformly. Passing to the limit and integrating by parts on the compact manifold $X$ gives ( 11.27 ). A partition of unity justifies this passage without a global regularization; the terms containing derivatives of the cutoff functions cancel after summation. Let $\sigma =w_*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T)$ and $
u =w_*E$. Equation ( 11.27 ) says that $
u ''=\sigma $ as distributions on $\mathbb R$. Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$ give \[  \sigma (\mathbb R)=\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0,\qquad \int _{\mathbb R}s\, \mathrm{d}\sigma (s)=\int _ Xw\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0.  \] Consequently $k(t)=\int (s-t)_+\, \mathrm{d}\sigma (s)$ is globally Lipschitz and vanishes outside $[a,b]$. It satisfies $k''=\sigma $, so the compactly supported distribution $
u -k(t)\, \mathrm{d} t$ has second derivative zero and therefore vanishes. Positivity of $
u $ and continuity of $k$ imply $k\geq 0$. This proves ( 11.28 ), and the assertion about level sets follows because $
u $ is absolutely continuous. We now prove ( 11.29 ). On a coordinate neighborhood of $\overline V$, set $ eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and choose $c_ V>0$ with $F\omega ^ n\geq c_ V eta ^ n$. Let $A_{\mathrm{ac}}$ denote the absolutely continuous part of the current $A$, whose coefficients are locally integrable functions. Applying lemma 1.7.7 with the constant function $g=c_ V^{1/n}$ and differentiating the coefficient measures, we obtain $\det _ eta A_{\mathrm{ac}}\geq c_ V$ almost everywhere. The local Sobolev regularity in section 1.6 gives $w_ho 	o w$ strongly in $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, so a subsequence of the gradients converges almost everywhere. Moreover, $A_ho 	o A_{\mathrm{ac}}$ almost everywhere, by differentiation of the coefficient measures. Since $T_ho $ contains the term $A_ho ^{n-1}$ and all its terms are positive, Fatou's lemma, applied to $E_ho $, yields the measure inequality 11.31  egin{equation} \label{eq:weak-energy-ac-lower} E\geq \mathrm{d} w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge A_{\mathrm{ac}}^{n-1}. \end{equation} The cofactor matrix of $A_{\mathrm{ac}}$ has smallest eigenvalue at least $\det A_{\mathrm{ac}}/\operatorname {tr}A_{\mathrm{ac}}\geq c_ V/\operatorname {tr}A_{\mathrm{ac}}$, where traces and determinants are taken with respect to $ eta $. The trace is locally integrable because $A$ has locally finite mass. The chain rule for Sobolev functions, ( 11.31 ) and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give \[  \int _ V|\mathrm{d}(p(w))|\, \mathrm{d}\lambda \leq C\left(\int _ V|p'(w)|^2\, \mathrm{d} Eight)^{1/2} \left(\int _ V rac{\operatorname {tr}A_{\mathrm{ac}}}{c_ V}\, \mathrm{d}\lambda ight)^{1/2}.  \] The last factor is finite and is absorbed into $C_ V$. The values of $p'$ at the finitely many corners of $p$ are immaterial, because $E$ charges no level set of $w$. $\square$ Lemma 11.4.4 . In the setting of proposition 11.4.3 , assume in addition that $F$ is continuous and that $U=\{ F>0\} $ is connected and dense. If $w=u-v$ is nonconstant, then \[  F\omega ^ n(\{ w=\min _ Xw\} )=F\omega ^ n(\{ w=\max _ Xw\} )=0.  \] Proof. Put $a=\min _ Xw<b=\max _ Xw$, and let $k$ be the function of proposition 11.4.3 . It is Lipschitz and nonnegative, and $k(a)=0$. Choose $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ with $a+\epsilon _ j<b$. For $\delta >0$, set \[  J_ j(\delta )=\int _ a^{a+\epsilon _ j} rac{\mathrm{d} t}{k(t)+\delta }.  \] If $L$ is a Lipschitz constant for $k$, then $k(t)\leq L(t-a)$ on this interval, so $J_ j(\delta )	o \infty $ as $\delta \downarrow 0$. Choose $\delta _ j>0$ with $J_ j=J_ j(\delta _ j)\geq j$. Let $p_ j=0$ on $(-\infty ,a]$, $p_ j=1$ on $[a+\epsilon _ j,\infty )$, and \[  p_ j'(t)= rac{1}{J_ j(k(t)+\delta _ j)}\quad (a<t<a+\epsilon _ j).  \] The pushforward identity ( 11.28 ) gives \[  \int _ X|p_ j'(w)|^2\, \mathrm{d} E = rac{1}{J_ j^2}\int _ a^{a+\epsilon _ j} rac{k(t)}{(k(t)+\delta _ j)^2}\, \mathrm{d} t \leq  rac1{J_ j}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Every point of $U$ has a coordinate neighborhood $V$ as in proposition 11.4.3 , since $F$ is continuous. By ( 11.29 ), therefore, $\mathrm{d}(p_ j(w))	o 0$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. The bounded functions $p_ j(w)$ converge pointwise and in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to $\mathbf1_{\{ w>a\} }$, whose distributional gradient therefore vanishes on $U$. Since $U$ is connected, this indicator function is almost everywhere constant on $U$. As $w$ is nonconstant, $\{ w>a\} $ is a nonempty open set, and its intersection with the dense open set $U$ is nonempty and open; hence the constant is one. Thus $\{ w=a\} \cap U$ has zero volume, and since $F=0$ off $U$, the first assertion follows. Applying the argument to $-w$ gives the assertion for the maximum set. $\square$

title: Lemma 11.4.4
text: Lemma 11.4.4 . In the setting of proposition 11.4.3 , assume in addition that $F$ is continuous and that $U=\{ F>0\} $ is connected and dense. If $w=u-v$ is nonconstant, then \[  F\omega ^ n(\{ w=\min _ Xw\} )=F\omega ^ n(\{ w=\max _ Xw\} )=0.  \] Proof. Put $a=\min _ Xw<b=\max _ Xw$, and let $k$ be the function of proposition 11.4.3 . It is Lipschitz and nonnegative, and $k(a)=0$. Choose $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ with $a+\epsilon _ j<b$. For $\delta >0$, set \[  J_ j(\delta )=\int _ a^{a+\epsilon _ j}\frac{\mathrm{d} t}{k(t)+\delta }.  \] If $L$ is a Lipschitz constant for $k$, then $k(t)\leq L(t-a)$ on this interval, so $J_ j(\delta )\to \infty $ as $\delta \downarrow 0$. Choose $\delta _ j>0$ with $J_ j=J_ j(\delta _ j)\geq j$. Let $p_ j=0$ on $(-\infty ,a]$, $p_ j=1$ on $[a+\epsilon _ j,\infty )$, and \[  p_ j'(t)=\frac{1}{J_ j(k(t)+\delta _ j)}\quad (a<t<a+\epsilon _ j).  \] The pushforward identity ( 11.28 ) gives \[  \int _ X|p_ j'(w)|^2\, \mathrm{d} E =\frac{1}{J_ j^2}\int _ a^{a+\epsilon _ j}\frac{k(t)}{(k(t)+\delta _ j)^2}\, \mathrm{d} t \leq \frac1{J_ j}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Every point of $U$ has a coordinate neighborhood $V$ as in proposition 11.4.3 , since $F$ is continuous. By ( 11.29 ), therefore, $\mathrm{d}(p_ j(w))\to 0$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. The bounded functions $p_ j(w)$ converge pointwise and in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to $\mathbf1_{\{ w>a\} }$, whose distributional gradient therefore vanishes on $U$. Since $U$ is connected, this indicator function is almost everywhere constant on $U$. As $w$ is nonconstant, $\{ w>a\} $ is a nonempty open set, and its intersection with the dense open set $U$ is nonempty and open; hence the constant is one. Thus $\{ w=a\} \cap U$ has zero volume, and since $F=0$ off $U$, the first assertion follows. Applying the argument to $-w$ gives the assertion for the maximum set. $\square$

title: 11.4.2 Concentrating smooth test potentials
text: 11.4.2 Concentrating smooth test potentials The next proposition produces smooth test potentials whose Monge–Ampère density dominates a fixed multiple of a prescribed function $g$, with a constant independent of $\sup _ Xg$ and of the derivatives of $g$. This uniformity allows the test densities to concentrate near a set of measure zero. Proposition 11.4.5 . For every $B_0>\| 1\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}$ there is $\varepsilon =\varepsilon (X,\omega ,B_0)>0$ such that every smooth function $g\geq 1$ with $\| g\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}\leq B_0$ admits a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $q$ satisfying 11.32 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-uniform-test-determinant} \omega _ q^ n\geq \varepsilon g \omega ^ n. \end{equation} Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ j=\{ |z_ j|<R_ j\} $, with closures in their charts, such that the concentric smaller balls $\{ |z_ j|<r_ j\} $ cover $X$. On $B_ j$, let $\psi _ j$ solve the Dirichlet problem 11.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-local-dirichlet} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j)^ n=g\omega ^ n,\qquad \psi _ j|_{\partial B_ j}=0. \end{equation} The density of $g\omega ^ n$ with respect to coordinate volume is smooth and strictly positive. The classical smooth Dirichlet theorem therefore applies, since $C_ j(|z_ j|^2-R_ j^2)$ is a smooth strict subsolution with zero boundary values for sufficiently large $C_ j>0$. Thus $\psi _ j$ is smooth and strictly plurisubharmonic on $\overline B_ j$, and the maximum principle gives $\psi _ j\leq 0$. We need a lower bound for $\psi _ j$ independent of $\sup _ Xg$. Write the coordinate equation as $\det (\partial _ a\bar\partial _ b\psi _ j)=D_ j$, and put $M_ j=-\min _{B_ j}\psi _ j$. Let $x_ j$ be a minimum point. For each real slope $p$ with $|p|<M_ j/(2R_ j)$, the function $\psi _ j-p\cdot (x-x_ j)$ attains its minimum at an interior point, because its value at $x_ j$ is $-M_ j$, while its boundary values are larger than $-M_ j$. At such a contact point the real Hessian $S$ of $\psi _ j$ is nonnegative, and the gradient of $\psi _ j$ maps the contact set onto the ball of these slopes. The area formula and the matrix inequality \[  \det _{\mathbb R}S\leq 4^ n\bigl (\det _{\mathbb C}(\partial _ a\bar\partial _ b\psi _ j)\bigr )^2=4^ nD_ j^2  \] therefore give $M_ j\leq C(n,R_ j)\| D_ j\| _{L^2(B_ j)}^{1/n}$. To prove the matrix inequality, let $J$ be the standard complex structure on the real coordinate space and average $S$ with $J^\mathsf TSJ$. Concavity of $\log \det $, and the fact that the eigenvalues of this $J$-invariant average occur in pairs, give the displayed factor; singular matrices are handled by approximation. Since the ratio of $\omega ^ n$ to coordinate volume is fixed and bounded, $\| D_ j\| _2$ is controlled by $B_0$. Consequently 11.34 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-local-uniform-sup} -M_0\leq \psi _ j\leq 0\quad \text{on every }B_ j, \end{equation} where $M_0$ depends only on $X,\omega ,B_0$ and the chosen finite cover. Next we glue the local solutions. Put $\beta _ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z_ j|^2$. Choose $a_ j>0$ such that $a_ j\beta _ j\leq \omega /2$ on $B_ j$, and let $t_ j=(R_ j^2+r_ j^2)/2$. If $0<c_0\leq F\leq C_0<\infty $ almost everywhere and bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions satisfy $\omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n$, then $u-v$ is constant. Proof. The functions $u,v$ are continuous by corollary 10.4.3 , and in dimension one the assertion follows from $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-v)=0$ and the maximum principle. The proof of lemma 11.4.4 applies with $U=X$, since proposition 11.4.3 gives the pushforward identity and local coercivity on every chart. Thus $K$ has zero volume. title: Corollary 11.4.6
text: Corollary 11.4.6 . If $0<c_0\leq F\leq C_0<\infty $ almost everywhere and bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions satisfy $\omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n$, then $u-v$ is constant. Proof. The functions $u,v$ are continuous by corollary 10.4.3 , and in dimension one the assertion follows from $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-v)=0$ and the maximum principle. Let $n\geq 2$, suppose that $w=u-v$ is nonconstant, and put $K=\{ w=\min _ Xw\} $. The proof of lemma 11.4.4 applies with $U=X$, since proposition 11.4.3 gives the pushforward identity and local coercivity on every chart. Thus $K$ has zero volume.
