title: 11.5 Comparison and invariant mass
text: 11.5 Comparison and invariant mass The preceding argument controls the extremal level sets of $u-v$ through connectedness of the set where the density is positive. When the background satisfies the Guan–Li condition below, invariance of the total mass gives the ordinary comparison principle instead. An auxiliary solution whose density is larger on a strict sublevel set of $u-v$ then forces this set to have zero mass for the common Monge–Ampère measure, and the domination principle proves uniqueness. Set $V=\int _ X\omega ^ n$. The Guan–Li condition 11.35 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0 \label{uni-eq:GL} \end{equation} is equivalent to invariance of the total mass $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)$ by lemma 2.1.2 , theorem 2.2.2 . In dimension one it holds automatically, for degree reasons. Theorem 11.5.1 . Assume ( 11.35 ), let $p>1$, and let $f\geq 0$ belong to $L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$ with positive integral. Then there is exactly one pair $(c,u)$, with $c>0$, $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $\sup _ Xu=0$, satisfying \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c f\, \omega ^ n.  \] Moreover \[  c=\frac{\int _ X\omega ^ n}{\int f\, \omega ^ n},  \] and $u$ is continuous. Thus two bounded solutions with the same $L^ p$ density differ by a constant, without any positive lower bound on $f$. We first show that the ordinary comparison principle is equivalent to invariance of the mass. Theorem 11.5.2 . Condition ( 11.35 ) holds if and only if every pair of bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $a,b$ satisfies 11.36 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:ordinaryCP} \int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (b) \leq \int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a). \end{equation} For the converse implication, it suffices to require this inequality for smooth potentials. Proof. Under ( 11.35 ), theorem 2.2.2 gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a)=V$ for every bounded potential $a$; for $n=1$ this is Stokes' theorem. Set $q=\max (a,b)$. On $\{ a<b\} $, plurifine locality gives $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q)=\mathrm{MA}_\omega (b)$. On $\{ a\geq b\} $, one has $a=q$, and $a\leq q$ everywhere, so bounded ordered contact (lemma 1.7.2 ) gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q).  \] The total masses of $a$, $b$ and $q$ all equal $V$. Hence \[  \int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (b)=V-\int _{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q) \leq V-\int _{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a)=\int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a),  \] which is ( 11.36 ). Conversely, comparison for smooth potentials implies that all smooth potentials have the same mass: given a smooth pair $a,b$, add to $b$ a constant so large that $\{ a<b\} =X$, apply ( 11.36 ), and then interchange the roles of $a$ and $b$. Comparison with the zero potential shows that the common mass is $V$. By theorem 2.2.2 , lemma 2.1.2 , this implies ( 11.35 ) when $n\geq 2$; for $n=1$ that condition holds for degree reasons. $\square$ For the uniqueness argument we need, in addition to comparison, auxiliary solutions and the mixed inequality ( 1.23 ). The auxiliary solutions come from continuous existence: if $G\geq 0$ lies in $L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$ and $\int _ XG\omega ^ n=V$, theorem 10.1.1 gives a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (\rho )=cG\omega ^ n$ with a constant $c>0$, and since all bounded potentials have mass $V$, this constant equals one. Thus 11.37 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:aux-solvability} \mathrm{MA}_\omega (\rho )=G\omega ^ n \end{equation} has a continuous solution $\rho $ for every such $G$, in particular for the density with an indicator factor used below. of 11.5.1 . We use the domination principle in the form of the case $c=0$ of theorem 10.2.2 : if $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a)(\{ a<b\} )=0$ for bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $a,b$, then $a\geq b$. We first prove that two bounded solutions $u,v$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)=\mu =F\omega ^ n$, with $F\in L^ p$, $p>1$, differ by a constant. The mass identity gives $\mu (X)=V$. If $u-v$ is nonconstant, add a constant to $u$ so that $u-v$ has supremum $s>0$ and infimum $-s$. Since $\{ v<u\} $ and $\{ u<v\} $ are disjoint, after interchanging $u$ and $v$ if necessary, the set $S=\{ v<u\} $ satisfies $\mu (S)\leq V/2$. Define \[  b_0=\frac{V-2\mu (S)}V\geq 0, \qquad G=2F\mathbf1_ S+b_0.  \] This nonnegative $L^ p$ function has total integral $V$, so we can choose a continuous solution $\rho $ of ( 11.37 ). Take $C_0$ with $\rho -C_0\leq u$, and set \[  q_\delta =(1-\delta )u+\delta (\rho -C_0),\qquad E_\delta =\{ v<q_\delta \} \subset S, \qquad 0<\delta <1.  \] Since $G\geq 2F$ on $S$, the mixed inequality ( 1.23 ) gives, on $S$, 11.38 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:mixed-bounded} \mathrm{MA}_\omega (q_\delta )\geq \bigl ((1-\delta )+\delta 2^{1/n}\bigr )^ n\mu =:A_\delta \mu , \qquad A_\delta >1. \end{equation} Ordinary comparison ( 11.36 ), applied to the pair $v,q_\delta $, yields \[  A_\delta \mu (E_\delta ) \leq \int _{E_\delta }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q_\delta ) \leq \int _{E_\delta }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)=\mu (E_\delta ).  \] Thus $\mu (E_\delta )=0$, that is, $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)(\{ v<q_\delta \} )=0$. Bounded domination gives $v\geq q_\delta $ everywhere, and letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $v\geq u$, which contradicts $\sup _ X(u-v)=s>0$. Therefore $u-v$ is constant. The argument never divides by $F$, so $F$ may vanish on an open set. Finally, for the density $f$ in the theorem, put $I=\int _ Xf\omega ^ n>0$ and $c=V/I$. By ( 11.37 ) with $G=cf$, there is a continuous solution, which we normalize by subtracting its supremum. Any other bounded solution, with constant $c'$, satisfies $V=c'I$ by mass invariance, hence $c'=c$; the uniqueness just proved and the common normalization then identify the potentials. In particular, every bounded solution with this $L^ p$ density is continuous, although continuity was not assumed. $\square$ Remark 11.5.3 . 11.5.2 is an equivalence between a differential condition, the comparison principle and mass invariance. It is not an equivalence between the Guan–Li condition and uniqueness: the other criteria in this chapter apply without that condition on the background. On the other hand, imposing the Guan–Li condition on an auxiliary metric rather than on $\omega $ does not give ( 11.36 ) for $\mathrm{MA}_\omega $.

title: 11.6 Smooth nonuniqueness for a degenerate density

text: 11.6 Smooth nonuniqueness for a degenerate density The first example places the freedom in the potential inside an open region where the density vanishes. Three independent semipositive forms of rank one reduce equality of the Monge–Ampère measures to equality of products of three scalar coefficients. We construct two semipositive forms with the same cube, and then add the same exact correction to both to obtain a strictly positive background. In this section and the following ones, $X=\mathbb P(\mathbb C^2\oplus \mathbb C^2)=\mathbb P^3$, with block homogeneous coordinates $[A:B]$, where $A,B\in \mathbb C^2$, and $\omega _ X$ is its Fubini–Study form. Here $A$ and $B$ denote coordinates, not the forms of ( 11.1 ); the two solution forms will be written $A_0$ and $B_0$. Theorem 11.6.1 . On $X=\mathbb P^3$ there exist a smooth Hermitian form $\omega $ with $\mathrm{d}\omega \ne 0$, a smooth nonnegative nonzero function $f$, and distinct smooth functions $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ such that \[  \sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv=0,\qquad (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=f\omega _ X^3=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^3.  \] The density vanishes on a nonempty open set, and both potentials have minimal singularities.

title: Theorem 11.6.1
text: Theorem 11.6.1 . On $X=\mathbb P^3$ there exist a smooth Hermitian form $\omega $ with $\mathrm{d}\omega \ne 0$, a smooth nonnegative nonzero function $f$, and distinct smooth functions $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ such that \[  \sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv=0,\qquad (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=f\omega _ X^3=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^3.  \] The density vanishes on a nonempty open set, and both potentials have minimal singularities. of theorem 11.6.1 . Set $\widetilde u=-w/2-\rho $ and $\widetilde v=w/2-\rho $. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=2H$, the construction gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u=A_0\geq 0,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v=B_0\geq 0.  \] Subtracting their respective suprema gives $u,v$. Their Hessians are unchanged, and $v-u=w+\text{constant}$ is nonconstant. The function $f=A_0^3/\omega _ X^3=B_0^3/\omega _ X^3$ is smooth, nonnegative and nonzero, and it vanishes on the nonempty open band $|r|<1$. Both potentials are smooth, hence bounded, so they have minimal singularities: for a Hermitian background, the envelope $V_\omega $ of section 1.19 is zero. $\square$

title: 11.6.1 Three rank-one directions
text: 11.6.1 Three rank-one directions On $U=\{ A\ne 0,B\ne 0\} $ put \[  r=\log \frac{|A|^2}{|B|^2},\qquad P=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |A|^2,\quad Q=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |B|^2,\quad R=\mathrm{d}r\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r.  \] The logarithms are computed in a local homogeneous lift, but their Hessians do not depend on the lift. The forms $P,Q$ are pullbacks of Fubini–Study forms from the two projective lines $\mathbb P(\mathbb C^2)$. All three forms are semipositive of rank one, and 11.39 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-rank-frame} P^2=Q^2=R^2=0,\qquad P\wedge Q\wedge R>0. \end{equation} Indeed, in local coordinates $A=(1,a)$ and $B=\tau (1,b)$, $P$ and $Q$ are positive multiples of $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}a\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar a$ and $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}b\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar b$, while \[  \partial r=\frac{\bar a\, \mathrm{d}a}{1+|a|^2} -\frac{\mathrm{d}\tau }{\tau } -\frac{\bar b\, \mathrm{d}b}{1+|b|^2}.  \] Its $\mathrm{d}\tau $ component is nonzero, so the three rank-one forms correspond to independent directions. In particular, for nonnegative $x,y,z$, 11.40 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-cube} (xP+yQ+zR)^3=6xyz\, P\wedge Q\wedge R, \end{equation} and the form is positive exactly when all three coefficients are positive. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=P-Q$, the chain rule gives, for a smooth function $G:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$, 11.41 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-chain} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G(r)=G'(r)(P-Q)+G''(r)R. \end{equation} Let $\sigma (r)=\mathrm{e}^ r/(1+\mathrm{e}^ r)$. Since $\log (|A|^2+|B|^2)=\log |B|^2+\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ r)$, we have 11.42 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-fs} \omega _ X=\sigma (r)P+\sigma (-r)Q+\sigma '(r)R. \end{equation} A function of $r$ that is constant near each end of $\mathbb R$ extends smoothly across $X\setminus U$. A form $xP+yQ+zR$ whose coefficients equal those of ( 11.42 ) for $|r|\geq 2$ extends smoothly by $\omega _ X$ across $X\setminus U$.

title: 11.6.2 The scalar coefficients
text: 11.6.2 The scalar coefficients On the central interval $-1\leq r\leq 1$, the coefficients will make a different rank-one factor vanish in each of the two solution forms. Outside a larger interval they coincide with the Fubini–Study coefficients, so the resulting forms extend across the omitted projective lines. Primes denote derivatives with respect to $r$. Choose an even smooth function $\beta $ supported in $[-1,1]$, strictly positive on $(-1,1)$, with $\beta '>0$ on $(-1,0)$, and normalized by $\int _{-1}^1\beta =2$; for instance, a positive multiple of $\exp (-1/(1-r^2))$ on $(-1,1)$, extended by zero. Define \[  F(r)=-1+\int _{-1}^ r\beta (t)\, \mathrm{d}t\quad (-1<r<1), \qquad F=-1\  (r\leq -1),\quad F=1\  (r\geq 1),  \] and put $p=\beta /2$, $q=\beta '/2$. Then $F$ is smooth and odd, $p$ is even, and $q$ is odd, positive on $(-1,0)$ and negative on $(0,1)$. Both $p$ and $q$ vanish to infinite order at the endpoints. Take smooth $a\geq 0$ with $a=1$ on $(-\infty ,-2/3]$ and $a=0$ on $[-1/3,\infty )$, and put $b(r)=a(-r)$. Choose an even nonnegative $\chi \in C_ c^\infty ((-1/3,1/3))$ with $\chi (0)>0$. On $[-1,1]$ set \[  z_0=(q^2+\chi ^2)^{1/2}.  \] It is smooth: the expression under the square root is positive in the interior, and near each endpoint $z_0=|q|$, where $q$ has a fixed sign. It is positive in the interior and vanishes to infinite order at the endpoints. Also, 11.43 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-coefficient-cancellation} z_0\geq |q|,\qquad a(z_0-q)=0,\qquad b(z_0+q)=0. \end{equation} The first cancellation holds because $\chi =0$ on the support of $a$ and $q\geq 0$ there; the second follows by reflection. On $(-\infty ,-1]$ choose smooth functions $\ell ,s$ such that $0\leq \ell \leq 1$, $\ell =0$ on $(-\infty ,-2]$, $\ell =1$ on $[-3/2,-1]$, while $s>0$ for $r<-1$, $s=1$ on $(-\infty ,-3/2]$, and $s$ vanishes to infinite order at $-1$. Such functions are easily obtained from smooth cutoff functions and a function like $\exp (-1/(r+1)^2)$. Define \[  \begin{aligned}  x& =(1-\ell )\sigma +\ell ,&  y& =(1-\ell )\sigma (-r)+\ell s,&  z& =(1-\ell )\sigma '+\ell s & & (r\leq -1),\\  x& =p+a,&  y& =p+b,&  z& =z_0 & & (-1\leq r\leq 1), \end{aligned}  \] and for $r\geq 1$ use $x(r)=y(-r)$, $y(r)=x(-r)$, $z(r)=z(-r)$. The definitions join smoothly: at $-1$ both definitions give the values $(1,0,0)$, and their differences vanish to infinite order there, since $a=1$ and $b=0$ near $-1$. The central definitions are symmetric under reflection, so the same holds at $1$. We have \[  x,y,z>0\quad \hbox{for }r\ne \pm 1,\qquad (x,y,z)(-1)=(1,0,0),\quad (x,y,z)(1)=(0,1,0).  \] For $|r|\geq 2$ their values are $(\sigma (r),\sigma (-r),\sigma '(r))$.
11.43 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-coefficient-cancellation} z_0\geq |q|,\qquad a(z_0-q)=0,\qquad b(z_0+q)=0. \end{equation}

title: 11.6.3 Two forms with the same cube
search_title: Two forms with the same cube
text: 11.6.3 Two forms with the same cube The cancellation identities now turn the scalar coefficients into two semipositive forms with the same cube. Their average is strictly positive except at the two ends of the central interval. By the extensions described above, the form and the function \[  \omega _0=x(r)P+y(r)Q+z(r)R,\qquad w=F(r)  \] are smooth on $X$. The form is semipositive, and positive except on the hypersurfaces $M_- =\{ r=-1\} $ and $M_+=\{ r=1\} $. Put \[  H=\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=p(P-Q)+qR,\qquad A_0=\omega _0-H,\quad B_0=\omega _0+H.  \] For $|r|\geq 1$ we have $H=0$. On $|r|<1$, \[  A_0=aP+(2p+b)Q+(z_0-q)R,\qquad B_0=(2p+a)P+bQ+(z_0+q)R.  \] All coefficients are nonnegative, and by ( 11.40 ) and ( 11.43 ), $A_0^3=B_0^3=0$ on this band. Outside it both cubes equal $\omega _0^3$. Thus $A_0,B_0$ are smooth semipositive forms on $X$ with equal cubes. This common top-degree form vanishes on the closed band $|r|\leq 1$ and is positive on its complement, including near $X\setminus U$.

title: 11.6.4 Restoring strict positivity of the background
search_title: Restoring strict positivity of the background
text: 11.6.4 Restoring strict positivity of the background The forms $A_0,B_0$ already have the required common measure. We obtain a Hermitian background by adding an exact correction $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ to their average $\omega _0$ and subtracting $\rho $ from both potentials. The correction must restore positivity at $M_\pm $ while preserving it in the transition regions. Take $\kappa \in C_ c^\infty ((-2,2))$, equal to one on $[-3/2,3/2]$. For a parameter $\varepsilon >0$ to be chosen, set \[  \rho (r)=\varepsilon (r^2-1)\kappa (r),\qquad \omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho .  \] By ( 11.41 ), its coefficients on $U$ are $x+\rho '$, $y-\rho '$ and $z+\rho ''$. On $[-3/2,3/2]$ one has $\rho '=2\varepsilon r$ and $\rho ''=2\varepsilon $, so the last coefficient is positive there. For $r\geq 0$, $x+2\varepsilon r$ is positive, including at $r=0$ since $x(0)=p(0)>0$. On $[-3/2,0]$, the function $x$ has a positive minimum $m$, so $x+2\varepsilon r\geq m-3\varepsilon >0$ for small $\varepsilon $. Reflection gives the corresponding estimate for $y-2\varepsilon r$. On the compact region $3/2\leq |r|\leq 2$, all three original coefficients have a positive minimum and the perturbations are $O(\varepsilon )$. For $|r|\geq 2$ and near $X\setminus U$, the form is exactly $\omega _ X$. Hence $\omega $ is strictly positive on $X$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. The form $\omega $ is not closed. Indeed, since $\mathrm{d}R=-\mathrm{d}r\wedge (P-Q)$, 11.46 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-differential} \mathrm{d}\omega =\mathrm{d}\omega _0 =\mathrm{d}r\wedge \bigl ((x'-z)P+(y'+z)Q\bigr ). \end{equation} At $r=0$, $x'=y'=0$ and $z=\chi (0)>0$. Hence $\mathrm{d}\omega =z\, \mathrm{d}r\wedge (Q-P)\ne 0$ there. The nonzero $\mathrm{d}\tau $ component used in ( 11.39 ) also shows that $\mathrm{d}r\wedge P$ and $\mathrm{d}r\wedge Q$ are linearly independent. of theorem 11.6.1 . Set $\widetilde u=-w/2-\rho $ and $\widetilde v=w/2-\rho $. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=2H$, the construction gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u=A_0\geq 0,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v=B_0\geq 0.  \] Subtracting their respective suprema gives $u,v$. Their Hessians are unchanged, and $v-u=w+\text{constant}$ is nonconstant. The function $f=A_0^3/\omega _ X^3=B_0^3/\omega _ X^3$ is smooth, nonnegative and nonzero, and it vanishes on the nonempty open band $|r|<1$. Both potentials are smooth, hence bounded, so they have minimal singularities: for a Hermitian background, the envelope $V_\omega $ of section 1.19 is zero. $\square$ Every Hermitian background on $\mathbb P^3$ has the bounded mass property of definition 6.5.1 : since the Fubini–Study form is closed, Stokes' theorem for bounded potentials shows that all its bounded potentials have the same mass, and proposition 6.5.2 shows that the property does not depend on the metric. This applies to all the backgrounds on $\mathbb P^3$ constructed below. The linearized equation also explains why the maximum principle argument fails. The form \[  T=A_0^2+A_0\wedge B_0+B_0^2  \] satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=B_0^3-A_0^3=0$, but $T=0$ on $M_\pm $, where $A_0=B_0=\omega _0$ has rank one. Thus the linear equation for $w$ is not elliptic everywhere, even though both potentials and their common density are smooth.
11.46 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-differential} \mathrm{d}\omega =\mathrm{d}\omega _0 =\mathrm{d}r\wedge \bigl ((x'-z)P+(y'+z)Q\bigr ). \end{equation}

title: 11.6.5 A continuum of radial solutions
text: 11.6.5 A continuum of radial solutions The open band where the density vanishes allows more solutions than the two smooth ones constructed above. Writing a further potential as $G(r)-\rho $, with $G$ a function of one real variable, reduces the equation on the band to choosing the slope $G'$ so that one of the three coefficients vanishes. Switching the vanishing coefficient at two suitable levels produces a continuum of $C^{1,1}$ solutions for the same background $\omega $ and density $f$. Recall that $q=p'$ and $z_0\geq |q|$. The strict inequality $z_0>|p'|$ near zero, where $\chi >0$, gives 11.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-half-excess} \int _0^1z_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r>\int _0^1|p'(r)|\, \mathrm{d}r=p(0). \end{equation} Proposition 11.6.2 . For the smooth background $\omega $ and the smooth density $f$ of theorem 11.6.1 , the equation \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=f\omega _ X^3  \] has uncountably many distinct $C^{1,1}$ solutions normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. If the cutoff $\kappa $ defining $\rho $ is chosen even, one of them, constructed explicitly, is invariant under the block exchange $\iota [A:B]=[B:A]$. Proof. Consider pairs $-1<I<0<J<1$ satisfying 11.48 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-transition-balance} \int _ I^ J z_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r=p(I)+p(J). \end{equation} We first show that such pairs exist, with $I$ ranging over an interval. Define \[  K(I,J)=\int _ I^ Jz_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r-p(I)-p(J).  \] We have $K(0,0)=-2p(0)<0$ and $K(0,1)>0$ by ( 11.47 ). By continuity, there is $\epsilon >0$ such that $K(I,0)<0<K(I,1)$ for every $I\in [-\epsilon ,0]$. For $0<J<1$, \[  \partial _ JK(I,J)=z_0(J)-p'(J)>0.  \] The intermediate value theorem therefore gives a unique $J=J(I)\in (0,1)$ satisfying ( 11.48 ) for every $I\in [-\epsilon ,0)$; we may assume $\epsilon <1$. For any pair satisfying ( 11.48 ), define the slope on $[-1,1]$ by \[  h_{I,J}(r)= \begin{cases}  p(r),& -1\leq r\leq I,\\  p(I)-\displaystyle \int _ I^ r z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s,& I\leq r\leq J,\\  -p(r),& J\leq r\leq 1, \end{cases}  \] and extend it by zero outside that interval. The balance identity makes it continuous at $J$, and continuity at $I$ is immediate. Each piece has bounded derivative, so $h_{I,J}$ is Lipschitz on $\mathbb R$; it vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. Let $G_{I,J}$ be a primitive of $h_{I,J}$. It is $C^{1,1}$ and constant near each end of the real line. Consequently $G_{I,J}(r)$ extends to a $C^{1,1}$ function on $X$ that is smooth near $X\setminus U$. On the middle interval $[I,J]$ the slope lies between $-p$ and $p$. Indeed, \[  (h_{I,J}-p)'=-z_0-p'\leq 0, \qquad (h_{I,J}+p)'=-z_0+p'\leq 0.  \] The first difference vanishes at $I$, and the second vanishes at $J$. Since both are nonincreasing, $h_{I,J}\leq p$ and $h_{I,J}\geq -p$ on $[I,J]$. Put $\widetilde u_{I,J}=G_{I,J}(r)-\rho $. By ( 11.41 ), almost everywhere on $U$, 11.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-slope-form} \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_{I,J} =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_{I,J}(r) =(x+h_{I,J})P+(y-h_{I,J})Q+(z+h_{I,J}')R. \end{equation} On $I<r<J$, the first two coefficients are nonnegative because $x=p+a$, $y=p+b$ and $-p\leq h_{I,J}\leq p$, and the third is zero. On $-1<r<I$, we have $h_{I,J}=p$ and $b=0$, since $I<0$; so the second coefficient is zero, and the others are nonnegative because $z_0+p'\geq 0$. On $J<r<1$, we have $h_{I,J}=-p$ and $a=0$; so the first coefficient is zero, and the others are nonnegative because $z_0-p'\geq 0$. Outside the band, $h_{I,J}=h_{I,J}'=0$, so the form equals $\omega _0$. Formula ( 11.52 ) has no additional term supported on the hypersurfaces $r=I$ and $r=J$: the function $G_{I,J}$ is $C^{1,1}$, so its first derivative is continuous at both transition points, and its distributional Hessian is its bounded almost-everywhere Hessian. The preceding coefficient inequalities therefore prove $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_{I,J}\geq 0$ as a current. By proposition 1.7.4 , its Monge–Ampère measure is the pointwise cube of ( 11.52 ), computed almost everywhere. By the rank-one identities ( 11.39 ) and ( 11.40 ), this cube is zero almost everywhere on the band, since one coefficient vanishes there, and it equals $\omega _0^3$ off the band. These are exactly the values of $f\omega _ X^3$ in the preceding construction. Thus $\widetilde u_{I,J}$ solves the equation, and subtracting its supremum gives a normalized solution $u_{I,J}$. Different values of $I\in [-\epsilon ,0)$ give different normalized solutions. If $I_1<I_2<0$ and $I_1<r<I_2$, then the slope belonging to $I_2$ is $p(r)$, whereas \[  p(r)-h_{I_1,J(I_1)}(r) =\int _{I_1}^ r(p'(s)+z_0(s))\, \mathrm{d}s>0,  \] because $p'>0$ on $(-1,0)$. The two primitives therefore do not differ by a constant. Since the interval $[-\epsilon ,0)$ is uncountable, this proves the first assertion. None of these slopes equals $p$ or $-p$ on all of $(-1,1)$, so the constructed solutions are also distinct from the two smooth solutions of theorem 11.6.1 . Finally, the function \[  L(t)=\int _0^ t z_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r-p(t),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1,  \] is negative at zero, positive at one, and strictly increasing on $(0,1)$. Its unique zero $t_*$ gives a symmetric pair $I=-t_*$, $J=t_*$ satisfying ( 11.48 ). Since $z_0$ and $p$ are even, $h_{I,J}$ is odd: on the middle interval it equals $-\int _0^ r z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$. Choose its primitive even. Since $\iota $ changes $r$ into $-r$, if $\rho $ is even, the potential $G_{I,J}(r)-\rho $ and its normalization are fixed by $\iota $. This proves the last assertion. $\square$ For these symmetric data, the normalized solutions of the equations with a positive exponent converge, as the exponent tends to zero, to the symmetric solution just constructed; see theorem 14.19.3 .
11.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-half-excess} \int _0^1z_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r>\int _0^1|p'(r)|\, \mathrm{d}r=p(0). \end{equation}

title: 11.7 Nonuniqueness with a zero set of empty interior
search_title: Nonuniqueness with a zero set of empty interior
text: 11.7 Nonuniqueness with a zero set of empty interior We now keep the Hermitian background of theorem 11.6.1 , but change the density so that it is positive off $M_-\cup M_+$, where $M_\pm =\{ r=\pm 1\} $. For potentials of the form $G(r)-\rho $, the equation on the middle band becomes a first-order ordinary differential equation for the slope $G'$. Barriers keep its solutions between the admissible slopes, and infinite-order vanishing at the endpoints then makes their extensions by zero smooth. Theorem 11.7.1 . There are a smooth nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ on $\mathbb P^3$ and a smooth nonnegative density $g$, positive off two disjoint smooth real hypersurfaces, such that the equation \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=g\omega _ X^3  \] has uncountably many distinct smooth solutions normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. The background $\omega $ has bounded mass. Thus a zero set with empty interior, even one of measure zero, does not ensure uniqueness of smooth normalized solutions. We use the coefficients of 11.6.2 , with the explicit choice \[  p(r)=C\exp \! \left(-\frac1{1-r^2}\right),\qquad -1<r<1, \qquad \int _{-1}^1p(r)\, \mathrm{d}r=1,  \] extended by zero, where the integral condition determines $C>0$; then $q=p'$. Fix $0<s<1$, and set \[  k_ s(r)=(x(r)+sp(r))(y(r)-sp(r))(z(r)+sq(r)).  \] For $|r|>1$ this is $xyz$. If $G'=sp$, then the potential $G(r)-\rho $ has $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(G(r)-\rho )=\omega _0+sH$. This form is strictly positive for $-1<r<1$, since \[  x+sp=a+(1+s)p>0,\quad y-sp=b+(1-s)p>0,\quad z_0+sq\geq (1-s)z_0>0.  \] It is also strictly positive outside the closed band, and at $r=\pm 1$ it equals the rank-one form $\omega _0$. Consequently 11.53 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-thin-density} g\omega _ X^3=(\omega _0+sH)^3 \end{equation} defines a smooth density $g$ that is positive exactly off $M_-\cup M_+$. These hypersurfaces have measure zero and empty interior. On the band $|r|<1$, a potential $G(r)-\rho $ with slope $h=G'$ solves the equation exactly when $(x+h)(y-h)(z+h')=k_ s$, which is the differential equation ( 11.54 ) below. Lemma 11.7.2 . There exists $\eta _0>0$ such that for every $0<\eta <\eta _0$ the initial-value problem 11.54 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-thin-ode} h'=\frac{k_ s(r)}{(x(r)+h)(y(r)-h)}-z(r), \qquad h(0)=sp(0)-\eta , \end{equation} has a smooth solution on $(-1,1)$ with $-x<h<y$ and $h<sp$. Moreover, on some fixed endpoint neighborhoods there are constants $0<c_ L<s<t<1$, independent of $\eta $, such that \[  c_ Lp<h<sp\quad \hbox{near }-1, \qquad -tp<h<sp\quad \hbox{near }1.  \] Proof. The function $h_ s=sp$ solves ( 11.54 ) and lies strictly between $-x$ and $y$ throughout $(-1,1)$. Write $F_ s(r,h)$ for the right-hand side of the equation, which is smooth on the open domain $-x(r)<h<y(r)$. Near $-1$ the coefficients are exactly \[  x=1+p,\qquad y=p,\qquad z=q>0.  \] For a constant $c\in (-1,1)$, the product of coefficients for the trial slope $cp$ is \[  k_ c=(1-c^2)\bigl (1+(1+c)p\bigr )pq.  \] Fix $c_ L\in (0,s)$. At $p=0$, the factor preceding $pq$ for $c=c_ L$ exceeds that for $c=s$ by $s^2-c_ L^2>0$. Thus, on a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood of the left endpoint, $k_{c_ L}>k_ s$ and 11.55 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-left-trap} F_ s(r,c_ Lp)-(c_ Lp)'= \frac{k_ s-k_{c_ L}}{(x+c_ Lp)(y-c_ Lp)}<0. \end{equation} Thus $c_ Lp$ is a lower barrier when the equation is solved backward, that is, toward $-1$. Near $1$ the exact coefficients are \[  x=p,\qquad y=1+p,\qquad z=-q>0,  \] and the trial slope $cp$ has product of coefficients \[  k_ c=(1-c^2)\bigl (1+(1-c)p\bigr )p(-q).  \] Fix $s<t<1$. At $p=0$, the factor for $c=s$ exceeds that for $c=-t$ by $t^2-s^2>0$. On a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood of the right endpoint, therefore, $k_ s>k_{-t}$, so 11.56 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-right-trap} F_ s(r,-tp)-(-tp)'= \frac{k_ s-k_{-t}}{(x-tp)(y+tp)}>0. \end{equation} Thus $-tp$ is a lower barrier when the equation is solved forward, toward $1$. Choose $r_ L<0<r_ R$ in these respective neighborhoods. The graph of $h_ s$ over $[r_ L,r_ R]$ is a compact subset of the domain of $F_ s$. Existence and continuous dependence on initial values for smooth ordinary differential equations therefore give $\eta _0>0$ such that, for every $0<\eta <\eta _0$, the solution with initial value $sp(0)-\eta $ exists on $[r_ L,r_ R]$, stays in the domain, and satisfies \[  h(r_ L)>c_ Lp(r_ L),\qquad h(r_ R)>-tp(r_ R).  \] By local uniqueness, two solutions of the equation cannot cross. Since $h(0)<h_ s(0)$, we have $h<h_ s$ wherever $h$ exists. Follow the solution backwards from $r_ L$; it cannot cross $c_ Lp$. Indeed, at a first crossing point the difference $h-c_ Lp$ would vanish and be positive immediately to its right, so its derivative there would be nonnegative, whereas ( 11.55 ) shows that this derivative is strictly negative. Thus $c_ Lp<h<sp$ on the part of the interval of existence to the left of $r_ L$. Likewise, ( 11.56 ) prevents a first downward crossing of $-tp$ to the right of $r_ R$, giving $-tp<h<sp$ there. These bounds also show that the maximal interval of existence is all of $(-1,1)$. Indeed, near a possible endpoint inside $(-1,1)$, the factors $x+h$ and $y-h$ stay bounded away from zero, so the graph of $h$ stays in a compact subset of the domain of $F_ s$, and the continuation theorem for ordinary differential equations extends the solution beyond that endpoint. Hence the solution exists on $(-1,1)$ and satisfies the claimed bounds. $\square$ Lemma 11.7.3 . Every solution furnished by lemma 11.7.2 , extended by zero outside $(-1,1)$, is smooth on $\mathbb R$ and vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. Proof. Let $h$ be one of the solutions in lemma 11.7.2 . On either endpoint neighborhood put $\xi =h/p$; since $p>0$ on $(-1,1)$, this quotient is smooth there, and the trapping bounds place $\xi $ in a fixed compact subinterval of $(-1,1)$. Define the rational functions \[  R_ L(p,\xi )= \frac{(1-s^2)(1+(1+s)p)}{(1+(1+\xi )p)(1-\xi )}-1,  \] \[  R_ R(p,\xi )=1- \frac{(1-s^2)(1+(1-s)p)}{(1+\xi )(1+(1-\xi )p)}.  \] The explicit formulas for the coefficients near the endpoints give \[  h'=q\, R_ L(p,\xi )\quad \hbox{on the left},\qquad h'=q\, R_ R(p,\xi )\quad \hbox{on the right}.  \] Both rational functions are smooth, with all derivatives bounded, on a neighborhood of the relevant set of pairs $(p,\xi )$ with $p\geq 0$ small and $\xi $ in the compact interval above. Writing $R_{L/R}$ for the function corresponding to the endpoint under consideration, we obtain from $h'=p'\xi +p\xi '$ and $q=p'$ 11.57 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-scaled-ode} \xi '=\frac{p'}p\bigl (R_{L/R}(p,\xi )-\xi \bigr ). \end{equation} For the chosen bump, \[  \frac{p'}p=-\frac{2r}{(1-r^2)^2}.  \] This rational function and each of its derivatives grow at most like a power of the inverse distance to the endpoint. Moreover, each derivative of $p$ is $p$ times a rational function with the same property. An induction using ( 11.57 ) shows that every derivative $\xi ^{(j)}$ grows at most polynomially in the inverse distance to the endpoint. The case $j=0$ is the trapping bound on $\xi $. For the induction step, differentiate the right-hand side of ( 11.57 ), including its term $-\xi $, $j$ times. Every resulting term is a product of a derivative of $p'/p$, a bounded partial derivative of $R_{L/R}$, and derivatives of $p$ and of $\xi $ of order at most $j$. All of these factors have polynomial bounds, by the induction hypothesis for the derivatives of $\xi $ and since every derivative of $p$ is bounded. This gives the bound for $\xi ^{(j+1)}$. Leibniz' rule for $h=p\xi $ now gives, for each $j$, constants $C_ j,N_ j$ such that \[  |h^{(j)}(r)|\leq C_ j p(r)(1-|r|)^{-N_ j}  \] near the endpoints. The right-hand side tends to zero at the endpoints, because $p$ decays exponentially in the inverse distance to the endpoint. Thus all derivatives of $h$ tend to zero at $\pm 1$. Extend each derivative by zero outside $(-1,1)$. By the mean value theorem, the difference quotient of $h^{(j)}$ at an endpoint tends to the limit of $h^{(j+1)}$, which is zero. Hence these extensions are the successive derivatives of the extension of $h$, which is therefore smooth and vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. $\square$ of theorem 11.7.1 . Let $\eta _0$ be as in lemma 11.7.2 , and for $0<\eta <\eta _0$ denote by $h_\eta $ the solution with initial value $sp(0)-\eta $. Extend $h_\eta $ by zero, which gives a smooth function by the preceding lemma, and take a primitive $G_\eta $. It is constant near each end of the real line, so $G_\eta (r)$ extends smoothly to all of $\mathbb P^3$, including the two omitted projective lines. Set \[  \widetilde u_\eta =G_\eta (r)-\rho .  \] On the open band, \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_\eta =(x+h_\eta )P+(y-h_\eta )Q+(z+h_\eta ')R.  \] The coefficients of $P$ and $Q$ are strictly positive by lemma 11.7.2 , while the equation gives \[  z+h_\eta '=\frac{k_ s}{(x+h_\eta )(y-h_\eta )}>0.  \] Outside the band the form is $\omega _0$, and on the two boundary hypersurfaces it is also the rank-one form $\omega _0$, since $h_\eta $ vanishes to infinite order there. It is therefore semipositive on $X$, and by ( 11.40 ) its cube equals $6k_ sP\wedge Q\wedge R=(\omega _0+sH)^3$ on the band and $\omega _0^3=(\omega _0+sH)^3$ elsewhere. Thus its cube is everywhere the measure $g\omega _ X^3$ of ( 11.53 ). Finally, normalize by subtracting $\sup _ X\widetilde u_\eta $. Distinct values of $\eta $ give different slopes at $r=0$, so the corresponding potentials do not differ by a constant, and their normalized versions are distinct. This gives an uncountable family. The background is that of theorem 11.6.1 , so it has bounded mass. $\square$ The density vanishes to infinite order on the two hypersurfaces. Their complement has three components, and on each of the two outer components, two different solutions differ by a constant, with different constants on the two components. The differential equation on the middle component joins these constants smoothly across the degenerate hypersurfaces. This is why ellipticity at every point of the positive-density set does not give a maximum principle argument across its boundary.

11.53 \begin{equation} \label{eq:numa-thin-density} g\omega _ X^3=(\omega _0+sH)^3 \end{equation}

title: Lemma 11.7.3
text: Lemma 11.7.3 . Every solution furnished by lemma 11.7.2 , extended by zero outside $(-1,1)$, is smooth on $\mathbb R$ and vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. Proof. Let $h$ be one of the solutions in lemma 11.7.2 . On either endpoint neighborhood put $\xi =h/p$; since $p>0$ on $(-1,1)$, this quotient is smooth there, and the trapping bounds place $\xi $ in a fixed compact subinterval of $(-1,1)$. For the induction step, differentiate the right-hand side of ( 11.57 ), including its term $-\xi $, $j$ times. title: 11.8 Quadratic density zeros
text: 11.8 Quadratic density zeros Infinite-order vanishing of the density is not needed for smooth nonuniqueness. We change the coefficients of $\omega _0$ so that its coefficient of $R$ stays positive and one of its coefficients of $P$ and $Q$ vanishes quadratically at each of the two hypersurfaces $M_\pm $. The resulting singular differential equation forces the slopes of differences of solutions to decay like $\exp (-A/d)$, where $d$ is the distance to the hypersurface and $A>0$. The slopes therefore extend smoothly by zero, even though the density vanishes only to finite order. Theorem 11.8.1 . On $\mathbb P^3$ there exist a smooth nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ and a smooth nonnegative density $g$ such that: The zero set of $g$ consists of two disjoint smooth real hypersurfaces. Near either hypersurface, $g$ is the square of a smooth defining function times a smooth strictly positive function. The equation $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=g\omega _ X^3$ has uncountably many distinct smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solutions normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. The background $\omega $ has bounded mass. We keep the rank-one forms $P,Q,R$ and the function $r$ of 11.6.1 , and use new scalar coefficients. Choose a smooth function $a$ valued in $[0,1]$, equal to one for $r\leq -2/3$ and zero for $r\geq -1/3$, and put $b(r)=a(-r)$. Choose a smooth even cutoff $\chi $ valued in $[0,1]$, zero for $|r|\leq 5/4$ and one for $|r|\geq 3/2$. Set $p(r)=(1-r^2)^2$ and 11.58 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-background} \begin{split}  x& =(1-\chi )(p+a)+\chi \sigma ,\\  y& =(1-\chi )(p+b)+\chi (1-\sigma ),\\  z& =1-\chi +\chi \sigma ',\qquad \omega _0=xP+yQ+zR. \end{split} \end{equation} Since these coefficients coincide with those of ( 11.42 ) for $|r|\geq 3/2$, the form $\omega _0$ extends by $\omega _ X$ across the two omitted projective lines. The coefficient $z$ is strictly positive, and $x,y$ are strictly positive except that $y(-1)=0$ and $x(1)=0$. Thus $\omega _0$ is positive off $M_\pm =\{ r=\pm 1\} $ and has rank two there. Choose a smooth cutoff $\kappa \in C_ c^\infty ((-2,2))$ equal to one on $[-3/2,3/2]$. For a parameter $\varepsilon >0$ to be chosen, define the correction \[  \rho =\varepsilon (r^2-1)\kappa (r),\qquad \omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho .  \] For sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, the form $\omega $ is strictly positive. Indeed, on $[-3/2,3/2]$ its coefficients are $x+2\varepsilon r$, $y-2\varepsilon r$ and $z+2\varepsilon $. The first is positive for $r\geq 0$, and on $[-3/2,0]$ the function $x$ has a positive minimum, so it remains positive for small $\varepsilon $. Reflection gives the positivity of the second coefficient, and that of the third is immediate. On $3/2\leq |r|\leq 2$, the form $\omega _0$ is strictly positive on a compact set and the correction is $O(\varepsilon )$. Near the projective ends there is no correction. The form $\omega $ is not closed: at $r=0$, $x'=y'=0$ and $z=1$, so by ( 11.46 ) \[  \mathrm{d}\omega =\mathrm{d}r\wedge \bigl ((x'-z)P+(y'+z)Q\bigr )\ne 0.  \] Define the density $g$ by \[  g\omega _ X^3=\omega _0^3.  \] It is smooth and positive exactly off $M_-\cup M_+$. By ( 11.42 ) and ( 11.40 ), $g=xyz/(\sigma (r)(1-\sigma (r))\sigma '(r))$. Near either hypersurface, $xyz=(1+p)p$, and hence \[  g(r)=\frac{(1+p(r))(1-r^2)^2}{\sigma (r)(1-\sigma (r))\sigma '(r)}.  \] The denominator is smooth and strictly positive at $\pm 1$, and $1-r^2$ is a defining function for $M_\pm $ near these hypersurfaces. This proves the asserted quadratic vanishing. The potential $-\rho $ is one smooth solution. Lemma 11.8.2 . For every sufficiently small $\eta >0$, the equation 11.62 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-density-ode} h'=\frac{xyz}{(x+h)(y-h)}-z,\qquad h(0)=-\eta \end{equation} has a smooth solution on $(-1,1)$ with $-x<h<y$ and $h<0$. There are a constant $0<c<1$ and fixed neighborhoods of both endpoints, independent of $\eta $, on which \[  -cp<h<0.  \] Every such solution, extended by zero, is a smooth function on $\mathbb R$ that vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. Proof. The right-hand side $F(r,h)$ is smooth on $-x<h<y$, and $h=0$ is a solution. Near $-1$, $(x,y,z)=(1+p,p,1)$; near $1$, $(x,y,z)=(p,1+p,1)$. Fix $0<c<1$. For the trial function $-cp$, near the left endpoint \[  F(r,-cp)+cp' =\frac{1+p}{(1+(1-c)p)(1+c)}-1+cp' \longrightarrow -\frac{c}{1+c}<0,  \] whereas near the right endpoint \[  F(r,-cp)+cp' =\frac{1+p}{(1-c)(1+(1+c)p)}-1+cp' \longrightarrow \frac{c}{1-c}>0.  \] as $r\to \pm 1$, since $p,p'\to 0$ at both endpoints. The strict inequalities therefore hold on fixed neighborhoods of the endpoints, and $-cp$ is a lower barrier for the equation solved backwards near $-1$ and forwards near $1$. Choose a compact interval $[r_ L,r_ R]\ni 0$ with endpoints in those neighborhoods. Continuous dependence on initial values, around the solution $h=0$, gives $\eta _0>0$ such that for every $0<\eta <\eta _0$ the solution exists on $[r_ L,r_ R]$, stays in the domain of $F$, and lies above $-cp$ at $r_ L$ and $r_ R$. By uniqueness of solutions, it cannot meet the solution zero, so $h<0$. The barrier argument used in the proof of lemma 11.7.2 then gives $-cp<h<0$ near both ends. On each compact subinterval of $(-1,1)$ the trapped graph stays at a positive distance from the boundary of the domain of $F$; hence, by the continuation theorem, the solution exists on all of $(-1,1)$. The equation factors as 11.63 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-density-logarithm} h'=h\, L(r,h),\qquad L(r,h)=\frac{z(x-y+h)}{(x+h)(y-h)}. \end{equation} Since $h<0$, we have $(\log (-h))'=L(r,h)$. Near the left endpoint, the trapping bounds and the explicit coefficients imply \[  L(r,h)=\frac{1+h}{(1+p+h)(p-h)}\geq \frac{C_1}{p}  \] after shrinking that neighborhood, with $C_1>0$. Near the right endpoint they give \[  L(r,h)=\frac{-1+h}{(p+h)(1+p-h)}\leq -\frac{C_2}{p}, \qquad C_2>0.  \] Indeed, on the left, $1+h\geq 1-cp\geq 1/2$ and the denominator is at most $(1+p)(1+c)p$; on the right, the numerator is at most $-1$, and the denominator is at most $p(1+(1+c)p)$. Since $p$ is comparable to the square of the distance $d=1-|r|$ to the endpoint, integrating these inequalities backwards on the left and forwards on the right gives, for some $A>0$, 11.64 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-density-exponential} |h(r)|\leq C \mathrm{e}^{-A/d} \end{equation} near either endpoint. The constants may depend on the solution; uniformity in $\eta $ is not needed for the smooth extension. It remains to control all derivatives. On the trapped graph, all partial derivatives in $(r,h)$ of the rational function $L$ grow at most polynomially in $d^{-1}$. Indeed, near an endpoint $x,y$ are polynomials in $r$, $z=1$, $h$ is bounded, and of the two factors in the denominator, one is bounded below by a positive constant and the other by $(1-c)p$. Repeated differentiation of the quotient therefore only introduces finite powers of $p^{-1}$. Inductively, for every $j\geq 0$ there are constants $C_ j,N_ j$ with \[  |h^{(j)}(r)|\leq C_ j \mathrm{e}^{-A/d}d^{-N_ j}.  \] The case $j=0$ is ( 11.64 ). Differentiate $h'=hL(r,h(r))$ $j$ times. Every resulting term is the product of a derivative of the factor $h$, of order at most $j$, and a derivative of the composite function $L(r,h(r))$. The latter involves only partial derivatives of $L$ and derivatives of $h$ of order at most $j$, which are polynomially bounded by the induction hypothesis, while the first factor has the exponential bound. This proves the case $j+1$. All derivatives of $h$ therefore tend to zero at $\pm 1$. Extending them by zero and applying the mean value theorem to the difference quotients at the endpoints, as in lemma 11.7.3 , shows that the extension of $h$ by zero is smooth and vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. $\square$ of theorem 11.8.1 . Let $\eta _0>0$ be such that lemma 11.8.2 applies for $0<\eta <\eta _0$, and let $h_\eta $ denote the solution with $h_\eta (0)=-\eta $. Take a primitive $G_\eta $ of its extension by zero. Since $G_\eta $ is constant near each end of the real line, $G_\eta (r)$ defines a smooth function on $X$. The potential $u_\eta =G_\eta (r)-\rho $ satisfies \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\eta =(x+h_\eta )P+(y-h_\eta )Q+(z+h_\eta ')R.  \] Inside the band, the first two coefficients are positive by the lemma, and the equation gives \[  z+h_\eta '=\frac{xyz}{(x+h_\eta )(y-h_\eta )}>0.  \] Outside the band the form is $\omega _0$, and on the two boundary hypersurfaces it is also the rank-two form $\omega _0$, since $h_\eta $ vanishes to infinite order there. Thus it is semipositive on $X$, and by ( 11.40 ) its cube is $6xyzP\wedge Q\wedge R=\omega _0^3=g\omega _ X^3$. Different initial values give potentials that do not differ by constants, so after normalization by the supremum we obtain an uncountable family. Bounded mass follows from proposition 6.5.2 , as for theorem 11.6.1 . $\square$ At each of the hypersurfaces $M_\pm $, the difference of two of these solutions agrees to infinite order with a constant, because its derivative is a difference of slopes that vanish to infinite order there. The constants at the two hypersurfaces need not agree. Thus the singular differential equation produces differences that are flat at $M_\pm $, even though the density has only quadratic zeros.

title: Theorem 11.8.1
text: Theorem 11.8.1 . title: Lemma 11.8.2
text: Lemma 11.8.2 . For every sufficiently small $\eta >0$, the equation 11.62 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-density-ode} h'=\frac{xyz}{(x+h)(y-h)}-z,\qquad h(0)=-\eta \end{equation} has a smooth solution on $(-1,1)$ with $-x<h<y$ and $h<0$. There are a constant $0<c<1$ and fixed neighborhoods of both endpoints, independent of $\eta $, on which \[  -cp<h<0.  \] Every such solution, extended by zero, is a smooth function on $\mathbb R$ that vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. The strict inequalities therefore hold on fixed neighborhoods of the endpoints, and $-cp$ is a lower barrier for the equation solved backwards near $-1$ and forwards near $1$. Choose a compact interval $[r_ L,r_ R]\ni 0$ with endpoints in those neighborhoods. Continuous dependence on initial values, around the solution $h=0$, gives $\eta _0>0$ such that for every $0<\eta <\eta _0$ the solution exists on $[r_ L,r_ R]$, stays in the domain of $F$, and lies above $-cp$ at $r_ L$ and $r_ R$. By uniqueness of solutions, it cannot meet the solution zero, so $h<0$. The barrier argument used in the proof of lemma 11.7.2 then gives $-cp<h<0$ near both ends. On each compact subinterval of $(-1,1)$ the trapped graph stays at a positive distance from the boundary of the domain of $F$; hence, by the continuation theorem, the solution exists on all of $(-1,1)$. The equation factors as 11.63 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-density-logarithm} h'=h\, L(r,h),\qquad L(r,h)=\frac{z(x-y+h)}{(x+h)(y-h)}. \end{equation} Since $h<0$, we have $(\log (-h))'=L(r,h)$. Near the left endpoint, the trapping bounds and the explicit coefficients imply \[  L(r,h)=\frac{1+h}{(1+p+h)(p-h)}\geq \frac{C_1}{p}  \] after shrinking that neighborhood, with $C_1>0$. Near the right endpoint they give \[  L(r,h)=\frac{-1+h}{(p+h)(1+p-h)}\leq -\frac{C_2}{p}, \qquad C_2>0.  \] Indeed, on the left, $1+h\geq 1-cp\geq 1/2$ and the denominator is at most $(1+p)(1+c)p$; on the right, the numerator is at most $-1$, and the denominator is at most $p(1+(1+c)p)$. Since $p$ is comparable to the square of the distance $d=1-|r|$ to the endpoint, integrating these inequalities backwards on the left and forwards on the right gives, for some $A>0$, 11.64 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-density-exponential} |h(r)|\leq C \mathrm{e}^{-A/d} \end{equation} near either endpoint. The constants may depend on the solution; uniformity in $\eta $ is not needed for the smooth extension. It remains to control all derivatives. On the trapped graph, all partial derivatives in $(r,h)$ of the rational function $L$ grow at most polynomially in $d^{-1}$. Indeed, near an endpoint $x,y$ are polynomials in $r$, $z=1$, $h$ is bounded, and of the two factors in the denominator, one is bounded below by a positive constant and the other by $(1-c)p$. Repeated differentiation of the quotient therefore only introduces finite powers of $p^{-1}$. Inductively, for every $j\geq 0$ there are constants $C_ j,N_ j$ with \[  |h^{(j)}(r)|\leq C_ j \mathrm{e}^{-A/d}d^{-N_ j}.  \] The case $j=0$ is ( 11.64 ). Differentiate $h'=hL(r,h(r))$ $j$ times. Every resulting term is the product of a derivative of the factor $h$, of order at most $j$, and a derivative of the composite function $L(r,h(r))$. The latter involves only partial derivatives of $L$ and derivatives of $h$ of order at most $j$, which are polynomially bounded by the induction hypothesis, while the first factor has the exponential bound. This proves the case $j+1$. All derivatives of $h$ therefore tend to zero at $\pm 1$. Extending them by zero and applying the mean value theorem to the difference quotients at the endpoints, as in lemma 11.7.3 , shows that the extension of $h$ by zero is smooth and vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. $\square$

title: 11.9 A real analytic density
text: 11.9 A real analytic density A globally real analytic density can occur in an equation with a smooth nonclosed Hermitian background and distinct smooth normalized solutions. We prescribe it as a polynomial in a real analytic function on projective space. Two symmetric radial perturbations give the required determinant on the middle band; patching the coefficients while preserving their product extends the construction across the projective ends. The two hypersurfaces where the density vanishes quadratically separate regions with different extremal values of the difference of the solutions. Theorem 11.9.1 . On $X=\mathbb P^3$, with block homogeneous coordinates $[A:B]$ and Fubini–Study form $\omega _ X$, put \[  t=\frac{|A|^2}{|A|^2+|B|^2},\qquad a=\frac1{1+\mathrm{e}},\qquad b=\frac{\mathrm{e}}{1+\mathrm{e}},\qquad f_*(t)=(t-a)^2(t-b)^2.  \] There exist a smooth nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ and distinct smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u,v$, normalized by $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv=0$, with 11.65 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:analytic-example} (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^3=f_*(t)\omega _ X^3. \end{equation} Both solution forms are positive away from the two connected real analytic hypersurfaces $\{ t=a\} $, $\{ t=b\} $, and have complex rank two on them. The density is real analytic on $X$, and it vanishes exactly to second order in the direction transverse to these hypersurfaces. For every $n\geq 4$ the same assertions hold on $\mathbb {P}^3\times \mathbb {P}^{n-3}$, with the pulled-back density and the product Fubini–Study volume, and with rank $n-1$ on the two product hypersurfaces. Proof. We use the forms $P,Q,R$ and the function $r$ of 11.6.1 . By ( 11.40 ), the construction reduces to finding scalar coefficients with a prescribed product. By ( 11.42 ), 11.66 \begin{equation} \label{eq:analytic-fs-cube} \omega _ X^3=6(\sigma ')^2P\wedge Q\wedge R, \qquad \sigma '=\sigma (r)\sigma (-r)>0. \end{equation} $\square$

title: 11.9.1 Prescribing the determinant
text: 11.9.1 Prescribing the determinant On $U$, one has $t=\sigma (r)$. We first construct two triples of coefficients, positive on the middle band, with product $f_*(\sigma )(\sigma ')^2$. At each endpoint of the band, exactly one of the coefficients of $P$ and $Q$ will vanish. Put $d_*(r)=f_*(\sigma (r))(\sigma '(r))^2$. Since $a=\sigma (-1)$, $b=\sigma (1)$, define the positive smooth divided differences \[  k_-(r)=\int _0^1\sigma '(-1+s(r+1))\, \mathrm{d}s,\qquad k_+(r)=\int _0^1\sigma '(1+s(r-1))\, \mathrm{d}s,  \] and $H_*(r)=k_-(r)k_+(r)\sigma '(r)>0$. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives 11.67 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:prescribed-det} \sigma (r)-a=(r+1)k_-(r),\quad \sigma (r)-b=(r-1)k_+(r),\quad d_*=(1-r^2)^2H_*^2. \end{equation} These formulas show that $H_*$ is smooth and positive also at the endpoints, without any division by a vanishing function. The symmetry $\sigma (-r)=1-\sigma (r)$ makes $d_*$, and hence $H_*$, even. Choose the function \[  p(r)= \begin{cases} \mathrm{e}^{-1/(1-r^2)},& |r|<1,\\ 0,& |r|\geq 1, \end{cases} \qquad q=p'.  \] All its derivatives vanish at $r=\pm 1$: each derivative is a finite sum of polynomials in $r$ times powers of $(1-r^2)^{-1}$, multiplied by the exponential, and the exponential factor dominates every such power. On $|r|<1$, $q=-2rp/(1-r^2)^2$. Define 11.70 \begin{align}  z_ b& =\sqrt{q^2+2H_*^2},\qquad S_* =\sqrt{r^2+4p^2+2z_ b(1-r^2)^2},\label{uni-eq:baseline1}\\  x_ b& =(S_*-r)/2,\qquad y_ b=(S_*+r)/2.\label{uni-eq:baseline2} \end{align} Both radicands are strictly positive everywhere, so these formulas define smooth functions on $\mathbb R$, including at the endpoints. They satisfy 11.72 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:baseline-identities} z_ b>|q|,\qquad x_ b-y_ b=-r,\qquad x_ by_ b=p^2+\frac{z_ b}2(1-r^2)^2. \end{equation} The coefficients $x_ b,y_ b$ are nonnegative, positive away from the endpoints, with values $(1,0)$ at $-1$ and $(0,1)$ at $1$. On the open band, \[  S_*^2-(2p+|r|)^2=2(1-r^2)^2(z_ b-|q|)>0,  \] so $x_ b>p$, $y_ b>p$. Consequently both triples 11.73 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:twotriples} (x_ b-p,y_ b+p,z_ b-q),\qquad (x_ b+p,y_ b-p,z_ b+q) \end{equation} are strictly positive there. We now verify that the two triples have the same product. Set $D_*=x_ by_ b-p^2$, $E_*=p(x_ b-y_ b)=-rp$. Equations ( 11.72 ) and the formula for $q$ give \[  D_*=(z_ b/2)(1-r^2)^2,\qquad qD_*=z_ bE_*.  \] The two products in ( 11.73 ) therefore equal 11.74 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:det-cancellation} (D_*+E_*)(z_ b-q)=(D_*-E_*)(z_ b+q) =\frac{D_*}{z_ b}(z_ b^2-q^2)=d_*. \end{equation} For $|r|\geq 1$, $p=q=0$ and the same identity reads $x_ by_ bz_ b=d_*$. Thus both triples have exactly the prescribed product, and at the endpoints exactly one of their entries vanishes.
11.67 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:prescribed-det} \sigma (r)-a=(r+1)k_-(r),\quad \sigma (r)-b=(r-1)k_+(r),\quad d_*=(1-r^2)^2H_*^2. \end{equation}
11.70 \begin{align}  z_ b& =\sqrt{q^2+2H_*^2},\qquad S_* =\sqrt{r^2+4p^2+2z_ b(1-r^2)^2},\label{uni-eq:baseline1}\\  x_ b& =(S_*-r)/2,\qquad y_ b=(S_*+r)/2.\label{uni-eq:baseline2} \end{align}
11.71 \[\begin{aligned}\begin{align}  x_ b& =(S_*-r)/2,\qquad y_ b=(S_*+r)/2.\label{uni-eq:baseline2} \end{align}\end{aligned}\]
11.72 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:baseline-identities} z_ b>|q|,\qquad x_ b-y_ b=-r,\qquad x_ by_ b=p^2+\frac{z_ b}2(1-r^2)^2. \end{equation}
11.73 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:twotriples} (x_ b-p,y_ b+p,z_ b-q),\qquad (x_ b+p,y_ b-p,z_ b+q) \end{equation}
11.74 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:det-cancellation} (D_*+E_*)(z_ b-q)=(D_*-E_*)(z_ b+q) =\frac{D_*}{z_ b}(z_ b^2-q^2)=d_*. \end{equation}

title: 11.9.2 Extension over the projective ends
text: 11.9.2 Extension over the projective ends The coefficients just constructed have the right product but need not extend across the projective ends. Away from the zero levels of $f_*(t)$, we interpolate the coefficients of $P$ and $Q$ to those of $f_*(t)^{1/3}\omega _ X$, and determine the coefficient of $R$ by the prescribed product. Choose a smooth even cutoff $0\leq \eta \leq 1$, equal to one on $|r|\leq 3/2$ and zero on $|r|\geq 2$. On $|r|<3/2$ set $(x,y,z)=(x_ b,y_ b,z_ b)$. On $|r|>5/4$, where $f_*(\sigma (r))>0$, put \begin{align*}  \kappa & =f_*(\sigma (r))^{1/3},\\  x& =\eta x_ b+(1-\eta )\kappa \sigma (r),\\  y& =\eta y_ b+(1-\eta )\kappa \sigma (-r),\qquad z=d_*/(xy). \end{align*} These coefficients are smooth and positive on the outer region. On the overlap $5/4<|r|<3/2$, we have $\eta =1$, $p=q=0$ and $x_ by_ bz_ b=d_*$, so the two definitions agree. For $|r|\geq 2$ they equal $\kappa (\sigma (r),\sigma (-r),\sigma '(r))$. Thus \[  \omega _0=xP+yQ+zR  \] extends smoothly across both omitted projective lines, being equal near them to $f_*(t)^{1/3}\omega _ X$, which is smooth and positive there since $f_*(0)=f_*(1)=a^2b^2>0$. On $X$, the form $\omega _0$ is semipositive, positive away from $r=\pm 1$, and of rank two on these levels. The function \[  F(r)=2\int _0^ r p(s)\, \mathrm{d}s  \] is constant on each of the intervals $(-\infty ,-1]$ and $[1,\infty )$, and so $F(r)$ extends to a smooth nonconstant function on $X$. By ( 11.41 ), half of its complex Hessian is $H_0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F/2=p(P-Q)+qR$. By ( 11.74 ) and ( 11.66 ), the forms $A_0=\omega _0-H_0$, $B_0=\omega _0+H_0$ satisfy \[  A_0^3=B_0^3=f_*(t)\omega _ X^3  \] on $U$, and hence on $X$. Their ranks and positivity were determined above, after ( 11.73 ). The construction is symmetric: $x(-r)=y(r)$, and $z$ is even.

title: 11.9.3 A positive equation background
text: 11.9.3 A positive equation background As in the first example, an exact correction makes the average form strictly positive without changing the two solution forms. Here the coefficient of $R$ is already positive, and the correction restores the missing coefficient of $P$ or $Q$ at each endpoint. Let $\varepsilon >0$ be a parameter, restricted below. Let $h(r)=(r^2-1)\eta (r)$, extend it by zero on the tails, and set $\rho =\varepsilon h$. The coefficients of $\omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ are 11.75 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:repair} (x+\varepsilon h',\  y-\varepsilon h',\  z+\varepsilon h''). \end{equation} On $|r|\leq 3/2$, we have $h'=2r$ and $h''=2$. For $0\leq r\leq 3/2$, $x+2\varepsilon r>0$, since the only zero of $x$ there is at $r=1$, where the correction is positive. On $[-3/2,0]$, $x$ has a positive minimum $m_0$, so positivity holds if $3\varepsilon <m_0$. Reflection proves positivity of the second coefficient, and the third is $z+2\varepsilon >0$. On the compact transition region $3/2\leq |r|\leq 2$, all original coefficients have a common positive lower bound $m_1$. If $M_1$ bounds $|h'|+|h''|$, taking also $\varepsilon <m_1/(M_1+1)$ preserves their positivity there. For $|r|\geq 2$, the background equals $f_*(t)^{1/3}\omega _ X>0$. Hence $\omega $ is strictly positive on $X$. The correction is exact, so $\mathrm{d}\omega =\mathrm{d}\omega _0$. At $r=0$, where $x=x_ b$ and $y=y_ b$, evenness of $S_*$ gives $x'(0)=-1/2$ and $y'(0)=1/2$. Hence ( 11.46 ) gives \[  \mathrm{d}\omega _0=(z_ b(0)+1/2)\, \mathrm{d}r\wedge (Q-P)\ne 0.  \] Indeed, if $\mathrm{d}r\wedge (Q-P)=0$, wedging with $P$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$ would contradict $P\wedge Q\wedge R>0$. Thus the Hermitian background $\omega $ is not closed. Now put $\widetilde u=-F/2-\rho $ and $\widetilde v=F/2-\rho $. Then $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u=A_0$, $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v=B_0$. Subtracting their respective suprema gives $u,v$ with $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv=0$, and ( 11.65 ) holds. Their difference is nonconstant because $F$ is nonconstant.
11.75 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:repair} (x+\varepsilon h',\  y-\varepsilon h',\  z+\varepsilon h''). \end{equation}

title: 11.9.4 Zeros and higher dimensions
text: 11.9.4 Zeros and higher dimensions It remains to examine the regularity of the density and the geometry of its zero levels. Taking a product with projective space then preserves the equality of the Monge–Ampère measures and gives examples in every higher dimension. The function $t$ is real analytic in every affine chart of $X$, being a quotient of real polynomials with positive denominator. Hence $f_*(t)$ is real analytic on $X$. Its two zero levels are regular hypersurfaces because $t=\sigma (r)$, $\sigma '>0$, and $\mathrm{d}r\ne 0$. Each level is connected, since it is the quotient of the product of two three-spheres of fixed nonzero radii by the diagonal action of the circle. Each level is compact and has zero volume. The divided differences in ( 11.67 ) show near the two levels that 11.76 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:quadratic-zero} f_*(\sigma (r))=(r+1)^2g_-(r),\qquad f_*(\sigma (r))=(r-1)^2g_+(r), \end{equation} respectively, with smooth strictly positive functions $g_\pm $. For $n\geq 4$, let $\theta $ be the Fubini–Study form on $Y=\mathbb {P}^{n-3}$, let $\pi _1:X\times Y\to X$ and $\pi _2:X\times Y\to Y$ be the projections, and set, on $X\times Y$, \[  \omega _ n=\pi _1^*\omega +\pi _2^*\theta ,\qquad \Omega _ n=\pi _1^*\omega _ X+\pi _2^*\theta ,\qquad u_ n=\pi _1^*u,\quad v_ n=\pi _1^*v.  \] In the expansion of an $n$-fold product, only the terms with exactly three factors pulled back from $X$ survive. Consequently \[  (\omega _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n)^ n =\binom n3\pi _1^*(A_0^3)\wedge \pi _2^*(\theta ^{n-3}) =f_*(\pi _1^*t)\Omega _ n^ n,  \] and the same holds for $v_ n$. On the two product levels, the solution forms have rank $2+(n-3)=n-1$. Restriction to a slice $X\times \{ y\} $ recovers $\mathrm{d}\omega \ne 0$, so $\omega _ n$ is not closed. Normalization, distinctness and real analyticity are preserved by pullback. Write $\operatorname {Vol}$ for the volume with respect to $\omega _ X^3$, or $\Omega _ n^ n$ in dimension $n$. The quadratic zeros complete the proof of the sharpness assertion in 11.1.4 . In finitely many tubular charts around the zero levels, the density is bounded above and below by positive multiples of the square of a real transverse coordinate, and the volume form has a bounded positive density with respect to coordinate volume. Away from these charts, the density is bounded below by a positive constant. Thus, for $s>0$ and $\alpha >0$, 11.77 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:sharp-asymptotic} \operatorname {Vol}\{ f_*\leq s\} \asymp \sqrt s\quad (s\downarrow 0), \qquad f_*^{-\alpha }\in L^1\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \alpha <\tfrac 12. \end{equation} Thus, for every $0<\alpha <1/2$ and every dimension $n\geq 3$, there are smooth examples of nonuniqueness whose density $f$ satisfies $f^{-\alpha }\in L^1$; this condition is weaker than the hypothesis $f^{-1/2}\in L^1$ of 11.1.4 . Remark 11.9.2 . For this example, the positive-density set $\{ f_*(t)>0\} $ has three components: the middle band and the two outer regions. The two solution forms have the same missing direction on each zero level, so $E_{\rm unif}=\{ f_*(t)>0\} $. The maximum and the minimum of the difference of the two potentials are attained on the two outer components, whose closures are disjoint, in accordance with 11.1.1 . Although the closure of the middle component meets both outer closures, the extremal values do not propagate through the middle component.
11.76 \begin{equation} \label{uni-eq:quadratic-zero} f_*(\sigma (r))=(r+1)^2g_-(r),\qquad f_*(\sigma (r))=(r-1)^2g_+(r), \end{equation}

title: 12 Complex Hessian equations
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: 12 Complex Hessian equations Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n$, let $\omega $ be a smooth positive Hermitian form, and fix $2\leq m<n$. The complex Hessian operator $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}$ replaces the determinant by an intermediate symmetric polynomial. Its admissible cone allows negative eigenvalues, so the product calculus for plurisubharmonic potentials from chapter 1 no longer applies directly. For a continuous admissible weak solution with smooth positive density depending on the potential, the difficulty is to obtain derivative estimates before smoothness is known. Proper exponential equations associate smooth solutions to its smooth admissible approximations. The complex-Hessian estimate is independent of derivatives of the prescribed approximation, so it survives passage to the limit. Uniform convergence defines the continuous mixed products, while obstacle envelopes give the domination principle that identifies the limit with the original solution. A concave uniformly elliptic extension then supplies classical interior regularity. The determinant case is treated in theorem 10.5.2 ; the argument here concerns the intermediate Hessian degrees. Uniform stability also constructs solutions for strictly increasing exponents, by contraction between constant barriers. Bounded admissible potentials require decreasing approximation. The recursion first gives currents with measure coefficients below degree $m$; local Hessian capacities control multiplication by their discontinuous potentials. Quasicontinuity and weighted convergence make the products symmetric and allow all approximation indices to tend to their limits together. At degree $m$, the positive product after wedging with $\omega ^{n-m}$ is a Radon measure. These weighted limits pass locality and the maximum inequality to bounded potentials. Truncation above the infimum then proves that the Hessian measure of each potential is nonzero on an arbitrary Hermitian background. In global comparison, the maximum inequality leaves a signed total-mass difference. The complex Hessians of the background powers determine when this difference vanishes for every bounded admissible list. On small sublevel sets, a modified comparison estimate absorbs the torsion error on arbitrary Hermitian backgrounds. It yields strict domination, bounded stability for proper equations and smoothness for their solutions with smooth data between constant barriers.

title: 12.1 The admissible cone
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: 12.1 The admissible cone For $\lambda \in \mathbb R^ n$, let $S_ j(\lambda )$ be the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree $j$, put $\sigma _ j=S_ j/\binom nj$ and $\sigma _0=1$, and set \[  \Gamma _ m=\{ \lambda :S_ j(\lambda )>0,\  1\leq j\leq m\} .  \] A real $(1,1)$-form belongs to $\Gamma _ m(\omega )$ if its eigenvalues relative to $\omega $ belong to $\Gamma _ m$. Write $C_{n,m}$ for the corresponding closed cone of Hermitian matrices. The algebraic assertions below also apply when $m=n$. We use the classical Gårding facts: the closed spectral cone is convex, contains the nonnegative matrices, and is preserved by adding them; adding a positive matrix puts a closed-cone matrix in its interior. The normalized root $F=\sigma _ m^{1/m}$ is concave and increasing there. Polarized products of $k$ forms in $\Gamma _ k(\omega )$ with $\omega ^{n-k}$ are positive, and Maclaurin's inequalities give $\sigma _ j^{1/j}\geq \sigma _ k^{1/k}$ for $j\leq k$. These algebraic facts will serve as inputs to the analytic arguments. A continuous real function $v$ on $X$ is admissible if 12.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hessian-continuous-admissibility} (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)\wedge \gamma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma _{m-1} \wedge \omega ^{n-m}\geq 0 \end{equation} in distributions for every smooth collection $\gamma _1,\ldots ,\gamma _{m-1}\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$. For smooth $v$ this is equivalent to the pointwise closed-cone condition; strict admissibility means membership in the open cone. Maxima and convex combinations preserve continuous admissibility. To check the maximum property, fix one smooth positive linear test in ( 12.1 ). Locally a smooth solution of its inhomogeneous linear equation reduces the assertion to the maximum property for subsolutions of a smooth elliptic operator. For a bounded upper semicontinuous function $v$, admissibility means that every local $C^2$ upper test $q$ at $x$ satisfies 12.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hessian-bounded-upper-tests} \omega (x)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q(x)\in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega (x))}. \end{equation} For continuous $v$, this agrees with ( 12.1 ): Gårding duality reduces both conditions to subsolution inequalities for smooth strictly elliptic linear operators. We use their classical viscosity–distributional equivalence, with the usual subharmonic representative in the bounded class. The first estimate controls a scalar shift of the cone. It will give lower bounds for every coefficient of the linearized Hessian operator. Lemma 12.1.1 . For $\lambda \in \Gamma _ m$, put \[  e_ m=\frac{\sigma _ m(\lambda )}{m\sigma _{m-1}(\lambda )}.  \] Then $\lambda -t\mathbf1\in \Gamma _ m$ for $0\leq t<e_ m$. If $m\geq 2$, the conclusion also holds for $t=e_ m$. For $m=1$, the endpoint lies on the boundary. Proof. The polynomial \[  P(x)=\sigma _ m(\lambda +x\mathbf1) =\sum _{j=0}^ m\binom mj\sigma _ j(\lambda )x^{m-j}  \] is a positive multiple of the $(n-m)$th derivative of $\prod _ i(x+\lambda _ i)$. Hence all its roots are real, by Rolle's theorem. Its coefficients are positive, so all its roots are strictly negative. Write $P(x)=\prod _{i=1}^ m(x+r_ i)$ with $r_ i>0$. Logarithmic differentiation at zero gives \[  \sum _{i=1}^ m r_ i^{-1} =\frac{m\sigma _{m-1}(\lambda )}{\sigma _ m(\lambda )} =e_ m^{-1}.  \] Thus $\min _ i r_ i\geq e_ m$, with strict inequality if $m\geq 2$. For $x> -\min _ i r_ i$, every derivative of $P$ is positive: differentiating its product expansion produces sums of products of positive factors. Since \[  P^{(m-j)}(x)=\frac{m!}{j!}\sigma _ j(\lambda +x\mathbf1), \qquad 1\leq j\leq m,  \] all the required symmetric polynomials are positive at $x=-t$. When $m=1$, the sole root is $-e_1$. $\square$ Lemma 12.1.2 . If $\alpha ,\gamma \in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$, then \[  \frac{\alpha ^{m-1}\wedge \gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} \frac{\alpha \wedge \omega ^{n-1}}{\omega ^ n} \geq \frac1{m!} \frac{\alpha ^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} \frac{\gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-1}}{\omega ^ n}.  \] The assertion extends to $\gamma \in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega )}$ by continuity. Proof. Write $\sigma _ k=\alpha ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k}/\omega ^ n$, and $M_ k=\alpha ^{k-1}\wedge \gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-k}/\omega ^ n$. For $1\leq k<m$, the cone shift with index $k+1$ and Gårding positivity give \[  M_{k+1}\geq tM_ k \quad \left(0\leq t<\frac{\sigma _{k+1}}{(k+1)\sigma _ k}\right).  \] Let $t$ increase to the displayed endpoint. Iterating, starting with $M_1=\gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-1}/\omega ^ n$, yields \[  M_ m\geq \frac{\sigma _ m}{m!\sigma _1}M_1.  \] All denominators are positive. Approximating a form in the closed cone by $\gamma +\delta \omega $, $\delta \downarrow 0$, gives the last assertion. $\square$ At a diagonal Hermitian matrix $\Lambda $ in the open cone, order its eigenvalues as $\lambda _1\geq \cdots \geq \lambda _ n$ and write \[  f=F(\Lambda ),\quad F_ i=\partial _{\lambda _ i}F,\quad S=\operatorname {tr}\Lambda ,\quad \mathcal F=\sum _ iF_ i, \quad Q=\sum _ iF_ i\lambda _ i^2.  \] The next inequalities use these derivatives of the normalized root, rather than derivatives of the polynomial $S_ m$. Lemma 12.1.3 . If $M$ belongs to the closed Hermitian $m$-cone, then \[  W:=\sum _ iF_ iM_{i\bar i}\geq \frac{f}{m!S}\operatorname {tr}M, \qquad F_ i\geq \frac{f}{m!S},\qquad |M_{1\bar1}|\leq \operatorname {tr}M.  \] No simultaneous diagonalization of $M$ and $\Lambda $ is required. Proof. In the wedge notation of the mixed-trace estimate, differentiation gives $DF_\Lambda (M)=fM_ m/\sigma _ m$. The estimate $M_ m\geq \sigma _ m M_1/(m!\sigma _1)$, with $M_1=\operatorname {tr}M/n$ and $\sigma _1=S/n$, proves the first inequality. The positive semidefinite rank-one coordinate projections belong to the closed $m$-cone; taking $M$ to be each projection proves the second inequality. The closed $m$-cone is contained in the closed $2$-cone. Its eigenvalues $\mu $ satisfy \[  \operatorname {tr}M\geq 0,\qquad \sum _ i\mu _ i^2=(\operatorname {tr}M)^2-2S_2(\mu ) \leq (\operatorname {tr}M)^2.  \] Thus the operator norm of $M$ is at most its trace, which proves the last inequality. The wedge pairing computes the derivative in the diagonal frame of $\Lambda $, regardless of the eigenvectors of $M$. $\square$ Lemma 12.1.4 . If $0<f_0\leq f\leq f_1$, then \[  Q:=\sum _ iF_ i\lambda _ i^2 \geq \frac{f_0}{m}S-\frac{n-m}{m}f_1^2, \qquad \mathcal F\geq 1.  \] Proof. The derivative of the normalized root is $F_ i=fS_{m-1}(\lambda |i)/(mS_ m)$. The splitting identity gives \[  Q=\frac fm S-\frac{(m+1)f}{mS_ m}S_{m+1}.  \] For $m=n$, set $S_{n+1}=0$. If $S_{m+1}\leq 0$, the second term is nonnegative. Otherwise $\lambda \in \Gamma _{m+1}$ and Maclaurin gives $S_{m+1}\leq \binom n{m+1}f^{m+1}$. Since $S_ m=\binom nm f^ m$, the subtracted term is at most $(n-m)f^2/m$. This proves the first assertion. Summing the derivatives gives $\mathcal F=f\sigma _{m-1}/\sigma _ m\geq 1$, again by Maclaurin. $\square$ When $m<n$, admissible forms need not be semipositive. Positivity of a mixed Hessian measure therefore does not directly bound every coefficient of its factors. For degrees below $m$, deleted-coordinate positivity supplies the required absolute bound: if $S_{j;I}$ means $S_ j$ with the coordinates indexed by $I$ omitted, then $S_{j;I}(\lambda )>0$ for $j+|I|\leq m$, by polarized Gårding positivity. Lemma 12.1.5 . If $0\leq r<m$, $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ r\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$, and $\Xi $ is a smooth complementary form, then \[  |\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ r\wedge \Xi | \leq C_{n,m,\Xi }(\alpha _1+\cdots +\alpha _ r)^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}.  \] For $r=0$ the right-hand side means $C_{n,m,\Xi }\omega ^ n$. Proof. First take a single form $\alpha $, diagonal in an $\omega $-unitary frame, with ordered eigenvalues $\lambda \in \Gamma _ m$. For $1\leq r<m$, repeated splitting and deleted-coordinate positivity give $S_ r(\lambda )\geq \lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ r$. The sum of the last $n-r$ eigenvalues is positive, so each negative eigenvalue has modulus at most $(n-r)\lambda _{r+1}$. Thus every product of $r$ distinct eigenvalues has modulus at most \[  (n-r)^ r\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ r\leq (n-r)^ r S_ r(\lambda ).  \] Indeed, replace its negative factors by this bound and its positive factors by the corresponding largest eigenvalues. In the diagonal frame only complementary diagonal coefficients of $\Xi $ contribute to $\alpha ^ r\wedge \Xi $. This proves $|\alpha ^ r\wedge \Xi |\leq C_{n,m,\Xi }\alpha ^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}$. Apply this bound to the polynomial $(\alpha _1+t_2\alpha _2+\cdots +t_ r\alpha _ r)^ r\wedge \Xi $, with $0\leq t_ i\leq 1$. Its absolute value is bounded by the stated right-hand side, by polarized positivity and monotonicity on the cone. A fixed invertible interpolation matrix on this finite-dimensional polynomial space bounds each coefficient by its supremum on the cube. The coefficient of $t_2\cdots t_ r$ is a fixed positive multiple of $\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ r\wedge \Xi $. This proves the mixed bound. The closed-cone case follows by adding $\varepsilon \omega $ to each form and taking the limit. $\square$ The next coefficient bound also controls a torsion form whose diagonal coefficients can have either sign. It compares each two-coordinate coefficient with the positive coefficients of the associated gradient pairing. Lemma 12.1.6 . If $\lambda \in \overline{\Gamma _ m}$, $1\leq q\leq \min \{ m-1,n-2\} $, and $i\ne j$, then, with $N=n-2$ and \[  c_{N,q}=\frac{q(N-q)}{(q+1)(N-q+1)}<1,  \] one has \[  |S_{q;ij}(\lambda )|^2 \leq \frac{S_{q;i}(\lambda )S_{q;j}(\lambda )}{1-c_{N,q}}.  \] This includes $q=N$, when $c_{N,N}=0$. Proof. First prove the unnormalized Newton inequality for an arbitrary real list $\mu $ of length $N$. For $1\leq q<N$, put $R(x)=\prod _{a=1}^ N(x+\mu _ a)$ and $G=R^{(N-q-1)}$. Repeated Rolle's theorem makes $G$ a real-rooted polynomial of degree $d=q+1$. Away from its roots $r_ a$, logarithmic differentiation and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[  G'^2-GG''=G^2\sum _{a=1}^ d\frac1{(x-r_ a)^2} \geq \frac1dG^2\left(\sum _{a=1}^ d\frac1{x-r_ a}\right)^2 =\frac1dG'^2.  \] Continuity extends this polynomial inequality to every real $x$. At zero, \[  G=(N-q-1)!S_{q+1}(\mu ),\quad G'=(N-q)!S_ q(\mu ),\quad G''=(N-q+1)!S_{q-1}(\mu ).  \] Consequently $S_{q-1}(\mu )S_{q+1}(\mu )\leq c_{N,q}S_ q(\mu )^2$. No sign restriction on $\mu $ or on these coefficients was used. For $q=N$, its left side is zero and the same assertion holds with $c_{N,N}=0$. Apply this to the list with $i,j$ deleted. Put $A=S_{q-1;ij}$, $B=S_{q;ij}$, $C=S_{q+1;ij}$ and $D_ i=S_{q;i}$, $D_ j=S_{q;j}$. Deleted-coordinate positivity gives $A,D_ i,D_ j\geq 0$: the required degrees are $q+1\leq m$. Splitting in the two omitted coordinates gives the exact identity \[  D_ iD_ j=A S_{q+1}(\lambda )+B^2-AC.  \] Since $S_{q+1}(\lambda )\geq 0$ and $AC\leq c_{N,q}B^2$, this is at least $(1-c_{N,q})B^2$. There is no division by $A$ or $D_ i$; all degenerate endpoints are therefore included. Equivalently one may first add $\epsilon \mathbf1$ and pass to the closed cone. $\square$ A smooth maximum preserves the cone condition and can be chosen monotone in its smoothing scale as well as in its two arguments. Lemma 12.1.7 . If smooth uniformly bounded admissible $u_ j\downarrow u$ and $v_ j\downarrow v$ are given, there are smooth uniformly bounded admissible $w_ j\downarrow \max \{ u,v\} $. For any chosen $\epsilon _ j>0$ decreasing to zero, they can be chosen to satisfy $w_ j=u_ j$ on $\{ u_ j-v_ j>\epsilon _ j\} $ and $w_ j=v_ j$ on $\{ v_ j-u_ j>\epsilon _ j\} $. For smooth functions $f,g$ on an open subset of $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega )}$, the regularized maximum $M_\epsilon (f,g)$ constructed below satisfies the same unshifted cone condition. Proof. Choose a nonnegative even smooth probability density $\zeta $ supported in $[-1,1]$, and set \[  r_\epsilon (t)=\int |t-\epsilon s|\zeta (s)\, \mathrm ds, \qquad M_\epsilon (x,y)=\tfrac 12(x+y+r_\epsilon (x-y)).  \] The function $r_\epsilon $ is smooth and convex, $|r_\epsilon '|\leq 1$, and $r_\epsilon (t)=|t|$ for $|t|\geq \epsilon $. Jensen's inequality and the triangle inequality give \[  \max \{ x,y\} \leq M_\epsilon (x,y) \leq \max \{ x,y\} +\epsilon /2.  \] Its partial derivatives in $x,y$ are nonnegative. For fixed $t$, $r_\epsilon (t)$ is an even convex function of $\epsilon $, since $\zeta $ is even. It is therefore nondecreasing for $\epsilon \geq 0$. Consequently $w_ j=M_{\epsilon _ j}(u_ j,v_ j)$ decreases pointwise to $\max \{ u,v\} $ and has the asserted equalities and bounds. Put $h_ j=u_ j-v_ j$ and $a_ j=(1+r_{\epsilon _ j}'(h_ j))/2$. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j =a_ j(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)+(1-a_ j)(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j) +\tfrac 12r_{\epsilon _ j}''(h_ j) \mathrm dh_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j.  \] Here $0\leq a_ j\leq 1$, and the last form is semipositive. Convexity of the cone and its stability under semipositive addition prove admissibility. For smooth local functions satisfying the unshifted cone condition, omit $\omega $ from this chain rule; the same argument proves preservation of that condition. The pointwise maximum is itself admissible: an upper test for it at a point is an upper test for a potential attaining the maximum there. Its canonical representative is thus the indicated pointwise maximum. $\square$ Lemma 12.1.8 . If bounded admissible $u,v$ satisfy $u\leq v$ almost everywhere with respect to $\omega ^ n$, then $u\leq v$ everywhere. Proof. By 12.1.7 , $w=\max \{ u,v\} $ is bounded admissible with its indicated canonical representative. Since $w=v$ almost everywhere, they represent the same distribution. The canonical subharmonic representative used in ( 12.2 ) is determined by that distribution. Thus $w=v$ pointwise, which is the assertion. $\square$

text: Lemma 12.1.5 .
