Thus every product of $r$ distinct eigenvalues has modulus at most \[  (n-r)^ r\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ r\leq (n-r)^ r S_ r(\lambda ).  \] Indeed, replace its negative factors by this bound and its positive factors by the corresponding largest eigenvalues. In the diagonal frame only complementary diagonal coefficients of $\Xi $ contribute to $\alpha ^ r\wedge \Xi $. This proves $|\alpha ^ r\wedge \Xi |\leq C_{n,m,\Xi }\alpha ^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}$. Apply this bound to the polynomial $(\alpha _1+t_2\alpha _2+\cdots +t_ r\alpha _ r)^ r\wedge \Xi $, with $0\leq t_ i\leq 1$. Its absolute value is bounded by the stated right-hand side, by polarized positivity and monotonicity on the cone. A fixed invertible interpolation matrix on this finite-dimensional polynomial space bounds each coefficient by its supremum on the cube. The coefficient of $t_2\cdots t_ r$ is a fixed positive multiple of $\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ r\wedge \Xi $. This proves the mixed bound. The closed-cone case follows by adding $\varepsilon \omega $ to each form and taking the limit. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.1.6
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 12.1.6 . If $\lambda \in \overline{\Gamma _ m}$, $1\leq q\leq \min \{ m-1,n-2\} $, and $i\ne j$, then, with $N=n-2$ and \[  c_{N,q}=\frac{q(N-q)}{(q+1)(N-q+1)}<1,  \] one has \[  |S_{q;ij}(\lambda )|^2 \leq \frac{S_{q;i}(\lambda )S_{q;j}(\lambda )}{1-c_{N,q}}.  \] This includes $q=N$, when $c_{N,N}=0$. Proof. First prove the unnormalized Newton inequality for an arbitrary real list $\mu $ of length $N$. For $1\leq q<N$, put $R(x)=\prod _{a=1}^ N(x+\mu _ a)$ and $G=R^{(N-q-1)}$. Repeated Rolle's theorem makes $G$ a real-rooted polynomial of degree $d=q+1$. Away from its roots $r_ a$, logarithmic differentiation and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[  G'^2-GG''=G^2\sum _{a=1}^ d\frac1{(x-r_ a)^2} \geq \frac1dG^2\left(\sum _{a=1}^ d\frac1{x-r_ a}\right)^2 =\frac1dG'^2.  \] Continuity extends this polynomial inequality to every real $x$. At zero, \[  G=(N-q-1)!S_{q+1}(\mu ),\quad G'=(N-q)!S_ q(\mu ),\quad G''=(N-q+1)!S_{q-1}(\mu ).  \] Consequently $S_{q-1}(\mu )S_{q+1}(\mu )\leq c_{N,q}S_ q(\mu )^2$. No sign restriction on $\mu $ or on these coefficients was used. For $q=N$, its left side is zero and the same assertion holds with $c_{N,N}=0$. Apply this to the list with $i,j$ deleted. Put $A=S_{q-1;ij}$, $B=S_{q;ij}$, $C=S_{q+1;ij}$ and $D_ i=S_{q;i}$, $D_ j=S_{q;j}$. Deleted-coordinate positivity gives $A,D_ i,D_ j\geq 0$: the required degrees are $q+1\leq m$. Splitting in the two omitted coordinates gives the exact identity \[  D_ iD_ j=A S_{q+1}(\lambda )+B^2-AC.  \] Since $S_{q+1}(\lambda )\geq 0$ and $AC\leq c_{N,q}B^2$, this is at least $(1-c_{N,q})B^2$. There is no division by $A$ or $D_ i$; all degenerate endpoints are therefore included. Equivalently one may first add $\epsilon \mathbf1$ and pass to the closed cone. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.1.7
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 12.1.7 . If smooth uniformly bounded admissible $u_ j\downarrow u$ and $v_ j\downarrow v$ are given, there are smooth uniformly bounded admissible $w_ j\downarrow \max \{ u,v\} $. For any chosen $\epsilon _ j>0$ decreasing to zero, they can be chosen to satisfy $w_ j=u_ j$ on $\{ u_ j-v_ j>\epsilon _ j\} $ and $w_ j=v_ j$ on $\{ v_ j-u_ j>\epsilon _ j\} $. For smooth functions $f,g$ on an open subset of $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega )}$, the regularized maximum $M_\epsilon (f,g)$ constructed below satisfies the same unshifted cone condition. Proof. Choose a nonnegative even smooth probability density $\zeta $ supported in $[-1,1]$, and set \[  r_\epsilon (t)=\int |t-\epsilon s|\zeta (s)\, \mathrm ds, \qquad M_\epsilon (x,y)=\tfrac 12(x+y+r_\epsilon (x-y)).  \] The function $r_\epsilon $ is smooth and convex, $|r_\epsilon '|\leq 1$, and $r_\epsilon (t)=|t|$ for $|t|\geq \epsilon $. Jensen's inequality and the triangle inequality give \[  \max \{ x,y\} \leq M_\epsilon (x,y) \leq \max \{ x,y\} +\epsilon /2.  \] Its partial derivatives in $x,y$ are nonnegative. For fixed $t$, $r_\epsilon (t)$ is an even convex function of $\epsilon $, since $\zeta $ is even. It is therefore nondecreasing for $\epsilon \geq 0$. Consequently $w_ j=M_{\epsilon _ j}(u_ j,v_ j)$ decreases pointwise to $\max \{ u,v\} $ and has the asserted equalities and bounds. Put $h_ j=u_ j-v_ j$ and $a_ j=(1+r_{\epsilon _ j}'(h_ j))/2$. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j =a_ j(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)+(1-a_ j)(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j) +\tfrac 12r_{\epsilon _ j}''(h_ j) \mathrm dh_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j.  \] Here $0\leq a_ j\leq 1$, and the last form is semipositive. Convexity of the cone and its stability under semipositive addition prove admissibility. For smooth local functions satisfying the unshifted cone condition, omit $\omega $ from this chain rule; the same argument proves preservation of that condition. The pointwise maximum is itself admissible: an upper test for it at a point is an upper test for a potential attaining the maximum there. Its canonical representative is thus the indicated pointwise maximum. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.1.8
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 12.1.8 . If bounded admissible $u,v$ satisfy $u\leq v$ almost everywhere with respect to $\omega ^ n$, then $u\leq v$ everywhere. Proof. By 12.1.7 , $w=\max \{ u,v\} $ is bounded admissible with its indicated canonical representative. Since $w=v$ almost everywhere, they represent the same distribution. The canonical subharmonic representative used in ( 12.2 ) is determined by that distribution. Thus $w=v$ pointwise, which is the assertion. $\square$

title: 12.2 Liouville and gradient estimates
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: 12.2 Liouville and gradient estimates The gradient estimate comes from rescaling a sequence at points of large gradient. The background then disappears, leaving a maximal function for a constant Euclidean cone. We first establish the Liouville theorem that rules out such a nonconstant limit. For this Euclidean argument allow $1\leq m\leq n$. Write $H(v)=(v_{i\bar j})$. A continuous real function $v$ on a Euclidean domain is admissible for $C_{n,m}$ if \[  \operatorname {tr}(QH(v))\geq 0 \quad \text{in distributions for every }Q\in C_{n,m}^*,  \] where $C_{n,m}^*=\{ Q:\operatorname {tr}(QA)\geq 0\text{ for all }A\in C_{n,m}\} $. For smooth functions this says $H(v)\in C_{n,m}$. Call $v$ maximal if every smooth lower test has Hessian outside the interior of $C_{n,m}$ at the contact point. Admissibility implies subharmonicity and is preserved by nonnegative convolution. The cone polynomial $S_ m$ increases under nonnegative matrix addition in the interior. Lemma 12.2.1 . Local uniform limits of admissible maximal functions are admissible and maximal. Suppose $v$ is admissible and maximal on a bounded open set $D$, and $h$ is smooth and admissible there. If both are continuous on $\overline D$ and $h\leq v$ on $\partial D$, then $h\leq v$ on $D$. Proof. The distributional inequalities pass to local uniform limits. If a lower test $h$ for the limit at $z_0$ has Hessian in the interior, subtract $\delta |z-z_0|^2$, for sufficiently small $\delta >0$, to make the contact strict while retaining interior admissibility near $z_0$. Interior minimum points for the approximants then tend to $z_0$. Adding the minimum value produces lower tests for them with Hessian in the interior, contradicting their maximality. For comparison choose $R$ with $\overline D\subset \{ |z|\leq R\} $. If $h>v$ somewhere, the function $h_\delta =h+\delta (|z|^2-R^2)$ still exceeds $v$ somewhere for small $\delta >0$ and is at most $v$ on the boundary. The negative minimum of $v-h_\delta $ is attained inside $D$. Since $H(h_\delta )=H(h)+\delta I$ belongs to the interior, adding the minimum value gives a forbidden lower test. This argument requires no regularity of the boundary. $\square$ Theorem 12.2.2 . Every bounded globally Lipschitz admissible function on $\mathbb C^ n$ that is maximal for $C_{n,m}$ is constant. Proof. For $m=1$, the distributional subharmonicity and the lower-test condition say that the function is a viscosity solution of the Laplace equation. The elementary equivalence with harmonicity and bounded harmonic Liouville give the conclusion. For $m=n$, admissibility is distributional plurisubharmonicity. The continuous representative is plurisubharmonic, and bounded plurisubharmonic Liouville applies. For a fixed $m\geq 2$, we therefore argue by induction on $n\geq m$. The reduction in dimension is particularly simple for this cone. For a Hermitian $(n-1)$-by-$(n-1)$ matrix $A$ and $m<n$, \[  S_ j(A\oplus 0)=S_ j(A),\qquad 1\leq j\leq m.  \] Consequently $A\oplus 0$ belongs to $C_{n,m}$, respectively its interior, exactly when $A$ belongs to $C_{n-1,m}$, respectively its interior. For the closed cones, the nonnegative inequalities characterize the closure: the expansion of $S_ j(\lambda +\delta \mathbf1)$ has nonnegative coefficients and a strictly positive $\delta ^ j$ term. If an admissible function is independent of $z_ n$, convolving it and using the block identity shows that the function in the remaining variables is admissible. Extending its lower tests independently of $z_ n$ shows that maximality also passes to dimension $n-1$. Suppose $v$ is nonconstant. Normalize $\inf v=0$, $\sup v=1$, and let $L$ be its Lipschitz constant. Choose a smooth radial nonnegative probability kernel $\eta $, supported in the closed unit ball and positive in its interior. Put \[  [f]_ r(x)=\int f(x+y)\eta _ r(y)\, \mathrm dy, \qquad \eta _ r(y)=r^{-2n}\eta (y/r),\qquad v_\epsilon =[v]_\epsilon .  \] Both $v$ and $v^2$ are subharmonic: for the second assertion use $\Delta (v_\epsilon ^2)=2v_\epsilon \Delta v_\epsilon +2|\nabla v_\epsilon |^2\geq 0$ and pass to the uniform limit. Their radial averages increase with $r$, by monotonicity of spherical means. For either $f=v$ or $f=v^2$, \[  |[f]_ r(x)-[f]_ r(y)| \leq \| f\| _\infty \| \eta _ r(\cdot -x)-\eta _ r(\cdot -y)\| _{L^1} \leq C\frac{|x-y|}{r}.  \] Thus the limiting average is independent of its center. The submean inequality makes it at least $f(x)$ for every $x$, and the upper bound is $\sup f=1$. Hence \[  [v]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1,\qquad [v^2]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1.  \] First suppose there are a fixed $\rho >0$, numbers $\epsilon _ k\downarrow 0$, $r_ k\to \infty $, points $x_ k$, and unit complex directions $\xi _ k$, such that \[  [v^2]_{r_ k}(x_ k)+[v]_\rho (x_ k)-2v(x_ k)\geq \frac43, \qquad \int _{B(x_ k,r_ k)}|\partial _{\xi _ k}v_{\epsilon _ k}|^2\, \mathrm dy\longrightarrow 0.  \] Translate and rotate to make $x_ k$ the origin and $\xi _ k$ the last complex direction. Compactness of uniformly bounded Lipschitz functions and the preceding lemma give a locally uniform limit $a$ that is admissible and maximal. The transformed mollifications have the same limit. Their last derivatives tend to zero in $L^2$ on every fixed ball, so $\partial _{z_ n}a=0$ in distributions. Since $a$ is real and continuous, it is independent of $z_ n$. The induction hypothesis gives $a=c\in [0,1]$. In the displayed gap inequality the first average is at most one, while the fixed-radius average and the value at the origin tend to $c$. This would give $4/3\leq 1-c\leq 1$, a contradiction. If this case does not occur, then for every fixed $\rho >0$ there is $C_\rho \geq 1$ such that \[  \int _{B(x,r)}|\partial _\xi v_\epsilon |^2\, \mathrm dy\geq C_\rho ^{-1}  \] for every unit complex direction $\xi $, whenever $0<\epsilon <C_\rho ^{-1}$, $r>C_\rho $ and $[v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_\rho (x)-2v(x)\geq 4/3$. Indeed, failure for every integer choice $C_\rho =k$ produces the sequences excluded above. The dependence on the fixed radius $\rho $ is retained. Translate so that $v(0)<1/12$. Choose $\rho $ with $[v]_\rho (0)>3/4$, then $r>C_\rho $ with $[v^2]_ r(0)>3/4$. The open set \[  D=\{ x:2v(x)<[v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_\rho (x)-4/3\}   \] contains the origin. On this set, $[v^2]_ r-c|z|^2$ is smooth and admissible for some fixed $c>0$. To prove this, decompose \[  H([v_\epsilon ^2]_ r) = [2v_\epsilon H(v_\epsilon )]_ r +[2(\partial _ i v_\epsilon \overline{\partial _ jv_\epsilon })_{ij}]_ r =A_\epsilon +B_\epsilon .  \] The matrix $A_\epsilon $ belongs to $C_{n,m}$ by convexity and $v_\epsilon \geq 0$. For every complex direction the unweighted energy on $B(x,r)$ is at least $C_\rho ^{-1}$. Since $|\nabla v_\epsilon |\leq L$, a sufficiently thin boundary annulus carries at most half that amount, uniformly in $x,\epsilon ,\xi $. On the remaining smaller closed ball $\eta _ r$ has a positive minimum. Therefore $B_\epsilon \geq c_0I$ on $D$, with $c_0>0$ independent of small $\epsilon $. Choose $0<c\leq c_0$. Then $A_\epsilon +B_\epsilon -cI\in C_{n,m}$. Uniform convergence of $v_\epsilon ^2$ and convolution at the fixed radius give convergence of every derivative to those of $[v^2]_ r$, proving the assertion. The smooth function \[  h=\tfrac 12\bigl ([v^2]_ r-c|z|^2+[v]_\rho -4/3\bigr )  \] is admissible on $D$. The set $D'=\{ v<h\} $ contains the origin, is bounded, and lies in $D$. Continuity gives $v=h$ on its boundary. The comparison lemma gives $h\leq v$ on $D'$, a contradiction. This completes the induction. $\square$ A trace bound now suffices to bound the gradient. The following statement permits a smooth background different from the metric. Proposition 12.2.3 . Fix a compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$, a smooth Hermitian form $\omega $, a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, an integer $2\leq m\leq n$, and constants $M,A,B>0$. There is a uniform bound for $\sup _ X|\partial u|_\omega $ over all smooth real $u$ such that $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$ and \[  |u|\leq M,\qquad \frac{\theta _ u^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n}\leq B, \qquad \operatorname {tr}_\omega \theta _ u \leq A\bigl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_\omega ^2\bigr ).  \] The bound requires no derivatives of the Hessian density. Proof. In local holomorphic coordinates write $\omega =\mathrm i g_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ and $\theta _ u=\mathrm i(b_{i\bar j}+\kappa u_{i\bar j})\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$, where the fixed constant $\kappa >0$ accounts for the convention for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. For eigenvalues $\lambda \in \Gamma _ m$, $m\geq 2$, one has \[  \sum _ i\lambda _ i^2 =\left(\sum _ i\lambda _ i\right)^2-2S_2(\lambda ) <\left(\sum _ i\lambda _ i\right)^2.  \] Thus the assumed trace estimate bounds every eigenvalue in absolute value by $A(1+\sup |\partial u|^2)$. Suppose contrary to the claim that a sequence $u_ j$ has maxima $R_ j=\sup |\partial u_ j|_\omega \to \infty $, attained at $x_ j$. Pass to $x_ j\to x_\infty $ and work in a fixed chart, changing coordinates linearly so that $g(x_\infty )=I$. If $y_ j$ is the coordinate of $x_ j$, set \begin{align*}  v_ j(z)& =u_ j(y_ j+z/R_ j),\qquad g_ j(z)=g(y_ j+z/R_ j),\\  E_ j(z)& =R_ j^{-2}b(y_ j+z/R_ j)+\kappa H(v_ j)(z). \end{align*} These are defined on balls with radii tending to infinity. On each fixed ball $g_ j\to I$, the smooth background term tends to zero, and $E_ j$ is uniformly bounded by the eigenvalue estimate. In particular $H(v_ j)$ and its Euclidean trace are uniformly bounded. Interior estimates for the fixed Euclidean Laplacian give local uniform $W^{2,q}$ bounds for every finite $q$. A diagonal subsequence converges in $C^1$ on compact subsets to a bounded globally Lipschitz $v$, with $|\partial v(0)|=1$. The Hermitian matrices $g_ j^{-1/2}E_ jg_ j^{-1/2}$ belong to the interior of $C_{n,m}$ and differ from $\kappa H(v_ j)$ by a term tending uniformly to zero on fixed balls. Pairing with any fixed matrix in the dual cone and passing in distributions proves that $v$ is admissible. Its equation is \[  \frac{S_ m(g_ j^{-1/2}E_ jg_ j^{-1/2})}{\binom nm} =R_ j^{-2m}\frac{\theta _{u_ j}^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} (y_ j+z/R_ j)\leq BR_ j^{-2m}.  \] We show maximality by lower tests, rather than by an unproved convergence assertion for variable-background Hessian measures. If a smooth lower test $\psi $ at $z_0$ had $H(\psi )(z_0)$ in the interior, choose a small $\delta >0$ so that $H(\psi )-\delta I$ remains there near $z_0$. Strictifying the contact by subtracting $\delta |z-z_0|^2$ gives interior minimum points $z_ j\to z_0$ for $v_ j$ minus this test. At those points \[  E_ j\geq R_ j^{-2}b+\kappa (H(\psi )-\delta I).  \] The matrix on the right, measured with $g_ j$, is uniformly inside the cone. Monotonicity of $S_ m$ under nonnegative addition gives a fixed positive lower bound for the left side of the preceding equation. This contradicts $BR_ j^{-2m}\to 0$. Hence $v$ is maximal. The Liouville theorem makes it constant, contradicting $|\partial v(0)|=1$. $\square$ On a fixed rescaled ball the metric varies by order $R_ j^{-1}$, whereas the background form enters with factor $R_ j^{-2}$. Thus this argument uses fixed smooth backgrounds and an upper bound for the Hessian density, without derivatives of that density.

On this set, $[v^2]_ r-c|z|^2$ is smooth and admissible for some fixed $c>0$. To prove this, decompose \[  H([v_\epsilon ^2]_ r) = [2v_\epsilon H(v_\epsilon )]_ r +[2(\partial _ i v_\epsilon \overline{\partial _ jv_\epsilon })_{ij}]_ r =A_\epsilon +B_\epsilon .  \] The matrix $A_\epsilon $ belongs to $C_{n,m}$ by convexity and $v_\epsilon \geq 0$. title: Proposition 12.2.3
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Proposition 12.2.3 . Fix a compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$, a smooth Hermitian form $\omega $, a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, an integer $2\leq m\leq n$, and constants $M,A,B>0$. There is a uniform bound for $\sup _ X|\partial u|_\omega $ over all smooth real $u$ such that $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$ and \[  |u|\leq M,\qquad \frac{\theta _ u^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n}\leq B, \qquad \operatorname {tr}_\omega \theta _ u \leq A\bigl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_\omega ^2\bigr ).  \] The bound requires no derivatives of the Hessian density. Proof. In local holomorphic coordinates write $\omega =\mathrm i g_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ and $\theta _ u=\mathrm i(b_{i\bar j}+\kappa u_{i\bar j})\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$, where the fixed constant $\kappa >0$ accounts for the convention for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. Suppose contrary to the claim that a sequence $u_ j$ has maxima $R_ j=\sup |\partial u_ j|_\omega \to \infty $, attained at $x_ j$. Pass to $x_ j\to x_\infty $ and work in a fixed chart, changing coordinates linearly so that $g(x_\infty )=I$. If $y_ j$ is the coordinate of $x_ j$, set \begin{align*}  v_ j(z)& =u_ j(y_ j+z/R_ j),\qquad g_ j(z)=g(y_ j+z/R_ j),\\  E_ j(z)& =R_ j^{-2}b(y_ j+z/R_ j)+\kappa H(v_ j)(z). \end{align*} These are defined on balls with radii tending to infinity. On each fixed ball $g_ j\to I$, the smooth background term tends to zero, and $E_ j$ is uniformly bounded by the eigenvalue estimate. In particular $H(v_ j)$ and its Euclidean trace are uniformly bounded. Interior estimates for the fixed Euclidean Laplacian give local uniform $W^{2,q}$ bounds for every finite $q$. A diagonal subsequence converges in $C^1$ on compact subsets to a bounded globally Lipschitz $v$, with $|\partial v(0)|=1$. The Hermitian matrices $g_ j^{-1/2}E_ jg_ j^{-1/2}$ belong to the interior of $C_{n,m}$ and differ from $\kappa H(v_ j)$ by a term tending uniformly to zero on fixed balls. Pairing with any fixed matrix in the dual cone and passing in distributions proves that $v$ is admissible. Its equation is \[  \frac{S_ m(g_ j^{-1/2}E_ jg_ j^{-1/2})}{\binom nm} =R_ j^{-2m}\frac{\theta _{u_ j}^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} (y_ j+z/R_ j)\leq BR_ j^{-2m}.  \] We show maximality by lower tests, rather than by an unproved convergence assertion for variable-background Hessian measures. If a smooth lower test $\psi $ at $z_0$ had $H(\psi )(z_0)$ in the interior, choose a small $\delta >0$ so that $H(\psi )-\delta I$ remains there near $z_0$. Strictifying the contact by subtracting $\delta |z-z_0|^2$ gives interior minimum points $z_ j\to z_0$ for $v_ j$ minus this test. At those points \[  E_ j\geq R_ j^{-2}b+\kappa (H(\psi )-\delta I).  \] The matrix on the right, measured with $g_ j$, is uniformly inside the cone. Monotonicity of $S_ m$ under nonnegative addition gives a fixed positive lower bound for the left side of the preceding equation. This contradicts $BR_ j^{-2m}\to 0$. Hence $v$ is maximal. The Liouville theorem makes it constant, contradicting $|\partial v(0)|=1$. $\square$

12.3 A trace estimate with a prescribed potential In a coordinate chart write $\omega =(\mathrm i/(2\pi ))g_{i ar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$. Covariant derivatives use the Chern connection of $g$. For a smooth strictly admissible $u$, put \[  H_{i ar j}=g_{i ar j}+u_{i ar j},\qquad W=g^{-1}H, \qquad L=\sum _ iF_ i
abla _{i ar i}  \] in a unitary frame diagonalizing $H$. Use $f,\mathcal F,S,Q$ from section 12.1 . Since $m\geq 2$, one has $|\lambda _ i|<S\leq n\lambda _1$. We shall estimate equations whose density involves another admissible potential $v$. In an approximation argument the derivatives of $v$ may diverge. The logarithmic weight below absorbs these derivatives using only uniform closeness to one fixed smooth comparison function. Lemma 12.3.1 . For $\epsilon >0$, let $\chi (t)=-(1/12)\log (2\epsilon -t)$ on $|t|\leq \epsilon $. Suppose $q=\chi '(t)\geq 8$. For any $a,b\in \mathbb C$, \[  \chi ''(t)|a-b|^2-(9q^2+2q)|a|^2-q|a| \geq q^2|a|^2-1-84q^2|b|^2.  \] In particular, let $v,\widetilde\varphi $ be smooth real functions with $|v-\widetilde\varphi |\leq \epsilon $, and take derivatives in an $\omega $-unitary frame. For a positive diagonal linearized operator with coefficients $B_ p$, setting $t=v-\widetilde\varphi $, $a=v_ p$, $b=\widetilde\varphi _ p$ and summing gives an error bounded by $(1+84q^2\sup |\partial \widetilde\varphi |_\omega ^2)\sum _ pB_ p$. The condition $q\geq 8$ holds throughout this interval if $\epsilon \leq 1/288$. Proof. Young's inequality gives $|a-b|^2\geq (7/8)|a|^2-7|b|^2$. Since $\chi ''=12q^2$, the coefficient of $|a|^2$ after subtracting $9q^2$ is $3q^2/2$. Moreover, $2q\leq q^2/4$ and $q|a|\leq q^2|a|^2/4+1$. The remaining coefficient is at least $q^2$, and the error involving $b$ is $84q^2|b|^2$. Finally $q\geq 1/(36\epsilon )$, which proves the last assertion. The weighted version follows by summing the scalar inequality with positive coefficients. $\square$ Lemma 12.3.2 . Suppose $f\geq f_0>0$, $C_ H,C_ G\geq 0$, and $q$ satisfies \[  q\geq 8,\qquad q\geq  rac{2nm!C_ H}{f_0},\qquad q^2\geq  rac{4m!C_ G}{f_0}.  \] For $0\leq r\leq 1/2$, $a,b\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $M\in C_{n,m}$, put $W_ M=\sum _ iF_ iM_{i ar i}$ and  egin{align*}  E={}& q(W_ M-\mathcal F)- rac{C_ H}{\lambda _1}|M_{1 ar1}| - rac{C_ G}{S}\sum _ i|a_ i|^2\ & +\sum _ iF_ i igl (12q^2|a_ i-b_ i|^2 -(9q^2+2q+rq^2)|a_ i|^2-q|a_ i| igr ). \end{align*} Then \[  E\geq  rac q2W_ M+ rac{q^2}{4}\sum _ iF_ i|a_ i|^2 -(q+1+84q^2\max _ i|b_ i|^2)\mathcal F.  \] Proof. 12.3.1 gives \[  12q^2|a_ i-b_ i|^2-(9q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2-q|a_ i| \geq q^2|a_ i|^2-1-84q^2|b_ i|^2.  \] Subtracting $rq^2|a_ i|^2$ leaves at least $q^2|a_ i|^2/2$. Since $S\leq n\lambda _1$, 12.1.3 and the hypothesis on $q$ imply \[   rac{C_ H}{\lambda _1}|M_{1 ar1}| \leq  rac{nC_ H}{S}\operatorname {tr}M\leq  rac q2 W_ M.  \] The lower bound for each $F_ i$ similarly gives \[   rac{C_ G}{S}\sum _ i|a_ i|^2 \leq  rac{q^2}{4}\sum _ iF_ i|a_ i|^2.  \] Combining these inequalities yields the assertion. The error depends on the fixed comparison vector $b$ and is not discarded. $\square$ For $\Psi (t)=-2At+(A	au /2)t^2$, $|t|\leq M$ and $	au M\leq 1$, one has $-3A\leq \Psi '\leq -A$. The two cases for the smallest eigenvalue will reduce to the following numerical estimate. Proposition 12.3.3 . Fix $a>0$, $b,d,e\geq 0$ and $0<\delta <1$. Let $K\geq 1$ and $0<f_0\leq f\leq f_1$. Suppose the following inequality holds according to the sign of $\lambda _ n+\delta \lambda _1$: If $\lambda _ n<-\delta \lambda _1$, then $0\geq aQ/K-bK\mathcal F-d\lambda _1\mathcal F-e$. If $\lambda _ n\geq -\delta \lambda _1$, then $0\geq aQ/K-bKF_1-e$. Then $S\leq CK$ and $\lambda _1\leq CK$, with $C$ depending only on the fixed displayed data and $n,m$. Proof. In the first case, symmetry and concavity of $F$ imply $F_ n\geq F_ i$ for every $i$, so $Q\geq \delta ^2\lambda _1^2\mathcal F/n$. To see the derivative ordering, apply monotonicity of the gradient of a concave function to $\lambda $ and the vector obtained by exchanging its $i$th and $n$th coordinates. Divide the assumed inequality by $K\mathcal F$, use $\mathcal F\geq 1$, and set $t=\lambda _1/K$. It yields $a\delta ^2t^2/n\leq b+dt+e$, which bounds $t$. Since $S\leq n\lambda _1$, the trace bound follows. In the second case, either $\lambda _1^2\leq 2bK^2/a$, which gives the same trace bound directly, or $aQ/(2K)\geq bKF_1$. The assumed inequality then gives $Q\leq 2eK/a$. 12.1.4 bounds $S$ by a multiple of $K$. Finally the $\Gamma _2$ identity gives $\lambda _1\leq (\sum _ i\lambda _ i^2)^{1/2}<S$. $\square$ The geometric computation uses a lower support for the largest eigenvalue, as in the second-order argument for the Gauduchon equation. The perturbation affects only this support; derivatives of $F$ remain evaluated at the original matrix $W$. Lemma 12.3.4 . At a point with $\lambda _1>1$, the largest eigenvalue has a smooth local lower support $\widetilde\lambda $, equal to $\lambda _1$ at the point, for which \[  L\log \widetilde\lambda \geq  rac{f_{1 ar1}}{\lambda _1}+N -\sum _ iF_ i|Z_ i|^2-C\mathcal F - rac{C}{\lambda _1^2}\sum _ iF_ i|H_{1 ar1;i}|,  \] where \[  N=- rac{D^2F_ W(
abla _1W,
abla _{ ar1}W)}{\lambda _1}, \qquad Z_ i= rac{H_{i ar1;1}}{\lambda _1}.  \] Here $C$ depends only on the fixed metric. Derivatives of $F$ are evaluated at $W$. Proof. Choose a smooth unitary frame parallel for the Chern connection at the point and diagonalizing $H$ there. The positive semidefinite tensor $B$, diagonal in this frame with entries $0, eta ,\ldots , eta $, satisfies $
abla B=0$ at the point and $|
abla ^2B|\leq C eta $. For $0< eta <1$, the largest eigenvalue of $W-B$ is simple, lies below that of $W$, and agrees with it at the point. This gives the required smooth support. Only its largest eigenvalue is perturbed; the equation still uses $F(W)$. Differentiating the normalized eigenvector equation gives \[  \widetilde\lambda _{;k}=H_{1 ar1;k},\qquad \widetilde\lambda _{;k ar k}\geq H_{1 ar1;k ar k} +\sum _{p>1} rac{|H_{p ar1;k}|^2+|H_{1 ar p;k}|^2}{\lambda _1-\lambda _ p+ eta }-C eta .  \] The denominators are at most $(n+1)\lambda _1$. Let $U=\partial  ar\partial u$, and take $T^ p_{ki}=\Gamma ^ p_{ki}-\Gamma ^ p_{ik}$. The first commutations are \[  U_{i ar j;k}=U_{k ar j;i}-T^ p_{ki}U_{p ar j},\qquad U_{i ar j; ar k}=U_{i ar k; ar j} -\overline{T^ p_{kj}}U_{i ar p}.  \] Apply the first identity, commute one mixed pair of covariant derivatives, and apply the conjugate identity. The result has the form \[  U_{1 ar1;k ar k}=U_{k ar k;1 ar1} -2\operatorname {Re}\sum _ p U_{k ar p;1}\overline{T^ p_{k1}}+E_ k, \qquad |E_ k|\leq C|U|.  \] Indeed the mixed commutator contracts curvature with $U$, differentiating the first torsion coefficient contracts $
abla T$ with $U$, and the second use of the first identities produces contractions of two torsion coefficients with $U$. Thus all the omitted terms satisfy the displayed bound. Since $g$ is parallel, the same derivative relations apply to $H$ apart from the explicit $g$ terms in the first commutation. At the diagonal point $|U|\leq C\lambda _1$. For $p>1$, rewrite $U_{k ar p;1}=U_{1 ar p;k}+T^ j_{k1}U_{j ar p}$. Young's inequality absorbs its third derivative into the positive eigenvalue square, at the cost of $C\lambda _1$. Consequently \[  \widetilde\lambda _{;k ar k}\geq H_{k ar k;1 ar1} -2\operatorname {Re}(H_{k ar1;1}\overline{T^1_{k1}})-C\lambda _1.  \] Differentiate $F(W)=f$ twice and sum this inequality with weights $F_ k$. Write $D_ k=H_{1 ar1;k}$ and $t_ k=T^1_{k1}$. The first commutation, using $U_{1 ar1}=\lambda _1-1$, gives \[  D_ k=\lambda _1Z_ k-(\lambda _1-1)t_ k.  \] The negative logarithmic square and the remaining torsion term therefore satisfy \[  - rac{|D_ k|^2}{\lambda _1^2}-2\operatorname {Re}(Z_ k ar t_ k) \geq -|Z_ k|^2-C-C\lambda _1^{-2}|D_ k|.  \] For example, expanding the left side leaves $-|Z_ k|^2-2\lambda _1^{-1}\operatorname {Re}(Z_ k ar t_ k)-(1-\lambda _1^{-1})^2|t_ k|^2$, and $\lambda _1|Z_ k|\leq |D_ k|+C\lambda _1$. This proves the claim, uniformly for small $ eta $. $\square$ Lemma 12.3.5 . Put $s=|\partial u|_ g^2$ and $K=1+\sup _ Xs$. For every $\eta >0$ one has \[  Ls\geq \sum _{i,k}F_ i(|u_{ki}|^2+|u_{k ar i}|^2) +2\operatorname {Re}\sum _ k f_ k u_{ ar k}-\eta Q-C_\eta K\mathcal F.  \] The constant depends only on the metric and $\eta $. Proof. Differentiate the squared norm using metric compatibility. Its quadratic part is the displayed sum. Commuting the remaining third derivatives gives \[  u_{ki ar i}=u_{i ar i;k}-T^ p_{ik}u_{p ar i} +R^ p_{i ar i k}u_ p, \qquad u_{ ar k i ar i}=u_{i ar i; ar k} -\overline{T^ p_{ik}}u_{i ar p}.  \] The first differentiated equation is $\sum _ iF_ i u_{i ar i;k}=f_ k$, because the background $g$ is parallel. At the diagonal point the torsion errors are bounded by $C\sqrt K\sum _ iF_ i(|\lambda _ i|+1)$, and the curvature errors by $CK\mathcal F$. Use \[  C\sqrt K F_ i|\lambda _ i| \leq \eta ' F_ i\lambda _ i^2+C_{\eta '}KF_ i  \] with a sufficiently small $\eta '$ for the finite sum. This gives the asserted bound. $\square$ Proposition 12.3.6 . Fix $M,B\geq 1$ and a smooth real $h(x,t)$ on a neighborhood of $X	imes [-B-1,B+1]$. There is $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, depending only on $M,B,h,\omega ,n,m$, with the following property. For every smooth real $\varphi $ with $\| \varphi \| _\infty \leq B$, there is $C<\infty $, depending also on its $C^2$ norm, such that if smooth real $u,v$ satisfy  egin{gather*}  W\in \Gamma _ m,\qquad I+v_{i ar j}\in \overline{\Gamma _ m},\  \| u\| _\infty \leq M,\qquad \| v-\varphi \| _\infty \leq \varepsilon ,\  F(W)=\exp  igl ((u+h(x,v))/m igr ), \end{gather*} then \[  \operatorname {tr}_\omega (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u) \leq C igl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_ g^2 igr ).  \] The cone condition on $v$ is understood in a unitary frame. The tolerance $\varepsilon $ uses no derivatives of $\varphi $; the constant $C$ uses no derivatives of $v$. Proof. For $\varepsilon \leq 1$ the density has fixed bounds $0<f_0\leq f\leq f_1$. Its first derivative is \[  f_ k= rac fm(u_ k+h_ k(x,v)+h_ t(x,v)v_ k).  \] The nonnegative $u_ k$ contribution can be dropped from the gradient lemma. At a point with $\lambda _1>1$, differentiating once more gives \[  f_{1 ar1}\geq -C(1+|\partial v|^2+|1+v_{1 ar1}|).  \] Here $u_{1 ar1}=\lambda _1-1>0$, the square from differentiating the exponential is nonnegative, and all derivatives of $h$ are bounded on the fixed interval. Set  egin{align*}  \Phi (s)& =-	frac 12\log (1-s/(2K)),\qquad \Psi (u)=-2Au+(A	au /2)u^2,\  \chi (t)& =-	frac 1{12}\log (2\varepsilon -t),\qquad 	au =(M+1)^{-1}. \end{align*} Then $(4K)^{-1}\leq \Phi '\leq (2K)^{-1}$, $\Phi ''=2(\Phi ')^2$, $-3A\leq \Psi '\leq -A$, $\Psi ''=A	au $, and $q=\chi '$ lies between $1/(36\varepsilon )$ and $1/(12\varepsilon )$, with $\chi ''=12q^2$. Take a maximum of $G=\log \lambda _1+\Phi (s)+\Psi (u)+\chi (v-\varphi )$ and use the smooth lower support from the eigenvalue lemma. At this point put \[  a_ i=v_ i,\quad b_ i=\varphi _ i,\quad P_ v=I+v_{i ar j},\quad W_ v=\sum _ iF_ i(P_ v)_{i ar i},\quad x_ i=\Phi 's_ i,\quad y_ i=\Psi 'u_ i.  \] The first derivative condition and the torsion identity give \[  H_{1 ar1;i}/\lambda _1=-x_ i-y_ i-q(a_ i-b_ i),\qquad Z_ i=-x_ i-y_ i-qa_ i+e_ i,\quad e_ i=qb_ i+(1-\lambda _1^{-1})T^1_{i1}.  \] Thus $|e_ i|\leq E_0$, with $E_0$ independent of $A$ and of derivatives of $v$. Its $y_ i$ term costs at most $\Psi ''\sum _ iF_ i|u_ i|^2/4+\mathcal F$ whenever $\lambda _1\geq L_0(A)$, where $L_0(A)$ is fixed independently of $K,v$. Its $qa_ i$ term costs at most $q\sum _ iF_ i|a_ i|$ when $\lambda _1$ exceeds a fixed metric constant; its $qb_ i$ term costs $C\mathcal F$. If either eigenvalue threshold fails, the required bound follows directly. Otherwise, with fixed $C_ H,C_ G,C_0$ independent of $A$, the second derivative condition gives  egin{align*}  0\geq {}& N-\sum _ iF_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _ iF_ i|x_ i|^2 +	frac 34\Psi ''\sum _ iF_ i|u_ i|^2+ rac{Q}{32K} +\Psi '(f-\mathcal F)-C_0\mathcal F\ & +q(W_ v-\mathcal F)- rac{C_ H}{\lambda _1}|(P_ v)_{1 ar1}| - rac{C_ G}S\sum _ i|a_ i|^2 +\sum _ iF_ i igl (12q^2|a_ i-b_ i|^2-q|a_ i| igr ). \end{align*} The fixed $qL\varphi $ term is included in $C_0$. This choice precedes that of $A$. First suppose $\lambda _ n<-\delta \lambda _1$. Concavity gives $N\geq 0$, and \[  -|Z_ i|^2+2|x_ i|^2 \geq -6|y_ i|^2-6q^2|a_ i|^2-6E_0^2.  \] The derivative-absorption lemma applies after decreasing the right side further by $(3q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$. For $i\in I$, $\lambda _ i<\lambda _1$ and \[   rac{F_ i-F_1}{\lambda _1-\lambda _ i} \geq  rac{(1-\delta )F_ i}{(1+\delta )\lambda _1} \geq  rac{(1-2\delta )F_ i}{\lambda _1}.  \] The spectral formula for $D^2F$, including its nonpositive diagonal part, therefore gives $N\geq (1-2\delta )\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2$. Then the first coefficient is at most $\Psi ''/2$, and $r\leq 1/2$. On the complementary indices the preceding elementary bound gives \[  -\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|x_ i|^2 \geq - rac{54A^2+6nE_0^2}{\delta }KF_1 -6q^2\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|a_ i|^2.  \] Apply the derivative-absorption lemma, with penalty $r$ on $I$ and zero outside it; adding the unused negative $(9q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$ on $I$, and $(3q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$ off $I$, only decreases its input. The constants in its fixed-comparison error and the high-index $rE_0^2$ error are bounded independently of $A,\delta $. Enlarge $C_*$ to include them. We obtain \[  0\geq  rac{Q}{32K}- rac{54A^2+6nE_0^2}{\delta }KF_1 +(A-C_*)\mathcal F-3Af_1.  \] Take $A\geq \max \{ 1,C_*+1\} $, then fix the displayed $\delta $ and the threshold $L_0(A)$. Both case inequalities now satisfy the hypotheses of the conditional eigenvalue proposition, with fixed data. Hence $\lambda _1\leq CK$ at the maximum point. Finally $\Phi ,\Psi ,\chi $ have oscillations bounded independently of $K$ and of derivatives of $v$. Comparing $G$ at any other point with its maximum gives the same bound for $\lambda _1$ everywhere. Since $S\leq n\lambda _1$, this proves the trace estimate. $\square$ Corollary 12.3.7 . Under the hypotheses of the proposition, one has \[  \sup _ X|\partial u|_ g+\sup _ X|\partial  ar\partial u|_ g\leq C,  \] with a constant depending on the same fixed data and no derivatives of $v$. Proof. The Hessian density is $F(W)^ m\leq f_1^ m$. Apply the trace-to-gradient blowup proposition to the fixed background $	heta =\omega $ and the preceding trace estimate. It gives the uniform gradient bound. The trace is then uniformly bounded, and the $\Gamma _2$ identity bounds the absolute value of every eigenvalue of $W$ by its trace. Subtracting the identity matrix gives the complex-Hessian bound. $\square$ The bound controls the complex Hessian. An estimate for all entries of the real Hessian is not needed: the Euclidean Laplacian supplies finite $L^ p$ estimates for those derivatives.

In the first case, symmetry and concavity of $F$ imply $F_ n\geq F_ i$ for every $i$, so $Q\geq \delta ^2\lambda _1^2\mathcal F/n$. To see the derivative ordering, apply monotonicity of the gradient of a concave function to $\lambda $ and the vector obtained by exchanging its $i$th and $n$th coordinates. Divide the assumed inequality by $K\mathcal F$, use $\mathcal F\geq 1$, and set $t=\lambda _1/K$. It yields $a\delta ^2t^2/n\leq b+dt+e$, which bounds $t$. Since $S\leq n\lambda _1$, the trace bound follows. In the second case, either $\lambda _1^2\leq 2bK^2/a$, which gives the same trace bound directly, or $aQ/(2K)\geq bKF_1$. The assumed inequality then gives $Q\leq 2eK/a$. 12.1.4 bounds $S$ by a multiple of $K$. Finally the $\Gamma _2$ identity gives $\lambda _1\leq (\sum _ i\lambda _ i^2)^{1/2}<S$. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.3.4
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text:
Lemma 12.3.4 . At a point with $\lambda _1>1$, the largest eigenvalue has a smooth local lower support $\widetilde\lambda $, equal to $\lambda _1$ at the point, for which \[  L\log \widetilde\lambda \geq  rac{f_{1 ar1}}{\lambda _1}+N -\sum _ iF_ i|Z_ i|^2-C\mathcal F - rac{C}{\lambda _1^2}\sum _ iF_ i|H_{1 ar1;i}|,  \] where \[  N=- rac{D^2F_ W(
abla _1W,
abla _{ ar1}W)}{\lambda _1}, \qquad Z_ i= rac{H_{i ar1;1}}{\lambda _1}.  \] Here $C$ depends only on the fixed metric. Derivatives of $F$ are evaluated at $W$. Proof. Choose a smooth unitary frame parallel for the Chern connection at the point and diagonalizing $H$ there. The positive semidefinite tensor $B$, diagonal in this frame with entries $0, eta ,\ldots , eta $, satisfies $
abla B=0$ at the point and $|
abla ^2B|\leq C eta $. For $0< eta <1$, the largest eigenvalue of $W-B$ is simple, lies below that of $W$, and agrees with it at the point. This gives the required smooth support. Only its largest eigenvalue is perturbed; the equation still uses $F(W)$. Differentiating the normalized eigenvector equation gives \[  \widetilde\lambda _{;k}=H_{1 ar1;k},\qquad \widetilde\lambda _{;k ar k}\geq H_{1 ar1;k ar k} +\sum _{p>1} rac{|H_{p ar1;k}|^2+|H_{1 ar p;k}|^2}{\lambda _1-\lambda _ p+ eta }-C eta .  \] The denominators are at most $(n+1)\lambda _1$. Let $U=\partial  ar\partial u$, and take $T^ p_{ki}=\Gamma ^ p_{ki}-\Gamma ^ p_{ik}$. The first commutations are \[  U_{i ar j;k}=U_{k ar j;i}-T^ p_{ki}U_{p ar j},\qquad U_{i ar j; ar k}=U_{i ar k; ar j} -\overline{T^ p_{kj}}U_{i ar p}.  \] Apply the first identity, commute one mixed pair of covariant derivatives, and apply the conjugate identity. The result has the form \[  U_{1 ar1;k ar k}=U_{k ar k;1 ar1} -2\operatorname {Re}\sum _ p U_{k ar p;1}\overline{T^ p_{k1}}+E_ k, \qquad |E_ k|\leq C|U|.  \] Indeed the mixed commutator contracts curvature with $U$, differentiating the first torsion coefficient contracts $
abla T$ with $U$, and the second use of the first identities produces contractions of two torsion coefficients with $U$. Thus all the omitted terms satisfy the displayed bound. Since $g$ is parallel, the same derivative relations apply to $H$ apart from the explicit $g$ terms in the first commutation. At the diagonal point $|U|\leq C\lambda _1$. For $p>1$, rewrite $U_{k ar p;1}=U_{1 ar p;k}+T^ j_{k1}U_{j ar p}$. Young's inequality absorbs its third derivative into the positive eigenvalue square, at the cost of $C\lambda _1$. Consequently \[  \widetilde\lambda _{;k ar k}\geq H_{k ar k;1 ar1} -2\operatorname {Re}(H_{k ar1;1}\overline{T^1_{k1}})-C\lambda _1.  \] Differentiate $F(W)=f$ twice and sum this inequality with weights $F_ k$. Write $D_ k=H_{1 ar1;k}$ and $t_ k=T^1_{k1}$. The first commutation, using $U_{1 ar1}=\lambda _1-1$, gives \[  D_ k=\lambda _1Z_ k-(\lambda _1-1)t_ k.  \] The negative logarithmic square and the remaining torsion term therefore satisfy \[  - rac{|D_ k|^2}{\lambda _1^2}-2\operatorname {Re}(Z_ k ar t_ k) \geq -|Z_ k|^2-C-C\lambda _1^{-2}|D_ k|.  \] For example, expanding the left side leaves $-|Z_ k|^2-2\lambda _1^{-1}\operatorname {Re}(Z_ k ar t_ k)-(1-\lambda _1^{-1})^2|t_ k|^2$, and $\lambda _1|Z_ k|\leq |D_ k|+C\lambda _1$. This proves the claim, uniformly for small $ eta $. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.3.5
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 12.3.5 . Put $s=|\partial u|_ g^2$ and $K=1+\sup _ Xs$. For every $\eta >0$ one has \[  Ls\geq \sum _{i,k}F_ i(|u_{ki}|^2+|u_{k\bar i}|^2) +2\operatorname {Re}\sum _ k f_ k u_{\bar k}-\eta Q-C_\eta K\mathcal F.  \] The constant depends only on the metric and $\eta $. Proof. Differentiate the squared norm using metric compatibility. Its quadratic part is the displayed sum. Commuting the remaining third derivatives gives \[  u_{ki\bar i}=u_{i\bar i;k}-T^ p_{ik}u_{p\bar i} +R^ p_{i\bar i k}u_ p, \qquad u_{\bar k i\bar i}=u_{i\bar i;\bar k} -\overline{T^ p_{ik}}u_{i\bar p}.  \] The first differentiated equation is $\sum _ iF_ i u_{i\bar i;k}=f_ k$, because the background $g$ is parallel. At the diagonal point the torsion errors are bounded by $C\sqrt K\sum _ iF_ i(|\lambda _ i|+1)$, and the curvature errors by $CK\mathcal F$. Use \[  C\sqrt K F_ i|\lambda _ i| \leq \eta ' F_ i\lambda _ i^2+C_{\eta '}KF_ i  \] with a sufficiently small $\eta '$ for the finite sum. This gives the asserted bound. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.3.6
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text:
Proposition 12.3.6 . Fix $M,B\geq 1$ and a smooth real $h(x,t)$ on a neighborhood of $X	imes [-B-1,B+1]$. There is $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, depending only on $M,B,h,\omega ,n,m$, with the following property. For every smooth real $\varphi $ with $\| \varphi \| _\infty \leq B$, there is $C<\infty $, depending also on its $C^2$ norm, such that if smooth real $u,v$ satisfy  egin{gather*}  W\in \Gamma _ m,\qquad I+v_{i ar j}\in \overline{\Gamma _ m},\  \| u\| _\infty \leq M,\qquad \| v-\varphi \| _\infty \leq \varepsilon ,\  F(W)=\exp  igl ((u+h(x,v))/m igr ), \end{gather*} then \[  \operatorname {tr}_\omega (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u) \leq C igl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_ g^2 igr ).  \] The cone condition on $v$ is understood in a unitary frame. The tolerance $\varepsilon $ uses no derivatives of $\varphi $; the constant $C$ uses no derivatives of $v$. Proof. For $\varepsilon \leq 1$ the density has fixed bounds $0<f_0\leq f\leq f_1$. Its first derivative is \[  f_ k= rac fm(u_ k+h_ k(x,v)+h_ t(x,v)v_ k).  \] The nonnegative $u_ k$ contribution can be dropped from the gradient lemma. At a point with $\lambda _1>1$, differentiating once more gives \[  f_{1 ar1}\geq -C(1+|\partial v|^2+|1+v_{1 ar1}|).  \] Here $u_{1 ar1}=\lambda _1-1>0$, the square from differentiating the exponential is nonnegative, and all derivatives of $h$ are bounded on the fixed interval. Set  egin{align*}  \Phi (s)& =-	frac 12\log (1-s/(2K)),\qquad \Psi (u)=-2Au+(A	au /2)u^2,\  \chi (t)& =-	frac 1{12}\log (2\varepsilon -t),\qquad 	au =(M+1)^{-1}. \end{align*} Then $(4K)^{-1}\leq \Phi '\leq (2K)^{-1}$, $\Phi ''=2(\Phi ')^2$, $-3A\leq \Psi '\leq -A$, $\Psi ''=A	au $, and $q=\chi '$ lies between $1/(36\varepsilon )$ and $1/(12\varepsilon )$, with $\chi ''=12q^2$. Take a maximum of $G=\log \lambda _1+\Phi (s)+\Psi (u)+\chi (v-\varphi )$ and use the smooth lower support from the eigenvalue lemma. At this point put \[  a_ i=v_ i,\quad b_ i=\varphi _ i,\quad P_ v=I+v_{i ar j},\quad W_ v=\sum _ iF_ i(P_ v)_{i ar i},\quad x_ i=\Phi 's_ i,\quad y_ i=\Psi 'u_ i.  \] The first derivative condition and the torsion identity give \[  H_{1 ar1;i}/\lambda _1=-x_ i-y_ i-q(a_ i-b_ i),\qquad Z_ i=-x_ i-y_ i-qa_ i+e_ i,\quad e_ i=qb_ i+(1-\lambda _1^{-1})T^1_{i1}.  \] Thus $|e_ i|\leq E_0$, with $E_0$ independent of $A$ and of derivatives of $v$. We make the initial maximum inequality explicit. The gradient lemma and the identity $u_{i ar j}=(\lambda _ i-1)\delta _{ij}$ give, after multiplication by $\Phi '$, \[  \Phi 'Ls\geq  rac1{8K}\sum _{i,k}F_ i(|u_{ki}|^2+|u_{k ar i}|^2) + rac{3}{64K}Q-C\mathcal F - rac{C_ G'}S\sum _ i|a_ i|^2.  \] To justify the constants, retain half of the positive quadratic term, use $(\lambda _ i-1)^2\geq \lambda _ i^2/2-1$, and choose the torsion parameter to cost at most $Q/(128K)$. The remaining density-gradient error is $C|a|/\sqrt K$. Young's inequality bounds it by $C_ G'|a|^2/S+cS/K$; choose $C_ G'$ large enough that the quadratic coercivity lemma absorbs $cS/K$ by $Q/(128K)$, with a fixed constant error. This leaves $3Q/(64K)$. The linear $H_{1 ar1;i}$ error in the eigenvalue lemma is estimated using the first derivative condition. Its $x_ i$ term costs at most half of the retained quadratic sum and $C\mathcal F$. Its $y_ i$ term costs at most $\Psi ''\sum _ iF_ i|u_ i|^2/4+\mathcal F$ whenever $\lambda _1\geq L_0(A)$, where $L_0(A)$ is fixed independently of $K,v$. Its $qa_ i$ term costs at most $q\sum _ iF_ i|a_ i|$ when $\lambda _1$ exceeds a fixed metric constant; its $qb_ i$ term costs $C\mathcal F$. If either eigenvalue threshold fails, the required bound follows directly. Otherwise, with fixed $C_ H,C_ G,C_0$ independent of $A$, the second derivative condition gives  egin{align*}  0\geq {}& N-\sum _ iF_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _ iF_ i|x_ i|^2 +	frac 34\Psi ''\sum _ iF_ i|u_ i|^2+ rac{Q}{32K} +\Psi '(f-\mathcal F)-C_0\mathcal F\ & +q(W_ v-\mathcal F)- rac{C_ H}{\lambda _1}|(P_ v)_{1 ar1}| - rac{C_ G}S\sum _ i|a_ i|^2 +\sum _ iF_ i igl (12q^2|a_ i-b_ i|^2-q|a_ i| igr ). \end{align*} The fixed $qL\varphi $ term is included in $C_0$. Choose $\varepsilon $ so the lower bound for $q$ meets all thresholds of the derivative-absorption lemma. These thresholds depend on $M,B,h$ and the metric, and not on derivatives of $\varphi $. This choice precedes that of $A$. First suppose $\lambda _ n<-\delta \lambda _1$. Concavity gives $N\geq 0$, and \[  -|Z_ i|^2+2|x_ i|^2 \geq -6|y_ i|^2-6q^2|a_ i|^2-6E_0^2.  \] The derivative-absorption lemma applies after decreasing the right side further by $(3q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$. Drop its nonnegative reserves and $\Psi ''$ term. Since $\Psi 'f\geq -3Af_1$, this gives \[  0\geq  rac{Q}{32K}-(54A^2+C_*)K\mathcal F-3Af_1,  \] where $C_*$ is fixed independently of $A,\delta $. Now suppose $\lambda _ n\geq -\delta \lambda _1$, and let $I=\{ i:F_ i>\delta ^{-1}F_1\} $. For $i\in I$, $\lambda _ i<\lambda _1$ and \[   rac{F_ i-F_1}{\lambda _1-\lambda _ i} \geq  rac{(1-\delta )F_ i}{(1+\delta )\lambda _1} \geq  rac{(1-2\delta )F_ i}{\lambda _1}.  \] The spectral formula for $D^2F$, including its nonpositive diagonal part, therefore gives $N\geq (1-2\delta )\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2$. This uses the original eigenvalues; repeated eigenvalues do not occur in $I$. Using $x_ i=-Z_ i-y_ i-qa_ i+e_ i$ and $|z+w|^2\geq \delta |z|^2-\delta |w|^2/(1-\delta )$, one obtains  egin{align*}  N-\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|x_ i|^2 & \geq - rac{4\delta (\Psi ')^2}{1-\delta }\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|u_ i|^2\ & \quad -r q^2\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|a_ i|^2-rE_0^2\mathcal F, \qquad r= rac{8\delta }{1-\delta }. \end{align*} Choose $\delta \leq \min \{ 1/17,	au /(72A+	au )\} $. Then the first coefficient is at most $\Psi ''/2$, and $r\leq 1/2$. On the complementary indices the preceding elementary bound gives \[  -\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|x_ i|^2 \geq - rac{54A^2+6nE_0^2}{\delta }KF_1 -6q^2\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|a_ i|^2.  \] Apply the derivative-absorption lemma, with penalty $r$ on $I$ and zero outside it; adding the unused negative $(9q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$ on $I$, and $(3q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$ off $I$, only decreases its input. The constants in its fixed-comparison error and the high-index $rE_0^2$ error are bounded independently of $A,\delta $. Enlarge $C_*$ to include them. We obtain \[  0\geq  rac{Q}{32K}- rac{54A^2+6nE_0^2}{\delta }KF_1 +(A-C_*)\mathcal F-3Af_1.  \] Take $A\geq \max \{ 1,C_*+1\} $, then fix the displayed $\delta $ and the threshold $L_0(A)$. Both case inequalities now satisfy the hypotheses of the conditional eigenvalue proposition, with fixed data. Hence $\lambda _1\leq CK$ at the maximum point. Finally $\Phi ,\Psi ,\chi $ have oscillations bounded independently of $K$ and of derivatives of $v$. Comparing $G$ at any other point with its maximum gives the same bound for $\lambda _1$ everywhere. Since $S\leq n\lambda _1$, this proves the trace estimate. $\square$

title: Corollary 12.3.7
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Corollary 12.3.7 . Under the hypotheses of the proposition, one has \[  \sup _ X|\partial u|_ g+\sup _ X|\partial \bar\partial u|_ g\leq C,  \] with a constant depending on the same fixed data and no derivatives of $v$. Proof. The Hessian density is $F(W)^ m\leq f_1^ m$. Apply the trace-to-gradient blowup proposition to the fixed background $\theta =\omega $ and the preceding trace estimate. It gives the uniform gradient bound. The trace is then uniformly bounded, and the $\Gamma _2$ identity bounds the absolute value of every eigenvalue of $W$ by its trace. Subtracting the identity matrix gives the complex-Hessian bound. $\square$

title: 12.4 Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions
search_title: Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: 12.4 Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions Uniform complex-Hessian bounds give enough compactness both to pass the nonlinear products to a limit and to make the Hessian root uniformly elliptic. In coordinates use the metric matrix $g$ of the preceding section and write $H(u)=(u_{i\bar j})$. Coefficient products with bounded measurable factors will be identified with currents by convolution. Lemma 12.4.1 . Suppose $u_ j$ is smooth, \[  \sup _ j\bigl (\| u_ j\| _\infty +\| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\| _{L^\infty }\bigr )<\infty , \qquad u_ j\longrightarrow u\quad \hbox{uniformly on }X.  \] Then $u\in W^{2,p}(X)$ for every $1<p<\infty $, its distributional complex Hessian has bounded coefficients, and $u_ j\to u$ in $C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ for every $0<\alpha <1$. The same hypotheses give uniform $W^{2,p}$ bounds for the sequence. Proof. On a coordinate ball the Euclidean Laplacian is $\Delta u_ j=4\sum _ i (u_ j)_{i\bar i}$, so it is uniformly bounded. The interior Laplace estimate on two nested balls gives \[  \| u_ j\| _{W^{2,p}(B')}\leq C_ p \bigl (\| \Delta u_ j\| _{L^ p(B)}+\| u_ j\| _{L^ p(B)}\bigr ).  \] A finite cover gives the global bound. Weak $W^{2,p}$ limits coincide with the uniform limit. The bounded complex Hessians have weak-star limits in $L^\infty $; testing against compactly supported smooth functions identifies them with $H(u)$. Choose $p$ with $1-2n/p>\alpha $. The compact Sobolev embedding into $C^{1,\alpha }$ gives convergence of subsequences. Every such limit is $u$, hence the whole sequence converges. This estimates the full real Hessian in every finite $L^ p$ space, without asserting that it is bounded. $\square$ Lemma 12.4.2 . For $1\leq a\leq k\leq n$, suppose $u_ j^ a$ and $u^ a$ satisfy the preceding lemma. Let $\theta _ a$ be fixed smooth real $(1,1)$-forms. Then \[  \bigwedge _{a=1}^ k(\theta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j^ a) \longrightarrow \bigwedge _{a=1}^ k(\theta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u^ a) \quad \hbox{as currents}.  \] The current on the right is the product of the almost-everywhere coefficients. No closedness or positivity of the $\theta _ a$ is required. For each compactly supported smooth complementary test form $\eta $, the difference of its pairings is bounded by $C_\eta \max _ a\| u_ j^ a-u^ a\| _\infty $. Proof. Set $D_ j^ a=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j^ a$ and $D^ a=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u^ a$. On a smaller coordinate ball, convolution gives smooth $u_\epsilon ^ a$ whose complex Hessians are uniformly bounded and converge to $H(u^ a)$ in every finite $L^ p$ space. Their coefficient products consequently converge in finite $L^ p$ spaces. In particular the products of the $D^ a$ are closed currents, since their smooth approximants are closed. Expand the smooth background factors and telescope each remaining product. Every difference has the form \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^ a-u^ a)\wedge T_ j,  \] where $T_ j$ is a product of $D_ j^ b$ and $D^ b$ with $b\ne a$. It has uniformly bounded coefficients and is closed. Local convolution, followed by strong convergence of its finite coefficient products, justifies integration by parts: \[  \left\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^ a-u^ a)\wedge T_ j,\xi \right\rangle =\int (u_ j^ a-u^ a)\, T_ j\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\xi .  \] Here $\xi $ includes the chosen smooth background factors and the test form, so their derivatives are retained. The right-hand side has the asserted uniform bound. A finite partition of unity proves the claim on $X$. This argument also proves that the coefficient product is the distributional limit; it does not identify a separately defined bounded Hessian operator for all nonsmooth admissible functions. $\square$ Lemma 12.4.3 . For $f_0>0$ and $L>0$, assume the set \[  K=\{ A\in C_{n,m}:\operatorname {tr}A\leq L, \  \sigma _ m(A)\geq f_0^ m\}   \] is nonempty. It is a compact subset of the interior, and there are $\vartheta ,\Theta >0$, depending only on $n,m,f_0,L$, such that \[  \vartheta I\leq DF_ A\leq \Theta I\qquad (A\in K).  \] The function on all Hermitian matrices defined by \[  \widehat F(B)=\inf _{A\in K} \bigl (F(A)+\operatorname {tr}(DF_ A(B-A))\bigr )  \] is concave, agrees with $F$ on $K$, and satisfies, for $P\geq 0$, \[  \vartheta \operatorname {tr}P\leq \widehat F(B+P)-\widehat F(B) \leq \Theta \operatorname {tr}P.  \] Proof. In the closed $2$-cone, \[  \sum _ i\lambda _ i^2=(\operatorname {tr}A)^2-2S_2(A) \leq L^2.  \] Thus $K$ is bounded and closed. Maclaurin gives $\sigma _ j(A)\geq \sigma _ m(A)^{j/m}\geq f_0^ j$ for $j\leq m$, so every matrix in $K$ is in the interior. In a unitary eigenframe, \[  F_ i=\frac{F^{1-m}S_{m-1}(\lambda |i)}{m\binom nm}, \qquad \frac{f_0}{m!L}\leq F_ i\leq \frac{L^{m-1}}{n f_0^{m-1}}.  \] The lower bound is 12.1.3 ; the upper bound uses $|\lambda _ i|\leq L$ in the polynomial numerator and its positivity. These bounds give possible values of $\vartheta $ and $\Theta $. Concavity places each tangent plane above $F$ on the cone; the plane at $B$ gives equality when $B\in K$. An infimum of affine functions is concave. Each plane increases under $P\geq 0$ by a number between the two displayed trace bounds; taking infima preserves these bounds. The same estimates give global Lipschitz continuity of $\widehat F$. $\square$ To interpret this as a real elliptic operator, let $\mathcal C(R)$ be the complex Hessian of the real quadratic function $q(x)=\frac12 x^{\mathsf T}Rx$, where $x\in \mathbb R^{2n}$. For $R\geq 0$, one has $\mathcal C(R)\geq 0$ and $\operatorname {tr}\mathcal C(R)=\operatorname {tr}R/4$. If $\mu I\leq g(x)\leq MI$, then \[  \mathcal G(x,R)=\widehat F \bigl (I+g(x)^{-1/2}\mathcal C(R)g(x)^{-1/2}\bigr )  \] is uniformly elliptic on real symmetric matrices, with constants $\vartheta /(4M)$ and $\Theta /(4\mu )$. Its dependence on $x$ satisfies on compact coordinate balls \[  |\mathcal G(x,R)-\mathcal G(y,R)| \leq C|x-y|(1+\| R\| ).  \] These follow respectively from the trace bound and the smooth dependence of the positive matrix square root of the fixed metric. We use the classical interior Evans–Krylov–Caffarelli estimate for a concave operator on all real symmetric matrices with fixed positive ellipticity constants and coefficient oscillation bounded by $C|x-y|^\gamma (1+\| R\| )$, where $\gamma >0$. A Hölder right-hand side then gives an interior $C^{2,\beta }$ estimate, for some $\beta >0$. This estimate applies also to continuous viscosity solutions. The real extension just constructed satisfies these conditions. Once its solution is $C^{2,\beta }$ and the attained complex Hessians remain in a compact subset of the open cone, the original smooth Hessian operator and Schauder estimates give the higher derivatives. We next identify the limit of the proper auxiliary equations that will be used for regularity. Proposition 12.4.4 . Suppose $v_ j\to \varphi $ uniformly on $X$, $h(x,t)$ is smooth on a fixed bounded interval containing their values, and smooth admissible $u_ j$ satisfy \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m} =e^{u_ j+h(x,v_ j)}\omega ^ n.  \] Assume $u_ j\to u$ uniformly and the complex Hessians of $u_ j$ are uniformly bounded. Then $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is admissible almost everywhere and its coefficient product satisfies \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m} =e^{u+h(x,\varphi )}\omega ^ n.  \] On every coordinate ball $u$ also solves the corresponding uniformly elliptic concave extension in the viscosity sense. Proof. The first lemma gives $u\in W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$ and a bounded complex Hessian. The matrices $A_ j=I+g^{-1/2}H(u_ j)g^{-1/2}$ converge weakly in $L^2$ to the analogous matrix $A$ for $u$. Mazur's lemma gives convex combinations of tails converging strongly in $L^2$, hence almost everywhere along a subsequence. The pointwise closed cone is convex, so $A\in C_{n,m}$ almost everywhere. The product lemma passes the equation to the limit as currents, since its right-hand side converges uniformly. Equality of the bounded densities then gives the equation almost everywhere. The right-hand sides are bounded above and away from zero. The complex Hessian bound gives a uniform upper bound $L$ for $\operatorname {tr}A_ j$. Choose $f_0>0$ below all their normalized roots. Thus every $A_ j$, and almost every $A$, belongs to the compact set $K$ of the preceding lemma. Every $u_ j$ is a classical solution of \[  \mathcal G(x,D^2u_ j)=r_ j(x),\qquad r_ j(x)=e^{(u_ j+h(x,v_ j))/m}.  \] For completeness, if a smooth test $q$ touches $u$ from above at an interior point $x_0$, add a small positive quartic term to make the local contact strict. Local maximum points of $u_ j-q$ tend to $x_0$. At these points $D^2u_ j\leq D^2q$, and ellipticity gives $\mathcal G(x,D^2q)\geq r_ j(x)$. Pass to the limit, then remove the quartic term. A test from below gives the reverse inequality. The extension is defined on every real Hessian, so no admissibility of a lower test has been assumed. This proves the viscosity statement. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.4.2
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 12.4.2 . For $1\leq a\leq k\leq n$, suppose $u_ j^ a$ and $u^ a$ satisfy the preceding lemma. Let $\theta _ a$ be fixed smooth real $(1,1)$-forms. Then \[  \bigwedge _{a=1}^ k(\theta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j^ a) \longrightarrow \bigwedge _{a=1}^ k(\theta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u^ a) \quad \hbox{as currents}.  \] The current on the right is the product of the almost-everywhere coefficients. No closedness or positivity of the $\theta _ a$ is required. For each compactly supported smooth complementary test form $\eta $, the difference of its pairings is bounded by $C_\eta \max _ a\| u_ j^ a-u^ a\| _\infty $. Proof. Set $D_ j^ a=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j^ a$ and $D^ a=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u^ a$. On a smaller coordinate ball, convolution gives smooth $u_\epsilon ^ a$ whose complex Hessians are uniformly bounded and converge to $H(u^ a)$ in every finite $L^ p$ space. Their coefficient products consequently converge in finite $L^ p$ spaces. In particular the products of the $D^ a$ are closed currents, since their smooth approximants are closed. Expand the smooth background factors and telescope each remaining product. Every difference has the form \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^ a-u^ a)\wedge T_ j,  \] where $T_ j$ is a product of $D_ j^ b$ and $D^ b$ with $b\ne a$. It has uniformly bounded coefficients and is closed. Local convolution, followed by strong convergence of its finite coefficient products, justifies integration by parts: \[  \left\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^ a-u^ a)\wedge T_ j,\xi \right\rangle =\int (u_ j^ a-u^ a)\, T_ j\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\xi .  \] Here $\xi $ includes the chosen smooth background factors and the test form, so their derivatives are retained. The right-hand side has the asserted uniform bound. A finite partition of unity proves the claim on $X$. This argument also proves that the coefficient product is the distributional limit; it does not identify a separately defined bounded Hessian operator for all nonsmooth admissible functions. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.4.3
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Lemma 12.4.3 . For $f_0>0$ and $L>0$, assume the set \[  K=\{ A\in C_{n,m}:\operatorname {tr}A\leq L, \  \sigma _ m(A)\geq f_0^ m\}   \] is nonempty. It is a compact subset of the interior, and there are $\vartheta ,\Theta >0$, depending only on $n,m,f_0,L$, such that \[  \vartheta I\leq DF_ A\leq \Theta I\qquad (A\in K).  \] The function on all Hermitian matrices defined by \[  \widehat F(B)=\inf _{A\in K} \bigl (F(A)+\operatorname {tr}(DF_ A(B-A))\bigr )  \] is concave, agrees with $F$ on $K$, and satisfies, for $P\geq 0$, \[  \vartheta \operatorname {tr}P\leq \widehat F(B+P)-\widehat F(B) \leq \Theta \operatorname {tr}P.  \] Proof. In the closed $2$-cone, \[  \sum _ i\lambda _ i^2=(\operatorname {tr}A)^2-2S_2(A) \leq L^2.  \] Thus $K$ is bounded and closed. Maclaurin gives $\sigma _ j(A)\geq \sigma _ m(A)^{j/m}\geq f_0^ j$ for $j\leq m$, so every matrix in $K$ is in the interior. In a unitary eigenframe, \[  F_ i=\frac{F^{1-m}S_{m-1}(\lambda |i)}{m\binom nm}, \qquad \frac{f_0}{m!L}\leq F_ i\leq \frac{L^{m-1}}{n f_0^{m-1}}.  \] The lower bound is 12.1.3 ; the upper bound uses $|\lambda _ i|\leq L$ in the polynomial numerator and its positivity. These bounds give possible values of $\vartheta $ and $\Theta $. Concavity places each tangent plane above $F$ on the cone; the plane at $B$ gives equality when $B\in K$. An infimum of affine functions is concave. Each plane increases under $P\geq 0$ by a number between the two displayed trace bounds; taking infima preserves these bounds. The same estimates give global Lipschitz continuity of $\widehat F$. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.4.4
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Proposition 12.4.4 . Suppose $v_ j\to \varphi $ uniformly on $X$, $h(x,t)$ is smooth on a fixed bounded interval containing their values, and smooth admissible $u_ j$ satisfy \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m} =e^{u_ j+h(x,v_ j)}\omega ^ n.  \] Assume $u_ j\to u$ uniformly and the complex Hessians of $u_ j$ are uniformly bounded. Then $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is admissible almost everywhere and its coefficient product satisfies \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m} =e^{u+h(x,\varphi )}\omega ^ n.  \] On every coordinate ball $u$ also solves the corresponding uniformly elliptic concave extension in the viscosity sense. Proof. The first lemma gives $u\in W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$ and a bounded complex Hessian. The matrices $A_ j=I+g^{-1/2}H(u_ j)g^{-1/2}$ converge weakly in $L^2$ to the analogous matrix $A$ for $u$. Mazur's lemma gives convex combinations of tails converging strongly in $L^2$, hence almost everywhere along a subsequence. The pointwise closed cone is convex, so $A\in C_{n,m}$ almost everywhere. The product lemma passes the equation to the limit as currents, since its right-hand side converges uniformly. Equality of the bounded densities then gives the equation almost everywhere. The right-hand sides are bounded above and away from zero. The complex Hessian bound gives a uniform upper bound $L$ for $\operatorname {tr}A_ j$. Choose $f_0>0$ below all their normalized roots. Thus every $A_ j$, and almost every $A$, belongs to the compact set $K$ of the preceding lemma. Every $u_ j$ is a classical solution of \[  \mathcal G(x,D^2u_ j)=r_ j(x),\qquad r_ j(x)=e^{(u_ j+h(x,v_ j))/m}.  \] For completeness, if a smooth test $q$ touches $u$ from above at an interior point $x_0$, add a small positive quartic term to make the local contact strict. Local maximum points of $u_ j-q$ tend to $x_0$. At these points $D^2u_ j\leq D^2q$, and ellipticity gives $\mathcal G(x,D^2q)\geq r_ j(x)$. Pass to the limit, then remove the quartic term. A test from below gives the reverse inequality. The extension is defined on every real Hessian, so no admissibility of a lower test has been assumed. This proves the viscosity statement. $\square$

title: 12.5 Proper equations and admissible approximation
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: 12.5 Proper equations and admissible approximation For a smooth potential write $H_ m(w)=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}$. The positive exponential coefficient controls additive constants by the maximum principle. The resulting smooth equations will also construct admissible approximations of bounded potentials, before any continuous Hessian product is defined. Lemma 12.5.1 . For every $a>0$ and smooth real $H$ on $X$, there is a unique smooth strictly admissible solution of \[  H_ m(w)=e^{aw+H}\omega ^ n.  \] It satisfies \[  -\frac{\max _ X H}{a}\leq w\leq -\frac{\min _ X H}{a}.  \] Proof. At a maximum of $w$, the admissible form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is at most $\omega $, hence $e^{aw+H}\leq 1$ there. At a minimum it is at least $\omega $, and the reverse inequality holds. These give the bounds. For two solutions, a positive maximum of their difference would imply $H_ m(w_1)\leq H_ m(w_2)$ there, contradicting the exponential factor. This proves uniqueness. First take $a=1$ and use the path $H_ m(w_ t)=e^{w_ t+tH}\omega ^ n$, starting with $w_0=0$. The trace estimate of 12.3.6 applies with prescribed potential $v=0$, fixed smooth comparison $0$, and $h(x,v)=tH(x)$; its constants are uniform for $t\in [0,1]$. 12.2.3 then gives a uniform gradient and complex-Hessian bound. 12.4.1 gives uniform $W^{2,p}$ and hence $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds, for any fixed $\alpha <1$. Consequently $r_ t=e^{(w_ t+tH)/m}$ has a uniform Hölder bound. The extension of 12.4.3 is uniformly elliptic and concave on all real Hessians, with coefficient oscillation bounded by $C|x-y|(1+\| R\| )$. The analytic estimate recalled in section 12.4 therefore gives uniform $C^{2,\beta }$ bounds on a finite cover. The original smooth Hessian operator is uniformly elliptic near the attained compact cone set. Differentiating and applying Schauder estimates gives bounds for every higher derivative. The linearization of $\log (H_ m(w)/\omega ^ n)-w-tH$ is $L_ w-1$, where \[  L_ w\xi =\frac{m\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\xi \wedge (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^{m-1} \wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{H_ m(w)}.  \] Its principal coefficients are positive definite. The maximum principle gives zero kernel; smooth elliptic Fredholm theory gives surjectivity and Schauder inversion. The implicit-function theorem proves openness. The uniform estimates prove closedness, so the path reaches $t=1$. For general $a$, use the metric $a\omega $ and potential $\widehat w=aw$. Both sides of its coefficient-one equation acquire the same factor $a^ n$, so it is exactly the stated equation after division by that factor. $\square$ An ordinary smooth approximation need not be admissible. To obtain an admissible one, choose a smooth obstacle above the continuous potential and penalize the solution's distance from that obstacle. Lemma 12.5.2 . Every continuous admissible $\varphi $ on $X$ is the uniform limit of smooth strictly admissible functions. Proof. Fix a smooth $h\geq \varphi $ and a constant \[  b>\max \left\{ 1,\left\| H_ m(h)/\omega ^ n\right\| _\infty \right\} .  \] For each positive integer $N$ solve, by the preceding lemma, \[  H_ m(w_ N)=b e^{N(w_ N-h)}\omega ^ n.  \] At a positive maximum of $w_ N-h$, the form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ lies above the strictly admissible form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ N$, hence is admissible there. Monotonicity would give $b e^{N(w_ N-h)}\leq H_ m(h)/\omega ^ n<b$, a contradiction. Thus $w_ N\leq h$. The preceding zero-order estimate also gives \[  \| w_ N\| _\infty \leq M_ N:=\| h\| _\infty +\frac{\log b}{N}.  \] Let $x_ N$ maximize $\varphi -(1+N^{-1})w_ N$. The smooth positive form $T_ N=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ N)^{m-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-m}$ defines a strictly elliptic linear operator. Admissibility gives $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge T_ N\geq 0$ in distributions. Its linear maximum principle, applied to the upper test $(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ plus the maximum value, gives at $x_ N$ \[  0\leq \bigl (\omega +(1+N^{-1})\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ N\bigr )\wedge T_ N.  \] This application is to a continuous distributional subsolution of a smooth strictly elliptic operator. It does not assume a second derivative of $\varphi $. Writing $d_ N=H_ m(w_ N)/\omega ^ n$, polarized Gårding positivity yields \[  (N+1)d_ N\geq \omega \wedge T_ N/\omega ^ n \geq d_ N^{(m-1)/m}.  \] Therefore, at this maximum point, \[  w_ N-h\geq -E_ N,\qquad E_ N=\frac{m\log (N+1)+\log b}{N}.  \] Since $\varphi \leq h$, the maximum of $\varphi -(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ is at most $E_ N+M_ N/N$. It follows on all of $X$ that \[  \varphi -E_ N-2M_ N/N\leq w_ N\leq h.  \] Given $\delta >0$, choose an ordinary smooth majorant $\varphi \leq h\leq \varphi +\delta $, and then $N$ so large that $E_ N+2M_ N/N\leq \delta $. The resulting $w_ N$ is strictly admissible and within $\delta $ of $\varphi $. Let $\delta \downarrow 0$. No monotonicity of the chosen approximants is needed. $\square$

title: 12.5.1 Decreasing approximation of bounded potentials
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: 12.5.1 Decreasing approximation of bounded potentials Upper semicontinuity supplies smooth obstacles decreasing to a bounded potential. The same penalty equation gives admissible functions between the potential and each obstacle, up to an error tending to zero. Choosing successive obstacles below the preceding smooth approximation makes the admissible approximations decrease as well. Lemma 12.5.3 . Every bounded upper semicontinuous real function $u$ on $X$ is the pointwise decreasing limit of smooth functions $h_ j>u$. Proof. Fix a Riemannian distance $d$ on $X$ and put \[  c_ j(x)=\sup _{y\in X}\{ u(y)-j d(x,y)\} .  \] Each $c_ j$ is Lipschitz, $c_ j\geq u$, and $c_{j+1}\leq c_ j$. The supremum is attained. If $y_ j$ attains it at a fixed $x$, then $j d(x,y_ j)\leq \sup _ X u-u(x)$, so $y_ j\to x$. Upper semicontinuity gives $\limsup _ j c_ j(x)\leq u(x)$, and hence $c_ j\downarrow u$ pointwise. Set $\delta _ j=4^{-j}$. Smooth approximation of continuous functions on a compact manifold gives $s_ j\in C^\infty (X)$ with $\| s_ j-c_ j\| _\infty \leq \delta _ j/4$. Take $h_ j=s_ j+\delta _ j$. Then \[  u+\tfrac 34\delta _ j\leq h_ j\leq c_ j+\tfrac 54\delta _ j, \qquad h_{j+1}\leq c_ j+\tfrac 5{16}\delta _ j < c_ j+\tfrac 34\delta _ j\leq h_ j.  \] The bounds also imply $h_ j(x)\to u(x)$ at every point. $\square$ Lemma 12.5.4 . Let $u$ be bounded admissible and $h\geq u$ smooth. Choose \[  b>\max \{ 1,\| H_ m(h)/\omega ^ n\| _\infty \} .  \] For each positive integer $N$, let $w_ N$ be the smooth strictly admissible solution of \[  H_ m(w_ N)=b e^{N(w_ N-h)}\omega ^ n.  \] With \[  M_ N=\| h\| _\infty +\frac{\log b}{N},\qquad E_ N=\frac{m\log (N+1)+\log b}{N},  \] one has $\| w_ N\| _\infty \leq M_ N$ and \[  u-E_ N-2M_ N/N\leq w_ N\leq h.  \] Proof. Existence follows from 12.5.1 . The maximum comparison with $h$ in the proof of 12.5.2 gives $w_ N\leq h$; it involves only the smooth obstacle and solution. The zero-order bound from 12.5.1 gives $\| w_ N\| _\infty \leq M_ N$. The upper semicontinuous function $u-(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ attains its maximum at some $x_ N$. The smooth function $(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ plus this maximum is an upper test for $u$ there. Put \[  T_ N=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ N)^{m-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-m}, \qquad d_ N=H_ m(w_ N)/\omega ^ n>0.  \] Condition ( 12.2 ) and polarized positivity yield, at $x_ N$, \[  (N+1)d_ N\geq \omega \wedge T_ N/\omega ^ n \geq d_ N^{(m-1)/m}.  \] Consequently $d_ N\geq (N+1)^{-m}$ and $w_ N-h\geq -E_ N$ there. Using $u\leq h$, the maximum is at most $E_ N+M_ N/N$. On all of $X$ this gives \[  u\leq (1+N^{-1})w_ N+E_ N+M_ N/N \leq w_ N+E_ N+2M_ N/N.  \] $\square$ Theorem 12.5.5 . Every bounded admissible potential $u$ on $X$ is the pointwise decreasing limit of smooth strictly admissible potentials. The sequence may be chosen uniformly bounded. Proof. Choose smooth $h_ k\downarrow u$ by 12.5.3 and put $\varepsilon _ j=8^{-j}$. We construct smooth strictly admissible $u_ j$ with $u_ j\geq u+\varepsilon _ j$. For $j=1$, take $k_1=1$. At a subsequent step choose $k_ j\geq \max \{ j,k_{j-1}+1\} $ so large that \[  h_{k_ j}<u_{j-1}-\tfrac 12\varepsilon _{j-1}\quad \hbox{on }X.  \] Such an index exists: the open sets $\{ h_ k<u_{j-1}-\varepsilon _{j-1}/2\} $ increase with $k$ and cover $X$, since $h_ k\downarrow u\leq u_{j-1}-\varepsilon _{j-1}$. Compactness gives a single index for all of $X$. For this fixed obstacle $h_{k_ j}$ choose $b_ j$ as in 12.5.4 , and then choose $N_ j$ so large that its error $E_{N_ j}+2M_{N_ j}/N_ j$ is at most $\varepsilon _ j$. The resulting smooth solution $w_ j$ satisfies \[  u-\varepsilon _ j\leq w_ j\leq h_{k_ j}.  \] Put $u_ j=w_ j+2\varepsilon _ j$. Adding a constant preserves strict admissibility, and $u_ j\geq u+\varepsilon _ j$. For $j\geq 2$, \[  u_ j\leq h_{k_ j}+2\varepsilon _ j <u_{j-1}-\tfrac 12\varepsilon _{j-1}+2\varepsilon _ j =u_{j-1}-\tfrac 14\varepsilon _{j-1}.  \] Finally, $u\leq u_ j\leq h_{k_ j}+2\varepsilon _ j$ and $k_ j\geq j$ give pointwise convergence to $u$. The bounds $\inf _ X u\leq u_ j\leq \sup _ X u_1$ give a common uniform bound. $\square$ For continuous $u$, Dini's theorem makes these decreasing approximations converge uniformly on $X$. This is the convergence used for the continuous mixed products in the next section.
