Against nonnegative continuous tests, lower semicontinuity of total variation preserves both bounds. They are consequently inequalities of measures and may be restricted to the Borel set $E$. Put $w=\max \{ u,V+b\} $ and $h=w-u$. The mixed maximum theorem 12.11.2 , with one moving slot and the fixed slots defining $T_{p,q}$, gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)T_{p,q} \geq \mathbf1_ E\sigma _ VT_{p,q} +\mathbf1_{X\setminus E}\sigma _ uT_{p,q}.  \] All products here are the corresponding positive mixed measures. After integration, this implies \[  b_{p,q+1}\leq b_{p+1,q} +\int _ X\bigl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)-\sigma _ u\bigr )T_{p,q}.  \] Regularized maxima of the smooth decreasing approximations give a uniformly bounded decreasing smooth list $w_ j\downarrow w$. Stokes' theorem on compact $X$ gives for these lists \[  \int _ X\bigl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)-\sigma _{u_ j}\bigr )T_{p,q}^ j =\int _ X(w_ j-u_ j)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}^ j.  \] Joint decreasing convergence passes the positive mixed measures on the left to their limits. The continuous two-variable weight $F(x,y)=y-x$ in 12.11.4 passes the right side to $\int _ Xh\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}$. No monotonicity of $w_ j-u_ j$ is needed. Since $h$ is zero outside $E$ and $0\leq h\leq s$, \[  \int _ Xh\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}\leq s|\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}|(E).  \] The torsion bounds prove both assertions. The argument never passes a varying measure to a weak limit after restriction to $E$. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.12.6
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text: Theorem 12.12.6 . There is $C\geq 1$, depending only on $X,\omega ,m,n$, with the following property. For bounded admissible $u,v$ and $0<\alpha <1$, put $\eta =1-\alpha $, $V=\alpha v$ and $S=\inf _ X(u-V)$. For $0<s<\eta ^3/C$, let $E_ s=\{ u<V+S+s\} $. Then \[  \int _{E_ s}H_ m(V) \leq \left(1+\frac{Cs}{\eta ^ m}\right) \int _{E_ s}H_ m(u).  \] No differential identity for a power of $\omega $ is assumed. Proof. Use the mixed measures above on $E_ s$, writing $b_{p,q}=M_{p,q}(E_ s)$ and $a_ k=b_{k,0}$. The definition of $S$ gives $0\leq \max \{ u,V+S+s\} -u\leq s$, so 12.12.5 applies. Repeatedly moving a $V$ slot to a $u$ slot gives, for $p+q=r$, \[  b_{p,q}\leq a_ r+C_1s\sum _{d=0}^{r-1}A_ d, \qquad A_ d=\max _{a+b=d}b_{a,b},\qquad 1\leq r\leq m.  \] Here there are at most $m$ moves, and the multiplicity $d+1$ in the lower-degree sum is absorbed in $C_1$. For $0<s\leq 1$, induction on $r$ shows \[  A_ r\leq a_ r+K_ rs\sum _{k<r}a_ k.  \] In fact $A_0=a_0$, and one may take $K_ r=C_1(1+\sum _{1\leq d<r}K_ d)$: insert the earlier bounds in the displayed recurrence and use $s^2\leq s$. Thus, for a constant $C_2$ depending only on the setting, \[  b_{0,m}\leq a_ m+C_2s\sum _{k<m}a_ k.  \] It remains to control the lower diagonal masses by $a_ m$. The identity $\sigma _ V=\alpha \sigma _ v+\eta \omega $ and mixed positivity give $b_{k,1}\geq \eta a_ k$; this identity and inequality pass from smooth approximations by joint convergence. The diagonal assertion of 12.12.5 gives \[  \eta a_ k\leq a_{k+1} +C_3s(a_ k+a_{k-1}+a_{k-2})\qquad (0\leq k<m),  \] with $a_{-1}=a_{-2}=0$. Set $B_ k=\eta ^{m-k}a_ k$ for $0\leq k\leq m$, and set $B_{-1}=B_{-2}=0$. Multiplying by $\eta ^{m-k-1}$ and using $0<\eta <1$ gives \[  B_ k\leq B_{k+1} +\delta (B_ k+B_{k-1}+B_{k-2}), \qquad \delta =C_3s\eta ^{-3}.  \] For $M=\max _{0\leq k<m}B_ k$, summing from any $j<m$ through $m-1$ gives $B_ j\leq B_ m+3m\delta M$. If $s<\eta ^3/(6mC_3)$, it follows that $M\leq 2B_ m$. Consequently \[  a_ k\leq 2\eta ^{-(m-k)}a_ m\quad (k<m),\qquad \sum _{k<m}a_ k\leq 2m\eta ^{-m}a_ m.  \] Choose $C\geq \max \{ 1,6mC_3,2mC_2\} $. Then the asserted range for $s$ supplies every preceding restriction, and substitution in the bound for $b_{0,m}$ proves the theorem. No division by $a_ m$ occurs, so zero top mass on $E_ s$ is included. $\square$

title: 12.12.2 Domination and proper equations
topic: Local Monge–Ampère theory and Hessian equations
text:
12.12.2 Domination and proper equations The weak modified comparison estimate makes strict domination possible on an arbitrary Hermitian background. A convex rescaling supplies a positive volume term, while choosing a sufficiently small sublevel set absorbs the torsion error. Canonical representatives detect its positive volume even when the set is not open. Theorem 12.12.7 . Let $u,v$ be bounded admissible. If, for some $0\leq c<1$, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(u) \leq c\mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(v),  \] then $u\geq v$ everywhere, on an arbitrary Hermitian background. In particular, $H_ m(u)(\{ u<v\} )=0$ implies $u\geq v$. Proof. Add the same constant to $u,v$ so that $v\geq 1$. This preserves the measure hypothesis and the desired conclusion. Choose $0<\alpha <1$ with $\alpha ^ m>c$ and put $V=\alpha v$, $\eta =1-\alpha $. Suppose $S=\inf _ X(u-V)<0$. For $0<s<-S$, the set $E_ s=\{ u<V+S+s\} $ is contained in $\{ u<V\} $ and hence in $\{ u<v\} $. It has positive volume. Indeed, if its volume were zero, then $u\geq V+S+s$ almost everywhere. Both functions are bounded admissible with their canonical representatives, so 12.1.8 would give this order everywhere, contradicting the definition of $S$. The argument does not require $E_ s$ to be open or the infimum to be attained. Choose also $s<\eta ^3/C$, where $C$ is from 12.12.6 . By 12.11.3 and the measure hypothesis, \[   egin{aligned}  \alpha ^ m H_ m(v)(E_ s)+\eta ^ m\int _{E_ s}\omega ^ n & \leq H_ m(V)(E_ s)\ & \leq (1+Cs\eta ^{-m})H_ m(u)(E_ s)\ & \leq c(1+Cs\eta ^{-m})H_ m(v)(E_ s). \end{aligned}  \] If $c>0$, take $s$ still smaller so that $c(1+Cs\eta ^{-m})<\alpha ^ m$. If $c=0$, this strict inequality already holds. All measures are finite and positive, so the display forces the positive-volume term to be zero, a contradiction. Hence $S\geq 0$ and $u\geq \alpha v$. Let $\alpha $ increase to one, with $\alpha ^ m>c$. Since $v$ is bounded, $\alpha v	o v$ uniformly, and therefore $u\geq v$. The final assertion is $c=0$. $\square$ Corollary 12.12.8 . Fix $a>0$. If bounded admissible $u,v$ satisfy \[  e^{-av}H_ m(v)\geq e^{-au}H_ m(u),  \] then $u\geq v$. Consequently, for any fixed finite positive Radon measure $
u $, the equation $H_ m(u)=e^{au}
u $ has at most one bounded admissible solution. Proof. For $\delta >0$, put $E_\delta =\{ u<v-\delta \} $. Multiplying the assumed measure inequality by the positive bounded Borel function $e^{au}$ gives on $E_\delta $ \[  H_ m(u)\leq e^{a(u-v)}H_ m(v) \leq e^{-a\delta }H_ m(v-\delta ).  \] The last identity uses invariance under constants. Since $e^{-a\delta }<1$, 12.12.7 applied to $u,v-\delta $ gives $u\geq v-\delta $ everywhere. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $u\geq v$. Two solutions of the stated equation have equal weighted measures $e^{-au}H_ m(u)=
u $. Applying the order assertion in both directions proves uniqueness. $\square$ A strictly increasing exponent also controls changes in logarithmic data for a fixed Radon right-hand measure. Proposition 12.12.9 . Let $A<B$ and $f$ be smooth near $X	imes [A,B]$, with $\partial _ t f\geq \kappa >0$ there, and let $
u $ be a finite positive Radon measure. Suppose bounded admissible $u,v$ have values in $[A,B]$ and satisfy \[  H_ m(u)=e^{f(x,u)+h_1}
u ,\qquad H_ m(v)=e^{f(x,v)+h_2}
u ,  \] where $h_1,h_2$ are bounded Borel functions. Then \[  \| u-v\| _\infty \leq \kappa ^{-1}\| h_1-h_2\| _{L^\infty (
u )}.  \] Proof. Put $K=\| h_1-h_2\| _{L^\infty (
u )}$ and fix $s>K/\kappa $. On $E_ s=\{ v+s<u\} $, the actual values $u,v$ lie in $[A,B]$, so $f(x,u)-f(x,v)\geq \kappa s$. The equations and the essential bound on $h_2-h_1$ therefore give, as restricted measures, \[  \mathbf1_{E_ s}H_ m(v+s) =\mathbf1_{E_ s}H_ m(v) \leq e^{K-\kappa s}\mathbf1_{E_ s}H_ m(u).  \] The constant is smaller than one. Applying 12.12.7 to $v+s,u$ gives $u\leq v+s$ pointwise. Let $s\downarrow K/\kappa $ and exchange $u,v$ to obtain the norm bound. The exponent is evaluated only at $u,v$; the shifted comparison potential need not take its values in $[A,B]$. $\square$ Corollary 12.12.10 . Under the hypotheses of 12.7.3 , every bounded admissible solution with values in $[A,B]$ is its smooth solution. In particular, for every $a>0$ and smooth real $H$, the equation $H_ m(u)=e^{au+H}\omega ^ n$ has exactly one bounded admissible solution, and that solution is smooth and strictly admissible. Proof. For a continuous admissible potential, smooth decreasing admissible approximations converge uniformly on compact $X$ by Dini's theorem. Thus 12.10.8 , 12.6.1 define the same Hessian measure on the continuous class. The smooth solution of 12.7.3 therefore solves the bounded equation as well. Apply 12.12.9 with $
u =\omega ^ n$ and $h_1=h_2=0$ to identify any other bounded solution in $[A,B]$ with it. For the final assertion, smooth existence is already 12.5.1 , and 12.12.8 with $
u =e^ H\omega ^ n$ gives uniqueness among all bounded solutions. $\square$

title: 3 Relative singularities and equations
text: 3 Relative singularities and equations

title: 13 Envelopes and volumes of singularities
text: 13 Envelopes and volumes of singularities Throughout this chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, with an auxiliary Hermitian metric $\omega $ and a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$, and $\theta $ denotes a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ whose positivity is specified in each section. In a closed background, the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère mass of a potential depends only on its singularity type; this is what makes mass a tool for comparing singularities. In a nonclosed background, a bounded change of the potential can change the mass, and a singularity type may contain potentials of different, even infinite, masses. This chapter opens the part of the book on relative singularities and the equations they govern, and introduces two kinds of invariants that take this into account. The first records the variation of mass: the lower and upper volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ of a potential $u$ are the infimum and the supremum of the masses of all potentials of the same singularity type. The second replaces a mass condition by a condition on envelopes. Fix a reference potential $\varphi $. Stretching a potential $u$ away from $\varphi $ by a factor $b\geq 1$ gives the obstacle $bu-(b-1)\varphi $, which is more singular than $u$ where $u$ lies below $\varphi $. The relative envelope class $\mathcal E_\varphi $ consists of the potentials $u$ at least as singular as $\varphi $ for which every such stretched obstacle lies above some $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function. This class is convex and stable under finite rooftops, its members have the same singularity envelope as $\varphi $, and its definition involves no mass. The main tool is the contact property of envelopes: the Monge–Ampère measure of an envelope is carried by the set where it touches its obstacle. Together with ordered contact, it gives the domination principle for bounded potentials in a semipositive background and bounds the measures of rooftop envelopes. For envelopes of logarithmic growth on $\mathbb C^ n$, which correspond to envelopes on $\mathbb P^ n$, we also examine how the contact of the regularized envelope with its obstacle depends on the growth allowance. In a semipositive big background, the contact property also produces positive mass. Let $\varphi $ be a model reference, that is, a fixed point of the singularity envelope that admits a competitor in a smaller background. Every member $u$ of $\mathcal E_\varphi $ then has a competitor in a background $a\theta $ with $0<a<1$, and an envelope in the remaining big background $(1-a)\theta $ has positive mass, which it transfers to $u$ on the contact set. The argument uses only that each bounded potential has positive mass, so it applies even when the infimum of these masses is zero. Conversely, if the Hermitian metric $\omega $ does not have the bounded mass property of definition 6.5.1 , the relative envelope class of the zero potential contains potentials of infinite mass. Envelope conditions and mass bounds are therefore different requirements, and this distinction is essential for the equations with prescribed singularities in the next chapter. We use the following notation from chapter 1 . For quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $u,v$, we write $u\preceq v$ if $u\leq v+C$ for a constant $C$, and $u\sim v$ if $u\preceq v$ and $v\preceq u$; the equivalence class of $u$ is its singularity type (definition 1.12.1 ). For an obstacle $f$, the envelope $P_\theta (f)$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of all $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\leq f$ quasi-everywhere; it may be identically $-\infty $, and then it does not belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the rooftop envelope is $P_\theta (u,v)=P_\theta (\min (u,v))$, and $V_\theta =P_\theta (0)$ is the potential with minimal singularities; see section 1.19 . The singularity envelope $P_\theta [u]$, its variant $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ with a smooth obstacle $F$, and envelope fixed points, that is, potentials with $P_\theta [u]=u$, are defined in definition 1.19.4 . We write $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ denotes the extended Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ of theorem 6.1.2 . It is the Bedford–Taylor measure $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ when $u$ is bounded, it puts no mass on pluripolar sets, and its total mass, the extended mass of $u$, may be infinite.

title: 13.1 Contact sets
text: 13.1 Contact sets The Monge–Ampère measure of an envelope is concentrated on the contact set, where the envelope meets its obstacle. For a smooth obstacle and a Hermitian background, the envelope is the uniform limit of solutions of exponential equations whose densities tend to zero wherever the envelope stays strictly below the obstacle. Continuity of bounded products then carries this property to quasi-continuous obstacles, first bounded ones, through monotone approximation, and then general ones, through truncation. Proposition 13.1.1 . Let $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. For $\beta >0$, denote by $u_\beta $ the smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solution of \[  \omega _{u_\beta }^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\beta (u_\beta -f)}\omega ^ n.  \] As $\beta \to +\infty $, these solutions converge uniformly to $p=P_\omega (f)$. Moreover, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\omega _ p^ n=0.  \] Proof. The solutions exist by theorem 9.6.2 . Choose $A\geq 0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\leq A\omega $. At a maximum point of $u_\beta -f$, the second derivative test gives \[  \omega _{u_\beta }\leq \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\leq (1+A)\omega .  \] Evaluating the equation at this point, we obtain \[  u_\beta \leq f+\frac{C_ f}{\beta },\qquad C_ f=n\log (1+A).  \] Thus $u_\beta -C_ f/\beta $ is a competitor for $P_\omega (f)$, and $u_\beta \leq p+C_ f/\beta $. For the lower bound, note that $p$ is continuous by proposition 1.19.3 , and choose smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ j\downarrow p$ by theorem 1.11.1 ; by Dini's theorem the convergence is uniform. For any $\delta >0$, choose $j$ so that \[  p\leq v_ j\leq p+\delta /2.  \] Then $v_ j-\delta \leq f$, since $p\leq f$. Since $\omega _{v_ j}>0$ and $X$ is compact, there is $c_ j>0$ such that $\omega _{v_ j}^ n\geq c_ j\omega ^ n$. Put $C_ j=\max (0,-\log c_ j)$. The function \[  w_{j,\beta }=v_ j-\delta -C_ j/\beta  \] satisfies \[  \omega _{w_{j,\beta }}^ n=\omega _{v_ j}^ n \geq \mathrm{e}^{-C_ j}\omega ^ n \geq \mathrm{e}^{\beta (w_{j,\beta }-f)}\omega ^ n.  \] Exponential comparison, corollary 10.2.4 with $\lambda =\beta $, gives $w_{j,\beta }\leq u_\beta $. Consequently \[  p-\delta -C_ j/\beta \leq u_\beta \leq p+C_ f/\beta .  \] Letting first $\beta \to \infty $ with $j$ fixed, so that no lower bound for $c_ j$ uniform in $j$ is needed, and then $\delta \downarrow 0$, we obtain uniform convergence. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity then gives weak convergence of the measures. On a compact subset of the open set $\{ p<f\} $, uniform convergence gives $u_\beta -f\leq -\epsilon $ for some $\epsilon >0$ and all large $\beta $. There the measures $\omega _{u_\beta }^ n$ have densities at most $\mathrm{e}^{-\beta \epsilon }$ with respect to $\omega ^ n$. Testing against continuous functions with compact support in $\{ p<f\} $ and passing to the limit gives $\omega _ p^ n=0$ on this open set. $\square$ Proposition 13.1.2 . If $f$ is bounded and lower semicontinuous, then $P_\omega (f)$ is bounded, lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, and its Monge–Ampère measure is concentrated on $\{ P_\omega (f)=f\} $. Proof. Suppose first that $f$ is continuous. Choose smooth functions $f_ j\to f$ uniformly. The Lipschitz bound for envelopes in proposition 1.19.3 gives $p_ j=P_\omega (f_ j)\to p=P_\omega (f)$ uniformly. Every compact subset of the open set $\{ p<f\} $ has a neighborhood on which $p_ j<f_ j$ for all large $j$. The preceding proposition and convergence of bounded products then give $\omega _ p^ n=0$ on $\{ p<f\} $. For lower semicontinuous $f$, choose continuous functions $f_ j\uparrow f$ with common upper and lower bounds. For example, for a fixed distance $d$ inducing the topology of $X$, one may take \[  f_ j(x)=\inf _{y\in X}\bigl (f(y)+j d(x,y)\bigr ).  \] These functions are Lipschitz and increase to $f$: if convergence failed at $x$, approximate minimizers $y$ would approach $x$, contradicting lower semicontinuity of $f$ at $x$. The functions $p_ j=P_\omega (f_ j)$ increase and stay bounded, so the regularized limit $p_\infty =(\lim _ jp_ j)^*$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. It agrees with $\lim _ jp_ j$ outside a pluripolar set, and since each $p_ j$ lies below $f_ j\leq f$ outside a pluripolar set, we obtain $p_\infty \leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Thus $p_\infty \leq P_\omega (f)$. For fixed $k$, the set $\{ p_\infty <f_ k\} $ is open, since $p_\infty $ is upper semicontinuous and $f_ k$ is continuous. If $j\geq k$, then $p_ j\leq p_\infty <f_ k\leq f_ j$ there, so the continuous case gives $\omega _{p_ j}^ n=0$ on that open set. Bedford–Taylor continuity along increasing sequences applies after adding a fixed smooth local function whose Hessian dominates $\omega $ and expanding with respect to the resulting smooth form. Together with the lower semicontinuity of the mass of open sets under weak convergence, it yields \[  \omega _{p_\infty }^ n(\{ p_\infty <f_ k\} )=0.  \] Taking the union over $k$ gives zero measure on $\{ p_\infty <f\} $, hence also on $\{ p_\infty <P_\omega (f)\} $ outside a pluripolar set, since $P_\omega (f)\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Bounded measures of this kind do not charge pluripolar sets, so the domination principle, theorem 10.2.2 , gives $p_\infty \geq P_\omega (f)$. The two functions are therefore equal, and the assertion follows. $\square$ Theorem 13.1.3 . Let $\theta \geq 0$ be smooth and let $f$ be bounded and quasi-continuous. Then $p=P_\theta (f)$ is bounded, $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere, and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0.  \] Proof. First suppose that $\theta =\omega $ is Hermitian. Choose bounded lower semicontinuous functions $f_ j\downarrow f$ quasi-everywhere, with common bounds, as in lemma 1.8.8 . The bounded functions $p_ j=P_\omega (f_ j)$ decrease to $p$. Indeed, their limit is a competitor for $p$, since it lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, and the reverse inequality follows from monotonicity. For fixed $k$, put $H_ k=\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} $, a bounded quasi-continuous function. Where $H_ k>0$ and $j\geq k$, we have $p_ j\leq p_ k<f\leq f_ j$ outside a pluripolar set. The lower semicontinuous case therefore gives \[  \int _ X H_ k\, \omega _{p_ j}^ n=0.  \] The convergence of bounded products against quasi-continuous weights in section 1.8 gives $\int _ XH_ k\, \omega _ p^ n=0$. Since the sets $\{ p_ k<f\} $ increase to $\{ p<f\} $, this proves the assertion for Hermitian $\theta $. For general semipositive $\theta $, set $\theta _ j=\theta +j^{-1}\omega $. The functions $p_ j=P_{\theta _ j}(f)$ have the common bounds $\inf _ Xf\leq p_ j\leq \sup _ Xf$ and decrease. Their limit is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic by distributional convergence and lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, so it is at most $p=P_\theta (f)$; since $p\leq p_ j$ for all $j$, it equals $p$. For each fixed $k$, the same coefficient $H_ k=\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} $ gives \[  \int _ XH_ k\, \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _ j}(p_ j)=0\qquad (j\geq k).  \] All $p_ j$ are bounded potentials for the fixed Hermitian form $\theta +\omega $. Expanding the products with background $\theta _ j$ with respect to this fixed background, we may use convergence of bounded products and uniform capacity bounds to pass the last identity to the limit, with the quasi-continuous weight $H_ k$; this gives $\int _ XH_ k\, \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0$. Exhausting $\{ p<f\} $ as before completes the proof. $\square$ Theorem 13.1.4 . Let $\theta $ be smooth and semipositive, and let $f$ be a quasi-continuous obstacle. If $p=P_\theta (f)$ is not identically $-\infty $, then $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0.  \] Here the total extended mass of $p$ may be infinite. Proof. The local envelope theorem, applied to a countable family realizing the supremum (Choquet's lemma), gives $p\leq f$ outside a pluripolar set. Choose $M>\sup _ Xp$ and replace $f$ by $\min (f,M)$. This does not change the envelope, since $p$ itself is a competitor for the smaller obstacle. Since $p<M$, the contact set is also unchanged, so it suffices to prove the theorem for the smaller obstacle; that is, we may assume that $f$ is bounded above. Set $f_ j=\max (f,-j)$ and $p_ j=P_\theta (f_ j)$. The constants $-j$ are competitors, so $p_ j$ is bounded. Theorem 13.1.3 gives $p_ j\leq f_ j$ quasi-everywhere and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p_ j<f_ j\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_ j)=0.  \] The sequence $p_ j$ decreases and stays above $p$. Its limit is therefore $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, it lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, and so it is a competitor for $p$. Hence $p_ j\downarrow p$. Fix an integer $k\geq 1$ and $C>0$, and define the bounded nonnegative quasi-continuous function \[  H_{k,C}=\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} \,  \min \{ 1,(p+C)_+\} .  \] Its values on pluripolar sets are immaterial. Where this coefficient is positive, $p_ k<f$ and $p>-C$. For $j\geq k$, we then have $p_ j\leq p_ k<f\leq f_ j$ and $p_ j\geq p>-C$ there. Plurifine locality and theorem 13.1.3 therefore imply \[  \int _ X H_{k,C}\,  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\max (p_ j,-C))=0.  \] The truncated potentials are uniformly bounded and decrease to $\max (p,-C)$, so their measures converge weakly by bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity. The uniform capacity bounds and the weighted convergence in section 1.8 also allow testing against $H_{k,C}$. Hence the last identity holds with $p$ in place of $p_ j$. By plurifine locality, this says that the extended measure of $p$ vanishes on $\{ p_ k<f\} \cap \{ p>-C\} $. Off the pole set of $p$, these sets increase to $\{ p<f\} $ as first $k$ and then $C$ tend to infinity. Continuity of positive measures along increasing sequences proves the assertion, even if the total extended mass is infinite. $\square$ For a smooth big background, constants need not be competitors, and a strictly $\theta $-plurisubharmonic barrier with poles replaces the constant lower truncations. The same contact property for quasi-continuous obstacles finite almost everywhere is proved in this setting in theorem 14.7.4 . Combined with ordered contact, either contact theorem controls the measures of rooftop envelopes. In the following bound, the strict inequality in the first term assigns the common contact set $\{ p=u=v\} $ to the second term. Proposition 13.1.5 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form that is semipositive or big, and let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. If $p=P_\theta (u,v)$ is not identically $-\infty $, then \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ p=u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) +\mathbf1_{\{ p=v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v).  \] Proof. The envelope lies below both obstacles quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere, since the obstacles are upper semicontinuous. By the contact theorem (theorem 13.1.4 or theorem 14.7.4 ), its measure is carried by $\{ p=\min (u,v)\} $. Partition this set into $\{ p=u<v\} $ and $\{ p=v\} $, and apply proposition 6.2.1 on each part. All measures vanish on the pluripolar pole sets, which can therefore be discarded throughout. $\square$ Proposition 13.1.6 . Let $\theta $ be smooth and semipositive. Every envelope fixed point $\varphi $ satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi ) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ \varphi =0\} }\theta ^ n.  \] In particular, its extended mass is finite. Proof. Since $\varphi =P_\theta [\varphi ]\leq 0$, the function $\varphi $ is a competitor for $P_\theta (\varphi +1,0)$. This rooftop is also a competitor for $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $, being at most $\varphi +1$ and at most zero, so it equals $\varphi $. Now apply proposition 13.1.5 with $u=\varphi +1$ and $v=0$. The contact set $\{ \varphi =\varphi +1<0\} $ is contained in the pole set of $\varphi $, which the extended measure does not charge. Only contact with zero contributes, and this gives the asserted bound. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.1.1
text: Proposition 13.1.1 . Let $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. For $\beta >0$, denote by $u_\beta $ the smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solution of \[  \omega _{u_\beta }^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\beta (u_\beta -f)}\omega ^ n.  \] As $\beta \to +\infty $, these solutions converge uniformly to $p=P_\omega (f)$. Moreover, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\omega _ p^ n=0.  \] Proof. The solutions exist by theorem 9.6.2 . Choose $A\geq 0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\leq A\omega $. At a maximum point of $u_\beta -f$, the second derivative test gives \[  \omega _{u_\beta }\leq \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\leq (1+A)\omega .  \] Evaluating the equation at this point, we obtain \[  u_\beta \leq f+\frac{C_ f}{\beta },\qquad C_ f=n\log (1+A).  \] Thus $u_\beta -C_ f/\beta $ is a competitor for $P_\omega (f)$, and $u_\beta \leq p+C_ f/\beta $. For the lower bound, note that $p$ is continuous by proposition 1.19.3 , and choose smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ j\downarrow p$ by theorem 1.11.1 ; by Dini's theorem the convergence is uniform. For any $\delta >0$, choose $j$ so that \[  p\leq v_ j\leq p+\delta /2.  \] Then $v_ j-\delta \leq f$, since $p\leq f$. Since $\omega _{v_ j}>0$ and $X$ is compact, there is $c_ j>0$ such that $\omega _{v_ j}^ n\geq c_ j\omega ^ n$. Put $C_ j=\max (0,-\log c_ j)$. The function \[  w_{j,\beta }=v_ j-\delta -C_ j/\beta  \] satisfies \[  \omega _{w_{j,\beta }}^ n=\omega _{v_ j}^ n \geq \mathrm{e}^{-C_ j}\omega ^ n \geq \mathrm{e}^{\beta (w_{j,\beta }-f)}\omega ^ n.  \] Exponential comparison, corollary 10.2.4 with $\lambda =\beta $, gives $w_{j,\beta }\leq u_\beta $. Consequently \[  p-\delta -C_ j/\beta \leq u_\beta \leq p+C_ f/\beta .  \] Letting first $\beta \to \infty $ with $j$ fixed, so that no lower bound for $c_ j$ uniform in $j$ is needed, and then $\delta \downarrow 0$, we obtain uniform convergence. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity then gives weak convergence of the measures. On a compact subset of the open set $\{ p<f\} $, uniform convergence gives $u_\beta -f\leq -\epsilon $ for some $\epsilon >0$ and all large $\beta $. There the measures $\omega _{u_\beta }^ n$ have densities at most $\mathrm{e}^{-\beta \epsilon }$ with respect to $\omega ^ n$. Testing against continuous functions with compact support in $\{ p<f\} $ and passing to the limit gives $\omega _ p^ n=0$ on this open set. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.1.2
text: Proposition 13.1.2 . If $f$ is bounded and lower semicontinuous, then $P_\omega (f)$ is bounded, lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, and its Monge–Ampère measure is concentrated on $\{ P_\omega (f)=f\} $. Proof. Suppose first that $f$ is continuous. Choose smooth functions $f_ j\to f$ uniformly. The Lipschitz bound for envelopes in proposition 1.19.3 gives $p_ j=P_\omega (f_ j)\to p=P_\omega (f)$ uniformly. Every compact subset of the open set $\{ p<f\} $ has a neighborhood on which $p_ j<f_ j$ for all large $j$. The preceding proposition and convergence of bounded products then give $\omega _ p^ n=0$ on $\{ p<f\} $. For lower semicontinuous $f$, choose continuous functions $f_ j\uparrow f$ with common upper and lower bounds. For example, for a fixed distance $d$ inducing the topology of $X$, one may take \[  f_ j(x)=\inf _{y\in X}\bigl (f(y)+j d(x,y)\bigr ).  \] These functions are Lipschitz and increase to $f$: if convergence failed at $x$, approximate minimizers $y$ would approach $x$, contradicting lower semicontinuity of $f$ at $x$. The functions $p_ j=P_\omega (f_ j)$ increase and stay bounded, so the regularized limit $p_\infty =(\lim _ jp_ j)^*$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. It agrees with $\lim _ jp_ j$ outside a pluripolar set, and since each $p_ j$ lies below $f_ j\leq f$ outside a pluripolar set, we obtain $p_\infty \leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Thus $p_\infty \leq P_\omega (f)$. For fixed $k$, the set $\{ p_\infty <f_ k\} $ is open, since $p_\infty $ is upper semicontinuous and $f_ k$ is continuous. If $j\geq k$, then $p_ j\leq p_\infty <f_ k\leq f_ j$ there, so the continuous case gives $\omega _{p_ j}^ n=0$ on that open set. Bedford–Taylor continuity along increasing sequences applies after adding a fixed smooth local function whose Hessian dominates $\omega $ and expanding with respect to the resulting smooth form. Together with the lower semicontinuity of the mass of open sets under weak convergence, it yields \[  \omega _{p_\infty }^ n(\{ p_\infty <f_ k\} )=0.  \] Taking the union over $k$ gives zero measure on $\{ p_\infty <f\} $, hence also on $\{ p_\infty <P_\omega (f)\} $ outside a pluripolar set, since $P_\omega (f)\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Bounded measures of this kind do not charge pluripolar sets, so the domination principle, theorem 10.2.2 , gives $p_\infty \geq P_\omega (f)$. The two functions are therefore equal, and the assertion follows. $\square$

title: Theorem 13.1.3
text: Theorem 13.1.3 . Let $\theta \geq 0$ be smooth and let $f$ be bounded and quasi-continuous. Then $p=P_\theta (f)$ is bounded, $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere, and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0.  \] Proof. First suppose that $\theta =\omega $ is Hermitian. Choose bounded lower semicontinuous functions $f_ j\downarrow f$ quasi-everywhere, with common bounds, as in lemma 1.8.8 . The bounded functions $p_ j=P_\omega (f_ j)$ decrease to $p$. Indeed, their limit is a competitor for $p$, since it lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, and the reverse inequality follows from monotonicity. For fixed $k$, put $H_ k=\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} $, a bounded quasi-continuous function. Where $H_ k>0$ and $j\geq k$, we have $p_ j\leq p_ k<f\leq f_ j$ outside a pluripolar set. The lower semicontinuous case therefore gives \[  \int _ X H_ k\, \omega _{p_ j}^ n=0.  \] The convergence of bounded products against quasi-continuous weights in section 1.8 gives $\int _ XH_ k\, \omega _ p^ n=0$. Since the sets $\{ p_ k<f\} $ increase to $\{ p<f\} $, this proves the assertion for Hermitian $\theta $. For general semipositive $\theta $, set $\theta _ j=\theta +j^{-1}\omega $. The functions $p_ j=P_{\theta _ j}(f)$ have the common bounds $\inf _ Xf\leq p_ j\leq \sup _ Xf$ and decrease. Their limit is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic by distributional convergence and lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, so it is at most $p=P_\theta (f)$; since $p\leq p_ j$ for all $j$, it equals $p$. For each fixed $k$, the same coefficient $H_ k=\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} $ gives \[  \int _ XH_ k\, \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _ j}(p_ j)=0\qquad (j\geq k).  \] All $p_ j$ are bounded potentials for the fixed Hermitian form $\theta +\omega $. Expanding the products with background $\theta _ j$ with respect to this fixed background, we may use convergence of bounded products and uniform capacity bounds to pass the last identity to the limit, with the quasi-continuous weight $H_ k$; this gives $\int _ XH_ k\, \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0$. Exhausting $\{ p<f\} $ as before completes the proof. $\square$

title: Theorem 13.1.4
text: Theorem 13.1.4 . Let $\theta $ be smooth and semipositive, and let $f$ be a quasi-continuous obstacle. If $p=P_\theta (f)$ is not identically $-\infty $, then $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0.  \] Here the total extended mass of $p$ may be infinite. Proof. The local envelope theorem, applied to a countable family realizing the supremum (Choquet's lemma), gives $p\leq f$ outside a pluripolar set. Choose $M>\sup _ Xp$ and replace $f$ by $\min (f,M)$. This does not change the envelope, since $p$ itself is a competitor for the smaller obstacle. Since $p<M$, the contact set is also unchanged, so it suffices to prove the theorem for the smaller obstacle; that is, we may assume that $f$ is bounded above. Theorem 13.1.3 gives $p_ j\leq f_ j$ quasi-everywhere and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p_ j<f_ j\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_ j)=0.  \] The sequence $p_ j$ decreases and stays above $p$. Where this coefficient is positive, $p_ k<f$ and $p>-C$. For $j\geq k$, we then have $p_ j\leq p_ k<f\leq f_ j$ and $p_ j\geq p>-C$ there. Plurifine locality and theorem 13.1.3 therefore imply \[  \int _ X H_{k,C}\,  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\max (p_ j,-C))=0.  \] The truncated potentials are uniformly bounded and decrease to $\max (p,-C)$, so their measures converge weakly by bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity. The uniform capacity bounds and the weighted convergence in section 1.8 also allow testing against $H_{k,C}$. Hence the last identity holds with $p$ in place of $p_ j$. By plurifine locality, this says that the extended measure of $p$ vanishes on $\{ p_ k<f\} \cap \{ p>-C\} $. Off the pole set of $p$, these sets increase to $\{ p<f\} $ as first $k$ and then $C$ tend to infinity. Continuity of positive measures along increasing sequences proves the assertion, even if the total extended mass is infinite. $\square$

text: Proposition 13.1.5 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form that is semipositive or big, and let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$.
