title: 13.4 Relative envelope classes
text: 13.4 Relative envelope classes Fix a reference potential $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For $b\geq 1$, the stretched obstacle $bu-(b-1)\varphi =\varphi +b(u-\varphi )$ magnifies the difference between $u$ and $\varphi $ by the factor $b$, and so becomes more singular where $u$ lies below $\varphi $. Requiring a competitor below every finite stretch defines a relative class that is stable under convex combinations and finite rooftops. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $b\geq 1$, define the family of competitors \[  \mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )= \left\{ h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})\varphi \leq u\right\} .  \] For $b=1$ the inequality means $h\leq u$. Away from the poles of $u$ and $\varphi $, the inequality means $h\leq bu-(b-1)\varphi $. The convex combination on the left is defined everywhere, so the definition does not require a value of $bu-(b-1)\varphi $ at common poles. When $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )$ is nonempty, we write \[  Q_ b(u,\varphi )=P_\theta (bu-(b-1)\varphi )  \] for its upper envelope. Since the obstacle is finite almost everywhere, the competitors have a common upper bound by section 1.19 , so $Q_ b(u,\varphi )$ is then a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function; in particular, it is not identically $-\infty $. The upper-envelope theorem gives its defining inequality almost everywhere, and lemma 1.3.3 makes it pointwise; thus $Q_ b(u,\varphi )$ is the largest member of $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )$. Definition 13.4.1 . The relative envelope class of $\varphi $ is \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\preceq \varphi , \  \mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )\ne \varnothing \text{ for every }b\geq 1\} .  \] When the background $\theta $ is fixed, we abbreviate $\mathcal E_\varphi =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. Proposition 13.4.2 . The class $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ is convex, contains all potentials of the singularity type of $\varphi $, and is stable under bounded changes of its members. If $u$ belongs to it, $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $u\leq v$ and $v\preceq \varphi $, then $v$ belongs to it. In particular, it is stable under maxima of two members. Replacing $\varphi $ by another member of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ of the same singularity type does not change the class. For every smooth real function $f$, \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u-f\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,\varphi -f).  \] Proof. If $u\geq \varphi -C$, then $h=\varphi -bC$ belongs to $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )$ for each $b$; hence every $u\sim \varphi $ belongs to the class. More generally, if $u'\geq u-C$ and $h\in \mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )$, then $h-bC\in \mathcal A_ b(u',\varphi )$. Since the condition $u\preceq \varphi $ is also unchanged by bounded changes of $u$, the class is stable under such changes. A convex combination of two competitors is a competitor for the same convex combination of the two potentials, which proves convexity. Finally, a competitor for $u$ is a competitor for any larger $v$, and the assumption $v\preceq \varphi $ gives the remaining condition. If $\varphi '\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi '\sim \varphi $, choose $C\geq 0$ with $|\varphi '-\varphi |\leq C$ off their common pole set. For $h\in \mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )$, the function $h-(b-1)C$ belongs to $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi ')$: the required inequality holds off the poles, and it extends everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . The reverse implication follows by interchanging the references, and $u\preceq \varphi $ is equivalent to $u\preceq \varphi '$. For the last assertion, note that $h\mapsto h-f$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)$. It preserves the order $\preceq $ and transforms each stretching inequality into \[  b^{-1}(h-f)+(1-b^{-1})(\varphi -f)\leq u-f.  \] This identity also holds at poles, because $f$ is smooth and finite. Thus the corresponding families of competitors are in bijection for every $b\geq 1$. $\square$ Lemma 13.4.3 . If $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $u\leq \varphi $, then $Q_ b(u,\varphi )\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ for every $b\geq 1$. More generally, if $u,w\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $u\leq w$, then $Q_ b(u,w)\in \mathcal E_\varphi $. Proof. Fix $b,s\geq 1$ and put $h=Q_{bs}(u,\varphi )$. Its defining inequality gives, off the pole sets, \[  s^{-1}h+(1-s^{-1})\varphi \leq bu-(b-1)\varphi .  \] The left-hand side is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, so it is at most $Q_ b(u,\varphi )$. Hence $h\in \mathcal A_ s(Q_ b(u,\varphi ),\varphi )$ for every $s$. Also $Q_ b(u,\varphi )\leq u\leq \varphi $, so $Q_ b(u,\varphi )\preceq \varphi $. The inequalities between convex combinations extend across the poles by lemma 1.3.3 , which proves the first assertion. For the second assertion, choose a constant $C$ such that $u-C\leq \varphi $ and $w-C\leq \varphi $. Since $Q_ b(u-C,w-C)=Q_ b(u,w)-C$ and class membership is unchanged by translation, we may assume $u,w\leq \varphi $. Because $u\leq w\leq \varphi $, the obstacle for $Q_ b(u,w)$ lies above that for $Q_ b(u,\varphi )$ and below $u$. Thus \[  Q_ b(u,\varphi )\leq Q_ b(u,w)\leq u\leq \varphi .  \] Since $Q_ b(u,\varphi )\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ by the first assertion, the stability under increase proved in proposition 13.4.2 gives the conclusion. $\square$ Proposition 13.4.4 . If $u_1,\ldots ,u_ N\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, $N\geq 1$, then the rooftop envelope $P_\theta (\min _ iu_ i)$ is not identically $-\infty $ and belongs to $\mathcal E_\varphi $. Proof. Adding a common constant to all $u_ i$, we may assume $u_ i\leq \varphi $. By lemma 13.4.3 , proposition 13.4.2 , \[  h=\frac1N\sum _{i=1}^ N Q_ N(u_ i,\varphi )\in \mathcal E_\varphi .  \] Each summand is at most $\varphi $. For every $i$, the defining inequality of $Q_ N(u_ i,\varphi )$ therefore gives \[  h\leq N^{-1}Q_ N(u_ i,\varphi )+(1-N^{-1})\varphi \leq u_ i.  \] These inequalities between convex combinations also hold at common poles. Thus $h$ is a competitor for $p=P_\theta (\min _ i u_ i)$, so $p$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $h\leq p\leq u_1\preceq \varphi $. Stability under increase gives $p\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, and undoing the translation preserves this conclusion. $\square$ The finiteness of the family is essential: every $\varphi -j$ belongs to $\mathcal E_\varphi $, whereas $P_\theta (\inf _{j\geq 1}(\varphi -j))\equiv -\infty $. The constructions of common envelopes for sequences in chapter 31 require additional estimates. Proposition 13.4.5 . If $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, then for every smooth real function $F$, \[  P_{\theta ,F}[u]=P_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ].  \] In particular, $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\varphi ]$. Proof. The relation $u\preceq \varphi $ gives $P_{\theta ,F}[u]\leq P_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ]$. For the reverse inequality, let $a\in (0,1)$ and choose $h_ a\in \mathcal A_{1/(1-a)}(u,\varphi )$, so that $a\varphi +(1-a)h_ a\leq u$. Combining competitors below $F$ gives \[  aP_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ]+(1-a)P_{\theta ,F}[h_ a] \leq P_{\theta ,F}[u].  \] Indeed, if $g_1$ and $g_2$ are competitors for $P_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ]$ and $P_{\theta ,F}[h_ a]$, then $ag_1+(1-a)g_2$ lies below $F$ and is at least as singular as $a\varphi +(1-a)h_ a\leq u$; taking the two upper envelopes preserves the inequality, by local regularization. Write $m=\min _ XF$ and $M=\max _ XF$. Translating competitors gives \[  P_\theta [h_ a]+m\leq P_{\theta ,F}[h_ a]\leq P_\theta [h_ a]+M.  \] Every $P_\theta [h_ a]$ has supremum zero, since it lies above $h_ a-\sup _ Xh_ a$ and below zero. The uniform $L^1$ bound for normalized potentials in theorem 1.4.2 therefore bounds the $L^1$ norms of the $P_{\theta ,F}[h_ a]$ uniformly in $a$. Letting $a\uparrow 1$ in the first inequality gives $P_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ]\leq P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ almost everywhere, and by lemma 1.3.3 the inequality holds everywhere. $\square$

title: Definition 13.4.1
text: Definition 13.4.1 . The relative envelope class of $\varphi $ is \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\preceq \varphi , \  \mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )\ne \varnothing \text{ for every }b\geq 1\} .  \]

text: Proposition 13.4.2 . If $\varphi '\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi '\sim \varphi $, choose $C\geq 0$ with $|\varphi '-\varphi |\leq C$ off their common pole set. For $h\in \mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )$, the function $h-(b-1)C$ belongs to $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi ')$: the required inequality holds off the poles, and it extends everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . Thus the corresponding families of competitors are in bijection for every $b\geq 1$. $\square$

title: Lemma 13.4.3
text: Lemma 13.4.3 . If $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $u\leq \varphi $, then $Q_ b(u,\varphi )\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ for every $b\geq 1$. More generally, if $u,w\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $u\leq w$, then $Q_ b(u,w)\in \mathcal E_\varphi $. Proof. Fix $b,s\geq 1$ and put $h=Q_{bs}(u,\varphi )$. Its defining inequality gives, off the pole sets, \[  s^{-1}h+(1-s^{-1})\varphi \leq bu-(b-1)\varphi .  \] The left-hand side is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, so it is at most $Q_ b(u,\varphi )$. Hence $h\in \mathcal A_ s(Q_ b(u,\varphi ),\varphi )$ for every $s$. Also $Q_ b(u,\varphi )\leq u\leq \varphi $, so $Q_ b(u,\varphi )\preceq \varphi $. The inequalities between convex combinations extend across the poles by lemma 1.3.3 , which proves the first assertion. For the second assertion, choose a constant $C$ such that $u-C\leq \varphi $ and $w-C\leq \varphi $. Since $Q_ b(u-C,w-C)=Q_ b(u,w)-C$ and class membership is unchanged by translation, we may assume $u,w\leq \varphi $. Because $u\leq w\leq \varphi $, the obstacle for $Q_ b(u,w)$ lies above that for $Q_ b(u,\varphi )$ and below $u$. Thus \[  Q_ b(u,\varphi )\leq Q_ b(u,w)\leq u\leq \varphi .  \] Since $Q_ b(u,\varphi )\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ by the first assertion, the stability under increase proved in proposition 13.4.2 gives the conclusion. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.4.4
text: Proposition 13.4.4 . If $u_1,\ldots ,u_ N\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, $N\geq 1$, then the rooftop envelope $P_\theta (\min _ iu_ i)$ is not identically $-\infty $ and belongs to $\mathcal E_\varphi $. Proof. Adding a common constant to all $u_ i$, we may assume $u_ i\leq \varphi $. By lemma 13.4.3 , proposition 13.4.2 , \[  h=\frac1N\sum _{i=1}^ N Q_ N(u_ i,\varphi )\in \mathcal E_\varphi .  \] Each summand is at most $\varphi $. For every $i$, the defining inequality of $Q_ N(u_ i,\varphi )$ therefore gives \[  h\leq N^{-1}Q_ N(u_ i,\varphi )+(1-N^{-1})\varphi \leq u_ i.  \] These inequalities between convex combinations also hold at common poles. Thus $h$ is a competitor for $p=P_\theta (\min _ i u_ i)$, so $p$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $h\leq p\leq u_1\preceq \varphi $. Stability under increase gives $p\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, and undoing the translation preserves this conclusion. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.4.5
text: Proposition 13.4.5 . If $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, then for every smooth real function $F$, \[  P_{\theta ,F}[u]=P_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ].  \] In particular, $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\varphi ]$. Proof. The relation $u\preceq \varphi $ gives $P_{\theta ,F}[u]\leq P_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ]$. For the reverse inequality, let $a\in (0,1)$ and choose $h_ a\in \mathcal A_{1/(1-a)}(u,\varphi )$, so that $a\varphi +(1-a)h_ a\leq u$. Combining competitors below $F$ gives \[  aP_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ]+(1-a)P_{\theta ,F}[h_ a] \leq P_{\theta ,F}[u].  \] Indeed, if $g_1$ and $g_2$ are competitors for $P_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ]$ and $P_{\theta ,F}[h_ a]$, then $ag_1+(1-a)g_2$ lies below $F$ and is at least as singular as $a\varphi +(1-a)h_ a\leq u$; taking the two upper envelopes preserves the inequality, by local regularization. Write $m=\min _ XF$ and $M=\max _ XF$. Translating competitors gives \[  P_\theta [h_ a]+m\leq P_{\theta ,F}[h_ a]\leq P_\theta [h_ a]+M.  \] Every $P_\theta [h_ a]$ has supremum zero, since it lies above $h_ a-\sup _ Xh_ a$ and below zero. The uniform $L^1$ bound for normalized potentials in theorem 1.4.2 therefore bounds the $L^1$ norms of the $P_{\theta ,F}[h_ a]$ uniformly in $a$. Letting $a\uparrow 1$ in the first inequality gives $P_{\theta ,F}[\varphi ]\leq P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ almost everywhere, and by lemma 1.3.3 the inequality holds everywhere. $\square$

title: 13.5 Model references and positive mass
text: 13.5 Model references and positive mass In this section $\theta $ is semipositive and big. Suppose that a potential $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has a competitor in a smaller background $a\theta $, $0<a<1$, that is, $P_{a\theta }(u)\not\equiv -\infty $. Then the big form $(1-a)\theta $ remains available: an envelope in this background has positive mass, and the contact property transfers this mass to $u$. To obtain such competitors for all members of a relative class, we use a reference $\varphi $ satisfying 13.26 \begin{equation} \label{eq:als-model-condition} P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi ,\qquad P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )\not\equiv -\infty \quad \text{for some }0<\varepsilon <1. \end{equation} We call such a $\varphi $ a model reference and fix one such $\varepsilon $. Note that $\varphi =P_\theta [\varphi ]\leq 0$. For $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, the envelope of $u-\varphi $ belongs to the relative envelope class $\mathcal E_0=\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,0)$ of the zero potential, and stretching realizes it in an arbitrarily small background. Under a bounded mass hypothesis, chapter 30 uses instead the condition ( 30.10 ), in which a positive lower volume replaces the condition on the smaller background; the two conditions are compared there. Lemma 13.5.1 . Let $\varphi $ be a model reference. If $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $u\leq \varphi $, then \[  w=P_\theta (u-\varphi )\in \mathcal E_0, \qquad w\leq 0, \qquad w+\varphi \leq u.  \] Proof. Since $\varphi \leq 0$, the potential $u$ lies below the obstacle $u-\varphi $ away from the pole set of $\varphi $, so it is a competitor. Hence the envelope $w$ is not identically $-\infty $. It is at most zero, since $u-\varphi \leq 0$, and it satisfies $w+\varphi \leq u$ off the poles, hence everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . For $b\geq 1$, let $h_ b=Q_ b(u,\varphi )$. Then, off the poles, \[  h_ b\leq bu-(b-1)\varphi \leq b(u-\varphi ).  \] Since $\theta \geq 0$, the function $b^{-1}h_ b$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and so it is a competitor for $w$. Hence $h_ b\leq bw$, so $\mathcal A_ b(w,0)$ is nonempty for every $b$. Since also $w\leq 0$, this means exactly that $w\in \mathcal E_0$. $\square$ Lemma 13.5.2 . Let $0<a<1$ and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. If $q=P_{a\theta }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $, then \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\geq (1-a)^ n v_-(\theta ),  \] and the mass on the left is strictly positive, even when $v_-(\theta )=0$. Proof. The obstacle $u-q$ is nonnegative away from the poles, so by lemma 1.19.2 the envelope $p=P_{(1-a)\theta }(u-q)$ is bounded. By the contact theorem, its measure is carried by $D=\{ p+q=u\} $, and $p+q\leq u$ everywhere. Since $p+q$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, positivity of mixed products and ordered contact imply \[  \mathrm{MA}_{(1-a)\theta }(p) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p+q) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u),  \] where all assertions are first restricted to the complement of the poles. Writing $p=(1-a)\widetilde p$ with $\widetilde p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and integrating, we obtain the lower bound from the definition of $v_-(\theta )$. Finally, the bounded potential $p$ has strictly positive mass by proposition 13.2.1 , since $(1-a)\theta $ is big. $\square$ Theorem 13.5.3 . Let $\varphi $ be a model reference, with $\varepsilon $ as in ( 13.26 ). For every $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and every $0<\delta <1-\varepsilon $, the envelope $P_{(\varepsilon +\delta )\theta }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $. Consequently, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\geq (1-\varepsilon )^ n v_-(\theta ), \qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)>0.  \] The mass may be infinite. Proof. After adding a constant to $u$, we may assume $u\leq \varphi $. Let $w\in \mathcal E_0$ be as in lemma 13.5.1 . Since $w\in \mathcal E_0$, the envelope $P_\theta (w/\delta )$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $\delta P_\theta (w/\delta )\leq w$. The potential \[  P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )+\delta P_\theta (w/\delta ) \leq \varphi +w\leq u  \] belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,(\varepsilon +\delta )\theta )$, so it is a competitor for $P_{(\varepsilon +\delta )\theta }(u)$. Applying lemma 13.5.2 with $a=\varepsilon +\delta $ and letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives the uniform estimate. The positivity follows from the same lemma with any one such $\delta $. $\square$
13.26 \begin{equation} \label{eq:als-model-condition} P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi ,\qquad P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )\not\equiv -\infty \quad \text{for some }0<\varepsilon <1. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 13.5.1

If $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $u\leq \varphi $, then \[  w=P_\theta (u-\varphi )\in \mathcal E_0, \qquad w\leq 0, \qquad w+\varphi \leq u.  \] Proof. title: Theorem 13.5.3
text: Theorem 13.5.3 . Let $\varphi $ be a model reference, with $\varepsilon $ as in ( 13.26 ). For every $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and every $0<\delta <1-\varepsilon $, the envelope $P_{(\varepsilon +\delta )\theta }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $. Consequently, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\geq (1-\varepsilon )^ n v_-(\theta ), \qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)>0.  \] The mass may be infinite. Proof. After adding a constant to $u$, we may assume $u\leq \varphi $. Let $w\in \mathcal E_0$ be as in lemma 13.5.1 . title: 13.6 Infinite mass inside the envelope class
search_title: Infinite mass inside the envelope class
text: 13.6 Infinite mass inside the envelope class We now take the Hermitian background $\theta =\omega $ and the reference $\varphi =0$. If $\omega $ does not have the bounded mass property, that is, if the upper mass $v_+(\omega )$ of definition 6.5.1 is infinite, then the series constructed in theorem 6.6.1 has infinite mass. It splits into a smooth finite sum and a tail whose curvature is bounded below by an arbitrarily small multiple of $-\omega $. Multiplying a sufficiently late tail by the stretching factor gives a competitor for that stretch, so the series lies in the relative envelope class of zero. Proposition 13.6.1 . If $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, the potential $U$ in theorem 6.6.1 can be chosen so that, in addition, \[  U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0),\qquad P_\omega [U]=0.  \] The same conclusions hold for $\varepsilon U$, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. Each of these potentials has infinite extended mass and trivial multiplier ideals at every positive weight. Proof. Use the smooth nonpositive $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u_ j$, $j\geq 1$, of theorem 6.6.1 and their convergent series $U=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}u_ j$. For each integer $N\geq 1$, write \[  U=A_ N+V_ N,\qquad A_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}u_ j,\qquad V_ N=\sum _{j>N}2^{-j}u_ j,\qquad \delta _ N=2^{-N}.  \] The head $A_ N$ is smooth, and since the finite partial sums of the tail decrease, $V_ N\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\delta _ N\omega )$; the tail is not identically $-\infty $, because $U=A_ N+V_ N$ is not. Fix $b>1$ and choose $N$ so large that $b\delta _ N\leq 1$. Then \[  h_ b=bV_ N+\min _ X(bA_ N)  \] is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ b\geq -b\delta _ N\omega \geq -\omega $. Moreover, $h_ b\leq bU$. Thus $h_ b\in \mathcal A_ b(U,0)$ for every $b$, and since $U\leq 0$, this proves $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0)$. For $\varepsilon U$, use the tails $\varepsilon V_ N$, and choose $N$ with $b\varepsilon \delta _ N\leq 1$. By proposition 13.4.5 , the singularity envelope of each of these potentials is $P_\omega [0]=0$. Their infinite mass and trivial multiplier ideals are given by corollary 6.6.2 . $\square$ The bound on the mass in proposition 13.1.6 concerns the envelope fixed point itself. This example shows that potentials with the same singularity envelope as a fixed point, even with trivial multiplier ideals at every positive weight, need not have finite mass. Corollary 13.6.2 . The following conditions on a Hermitian metric $\omega $ are equivalent: $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $; every member of $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0)$ has finite extended mass; every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $P_\omega [u]=0$ has finite extended mass. Proof. If $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $, all $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions have finite extended mass by proposition 6.5.3 . If $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, proposition 13.6.1 contradicts each of the other two conditions. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.6.1
text: Proposition 13.6.1 . If $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, the potential $U$ in theorem 6.6.1 can be chosen so that, in addition, \[  U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0),\qquad P_\omega [U]=0.  \] The same conclusions hold for $\varepsilon U$, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. Each of these potentials has infinite extended mass and trivial multiplier ideals at every positive weight. Proof. Use the smooth nonpositive $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u_ j$, $j\geq 1$, of theorem 6.6.1 and their convergent series $U=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}u_ j$. For each integer $N\geq 1$, write \[  U=A_ N+V_ N,\qquad A_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}u_ j,\qquad V_ N=\sum _{j>N}2^{-j}u_ j,\qquad \delta _ N=2^{-N}.  \] The head $A_ N$ is smooth, and since the finite partial sums of the tail decrease, $V_ N\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\delta _ N\omega )$; the tail is not identically $-\infty $, because $U=A_ N+V_ N$ is not. Fix $b>1$ and choose $N$ so large that $b\delta _ N\leq 1$. Then \[  h_ b=bV_ N+\min _ X(bA_ N)  \] is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ b\geq -b\delta _ N\omega \geq -\omega $. Moreover, $h_ b\leq bU$. Thus $h_ b\in \mathcal A_ b(U,0)$ for every $b$, and since $U\leq 0$, this proves $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0)$. For $\varepsilon U$, use the tails $\varepsilon V_ N$, and choose $N$ with $b\varepsilon \delta _ N\leq 1$. title: Corollary 13.6.2
text: Corollary 13.6.2 . The following conditions on a Hermitian metric $\omega $ are equivalent: $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $; every member of $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0)$ has finite extended mass; every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $P_\omega [u]=0$ has finite extended mass. Proof. If $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $, all $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions have finite extended mass by proposition 6.5.3 . If $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, proposition 13.6.1 contradicts each of the other two conditions. $\square$

title: 14 Equations with prescribed singularities
text: 14 Equations with prescribed singularities Throughout this chapter we fix a Hermitian metric $\omega $ on $X$ and a smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$. Unless another measure is named, $L^ p$ norms, volumes and the phrase “almost everywhere” refer to $\mathrm{d}V$, while capacity and convergence in capacity refer to $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ from section 1.8 . The background $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form whose positivity is specified in each section. For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\alpha $ and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\alpha )$ we write $\alpha _ u=\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and we call $\{ u=-\infty \} $ the pole set of $u$; it is pluripolar and has zero volume. We write $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ for the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ of theorem 6.1.2 . It equals $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ when $u$ is bounded, charges no pluripolar set, and may have infinite total mass; we keep the superscript where this possibility matters. Finally, $s_+=\max (s,0)$ for real $s$. We use the following notation from earlier chapters. As in definition 1.12.1 , $u\preceq v$ means that $u\leq v+C$ for some constant $C$, and $u\sim v$ means that $u\preceq v$ and $v\preceq u$; the equivalence classes of $\sim $ are the ordinary singularity types. For an obstacle $f$, $P_\theta (f)$ is the largest $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function lying below $f$ quasi-everywhere, $P_\theta (u,v)=P_\theta (\min (u,v))$ is the rooftop envelope, and $V_\theta =P_\theta (0)$; a potential has minimal singularities if it is equivalent to $V_\theta $ (section 1.19 ). The ordinary envelope $P_\theta [u]$ and the envelope fixed points, those $u$ with $P_\theta [u]=u$, are defined in definition 1.19.4 . Recall that $\theta $ is big if some $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $\theta _\rho \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$. We call such a $\rho $ a strict barrier ; by theorem 1.15.3 it can be chosen with analytic singularities. We seek potentials $u$ in the ordinary singularity type of a given reference $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ solving \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu \quad (\lambda >0) \qquad \text{or}\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu ,  \] where $\mu $ is a given measure, typically $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $f\in L^ p$ and $p>1$, and the constant $c>0$ is part of the unknown. When $\varphi $ is unbounded, the comparison principles for bounded potentials no longer apply, and a limit of approximate solutions may leave the prescribed type. For a semipositive big background, both difficulties are overcome by a smaller background. If $P_{\delta \theta }(\varphi )\not\equiv -\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$, then the part $\delta \theta $ of the background can carry the singularity of $\varphi $, while bounded envelopes in the remaining big background $(1-\delta )\theta $ have Monge–Ampère measures of positive mass. This gives a domination principle for singular potentials (theorem 14.1.2 ), and hence uniqueness. Existence starts from bounded equations with $L^ p$ densities, solved with a subsolution built from a strict barrier. A compactness criterion with a common lower barrier identifies limits of Monge–Ampère measures, and an addition theorem for weighted measures in a fixed type removes a possible deficit of mass in a limit. Together with a uniform estimate relative to the reference (theorem 14.11.3 ), these results solve both equations in the type of an envelope fixed point that admits such a smaller-background envelope (theorem 14.11.1 ). At exponent zero, comparison determines the constant $c$ but, in general, not the potential. If $\theta $ is big but not semipositive, $V_\theta $ may be unbounded and the smaller-background construction is not available. A strict analytic barrier $\rho $ takes over its role. For two potentials bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant, a small perturbation by $\rho $ forces a negative infimum of their difference to be attained away from the poles of $\rho $, where a local comparison applies. Resolving the singularities of analytic approximants of $V_\theta $ reduces the equations to semipositive big backgrounds. Stability above the barrier then produces solutions with minimal singularities which are locally Hölder continuous off the poles of $\rho $ (theorem 14.15.2 , theorem 14.15.4 , theorem 14.16.1 ). They are smooth off these poles when the density is smooth and strictly positive on the whole complement (theorem 14.17.1 ). The same barrier controls smooth equations as a semipositive background degenerates (theorem 14.18.3 ). For small resolutions of threefold nodes with a closed background, the potentials converge smoothly away from the exceptional curves, and comparing the limiting and approximating metrics reduces to controlling the diameters of neighborhoods of these curves. In the projective example of theorem 11.6.1 , where the normalized potential is not unique, symmetry selects the zero-exponent limit, while local examples show that a positive density on a small open set does not by itself give regularity. Resolved logarithmic poles and minimal types on blowups give explicit equations whose data are determined by the residual form and the Jacobian of the modification. The last part of the chapter concerns a Hermitian background $h$ and general right-hand sides. Solvability of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=c\mu $ for every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $ is equivalent to a positive lower bound for the masses of bounded $h$-plurisubharmonic functions. For singular data supported on shrinking coordinate spheres, a bounded-density test against a fixed probability supplies a strict Hölder reference, a normalized Hölder solution of the homogeneous equation and bounded exponential solutions (proposition 14.25.1 , corollary 14.25.2 , theorem 14.25.3 ), even when the lower mass vanishes. For an individual nonnegative density $f\in L^1$, bounded truncations and Gauduchon tests determine the largest coefficient $a$ for which $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a solution. Passing from this threshold to an exact equation at exponent zero requires control of the potentials as well as of their measures. At a positive exponent, exponential decay controls the mass on deep sublevels (theorem 14.33.1 ); this control is lost as the exponent tends to zero.

title: 14.1 Domination with a smaller background
text:
14.1 Domination with a smaller background Throughout this section $	heta $ is semipositive and big. Let $0<\delta <1$. When a singular potential lies above a $\delta 	heta $-plurisubharmonic function, the gap between them can be measured by an envelope in the remaining background $(1-\delta )	heta $. This background is again semipositive and big, so its bounded potentials have Monge–Ampère measures of positive mass by proposition 13.2.1 , and bounded domination applies to them. It bounds the envelope from below. A family of stretched envelopes then converts a strict measure inequality into a pointwise inequality, as in the bounded case of theorem 13.2.2 . We say that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ admits a smaller-background envelope if $P_{\delta 	heta }(u)
ot\equiv -\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$. This property depends only on the ordinary singularity type of $u$: if $u'\geq u-C$, then $P_{\delta 	heta }(u)-C$ is a competitor for $P_{\delta 	heta }(u')$. Lemma 14.1.1 . Suppose $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, $v\preceq u$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u)(\{ u<v\} )=0$. If $0<\delta <1$ and $v_\delta =P_{\delta 	heta }(v)
ot\equiv -\infty $, then $u\geq v_\delta $. Proof. Choose $C$ with $v-C\leq u$. Since $v_\delta \leq v$, the obstacle $u-v_\delta $ is bounded below by $-C$ off the pole sets, and it is finite almost everywhere. Hence the envelope \[  p=P_{(1-\delta )	heta }(u-v_\delta )  \] is bounded by lemma 1.19.2 , and by contact support (theorem 13.1.4 ) its measure is carried by $D=\{ p+v_\delta =u\} $. Moreover $p+v_\delta \leq u$ everywhere, and \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p+v_\delta ) =((1-\delta )	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)+(\delta 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta )  \] is a sum of two positive currents. Positivity of mixed products and ordered contact therefore give \[  \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_{(1-\delta )	heta }(p) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u);  \] this inequality is first proved on common finite truncation levels and then extended by exhaustion. Off the pole sets, every point of $D\cap \{ p<0\} $ satisfies $u=p+v_\delta <v_\delta \leq v$. The hypothesis therefore gives $\mathrm{MA}_{(1-\delta )	heta }(p)(\{ p<0\} )=0$. Since $(1-\delta )	heta $ is semipositive and big, bounded domination (theorem 13.2.2 , with proposition 13.2.1 ), applied to $p$ and the constant $0$ with coefficient zero, yields $p\geq 0$. Hence $u\geq p+v_\delta \geq v_\delta $. $\square$ Theorem 14.1.2 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $P_{\delta 	heta }(u)
ot\equiv -\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$. Suppose $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, $v\preceq u$, and $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u) \leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (v),  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. Since $\max (u,v)=v$ on the plurifine open set $\{ u<v\} $, plurifine locality shows that replacing $v$ by $\max (u,v)$ preserves the hypothesis; it does not change the conclusion. We may therefore assume $u\leq v$, and since $v\preceq u$ there is $C\geq 0$ with $u\leq v\leq u+C$. For $b>1$ consider the stretched envelopes \[  p_ b=P_	heta (bu-(b-1)v),\qquad D_ b=\{ p_ b=bu-(b-1)v\} .  \] The function $u-(b-1)C$ is a competitor, so $p_ b
ot\equiv -\infty $; and since $bu-(b-1)v\leq u$, we have $u-(b-1)C\leq p_ b\leq u$. By contact support, the measure of $p_ b$ is concentrated on $D_ b$. The potential $b^{-1}p_ b+(1-b^{-1})v$ lies below $u$ and agrees with it on $D_ b$, so ordered contact and positivity of mixed products give \[  \mathbf1_{D_ b} igl [b^{-n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p_ b) +(1-b^{-1})^ n\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (v) igr ] \leq \mathbf1_{D_ b}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u).  \] Choose $b$ so large that $(1-b^{-1})^ n>c$. On $D_ b\cap \{ u<v\} $ the hypothesis then forces $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p_ b)$ to vanish. Since the masses may be infinite, we justify this subtraction as follows. On each set where $u,v,p_ b>-k$, every measure involved is finite, being bounded by the mass of the corresponding bounded truncation. We subtract the finite terms on each such set and then take the union over $k$, so no infinite masses are ever subtracted. It follows that the measure of $p_ b$ is carried by $D_ b\cap \{ u=v\} \subset \{ p_ b=u\} $. We apply lemma 14.1.1 to the pair $(p_ b,u)$: their singularities are equivalent, $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p_ b)(\{ p_ b<u\} )=0$, and $P_{\delta 	heta }(u)
ot\equiv -\infty $. We obtain \[  p_ b\geq P_{\delta 	heta }(u)  \] for all sufficiently large $b$. Suppose now that $u\geq v$ fails. By lemma 1.3.3 , the set $\{ u<v\} $ has positive volume. Since both potentials are finite almost everywhere, some set $E=\{ u<v-a\} $ with $a>0$ has positive volume and both functions are finite on $E$. On $E$ the obstacle inequality gives \[  P_{\delta 	heta }(u)\leq p_ b\leq v-ba  \] quasi-everywhere. Letting $b$ tend to infinity through the integers shows that the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $P_{\delta 	heta }(u)
ot\equiv -\infty $ equals $-\infty $ on a set of positive volume, a contradiction. Thus $u\geq v$ off the pole sets, and lemma 1.3.3 gives the inequality everywhere. $\square$ Corollary 14.1.3 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $v\preceq u$, and suppose that $u$ admits a smaller-background envelope. If $\lambda >0$ and \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (v)  \] off the pole sets, then $u\geq v$. In particular, for every $\lambda >0$ and every positive measure $\mu $, the equation $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $ has at most one solution in an ordinary singularity type admitting a smaller-background envelope. Proof. Fix $t>0$. On $\{ u<v-t\} $ the assumed inequality gives $\mathrm{MA}_	heta ^{\mathrm{ext}}(u)\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\mathrm{MA}_	heta ^{\mathrm{ext}}(v-t)$. The theorem, applied to $u$ and $v-t$ with $c=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}$, gives $u\geq v-t$; now let $t\downarrow 0$. For two solutions of the same equation in the stated type, apply this result in both directions. The weighted measures are compared off the common pole sets, which these measures do not charge, so no value of an infinite weight is needed. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.1.1
text: Lemma 14.1.1 . Suppose $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $v\preceq u$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)(\{ u<v\} )=0$. If $0<\delta <1$ and $v_\delta =P_{\delta \theta }(v)\not\equiv -\infty $, then $u\geq v_\delta $. Proof. Choose $C$ with $v-C\leq u$. Since $v_\delta \leq v$, the obstacle $u-v_\delta $ is bounded below by $-C$ off the pole sets, and it is finite almost everywhere. Hence the envelope \[  p=P_{(1-\delta )\theta }(u-v_\delta )  \] is bounded by lemma 1.19.2 , and by contact support (theorem 13.1.4 ) its measure is carried by $D=\{ p+v_\delta =u\} $. Moreover $p+v_\delta \leq u$ everywhere, and \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p+v_\delta ) =((1-\delta )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)+(\delta \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta )  \] is a sum of two positive currents. Positivity of mixed products and ordered contact therefore give \[  \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_{(1-\delta )\theta }(p) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u);  \] this inequality is first proved on common finite truncation levels and then extended by exhaustion. Off the pole sets, every point of $D\cap \{ p<0\} $ satisfies $u=p+v_\delta <v_\delta \leq v$. The hypothesis therefore gives $\mathrm{MA}_{(1-\delta )\theta }(p)(\{ p<0\} )=0$. Since $(1-\delta )\theta $ is semipositive and big, bounded domination (theorem 13.2.2 , with proposition 13.2.1 ), applied to $p$ and the constant $0$ with coefficient zero, yields $p\geq 0$. Hence $u\geq p+v_\delta \geq v_\delta $. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.1.2
text:
Theorem 14.1.2 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $P_{\delta 	heta }(u)
ot\equiv -\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$. Suppose $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, $v\preceq u$, and $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u) \leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (v),  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. Since $\max (u,v)=v$ on the plurifine open set $\{ u<v\} $, plurifine locality shows that replacing $v$ by $\max (u,v)$ preserves the hypothesis; it does not change the conclusion. We may therefore assume $u\leq v$, and since $v\preceq u$ there is $C\geq 0$ with $u\leq v\leq u+C$. For $b>1$ consider the stretched envelopes \[  p_ b=P_	heta (bu-(b-1)v),\qquad D_ b=\{ p_ b=bu-(b-1)v\} .  \] The function $u-(b-1)C$ is a competitor, so $p_ b
ot\equiv -\infty $; and since $bu-(b-1)v\leq u$, we have $u-(b-1)C\leq p_ b\leq u$. By contact support, the measure of $p_ b$ is concentrated on $D_ b$. The potential $b^{-1}p_ b+(1-b^{-1})v$ lies below $u$ and agrees with it on $D_ b$, so ordered contact and positivity of mixed products give \[  \mathbf1_{D_ b} igl [b^{-n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p_ b) +(1-b^{-1})^ n\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (v) igr ] \leq \mathbf1_{D_ b}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u).  \] Choose $b$ so large that $(1-b^{-1})^ n>c$. On $D_ b\cap \{ u<v\} $ the hypothesis then forces $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p_ b)$ to vanish. Since the masses may be infinite, we justify this subtraction as follows. On each set where $u,v,p_ b>-k$, every measure involved is finite, being bounded by the mass of the corresponding bounded truncation. We subtract the finite terms on each such set and then take the union over $k$, so no infinite masses are ever subtracted. It follows that the measure of $p_ b$ is carried by $D_ b\cap \{ u=v\} \subset \{ p_ b=u\} $. We apply lemma 14.1.1 to the pair $(p_ b,u)$: their singularities are equivalent, $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p_ b)(\{ p_ b<u\} )=0$, and $P_{\delta 	heta }(u)
ot\equiv -\infty $. We obtain \[  p_ b\geq P_{\delta 	heta }(u)  \] for all sufficiently large $b$. Suppose now that $u\geq v$ fails. By lemma 1.3.3 , the set $\{ u<v\} $ has positive volume. Since both potentials are finite almost everywhere, some set $E=\{ u<v-a\} $ with $a>0$ has positive volume and both functions are finite on $E$. On $E$ the obstacle inequality gives \[  P_{\delta 	heta }(u)\leq p_ b\leq v-ba  \] quasi-everywhere. Letting $b$ tend to infinity through the integers shows that the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $P_{\delta 	heta }(u)
ot\equiv -\infty $ equals $-\infty $ on a set of positive volume, a contradiction. Thus $u\geq v$ off the pole sets, and lemma 1.3.3 gives the inequality everywhere. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.1.3
text: Corollary 14.1.3 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $v\preceq u$, and suppose that $u$ admits a smaller-background envelope. If $\lambda >0$ and \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v)  \] off the pole sets, then $u\geq v$. In particular, for every $\lambda >0$ and every positive measure $\mu $, the equation $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $ has at most one solution in an ordinary singularity type admitting a smaller-background envelope. Proof. Fix $t>0$. On $\{ u<v-t\} $ the assumed inequality gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta ^{\mathrm{ext}}(u)\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\mathrm{MA}_\theta ^{\mathrm{ext}}(v-t)$. The theorem, applied to $u$ and $v-t$ with $c=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}$, gives $u\geq v-t$; now let $t\downarrow 0$. For two solutions of the same equation in the stated type, apply this result in both directions. The weighted measures are compared off the common pole sets, which these measures do not charge, so no value of an infinite weight is needed. $\square$

title: 14.2 Bounded equations in a semipositive big background
search_title: Bounded equations in a semipositive big background
text: 14.2 Bounded equations in a semipositive big background In this section $\theta $ is again semipositive and big, and we solve the exponential and the normalized equations with $L^ p$ densities by bounded potentials. The basic tool is a bounded subsolution. A strict barrier, corrected by the solution of a Hermitian equation, is composed with a bounded convex function; the result is a bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function whose Monge–Ampère measure dominates a prescribed density. The derivative of the convex function decays polynomially near the poles of the barrier, and we compensate for this decay by multiplying the auxiliary density by the reciprocal weight. Fix a strict barrier $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $0<a\leq 1$ such that \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq a\omega ,\qquad \rho \leq -1.  \] No property of $\rho $ other than these two inequalities will be used. Lemma 14.2.1 . Fix $p>1$ and $L>0$. There is $b>0$ such that, for every $f\geq 0$ with $\| f\| _{L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq L$, one can find $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfying \[  -1\leq s\leq 0,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (s)\geq b f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The constant $b$ depends only on the fixed geometry and on $\rho ,a,p,L$. Proof. Choose $1<q<p$. Since a fixed quasi-plurisubharmonic function belongs to every finite $L^ r$ space, Hölder's inequality gives a uniform $L^ q$ bound for \[  g=(-\rho )^{2n}f.  \] By theorem 10.1.1 there are $c>0$ and a continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $v$, normalized by $\sup _ Xv=-1$, such that \[  \omega _ v^ n=c(1+g)\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The construction in that theorem gives a uniform upper bound for $c$, because in its Gauduchon trace estimate the root integral of $1+g$ is bounded below by the root integral of $1$. The lower-density estimate of theorem 10.3.3 gives $c\| 1+g\| _ q\geq c_ q>0$, so $c$ is also bounded below. The potential estimate of the same theorem then gives $-C\leq v\leq -1$ with a uniform $C$. Put $h=\rho +av\leq -1$. Then $\theta _ h\geq a\omega _ v$. On $(-\infty ,-1]$ define \[  \chi (t)=-t^{-1}-1,\qquad \chi '(t)=t^{-2}\in (0,1],\qquad \chi ''(t)=-2t^{-3}>0,  \] and set $s=\chi (h)$, with value $-1$ at the poles of $h$. To justify both the positivity of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ and the computation of its Monge–Ampère measure, we first work with the bounded functions $h_ k=\max (h,-k)$, $k\geq 1$. The chain rule for bounded potentials and $\theta \geq 0$ give \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi (h_ k) =(1-\chi '(h_ k))\theta +\chi '(h_ k)\theta _{h_ k} +\chi ''(h_ k)\, \mathrm{d}h_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ k\geq 0.  \] These bounded potentials decrease to $s$, so $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $-1\leq s\leq 0$. On $\{ h>-k\} $, locality and positivity of mixed products give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (s) \geq a^ n|h|^{-2n}\omega _ v^ n \geq a^ nc|h|^{-2n}(-\rho )^{2n}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Letting $k\to \infty $, we obtain this inequality on the set where $h$ is finite; its complement is pluripolar and has zero volume. Since $|h|\leq (-\rho )+aC\leq (1+aC)(-\rho )$, the assertion follows with any common lower bound for $a^ nc(1+aC)^{-2n}$. $\square$ The lemma gives a subsolution for each density in an $L^ p$-bounded family. It does not give a lower bound for the masses of all bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions.

title: 14.2.1 The exponential equation
text: 14.2.1 The exponential equation We approximate $\theta $ from above by the Hermitian forms $\theta +\varepsilon \omega $. The bounded subsolution provides a common lower barrier for the corresponding solutions, and exponential comparison shows that they decrease as $\varepsilon $ decreases. Their limit solves the equation in the original background. Theorem 14.2.2 . Let $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero, and let $\lambda >0$. There is a unique bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] For fixed $\lambda $, these solutions are uniformly bounded when $\| f\| _ p$ is bounded above and $\int _ X f^{1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V$ is bounded away from zero. Proof. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, set $\theta _\varepsilon =\theta +\varepsilon \omega $. By the Hermitian existence theorem theorem 10.1.2 , there is a continuous solution $v_\varepsilon $ of \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _\varepsilon }(v_\varepsilon ) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\varepsilon }f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Take $s,b$ from lemma 14.2.1 , and put $w=s+\lambda ^{-1}\log b$. Positivity of bounded products gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _\varepsilon }(w) \geq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (s)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V \geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w}f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] and bounded exponential comparison (corollary 10.2.4 ) yields $w\leq v_\varepsilon $. If $0<\varepsilon '<\varepsilon $, then $v_{\varepsilon '}$ is also $\theta _\varepsilon $-plurisubharmonic and \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _\varepsilon }(v_{\varepsilon '}) \geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_{\varepsilon '}}f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] so the same comparison gives $v_{\varepsilon '}\leq v_\varepsilon $. Hence $v_\varepsilon $ decreases to a bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $v$ with $w\leq v\leq v_1$. To pass to the limit in the equation, we use the fixed Hermitian background $\Omega =\theta +\omega $ and the expansion \[  (\theta _\varepsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n =\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk (\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ k \wedge \bigl (-(1-\varepsilon )\omega \bigr )^{n-k}.  \] Continuity of bounded products along monotone sequences applies to every term, and the smooth coefficients converge. Dominated convergence applies to the right-hand sides. This proves the equation. Uniqueness follows from bounded domination in the semipositive big background (theorem 13.2.2 , proposition 13.2.1 ) by the usual exponential comparison argument. For the uniform assertion, note first that the lower barrier $w$ is uniform by lemma 14.2.1 . The upper barrier $v_1$ solves an equation in the fixed Hermitian background $\Omega $. The proof of lemma 10.4.1 bounds its supremum using only an upper bound for the density norm and a positive lower bound for the root integral: these two bounds control, respectively, the Hölder term and the denominator in ( 10.16 ), and they survive the smooth approximation used there. Thus $v_1$, and hence $v$, has a uniform upper bound. $\square$ Local continuity of this bounded solution will follow from theorem 14.5.1 .

title: 14.2.2 The normalized equation
text: 14.2.2 The normalized equation For the normalized equation the approximating potentials need not be monotone. Upper envelopes and lower envelopes of their tails provide monotone sequences on either side of an $L^1$ cluster limit. Comparison identifies the two limits, and hence the equation, while the constant is controlled by the Gauduchon trace and the bounded subsolution. Theorem 14.2.3 . For every nonzero $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, there are a bounded $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a uniquely determined $c>0$ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi )=cf\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \sup _ X\varphi =0.  \] The construction gives uniform bounds for $\| \varphi \| _\infty $, $c$ and $c^{-1}$ when $\| f\| _ p$ is bounded above and $\int _ Xf^{1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V$ is bounded away from zero. Only the constant $c$ is asserted to be unique; the normalized potential need not be unique, as theorem 11.6.1 shows already for a Hermitian background. Proof. Step 1: approximating equations and their constants. For integers $j\geq 1$, put $\omega _ j=\theta +2^{-j}\omega $, and choose continuous normalized solutions \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\varphi _ j)=c_ jf\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \sup _ X\varphi _ j=0.  \] We first bound $c_ j$. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma _0$; when $n=1$ any Hermitian form will do, and the calculation below reduces to Stokes' theorem. The smooth approximation in the proof of theorem 10.1.1 , together with the Gauduchon trace, gives a common upper bound: the numerator $\int _ X\omega _ j\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}$ is bounded above by $\int _ X(\theta +\omega )\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}$, and the root integral of $f$ is positive and fixed. Here the estimate is applied to the smooth approximating equations before passing to their continuous limits. For a lower bound, take $s,b$ from lemma 14.2.1 . If $c_ j<b$, then \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\varphi _ j) \leq (c_ j/b)\mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(s+A)  \] for every constant $A$, and strict domination in the Hermitian background $\omega _ j$ (theorem 10.2.2 ) would give $\varphi _ j\geq s+A$ for every $A$, which is absurd. Thus $c_ j\geq b$. In fact the constants decrease with $j$: if $k>j$, positivity gives $\mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\varphi _ k)\geq c_ kf\, \mathrm{d}V$, and the same argument excludes $c_ j<c_ k$. Hence $c_ j\downarrow c>0$. Step 2: a uniform bound for the potentials. For the Hermitian form $\Omega =\theta +\omega $, all $\varphi _ j$ are normalized $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic functions. Using uniform exponential integrability (lemma 1.5.1 ) and Hölder's inequality, choose $\gamma >0$ small and $1<q<p$ such that \[  g_ j=\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma \varphi _ j}f  \] is bounded in $L^ q$. Since $\varphi _ j\leq 0$, we have $g_ j\geq f$. Theorem 14.2.2 , applied with integrability exponent $q$ and exponential exponent $\gamma $, therefore gives uniformly bounded $w_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ j)=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma w_ j}g_ j\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Choose $C_0\geq \max \{ 1,\sup _ jc_ j\} $ and set $z_ j=w_ j-\gamma ^{-1}\log C_0$. Then \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(z_ j) \geq \mathrm{e}^{\gamma z_ j}c_ jg_ j\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\varphi _ j) =\mathrm{e}^{\gamma \varphi _ j}c_ jg_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] and exponential comparison gives $z_ j\leq \varphi _ j\leq 0$. Thus all $\varphi _ j$ take values in a common bounded interval. Step 3: the upper envelopes. Extract a subsequence converging in $L^1$ and almost everywhere to the canonical $\theta $-plurisubharmonic representative $\varphi $. We keep the indices $j$; the coefficients of $\omega $ in $\omega _ j$ still decrease to zero. Define \[  \Phi _ j^+=\left(\sup _{\ell \geq j}\varphi _\ell \right)^*, \qquad h_ j=\inf _{\ell \geq j}\varphi _\ell , \qquad p_ j=P_\theta (h_ j).  \] All these functions take values in a common bounded interval. The upper envelopes are $\omega _ j$-plurisubharmonic and decrease to $\varphi $, since the regularized upper envelope agrees almost everywhere with the $L^1$ limit; this also follows from the local Hartogs lemma applied to the bounded tails. For $\ell \geq j$, positivity gives $\mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\varphi _\ell )\geq c_\ell f\, \mathrm{d}V\geq cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. By ordered contact (lemma 1.7.2 ), finite maxima of these functions satisfy the same lower bound. Continuity of bounded products along increasing sequences, followed by the decreasing limit in $j$ and the expansion in the smooth background, gives 14.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-normalized-upper-tail} \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\Phi _ j^+)\geq cf\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi )\geq cf\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} Step 4: the lower envelopes. For the reverse inequality we use lower envelopes, which carry a useful exponential weight. For $N\geq j$ put \[  p_{j,N}=P_\theta \left(\min _{j\leq \ell \leq N}\varphi _\ell \right).  \] The obstacle is continuous and bounded, so the measure of $p_{j,N}$ is carried by its contact set. Partition this set into disjoint Borel pieces according to the first index $\ell $ at which $p_{j,N}=\varphi _\ell $. On such a piece, positivity and ordered contact in the background $\omega _\ell $ give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_{j,N}) \leq \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _\ell }(p_{j,N}) \leq c_\ell f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Moreover $p_{j,N}=\varphi _\ell \geq h_ j$ there, and $c_\ell \leq c_ j$. Summing over the pieces therefore yields the global inequality \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_{j,N}) \leq \mathrm{e}^{p_{j,N}-h_ j}c_ jf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] As $N\to \infty $, the envelopes decrease to $p_ j$. Indeed, their limit lies below each tail obstacle quasi-everywhere and is thus a competitor for $P_\theta (h_ j)$, while the reverse inequality is immediate. Continuity of bounded products along monotone sequences and dominated convergence give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_ j)\leq \mathrm{e}^{p_ j-h_ j}c_ jf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The functions $p_ j$ increase. Let $\varphi '=(\lim _ jp_ j)^*$. Since $h_ j\to \varphi $ almost everywhere, we have $\varphi '\leq \varphi $ for the canonical representatives. Passing to the increasing limit and using ( 14.1 ), we obtain \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi ') \leq \mathrm{e}^{\varphi '-\varphi }cf\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \mathrm{e}^{\varphi '-\varphi }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi ).  \] Bounded exponential comparison forces $\varphi '\geq \varphi $. Thus $\varphi '=\varphi $, and the last inequality, together with ( 14.1 ), proves the equation. If necessary, subtracting $\sup _ X\varphi $ gives the required normalization. Step 5: uniformity and uniqueness of $c$. All bounds used above depend only on the two stated density bounds and the fixed data, which proves the uniform assertion for the constructed solution. Finally, two different positive constants for the same $f$ would contradict strict domination after an arbitrary translation of one of the bounded solutions, exactly as in the lower bound for $c_ j$. This proves the uniqueness of $c$. $\square$ For $\lambda >0$, let $v_\lambda $ be the bounded solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V$, and let $(\varphi ,c)$ be a normalized solution given by theorem 14.2.3 . The two exponential barriers used in proposition 10.6.1 give \[  \| \lambda v_\lambda -\log c\| _\infty \leq \lambda \operatorname {osc}_ X\varphi  \] also in this semipositive background.

The smooth approximation in the proof of theorem 10.1.1 , together with the Gauduchon trace, gives a common upper bound: the numerator $\int _ X\omega _ j\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}$ is bounded above by $\int _ X(\theta +\omega )\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}$, and the root integral of $f$ is positive and fixed. Here the estimate is applied to the smooth approximating equations before passing to their continuous limits. For a lower bound, take $s,b$ from lemma 14.2.1 . If $c_ j<b$, then \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\varphi _ j) \leq (c_ j/b)\mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(s+A)  \] for every constant $A$, and strict domination in the Hermitian background $\omega _ j$ (theorem 10.2.2 ) would give $\varphi _ j\geq s+A$ for every $A$, which is absurd. Thus $c_ j\geq b$. In fact the constants decrease with $j$: if $k>j$, positivity gives $\mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\varphi _ k)\geq c_ kf\, \mathrm{d}V$, and the same argument excludes $c_ j<c_ k$. Hence $c_ j\downarrow c>0$. Step 2: a uniform bound for the potentials. For the Hermitian form $\Omega =\theta +\omega $, all $\varphi _ j$ are normalized $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic functions. Using uniform exponential integrability (lemma 1.5.1 ) and Hölder's inequality, choose $\gamma >0$ small and $1<q<p$ such that \[  g_ j=\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma \varphi _ j}f  \] is bounded in $L^ q$. Since $\varphi _ j\leq 0$, we have $g_ j\geq f$. Theorem 14.2.2 , applied with integrability exponent $q$ and exponential exponent $\gamma $, therefore gives uniformly bounded $w_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ j)=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma w_ j}g_ j\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Choose $C_0\geq \max \{ 1,\sup _ jc_ j\} $ and set $z_ j=w_ j-\gamma ^{-1}\log C_0$. Then \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(z_ j) \geq \mathrm{e}^{\gamma z_ j}c_ jg_ j\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\varphi _ j) =\mathrm{e}^{\gamma \varphi _ j}c_ jg_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] and exponential comparison gives $z_ j\leq \varphi _ j\leq 0$. Thus all $\varphi _ j$ take values in a common bounded interval. Step 3: the upper envelopes. Extract a subsequence converging in $L^1$ and almost everywhere to the canonical $\theta $-plurisubharmonic representative $\varphi $. We keep the indices $j$; the coefficients of $\omega $ in $\omega _ j$ still decrease to zero. Define \[  \Phi _ j^+=\left(\sup _{\ell \geq j}\varphi _\ell \right)^*, \qquad h_ j=\inf _{\ell \geq j}\varphi _\ell , \qquad p_ j=P_\theta (h_ j).  \] All these functions take values in a common bounded interval. The upper envelopes are $\omega _ j$-plurisubharmonic and decrease to $\varphi $, since the regularized upper envelope agrees almost everywhere with the $L^1$ limit; this also follows from the local Hartogs lemma applied to the bounded tails. For $\ell \geq j$, positivity gives $\mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\varphi _\ell )\geq c_\ell f\, \mathrm{d}V\geq cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. By ordered contact (lemma 1.7.2 ), finite maxima of these functions satisfy the same lower bound. Continuity of bounded products along increasing sequences, followed by the decreasing limit in $j$ and the expansion in the smooth background, gives 14.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-normalized-upper-tail} \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\Phi _ j^+)\geq cf\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi )\geq cf\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} Step 4: the lower envelopes. For the reverse inequality we use lower envelopes, which carry a useful exponential weight. For $N\geq j$ put \[  p_{j,N}=P_\theta \left(\min _{j\leq \ell \leq N}\varphi _\ell \right).  \] The obstacle is continuous and bounded, so the measure of $p_{j,N}$ is carried by its contact set. Partition this set into disjoint Borel pieces according to the first index $\ell $ at which $p_{j,N}=\varphi _\ell $. On such a piece, positivity and ordered contact in the background $\omega _\ell $ give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_{j,N}) \leq \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _\ell }(p_{j,N}) \leq c_\ell f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Moreover $p_{j,N}=\varphi _\ell \geq h_ j$ there, and $c_\ell \leq c_ j$. Summing over the pieces therefore yields the global inequality \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_{j,N}) \leq \mathrm{e}^{p_{j,N}-h_ j}c_ jf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] As $N\to \infty $, the envelopes decrease to $p_ j$. Indeed, their limit lies below each tail obstacle quasi-everywhere and is thus a competitor for $P_\theta (h_ j)$, while the reverse inequality is immediate. Continuity of bounded products along monotone sequences and dominated convergence give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_ j)\leq \mathrm{e}^{p_ j-h_ j}c_ jf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The functions $p_ j$ increase. Let $\varphi '=(\lim _ jp_ j)^*$. Since $h_ j\to \varphi $ almost everywhere, we have $\varphi '\leq \varphi $ for the canonical representatives. Passing to the increasing limit and using ( 14.1 ), we obtain \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi ') \leq \mathrm{e}^{\varphi '-\varphi }cf\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \mathrm{e}^{\varphi '-\varphi }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi ).  \] Bounded exponential comparison forces $\varphi '\geq \varphi $. Thus $\varphi '=\varphi $, and the last inequality, together with ( 14.1 ), proves the equation. If necessary, subtracting $\sup _ X\varphi $ gives the required normalization. Step 5: uniformity and uniqueness of $c$. All bounds used above depend only on the two stated density bounds and the fixed data, which proves the uniform assertion for the constructed solution. Finally, two different positive constants for the same $f$ would contradict strict domination after an arbitrary translation of one of the bounded solutions, exactly as in the lower bound for $c_ j$. This proves the uniqueness of $c$. $\square$
14.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-normalized-upper-tail} \mathrm{MA}_{\omega _ j}(\Phi _ j^+)\geq cf\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi )\geq cf\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation}

title: 14.3 A quantitative stability estimate
text: 14.3 A quantitative stability estimate If a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function exceeds a bounded solution only by a small amount in $L^1$, the excess is also uniformly small. To prove this, we restrict the density of the solution to a strict superlevel set of the difference and construct a subsolution for the restricted density. Domination bounds the height of the superlevel set in terms of the norm of the restricted density, and Hölder's inequality converts its volume into a power of the $L^1$ error. Throughout this section $\theta $ is semipositive and big, and $p>1$ is fixed. Theorem 14.3.1 . Fix $L,C_0>0$. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy \[  -C_0\leq u\leq 0,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad 0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V),\quad \| f\| _ p\leq L.  \] For every \[  0<\eta <\frac{p-1}{np+p-1}  \] there is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data and $\eta $, such that every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\leq 0$ satisfies \[  \sup _ X(v-u)_+ \leq C\left(\int _ X(v-u)_+\, \mathrm{d}V\right)^\eta .  \] The comparison potential $v$ need not be bounded. Proof. Replacing $v$ by $\max (v,u)$ leaves both sides unchanged, so we may assume $-C_0\leq u\leq v\leq 0$. Put $I=\int _ X(v-u)\, \mathrm{d}V$. If $I=0$, the two canonical potentials agree everywhere and there is nothing to prove, so we assume $I>0$. Choose $q\in (1,p)$, to be specified at the end. For $\delta >0$ put \[  E_\delta =\{ u<v-\delta \} ,\qquad g_\delta =\mathbf1_{E_\delta }f,\qquad m_\delta =\| g_\delta \| _ q.  \] If $m_\delta >0$, apply lemma 14.2.1 to $g_\delta /m_\delta $. It gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $b>0$ such that \[  -1\leq h\leq 0,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (h)\geq b\, g_\delta /m_\delta \, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The constant $b$ does not depend on $\delta ,f,u,v$, since the auxiliary density has $L^ q$ norm one. First suppose $0<m_\delta <b/2$, and take \[  t=(2m_\delta /b)^{1/n}\in (0,1),\qquad w=(1-t)v+th-\delta -C_0t.  \] Because $h-v\leq C_0$, we have $w\leq v-\delta $, and hence $\{ u<w\} \subset E_\delta $. Positivity of bounded mixed products gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)\geq t^ n\mathrm{MA}_\theta (h) \geq 2g_\delta \, \mathrm{d}V.  \] On $\{ u<w\} $ the last measure equals $2\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$. Bounded strict domination in the semipositive big background (theorem 13.2.2 ) therefore implies $u\geq w$. Consequently \[  v-u\leq v-w =\delta +C_0t+t(v-h)\leq \delta +(C_0+1)t.  \] If $m_\delta =0$, the measure of $u$ vanishes on $E_\delta $, and the same domination theorem with coefficient zero, applied to $u$ and $v-\delta $, gives $v-u\leq \delta $. If $m_\delta \geq b/2$, the bound $v-u\leq C_0$ gives the following inequality after an increase of its constant. Thus in every case 14.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:stability-small-set} \sup _ X(v-u)\leq \delta +C_1m_\delta ^{1/n}. \end{equation} Hölder's inequality and Chebyshev's inequality give \[  m_\delta \leq \| f\| _ p\, \mathrm{d}V(E_\delta )^{1/q-1/p} \leq L(I/\delta )^{(p-q)/(pq)}.  \] Set $a=(p-q)/(npq)>0$. For $0<I\leq 1$, choose $\delta =I^{a/(1+a)}$. Substituting in ( 14.2 ) yields \[  \sup _ X(v-u)\leq C_2 I^{\eta _ q}, \qquad \eta _ q=\frac{p-q}{npq+p-q}.  \] As $q\downarrow 1$, the exponent $\eta _ q$ tends to $(p-1)/(np+p-1)$. For the prescribed $\eta $ we choose $q>1$ so close to $1$ that $\eta _ q>\eta $; then $I^{\eta _ q}\leq I^\eta $ on $(0,1]$. When $I>1$, the bound $v-u\leq C_0$ gives the same conclusion after increasing $C$. This proves the theorem. $\square$ Corollary 14.3.2 . Fix $C_0>0$. Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $-C_0\leq u_ j,u\leq 0$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_ j)=f_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \sup _ j\| f_ j\| _ p+\| f\| _ p<+\infty .  \] If $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1$, then $u_ j\to u$ uniformly. More precisely, for every exponent $\eta $ as in the theorem, \[  \| u_ j-u\| _\infty \leq C\| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(\mathrm{d}V)}^\eta .  \] Proof. Apply the theorem first with solution $u$ and comparison potential $u_ j$, and then with solution $u_ j$ and comparison potential $u$. The constants are uniform because of the common range and the common density bound. The larger of the two suprema is the uniform norm, and each integral of a positive part is at most the full $L^1$ difference. $\square$ The corollary assumes that the limit $u$ already solves an equation with an $L^ p$ density. In an existence proof, this must be established before the corollary can be applied.

title: 14.4 Hölder continuity from bounded stability
text: 14.4 Hölder continuity from bounded stability Bounded stability also gives a Hölder modulus. We apply it to Demailly's Chern-connection regularization of a solution: the $L^1$ error of the regularization controls its pointwise error, and a gradient estimate for the smooth averages then gives the modulus. We use the averaging operators $R_ t$ and the transforms $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ of lemma 1.21.1 , with the constants $A,K$ given there, together with the estimates of lemma 1.21.2 . Interpolating between the smoothing error and the gradient bound yields the exponent below. Theorem 14.4.1 . Let $p>1$ and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ solve \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad 0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V).  \] Then $u$ is Hölder continuous with every exponent \[  0<\beta <\frac{2(p-1)}{np+3(p-1)}.  \] The Hölder constants are uniform for a fixed bound $-C_0\leq u\leq 0$ and a fixed bound for $\| f\| _ p$. In particular, the continuous solutions constructed in theorem 10.1.1 have this regularity. Proof. After adding a constant we may assume $-C_0\leq u\leq 0$. Choose \[  0<\eta <\frac{p-1}{np+p-1},\qquad \alpha =2\eta <1.  \] For small $\delta >0$ set \[  c=\delta ^\alpha ,\qquad e=Ac+2K\delta ,\qquad r=-C_0-1,\qquad v_\delta =\frac{\Phi _{c,\delta }+er}{1+e}.  \] The curvature estimate of lemma 1.21.1 gives $v_\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Evaluating the infimum defining $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ at $t=\delta $ gives $\Phi _{c,\delta }\leq R_\delta u\leq 0$. On the other hand, \[  \Phi _{c,\delta }\geq u-K(\delta ^2+\delta ),  \] since $R_ tu+Kt^2\geq u$, $Kt\geq 0$ and $-c\log (t/\delta )\geq 0$ for $0<t\leq \delta $. For small $\delta $ this lower bound is at least $r$, and therefore \[  v_\delta \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }\leq R_\delta u\leq 0.  \] The Hermitian form $\omega $ is semipositive and big, so theorem 14.3.1 applies in the background $\omega $. Together with the $L^1$ estimate of lemma 1.21.2 , it gives \[  \sup _ X(v_\delta -u)_+ \leq C\left(\int _ X(v_\delta -u)_+\, \mathrm{d}V\right)^\eta \leq C\| R_\delta u-u\| _1^\eta \leq C\delta ^\alpha .  \] Since $e\leq C\delta ^\alpha $ and $u-r\leq C_0+1$, it follows that 14.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:holder-transform-bound} \Phi _{c,\delta }-u =(1+e)(v_\delta -u)+e(u-r)\leq C\delta ^\alpha . \end{equation} We now bound the minimizing radius from below. Fix $z$ and a radius $t=t(z)\in (0,\delta ]$ at which the infimum is attained. The lower estimate at this radius and ( 14.3 ) give \[  -c\log (t/\delta ) \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }(z)-u(z)+K(\delta ^2+\delta ) \leq C\delta ^\alpha =Cc.  \] Thus $t(z)\geq a\delta $ with the constant $a=\mathrm{e}^{-C}>0$, which is independent of $z$ and $\delta $. Since $R_ su+Ks^2$ is increasing in $s$, \[  \begin{split}  R_{a\delta }u+K(a\delta )^2 & \leq R_ tu+Kt^2\\ & =\Phi _{c,\delta }+K\delta ^2+K\delta -Kt+c\log (t/\delta )\\ & \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }+K\delta ^2+K\delta . \end{split}  \] Combining this with ( 14.3 ) and the lower bound $R_ su-u\geq -Ks^2$, and setting $s=a\delta $, we obtain \[  \| R_ su-u\| _\infty \leq Cs^\alpha  \] for every sufficiently small $s>0$. Finally, let $x,y$ be points at a small distance $d$. The gradient estimate $\| \nabla R_ su\| _\infty \leq C/s$ gives \[  |u(x)-u(y)|\leq 2Cs^\alpha +C d/s.  \] With $s=d^{1/(1+\alpha )}$, both terms are bounded by a constant times $d^{\alpha /(1+\alpha )}$, and larger distances are controlled by the bound on the oscillation. This proves Hölder continuity with exponent $\alpha /(1+\alpha )$. Letting $\eta $ approach its upper endpoint gives every $\beta $ in the theorem; smaller exponents follow on compact $X$ by changing the constant. $\square$

title: 14.4.1 Regularity for a measure with a Hölder reference
search_title: Regularity for a measure with a Hölder reference
text: 14.4.1 Regularity for a measure with a Hölder reference The same smoothing argument applies to a singular solution measure dominated by the product of a Hölder potential. Its square-capacity bound supplies stability, and the weighted Chern estimate supplies the smoothing error. Theorem 14.4.2 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C^{0,\alpha }(X)$, $0<\alpha \leq 1$, and suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ satisfies \[  \omega _\varphi ^ n=\mu \leq A\omega _ u^ n, \qquad A>0.  \] Then $\varphi $ is Hölder continuous with exponent \[  \beta =\frac{\alpha }{(\alpha +2n)(6n+1)+\alpha }>0.  \] Its Hölder constant is uniform for fixed bounds on $A$, $\| u\| _{C^{0,\alpha }}$ and the oscillation of $\varphi $. Proof. Normalize $\sup _ X\varphi =0$ and write $M=\| \varphi \| _\infty $. By proposition 1.8.7 , the measure $\mu $ has a square-capacity bound with a fixed constant. Put \[  \eta =\frac{2\alpha }{\alpha +2n},\qquad \gamma =\frac1{6n+1},\qquad q=\eta \gamma /2<1.  \] The weighted estimate of lemma 1.21.6 gives $\| R_\delta \varphi -\varphi \| _{L^1(\mu )}\leq C\delta ^\eta $. Use the constants $A_0,K$ of lemma 1.21.1 , taking $A_0\geq 1$, and define the unshifted transform \[  F=\inf _{0<t\leq \delta } \{ R_ t\varphi +Kt^2+Kt-b\log (t/\delta )\} .  \] It differs from $\Phi _{b,\delta }$ by the constant $K(\delta ^2+\delta )$, so \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F\geq -(A_0b+2K\delta )\omega , \qquad \varphi \leq F\leq R_\delta \varphi +2K\delta  \] when $\delta \leq 1$. Choose $\varepsilon =\delta ^ q$ and $b=(\varepsilon -2K\delta )/A_0$. For small $\delta $, $\varepsilon \leq 1/2$ and $\varepsilon /(2A_0)\leq b\leq \varepsilon /A_0$. Set $T=(1-\varepsilon )F$. Then $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq \varepsilon ^2\omega $. The transform is continuous: its positive logarithmic penalty excludes radii near zero uniformly in the base point for each fixed $\delta ,b$, and the minimum of its continuous defining function on the resulting compact interval depends continuously on the base point. Take $B\geq M+2K+1$ and set $\psi =T-B\varepsilon $. Since $R_\delta \varphi \leq 0$, we have $-M-B\leq \psi \leq 0$. title: 14.5 Local continuity in a semipositive big background
search_title: Local continuity in a semipositive big background
text: 14.5 Local continuity in a semipositive big background We return to a semipositive big background $\theta $. Where $\theta $ degenerates, regularization loses some positivity, and this curvature error can be repaired by adding a small multiple of a strict barrier. Bounded stability then shows that a bounded solution is continuous wherever the barrier is locally bounded. Fix $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa \omega $ for some $\kappa >0$. For bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ we use the averages $R_ tu$, the transforms $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ and the curvature modulus $\epsilon (\delta )$, with the constants $A,K$, from 1.21.1 , lemma 1.21.3 . Theorem 14.5.1 . Let $p>1$ and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cap L^\infty (X)$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad 0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V).  \] Then $u$ is continuous on every open set $U\subseteq X$ on which $\rho $ is locally bounded. Proof. After adding constants we may assume $-C_0\leq u\leq 0$ and $\rho \leq -C_0-1$. Choose \[  0<\eta <\frac{p-1}{np+p-1},\qquad \alpha =2\eta <1,  \] and set, for small $\delta >0$, \[  c=\delta ^\alpha +\epsilon (\delta ),\qquad e=Ac+\epsilon (\delta ),\qquad s=e/\kappa ,\qquad v_\delta =\frac{\Phi _{c,\delta }+s\rho }{1+s}.  \] Since $s\kappa =e$, the curvature bounds for $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ and $\rho $ give $v_\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Moreover \[  \rho \leq -C_0-1\leq \Phi _{c,\delta } \leq R_\delta u\leq 0  \] for small $\delta $: the lower bound follows from $\Phi _{c,\delta }\geq u-K(\delta ^2+\delta )$, exactly as in the proof of theorem 14.4.1 . Hence $v_\delta \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }\leq R_\delta u\leq 0$. Theorem 14.3.1 allows an unbounded comparison potential, so it applies to $v_\delta $. Together with the $L^1$ smoothing estimate, it gives \[  \sup _ X(v_\delta -u)_+ \leq C\left(\int _ X(v_\delta -u)_+\, \mathrm{d}V\right)^\eta \leq C\delta ^\alpha .  \] Fix $M$ and consider the points where $\rho \geq -M$. Since $s\leq Cc$ and $c\to 0$, the identity \[  \Phi _{c,\delta }-u=(1+s)(v_\delta -u)+s(u-\rho )  \] gives $\Phi _{c,\delta }-u\leq C_ Mc$ there. At a radius $t$ where the infimum defining $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ is attained, the same lower estimate yields \[  -c\log (t/\delta ) \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }-u+K(\delta ^2+\delta ) \leq C_ Mc.  \] Thus $t\geq a_ M\delta $ with $a_ M>0$ independent of the point and of $\delta $. Since $R_ tu+Kt^2$ is increasing in $t$, we obtain \[  R_{a_ M\delta }u+K(a_ M\delta )^2 \leq R_ tu+Kt^2 \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }+K\delta ^2+K\delta .  \] This upper bound and the lower bound $R_ su\geq u-Ks^2$ imply \[  \sup _{\{ \rho \geq -M\} } |R_{a_ M\delta }u-u| \leq C_ M\bigl (\delta ^\alpha +\epsilon (\delta )\bigr ) \longrightarrow 0.  \] On every compact subset of $U$, the function $\rho $ is bounded below. The smooth functions $R_{a_ M\delta }u$ therefore converge uniformly to $u$ on each such compact set, which proves that $u$ is continuous on $U$. $\square$ The proof also gives a modulus of continuity on each compact subset of $U$, obtained by combining the uniform smoothing error with the gradient bound $C/t$. A Hölder exponent would require a power bound for the modulus $\epsilon (\delta )$. For potentials that are locally bounded off the poles of a strict analytic barrier, lemma 1.21.7 refines the classical expansion and gives a curvature error linear in $\delta $. Combined with stability above a strict barrier, this yields local Hölder continuity even for solutions with minimal singularities (theorem 14.16.1 ). Neither argument gives continuity across the pole set of the barrier.
