title: 14.6 Homogeneous replacement on a coordinate ball
search_title: Homogeneous replacement on a coordinate ball
text: 14.6 Homogeneous replacement on a coordinate ball To show that the Monge–Ampère measure of an envelope vanishes off the contact set, we shall replace the envelope on small balls by a solution of the homogeneous equation with the same boundary values. We first recall the smooth Dirichlet problem with a smooth positive density; the replacement is obtained by letting a constant density tend to zero, and continuous boundary values are then handled by uniform approximation. In this section we work on the ball $B=B_ R=\{ |z|<R\} \subset \mathbb C^ n$, put $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$, and let $\theta $ be any smooth real $(1,1)$-form defined near $\overline B$. Distances and the Laplacian $\Delta $ are Euclidean. Lemma 14.6.1 . Let $\varphi \in C^\infty (\partial B)$, and let $F$ be a smooth strictly positive function on $\overline B$. There is a unique smooth function $v$ on $\overline B$ such that \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0,\qquad (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=F\beta ^ n, \qquad v|_{\partial B}=\varphi .  \] Proof. Extend $\varphi $ to a smooth function $\widetilde\varphi $ on $\overline B$. For sufficiently large $A$, the function $\underline v=\widetilde\varphi +A(|z|^2-R^2)$ is a smooth strict subsolution with the prescribed boundary values: $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline v$ is positive and its determinant is at least $(\max _{\overline B}F)\beta ^ n$. For $n\geq 2$, the classical smooth Dirichlet theorem of Guan–Li therefore applies on the ball, with the arbitrary smooth background $\chi =\theta $ and the smooth positive right-hand side $F$. Their operator is $(\mathrm{i}/2)\partial \bar\partial $, so our potential is $\pi $ times theirs. No closedness condition is needed here; such conditions enter only in their separate theorems on compact manifolds. For $n=1$ the lemma is the Dirichlet problem for the Poisson equation. For uniqueness, integrate the derivative of $\log \det $ along the segment between the two positive matrices: the difference of the logarithms of the two determinants becomes a uniformly elliptic linear operator with smooth coefficients applied to the difference of the solutions, and the maximum principle applies. $\square$ The same argument gives smooth comparison on subdomains $D$ of the ball. Let $a,b$ be smooth functions on $\overline D$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a>0$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b>0$. If $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a)^ n\geq (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b)^ n$ in $D$ and $a\leq b$ on $\partial D$, then $a\leq b$ in $D$. Indeed, integrating the derivative of the logarithm of the determinant along the segment between the two positive matrices gives a linear elliptic inequality for $a-b$, and the maximum principle proves the assertion. The boundary of $D$ need not be smooth for this argument. Theorem 14.6.2 . For every $\varphi \in C(\partial B)$ there exists a continuous $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $H_\varphi $ on $\overline B$ such that \[  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_\varphi )^ n=0\quad \hbox{on }B, \qquad H_\varphi |_{\partial B}=\varphi .  \] It dominates every continuous $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $p$ on $\overline B$ with $p|_{\partial B}\leq \varphi $. For $\varphi ,\psi \in C(\partial B)$, the construction satisfies \[  \| H_\varphi -H_\psi \| _{C(\overline B)} \leq \| \varphi -\psi \| _{C(\partial B)}.  \] For smooth boundary data the constructed function is Lipschitz on $\overline B$. Proof. Step 1: boundary barriers. We first take $\varphi $ smooth and $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, and let $v_\varepsilon $ be the solution of lemma 14.6.1 with the constant density $F\equiv \varepsilon $. The strict subsolution $\underline v$ constructed there for $F\equiv 1$ lies below every $v_\varepsilon $, by smooth comparison. Choose a smooth function $q$ with $q=\varphi $ on the boundary and $\Delta q=-C$, where $C$ is so large that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon \geq 0$ implies $\Delta v_\varepsilon \geq -C$. The maximum principle for the Laplacian gives $v_\varepsilon \leq q$. Both barriers are smooth and equal $\widetilde\varphi $ on the boundary. Consequently 14.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ball-boundary-distance} |v_\varepsilon (z)-\widetilde\varphi (z)| \leq C_1\operatorname {dist}(z,\partial B), \end{equation} with $C_1$ independent of $\varepsilon $. Step 2: a Lipschitz bound independent of $\varepsilon $. Let $h\in \mathbb C^ n$ be small, and set $D_ h=\{ z\in B:z+h\in B\} $. Since $\theta $ is smooth, there is $C_2>0$, independent of the translation $h$, such that \[  \theta (z)-\theta (z+h)+C_2|h|\beta \geq 0.  \] For a constant $C_3>0$ to be fixed, define on $D_ h$ \[  w(z)=v_\varepsilon (z+h) +C_2|h|(|z|^2-R^2)-C_3|h|.  \] Then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \theta (z+h)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon (z+h)>0$, and the determinant of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is at least $\varepsilon \beta ^ n$, because the Euclidean volume form is translation invariant. On $\partial D_ h$, one of the points $z$ and $z+h$ lies on $\partial B$, and the other has distance at most $|h|$ from $\partial B$. Estimate ( 14.7 ) and the Lipschitz bound for $\widetilde\varphi $ therefore give $w\leq v_\varepsilon $ on $\partial D_ h$ if $C_3$ is chosen sufficiently large, and smooth comparison extends this inequality to all of $D_ h$. Together with the same argument for $-h$, this gives \[  |v_\varepsilon (z+h)-v_\varepsilon (z)|\leq C_4|h|,  \] with constants independent of $\varepsilon $. The same bound for arbitrary pairs of points follows by subdividing the segment joining them inside the convex ball, and it extends to $\overline B$ because each $v_\varepsilon $ is continuous there. Step 3: the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$. Smooth comparison also shows that $v_\varepsilon $ increases as $\varepsilon $ decreases. By the barriers and the common Lipschitz bound, the limit $H_\varphi $ is Lipschitz and the convergence is uniform on $\overline B$. The inequality $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon >0$ of currents passes to the limit, and continuity of local bounded products under uniform convergence gives $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_\varphi )^ n=0$. For smooth boundary values $\varphi ,\psi $, denote the solutions of lemma 14.6.1 with $F\equiv \varepsilon $ by $v_{\varepsilon ,\varphi }$ and $v_{\varepsilon ,\psi }$. Smooth comparison gives $\| v_{\varepsilon ,\varphi }-v_{\varepsilon ,\psi }\| _\infty \leq \| \varphi -\psi \| _\infty $, and passing to the limit proves the contraction for smooth data. Step 4: continuous boundary values. For continuous $\varphi $, choose smooth $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ uniformly on $\partial B$. By the contraction, $H_{\varphi _ j}$ is uniformly Cauchy. Its limit $H_\varphi $ is continuous and $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, has the prescribed boundary values, and satisfies the homogeneous equation, again by continuity of bounded products under uniform convergence. Passing to the limit also proves the contraction for all continuous boundary data. Step 5: domination. It remains to prove the domination property, which does not follow from a comparison of total masses. First take $\varphi $ smooth and $p$ as in the statement. For $\delta >0$ put $p_\delta =p+\delta (|z|^2-R^2)$, so that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_\delta \geq \delta \beta $. By lemma 1.3.9 , every $C^2$ function $a$ touching $p_\delta $ from above at an interior point $z_0$ satisfies \[  \theta (z_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a(z_0)\geq \delta \beta .  \] Suppose that $p_\delta -v_\varepsilon $ had a positive maximum. Since this difference is nonpositive on the boundary, the maximum would be attained at an interior point, where $v_\varepsilon $ plus the maximum touches $p_\delta $ from above. The determinant of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon $ at that point would then be at least $\delta ^ n\beta ^ n$, contradicting the equation for $v_\varepsilon $ when $\varepsilon <\delta ^ n$. Hence $p_\delta \leq v_\varepsilon $ for small $\varepsilon $. Letting first $\varepsilon $ and then $\delta $ decrease to zero, we obtain $p\leq H_\varphi $. Finally, for continuous $\varphi $, take the smooth approximants $\varphi _ j$ above and set $a_ j=\| \varphi _ j-\varphi \| _\infty $. The boundary values of $p-a_ j$ are at most $\varphi _ j$, so the result for smooth data gives $p-a_ j\leq H_{\varphi _ j}$. Uniform convergence proves $p\leq H_\varphi $. $\square$ By the domination property, $H_\varphi $ is the largest continuous $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function on $\overline B$ whose boundary values are at most $\varphi $. This is the property needed for replacing an envelope locally.

text: 14.7 Contact support in a big background Throughout this section, $\theta $ is an arbitrary smooth big background, not necessarily semipositive. For a continuous obstacle, regularization shows that the envelope is continuous off the poles of a strict analytic barrier. On a small ball where the envelope stays below the obstacle, a homogeneous replacement then shows that the envelope already solves the homogeneous equation, so its Monge–Ampère measure vanishes away from the contact set. By theorem 1.15.3 , applied to a strict barrier with a sufficiently small curvature error, we may fix $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities and a smooth remainder after resolution such that \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa \omega ,\qquad \kappa >0.  \] Its pole set $Z=\{ \rho =-\infty \} $ is an analytic, hence pluripolar, subset of $X$. Theorem 14.7.1 . Let $h\in C(X)$. Then $p=P_\theta (h)$ is a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function, continuous on $X\setminus Z$, whose Monge–Ampère measure satisfies \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<h\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0.  \] Here $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ is allowed to have infinite total mass. Proof. Subtract a constant from $\rho $ so that $\rho +2\leq h$. Then $\rho +2$ is a competitor, and since the obstacle is continuous, the envelope lies below it everywhere; thus \[  \rho +2\leq p\leq h.  \] In particular, $p$ is locally bounded off $Z$. We first prove that $p$ is continuous there; this part does not use the contact assertion. Apply lemma 1.21.7 to $p-\sup _ Xp$ and add back the constant. The transforms $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ of that lemma are defined on $X$ and, with fixed constants $A,K,C>0$ and $\epsilon (\delta )=C\delta $, satisfy 14.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-envelope-regularization} \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _{c,\delta }\geq -(Ac+\epsilon (\delta ))\omega . \end{equation} Off $Z$ the infimum defining $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ is attained at a positive radius, and \[  p-K(\delta ^2+\delta )\leq \Phi _{c,\delta } \leq R_\delta p\leq R_\delta h.  \] For small $\delta $ the first inequality gives $\Phi _{c,\delta }\geq \rho +1$, hence $\rho \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }$ on $X$. Set \[  m(\delta )=\sup _{0<t\leq \delta }\| R_ th-h\| _\infty , \qquad c=m(\delta )+\epsilon (\delta )+\delta , \qquad s=\frac{Ac+\epsilon (\delta )}{\kappa }.  \] The averaging kernels are positive, have integral one and are supported in balls of radius comparable to $t$, so uniform continuity of $h$ gives $m(\delta )\to 0$. Define \[  v_\delta =\frac{\Phi _{c,\delta }+s\rho }{1+s}.  \] By the choice of $s$, the strict barrier and ( 14.8 ) show that $v_\delta $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. Since $\rho \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }$, \[  v_\delta \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }\leq R_\delta h\leq h+m(\delta ).  \] Thus $v_\delta -m(\delta )$ is a competitor for the envelope, and $v_\delta \leq p+m(\delta )$. Let $L\Subset X\setminus Z$ be compact. On $L$ the difference $p-\rho $ is bounded above. Since $s\leq Cc$, the identity \[  \Phi _{c,\delta }-p=(1+s)(v_\delta -p)+s(p-\rho )  \] therefore gives $\Phi _{c,\delta }-p\leq C_ Lc$ on $L$. At a radius $t$ where the infimum is attained, \[  -c\log (t/\delta ) \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }-p+K(\delta ^2+\delta )\leq C_ Lc.  \] Since $c\geq \delta $, this yields $t\geq a_ L\delta $ with a fixed $a_ L>0$. Because $R_ tp+Kt^2$ is increasing in $t$, it follows that \[  p-K(a_ L\delta )^2\leq R_{a_ L\delta }p \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }+K\delta ^2+K\delta .  \] Consequently $R_{a_ L\delta }p\to p$ uniformly on $L$. These averages are smooth for positive radius, even though $p$ is unbounded on $X$. Applying this to compact neighborhoods of the points of $X\setminus Z$ proves that $p$ is continuous on $X\setminus Z$. We turn to the contact assertion. By the continuity just proved, the set $\{ p<h\} \setminus Z$ is open. Let $x$ be one of its points, and choose a small coordinate ball $B_ r$ centered at $x$ whose closure lies in this set. Let $H$ be the homogeneous replacement of theorem 14.6.2 with boundary values $p|_{\partial B_ r}$. Its domination property gives $H\geq p$ on the ball. We claim that $H\leq h$ on $B_ r$ if $r$ is small enough. Indeed, in the chosen Euclidean coordinates $z$, with Laplacian $\Delta $, the inequality $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H\geq 0$ implies a fixed bound $\Delta H\geq -C$. Comparison with the function $\sup _{\partial B_ r}p+C'(r^2-|z-x|^2)$, with $C'$ fixed large enough, gives \[  H\leq \sup _{\partial B_ r}p+C'r^2.  \] As $r\to 0$, the right-hand side tends to $p(x)$, whereas $\inf _{B_ r}h\to h(x)>p(x)$. This proves the claim for sufficiently small $r$. Now replace $p$ by $H$ on the ball. The resulting function is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. To see this, fix $a>0$ and take $\max \{ p,H-a\} $ inside the ball and $p$ outside. Since $H$ and $p$ are continuous with equal boundary values, $H-a<p$ on a collar of $\partial B_ r$, so this is an ordinary local maximum construction. Letting $a\downarrow 0$ gives the function equal to $H$ on $B_ r$ and to $p$ outside, with locally uniform convergence near the boundary of the ball. This function is bounded above by $h$ on all of $X$, so the definition of the envelope forces it to be at most $p$. Thus $p=H$ on $B_ r$, and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ vanishes there. These balls cover $\{ p<h\} \setminus Z$. There the extended measure agrees with the local bounded product, and it does not charge the pluripolar set $Z$. This proves the contact assertion on $X$; no bound on the total mass of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ was needed. $\square$

title: 14.7.1 Quasi-continuous obstacles
text:
14.7.1 Quasi-continuous obstacles We now extend the contact property to discontinuous obstacles. Continuous approximations of an obstacle need not preserve every competitor of its envelope pointwise. For lower semicontinuous obstacles, the approximation of lemma 1.19.5 repairs this, and quasi-continuity then allows us to pass to limits of weighted measures. An unbounded obstacle is truncated at finite levels; in an arbitrary smooth background this produces signed products, whose limits are controlled by lemma 1.8.10 before we restrict to the region where the product is positive. The strict analytic barrier $ho $ and its pole set $Z$ are those fixed above. Proposition 14.7.2 . If $f$ is bounded and lower semicontinuous, then $p=P_	heta (f)$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus Z$, and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)=0.  \] Proof. Using the infimum construction in the proof of proposition 13.1.2 , take continuous $f_ j\uparrow f$ with common bounds $m\leq f_ j\leq M$, and shift $ho $ below $m$. The envelopes $p_ j=P_	heta (f_ j)$ increase and satisfy \[  ho \leq p_ j\leq M.  \] Their regularized limit $q=(\lim _ jp_ j)^*$ is therefore $	heta $-plurisubharmonic. Outside a pluripolar set it equals the pointwise limit, which is at most $f$; hence $q\leq p=P_	heta (f)$. We prove the reverse inequality without using a domination theorem. Let $u$ be any competitor for $P_	heta (f)$, and let $u_ t\leq f$ be the potentials given by lemma 1.19.5 , which satisfy this inequality everywhere. For fixed $t,\eta >0$, the sets \[  \{ u_ t<f_ j+\eta \} ,\qquad j\geq 1,  \] are open, increase with $j$, and cover $X$. By compactness, $u_ t\leq f_ j+\eta $ everywhere for all large $j$. Thus $u_ t-\eta $ is a competitor for $p_ j$, and $q\geq u_ t-\eta $. Letting first $\eta \downarrow 0$ and then $t\downarrow 0$, we obtain $q\geq u$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . Taking the supremum over all competitors $u$ gives $q\geq p$, so $q=p$. For fixed $k$, the set $U_ k=\{ p<f_ k\} $ is open. If $j\geq k$, then $p_ j\leq p<f_ k\leq f_ j$ on $U_ k$, so theorem 14.7.1 gives $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p_ j)=0$ there. On every relatively compact open subset of $X\setminus Z$ the functions $p_ j$ have common bounds. After a common smooth correction and a finite expansion, the local Bedford–Taylor continuity along increasing sequences shows that their measures converge to $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)$ there. Since the measure of an open set is at most the lower limit of the measures of the approximating sequence, $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)$ vanishes on $U_ k\setminus Z$. The union of these sets is $\{ p<f\} \setminus Z$, and the extended measure does not charge the pluripolar set $Z$. $\square$ Proposition 14.7.3 . The conclusion of proposition 14.7.2 holds for every bounded quasi-continuous obstacle $f$. Proof. By lemma 1.8.8 , there are bounded lower semicontinuous $f_ j$ with common bounds and $f_ j\downarrow f$ quasi-everywhere. The envelopes $p_ j=P_	heta (f_ j)$ decrease to $p=P_	heta (f)$. Indeed, the common lower barrier shows that the limit is not identically $-\infty $; the limit lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere and is thus a competitor for $P_	heta (f)$, while monotonicity gives the other inequality. All these functions have common local bounds off $Z$. For fixed $k$, put $H_ k=\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} $ on $X\setminus Z$, a bounded quasi-continuous function there. If $j\geq k$, then on $\{ H_ k>0\} $ we have $p_ j\leq p_ k<f\leq f_ j$ outside a pluripolar set, so proposition 14.7.2 gives $H_ k\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p_ j)=0$ off $Z$. Let $g$ be continuous with compact support in $X\setminus Z$. The continuity of bounded products against quasi-continuous weights from section 1.6 applies to the fixed quasi-continuous coefficient $gH_ k$. Consequently $H_ k\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)=0$ off $Z$. As $k	o \infty $, the sets $\{ H_ k>0\} $ exhaust $\{ p<f\} \setminus Z$, and $Z$ is not charged because it is pluripolar. $\square$ For an unbounded obstacle, we truncate and use the convergence of signed products in lemma 1.8.10 . Theorem 14.7.4 . Let $	heta $ be smooth and big. Let $f$ be a quasi-continuous obstacle, finite almost everywhere, such that $p=P_	heta (f)
ot\equiv -\infty $. Then $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)=0.  \] As before, the measure $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)$ may have infinite total mass. Proof. As in the proof of theorem 13.1.4 , the local envelope theorem and a countable Choquet family give $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Set $f_ j=\max (f,-j)$ and $p_ j=P_	heta (f_ j)$. Then $p$ is a competitor for every $f_ j$. Since $f_ j\leq f_1$ and $f_1$ is finite almost everywhere, the finite-sublevel argument in section 1.19 gives a common upper bound for all competitors. Thus the envelopes $p_ j$ are $	heta $-plurisubharmonic and uniformly bounded above. Choose $M$ strictly larger than this bound. The obstacle $g_ j=\min (f_ j,M)$ is bounded and quasi-continuous. Since $p_ j<M$ and $p_ j\leq f_ j$ quasi-everywhere, $p_ j$ is a competitor for $P_	heta (g_ j)$; the reverse inequality follows from $g_ j\leq f_ j$. Thus $p_ j=P_	heta (g_ j)$, and proposition 14.7.3 gives contact support for $p_ j$ with respect to $g_ j$. Because $p_ j<M$, no contact occurs at the artificial upper cutoff, so 14.9  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-truncated-obstacle-contact} \mathbf1_{\{ p_ j<f_ j\} }\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p_ j)=0. \end{equation} Each $p_ j$ is locally bounded off $Z$, with a lower barrier of the form $ho -C_ j$. The sequence decreases to $p$: its limit is not identically $-\infty $ because it dominates $p$, and it lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, so it is itself a competitor for $P_	heta (f)$. Fix a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq 	heta $. For integers $C,k\geq 1$, consider the bounded $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic functions \[  v_{j,C}=\max (p_ j,-C),\qquad v_ C=\max (p,-C),  \] and set \[  H_{k,C} =\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} \min \{ 1,(p+C)_+\}  \quad \hbox{on }X\setminus Z,  \] extended by zero on $Z$. This function is bounded and quasi-continuous. Indeed, off $Z$ the function $p_ k$ is a finite quasi-plurisubharmonic function, truncation by bounded continuous functions preserves quasi-continuity, and the pluripolar set $Z$ can be removed by an open set of arbitrarily small capacity. At a pole of $p$ the second factor vanishes. For $j\geq k$, on $\{ H_{k,C}>0\} $ we have, outside pluripolar sets, \[  p_ j\geq p>-C,\qquad p_ j\leq p_ k<f\leq f_ j.  \] By plurifine locality, the signed measure $
u _{j,C}=(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{j,C})^ n$ therefore agrees there with $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p_ j)$, and ( 14.9 ) gives \[  H_{k,C}
u _{j,C}=0.  \] For fixed $C$, the potentials $v_{j,C}$ have common global bounds and decrease to $v_ C$, so lemma 1.8.10 yields \[  \int _ X H_{k,C}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ C)^ n=0.  \] On the set where $H_{k,C}$ is positive we have $p>-C$, so the restricted product in theorem 6.1.2 identifies $H_{k,C}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ C)^ n$ with the positive measure $H_{k,C}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)$; on the complement the coefficient is zero. Hence $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)$ vanishes on $\{ H_{k,C}>0\} $. Finally, if $p(x)$ is finite and $p(x)<f(x)$, then $p_ k(x)<f(x)$ for large $k$ and $p(x)>-C$ for large $C$. The countable union of the sets $\{ H_{k,C}>0\} $ therefore covers $\{ p<f\} $ outside $Z\cup \{ p=-\infty \} $. Both excluded sets are pluripolar, and the theorem follows. $\square$

14.8 Compactness with a common lower barrier We return to a semipositive big background $	heta $. Convergence of potentials in $L^1$ does not by itself imply convergence of their Monge–Ampère measures. We give a criterion for convergence in capacity when the potentials stay within a bounded distance of a reference admitting a smaller-background envelope. This common lower barrier ensures that all finite and infinite rooftop envelopes of the sequence are $	heta $-plurisubharmonic. A small error integral of each potential against its own Monge–Ampère measure bounds the corresponding error of the rooftops by a summable tail. Weighted lower semicontinuity passes this bound to the limit, and singular domination identifies the limit of the lower envelopes with the $L^1$ limit. Squeezing the sequence between lower and upper envelopes then gives convergence in capacity, and a domination of the measures also controls their mass on deep sublevels. Theorem 14.8.1 . Let $	heta \geq 0$ be big. Suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfies $P_{\delta 	heta }(\varphi )
ot\equiv -\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$. Proof. The canonical representative of the limit also lies between $\varphi -C$ and $\varphi +C$. It suffices to show that every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in capacity. We may therefore assume that $I_ j\leq 2^{-j}$ and that $u_ j	o u$ almost everywhere. For $N\geq j$ define \[  p_{j,N}=P_	heta (\min \{ u_ j,\ldots ,u_ N\} ),\qquad p_ j=P_	heta \left(\inf _{\ell \geq j}u_\ell ight).  \] All these envelopes lie between $\varphi -C$ and $\varphi +C$. The contact theorem and ordered contact give an inequality for the finite rooftops. Partition the contact set of $p_{j,N}$ according to the first index $\ell $ for which $p_{j,N}=u_\ell $. On the corresponding piece, the measure of $p_{j,N}$ is bounded by that of $u_\ell $, and $\mathrm{e}^{p_{j,N}}=\mathrm{e}^{u_\ell }$. Therefore \[  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{p_{j,N}}-\mathrm{e}^ u|\,  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p_{j,N}) \leq \sum _{\ell =j}^ N I_\ell \leq 2^{1-j}.  \] Only positive measures enter this argument, so it applies also when their total masses are infinite. The sequence $p_ j$ increases, and its canonical limit $p$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic. By lemma 1.8.12 , both monotone limits hold in capacity. 14.10 Adding weighted Monge–Ampère measures Let $u$ and $v$ be potentials of the same ordinary singularity type. We show that the sum of their weighted measures $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)+\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (v)$ is again of the form $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda a}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (a)$ for a potential $a$ of that type. Truncating $u$ and $v$ gives bounded equations, solved by the bounded subsolution theorem, whose solutions have a common lower barrier. Their exponential error tends to zero even though the approximating masses may grow, so the lower-barrier criterion identifies the limit. This addition step will remove a deficit of mass in the existence proof of section 14.11 . Theorem 14.10.1 . Let $	heta \geq 0$ be big, and suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfies $P_{\delta 	heta }(\varphi )
ot\equiv -\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$. Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $u,v\sim \varphi $, and let $\lambda >0$. The solution $a$ is unique in the ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $. Proof. Step 1: truncated equations and barriers. Choose $S\geq \max (\sup _ Xu,\sup _ Xv)$. A common translation reduces the theorem to the case $u,v\leq 0$: translating $u$ and $v$ by $-S$ multiplies $\mu $ by $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda S}$, and the resulting solution is then translated back by $S$. For integers $j\geq 1$, set $u_ j=\max (u,-j)$, $v_ j=\max (v,-j)$ and \[  \mu _ j=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u_ j}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u_ j) +\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v_ j}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (v_ j).  \] For $s_ j=(u_ j+v_ j)/2$, positivity of mixed products gives \[  \mu _ j\leq 2^ n \mathrm{e}^{\lambda j}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (s_ j).  \] Thus $\mu _ j$ has a bounded density with respect to the Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded potential $s_ j$, and $\mu _ j
eq 0$ by proposition 13.2.1 . The bounded subsolution theorem theorem 14.9.1 therefore gives bounded $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (a_ j)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda a_ j}\mu _ j$, and bounded exponential comparison yields \[  a_ j\leq \min (u_ j,v_ j)\leq 0.  \] Choose $C$ with $|u-v|\leq C$ off the common pole set; then $|u_ j-v_ j|\leq C$. Put \[  D=C/2+n\lambda ^{-1}\log 2,\qquad b_ j=s_ j-D.  \] Because $|u_ j-v_ j|\leq C$, positivity of mixed products gives \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda b_ j}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (b_ j) \geq 2^{-n}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda D-\lambda s_ j}  igl (\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u_ j)+\mathrm{MA}_	heta (v_ j) igr ) \geq \mu _ j.  \] Hence $a_ j\geq b_ j\geq w$, where \[  w=(u+v)/2-D\sim \varphi  \] is a fixed $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function. If $j>2T$ and $x
otin E_ j$, the inequalities $w(x)\leq a_ j(x)\leq -j$ force $\zeta _ T(x)=0$. On the left we may replace $a_ j$ by $\max (a_ j,-2T)$ and use continuity of bounded products under convergence in capacity, with the fixed bounded quasi-continuous weight $\zeta _ T$. On the right, the exponentials converge against the fixed measure $\mu $, which gives convergence in total variation. Therefore \[  \zeta _ T\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (a) =\zeta _ T\mathrm{e}^{\lambda a}\mu .  \] As $T	o \infty $, the cutoffs increase to one off the pole set of $w$, which no measure involved charges. This proves the equation and, in particular, shows that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (a)$ has finite mass. Uniqueness follows from corollary 14.1.3 . $\square$

text: 14.11 Equations in a prescribed ordinary type We return to a semipositive big background $\theta $ and now require the solution to have the ordinary singularity type of a fixed reference $\varphi $. Throughout this section, $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is an envelope fixed point admitting a smaller-background envelope; that is, ( 13.26 ) holds: \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi ,\qquad P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )\not\equiv -\infty \quad \text{for some }0<\varepsilon <1.  \] We fix such an $\varepsilon $. Note that $\varphi \leq 0$, since every competitor for $P_\theta [\varphi ]$ is nonpositive. For a normalized solution $u$, the fixed-point property gives the upper bound $u\leq \varphi $, while the smaller-background envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ yields a uniform lower bound $u\geq \varphi -C$. A supersolution and the addition theorem then prove existence in this type. Theorem 14.11.1 . Let $\theta $ and $\varphi $ be as above, and let $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and $\mu (X)>0$. Then: For every $\lambda >0$ there is a unique $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu .  \] There are $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $ and a uniquely determined constant $c>0$ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu .  \] The potential in part (2) need not be unique up to an additive constant, even for a Hermitian background and the reference $\varphi =0$; see the counterexample in theorem 11.6.1 . The proof uses two estimates in the prescribed type. The first is a lower bound for the norm of a Monge–Ampère density. Lemma 14.11.2 . Fix $q>1$. There is $b_ q>0$ such that every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=F\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad 0\leq F\in L^ q(\mathrm{d}V),  \] satisfies $\| F\| _ q\geq b_ q$. For fixed $\theta $ and $\varepsilon $, the constant $b_ q$ is independent of $\varphi $. Proof. Since $u\sim \varphi $, the smaller-background envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $. If $F=0$, then theorem 14.1.2 , applied to $u$ and $u+1$ with coefficient zero, would give $u\geq u+1$; hence $N=\| F\| _ q>0$. Apply lemma 14.2.1 in the semipositive big background $(1-\varepsilon )\theta $ to $F/N$, whose $L^ q$ norm is one. It gives a bounded $s$ with $-1\leq s\leq 0$ and a constant $b_ q>0$, depending only on this fixed background and on $q$, such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_{(1-\varepsilon )\theta }(s)\geq (b_ q/N)F\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Put $h=P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )+s$. This is a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function with $h\preceq u$. Since $\theta _ h$ is the sum of the positive currents $\varepsilon \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ and $(1-\varepsilon )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$, the same density bound holds for $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h)$. To justify this, we truncate $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ at finite levels, use positivity of bounded mixed products, and exhaust the set where $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ is finite; its pole set has zero volume. If $N<b_ q$, we would have \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq (N/b_ q)\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h+t) \quad \text{for every }t\in \mathbb R.  \] Since $N/b_ q<1$, theorem 14.1.2 would then imply $u\geq h+t$ for every $t$, which is impossible at a point where both potentials are finite. Thus $N\geq b_ q$. The construction of $s$ used no property of $\varphi $, which proves the last assertion. $\square$ The lemma bounds the $L^ q$ norm of the density from below; it gives no positive lower bound for the total mass $\int _ XF\, \mathrm{d}V$. The second estimate bounds a normalized solution from below by $\varphi $ minus a uniform constant. It is what keeps limits of solutions in the ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $. Theorem 14.11.3 . Let $\theta $ and $\varphi $ be as above. Suppose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $u\sim \varphi $, $\sup _ Xu=0$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad 0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V),\quad p>1.  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed geometry, $\varphi $, $p$, and an upper bound for $\| f\| _{L^ p}$, such that \[  \varphi -C\leq u\leq \varphi .  \] Proof. The upper bound follows directly from the fixed-point property: since $u\leq 0$ and $u\preceq \varphi $, the function $u$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $. For the lower bound we construct a subsolution $\psi $ of the type of $\varphi $ whose measure dominates a multiple of $\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, and then apply singular domination. Put $\varphi _\varepsilon =P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$, so that $\varphi _\varepsilon \leq \varphi \leq 0$. Uniform exponential integrability (lemma 1.5.1 ) for the normalized potentials $u$ and exponential integrability for the fixed function $\varphi _\varepsilon $ allow us to choose $\gamma >0$ and $1<q<p$ such that \[  g=\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma (\varphi _\varepsilon +u)}f  \] has a uniform $L^ q$ bound. Explicitly, we first choose $q<p$ and apply Hölder's inequality with exponents $p/q$ and $p/(p-q)$; then we choose $\gamma $ so small that the exponential factor is controlled by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the two exponential integrability estimates. Theorem 14.2.3 , applied in the semipositive big background $(1-\varepsilon )\theta $ to the density $1+g$, gives a bounded $v$ with $\sup _ Xv=0$ and a constant $c>0$ such that \[  ((1-\varepsilon )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=c(1+g)\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Both $\| v\| _\infty $ and $c^{-1}$ are uniformly bounded. Adding the constant one to $g$ makes the root integral of the density at least one, so no lower bound for the integral of $f$ is needed. Put $h=\varphi _\varepsilon +v\leq \varphi $, which is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and define \[  \chi (t)=\frac1{1-t}\quad (t\leq 0),\qquad \psi =\varphi +\chi (h-\varphi ),  \] where the formula for $\psi $ is evaluated off the pole sets. Then $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, $0<\chi '\leq 1$, and $\chi ''>0$. For bounded potentials with $h\leq \varphi $, lemma 1.7.9 , applied with $G(x,y)=x+\chi (y-x)$, gives \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G(\varphi ,h) \geq (1-\chi '(h-\varphi ))\theta _\varphi +\chi '(h-\varphi )\theta _ h\geq 0.  \] For unbounded potentials we apply this bounded assertion to $\varphi _ k=\max (\varphi ,-k)$ and $h_ k=\max (h,-k)\leq \varphi _ k$. Since $G$ is nondecreasing in both variables, $G(\varphi _ k,h_ k)$ decreases as $k$ increases. Its limit is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and lies between $\varphi $ and $\varphi +1$; hence it is not identically $-\infty $, and it equals $\psi $. Locality on common finite levels and positivity of bounded products give \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi ) \geq (\varphi -h+1)^{-2n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h) \geq c(\varphi -h+1)^{-2n}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma \varphi _\varepsilon } \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where the second inequality uses $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h)\geq ((1-\varepsilon )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq cg\, \mathrm{d}V$. These inequalities are first obtained off the pole sets; since pole sets have zero volume, they extend by exhaustion to all Borel sets. Write $T=-\varphi _\varepsilon \geq 0$. If $C_1\geq 1+\| v\| _\infty $, then $\varphi -h+1\leq T+C_1$. Since \[  A:=\inf _{T\geq 0}\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\gamma T}}{(T+C_1)^{2n}}>0,  \] we obtain, with a uniform $d>0$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi ) \geq d \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u).  \] Choose $K=2+\gamma ^{-1}|\log d|$. On $\{ u<\psi -K\} $ we have $u<1-K$, because $\psi \leq \varphi +1\leq 1$; hence \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq d^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{\gamma (1-K)} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi -K) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi -K).  \] The potentials $u$ and $\psi -K$ have the same ordinary singularity type. Moreover, $u\geq \varphi -C_ u$ for some constant $C_ u$, so $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(u)\geq \varphi _\varepsilon -C_ u$ is not identically $-\infty $. Theorem 14.1.2 therefore yields $u\geq \psi -K\geq \varphi -K$. All constants used to choose $K$ are uniform over the family in the theorem; the possibly nonuniform constant $C_ u$ serves only to show that the smaller-background envelope of $u$ is not identically $-\infty $, and it enters no estimate. $\square$ The existence proof starts from a supersolution in the prescribed type. It is obtained from a bounded solution by a rooftop envelope with $\varphi $. Lemma 14.11.4 . For nonzero $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and $\lambda >0$, there exists $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim \varphi $ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (w)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Let $v$ be the bounded solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ given by theorem 14.2.2 , and write $M=\sup _ Xv$ and $a=v-M\leq 0$. The rooftop envelope $p=P_\theta (a,\varphi )$ satisfies $\varphi -\| a\| _\infty \leq p\leq \varphi $, so $p\sim \varphi $. By the rooftop inequality of proposition 13.1.5 , \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (p) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ p=a\leq \varphi \} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a) +\mathbf1_{\{ p=\varphi <a\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\varphi ).  \] The second term vanishes: by proposition 13.1.6 , the measure of $\varphi $ is carried by $\{ \varphi =0\} $, whereas $\varphi <a\leq 0$ on the set in question. On the first contact set, $a=p$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (a+M)}f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Thus $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda (p+M)}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, and $w=p+M$ has the required properties. $\square$

text: Lemma 14.11.4 . For nonzero $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and $\lambda >0$, there exists $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim \varphi $ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (w)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Let $v$ be the bounded solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ given by theorem 14.2.2 , and write $M=\sup _ Xv$ and $a=v-M\leq 0$. The rooftop envelope $p=P_\theta (a,\varphi )$ satisfies $\varphi -\| a\| _\infty \leq p\leq \varphi $, so $p\sim \varphi $. By the rooftop inequality of proposition 13.1.5 , \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (p) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ p=a\leq \varphi \} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a) +\mathbf1_{\{ p=\varphi <a\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\varphi ).  \] The second term vanishes: by proposition 13.1.6 , the measure of $\varphi $ is carried by $\{ \varphi =0\} $, whereas $\varphi <a\leq 0$ on the set in question. On the first contact set, $a=p$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (a+M)}f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Thus $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda (p+M)}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, and $w=p+M$ has the required properties. $\square$

title: 14.11.2 The normalized equation
text: 14.11.2 The normalized equation For the normalized equation we let the positive exponent tend to zero. Bounded comparison controls the normalizing constants from above, while the lower density estimate of lemma 14.11.2 keeps them away from zero. The common barriers then give convergence of the Monge–Ampère measures and keep the limit in the prescribed type. of theorem 14.11.1 , part (2). For each $j\geq 1$, part (1) gives $u_ j\sim \varphi $ with \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)=\mathrm{e}^{u_ j/j}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Write $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$, $v_ j=u_ j-M_ j$ and $c_ j=\mathrm{e}^{M_ j/j}$. Let $h$ be a bounded normalized solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (h)=\alpha f\, \mathrm{d}V$, with $\alpha >0$, given by theorem 14.2.3 . For $H_ j=h+\| h\| _\infty +j\log \alpha $ we have \[  \mathrm{e}^{-H_ j/j}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (H_ j) =\mathrm{e}^{-(h+\| h\| _\infty )/j}f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq f\, \mathrm{d}V =\mathrm{e}^{-u_ j/j}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j).  \] The bounded function $H_ j$ admits a smaller-background envelope, and $u_ j\preceq H_ j$, so corollary 14.1.3 gives $u_ j\leq H_ j$. In particular, \[  0<c_ j\leq \alpha \exp (2\| h\| _\infty /j).  \] The lower density bound of lemma 14.11.2 , applied to $v_ j$ with $q=p$, gives \[  b_ p\leq \| c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f\| _ p\leq c_ j\| f\| _ p,  \] so the $c_ j$ are also bounded away from zero. Since $\sup _ Xv_ j=0$ and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v_ j)=c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f\, \mathrm{d}V\leq C f\, \mathrm{d}V$, theorem 14.11.3 gives $\varphi -C'\leq v_ j\leq \varphi $. Extract a subsequence with $v_ j\to v$ in $L^1(X)$ and $c_ j\to c>0$. By corollary 14.8.3 , the convergence holds in capacity, $v\sim \varphi $, and the Monge–Ampère measures converge weakly. Meanwhile, lemma 1.23.3 gives \[  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}-1|f\, \mathrm{d}V\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus the right-hand sides converge in total variation to $cf\, \mathrm{d}V$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. For the uniqueness of the constant, suppose that $a,b\sim \varphi $ solve the normalized equation with constants $c_ a<c_ b$. For every real $t$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (a) =\frac{c_ a}{c_ b}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (b+t),  \] so theorem 14.1.2 gives $a\geq b+t$. This is impossible as $t\to +\infty $, at any point where both potentials are finite. Interchanging the roles of the two constants proves that $c$ is unique. $\square$

title: 14.12 Comparison above a strict singular barrier
search_title: Comparison above a strict singular barrier
text: 14.12 Comparison above a strict singular barrier From now on, $\theta $ is an arbitrary smooth big real $(1,1)$-form. Then $V_\theta $ may be unbounded, and the smaller-background construction used above is no longer available. Its role is taken by a strict analytic barrier. When two potentials bounded below by the barrier are compared, adding a small multiple of the barrier forces a negative infimum of their difference to be attained away from its pole set, and there a local comparison principle rules it out. Since $\theta $ is big, theorem 1.15.3 provides $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities and a smooth remainder after resolution such that $\theta _\rho \geq \kappa \omega $ for some $\kappa >0$. Replacing $\omega $ by a small positive multiple and subtracting a constant from $\rho $, we fix such a $\rho $ with $\rho \leq 0$ and $\theta _\rho \geq \omega $. Put $Z=\{ \rho =-\infty \} $ and $\Omega =X\setminus Z$. From now on until the end of section 14.17 , these data remain fixed, and $\Omega $ always denotes this open set rather than an auxiliary Hermitian form. A potential bounded below by $\rho -C$ is locally bounded on $\Omega $, and there its extended Monge–Ampère measure agrees with the local bounded product. Lemma 14.12.1 . Let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a coordinate ball, and let $u,v$ be bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions on $B$. Assume \[  \liminf _{x\to \partial B}(u-v)(x)\geq 0, \qquad \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v).  \] Then $u\geq v$ on $B$. Proof. Fix $\varepsilon >0$ and set $v_\varepsilon =\max (u,v-\varepsilon )$, which equals $u$ near the boundary. We claim that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\varepsilon )  \] throughout $B$. On $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ this follows from locality, since $v_\varepsilon =u$ there. On $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $ it follows from ordered contact and from the assumed inequality, which applies because this set is contained in $\{ u<v\} $. Let $q$ be the plurisubharmonic envelope on $B$ of the obstacle $u-v_\varepsilon $, in the sense of ( 1.9 ). This obstacle is bounded, quasi-continuous and zero near the boundary. Hence it lies between $Ah$ and zero for a sufficiently large $A$, where $h<0$ is a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic defining function for the ball. Thus $q$ tends to zero at the boundary, and ( 1.9 ) shows that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$ is carried by $D=\{ q=u-v_\varepsilon \} $. Since $q\leq u-v_\varepsilon $ quasi-everywhere, the canonical representatives satisfy $q+v_\varepsilon \leq u$. Ordered contact, followed by the measure inequality above, yields \[  \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (q+v_\varepsilon ) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\varepsilon ).  \] The positive expansion of $(\theta _{v_\varepsilon }+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$ contains both $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\varepsilon )$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$. Thus $\mathbf1_ D(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=0$, and since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$ is carried by $D$, we get $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=0$. The classical Bedford–Taylor comparison principle for bounded plurisubharmonic functions with zero boundary values implies $q=0$. Consequently $u\geq v_\varepsilon $, first quasi-everywhere and then everywhere. Finally let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$ Theorem 14.12.2 . Suppose $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy, for constants $C_0,C_1\geq 0$, \[  \min (u,v)\geq \rho -C_0,\qquad v\leq u+C_1.  \] If, for some $0\leq c<1$, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v),  \] then $u\geq v$. The measures in the theorem need not have finite total mass. Proof. We first modify the barrier. Let $r=a\rho -A$, where $a>1$ is sufficiently close to one and $A$ is sufficiently large. Since \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\rho )=a\theta _\rho +(1-a)\theta ,  \] we can arrange $\theta _ r\geq \omega /2$ and $r-v\leq -1$, and moreover $u-r\to +\infty $ at $Z$, because $u-r\geq (a-1)(-\rho )+A-C_0$. When $Z$ is empty, the last property is not needed. Choose $0<\delta <1$ with $(1-\delta )^ n>c$, and put $v_\delta =(1-\delta )v+\delta r$. Then \[  u-v_\delta \geq \delta (u-r)-(1-\delta )C_1.  \] Suppose that the infimum $m$ of $u-v_\delta $ on $\Omega $ were negative. Since $u-v_\delta \to +\infty $ at $Z$, a sequence $x_ j$ along which $u-v_\delta $ tends to $m$ has a subsequence converging to a point $x_0\in \Omega $. Choose a coordinate ball $B\Subset \Omega $ centered at $x_0$, identify it with $\{ |z|<1\} $, and take \[  \eta (z)=b(1-|z|^2),\qquad 0<b<1, \qquad \omega /2+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta \geq 0.  \] The function $w=v_\delta +\delta \eta +m$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic on $B$, and $\liminf _{\partial B}(u-w)\geq 0$ because $\eta $ vanishes on $\partial B$. Also \[  w-v=\delta (r-v+\eta )+m<0.  \] Thus $\{ u<w\} \subset \{ u<v\} $, and positivity of mixed products gives on this set \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq c\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\leq (1-\delta )^ n\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\leq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w).  \] By lemma 14.12.1 , $u\geq w$ on $B$. Evaluating at $x_ j$ gives $u(x_ j)-v_\delta (x_ j)\geq m+\delta \eta (x_ j)$, which contradicts $\eta (x_0)>0$ in the limit. Hence $u\geq v_\delta $ on $\Omega $. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ along values with $(1-\delta )^ n>c$, we obtain $u\geq v$ on $\Omega $, and lemma 1.3.3 extends this inequality to $X$. $\square$ Corollary 14.12.3 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u,v\geq \rho -C$ for some $C\geq 0$ and $u\sim v$. If $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq c\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$ for some $c\geq 0$, then $c\geq 1$. If $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda (u-v)}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$ for some $\lambda >0$, then $u\geq v$. In particular, let $\mu $ be a positive measure. Among potentials bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant, each ordinary singularity type contains at most one solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $, and the constant $c>0$ in $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu $ is uniquely determined within each type. Proof. If $c<1$, apply the theorem to $u$ and $v+A$ for every constant $A>0$; the constants in its hypotheses may depend on $A$. The resulting inequality $u\geq v+A$ for all $A$ is impossible. For the second assertion, fix $a>0$ and restrict the measure inequality to $\{ u<v-a\} $. There the factor is at most $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda a}<1$, so the theorem gives $u\geq v-a$; now let $a\downarrow 0$. For two solutions of the exponential equation, apply the second assertion in both orders; for two solutions of the normalized equation, apply the first. $\square$

title: 14.13 Subsolutions and the Gauduchon trace
text: 14.13 Subsolutions and the Gauduchon trace The strict barrier also yields subsolutions within a bounded distance of any reference between $\rho $ and zero. The curvature estimate comes from composing a convex function with the difference between the reference and a barrier-based subsolution, which produces a convex combination of positive currents. Pairing the equation with a Gauduchon metric then bounds the normalizing constants through a linear trace. Lemma 14.13.1 . Fix $p>1$ and $L>0$. There is $m>0$ such that, whenever \[  \rho \leq \eta \leq 0,\quad \eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ), \qquad g\geq 0,\quad \| g\| _{L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq L,  \] there exists $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  \eta \leq v\leq \eta +1,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\geq m g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The constant $m$ depends only on the fixed geometry and on $\rho ,p,L$. Proof. Choose $1<q<p$. By Hölder's inequality and the finiteness of all polynomial moments of the fixed quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\rho $, the functions $h=g(2-\rho )^{2n}$ have uniformly bounded $L^ q$ norms. Lemma 14.2.1 , applied in the Hermitian background $\omega $, gives $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $-1\leq s\leq 0$ and \[  \omega _ s^ n\geq m h\, \mathrm{d}V  \] for a fixed $m>0$. Put $u_1=\rho +s$. Then $\theta _{u_1}\geq \omega _ s$ and $u_1\leq \rho \leq \eta $. On $\Omega $ define \[  t=1+\eta -u_1,\qquad v=\eta +t^{-1},  \] so that $1\leq t\leq 2-\rho $. Lemma 1.7.9 , applied on relatively compact subsets of $\Omega $ with $a=\eta $, $h=u_1$ and $\chi (x)=(1-x)^{-1}$, gives \[  \theta _ v=(1-t^{-2})\theta _\eta +t^{-2}\theta _{u_1} +2t^{-3}\, \mathrm{d}(\eta -u_1)\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\eta -u_1) \geq t^{-2}\theta _{u_1}.  \] Since $\eta \leq v\leq \eta +1$, lemma 1.3.7 extends $v$ across $Z$, and the bounds extend by lemma 1.3.3 . On $\Omega $, positivity of the local products gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\geq t^{-2n}\theta _{u_1}^ n \geq (2-\rho )^{-2n}\omega _ s^ n \geq m g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Neither side charges $Z$, so the inequality holds on $X$. $\square$ Proposition 14.13.2 . Let $\gamma $ be a Gauduchon metric on $X$, write $\gamma ^ n=G\, \mathrm{d}V$, and put \[  T_\gamma =\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Then $T_\gamma >0$. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $u\geq \rho -C$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\geq F\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $F\geq 0$, then 14.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-singular-gauduchon-trace} \int _ X F^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V\leq T_\gamma . \end{equation} Consequently, let $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero, and let $\lambda >0$. Every solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ that is bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant satisfies $\sup _ Xu\leq C'$, where $C'$ depends only on $\theta $, $\gamma $, $f$ and $\lambda $. Moreover, if $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $j\geq 1$, and constants $C_ j\geq 0$ and $c_ j>0$ satisfy \[  \sup _ Xv_ j=0,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_ j)=c_ j \mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad v_ j\geq \rho -C_ j,  \] then the constants $c_ j$ are uniformly bounded above. Proof. The current $\theta _ u\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is linear in $\theta _ u$, so it is a globally defined positive current, even at $Z$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma ^{n-1}=0$, Stokes' theorem in the sense of currents gives \[  \int _ X\theta _ u\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Applied to $\rho $, this identity proves $T_\gamma \geq \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}>0$. On $\Omega $, lemma 1.7.6 , applied to $\theta _ u$ and $\gamma $, gives \[  \theta _ u\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq F^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Exhausting $\Omega $ and using positivity of the global trace measure, we obtain ( 14.12 ), since the complement $Z$ has zero volume. For the exponential equation, write $a=\sup _ Xu$ and $w=u-a$. The estimate becomes \[  \mathrm{e}^{\lambda a/n}\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{\lambda w/n}f^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V \leq T_\gamma .  \] The integral has a positive lower bound over all normalized $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Otherwise, normalized compactness would give a sequence of such $w$ with integrals tending to zero and converging almost everywhere to a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function; since $w\leq 0$ and $f^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}$ is integrable, dominated convergence would give a strictly positive limit integral, a contradiction. This bounds $a$ from above. For the last assertion, the same estimate contains the factors $c_ j^{1/n}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/(jn)}$. If the integrals $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/(jn)}f^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V$ tended to zero along a subsequence with $j\to \infty $, normalized compactness and almost-everywhere convergence would give $v_ j/j\to 0$ almost everywhere along a further subsequence. Dominated convergence would then give the positive limit $\int _ Xf^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V$. This contradiction bounds $c_ j$ for all large $j$, and each of the finitely many remaining constants is finite. Neither argument uses the total Monge–Ampère mass. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.13.1
text: Lemma 14.13.1 . Fix $p>1$ and $L>0$. There is $m>0$ such that, whenever \[  \rho \leq \eta \leq 0,\quad \eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ), \qquad g\geq 0,\quad \| g\| _{L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq L,  \] there exists $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  \eta \leq v\leq \eta +1,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\geq m g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The constant $m$ depends only on the fixed geometry and on $\rho ,p,L$. Proof. Choose $1<q<p$. Put $u_1=\rho +s$. Then $\theta _{u_1}\geq \omega _ s$ and $u_1\leq \rho \leq \eta $. On $\Omega $ define \[  t=1+\eta -u_1,\qquad v=\eta +t^{-1},  \] so that $1\leq t\leq 2-\rho $. On $\Omega $, positivity of the local products gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\geq t^{-2n}\theta _{u_1}^ n \geq (2-\rho )^{-2n}\omega _ s^ n \geq m g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Neither side charges $Z$, so the inequality holds on $X$. $\square$

title: 14.14 Stability above a strict barrier
text: 14.14 Stability above a strict barrier The subsolutions of lemma 14.13.1 stay within a bounded distance of a given reference. With them, the proof of theorem 14.3.1 extends to unbounded potentials lying above $\rho $, and the resulting estimate is uniform over all references between $\rho $ and zero. For a fixed reference, it upgrades $L^1$ compactness of solutions to uniform convergence of their differences on $\Omega $. Theorem 14.14.1 . Fix $C_0,L>0$, $p>1$, and \[  0<\gamma <\frac{p-1}{np+p-1}.  \] Let $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $\rho \leq \eta \leq 0$, and suppose that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies \[  \eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad 0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V), \quad \| f\| _ p\leq L.  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed geometry and on $\rho ,C_0,L,p,\gamma $, such that every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\leq \eta $ satisfies 14.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-reference-stability} \sup _\Omega (v-u)_+ \leq C\left(\int _\Omega (v-u)_+\, \mathrm{d}V\right)^\gamma . \end{equation} In particular, the constant does not depend on the reference $\eta $, and the comparison potential $v$ need not have the ordinary singularity type of $\eta $. The difference $v-u$ is evaluated on $\Omega $, where $u$ and $\eta $ are locally bounded; since $Z$ has zero volume, the integral is the same as over $X$. Since $Z$ is pluripolar, the resulting inequality $v\leq u+C\bigl (\int _\Omega (v-u)_+\, \mathrm{d}V\bigr )^\gamma $ on $\Omega $ extends to the canonical representatives on all of $X$. Proof. Replacing $v$ by $\max (v,u)$, we may assume $\eta -C_0\leq u\leq v\leq \eta $, so that $0\leq v-u\leq C_0$ on $\Omega $.  Fix $q\in (1,p)$ and $\delta >0$, and put \[  E_\delta =\{ u<v-\delta \} \cap \Omega ,\qquad g_\delta =\mathbf1_{E_\delta }f,\qquad m_\delta =\| g_\delta \| _ q.  \] When $m_\delta >0$, lemma 14.13.1 , followed by subtracting one from its potential, gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a fixed $b>0$ such that \[  \eta -1\leq h\leq \eta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (h)\geq b\, g_\delta /m_\delta \, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The constant $b$ is uniform in $\eta $, because the auxiliary density has $L^ q$ norm one and the strict barrier is fixed. If $0<m_\delta <b/2$, set \[  t=(2m_\delta /b)^{1/n},\qquad w=(1-t)v+th-\delta -C_0t.  \] Since $h-v\leq C_0$, we have $w\leq v-\delta $, so the set $\{ u<w\} \cap \Omega $ is contained in $E_\delta $. On this set the local expansion into positive mixed products gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)\geq t^ n\mathrm{MA}_\theta (h)\geq 2\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$. Both potentials are bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant, and $w\leq u+C_0$, so theorem 14.12.2 applies and gives $u\geq w$. It follows that \[  v-u\leq \delta +C_0t+t(v-h)\leq \delta +(C_0+1)t.  \] If $m_\delta =0$, we apply the same domination theorem with coefficient zero to $u$ and $v-\delta $. If $m_\delta \geq b/2$, we use $v-u\leq C_0$. In all cases, \[  \sup _\Omega (v-u)\leq \delta +C_1m_\delta ^{1/n}.  \] Write $I=\int _\Omega (v-u)\, \mathrm{d}V$. If $I=0$, the canonical potentials agree. Otherwise Hölder's and Chebyshev's inequalities give \[  m_\delta \leq L(I/\delta )^{(p-q)/(pq)}.  \] For $0<I\leq 1$, the choice $\delta =I^{(p-q)/(npq+p-q)}$ yields the exponent $\gamma _ q=(p-q)/(npq+p-q)$. We choose $q>1$ so close to one that $\gamma _ q>\gamma $. The case $I>1$ follows from the bound $v-u\leq C_0$. This proves ( 14.13 ). $\square$ Corollary 14.14.2 . Fix $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\rho \leq \eta \leq 0$, constants $C_0,L>0$, and $p>1$. Consider the family of potentials $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfying \[  \eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f_ u\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad 0\leq f_ u\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V), \quad \| f_ u\| _ p\leq L.  \] This family is compact for uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $. If $u_ j$ belong to the family and $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1$, then $u$ belongs to the family and \[  \sup _\Omega |u_ j-u|\leq C\| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(\mathrm{d}V)}^\gamma \longrightarrow 0  \] for every exponent $\gamma $ as in theorem 14.14.1 . Moreover, $f_{u_ j}$ converges weakly to $f_ u$ in $L^ p$. Proof. Applying the theorem in both orders to $u_ j$ and $u_ k$, with the common reference $\eta $, we see that an $L^1$-Cauchy sequence in the family is uniformly Cauchy in differences on $\Omega $. Its uniform limit on $\Omega $ is locally $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and agrees almost everywhere, hence everywhere for the canonical representatives, with the $L^1$ limit $u$. The bounds $\eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta $ hold on all of $X$. Letting $k\to \infty $ in the pairwise estimate proves the quantitative bound, before any equation for $u$ is used. The densities form a bounded set in the reflexive space $L^ p$. Let $f$ be the weak limit of a subsequence $f_{u_{j_ k}}$. Since the potentials are locally bounded and converge locally uniformly on $\Omega $, Bedford–Taylor continuity, which holds also for the smooth nonclosed background, gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ on $\Omega $. Neither measure charges the analytic set $Z$, so this equality holds on $X$. Positivity and weak lower semicontinuity of the norm give $f\geq 0$ and $\| f\| _ p\leq L$. Thus every weak cluster point equals the density $f_ u$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, which proves weak convergence of the whole sequence. Finally, the common bounds by $\eta $ and $\eta -C_0$ give $L^1$ compactness of the family, by the compactness of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, and the preceding argument upgrades each convergent subsequence to uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $. $\square$ For solutions with minimal singularities, normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, we take $\eta =V_\theta $. Then $\rho \leq V_\theta \leq 0$, and every normalized comparison potential $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $v\leq V_\theta $, as the theorem requires.

title: 14.15 Minimal singularities in an arbitrary big background
search_title: Minimal singularities in an arbitrary big background
text: 14.15 Minimal singularities in an arbitrary big background We now solve the equations in the ordinary singularity type of $V_\theta $. Demailly's regularization approximates $V_\theta $ by strict potentials with analytic singularities. On a resolution of these singularities, the corresponding equations become equations in a semipositive big background, which we have already solved. The solutions satisfy bounds relative to the approximating singularities that are uniform in the approximation, and upper and lower envelopes then produce a solution with minimal singularities. For the normalized equation, the normalized exponential solutions lie in a common interval below $V_\theta $, so the compactness theorem of the preceding section applies directly. Since $\rho \leq 0$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, it is a competitor for $V_\theta $, and hence $\rho \leq V_\theta \leq 0$. We use the analytic regularization of theorem 1.15.3 in its resolved form. Lemma 14.15.1 . Let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $\theta _\psi \geq a\omega $ for some $a>0$, and suppose that $\psi $ has a smooth remainder after resolution, as in theorem 1.15.3 . For every nonzero $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and every $\lambda >0$, there exists $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \psi $ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification resolving the singularities of $\psi $. The pulled-back current has the form \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\pi ^*\psi =\beta +[D],  \] where $D$ is an effective real divisor, $[D]$ is its current of integration, and $\beta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $Y$. Off $D$ we have $\beta \geq a\pi ^*\omega $, and by continuity this inequality holds everywhere. In particular, $\beta $ is semipositive. We check that $\beta $ is big. For a blowup with smooth center and exceptional divisor $E$, choose a metric on $\mathcal O(-E)$ whose curvature is positive in the directions tangent to the projective fibers. Along $E$, the pullback of a Hermitian metric is positive in the complementary directions. Consequently, its sum with a sufficiently small positive multiple of this curvature form is a Hermitian metric: positivity holds first along $E$, then on a neighborhood of $E$, and finally on the compact complement, where the pullback is already positive. Iterating over the blowups, we obtain an effective real exceptional divisor $F$, with logarithmic potential $\zeta $, and a smooth Hermitian form $\kappa $ such that \[  \pi ^*\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta =\kappa +[F].  \] At each step of the iteration, we pull back the smooth positive form obtained so far, apply the construction for one blowup, and add the pullback of the previous divisor to the new positive multiple of $E$. Hence $\beta +a\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta \geq a\kappa $, so $\beta $ is big. This argument only involves Hermitian metrics and never requires a closed positive form on $Y$. Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ on $Y$, and write $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}V=J\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y$. The function $J$ is smooth, nonnegative and bounded, and it is positive off the exceptional locus. Define \[  H=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \pi ^*\psi }(f\circ \pi )J.  \] This function is nonzero and belongs to $L^ p(\mathrm{d}V_ Y)$. Indeed, $\psi $ is bounded above, and the change of variables formula gives \[  \int _ Y|(f\circ \pi )J|^ p\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \leq \| J\| _\infty ^{p-1}\int _ X|f|^ p\, \mathrm{d}V;  \] the analytic exceptional sets do not affect these integrals. Theorem 14.2.2 , applied on $Y$ in the semipositive big background $\beta $, gives a bounded $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\beta )$ with \[  \mathrm{MA}_\beta (s)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}H\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y.  \] The function $\pi ^*\psi +s$ is $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic, because the corresponding current is $\beta _ s+[D]\geq 0$, where $\beta _ s=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$. By theorem A.2.1 it descends to some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $u\sim \psi $ because $s$ is bounded. Off the exceptional set and the pole set of $\psi $, the change of variables formula gives the required equation. Neither the extended measure on the left nor the measure $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ on the right charges these analytic sets, so the equation holds on all of $X$. $\square$ Theorem 14.15.2 . Let $\theta $ be any smooth big real $(1,1)$-form and let $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero. For every $\lambda >0$ there is a unique $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that \[  u\sim V_\theta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Step 1: approximating singularity types. Apply theorem 1.15.3 to $V_\theta $. Set $\delta _ j=2^{-j}$ and pass to a subsequence whose curvature errors are at most $\delta _ j$. Denote its potentials by $\widetilde\psi _ j$; thus $\widetilde\psi _ j\downarrow V_\theta $ and $\theta _{\widetilde\psi _ j}\geq -\delta _ j\omega $. Set \[  a_ j=(1-\delta _ j)\sup _ X\widetilde\psi _ j\geq 0, \qquad \psi _ j=(1-\delta _ j)\widetilde\psi _ j+\delta _ j\rho -a_ j.  \] By Hartogs' lemma, $\sup _ X\widetilde\psi _ j\to \sup _ XV_\theta =0$, so $a_ j\to 0$. A common resolution of the singularities of $\widetilde\psi _ j$ and $\rho $ shows that $\psi _ j$ has a smooth remainder after resolution. Moreover, 14.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-minimal-approximation} \theta _{\psi _ j}\geq \delta _ j^2\omega , \qquad (1-\delta _ j)V_\theta +\delta _ j\rho -a_ j \leq \psi _ j\leq V_\theta . \end{equation} The upper inequality holds because $\psi _ j$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and nonpositive. Subtracting $a_ j$ explicitly keeps the normalization separate from the fixed barrier $\rho $. Step 2: uniform bounds. By lemma 14.15.1 there are $u_ j\sim \psi _ j$ satisfying \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_ j)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Each $u_ j$ is bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant depending on $j$, so proposition 14.13.2 gives a uniform upper bound for $\sup _ Xu_ j$. There is also a uniform lower bound. We apply lemma 14.13.1 with the barrier $\rho $ replaced by $\rho -1-\sup _ ja_ j$ and with the reference $\psi _ j-1$, which lies between this barrier and zero. The lemma gives $v_ j$ with $\psi _ j-1\leq v_ j\leq \psi _ j\leq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_ j)\geq mf\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $m>0$ is independent of $j$. Put $w_ j=v_ j+\lambda ^{-1}\log m$. Then \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ j)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w_ j}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad u_ j\sim w_ j\sim \psi _ j,  \] and the exponential order in corollary 14.12.3 gives $u_ j\geq w_ j$. Thus, for a uniform constant $C$, 14.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-minimal-solution-bounds} \psi _ j-C\leq u_ j\leq V_\theta +C. \end{equation} After extraction, $u_ j$ converges in $L^1$ and almost everywhere to a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, and the preceding bounds give $V_\theta -C\leq u\leq V_\theta +C$. Step 3: the equation for the limit. We identify the equation using envelopes. Put $A_ j=\sup _{k\geq j}a_ k$ and, for $N\geq j$, define \[  p_{j,N}=P_\theta (\min \{ u_ j,\ldots ,u_ N\} ),\qquad t_{j,N}=\max _{j\leq k\leq N}u_ k.  \] Both functions lie above the $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function \[  b_ j=(1-\delta _ j)V_\theta +\delta _ j\rho -C-A_ j,  \] which is a competitor for every $p_{j,N}$; in particular, no envelope is identically $-\infty $. All these functions are locally bounded on $\Omega $, uniformly in $j$ and $N$. Contact support (theorem 14.7.4 ), together with a partition of the contact set according to the first index of contact, gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_{j,N})\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda p_{j,N}}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] No factor $N$ appears here: on each piece the envelope equals a single $u_ k$, and ordered contact bounds its measure by the measure of that $u_ k$. Similarly, locality and ordered contact for a finite maximum give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (t_{j,N})\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t_{j,N}}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Now let $N\to \infty $, and set $p_ j=\lim _ Np_{j,N}$ and $t_ j=(\lim _ Nt_{j,N})^*$. Continuity of local bounded products along monotone sequences passes both inequalities to these limits. Next, $p_ j$ increases to a regularized limit $p$, while $t_ j$ decreases to $u$ by Hartogs' lemma. The bound by $b_ j$ gives $p\sim V_\theta $, and $p\leq u$. A second application of the monotone continuity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda p}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] These inequalities hold on $\Omega $, and they extend across $Z$ because no measure involved charges $Z$. Thus $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda (p-u)}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, and the exponential order in corollary 14.12.3 gives $p\geq u$. Hence $p=u$, and the equation follows. Applying the same order in both directions proves uniqueness. Note that the Monge–Ampère operator was only ever applied along monotone sequences that are locally bounded on $\Omega $. $\square$ Lemma 14.15.3 . Under the hypotheses of theorem 14.15.2 , let $u_\lambda $ be the solution given there, and put \[  v_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda , \qquad c_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \sup _ Xu_\lambda }.  \] There are constants $B,C,m>0$, independent of $0<\lambda \leq 1$, such that 14.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-normalized-uniform-type} V_\theta -B\leq v_\lambda \leq V_\theta , \qquad m\leq c_\lambda \leq C. \end{equation} Proof. The normalized potential satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda )=c_\lambda \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda } f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and write $\gamma ^ n=G\, \mathrm{d}V$. Since $v_\lambda \leq 0$ and $0<\lambda \leq 1$, ( 14.12 ) gives \[  c_\lambda ^{1/n} \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{v_\lambda /n}f^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] The integrals on the left have a positive lower bound independent of $\lambda $. Otherwise, the compactness of normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions would give an almost everywhere convergent sequence of the normalized $v_\lambda $ whose integrals tend to zero, with a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic limit; since $f$ is nonzero, dominated convergence would give a positive limit integral. Thus $c_\lambda \leq C$. To control the singularity type, we use uniform exponential integrability (lemma 1.5.1 ) and Hölder's inequality to choose $\varepsilon >0$ and $1<q<p$ such that $\| \mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon v_\lambda }f\| _ q$ is uniformly bounded. Lemma 14.13.1 , applied with the reference $V_\theta -1$ and the barrier $\rho -1$, gives $\eta _\lambda \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  V_\theta -1\leq \eta _\lambda \leq V_\theta , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\eta _\lambda )\geq m\mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon v_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V \geq mf\, \mathrm{d}V  \] for a fixed $m>0$. The scalar order in corollary 14.12.3 , together with $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda )\leq c_\lambda f\, \mathrm{d}V$, gives $c_\lambda \geq m$. Set $D=\varepsilon ^{-1}\max \{ 0,\log (C/m)\} $ and $w_\lambda =\eta _\lambda -D$. Then \[  \mathrm{e}^{\varepsilon (w_\lambda -v_\lambda )}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda ) \leq m\mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon v_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_\lambda ),  \] since $\lambda v_\lambda \leq 0$ and $\eta _\lambda \leq 0$. The exponential order in corollary 14.12.3 gives $v_\lambda \geq w_\lambda $, which proves the uniform bounds with $B=1+D$. $\square$ Theorem 14.15.4 . Under the assumptions of theorem 14.15.2 , there are $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, a constant $C>0$ and a uniquely determined $c>0$ such that \[  \sup _ Xv=0, \qquad V_\theta -C\leq v\leq V_\theta , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] As in the semipositive case, only the constant $c$ is asserted to be unique, not the normalized potential. Proof. Apply lemma 14.15.3 with $\lambda =1/j$, and write $v_ j=v_{1/j}$ and $c_ j=c_{1/j}$. Extract a subsequence with $v_ j\to v$ in $L^1$ and almost everywhere, and with $c_ j\to c\in [m,C]$. The limit is normalized, $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and has minimal singularities. The densities $c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f$ have a common $L^ p$ bound. Hence corollary 14.14.2 , applied with the reference $V_\theta $, upgrades the convergence to uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $ and identifies the weak $L^ p$ limit of these densities with the density of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$. At almost every point, $v_ j$ converges to a finite value, so $v_ j/j\to 0$. Since $v_ j\leq 0$ and $c_ j\leq C$, dominated convergence gives $c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f\to cf$ in $L^ p$. Therefore $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. The uniqueness of the constant follows from corollary 14.12.3 . $\square$

title: Lemma 14.15.1
text: Lemma 14.15.1 . Let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $\theta _\psi \geq a\omega $ for some $a>0$, and suppose that $\psi $ has a smooth remainder after resolution, as in theorem 1.15.3 . For every nonzero $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and every $\lambda >0$, there exists $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \psi $ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification resolving the singularities of $\psi $. The pulled-back current has the form \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\pi ^*\psi =\beta +[D],  \] where $D$ is an effective real divisor, $[D]$ is its current of integration, and $\beta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $Y$. Off $D$ we have $\beta \geq a\pi ^*\omega $, and by continuity this inequality holds everywhere. In particular, $\beta $ is semipositive. We check that $\beta $ is big. For a blowup with smooth center and exceptional divisor $E$, choose a metric on $\mathcal O(-E)$ whose curvature is positive in the directions tangent to the projective fibers. Along $E$, the pullback of a Hermitian metric is positive in the complementary directions. Consequently, its sum with a sufficiently small positive multiple of this curvature form is a Hermitian metric: positivity holds first along $E$, then on a neighborhood of $E$, and finally on the compact complement, where the pullback is already positive. Iterating over the blowups, we obtain an effective real exceptional divisor $F$, with logarithmic potential $\zeta $, and a smooth Hermitian form $\kappa $ such that \[  \pi ^*\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta =\kappa +[F].  \] At each step of the iteration, we pull back the smooth positive form obtained so far, apply the construction for one blowup, and add the pullback of the previous divisor to the new positive multiple of $E$. Hence $\beta +a\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta \geq a\kappa $, so $\beta $ is big. This argument only involves Hermitian metrics and never requires a closed positive form on $Y$. Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ on $Y$, and write $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}V=J\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y$. The function $J$ is smooth, nonnegative and bounded, and it is positive off the exceptional locus. Define \[  H=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \pi ^*\psi }(f\circ \pi )J.  \] This function is nonzero and belongs to $L^ p(\mathrm{d}V_ Y)$. Indeed, $\psi $ is bounded above, and the change of variables formula gives \[  \int _ Y|(f\circ \pi )J|^ p\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \leq \| J\| _\infty ^{p-1}\int _ X|f|^ p\, \mathrm{d}V;  \] the analytic exceptional sets do not affect these integrals. Theorem 14.2.2 , applied on $Y$ in the semipositive big background $\beta $, gives a bounded $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\beta )$ with \[  \mathrm{MA}_\beta (s)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}H\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y.  \] The function $\pi ^*\psi +s$ is $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic, because the corresponding current is $\beta _ s+[D]\geq 0$, where $\beta _ s=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$. By theorem A.2.1 it descends to some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $u\sim \psi $ because $s$ is bounded. Off the exceptional set and the pole set of $\psi $, the change of variables formula gives the required equation. Neither the extended measure on the left nor the measure $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ on the right charges these analytic sets, so the equation holds on all of $X$. $\square$

Next, $p_ j$ increases to a regularized limit $p$, while $t_ j$ decreases to $u$ by Hartogs' lemma. The bound by $b_ j$ gives $p\sim V_\theta $, and $p\leq u$. A second application of the monotone continuity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda p}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] These inequalities hold on $\Omega $, and they extend across $Z$ because no measure involved charges $Z$. 14.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-minimal-approximation} \theta _{\psi _ j}\geq \delta _ j^2\omega , \qquad (1-\delta _ j)V_\theta +\delta _ j\rho -a_ j \leq \psi _ j\leq V_\theta . \end{equation}

title: Lemma 14.15.3
text: Lemma 14.15.3 . Under the assumptions of theorem 14.15.2 , there are $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, a constant $C>0$ and a uniquely determined $c>0$ such that \[  \sup _ Xv=0, \qquad V_\theta -C\leq v\leq V_\theta , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof.
