title: 14.16 Local Hölder continuity in a big background
search_title: Local Hölder continuity in a big background
text: 14.16 Local Hölder continuity in a big background We now combine the stability estimate above $\rho $ with the regularization of lemma 1.21.7 , whose curvature error is linear in the regularization parameter. As in the proof of theorem 14.4.1 , a small multiple of the strict barrier absorbs the curvature error of the transforms, and a lower bound for the minimizing radius converts the estimate for the transforms into an estimate for the smoothing on compact subsets of $\Omega $. This gives a local Hölder modulus for solutions with minimal singularities. Theorem 14.16.1 . Fix $C_0>0$. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy \[  \sup _ Xu=0,\qquad V_\theta -C_0\leq u\leq V_\theta , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ and $p>1$. Then $u$ is locally Hölder continuous on $\Omega $, with every exponent \[  0<\beta <\frac{2(p-1)}{np+3(p-1)}.  \] For fixed bounds on $C_0$ and $\| f\| _ p$, the Hölder constants are uniform on each fixed compact subset of $\Omega $. Proof. Since $u\geq V_\theta -C_0\geq \rho -C_0$, we may subtract a constant from the strict barrier so that $\rho \leq u-1$; it still satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa \omega $ for a fixed $\kappa >0$. Choose $0<\gamma <(p-1)/(np+p-1)$ and set $\alpha =2\gamma <1$. Apply lemma 1.21.7 with $a=u$, and let $A,K,C$ and $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ be the constants and transforms given there. For small $\delta >0$ set \[  c=\delta ^\alpha ,\qquad e=Ac+C\delta ,\qquad s=e/\kappa , \qquad v_\delta =\frac{\Phi _{c,\delta }+s\rho }{1+s}.  \] By the curvature bound of lemma 1.21.7 , $v_\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The lower bound for $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ in that lemma implies $\rho \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }$ when $\delta $ is small. Thus \[  v_\delta \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }\leq R_\delta u\leq 0.  \] In particular $v_\delta \leq V_\theta $, so theorem 14.14.1 applies with the reference $V_\theta $ and the comparison potential $v_\delta $. Together with the $L^1$ smoothing estimate, it gives \[  \sup _\Omega (v_\delta -u)_+ \leq C\| (R_\delta u-u)_+\| _1^\gamma \leq C\delta ^\alpha .  \] Fix a compact subset of $\Omega $ on which $\rho \geq -M$. Since $s\leq C\delta ^\alpha $ and $u\leq 0$, the identity \[  \Phi _{c,\delta }-u=(1+s)(v_\delta -u)+s(u-\rho )  \] gives $\Phi _{c,\delta }-u\leq C_ M\delta ^\alpha $ there. At a radius $t$ where the infimum defining $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ is attained, the monotone lower bound yields \[  -c\log (t/\delta )\leq \Phi _{c,\delta }-u+K(\delta ^2+\delta ) \leq C_ Mc.  \] Hence $t\geq a_ M\delta $ for a fixed $a_ M>0$. As in the proof of theorem 14.4.1 , monotonicity of the smoothing now gives \[  R_{a_ M\delta }u-u\leq C_ M\delta ^\alpha , \qquad R_{a_ M\delta }u-u\geq -K(a_ M\delta )^2  \] on the chosen compact set. Since every small radius has the form $a_ M\delta $, we obtain $|R_ tu-u|\leq C_ Mt^\alpha $ there for all small $t>0$, with constants uniform on that compact set.  We apply this to a slightly larger compact neighborhood, on which also $\| \nabla R_ tu\| \leq C_ M/t$. For nearby points $x,y$ at distance $d>0$, the smooth function $R_ tu$ and a short path in that neighborhood give \[  |u(x)-u(y)|\leq C_ M(t^\alpha +d/t).  \] The choice $t=d^{1/(1+\alpha )}$ gives the exponent $\alpha /(1+\alpha )$, and letting $\gamma $ approach its upper endpoint gives the asserted range. Pairs of points farther apart are handled by the boundedness of $u$ on the compact neighborhood. $\square$ It suffices that the equation hold on $\Omega $. Suppose that $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ on $\Omega $, where $c>0$ and $0\leq f\in L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V)$, and that $u$ satisfies the same bounds as in the theorem. The lower bound $u\geq V_\theta -C_0\geq \rho -C_0$ shows that $u$ is locally bounded on $\Omega $, so there $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ is the local bounded product. Since $Z$ has zero volume and is not charged by $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, the equation holds on $X$, and the theorem applies with $cf$ in place of $f$. The uniform estimates then depend on a bound for $\| cf\| _ p$, which includes the constant $c$.

title: Theorem 14.16.1

Then $u$ is locally Hölder continuous on $\Omega $, with every exponent \[  0<\beta <\frac{2(p-1)}{np+3(p-1)}.  \] For fixed bounds on $C_0$ and $\| f\| _ p$, the Hölder constants are uniform on each fixed compact subset of $\Omega $. Proof. Since $u\geq V_\theta -C_0\geq \rho -C_0$, we may subtract a constant from the strict barrier so that $\rho \leq u-1$; it still satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa \omega $ for a fixed $\kappa >0$. Choose $0<\gamma <(p-1)/(np+p-1)$ and set $\alpha =2\gamma <1$. Apply lemma 1.21.7 with $a=u$, and let $A,K,C$ and $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ be the constants and transforms given there. For small $\delta >0$ set \[  c=\delta ^\alpha ,\qquad e=Ac+C\delta ,\qquad s=e/\kappa , \qquad v_\delta =\frac{\Phi _{c,\delta }+s\rho }{1+s}.  \] By the curvature bound of lemma 1.21.7 , $v_\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The lower bound for $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ in that lemma implies $\rho \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }$ when $\delta $ is small. Thus \[  v_\delta \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }\leq R_\delta u\leq 0.  \] In particular $v_\delta \leq V_\theta $, so theorem 14.14.1 applies with the reference $V_\theta $ and the comparison potential $v_\delta $. Together with the $L^1$ smoothing estimate, it gives \[  \sup _\Omega (v_\delta -u)_+ \leq C\| (R_\delta u-u)_+\| _1^\gamma \leq C\delta ^\alpha .  \] Fix a compact subset of $\Omega $ on which $\rho \geq -M$. Since $s\leq C\delta ^\alpha $ and $u\leq 0$, the identity \[  \Phi _{c,\delta }-u=(1+s)(v_\delta -u)+s(u-\rho )  \] gives $\Phi _{c,\delta }-u\leq C_ M\delta ^\alpha $ there. At a radius $t$ where the infimum defining $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ is attained, the monotone lower bound yields \[  -c\log (t/\delta )\leq \Phi _{c,\delta }-u+K(\delta ^2+\delta ) \leq C_ Mc.  \] Hence $t\geq a_ M\delta $ for a fixed $a_ M>0$. As in the proof of theorem 14.4.1 , monotonicity of the smoothing now gives \[  R_{a_ M\delta }u-u\leq C_ M\delta ^\alpha , \qquad R_{a_ M\delta }u-u\geq -K(a_ M\delta )^2  \] on the chosen compact set. Since every small radius has the form $a_ M\delta $, we obtain $|R_ tu-u|\leq C_ Mt^\alpha $ there for all small $t>0$, with constants uniform on that compact set.  We apply this to a slightly larger compact neighborhood, on which also $\| \nabla R_ tu\| \leq C_ M/t$. For nearby points $x,y$ at distance $d>0$, the smooth function $R_ tu$ and a short path in that neighborhood give \[  |u(x)-u(y)|\leq C_ M(t^\alpha +d/t).  \] The choice $t=d^{1/(1+\alpha )}$ gives the exponent $\alpha /(1+\alpha )$, and letting $\gamma $ approach its upper endpoint gives the asserted range. Pairs of points farther apart are handled by the boundedness of $u$ on the compact neighborhood. $\square$

title: 14.16.1 Limits of normalized exponential solutions
text: 14.16.1 Limits of normalized exponential solutions For the normalized exponential family $(v_\lambda ,c_\lambda )$ of lemma 14.15.3 , the reference interval $[V_\theta -B,V_\theta ]$ is uniform in $0<\lambda \leq 1$. Stability therefore controls differences on all of $\Omega $, and the local Hölder estimates strengthen the convergence on compact subsets. We fix the nonzero density $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and use the constants $B,C,m$ of that lemma. Proposition 14.16.2 . For the family $(v_\lambda ,c_\lambda )$ of lemma 14.15.3 , the normalized potentials are relatively compact for uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $. As $\lambda \downarrow 0$, every cluster limit $v$ is normalized, has minimal singularities, and satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where $c>0$ is the unique constant of theorem 14.15.4 . Moreover, \[  c_\lambda \longrightarrow c, \qquad c_\lambda \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f \longrightarrow cf\quad \text{in }L^ p(\mathrm{d}V).  \] Every sequence of parameters in $(0,1]$ has a subsequence for which the potentials converge in $C^\beta $ on each compact subset of $\Omega $, for all \[  0<\beta <\frac{2(p-1)}{np+3(p-1)}.  \] Proof. By lemma 14.15.3 , all $v_\lambda $ lie in a common reference interval, and their densities are bounded in $L^ p$ by $C\| f\| _ p$. We may therefore apply corollary 14.14.2 with $\eta =V_\theta $. Given any sequence $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$, we pass to a subsequence with $v_{\lambda _ j}\to v$ uniformly in differences on $\Omega $ and in $L^1(X)$, and with $c_{\lambda _ j}\to c_*\in [m,C]$. The limit satisfies the same reference bounds and is normalized. Off the pole set, \[  0\leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda } \leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (V_\theta -B)}\longrightarrow 0  \] as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Multiplying by $f$ and using dominated convergence, we obtain $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f\to f$ in $L^ p$ for the whole family. The compactness corollary therefore identifies the limit equation as $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=c_*f\, \mathrm{d}V$, and the uniqueness of the constant gives $c_*=c$. Since every subsequential limit of $c_\lambda $ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ equals $c$, we conclude that $c_\lambda \to c$, and the stated convergence of the densities follows. Finally, theorem 14.16.1 gives uniform local $C^\alpha $ bounds for every $\alpha $ below its endpoint, and the uniform limit inherits these bounds by pointwise convergence. For $0<\beta <\alpha $, uniform convergence and the elementary interpolation inequality on smaller coordinate balls give \[  [v_{\lambda _ j}-v]_{C^\beta } \leq C\| v_{\lambda _ j}-v\| _\infty ^{1-\beta /\alpha } [v_{\lambda _ j}-v]_{C^\alpha }^{\beta /\alpha } \longrightarrow 0,  \] where the Hölder bounds are taken on slightly larger compact neighborhoods. The uniformly convergent subsequence given by compactness thus converges in $C^\beta $ on every compact subset of $\Omega $ and for every exponent below the endpoint; no further extraction depending on the exponent is needed. $\square$ Corollary 14.16.3 . Suppose a group $G$ of biholomorphisms of $X$ preserves $\theta $ and the measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Then every $v_\lambda $ and every cluster limit as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ is $G$-invariant. If the normalized zero-exponent equation has only one $G$-invariant solution with minimal singularities, then the whole family $v_\lambda $ converges to it as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, uniformly in differences on $\Omega $ and in each local $C^\beta $ topology of the proposition. Proof. For $g\in G$, pullback by $g$ preserves $\theta $-plurisubharmonicity, and $V_\theta \circ g=V_\theta $ by the definition of the envelope. Pullback also preserves the positive-exponent equation, so its uniqueness gives $u_\lambda \circ g=u_\lambda $, and the normalization preserves this equality. Pullback by a fixed smooth biholomorphism is continuous on $L^1(X)$, since its Jacobian relative to the fixed smooth volume is bounded. Hence every cluster limit is invariant almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere for the canonical representatives. This argument does not require $g$ to preserve the barrier $\rho $ or the set $\Omega $. If the invariant solution is unique, every cluster limit is the same potential. Relative compactness then implies convergence of the whole family for uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $: a sequence staying at a fixed positive distance from that potential would have a convergent subsequence, a contradiction. The interpolation argument above upgrades this to the asserted local $C^\beta $ convergence. $\square$ The proposition gives compactness and identifies the equation of every cluster limit, and the symmetry criterion is one way to identify the limit itself. In general, theorem 15.12.1 shows that the whole family converges, and it describes the limit through the greatest subsolution of the zero-exponent equation that satisfies a family of integral normalizations determined by how the constant $c$ depends on the density. This holds even when the zero-exponent equation has several normalized solutions.

title: 14.17 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
search_title: Interior smoothness on the regular locus
text: 14.17 Interior smoothness on the regular locus Throughout this section, $\theta $ is a smooth big real $(1,1)$-form, and $\rho $, $Z=\{ \rho =-\infty \} $ and $\Omega =X\setminus Z$ are the strict analytic barrier and its regular locus fixed in section 14.12 . Thus $\rho \leq 0$ has analytic singularities with smooth remainder, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \omega $. If $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities, then $\varphi \geq V_\theta -C\geq \rho -C$ for a constant $C$. Hence $\varphi $ is locally bounded on $\Omega $, and its Monge–Ampère measure there is the bounded-potential product. For such a potential, theorem 14.16.1 gives local Hölder continuity on $\Omega $ when the density belongs to $L^ p$ for some $p>1$. We show that a smooth strictly positive density on the whole of $\Omega $ then makes the potential smooth on $\Omega $. Local information alone cannot give this: example 14.20.5 below is a locally Lipschitz plurisubharmonic function with constant Monge–Ampère density that is not $C^1$. The argument therefore uses the barrier globally. By the proper gap of lemma 1.19.7 , the difference between the solution and the barrier attains a minimum on the closed set where smoothness fails, and strict positivity of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ turns this minimum into a quadratic separation. Near the minimum, smooth Dirichlet approximants have traces of polynomial growth; the separation improves this growth until a uniform trace bound yields elliptic regularity. Theorem 14.17.1 . Suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities and is locally Hölder continuous on $\Omega $. Let $c>0$ and let $f$ be smooth and strictly positive on $\Omega $. Assume \[  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n\quad \text{on }\Omega .  \] Then $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$ there. The Hölder hypothesis holds when, in addition, $f\in L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$ for some $p>1$, by theorem 14.16.1 ; see corollary 14.17.11 . The theorem also applies when local Hölder continuity is obtained by another argument. The proof is by contradiction and occupies the rest of the section. Let $\mathcal S\subset \Omega $ be the closed set of points near which $\varphi $ is not smooth, suppose that $\mathcal S\neq \varnothing $, and let $p\in \mathcal S$ minimize $\varphi -\rho $ on $\mathcal S$. On a small ball centered at $p$ the argument has four steps. A comparison principle for continuous solutions (section 14.17.1 ) and the smooth Dirichlet problem give smooth solutions $u_ j$ of the equation that converge uniformly to $\varphi $ at a polynomial rate in $j$, while the traces of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$, measured in Euclidean coordinates, grow at most polynomially in $j$ (section 14.17.3 ). Near $p$, the quadratic separation along $\mathcal S$, together with uniform trace bounds on compact sets where $\varphi $ is already smooth, improves the trace growth to $O(j^\gamma )$ for every $\gamma >0$. Interpolation with the convergence rate then gives uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds for every $\alpha <1$ (section 14.17.4 ). A third-order estimate whose constants depend polynomially on the ellipticity turns uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds, for $\alpha $ close to one, into a uniform trace bound (section 14.17.5 ). A continuous solution with bounded trace is smooth (section 14.17.2 ). Hence $\varphi $ is smooth near $p$, contradicting $p\in \mathcal S$ (section 14.17.6 ).

title: Theorem 14.17.1
text: Theorem 14.17.1 . Suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities and is locally Hölder continuous on $\Omega $. Let $c>0$ and let $f$ be smooth and strictly positive on $\Omega $. Assume \[  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n\quad \text{on }\Omega .  \] Then $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$ there. of theorem 14.17.1 . If $n=1$, the equation is the linear identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =cf\, \omega -\theta \quad \text{on }\Omega .  \] Its right-hand side is smooth, so interior elliptic regularity gives $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$, and the original equation gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =cf\, \omega >0$. We henceforth assume $n\geq 2$. Let \[  \mathcal S=\{ p\in \Omega :\varphi \text{ is not smooth on any neighborhood of }p\} .  \] This is closed in $\Omega $. Suppose $\mathcal S\neq \varnothing $. By lemma 1.19.7 , the restriction of $\varphi -\rho $ to $\mathcal S$ attains its minimum $m$ at some $p\in \mathcal S$. Choose nested coordinate balls \[  B\Subset B_0\Subset \Omega  \] centered at $p$. On $B_0$, proposition 14.17.6 gives smooth exact Dirichlet solutions $u_ j$ converging uniformly to $\varphi $ at a polynomial rate and having polynomial global trace growth. On the open set $\Omega \setminus \mathcal S$ the function $\varphi $ is smooth, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is semipositive with positive determinant, hence positive definite. Proposition 14.17.8 therefore gives a uniform trace bound for the $u_ j$ on every compact subset of $B_0\setminus \mathcal S$. In coordinates centered at $p$, take $\kappa >0$ small and set \[  q(z)=\rho (z)-\kappa |z|^2.  \] After shrinking $B$, the lower bound $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \omega $ gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q>0$ on $\overline B$. If $v=\varphi -q$, then the minimizing property of $p$ gives \[  v(p)=m, \qquad v(z)=(\varphi -\rho )(z)+\kappa |z|^2 \geq m+\kappa |z|^2 \quad (z\in \mathcal S\cap \overline B).  \] Thus proposition 14.17.7 applies on $B$ with the closed set $\mathcal S\cap \overline B$: the approximation rate and global polynomial trace bound come from proposition 14.17.6 , and the bound away from $\mathcal S$ comes from proposition 14.17.8 . Its second assertion gives, for every $0<\alpha <1$, a neighborhood of $p$ on which the approximants have a uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound. Choose $\alpha >\alpha _*$ as in proposition 14.17.10 , and apply that proposition on a ball centered at $p$ inside this neighborhood. It yields \[  \sup _ j\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)<\infty  \] on a still smaller neighborhood of $p$. Since $u_ j\to \varphi $ uniformly, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ as currents. The trace bound passes to the limit, so $\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ has a bounded density near $p$. Proposition 14.17.3 now implies that $\varphi $ is smooth near $p$, contradicting $p\in \mathcal S$. Hence $\mathcal S=\varnothing $ and $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$. The form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is smooth and semipositive there, while \[  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n>0.  \] Its nonnegative eigenvalues have positive product, so every eigenvalue is positive. Therefore $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$ on $\Omega $. $\square$

title: 14.17.1 Local comparison
text: 14.17.1 Local comparison The comparison principle below, for continuous sub- and supersolutions on a bounded domain, identifies the given continuous potential with limits of smooth Dirichlet solutions. Since the background need not be closed, the classical Bedford–Taylor comparison does not apply directly. We freeze the background at a point, apply the closed-current comparison formula ( 1.8 ) to quadratic modifications, and control the error by the mixed inequalities of lemma 1.7.6 , lemma 1.7.7 . The local arguments of this section take place in coordinate balls, always with compact closure in a larger coordinate chart. There we put $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$, write $\partial _ i=\partial /\partial z_ i$ and $\partial _{\bar i}=\partial /\partial \bar z_ i$, and take coefficient matrices of real $(1,1)$-forms relative to $\beta $. For such a form $A$, $\operatorname {tr}_\beta A$ and $\det _\beta A$ denote the trace and the determinant of its coefficient matrix, so that $A^ n=(\det _\beta A)\beta ^ n$, and $\Delta _\beta =\operatorname {tr}_\beta \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. For a positive form $T$, $\operatorname {tr}_ T$ is the trace computed with the inverse of the coefficient matrix of $T$. Indices run from $1$ to $n$, repeated indices in tensor expressions are summed, and $I$ denotes the identity matrix. In local statements, $\vartheta $ denotes a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, not necessarily closed, which plays the role of $\theta $. Proposition 14.17.2 . Let $D\Subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded domain and let $\vartheta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form near $\overline D$. Suppose $u,v\in C(\overline D)$ are $\vartheta $-plurisubharmonic, \[  (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\geq F\beta ^ n, \qquad (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\leq F\beta ^ n,  \] where $F>0$ is continuous on $D$. If $u\leq v$ on $\partial D$, then $u\leq v$ in $D$. Proof. Step 1: $v$ admits no strict smooth lower test. Suppose, to the contrary, that a $C^2$ function $q$ touches $v$ from below at a point $p\in D$ and that, at $p$, \[  \vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q>0, \qquad \det _\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)>F.  \] Choose a sufficiently small $a>0$. After replacing $q$ by $q-a|z-p|^2$, which makes the contact strict, and restricting to a small ball $B_ r(p)$, there are fixed $\lambda ,\eta >0$ such that \[  A:=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \lambda \beta , \qquad A^ n\geq (F+\eta )\beta ^ n.  \] To compare with closed currents, freeze the background at $p$: put $\kappa =\sup _{B_ r}\lVert \vartheta -\vartheta (p)\rVert _\beta $ and $B_0=\vartheta (p)+\kappa \beta $. Then $S=B_0-\vartheta $ satisfies $0\leq S\leq 2\kappa \beta $. For small $s>0$ the set $E=\{ v<q+s\} $ is nonempty and relatively compact in $B_ r$. If $Q_0$ is a quadratic potential for the constant form $B_0$, then \[  P=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+Q_0)=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+S, \qquad Q=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q+s+Q_0)=A+S\geq \lambda \beta  \] are closed positive Hessians. Applying ( 1.8 ), expanding $P$, and using $S\leq 2\kappa \beta \leq 2\kappa \lambda ^{-1}Q$, we obtain \[  \int _ E P^ n\leq \int _ E F\beta ^ n+e_\kappa \int _ E P^ n, \qquad e_\kappa =\left(1+\frac{2\kappa }{\lambda }\right)^ n-1.  \] On the other hand, ( 1.8 ) with $j=n$ gives \[  \int _ E P^ n\geq \int _ E Q^ n\geq \int _ E(F+\eta )\beta ^ n.  \] If $M$ bounds $F$ on the ball, the two estimates give $(1-e_\kappa )\eta \leq e_\kappa M$. Since $\kappa \to 0$, and hence $e_\kappa \to 0$, as $r\downarrow 0$, this is impossible for small $r$. Thus no such lower test exists. Step 2: comparison. Suppose that $\max _ D(u-v)>0$. We regularize $u$ to produce a forbidden lower test for $v$. Let $\chi _\delta $ be a nonnegative smooth mollifier of mass one and radius $\delta >0$. For small $t>0$ and $C\geq \sup _ D|z|^2$, set \[  u_ t=u+t(|z|^2-C).  \] Then $u_ t\leq v$ on $\partial D$, the positive maximum persists, and $T_ t=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t\geq t\beta $. Lemma 1.7.6 gives \[  T_ t^ n\geq (F^{1/n}+t)^ n\beta ^ n.  \] Choose a relatively compact neighborhood $W$ of the positive maximum set. By lemma 1.7.7 , \[  (T_ t*\chi _\delta )^ n \geq \bigl ((F^{1/n}+t)*\chi _\delta \bigr )^ n\beta ^ n.  \] Since \[  \vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ t*\chi _\delta ) =T_ t*\chi _\delta +(\vartheta -\vartheta *\chi _\delta ),  \] the convolution satisfies $T_ t*\chi _\delta \geq t\beta $. If $\epsilon _\delta =\| \vartheta -\vartheta *\chi _\delta \| _{C^0(W)}$, then \[  \vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ t*\chi _\delta ) \geq (1-\epsilon _\delta /t)(T_ t*\chi _\delta ).  \] For fixed $t>0$, uniform convergence of the convolved density and $\epsilon _\delta \to 0$ show that the left-hand side is positive and has determinant strictly larger than $F$ on $W$ for small $\delta $. Since $u_ t*\chi _\delta \to u_ t$ uniformly on $W$, the difference $u_ t*\chi _\delta -v$ still attains its maximum over $\overline W$ at an interior point of $W$ for small $\delta $. Subtracting this maximum from $u_ t*\chi _\delta $ produces a smooth function touching $v$ from below with the properties excluded in Step 1, a contradiction. $\square$

title: 14.17.2 Bounded traces and smoothness
text: 14.17.2 Bounded traces and smoothness We begin with the criterion used in the last step of the proof. A bounded trace of a positive current bounds all its coefficient measures, so a continuous solution with bounded trace is a strong solution with $W^{2,q}$ regularity for every finite $q$. The equation then bounds the eigenvalues from below, so it becomes uniformly elliptic. Since the solution is not yet known to be $C^2$, the Evans–Krylov theory is applied to it as a viscosity solution of a concave extension of the operator. Proposition 14.17.3 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a coordinate ball, let $\vartheta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form there and let $F\in C^\infty (B)$ be strictly positive. Suppose $u$ is continuous, $T=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$, and 14.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-local-ma} T^ n=F\beta ^ n. \end{equation} For a point $p\in B$, the following conditions, each required on some neighborhood of $p$, are equivalent: $u$ is smooth; $T\geq \delta \beta $ for some $\delta >0$; $\operatorname {tr}_\beta T$ has a locally bounded measure density. Proof. Choose $C$ so that $v=u+C|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic, and use nonnegative radial mollifiers for which $v_\eta \downarrow v$. The smooth matrix convolutions $T_\eta =T*\chi _\eta $ can be written as \[  T_\eta =(\vartheta *\chi _\eta -C\beta )+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\eta .  \] Bedford–Taylor monotone continuity and smooth convergence of the background imply $T_\eta ^ k\to T^ k$ for every $k$. (2)$\Rightarrow $(3). Assume (2). For every Hermitian matrix $M\geq \delta I$, \[  \det M\geq \delta ^{n-1}\bigl (\operatorname {tr} M-(n-1)\delta \bigr ).  \] Apply this to the regularizations and pass to currents. Equation ( 14.17 ) gives \[  \operatorname {tr}_\beta T\leq \delta ^{1-n}F+(n-1)\delta ,  \] which is (3). (3)$\Rightarrow $(1). Assume (3), say $\operatorname {tr}_\beta T\leq L$. Positivity makes every coefficient of the matrix-valued current $T$ a bounded density. Hence the Euclidean Laplacian of $u$ is locally bounded, and interior Poisson estimates give $u\in W^{2,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $q$. Mollification converges in $W^{2,q}$; taking $q>2n$ identifies the bounded-potential determinant with the ordinary almost-everywhere determinant. Thus $\det _\beta T=F$ almost everywhere. On a smaller ball with $F\geq m>0$, all eigenvalues of $T$ are at most $L$ and their product is at least $m$, so \[  \frac{m}{L^{n-1}}I\leq T\leq LI  \] almost everywhere. It remains to show that this strong solution is smooth. Let $P$ be the real linear map from real symmetric $2n\times 2n$ Hessian matrices to Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices, sending $D^2u$ to the coefficient matrix of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ relative to $\beta $, and let $\Theta (x)$ be the matrix of $\vartheta $. With $\delta =mL^{1-n}$, define the concave extension \[  G(x,M)=\inf _{\delta I\leq A\leq LI} \left\{ \log \det A+\operatorname {tr}\! \left[A^{-1}\bigl (\Theta (x)+P(M)-A\bigr )\right]\right\} -\log F(x).  \] For fixed $A$, write $\mathcal E_ A(x,M)$ for the expression in braces minus $\log F(x)$. The tangent-plane formula for $\log \det $ gives \[  G(x,D^2u)=0\quad \text{almost everywhere}.  \] The operator $G$ is concave and uniformly elliptic on real symmetric matrices. The affine operators $\mathcal E_ A$ have constant principal matrices with eigenvalues bounded above and below in terms of $\delta $ and $L$. Their $x$-dependence is smooth uniformly in $A$, so $G$ has a uniform local Lipschitz modulus in $x$. We claim that $u$ is a viscosity solution of $G(x,D^2u)=0$. Suppose that a smooth function $\psi $ touches $u$ from above at $x_0$ and that $G(x_0,D^2\psi )<0$. Some fixed matrix $A$ then satisfies $\mathcal E_ A(x,D^2\psi )<-\eta $ on a small ball. Since $G(x,D^2u)=0$ almost everywhere, $\mathcal E_ A(x,D^2u)\geq 0$ there. Thus $u-\psi $ has an interior maximum and satisfies \[  \operatorname {tr}\! \left(A^{-1}P(D^2(u-\psi ))\right)\geq \eta \quad \text{almost everywhere}.  \] After a small quadratic perturbation makes the contact strict, this contradicts the Aleksandrov maximum principle [ Chapter 9, Theorem 9.1 , GT01 ] . If instead $\psi $ touches $u$ from below and $G(x_0,D^2\psi )>0$, then $\mathcal E_ A(x,D^2\psi )>\eta $ for every admissible $A$ on a small ball. At almost every point choose an admissible $A(x)$ with $\mathcal E_{A(x)}(x,D^2u)<\eta /2$. A measurable choice is obtained by taking the first qualifying element of a countable dense family. The function $\psi -u$ then violates the same maximum principle for the measurable uniformly elliptic coefficients $A(x)^{-1}$. This proves the claim. The classical variable-coefficient Evans–Krylov theorem gives $u\in C^{2,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for some $0<\alpha <1$. The original equation is now uniformly elliptic with smooth data. Difference quotients satisfy linear equations whose principal coefficients are averages of inverse matrices along positive definite segments. Interior Schauder estimates first give $u\in C^{3,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and then, by iteration, $u\in C^\infty $. This proves (3)$\Rightarrow $(1). (1)$\Rightarrow $(2). If $u$ is smooth, then $T$ is a smooth semipositive form with determinant $F>0$, so it is positive definite; on a smaller neighborhood this gives (2). $\square$

title: 14.17.3 Smooth exact approximants

14.17.3 Smooth exact approximants We now construct the approximants of the first step. The smooth Dirichlet theorem, lemma 14.6.1 , applies to every smooth positive density $F$. Approximating the Hölder boundary values of $\varphi $ by smooth functions therefore gives smooth solutions, and the point is to control them quantitatively. The estimates below bound the trace of a smooth solution by a power of the $C^4$ norm of its boundary value. The $C^4$ norms of the boundary approximations grow polynomially while their uniform errors decay polynomially, so both the convergence and the trace growth have polynomial rates. From ( 14.19 ), 14.20 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-log-trace} \Delta _ T\log S \geq -\frac{C_0(1+H)}S- \frac2S\operatorname {Re}\langle \partial \log S,E\rangle _ T. \end{equation} Set $g_ A(s)=-As+\mathrm{e}^{-s}$. At a local maximum of $Q_ A$, $\partial \log S=-g_ A'(v)\partial v$ and $\Delta _ Tv=n-\operatorname {tr}_ TR$. Combining these identities with ( 14.20 ), then completing the square in $\partial v$, yields 14.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-peak-inequality} 0\geq \left[\varepsilon A-\frac{C_2}{S}-\frac{C_2(A+1)^2}{S^2}\right]H -C_3(A+1)-\frac{C_2}{S}. \end{equation} Here $|E|_ T^2\leq CH$ and the bounds for $v$ have been used. If $S\geq K\sqrt A$ and $K$ is large, the bracket is at least $\varepsilon A/2$. Thus $H\leq C$ independently of $A$ and $u$. The determinant upper bound then gives $S\leq C'$. Enlarging $K$ makes this incompatible with $S\geq K\sqrt A$, proving ( 14.18 ). $\square$
14.18 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-trace-peak} S\leq C\sqrt A. \end{equation}

title: A polynomial boundary trace estimate
text:
A polynomial boundary trace estimate Proposition 14.17.5 . Let $B$ be the unit ball. Fix smooth $\vartheta $, smooth $F>0$ near $\overline B$, and $M<\infty $. There are $C,N<\infty $, depending only on these fixed data, such that every smooth solution $u$ with boundary value $g\in C^\infty (\partial B)$ of \[  T=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0, \qquad T^ n=F\beta ^ n, \qquad \lVert u\rVert _{L^\infty (B)}\leq M, \qquad u|_{\partial B}=g,  \] satisfies 14.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-polynomial-global-trace} \sup _{\overline B}\operatorname {tr}_\beta T \leq C\bigl (1+\lVert g\rVert _{C^4(\partial B)}\bigr )^ N. \end{equation} Proof. We follow the classical boundary estimates for the Dirichlet problem on a ball and keep track of the dependence on $L=1+\lVert g\rVert _{C^4}$. Barriers bound the first derivatives, and differentiation along rotations bounds the mixed normal–tangential second derivatives on the boundary. A lower bound for the tangential block of $T$ then bounds the double normal derivative through the equation, and lemma 14.17.4 reduces the interior bound to the boundary bound. Step 1: first derivatives. Fix a sufficiently large constant $K>0$, depending only on the fixed data. Extend $g$ to $G$ on $\overline B$ with $\lVert G\rVert _{C^4}\leq CL$. For $A=CL$ large enough, \[  \underline u=G+A(|z|^2-1), \qquad \underline T=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline u\geq K\beta , \qquad \underline T^ n\geq F\beta ^ n.  \] Proposition 14.17.2 gives $\underline u\leq u$. If $h$ solves $\Delta _\beta h=-C_\vartheta $ with $h=g$ on $\partial B$ and $C_\vartheta \geq \sup \operatorname {tr}_\beta \vartheta $, then $u\leq h$. Boundary differentiation of these barriers gives 14.23 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-first-boundary} |\partial _\nu u|+|\nabla _{\tan }u|\leq CL \quad \text{on }\partial B. \end{equation} Let $H=\operatorname {tr}_ T\beta $, $\mathcal L=\operatorname {tr}_ T\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, and $w=u-\underline u\geq 0$, the linearized operator and the barrier function used below. Taking $K$ fixed and sufficiently large gives 14.24 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-w-barrier} \mathcal Lw=n-\operatorname {tr}_ T\underline T\leq -(1+H). \end{equation} Let $E=\sum _ k(z_ k\partial _{z_ k}+\bar z_ k\partial _{\bar z_ k})$ be the real radial field. Write $\Theta $ for the coefficient matrix of $\vartheta $. Differentiating $\log \det T=\log F$ and commuting $E$ with complex second derivatives yields \[  \mathcal L(Eu)=E(\log F)+2n-\operatorname {tr}_ T(E\Theta +2\Theta ).  \] Hence $|\mathcal L(Eu)|\leq C(1+H)$. The same estimate holds for $Zu$ when $Z$ is an infinitesimal unitary rotation. Applying the minimum principle to $CL+C'w\pm Yu$, with $Y=E$ or $Z$, gives 14.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-first-fields} |Eu|+|Zu|\leq CL\quad \text{on }B. \end{equation} Step 2: mixed second derivatives on the boundary. For a rotation $Z$, the function $R_ Z=Z(u-G)$ vanishes on $\partial B$ and satisfies $|\mathcal LR_ Z|\leq CL(1+H)$. The barriers $CLw\pm R_ Z$ and ( 14.24 ) imply $|\partial _\nu R_ Z|\leq CL^2$ on the boundary. Rotations span the real tangent space of $\partial B$, so all real mixed normal–tangential second derivatives are $O(L^2)$. Pure tangential second derivatives are $O(L)$ by differentiating $u=g$ twice and using ( 14.23 ). Thus all complex Hessian entries except the complex normal–normal entry are $O(L^2)$. Step 3: the double normal derivative. It remains to bound the tangential block of $T$ from below. For $n\geq 2$, let \[  \lambda _0=\min \{ T_ p(\xi ,\bar\xi ):p\in \partial B, \  \xi \in T_ p^{1,0}(\partial B),\  |\xi |_\beta =1\} .  \] Choose a minimizing pair $(p,\xi )$ and extend $\xi $ to a smooth unit tangential field near $p$, with uniformly bounded derivatives. On the sphere, any smooth function vanishing there satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-G)(\xi ,\bar\xi )=\frac12E(u-G).  \] Define \[  a(z)=(\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G)_ z(\xi (z),\overline{\xi (z)})-\frac12EG(z), \qquad P=a+\frac12Eu-\lambda _0.  \] Then $P\geq 0$ on the nearby spherical boundary and $P(p)=0$. The boundary first-derivative bound also gives $\lambda _0\leq CL$ by the tangential identity above. Consequently \[  |P|\leq CL, \qquad |\mathcal LP|\leq CL(1+H).  \] On a fixed cap $D=B\cap B_ r(p)$ consider \[  \Psi =P+C_1Lw+C_2L|z-p|^2.  \] Choose $C_2$ so that $\Psi \geq 0$ on the interior spherical part of $\partial D$, and then $C_1$ so that $\mathcal L\Psi \leq 0$ by ( 14.24 ). The minimum principle yields $\Psi \geq 0$. At $p$ the normal derivative of $|z-p|^2$ vanishes, and therefore \[  \partial _\nu P+C_1L\partial _\nu w\leq 0.  \] Equations ( 14.23 )–( 14.25 ) now give $D^2u(\nu ,\nu )(p)\leq CL^2$, hence $\operatorname {tr}_\beta T(p)\leq CL^2$. Positivity and $\det _\beta T=F$ imply 14.26 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-tangential-lower} \lambda _0\geq cL^{-2(n-1)}. \end{equation} At any boundary point write \[  T=\begin{pmatrix} B_0

& b

\\  b^*

& d

\end{pmatrix}  \] in tangential–normal blocks, with $B_0$ an $(n-1)\times (n-1)$ Hermitian matrix, $b\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$ and $d\in \mathbb R$. We have $|b|\leq CL^2$ and $B_0\geq \lambda _0I$. The determinant equation and the Schur complement give \[  d=\frac{F}{\det B_0}+b^*B_0^{-1}b \leq (\sup F)\lambda _0^{-(n-1)}+CL^4\lambda _0^{-1},  \] which is polynomial in $L$. For $n=1$, the trace is $F$ and this argument is unnecessary. Step 4: the interior. Choose a fixed quadratic $q$ with $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \varepsilon \beta $. Apply lemma 14.17.4 with one fixed $A$. At an interior maximum of its auxiliary function the trace is uniformly bounded, while at a boundary maximum the preceding estimate applies. Since the remaining terms are uniformly bounded, ( 14.22 ) follows. $\square$

title: Exact approximation
text: Exact approximation We apply these estimates to smooth approximations of the boundary values of $\varphi $ on a ball in $\Omega $. Recall that $\theta $, $\omega $, $c$ and $f$ are the data of theorem 14.17.1 . Proposition 14.17.6 . Let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a coordinate ball, identified with $\{ |z|<r_0\} $, with closure in a larger coordinate chart, and put \[  F=\frac{cf\, \omega ^ n}{\beta ^ n}.  \] There are $a>0$, $b,C<\infty $, and $u_ j\in C^\infty (\overline B)$ such that 14.27 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-exact-approximants} \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0, \qquad (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n=F\beta ^ n, \end{equation} and 14.28 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-tame-rates} \lVert u_ j-\varphi \rVert _{L^\infty (B)}\leq Cj^{-a}, \qquad \sup _{\overline B}\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\leq Cj^ b. \end{equation} Proof. Since $\varphi $ is Hölder continuous near $\overline B$, mollification at scale $1/j$ gives smooth boundary approximations $g_ j$ with \[  \lVert g_ j-\varphi \rVert _{L^\infty (\partial B)}\leq Cj^{-a}, \qquad \lVert g_ j\rVert _{C^4(\partial B)}\leq Cj^4.  \] Choose a fixed quadratic $q$ with $\eta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q>0$ near $\overline B$. Extend $g_ j$ smoothly to $G_ j$. For a sufficiently large, polynomially bounded $A_ j$, the function \[  \underline w_ j=G_ j-q+A_ j(|z|^2-r_0^2)  \] has boundary value $g_ j-q$ and satisfies \[  \eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline w_ j =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ j+A_ j\beta >0, \qquad (\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline w_ j)^ n\geq F\beta ^ n.  \] Apply the smooth Dirichlet theorem recalled at the beginning of this subsection, with density $H=F\beta ^ n/\eta ^ n$ to obtain a solution $w_ j$ for the Hermitian background $\eta $; put $u_ j=w_ j+q$. Comparing $u_ j$ with $\varphi \pm \lVert g_ j-\varphi \rVert _\infty $ by proposition 14.17.2 proves the first bound in ( 14.28 ). The functions $u_ j$ are therefore uniformly bounded. Proposition 14.17.5 and the polynomial $C^4$ boundary norm give the second bound. $\square$

title: 14.17.4 Localization near the nonregular set
text: 14.17.4 Localization near the nonregular set In the auxiliary function of lemma 14.17.4 , the term $-A(u_ j-q)$ penalizes points where $u_ j-q$ is large. A quadratic gap of $u-q$ along the nonregular set therefore suppresses the contribution of the boundary of a neighborhood of that set. Taking $A$ proportional to $\log j$ makes this suppression beat the polynomial growth of the boundary trace, and near the point of minimal $u-q$ the trace then grows more slowly than every positive power of $j$. Interpolation with the polynomial approximation rate gives uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds. Distances and norms below are Euclidean. By a smooth exact solution for $(\vartheta ,F)$ we mean a smooth function $u_ j$ with $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0$ and $(\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n=F\beta ^ n$. Proposition 14.17.7 . For $R>0$, let $B=B_ R(0)$, let $\vartheta $ and $F>0$ be smooth near $\overline B$, and let $u\in C(\overline B)$. Suppose $q$ is smooth and $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \varepsilon \beta $ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Put $v=u-q$ and $m=v(0)$, and fix $\kappa >0$. Let $\mathcal S\subset \overline B$ be closed, contain $0$, and satisfy 14.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-quadratic-separation} v(0)=m, \qquad v(z)\geq m+\kappa |z|^2\quad (z\in \mathcal S). \end{equation} Assume that smooth exact solutions $u_ j$, $j\geq 2$, satisfy, for fixed constants $a>0$, $b\geq 0$ and $C>0$, 14.30 \begin{align}  \lVert u_ j-u\rVert _\infty & \leq Cj^{-a}, \label{eq:interior-localization-a}\\  \sup _{\overline B}\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)& \leq Cj^ b, \label{eq:interior-localization-b}\\  \sup _ j\sup _ K\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)& <\infty \quad \text{for every }K\Subset \overline B\setminus \mathcal S. \label{eq:interior-localization-c} \end{align} Then for every $\gamma >0$ there are a neighborhood $U_\gamma $ of $0$ and $C_\gamma $ such that 14.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-subpower-trace} \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\leq C_\gamma j^\gamma \quad \text{on }U_\gamma . \end{equation} For every $0<\alpha <1$, there is also a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ on which $u_ j\to u$ in $C^{1,\alpha }$. In particular the approximants are uniformly bounded in that norm and $u\in C^{1,\alpha }(U)$. Proof. Step 1: the trace bound ( 14.33 ). Write $e_ j=Cj^{-a}$, fix $d=\kappa R^2/2$, and choose $D>(b+1)/d$. Choose $\eta >0$ so that $2D\eta <\gamma /2$. For small $\delta >0$, the neighborhood \[  W_\delta =\{ z\in B:\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathcal S)<\delta \}   \] contains $0$, has $v\geq m-\eta $ on its closure, and satisfies $v\geq m+d$ on $\partial B\cap \overline W_\delta $ with the fixed $d$ above. These properties follow from ( 14.29 ), continuity, and compactness. The remaining part of the boundary of $W_\delta $ is a compact subset of $\overline B\setminus \mathcal S$, where ( 14.32 ) applies. Set $A_ j=D\log j$. Apply the maximum principle on $\overline W_\delta $ to \[  Q_ j=\log \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)-A_ j(u_ j-q)+\mathrm{e}^{-(u_ j-q)}.  \] At an interior maximum, lemma 14.17.4 gives $\log \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\leq C+\frac12\log A_ j$. On the part of $\partial W_\delta $ inside $B$, which stays away from $\mathcal S$, the trace has a bound independent of $j$. On the outer part $\partial B\cap \overline W_\delta $, ( 14.31 ) and the gap $d$ give \[  Q_ j\leq C+b\log j-A_ j(m+d-e_ j),  \] and the choice $Dd>b+1$ makes this smaller than the bound below for large $j$. Hence throughout $W_\delta $, \[  Q_ j\leq C_\delta +\tfrac 12\log A_ j-A_ j(m-\eta -e_ j).  \] On a small ball about $0$ where $v\leq m+\eta $, this implies \[  \log \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j) \leq C_\delta +\tfrac 12\log A_ j+A_ j(2\eta +2e_ j).  \] By the choice of $\eta $, the logarithmic factor and $A_ je_ j$ are absorbed into the remaining power. This proves ( 14.33 ). Step 2: $C^{1,\alpha }$ convergence. On a smaller ball, the real Laplacian of $u_ j$ is bounded by $Cj^\gamma $. Interior Poisson estimates give a $W^{2,q_0}$ bound for every finite $q_0$, and Sobolev embedding with $q_0$ large then gives, for every $\sigma <1$, \[  \lVert u_ j\rVert _{W^{2,q_0}}+\lVert u_ j\rVert _{C^{1,\sigma }} \leq Cj^\gamma .  \] For $d_ k=u_{2^{k+1}}-u_{2^ k}$, \[  \lVert d_ k\rVert _\infty \leq C2^{-ka}, \qquad \lVert d_ k\rVert _{C^{1,\sigma }}\leq C2^{k\gamma }.  \] If $\alpha <\sigma $ and $t=(1+\alpha )/(1+\sigma )$, Hölder interpolation gives \[  \lVert d_ k\rVert _{C^{1,\alpha }} \leq C2^{k[-a(1-t)+\gamma t]}.  \] Since $\gamma $ may be arbitrarily small, the exponent can be made negative. The dyadic series converges in $C^{1,\alpha }$ to its uniform limit $u$. If $2^ k\leq j<2^{k+1}$, interpolation applied to $u_ j-u_{2^ k}$ gives the same decaying bound. Hence the full sequence converges to $u$ in $C^{1,\alpha }$ on a smaller ball. $\square$ Proposition 14.17.8 . Suppose $u_ j$ solve the same smooth equation as in proposition 14.17.7 , satisfy ( 14.30 )–( 14.31 ), and $u$ is smooth with $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ on an open set $O\subset B$. Then, for every $K\Subset O$, 14.34 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-regular-stability} \sup _ j\sup _ K\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)<\infty . \end{equation} Proof. Where $u$ is smooth and strictly $\vartheta $-plurisubharmonic, it provides its own quadratic separation, so the argument of proposition 14.17.7 applies around every point of $O$. A first application gives trace growth of order $\sqrt{\log j}$; the resulting gradient convergence then allows the variant of lemma 14.17.4 with a gradient bound, which removes this growth. For $p$ in a fixed compact subset of $O$, take a uniformly sized ball $B_ r(p)\Subset O$ and set \[  q_ p(z)=u(z)-\kappa |z-p|^2  \] with $\kappa >0$ small, so $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ p\geq \varepsilon \beta $. If $e_ j=Cj^{-a}$ and $v_{j,p}=u_ j-q_ p$, then \[  v_{j,p}\geq -e_ j, \quad v_{j,p}(p)\leq e_ j, \quad v_{j,p}\geq \kappa r^2-e_ j\text{ on }\partial B_ r(p).  \] With $A_ j=D\log j$ and $D\kappa r^2>b+1$, the same maximum argument as above gives 14.35 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-sqrtlog-trace} \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)(p)\leq C\sqrt{\log j}. \end{equation} The constants are uniform on compact subsets of $O$. Put $T_ j=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ and $w_ j=u_ j-u$. On slightly larger compact sets, ( 14.35 ) bounds $|\Delta w_ j|$ by $C\sqrt{\log j}$. Poisson estimates and Sobolev embedding give \[  \lVert w_ j\rVert _{C^{1,\sigma }}\leq C_\sigma \sqrt{\log j}, \qquad \sigma <1.  \] Interpolating with $\lVert w_ j\rVert _\infty \leq Cj^{-a}$ shows $\nabla w_ j\to 0$ uniformly on smaller compact sets. The gradients of $v_{j,p}$ are therefore uniformly bounded. Repeat the maximum argument with $\log \operatorname {tr}_\beta T_ j-A_ jv_{j,p}$, now using the variant of lemma 14.17.4 with a gradient bound. Its interior trace bound is now independent of $A_ j$, while the boundary term is suppressed as before. Evaluation at $p$ gives \[  \operatorname {tr}_\beta T_ j(p)\leq C\exp (2A_ je_ j)\leq C,  \] proving ( 14.34 ). $\square$

text: Proposition 14.17.7 . For $R>0$, let $B=B_ R(0)$, let $\vartheta $ and $F>0$ be smooth near $\overline B$, and let $u\in C(\overline B)$. Suppose $q$ is smooth and $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \varepsilon \beta $ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Put $v=u-q$ and $m=v(0)$, and fix $\kappa >0$. Write $e_ j=Cj^{-a}$, fix $d=\kappa R^2/2$, and choose $D>(b+1)/d$. Choose $\eta >0$ so that $2D\eta <\gamma /2$. For small $\delta >0$, the neighborhood \[  W_\delta =\{ z\in B:\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathcal S)<\delta \}   \] contains $0$, has $v\geq m-\eta $ on its closure, and satisfies $v\geq m+d$ on $\partial B\cap \overline W_\delta $ with the fixed $d$ above. These properties follow from ( 14.29 ), continuity, and compactness. The remaining part of the boundary of $W_\delta $ is a compact subset of $\overline B\setminus \mathcal S$, where ( 14.32 ) applies. Set $A_ j=D\log j$. On the part of $\partial W_\delta $ inside $B$, which stays away from $\mathcal S$, the trace has a bound independent of $j$. Hence throughout $W_\delta $, \[  Q_ j\leq C_\delta +\tfrac 12\log A_ j-A_ j(m-\eta -e_ j).  \] On a small ball about $0$ where $v\leq m+\eta $, this implies \[  \log \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j) \leq C_\delta +\tfrac 12\log A_ j+A_ j(2\eta +2e_ j).  \] By the choice of $\eta $, the logarithmic factor and $A_ je_ j$ are absorbed into the remaining power. This proves ( 14.33 ). Step 2: $C^{1,\alpha }$ convergence. On a smaller ball, the real Laplacian of $u_ j$ is bounded by $Cj^\gamma $. Interior Poisson estimates give a $W^{2,q_0}$ bound for every finite $q_0$, and Sobolev embedding with $q_0$ large then gives, for every $\sigma <1$, \[  \lVert u_ j\rVert _{W^{2,q_0}}+\lVert u_ j\rVert _{C^{1,\sigma }} \leq Cj^\gamma .  \] For $d_ k=u_{2^{k+1}}-u_{2^ k}$, \[  \lVert d_ k\rVert _\infty \leq C2^{-ka}, \qquad \lVert d_ k\rVert _{C^{1,\sigma }}\leq C2^{k\gamma }.  \] If $\alpha <\sigma $ and $t=(1+\alpha )/(1+\sigma )$, Hölder interpolation gives \[  \lVert d_ k\rVert _{C^{1,\alpha }} \leq C2^{k[-a(1-t)+\gamma t]}.  \] Since $\gamma $ may be arbitrarily small, the exponent can be made negative. The dyadic series converges in $C^{1,\alpha }$ to its uniform limit $u$. If $2^ k\leq j<2^{k+1}$, interpolation applied to $u_ j-u_{2^ k}$ gives the same decaying bound. Hence the full sequence converges to $u$ in $C^{1,\alpha }$ on a smaller ball. $\square$

title: 14.17.5 Derivative estimates and bounded traces
text:
14.17.5 Derivative estimates and bounded traces Uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds control averages of the trace $\operatorname {tr}_ eta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)=\operatorname {tr}_ eta \vartheta +\Delta _ eta u_ j$ over small balls. To pass from averages to pointwise values we need a bound for the gradient of the trace, that is, a third-order estimate, whose dependence on the ellipticity constants is polynomial. We prove it by Calabi's maximum-principle argument, computed with the Chern connection of the solution so that the torsion of the nonclosed background appears explicitly. The resulting averaging inequality is nonlinear in the trace, and it closes under iteration when $\alpha $ is sufficiently close to one. In this subsection $B$ is the unit ball and $B_ r(p)$ is the Euclidean ball of radius $r$ centered at $p$. For a Hermitian metric $g$, $\partial g$ denotes the ordinary coordinate derivatives of its coefficient matrix, while tensor derivatives in the proofs are taken with respect to the Chern connection of $g$. Proposition 14.17.9 . Fix smooth $\vartheta $ and smooth $F>0$ near the closed unit ball. There are $C,N<\infty $, depending only on finitely many derivatives of the fixed data, such that any smooth solution \[  g=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u, \qquad g^ n=F eta ^ n, \qquad M^{-1} eta \leq g\leq M eta , \qquad M\geq 1,  \] satisfies 14.36  egin{equation} \label{eq:interior-calabi-polynomial} \sup _{B_{1/2}}|\partial g|_ eta \leq CM^ N. \end{equation} If only $\sup _ B\operatorname {tr}_ eta g\leq L$ is given, the same bound holds with a fixed power of $1+L$. On a ball of radius $r\leq 1$, 14.37  egin{equation} \label{eq:interior-gradient-trace-scaled} \sup _{B_{r/2}}|
abla \operatorname {tr}_ eta g|_ eta \leq Cr^{-1}(1+L)^ N. \end{equation} Proof. Since $|\partial g|_ eta ^2\leq M^3\mathcal R$, this proves ( 14.36 ). If $s\leq L$, the determinant lower bound gives $\lambda _{\min }(g)\geq (\inf F)L^{1-n}$, so $M$ is a fixed power of $1+L$. For a ball $B_ r(p)$, set $u_ r(z)=r^{-2}u(p+rz)$ and use the coefficient matrices $\vartheta _ r(z)=\vartheta (p+rz)$, $g_ r(z)=g(p+rz)$ and $F_ r(z)=F(p+rz)$. Then $g_ r=\vartheta _ r+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ r$ in the unit coordinates and $\det g_ r=F_ r$. For $r\leq 1$ the derivatives of the fixed data remain uniformly bounded. The unit-ball estimate for the ordinary coefficient derivatives $\partial g_ r$ and their conjugates gives the factor $r^{-1}$ in ( 14.37 ). $\square$ Proposition 14.17.10 . There is $\alpha _*<1$, depending only on $n$ and the exponent $N$ in proposition 14.17.9 , with the following property. Let $B_0$ be a Euclidean ball, fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\vartheta $ and a smooth function $F>0$ near $\overline{B_0}$, and let $u_ j$ be smooth exact solutions of $(\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n=F eta ^ n$ with $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0$. If \[  \sup _ j\lVert u_ jVert _{C^{1,\alpha }(B_0)}<\infty \qquad 	ext{for some }\alpha _*<\alpha <1,  \] then $\operatorname {tr}_ eta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)$ is uniformly bounded on every smaller ball. Proof. Fix a center for concentric balls $B_ r\Subset B_0$, put $s_ j=\operatorname {tr}_ eta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)$, and set \[  M_ j(r)=1+\sup _{B_ r}s_ j.  \] For concentric balls $B_ r\Subset B_ R\Subset B_0$, $d=R-r\leq 1$, proposition 14.17.9 gives 14.47  egin{equation} \label{eq:interior-trace-gradient-M} |
abla s_ j|\leq Cd^{-1}M_ j(R)^ N \quad 	ext{on }B_{r+d/2}. \end{equation} Fix $p\in B_ r$ and let $\chi _ h$ be a nonnegative mollifier of radius $h\leq d/4$. Since \[  s_ j=\operatorname {tr}_ eta \vartheta +\Delta _ eta u_ j,  \] integration by parts, after subtracting the constant vector $
abla u_ j(p)$, and the uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound give \[  (s_ j*\chi _ h)(p)\leq C(1+h^{\alpha -1}).  \] Equation ( 14.47 ) gives \[  |s_ j(p)-(s_ j*\chi _ h)(p)| \leq Cd^{-1}M_ j(R)^ Nh.  \] Choose \[  h= rac d4M_ j(R)^{-N/(2-\alpha )}.  \] Taking the supremum over $p\in B_ r$ and absorbing fixed powers of $d^{-1}$, we obtain 14.48  egin{equation} \label{eq:interior-nonlinear-iteration} M_ j(r)\leq Cd^{-1}M_ j(R)^ q, \qquad q= rac{N(1-\alpha )}{2-\alpha }. \end{equation} Choose $\alpha _*$ so close to one that $q<1$ for $\alpha >\alpha _*$. Choose $0<r_0<R_0$ with $B_{R_0}\Subset B_0$. Let $r_ k\uparrow R_0$ with $r_{k+1}-r_ k=(R_0-r_0)2^{-k-1}$. Iterating ( 14.48 ) gives \[  M_ j(r_0) \leq \prod _{k=0}^{m-1}\left[C(r_{k+1}-r_ k)^{-1}ight]^{q^ k} M_ j(r_ m)^{q^ m}.  \] The infinite product converges because $\sum q^ k(1+k)<\infty $. For each fixed $j$, the final factor tends to one as $m	o \infty $. The resulting bound is independent of $j$. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.17.10
text: Proposition 14.17.10 . There is $\alpha _*<1$, depending only on $n$ and the exponent $N$ in proposition 14.17.9 , with the following property. Let $B_0$ be a Euclidean ball, fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\vartheta $ and a smooth function $F>0$ near $\overline{B_0}$, and let $u_ j$ be smooth exact solutions of $(\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n=F\beta ^ n$ with $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0$. If \[  \sup _ j\lVert u_ j\rVert _{C^{1,\alpha }(B_0)}<\infty \qquad \text{for some }\alpha _*<\alpha <1,  \] then $\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)$ is uniformly bounded on every smaller ball. Proof. Fix a center for concentric balls $B_ r\Subset B_0$, put $s_ j=\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)$, and set \[  M_ j(r)=1+\sup _{B_ r}s_ j.  \] For concentric balls $B_ r\Subset B_ R\Subset B_0$, $d=R-r\leq 1$, proposition 14.17.9 gives 14.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-trace-gradient-M} |\nabla s_ j|\leq Cd^{-1}M_ j(R)^ N \quad \text{on }B_{r+d/2}. \end{equation} Fix $p\in B_ r$ and let $\chi _ h$ be a nonnegative mollifier of radius $h\leq d/4$. Since \[  s_ j=\operatorname {tr}_\beta \vartheta +\Delta _\beta u_ j,  \] integration by parts, after subtracting the constant vector $\nabla u_ j(p)$, and the uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound give \[  (s_ j*\chi _ h)(p)\leq C(1+h^{\alpha -1}).  \] Equation ( 14.47 ) gives \[  |s_ j(p)-(s_ j*\chi _ h)(p)| \leq Cd^{-1}M_ j(R)^ Nh.  \] Choose \[  h=\frac d4M_ j(R)^{-N/(2-\alpha )}.  \] Taking the supremum over $p\in B_ r$ and absorbing fixed powers of $d^{-1}$, we obtain 14.48 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-nonlinear-iteration} M_ j(r)\leq Cd^{-1}M_ j(R)^ q, \qquad q=\frac{N(1-\alpha )}{2-\alpha }. \end{equation} Choose $\alpha _*$ so close to one that $q<1$ for $\alpha >\alpha _*$. Choose $0<r_0<R_0$ with $B_{R_0}\Subset B_0$. Let $r_ k\uparrow R_0$ with $r_{k+1}-r_ k=(R_0-r_0)2^{-k-1}$. Iterating ( 14.48 ) gives \[  M_ j(r_0) \leq \prod _{k=0}^{m-1}\left[C(r_{k+1}-r_ k)^{-1}\right]^{q^ k} M_ j(r_ m)^{q^ m}.  \] The infinite product converges because $\sum q^ k(1+k)<\infty $. For each fixed $j$, the final factor tends to one as $m\to \infty $. The resulting bound is independent of $j$. $\square$
14.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-trace-gradient-M} |\nabla s_ j|\leq Cd^{-1}M_ j(R)^ N \quad \text{on }B_{r+d/2}. \end{equation}
14.48 \begin{equation} \label{eq:interior-nonlinear-iteration} M_ j(r)\leq Cd^{-1}M_ j(R)^ q, \qquad q=\frac{N(1-\alpha )}{2-\alpha }. \end{equation}

title: 14.17.6 Proof of the main theorem
text: 14.17.6 Proof of the main theorem We now assemble the four steps outlined after theorem 14.17.1 . The barrier enters only once, but globally: it locates a point of the nonsmooth set at which the quadratic separation required in proposition 14.17.7 holds. of theorem 14.17.1 . If $n=1$, the equation is the linear identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =cf\, \omega -\theta \quad \text{on }\Omega .  \] Its right-hand side is smooth, so interior elliptic regularity gives $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$, and the original equation gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =cf\, \omega >0$. We henceforth assume $n\geq 2$. Let \[  \mathcal S=\{ p\in \Omega :\varphi \text{ is not smooth on any neighborhood of }p\} .  \] This is closed in $\Omega $. Suppose $\mathcal S\neq \varnothing $. By lemma 1.19.7 , the restriction of $\varphi -\rho $ to $\mathcal S$ attains its minimum $m$ at some $p\in \mathcal S$. Choose nested coordinate balls \[  B\Subset B_0\Subset \Omega  \] centered at $p$. On $B_0$, proposition 14.17.6 gives smooth exact Dirichlet solutions $u_ j$ converging uniformly to $\varphi $ at a polynomial rate and having polynomial global trace growth. On the open set $\Omega \setminus \mathcal S$ the function $\varphi $ is smooth, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is semipositive with positive determinant, hence positive definite. Proposition 14.17.8 therefore gives a uniform trace bound for the $u_ j$ on every compact subset of $B_0\setminus \mathcal S$. In coordinates centered at $p$, take $\kappa >0$ small and set \[  q(z)=\rho (z)-\kappa |z|^2.  \] After shrinking $B$, the lower bound $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \omega $ gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q>0$ on $\overline B$. If $v=\varphi -q$, then the minimizing property of $p$ gives \[  v(p)=m, \qquad v(z)=(\varphi -\rho )(z)+\kappa |z|^2 \geq m+\kappa |z|^2 \quad (z\in \mathcal S\cap \overline B).  \] Thus proposition 14.17.7 applies on $B$ with the closed set $\mathcal S\cap \overline B$: the approximation rate and global polynomial trace bound come from proposition 14.17.6 , and the bound away from $\mathcal S$ comes from proposition 14.17.8 . Its second assertion gives, for every $0<\alpha <1$, a neighborhood of $p$ on which the approximants have a uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound. Choose $\alpha >\alpha _*$ as in proposition 14.17.10 , and apply that proposition on a ball centered at $p$ inside this neighborhood. It yields \[  \sup _ j\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)<\infty  \] on a still smaller neighborhood of $p$. Since $u_ j\to \varphi $ uniformly, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ as currents. The trace bound passes to the limit, so $\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ has a bounded density near $p$. Proposition 14.17.3 now implies that $\varphi $ is smooth near $p$, contradicting $p\in \mathcal S$. Hence $\mathcal S=\varnothing $ and $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$. The form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is smooth and semipositive there, while \[  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n>0.  \] Its nonnegative eigenvalues have positive product, so every eigenvalue is positive. Therefore $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$ on $\Omega $. $\square$ Corollary 14.17.11 . Let $0\leq f\in L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$, $p>1$, be smooth and strictly positive on $\Omega $. Every minimal-singularity solution of $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n$, $c>0$, is smooth and strictly $\theta $-plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. Proof. The analytic complement of $\Omega $ has zero mass for both measures, so it suffices to know the equation in the bounded-potential sense on $\Omega $. Apply theorem 14.16.1 with density $cf$ to obtain local Hölder continuity. All hypotheses of theorem 14.17.1 are now satisfied. $\square$ By theorem 14.15.4 , such a solution exists, with a uniquely determined $c>0$. For a smooth closed big representative on a compact Kähler manifold, theorem 28.10.1 applies this conclusion to the classical full-mass solution and identifies the regular open set with the ample locus.

title: Corollary 14.17.11
text: Corollary 14.17.11 . Let $0\leq f\in L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$, $p>1$, be smooth and strictly positive on $\Omega $. Every minimal-singularity solution of $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n$, $c>0$, is smooth and strictly $\theta $-plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. Proof. The analytic complement of $\Omega $ has zero mass for both measures, so it suffices to know the equation in the bounded-potential sense on $\Omega $. Apply theorem 14.16.1 with density $cf$ to obtain local Hölder continuity. All hypotheses of theorem 14.17.1 are now satisfied. $\square$

title: 14.18 Degenerating semipositive backgrounds
text: 14.18 Degenerating semipositive backgrounds Adding a small multiple of a Hermitian form makes a semipositive background strictly positive, and the smooth theory then solves the normalized equation with a smooth positive density. We study these smooth solutions as the added multiple tends to zero. Bounded subsolutions give uniform bounds for the potentials and the normalizing constants, and a strict analytic barrier gives uniform bounds for the trace on compact sets away from its poles. Smooth local convergence then identifies the limiting equation, without any global continuity property of the Monge–Ampère operator. The main example is a small resolution of a threefold with nodes ( 14.18.1 ). There the background is the pullback of a positive form from the singular threefold, and it degenerates exactly along the exceptional curves. When this background is closed, the limit is unique and the whole family converges smoothly away from the exceptional curves. Convergence of the associated metric spaces then reduces to controlling the diameters of neighborhoods of these curves, in the limiting metric and in the approximating metrics ( 14.18.3 ). Throughout this section $n\geq 2$. The background $\theta $, the barrier $\rho $ and its pole set $Z$ are new data, independent of those fixed in section 14.12 . Let $\theta \geq 0$ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, and fix a Hermitian form $\eta $ and a smooth positive probability volume form $\mu $ on $X$. Suppose that there are $\delta >0$ and $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities such that 14.49 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degeneration-strict-barrier} \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \eta , \qquad \sup _ X\rho =0. \end{equation} Write $Z=\{ \rho =-\infty \} $ and assume that $\rho $ is smooth on $X\setminus Z$. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, the form $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ is Hermitian, and theorem 9.1.1 gives $u_\varepsilon \in C^\infty (X)$ and $c_\varepsilon >0$ with 14.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:semipositive-smooth-approximation} \omega _\varepsilon :=\theta +\varepsilon \eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon >0, \qquad \omega _\varepsilon ^ n=c_\varepsilon \mu , \qquad \sup _ Xu_\varepsilon =0. \end{equation} Lemma 14.18.1 . There are constants $b,B,C>0$, independent of $\varepsilon $, such that \[  b\leq c_\varepsilon \leq B, \qquad -C\leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0.  \] Proof. Write $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f$ is smooth and positive. The strict barrier makes $\theta $ big. By lemma 14.2.1 , there is a bounded $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $-1\leq s\leq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (s)\geq b\mu $ for some fixed $b>0$. If $c_\varepsilon <b$, positivity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(u_\varepsilon ) \leq (c_\varepsilon /b)\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(s+A)  \] for every constant $A$. Strict bounded domination would imply $u_\varepsilon \geq s+A$ for every $A$, which is absurd. Hence $c_\varepsilon \geq b$. For an upper bound, choose a fixed Gauduchon form $\gamma $. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and Stokes give \[  c_\varepsilon ^{1/n} \int _ X\left(\frac{\mu }{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ X\omega _\varepsilon \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X(\theta +\varepsilon \eta )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \leq \int _ X(\theta +\eta )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] The first integral is fixed and positive, giving $c_\varepsilon \leq B$. For the lower bound on $u_\varepsilon $, note that all $u_\varepsilon $ are normalized $(\theta +\eta )$-plurisubharmonic functions. Uniform exponential integrability, lemma 1.5.1 , gives $a>0$ such that $g_\varepsilon =\mathrm{e}^{-a u_\varepsilon }f$ has a common $L^2$ bound. Also $g_\varepsilon \geq f$. By theorem 14.2.2 , the solutions \[  w_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ), \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_\varepsilon ) =\mathrm{e}^{a w_\varepsilon }g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V  \] are uniformly bounded. Put $B_0=\max \{ 1,B\} $ and $z_\varepsilon =w_\varepsilon -a^{-1}\log B_0$. Then \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(z_\varepsilon ) \geq \mathrm{e}^{a z_\varepsilon }c_\varepsilon g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(u_\varepsilon ) =\mathrm{e}^{a u_\varepsilon }c_\varepsilon g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The comparison principle for the exponential equation in the background $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ gives $z_\varepsilon \leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0$, and $z_\varepsilon $ is bounded below uniformly in $\varepsilon $. $\square$ Since $\theta $ may degenerate along $Z$, we do not estimate the trace by local arguments. Instead we apply the maximum principle on all of $X\setminus Z$ to the logarithm of the trace minus a multiple of $u_\varepsilon -\rho $. This function tends to $-\infty $ at $Z$, so its maximum is attained off $Z$, where $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \eta $ provides positivity. An additional logarithmic term in the weight absorbs the torsion term without a gradient bound for $\rho $. Lemma 14.18.2 . For every compact $K\Subset X\setminus Z$, there is $C_ K>1$, independent of $\varepsilon $, such that \[  C_ K^{-1}\eta \leq \omega _\varepsilon \leq C_ K\eta \quad \hbox{on }K.  \] Proof. For the differentiated calculation write $U=u_\varepsilon /(2\pi )$ and $P=\rho /(2\pi )$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial U$. Put \[  S=\operatorname {tr}_\eta \omega _\varepsilon , \quad R=\operatorname {tr}_{\omega _\varepsilon }\eta , \quad D=\omega _\varepsilon ^ n/\eta ^ n.  \] The previous lemma and the smooth positive density give $0<d_1\leq D\leq d_2$. Choose a fixed $C_0$ so that $v=U-P+C_0>1$, and set \[  H=\log S-\gamma (v),\qquad \gamma (v)=Av+\log v,  \] where $A$ will be fixed below. For each $\varepsilon $, $S$ is smooth on $X$ and $v$ tends to infinity at $Z$. Thus $H\to -\infty $ there, and $H$ attains its maximum on $X\setminus Z$. We bound this maximum independently of $\varepsilon $. In local holomorphic coordinates, $h$ and $g$ denote the coefficient matrices of $\eta $ and $\omega _\varepsilon $ with respect to $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$, and commas denote coordinate derivatives, as in $h_{i\bar j,k}=\partial _ kh_{i\bar j}$ and $h_{i\bar j,\bar k}=\partial _{\bar k}h_{i\bar j}$. At a maximum point choose holomorphic coordinates in which \[  h_{i\bar j}=\delta _{ij},\qquad h_{i\bar i,k}=0, \qquad g_{i\bar j}=\lambda _ i\delta _{ij}.  \] A linear change first normalizes $h$ and diagonalizes $g$. In these coordinates, the quadratic change $z_ i=w_ i+\frac12\sum _{j,k}a^ i_{jk}w_ jw_ k$, with symmetric coefficients chosen so that $a^ i_{ik}=-h_{i\bar i,k}$, then kills $h_{i\bar i,k}$. Its coefficients are uniformly bounded on a fixed finite cover. Write \[  \Delta _ g=\sum _ i\lambda _ i^{-1}\partial _ i\partial _{\bar i}, \quad T_{ij\bar k}=g_{j\bar k,i}-g_{i\bar k,j}, \quad E_ i=\sum _ jT_{ij\bar j}.  \] The lowered torsion coefficients $T_{ij\bar k}$ and their first derivatives are uniformly bounded: the potential Hessian cancels, leaving only derivatives of $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $. Let $\mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ be the density of $\mu $ with respect to the coordinate volume form. Differentiating $S=h^{k\bar\ell }g_{k\bar\ell }$ and the equation $\log \det g=\log c_\varepsilon +\log \mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ gives 14.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degeneration-trace-calculus} \Delta _ g S\geq Q-CRS-CR, \qquad Q=\sum _{i,j}\frac{|g_{i\bar j,j}|^2}{\lambda _ i\lambda _ j}. \end{equation} The second derivatives of $g$ contribute $\sum _{i,j,k}|g_{i\bar j,k}|^2/(\lambda _ i\lambda _ j)$, up to $-CR-C$, by commuting the potential derivatives. The first derivatives of $h$ contribute $-2\operatorname {Re}\sum _{i,j,k}\lambda _ i^{-1}h_{j\bar k,\bar i}g_{k\bar j,i}$. Its terms with $j=k$ vanish. Replace $g_{k\bar j,i}$ by $g_{i\bar j,k}+T_{ik\bar j}$ and apply weighted Cauchy–Schwarz. This consumes exactly the terms of the preceding square with $j\ne k$ and costs at most $CRS+CR$. The second derivatives of $h^{-1}$ cost $CRS$. Finally the fixed density term $-C$ is absorbed using $SR\geq n^2$. Since $\partial _ iS=\sum _ jg_{i\bar j,j}+E_ i$ at the maximum point, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz also gives \[  |\partial S|_ g^2 \leq SQ+2\operatorname {Re}\langle E,\partial S\rangle _ g.  \] Indeed expand around $\partial S-E$ and discard the resulting term $-|E|_ g^2$. Combining with ( 14.51 ) yields \[  \Delta _ g\log S\geq -CR-CR/S -\frac2S\operatorname {Re}\langle E,\partial \log S\rangle _ g.  \] At the maximum, $\partial \log S=\gamma '\partial v$. Moreover ( 14.49 ) gives $\Delta _ gv\leq n-\delta R$, and $|E|_ g^2\leq CR$. Young's inequality with the positive coefficient $-\gamma ''=v^{-2}$ therefore gives \[  0\geq \Delta _ g H \geq (\delta \gamma '-C)R-n\gamma '-CR/S -\frac{CR}{S^2}\frac{\gamma '^2}{-\gamma ''}.  \] Since $\gamma '=A+v^{-1}$, choose $A$ with $\delta A-C\geq 1$. The resulting inequality is 14.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degeneration-maximum-trace} 0\geq R-C\left(1+\frac RS+\frac{R(1+v^2)}{S^2}\right). \end{equation} All constants are independent of $\varepsilon $. If the maxima of $H$ were unbounded, then at a sequence of maximizing points \[  \log (S/v)=H+Av\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Thus $S/v\to \infty $ and $S\to \infty $. Inequality ( 14.52 ) would imply $R\leq 2C$ along this sequence. But \[  S=D\sum _ i\prod _{j\ne i}\lambda _ j^{-1} \leq nDR^{n-1}\leq nd_2(2C)^{n-1},  \] a contradiction. Hence $H$ is uniformly bounded. On $K$, both $U$ and $P$ are bounded, so $S\leq C_ K$. The determinant lower bound then gives $\lambda _ i\geq d_1/C_ K^{n-1}$, completing the proof. $\square$ Theorem 14.18.3 . In the preceding setting, $c_\varepsilon $ decreases to a positive number $c_0$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. This number is independent of the perturbing Hermitian form $\eta $. For every sequence $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, a subsequence satisfies \[  u_{\varepsilon _ j}\longrightarrow u_0 \quad \hbox{in }L^1(X)\cap C^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(X\setminus Z),  \] where $u_0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cap L^\infty (X)$, $\sup _ Xu_0=0$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)=c_0\mu .  \] If $\theta $ is closed, then $c_0=\int _ X\theta ^ n$. Proof. Monotonicity of the constants. Let $\alpha \leq \beta $ be Hermitian forms, and let $(u_\alpha ,c_\alpha )$ and $(u_\beta ,c_\beta )$ be the normalized smooth solutions of $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha )^ n=c_\alpha \mu $ and $(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\beta )^ n=c_\beta \mu $. At a maximum point of $u_\alpha -u_\beta $, \[  \alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \leq \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\beta ,  \] so $c_\alpha \leq c_\beta $. Hence $c_\varepsilon $ decreases as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, and lemma 14.18.1 gives $c_0\geq b>0$. Write $c_\eta (\varepsilon )$ for the constant $c_\varepsilon $ defined with the perturbation $\eta $. For two perturbations with $M^{-1}\eta _1\leq \eta _2\leq M\eta _1$, the same comparison gives \[  c_{\eta _1}(\varepsilon /M) \leq c_{\eta _2}(\varepsilon ) \leq c_{\eta _1}(M\varepsilon ).  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $c_0$ does not depend on $\eta $. Local estimates. The trace bound of lemma 14.18.2 gives uniform ellipticity on compact subsets of $X\setminus Z$. The smooth coefficients of $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ and all derivatives of $\log \mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ have common bounds there. Interior complex Evans–Krylov and Schauder estimates, as in the ellipticity argument of proposition 14.17.3 , give uniform $C^ k$ bounds on smaller compact subsets for every $k$. Convergence and the limiting equation. Normalized compactness in the fixed background $\theta +\eta $, followed by a diagonal extraction over an exhaustion of $X\setminus Z$, gives the stated convergence. The uniform bound $-C\leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ passes to the canonical limit, and normalized compactness preserves the supremum zero. Current convergence gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0\geq 0$, and smooth convergence identifies the equation on $X\setminus Z$. The bounded non-pluripolar measure $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)$ and the smooth measure $\mu $ both vanish on the analytic set $Z$. This proves the equation on all of $X$. For closed $\theta $, bounded closed-background Stokes gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)=\int _ X\theta ^ n$, proving the last assertion. $\square$ Since $\theta \geq 0$ is nef, theorem 26.10.1 identifies $c_0$ with the Gauduchon variational volume $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )$. The proof uses no bound on Monge–Ampère masses: all estimates concern the solutions for the fixed smooth density $\mu $. If the bounded normalized limiting equation has a unique solution, all cluster limits coincide, and the whole family converges in $L^1(X)\cap C^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(X\setminus Z)$.
