title: Lemma 14.18.1
text: Lemma 14.18.1 . There are constants $b,B,C>0$, independent of $\varepsilon $, such that \[  b\leq c_\varepsilon \leq B, \qquad -C\leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0.  \] Proof. Write $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f$ is smooth and positive. The strict barrier makes $\theta $ big. By lemma 14.2.1 , there is a bounded $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $-1\leq s\leq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (s)\geq b\mu $ for some fixed $b>0$. If $c_\varepsilon <b$, positivity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(u_\varepsilon ) \leq (c_\varepsilon /b)\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(s+A)  \] for every constant $A$. Strict bounded domination would imply $u_\varepsilon \geq s+A$ for every $A$, which is absurd. Hence $c_\varepsilon \geq b$. For an upper bound, choose a fixed Gauduchon form $\gamma $. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and Stokes give \[  c_\varepsilon ^{1/n} \int _ X\left(\frac{\mu }{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ X\omega _\varepsilon \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X(\theta +\varepsilon \eta )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \leq \int _ X(\theta +\eta )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] The first integral is fixed and positive, giving $c_\varepsilon \leq B$. For the lower bound on $u_\varepsilon $, note that all $u_\varepsilon $ are normalized $(\theta +\eta )$-plurisubharmonic functions. Uniform exponential integrability, lemma 1.5.1 , gives $a>0$ such that $g_\varepsilon =\mathrm{e}^{-a u_\varepsilon }f$ has a common $L^2$ bound. Also $g_\varepsilon \geq f$. By theorem 14.2.2 , the solutions \[  w_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ), \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_\varepsilon ) =\mathrm{e}^{a w_\varepsilon }g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V  \] are uniformly bounded. Put $B_0=\max \{ 1,B\} $ and $z_\varepsilon =w_\varepsilon -a^{-1}\log B_0$. Then \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(z_\varepsilon ) \geq \mathrm{e}^{a z_\varepsilon }c_\varepsilon g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(u_\varepsilon ) =\mathrm{e}^{a u_\varepsilon }c_\varepsilon g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The comparison principle for the exponential equation in the background $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ gives $z_\varepsilon \leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0$, and $z_\varepsilon $ is bounded below uniformly in $\varepsilon $. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.18.2
text: Lemma 14.18.2 . For every compact $K\Subset X\setminus Z$, there is $C_ K>1$, independent of $\varepsilon $, such that \[  C_ K^{-1}\eta \leq \omega _\varepsilon \leq C_ K\eta \quad \hbox{on }K.  \] Proof. For the differentiated calculation write $U=u_\varepsilon /(2\pi )$ and $P=\rho /(2\pi )$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial U$. Put \[  S=\operatorname {tr}_\eta \omega _\varepsilon , \quad R=\operatorname {tr}_{\omega _\varepsilon }\eta , \quad D=\omega _\varepsilon ^ n/\eta ^ n.  \] The previous lemma and the smooth positive density give $0<d_1\leq D\leq d_2$. Choose a fixed $C_0$ so that $v=U-P+C_0>1$, and set \[  H=\log S-\gamma (v),\qquad \gamma (v)=Av+\log v,  \] where $A$ will be fixed below. For each $\varepsilon $, $S$ is smooth on $X$ and $v$ tends to infinity at $Z$. Thus $H\to -\infty $ there, and $H$ attains its maximum on $X\setminus Z$. We bound this maximum independently of $\varepsilon $. In local holomorphic coordinates, $h$ and $g$ denote the coefficient matrices of $\eta $ and $\omega _\varepsilon $ with respect to $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$, and commas denote coordinate derivatives, as in $h_{i\bar j,k}=\partial _ kh_{i\bar j}$ and $h_{i\bar j,\bar k}=\partial _{\bar k}h_{i\bar j}$. At a maximum point choose holomorphic coordinates in which \[  h_{i\bar j}=\delta _{ij},\qquad h_{i\bar i,k}=0, \qquad g_{i\bar j}=\lambda _ i\delta _{ij}.  \] A linear change first normalizes $h$ and diagonalizes $g$. In these coordinates, the quadratic change $z_ i=w_ i+\frac12\sum _{j,k}a^ i_{jk}w_ jw_ k$, with symmetric coefficients chosen so that $a^ i_{ik}=-h_{i\bar i,k}$, then kills $h_{i\bar i,k}$. Its coefficients are uniformly bounded on a fixed finite cover. Write \[  \Delta _ g=\sum _ i\lambda _ i^{-1}\partial _ i\partial _{\bar i}, \quad T_{ij\bar k}=g_{j\bar k,i}-g_{i\bar k,j}, \quad E_ i=\sum _ jT_{ij\bar j}.  \] The lowered torsion coefficients $T_{ij\bar k}$ and their first derivatives are uniformly bounded: the potential Hessian cancels, leaving only derivatives of $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $. Let $\mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ be the density of $\mu $ with respect to the coordinate volume form. Differentiating $S=h^{k\bar\ell }g_{k\bar\ell }$ and the equation $\log \det g=\log c_\varepsilon +\log \mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ gives 14.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degeneration-trace-calculus} \Delta _ g S\geq Q-CRS-CR, \qquad Q=\sum _{i,j}\frac{|g_{i\bar j,j}|^2}{\lambda _ i\lambda _ j}. \end{equation} The second derivatives of $g$ contribute $\sum _{i,j,k}|g_{i\bar j,k}|^2/(\lambda _ i\lambda _ j)$, up to $-CR-C$, by commuting the potential derivatives. The first derivatives of $h$ contribute $-2\operatorname {Re}\sum _{i,j,k}\lambda _ i^{-1}h_{j\bar k,\bar i}g_{k\bar j,i}$. Its terms with $j=k$ vanish. Replace $g_{k\bar j,i}$ by $g_{i\bar j,k}+T_{ik\bar j}$ and apply weighted Cauchy–Schwarz. This consumes exactly the terms of the preceding square with $j\ne k$ and costs at most $CRS+CR$. The second derivatives of $h^{-1}$ cost $CRS$. Finally the fixed density term $-C$ is absorbed using $SR\geq n^2$. Since $\partial _ iS=\sum _ jg_{i\bar j,j}+E_ i$ at the maximum point, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz also gives \[  |\partial S|_ g^2 \leq SQ+2\operatorname {Re}\langle E,\partial S\rangle _ g.  \] Indeed expand around $\partial S-E$ and discard the resulting term $-|E|_ g^2$. Combining with ( 14.51 ) yields \[  \Delta _ g\log S\geq -CR-CR/S -\frac2S\operatorname {Re}\langle E,\partial \log S\rangle _ g.  \] At the maximum, $\partial \log S=\gamma '\partial v$. Moreover ( 14.49 ) gives $\Delta _ gv\leq n-\delta R$, and $|E|_ g^2\leq CR$. Young's inequality with the positive coefficient $-\gamma ''=v^{-2}$ therefore gives \[  0\geq \Delta _ g H \geq (\delta \gamma '-C)R-n\gamma '-CR/S -\frac{CR}{S^2}\frac{\gamma '^2}{-\gamma ''}.  \] Since $\gamma '=A+v^{-1}$, choose $A$ with $\delta A-C\geq 1$. The resulting inequality is 14.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degeneration-maximum-trace} 0\geq R-C\left(1+\frac RS+\frac{R(1+v^2)}{S^2}\right). \end{equation} All constants are independent of $\varepsilon $. If the maxima of $H$ were unbounded, then at a sequence of maximizing points \[  \log (S/v)=H+Av\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Thus $S/v\to \infty $ and $S\to \infty $. Inequality ( 14.52 ) would imply $R\leq 2C$ along this sequence. But \[  S=D\sum _ i\prod _{j\ne i}\lambda _ j^{-1} \leq nDR^{n-1}\leq nd_2(2C)^{n-1},  \] a contradiction. Hence $H$ is uniformly bounded. On $K$, both $U$ and $P$ are bounded, so $S\leq C_ K$. The determinant lower bound then gives $\lambda _ i\geq d_1/C_ K^{n-1}$, completing the proof. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.18.3
text: Theorem 14.18.3 . In the preceding setting, $c_\varepsilon $ decreases to a positive number $c_0$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. This number is independent of the perturbing Hermitian form $\eta $. For every sequence $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, a subsequence satisfies \[  u_{\varepsilon _ j}\longrightarrow u_0 \quad \hbox{in }L^1(X)\cap C^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(X\setminus Z),  \] where $u_0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cap L^\infty (X)$, $\sup _ Xu_0=0$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)=c_0\mu .  \] If $\theta $ is closed, then $c_0=\int _ X\theta ^ n$. Proof. Monotonicity of the constants. Let $\alpha \leq \beta $ be Hermitian forms, and let $(u_\alpha ,c_\alpha )$ and $(u_\beta ,c_\beta )$ be the normalized smooth solutions of $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha )^ n=c_\alpha \mu $ and $(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\beta )^ n=c_\beta \mu $. At a maximum point of $u_\alpha -u_\beta $, \[  \alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \leq \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\beta ,  \] so $c_\alpha \leq c_\beta $. Hence $c_\varepsilon $ decreases as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, and lemma 14.18.1 gives $c_0\geq b>0$. Write $c_\eta (\varepsilon )$ for the constant $c_\varepsilon $ defined with the perturbation $\eta $. For two perturbations with $M^{-1}\eta _1\leq \eta _2\leq M\eta _1$, the same comparison gives \[  c_{\eta _1}(\varepsilon /M) \leq c_{\eta _2}(\varepsilon ) \leq c_{\eta _1}(M\varepsilon ).  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $c_0$ does not depend on $\eta $. Local estimates. The trace bound of lemma 14.18.2 gives uniform ellipticity on compact subsets of $X\setminus Z$. The smooth coefficients of $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ and all derivatives of $\log \mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ have common bounds there. Interior complex Evans–Krylov and Schauder estimates, as in the ellipticity argument of proposition 14.17.3 , give uniform $C^ k$ bounds on smaller compact subsets for every $k$. Convergence and the limiting equation. Normalized compactness in the fixed background $\theta +\eta $, followed by a diagonal extraction over an exhaustion of $X\setminus Z$, gives the stated convergence. The uniform bound $-C\leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ passes to the canonical limit, and normalized compactness preserves the supremum zero. For closed $\theta $, bounded closed-background Stokes gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)=\int _ X\theta ^ n$, proving the last assertion. $\square$

title: 14.18.1 Small resolutions of nodes
text: 14.18.1 Small resolutions of nodes The pullback of a positive form from a singular space loses positivity along the contracted curves. In the standard small resolution of a node, the logarithm of the norm in the normal bundle of the exceptional curve provides the missing curvature along the curve. Cutting this logarithm off where the pullback is already positive gives a global strict barrier, so the results above apply. Assume now $n=3$. Let $Y$ be a connected compact normal complex threefold, smooth outside a finite set $\Sigma $ of nodes. A node is locally the hypersurface \[  \{ x_1x_4-x_2x_3=0\} \subset \mathbb C^4.  \] Let $\pi :X\to Y$ be a proper holomorphic map that is biholomorphic over $Y\setminus \Sigma $. Assume each local resolution is the standard small resolution: a neighborhood of its exceptional curve is identified with a neighborhood of the zero section of \[  \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)\oplus \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1),  \] and the contraction, in bundle coordinates $(z,y_1,y_2)$, is 14.53 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nodal-contraction-chart} \pi (z,y_1,y_2)=(y_1,zy_1,y_2,zy_2). \end{equation} Interchanging the two rulings gives the other standard model. Write $E=\pi ^{-1}(\Sigma )$; its components $E_ j$ are disjoint copies of $\mathbb P^1$. Fix a positive form $\omega _ Y$ on $Y$ in the local embedding sense: in each ambient chart it is induced by a smooth strictly positive real $(1,1)$-form. Set $\theta =\pi ^*\omega _ Y$, and let $\eta $ be an arbitrary Hermitian form on $X$. Lemma 14.18.4 . The form $\theta $ is smooth and semipositive, positive on $X\setminus E$. There are $\delta >0$ and $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic poles precisely on $E$, smooth on $X\setminus E$, such that \[  \sup _ X\rho =0,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \eta .  \] Proof. Smoothness and positivity off $E$ follow from the pullback and the biholomorphism. In one standard model put \[  r^2=(1+|z|^2)(|y_1|^2+|y_2|^2),\qquad b=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2).  \] The function $r^2$ is the sum of the squared absolute values of the four contracted coordinates. It is therefore globally defined on the bundle; $b$ is the pullback of the Fubini–Study form from its base. In the chart ( 14.53 ), 14.54 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nodal-logarithmic-curvature} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log r^2 =b+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (|y_1|^2+|y_2|^2)\geq b. \end{equation} This is an inequality of currents across the zero section as well as a smooth inequality off it. Ambient positivity gives $\theta \geq c\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r^2$ on a sufficiently small tube, for some $c>0$. The smooth form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r^2+b$ is positive definite there. Indeed the contraction is an immersion off the zero section, and on that section $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r^2$ is positive in both fiber directions while $b$ is positive along the base. Compactness of the zero section and a smaller closed tube give a uniform lower bound by a positive multiple of $\eta $. Thus, for every fixed $a>0$, \[  \theta +a\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log r^2 \geq c\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r^2+ab \geq \delta _ a\eta  \] near the zero section, with $\delta _ a>0$. Choose disjoint model tubes with nonempty complement and numbers $0<t_1<t_2<1$ in each. Let $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ be a smooth cutoff of $r^2$, equal to one for $r^2\leq t_1$ and zero for $r^2\geq t_2$. Extend $\chi (r^2)\log r^2$ by zero outside its tube. On the compact transition annuli, the pullback $\theta $ is uniformly positive and the second derivatives of this cutoff potential are bounded. A sufficiently small positive rational $a$ therefore makes \[  \rho =a\sum _ j\chi _ j(r_ j^2)\log r_ j^2  \] satisfy $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \eta $ there and near every $E_ j$. On the remaining compact set, $\rho =0$ and $\theta $ is positive, so decreasing $\delta $ proves the global inequality. Near $E_ j$ the function is $a\log (|y_1|^2+|y_2|^2)+a\log (1+|z|^2)$, hence has analytic singularities with rational coefficient and pole set exactly $E_ j$. It is smooth elsewhere and nonpositive; its zero extension gives supremum zero. If $E$ is empty, take $\rho =0$ and use the positivity of $\theta $ on compact $X$. $\square$ Corollary 14.18.5 . For the preceding geometric data and every smooth positive probability volume form $\mu $ on $X$, the solutions of ( 14.50 ) have the bounds and subsequential convergence of theorem 14.18.3 , with $Z=E$. Moreover, for each exceptional curve, \[  \int _{E_ j}\omega _\varepsilon =\varepsilon \int _{E_ j}\eta \longrightarrow 0.  \] Proof. Apply the theorem using lemma 14.18.4 . Since $\pi $ contracts $E_ j$, the restriction of $\theta $ to it is zero. Stokes on the compact smooth curve gives $\int _{E_ j}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =0$, proving the area identity. $\square$ When $K_ X$ is torsion, the density can be chosen so that these metrics are Chern–Ricci flat. Recall that the Chern–Ricci form $\operatorname {Ric}^{\mathrm{Ch}}(\omega )$ of a Hermitian metric $\omega $ is $-\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial $ of the logarithm of the density of $\omega ^ n$ with respect to a coordinate volume form. Choose a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $K_ X^{\otimes m}$ for some $m\geq 1$. If its local expression is $f(\mathrm{d}z_1\wedge \mathrm{d}z_2\wedge \mathrm{d}z_3)^{\otimes m}$, use $|f|^{2/m}$ as the density relative to the standard coordinate volume form. The coordinate Jacobians cancel, so this defines a smooth positive volume form on $X$; normalize it to total mass one and take it as $\mu $. Its logarithmic density is pluriharmonic. Applying $-\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial \log $ to $\omega _\varepsilon ^3=c_\varepsilon \mu $ therefore gives $\operatorname {Ric}^{\mathrm{Ch}}(\omega _\varepsilon )=0$, and the same holds for the smooth limiting metric on $X\setminus E$.
14.53 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nodal-contraction-chart} \pi (z,y_1,y_2)=(y_1,zy_1,y_2,zy_2). \end{equation}

Choose disjoint model tubes with nonempty complement and numbers $0<t_1<t_2<1$ in each. Let $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ be a smooth cutoff of $r^2$, equal to one for $r^2\leq t_1$ and zero for $r^2\geq t_2$. 14.54 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nodal-logarithmic-curvature} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log r^2 =b+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (|y_1|^2+|y_2|^2)\geq b. \end{equation}

title: Corollary 14.18.5
text: Corollary 14.18.5 . For the preceding geometric data and every smooth positive probability volume form $\mu $ on $X$, the solutions of ( 14.50 ) have the bounds and subsequential convergence of theorem 14.18.3 , with $Z=E$. Moreover, for each exceptional curve, \[  \int _{E_ j}\omega _\varepsilon =\varepsilon \int _{E_ j}\eta \longrightarrow 0.  \] Proof. Apply the theorem using lemma 14.18.4 . Since $\pi $ contracts $E_ j$, the restriction of $\theta $ to it is zero. Stokes on the compact smooth curve gives $\int _{E_ j}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =0$, proving the area identity. $\square$

Descent and the zero exceptional mass identify bounded solutions upstairs and downstairs, proving the final assertion. $\square$

title: 14.18.3 Distances across finitely many contracting regions
search_title: Distances across finitely many contracting regions
text: 14.18.3 Distances across finitely many contracting regions On the small resolutions above, the potential limit for a closed background gives smooth convergence of the metrics away from the exceptional curves. Global distances, however, are also affected by paths through neighborhoods of these curves, so their convergence requires control of the diameters of such neighborhoods. The criterion of proposition 14.18.11 separates the two controls: uniform convergence on compact subsets of the regular part, and small diameters of neighborhoods of the contracted sets, in the limiting metric and uniformly in the approximating metrics. We first recall the Gromov–Hausdorff distance. Definition 14.18.8 . For nonempty subsets $E,F$ of a metric space $(W,d_ W)$, their Hausdorff distance is \[  d_{\mathrm H}^ W(E,F)=\max \left\{  \sup _{x\in E}\inf _{y\in F}d_ W(x,y), \sup _{y\in F}\inf _{x\in E}d_ W(x,y)\right\} .  \] For nonempty bounded metric spaces $E,F$, put \[  d_{\mathrm{GH}}(E,F) =\inf _{W,\iota ,\jmath }d_{\mathrm H}^ W(\iota (E),\jmath (F)),  \] where $\iota ,\jmath $ are isometric embeddings into a common metric space $W$. A correspondence is a subset $R\subset E\times F$ whose two coordinate projections are surjective. Its distortion is \[  \operatorname {dis}R =\sup _{(x,y),(x',y')\in R} |d_ E(x,x')-d_ F(y,y')|.  \] Lemma 14.18.9 . For any correspondence $R$ between nonempty bounded metric spaces, \[  \frac12|\operatorname {diam}E-\operatorname {diam}F| \leq d_{\mathrm{GH}}(E,F) \leq \frac12\operatorname {dis}R.  \] Proof. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ with $2\varepsilon \geq \operatorname {dis}R$. Give the disjoint union $E\sqcup F$ its original distances within each space, and use the symmetric cross distance \[  D(x,y)=\inf _{(x_0,y_0)\in R} \bigl (d_ E(x,x_0)+\varepsilon +d_ F(y_0,y)\bigr ), \qquad x\in E,\  y\in F.  \] It is finite and at least $\varepsilon $. The triangle inequalities involving one cross distance follow from the triangle inequality within the corresponding space and the infimum. For two cross distances, take $(x_0,y_0),(x_1,y_1)\in R$. The distortion bound gives \[  \begin{split}  d_ E(x,x') & \leq d_ E(x,x_0)+d_ F(y_0,y_1) +2\varepsilon +d_ E(x_1,x')\\ & \leq d_ E(x,x_0)+d_ F(y_0,y)+\varepsilon +\varepsilon +d_ F(y,y_1)+d_ E(x_1,x'). \end{split}  \] Taking the two infima gives $d_ E(x,x')\leq D(x,y)+D(y,x')$. The same argument with $E,F$ exchanged treats the other case. Hence $D$ is a metric extending both metrics. Each point has a correspondent at cross distance $\varepsilon $, so the Hausdorff distance between $E$ and $F$ in $(E\sqcup F,D)$ is at most $\varepsilon $. Letting $\varepsilon $ decrease to half the distortion proves the upper bound, including zero distortion. For the lower bound, suppose two isometric images have Hausdorff distance $h$. For every $\delta >0$, two points in the first image have points in the second within $h+\delta $. Their distance is at most $\operatorname {diam}F+2h+2\delta $. Taking the supremum and then $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $\operatorname {diam}E\leq \operatorname {diam}F+2h$. Exchanging the images and taking the infimum over embeddings proves the lower bound. $\square$ We now work in a purely metric setting, which contains the nodal one. Let $Y$ be a compact metrizable space and let $S=\{ s_1,\ldots ,s_ N\} \subset Y$ be finite. Assume $Y^\circ =Y\setminus S$ is a dense connected smooth manifold. Let $g_0$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $Y^\circ $, and denote its intrinsic length distance by $d_0$. Lemma 14.18.10 . Suppose every $s_ a$ has a neighborhood basis of open sets $V_{a,r}$ such that \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\operatorname {diam}_{d_0}(V_{a,r}\setminus S)=0.  \] Then the metric completion $(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0)$ of $(Y^\circ ,d_0)$ is compact, and the identity on $Y^\circ $ extends to a homeomorphism $\iota :Y\to \widehat Y$. Proof. The neighborhoods can be chosen nested, with closures avoiding the other points of $S$. Every sequence of regular points converging to $s_ a$ is $d_0$-Cauchy: its tail lies in each prescribed neighborhood, whose punctured diameter tends to zero. Interleaving two such sequences shows that they define the same completion point, denoted by $\widehat s_ a$. Density of $Y^\circ $ guarantees the existence of these sequences. For each prescribed positive diameter, remove sufficiently small neighborhoods of all the points of $S$. Their complement is a compact subset of $Y^\circ $ and hence is totally bounded for $d_0$. The removed punctured neighborhoods each have the prescribed small diameter. Thus $Y^\circ $ is totally bounded, and its completion is compact. The points $\widehat s_ a$ are distinct from one another and from the regular points. To see this, fix $s_ a$ and a different point $y\in Y$. Choose an open neighborhood $V$ of $s_ a$ whose closure avoids $y$ and $S\setminus \{ s_ a\} $, and choose $W\Subset V$ containing $s_ a$. There is a smooth function $\chi $ on $Y^\circ $, equal to one on $W\setminus S$ and zero outside $V$, whose derivative has compact support in $Y^\circ $. Indeed the transition takes place in the compact regular set $\overline V\setminus W$, where smooth cutoffs exist. Therefore $|\mathrm{d}\chi |_{g_0}\leq C$ for some finite $C$. Integration along curves gives \[  |\chi (p)-\chi (q)|\leq C d_0(p,q),\qquad p,q\in Y^\circ .  \] The Lipschitz extension of $\chi $ to the completion has value one at $\widehat s_ a$ and zero at the regular point $y$, or at $\widehat s_ b$ if $y=s_ b$. This proves the assertion. Define $\iota $ by the identity on the regular locus and by $\iota (s_ a)=\widehat s_ a$. The intrinsic distance induces the smooth topology at each regular point. At $s_ a$, adjoining $\widehat s_ a$ to a punctured neighborhood does not increase its diameter, so the diameter hypothesis proves continuity of $\iota $. Every completion point is represented by a Cauchy sequence in $Y^\circ $. Compact metrizability of $Y$ gives a subsequence converging topologically either to a regular point or to some $s_ a$; the preceding arguments give its metric limit. Hence $\iota $ is surjective as well as injective. A continuous bijection from compact $Y$ to Hausdorff $\widehat Y$ is a homeomorphism. $\square$ Let $X$ be a compact connected smooth manifold and let $\pi :X\to Y$ be a continuous surjection, with $E=\pi ^{-1}(S)$ and with $\pi :X\setminus E\to Y^\circ $ a diffeomorphism. Assume that the identity of $Y^\circ $ extends to a homeomorphism $\iota :Y\to \widehat Y$, for instance under the hypothesis of lemma 14.18.10 , and write $G=\iota \circ \pi $. For a smooth Riemannian metric $g$ on $X$ and an open subset $U$, let $\operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U,g)$ denote the intrinsic diameter of $U$, computed with the lengths of piecewise smooth curves contained in $U$. Proposition 14.18.11 . Let $g_ j$ be smooth Riemannian metrics on $X$ such that $g_ j\to \pi ^*g_0$ uniformly on every compact subset of $X\setminus E$. Suppose each $s_ a$ has a nested neighborhood basis $V_{a,r}$, with $U_{a,r}=\pi ^{-1}(V_{a,r})$, satisfying \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\operatorname {diam}_{\widehat d_0}(\iota (V_{a,r}))=0, \qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\limsup _{j\to \infty } \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_{a,r},g_ j)=0.  \] Then, for the global length distances $d_ j$ of $g_ j$, \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\sup _{x,x'\in X} |d_ j(x,x')-\widehat d_0(G(x),G(x'))|=0.  \] Consequently $(X,d_ j)$ converges to $(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0)$ in Gromov–Hausdorff distance. Proof. If $S$ is empty, uniform metric comparison on compact $X$ proves the distance convergence. Assume $N\geq 1$. Fix $\tau >0$. Choose pairwise disjoint neighborhoods $V_ a$ from the specified bases with \[  \operatorname {diam}_{\widehat d_0}(\iota (V_ a))<\tau , \qquad \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_ a,g_ j)<\tau  \] for all sufficiently large $j$, where $U_ a=\pi ^{-1}(V_ a)$. Pick $q_ a\in V_ a\setminus S$, and then choose open neighborhoods $W_ a$ of $s_ a$ with $\overline W_ a\subset V_ a$ and $q_ a\notin \overline W_ a$. The regular cores \[  K_ Y=Y\setminus \bigcup _ a W_ a, \qquad K_ X=\pi ^{-1}(K_ Y)  \] are compact and identified by $\pi $. Uniform convergence and positivity of $g_0$ on this core give numbers $A_ j\geq 1$, with $A_ j\to 1$, such that lengths of curves contained in the cores compare in both directions by the factor $A_ j$. Consider a piecewise smooth path in $Y^\circ $ joining two points of $K_ Y$. The preimages of the closed sets $\overline W_ a$ are compact subsets of its parameter interval. At its first visit to any such set, delete the portion from that visit through its last visit to the same set. Resume with the remaining tail. That set is never visited again; thus there are at most $N$ deleted portions. Each retained segment lies in $K_ Y$, and each deleted portion has endpoints in a single $\overline W_ a\subset V_ a$. The lifts of those endpoints can be joined in $U_ a$ with $g_ j$-length less than $\tau $, up to an arbitrarily small error. Applying this procedure to almost minimizing paths, comparing retained lengths, and letting the errors tend to zero gives, for $x,x'\in K_ X$, \[  d_ j(x,x')\leq A_ j\widehat d_0(G(x),G(x'))+N\tau .  \] Conversely start with an almost minimizing $g_ j$-path in $X$ and apply the same deletion procedure to the closed sets $\pi ^{-1}(\overline W_ a)$. Project its retained segments, which avoid $E$, to $K_ Y$. The two images of each deleted portion have completion distance less than $\tau $. The triangle inequality in $\widehat Y$ therefore gives \[  \widehat d_0(G(x),G(x'))\leq A_ j d_ j(x,x')+N\tau , \qquad x,x'\in K_ X.  \] For any $x\notin K_ X$ with $\pi (x)\in W_ a$, replace $x$ by $p=\pi ^{-1}(q_ a)\in U_ a\cap K_ X$. Then $d_ j(x,p)<\tau $ and $\widehat d_0(G(x),G(p))<\tau $. Leave points of $K_ X$ fixed. Replacing both endpoints extends the two inequalities to all $x,x'\in X$, with the same error \[  C_ j=(N+2+2A_ j)\tau .  \] If $D=\operatorname {diam}(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0)$, the first inequality gives $\operatorname {diam}(X,d_ j)\leq A_ jD+C_ j$. The positive and negative distance errors are consequently bounded by \[  (A_ j-1)D+C_ j, \qquad (A_ j-1)(A_ jD+C_ j)+C_ j,  \] respectively. Their upper limits are at most $(N+4)\tau $. Letting $\tau \downarrow 0$ proves uniform convergence. The graph of $G$ is a correspondence between $X$ and $\widehat Y$, and its distortion $b_ j$ for the distances $d_ j$ and $\widehat d_0$ is the supremum in the statement. By lemma 14.18.9 , \[  d_{\mathrm{GH}}((X,d_ j),(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0))\leq b_ j/2\longrightarrow 0.  \] $\square$ For the standard nodal small resolutions of 14.18.1 with closed $\theta $, the smooth convergence of the whole family off $E$ in theorem 14.18.7 gives the uniform convergence on compact subsets of $X\setminus E$ required in proposition 14.18.11 . What remains are the two conditions on the diameters of neighborhoods. The next estimates control the approximating neighborhoods by metric bounds along and normal to the exceptional curves.

At $s_ a$, adjoining $\widehat s_ a$ to a punctured neighborhood does not increase its diameter, so the diameter hypothesis proves continuity of $\iota $. Every completion point is represented by a Cauchy sequence in $Y^\circ $. Compact metrizability of $Y$ gives a subsequence converging topologically either to a regular point or to some $s_ a$; the preceding arguments give its metric limit. Hence $\iota $ is surjective as well as injective. A continuous bijection from compact $Y$ to Hausdorff $\widehat Y$ is a homeomorphism. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.18.11
text: Proposition 14.18.11 . Let $g_ j$ be smooth Riemannian metrics on $X$ such that $g_ j\to \pi ^*g_0$ uniformly on every compact subset of $X\setminus E$. Suppose each $s_ a$ has a nested neighborhood basis $V_{a,r}$, with $U_{a,r}=\pi ^{-1}(V_{a,r})$, satisfying \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\operatorname {diam}_{\widehat d_0}(\iota (V_{a,r}))=0, \qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\limsup _{j\to \infty } \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_{a,r},g_ j)=0.  \] Then, for the global length distances $d_ j$ of $g_ j$, \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\sup _{x,x'\in X} |d_ j(x,x')-\widehat d_0(G(x),G(x'))|=0.  \] Consequently $(X,d_ j)$ converges to $(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0)$ in Gromov–Hausdorff distance. Proof. If $S$ is empty, uniform metric comparison on compact $X$ proves the distance convergence. Assume $N\geq 1$. Fix $\tau >0$. Choose pairwise disjoint neighborhoods $V_ a$ from the specified bases with \[  \operatorname {diam}_{\widehat d_0}(\iota (V_ a))<\tau , \qquad \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_ a,g_ j)<\tau  \] for all sufficiently large $j$, where $U_ a=\pi ^{-1}(V_ a)$. Pick $q_ a\in V_ a\setminus S$, and then choose open neighborhoods $W_ a$ of $s_ a$ with $\overline W_ a\subset V_ a$ and $q_ a\notin \overline W_ a$. The regular cores \[  K_ Y=Y\setminus \bigcup _ a W_ a, \qquad K_ X=\pi ^{-1}(K_ Y)  \] are compact and identified by $\pi $. Uniform convergence and positivity of $g_0$ on this core give numbers $A_ j\geq 1$, with $A_ j\to 1$, such that lengths of curves contained in the cores compare in both directions by the factor $A_ j$. Consider a piecewise smooth path in $Y^\circ $ joining two points of $K_ Y$. The preimages of the closed sets $\overline W_ a$ are compact subsets of its parameter interval. At its first visit to any such set, delete the portion from that visit through its last visit to the same set. Resume with the remaining tail. That set is never visited again; thus there are at most $N$ deleted portions. Each retained segment lies in $K_ Y$, and each deleted portion has endpoints in a single $\overline W_ a\subset V_ a$. The lifts of those endpoints can be joined in $U_ a$ with $g_ j$-length less than $\tau $, up to an arbitrarily small error. Applying this procedure to almost minimizing paths, comparing retained lengths, and letting the errors tend to zero gives, for $x,x'\in K_ X$, \[  d_ j(x,x')\leq A_ j\widehat d_0(G(x),G(x'))+N\tau .  \] Conversely start with an almost minimizing $g_ j$-path in $X$ and apply the same deletion procedure to the closed sets $\pi ^{-1}(\overline W_ a)$. Project its retained segments, which avoid $E$, to $K_ Y$. The two images of each deleted portion have completion distance less than $\tau $. The triangle inequality in $\widehat Y$ therefore gives \[  \widehat d_0(G(x),G(x'))\leq A_ j d_ j(x,x')+N\tau , \qquad x,x'\in K_ X.  \] For any $x\notin K_ X$ with $\pi (x)\in W_ a$, replace $x$ by $p=\pi ^{-1}(q_ a)\in U_ a\cap K_ X$. Then $d_ j(x,p)<\tau $ and $\widehat d_0(G(x),G(p))<\tau $. Leave points of $K_ X$ fixed. Replacing both endpoints extends the two inequalities to all $x,x'\in X$, with the same error \[  C_ j=(N+2+2A_ j)\tau .  \] If $D=\operatorname {diam}(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0)$, the first inequality gives $\operatorname {diam}(X,d_ j)\leq A_ jD+C_ j$. The positive and negative distance errors are consequently bounded by \[  (A_ j-1)D+C_ j, \qquad (A_ j-1)(A_ jD+C_ j)+C_ j,  \] respectively. Their upper limits are at most $(N+4)\tau $. Letting $\tau \downarrow 0$ proves uniform convergence. The graph of $G$ is a correspondence between $X$ and $\widehat Y$, and its distortion $b_ j$ for the distances $d_ j$ and $\widehat d_0$ is the supremum in the statement. By lemma 14.18.9 , \[  d_{\mathrm{GH}}((X,d_ j),(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0))\leq b_ j/2\longrightarrow 0.  \] $\square$

title: Curve areas and radial tube lengths
search_title: Curve areas and radial tube lengths
text: None Curve areas and radial tube lengths The approximating metrics give each exceptional curve an area tending to zero, by corollary 14.18.5 . Along the curve, small area forces small diameter as long as the metrics are bounded above; in the normal directions, an integrable bound for the speed of radial rays has the same effect. Let $C$ be a connected compact Riemann surface. Fix a smooth Hermitian metric $h$ of area one on $C$, and use the associated Riemannian metrics for lengths and areas. Lemma 14.18.12 . There is $K_ h>0$ such that every smooth Hermitian metric $g\leq M h$, with $M>0$ and $A=\operatorname {Area}_ g(C)$, satisfies \[  \operatorname {diam}(C,g) \leq K_ h\sqrt{A\bigl (1+\log (M/A)\bigr )}.  \] Here $0<A\leq M$. In particular, for a fixed upper bound $M$, area tending to zero implies diameter tending to zero. Proof. Replace $g$ by $g/M$. Its area is $a=A/M\leq 1$, and it is bounded above by $h$. We prove the estimate for this normalized metric. Choose a finite cover by holomorphic coordinate disks $U_ i$ represented by $\{ |z|<1\} $, with each coordinate defined on the larger disk $\{ |z|<2\} $. Write $g=\rho _ i|\mathrm{d}z|^2$ there. There is a common $L>0$ such that $0<\rho _ i\leq L$ on all the closed unit disks, and \[  \int _{U_ i}\rho _ i\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2\leq a,  \] where $\lambda _2$ is Euclidean area. For $p,z\in U_ i$, let $\ell _ p(z)$ be the $g$-length of their straight coordinate segment, which stays in $U_ i$. Polar coordinates about $p$ and Fubini give \[  \int _{U_ i}\ell _ p(z)\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2(z) \leq 2\int _{U_ i}\frac{\sqrt{\rho _ i(w)}}{|w-p|} \, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2(w).  \] Indeed each ray meets the convex unit disk in an interval of length $R\leq 2$. Interchanging the radial integrals multiplies the length integrand at radius $s$ by $(R^2-s^2)/2\leq 2$. For $0<a\leq 1/4$, put $t=\sqrt a$. The integral on the right, without its factor two, is bounded by \[  \begin{split}  \sqrt L\int _{\{ |w-p|<t\} }\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda _2(w)}{|w-p|} & +\left(\int _{U_ i}\rho _ i\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2\right)^{1/2} \left(\int _{\{ t<|w-p|<2\} }\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda _2(w)}{|w-p|^2}\right)^{1/2}\\ & \leq 2\pi \sqrt L\, t+\sqrt{2\pi a\log (2/t)} \leq K\sqrt{a\bigl (1+\log (1/a)\bigr )}. \end{split}  \] Thus for any $p,q\in U_ i$, averaging $\ell _ p(z)+\ell _ q(z)$ over $z\in U_ i$ gives a two-segment path of length at most $K\sqrt{a(1+\log (1/a))}$. The constant is common to the finite cover. The overlap graph of this cover is connected because $C$ is connected. Choose points in consecutive overlaps along a simple path in this finite graph. The local estimates join any two points of $C$ through at most the number of covering disks, proving the global bound for $a\leq 1/4$. For $1/4\leq a\leq 1$, the comparison $g\leq h$ gives $\operatorname {diam}(C,g)\leq \operatorname {diam}(C,h)$, and increasing $K_ h$ gives the same estimate. Restoring the factor $M$ scales lengths by $\sqrt M$ and proves the assertion. $\square$ Example 14.18.13 . On every such $(C,h)$ there are smooth Hermitian metrics $g_\varepsilon \leq h$, for $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, such that \[  \begin{aligned}  A_\varepsilon :=\operatorname {Area}_{g_\varepsilon }(C) & \asymp \varepsilon ^2\log (1/\varepsilon ),\\  \operatorname {diam}(C,g_\varepsilon ) & \asymp \varepsilon \log (1/\varepsilon ). \end{aligned}  \] Consequently the preceding diameter bound has sharp order under its uniform upper bound. Without that bound, area can tend to zero while diameter stays bounded below by a positive constant. Proof. Choose a coordinate disk $\{ |z|<R\} $ with $0<R<1$, on whose closure $h=\lambda (z)|\mathrm{d}z|^2$ with $\lambda >0$ smooth. Choose a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, supported in this disk and equal to one for $|z|\leq R/2$, and a constant $c>0$ with $c\leq \min \lambda $. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, set \[  g_\varepsilon = \left(\chi \frac{c\varepsilon ^2}{\lambda (z)(\varepsilon ^2+|z|^2)} +(1-\chi )\varepsilon ^2\right)h  \] in the disk, and set $g_\varepsilon =\varepsilon ^2h$ outside it. The cutoff makes this a smooth positive metric, and both coefficients in its convex combination are at most one. On $|z|\leq R/2$ its metric density is $c\varepsilon ^2/(\varepsilon ^2+|z|^2)$, whose area is \[  \pi c\varepsilon ^2 \log \left(1+\frac{R^2}{4\varepsilon ^2}\right).  \] The remaining area is $O(\varepsilon ^2)$, proving the asserted area comparison. Any path from the origin to a point outside this smaller disk must first cross its boundary. Radial variation is bounded by Euclidean speed, so that initial portion has length at least \[  \sqrt c\, \varepsilon \int _0^{R/2} \frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\sqrt{\varepsilon ^2+r^2}} =\sqrt c\, \varepsilon \operatorname {arsinh}(R/(2\varepsilon )) \asymp \varepsilon \log (1/\varepsilon ).  \] This gives the diameter lower bound. The upper bound follows from lemma 14.18.12 , since $A_\varepsilon (1+\log (1/A_\varepsilon ))\asymp \varepsilon ^2\log ^2(1/\varepsilon )$. Finally rescale by \[  \widetilde g_\varepsilon =\frac{g_\varepsilon }{\varepsilon ^2\log ^2(1/\varepsilon )}.  \] Its area is comparable to $1/\log (1/\varepsilon )$ and tends to zero, whereas its diameter is comparable to one. At the origin its ratio to $h$ tends to infinity, so it has no uniform upper bound. $\square$ Let $V\to C$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of positive rank with a fixed smooth Hermitian fiber norm. Write $U_\delta =\{ v\in V:|v|<\delta \} $ and identify its zero section with $C$. Proposition 14.18.14 . Let $g_ j$ be smooth Hermitian metrics on $U_{\delta _0}$. Suppose their restrictions to $C$ satisfy \[  g_ j|_ C\leq M h,\qquad A_ j=\operatorname {Area}_{g_ j|_ C}(C)\longrightarrow 0  \] for a fixed $M>0$. Suppose also that there are $B>0$ and $0<\alpha \leq 1$ such that, for every unit fiber vector $v$ over any $x\in C$, the ray $\gamma _{x,v}(s)=sv$ satisfies \[  g_ j(\gamma _{x,v}'(s),\gamma _{x,v}'(s)) \leq B s^{2\alpha -2}, \qquad 0<s<\delta _0,  \] uniformly in $j,x,v$. Then \[  \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j) \leq \frac{2\sqrt B}{\alpha }\delta ^\alpha +K_ h\sqrt{A_ j\bigl (1+\log (M/A_ j)\bigr )}, \qquad 0<\delta <\delta _0.  \] In particular, \[  \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\limsup _{j\to \infty } \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j)=0.  \] Proof. A point of fiber radius $r<\delta $ joins its base point on the zero section along the radial segment, entirely inside $U_\delta $. Its length is at most \[  \sqrt B\int _0^ r s^{\alpha -1}\, \mathrm{d}s =\frac{\sqrt B}{\alpha }r^\alpha .  \] The metric is smooth at the zero section for each $j$; the integrable uniform bound controls the whole segment. Join the two base points by an almost minimizing path in $(C,g_ j|_ C)$. This path also lies in $U_\delta $, and up to an arbitrarily small excess its length is bounded by lemma 14.18.12 . Together with the two radial segments, this gives the asserted bound for the intrinsic diameter. Since $A_ j(1+\log (M/A_ j))\to 0$, taking $j\to \infty $ and then $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the final assertion. $\square$ Return to the standard nodal small resolutions of 14.18.1 . On a nodal tube put $r^2=\sum _{k=1}^4|x_ k\circ \pi |^2$, the squared bundle norm used in lemma 14.18.4 . Let $V_\delta \subset Y$ be the nodal coordinate ball $\sum _ k|x_ k|^2<\delta ^2$. For sufficiently small $\delta $, properness gives $\pi ^{-1}(V_\delta )=\{ r<\delta \} $. Write $g_\varepsilon $ for the Riemannian metric associated to $\omega _\varepsilon $. Its area on $E_ a$ is $\varepsilon \int _{E_ a}\eta $ by corollary 14.18.5 . Fix an area-one Hermitian metric $h_ a$ on $E_ a$. If $g_\varepsilon |_{E_ a}\leq M h_ a$ uniformly and the radial bound of proposition 14.18.14 holds with $\alpha =1/2$, substitution in that proposition gives \[  \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(\{ r<\delta \} ,g_\varepsilon ) \leq K\delta ^{1/2} +K\sqrt{\varepsilon \bigl (1+\log (1/\varepsilon )\bigr )}  \] for sufficiently small $\varepsilon $ and $\delta $, with $K$ independent of both. Under these two pointwise metric bounds, the condition on approximating neighborhoods in proposition 14.18.11 therefore holds. The condition on punctured neighborhoods in the limiting metric does not follow from it, as the next example shows. In the following surface example the volume form is fixed and the approximating tubes shrink, but the punctured neighborhoods of the contracted point keep a positive diameter in the limiting metric. Example 14.18.15 . There are a compact complex surface $X$, a holomorphic map $\pi :X\to Y=\mathbb P^2$ contracting a curve $E$ to a point $p$, and smooth Hermitian metrics $g_ j,g_*$ on $X$ with the following properties. The map is biholomorphic from $X\setminus E$ to $Y\setminus \{ p\} $, and $g_ j=g_*$ eventually on each compact subset of $X\setminus E$. Their associated Hermitian forms satisfy \[  \omega _ j^2=\omega _*^2.  \] The curve areas tend to zero, and the metrics have a uniform integrable radial bound near $E$. For a neighborhood basis $V_\delta $ of $p$, with $U_\delta =\pi ^{-1}(V_\delta )$, \[  \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\limsup _{j\to \infty } \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j)=0.  \] Nevertheless, for the intrinsic distance $d_0$ of $g_0=(\pi ^{-1})^*g_*$ on $Y\setminus \{ p\} $, there is $c>0$ such that \[  \operatorname {diam}_{d_0}(V_\delta \setminus \{ p\} )\geq c  \] for every sufficiently small $\delta $. Proof. Put $p=[1:0:0]$ and take the incidence surface \[  \begin{gathered} X=\bigl \{ ([z_0:z_1:z_2],[u:v])\in \mathbb P^2\times \mathbb P^1: z_1v=z_2u\bigr \} ,\\ \pi ([z],[u:v])=[z]. \end{gathered}  \] Off $p$, the second coordinate is $[z_1:z_2]$, so $\pi $ is biholomorphic there. Its exceptional curve is $E=\{ p\} \times \mathbb P^1$. In the affine chart $z_0=1$, a chart of $X$ is \[  (t,w)\longmapsto ([1:w:tw],[1:t]).  \] The other chart is $([1:t'w':w'],[t':1])$, with $t'=1/t$ and $w'=tw$ on their overlap. These are the charts of the tautological line bundle $L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$. They also show smoothness along $E$; smoothness elsewhere follows from the biholomorphism. Thus $X$ is a compact smooth complex surface. Its connected dense complement $X\setminus E$ makes it connected. Let $q:L\to \mathbb P^1$ be the bundle projection. Give $L$ the norm induced by its tautological inclusion into $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb C^2$. In the first chart its squared norm is \[  r^2=(1+|t|^2)|w|^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2.  \] Fix an area-one Hermitian metric $h$ on $\mathbb P^1$. The Chern connection of the fiber norm defines a smooth semipositive Hermitian tensor $k$ on $L$ by the squared norm of the covariant fiber differential. Explicitly, with $\lambda =1+|t|^2$, \[  k=\lambda \left|\mathrm{d}w+w\partial \log \lambda \right|^2.  \] Under $t'=1/t$, $w'=tw$, the differential in this formula multiplies by $t$ and $\lambda $ divides by $|t|^2$, so the tensor is globally defined. It has complex rank one, is positive on nonzero vertical tangent vectors, and restricts to zero on $TE$. Consequently $q^*h+k$ is a smooth positive Hermitian metric on $L$. Choose $0<\delta _0<1$ and extend this metric from $U_{\delta _0}=\{ r<\delta _0\} $ to a smooth Hermitian metric $g_*$ on $X$. Such an extension follows by a smooth cutoff supported in a slightly larger bundle tube and a convex combination with any global Hermitian metric. It agrees exactly with $q^*h+k$ on $U_{\delta _0}$. Choose $0<\varepsilon _ j<1$ tending to zero, with $2\varepsilon _ j^2<\delta _0$, and a smooth function $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ on $[0,\infty )$, equal to zero on $[0,1]$ and to one on $[4,\infty )$. Set \[  \begin{aligned}  f_ j(r)& =\varepsilon _ j^2+(1-\varepsilon _ j^2) \chi (r^2/\varepsilon _ j^4),\\  g_ j& =f_ jq^*h+f_ j^{-1}k, \end{aligned}  \] on $U_{\delta _0}$, and set $g_ j=g_*$ elsewhere. The function $f_ j$ is smooth at $E$, is at least $\varepsilon _ j^2$, and equals one for $r\geq 2\varepsilon _ j^2$. Hence the metrics glue smoothly and are positive. They equal $g_*$ eventually on every compact subset of $X\setminus E$. Let $\beta ,\kappa $ be the Hermitian forms of $q^*h,k$. Their complex rank one gives $\beta ^2=\kappa ^2=0$. On the tube, \[  (f_ j\beta +f_ j^{-1}\kappa )^2 =2\beta \wedge \kappa =(\beta +\kappa )^2.  \] Outside it the metrics coincide. This proves the global volume identity. On $E$, the restriction is $g_ j|_ E=\varepsilon _ j^2h$, so its area is $\varepsilon _ j^2$. For any unit fiber vector $a$, a radial ray $\gamma (s)=sa$ has $k$-squared speed one and zero base component. Thus its $g_ j$-squared speed is $f_ j(s)^{-1}$. If $s<2\varepsilon _ j^2$, this is at most $\varepsilon _ j^{-2}\leq 2/s$; otherwise it is one, still at most $2/s$ for $s<\delta _0$. This is the uniform integrable radial bound with exponent $1/2$. A radial segment of radius $r<\delta $ has length at most $r+2\varepsilon _ j$: its portion below $2\varepsilon _ j^2$ has speed at most $\varepsilon _ j^{-1}$ and length at most $2\varepsilon _ j$, and its remaining speed is one. Connect two points by their radial segments and an almost minimizing path on $E$. All three segments stay inside $U_\delta $, giving \[  \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j) \leq 2\delta +\varepsilon _ j\bigl (4+\operatorname {diam}(\mathbb P^1,h)\bigr ).  \] Taking $j\to \infty $ before $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the asserted shrinking condition. The affine balls \[  V_\delta =\{ [1:z_1:z_2]:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2<\delta ^2\}   \] have precisely these tubes as their preimages. Let $d_*$ be the global distance of the fixed smooth metric $g_*$. Choose distinct points $a,b\in E$, and put $c=d_*(a,b)>0$. Choose points $a_ r,b_ r$ of fiber norm $r>0$ over these base points. They tend to $a,b$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Every path in $Y\setminus \{ p\} $ lifts to a path in $X\setminus E$ with the same $g_0$-length as its $g_*$-length. Therefore \[  d_0(\pi (a_ r),\pi (b_ r))\geq d_*(a_ r,b_ r)\longrightarrow c.  \] For any fixed $\delta >0$, these two images lie in $V_\delta $ when $r<\delta $. Taking the supremum and then $r\downarrow 0$ gives its punctured diameter at least $c$. $\square$

There are a compact complex surface $X$, a holomorphic map $\pi :X\to Y=\mathbb P^2$ contracting a curve $E$ to a point $p$, and smooth Hermitian metrics $g_ j,g_*$ on $X$ with the following properties. The map is biholomorphic from $X\setminus E$ to $Y\setminus \{ p\} $, and $g_ j=g_*$ eventually on each compact subset of $X\setminus E$. Their associated Hermitian forms satisfy \[  \omega _ j^2=\omega _*^2.  \] The curve areas tend to zero, and the metrics have a uniform integrable radial bound near $E$. For a neighborhood basis $V_\delta $ of $p$, with $U_\delta =\pi ^{-1}(V_\delta )$, \[  \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\limsup _{j\to \infty } \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j)=0.  \] Nevertheless, for the intrinsic distance $d_0$ of $g_0=(\pi ^{-1})^*g_*$ on $Y\setminus \{ p\} $, there is $c>0$ such that \[  \operatorname {diam}_{d_0}(V_\delta \setminus \{ p\} )\geq c  \] for every sufficiently small $\delta $. Proof. Put $p=[1:0:0]$ and take the incidence surface \[  \begin{gathered} X=\bigl \{ ([z_0:z_1:z_2],[u:v])\in \mathbb P^2\times \mathbb P^1: z_1v=z_2u\bigr \} ,\\ \pi ([z],[u:v])=[z]. \end{gathered}  \] Off $p$, the second coordinate is $[z_1:z_2]$, so $\pi $ is biholomorphic there. Its exceptional curve is $E=\{ p\} \times \mathbb P^1$. In the affine chart $z_0=1$, a chart of $X$ is \[  (t,w)\longmapsto ([1:w:tw],[1:t]).  \] The other chart is $([1:t'w':w'],[t':1])$, with $t'=1/t$ and $w'=tw$ on their overlap. These are the charts of the tautological line bundle $L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$. They also show smoothness along $E$; smoothness elsewhere follows from the biholomorphism. Thus $X$ is a compact smooth complex surface. Its connected dense complement $X\setminus E$ makes it connected. Let $q:L\to \mathbb P^1$ be the bundle projection. Give $L$ the norm induced by its tautological inclusion into $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb C^2$. In the first chart its squared norm is \[  r^2=(1+|t|^2)|w|^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2.  \] Fix an area-one Hermitian metric $h$ on $\mathbb P^1$. The Chern connection of the fiber norm defines a smooth semipositive Hermitian tensor $k$ on $L$ by the squared norm of the covariant fiber differential. Explicitly, with $\lambda =1+|t|^2$, \[  k=\lambda \left|\mathrm{d}w+w\partial \log \lambda \right|^2.  \] Under $t'=1/t$, $w'=tw$, the differential in this formula multiplies by $t$ and $\lambda $ divides by $|t|^2$, so the tensor is globally defined. It has complex rank one, is positive on nonzero vertical tangent vectors, and restricts to zero on $TE$. Consequently $q^*h+k$ is a smooth positive Hermitian metric on $L$. Choose $0<\delta _0<1$ and extend this metric from $U_{\delta _0}=\{ r<\delta _0\} $ to a smooth Hermitian metric $g_*$ on $X$. Such an extension follows by a smooth cutoff supported in a slightly larger bundle tube and a convex combination with any global Hermitian metric. It agrees exactly with $q^*h+k$ on $U_{\delta _0}$. Choose $0<\varepsilon _ j<1$ tending to zero, with $2\varepsilon _ j^2<\delta _0$, and a smooth function $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ on $[0,\infty )$, equal to zero on $[0,1]$ and to one on $[4,\infty )$. Set \[  \begin{aligned}  f_ j(r)& =\varepsilon _ j^2+(1-\varepsilon _ j^2) \chi (r^2/\varepsilon _ j^4),\\  g_ j& =f_ jq^*h+f_ j^{-1}k, \end{aligned}  \] on $U_{\delta _0}$, and set $g_ j=g_*$ elsewhere. The function $f_ j$ is smooth at $E$, is at least $\varepsilon _ j^2$, and equals one for $r\geq 2\varepsilon _ j^2$. Hence the metrics glue smoothly and are positive. They equal $g_*$ eventually on every compact subset of $X\setminus E$. Let $\beta ,\kappa $ be the Hermitian forms of $q^*h,k$. Their complex rank one gives $\beta ^2=\kappa ^2=0$. On the tube, \[  (f_ j\beta +f_ j^{-1}\kappa )^2 =2\beta \wedge \kappa =(\beta +\kappa )^2.  \] Outside it the metrics coincide. This proves the global volume identity. On $E$, the restriction is $g_ j|_ E=\varepsilon _ j^2h$, so its area is $\varepsilon _ j^2$. For any unit fiber vector $a$, a radial ray $\gamma (s)=sa$ has $k$-squared speed one and zero base component. Thus its $g_ j$-squared speed is $f_ j(s)^{-1}$. If $s<2\varepsilon _ j^2$, this is at most $\varepsilon _ j^{-2}\leq 2/s$; otherwise it is one, still at most $2/s$ for $s<\delta _0$. This is the uniform integrable radial bound with exponent $1/2$. A radial segment of radius $r<\delta $ has length at most $r+2\varepsilon _ j$: its portion below $2\varepsilon _ j^2$ has speed at most $\varepsilon _ j^{-1}$ and length at most $2\varepsilon _ j$, and its remaining speed is one. Connect two points by their radial segments and an almost minimizing path on $E$. All three segments stay inside $U_\delta $, giving \[  \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j) \leq 2\delta +\varepsilon _ j\bigl (4+\operatorname {diam}(\mathbb P^1,h)\bigr ).  \] Taking $j\to \infty $ before $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the asserted shrinking condition. The affine balls \[  V_\delta =\{ [1:z_1:z_2]:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2<\delta ^2\}   \] have precisely these tubes as their preimages. Let $d_*$ be the global distance of the fixed smooth metric $g_*$. Choose distinct points $a,b\in E$, and put $c=d_*(a,b)>0$. Choose points $a_ r,b_ r$ of fiber norm $r>0$ over these base points. They tend to $a,b$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Every path in $Y\setminus \{ p\} $ lifts to a path in $X\setminus E$ with the same $g_0$-length as its $g_*$-length. Therefore \[  d_0(\pi (a_ r),\pi (b_ r))\geq d_*(a_ r,b_ r)\longrightarrow c.  \] For any fixed $\delta >0$, these two images lie in $V_\delta $ when $r<\delta $. Taking the supremum and then $r\downarrow 0$ gives its punctured diameter at least $c$. $\square$

text: 14.19 Symmetry and the selected projective limit Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form and $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, a nonzero density. When the normalized equation $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has several solutions, the positive-exponent equations $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ still have unique solutions, and their normalized limits as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ single out particular solutions of the normalized equation. We study this selection in the projective example of theorem 11.6.1 , whose density vanishes on an open band. The starting point is a general observation: uniqueness at positive exponent preserves the symmetries of the data, and uniform compactness carries them to every normalized cluster limit. For the projective data this already gives a solution distinct from the two smooth solutions exchanged by the involution. The radial form of the equation then identifies the selected limit (theorem 14.19.3 ) and shows that the positive-exponent solutions fail to be $C^2$ along the same hypersurfaces (proposition 14.19.5 ). Proposition 14.19.1 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$, let $\mathrm{d}V$ be a smooth positive volume form, and let $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero. Let $c>0$ be the unique scalar for the bounded equation $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ (theorem 10.1.1 ). For $\lambda >0$ denote by $u_\lambda $ the unique bounded solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad a_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda .  \] The family $\{ a_\lambda :0<\lambda \leq 1\} $ is relatively compact in $C(X)$. Every cluster limit as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ is a normalized bounded solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Suppose a group $G$ of biholomorphisms of $X$ preserves $\omega $ and the measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Then every $a_\lambda $ and every such cluster limit is $G$-invariant. In particular, the zero-exponent equation has a $G$-invariant normalized solution. Proof. The barriers of proposition 10.6.1 give a uniform oscillation bound for $u_\lambda $ and uniform convergence $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }\to c$. Thus the equation densities are uniformly bounded in $L^ p$ for $0<\lambda \leq 1$ and tend to $cf$ in $L^ p$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Apply theorem 10.3.4 to obtain relative compactness of $a_\lambda $ in $C(X)$ and the asserted equation for every cluster limit. For each $g\in G$, pullback of the positive-exponent equation shows that $u_\lambda \circ g$ solves the same equation. Its uniqueness gives $u_\lambda \circ g=u_\lambda $. Surjectivity of $g$ preserves the supremum, so $a_\lambda \circ g=a_\lambda $. Uniform convergence preserves these equalities for every $g$. Compactness gives at least one cluster limit as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, yielding the invariant solution. $\square$ Corollary 14.19.2 . On $\mathbb P(\mathbb C^2\oplus \mathbb C^2)$, with block homogeneous coordinates $[A:B]$, the data in theorem 11.6.1 can be chosen so that the same zero-exponent equation has at least three distinct normalized bounded solutions. Two are smooth, and a third is Hölder continuous and fixed by the involution $\iota [A:B]=[B:A]$. Proof. Use the radial coordinate $r$, rank-one forms $P,Q,R$, Fubini–Study form $\omega _ X$, and scalar functions $F,x,y,z$ from 11.6.1 , 11.6.2 . Set $w=F(r)$, $\omega _0=xP+yQ+zR$, $H=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w/2$, $A_0=\omega _0-H$ and $B_0=\omega _0+H$ as in 11.6.3 . The Hermitian form is $\omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $, with $\rho =\varepsilon (r^2-1)\kappa (r)$ from 11.6.4 . Choose the cutoff $\kappa $ even; all its required support and plateau properties are preserved by this choice. Then $\rho $ is even, while $w=F(r)$ is odd. The involution sends $r$ to $-r$, interchanges $P,Q$, and fixes $R$. The coefficient identities $x(-r)=y(r)$ and $z(-r)=z(r)$ show that $\iota ^*\omega _0=\omega _0$. Thus $\iota ^*\omega =\omega $, and $\iota ^*\omega _ X=\omega _ X$. Since $\iota ^*H=-H$, the involution interchanges $A_0$ and $B_0$. Their cubes are equal, so $f\omega _ X^3$ is invariant. It also interchanges $\widetilde u=-w/2-\rho $ and $\widetilde v=w/2-\rho $. These functions therefore have the same supremum, and the normalized solutions $u,v$ are interchanged. They are distinct, so neither is invariant. Apply proposition 14.19.1 to the group generated by $\iota $. Here $c=1$, as the two constructed solutions already have that scalar. An invariant cluster solution $a$ cannot equal either $u$ or $v$. Its bounded equation with smooth density gives Hölder regularity by theorem 14.4.1 . This gives a third solution. Its regularity is determined in section 14.19.1 , section 14.19.2 : it is $C^{1,1}$ but not $C^2$. $\square$ To identify the whole normalized limit for these symmetric data, we now use the radial form of the equation. It determines the invariant solution even among bounded potentials whose differentiability is not known in advance.

14.19.1 The invariant projective solution We keep the symmetric projective data of corollary 14.19.2 . Thus $X=\mathbb P^3$ with block coordinates $[A:B]$ and Fubini–Study form $\omega _ X$; on $U=\{ A
e 0,\  B
e 0\} $ we use the radial coordinate $r$, the rank-one forms $P,Q,R$ and the coefficients $x,y,z,p,z_0$ of 11.6.1 , 11.6.2 . The function $ho (r)$ is the even correction of 11.6.4 , not a barrier, and $\omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho $ is the resulting Hermitian form, with $\omega _0=xP+yQ+zR$; the density $f$ is that of theorem 11.6.1 . Let $K$ be the group generated by the block unitary group $U(2)	imes U(2)$ and the exchange $\iota [A:B]=[B:A]$. Both preserve $\omega $ and $f\omega _ X^3$. Denote by $u_*$ the normalized $\iota $-invariant solution of proposition 11.6.2 , given by the symmetric transition pair $(-t_*,t_*)$. Theorem 14.19.3 . For the symmetric projective data, $u_*$ is the unique normalized bounded $K$-invariant solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=f\omega _ X^3.  \] If $u_\lambda $ is the unique solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda ) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\omega _ X^3,\qquad \lambda >0,  \] then \[  u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda \longrightarrow u_* \quad \hbox{uniformly as }\lambda \downarrow 0.  \] The selected limit $u_*$ is $C^{1,1}$. Uniqueness holds only within the $K$-invariant class: by proposition 11.6.2 , the same equation has uncountably many normalized solutions. Since a cluster limit is a priori only bounded, the proof needs the radial form of the equation for bounded invariant solutions, which we derive first. For a real scalar $s$, define the coefficient polynomial $A(r,s)$ and its primitive $\Phi (r,s)$ by \[  A(r,s)=(x(r)+s)(y(r)-s),\qquad \Phi (r,s)=\int _0^ s A(r,t)\, \mathrm{d}t.  \] Partial derivatives of $\Phi $ with respect to $r$ below keep $s$ fixed. Lemma 14.19.4 . Suppose $u$ is a bounded block-unitary-invariant solution of the zero-exponent equation. On $U$ write $u+ho =G(r)$. Then $G$ is locally Lipschitz, its derivative $h=G'$ has locally bounded variation, and its one-sided representatives satisfy \[  -x(r)\leq h(r\pm )\leq y(r),\qquad \mathrm{d}h+z\, \mathrm{d}r\geq 0.  \] In fact $h$ is continuous. With \[  k(r)= egin{cases} 0,& |r|\leq 1,\ x(r)y(r)z(r),& |r|>1,\end{cases}  \] it satisfies the distributional identity on $\mathbb R$ 14.67  egin{equation} \label{eq:numa-flux-identity} \mathrm{d} igl (\Phi (r,h(r)) igr ) = igl (k(r)-A(r,h(r))z(r) +\partial _ r\Phi (r,h(r)) igr )\, \mathrm{d}r. \end{equation} On every open interval where $A(r,h(r))>0$, $h$ is smooth and \[  h'= rac{k(r)}{A(r,h)}-z.  \] Proof. Reduction to one variable. Block-unitary orbits in $U$ are exactly the level sets of $r$: normalize the sum of the squared norms of the two coordinate blocks, and map the two vectors of the same respective lengths by their unitary groups. Thus invariance gives a function $G$ of one real variable. On a compact $r$-interval, the radial direction annihilates $P,Q$, while $R$ is strictly positive in that direction. Testing positivity of $\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G(r)$ in this direction gives $G''+z\geq 0$ as a one-dimensional distribution. One may obtain this first by smooth approximation of the scalar distribution and then by testing with nonnegative functions. Adding a twice integrated primitive of $z$ makes $G$ convex. A finite bounded convex function on an interval is locally Lipschitz, and its derivative is locally of bounded variation. The quasi-plurisubharmonic representative is the corresponding continuous representative. The horizontal directions give $x+h\geq 0$, $y-h\geq 0$ almost everywhere. Continuity of $x,y$ and the one-sided limits of a function of bounded variation give these bounds for both one-sided representatives. The radial inequality is precisely $\mathrm{d}h+z\, \mathrm{d}r\geq 0$; in particular jumps of $h$ can only be upward. The radial form of the measure. We next justify the formula for the measure, including possible jumps. Identify $U$ smoothly with $\mathbb R	imes Y$, where $Y=\{ r=0\} $, by real scaling of one block. The forms $P,Q$ are independent of $r$ in this identification. So is $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$: in local coordinates it is the angular differential of the relative complex scale plus fixed base terms. Therefore \[  P\wedge Q\wedge R=\mathrm{d}r\wedge 
u ,  \] where $
u $ is a fixed smooth positive volume form on the compact orbit $Y$, with the orientation chosen by this equality. For smooth $G$, the rank-one wedge formula gives the radial coefficient of its Monge–Ampère measure, after dividing by $6
u $, as \[  A(r,h)(z+h')\, \mathrm{d}r =A(r,h)z\, \mathrm{d}r+\mathrm{d} igl (\Phi (r,h) igr ) -\partial _ r\Phi (r,h)\, \mathrm{d}r.  \] This identity passes to a locally Lipschitz $G$ with the preceding lower Hessian bound. Indeed, convolve $G$ on a slightly larger compact interval. The derivatives $h_\epsilon $ are uniformly bounded and converge to $h$ almost everywhere and in every finite $L^ q$ space. Their second derivatives have a uniform lower bound. Consequently the functions $G_\epsilon (r)$ have a common quasi-plurisubharmonic lower Hessian bound on compact subsets of $U$, and converge uniformly to $G(r)$. A fixed smooth local correction and bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity give convergence of their signed products. On the right-hand side of the formula, the two ordinary terms converge in $L^1$, and $\Phi (r,h_\epsilon )	o \Phi (r,h)$ in $L^1$, giving distributional convergence of its derivative. This proves the same formula for the bounded product of $G$. Continuity of $h$. After the same division by $6
u $, the right-hand side $f\omega _ X^3$ has radial coefficient $k(r)\, \mathrm{d}r$. This gives ( 14.67 ), initially for the almost-everywhere representative of $h$. If $h$ jumped at $r_0$, the atom of its left side would be \[  \Phi (r_0,h(r_0+))-\Phi (r_0,h(r_0-)) =\int _{h(r_0-)}^{h(r_0+)}(x(r_0)+s)(y(r_0)-s)\, \mathrm{d}s.  \] The right side has no atom. An upward jump of positive size lies in $[-x(r_0),y(r_0)]$, where the integrand is strictly positive in the interior. Since $x+y>0$ everywhere, such an integral is strictly positive. Thus there are no jumps. A locally bounded-variation function whose jumps all vanish has a continuous representative here: its distributional derivative consists of an absolutely continuous measure and a nonnegative singular measure, so its one-sided representatives coincide at every point. We henceforth use this representative. In particular $G$ is $C^1$ and $G'=h$ everywhere. All coefficients on the right of ( 14.67 ) are now continuous, so $\Phi (r,h(r))$ is $C^1$. Where $\partial _ s\Phi =A>0$, the implicit function theorem gives $h\in C^1$ and the stated ordinary differential equation. Smoothness then follows by the smooth coefficients of that equation. The function $k$ is smooth, since the original density and its flat joins are smooth. $\square$ of theorem 14.19.3 . We first show that a normalized bounded $K$-invariant solution $u$ coincides with $u_*$, by computing its slope $h$ on the band $|r|\leq 1$ and outside it. Apply lemma 14.19.4 . Because $ho $ and $u$ are invariant under block exchange, $G$ is even, so $h$ is odd and $h(0)=0$. The slope on the band. On $0<r<1$ we have $x=p>0$ and $y=p+b\geq p>0$. Starting from zero, as long as $-p<h<y$, the equation is $h'=-z_0$. Thus $h(r)=-\int _0^ r z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$. This decreasing function cannot meet the positive upper boundary $y$. Its first meeting with the lower boundary $-p$ occurs at the unique $t_*\in (0,1)$ satisfying \[  \int _0^{t_*}z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s=p(t_*),  \] whose existence and uniqueness were proved in proposition 11.6.2 . After that meeting, $h$ must stay on $-p$ until $r=1$. To prove it, suppose a connected component $(a_0,b_0)$ of $\{ h+p>0\} $ lies to its right. Its left endpoint has $a_0\geq t_*$ and $h(a_0)=-p(a_0)<0$. Near that endpoint, $h<0<y$; hence on the component the interior equation applies for as long as $h<0$. It forces $h'=-z_0<0$, so $h$ cannot first reach zero. The equation therefore holds throughout the component. But then \[  (h+p)'=p'-z_0<0,  \] contradicting positivity of $h+p$ immediately to the right of its zero at $a_0$. Thus $h=-p$ on $[t_*,1]$. Oddness determines the entire negative half of the band. The slope on $[-1,1]$ is exactly that of the symmetric explicit solution. The slope outside the band. Here boundedness of $u$ at the projective ends matters. On $r>1$, $k=xyz>0$. Neither horizontal coefficient can vanish at a finite point of this interval. For the lower one define \[  \Psi (r)=\int _{-x(r)}^{h(r)}A(r,s)\, \mathrm{d}s\geq 0.  \] Equation ( 14.67 ) and the smooth lower endpoint show that $\Psi $ is $C^1$. If $h(r_0)=-x(r_0)$, its derivative at that point is $k(r_0)>0$: the $Az$ term vanishes, and the two partial-$r$ terms agree at the common endpoint. This contradicts that the nonnegative $C^1$ function $\Psi $ has an interior minimum zero there. The upper-endpoint integral $\int _{h(r)}^{y(r)}A(r,s)\, \mathrm{d}s$ gives the same contradiction, with derivative $-k(r_0)$, when $h=y$. Thus $-x<h<y$ everywhere on $r>1$, and the smooth ordinary differential equation of the lemma applies. For $r\geq 2$ the background is Fubini–Study: \[  x=\sigma ,\qquad y=1-\sigma ,\qquad z=\sigma ', \qquad \sigma = rac{\mathrm{e}^ r}{1+\mathrm{e}^ r}.  \] Set $a=\sigma +h\in (0,1)$. Its equation is \[  a(1-a)a'=\sigma (1-\sigma )\sigma '>0.  \] Hence $a$ is increasing and has a limit in $(0,1]$ at $+\infty $. If that limit were less than one, $h=a-\sigma $ would approach a negative constant and its primitive $G$ would be unbounded below, contrary to boundedness of $u$ and $ho $. The limit is therefore one. Integrating the equation gives \[   rac{a^2}{2}- rac{a^3}{3} = rac{\sigma ^2}{2}- rac{\sigma ^3}{3}+C.  \] Taking the limit at infinity gives $C=0$. The scalar function $s^2/2-s^3/3$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$, so $a=\sigma $ and $h=0$ for $r\geq 2$. Ordinary uniqueness propagates this zero solution throughout $r>1$, since the coefficients are smooth and the two horizontal coefficients stay positive there. Oddness gives $h=0$ on $r<-1$ as well. We have proved that $G'$ agrees everywhere with the symmetric explicit slope. Thus $u$ differs from $u_*$ by a constant on $U$. The two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions then agree up to that constant on $X$ by their canonical representatives. Their supremum normalization removes the constant. This proves uniqueness within the bounded $K$-invariant class. Convergence. Finally proposition 14.19.1 gives uniform precompactness of the normalized positive-exponent family. Every cluster limit solves the zero-exponent equation and is $K$-invariant, because the data are $K$-invariant. The scalar is one for these data. The uniqueness just proved identifies every cluster limit with $u_*$. If convergence of the whole family failed, a sequence staying a fixed positive uniform distance from $u_*$ would have a convergent subsequence, contradicting that identification. This proves uniform convergence and the asserted $C^{1,1}$ regularity of the limit. $\square$

For the symmetric projective data, $u_*$ is the unique normalized bounded $K$-invariant solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=f\omega _ X^3.  \] If $u_\lambda $ is the unique solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda ) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\omega _ X^3,\qquad \lambda >0,  \] then \[  u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda \longrightarrow u_* \quad \hbox{uniformly as }\lambda \downarrow 0.  \] The selected limit $u_*$ is $C^{1,1}$. of theorem 14.19.3 . We first show that a normalized bounded $K$-invariant solution $u$ coincides with $u_*$, by computing its slope $h$ on the band $|r|\leq 1$ and outside it. Apply lemma 14.19.4 . Because $\rho $ and $u$ are invariant under block exchange, $G$ is even, so $h$ is odd and $h(0)=0$. The slope on the band. On $0<r<1$ we have $x=p>0$ and $y=p+b\geq p>0$. Starting from zero, as long as $-p<h<y$, the equation is $h'=-z_0$. Thus $h(r)=-\int _0^ r z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$. This decreasing function cannot meet the positive upper boundary $y$. Its first meeting with the lower boundary $-p$ occurs at the unique $t_*\in (0,1)$ satisfying \[  \int _0^{t_*}z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s=p(t_*),  \] whose existence and uniqueness were proved in proposition 11.6.2 . After that meeting, $h$ must stay on $-p$ until $r=1$. To prove it, suppose a connected component $(a_0,b_0)$ of $\{ h+p>0\} $ lies to its right. Its left endpoint has $a_0\geq t_*$ and $h(a_0)=-p(a_0)<0$. Near that endpoint, $h<0<y$; hence on the component the interior equation applies for as long as $h<0$. It forces $h'=-z_0<0$, so $h$ cannot first reach zero. The equation therefore holds throughout the component. But then \[  (h+p)'=p'-z_0<0,  \] contradicting positivity of $h+p$ immediately to the right of its zero at $a_0$. Thus $h=-p$ on $[t_*,1]$. Oddness determines the entire negative half of the band. The slope on $[-1,1]$ is exactly that of the symmetric explicit solution. The slope outside the band. Here boundedness of $u$ at the projective ends matters. On $r>1$, $k=xyz>0$. Neither horizontal coefficient can vanish at a finite point of this interval. For the lower one define \[  \Psi (r)=\int _{-x(r)}^{h(r)}A(r,s)\, \mathrm{d}s\geq 0.  \] Equation ( 14.67 ) and the smooth lower endpoint show that $\Psi $ is $C^1$. If $h(r_0)=-x(r_0)$, its derivative at that point is $k(r_0)>0$: the $Az$ term vanishes, and the two partial-$r$ terms agree at the common endpoint. This contradicts that the nonnegative $C^1$ function $\Psi $ has an interior minimum zero there. The upper-endpoint integral $\int _{h(r)}^{y(r)}A(r,s)\, \mathrm{d}s$ gives the same contradiction, with derivative $-k(r_0)$, when $h=y$. Thus $-x<h<y$ everywhere on $r>1$, and the smooth ordinary differential equation of the lemma applies. For $r\geq 2$ the background is Fubini–Study: \[  x=\sigma ,\qquad y=1-\sigma ,\qquad z=\sigma ', \qquad \sigma =\frac{\mathrm{e}^ r}{1+\mathrm{e}^ r}.  \] Set $a=\sigma +h\in (0,1)$. Its equation is \[  a(1-a)a'=\sigma (1-\sigma )\sigma '>0.  \] Hence $a$ is increasing and has a limit in $(0,1]$ at $+\infty $. If that limit were less than one, $h=a-\sigma $ would approach a negative constant and its primitive $G$ would be unbounded below, contrary to boundedness of $u$ and $\rho $. The limit is therefore one. Integrating the equation gives \[  \frac{a^2}{2}-\frac{a^3}{3} =\frac{\sigma ^2}{2}-\frac{\sigma ^3}{3}+C.  \] Taking the limit at infinity gives $C=0$. The scalar function $s^2/2-s^3/3$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$, so $a=\sigma $ and $h=0$ for $r\geq 2$. Ordinary uniqueness propagates this zero solution throughout $r>1$, since the coefficients are smooth and the two horizontal coefficients stay positive there. Oddness gives $h=0$ on $r<-1$ as well. We have proved that $G'$ agrees everywhere with the symmetric explicit slope. Thus $u$ differs from $u_*$ by a constant on $U$. The two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions then agree up to that constant on $X$ by their canonical representatives. Their supremum normalization removes the constant. This proves uniqueness within the bounded $K$-invariant class. Convergence. Finally proposition 14.19.1 gives uniform precompactness of the normalized positive-exponent family. Every cluster limit solves the zero-exponent equation and is $K$-invariant, because the data are $K$-invariant. The scalar is one for these data. The uniqueness just proved identifies every cluster limit with $u_*$. If convergence of the whole family failed, a sequence staying a fixed positive uniform distance from $u_*$ would have a convergent subsequence, contradicting that identification. This proves uniform convergence and the asserted $C^{1,1}$ regularity of the limit. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.19.4
text:
Lemma 14.19.4 . Suppose $u$ is a bounded block-unitary-invariant solution of the zero-exponent equation. On $U$ write $u+ho =G(r)$. Then $G$ is locally Lipschitz, its derivative $h=G'$ has locally bounded variation, and its one-sided representatives satisfy \[  -x(r)\leq h(r\pm )\leq y(r),\qquad \mathrm{d}h+z\, \mathrm{d}r\geq 0.  \] In fact $h$ is continuous. With \[  k(r)= egin{cases} 0,& |r|\leq 1,\ x(r)y(r)z(r),& |r|>1,\end{cases}  \] it satisfies the distributional identity on $\mathbb R$ 14.67  egin{equation} \label{eq:numa-flux-identity} \mathrm{d} igl (\Phi (r,h(r)) igr ) = igl (k(r)-A(r,h(r))z(r) +\partial _ r\Phi (r,h(r)) igr )\, \mathrm{d}r. \end{equation} On every open interval where $A(r,h(r))>0$, $h$ is smooth and \[  h'= rac{k(r)}{A(r,h)}-z.  \] Proof. Reduction to one variable. Block-unitary orbits in $U$ are exactly the level sets of $r$: normalize the sum of the squared norms of the two coordinate blocks, and map the two vectors of the same respective lengths by their unitary groups. Thus invariance gives a function $G$ of one real variable. On a compact $r$-interval, the radial direction annihilates $P,Q$, while $R$ is strictly positive in that direction. Testing positivity of $\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G(r)$ in this direction gives $G''+z\geq 0$ as a one-dimensional distribution. One may obtain this first by smooth approximation of the scalar distribution and then by testing with nonnegative functions. Adding a twice integrated primitive of $z$ makes $G$ convex. A finite bounded convex function on an interval is locally Lipschitz, and its derivative is locally of bounded variation. The quasi-plurisubharmonic representative is the corresponding continuous representative. The horizontal directions give $x+h\geq 0$, $y-h\geq 0$ almost everywhere. Continuity of $x,y$ and the one-sided limits of a function of bounded variation give these bounds for both one-sided representatives. The radial inequality is precisely $\mathrm{d}h+z\, \mathrm{d}r\geq 0$; in particular jumps of $h$ can only be upward. The radial form of the measure. We next justify the formula for the measure, including possible jumps. Identify $U$ smoothly with $\mathbb R	imes Y$, where $Y=\{ r=0\} $, by real scaling of one block. The forms $P,Q$ are independent of $r$ in this identification. So is $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$: in local coordinates it is the angular differential of the relative complex scale plus fixed base terms. Therefore \[  P\wedge Q\wedge R=\mathrm{d}r\wedge 
u ,  \] where $
u $ is a fixed smooth positive volume form on the compact orbit $Y$, with the orientation chosen by this equality. For smooth $G$, the rank-one wedge formula gives the radial coefficient of its Monge–Ampère measure, after dividing by $6
u $, as \[  A(r,h)(z+h')\, \mathrm{d}r =A(r,h)z\, \mathrm{d}r+\mathrm{d} igl (\Phi (r,h) igr ) -\partial _ r\Phi (r,h)\, \mathrm{d}r.  \] This identity passes to a locally Lipschitz $G$ with the preceding lower Hessian bound. Indeed, convolve $G$ on a slightly larger compact interval. The derivatives $h_\epsilon $ are uniformly bounded and converge to $h$ almost everywhere and in every finite $L^ q$ space. Their second derivatives have a uniform lower bound. Consequently the functions $G_\epsilon (r)$ have a common quasi-plurisubharmonic lower Hessian bound on compact subsets of $U$, and converge uniformly to $G(r)$. u $, the right-hand side $f\omega _ X^3$ has radial coefficient $k(r)\, \mathrm{d}r$. This gives ( 14.67 ), initially for the almost-everywhere representative of $h$.
