title: 14.19.2 Second derivatives at positive exponent
text: 14.19.2 Second derivatives at positive exponent On the band where the density vanishes, the exponential factor plays no role, and the radial equation determines the slope of the solution independently of the exponent. Consequently the positive-exponent solutions have the same failure of second differentiability as the selected limit $u_*$. We keep the notation $A$, $\Phi $, $k$ and the transition radius $t_*$ of section 14.19.1 . Proposition 14.19.5 . For the symmetric projective data of theorem 14.19.3 , let $u_\lambda $ solve \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda ) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\omega _ X^3, \qquad \lambda >0.  \] On the open band $\{ -1<r<1\} $, $u_\lambda -u_*$ is constant. Both potentials are $C^{1,1}$ there and fail to be $C^2$ at every point of the two hypersurfaces $r=\pm t_*$. In particular, none of these positive-exponent solutions is a globally $C^2$ potential. Proof. Uniqueness and invariance of the data imply that $u_\lambda $ is $K$-invariant. Write $u_\lambda +\rho =G_\lambda (r)$ on $U$. The positivity argument in lemma 14.19.4 uses only boundedness and invariance, so $G_\lambda $ is locally Lipschitz and $h_\lambda =G_\lambda '$ is locally of bounded variation, with \[  -x\leq h_\lambda (r\pm )\leq y, \qquad \mathrm{d}h_\lambda +z\, \mathrm{d}r\geq 0.  \] Its weak flux equation is the same one, with the prescribed coefficient replaced by \[  k_\lambda (r)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (G_\lambda (r)-\rho (r))}k(r).  \] Indeed, the scalar convolution and signed-product argument of that lemma is unchanged, and $k_\lambda $ is exactly the radial coefficient of the right-hand measure. Since $G_\lambda $ is bounded on compact $r$-intervals, $k_\lambda $ is locally bounded. Hence the right side of the flux equation has no atoms. The same strictly positive jump integral eliminates every jump of $h_\lambda $. Thus $h_\lambda $ is continuous and $G_\lambda $ is $C^1$. The coefficient $k_\lambda $ is consequently continuous. Where $A(r,h_\lambda )>0$, inversion of the $C^1$ flux gives \[  h_\lambda '=\frac{k_\lambda (r)}{A(r,h_\lambda )}-z.  \] On $-1<r<1$ the coefficient $k_\lambda $ is identically zero. Exchange invariance gives $h_\lambda (0)=0$ and oddness. On the positive half-band, the first-contact and no-departure arguments in the proof of theorem 14.19.3 apply verbatim: the first branch solves $h'=-z_0$, reaches $-p$ at $t_*$, and cannot leave that lower boundary to its right because $(h+p)'=p'-z_0<0$ on every proposed departure interval. Therefore \[  h_\lambda (r)= \begin{cases}  p(r),& -1<r\leq -t_*,\\  -\displaystyle \int _0^ r z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s,& -t_*\leq r\leq t_*,\\  -p(r),& t_*\leq r<1. \end{cases}  \] This is the derivative of $u_*+\rho $. Its primitive differs from $G_\lambda $ by one constant on the connected band. The claimed local $C^{1,1}$ regularity follows from the explicit slope. At $t_*\in (0,1)$ the two one-sided derivatives of this slope are \[  h_\lambda '(t_*-)=-z_0(t_*)<0, \qquad h_\lambda '(t_*+)=-p'(t_*)>0.  \] These unequal derivatives prevent the scalar primitive from having a second derivative at $t_*$. Through every point of that level set, the submersion $r$ provides a smooth curve parametrized by $r$, transferring the failure to $u_\lambda $. Smooth $\rho $ cannot cancel the jump. Oddness gives the conclusion at $-t_*$, and the identical slope proves it for $u_*$. $\square$ The zero set of $f$ contains the whole band. This example therefore does not concern the smooth strictly positive densities in the Hermitian Calabi–Yau theorem. It does show why smoothness of a nonnegative density alone is insufficient for second-order regularity, even when the equation includes a strictly increasing exponential factor.

title: 14.20 Local density and boundary control
text: 14.20 Local density and boundary control Theorem 14.17.1 requires a smooth positive density on the whole regular locus of a global strict barrier, and the global minimum of the difference between the solution and the barrier drives its proof. If the density is smooth and positive only on a smaller open set, smoothness can fail there. A bounded solution with minimal singularities can be discontinuous on a ball where its density is constant (theorem 14.20.4 ), and a locally Lipschitz plurisubharmonic function with constant density need not be $C^1$ (example 14.20.5 ). Boundary data give a different route to regularity: if the solution has smooth boundary values on small balls, uniqueness for the bounded Dirichlet problem identifies it with the smooth Dirichlet solution. In this section $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\varepsilon >0$; in particular $\theta $ is big. We fix an open set $\Omega \subset X$ on which $\rho $ is smooth and $\mathrm{d}\theta =0$.

title: 14.20.1 Smooth boundary traces
text: 14.20.1 Smooth boundary traces Let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a coordinate ball. A function $u$ on $B$ has boundary trace $g$, a function on $\partial B$, if $u(z)\to g(\xi )$ as $B\ni z\to \xi $, for every $\xi \in \partial B$. Theorem 14.20.1 . Suppose that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal ordinary singularities and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V\quad \text{on }\Omega , \qquad f\in C^\infty (\Omega ),\quad f>0.  \] Assume that $\Omega $ is covered by coordinate Euclidean balls $B_ j\Subset \Omega $ such that $\theta $ has a smooth local potential near $\overline{B_ j}$ and $u$ has a smooth boundary trace on $\partial B_ j$. Then $u\in C^\infty (\Omega )$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ there. Proof. Since $\rho -\sup _ X\rho \leq V_\theta $, minimal singularities give $u\geq \rho -C$ for a constant $C$. Thus $u$ is locally bounded on $\Omega $. Fix one of the balls, write it as $B=B_ R(z_0)$, let $g$ be the boundary trace of $u$ on $\partial B$, and choose a smooth function $h$ near $\overline B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\theta $. By proposition 1.7.1 , the bounded plurisubharmonic function $v=u+h$ has Bedford–Taylor measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ and smooth boundary trace $\varphi =g+h|_{\partial B}$. For a smooth function $V$ and the Euclidean volume $\mathrm{d}\Lambda $, 14.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:local-density-determinant} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det (V_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm{d}\Lambda . \end{equation} The smooth Dirichlet theorem recalled in section 14.17.3 , with zero background and density $f\, \mathrm{d}V$, gives a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic $V$ on $\overline B$ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ and boundary value $\varphi $; a smooth extension $\Phi $ of $\varphi $ gives the required strict subsolution $\Phi +A(|z-z_0|^2-R^2)$ for large $A$. In dimension one this is the Dirichlet problem for the Poisson equation. The difference $v-V$ tends to zero at every boundary point. Compactness of $\partial B$ makes this convergence uniform near the boundary: otherwise a sequence approaching the boundary with difference bounded away from zero would have a subsequence approaching one fixed boundary point. Uniqueness for the bounded Dirichlet problem, that is, the Bedford–Taylor comparison principle, gives $v=V$. Therefore $u=V-h$ is smooth on $B$, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V>0$ there. Since the balls cover $\Omega $, the theorem follows. $\square$ The proof uses minimal singularities only to obtain the local lower bound by $\rho $. Consequently the same conclusion holds for any solution already known to be locally bounded on $\Omega $ and satisfying the same trace condition. Closedness of $\theta $ on $\Omega $ provides the local potentials $h$ once the coordinate balls are small enough; the background may be nonclosed elsewhere. Example 14.20.2 . For every $n\geq 1$, the trace criterion applies to a bounded continuous solution whose global density belongs to $L^1$ but to no $L^ p$ with $p>1$, and which is not Hölder continuous at the points of $X\setminus \Omega $. Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z)$, $X=E^ n$, and \[  \omega _ j=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j, \qquad \theta =\sum _{j=1}^ n\omega _ j, \qquad D=\{ 0\} \times E^{n-1}.  \] Take $\mathrm{d}V=\theta ^ n$ and $\rho =0$. Choose a nonnegative smooth cutoff $\chi $ supported in a coordinate disk $|z|<r_0<1$ of $E$ and equal to one near zero. For $\beta >0$, define \[  \psi (z)=\chi (z)(-\log |z|^2)^{-\beta }\quad (z\ne 0), \qquad \psi (0)=0,  \] and extend by zero. On the smaller punctured disk put $t=|z|^2$ and $L=-\log t$. Differentiation gives 14.72 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-logarithmic-profile} \psi _{z\bar z}=\frac{\beta (\beta +1)}{tL^{\beta +2}}, \qquad t\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}L^{-\beta } =\beta L^{-\beta -1}\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} The first expression is integrable and the second is the radial flux. Integration by parts on punctured disks, using also $\psi \to 0$, shows that the distributional Hessian has no atom at zero. On the cutoff annulus its negative part is bounded. Hence, for a sufficiently small fixed $\eta >0$, $u=\eta \psi (z_1)$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \theta /2$. Only one coordinate contributes to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Locally approximate the bounded subharmonic potential in that coordinate from above and use theorem 1.6.1 ; the smooth diagonal determinant identity passes to the limit and yields \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\theta ^ n, \qquad f=1+\eta \psi _{z\bar z}(z_1).  \] Give $f$ any positive value on the null set $D$. It is smooth and positive on $\Omega =X\setminus D$, where $u$ is smooth and has smooth traces on all relatively compact coordinate balls. Near $D$ its singular term is comparable to $|z_1|^{-2}(-\log |z_1|^2)^{-\beta -2}$. Its radial $L^1$ integral converges, whereas \[  \int _0^{r_0}s^{1-2p}(-\log s^2)^{-p(\beta +2)}\, \mathrm{d}s=+\infty \qquad (p>1).  \] Also $(-\log |z|^2)^{-\beta }/|z|^\alpha \to +\infty $ for every $\alpha >0$, so $u$ is not Hölder at $D$. Finally, boundedness gives minimal ordinary singularities, since every global $\theta $-plurisubharmonic competitor is bounded above.

title: Example 14.20.2
text: Example 14.20.2 . For every $n\geq 1$, the trace criterion applies to a bounded continuous solution whose global density belongs to $L^1$ but to no $L^ p$ with $p>1$, and which is not Hölder continuous at the points of $X\setminus \Omega $. For $\beta >0$, define \[  \psi (z)=\chi (z)(-\log |z|^2)^{-\beta }\quad (z\ne 0), \qquad \psi (0)=0,  \] and extend by zero. On the smaller punctured disk put $t=|z|^2$ and $L=-\log t$. Integration by parts on punctured disks, using also $\psi \to 0$, shows that the distributional Hessian has no atom at zero. On the cutoff annulus its negative part is bounded. Hence, for a sufficiently small fixed $\eta >0$, $u=\eta \psi (z_1)$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \theta /2$. Only one coordinate contributes to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Locally approximate the bounded subharmonic potential in that coordinate from above and use theorem 1.6.1 ; the smooth diagonal determinant identity passes to the limit and yields \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\theta ^ n, \qquad f=1+\eta \psi _{z\bar z}(z_1).  \] Give $f$ any positive value on the null set $D$. It is smooth and positive on $\Omega =X\setminus D$, where $u$ is smooth and has smooth traces on all relatively compact coordinate balls. Near $D$ its singular term is comparable to $|z_1|^{-2}(-\log |z_1|^2)^{-\beta -2}$. Its radial $L^1$ integral converges, whereas \[  \int _0^{r_0}s^{1-2p}(-\log s^2)^{-p(\beta +2)}\, \mathrm{d}s=+\infty \qquad (p>1).  \] Also $(-\log |z|^2)^{-\beta }/|z|^\alpha \to +\infty $ for every $\alpha >0$, so $u$ is not Hölder at $D$. Finally, boundedness gives minimal ordinary singularities, since every global $\theta $-plurisubharmonic competitor is bounded above.

title: 14.20.2 A bounded discontinuous potential
text: 14.20.2 A bounded discontinuous potential We construct a bounded plurisubharmonic function on a bidisk whose Monge–Ampère measure is a constant multiple of Lebesgue measure, but which is discontinuous. The construction places logarithmic poles with summable weights at points accumulating at the origin; the resulting weight $b$ vanishes at the poles but not at their limit. It is the local model for theorem 14.20.4 . Let $U=W=\{ |z|<1/4\} \subset \mathbb C$, with coordinates $z$ and $w$ on the two factors. Write $\mathrm{d}A$ for planar Lebesgue measure and set \[  a_ k=\alpha _ k=2^{-k-4},\qquad A=\sum _{k\geq 1}\alpha _ k=\frac1{16},\qquad S=\{ 0\} \cup \{ a_ k:k\geq 1\} .  \] Define on $U$ 14.73 \begin{equation} \label{eq:accumulating-polar-weight} h(z)=\sum _{k\geq 1}\alpha _ k\log |z-a_ k|^2, \qquad b(z)=\mathrm{e}^{h(z)}, \end{equation} with $b=0$ where $h=-\infty $. Lemma 14.20.3 . The function \[  a(z)=\frac1\pi \int _ U\log |z-\zeta |^2\, b(\zeta )^{-1}\, \mathrm{d}A(\zeta )  \] is bounded and continuous on $U$. The bounded function \[  P(z,w)=a(z)+b(z)|w|^2  \] is plurisubharmonic on $U\times W$, is smooth off $S\times W$, and satisfies 14.74 \begin{equation} \label{eq:discontinuous-constant-measure} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P)^2=\frac2{\pi ^2}\, \mathrm{d}A(z)\, \mathrm{d}A(w). \end{equation} It is discontinuous at every $(0,w_0)$ with $w_0\ne 0$. Proof. The summands defining $h$ are negative on $U$, so their partial sums decrease. Since $h(0)=2\sum _ k\alpha _ k\log a_ k> -\infty $, the limit is subharmonic. On compact subsets of $U\setminus S$, the series and its derivatives converge uniformly, making $h$ harmonic there. Moreover $0\leq b\leq 1$, $b(a_ k)=0$, and $b(0)>0$. Weighted arithmetic–geometric mean gives, almost everywhere, 14.75 \begin{equation} \label{eq:polar-reciprocal-integrability} b(z)^{-2}\leq \sum _{k\geq 1}\frac{\alpha _ k}{A}|z-a_ k|^{-4A}. \end{equation} For the countable inequality, first use the first $N$ weights and assign the remaining weight to the factor $1$; then let $N$ increase. Since $4A=1/4<2$, the integrals of the terms $|z-a_ k|^{-4A}$ on $U$ are bounded uniformly in $k$. Thus $b^{-1}\in L^2(U)$. The logarithmic kernel has uniformly bounded $L^2$ norm on the translates of $U$ that occur in the definition of $a$. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds $a$ uniformly. Choose a compactly supported $L^2(\mathbb C)$ kernel agreeing with $\log |z|^2$ on $U-U$. Translation continuity in $L^2$, paired with $b^{-1}\mathbf1_ U\in L^2$, proves continuity of $a$. The distribution identity $\partial _ z\partial _{\bar z}\log |z|^2=\pi \delta _0$ gives $a_{z\bar z}=b^{-1}$. In particular $a$ is subharmonic and, by local elliptic regularity, smooth off $S$. The second summand of $P$ is $\exp (h(z)+\log |w|^2)$, a convex increasing composition of a plurisubharmonic function, extended by zero at its poles. Thus $P$ is bounded and plurisubharmonic. At smooth points the harmonicity of $h=\log b$ gives $bb_{z\bar z}=|b_ z|^2$, and hence \[  \det (P_{j\bar k}) =ba_{z\bar z}+|w|^2\bigl (bb_{z\bar z}-|b_ z|^2\bigr )=1.  \] The set $S\times W$ is contained in the pole set of $h(z)+\log |z|$, a plurisubharmonic function not identically $-\infty $. It is also Lebesgue-null. Pluripolar nullity in theorem 1.6.1 and ( 14.71 ) prove ( 14.74 ) throughout the bidisk. Finally, \[  P(a_ k,w_0)=a(a_ k)\longrightarrow a(0) <a(0)+b(0)|w_0|^2=P(0,w_0)  \] when $w_0\ne 0$. $\square$

title: 14.20.3 Compact gluing
text:
14.20.3 Compact gluing We now glue the local example into a compact torus by a regularized maximum with a quadratic function. The result is a bounded solution with minimal singularities whose density is constant on a ball, where the solution is discontinuous; in the transition region the density acquires singularities that destroy every $L^ p$ bound with $p>1$. We work on the flat complex torus $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z))^2$, identifying a small coordinate ball with a ball in $U	imes W$. For a smooth function $v$ on the ball write $H_ v=(v_{j ar k})$ for its complex Hessian and $I$ for the two-dimensional identity matrix. Theorem 14.20.4 . There are a positive flat Kähler form $	heta $ on $X$, a bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with minimal ordinary singularities, and a density $F>0$ almost everywhere such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=F	heta ^2,\qquad F\in L^1(X,	heta ^2),\qquad F
otin L^ p(X,	heta ^2)\quad (p>1).  \] On an open coordinate ball $\Omega $, $F$ is a positive constant and $u$ is discontinuous. The constant function $ho =0$ is a smooth strict barrier on $X$. Proof. Set $R=1/8$ and choose $M$ so that $P_0=P+M$ satisfies $0\leq P_0\leq L$ on $B_ R\Subset U	imes W$ for some finite $L$. Choose $C>0$ with 14.76  egin{equation} \label{eq:compact-gluing-collar}  rac{3CR^2}{16}\geq 2,\qquad  rac{5CR^2}{16}>L+2, \end{equation} and put $Q(Z)=C(|Z|^2-R^2/4)$ for $Z=(z,w)$. Let $\chi $ be the convolution of $|t|$ with an even nonnegative smooth probability kernel supported in $(-1,1)$. Then $\chi $ is smooth and convex, $|\chi '|\leq 1$, $\chi '(0)=0$, and $\chi (t)=|t|$ for $|t|\geq 1$. The function \[  m(s,t)= rac{s+t+\chi (s-t)}2,\qquad v=m(P_0,Q)  \] is bounded and plurisubharmonic, because $m$ is convex and nondecreasing in each variable. The collar inequalities imply \[  v=P_0\quad 	ext{on }B_{R/4},\qquad v=Q\quad 	ext{when }3R/4\leq |Z|<R.  \] Indeed, $Q\leq -2\leq P_0-2$ on the first ball and $Q>L+2\geq P_0+2$ on the collar. Define \[  	heta = rac{\mathrm{i}C}{2\pi } (\mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d} ar z+\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm{d} ar w), \qquad u= egin{cases} v-Q& 	ext{on }B_ R,\ 0& 	ext{outside }B_ R.\end{cases}  \] The collar identity makes $u$ identically zero near $\partial B_ R$ and gives a global bounded potential with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ on the ball and $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=	heta $ outside. Thus $u$ is admissible and has minimal ordinary singularities. Outside the pluripolar set $(S	imes W)\cap B_ R$, set $\lambda =(1+\chi '(P_0-Q))/2$. Differentiating the regularized maximum gives 14.79  egin{equation} \label{eq:regularized-max-hessian-density} H_ v=\lambda H_ P+(1-\lambda )CI + rac{\chi ''(P_0-Q)}2 \partial (P_0-Q)\otimes \overline{\partial (P_0-Q)}. \end{equation} Both $H_ P$ and $CI$ are positive definite there; the final term is positive semidefinite. Hence the classical density is positive. Bounded products charge no pluripolar sets, so there is no further measure on the exceptional set. Their mass on compact $X$ is finite by proposition 1.7.1 . This proves $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=F	heta ^2$ for an almost-everywhere positive $F\in L^1$. On $\Omega =B_{R/4}$, ( 14.74 ) gives the representative $F=C^{-2}$. There $u=P+M-Q$ is discontinuous at $(0,w_0)$ for $0<|w_0|<R/4$. We prove failure of every global $L^ p$ directly in the transition region. For large $k$, set \[  m_ k=a(a_ k)+M\in [0,L],\qquad w_ k= igl (R^2/4+m_ k/C-|a_ k|^2 igr )^{1/2}, \qquad Z_ k=(a_ k,w_ k).  \] Then $w_ k>0$, $P_0(Z_ k)=Q(Z_ k)=m_ k$, and ( 14.76 ) gives $|Z_ k|^2<9R^2/16$. Near the isolated pole $a_ k$, \[  h(z)=\alpha _ k\log |z-a_ k|^2+H_ k(z),  \] where $H_ k$ is smooth and harmonic. Consequently $b$ and $P_0$ are continuous near $Z_ k$. There is a product neighborhood $V_ k\Subset B_ R$ of $Z_ k$, with $|w|$ bounded below by a positive number, on which $1/4\leq \lambda \leq 3/4$. At smooth points of $V_ k$, positivity and the two-dimensional determinant expansion give \[   egin{split}  \det H_ v& \geq \det  igl (\lambda H_ P+(1-\lambda )CI igr )\ & \geq \lambda (1-\lambda )C\operatorname {tr}H_ P \geq c_ k b_{z ar z}, \end{split}  \] where $c_ k>0$ may depend on $k$ and $C$. Here $P_{z ar z}=b^{-1}+|w|^2b_{z ar z}$. With $\zeta =z-a_ k$, shrink the first factor of $V_ k$ so that \[  b_{z ar z}=|\zeta |^{2\alpha _ k}\mathrm{e}^{H_ k} \left| rac{\alpha _ k}{\zeta }+\partial _ zH_ kight|^2 \geq c'_ k|\zeta |^{2\alpha _ k-2}  \] for some $c'_ k>0$. Since $F=C^{-2}\det H_ v$, this lower bound implies $F
otin L^ p$ whenever $p(1-\alpha _ k)\geq 1$: the $w$-disk has positive area and the radial integral in $z$ contains \[  \int _0^{\delta _ k}r^{1-2p(1-\alpha _ k)}\, \mathrm{d}r=+\infty .  \] For each $p>1$ such a $k$ exists because $\alpha _ k\downarrow 0$. $\square$ The bounded-product capacity estimate in section 1.6 also holds for the discontinuous potential $P$. Thus a first-order capacity bound, even together with a constant positive density, cannot supply the missing boundary control. Example 14.20.5 . On the bidisk in $\mathbb C^2$ with coordinates $(z,w)$, the function \[  H(z,w)=2|z|(1+|w|^2)  \] is locally Lipschitz, plurisubharmonic and not $C^1$ along $\{ z=0\} $. Plurisubharmonicity follows by writing its two summands as convex exponential compositions of $\log |z|$ and $\log |z|+\log |w|^2$. At $z
e 0$, \[  H_{z ar z}= rac{1+|w|^2}{2|z|},\qquad H_{w ar w}=2|z|,\qquad |H_{z ar w}|^2=|w|^2.  \] Hence $\det (H_{j ar k})=1$, and pluripolar nullity gives $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^2=2\pi ^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}\Lambda $ on the entire bidisk. The last example rules out a purely local implication from Hölder continuity and a smooth positive density to smoothness; being local, it says nothing about the global hypotheses of theorem 14.17.1 . Nor does theorem 14.20.4 contradict that theorem: there the solution is not locally Hölder continuous on the ball $\Omega $, and its density is not smooth on the rest of $X$, which is the regular locus of the barrier $ho =0$. The trace criterion of theorem 14.20.1 avoids both global hypotheses by identifying the bounded solution with a smooth Dirichlet solution on each ball.

title: Theorem 14.20.4
text: Theorem 14.20.4 . There are a positive flat Kähler form $\theta $ on $X$, a bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with minimal ordinary singularities, and a density $F>0$ almost everywhere such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=F\theta ^2,\qquad F\in L^1(X,\theta ^2),\qquad F\notin L^ p(X,\theta ^2)\quad (p>1).  \] On an open coordinate ball $\Omega $, $F$ is a positive constant and $u$ is discontinuous. The constant function $\rho =0$ is a smooth strict barrier on $X$. Proof. Set $R=1/8$ and choose $M$ so that $P_0=P+M$ satisfies $0\leq P_0\leq L$ on $B_ R\Subset U\times W$ for some finite $L$. Choose $C>0$ with 14.76 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-gluing-collar} \frac{3CR^2}{16}\geq 2,\qquad \frac{5CR^2}{16}>L+2, \end{equation} and put $Q(Z)=C(|Z|^2-R^2/4)$ for $Z=(z,w)$. Let $\chi $ be the convolution of $|t|$ with an even nonnegative smooth probability kernel supported in $(-1,1)$. Then $\chi $ is smooth and convex, $|\chi '|\leq 1$, $\chi '(0)=0$, and $\chi (t)=|t|$ for $|t|\geq 1$. The function \[  m(s,t)=\frac{s+t+\chi (s-t)}2,\qquad v=m(P_0,Q)  \] is bounded and plurisubharmonic, because $m$ is convex and nondecreasing in each variable. The collar inequalities imply \[  v=P_0\quad \text{on }B_{R/4},\qquad v=Q\quad \text{when }3R/4\leq |Z|<R.  \] Indeed, $Q\leq -2\leq P_0-2$ on the first ball and $Q>L+2\geq P_0+2$ on the collar. Define \[  \theta =\frac{\mathrm{i}C}{2\pi } (\mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z+\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w), \qquad u=\begin{cases} v-Q& \text{on }B_ R,\\ 0& \text{outside }B_ R.\end{cases}  \] The collar identity makes $u$ identically zero near $\partial B_ R$ and gives a global bounded potential with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ on the ball and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\theta $ outside. Thus $u$ is admissible and has minimal ordinary singularities. Outside the pluripolar set $(S\times W)\cap B_ R$, set $\lambda =(1+\chi '(P_0-Q))/2$. Differentiating the regularized maximum gives 14.79 \begin{equation} \label{eq:regularized-max-hessian-density} H_ v=\lambda H_ P+(1-\lambda )CI +\frac{\chi ''(P_0-Q)}2 \partial (P_0-Q)\otimes \overline{\partial (P_0-Q)}. \end{equation} Both $H_ P$ and $CI$ are positive definite there; the final term is positive semidefinite. Hence the classical density is positive. Bounded products charge no pluripolar sets, so there is no further measure on the exceptional set. Their mass on compact $X$ is finite by proposition 1.7.1 . This proves $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=F\theta ^2$ for an almost-everywhere positive $F\in L^1$. On $\Omega =B_{R/4}$, ( 14.74 ) gives the representative $F=C^{-2}$. There $u=P+M-Q$ is discontinuous at $(0,w_0)$ for $0<|w_0|<R/4$. We prove failure of every global $L^ p$ directly in the transition region. For large $k$, set \[  m_ k=a(a_ k)+M\in [0,L],\qquad w_ k=\bigl (R^2/4+m_ k/C-|a_ k|^2\bigr )^{1/2}, \qquad Z_ k=(a_ k,w_ k).  \] Then $w_ k>0$, $P_0(Z_ k)=Q(Z_ k)=m_ k$, and ( 14.76 ) gives $|Z_ k|^2<9R^2/16$. Near the isolated pole $a_ k$, \[  h(z)=\alpha _ k\log |z-a_ k|^2+H_ k(z),  \] where $H_ k$ is smooth and harmonic. Consequently $b$ and $P_0$ are continuous near $Z_ k$. There is a product neighborhood $V_ k\Subset B_ R$ of $Z_ k$, with $|w|$ bounded below by a positive number, on which $1/4\leq \lambda \leq 3/4$. At smooth points of $V_ k$, positivity and the two-dimensional determinant expansion give \[  \begin{split}  \det H_ v& \geq \det \bigl (\lambda H_ P+(1-\lambda )CI\bigr )\\ & \geq \lambda (1-\lambda )C\operatorname {tr}H_ P \geq c_ k b_{z\bar z}, \end{split}  \] where $c_ k>0$ may depend on $k$ and $C$. Here $P_{z\bar z}=b^{-1}+|w|^2b_{z\bar z}$. With $\zeta =z-a_ k$, shrink the first factor of $V_ k$ so that \[  b_{z\bar z}=|\zeta |^{2\alpha _ k}\mathrm{e}^{H_ k} \left|\frac{\alpha _ k}{\zeta }+\partial _ zH_ k\right|^2 \geq c'_ k|\zeta |^{2\alpha _ k-2}  \] for some $c'_ k>0$. Since $F=C^{-2}\det H_ v$, this lower bound implies $F\notin L^ p$ whenever $p(1-\alpha _ k)\geq 1$: the $w$-disk has positive area and the radial integral in $z$ contains \[  \int _0^{\delta _ k}r^{1-2p(1-\alpha _ k)}\, \mathrm{d}r=+\infty .  \] For each $p>1$ such a $k$ exists because $\alpha _ k\downarrow 0$. $\square$
14.76 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-gluing-collar} \frac{3CR^2}{16}\geq 2,\qquad \frac{5CR^2}{16}>L+2, \end{equation}
14.79 \begin{equation} \label{eq:regularized-max-hessian-density} H_ v=\lambda H_ P+(1-\lambda )CI +\frac{\chi ''(P_0-Q)}2 \partial (P_0-Q)\otimes \overline{\partial (P_0-Q)}. \end{equation}

title: Example 14.20.5
text: Example 14.20.5 . On the bidisk in $\mathbb C^2$ with coordinates $(z,w)$, the function \[  H(z,w)=2|z|(1+|w|^2)  \] is locally Lipschitz, plurisubharmonic and not $C^1$ along $\{ z=0\} $. Plurisubharmonicity follows by writing its two summands as convex exponential compositions of $\log |z|$ and $\log |z|+\log |w|^2$. At $z\ne 0$, \[  H_{z\bar z}=\frac{1+|w|^2}{2|z|},\qquad H_{w\bar w}=2|z|,\qquad |H_{z\bar w}|^2=|w|^2.  \] Hence $\det (H_{j\bar k})=1$, and pluripolar nullity gives $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^2=2\pi ^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}\Lambda $ on the entire bidisk.

title: 14.21 Equations with resolved logarithmic poles
text: 14.21 Equations with resolved logarithmic poles We now prescribe a singularity type with logarithmic poles. If the poles become a divisor on a modification, the singular part can be removed there, and what remains is a smooth residual form. When this residual form is strictly positive, the bounded Hermitian theory on the modification provides the remaining bounded potential, and pushing forward solves the equation in the prescribed type. In this section $n\geq 2$, and the background is a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$. Let $\psi \leq 0$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function that is smooth outside a nonempty analytic set $A$, its pole set. Assume that there is a modification $\pi :Y\to X$, biholomorphic over $X\setminus A$, such that $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is the support $|D|$ of a simple normal crossing divisor $D=\sum _ jD_ j$ and 14.82 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-type} \psi \circ \pi =\sum _ j c_ j\log |s_ j|^2+b, \qquad \beta =\pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b-\sum _ jc_ j\Theta _ j>0, \end{equation} where $c_ j>0$, $b$ is smooth on $Y$, $s_ j$ is a holomorphic section of $\mathcal O(D_ j)$ defining $D_ j$, and $\Theta _ j$ is the curvature form of a smooth Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O(D_ j)$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_ j|^2=[D_ j]-\Theta _ j$. Thus $\beta $ is the smooth part of the current $\pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi \circ \pi )$, which we call the residual form . Theorem 14.21.1 . For every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p(X,h^ n)$, $p>1$, there are $\kappa >0$ and a normalized $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ such that 14.83 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-equation} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=\kappa f h^ n, \qquad u=\psi +O(1). \end{equation} The lifted remainder $v=(u-\psi )\circ \pi $ extends Hölder continuously over $Y$, so $u$ is locally Hölder on $X\setminus A$. Its current is 14.84 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-current} \pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ) =\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]+\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v. \end{equation} The positive residual current $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ has zero Lelong numbers. If $h$ is Kähler, then $\kappa =\int _ Y\beta ^ n/\int _ X f h^ n$, and the normalized solution is unique among all normalized solutions $u'$ of ( 14.83 ) with $u'=\psi +O(1)$, continuous or not. If the density $g=(f\circ \pi )\, \pi ^*h^ n/\beta ^ n$ is smooth and strictly positive on $Y$, the residual current $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ may be chosen smooth and strictly positive. Proof. Define $J=\pi ^*h^ n/\beta ^ n$ and $g=(f\circ \pi )J$ off the exceptional set, assigning any value to $g$ on that volume-zero set. The smooth nonnegative $J$ is bounded. Change of variables on the biholomorphic locus gives 14.85 \begin{equation} \label{eq:prescribed-transport} \int _ Yg\beta ^ n=\int _ Xfh^ n, \qquad \int _ Yg^ p\beta ^ n\leq \| J\| _\infty ^{p-1}\int _ Xf^ ph^ n. \end{equation} Thus $g$ is a nonzero $L^ p$ density. Theorem 10.1.1 , Theorem 14.4.1 give a bounded Hölder $\beta $-plurisubharmonic $v$ and $\kappa >0$ with $(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=\kappa g\beta ^ n$. If $h$ is Kähler, then $\beta $ is Kähler and the mass identity fixes the stated scalar. For smooth positive $g$, theorem 9.1.1 gives a smooth solution instead. Set $u=\psi +v\circ \pi ^{-1}$ on $X\setminus A$ and $u=-\infty $ on $A$. Push forward the positive current $\sum c_ j[D_ j]+\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. Pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, $\pi _*\pi ^*h=h$, and the pushed locally integrable potential is $u$ almost everywhere. Its quasi-plurisubharmonic representative equals $\psi +v\circ \pi ^{-1}$ off $A$ and tends to $-\infty $ at $A$ because $v$ is bounded. Hence $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ and $u=\psi +O(1)$ in the two-sided ordinary sense. The pulled-back identity is ( 14.84 ); bounded residuals have zero Lelong number. The equation holds off $A$ by ( 14.85 ), and theorem 6.1.2 extends it as ( 14.83 ). Subtracting $\sup _ Xu$ changes neither the equation nor the ordinary type. For uniqueness when $h$ is Kähler, let $u'$ be a normalized solution with $u'=\psi +O(1)$. On $Y\setminus D$, $w=(u'-\psi )\circ \pi $ is bounded and $\beta $-plurisubharmonic. Since $w$ is bounded, lemma 1.3.7 extends it across $D$ to a bounded $\beta $-plurisubharmonic function on $Y$. On each relatively compact subset of $Y\setminus D$, sufficiently deep truncations of $u'$ equal $u'$. Thus locality in theorem 6.1.2 gives the bounded equation $\kappa g\beta ^ n$ there; both sides give $D$ zero mass. The global equation follows, its mass fixes $\kappa $, and closed full-mass uniqueness gives $w=v+$constant as recalled in section 34.19 . Normalization fixes that constant. $\square$ The Hölder constants depend on the fixed geometry and divisor metrics, the $c_ j$, a lower bound for the positivity of $\beta $, $p$, and the $L^ p$ norm of the density $\kappa g$ itself. In particular, the argument gives no estimate that is uniform as $\beta $ degenerates or as $\kappa $ becomes unbounded. In simple normal crossing coordinates a density comparable to $\prod _ j|z_ j|^{-2a_ j}$ belongs locally to $L^ p$ exactly when 14.86 \begin{equation} \label{eq:snc-integrability} pa_ j<1\quad \hbox{for every }j, \end{equation} by the factors $\int _0^\epsilon r_ j^{1-2pa_ j}\, \mathrm{d} r_ j$. A smooth positive density $f$ on $X$ need not give a strictly positive $g$ on $Y$, since the Jacobian factor $J=\pi ^*h^ n/\beta ^ n$ of the proof can vanish on the exceptional set. Example 14.21.2 . Take $X=\mathbb P^ n$, $h=\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, $\int _ X\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^ n=1$, and $0<c<\lambda $. Put \[  \psi _ c=c\log \frac{\sum _{j=1}^ n|Z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ n|Z_ j|^2}.  \] Its pole is $P=[1:0:\cdots :0]$. On the point blowup $\pi :Y\to X$, let $q:Y\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$ be the direction map. In affine blowup coordinates $x=(z,zw)$, Poincaré–Lelong gives \[  \pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _ c\circ \pi ) =c[E]+(\lambda -c)\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+cq^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}.  \] The residual form $\beta =(\lambda -c)\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+cq^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is positive: $\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is positive in the directions normal to $E$, and $q^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ in the directions tangent to $E$. Write $H=\pi ^*[\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}]$. Since $H|_ E=0$ and $E^ n=(-1)^{n-1}$, its mass is 14.87 \begin{equation} \label{eq:point-residual-mass} \int _ Y\bigl ((\lambda -c)\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+cq^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}\bigr )^ n=\lambda ^ n-c^ n. \end{equation} Hence, for every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p$ with $\int _ Xfh^ n=\lambda ^ n-c^ n$, theorem 14.21.1 gives $\kappa =1$ and a solution of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=fh^ n$ with the nonminimal type $u=\psi _ c+O(1)$. For an explicit solution, choose a smooth function $v$ on $Y$ with $v|_ E$ nonconstant, small enough that $S=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is still positive, and put $u=\psi _ c+v\circ \pi ^{-1}$ off $P$. The density $f$ of its measure, given by $f\circ \pi =S^ n/\pi ^*h^ n$ off $E$, lies in every $L^ p$ with $1<p<n/(n-1)$: $\pi ^*h^ n$ vanishes to order $|z|^{2(n-1)}$ along $E$, so the local integral of $f^ p$ is finite precisely when $(n-1)(p-1)<1$. Different directions of approach to $P$ give different limits of $u-\psi _ c$. The divisor $c[E]$ of the current upstairs leaves no divisor downstairs, since $E$ is contracted to a point. On $X\setminus \{ P\} $, where $u$ is smooth and strictly $h$-plurisubharmonic, the Hermitian metric $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is isometric to $(Y\setminus E,S)$. Its metric completion is $Y$ with the metric $S$, so the whole divisor $E$ is restored: removing the smooth real codimension-two submanifold $E$ does not change the infimum of path lengths in $Y$. Finally, if $h$ is replaced by a sufficiently small nonclosed perturbation, both $h$ and the residual form remain positive, so the existence part of theorem 14.21.1 still applies.
14.82 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-type} \psi \circ \pi =\sum _ j c_ j\log |s_ j|^2+b, \qquad \beta =\pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b-\sum _ jc_ j\Theta _ j>0, \end{equation}

title: Theorem 14.21.1
text: Theorem 14.21.1 . Its current is 14.84 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-current} \pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ) =\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]+\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v. \end{equation} The positive residual current $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ has zero Lelong numbers. If $h$ is Kähler, then $\kappa =\int _ Y\beta ^ n/\int _ X f h^ n$, and the normalized solution is unique among all normalized solutions $u'$ of ( 14.83 ) with $u'=\psi +O(1)$, continuous or not. Change of variables on the biholomorphic locus gives 14.85 \begin{equation} \label{eq:prescribed-transport} \int _ Yg\beta ^ n=\int _ Xfh^ n, \qquad \int _ Yg^ p\beta ^ n\leq \| J\| _\infty ^{p-1}\int _ Xf^ ph^ n. \end{equation} Thus $g$ is a nonzero $L^ p$ density. Theorem 10.1.1 , Theorem 14.4.1 give a bounded Hölder $\beta $-plurisubharmonic $v$ and $\kappa >0$ with $(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=\kappa g\beta ^ n$. If $h$ is Kähler, then $\beta $ is Kähler and the mass identity fixes the stated scalar. For smooth positive $g$, theorem 9.1.1 gives a smooth solution instead. Set $u=\psi +v\circ \pi ^{-1}$ on $X\setminus A$ and $u=-\infty $ on $A$. Push forward the positive current $\sum c_ j[D_ j]+\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. Pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, $\pi _*\pi ^*h=h$, and the pushed locally integrable potential is $u$ almost everywhere. Its quasi-plurisubharmonic representative equals $\psi +v\circ \pi ^{-1}$ off $A$ and tends to $-\infty $ at $A$ because $v$ is bounded. Hence $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ and $u=\psi +O(1)$ in the two-sided ordinary sense. The pulled-back identity is ( 14.84 ); bounded residuals have zero Lelong number. The equation holds off $A$ by ( 14.85 ), and theorem 6.1.2 extends it as ( 14.83 ). Subtracting $\sup _ Xu$ changes neither the equation nor the ordinary type. For uniqueness when $h$ is Kähler, let $u'$ be a normalized solution with $u'=\psi +O(1)$. On $Y\setminus D$, $w=(u'-\psi )\circ \pi $ is bounded and $\beta $-plurisubharmonic. Since $w$ is bounded, lemma 1.3.7 extends it across $D$ to a bounded $\beta $-plurisubharmonic function on $Y$. On each relatively compact subset of $Y\setminus D$, sufficiently deep truncations of $u'$ equal $u'$. Thus locality in theorem 6.1.2 gives the bounded equation $\kappa g\beta ^ n$ there; both sides give $D$ zero mass. The global equation follows, its mass fixes $\kappa $, and closed full-mass uniqueness gives $w=v+$constant as recalled in section 34.19 . Normalization fixes that constant. $\square$
14.83 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-equation} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=\kappa f h^ n, \qquad u=\psi +O(1). \end{equation}
14.84 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-current} \pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ) =\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]+\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v. \end{equation}
14.85 \begin{equation} \label{eq:prescribed-transport} \int _ Yg\beta ^ n=\int _ Xfh^ n, \qquad \int _ Yg^ p\beta ^ n\leq \| J\| _\infty ^{p-1}\int _ Xf^ ph^ n. \end{equation}
14.86 \begin{equation} \label{eq:snc-integrability} pa_ j<1\quad \hbox{for every }j, \end{equation}

title: 14.21.1 Residual mass
text: 14.21.1 Residual mass When $h$ is not Kähler, the scalar in theorem 14.21.1 is still determined by masses if $h$ satisfies the power condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h^ k)=0$, $1\leq k\leq n-1$, of theorem 2.2.2 , which fixes the mass of every bounded solution. The condition persists under pullback and under addition of a smooth closed form: expand each power and apply the original identities to its terms. For $n=2$ the condition is simply $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=0$, so it includes the nonclosed Hopf metric of proposition 20.6.1 . The residual form then has strictly smaller mass than $h$, the difference being carried by the divisor. Proposition 14.21.3 . Under ( 14.82 ), assume $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h^ k)=0$ for $1\leq k\leq n-1$, and put $H=\pi ^*h$. Then 14.88 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mass-deficit} \int _ Xh^ n-\int _ Y\beta ^ n =\sum _ jc_ j\sum _{i=0}^{n-1} \int _{D_ j}H^ i\wedge \beta ^{n-1-i}>0. \end{equation} Thus the constructed solution of theorem 14.21.1 has $\kappa =\int _ Y\beta ^ n/\int _ Xfh^ n$. If $\int _ Xfh^ n=\int _ Xh^ n$, its scalar is strictly less than one. Proof. Let $C=\sum _ jc_ j\Theta _ j-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b$, so $\beta =H-C$ with $C$ closed. The mixed forms $Q_ i=H^ i\wedge \beta ^{n-1-i}$ satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_ i=0$: expand $\beta =H-C$ and apply the power condition to each $H^ k$. With $\Psi =\psi \circ \pi $, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]-C$. Distributional integration by parts against the smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $Q_ i$ gives \[  \int _ Y(H^ n-\beta ^ n)=\sum _ i\int _ Y C\wedge Q_ i =\sum _ jc_ j\sum _ i\int _{D_ j}Q_ i.  \] Change of variables gives $\int _ YH^ n=\int _ Xh^ n$. Every integrand on the right is nonnegative, since $H$ is semipositive and $\beta $ positive; the $i=0$ term on each nonempty $D_ j$ is strictly positive. This includes exceptional divisors. By theorem 2.2.2 , the residual solution has mass $\int _ Y\beta ^ n$, giving the scalar. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.21.3
text: Proposition 14.21.3 . Under ( 14.82 ), assume $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h^ k)=0$ for $1\leq k\leq n-1$, and put $H=\pi ^*h$. Then 14.88 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mass-deficit} \int _ Xh^ n-\int _ Y\beta ^ n =\sum _ jc_ j\sum _{i=0}^{n-1} \int _{D_ j}H^ i\wedge \beta ^{n-1-i}>0. \end{equation} Thus the constructed solution of theorem 14.21.1 has $\kappa =\int _ Y\beta ^ n/\int _ Xfh^ n$. The mixed forms $Q_ i=H^ i\wedge \beta ^{n-1-i}$ satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_ i=0$: expand $\beta =H-C$ and apply the power condition to each $H^ k$. With $\Psi =\psi \circ \pi $, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]-C$. Distributional integration by parts against the smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $Q_ i$ gives \[  \int _ Y(H^ n-\beta ^ n)=\sum _ i\int _ Y C\wedge Q_ i =\sum _ jc_ j\sum _ i\int _{D_ j}Q_ i.  \] Change of variables gives $\int _ YH^ n=\int _ Xh^ n$. 14.88 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mass-deficit} \int _ Xh^ n-\int _ Y\beta ^ n =\sum _ jc_ j\sum _{i=0}^{n-1} \int _{D_ j}H^ i\wedge \beta ^{n-1-i}>0. \end{equation}

title: 14.22 Minimal singularities on blowups
text: 14.22 Minimal singularities on blowups On a blowup, the background itself can force an exceptional divisor into every positive current. The coefficient of this divisor is then part of the minimal ordinary type, while the rest of the potential descends to the target of the blowup, so the equation reduces to one on the target. The density changes by the Jacobian of the blowup, which determines the loss of integrability. In this section the roles of the letters differ from those in section 14.21 : $X$ is a blowup and $Y$ its target. Let $(Y,h)$ be a connected compact Hermitian $n$-fold, $n\geq 2$, let $Z\subset Y$ be a connected smooth center of codimension $r\geq 2$, and write $\pi :X=\operatorname {Bl}_ ZY\to Y$ for the blowup, with exceptional divisor $E$. Let $s_ E$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O(E)$, choose a smooth Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O(E)$ with curvature form $\Theta _ E$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_ E|^2=[E]-\Theta _ E$, put $L=\log |s_ E|^2$, and fix $c>0$. The smooth background 14.89 \begin{equation} \label{eq:blowup-background} \theta =\pi ^*h+c\Theta _ E \end{equation} can be indefinite, and it is nonclosed when $h$ is nonclosed. Positivity is imposed on $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, not on $\theta $. Proposition 14.22.1 . Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has, up to an additive constant, a unique $h$-plurisubharmonic target potential $q$ such that 14.90 \begin{equation} \label{eq:blowup-representation} u=cL+q\circ \pi +C, \qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\pi ^*(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)+c[E]. \end{equation} The potentials with minimal ordinary singularities are exactly those of the form $cL+O(1)$, and $u$ is one of them if and only if $q$ is bounded. There is a strict $\theta $-plurisubharmonic barrier with logarithmic coefficient $c+\delta $ for some $\delta >0$. Proof. Put $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $q=\pi _*(u-cL)$ as a scalar distribution. The latter is locally integrable: off $Z$ it is the inverse-coordinate function, and a smooth target volume pulls back with bounded Jacobian, so its absolute integral is controlled by that of $u-cL$ on $X$. Since $\pi _*[E]=0$, \[  S=\pi _*T=h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq 0.  \] A smooth local strictly plurisubharmonic shift gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative of $q$. Its pullback $q\circ \pi $ is not identically $-\infty $ and satisfies $\pi ^*(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)\geq 0$, by lemma 1.22.1 : since $\pi $ is dominant, the composition of a local plurisubharmonic function with $\pi $ is again plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $. Off $E$, $T=\pi ^*S$. The difference is an order-zero current supported on $E$, and it is closed: both derivatives equal $\pi ^*\mathrm{d} h$. To identify it, write $R=T-\pi ^*S$. In a chart where $E=\{ z=0\} $, order zero gives $zR=\bar zR=0$. Closedness then gives $\mathrm{d}z\wedge R=\mathrm{d}\bar z\wedge R=0$. Thus only its normal $(1,1)$ coefficient remains, a measure on $E$; the tangential equations in $\mathrm{d}R=0$ make that measure a constant multiple of integration on $E$. Connectedness of $E$ identifies one constant $a$ globally, so $R=a[E]$. Its cohomology class is $c[E]$. On a line in an exceptional fiber, $\mathcal O(E)$ has degree $-1$, so $[E]$ is nonzero and $a=c$. The difference between the two scalar potentials in ( 14.90 ) has $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ zero. Local elliptic regularity makes it pluriharmonic; compactness and connectedness make it constant. Since $h>0$, $q=0$ is admissible, and every $h$-plurisubharmonic $q$ is bounded above on compact $Y$. Hence $cL$ is minimal and two-sided bounded comparison with it is exactly boundedness of $q$. For the barrier choose another divisor metric, with logarithmic norm $L'=L+\sigma $ and curvature $\Theta '_ E=\Theta _ E-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma $ for a smooth real function $\sigma $, so that $-\Theta '_ E$ is positive on the vertical tangent bundle of $E\to Z$, using the tautological $\mathcal O(-1)$. In adapted coordinates 14.91 \begin{equation} \label{eq:blowup-chart} \pi (y,z,w)=(y,z,zw), \end{equation} $\pi ^*h$ controls the nonvertical directions and $|z|^2|\mathrm{d} w|^2$. For small $\delta >0$, the vertical positivity of $-\delta \Theta '_ E$ dominates its mixed errors by completing the square; away from $E$, compactness allows the same $\delta $. Thus $\pi ^*h-\delta \Theta '_ E>0$. For the fixed background $\theta $ in ( 14.89 ), take \[  w=(c+\delta )L'-c\sigma =(c+\delta )L+\delta \sigma .  \] Then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=(c+\delta )[E]+\pi ^*h-\delta \Theta '_ E$ dominates a positive Hermitian form. The smooth correction $\delta \sigma $ preserves the stated logarithmic coefficient. $\square$ Theorem 14.22.2 . Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mu $ on $X$ and a nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p(X,\mu )$, $p>1$. There exist $\kappa >0$ and a normalized minimal-type solution of 14.92 \begin{equation} \label{eq:minimal-blowup-equation} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=\kappa f\mu , \qquad u=cL+q\circ \pi +C, \end{equation} where $q$ is Hölder on $Y$. The divisor coefficient is exactly $c$. In ( 14.91 ), $u-cL=q(y,0)+C+O(|z|^\alpha )$ on smaller charts for some $\alpha >0$, so its limit is constant along each exceptional fiber. If $\pi _*(f\mu )=Fh^ n$, then $F\in L^ s(Y,h^ n)$ for every 14.93 \begin{equation} \label{eq:pushforward-exponent} 1<s<\frac{rp}{(r-1)p+1}. \end{equation} For a point center, data bounded above and below by positive constants near $E$ attain the strict threshold $s<n/(n-1)$, and for finite $p$ no strictly larger universal exponent than $np/((n-1)p+1)$ can be guaranteed. If $h$ is Kähler, the class $[\theta ]$ is big and non-nef, has volume $\int _ Yh^ n$, and $\kappa =\int _ Yh^ n/\int _ Xf\mu $; the normalized solution is unique among all normalized solutions of ( 14.92 ) with minimal ordinary singularities. Under $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h^ j)=0$, $1\leq j\leq n-1$, the scalar of the constructed solution has the same integral formula. Proof. Integrability and existence. In ( 14.91 ) the complex Jacobian is $z^{r-1}$. Put $J=\pi ^*h^ n/\mu $, so $J\asymp |z|^{2(r-1)}$ on nested charts and $F\circ \pi =f/J$ off $E$. For $1<s<p$, change of variables and Hölder's inequality give 14.94 \begin{align} \label{eq:pushforward-holder} \int _ YF^ s h^ n & =\int _ X f^ sJ^{1-s}\mu \\ & \leq \| f\| _{L^ p(\mu )}^ s \left(\int _ XJ^{-(s-1)p/(p-s)}\mu \right)^{(p-s)/p}. \end{align} The normal complex integral is finite precisely if $(r-1)(s-1)p/(p-s)<1$, which is ( 14.93 ). Theorem 10.1.1 , Theorem 14.4.1 on $(Y,h)$ supply $q$ and $\kappa $ with $(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=\kappa Fh^ n$. Use ( 14.90 ) off $E$ and theorem 6.1.2 across it. Hölder continuity gives $q(\pi (y,z,w))=q(y,0)+O(|z|^\alpha )$ uniformly on smaller charts. Sharpness of the exponent. For $f$ bounded above and below by positive constants near the exceptional divisor of a point center, $F$ is comparable to $\operatorname {dist}_ h(\cdot ,Z)^{-2(n-1)}$ near $Z$, giving the strict threshold. More generally, $f\asymp |s_ E|^{-2a}$ with $0\leq a<1/p$ belongs to $L^ p$ upstairs, while its pushforward has threshold $s<n/(n-1+a)$. Letting $a\uparrow 1/p$ proves the stated limitation; it makes no finite-$p$ endpoint assertion. The Kähler case. When $h$ is Kähler, the strict barrier current $(c+\delta )[E]+\pi ^*h-\delta \Theta '_ E$ constructed in proposition 14.22.1 makes $[\theta ]$ big. Its degree on an exceptional-fiber line is $-c$, so it is not nef. The minimal current $c[E]+\pi ^*h$ has non-pluripolar top mass $\int _ Yh^ n$, and the minimal mass theorem identifies this with $\operatorname {vol}([\theta ])$ as recalled in section 34.16 . Full-mass uniqueness and mass integration fix the scalar and normalized current as recalled in section 34.19 . A normalized solution of minimal ordinary type, possibly discontinuous, still has bounded $q$ by proposition 14.22.1 ; on every relatively compact set off $E$, deep truncations equal that competitor, so locality in theorem 6.1.2 gives the bounded target equation off $Z$. Both target measures give $Z$ zero mass, so closed uniqueness applies globally. If only the power conditions hold, theorem 2.2.2 fixes the scalar of the constructed solution. Quantitative Hölder bounds depend on $\kappa F$, not on an unnormalized $F$ alone. $\square$ For the prescribed pullback measure $\pi ^*(h^ n)$, choose $q=0$ and $\kappa =1$. The current is $c[E]+\pi ^*h$. Its smooth part $\pi ^*h$ is degenerate on $E$ exactly in the directions tangent to the exceptional fibers, and its density relative to a smooth volume form is $|z|^{2(r-1)}$ times a smooth positive factor. On $X\setminus E$, where the solution $u=cL$ is smooth and strictly $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, the metric $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\pi ^*h$ is isometric to $(Y\setminus Z,h)$; its metric completion is $Y$, so each exceptional fiber collapses to a point of $Z$. The distance to $E$ is comparable to $|z|$ on bounded adapted charts. Neither the density order nor this distance exponent depends on $c$. Example 14.22.3 . If $n=2$ and $Z$ is a point on a compact Kähler surface, $[\theta ]=\pi ^*[h]+c[E]$ has Zariski positive part $\pi ^*[h]$ and negative part $cE$: $E^2=-1$ and $\pi ^*[h]\cdot E=0$. Let $\pi :Y_ m\to Y_0$ be a finite nonempty sequence of blowups of connected smooth centers of codimensions $r_ j\geq 2$ over a compact Hermitian $(Y_0,h_0)$. title: Proposition 14.22.1
text: Proposition 14.22.1 . Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has, up to an additive constant, a unique $h$-plurisubharmonic target potential $q$ such that 14.90 \begin{equation} \label{eq:blowup-representation} u=cL+q\circ \pi +C, \qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\pi ^*(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)+c[E]. \end{equation} The potentials with minimal ordinary singularities are exactly those of the form $cL+O(1)$, and $u$ is one of them if and only if $q$ is bounded. There is a strict $\theta $-plurisubharmonic barrier with logarithmic coefficient $c+\delta $ for some $\delta >0$. Proof. Put $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $q=\pi _*(u-cL)$ as a scalar distribution. The latter is locally integrable: off $Z$ it is the inverse-coordinate function, and a smooth target volume pulls back with bounded Jacobian, so its absolute integral is controlled by that of $u-cL$ on $X$. Since $\pi _*[E]=0$, \[  S=\pi _*T=h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq 0.  \] A smooth local strictly plurisubharmonic shift gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative of $q$. Its pullback $q\circ \pi $ is not identically $-\infty $ and satisfies $\pi ^*(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)\geq 0$, by lemma 1.22.1 : since $\pi $ is dominant, the composition of a local plurisubharmonic function with $\pi $ is again plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $. Off $E$, $T=\pi ^*S$. The difference is an order-zero current supported on $E$, and it is closed: both derivatives equal $\pi ^*\mathrm{d} h$. To identify it, write $R=T-\pi ^*S$. In a chart where $E=\{ z=0\} $, order zero gives $zR=\bar zR=0$. Closedness then gives $\mathrm{d}z\wedge R=\mathrm{d}\bar z\wedge R=0$. Thus only its normal $(1,1)$ coefficient remains, a measure on $E$; the tangential equations in $\mathrm{d}R=0$ make that measure a constant multiple of integration on $E$. Connectedness of $E$ identifies one constant $a$ globally, so $R=a[E]$. Its cohomology class is $c[E]$. On a line in an exceptional fiber, $\mathcal O(E)$ has degree $-1$, so $[E]$ is nonzero and $a=c$. The difference between the two scalar potentials in ( 14.90 ) has $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ zero. Local elliptic regularity makes it pluriharmonic; compactness and connectedness make it constant. Since $h>0$, $q=0$ is admissible, and every $h$-plurisubharmonic $q$ is bounded above on compact $Y$. Hence $cL$ is minimal and two-sided bounded comparison with it is exactly boundedness of $q$. For the barrier choose another divisor metric, with logarithmic norm $L'=L+\sigma $ and curvature $\Theta '_ E=\Theta _ E-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma $ for a smooth real function $\sigma $, so that $-\Theta '_ E$ is positive on the vertical tangent bundle of $E\to Z$, using the tautological $\mathcal O(-1)$. In adapted coordinates 14.91 \begin{equation} \label{eq:blowup-chart} \pi (y,z,w)=(y,z,zw), \end{equation} $\pi ^*h$ controls the nonvertical directions and $|z|^2|\mathrm{d} w|^2$. For small $\delta >0$, the vertical positivity of $-\delta \Theta '_ E$ dominates its mixed errors by completing the square; away from $E$, compactness allows the same $\delta $. Thus $\pi ^*h-\delta \Theta '_ E>0$. For the fixed background $\theta $ in ( 14.89 ), take \[  w=(c+\delta )L'-c\sigma =(c+\delta )L+\delta \sigma .  \] Then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=(c+\delta )[E]+\pi ^*h-\delta \Theta '_ E$ dominates a positive Hermitian form. The smooth correction $\delta \sigma $ preserves the stated logarithmic coefficient. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.22.2
text: Theorem 14.22.2 . Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mu $ on $X$ and a nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p(X,\mu )$, $p>1$. There exist $\kappa >0$ and a normalized minimal-type solution of 14.92 \begin{equation} \label{eq:minimal-blowup-equation} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=\kappa f\mu , \qquad u=cL+q\circ \pi +C, \end{equation} where $q$ is Hölder on $Y$. The divisor coefficient is exactly $c$. In ( 14.91 ), $u-cL=q(y,0)+C+O(|z|^\alpha )$ on smaller charts for some $\alpha >0$, so its limit is constant along each exceptional fiber. If $\pi _*(f\mu )=Fh^ n$, then $F\in L^ s(Y,h^ n)$ for every 14.93 \begin{equation} \label{eq:pushforward-exponent} 1<s<\frac{rp}{(r-1)p+1}. \end{equation} For a point center, data bounded above and below by positive constants near $E$ attain the strict threshold $s<n/(n-1)$, and for finite $p$ no strictly larger universal exponent than $np/((n-1)p+1)$ can be guaranteed. If $h$ is Kähler, the class $[\theta ]$ is big and non-nef, has volume $\int _ Yh^ n$, and $\kappa =\int _ Yh^ n/\int _ Xf\mu $; the normalized solution is unique among all normalized solutions of ( 14.92 ) with minimal ordinary singularities. Under $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h^ j)=0$, $1\leq j\leq n-1$, the scalar of the constructed solution has the same integral formula. Proof. Integrability and existence. In ( 14.91 ) the complex Jacobian is $z^{r-1}$. Put $J=\pi ^*h^ n/\mu $, so $J\asymp |z|^{2(r-1)}$ on nested charts and $F\circ \pi =f/J$ off $E$. For $1<s<p$, change of variables and Hölder's inequality give 14.94 \begin{align} \label{eq:pushforward-holder} \int _ YF^ s h^ n & =\int _ X f^ sJ^{1-s}\mu \\ & \leq \| f\| _{L^ p(\mu )}^ s \left(\int _ XJ^{-(s-1)p/(p-s)}\mu \right)^{(p-s)/p}. \end{align} The normal complex integral is finite precisely if $(r-1)(s-1)p/(p-s)<1$, which is ( 14.93 ). Theorem 10.1.1 , Theorem 14.4.1 on $(Y,h)$ supply $q$ and $\kappa $ with $(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=\kappa Fh^ n$. Use ( 14.90 ) off $E$ and theorem 6.1.2 across it. Hölder continuity gives $q(\pi (y,z,w))=q(y,0)+O(|z|^\alpha )$ uniformly on smaller charts. Sharpness of the exponent. For $f$ bounded above and below by positive constants near the exceptional divisor of a point center, $F$ is comparable to $\operatorname {dist}_ h(\cdot ,Z)^{-2(n-1)}$ near $Z$, giving the strict threshold. More generally, $f\asymp |s_ E|^{-2a}$ with $0\leq a<1/p$ belongs to $L^ p$ upstairs, while its pushforward has threshold $s<n/(n-1+a)$. Its degree on an exceptional-fiber line is $-c$, so it is not nef. The minimal current $c[E]+\pi ^*h$ has non-pluripolar top mass $\int _ Yh^ n$, and the minimal mass theorem identifies this with $\operatorname {vol}([\theta ])$ as recalled in section 34.16 . Full-mass uniqueness and mass integration fix the scalar and normalized current as recalled in section 34.19 . A normalized solution of minimal ordinary type, possibly discontinuous, still has bounded $q$ by proposition 14.22.1 ; on every relatively compact set off $E$, deep truncations equal that competitor, so locality in theorem 6.1.2 gives the bounded target equation off $Z$. Both target measures give $Z$ zero mass, so closed uniqueness applies globally. If only the power conditions hold, theorem 2.2.2 fixes the scalar of the constructed solution. Quantitative Hölder bounds depend on $\kappa F$, not on an unnormalized $F$ alone. $\square$
14.92 \begin{equation} \label{eq:minimal-blowup-equation} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=\kappa f\mu , \qquad u=cL+q\circ \pi +C, \end{equation}
14.93 \begin{equation} \label{eq:pushforward-exponent} 1<s<\frac{rp}{(r-1)p+1}. \end{equation}
14.94 \begin{align} \label{eq:pushforward-holder} \int _ YF^ s h^ n & =\int _ X f^ sJ^{1-s}\mu \\ & \leq \| f\| _{L^ p(\mu )}^ s \left(\int _ XJ^{-(s-1)p/(p-s)}\mu \right)^{(p-s)/p}. \end{align}

text:
14.23 Representing measures in an ordinary type We return to the general setting of the chapter, with the Hermitian form $\omega $ fixed at its beginning. Locally, every finite non-pluripolar measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the Monge–Ampère measure of a bounded plurisubharmonic function (lemma 1.6.5 ). We globalize this statement in a prescribed ordinary type. The local potentials are glued to a strictly $	heta $-plurisubharmonic potential lying below the reference and are then truncated relative to the reference. A decreasing convex sum of the resulting countable family has a Monge–Ampère measure that dominates every local piece in the sense of absolute continuity. Its potential has the prescribed ordinary type, and the given measure has an integrable density with respect to its Monge–Ampère measure. Proposition 14.23.1 . Let $	heta \geq 0$ be a smooth big real $(1,1)$-form, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be such that the envelope $P_{\epsilon 	heta }(\varphi )$ of section 1.19 is not identically $-\infty $ for some $0<\epsilon <1$. For every finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $ there are \[  \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ),\qquad \psi \sim \varphi , \qquad 0\leq f\in L^1 igl (\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi ) igr )  \] such that \[  \mu =f\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi ).  \] The measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi )$ may have infinite mass, but the density $f$ is integrable with respect to it. Proof. Translate $\varphi $ below zero. Put $q=P_{\epsilon 	heta }(\varphi )\leq \varphi $, and choose a strict big potential $ho \leq 0$ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq a\omega $, where $a>0$. Then \[  s=q+(1-\epsilon )ho \leq \varphi ,\qquad 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s\geq (1-\epsilon )a\omega .  \] In particular $s$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $. Its pole set is pluripolar, as is that of $\varphi $, so both are negligible for $\mu $. Cover $X$ by finitely many closed coordinate balls $K_ i$, each contained in a larger coordinate ball $B_ i$. Apply lemma 1.6.5 to $\mu _ i=\mathbf1_{K_ i}\mu $. This gives bounded local plurisubharmonic $v_ i$, normalized by $1\leq v_ i\leq 2$, with \[  \mu _ i\ll 
u _ i:=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ i)^ n.  \] Take a smooth cutoff $\chi _ i$ which is zero near $K_ i$ and $-3$ on a boundary collar of $B_ i$. Choose $\delta _ i>0$ so small that \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} igl (s+\delta _ i(v_ i+\chi _ i) igr ) \geq 	frac 12(1-\epsilon )a\omega +\delta _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ i.  \] Let $S_ i$ equal $\max (s,s+\delta _ i(v_ i+\chi _ i))$ on $B_ i$ and $s$ elsewhere. The boundary collar makes this a global $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function. Since $\chi _ i\leq 0$ may be arranged, \[  s\leq S_ i\leq s+2\delta _ i\leq \varphi +2\delta _ i.  \] For every positive integer $m$, set \[  q_{i,m}=\max (\varphi -m,S_ i)-2\delta _ i.  \] These potentials have the same ordinary type as $\varphi $, and 14.97  egin{equation} \label{eq:relative-carrier-bounds} \varphi -m-2\delta _ i\leq q_{i,m}\leq \varphi . \end{equation} On a neighborhood of $K_ i$, $S_ i=s+\delta _ i v_ i$ away from the pole set of $s$. Let \[  D_{i,m}=\{ s+\delta _ i v_ i>\varphi -m\}   \] in that neighborhood, restricting to points where the potentials are finite. This is a plurifinely open set there. Locality and positive mixed products give 14.98  egin{equation} \label{eq:relative-carrier-local-domination} \mathbf1_{D_{i,m}}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (q_{i,m}) \geq \delta _ i^ n\mathbf1_{D_{i,m}}
u _ i. \end{equation} Here $s$ need not be bounded. After a local smooth correction, the positive product inequality holds at every common finite truncation level of $s$ and the bounded potential $v_ i$. Exhaust the complement of the pole set of $s$. The measure $
u _ i$ is non-pluripolar, so it loses no mass in that exhaustion. Then restrict the resulting inequality by plurifine locality. This proves ( 14.98 ) for the extended measures. For $\mu _ i$-almost every point of $K_ i$, both $s$ and $\varphi $ are finite, and hence that point belongs to $D_{i,m}$ for some $m$. Consequently, a Borel set which is null for every $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (q_{i,m})$ is null for every $\mu _ i$, and therefore for $\mu $. Enumerate the countable family $q_{i,m}$ as $q_ k$, and write its bounds as $\varphi -C_ k\leq q_ k\leq \varphi $ with $C_ k<\infty $. Choose positive $t_ k$ such that \[  \sum _ k t_ k<1,\qquad B:=\sum _ k t_ kC_ k<\infty .  \] The finite convex combinations \[  \psi _ N=\sum _{k=1}^ N t_ kq_ k +\left(1-\sum _{k=1}^ N t_ kight)\varphi  \] decrease and lie between $\varphi -B$ and $\varphi $. Their limit $\psi $ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic, satisfies $\psi \geq \varphi -B$, and hence $\psi \sim \varphi $. For any fixed $k$, separate its summand to write \[  \psi =t_ kq_ k+(1-t_ k)w_ k, \qquad w_ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ),\qquad w_ k\sim \varphi .  \] The remainder is obtained by the same decreasing convex-sum construction. Positive non-pluripolar mixed products give \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi ) \geq t_ k^ n\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (q_ k).  \] This is valid also for infinite measures: first restrict away from the common pole set, which is the pole set of $\varphi $ by the ordinary-type bounds, and then exhaust by finite truncations. All measures ignore that pole set. The preceding null-set conclusion now gives $\mu \ll \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi )$. By theorem 6.1.2 , the measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi )$ is $\sigma $-finite. The Radon–Nikodym theorem applies to this $\sigma $-finite measure and the finite $\mu $. It gives a nonnegative density $f$ with \[  \int _ X f\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi )=\mu (X)<\infty ,  \] as claimed. If $\mu =0$, one may simply take $\psi =\varphi $ and $f=0$. $\square$ Lemma 14.23.2 . Let $	heta \geq 0$ be a smooth big real $(1,1)$-form, and let $\mu $ be a finite non-pluripolar measure on $X$. There are a bounded $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and a nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{MA}_	heta (\psi ))$ such that \[  \mu =f\, \mathrm{MA}_	heta (\psi ).  \] Proof. Apply proposition 14.23.1 with $\varphi =0$. Semipositivity of $	heta $ gives $P_{\epsilon 	heta }(0)=0$ for every $0<\epsilon <1$, and $\psi \sim 0$ means that $\psi $ is bounded. $\square$ These representations give only an $L^1$ density, whereas theorem 14.9.1 requires a bounded density with respect to the measure of a bounded potential; for an unbounded prescribed type, moreover, the representing potential is itself unbounded. The existence argument for general measures in section 31.6 therefore uses a bounded Hermitian reference and relative compactness instead.

title: Lemma 14.23.2
text: Lemma 14.23.2 . Let $\theta \geq 0$ be a smooth big real $(1,1)$-form, and let $\mu $ be a finite non-pluripolar measure on $X$. There are a bounded $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi ))$ such that \[  \mu =f\, \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi ).  \] Proof. Apply proposition 14.23.1 with $\varphi =0$. Semipositivity of $\theta $ gives $P_{\epsilon \theta }(0)=0$ for every $0<\epsilon <1$, and $\psi \sim 0$ means that $\psi $ is bounded. $\square$

14.25 Singular measures on shrinking spheres A bounded density with respect to the measure of a bounded potential gives an exponential equation by theorem 14.9.1 . The following construction turns this analytic hypothesis into a test against a probability measure fixed by a coordinate ball. Fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, with $n\geq 2$, a holomorphic coordinate ball centered at a point $p$, and a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ supported in that ball and equal to one near a smaller closed ball. Choose $r_0>0$ so small that all spheres of radii $r_ j=r_0 2^{-j}$, $j\geq 1$, lie in the smaller ball. Let $\sigma _ j$ denote their normalized Euclidean surface probabilities, extended by zero to $X$, and put 14.99  egin{equation} \label{eq:fixed-spherical-probability} S_ n=\sum _{j\geq 1}r_ j^{n/2},\qquad ho = rac1{S_ n}\sum _{j\geq 1}r_ j^{n/2}\sigma _ j. \end{equation} For a finite positive measure $

Allowing the existence of some coordinate ball with this construction gives a sufficient condition independent of a specified chart. Proposition 14.25.1 . The measure $ho $ is a singular non-pluripolar probability. In the coordinate ball write $R=|z|$ and set \[  \psi _ j=\chi \log \max \{ R^2,r_ j^2\} +(1-\chi ),  \] extending $\psi _ j$ by one outside it. On the transition region of $\chi $, $R$ is bounded away from zero and exceeds all $r_ j$. Hence all $\psi _ j$ agree there with the same smooth function. Where $\chi =1$ they are plurisubharmonic, and outside its support they are constant. One fixed $K\geq 1$ therefore satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j\geq -Kh$ for every $j$. Put \[  Z=2K\sum _{j\geq 1}\sqrt{r_ j},\qquad d_ j= rac{\sqrt{r_ j}}Z,\qquad u_0=\sum _{j\geq 1}d_ j\psi _ j.  \] The estimate $\| \psi _ j\| _\infty \leq C(1+|\log r_ j|)$ gives uniform convergence, and $\sum d_ j=1/(2K)$ yields $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0\geq h/2$. For two points of the inner ball at Euclidean distance $t$, the reverse triangle inequality gives \[  |\log \max \{ |z|^2,r_ j^2\} -\log \max \{ |z'|^2,r_ j^2\} | \leq 2\log (1+t/r_ j).  \] The contribution of $r_ j\geq t$ is at most $Ct\sum _{r_ j\geq t}r_ j^{-1/2}\leq C\sqrt t$. title: 14.26 Lower mass and solvability for all measures
search_title: Lower mass and solvability for all measures
text:
14.26 Lower mass and solvability for all measures Throughout the rest of the chapter, $h$ denotes a Hermitian form on $X$, used as the background, and densities are taken with respect to the fixed smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$; the sections that use another background say so explicitly. No singularity type is prescribed: the unknown potentials range over all of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. Constants belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$, and every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ is bounded above, so $u\preceq v$ for every bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. The masses of bounded potentials are measured by the lower and upper masses of definition 6.5.1 , \[  v_-(h)=\inf _ v\int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n,\qquad v_+(h)=\sup _ v\int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n,  \] where $v$ ranges over the bounded functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. The form $h$ has positive lower mass if $v_-(h)>0$. If $h$ is Kähler, Stokes' theorem gives $v_-(h)=v_+(h)=\int _ Xh^ n$; on a non-Kähler manifold the lower mass can vanish (theorem 26.18.1 ). For a nonzero nonnegative $q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ with $p>1$, theorem 10.1.1 gives a constant $c>0$ and a continuous $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=cq\, \mathrm{d}V$, and proposition 10.6.1 shows that $c$ is determined by $q$. We call $c_ h(q)=c$ the normalization scalar of $q$, and for the measure $
u =q\, \mathrm{d}V$ we also write $c_ h(
u )=c_ h(q)$. We say that a finite measure $
u $ admits a positive scaled subsolution if there are $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and a constant $a>0$ such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq a
u $. If $
u $ admits a solution of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=c
u $ with $c>0$, then it admits in particular a positive scaled subsolution. We show that every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure admits such a solution if and only if $h$ has positive lower mass. The key estimate is a consequence of strict domination: if $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq aq\, \mathrm{d}V$, then $a\leq c_ h(q)$. When $v_-(h)=0$, there are smooth probability densities with arbitrarily small normalization scalars, and a weighted sum of such densities, with scalars decreasing fast enough, is a single probability density admitting no positive scaled subsolution. Lemma 14.26.1 . Let $0\leq q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq aq\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] then $a\leq c_ h(q)$. Consequently, for nonzero nonnegative bounded densities $q,r$, \[  q\leq r\  \Longrightarrow \  c_ h(q)\geq c_ h(r), \qquad c_ h(tq)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)\quad (t>0).  \] Proof. Let $v$ be a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V$, and suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $a>c_ h(q)$. Then $	au =c_ h(q)/a<1$ and, for every real $A$, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(v+A)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V \leq 	au \, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u).  \] The translate $v+A$ is bounded, so $P_{h/2}(v+A)\geq \inf _ Xv+A$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $u\preceq v+A$. Theorem 14.1.2 , with $\delta =1/2$ and $c=	au $, therefore gives $v+A\geq u$ for every real $A$. Letting $A	o -\infty $ at a point where $u$ is finite gives a contradiction. Hence $a\leq c_ h(q)$. If $q\leq r$, a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)=c_ h(r)r\, \mathrm{d}V$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)\geq c_ h(r)q\, \mathrm{d}V$, so the first assertion gives $c_ h(r)\leq c_ h(q)$. Finally, the equation $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V$ can be written as $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)\, (tq)\, \mathrm{d}V$, and uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ h(tq)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)$. $\square$ The proof uses only that $v$ is bounded. Hence, more generally, if a nonnegative density $g$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c\, g\, \mathrm{d}V$ for some bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and some $c>0$, then every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq ag\, \mathrm{d}V$ satisfy $a\leq c$. Lemma 14.26.2 . Fix $p>1$. If nonzero nonnegative densities $q_ j,q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ satisfy $q_ j	o q$ in $L^ p$, then $c_ h(q_ j)	o c_ h(q)$. Proof. We first show that the scalars $c_ h(q_ j)$ lie in a compact subset of $(0,+\infty )$. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $X$ (definition 4.1.1 ; in dimension one, any Hermitian metric). Pairing the equation for $q_ j$ with $\gamma ^{n-1}$, as in proposition 14.13.2 with $	heta =h$ and barrier $ho =0$, gives \[  c_ h(q_ j)^{1/n}\int _ X\left( rac{q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}ight)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Since $q_ j^{1/n}	o q^{1/n}$ in $L^ n$, the integrals on the left converge to the corresponding integral for $q$, which is positive. Hence the scalars are bounded above. The lower-density estimate of theorem 10.3.3 gives $c_ h(q_ j)\| q_ j\| _{L^ p}\geq c_ p>0$, so they are also bounded away from zero. Consequently, the normalized continuous solutions $u_ j$ of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ j)=c_ h(q_ j)q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ have uniformly bounded $L^ p$ densities. By theorem 10.3.4 , every subsequence has a further subsequence along which $u_ j$ converges uniformly to some $u$ and $c_ h(q_ j)$ converges to some $c>0$. Continuity of bounded Monge–Ampère products under uniform convergence gives $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=cq\, \mathrm{d}V$, and uniqueness of the scalar gives $c=c_ h(q)$. Since every subsequence of $(c_ h(q_ j))$ has a further subsequence converging to $c_ h(q)$, the whole sequence converges to $c_ h(q)$. $\square$ Theorem 14.26.3 . Suppose $v_-(h)=0$. There is a probability measure $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$, with $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and $f\geq m$ almost everywhere for a constant $m>0$, such that no $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ satisfy 14.100  egin{equation} \label{eq:lower-mass-impossible-subsolution} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq a\mu . \end{equation} In particular, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=c\mu $ has no solution $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ for any $c>0$; neither a singularity type nor finiteness of the mass of $u$ is imposed. Proof. By theorem 26.14.3 , theorem 26.1.3 , $v_-(h)$ is the infimum of the normalization scalars $c_ h(
u )$ over smooth strictly positive probability measures $
u $. Since $v_-(h)=0$, we can choose such measures $
u _ j=f_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ with \[  c_ h(
u _ j)\leq 2^{-2j}\qquad (j\geq 1).  \] Set \[  \mu =\sum _{j=1}^{\infty }2^{-j}
u _ j, \qquad f=\sum _{j=1}^{\infty }2^{-j}f_ j.  \] By monotone convergence, $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V=1$, so $f\in L^1$. Moreover $f\geq 	frac 12\min _ X f_1=:m>0$, and $\mu $ is non-pluripolar, being absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$. Suppose that ( 14.100 ) held for some $u$ and $a>0$. Since $\mu \geq 2^{-j}
