u _ j)\leq 2^{-2j}$. Thus $a\leq 2^{-j}$ for every $j$, contradicting $a>0$. $\square$ For the reference $0$, definition 13.4.1 says that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ belongs to the relative envelope class $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ if, for every $b\geq 1$, some $g\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ satisfies $g\leq bu$. Corollary 14.26.4 . The following conditions are equivalent: $v_-(h)>0$. For every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $ there are $c>0$ and $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=c\mu $. For every probability density $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ bounded below by a positive constant, there are $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$. Proof. The Hermitian form $h$ is semipositive and big, and the reference $0$ satisfies ( 13.26 ), since $P_ h[0]=0$ and $P_{\varepsilon h}(0)=0$ for every $0<\varepsilon <1$. Hence, if $v_-(h)>0$, theorem 31.1.1 , applied with $	heta =h$ and $\varphi =0$, gives (2). Condition (2) implies (3), because a finite measure that is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$ is non-pluripolar. Finally, if $v_-(h)=0$, the density of theorem 14.26.3 violates (3); thus (3) implies (1). $\square$ Corollary 14.26.5 . Assume $v_-(h)=0$, and let $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$ be the measure of theorem 14.26.3 . Then $f
otin L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for every $p>1$. Moreover, for every probability density $g\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and every $0<t<1$, the probability density \[  g_ t=(1-t)g+tf  \] admits no positive scaled subsolution, although $\| g_ t-g\| _{L^1}\leq 2t$. In particular, the probability densities admitting no positive scaled subsolution are dense among all probability densities in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Proof. If $f\in L^ p$ for some $p>1$, theorem 10.1.1 would give a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $c>0$, contradicting the theorem. Since $g_ t\, \mathrm{d}V\geq t\mu $, a positive scaled subsolution for $g_ t\, \mathrm{d}V$ would also give one for $\mu $. Finally, $\| g_ t-g\| _{L^1}=t\| f-g\| _{L^1}\leq 2t$. $\square$ Smooth strictly positive probability densities are also dense in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, and each of them admits a smooth solution of the normalized equation. Thus, when the lower mass vanishes, solvability is not preserved under $L^1$ approximation. The obstruction comes from the way the density concentrates, not from its size: the density in theorem 14.26.3 is bounded below by a positive constant. It occurs, for instance, on the compact threefold of theorem 26.18.1 , where every Hermitian form has zero lower mass. Theorem 14.26.3 does not exclude unbounded solutions of the exponential equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $ with $\lambda >0$, because the factor $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ need not have a positive lower bound. It does exclude bounded solutions, since a bounded solution would satisfy $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda \inf _ Xu}\mu $. On suitable products, theorem 14.34.6 chooses the concentrating components of such a density so that its exponential equation has a solution for every positive exponent. We do not know whether this holds for every density admitting no positive scaled subsolution, nor which individual measures admit a solution of the normalized equation when $v_-(h)=0$.

title: Lemma 14.26.1
text: Lemma 14.26.1 . Let $0\leq q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq aq\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] then $a\leq c_ h(q)$. Consequently, for nonzero nonnegative bounded densities $q,r$, \[  q\leq r\  \Longrightarrow \  c_ h(q)\geq c_ h(r), \qquad c_ h(tq)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)\quad (t>0).  \] Proof. Let $v$ be a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V$, and suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $a>c_ h(q)$. Then $\tau =c_ h(q)/a<1$ and, for every real $A$, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(v+A)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \tau \, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u).  \] The translate $v+A$ is bounded, so $P_{h/2}(v+A)\geq \inf _ Xv+A$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $u\preceq v+A$. Theorem 14.1.2 , with $\delta =1/2$ and $c=\tau $, therefore gives $v+A\geq u$ for every real $A$. Letting $A\to -\infty $ at a point where $u$ is finite gives a contradiction. Hence $a\leq c_ h(q)$. If $q\leq r$, a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)=c_ h(r)r\, \mathrm{d}V$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)\geq c_ h(r)q\, \mathrm{d}V$, so the first assertion gives $c_ h(r)\leq c_ h(q)$. Finally, the equation $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V$ can be written as $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)\, (tq)\, \mathrm{d}V$, and uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ h(tq)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)$. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.26.2
text: Lemma 14.26.2 . Fix $p>1$. If nonzero nonnegative densities $q_ j,q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ satisfy $q_ j\to q$ in $L^ p$, then $c_ h(q_ j)\to c_ h(q)$. Proof. We first show that the scalars $c_ h(q_ j)$ lie in a compact subset of $(0,+\infty )$. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $X$ (definition 4.1.1 ; in dimension one, any Hermitian metric). Pairing the equation for $q_ j$ with $\gamma ^{n-1}$, as in proposition 14.13.2 with $\theta =h$ and barrier $\rho =0$, gives \[  c_ h(q_ j)^{1/n}\int _ X\left(\frac{q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Since $q_ j^{1/n}\to q^{1/n}$ in $L^ n$, the integrals on the left converge to the corresponding integral for $q$, which is positive. Hence the scalars are bounded above. The lower-density estimate of theorem 10.3.3 gives $c_ h(q_ j)\| q_ j\| _{L^ p}\geq c_ p>0$, so they are also bounded away from zero. Consequently, the normalized continuous solutions $u_ j$ of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ j)=c_ h(q_ j)q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ have uniformly bounded $L^ p$ densities. By theorem 10.3.4 , every subsequence has a further subsequence along which $u_ j$ converges uniformly to some $u$ and $c_ h(q_ j)$ converges to some $c>0$. Continuity of bounded Monge–Ampère products under uniform convergence gives $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=cq\, \mathrm{d}V$, and uniqueness of the scalar gives $c=c_ h(q)$. Since every subsequence of $(c_ h(q_ j))$ has a further subsequence converging to $c_ h(q)$, the whole sequence converges to $c_ h(q)$. $\square$

text: Corollary 14.26.5 . Assume $v_-(h)=0$, and let $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$ be the measure of theorem 14.26.3 . Then $f\notin L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for every $p>1$. Moreover, for every probability density $g\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and every $0<t<1$, the probability density \[  g_ t=(1-t)g+tf  \] admits no positive scaled subsolution, although $\| g_ t-g\| _{L^1}\leq 2t$. title: 14.27 Subsolutions for an individual density
text: 14.27 Subsolutions for an individual density When $v_-(h)=0$, some densities admit no positive scaled subsolution. For one fixed density $f$, we now determine the largest coefficient $a$ for which $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a solution. The bounded truncations of $f$ have normalization scalars, and their limit is the answer. Moreover, the largest coefficient is attained: the normalized continuous solutions for the truncations have an $L^1$ cluster limit, and a lower bound for Monge–Ampère densities passes to $L^1$ limits of potentials by means of monotone upper envelopes. Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ have positive integral. Its truncations are bounded and nonzero, and we put 14.101 \begin{equation} \label{eq:individual-truncated-normalizer} f_ k=\min (f,k),\qquad b_ h(f)=\lim _{k\to \infty }c_ h(f_ k). \end{equation} By lemma 14.26.1 , the scalars $c_ h(f_ k)$ decrease as $k$ increases, so the limit exists in $[0,c_ h(f_1)]$. We call $b_ h(f)$ the subsolution threshold of $f$; theorem 14.27.2 below justifies the name. The same lemma gives 14.102 \begin{equation} \label{eq:individual-bounded-tests} b_ h(f)=\inf \{ c_ h(q):0\leq q\leq f,\  q\in L^\infty , \  \textstyle \int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}V>0\} . \end{equation} Indeed, every such $q$ satisfies $q\leq f_ k$ for $k\geq \| q\| _{L^\infty }$, hence $c_ h(q)\geq c_ h(f_ k)\geq b_ h(f)$, while the truncations $f_ k$ are themselves admissible. The Monge–Ampère operator is not continuous under $L^1$ convergence of potentials, but a lower bound for a Monge–Ampère density survives such convergence. The proof replaces the sequence by monotone upper envelopes, which converge in capacity, and uses the continuity of damped measures, theorem 7.3.1 , applied with the Hermitian form $h$ and the weight $t\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-t}$. For nonpositive $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$, the corresponding damped measure is $\mathrm{e}^{v}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v)$, with weight zero on the pole set; it has finite mass and depends weakly continuously on $v$ under convergence in capacity. Lemma 14.27.1 . Let $s_ j,s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ be bounded above by a common constant and satisfy $s_ j\to s$ in $L^1(X)$. Suppose $g_ j,g\geq 0$, $g_ j\to g$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s_ j)\geq g_ j\, \mathrm{d}V \quad \text{for every }j.  \] Then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Subtracting a common constant, which does not change the extended measures, we may assume that all potentials are nonpositive. Pass to a subsequence along which $s_ j\to s$ and $g_ j\to g$ almost everywhere, and set \[  a_ j=\inf _{\ell \geq j}g_\ell ,\qquad w_ j=\left(\sup _{\ell \geq j}s_\ell \right)^*.  \] Then $0\leq a_ j\uparrow g$ almost everywhere, and $w_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ decreases to $s$. Step 1: $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. Fix $j$. For $N\geq j$, the finite maximum $m_ N=\max _{j\leq \ell \leq N}s_\ell $ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$: on the set $\{ m_ N=s_\ell \} $, proposition 6.2.1 gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s_\ell )\geq g_\ell \, \mathrm{d}V\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and these sets cover $X$. As $N\to \infty $, the functions $m_ N$ increase, are bounded above by zero, and have regularized limit $w_ j$. By lemma 1.8.12 , $m_ N\to w_ j$ in capacity, so the damped measures $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)$ converge weakly to $\mathrm{e}^{w_ j}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)$. Since $m_ N\to w_ j$ almost everywhere and $a_ j\leq g$, dominated convergence gives $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}a_ j\to \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Passing to the limit in $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq \mathrm{e}^{m_ N}a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ gives \[  \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j) \geq \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The pole set of $w_ j$ has zero volume and is not charged by $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)$. Dividing by the positive weight off this set gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. Step 2: passage to $s$. Since $w_ j$ decreases to $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$, lemma 1.8.12 gives $w_ j\to s$ in capacity, and the damped measures of $w_ j$ converge weakly to $\mathrm{e}^ s\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)$. Moreover $0\leq \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\leq g$ and $\mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\to \mathrm{e}^ sg$ almost everywhere, so dominated convergence and Step 1 give \[  \mathrm{e}^ s\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s) \geq \mathrm{e}^ s g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Dividing by $\mathrm{e}^ s$ on $\{ s>-N\} $ and letting $N\to \infty $ gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V$ off the pole set of $s$. Both measures give zero mass to the pole set, which proves the lemma. $\square$ Theorem 14.27.2 . For every nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ with positive integral, \[  b_ h(f)=\max \{ a\geq 0:\text{there exists }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h) \text{ with }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u) \geq af\, \mathrm{d}V\} .  \] In particular, $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ admits a positive scaled subsolution if and only if $b_ h(f)>0$. Proof. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then also $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af_ k\, \mathrm{d}V$ for every $k$, and lemma 14.26.1 gives $a\leq c_ h(f_ k)$. Letting $k\to \infty $ gives $a\leq b_ h(f)$. If $b_ h(f)=0$, the coefficient zero is attained by the zero potential. Suppose now that $b=b_ h(f)>0$, and let $u_ k$ be continuous solutions of \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ k)=c_ h(f_ k)f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ k=0.  \] By theorem 1.4.2 , a subsequence $u_{k_ j}$ converges in $L^1$ to some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$. The densities $c_ h(f_{k_ j})f_{k_ j}$ are dominated by $c_ h(f_1)f$ and converge to $bf$ almost everywhere, hence in $L^1$. Lemma 14.27.1 now gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, so the maximum is attained at $a=b$. $\square$ When $b_ h(f)>0$, a function $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is called a threshold subsolution for $f$, and a threshold subsolution with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is called a threshold solution ; the theorem shows that threshold subsolutions exist. Its proof preserves only a lower bound for the density. It shows neither that the normalized solutions $u_ k$ converge in capacity, nor that their limit has finite mass, nor that equality holds in the limit; these are the additional difficulties of the exact equation for an individual density. The threshold does not depend on the choice of truncations. If $(q_ k)$ is any increasing sequence of nonzero bounded densities converging to $f$ almost everywhere, then $c_ h(q_ k)\geq b_ h(f)$ by ( 14.102 ); conversely, the second half of the proof, applied to normalized solutions for $q_ k$, gives a subsolution with coefficient $\lim _ kc_ h(q_ k)$, which is therefore at most $b_ h(f)$. Hence $\lim _ kc_ h(q_ k)=b_ h(f)$.
14.101 \begin{equation} \label{eq:individual-truncated-normalizer} f_ k=\min (f,k),\qquad b_ h(f)=\lim _{k\to \infty }c_ h(f_ k). \end{equation}
14.102 \begin{equation} \label{eq:individual-bounded-tests} b_ h(f)=\inf \{ c_ h(q):0\leq q\leq f,\  q\in L^\infty , \  \textstyle \int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}V>0\} . \end{equation}

title: Lemma 14.27.1
text: Lemma 14.27.1 . Let $s_ j,s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ be bounded above by a common constant and satisfy $s_ j\to s$ in $L^1(X)$. Suppose $g_ j,g\geq 0$, $g_ j\to g$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s_ j)\geq g_ j\, \mathrm{d}V \quad \text{for every }j.  \] Then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Subtracting a common constant, which does not change the extended measures, we may assume that all potentials are nonpositive. Pass to a subsequence along which $s_ j\to s$ and $g_ j\to g$ almost everywhere, and set \[  a_ j=\inf _{\ell \geq j}g_\ell ,\qquad w_ j=\left(\sup _{\ell \geq j}s_\ell \right)^*.  \] Then $0\leq a_ j\uparrow g$ almost everywhere, and $w_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ decreases to $s$. Step 1: $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. Fix $j$. For $N\geq j$, the finite maximum $m_ N=\max _{j\leq \ell \leq N}s_\ell $ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$: on the set $\{ m_ N=s_\ell \} $, proposition 6.2.1 gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s_\ell )\geq g_\ell \, \mathrm{d}V\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and these sets cover $X$. As $N\to \infty $, the functions $m_ N$ increase, are bounded above by zero, and have regularized limit $w_ j$. By lemma 1.8.12 , $m_ N\to w_ j$ in capacity, so the damped measures $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)$ converge weakly to $\mathrm{e}^{w_ j}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)$. Since $m_ N\to w_ j$ almost everywhere and $a_ j\leq g$, dominated convergence gives $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}a_ j\to \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Passing to the limit in $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq \mathrm{e}^{m_ N}a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ gives \[  \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j) \geq \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The pole set of $w_ j$ has zero volume and is not charged by $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)$. Dividing by the positive weight off this set gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. Step 2: passage to $s$. Since $w_ j$ decreases to $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$, lemma 1.8.12 gives $w_ j\to s$ in capacity, and the damped measures of $w_ j$ converge weakly to $\mathrm{e}^ s\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)$. Moreover $0\leq \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\leq g$ and $\mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\to \mathrm{e}^ sg$ almost everywhere, so dominated convergence and Step 1 give \[  \mathrm{e}^ s\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s) \geq \mathrm{e}^ s g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Dividing by $\mathrm{e}^ s$ on $\{ s>-N\} $ and letting $N\to \infty $ gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V$ off the pole set of $s$. Both measures give zero mass to the pole set, which proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.27.2
text: Theorem 14.27.2 . For every nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ with positive integral, \[  b_ h(f)=\max \{ a\geq 0:\text{there exists }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h) \text{ with }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u) \geq af\, \mathrm{d}V\} .  \] In particular, $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ admits a positive scaled subsolution if and only if $b_ h(f)>0$. Proof. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then also $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af_ k\, \mathrm{d}V$ for every $k$, and lemma 14.26.1 gives $a\leq c_ h(f_ k)$. Letting $k\to \infty $ gives $a\leq b_ h(f)$. If $b_ h(f)=0$, the coefficient zero is attained by the zero potential. Suppose now that $b=b_ h(f)>0$, and let $u_ k$ be continuous solutions of \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ k)=c_ h(f_ k)f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ k=0.  \] By theorem 1.4.2 , a subsequence $u_{k_ j}$ converges in $L^1$ to some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$. The densities $c_ h(f_{k_ j})f_{k_ j}$ are dominated by $c_ h(f_1)f$ and converge to $bf$ almost everywhere, hence in $L^1$. Lemma 14.27.1 now gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, so the maximum is attained at $a=b$. $\square$

title: 14.27.1 The greatest normalized threshold subsolution
text: 14.27.1 The greatest normalized threshold subsolution Suppose $b_ h(f)>0$. The threshold subsolutions with supremum zero form a family that is stable under finite maxima and under $L^1$ limits. Its upper envelope is therefore again a normalized threshold subsolution, and it dominates all the others. Proposition 14.27.3 . Suppose $b=b_ h(f)>0$. The family \[  \mathcal S_ f=\{ s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h):\sup _ Xs=0, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V\}   \] is nonempty and compact in $L^1(X)$. Its upper envelope \[  \Phi _ f=\left(\sup _{s\in \mathcal S_ f}s\right)^*  \] belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$ and is therefore its greatest member. Moreover, let $u_\lambda $ be the greatest exponential solutions of corollary 14.34.2 and $v_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $. Every $L^1$ limit of a sequence $v_{\lambda _ j}$ with $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$ belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$, and hence lies below $\Phi _ f$. Proof. The family is nonempty by theorem 14.27.2 . By theorem 1.4.2 , an $L^1$ limit of members of $\mathcal S_ f$ is $h$-plurisubharmonic with supremum zero, and lemma 14.27.1 , with $g_ j=g=bf$, shows that it satisfies the measure inequality. Thus $\mathcal S_ f$ is a closed subset of the compact set of normalized $h$-plurisubharmonic functions, hence compact. It is also stable under finite maxima: if $s_1,s_2\in \mathcal S_ f$, then $\max (s_1,s_2)$ has supremum zero, and proposition 6.2.1 , applied on the sets where the maximum equals $s_1$ or $s_2$, gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(\max (s_1,s_2))\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. By Choquet's lemma there is a sequence $(s_ i)_{i\geq 1}$ in $\mathcal S_ f$ with $(\sup _ is_ i)^*=\Phi _ f$. Fix $s_0\in \mathcal S_ f$. The finite maxima $t_ N=\max (s_0,s_1,\ldots ,s_ N)$ belong to $\mathcal S_ f$, increase with $N$, and satisfy $s_0\leq t_ N\leq 0$; their regularized limit is $\Phi _ f$. Hence $t_ N\to \Phi _ f$ almost everywhere and, by dominated convergence, in $L^1$. Lemma 14.27.1 gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(\Phi _ f)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, and $s_0\leq \Phi _ f\leq 0$ forces $\sup _ X\Phi _ f=0$. Thus $\Phi _ f\in \mathcal S_ f$, and by construction it dominates every member of $\mathcal S_ f$. Finally, suppose $v_{\lambda _ j}\to v$ in $L^1$ with $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$. The measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_{\lambda _ j})=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ ju_{\lambda _ j}}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ have densities converging in $L^1$ to $bf$, by corollary 14.34.2 . Applying lemma 14.27.1 to these densities and potentials shows that $v\in \mathcal S_ f$. $\square$ The proposition gives a greatest normalized threshold subsolution, but not the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(\Phi _ f)=bf\, \mathrm{d}V$; in particular, it does not show that $\Phi _ f$ has finite mass. Proposition 14.27.4 . Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ have positive integral. If $f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for some $p>1$, then $b_ h(f)=c_ h(f)$. In general, \[  b_ h(f)\geq \frac{v_-(h)}{\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V}.  \] If $h$ is Kähler, then $b_ h(f)=\int _ Xh^ n/\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Suppose that $f\in L^ p$ with $p>1$, and let $v$ be a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$. It is a subsolution with coefficient $c_ h(f)$, so theorem 14.27.2 gives $c_ h(f)\leq b_ h(f)$. Conversely, lemma 14.26.1 , applied to a threshold subsolution, gives $b_ h(f)\leq c_ h(f)$. For general $f$, the continuous solution for $f_ k$ has total mass $c_ h(f_ k)\int _ Xf_ k\, \mathrm{d}V$, which is at least $v_-(h)$ by the definition of the lower mass. Letting $k\to \infty $ and using monotone convergence gives the lower bound for $b_ h(f)$. If $h$ is Kähler, Stokes' theorem for bounded potentials gives instead the identity $c_ h(f_ k)\int _ Xf_ k\, \mathrm{d}V=\int _ Xh^ n$, and the same limit proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: 14.27.2 Smooth comparison tests
text: 14.27.2 Smooth comparison tests The infimum ( 14.102 ) runs over bounded measurable densities below $f$. One may ask whether smooth densities suffice to compute the threshold. A smooth test $g$ is in general not below $f$, so we compare it with $f$ through the ratio $\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }$. Thus let $f$ be a probability density bounded below by a positive constant, and define \[  C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f)=\inf _ g c_ h(g)\| g/f\| _{L^\infty },  \] where $g$ ranges over smooth strictly positive probability densities. For each such $g$, with $R=\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }$, a subsolution with coefficient $a$ for $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is a subsolution with coefficient $a/R$ for $g\, \mathrm{d}V$, so $a\leq Rc_ h(g)$ by lemma 14.26.1 . Hence $b_ h(f)\leq C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f)$, with equality if $f$ is smooth (take $g=f$). When the lower mass vanishes, the two quantities can differ even in their positivity. Theorem 14.27.5 . If $v_-(h)=0$, there is a probability density $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ bounded below by a positive constant such that \[  b_ h(f)=0<C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f).  \] Thus $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ admits no positive scaled subsolution, although $c_ h(g)\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }$ is bounded below by a positive constant for all smooth strictly positive probability densities $g$. Proof. We construct $f=(1+Q)/M$, where $Q\geq 0$ concentrates on closed nowhere dense sets in such a way that it has essential infimum zero on every nonempty open set. Step 1: the pieces. Let $(U_ i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a countable basis of nonempty open subsets of $X$. We construct inductively numbers $\alpha _ j>0$, nonzero bounded densities $q_ j$, and closed nowhere dense sets $K_ j\subset X$ such that \[  \int _ Xq_ j\, \mathrm{d}V\leq 1,\qquad q_ j=0\text{ outside }K_ j,\qquad c_ h(q_ j)\leq \alpha _ j2^{-j}.  \] Start with $\alpha _1=1/4$. Once $\alpha _ j$ has been chosen, theorem 26.14.3 , theorem 26.1.3 and $v_-(h)=0$ give a smooth strictly positive probability density $g_ j$ with $c_ h(g_ j)<\alpha _ j2^{-j}$. Removing from $X$ an open dense set of small volume, we obtain a closed nowhere dense set $K_ j$ for which $q_ j=g_ j\mathbf1_{K_ j}$ is nonzero and, since $g_ j$ is bounded, arbitrarily close to $g_ j$ in $L^2$. By lemma 14.26.2 with $p=2$, we can therefore choose $K_ j$ so that $c_ h(q_ j)\leq \alpha _ j2^{-j}$. After $K_1,\ldots ,K_ N$ have been chosen, put \[  m_ N=\min _{1\leq i\leq N} \mathrm{d}V\left(U_ i\setminus \bigcup _{j=1}^ NK_ j\right)>0;  \] each set inside the minimum is open and nonempty, since a finite union of closed nowhere dense sets is closed and nowhere dense. Choose \[  0<\alpha _{N+1}\leq \min \{ \alpha _ N/2,\  2^{-N-2}m_ N\} ,  \] and continue. In particular, \[  \sum _{j>N}\alpha _ j\leq 2\alpha _{N+1} \leq 2^{-N-1}m_ N.  \] Step 2: the concentrating part. The function $Q=\sum _ j\alpha _ jq_ j$ is nonnegative and integrable. We claim that its essential infimum on every nonempty open set is zero. Since every nonempty open set contains some $U_ i$, it suffices to consider $U_ i$. Take $N\geq i$ and remove $K_1,\ldots ,K_ N$ from $U_ i$. On the remaining set, whose volume is at least $m_ N$, the first $N$ summands of $Q$ vanish. By Markov's inequality, the set where the tail $\sum _{j>N}\alpha _ jq_ j$ exceeds $2^{-N}$ has volume at most \[  2^ N\sum _{j>N}\alpha _ j\int _ Xq_ j\, \mathrm{d}V \leq m_ N/2.  \] Hence $Q\leq 2^{-N}$ on a subset of $U_ i$ of positive volume. Letting $N\to \infty $ proves the claim. Step 3: $b_ h(f)=0$. Set $M=\int _ X(1+Q)\, \mathrm{d}V$ and $f=(1+Q)/M$, a probability density with $f\geq 1/M$. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq (a\alpha _ j/M)q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and lemma 14.26.1 gives \[  \frac{a\alpha _ j}{M}\leq c_ h(q_ j)\leq \alpha _ j2^{-j} \quad \text{for every }j.  \] This is impossible. Hence $b_ h(f)=0$ by theorem 14.27.2 . Step 4: $C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f)>0$. Let $g$ be a smooth strictly positive probability density and put $R=\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }$. Then $g\leq R(1+Q)/M$ almost everywhere, and this forces $g\leq R/M$ everywhere. Otherwise, by continuity, $g>R(1+\varepsilon )/M$ on a nonempty open set for some $\varepsilon >0$, while $Q<\varepsilon $ on a subset of positive volume of this set by Step 2, a contradiction. The order and homogeneity of the scalar in lemma 14.26.1 now give $c_ h(g)\geq c_ h(R/M)=(M/R)c_ h(1)$, that is, \[  R c_ h(g)\geq M c_ h(1).  \] The constant density $g=1$ attains this value, since $\operatorname *{ess\, inf}_ XQ=0$ gives $\| 1/f\| _{L^\infty }=M$. Thus $C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f)=M c_ h(1)>0$, as required. $\square$ The point is that a smooth test $g$ with $\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }\leq R$ is controlled by the essential infimum of $f$ on open sets. It therefore cannot detect an increase of $f$ that leaves this essential infimum unchanged on every open set, whereas bounded measurable tests below $f$ do detect it. The theorem concerns only the existence of subsolutions. Exact solutions of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$, the singularity class in which they should be sought, and compactness of their normalized solutions are further problems; see 33.1.1 .

title: 14.28 Gauduchon tests for integrable densities
text: 14.28 Gauduchon tests for integrable densities For a smooth strictly positive probability density, the normalization scalar is an infimum of Gauduchon quotients by theorem 26.1.3 . We extend this dual formula to the threshold of an arbitrary integrable density. A uniform bound for all Gauduchon tests in a single $L^ r$ norm allows the passage from smooth to bounded densities, and monotone truncation then reaches all integrable densities, including those with zero threshold. The formula is most naturally written for the $n$th root of the density. Recall that a Hermitian form $\gamma $ is Gauduchon if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$ (definition 4.1.1 ); in dimension one every Hermitian form is Gauduchon. For a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ and a nonnegative measurable function $p$, put \[  L_{h,\gamma }(p)= \frac{\displaystyle \int _ Xp(\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n}{\displaystyle \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}} =\int _ Xp\, a_\gamma \, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad a_\gamma =\frac{(\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)^{(n-1)/n}}{\int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}.  \] Since the coefficient $a_\gamma $ is smooth and strictly positive, each individual test $L_{h,\gamma }$ is finite on $L^ n$; the supremum over $\gamma $ may be infinite. In dimension one the test is $\int _ Xp\, \mathrm{d}V/\int _ Xh$. For real or complex $p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$, define the root functional \[  \rho _ h(p)=b_ h(|p|^ n)^{-1/n}\quad (p\ne 0),\qquad \rho _ h(0)=0,  \] with the convention $0^{-1/n}=+\infty $. Theorem 14.28.1 . For every real or complex $p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$, 14.103 \begin{equation} \label{eq:integrable-gauduchon-root} \rho _ h(p)=\sup _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}}L_{h,\gamma }(|p|). \end{equation} Equivalently, for every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, 14.104 \begin{equation} \label{eq:integrable-gauduchon-threshold} b_ h(f)^{1/n}= \inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\displaystyle \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\displaystyle \int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n}. \end{equation} Both sides of ( 14.103 ) may be $+\infty $, and both sides of ( 14.104 ) may vanish. Proof. It suffices to prove ( 14.103 ) for $p\geq 0$, since both sides depend only on $|p|$; the case $p=0$ is immediate. Step 1: smooth strictly positive $p$. Apply theorem 26.1.3 , with background $h$, to the probability measure $\mu =p^ n\mathrm{d}V/Z$, where $Z=\int _ Xp^ n\, \mathrm{d}V$. By homogeneity (lemma 14.26.1 ) its scalar is $c_ h(\mu )=Zc_ h(p^ n)$, while the denominator of each Gauduchon quotient is $Z^{-1/n}\int _ Xp(\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. The factors of $Z$ cancel, and the dual formula becomes \[  c_ h(p^ n)^{-1/n}=\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p).  \] Since $b_ h(p^ n)=c_ h(p^ n)$ by proposition 14.27.4 , this proves ( 14.103 ) for such $p$. Step 2: a uniform bound for the tests. The lower-density estimate of theorem 10.3.3 , with exponent two, gives a constant $m_ h>0$ such that \[  c_ h(p^ n)\| p^ n\| _{L^2}\geq m_ h  \] for smooth strictly positive $p$. By Step 1, therefore, 14.105 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gauduchon-test-uniform-bound} L_{h,\gamma }(p)\leq m_ h^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^{2n}} \quad \text{for every }\gamma . \end{equation} Approximating nonnegative functions in $L^{2n}$ by smooth strictly positive ones extends this bound to all nonnegative $p\in L^{2n}$. Since $a_\gamma >0$, duality gives $\| a_\gamma \| _{L^{2n/(2n-1)}}\leq m_ h^{-1/n}$ for every $\gamma $. In particular, $p\mapsto \sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p)$ is Lipschitz on the cone of nonnegative functions in $L^{2n}$, with the same constant. Step 3: bounded $p$. Let $p\geq 0$ be bounded and nonzero, and approximate it in $L^{2n}$ by smooth strictly positive functions $p_ j$. By Hölder's inequality, $p_ j^ n\to p^ n$ in $L^2$, so lemma 14.26.2 gives \[  c_ h(p_ j^ n)\longrightarrow c_ h(p^ n)>0.  \] By the Lipschitz bound derived from ( 14.105 ), \[  \sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p_ j) \longrightarrow \sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p).  \] Passing to the limit in the identity of Step 1 for $p_ j$, and using $b_ h(p^ n)=c_ h(p^ n)$ (proposition 14.27.4 ), we obtain ( 14.103 ) for bounded $p$. Step 4: general $p$. For nonnegative $p\in L^ n$, put $p_ k=\min (p,k)$. Then $p_ k^ n=\min (p^ n,k^ n)$ are truncations of $p^ n$, so the definition of $b_ h$ and Step 3 give \[  \rho _ h(p)=\lim _{k\to \infty }c_ h(p_ k^ n)^{-1/n} =\sup _ k\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p_ k).  \] For each fixed $\gamma $, monotone convergence gives $\sup _ kL_{h,\gamma }(p_ k)=L_{h,\gamma }(p)$. Interchanging the two suprema proves ( 14.103 ). Finally, every denominator in ( 14.104 ) is positive; taking reciprocals in ( 14.103 ) with $p=f^{1/n}$ proves ( 14.104 ), including the case $b_ h(f)=0$. $\square$ For a nonsmooth density we do not claim that the infimum in ( 14.104 ) is attained by a Gauduchon form; attainment by Gauduchon currents is studied in section 26.9 . For $n\geq 2$, the coefficient of the test has norm \[  \| a_\gamma \| _{L^{n/(n-1)}} =\frac{(\int _ X\gamma ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}}{\int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}  \] in the exponent dual to $n$. By ( 26.89 ) in theorem 26.14.3 , positive lower mass is therefore equivalent to a uniform bound for these norms, that is, for all tests on $L^ n$ simultaneously. Without positive lower mass, Step 2 of the proof still bounds the coefficients uniformly in the weaker norm of $L^{2n/(2n-1)}$, on every compact Hermitian manifold. This suffices to pass from smooth to bounded densities, and monotone truncation then treats all integrable densities. Proposition 14.28.2 . Let $f$ be a nonzero nonnegative function in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and let $p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$ be real or complex. If $h_1,h_2$ are Hermitian forms on $X$ and $m h_1\leq h_2\leq M h_1$ for positive constants $m,M$, then \[  m^ n b_{h_1}(f)\leq b_{h_2}(f)\leq M^ n b_{h_1}(f), \qquad M^{-1}\rho _{h_1}(p)\leq \rho _{h_2}(p)\leq m^{-1}\rho _{h_1}(p).  \] If $h_2-h_1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ for a smooth real function $a$, then $b_{h_1}(f)=b_{h_2}(f)$ and $\rho _{h_1}(p)=\rho _{h_2}(p)$. Proof. For every Gauduchon form $\gamma $, the numerators in ( 14.104 ) satisfy \[  m\int _ Xh_1\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\leq \int _ Xh_2\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \leq M\int _ Xh_1\wedge \gamma ^{n-1},  \] while the denominators do not depend on the background. Taking the infimum over $\gamma $ and then $n$th powers proves the bounds for the thresholds; taking reciprocal $n$th roots gives the bounds for $\rho $, with the stated conventions at zero and infinity. If $h_2-h_1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$, the numerators agree by Stokes' theorem, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$. $\square$ Any two Hermitian metrics on the compact manifold $X$ are comparable. Hence the positivity of $b_ h(f)$, and the set of real or complex $p\in L^ n$ with $\rho _ h(p)<+\infty $, do not depend on the choice of $h$. The dependence on the reference volume is equally simple. If $\mathrm{d}V$ is replaced by $\mathrm{d}V'=\sigma \, \mathrm{d}V$ with a smooth function $\sigma >0$, the measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ has density $f'=f/\sigma $ with respect to $\mathrm{d}V'$, and theorem 14.27.2 shows that the threshold of $f'$ relative to $\mathrm{d}V'$ equals $b_ h(f)$. Correspondingly, the map $p\mapsto \sigma ^{-1/n}p$ from $L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$ to $L^ n(\mathrm{d}V')$ preserves both the $L^ n$ norm and the root functional.

title: Theorem 14.28.1
text: Theorem 14.28.1 . For every real or complex $p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$, 14.103 \begin{equation} \label{eq:integrable-gauduchon-root} \rho _ h(p)=\sup _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}}L_{h,\gamma }(|p|). \end{equation} Equivalently, for every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, 14.104 \begin{equation} \label{eq:integrable-gauduchon-threshold} b_ h(f)^{1/n}= \inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\displaystyle \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\displaystyle \int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n}. \end{equation} Both sides of ( 14.103 ) may be $+\infty $, and both sides of ( 14.104 ) may vanish. Proof. It suffices to prove ( 14.103 ) for $p\geq 0$, since both sides depend only on $|p|$; the case $p=0$ is immediate. Step 1: smooth strictly positive $p$. Apply theorem 26.1.3 , with background $h$, to the probability measure $\mu =p^ n\mathrm{d}V/Z$, where $Z=\int _ Xp^ n\, \mathrm{d}V$. By homogeneity (lemma 14.26.1 ) its scalar is $c_ h(\mu )=Zc_ h(p^ n)$, while the denominator of each Gauduchon quotient is $Z^{-1/n}\int _ Xp(\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. The factors of $Z$ cancel, and the dual formula becomes \[  c_ h(p^ n)^{-1/n}=\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p).  \] Since $b_ h(p^ n)=c_ h(p^ n)$ by proposition 14.27.4 , this proves ( 14.103 ) for such $p$. Step 2: a uniform bound for the tests. The lower-density estimate of theorem 10.3.3 , with exponent two, gives a constant $m_ h>0$ such that \[  c_ h(p^ n)\| p^ n\| _{L^2}\geq m_ h  \] for smooth strictly positive $p$. By Step 1, therefore, 14.105 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gauduchon-test-uniform-bound} L_{h,\gamma }(p)\leq m_ h^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^{2n}} \quad \text{for every }\gamma . \end{equation} Approximating nonnegative functions in $L^{2n}$ by smooth strictly positive ones extends this bound to all nonnegative $p\in L^{2n}$. Since $a_\gamma >0$, duality gives $\| a_\gamma \| _{L^{2n/(2n-1)}}\leq m_ h^{-1/n}$ for every $\gamma $. In particular, $p\mapsto \sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p)$ is Lipschitz on the cone of nonnegative functions in $L^{2n}$, with the same constant. Step 3: bounded $p$. Let $p\geq 0$ be bounded and nonzero, and approximate it in $L^{2n}$ by smooth strictly positive functions $p_ j$. By Hölder's inequality, $p_ j^ n\to p^ n$ in $L^2$, so lemma 14.26.2 gives \[  c_ h(p_ j^ n)\longrightarrow c_ h(p^ n)>0.  \] By the Lipschitz bound derived from ( 14.105 ), \[  \sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p_ j) \longrightarrow \sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p).  \] Passing to the limit in the identity of Step 1 for $p_ j$, and using $b_ h(p^ n)=c_ h(p^ n)$ (proposition 14.27.4 ), we obtain ( 14.103 ) for bounded $p$. Step 4: general $p$. For nonnegative $p\in L^ n$, put $p_ k=\min (p,k)$. Then $p_ k^ n=\min (p^ n,k^ n)$ are truncations of $p^ n$, so the definition of $b_ h$ and Step 3 give \[  \rho _ h(p)=\lim _{k\to \infty }c_ h(p_ k^ n)^{-1/n} =\sup _ k\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p_ k).  \] For each fixed $\gamma $, monotone convergence gives $\sup _ kL_{h,\gamma }(p_ k)=L_{h,\gamma }(p)$. Interchanging the two suprema proves ( 14.103 ). Finally, every denominator in ( 14.104 ) is positive; taking reciprocals in ( 14.103 ) with $p=f^{1/n}$ proves ( 14.104 ), including the case $b_ h(f)=0$. $\square$

title: 14.29 Exact equations on products with zero lower mass
search_title: Exact equations on products with zero lower mass
text: 14.29 Exact equations on products with zero lower mass Positive lower mass guarantees solvability for all measures, but an individual density can have a positive threshold and an exact equation even when the lower mass vanishes. We construct explicit examples on products. Let $(X_0,h_0)$ be a connected compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $m\geq 1$ with $v_-(h_0)=0$. On its product with a projective space, a singular potential pulled back from the projective factor solves an explicit equation whose density has a sublogarithmic singularity. The coefficient is computed from the normalization scalars of bounded truncations, the equation itself follows from the product structure of the Monge–Ampère measure, and the product background again has zero lower mass. Throughout this section, $Y=\mathbb P^ k$ with $k\geq 1$, $\kappa $ is the Fubini–Study form normalized by $\int _ Y\kappa ^ k=1$, and $X=X_0\times Y$, a compact complex manifold of dimension $N=m+k$ with the Hermitian background $H=h_0+\kappa $. Forms and functions on the factors are identified with their pullbacks to $X$. Put \[  V_0=\int _{X_0}h_0^ m,\qquad C=\binom Nm,\qquad \mu =V_0^{-1}h_0^ m\wedge \kappa ^ k,\qquad R=\frac{\mu }{\mathrm{d}V},  \] where $\mathrm{d}V$ is any smooth positive probability volume form on $X$. Then $\mu $ is a smooth positive probability volume form, and $R$ is smooth and bounded above and below by positive constants. The normalization scalar $c_ H$ and the threshold $b_ H$ are those of section 14.26 , section 14.27 , now on the $N$-dimensional manifold $X$ with background $H$. For $0<\alpha <1$ define, on $Y$, \[  \psi ([z_0:\cdots :z_ k])=\log \frac{\sum _{i=1}^ k|z_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ k|z_ i|^2}, \qquad u_\alpha =1-(1-\psi )^\alpha .  \] The function $\psi $ is smooth on $Y\setminus \{ o\} $, where $o=[1:0:\cdots :0]$, and tends to $-\infty $ at $o$; moreover $\psi \leq 0$, with equality exactly on the hyperplane $\{ z_0=0\} $. Thus $u_\alpha \leq 0$, and $u_\alpha $ has a single pole at $o$, where $u_\alpha (o)=-\infty $. Lemma 14.29.1 . The function $u_\alpha $ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic with supremum zero, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (u_\alpha )=q_\alpha \kappa ^ k, \qquad \int _ Yq_\alpha \kappa ^ k=1.  \] The density $q_\alpha $ is smooth and strictly positive on $Y\setminus \{ o\} $, belongs to $L^1(\kappa ^ k)$, and belongs to no $L^ p(\kappa ^ k)$ with $p>1$. If we set $q_\alpha (o)=+\infty $, then every truncation $\min (q_\alpha ,s)$, $s>0$, is strictly positive and continuous on $Y$. Proof. In homogeneous coordinates, $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _{i=1}^ k|z_ i|^2\geq 0$ on $Y\setminus \{ o\} $. The function $\chi (t)=1-(1-t)^\alpha $, $t\leq 0$, is increasing and convex, with $0<\chi '\leq \alpha $. Hence, off $o$, \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \geq (1-\chi '(\psi ))\kappa +\chi '(\psi )(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi ) \geq (1-\alpha )\kappa .  \] Since $u_\alpha $ is bounded above, it extends across $o$ as a $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function, with value $-\infty $ at $o$. On the hyperplane $\{ z_0=0\} $ we have $\psi =0$, hence $u_\alpha =0$, so $\sup _ Yu_\alpha =0$. To compute the measure, work in the affine chart $z_0=1$ and put $r=\sum _{i=1}^ k|z_ i|^2$. On this chart $\kappa =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+r)$ and $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F$, where $s(r)=1-\log (r/(1+r))$ and \[  F(r)=\log (1+r)+1-s(r)^\alpha ,\qquad Q(r)=rF'(r)=\frac{r+\alpha s(r)^{\alpha -1}}{1+r}.  \] For a radial function, the Levi form has the tangential eigenvalue $F'(r)=Q(r)/r$, with multiplicity $k-1$, and the radial eigenvalue \[  Q'(r)=\frac{1-\alpha s(r)^{\alpha -1}+\alpha (1-\alpha )r^{-1}s(r)^{\alpha -2}}{(1+r)^2}>0.  \] Integrating in the radial variable gives $\int _{\{ a<r<b\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^ k=Q(b)^ k-Q(a)^ k$; the constant of proportionality is fixed by the case $F=\log (1+r)$, for which $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^ k=\kappa ^ k$ has mass one on the chart and $Q(r)=r/(1+r)$. Since again $Q(0)=0$ and $Q(\infty )=1$, the punctured chart has mass one. The complement of the chart is a hyperplane, which has zero volume, and the non-pluripolar measure does not charge $o$. Hence $\int _ Yq_\alpha \kappa ^ k=1$. Relative to $\kappa ^ k$, whose tangential and radial eigenvalues are $1/(1+r)$ and $1/(1+r)^2$, the density on this chart is \[  q_\alpha (r)=(1+r)^{k+1}(Q(r)/r)^{k-1}Q'(r) \asymp r^{-k}(1-\log r)^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}\quad (r\downarrow 0).  \] Near $r=0$ the smooth volume is comparable to $r^{k-1}\mathrm{d}r$ in the radial variable, so $q_\alpha $ is integrable. For $p>1$, the substitution $L=1-\log r$ turns the integral of $q_\alpha ^ p$ into the integral of $\mathrm{e}^{k(p-1)L}$ times a power of $L$, which diverges. The same asymptotics show that $q_\alpha (r)\to +\infty $ uniformly as $r\downarrow 0$, so every truncation $\min (q_\alpha ,s)$ is continuous at $o$. Finally, $q_\alpha \geq (1-\alpha )^ k>0$ by the lower bound $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \geq (1-\alpha )\kappa $. $\square$ Lemma 14.29.2 . Let $g$ be a strictly positive continuous function on $Y$, and put $M_ g=\int _ Yg\kappa ^ k$. Then \[  c_ H(Rg)=\frac{CV_0}{M_ g}.  \] Proof. Suppose first that $g$ is smooth. Since $\kappa $ is Kähler, theorem 9.1.1 on $Y$ gives a smooth $\phi _ g$ with $A_ g=\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ g>0$ and $A_ g^ k=(g/M_ g)\kappa ^ k$; the scalar is determined by integration, since both sides have mass one. On $X$, since $h_0^{m+1}=0$ and $A_ g^{k+1}=0$ for dimensional reasons, \[  (H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ g)^ N=C h_0^ m\wedge A_ g^ k =(CV_0/M_ g)Rg\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ H(Rg)=CV_0/M_ g$. For continuous $g>0$, choose smooth $g_ l>0$ converging uniformly to $g$. Since $g$ has a positive minimum, $(1-\varepsilon _ l)g\leq g_ l\leq (1+\varepsilon _ l)g$ for some $\varepsilon _ l\in (0,1)$ tending to zero. The order and homogeneity of the scalar in lemma 14.26.1 give \[  (1-\varepsilon _ l)c_ H(Rg_ l)\leq c_ H(Rg) \leq (1+\varepsilon _ l)c_ H(Rg_ l).  \] Since $M_{g_ l}\to M_ g$, the smooth case proves the formula. $\square$ Theorem 14.29.3 . The Hermitian form $H$ is not closed and satisfies $v_-(H)=0$. For every $0<\alpha <1$, the function $f=Rq_\alpha $ is a probability density in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, belonging to no $L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ with $p>1$, and \[  b_ H(f)=CV_0>0,\qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=b_ H(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The potential $u_\alpha $, pulled back to $X$, has supremum zero and finite mass $CV_0$. It belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,0)$, and $P_{\delta H}(u_\alpha )\not\equiv -\infty $ for every $0<\delta <1$. Proof. Step 1: the threshold. Write $a=\min _ XR>0$, $A=\max _ XR$, and $M_ s=\int _ Y\min (q_\alpha ,s)\kappa ^ k$ for $s>0$. By lemma 14.29.1 , the truncations $\min (q_\alpha ,s)$ are continuous and strictly positive, and $M_ s\uparrow 1$ as $s\to \infty $. The truncations of $f$ satisfy \[  R\min (q_\alpha ,j/A)\leq \min (Rq_\alpha ,j) \leq R\min (q_\alpha ,j/a).  \] Hence lemma 14.29.2 and the monotonicity of the scalar give \[  \frac{CV_0}{M_{j/a}}\leq c_ H(\min (f,j)) \leq \frac{CV_0}{M_{j/A}}.  \] Both bounds tend to $CV_0$ as $j\to \infty $, so $b_ H(f)=CV_0$, whatever the reference volume $\mathrm{d}V$. Step 2: the equation. For $u_{\alpha ,j}=\max (u_\alpha ,-j)$, the binomial expansion of bounded local products, with factor forms of degrees $m$ and $k$, gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_ H(u_{\alpha ,j}) =C h_0^ m\wedge \mathrm{MA}_\kappa (u_{\alpha ,j}).  \] Multiplying by $\mathbf1_{\{ u_\alpha >-j\} }$ and letting $j\to \infty $, as in the definition ( 6.1 ) of the extended measure, we obtain \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=Ch_0^ m\wedge q_\alpha \kappa ^ k =CV_0\, q_\alpha \mu =CV_0f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] a measure of mass $CV_0$. The bounds $a\leq R\leq A$ transfer the integrability properties of $q_\alpha $ to $f$. Step 3: lower mass and nonclosedness. Pull back bounded $h_0$-plurisubharmonic functions whose masses on $X_0$ tend to zero. The same expansion shows that their $H$-masses are $C$ times their masses on $X_0$, so $v_-(H)=0$. If $h_0$ were closed, Stokes' theorem would give every bounded $h_0$-plurisubharmonic function the mass $V_0>0$, contradicting $v_-(h_0)=0$. Hence $h_0$, and therefore $H$, is not closed. Step 4: the envelopes. Choose $\alpha <\beta <1$. For $b\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon >0$ with $\varepsilon \beta \leq 1$, the number \[  K_ b=\sup _{s\geq 1}\{ b s^\alpha -\varepsilon s^\beta \} -b  \] is finite, since $\beta >\alpha $. The function $g_ b=-\varepsilon (1-\psi )^\beta -K_ b$ on $Y$ satisfies $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ b\geq (1-\varepsilon \beta )\kappa \geq 0$, by the chain-rule computation in the proof of lemma 14.29.1 , applied to the increasing convex function $t\mapsto -\varepsilon (1-t)^\beta $, whose derivative is at most $\varepsilon \beta $ for $t\leq 0$. With $L=1-\psi \geq 1$, the inequality $g_ b\leq bu_\alpha $ reads $bL^\alpha -\varepsilon L^\beta -b\leq K_ b$, so it holds on $Y\setminus \{ o\} $, and also at $o$, where both sides are $-\infty $. Thus the pullback of $g_ b$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,H)$ and lies below $bu_\alpha $. Since $b\geq 1$ is arbitrary, $u_\alpha \in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,0)$ by definition 13.4.1 . For $0<\delta <1$, take $b=1$ and $\varepsilon \beta \leq \delta $. Then $g_1$ is $\delta H$-plurisubharmonic and lies below $u_\alpha $, so $P_{\delta H}(u_\alpha )\geq g_1$ is not identically $-\infty $. $\square$ Corollary 14.29.4 . Let $X_0$ be the elliptic threefold of theorem 26.18.1 , with the balanced metric $\omega $ of proposition 26.18.7 . On $X_0\times \mathbb P^2$, with background $H=\omega +\kappa $, the densities $f=Rq_\alpha $ of the preceding theorem satisfy \[  v_-(H)=0,\qquad b_ H(f)=240\pi , \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=240\pi f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Theorem 26.18.1 gives $v_-(\omega )=0$, and proposition 26.18.7 gives $V_0=24\pi $. The product theorem applies with $m=3$, $k=2$ and $C=\binom 53=10$. $\square$ These examples show that an individual density can have a positive threshold and an exact equation even though the background has zero lower mass. The exactness comes from the product structure. For $k\geq 2$, the radial flux also identifies the normalized exponential limit in theorem 14.35.2 ; the first moment determines whether scalar centering has a finite limit. 33.1.1 asks for an exact equation for every integrable density with positive threshold.

title: Lemma 14.29.2
text: Lemma 14.29.2 . Let $g$ be a strictly positive continuous function on $Y$, and put $M_ g=\int _ Yg\kappa ^ k$. Then \[  c_ H(Rg)=\frac{CV_0}{M_ g}.  \] Proof. Suppose first that $g$ is smooth. Since $\kappa $ is Kähler, theorem 9.1.1 on $Y$ gives a smooth $\phi _ g$ with $A_ g=\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ g>0$ and $A_ g^ k=(g/M_ g)\kappa ^ k$; the scalar is determined by integration, since both sides have mass one. On $X$, since $h_0^{m+1}=0$ and $A_ g^{k+1}=0$ for dimensional reasons, \[  (H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ g)^ N=C h_0^ m\wedge A_ g^ k =(CV_0/M_ g)Rg\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ H(Rg)=CV_0/M_ g$. For continuous $g>0$, choose smooth $g_ l>0$ converging uniformly to $g$. Since $g$ has a positive minimum, $(1-\varepsilon _ l)g\leq g_ l\leq (1+\varepsilon _ l)g$ for some $\varepsilon _ l\in (0,1)$ tending to zero. The order and homogeneity of the scalar in lemma 14.26.1 give \[  (1-\varepsilon _ l)c_ H(Rg_ l)\leq c_ H(Rg) \leq (1+\varepsilon _ l)c_ H(Rg_ l).  \] Since $M_{g_ l}\to M_ g$, the smooth case proves the formula. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.29.3
text: Theorem 14.29.3 . The Hermitian form $H$ is not closed and satisfies $v_-(H)=0$. For every $0<\alpha <1$, the function $f=Rq_\alpha $ is a probability density in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, belonging to no $L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ with $p>1$, and \[  b_ H(f)=CV_0>0,\qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=b_ H(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The potential $u_\alpha $, pulled back to $X$, has supremum zero and finite mass $CV_0$. It belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,0)$, and $P_{\delta H}(u_\alpha )\not\equiv -\infty $ for every $0<\delta <1$. Proof. Step 1: the threshold. Write $a=\min _ XR>0$, $A=\max _ XR$, and $M_ s=\int _ Y\min (q_\alpha ,s)\kappa ^ k$ for $s>0$. By lemma 14.29.1 , the truncations $\min (q_\alpha ,s)$ are continuous and strictly positive, and $M_ s\uparrow 1$ as $s\to \infty $. The truncations of $f$ satisfy \[  R\min (q_\alpha ,j/A)\leq \min (Rq_\alpha ,j) \leq R\min (q_\alpha ,j/a).  \] Hence lemma 14.29.2 and the monotonicity of the scalar give \[  \frac{CV_0}{M_{j/a}}\leq c_ H(\min (f,j)) \leq \frac{CV_0}{M_{j/A}}.  \] Both bounds tend to $CV_0$ as $j\to \infty $, so $b_ H(f)=CV_0$, whatever the reference volume $\mathrm{d}V$. Step 2: the equation. For $u_{\alpha ,j}=\max (u_\alpha ,-j)$, the binomial expansion of bounded local products, with factor forms of degrees $m$ and $k$, gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_ H(u_{\alpha ,j}) =C h_0^ m\wedge \mathrm{MA}_\kappa (u_{\alpha ,j}).  \] Multiplying by $\mathbf1_{\{ u_\alpha >-j\} }$ and letting $j\to \infty $, as in the definition ( 6.1 ) of the extended measure, we obtain \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=Ch_0^ m\wedge q_\alpha \kappa ^ k =CV_0\, q_\alpha \mu =CV_0f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] a measure of mass $CV_0$. The bounds $a\leq R\leq A$ transfer the integrability properties of $q_\alpha $ to $f$. Step 3: lower mass and nonclosedness. Pull back bounded $h_0$-plurisubharmonic functions whose masses on $X_0$ tend to zero. The same expansion shows that their $H$-masses are $C$ times their masses on $X_0$, so $v_-(H)=0$. If $h_0$ were closed, Stokes' theorem would give every bounded $h_0$-plurisubharmonic function the mass $V_0>0$, contradicting $v_-(h_0)=0$. Hence $h_0$, and therefore $H$, is not closed. Step 4: the envelopes. Choose $\alpha <\beta <1$. For $b\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon >0$ with $\varepsilon \beta \leq 1$, the number \[  K_ b=\sup _{s\geq 1}\{ b s^\alpha -\varepsilon s^\beta \} -b  \] is finite, since $\beta >\alpha $. The function $g_ b=-\varepsilon (1-\psi )^\beta -K_ b$ on $Y$ satisfies $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ b\geq (1-\varepsilon \beta )\kappa \geq 0$, by the chain-rule computation in the proof of lemma 14.29.1 , applied to the increasing convex function $t\mapsto -\varepsilon (1-t)^\beta $, whose derivative is at most $\varepsilon \beta $ for $t\leq 0$. With $L=1-\psi \geq 1$, the inequality $g_ b\leq bu_\alpha $ reads $bL^\alpha -\varepsilon L^\beta -b\leq K_ b$, so it holds on $Y\setminus \{ o\} $, and also at $o$, where both sides are $-\infty $. Thus the pullback of $g_ b$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,H)$ and lies below $bu_\alpha $. Since $b\geq 1$ is arbitrary, $u_\alpha \in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,0)$ by definition 13.4.1 . For $0<\delta <1$, take $b=1$ and $\varepsilon \beta \leq \delta $. Then $g_1$ is $\delta H$-plurisubharmonic and lies below $u_\alpha $, so $P_{\delta H}(u_\alpha )\geq g_1$ is not identically $-\infty $. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.29.4
text: Corollary 14.29.4 . Let $X_0$ be the elliptic threefold of theorem 26.18.1 , with the balanced metric $\omega $ of proposition 26.18.7 . On $X_0\times \mathbb P^2$, with background $H=\omega +\kappa $, the densities $f=Rq_\alpha $ of the preceding theorem satisfy \[  v_-(H)=0,\qquad b_ H(f)=240\pi , \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=240\pi f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Theorem 26.18.1 gives $v_-(\omega )=0$, and proposition 26.18.7 gives $V_0=24\pi $. The product theorem applies with $m=3$, $k=2$ and $C=\binom 53=10$. $\square$

title: 14.29.1 Closed factors and arbitrary integrable densities
search_title: Closed factors and arbitrary integrable densities
text: 14.29.1 Closed factors and arbitrary integrable densities The preceding examples use an explicit potential on projective space. On a closed factor, the mass bound from Stokes' theorem instead makes every threshold subsolution exact. This gives equations for arbitrary integrable densities on that factor, with no assumption that they are bounded below. For this subsection let $(X_0,h_0)$ be any connected compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $m\geq 1$, and let $(Y,\kappa )$ be connected compact Kähler of dimension $k\geq 2$, normalized by $\int _ Y\kappa ^ k=1$. On $X=X_0\times Y$ put \[  N=m+k,\qquad H=h_0+\kappa ,\qquad C=\binom Nm,\qquad V_0=\int _{X_0}h_0^ m,\qquad c_0=CV_0.  \] Forms and functions on the factors are pulled back when used on $X$. For any smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm dV$ on $X$, put \[  \mu =V_0^{-1}h_0^ m\wedge \kappa ^ k,\qquad R=\frac\mu {\mathrm dV},\qquad a=\min _ XR>0,\qquad A=\max _ XR.  \] Theorem 14.29.5 . For every nonzero nonnegative $g\in L^1(Y,\kappa ^ k)$, with $M_ g=\int _ Yg\kappa ^ k$, one has \[  b_ H(Rg)=\frac{c_0}{M_ g}.  \] There is $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ with $\sup _ Yv=0$ and $\int _ Y\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (v)=1$ whose pullback $u$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u) =\frac{c_0}{M_ g}Rg\, \mathrm dV,\qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)=c_0.  \] If $v_-(h_0)=0$, then $v_-(H)=0$ and $H$ is not closed. Proof. We first compute the scalars of bounded densities, then use the closed factor's mass bound to identify the equation for an unbounded density. Step 1: bounded densities. If $g$ is bounded and nonzero, theorem 10.1.1 on $Y$ gives a bounded continuous $v$ with $\mathrm{MA}_\kappa (v)=c_\kappa (g)g\kappa ^ k$. Closed Stokes gives $c_\kappa (g)=1/M_ g$. The bounded product expansion gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_ H(v)=C h_0^ m\wedge \mathrm{MA}_\kappa (v) =\frac{c_0}{M_ g}Rg\, \mathrm dV.  \] Uniqueness of the bounded normalization scalar therefore gives $c_ H(Rg)=c_0/M_ g$, including densities with zeros. Step 2: the threshold. For general $g\in L^1$, the original truncations on $X$ satisfy \[  R\min (g,j/A)\leq \min (Rg,j)\leq R\min (g,j/a).  \] By Step 1 and lemma 14.26.1 , \[  \frac{c_0}{\int _ Y\min (g,j/a)\kappa ^ k} \leq c_ H(\min (Rg,j)) \leq \frac{c_0}{\int _ Y\min (g,j/A)\kappa ^ k}.  \] Both bounds tend to $c_0/M_ g$. Step 3: the exact equation. By proposition 14.27.4 , $b_\kappa (g)=1/M_ g$. Thus theorem 14.27.2 on $Y$ gives $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ with supremum zero and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (v)\geq (g/M_ g)\kappa ^ k.  \] For $v_ j=\max (v,-j)$, closed Stokes gives $\int _ Y\mathrm{MA}_\kappa (v_ j)=1$. The defining non-pluripolar truncations consequently give $\int _ Y\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (v)\leq 1$. The prescribed lower measure has mass one, so equality holds both in mass and in the measure inequality. The pullback $u$ is $H$-plurisubharmonic, and $\max (u,-j)$ is the pullback of $v_ j$. Multiplying the bounded product expansion by the pullback of $\mathbf1_{\{ v>-j\} }$ and passing to the defining non-pluripolar limit gives \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u) =C h_0^ m\wedge \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (v) =\frac{c_0}{M_ g}Rg\, \mathrm dV.  \] Its mass is $c_0$. Finally, when $v_-(h_0)=0$, pulling back bounded potentials from $X_0$ whose masses tend to zero proves $v_-(H)=0$ by the same expansion. Closedness of $h_0$ would contradict that vanishing by Stokes' theorem, so $H$ is not closed. $\square$ On the elliptic threefold of theorem 26.18.1 , with the balanced metric of proposition 26.18.7 , the product with $\mathbb P^2$ has $c_0=240\pi $. Thus every probability density from the projective factor has this threshold and a finite-mass threshold solution. The theorem concerns factor densities; it does not give an exact equation for an arbitrary density on $X$ or identify limits of normalized exponential solutions.

title: 14.30 Singular measures on products with a curve
search_title: Singular measures on products with a curve
text: 14.30 Singular measures on products with a curve The closed-factor equations above concern integrable densities. A curve factor also allows a direct test on a measure: its logarithmic potential determines an exact equation, and continuity of that potential supplies the energy control needed for every positive exponent. The resulting product measure may be singular with respect to smooth volume, even when the solution is continuous. Let $Y=\mathbb P^1$ and let $\kappa $ be the Fubini–Study form of mass one. For the chordal distance $d_{\mathrm{ch}}$, put \[  G(x,y)=\log d_{\mathrm{ch}}(x,y)^2+1,\qquad K(x,y)=1-G(x,y)\geq 0.  \] For a Borel probability $\mu $ on $Y$, define 14.106 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-measure-green-potential} Q_\mu (x)=\int _ YG(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y). \end{equation} We say that $\mu $ is non-polar if it gives every polar Borel set mass zero.
14.106 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-measure-green-potential} Q_\mu (x)=\int _ YG(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y). \end{equation}

title: 14.30.1 The logarithmic potential and its measure trace
search_title: The logarithmic potential and its measure trace
text: 14.30.1 The logarithmic potential and its measure trace Lemma 14.30.1 . For every probability $\mu $, the function $Q_\mu $ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic, has $\kappa $-mean zero, and satisfies \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_\mu =\mu ,\qquad Q_\mu \leq 1.  \] If $\mu $ is non-polar, then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (Q_\mu )=\mu $. Every $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (p)\geq \mu $ is of the form $Q_\mu +C$. Proof. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ xG(x,y)=\delta _ y-\kappa $. After a rotation sending $y$ to $[1:0]$, the variable $t=d_{\mathrm{ch}}(x,y)^2$ is uniformly distributed on $[0,1]$ for the measure $\kappa $. Thus \[  \int _ YG(x,y)\kappa (x)=\int _0^1(\log t+1)\, \mathrm dt=0, \qquad \sup _ y\int _ Y|G(x,y)|\kappa (x)<\infty .  \] The continuous potentials $\int \max (G(x,y),-L)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)$ are $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic by lemma 1.3.1 and averaging, and decrease to $Q_\mu $. Tonelli's theorem gives its integrability and mean zero; the decreasing-limit property gives its canonical values. Distributional Fubini proves the curvature identity. In degree one the extended measure of $p$ is \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (p) =\mathbf1_{\{ p>-\infty \} }(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p).  \] The pole set of $Q_\mu $ is polar, so non-polarity gives its asserted measure. For any $p$, distributional Stokes gives the full current $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p$ mass one, and its extended measure has mass at most one. Domination of the probability $\mu $ therefore forces both measures to equal $\mu $. The distribution $p-Q_\mu $ is harmonic on the compact connected curve, hence constant, and canonical equality gives the assertion everywhere. $\square$ For real Sobolev functions on $Y$ use the Dirichlet form \[  E(p,q)=\int _ Y\mathrm dp\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q.  \] It is symmetric and nonnegative on the diagonal. The space $H^1(Y)$ and its norm are taken for the Fubini–Study Riemannian metric. Lemma 14.30.2 . Suppose $Q=Q_\mu $ is finite and continuous. Then $\mu $ is non-polar, $Q\in H^1(Y)$, and smooth restriction extends to a continuous linear map \[  \operatorname {Tr}_\mu :H^1(Y)\longrightarrow L^1(\mu ).  \] For every $h\in H^1(Y)$, 14.107 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-potential-trace} \int _ Y\operatorname {Tr}_\mu h\, \mathrm d\mu =\int _ Yh\kappa -E(h,Q). \end{equation} For $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )\cap H^1(Y)$ this trace agrees $\mu $-almost everywhere with its canonical values. The trace commutes with Lipschitz real compositions. Proof. Continuity gives the uniform kernel bound 14.108 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-potential-kernel-bound} A_\mu :=\sup _ x\int _ YK(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y) =1-\inf _ YQ<\infty . \end{equation} To prove non-polarity, take a nontrivial subharmonic function on a coordinate disk. Cut off its positive Hessian measure on a slightly larger disk. The logarithmic potential of this finite measure has the same Hessian on the smaller disk, so their difference is harmonic there. This is the local Riesz decomposition: it also follows directly from the distributional fundamental solution and harmonic regularity. On compact subdisks the kernel $-\log |z-a|^2$ differs from $K(z,a)$ by a bounded smooth term. Symmetry of $K$, Tonelli's theorem and ( 14.108 ) make the logarithmic potential integrable against $\mu $; its harmonic remainder is bounded. The pole set consequently has $\mu $-mass zero. A countable disk cover proves the claim for polar Borel sets. The group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ acts on $Y$ by Fubini–Study isometries. Average with smooth nonnegative conjugation-invariant kernels of mass one supported near the identity. This gives smooth $Q_\epsilon $, probability measures $\mu _\epsilon $, and \[  Q_\epsilon \longrightarrow Q\  \text{uniformly},\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_\epsilon =\mu _\epsilon -\kappa ,\qquad \int _ YQ_\epsilon \kappa =0.  \] Smooth Stokes gives $E(Q_\epsilon ,Q_\epsilon )=-\int Q_\epsilon \, \mathrm d\mu _\epsilon \leq \| Q\| _\infty $. Poincaré's inequality and weak Hilbert compactness show that $Q\in H^1$. Its distributional curvature identity gives ( 14.107 ) first for smooth $h$. Apply this identity to $\sqrt{h^2+\epsilon ^2}$, whose gradient has magnitude at most $|\mathrm dh|$. Letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ yields \[  \int _ Y|h|\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \| h\| _{L^1(\kappa )}+E(h,h)^{1/2}E(Q,Q)^{1/2} \leq C_\mu \| h\| _{H^1}.  \] Completion defines the trace and extends the identity. These group averages converge strongly in $H^1$: rotations act continuously and isometrically on that space, and the averaging kernels approach the identity. They also converge pointwise to every canonical quasi-subharmonic function. Indeed their induced averages about a point are radial by conjugation invariance. In a coordinate centered at that point they are positive averages of circular means; after a smooth quadratic correction, the submean inequality and upper semicontinuity give the required limit. The correction error tends to zero, and upper semicontinuity gives the limit also at a pole. For a $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic $H^1$ function, strong convergence and the trace bound give $L^1(\mu )$ convergence, while a subsequence converges $\mu $-almost everywhere to the trace. Non-polarity makes the canonical value finite there and identifies the two. Finally, the Sobolev chain rule and smooth approximation show that Lipschitz compositions are continuous in $H^1$; the corresponding $L^1(\mu )$ limits prove the composition assertion. $\square$

title: 14.30.2 Exponential equations and uniform selection on the curve
search_title: Exponential equations and uniform selection on the curve
text: 14.30.2 Exponential equations and uniform selection on the curve Theorem 14.30.3 . Suppose $Q=Q_\mu $ is finite and continuous. For every $\lambda >0$ there is a unique bounded $w_\lambda \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ satisfying 14.109 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-potential-curve-exponential} \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\lambda =\mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda }\mu , \qquad \int _ Y\mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda }\, \mathrm d\mu =1. \end{equation} It is continuous and obeys 14.110 \begin{equation} \label{eq:continuous-potential-curve-barriers} Q-\sup _ YQ\leq w_\lambda \leq Q-\inf _ YQ. \end{equation} The entire family satisfies, as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, \[  \left\| w_\lambda -Q+\int _ YQ\, \mathrm d\mu \right\| _\infty =O(\lambda ).  \] The limit is the greatest $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (p)\geq \mu $ and $\int _ Yp\, \mathrm d\mu \leq 0$. Proof. Variational existence. title: 14.31 Stability of the subsolution threshold
text: 14.31 Stability of the subsolution threshold We now study how the threshold $b_ h(f)$ depends on $f$. By ( 14.104 ), $b_ h^{1/n}$ is an infimum of functions that are continuous on $L^1$, and is therefore upper semicontinuous. It is not continuous in general: when $v_-(h)=0$, every density with positive threshold is an $L^1$ limit of densities with zero threshold. For density roots, ( 14.103 ) expresses $\rho _ h$ as a supremum of positive linear functionals. Hence $\rho _ h$ is a norm on the space where it is finite, this space is complete for a suitable norm, and the threshold depends continuously on the root in that norm. Theorem 14.31.1 . Suppose $f_ j,f$ are nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ densities and $f_ j\to f$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Then \[  \limsup _{j\to \infty }b_ h(f_ j)\leq b_ h(f).  \] Moreover, 14.113 \begin{equation} \label{eq:individual-threshold-relaxation} b_ h(f)=\lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\sup \{ c_ h(q):q\in L^\infty ,\  q\geq 0,\  q\not\equiv 0, \  \| q-f\| _{L^1}<\delta \} , \end{equation} and the suprema are finite for sufficiently small $\delta $. Proof. For a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ on $X$, write $A_\gamma (f)=\int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. Since $|s^{1/n}-t^{1/n}|\leq |s-t|^{1/n}$ for $s,t\geq 0$, Hölder's inequality shows that $A_\gamma $ is continuous on $L^1$; it is positive at every nonzero nonnegative density. By theorem 14.28.1 , $b_ h^{1/n}$ is the infimum over $\gamma $ of the continuous positive functions $f\mapsto \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}/A_\gamma (f)$. It is therefore upper semicontinuous, and testing a single $\gamma $ bounds it above on an $L^1$ neighborhood of $f$. For the second assertion, recall that $b_ h(q)=c_ h(q)$ for bounded $q$ (proposition 14.27.4 ). By the first assertion, $\limsup _ jc_ h(q_ j)\leq b_ h(f)$ for every sequence of nonzero nonnegative bounded densities $q_ j\to f$ in $L^1$. Hence the limit in ( 14.113 ) is at most $b_ h(f)$, and the local upper bound makes the suprema finite for small $\delta $. Conversely, the truncations $f_ k$ converge to $f$ in $L^1$ and satisfy $c_ h(f_ k)\geq b_ h(f)$, so every supremum in ( 14.113 ) is at least $b_ h(f)$. $\square$ Since $b_ h\geq 0$, upper semicontinuity makes $b_ h$ continuous at every density where it vanishes. If $v_-(h)=0$, these are its only points of continuity. Indeed, let $b_ h(f)>0$ and $g=f/\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$. By corollary 14.26.5 and theorem 14.27.2 , the densities $(1-t)g+tf_0$, where $f_0$ is the density of theorem 14.26.3 , have zero threshold and converge to $g$ in $L^1$ as $t\downarrow 0$; multiplying them by $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$ gives densities with zero threshold converging to $f$. These statements concern only the scalar $b_ h$; they say nothing about capacity convergence of the corresponding potentials or about the limits of their Monge–Ampère measures.

title: Theorem 14.31.1
text: Theorem 14.31.1 . Suppose $f_ j,f$ are nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ densities and $f_ j\to f$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Then \[  \limsup _{j\to \infty }b_ h(f_ j)\leq b_ h(f).  \] Moreover, 14.113 \begin{equation} \label{eq:individual-threshold-relaxation} b_ h(f)=\lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\sup \{ c_ h(q):q\in L^\infty ,\  q\geq 0,\  q\not\equiv 0, \  \| q-f\| _{L^1}<\delta \} , \end{equation} and the suprema are finite for sufficiently small $\delta $. Proof. For a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ on $X$, write $A_\gamma (f)=\int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. Since $|s^{1/n}-t^{1/n}|\leq |s-t|^{1/n}$ for $s,t\geq 0$, Hölder's inequality shows that $A_\gamma $ is continuous on $L^1$; it is positive at every nonzero nonnegative density. By theorem 14.28.1 , $b_ h^{1/n}$ is the infimum over $\gamma $ of the continuous positive functions $f\mapsto \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}/A_\gamma (f)$. It is therefore upper semicontinuous, and testing a single $\gamma $ bounds it above on an $L^1$ neighborhood of $f$. For the second assertion, recall that $b_ h(q)=c_ h(q)$ for bounded $q$ (proposition 14.27.4 ). By the first assertion, $\limsup _ jc_ h(q_ j)\leq b_ h(f)$ for every sequence of nonzero nonnegative bounded densities $q_ j\to f$ in $L^1$. Hence the limit in ( 14.113 ) is at most $b_ h(f)$, and the local upper bound makes the suprema finite for small $\delta $. Conversely, the truncations $f_ k$ converge to $f$ in $L^1$ and satisfy $c_ h(f_ k)\geq b_ h(f)$, so every supremum in ( 14.113 ) is at least $b_ h(f)$. $\square$
