title: 14.31.1 Finite sums of densities
text:
14.31.1 Finite sums of densities Since ( 14.103 ) expresses $ho _ h(p)$ as a supremum of positive linear functionals evaluated at $|p|$, the root functional is homogeneous, monotone and subadditive. Subadditivity shows that the sum of two densities with positive threshold again has positive threshold. In the statements below, $f$ and $g$ are nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ densities, and $p$ and $q$ are real or complex functions in $L^ n$. Proposition 14.31.2 . The functional $ho _ h$ satisfies $ho _ h(tp)=|t|ho _ h(p)$ for scalars $t
e 0$, $ho _ h(p)\leq ho _ h(q)$ whenever $|p|\leq |q|$, and \[  ho _ h(p+q)\leq ho _ h(p)+ho _ h(q).  \] In particular, if $b_ h(f),b_ h(g)>0$, then \[  b_ h(f+g)\geq  igl (b_ h(f)^{-1/n}+b_ h(g)^{-1/n} igr )^{-n}>0.  \] Proof. By ( 14.103 ), $ho _ h(p)=\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(|p|)$ is a supremum of positive linear functionals evaluated at $|p|$. This gives homogeneity and monotonicity, and, together with $|p+q|\leq |p|+|q|$, the triangle inequality. Finally, $(f+g)^{1/n}\leq f^{1/n}+g^{1/n}$ gives \[  b_ h(f+g)^{-1/n}=ho _ h igl ((f+g)^{1/n} igr )\leq ho _ h(f^{1/n})+ho _ h(g^{1/n}) =b_ h(f)^{-1/n}+b_ h(g)^{-1/n},  \] which is equivalent to the asserted lower bound for $b_ h(f+g)$. $\square$ Proposition 14.31.3 . The real or complex vector space \[  \mathcal D_ h=\{ p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V):ho _ h(p)<+\infty \}   \] is complete for the norm $\| p\| _{\mathcal D_ h}=\| p\| _{L^ n}+ho _ h(p)$. It is an order ideal in $L^ n$: if $q\in \mathcal D_ h$ and $|p|\leq |q|$, then $p\in \mathcal D_ h$. It contains $L^\infty $ and is therefore dense in $L^ n$ for the $L^ n$ norm. Moreover, $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ if and only if $v_-(h)>0$, and in that case the norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is equivalent to the $L^ n$ norm. If $h$ is Kähler, then \[  ho _ h(p)=\left(\int _ Xh^ night)^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n}.  \] Proof. By proposition 14.31.2 , $\mathcal D_ h$ is a vector space and an order ideal, and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is a norm on it. Bounded functions belong to $\mathcal D_ h$, because $b_ h(|p|^ n)=c_ h(|p|^ n)>0$ for bounded nonzero $p$. We next show that $ho _ h$ is lower semicontinuous on $L^ n$. If $p_ j	o p$ in $L^ n$, then $|p_ j|^ n	o |p|^ n$ in $L^1$, and the upper semicontinuity of $b_ h$ in theorem 14.31.1 gives \[  ho _ h(p)\leq \liminf _ jho _ h(p_ j).  \] This includes the case $b_ h(|p|^ n)=0$, in which the right side must be infinite; for $p=0$ the inequality is trivial. Now let $(p_ j)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_ h$. It converges in $L^ n$ to some $p$, and lower semicontinuity gives $ho _ h(p)\leq \liminf _ jho _ h(p_ j)<+\infty $, so $p\in \mathcal D_ h$. Applied to $p_ j-p_ k$ as $k	o \infty $, lower semicontinuity also gives \[  ho _ h(p_ j-p)\leq \liminf _{k	o \infty }ho _ h(p_ j-p_ k),  \] which tends to zero as $j	o \infty $. Together with $L^ n$ convergence, this proves completeness. If $v_-(h)>0$, proposition 14.27.4 gives $ho _ h(p)\leq v_-(h)^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n}$, so $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ with an equivalent norm. If $v_-(h)=0$, the density $f$ of theorem 14.26.3 has $b_ h(f)=0$ by theorem 14.27.2 ; thus $f^{1/n}$ belongs to $L^ n$ but not to $\mathcal D_ h$. The Kähler formula follows from the same proposition. $\square$ Thus, when the lower mass vanishes, $\mathcal D_ h$ is a proper dense subspace of $L^ n$, complete for the stronger norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$; its nonnegative elements are the $n$th roots of the densities admitting a positive scaled subsolution. A finite sum of such densities again admits a positive scaled subsolution, but a convergent infinite sum need not: the smooth summands in theorem 14.26.3 give an example. By proposition 14.28.2 , the space $\mathcal D_ h$ does not depend on the Hermitian form $h$, and the norms $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ for different Hermitian forms are equivalent. The closure of the bounded functions for this norm is studied in 14.31.2 . The restriction of $ho _ h$ to $\mathcal D_ h$ is itself a norm: if $p
e 0$, then $ho _ h(p)\geq L_{h,\gamma }(|p|)>0$ for any Gauduchon form $\gamma $. Whether this weaker norm is complete depends on the upper mass. Proposition 14.31.4 . The norm $ho _ h$ is complete on $\mathcal D_ h$ if and only if $v_+(h)<+\infty $. When the upper mass is finite, \[  \| p\| _{L^ n}\leq v_+(h)^{1/n}ho _ h(p)\qquad (p\in \mathcal D_ h),  \] so $ho _ h$ and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ are equivalent norms. Proof. Suppose $v_+(h)<+\infty $. A continuous solution for a bounded density $q$ has mass $c_ h(q)\int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}V\leq v_+(h)$. Applying this to the truncations of $|p|^ n$ and letting the truncation level increase gives $b_ h(|p|^ n)\| p\| _{L^ n}^ n\leq v_+(h)$, which is the asserted inequality. Hence $ho _ h$ and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ are equivalent, and completeness follows from proposition 14.31.3 . Suppose instead that $v_+(h)=+\infty $. By theorem 26.14.3 , theorem 26.1.3 , the normalization scalars of smooth strictly positive probability densities are unbounded above. For each $j$, choose such a density $f_ j$ with \[  c_ h(f_ j)\geq (j2^ j)^ n, \qquad 	ext{and put}\qquad p_ j=jf_ j^{1/n}.  \] Then $\| p_ j\| _{L^ n}=j$ and $ho _ h(p_ j)=jc_ h(f_ j)^{-1/n}\leq 2^{-j}$, so the partial sums $P_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}p_ j$ form a Cauchy sequence for $ho _ h$. Fix a Gauduchon form $\gamma $. Its coefficient $a_\gamma $ is bounded below by a positive constant, so ( 14.103 ) gives $ho _ h(p)\geq c\| p\| _{L^1}$ with a constant $c>0$. Hence $\sum _ jp_ j$ converges in $L^1$ to a nonnegative function $P$. If $P_ N$ converged for $ho _ h$ to an element of $\mathcal D_ h$, that element would also be the $L^1$ limit, hence equal to $P$ almost everywhere. But $P\geq p_ j$ gives $\| P\| _{L^ n}\geq j$ for every $j$, so $P
otin L^ n$. Therefore $ho _ h$ is not complete. $\square$ The two mass properties play separate roles: positive lower mass makes every $L^ n$ function admissible, whereas finite upper mass makes the root norm control the $L^ n$ norm. The norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is complete without either assumption. All four combinations occur. On a compact Kähler manifold both mass properties hold. The Hopf threefold has positive lower mass and infinite upper mass (corollary 8.7.2 ). The elliptic threefold of theorem 26.18.1 has zero lower mass, and finite upper mass for its balanced metric (proposition 26.18.7 ). The product manifolds of corollary 26.18.6 have zero lower mass and infinite upper mass. Since neither $\mathcal D_ h$ nor the completeness of $ho _ h$ depends on the choice of $h$ (proposition 14.28.2 , proposition 6.5.2 ), we obtain the following table. Manifold Domain $\mathcal D_ h$ Is $ho _ h$ complete? Kähler manifold $L^ n$ Yes Hopf threefold $L^ n$ No Elliptic threefold $\mathcal D_ h\subsetneq L^ n$ Yes Product example $\mathcal D_ h\subsetneq L^ n$ No

title: Proposition 14.31.2
text: Proposition 14.31.2 . The functional $\rho _ h$ satisfies $\rho _ h(tp)=|t|\rho _ h(p)$ for scalars $t\ne 0$, $\rho _ h(p)\leq \rho _ h(q)$ whenever $|p|\leq |q|$, and \[  \rho _ h(p+q)\leq \rho _ h(p)+\rho _ h(q).  \] In particular, if $b_ h(f),b_ h(g)>0$, then \[  b_ h(f+g)\geq \bigl (b_ h(f)^{-1/n}+b_ h(g)^{-1/n}\bigr )^{-n}>0.  \] Proof. By ( 14.103 ), $\rho _ h(p)=\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(|p|)$ is a supremum of positive linear functionals evaluated at $|p|$. This gives homogeneity and monotonicity, and, together with $|p+q|\leq |p|+|q|$, the triangle inequality. Finally, $(f+g)^{1/n}\leq f^{1/n}+g^{1/n}$ gives \[  b_ h(f+g)^{-1/n}=\rho _ h\bigl ((f+g)^{1/n}\bigr )\leq \rho _ h(f^{1/n})+\rho _ h(g^{1/n}) =b_ h(f)^{-1/n}+b_ h(g)^{-1/n},  \] which is equivalent to the asserted lower bound for $b_ h(f+g)$. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.31.3
text: Proposition 14.31.3 . The real or complex vector space \[  \mathcal D_ h=\{ p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V):\rho _ h(p)<+\infty \}   \] is complete for the norm $\| p\| _{\mathcal D_ h}=\| p\| _{L^ n}+\rho _ h(p)$. It is an order ideal in $L^ n$: if $q\in \mathcal D_ h$ and $|p|\leq |q|$, then $p\in \mathcal D_ h$. It contains $L^\infty $ and is therefore dense in $L^ n$ for the $L^ n$ norm. Moreover, $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ if and only if $v_-(h)>0$, and in that case the norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is equivalent to the $L^ n$ norm. If $h$ is Kähler, then \[  \rho _ h(p)=\left(\int _ Xh^ n\right)^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n}.  \] Proof. By proposition 14.31.2 , $\mathcal D_ h$ is a vector space and an order ideal, and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is a norm on it. Bounded functions belong to $\mathcal D_ h$, because $b_ h(|p|^ n)=c_ h(|p|^ n)>0$ for bounded nonzero $p$. We next show that $\rho _ h$ is lower semicontinuous on $L^ n$. If $p_ j\to p$ in $L^ n$, then $|p_ j|^ n\to |p|^ n$ in $L^1$, and the upper semicontinuity of $b_ h$ in theorem 14.31.1 gives \[  \rho _ h(p)\leq \liminf _ j\rho _ h(p_ j).  \] This includes the case $b_ h(|p|^ n)=0$, in which the right side must be infinite; for $p=0$ the inequality is trivial. Now let $(p_ j)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_ h$. It converges in $L^ n$ to some $p$, and lower semicontinuity gives $\rho _ h(p)\leq \liminf _ j\rho _ h(p_ j)<+\infty $, so $p\in \mathcal D_ h$. Applied to $p_ j-p_ k$ as $k\to \infty $, lower semicontinuity also gives \[  \rho _ h(p_ j-p)\leq \liminf _{k\to \infty }\rho _ h(p_ j-p_ k),  \] which tends to zero as $j\to \infty $. Together with $L^ n$ convergence, this proves completeness. If $v_-(h)>0$, proposition 14.27.4 gives $\rho _ h(p)\leq v_-(h)^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n}$, so $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ with an equivalent norm. If $v_-(h)=0$, the density $f$ of theorem 14.26.3 has $b_ h(f)=0$ by theorem 14.27.2 ; thus $f^{1/n}$ belongs to $L^ n$ but not to $\mathcal D_ h$. The Kähler formula follows from the same proposition. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.31.4
text: Proposition 14.31.4 . The norm $\rho _ h$ is complete on $\mathcal D_ h$ if and only if $v_+(h)<+\infty $. When the upper mass is finite, \[  \| p\| _{L^ n}\leq v_+(h)^{1/n}\rho _ h(p)\qquad (p\in \mathcal D_ h),  \] so $\rho _ h$ and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ are equivalent norms. Proof. Suppose $v_+(h)<+\infty $. A continuous solution for a bounded density $q$ has mass $c_ h(q)\int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}V\leq v_+(h)$. Applying this to the truncations of $|p|^ n$ and letting the truncation level increase gives $b_ h(|p|^ n)\| p\| _{L^ n}^ n\leq v_+(h)$, which is the asserted inequality. Hence $\rho _ h$ and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ are equivalent, and completeness follows from proposition 14.31.3 . Suppose instead that $v_+(h)=+\infty $. By theorem 26.14.3 , theorem 26.1.3 , the normalization scalars of smooth strictly positive probability densities are unbounded above. For each $j$, choose such a density $f_ j$ with \[  c_ h(f_ j)\geq (j2^ j)^ n, \qquad \text{and put}\qquad p_ j=jf_ j^{1/n}.  \] Then $\| p_ j\| _{L^ n}=j$ and $\rho _ h(p_ j)=jc_ h(f_ j)^{-1/n}\leq 2^{-j}$, so the partial sums $P_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}p_ j$ form a Cauchy sequence for $\rho _ h$. Fix a Gauduchon form $\gamma $. Its coefficient $a_\gamma $ is bounded below by a positive constant, so ( 14.103 ) gives $\rho _ h(p)\geq c\| p\| _{L^1}$ with a constant $c>0$. Hence $\sum _ jp_ j$ converges in $L^1$ to a nonnegative function $P$. If $P_ N$ converged for $\rho _ h$ to an element of $\mathcal D_ h$, that element would also be the $L^1$ limit, hence equal to $P$ almost everywhere. But $P\geq p_ j$ gives $\| P\| _{L^ n}\geq j$ for every $j$, so $P\notin L^ n$. Therefore $\rho _ h$ is not complete. $\square$

title: 14.31.2 Approximation by bounded density roots
text: 14.31.2 Approximation by bounded density roots Bounded functions are dense in $\mathcal D_ h$ for the $L^ n$ norm, but not obviously for the norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$. Let $\mathcal D_ h^0$ denote the closure of $L^\infty $ in $\mathcal D_ h$ for this norm. We show that a function belongs to $\mathcal D_ h^0$ exactly when its tails are small uniformly over all Gauduchon tests. The basic tool is a subcritical estimate. For every $r>n$, 14.114 \begin{equation} \label{eq:root-subcritical-bound} \rho _ h(p)\leq C_ r\| p\| _{L^ r}\qquad (p\in L^ r), \end{equation} where the constant $C_ r$ depends on $h$, the reference volume and $r$, but not on $p$. Indeed, for nonzero $p\in L^ r$ the density $|p|^ n$ belongs to $L^{r/n}$, so $b_ h(|p|^ n)=c_ h(|p|^ n)$ by proposition 14.27.4 , and the lower-density estimate of theorem 10.3.3 , with exponent $r/n$, gives $c_ h(|p|^ n)\| |p|^ n\| _{L^{r/n}}\geq c_{r/n}>0$. Proposition 14.31.5 . For $p\in \mathcal D_ h$, the following conditions are equivalent: $p\in \mathcal D_ h^0$; $\rho _ h(|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })\to 0$ as $K\to \infty $; whenever $|q_ j|\leq |p|$ and $q_ j\to 0$ in measure, one has $\| q_ j\| _{\mathcal D_ h}\to 0$. By ( 14.103 ), the second condition can be written as \[  \sup _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} L_{h,\gamma }(|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })\longrightarrow 0 \qquad (K\to \infty ).  \] The space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ is a closed order ideal in $\mathcal D_ h$. It contains $L^ r$ for every $r>n$, and smooth functions are dense in it. If $v_-(h)>0$, then $\mathcal D_ h^0=\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$. Proof. For $K>0$, set $p_ K=p\min (1,K/|p|)$ where $p\ne 0$, and $p_ K=0$ where $p=0$. Then $|p-p_ K|=(|p|-K)_+$ and \[  (|p|-K)_+\leq |p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} },\qquad |p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>2K\} }\leq 2(|p|-K)_+.  \] Since the $L^ n$ norms of the tails tend to zero, these inequalities and the monotonicity of $\rho _ h$ show that the second condition is equivalent to $p_ K\to p$ in $\mathcal D_ h$; in particular, it implies the first. Conversely, if $a$ is bounded and $K\geq \| a\| _{L^\infty }$, then $(|p|-K)_+\leq |p-a|$, so $\| p-p_ K\| _{\mathcal D_ h}\leq \| p-a\| _{\mathcal D_ h}$. Approximating $p$ by bounded functions $a$ shows that the first condition implies $p_ K\to p$, hence the second. Assume the second condition, and let $q_ j$ be as in the third. Fix $K$. On $\{ |p|\leq K\} $, the functions $q_ j$ are bounded by $K$ and tend to zero in measure, hence in $L^{2n}$; by ( 14.114 ) with $r=2n$, the root functional of $q_ j\mathbf1_{\{ |p|\leq K\} }$ tends to zero. On the complementary set, $\rho _ h(q_ j\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })\leq \rho _ h(|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })$. Letting first $j$ and then $K$ tend to infinity gives $\rho _ h(q_ j)\to 0$, and dominated convergence gives $\| q_ j\| _{L^ n}\to 0$. Conversely, the third condition applied to $q_ j=|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>j\} }$ gives the second. Since the second condition passes from $p$ to every function dominated by $|p|$, the space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ is an order ideal; it is closed by definition. For $p\in L^ r$ with $r>n$, the truncations $p_ K$ converge to $p$ in $L^ r$, hence in $\mathcal D_ h$ by ( 14.114 ). Bounded functions can be approximated in $L^{2n}$ by smooth functions, which then converge in $\mathcal D_ h$ by the same estimate; hence smooth functions are dense in $\mathcal D_ h^0$. Under positive lower mass, proposition 14.31.3 shows that $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ with an equivalent norm, and bounded functions are dense in $L^ n$; hence $\mathcal D_ h^0=\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$. $\square$ By proposition 14.28.2 , the space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ does not depend on the choice of the Hermitian form $h$. Convergence in $\mathcal D_ h$ controls the threshold: if $p_ j\to p\ne 0$ in $\mathcal D_ h$, then \[  |\rho _ h(p_ j)-\rho _ h(p)|\leq \rho _ h(p_ j-p)\longrightarrow 0, \qquad b_ h(|p_ j|^ n)\longrightarrow b_ h(|p|^ n)>0.  \] For $p\in \mathcal D_ h^0$, the uniform tail condition also gives a uniform modulus for exponential damping and error bounds for the scalars of the exponential equations; see proposition 14.34.3 . It does not by itself give capacity convergence of the solutions. We do not know whether $\mathcal D_ h^0=\mathcal D_ h$ when $v_-(h)=0$.
14.114 \begin{equation} \label{eq:root-subcritical-bound} \rho _ h(p)\leq C_ r\| p\| _{L^ r}\qquad (p\in L^ r), \end{equation}

title: Proposition 14.31.5
text: Proposition 14.31.5 . For $p\in \mathcal D_ h$, the following conditions are equivalent: $p\in \mathcal D_ h^0$; $\rho _ h(|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })\to 0$ as $K\to \infty $; whenever $|q_ j|\leq |p|$ and $q_ j\to 0$ in measure, one has $\| q_ j\| _{\mathcal D_ h}\to 0$. By ( 14.103 ), the second condition can be written as \[  \sup _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} L_{h,\gamma }(|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })\longrightarrow 0 \qquad (K\to \infty ).  \] The space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ is a closed order ideal in $\mathcal D_ h$. It contains $L^ r$ for every $r>n$, and smooth functions are dense in it. If $v_-(h)>0$, then $\mathcal D_ h^0=\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$. Proof. For $K>0$, set $p_ K=p\min (1,K/|p|)$ where $p\ne 0$, and $p_ K=0$ where $p=0$. Then $|p-p_ K|=(|p|-K)_+$ and \[  (|p|-K)_+\leq |p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} },\qquad |p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>2K\} }\leq 2(|p|-K)_+.  \] Since the $L^ n$ norms of the tails tend to zero, these inequalities and the monotonicity of $\rho _ h$ show that the second condition is equivalent to $p_ K\to p$ in $\mathcal D_ h$; in particular, it implies the first. Conversely, if $a$ is bounded and $K\geq \| a\| _{L^\infty }$, then $(|p|-K)_+\leq |p-a|$, so $\| p-p_ K\| _{\mathcal D_ h}\leq \| p-a\| _{\mathcal D_ h}$. Approximating $p$ by bounded functions $a$ shows that the first condition implies $p_ K\to p$, hence the second. Assume the second condition, and let $q_ j$ be as in the third. Fix $K$. On $\{ |p|\leq K\} $, the functions $q_ j$ are bounded by $K$ and tend to zero in measure, hence in $L^{2n}$; by ( 14.114 ) with $r=2n$, the root functional of $q_ j\mathbf1_{\{ |p|\leq K\} }$ tends to zero. On the complementary set, $\rho _ h(q_ j\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })\leq \rho _ h(|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })$. Letting first $j$ and then $K$ tend to infinity gives $\rho _ h(q_ j)\to 0$, and dominated convergence gives $\| q_ j\| _{L^ n}\to 0$. Conversely, the third condition applied to $q_ j=|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>j\} }$ gives the second. Since the second condition passes from $p$ to every function dominated by $|p|$, the space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ is an order ideal; it is closed by definition. For $p\in L^ r$ with $r>n$, the truncations $p_ K$ converge to $p$ in $L^ r$, hence in $\mathcal D_ h$ by ( 14.114 ). Bounded functions can be approximated in $L^{2n}$ by smooth functions, which then converge in $\mathcal D_ h$ by the same estimate; hence smooth functions are dense in $\mathcal D_ h^0$. Under positive lower mass, proposition 14.31.3 shows that $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ with an equivalent norm, and bounded functions are dense in $L^ n$; hence $\mathcal D_ h^0=\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$. $\square$

title: 14.31.3 Density roots from a closed factor
search_title: Density roots from a closed factor
text: 14.31.3 Density roots from a closed factor The product formula of theorem 14.29.5 identifies a complete subspace of density roots with uniformly vanishing tails even when the ambient lower mass is zero. Use the product data $X_0,Y,N,H,c_0,\mu ,R$ of 14.29.1 . The spaces $\mathcal D_ H$ and $\mathcal D_ H^0$ are now taken on the $N$-dimensional product with reference volume $\mathrm dV$. Proposition 14.31.6 . For real or complex $\xi \in L^ N(Y,\kappa ^ k)$, put $J\xi =R^{1/N}\pi _ Y^*\xi $. Then \[  \| J\xi \| _{L^ N(\mathrm dV)}=\| \xi \| _{L^ N(\kappa ^ k)},\qquad \rho _ H(J\xi )=c_0^{-1/N}\| \xi \| _{L^ N(\kappa ^ k)}.  \] The image of $J$ is a closed linear subspace of $\mathcal D_ H^0$. If $g=|\xi |^ N$ and $A=\max _ XR$, then \[  \rho _ H\bigl (J\xi \mathbf1_{\{ |J\xi |>K\} }\bigr ) \leq \left(\frac1{c_0}\int _{\{ g>K^ N/A\} }g\kappa ^ k\right)^{1/N} \longrightarrow 0.  \] For $\mathrm dV=\mu $, so that $R=1$, the exact tail formula is \[  \rho _ H\bigl (\pi _ Y^*\xi \mathbf1_{\{ |\xi |>K\} }\bigr ) =\left(\frac1{c_0}\int _{\{ |\xi |>K\} }|\xi |^ N\kappa ^ k\right)^{1/N}.  \] Proof. Since $|J\xi |^ N=R|\xi |^ N$, integration against $\mathrm dV$ gives the first norm identity. For nonzero $\xi $, theorem 14.29.5 applied to $g=|\xi |^ N$ gives the root-functional identity; for $\xi =0$ it holds by definition. Applying the two identities to differences yields \[  \| J\xi -J\eta \| _{\mathcal D_ H} =(1+c_0^{-1/N})\| \xi -\eta \| _{L^ N(\kappa ^ k)}.  \] Bounded approximations of $\xi $ in $L^ N$ have bounded images because $R$ is bounded, so $J\xi \in \mathcal D_ H^0$. Completeness of $L^ N(Y,\kappa ^ k)$ and the displayed identity make the image closed. On $\{ |J\xi |>K\} $ one has $g>K^ N/A$, and hence \[  |J\xi |\mathbf1_{\{ |J\xi |>K\} } \leq \bigl (Rg\mathbf1_{\{ g>K^ N/A\} }\bigr )^{1/N}.  \] Monotonicity of the root functional and its identity for factor roots give the estimate, with the value zero when the tail vanishes. Integrability of $g$ makes the bound tend to zero; the $L^ N$ tails also vanish. When $R=1$, the amplitude cutoff itself is pulled back from $Y$, so the same norm identity gives equality. $\square$ For $Y=\mathbb P^ k$ and $\mathrm dV=\mu $, take $p_\alpha =\pi _ Y^*(q_\alpha ^{1/N})$ with $q_\alpha $ from lemma 14.29.1 . title: Proposition 14.31.6
text: Proposition 14.31.6 . For real or complex $\xi \in L^ N(Y,\kappa ^ k)$, put $J\xi =R^{1/N}\pi _ Y^*\xi $. Then \[  \| J\xi \| _{L^ N(\mathrm dV)}=\| \xi \| _{L^ N(\kappa ^ k)},\qquad \rho _ H(J\xi )=c_0^{-1/N}\| \xi \| _{L^ N(\kappa ^ k)}.  \] The image of $J$ is a closed linear subspace of $\mathcal D_ H^0$. If $g=|\xi |^ N$ and $A=\max _ XR$, then \[  \rho _ H\bigl (J\xi \mathbf1_{\{ |J\xi |>K\} }\bigr ) \leq \left(\frac1{c_0}\int _{\{ g>K^ N/A\} }g\kappa ^ k\right)^{1/N} \longrightarrow 0.  \] For $\mathrm dV=\mu $, so that $R=1$, the exact tail formula is \[  \rho _ H\bigl (\pi _ Y^*\xi \mathbf1_{\{ |\xi |>K\} }\bigr ) =\left(\frac1{c_0}\int _{\{ |\xi |>K\} }|\xi |^ N\kappa ^ k\right)^{1/N}.  \] Proof. Since $|J\xi |^ N=R|\xi |^ N$, integration against $\mathrm dV$ gives the first norm identity. For nonzero $\xi $, theorem 14.29.5 applied to $g=|\xi |^ N$ gives the root-functional identity; for $\xi =0$ it holds by definition. Applying the two identities to differences yields \[  \| J\xi -J\eta \| _{\mathcal D_ H} =(1+c_0^{-1/N})\| \xi -\eta \| _{L^ N(\kappa ^ k)}.  \] Bounded approximations of $\xi $ in $L^ N$ have bounded images because $R$ is bounded, so $J\xi \in \mathcal D_ H^0$. Completeness of $L^ N(Y,\kappa ^ k)$ and the displayed identity make the image closed. On $\{ |J\xi |>K\} $ one has $g>K^ N/A$, and hence \[  |J\xi |\mathbf1_{\{ |J\xi |>K\} } \leq \bigl (Rg\mathbf1_{\{ g>K^ N/A\} }\bigr )^{1/N}.  \] Monotonicity of the root functional and its identity for factor roots give the estimate, with the value zero when the tail vanishes. Integrability of $g$ makes the bound tend to zero; the $L^ N$ tails also vanish. When $R=1$, the amplitude cutoff itself is pulled back from $Y$, so the same norm identity gives equality. $\square$

title: 14.32 Power capacity bounds and threshold equations
search_title: Power capacity bounds and threshold equations
text: 14.32 Power capacity bounds and threshold equations In this section, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 3$, with a Hermitian form $h$ and a smooth positive probability volume $\mathrm dV$. The root-tail condition of proposition 14.31.5 controls the scalar threshold. A power bound for one density's measure supplies the missing control of its approximating potentials: the capacity estimates give a common bound, and stability against the solution measure gives uniform convergence. Theorem 14.32.1 . Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm dV)$ have positive integral. Suppose that $A,\alpha >0$ satisfy 14.115 \begin{equation} \label{eq:datum-power-capacity} \int _ Ef\, \mathrm dV\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_ h(E)^{1+\alpha } \qquad (E\subset X\text{ Borel}). \end{equation} There is $C>0$, depending only on $(X,h),A,\alpha $, such that every measurable $0\leq g\leq f$ with positive integral satisfies 14.116 \begin{equation} \label{eq:power-capacity-critical-bound} b_ h(g)\geq C\left(\int _ Xg\, \mathrm dV\right)^{-\alpha /(1+\alpha )}, \qquad \rho _ h(g^{1/n})\leq C^{-1/n} \left(\int _ Xg\, \mathrm dV\right)^{\alpha /(n(1+\alpha ))}. \end{equation} In particular, $f^{1/n}\in \mathcal D_ h^0$. There is $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)\cap C(X)$, with $\sup _ X\phi =0$, such that 14.117 \begin{equation} \label{eq:power-capacity-exact-threshold} \mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi )=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} The coefficient $b_ h(f)$ and the mass of this measure are finite and strictly positive. Proof. Step 1: the coefficient and root tails. Put $g_ j=\min (g,j)$ and let $\phi _ j$ be normalized continuous solutions of \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi _ j)=c_ jg_ j\, \mathrm dV, \qquad c_ j=c_ h(g_ j),\qquad \sup _ X\phi _ j=0,  \] given by theorem 10.1.1 . The definition ( 14.101 ) gives $c_ j\downarrow b_ h(g)$. Their measures satisfy a power capacity bound with constant $c_ jA$. Take competitor zero, $H=1$ and $\varepsilon =1/2$ in lemma 10.3.2 , lemma 10.3.1 . Choose $D>0$ fixed with $2D<\delta _{1/2}$ and put $U_ D=\{ \phi _ j<\inf _ X\phi _ j+D\} $. These estimates give \[  D\leq C_\alpha (C_1c_ jA)^{1/n} \operatorname {Cap}_ h(U_ D)^{\alpha /n}, \qquad D^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ h(U_ D) \leq C_1c_ j\int _ Xg_ j\, \mathrm dV.  \] Combining them yields \[  c_ j^{1+\alpha }\left(\int _ Xg_ j\, \mathrm dV\right)^\alpha \geq c>0.  \] Taking the limit proves the lower bound for $b_ h(g)$. The identity ( 14.103 ), with its full family of Gauduchon tests, gives the root estimate. Apply it to $g=f\mathbf1_{\{ f>K^ n\} }$ whenever this density is nonzero. Its mass tends to zero; the zero density has root norm zero. Thus the tails of $f^{1/n}$ tend to zero in both $L^ n$ and $\rho _ h$, and proposition 14.31.5 gives $f^{1/n}\in \mathcal D_ h^0$. Step 2: uniform convergence of a subsequence. Now use $f_ j=\min (f,j)$, $c_ j=c_ h(f_ j)$ and normalized continuous solutions $\phi _ j$. Step 1 gives $b_ h(f)>0$, while $c_ j\leq c_1<\infty $. Hence \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi _ j)(E) \leq Ac_1\operatorname {Cap}_ h(E)^{1+\alpha }.  \] The first part of the proof of proposition 10.3.5 , using the capacity tail estimate, gives one $M\geq 1$ with $-M\leq \phi _ j\leq 0$ for all $j$. By theorem 1.4.2 , extract a subsequence converging in $L^1(\mathrm dV)$ and almost everywhere. Since $f\, \mathrm dV$ is a fixed finite absolutely continuous measure and the potentials have a common bound, dominated convergence gives \[  \int _ X|\phi _ j-\phi _ k|\, \mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi _ j) \leq c_1\int _ X|\phi _ j-\phi _ k|f\, \mathrm dV\longrightarrow 0  \] along this subsequence as both indices tend to infinity. Apply proposition 10.3.5 in both orders, with $H=M$. The subsequence is uniformly Cauchy. Its limit $\phi $ is continuous, $h$-plurisubharmonic by distributional positivity, and has supremum zero. Step 3: passage of the products. On a coordinate ball choose a fixed smooth $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq h$, and put $S_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi _ j+q)$ and $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi +q)$. For every $\ell \geq 1$, the calculus of bounded products gives \[  S_ j^\ell -S^\ell =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\left[(\phi _ j-\phi ) \sum _{a=0}^{\ell -1}S_ j^ a\wedge S^{\ell -1-a}\right].  \] The local Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate bounds its pairing with a compactly supported smooth test form by $C\| \phi _ j-\phi \| _\infty $. Expand the Hermitian products as in proposition 1.7.1 : \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi _ j) =\sum _{\ell =0}^ n\binom n\ell S_ j^\ell \wedge (h-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^{n-\ell }.  \] Every term converges, with its smooth correction factor, to the corresponding term for $\phi $. On the other hand, $c_ jf_ j\to b_ h(f)f$ in $L^1(\mathrm dV)$. title: 14.32.1 A logarithmic density with critical coefficient one
search_title: A logarithmic density with critical coefficient one
text: 14.32.1 A logarithmic density with critical coefficient one The power capacity condition can hold for a density outside every $L^ p$ class with $p>1$. A bounded continuous potential with logarithmic modulus at one point gives such a datum on each fixed Hermitian background. Theorem 14.32.2 . In the setting of theorem 14.32.1 , fix $\alpha >0$. There is $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)\cap C(X)$ with $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq h/2$ whose measure $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=f\, \mathrm dV$ satisfies \[  f\in L^1(\mathrm dV),\qquad f\notin L^ p(\mathrm dV)\quad \text{for every }p>1.  \] For some $A>0$ it satisfies ( 14.115 ), and $b_ h(f)=1$. For all sufficiently large $K$, 14.118 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-root-tail} \rho _ h\bigl (f^{1/n}\mathbf1_{\{ f>K\} }\bigr ) \leq C(\log K)^{-\alpha }. \end{equation} Proof. Choose a holomorphic ball with coordinates centred at $x_0$ and $R=|z|<1$, and a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ supported in it and equal to one on a smaller ball. Put \[  q(s)=(1-s)^{-\alpha },\qquad s=\log R^2, \qquad \psi =\chi q(\log R^2)+1-\chi .  \] Set $\psi (x_0)=0$ and extend $\psi =1$ outside the ball. In the smaller ball, $q'=\alpha (1-s)^{-\alpha -1}>0$ and $q''=\alpha (\alpha +1)(1-s)^{-\alpha -2}>0$, so $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic there, including its continuous extension at $x_0$. The transition is smooth and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq -K_0h$ globally for a fixed $K_0$. For sufficiently small $\delta >0$, the normalized potential $u=\delta \psi -\sup _ X\delta \psi $ satisfies $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq h/2$. The bounded product gives zero mass to $x_0$. Indeed, after a smooth local correction, its expansion is dominated in total variation by a constant times the top product of a bounded plurisubharmonic function plus a strictly plurisubharmonic quadratic function. Rescaling this sum into $[0,1]$ bounds that top product by local capacity, and a pluripolar point has capacity zero. Off $x_0$ the potential is smooth. Thus the measure is absolutely continuous; write it as $f\, \mathrm dV$. The strict lower bound implies $f\geq c>0$ almost everywhere. In the smaller ball the tangential and radial eigenvalues of the Hessian of $q(\log R^2)$ are $q'/R^2$ and $q''/R^2$. In the operator convention of the book this gives 14.119 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-density-radial} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n =\frac{\delta ^ nn!\alpha ^ n(\alpha +1)}{\pi ^ n} R^{-2n}(1-\log R^2)^{-n(\alpha +1)-1}\, \mathrm d\lambda , \end{equation} where $\mathrm d\lambda $ is Euclidean volume. Integration over the ball gives \[  \int _{B_ r}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n =\delta ^ n\alpha ^ n(1-\log r^2)^{-n(\alpha +1)}.  \] For $k<n$, the degree-$k$ mixed terms with the smooth positive form $h$ have density bounded by $CR^{-2k}(1-\log R^2)^{-k(\alpha +1)}$ and mass $O(r^2)$ on $B_ r$. The expansion has positive terms in this ball. Hence $f\in L^1$. For $p>1$, the pure top term gives a positive multiple of the divergent integral \[  \int _0^ r R^{2n(1-p)-1} (1-\log R^2)^{-p(n(\alpha +1)+1)}\, \mathrm dR  \] as a lower bound for $\int _{B_ r}f^ p\, \mathrm dV$, since smooth volume densities are comparable. Thus $f\notin L^ p$. For all sufficiently small $r$, 14.120 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-density-ball} \int _{B_ r}f\, \mathrm dV \leq C\bigl [(1-\log r^2)^{-n(\alpha +1)}+r^2\bigr ], \qquad \mathop{\rm ess\, sup}_{X\setminus B_ r}f\leq Cr^{-2n}. \end{equation} By ( 1.25 ), \[  \mathrm dV(E)\leq C\exp \bigl (-a\operatorname {Cap}_ h(E)^{-1/n}\bigr ).  \] Let $s=\operatorname {Cap}_ h(E)>0$ be small and choose $r=\exp [-as^{-1/n}/(4n)]$. Splitting $E$ inside and outside $B_ r$ and applying ( 14.120 ), we obtain \[  \int _ Ef\, \mathrm dV \leq Cs^{1+\alpha } +C\exp [-as^{-1/n}/(2n)] +C\exp [-as^{-1/n}/2] \leq C's^{1+\alpha }.  \] For larger $s$ use the finite total mass; for $s=0$ the volume estimate gives $\mathrm dV(E)=0$. This proves ( 14.115 ) for every Borel set. By theorem 14.32.1 , there is a normalized continuous $\phi $ with $\mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi )=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm dV$. The explicit potential $u$ is a subsolution with coefficient one, so theorem 14.27.2 gives $b_ h(f)\geq 1$. Suppose $b_ h(f)>1$, and choose $0<\varepsilon <1$ with $(1-\varepsilon )^ nb_ h(f)>1$. Positive multilinearity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h((1-\varepsilon )\phi ) \geq (1-\varepsilon )^ nb_ h(f)f\, \mathrm dV.  \] Apply theorem 10.2.1 to $u,\phi $ on \[  U_ s=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )\phi + \inf _ X(u-(1-\varepsilon )\phi )+s\} .  \] For sufficiently small $s>0$ its reverse factor $Q_\varepsilon (s)$ is defined, tends to one as $s\downarrow 0$, and satisfies \[  (1-\varepsilon )^ nb_ h(f)\int _{U_ s}f\, \mathrm dV \leq Q_\varepsilon (s)\int _{U_ s}f\, \mathrm dV.  \] Choose $s$ so that $Q_\varepsilon (s)<(1-\varepsilon )^ nb_ h(f)$. The set $U_ s$ is open and nonempty, and $f\geq c>0$ almost everywhere, so its $f\, \mathrm dV$ measure is positive. This contradiction proves $b_ h(f)=1$. Finally take $r_ K=K^{-1/(4n)}$. The outside bound in ( 14.120 ) gives $f\leq CK^{1/2}<K$ almost everywhere on $X\setminus B_{r_ K}$ for large $K$. Therefore \[  \int _{\{ f>K\} }f\, \mathrm dV \leq C(\log K)^{-n(\alpha +1)}+CK^{-1/(2n)} \leq C'(\log K)^{-n(\alpha +1)}.  \] Apply ( 14.116 ) to $g=f\mathbf1_{\{ f>K\} }$ to get ( 14.118 ). $\square$ The potential has logarithmic modulus at $x_0$ and is not Hölder there. Its root-tail estimate follows from the capacity bound despite the failure of higher $L^ p$ integrability. The construction applies to each fixed background, including one with $v_-(h)=0$.

The outside bound in ( 14.120 ) gives $f\leq CK^{1/2}<K$ almost everywhere on $X\setminus B_{r_ K}$ for large $K$. Therefore \[  \int _{\{ f>K\} }f\, \mathrm dV \leq C(\log K)^{-n(\alpha +1)}+CK^{-1/(2n)} \leq C'(\log K)^{-n(\alpha +1)}.  \] Apply ( 14.116 ) to $g=f\mathbf1_{\{ f>K\} }$ to get ( 14.118 ). $\square$
14.118 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-root-tail} \rho _ h\bigl (f^{1/n}\mathbf1_{\{ f>K\} }\bigr ) \leq C(\log K)^{-\alpha }. \end{equation}

14.119 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-density-radial} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n =\frac{\delta ^ nn!\alpha ^ n(\alpha +1)}{\pi ^ n} R^{-2n}(1-\log R^2)^{-n(\alpha +1)-1}\, \mathrm d\lambda , \end{equation}

14.120 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-density-ball} \int _{B_ r}f\, \mathrm dV \leq C\bigl [(1-\log r^2)^{-n(\alpha +1)}+r^2\bigr ], \qquad \mathop{\rm ess\, sup}_{X\setminus B_ r}f\leq Cr^{-2n}. \end{equation}

title: 14.33 Limits of exponential equations
text: 14.33 Limits of exponential equations In this section $\theta $ is an arbitrary smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $\mu $ a finite non-pluripolar measure. We consider solutions $u_\lambda \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }\mu \qquad (\lambda >0).  \] As $\lambda \downarrow 0$, one expects suitably normalized solutions to converge to a solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu $ with a scalar $c>0$. For an $L^ p$ density with $p>1$ and a Hermitian background, the continuous solutions satisfy $\lambda u_\lambda \to \log c$ uniformly (proposition 10.6.1 ). For solutions in a fixed unbounded ordinary type, no such uniform convergence is possible: by proposition 1.23.2 , the $L^\infty $ distance from $\lambda u_\lambda $ to every finite constant is infinite for each $\lambda >0$. The limit must instead be formulated through normalized potentials and their measures. Write \[  v_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda ,\qquad c_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \sup _ Xu_\lambda },  \] so that $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda )=c_\lambda \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }\mu $. By lemma 1.23.3 , $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }\to 1$ in $L^1(\mu )$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$; hence, if $c_\lambda \to c<+\infty $, the right-hand sides converge in total variation to $c\mu $. If $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $f\in L^ p$ for some $p>1$, lemma 1.23.3 gives an error linear in $\lambda $. To identify the Monge–Ampère measure of an $L^1$ limit of the $v_\lambda $, one needs in addition a continuity theorem for the Monge–Ampère operator. For potentials of a fixed ordinary type, corollary 14.8.3 identifies the limiting measure under a common barrier and a domination hypothesis. In a relative envelope class, theorem 31.3.3 instead constructs a common lower envelope under positive lower mass: for a semipositive big $\theta $ and a reference satisfying ( 13.26 ), an $L^1$-convergent sequence in the class whose measures are dominated by one finite non-pluripolar measure converges in capacity, and its measures converge weakly. That argument, with its mass hypothesis, is developed in chapter 31 .

title: 14.33.1 A positive limiting exponent
text: 14.33.1 A positive limiting exponent When the exponents converge to a positive limit, the factor $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ makes the Monge–Ampère mass of deep sublevels uniformly small. If the potentials converge in capacity, the tail criterion of theorem 7.4.1 then identifies the limit of their Monge–Ampère measures, and convergence of the right-hand sides identifies the equation. Theorem 14.33.1 . Let $\theta $ be any smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $\mu $ a finite non-pluripolar measure. Suppose $f_ j\geq 0$, $f_ j\to f$ in $L^1(\mu )$, and $\lambda _ j>0$ with $\lambda _ j\to \lambda >0$. Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be nonpositive, suppose $u_ j\to u$ in capacity, and assume \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}f_ j\, \mu .  \] Then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ is finite and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mu .  \] Moreover, $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)\rightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ weakly, and the right-hand sides converge in total variation. Proof. Discarding finitely many indices, we may assume that $\lambda _ j\geq \lambda /2$. The measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)$ have masses at most $\| f_ j\| _{L^1(\mu )}$, which are uniformly bounded, and since $u_ j\leq 0$, their deep sublevels satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)(\{ u_ j<-T\} ) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda T/2}\| f_ j\| _{L^1(\mu )}.  \] The tail criterion theorem 7.4.1 , which holds for an arbitrary smooth background by theorem 7.6.1 , therefore shows that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ is finite and that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)\rightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$. It remains to identify this limit with $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mu $. By lemma 1.8.11 , $u_ j\to u$ in $\mu $-measure. Since $t\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}$ is $\lambda $-Lipschitz for $t\leq 0$, the functions $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}$, which are bounded by one, converge in $\mu $-measure to $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$. The change of exponent is uniform for nonpositive arguments, because the mean value theorem gives \[  \sup _{t\leq 0}|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jt}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}| \leq |\lambda _ j-\lambda | \sup _{s\geq 0}s \mathrm{e}^{-(\lambda /2)s}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ in $\mu $-measure, and hence in $f\mu $-measure, since the finite measure $f\mu $ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu $. As these functions are bounded by one, the convergence also holds in $L^1(f\mu )$. Therefore \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}f_ j-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f|\, \mathrm{d}\mu & \leq \| f_ j-f\| _{L^1(\mu )}\\ & \quad +\int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}|f\, \mathrm{d}\mu \longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] This proves the total-variation convergence of the right-hand sides, and comparing the two limits gives the equation for $u$. $\square$ Additive normalizations of the potentials can be absorbed into the densities: translating each $u_ j$ by a constant multiplies $f_ j$ by an exponential factor, and the theorem applies as long as the modified densities still converge in $L^1(\mu )$. Convergence in capacity is a hypothesis; the theorem says nothing about sequences that converge only in $L^1$, and it does not keep the limit in a prescribed envelope class. The proof also shows where the difficulty lies as $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$: the tail bound $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda _ jT}\| f_ j\| _{L^1(\mu )}$ no longer tends to zero uniformly in $j$ as $T\to \infty $. A zero-exponent limit therefore needs another source of uniform tail control, such as the integrability condition of corollary 7.4.2 ; a uniform bound on the total masses does not by itself control these tails.

title: Theorem 14.33.1
text: Theorem 14.33.1 . Let $\theta $ be any smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $\mu $ a finite non-pluripolar measure. Suppose $f_ j\geq 0$, $f_ j\to f$ in $L^1(\mu )$, and $\lambda _ j>0$ with $\lambda _ j\to \lambda >0$. Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be nonpositive, suppose $u_ j\to u$ in capacity, and assume \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}f_ j\, \mu .  \] Then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ is finite and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mu .  \] Moreover, $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)\rightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ weakly, and the right-hand sides converge in total variation. It remains to identify this limit with $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mu $. By lemma 1.8.11 , $u_ j\to u$ in $\mu $-measure. Since $t\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}$ is $\lambda $-Lipschitz for $t\leq 0$, the functions $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}$, which are bounded by one, converge in $\mu $-measure to $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$. The change of exponent is uniform for nonpositive arguments, because the mean value theorem gives \[  \sup _{t\leq 0}|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jt}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}| \leq |\lambda _ j-\lambda | \sup _{s\geq 0}s \mathrm{e}^{-(\lambda /2)s}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ in $\mu $-measure, and hence in $f\mu $-measure, since the finite measure $f\mu $ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu $. As these functions are bounded by one, the convergence also holds in $L^1(f\mu )$. Therefore \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}f_ j-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f|\, \mathrm{d}\mu & \leq \| f_ j-f\| _{L^1(\mu )}\\ & \quad +\int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}|f\, \mathrm{d}\mu \longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] This proves the total-variation convergence of the right-hand sides, and comparing the two limits gives the equation for $u$. $\square$

title: 14.34 Exponential equations for an individual density
search_title: Exponential equations for an individual density
text: 14.34 Exponential equations for an individual density We return to the Hermitian background $h$ and a fixed nonzero density $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, and consider, for $\lambda >0$, the exponential equation 14.123 \begin{equation} \label{eq:individual-exponential-equation} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h). \end{equation} A solution is a function $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ satisfying ( 14.123 ), and an exponential subsolution at exponent $\lambda $ is a function $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}f\, \mathrm{d}V$. For the truncations $f_ k=\min (f,k)$, theorem 10.1.2 gives continuous solutions $u_ k$ of the truncated equations, and these decrease as $k$ increases. Strict domination shows that every exponential subsolution is a common lower bound for the $u_ k$. Hence, as soon as one subsolution exists, the decreasing limit is not identically $-\infty $, and theorem 14.33.1 shows that it solves ( 14.123 ); it is the greatest subsolution. A positive threshold $b_ h(f)$ provides exponential subsolutions for every exponent, and the normalized greatest solutions then recover $b_ h(f)$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Theorem 14.34.1 . Fix $\lambda >0$, and suppose that ( 14.123 ) has an exponential subsolution $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. For $k\geq 1$, let $u_ k$ be the continuous solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ k)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ k}f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad f_ k=\min (f,k),  \] given by theorem 10.1.2 . Then $u_ k$ decreases to a solution $u_\lambda $ of ( 14.123 ), and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_\lambda )$ has finite mass. Moreover, $u_\lambda $ is the greatest exponential subsolution: every exponential subsolution $v$ at exponent $\lambda $ satisfies $v\leq u_\lambda $. In particular, $u_\lambda $ is the greatest solution of ( 14.123 ). Proof. Since $f_ k\leq f_{k+1}$, lemma 10.4.2 gives $u_{k+1}\leq u_ k$. We first show that every exponential subsolution $v$ lies below each $u_ k$. Let $t>0$. On the set $\{ u_ k<v-t\} $, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ k)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ k}f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v}f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v-t).  \] Since $u_ k$ is bounded, $P_{h/2}(u_ k)\geq \inf _ Xu_ k$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $v-t\preceq u_ k$. Strict domination, theorem 14.1.2 , therefore gives $u_ k\geq v-t$. Letting $t\downarrow 0$ gives $u_ k\geq v$. In particular $s\leq u_ k\leq u_1$ for every $k$, so the decreasing limit $u_\lambda \geq s$ is not identically $-\infty $ and belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. By lemma 1.8.12 , $u_ k\to u_\lambda $ in capacity. Choose a constant $A\geq \sup _ Xu_1$. The nonpositive functions $u_ k-A$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_ k-A)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (u_ k-A)}\, \mathrm{e}^{\lambda A}f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] and $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda A}f_ k\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda A}f$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Theorem 14.33.1 , applied with $\mu =\mathrm{d}V$ and constant exponents, shows that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_\lambda )$ is finite and that $u_\lambda $ solves ( 14.123 ). Finally, every exponential subsolution lies below all $u_ k$, hence below $u_\lambda $, which is itself a subsolution. $\square$ Being the greatest subsolution, $u_\lambda $ does not depend on the approximation used to construct it. The equation may have other, smaller solutions with different singularities. If $f\in L^ p$ for some $p>1$, the continuous solution of theorem 10.1.2 is a subsolution and therefore lies below $u_\lambda $. Thus $u_\lambda $ is bounded, and bounded exponential comparison (corollary 10.2.4 ) shows that it coincides with the continuous solution. Corollary 14.34.2 . Suppose $b=b_ h(f)>0$. Then ( 14.123 ) has a greatest solution $u_\lambda $ for every $\lambda >0$. If $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ satisfies $\sup _ Xv=0$ and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, then \[  u_\lambda \geq v+\lambda ^{-1}\log b.  \] Put \[  M_\lambda =\sup _ Xu_\lambda ,\qquad v_\lambda =u_\lambda -M_\lambda ,\qquad c_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda M_\lambda }.  \] Then, as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, \[  c_\lambda \longrightarrow b_ h(f),\qquad \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\longrightarrow b_ h(f)f \quad \text{in }L^1(\mathrm{d}V).  \] Proof. By theorem 14.27.2 , a function $v$ as in the statement exists. Since $v\leq 0$, the function $s=v+\lambda ^{-1}\log b$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V \geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] so it is an exponential subsolution. Theorem 14.34.1 gives the greatest solution $u_\lambda $ and the bound $u_\lambda \geq s$; in particular, $c_\lambda \geq b$. Set $g_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f$. By lemma 1.23.3 , applied to the finite measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$, we have $g_\lambda \to f$ in $L^1$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Each $g_\lambda $ is nonzero, since $v_\lambda $ is finite almost everywhere. The equation for $u_\lambda $ reads $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_\lambda )=c_\lambda g_\lambda \, \mathrm{d}V$, so theorem 14.27.2 , applied to the density $g_\lambda $, gives \[  c_\lambda \leq b_ h(g_\lambda ).  \] The upper semicontinuity of the threshold (theorem 14.31.1 ) therefore gives \[  b\leq \liminf _{\lambda \downarrow 0}c_\lambda \leq \limsup _{\lambda \downarrow 0}c_\lambda \leq b_ h(f)=b.  \] This proves $c_\lambda \to b$. Since $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f=c_\lambda g_\lambda $ and $g_\lambda \to f$ in $L^1$, it also proves $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\to bf$ in $L^1$. $\square$ Since $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V$, the Monge–Ampère measures of the normalized greatest solutions converge in total variation to $b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$. This answers the questions about the scalar and the measure raised in section 14.33 ; the potentials $v_\lambda $ themselves are harder to control. Under positive lower mass, corollary 31.7.1 shows that every $L^1$-convergent sequence $v_{\lambda _ j}$ with $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$ converges in capacity to a solution of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v)=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$. For $L^ p$ data with $p>1$, proposition 14.19.1 gives uniform precompactness. In both cases, convergence of the whole family $(v_\lambda )$ requires that all its cluster limits coincide. This holds when the dual problem for $f^{1/n}$ over Gauduchon currents, studied in section 26.9 , has a smooth strictly positive maximizer: the whole family then converges uniformly (corollary 26.9.7 ). If the maximizer is smooth and semipositive, and strictly positive outside a proper analytic set, proposition 26.9.11 gives $L^1$ convergence of the whole family and a fixed lower barrier, and corollary 26.9.18 strengthens this to uniform convergence for $L^ p$ data with $p>1$. For a general positive threshold, the corollary gives the lower bound \[  v_\lambda \geq v-\lambda ^{-1}\log (c_\lambda /b_ h(f))  \] for every normalized threshold subsolution $v$. The next subsection estimates the scalar error $\log (c_\lambda /b_ h(f))$ when $f^{1/n}$ can be approximated by bounded functions in the norm of $\mathcal D_ h$. When $b_ h(f)=0$, theorem 14.34.1 still applies whenever an exponential subsolution exists; examples are constructed in 14.34.2 .
14.123 \begin{equation} \label{eq:individual-exponential-equation} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h). \end{equation}

title: 14.34.1 An error bound for the scalar limit
search_title: An error bound for the scalar limit
text: 14.34.1 An error bound for the scalar limit Suppose that $f^{1/n}$ belongs to the space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ of 14.31.2 . The uniform tail condition of proposition 14.31.5 then gives a rate for the convergence $c_\lambda \to b_ h(f)$ in corollary 14.34.2 . Split the root $p=f^{1/n}$ at a height $K$. On $\{ p\leq K\} $, the error $p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})$ of the damped root has norm $O(K\lambda )$ in $\mathcal D_ h$, uniformly over normalized potentials $v$, while on $\{ p>K\} $ it is bounded by the tail of $p$, which is small in that norm. Optimizing over $K$ gives a modulus valid for every normalized potential. Proposition 14.34.3 . Let $0\leq p\in \mathcal D_ h^0$ be nonzero, and put $f=p^ n$, $R=\rho _ h(p)$ and $b=R^{-n}=b_ h(f)$. There is a constant $C_ h$, depending only on $h$ and $\mathrm{d}V$, such that the function \[  \eta _ p(\lambda )=\inf _{K>0} \left(\| p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }\| _{\mathcal D_ h}+C_ hK\lambda \right)  \] tends to zero as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ and satisfies 14.124 \begin{equation} \label{eq:uniform-root-damping} \big \| p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})\big \| _{\mathcal D_ h} \leq \eta _ p(\lambda ) \qquad \bigl (v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h),\  \sup _ Xv=0\bigr ). \end{equation} Let $u_\lambda $, $v_\lambda $ and $c_\lambda $ be the greatest exponential solutions and their normalizations from corollary 14.34.2 . If $\eta _ p(\lambda )<R$, then \[  b\leq c_\lambda \leq \bigl (R-\eta _ p(\lambda )\bigr )^{-n}  \] and \begin{align*}  \big \| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_\lambda ) -bf\, \mathrm{d}V\big \| _{\mathrm{TV}} & \leq (c_\lambda -b)\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n} +nb\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n-1}\eta _ p(\lambda ). \end{align*} If $p\in L^ r$ for some finite $r>n$, the same bounds hold with $\eta _ p(\lambda )$ replaced by $C_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}\lambda $, where $C_{h,r}$ depends only on $h$, $\mathrm{d}V$ and $r$. In particular, for each such $p$ the scalar and total-variation errors are $O(\lambda )$. Proof. By lemma 1.5.1 , normalized $h$-plurisubharmonic functions are uniformly bounded in every $L^ s$ with $s<+\infty $. By ( 14.114 ) with $r=2n$, their norms $\| v\| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ are therefore uniformly bounded; let $C_ h$ be $1/n$ times this bound. Let $v$ be normalized and $K>0$. On $\{ p\leq K\} $ we have \[  0\leq p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n}) \leq K\lambda (-v)/n,  \] since $1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}\leq x$ for $x\geq 0$, while on $\{ p>K\} $ we use the bound $p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})\leq p$. The monotonicity of $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ and the triangle inequality give \[  \big \| p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})\big \| _{\mathcal D_ h} \leq \| p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }\| _{\mathcal D_ h}+C_ hK\lambda ,  \] and taking the infimum over $K$ proves ( 14.124 ). By proposition 14.31.5 , and since the $L^ n$ tails of $p$ tend to zero, $\| p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }\| _{\mathcal D_ h}\to 0$ as $K\to \infty $. Choosing $K$ first and then letting $\lambda \downarrow 0$ shows that $\eta _ p(\lambda )\to 0$. Now set $q_\lambda =p\, \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda /n}$, so that $q_\lambda ^ n=g_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f$, with $g_\lambda $ as in the proof of corollary 14.34.2 . Since $0\leq q_\lambda \leq p$ and $\rho _ h(p-q_\lambda )\leq \eta _ p(\lambda )$ by ( 14.124 ), the triangle inequality and monotonicity give \[  R-\eta _ p(\lambda )\leq \rho _ h(q_\lambda )\leq R.  \] The same proof gives $b\leq c_\lambda \leq b_ h(g_\lambda )=\rho _ h(q_\lambda )^{-n}$, which yields the scalar bound. For the measures, the factorization of $p^ n-q_\lambda ^ n$ gives $0\leq p^ n-q_\lambda ^ n\leq np^{n-1}(p-q_\lambda )$, and Hölder's inequality implies \[  \| f-g_\lambda \| _{L^1} \leq n\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n-1}\| p-q_\lambda \| _{L^ n} \leq n\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n-1}\eta _ p(\lambda ).  \] Since $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_\lambda )=c_\lambda g_\lambda \, \mathrm{d}V$, the identity $c_\lambda g_\lambda -bf=(c_\lambda -b)g_\lambda -b(f-g_\lambda )$, together with $\| g_\lambda \| _{L^1}\leq \| f\| _{L^1}=\| p\| _{L^ n}^ n$, proves the total-variation bound. Finally, suppose $p\in L^ r$ with $n<r<+\infty $, and choose $n<s<r$. By ( 14.114 ) with exponent $s$, and since $\| \cdot \| _{L^ n}\leq \| \cdot \| _{L^ s}$, we have $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}\leq (1+C_ s)\| \cdot \| _{L^ s}$. Hölder's inequality and lemma 1.5.1 then give, for every normalized $v$, \[  \| p(-v)\| _{\mathcal D_ h} \leq (1+C_ s)\| p(-v)\| _{L^ s} \leq (1+C_ s)\| p\| _{L^ r}\| v\| _{L^{rs/(r-s)}} \leq nC_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}.  \] Since $0\leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n}\leq \lambda (-v)/n$, the left side of ( 14.124 ) is therefore at most $C_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}\lambda $, and the two estimates above can be repeated with this bound in place of $\eta _ p(\lambda )$. For $\lambda $ so small that $C_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}\lambda \leq R/2$, the function $t\mapsto (R-t)^{-n}$ has bounded derivative on $[0,R/2]$, so the scalar error $c_\lambda -b$, and hence the total-variation error, is $O(\lambda )$. $\square$ For a general $p\in \mathcal D_ h^0$ the modulus $\eta _ p(\lambda )$ tends to zero, but we do not know whether it is $O(\lambda )$. Combined with the lower bound $v_\lambda \geq v-\lambda ^{-1}\log (c_\lambda /b)$ for normalized threshold subsolutions $v$, the proposition gives \[  0\leq \lambda ^{-1}\log (c_\lambda /b) \leq -\frac n\lambda \log \bigl (1-\eta _ p(\lambda )/R\bigr ),  \] which stays bounded as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ when $\eta _ p(\lambda )=O(\lambda )$, in particular for $p\in L^ r$ with $r>n$; root tails alone do not give such a bound. Even when a uniform lower barrier for $v_\lambda $ is available, passing to the limit in capacity requires the singularity-type or lower-mass hypotheses of a continuity theorem. The proposition estimates only scalars and measures; when the lower mass vanishes, it does not give an exact equation at the threshold.

Finally, suppose $p\in L^ r$ with $n<r<+\infty $, and choose $n<s<r$. By ( 14.114 ) with exponent $s$, and since $\| \cdot \| _{L^ n}\leq \| \cdot \| _{L^ s}$, we have $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}\leq (1+C_ s)\| \cdot \| _{L^ s}$. Hölder's inequality and lemma 1.5.1 then give, for every normalized $v$, \[  \| p(-v)\| _{\mathcal D_ h} \leq (1+C_ s)\| p(-v)\| _{L^ s} \leq (1+C_ s)\| p\| _{L^ r}\| v\| _{L^{rs/(r-s)}} \leq nC_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}.  \] Since $0\leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n}\leq \lambda (-v)/n$, the left side of ( 14.124 ) is therefore at most $C_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}\lambda $, and the two estimates above can be repeated with this bound in place of $\eta _ p(\lambda )$.
