title: 14.34.2 Exponential equations at zero threshold
text: 14.34.2 Exponential equations at zero threshold When $b_ h(f)=0$, no positive multiple of $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is dominated by a Monge–Ampère measure. An exponential subsolution $s$ only needs $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, however, and the factor $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}$ is small where $s$ is very negative. A density concentrating near the pole of a singular potential can therefore admit exponential subsolutions although its threshold vanishes. We construct such densities on the products of section 14.29 . We keep the notation of that section: $X=X_0\times Y$ with $Y=\mathbb P^ k$, the background $H=h_0+\kappa $, the constants $N$, $C$ and $V_0$, the probability volume form $\mu =V_0^{-1}h_0^ m\wedge \kappa ^ k$ with density $R=\mu /\mathrm{d}V$, and the potential $u_\alpha $ with density $q_\alpha $ from lemma 14.29.1 , for a fixed $0<\alpha <1$. On $Y\setminus \{ o\} $ put $L=1-\psi \geq 1$, so that $u_\alpha =1-L^\alpha $, and $t=\mathrm e^{1-L}$. As functions of $L$, define \[  a=\alpha L^{\alpha -1},\qquad Q=t+(1-t)a,\qquad D=t(1-a)+(1-t)\alpha (1-\alpha )L^{\alpha -2},  \] \[  W=kQ^{k-1}D,\qquad B_\tau =q_\alpha \mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}\quad (\tau >0),\qquad b_0=(1-\alpha )^ k.  \] Here $Q$ is the function $Q(r)$ of lemma 14.29.1 , written in terms of $L$, and $D=-\mathrm{d}Q/\mathrm{d}L$. The weight $B_\tau $ is chosen so that $\mathrm e^{\tau u_\alpha }B_\tau =q_\alpha $ off $o$. Lemma 14.34.4 . As functions of $L$, \[  q_\alpha =Q^{k-1}D\, \mathrm e^{k(L-1)},\qquad q_\alpha \geq b_0,  \] and $W(L)\sim k\alpha ^ k(1-\alpha )L^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}$ as $L\to +\infty $. For every $\tau >0$, $\mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}W(L)\to +\infty $ as $L\to +\infty $. In particular, $B_\tau \kappa ^ k$ has infinite mass on every punctured neighborhood of $o$. Proof. In the notation of the proof of lemma 14.29.1 , $t=r/(1+r)$ and $s(r)=L$. Since the mass of $q_\alpha \kappa ^ k$ on $\{ r_1<r<r_2\} $ is $Q(r_2)^ k-Q(r_1)^ k$, this measure has radial distribution $-\mathrm{d}(Q^ k)/\mathrm{d}L=W(L)\, \mathrm{d}L$. The Fubini–Study measure $\kappa ^ k$ corresponds to $Q=t$, so its radial distribution is $k\mathrm e^{-k(L-1)}\mathrm{d}L$. Both measures are invariant under the unitary group of the chart, so $q_\alpha $ is the ratio of the two distributions, which is the stated formula. The lower bound $q_\alpha \geq b_0$ follows from $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \geq (1-\alpha )\kappa $ off $o$. As $L\to +\infty $, $t$ tends to zero exponentially, so $Q\sim \alpha L^{\alpha -1}$ and $D\sim \alpha (1-\alpha )L^{\alpha -2}$; this gives the asymptotics of $W$. Consequently, \[  \log \bigl (\mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}W(L)\bigr )=\tau L^\alpha -[1+k(1-\alpha )]\log L+O(1)\longrightarrow +\infty ,  \] and the mass of $B_\tau \kappa ^ k$ on $\{ L>T\} $, which equals $\int _ T^\infty \mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}W(L)\, \mathrm{d}L$, is infinite for every $T$. $\square$ Theorem 14.34.5 . Let $f\geq 0$ be a nonzero integrable function on $X$, and put $F=f/R$. If $\lambda >0$ and $F\leq AB_\lambda $ almost everywhere for a constant $A>0$, then \[  s_\lambda =u_\alpha +\lambda ^{-1}\log (CV_0/A)  \] is an exponential subsolution at exponent $\lambda $, of mass $CV_0$, and the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a greatest solution, whose mass is finite and positive. Suppose that $F$ is locally essentially bounded on $X\setminus (X_0\times \{ o\} )$ and \[  \lim _{T\to +\infty }\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{x\in X_0,\  L(y)>T} \frac{\log ^+(F(x,y)/q_\alpha (y))}{L(y)^\alpha }=0,  \] where $\log ^+r=\log \max (1,r)$ for $r\geq 0$. Then the hypothesis of (1), and hence its conclusion, holds for every $\lambda >0$. Proof. (1) By theorem 14.29.3 , $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=CV_0q_\alpha \mu $. Off the pole fiber $X_0\times \{ o\} $ we have $\mathrm e^{\lambda u_\alpha }B_\lambda =q_\alpha $ and $f\, \mathrm{d}V=F\mu \leq AB_\lambda \mu $, hence \[  \mathrm e^{\lambda s_\lambda }f\, \mathrm dV \leq (CV_0/A)\mathrm e^{\lambda u_\alpha }AB_\lambda \mu =CV_0q_\alpha \mu =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(s_\lambda ),  \] and both measures vanish on the pole fiber. Thus $s_\lambda $ is an exponential subsolution, and its mass is $CV_0$, since adding a constant does not change the Monge–Ampère measure. Theorem 14.34.1 now gives the greatest solution $u$ and the finiteness of its mass. The mass $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is positive because $u$ is finite almost everywhere and $f$ has positive integral. (2) Fix $\lambda >0$. By hypothesis, there is $T$ such that $F/q_\alpha \leq \mathrm e^{(\lambda /2)L^\alpha }$ almost everywhere on $\{ L>T\} $. Since $\mathrm e^{(\lambda /2)L^\alpha }\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda }\mathrm e^{\lambda (L^\alpha -1)}$ for $L\geq 1$, we have $F\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda }B_\lambda $ there. On the complement $\{ L\leq T\} $, which is compact and disjoint from the pole fiber, $F$ is essentially bounded, while $B_\lambda \geq q_\alpha \geq b_0>0$. Increasing the constant, we obtain $F\leq AB_\lambda $ almost everywhere on $X$. $\square$ Theorem 14.34.6 . Let $F_ j$, $j\geq 1$, be smooth strictly positive probability densities on $X_0$ with respect to $\mathrm dV_0=V_0^{-1}h_0^ m$, whose normalization scalars on $X_0$, relative to $h_0$ and $\mathrm dV_0$, satisfy $c_{h_0}(F_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}/C$. There are smooth strictly positive probability densities $g_ j$ on $Y$ with respect to $\kappa ^ k$ such that the probability densities \[  f_ j=RF_ jg_ j,\qquad f=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}f_ j  \] on $X$ satisfy $c_ H(f_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}$ and $b_ H(f)=0$. The function $f$ is finite everywhere, smooth off the pole fiber $X_0\times \{ o\} $, has integral one and is bounded below by a positive constant. For every $\lambda >0$, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ has an exponential subsolution and a greatest solution, of finite mass, and every solution is unbounded. Proof. Put $w_ j=2^{-j}$ and $M_ j=\max _{X_0}F_ j$. Step 1: a smooth baseline. Fix $C^ j$ norms $\| \cdot \| _{C^ j}$ on $X_0$, computed in a fixed finite atlas, so that they increase with $j$. Choose $0<\varepsilon _ j\leq 1/2$ with \[  w_ j\varepsilon _ jM_ j\leq b_0 2^{-j-2},\qquad w_ j\varepsilon _ j\| F_ j\| _{C^ j}\leq 2^{-j}.  \] Then $E=\sum _ jw_ j\varepsilon _ jF_ j$ converges in every $C^ l$ norm, so $E$ is smooth on $X_0$, and $0<E\leq b_0/4$. Step 2: bumps escaping to the pole. Choose a smooth function $\chi :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, supported in $[0,1]$, positive on $(0,1)$ and flat at $0$ and $1$. Starting with $T_0=0$, choose inductively $T_ j\geq 2$ with $T_ j>T_{j-1}+2$ and \[  Z_ j=\int _{T_ j}^{T_ j+1}\chi (L-T_ j) \mathrm e^{(L^\alpha -1)/j}W(L)\, \mathrm dL \geq 2w_ jM_ j.  \] This is possible because, by lemma 14.34.4 with $\tau =1/j$, the factor $\mathrm e^{(L^\alpha -1)/j}W(L)$ is uniformly large on sufficiently distant intervals. On the annulus $\{ T_ j\leq L\leq T_ j+1\} $ put $\beta _ j=\chi (L-T_ j)B_{1/j}/Z_ j$, extend $\beta _ j$ by zero, and set $g_ j=\varepsilon _ j+(1-\varepsilon _ j)\beta _ j$. Since $\chi $ is flat at the endpoints, $\beta _ j$ is smooth; it vanishes near $o$ and near the hyperplane $\{ L=1\} $. Its integral against $\kappa ^ k$ is one, so $g_ j$ is a smooth strictly positive probability density with respect to $\kappa ^ k$. Moreover, \[  w_ jM_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)\beta _ j\leq B_{1/j}/2.  \] Step 3: the scalars $c_ H(f_ j)$. By theorem 9.1.1 on $Y$, there is a smooth $\phi _ j$ with $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ j>0$ and $(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ j)^ k=g_ j\kappa ^ k$; the scalar is one because both sides have mass one. On $X_0$, the same theorem gives a smooth $v_ j$ with $h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j>0$ and $(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ m=c_{h_0}(F_ j)F_ j\, \mathrm dV_0$. Since only one term of the binomial expansion survives for dimensional reasons, \[  (H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ j+\phi _ j))^ N =C c_{h_0}(F_ j)F_ jg_ j\mu =C c_{h_0}(F_ j)f_ j\, \mathrm dV.  \] Uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ H(f_ j)=C c_{h_0}(F_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}$. Step 4: properties of $f$. By Tonelli's theorem, $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm dV=\sum _ jw_ j=1$. The density of $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with respect to $\mu $ is \[  F=f/R=\sum _ jw_ jF_ jg_ j=E+\sum _ jw_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)F_ j\beta _ j.  \] The annuli are disjoint and escape to the pole, so only finitely many bumps meet any compact subset of $Y\setminus \{ o\} $; hence $F$, and therefore $f$, is smooth off the pole fiber. On the pole fiber all bumps vanish and $F=E$, so $f$ is finite everywhere. Also $f\geq w_1f_1\geq \frac12\min _ Xf_1>0$. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq aw_ jf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and lemma 14.26.1 gives \[  aw_ j\leq c_ H(f_ j)\leq 2^{-2j},\quad \text{that is,}\quad a\leq 2^{-j}, \quad \text{for every }j.  \] This is impossible, so $b_ H(f)=0$ by theorem 14.27.2 . Step 5: exponential subsolutions. Fix $\lambda >0$, and choose $J$ with $1/j\leq \lambda $ for $j\geq J$. Since $L^\alpha -1\geq 0$, we have $B_{1/j}\leq B_\lambda $ for these $j$. As the bumps have disjoint supports, Step 2 bounds their total contribution $\sum _{j\geq J}w_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)F_ j\beta _ j$ by $B_\lambda /2$. The baseline satisfies $E\leq b_0/4\leq B_\lambda /4$, because $B_\lambda \geq q_\alpha \geq b_0$. The remaining finitely many bumps are bounded by the constant \[  K_\lambda =\max _ Y\sum _{j<J}w_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)M_ j\beta _ j,  \] and $K_\lambda \leq (K_\lambda /b_0)B_\lambda $. Hence $F\leq A_\lambda B_\lambda $ with $A_\lambda =3/4+K_\lambda /b_0$, and theorem 14.34.5 gives the exponential subsolution $u_\alpha +\lambda ^{-1}\log (CV_0/A_\lambda )$ and the greatest solution. Finally, a bounded solution $u$ would satisfy $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda \inf _ Xu}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, a positive scaled subsolution, contradicting $b_ H(f)=0$. Hence every solution is unbounded. $\square$ The density just constructed also satisfies the criterion in part (2) of theorem 14.34.5 : on the $j$th annulus, $F/q_\alpha \leq 1/4+\frac12\mathrm e^{(L^\alpha -1)/j}$, and away from all annuli the ratio is at most $1/4$. Approaching the pole through the annuli forces $j\to \infty $, so the required limit is zero. Since $b_ H(f)=0$, proposition 14.27.4 also shows that $f$ belongs to no $L^ p$ with $p>1$. Densities $F_ j$ as in the theorem exist whenever $v_-(h_0)=0$, by theorem 26.14.3 , theorem 26.1.3 . For instance, on the elliptic threefold, theorem 26.18.1 gives smooth functions $v_\ell $ with $h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\ell >0$ and masses $\delta _\ell =\int _{X_0}(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\ell )^3\to 0$. The probability densities $F_\ell =(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\ell )^3/(\delta _\ell \, \mathrm dV_0)$ satisfy $c_{h_0}(F_\ell )=\delta _\ell $ by uniqueness of the scalar, and a subsequence with $\delta _{\ell _ j}\leq 2^{-2j}/C$ gives the required densities. Thus the construction applies to this threefold times $\mathbb P^ k$ for every $k\geq 1$. With the balanced metric of proposition 26.18.7 , $V_0=24\pi $, so the explicit subsolutions have mass $CV_0$, equal to $96\pi $ on the fourfold ($k=1$) and $240\pi $ on the fivefold ($k=2$). These values concern the subsolutions; the greatest solutions have their own finite positive masses. In this construction the projective components $g_ j$ are chosen after the densities $F_ j$, to fit them. We do not know whether the exponential equation is solvable for every prescribed concentration family of this kind, and we have no necessary criterion for solvability at zero threshold.

title: Lemma 14.34.4
text: Lemma 14.34.4 . As functions of $L$, \[  q_\alpha =Q^{k-1}D\, \mathrm e^{k(L-1)},\qquad q_\alpha \geq b_0,  \] and $W(L)\sim k\alpha ^ k(1-\alpha )L^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}$ as $L\to +\infty $. For every $\tau >0$, $\mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}W(L)\to +\infty $ as $L\to +\infty $. In particular, $B_\tau \kappa ^ k$ has infinite mass on every punctured neighborhood of $o$. Proof. In the notation of the proof of lemma 14.29.1 , $t=r/(1+r)$ and $s(r)=L$. Since the mass of $q_\alpha \kappa ^ k$ on $\{ r_1<r<r_2\} $ is $Q(r_2)^ k-Q(r_1)^ k$, this measure has radial distribution $-\mathrm{d}(Q^ k)/\mathrm{d}L=W(L)\, \mathrm{d}L$. The Fubini–Study measure $\kappa ^ k$ corresponds to $Q=t$, so its radial distribution is $k\mathrm e^{-k(L-1)}\mathrm{d}L$. Both measures are invariant under the unitary group of the chart, so $q_\alpha $ is the ratio of the two distributions, which is the stated formula. The lower bound $q_\alpha \geq b_0$ follows from $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \geq (1-\alpha )\kappa $ off $o$. As $L\to +\infty $, $t$ tends to zero exponentially, so $Q\sim \alpha L^{\alpha -1}$ and $D\sim \alpha (1-\alpha )L^{\alpha -2}$; this gives the asymptotics of $W$. Consequently, \[  \log \bigl (\mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}W(L)\bigr )=\tau L^\alpha -[1+k(1-\alpha )]\log L+O(1)\longrightarrow +\infty ,  \] and the mass of $B_\tau \kappa ^ k$ on $\{ L>T\} $, which equals $\int _ T^\infty \mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}W(L)\, \mathrm{d}L$, is infinite for every $T$. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.34.5
text: Theorem 14.34.5 . Let $f\geq 0$ be a nonzero integrable function on $X$, and put $F=f/R$. If $\lambda >0$ and $F\leq AB_\lambda $ almost everywhere for a constant $A>0$, then \[  s_\lambda =u_\alpha +\lambda ^{-1}\log (CV_0/A)  \] is an exponential subsolution at exponent $\lambda $, of mass $CV_0$, and the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a greatest solution, whose mass is finite and positive. Suppose that $F$ is locally essentially bounded on $X\setminus (X_0\times \{ o\} )$ and \[  \lim _{T\to +\infty }\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{x\in X_0,\  L(y)>T} \frac{\log ^+(F(x,y)/q_\alpha (y))}{L(y)^\alpha }=0,  \] where $\log ^+r=\log \max (1,r)$ for $r\geq 0$. Then the hypothesis of (1), and hence its conclusion, holds for every $\lambda >0$. Proof. (1) By theorem 14.29.3 , $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=CV_0q_\alpha \mu $. Off the pole fiber $X_0\times \{ o\} $ we have $\mathrm e^{\lambda u_\alpha }B_\lambda =q_\alpha $ and $f\, \mathrm{d}V=F\mu \leq AB_\lambda \mu $, hence \[  \mathrm e^{\lambda s_\lambda }f\, \mathrm dV \leq (CV_0/A)\mathrm e^{\lambda u_\alpha }AB_\lambda \mu =CV_0q_\alpha \mu =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(s_\lambda ),  \] and both measures vanish on the pole fiber. Thus $s_\lambda $ is an exponential subsolution, and its mass is $CV_0$, since adding a constant does not change the Monge–Ampère measure. Theorem 14.34.1 now gives the greatest solution $u$ and the finiteness of its mass. The mass $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is positive because $u$ is finite almost everywhere and $f$ has positive integral. (2) Fix $\lambda >0$. By hypothesis, there is $T$ such that $F/q_\alpha \leq \mathrm e^{(\lambda /2)L^\alpha }$ almost everywhere on $\{ L>T\} $. Since $\mathrm e^{(\lambda /2)L^\alpha }\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda }\mathrm e^{\lambda (L^\alpha -1)}$ for $L\geq 1$, we have $F\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda }B_\lambda $ there. On the complement $\{ L\leq T\} $, which is compact and disjoint from the pole fiber, $F$ is essentially bounded, while $B_\lambda \geq q_\alpha \geq b_0>0$. Increasing the constant, we obtain $F\leq AB_\lambda $ almost everywhere on $X$. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.34.6
text: Theorem 14.34.6 . Let $F_ j$, $j\geq 1$, be smooth strictly positive probability densities on $X_0$ with respect to $\mathrm dV_0=V_0^{-1}h_0^ m$, whose normalization scalars on $X_0$, relative to $h_0$ and $\mathrm dV_0$, satisfy $c_{h_0}(F_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}/C$. There are smooth strictly positive probability densities $g_ j$ on $Y$ with respect to $\kappa ^ k$ such that the probability densities \[  f_ j=RF_ jg_ j,\qquad f=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}f_ j  \] on $X$ satisfy $c_ H(f_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}$ and $b_ H(f)=0$. The function $f$ is finite everywhere, smooth off the pole fiber $X_0\times \{ o\} $, has integral one and is bounded below by a positive constant. For every $\lambda >0$, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ has an exponential subsolution and a greatest solution, of finite mass, and every solution is unbounded. Proof. Put $w_ j=2^{-j}$ and $M_ j=\max _{X_0}F_ j$. Step 1: a smooth baseline. Fix $C^ j$ norms $\| \cdot \| _{C^ j}$ on $X_0$, computed in a fixed finite atlas, so that they increase with $j$. Choose $0<\varepsilon _ j\leq 1/2$ with \[  w_ j\varepsilon _ jM_ j\leq b_0 2^{-j-2},\qquad w_ j\varepsilon _ j\| F_ j\| _{C^ j}\leq 2^{-j}.  \] Then $E=\sum _ jw_ j\varepsilon _ jF_ j$ converges in every $C^ l$ norm, so $E$ is smooth on $X_0$, and $0<E\leq b_0/4$. Step 2: bumps escaping to the pole. Choose a smooth function $\chi :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, supported in $[0,1]$, positive on $(0,1)$ and flat at $0$ and $1$. Starting with $T_0=0$, choose inductively $T_ j\geq 2$ with $T_ j>T_{j-1}+2$ and \[  Z_ j=\int _{T_ j}^{T_ j+1}\chi (L-T_ j) \mathrm e^{(L^\alpha -1)/j}W(L)\, \mathrm dL \geq 2w_ jM_ j.  \] This is possible because, by lemma 14.34.4 with $\tau =1/j$, the factor $\mathrm e^{(L^\alpha -1)/j}W(L)$ is uniformly large on sufficiently distant intervals. On the annulus $\{ T_ j\leq L\leq T_ j+1\} $ put $\beta _ j=\chi (L-T_ j)B_{1/j}/Z_ j$, extend $\beta _ j$ by zero, and set $g_ j=\varepsilon _ j+(1-\varepsilon _ j)\beta _ j$. Since $\chi $ is flat at the endpoints, $\beta _ j$ is smooth; it vanishes near $o$ and near the hyperplane $\{ L=1\} $. Its integral against $\kappa ^ k$ is one, so $g_ j$ is a smooth strictly positive probability density with respect to $\kappa ^ k$. Moreover, \[  w_ jM_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)\beta _ j\leq B_{1/j}/2.  \] Step 3: the scalars $c_ H(f_ j)$. By theorem 9.1.1 on $Y$, there is a smooth $\phi _ j$ with $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ j>0$ and $(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ j)^ k=g_ j\kappa ^ k$; the scalar is one because both sides have mass one. On $X_0$, the same theorem gives a smooth $v_ j$ with $h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j>0$ and $(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ m=c_{h_0}(F_ j)F_ j\, \mathrm dV_0$. Since only one term of the binomial expansion survives for dimensional reasons, \[  (H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ j+\phi _ j))^ N =C c_{h_0}(F_ j)F_ jg_ j\mu =C c_{h_0}(F_ j)f_ j\, \mathrm dV.  \] Uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ H(f_ j)=C c_{h_0}(F_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}$. Step 4: properties of $f$. By Tonelli's theorem, $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm dV=\sum _ jw_ j=1$. The density of $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with respect to $\mu $ is \[  F=f/R=\sum _ jw_ jF_ jg_ j=E+\sum _ jw_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)F_ j\beta _ j.  \] The annuli are disjoint and escape to the pole, so only finitely many bumps meet any compact subset of $Y\setminus \{ o\} $; hence $F$, and therefore $f$, is smooth off the pole fiber. On the pole fiber all bumps vanish and $F=E$, so $f$ is finite everywhere. Also $f\geq w_1f_1\geq \frac12\min _ Xf_1>0$. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq aw_ jf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and lemma 14.26.1 gives \[  aw_ j\leq c_ H(f_ j)\leq 2^{-2j},\quad \text{that is,}\quad a\leq 2^{-j}, \quad \text{for every }j.  \] This is impossible, so $b_ H(f)=0$ by theorem 14.27.2 . Step 5: exponential subsolutions. Fix $\lambda >0$, and choose $J$ with $1/j\leq \lambda $ for $j\geq J$. Since $L^\alpha -1\geq 0$, we have $B_{1/j}\leq B_\lambda $ for these $j$. As the bumps have disjoint supports, Step 2 bounds their total contribution $\sum _{j\geq J}w_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)F_ j\beta _ j$ by $B_\lambda /2$. The baseline satisfies $E\leq b_0/4\leq B_\lambda /4$, because $B_\lambda \geq q_\alpha \geq b_0$. The remaining finitely many bumps are bounded by the constant \[  K_\lambda =\max _ Y\sum _{j<J}w_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)M_ j\beta _ j,  \] and $K_\lambda \leq (K_\lambda /b_0)B_\lambda $. Hence $F\leq A_\lambda B_\lambda $ with $A_\lambda =3/4+K_\lambda /b_0$, and theorem 14.34.5 gives the exponential subsolution $u_\alpha +\lambda ^{-1}\log (CV_0/A_\lambda )$ and the greatest solution. Finally, a bounded solution $u$ would satisfy $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda \inf _ Xu}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, a positive scaled subsolution, contradicting $b_ H(f)=0$. Hence every solution is unbounded. $\square$

title: 14.34.3 Solvable exponents and collapse at zero threshold
search_title: Solvable exponents and collapse at zero threshold
text: 14.34.3 Solvable exponents and collapse at zero threshold We return to a general Hermitian form $h$ on $X$ and a nonzero density $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm dV)$. Let $\Lambda _ h(f)$ be the set of exponents $\lambda >0$ for which ( 14.123 ) has a solution. By theorem 14.34.1 , $\lambda \in \Lambda _ h(f)$ if and only if the equation has an exponential subsolution at exponent $\lambda $. Proposition 14.34.7 . If $\lambda _0\in \Lambda _ h(f)$, then $[\lambda _0,+\infty )\subset \Lambda _ h(f)$. Consequently, $\Lambda _ h(f)$ is empty, or equals $(a,+\infty )$ for some $a\geq 0$, or equals $[a,+\infty )$ for some $a>0$. If $b_ h(f)>0$, then $\Lambda _ h(f)=(0,+\infty )$. Proof. Let $u$ be a solution at $\lambda _0$, and put $s=u-\max (0,\sup _ Xu)$. Then $s\leq \min (u,0)$, so for $\lambda \geq \lambda _0$, \begin{align*}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s) & =\mathrm e^{\lambda _0u}f\, \mathrm dV\\ & \geq \mathrm e^{\lambda _0s}f\, \mathrm dV \geq \mathrm e^{\lambda s}f\, \mathrm dV. \end{align*} Thus $s$ is an exponential subsolution at every $\lambda \geq \lambda _0$, and theorem 14.34.1 gives a solution. Hence $\Lambda _ h(f)$ contains $[\lambda _0,+\infty )$ together with each of its points $\lambda _0$. A nonempty subset of $(0,+\infty )$ with this property is determined by its infimum $a$ and by whether $a$ belongs to it, which gives the stated forms. If $b_ h(f)>0$, corollary 14.34.2 gives $\Lambda _ h(f)=(0,+\infty )$. $\square$ Proposition 14.34.8 . Suppose $b_ h(f)=0$. Let $\lambda _ j>0$ decrease to zero, and let $u_ j$ be any solution of ( 14.123 ) at exponent $\lambda _ j$. Put \[  M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j,\qquad v_ j=u_ j-M_ j,\qquad c_ j=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jM_ j}.  \] Then \begin{gather*}  c_ j\longrightarrow 0,\qquad \lambda _ jM_ j\longrightarrow -\infty ,\\  \| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_ j)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_ j)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0. \end{gather*} Moreover, $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}\to 0$ uniformly on $X$, where the exponential is zero on the pole set, and $u_ j\to -\infty $ uniformly, that is, $\sup _ Xu_ j\to -\infty $. Proof. Set $g_ j=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jv_ j}f$. By lemma 1.23.3 , applied to the finite non-pluripolar measure $f\, \mathrm dV$, $g_ j\to f$ in $L^1$; each $g_ j$ is nonzero, since $v_ j$ is finite almost everywhere. Since the Monge–Ampère measure is unchanged by adding constants, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_ j)=c_ jg_ j\, \mathrm dV, \qquad \text{hence}\qquad 0<c_ j\leq b_ h(g_ j)  \] by theorem 14.27.2 . The upper semicontinuity of the threshold, theorem 14.31.1 , gives $\limsup _ jc_ j\leq b_ h(f)=0$. Since $0\leq g_ j\leq f$, the total masses are at most $c_ j\| f\| _{L^1}$ and tend to zero. Moreover $\lambda _ jM_ j=\log c_ j\to -\infty $, and $0\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda _ jM_ j}=c_ j$. Finally, once $\lambda _ j<1$ and $\log c_ j<0$, we have $M_ j=\lambda _ j^{-1}\log c_ j\leq \log c_ j$, so $M_ j\to -\infty $. $\square$ For the density of theorem 14.34.6 , solutions exist for every positive exponent, so the collapse applies as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ to every choice of solutions, in particular to the greatest ones. By contrast, the subsolutions of theorem 14.34.5 keep the mass $CV_0$ for every exponent, while the masses of the solutions above them tend to zero: on a nonclosed background, the order of two potentials does not give an order of their total Monge–Ampère masses. Whether the normalized potentials converge in capacity, and which equation a normalized cluster limit satisfies at exponent zero, are not decided by this argument. Positive endpoints of $\Lambda _ h(f)$ are governed instead by the compactness criterion below.

Put \[  M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j,\qquad v_ j=u_ j-M_ j,\qquad c_ j=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jM_ j}.  \] Then \begin{gather*}  c_ j\longrightarrow 0,\qquad \lambda _ jM_ j\longrightarrow -\infty ,\\  \| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_ j)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_ j)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0. \end{gather*} Moreover, $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}\to 0$ uniformly on $X$, where the exponential is zero on the pole set, and $u_ j\to -\infty $ uniformly, that is, $\sup _ Xu_ j\to -\infty $. title: 14.34.4 Positive endpoints and one-sided limits
text:
14.34.4 Positive endpoints and one-sided limits For $\lambda \in \Lambda _ h(f)$, write $U_\lambda $ for the greatest solution given by theorem 14.34.1 . When the exponents stay above a fixed $	au >0$, the solution of a bounded truncated equation at exponent $	au $ is a common upper barrier for all subsolutions. Together with the maximality of greatest solutions, this barrier gives an order estimate between $U_{\lambda _1}$ and $U_{\lambda _2}$, which controls the positive endpoint of $\Lambda _ h(f)$ and the limits of $U_\lambda $ from the right. Lemma 14.34.9 . For every $	au >0$, there is a nonnegative $t_	au \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)\cap C(X)$ such that every exponential subsolution at an exponent $\lambda \geq 	au $ lies below $t_	au $. Put $K_	au =\sup _ Xt_	au $. If $	au \leq \lambda _1\leq \lambda _2$ belong to $\Lambda _ h(f)$, then \[  U_{\lambda _2}\geq U_{\lambda _1} -K_	au  rac{\lambda _2-\lambda _1}{\lambda _2}.  \] Consequently, $\lambda \mapsto U_\lambda +K_	au \log (\lambda /	au )$ is nondecreasing on $\Lambda _ h(f)\cap [	au ,+\infty )$. Proof. Set $q=\min (f,1)$, a nonzero bounded density. By theorem 10.1.2 , there is a continuous $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)=\mathrm e^{	au w}q\, \mathrm dV$. Put $t_	au =w+\max (0,-\inf _ Xw)$. Then $t_	au \geq 0$ and $t_	au \geq w$, so for $\lambda \geq 	au $, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(t_	au )=\mathrm e^{	au w}q\, \mathrm dV \leq \mathrm e^{\lambda t_	au }f\, \mathrm dV.  \] Let $u$ be an exponential subsolution at an exponent $\lambda \geq 	au $, and let $\epsilon >0$. On $\{ t_	au <u-\epsilon \} $, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(t_	au ) \leq \mathrm e^{\lambda (u-\epsilon )}f\, \mathrm dV \leq \mathrm e^{-\lambda \epsilon } \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u-\epsilon ).  \] The bounded function $t_	au $ satisfies $P_{h/2}(t_	au )
ot\equiv -\infty $, and $u-\epsilon \preceq t_	au $. Thus theorem 14.1.2 gives $t_	au \geq u-\epsilon $, and letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $t_	au \geq u$. For the order estimate, put $\delta =K_	au (\lambda _2-\lambda _1)/\lambda _2$. By the first part, $U_{\lambda _1}\leq t_	au \leq K_	au $, so $(\lambda _2-\lambda _1)U_{\lambda _1}\leq \lambda _2\delta $, that is, $\lambda _1U_{\lambda _1}\geq \lambda _2(U_{\lambda _1}-\delta )$. Since the Monge–Ampère measure is unchanged by adding constants,  egin{align*}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(U_{\lambda _1}-\delta ) & =\mathrm e^{\lambda _1U_{\lambda _1}}f\, \mathrm dV\ & \geq \mathrm e^{\lambda _2(U_{\lambda _1}-\delta )}f\, \mathrm dV. \end{align*} Thus $U_{\lambda _1}-\delta $ is an exponential subsolution at $\lambda _2$, and the maximality of $U_{\lambda _2}$ gives $U_{\lambda _2}\geq U_{\lambda _1}-\delta $. Finally, $1-x^{-1}\leq \log x$ for $x\geq 1$; with $x=\lambda _2/\lambda _1$ this gives $\delta \leq K_	au \log (\lambda _2/\lambda _1)$, which proves the monotonicity. $\square$ Proposition 14.34.10 . Suppose $\Lambda _ h(f)
e \varnothing $ and $a=\inf \Lambda _ h(f)>0$. Then $a\in \Lambda _ h(f)$ if and only if there are exponents $\lambda _ j>a$ decreasing to $a$ and solutions $u_ j$ at exponent $\lambda _ j$ with $\inf _ j\sup _ Xu_ j> -\infty $. If $a
otin \Lambda _ h(f)$, then every sequence of solutions $u_ j$ at exponents $\lambda _ j>a$ decreasing to $a$ satisfies  egin{gather*}  \sup _ Xu_ j\longrightarrow -\infty ,\qquad \mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}\longrightarrow 0\  	ext{uniformly on }X,\  \| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_ j)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0, \end{gather*} where the exponential is zero on the pole sets. Proof. Suppose first that $a\in \Lambda _ h(f)$, let $u_ a$ be a solution at $a$, and put $s=u_ a-\max (0,\sup _ Xu_ a)$. As in the proof of proposition 14.34.7 , $s$ is an exponential subsolution at every $\lambda \geq a$, so $U_\lambda \geq s$. Hence the greatest solutions at any exponents $\lambda _ j\downarrow a$ have suprema at least $\sup _ Xs>-\infty $. Conversely, let $\lambda _ j$ and $u_ j$ be as in the statement. The lemma with $	au =a$ gives the common upper bound $u_ j\leq K_ a$. Write $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$. After extraction, $M_ j	o M\in \mathbb R$ and, by theorem 1.4.2 , $u_ j-M_ j	o v$ in $L^1$ for some $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. Then $u_ j	o u=v+M$ in $L^1$ and, after a further extraction, almost everywhere. Since $a\leq \lambda _ j\leq \lambda _1$, $u_ j\leq K_ a$ and $K_ a\geq 0$, the densities $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}f$ are bounded by $\mathrm e^{\lambda _1K_ a}f$, and dominated convergence gives \[  \mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}f\longrightarrow \mathrm e^{au}f \quad 	ext{in }L^1(\mathrm dV).  \] Lemma 14.27.1 now gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq \mathrm e^{au}f\, \mathrm dV$. Thus $u$ is an exponential subsolution at $a$, and theorem 14.34.1 gives a solution at $a$. Finally, suppose $a
otin \Lambda _ h(f)$, and let $u_ j$ be solutions at exponents $\lambda _ j\downarrow a$. If $\sup _ Xu_ j$ did not tend to $-\infty $, a subsequence would satisfy the condition just shown to imply $a\in \Lambda _ h(f)$. Hence $M_ j	o -\infty $. Once $M_ j<0$, since $\lambda _ j\geq a>0$, \[  0\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda _ jM_ j}\leq \mathrm e^{aM_ j} \longrightarrow 0,  \] and the total mass $\int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}f\, \mathrm dV$ is at most $\mathrm e^{aM_ j}\| f\| _{L^1}$. $\square$ Proposition 14.34.11 . For every $a\in \Lambda _ h(f)$, the greatest solutions satisfy \[  U_\lambda \longrightarrow U_ a \quad 	ext{in }L^1	ext{ and in capacity}\quad (\lambda \downarrow a),  \] and their Monge–Ampère measures converge in total variation to $\mathrm e^{aU_ a}f\, \mathrm dV$. Proof. Let $K=K_ a$ be the constant of the lemma with $	au =a$, and let $\lambda _ j>a$ decrease to $a$. By the lemma, the functions \[  V_ j=U_{\lambda _ j}+K\log (\lambda _ j/a)  \] decrease and satisfy $V_ j\geq U_ a$. Their limit $V$ therefore belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and satisfies $V\geq U_ a$. Dominated convergence between the integrable bounds $U_ a$ and $V_1$ gives $V_ j	o V$ in $L^1$, and lemma 1.8.12 gives convergence in capacity. Since the added constants tend to zero, $U_{\lambda _ j}	o V$ in both senses. The nonpositive functions $U_{\lambda _ j}-K$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(U_{\lambda _ j}-K)=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ j(U_{\lambda _ j}-K)}\, \mathrm e^{\lambda _ jK}f\, \mathrm dV,  \] and $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jK}f	o \mathrm e^{aK}f$ in $L^1$. Theorem 14.33.1 therefore gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(V)=\mathrm e^{aV}f\, \mathrm dV$, together with total-variation convergence of the measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(U_{\lambda _ j})$. Hence $V$ is a solution at $a$, so $V\leq U_ a$ by maximality, while $V\geq U_ a$ by construction. Thus $V=U_ a$. Since every sequence of exponents converging to $a$ from above has a decreasing subsequence, this proves the assertions. $\square$ The corrected order also controls approach from the left. The limit solves the equation at the limiting exponent; maximality gives an inequality with the greatest solution there, but does not force equality. Proposition 14.34.12 . Suppose $\Lambda _ h(f)
e \varnothing $, and put $a_0=\inf \Lambda _ h(f)$. For every $a>a_0$, there is $L_ a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ such that \[  U_\lambda \longrightarrow L_ a \quad 	ext{in }L^1	ext{ and in capacity}\quad (\lambda \uparrow a).  \] It satisfies \[  L_ a\leq U_ a,\qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(L_ a)=\mathrm e^{aL_ a}f\, \mathrm dV.  \] The equation measures converge in total variation to this finite measure. The left limit is independent of the auxiliary exponent and of the cofinal sequence used to construct it. Proof. Choose $	au \in \Lambda _ h(f)$ with $0<	au <a$; the upper-interval property gives such a choice. Put $K=K_	au $ from lemma 14.34.9 and \[  V_\lambda =U_\lambda +K\log (\lambda /	au ) \qquad (\lambda \in \Lambda _ h(f),\  \lambda \geq 	au ).  \] This family is increasing. For a sequence $\lambda _ j\uparrow a$ with $	au \leq \lambda _ j<a$, its members lie between the integrable potentials $V_	au $ and $V_ a$. The upper-envelope construction in section 1.19 gives \[  V^-_ a=\left(\sup _{	au \leq \lambda <a}V_\lambda ight)^* =\left(\lim _ jV_{\lambda _ j}ight)^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h).  \] Indeed cofinality and the order give the same pointwise supremum for every such sequence. Since the added constants converge, set \[  L_ a=V^-_ a-K\log (a/	au ).  \] Then $U_{\lambda _ j}	o L_ a$ in both topologies and $L_ a\leq U_ a$; the latter inequality survives regularization because $V_ a$ is upper semicontinuous. The potentials $U_{\lambda _ j}-K$ and their limit $L_ a-K$ are nonpositive. Apply theorem 14.33.1 with exponents tending to $a>0$ and densities $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jK}f	o \mathrm e^{aK}f$ in $L^1$. It proves the exact equation and total-variation convergence. Every sequence approaching $a$ from the left has a cofinal increasing subsequence. If potential convergence in either topology, or total-variation convergence of the equation measures, failed, a sequence staying outside a fixed neighbourhood of the proposed limit would therefore have an increasing subsequence, contrary to the preceding argument. This proves the full left limit and measure convergence. Repeating the construction with another $	au $ gives the same $L^1$ limit; canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere. Thus the auxiliary choice does not change $L_ a$. $\square$ Proposition 14.34.13 . Suppose $\Lambda _ h(f)
e \varnothing $, put $a_0=\inf \Lambda _ h(f)$, and let $L_ a$ be the left limit of proposition 14.34.12 . The set \[  D=\{ a>a_0:L_ a
e U_ a\}   \] is at most countable. At every $a>a_0$ with $a
otin D$, the greatest solutions are continuous in $L^1$ and in capacity as $\lambda 	o a$, and their equation measures converge in total variation to $\mathrm e^{aU_ a}f\, \mathrm dV$. Proof. Fix $a_0<\alpha < eta $, choose an admitted $0<	au <\alpha $, and use the corrected family $V_\lambda $ from the preceding proof on $[\alpha , eta ]$. Its integrals \[  I(\lambda )=\int _ XV_\lambda \, \mathrm dV  \] form a finite bounded increasing real function. For $a\in (\alpha , eta ]$, the left-limit proposition gives \[  I(a)-I(a-)=\int _ X(U_ a-L_ a)\, \mathrm dV.  \] If $L_ a
e U_ a$, this quantity is positive: the integrable nonnegative difference cannot vanish almost everywhere without equality of the canonical potentials. For any finite ordered collection of such points, the sum of their jumps is at most $I( eta )-I(\alpha )$. Consequently there are only finitely many jumps at least $1/m$ for each positive integer $m$, and at most countably many positive jumps. A countable cover by intervals with rational endpoints inside $(a_0,+\infty )$ proves the assertion about $D$. If $a
otin D$, the left limit is $U_ a$, and proposition 14.34.11 supplies the same right limit in both topologies and for the equation measures. Splitting an arbitrary approaching sequence into its two sides proves the stated two-sided convergence. $\square$ Whether an actual jump occurs, or all left limits equal the greatest solution, remains undecided. An intrinsic criterion on $f$ and the existence or nonexistence of a positive excluded endpoint remain separate questions. These one-sided limits concern greatest solutions at positive exponents; they do not identify limits of arbitrary solutions with other singularities or supply a zero-exponent limit.

title: Lemma 14.34.9
text: Lemma 14.34.9 . For every $\tau >0$, there is a nonnegative $t_\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)\cap C(X)$ such that every exponential subsolution at an exponent $\lambda \geq \tau $ lies below $t_\tau $. Put $K_\tau =\sup _ Xt_\tau $. If $\tau \leq \lambda _1\leq \lambda _2$ belong to $\Lambda _ h(f)$, then \[  U_{\lambda _2}\geq U_{\lambda _1} -K_\tau \frac{\lambda _2-\lambda _1}{\lambda _2}.  \] Consequently, $\lambda \mapsto U_\lambda +K_\tau \log (\lambda /\tau )$ is nondecreasing on $\Lambda _ h(f)\cap [\tau ,+\infty )$. Proof. Set $q=\min (f,1)$, a nonzero bounded density. By theorem 10.1.2 , there is a continuous $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)=\mathrm e^{\tau w}q\, \mathrm dV$. Put $t_\tau =w+\max (0,-\inf _ Xw)$. Then $t_\tau \geq 0$ and $t_\tau \geq w$, so for $\lambda \geq \tau $, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(t_\tau )=\mathrm e^{\tau w}q\, \mathrm dV \leq \mathrm e^{\lambda t_\tau }f\, \mathrm dV.  \] Let $u$ be an exponential subsolution at an exponent $\lambda \geq \tau $, and let $\epsilon >0$. On $\{ t_\tau <u-\epsilon \} $, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(t_\tau ) \leq \mathrm e^{\lambda (u-\epsilon )}f\, \mathrm dV \leq \mathrm e^{-\lambda \epsilon } \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u-\epsilon ).  \] The bounded function $t_\tau $ satisfies $P_{h/2}(t_\tau )\not\equiv -\infty $, and $u-\epsilon \preceq t_\tau $. Thus theorem 14.1.2 gives $t_\tau \geq u-\epsilon $, and letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $t_\tau \geq u$. For the order estimate, put $\delta =K_\tau (\lambda _2-\lambda _1)/\lambda _2$. By the first part, $U_{\lambda _1}\leq t_\tau \leq K_\tau $, so $(\lambda _2-\lambda _1)U_{\lambda _1}\leq \lambda _2\delta $, that is, $\lambda _1U_{\lambda _1}\geq \lambda _2(U_{\lambda _1}-\delta )$. Since the Monge–Ampère measure is unchanged by adding constants, \begin{align*}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(U_{\lambda _1}-\delta ) & =\mathrm e^{\lambda _1U_{\lambda _1}}f\, \mathrm dV\\ & \geq \mathrm e^{\lambda _2(U_{\lambda _1}-\delta )}f\, \mathrm dV. \end{align*} Thus $U_{\lambda _1}-\delta $ is an exponential subsolution at $\lambda _2$, and the maximality of $U_{\lambda _2}$ gives $U_{\lambda _2}\geq U_{\lambda _1}-\delta $. Finally, $1-x^{-1}\leq \log x$ for $x\geq 1$; with $x=\lambda _2/\lambda _1$ this gives $\delta \leq K_\tau \log (\lambda _2/\lambda _1)$, which proves the monotonicity. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.34.10
text:
Proposition 14.34.10 . Suppose $\Lambda _ h(f)
e \varnothing $ and $a=\inf \Lambda _ h(f)>0$. Then $a\in \Lambda _ h(f)$ if and only if there are exponents $\lambda _ j>a$ decreasing to $a$ and solutions $u_ j$ at exponent $\lambda _ j$ with $\inf _ j\sup _ Xu_ j> -\infty $. If $a
otin \Lambda _ h(f)$, then every sequence of solutions $u_ j$ at exponents $\lambda _ j>a$ decreasing to $a$ satisfies  egin{gather*}  \sup _ Xu_ j\longrightarrow -\infty ,\qquad \mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}\longrightarrow 0\  	ext{uniformly on }X,\  \| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_ j)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0, \end{gather*} where the exponential is zero on the pole sets. Proof. Suppose first that $a\in \Lambda _ h(f)$, let $u_ a$ be a solution at $a$, and put $s=u_ a-\max (0,\sup _ Xu_ a)$. As in the proof of proposition 14.34.7 , $s$ is an exponential subsolution at every $\lambda \geq a$, so $U_\lambda \geq s$. Hence the greatest solutions at any exponents $\lambda _ j\downarrow a$ have suprema at least $\sup _ Xs>-\infty $. Conversely, let $\lambda _ j$ and $u_ j$ be as in the statement. The lemma with $	au =a$ gives the common upper bound $u_ j\leq K_ a$. Write $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$. After extraction, $M_ j	o M\in \mathbb R$ and, by theorem 1.4.2 , $u_ j-M_ j	o v$ in $L^1$ for some $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. Then $u_ j	o u=v+M$ in $L^1$ and, after a further extraction, almost everywhere. Since $a\leq \lambda _ j\leq \lambda _1$, $u_ j\leq K_ a$ and $K_ a\geq 0$, the densities $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}f$ are bounded by $\mathrm e^{\lambda _1K_ a}f$, and dominated convergence gives \[  \mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}f\longrightarrow \mathrm e^{au}f \quad 	ext{in }L^1(\mathrm dV).  \] Lemma 14.27.1 now gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq \mathrm e^{au}f\, \mathrm dV$. Thus $u$ is an exponential subsolution at $a$, and theorem 14.34.1 gives a solution at $a$. Finally, suppose $a
otin \Lambda _ h(f)$, and let $u_ j$ be solutions at exponents $\lambda _ j\downarrow a$. If $\sup _ Xu_ j$ did not tend to $-\infty $, a subsequence would satisfy the condition just shown to imply $a\in \Lambda _ h(f)$. Hence $M_ j	o -\infty $. Once $M_ j<0$, since $\lambda _ j\geq a>0$, \[  0\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda _ jM_ j}\leq \mathrm e^{aM_ j} \longrightarrow 0,  \] and the total mass $\int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}f\, \mathrm dV$ is at most $\mathrm e^{aM_ j}\| f\| _{L^1}$. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.34.11
text: Proposition 14.34.11 . For every $a\in \Lambda _ h(f)$, the greatest solutions satisfy \[  U_\lambda \longrightarrow U_ a \quad \text{in }L^1\text{ and in capacity}\quad (\lambda \downarrow a),  \] and their Monge–Ampère measures converge in total variation to $\mathrm e^{aU_ a}f\, \mathrm dV$. Proof. Let $K=K_ a$ be the constant of the lemma with $\tau =a$, and let $\lambda _ j>a$ decrease to $a$. By the lemma, the functions \[  V_ j=U_{\lambda _ j}+K\log (\lambda _ j/a)  \] decrease and satisfy $V_ j\geq U_ a$. Their limit $V$ therefore belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and satisfies $V\geq U_ a$. Dominated convergence between the integrable bounds $U_ a$ and $V_1$ gives $V_ j\to V$ in $L^1$, and lemma 1.8.12 gives convergence in capacity. Since the added constants tend to zero, $U_{\lambda _ j}\to V$ in both senses. The nonpositive functions $U_{\lambda _ j}-K$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(U_{\lambda _ j}-K)=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ j(U_{\lambda _ j}-K)}\, \mathrm e^{\lambda _ jK}f\, \mathrm dV,  \] and $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jK}f\to \mathrm e^{aK}f$ in $L^1$. Theorem 14.33.1 therefore gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(V)=\mathrm e^{aV}f\, \mathrm dV$, together with total-variation convergence of the measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(U_{\lambda _ j})$. Hence $V$ is a solution at $a$, so $V\leq U_ a$ by maximality, while $V\geq U_ a$ by construction. Thus $V=U_ a$. Since every sequence of exponents converging to $a$ from above has a decreasing subsequence, this proves the assertions. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.34.12
text: Proposition 14.34.12 . Suppose $\Lambda _ h(f)\ne \varnothing $, and put $a_0=\inf \Lambda _ h(f)$. For every $a>a_0$, there is $L_ a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ such that \[  U_\lambda \longrightarrow L_ a \quad \text{in }L^1\text{ and in capacity}\quad (\lambda \uparrow a).  \] It satisfies \[  L_ a\leq U_ a,\qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(L_ a)=\mathrm e^{aL_ a}f\, \mathrm dV.  \] The equation measures converge in total variation to this finite measure. The left limit is independent of the auxiliary exponent and of the cofinal sequence used to construct it. Proof. Choose $\tau \in \Lambda _ h(f)$ with $0<\tau <a$; the upper-interval property gives such a choice. Put $K=K_\tau $ from lemma 14.34.9 and \[  V_\lambda =U_\lambda +K\log (\lambda /\tau ) \qquad (\lambda \in \Lambda _ h(f),\  \lambda \geq \tau ).  \] This family is increasing. For a sequence $\lambda _ j\uparrow a$ with $\tau \leq \lambda _ j<a$, its members lie between the integrable potentials $V_\tau $ and $V_ a$. The upper-envelope construction in section 1.19 gives \[  V^-_ a=\left(\sup _{\tau \leq \lambda <a}V_\lambda \right)^* =\left(\lim _ jV_{\lambda _ j}\right)^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h).  \] Indeed cofinality and the order give the same pointwise supremum for every such sequence. Regularization changes it only on a pluripolar set. Dominated convergence between the integrable bounds gives $L^1$ convergence to $V^-_ a$, and lemma 1.8.12 gives convergence in capacity. Since the added constants converge, set \[  L_ a=V^-_ a-K\log (a/\tau ).  \] Then $U_{\lambda _ j}\to L_ a$ in both topologies and $L_ a\leq U_ a$; the latter inequality survives regularization because $V_ a$ is upper semicontinuous. The potentials $U_{\lambda _ j}-K$ and their limit $L_ a-K$ are nonpositive. Apply theorem 14.33.1 with exponents tending to $a>0$ and densities $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jK}f\to \mathrm e^{aK}f$ in $L^1$. It proves the exact equation and total-variation convergence. Every sequence approaching $a$ from the left has a cofinal increasing subsequence. If potential convergence in either topology, or total-variation convergence of the equation measures, failed, a sequence staying outside a fixed neighbourhood of the proposed limit would therefore have an increasing subsequence, contrary to the preceding argument. This proves the full left limit and measure convergence. Repeating the construction with another $\tau $ gives the same $L^1$ limit; canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere. Thus the auxiliary choice does not change $L_ a$. $\square$

title: 14.35 Radial selection for integrable densities
text: 14.35 Radial selection for integrable densities The scalar and measure limits in corollary 14.34.2 do not by themselves determine a limit potential. For the sublogarithmic densities of lemma 14.29.1 , the radial flux supplies the missing information. It also distinguishes convergence after subtracting the supremum from convergence after subtracting $\lambda ^{-1}\log b$, where $b$ is the critical scalar: the latter depends on a first moment of the limiting measure. Use the product $X=X_0\times Y$, $Y=\mathbb P^ k$, $H=h_0+\kappa $, and the probability volume $\mu =V_0^{-1}h_0^ m\wedge \kappa ^ k$ of section 14.29 , with $\dim X_0=m$, $v_-(h_0)=0$ and $k\geq 2$. Put $b=\binom NmV_0$, where $N=m+k$. For $0<\alpha <1$, let $U_{\lambda ,\alpha }$ be the greatest solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(U_{\lambda ,\alpha }) =\mathrm e^{\lambda U_{\lambda ,\alpha }}q_\alpha \mu , \qquad \lambda >0.  \] The threshold of this forcing measure is $b>0$, by theorem 14.29.3 , so the solutions exist by corollary 14.34.2 .

title: 14.35.1 Separation and the radial flux
text: 14.35.1 Separation and the radial flux Lemma 14.35.1 . There is a $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function $w_{\lambda ,\alpha }$ on $Y$ such that \[  U_{\lambda ,\alpha }=\lambda ^{-1}\log b+w_{\lambda ,\alpha },\qquad w_{\lambda ,\alpha }\geq u_\alpha , \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (w_{\lambda ,\alpha }) =\mathrm e^{\lambda w_{\lambda ,\alpha }}q_\alpha \kappa ^ k.  \] The last measure has mass one. On the affine chart centered at $o$, set $s=\log |z|^2$, $\rho (s)=\log (1+\mathrm e^ s)$ and $m(s)=\rho '(s)$. The function $w=w_{\lambda ,\alpha }$ is radial and satisfies 14.125 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-selection-flux} \begin{aligned}  Q_{\lambda ,\alpha }(s) & =\int _{-\infty }^ s\mathrm e^{\lambda w(r)}q_\alpha (r)\,  \mathrm d(m(r)^ k),\\  w'(s)& =Q_{\lambda ,\alpha }(s)^{1/k}-m(s), \qquad Q_{\lambda ,\alpha }(-\infty )=0, \quad Q_{\lambda ,\alpha }(+\infty )=1. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Proof. Choose a smooth nondecreasing concave function $\chi $ on $[0,+\infty )$, equal to the identity on $[0,1]$ and constant on $[2,+\infty )$, and put $q_ j=j\chi (q_\alpha /j)$. Concavity gives $q_ j\uparrow q_\alpha $ and \[  \min (q_\alpha ,j)\leq q_ j\leq \min (q_\alpha ,2j).  \] The functions $q_ j$ are smooth and positive on $Y$: near $o$ they are constant, and elsewhere the density is smooth. Let $w_ j$ be the continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\kappa (w_ j)=\mathrm e^{\lambda w_ j}q_ j\kappa ^ k$ from theorem 10.1.2 . It is the greatest subsolution by theorem 14.34.1 and bounded uniqueness. Since $u_\alpha \leq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (u_\alpha )=q_\alpha \kappa ^ k$, it is a subsolution for every $q_ j$, whence $u_\alpha \leq w_ j$. Density comparison gives $w_ j\downarrow w$. The pullback $W_ j=\lambda ^{-1}\log b+w_ j$ is a bounded solution on $X$, by the product expansion in theorem 14.29.3 . For the smooth density $q_ j\mu $ it is therefore also the greatest subsolution. Every subsolution for $q_\alpha \mu $ is a subsolution for $q_ j\mu $, so $U_{\lambda ,\alpha }\leq W_ j$. Monotone convergence in capacity and theorem 14.33.1 on $Y$ identify the equation for $w\geq u_\alpha $. Moreover, Stokes gives $\int _ Y\mathrm e^{\lambda w_ j}q_ j\kappa ^ k=1$. The integrands are dominated by $\mathrm e^{\lambda \sup _ Yw_1}q_\alpha $, so dominated convergence gives the same identity for $w$. Its pullback is a product solution, hence lies below the greatest solution on $X$. Together with $U_{\lambda ,\alpha }\leq \lim _ jW_ j$, this proves separation and all measure assertions. Uniqueness makes each $w_ j$ invariant under the unitary action on the affine coordinates $z\in \mathbb C^ k$, and the limit has the same invariance. A radial $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function has a convex nondecreasing profile $\rho +w$. Symmetric convolution of this convex profile on compact $s$ intervals, decreasing as the scale decreases, and bounded-product continuity give its radial measure $\mathrm d((\rho +w)'^ k)$, as in lemma 14.29.1 . The bound $w\geq u_\alpha $, whose growth is $o(|s|)$ at $-\infty $, forces the initial derivative to vanish. The positive density makes the flux continuous and positive at finite $s$, yielding ( 14.125 ). Its final value is the mass one already proved. The profile is consequently smooth on finite $s$ intervals. $\square$

title: 14.35.2 The normalized limit
text: 14.35.2 The normalized limit Set \[  a_{\lambda ,\alpha }=\sup _ Yw_{\lambda ,\alpha },\qquad v_{\lambda ,\alpha }=w_{\lambda ,\alpha }-a_{\lambda ,\alpha },\qquad c_{\lambda ,\alpha }=\mathrm e^{\lambda \sup _ XU_{\lambda ,\alpha }} =b\mathrm e^{\lambda a_{\lambda ,\alpha }}.  \] In particular $a_{\lambda ,\alpha }\geq 0$. Theorem 14.35.2 . Let $\alpha _ j\to \alpha \in (0,1)$ and $\lambda _ j\to 0$ with $\lambda _ j>0$, at arbitrary relative rates. Then \[  v_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\longrightarrow u_\alpha \quad \text{in }L^1(Y),\text{ in capacity, and locally uniformly on }Y\setminus \{ o\} .  \] Their pullbacks converge in $L^1(X)$, in capacity on $X$, and locally uniformly off $X_0\times \{ o\} $. Furthermore $q_{\alpha _ j}\to q_\alpha $ in $L^1(\kappa ^ k)$, $c_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\to b$, and the equation measures converge in total variation to $bq_\alpha \mu $. The limiting pullback has finite mass $b$ and belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,0)$. Proof. Choose $[\alpha _-,\alpha _+]\Subset (0,1)$ containing all late parameters. The density formula in lemma 14.29.1 gives, uniformly for $\delta $ in this interval and $t=-s$ large, \[  q_\delta (s)\leq C\mathrm e^{kt}(1+t)^{-1-k(1-\alpha _+)}.  \] Away from $o$ the densities are jointly smooth, including on the hyperplane at infinity. Thus one integrable density $g$ dominates all $q_\delta $, and dominated convergence gives $q_{\alpha _ j}\to q_\alpha $ in $L^1$. For every normalized $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic $v$, theorem 1.4.2 gives $\int _ Y(-v)\kappa ^ k\leq C_ k$. Absolute continuity of the integral of $g$ therefore implies \[  \sup _{\sup _ Yv=0}\int _{\{ v<-T\} }g\kappa ^ k\longrightarrow 0 \quad (T\to \infty ).  \] Taking $T=\lambda ^{-1/2}$ shows that \[  \int _ Y(1-\mathrm e^{\lambda v})q_\delta \kappa ^ k \leq \lambda T+\int _{\{ v<-T\} }g\kappa ^ k\longrightarrow 0  \] uniformly in $\delta $ and $v$. Write $v_ j=v_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}$ and $a_ j=a_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}$. The exact mass identity of the lemma is 14.128 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-selection-mass} 1=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ja_ j} \int _ Y\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jv_ j}q_{\alpha _ j}\kappa ^ k. \end{equation} It gives $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ja_ j}\to 1$, hence $\lambda _ ja_ j\to 0$. The actual densities $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ja_ j}\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jv_ j}q_{\alpha _ j}$ converge in $L^1$ to $q_\alpha $ and are bounded by $2g$ for all late $j$. Their cumulative radial fluxes $Q_ j$ consequently converge uniformly to the flux $Q_\alpha $ of $u_\alpha $. By ( 14.125 ), $v_ j'\to u_\alpha '$ uniformly on compact $s$ intervals. The normalized $L^1$ bound controls one value of each profile on a fixed annulus; thus every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact $s$ intervals to $u_\alpha +d$ for some finite constant $d$. Near infinity the common bound for the densities is smooth and bounded. Hence $1-Q_ j(s)\leq C\mathrm e^{-s}$ and $|v_ j'(s)|\leq C\mathrm e^{-s}$ for large $s$. Integrating gives uniform convergence up to the hyperplane at infinity. At the other end, monotonicity of $\rho +v_ j$ gives, for $s<s_0$, \[  v_ j(s)\leq v_ j(s_0)+\rho (s_0).  \] Choose $s_0$ so negative that the right side is negative for all late members of the subsequence. The supremum zero is then attained outside this inner ball. Uniform convergence on its compact complement gives $\sup _ Y(u_\alpha +d)=0$, so $d=0$. Normalized compactness identifies every $L^1$ cluster limit with $u_\alpha $; this proves convergence of the entire family and its local uniform convergence off $o$. For capacity convergence, fix $T>0$. The sublevel $\{ u_\alpha <-T\} $ is a neighborhood of $o$, and its complement is a compact set on which convergence is uniform. Its capacity is at most $C/T$ by ( 1.26 ). Let $j\to \infty $ and then $T\to \infty $. The same argument on $X$ uses the normalized pullback of $u_\alpha $ and proves convergence in Hermitian capacity there; comparison sets omit pole sets. Pullback also preserves the $L^1$ and local uniform limits. The product expansion proves total-variation convergence of the measures, and theorem 14.29.3 supplies the exact limiting mass and envelope class. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.35.2

Thus one integrable density $g$ dominates all $q_\delta $, and dominated convergence gives $q_{\alpha _ j}\to q_\alpha $ in $L^1$. For every normalized $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic $v$, theorem 1.4.2 gives $\int _ Y(-v)\kappa ^ k\leq C_ k$. Absolute continuity of the integral of $g$ therefore implies \[  \sup _{\sup _ Yv=0}\int _{\{ v<-T\} }g\kappa ^ k\longrightarrow 0 \quad (T\to \infty ).  \] Taking $T=\lambda ^{-1/2}$ shows that \[  \int _ Y(1-\mathrm e^{\lambda v})q_\delta \kappa ^ k \leq \lambda T+\int _{\{ v<-T\} }g\kappa ^ k\longrightarrow 0  \] uniformly in $\delta $ and $v$. Write $v_ j=v_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}$ and $a_ j=a_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}$. The exact mass identity of the lemma is 14.128 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-selection-mass} 1=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ja_ j} \int _ Y\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jv_ j}q_{\alpha _ j}\kappa ^ k. \end{equation} It gives $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ja_ j}\to 1$, hence $\lambda _ ja_ j\to 0$. The actual densities $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ja_ j}\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jv_ j}q_{\alpha _ j}$ converge in $L^1$ to $q_\alpha $ and are bounded by $2g$ for all late $j$. Their cumulative radial fluxes $Q_ j$ consequently converge uniformly to the flux $Q_\alpha $ of $u_\alpha $. By ( 14.125 ), $v_ j'\to u_\alpha '$ uniformly on compact $s$ intervals. The normalized $L^1$ bound controls one value of each profile on a fixed annulus; thus every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact $s$ intervals to $u_\alpha +d$ for some finite constant $d$. Near infinity the common bound for the densities is smooth and bounded. Hence $1-Q_ j(s)\leq C\mathrm e^{-s}$ and $|v_ j'(s)|\leq C\mathrm e^{-s}$ for large $s$. Integrating gives uniform convergence up to the hyperplane at infinity. At the other end, monotonicity of $\rho +v_ j$ gives, for $s<s_0$, \[  v_ j(s)\leq v_ j(s_0)+\rho (s_0).  \] Choose $s_0$ so negative that the right side is negative for all late members of the subsequence. The supremum zero is then attained outside this inner ball. Uniform convergence on its compact complement gives $\sup _ Y(u_\alpha +d)=0$, so $d=0$. Normalized compactness identifies every $L^1$ cluster limit with $u_\alpha $; this proves convergence of the entire family and its local uniform convergence off $o$. For capacity convergence, fix $T>0$. The sublevel $\{ u_\alpha <-T\} $ is a neighborhood of $o$, and its complement is a compact set on which convergence is uniform. Its capacity is at most $C/T$ by ( 1.26 ). Let $j\to \infty $ and then $T\to \infty $. The same argument on $X$ uses the normalized pullback of $u_\alpha $ and proves convergence in Hermitian capacity there; comparison sets omit pole sets. Pullback also preserves the $L^1$ and local uniform limits. The product expansion proves total-variation convergence of the measures, and theorem 14.29.3 supplies the exact limiting mass and envelope class. $\square$

text: 14.35.3 Scalar centering and its moment boundary Proposition 14.35.3 . The first moment \[  M_\alpha =\int _ Yu_\alpha q_\alpha \kappa ^ k  \] is finite exactly when $\alpha <k/(k+1)$. In this range, 14.129 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-centering-constant} -M_\alpha =\alpha \int _1^\infty x^{\alpha -1} \left[\alpha x^{\alpha -1}+(1-\alpha x^{\alpha -1})\mathrm e^{1-x}\right]^ k\, \mathrm dx. \end{equation} For the joint limits of theorem 14.35.2 , if $\alpha <k/(k+1)$, then \[  a_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\to -M_\alpha ,\qquad U_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}-\lambda _ j^{-1}\log b \to u_\alpha -M_\alpha  \] in $L^1$, in capacity, and locally uniformly away from the pole fiber. If $\alpha \geq k/(k+1)$, then $a_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\to +\infty $ and the latter translated potentials tend to $+\infty $ locally uniformly off the pole fiber, although $\lambda _ ja_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\to 0$. In both cases the exact scalar error is \[  \lambda _ j^{-1}\log (c_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}/b) =a_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}.  \] Proof. As $t=-s\to \infty $, the radial profile of lemma 14.29.1 satisfies \[  u_\alpha \sim -t^\alpha ,\qquad Q_\alpha '(s)\sim k(1-\alpha )\alpha ^ k t^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}.  \] Thus the first moment is finite precisely when $(k+1)\alpha <k$. In that case, write $x=1-\psi $. Its cumulative flux is \[  Q_\alpha =\left[\alpha x^{\alpha -1} +(1-\alpha x^{\alpha -1})\mathrm e^{1-x}\right]^ k.  \] Integration by parts gives ( 14.129 ); the pole boundary term vanishes since $(k+1)\alpha -k<0$. Suppose $\alpha <k/(k+1)$ and choose the parameter interval in the preceding proof with $\alpha _+<k/(k+1)$. Its dominating density $g$ satisfies $(-u_{\alpha _+})g\in L^1$. Write $w_ j=w_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}=v_ j+a_ j$. Since $w_ j\geq u_{\alpha _ j}\geq u_{\alpha _+}$, the mass identity and $\mathrm e^ r\geq 1+r$ give $\int _ Yw_ jq_{\alpha _ j}\kappa ^ k\leq 0$. On a fixed annulus $A$ away from $o$, the normalized smooth-volume $L^1$ bound gives \[  \int _ Aw_ jq_{\alpha _ j}\kappa ^ k \geq a_ j\int _ Aq_{\alpha _ j}\kappa ^ k-C.  \] On the complement, use $w_ j\geq u_{\alpha _+}$ and the integrable lower bound. The annulus has uniformly positive measure, so $0\leq a_ j\leq C_*$. Along any subsequence with $a_ j\to a$, local uniform convergence gives $w_ j\to u_\alpha +a$ off $o$. In the exact identity \[  \int _ Y\frac{\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jw_ j}-1}{\lambda _ j} q_{\alpha _ j}\kappa ^ k=0,  \] the negative part is dominated by $(-u_{\alpha _+})g$ and the positive part by $C_*\mathrm e^{C_*}g$. Dominated convergence gives $M_\alpha +a=0$. Every subsequence therefore has the asserted scalar limit. Adding these convergent constants to the normalized potentials gives all three claimed topologies. If $\alpha \geq k/(k+1)$, use instead \[  \int _ Y\frac{1-\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jv_ j}}{\lambda _ j} q_{\alpha _ j}\kappa ^ k =\frac{1-\mathrm e^{-\lambda _ ja_ j}}{\lambda _ j}\leq a_ j.  \] The integrands are nonnegative and tend off $o$ to $(-u_\alpha )q_\alpha $. Fatou's lemma forces $a_ j\to +\infty $. The preceding theorem gives $\lambda _ ja_ j\to 0$; local uniform convergence of $v_ j$ gives the stated divergence of $w_ j$. This includes sequences approaching the moment boundary from below. $\square$ For the elliptic fivefold of corollary 14.29.4 , $b=240\pi $ and the moment boundary is $\alpha =2/3$. The choice $\alpha =1/2$ has a finite centering constant. For $2/3\leq \alpha <1$, the supremum-normalized family still converges to the exact threshold solution, while its scalar-centered version diverges off the pole fiber. Thus convergence of the normalization scalars alone does not give a bounded first-order scalar error.

title: 14.35.4 Order in the separated class
text: 14.35.4 Order in the separated class We use here the closed-class uniqueness theorem: on a compact connected Kähler manifold, two potentials whose non-pluripolar measures have full mass and are equal differ by a constant. This is an external input; its source is identified in 34.11 . Corollary 14.35.4 . Every separated threshold subsolution $r=r(y)$ with $r\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(r)\geq bq_\alpha \mu $ equals $u_\alpha +d$ for some constant $d$. In particular $u_\alpha $ is its unique supremum-zero member. If $\alpha <k/(k+1)$, then $u_\alpha -M_\alpha $ is the greatest such subsolution whose $q_\alpha $-mean on $Y$ is nonpositive. Proof. The product formula reduces the inequality to $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (r)\geq q_\alpha \kappa ^ k$. Closed Stokes gives each bounded truncation mass one, so the extended measure of $r$ has mass at most one. The inequality therefore gives equality and full mass. Closed-class uniqueness yields $r=u_\alpha +d$. In the finite-moment range its mean is $M_\alpha +d$, which is nonpositive exactly when $d\leq -M_\alpha $. $\square$ At and beyond the moment boundary every constant translate has mean $-\infty $, so that mean condition no longer chooses a greatest translate. The order assertion concerns separated potentials. Selection for arbitrary integrable densities and uniqueness of arbitrary critical potentials on the nonclosed product remain the questions of 33.1.1 and section 14.33 .

title: 15 Normalization and weak adjoint measures
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15 Normalization and weak adjoint measures Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$. Function spaces are real, and Lebesgue norms are taken with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$. Until section 15.8 , $\theta $ is a smooth semipositive big real $(1,1)$-form and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is a model reference in the sense of ( 13.26 ): it is a fixed point of the ordinary singularity envelope $P_\theta [\cdot ]$ of definition 1.19.4 , and its envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ in a smaller background is not identically $-\infty $ for some $0<\varepsilon <1$. We write $u\sim \varphi $ when $u$ has the ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $ (definition 1.12.1 ), and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta $ for the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 6.1.2 ; when its total mass is finite, it is the usual non-pluripolar measure, which we also denote by $\mathrm{MA}_\theta $. In the ordinary type of $\varphi $, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=c\, \mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$ determines the constant $c>0$ uniquely, even when it has several normalized solutions. As a function of the logarithmic density $F$, the logarithm of this constant is concave. Its supporting functionals are probability measures that describe the first-order response of the constant to a change of density; for smooth Hermitian equations they are the Gauduchon adjoint probabilities of the linearized operator. The convex dual of the functional controls the concentration of these measures through entropy, and this gives compactness when the density, the reference or the positive background varies. The same measures provide the integral normalizations that single out the limit of the exponential equations as the exponent tends to zero. The scalar functional does not, however, determine the singularities of the solutions: examples with moving divisors have identical functionals but different limiting potentials. On closed projective backgrounds, convex geometry gives quantitative criteria for varying references, including references with nonanalytic poles or degenerate residuals.

title: 15.1 The scalar functional
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.1 The scalar functional The domination principle makes the constant decrease as the density increases, and mixed Monge–Ampère products strengthen this monotonicity to concavity in the logarithmic density. Compactness of the solutions then gives continuity under uniformly bounded $L^1$ perturbations. For a bounded real measurable function $F$, part (2) of theorem 14.11.1 , applied to the bounded density $\mathrm{e}^ F$, gives $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $ and a unique constant $c_\varphi (F)>0$ such that 15.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-normalization} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) =c_\varphi (F)\mathrm{e}^ F\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} The normalization scalar is \[  B_\varphi (F)=\log c_\varphi (F).  \] Since the constant is unique, $B_\varphi $ is well defined; it depends on $\varphi $ only through its ordinary singularity type. Proposition 15.1.1 . Let $F,G\in L^\infty (\mathrm{d}V)$ be real. The functional $B_\varphi $ is decreasing, and for every constant $a\in \mathbb R$, \[  B_\varphi (F+a)=B_\varphi (F)-a.  \] Consequently 15.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-normalization-lipschitz} -\mathop{\rm ess\, sup}_ X(G-F) \leq B_\varphi (G)-B_\varphi (F) \leq -\mathop{\rm ess\, inf}_ X(G-F), \end{equation} and $|B_\varphi (G)-B_\varphi (F)|\leq \| G-F\| _\infty $. Proof. Suppose that $F\leq G$ almost everywhere and, to reach a contradiction, that $c_\varphi (F)<c_\varphi (G)$. Let $u,v\sim \varphi $ solve the two equations. Since $F\leq G$ and the extended measure is unchanged by adding constants, for every constant $a$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq \frac{c_\varphi (F)}{c_\varphi (G)} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v+a),  \] and the ratio is strictly less than one. As $u\sim \varphi $, the envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(u)$ dominates a translate of $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ and is therefore not identically $-\infty $; moreover $v+a\preceq u$. The singular strict domination principle, theorem 14.1.2 , gives $u\geq v+a$ for every $a$, which is impossible at any point where both potentials are finite. Thus $B_\varphi (F)\geq B_\varphi (G)$. Replacing $F$ by $F+a$ and the constant by $\mathrm{e}^{-a}c_\varphi (F)$ leaves the right-hand side of ( 15.1 ) unchanged, so uniqueness of the constant proves the translation rule. Finally, $G$ lies between the constant translates $F+\mathop{\rm ess\, inf}_ X(G-F)$ and $F+\mathop{\rm ess\, sup}_ X(G-F)$; monotonicity and the translation rule give ( 15.2 ). $\square$ The scalar does not depend on the smooth representative of the background: for a smooth real $h$, replacing $\theta $ by $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ and each potential $u$, including $\varphi $, by $u-h$ preserves the currents and the prescribed ordinary type, and hence leaves the equation and its constant unchanged. Concavity comes from mixed products. A convex combination of two solutions stays in the prescribed ordinary type, and lemma 6.4.1 bounds its measure below by the corresponding mixed density. Theorem 15.1.2 . The functional $B_\varphi $ is concave on the real space $L^\infty (\mathrm{d}V)$: for $F,G$ in that space, \[  B_\varphi (tF+(1-t)G) \geq tB_\varphi (F)+(1-t)B_\varphi (G),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] Proof. Let $u,v\sim \varphi $ solve the equations for $F$ and $G$, and set $H=tF+(1-t)G$ and $D=c_\varphi (F)^ t c_\varphi (G)^{1-t}$. Lemma 6.4.1 and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality give \[  \begin{split}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (tu+(1-t)v) & \geq \bigl (t(c_\varphi (F)\mathrm{e}^ F)^{1/n} +(1-t)(c_\varphi (G)\mathrm{e}^ G)^{1/n}\bigr )^ n\, \mathrm{d}V\\ & \geq D \mathrm{e}^ H\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{split}  \] The averaged potential $tu+(1-t)v$ has the ordinary type of $\varphi $. If $c_\varphi (H)<D$, its measure dominates the measure of a solution $w\sim \varphi $ for $H$ by the factor $D/c_\varphi (H)>1$. Applying the singular strict domination principle to $w$ and to every constant translate of the averaged potential, as in the proof of proposition 15.1.1 , leads to the same contradiction. Hence $c_\varphi (H)\geq D$, and taking logarithms proves concavity. $\square$ For smooth Hermitian data, this concavity agrees with the second-variation formula of theorem 9.7.1 . Uniformly bounded logarithmic densities give the solutions a common lower barrier, and compactness of the solutions identifies the limiting scalar even when the densities converge only in $L^1$. Theorem 15.1.3 . If $F_ j,F$ are uniformly bounded real measurable functions and $F_ j\to F$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, then \[  B_\varphi (F_ j)\longrightarrow B_\varphi (F).  \] Proof. Choose solutions $u_ j\sim \varphi $ normalized by $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$, and write $c_ j=c_\varphi (F_ j)$. If $|F_ j|\leq M$, monotonicity and the translation rule of proposition 15.1.1 give \[  \mathrm{e}^{-M}c_\varphi (0)\leq c_ j\leq \mathrm{e}^ M c_\varphi (0).  \] In particular, the Monge–Ampère measures of the $u_ j$ are dominated by a fixed multiple of $\mathrm{d}V$, and theorem 14.11.3 gives a constant $C$ such that \[  \varphi -C\leq u_ j\leq \varphi .  \] From any subsequence, extract a further subsequence with $c_ j\to c>0$ and $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1(X)$. By corollary 14.8.3 , the convergence also holds in capacity, $u\sim \varphi $, and the measures converge weakly. On the other hand, the exponential function is Lipschitz on the common range of the $F_ j$, so $c_ j\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}\to c\mathrm{e}^ F$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Therefore \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=c\mathrm{e}^ F\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] and uniqueness of the constant gives $c=c_\varphi (F)$. Since every subsequence has a further subsequence along which $c_ j\to c_\varphi (F)$, the whole sequence converges, and so do the logarithms. $\square$

title: Theorem 15.2.1

text:
Theorem 15.2.1 . For every $F\in C(X)$, the set $\mathcal A_\varphi (F)$ is nonempty, convex and weakly compact. Every one of its measures is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$. Proof. The function $C_\varphi =-B_\varphi $ is convex and Lipschitz. Fix $F\in C(X)$. For a direction $h\in C(X)$, the limit \[  p(h)=\lim _{t\downarrow 0}  rac{C_\varphi (F+th)-C_\varphi (F)}{t}  \] exists and is finite: convexity makes the difference quotients monotone in $t>0$, and their absolute values are at most $\| h\| _\infty $. Clearly $p$ is positively homogeneous. Given another direction $k\in C(X)$, apply convexity at the midpoint of $F+2th$ and $F+2tk$ and let $t\downarrow 0$; this gives $p(h+k)\leq p(h)+p(k)$. Thus $p$ is sublinear. By the Hahn–Banach theorem, the zero functional on $\{ 0\} $ extends to a linear functional $\ell \leq p$. Since $p(h)\leq \| h\| _\infty $, applying this bound to $h$ and $-h$ shows that $\ell $ is continuous. Monotonicity of the convex difference quotients gives \[  C_\varphi (F+h)\geq C_\varphi (F)+\ell (h),  \] which is ( 15.5 ) once $\ell $ is represented by a probability. Testing the translation rule with positive and negative constants gives $\ell (1)=1$. If $h\geq 0$, monotonicity of $B_\varphi $ gives $C_\varphi (F-th)\leq C_\varphi (F)$ for $t>0$, whereas the inequality just proved gives the lower bound $C_\varphi (F)-t\ell (h)$. Hence $\ell (h)\geq 0$. By the Riesz representation theorem, $\ell (h)=\int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}
u $ for a probability measure $
u $, and $
u \in \mathcal A_\varphi (F)$. Each inequality in ( 15.5 ) defines a weakly closed half-space in the compact space of probability measures, so their intersection is closed and convex, hence weakly compact. It remains to prove absolute continuity. Let $K$ be compact with $\mathrm{d}V(K)=0$, and choose continuous functions $0\leq \chi _ j\leq 1$, equal to one on $K$, whose supports have volumes tending to zero. For any $
u \in \mathcal A_\varphi (F)$, the supporting inequality with $G=F+\chi _ j$ gives \[  0\leq 
u (K)\leq \int _ X\chi _ j\, \mathrm{d}
u \leq B_\varphi (F)-B_\varphi (F+\chi _ j).  \] The right-hand side tends to zero by theorem 15.1.3 , so $
u (K)=0$. By inner regularity of finite Borel measures on $X$, the same holds for every Borel set of zero volume. The Radon–Nikodym theorem now gives $\mathrm{d}
u =h_
u \mathrm{d}V$ with $h_
u \geq 0$ and $\int _ Xh_
u \mathrm{d}V=1$. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.2.2
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
Proposition 15.2.2 . Let $F_ j,F\in C(X)$ with $F_ j	o F$ uniformly, and let $
u _ j\in \mathcal A_\varphi (F_ j)$. Then every weak cluster point of $(
u _ j)$ belongs to $\mathcal A_\varphi (F)$. In particular, if the latter set consists of a single measure, $
u _ j$ converges weakly to it. Proof. Take a weakly convergent subsequence and fix $G\in C(X)$. In the inequality \[  B_\varphi (G)\leq B_\varphi (F_ j)-\int _ X(G-F_ j)\, \mathrm{d}
u _ j,  \] the Lipschitz continuity of $B_\varphi $, the uniform convergence of $F_ j$ and the weak convergence of the probabilities allow passage to the limit. If that set is a singleton, every convergent subsequence has the same limit, and compactness of the space of probability measures proves the final assertion. $\square$

text:
15.2.3 Gauduchon adjoints For a smooth Hermitian equation, differentiating the scalar identifies the supporting probability with the adjoint probability of the linearized operator. Theorem 15.2.5 . Let $	heta =\omega $ be a Hermitian form, let $\varphi =0$, and let $F$ be a smooth real function. Let $u$ be the smooth solution of ( 15.1 ), unique up to an additive constant by corollary 11.4.6 , and let $\mu _ u$ be its Gauduchon adjoint probability from proposition 4.8.1 ; for $n=1$, this is $\mu _ u=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)/\int _ X\omega $. Then \[  \mathcal A_0(F)=\{ \mu _ u\} .  \] Proof. Suppose first that $n\geq 2$. By uniqueness of the constant, the normalization scalar of the smooth equation in theorem 9.7.1 is $B_0$, and that theorem gives, for every smooth real $G$, \[  \left. rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}ight|_{t=0}B_0(F+tG) =-\int _ XG\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u.  \] Let $
u \in \mathcal A_0(F)$. Testing the supporting inequality at $F+tG$ for both signs of $t$ and letting $t	o 0$ shows that $G$ has the same integral against $
u $ and $\mu _ u$. Since smooth functions are uniformly dense in $C(X)$, it follows that $
u =\mu _ u$, and the assertion follows from nonemptiness of $\mathcal A_0(F)$. In dimension one, Stokes' theorem gives $c_0(F)=\int _ X\omega /\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F \mathrm{d}V$; differentiating its logarithm in the same way yields the stated measure, since $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=c_0(F)\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$. $\square$ Consequently, in the Hermitian case the supporting probabilities at a continuous $F$ can be approached through smooth data. If smooth $F_ j$ converge uniformly to $F$, then by proposition 15.2.2 every weak cluster point of the Gauduchon adjoint probabilities of the solutions for $F_ j$ belongs to $\mathcal A_0(F)$, and is therefore absolutely continuous. If $\mathcal A_0(F)$ is a singleton, which holds in particular for every $F\in \mathscr U_0$ and under the continuous positive Hessian hypothesis of theorem 15.2.6 , these probabilities converge to its unique member, independently of the approximation. We do not know whether $\mathcal A_0(F)$ is a singleton for every continuous $F$, even in this Hermitian setting; the same question is open for the singular references considered above. For $n\geq 2$, the Hermitian zero-reference case admits a quantitative strengthening: corollary 26.8.3 bounds the densities of all supporting probabilities uniformly in $L^ q$, for $1<q<n/(n-1)$, when $\| F\| _\infty $ is bounded, and also for $q=n/(n-1)$ when $\omega $ has positive lower mass $v_-(\omega )>0$ in the sense of definition 6.5.1 . The proof uses the Gauduchon-current formulation of chapter 26 , and we do not claim such a bound for an arbitrary singular reference. A weak linearized operator requires more than a supporting probability. In the same Hermitian zero-reference setting, theorem 26.7.2 represents each supporting probability by a determinant-weighted positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed current. Identifying that current with a scalar multiple of a weak power $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-1}$ would require a well-defined product and its compatibility with approximation. A similar representation holds for a functional defined by subsolutions rather than by an equation in a prescribed singularity type. Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero with $f^{1/n}\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$, the space of densities with uniformly vanishing Gauduchon tails from 14.31.2 . Then proposition 26.9.4 describes the supporting probabilities of $F\mapsto \log b_\omega (\mathrm{e}^ Ff)$, where $b_\omega (\cdot )$ is the density threshold of theorem 14.27.2 .
