title: 15.2.4 Continuous positive complex Hessians
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
15.2.4 Continuous positive complex Hessians The smooth recovery theorem extends to a bounded solution whose complex Hessian is continuous and everywhere positive. In this case one can vary the potential in both directions, and the resulting densities force every supporting probability to annihilate the same elliptic operator. The Sobolev range theorem then gives uniqueness. Theorem 15.2.6 . Let $n\geq 2$, let $	heta =\omega $ be a Hermitian form, and let $\varphi =0$. Suppose $F\in C(X)$ and a bounded solution $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ of ( 15.1 ) has distributional complex Hessian represented by a continuous form \[  \sigma =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0  \] everywhere on $X$. Then $\mathcal A_0(F)$ consists of one probability $
u _ F$. It satisfies  egin{align*}  \int _ X L_\sigma h\, \mathrm d
u _ F& =0\quad (h\in C^\infty (X)),\  DB_0(F)[H]& =-\int _ XH\, \mathrm d
u _ F\quad (H\in C(X)). \end{align*} The derivative is taken in the Gâteaux sense. Proof. The continuous trace of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is the Euclidean Laplacian of $u$, up to the fixed normalization. Local constant-coefficient elliptic regularity gives $u\in W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$. Indeed, subtract the Newtonian potential of a cutoff of this trace. Its second high-frequency derivatives are order-zero multipliers, and the low-frequency kernels are locally bounded; the remaining distribution is harmonic. Sobolev embedding gives a $C^{1,\alpha }$ representative for every $\alpha <1$, which agrees with the quasi-psh representative. On a coordinate ball choose smooth $ho $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \omega $. The radial regularizations of the bounded psh function $u+ho $ decrease to it, and their complex Hessians converge uniformly on smaller balls. Continuity of bounded products and the finite smooth-background expansion identify $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ with $\sigma ^ n$. For smooth real $h$, the same argument applies to $u+th$, which is admissible for all sufficiently small signed $t$ by uniform positivity. Define \[  F_ t=F+\log  rac{(\sigma +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n}{\sigma ^ n}.  \] Its equation has the same normalization scalar as the equation for $u$, so $B_0(F_ t)=B_0(F)$. The supporting inequality gives $\int _ X(F_ t-F)\, \mathrm d
u \leq 0$ for each $
u \in \mathcal A_0(F)$. Since $F_ t-F=tL_\sigma h+O(t^2)$ uniformly, using both signs yields stationarity. Choose $p=4n+1$ and $q=p/(p-1)=1+1/(4n)$. By corollary 26.8.3 , every supporting probability has an $L^ q$ density, since $q<n/(n-1)$. Smooth density in $W^{2,p}$ extends its stationarity to every $W^{2,p}$ test. By lemma 4.9.1 , all these densities lie in a one-dimensional space. Their integrals equal one, so they coincide. Nonemptiness is theorem 15.2.1 , and the derivative formula follows from proposition 15.2.3 . $\square$

title: 15.2.5 Products with a Hermitian factor
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
15.2.5 Products with a Hermitian factor An explicit product construction exhibits the criterion for densities with an arbitrary continuous modulus. Let $(Y,\kappa )$ be a connected compact Hermitian $k$-fold, $k\geq 1$, with $\int _ Y\kappa ^ k=1$. Denote by $
u _\kappa $ the smooth stationary probability of $L_\kappa =\operatorname {tr}_\kappa \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, given by the Gauduchon multiplier when $k\geq 2$; for $k=1$ it is $\kappa $. Write $w$ for the Fubini–Study area of mass one on $\mathbb P^1$. All factor forms and functions below are pulled back to $X=\mathbb P^1	imes Y$. Proposition 15.2.7 . Let $a>0$, let $b$ be smooth and positive on $\mathbb P^1$, and let $A$ be continuous and positive there, with $\int _{\mathbb P^1}Aw=a$. For \[  \omega =aw+b\kappa ,\qquad \mathrm dV=w\wedge \kappa ^ k, \qquad F=\log ((k+1)Ab^ k),  \] one has \[  c_0(F)=1,\qquad \mathcal A_0(F)=\left\{  rac Aa\, w\otimes 
u _\kappa ight\} .  \] Proof. The Green solution of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(A-a)w$ on $\mathbb P^1$ has continuous complex Hessian and is bounded. Its pullback yields $\sigma =Aw+b\kappa >0$, and $\sigma ^{k+1}=(k+1)Ab^ kw\wedge \kappa ^ k$. Thus scalar uniqueness gives $c_0(F)=1$, and theorem 15.2.6 gives a unique support. For every smooth $h$ depending on all variables, the block decomposition \[  L_\sigma h=A^{-1}L_ wh+b^{-1}L_\kappa h  \] shows that $(A/a)w\otimes 
u _\kappa $ is stationary: the first term integrates to zero by Stokes on $\mathbb P^1$, and the second by stationarity on $Y$ and Fubini. This candidate has a bounded density with respect to $\mathrm dV$. The one-dimensional annihilator of lemma 4.9.1 and probability normalization therefore identify it with the supporting probability. $\square$ Example 15.2.8 . There is a non-Kähler threefold with a nonclosed Hermitian background and a positive continuous density whose logarithm is neither Dini continuous nor Hölder continuous of any positive order, but whose supporting probability is explicit and unique. Proof. Take the Hopf surface $Y=(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto 2zangle $ and its unit-volume metric $\kappa =c|z|^{-2}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$, where $c>0$ is chosen so that $\int _ Y\kappa ^2=1$. Put $s=\log |z|^2$, $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ and $ eta =\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s$, so that $\kappa =c(\alpha + eta )$. The differentiation in ( 8.1 ) applies in this dimension. Here $\alpha $ has rank one, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa =-c\alpha ^2=0$ and $
u _\kappa =\kappa ^2$. Polar coordinates identify $Y$ with $S^3	imes S^1$, hence $H^2(Y,\mathbb R)=0$. A closed positive form would be exact and have positive square integral, contradicting Stokes. Thus $Y$ is non-Kähler, and so is $\mathbb P^1	imes Y$, by restriction. Let $	au \in [-1,1]$ be the height on $\mathbb P^1$, set $b=2+	au $, and put \[  f(t)= egin{cases}  1/\log (e/|t|),& 0<|t|\leq 1,\  0,& t=0, \end{cases}  \] \[  A=a+\varepsilon \left(f(	au )-\int _{\mathbb P^1}f(	au )wight), \quad 0<\varepsilon <a.  \] Since $0\leq f\leq 1$, this is a positive continuous function of mean $a$. Along a normal segment to the equator, $|	au |$ is comparable to the distance $r$. The oscillation of $A$ is therefore bounded below by a positive multiple of $1/\log (e/r)$. Its Dini integral $\int _0^{r_0}\mathrm dr/(r\log (e/r))$ diverges, and this modulus is larger than every $r^\gamma $, $\gamma >0$, as $r\downarrow 0$. The logarithm of $A$ has the same lower bound, because $A$ is uniformly positive and bounded. The smooth term $2\log b$ contributes only $O(r)$, so $F=\log (3Ab^2)$ has neither regularity. The mixed component $\mathrm db\wedge \kappa $ shows that $\omega =aw+b\kappa $ is nonclosed. By proposition 15.2.7 , its supporting probability is $(A/a)w\wedge \kappa ^2$. $\square$ The theorem assumes a continuous positive complex Hessian for a bounded solution. It does not establish that hypothesis for every continuous $F$; the uniqueness question for arbitrary continuous data remains open.

title: Proposition 15.2.7
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 15.2.7 . Let $a>0$, let $b$ be smooth and positive on $\mathbb P^1$, and let $A$ be continuous and positive there, with $\int _{\mathbb P^1}Aw=a$. For \[  \omega =aw+b\kappa ,\qquad \mathrm dV=w\wedge \kappa ^ k, \qquad F=\log ((k+1)Ab^ k),  \] one has \[  c_0(F)=1,\qquad \mathcal A_0(F)=\left\{ \frac Aa\, w\otimes \nu _\kappa \right\} .  \] Proof. The Green solution of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(A-a)w$ on $\mathbb P^1$ has continuous complex Hessian and is bounded. Its pullback yields $\sigma =Aw+b\kappa >0$, and $\sigma ^{k+1}=(k+1)Ab^ kw\wedge \kappa ^ k$. Thus scalar uniqueness gives $c_0(F)=1$, and theorem 15.2.6 gives a unique support. For every smooth $h$ depending on all variables, the block decomposition \[  L_\sigma h=A^{-1}L_ wh+b^{-1}L_\kappa h  \] shows that $(A/a)w\otimes \nu _\kappa $ is stationary: the first term integrates to zero by Stokes on $\mathbb P^1$, and the second by stationarity on $Y$ and Fubini. This candidate has a bounded density with respect to $\mathrm dV$. The one-dimensional annihilator of lemma 4.9.1 and probability normalization therefore identify it with the supporting probability. $\square$

Proof. title: 15.2.6 Divisorial smoothing
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
15.2.6 Divisorial smoothing For a singular reference, the supporting probability can be unique while smoothings of the solution have different limiting adjoint probabilities. The reason is that the non-pluripolar product discards the mass on a divisor that the smoothings keep. On a product of two projective lines, explicit formulas exhibit both the lost mass and its dependence on the smoothing. In this subsection, $X=\mathbb P^1	imes \mathbb P^1$. Let $\omega _1$ and $\omega _2$ be the pullbacks of the Fubini–Study forms of the two factors, normalized to have integral one on their factors, and put \[  	heta =2\omega _1+2\omega _2,\qquad  eta =\omega _1+2\omega _2,\qquad \omega =\omega _1+\omega _2,\qquad \mathrm dV=\omega _1\wedge \omega _2.  \] Thus $\mathrm dV$ is a probability volume form, $	heta ^2=8\mathrm dV$ and $ eta ^2=4\mathrm dV$. Let $z$ be the affine coordinate on the first factor, and put \[  r= rac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2},\qquad \psi =\log r,\qquad D=\{ 0\} 	imes \mathbb P^1.  \] The function $r$ extends smoothly to the first factor, with value one at infinity, and $\psi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic with value $-\infty $ exactly on $D$. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =[D]-\omega _1$, so $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi = eta +[D]$. For a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form $\Omega $ on the surface $X$, the linearization $v\mapsto 2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Omega /\Omega ^2$ of the logarithmic Monge–Ampère operator has the adjoint probability $ho \Omega ^2$, where the Gauduchon multiplier $ho >0$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ho \Omega )=0$ and $\int _ Xho \Omega ^2=1$ (proposition 4.8.1 ). We call $Q=ho \Omega $ the adjoint cofactor of $\Omega $: it is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, and $\Omega \wedge Q$ is the adjoint probability. Lemma 15.2.9 . Write $x=\log |z|^2$ and $\chi (x)=\log (1+\mathrm e^ x)$. The envelope $\varphi =P_	heta [\psi ]$ is 15.8  egin{equation} \label{eq:divisorial-adjoint-model} \varphi =W(x)-2\chi (x),\qquad W(x)= egin{cases} x+2\log 2,& x\leq 0,\ 2\chi (x),& x\geq 0.\end{cases} \end{equation} It satisfies $\psi \leq \varphi \leq 0$, $0\leq \varphi -\psi \leq 2\log 2$, and the model condition ( 13.26 ) with $\varepsilon =3/4$. Proof. The function $W$ is convex: both one-sided derivatives at zero equal one, and the derivative of $2\chi $ increases from one to two on $[0,\infty )$. Since $\omega _1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi (x)$ on the affine chart, $W-2\chi $ is $2\omega _1$-plurisubharmonic there. Since $W$ has slope one for $x\leq 0$ and agrees with $2\chi $ for $x\geq 0$, the function $W-2\chi $ extends to a global $2\omega _1$-plurisubharmonic function, with a logarithmic pole along $D$ and equal to zero where $|z|\geq 1$. The asserted bounds follow from $\psi =x-\chi $: the difference $\varphi -\psi $ equals $2\log 2-\chi $ for $x\leq 0$ and $\chi -x$ for $x\geq 0$. For $C>0$ write $v_ C=P_	heta (\min \{ \psi +C,0\} )$. Rotations of the first factor and the transitive unitary action on the second preserve the whole competitor class, so the envelope is radial and independent of the second factor. The function $V_ C=2\chi +v_ C$ is then convex in $x$ and satisfies $V_ C\leq \chi +x+C$. This upper bound as $x	o -\infty $ forces the slope of $V_ C$ at $-\infty $ to be at least one, and by convexity all its slopes are at least one. For $x<0$, \[  V_ C(x)\leq V_ C(0)+x\leq 2\log 2+x=W(x).  \] For $x\geq 0$, the zero obstacle gives $V_ C\leq 2\chi =W$. Consequently $v_ C\leq \varphi $. If $C\geq 2\log 2$, the bounds already proved make $\varphi $ a competitor, so $v_ C=\varphi $. Letting $C	o \infty $ proves $P_	heta [\psi ]=\varphi $. Since $\varphi \sim \psi $ and the ordinary envelope depends only on the singularity type, also $P_	heta [\varphi ]=\varphi $. Finally \[  	frac 34	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =	frac 12\omega _1+	frac 32\omega _2+[D]\geq 0.  \] Since $\psi \leq \varphi $, the function $\psi $ is a competitor for $P_{(3/4)	heta }(\varphi )$, which is therefore not identically $-\infty $. $\square$ Proposition 15.2.10 . text: Lemma 15.2.9 . Write $x=\log |z|^2$ and $\chi (x)=\log (1+\mathrm e^ x)$. Proof. The function $W$ is convex: both one-sided derivatives at zero equal one, and the derivative of $2\chi $ increases from one to two on $[0,\infty )$. Since $\omega _1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi (x)$ on the affine chart, $W-2\chi $ is $2\omega _1$-plurisubharmonic there. Since $W$ has slope one for $x\leq 0$ and agrees with $2\chi $ for $x\geq 0$, the function $W-2\chi $ extends to a global $2\omega _1$-plurisubharmonic function, with a logarithmic pole along $D$ and equal to zero where $|z|\geq 1$. The asserted bounds follow from $\psi =x-\chi $: the difference $\varphi -\psi $ equals $2\log 2-\chi $ for $x\leq 0$ and $\chi -x$ for $x\geq 0$. For $C>0$ write $v_ C=P_\theta (\min \{ \psi +C,0\} )$. Rotations of the first factor and the transitive unitary action on the second preserve the whole competitor class, so the envelope is radial and independent of the second factor. The function $V_ C=2\chi +v_ C$ is then convex in $x$ and satisfies $V_ C\leq \chi +x+C$. The adjoint cofactors and adjoint probabilities of the forms $\Omega _{\delta ,g}$ are \[  Q_{\delta ,g}=\Omega _{\delta ,g}/8,\qquad \nu _{\delta ,g}=\Omega _{\delta ,g}^2/8,  \] and they have the weak limits 15.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:divisorial-adjoint-limits} \begin{split}  Q_{\delta ,g}& \longrightarrow (\beta +[D])/8,\\  \nu _{\delta ,g}& \longrightarrow \tfrac 12\mathrm dV+\tfrac 12[D]\wedge \omega _2 +\tfrac 18[D]\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g. \end{split} \end{equation} The limiting probability has mass $1/2$ on $D$ and depends on $g$, although $\mathcal A_\varphi (0)=\{ \mathrm dV\} $. The cofactors do not approach $\beta /4$, and their limit is not $\rho \beta $ for any locally integrable scalar $\rho $. Proof. Smoothness and monotone convergence follow directly from the defining formula, also on $D$, where $\psi =-\infty $. Off $D$, set \[  \lambda =\frac{r}{r+\delta \mathrm e^ g},\qquad h=\psi -g-\log \delta .  \] The chain rule gives $\Omega _{\delta ,g}=A_\delta +R_\delta $, where \[  A_\delta =(2-\lambda )\omega _1+2\omega _2+(1-\lambda )\gamma , \qquad R_\delta =\lambda (1-\lambda )\mathrm dh\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h.  \] Thus $A_\delta \geq \omega _1+\omega _2$ and $R_\delta \geq 0$, and the inequality $\Omega _{\delta ,g}\geq \omega $ extends across $D$ by continuity. Closedness of $\theta $ and Stokes' theorem give the mass eight. Since $\Omega _{\delta ,g}$ is closed, the Gauduchon condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \Omega _{\delta ,g})=0$ reduces to the elliptic equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \wedge \Omega _{\delta ,g}=0$ on the connected surface, whose smooth solutions are constant by the maximum principle. Normalization against $\Omega _{\delta ,g}^2$ gives $\rho =1/8$ and the stated adjoint cofactors and probabilities. The rank-one form $R_\delta $ has square zero, hence $\Omega _{\delta ,g}^2=A_\delta ^2+2A_\delta \wedge R_\delta $. The bounded coefficients of $A_\delta $ converge off $D$ to those of $\beta $, which gives $A_\delta ^2\to 4\mathrm dV$. Write $N=\mathrm d\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\psi $. In $A_\delta \wedge R_\delta $, the part in which $R_\delta $ contributes only derivatives along the first factor (the normal part) is \[  \lambda (1-\lambda )N\wedge \bigl (2\omega _2+(1-\lambda )\gamma \bigr ).  \] Terms mixing a derivative along the first factor with one along the second vanish for degree reasons. The remaining tangential term is $\lambda (1-\lambda )(2-\lambda )\omega _1\wedge \mathrm dg\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g$, which tends to zero by dominated convergence. The normal coefficients can be computed in polar coordinates. Put $s=\delta \mathrm e^{g}$ and $t=|z|^2$. Then \[  \lambda =\frac{t}{s+(1+s)t},\qquad N=\frac{\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\bar z}{2\pi t(1+t)^2}.  \] After angular integration the radial measure of $\lambda (1-\lambda )N$ is \[  \frac{s\, \mathrm dt}{(1+t)(s+(1+s)t)^2} =\frac{\mathrm dy}{(1+sy)(1+(1+s)y)^2},\qquad t=sy.  \] It is bounded by $\mathrm dy/(1+y)^2$ and tends to that measure, whose integral is one. With an additional factor $1-\lambda $, the rescaled measure becomes $\mathrm dy/(1+(1+s)y)^3$, which is bounded by $\mathrm dy/(1+y)^3$ and has limiting integral $1/2$. The mass of both measures outside every fixed tube around $D$ tends to zero, uniformly in the point of the second factor because $g$ is bounded. Testing against continuous functions therefore gives \[  \lambda (1-\lambda )N\longrightarrow [D],\qquad \lambda (1-\lambda )^2N\longrightarrow \tfrac 12[D].  \] Combining the normal and the remaining terms proves 15.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:divisorial-square-limit} \Omega _{\delta ,g}^2\longrightarrow 4\mathrm dV+[D]\wedge (4\omega _2+\gamma ). \end{equation} Dividing by eight gives the second line of ( 15.13 ). The limit is positive since $4\omega _2+\gamma \geq 3\omega _2$, and its mass on $D$ is $4/8=1/2$ by Stokes' theorem on the second factor. Taking $g=0$ and a small nonconstant smooth $g$ gives different limits, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ vanishes identically only for constant $g$. The difference of the potentials satisfies \[  0\leq u_{\delta ,g}-\psi \leq \log \bigl (1+\delta \mathrm e^{\max g}/r\bigr )  \] off $D$. The right-hand side tends to zero and is dominated by an integrable logarithmic pole, which proves $L^1$ convergence. Continuity of distributional differentiation then gives the limit of the cofactors. A locally integrable function times the smooth form $\beta $ has absolutely continuous coefficients, so it cannot produce the singular coefficients of $[D]$. For convergence in capacity, use the capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ of section 1.8 ; after subtracting one, its test potentials range over $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $-1\leq v\leq 0$. For such $v$, apply the cutoff argument of ( 15.12 ) with $\beta $ replaced by $\omega $ and $w=v+1$. Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ X\omega _1\wedge (2\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)=2$, so \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega \{ \psi <-t\}  \leq \int _ X(-f_ t)\omega ^2+2/t\longrightarrow 0.  \] The same bound shows that $D$ has capacity zero. For $\eta >0$, the set of points off $D$ where $u_{\delta ,g}-\psi >\eta $ is contained in \[  \left\{ r<\frac{\delta \mathrm e^{\max g}}{\mathrm e^\eta -1}\right\} .  \] This is a sublevel set of $\psi $ whose level tends to $-\infty $ as $\delta \downarrow 0$. The capacity bound for such sublevel sets, together with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (D)=0$, proves convergence in capacity. Finally, $\Omega _{\delta ,g}\geq \omega $ gives $F_{\delta ,g}\geq -\log 2$. In the affine chart $|\mathrm d\psi |_\omega ^2\leq C/r$, while $g$ and its first two derivatives are bounded. The decomposition above yields $\Omega _{\delta ,g}\leq C_ g(1+r^{-1})\omega $, hence \[  |F_{\delta ,g}|\leq C_ g+2|\log r|.  \] Every finite power of this logarithmic bound is integrable. Smooth convergence off $D$ gives $F_{\delta ,g}\to 0$ there, and dominated convergence proves convergence in $L^ p$. $\square$

15.6 Entropy bounds For a Hermitian background and the zero reference, a lower bound for the $L^ q$ norm of the density in the equation and an upper bound coming from a Gauduchon trace place $B_0$ between two logarithmic integrals. Dualizing gives two-sided entropy estimates, which identify the set where $H_0$ is finite. Throughout this section, $\mathrm{d}V$ is normalized by $\mathrm{d}V(X)=1$. Proposition 15.6.1 . Let $	heta =\omega $ be a Hermitian form, and let $\varphi =0$. There are real constants $A$ and, for every $q>1$, $a_ q$ such that every Borel probability measure $
u $ satisfies \[  a_ q+ rac1q\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u ) \leq H_0(
u ) \leq A+n\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u ).  \] The inequalities include the value $+\infty $. Thus $H_0(
u )<\infty $ if and only if $
u $ has finite entropy, and a family of probability measures has uniformly bounded values of $H_0$ if and only if its entropies are uniformly bounded. Proof. In dimension one, $\omega $ is a Kähler form, and proposition 15.5.2 , which rests on ( 15.25 ), gives $H_0=\log \int _ X\omega +\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}$, so the assertions follow. It gives a constant $c_ q>0$, independent of $G$, such that \[  B_0(G)\geq \log c_ q- rac1q\log \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{qG}\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] For the upper bound, fix a smooth Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, rescaled so that $\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=1$, and write \[  k_\gamma =\left( rac{\gamma ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}ight)^{(n-1)/n}, \qquad m=\min _ X k_\gamma >0.  \] For smooth $G$, the trace bound ( 4.3 ) gives \[  \mathrm{e}^{B_0(G)/n}\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{G/n}k_\gamma \, \mathrm{d}V\leq 1.  \] Uniform approximation and continuity of $B_0$ extend this inequality to continuous $G$. 15.6.1 The mass bounds as entropy differences In a closed background the difference between $H_0$ and the entropy is constant. In general it measures how much the total Monge–Ampère mass of bounded potentials varies: its infimum and supremum recover the lower and upper masses $v_-(\omega )$ and $v_+(\omega )$ of definition 6.5.1 . Let $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{ent}}(X)$ denote the set of probability measures of finite entropy relative to the fixed smooth probability volume $\mathrm{d}V$. By proposition 15.6.1 , the difference $H_0(
u )-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u )$ is a finite real number for every $
u $ in this set. Proposition 15.6.2 . For every Hermitian background $\omega $, \[   egin{split}  \inf _{
u \in \mathcal P_{\mathrm{ent}}(X)}  igl (H_0(
u )-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u ) igr ) & =\log v_-(\omega ),\  \sup _{
u \in \mathcal P_{\mathrm{ent}}(X)}  igl (H_0(
u )-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u ) igr ) & =\log v_+(\omega ). \end{split}  \] The same extrema are obtained over smooth strictly positive probability measures. Here $\log 0=-\infty $ and $\log (+\infty )=+\infty $. Thus the difference is bounded above if and only if $X$ has the bounded mass property, and bounded below if and only if $\omega $ has positive lower mass. Proof. Write $Z_ G=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ G\, \mathrm{d}V$. A bounded solution for $G\in C(X)$ has mass $\mathrm{e}^{B_0(G)}Z_ G$. If $v_-(\omega )>0$, the lower mass bound gives \[  B_0(G)\geq \log v_-(\omega )-\log Z_ G.  \] Taking the defining supremum for $H_0$ and using lemma 15.5.1 gives $H_0-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}\geq \log v_-(\omega )$ on $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{ent}}(X)$. In the same way, if $v_+(\omega )<\infty $, the upper mass bound gives $H_0-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}\leq \log v_+(\omega )$. These bounds hold trivially when $v_-(\omega )=0$ or $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. To prove sharpness, first take a smooth real $G$ and its Gibbs probability $
u _ G=Z_ G^{-1}\mathrm{e}^ G\, \mathrm{d}V$, which has finite entropy. Testing the supremum defining $H_0$ with $G$ gives \[  H_0(
u _ G)-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u _ G) \geq B_0(G)+\log Z_ G.  \] In the other direction, let $\sigma _ G$ be the smooth strictly positive Gauduchon adjoint probability of theorem 15.2.5 . It lies in $\mathcal A_0(G)$, so its dual value is $B_0(G)+\int _ XG\, \mathrm{d}\sigma _ G$, and lemma 15.5.1 yields \[  H_0(\sigma _ G)-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(\sigma _ G) \leq B_0(G)+\log Z_ G.  \] As $G$ runs over smooth real functions, the masses $\mathrm{e}^{B_0(G)}Z_ G$ run over the masses $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ of all smooth $u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, since such a $u$ solves the equation for $G=\log ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n/\mathrm{d}V)$. By theorem 1.11.1 , the mass of every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function is a limit of such masses. Hence the infimum and supremum of $\mathrm{e}^{B_0(G)}Z_ G$ over smooth $G$ are $v_-(\omega )$ and $v_+(\omega )$. Since $
u _ G$ and $\sigma _ G$ are smooth and strictly positive, the last two inequalities prove sharpness on this smaller domain, including the cases $v_-(\omega )=0$ and $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. The two equivalences follow. $\square$ The difference does not depend on the smooth positive reference volume. For smooth real $a$, replacing $\mathrm{d}V$ by $\mathrm{d}V'=\mathrm{e}^ a\mathrm{d}V$ changes both $H_0(
u )$ and $\operatorname {Ent}(
u )$ by $-\int _ Xa\, \mathrm{d}
u $, by the transformation formula preceding proposition 15.6.1 , and finiteness of the entropy is unchanged because $a$ is bounded. Similarly, if $h$ is a smooth real function and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ is also Hermitian, transporting bounded solutions by $u\mapsto u-h$ preserves $B_0$, and hence this difference. Finally, the difference is constant on $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{ent}}(X)$ exactly when $v_-(\omega )=v_+(\omega )$, that is, when all bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions have the same mass.

15.6.2 Entropy for a prescribed ordinary type Return to the standing setting: $	heta $ is semipositive and big, and $\varphi $ is a model reference, with $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ as in ( 13.26 ). The part $(1-\varepsilon )	heta $ of the background left over by the smaller-background envelope gives a uniform lower bound for the density norm, while comparison in a larger Hermitian background gives the upper bound. Together they extend the entropy estimates to the prescribed type. Corollary 15.6.3 . For every $q>1$ there is a finite real $a_ q$, and there is a finite real $A$, such that \[  a_ q+ rac1q\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u ) \leq H_\varphi (
u ) \leq A+n\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u )  \] for every Borel probability measure $
u $, including infinite values. Thus $H_\varphi (
u )$ is finite exactly when $
u $ has finite entropy, and uniformly bounded dual values are equivalent to uniformly bounded entropies. For fixed $	heta $ and $\varepsilon $, the constants can be chosen independently of the model reference $\varphi $. Proof. For $G\in C(X)$, let $u\sim \varphi $ solve the equation with density $c\mathrm{e}^ G$, where $c=\mathrm{e}^{B_\varphi (G)}$. The lower bound $b_ q>0$ of lemma 14.11.2 for the $L^ q$ norm of the density gives $c\| \mathrm{e}^ G\| _ q\geq b_ q$, hence \[  B_\varphi (G)\geq \log b_ q- rac1q \log \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{qG}\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] For the upper bound, choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq 	heta $, and let $B_{\Omega ,0}$ and $H_{\Omega ,0}$ denote its normalization scalar and dual functional for the zero reference. Let $v$ be a bounded solution for $G$ in this background; being bounded, it has a smaller-background envelope $P_{\delta \Omega }(v)\geq \inf _ Xv$ for every $0<\delta <1$. Moreover $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Omega )$, $u\preceq v$, and positivity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Omega (u) \geq \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u) =c\mathrm{e}^ G\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] If $c>\mathrm{e}^{B_{\Omega ,0}(G)}$, the singular strict domination principle, applied in the background $\Omega $ to $v$ and $u+t$ for every real $t$, would give $v\geq u+t$ for all $t$, which is impossible. 15.7.1 Uniform comparison of the scalar functionals When two scalar functionals are uniformly close, their supporting probabilities are close as well. To make this precise, define for two model references $\varphi ,\psi $ in the preceding setting 15.28  egin{equation} \label{eq:normalization-distance} \Delta (\varphi ,\psi ) =\sup _{G\in C(X)}|B_\varphi (G)-B_\psi (G)|. \end{equation} The comparison with $B_0$ in proposition 15.7.1 makes this number finite for every such pair. It is a pseudometric: symmetry, vanishing on the diagonal and the triangle inequality follow from the properties of the uniform norm. Distinct singularity types can have distance zero, as example 15.10.2 shows. Proposition 15.7.2 . For these model references, \[  \Delta (\varphi ,\psi ) =\sup _{\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u )<\infty } |H_\varphi (
u )-H_\psi (
u )|,  \] where the supremum is over probability measures of finite entropy. The same value is obtained if ( 15.28 ) uses all bounded measurable $G$, and it does not depend on the smooth positive reference volume. Proof. By corollary 15.6.3 , both duals are finite exactly on the probability measures of finite entropy; rescaling the reference volume to have mass one does not affect finiteness. A uniform bound for $|B_\varphi -B_\psi |$ passes to the defining suprema, so the supremum in the statement is at most $\Delta (\varphi ,\psi )$. Conversely, denote that supremum by $D$. If $
u \in \mathcal A_\psi (G)$, then $

title: Theorem 15.8.1
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 15.8.1 . Suppose $0<\varepsilon <1$ and $(1-\varepsilon )\beta \leq \beta '\leq (1+\varepsilon )\beta $. For every bounded measurable $F$, 15.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:geometric-normalization-comparison} n\log (1-\varepsilon )\leq B_{\beta '}(F)-B_\beta (F)\leq n\log (1+\varepsilon ). \end{equation} In particular, $d(B_\beta ,B_{\beta '})\leq -n\log (1-\varepsilon )$. The same conclusion holds if the two inequalities between forms are satisfied by positive representatives $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ and $\beta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h'$, with $h,h'$ smooth real functions. Proof. First let $F$ be smooth, and let $v,v'$ be smooth solutions in the two backgrounds. At a maximum point of $v'-(1+\varepsilon )v$, \[  0<\beta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v'\leq (1+\varepsilon )(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v).  \] Taking determinants and canceling $\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$ gives the upper bound. At a minimum point of $v'-(1-\varepsilon )v$, the reverse inequality between forms gives the lower bound. For bounded measurable $F$, choose smooth uniformly bounded approximations converging in $L^1$ and apply theorem 15.1.3 in each of the two backgrounds. Finally, the correspondence $v\mapsto v-h$ preserves both boundedness and the current, so $B_{\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h}=B_\beta $ whenever both backgrounds are positive. This proves the assertion about representatives. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.8.3
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 15.8.3 . Let $\beta _ j,\beta $ be Hermitian forms and $F_ j,F$ smooth real functions with $\beta _ j\to \beta $ and $F_ j\to F$ in $C^\infty $. Then the solutions $v_ j$ for $(\beta _ j,F_ j)$ normalized by $\int _ Xv_ j\, \mathrm{d}V=0$ converge in $C^\infty $ to the similarly normalized solution $v$ for $(\beta ,F)$, and their scalars converge as well. Proof. Fix $k\geq 0$ and $0<\alpha <1$. On the open set where $\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w>0$, consider the smooth map \[  (\eta ,G,w,a)\longmapsto \log \frac{(\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}-a-G  \] defined for $C^{k,\alpha }$ forms $\eta $ and functions $G$, mean-zero $C^{k+2,\alpha }$ potentials $w$ and $a\in \mathbb R$, with values in $C^{k,\alpha }$. At the limiting solution its derivative in $(w,a)$ is $(h,q)\mapsto \Delta _\Omega h-q$, where $\Omega =\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ and $\Delta _\Omega h=n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \Omega ^{n-1}/\Omega ^ n$. Given a target $g$, choose $q=-\int _ Xg\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ v$, where $\mu _ v$ is the adjoint probability of proposition 4.8.1 . The Fredholm alternative then gives a unique mean-zero $h$ with $\Delta _\Omega h=g+q$, and the inverse is bounded as in proposition 9.3.1 . In dimension one this is the Fredholm alternative for the Poisson equation. The implicit function theorem gives a local branch of solutions depending continuously on the parameters in these spaces. For smooth parameters, uniqueness of bounded solutions modulo constants, corollary 11.4.6 , identifies this branch with the global smooth solution. Thus $v_ j\to v$ in $C^{k+2,\alpha }$ for every $k$, which proves the assertion. $\square$

title: 15.9 Divisorial types and moving sections
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.9 Divisorial types and moving sections For a reference given by logarithms of holomorphic sections, removing its divisorial part identifies its ordinary singularity type with the bounded potentials of the residual background. The normalization scalar therefore depends only on the residual form, whereas convergence of the full potentials also requires control of the sections defining the divisors. In this section, $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Fix finitely many holomorphic line bundles $L_ r$ on $X$ with smooth Hermitian metrics $h_ r$, nonzero holomorphic sections $s_ r$, and weights $t_ r>0$. Put \[  \varphi =\sum _ r t_ r\log |s_ r|_{h_ r}^2,\qquad \Gamma =\sum _ r t_ r\operatorname {div}(s_ r),\qquad \beta =\theta -\sum _ r t_ rc_1(L_ r,h_ r),  \] where $c_1(L_ r,h_ r)$ is the Chern curvature form, and assume that the residual form $\beta $ is positive. The empty family is allowed, with $\varphi =0$ and $\beta =\theta $. Theorem 15.9.1 . The ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $ is described by \[  \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\sim \varphi \}  =\{ \varphi +w:w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )\cap L^\infty (X)\} ,  \] and for each such $w$, 15.31 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ordinary-divisor-measure} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\varphi +w)=(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n. \end{equation} For every bounded measurable $F$, the equation ( 15.1 ) in this ordinary type has a unique constant and a solution unique modulo constants. Its normalization scalar $B_{\theta ,[\varphi ]}$ satisfies \[  B_{\theta ,[\varphi ]}(F)=B_\beta (F),  \] so its dual functional and supporting sets coincide with $H_\beta $ and $\mathcal A_\beta $. Proof. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =[\Gamma ]+\beta $, so every function on the right is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and has the type of $\varphi $. Conversely, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $. Then $u$ has the same generic Lelong numbers as $\varphi $ along the components of $\Gamma $, namely the coefficients of $\Gamma $, and lemma 1.17.1 gives \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-[\Gamma ]\geq 0.  \] The locally integrable difference $w=u-\varphi $ therefore has a $\beta $-plurisubharmonic representative. It is bounded off the divisor because $u\sim \varphi $, and the local submean property preserves both bounds across the divisor. Since $u$ and $\varphi +w$ agree almost everywhere, they are equal as quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. Off the divisor, the currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi +w)$ and $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ agree, and locality identifies their Monge–Ampère products there. The extended measure on the left gives the divisor zero mass, and so does the bounded product on the right, which is finite and charges no analytic set by section 1.7 . This proves ( 15.31 ). In the background $\beta $, the equation with bounded density has a continuous solution and a unique constant by theorem 10.1.1 , proposition 10.6.1 . The density $\mathrm{e}^ F$ is bounded above and below by positive constants, so corollary 11.4.6 gives uniqueness modulo constants. The correspondence transfers these assertions to the whole ordinary type and identifies the functionals. $\square$ In particular, the comparison of backgrounds and the stability of supporting probabilities in theorem 15.8.1 , corollary 15.8.2 apply whenever the positive residual forms satisfy the two-sided inequalities there; the location of the divisors does not enter these estimates. This statement concerns ordinary types. To interpret it in terms of model references, one also needs the envelope $P_\theta [\varphi ]$ to differ from $\varphi $ by a bounded function. For a Hermitian $\theta $, lemma 15.9.3 below proves this bounded difference and the smaller-background model condition. For a fixed positive residual $\beta $, uniformly bounded $F_ j\to F$ in $L^1$ give uniform convergence of the residual solutions normalized by $\sup _ Xv_ j=0$. Indeed, continuity of the scalar gives uniformly bounded densities $\mathrm{e}^{B_\beta (F_ j)+F_ j}$ converging in every $L^ p$, $p<\infty $. The compactness theorem theorem 10.3.4 gives uniform convergence of subsequences, continuity of bounded products identifies the limiting equation, and corollary 11.4.6 identifies every limit. Subtracting the means gives the same conclusion for solutions normalized to have mean zero. Theorem 15.9.2 . Keep the line bundles and metrics fixed. Let nonzero sections $s_{jr}$ converge to $s_ r\ne 0$ in the finite-dimensional spaces of global sections, and let positive weights satisfy $t_{jr}\to t_ r>0$. Given Hermitian forms $\beta _ j$, define $\varphi _ j$ and $\theta _ j=\beta _ j+\sum _ rt_{jr}c_1(L_ r,h_ r)$ by the preceding formulas. Suppose either that $\beta _ j\to \beta $ in $C^\infty $ for a Hermitian form $\beta >0$ and $F_ j\to F$ in $C^\infty $, or that $\beta _ j=\beta $ for all $j$ and the tests $F_ j$ converge to $F$ in $L^1$ with a common $L^\infty $ bound. Then $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ in $L^1$, and the solutions $u_ j\sim \varphi _ j$ for $(\theta _ j,F_ j)$, normalized by $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$, converge in $L^1$ to the similarly normalized solution $u\sim \varphi $. For the residual solutions $v_ j$ normalized to have mean zero, one also has \[  \sup _ X(\varphi _ j+v_ j)\longrightarrow \sup _ X(\varphi +v).  \] The residuals converge smoothly in the first regime and uniformly in the second. Proof. The convergence of the residual solutions follows from proposition 15.8.3 in the first case and from the preceding compactness argument in the second. The fixed metrics and bounded weights give a common smooth lower bound for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$. The convergent sections give a common upper bound for $\varphi _ j$ and convergence at a point outside all limiting divisors, so the suprema of the $\varphi _ j$ are bounded above and below. By theorem 1.4.2 , every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $L^1$. Off the limiting divisors, convergence of the sections and weights gives local uniform convergence to $\varphi $; since those divisors have zero volume, every $L^1$ cluster point equals $\varphi $. Thus $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. Put $C_ j=\sup _ X(\varphi _ j+v_ j)$ and $C=\sup _ X(\varphi +v)$. The sums converge in $L^1$ and have a common smooth lower bound for their complex Hessians, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq -\beta _ j$ and the residual forms are uniformly bounded. Applying lemma 1.4.1 at maximum points gives $\limsup _ jC_ j\leq C$. A maximum point of $\varphi +v$ lies off the poles of $\varphi $, and evaluation there, using local uniform convergence, gives $\liminf _ jC_ j\geq C$. It follows that $u_ j=\varphi _ j+v_ j-C_ j\to \varphi +v-C=u$ in $L^1$. For an empty family of divisors, the assertion reduces to the convergence of the residual solutions and of their suprema. $\square$

text:
15.9.1 One-sided divisorial classes and sharp thresholds The ordinary-type correspondence extends to potentials with additional poles. It then identifies the largest subsolution coefficient in the whole one-sided class, even for merely integrable data. For smooth positive data, the prescribed divisor causes a strict loss relative to the global coefficient. Keep the divisorial setting above, assume also that $	heta $ is a Hermitian form and $n\ge 2$, and subtract a constant from $\varphi $ so that $\sup _ X\varphi =0$. Write $S=\operatorname {Supp}\Gamma $ and $\psi =P_	heta [\varphi ]$. For a nonempty class $\mathcal A\subset \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and nonzero $0\le f\in L^1(\mathrm dV)$, define \[  b_{	heta ,\mathcal A}(f)=\sup \{ c\ge 0:	ext{some }u\in \mathcal A 	ext{ satisfies }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u) \ge cf\, \mathrm dV\} .  \] The three classes considered here are \[   egin{aligned}  \mathcal A_{\preceq }& =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\preceq \varphi \} ,\  \mathcal A_{\sim }& =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\sim \varphi \} ,\  \mathcal A_{\mathrm{env}}& =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,\psi ). \end{aligned}  \] The following lemma supplies the genuine reference $\psi $ used in the last definition. Lemma 15.9.3 . The map $w\mapsto \varphi +w$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X, eta )$ onto $\mathcal A_{\preceq }$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\varphi +w) =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ eta (w).  \] Its bounded members correspond to $\mathcal A_{\sim }$. The envelope $\psi $ is genuine, satisfies $\varphi \le \psi \le \varphi +K$ for some finite $K$, meets the model condition ( 13.26 ), and \[  \mathcal A_{\sim }\subset \mathcal A_{\mathrm{env}} \subset \mathcal A_{\preceq }.  \] Proof. If $u\preceq \varphi $, its generic Lelong numbers dominate the coefficients of $\Gamma $. By lemma 1.17.1 , $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-[\Gamma ]\ge 0$. The locally integrable distribution $w=u-\varphi $ therefore has a canonical $ eta $-psh representative. Off $S$ it equals the difference and is bounded above. The identity $u=\varphi +w$ holds almost everywhere, hence everywhere for the canonical quasi-psh functions. Conversely, $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X, eta )$ has finite supremum, and \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi +w)= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+[\Gamma ]\ge 0, \qquad \varphi +w\preceq \varphi .  \] These maps are inverse. The bounded correspondence is theorem 15.9.1 . Off $S$ the currents agree; locality of the extended products identifies their measures there. For every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm dV)$, \[  b_{	heta ,\mathcal A_{\preceq }}(f)=b_ eta (f),  \] and this coefficient is attained. title: 15.10 The mass determined by the functional
search_title: The mass determined by the functional
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.10 The mass determined by the functional In a closed background, the information lost by the scalar functional can be described exactly: for the model references below, two functionals agree precisely when the masses agree. This also gives examples in which the supporting probabilities stay fixed while the potentials have different limits. In this section $X$ is a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ is any smooth closed big real $(1,1)$-form. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $, have small unbounded locus in the sense of section 1.12 , and have positive mass \[  m_\varphi =\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi )>0.  \] Write $B_{\theta ,\varphi }$ and $\mathcal A_{\theta ,\varphi }$ for the normalization scalar and the supporting sets of the equation ( 15.1 ) in the ordinary type of $\varphi $, and put $Z_ F=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F\, \mathrm{d}V$. Theorem 15.10.1 . For every such pair $(\theta ,\varphi )$ and every bounded measurable $F$, the equation in the ordinary type of $\varphi $ has a unique constant and a solution unique modulo constants. Its normalization scalar is \[  B_{\theta ,\varphi }(F)=\log m_\varphi -\log Z_ F.  \] For continuous real $F$, its supporting set is \[  \mathcal A_{\theta ,\varphi }(F)=\{ \mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V/Z_ F\} .  \] For two such pairs on the same $X$, with the same $\mathrm{d}V$ and possibly in different classes, 15.37 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normalization-mass-distance} \sup _{F\in L^\infty }|B_{\theta ,\varphi }(F)-B_{\theta ',\psi }(F)| =|\log m_\varphi -\log m_\psi |. \end{equation} Thus an invariant of these pairs is determined by the whole functional if and only if it is constant on every fiber of the map $(\theta ,\varphi )\mapsto m_\varphi $. Proof. Existence follows from corollary 32.8.3 . Indeed, a Kähler manifold has the bounded mass property by lemma 21.4.1 , and since in a closed background all potentials of the ordinary type of $\varphi $ have the same mass $m_\varphi >0$, the reference satisfies the positive-volume model condition ( 30.10 ). Uniqueness modulo constants is the classical theorem on equations with prescribed singularities in closed big classes, which applies under the model and small-unbounded-locus hypotheses; see the notes in section 34.11 . Every potential of the ordinary type of $\varphi $ has mass $m_\varphi $, so integrating the equation forces $cZ_ F=m_\varphi $, which is the scalar formula. For continuous $F$, Jensen's inequality shows, as for ( 15.25 ), that the normalized exponential measure is a supporting probability, and differentiating at zero in both signs of every continuous direction shows that it is the only one. Subtracting the scalar formulas gives ( 15.37 ). Finally, $m_\varphi =\mathrm{d}V(X)\exp B_{\theta ,\varphi }(0)$, so the functional and the mass determine each other, and an invariant factors through either one exactly when it is constant on the fibers of the mass map. $\square$ For an ordinary divisorial type whose residual form $\beta $ is positive and closed, theorem 15.9.1 gives the same formula with mass $\int _ X\beta ^ n$, since Stokes' theorem for bounded products in a closed background fixes the mass of every bounded $\beta $-plurisubharmonic function. This computation does not require the real weighted sum of divisors to have a model representative. If $\beta _ j\to \beta $ uniformly, the masses converge by continuity of $\beta \mapsto \int _ X\beta ^ n$; under the two-sided bounds $(1-\varepsilon _ j)\beta \leq \beta _ j\leq (1+\varepsilon _ j)\beta $ one has the sharper inequalities $(1-\varepsilon _ j)^ n\int \beta ^ n\leq \int \beta _ j^ n\leq (1+\varepsilon _ j)^ n\int \beta ^ n$. Example 15.10.2 . Let $X=\mathbb P^ n$ with $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be the Fubini–Study form, normalized by $\int _ X\theta ^ n=1$, and let $D$ be a hyperplane. Let $s_ D$ be a section of $\mathcal O(1)$ defining $D$, measured with the Fubini–Study metric and rescaled so that $a_ D=\log |s_ D|^2\leq 0$, and choose $t\in (0,1)$. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ D=[D]-\theta ,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ta_ D)=(1-t)\theta +t[D].  \] Put $\varphi _{t,D}=P_\theta [ta_ D]$. By proposition 16.2.7 , this envelope fixed point has the ordinary type of $ta_ D$. Moreover $ta_ D\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,t\theta )$ and $ta_ D\leq \varphi _{t,D}$, so $\varphi _{t,D}$ satisfies ( 13.26 ) with $\varepsilon =t$. Off $D$, the potential $ta_ D$ has Monge–Ampère measure $(1-t)^ n\theta ^ n$, and its non-pluripolar measure puts no mass on $D$. Since mass is invariant under bounded changes of the potential in a closed background, \[  m_{\varphi _{t,D}}=(1-t)^ n,\qquad B_{\varphi _{t,D}}(G)-B_0(G)=n\log (1-t)\quad (G\in C(X,\mathbb R)).  \] Thus the constant in proposition 15.7.1 is sharp. Now let $n=1$, and take for $D$ two distinct points $p,q\in \mathbb P^1$. The corresponding references have distance zero, although $\varphi _{t,p}$ is unbounded near $p$ and bounded near $q$, while $\varphi _{t,q}$ behaves in the opposite way; in particular they are not ordinarily equivalent. For every positive integer $m$, \[  \mathcal I(m\varphi _{t,p})=\mathcal O(-\lfloor mt\rfloor p),\qquad \mathcal I(m\varphi _{t,q})=\mathcal O(-\lfloor mt\rfloor q),  \] by lemma 1.16.1 , and for $mt\geq 1$ these ideals differ. Thus the distance $\Delta $ of ( 15.28 ) does not even separate multiplier-ideal types, and it determines neither the ordinary nor the ideal singularity type. Fix a smooth real function $F$ on $\mathbb P^1$, and let $w_ F$ be the solution of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ F=\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V/Z_ F$ with $\int _ Xw_ F\, \mathrm{d}V=0$. The normalized solutions for $D=p$ and $D=q$ are \[  u_{t,D}=ta_ D+(1-t)w_ F-\sup _ X\bigl (ta_ D+(1-t)w_ F\bigr ).  \] Their difference satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_{t,p}-u_{t,q})=t([p]-[q])\ne 0$. Hence the sequence of solutions obtained by alternating between $D=p$ and $D=q$ has two different $L^1$ cluster points, although the scalar functional and all its supporting sets are the same at every step. Within this one-parameter family, the functional does recover $t$, since $t\mapsto (1-t)^ n$ is injective. Example 15.10.3 . On $\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 2$, let $\omega $ be the Fubini–Study form, normalized as in example 15.10.2 , and let $f$ be a nonconstant smooth real function. Fix $0<t<1$ and put \[  \beta =\mathrm{e}^ f\omega ,\qquad \theta =\beta +t\omega ,\qquad \varphi _ D=t\log |s_ D|^2.  \] Here $s_ D$ defines a hyperplane $D$ as in example 15.10.2 , and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ D=\beta +t[D]$, so every hyperplane has the same positive residual form $\beta $. This form is not closed: $\mathrm{d}\beta =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm{d}f\wedge \omega \not\equiv 0$, since $\mathrm{d}f$ is nonzero somewhere and wedging a one-form with $\omega ^{n-1}$ is injective. By theorem 15.9.1 , the ordinary types of all $\varphi _ D$ have the same functional $B_\beta $ on bounded tests, hence the same supporting sets. At a smooth test, the common supporting probability is the Gauduchon adjoint probability of theorem 15.2.5 . If $v_ F$ is the common smooth residual solution, the normalized solutions are the functions $\varphi _ D+v_ F-\sup _ X(\varphi _ D+v_ F)$. Two distinct hyperplanes $D_1,D_2$ give different poles, different divisorial coefficients and, for sufficiently large $k$, different multiplier ideals $\mathcal O(-\lfloor kt\rfloor D_ i)$, by the calculation in normal coordinates of lemma 1.16.1 . The potentials differ by more than a constant, since the difference of their complex Hessians is $t([D_1]-[D_2])$, and alternating between the two hyperplanes again produces two distinct $L^1$ limits. These conclusions come from the common residual form; for general nonclosed backgrounds we do not claim that the functional is determined by a mass.

text: Example 15.10.2 . Let $X=\mathbb P^ n$ with $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be the Fubini–Study form, normalized by $\int _ X\theta ^ n=1$, and let $D$ be a hyperplane. Let $s_ D$ be a section of $\mathcal O(1)$ defining $D$, measured with the Fubini–Study metric and rescaled so that $a_ D=\log |s_ D|^2\leq 0$, and choose $t\in (0,1)$. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ D=[D]-\theta ,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ta_ D)=(1-t)\theta +t[D].  \] Put $\varphi _{t,D}=P_\theta [ta_ D]$. By proposition 16.2.7 , this envelope fixed point has the ordinary type of $ta_ D$. Moreover $ta_ D\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,t\theta )$ and $ta_ D\leq \varphi _{t,D}$, so $\varphi _{t,D}$ satisfies ( 13.26 ) with $\varepsilon =t$. Off $D$, the potential $ta_ D$ has Monge–Ampère measure $(1-t)^ n\theta ^ n$, and its non-pluripolar measure puts no mass on $D$. Since mass is invariant under bounded changes of the potential in a closed background, \[  m_{\varphi _{t,D}}=(1-t)^ n,\qquad B_{\varphi _{t,D}}(G)-B_0(G)=n\log (1-t)\quad (G\in C(X,\mathbb R)).  \] Thus the constant in proposition 15.7.1 is sharp. Now let $n=1$, and take for $D$ two distinct points $p,q\in \mathbb P^1$. The corresponding references have distance zero, although $\varphi _{t,p}$ is unbounded near $p$ and bounded near $q$, while $\varphi _{t,q}$ behaves in the opposite way; in particular they are not ordinarily equivalent. For every positive integer $m$, \[  \mathcal I(m\varphi _{t,p})=\mathcal O(-\lfloor mt\rfloor p),\qquad \mathcal I(m\varphi _{t,q})=\mathcal O(-\lfloor mt\rfloor q),  \] by lemma 1.16.1 , and for $mt\geq 1$ these ideals differ. Thus the distance $\Delta $ of ( 15.28 ) does not even separate multiplier-ideal types, and it determines neither the ordinary nor the ideal singularity type. Fix a smooth real function $F$ on $\mathbb P^1$, and let $w_ F$ be the solution of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ F=\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V/Z_ F$ with $\int _ Xw_ F\, \mathrm{d}V=0$. The normalized solutions for $D=p$ and $D=q$ are \[  u_{t,D}=ta_ D+(1-t)w_ F-\sup _ X\bigl (ta_ D+(1-t)w_ F\bigr ).  \] Their difference satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_{t,p}-u_{t,q})=t([p]-[q])\ne 0$. Hence the sequence of solutions obtained by alternating between $D=p$ and $D=q$ has two different $L^1$ cluster points, although the scalar functional and all its supporting sets are the same at every step. Within this one-parameter family, the functional does recover $t$, since $t\mapsto (1-t)^ n$ is injective.

title: Example 15.10.3
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Example 15.10.3 . On $\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 2$, let $\omega $ be the Fubini–Study form, normalized as in example 15.10.2 , and let $f$ be a nonconstant smooth real function. Fix $0<t<1$ and put \[  \beta =\mathrm{e}^ f\omega ,\qquad \theta =\beta +t\omega ,\qquad \varphi _ D=t\log |s_ D|^2.  \] Here $s_ D$ defines a hyperplane $D$ as in example 15.10.2 , and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ D=\beta +t[D]$, so every hyperplane has the same positive residual form $\beta $. This form is not closed: $\mathrm{d}\beta =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm{d}f\wedge \omega \not\equiv 0$, since $\mathrm{d}f$ is nonzero somewhere and wedging a one-form with $\omega ^{n-1}$ is injective. By theorem 15.9.1 , the ordinary types of all $\varphi _ D$ have the same functional $B_\beta $ on bounded tests, hence the same supporting sets. At a smooth test, the common supporting probability is the Gauduchon adjoint probability of theorem 15.2.5 . If $v_ F$ is the common smooth residual solution, the normalized solutions are the functions $\varphi _ D+v_ F-\sup _ X(\varphi _ D+v_ F)$. Two distinct hyperplanes $D_1,D_2$ give different poles, different divisorial coefficients and, for sufficiently large $k$, different multiplier ideals $\mathcal O(-\lfloor kt\rfloor D_ i)$, by the calculation in normal coordinates of lemma 1.16.1 . The potentials differ by more than a constant, since the difference of their complex Hessians is $t([D_1]-[D_2])$, and alternating between the two hyperplanes again produces two distinct $L^1$ limits. These conclusions come from the common residual form; for general nonclosed backgrounds we do not claim that the functional is determined by a mass.

title: 15.11 Convex-body criteria for varying references
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.11 Convex-body criteria for varying references When the singularities of a torus-invariant reference are described by a convex body, the closed mass formula of theorem 15.10.1 turns convergence of the convex bodies into convergence of the functionals. A translated simplex contained in all the bodies keeps the limiting reference solvable, and the Hausdorff distance then controls the functionals uniformly over all continuous tests, even though the ordinary types vary. Let $n\geq 2$, and let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ n$, normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^ n}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^ n=1$. In homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ n]$, consider the torus $T=\{ Z_0\cdots Z_ n\ne 0\} $, and put \[  x_ i=\log |Z_ i/Z_0|^2,\qquad L(x)=\log \bigl (1+\textstyle \sum _ i\mathrm{e}^{x_ i}\bigr ),\qquad \Sigma =\{ p_ i\geq 0:\textstyle \sum _ i p_ i\leq 1\} ,  \] where $1\leq i\leq n$ and $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^ n$ is the standard simplex. Functions of $x=(x_1,\ldots ,x_ n)$ are regarded as functions on $T$; thus $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L$ on $T$. Define the continuous function $\ell $ on $\Sigma $ by \[  \ell (p)=\sum _ i p_ i\log p_ i+ (1-\textstyle \sum _ i p_ i)\log (1-\textstyle \sum _ i p_ i), \qquad 0\log 0=0.  \] For a convex body $K\subset \Sigma $, that is, a compact convex set with nonempty interior, set \[  h_ K(x)=\sup _{p\in K}p\cdot x,\qquad g_ K(x)=\sup _{p\in K}\{ p\cdot x-\ell (p)\} .  \]

15.11.1 Canonical models and their mass Lemma 15.11.1 . The functions $h_ K-L$ and $g_ K-L$ on $T$ extend uniquely to $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic functions $\psi _ K,\Phi _ K$ on $\mathbb P^ n$. They satisfy \[   egin{aligned} & \psi _ K\leq \Phi _ K\leq \psi _ K+\log (n+1),\qquad \sup \Phi _ K=0,\ & P_{\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}}[\psi _ K]=\Phi _ K =P_{\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}}[\Phi _ K]. \end{aligned}  \] If $p_*+\delta \Sigma \subset K$ for some $p_*\in \mathbb R^ n$ and $0<\delta <1$, then $P_{(1-\delta )\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}}(\Phi _ K)
ot\equiv -\infty $. Proof. The Legendre transform of $L$ is $L^*=\ell $ on $\Sigma $ and $+\infty $ outside it. Since $-\log (n+1)\leq \ell \leq 0$, \[  h_ K\leq g_ K\leq h_ K+\log (n+1),\qquad g_ K\leq L,\qquad h_ K\leq h_\Sigma \leq L.  \] A finite convex function of the logarithmic moduli is plurisubharmonic: for a smooth convex function the complex Hessian is positive, and convolution gives the general case. On $T\cap \{ Z_ j
e 0\} $, add the local Fubini–Study potential $\log \sum _ i|Z_ i/Z_ j|^2$; the resulting functions are again convex functions of the logarithmic moduli of the affine coordinates, and they are bounded above by that smooth potential because $h_ K,g_ K\leq L$. Lemma 1.3.7 therefore gives the extensions across the coordinate hyperplanes and the stated bounds. If $p\in \operatorname {int}K$, then $p\in \operatorname {int}\Sigma $, and at $x_ i=\log (p_ i/(1-\sum _ k p_ k))$ the supremum defining $L=\ell ^*$ is attained at $p\in K$, so $g_ K(x)=L(x)$. This proves $\sup \Phi _ K=0$. For $C\geq \log (n+1)$, let $v_ C=P_{\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}}(\psi _ K+C,0)$, the envelope of the obstacle $\min (\psi _ K+C,0)$. Since $\Phi _ K$ is a competitor, $\Phi _ K\leq v_ C\leq 0$. The obstacle is upper semicontinuous, so $v_ C\leq \psi _ K+C$ everywhere. The compact torus acting by rotations of the coordinates preserves the obstacle, so $v_ C$ is invariant, and on $T$ the function $f=v_ C+L$ is a finite convex function of $x$ with $f\leq L$ and $f\leq h_ K+C$. The second inequality shows that the Legendre transform $f^*$ is $+\infty $ outside $K$, and the first gives $f^*\geq \ell $. Thus \[  f(x)=\sup _{p\in \operatorname {dom}f^*}\{ p\cdot x-f^*(p)\}  \leq g_ K(x).  \] Hence $v_ C\leq \Phi _ K$ on $T$, and since both functions are quasi-plurisubharmonic and $T$ is the complement of an analytic set, $v_ C=\Phi _ K$ on $\mathbb P^ n$. Letting $C	o \infty $ gives $P_{\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}}[\psi _ K]=\Phi _ K$. Since $\psi _ K\leq \Phi _ K\leq \psi _ K+\log (n+1)$, the envelopes of $\min (\Phi _ K+C,0)$ and $\min (\psi _ K+C,0)$ interlace as $C	o \infty $, so also $P_{\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}}[\Phi _ K]=\Phi _ K$. For the final assertion put $\varepsilon =1-\delta $, $b=\sum _ i p_{*,i}$ and $\chi =p_*\cdot x-\varepsilon L$ on $T$. The inclusion $p_*+\delta \Sigma \subset \Sigma $ implies $p_{*,i}\geq 0$ and $b\leq \varepsilon $, and the extension of $\chi $ to $\mathbb P^ n$ satisfies \[  \varepsilon \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi =\sum _ i p_{*,i}[Z_ i=0]+(\varepsilon -b)[Z_0=0]\geq 0.  \] Since $h_ K\geq p_*\cdot x+\delta h_\Sigma $ and $L-h_\Sigma \leq \log (n+1)$, one has $\chi -\delta \log (n+1)\leq \Phi _ K$. Lemma 15.11.2 . The manifold $X$ is Kähler, and $\Theta $ is smooth, closed, semipositive and big. For $r>0$, the reference $r\pi ^*\Phi _ K$ satisfies $P_{r\Theta }[r\pi ^*\Phi _ K]=r\pi ^*\Phi _ K$, has small unbounded locus, and satisfies 15.40  egin{equation} \label{eq:convex-body-mass} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{r\Theta }(r\pi ^*\Phi _ K) =r^ n n!\operatorname {Vol}_ n(K). \end{equation} If $p_*+\delta \Sigma \subset K$ with $0<\delta <1$, then $P_{(1-\delta )r\Theta }(r\pi ^*\Phi _ K)
ot\equiv -\infty $. Proof. On $\mathbb P^ n$, the envelope identity is lemma 15.11.1 . In the blowup case, every $\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function descends to $\mathbb P^ n$. Indeed, off $E_ q$ add a local potential of $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$; the resulting plurisubharmonic function is bounded above near $q$, because the original function is bounded above near the compact fiber $E_ q$, and therefore extends across $q$. The pullback of the extension agrees with the original function off $E_ q$, hence everywhere. For bigness in the blowup case, choose unitary homogeneous coordinates $[W_0:\cdots :W_ n]$, used only in this paragraph, in which $q=[1:0:\cdots :0]$, set \[  \psi _ q=\log  rac{\sum _{i=1}^ n|W_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ n|W_ i|^2},  \] and let $Q:X	o \mathbb P^{n-1}$ be the map induced by the linear projection from $q$. This proves the assertions about the manifold and the form $\Theta $. For a smooth convex $g$, the coordinates $z_ i=\mathrm{e}^{x_ i/2+\mathrm{i}\vartheta _ i}$ give \[  \mathrm{d}^{\mathrm c}g= rac1{2\pi }\sum _ i g_ i\, \mathrm{d}\vartheta _ i, \qquad \int _ T(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)^ n=n!\int _{\mathbb R^ n}\det (D^2g)\, \mathrm{d}x.  \] For a finite convex $g$, convolution and the continuity of bounded Monge–Ampère products under local uniform convergence identify $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)^ n$ on $T$ in the same way: its image under $z\mapsto x$ is $n!M_ g$, where $M_ g$ is the Alexandrov measure, which assigns to a Borel set of $\mathbb R^ n$ the Euclidean volume of its subgradient image. For $g_ K$, the bound $g_ K\leq h_ K+\log (n+1)$ and a separation argument put every subgradient in $K$. Conversely, if $p\in \operatorname {int}K$ and $p+c\mathbb B\subset K$, where $\mathbb B$ is the closed unit ball of $\mathbb R^ n$ and $c>0$, then $g_ K(x)-p\cdot x\geq c|x|$; this function attains a minimum, so $p$ is a subgradient of $g_ K$ at some point. 15.11.3 A family with nonanalytic isolated poles The hypothesis of a common simplex allows ordinary singularity types that contain no potential with analytic singularities. Let $o=[1:0:\cdots :0]$ be the origin of the affine chart $Z_0
e 0$, with affine coordinates $z_ i=Z_ i/Z_0$. For $0<a\leq 1$, define \[  P_ a=\{ p\in \Sigma :	extstyle \sum _ i\sqrt{p_ i}\geq \sqrt a\} , \qquad \kappa _ n= rac{2^ n n!}{(2n)!}= rac1{(2n-1)!!}.  \] Proposition 15.11.4 . The function $\Phi _{P_ a}$ is locally bounded outside the single point $o$, where it has a pole, and it does not have the ordinary singularity type of any function with analytic singularities. Its generic Lelong number along every prime divisor of $\mathbb P^ n$ is zero, and 15.43  egin{equation} \label{eq:curved-nonanalytic-mass} \int _{\mathbb P^ n}\mathrm{MA}_{\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}}(\Phi _{P_ a}) =1-\kappa _ n a^ n>0. \end{equation} The same assertions about the pole, nonanalyticity and generic Lelong numbers hold for $\pi ^*\Phi _{P_ a}$ on the blowup $\operatorname {Bl}_ q\mathbb P^ n$ at a fixed point $q
e o$. Proof. The function $p\mapsto \sum _ i\sqrt{p_ i}$ is concave, so $P_ a$ is convex. Set \[  b= rac{n+1}{2n},\qquad p_{*,i}= rac bn, \qquad \delta = rac{n-1}{4n}.  \] Then $b+\delta <1$ and $\sum _ i\sqrt{p_{*,i}}=\sqrt{(n+1)/2}>1$. Adding a point of $\delta \Sigma $ preserves the last inequality and keeps the sum of the coordinates below one, so $p_*+\delta \Sigma $ lies in every $P_ a$. All the standard basis vectors $e_ i$ belong to $P_ a$, and therefore \[  \psi _{P_ a}\geq \log  rac{\max _{1\leq i\leq n}|Z_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ n|Z_ i|^2}.  \] Hence the reference is locally bounded away from $o$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $\sum _ ip_ i\geq a/n$ on $P_ a$. When all $x_ i<0$, this yields $h_{P_ a}(x)\leq (a/n)\max _ i x_ i$, which tends to $-\infty $ as $z	o o$, and lemma 15.11.1 gives the pole at $o$. Local boundedness outside one point implies that all generic Lelong numbers along prime divisors vanish, and pulling back to the blowup at a different point introduces no pole. To test analyticity, fix positive $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n$ and approach $o$ along $|z_ i|^2=\mathrm{e}^{-R\lambda _ i}$, $R	o \infty $. Writing $y_ i=\sqrt{p_ i}$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives 15.44  egin{equation} \label{eq:curved-directional-coefficient} \min _{p\in P_ a}\sum _ i\lambda _ i p_ i = rac a{\sum _ i\lambda _ i^{-1}}=:d_ a(\lambda ),\qquad y_ i= rac{\sqrt a}{\lambda _ i\sum _ k\lambda _ k^{-1}}, \end{equation} where the minimizer satisfies $\sum _ ip_ i\leq a\leq 1$, so that it lies in $P_ a$. text: 15.11.4 Positive mass with a degenerate smooth residual A second family has a logarithmic pole whose resolution leaves a smooth residual form degenerating along a different exceptional divisor. Let $o=[1:0:\cdots :0]$ as in section 15.11.3 , and fix $q\ne o$ in $\mathbb P^ n$. On $X=\operatorname {Bl}_ q\mathbb P^ n$, keep $\Theta =\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. For $0<t<1$, put \[  \psi _ t=t\log \frac{\sum _{i=1}^ n|Z_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ n|Z_ i|^2}, \qquad K_ t=\{ p\in \Sigma :\textstyle \sum _ i p_ i\geq t\} .  \] On $T$, the function $\psi _ t+L$, a potential of $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ t$, equals $(1-t)L+t\log \sum _ i\mathrm{e}^{x_ i}$. It differs by a bounded function from \[  (1-t)h_\Sigma +t\max _ i x_ i=h_{K_ t},\qquad K_ t=(1-t)\Sigma +t\operatorname {conv}(e_1,\ldots ,e_ n).  \] Thus $\psi _ t\sim \psi _{K_ t}\sim \Phi _{K_ t}$, and $n!\operatorname {Vol}_ n(K_ t)=1-t^ n$. We call $\psi _ t$ the prototype of this ordinary type. Proposition 15.11.6 . Let $\tau :Z\to X$ be the blowup of the point of $X$ above $o$, with exceptional divisor $E_ o$, and denote the inverse image of $E_ q$ in $Z$ again by $E_ q$. There is a smooth semipositive closed form $\alpha _ t$ on $Z$ such that 15.45 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degenerate-projective-residual} (\pi \circ \tau )^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}} +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _ t\circ \pi \circ \tau )=\alpha _ t+t[E_ o]. \end{equation} It is positive away from $E_ q$, has rank exactly one at every point of $E_ q$, and satisfies $\int _ Z\alpha _ t^ n=1-t^ n>0$. Moreover, for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Theta )$ with the ordinary type of $\pi ^*\Phi _{K_ t}$, in particular for every solution of the equation in this type, the function $u\circ \tau -\psi _ t\circ \pi \circ \tau $ extends from $Z\setminus E_ o$ to a bounded $\alpha _ t$-plurisubharmonic function on $Z$. Proof. On $Y=\operatorname {Bl}_ o\mathbb P^ n$, let $\pi _ o$ be the blowdown map and $Q_ o:Y\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$ the map induced by the linear projection from $o$. As in the proof of lemma 15.11.2 , the incidence graph embedding shows that \[  \beta _ t=(1-t)\pi _ o^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}} +tQ_ o^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS},n-1}  \] is a Kähler form, where $\omega _{\mathrm{FS},n-1}$ is the Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^{n-1}$. Since the two centers are distinct, $Z$ is also the blowup $\sigma :Z\to Y$ of the point above $q$. Put $\alpha _ t=\sigma ^*\beta _ t$. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives ( 15.45 ); there is no term along $E_ q$, since $\psi _ t$ is locally bounded near $q$. In a blowup chart, $\sigma $ is $(s,w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)\mapsto (s,sw_2,\ldots ,sw_ n)$. At $s=0$ its differential has rank one and kills the $n-1$ tangent directions of $E_ q$. Positivity of $\beta _ t$ therefore gives the assertion about the rank; off $E_ q$ the map is biholomorphic. Write $H=\pi _ o^*[\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}]$ and $E=[E_ o]$ for the cohomology classes on $Y$. The current identity gives $[\beta _ t]=H-tE$. Since $H|_{E_ o}=0$, all mixed top intersections vanish. The normal bundle of $E_ o\cong \mathbb P^{n-1}$ is $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{n-1}}(-1)$, so $\int _ YE^ n=(-1)^{n-1}$. Therefore \[  \int _ Z\alpha _ t^ n=\int _ Y(H-tE)^ n=1-t^ n.  \] The first equality holds because $\sigma $ has degree one. Finally, if $u\sim \pi ^*\Phi _{K_ t}\sim \pi ^*\psi _ t$, then $u\circ \tau $ differs from the pulled-back prototype $\psi _ t\circ \pi \circ \tau $ by a bounded function off $E_ o$. By ( 15.45 ), after adding a local potential of $\alpha _ t$ this bounded difference becomes plurisubharmonic off $E_ o$, and it extends across $E_ o$ by lemma 1.3.7 . No Monge–Ampère product of unbounded potentials is involved. $\square$ Corollary 15.11.7 . Let $t_ j,t\in [t_{\min },t_{\max }]\subset (0,1)$ with $t_ j\to t$, and let $r_ j>0$ tend to $r>0$. The references $r_ j\pi ^*\Phi _{K_{t_ j}}$ satisfy the hypotheses of theorem 15.11.3 , so in particular the equation is solvable in the limiting ordinary type, and \[  \sup _ G|B_ j(G)-B(G)| \leq n|\log (r_ j/r)|+ \frac{nt_{\max }^{n-1}}{1-t_{\max }^ n}|t_ j-t|.  \] At continuous tests, all supporting sets consist of the normalized exponential probabilities of that theorem. At the endpoint $t=1$, where the mass vanishes, no equation with a positive bounded density is solvable in the ordinary type of the prototype $\pi ^*\psi _1$. Proof. Choose $p_{*,i}=t_{\max }/n$ and $\delta =(1-t_{\max })/2$; then $p_*+\delta \Sigma $ lies in every $K_ t$ with $t\leq t_{\max }$. For $s\geq t$, moving a point of $K_ t$ toward a vertex $e_ i$ until its coordinate sum reaches $s$ gives \[  d_ H(K_ s,K_ t)\leq \frac{\sqrt2}{1-t_{\max }}|s-t|.  \] Hence the stability theorem applies. Instead of its general bound, the derivative bound for $\log (1-t^ n)$ on $[t_{\min },t_{\max }]$ and the mass formula give the sharper estimate for the functionals. At $t=1$, the resolved residual form $\alpha _1$ is pulled back from $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, so $\int _ Z\alpha _1^ n=0$. The argument of proposition 15.11.6 shows that every potential of the ordinary type of $\pi ^*\psi _1$ has a bounded $\alpha _1$-plurisubharmonic remainder. Stokes' theorem for bounded products in a closed background gives this remainder mass zero, and positivity forces its Monge–Ampère measure to vanish. Thus no such potential can solve the equation with density $c\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$ for bounded $F$ and $c>0$. In contrast, the endpoint $a=1$ in corollary 15.11.5 has positive mass and remains solvable. $\square$ Scaling by $r>0$ multiplies both the resolved residual form and the divisor coefficient by $r$. Solvability is obtained on $X$ through the criterion of theorem 15.10.1 , without requiring the resolved residual form to be strictly positive. These criteria use closed projective backgrounds and fixed modifications; we do not know analogous convergence criteria for general nonclosed Hermitian backgrounds, for moving modifications, or for unrestricted degenerations of the singularities. Moreover, the supporting probabilities here only identify the limiting functional: we make no claim about convergence of the solutions or of weighted adjoint products.

text: 15.12.1 A norm defined by the critical scalar Mixed products turn the comparison of critical scalars into a triangle inequality for $n$th roots of densities, and the subsolution estimate associated with the strict barrier gives continuity in the corresponding Lebesgue norm. Fix $1<q<p$ and set $\ell =nq$. On real $L^\ell (\mathrm{d}V)$ define \[  N(a)= \begin{cases}  c(|a|^ n)^{-1/n},& a\ne 0,\\  0,& a=0. \end{cases}  \] Proposition 15.12.2 . The function $N$ is a lattice norm on $L^\ell (\mathrm{d}V)$, that is, a norm satisfying $N(a)\leq N(b)$ whenever $|a|\leq |b|$. There is $C_ q<\infty $, depending only on $X,\theta ,\mathrm{d}V$ and $q$, such that 15.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:critical-scalar-norm-bound} N(a)\leq C_ q\| a\| _\ell ,\qquad |N(a)-N(b)|\leq C_ q\| a-b\| _\ell . \end{equation} Consequently, for nonzero $g,h\geq 0$ in $L^ q$, \[  |c(g)^{-1/n}-c(h)^{-1/n}| \leq C_ q\| g-h\| _ q^{1/n}.  \] Proof. If a potential $v$ of minimal type satisfies $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\geq d g\, \mathrm{d}V$, then $d\leq c(g)$, since otherwise comparison with a critical potential for $g$ contradicts part (1) of corollary 14.12.3 . Hence $g\leq h$ implies $c(g)\geq c(h)$. Uniqueness of the critical scalar also gives $c(tg)=c(g)/t$ for $t>0$. These facts prove that $N$ is monotone and absolutely homogeneous, and positivity follows from $0<c(g)<\infty $. For the triangle inequality, let $a,b\geq 0$ be nonzero, put $A=N(a)$ and $B=N(b)$, and choose critical potentials $v_ a,v_ b$ with measures $(a/A)^ n\mathrm{d}V$ and $(b/B)^ n\mathrm{d}V$. On every relatively compact subset of $\Omega $, ( 1.23 ) gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta \left(\frac{A v_ a+B v_ b}{A+B}\right) \geq \left(\frac{a+b}{A+B}\right)^ n\mathrm{d}V,  \] where both potentials are locally bounded. Exhausting $\Omega $ gives the inequality on $X$, since $X\setminus \Omega $ has zero smooth volume. The averaged potential has minimal type, so the first paragraph gives $N(a+b)\leq A+B$. The cases where $a$ or $b$ vanishes are trivial, and for real functions we use $|a+b|\leq |a|+|b|$ and monotonicity. Next, apply lemma 14.13.1 with $\eta =V_\theta $ to nonnegative densities of $L^ q$ norm at most one. It gives a uniform $m>0$ and subsolutions of minimal type, hence $c(g)\geq m$ for each such nonzero density. For $a\ne 0$, take $g=|a|^ n/\| a\| _\ell ^ n$, which has $L^ q$ norm one. Homogeneity gives $N(a)\leq m^{-1/n}\| a\| _\ell $, which is the first bound in ( 15.52 ), and the reverse triangle inequality gives the second. text: Proposition 15.12.2 . The function $N$ is a lattice norm on $L^\ell (\mathrm{d}V)$, that is, a norm satisfying $N(a)\leq N(b)$ whenever $|a|\leq |b|$. There is $C_ q<\infty $, depending only on $X,\theta ,\mathrm{d}V$ and $q$, such that 15.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:critical-scalar-norm-bound} N(a)\leq C_ q\| a\| _\ell ,\qquad |N(a)-N(b)|\leq C_ q\| a-b\| _\ell . \end{equation} Consequently, for nonzero $g,h\geq 0$ in $L^ q$, \[  |c(g)^{-1/n}-c(h)^{-1/n}| \leq C_ q\| g-h\| _ q^{1/n}.  \] Proof. If a potential $v$ of minimal type satisfies $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\geq d g\, \mathrm{d}V$, then $d\leq c(g)$, since otherwise comparison with a critical potential for $g$ contradicts part (1) of corollary 14.12.3 . Hence $g\leq h$ implies $c(g)\geq c(h)$. Uniqueness of the critical scalar also gives $c(tg)=c(g)/t$ for $t>0$. These facts prove that $N$ is monotone and absolutely homogeneous, and positivity follows from $0<c(g)<\infty $. For the triangle inequality, let $a,b\geq 0$ be nonzero, put $A=N(a)$ and $B=N(b)$, and choose critical potentials $v_ a,v_ b$ with measures $(a/A)^ n\mathrm{d}V$ and $(b/B)^ n\mathrm{d}V$. On every relatively compact subset of $\Omega $, ( 1.23 ) gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta \left(\frac{A v_ a+B v_ b}{A+B}\right) \geq \left(\frac{a+b}{A+B}\right)^ n\mathrm{d}V,  \] where both potentials are locally bounded. Exhausting $\Omega $ gives the inequality on $X$, since $X\setminus \Omega $ has zero smooth volume. The averaged potential has minimal type, so the first paragraph gives $N(a+b)\leq A+B$. The cases where $a$ or $b$ vanishes are trivial, and for real functions we use $|a+b|\leq |a|+|b|$ and monotonicity. Next, apply lemma 14.13.1 with $\eta =V_\theta $ to nonnegative densities of $L^ q$ norm at most one. It gives a uniform $m>0$ and subsolutions of minimal type, hence $c(g)\geq m$ for each such nonzero density. For $a\ne 0$, take $g=|a|^ n/\| a\| _\ell ^ n$, which has $L^ q$ norm one. Homogeneity gives $N(a)\leq m^{-1/n}\| a\| _\ell $, which is the first bound in ( 15.52 ), and the reverse triangle inequality gives the second. Applying the second bound to $g^{1/n},h^{1/n}$ and using $|g^{1/n}-h^{1/n}|^ n\leq |g-h|$ proves the last assertion. $\square$

Lemma 15.12.5 . The functional $\mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}$ is finite, concave, decreasing and $\lambda ^{-1}$-Lipschitz for the uniform norm on $C(X)$. It satisfies \[  \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(0)=w_\lambda (x),\qquad \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r+b) =\mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r)-b/\lambda .  \] There is a probability measure $
u _{\lambda ,x}$ such that, for every $r\in C(X)$ and every $s$ admissible for $r$ in ( 15.59 ), 15.60  egin{equation} \label{eq:selection-forcing-support} \lambda s(x)+\int _ Xr\, \mathrm{d}
u _{\lambda ,x} \leq \lambda w_\lambda (x). \end{equation} Proof. By part (2) of corollary 14.12.3 , $w_\lambda $ is the greatest admissible potential for $r=0$. If $m=\min _ Xr$ and $M=\max _ Xr$, then $w_\lambda -M/\lambda $ is admissible for $r$, and translating any potential admissible for $r$ by $m/\lambda $ makes it admissible for $r=0$. Hence \[  w_\lambda (x)-M/\lambda \leq \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r) \leq w_\lambda (x)-m/\lambda .  \] The mixed density inequality on $\Omega $ and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality show that a convex combination of potentials admissible for $r_0$ and $r_1$ is admissible for the same convex combination of the forcing terms. Approximating the two suprema at $x$ proves concavity. Inclusion of the admissible classes proves monotonicity, and translation by constants proves the translation rule and the Lipschitz bound. Now apply the Hahn–Banach construction in the proof of theorem 15.2.1 to $-\lambda \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}$ at zero. This functional is finite, continuous, convex and increasing, and it satisfies $-\lambda \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r+b)=-\lambda \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r)+b$ for constants $b$. The same tests with nonnegative functions and constants show that its subgradient is a probability measure $
u _{\lambda ,x}$. The resulting supporting inequality, combined with $s(x)\leq \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r)$, gives ( 15.60 ); it is not necessary that the supremum be attained. $\square$

title: 15.13 Selection for logarithmic models on products
