text: 15.13 Selection for logarithmic models on products For a logarithmic reference with a positive residual background, removing the divisor turns the singular exponential equation into a bounded equation. On a product with a curve, the selected residual can then be determined by the Green operator. This also controls simultaneous changes of the reference, background and density, for which the centering constant must follow the changing data. Let $(Y,\kappa )$ be a connected compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $k\geq 1$, with $\int _ Y\kappa ^ k=1$, and put $X=\mathbb P^1\times Y$, $N=k+1$. Write $\omega _1$ for the mass-one Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^1$ and $\mathrm{d}W=\omega _1\wedge \kappa ^ k$; pullbacks to $X$ are implicit. Fix $a,d>0$, a smooth positive nonconstant function $b$ on $\mathbb P^1$, and a continuous positive function $H$ on $\mathbb P^1$. Set \[  \begin{aligned}  \theta & =(a+d)\omega _1+b\kappa ,& \eta & =a\omega _1+b\kappa ,\\  f& =N b^ kH,& m& =\int _{\mathbb P^1}H\omega _1,\qquad c_0=\frac am. \end{aligned}  \] Both forms are positive and nonclosed: the component $\mathrm{d}b\wedge \kappa $ of horizontal degree one cannot cancel the vertical component $b\, \mathrm{d}\kappa $. For homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:Z_1]$, put \[  \ell =\frac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2},\qquad D=\{ Z_0=0\} \times Y,\qquad \psi =d\log \ell .  \] The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\eta +d[D]$.

title: 15.13.1 The ordinary model and the greatest solutions
search_title: The ordinary model and the greatest solutions
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.13.1 The ordinary model and the greatest solutions Put $K=a+d$, $R=a/d$ and $C_*=K\log (K/d)-a\log (a/d)$. In the coordinate $z=Z_1/Z_0$ define 15.65 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-product-model} \phi _{a,d}=\begin{cases}  0,& |z|^2\leq R,\\  a\log |z|^2+C_*-K\log (1+|z|^2),& |z|^2>R, \end{cases} \qquad \phi _{a,d}|_ D=-\infty . \end{equation} Proposition 15.13.1 . The function $\phi _{a,d}$ is an ordinary model reference for $\theta $, with \[  P_\theta [\psi ]=P_\theta [\phi _{a,d}]=\phi _{a,d},\qquad \psi \leq \phi _{a,d}\leq \psi +C_*,\qquad \sup _ X\phi _{a,d}=0.  \] For $d/(a+d)<\delta <1$, the envelope $P_{\delta \theta }(\phi _{a,d})$ is not identically $-\infty $. The model has finite positive Monge–Ampère measure \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\phi _{a,d}) =N b^ kK\mathbf1_{\{ |z|^2<R\} }\, \mathrm{d}W.  \] The difference $\phi _{a,d}-\psi $ extends continuously across $D$. If $(a_ j,d_ j)\to (a,d)$ in $(0,+\infty )^2$, these residual extensions converge uniformly. Proof. First take the ordinary envelope on the curve with background $K\omega _1$ and obstacle $\min (\psi +C,0)$. Rotation of $z$ preserves both the obstacle and the admissible family, so the envelope is rotation invariant. With $s=\log |z|^2$ and $F(s)=K\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ s)$, its profile plus $F$ is convex and lies below $F$. The comparison with $\psi +C$ bounds its final slope by $a$. At $s_*=\log R$, one has $F'(s_*)=a$. Above $s_*$, convexity and the final slope bound give \[  u(s)+F(s)\leq F(s_*)+a(s-s_*),  \] and below $s_*$ the obstacle gives $u\leq 0$. The function in ( 15.65 ) attains both bounds. Its convex profile, including its logarithmic value at infinity, gives a curve potential, and direct calculation gives $\psi \leq \phi _{a,d}\leq \psi +C_*$. It is therefore a competitor for every $C\geq C_*$, so the curve envelope is exactly $\phi _{a,d}$. A product competitor restricts to each curve $\mathbb P^1\times \{ y\} $ as either the constant $-\infty $ or a curve competitor. It is thus bounded above by $\phi _{a,d}$. Conversely, the curve model is a product competitor because the vertical form $b\kappa $ is positive. Hence the product envelope is the same function. Ordinary-type invariance of the singularity envelope gives its model property. Moreover, \[  \delta \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =(\delta K-d)\omega _1+\delta b\kappa +d[D]\geq 0,  \] which proves the smaller-background assertion. Off $D$, the horizontal curvature of $\phi _{a,d}$ is $K\mathbf1_{\{ |z|^2<R\} }\omega _1$. The first derivatives of its convex profile agree at $R$, so there is no boundary-circle atom. Expanding the product off $D$ gives the displayed measure, and the non-pluripolar product assigns $D$ zero mass. Finally, in terms of $\ell $ the residual extension is \[  \phi _{a,d}-\psi =\begin{cases}  -d\log \ell ,& \ell \geq d/K,\\  a\log (1-\ell )+C_*,& \ell <d/K. \end{cases}  \] The formulas agree at the moving interface and extend to both endpoints. On compact positive parameter ranges each logarithm is used away from its singular endpoint. Joint continuity on the resulting compact set proves uniform variation. $\square$ Lemma 15.13.2 . For every $\sigma >0$, the equation 15.70 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-product-exponential} \mathrm{MA}_\theta (s_\sigma )=\mathrm{e}^{\sigma s_\sigma }f\, \mathrm{d}W \end{equation} has a solution of ordinary type $\phi _{a,d}$, unique in that type. It is the greatest exponential subsolution among all $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi _{a,d}$, and its measure has finite mass. Proof. The one-sided ordinary class has the description 15.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-one-sided-removal} u\preceq \psi \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u=\psi +r,\quad r\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta ),\qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi +r) =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\eta (r). \end{equation} Indeed, $u\preceq \psi $ gives $\nu (u,D)\geq d$. Divisorial removal, lemma 1.17.1 , shows that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-d[D]\geq 0$. Thus the locally integrable difference $u-\psi $ has an $\eta $-plurisubharmonic representative $r$. The equality $u=\psi +r$ holds off $D$ by canonical equality and on $D$ because both sides equal $-\infty $. Conversely, adding $\psi $ to $r$ adds the positive current $d[D]$; since $r$ has a finite compact upper bound, the one-sided comparison follows. Off $D$ the currents agree, so finite-level locality identifies their extended products, including at any additional poles of $r$. Both measures give $D$ zero mass, proving the global equality. The bounded ordinary type corresponds exactly to bounded $r$, as in theorem 15.9.1 . The function $g_\sigma =\mathrm{e}^{\sigma \psi }f$ extends continuously by zero on $D$ and is positive elsewhere. Since $\eta >0$, theorem 10.1.2 gives a continuous solution $R_\sigma $ of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\eta (R_\sigma )=\mathrm{e}^{\sigma R_\sigma }g_\sigma \, \mathrm{d}W.  \] For this bounded density, the greatest solution of theorem 14.34.1 is bounded and coincides with $R_\sigma $ by corollary 10.2.4 . Thus it dominates every $\eta $-plurisubharmonic exponential subsolution. The correspondence ( 15.71 ) transfers this order to the entire one-sided ordinary class and gives $s_\sigma =\psi +R_\sigma $. Bounded residual uniqueness gives uniqueness in the ordinary type. The bounded residual equation has finite mass, so the singular equation does too. $\square$

title: Theorem 15.13.3
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 15.13.3 . Let $a_ j,d_ j>0$ converge to $a,d>0$, let smooth positive functions $b_ j$ converge uniformly to $b$, and let continuous positive functions $H_ j$ converge uniformly to $H$. For any $\sigma _ j>0$ tending to zero, put \[  \begin{aligned}  \theta _ j& =(a_ j+d_ j)\omega _1+b_ j\kappa ,& \psi _ j& =d_ j\log \ell ,& \phi _ j& =\phi _{a_ j,d_ j},\\  f_ j& =N b_ j^ kH_ j,& m_ j& =\int _{\mathbb P^1}H_ j\omega _1,& c_{0,j}& =a_ j/m_ j. \end{aligned}  \] Let $s_ j$ be the greatest solution of ( 15.70 ) for these data, and set $v_ j=s_ j-\sup _ Xs_ j$, $c_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j\sup _ Xs_ j}$. Then \[  v_ j\longrightarrow v_0=\psi +w_0-S_0,\qquad s_ j-\sigma _ j^{-1}\log c_{0,j}\longrightarrow s_0=\psi +w_0-J  \] in $L^1(X)$, in capacity, and locally uniformly on $X\setminus D$. Moreover, 15.77 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-scalar-error} c_ j\longrightarrow c_0,\qquad \sigma _ j^{-1}\log (c_ j/c_{0,j})\longrightarrow S_0-J, \end{equation} and $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _ j}(v_ j)\to c_0 f\, \mathrm{d}W$ in total variation. The limit has ordinary type $\phi _{a,d}$ and belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\phi _{a,d})$, with \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_0)=c_0 f\, \mathrm{d}W.  \] There is no restriction on the relative rates of parameter and exponent convergence. Proof. We construct uniformly bounded residuals on the curve, then use their equation to determine both the normalized limit and the scalar error. Uniform construction. The kernel has uniformly integrable logarithmic tails and $C_ G=\sup _ x\int |G(x,z)|\omega _1(z)<\infty $. These facts follow by rotation invariance and the radial integral of $|\log \ell +1|$ on $0<\ell <1$; the Poincaré–Lelong formula and $\int _0^1\log \ell \, \mathrm{d}\ell =-1$ give its curvature and mean. Truncating the kernel shows that convolution of bounded densities is continuous. Temporarily omit subscripts. On continuous mean-zero functions on the curve define \[  T_\sigma (w)=G*(A(w)-a),\qquad A(w)=\frac{aH\mathrm{e}^{\sigma (\psi +w)}}{Z(w)},\qquad Z(w)=\int _{\mathbb P^1}H\mathrm{e}^{\sigma (\psi +w)}\omega _1.  \] For all late parameters choose fixed bounds $a\leq a_{\max }$, $d\leq d_{\max }$ and $0<h_{\min }\leq H\leq h_{\max }$. Put $B=4a_{\max }h_{\max }/h_{\min }$ and choose $R_0>C_ G(B+a_{\max })$. On the ball $\| w\| _\infty \leq R_0$, for sufficiently small $\sigma $, \[  Z(w)\geq \frac{h_{\min }\mathrm{e}^{-\sigma R_0}}{1+\sigma d_{\max }} \geq h_{\min }/2,\qquad 0\leq A(w)\leq B.  \] Here $\int \ell ^{\sigma d}\omega _1=(1+\sigma d)^{-1}$. Thus $T_\sigma $ maps the mean-zero ball into itself. Since $\int A(w)\omega _1=a$, its density derivative in direction $h$ is \[  \sigma A(w)\left(h-a^{-1}\int hA(w)\omega _1\right).  \] It follows that $\| T_\sigma (w)-T_\sigma (v)\| _\infty \leq 2\sigma B C_ G\| w-v\| _\infty $. The map is a contraction for all sufficiently small exponents, uniformly over the late parameters. Its fixed point $w_ j$ has mean zero and $\| w_ j\| _\infty \leq R_0$. Write $Z_ j=Z(w_ j)$ and $A_ j=A(w_ j)$. The fixed-point equation gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j=(A_ j-a_ j)\omega _1$, and the potential 15.78 \begin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-exponential-residual} \psi _ j+w_ j+\sigma _ j^{-1}\log (a_ j/Z_ j) \end{equation} has residual form $A_ j\omega _1+b_ j\kappa $, continuous and semipositive. On coordinate balls, mollification of $w_ j$ converges together with its continuous complex Hessian. The local bounded product, expanded after a common strict smooth correction, therefore equals $N b_ j^ kA_ j\, \mathrm{d}W$. Removing $D$ identifies the singular product with the same measure. The identity \[  N b_ j^ kA_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j(\psi _ j+w_ j)}(a_ j/Z_ j)f_ j  \] shows that ( 15.78 ) solves the exponential equation in the ordinary type. By lemma 15.13.2 , it is $s_ j$. Residual and normalized limits. Uniform boundedness and dominated convergence give $Z_ j\to m$ and $A_ j\to A_0$ in $L^1(\omega _1)$, with a common bound on $A_ j$. For uniformly bounded densities $F_ j\to 0$ in $L^1$, one has \[  \| G*F_ j\| _\infty \leq \| F_ j\| _\infty \sup _ x\int _{\{ |G(x,z)|>M\} }|G(x,z)|\omega _1(z) +M\| F_ j\| _1.  \] First letting $j\to \infty $ and then $M\to \infty $ proves $w_ j\to w_0$ uniformly. Although $A_ j=0$ on $D$ and $A_0>0$ there, the $L^1$ convergence suffices for this argument. Put $S_ j=\sup _ X(\psi _ j+w_ j)$. A point with $\ell =1$ supplies a uniformly bounded competing value. Since $d_ j\geq d_{\min }>0$, the upper bound $d_{\min }\log \ell +R_0$ tends uniformly to $-\infty $ near $D$, so all maximizing points stay in a fixed compact subset of $X\setminus D$. Uniform convergence there gives $S_ j\to S_0$. Hence $v_ j=\psi _ j+w_ j-S_ j$ has the asserted $L^1$ and local uniform limits. For capacity convergence, the complements of $\{ \psi <-T\} $ are compact subsets of $X\setminus D$. Choose a fixed Hermitian form for which $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic and apply ( 1.26 ); their omitted sublevels have capacity at most $C/T$. Local uniform convergence, followed by $T\to \infty $, proves convergence in capacity, with the common poles omitted. The measure formula and uniform convergence of $b_ j$ give total-variation convergence to $N b^ kA_0\, \mathrm{d}W=c_0 f\, \mathrm{d}W$. The same bounded product calculation gives this equation for $v_0$. The residual extensions in proposition 15.13.1 show directly that $v_0\sim \phi _{a,d}$. Choose $C$ with $v_0\geq \phi _{a,d}-C$. For every $t\geq 1$, the potential $q_ t=\phi _{a,d}-tC$ satisfies \[  t^{-1}q_ t+(1-t^{-1})\phi _{a,d}\leq v_0,  \] which proves membership in the relative envelope class by definition 13.4.1 . Scalar centering. The exact formula is $c_ j=a_ j\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j S_ j}/Z_ j$. In the difference quotient \[  \frac{Z_ j-m_ j}{\sigma _ j} =\int H_ j\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j(\psi _ j+w_ j)}-1}{\sigma _ j}\omega _1,  \] the negative part is bounded by $h_{\max }(d_{\max }|\log \ell |+R_0)$ and the positive part by a constant. Dominated convergence gives a limit $\int H(\psi +w_0)\omega _1=mJ$. Since $m_ j\to m>0$, \[  \sigma _ j^{-1}\log (Z_ j/m_ j)\longrightarrow J.  \] The identity $c_ j/c_{0,j}=m_ j\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j S_ j}/Z_ j$ proves ( 15.77 ). Subtracting $\sigma _ j^{-1}\log c_{0,j}$ in ( 15.78 ) leaves $\psi _ j+w_ j-\sigma _ j^{-1}\log (Z_ j/m_ j)$, proving the centered limit in all three topologies. $\square$

title: 15.13.3 The critical coefficient and separated order

text: 15.13.3 The critical coefficient and separated order Corollary 15.13.4 . For the fixed data, $c_0$ is the largest coefficient $c>0$ for which $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi _{a,d}$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)\geq c f\, \mathrm{d}W$. Among separated potentials $u=\psi +r(x)\preceq \phi _{a,d}$, the critical subsolutions are exactly the translates of $\psi +w_0$. Thus $v_0$ is their unique supremum-zero member, and $s_0$ is their greatest member with $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}\nu _0\leq 0$. Proof. For a separated critical subsolution, ( 15.71 ) and the product expansion give $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{a\omega _1}(r)\geq A_0\omega _1$. Closed curve truncations have mass $a$, so the non-pluripolar measure has mass at most $a$. Since $\int A_0\omega _1=a$, it must equal $A_0\omega _1$. The positive closed current $a\omega _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r$ also has mass $a$, so it has no remaining measure on the pole set. Consequently $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=(A_0-a)\omega _1$ as distributions, and $r=w_0+C$ because harmonic distributions on $\mathbb P^1$ are constant. Supremum zero gives $C=-S_0$, while the mean condition gives $C\leq -J$. For a general $u\preceq \phi _{a,d}$ with coefficient $c>0$, write $u=\psi +r$ by ( 15.71 ) and put $B_ r=\sup _ Xr$. Since $\psi \leq 0$, the potential $u+\sigma ^{-1}\log c-B_ r$ is an exponential subsolution for every $\sigma >0$. Greatestness gives \[  u+\sigma ^{-1}\log c-B_ r\leq s_\sigma .  \] At a point off $D$ where $r$ is finite, subtract $\sigma ^{-1}\log c_0$, multiply by $\sigma $ and use the fixed-data case of theorem 15.13.3 . This yields $\log c\leq \log c_0$. The potential $v_0$ attains $c_0$. $\square$ The scalar in the centering follows the varying data. Replacing $c_{0,j}$ by $c_0$ adds $\sigma _ j^{-1}\log (c_{0,j}/c_0)$ to the centered potential, and this term need not vanish. For example, take $a=1$, $d=1/4$, $H=1$ and $b=2+t$, where $t$ is the sphere height. Then $w_0=0$, $S_0=0$, $J=-1/4$ and $c_0=1$, so $s_0=\psi +1/4$ and the scalar-error limit is $1/4$. If $a_ j=1+\sqrt{\sigma _ j}$ and the other data are fixed, the appropriate centering uses $c_{0,j}=a_ j$. Centering by $1$ instead adds \[  \frac{\log (1+\sqrt{\sigma _ j})}{\sigma _ j}\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] These examples can be taken on a non-Kähler manifold by choosing $Y$ to be the scalar Hopf surface with its Hermitian form rescaled to unit volume. The product cannot be Kähler, since a Kähler form would restrict to one on the Hopf fiber. The pole divisor remains present in the selected ordinary type.

title: Lemma 15.13.5
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Lemma 15.13.5 . Let $V>0$ be continuous on $\mathbb P^1$, and let $T$ be a finite signed measure such that \[  \int _{\mathbb P^1}(\Delta f-Vf)\, \mathrm{d}T=0 \qquad (f\in C^\infty (\mathbb P^1)).  \] Then $T=0$. Proof. Let $H_ t$ be the sphere heat operator. On spherical harmonics of degree $\ell $, it acts by $\mathrm{e}^{-t\ell (\ell +1)}$. The harmonic series defines a smooth heat solution for $t>0$; for smooth initial functions, the maximum principle gives positivity and contraction in the uniform norm. Density of smooth functions extends $H_ t$ to a positive, strongly continuous contraction on $C(\mathbb P^1)$. Choose $M\geq \max V$ and define \[  R_ Mg=\int _0^\infty \mathrm{e}^{-Mt}H_ tg\, \mathrm{d}t.  \] Then $\| R_ M\| \leq M^{-1}$ and $(M-\Delta )R_ Mg=g$ in distributions. For any $g\in C(\mathbb P^1)$, the map \[  f\longmapsto R_ M((M-V)f-g)  \] contracts by at most $1-\min V/M<1$. Its continuous fixed point satisfies $\Delta f=Vf+g$ in distributions, with a continuous right-hand side. The functions $f_\varepsilon =H_\varepsilon f$ are smooth and satisfy \[  f_\varepsilon \longrightarrow f,\qquad \Delta f_\varepsilon =H_\varepsilon (Vf+g)\longrightarrow Vf+g  \] uniformly. Thus $(\Delta -V)f_\varepsilon \to g$ uniformly. Testing against the finite measure $T$ gives $\int g\, \mathrm{d}T=0$ for every continuous $g$, hence $T=0$. $\square$

Example 15.13.8 . Take $a=1$, $d=1/4$, $q=1$, and let $t$ be the sphere height \[  t= rac{|Z_0|^2-|Z_1|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2},\qquad b=2+t,\qquad H=A=	frac 12+|t|.  \] Here $c_0=1$ and $F=\log (2bA)$ is Lipschitz but not $C^1$. The residual has continuous positive coefficients with the same loss of differentiability. Its supporting probability differs from normalized Monge–Ampère volume: \[  \int _ X\Omega ^2=4,\qquad \int _ Xt\, \mathrm{d}
u =0,\qquad \int _ Xt\,  rac{\Omega ^2}{4}= rac5{24}.  \] Even for smooth constant $H$, approximation of the pole by globally smooth potentials need not recover the weak adjoint. For $H=a$, so that $w_0=0$ and $
u =\mathrm{d}W$, put \[  \psi _\delta =d\log (\ell +\delta (1-\ell )),\qquad P_\delta =\omega _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _\delta /d),\qquad 0<\delta \leq 1.  \] The smooth potentials $\psi _\delta $ decrease pointwise to $\psi $, converge in $L^1$ and smoothly off $D$, but the classical adjoint probabilities of $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta $ converge to \[   rac{a\omega _1+d\delta _ p}{a+d}\wedge \omega _2, \qquad p=\{ Z_0=0\} .  \] This limit assigns mass $d/(a+d)>0$ to $D$, and the weighted currents also retain a nonzero divisor component. Proof. The height $t$ is uniform on $[-1,1]$, so $\int A\omega _1=1$ and $\int tA\omega _1=0$. Since $\Omega ^2=2bA\, \mathrm{d}W$, its mass is four and its normalized height moment is \[   rac12\int _{-1}^1 t^2(	frac 12+|t|)\,  rac{\mathrm{d}t}{2} = rac5{24}.  \] The weight is $1/(2b)$ and $
u =A\, \mathrm{d}W$. Moreover, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	heta =-2t\, \mathrm{d}W$, so the background has no smooth positive Gauduchon potential perturbation. For the smoothing family, direct differentiation gives \[   rac{P_\delta }{\omega _1} = rac{4\delta }{((1+\delta )+(1-\delta )t)^2}.  \] It is positive of mass one and converges weakly to $\delta _ p$. Thus the positive smooth forms are $\widehat\Omega _\delta =a\omega _1+dP_\delta +b\omega _2$. Their classical weights and probabilities are \[  \widehatho _\delta = rac1{2(a+d)b},\qquad \widehat
u _\delta = rac{a\omega _1+dP_\delta }{a+d}\wedge \omega _2.  \] The weighted forms are closed, so these are the normalized classical adjoints. Their limits follow from the curve measure convergence. In particular, the weighted-current limit contains $d[D]/(2(a+d)b(p))$. These smoothings fill the pole and do not satisfy the fixed-divisor and uniform-residual hypotheses of proposition 15.13.7 . $\square$

text: 15.14 Residual regularity in radial singularity types Subtracting a prescribed singularity separates regularity of the residual from the pole of the solution. On projective space, central radial mass gives an exact inverse for the equation. A relative density error then controls the residual through two derivatives, even when the density is merely integrable at the pole. The inverse also permits smooth crossing of density zeros away from it. The pole is the one used in lemma 14.29.1 ; here its ordinary type is fixed while the density varies.

title: 15.14.1 The prescribed ordinary type
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.14.1 The prescribed ordinary type Let $k\geq 2$, let $\kappa $ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ k$ with $\int \kappa ^ k=1$, and put $o=[1:0:\cdots :0]$. On the chart $Z_0\ne 0$ write $z_ i=Z_ i/Z_0$ and set \[  r=\sum _{j=1}^ k|z_ j|^2,\qquad P=\frac r{1+r},\qquad T=1-\log P, \qquad u_\alpha =1-T^\alpha \quad (0<\alpha <1).  \] The ratio $P=\sum _{i=1}^ k|Z_ i|^2/\sum _{i=0}^ k|Z_ i|^2$ is global. Give $u_\alpha $ its canonical value $-\infty $ at $o$ and value zero on the hyperplane $Z_0=0$. Primes denote differentiation in $r$, and $b_\alpha =k(1-\alpha )>0$ throughout this section. Lemma 15.14.1 . The canonical $u_\alpha $ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic and smooth off $o$. Its non-pluripolar measure has a positive density $q_\alpha $ of mass one, in $L^1$ and in no $L^ p$, $p>1$. Distinct $\alpha $ give distinct ordinary types, although all their multiplier ideals are trivial. Proof. Plurisubharmonicity, smoothness off the pole, unit mass and the $L^ p$ assertions are those of lemma 14.29.1 . To fix the profile used in the inverse below, put 15.80 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-residual-baseline} \Phi _\alpha =\log (1+r)+u_\alpha ,\qquad Q_\alpha =r\Phi _\alpha '=P+\alpha (1-P)T^{\alpha -1}. \end{equation} The tangential and radial eigenvalues are $Q_\alpha /r$ and $Q_\alpha '$, both positive. Radial determinant integration, with the constant fixed by $\Phi =\log (1+r)$, gives 15.81 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-residual-flux} \int _{a<|z|^2<b}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )^ k=Q(b)^ k-Q(a)^ k, \qquad Q=r\Phi '. \end{equation} Since $Q_\alpha (0)=0$ and $Q_\alpha (\infty )=1$, the density is 15.82 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-residual-baseline-density} q_\alpha =\frac{(Q_\alpha ^ k)'}{(P^ k)'}>0. \end{equation} Smoothness on the hyperplane and the exclusion of the canonical pole in the product leave no further measure. Near $r=0$, with $L=1-\log r$, direct differentiation gives 15.83 \begin{align} \label{eq:radial-residual-asymptotics} Q_\alpha & \sim \alpha L^{\alpha -1},&  Q_\alpha '& \sim \frac{\alpha (1-\alpha )}rL^{\alpha -2},\\  (Q_\alpha ^ k)'& \sim \frac{k\alpha ^ k(1-\alpha )}rL^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}.\nonumber \end{align} In particular $q_\alpha \sim \alpha ^ k(1-\alpha )r^{-k}L^{-1-b_\alpha }$; the radial volume has order $r^{k-1}\, \mathrm{d}r$, recovering these integrability assertions. The types for different $\alpha $ are ordinarily distinct, since their difference is unbounded at $o$. Yet every $\mathcal I(tu_\alpha )$ is trivial for finite $t>0$: integrability of the constant function reduces near $o$ to $\int ^\infty \mathrm{e}^{-kL+tL^\alpha }\, \mathrm{d}L<\infty $. Ordinary type information here is strictly finer than this ideal information. $\square$

title: 15.14.2 Density criterion and exact inverse
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
15.14.2 Density criterion and exact inverse Here “radial” means depending only on $r$ in the displayed chart. The smoothness assumption along the hyperplane includes a smooth profile in $t=1/r$ near $t=0$. Theorem 15.14.2 . Let $q\ge 0$ be radial, smooth on $\mathbb P^ k\setminus \{ o\} $, including the hyperplane at infinity, and satisfy $\int q\kappa ^ k=1$. Suppose that for some $\delta ,A,r_0>0$, 15.84  egin{equation} \label{eq:radial-residual-density-error} \left| rac{q(r)}{q_\alpha (r)}-1ight|\le Ar^\delta \quad (0<r<r_0). \end{equation} Then there is a genuine radial $\kappa $-psh potential $U$, normalized to have value zero on the hyperplane, with \[  \mathrm{MA}_\kappa (U)=q\kappa ^ k, \qquad U\sim u_\alpha .  \] Its residual $R=U-u_\alpha $ off $o$ extends continuously across $o$, with value $R_0$, and for small $r$ satisfies 15.85  egin{equation} \label{eq:radial-residual-estimates}  egin{aligned}  |R-R_0|& \le Cr^\delta L^{\alpha -2},\  |R'|& \le Cr^{\delta -1}L^{\alpha -2},\qquad |R''|\le Cr^{\delta -2}L^{\alpha -2}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} It is locally $C^{0,\min \{ 1,2\delta \} }$. For $\delta \ge  rac12$ it extends $C^1$ with zero gradient at $o$; for $\delta \ge 1$ it extends $C^2$ with zero Hessian at $o$. No derivative hypothesis on the error in ( 15.84 ) is needed for these conclusions. The potential and its residual are smooth on $\mathbb P^ k\setminus \{ o\} $, including every density zero there. The tail condition ensures positive cumulative central mass; local density smoothness alone is not the criterion. Proof. Let 15.88  egin{equation} \label{eq:radial-residual-inverse}  egin{aligned}  M(r)& =\int _{|z|^2<r}q\kappa ^ k,&  Q(r)& =M(r)^{1/k},\  U'(r)& = rac{Q(r)-P(r)}r,&  U(\infty )& =0. \end{aligned} \end{equation} The tail condition makes $q$ positive near $o$, so $M(r)>0$ for every $r>0$. One has $M'=q(P^ k)'\ge 0$, $Q'\ge 0$ and $M(\infty )=1$. Thus the positive root defining $Q$ is smooth for every finite $r>0$, even where $q$ vanishes. This proves smoothness across all finite density zeros without a vanishing-order assumption. In $t=1/r$, the tail $1-M$ is the integral from $0$ to $t$ of the smooth density profile times $-\mathrm{d}(1+t)^{-k}/\mathrm{d}t$. Thus $M$ and $Q$ are smooth there, with $Q(0)=1$ in that coordinate. The equation $\mathrm{d}U/\mathrm{d}t=-(Q-P)/t$ is smooth there, since $Q-P$ vanishes at $t=0$. This both defines the normalization and proves smoothness along the full hyperplane. From ( 15.84 ) and ( 15.83 ), 15.91  egin{equation} \label{eq:radial-residual-tail} |M-Q_\alpha ^ k| \le C\int _0^ r s^{\delta -1}(1-\log s)^{-1-b_\alpha }\, \mathrm{d}s \le Cr^\delta L^{-1-b_\alpha }. \end{equation} The last inequality follows by writing $s=r\mathrm{e}^{-y}$ and bounding $\int _0^\infty \mathrm{e}^{-\delta y}(L+y)^{-1-b_\alpha }\, \mathrm{d}y$. Dividing by $Q_\alpha ^ k\asymp L^{-b_\alpha }$ shows that $Q/Q_\alpha $ tends to one; the mean value theorem for the positive $k$th root then gives 15.92  egin{equation} \label{eq:radial-residual-flux-error} |Q-Q_\alpha |\le Cr^\delta L^{\alpha -2}. \end{equation} Moreover the exact identity \[   rac{Q'}{Q_\alpha '}=  rac q{q_\alpha }\left( rac{Q_\alpha }{Q}ight)^{k-1}  \] gives $|Q'-Q_\alpha '|\le Cr^{\delta -1}L^{\alpha -2}$. Since $R'=(Q-Q_\alpha )/r$, integration to the origin gives a finite $R_0$ and the first two inequalities in ( 15.85 ). Differentiating this formula gives the last inequality. The local potential $\Phi =\log (1+r)+U$ has semipositive Hessian away from $o$ because $Q/r>0$ and $Q'\ge 0$. Also $U=u_\alpha +R_0+o(1)$ near $o$, so $\Phi $ tends to $-\infty $. The local profile has nonnegative increasing slope in $\log r$, so its maxima with its value at $r=\varepsilon $ are plurisubharmonic. They decrease to the locally integrable profile; the local decreasing-limit property gives its genuine plurisubharmonic extension with the canonical pole retained. Thus $U$ is globally $\kappa $-psh. Formula ( 15.81 ) or the local determinant ratio gives its measure $q\kappa ^ k$ away from $o$; the defining non-pluripolar truncations exclude $o$ and are locally identical to this smooth product elsewhere. The measure has exactly total mass one. The bounded global residual proves the ordinary type. In real coordinates, with $ho =|z|=\sqrt r$, \[  |

title: 15.14.3 Smooth residuals from flat errors
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.14.3 Smooth residuals from flat errors Proposition 15.14.3 . Under the hypotheses of Theorem 15.14.2 , suppose $g=q/q_\alpha -1$ satisfies \[  (r\partial _ r)^ jg=O(r^ N) \quad \text{for every }N,j\ge 0.  \] Then $R-R_0$ extends smoothly across $o$, with every derivative zero there. Proof. Put $x=-\log r$, $a(x)=Q_\alpha (\mathrm{e}^{-x})^ k$ and $E(x)=M(\mathrm{e}^{-x})-a(x)$. The exact central integral is \[  E(x)=\int _ x^\infty g(\mathrm{e}^{-y})[-a'(y)]\, \mathrm{d}y, \qquad E'(x)=g(\mathrm{e}^{-x})a'(x).  \] Every derivative of $a$ has at most polynomial growth in $1+x$, and $a\asymp (1+x)^{-b_\alpha }$. The integral bounds $E$ by an exponential of arbitrarily large rate. Repeated differentiation of $E'$ expresses each derivative as a finite Leibniz sum of flat derivatives of $g$ and polynomially bounded derivatives of $a$; all derivatives of $E$ are therefore exponentially flat. Every derivative of $1/a$ has at most polynomial growth, by ( 15.80 ). Thus $E/a$ has the same flatness. Applying smooth composition near one to \[  Q-Q_\alpha =Q_\alpha \bigl [(1+E/a)^{1/k}-1\bigr ]  \] proves flatness of every $x$ derivative of $Q-Q_\alpha $. Since $\mathrm{d}R/\mathrm{d}x=-(Q-Q_\alpha )$, integration from $x$ to infinity proves the same for $R-R_0$, including its zeroth derivative. An ordinary $j$th derivative in $r$ is $r^{-j}$ times a polynomial in $\partial _ x$; arbitrarily strong exponential decay absorbs that factor. All ordinary derivatives extend continuously as zero at $r=0$, and repeated one-dimensional integration verifies smoothness there. Composition with $r=|z|^2$ gives the conclusion. $\square$

title: 15.14.4 Compact examples and sharp derivative thresholds

text: 15.14.4 Compact examples and sharp derivative thresholds Proposition 15.14.4 . The $C^1$ threshold $\delta =1/2$ and $C^2$ threshold $\delta =1$ are sharp. When $2\delta <1$, the stated Hölder exponent is also sharp. Nontrivial probability-density perturbations with smoothly flat residuals exist. Proof. Choose smooth nonnegative radial cutoffs $\chi _0,\chi _1$ with disjoint supports: $\chi _0=1$ near $r=0$ and vanishes outside a finite small ball; $\chi _1$ is nonzero in a finite annulus. Put 15.93 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-residual-sharp-examples} B=\frac{\int r^\delta \chi _0q_\alpha \kappa ^ k}{\int \chi _1q_\alpha \kappa ^ k},\qquad q_ c=q_\alpha \bigl [1+c(r^\delta \chi _0-B\chi _1)\bigr ]. \end{equation} For sufficiently small $c>0$, $q_ c$ is positive, smooth off $o$ and along the hyperplane, and has total mass exactly one. It is comparable to $q_\alpha $ near $o$, hence is in no $L^ p$, $p>1$. Theorem 15.14.2 gives a compact solution in the prescribed ordinary type. Near $o$ its central flux difference is exactly $c\int _0^ r s^\delta (Q_\alpha ^ k)'\, \mathrm{d}s$. The substitution $s=r\mathrm{e}^{-y}$ and dominated convergence give \[  \int _0^ r s^{\delta -1}(1-\log s)^{-1-b_\alpha }\, \mathrm{d}s \sim \delta ^{-1}r^\delta L^{-1-b_\alpha }.  \] Using ( 15.83 ) and the $k$th-root expansion yields \begin{align*}  R_ c'(r)& \sim \frac{c\alpha (1-\alpha )}\delta r^{\delta -1}L^{\alpha -2},\\  R_ c(r)-R_ c(0)& \sim \frac{c\alpha (1-\alpha )}{\delta ^2} r^\delta L^{\alpha -2}. \end{align*} For $\delta <\frac12$, the radial gradient $2\sqrt r\, R_ c'$ diverges, ruling out $C^1$ extension. For $\delta <1$, a tangential real Hessian eigenvalue $2R_ c'$ diverges, ruling out $C^2$ extension. The annular compensation changes no central flux. For $2\delta <1$ the displayed asymptotic also rules out any larger Hölder exponent. The critical derivative thresholds in Theorem 15.14.2 are therefore sharp for this family. Replacing $r^\delta \chi _0$ in ( 15.93 ) by $\mathrm{e}^{-1/r}\chi _0$ and adjusting $B$ by the same integral formula gives a nonzero mass-preserving perturbation satisfying every flat-error hypothesis. Proposition 15.14.3 then supplies a smoothly flat residual across the pole. $\square$

title: 15.14.5 Smooth residuals with an open density-zero annulus
search_title: Smooth residuals with an open density-zero annulus

text: 15.14.5 Smooth residuals with an open density-zero annulus Proposition 15.14.5 . For every $k\ge 2$ and $0<\alpha <1$, there is a nonnegative radial probability density $q_0$, smooth off $o$ and along the hyperplane, which equals $q_\alpha $ near $o$ and vanishes on a nonempty open annulus. Its solution has ordinary type $u_\alpha $ and a globally smooth residual, constant near $o$. Proof. Choose a smooth radial $h$ with $0\le h\le 1$, equal to zero on a nonempty finite annulus and equal to one near $o$ and outside a larger finite annulus. Choose a nonzero nonnegative smooth radial cutoff $\chi $ supported in a disjoint finite annulus where $h=1$. Set \[  C=\frac{\int (1-h)q_\alpha \kappa ^ k}{\int \chi q_\alpha \kappa ^ k}>0, \qquad q_0=q_\alpha (h+C\chi ).  \] This is nonnegative and has integral one. It is smooth at every point off $o$, including the hyperplane, and equals $q_\alpha $ near $o$. It vanishes on the chosen open annulus and is still in no $L^ p$, $p>1$. Theorem 15.14.2 applies, with zero relative density error on a neighborhood of $o$. There the exact central fluxes agree, so $Q=Q_\alpha $ and $R'=0$. Hence $R$ is constant near $o$ and extends smoothly across it. It is smooth everywhere else by the positive-root inverse, including the entire zero annulus. The solution retains its genuine pole; this smoothness assertion concerns the residual. $\square$

title: 15.14.6 Products with a zero-lower-mass factor
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.14.6 Products with a zero-lower-mass factor Let $(X_0,h_0)$ be any connected compact Hermitian $m$-fold with $v_-(h_0)=0$, and write $V_0=\int _{X_0}h_0^ m>0$. On $X=X_0\times \mathbb P^ k$ put $N=m+k$ and $H=\operatorname {pr}_0^*h_0+\operatorname {pr}_ Y^*\kappa $, where $\operatorname {pr}_0$ and $\operatorname {pr}_ Y$ are the two projections. In the product formulas below, $U$ and $R$ denote their pullbacks. Corollary 15.14.6 . The pullback of $U$ has the pulled-back ordinary type and relative envelope-class membership. Its residual retains the proved regularity across $X_0\times \{ o\} $, and its finite Monge–Ampère mass is $\binom Nm V_0$. The background $H$ is nonclosed and $v_-(H)=0$. Proof. The pullback of $U$ obeys \[  \mathrm{MA}_ H(U)=\binom Nm\operatorname {pr}_0^*(h_0^ m) \wedge \operatorname {pr}_ Y^*(q\kappa ^ k), \qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_ H(U)=\binom Nm V_0.  \] Indeed the bounded truncation $\max \{ U,-j\} $ is a pullback. The bounded corrected-product expansion of proposition 1.7.1 , lemma 1.7.3 leaves only the displayed binomial term by dimensions; multiplication by $1_{\{ U>-j\} }$ and increasing $j$ give the exact formula and finite mass. The residual is the pullback of $R$, so its proved regularity extends across $X_0\times \{ o\} $. It is ordinarily equivalent to the pullback of $u_\alpha $ and belongs to the corresponding relative stretching class by the same explicit $v_ t$. Also $v_-(H)=0$: bounded $h_0$-psh potentials with masses tending to zero have pullbacks of mass $\binom Nm$ times those masses. The background is genuinely nonclosed, since a closed positive $h_0$ would have all bounded masses equal to $V_0>0$ by Stokes. The zero-lower-mass conclusion retains the stated factor hypothesis; the calculation does not determine an individual density threshold. $\square$

title: 15.15 Envelopes for singular radial obstacles
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.15 Envelopes for singular radial obstacles The radial inverse of section 15.14 starts with a density. One can instead perturb the singular reference as an obstacle and let the envelope select its measure. The resulting total profile is a convex minorant. Its affine intervals give open regions of zero density, while its contact with the reference at both ends controls the residual across the pole and the hyperplane at infinity. Keep $k\geq 2$, $0<\alpha <1$, the normalized Fubini–Study form $\kappa $ on $\mathbb P^ k$ and the potential $u_\alpha $ of lemma 15.14.1 . Write $r=|z|^2$ on the chart $Z_0\ne 0$, put $x=\log r$, and define \[  A(x)=\log (1+\mathrm e^ x)+u_\alpha (x).  \] Here $u_\alpha (x)$ denotes its radial profile. Throughout this section primes denote derivatives in $x$. For $F\in C_ c^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$, extend $F(\log r)$ by zero near the pole $o$ and the hyperplane at infinity, and set 15.94 \begin{equation} \label{eq:singular-radial-envelope} E_ F=\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^ k,\kappa ): v\leq u_\alpha +F\  \text{everywhere},\  v\preceq u_\alpha \} \right)^*. \end{equation} The obstacle takes the value $-\infty $ at $o$. Since $F$ is bounded, its pointwise constraint already implies ordinary domination for each competitor. Lemma 15.15.1 . The profile $A$ is smooth and strictly convex, with $0<A'<1$, bounded $A''$ and asymptotic slopes $0,1$. Its tangents tend uniformly to $-\infty $ on each compact interval as their point of tangency tends to $-\infty $, and uniformly to the line $y\mapsto y$ as that point tends to $+\infty $. Moreover, $A(x)-x\searrow 0$ at the right end. Proof. Put $p=\mathrm e^ x/(1+\mathrm e^ x)$, $T=1-\log p$ and $a=\alpha T^{\alpha -1}$. Differentiating ( 15.80 ) gives \[  A'=p+(1-p)a,\qquad A''=p(1-p)(1-a)+\alpha (1-\alpha )(1-p)^2T^{\alpha -2}.  \] Since $T\geq 1$ and $0<a\leq \alpha <1$, these formulas give the asserted positivity and bounds. On the left, $A(x)=1-(1-x)^\alpha +o(1)$ and $A-xA'$ has leading term $-(1-\alpha )(-x)^\alpha $. On the right, $A=x+(1-\alpha )\mathrm e^{-x}+O(\mathrm e^{-2x})$ and $A'=1-(1-\alpha )\mathrm e^{-x}+O(\mathrm e^{-2x})$. The tangent at $x$ is $y\mapsto A'(x)y+A(x)-xA'(x)$, so both uniform limits follow. Finally $A'-1<0$ gives the decreasing right-end limit. $\square$

text: Lemma 15.15.1 . The profile $A$ is smooth and strictly convex, with $0<A'<1$, bounded $A''$ and asymptotic slopes $0,1$. Its tangents tend uniformly to $-\infty $ on each compact interval as their point of tangency tends to $-\infty $, and uniformly to the line $y\mapsto y$ as that point tends to $+\infty $. Moreover, $A(x)-x\searrow 0$ at the right end. Proof. Put $p=\mathrm e^ x/(1+\mathrm e^ x)$, $T=1-\log p$ and $a=\alpha T^{\alpha -1}$. Differentiating ( 15.80 ) gives \[  A'=p+(1-p)a,\qquad A''=p(1-p)(1-a)+\alpha (1-\alpha )(1-p)^2T^{\alpha -2}.  \] Since $T\geq 1$ and $0<a\leq \alpha <1$, these formulas give the asserted positivity and bounds. On the left, $A(x)=1-(1-x)^\alpha +o(1)$ and $A-xA'$ has leading term $-(1-\alpha )(-x)^\alpha $. On the right, $A=x+(1-\alpha )\mathrm e^{-x}+O(\mathrm e^{-2x})$ and $A'=1-(1-\alpha )\mathrm e^{-x}+O(\mathrm e^{-2x})$. The tangent at $x$ is $y\mapsto A'(x)y+A(x)-xA'(x)$, so both uniform limits follow. Finally $A'-1<0$ gives the decreasing right-end limit. $\square$

title: 15.15.1 The convex minorant and its residual
search_title: The convex minorant and its residual
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 15.15.1 The convex minorant and its residual Put $g=A+F$, $K_ F=\| F\| _\infty $, and let $C_ F$ be the supremum of all affine functions below $g$ on $\mathbb R$. Since $A-K_ F$ is convex and is the supremum of its supporting lines, 15.95 \begin{equation} \label{eq:singular-radial-sandwich} A-K_ F\leq C_ F\leq A+F\leq A+K_ F. \end{equation} In particular $C_ F$ is a finite convex function. Theorem 15.15.2 . The envelope ( 15.94 ) is \[  E_ F=C_ F(\log r)-\log (1+r)  \] on the punctured affine chart, with its canonical extensions at both ends. It has ordinary type $u_\alpha $. The residual $R_ F=E_ F-u_\alpha $ off $o$ extends to $C^{1,1}(\mathbb P^ k)$, is zero near $o$ and is smooth near infinity. The function $C_ F$ is affine on each component of $\{ C_ F<g\} $, and, with $L_2=\sup _{\mathbb R}\max (g'',0)$, 15.96 \begin{equation} \label{eq:singular-radial-slope-bound} 0\leq C_ F'(b)-C_ F'(a)\leq L_2(b-a)\qquad (a<b). \end{equation} Proof. We first identify the full envelope, then examine contact and the two ends. Every supporting slope of $C_ F$ lies in $[0,1]$, by the left growth $g\to -\infty $ and the right growth $g=x+o(1)$. The sandwich forces its asymptotic slopes to be $0,1$. The competitor family is invariant under the unitary group $U(k)$ acting on the affine coordinates. Its regularized supremum is therefore radial. Adding smooth local potentials of $\kappa $ gives a locally upper-bounded family of plurisubharmonic functions, so the envelope is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic. The competitor $u_\alpha -K_ F$ prevents collapse, and upper semicontinuity of the obstacle preserves the everywhere bound after regularization, including at $o$. A radial plurisubharmonic total potential $B(\log r)$ has convex profile $B$: restriction to a complex line gives this from radial subharmonicity. Positivity in a direction orthogonal to $z$ gives $B'\geq 0$. Conversely a convex nondecreasing profile has nonnegative tangential and radial Hessian eigenvalues $B'/r$ and $B''/r$, first for smooth profiles and then by convex smoothing on annuli. The envelope's total profile is consequently a convex minorant of $g$, and is at most $C_ F$. The same criterion makes $C_ F(\log r)$ plurisubharmonic on the punctured chart. Its upper bound near $o$ and ( 15.95 ) give a removable extension with value $-\infty $. Since $C_ F'\leq 1$, the function $C_ F-x$ is nonincreasing and, by the sandwich, has a finite right-end limit. The proposed $E_ F$ is thus locally bounded above near infinity. Add a local smooth potential of $\kappa $ and apply lemma 1.3.7 across the hyperplane. This gives a global competitor, hence the formula. The sandwich proves ordinary equivalence without subtracting the infinite values at $o$. On a compact interval in the free set the gap $g-C_ F$ is positive. Replacing $C_ F$ on a sufficiently short subinterval by its chord preserves convexity at both endpoints and stays below $g$. Unless $C_ F$ is locally affine this would give a larger minorant. It follows that it is affine on each free component. At a contact point $y$, domination by $g$ gives $C'_{F,-}(y)\geq g'(y)\geq C'_{F,+}(y)$, and convexity reverses the outer inequality. Thus $C_ F$ is differentiable at contacts, with derivative $g'$, and it is differentiable on free intervals as well. Its derivative is continuous. For $a<b$ outside one common free interval, move $a$ to its right contact endpoint and $b$ to its left contact endpoint whenever necessary. These points $a',b'\in [a,b]$ have the same respective derivatives. An unbounded free interval lacking the needed endpoint contains both original points, in which case the difference is zero. Otherwise \[  0\leq C_ F'(b)-C_ F'(a)=g'(b')-g'(a') \leq L_2(b'-a')\leq L_2(b-a),  \] which proves ( 15.96 ). For all sufficiently negative $x$, the tangent to $A$ at $x$ lies below $g$ on $\operatorname {supp}F$, by lemma 15.15.1 , and below $A=g$ elsewhere. Hence $C_ F=A$ on a left tail. The residual is zero near $o$. For the other end, put $L_ F=\inf _{\mathbb R}(g(x)-x)\leq 0$. If this infimum is attained at $y$, the affine minorant $x+L_ F$ touches $g$ there. The bound $C_ F'\leq 1$ forces $C_ F=x+L_ F$ for $x\geq y$. A negative infimum is always attained, since $g-x$ tends to $+\infty $ on the left and to zero on the right. With $R=1/r$, the envelope on this tail is 15.97 \begin{equation} \label{eq:singular-radial-infinity-tail} E_ F=L_ F-\log (1+R). \end{equation} If $L_ F=0$ is not attained and $F\ne 0$, the continuous function $g(y)-y$ has a positive minimum on $\operatorname {supp}F$. The right tangents of $A$ approach the line $y$ uniformly there, so every sufficiently late tangent lies below $g$ and gives $C_ F=A$ at its contact point. Thus $C_ F=A$ on a right tail; for $F=0$ this holds everywhere. Both alternatives give a smooth residual near infinity, because $R$ and $u_\alpha $ are smooth there. On the intervening finite annulus, \[  |C_ F-A|\leq K_ F,\qquad |C_ F'-A'|\leq 1, \qquad |(C_ F-A)''|\leq L_2+\| A''\| _\infty \quad \text{a.e.}  \] Composing with the smooth coordinate function $x=\log r$ gives $C^{1,1}$ regularity. The exact end formulas extend it over the whole projective space. $\square$ Corollary 15.15.3 . The non-pluripolar measure of $E_ F$ has mass one and satisfies \[  \operatorname{MA}_\kappa (E_ F)(\{ a<\log r<b\} )=C_ F'(b)^ k-C_ F'(a)^ k \qquad (-\infty <a<b<\infty ).  \] It vanishes on every free interval. For any $F,G\in C_ c^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$, 15.98 \begin{equation} \label{eq:singular-radial-value-stability} \| R_ F-R_ G\| _{C^0(\mathbb P^ k)}\leq \| F-G\| _\infty . \end{equation} Proof. On an annulus, the radial flux formula ( 15.81 ), followed by convex smoothing and bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity, gives the displayed measure. Continuity of $C_ F'$ excludes boundary atoms. The non-pluripolar truncations discard $o$, and smoothness at infinity excludes hyperplane mass. The asymptotic slopes $0,1$ therefore give mass one. An affine profile has zero radial eigenvalue and hence zero top-degree measure. Finally, if $\delta =\| F-G\| _\infty $, subtracting $\delta $ from a competitor for $F$ gives a competitor for $G$, and conversely. The resulting value bound for the envelopes gives ( 15.98 ) off $o$, and continuity of the residuals extends it across both ends. $\square$ For example, take a nonnegative smooth compactly supported bump $\chi $ with $\chi (x_0)=1$ and $F=-M\chi $, where $M>A(x_0)-x_0$. Then $L_ F<0$, and ( 15.97 ) gives an open free region of zero density. The envelope still has its sublogarithmic pole, while its residual is globally $C^{1,1}$.

15.15.2 Uniform bounds through moving contact For a fixed interval $[a,b]$ and $M>0$, let $\mathcal F_{a,b,M}$ consist of real $C^2$ functions supported in $[a,b]$ with $\| F\| _\infty +\| F''\| _\infty \leq M$. Take all norms in one fixed finite smooth projective atlas. Theorem 15.15.4 . There is $K=K(k,\alpha ,a,b,M)$ such that \[  \| R_ F\| _{C^{1,1}}\leq K\qquad (F\in \mathcal F_{a,b,M}).  \] For every $0<\gamma <1$ and $F,G\in \mathcal F_{a,b,M}$ with $\delta =\| F-G\| _\infty \leq 1$, \[  \| R_ F-R_ G\| _{C^{1,\gamma }} \leq K_\gamma \delta ^{(1-\gamma )/2},  \] where $K_\gamma $ has the same fixed-parameter dependence. These bounds hold across changes of the infinity alternative in theorem 15.15.2 . Proof. The left tangents of $A$ lie below $A-M$ on $[a,b]$ once their contact point is less than a common $a_0<a$. They are minorants of every $A+F$, so all residuals vanish on the same neighborhood of $o$. The sandwich and slope bound give uniform real Hessian bounds on any fixed finite annulus, since $L_2\leq \| A''\| _\infty +M$. It remains to control infinity, where the right contact point need not stay bounded. Put $B=\max (b,0)+1$. For $x>B$, the obstacle is $A$. At contact $C_ F'=A'$. On a free interval with finite right contact endpoint $d$, its constant slope is $A'(d)\geq A'(x)$; an unbounded right free interval has slope one. Thus \[  0\leq d_ F(x):=1-C_ F'(x)\leq 1-A'(x)\leq \mathrm e^{-x}.  \] The locally Lipschitz functions $C_ F',A'$ agree on the contact set, so their derivatives agree almost everywhere there. Indeed, a differentiable Lipschitz function has derivative zero at almost every density point of its zero set. On the free set $C_ F''=0$. The reference formula consequently gives 15.99  egin{equation} \label{eq:singular-radial-weighted-tail} 0\leq C_ F''(x)\leq A''(x) \leq (1+\alpha (1-\alpha ))\mathrm e^{-x} \quad 	ext{a.e. on }x>B. \end{equation} In a chart $Z_ j

e j}$. Then \[  R= rac{|\zeta |^2}{1+\sum |y_ i|^2},\qquad x=-\log R.  \] On fixed relatively compact chart pieces, $|
abla R|\leq c\sqrt R$ and $|
abla ^2R|\leq c$. Write the envelope as $\mathcal E_ F(R)=C_ F(-\log R)+\log R-\log (1+R)$ for $R>0$. Its derivatives are \[  (\mathcal E_ F)_ R= rac{d_ F}{R}- rac1{1+R},\qquad (\mathcal E_ F)_{RR}= rac{C_ F''-d_ F}{R^2}+ rac1{(1+R)^2} \quad 	ext{a.e.}  \] The tail bounds give $|(\mathcal E_ F)_ R|\leq 2$ and $|(\mathcal E_ F)_{RR}|\leq c_\alpha /R+1$. The real chain rule therefore bounds its Hessian uniformly, and its gradient tends to zero as $\zeta 	o 0$. Also $L_ F=\lim (C_ F-x)\in [-M,0]$, and integrating $d_ F\leq \mathrm e^{-x}$ gives $|C_ F(x)-x-L_ F|\leq \mathrm e^{-x}$. Hence $\mathcal E_ F-L_ F=O(R)$, so the extended envelope is differentiable on the hyperplane with zero gradient. The Hessian bound makes the gradient Lipschitz off the hyperplane. Apply it along straight coordinate segments and use the continuous zero gradient at a crossing; on segments contained in the hyperplane the gradient is zero. This proves a uniform $C^{1,1}$ extension. Subtract the fixed smooth $u_\alpha $ near infinity and join this estimate to the common pole neighborhood and a fixed annulus. On a smaller fixed chart, a real directional increment of length $h$ gives $|\partial _ e Z|\leq 2\delta /h+Kh$. Taking $h$ of order $\sqrt\delta $, or enlarging the constant when limited by the chart radius, yields $\| 
abla Z\| _\infty \leq c\sqrt\delta $. For points a distance $t$ apart, \[  |

abla Z(y)|\leq \min (c\sqrt\delta ,2Kt).  \] Dividing by $t^\gamma $ and splitting at $t=\sqrt\delta $ gives the estimate in a finite atlas. When $\delta =0$, the value bound gives equality. This argument does not assert convergence in $C^{1,1}$. $\square$

title: 15.15.3 The full envelope on a Hermitian product

text: 15.15.3 The full envelope on a Hermitian product Let $(Y,h_0)$ be a connected compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $m\geq 1$, and on $X=\mathbb P^ k\times Y$ put $H=\operatorname {pr}_1^*\kappa +\operatorname {pr}_2^*h_0$, $N=k+m$ and $V_0=\int _ Yh_0^ m$. Pull $u_\alpha $ and $F$ back to $X$, and define $E_ F^ H$ by ( 15.94 ) using the full family $\mathrm{PSH}(X,H)$. Proposition 15.15.5 . One has $E_ F^ H=\operatorname {pr}_1^*E_ F$ and \[  \operatorname{MA}_ H(E_ F^ H)=\binom Nk\, \operatorname{MA}_\kappa (E_ F)\otimes h_0^ m, \qquad \operatorname{MA}_ H(E_ F^ H)(X)=\binom Nk V_0.  \] The pulled-back residual is globally $C^{1,1}$, and $E_ F^ H$ belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,u_\alpha )$. On each fixed product the uniform bounds and derivative stability of theorem 15.15.4 hold for these residuals. Proof. Every competitor restricts to a projective slice as a $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function or as $-\infty $ identically. To check the exact lower bound when $H$ is nonclosed, choose a smooth quadratic correction $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq H$ on a coordinate polydisk and let $v_\epsilon =(v+q)*\eta _\epsilon -q$ on a smaller polydisk, where $\eta _\epsilon $ is the rescaling of a fixed smooth nonnegative radial probability kernel. Radial plurisubharmonic convolutions decrease to the canonical $v+q$, and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\epsilon \geq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q-H)*\eta _\epsilon -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q \geq -H-o(1)\omega _{\mathrm{Eucl}}.  \] Restrict this smooth inequality to a fixed slice. The corrected restrictions decrease either to $-\infty $ or to a plurisubharmonic function in local $L^1$; in the latter case the background error tends to zero distributionally. Subtracting $q$ gives the exact $\kappa $ bound, and these canonical restrictions patch on the connected slice. The everywhere obstacle constraint now gives $v\leq \operatorname {pr}_1^*E_ F$ on every slice. Upper regularization preserves this bound. Conversely every base competitor lifts, since $h_0>0$, proving equality of the full envelopes. The bounded truncations $\max (E_ F^ H,-j)$ are pullbacks. By proposition 1.7.1 , lemma 1.7.3 , dimensional multilinearity leaves only the term with $k$ projective factors and $m$ factor entries. Restrict to strict superlevel sets and let $j\to \infty $ to obtain the stated non-pluripolar measure and its finite mass. The residual regularity and uniform estimates pull back in a fixed smooth product atlas. Finally $E_ F^ H\geq u_\alpha -K_ F$. At $t=1$ take the stretching witness $v_1=E_ F^ H$; for $t>1$ take $v_ t=u_\alpha -tK_ F$, so that \[  t^{-1}v_ t+(1-t^{-1})u_\alpha =u_\alpha -K_ F\leq E_ F^ H.  \] Together with ordinary domination this is definition 13.4.1 , including the canonical values at the common pole. $\square$ Example 15.15.6 . There is a nonclosed positive background on a non-Kähler fourfold for which the preceding full envelope formula and uniform residual estimates hold. Proof. Take $Y=(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle \zeta \mapsto \mathrm e\zeta \rangle $. With $s=\log |\zeta |^2$, the form $h_0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s+\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s$ is invariant under the quotient. Its two summands are positive on the tangential and radial complex directions, respectively, so it is Hermitian. Moreover $\mathrm dh_0=-\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s\ne 0$. The Hopf surface is diffeomorphic to $S^3\times S^1$ and has odd first Betti number. Thus $X=\mathbb P^2\times Y$ is a non-Kähler fourfold with $\mathrm dH\ne 0$, and proposition 15.15.5 applies. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.15.5
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 15.15.5 . One has $E_ F^ H=\operatorname {pr}_1^*E_ F$ and \[  \operatorname{MA}_ H(E_ F^ H)=\binom Nk\, \operatorname{MA}_\kappa (E_ F)\otimes h_0^ m, \qquad \operatorname{MA}_ H(E_ F^ H)(X)=\binom Nk V_0.  \] The pulled-back residual is globally $C^{1,1}$, and $E_ F^ H$ belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,u_\alpha )$. On each fixed product the uniform bounds and derivative stability of theorem 15.15.4 hold for these residuals. Proof. Every competitor restricts to a projective slice as a $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function or as $-\infty $ identically. To check the exact lower bound when $H$ is nonclosed, choose a smooth quadratic correction $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq H$ on a coordinate polydisk and let $v_\epsilon =(v+q)*\eta _\epsilon -q$ on a smaller polydisk, where $\eta _\epsilon $ is the rescaling of a fixed smooth nonnegative radial probability kernel. Radial plurisubharmonic convolutions decrease to the canonical $v+q$, and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\epsilon \geq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q-H)*\eta _\epsilon -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q \geq -H-o(1)\omega _{\mathrm{Eucl}}.  \] Restrict this smooth inequality to a fixed slice. The corrected restrictions decrease either to $-\infty $ or to a plurisubharmonic function in local $L^1$; in the latter case the background error tends to zero distributionally. Subtracting $q$ gives the exact $\kappa $ bound, and these canonical restrictions patch on the connected slice. The everywhere obstacle constraint now gives $v\leq \operatorname {pr}_1^*E_ F$ on every slice. Upper regularization preserves this bound. Conversely every base competitor lifts, since $h_0>0$, proving equality of the full envelopes. The bounded truncations $\max (E_ F^ H,-j)$ are pullbacks. By proposition 1.7.1 , lemma 1.7.3 , dimensional multilinearity leaves only the term with $k$ projective factors and $m$ factor entries. Restrict to strict superlevel sets and let $j\to \infty $ to obtain the stated non-pluripolar measure and its finite mass. The residual regularity and uniform estimates pull back in a fixed smooth product atlas. Finally $E_ F^ H\geq u_\alpha -K_ F$. At $t=1$ take the stretching witness $v_1=E_ F^ H$; for $t>1$ take $v_ t=u_\alpha -tK_ F$, so that \[  t^{-1}v_ t+(1-t^{-1})u_\alpha =u_\alpha -K_ F\leq E_ F^ H.  \] Together with ordinary domination this is definition 13.4.1 , including the canonical values at the common pole. $\square$

title: 16 Multiplier-ideal envelopes and -goodness
text: 16 Multiplier-ideal envelopes and $\mathcal I$-goodness Throughout this chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n$ and $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, which need not be closed. We fix a smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$ and take $L^1$ norms with respect to it. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ denotes the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ of theorem 6.1.2 ; its total mass may be infinite. We write $u\preceq v$ and $u\sim v$ for the ordinary singularity order and equivalence of definition 1.12.1 , and $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$ and $u\sim _{\mathcal I}v$ for inclusion and equality of the multiplier ideals $\mathcal I(ku)$ and $\mathcal I(kv)$ at every weight $k>0$, as in section 1.12 . Finally, $P_\theta [u]$ and $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ denote the ordinary singularity envelopes of definition 1.19.4 , below zero and below a smooth obstacle $F$, and $V_\theta =P_\theta (0)$ is the potential with minimal singularities of section 1.19 . Multiplier ideals record weighted holomorphic integrability. Two potentials can have the same multiplier ideals at every weight although their ordinary envelopes differ, so passing from the ordinary singularity type of a potential to its multiplier-ideal class loses information. Analytic approximation makes this loss visible: along dyadic Demailly approximations, the envelopes converge to the greatest nonpositive representative of the multiplier-ideal class, which may exceed the ordinary envelope of the original potential. In the Kähler theory, equality of these two envelopes is also characterized by a mass condition. In a nonclosed background the equality remains meaningful even when the potential has infinite mass, and we therefore study both envelopes along analytic approximations. Examples on curves show that this still does not give continuity of mass or completeness, because diffuse polar curvature can disappear in the limit. The same examples explain why the obstacle has to be taken into account when the background changes.

title: 16.1 The Kähler characterization
text: 16.1 The Kähler characterization First suppose that $X$ is Kähler, that $\theta $ is a smooth closed big real $(1,1)$-form, and that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has positive non-pluripolar mass. Let $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ be the multiplier-ideal envelope of definition 16.2.1 below, and let $d_ S$ be the singularity pseudometric of [ Section 6.2 , SGPT ] . The characterization of $\mathcal I$-good singularities in [ Theorem 7.1.1 , SGPT ] states that the following three conditions are equivalent: \[  \begin{gathered} u\text{ lies in the }d_ S\text{-closure of analytic singularities},\\ \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) =\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}),\\ P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}. \end{gathered}  \] The last condition involves only envelopes. It therefore offers a starting point for the Hermitian problem even where the metric and the mass characterizations are unavailable. The integral on the right of the middle condition is the multiplier-ideal volume of [ SGPT ] . The upper and lower volumes of definition 13.3.1 , by contrast, vary the potential within its ordinary singularity type. The distinction matters in a nonclosed background, where even a bounded change of the potential can alter its total mass.

title: 16.2 Ideal projection
text: 16.2 Ideal projection We return to the general setting fixed at the beginning of the chapter. The multiplier-ideal envelope is the greatest nonpositive potential in a multiplier-ideal class. Taking a supremum over the class could a priori enlarge the multiplier ideals; the increasing-limit form of strong openness rules this out, and the envelope is then a projection onto the class. Definition 16.2.1 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ define \[  P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I} :=\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):v\leq 0, \  v\sim _{\mathcal I}u\} \right)^*.  \] As for ordinary envelopes, the members of the defining family are called competitors . The family is nonempty because it contains $u-\sup _ Xu$; bounded perturbations do not change multiplier ideals. Since it is bounded above by zero, its regularized supremum is a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function. The envelope depends only on the multiplier-ideal class of $u$. Theorem 16.2.2 . For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\sim _{\mathcal I}u,\qquad P_\theta [P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}]_{\mathcal I}=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The regularization in definition 16.2.1 does not change the pointwise supremum. Moreover, \[  \sup _ X P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=0.  \] Proof. Write $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. By Choquet's lemma, some sequence from the defining family has regularized supremum $q$. Replacing its terms by successive finite maxima, we obtain by lemma 1.16.4 an increasing sequence $v_ j$ that remains in the family and converges to $q$ almost everywhere. Fix $x\in X$ and $\lambda >0$. On a coordinate ball about $x$, choose one smooth function $r$ such that every $v_ j+r$ and $q+r$ is plurisubharmonic; this is possible because all these functions have complex Hessian bounded below by the same smooth form $-\theta $. The increasing-limit assertion of theorem 1.16.3 gives \[  \mathcal I(\lambda (q+r))_ x =\mathcal I(\lambda (v_ j+r))_ x =\mathcal I(\lambda u)_ x  \] for all large $j$; the second equality holds because smooth additions do not change multiplier ideals. Hence $q\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. Since $q\leq 0$, it belongs to its own defining family. The pointwise supremum is therefore at least $q$, and it is at most its regularization $q$; this proves the assertion about regularization. The defining families for $P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I}$ and $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ coincide, which proves idempotence. Finally, if $\sup _ Xq<0$, then $q-\sup _ Xq$ would be a larger competitor, which is impossible. $\square$ Ideal projection commutes with pullback by a modification because both the potential class and the all-weight ideal class descend. Proposition 16.2.3 . Let $\mu :Y\to X$ be a modification of connected compact complex manifolds. For every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ and every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  P_{\mu ^*\theta }[u\circ \mu ]_{\mathcal I} =P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\circ \mu .  \] Proof. By proposition 1.22.12 , pullback identifies the potentials in the two backgrounds. Surjectivity of $\mu $ identifies their nonpositivity constraints, and lemma 1.22.17 identifies their all-weight multiplier-ideal classes. Hence pullback gives a bijection of the complete competitor families. The ideal envelope is itself a competitor and is their greatest member by theorem 16.2.2 . Its pullback is therefore the greatest competitor upstairs, which proves the identity. $\square$ Proposition 16.2.4 . For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  u-\sup _ Xu\leq P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\leq V_\theta .  \] Moreover, \[  \begin{gathered} P_\theta [u]\sim _{\mathcal I}u,\qquad P_\theta [P_\theta [u]]_{\mathcal I}=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I},\\ P_\theta [P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}. \end{gathered}  \] Proof. Let $h\leq 0$ be a competitor for the ordinary envelope, so that $h\preceq u$. The function $\max (h,u-\sup _ Xu)$ is nonpositive, ordinarily equivalent to $u$, and dominates $h$. Since ordinarily equivalent potentials have the same multiplier ideals, it is a competitor for the ideal envelope. Taking regularized suprema gives $P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$; the two outer inequalities follow directly from the defining families. Projection and monotonicity of local integrability now give, for every $\lambda >0$, \[  \mathcal I(\lambda u) \subseteq \mathcal I(\lambda P_\theta [u]) \subseteq \mathcal I(\lambda P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}) =\mathcal I(\lambda u).  \] Thus the ordinary envelope preserves all multiplier ideals, and it has the same ideal envelope as $u$. For $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, the inequalities already proved and idempotence give $q\leq P_\theta [q]\leq P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I}=q$. $\square$ We call $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ normalized if $\sup _ Xu=0$. Recall from definition 1.19.4 that $u$ is an ordinary model, or envelope fixed point, if $P_\theta [u]=u$; we call $u$ an ideal model if $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=u$. Models of either kind are normalized, and by the last identity in proposition 16.2.4 every ideal model is an ordinary model. The map $u\mapsto P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ is called ideal projection . Corollary 16.2.5 . If $\theta $ is semipositive and big, then $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ has finite extended Monge–Ampère mass for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proof. By the last identity in corollary 16.2.4 , $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ is an ordinary model, that is, an envelope fixed point. The mass estimate for envelope fixed points in proposition 13.1.6 applies. $\square$ Proposition 16.2.6 . For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v\quad \Longrightarrow \quad P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\leq P_\theta [v]_{\mathcal I}.  \] For $a>0$ one has $P_{a\theta }[a u]_{\mathcal I}=aP_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. For smooth real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ i$ and potentials $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$, $i=1,2$, \[  P_{\theta _1}[u_1]_{\mathcal I}+P_{\theta _2}[u_2]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[u_1+u_2]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Proof. Let $h$ be a competitor for $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. Since $h\sim _{\mathcal I}u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$, the Lelong-number criterion in theorem 1.16.3 shows that $\max (h,v-\sup _ Xv)$ is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $v$. This function is nonpositive and dominates $h$, so it is a competitor for $P_\theta [v]_{\mathcal I}$; taking the supremum over $h$ proves that the envelope preserves the order. Multiplication by $a$ is a bijection between the defining families in the scaling identity. For the sum, $P_{\theta _1}[u_1]_{\mathcal I}+P_{\theta _2}[u_2]_{\mathcal I}$ is nonpositive and $(\theta _1+\theta _2)$-plurisubharmonic, and it is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u_1+u_2$ by projection and lemma 1.16.4 . It is therefore a competitor for the envelope on the right. $\square$

text: Proposition 16.2.6 . title: 16.2.1 Analytic and divisorial singularities
text: 16.2.1 Analytic and divisorial singularities For a potential $a$ with analytic singularities, the multiplier-ideal order controls the ordinary order: by lemma 1.17.10 , every quasi-plurisubharmonic $v$ with $v\preceq _{\mathcal I}a$ satisfies $v\preceq a$. The ideal envelope of $a$ is then a competitor for its ordinary envelope, and the two envelopes coincide. This extends [ Proposition 3.2.10 , SGPT ] to smooth backgrounds. Proposition 16.2.7 . Let $a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have analytic singularities. Then \[  a\sim P_\theta [a]=P_\theta [a]_{\mathcal I}.  \] In particular the common envelope has analytic singularities with the same coefficient and ideal as $a$, up to a bounded remainder. Proof. Set $q=P_\theta [a]_{\mathcal I}$. Projection gives $q\sim _{\mathcal I}a$, so lemma 1.17.10 gives $q\preceq a$. Since $q\leq 0$, it is a competitor for $P_\theta [a]$. Together with proposition 16.2.4 , this yields \[  a-\sup _ Xa\leq P_\theta [a]\leq q\leq P_\theta [a].  \] Hence the two envelopes are equal and ordinarily equivalent to $a$. Since they differ from $a$ by a bounded function, they inherit its analytic presentation. $\square$ The same argument applies to the potential of a countable divisorial current of finite mass, with lemma 1.17.4 in place of lemma 1.17.10 . Corollary 16.2.8 . Let $S$ be a closed positive divisorial current of finite mass on a connected compact complex manifold $Z$, and choose a smooth residual decomposition $S=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ as in corollary 1.17.5 . For every Hermitian form $\Omega $ with $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Z,\Omega )$, \[  P_\Omega [v]=P_\Omega [v]_{\mathcal I}\sim v.  \] Proof. Set $q=P_\Omega [v]_{\mathcal I}$. Projection gives $q\sim _{\mathcal I}v$, and lemma 1.17.4 gives $q\preceq v$. Thus $q$ is a competitor for $P_\Omega [v]$. Together with proposition 16.2.4 , this yields $v-\sup _ Zv\leq P_\Omega [v]=q\preceq v$. $\square$

title: 16.3 Changes of background and envelope mass
search_title: Changes of background and envelope mass
text: 16.3 Changes of background and envelope mass A smooth change of representative $(\theta ,u)\mapsto (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,u-f)$ preserves the current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ but moves the zero obstacle. The resulting envelopes remain ordinarily equivalent after transport. In a nonclosed background, however, their masses can differ. Proposition 16.3.1 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. Set $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, $u'=u-f$, $m=\min _ Xf$ and $M=\max _ Xf$. Then \[  P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}+m \leq P_{\theta '}[u']_{\mathcal I}+f \leq P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}+M.  \] The same inequalities hold for the ordinary envelopes. Proof. If $v$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, then $v-f+m$ is $\theta '$-plurisubharmonic, nonpositive and multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u'$. Therefore $v\leq P_{\theta '}[u']_{\mathcal I}+f-m$, and taking the envelope gives the first inequality. Conversely, a competitor $v'$ in the new background gives the competitor $v'+f-M$ in the old one, which proves the second inequality. For the ordinary envelopes, the same calculation applies with the ordinary singularity order in place of multiplier-ideal equivalence. $\square$ For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, put \[  W_\theta (u)=\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})\in [0,+\infty ].  \] This quantity depends on the decomposition of the current, even for smooth potentials. Proposition 16.3.2 . There are two smooth decompositions of the same positive current for which the corresponding values of $W$ are different. Proof. Use the Hermitian form $\omega $ and the smooth function $g=u_ t$ of example 2.3.1 , with $t\ne 0$ sufficiently small. Both $\omega $ and $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ are Hermitian, and \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}0=\omega '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(-g).  \] For a smooth potential in a Hermitian background, all multiplier ideals are trivial and zero is a competitor for its multiplier-ideal envelope, so that envelope is zero. Consequently \[  W_\omega (0)=\int _ X\omega ^2,\qquad W_{\omega '}(-g)=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)^2.  \] By the explicit formula ( 2.3 ), the two integrals differ. $\square$ The underlying torus is Kähler; the dependence comes from the chosen nonclosed background. In the closed theory, the invariance of mass under bounded changes of the potential gives the missing step after proposition 16.3.1 . Singularity volumes, on the other hand, range over the entire ordinary type, so the bijection of competitors in the gauge change preserves them. Under bounded mass, proposition 30.9.1 accordingly transports ordinary models of positive volume and preserves their upper-volume comparison.

title: Proposition 16.3.1
text: Proposition 16.3.1 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. Set $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, $u'=u-f$, $m=\min _ Xf$ and $M=\max _ Xf$. Then \[  P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}+m \leq P_{\theta '}[u']_{\mathcal I}+f \leq P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}+M.  \] The same inequalities hold for the ordinary envelopes. Proof. If $v$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, then $v-f+m$ is $\theta '$-plurisubharmonic, nonpositive and multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u'$. Therefore $v\leq P_{\theta '}[u']_{\mathcal I}+f-m$, and taking the envelope gives the first inequality. Conversely, a competitor $v'$ in the new background gives the competitor $v'+f-M$ in the old one, which proves the second inequality. For the ordinary envelopes, the same calculation applies with the ordinary singularity order in place of multiplier-ideal equivalence. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.3.2
text: Proposition 16.3.2 . There are two smooth decompositions of the same positive current for which the corresponding values of $W$ are different. Proof. Use the Hermitian form $\omega $ and the smooth function $g=u_ t$ of example 2.3.1 , with $t\ne 0$ sufficiently small. Both $\omega $ and $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ are Hermitian, and \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}0=\omega '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(-g).  \] For a smooth potential in a Hermitian background, all multiplier ideals are trivial and zero is a competitor for its multiplier-ideal envelope, so that envelope is zero. Consequently \[  W_\omega (0)=\int _ X\omega ^2,\qquad W_{\omega '}(-g)=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)^2.  \] By the explicit formula ( 2.3 ), the two integrals differ. $\square$

title: 16.3.1 Envelope equality and infinite mass
text: 16.3.1 Envelope equality and infinite mass For each $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the equality 16.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:background-goodness} P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I} \end{equation} is meaningful. If a Hermitian metric $\omega $ fails the bounded mass property of definition 6.5.1 , there exists $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ such that \[  P_\omega [U]=P_\omega [U]_{\mathcal I}=0, \qquad U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0), \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)(X)=+\infty ,  \] where $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0)$ is the relative envelope class of definition 13.4.1 . Since $P_\omega [U]=V_\omega =0$, proposition 16.2.4 gives $P_\omega [U]_{\mathcal I}=0$. $\square$

title: 16.4 geometry of ideal classes
text: 16.4 $L^1$ geometry of ideal classes Ideal projection selects a canonical representative of each multiplier-ideal class, so the $L^1$ distance between these representatives defines a metric on the classes. Since the representatives have supremum zero, normalized compactness makes this metric totally bounded and its completion compact. The points added in the completion, however, need not be ideal models. On a curve this happens as badly as possible: approximating curvature measures by finite atomic measures shows that the completion contains every normalized potential. Let \[  \mathfrak S_{\mathcal I}(X,\theta ) =\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )/{\sim _{\mathcal I}},\qquad \mathfrak M_{\mathcal I}(X,\theta ) =\{ q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I}=q\}   \] be the set of multiplier-ideal classes and the set of ideal models, and write $[u]_{\mathcal I}$ for the multiplier-ideal class of $u$. By theorem 16.2.2 , the map $[u]_{\mathcal I}\mapsto P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ identifies these two sets, and every ideal envelope has supremum zero. Proposition 16.4.1 . The formula 16.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ideal-lone-metric} d_{\mathcal I,\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}([u]_{\mathcal I},[v]_{\mathcal I}) =\int _ X|P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}-P_\theta [v]_{\mathcal I}|\, \mathrm{d}V \end{equation} defines a finite metric on $\mathfrak S_{\mathcal I}(X,\theta )$. This metric space is totally bounded. Its metric completion is canonically the $L^1$ closure of $\mathfrak M_{\mathcal I}(X,\theta )$ inside the compact space $\mathcal K_\theta $ of normalized $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions in theorem 1.4.2 . Changing $\mathrm{d}V$ to another smooth positive probability volume form gives a bi-Lipschitz equivalent metric. Proof. The ideal envelopes are integrable and depend only on the ideal classes, so the formula is well defined and finite; symmetry and the triangle inequality are those of the $L^1$ norm. If the distance is zero, the two envelopes agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 , and projection shows that the two ideal classes coincide. Conversely, equal ideal classes have the same envelope. By the normalized compactness theorem, $\mathfrak M_{\mathcal I}$ lies in the compact space $\mathcal K_\theta $. Every subset of a compact metric space is totally bounded, and its completion is its closure in that space. Finally, the ratio of two smooth positive volume forms on the compact manifold $X$ is bounded above and below by positive constants, and multiplying the integral by these bounds proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: 16.4.2 Mass and capacity convergence
text:
16.4.2 Mass and capacity convergence The approximation in theorem 16.4.2 loses all non-pluripolar mass. For the nonconstant smooth $u$ at the end of its proof, the approximants $q_ j$ have zero non-pluripolar measure, whereas $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. After normalization to mean zero, the same sequence converges in the Gauduchon trace metric of corollary 5.2.1 . Nevertheless, the sequence $q_ j$ does not converge to $u$ in capacity. Otherwise, since $q_ j,u\leq 0$, theorem 7.3.1 would give \[  0=\mathrm{e}^{q_ j}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (q_ j) ightharpoonup \mathrm{e}^{u}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u),  \] contradicting the strict positivity of the limiting measure. Thus weak convergence of traces and $L^1$ convergence do not imply convergence in capacity, even on a curve. The same sequence shows that ideal projection is not continuous for the $L^1$ topology: $P_	heta [q_ j]_{\mathcal I}=q_ j	o u$, whereas $P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I}=0$. The completion therefore distinguishes smooth normalized potentials that the quotient by multiplier-ideal equivalence identifies. The loss of mass also occurs along sequences of fixed positive mass. Proposition 16.4.3 . In the curve setting above, for every rational $0<	au <1$ there are ideal models $r_ j$ with analytic singularities such that \[   egin{gathered} d_{\mathcal I,	heta ,\mathrm{d}V}([r_ j]_{\mathcal I},[0]_{\mathcal I})\longrightarrow 0,\ \mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)(Y)=	au , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)ightharpoonup 	au 	heta . \end{gathered}  \] In particular, non-pluripolar mass is not continuous for this metric, even on a family whose masses have a fixed positive lower bound. Proof. Choose finitely supported probability measures $
u _ j$ with rational weights converging weakly to $	heta $, and let $q_ j$ be their normalized Green potentials; the preceding proof gives $q_ j	o 0$ in $L^1$. Put $a=1-	au $ and $r_ j=P_	heta [a q_ j]_{\mathcal I}$. The scaled potential lies in the same background, since \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(aq_ j)=(1-a)	heta +a
u _ j\geq 0.  \] Since $aq_ j$ is a competitor, $aq_ j\leq r_ j\leq 0$, and hence $r_ j	o 0$ in $L^1$. By projection, $r_ j$ is an ideal model. By proposition 16.2.7 , it has exactly the logarithmic coefficients of $aq_ j$, which are rational, with bounded local remainders, and it is locally bounded away from the finite pole set. On the curve, removing the polar part of the curvature therefore gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r_ j-a
u _ j.  \] By distributional Stokes, this measure has total mass $1-a=	au $. The positive curvature measures $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r_ j$ have mass one and converge as distributions, hence weakly, to $	heta $. Since $
u _ jightharpoonup 	heta $, the last identity gives $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)ightharpoonup 	au 	heta $.
