Finally, if $\rho _\Psi (\Phi (q_ j),\Phi (q))\to 0$, then theorem 30.12.4 gives $q_ j\to q$ in $L^1(C)$. Off the pole sets, which have smooth volume zero, the difference of the two product potentials is $(q_ j-q)\circ p$. For a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm dV$ on $M$, integration along the compact fibers makes $p_*\mathrm dV$ a smooth positive density on $C$, and Fubini's theorem gives \[  \int _ M|\Phi (q_ j)-\Phi (q)|\, \mathrm dV \leq C_{\mathrm dV}\| q_ j-q\| _{L^1(C,\eta )}\longrightarrow 0,  \] where $C_{\mathrm dV}$ bounds the density of $p_*\mathrm dV$ with respect to $\eta $. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.6.27
text: Corollary 16.6.27 . Let $M=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^ k$, $k\geq 1$, with projections $h,s,r$. Let $\sigma $ and $\kappa $ be the probability Fubini–Study forms on $\mathbb P^1$ and $\mathbb P^ k$, respectively, and let $f$ be a positive nonconstant smooth real function on the first factor. Set \[  \Theta =h^*\sigma +(f\circ h)s^*\sigma +r^*\kappa , \qquad \Psi =\psi \circ r,  \] where $\psi $ is the normalized hyperplane potential with $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =[D]$. For every normalized ordinary model $q$ on $(\mathbb P^1,\sigma )$, put $\Phi _ f(q)=\Psi +q\circ h$. Then \[  P_\Theta [\Phi _ f(q)]=\Phi _ f(q),\qquad P_\Theta [\Phi _ f(q)]_{\mathcal I} =\Phi _ f(P_\sigma [q]_{\mathcal I}).  \] On $\mathcal T_\Psi =\{ \Phi _ f(q):P_\sigma [q]=q\} $, define \[  \begin{gathered} \rho _{\Psi ,f}(\Phi _ f(q_1),\Phi _ f(q_2)) =\| \mu _{q_1}-\mu _{q_2}\| _{\mathrm{TV}},\\ \mu _ q=\mathbf1_{\{ q=-\infty \} }(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q). \end{gathered}  \] All the conclusions of proposition 16.6.26 hold on this locus: completeness and geodesics, vanishing of the upper-volume comparison, a closed ideal subspace in which analytic models are dense, ideal projection as the nearest-point retraction, and $L^1$ convergence upstairs. Proof. On $Y=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, write $\pi _1,\pi _2$ for the projections and put $\beta =\pi _1^*\sigma +(f\circ \pi _1)\pi _2^*\sigma $. The restriction argument of example 16.6.24 applies to every normalized ordinary curve model and gives \[  P_\beta [q\circ \pi _1]=q\circ \pi _1.  \] Indeed, the maximum of an ordinary competitor with $q\circ \pi _1$ restricts on every horizontal section to a competitor for $P_\sigma [q]=q$ that is $\sigma $-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $. Put $q_{\mathcal I}=P_\sigma [q]_{\mathcal I}$ and let $E$ be the atomic part of $\mu _ q$. The Green potential $w_ E$ of lemma 19.5.2 satisfies $q_{\mathcal I}\sim w_ E$ and $q\sim _{\mathcal I}w_ E$. Its pullback satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w_ E\circ \pi _1) =\sum _ xE(\{ x\} )[\{ x\} \times \mathbb P^1] -E(\mathbb P^1)\pi _1^*\sigma .  \] The divisor current is closed and has finite mass, and $w_ E\circ \pi _1$ is $\beta $-plurisubharmonic because $E(\mathbb P^1)\leq 1$. By corollary 16.2.8 , its ordinary and ideal envelopes are equal. Multiplier ideals pull back by lemma 1.16.6 , so ordinary equivalence and the ordinary identity just proved give \[  P_\beta [q\circ \pi _1]_{\mathcal I} =P_\beta [w_ E\circ \pi _1]_{\mathcal I} =P_\beta [w_ E\circ \pi _1] =q_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi _1.  \] This includes the cases $E=0$ and $E$ with countably many atoms. Apply proposition 16.6.13 to $M\to Y$ and the divisor $Y\times D$, whose induced zero obstacle is zero. The two identities on the base give the asserted identities upstairs. Thus $\Phi _ f$ identifies the locus isometrically with the whole space of curve models, and ideal projection again takes the atomic part. The metric, nearest-point and analytic-closure arguments of proposition 16.6.26 apply unchanged; rational atomic coefficients and the unit coefficient of the hyperplane give local analytic monomials. Each pairwise maximum still has the form $\Psi +\max (q_1,q_2)\circ h$, so the fibration proposition makes all three upper volumes zero. Finally, integration of a smooth volume form along the compact fibers of $h$ transfers $L^1$ convergence on the curve to $M$, as in that proposition. The background is positive and not closed, and, as in example 16.6.24 , a dominating closed product form gives the bounded mass property. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.6.28
text: Corollary 16.6.28 . Keep $M,h,s,r,\sigma ,\kappa ,D,\Psi $ from corollary 16.6.27 . For any smooth real function $f\geq 0$ on the first curve, put \[  \Theta _ f=h^*\sigma +(f\circ h)s^*\sigma +r^*\kappa , \qquad \Phi (q)=\Psi +q\circ h.  \] For every normalized ordinary curve model $q$, one has \[  P_{\Theta _ f}[\Phi (q)]=\Phi (q),\qquad P_{\Theta _ f}[\Phi (q)]_{\mathcal I} =\Phi (P_\sigma [q]_{\mathcal I}).  \] All the metric conclusions of corollary 16.6.27 hold on the same set $\mathcal T_\Psi $, with the same distance given by total variation of polar curvature. The identity map of this set is an isometry between any two of the backgrounds $\Theta _ f$ and commutes with ideal projection. This includes uniformly convergent families $f_ j\to 0$, whose limiting background $\Theta _0$ is not big. Proof. On $Y=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, put $\beta _ f=\pi _1^*\sigma +(f\circ \pi _1)\pi _2^*\sigma $. This form is semipositive, and the argument with horizontal sections in corollary 16.6.27 still gives \[  P_{\beta _ f}[q\circ \pi _1]=q\circ \pi _1.  \] Indeed, the pullback of $q$ is $\beta _ f$-plurisubharmonic, and every horizontal section has background $\sigma $, also where $f$ vanishes. Write $q_{\mathcal I}=P_\sigma [q]_{\mathcal I}$, let $E$ be the atomic part of $\mu _ q$, and set $g=w_ E\circ \pi _1$, with the Green potential of the preceding proof. Then $g$ is $\beta _ f$-plurisubharmonic, $q\circ \pi _1\sim _{\mathcal I}g$, and $g\sim q_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi _1$. Its complex Hessian is the same countable divisor current of finite mass minus $E(\mathbb P^1)\pi _1^*\sigma $. For every ideal competitor $v\leq 0$ for $q\circ \pi _1$, lemma 1.17.4 gives $v\preceq g$. Therefore \[  v\leq P_{\beta _ f}[g] =P_{\beta _ f}[q_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi _1] =q_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi _1.  \] The last equality uses the ordinary identity just proved, since $q_{\mathcal I}$ is an ordinary curve model. Conversely, $q_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi _1$ is a normalized $\beta _ f$-plurisubharmonic ideal competitor, because ideal projection preserves the ideal type on the curve and multiplier ideals pull back. This proves the ideal identity on the base, including the cases $E=0$ and $E$ with countably many atoms. Proposition 16.6.13 allows this semipositive background on the base and gives both identities upstairs. Normalization follows because the factors are independent. The metric space is the same isometric copy of the whole space of curve models, and ideal projection, analytic closure, geodesics and $L^1$ convergence upstairs follow as in the preceding proof. Since the relevant currents are still pulled back from the surface $Y$, the same proposition gives zero upper volumes, so the upper-volume comparison vanishes. Both $\Phi (q)$ and its polar measure are independent of $f$, so the stated identifications and the compatibility with ideal projection hold exactly, including at the limiting background. Analytic singularities depend only on the functions, so their closure is also unchanged. To see that $\Theta _0$ is not big, let $n=k+2$, and take the smooth closed positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form and the Hermitian form \[  T=h^*\sigma \wedge r^*(\kappa ^ k),\qquad \Omega =h^*\sigma +s^*\sigma +r^*\kappa .  \] One has $\int _ M\Theta _0\wedge T=0$ and $\int _ M\Omega \wedge T=1$. If $\Theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \varepsilon \Omega $ for some $u\in \mathrm{QPSH}(M)$ and $\varepsilon >0$, pairing with $T$ and using Stokes' theorem would give $0\geq \varepsilon $. Thus $\Theta _0$ is not big, although the model locus keeps its complete metric. $\square$

title: 16.6.8 Several curve factors
text:
16.6.8 Several curve factors A single curve factor produces a model space isometric to the space of models on one curve. Products of several curves give larger complete model spaces at zero volume. The envelopes of a sum of curve models are again computed coordinatewise: the supremum of a competitor over all factors but one is a potential on the remaining curve, and restriction to slices treats the other factors by induction. The sum of the polar distances of the factors is then a complete metric on the induced product models. Let $C_1,\ldots ,C_ m$ be connected compact curves with smooth positive forms $\eta _ i$, where $m\geq 2$, and put $A_ i=\int _{C_ i}\eta _ i$. Set \[  Y=\prod _{i=1}^ m C_ i,\qquad  eta =\sum _{i=1}^ m\pi _ i^*\eta _ i,  \] where $\pi _ i:Y	o C_ i$ are the projections. For normalized ordinary models $q_ i$ on $(C_ i,\eta _ i)$, write \[  w=\sum _{i=1}^ m q_ i\circ \pi _ i,\qquad q_{i,\mathcal I}=P_{\eta _ i}[q_ i]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Lemma 16.6.29 . The function $w$ is a normalized ordinary model on $(Y, eta )$, and \[  P_ eta [w]_{\mathcal I} =\sum _{i=1}^ m q_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i.  \] Proof. The function $w$ is $ eta $-plurisubharmonic and has supremum zero. We prove $P_ eta [w]=w$ by induction on the number of factors, the case of one factor being the identity $P_{\eta _1}[q_1]=q_1$. Let $v\leq 0$ be an ordinary competitor, and replace it by $\max (v,w)$. This preserves $v\preceq w$ and ensures that the restrictions of $v$ to slices are not identically $-\infty $ wherever the corresponding curve potentials are finite. Write $Y=Y'	imes C_ m$, and take the regularized partial supremum \[  a(t)=\left(\sup _{y'\in Y'}v(y',t)ight)^*.  \] The restrictions of $v$ to the slices $\{ y'\} 	imes C_ m$ are $\eta _ m$-plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. They are bounded above by zero, and at least one of them is not identically $-\infty $, since $v\geq w$. The local upper-envelope theorem from chapter 1 therefore makes $a$ an $\eta _ m$-plurisubharmonic function. The global inequality $v\leq w+C$ gives $a\leq q_ m+C$, because the other normalized potentials have supremum zero. Thus $a$ is a competitor for $P_{\eta _ m}[q_ m]$, and $a\leq P_{\eta _ m}[q_ m]=q_ m$. For $t$ with $q_ m(t)$ finite, the function $v(\cdot ,t)-q_ m(t)$ is a potential in the product background on $Y'$, not identically $-\infty $; it is nonpositive and at least as singular as $\sum _{i<m}q_ i\circ \pi _ i$. The induction hypothesis bounds it by that sum. Hence $v\leq w$ off the poles of $q_ m$. At those poles the original bound $v\leq w+C$ gives the same inequality. Taking the envelope proves the ordinary identity. For the ideal identity, let $E_ i$ be the atomic part of the polar curvature of $q_ i$, and take the Green potentials $g_ i$ of lemma 19.5.2 . They satisfy \[  q_ i\sim _{\mathcal I}g_ i,\qquad q_{i,\mathcal I}\sim g_ i,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ i=E_ i- rac{E_ i(C_ i)}{A_ i}\eta _ i.  \] By lemma 1.16.6 , lemma 1.16.4 , $g=\sum _ i g_ i\circ \pi _ i$ is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $w$. Its complex Hessian is a closed countable sum of the divisors $\pi _ i^{-1}(x)$ minus the smooth form $\sum _ i E_ i(C_ i)\pi _ i^*\eta _ i/A_ i$. Each coordinate fiber has constant mass for the product metric, so the divisor part has finite mass. Moreover $g$ is $ eta $-plurisubharmonic since $E_ i(C_ i)\leq A_ i$. Therefore corollary 16.2.8 gives $P_ eta [g]_{\mathcal I}=P_ eta [g]$. Since $g$ is ordinarily equivalent to $\sum _ iq_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i$, the ordinary identity, applied to the models $q_{i,\mathcal I}$, shows that this envelope is $\sum _ iq_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i$. As $w\sim _{\mathcal I}g$, the ideal envelope of $w$ is the same, which proves the assertion. $\square$ The same coordinatewise computation applies to arbitrary curve potentials, to curve backgrounds that need not be positive, and to smooth obstacles that are sums of functions of the separate coordinates. Keep the curves $C_ i$, the product $Y$ and its projections $\pi _ i$. Let $\sigma _ i$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms on $C_ i$ with $\mathrm{PSH}(C_ i,\sigma _ i)
e \varnothing $, that is, with $\int _{C_ i}\sigma _ i\geq 0$ by lemma 1.8.14 , and choose $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(C_ i,\sigma _ i)$ and $F_ i\in C^\infty (C_ i,\mathbb R)$. Put \[  \gamma =\sum _ i\pi _ i^*\sigma _ i,\qquad u=\sum _ i u_ i\circ \pi _ i,\qquad F=\sum _ i F_ i\circ \pi _ i.  \] Proposition 16.6.30 . For the preceding data, 16.27  egin{equation} \label{eq:separated-curve-obstacle-projections}  egin{aligned}  P_{\gamma ,F}[u] & =\sum _ i P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]\circ \pi _ i,\  P_{\gamma ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} & =\sum _ i P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i. \end{aligned} \end{equation} These identities also hold when some of the curve backgrounds have zero area. Proof. Write $e_ i=P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]$. Sums of ordinary competitors in the separate coordinates are ordinary competitors on the product, and their regularized supremum is $\sum _ i e_ i\circ \pi _ i$. This gives the lower bound in the first identity. For the upper bound we use induction on the number of factors, the case of one factor being trivial. Let $v\leq F$ be an ordinary competitor, so that $v\leq u+C$ for some constant $C$. Choose a constant $K$ with $u-K\leq F$ and replace $v$ by $\max (v,u-K)$. This preserves both bounds and ensures that the restrictions of $v$ to the slices used below are not identically $-\infty $. Write $Y=Y'	imes C_ m$, and on $Y'$ put $u'=\sum _{i<m}u_ i\circ \pi _ i$ and $F'=\sum _{i<m}F_ i\circ \pi _ i$. The regularized partial supremum \[  a(t)=\left(\sup _{y'\in Y'} igl (v(y',t)-F'(y') igr )ight)^*  \] is $\sigma _ m$-plurisubharmonic by the local upper-envelope theorem of chapter 1 : the functions $t\mapsto v(y',t)-F'(y')$ have the common upper bound $F_ m$, and at least one of them is not identically $-\infty $, by the lower bound $v\geq u-K$. The bound $v\leq u+C$ gives \[  a\leq u_ m+C+\sup _{Y'}(u'-F'),\qquad a\leq F_ m.  \] Thus $a$ is a competitor for $e_ m$, and $a\leq e_ m$. If $u_ m(t)$ is finite, so is $e_ m(t)$, since a sufficiently low translate of $u_ m$ is a competitor for $e_ m$. The function $v(\cdot ,t)-e_ m(t)$ is then a potential in the product background on $Y'$, not identically $-\infty $, lying below $F'$ and at least as singular as $u'$. By induction, $v(\cdot ,t)\leq \sum _{i<m}e_ i\circ \pi _ i+e_ m(t)$. At a pole of $u_ m$, the bound $v\leq u+C$ already gives $v=-\infty $. Every competitor is therefore bounded by $\sum _ i e_ i\circ \pi _ i$, and taking the regularized supremum proves the ordinary identity. For the ideal identity, put $B_ i=\int _{C_ i}\sigma _ i\geq 0$ and $\widehat\eta _ i=\eta _ i/A_ i$. By lemma 1.8.14 , choose smooth functions $\chi _ i$ with \[  \sigma _ i=B_ i\widehat\eta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ i.  \] Let $E_ i$ be the atomic part of $\sigma _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$. If $B_ i>0$, apply lemma 19.5.2 to $u_ i+\chi _ i$ in the positive background $B_ i\widehat\eta _ i$. Subtracting $\chi _ i$ from the resulting atomic Green potential gives a $\sigma _ i$-plurisubharmonic function $g_ i$ such that \[   egin{gathered} u_ i\sim _{\mathcal I}g_ i,\qquad P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}\sim g_ i,\ \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ i=E_ i-E_ i(C_ i)\widehat\eta _ i-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ i; \end{gathered}  \] the second relation uses the smooth gauge bounds of proposition 16.3.1 . If $B_ i=0$, lemma 1.8.14 gives $u_ i=-\chi _ i+c_ i$ for a constant $c_ i$, and $E_ i=0$; taking $g_ i=-\chi _ i$ gives the same conclusions. In either case, \[  \sigma _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ i =E_ i+(B_ i-E_ i(C_ i))\widehat\eta _ i\geq 0.  \] Put $g=\sum _ i g_ i\circ \pi _ i$. Pullback and addition, lemma 1.16.6 , lemma 1.16.4 , give $g\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. The complex Hessian of $g$ is a countable sum of divisor currents supported on coordinate fibers, minus a smooth form. This divisor current has finite mass, because each coordinate fiber has constant mass for a fixed product metric and each $E_ i$ has finite mass. Thus lemma 1.17.4 applies, even when some $B_ i$ vanish. Every ideal competitor $v\leq F$ for $u$ therefore satisfies $v\preceq g$, and is bounded by $P_{\gamma ,F}[g]$. Set $r_ i=P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}$. Invariance of the ordinary envelope under ordinary equivalence and proposition 16.6.8 give \[  P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[g_ i] =P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}] =r_ i.  \] By the ordinary identity already proved, applied to $g$, the ideal envelope of $u$ is therefore at most $\sum _ i r_ i\circ \pi _ i$. Conversely, each $r_ i$ lies below $F_ i$ and is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u_ i$, again by proposition 16.6.8 . Their sum is a $\gamma $-plurisubharmonic ideal competitor for $u$ below $F$, which proves the reverse inequality. No strict positivity of the backgrounds is needed in this comparison. $\square$ The proof of ( 16.27 ) uses that the obstacle is a sum of functions of the separate coordinates; for an arbitrary smooth obstacle on $Y$, the coordinatewise bounds are not available. Equality of the two envelopes below such mixed obstacles is treated in 16.6.11 . We now return to the positive product background $ eta $ and the normalized curve models $q_ i$, and add a divisorial factor as in 16.6.7 . Let $Z$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $k\geq 1$, and let $D\subset Z$ be a nonempty smooth reduced divisor, with a Kähler form $\kappa $ and a normalized potential $\psi $ satisfying $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =[D]$. On $M=Y	imes Z$, write $p,r$ for the projections, set $h_ i=\pi _ i\circ p$, and put \[  \Theta =p^* eta +r^*\kappa ,\qquad \Psi =\psi \circ r,\qquad \Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)=\Psi +\sum _ i q_ i\circ h_ i.  \] Let $\mathcal S_\Psi ^{(m)}$ be the set of these potentials. For the polar curvatures $\mu _ i=\mathbf1_{\{ q_ i=-\infty \} }(\eta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ i)$ and the analogous measures $
u _ i$ of models $b_ i$, define 16.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:separated-product-polar-metric} ho _\Psi ^{(m)}(\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m),\Phi (b_1,\ldots ,b_ m)) =\sum _ i\| \mu _ i-
u _ i\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Proposition 16.6.31 . The set $\mathcal S_\Psi ^{(m)}$ consists of normalized ordinary models and is a complete geodesic metric space for $ho _\Psi ^{(m)}$. Its ideal models form a closed geodesically convex subspace, equal to the metric closure of its models with analytic singularities. Ideal projection is the unique nearest-point retraction onto this subspace and is $1$-Lipschitz, and the distance to the subspace is the sum of the nonatomic polar masses. Metric convergence implies $L^1(M)$ convergence for every smooth positive volume form. The upper-volume comparison $d_\Theta $ vanishes on every pair of points of this locus. Proof. The preceding lemma and proposition 16.6.13 give \[   egin{gathered} P_\Theta [\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)]=\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m),\ P_\Theta [\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)]_{\mathcal I} =\Phi (q_{1,\mathcal I},\ldots ,q_{m,\mathcal I}), \end{gathered}  \] since the induced zero obstacle is zero; independence of the factors gives normalization. Restricting to sections on which the other potentials are finite shows that if two product potentials are equal, then each coordinate difference is constant, and normalization makes every such constant zero. Thus $\Phi $ identifies this locus with the finite product of the spaces of curve models, equipped with the sum of their metrics. Completeness follows coordinate by coordinate from corollary 30.12.3 . Interpolating all polar measures linearly with the same parameter gives a constant-speed geodesic for the sum metric. Ideal projection takes the atomic part in each coordinate, so the assertions on closedness, convexity, unique nearest points and the Lipschitz bound follow coordinate by coordinate from corollary 30.12.3 , proposition 30.12.6 , and the distances add. Finite atomic approximations with rational coefficients in each coordinate have local logarithmic coefficients whose denominators, together with the unit coefficient of $D$, can be cleared in a product monomial. They give analytic models that are dense in the ideal subspace. Conversely, every ordinary model with analytic singularities is its own ideal projection by proposition 16.2.7 , so the closure of these models is exactly the ideal subspace. By theorem 30.12.4 , metric convergence gives $L^1$ convergence on each curve. Off the pole sets, the difference of two product potentials is the sum of the pulled-back coordinate differences. Integrating each term along the compact fibers of $h_ i$ bounds its $L^1$ norm on $M$ by a constant times its $L^1$ norm on the curve, as in proposition 16.6.26 , and the finite sum tends to zero. Finally, since $\dim Y=m<\dim M$, proposition 16.6.13 shows that every model in this locus has zero upper singularity volume. A pairwise maximum is still $\Psi $ plus the pullback of a $ eta $-plurisubharmonic function on $Y$, so the same proposition gives zero upper volume for it. All three terms of $d_\Theta $ therefore vanish. $\square$ As in corollary 16.6.27 , corollary 16.6.28 , an auxiliary curve factor with a variable coefficient makes the background nonclosed, and lets it degenerate, without changing this metric locus. Keep $Y, eta ,\pi _ i$ and $Z,\kappa ,D,\psi $ from above. Let $C_0$ be another connected compact curve with a smooth positive form $	au $. On $M=Y	imes C_0	imes Z$, write $p,s,r$ for the projections. For a smooth real function $f\geq 0$ on $Y$, put \[  \Theta _ f=p^* eta +(f\circ p)s^*	au +r^*\kappa , \qquad \Psi =\psi \circ r,  \] and set $\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)=\Psi +\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p$. Corollary 16.6.32 . For every tuple of normalized ordinary curve models, one has \[   egin{gathered} P_{\Theta _ f}[\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)]=\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m),\ P_{\Theta _ f}[\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)]_{\mathcal I} =\Phi (q_{1,\mathcal I},\ldots ,q_{m,\mathcal I}). \end{gathered}  \] On the locus of these potentials, use the sum of polar distances ( 16.30 ). All the metric conclusions of proposition 16.6.31 hold, and the diameter is $2\sum _ i A_ i$. The locus, its metric, ideal projection and the analytic closure are independent of $f$, including at $f=0$. The background is positive and not closed when $f$ is positive and nonconstant. The background $\Theta _0$ obtained for $f=0$ is not big. Proof. On $B=Y	imes C_0$, let $\pi ,s_0$ be the projections and put $ eta _ f=\pi ^* eta +(f\circ \pi )s_0^*	au $. For $w=\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i$, an ordinary competitor $v\leq 0$ for $w\circ \pi $ may be replaced by its maximum with $w\circ \pi $. Its restriction to every section $Y	imes \{ z\} $ is then a $ eta $-plurisubharmonic competitor for $P_ eta [w]=w$, not identically $-\infty $, by lemma 16.6.29 . Thus \[  P_{ eta _ f}[w\circ \pi ]=w\circ \pi .  \] Take the atomic Green potentials $g_ i$ from the proof of the lemma and put $g=\sum _ i g_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $. Its complex Hessian is a closed countable divisor current of finite mass minus a smooth form. It is $ eta _ f$-plurisubharmonic for every $f\geq 0$, and it is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $w\circ \pi $. Put $w_{\mathcal I}=\sum _ iq_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i$. Since $g\sim w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi $, every ideal competitor $v\leq 0$ is bounded above by \[  P_{ eta _ f}[g] =P_{ eta _ f}[w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi ] =w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi .  \] Here lemma 1.17.4 gives $v\preceq g$, and the ordinary identity applies to $w_{\mathcal I}$. Conversely, $w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi $ is a normalized ideal competitor, because ideal projection preserves the ideal type on each curve and the ideal type is compatible with pullback and addition. This computes the ideal envelope on $B$ without requiring $ eta _ f$ to be positive. Apply proposition 16.6.13 to $M	o B$ and the divisor $B	imes D$. Its induced zero obstacle is zero, which gives the two identities upstairs and normalization. Restriction to a fixed section of the auxiliary curve identifies this locus isometrically with the finite product of the spaces of curve models. Completeness, geodesics and the nearest-point property of ideal projection therefore follow as in proposition 16.6.31 , and the same rational atomic monomials give analytic density. For $f=1$, the background is positive and proposition 16.2.7 shows that every analytic model lies in the ideal subspace. Analytic singularities and the computed ideal projection are independent of $f$, so this analytic-closure assertion holds for every nonnegative coefficient. Fiber integration, now including the factor $C_0$, gives the same $L^1$ convergence upstairs. Each model and each pairwise maximum is $\Psi $ plus a pullback from $B$, whose dimension is smaller than that of $M$, so their upper volumes vanish by proposition 16.6.13 ; the upper-volume comparison of definition 30.6.1 therefore vanishes for every $f$. Each polar measure $\mu _ i$ has mass at most $A_ i$, so the sum distance is at most $2\sum _ iA_ i$. By lemma 30.12.1 , this bound is attained by placing mass $A_ i$ at two distinct points of each $C_ i$. Hence the diameter does not change, even at the limiting coefficient. Finally, $\mathrm d\Theta _ f=p^*(\mathrm df)\wedge s^*	au $ is nonzero for nonconstant $f$, and $\Theta _ f$ is strictly positive when $f>0$. To see that $\Theta _0$ is not big, put $n=m+1+k$ and use the smooth closed positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form $T$ and the Hermitian form $\Omega $ given by \[  T=p^*\left( igwedge _ i\pi _ i^*\eta _ iight)\wedge r^*(\kappa ^ k), \qquad \Omega =p^* eta +s^*	au +r^*\kappa .  \] Then $\int _ M\Theta _0\wedge T=0$, whereas $\int _ M\Omega \wedge T>0$. By Stokes' theorem, a lower bound $\Theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \varepsilon \Omega $ with $\varepsilon >0$ would contradict these identities. Thus the background $\Theta _0$ is not big. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.6.29
text: Lemma 16.6.29 . The function $w$ is a normalized ordinary model on $(Y,\beta )$, and \[  P_\beta [w]_{\mathcal I} =\sum _{i=1}^ m q_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i.  \] Proof. The function $w$ is $\beta $-plurisubharmonic and has supremum zero. We prove $P_\beta [w]=w$ by induction on the number of factors, the case of one factor being the identity $P_{\eta _1}[q_1]=q_1$. Let $v\leq 0$ be an ordinary competitor, and replace it by $\max (v,w)$. This preserves $v\preceq w$ and ensures that the restrictions of $v$ to slices are not identically $-\infty $ wherever the corresponding curve potentials are finite. Write $Y=Y'\times C_ m$, and take the regularized partial supremum \[  a(t)=\left(\sup _{y'\in Y'}v(y',t)\right)^*.  \] The restrictions of $v$ to the slices $\{ y'\} \times C_ m$ are $\eta _ m$-plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. They are bounded above by zero, and at least one of them is not identically $-\infty $, since $v\geq w$. The local upper-envelope theorem from chapter 1 therefore makes $a$ an $\eta _ m$-plurisubharmonic function. The global inequality $v\leq w+C$ gives $a\leq q_ m+C$, because the other normalized potentials have supremum zero. Thus $a$ is a competitor for $P_{\eta _ m}[q_ m]$, and $a\leq P_{\eta _ m}[q_ m]=q_ m$. For $t$ with $q_ m(t)$ finite, the function $v(\cdot ,t)-q_ m(t)$ is a potential in the product background on $Y'$, not identically $-\infty $; it is nonpositive and at least as singular as $\sum _{i<m}q_ i\circ \pi _ i$. The induction hypothesis bounds it by that sum. Hence $v\leq w$ off the poles of $q_ m$. At those poles the original bound $v\leq w+C$ gives the same inequality. Taking the envelope proves the ordinary identity. For the ideal identity, let $E_ i$ be the atomic part of the polar curvature of $q_ i$, and take the Green potentials $g_ i$ of lemma 19.5.2 . They satisfy \[  q_ i\sim _{\mathcal I}g_ i,\qquad q_{i,\mathcal I}\sim g_ i,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ i=E_ i-\frac{E_ i(C_ i)}{A_ i}\eta _ i.  \] By lemma 1.16.6 , lemma 1.16.4 , $g=\sum _ i g_ i\circ \pi _ i$ is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $w$. Its complex Hessian is a closed countable sum of the divisors $\pi _ i^{-1}(x)$ minus the smooth form $\sum _ i E_ i(C_ i)\pi _ i^*\eta _ i/A_ i$. Each coordinate fiber has constant mass for the product metric, so the divisor part has finite mass. Moreover $g$ is $\beta $-plurisubharmonic since $E_ i(C_ i)\leq A_ i$. Therefore corollary 16.2.8 gives $P_\beta [g]_{\mathcal I}=P_\beta [g]$. Since $g$ is ordinarily equivalent to $\sum _ iq_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i$, the ordinary identity, applied to the models $q_{i,\mathcal I}$, shows that this envelope is $\sum _ iq_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i$. As $w\sim _{\mathcal I}g$, the ideal envelope of $w$ is the same, which proves the assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.6.30
text: Proposition 16.6.30 . For the preceding data, 16.27 \begin{equation} \label{eq:separated-curve-obstacle-projections} \begin{aligned}  P_{\gamma ,F}[u] & =\sum _ i P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]\circ \pi _ i,\\  P_{\gamma ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} & =\sum _ i P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i. \end{aligned} \end{equation} These identities also hold when some of the curve backgrounds have zero area. Proof. Write $e_ i=P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]$. Sums of ordinary competitors in the separate coordinates are ordinary competitors on the product, and their regularized supremum is $\sum _ i e_ i\circ \pi _ i$. This gives the lower bound in the first identity. For the upper bound we use induction on the number of factors, the case of one factor being trivial. Let $v\leq F$ be an ordinary competitor, so that $v\leq u+C$ for some constant $C$. Choose a constant $K$ with $u-K\leq F$ and replace $v$ by $\max (v,u-K)$. This preserves both bounds and ensures that the restrictions of $v$ to the slices used below are not identically $-\infty $. Write $Y=Y'\times C_ m$, and on $Y'$ put $u'=\sum _{i<m}u_ i\circ \pi _ i$ and $F'=\sum _{i<m}F_ i\circ \pi _ i$. The regularized partial supremum \[  a(t)=\left(\sup _{y'\in Y'}\bigl (v(y',t)-F'(y')\bigr )\right)^*  \] is $\sigma _ m$-plurisubharmonic by the local upper-envelope theorem of chapter 1 : the functions $t\mapsto v(y',t)-F'(y')$ have the common upper bound $F_ m$, and at least one of them is not identically $-\infty $, by the lower bound $v\geq u-K$. The bound $v\leq u+C$ gives \[  a\leq u_ m+C+\sup _{Y'}(u'-F'),\qquad a\leq F_ m.  \] Thus $a$ is a competitor for $e_ m$, and $a\leq e_ m$. If $u_ m(t)$ is finite, so is $e_ m(t)$, since a sufficiently low translate of $u_ m$ is a competitor for $e_ m$. The function $v(\cdot ,t)-e_ m(t)$ is then a potential in the product background on $Y'$, not identically $-\infty $, lying below $F'$ and at least as singular as $u'$. By induction, $v(\cdot ,t)\leq \sum _{i<m}e_ i\circ \pi _ i+e_ m(t)$. At a pole of $u_ m$, the bound $v\leq u+C$ already gives $v=-\infty $. Every competitor is therefore bounded by $\sum _ i e_ i\circ \pi _ i$, and taking the regularized supremum proves the ordinary identity. For the ideal identity, put $B_ i=\int _{C_ i}\sigma _ i\geq 0$ and $\widehat\eta _ i=\eta _ i/A_ i$. By lemma 1.8.14 , choose smooth functions $\chi _ i$ with \[  \sigma _ i=B_ i\widehat\eta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ i.  \] Let $E_ i$ be the atomic part of $\sigma _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$. If $B_ i>0$, apply lemma 19.5.2 to $u_ i+\chi _ i$ in the positive background $B_ i\widehat\eta _ i$. Subtracting $\chi _ i$ from the resulting atomic Green potential gives a $\sigma _ i$-plurisubharmonic function $g_ i$ such that \[  \begin{gathered} u_ i\sim _{\mathcal I}g_ i,\qquad P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}\sim g_ i,\\ \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ i=E_ i-E_ i(C_ i)\widehat\eta _ i-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ i; \end{gathered}  \] the second relation uses the smooth gauge bounds of proposition 16.3.1 . If $B_ i=0$, lemma 1.8.14 gives $u_ i=-\chi _ i+c_ i$ for a constant $c_ i$, and $E_ i=0$; taking $g_ i=-\chi _ i$ gives the same conclusions. In either case, \[  \sigma _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ i =E_ i+(B_ i-E_ i(C_ i))\widehat\eta _ i\geq 0.  \] Put $g=\sum _ i g_ i\circ \pi _ i$. Pullback and addition, lemma 1.16.6 , lemma 1.16.4 , give $g\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. The complex Hessian of $g$ is a countable sum of divisor currents supported on coordinate fibers, minus a smooth form. This divisor current has finite mass, because each coordinate fiber has constant mass for a fixed product metric and each $E_ i$ has finite mass. Thus lemma 1.17.4 applies, even when some $B_ i$ vanish. Every ideal competitor $v\leq F$ for $u$ therefore satisfies $v\preceq g$, and is bounded by $P_{\gamma ,F}[g]$. Set $r_ i=P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}$. Invariance of the ordinary envelope under ordinary equivalence and proposition 16.6.8 give \[  P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[g_ i] =P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}] =r_ i.  \] By the ordinary identity already proved, applied to $g$, the ideal envelope of $u$ is therefore at most $\sum _ i r_ i\circ \pi _ i$. Conversely, each $r_ i$ lies below $F_ i$ and is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u_ i$, again by proposition 16.6.8 . Their sum is a $\gamma $-plurisubharmonic ideal competitor for $u$ below $F$, which proves the reverse inequality. No strict positivity of the backgrounds is needed in this comparison. $\square$

16.27 \begin{equation} \label{eq:separated-curve-obstacle-projections} \begin{aligned}  P_{\gamma ,F}[u] & =\sum _ i P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]\circ \pi _ i,\\  P_{\gamma ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} & =\sum _ i P_{\sigma _ i,F_ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
16.30 \begin{equation} \label{eq:separated-product-polar-metric} \rho _\Psi ^{(m)}(\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m),\Phi (b_1,\ldots ,b_ m)) =\sum _ i\| \mu _ i-\nu _ i\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 16.6.31
text: Proposition 16.6.31 . The set $\mathcal S_\Psi ^{(m)}$ consists of normalized ordinary models and is a complete geodesic metric space for $\rho _\Psi ^{(m)}$. Its ideal models form a closed geodesically convex subspace, equal to the metric closure of its models with analytic singularities. Ideal projection is the unique nearest-point retraction onto this subspace and is $1$-Lipschitz, and the distance to the subspace is the sum of the nonatomic polar masses. Metric convergence implies $L^1(M)$ convergence for every smooth positive volume form. The upper-volume comparison $d_\Theta $ vanishes on every pair of points of this locus. Proof. The preceding lemma and proposition 16.6.13 give \[  \begin{gathered} P_\Theta [\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)]=\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m),\\ P_\Theta [\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)]_{\mathcal I} =\Phi (q_{1,\mathcal I},\ldots ,q_{m,\mathcal I}), \end{gathered}  \] since the induced zero obstacle is zero; independence of the factors gives normalization. Restricting to sections on which the other potentials are finite shows that if two product potentials are equal, then each coordinate difference is constant, and normalization makes every such constant zero. Thus $\Phi $ identifies this locus with the finite product of the spaces of curve models, equipped with the sum of their metrics. Completeness follows coordinate by coordinate from corollary 30.12.3 . Interpolating all polar measures linearly with the same parameter gives a constant-speed geodesic for the sum metric. Ideal projection takes the atomic part in each coordinate, so the assertions on closedness, convexity, unique nearest points and the Lipschitz bound follow coordinate by coordinate from corollary 30.12.3 , proposition 30.12.6 , and the distances add. Finite atomic approximations with rational coefficients in each coordinate have local logarithmic coefficients whose denominators, together with the unit coefficient of $D$, can be cleared in a product monomial. They give analytic models that are dense in the ideal subspace. Conversely, every ordinary model with analytic singularities is its own ideal projection by proposition 16.2.7 , so the closure of these models is exactly the ideal subspace. By theorem 30.12.4 , metric convergence gives $L^1$ convergence on each curve. Off the pole sets, the difference of two product potentials is the sum of the pulled-back coordinate differences. Integrating each term along the compact fibers of $h_ i$ bounds its $L^1$ norm on $M$ by a constant times its $L^1$ norm on the curve, as in proposition 16.6.26 , and the finite sum tends to zero. Finally, since $\dim Y=m<\dim M$, proposition 16.6.13 shows that every model in this locus has zero upper singularity volume. A pairwise maximum is still $\Psi $ plus the pullback of a $\beta $-plurisubharmonic function on $Y$, so the same proposition gives zero upper volume for it. All three terms of $d_\Theta $ therefore vanish. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.6.32
text: Corollary 16.6.32 . For every tuple of normalized ordinary curve models, one has \[  \begin{gathered} P_{\Theta _ f}[\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)]=\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m),\\ P_{\Theta _ f}[\Phi (q_1,\ldots ,q_ m)]_{\mathcal I} =\Phi (q_{1,\mathcal I},\ldots ,q_{m,\mathcal I}). \end{gathered}  \] On the locus of these potentials, use the sum of polar distances ( 16.30 ). All the metric conclusions of proposition 16.6.31 hold, and the diameter is $2\sum _ i A_ i$. The locus, its metric, ideal projection and the analytic closure are independent of $f$, including at $f=0$. The background is positive and not closed when $f$ is positive and nonconstant. The background $\Theta _0$ obtained for $f=0$ is not big. Proof. On $B=Y\times C_0$, let $\pi ,s_0$ be the projections and put $\beta _ f=\pi ^*\beta +(f\circ \pi )s_0^*\tau $. For $w=\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i$, an ordinary competitor $v\leq 0$ for $w\circ \pi $ may be replaced by its maximum with $w\circ \pi $. Its restriction to every section $Y\times \{ z\} $ is then a $\beta $-plurisubharmonic competitor for $P_\beta [w]=w$, not identically $-\infty $, by lemma 16.6.29 . Thus \[  P_{\beta _ f}[w\circ \pi ]=w\circ \pi .  \] Take the atomic Green potentials $g_ i$ from the proof of the lemma and put $g=\sum _ i g_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $. Its complex Hessian is a closed countable divisor current of finite mass minus a smooth form. It is $\beta _ f$-plurisubharmonic for every $f\geq 0$, and it is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $w\circ \pi $. Put $w_{\mathcal I}=\sum _ iq_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i$. Since $g\sim w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi $, every ideal competitor $v\leq 0$ is bounded above by \[  P_{\beta _ f}[g] =P_{\beta _ f}[w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi ] =w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi .  \] Here lemma 1.17.4 gives $v\preceq g$, and the ordinary identity applies to $w_{\mathcal I}$. Conversely, $w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi $ is a normalized ideal competitor, because ideal projection preserves the ideal type on each curve and the ideal type is compatible with pullback and addition. This computes the ideal envelope on $B$ without requiring $\beta _ f$ to be positive. Apply proposition 16.6.13 to $M\to B$ and the divisor $B\times D$. Its induced zero obstacle is zero, which gives the two identities upstairs and normalization. Restriction to a fixed section of the auxiliary curve identifies this locus isometrically with the finite product of the spaces of curve models. Completeness, geodesics and the nearest-point property of ideal projection therefore follow as in proposition 16.6.31 , and the same rational atomic monomials give analytic density. For $f=1$, the background is positive and proposition 16.2.7 shows that every analytic model lies in the ideal subspace. Analytic singularities and the computed ideal projection are independent of $f$, so this analytic-closure assertion holds for every nonnegative coefficient. Fiber integration, now including the factor $C_0$, gives the same $L^1$ convergence upstairs. Each model and each pairwise maximum is $\Psi $ plus a pullback from $B$, whose dimension is smaller than that of $M$, so their upper volumes vanish by proposition 16.6.13 ; the upper-volume comparison of definition 30.6.1 therefore vanishes for every $f$. Each polar measure $\mu _ i$ has mass at most $A_ i$, so the sum distance is at most $2\sum _ iA_ i$. By lemma 30.12.1 , this bound is attained by placing mass $A_ i$ at two distinct points of each $C_ i$. Hence the diameter does not change, even at the limiting coefficient. Finally, $\mathrm d\Theta _ f=p^*(\mathrm df)\wedge s^*\tau $ is nonzero for nonconstant $f$, and $\Theta _ f$ is strictly positive when $f>0$. To see that $\Theta _0$ is not big, put $n=m+1+k$ and use the smooth closed positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form $T$ and the Hermitian form $\Omega $ given by \[  T=p^*\left(\bigwedge _ i\pi _ i^*\eta _ i\right)\wedge r^*(\kappa ^ k), \qquad \Omega =p^*\beta +s^*\tau +r^*\kappa .  \] Then $\int _ M\Theta _0\wedge T=0$, whereas $\int _ M\Omega \wedge T>0$. By Stokes' theorem, a lower bound $\Theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \varepsilon \Omega $ with $\varepsilon >0$ would contradict these identities. Thus the background $\Theta _0$ is not big. $\square$

title: 16.6.9 Varying the curve coefficients
text:
16.6.9 Varying the curve coefficients The coefficient $f$ of the auxiliary curve in corollary 16.6.32 does not affect the metric on the model locus. Scaling the curve forms themselves has a different effect: a positive coefficient rescales the polar distance in its coordinate, whereas a zero coefficient removes the coordinate altogether, so the diameter depends on the remaining curve areas. We describe the resulting family of model spaces and then compare its members. Keep the product $M=Y	imes C_0	imes Z$, its projections and the forms of that corollary. For $a=(a_1,\ldots ,a_ m)\in [0,\infty )^ m$ and a smooth function $f\geq 0$ on $Y$, put \[  J(a)=\{ i:a_ i>0\} ,\qquad  eta _ a=\sum _ i a_ i\pi _ i^*\eta _ i,\qquad \Theta _{a,f}=p^* eta _ a+(f\circ p)s^*	au +r^*\kappa .  \] The coordinates $i\in J(a)$ are called active . For normalized ordinary models $q_ i$ in the fixed curve backgrounds $\eta _ i$, define \[  \Phi _ a(q)=\Psi +\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p, \qquad \Psi =\psi \circ r.  \] Terms with zero coefficient are omitted, also on their pole sets, so $\Phi _ a(q)$ depends only on the active coordinates. Write $\mathcal S_ a$ for this locus of potentials, and $q_{i,\mathcal I}=P_{\eta _ i}[q_ i]_{\mathcal I}$. Lemma 16.6.33 . For every $a$ and $f$ as above, \[  P_{\Theta _{a,f}}[\Phi _ a(q)]=\Phi _ a(q),\qquad P_{\Theta _{a,f}}[\Phi _ a(q)]_{\mathcal I}=\Phi _ a(q_{\mathcal I}).  \] Both potentials have supremum zero. In particular, $\mathcal S_0=\{ \Psi \} $. Proof. For $a_ i>0$, scaling the ordinary competitors shows that $a_ iq_ i$ is an ordinary model for $a_ i\eta _ i$. Its polar curvature is $a_ i\mu _ i$, where $\mu _ i$ is the polar curvature of $q_ i$. Taking atomic parts and applying theorem 30.13.3 , we see that its ideal model is $a_ iq_{i,\mathcal I}$. Put $w_ a=\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i$. If there are at least two active factors, lemma 16.6.29 makes the corresponding sum an ordinary model on the product of the active curves, with its positive product background. For one active factor, this is the identity on the curve. The identity is preserved under pullback to $Y$, by proposition 1.22.3 : every competitor in the pulled-back background descends, and so do its obstacle bound and its ordinary order, since the projection is surjective. If there are no active factors, the normalized model is zero by the maximum principle. Hence $P_{ eta _ a}[w_ a]=w_ a$ in all cases. On $B=Y	imes C_0$, use the background $ eta _{a,f}=\pi ^* eta _ a+(f\circ \pi )s_0^*	au $. As in corollary 16.6.32 , replace an ordinary competitor by its maximum with $w_ a\circ \pi $ and restrict it to each section $Y	imes \{ z\} $. This gives $P_{ eta _{a,f}}[w_ a\circ \pi ]=w_ a\circ \pi $. For the ideal identity, take $g_ a=\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ i g_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $, with the atomic Green potentials $g_ i$ of lemma 19.5.2 . Scaling, addition and pullback preserve multiplier-ideal equivalence by lemma 1.16.4 , lemma 1.16.6 . The complex Hessian of $g_ a$ is a closed countable divisor current of finite mass minus a smooth form, and $g_ a$ is $ eta _{a,f}$-plurisubharmonic. It is ordinarily equivalent to $w_{a,\mathcal I}\circ \pi $, where $w_{a,\mathcal I}=\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ iq_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i$. By lemma 1.17.4 , every ideal competitor is an ordinary competitor for $g_ a$, so by the ordinary identity applied to the models $a_ iq_{i,\mathcal I}$ it is bounded by $w_{a,\mathcal I}\circ \pi $. The latter is itself an ideal competitor, so the ideal envelope equals it. When $J(a)$ is empty, both envelopes on $B$ are zero directly. Finally, proposition 16.6.13 , applied to $M	o B$ and the divisor $B	imes D$ with weight one, gives the identities upstairs, and independence of the factors gives normalization. $\square$ For two tuples $q,\widetilde q$, let $\mu _ i,
u _ i$ be their polar curvature measures in the fixed backgrounds $\eta _ i$, and set 16.31  egin{equation} \label{eq:weighted-product-polar-metric} ho _ a(\Phi _ a(q),\Phi _ a(\widetilde q)) =\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ i\| \mu _ i-
u _ i\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} On the singleton $\mathcal S_0$ this distance is zero. Proposition 16.6.34 . For every $a$, the locus $\mathcal S_ a$ is a complete geodesic metric space for $ho _ a$, independently of $f$. Its ideal subspace is closed, geodesically convex and equal to the metric closure of its models with analytic singularities. Ideal projection is the unique nearest-point retraction onto this subspace and is $1$-Lipschitz, with distance \[  ho _ a igl (\Phi _ a(q),\Phi _ a(q_{\mathcal I}) igr ) =\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ i\mu _ i^{\mathrm{na}}(C_ i),  \] where $\mu _ i^{\mathrm{na}}$ is the nonatomic part of $\mu _ i$. The diameter is $2\sum _ i a_ iA_ i$, and metric convergence implies $L^1(M)$ convergence for every smooth positive volume form. The upper-volume comparison vanishes on this locus. If $a,b$ have the same nonempty active set $J$, the correspondence $T_{ba}\Phi _ a(q)=\Phi _ b(q)$ is well defined, commutes with ideal projection and satisfies \[  \min _{i\in J} rac{b_ i}{a_ i}\, ho _ a(u,v) \leq ho _ b(T_{ba}u,T_{ba}v) \leq \max _{i\in J} rac{b_ i}{a_ i}\, ho _ a(u,v).  \] For a fixed smooth positive volume form on $M$, there are constants $K_ i$, independent of $a,b$ and of the normalized model tuple $q$, such that \[  \| \Phi _ a(q)-\Phi _ b(q)\| _{L^1(M)} \leq \sum _ i K_ i|a_ i-b_ i|.  \] Consequently, as all $a_ i$ tend to zero, the diameter tends to zero and every potential in $\mathcal S_ a$ tends to $\Psi $ in $L^1(M)$, uniformly over the normalized model tuples. Proof. Restriction to coordinate sections on which the other potentials are finite determines every active term $a_ iq_ i$ up to a constant, and normalization makes these constants zero. Thus ( 16.31 ) is well defined, and it identifies $\mathcal S_ a$ with the product of the spaces of curve models in the active coordinates, with their distances multiplied by $a_ i$. Coordinates with $a_ i=0$ do not appear, and for $J(a)=\varnothing $ the empty product is a single point. The completeness, geodesic and atomic-projection results of corollary 30.12.3 , proposition 30.12.6 apply coordinate by coordinate, and the weighted distances add; this proves the metric assertions and the distance formula. The diameter bound is attained by choosing polar measures $A_ i\delta _{x_ i}$ and $A_ i\delta _{y_ i}$ with $x_ i
e y_ i$ on each active curve. Fiber integration and theorem 30.12.4 give $L^1$ convergence upstairs. The preceding lemma shows that ideal projection does not depend on $f$. Since every model and every pairwise maximum is $\Psi $ plus a pullback from $B$, proposition 16.6.13 gives zero upper volumes, so the upper-volume comparison vanishes. For analytic density, approximate the atomic part $a_ i\mu _ i^{\mathrm{at}}$ of each scaled polar measure, where $\mu _ i^{\mathrm{at}}=\mu _ i-\mu _ i^{\mathrm{na}}$, by finite atomic measures with rational coefficients and mass at most $a_ iA_ i$. These approximations converge in total variation. Their curve models in the background $a_ i\eta _ i$ have finitely many logarithmic poles with rational coefficients, whose denominators, together with the unit coefficient of $D$, can be cleared in local product monomials. They therefore give analytic models in $\mathcal S_ a$ converging to every ideal model. Conversely, suppose that $\Phi _ a(q)$ has analytic singularities. Restrict it to a section along an active curve on which all other potentials are finite and whose $Z$-coordinate lies outside $D$. By proposition 1.13.1 , the restriction, which is $a_ iq_ i$ plus a constant and not identically $-\infty $, has analytic singularities. It is an ordinary model in the positive background $a_ i\eta _ i$, so proposition 16.2.7 shows that it equals its ideal projection. The preceding lemma now shows that $\Phi _ a(q)$ is an ideal model, and closedness gives the analytic-closure assertion. The argument uses rational coefficients for the scaled poles $a_ iq_ i$ themselves. With the rational-coefficient convention of section 1.13 , an irrational scaling need not preserve an analytic curve model, since it can give a pole an irrational Lelong number. For a common active set, the normalized tuple is determined by the potential. The two bounds for $T_{ba}$ follow by comparing each positive weight $b_ i$ with $a_ i$, and atomic projection in each coordinate commutes with this correspondence. Finally, normalized compactness, theorem 1.4.2 , bounds the $L^1(C_ i)$ norms of all the $q_ i$ uniformly. Integration along the compact fibers of $\pi _ i\circ p$ gives constants $K_ i$ bounding the $L^1(M)$ norms of their pullbacks. Off the pole sets, which have smooth volume zero, the difference of the two potentials is the sum of the functions $(a_ i-b_ i)q_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p$. The triangle inequality proves the uniform estimate, also when some coefficients vanish. Taking $b=0$ gives uniform convergence to $\Psi $, and the diameter formula shows that the diameters tend to zero. $\square$ Thus letting the auxiliary coefficient vanish leaves the metric of corollary 16.6.32 unchanged, whereas letting a curve coefficient vanish removes its coordinate and decreases the diameter. These computations concern only the specified product loci, not general ordinary models in higher dimension.

title: Lemma 16.6.33
text: Lemma 16.6.33 . For every $a$ and $f$ as above, \[  P_{\Theta _{a,f}}[\Phi _ a(q)]=\Phi _ a(q),\qquad P_{\Theta _{a,f}}[\Phi _ a(q)]_{\mathcal I}=\Phi _ a(q_{\mathcal I}).  \] Both potentials have supremum zero. In particular, $\mathcal S_0=\{ \Psi \} $. Proof. For $a_ i>0$, scaling the ordinary competitors shows that $a_ iq_ i$ is an ordinary model for $a_ i\eta _ i$. Its polar curvature is $a_ i\mu _ i$, where $\mu _ i$ is the polar curvature of $q_ i$. Taking atomic parts and applying theorem 30.13.3 , we see that its ideal model is $a_ iq_{i,\mathcal I}$. Put $w_ a=\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i$. If there are at least two active factors, lemma 16.6.29 makes the corresponding sum an ordinary model on the product of the active curves, with its positive product background. For one active factor, this is the identity on the curve. The identity is preserved under pullback to $Y$, by proposition 1.22.3 : every competitor in the pulled-back background descends, and so do its obstacle bound and its ordinary order, since the projection is surjective. If there are no active factors, the normalized model is zero by the maximum principle. Hence $P_{\beta _ a}[w_ a]=w_ a$ in all cases. On $B=Y\times C_0$, use the background $\beta _{a,f}=\pi ^*\beta _ a+(f\circ \pi )s_0^*\tau $. As in corollary 16.6.32 , replace an ordinary competitor by its maximum with $w_ a\circ \pi $ and restrict it to each section $Y\times \{ z\} $. This gives $P_{\beta _{a,f}}[w_ a\circ \pi ]=w_ a\circ \pi $. For the ideal identity, take $g_ a=\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ i g_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $, with the atomic Green potentials $g_ i$ of lemma 19.5.2 . Scaling, addition and pullback preserve multiplier-ideal equivalence by lemma 1.16.4 , lemma 1.16.6 . The complex Hessian of $g_ a$ is a closed countable divisor current of finite mass minus a smooth form, and $g_ a$ is $\beta _{a,f}$-plurisubharmonic. It is ordinarily equivalent to $w_{a,\mathcal I}\circ \pi $, where $w_{a,\mathcal I}=\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ iq_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i$. By lemma 1.17.4 , every ideal competitor is an ordinary competitor for $g_ a$, so by the ordinary identity applied to the models $a_ iq_{i,\mathcal I}$ it is bounded by $w_{a,\mathcal I}\circ \pi $. The latter is itself an ideal competitor, so the ideal envelope equals it. When $J(a)$ is empty, both envelopes on $B$ are zero directly. Finally, proposition 16.6.13 , applied to $M\to B$ and the divisor $B\times D$ with weight one, gives the identities upstairs, and independence of the factors gives normalization. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.6.34
text: Proposition 16.6.34 . For every $a$, the locus $\mathcal S_ a$ is a complete geodesic metric space for $\rho _ a$, independently of $f$. Its ideal subspace is closed, geodesically convex and equal to the metric closure of its models with analytic singularities. Ideal projection is the unique nearest-point retraction onto this subspace and is $1$-Lipschitz, with distance \[  \rho _ a\bigl (\Phi _ a(q),\Phi _ a(q_{\mathcal I})\bigr ) =\sum _{i\in J(a)}a_ i\mu _ i^{\mathrm{na}}(C_ i),  \] where $\mu _ i^{\mathrm{na}}$ is the nonatomic part of $\mu _ i$. The diameter is $2\sum _ i a_ iA_ i$, and metric convergence implies $L^1(M)$ convergence for every smooth positive volume form. The upper-volume comparison vanishes on this locus. If $a,b$ have the same nonempty active set $J$, the correspondence $T_{ba}\Phi _ a(q)=\Phi _ b(q)$ is well defined, commutes with ideal projection and satisfies \[  \min _{i\in J}\frac{b_ i}{a_ i}\, \rho _ a(u,v) \leq \rho _ b(T_{ba}u,T_{ba}v) \leq \max _{i\in J}\frac{b_ i}{a_ i}\, \rho _ a(u,v).  \] For a fixed smooth positive volume form on $M$, there are constants $K_ i$, independent of $a,b$ and of the normalized model tuple $q$, such that \[  \| \Phi _ a(q)-\Phi _ b(q)\| _{L^1(M)} \leq \sum _ i K_ i|a_ i-b_ i|.  \] Consequently, as all $a_ i$ tend to zero, the diameter tends to zero and every potential in $\mathcal S_ a$ tends to $\Psi $ in $L^1(M)$, uniformly over the normalized model tuples. Proof. Restriction to coordinate sections on which the other potentials are finite determines every active term $a_ iq_ i$ up to a constant, and normalization makes these constants zero. Thus ( 16.31 ) is well defined, and it identifies $\mathcal S_ a$ with the product of the spaces of curve models in the active coordinates, with their distances multiplied by $a_ i$. Coordinates with $a_ i=0$ do not appear, and for $J(a)=\varnothing $ the empty product is a single point. The completeness, geodesic and atomic-projection results of corollary 30.12.3 , proposition 30.12.6 apply coordinate by coordinate, and the weighted distances add; this proves the metric assertions and the distance formula. The diameter bound is attained by choosing polar measures $A_ i\delta _{x_ i}$ and $A_ i\delta _{y_ i}$ with $x_ i\ne y_ i$ on each active curve. Fiber integration and theorem 30.12.4 give $L^1$ convergence upstairs. The preceding lemma shows that ideal projection does not depend on $f$. Since every model and every pairwise maximum is $\Psi $ plus a pullback from $B$, proposition 16.6.13 gives zero upper volumes, so the upper-volume comparison vanishes. For analytic density, approximate the atomic part $a_ i\mu _ i^{\mathrm{at}}$ of each scaled polar measure, where $\mu _ i^{\mathrm{at}}=\mu _ i-\mu _ i^{\mathrm{na}}$, by finite atomic measures with rational coefficients and mass at most $a_ iA_ i$. These approximations converge in total variation. Their curve models in the background $a_ i\eta _ i$ have finitely many logarithmic poles with rational coefficients, whose denominators, together with the unit coefficient of $D$, can be cleared in local product monomials. They therefore give analytic models in $\mathcal S_ a$ converging to every ideal model. Conversely, suppose that $\Phi _ a(q)$ has analytic singularities. Restrict it to a section along an active curve on which all other potentials are finite and whose $Z$-coordinate lies outside $D$. By proposition 1.13.1 , the restriction, which is $a_ iq_ i$ plus a constant and not identically $-\infty $, has analytic singularities. It is an ordinary model in the positive background $a_ i\eta _ i$, so proposition 16.2.7 shows that it equals its ideal projection. The preceding lemma now shows that $\Phi _ a(q)$ is an ideal model, and closedness gives the analytic-closure assertion. The argument uses rational coefficients for the scaled poles $a_ iq_ i$ themselves. With the rational-coefficient convention of section 1.13 , an irrational scaling need not preserve an analytic curve model, since it can give a pole an irrational Lelong number. For a common active set, the normalized tuple is determined by the potential. The two bounds for $T_{ba}$ follow by comparing each positive weight $b_ i$ with $a_ i$, and atomic projection in each coordinate commutes with this correspondence. Finally, normalized compactness, theorem 1.4.2 , bounds the $L^1(C_ i)$ norms of all the $q_ i$ uniformly. Integration along the compact fibers of $\pi _ i\circ p$ gives constants $K_ i$ bounding the $L^1(M)$ norms of their pullbacks. Off the pole sets, which have smooth volume zero, the difference of the two potentials is the sum of the functions $(a_ i-b_ i)q_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p$. The triangle inequality proves the uniform estimate, also when some coefficients vanish. Taking $b=0$ gives uniform convergence to $\Psi $, and the diameter formula shows that the diameters tend to zero. $\square$

title: Comparing bounded model spaces
text: None Comparing bounded model spaces When the active sets differ, the coordinatewise correspondence $T_{ba}$ no longer defines a bijection between $\mathcal S_ a$ and $\mathcal S_ b$. We compare them as abstract metric spaces. They are bounded, but they are not compact as soon as some coefficient is positive. The Gromov–Hausdorff distance $d_{\mathrm{GH}}$ of bounded metric spaces from definition 14.18.8 , together with its estimate through correspondences in lemma 14.18.9 , applies without a compactness hypothesis. Write $\mathcal I_ a\subset \mathcal S_ a$ for the ideal subspace of proposition 16.6.34 , with the restricted metric $\rho _ a$. Proposition 16.6.35 . For all nonnegative coefficient vectors $a,b$, including vectors with different active sets, 16.32 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weighted-product-gh-bounds} \left|\sum _ i(a_ i-b_ i)A_ i\right| \leq d_{\mathrm{GH}}(\mathcal S_ a,\mathcal S_ b) \leq \sum _ i|a_ i-b_ i|A_ i. \end{equation} The same bounds hold for $d_{\mathrm{GH}}(\mathcal I_ a,\mathcal I_ b)$. If $b_ i\leq a_ i$ for every $i$, both distances equal $\sum _ i(a_ i-b_ i)A_ i$. In particular, the distance from $\mathcal S_ a$ to the singleton $\mathcal S_0=\mathcal I_0=\{ \Psi \} $ equals $\sum _ i a_ iA_ i$. For $b\leq a$, the map $T_{ba}\Phi _ a(q)=\Phi _ b(q)$ is a surjective $1$-Lipschitz map and commutes with ideal projection. Every fiber has diameter \[  2\sum _{\{ i:a_ i>0,\  b_ i=0\} }a_ iA_ i.  \] If some $a_ i>0$, then $\mathcal S_ a$ and $\mathcal I_ a$ are not totally bounded, and hence not compact. Proof. Use the correspondence \[  R_{ab}=\{ (\Phi _ a(q),\Phi _ b(q)):q_ i \text{ are normalized ordinary curve models}\} .  \] Every potential in either locus arises from such a tuple, with arbitrary normalized models in its coordinates of zero coefficient, so both projections of $R_{ab}$ are surjective. For any two tuples, put $d_ i=\| \mu _ i-\nu _ i\| _{\mathrm{TV}}$. By ( 16.31 ), the difference of their two distances is $\sum _ i(a_ i-b_ i)d_ i$, with $0\leq d_ i\leq 2A_ i$. Thus the distortion of this correspondence satisfies $\operatorname {dis}R_{ab}\leq 2\sum _ i|a_ i-b_ i|A_ i$, and lemma 14.18.9 gives the upper bound in ( 16.32 ). The diameter formula in proposition 16.6.34 and the same lemma give the lower bound. Restricting the correspondence to tuples of ideal curve models, we obtain a correspondence between the two ideal subspaces with the same distortion bound. The atomic measures $A_ i\delta _{x_ i}$ and $A_ i\delta _{y_ i}$ show that the ideal subspaces have the same diameters as the full spaces, so the lower bound also holds for them. When $b\leq a$, the upper and lower bounds coincide, including when $b=0$. For the transition map, every active coordinate of $b$ is active for $a$, and uniqueness of the normalized active tuple makes the map well defined. Every $b$-tuple extends to an $a$-tuple, so the map is surjective, and $\sum _ i b_ i d_ i\leq \sum _ i a_ i d_ i$ proves the Lipschitz bound. Atomic projection in each coordinate commutes with discarding and rescaling coordinates. In a fiber, every coordinate with $b_ i>0$ is fixed, while the coordinates with $a_ i>0$ and $b_ i=0$ vary freely. The diameter of the fiber is therefore the sum above, by the calculation of the diameter on each curve. Finally, fix an active coordinate $i$ and all other coordinates at their zero models. Let $q_ i$ have polar measure $A_ i\delta _ x$, with $x$ ranging over infinitely many distinct points of $C_ i$. The resulting potentials are ideal models, and any two of them are at distance $2a_ iA_ i$. This infinite separated set excludes total boundedness of both spaces. In particular, the comparison above is between complete bounded spaces that are not compact. $\square$

title: 16.6.10 Arbitrary curve backgrounds
text:
16.6.10 Arbitrary curve backgrounds Scaling by coefficients is a special case of changing the curve backgrounds. By proposition 16.6.30 , the coordinatewise computation of the envelopes holds for arbitrary smooth curve backgrounds of nonnegative area, so the product metric depends on the areas of the curve backgrounds rather than on their positivity. A curve background of area zero has a unique normalized potential, which is smooth. Its coordinate no longer contributes to the metric, but its smooth potential remains a summand of the product potentials. Keep $M=Y	imes C_0	imes Z$, the projections $p,s,r$ and $\Psi $ from corollary 16.6.32 . On each $C_ i$, choose a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\sigma _ i$ with $\mathrm{PSH}(C_ i,\sigma _ i)
e \varnothing $, and put $B_ i=\int _{C_ i}\sigma _ i\geq 0$. For a smooth function $f\geq 0$ on $Y$, set \[  \gamma _\sigma =\sum _ i\pi _ i^*\sigma _ i,\qquad \Theta _{\sigma ,f}=p^*\gamma _\sigma +(f\circ p)s^*	au +r^*\kappa .  \] For normalized ordinary models $q_ i$ in the curve backgrounds $\sigma _ i$, write \[  \Phi _\sigma (q)=\Psi +\sum _ i q_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p, \qquad q_{i,\mathcal I}=P_{\sigma _ i}[q_ i]_{\mathcal I},  \] and let $\mathcal S_\sigma $ be the locus of these potentials. All coordinates are included: when $B_ i=0$, $q_ i$ is the unique normalized potential $u_{\sigma _ i}$ of lemma 1.8.14 , which is smooth. Lemma 16.6.36 . Every $\Phi _\sigma (q)$ is a normalized ordinary model, and \[  P_{\Theta _{\sigma ,f}}[\Phi _\sigma (q)]_{\mathcal I} =\Phi _\sigma (q_{\mathcal I}).  \] The background is not big if $f=0$ or some $B_ i=0$. If $f>0$ everywhere and all $B_ i>0$, it is big. It is not closed whenever $f$ is nonconstant. Proof. On $B=Y	imes C_0$, let $\pi ,s_0$ be the projections and put \[  \gamma _{\sigma ,f}=\pi ^*\gamma _\sigma +(f\circ \pi )s_0^*	au , \qquad w=\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i.  \] The case of the zero obstacle in proposition 16.6.30 gives $P_{\gamma _\sigma }[w]=w$. Replace an ordinary competitor for $w\circ \pi $ by its maximum with $w\circ \pi $. Its restriction to every section $Y	imes \{ z\} $ is then a competitor for $P_{\gamma _\sigma }[w]$ that is not identically $-\infty $, so \[  P_{\gamma _{\sigma ,f}}[w\circ \pi ]=w\circ \pi .  \] Use the atomic Green representatives $g_ i$ constructed in the proof of proposition 16.6.30 , which are smooth in the coordinates of zero area. Their sum $g=\sum _ i g_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $ is $\gamma _{\sigma ,f}$-plurisubharmonic and multiplier-ideal equivalent to $w\circ \pi $, and its complex Hessian is a closed countable divisor current of finite mass minus a smooth form. If $w_{\mathcal I}=\sum _ iq_{i,\mathcal I}\circ \pi _ i$, then $g\sim w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi $. By lemma 1.17.4 , every ideal competitor is ordinarily dominated by $g$, hence bounded by \[  P_{\gamma _{\sigma ,f}}[g] =P_{\gamma _{\sigma ,f}}[w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi ] =w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi .  \] Here the last equality holds because each ideal projection $q_{i,\mathcal I}$ on a curve is an ordinary model, so the argument with sections just given applies to $w_{\mathcal I}$. By pullback and addition, $w_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi $ is itself an ideal competitor, which proves the ideal identity on $B$. Now apply proposition 16.6.13 to $M	o B$ and the divisor $B	imes D$ with weight one, whose induced zero obstacle is zero. The two identities upstairs and the independence of the factors give the assertion and normalization. For the statements on bigness, put $n=m+1+k$ and $\Omega =p^* eta +s^*	au +r^*\kappa >0$, with the positive product form $ eta $ fixed earlier. For $f=0$, the closed positive test form \[  T_0=p^*\left( igwedge _ j\pi _ j^*\eta _ jight)\wedge r^*(\kappa ^ k)  \] satisfies $\int _ M\Theta _{\sigma ,0}\wedge T_0=0$ and $\int _ M\Omega \wedge T_0>0$. If $B_ i=0$, use instead \[  T_ i=p^*\left( igwedge _{j
e i}\pi _ j^*\eta _ jight) \wedge s^*	au \wedge r^*(\kappa ^ k).  \] Then $\int _ M\Theta _{\sigma ,f}\wedge T_ i=0$ for every $f$, since the only nonzero term contains the factor $\int _{C_ i}\sigma _ i=B_ i$, while $\int _ M\Omega \wedge T_ i>0$. In either case, Stokes' theorem against the closed test form shows that no current $\Theta _{\sigma ,f}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ quasi-plurisubharmonic is bounded below by a positive multiple of $\Omega $, so the background is not big. Finally, write $\sigma _ i=B_ i\eta _ i/A_ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ i$ by lemma 1.8.14 . The smooth potential $-\sum _ i\chi _ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p$ has strictly positive current when every $B_ i>0$ and $f>0$, which proves bigness in that case. The identity $\mathrm d\Theta _{\sigma ,f}=p^*(\mathrm df)\wedge s^*	au $ shows that the background is not closed for nonconstant $f$. $\square$ For the polar curvatures $\mu _ i$ of $q_ i$ and $
u _ i$ of another tuple $\widetilde q$, taken in the backgrounds $\sigma _ i$, set 16.33  egin{equation} \label{eq:arbitrary-product-polar-metric} ho _\sigma (\Phi _\sigma (q),\Phi _\sigma (\widetilde q)) =\sum _ i\| \mu _ i-
u _ i\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Write $\mathcal I_\sigma \subset \mathcal S_\sigma $ for the ideal subspace and $\mu _ i^{\mathrm{na}}$ for the nonatomic part of $\mu _ i$. Proposition 16.6.37 . The metric space $(\mathcal S_\sigma ,ho _\sigma )$ is complete and geodesic, with diameter $2\sum _ i B_ i$. The ideal subspace is closed, geodesically convex and equal to the metric closure of the models with analytic singularities. Ideal projection is the unique nearest-point retraction onto it and is $1$-Lipschitz, and the distance to the subspace is $\sum _ i\mu _ i^{\mathrm{na}}(C_ i)$. Metric convergence implies $L^1(M)$ convergence for every smooth positive volume form. These assertions are independent of $f$, and the upper-volume comparison vanishes on this locus. Let $\sigma '_ i$ be another tuple of smooth real forms with $\mathrm{PSH}(C_ i,\sigma '_ i)
e \varnothing $, with areas $B'_ i$. Then 16.34  egin{equation} \label{eq:arbitrary-product-area-comparison} \left|\sum _ i(B_ i-B'_ i)ight| \leq d_{\mathrm{GH}}(\mathcal S_\sigma ,\mathcal S_{\sigma '}) \leq \sum _ i|B_ i-B'_ i|. \end{equation} The same bounds hold for the ideal subspaces. If $B'_ i\leq B_ i$ for every $i$, both distances equal $\sum _ i(B_ i-B'_ i)$. In this case, rescaling the polar measures by the area ratios, with the unique normalized potential in each target coordinate of zero area, gives a surjective $1$-Lipschitz map that commutes with ideal projection. Its fibers have diameter $2\sum _{\{ i:B_ i>0,\  B'_ i=0\} }B_ i$. Both $\mathcal S_\sigma $ and $\mathcal I_\sigma $ are noncompact if some $B_ i>0$. If all $B_ i=0$, they coincide with the singleton $\{ \Psi +\sum _ i u_{\sigma _ i}\circ \pi _ i\circ p\} $. Proof. Restriction to coordinate sections on which the other potentials are finite determines each $q_ i$ up to a constant, and normalization fixes that constant. The preceding lemma and proposition 30.13.1 therefore identify the locus with the finite product of the spaces of curve models, with the sum of their polar metrics; factors of zero area are single points. Completeness, geodesics and the diameter formula follow coordinatewise. Under this identification, corollary 30.12.3 , proposition 30.12.6 give closedness, geodesic convexity and the unique nearest-point retraction onto the ideal subspace, and the distances add. Fiber integration transfers $L^1$ convergence on the curves to $M$. For analytic density, approximate each atomic polar measure by finite atomic measures with rational coefficients and mass at most $B_ i$. By the atomic Green construction and transport under smooth gauge changes, their models in background $\sigma _ i$ have the corresponding finitely many poles with rational coefficients, up to bounded remainders. Coordinates of zero area are smooth. Together with the unit coefficient of $D$, the poles in the coordinates of positive area allow the denominators to be cleared in local product monomials, which gives analytic models in the locus. They converge for the metric ( 16.33 ). Conversely, by proposition 1.13.1 , a product model with analytic singularities restricts, on every coordinate curve section on which the other potentials are finite and whose $Z$-coordinate lies outside $D$, to a function with analytic singularities that is not identically $-\infty $. Each $q_ i$ therefore has polar curvature with finitely many atoms, and it is an ideal model by the classification of curve models. Closedness proves the analytic-closure assertion. By proposition 16.6.13 , applied to the divisor $B	imes D$ with weight one, every model and every pairwise maximum in this locus has zero upper volume; for a maximum, use $\Psi $ plus the pullback of the maximum of the two potentials on $B$. Thus all three terms of the upper-volume comparison vanish, even in the backgrounds that are not big by the lemma. To compare different backgrounds, put $a_ i=B_ i/A_ i$, and for a positive polar measure $\mu $ on $C_ i$ of mass at most $B_ i$ write $p_{\sigma _ i}(\mu )$ for the ordinary model in background $\sigma _ i$ with polar curvature $\mu $, as in proposition 30.13.1 . Sending a curve model for $\eta _ i$ with polar measure $\mu _ i$, of mass at most $A_ i$, to $p_{\sigma _ i}(a_ i\mu _ i)$, which for $a_ i=0$ is the unique normalized potential, defines an isometry from the weighted locus $\mathcal S_ a$ of proposition 16.6.34 onto $\mathcal S_\sigma $ that maps the ideal subspaces onto each other. Applying proposition 16.6.35 with $a_ i=B_ i/A_ i$ and $b_ i=B'_ i/A_ i$ gives ( 16.34 ), the exact value for ordered areas, the contractions and the diameters of their fibers. In curve coordinates the contraction is \[  p_{\sigma _ i}(\mu )\longmapsto  egin{cases}  p_{\sigma '_ i}((B'_ i/B_ i)\mu ),& B_ i>0,\  p_{\sigma '_ i}(0),& B_ i=0. \end{cases}  \] In the second case $B'_ i=0$, because $B'_ i\leq B_ i$. Atomic projection commutes with both operations. As in theorem 30.13.3 , irrational area ratios need not preserve individual analytic models, but the ideal subspaces are preserved for every ratio. If $B_ i>0$, the models with polar measure $B_ i\delta _ x$ for infinitely many distinct points $x\in C_ i$, with all other coordinates fixed at their models with zero polar curvature, form an infinite set of ideal product models with mutual distances $2B_ i$. This excludes total boundedness of both loci. If all areas are zero, every curve coordinate is fixed at its unique normalized smooth potential, which proves the last assertion. $\square$ Corollary 16.6.38 . For each $i$, let $\sigma _{i,j}$ be smooth real forms on $C_ i$ of nonnegative area that converge uniformly, as $j	o \infty $, to a smooth form $\sigma _{i,0}$ of area zero, and write $\sigma _ j=(\sigma _{1,j},\ldots ,\sigma _{m,j})$. For any nonnegative smooth auxiliary coefficients $f_ j$, the diameters of $\mathcal S_{\sigma _ j}$ tend to zero. For every fixed smooth positive volume form on $M$, the potentials in $\mathcal S_{\sigma _ j}$ converge in $L^1(M)$ to \[  \Psi +\sum _ i u_{\sigma _{i,0}}\circ \pi _ i\circ p,  \] uniformly over all normalized model tuples. Proof. The areas $B_{i,j}$ tend to zero, so the diameter formula applies. By theorem 1.8.15 , all normalized $\sigma _{i,j}$-plurisubharmonic potentials converge in $L^1(C_ i)$ to $u_{\sigma _{i,0}}$, uniformly over this family. Integration along the fixed compact fibers bounds each pulled-back norm by a constant times the norm on the curve, and the finite sum gives the asserted uniform limit on $M$. The auxiliary coefficients do not enter these potentials or their metrics. $\square$ Thus the metric comparison sees only the areas of the curve backgrounds, while the limiting potential still records their smooth gauges. These statements concern the separated product locus; extending the metric to general ordinary models is part of 16.6.79 .

title: Lemma 16.6.36
text: Lemma 16.6.36 . Now apply proposition 16.6.13 to $M\to B$ and the divisor $B\times D$ with weight one, whose induced zero obstacle is zero.
