The identity $\mathrm d\Theta _{\sigma ,f}=p^*(\mathrm df)\wedge s^*\tau $ shows that the background is not closed for nonconstant $f$. $\square$
16.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:arbitrary-product-polar-metric} \rho _\sigma (\Phi _\sigma (q),\Phi _\sigma (\widetilde q)) =\sum _ i\| \mu _ i-\nu _ i\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 16.6.37
text: Proposition 16.6.37 . The metric space $(\mathcal S_\sigma ,\rho _\sigma )$ is complete and geodesic, with diameter $2\sum _ i B_ i$. The ideal subspace is closed, geodesically convex and equal to the metric closure of the models with analytic singularities. Ideal projection is the unique nearest-point retraction onto it and is $1$-Lipschitz, and the distance to the subspace is $\sum _ i\mu _ i^{\mathrm{na}}(C_ i)$. Metric convergence implies $L^1(M)$ convergence for every smooth positive volume form. These assertions are independent of $f$, and the upper-volume comparison vanishes on this locus. Let $\sigma '_ i$ be another tuple of smooth real forms with $\mathrm{PSH}(C_ i,\sigma '_ i)\ne \varnothing $, with areas $B'_ i$. Then 16.34 \begin{equation} \label{eq:arbitrary-product-area-comparison} \left|\sum _ i(B_ i-B'_ i)\right| \leq d_{\mathrm{GH}}(\mathcal S_\sigma ,\mathcal S_{\sigma '}) \leq \sum _ i|B_ i-B'_ i|. \end{equation} The same bounds hold for the ideal subspaces. If $B'_ i\leq B_ i$ for every $i$, both distances equal $\sum _ i(B_ i-B'_ i)$. In this case, rescaling the polar measures by the area ratios, with the unique normalized potential in each target coordinate of zero area, gives a surjective $1$-Lipschitz map that commutes with ideal projection. Its fibers have diameter $2\sum _{\{ i:B_ i>0,\  B'_ i=0\} }B_ i$. Both $\mathcal S_\sigma $ and $\mathcal I_\sigma $ are noncompact if some $B_ i>0$. If all $B_ i=0$, they coincide with the singleton $\{ \Psi +\sum _ i u_{\sigma _ i}\circ \pi _ i\circ p\} $. Proof. Restriction to coordinate sections on which the other potentials are finite determines each $q_ i$ up to a constant, and normalization fixes that constant. The preceding lemma and proposition 30.13.1 therefore identify the locus with the finite product of the spaces of curve models, with the sum of their polar metrics; factors of zero area are single points. Completeness, geodesics and the diameter formula follow coordinatewise. Under this identification, corollary 30.12.3 , proposition 30.12.6 give closedness, geodesic convexity and the unique nearest-point retraction onto the ideal subspace, and the distances add. Fiber integration transfers $L^1$ convergence on the curves to $M$. For analytic density, approximate each atomic polar measure by finite atomic measures with rational coefficients and mass at most $B_ i$. By the atomic Green construction and transport under smooth gauge changes, their models in background $\sigma _ i$ have the corresponding finitely many poles with rational coefficients, up to bounded remainders. Coordinates of zero area are smooth. Together with the unit coefficient of $D$, the poles in the coordinates of positive area allow the denominators to be cleared in local product monomials, which gives analytic models in the locus. They converge for the metric ( 16.33 ). Conversely, by proposition 1.13.1 , a product model with analytic singularities restricts, on every coordinate curve section on which the other potentials are finite and whose $Z$-coordinate lies outside $D$, to a function with analytic singularities that is not identically $-\infty $. Each $q_ i$ therefore has polar curvature with finitely many atoms, and it is an ideal model by the classification of curve models. Closedness proves the analytic-closure assertion. By proposition 16.6.13 , applied to the divisor $B\times D$ with weight one, every model and every pairwise maximum in this locus has zero upper volume; for a maximum, use $\Psi $ plus the pullback of the maximum of the two potentials on $B$. Thus all three terms of the upper-volume comparison vanish, even in the backgrounds that are not big by the lemma. To compare different backgrounds, put $a_ i=B_ i/A_ i$, and for a positive polar measure $\mu $ on $C_ i$ of mass at most $B_ i$ write $p_{\sigma _ i}(\mu )$ for the ordinary model in background $\sigma _ i$ with polar curvature $\mu $, as in proposition 30.13.1 . Sending a curve model for $\eta _ i$ with polar measure $\mu _ i$, of mass at most $A_ i$, to $p_{\sigma _ i}(a_ i\mu _ i)$, which for $a_ i=0$ is the unique normalized potential, defines an isometry from the weighted locus $\mathcal S_ a$ of proposition 16.6.34 onto $\mathcal S_\sigma $ that maps the ideal subspaces onto each other. Applying proposition 16.6.35 with $a_ i=B_ i/A_ i$ and $b_ i=B'_ i/A_ i$ gives ( 16.34 ), the exact value for ordered areas, the contractions and the diameters of their fibers. In curve coordinates the contraction is \[  p_{\sigma _ i}(\mu )\longmapsto \begin{cases}  p_{\sigma '_ i}((B'_ i/B_ i)\mu ),& B_ i>0,\\  p_{\sigma '_ i}(0),& B_ i=0. \end{cases}  \] In the second case $B'_ i=0$, because $B'_ i\leq B_ i$. Atomic projection commutes with both operations. As in theorem 30.13.3 , irrational area ratios need not preserve individual analytic models, but the ideal subspaces are preserved for every ratio. If $B_ i>0$, the models with polar measure $B_ i\delta _ x$ for infinitely many distinct points $x\in C_ i$, with all other coordinates fixed at their models with zero polar curvature, form an infinite set of ideal product models with mutual distances $2B_ i$. This excludes total boundedness of both loci. If all areas are zero, every curve coordinate is fixed at its unique normalized smooth potential, which proves the last assertion. $\square$

16.34 \begin{equation} \label{eq:arbitrary-product-area-comparison} \left|\sum _ i(B_ i-B'_ i)\right| \leq d_{\mathrm{GH}}(\mathcal S_\sigma ,\mathcal S_{\sigma '}) \leq \sum _ i|B_ i-B'_ i|. \end{equation}

title: Corollary 16.6.38
text: Corollary 16.6.38 . For each $i$, let $\sigma _{i,j}$ be smooth real forms on $C_ i$ of nonnegative area that converge uniformly, as $j\to \infty $, to a smooth form $\sigma _{i,0}$ of area zero, and write $\sigma _ j=(\sigma _{1,j},\ldots ,\sigma _{m,j})$. For any nonnegative smooth auxiliary coefficients $f_ j$, the diameters of $\mathcal S_{\sigma _ j}$ tend to zero. For every fixed smooth positive volume form on $M$, the potentials in $\mathcal S_{\sigma _ j}$ converge in $L^1(M)$ to \[  \Psi +\sum _ i u_{\sigma _{i,0}}\circ \pi _ i\circ p,  \] uniformly over all normalized model tuples. Proof. The areas $B_{i,j}$ tend to zero, so the diameter formula applies. By theorem 1.8.15 , all normalized $\sigma _{i,j}$-plurisubharmonic potentials converge in $L^1(C_ i)$ to $u_{\sigma _{i,0}}$, uniformly over this family. Integration along the fixed compact fibers bounds each pulled-back norm by a constant times the norm on the curve, and the finite sum gives the asserted uniform limit on $M$. The auxiliary coefficients do not enter these potentials or their metrics. $\square$

title: 16.6.11 Equality below all obstacles on separated products

16.6.11 Equality below all obstacles on separated products We return to the question raised in 16.6.4 : does equality of the two envelopes below zero imply their equality below every smooth obstacle? For sums of curve potentials the answer is yes, even for obstacles that mix the coordinates. By proposition 16.6.8 , membership in the relative envelope class of the ideal model implies equality below every obstacle, and this membership can be tested coordinatewise, because stretching competitors can be added before any obstacle is imposed. Lemma 16.6.39 . Let $N\geq 1$, let $X_ j$, $1\leq j\leq N$, be connected compact complex manifolds with smooth real $(1,1)$-forms $	heta _ j$, and let $u_ j,\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X_ j,	heta _ j)$. On $X=\prod _ jX_ j$, with projections $\operatorname {pr}_ j$, put \[  \vartheta =\sum _ j\operatorname {pr}_ j^*	heta _ j,\qquad u=\sum _ j u_ j\circ \operatorname {pr}_ j,\qquad \varphi =\sum _ j\varphi _ j\circ \operatorname {pr}_ j.  \] Then \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\vartheta ,\varphi ) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u_ j\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X_ j,	heta _ j,\varphi _ j) \quad 	ext{for every }j.  \] Proof. The ordinary order between the sums is equivalent to the ordinary order in each coordinate. Indeed, the latter follows from the former by fixing the other coordinates at points where their potentials are finite and restricting the inequality, and the converse follows by adding the coordinate inequalities. Suppose that each $u_ j$ belongs to its relative class. For $b>1$, choose stretching competitors $h_ j$ as in definition 13.4.1 . The sum $h=\sum _ jh_ j\circ \operatorname {pr}_ j$ is $\vartheta $-plurisubharmonic and satisfies \[  b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})\varphi \leq u.  \] This convex inequality is meaningful at poles. For $b=1$, use $h=u$. Thus $u$ belongs to the relative class on the product. Conversely, fix $b>1$ and a stretching competitor $h$ on the product. Choose a point $x=(x_1,\ldots ,x_ N)$ at which $h$ and all the coordinate potentials are finite; such points have full smooth volume. For each $j$, let $h^{(j)}$ be the restriction of $h$ to the slice through $x$ in the $j$th factor. It is $	heta _ j$-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $, since it is finite at $x_ j$. Put \[  c_ j=\sum _{\ell 
e j}u_\ell (x_\ell ),\qquad d_ j=\sum _{\ell 
e j}\varphi _\ell (x_\ell ).  \] Restricting the product inequality to the slice gives \[  b^{-1} igl (h^{(j)}-bc_ j+(b-1)d_ j igr ) +(1-b^{-1})\varphi _ j\leq u_ j.  \] This gives a stretching competitor in the $j$th coordinate for every $b>1$. Together with the ordinary order and the competitor $u_ j$ for $b=1$, it proves the converse. $\square$ Keep the curves $C_ i$ and the smooth forms $\sigma _ i$ with $\mathrm{PSH}(C_ i,\sigma _ i)
e \varnothing $ from 16.6.10 , and choose arbitrary $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(C_ i,\sigma _ i)$. Put \[  u=\sum _ i u_ i\circ \pi _ i,\qquad q_ i=P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i],\qquad r_ i=P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I},\qquad Q=\sum _ i r_ i\circ \pi _ i.  \] Write $\mu _ i$ and $E_ i$ for the polar and the atomic parts of the positive curvature measure $\sigma _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$, respectively. Proposition 16.6.40 . For these data, $Q=P_{\gamma _\sigma }[u]_{\mathcal I}$. The following are equivalent: \[   egin{gathered} P_{\gamma _\sigma }[u]=P_{\gamma _\sigma }[u]_{\mathcal I}, \qquad \mu _ i=E_ i\quad 	ext{for every }i,\ u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\gamma _\sigma ,Q),\ P_{\gamma _\sigma ,F}[u]=P_{\gamma _\sigma ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \quad 	ext{for every smooth real }F	ext{ on }Y. \end{gathered}  \] The obstacle in the last condition may mix the curve coordinates. Curve backgrounds of zero area are allowed, and the models may have zero volume. Proof. For the zero obstacle, proposition 16.6.30 identifies the two envelopes with $\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i$ and $Q$, respectively. Since the coordinates are independent and all these functions have supremum zero, the two sums are equal if and only if $q_ i=r_ i$ for every $i$. By corollary 30.13.2 , this is equivalent to $\mu _ i=E_ i$, and also to $u_ i\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(C_ i,\sigma _ i,r_ i)$, for every $i$, including backgrounds of zero area. The preceding lemma identifies these memberships with membership in the relative class on the product. Finally, proposition 16.6.8 gives equality below every smooth obstacle, and taking $F=0$ gives the reverse implication. This proves all four equivalences. $\square$ Corollary 16.6.41 . On $M=Y	imes C_0	imes Z$ with the background $\Theta _{\sigma ,f}$, for any smooth $f\geq 0$, put $U=\Psi +u\circ p$. Then \[   egin{aligned}  P_{\Theta _{\sigma ,f}}[U]& =\Psi +\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p,\  P_{\Theta _{\sigma ,f}}[U]_{\mathcal I}& =\Psi +Q\circ p. \end{aligned}  \] The following are equivalent: equality of these two envelopes; $\mu _ i=E_ i$ for every $i$; $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta _{\sigma ,f},\Psi +Q\circ p)$; and equality of the ordinary and ideal envelopes of $U$ below every smooth real obstacle on $M$. These statements include the case $f=0$ and curve backgrounds of zero area. Proof. On $B=Y	imes C_0$, with projection $\pi $ to $Y$, use the background $\gamma _{\sigma ,f}$ of the proof of lemma 16.6.36 . Sums of ordinary competitors in the separate coordinates give $P_{\gamma _{\sigma ,f}}[u\circ \pi ]\geq \sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $. For the reverse inequality, replace an ordinary competitor by its maximum with a sufficiently low translate of $u\circ \pi $. Its restriction to every section $Y	imes \{ z\} $ is then not identically $-\infty $, nonpositive and at least as singular as $u$, so the separation for the zero obstacle bounds it by $\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i$. The reduction of proposition 16.6.13 , applied to the divisor $B	imes D$ with weight one, proves the ordinary identity upstairs. By corollary 16.2.4 , each $q_ i$ has the multiplier ideals of $u_ i$, so pullback and addition give $U\sim _{\mathcal I}\Phi _\sigma (q)$. These two potentials therefore have the same ideal envelope, which lemma 16.6.36 identifies with $\Psi +Q\circ p$. If $\mu _ i=E_ i$ for every $i$, then $u_ i\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(C_ i,\sigma _ i,r_ i)$ by corollary 30.13.2 , and we choose stretching competitors in these curve classes. The sum of their pullbacks plus $\Psi $ is $\Theta _{\sigma ,f}$-plurisubharmonic: its current is the sum of the pulled-back positive curve currents, the form $(f\circ p)s^*	au $ and the current of the divisor with weight one. Adding the stretching inequalities gives the one for $U$ relative to $\Psi +Q\circ p$, also at poles, and the ordinary order follows in the same way. Thus $U$ belongs to that relative class, and proposition 16.6.8 gives equality below all obstacles. Taking the zero obstacle and using the two identities above recovers $q_ i=r_ i$, hence $\mu _ i=E_ i$. This closes the chain of equivalences. $\square$ These criteria concern sums of curve potentials and their extensions to the product $M$. They give neither coordinatewise formulas for the envelopes below mixed obstacles nor the implication for general potentials of zero volume.

title: Lemma 16.6.39
text: Lemma 16.6.39 . Let $N\geq 1$, let $X_ j$, $1\leq j\leq N$, be connected compact complex manifolds with smooth real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ j$, and let $u_ j,\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X_ j,\theta _ j)$. On $X=\prod _ jX_ j$, with projections $\operatorname {pr}_ j$, put \[  \vartheta =\sum _ j\operatorname {pr}_ j^*\theta _ j,\qquad u=\sum _ j u_ j\circ \operatorname {pr}_ j,\qquad \varphi =\sum _ j\varphi _ j\circ \operatorname {pr}_ j.  \] Then \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\vartheta ,\varphi ) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u_ j\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X_ j,\theta _ j,\varphi _ j) \quad \text{for every }j.  \] Proof. The ordinary order between the sums is equivalent to the ordinary order in each coordinate. Indeed, the latter follows from the former by fixing the other coordinates at points where their potentials are finite and restricting the inequality, and the converse follows by adding the coordinate inequalities. Suppose that each $u_ j$ belongs to its relative class. For $b>1$, choose stretching competitors $h_ j$ as in definition 13.4.1 . The sum $h=\sum _ jh_ j\circ \operatorname {pr}_ j$ is $\vartheta $-plurisubharmonic and satisfies \[  b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})\varphi \leq u.  \] This convex inequality is meaningful at poles. For $b=1$, use $h=u$. Thus $u$ belongs to the relative class on the product. Conversely, fix $b>1$ and a stretching competitor $h$ on the product. Choose a point $x=(x_1,\ldots ,x_ N)$ at which $h$ and all the coordinate potentials are finite; such points have full smooth volume. For each $j$, let $h^{(j)}$ be the restriction of $h$ to the slice through $x$ in the $j$th factor. It is $\theta _ j$-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $, since it is finite at $x_ j$. Put \[  c_ j=\sum _{\ell \ne j}u_\ell (x_\ell ),\qquad d_ j=\sum _{\ell \ne j}\varphi _\ell (x_\ell ).  \] Restricting the product inequality to the slice gives \[  b^{-1}\bigl (h^{(j)}-bc_ j+(b-1)d_ j\bigr ) +(1-b^{-1})\varphi _ j\leq u_ j.  \] This gives a stretching competitor in the $j$th coordinate for every $b>1$. Together with the ordinary order and the competitor $u_ j$ for $b=1$, it proves the converse. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.6.41
text: Corollary 16.6.41 . On $M=Y\times C_0\times Z$ with the background $\Theta _{\sigma ,f}$, for any smooth $f\geq 0$, put $U=\Psi +u\circ p$. Then \[  \begin{aligned}  P_{\Theta _{\sigma ,f}}[U]& =\Psi +\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p,\\  P_{\Theta _{\sigma ,f}}[U]_{\mathcal I}& =\Psi +Q\circ p. \end{aligned}  \] The following are equivalent: equality of these two envelopes; $\mu _ i=E_ i$ for every $i$; $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta _{\sigma ,f},\Psi +Q\circ p)$; and equality of the ordinary and ideal envelopes of $U$ below every smooth real obstacle on $M$. These statements include the case $f=0$ and curve backgrounds of zero area. Proof. On $B=Y\times C_0$, with projection $\pi $ to $Y$, use the background $\gamma _{\sigma ,f}$ of the proof of lemma 16.6.36 . Sums of ordinary competitors in the separate coordinates give $P_{\gamma _{\sigma ,f}}[u\circ \pi ]\geq \sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $. For the reverse inequality, replace an ordinary competitor by its maximum with a sufficiently low translate of $u\circ \pi $. Its restriction to every section $Y\times \{ z\} $ is then not identically $-\infty $, nonpositive and at least as singular as $u$, so the separation for the zero obstacle bounds it by $\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i$. The reduction of proposition 16.6.13 , applied to the divisor $B\times D$ with weight one, proves the ordinary identity upstairs. By corollary 16.2.4 , each $q_ i$ has the multiplier ideals of $u_ i$, so pullback and addition give $U\sim _{\mathcal I}\Phi _\sigma (q)$. These two potentials therefore have the same ideal envelope, which lemma 16.6.36 identifies with $\Psi +Q\circ p$. If $\mu _ i=E_ i$ for every $i$, then $u_ i\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(C_ i,\sigma _ i,r_ i)$ by corollary 30.13.2 , and we choose stretching competitors in these curve classes. The sum of their pullbacks plus $\Psi $ is $\Theta _{\sigma ,f}$-plurisubharmonic: its current is the sum of the pulled-back positive curve currents, the form $(f\circ p)s^*\tau $ and the current of the divisor with weight one. Adding the stretching inequalities gives the one for $U$ relative to $\Psi +Q\circ p$, also at poles, and the ordinary order follows in the same way. Taking the zero obstacle and using the two identities above recovers $q_ i=r_ i$, hence $\mu _ i=E_ i$. This closes the chain of equivalences. $\square$

title: 16.6.12 Auxiliary compact complex factors
text: 16.6.12 Auxiliary compact complex factors So far, the auxiliary factor that makes the background nonclosed has been a curve. The arguments only used that the auxiliary term in the background is semipositive and vanishes on the slices parallel to the curve product. The auxiliary factor can therefore be any compact complex manifold of positive dimension, Kähler or not, and the potentials and their polar metric still depend only on the curve coordinates and the fixed divisor of weight one. Keep $Y$, $\sigma _ i$, $B_ i$ and $\gamma _\sigma $, as well as the data $(Z,\kappa ,D,\psi )$ of the divisor of weight one. Let $T$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $\ell \geq 1$, and put $B=Y\times T$, with projections $\pi $ to $Y$ and $\operatorname {pr}_ T$ to $T$. Choose a smooth semipositive real $(1,1)$-form $\alpha $ on $B$ whose restriction to every slice $Y\times \{ t\} $ is zero. By semipositivity, the tangent spaces of these slices lie in the kernel of $\alpha $, so in product coordinates $\alpha $ has only coefficients in the $T$-directions. On $M=B\times Z$, let $\varpi ,r$ be the projections, and put $p=\pi \circ \varpi $ and \[  \Gamma _\alpha =\pi ^*\gamma _\sigma +\alpha ,\qquad \Theta _\alpha =\varpi ^*\Gamma _\alpha +r^*\kappa , \qquad \Psi =\psi \circ r.  \] We assume neither that $\alpha $ is closed nor that $M$ has the bounded mass property. Lemma 16.6.42 . For $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(C_ i,\sigma _ i)$ put \[  u=\sum _ i u_ i\circ \pi _ i,\qquad U=\Psi +u\circ p, \qquad q_ i=P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i],\quad r_ i=P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Then \[  \begin{aligned}  P_{\Theta _\alpha }[U]& =\Psi +\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p,\\  P_{\Theta _\alpha }[U]_{\mathcal I} & =\Psi +\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p. \end{aligned}  \] Every ordinary representative of either of these envelopes has zero extended mass, so their upper and lower singularity volumes are zero. Proof. On $B$, sums of ordinary competitors on the curves give the lower bound $P_{\Gamma _\alpha }[u\circ \pi ]\geq \sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $. For the upper bound, replace a competitor by its maximum with a sufficiently low translate of $u\circ \pi $. Its restriction to every slice $Y\times \{ t\} $ is then not identically $-\infty $, and since $\alpha $ restricts to zero there, it is a $\gamma _\sigma $-plurisubharmonic ordinary competitor for $u$. The case of the zero obstacle in proposition 16.6.30 bounds it by $\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i$. This proves the identity for the ordinary envelope on $B$. Take the atomic Green representatives $g_ i$ of the proof of proposition 16.6.30 . The pullback $g$ of their sum to $B$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(B,\Gamma _\alpha )$, is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u\circ \pi $, and is ordinarily equivalent to $\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $. Its complex Hessian is a countable current of divisors along coordinate fibers, minus a smooth form; this divisor current has finite mass, as one sees with a fixed product Hermitian metric and the finite atomic masses on the curves. By lemma 1.17.4 , every ideal competitor is therefore at least as singular as $g$; if the divisor current is zero, $g$ is smooth and this is immediate by compactness. Thus every such competitor is bounded by $P_{\Gamma _\alpha }[g]=P_{\Gamma _\alpha }[\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi ]$, which equals $\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $ by the ordinary identity just proved and $P_{\sigma _ i}[r_ i]=r_ i$. This sum is itself an ideal competitor, which proves the identity for the ideal envelope on $B$. Apply proposition 16.6.13 to $M\to B$ and the divisor $B\times D$ with weight one. Its induced zero obstacle is zero because $\sup _ Z\psi =0$, which gives both identities upstairs. The mass assertion of the same proposition, applied to each of the two envelopes, shows that every representative of its ordinary type has zero mass, so both singularity volumes are zero. $\square$ For normalized ordinary curve models $q_ i$, write \[  \Phi _\alpha (q)=\Psi +\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p,  \] let $\mathcal S_\alpha $ be the locus of these potentials, and give it the metric \[  \rho _\alpha (\Phi _\alpha (q),\Phi _\alpha (\widetilde q)) =\sum _ i\| \mu _ i-\widetilde\mu _ i\| _{\mathrm{TV}},  \] where $\mu _ i,\widetilde\mu _ i$ are the polar curvatures of $q_ i,\widetilde q_ i$. Proposition 16.6.43 . The map $\Phi _\alpha (q)\mapsto \Phi _\sigma (q)$ is an isometry from $\mathcal S_\alpha $ onto the locus $\mathcal S_\sigma $ of proposition 16.6.37 , and it maps the ideal subspaces and the models with analytic singularities onto each other. Consequently $\mathcal S_\alpha $ is complete and geodesic, with diameter $2\sum _ iB_ i$. Its ideal subspace is closed, geodesically convex and equal to the metric closure of the models with analytic singularities. Ideal projection is the unique nearest-point retraction onto this subspace and is $1$-Lipschitz, and the distance to the subspace is the sum of the nonatomic polar masses. Changing $T$ or $\alpha $ does not change this abstract metric space. All the area comparisons and the contractions commuting with ideal projection of proposition 16.6.37 hold, even for different auxiliary data. The upper-volume comparison vanishes on the locus, and metric convergence implies $L^1(M)$ convergence for every smooth positive volume form. If $T$ and $Z$ are fixed and the curve backgrounds converge uniformly to backgrounds of zero area, then, for any choice of the semipositive terms $\alpha $, the potentials converge in $L^1(M)$, uniformly over the model tuples, to the sum of $\Psi $ and the pullbacks of the normalized smooth potentials of the limiting curve backgrounds, as in corollary 16.6.38 . Proof. Applied to model tuples, the lemma shows that every $\Phi _\alpha (q)$ is a normalized ordinary model and computes its ideal projection coordinatewise. Restrictions to curve sections on which the other potentials are finite determine the tuple up to constants, and the normalization of the coordinates determines these constants. Thus the map is well defined and bijective, and the formulas for the polar curvatures make it an isometry preserving ideal projection. Each potential in either locus is pulled back from $Y\times Z$. Analytic presentations pull back under the projection that forgets the auxiliary factor. Conversely, by proposition 1.13.1 , the restriction of a potential with analytic singularities to a section with fixed auxiliary coordinate has analytic singularities and is not identically $-\infty $. Hence a potential in either locus has analytic singularities exactly when the common potential on $Y\times Z$ does, and the isometry maps the analytic models onto each other. The statements on the complete metric, the ideal closure, geodesics, nearest points and area comparisons now follow from proposition 16.6.37 . A pairwise maximum is $\Psi $ plus the pullback of the maximum of two $\Gamma _\alpha $-plurisubharmonic functions on $B$. The reduction along the divisor of weight one gives zero upper volume for it and for both models, so the upper-volume comparison vanishes. For $L^1$ convergence, integration along the fixed compact fibers bounds the norm of each pulled-back curve potential by a constant times its norm on the curve. The same estimate and theorem 1.8.15 give the asserted uniform limit at zero area. Neither estimate involves $\alpha $. $\square$ Corollary 16.6.44 . For the arbitrary curve potentials $u_ i$ of the lemma, put $R=\Psi +\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p$. The following are equivalent: $P_{\Theta _\alpha }[U]=P_{\Theta _\alpha }[U]_{\mathcal I}$; for each $i$, the polar part of the curvature measure of $u_ i$ equals its atomic part; $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta _\alpha ,R)$; and the ordinary and ideal envelopes of $U$ agree below every smooth real obstacle on $M$. Proof. By the lemma and the normalization of the coordinates, equality of the envelopes below zero is equivalent to $q_ i=r_ i$ for every $i$. By corollary 30.13.2 , this is equivalent to equality of the polar and atomic measures, and in that case $u_ i\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(C_ i,\sigma _ i,r_ i)$. Choose stretching competitors in these curve classes. The sum of their pullbacks plus $\Psi $ has positive current, since the contributions of the curves, the form $\varpi ^*\alpha $ and the current of the divisor are all positive. Adding the convex stretching inequalities, which is possible also at poles, gives a stretching competitor relative to $R$ for every finite stretch, and adding the ordinary bounds gives $U\preceq R$. Thus $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta _\alpha ,R)$, and proposition 16.6.8 gives equality below every smooth obstacle. Taking the zero obstacle recovers the first condition, which proves the equivalence. $\square$ Corollary 16.6.45 . If $\alpha =0$ or some $B_ i=0$, the background $\Theta _\alpha $ is not big. If all $B_ i>0$ and $\alpha $ is positive on every nonzero vector tangent to the factor $T$, it is big. In particular, for a Hermitian form $\omega _ T$ on $T$ and a positive nonconstant smooth function $h$ on $Y$, the choice $\alpha =(h\circ \pi )\operatorname {pr}_ T^*\omega _ T$ gives a big background that is not closed whenever all $B_ i>0$. Proof. For $\alpha =0$, the background is pulled back from $Y\times Z$, and by proposition 1.22.3 every potential in it descends to $Y\times Z$. The corresponding currents have no component in the $T$-directions, so they cannot dominate a positive multiple of a Hermitian form on $M$. Thus the background is not big. If $B_ i=0$, choose any Hermitian form $\omega _ T$ on $T$ and write $s:M\to T$ for the projection. The positive $(m+\ell +k-1,m+\ell +k-1)$-form \[  L_ i=p^*\left(\bigwedge _{j\ne i}\pi _ j^*\eta _ j\right) \wedge s^*(\omega _ T^\ell )\wedge r^*(\kappa ^ k)  \] is closed, because $\omega _ T^\ell $ has top degree on $T$. Its pairing with $\Theta _\alpha $ is zero, since the only possible contribution contains the integral of $\sigma _ i$, whereas its pairing with a positive product Hermitian form is strictly positive. By Stokes' theorem, no current in the background is bounded below by a positive multiple of a Hermitian form. When all areas are positive, write $\sigma _ i=B_ i\eta _ i/A_ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ i$. Subtracting the smooth pullback of $\sum _ i\chi _ i\circ \pi _ i$ gives the current $p^*\sum _ i(B_ i/A_ i)\pi _ i^*\eta _ i+\varpi ^*\alpha +r^*\kappa $. Positivity of $\alpha $ in the $T$-directions makes this form strictly positive, which proves bigness. For the stated choice of $\alpha $, the exterior derivative of $\Theta _\alpha $ has the component $\mathrm dh\wedge \omega _ T$, with one direction in $Y$ and two in $T$. Hence $\mathrm d\Theta _\alpha \ne 0$. $\square$ The proofs use no bound on the ambient masses, so the auxiliary manifold may fail the bounded mass property; an explicit example follows. The complete metric and the criterion for all obstacles concern only the specified product locus.

title: Lemma 16.6.42
text: Lemma 16.6.42 . For $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(C_ i,\sigma _ i)$ put \[  u=\sum _ i u_ i\circ \pi _ i,\qquad U=\Psi +u\circ p, \qquad q_ i=P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i],\quad r_ i=P_{\sigma _ i}[u_ i]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Then \[  \begin{aligned}  P_{\Theta _\alpha }[U]& =\Psi +\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p,\\  P_{\Theta _\alpha }[U]_{\mathcal I} & =\Psi +\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p. \end{aligned}  \] Every ordinary representative of either of these envelopes has zero extended mass, so their upper and lower singularity volumes are zero. Proof. On $B$, sums of ordinary competitors on the curves give the lower bound $P_{\Gamma _\alpha }[u\circ \pi ]\geq \sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $. For the upper bound, replace a competitor by its maximum with a sufficiently low translate of $u\circ \pi $. Its restriction to every slice $Y\times \{ t\} $ is then not identically $-\infty $, and since $\alpha $ restricts to zero there, it is a $\gamma _\sigma $-plurisubharmonic ordinary competitor for $u$. The case of the zero obstacle in proposition 16.6.30 bounds it by $\sum _ iq_ i\circ \pi _ i$. This proves the identity for the ordinary envelope on $B$. Take the atomic Green representatives $g_ i$ of the proof of proposition 16.6.30 . The pullback $g$ of their sum to $B$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(B,\Gamma _\alpha )$, is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u\circ \pi $, and is ordinarily equivalent to $\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $. Its complex Hessian is a countable current of divisors along coordinate fibers, minus a smooth form; this divisor current has finite mass, as one sees with a fixed product Hermitian metric and the finite atomic masses on the curves. By lemma 1.17.4 , every ideal competitor is therefore at least as singular as $g$; if the divisor current is zero, $g$ is smooth and this is immediate by compactness. Thus every such competitor is bounded by $P_{\Gamma _\alpha }[g]=P_{\Gamma _\alpha }[\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi ]$, which equals $\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ \pi $ by the ordinary identity just proved and $P_{\sigma _ i}[r_ i]=r_ i$. This sum is itself an ideal competitor, which proves the identity for the ideal envelope on $B$. Apply proposition 16.6.13 to $M\to B$ and the divisor $B\times D$ with weight one. Its induced zero obstacle is zero because $\sup _ Z\psi =0$, which gives both identities upstairs. The mass assertion of the same proposition, applied to each of the two envelopes, shows that every representative of its ordinary type has zero mass, so both singularity volumes are zero. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.6.43
text: Proposition 16.6.43 . The map $\Phi _\alpha (q)\mapsto \Phi _\sigma (q)$ is an isometry from $\mathcal S_\alpha $ onto the locus $\mathcal S_\sigma $ of proposition 16.6.37 , and it maps the ideal subspaces and the models with analytic singularities onto each other. Consequently $\mathcal S_\alpha $ is complete and geodesic, with diameter $2\sum _ iB_ i$. Its ideal subspace is closed, geodesically convex and equal to the metric closure of the models with analytic singularities. Ideal projection is the unique nearest-point retraction onto this subspace and is $1$-Lipschitz, and the distance to the subspace is the sum of the nonatomic polar masses. Changing $T$ or $\alpha $ does not change this abstract metric space. All the area comparisons and the contractions commuting with ideal projection of proposition 16.6.37 hold, even for different auxiliary data. The upper-volume comparison vanishes on the locus, and metric convergence implies $L^1(M)$ convergence for every smooth positive volume form. If $T$ and $Z$ are fixed and the curve backgrounds converge uniformly to backgrounds of zero area, then, for any choice of the semipositive terms $\alpha $, the potentials converge in $L^1(M)$, uniformly over the model tuples, to the sum of $\Psi $ and the pullbacks of the normalized smooth potentials of the limiting curve backgrounds, as in corollary 16.6.38 . Proof. Applied to model tuples, the lemma shows that every $\Phi _\alpha (q)$ is a normalized ordinary model and computes its ideal projection coordinatewise. Restrictions to curve sections on which the other potentials are finite determine the tuple up to constants, and the normalization of the coordinates determines these constants. Thus the map is well defined and bijective, and the formulas for the polar curvatures make it an isometry preserving ideal projection. Each potential in either locus is pulled back from $Y\times Z$. Analytic presentations pull back under the projection that forgets the auxiliary factor. Conversely, by proposition 1.13.1 , the restriction of a potential with analytic singularities to a section with fixed auxiliary coordinate has analytic singularities and is not identically $-\infty $. Hence a potential in either locus has analytic singularities exactly when the common potential on $Y\times Z$ does, and the isometry maps the analytic models onto each other. The statements on the complete metric, the ideal closure, geodesics, nearest points and area comparisons now follow from proposition 16.6.37 . A pairwise maximum is $\Psi $ plus the pullback of the maximum of two $\Gamma _\alpha $-plurisubharmonic functions on $B$. The reduction along the divisor of weight one gives zero upper volume for it and for both models, so the upper-volume comparison vanishes. For $L^1$ convergence, integration along the fixed compact fibers bounds the norm of each pulled-back curve potential by a constant times its norm on the curve. The same estimate and theorem 1.8.15 give the asserted uniform limit at zero area. Neither estimate involves $\alpha $. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.6.44
text: Corollary 16.6.44 . For the arbitrary curve potentials $u_ i$ of the lemma, put $R=\Psi +\sum _ ir_ i\circ \pi _ i\circ p$. The following are equivalent: $P_{\Theta _\alpha }[U]=P_{\Theta _\alpha }[U]_{\mathcal I}$; for each $i$, the polar part of the curvature measure of $u_ i$ equals its atomic part; $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta _\alpha ,R)$; and the ordinary and ideal envelopes of $U$ agree below every smooth real obstacle on $M$. Proof. By the lemma and the normalization of the coordinates, equality of the envelopes below zero is equivalent to $q_ i=r_ i$ for every $i$. By corollary 30.13.2 , this is equivalent to equality of the polar and atomic measures, and in that case $u_ i\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(C_ i,\sigma _ i,r_ i)$. Choose stretching competitors in these curve classes. The sum of their pullbacks plus $\Psi $ has positive current, since the contributions of the curves, the form $\varpi ^*\alpha $ and the current of the divisor are all positive. Adding the convex stretching inequalities, which is possible also at poles, gives a stretching competitor relative to $R$ for every finite stretch, and adding the ordinary bounds gives $U\preceq R$. Thus $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta _\alpha ,R)$, and proposition 16.6.8 gives equality below every smooth obstacle. Taking the zero obstacle recovers the first condition, which proves the equivalence. $\square$

title: 16.6.13 A polar metric in a background with unbounded mass
search_title: A polar metric in a background with unbounded mass
text: 16.6.13 A polar metric in a background with unbounded mass Taking the Hopf threefold of theorem 8.0.1 as the auxiliary factor makes the ambient masses unbounded, while the complete metric on the product models is unchanged. Letting the coefficient of the Hopf factor vary over the curve product also makes the background nonclosed. Example 16.6.46 . There is a compact complex sixfold with a smooth positive background $\Theta $ that is not closed and has infinite upper mass $v_+(\Theta )=+\infty $ in the sense of definition 6.5.1 , while the locus of separated product models of proposition 16.6.43 , along a divisor of weight one, has a complete geodesic polar metric of diameter $4$. The ideal subspace is closed and is the metric closure of the models with analytic singularities, and ideal projection is the unique nearest-point retraction onto it and is $1$-Lipschitz. The upper-volume comparison vanishes on this locus. The locus contains distinct ideal models with analytic singularities at polar distance $1$. Proof. Take $Y=C_1\times C_2$ with $C_1=C_2=\mathbb P^1$ and normalized Fubini–Study forms $\omega _ i$ of area one, and write $\pi _ i:Y\to C_ i$ for the projections. Let $(T,\omega _ T,V_ j)$ be the Hopf threefold, its Gauduchon form and the smooth potentials of theorem 8.0.1 . Take $Z=\mathbb P^1$ with its normalized Fubini–Study form $\kappa $, a point $D$ and its normalized potential $\psi $ satisfying $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =[D]$. On $M=Y\times T\times Z$, write $p,s,r$ for the projections. Choose a positive nonconstant smooth function $h$ on $Y$ and put \[  \Theta =p^*(\pi _1^*\omega _1+\pi _2^*\omega _2) +(h\circ p)s^*\omega _ T+r^*\kappa , \qquad \Psi =\psi \circ r.  \] This form is strictly positive. The component $\mathrm dh\wedge \omega _ T$ of its exterior derivative, with one direction in $Y$ and two in $T$, is nonzero and cannot be canceled by the component with three directions in $T$. Thus $\Theta $ is not closed. Put $c=\min _ Yh>0$. The smooth functions $W_ j=cV_ j\circ s$ are strictly $\Theta $-plurisubharmonic, since their current in the $T$-directions is \[  h\omega _ T+c\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j =c(\omega _ T+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)+(h-c)\omega _ T>0.  \] Only the part of degree three in the $T$-directions contributes to the top-degree product. The three curve forms have integral one, so positivity of smooth mixed products and Fubini's theorem give \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ M(\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W_ j)^6 & =120\int _ Y\pi _1^*\omega _1\wedge \pi _2^*\omega _2 \int _ T(h(y)\omega _ T+c\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^3\\ & \geq 120c^3\int _ T(\omega _ T+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^3 \longrightarrow +\infty . \end{aligned}  \] The factor $120=6!/3!$ counts the ways of choosing one factor for each curve direction and three for $T$. Each $W_ j$ is bounded, so definition 6.5.1 gives $v_+(\Theta )=+\infty $, and the bounded mass property fails. Apply proposition 16.6.43 to this product, with both curve areas equal to one. On the locus of potentials $\Psi +q_1\circ \pi _1\circ p+q_2\circ \pi _2\circ p$, where each $q_ i$ ranges over the ordinary $\omega _ i$-models with supremum zero, it gives a complete metric $\rho $ of diameter $4$, the analytic closure of the ideal subspace, the nearest-point retraction and the vanishing of the upper-volume comparison. These conclusions use no bound on the ambient masses. For $x\in C_1$, let $g_ x$ be the normalized Green potential of the point $x$, with $\omega _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ x=[x]$. By lemma 16.6.42 , the potentials \[  \Phi _0=\Psi ,\qquad \Phi _ x=\Psi +g_ x\circ \pi _1\circ p  \] are ordinary and ideal models, and their divisorial poles with coefficient one give analytic singularities. Their tuples of polar curvatures are $(0,0)$ and $(\delta _ x,0)$, so $\rho (\Phi _0,\Phi _ x)=\| \delta _ x\| _{\mathrm{TV}}=1$. Nevertheless, by the same lemma, every representative of either ordinary type has zero extended mass; in particular, all their upper and lower singularity volumes are zero. $\square$

title: 16.6.14 Models over a curve
text:
16.6.14 Models over a curve The polar metric on a curve also describes models on a compact manifold that maps onto it with connected fibers, including critical fibers. A background pulled back from the curve has no vertical curvature, so every potential descends. Gauduchon volumes of the fiber divisors are constant, with their multiplicities included. The normalized polar trace therefore recovers the curve metric without choosing a product structure. Let $p:X	o C$ be a surjective holomorphic map with connected fibers, where $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$ and $C$ is a connected compact Riemann surface. Fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $ eta $ on $C$, put $A=\int _ C eta $ and $	heta =p^* eta $, and choose a smooth positive area-one form $\eta $ on $C$. For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(C, eta )$ write \[  T_ v= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v,\qquad \mu _ v=\mathbf1_{\{ v=-\infty \} }T_ v.  \] Thus $\mu _ v$ is the polar curvature of the curve potential. Lemma 16.6.47 . The class $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is nonempty if and only if $A\geq 0$. For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(C, eta )$ and $U=v\circ p$, one has \[  P_	heta [U]=P_ eta [v]\circ p,\qquad P_	heta [U]_{\mathcal I}=P_ eta [v]_{\mathcal I}\circ p.  \] Pullback is a bijection between the ordinary model spaces and between their ideal subspaces. Every potential in this background has zero extended Monge–Ampère measure, and every ordinary type has zero upper and lower singularity volumes. If $A=0$ and $ eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$, the only normalized potential is $-h\circ p+\min _ Ch$. It is smooth and is the unique ordinary and ideal model. Proof. By 1.22.4 , every potential descends, even for this possibly indefinite background. Thus nonemptiness is equivalent to the curve condition in lemma 1.8.14 . Descent preserves the ordinary order, and 1.22.6 preserves and reflects the all-weight ideal order. At each $x\in X$, choose coordinates centered at $x$ and $p(x)$. A complex line detects the first nonzero homogeneous term of $p$. Its restriction to that line is open, so $p$ is open. Upper regularization therefore commutes with pullback, proving the envelope identities and the model bijections. Write $ eta =A\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ with $h$ smooth, using lemma 1.8.14 . For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(C, eta )$, put $w=v+h\in \mathrm{PSH}(C,A\eta )$. Then \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ p) =A p^*\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w\circ p).  \] When $A>0$, put $W=w\circ p$. Its bounded truncations are $\max (W,-j)=\max (w,-j)\circ p$. Locally choose a smooth $a$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a=A\eta $. The bounded subharmonic function $a+\max (w,-j)$ has smooth decreasing local approximants. Their pullbacks have complex Hessian rank at most one, including at critical points, so their $n$th powers vanish. Bounded product continuity makes each truncation have zero top product, and hence $W$ has zero extended measure in the positive background. The current invariance in theorem 6.1.2 gives zero extended measure in the original decomposition as well. When $A=0$, the curve lemma gives $v=-h+c$. Its pullback is smooth with zero curvature current, so its top product is zero. Surjectivity gives the stated normalization. Every potential differs from this one by a constant, and both envelopes fix its normalized representative. Since descent applies to every representative of every ordinary type, both singularity volumes are zero in all cases. $\square$ Henceforth assume $A\geq 0$. Fix a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ on $X$. For a finite positive measure $\mu $ of mass $M$, let $q_\mu $ be the solution normalized by $\int _ Cq_\mu \, \eta =0$ to \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_\mu =\mu -M\eta .  \] The curve Green kernel of section 19.3 gives this quasi-subharmonic solution. Define the positive current \[  p^*\mu =M p^*\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q_\mu \circ p),\qquad L_\gamma (\mu )=p^*\mu \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Locally this is the pullback of a subharmonic potential of $\mu $; changing that potential adds a harmonic function and does not change the current. Extend both operators to signed measures by linearity. Write $F_ s=p^{-1}(s)$ for the fiber divisor with its scheme multiplicities. Lemma 16.6.48 . There is a positive constant $\kappa _\gamma $ such that, for every finite signed measure $\mu $ and every Borel set $B\subset C$, \[   egin{gathered} p_*L_\gamma (\mu )=\kappa _\gamma \mu ,\qquad \| L_\gamma (\mu )\| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\kappa _\gamma \| \mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}},\ L_\gamma (\mathbf1_ B\mu ) =\mathbf1_{p^{-1}(B)}L_\gamma (\mu ),\qquad \int _{F_ s}\gamma ^{n-1}=\kappa _\gamma \quad (s\in C). \end{gathered}  \] The last integral includes the multiplicities of the fiber. Proof. The positive $(0,0)$-current $S=p_*(\gamma ^{n-1})$ on $C$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=p_*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$. A harmonic distribution is smooth, so $S$ is a constant $\kappa _\gamma $. On the complement of the critical values, smooth fiber integration identifies it with the positive integral of $\gamma ^{n-1}$ on a regular fiber. Thus $\kappa _\gamma >0$. First let $\mu $ be positive with mass $M>0$. Choose smooth positive measures $\mu _ j$ with the same mass and $\mu _ jightharpoonup \mu $. Their mean-zero solutions $q_ j$ have a common lower curvature bound $-M\eta $. Normalized compactness bounds $\sup _ Cq_ j$: their mean-zero condition makes this supremum the negative mean of their supremum-zero normalization. Hence $(q_ j)$ is precompact in $L^1(C)$. Every limit has mean zero and Hessian $\mu -M\eta $. Two such limits differ by a harmonic function, hence by a constant, which their means force to be zero. Therefore $q_ j	o q_\mu $ in $L^1(C)$. By 1.22.7 , $q_ j\circ p	o q_\mu \circ p$ in $L^1(X)$. Thus $p^*\mu _ j	o p^*\mu $ as currents and their smooth Hermitian traces converge weakly. For smooth $\mu _ j$, the definition of $S$ gives $p_*L_\gamma (\mu _ j)=\kappa _\gamma \mu _ j$. Passing to the limit proves the identity for $\mu $. The case $M=0$ is zero, and linearity proves the signed identity. For a positive $\mu $, split it into $\mathbf1_ B\mu $ and $\mathbf1_{C\setminus B}\mu $. Their traces are positive; the pushforward identity shows that they are respectively carried by $p^{-1}(B)$ and its complement. Additivity then gives the restriction identity. Apply the same argument to the positive and negative Jordan parts of a signed measure. Their disjoint Borel carriers pull back to disjoint carriers, so their traces are the Jordan parts upstairs. The pushforward identity gives the asserted total-variation norm. Finally the Poincaré–Lelong formula in the book normalization gives $p^*\delta _ s=[F_ s]$, including every zero multiplicity of a local equation of the fiber. Its trace has total mass $\kappa _\gamma $, by the pushforward identity with $\mu =\delta _ s$. $\square$ Let $\mathcal M(	heta )$ be the ordinary model space. For $U=v\circ p\in \mathcal M(	heta )$, its polar trace measure is \[  \lambda _ U^\gamma =\mathbf1_{\{ U=-\infty \} } (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =L_\gamma (\mu _ v).  \] The last identity follows from the Borel restriction formula of 16.6.48 , including at critical fibers and for a nonatomic polar measure. Define \[  ho _	heta (U,V)=\kappa _\gamma ^{-1} \| \lambda _ U^\gamma -\lambda _ V^\gamma \| _{\mathrm{TV}}.  \] Proposition 16.6.49 . The metric $ho _	heta $ is independent of the Gauduchon form $\gamma $. Pullback is an isometry from the complete geodesic curve model space onto $(\mathcal M(	heta ),ho _	heta )$, which has diameter $2A$. The ideal models form a closed geodesically convex subspace equal to the metric closure of the models with analytic singularities. Ideal projection is its unique nearest-point retraction and is $1$-Lipschitz. If $U=v\circ p$ is a model, its distance to that subspace is the nonatomic polar mass of $v$. Metric convergence implies $L^1(X)$ convergence for every smooth positive volume form. The upper-volume comparison on $\mathcal M(	heta )$ vanishes identically. At $A=0$ this is the one-point metric space of the unique smooth model. Proof. The definition of pullback measure gives $p^*T_ v=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ p)$: in the smooth decomposition $ eta =A\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$, both sides are $A p^*\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((v+h)\circ p)$. e t$, attain this bound. For $A=0$, 16.6.47 gives the singleton. Ideal projection corresponds to the atomic part of the polar measure by the same curve classification. If $\mu =\mu _{\mathrm{at}}+\mu _{\mathrm{diff}}$ and $
u $ is atomic, the measures $\mu _{\mathrm{diff}}$ and $\mu _{\mathrm{at}}-

title: Lemma 16.6.47
text: Lemma 16.6.47 . The class $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is nonempty if and only if $A\geq 0$. For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(C,\beta )$ and $U=v\circ p$, one has \[  P_\theta [U]=P_\beta [v]\circ p,\qquad P_\theta [U]_{\mathcal I}=P_\beta [v]_{\mathcal I}\circ p.  \] Pullback is a bijection between the ordinary model spaces and between their ideal subspaces. Every potential in this background has zero extended Monge–Ampère measure, and every ordinary type has zero upper and lower singularity volumes. If $A=0$ and $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$, the only normalized potential is $-h\circ p+\min _ Ch$. It is smooth and is the unique ordinary and ideal model. Proof. By 1.22.4 , every potential descends, even for this possibly indefinite background. Thus nonemptiness is equivalent to the curve condition in lemma 1.8.14 . Descent preserves the ordinary order, and 1.22.6 preserves and reflects the all-weight ideal order. At each $x\in X$, choose coordinates centered at $x$ and $p(x)$. A complex line detects the first nonzero homogeneous term of $p$. Its restriction to that line is open, so $p$ is open. Upper regularization therefore commutes with pullback, proving the envelope identities and the model bijections. Write $\beta =A\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ with $h$ smooth, using lemma 1.8.14 . For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(C,\beta )$, put $w=v+h\in \mathrm{PSH}(C,A\eta )$. Then \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ p) =A p^*\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w\circ p).  \] When $A>0$, put $W=w\circ p$. Its bounded truncations are $\max (W,-j)=\max (w,-j)\circ p$. Locally choose a smooth $a$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a=A\eta $. The bounded subharmonic function $a+\max (w,-j)$ has smooth decreasing local approximants. title: Lemma 16.6.48
text: Lemma 16.6.48 . There is a positive constant $\kappa _\gamma $ such that, for every finite signed measure $\mu $ and every Borel set $B\subset C$, \[  \begin{gathered} p_*L_\gamma (\mu )=\kappa _\gamma \mu ,\qquad \| L_\gamma (\mu )\| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\kappa _\gamma \| \mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}},\\ L_\gamma (\mathbf1_ B\mu ) =\mathbf1_{p^{-1}(B)}L_\gamma (\mu ),\qquad \int _{F_ s}\gamma ^{n-1}=\kappa _\gamma \quad (s\in C). \end{gathered}  \] The last integral includes the multiplicities of the fiber. Proof. The positive $(0,0)$-current $S=p_*(\gamma ^{n-1})$ on $C$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=p_*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$. A harmonic distribution is smooth, so $S$ is a constant $\kappa _\gamma $. On the complement of the critical values, smooth fiber integration identifies it with the positive integral of $\gamma ^{n-1}$ on a regular fiber. Thus $\kappa _\gamma >0$. First let $\mu $ be positive with mass $M>0$. Choose smooth positive measures $\mu _ j$ with the same mass and $\mu _ j\rightharpoonup \mu $. Their mean-zero solutions $q_ j$ have a common lower curvature bound $-M\eta $. Normalized compactness bounds $\sup _ Cq_ j$: their mean-zero condition makes this supremum the negative mean of their supremum-zero normalization. Hence $(q_ j)$ is precompact in $L^1(C)$. Every limit has mean zero and Hessian $\mu -M\eta $. Two such limits differ by a harmonic function, hence by a constant, which their means force to be zero. Therefore $q_ j\to q_\mu $ in $L^1(C)$. By 1.22.7 , $q_ j\circ p\to q_\mu \circ p$ in $L^1(X)$. Thus $p^*\mu _ j\to p^*\mu $ as currents and their smooth Hermitian traces converge weakly. For smooth $\mu _ j$, the definition of $S$ gives $p_*L_\gamma (\mu _ j)=\kappa _\gamma \mu _ j$. Passing to the limit proves the identity for $\mu $. The case $M=0$ is zero, and linearity proves the signed identity. For a positive $\mu $, split it into $\mathbf1_ B\mu $ and $\mathbf1_{C\setminus B}\mu $. Their traces are positive; the pushforward identity shows that they are respectively carried by $p^{-1}(B)$ and its complement. Additivity then gives the restriction identity. Apply the same argument to the positive and negative Jordan parts of a signed measure. Their disjoint Borel carriers pull back to disjoint carriers, so their traces are the Jordan parts upstairs. The pushforward identity gives the asserted total-variation norm. Finally the Poincaré–Lelong formula in the book normalization gives $p^*\delta _ s=[F_ s]$, including every zero multiplicity of a local equation of the fiber. Its trace has total mass $\kappa _\gamma $, by the pushforward identity with $\mu =\delta _ s$. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.6.50
text: Corollary 16.6.50 . Let $U=v\circ p$ and $R=P_\theta [U]_{\mathcal I}$. The following are equivalent: $P_\theta [U]=P_\theta [U]_{\mathcal I}$; $\mu _ v$ is atomic; $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,R)$; and the ordinary and ideal envelopes of $U$ agree below every smooth real obstacle on $X$. title: 16.6.15 Finite curve factors
text: 16.6.15 Finite curve factors Keep $X$ and $C$ as above, but now allow $p:X\to C$ to have disconnected fibers. By 1.22.9 , it has the component factorization \[  X\xrightarrow {q}C'\xrightarrow {r}C, \qquad p=r\circ q,  \] where $q$ is surjective and holomorphic with connected fibers, $C'$ is a connected compact Riemann surface, and $r$ is finite and holomorphic of degree $d\geq 1$. Let $\beta $ be any smooth real form on $C$, put $A=\int _ C\beta $, and set $\sigma =r^*\beta $ and $\theta =p^*\beta =q^*\sigma $. Proposition 16.6.51 . The class $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is nonempty exactly when $A\geq 0$. For $A\geq 0$, the entire ordinary $\theta $-model space is isometric, using the $q$-fiber normalization, to the curve model space in background $\sigma $, whose area is $dA$. Its diameter is $2dA$; it has the analytic closure, ideal retraction, convergence and all-obstacle properties above. Every potential has zero extended top-degree measure and every ordinary type has zero upper and lower singularity volumes. At $A=0$ the model space is a smooth singleton. If $\kappa _ q^\gamma $ and $\kappa _ p^\gamma $ are the constants defined by the pushforwards of $\gamma ^{n-1}$ to $C'$ and $C$, then \[  \kappa _ p^\gamma =d\kappa _ q^\gamma .  \] For $A\geq 0$, normalizing the same polar-trace variation by $\kappa _ p^\gamma $ gives $d^{-1}$ times the $q$-normalized metric, with diameter $2A$. This rescaled metric is also independent of $\gamma $. For a model $U=v\circ q$ with polar measure $\mu _ v$, \[  p_*\lambda _ U^\gamma =\kappa _ q^\gamma r_*\mu _ v.  \] Proof. Away from the finitely many critical values, $r$ is a covering with $d$ sheets. Change of variables on these sheets gives \[  \int _{C'}r^*\alpha =d\int _ C\alpha  \] for every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\alpha $; the branch points and their inverse images have smooth area zero. In particular $\int _{C'}\sigma =dA$. The envelope lemma 16.6.47 , applied to $q$, gives nonemptiness exactly for $dA\geq 0$, equivalent to $A\geq 0$, and proves the zero-mass and zero-area assertions. In this nonempty case, apply 16.6.49 , 16.6.50 to $q$ and the smooth background $\sigma $, which may vanish at branch points or be indefinite. The Gauduchon trace lemma for $q$ gives $q_*(\gamma ^{n-1})=\kappa _ q^\gamma $. For a smooth test form $\alpha $ on $C$, the projection formula and the covering calculation yield \[  \int _ Xp^*\alpha \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\kappa _ q^\gamma \int _{C'}r^*\alpha =d\kappa _ q^\gamma \int _ C\alpha .  \] Thus $p_*(\gamma ^{n-1})$ is the constant $d\kappa _ q^\gamma $. The ratio of the two normalizations is $d^{-1}$, giving every metric assertion. Finally $q_*\lambda _ U^\gamma =\kappa _ q^\gamma \mu _ v$, so composing pushforwards proves the last identity. $\square$ Example 16.6.52 . Let $X=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, let $q$ be its first projection and let $r:\mathbb P^1\to \mathbb P^1$ be $r([z_0:z_1])=[z_0^2:z_1^2]$. Put $p=r\circ q$ and $\theta =p^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, with $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=1$. There are two distinct analytic ideal $\theta $-models $U_+,U_-$ which do not descend through $p$. Their $q$-normalized polar distance is four and their $p$-normalized distance is two, yet \[  p_*\lambda _{U_+}^\gamma =p_*\lambda _{U_-}^\gamma  \] for every Gauduchon form $\gamma $. Thus the pushforward of polar trace to the original base does not separate the models. Proof. The finite map $r$ has degree two and is branched at zero and infinity. In the affine coordinate it is $r(z)=z^2$, so the smooth semipositive form $\sigma =r^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ has area two. For $s\in \{ 1,-1\} $, set \[  v_ s(z)=2\log |z-s|^2-\log (1+|z|^4)-\log 8.  \] This extends smoothly across infinity and has curvature $\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ s=2\delta _ s$. The inequality $|z-s|^4\leq (|z|+1)^4\leq 8(1+|z|^4)$, with equality at $z=-s$, shows that its supremum is zero. The model of $2\delta _ s$ from proposition 30.13.1 has precisely this total curvature, since its polar measure already has the full mass two. Harmonic uniqueness and normalization identify it with $v_ s$. Write $v_+=v_1$ and $v_-=v_{-1}$. Both have analytic singularities, hence are ideal by proposition 16.2.7 . The model pullback bijection makes $U_\pm =v_\pm \circ q$ analytic ideal $\theta $-models. The function $U_+$ is $-\infty $ on $q^{-1}(1)$ and finite on $q^{-1}(-1)$, although both divisors are mapped by $p$ to the same base point $1$. It therefore cannot descend through $p$; the same argument with the divisors exchanged applies to $U_-$. The variation of $2\delta _1-2\delta _{-1}$ is four. The finite factor proposition gives the two distances and \[  p_*\lambda _{U_\pm }^\gamma =2\kappa _ q^\gamma \delta _1.  \] The upstairs polar traces are distinct, while this common pushforward loses which component carries the pole. $\square$

title: 16.6.16 Models pulled back by a finite curve map
search_title: Models pulled back by a finite curve map
text: 16.6.16 Models pulled back by a finite curve map Let $r:C'\to C$ be a finite surjective holomorphic map of degree $d$ between connected compact Riemann surfaces. Fix a smooth real form $\beta $ of area $A\geq 0$ on $C$ and put $\sigma =r^*\beta $. The models pulled back from $C$ occupy a proper subspace of the full model space on $C'$ in general. The fiber maximum of 1.22.10 compares envelope competitors on the two curves. The weighted measure pullback then identifies the metric on this subspace and gives a retraction from the full space. Proposition 16.6.53 . For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(C,\beta )$ and every smooth real obstacle $F$ on $C$, \[  \begin{aligned}  P_{\sigma ,F\circ r}[v\circ r] & =P_{\beta ,F}[v]\circ r,\\  P_{\sigma ,F\circ r}[v\circ r]_{\mathcal I} & =P_{\beta ,F}[v]_{\mathcal I}\circ r. \end{aligned}  \] In particular, $J(v)=v\circ r$ embeds the ordinary model space $\mathcal M(\beta )$ into $\mathcal M(\sigma )$ and preserves ideal projection. Proof. Pullback sends every base competitor to an upstairs competitor: it preserves positivity, the obstacle inequality, the ordinary order and, by the Lelong formula and the curve valuative criterion, the all-weight ideal order. Conversely, if $h$ is an upstairs competitor, its fiber maximum $m_ h$ is a base competitor by 1.22.10 , since $h\leq F\circ r$ implies $m_ h\leq F$. Also $h\leq m_ h\circ r$. Thus the two unregularized suprema are equal after pullback. A finite nonconstant holomorphic map of curves is open; upper regularization commutes with its pullback, as is seen in the coordinates $t=z^ e$. This proves both identities. Take $F=0$. An ordinary model is fixed by its ordinary envelope, so its pullback is a model; surjectivity of $r$ gives injectivity. Applying the ideal identity to a model proves preservation of ideal projection. $\square$ Let $d_\beta $ and $d_\sigma $ be the polar metrics from proposition 30.13.1 . If $q$ is a model on $C'$, denote its polar curvature by $\mu _ q=\mathbf1_{\{ q=-\infty \} }(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)$. Write $p_\beta (\nu )$ for the base model with polar measure $\nu $, using the same classification. Write $U_\beta (v)=\int _ C\mathrm{MA}_\beta (v)$ and $U_\sigma (q)=\int _{C'}\mathrm{MA}_\sigma (q)$ for their non-pluripolar volumes. Proposition 16.6.54 . For $u,v\in \mathcal M(\beta )$, \[  d_\sigma (J(u),J(v))=d\, d_\beta (u,v),\qquad U_\sigma (J(u))=d\, U_\beta (u).  \] The image $J(\mathcal M(\beta ))$ is closed and contains the linear polar-measure geodesic between each pair of its members. The map \[  R(q)=J\! \left(p_\beta \! \left(d^{-1}r_*\mu _ q\right)\right)  \] is a $1$-Lipschitz retraction onto this image. Its polar measure is \[  \mu _{R(q)}=d^{-1}r^*r_*\mu _ q.  \] It preserves the polar mass and the non-pluripolar volume, and commutes with ideal projection on $\mathcal M(\sigma )$. At $A=0$ both model spaces are smooth singletons. Proof. Change of variables off the finite branch sets gives $\int _{C'}\sigma =dA$. By 1.22.11 , the polar measure of $J(v)$ is $r^*\mu _ v$, with total mass $d\mu _ v(C)$. The curve classification gives \[  \begin{aligned}  d_\sigma (J(u),J(v)) & =\| r^*(\mu _ u-\mu _ v)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} =d\| \mu _ u-\mu _ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}},\\  U_\sigma (J(v)) & =dA-d\mu _ v(C)=d\, U_\beta (v). \end{aligned}  \] Completeness of the base model space proves closedness of the image: a convergent sequence in the image comes from a Cauchy sequence downstairs. Linear interpolation of polar measures commutes with $r^*$, giving the stated geodesics. For any $q\in \mathcal M(\sigma )$, its polar measure has mass at most $dA$. Its pushforward is polar by the image assertion of 1.22.11 , so $d^{-1}r_*\mu _ q$ has mass at most $A$ and defines a base model. This proves that $R$ is well defined and gives its displayed polar measure. The identity $r_*r^*=d$ makes $R\circ J=J$. For any finite signed measure $\tau $ on $C'$, pushforward does not increase total variation, hence \[  \| d^{-1}r^*r_*\tau \| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\| r_*\tau \| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \| \tau \| _{\mathrm{TV}}.  \] Apply this to the difference of two polar measures to obtain the Lipschitz estimate. The averaging operator preserves their total mass, so the formula $U_\sigma (q)=dA-\mu _ q(C')$ gives volume preservation. Both measure operations commute with taking the atomic part, which is ideal projection by the curve classification. This proves the commutation assertion. At zero area all polar measures vanish and both spaces are singletons. $\square$ Corollary 16.6.55 . Let $p:X\to C$ be a surjective holomorphic map from a connected compact complex manifold of dimension at least two, with component factorization $p=r\circ q$, $q:X\to C'$. For $\theta =p^*\beta $, the ordinary models that are constant on each $p$-fiber form a closed complete subspace. With the $p$-fiber normalization of 16.6.51 , the map $v\mapsto v\circ p$ is an isometry from $(\mathcal M(\beta ),d_\beta )$ onto this subspace. Every model has the form $U=u\circ q$, and \[  R_ X(U)=R(u)\circ q  \] is a $1$-Lipschitz retraction onto the subspace. It commutes with ideal projection. The subspace contains the linear polar-measure geodesic between each pair of its members. Proof. The full model correspondence for $q$ is 16.6.47 . A model $u\circ q$ is constant on $p$-fibers exactly when $u$ is constant on $r$-fibers. In that case $u=m_ u\circ r$, and 1.22.10 makes $m_ u$ a base potential. The envelope identity and injectivity of $J$ then show that $m_ u$ is a model. Thus this subspace is exactly the pullback image of $\mathcal M(\beta )$. By 16.6.51 , the $p$-normalized metric is $d^{-1}$ times the polar metric on $C'$. The preceding proposition proves the isometry, closedness, completeness, retraction and geodesic assertions. The ideal-envelope correspondence for $q$ transfers the commutation with ideal projection. $\square$ This retraction averages the singularity data over a fiber. Unlike the ideal retraction, it need not select a nearest model. Example 16.6.56 . For $r:\mathbb P^1\to \mathbb P^1$, $r(z)=z^3$, and the Fubini–Study background $\beta $ of area one, the retraction $R$ above is not a nearest-point retraction, even on ideal models with analytic singularities. Proof. Put $\sigma =r^*\beta $, of area three, and let $q$ be its model with polar measure $\delta _1$. This is an analytic ideal model: in the affine coordinate, the global function \[  h(z)=\log |z-1|^2-\tfrac 13\log (1+|z|^6)  \] extends smoothly across infinity and satisfies $\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\delta _1+\tfrac 23\sigma $. Thus $h$ is $\sigma $-plurisubharmonic with one logarithmic pole, and the curve classification identifies its envelope with $q$; proposition 16.2.7 preserves its analytic type. Writing $\zeta =\exp (2\pi \mathrm i/3)$, one has \[  \mu _{R(q)}=\tfrac 13(\delta _1+\delta _\zeta +\delta _{\zeta ^2}).  \] The three atoms are distinct, so \[  d_\sigma (q,R(q))=\tfrac 23+\tfrac 13+\tfrac 13=\tfrac 43.  \] The zero model is $J(0)$ and has zero polar measure, giving $d_\sigma (q,J(0))=1$. Hence the averaged model is strictly farther from $q$ than a member of the same pullback subspace. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.6.53
text: Proposition 16.6.53 . For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(C,\beta )$ and every smooth real obstacle $F$ on $C$, \[  \begin{aligned}  P_{\sigma ,F\circ r}[v\circ r] & =P_{\beta ,F}[v]\circ r,\\  P_{\sigma ,F\circ r}[v\circ r]_{\mathcal I} & =P_{\beta ,F}[v]_{\mathcal I}\circ r. \end{aligned}  \] In particular, $J(v)=v\circ r$ embeds the ordinary model space $\mathcal M(\beta )$ into $\mathcal M(\sigma )$ and preserves ideal projection. Proof. Pullback sends every base competitor to an upstairs competitor: it preserves positivity, the obstacle inequality, the ordinary order and, by the Lelong formula and the curve valuative criterion, the all-weight ideal order. Conversely, if $h$ is an upstairs competitor, its fiber maximum $m_ h$ is a base competitor by 1.22.10 , since $h\leq F\circ r$ implies $m_ h\leq F$. Also $h\leq m_ h\circ r$. Thus the two unregularized suprema are equal after pullback. A finite nonconstant holomorphic map of curves is open; upper regularization commutes with its pullback, as is seen in the coordinates $t=z^ e$. This proves both identities. Take $F=0$. An ordinary model is fixed by its ordinary envelope, so its pullback is a model; surjectivity of $r$ gives injectivity. Applying the ideal identity to a model proves preservation of ideal projection. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.6.54
text: Proposition 16.6.54 . For $u,v\in \mathcal M(\beta )$, \[  d_\sigma (J(u),J(v))=d\, d_\beta (u,v),\qquad U_\sigma (J(u))=d\, U_\beta (u).  \] The image $J(\mathcal M(\beta ))$ is closed and contains the linear polar-measure geodesic between each pair of its members. The map \[  R(q)=J\! \left(p_\beta \! \left(d^{-1}r_*\mu _ q\right)\right)  \] is a $1$-Lipschitz retraction onto this image. Its polar measure is \[  \mu _{R(q)}=d^{-1}r^*r_*\mu _ q.  \] It preserves the polar mass and the non-pluripolar volume, and commutes with ideal projection on $\mathcal M(\sigma )$. At $A=0$ both model spaces are smooth singletons. Proof. Change of variables off the finite branch sets gives $\int _{C'}\sigma =dA$. By 1.22.11 , the polar measure of $J(v)$ is $r^*\mu _ v$, with total mass $d\mu _ v(C)$. The curve classification gives \[  \begin{aligned}  d_\sigma (J(u),J(v)) & =\| r^*(\mu _ u-\mu _ v)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} =d\| \mu _ u-\mu _ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}},\\  U_\sigma (J(v)) & =dA-d\mu _ v(C)=d\, U_\beta (v). \end{aligned}  \] Completeness of the base model space proves closedness of the image: a convergent sequence in the image comes from a Cauchy sequence downstairs. Linear interpolation of polar measures commutes with $r^*$, giving the stated geodesics. For any $q\in \mathcal M(\sigma )$, its polar measure has mass at most $dA$. Its pushforward is polar by the image assertion of 1.22.11 , so $d^{-1}r_*\mu _ q$ has mass at most $A$ and defines a base model. This proves that $R$ is well defined and gives its displayed polar measure. The identity $r_*r^*=d$ makes $R\circ J=J$. For any finite signed measure $\tau $ on $C'$, pushforward does not increase total variation, hence \[  \| d^{-1}r^*r_*\tau \| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\| r_*\tau \| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \| \tau \| _{\mathrm{TV}}.  \] Apply this to the difference of two polar measures to obtain the Lipschitz estimate. The averaging operator preserves their total mass, so the formula $U_\sigma (q)=dA-\mu _ q(C')$ gives volume preservation. Both measure operations commute with taking the atomic part, which is ideal projection by the curve classification. This proves the commutation assertion. At zero area all polar measures vanish and both spaces are singletons. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.6.55
text: Corollary 16.6.55 . Let $p:X\to C$ be a surjective holomorphic map from a connected compact complex manifold of dimension at least two, with component factorization $p=r\circ q$, $q:X\to C'$. For $\theta =p^*\beta $, the ordinary models that are constant on each $p$-fiber form a closed complete subspace. With the $p$-fiber normalization of 16.6.51 , the map $v\mapsto v\circ p$ is an isometry from $(\mathcal M(\beta ),d_\beta )$ onto this subspace. Every model has the form $U=u\circ q$, and \[  R_ X(U)=R(u)\circ q  \] is a $1$-Lipschitz retraction onto the subspace. It commutes with ideal projection. The subspace contains the linear polar-measure geodesic between each pair of its members. Proof. The full model correspondence for $q$ is 16.6.47 . A model $u\circ q$ is constant on $p$-fibers exactly when $u$ is constant on $r$-fibers. In that case $u=m_ u\circ r$, and 1.22.10 makes $m_ u$ a base potential. The envelope identity and injectivity of $J$ then show that $m_ u$ is a model. Thus this subspace is exactly the pullback image of $\mathcal M(\beta )$. By 16.6.51 , the $p$-normalized metric is $d^{-1}$ times the polar metric on $C'$. The preceding proposition proves the isometry, closedness, completeness, retraction and geodesic assertions. The ideal-envelope correspondence for $q$ transfers the commutation with ideal projection. $\square$

16.6.17 Hopf surface fibers and unbounded ambient mass The complete model space of a curve submersion can occur on a manifold whose ambient Hermitian masses are unbounded. Blowing up the elliptic base locus of the projection $[z_0:z_1]$ on the scalar Hopf threefold turns this projection into a submersion with Hopf surface fibers. The rank-one background then retains only the curve singularities, while the smooth potentials of the Hopf threefold still force unbounded mass in a positive ambient background. Example 16.6.57 . There is a connected compact complex threefold $Z$ with a surjective holomorphic submersion $p:Z	o \mathbb P^1$ whose fibers are scalar Hopf surfaces. The manifold $Z$ does not have the bounded mass property. For the pullback $	heta =p^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ of the Fubini–Study form of area one, the entire ordinary model space has the complete geodesic polar metric of 16.6.49 , with diameter two. Its ideal subspace is the analytic closure, with the unique nearest-point, $1$-Lipschitz ideal retraction. All potentials in this background have zero extended Monge–Ampère measure, yet it contains analytic ideal models at polar distance one. Proof. Put $\lambda =\mathrm e^{-1}$ and consider the vector bundle \[  \mathcal V=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1) \oplus \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}.  \] Let $\mathcal V^	imes $ be its total space with the zero section removed, and define \[  Z=\mathcal V^	imes /\langle v\mapsto \lambda vangle .  \] The bundle projection descends to a holomorphic map $p:Z	o \mathbb P^1$. A Hermitian norm on the bundle satisfies $\| \lambda ^ kv\| =\lambda ^ k\| v\| $. The action is free and proper: on compact subsets of $\mathcal V^	imes $ the norms have positive lower and finite upper bounds, so only finitely many powers can move one such subset to meet another. Thus the quotient is a complex threefold. The annulus bundle $\{ \lambda \leq \| v\| \leq 1\} $ is compact over $\mathbb P^1$ and meets every orbit, so $Z$ is compact. Bundle charts identify $p^{-1}(U)$ with \[  U	imes  igl ((\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )/ \langle w\mapsto \lambda wangle  igr ).  \] Hence $p$ is a holomorphic submersion with connected compact Hopf surface fibers, and $Z$ is connected. The tautological inclusion into $\mathbb C^2$ identifies $\mathcal V^	imes $ with the incidence manifold \[  \left\{ ([s:t],z)\in \mathbb P^1	imes (\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} ):\  t z_0=s z_1ight\} .  \] The last coordinate $z_2$ comes from the trivial summand. This is the blowup of $\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} $ along $L=\{ z_0=z_1=0,\  z_2
e 0\} $: in the chart $s
e 0$, write $a=t/s$ and $z_1=az_0$, while in the chart $t
e 0$ write $b=s/t$ and $z_0=bz_1$. These are the two usual blowup charts of the ideal $(z_0,z_1)$. The scalar contraction preserves the incidence relation and commutes with projection to $z$. It therefore descends to a modification \[  \mu :Z\longrightarrow H=(\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} )/ \langle z\mapsto \lambda zangle .  \] The map is an isomorphism away from the elliptic curve $L/\langle \lambda angle $. Local quotient charts show that it is its blowup; in particular it has degree one. Take the Gauduchon form $\omega $ and smooth potentials $V_ j$ on $H$ from theorem 8.0.1 . Since $Z$ is compact, a sufficiently large multiple $\Omega $ of any Hermitian form satisfies $\Omega -\mu ^*\omega >0$. Put $W_ j=V_ j\circ \mu $. Then \[  \Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W_ j =\Omega -\mu ^*\omega +\mu ^*(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)>0.  \] Positivity of smooth mixed products and the degree-one change of variables off the exceptional divisor give \[   egin{aligned}  \int _ Z(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W_ j)^3 & \geq \int _ Z\mu ^*(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^3\ & =\int _ H(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^3\longrightarrow +\infty . \end{aligned}  \] The exceptional divisor and its image have zero measure for smooth top-degree forms, so they do not affect the equality. To see the stated distance explicitly, fix $x\in \mathbb P^1$ and let $g_ x$ be its normalized Green model, with $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ x=\delta _ x$. The models $0$ and $g_ x\circ p$ are ordinary and ideal, and the latter has a logarithmic pole of coefficient one along the smooth reduced fiber $p^{-1}(x)$. Thus both have analytic singularities. Their base polar measures are $0$ and $\delta _ x$, so their polar distance is one, although their top-degree measures vanish. $\square$
