text:
20.3 Restricted sections and trace data Let $Y\subset X$ be a connected compact complex submanifold of dimension $r\geq 1$, and suppose that the generic Lelong number $
u (u,Y)=\inf _{y\in Y}
u (u,y)$ vanishes. Recall from section 19.1 the image ideals $\mathfrak a_ m=\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y)=\mathcal I(mu)\mathcal O_ Y$ and the divisorial trace data $	au _{Y,u}(E)$ of a prime divisor $E$ on a smooth compact modification of $Y$, defined in ( 19.1 ) as the limit of $\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ m/m$. Put \[  V_ m=\operatorname {im} igl (\mathcal H_ m(u)\longrightarrow H^0(Y,L^ m|_ Y) igr ).  \] The local coefficients of a restricted section lie in $\mathfrak a_ m$, so $V_ m\subseteq H^0(Y,L^ m|_ Y\otimes \mathfrak a_ m)$; the right-hand space can contain sections that do not extend to $X$. On a modification of $Y$, the pullback of a nonzero restricted section vanishes along each prime divisor at least to the order imposed by the image ideal. Subtracting finitely many of these orders still leaves an effective divisor, which the Poincaré–Lelong formula turns into a positive current. If such sections exist in arbitrarily large degrees, normalized compactness produces a positive current in the class obtained by subtracting the trace data from the curvature class, and pairing it with a Gauduchon metric gives a degree inequality. Below, $c_1$ denotes the first Chern class in real Bott–Chern cohomology (section 23.4 ); it is represented by the curvature form of any smooth Hermitian metric. Theorem 20.3.1 . Suppose that $V_ m
eq 0$ for arbitrarily large integers $m$. Let $\pi :Z	o Y$ be any smooth compact modification, let $E_1,\ldots ,E_ q$ be distinct prime divisors on $Z$, and let $\gamma $ be a Gauduchon metric on $Z$. Then \[  \deg _\gamma (\pi ^*(L|_ Y)) \geq \sum _{i=1}^ q	au _{Y,u}(E_ i)\int _{E_ i}\gamma ^{r-1}.  \] Moreover, the real closed $(1,1)$ class \[  c_1(\pi ^*(L|_ Y))- \sum _{i=1}^ q	au _{Y,u}(E_ i)c_1(\mathcal O_ Z(E_ i))  \] is pseudoeffective: it contains a closed positive current. Proof. Choose an unbounded set of degrees $m$ and nonzero sections $s_ m\in V_ m$, and put $b_ i(m)=\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}\mathfrak a_ m$. The pullback $\pi ^*s_ m$ is nonzero, and its local coefficients belong to the pulled-back ideal $\mathfrak a_ m\mathcal O_ Z$, so it vanishes to order at least $b_ i(m)$ along $E_ i$. Thus \[  D_ m:=\operatorname {div}(\pi ^*s_ m)-\sum _{i=1}^ q b_ i(m)E_ i \geq 0.  \] Choose smooth Hermitian metrics on the line bundles $\mathcal O_ Z(E_ i)$, with curvature forms $ eta _ i$, and set \[  \Theta _ m=\pi ^*( eta |_ Y)-\sum _{i=1}^ q rac{b_ i(m)}m eta _ i, \qquad \Theta =\pi ^*( eta |_ Y)-\sum _{i=1}^ q	au _{Y,u}(E_ i) eta _ i.  \] Dividing $\pi ^*s_ m$ by the corresponding powers of the canonical sections of the bundles $\mathcal O_ Z(E_ i)$ gives a nonzero holomorphic section of $\pi ^*(L^ m|_ Y)\otimes \mathcal O_ Z(-\sum _ i b_ i(m)E_ i)$ with divisor $D_ m$. Equip this line bundle with the metric induced by $h$ and the chosen metrics. One $m$th of the logarithm of the squared norm of this section is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $w_ m$ on $Z$, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \Theta _ m+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ m= rac1m[D_ m]\geq 0.  \] By theorem 19.1.1 , $b_ i(m)/m	o 	au _{Y,u}(E_ i)$ as $m	o \infty $ through all integers, hence also along the chosen degrees, so $\Theta _ m	o \Theta $ smoothly. Consequently a single Hermitian form $\Lambda $ on $Z$ dominates all the forms $\Theta _ m$, and every $w_ m$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(Z,\Lambda )$. Normalize $\sup _ Zw_ m=0$. By theorem 1.4.2 , a subsequence converges in $L^1$, and its limit $w$ satisfies \[  \Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0.  \] Since $\Theta $ is closed and represents the class in the statement, this positive current proves the asserted pseudoeffectivity. Finally, pair this current with $\gamma ^{r-1}$, where $\gamma ^{r-1}=1$ if $r=1$. Integration by parts removes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ because $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula for the canonical section of $\mathcal O_ Z(E_ i)$ gives $\int _ Z eta _ i\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}=\int _{E_ i}\gamma ^{r-1}$. The nonnegativity of the pairing is exactly the stated degree inequality. $\square$ Equivalently, if one of these inequalities fails for some choice of $Z$, $E_1,\ldots ,E_ q$ and $\gamma $, then $V_ m=0$ for all sufficiently large $m$. The converse of the theorem fails in general. Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z)$ be the square elliptic curve, choose an irrational real number $a$, and let $L$ be the flat line bundle on $E$ with multipliers $\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm{i} a}$ and $1$ along the two generators: its sections lift to holomorphic functions $f$ on $\mathbb C$ with $f(z+1)=\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm{i} a}f(z)$ and $f(z+\mathrm{i})=f(z)$. The constant metric on $L$ has curvature zero. Take $u=0$ and $Y=X=E$. Then every trace number is zero, and the class in the theorem is zero, hence pseudoeffective. Nevertheless no positive tensor power of $L$ has a nonzero holomorphic section. Indeed, a nonzero section of $L^ m$ would have a zero divisor of degree zero and would therefore be nowhere zero. The logarithm of its norm would be harmonic on $E$, hence constant, so its lift $f$ would be a holomorphic function of constant modulus on $\mathbb C$, and thus constant. Since $ma
otin \mathbb Z$, the relation $f(z+1)=\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm{i} ma}f(z)$ then forces $f=0$, a contradiction.

title: Theorem 20.3.1
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Theorem 20.3.1 . Suppose that $V_ m\neq 0$ for arbitrarily large integers $m$. Let $\pi :Z\to Y$ be any smooth compact modification, let $E_1,\ldots ,E_ q$ be distinct prime divisors on $Z$, and let $\gamma $ be a Gauduchon metric on $Z$. Then \[  \deg _\gamma (\pi ^*(L|_ Y)) \geq \sum _{i=1}^ q\tau _{Y,u}(E_ i)\int _{E_ i}\gamma ^{r-1}.  \] Moreover, the real closed $(1,1)$ class \[  c_1(\pi ^*(L|_ Y))- \sum _{i=1}^ q\tau _{Y,u}(E_ i)c_1(\mathcal O_ Z(E_ i))  \] is pseudoeffective: it contains a closed positive current. Proof. Choose an unbounded set of degrees $m$ and nonzero sections $s_ m\in V_ m$, and put $b_ i(m)=\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}\mathfrak a_ m$. The pullback $\pi ^*s_ m$ is nonzero, and its local coefficients belong to the pulled-back ideal $\mathfrak a_ m\mathcal O_ Z$, so it vanishes to order at least $b_ i(m)$ along $E_ i$. Thus \[  D_ m:=\operatorname {div}(\pi ^*s_ m)-\sum _{i=1}^ q b_ i(m)E_ i \geq 0.  \] Choose smooth Hermitian metrics on the line bundles $\mathcal O_ Z(E_ i)$, with curvature forms $\beta _ i$, and set \[  \Theta _ m=\pi ^*(\beta |_ Y)-\sum _{i=1}^ q\frac{b_ i(m)}m\beta _ i, \qquad \Theta =\pi ^*(\beta |_ Y)-\sum _{i=1}^ q\tau _{Y,u}(E_ i)\beta _ i.  \] Dividing $\pi ^*s_ m$ by the corresponding powers of the canonical sections of the bundles $\mathcal O_ Z(E_ i)$ gives a nonzero holomorphic section of $\pi ^*(L^ m|_ Y)\otimes \mathcal O_ Z(-\sum _ i b_ i(m)E_ i)$ with divisor $D_ m$. Equip this line bundle with the metric induced by $h$ and the chosen metrics. One $m$th of the logarithm of the squared norm of this section is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $w_ m$ on $Z$, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \Theta _ m+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ m=\frac1m[D_ m]\geq 0.  \] By theorem 19.1.1 , $b_ i(m)/m\to \tau _{Y,u}(E_ i)$ as $m\to \infty $ through all integers, hence also along the chosen degrees, so $\Theta _ m\to \Theta $ smoothly. Consequently a single Hermitian form $\Lambda $ on $Z$ dominates all the forms $\Theta _ m$, and every $w_ m$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(Z,\Lambda )$. Normalize $\sup _ Zw_ m=0$. By theorem 1.4.2 , a subsequence converges in $L^1$, and its limit $w$ satisfies \[  \Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0.  \] Since $\Theta $ is closed and represents the class in the statement, this positive current proves the asserted pseudoeffectivity. Finally, pair this current with $\gamma ^{r-1}$, where $\gamma ^{r-1}=1$ if $r=1$. Integration by parts removes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ because $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula for the canonical section of $\mathcal O_ Z(E_ i)$ gives $\int _ Z\beta _ i\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}=\int _{E_ i}\gamma ^{r-1}$. The nonnegativity of the pairing is exactly the stated degree inequality. $\square$

title: 20.4 Bounded weighted sections
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: 20.4 Bounded weighted sections The spaces $\mathcal H_ m(u)$ need not be closed under multiplication: the product of two sections with integrable weighted squared norms need not have an integrable weighted squared norm, as the following logarithmic example shows. Requiring the weighted pointwise norm to be bounded rather than integrable gives spaces that do multiply. They form the graded algebra used in chapter 21 . Example 20.4.1 . Let $X=\mathbb P^1$ with affine coordinate $z$, and let $\delta _0$ be the Dirac mass at the origin. Take $L=\mathcal O(1)$ with its Fubini–Study metric, whose curvature form is $\beta $, and let \[  u(z)=\frac35\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}.  \] Then $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\frac25\beta +\frac35\delta _0\geq 0$, $\mathcal I(u)=\mathcal O$ and $\mathcal I(2u)=\mathcal O(-[0])$. A section of $L$ that does not vanish at $0$ belongs to $\mathcal H_1(u)$, but its square does not belong to $\mathcal H_2(u)$. Proof. The curvature formula follows from the Poincaré–Lelong formula $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=\delta _0$ and from $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$ on $\mathbb C$. The weight is bounded near infinity and equals $\frac35\log |z|^2+O(1)$ near zero, its only singularity. The one-variable calculation of example 1.12.5 therefore gives the two stated ideals: $\mathcal I(u)$ is trivial, while $\mathcal I(2u)$ consists of the functions vanishing at the origin. A section of $L$ with $s(0)\neq 0$ thus lies in $\mathcal H_1(u)$, whereas $s^2$ does not vanish at the origin and so does not lie in $\mathcal H_2(u)$. $\square$ We return to the general data $(X,L,h,u)$. Define $\mathcal W_0=\mathbb C$ and, for $m\geq 1$, \[  \mathcal W_ m(u)=\{ s\in H^0(X,L^ m): |s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mu}\text{ is bounded off }\{ u=-\infty \} \} .  \] These are vector spaces, since $|s+t|^2\leq 2|s|^2+2|t|^2$; they are finite-dimensional and do not depend on the smooth metric, because the ratio of two smooth metrics is bounded above and below on $X$. Since $X$ has finite volume, they are contained in $\mathcal H_ m(u)$. For positive integers $m,k$, $s\in \mathcal W_ m(u)$ and $t\in \mathcal W_ k(u)$, the identity \[  |st|_{h^{m+k}}^2\mathrm{e}^{-(m+k)u} =\bigl (|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mu}\bigr ) \bigl (|t|_{h^ k}^2\mathrm{e}^{-ku}\bigr )  \] proves $\mathcal W_ m(u)\mathcal W_ k(u)\subseteq \mathcal W_{m+k}(u)$. Thus $\bigoplus _ m\mathcal W_ m(u)$ is a graded subalgebra of the section ring $\bigoplus _{m\geq 0}H^0(X,L^ m)$ of $L$. On a smooth projective variety, for big line bundles with metrics of positive curvature current and positive multiplier-ideal volume, the almost-semigroup construction of [ Section 10.3 , SGPT ] works with the integrable section spaces themselves.

title: 20.5 Section growth on a curve
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: 20.5 Section growth on a curve On a curve, a weight with logarithmic poles imposes vanishing orders at the poles. Integrability rounds the required order down and boundedness rounds it up, so the two resulting divisors differ by a bounded amount, and Riemann–Roch gives the same leading growth for both section spaces. Throughout this section, $X$ is a compact Riemann surface and $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Let $p_1,\ldots ,p_ r$ be distinct points such that $u$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus \{ p_1,\ldots ,p_ r\} $ and, in coordinates $z_ i$ centered at $p_ i$, \[  u=c_ i\log |z_ i|^2+O(1),\qquad c_ i>0.  \] Set $\ell =\deg L=\int _ X\beta $ and $d=\sum _ i c_ i$. Recall that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\beta (u)$ denotes the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 6.1.2 . Theorem 20.5.1 . In this situation $0\leq d\leq \ell $, and \[  \begin{split}  \mathcal H_ m(u)& =H^0\left(X,L^ m\Bigl (-\sum _ i\lfloor mc_ i\rfloor p_ i\Bigr )\right),\\  \mathcal W_ m(u)& =H^0\left(X,L^ m\Bigl (-\sum _ i\lceil mc_ i\rceil p_ i\Bigr )\right). \end{split}  \] Moreover, \[  \lim _{m\to \infty }\frac{\dim \mathcal H_ m(u)}m =\lim _{m\to \infty }\frac{\dim \mathcal W_ m(u)}m =\ell -d =\int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\beta (u).  \] Proof. Step 1: the section spaces. A germ of a section of $L^ m$ vanishing to order $k$ at $p_ i$ has weighted squared norm comparable to $|z_ i|^{2(k-mc_ i)}$. As in example 1.12.5 , it is locally integrable if and only if $k-mc_ i>-1$, that is, $k\geq \lfloor mc_ i\rfloor $; it is bounded if and only if $k\geq mc_ i$, that is, $k\geq \lceil mc_ i\rceil $. Away from the points $p_ i$ the weight is locally bounded and imposes no condition. Since $X$ is compact, this gives the displayed global identifications. Step 2: the mass. The positive measure $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has total mass $\ell $, and it has an atom of mass $c_ i$ at $p_ i$. Subtracting these atoms leaves a positive measure, which proves $d\leq \ell $. This remaining measure does not charge polar sets: after subtraction of the logarithmic singularity, its local potential has a bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic representative, and by proposition 1.7.1 its curvature gives polar sets zero mass. Thus the remaining measure is exactly the extended measure, and its mass is $\ell -d$. Step 3: growth. If $\ell >d$, the degrees of both line bundles in the display equal $m(\ell -d)+O(1)$ and tend to infinity. Let $g$ be the genus of $X$. By Riemann–Roch and Serre duality, $h^0=\deg +1-g$ once the degree exceeds $2g-2$. Dividing by $m$ proves both limits. If $\ell =d$, both degrees remain bounded. A line bundle of negative degree has no nonzero section, and one of nonnegative degree $k$ has at most $k+1$ independent sections: the sections vanishing at $k+1$ given distinct points are sections of a line bundle of negative degree, hence zero. Therefore both dimensions are uniformly bounded, and both limits vanish. These arguments include the case $r=0$. $\square$

title: 20.6 Homogeneous sections on a Hopf manifold
search_title: Homogeneous sections on a Hopf manifold
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: 20.6 Homogeneous sections on a Hopf manifold On a scalar Hopf manifold, a holomorphic section of a line bundle lifts to a function on $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ with an exact homogeneity property under the contraction. Hartogs extension reduces the section spaces to spaces of homogeneous polynomials, and the invariance of the metric makes the Bergman kernel constant. The resulting growth is of order $m^{n-1}$, reflecting the dimension of the projective base rather than that of the manifold. Let $n\geq 2$, let $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ be the coordinates on $\mathbb C^ n$, and set \[  X_ n=(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-1}z\rangle .  \] On the covering space put \[  s=\log |z|^2,\qquad \alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s,\qquad \zeta =\mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s,\qquad \omega =\alpha +\zeta .  \] The contraction changes $s$ by the constant $-2$, so these forms descend to $X_ n$. The calculation proving ( 8.1 ), written in chapter 8 for $n=3$ and with $\beta $ in place of $\zeta $, applies in every dimension and gives \[  \alpha ^ n=0,\qquad \zeta ^2=0,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta =-\alpha ^2, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-1})=-(n-1)\alpha ^ n=0.  \] Thus $\omega $ is a Gauduchon form. Projectivization defines a holomorphic map $\pi :X_ n\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$ with elliptic fibers, and $\alpha $ is the pullback of the Fubini–Study form normalized to have total mass one. Since $\zeta $ restricts to twice the normalized area form on each fiber, as in the proof of proposition 8.1.1 , and $\omega ^ n=n\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta $, we obtain \[  \int _{X_ n}\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta =2, \qquad \int _{X_ n}\omega ^ n=2n.  \] Set $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n/(2n)$, a probability measure. For an integer $k\geq 0$, let $L_ k$ be the line bundle on $X_ n$ obtained from $(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} )\times \mathbb C$ through the identification \[  (z,t)\sim (\mathrm{e}^{-1}z,\mathrm{e}^{-k}t).  \] Give it the metric $|t|_{h_ k}^2=|t|^2|z|^{-2k}$. Under the identification the two factors change by $\mathrm{e}^{-2k}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{2k}$, so this metric descends. In the frame $t=1$ the squared norm is $|z|^{-2k}$, and the curvature form is $k\alpha $. We apply the constructions of section 20.1 with $X=X_ n$, $L=L_ k$, $h=h_ k$ and this probability volume form. Proposition 20.6.1 . For $m\geq 1$ and the weight $u=0$, \[  N_ m:=h^0(X_ n,L_ k^ m)=\binom {km+n-1}{n-1}, \qquad B_{m,0}=N_ m.  \] The Bergman potential is the constant $m^{-1}\log N_ m$, and the Bergman current is $k\alpha $. Moreover, \[  \deg _\omega L_ k=2k(n-1),\qquad \lim _{m\to \infty }m^{-n}N_ m=0, \qquad (k\alpha )^ n=0,  \] whereas $\int _{X_ n}\omega ^ n=2n>0$. Proof. A section of $L_ k^ m$ lifts to a holomorphic function $f$ on $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ satisfying \[  f(\mathrm{e}^{-1}z)=\mathrm{e}^{-km}f(z).  \] Since $n\geq 2$, Hartogs' theorem extends $f$ holomorphically to $\mathbb C^ n$. In its Taylor series, a monomial of total degree $j$ is multiplied by $\mathrm{e}^{-j}$ under the contraction, so comparing coefficients shows that only monomials of degree $km$ occur. Conversely, every homogeneous polynomial of that degree has the required equivariance. Counting monomials gives the binomial coefficient; when $k=0$, only the constant polynomials remain. The inner product defined by $h_ k^ m$ and $\mathrm{d}V$ is invariant under the unitary group $U(n)$, so the basis-independent function $K_{m,0}$ is $U(n)$-invariant. It is also invariant under positive radial dilations: every section is homogeneous of degree $km$, and the factor $|z|^{-2km}$ in its squared norm cancels the effect of a dilation. Unitary transformations and positive radial dilations act transitively on $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, so $K_{m,0}$ is constant. By proposition 20.1.2 its integral is $N_ m$, and $\mathrm{d}V$ has mass one. Thus $K_{m,0}=B_{m,0}=N_ m$. The statements about the Bergman potential and current follow immediately. Since $\alpha ^ n=0$ and $\zeta ^2=0$, \[  \int _{X_ n}k\alpha \wedge \omega ^{n-1} =k(n-1)\int _{X_ n}\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta =2k(n-1).  \] The binomial coefficient grows at most like $m^{n-1}$, which proves the normalized limit, and $\alpha ^ n=0$ proves the vanishing of the curvature mass. $\square$ For $n=3$, $X_3$ is the Gauduchon threefold of theorem 8.0.1 , on which Hermitian Monge–Ampère masses are unbounded; for $k>0$, the line bundles $L_ k$ nevertheless have positive degree and quadratic section growth. In the notation of example 4.6.55 , $L_ k$ is the line bundle $E_ a$ on $X_ q$ with $q=\mathrm e^{-1}$ and $a=\mathrm e^{-k}$. Hence, for every $n\geq 2$ and $k>0$, the complement $\mathbb P(\mathcal O\oplus L_ k)\setminus \mathbb P(\mathcal O)$ of 4.6.12 has least smooth convexity index two, that is, it is $2$-convex but not $1$-convex in the sense of 4.6.8 . When $k=0$, the line bundle is trivial and the least smooth convexity index of its complement is $n+1$, by the same example.

title: 20.7 Section counts and infinite Hermitian mass

text: 20.7 Section counts and infinite Hermitian mass We return to a connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$ and fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$. A weight with trivial multiplier ideals leaves every integrable section space unchanged. When $X$ fails the bounded mass property of definition 6.5.1 , theorem 6.6.1 provides such a weight $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with infinite extended mass. For the trivial line bundle with constant metric, $\mathcal H_ m(U)$ consists of constants and every Bergman current vanishes. Thus section growth in a closed curvature class does not determine the mass in an unrelated Hermitian background. Proposition 20.7.1 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian metric on $X$ with $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. There is a potential $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ such that, with $L=\mathcal O_ X$ and its constant metric, \[  \dim \mathcal H_ m(U)=1\quad \hbox{for every }m\geq 1, \qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)=+\infty .  \] All Bergman currents of $U$ are identically zero. Proof. Take $U$ from theorem 6.6.1 ; its extended mass is infinite, and $\mathcal I(tU)=\mathcal O_ X$ for every $t>0$. Global holomorphic functions on $X$ are constant, and the constant function $1$ lies in $\mathcal H_ m(U)$ because $\mathcal I(mU)=\mathcal O_ X$ and $X$ is compact. Hence every weighted section space is one-dimensional, and its orthonormal basis consists of a nonzero constant. Each Bergman potential $\Phi _ m$ is therefore constant. Since the trivial metric has curvature zero, every Bergman current is zero. $\square$

section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: 21 Flags, convex bodies and section growth Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n$, and let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$. Along a complete flag of compact complex submanifolds, successive vanishing orders turn each section of $L^ m$ into a lattice point, and the Gauduchon degree bounds of chapter 20 keep the normalized points in a compact convex body. For a graded algebra of sections with some nonzero piece of positive degree, counting these points gives the growth exponent and the leading coefficient of its graded pieces: the exponent is the transcendence degree of the field of section ratios, and the coefficient is an intrinsic lattice volume of the body. A smooth metric on $L$ supplies an additional bound: its maximal curvature rank on the semipositive locus bounds the growth dimension, even if its curvature has no global sign. Not every compact complex manifold carries such a flag, but the blowup of a point does, and Hartogs extension identifies the sections on the blowup with those on $X$; the count therefore applies to every compact complex manifold. Growth of the maximal order $m^ n$ forces $X$ to admit a modification from a projective manifold, and hence to have the bounded mass property. On the Hopf threefold, where Hermitian masses are unbounded, positive-degree line bundles still have bodies that are triangles: their area detects quadratic section growth, although their three-dimensional volume vanishes.

title: 21.1 Flag valuations and degree bounds

section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text:
21.1 Flag valuations and degree bounds Successive vanishing orders along a flag compute the lexicographically smallest exponent in a local Taylor expansion. The coefficient of that exponent is a linear functional on sections, and this shows that the number of distinct values on a space of sections equals its dimension. At each step, the effective divisor that remains gives, through a Gauduchon degree, a linear bound for the next order. Until section 21.5 , suppose that $X$ carries a complete flag , that is, a chain \[  X=Y_0\supset Y_1\supset \cdots \supset Y_ n=\{ p\} ,  \] where $p$ is a point and each $Y_ i$, $1\leq i\leq n$, is a smooth connected compact prime divisor in $Y_{i-1}$. For a nonnegative integer $m$ and a nonzero section $s\in H^0(X,L^ m)$, let $

21.2 The body of a graded section algebra The valuations of the nonzero homogeneous elements of a graded algebra of sections form a semigroup whose part in degree $m$ has exactly as many elements as the dimension of the degree-$m$ piece. The linear bound of theorem 21.1.2 places this semigroup in a cone with compact height-one slice, and a semigroup counting theorem relates the asymptotic count to the volume of this slice. Let $W_ ullet = igoplus _{m\geq 0}W_ m$ be a graded subalgebra of the section ring $ igoplus _{m\geq 0}H^0(X,L^ m)$, with $W_0=\mathbb C$. For a weight $u\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, the bounded weighted section algebra $\mathcal W_ ullet (u)$ of section 20.4 is an example. Set \[  S=\{ (0,0)\} \cup \{ (
u (s),m):m\geq 1,\  0
eq s\in W_ m\} .  \] This is an additive semigroup, because the product of two nonzero sections on the connected manifold $X$ is nonzero and valuations add. Choose constants $C_ i$ as in theorem 21.1.2 . Then $S$ lies in the closed cone \[  \{ (x,t)\in \mathbb R^ n	imes \mathbb R:t\geq 0,\  0\leq x_ i\leq C_ i t\} ,  \] whose only point at height zero is the origin. Define \[  \Delta (W_ ullet )= \overline{\operatorname {conv}} \{ m^{-1}
u (s):m\geq 1,\  0
eq s\in W_ m\} ,  \] where $\overline{\operatorname {conv}}$ denotes the closed convex hull. If some positive-degree piece of $W_ ullet $ is nonzero, this is a compact convex subset of $\mathbb R^ n$; equivalently, it is the height-one slice of the closed convex cone generated by $S$. If every positive-degree piece is zero, $\Delta (W_ ullet )=\varnothing $. Write $\operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ n}$ for Euclidean volume. Proposition 21.2.1 . For every such algebra, \[  \limsup _{m	o \infty }m^{-n}\dim W_ m \leq \operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ n}\Delta (W_ ullet ).  \] In particular, if $\Delta (W_ ullet )$ has empty interior, then $\dim W_ m=o(m^ n)$. Proof. The empty case is immediate. Otherwise, let $S_ m=\{ 
u (s):0
eq s\in W_ m\} $. By lemma 21.1.1 , $S_ m$ has $\dim W_ m$ elements, and $m^{-1}S_ m\subseteq \Delta (W_ ullet )$. Attach to each $a\in S_ m$ the half-open cube $m^{-1}(a+[0,1)^ n)$. These cubes are disjoint, their total volume is $m^{-n}\dim W_ m$, and their union is contained in \[  \Delta (W_ ullet )+[0,m^{-1}]^ n.  \] These compact neighborhoods decrease to $\Delta (W_ ullet )$ as $m	o \infty $, so their volumes converge to its volume. This proves the inequality. A compact convex set has positive $n$-dimensional volume exactly when it has nonempty interior, which gives the last statement. $\square$ We use the following semigroup counting theorem, recalled in [ Theorem C.2.1 , SGPT ] . Let $r\geq 0$, and let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb Z^{r+1}$ be an additive semigroup that generates $\mathbb Z^{r+1}$ as a group and lies in a closed convex cone in $\mathbb R^ r	imes \mathbb R_{\geq 0}$ whose height-one slice is compact and whose only point at height zero is the origin. Then the number of points of $\Sigma $ at height $m$, divided by $m^ r$, converges to the Euclidean volume of the height-one slice of the closed convex cone generated by $\Sigma $. Corollary 21.2.2 . If the subgroup generated by $S$ is all of $\mathbb Z^{n+1}$, then \[  \lim _{m	o \infty }m^{-n}\dim W_ m =\operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ n}\Delta (W_ ullet ).  \] Proof. The semigroup $S$ satisfies the cone conditions established above and, by hypothesis, generates $\mathbb Z^{n+1}$. The semigroup counting theorem therefore applies to it. By lemma 21.1.1 , the number of points of $S$ at height $m$ is $\dim W_ m$, and the height-one slice of the closed convex cone generated by $S$ is $\Delta (W_ ullet )$. $\square$

21.3 Intrinsic dimension, lattice and growth A body of zero volume in $\mathbb R^ n$ can still detect growth of lower order. The group generated by the valuation semigroup determines a degree period and a lattice in which the body is full-dimensional, and counting in this lattice gives the growth exponent and the leading coefficient. Ratios of sections identify the exponent with a transcendence degree, and since the coefficient is a limit of graded dimensions, it does not depend on the flag. Throughout this section, some positive-degree piece of $W_ ullet $ is nonzero. Let $G\subset \mathbb Z^{n+1}$ be the subgroup generated by $S$, and let $\operatorname {pr}_{n+1}$ be the projection to the last coordinate. Define the degree period $e\geq 1$ by \[  \operatorname {pr}_{n+1}(G)=e\mathbb Z.  \] Thus $e$ is the greatest common divisor of the degrees $m$ with $W_ m
eq 0$. Set \[  \Lambda =G\cap (\mathbb R^ n	imes \{ 0\} ), \qquad d=\operatorname {rank}\Lambda .  \] We regard $\Lambda $ as a lattice in its real span, a $d$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb R^ n	imes \{ 0\} $. Its lattice measure assigns volume one to a fundamental parallelepiped. On each translate of this span we use the translated measure, denoted by $\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda $; when $d=0$, a point has volume one. Theorem 21.3.1 . The affine dimension of $\Delta (W_ ullet )$ is $d$. Its lattice volume is finite and strictly positive, and \[  \lim _{q	o \infty } rac{\dim W_{eq}}{(eq)^ d} =\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda \Delta (W_ ullet ).  \] If $e$ does not divide $m$, then $W_ m=0$. In particular, $W_ m
eq 0$ for all sufficiently large multiples $m$ of $e$. Proof. Choose $g_0=(b,e)\in G$ and an integral basis $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ d$ of $\Lambda $. Every element of $G$ has a unique expression \[  \sum _{i=1}^ d a_ i\lambda _ i+qg_0, \qquad (a,q)\in \mathbb Z^ d	imes \mathbb Z.  \] These coordinates identify $G$ with $\mathbb Z^{d+1}$. Let $S'$ be the image of $S$ under this identification. It generates $\mathbb Z^{d+1}$, and the height of the image of $(x,m)\in S$ is $q=m/e\geq 0$. The points $(m^{-1}x,1)$, for $(x,m)\in S$ with $m>0$, span the $(d+1)$-dimensional real vector space $\operatorname {span}_{\mathbb R}G$. Since they all have height one, their affine span has dimension $d$. Taking the convex hull and the closure does not change this affine span, which proves the dimension assertion. Intersect the cone containing $S$ with $\operatorname {span}_{\mathbb R}G$. The linear change of coordinates carries this intersection to a closed cone with compact height-one slice whose only point at height zero is the origin. Indeed, a vector $(x,m)$ with $|x|\leq Cm$ has horizontal coordinates bounded by a constant times $m$, hence by a constant times $q$. The height-one body of $S'$ is \[  \Delta '=e igl (\Delta (W_ ullet )-b/e igr ),  \] where the right-hand side is expressed in the basis $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ d$. It is full-dimensional in $\mathbb R^ d$, and therefore \[  \operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ d}\Delta ' =e^ d\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda \Delta (W_ ullet )>0.  \] Apply the semigroup counting theorem of section 21.2 to $S'$, which generates its full lattice. The points of $S'$ at height $q$ correspond bijectively to the valuations of the nonzero elements of $W_{eq}$, and by lemma 21.1.1 there are $\dim W_{eq}$ of them. Hence \[  \lim _{q	o \infty } rac{\dim W_{eq}}{q^ d} =\operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ d}\Delta '.  \] Dividing by $e^ d$ gives the asserted limit, and its positivity gives eventual nonvanishing. For $d=0$ the body is a point of volume one, so the integer dimensions converge to one and are eventually equal to one. Finally, every degree with a nonzero section lies in the projection $e\mathbb Z$ of $G$, which proves the vanishing outside these multiples. $\square$ The growth dimension also has a description independent of the flag. Write $\mathcal M(X)$ for the field of meromorphic functions on $X$ and define the section-ratio field \[  K(W_ ullet )=\{ s/t:s,t\in W_ m	ext{ for some }m\geq 0, \  t
eq 0\} \subset \mathcal M(X).  \] It is a field: sums and products of two such ratios, with denominators $t_1\in W_{m_1}$ and $t_2\in W_{m_2}$, can be written with the common denominator $t_1t_2$ in degree $m_1+m_2$, and inversion exchanges numerator and denominator. It contains $\mathbb C$ because $W_0=\mathbb C$. Proposition 21.3.2 . The transcendence degree of $K(W_ ullet )$ over $\mathbb C$ is exactly $d$. If $\Delta (W_ ullet )$ has nonempty interior in $\mathbb R^ n$, then $X$ has $n$ algebraically independent meromorphic functions. Moreover, $d$, the period $e$ and the intrinsic volume in theorem 21.3.1 are the same for any two complete flags on $X$. Proof. Suppose first that $d>0$. Choose sections $s_0,\ldots ,s_ d$ of positive degrees $m_0,\ldots ,m_ d$ whose normalized valuations $
u (s_ i)/m_ i$ are affinely independent. Let $M$ be a common multiple of their degrees and put $t_ i=s_ i^{M/m_ i}\in W_ M$. The ratios $f_ i=t_ i/t_0$ belong to $K(W_ ullet )$. The flag valuation extends to quotients by subtraction, giving \[  
u (f_ i)=M\left( rac{
u (s_ i)}{m_ i} - rac{
u (s_0)}{m_0}ight), \qquad 1\leq i\leq d.  \] These vectors are linearly independent. Distinct monomials in the $f_ i$ therefore have distinct valuations, so the term of smallest valuation in a nonzero polynomial expression cannot cancel, and the ratios are algebraically independent. Thus the transcendence degree is at least $d$; this is trivial when $d=0$. Conversely, let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$, with $r\geq 1$, be algebraically independent elements of the field. Using the product of their denominators, write $f_ i=A_ i/B$ with $A_ i,B\in W_ M$ and $B
eq 0$ for a common positive degree $M$. For every integer $q\geq 1$ and every multi-index $a=(a_1,\ldots ,a_ r)\in \mathbb N^ r$ with $|a|=a_1+\cdots +a_ r\leq q$, the sections \[  B^{q-|a|}A_1^{a_1}\cdots A_ r^{a_ r}\in W_{Mq}  \] are linearly independent, because division by $B^ q$ turns a linear relation among them into a polynomial relation among the $f_ i$. There are $ inom {q+r}{r}$ such sections. Since $W_ M
eq 0$, the degree $M$ is a multiple of $e$, and theorem 21.3.1 gives $\dim W_{Mq}=O(q^ d)$. Comparing with the binomial lower bound forces $r\leq d$, which proves equality of the transcendence degree with $d$. A body with nonempty interior has $d=n$, and this gives the stated consequence for $X$. The field and the set of degrees with nonzero sections do not depend on the flag, so neither $d$ nor $e$ does. By theorem 21.3.1 , the lattice volume is, for either flag, the limit of the same dimensions with the same normalization. It is therefore independent of the flag as well, although the bodies and their lattices may differ. $\square$

title: 21.4 Moishezon manifolds and bounded mass
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: 21.4 Moishezon manifolds and bounded mass A compact complex manifold of dimension $n$ is Moishezon if it has $n$ algebraically independent meromorphic functions. By Moishezon's theorem, a compact irreducible complex space of dimension $n$ with $n$ algebraically independent meromorphic functions admits a modification from a smooth projective manifold; the source of this form of the theorem is given in section 34.14 . Such a modification bounds the masses of Hermitian potentials on $X$: the pulled-back Hermitian form is dominated by a fixed Kähler form, whose Monge–Ampère mass does not change when a smooth potential is added. Recall that $X$ has the bounded mass property if the masses $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ of bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $v$ are uniformly bounded for one, equivalently every, Hermitian form $\omega $ (definition 6.5.1 , proposition 6.5.2 ). Lemma 21.4.1 . If a compact complex manifold $X$ admits a modification $\pi :Z\to X$ from a compact Kähler manifold, then $X$ has the bounded mass property. Proof. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$ and a Kähler form $\kappa $ on $Z$, and choose $C>0$ with $\pi ^*\omega \leq C\kappa $. By proposition 6.5.2 , it suffices to bound the masses of smooth functions $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Their pullbacks satisfy \[  0\leq \pi ^*\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ) \leq C\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ).  \] Taking top powers and integrating gives \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n & =\int _ Z(\pi ^*\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ))^ n\\ & \leq \int _ Z(C\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ))^ n =C^ n\int _ Z\kappa ^ n. \end{split}  \] The first equality follows by change of variables on the set where $\pi $ is biholomorphic, since smooth top-degree forms give the exceptional analytic sets zero mass. The inequality follows by expanding in the smooth semipositive difference $C\kappa -\pi ^*\omega $, and the last equality follows from Stokes' theorem because $\kappa $ is closed. The bound does not depend on $u$, which proves the bounded mass property. $\square$ Theorem 21.4.2 . If $X$ fails the bounded mass property, then for every complete flag on $X$, every holomorphic line bundle $L$ and every graded subalgebra $W_\bullet $ of its section ring as above, \[  \operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ n}\Delta (W_\bullet )=0, \qquad \dim W_ m=o(m^ n).  \] Proof. title: 21.5 Flags on a point blowup
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text:
21.5 Flags on a point blowup We now remove the assumption that $X$ carries a complete flag. A curve always does, since any point completes the flag. In dimension at least two, the exceptional divisor of the blowup of a point is a projective space and carries a complete flag of linear subspaces, while Hartogs extension identifies the sections on the blowup with those on $X$. The growth formula on the blowup therefore counts the original section spaces. Lemma 21.5.1 . Every connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n\geq 1$ admits a smooth compact modification $\pi :\widetilde X	o X$ such that $\widetilde X$ carries a complete flag and, for every holomorphic line bundle $L$ on $X$ and every $m\geq 0$, pullback is an isomorphism \[  H^0(X,L^ m)\simeq H^0(\widetilde X,\pi ^*L^ m).  \] These isomorphisms are compatible with products. Proof. If $n=1$, take $\pi $ to be the identity and any point as the last member of the flag; the remaining assertions are then immediate. If $n\geq 2$, blow up a point $p\in X$. The local description of the blowup of $\mathbb C^ n$ at the origin shows that $\widetilde X$ is smooth and that its exceptional divisor is $E\simeq \mathbb P^{n-1}$. A nested sequence of linear subspaces of $E$, together with $\widetilde X$, gives a flag \[  \widetilde X\supset E\supset \mathbb P^{n-2} \supset \cdots \supset \mathbb P^0.  \] Each member is smooth, compact and connected, and is a prime divisor in the preceding member. The modification is an isomorphism off $E$. Let $s$ be a section of $\pi ^*L^ m$. Off $E$, it gives a section of $L^ m$ on $X\setminus \{ p\} $. In a trivialization of $L^ m$ on a coordinate ball centered at $p$, its coefficient is holomorphic on the punctured ball, and by Hartogs' extension theorem, valid since $n\geq 2$, it extends holomorphically across $p$. The extension glues with the section away from $p$ to a section of $L^ m$ on $X$. Its pullback agrees with $s$ off $E$, hence everywhere by the identity theorem. This proves surjectivity; injectivity and compatibility with products follow because pullback is an isomorphism on the dense open set $\widetilde X\setminus E$. $\square$ Given a graded subalgebra $W_ ullet $ of the section ring of $L$, choose a complete flag on the modification of lemma 21.5.1 and apply the constructions of section 21.2 on $\widetilde X$ to the pulled-back algebra $\widetilde W_ m=\pi ^*W_ m\subseteq H^0(\widetilde X,\pi ^*L^ m)$. The shape of the resulting body may depend on the point and on the flag, but its dimension and its normalized count are determined by $W_ ullet $. Theorem 21.5.2 . Assume that some positive-degree piece of $W_ ullet $ is nonzero. There are an integer $0\leq d\leq n$, a degree period $e\geq 1$, and a number $V(W_ ullet )>0$ such that \[  \lim _{q	o \infty } rac{\dim W_{eq}}{(eq)^ d}=V(W_ ullet ), \qquad W_ m=0\quad \hbox{if }e
mid m.  \] Here $d$ is the transcendence degree of the section-ratio field $K(W_ ullet )$, $e$ is the greatest common divisor of the degrees $m$ with $W_ m
eq 0$, and $V(W_ ullet )$ is the intrinsic lattice volume of every body constructed on such a modification. In particular, these three quantities do not depend on the choice of the modification or the flag. Proof. Pullback preserves the graded dimensions and the degrees with nonzero sections. Applying theorem 21.1.2 , theorem 21.3.1 on $\widetilde X$ gives the displayed limit and the positivity of the lattice volume. Pullback also identifies the section-ratio fields, since their elements are the corresponding ratios and pullback is injective on the dense set where $\pi $ is an isomorphism. Thus proposition 21.3.2 identifies $d$ with the transcendence degree of the original field. The unchanged degrees with nonzero sections determine $e$, and the limit of the unchanged dimensions determines $V(W_ ullet )$. None of the three depends on the auxiliary choices. $\square$ Corollary 21.5.3 . For every holomorphic line bundle $L$ on a connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$, \[  h^0(X,L^ m)=O(m^ n).  \] If $X$ is not Moishezon, then, for each $L$, either all positive-degree section spaces of $L$ vanish, or there is an integer $d<n$ for which \[  h^0(X,L^ m)=O(m^ d).  \] In particular $m^{-n}h^0(X,L^ m)	o 0$. Otherwise, apply the theorem to the full section ring. Since $W_ m=0$ for $e
mid m$, the limit gives $h^0(X,L^ m)=O(m^ d)$ for all degrees, with $d\leq n$. title: 21.6 Curvature rank and section growth
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text:
21.6 Curvature rank and section growth The dimension of a section-ratio field can be bounded by a smooth curvature form, even when that form changes rank and has no global sign. The key is to arrange that a maximum of a section norm occurs where the section map has its maximal rank. This gives a pointwise restriction on the growth counted by the preceding sections. Keep the connected compact complex manifold $X$ and line bundle $L$, and choose a smooth Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$. In a local frame write $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm e^{-\chi }$ and put $ eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $, with the normalization of section 20.1 . Let $r=\max _ X\operatorname {rank} eta $. No positivity of $ eta $, constant-rank condition or Kähler metric is assumed. Set $S_ h=\{ x: eta _ x\geq 0\} $; when $S_ h$ is nonempty, let $r_ h^+=\max _{S_ h}\operatorname {rank} eta $. Proposition 21.6.1 . For a nonzero subspace $W\subset H^0(X,L^ p)$, $p\geq 1$, let $B_ W$ be its common zero set and let $\Phi _ W:X\setminus B_ W	o \mathbb P(W^*)$ be its section map. If $d$ is the maximal rank of its differential, there is $x_*
otin B_ W$ such that \[  \operatorname {rank}\mathrm d\Phi _ W|_{x_*}=d, \qquad  eta _{x_*}\geq 0, \qquad \operatorname {rank} eta _{x_*}\geq d.  \] Proof. Choose a basis $s_0,\ldots ,s_ N$ of $W$. Principalizing the ideal of their local coefficients gives a smooth compact modification $\pi :Y	o X$, isomorphic over $X\setminus B_ W$, and an effective divisor $D$ with \[  \pi ^*s_ j=s_ Dv_ j,\qquad v_ j\in H^0(Y,\pi ^*L^ p(-D)),  \] where the $v_ j$ have no common zero. The resolved map $f=[v_0:\cdots :v_ N]:Y	o \mathbb P^ N$ has maximal differential rank $d$, since it agrees with $\Phi _ W\circ \pi $ on a dense open set. The critical set $C=\{ y:\operatorname {rank}\mathrm df_ y<d\} $ is analytic. Proper mapping and the image-dimension theorem imply that $Z=f(Y)$ and $T=f(C)$ are compact analytic sets, with $\dim Z=d$ and $\dim T\leq d-1$ when $T$ is nonempty. For the last inequality apply the rank bound to the smooth locus of every irreducible component of $C$. By Chow's theorem $T$ is algebraic. Choose a homogeneous polynomial $P$ of degree $a\geq 1$ that vanishes on $T$ and does not vanish identically on $Z$. If $T$ is empty, take $P=1$ and $a=0$, which also covers $d=0$. Then $\sigma =P(s_0,\ldots ,s_ N)$ is a nonzero section of $L^{pa}$. Indeed, the set where $P(v_0,\ldots ,v_ N)
e 0$ meets the dense locus where $\pi $ is an isomorphism. The smooth function \[  \Psi =\sum _ j|\sigma s_ j|_{h^{p(a+1)}}^2  \] has a positive maximum $x_*$. At that point $\sigma 
e 0$ and some $s_ j
e 0$, so $x_*
otin B_ W$ and its lift is outside $C$. The tuples $(\sigma s_ j)$ and $(s_ j)$ define the same projective map near $x_*$. For $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|w|^2)$ in an affine chart, the Hessian test gives \[  0\geq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \Psi |_{x_*} =\Phi _ W^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}|_{x_*} -p(a+1) eta _{x_*}.  \] The first form on the right is semipositive of rank $d$. Thus $ eta _{x_*}$ is semipositive and its kernel is contained in the kernel of that form, proving the assertion. The polynomial degree may depend on $p$ and $W$; no bound on it is needed. $\square$ For the complete section ring with a nonzero positive-degree piece, denote its section-ratio transcendence degree by $\kappa (L)$, the Kodaira–Iitaka dimension ; put $\kappa (L)=-\infty $ when all positive powers have no sections. Corollary 21.6.2 . If $S_ h$ is empty, then $H^0(X,L^ p)=0$ for every $p\geq 1$. Otherwise \[  \kappa (L)\leq r_ h^+\leq r, \qquad h^0(X,L^ p)=O(p^{r_ h^+}).  \] In this second case, every graded section algebra with a nonzero positive-degree piece has growth dimension at most $r_ h^+$, as do all its flag bodies, including those constructed on a point blowup. For every fixed weight $u\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, the integrable spaces satisfy $\dim \mathcal H_ p(u)=O(p^{r_ h^+})$. Proof. The proposition applied to a single section excludes every positive power if $S_ h$ is empty. If all positive-degree section spaces vanish, the remaining section bounds are immediate and $\kappa (L)=-\infty $. Otherwise, suppose a graded algebra has a nonzero positive-degree piece. Write any finitely many algebraically independent elements of its ratio field with a common denominator in one positive degree, as in proposition 21.3.2 . They are coordinate ratios of a section map. Its resolved image is projective algebraic by proper mapping and Chow's theorem; its dimension is therefore at least their number. The proposition bounds this dimension by $r_ h^+$, so the field's transcendence degree is at most $r_ h^+$. Apply theorem 21.5.2 to this algebra and to the full section ring. The degree-period formula gives the growth bound in every degree, including the zero spaces outside the period. The earlier flag identification gives the body dimensions. Finally, $\mathcal H_ p(u)\subseteq H^0(X,L^ p)$, so the same upper bound holds even though the integrable spaces need not form a graded algebra. $\square$ Lemma 21.6.3 . For every fixed holomorphic line bundle $A$ on $X$, \[  h^0(X,L^ p\otimes A)=O(p^ r).  \] Proof. Induct on the dimension, simultaneously for all compact complex manifolds and all integer upper bounds on curvature rank. Dimension zero is immediate. If all these section spaces vanish, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise fix a nonzero section in degree $a\geq 1$ and resolve its zero divisor on a smooth compact modification $\mu :Y	o X$. With $M=\mu ^*L$, the pulled-back twist is $M^{-a}(D)$ for a fixed effective divisor $D$ whose components are smooth. Pullback is injective on sections, and the pulled-back curvature has rank at most $r$. Write $D=H_1+\cdots +H_ s$, allowing repeated components, and put $D_ j=H_1+\cdots +H_ j$. For $m=p-a>0$, the divisor sequences give \[  h^0(Y,M^ m(D)) \leq h^0(Y,M^ m)+\sum _{j=1}^ s h^0 igl (H_ j,(M|_{H_ j})^ m\otimes \mathcal O_ Y(D_ j)|_{H_ j} igr ).  \] The first term is $O(m^ r)$ by the preceding corollary; every other term is $O(m^ r)$ by induction, since curvature rank cannot increase on restriction. The number of terms and their twists are fixed. Absorb the finitely many $p\leq a$ in the constant. On disconnected manifolds apply this argument componentwise; this also makes the induction valid for disconnected divisor components. $\square$ Corollary 21.6.4 . For every fixed holomorphic vector bundle $E$ on $X$, \[  h^0(X,L^ p\otimes E)=O(p^ r), \qquad h^ n(X,L^ p\otimes E)=O(p^ r).  \] Proof. For $E$ of positive rank, let $\pi :Y=\mathbb P(E^*)	o X$ parametrize lines, and let $\mathcal O_ Y(1)$ be dual tautological. Fiberwise linear forms give $\pi _*\mathcal O_ Y(1)=E$, hence \[  H^0(X,L^ p\otimes E) =H^0(Y,(\pi ^*L)^ p\otimes \mathcal O_ Y(1)).  \] The pulled-back curvature has rank at most $r$, so the fixed-line-twist lemma, proved in all dimensions, gives the first bound. Serre duality identifies the dual of the top cohomology with \[  H^0(X,(L^*)^ p\otimes E^*\otimes K_ X).  \] The dual curvature is $- eta $ and has the same rank; apply the degree-zero bound to $L^*$. A bundle of rank zero has zero cohomology and satisfies both bounds. $\square$ Proposition 21.6.5 . For every fixed holomorphic vector bundle $E$, the Euler characteristic $\chi (X,L^ p\otimes E)$ is a polynomial in $p$ of degree at most $r$. Proof. The analytic Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem gives \[  \chi (X,L^ p\otimes E) =\int _ X\mathrm e^{p eta }\operatorname {ch}(E) \operatorname {td}(T^{1,0}X) =\sum _{j=0}^{r} rac{p^ j}{j!} \int _ X eta ^ j\wedge \operatorname {ch}(E) \wedge \operatorname {td}(T^{1,0}X).  \] Here the integral selects real degree $2n$, and the Chern character and Todd forms are computed with fixed Hermitian metrics. The curvature normalization represents $c_1(L)$, and $ eta ^{r+1}=0$ pointwise by its rank bound. Every coefficient is independent of $p$. $\square$ Corollary 21.6.6 . If $\dim X=2$, then $h^ q(X,L^ p\otimes E)=O(p^ r)$ for every fixed holomorphic vector bundle $E$ and $0\leq q\leq 2$. Proof. The endpoints have already been bounded. Since $\chi =h^0-h^1+h^2$, the middle dimension is at most $h^0+h^2+|\chi |=O(p^ r)$ by the Euler polynomial. $\square$ Example 21.6.7 . Let $0\leq r\leq n$, let $Y$ be any connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n-r$, and take $X=\mathbb P^ r	imes Y$ and $L=\operatorname {pr}_1^*\mathcal O(1)$ with the pulled-back Fubini–Study metric. Its curvature has rank $r$, and \[  h^0(X,L^ p)= inom {p+r}{r}.  \] Thus the section-growth exponent cannot be reduced, including when $Y$ is non-Kähler. Proof. A section, expressed in a line-bundle frame on the projective factor, is a holomorphic function of $Y$ and hence is constant there. Restriction to any slice $\mathbb P^ r	imes \{ y_0\} $ is therefore inverse to pullback on sections. Counting degree-$p$ homogeneous monomials in $r+1$ variables gives the formula; for $r=0$ it equals one. $\square$ These bounds concern the closed curvature of a line bundle. They do not estimate the mass of a potential in an unrelated nonclosed Hermitian background, as proposition 20.7.1 shows. In dimension at least three, the endpoint bounds and the Euler polynomial alone do not control the individual intermediate cohomology dimensions. The Hopf body computed next realizes the rank bound $n-1$ for the pulled-back positive line bundles of proposition 21.7.1 .

Finally, $\mathcal H_ p(u)\subseteq H^0(X,L^ p)$, so the same upper bound holds even though the integrable spaces need not form a graded algebra. $\square$

title: Lemma 21.6.3
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: Lemma 21.6.3 . For every fixed holomorphic line bundle $A$ on $X$, \[  h^0(X,L^ p\otimes A)=O(p^ r).  \] Proof. Induct on the dimension, simultaneously for all compact complex manifolds and all integer upper bounds on curvature rank. Dimension zero is immediate. If all these section spaces vanish, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise fix a nonzero section in degree $a\geq 1$ and resolve its zero divisor on a smooth compact modification $\mu :Y\to X$. With $M=\mu ^*L$, the pulled-back twist is $M^{-a}(D)$ for a fixed effective divisor $D$ whose components are smooth. Pullback is injective on sections, and the pulled-back curvature has rank at most $r$. Write $D=H_1+\cdots +H_ s$, allowing repeated components, and put $D_ j=H_1+\cdots +H_ j$. For $m=p-a>0$, the divisor sequences give \[  h^0(Y,M^ m(D)) \leq h^0(Y,M^ m)+\sum _{j=1}^ s h^0\bigl (H_ j,(M|_{H_ j})^ m\otimes \mathcal O_ Y(D_ j)|_{H_ j}\bigr ).  \] The first term is $O(m^ r)$ by the preceding corollary; every other term is $O(m^ r)$ by induction, since curvature rank cannot increase on restriction. The number of terms and their twists are fixed. Absorb the finitely many $p\leq a$ in the constant. On disconnected manifolds apply this argument componentwise; this also makes the induction valid for disconnected divisor components. $\square$

title: Corollary 21.6.4
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: Corollary 21.6.4 . For every fixed holomorphic vector bundle $E$ on $X$, \[  h^0(X,L^ p\otimes E)=O(p^ r), \qquad h^ n(X,L^ p\otimes E)=O(p^ r).  \] Proof. For $E$ of positive rank, let $\pi :Y=\mathbb P(E^*)\to X$ parametrize lines, and let $\mathcal O_ Y(1)$ be dual tautological. Fiberwise linear forms give $\pi _*\mathcal O_ Y(1)=E$, hence \[  H^0(X,L^ p\otimes E) =H^0(Y,(\pi ^*L)^ p\otimes \mathcal O_ Y(1)).  \] The pulled-back curvature has rank at most $r$, so the fixed-line-twist lemma, proved in all dimensions, gives the first bound. Serre duality identifies the dual of the top cohomology with \[  H^0(X,(L^*)^ p\otimes E^*\otimes K_ X).  \] The dual curvature is $-\beta $ and has the same rank; apply the degree-zero bound to $L^*$. A bundle of rank zero has zero cohomology and satisfies both bounds. $\square$

title: Proposition 21.6.5
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: Proposition 21.6.5 . For every fixed holomorphic vector bundle $E$, the Euler characteristic $\chi (X,L^ p\otimes E)$ is a polynomial in $p$ of degree at most $r$. Proof. The analytic Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem gives \[  \chi (X,L^ p\otimes E) =\int _ X\mathrm e^{p\beta }\operatorname {ch}(E) \operatorname {td}(T^{1,0}X) =\sum _{j=0}^{r}\frac{p^ j}{j!} \int _ X\beta ^ j\wedge \operatorname {ch}(E) \wedge \operatorname {td}(T^{1,0}X).  \] Here the integral selects real degree $2n$, and the Chern character and Todd forms are computed with fixed Hermitian metrics. The curvature normalization represents $c_1(L)$, and $\beta ^{r+1}=0$ pointwise by its rank bound. Every coefficient is independent of $p$. $\square$

title: Corollary 21.6.6
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: Corollary 21.6.6 . If $\dim X=2$, then $h^ q(X,L^ p\otimes E)=O(p^ r)$ for every fixed holomorphic vector bundle $E$ and $0\leq q\leq 2$. Proof. The endpoints have already been bounded. Since $\chi =h^0-h^1+h^2$, the middle dimension is at most $h^0+h^2+|\chi |=O(p^ r)$ by the Euler polynomial. $\square$

title: Example 21.6.7
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: Example 21.6.7 . Let $0\leq r\leq n$, let $Y$ be any connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n-r$, and take $X=\mathbb P^ r\times Y$ and $L=\operatorname {pr}_1^*\mathcal O(1)$ with the pulled-back Fubini–Study metric. Its curvature has rank $r$, and \[  h^0(X,L^ p)=\binom {p+r}{r}.  \] Thus the section-growth exponent cannot be reduced, including when $Y$ is non-Kähler. Proof. A section, expressed in a line-bundle frame on the projective factor, is a holomorphic function of $Y$ and hence is constant there. Restriction to any slice $\mathbb P^ r\times \{ y_0\} $ is therefore inverse to pullback on sections. Counting degree-$p$ homogeneous monomials in $r+1$ variables gives the formula; for $r=0$ it equals one. $\square$

title: 21.7 The Hopf flag and its lower-dimensional body
search_title: The Hopf flag and its lower-dimensional body
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 16.4 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: 21.7 The Hopf flag and its lower-dimensional body On a scalar Hopf manifold, the coordinate subspaces give a complete flag ending at a point of an elliptic fiber. Along this flag, a homogeneous section reduces to a nowhere-vanishing section on the elliptic fiber, so the last coordinate of its valuation is zero; the remaining coordinates fill a simplex whose intrinsic volume gives the section growth. Let $X_ n$ and $L_ k$, with $n\geq 2$ and $k\geq 0$, be as in section 20.6 . In the covering coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ n$, the image of $\{ z_1=\cdots =z_{n-1}=0\} \setminus \{ 0\} $ in $X_ n$ is an elliptic curve; choose a point $p$ on it. Consider the flag $Y_0=X_ n$, \[  Y_ i=\{ z_1=\cdots =z_ i=0\} /\langle \mathrm{e}^{-1}\rangle \quad (1\leq i\leq n-1),\qquad Y_ n=\{ p\} \subset Y_{n-1},  \] where $/\langle \mathrm e^{-1}\rangle $ denotes the quotient of the punctured linear subspace by the contraction $z\mapsto \mathrm e^{-1}z$. Each member is smooth, compact and connected, and is a prime divisor in the preceding member. Take $W_ m=H^0(X_ n,L_ k^ m)$. Proposition 21.7.1 . For this flag, \[  \{ \nu (s):0\neq s\in W_ m\}  =\{ (a_1,\ldots ,a_{n-1},0):a_ i\in \mathbb N, \  \textstyle \sum _ i a_ i\leq km\} .  \] Consequently \[  \Delta (W_\bullet )= \{ (x_1,\ldots ,x_{n-1},0):x_ i\geq 0, \  \textstyle \sum _ i x_ i\leq k\} .  \] Its $n$-dimensional volume is zero. When $k>0$, its volume in the coordinate hyperplane $x_ n=0$, with the Euclidean measure for which the coordinate lattice has covolume one, is \[  \frac{k^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} =\lim _{m\to \infty }\frac{\dim W_ m}{m^{n-1}}.  \] For $k=0$ the body is a point and $\dim W_ m=1$. Proof. By proposition 20.6.1 , sections of $L_ k^ m$ are homogeneous polynomials of degree $km$. Dividing successively by the highest powers of $z_1,\ldots ,z_{n-1}$ that divide the section, and restricting at each step, leaves a nonzero multiple of $z_ n^{km-a_1-\cdots -a_{n-1}}$, where $a_ i$ is the $i$th valuation. This residual section has no zeros on $Y_{n-1}$, so the last valuation is zero, and the preceding ones are nonnegative with sum at most $km$. Conversely, every such tuple is the valuation of the monomial \[  z_1^{a_1}\cdots z_{n-1}^{a_{n-1}} z_ n^{km-a_1-\cdots -a_{n-1}}.  \] The normalized values lie in the displayed simplex and, for $m=1$, include all its vertices, so their closed convex hull is the simplex. For $k>0$, its coordinate-lattice volume is $k^{n-1}/(n-1)!$, the leading coefficient of the binomial count in proposition 20.6.1 . For $k=0$, only the constant polynomials remain. $\square$ 21.1 For the Hopf threefold and $k>0$, the body is a triangle in a coordinate plane. Its area gives the quadratic section growth, while its ambient volume vanishes.

title: 22 Hopf fibrations and toric potentials
text: 22 Hopf fibrations and toric potentials Let $n\geq 2$ and let $X_ n$ be the scalar Hopf manifold of section 20.6 , which fibers over $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ with compact elliptic fibers. A potential in a pulled-back closed class is constant on each fiber and therefore descends to the base. For such a weight, the weighted section integrands also descend, and fiber integration identifies the section norms and Bergman kernels on the two spaces. A potential of the standard Gauduchon form may vary along the fibers. For one that descends, the vertical part of this form supplies a single factor in the Hermitian Monge–Ampère measure, and fiber integration reduces the equation to the projective base. For bounded descended potentials, closedness on the base determines the normalizing constant and gives uniqueness up to additive constants. On the Hopf threefold, the descended masses are at most six, so unbounded masses require variation along the fibers. On the base, invariance under separate rotations of the homogeneous coordinates gives a real convex description in logarithmic coordinates. Strict positivity of the curvature makes the gradient a parametrization of the relative interior of a simplex. Write $\pi :X_ n\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$ for the projection. The forms $\alpha ,\zeta ,\omega $ and the probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n/(2n)$ are as in section 20.6 . Write $\sigma $ for the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}\sigma ^{n-1}=1$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ for the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 6.1.2 . The fiber calculations use the following identities, where $y\in \mathbb P^{n-1}$: \[  \alpha =\pi ^*\sigma ,\qquad \omega =\alpha +\zeta ,\qquad \zeta ^2=0,\qquad \mathrm{d}V=\tfrac 12\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta ,\qquad \int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}\zeta =2.  \]

title: 22.1 Weighted sections on the projective base
search_title: Weighted sections on the projective base
text: 22.1 Weighted sections on the projective base For an integer $k\geq 0$, the line bundle $L_ k$ of section 20.6 , with its metric $h_ k$, is the pullback of $\mathcal O(k)$ with its Fubini–Study metric. By the proof of proposition 20.6.1 , sections of $L_ k^ m$ are represented by homogeneous polynomials $f$ of degree $km$ in the covering coordinates $z\in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, exactly as sections of $\mathcal O(km)$ on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, and the pointwise squared norm $|f(z)|^2|z|^{-2km}$ is invariant under every nonzero complex scalar. If the weight also descends, the weighted integrand is a function on the base, and fiber integration identifies the norms and Bergman kernels of section 20.1 on the two spaces. Theorem 22.1.1 . Let $k\geq 0$ be an integer and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X_ n,k\alpha )$. Then $u=\pi ^*v$ for a unique $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},k\sigma )$. For every positive integer $m$, pullback identifies the weighted section spaces isometrically: for a section $s$ in the space on the base, \[  \begin{split}  H^0\bigl (\mathbb P^{n-1},\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathcal I(mv)\bigr ) & \simeq H^0\bigl (X_ n,L_ k^ m\otimes \mathcal I(mu)\bigr ),\\  \| \pi ^*s\| _{X_ n,m,u}^2& =\| s\| _{\mathbb P^{n-1},m,v}^2. \end{split}  \] Here the norm on the base is defined with the Fubini–Study metric and the volume form $\sigma ^{n-1}$. The kernels $K$ and, off their pole sets, $B$ on $X_ n$ are the pullbacks of the corresponding kernels on the base. Pullback also identifies the bounded weighted section algebras $\mathcal W_\bullet (v)$ and $\mathcal W_\bullet (u)$. Proof. The descent of the potential follows from proposition 1.22.3 . By the proof of proposition 20.6.1 , the unweighted section spaces on both manifolds consist of the same homogeneous polynomials of degree $km$, and the pointwise norms of corresponding sections agree because the metrics correspond. For every nonnegative Borel function $F$ on the base, fiber integration gives \[  \int _{X_ n}(F\circ \pi )\, \mathrm{d}V =\frac12\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}F\sigma ^{n-1} \int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}\zeta =\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}F\sigma ^{n-1}.  \] Applied to $F=|s|^2\mathrm{e}^{-mv}$, with arbitrary values on the pole set, this formula gives equality of the two possibly infinite integrals. Since finiteness of the weighted norm characterizes the multiplier-ideal section spaces, this proves the asserted isometry. An orthonormal basis therefore pulls back to an orthonormal basis, which proves the kernel identities. Finally, a nonnegative function on the base is bounded if and only if its pullback is bounded, so pullback also identifies the bounded weighted sections, compatibly with multiplication. $\square$

title: 22.2 Descended measures and equations
text:
22.2 Descended measures and equations The pulled-back curvature of a descended potential has no component in the fiber direction; the form $\zeta $ supplies it. Since $\zeta ^2=0$, the Hermitian top power of a descended potential consists of a single mixed term, and fiber integration of this term determines the mass and reduces the Monge–Ampère equation for descended potentials to the base. For a positive Borel measure $
u $ on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, we write $\pi ^*
u \wedge \zeta $ for the measure on $X_ n$ defined, on nonnegative Borel functions $F$, by \[  \int _{X_ n}F\, \pi ^*
u \wedge \zeta =\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}} \left(\int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}F\zeta ight)\mathrm{d}
u (y).  \] When $
u $ is given by a smooth top-degree form, this agrees with the pullback of the form wedged with $\zeta $. Theorem 22.2.1 . For a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, the pullback $u=\pi ^*v$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X_ n,\omega )$ if and only if $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$. In this case \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u) =n\, \pi ^*\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\sigma (v)\wedge \zeta .  \] Consequently \[  \int _{X_ n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u) =2n\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\sigma (v) \leq 2n,  \] with equality for bounded $v$. For an integer $k\geq 0$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},k\sigma )$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k\alpha }(\pi ^*v)=0  \] as a measure on the $n$-dimensional manifold $X_ n$. Proof. If $v$ is $\sigma $-plurisubharmonic, then \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\pi ^*(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+\zeta \geq 0.  \] Conversely, suppose that the left-hand side is positive. Wedge it with the smooth semipositive form $\zeta $ and push the result forward to the base. Since $\zeta ^2=0$ and the fiber integral of $\zeta $ is two, \[  \pi _* igl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \zeta  igr ) =2(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)\geq 0;  \] this identity of currents follows by testing against smooth forms on the base and integrating over the fibers. It proves the converse. For the measure formula, first let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$ be bounded. By lemma 1.7.3 , its bounded products commute with $\pi ^*$. Since $\zeta ^2=0$ and the base has dimension $n-1$, expanding the power gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n =n\, \pi ^*(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}\wedge \zeta ,  \] and fiber integration identifies the right-hand side with the measure defined above. For general $v$, normalize $v\leq 0$ and set $v_ j=\max (v,-j)$. Since $\sigma $ is positive, these are bounded $\sigma $-plurisubharmonic functions, and their pullbacks are exactly $u_ j=\max (u,-j)$. Multiply the bounded identity by the common indicator function $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-j\} }=\pi ^*\mathbf1_{\{ v>-j\} }$ and pass to the increasing limits defining the extended measures. Fiber integration of nonnegative functions justifies the limit on the right-hand side, including over the poles. The mass formula follows because each fiber has $\zeta $-mass two. The extended mass on the base is at most one: on $\{ v>-j\} $, its truncated measure is bounded above by the full bounded product, whose mass is $\int \sigma ^{n-1}=1$ by Stokes' theorem for the closed form $\sigma $. For bounded $v$ nothing is removed, and equality holds. For the last assertion, take bounded truncations of $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},k\sigma )$. By lemma 1.7.3 , the $n$th powers of their pulled-back currents vanish. Restricting to the truncation levels and taking the increasing limit shows that the extended measure is zero; this includes the case $k=0$. $\square$ If an $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potential is constant on the fibers, the local-section argument in proposition 1.22.3 shows that it descends to a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on the base. The theorem therefore bounds its Hermitian mass by $2n$. On the Hopf threefold this bound is six, so the unbounded masses of chapter 8 require potentials that vary along the fibers. For the equation, let $p>1$ and let $f\geq 0$ belong to $L^ p(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma ^{n-1})$, with $\int f\sigma ^{n-1}>0$. For potentials $u=\pi ^*v$ with bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$, the equation 22.3  egin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-reduced-equation}\index{Monge--Ampere equation@Monge--Amp\` ere equation!Hopf reduction} (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c(f\circ \pi )\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad c>0, \end{equation} is equivalent to the base equation \[  (\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}= rac{c}{2n}f\sigma ^{n-1}.  \] Indeed, the base equation implies ( 22.3 ) by theorem 22.2.1 and the formula for $\mathrm{d}V$. Conversely, pushing ( 22.3 ) forward to the base gives $2n(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}=cf\sigma ^{n-1}$. Integrating the base equation determines the constant: \[  c= rac{2n}{\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}f\sigma ^{n-1}}.  \] Since $\sigma $ is closed, it satisfies the Guan–Li condition ( 11.35 ). Applied to $(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$, 11.5.1 gives a continuous solution of the base equation with this constant, unique up to additive constants among bounded $\sigma $-plurisubharmonic functions. Consequently ( 22.3 ) has a continuous solution, unique up to additive constants among bounded descended potentials. For smooth positive $f$, theorem 9.1.1 on the base gives a smooth solution $v$, and the constant is again determined by Stokes' theorem. For a real parameter $\lambda $, the same calculation shows that the equation with right-hand side $c\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}(f\circ \pi )\mathrm{d}V$ is equivalent to the base equation with right-hand side $(c/(2n))\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v}f\sigma ^{n-1}$.

title: 22.3 Logarithmic coordinates and the gradient simplex
search_title: Logarithmic coordinates and the gradient simplex
text:
22.3 Logarithmic coordinates and the gradient simplex For potentials invariant under rotations of the individual coordinates, the complex Hessian becomes the real Hessian of a function of the logarithmic coordinates. Invariance under complex scaling gives this Hessian a null direction; transverse to it, positivity becomes convexity, and boundedness of the potential confines the gradient to a simplex. Logarithmic growth makes every interior point of the simplex a gradient value, and strict positivity on the base makes the gradient injective modulo the null direction. In this section, $k>0$ is a real number. Let $v$ be a smooth real function on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ that is invariant under the torus action \[  [z_1:\cdots :z_ n]\longmapsto [\mathrm e^{\mathrm it_1}z_1:\cdots :\mathrm e^{\mathrm it_ n}z_ n], \qquad t\in \mathbb R^ n,  \] and put $u=\pi ^*v$. On the locus where all covering coordinates $z_ i$ are nonzero, set $x_ i=\log |z_ i|^2$. By this invariance, $u$ is a function of $x=(x_1,\ldots ,x_ n)$, which we denote by $u(x)$, and we set \[  F(x)=k\log \left(\sum _{i=1}^ n \mathrm{e}^{x_ i}ight)+u(x).  \] Write $

title: 23 Divisorial currents on compact modifications
text: 23 Divisorial currents on compact modifications Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold and $Y\subset X$ a connected compact complex submanifold of dimension $r\geq 1$. Fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ and a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have generic Lelong number $\nu (u,Y)=\inf _{y\in Y}\nu (u,y)=0$. The divisorial trace data of $u$ along $Y$ (chapter 19 ) assign a number to every prime divisor on every smooth compact modification of $Y$. A single model sees only part of these data, since blowing up can reveal vanishing that had higher codimension on $Y$. Summing the coefficients visible on one model gives a closed positive current, whose mass is controlled by a Gauduchon degree. These currents agree under pushforward, while their pullbacks acquire an effective exceptional correction. The trace envelope, which imposes the trace inequalities on all models at once, pulls back exactly. This discrepancy explains why the ordinary singularity type of the divisorial part on one model need not realize the full trace data. The divisorial currents are closed even when the background is not. In a closed restricted background, subtracting them gives residual Bott–Chern classes that are compatible between models. To identify the exceptional correction for an infinite divisorial sum, we need pullback to be continuous on closed positive currents; this continuity comes from choosing, in each Bott–Chern class, the representative of constant Gauduchon trace. Residual classes with a nonzero prescribed exterior derivative belong to the affine spaces of chapter 24 . Let $u_ m$ and $\epsilon _ m$ be the analytic approximants and curvature errors of corollary 1.15.2 : $u_ m$ has analytic singularities of type $(1/m,\mathcal I(mu))$, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ m\geq -\epsilon _ m\omega $ with $\epsilon _ m\to 0$. For a smooth compact modification $\pi :Z\to Y$, put \[  \theta _ Z=\pi ^*(\theta |_ Y),\qquad \omega _ Z^0=\pi ^*(\omega |_ Y),\qquad b_ m(E)=\operatorname {ord}_ E\bigl (\mathcal I(mu)\mathcal O_ Y\bigr ) \quad (m\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 1}).  \] Here $E$ is a prime divisor on $Z$, $[E]$ denotes its integration current, and $b_ m(E)$ is the vanishing order along $E$ of the image ideal $\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y)=\mathcal I(mu)\mathcal O_ Y$ pulled back to $Z$. By theorem 19.1.1 , the trace numbers satisfy \[  \frac{b_ m(E)}m\longrightarrow \tau _{Y,u}(E),\qquad \tau _{Y,u}(E)=\sup _{m\geq 1}\frac{b_ m(E)}m.  \] By corollary 1.22.18 , the restrictions $u_ m|_ Y$ are not identically $-\infty $, and the curvature bound pulls back to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((u_ m|_ Y)\circ \pi )\geq -\theta _ Z-\epsilon _ m\omega _ Z^0$.

title: 23.1 Divisorial trace currents
text: 23.1 Divisorial trace currents On a model $Z$, the curvature current of the pulled-back analytic approximant dominates the divisor of the image ideal of $\mathcal I(mu)$. Pairing with a Gauduchon metric removes the potential from this inequality, and the resulting bound passes to the limit in each coefficient and controls the sum of all trace coefficients. For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $Z$, we call $\int _ ZT\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}$ the trace mass of a positive $(1,1)$-current $T$; when $r=1$, $\gamma ^{r-1}=1$ and $\gamma $ may be any Hermitian metric. For a positive integer $m$, with $E$ ranging over the prime divisors on $Z$, define the finite divisorial current \[  D_{m,Z}=\frac1m\sum _ E b_ m(E)[E].  \] The sum is finite: the pulled-back image ideal is a nonzero coherent ideal on the compact manifold $Z$, so its zero set has only finitely many components of codimension one. We also consider the possibly infinite sum \[  S_ Z(u;Y)=\sum _ E\tau _{Y,u}(E)[E],  \] which a priori is defined only through its finite subsums. Theorem 23.1.1 . The sum $S_ Z(u;Y)$ defines a closed positive $(1,1)$-current of finite mass on $Z$. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $Z$, 23.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:trace-divisorial-linear-budget} \int _ Z S_ Z(u;Y)\wedge \gamma ^{r-1} \leq \int _ Z\theta _ Z\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}, \end{equation} where $\gamma ^{r-1}=1$ if $r=1$. Moreover, \[  0\leq D_{m,Z}\leq S_ Z(u;Y),\qquad \int _ Z\bigl (S_ Z(u;Y)-D_{m,Z}\bigr )\wedge \gamma ^{r-1} \longrightarrow 0.  \] In particular, $D_{m,Z}$ converges weakly to $S_ Z(u;Y)$ as currents, and the dyadic sequence $D_{2^ j,Z}$ is increasing. Proof. Set $w_ m=(u_ m|_ Y)\circ \pi $. By corollary 1.22.18 , these functions are not identically $-\infty $. Moreover, $u_ m|_ Y$ has analytic type $(1/m,\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y))$ by proposition 1.13.1 , as in the proof of that corollary, so its pullback $w_ m$ has generic Lelong number $b_ m(E)/m$ along $E$. Thus \[  T_ m=\theta _ Z+\epsilon _ m\omega _ Z^0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ m\geq 0, \qquad \nu (w_ m,E)=b_ m(E)/m.  \] Lemma 1.17.1 gives $D_{m,Z}\leq T_ m$. Integration by parts for currents and the Gauduchon condition therefore give \[  \int _ ZD_{m,Z}\wedge \gamma ^{r-1} \leq \int _ Z\theta _ Z\wedge \gamma ^{r-1} +\epsilon _ m\int _ Z\omega _ Z^0\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}.  \] For any fixed finite set of prime divisors, let $m\to \infty $ in the coefficients of these divisors, using theorem 19.1.1 , and then take the supremum over all finite sets. This proves ( 23.1 ) for every finite subsum. Every prime divisor has strictly positive $\gamma $-area. Hence at most countably many coefficients are positive: for each positive integer $k$, only finitely many terms can have trace mass at least $1/k$, and every positive term is among these for some $k$. Enumerate the corresponding divisors. The finite partial sums are increasing positive closed currents with uniformly bounded trace mass. They therefore converge, in the sense of coefficient measures and weakly as currents, to a positive current of finite mass, which is closed because differentiation is continuous on currents. This constructs $S_ Z(u;Y)$ and proves the integral inequality. The supremum formula for $\tau _{Y,u}(E)$ gives $b_ m(E)/m\leq \tau _{Y,u}(E)$ for every $m$ and $E$, and the limit along the integers gives coefficientwise convergence. Dominated convergence for the countable series with summable weights $\tau _{Y,u}(E)\int _ E\gamma ^{r-1}$ shows that the trace mass of $S_ Z-D_{m,Z}$ tends to zero. Since a fixed smooth test form is bounded in absolute value, on positive $(1,1)$-currents, by a constant times the trace mass, this gives weak convergence. Finally, $b_{2m}(E)\geq 2b_ m(E)$ gives $D_{2m,Z}\geq D_{m,Z}$. $\square$

title: 23.2 Compatibility between models
text: 23.2 Compatibility between models Under a further modification, a prime divisor and its strict transform define the same vanishing order on the image ideals, while exceptional divisors disappear under pushforward. Hence the trace currents are compatible with pushforward. Under pullback, exceptional divisors can carry additional vanishing, and divisibility of the pulled-back ideals shows that this additional vanishing is nonnegative. Theorem 23.2.1 . Let $g:Z'\to Z$ be a smooth compact modification, and regard $Z'$ as a model over $Y$ through $\pi \circ g$. Then \[  g_*S_{Z'}(u;Y)=S_ Z(u;Y).  \] The current $S_ Z(u;Y)$ is additive and positively homogeneous in $u$. For every finite set $\mathcal F$ of prime divisors on $Z$, the finite effective real divisor \[  A_{\mathcal F}=\sum _{E\in \mathcal F}\tau _{Y,u}(E)E  \] satisfies \[  [g^*A_{\mathcal F}]\leq S_{Z'}(u;Y).  \] Proof. Every prime divisor on $Z'$ is either the strict transform of a prime divisor on $Z$ or exceptional for $g$. If $E'$ is the strict transform of a prime divisor $E\subset Z$, then $g$ is biholomorphic near generic points of $E'$. Hence $E'$ and $E$ define the same vanishing order on the image ideals from $Y$, so $\tau _{Y,u}(E')=\tau _{Y,u}(E)$, and $g_*[E']=[E]$. The image of an exceptional prime divisor $F$ has codimension at least two. The pullback of a smooth $(r-1,r-1)$ test form therefore restricts to zero on the regular locus of $F$, where the restriction of $g$ has complex rank at most $r-2$; thus $g_*[F]=0$. In dimension one, a modification between smooth compact curves is an isomorphism, and there are no exceptional divisors. Pushforward under the proper map $g$ is continuous on currents. Applying it to the increasing finite partial sums, or equivalently testing their summable positive coefficient measures, proves the displayed compatibility. Additivity and homogeneity follow coefficientwise from proposition 19.1.2 . For the inequality, fix a positive integer $m$ and let $\mathfrak a_{m,Z}=\mathcal I(mu)\mathcal O_ Z$ denote the image ideal on $Z$. Its divisorial vanishing gives \[  \mathfrak a_{m,Z}\subseteq \mathcal O_ Z\left(-\sum _{E\in \mathcal F}b_ m(E)E\right).  \] Indeed, on a manifold, a holomorphic function vanishing to the indicated generic orders is divisible by the corresponding powers of the local equations of the divisors. Pulling back this inclusion and taking the order along a prime divisor $F\subset Z'$ gives 23.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:trace-ideal-model-inequality} b_ m(F)\geq \sum _{E\in \mathcal F} b_ m(E)\operatorname {ord}_ F(g^*E). \end{equation} Divide by $m$ and let $m\to \infty $; the sum is finite. Thus every coefficient of $g^*A_{\mathcal F}$ is at most the corresponding coefficient $\tau _{Y,u}(F)$ of $S_{Z'}(u;Y)$. Since both sides are positive divisorial currents, this proves the asserted inequality of currents. $\square$
