title: 23.3 The trace envelope as a common majorant
search_title: The trace envelope as a common majorant
text: 23.3 The trace envelope as a common majorant The trace envelope of section 19.6 imposes the trace inequalities along all divisors over $Y$, including those that do not appear on a given model. It therefore gives a single potential on $Y$, in the original background $\theta |_ Y$, whose pulled-back curvature current dominates the trace current on every model. Proposition 23.3.1 . There exists $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta |_ Y)$ such that, for every smooth compact modification $\pi :Z\to Y$, \[  \nu (v\circ \pi ,E)\geq \tau _{Y,u}(E) \quad \hbox{for every prime divisor }E\subset Z,  \] and \[  \pi ^*(\theta |_ Y)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ \pi )\geq S_ Z(u;Y).  \] Proof. Take for $v$ the trace envelope $\mathcal T_{\theta |_ Y}(u;Y)$ of ( 19.7 ). By theorem 19.6.2 , it belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta |_ Y)$ and satisfies every defining trace inequality. On a fixed model $Z$, lemma 1.17.1 therefore allows us to subtract every finite partial sum of $S_ Z(u;Y)$ from $\theta _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ \pi )$ while preserving positivity. Passing to the limit of these partial sums, constructed in theorem 23.1.1 , preserves positivity and proves the second assertion. $\square$ The potential in the proof is canonical: by theorem 19.6.3 , $v\circ \pi $ is the trace envelope on $Z$ in the background $\theta _ Z$ for the same trace data. Its generic Lelong numbers may nevertheless exceed the prescribed trace numbers. Exact realization of the trace data requires the reverse inequality, which chapter 19 establishes for analytic singularities, for Kähler $Y$ in sufficiently large closed backgrounds, and for pullbacks from curves. By contrast, the ordinary singularity type attached to $S_ Z$ by corollary 1.17.5 records only the divisorial part on the particular model $Z$.

title: 23.4 Bott–Chern classes and closed currents
text: 23.4 Bott–Chern classes and closed currents Bott–Chern cohomology records a closed $(1,1)$-current modulo $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of global functions, and so separates the smooth background of the current from its potential. When $\theta $ is closed, subtracting the trace current from the pulled-back background gives a residual class on each model, and compatibility with pushforward organizes these classes into a b-divisor class in the sense of [ section The notion of b-divisors , SGPT ] . For a complex manifold $Z$, let $\Lambda ^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}$ denote the bundle of real $(1,1)$-forms and define \[  H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R) =\frac{\{ \beta \in C^\infty (Z,\Lambda ^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}):\mathrm{d}\beta =0\} }{\{ \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f:f\in C^\infty (Z,\mathbb R)\} }.  \] Lemma 23.4.1 . Replacing smooth forms and smooth functions in this quotient by real currents and real distributions gives the same space. In particular, every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $Z$ can be written \[  T=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w  \] with $\beta $ smooth and closed and $w$ a global quasi-plurisubharmonic function. Proof. The decomposition of lemma 1.17.3 shows that the natural map from the smooth quotient to the current quotient is surjective, and it gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic potential for positive currents. The same lemma shows that two distributional potentials in such decompositions differ by a smooth function; equivalently, a distribution whose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is smooth is itself smooth. Hence two smooth forms that are identified in the current quotient are already identified in the smooth quotient, and the map is injective. $\square$ From now on, $Z$ is connected and compact. By the lemma, every closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ has a Bott–Chern class, written $\{ T\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$; the class is pseudoeffective if it contains a closed positive current. Pullback of classes is defined on smooth representatives. Pushforward of classes under a modification is defined on current representatives; it is well defined because pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, and by the lemma the resulting class is again a smooth Bott–Chern class. For a modification $g$ and every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\beta $ on its target, $g_*g^*\beta =\beta $ as currents, by the change of variables formula for the degree-one map $g$. A Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ defines a linear functional on this cohomology: \[  \ell _\gamma (\{ T\} _{\mathrm{BC}})=\int _ ZT\wedge \gamma ^{\dim Z-1}.  \] Integration by parts for currents shows that it does not depend on the representative. On a positive representative it is nonnegative, and it vanishes only if that representative is zero, by the strict positivity of the metric. In particular, the pseudoeffective cone contains no line: if $T_1,T_2\geq 0$ represent opposite classes, their sum has zero Gauduchon pairing, hence $T_1=T_2=0$. Gauduchon pairings detect closed curvature information that is invisible in de Rham cohomology. Consider the Hopf manifold $X_ n$, $n\geq 2$, with its Gauduchon form $\omega $ and covering coordinates $z\in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, as in section 20.6 . The form $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2$ is exact as a de Rham form, because $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\log |z|^2$ descends to the quotient: the logarithm changes only by a constant under the contraction. Nevertheless, by the calculation in proposition 20.6.1 , \[  \ell _\omega (\{ \alpha \} _{\mathrm{BC}}) =\int _{X_ n}\alpha \wedge \omega ^{n-1}=2(n-1)>0,  \] so the Bott–Chern class of $\alpha $ is nonzero. We return to the smooth compact modifications of the manifold $Y$ fixed at the beginning of the chapter. Two such modifications $\pi :Z\to Y$ and $\pi ':Z'\to Y$ are compared through modifications $g:Z'\to Z$ with $\pi '=\pi \circ g$; we then say that $Z'$ dominates $Z$. Definition 23.4.2 . A Bott–Chern b-divisor class over $Y$ is a family \[  \mathbb A=(\mathbb A_ Z)_{\pi :Z\to Y},\qquad \mathbb A_ Z\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R),  \] indexed by the smooth compact modifications of $Y$ and compatible with pushforward: $g_*\mathbb A_{Z'}=\mathbb A_ Z$ whenever $g:Z'\to Z$ is a modification over $Y$. It is pseudoeffective if every $\mathbb A_ Z$ is pseudoeffective. It is Cartier if there are a model $Z$ and a class $a_ Z\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R)$ such that $\mathbb A_{Z'}=g^*a_ Z$ for every model $g:Z'\to Z$ dominating $Z$; the pair $(Z,a_ Z)$ is then called a Cartier realization of $\mathbb A$. When the models are Kähler, the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma identifies this cohomology with the real $(1,1)$-cohomology used in [ section The notion of b-divisors , SGPT ] , and the definition agrees with the one given there. We now return to the trace data fixed at the beginning of the chapter. When $\theta $ is closed, the common majorant of proposition 23.3.1 provides positive representatives of the residual classes. Proposition 23.4.3 . If the ambient background $\theta $ is closed, the classes \[  \mathbb A_ Z(u;Y,\theta ) =\{ \pi ^*(\theta |_ Y)-S_ Z(u;Y)\} _{\mathrm{BC}}  \] form a pseudoeffective Bott–Chern b-divisor class. They depend only on the ambient multiplier-ideal class of $u$ and the Bott–Chern class of $\theta |_ Y$. Proof. By proposition 23.3.1 , there is one $v$ on $Y$ such that \[  R_ Z=\pi ^*(\theta |_ Y)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ \pi )-S_ Z(u;Y)\geq 0  \] on every model. Since $\theta $ and $S_ Z$ are closed, $R_ Z$ is closed, and its class is the class in the statement. This proves pseudoeffectivity. Compatibility with pushforward follows from theorem 23.2.1 together with $g_*g^*(\theta _ Z)=\theta _ Z$. Finally, the trace data do not change under ambient multiplier-ideal equivalence, and replacing $\theta |_ Y$ by $\theta |_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth changes no class; this proves the last assertion. $\square$ If $\theta $ is not closed, the same expression $R_ Z$ is still a positive current, but \[  \mathrm{d}R_ Z=\pi ^*(\mathrm{d}\theta |_ Y).  \] It is therefore not closed in general and defines no Bott–Chern class. Classes whose representatives have a prescribed nonzero exterior derivative are treated in chapter 24 .

title: Lemma 23.4.1
text: Lemma 23.4.1 . Replacing smooth forms and smooth functions in this quotient by real currents and real distributions gives the same space. In particular, every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $Z$ can be written \[  T=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w  \] with $\beta $ smooth and closed and $w$ a global quasi-plurisubharmonic function. Proof. The decomposition of lemma 1.17.3 shows that the natural map from the smooth quotient to the current quotient is surjective, and it gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic potential for positive currents. The same lemma shows that two distributional potentials in such decompositions differ by a smooth function; equivalently, a distribution whose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is smooth is itself smooth. Hence two smooth forms that are identified in the current quotient are already identified in the smooth quotient, and the map is injective. $\square$

The trace coefficients then become the generic Lelong numbers of the pulled-back potential along divisors, and divisorial removal gives the positive residual currents directly. u _ E.  \] The limit along the integers defining $	au _{Y,w}(E)$ is therefore $

title: 23.6 Nef Cartier realizations
text: 23.6 Nef Cartier realizations If $T$ has analytic singularities, a log resolution splits its pullback into a finite divisor and a current with bounded potentials. The bounded part acquires no divisorial component on higher models, so its class determines the whole b-divisor class there, and smooth regularization of its bounded potential shows that this class is nef. A class $a\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R)$ is nef if, for one Hermitian metric $\gamma $, it has for every $\epsilon >0$ a smooth representative $\beta _\epsilon \geq -\epsilon \gamma $. Since any two Hermitian metrics are comparable, this does not depend on the metric. A Cartier b-divisor class is called nef if it has a Cartier realization $(Z,a_ Z)$ with $a_ Z$ nef. Lemma 23.6.1 . On a connected compact complex manifold $Z$, let $\beta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $v$ a bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic function. If $R=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0$ is closed, then $\{ R\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$ is nef. Proof. Since $R$ is closed, so is $\beta $. Fix a Hermitian metric $\gamma $. By proposition 1.10.1 , there are smooth functions $v_ j$ and numbers $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ such that \[  \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq -\epsilon _ j\gamma .  \] These forms are closed representatives of $\{ R\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$. Given $\epsilon >0$, choosing $j$ with $\epsilon _ j\leq \epsilon $ gives the estimate required in the definition of nefness. $\square$ Theorem 23.6.2 . If the closed positive current $T$ has analytic singularities, then $\mathbb D(T)$ is Cartier and has a nef Cartier realization on a smooth compact modification. Proof. Resolve the analytic singularity ideal, using the log-resolution theorem in [ section on analytic singularities, theorem on existence of log resolutions , SGPT ] . On a suitable smooth compact model $\pi :Z\to Y$, \[  \pi ^*T=[D]+R,  \] where $D$ is a finite effective rational divisor and $R$ is a closed positive current with locally bounded potentials. To obtain a global bounded potential, choose smooth metrics on the line bundles of the components of $D$ and subtract the corresponding logarithms of squared norms of the canonical sections from $w\circ \pi $. The remainder $v$ is globally bounded, and \[  R=\beta _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v  \] for a smooth closed form $\beta _ Z$. By the lemma, the class of $R$ is nef. On every further compact modification $g:Z'\to Z$, the current $g^*R$ still has bounded local potentials and therefore zero Lelong numbers. Hence the divisorial part of $g^*\pi ^*T$ is exactly $[g^*D]$, and its regular part is $g^*R$. It follows that $\mathbb D(T)_{Z'}=g^*\{ R\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$. Thus $(Z,\{ R\} _{\mathrm{BC}})$ is a nef Cartier realization. $\square$ For a general current, analytic regularization gives closed approximants bounded below by $-\epsilon _ m\gamma $. Adding $\epsilon _ m\gamma $ makes them positive but, when $\gamma $ is not closed, changes their exterior derivative. The approximation then takes place in the larger spaces of chapter 24 , and does not by itself approximate the original Bott–Chern b-divisor class by nef Cartier classes.

title: 23.7 Continuous representatives and pullback
text: 23.7 Continuous representatives and pullback A finite divisorial sum is pulled back through the local equations of its divisors. For an infinite sum we need pullback to be continuous on closed positive currents whose Bott–Chern classes vary. Solving a scalar equation for the Gauduchon trace selects a smooth representative in each class; the complementary normalized potentials then converge in $L^1$, and lemma 1.22.13 shows that their pullbacks converge as well. In this section, $Y$ denotes an arbitrary connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and $\gamma $ is a Gauduchon metric on $Y$; in dimension one, any Hermitian metric will do. Fix smooth norms on tensor fields induced by $\gamma $. Put $V_\gamma =\int _ Y\gamma ^ n$ and, for a real $(1,1)$-form or current $B$, define its scalar trace $\sigma _\gamma (B)$ by \[  \sigma _\gamma (B)\, \gamma ^ n=B\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] For a current this is an identity of distributions. As in the proof of theorem 4.1.2 , we use the classical elliptic Fredholm theorem, elliptic regularity, and the continuity on distributions of the normalized elliptic inverse. Lemma 23.7.1 . Every closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ has a unique decomposition \[  T=B_\gamma (T)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T),\qquad \int _ Yv_\gamma (T)\, \gamma ^ n=0,  \] where $v_\gamma (T)$ is a real distribution and $B_\gamma (T)$ is a smooth closed real form with constant scalar trace. Both assignments are linear and continuous from weak convergence of currents to convergence of distributions. The forms $B_\gamma (T)$ lie in a finite-dimensional space, and their convergence takes place in $C^\infty $. This space maps isomorphically onto $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Y,\mathbb R)$. If $T\geq 0$, then $v_\gamma (T)$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic. On the cone of positive closed currents, $v_\gamma (T)$ depends continuously on $T$ in $L^1$, and for every nonnegative integer $l$, 23.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:constant-trace-representative-bound} \| B_\gamma (T)\| _{C^ l}+\| v_\gamma (T)\| _{L^1(\gamma ^ n)} \leq C_ l\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}, \end{equation} where the constants $C_ l$ depend only on the fixed metric and norms. Proof. Set $L_\gamma f=\sigma _\gamma (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)$. We use the inverse $G_\gamma $ of ( 5.1 ), normalized with the volume form $\gamma ^ n/V_\gamma $. It acts on top-degree distributions of total mass zero and is continuous by the elliptic estimates for the operator and its transpose. Step 1: construction. Define \[  c_ T=\frac{\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{V_\gamma },\qquad v_\gamma (T)=G_\gamma \bigl ((\sigma _\gamma (T)-c_ T)\gamma ^ n\bigr ),\qquad B_\gamma (T)=T-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T).  \] The current $B_\gamma (T)$ is closed and has scalar trace $c_ T$. We now prove its smoothness and the finite-dimensionality assertion without using any Kähler identity. Step 2: an elliptic system. Let $J$ be the complex structure acting on real covectors. On real $(1,1)$-forms consider the first-order operator \[  \mathscr P B=(\mathrm{d}B,\mathrm{d}\sigma _\gamma (B)).  \] Its principal symbol at a nonzero real covector $\xi $ is $B\mapsto (\xi \wedge B,\xi \, \sigma _\gamma (B))$, and we claim that it is injective. If $\xi \wedge B=0$, then the $(1,1)$ condition forces $B$ to be a real multiple of $\xi \wedge J\xi $. To check this, choose unitary real coordinates with $\xi =\mathrm{d}x_1$: every term of $B$ contains $\mathrm{d}x_1$, and invariance under $J$ forces every term to contain $\mathrm{d}y_1$ as well. If moreover $\xi \, \sigma _\gamma (B)=0$, then $\sigma _\gamma (B)=0$; since the scalar trace of $\xi \wedge J\xi $ is nonzero, the multiple is zero. Let $\mathscr P^*$ be the formal adjoint of $\mathscr P$ for the fixed metric and volume. Since the symbol of $\mathscr P$ is injective, $\mathscr P^*\mathscr P$ is elliptic. By elliptic regularity and compactness, its distributional kernel is a finite-dimensional space of smooth forms. Since $\mathscr P B_\gamma (T)=0$, the form $B_\gamma (T)$ belongs to this space. Conversely, the kernel consists exactly of the closed forms with constant scalar trace: integrating $\langle \mathscr P^*\mathscr P B,B\rangle $ gives $\mathscr P B=0$, and connectedness makes the trace constant. Denote this kernel by $\mathscr H_\gamma $. Step 3: Bott–Chern representatives. The construction is linear and continuous on distributions. Convergence of the components $B_\gamma (T)$ therefore takes place in the finite-dimensional space $\mathscr H_\gamma $, hence in every smooth norm. If $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a distribution $f$, then $c_ T=0$ and the inverse gives $v_\gamma (T)=f-V_\gamma ^{-1}\int _ Yf\gamma ^ n$, so $B_\gamma (T)=0$. Applied to smooth closed forms, this shows that $\mathscr H_\gamma $ contains exactly one representative of each Bott–Chern class. Uniqueness of the decomposition can also be seen directly: if two decompositions are given, $L_\gamma $ of the difference of the two potentials is a constant, integration forces this constant to be zero, and the normalized kernel of $L_\gamma $ is zero. Step 4: positive currents. Suppose now that $T\geq 0$. The inequality $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T)\geq -B_\gamma (T)$ gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative of the distribution $v_\gamma (T)$. Let positive closed currents $T_ j$ converge weakly to $T$. Their components $B_\gamma (T_ j)$ converge smoothly, so the potentials $v_\gamma (T_ j)$ have a common smooth lower curvature bound. By theorem 1.4.2 , after subtracting their suprema they form an $L^1$-precompact family. If $a_ j=\sup _ Yv_\gamma (T_ j)$, the zero-mean normalization gives \[  0\leq a_ j V_\gamma =\int _ Y\bigl (a_ j-v_\gamma (T_ j)\bigr )\, \gamma ^ n,  \] and the right-hand side is uniformly bounded. Hence the potentials $v_\gamma (T_ j)$ themselves are $L^1$-precompact. Every cluster point equals their distributional limit $v_\gamma (T)$, so the whole sequence converges in $L^1$. Finally, the positive closed currents with trace mass $\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=1$ form a weakly compact set: positivity bounds their coefficient measures, weak limits remain positive and closed, and testing with $\gamma ^{n-1}$ preserves the trace mass. The smooth and $L^1$ continuity just proved bounds both norms on this set, and positive homogeneity gives ( 23.3 ). A positive current of trace mass zero is zero, so this case is included. $\square$ The smooth representatives give a common curvature bound for converging normalized potentials. This is exactly the hypothesis needed to pull back their $L^1$ convergence. Proposition 23.7.2 . Let $g:Z\to Y$ be a smooth compact modification, and fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma '$ on $Z$. Pullback of positive closed $(1,1)$-currents, defined through their local potentials, is weakly continuous. Moreover, there is a constant $C_ g$, depending only on the modification and the fixed metrics, such that 23.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:modification-linear-mass-bound} \int _ Zg^*T\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1} \leq C_ g\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \qquad (T\geq 0,\  \mathrm{d}T=0). \end{equation} Proof. Write $T=B_\gamma (T)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T)$. The pullback is \[  g^*T=g^*B_\gamma (T)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_\gamma (T)\circ g).  \] This current is positive and closed, since it is locally $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of plurisubharmonic functions, and the composed potential is not identically $-\infty $ because $g$ is surjective. The formula agrees with the definition through local potentials, so it does not depend on the decomposition. If $T_ j\to T$, the smooth parts converge in $C^\infty $, and the potentials converge in $L^1(Y)$ with a common lower curvature bound. By lemma 1.22.13 , their compositions with $g$ converge in $L^1(Z)$, and taking $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ proves the weak convergence of the pullbacks. Integration by parts on $Z$ gives \[  \int _ Zg^*T\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1} =\int _ Zg^*B_\gamma (T)\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1}.  \] The absolute value of the right-hand side is at most a fixed constant times $\| B_\gamma (T)\| _{C^0}$. Since the left-hand side is nonnegative, ( 23.3 ) gives ( 23.4 ). $\square$ Corollary 23.7.3 . Let $g:Z\to Y$, $\gamma $ and $\gamma '$ be as in proposition 23.7.2 . Let $D_ j$ be prime divisors on $Y$, with integration currents $[D_ j]$, and let $c_ j>0$. If $S=\sum _ j c_ j[D_ j]$ is a positive closed current of finite mass, then \[  g^*S=\sum _ j c_ j[g^*D_ j]  \] as positive currents of finite mass. The trace masses on $Z$ of the positive tails of this series tend to zero. In particular, $g^*S$ is again purely divisorial. Proof. Apply the proposition to the increasing finite partial sums $S_ N$ and to their positive closed tails $S-S_ N$. Pullback is additive on positive closed currents, by addition of local potentials. Thus $g^*S-g^*S_ N=g^*(S-S_ N)\geq 0$, and its trace mass is at most $C_ g$ times the trace mass of $S-S_ N$, which tends to zero. The pullback of a finite divisor is the usual pullback of its local equations, which identifies $g^*S_ N$ with the corresponding partial sum of the series, and hence $g^*S$ with its limit. Its terms are integration currents of prime divisors with nonnegative coefficients, and regrouping this countable positive sum of finite mass does not change it. $\square$

The forms $B_\gamma (T)$ lie in a finite-dimensional space, and their convergence takes place in $C^\infty $. This space maps isomorphically onto $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Y,\mathbb R)$. If $T\geq 0$, then $v_\gamma (T)$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic. On the cone of positive closed currents, $v_\gamma (T)$ depends continuously on $T$ in $L^1$, and for every nonnegative integer $l$, 23.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:constant-trace-representative-bound} \| B_\gamma (T)\| _{C^ l}+\| v_\gamma (T)\| _{L^1(\gamma ^ n)} \leq C_ l\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}, \end{equation} where the constants $C_ l$ depend only on the fixed metric and norms. Proof. Set $L_\gamma f=\sigma _\gamma (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)$. We use the inverse $G_\gamma $ of ( 5.1 ), normalized with the volume form $\gamma ^ n/V_\gamma $. It acts on top-degree distributions of total mass zero and is continuous by the elliptic estimates for the operator and its transpose. Step 1: construction. Define \[  c_ T=\frac{\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{V_\gamma },\qquad v_\gamma (T)=G_\gamma \bigl ((\sigma _\gamma (T)-c_ T)\gamma ^ n\bigr ),\qquad B_\gamma (T)=T-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T).  \] The current $B_\gamma (T)$ is closed and has scalar trace $c_ T$. We now prove its smoothness and the finite-dimensionality assertion without using any Kähler identity. Step 2: an elliptic system. Let $J$ be the complex structure acting on real covectors. On real $(1,1)$-forms consider the first-order operator \[  \mathscr P B=(\mathrm{d}B,\mathrm{d}\sigma _\gamma (B)).  \] Its principal symbol at a nonzero real covector $\xi $ is $B\mapsto (\xi \wedge B,\xi \, \sigma _\gamma (B))$, and we claim that it is injective. If $\xi \wedge B=0$, then the $(1,1)$ condition forces $B$ to be a real multiple of $\xi \wedge J\xi $. To check this, choose unitary real coordinates with $\xi =\mathrm{d}x_1$: every term of $B$ contains $\mathrm{d}x_1$, and invariance under $J$ forces every term to contain $\mathrm{d}y_1$ as well. If moreover $\xi \, \sigma _\gamma (B)=0$, then $\sigma _\gamma (B)=0$; since the scalar trace of $\xi \wedge J\xi $ is nonzero, the multiple is zero. Let $\mathscr P^*$ be the formal adjoint of $\mathscr P$ for the fixed metric and volume. Since the symbol of $\mathscr P$ is injective, $\mathscr P^*\mathscr P$ is elliptic. By elliptic regularity and compactness, its distributional kernel is a finite-dimensional space of smooth forms. Since $\mathscr P B_\gamma (T)=0$, the form $B_\gamma (T)$ belongs to this space. Conversely, the kernel consists exactly of the closed forms with constant scalar trace: integrating $\langle \mathscr P^*\mathscr P B,B\rangle $ gives $\mathscr P B=0$, and connectedness makes the trace constant. Denote this kernel by $\mathscr H_\gamma $. Step 3: Bott–Chern representatives. The construction is linear and continuous on distributions. Convergence of the components $B_\gamma (T)$ therefore takes place in the finite-dimensional space $\mathscr H_\gamma $, hence in every smooth norm. If $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a distribution $f$, then $c_ T=0$ and the inverse gives $v_\gamma (T)=f-V_\gamma ^{-1}\int _ Yf\gamma ^ n$, so $B_\gamma (T)=0$. Applied to smooth closed forms, this shows that $\mathscr H_\gamma $ contains exactly one representative of each Bott–Chern class. Uniqueness of the decomposition can also be seen directly: if two decompositions are given, $L_\gamma $ of the difference of the two potentials is a constant, integration forces this constant to be zero, and the normalized kernel of $L_\gamma $ is zero. Step 4: positive currents. Suppose now that $T\geq 0$. The inequality $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T)\geq -B_\gamma (T)$ gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative of the distribution $v_\gamma (T)$. Let positive closed currents $T_ j$ converge weakly to $T$. Their components $B_\gamma (T_ j)$ converge smoothly, so the potentials $v_\gamma (T_ j)$ have a common smooth lower curvature bound. By theorem 1.4.2 , after subtracting their suprema they form an $L^1$-precompact family. If $a_ j=\sup _ Yv_\gamma (T_ j)$, the zero-mean normalization gives \[  0\leq a_ j V_\gamma =\int _ Y\bigl (a_ j-v_\gamma (T_ j)\bigr )\, \gamma ^ n,  \] and the right-hand side is uniformly bounded. Hence the potentials $v_\gamma (T_ j)$ themselves are $L^1$-precompact. Every cluster point equals their distributional limit $v_\gamma (T)$, so the whole sequence converges in $L^1$. Finally, the positive closed currents with trace mass $\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=1$ form a weakly compact set: positivity bounds their coefficient measures, weak limits remain positive and closed, and testing with $\gamma ^{n-1}$ preserves the trace mass. The smooth and $L^1$ continuity just proved bounds both norms on this set, and positive homogeneity gives ( 23.3 ). A positive current of trace mass zero is zero, so this case is included. $\square$
23.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:constant-trace-representative-bound} \| B_\gamma (T)\| _{C^ l}+\| v_\gamma (T)\| _{L^1(\gamma ^ n)} \leq C_ l\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}, \end{equation}

title: Proposition 23.7.2
text: Proposition 23.7.2 . Let $g:Z\to Y$ be a smooth compact modification, and fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma '$ on $Z$. Pullback of positive closed $(1,1)$-currents, defined through their local potentials, is weakly continuous. Moreover, there is a constant $C_ g$, depending only on the modification and the fixed metrics, such that 23.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:modification-linear-mass-bound} \int _ Zg^*T\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1} \leq C_ g\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \qquad (T\geq 0,\  \mathrm{d}T=0). \end{equation} Proof. Write $T=B_\gamma (T)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T)$. The pullback is \[  g^*T=g^*B_\gamma (T)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_\gamma (T)\circ g).  \] This current is positive and closed, since it is locally $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of plurisubharmonic functions, and the composed potential is not identically $-\infty $ because $g$ is surjective. The formula agrees with the definition through local potentials, so it does not depend on the decomposition. If $T_ j\to T$, the smooth parts converge in $C^\infty $, and the potentials converge in $L^1(Y)$ with a common lower curvature bound. By lemma 1.22.13 , their compositions with $g$ converge in $L^1(Z)$, and taking $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ proves the weak convergence of the pullbacks. Integration by parts on $Z$ gives \[  \int _ Zg^*T\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1} =\int _ Zg^*B_\gamma (T)\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1}.  \] The absolute value of the right-hand side is at most a fixed constant times $\| B_\gamma (T)\| _{C^0}$. Since the left-hand side is nonnegative, ( 23.3 ) gives ( 23.4 ). $\square$
23.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:modification-linear-mass-bound} \int _ Zg^*T\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1} \leq C_ g\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \qquad (T\geq 0,\  \mathrm{d}T=0). \end{equation}

title: Corollary 23.7.3
text: Corollary 23.7.3 . Let $g:Z\to Y$, $\gamma $ and $\gamma '$ be as in proposition 23.7.2 . Let $D_ j$ be prime divisors on $Y$, with integration currents $[D_ j]$, and let $c_ j>0$. If $S=\sum _ j c_ j[D_ j]$ is a positive closed current of finite mass, then \[  g^*S=\sum _ j c_ j[g^*D_ j]  \] as positive currents of finite mass. The trace masses on $Z$ of the positive tails of this series tend to zero. In particular, $g^*S$ is again purely divisorial. Proof. Apply the proposition to the increasing finite partial sums $S_ N$ and to their positive closed tails $S-S_ N$. Pullback is additive on positive closed currents, by addition of local potentials. Thus $g^*S-g^*S_ N=g^*(S-S_ N)\geq 0$, and its trace mass is at most $C_ g$ times the trace mass of $S-S_ N$, which tends to zero. The pullback of a finite divisor is the usual pullback of its local equations, which identifies $g^*S_ N$ with the corresponding partial sum of the series, and hence $g^*S$ with its limit. Its terms are integration currents of prime divisors with nonnegative coefficients, and regrouping this countable positive sum of finite mass does not change it. $\square$

title: 23.8 Exceptional divisors between trace models
text: 23.8 Exceptional divisors between trace models We return to the trace data fixed at the beginning of the chapter, with $\dim Y=r$, and write $S_ Z=S_ Z(u;Y)$. By corollary 23.7.3 , the full trace current can now be pulled back under a modification $g:Z'\to Z$. The pullback is bounded above by the trace current on $Z'$, with equal coefficients along strict transforms, so the difference is a finite effective divisor supported on the exceptional locus. Its logarithmic potential measures the change in the ordinary singularity types of the divisorial parts. Theorem 23.8.1 . For a smooth compact modification $g:Z'\to Z$ over $Y$, there is a unique finite effective real divisor $E_ g$ supported on the exceptional locus of $g$ such that 23.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:trace-exceptional-difference} S_{Z'}=g^*S_ Z+[E_ g]. \end{equation} For a further smooth compact modification $h:Z''\to Z'$, these divisors satisfy 23.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:trace-exceptional-cocycle} E_{g\circ h}=E_ h+h^*E_ g. \end{equation} Their coefficients are additive and positively homogeneous in the ambient potential $u$. For every $m$, the analytic-ideal divisors on the two models differ by a finite effective divisor $E_{m,g}$ supported on the exceptional locus: \[  [E_{m,g}]=D_{m,Z'}-g^*D_{m,Z}.  \] For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma '$ on $Z'$, the measures \[  [E_{m,g}]\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1} \longrightarrow [E_ g]\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1}  \] converge in total variation. Proof. Step 1: the exceptional divisor. Enumerate the prime divisors on $Z$ with positive trace coefficient. By theorem 23.2.1 , the pullback of every finite partial sum of $S_ Z$ is at most $S_{Z'}$, and corollary 23.7.3 identifies the increasing limit of these pullbacks with $g^*S_ Z$. Thus $S_{Z'}-g^*S_ Z$ is a positive closed divisorial current. The two currents have equal coefficients along the strict transform of every prime divisor on $Z$, because these coefficients are computed by the same valuation. Every other prime divisor on $Z'$ is exceptional for $g$, and the exceptional analytic set has only finitely many irreducible components on the compact manifold $Z'$. Hence the difference is the integration current of a finite effective real divisor $E_ g$ supported on its divisorial components, and the coefficients of integration currents determine $E_ g$ uniquely. Step 2: the cocycle identity. Pullback of positive closed $(1,1)$-currents is functorial, since it is defined by composing local plurisubharmonic potentials. Using ( 23.5 ) for $h$ and for $g$ gives \[  S_{Z''}=h^*S_{Z'}+[E_ h] =(g\circ h)^*S_ Z+[h^*E_ g]+[E_ h],  \] and uniqueness gives ( 23.6 ). Additivity and positive homogeneity follow from the same properties of the trace coefficients and the linearity of pullback. Step 3: approximation. For fixed $m$, apply ( 23.2 ) to the finitely many prime divisors in the support of the image ideal on $Z$. After division by $m$, it gives $D_{m,Z'}-g^*D_{m,Z}\geq 0$. The coefficients along strict transforms vanish, so this difference is the integration current of an effective real divisor $E_{m,g}$ supported on the exceptional locus. Choose also a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $Z$. By theorem 23.1.1 , the currents $S_ Z-D_{m,Z}$ and $S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'}$ are positive, and their trace masses tend to zero. Subtracting the two identities for the exceptional currents gives \[  [E_{m,g}]-[E_ g] =-(S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'})+g^*(S_ Z-D_{m,Z}),  \] where both $S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'}$ and $g^*(S_ Z-D_{m,Z})$ are positive. By ( 23.4 ), the total variation of the signed measure $([E_{m,g}]-[E_ g])\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1}$ is therefore at most \[  \int _{Z'}(S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'})\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1} +C_ g\int _ Z(S_ Z-D_{m,Z})\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}.  \] Both terms tend to zero, which proves convergence in total variation. $\square$ For a modification $g:Z'\to Z$ as in the theorem, the coefficient of $E_ g$ along an exceptional prime divisor $F\subset Z'$ is 23.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:trace-exceptional-coefficient} \tau _{Y,u}(F) -\sum _{D\subset Z}\tau _{Y,u}(D)\operatorname {ord}_ F(g^*D), \end{equation} where $D$ ranges over the prime divisors on $Z$ with positive trace coefficient. This countable sum converges: it is the coefficient of $g^*S_ Z$ along $F$ in the positive divisorial series of corollary 23.7.3 , and it is at most $\tau _{Y,u}(F)$. The same current identity compares the ordinary singularity types attached to $S_ Z$ and $S_{Z'}$ by corollary 1.17.5 . Corollary 23.8.2 . Choose decompositions $S_ Z=B_ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ Z$ and $S_{Z'}=B_{Z'}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{Z'}$ with smooth closed forms $B_ Z,B_{Z'}$, as in corollary 1.17.5 . Let $\rho _{E_ g}$ be a global logarithmic potential of $E_ g$, that is, a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $Z'$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho _{E_ g}-[E_ g]$ is smooth. Then \[  v_{Z'}-(v_ Z\circ g)-\rho _{E_ g}  \] is represented by a smooth function. In particular, \[  v_{Z'}\preceq v_ Z\circ g  \] in the sense of definition 1.12.1 , and the two ordinary singularity types are equal if and only if $E_ g=0$. Proof. Global logarithmic potentials exist: choose smooth Hermitian metrics on the line bundles of the prime components of $E_ g$, let $\alpha _{E_ g}$ be the corresponding weighted sum of their curvature forms, and let $\rho _{E_ g}$ be the weighted sum of the logarithms of the squared norms of the canonical sections. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho _{E_ g}=[E_ g]-\alpha _{E_ g},  \] and any two global logarithmic potentials differ by a smooth function, by lemma 1.17.3 . We may therefore use this choice. The function $\rho _{E_ g}$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic and bounded above on the compact manifold $Z'$. The chosen decompositions and ( 23.5 ) give \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (v_{Z'}-v_ Z\circ g-\rho _{E_ g}\bigr ) =g^*B_ Z+\alpha _{E_ g}-B_{Z'},  \] which is smooth. By lemma 1.17.3 , this difference of locally integrable functions is represented by a smooth function. The resulting equality of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions extends from almost everywhere to everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . Since $\rho _{E_ g}$ is bounded above, this gives the ordinary domination. If $E_ g=0$, the smooth difference gives ordinary equivalence. Conversely, ordinary equivalence would give equal generic Lelong numbers along every prime divisor of $Z'$, whereas the identity just proved shows that along a prime component of $E_ g$ these numbers differ by its positive coefficient. Hence ordinary equivalence forces $E_ g=0$. $\square$ When $\theta $ is closed, the positive residual currents $R_ Z$ constructed in the proof of proposition 23.4.3 , and their Bott–Chern classes, satisfy \[  \begin{split}  R_{Z'}& =g^*R_ Z-[E_ g],\\  \mathbb A_{Z'}(u;Y,\theta ) & =g^*\mathbb A_ Z(u;Y,\theta )-\{ [E_ g]\} _{\mathrm{BC}}. \end{split}  \] Indeed, the smooth background and the common trace potential pull back, while ( 23.5 ) gives the change in the subtracted divisorial current. The correction $\{ [E_ g]\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$ accounts for the additional divisorial vanishing prescribed on the higher model. This is consistent with the exact pullback of the trace envelope in theorem 19.6.3 , since the envelope imposes the trace inequalities on all models at once. The following example shows that the correction can be nonzero even when the trace data are realized exactly by a potential. Example 23.8.3 . Let $Y=\mathbb P^2$ with homogeneous coordinates $[t_0:t_1:t_2]$, let $\sigma $ be the Fubini–Study form normalized by $\int _ Y\sigma ^2=1$, and choose $a\in \mathbb Q_{>0}$. Put \[  u=a\log \frac{|t_1|^2+|t_2|^2}{|t_0|^2+|t_1|^2+|t_2|^2},  \] and take the ambient manifold to be $Y$ itself. Then $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,a\sigma )$. It has analytic singularities, with its only pole at $p=[1:0:0]$, and zero generic Lelong number on $Y$. By proposition 19.2.1 , its trace data are given by the generic Lelong numbers of its pullbacks: $\tau _{Y,u}(E)=\nu (u\circ \pi ,E)$ for every prime divisor $E$ on a smooth compact modification $\pi $ of $Y$. Since $u$ has no divisorial poles on $Y$, we have $S_ Y=0$, whose canonical ordinary type is that of a smooth function. If $\pi :\widetilde Y\to Y$ is the blowup at $p$ with exceptional curve $F$, then \[  S_{\widetilde Y}=a[F],\qquad E_\pi =aF.  \] Indeed, on either standard chart of the blowup, the numerator is the squared modulus of the exceptional coordinate times a smooth positive function, so the pole order is $a$ along $F$ and zero along every other prime divisor. Thus the trace data are realized exactly by $u$, although $E_\pi \neq 0$. The exceptional difference does not obstruct exact realization; it prevents the identification of the realizing potential with the canonical ordinary type of the divisorial part on the original model, which here is smooth. The same phenomenon occurs on a manifold without the bounded mass property. Let $(W,\omega _ W)$ be a compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $k$ that fails the bounded mass property, such as the Hopf threefold of theorem 8.0.1 , and pull $u$ back to $Y\times W$; take both the ambient manifold and the submanifold to be $Y\times W$. The pole set of the pullback is $\{ p\} \times W$, of codimension two, and the modification $\widetilde Y\times W\to Y\times W$ has exceptional coefficient $a$ along $F\times W$. Analytic restriction again shows that the trace data are realized exactly. Let $\operatorname {pr}_ Y$ and $\operatorname {pr}_ W$ be the two product projections. Choose smooth $\omega _ W$-plurisubharmonic functions $H_ j$ whose masses tend to infinity. For the Hermitian form $\Omega =\operatorname {pr}_ Y^*\sigma +\operatorname {pr}_ W^*\omega _ W$, the pullbacks of the $H_ j$ have masses \[  \binom {k+2}{2}\left(\int _ Y\sigma ^2\right) \left(\int _ W(\omega _ W+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ k\right)\longrightarrow +\infty ,  \] by the binomial expansion of smooth forms and the dimensions of the two factors. Hence the product also fails the bounded mass property. The pulled-back potential belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(Y\times W,C\Omega )$ for every $C\geq \max \{ a,1\} $, since its curvature is bounded below by $-a\operatorname {pr}_ Y^*\sigma $. Scaling the smooth functions $H_ j$ by $C$ shows that $C\Omega $ also has unbounded mass.

title: 24 Classes with a nonclosed background
text: 24 Classes with a nonclosed background Let $Y$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $Y$, and let $\pi :Z\to Y$ denote a smooth compact modification. When the background $\theta $ is not closed, subtracting a closed divisorial current from its pullback leaves the exterior derivative unchanged, so the residual currents of chapter 23 are not closed and define no Bott–Chern class. They do define classes in an affine space over Bott–Chern cohomology, since two representatives with the same exterior derivative differ by a closed current. The trace envelope still gives positive residual representatives, and the exceptional divisors of section 23.8 describe how the classes change between models. Analytic singularities give nef Cartier realizations in these affine spaces. For a general potential, analytic regularization gives such realizations in slightly larger backgrounds, and on each fixed model the positive residual currents converge weakly. The error in the background tends to zero smoothly, but removing it can destroy nefness. Nor does this linear convergence control Monge–Ampère mass: for a Hermitian background with unbounded upper mass, a potential of infinite mass can have the same residual classes as the zero potential, whose classes are realized by a smooth positive form.

title: 24.1 Affine classes with prescribed derivative
text: 24.1 Affine classes with prescribed derivative Two real $(1,1)$-currents on $Z$ with exterior derivative $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $ differ by a closed current, and modulo $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of global distributions such differences are Bott–Chern classes. Let $\mathcal D'(Z,\mathbb R)$ denote the space of real distributions on $Z$, and set \[  \mathscr A_ Z(\theta )= \frac{\{ \pi ^*\theta +C:C\text{ is a closed real }(1,1)\text{-current on }Z\} }{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\mathcal D'(Z,\mathbb R)}.  \] Write $\{ T\} $ for the class of $T$ in this space. By lemma 23.4.1 , every class has a smooth representative, and translation by Bott–Chern classes gives \[  \mathscr A_ Z(\theta )=\{ \pi ^*\theta \} +H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R).  \] A smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ represents an element of $\mathscr A_ Z(\theta )$ exactly when $\mathrm{d}\eta =\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $. As for Bott–Chern classes, pullback of a class is defined on a smooth representative and pushforward on current representatives. Proposition 24.1.1 . If $g:Z'\to Z$ is a compact modification over $Y$, pushforward and pullback induce maps \[  g_*:\mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta )\to \mathscr A_ Z(\theta ), \qquad g^*:\mathscr A_ Z(\theta )\to \mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta ), \qquad g_*g^*=\mathrm{id}.  \] Pushforward preserves classes with positive current representatives. Proof. Write $\pi '=\pi \circ g$. Translation by the pulled-back background identifies the required maps with the Bott–Chern maps of section 23.4 . Indeed, for a closed current $C'$ on $Z'$ and a smooth closed form $\beta $ on $Z$, \[  g_*(\pi '^*\theta +C')=\pi ^*\theta +g_*C',\qquad g^*(\pi ^*\theta +\beta )=\pi '^*\theta +g^*\beta ,  \] where the first equality uses the change of variables formula for the degree-one map $g$ on the smooth background. Since the Bott–Chern maps are well defined on the closed terms, these identities define the affine maps independently of the representatives. Their composition is the identity because $g_*g^*$ is the identity both on the background and on Bott–Chern classes. Finally, pushforward under a proper map preserves positive currents. $\square$ The prescribed derivative is essential for this pushforward: $g_*\pi '^*\mathrm{d}\theta =\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $ is smooth, whereas the pushforward of an arbitrary smooth exact form can be a singular current. We call a family $(\mathbb A_ Z)$, with $\mathbb A_ Z\in \mathscr A_ Z(\theta )$ for every model $Z$ and compatible with pushforward, a b-divisor class over the background $\theta $ . Pseudoeffectivity and Cartier realizations are defined as in definition 23.4.2 , with affine classes in place of Bott–Chern classes. A class in $\mathscr A_ Z(\theta )$ is nef if, for a Hermitian form $\gamma $ on $Z$, it has for every $\epsilon >0$ a smooth representative bounded below by $-\epsilon \gamma $, as in section 23.6 .

title: 24.2 Residual trace classes
text: 24.2 Residual trace classes Since the trace envelope dominates the trace currents on every model, subtracting them from its curvature current gives positive residual representatives, with exterior derivative $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $. The classes are determined by the prescribed trace currents, even when the envelope has larger Lelong numbers. In this section, $Y$ is a complex submanifold of a connected compact complex manifold $X$. Let $\Theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ with $\Theta |_ Y=\theta $, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Theta )$ have generic Lelong number $\nu (u,Y)=0$. We use the trace currents $S_ Z(u;Y)$ of section 23.1 , now with $\Theta $ in the role of the ambient background. Theorem 24.2.1 . The family defined by \[  \mathbb B_ Z(u;Y,\theta ) =\{ \pi ^*\theta -S_ Z(u;Y)\} \in \mathscr A_ Z(\theta )  \] is a pseudoeffective b-divisor class over $\theta $. It is unchanged by ambient multiplier-ideal equivalence and, after the resulting affine spaces are identified, by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of the restricted background. Proof. The currents $S_ Z$ are closed, so the classes belong to the indicated affine spaces, and their compatibility follows from theorem 23.2.1 , proposition 24.1.1 . Take $v=\mathcal T_\theta (u;Y)$, the trace envelope of ( 19.7 ). By proposition 23.3.1 , \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ \pi )-S_ Z(u;Y)\geq 0  \] on every model, which proves pseudoeffectivity in the original restricted background. The currents $S_ Z$ depend only on the ambient multiplier ideals. For a smooth real function $f$ on $Y$, the change $\theta \mapsto \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ adds $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f\circ \pi )$ to every representative, which is zero in the quotient. This proves both invariances. $\square$ When $\theta $ is closed, this family is the Bott–Chern family of proposition 23.4.3 . On a higher model, the trace current can exceed the pullback of the trace current from a lower model. The effective exceptional difference of theorem 23.8.1 therefore translates the residual class, and the translation preserves the prescribed exterior derivative. Corollary 24.2.2 . Let $g:Z'\to Z$ be a compact modification over $Y$, and let $E_ g$ be the effective exceptional divisor of theorem 23.8.1 . The trace classes of theorem 24.2.1 satisfy \[  \mathbb B_{Z'}(u;Y,\theta ) =g^*\mathbb B_ Z(u;Y,\theta )-\{ [E_ g]\} _{\mathrm{BC}},  \] where the Bott–Chern class on the right acts by translation on the affine space $\mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta )$. Proof. Let $\pi :Z\to Y$ be the structure map and put $\pi '=\pi \circ g$. Abbreviate $S_ Z=S_ Z(u;Y)$, and use lemma 1.17.3 to write $S_ Z=B_ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ Z$ with $B_ Z$ smooth and closed and $v_ Z$ quasi-plurisubharmonic. The affine class $\mathbb B_ Z$ has the smooth representative $\pi ^*\theta -B_ Z$. Its pullback is therefore the class of $\pi '^*\theta -g^*S_ Z$, since the two representatives differ by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ Z\circ g)$. Substituting $S_{Z'}=g^*S_ Z+[E_ g]$ gives the asserted identity. Both representatives have exterior derivative $\pi '^*\mathrm{d}\theta $, because the subtracted currents are closed, so the subtraction takes place within $\mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta )$. $\square$ The cocycle identity ( 23.6 ) makes these translations compatible with composition of modifications, and by theorem 23.8.1 their analytic-ideal approximants converge in total variation of the trace measures. On the other hand, theorem 19.6.3 identifies the trace envelopes on the models with pullbacks of the original trace envelope. The exceptional translation accounts for the additional divisorial subtraction on the higher model; it is consistent with this exact pullback of the envelope, and it can be nonzero even when the trace data are realized exactly, as in example 23.8.3 . For the rest of the chapter, the ambient manifold is $Y$ itself, and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$. For a smooth compact modification $\pi :Z\to Y$, we write $N_ Z(u)$ for the divisorial current of $u\circ \pi $ and $\mathbb D_\theta (u)$ for the resulting residual family. By the self-trace identity of lemma 23.5.1 , \[  N_ Z(u)=\sum _ E\nu (u\circ \pi ,E)[E]=S_ Z(u;Y), \qquad \mathbb D_\theta (u)_ Z=\{ \pi ^*\theta -N_ Z(u)\} ,  \] where $E$ ranges over the prime divisors on $Z$. By theorem 24.2.1 , $\mathbb D_\theta (u)$ is pseudoeffective. In this case divisorial removal gives the positive representative $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi )-N_ Z(u)\geq 0$ directly, by lemma 1.17.1 and passage to the limit of increasing finite sums.

title: 24.3 Nef realizations and residual-current limits
text: 24.3 Nef realizations and residual-current limits On a resolution of an analytic singularity, the bounded residual potential has smooth approximants with arbitrarily small curvature error, and these prove nefness within the same affine class. Boundedness also prevents new divisorial terms on further modifications, which gives the Cartier realization. Proposition 24.3.1 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ has analytic singularities, then $\mathbb D_\theta (u)$ has a nef Cartier realization on a smooth compact modification. Proof. Resolve the analytic singularity ideal as in the proof of theorem 23.6.2 . On a suitable model $\pi :Z\to Y$ we obtain \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi )=[D]+R, \qquad R=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0,  \] where $D$ is a finite effective rational divisor, $\beta $ is smooth with $\mathrm{d}\beta =\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $, and $v$ is globally bounded after the choice of metrics on the line bundles of the components of $D$. Positivity of $R$ follows from divisorial removal. Fix a Hermitian form $\gamma $ on $Z$ and apply proposition 1.10.1 to $v$ in the smooth background $\beta $. It gives smooth functions $v_ j$ with $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq -\epsilon _ j\gamma $ and $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. These forms represent the same affine class and have exterior derivative $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $, which proves nefness. On every further modification $g:Z'\to Z$, the current $g^*\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ g)$ is positive by lemma 1.22.1 . Its bounded potential has zero Lelong numbers, so the divisorial part of the full pullback is exactly $g^*D$. The residual affine class on $Z'$ is therefore $g^*\{ R\} $, which proves the Cartier realization. $\square$ For general $u$, add twice the curvature error of analytic regularization to the background. This gives positive currents with analytic singularities, to which the proposition applies, while the ideal orders identify the limiting residual family. Theorem 24.3.2 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ and fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $Y$. There are potentials $u_ m$ with analytic singularities, converging to $u$ in $L^1(Y)$, and positive numbers $\epsilon _ m\downarrow 0$, indexed by sufficiently large positive integers $m$, such that \[  \theta _ m=\theta +2\epsilon _ m\omega , \qquad \theta _ m+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ m\geq \epsilon _ m\omega .  \] For each $m$, the family $\mathbb D_{\theta _ m}(u_ m)$ has a nef Cartier realization. On every fixed compact model $\pi :Z\to Y$, its class has the current representative \[  C_{m,Z}=\pi ^*\theta +2\epsilon _ m\pi ^*\omega -D_{m,Z}, \qquad D_{m,Z}=\frac1m\sum _ E\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(mu)[E],  \] where $E$ ranges over the prime divisors on $Z$ and the order is computed after pulling the ideal back to $Z$. These representatives satisfy \[  C_{m,Z}\longrightarrow \pi ^*\theta -N_ Z(u) \quad \hbox{weakly as currents},  \] and the positive residual representatives satisfy \[  R_{m,Z}:=C_{m,Z}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ m\circ \pi ) \longrightarrow \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi )-N_ Z(u)\geq 0 \quad \hbox{weakly as currents}.  \] The exterior derivatives of both $C_{m,Z}$ and $R_{m,Z}$ converge smoothly to $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $. Proof. Take $u_ m$ from corollary 1.15.2 ; they converge to $u$ in $L^1$. If $e_ m\to 0$ are their curvature errors, put $\epsilon _ m=\sup _{\ell \geq m}e_\ell +1/m$. These numbers are positive and decrease to zero, and the indices $m$ are unchanged. Adding $2\epsilon _ m\omega $ to the background turns the lower bound $-\epsilon _ m\omega $ into $\epsilon _ m\omega $. Since each $u_ m$ has analytic type $(1/m,\mathcal I(mu))$, proposition 24.3.1 gives a nef Cartier realization in the background $\theta _ m$. On a fixed model, the generic divisorial Lelong numbers of $u_ m\circ \pi $ are exactly $m^{-1}\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(mu)$, so $N_ Z(u_ m)=D_{m,Z}$ and $C_{m,Z}=\pi ^*\theta _ m-N_ Z(u_ m)$ represents the class of $\mathbb D_{\theta _ m}(u_ m)$ on $Z$. The self-trace identity and theorem 23.1.1 give $D_{m,Z}\to N_ Z(u)$ in the trace mass of section 23.1 , hence weakly as currents. Since the smooth error $2\epsilon _ m\pi ^*\omega $ tends to zero with all its derivatives, $C_{m,Z}$ converges as stated. Divisorial removal gives $R_{m,Z}\geq 0$. All the $u_ m$ and $u$ have a common smooth lower curvature bound: choose $A>0$ with $\theta +\epsilon _ m\omega \leq A\omega $ for every index $m$ considered. By lemma 1.22.13 , the convergence in $L^1(Y)$ implies $u_ m\circ \pi \to u\circ \pi $ in $L^1(Z)$. Applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ and adding the convergent currents $C_{m,Z}$ proves the convergence of the residual currents, and positivity persists in the weak limit. Finally, since each $D_{m,Z}$ is closed, \[  \mathrm{d}R_{m,Z}=\mathrm{d}C_{m,Z} =\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta +2\epsilon _ m\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\omega ,  \] which proves the smooth convergence of the exterior derivatives. $\square$ The classes $\mathbb D_{\theta _ m}(u_ m)_ Z$ lie in $\mathscr A_ Z(\theta _ m)$. Translation by $-2\epsilon _ m\pi ^*\omega $ identifies this space with $\mathscr A_ Z(\theta )$, but subtracting this form need not preserve nefness. Thus the convergence of currents above does not give an approximation by nef Cartier classes with exactly the prescribed exterior derivative.

title: 24.4 Divisorial classes and infinite mass
text: 24.4 Divisorial classes and infinite mass Now let the background be a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $Y$, with upper mass $v_+(\omega )$ (definition 6.5.1 ) and extended Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega $ (theorem 6.1.2 ). When $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, the potential of theorem 6.6.1 has the same multiplier ideals as a smooth potential. The two potentials therefore have the same residual classes on every model, while their extended masses differ. Proposition 24.4.1 . If $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, there is $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\omega )$ such that \[  \mathbb D_\omega (U)=\mathbb D_\omega (0),\qquad \int _ Y\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)=+\infty , \qquad \int _ Y\omega ^ n<+\infty .  \] The common family has the nef Cartier realization $(Y,\{ \omega \} )$. Proof. Take $U$ from theorem 6.6.1 . All its multiplier ideals at positive weights are trivial, so every divisorial order in $D_{m,Z}$ vanishes on every model. The self-trace identity gives $N_ Z(U)=0$, which is also the divisorial part of the zero potential. Both families therefore consist of the pullbacks of the class of $\omega $. Since $\omega $ is smooth and positive, its affine class is nef and realizes the family on $Y$ itself. The extended mass of $U$ is infinite by construction, whereas the smooth measure $\omega ^ n$ has finite mass because $Y$ is compact. $\square$

title: 25 Envelope systems over Hermitian perturbations
text: 25 Envelope systems over Hermitian perturbations Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and fix real numbers $a<c$. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the multiplier-ideal envelope $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ of definition 16.2.1 is the regularized supremum of the nonpositive $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions with the multiplier ideals of $u$. It depends on the background $\theta $. When $\theta $ is perturbed by Hermitian forms, the envelopes of one multiplier-ideal class in the perturbed backgrounds form a compatible family, and as the perturbation tends to zero these normalized representatives decrease to a potential in the original background. Projecting the limit back to the perturbed backgrounds recovers the family exactly when the limit keeps the multiplier ideals of the family; otherwise it gives the greatest family below it that comes from the original background. We apply this to test curves that are constant for parameters $\tau \leq a$ and have cutoff $c$. Recovery can fail even in a Kähler background: on a ruled surface, at zero volume, the limit acquires an additional divisorial pole. On the other hand, for big backgrounds on manifolds with the bounded mass property, recovery holds by theorem 30.5.6 when the lower volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}$ of the initial slices (definition 13.3.1 ) have a positive limit. On the Hopf threefold, scalar invariance along the elliptic fibers instead allows recovery from positive lower volume on the projective base, by theorem 25.6.3 , even though ambient upper mass is unbounded. Smooth changes of the background commute with recovery, whereas the limiting Monge–Ampère mass can change when the background is not closed. We also use the ordinary singularity envelope $P_\theta [u]$ of definition 1.19.4 , the ordinary and multiplier-ideal singularity orders of section 1.12 , and the extended Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ of theorem 6.1.2 . A potential $u$ with $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=u$ is called $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed.

title: 25.1 Curves constant on a left half-line
search_title: Curves constant on a left half-line
text: 25.1 Curves constant on a left half-line We restrict the envelope test curves of definition 18.1.1 by requiring that each slice be fixed by the multiplier-ideal envelope and that the curve be constant for $\tau \leq a$. Constancy identifies the initial potential explicitly as $\Gamma _ a$, and it confines the associated ray between the translates of this potential by $at$ and by $ct$. Definition 25.1.1 . Let $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$ be the set of families $\Gamma =(\Gamma _\tau )_{\tau <c}$ such that $\Gamma _\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $P_\theta [\Gamma _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}=\Gamma _\tau $ for every $\tau <c$; the family is pointwise concave and decreasing in $\tau $; $\Gamma _\tau =\Gamma _ a$ for $\tau \leq a$. The cutoff of $\Gamma $ is $c$, and we extend $\Gamma $ by $\Gamma _ c=\lim _{\tau \uparrow c}\Gamma _\tau $ and $\Gamma _\tau =-\infty $ for $\tau >c$. Such curves are ordered by the pointwise order of their slices $\Gamma _\tau $, $\tau <c$. Every slice has supremum zero by theorem 16.2.2 . Hence, by theorem 1.4.2 , corollary 1.4.3 , the decreasing limit $\Gamma _ c$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; in particular, it is not identically $-\infty $. It is also $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed. Indeed, $\Gamma _ c\leq 0$ is a competitor for its own envelope, and $\Gamma _ c\leq \Gamma _\tau $, so the order preservation of proposition 16.2.6 gives \[  \Gamma _ c\leq P_\theta [\Gamma _ c]_{\mathcal I}\leq \Gamma _\tau \quad (\tau <c).  \] Taking the infimum over $\tau $ proves equality. Its Legendre transform \[  U_ t=\Bigl (\sup _{\tau <c}(\Gamma _\tau +t\tau )\Bigr )^*\qquad (t>0)  \] is an envelope ray with initial potential $\varphi $ and slope $c$, in the sense of definition 18.1.2 , and satisfies \[  \varphi +at\leq U_ t\leq \varphi +ct\qquad (t>0).  \] In particular $U_ t\sim \varphi $ for every $t>0$. title: Definition 25.1.1
text: Definition 25.1.1 . title: 25.2 Transition maps and envelope systems
text: 25.2 Transition maps and envelope systems Curves over different backgrounds are related by projecting each slice to the ideal envelope in the larger background. For these projections to form a consistent system, projecting in two steps must agree with projecting directly. This follows because each projection preserves multiplier ideals, while in each background a multiplier-ideal class has a unique representative fixed by the ideal envelope. The same fact gives injectivity: equal projected slices have equal multiplier ideals, hence come from equal fixed representatives. Proposition 25.2.1 . Let $\beta \geq \theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Slicewise projection, $\Gamma \mapsto (P_\beta [\Gamma _\tau ]_{\mathcal I})_{\tau <c}$, defines an injective and order-preserving map \[  P_\beta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}:\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )\longrightarrow \mathscr T_{a,c}(\beta ).  \] For every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\beta '$ with $\beta \geq \beta '\geq \theta $, these maps satisfy \[  P_\beta \bigl [P_{\beta '}[\Gamma ]_{\mathcal I}\bigr ]_{\mathcal I}=P_\beta [\Gamma ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Proof. Since $\beta \geq \theta $, every slice is $\beta $-plurisubharmonic, and by theorem 16.2.2 its projection is a $\beta $-plurisubharmonic function fixed by $P_\beta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$. Decreasingness, constancy for $\tau \leq a$, and order preservation follow from proposition 16.2.6 . For concavity, let $r,t<c$ and $0<s<1$, and put $\tau =(1-s)r+s t$. By the same proposition and the concavity of the original curve, \[  \begin{split}  (1-s)P_\beta [\Gamma _ r]_{\mathcal I}+sP_\beta [\Gamma _ t]_{\mathcal I} & \leq P_\beta [(1-s)\Gamma _ r+s\Gamma _ t]_{\mathcal I}\\ & \leq P_\beta [\Gamma _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}. \end{split}  \] Here the first inequality follows by combining the scaling and addition formulas of that proposition, with backgrounds $(1-s)\beta $ and $s\beta $. Each projection preserves the multiplier ideals at every weight. Hence the two sides of the transition identity are $P_\beta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed representatives of the same multiplier-ideal class, and they are equal. If two projected curves agree, their original slices have the same multiplier ideals; since those slices are $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed, they agree as well. This proves injectivity. $\square$ Let $\mathscr H(X)$ denote the set of Hermitian forms on $X$; for $\eta \in \mathscr H(X)$ we also write $\eta >0$. Definition 25.2.2 . An envelope system over $\theta $ , with parameters $a<c$, is a family \[  \boldsymbol \Gamma =(\Gamma ^\eta )_{\eta \in \mathscr H(X)}, \qquad \Gamma ^\eta \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta +\eta ),  \] such that 25.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hermitian-system-compatibility} \Gamma ^\eta =P_{\theta +\eta }[\Gamma ^{\eta '}]_{\mathcal I} \quad \hbox{whenever }\eta \geq \eta '. \end{equation} Write $\mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )$ for the set of these systems, ordered componentwise. For $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$, set \[  \mathsf E(\Gamma )^\eta =P_{\theta +\eta }[\Gamma ]_{\mathcal I} \qquad (\eta \in \mathscr H(X)).  \] A system is realized in the background $\theta $ if it equals $\mathsf E(\Gamma )$ for some $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$. By the transition proposition, $\mathsf E(\Gamma )$ is an envelope system, and the map $\mathsf E$ is injective. All components of an envelope system have the same multiplier ideals at each $\tau <c$: compare two components $\Gamma ^\eta $ and $\Gamma ^{\eta '}$ with the component indexed by $\eta +\eta '$. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the constant family $\Gamma _\tau =P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, $\tau <c$, with cutoff $c$, lies in $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$, and its projections form the envelope system $\mathsf E(\Gamma )$.

title: 25.3 The limiting curve and recovery
text: 25.3 The limiting curve and recovery Every Hermitian form dominates all sufficiently small multiples of a fixed Hermitian form. A single decreasing sequence of components therefore determines the limit of the whole system. Projecting the resulting curve back gives the greatest realized system below the original one, and strict inequality means that recovery fails. Theorem 25.3.1 . Fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, and let $j$ range over the positive integers. For every $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )$ and every $\tau <c$, the sequence $\Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau $ decreases, and its limit \[  (\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau =\lim _{j\to \infty }\Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau  \] is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, in particular not identically $-\infty $. These limits define an element $\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $ of $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$, which does not depend on $h$. The maps $\mathsf E$ and $\mathsf R$ satisfy \[  \mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}, \qquad \mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma ) \leq \boldsymbol \Gamma .  \] Both maps preserve order. More precisely, 25.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hermitian-system-order-adjunction} \mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \boldsymbol \Gamma \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \Gamma \leq \mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma . \end{equation} Thus $\mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma )$ is the greatest system below $\boldsymbol \Gamma $ that is realized in the original background. Proof. Step 1: the limit. Fix $\tau <c$ and put $q_ j=\Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau $. By compatibility, $q_ j=P_{\theta +h/j}[q_{j+1}]_{\mathcal I}$, and $q_{j+1}\leq 0$ is a competitor for this envelope; hence $q_ j\geq q_{j+1}$. The functions $q_ j$ have supremum zero and a common smooth lower curvature bound. By theorem 1.4.2 , corollary 1.4.3 , their decreasing limit $q$ is not identically $-\infty $ and has supremum zero. Passing to the limit in the distributional inequalities \[  \theta +h/j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ j\geq 0  \] gives $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The defining family of an ideal envelope grows when the background increases. Together with $q\leq q_ j$ and order preservation, this gives \[  q\leq P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_{\theta +h/j}[q]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_{\theta +h/j}[q_ j]_{\mathcal I}=q_ j.  \] Taking the infimum over $j$ proves $P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I}=q$. Concavity, decreasingness and constancy on the left half-line pass to the pointwise limits, so these limits form a curve in $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$. Step 2: independence of $h$. For every $\eta >0$ there is $j$ with $h/j\leq \eta $, and compatibility then gives $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau \geq \Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau $. Consequently \[  (\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau =\inf _{\eta \in \mathscr H(X)}\Gamma ^\eta _\tau ,  \] which proves that $\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $ does not depend on $h$. This formula also shows that $\mathsf R$ preserves order. Step 3: the two compositions. Write $q=(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau $. Since $q\leq \Gamma ^\eta _\tau $ and $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $ is fixed by its envelope, order preservation gives $P_{\theta +\eta }[q]_{\mathcal I}\leq \Gamma ^\eta _\tau $. This proves $\mathsf E\mathsf R\leq \mathrm{id}$. Now start with a curve $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$. Its slice $\Gamma _\tau $ is a competitor in every larger background, so \[  \Gamma _\tau \leq (\mathsf R\mathsf E\Gamma )_\tau \leq P_{\theta +\eta }[\Gamma _\tau ]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\eta >0).  \] The two outer terms have the same multiplier ideals, so the two ideal inclusions given by these inequalities show that the middle term has those ideals as well. Since both the middle term and $\Gamma _\tau $ are $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed, they are equal. This proves $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$. Step 4: the adjunction. By the transition proposition, $\mathsf E$ preserves order. If $\mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \boldsymbol \Gamma $, applying $\mathsf R$ gives $\Gamma =\mathsf R\mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $. Conversely, if $\Gamma \leq \mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $, applying $\mathsf E$ and using $\mathsf E\mathsf R\leq \mathrm{id}$ gives $\mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \boldsymbol \Gamma $. This proves ( 25.4 ), and the final maximality assertion follows from it. $\square$ Proposition 25.3.2 . A system $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )$ is realized in $\theta $ if and only if, for every $\tau <c$, its limiting slice $(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau $ is multiplier-ideal equivalent to one, and hence every, slice $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $. Proof. For a realized system, this follows from $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$ and the preservation of multiplier ideals by each projection. Conversely, the assumed equivalence and the fact that $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $ is fixed by its envelope in the larger background give \[  P_{\theta +\eta }[(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau ]_{\mathcal I} =\Gamma ^\eta _\tau .  \] Thus the system equals $\mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma )$. $\square$ By theorem 1.16.3 , multiplier-ideal equivalence means equality of all Lelong numbers on all local modifications. Recovery therefore holds exactly when the limiting slices keep these Lelong numbers. They are the same for all components of a system, whereas the limiting slice can have larger values: in the ruled-surface example of section 25.5 , one of them increases from zero to one. For big backgrounds on manifolds with the bounded mass property, theorem 30.5.6 excludes such an increase when the initial slices have positive limiting lower volume. When $X$ is Kähler, the Kähler forms are cofinal among the Hermitian forms: a sufficiently small positive multiple of a fixed Kähler form lies below any given Hermitian form. The compatibility condition therefore determines a system by its components indexed by Kähler forms. Conversely, every compatible family indexed by Kähler forms extends uniquely to a system: for $\eta >0$, choose a Kähler form $\kappa \leq \eta $ and set $\Gamma ^\eta =P_{\theta +\eta }[\Gamma ^\kappa ]_{\mathcal I}$. Two choices of $\kappa $ give the same result, as one sees by passing to a common smaller Kähler form and using the transition identity.

title: 25.4 Changes of representative and limiting mass
search_title: Changes of representative and limiting mass
text: 25.4 Changes of representative and limiting mass Subtracting a smooth function transports a curve to a new background, and projection restores the envelope normalization. The gauge estimate is uniform in the perturbation, so this transport also respects the limiting curve. The limiting Monge–Ampère mass behaves differently: in a nonclosed background, it can change even for the system all of whose slices are zero. Proposition 25.4.1 . Let $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. For $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$ and $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )$, the formulas \[  (\mathsf G_ f\Gamma )_\tau =P_{\theta '}[\Gamma _\tau -f]_{\mathcal I}, \qquad (\mathsf G_ f\boldsymbol \Gamma )^\eta _\tau =P_{\theta '+\eta }[\Gamma ^\eta _\tau -f]_{\mathcal I}  \] define bijections $\mathsf G_ f:\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )\to \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta ')$ and $\mathsf G_ f:\mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )\to \mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta ')$. They satisfy the cocycle law $\mathsf G_ g\mathsf G_ f=\mathsf G_{f+g}$, where $\mathsf G_ g$ is formed in the background $\theta '$, and they commute with $\mathsf E$ and $\mathsf R$. Proof. Subtracting $f$ changes the background from $\theta $ to $\theta '$ and preserves concavity, decreasingness and constancy on the left half-line. Slicewise projection preserves these properties by the argument of proposition 25.2.1 . Since $f$ is smooth, every new slice has the multiplier ideals of the original one. Applying the construction with $-f$ therefore gives a $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed slice with the same ideals as the original slice, hence the original slice itself. This proves that $\mathsf G_{-f}$ is the inverse of $\mathsf G_ f$; the same uniqueness of fixed representatives proves the cocycle law. Compatibility of the transformed system and commutation with $\mathsf E$ follow by comparing multiplier ideals in the common final background. For commutation with $\mathsf R$, the gauge estimate of proposition 16.3.1 , applied in each background $\theta +\eta $, gives \[  \Gamma ^\eta _\tau +\min _ Xf \leq (\mathsf G_ f\boldsymbol \Gamma )^\eta _\tau +f \leq \Gamma ^\eta _\tau +\max _ Xf,  \] with constants independent of $\eta $. Pass to the decreasing limits along a cofinal sequence. The new limit has the same ordinary singularity type as the old limit minus $f$, and hence the same multiplier ideals. It is $P_{\theta '}[\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed by theorem 25.3.1 , so it equals $P_{\theta '}[(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau -f]_{\mathcal I}$. This proves commutation with $\mathsf R$. $\square$ For closed backgrounds on a compact Kähler manifold, [ chapter “Non-Archimedean pluripotential theory”, section “The definition of non-Archimedean metrics” , SGPT ] indexes such systems by Kähler perturbations, as above, and defines their volume as a limit of the masses of the initial potentials. Its components are general test curves fixed by the ideal envelope, with initial potentials of positive mass, whereas our curves are constant on a prescribed left half-line and our system spaces impose no mass condition. For nonclosed positive backgrounds, the corresponding limit of masses is not invariant under the gauge bijections. Proposition 25.4.2 . There are a compact complex surface $X$, Hermitian forms $\omega ,h$ on $X$, and a smooth real function $f$ with $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f>0$, with the following property. For every $a<c$ there is a system $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\omega )$ such that the limits \[  \lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\omega +\epsilon h} (\Gamma ^{\epsilon h}_ a), \qquad \lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\omega '+\epsilon h} ((\mathsf G_ f\boldsymbol \Gamma )^{\epsilon h}_ a)  \] both exist and are different. Proof. Take the torus $X$ and the smooth perturbation of proposition 16.3.2 , so that $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is Hermitian and $\int _ X(\omega ')^2\neq \int _ X\omega ^2$, and fix any Hermitian form $h$. In every background $\omega +\eta $, let every slice with $\tau <c$ be zero. This is an envelope system for every $a<c$, since zero is the multiplier-ideal envelope of the unit-ideal class in a positive background. Its first limit is \[  \lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}\int _ X(\omega +\epsilon h)^2 =\int _ X\omega ^2.  \] The gauge bijection sends every slice to $P_{\omega '+\eta }[-f]_{\mathcal I}=0$, since $f$ is smooth and the new background is positive. The second limit is therefore $\int _ X(\omega ')^2$, which is different. $\square$
