There are a compact complex surface $X$, Hermitian forms $\omega ,h$ on $X$, and a smooth real function $f$ with $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f>0$, with the following property. For every $a<c$ there is a system $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\omega )$ such that the limits \[  \lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\omega +\epsilon h} (\Gamma ^{\epsilon h}_ a), \qquad \lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\omega '+\epsilon h} ((\mathsf G_ f\boldsymbol \Gamma )^{\epsilon h}_ a)  \] both exist and are different. Proof. Take the torus $X$ and the smooth perturbation of proposition 16.3.2 , so that $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is Hermitian and $\int _ X(\omega ')^2\neq \int _ X\omega ^2$, and fix any Hermitian form $h$. In every background $\omega +\eta $, let every slice with $\tau <c$ be zero. This is an envelope system for every $a<c$, since zero is the multiplier-ideal envelope of the unit-ideal class in a positive background. Its first limit is \[  \lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}\int _ X(\omega +\epsilon h)^2 =\int _ X\omega ^2.  \] The gauge bijection sends every slice to $P_{\omega '+\eta }[-f]_{\mathcal I}=0$, since $f$ is smooth and the new background is positive. The second limit is therefore $\int _ X(\omega ')^2$, which is different. $\square$

title: 25.5 Failure of recovery in a positive background
search_title: Failure of recovery in a positive background
text:
25.5 Failure of recovery in a positive background We construct a Kähler background on a ruled surface over an elliptic curve and an envelope system that is not realized in this background. The obstruction is a section $D$ of the ruling whose class is nef but contains only one closed positive current, namely $[D]$. Prescribing a logarithmic pole along one fiber in the Kähler background leaves the class of $D$ as the residual class. In every positive perturbation of the background, this class has smooth positive representatives, so the perturbed envelopes have only the fiber pole. In the limit, however, the only positive representative left is $[D]$, so the limiting envelope acquires $D$ as an additional pole, and the residual volume tends to zero. In this section, $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$, and $X$ is the compact ruled surface \[  X=(\mathbb C_ z\times \mathbb P^1_ w)/\sim , \qquad (z,w)\sim (z+1,w),\qquad (z,w)\sim (z+\mathrm i,w+1).  \] These commuting transformations define a holomorphic $\mathbb P^1$-bundle $\pi :X\to E$. Let $D$ be its section $w=\infty $. The function $v=w-\operatorname {Im}z$ is invariant under both transformations and descends to a smooth function on $X\setminus D$. Lemma 25.5.1 . Let $\sigma _0=(\mathrm i/2)\, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z$ be the flat probability form on $E$. There is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta \in c_1(\mathcal O_ X(D))$ whose class is nef and for which \[  \kappa =\theta +\pi ^*\sigma _0  \] is a Kähler form. The only closed positive current of the form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is $[D]$. Proof. Let $s_ D$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O_ X(D)$, with zero divisor $D$. For a real parameter $t>0$, define a smooth Hermitian metric on this line bundle by prescribing the norm of $s_ D$: \[  |s_ D|_ t^2=(1+t|v|^2)^{-1}\quad \hbox{on }X\setminus D.  \] To check that it extends smoothly, use the coordinate $\xi =1/w$ near $D$. The squared norm of a local nonvanishing frame is \[  \bigl (|\xi |^2+t|1-(\operatorname {Im}z)\xi |^2\bigr )^{-1},  \] which is smooth and positive. The prescribed norm is invariant under the transformations on the complement of $D$, so these local extensions define a global metric. Its curvature form is \[  \theta _ t=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+t|v|^2) \quad \hbox{on }X\setminus D.  \] Set $\theta =\theta _1$, and let $\sigma =\sigma _0/\pi $ on $E$, where the denominator is the number $\pi $. We now estimate the curvature from below. Put $r=|v|^2$ and let $H$ be the complex Hessian of $\log (1+tr)$ in the coordinates $(z,w)$. Direct differentiation gives \[  \begin{split}  H_{w\bar w}& =\frac{t}{(1+tr)^2},\\  H_{z\bar w}& =\frac{\mathrm i t(1-tv^2)}{2(1+tr)^2},\\  H_{z\bar z}& =\frac{t}{2(1+tr)} -\frac{t^2(\operatorname {Re}v)^2}{(1+tr)^2}. \end{split}  \] Consequently \[  H_{z\bar z}-\frac{|H_{z\bar w}|^2}{H_{w\bar w}} =\frac{t(1-tr)}{4(1+tr)}\geq -\frac t4.  \] Completing the square gives $\theta _ t\geq -(t/4)\pi ^*\sigma $ on $X\setminus D$, and by continuity this inequality extends across $D$. The restriction of $\theta _ t$ to every fiber is a positive Fubini–Study form, including at infinity. Thus $\theta _ t+A\pi ^*\sigma $ is strictly positive off $D$ whenever $A>t/4$. At $\xi =0$, its coefficient matrix, with the common factor $\mathrm i/(2\pi )$ omitted, is \[  \begin{pmatrix}  A

& \mathrm i/2

\\ -\mathrm i/2

& 1/t

\end{pmatrix}.  \] Its vertical coefficient is positive and its Schur complement is $A-t/4>0$, so the form is strictly positive along $D$ as well. In particular, $\kappa =\theta +\pi ^*\sigma _0$ is Kähler. The function \[  f_ t=\log \frac{1+t|v|^2}{1+|v|^2}  \] extends smoothly across $D$ and satisfies $\theta _ t=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ t$. Letting $t\downarrow 0$ in the curvature lower bound shows that the class of $\theta $ is nef in the sense of section 23.6 . Write $\psi _ D=\log |s_ D|_1^2$. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ D=[D]$. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then $u-\psi _ D$ is plurisubharmonic on $X\setminus D$. Its lift $\Phi (z,w)$ to $\mathbb C^2$ is invariant under the two deck transformations and, since $u$ is bounded above on the compact surface $X$, satisfies \[  \Phi (z,w)\leq C+\log \bigl (1+|w-\operatorname {Im}z|^2\bigr )  \] for some real constant $C$. For each fixed $w$, the function $z\mapsto \Phi (z,w)$ is either identically $-\infty $ or subharmonic. It is $1$-periodic and has logarithmic upper growth, so lemma 1.3.6 makes it constant. Thus $\Phi (z,w)=\phi (w)$, where $\phi $ is a subharmonic function of $w$, not identically $-\infty $. The second deck transformation gives $\phi (w+1)=\phi (w)$, and the bound at $z=0$ gives logarithmic growth, so the same lemma makes $\phi $ constant. Therefore $u=\psi _ D+C$ off $D$, and lemma 1.3.3 extends this equality across $D$. Hence $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=[D]$. $\square$ Fix a point $p\in E$ and let $F=\pi ^{-1}(p)$. The Green-kernel construction in the proof of theorem 19.3.1 gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $g$ on $E$ with $\sigma _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\delta _ p$. Its pullback $\psi _ F=g\circ \pi $ has a logarithmic pole of coefficient one along $F$, and \[  \pi ^*\sigma _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ F=[F].  \] Theorem 25.5.2 . For the Kähler background $\kappa $ of lemma 25.5.1 and every $a<c$, there is a system $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\kappa )$ for which \[  \mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma ) \neq \boldsymbol \Gamma .  \] Every slice $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $, $\tau <c$, of every component has multiplier ideals \[  \mathcal I(t\Gamma ^\eta _\tau ) =\mathcal O_ X(-\lfloor t\rfloor F)\qquad (t>0),  \] whereas its limiting slices have multiplier ideals \[  \mathcal I\bigl (t(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau \bigr ) =\mathcal O_ X(-\lfloor t\rfloor (F+D)).  \] In particular, on the system space $\mathscr S_{a,c}(\kappa )$, which carries no mass condition, $\mathsf E$ is not surjective and $\mathsf R$ is not injective. Proof. For each Hermitian form $\eta $, the nef approximation of lemma 25.5.1 gives a smooth function $f_\eta $ such that $\theta +\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_\eta \geq 0$. Then \[  u_\eta =\psi _ F+f_\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa +\eta ).  \] Let every slice $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $, $\tau <c$, of the component $\Gamma ^\eta $ be $q_\eta =P_{\kappa +\eta }[u_\eta ]_{\mathcal I}$, with cutoff $c$. The multiplier ideals of $q_\eta $ are those of $\psi _ F$ and do not depend on the smooth function $f_\eta $. Hence the compatibility condition follows by comparing these ideals in the larger background, and the constant curves form a system with the required parameters. Let $q$ be its limiting slice under $\mathsf R$, and let $\nu (q,F)$ be its generic Lelong number along $F$. Each $q_\eta $ has generic Lelong number one along $F$, so lemma 1.17.6 , applied to a decreasing cofinal sequence, gives $\nu (q,F)\geq 1$. By lemma 1.17.1 , \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q-[F]\geq 0.  \] By the Poincaré–Lelong identity for $\psi _ F$, this current equals $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q-\psi _ F)$, where the difference $q-\psi _ F$ is first taken as a locally integrable function. Since the current is positive, this difference has a canonical $\theta $-plurisubharmonic representative, and by lemma 25.5.1 it differs from $\psi _ D$ by a constant. Hence \[  q=\psi _ F+\psi _ D+C.  \] The divisors $F$ and $D$ are smooth and meet transversely, since one is a fiber and the other a section. A direct integrability calculation in local product coordinates therefore gives the stated ideals for every real $t>0$. In particular, the Lelong number at a generic point of $D$ has increased from zero to one, and proposition 25.3.2 shows that recovery fails. Finally, since $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$, the system $\boldsymbol \Gamma $ and the realized system $\mathsf E\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma \neq \boldsymbol \Gamma $ have the same image under $\mathsf R$. Thus $\mathsf R$ is not injective, and $\boldsymbol \Gamma $ is not in the image of $\mathsf E$. $\square$ Proposition 25.5.3 . Let $q_\eta $ be the common slice of the component $\Gamma ^\eta $ constructed in the preceding proof. Along the closed perturbations $\eta =\epsilon \kappa $, with real $\epsilon >0$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\kappa +\epsilon \kappa }(q_{\epsilon \kappa }) =2\epsilon \int _ X\theta \wedge \kappa +\epsilon ^2\int _ X\kappa ^2\longrightarrow 0.  \] The limiting slice has zero non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure. Proof. The potential $u_\eta =\psi _ F+f_\eta $ has analytic singularities, so proposition 16.2.7 gives $q_\eta \sim u_\eta \sim \psi _ F$. Removing the divisorial component $[F]$ gives a positive current in the background $\theta +\eta $, whose global potential $w_\eta =q_\eta -\psi _ F$ is bounded by this ordinary equivalence. Off $F$, plurifine locality identifies the Monge–Ampère measure of $q_\eta $ with $(\theta +\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\eta )^2$. This bounded product gives no mass to $F$ by proposition 1.7.1 . For closed $\eta =\epsilon \kappa $, Stokes' theorem gives its total mass as $\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon \kappa )^2$. The normal bundle of $D$ is trivial. Indeed, the transformation $w\mapsto w+1$ becomes $\xi \mapsto \xi /(1+\xi )$, whose derivative at $\xi =0$ is one, and the other transformation fixes $w$. Hence $\int _ X\theta ^2=D^2=0$, and expanding the square gives the formula. The limiting potential has curvature current $[F]+[D]$, which vanishes away from the pluripolar set $F\cup D$; its non-pluripolar measure is therefore zero. $\square$

title: 25.6 Recovery through the Hopf fibration
text: 25.6 Recovery through the Hopf fibration Positive lower volume on a closed base can force recovery even when the ambient manifold has unbounded upper mass. We now take \[  X=(\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \mathrm e^{-1}z\rangle , \qquad B=\mathbb P^2,\qquad \pi :X\to B,  \] and use the geometry of chapter 8 . Write $\kappa =\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, with $\int _ B\kappa ^2=1$, and put \[  s=\log |z|^2,\qquad \alpha =\pi ^*\kappa =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s,\qquad \beta =\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s,\qquad h=\alpha +\beta .  \] The derivatives of $s$ descend to $X$. Scalar multiplication gives an action of the elliptic group $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+2\pi \mathrm i\mathbb Z)$, transitive on each fiber of $\pi $ and preserving $h$. By theorem 8.0.1 , $h$ has unbounded upper mass. Invariant potentials nevertheless reduce to potentials on $B$ because the horizontal part of $h$ is the pullback of $\kappa $. Proposition 25.6.1 . For every $b>0$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,b\kappa )$, \[  P_{bh}[\pi ^*v]_{\mathcal I} =\pi ^*P_{b\kappa }[v]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The envelope on the left uses all ambient competitors. Proof. First, an $E$-invariant $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,bh)$ descends to an upper semicontinuous function $w$ on $B$, since $\pi $ is proper and $q$ is constant on its fibers. In a product chart, Fubini gives $w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, and \[  bh+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=\pi ^*(b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)+b\beta .  \] Lift a smooth base vector to a vector annihilated by $\partial s$. Its pairing with $\beta $ is zero. Testing the positive current above against these lifts and a nonnegative smooth fiber density of integral one proves $b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0$ distributionally. A local potential of $b\kappa $ gives its canonical plurisubharmonic representative. Its pullback agrees almost everywhere with $q$, hence everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . Thus $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,b\kappa )$. Conversely, every such $w$ lifts to a $bh$-plurisubharmonic function by the displayed identity. Now set $q=P_{bh}[\pi ^*v]_{\mathcal I}$. Translation by any $g\in E$ preserves its complete competitor family: it preserves the background, the obstacle zero, and the ideals of the invariant input. The envelope is their greatest member, so $q\circ g=q$. Descend $q=\pi ^*w$ as above. By lemma 1.16.6 , its ideal equivalence to $\pi ^*v$ implies $w\sim _{\mathcal I}v$: a germ pulled back from the base is weighted-integrable in a product chart if and only if the base germ is, by Fubini. Hence $w$ is a base competitor. Every base competitor also lifts to an ambient competitor by the same lemma and the current identity. Taking the greatest members gives equality. $\square$ Fix real numbers $a<c$. For an envelope system $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(h)$, scalar invariance alone supplies the whole transverse system, including its components over nonclosed base perturbations. Lemma 25.6.2 . Suppose $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}$ is $E$-invariant for every $\epsilon >0$ and $\tau <c$. There is a unique envelope system $\boldsymbol \Psi \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\kappa )$ such that \[  \Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=\pi ^*\Psi _\tau ^{\epsilon \kappa } \quad (\epsilon >0,\  \tau <c).  \] Writing $\Gamma =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $ and $\psi =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Psi $, we have $\Gamma _\tau =\pi ^*\psi _\tau $ for every $\tau <c$. Proof. The descent in proposition 25.6.1 gives $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=\pi ^*\phi _\tau ^\epsilon $ with $\phi _\tau ^\epsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,(1+\epsilon )\kappa )$. Normalization, decrease, concavity and constancy for $\tau \leq a$ descend pointwise. The fiber-envelope identity descends both ideal-model fixedness and scalar compatibility: \[  \phi _\tau ^{\epsilon _2} =P_{(1+\epsilon _2)\kappa } [\phi _\tau ^{\epsilon _1}]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\epsilon _2\geq \epsilon _1>0).  \] In particular, the positive scalar slices have the same ideals at every weight. For a Hermitian form $\xi >0$ on $B$, choose $\delta >0$ with $\delta \kappa \leq \xi $, fixed for the whole parameter interval, and define \[  \Psi _\tau ^\xi =P_{\kappa +\xi } [\phi _\tau ^\delta ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The definition is independent of $\delta $ because the scalar inputs have the same ideals. It reproduces the scalar components, and proposition 25.2.1 proves that each component is a curve in $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\kappa +\xi )$. Projection preserves the ideals, so comparing the complete competitor families proves compatibility for $\xi \geq \xi '$. Thus $\boldsymbol \Psi $ is a full envelope system. Every possible extension is forced by this formula, which proves uniqueness. The retraction theorem applies to both systems. Taking their decreasing limits along $h/j$ and $\kappa /j$ in the scalar identity gives $\Gamma _\tau =\pi ^*\psi _\tau $. In particular the limits, including their values at poles, agree. For any other Hermitian metric $k$ on $B$, constants $0<l\leq r$ with $l\kappa \leq k\leq r\kappa $ give \[  \phi _\tau ^{l/j}\leq \Psi _\tau ^{k/j}\leq \phi _\tau ^{r/j}.  \] Both outer sequences decrease to $\psi _\tau $. This also identifies the transverse limit directly, without assuming that it keeps the ideals of the positive scalar slices. $\square$ Theorem 25.6.3 . Let $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(h)$ have $E$-invariant scalar components as in lemma 25.6.2 . Let $\psi =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Psi $ be the transverse limiting curve. If \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\kappa (\psi _ a)>0,  \] then for every $\tau <c$ and every Hermitian form $\eta >0$ on $X$, \[  \Gamma _\tau ^\eta =P_{h+\eta }[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Thus $\boldsymbol \Gamma =\mathsf E(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )$. Proof. The closed Kähler background $\kappa $ is big and $B$ has the bounded mass property. Apply theorem 30.5.6 to the full transverse system. Its initial-volume hypothesis is exactly the displayed one, and it gives \[  \Psi _\tau ^{\epsilon \kappa } =P_{(1+\epsilon )\kappa }[\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\epsilon >0,\  \tau <c).  \] The fiber-envelope identity yields $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=P_{(1+\epsilon )h}[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$. For a general $\eta >0$, choose $\epsilon h\leq \eta $. Compatibility and the nested-background identity of proposition 25.2.1 then give \[  \Gamma _\tau ^\eta =P_{h+\eta }[\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}]_{\mathcal I} =P_{h+\eta }[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] $\square$ The positivity condition is a lower ordinary-type volume on the closed base. It does not use an ambient upper-volume deficit or identify the ideals of the limit in advance. The conclusion holds at every finite $\tau <c$; it gives no uniform positive-volume bound as $\tau $ approaches $c$.

Testing the positive current above against these lifts and a nonnegative smooth fiber density of integral one proves $b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0$ distributionally. Thus $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,b\kappa )$. Conversely, every such $w$ lifts to a $bh$-plurisubharmonic function by the displayed identity. Now set $q=P_{bh}[\pi ^*v]_{\mathcal I}$. Translation by any $g\in E$ preserves its complete competitor family: it preserves the background, the obstacle zero, and the ideals of the invariant input. The envelope is their greatest member, so $q\circ g=q$. Descend $q=\pi ^*w$ as above. By lemma 1.16.6 , its ideal equivalence to $\pi ^*v$ implies $w\sim _{\mathcal I}v$: a germ pulled back from the base is weighted-integrable in a product chart if and only if the base germ is, by Fubini. Hence $w$ is a base competitor. Every base competitor also lifts to an ambient competitor by the same lemma and the current identity. Taking the greatest members gives equality. $\square$

title: Lemma 25.6.2
text: Lemma 25.6.2 . Suppose $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}$ is $E$-invariant for every $\epsilon >0$ and $\tau <c$. There is a unique envelope system $\boldsymbol \Psi \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\kappa )$ such that \[  \Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=\pi ^*\Psi _\tau ^{\epsilon \kappa } \quad (\epsilon >0,\  \tau <c).  \] Writing $\Gamma =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $ and $\psi =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Psi $, we have $\Gamma _\tau =\pi ^*\psi _\tau $ for every $\tau <c$. Proof. The descent in proposition 25.6.1 gives $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=\pi ^*\phi _\tau ^\epsilon $ with $\phi _\tau ^\epsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,(1+\epsilon )\kappa )$. Normalization, decrease, concavity and constancy for $\tau \leq a$ descend pointwise. The fiber-envelope identity descends both ideal-model fixedness and scalar compatibility: \[  \phi _\tau ^{\epsilon _2} =P_{(1+\epsilon _2)\kappa } [\phi _\tau ^{\epsilon _1}]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\epsilon _2\geq \epsilon _1>0).  \] In particular, the positive scalar slices have the same ideals at every weight. For a Hermitian form $\xi >0$ on $B$, choose $\delta >0$ with $\delta \kappa \leq \xi $, fixed for the whole parameter interval, and define \[  \Psi _\tau ^\xi =P_{\kappa +\xi } [\phi _\tau ^\delta ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The definition is independent of $\delta $ because the scalar inputs have the same ideals. It reproduces the scalar components, and proposition 25.2.1 proves that each component is a curve in $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\kappa +\xi )$. Projection preserves the ideals, so comparing the complete competitor families proves compatibility for $\xi \geq \xi '$. Thus $\boldsymbol \Psi $ is a full envelope system. Every possible extension is forced by this formula, which proves uniqueness. The retraction theorem applies to both systems. Taking their decreasing limits along $h/j$ and $\kappa /j$ in the scalar identity gives $\Gamma _\tau =\pi ^*\psi _\tau $. In particular the limits, including their values at poles, agree. For any other Hermitian metric $k$ on $B$, constants $0<l\leq r$ with $l\kappa \leq k\leq r\kappa $ give \[  \phi _\tau ^{l/j}\leq \Psi _\tau ^{k/j}\leq \phi _\tau ^{r/j}.  \] Both outer sequences decrease to $\psi _\tau $. This also identifies the transverse limit directly, without assuming that it keeps the ideals of the positive scalar slices. $\square$

title: Theorem 25.6.3
text: Theorem 25.6.3 . Let $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(h)$ have $E$-invariant scalar components as in lemma 25.6.2 . Let $\psi =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Psi $ be the transverse limiting curve. If \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\kappa (\psi _ a)>0,  \] then for every $\tau <c$ and every Hermitian form $\eta >0$ on $X$, \[  \Gamma _\tau ^\eta =P_{h+\eta }[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Thus $\boldsymbol \Gamma =\mathsf E(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )$. Proof. The closed Kähler background $\kappa $ is big and $B$ has the bounded mass property. Apply theorem 30.5.6 to the full transverse system. Its initial-volume hypothesis is exactly the displayed one, and it gives \[  \Psi _\tau ^{\epsilon \kappa } =P_{(1+\epsilon )\kappa }[\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\epsilon >0,\  \tau <c).  \] The fiber-envelope identity yields $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=P_{(1+\epsilon )h}[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$. For a general $\eta >0$, choose $\epsilon h\leq \eta $. Compatibility and the nested-background identity of proposition 25.2.1 then give \[  \Gamma _\tau ^\eta =P_{h+\eta }[\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}]_{\mathcal I} =P_{h+\eta }[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] $\square$

title: 25.6.1 A nonanalytic family
text: 25.6.1 A nonanalytic family The countable hyperplane series of 30.8.5 , 30.8.6 supplies an explicit family satisfying the transverse condition. Choose infinitely many distinct hyperplanes $H_ j\subset B$, positive coefficients $q_ j$ with $\sum _ jq_ j=1$, and their standard logarithms $\ell _ j\leq 0$. Put \[  u_0=\sum _{j\geq 1}q_ j\ell _ j -\sup _ B\sum _{j\geq 1}q_ j\ell _ j.  \] Then $u_0\leq 0$ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic and $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0=\sum _ jq_ j[H_ j]$. Example 25.6.4 . Fix $0<\lambda _0<\lambda _*<1$ and $r>0$ with $r(c-a)<\lambda _*-\lambda _0$. For $\tau <c$, set \[  \lambda (\tau )=\lambda _0+r\max (\tau -a,0),\qquad u_\tau =\lambda (\tau )u_0,  \] and, for every Hermitian form $\eta >0$ on $X$, define \[  \Gamma _\tau ^\eta =P_{h+\eta }[\pi ^*u_\tau ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] These components form an envelope system with $E$-invariant scalar slices. Its transverse limiting curve is $\psi _\tau =P_\kappa [u_\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$, and \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\kappa (\psi _\tau ) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\kappa (\psi _\tau ) =(1-\lambda (\tau ))^2>0.  \] The system is recovered from its limit. Its ideal data cannot be represented by analytic singularities. Proof. The function $\lambda $ is positive, increasing and convex, and $u_0\leq 0$, so $u_\tau $ decreases, is pointwise concave and is constant for $\tau \leq a$. Moreover, \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\tau =(1-\lambda (\tau ))\kappa +\lambda (\tau )\sum _ jq_ j[H_ j]>0, \qquad h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\pi ^*u_\tau \geq (1-\lambda _*)h.  \] Set $q_\tau =P_\kappa [u_\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$. The order, scaling and addition inequalities of proposition 16.2.6 show that $q_\tau $ remains decreasing and concave; it is constant on the same left half-line. Thus $q\in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\kappa )$. Apply the same argument upstairs to $Q_\tau =P_ h[\pi ^*u_\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$. The fiber-envelope identity gives $Q_\tau =\pi ^*q_\tau $, and the nested-background identity identifies the displayed family with $\mathsf E(Q)$. It is therefore an envelope system, its limit is $Q$ by $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$, and its scalar slices are invariant. Apply 30.8.6 with background $\kappa $, coefficients $a_ j=\lambda (\tau )q_ j$ and residual $(1-\lambda (\tau ))\kappa $. It gives the asserted exact lower and upper volumes of $q_\tau $. The transverse recovery theorem applies, also confirming recovery directly. For every $j$, the divisorial coefficient of $u_\tau $ along $H_ j$ is positive. Projection preserves all ideals and hence these coefficients. Analytic singularities on a compact manifold have only finitely many divisorial components, since their defining coherent ideals have this property. Thus no analytic singularity type has the same all-weight ideals. The same conclusion holds upstairs along the distinct divisors $\pi ^{-1}(H_ j)$, by submersion pullback. $\square$

title: 26 A Gauduchon variational volume
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26 A Gauduchon variational volume Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, which we call the background , and let $\mu $ be a smooth strictly positive probability form on $X$. If $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$ for some smooth real function $v$, there is exactly one constant $c>0$ for which the Monge–Ampère equation $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c\mu $ has a smooth solution $u$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. When $\theta $ is closed, Stokes' theorem gives $c=\int _ X\theta ^ n$, independently of $\mu $. For a nonclosed background the total mass $\int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ can depend on the potential, and the constant $c$ is the one number that the equation attaches to the pair $(\theta ,\mu )$. This chapter studies it as a function of the background. The starting point is a dual formula. Integrating the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality against the $(n-1)$st power of a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, that is, of a Hermitian form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$, shows that $c^{1/n}$ is the infimum of a quotient whose numerator $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is linear in $\theta $ and unchanged by smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ changes of $\theta $. Taking this infimum for every pseudoeffective background defines the root of the Gauduchon variational volume. The root volume is concave. On the positive cone, a minimizing Gauduchon metric computes its derivative, and the Hessian of its negative logarithm defines a Riemannian metric on background classes in each finite-dimensional family. Invariant forms on compact quotients of complex Lie groups and warped products with a curve show that the unit-volume hypersurface of this metric may be complete or may acquire a boundary at finite distance. For $n\geq 2$, the same quotient computes the subsolution threshold $b_\omega (f)$ for a Hermitian background $\omega $ and an integrable density $f$. Allowing positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed currents as tests makes this dual problem compact. For continuous densities the maximizing currents represent exactly the supporting probabilities of the normalization functional; for integrable densities, a uniform tail condition passes the determinant integral to weak limits and again gives a maximizing current. A maximizing test that is a smooth strictly positive form gives more: equality in the trace inequality determines the solution current and forces an exact smooth equation. The exact equation persists when the maximizing form degenerates along a proper analytic set, whereas a threshold solution with a point pole can admit no smooth maximizing test at all. The last part of the chapter concerns the boundary of the positive cone and the dependence on $\mu $. At a nef background the variational volume is the limit of the smooth equation constants of nearby positive backgrounds. A projective radial model gives positive variational volume without bigness, even at the finite maximal time of a Chern–Ricci flow. Varying $\mu $ recovers the upper and lower Monge–Ampère masses. A threefold with zero lower mass shows that positivity for each smooth density need not be uniform over densities, whereas on an elliptic threefold a nonnegative sum of curvature squares gives a bounded cubic energy identity and hence a positive lower bound for every potential, even when the manifold admits no pluriclosed metric. Finally, nef degeneration gives a further contrast with closed Kähler classes: intersection polynomials are replaced by fractional, logarithmic or oscillating decay, and a single blowup can change its order. Throughout the chapter, a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ is called pseudoeffective if $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing $, that is, if $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ for some quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$; by theorem 4.3.1 this holds exactly when $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq 0$ for every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. Bigness is defined in section 1.19 , and $\theta $ is nef if, for a Hermitian form $h$ and every $\epsilon >0$, there is a smooth real $f_\epsilon $ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_\epsilon \geq -\epsilon h$; this is the condition of section 23.6 for the affine class of $\theta $ in section 24.1 . None of these notions requires $\theta $ to be closed, and each is unchanged by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of $\theta $.

title: 26.1 The quotient and the smooth equation
search_title: The quotient and the smooth equation
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.1 The quotient and the smooth equation For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, Stokes' theorem shows that the pairing $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is unchanged by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of $\theta $; this pairing will be the numerator of our quotient. For the denominator, put \[  D_\mu (\gamma )=\int _ X \left(\frac{\mu }{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] This number is positive. Like the numerator, it is multiplied by $r^{n-1}$ when $\gamma $ is multiplied by a positive constant $r$, so the quotient below depends only on the ray of $\gamma $. Definition 26.1.1 . For a pseudoeffective smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$, define \[  \lambda _\mu (\theta )= \inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\displaystyle \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma )}, \qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=\lambda _\mu (\theta )^ n.  \] We call $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )$ the Gauduchon variational volume of $\theta $ with respect to $\mu $, and $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ its root volume . In dimension one every Hermitian metric is Gauduchon, and every quotient equals $\int _ X\theta $. Proposition 26.1.2 . For a pseudoeffective $\theta $, the number $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ is finite and nonnegative. It is unchanged by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of $\theta $, positively homogeneous of degree one, and concave on the cone of pseudoeffective forms. If $\beta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $\beta -\theta $ is pseudoeffective, then \[  \lambda _\mu (\beta )\geq \lambda _\mu (\theta ).  \] Finally, $\lambda _\mu $ is upper semicontinuous under smooth convergence within this cone. Proof. Choose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, Stokes' theorem for currents and the Gauduchon condition give \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq 0.  \] Thus every quotient is nonnegative, and testing one fixed Gauduchon metric gives a finite upper bound. The same identity shows that each quotient is unchanged by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of the background, and, applied to $\beta -\theta $, it proves the monotonicity. Each quotient is a linear function of the background, so their infimum is concave and positively homogeneous. Each individual quotient is also continuous in the smooth topology. Given a smoothly converging sequence, we bound the infimum by any one quotient, take the upper limit, and finally take the infimum over the test metric. This proves upper semicontinuity. $\square$ The smooth equation identifies both the value of the quotient and every minimizing metric. Let $\mathscr P$ be the set of backgrounds $\theta $ admitting a smooth real function $u$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Choosing such a Hermitian representative of $\theta $ and writing $\mu $ as a smooth positive density relative to its volume form, we may apply theorem 9.1.1 . It gives, for each $\theta \in \mathscr P$, a unique positive form $\Omega _\theta $, which we call the solution form , and a unique constant $c_\theta (\mu )>0$ such that \[  \Omega _\theta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\theta , \qquad \Omega _\theta ^ n=c_\theta (\mu )\mu .  \] The potential $u_\theta $ is unique after any fixed additive normalization. Theorem 26.1.3 . For every $\theta \in \mathscr P$, \[  \lambda _\mu (\theta )=c_\theta (\mu )^{1/n}, \qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=c_\theta (\mu ).  \] The infimum in definition 26.1.1 is attained. When $n\geq 2$, its minimizing Gauduchon metrics are precisely the constant multiples of the Gauduchon metric conformal to $\Omega _\theta $. Proof. For any Hermitian metric $\gamma $, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for the eigenvalues of $\Omega _\theta $ relative to $\gamma $ gives the pointwise inequality \[  \Omega _\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq \left(\frac{\Omega _\theta ^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n =c_\theta (\mu )^{1/n} \left(\frac{\mu }{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] If $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, integration and Stokes' theorem replace $\Omega _\theta $ in the numerator by $\theta $. Every test quotient is therefore at least $c_\theta (\mu )^{1/n}$. For $n\geq 2$, take the Gauduchon metric $\gamma =\mathrm{e}^ g\Omega _\theta $ conformal to $\Omega _\theta $, given by theorem 4.1.2 , where $g$ is a smooth real function. Since all eigenvalues of $\Omega _\theta $ relative to $\gamma $ are equal at every point, equality holds pointwise and hence in the quotient. This proves the formula and attainment. Conversely, if a Gauduchon metric attains the infimum, the nonnegative smooth difference of the two sides of the pointwise inequality has zero integral. It therefore vanishes everywhere, and the equality case of the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality makes $\gamma $ conformal to $\Omega _\theta $. Since the Gauduchon metric in a conformal class is unique up to a constant factor, this proves the last assertion. For $n=1$, we integrate the equation and use $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\theta =0$. This gives $c_\theta (\mu )=\int _ X\theta $, which equals every quotient in the definition. $\square$ For a Hermitian background $\omega $, a smooth positive probability volume $\mathrm{d}V$ and a nonzero nonnegative density $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, the analogous quotient, with $\mu $ replaced by $f\, \mathrm{d}V$, computes the subsolution threshold $b_\omega (f)$ of section 14.27 ; see theorem 14.28.1 . Attainment in this extremal problem, and the regularity of the extremal tests, are studied from section 26.6 on. Corollary 26.1.4 . If $\theta $ is big, then $\lambda _\mu (\theta )>0$. Proof. By the definition of bigness, there are a Hermitian form $h$ and $\delta >0$ such that $\theta -\delta h$ is pseudoeffective. Monotonicity, homogeneity and the theorem, applied to $h\in \mathscr P$, give $\lambda _\mu (\theta )\geq \delta \lambda _\mu (h)>0$. $\square$ The converse fails for nef nonclosed backgrounds: theorem 26.13.2 gives, on a projective manifold, a nef background of positive volume that is not big.

title: 26.2 The equality case of concavity and the first variation

text: 26.2 The equality case of concavity and the first variation Since $\lambda _\mu $ is an infimum of linear functions, each minimizing Gauduchon metric at $\theta $ defines a linear functional that supports $\lambda _\mu $ at $\theta $. If equality holds in the concavity inequality along a segment, a metric minimizing at an interior point must minimize at both endpoints, and theorem 26.1.3 then makes the two endpoint solution forms proportional. Differentiating the smooth equation shows that the supporting functional is the derivative of $\lambda _\mu $. For $\theta \in \mathscr P$ we write $\gamma _\theta $ for a minimizing Gauduchon metric, which exists by theorem 26.1.3 ; variation directions are smooth real $(1,1)$-forms. Theorem 26.2.1 . Let $\theta _0,\theta _1\in \mathscr P$ and $0<s<1$. Then \[  \lambda _\mu ((1-s)\theta _0+s\theta _1) \geq (1-s)\lambda _\mu (\theta _0)+s\lambda _\mu (\theta _1).  \] Equality holds if and only if, for some $r>0$ and some smooth real $f$, \[  \theta _1=r\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f.  \] Proof. Concavity was proved in proposition 26.1.2 . Suppose first that $n\geq 2$ and that equality holds. Take a minimizing Gauduchon metric for the middle background $(1-s)\theta _0+s\theta _1$. Its quotient at the middle background is the same convex combination of its quotients at $\theta _0$ and $\theta _1$, and each of these is at least the corresponding infimum. Equality therefore forces this metric to minimize both endpoint quotients. By theorem 26.1.3 , the solution forms $\Omega _ i=\Omega _{\theta _ i}$, with constants $c_ i=c_{\theta _ i}(\mu )$ for $i=0,1$, are then both conformal to this metric. Their volume forms are $c_0\mu $ and $c_1\mu $, so their pointwise proportionality factor is the constant $r=(c_1/c_0)^{1/n}$. Hence $\Omega _1=r\Omega _0$, which gives the stated smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ relation. Conversely, if that relation holds, invariance under smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ changes and homogeneity give equality. When $n=1$, the function is $\theta \mapsto \int _ X\theta $. Take $r=\int _ X\theta _1/\int _ X\theta _0$. The difference $\theta _1-r\theta _0$ has integral zero, so the Green operator of the compact curve writes it as $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth. Thus the same equivalence holds. $\square$ Proposition 26.2.2 . The function $\lambda _\mu $ is smooth along smooth finite-dimensional families in $\mathscr P$. For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\chi $ and $n\geq 2$, its derivative at $\theta $ is \[  (\mathrm{d}\lambda _\mu )_\theta (\chi ) =\frac{\displaystyle \int _ X\chi \wedge \gamma _\theta ^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma _\theta )},  \] where $\gamma _\theta $ is any minimizing Gauduchon metric. In dimension one the derivative is $\int _ X\chi $. Proof. Choose a smooth potential $u_*$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_*>0$. Backgrounds $\theta _ t$ near $\theta $ then have the positive representatives $\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_*$. The implicit-function argument in the proof of proposition 15.8.3 applies to this family and shows that the solution and its constant depend smoothly on the parameters. Adding $u_*$ to these solution potentials and fixing the mean gives the normalized solutions for $\theta _ t$, so $\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)=c_{\theta _ t}(\mu )^{1/n}$ is smooth. To compute the derivative, write $\lambda =\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ and $\Omega =\Omega _\theta $, and write the minimizing metric as $\gamma _\theta =\mathrm{e}^ g\Omega $ with $g$ smooth and real, as theorem 26.1.3 permits. Along $\theta _ t=\theta +t\chi $ for small real $t$, put $\Omega _ t=\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t$ and $\lambda _ t=\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)$, and let dots denote derivatives at $t=0$. In dimension one the formula follows directly from the definition. $\square$

text: Theorem 26.2.1 . Let $\theta _0,\theta _1\in \mathscr P$ and $0<s<1$. Then \[  \lambda _\mu ((1-s)\theta _0+s\theta _1) \geq (1-s)\lambda _\mu (\theta _0)+s\lambda _\mu (\theta _1).  \] Equality holds if and only if, for some $r>0$ and some smooth real $f$, \[  \theta _1=r\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f.  \] Proof. title: 26.4 Recovering a positive class from its Gauduchon derivative
search_title: Recovering a positive class from its Gauduchon derivative
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.4 Recovering a positive class from its Gauduchon derivative By proposition 26.2.2 , the derivative of $\lambda _\mu $ at $\theta \in \mathscr P$ is represented by a minimizing Gauduchon metric, which is determined up to a constant factor. The solution form is conformal to this metric and has a prescribed volume form, so the value and the derivative of $\lambda _\mu $ together reconstruct the solution form, and hence the background class. Fix $\theta \in \mathscr P$ and a minimizing metric $\gamma _\theta $. For $n\geq 2$ define the smooth positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form \[  \Xi _\theta =\frac{\gamma _\theta ^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma _\theta )}.  \] Since numerator and denominator are both homogeneous of degree $n-1$ in $\gamma _\theta $, this form does not depend on the choice of the minimizing metric. It is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, and by proposition 26.2.2 it represents the derivative in every smooth real $(1,1)$-direction $\chi $: \[  (\mathrm{d}\lambda _\mu )_\theta (\chi )=\int _ X\chi \wedge \Xi _\theta .  \] Proposition 26.4.1 . Let $n\geq 2$ and $\theta \in \mathscr P$. The value $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ and the derivative of $\lambda _\mu $ at $\theta $ on all smooth real $(1,1)$-forms together determine the background class of $\theta $, and the derivative alone determines this class up to multiplication by a positive constant. More precisely, if $\widehat\gamma $ is the positive $(1,1)$-form with $\widehat\gamma ^{n-1}=\Xi _\theta $, then \[  D_\mu (\widehat\gamma )=1, \qquad \Omega _\theta = \lambda _\mu (\theta ) \left(\frac{\mu }{\widehat\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n} \widehat\gamma .  \] Moreover, assigning to a background class in $\mathscr P$ with $\lambda _\mu =1$ the ray of its minimizing Gauduchon metrics is a bijection onto the set of rays of Gauduchon metrics. Proof. The values of the derivative on all smooth $(1,1)$-forms determine the smooth form $\Xi _\theta $. Its positive root exists and is unique by the positive-root construction preceding the proof of theorem 4.3.1 . If $D=D_\mu (\gamma _\theta )$, this root is $\widehat\gamma =D^{-1/(n-1)}\gamma _\theta $, and the homogeneity of $D_\mu $ gives $D_\mu (\widehat\gamma )=1$. By theorem 26.1.3 , the solution form $\Omega _\theta $ is conformal to $\widehat\gamma $, and its volume form is $\lambda _\mu (\theta )^ n\mu $. These two requirements determine the conformal factor pointwise and give the formula for $\Omega _\theta $. Thus the value and the derivative recover $\Omega _\theta $, a representative of the class of $\theta $. Without the value, the same formula recovers $\Omega _\theta $ up to a positive constant factor. Conversely, multiplying the class by a positive constant multiplies $\Omega _\theta $ by the same constant and leaves its minimizing Gauduchon ray, and hence $\Xi _\theta $, unchanged; so the derivative cannot determine more than the ray of the class. For the surjectivity in the last assertion, take any Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and set \[  \Omega _\gamma =\left(\frac\mu {\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma .  \] This Hermitian form is unchanged by constant rescaling of $\gamma $ and satisfies $\Omega _\gamma ^ n=\mu $. The zero potential therefore solves the equation for the background $\Omega _\gamma $ with constant one, so its class has $\lambda _\mu =1$, and $\gamma $ is a minimizing Gauduchon metric by theorem 26.1.3 . Injectivity follows from the recovery formula: two classes with $\lambda _\mu =1$ and the same Gauduchon ray have the same solution form. This proves the bijection. $\square$ In dimension one, a background class is determined by its integral, by the Green operator of the curve. The derivative is then the fixed functional $\chi \mapsto \int _ X\chi $, and the value alone determines the class.

title: 26.5 The Hessian metric and its completion
search_title: The Hessian metric and its completion
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.5 The Hessian metric and its completion We now study the metric $\mathfrak g$ of ( 26.3 ) on finite-dimensional cones of backgrounds, where it defines an ordinary Riemannian path distance. Homogeneity of $\lambda _\mu $ separates the scale of a positive class from its position on a level set of $\lambda _\mu $, and the logarithm of this scale turns out to be a Euclidean coordinate orthogonal to the level sets. The metric is therefore a product, and its completeness reduces to that of the unit-volume hypersurface. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space of smooth real $(1,1)$-forms such that \[  V\cap \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)=\{ 0\} , \qquad \mathscr C=V\cap \mathscr P\ne \varnothing .  \] Then $\mathscr C$ is an open convex cone in $V$. Write $\lambda =\lambda _\mu |_{\mathscr C}$, and let $g=-D^2\log \lambda $ be the restriction to $\mathscr C$ of the metric ( 26.3 ); it is a smooth Riemannian metric on $\mathscr C$ because $V$ meets $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ only in zero. Put \[  \mathscr S=\{ \theta \in \mathscr C:\lambda (\theta )=1\} ,  \] and equip this smooth hypersurface with the induced metric $g_{\mathscr S}$. Proposition 26.5.1 . The map \[  \Phi :\mathbb R\times \mathscr S\longrightarrow \mathscr C, \qquad (r,q)\longmapsto \mathrm{e}^ r q  \] is an isometry from the product metric $\mathrm{d}r^2+g_{\mathscr S}$ onto $g$. In particular, if $d_ g$ and $d_{\mathscr S}$ are the intrinsic distances, then \[  d_ g(\mathrm{e}^{r_0}q_0,\mathrm{e}^{r_1}q_1)^2 =|r_1-r_0|^2+d_{\mathscr S}(q_0,q_1)^2.  \] The metric on $\mathscr C$ is complete if and only if the induced metric on $\mathscr S$ is complete. Every path for which $\lambda $ tends to zero or to infinity has infinite length. Proof. Homogeneity gives $\lambda (s\theta )=s\lambda (\theta )$ for $s>0$. Hence $r=\log \lambda (\theta )$ and $q=\theta /\lambda (\theta )$ define the smooth inverse of $\Phi $. The level set is smooth because the Euler identity gives $D\lambda _\theta (\theta )=\lambda (\theta )>0$. Differentiating the Euler identity $D\log \lambda _\theta (\theta )=1$ in a direction $\chi \in V$ gives \[  g_\theta (\theta ,\chi )=D\log \lambda _\theta (\chi ), \qquad g_\theta (\theta ,\theta )=1.  \] For directions $\chi ,\eta \in V$, differentiating homogeneity twice also gives \[  g_{s\theta }(s\chi ,s\eta )=g_\theta (\chi ,\eta ).  \] Let $q\in \mathscr S$, let $\xi ,\eta \in T_ q\mathscr S$, and let $a,b,r$ be real numbers. Since $\xi $ and $\eta $ are tangent to a level set of $\lambda $, the first of these identities shows that both are $g_ q$-orthogonal to the radial vector $q$. Using also the second identity and the scaling rule, we obtain \[  g_{\mathrm{e}^ rq}\bigl (\mathrm{e}^ r(aq+\xi ),\mathrm{e}^ r(bq+\eta )\bigr ) =ab+g_ q(\xi ,\eta ),  \] which proves the metric identity. It remains to prove the distance formula and its consequences. A path $(r(t),q(t))$ in the product has length $\int \sqrt{|r'|^2+|q'|_{g_{\mathscr S}}^2}\, \mathrm{d}t$. The triangle inequality in $\mathbb R^2$ (applied to the integral of the vector $(|r'|,|q'|_{g_{\mathscr S}})$) bounds this below by the square root of the sum of the squared endpoint difference in $r$ and the squared length of the projected path in $\mathscr S$. For the opposite bound, choose a path in $\mathscr S$ of length within $\epsilon $ of the distance of its endpoints, parametrize it with constant speed, and let $r$ vary linearly; then let $\epsilon $ decrease to zero. This proves the distance formula. It identifies Cauchy sequences in $\mathscr C$ with pairs of Cauchy sequences in the two factors; since $\mathbb R$ is complete, the completeness assertion follows. Finally, the length of any path is at least the total change of $\log \lambda $ along it, and this change is infinite when $\lambda $ tends to zero or to infinity. $\square$

title: 26.5.1 Product and blowup examples
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.5.1 Product and blowup examples The following two examples of closed classes show that the unit-volume hypersurface may be complete or may have a boundary at finite distance. The first also shows why the derivative is needed in proposition 26.4.1 : knowing the volume for every smooth probability measure need not identify the class. For the first example take $X=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, and let $\alpha ,\beta $ be the pulled-back Fubini–Study forms of integral one on their respective factors. They satisfy \[  \alpha ^2=\beta ^2=0,\qquad \int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta =1.  \] For $a,b>0$ the form $\theta _{a,b}=a\alpha +b\beta $ is Kähler. Since it is closed, integrating the smooth equation gives, for every smooth positive probability measure $\mu $, \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _{a,b})=2ab, \qquad \lambda _\mu (\theta _{a,b})=\sqrt{2ab}.  \] Consequently, for real $t$, all the forms $\theta _{\mathrm{e}^ t,\mathrm{e}^{-t}}$ have volume $2$ for every $\mu $. Their background classes are nevertheless distinct: for any fixed point $p$ of the second factor, integration over $\mathbb P^1\times \{ p\} $ gives $\mathrm{e}^ t$, and this integral is unchanged by the addition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. By direct differentiation, the restriction of ( 26.3 ) to this two-dimensional cone is \[  \mathfrak g=\frac12\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}a^2}{a^2}+\frac{\mathrm{d}b^2}{b^2}\right).  \] The coordinates $((\log a)/\sqrt2,(\log b)/\sqrt2)$ identify this metric with the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb R^2$, so the metric on this family is complete. The curve $a=\mathrm{e}^ t$, $b=\mathrm{e}^{-t}$ has unit speed. All distances here are intrinsic to this two-dimensional family. In the second example, the blowup of $\mathbb P^2$ at a point, the cone is incomplete, and the boundary added by the completion consists of classes of positive volume. Example 26.5.2 . Let $\pi :X\to \mathbb P^2$ be the blowup at one point. Write $H$ for the pullback of the hyperplane class and $E$ for the exceptional divisor class. In the two-dimensional space they span, the cone of classes with a positive smooth representative is \[  \mathscr C=\{ aH-bE:a>b>0\} .  \] These are closed classes, and we represent them by fixed smooth forms in order to apply proposition 26.5.1 . Their intersection numbers are $H^2=1$, $H\cdot E=0$, $E^2=-1$. Consequently, for every smooth positive probability measure $\mu $, \[  \lambda _\mu (aH-bE)=\sqrt{a^2-b^2}.  \] In the coordinates \[  a=\mathrm{e}^ r\cosh s,\qquad b=\mathrm{e}^ r\sinh s, \qquad r\in \mathbb R,\quad s>0,  \] the Hessian metric is $\mathrm{d}r^2+\mathrm{d}s^2$. Its completion is therefore the Euclidean closed half-plane. The added boundary $s=0$ consists of the nef classes $\mathrm{e}^ rH$, each of positive volume $\mathrm{e}^{2r}$. Proof. The projection from the blown-up point extends to a morphism $f:X\to \mathbb P^1$ with class $L=H-E$. The incidence map $(\pi ,f):X\to \mathbb P^2\times \mathbb P^1$ is an embedding. If $h$ and $\ell $ are pullbacks of Fubini–Study forms of integral one, then \[  (a-b)h+b\ell  \] is positive for $a>b>0$, by the product embedding. Conversely, a positive representative has positive integrals over the exceptional curve and the strict transform of a line through the blown-up point. These integrals are respectively $b$ and $a-b$, proving the cone description. The same curves show that no nonzero linear combination in this two-dimensional space is smoothly $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. The intersection numbers follow from the hyperplane pullback and the normal bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$ of the exceptional curve; equivalently $H^2=H\cdot L=1$ and $L^2=0$. Since the classes are closed, integrating the smooth equation gives $\mathcal V_\mu =a^2-b^2$, independently of $\mu $. Direct differentiation of $-\log \sqrt{a^2-b^2}$ gives \[  g=\frac{(a^2+b^2)(\mathrm{d}a^2+\mathrm{d}b^2)-4ab\, \mathrm{d}a\, \mathrm{d}b}{(a^2-b^2)^2}.  \] Substituting the stated coordinates gives $\mathrm{d}r^2+\mathrm{d}s^2$. The coordinate domain is exactly $\mathbb R\times (0,\infty )$, so the intrinsic distance and completion are those of that Euclidean half-plane. Finally, $H$ has a semipositive pullback representative and is a limit of positive classes, hence is nef. Its square is one, but its integral over $E$ is zero, so it has no positive representative. This proves all assertions about the added boundary. $\square$

Conversely, a positive representative has positive integrals over the exceptional curve and the strict transform of a line through the blown-up point. These integrals are respectively $b$ and $a-b$, proving the cone description. The same curves show that no nonzero linear combination in this two-dimensional space is smoothly $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. The intersection numbers follow from the hyperplane pullback and the normal bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$ of the exceptional curve; equivalently $H^2=H\cdot L=1$ and $L^2=0$. Since the classes are closed, integrating the smooth equation gives $\mathcal V_\mu =a^2-b^2$, independently of $\mu $. Direct differentiation of $-\log \sqrt{a^2-b^2}$ gives \[  g=\frac{(a^2+b^2)(\mathrm{d}a^2+\mathrm{d}b^2)-4ab\, \mathrm{d}a\, \mathrm{d}b}{(a^2-b^2)^2}.  \] Substituting the stated coordinates gives $\mathrm{d}r^2+\mathrm{d}s^2$. The coordinate domain is exactly $\mathbb R\times (0,\infty )$, so the intrinsic distance and completion are those of that Euclidean half-plane. Finally, $H$ has a semipositive pullback representative and is a limit of positive classes, hence is nef. Its square is one, but its integral over $E$ is zero, so it has no positive representative. This proves all assertions about the added boundary. $\square$

26.5.2 Invariant backgrounds on compact Lie-group quotients On a compact quotient of a complex Lie group, the backgrounds with constant coefficients in an invariant coframe form a cone of nonclosed backgrounds on which everything can be computed explicitly. With respect to the normalized invariant volume, the root volume is the $n$th root of a determinant, the minimizing metric is the background itself, and the Hessian metric is the trace metric on positive Hermitian matrices. Its unit-volume hypersurface is complete, so the boundary of the cone of coefficient matrices lies at infinite distance after normalization. Let $G$ be a connected complex Lie group of dimension $n\geq 2$, and let $X=\Gamma  ackslash G$ be compact, where the discrete subgroup $\Gamma $ acts on the left. Choose a left-invariant holomorphic coframe $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ n$, which descends to $X$. For a Hermitian matrix $A$ put \[   egin{gathered} 	heta _ A= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}A_{jk}\alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ k, \qquad h_0=	heta _ I,\ H=\int _ Xh_0^ n,\qquad \mu = rac{h_0^ n}{H}. \end{gathered}  \] Here $\operatorname {Herm}(n)$ is the real vector space of Hermitian $n	imes n$ matrices, and $A>0$ (respectively $A\geq 0$) means that $A$ is positive definite (respectively semidefinite). Fix a real linear subspace $W\subset \operatorname {Herm}(n)$ containing a positive matrix, and write $V_ W=\{ 	heta _ A:A\in W\} $. Throughout this subsection, the probability form is the normalized invariant volume $\mu $ just defined. Proposition 26.5.3 . The backgrounds in $V_ W\cap \mathscr P$ are exactly the forms $	heta _ A$ with $A\in W$ and $A>0$. Moreover, \[  V_ W\cap \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)=\{ 0\} .  \] Every positive $	heta _ A$ is balanced, and its unique minimizing Gauduchon metric normalized by $D_\mu =1$ is 26.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:parallelizable-gaud-volume} \lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)=(H\det A)^{1/n},\qquad \gamma _ A= rac{	heta _ A}{\lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)},\qquad \gamma _ A^ n=\mu . \end{equation} On this coefficient cone the Hessian metric is 26.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:parallelizable-gaud-hessian} g_ A(U,Z)= rac1n\operatorname {tr}(A^{-1}UA^{-1}Z), \qquad U,Z\in W. \end{equation} For $A\in W$, there is a real distribution $u$ with $	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ exactly when $A\geq 0$. The closure of $\{ A\in W:A>0\} $ is $W\cap \{ A\geq 0\} $, and each of its points $A$ is represented by the smooth semipositive form $	heta _ A$. For $A=0$, the only positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is zero. If $G$ is nonabelian, every positive background in this cone is nonclosed, and adding a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ term never makes it closed. Proof. Invariant averages and balancedness. Let $Z_1,\ldots ,Z_ n$ be the invariant holomorphic vector fields dual to $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ n$, and set $\Upsilon =\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ n$. This holomorphic top-degree form and its conjugate are closed. For an invariant holomorphic vector field $Z$, evaluation on the invariant frame gives \[  \mathcal L_ Z\Upsilon =-\operatorname {tr}(\operatorname {ad}Z)\Upsilon , \qquad \mathcal L_ Z ar\Upsilon =0.  \] The second identity also follows from Cartan's formula. Since $h_0^ n$ is a positive constant multiple of the appropriately oriented form $\Upsilon \wedge  ar\Upsilon $, Stokes' theorem on compact $X$ gives \[  0=\int _ X\mathcal L_ Zh_0^ n=-H\operatorname {tr}(\operatorname {ad}Z).  \] Thus the fields $Z_ j$ and their conjugates have zero divergence with respect to $\mu $. In particular, 26.6  egin{equation} \label{eq:parallelizable-zero-mean} \int _ XZ_ jf\, \mu =\int _ X ar Z_ jf\, \mu =0 \qquad (f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb C)). \end{equation} Cartan's formula also gives $\mathrm d(\iota _{Z_ j}\Upsilon )=0$. These contractions span the invariant $(n-1,0)$-forms. The form $	heta _ A^{n-1}$ is a constant linear combination of their wedges with conjugates, so $\mathrm d	heta _ A^{n-1}=0$. The holomorphic fields commute with the antiholomorphic fields, and $\mathrm d\alpha _ j$ has type $(2,0)$. The coefficient matrix of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is therefore $(Z_ j ar Z_ k u)$. For smooth $u$ its entries have $\mu $-mean zero by ( 26.6 ), so the matrix of $\mu $-means of the coefficients of $	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is $A$. If $	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, averaging the positive coefficient matrix gives $A>0$. The converse follows by taking $u=0$. The same average shows that $V_ W$ contains no nonzero smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ direction. For a distribution $u$, the adjoints of $Z_ j$ and $ ar Z_ k$ with respect to $\mu $ annihilate constants, so the mean of each $Z_ j ar Z_ k u$ is still zero. The coefficients of a positive current in this global frame form a positive matrix of measures, whose matrix of total masses is semipositive; for $	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ this gives $A\geq 0$. Conversely, $	heta _ A$ itself is a positive current when $A\geq 0$. If $A=0$, the positive trace measure of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has total mass zero, and polarization then makes the entire current zero. Finally, for a fixed positive $A_+\in W$, the matrices $A+\varepsilon A_+$ with $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ approximate every semipositive $A\in W$ from the positive cone. This proves the closure assertion. The quotient and its equality case. Put $Q=H\det A$, so that $	heta _ A^ n=Q\mu $. For every smooth positive Hermitian form $\gamma $, the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[   rac{	heta _ A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\gamma ^ n} = rac1n\operatorname {tr}_\gamma 	heta _ A \geq \left( rac{	heta _ A^ n}{\gamma ^ n}ight)^{1/n}.  \] Integration yields $\int _ X	heta _ A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq Q^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma )$, which bounds every Gauduchon quotient in definition 26.1.1 from below. The balanced, hence Gauduchon, metric $\gamma =	heta _ A$ has $D_\mu (	heta _ A)=Q^{(n-1)/n}$ and attains equality. This proves the formula for $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)$. For a minimizing Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, the continuous nonnegative difference of the two sides of the pointwise inequality has integral zero. Pointwise equality then forces $\gamma =f	heta _ A$ for a smooth positive function $f$. Set $q=f^{n-1}$ and $T=	heta _ A^{n-1}$. Since $\mathrm dT=0$, the Gauduchon equation becomes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\wedge T=0$, and \[  0=\int _ Xq\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\wedge T=-\int _ X\mathrm dq\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q\wedge T.  \] The last integrand is nonnegative and vanishes exactly where $\mathrm dq=0$. Thus $f$ is constant. As $n\geq 2$ and \[  D_\mu (c	heta _ A)=c^{n-1}\lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)^{n-1},  \] normalization determines $c=\lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)^{-1}$. This proves the unique minimizer and its volume identity. Differentiating $-\log \lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)=-(\log H+\log \det A)/n$ twice gives ( 26.5 ). The corresponding squared norm of $U$ is $\| A^{-1/2}UA^{-1/2}\| _{\mathrm F}^2/n$, which is positive for $U
e 0$; here $\| B\| _{\mathrm F}^2=\operatorname {tr}(B^*B)$ denotes the squared Frobenius norm. Finally, \[  \partial 	heta _ A= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}A_{jk}\, \mathrm d\alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ k.  \] For invertible $A$, the vanishing of this form forces every $\mathrm d\alpha _ j=0$, by independence of the conjugate coframe, and the Lie algebra would then be abelian. Since adding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ does not change $\mathrm d	heta _ A$, this proves the last assertion. $\square$ Lemma 26.5.4 . On the cone of all positive definite Hermitian $n	imes n$ matrices, the Riemannian distance of the metric ( 26.5 ) is 26.7  egin{equation} \label{eq:positive-matrix-hessian-distance} d_{\mathrm{full}}(A,B)= rac1{\sqrt n} \| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F}. \end{equation} For endpoints with equal determinant, this is also the intrinsic distance in the hypersurface of all positive definite matrices with that determinant. Proof. By the trace formula, the congruence $M\mapsto P^*MP$ by a fixed invertible matrix $P$ is an isometry. Taking $P=A^{-1/2}$, we may assume that the endpoints are $I$ and $C=A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}>0$. The curve $\exp (t\log C)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, has constant speed $\| \log C\| _{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n$, which gives the upper bound for the distance. For the reverse inequality, diagonalization gives the convergent resolvent formula for the matrix logarithm and its derivative  egin{align*}  \log M& =\int _0^\infty  igl ((1+s)^{-1}I-(M+sI)^{-1} igr )\, \mathrm ds,\  D\log _ M[U]& =\int _0^\infty (M+sI)^{-1}U(M+sI)^{-1}\, \mathrm ds. \end{align*} On a neighborhood of $M$ where the spectrum is bounded below by a positive constant, differentiation under the integral sign is justified by an integrable bound. In a unitary basis diagonalizing $M$, with eigenvalues $d_ i>0$, the derivative has entries $c_{ij}U_{ij}$, where \[  c_{ij}= rac{\log d_ i-\log d_ j}{d_ i-d_ j}\quad (d_ i
e d_ j), \qquad c_{ij}= rac1{d_ i}\quad (d_ i=d_ j).  \] Writing $d_ i/d_ j=\mathrm e^{2s}$ gives $\sqrt{d_ id_ j}|c_{ij}|=|s/\sinh s|\leq 1$, including the limiting value at $s=0$. Hence \[  \| D\log _ M[U]\| _{\mathrm F} \leq \| M^{-1/2}UM^{-1/2}\| _{\mathrm F}.  \] Applying this along a piecewise $C^1$ path of positive matrices from $I$ to $C$ and integrating, we bound its length below by $\| \log C\| _{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n$. This proves the distance formula. In terms of the original endpoints, the length-minimizing curve is 26.8  egin{equation} \label{eq:positive-matrix-exponential-path} M(t)=A^{1/2}(A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})^ tA^{1/2}. \end{equation} Its determinant is $(\det A)^{1-t}(\det B)^ t$, so for endpoints with equal determinant it stays in the fixed-determinant hypersurface. $\square$ Write $\lambda (A)=\lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)$ and \[  S_ W=\{ A\in W:A>0,\  H\det A=1\} .  \] The radial derivative of $\lambda $ is positive, so $S_ W$ is a smooth hypersurface of the cone $\{ A\in W:A>0\} $. We write $d_ W$ for the intrinsic path distance of $S_ W$ with the metric induced by ( 26.5 ). Theorem 26.5.5 . The metric space $(S_ W,d_ W)$ is complete and proper, and a sequence in $S_ W$ is Cauchy exactly when its coefficient matrices converge to a positive matrix in $S_ W$. For $A,B\in S_ W$, 26.9  egin{align}  d_ W(A,B)& \geq  rac1{\sqrt n} \| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F},\label{eq:parallelizable-intrinsic-lower}\  d_ W(A,B)& \leq  rac{\| A-B\| _{\mathrm F}}{\sqrt n\min \{ \lambda _{\min }(A),\lambda _{\min }(B)\} }. \label{eq:parallelizable-intrinsic-upper} \end{align} The normalized minimizing metrics of ( 26.4 ) satisfy, pointwise on $X$, 26.11  egin{equation} \label{eq:parallelizable-minimizer-order} \mathrm e^{-\sqrt n d_ W(A,B)}\gamma _ A \leq \gamma _ B\leq \mathrm e^{\sqrt n d_ W(A,B)}\gamma _ A. \end{equation} In particular, the completion of $S_ W$ adds no point, and no point of the boundary of the coefficient cone is a limit of a Cauchy sequence. If $A_ j>0$ in $W$ converges to a nonzero singular semipositive $A_0$, then $\widehat A_ j=A_ j/\lambda (A_ j)$ lies in $S_ W$ and, for fixed $A_\star \in S_ W$, 26.12  egin{equation} \label{eq:parallelizable-singular-boundary-rate} d_ W(A_\star ,\widehat A_ j) \geq  rac{|\log \det A_ j|}{n\sqrt n}+O(1) \longrightarrow \infty . \end{equation} By contrast, a sequence of coefficient matrices tending to zero can normalize to a point of $S_ W$. Proof. Paths in $W$. Every path in $S_ W$ is a path in the hypersurface of all positive matrices with $H\det A=1$, so lemma 26.5.4 gives ( 26.9 ). To obtain an upper bound by paths inside $W$, put \[  U=B-A,\qquad C(t)=A+tU,\qquad N(t)= rac{C(t)}{\lambda (C(t))}.  \] Since the positive cone is convex and $W$ is linear, $N(t)$ stays in $S_ W$ and joins $A$ to $B$. With $K=C^{-1/2}UC^{-1/2}$, differentiation gives \[   egin{gathered} g_ N(N',N')= rac1n\operatorname {tr}(K^2) - rac1{n^2}(\operatorname {tr}K)^2 \leq  rac{\| U\| _{\mathrm F}^2}{nm^2},\ m=\min \{ \lambda _{\min }(A),\lambda _{\min }(B)\} . \end{gathered}  \] Indeed $C(t)\geq mI$ and $(\log \lambda (C))'=\operatorname {tr}(C^{-1}U)/n$. Integrating proves ( 26.10 ), and shows in particular that $S_ W$ is connected. Put $d=d_ W(A,B)$. Every eigenvalue of $A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}$ has a logarithm of absolute value at most $\| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F}\leq \sqrt n\, d$, by ( 26.9 ). Hence 26.13  egin{equation} \label{eq:parallelizable-coefficient-order} \mathrm e^{-\sqrt n d}A\leq B\leq \mathrm e^{\sqrt n d}A. \end{equation} Since $\gamma _ A=	heta _ A$ on $S_ W$, this proves ( 26.11 ). Cauchy sequences and bounded balls. For a Cauchy sequence $(A_ j)$ in $(S_ W,d_ W)$, comparison with one fixed element of the sequence, using ( 26.13 ), gives $mI\leq A_ j\leq MI$ with fixed positive $m,M$. Comparing two elements then gives \[  \| A_ j-A_ k\| _{\mathrm{op}} \leq M igl (\mathrm e^{\sqrt n d_ W(A_ j,A_ k)}-1 igr ),  \] where $\| \cdot \| _{\mathrm{op}}$ is the operator norm. The coefficient matrices therefore form a Cauchy sequence. Their limit lies in the closed linear space $W$, is positive, and satisfies $H\det A=1$, and the upper bound ( 26.10 ) proves convergence to that point in $d_ W$. Conversely, coefficient convergence to a positive point gives convergence in $d_ W$ by the same bound. This proves completeness and the Cauchy criterion. The minimizing forms then converge in $C^\infty $, because their coefficients multiply a fixed smooth coframe. By these estimates, $d_ W$ induces the topology of coefficient convergence. A closed ball of radius $R$ around $A_\star $ is contained in the compact matrix interval \[   egin{gathered} \mathrm e^{-\sqrt nR}A_\star \leq A\leq \mathrm e^{\sqrt nR}A_\star ,\ A\in W,\qquad H\det A=1. \end{gathered}  \] The ball is closed in that interval, hence compact. This proves properness. In particular, distances from a fixed reference point are bounded exactly when the eigenvalues relative to that point are bounded above and away from zero. The coefficient boundary. Write $\lambda _{\max }$ for the largest eigenvalue. If $A_ j	o A_0$ with $A_0\geq 0$ singular and nonzero, then $\lambda (A_ j)	o 0$ while $\lambda _{\max }(A_ j)$ has a positive limit, so the largest eigenvalue of $\widehat A_ j$ tends to infinity. Applying ( 26.13 ) to $A_\star ,\widehat A_ j$ gives \[   egin{aligned}  d_ W(A_\star ,\widehat A_ j) & \geq  rac1{\sqrt n}\log  rac{\lambda _{\max }(A_ j)}{\lambda (A_ j)\lambda _{\max }(A_\star )}\ & = rac{|\log \det A_ j|}{n\sqrt n}+O(1). \end{aligned}  \] The error term is bounded because $A_0
e 0$. This proves ( 26.12 ). For comparison, $A_ j=t_ jA_\star $ with $t_ j\downarrow 0$ normalizes to $A_\star $ for every $j$; its coefficient limit, the zero matrix, gives no new point of the completion. $\square$ By proposition 26.5.1 , the whole cone $\{ 	heta _ A:A\in W,\  A>0\} $ is then complete as well. The argument uses the invariant probability and the linearity of $W$; in other geometries the unit-volume hypersurface can have a boundary at finite distance, as in example 26.5.2 . The length-minimizing path ( 26.8 ) need not stay in a proper subspace $W$. For $n=3$, take \[  W=\operatorname {span}_{\mathbb R}\{ I,\operatorname {diag}(0,1,2)\} , \qquad a=H^{-1/3}.  \] The points $aI$ and $a6^{-1/3}\operatorname {diag}(1,2,3)$ of $S_ W$ have, on the path ( 26.8 ), the midpoint $a6^{-1/6}\operatorname {diag}(1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$. The diagonal entries fail the relation $x_1-2x_2+x_3=0$, since $1-2\sqrt2+\sqrt3
e 0$. Thus this path leaves $W$, whereas the normalized segment $N(t)$ used in the proof remains in it. Example 26.5.6 . On $G=\mathbb C^3$ take the multiplication \[  z\cdot w=(z_1+w_1,z_2+w_2,z_3+w_3+z_1w_2),  \] the Gaussian lattice $\Gamma =\mathbb Z[\mathrm i]^3$, and $X=\Gamma  ackslash G$. This is a compact non-Kähler manifold of dimension three, with invariant coframe \[  \alpha _1=\mathrm dz_1,\qquad \alpha _2=\mathrm dz_2,\qquad \alpha _3=\mathrm dz_3-z_1\mathrm dz_2.  \] For its full nine-dimensional cone $W=\operatorname {Herm}(3)$ and the normalized invariant probability, \[  H= rac6{\pi ^3},\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (	heta _ A)= rac6{\pi ^3}\det A,\qquad S=\{ A>0:\det A=\pi ^3/6\} .  \] Every positive background is nonclosed. The eight-dimensional unit-volume hypersurface is complete and proper, and its intrinsic distance is 26.16  egin{equation} \label{eq:iwasawa-unit-volume-distance} d_ S(A,B)= rac1{\sqrt3}\| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F}. \end{equation} Proof. The bilinear cross term makes the multiplication associative, with identity zero and inverse $(-z_1,-z_2,-z_3+z_1z_2)$. These operations preserve the Gaussian lattice. Its action by left multiplication is free and properly discontinuous: for a compact set $K\subset G$, elements $\gamma $ with $\gamma K\cap K
e \varnothing $ belong to the compact set $KK^{-1}$, containing only finitely many lattice elements. Choose Gaussian integers $\gamma _1,\gamma _2$ that move $z_1,z_2$ into the half-open unit square, and then $\gamma _3$ that moves $z_3+\gamma _1z_2$ into it. This gives a representative in the real six-dimensional unit cube. If two points of the half-open cube are equivalent, then $\gamma _1=\gamma _2=0$ and then $\gamma _3=0$. The cube is therefore a measurable fundamental domain, and $X$ is compact, being the image of its closure. This coframe is left-invariant, descends to $X$, and has \[  \mathrm d\alpha _3=-\alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2,\qquad \alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2\wedge \alpha _3 =\mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm dz_3.  \] The density of $h_0^3$ is $6/\pi ^3$ times real Lebesgue volume on the fundamental cube, giving the stated $H$. The coefficient of $\alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2\wedge  ar\alpha _3$ in $\partial 	heta _ A$ is $-\mathrm iA_{33}/(2\pi )$, so positivity makes every such background nonclosed. To see that $X$ admits no Kähler metric at all, suppose that a positive closed $(1,1)$-form $\kappa $ existed, and average its coefficient functions in this coframe against $\mu $. Their mean is a positive matrix $A$. In the coefficients of $\partial \kappa $, derivative terms have mean zero by ( 26.6 ); the remaining means are exactly the coefficients of $\partial 	heta _ A$. Closedness would force them to vanish, contradicting $A_{33}>0$. Thus $X$ is non-Kähler. The assertions about the volume, the minimizers and completeness follow from proposition 26.5.3 , theorem 26.5.5 . As $W$ is the full matrix space, the equal-determinant exponential path stays in $S$, and lemma 26.5.4 gives ( 26.16 ). For $A_\star =aI$, $a=(\pi ^3/6)^{1/3}$, this becomes \[  d_ S(A_\star ,A)^2= rac13\sum _{j=1}^3 \left(\log  rac{\lambda _ j(A)}aight)^2.  \] The three logarithms sum to zero. For a concrete degeneration, take $A_\varepsilon =\operatorname {diag}(1,1,\varepsilon )$, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. As $\varepsilon 	o 0$, the coefficients converge to the nonzero smooth semipositive form $	heta _{\operatorname {diag}(1,1,0)}$. The normalized matrices and their distances, on the other hand, are 26.17  egin{equation} \label{eq:iwasawa-diagonal-degeneration}  egin{gathered} \widehat A_\varepsilon =a\operatorname {diag}(\varepsilon ^{-1/3},\varepsilon ^{-1/3},\varepsilon ^{2/3}),\ d_ S(A_\star ,\widehat A_\varepsilon )= rac{\sqrt2}{3}|\log \varepsilon |. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Thus, after normalization, the boundary form $	heta _{\operatorname {diag}(1,1,0)}$ lies at infinite distance. $\square$

For every smooth positive Hermitian form $\gamma $, the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  \frac{\theta _ A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\gamma ^ n} =\frac1n\operatorname {tr}_\gamma \theta _ A \geq \left(\frac{\theta _ A^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}.  \] Integration yields $\int _ X\theta _ A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq Q^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma )$, which bounds every Gauduchon quotient in definition 26.1.1 from below. The balanced, hence Gauduchon, metric $\gamma =\theta _ A$ has $D_\mu (\theta _ A)=Q^{(n-1)/n}$ and attains equality. This proves the formula for $\lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)$. For a minimizing Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, the continuous nonnegative difference of the two sides of the pointwise inequality has integral zero. Pointwise equality then forces $\gamma =f\theta _ A$ for a smooth positive function $f$. Set $q=f^{n-1}$ and $T=\theta _ A^{n-1}$. Since $\mathrm dT=0$, the Gauduchon equation becomes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\wedge T=0$, and \[  0=\int _ Xq\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\wedge T=-\int _ X\mathrm dq\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q\wedge T.  \] The last integrand is nonnegative and vanishes exactly where $\mathrm dq=0$. Thus $f$ is constant. As $n\geq 2$ and \[  D_\mu (c\theta _ A)=c^{n-1}\lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)^{n-1},  \] normalization determines $c=\lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)^{-1}$. This proves the unique minimizer and its volume identity. Differentiating $-\log \lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)=-(\log H+\log \det A)/n$ twice gives ( 26.5 ). The corresponding squared norm of $U$ is $\| A^{-1/2}UA^{-1/2}\| _{\mathrm F}^2/n$, which is positive for $U\ne 0$; here $\| B\| _{\mathrm F}^2=\operatorname {tr}(B^*B)$ denotes the squared Frobenius norm. Finally, \[  \partial \theta _ A=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}A_{jk}\, \mathrm d\alpha _ j\wedge \bar\alpha _ k.  \] For invertible $A$, the vanishing of this form forces every $\mathrm d\alpha _ j=0$, by independence of the conjugate coframe, and the Lie algebra would then be abelian. Since adding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ does not change $\mathrm d\theta _ A$, this proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Lemma 26.5.4
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Lemma 26.5.4 . On the cone of all positive definite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices, the Riemannian distance of the metric ( 26.5 ) is 26.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-matrix-hessian-distance} d_{\mathrm{full}}(A,B)=\frac1{\sqrt n} \| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F}. \end{equation} For endpoints with equal determinant, this is also the intrinsic distance in the hypersurface of all positive definite matrices with that determinant. Proof. By the trace formula, the congruence $M\mapsto P^*MP$ by a fixed invertible matrix $P$ is an isometry. Taking $P=A^{-1/2}$, we may assume that the endpoints are $I$ and $C=A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}>0$. The curve $\exp (t\log C)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, has constant speed $\| \log C\| _{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n$, which gives the upper bound for the distance. For the reverse inequality, diagonalization gives the convergent resolvent formula for the matrix logarithm and its derivative \begin{align*}  \log M& =\int _0^\infty \bigl ((1+s)^{-1}I-(M+sI)^{-1}\bigr )\, \mathrm ds,\\  D\log _ M[U]& =\int _0^\infty (M+sI)^{-1}U(M+sI)^{-1}\, \mathrm ds. \end{align*} On a neighborhood of $M$ where the spectrum is bounded below by a positive constant, differentiation under the integral sign is justified by an integrable bound. In a unitary basis diagonalizing $M$, with eigenvalues $d_ i>0$, the derivative has entries $c_{ij}U_{ij}$, where \[  c_{ij}=\frac{\log d_ i-\log d_ j}{d_ i-d_ j}\quad (d_ i\ne d_ j), \qquad c_{ij}=\frac1{d_ i}\quad (d_ i=d_ j).  \] Writing $d_ i/d_ j=\mathrm e^{2s}$ gives $\sqrt{d_ id_ j}|c_{ij}|=|s/\sinh s|\leq 1$, including the limiting value at $s=0$. Hence \[  \| D\log _ M[U]\| _{\mathrm F} \leq \| M^{-1/2}UM^{-1/2}\| _{\mathrm F}.  \] Applying this along a piecewise $C^1$ path of positive matrices from $I$ to $C$ and integrating, we bound its length below by $\| \log C\| _{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n$. This proves the distance formula. In terms of the original endpoints, the length-minimizing curve is 26.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-matrix-exponential-path} M(t)=A^{1/2}(A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})^ tA^{1/2}. \end{equation} Its determinant is $(\det A)^{1-t}(\det B)^ t$, so for endpoints with equal determinant it stays in the fixed-determinant hypersurface. $\square$
