title: Theorem 26.5.5
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 26.5.5 . The metric space $(S_ W,d_ W)$ is complete and proper, and a sequence in $S_ W$ is Cauchy exactly when its coefficient matrices converge to a positive matrix in $S_ W$. For $A,B\in S_ W$, 26.9 \begin{align}  d_ W(A,B)& \geq \frac1{\sqrt n} \| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F},\label{eq:parallelizable-intrinsic-lower}\\  d_ W(A,B)& \leq \frac{\| A-B\| _{\mathrm F}}{\sqrt n\min \{ \lambda _{\min }(A),\lambda _{\min }(B)\} }. \label{eq:parallelizable-intrinsic-upper} \end{align} The normalized minimizing metrics of ( 26.4 ) satisfy, pointwise on $X$, 26.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:parallelizable-minimizer-order} \mathrm e^{-\sqrt n d_ W(A,B)}\gamma _ A \leq \gamma _ B\leq \mathrm e^{\sqrt n d_ W(A,B)}\gamma _ A. \end{equation} In particular, the completion of $S_ W$ adds no point, and no point of the boundary of the coefficient cone is a limit of a Cauchy sequence. If $A_ j>0$ in $W$ converges to a nonzero singular semipositive $A_0$, then $\widehat A_ j=A_ j/\lambda (A_ j)$ lies in $S_ W$ and, for fixed $A_\star \in S_ W$, 26.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:parallelizable-singular-boundary-rate} d_ W(A_\star ,\widehat A_ j) \geq \frac{|\log \det A_ j|}{n\sqrt n}+O(1) \longrightarrow \infty . \end{equation} By contrast, a sequence of coefficient matrices tending to zero can normalize to a point of $S_ W$. Proof. Paths in $W$. Every path in $S_ W$ is a path in the hypersurface of all positive matrices with $H\det A=1$, so lemma 26.5.4 gives ( 26.9 ). To obtain an upper bound by paths inside $W$, put \[  U=B-A,\qquad C(t)=A+tU,\qquad N(t)=\frac{C(t)}{\lambda (C(t))}.  \] Since the positive cone is convex and $W$ is linear, $N(t)$ stays in $S_ W$ and joins $A$ to $B$. With $K=C^{-1/2}UC^{-1/2}$, differentiation gives \[  \begin{gathered} g_ N(N',N')=\frac1n\operatorname {tr}(K^2) -\frac1{n^2}(\operatorname {tr}K)^2 \leq \frac{\| U\| _{\mathrm F}^2}{nm^2},\\ m=\min \{ \lambda _{\min }(A),\lambda _{\min }(B)\} . \end{gathered}  \] Indeed $C(t)\geq mI$ and $(\log \lambda (C))'=\operatorname {tr}(C^{-1}U)/n$. Integrating proves ( 26.10 ), and shows in particular that $S_ W$ is connected. Put $d=d_ W(A,B)$. Every eigenvalue of $A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}$ has a logarithm of absolute value at most $\| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F}\leq \sqrt n\, d$, by ( 26.9 ). Hence 26.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:parallelizable-coefficient-order} \mathrm e^{-\sqrt n d}A\leq B\leq \mathrm e^{\sqrt n d}A. \end{equation} Since $\gamma _ A=\theta _ A$ on $S_ W$, this proves ( 26.11 ). Cauchy sequences and bounded balls. For a Cauchy sequence $(A_ j)$ in $(S_ W,d_ W)$, comparison with one fixed element of the sequence, using ( 26.13 ), gives $mI\leq A_ j\leq MI$ with fixed positive $m,M$. Comparing two elements then gives \[  \| A_ j-A_ k\| _{\mathrm{op}} \leq M\bigl (\mathrm e^{\sqrt n d_ W(A_ j,A_ k)}-1\bigr ),  \] where $\| \cdot \| _{\mathrm{op}}$ is the operator norm. The coefficient matrices therefore form a Cauchy sequence. Their limit lies in the closed linear space $W$, is positive, and satisfies $H\det A=1$, and the upper bound ( 26.10 ) proves convergence to that point in $d_ W$. Conversely, coefficient convergence to a positive point gives convergence in $d_ W$ by the same bound. This proves completeness and the Cauchy criterion. The minimizing forms then converge in $C^\infty $, because their coefficients multiply a fixed smooth coframe. By these estimates, $d_ W$ induces the topology of coefficient convergence. A closed ball of radius $R$ around $A_\star $ is contained in the compact matrix interval \[  \begin{gathered} \mathrm e^{-\sqrt nR}A_\star \leq A\leq \mathrm e^{\sqrt nR}A_\star ,\\ A\in W,\qquad H\det A=1. \end{gathered}  \] The ball is closed in that interval, hence compact. This proves properness. In particular, distances from a fixed reference point are bounded exactly when the eigenvalues relative to that point are bounded above and away from zero. The coefficient boundary. Write $\lambda _{\max }$ for the largest eigenvalue. If $A_ j\to A_0$ with $A_0\geq 0$ singular and nonzero, then $\lambda (A_ j)\to 0$ while $\lambda _{\max }(A_ j)$ has a positive limit, so the largest eigenvalue of $\widehat A_ j$ tends to infinity. Applying ( 26.13 ) to $A_\star ,\widehat A_ j$ gives \[  \begin{aligned}  d_ W(A_\star ,\widehat A_ j) & \geq \frac1{\sqrt n}\log \frac{\lambda _{\max }(A_ j)}{\lambda (A_ j)\lambda _{\max }(A_\star )}\\ & =\frac{|\log \det A_ j|}{n\sqrt n}+O(1). \end{aligned}  \] The error term is bounded because $A_0\ne 0$. This proves ( 26.12 ). For comparison, $A_ j=t_ jA_\star $ with $t_ j\downarrow 0$ normalizes to $A_\star $ for every $j$; its coefficient limit, the zero matrix, gives no new point of the completion. $\square$

title: Example 26.5.6
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Example 26.5.6 . On $G=\mathbb C^3$ take the multiplication \[  z\cdot w=(z_1+w_1,z_2+w_2,z_3+w_3+z_1w_2),  \] the Gaussian lattice $\Gamma =\mathbb Z[\mathrm i]^3$, and $X=\Gamma \backslash G$. This is a compact non-Kähler manifold of dimension three, with invariant coframe \[  \alpha _1=\mathrm dz_1,\qquad \alpha _2=\mathrm dz_2,\qquad \alpha _3=\mathrm dz_3-z_1\mathrm dz_2.  \] For its full nine-dimensional cone $W=\operatorname {Herm}(3)$ and the normalized invariant probability, \[  H=\frac6{\pi ^3},\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ A)=\frac6{\pi ^3}\det A,\qquad S=\{ A>0:\det A=\pi ^3/6\} .  \] Every positive background is nonclosed. The eight-dimensional unit-volume hypersurface is complete and proper, and its intrinsic distance is 26.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:iwasawa-unit-volume-distance} d_ S(A,B)=\frac1{\sqrt3}\| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F}. \end{equation} Proof. The bilinear cross term makes the multiplication associative, with identity zero and inverse $(-z_1,-z_2,-z_3+z_1z_2)$. These operations preserve the Gaussian lattice. Its action by left multiplication is free and properly discontinuous: for a compact set $K\subset G$, elements $\gamma $ with $\gamma K\cap K\ne \varnothing $ belong to the compact set $KK^{-1}$, containing only finitely many lattice elements. Choose Gaussian integers $\gamma _1,\gamma _2$ that move $z_1,z_2$ into the half-open unit square, and then $\gamma _3$ that moves $z_3+\gamma _1z_2$ into it. This gives a representative in the real six-dimensional unit cube. If two points of the half-open cube are equivalent, then $\gamma _1=\gamma _2=0$ and then $\gamma _3=0$. The cube is therefore a measurable fundamental domain, and $X$ is compact, being the image of its closure. This coframe is left-invariant, descends to $X$, and has \[  \mathrm d\alpha _3=-\alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2,\qquad \alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2\wedge \alpha _3 =\mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm dz_3.  \] The density of $h_0^3$ is $6/\pi ^3$ times real Lebesgue volume on the fundamental cube, giving the stated $H$. The coefficient of $\alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2\wedge \bar\alpha _3$ in $\partial \theta _ A$ is $-\mathrm iA_{33}/(2\pi )$, so positivity makes every such background nonclosed. To see that $X$ admits no Kähler metric at all, suppose that a positive closed $(1,1)$-form $\kappa $ existed, and average its coefficient functions in this coframe against $\mu $. Their mean is a positive matrix $A$. In the coefficients of $\partial \kappa $, derivative terms have mean zero by ( 26.6 ); the remaining means are exactly the coefficients of $\partial \theta _ A$. Closedness would force them to vanish, contradicting $A_{33}>0$. Thus $X$ is non-Kähler. The assertions about the volume, the minimizers and completeness follow from proposition 26.5.3 , theorem 26.5.5 . As $W$ is the full matrix space, the equal-determinant exponential path stays in $S$, and lemma 26.5.4 gives ( 26.16 ). For $A_\star =aI$, $a=(\pi ^3/6)^{1/3}$, this becomes \[  d_ S(A_\star ,A)^2=\frac13\sum _{j=1}^3 \left(\log \frac{\lambda _ j(A)}a\right)^2.  \] The three logarithms sum to zero. For a concrete degeneration, take $A_\varepsilon =\operatorname {diag}(1,1,\varepsilon )$, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. As $\varepsilon \to 0$, the coefficients converge to the nonzero smooth semipositive form $\theta _{\operatorname {diag}(1,1,0)}$. The normalized matrices and their distances, on the other hand, are 26.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:iwasawa-diagonal-degeneration} \begin{gathered} \widehat A_\varepsilon =a\operatorname {diag}(\varepsilon ^{-1/3},\varepsilon ^{-1/3},\varepsilon ^{2/3}),\\ d_ S(A_\star ,\widehat A_\varepsilon )=\frac{\sqrt2}{3}|\log \varepsilon |. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Thus, after normalization, the boundary form $\theta _{\operatorname {diag}(1,1,0)}$ lies at infinite distance. $\square$

None Masses and reference densities in dimension three In dimension three, an invariant positive background has a nonnegative complex Hessian. Together with the mass identities for Gauduchon backgrounds, this determines its upper Monge–Ampère mass and shows that the singular semipositive coefficient limits have zero top mass. On the Iwasawa quotient, the same calculation identifies exactly which smooth reference probabilities keep the determinant formula for the volume. We keep the invariant coframe, $h_0$, $H$ and $	heta _ A$ of section 26.5.2 , and now assume $n=3$. Write $\mu _0=h_0^3/H$ to distinguish this invariant probability from other reference measures, and let $\mathscr M$ be the set of smooth strictly positive probability forms on $X$. Recall that $v_+$ denotes the upper Monge–Ampère mass of definition 6.5.1 . Proposition 26.5.7 . For $A>0$ on any such compact complex Lie-group quotient, 26.18  egin{equation} \label{eq:invariant-threefold-upper-mass} v_+(	heta _ A)=H\det A =\max _{
u \in \mathscr M}\mathcal V_
u (	heta _ A). \end{equation} The invariant probability $\mu _0$ attains this maximum. In particular the quotient has the bounded mass property. Proof. Since the forms $\mathrm d\alpha _ j$ are holomorphic, we have 26.19  egin{equation} \label{eq:invariant-pluripositive-form} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	heta _ A= rac1{4\pi ^2} \sum _{j,k}A_{jk}\, \mathrm d\alpha _ j\wedge \mathrm d ar\alpha _ k\geq 0. \end{equation} Indeed $ ar\partial (\alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ k) =-\alpha _ j\wedge \mathrm d ar\alpha _ k$, and applying $\partial $ and multiplying by $(\mathrm i/(2\pi ))^2$ gives the identity in ( 26.19 ). Diagonalizing the positive coefficient matrix expresses the result as a sum of nonnegative multiples of $ eta \wedge  ar eta $ for invariant $(2,0)$-forms $ eta $. In dimension three these are nonnegative $(2,2)$-forms: the wedge product with $\mathrm i\xi \wedge  ar\xi $, for a $(1,0)$-form $\xi $, has the squared modulus of $\xi \wedge  eta $ as coefficient. By proposition 26.5.3 , $	heta _ A$ is balanced, hence Gauduchon. The maximum case of theorem 26.15.3 therefore gives $v_+(	heta _ A)=\int _ X	heta _ A^3=H\det A$. The supremum of $\mathcal V_
u (	heta _ A)$ over $
u \in \mathscr M$ equals this upper mass by theorem 26.14.3 , and ( 26.4 ) shows that it is attained at $\mu _0$. Finally, proposition 6.5.2 makes the finiteness of the upper mass a property of the manifold. $\square$ Corollary 26.5.8 . If $A\geq 0$ is singular, then every bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ A)$ satisfies \[  \int _ X(	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=0.  \] For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ A)$, bounded or not, the non-pluripolar top power of $	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is also zero. Thus the nonzero semipositive boundary forms $	heta _ A$ of proposition 26.5.3 have zero non-pluripolar top mass. Proof. For $\varepsilon >0$, the same bounded $u$ is $	heta _{A+\varepsilon I}$-plurisubharmonic, so the preceding proposition bounds its mass by $H\det (A+\varepsilon I)$, which tends to zero with $\varepsilon $. By the multilinear construction of bounded products in proposition 1.7.1 , \[  (	heta _{A+\varepsilon I}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 = igl (	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+\varepsilon h_0 igr )^3  \] is a polynomial in $\varepsilon $ whose coefficients are mixed products of finite mass. Its total mass therefore converges to $\int _ X(	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, so this mass is zero, and positivity makes the measure zero. For unbounded $u$, we subtract a constant so that $u\leq 0$. Since $	heta _ A\geq 0$, the truncations $u_ k=\max (u,-k)$ are bounded and $	heta _ A$-plurisubharmonic, so their top products vanish by the bounded case. Restricting them to $\{ u>-k\} $ and passing to the limit that defines the non-pluripolar product gives zero as well. $\square$ We now specialize to the Iwasawa quotient of example 26.5.6 . Put \[  E=\mathbb C/\mathbb Z[\mathrm i],\qquad B=E^2,\qquad p:X\longrightarrow B,\quad [z]\longmapsto ([z_1],[z_2]).  \] This is a holomorphic submersion with connected elliptic fibers, and the coordinate description of the fundamental cube gives $p_*\mu _0=\mu _ B$, where $\mu _ B$ is the Haar probability on $B$. A smooth probability is called fiber invariant if it has the form \[  \mu _ f=(f\circ p)\mu _0,\qquad f\in C^\infty (B),\quad f>0,\quad \int _ B f\, \mu _ B=1.  \] Thus a smooth probability is fiber invariant when its density relative to $\mu _0$ is constant along the elliptic fibers of $p$; no invariance in the base directions is required. Theorem 26.5.9 . For every $A>0$ and fiber-invariant $\mu _ f$, 26.20  egin{equation} \label{eq:iwasawa-fiber-invariant-volume} \mathcal V_{\mu _ f}(	heta _ A)=H\det A, \qquad H= rac6{\pi ^3}. \end{equation} Its unique minimizing Gauduchon metric normalized by $D_{\mu _ f}=1$ is 26.21  egin{equation} \label{eq:iwasawa-fiber-invariant-minimizer} \gamma _{A,f}= rac{	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p^*v_{A,f})}{(H\det A)^{1/3}}, \qquad \gamma _{A,f}^3=\mu _ f, \end{equation} where $v_{A,f}$ is the solution of the Monge–Ampère equation ( 26.22 ) on the torus $B$, with a closed background, constructed in the proof. Conversely, for a fixed $A>0$, the probabilities $
u \in \mathscr M$ maximizing $\mathcal V_
u (	heta _ A)$ are exactly the fiber-invariant ones. For each fixed real linear $W\subset \operatorname {Herm}(3)$ containing a positive matrix, the Hessian metric for $\mu _ f$ is \[  g_ A(U,Z)= rac13\operatorname {tr}(A^{-1}UA^{-1}Z).  \] Its unit-volume hypersurface $S_ W=\{ A\in W:A>0,\  H\det A=1\} $ is complete and proper, and the Cauchy criterion and the distance bounds of theorem 26.5.5 hold with $n=3$. Proof. The map $p$ is well defined because multiplication by lattice elements adds Gaussian integers to the first two coordinates. It is a submersion, and fixing representatives of those coordinates identifies each fiber with the central quotient $E$. Integrating first in the third coordinate over the fundamental cube proves the pushforward identity. The closed equation on the base. Write the positive Hermitian matrix in block form and take its Schur complement: \[   egin{gathered} A= egin{pmatrix} C

& b

\  b^*

& a

\end{pmatrix},\ a=A_{33}>0,\qquad S=C-a^{-1}bb^*>0. \end{gathered}  \] On $B$, let \[  \omega _ S= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k=1}^2 S_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ k, \qquad Q_ B=\int _ B\omega _ S^2= rac2{\pi ^2}\det S.  \] We apply theorem 9.1.1 to this closed background with the density $Q_ Bf\mu _ B$. Since $\omega _ S$ is closed and the density has total mass $Q_ B$, Stokes' theorem forces the constant in the equation to be one. We obtain a smooth real $v=v_{A,f}$, unique up to an additive constant, such that 26.22  egin{equation} \label{eq:iwasawa-schur-base-equation} (\omega _ S+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^2=Q_ Bf\mu _ B, \qquad \omega _ S+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0. \end{equation} If $K$ is the coefficient matrix of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ in the base coframe, this says $\det (S+K)=(\det S)f$. The form \[  \Omega =	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p^*v)  \] has coefficient matrix $\left( egin{smallmatrix}C+K& b\ b^*& a\end{smallmatrix}ight)$ in the invariant coframe. Since $a>0$ and the Schur complement $S+K$ is positive, $\Omega >0$; its determinant is $a\det (S+K)=(\det A)(f\circ p)$. Consequently $\Omega ^3=(H\det A)\mu _ f$. This solution form is also balanced. Put $ eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p^*v)$, which is closed and uses only $\alpha _1,\alpha _2$ and their conjugates. Since $\mathrm d\alpha _3=-\alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2$, every term of $\partial 	heta _ A$ contains $\alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2$, and every conjugate term contains $ ar\alpha _1\wedge  ar\alpha _2$. Thus $\mathrm d	heta _ A\wedge  eta =0$. Together with $\mathrm d	heta _ A^2=0$, this proves \[  \mathrm d\Omega ^2=\mathrm d	heta _ A^2+2\mathrm d	heta _ A\wedge  eta =0.  \] Theorem 26.1.3 now gives ( 26.20 ). text: Corollary 26.5.8 . If $A\geq 0$ is singular, then every bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ A)$ satisfies \[  \int _ X(\theta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=0.  \] For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ A)$, bounded or not, the non-pluripolar top power of $\theta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is also zero. Thus the nonzero semipositive boundary forms $\theta _ A$ of proposition 26.5.3 have zero non-pluripolar top mass. Proof. For $\varepsilon >0$, the same bounded $u$ is $\theta _{A+\varepsilon I}$-plurisubharmonic, so the preceding proposition bounds its mass by $H\det (A+\varepsilon I)$, which tends to zero with $\varepsilon $. By the multilinear construction of bounded products in proposition 1.7.1 , \[  (\theta _{A+\varepsilon I}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =\bigl (\theta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+\varepsilon h_0\bigr )^3  \] is a polynomial in $\varepsilon $ whose coefficients are mixed products of finite mass. Its total mass therefore converges to $\int _ X(\theta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, so this mass is zero, and positivity makes the measure zero. For unbounded $u$, we subtract a constant so that $u\leq 0$. Since $\theta _ A\geq 0$, the truncations $u_ k=\max (u,-k)$ are bounded and $\theta _ A$-plurisubharmonic, so their top products vanish by the bounded case. Restricting them to $\{ u>-k\} $ and passing to the limit that defines the non-pluripolar product gives zero as well. $\square$

text: Theorem 26.5.10 . This span contains no nonzero smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ direction, and its intersection with $\mathscr P$ is the cone \[  \mathscr C=\{ b>0,\  e>0,\  e+cM>0\} .  \] For $\theta =\theta _{b,c,e}\in \mathscr C$, let $H(c,e)=\int _ B\sigma /L$. Then 26.24 \begin{equation} \label{eq:warped-gauduchon-volume} \mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=\frac{nb^ m}{H(c,e)}. \end{equation} A minimizing Gauduchon metric is \[  \gamma =L^{-1/m}(A+Lw),\qquad A=b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi >0,\qquad A^ m=\frac{b^ m}{H}\frac{\sigma }{L},  \] where $\phi $ is a smooth real function on $B$. This metric is balanced. Backgrounds with $c\ne 0$ are nonclosed. Proof. Pairing a smooth positive representative $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with the closed semipositive form $\kappa ^{m-1}\wedge w$ gives $b>0$, and its integral over the compact fiber $\{ y\} \times C$ is $L(y)>0$, by Stokes' theorem. These are exactly the stated inequalities; conversely, they make $\theta $ itself positive. The same tests applied to a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ direction give $b=0$ and $ca+e=0$ everywhere, and since $a$ is nonconstant, $c=e=0$. Also $\mathrm{d}\theta =c\, \mathrm{d}a\wedge w$, which is not identically zero when $c\ne 0$. Next we apply theorem 9.1.1 on $B$ to the closed positive background $b\kappa $ and the density $(b^ m/H)\sigma /L$. Since this density has integral $b^ m=\int _ B(b\kappa )^ m$, Stokes' theorem forces the constant in the equation to be one, and we obtain $A$. Put $\Omega =A+Lw$. Since $A^{m+1}=0$ and $(Lw)^2=0$, the binomial expansion gives 26.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:warped-balanced-cofactor} \Omega ^ n=\frac{nb^ m}{H}\mu ,\qquad \gamma ^ m=L^{-1}A^ m+mA^{m-1}\wedge w. \end{equation} The first summand is the pullback of a top-degree form on $B$, and the second is closed. Hence $\gamma $ is balanced, and in particular Gauduchon. For every Gauduchon metric $\eta $ on $X$, Stokes' theorem and the pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality give \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge \eta ^ m =\int _ X\Omega \wedge \eta ^ m \geq \left(\frac{nb^ m}{H}\right)^{1/n}D_\mu (\eta ).  \] For $\eta =\gamma $ the numerator is $nb^ m$, while $D_\mu (\gamma )=(nb^ m/H)^{m/n}H$. The quotient of $\gamma $ therefore attains the lower bound, which proves ( 26.24 ) and the minimizing property of $\gamma $. $\square$

title: Theorem 26.5.13
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 26.5.13 . Under the hypotheses of lemma 26.5.12 on the extreme sets, the metric completion of $\mathscr S$ is a closed Euclidean strip if $r_0,r_ M>1$, a closed Euclidean half-plane if exactly one of them exceeds one, and the whole Euclidean plane otherwise. Each boundary line of the completion is parametrized by $b>0$, and its points are represented by the forms \begin{align*}  \theta _+(b)& =b\kappa +\frac{H_ a}{nb^ m}a w, & H_ a& =\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{a}\quad (r_0>1),\\  \theta _-(b)& =b\kappa +\frac{H_-}{nb^ m}(1-a/M)w, & H_-& =\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{1-a/M}\quad (r_ M>1). \end{align*} These forms are smooth, semipositive, nef, nonclosed and not big, and their variational volume is one. The completion has no other boundary points. Proof. The completion of the convex product $\mathbb R\times I$ of proposition 26.5.11 is its Euclidean closure. Along a Cauchy sequence, $Y$ converges, so $b$ has a finite positive limit, and $R$ converges to a point of $I$ or to a finite endpoint of $I$. Lemma 26.5.12 decides which endpoints are finite and gives the three alternatives. On $\mathscr S$ we have $e=Q(v)/(nb^ m)$ and $c=ve$. At the end $v\to \infty $, $vQ(v)\to H_ a$ by monotone convergence, which gives the coefficient limit $\theta _+(b)$. At the end $v\to -1/M$, write $1+va=1-a/M+(v+1/M)a$; dominated convergence gives $Q(v)\to H_-$, and hence the limit $\theta _-(b)$. These are the coefficient limits at all finite ends. The forms are semipositive, hence nef, and they are nonclosed. Increasing their fiber coefficient by $\epsilon >0$ makes them positive, and ( 26.24 ) shows that the resulting volumes tend to one as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Monotonicity bounds the root volume of the limit form by this limit. Conversely, each fixed Gauduchon quotient is continuous in $\epsilon $, so the limit of the root volumes is at most every quotient of the limit form, hence at most its root volume. Thus the variational volume of $\theta _\pm (b)$ is one. Suppose that some quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$ satisfied \[  \theta _\pm +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta (\kappa +w),\qquad \delta >0.  \] For every smooth nonnegative top-degree form $\eta $ on $B$, its pullback is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed for degree reasons, and $\kappa \wedge \eta =0$. Stokes' theorem for currents therefore gives \[  \int _ B(L_\pm -\delta )\eta \geq 0.  \] where $L_\pm $ is the fiber coefficient of $\theta _\pm $. But $L_\pm $ vanishes somewhere, and a nonzero $\eta $ supported where $L_\pm <\delta $ contradicts this inequality. Thus $\theta _\pm $ is not big. $\square$

title: Current cones and endpoint equations
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: None Current cones and endpoint equations We keep the product $X=B\times C$, the backgrounds $\theta =b\kappa +(ca+e)w$ with real parameters $b,c,e$, and the probability $\mu =\sigma \wedge w$ of section 26.5.3 , and write $h=\kappa +w$ for the product Hermitian form. Pullbacks of nonnegative top-degree forms on $B$ are closed, and testing against them determines which backgrounds have positive current representatives, not only which have smooth positive ones. At a finite end of the unit-volume hypersurface, the reciprocal of the fiber coefficient is integrable with an exponent greater than one, so the equation on the base still has a continuous solution. Proposition 26.5.14 . In this real span, the pseudoeffective and nef cones both equal \[  \{ b\geq 0,\  e\geq 0,\  e+cM\geq 0\} .  \] A background in this span is big, that is, admits a representative $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta h$ with $\delta >0$, if and only if $b>0$, $e>0$ and $e+cM>0$. Thus the big backgrounds in this span form exactly the cone $\mathscr C$ of theorem 26.5.10 . Proof. Put $L=ca+e$, and suppose that a quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta h$ for some $\delta \geq 0$. Pairing with the closed semipositive form $\kappa ^{m-1}\wedge w$ and using Stokes' theorem for currents gives $b\geq \delta $. For every smooth nonnegative top-degree form $\eta $ on $B$, its pullback to $X$ is closed for degree reasons, and \[  \int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\delta h)\wedge \eta =\int _ B(L-\delta )\eta \geq 0.  \] If $L<\delta $ at some point, a nonzero form $\eta $ supported in the open set where $L<\delta $ contradicts this inequality. Hence $L\geq \delta $ everywhere. For $\delta =0$ these conditions are exactly $b\geq 0$, $e\geq 0$ and $e+cM\geq 0$; conversely, they make $\theta $ semipositive, and such forms are nef because $\theta +\varepsilon h>0$ for every $\varepsilon >0$. Conversely, if $\theta $ is nef, applying the same tests to smooth positive representatives of $\theta +\varepsilon h$ and letting $\varepsilon $ tend to zero gives these inequalities. For $\delta >0$ the conditions force the three strict inequalities, and conversely these make $\theta $ itself strictly positive. $\square$ Proposition 26.5.15 . Under the hypotheses of lemma 26.5.12 on the extreme sets, let $\theta =b\kappa +L_0w$, with $b>0$, be one of the boundary forms $\theta _+(b)$ or $\theta _-(b)$ of theorem 26.5.13 at a finite end. There is a continuous $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, pulled back from $B$, such that 26.37 \begin{equation} \label{eq:warped-continuous-endpoint-equation} (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu . \end{equation} Here the product is the usual product of bounded potentials. No solution of this equation is of class $C^{1,1}$ on $X$. Proof. Let $f=a$ for $\theta _+(b)$ and $f=1-a/M$ for $\theta _-(b)$, and let $r>1$ be the corresponding ratio $r_0$ or $r_ M$. The coefficient $L_0$ is a positive constant multiple of $f$. In each tube around an extreme component, the integral of $f^{-p}$ converges exactly when \[  \int _0^{s_0}s^{\operatorname {codim}_{\mathbb R}Z_ i-1-k_ ip}\, \mathrm{d}s  \] converges, where $s$ is the normal radius and $s_0>0$ is small. Thus $1/L_0\in L^ p(B,\sigma )$ for every $1<p<r$. The zero set of $L_0$ has volume zero, so the value assigned to the density there is irrelevant. The formulas for $\theta _\pm (b)$ give \[  H_0:=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{L_0}=nb^ m.  \] We apply theorem 10.1.1 on $B$ to the positive closed background $b\kappa $ and obtain a continuous $\phi $ with $A=b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi \geq 0$ and $A^ m=c_0\sigma /L_0$ for a constant $c_0>0$. Since $b\kappa $ is closed, bounded potentials do not change its mass, by theorem 2.2.2 ; hence $\int _ BA^ m=b^ m$ and $c_0=b^ m/H_0$. Set $u=\phi \circ p_ B$, where $p_ B:X\to B$ is the projection. Then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=A+L_0w\geq 0$. The pullback identity of lemma 1.7.3 gives $A^{m+1}=0$ on $X$, and $(L_0w)^2=0$. title: Proposition 26.5.14
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.5.14 . In this real span, the pseudoeffective and nef cones both equal \[  \{ b\geq 0,\  e\geq 0,\  e+cM\geq 0\} .  \] A background in this span is big, that is, admits a representative $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta h$ with $\delta >0$, if and only if $b>0$, $e>0$ and $e+cM>0$. Thus the big backgrounds in this span form exactly the cone $\mathscr C$ of theorem 26.5.10 . Proof. Put $L=ca+e$, and suppose that a quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta h$ for some $\delta \geq 0$. Pairing with the closed semipositive form $\kappa ^{m-1}\wedge w$ and using Stokes' theorem for currents gives $b\geq \delta $. For every smooth nonnegative top-degree form $\eta $ on $B$, its pullback to $X$ is closed for degree reasons, and \[  \int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\delta h)\wedge \eta =\int _ B(L-\delta )\eta \geq 0.  \] If $L<\delta $ at some point, a nonzero form $\eta $ supported in the open set where $L<\delta $ contradicts this inequality. Hence $L\geq \delta $ everywhere. For $\delta =0$ these conditions are exactly $b\geq 0$, $e\geq 0$ and $e+cM\geq 0$; conversely, they make $\theta $ semipositive, and such forms are nef because $\theta +\varepsilon h>0$ for every $\varepsilon >0$. Conversely, if $\theta $ is nef, applying the same tests to smooth positive representatives of $\theta +\varepsilon h$ and letting $\varepsilon $ tend to zero gives these inequalities. For $\delta >0$ the conditions force the three strict inequalities, and conversely these make $\theta $ itself strictly positive. $\square$

topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.5.15 . There is a continuous $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, pulled back from $B$, such that 26.37 \begin{equation} \label{eq:warped-continuous-endpoint-equation} (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu . \end{equation} Here the product is the usual product of bounded potentials. title: Limits of the base potentials
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: None Limits of the base potentials The base potentials used in theorem 26.5.10 to construct the minimizing balanced metrics converge uniformly at each finite end, and the limit solves the endpoint equation ( 26.37 ). Both the compactness and the uniqueness needed here concern only the equation on $B$, whose background is closed. Proposition 26.5.16 . Under the hypotheses of theorem 26.5.13 , let $\theta _ j=b_ j\kappa +L_ jw\in \mathscr S$ converge in coefficients to a boundary form $\theta _0=b\kappa +L_0w$ at a finite end. Normalize the smooth base potentials $\phi _ j$ of theorem 26.5.10 by $\sup _ B\phi _ j=0$ and put $u_ j=\phi _ j\circ p_ B$. Then the $u_ j$ converge uniformly on $X$ to a continuous solution $u_0$ of ( 26.37 ) pulled back from $B$. For every $1\leq k\leq n$, \[  (\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ k\rightharpoonup (\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0)^ k.  \] Moreover, $u_0$ is the unique bounded solution of ( 26.37 ) that is pulled back from $B$ and has supremum zero. Proof. Write $v_ j=c_ j/e_ j$ and $\psi _ j=\phi _ j/b_ j$. On $\mathscr S$ the equation for $\phi _ j$ on $B$ becomes \[  (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j)^ m=F_{v_ j}\sigma , \qquad F_ v=\frac1{Q(v)(1+va)},\qquad \sup _ B\psi _ j=0.  \] At the end where $\theta _0=\theta _+(b)$, $v_ j\to \infty $. Set $\epsilon =1/v$ and $H_\epsilon =\int _ B\sigma /(a+\epsilon )$. Then $F_ v=[H_\epsilon (a+\epsilon )]^{-1}$ and $H_\epsilon \to H_ a$. At the end where $\theta _0=\theta _-(b)$, $v_ j\to -1/M$. With $f=1-a/M$ and $t=v+1/M>0$, the denominator of $F_ v$ is $Q(v)(f+ta)$, and $Q(v)\to H_-$. Thus the respective limits of $F_{v_ j}$ are \[  F_+=\frac1{H_ a a},\qquad F_-=\frac1{H_-(1-a/M)}.  \] Choose $1<p<r$, where $r>1$ is the ratio $r_0$ or $r_ M$ of that end. Integration over tubes as in the proof of proposition 26.5.15 gives $a^{-1}\in L^ p(B,\sigma )$, respectively $f^{-1}\in L^ p(B,\sigma )$. Near the first end $F_ v\leq C/a$, and near the second $F_ v\leq C/f$. Since the extreme sets have volume zero, dominated convergence gives $F_{v_ j}\to F_\pm $ in $L^ p(B,\sigma )$, and each limiting density has integral one. Since $\sigma /\kappa ^ m$ is smooth and strictly positive on compact $B$, the densities of the equations also have a common bound in $L^ p(B,\kappa ^ m)$. We apply theorem 10.3.4 to the fixed background $\kappa $: every subsequence of $(\psi _ j)$ has a uniformly convergent further subsequence. Continuity of bounded products under uniform convergence identifies its limit with a normalized solution of $(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _0)^ m=F_\pm \sigma $. Since $\kappa $ is closed, it satisfies the Guan–Li condition, so 11.5.1 makes this solution unique. Every cluster limit is consequently the same, which proves uniform convergence of the whole sequence. Since $b_ j\to b>0$, we obtain $u_ j\to u_0=(b\psi _0)\circ p_ B$ uniformly. To prove convergence of the products, note that on each coordinate ball the convergence of the background coefficients provides a common smooth function $q$, a quadratic polynomial, such that all $u_ j+q$ are plurisubharmonic. These corrected potentials are uniformly bounded and converge uniformly. The continuity of bounded products under convergence in capacity (section 1.6 ) gives weak convergence of all their products, with uniform local mass bounds. Expanding the products as in ( 1.21 ), and using smooth convergence of the remaining background factors, we obtain the asserted convergence of currents. In top degree, $(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n=\mu $ for all $j$, so the limit solves the endpoint equation. For uniqueness, let $v=\chi \circ p_ B$ be a bounded solution pulled back from $B$, with $\sup _ B\chi =0$. The current $A_\chi =b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ on $B$ is positive, as one sees by pairing the pulled-back current $\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ with $w$ and with pullbacks of positive forms on $B$. The product expansion gives $nL_0A_\chi ^ m\wedge w=\sigma \wedge w$, which determines $A_\chi ^ m=\sigma /(nL_0)$ off the extreme set. That density already has total mass $H_0/n=b^ m$, whereas mass invariance for the closed background $b\kappa $ gives $\int _ BA_\chi ^ m=b^ m$. Positivity therefore excludes any mass of $A_\chi ^ m$ on the extreme set. Thus $\chi /b$ satisfies the same normalized equation on $B$ as $\psi _0$, and 11.5.1 proves the asserted uniqueness. $\square$ The proposition concerns the limit of the base potentials constructed above. It does not describe solutions of the endpoint equation that are not pulled back from $B$, nor does it give a pointwise limit of the balanced metrics $\gamma _ j=L_ j^{-1/m}(b_ j\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ j+L_ jw)$.

title: Projective and torus examples
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Projective and torus examples Example 26.5.19 . On $B=\mathbb P^2$, take normalized Fubini–Study $\kappa $, $\sigma =\kappa ^2$, $C=\mathbb P^1$, and \[  a([Z])=\frac{|Z_1|^2/2+|Z_2|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2}.  \] Then $M=1$, $r_0=r_ M=2$, and the completion is a closed strip with finite faces \[  b\kappa +\frac{4\log 2}{3b^2}a w,\qquad b\kappa +\frac{4\log 2}{3b^2}(1-a)w.  \] For $v\ne 0$, \[  Q(v)=\frac4{v^2}\bigl [(v+1)\log (1+v) -(v+2)\log (1+v/2)\bigr ], \qquad Q(0)=1.  \] The width of the strip is the finite positive integral \[  \int _{-1}^{\infty } \sqrt{\frac{Q''/Q-2(Q'/Q)^2}{3}}\, \mathrm{d}v.  \] Proof. The extreme sets are the points $[1:0:0]$ and $[0:0:1]$. In affine coordinates, $a$ and $1-a$ vanish there to exactly second order, so both real codimensions are four and both orders are two. To compute the law of $a$ under $\sigma $, polar integration in the chart $Z_0=1$ gives $2\, \mathrm{d}s_1\mathrm{d}s_2/(1+s_1+s_2)^3$, where $s_ j=|z_ j|^2$. The transformation $u_ j=s_ j/(1+s_1+s_2)$ gives the uniform density two on the triangle $u_1,u_2\geq 0$, $u_1+u_2\leq 1$, and $a=u_1/2+u_2$. For $0\leq s\leq 1/2$, the triangle $u_1/2+u_2\leq s$ has area $s^2$, so the law of $a$ has density $4s$ on $[0,1/2]$. With $u_0=1-u_1-u_2$, exchanging $u_0$ and $u_2$ preserves the uniform measure and replaces $a$ by $1-a$; hence the law has density $4(1-s)$ on $[1/2,1]$. Integrating against these two densities gives $H_ a=H_-=4\log 2$ and the formula for $Q$, and the integral definition of $Q$ shows that $Q(0)=1$ is its continuous extension. Theorem 26.5.13 gives the boundary lines and the finite width, with Euclidean coordinates $Y=\sqrt2\log b$ and $R(v)$. $\square$ Example 26.5.20 . Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$, $B=E^ m$, and write $z_ j=u_ j+i\tau _ j$. Put \[  \eta _ j=\frac i2\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j, \qquad s=(m!)^{-1/m},\qquad \kappa =s\sum _ j\eta _ j,\qquad \sigma =\kappa ^ m.  \] For $a=\sin ^2(\pi u_1)$, the unit-volume hypersurface is itself a complete Euclidean plane, with Euclidean coordinates \[  Y=\sqrt m\log b,\qquad R=\frac{\log (1+v)}{2\sqrt n},\qquad v>-1.  \] Its minimizing balanced metrics can be written down by integrating a periodic function twice. Proof. The forms descend to $B$, and $\sigma =\eta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \eta _ m$ is a probability form. Both extreme sets are real hypersurfaces along which $a$, respectively $1-a$, vanishes to second order, so $r_0=r_ M=1/2$. Splitting the period and substituting $t=\tan (\pi u)$ gives \begin{align*}  Q(v)& =\int _0^1\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{1+v\sin ^2(\pi u)}\\ & =\frac2\pi \int _0^\infty \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{1+(1+v)t^2} =\frac1{\sqrt{1+v}}. \end{align*} Let $F_ v(u)=[Q(v)(1+v\sin ^2(\pi u))]^{-1}$, which has mean one over a period. Integrating the equation \[  \phi _ v''=4\pi bs(F_ v-1)  \] twice, whose right side has mean zero, gives a smooth periodic potential $\phi _ v$ of $u=u_1$; the first integration constant is chosen so that $\phi _ v'$ has mean zero. In our normalization $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ v=\phi _ v''\eta _1/(4\pi )$, hence \[  A=bs\left(F_ v\eta _1+\sum _{j=2}^ m\eta _ j\right)>0, \qquad A^ m=b^ mF_ v\sigma =\frac{b^ m}{H}\frac{\sigma }{L}.  \] Thus the minimizer of theorem 26.5.10 , with its cofactor formula ( 26.25 ), is explicit in this example, without an appeal to theorem 9.1.1 . Differentiating $Q$ gives \[  \rho (v)=\frac1{4n(1+v)^2},\qquad g_{\mathscr S}=m\, \mathrm{d}U^2+ \frac1{4n}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{1+v}\right)^2.  \] As $U$ and $v$ range over $\mathbb R$ and $(-1,\infty )$, the coordinates $(Y,R)$ range over all of $\mathbb R^2$. Both boundary faces of the coefficient cone are therefore at infinite distance on the unit-volume hypersurface. $\square$ These distances are those of the fixed three-parameter cone with the product probability $\mu =\sigma \wedge w$. The endpoint criterion of lemma 26.5.12 uses the hypothesis that the extreme sets are disjoint unions of submanifolds along which $a$ vanishes to finite power order; intersecting extreme strata or vanishing of infinite order would require further estimates. The variances are computed from the minimizing metrics, but we do not assert that these metrics have a pointwise limit at a finite end.

title: 26.6 A compact dual problem over Gauduchon currents
search_title: A compact dual problem over Gauduchon currents
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.6 A compact dual problem over Gauduchon currents We now fix a Hermitian background and vary the density. For a smooth positive density, theorem 26.1.3 provides a minimizing Gauduchon metric; for a density that is only continuous or integrable, there is no smooth equation to produce one. The extremal problem becomes compact when positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-currents are allowed as tests, provided the denominator $D_\mu $ is extended to currents. For this we take the determinant of the matrix density of a current relative to its trace measure. The integral of its $n$th root is an infimum of continuous linear functionals, hence upper semicontinuous under weak convergence, and its maximum over normalized currents is attained. The smooth equation identifies this maximum with the supremum over smooth tests. From here until section 26.10 , we assume $n\geq 2$, and we fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ and a smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$; integrability and convergence in measure refer to $\mathrm{d}V$. As in chapter 6 , $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ for bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)$ is the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 6.1.2 . Let $\mathscr G_\omega $ be the compact convex set of normalized Gauduchon currents of section 4.4 , that is, of positive $(n-1,n-1)$-currents $T$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ and $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$. Finally, let $F\in C(X,\mathbb R)$. For $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, the trace measure $\sigma _ T=\omega \wedge T$ is a probability measure, and all coefficient measures of $T$ are absolutely continuous with respect to it. In a unitary frame for $\omega $, let $B$ be the matrix of a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\beta $ relative to $\omega $. The coefficient densities of $T$ form a measurable positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix $P_ T$, determined $\sigma _ T$-almost everywhere by \[  \beta \wedge T=\frac1n\operatorname {tr}(B P_ T)\, \mathrm{d}\sigma _ T, \qquad \operatorname {tr}P_ T=n\quad \sigma _ T\text{-almost everywhere}.  \] The matrix $P_ T$ transforms by unitary conjugation when the frame changes, so its determinant is well defined. Define 26.39 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-gaud-functional} f_ F=\left(\frac{\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V}{\omega ^ n}\right)^{1/n},\qquad \Gamma _ F(T)=f_ F(\det P_ T)^{1/n}\sigma _ T,\qquad \mathfrak D_ F(T)=\Gamma _ F(T)(X). \end{equation} These quantities are finite, since the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives $(\det P_ T)^{1/n}\leq 1$; the measure $\Gamma _ F(T)$ may vanish for some currents. The same definitions apply to every positive $(n-1,n-1)$-current $T$ of finite mass, with the finite measure $\sigma _ T=\omega \wedge T$ and $\operatorname {tr}P_ T=n$, and $\Gamma _ F$ is positively homogeneous of degree one in $T$. If the coefficient measures of $T$ are written instead as a matrix density $P'$ relative to another positive measure $\sigma '$ with respect to which they are absolutely continuous, then $(\det P_ T)^{1/n}\sigma _ T=(\det P')^{1/n}\sigma '$, by homogeneity of the determinant. For a smooth positive $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$, we may therefore use the reference measure $\omega ^ n$. The coefficient matrix of $T$ relative to $\omega ^ n$ is the cofactor matrix of the matrix of $\gamma $, and its determinant is $(\gamma ^ n/\omega ^ n)^{n-1}$. The definition therefore gives \[  \mathfrak D_ F(\gamma ^{n-1}) =\int _ X\left(\frac{\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Thus $\mathfrak D_ F$ extends the denominator $D_\mu $ of definition 26.1.1 to currents, with $\mu $ replaced by the possibly unnormalized density $\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$. Lemma 26.6.1 . For every positive $(n-1,n-1)$-current $T$ of finite mass on $X$, \[  \mathfrak D_ F(T) =\inf _{\substack {\beta >0\  \mathrm{continuous}\\ \beta ^ n=\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V}} \int _ X\beta \wedge T.  \] In particular, $\mathfrak D_ F$ is concave, positively homogeneous and weakly upper semicontinuous on $\mathscr G_\omega $, and its value does not depend on the auxiliary frame or on the metric used to express the matrix density. Proof. Let $I$ be the identity matrix of size $n$. For any positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix $P$ of that size, \[  (\det P)^{1/n} =\inf _{Q>0,\  \det Q=1}\frac1n\operatorname {tr}(QP).  \] The inequality $\leq $ is the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. For the reverse inequality, take, for real $\varepsilon >0$, \[  Q_\varepsilon = \det (P+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}(P+\varepsilon I)^{-1}.  \] Its determinant is one. If $P$ is positive definite, the trace expression $\frac1n\operatorname {tr}(Q_\varepsilon P)$ converges to $(\det P)^{1/n}$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. If $P$ is singular, it converges to zero: each ratio of an eigenvalue of $P$ to that eigenvalue plus $\varepsilon $ is bounded, while the prefactor tends to zero. When $\operatorname {tr}P=n$, the trace expression is at most $1+\varepsilon $. We apply this formula to $P_ T$ and multiply by $f_ F$. Every continuous positive $\beta $ in the asserted infimum has matrix $f_ FQ$ with $\det Q=1$, so it gives an upper bound for $\mathfrak D_ F(T)$. Conversely, for fixed $\varepsilon >0$ the measurable field $Q_\varepsilon $ formed with $P=P_ T$ is bounded above and below by positive constants. It can be approximated in $L^1(\sigma _ T)$ by continuous positive definite Hermitian fields with bounds of the same type. One way to construct them is to apply Lusin's theorem in finitely many bundle charts, extend the continuous fields from the resulting compact sets, and glue with a partition of unity; spectral truncation to a fixed positive interval preserves the bounds. Finally we divide each approximating field by the $n$th root of its determinant. This normalization is uniformly continuous on fields with spectrum in a fixed compact positive interval, so the normalized fields still converge in $L^1(\sigma _ T)$ and have determinant one. Their trace integrals converge to that of $Q_\varepsilon $. Now let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. The bound $1+\varepsilon $ permits dominated convergence, and we obtain equality of the infimum and the integral. For a current of arbitrary positive finite trace mass we use homogeneity, and the zero current is immediate. The infimum is taken over functionals $T\mapsto \int _ X\beta \wedge T$ that are linear and weakly continuous, which proves concavity and upper semicontinuity. It also expresses $\mathfrak D_ F(T)$ without a matrix frame or an auxiliary metric, which proves the final assertion. $\square$ Let $B_0(F)$ be the normalization scalar of section 15.1 for the background $\omega $ and the reference potential zero. Thus the equation $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=\mathrm{e}^{B_0(F)+F}\mathrm{d}V$ has a bounded solution $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and $B_0(F)$ is the only constant with this property. Theorem 26.6.2 . For every $F\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, 26.40 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weak-gaud-max-formula} M(F):=\max _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }\mathfrak D_ F(T) =\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(F)/n}>0. \end{equation} The maximum equals the supremum over the smooth strictly positive members of $\mathscr G_\omega $. The set $\mathscr M(F)$ of maximizing currents is nonempty, compact and convex. If $F$ is smooth, there is exactly one maximizing current, namely the normalized $(n-1)$st power of the Gauduchon metric conformal to the smooth solution form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=\mathrm{e}^{B_0(F)+F}\mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Upper semicontinuity of $\mathfrak D_ F$ on the compact set $\mathscr G_\omega $ gives attainment, and testing a smooth positive member gives a positive value. Concavity makes the set of maximizers convex, and upper semicontinuity makes it closed. Suppose first that $F$ is smooth, and let $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ be the smooth solution form with $\Omega ^ n=\mathrm{e}^{B_0(F)+F}\mathrm{d}V$. The form $\beta =\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(F)/n}\Omega $ is an admissible test in the preceding lemma, so Stokes' theorem for currents gives, for every $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, \[  \mathfrak D_ F(T)\leq \int _ X\beta \wedge T =\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(F)/n}\int _ X\omega \wedge T=\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(F)/n}.  \] If $\gamma $ is the Gauduchon metric conformal to $\Omega $, equality holds in the pointwise matrix inequality for $T$ proportional to $\gamma ^{n-1}$; normalizing $T$ so that $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$, we obtain the formula and its attainment by a smooth test. For uniqueness, let $T$ be a maximizer. Equality in the integrated inequalities forces equality in the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality $\sigma _ T$-almost everywhere. Since the matrix of $\beta $ is positive definite and $\operatorname {tr}P_ T=n$, this means that the coefficient measures of $T$ are a nonnegative scalar measure times the smooth coefficients of $\gamma ^{n-1}$. Thus $T=a\gamma ^{n-1}$, where $a$ is a positive measure, regarded as a distribution. The equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\gamma ^{n-1})=0$ is the adjoint of a scalar elliptic equation, so elliptic regularity makes $a$ smooth. Since $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, proposition 4.8.1 identifies the kernel of this adjoint operator with the constants: the trace operator $v\mapsto n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}/\gamma ^ n$ has the constants as kernel and index zero, and integration against $\gamma ^ n$ annihilates its range. Thus $a$ is constant, and the normalization fixes the constant. This proves uniqueness. For continuous $F,G$, the pointwise definition gives \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\| F-G\| _\infty /n}\mathfrak D_ G(T) \leq \mathfrak D_ F(T) \leq \mathrm{e}^{\| F-G\| _\infty /n}\mathfrak D_ G(T).  \] The same bounds hold for the maxima, and for the suprema over smooth positive members. We approximate $F$ uniformly by smooth functions. Since $B_0$ is $1$-Lipschitz for the uniform norm by proposition 15.1.1 , the formula just proved for smooth data gives ( 26.40 ) in the limit, including the equality with the smooth supremum. Note that only $F$ is approximated here: some normalized Gauduchon currents are not limits of smooth positive ones, as example 28.8.2 shows. $\square$

The equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\gamma ^{n-1})=0$ is the adjoint of a scalar elliptic equation, so elliptic regularity makes $a$ smooth. Since $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, proposition 4.8.1 identifies the kernel of this adjoint operator with the constants: the trace operator $v\mapsto n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}/\gamma ^ n$ has the constants as kernel and index zero, and integration against $\gamma ^ n$ annihilates its range. Thus $a$ is constant, and the normalization fixes the constant. This proves uniqueness. For continuous $F,G$, the pointwise definition gives \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\| F-G\| _\infty /n}\mathfrak D_ G(T) \leq \mathfrak D_ F(T) \leq \mathrm{e}^{\| F-G\| _\infty /n}\mathfrak D_ G(T).  \] The same bounds hold for the maxima, and for the suprema over smooth positive members. We approximate $F$ uniformly by smooth functions. Since $B_0$ is $1$-Lipschitz for the uniform norm by proposition 15.1.1 , the formula just proved for smooth data gives ( 26.40 ) in the limit, including the equality with the smooth supremum. Note that only $F$ is approximated here: some normalized Gauduchon currents are not limits of smooth positive ones, as example 28.8.2 shows. $\square$

title: Lemma 26.7.1
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Lemma 26.7.1 . Suppose $T_ j\to T$ weakly in $\mathscr G_\omega $ and $\mathfrak D_ F(T_ j)\to M(F)$. Then $T\in \mathscr M(F)$ and $\Gamma _ F(T_ j)\rightharpoonup \Gamma _ F(T)$. On $\mathscr M(F)$ the map $T\mapsto \Gamma _ F(T)$ is affine and continuous. Proof. Upper semicontinuity gives $\mathfrak D_ F(T)\geq M(F)$, hence equality. The measures $\Gamma _ F(T_ j)$ have bounded mass; let $\Gamma '$ be a weak cluster point, whose mass is $M(F)$. For a continuous real function $h$, choose $\varepsilon >0$ with $1\pm \varepsilon h>0$. Since $\Gamma _{F+n\log (1\pm \varepsilon h)}=(1\pm \varepsilon h)\Gamma _ F$, upper semicontinuity of $\mathfrak D$ for these two continuous logarithmic densities gives \[  \int _ X(1\pm \varepsilon h)\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma ' \leq \int _ X(1\pm \varepsilon h)\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _ F(T).  \] Since both measures have mass $M(F)$, the two signs give equality of the integrals of $h$. Thus every cluster point equals $\Gamma _ F(T)$, which proves the convergence. For affineness, take $T_1,T_2\in \mathscr G_\omega $ and $t\in [0,1]$, and express the coefficient measures of both currents through densities with respect to the sum of their trace measures. Concavity and homogeneity of the $n$th root of the determinant, applied to these matrix densities, give \[  \Gamma _ F(tT_1+(1-t)T_2) \geq t\Gamma _ F(T_1)+(1-t)\Gamma _ F(T_2),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] If $T_1$ and $T_2$ maximize, so does the current on the left, by concavity of $\mathfrak D_ F$. Both measures in the inequality then have mass $M(F)$, so equality holds. This proves affineness, and continuity is the special case of the first assertion in which every $T_ j$ is a maximizer. $\square$

title: 26.8 Integrability of Gauduchon determinant measures
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
26.8 Integrability of Gauduchon determinant measures A lower bound for the constants of smooth equations in terms of an $L^ p$ norm of the density gives, by duality, a uniform $L^ q$ bound for the determinant measures of all normalized Gauduchon currents, for every exponent $q<n/(n-1)$. At the endpoint $q=n/(n-1)$, the optimal constant is exactly $v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}$, where $v_-(\omega )$ is the lower Monge–Ampère mass of definition 6.5.1 . Thus integrability of the dual tests at the critical exponent is equivalent to positive lower mass of the background. Write $\Gamma _0(T)$ for the determinant measure $\Gamma _ F(T)$ of ( 26.39 ) with $F=0$. Theorem 26.8.1 . For every $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, the measure $\Gamma _0(T)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$; we write $\Gamma _0(T)=k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V$ and call $k_ T\geq 0$ the determinant density of $T$. For every $1<q<n/(n-1)$ there is $C_ q>0$ such that \[  \| k_ T\| _{L^ q(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq C_ q \qquad (T\in \mathscr G_\omega ).  \] Proof. Fix $p>1$ and a smooth strictly positive function $h$. By theorem 9.1.1 there are a smooth form $\Omega _ h=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ h>0$ and a constant $c_ h>0$ such that \[  \Omega _ h^ n=c_ hh^ n\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The lower-density estimate of theorem 10.3.3 gives a constant $c_ p>0$, independent of $h$, such that \[  c_ h\| h^ n\| _{L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)}\geq c_ p.  \] The pointwise matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, applied to $\Omega _ h$ and the coefficient density of $T$, gives the inequality of measures \[  c_ h^{1/n}h\, \Gamma _0(T)\leq \Omega _ h\wedge T.  \] Integrating and using $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ yields \[  \int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _0(T) \leq c_ h^{-1/n}\int _ X\Omega _ h\wedge T =c_ h^{-1/n} \leq c_ p^{-1/n}\| h\| _{L^{np}(\mathrm{d}V)}.  \] Approximation by smooth strictly positive functions extends this bound to every continuous nonnegative $h$, and applied to $|h|$ it bounds the integral of every continuous function against $\Gamma _0(T)$ by its $L^{np}$ norm. Since continuous functions are dense in $L^{np}$, the duality between $L^{np}$ and $L^{np/(np-1)}$ shows that $\Gamma _0(T)$ has a density in $L^{np/(np-1)}$, with norm at most $c_ p^{-1/n}$. As $p$ ranges over $(1,+\infty )$, the exponent $np/(np-1)$ ranges over $(1,n/(n-1))$. This proves the theorem. $\square$ In particular, the determinant of the matrix density vanishes on the singular part of the trace measure: if $\sigma _ T=\sigma _{T,\mathrm{ac}}+\sigma _{T,\mathrm{s}}$ is its Lebesgue decomposition with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$, then \[  \det P_ T=0\quad \sigma _{T,\mathrm{s}}	ext{-almost everywhere}.  \] Indeed, $f_0=(\mathrm{d}V/\omega ^ n)^{1/n}$ is everywhere positive and $\Gamma _0(T)=f_0(\det P_ T)^{1/n}\sigma _ T$ is absolutely continuous. This says nothing about a possible singular part of the current $T$ itself. Theorem 26.8.2 . With the extended value $+\infty $ allowed, one has \[  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega } \| k_ T\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathrm{d}V)}=v_-(\omega )^{-1/n},  \] where the right side is interpreted as $+\infty $ when $v_-(\omega )=0$. The supremum does not change if $T$ is restricted to the smooth strictly positive members of $\mathscr G_\omega $. Thus a uniform estimate at the endpoint exponent holds if and only if $v_-(\omega )>0$. Proof. Suppose first that $v_-(\omega )>0$. For the smooth equation in the preceding proof, the definition of $v_-$ gives \[  c_ h\int _ Xh^ n\, \mathrm{d}V=\int _ X\Omega _ h^ n\geq v_-(\omega ).  \] The same pointwise inequality and Stokes' theorem therefore give \[  \int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _0(T) \leq v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}\| h\| _{L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)}.  \] By duality, $\| k_ T\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}}\leq v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}$ for every $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $. For the reverse bound, let $g$ be any smooth positive probability density relative to $\mathrm{d}V$, and solve \[  \Omega _ g^ n=c(g)g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Let $T_ g$ be the trace-normalized $(n-1)$st power of the Gauduchon metric conformal to $\Omega _ g$. Equality in the pointwise matrix inequality gives \[  \int _ Xg^{1/n}\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _0(T_ g)=c(g)^{-1/n}.  \] Since $\| g^{1/n}\| _{L^ n}=1$, Hölder's inequality gives $\| k_{T_ g}\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}}\geq c(g)^{-1/n}$. By theorem 26.14.3 , theorem 26.1.3 , \[  \inf _{g>0\  \mathrm{smooth},\  \int _ Xg\, \mathrm{d}V=1}c(g)=v_-(\omega ).  \] Taking the supremum over these smooth currents $T_ g$ proves the matching lower bound; if $v_-(\omega )=0$, the same argument makes this supremum infinite. Since the currents $T_ g$ are smooth, this also proves that allowing nonsmooth currents does not change the supremum. $\square$ The formula shows that the optimal endpoint constant does not depend on the choice of $\mathrm{d}V$, whereas the subcritical constants $C_ q$ may depend on it. Corollary 26.8.3 . For every $R>0$ and $1<q<n/(n-1)$ there is a constant $C_{R,q}$ with the following property. If $F\in C(X)$ and $\| F\| _\infty \leq R$, every supporting probability $
u \in \mathcal A_0(F)$ of theorem 26.7.2 has a density $a$ satisfying \[  
u =a\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \| a\| _{L^ q(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq C_{R,q}.  \] If $v_-(\omega )>0$, this holds also for $q=n/(n-1)$. Proof. Recall that $M(F)=\exp (-B_0(F)/n)$, and represent $
u $ by a maximizing current $T\in \mathscr M(F)$, using theorem 26.7.2 . Since $\Gamma _ F(T)=\mathrm{e}^{F/n}\Gamma _0(T)$ and $B_0$ is $1$-Lipschitz, \[  
u = rac{\mathrm{e}^{F/n}k_ T}{M(F)}\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad M(F)\geq \mathrm{e}^{-R/n}M(0)>0.  \] Theorem 26.8.1 therefore gives the subcritical bound with constant $\mathrm{e}^{2R/n}M(0)^{-1}C_ q$. When $v_-(\omega )>0$, the same argument with the endpoint constant $v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}$ of theorem 26.8.2 gives the case $q=n/(n-1)$. $\square$ On the threefold of theorem 26.18.1 , every Hermitian form has zero lower mass, so the endpoint estimate fails for the whole family $\mathscr G_\omega $, while all the subcritical estimates above remain valid. For a fixed smooth density, theorem 26.6.2 gives a unique smooth maximizing current, and its determinant density is bounded. Sequences of currents whose values approach the maximum need not, however, have uniformly bounded higher moments, as proposition 26.17.2 shows. On the other hand, the endpoint estimate can hold on a manifold with infinite upper mass. On the Hopf threefold of chapter 8 , take the Gauduchon metric $\omega $ of that chapter, for which $v_-(\omega )=6$ and $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, and set $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^3/6$. The normalized Gauduchon form $T_0=\omega ^2/6$ has $\sigma _{T_0}=\mathrm{d}V$ and $P_{T_0}=I$. Hence $k_{T_0}=6^{-1/3}$, and \[  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }\| k_ T\| _{L^{3/2}(\mathrm{d}V)}=6^{-1/3}.  \] Thus an endpoint determinant estimate, with its optimal constant attained, can coexist with infinite upper Monge–Ampère mass.

26.8.1 Uniform bounds near a smooth density The endpoint estimate can fail for the family of all tests while the maximizing tests for a family of densities remain uniformly controlled. For smooth densities close in $C^{2,\alpha }$ to the normalized volume form $\omega ^ n/\int _ X\omega ^ n$ of the background, a fixed-point argument keeps the solution forms close to $\omega $ and their Gauduchon factors close to that of $\omega $. This gives uniform bounds for both the determinant density of the maximizing current and the density of the supporting probability. In this subsection we assume $n\geq 3$ and fix $0<\alpha <1$. All Hölder norms are defined using a fixed finite atlas and fixed smooth connections. Put \[  H= rac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V},\qquad V=\int _ X\omega ^ n,\qquad F_*=\log (H/V).  \] Thus $\mathrm{e}^{F_*}\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n/V$ is a probability measure. By theorem 4.1.2 , there is a unique smooth positive function $\chi _0$, the normalized Gauduchon factor of $\omega $, such that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi _0\omega ^{n-1})=0,\qquad \int _ X\chi _0\omega ^ n=1.  \] Write $m=\min _ X\chi _0$, $a=\max _ X\chi _0$ and $C_0=\| \chi _0\| _{C^{2,\alpha }}$. We first specify the constants that determine the size of the neighborhood. For a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form $\Omega $, set \[  L_\omega v= rac{n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \omega ^{n-1}}{\omega ^ n}, \qquad A_\Omega \eta = rac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\eta \Omega ^{n-1})}{\mathrm{d}V}.  \] The compatibility argument of proposition 4.8.1 , proposition 9.3.1 shows that \[  \mathcal L(v,c)=L_\omega v-c, \qquad \int _ Xv\, \mathrm{d}V=0,  \] is an isomorphism from the space of pairs $(v,c)\in C^{4,\alpha }	imes \mathbb R$ with this normalization onto $C^{2,\alpha }$. Let $K\geq 1$ bound its inverse for the norm $\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}+|c|$. The formal adjoint of $A_\omega $ with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$ is $(H/n)L_\omega $, whose kernel consists of the constants and whose index is zero. Consequently $A_\omega $ has kernel $\mathbb R\chi _0$ and range \[  Z_0=\left\{ g\in C^{0,\alpha }:\int _ Xg\, \mathrm{d}V=0ight\} .  \] Its restriction to \[  E_\chi =\left\{ \eta \in C^{2,\alpha }:\int _ X\eta \omega ^ n=0ight\}   \] has a bounded inverse $\mathcal R:Z_0	o E_\chi $. Fix $G\geq 1$ bounding this inverse. We normalize the Hölder norms of forms and of endomorphism fields so that they dominate pointwise operator norms and are submultiplicative under composition of endomorphisms; the subscript $\mathrm{alg}$ below refers to this norm on endomorphism fields. Choose $D\geq 1$ so that \[  \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\| _{C^{2,\alpha }}\leq D\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }},\qquad \| \omega ^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\| _{C^{2,\alpha },\mathrm{alg}} \leq D\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}.  \] Let $C_{\mathrm{tr}}\geq 1$ be a bound for the trace map on endomorphism fields, and put $Q=2C_{\mathrm{tr}}D^2$. Expanding $\Omega ^{n-1}-\omega ^{n-1}$ gives a constant $C_ A\geq 1$ such that \[  \| A_\Omega -A_\omega \| _{C^{2,\alpha }	o C^{0,\alpha }} \leq C_ A\| \Omega -\omega \| _{C^{2,\alpha }} \quad 	ext{if }\| \Omega -\omega \| _{C^{2,\alpha }}\leq 1.  \] Only two derivatives of $\Omega $ enter this polynomial estimate. Define 26.41  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-local-adjoint-radius} r=\min \left\{  rac1{2D}, rac1{4KQ},  rac{m}{4GC_ ADC_0}ight\} , \qquad \varepsilon = rac r{2K}. \end{equation} These constants depend only on $\omega $, $\mathrm{d}V$, $\alpha $ and the chosen norms. The solution form $\Omega _ F=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ F$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_ F)=\mathrm{e}^{B_0(F)+F}\mathrm{d}V$ and its Gauduchon factor $\chi _ F$, normalized as below, satisfy  egin{gather*}  	frac 12\omega \leq \Omega _ F\leq 	frac 32\omega , \qquad  rac m2\leq \chi _ F\leq  rac{3a}2,\  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi _ F\Omega _ F^{n-1})=0, \qquad \int _ X\chi _ F\omega ^ n=1. \end{gather*} The potential can be normalized by $\int _ Xu_ F\, \mathrm{d}V=0$ with $\| u_ F\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}+|B_0(F)-\log V|\leq r$. Proof. For $\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}\leq 1/(2D)$ put \[  N(v)=\log \det (I+\omega ^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)-L_\omega v.  \] The logarithm series starts at degree two. If the endomorphism norms of $\omega ^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ and $\omega ^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ are at most $ho \leq 1/2$, telescoping their powers bounds the difference series by $C_{\mathrm{tr}}ho /(1-ho )$ times the endomorphism difference. Hence  egin{align*}  \| N(v)\| _{C^{2,\alpha }}& \leq Q\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}^2,\  \| N(v)-N(w)\| _{C^{2,\alpha }} & \leq Q(\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}+\| w\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}) \| v-w\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}. \end{align*} On the closed radius-$r$ ball of normalized pairs $(v,c)$, the map \[  (v,c)\longmapsto \mathcal L^{-1}(F-F_*-N(v))  \] has image norm at most $K\varepsilon +KQr^2\leq 3r/4$ and Lipschitz constant at most $2KQr\leq 1/2$. Its fixed point $(u,c)$ satisfies \[  \log  rac{(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n}{\omega ^ n}-c=F-F_*.  \] The estimate $Dr\leq 1/2$ gives the form comparison. The scalar is $b=\log V+c$. Differentiating the local equation gives a uniformly elliptic equation for each first derivative of $u$, with coefficients initially in $C^{2,\alpha }$. Interior Schauder estimates improve the regularity one order at a time, so $u$ is smooth. Uniqueness in theorem 9.1.1 identifies it with $u_ F$ and gives $b=B_0(F)$. No uniform higher-derivative bounds on $F$ enter the estimates above. Put $\Delta A=A_{\Omega _ F}-A_\omega $. Stokes' theorem makes its image lie in $Z_0$. On the complete space $E_\chi $, the affine map \[  \eta \longmapsto -\mathcal R\Delta A(\chi _0+\eta )  \] has Lipschitz constant $\kappa =GC_ ADr\leq m/(4C_0)\leq 1/4$. Its fixed point obeys \[  \| \eta \| _{C^{2,\alpha }} \leq  rac{\kappa C_0}{1-\kappa } \leq 2\kappa C_0\leq m/2.  \] Since $A_\omega \chi _0=0$ and $A_\omega \mathcal R$ is the identity on $Z_0$, the function $\chi _ F=\chi _0+\eta $ satisfies $A_{\Omega _ F}\chi _ F=0$, and it has the stated normalization and bounds. Elliptic regularity makes it smooth. Every Gauduchon factor of $\Omega _ F$ with the same normalization satisfies the same affine fixed-point equation, so this factor is the one given by theorem 4.1.2 . $\square$ Theorem 26.8.5 . For every smooth $F$ in the ball of lemma 26.8.4 , let $T_ F$ be the maximizing current of theorem 26.6.2 and $
u _ F$ the supporting probability of $B_0$ at $F$; both are unique. With \[  H_{\max }=\max _ XH,\qquad C_
u = rac{3^{n+1}}4aH_{\max },\qquad C_ k= rac{3^ n}2aH_{\max }^{(n-1)/n},  \] their densities satisfy \[  
u _ F=q_ F\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \| q_ F\| _{L^\infty }\leq C_
u ,\qquad \| k_{T_ F}\| _{L^\infty }\leq C_ k.  \] In particular, for $p=n/(n-1)$, \[  \| q_ F\| _{L^ p}\leq C_
u ^{1/n},\qquad \| k_{T_ F}\| _{L^ p}\leq C_ k.  \] The constants do not involve $v_-(\omega )$; in particular, these bounds hold also when $v_-(\omega )=0$. Proof. Set $\Omega =\Omega _ F$, $\chi =\chi _ F$ and \[  Z=\int _ X\chi \omega \wedge \Omega ^{n-1}.  \] The form comparison and $\int _ X\chi \omega ^ n=1$ give 26.42  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-local-factor-normalization} 2^{-(n-1)}\leq Z\leq (3/2)^{n-1}. \end{equation} Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi \Omega ^{n-1})=0$, Stokes' theorem also gives $Z=\int _ X\chi \Omega ^ n$. By theorem 26.6.2 , it is the unique maximizing current, so $T=T_ F$. The equality case in the proof of that theorem gives $
u _ F=\Omega \wedge T_ F$, and hence 26.43  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-local-adjoint-densities}  egin{aligned}  T_ F& = rac\chi Z\Omega ^{n-1},\  
u _ F& =\Omega \wedge T_ F= rac\chi Z\Omega ^ n,\  q_ F& = rac\chi Z rac{\Omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V},\  k_{T_ F}& = rac\chi Z \left( rac{\Omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}ight)^{(n-1)/n}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} The last identity uses the positive root $\gamma =(\chi /Z)^{1/(n-1)}\Omega $, for which $T_ F=\gamma ^{n-1}$. Uniqueness of the supporting probability follows from theorem 26.7.2 . Now $\chi /Z\leq (3a/2)2^{n-1}$ and $\Omega ^ n/\mathrm{d}V\leq (3/2)^ nH_{\max }$, and multiplying gives exactly $q_ F\leq C_
u $ and $k_{T_ F}\leq C_ k$. Since $\int _ Xq_ F\, \mathrm{d}V=1$, we have $\int _ Xq_ F^ p\, \mathrm{d}V\leq C_
u ^{p-1}$, which gives the sharper $L^ p$ estimate for $q_ F$. The $L^ p$ estimate for $k_{T_ F}$ follows from $\int _ X\mathrm{d}V=1$. $\square$ Corollary 26.8.6 . The ball of lemma 26.8.4 contains smooth injectively parametrized families, of arbitrarily large finite dimension, of data $F$ normalized by $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V=1$. It also contains a smooth path of such data whose maximizing currents are pairwise distinct. Proof. For a small smooth function $f$, put \[  F(f)=F_*+f-\log \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{F_*+f}\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] If $F(f)=F(g)$, then $f-g$ is constant, so the map $f\mapsto F(f)$ is injective on functions of zero $\mathrm{d}V$-mean. By its continuity in $C^{2,\alpha }$, it maps a sufficiently small neighborhood of zero in any fixed finite-dimensional space of such smooth functions into the ball, and these spaces can have arbitrary dimension. For the path, choose a smooth real $\psi $ of zero $\mathrm{d}V$-mean whose complex Hessian at some point $x_0$ has, in an $\omega $-unitary frame, a matrix $Q_0$ that is not a multiple of the identity. A cutoff of $|z_1|^2-|z_2|^2$ in local coordinates, minus its mean, is such a function. For small real $t$ put \[  \Omega _ t=\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi ,\qquad V_ t=\int _ X\Omega _ t^ n,\qquad F_ t=\log  rac{\Omega _ t^ n}{V_ t\, \mathrm{d}V}.  \] These normalized data tend to $F_*$ in $C^{2,\alpha }$ as $t	o 0$, and by uniqueness in theorem 9.1.1 their solution forms are the forms $\Omega _ t$. If $F_ s=F_ t$, then $\log (\Omega _ s^ n/\Omega _ t^ n)$ is the constant $\log (V_ s/V_ t)$. The signs of the complex Hessian of $(s-t)\psi $ at a maximum and at a minimum force this constant to be zero. Integrating the derivative of $\log \det $ along the segment between $\Omega _ t$ and $\Omega _ s$ then gives a uniformly elliptic equation for $(s-t)\psi $ without zeroth-order term, and the maximum principle forces $(s-t)\psi $ to be constant. Since $\psi $ is not constant, $s=t$. If the maximizing currents for $F_ s$ and $F_ t$ agree, ( 26.43 ) makes $\Omega _ s^{n-1}$ and $\Omega _ t^{n-1}$ proportional at $x_0$. Positive cofactor matrices determine positive forms up to scale, so $I+sQ_0$ and $I+tQ_0$ are proportional. Since $I$ and $Q_0$ are linearly independent, comparing coefficients gives $s=t$. $\square$ The small $C^{2,\alpha }$ neighborhood gives a condition directly on the prescribed density. The next estimate instead assumes uniform bounds for the solution forms and covers a larger smooth family without derivative bounds on its densities. The question for arbitrary bounded families of continuous densities remains open when $v_-(\omega )=0$. The concentrating sequences of proposition 26.17.2 consist of near-maximizers, so these estimates do not apply to them.

text: Lemma 26.8.4 . Let $F$ be smooth with $\| F-F_*\| _{C^{2,\alpha }}\leq \varepsilon $. The solution form $\Omega _ F=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ F$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_ F)=\mathrm{e}^{B_0(F)+F}\mathrm{d}V$ and its Gauduchon factor $\chi _ F$, normalized as below, satisfy \begin{gather*}  \tfrac 12\omega \leq \Omega _ F\leq \tfrac 32\omega , \qquad \frac m2\leq \chi _ F\leq \frac{3a}2,\\  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi _ F\Omega _ F^{n-1})=0, \qquad \int _ X\chi _ F\omega ^ n=1. \end{gather*} The potential can be normalized by $\int _ Xu_ F\, \mathrm{d}V=0$ with $\| u_ F\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}+|B_0(F)-\log V|\leq r$. Proof. For $\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}\leq 1/(2D)$ put \[  N(v)=\log \det (I+\omega ^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)-L_\omega v.  \] The logarithm series starts at degree two. If the endomorphism norms of $\omega ^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ and $\omega ^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ are at most $\rho \leq 1/2$, telescoping their powers bounds the difference series by $C_{\mathrm{tr}}\rho /(1-\rho )$ times the endomorphism difference. Hence \begin{align*}  \| N(v)\| _{C^{2,\alpha }}& \leq Q\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}^2,\\  \| N(v)-N(w)\| _{C^{2,\alpha }} & \leq Q(\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}+\| w\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}) \| v-w\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}. \end{align*} On the closed radius-$r$ ball of normalized pairs $(v,c)$, the map \[  (v,c)\longmapsto \mathcal L^{-1}(F-F_*-N(v))  \] has image norm at most $K\varepsilon +KQr^2\leq 3r/4$ and Lipschitz constant at most $2KQr\leq 1/2$. Its fixed point $(u,c)$ satisfies \[  \log \frac{(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n}{\omega ^ n}-c=F-F_*.  \] The estimate $Dr\leq 1/2$ gives the form comparison. The scalar is $b=\log V+c$. Differentiating the local equation gives a uniformly elliptic equation for each first derivative of $u$, with coefficients initially in $C^{2,\alpha }$. Interior Schauder estimates improve the regularity one order at a time, so $u$ is smooth. Uniqueness in theorem 9.1.1 identifies it with $u_ F$ and gives $b=B_0(F)$. No uniform higher-derivative bounds on $F$ enter the estimates above. Put $\Delta A=A_{\Omega _ F}-A_\omega $. Stokes' theorem makes its image lie in $Z_0$. On the complete space $E_\chi $, the affine map \[  \eta \longmapsto -\mathcal R\Delta A(\chi _0+\eta )  \] has Lipschitz constant $\kappa =GC_ ADr\leq m/(4C_0)\leq 1/4$. Its fixed point obeys \[  \| \eta \| _{C^{2,\alpha }} \leq \frac{\kappa C_0}{1-\kappa } \leq 2\kappa C_0\leq m/2.  \] Since $A_\omega \chi _0=0$ and $A_\omega \mathcal R$ is the identity on $Z_0$, the function $\chi _ F=\chi _0+\eta $ satisfies $A_{\Omega _ F}\chi _ F=0$, and it has the stated normalization and bounds. Elliptic regularity makes it smooth. Every Gauduchon factor of $\Omega _ F$ with the same normalization satisfies the same affine fixed-point equation, so this factor is the one given by theorem 4.1.2 . $\square$
