title: 26.8.2 Uniformly controlled complex Hessians
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
26.8.2 Uniformly controlled complex Hessians The preceding construction bounds the solution form and its Gauduchon factor by controlling derivatives of the logarithmic density. A bound on the solution form itself leads to a different estimate. If $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$, then $d\Omega =d\omega $, so the divergence of its cofactor depends only on the fixed torsion and the size of $\Omega $. This permits uniform bounds for the factor even when derivatives of the varying complex Hessian are unbounded. We continue to assume $n\geq 3$ and that $\mathrm{d}V$ is a probability volume form. We first give the real elliptic estimate used below. A cube denoted by $tQ$ has the same center as $Q$ and $t$ times its side length, and $ int _ Q$ denotes its Euclidean average. Lemma 26.8.7 . Let $Q\subset \mathbb R^ m$, $m>2$, be a cube. Suppose that $u$ is a smooth strictly positive solution on a neighborhood of $3Q$ of \[  \operatorname {div}(A
abla u+Bu)=0, \qquad \lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I,\qquad |B|\leq K,  \] where $A$ is a smooth symmetric matrix field and $B$ is a smooth vector field. Then \[  \sup _{Q/2}u\leq C\inf _{Q/2}u,  \] where $C$ depends only on $m,\lambda ,\Lambda ,K$ and the side length of $Q$. Derivatives of $A$ and $B$ do not enter $C$. Proof. We first estimate positive and negative powers, then compare their small moments by an estimate for $\log u$. For $p
e 0,1$, test the weak equation by $\eta ^2u^{p-1}$, where $\eta $ is a smooth cutoff. The principal term is \[  (p-1)\int \eta ^2u^{p-2}\langle A
abla u,
abla uangle .  \] The other terms contain respectively $2\eta u^{p-1}A
abla u\cdot 
abla \eta $, $(p-1)\eta ^2u^{p-1}B\cdot 
abla u$, and $2\eta u^ pB\cdot 
abla \eta $. Taking absolute values after moving the principal term to one side and applying Young's inequality absorbs half of its energy. Thus, for either sign of $p$, 26.48  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-harnack-power} \int \eta ^2|
abla u^{p/2}|^2 \leq C_1p^2(1+|p-1|^{-2}) \int (|
abla \eta |^2+K^2\eta ^2)u^ p, \end{equation} with $C_1$ depending only on the ellipticity bounds. Each test is legitimate since this individual smooth positive solution is bounded above and away from zero on the cutoff support. Put $ eta =m/(m-2)>1$ and choose $p_0= eta ^{-k-1/2}$, with $k$ to be fixed later. Apply the Euclidean Sobolev inequality to $\eta u^{p/2}$ on nested cubes shrinking from $Q$ to $Q/2$. Choose the cutoff gaps proportional to $2^{-j}$ and the powers $p_ j=p_0 eta ^ j$. The positive powers never equal one: the closest two are $ eta ^{-1/2}$ and $ eta ^{1/2}$. Consequently the constants in ( 26.48 ), together with the cutoff terms from $
abla (\eta u^{p/2})$, grow at most polynomially in $p_ j$ and exponentially in $j$. Since $\sum _ j(j+1) eta ^{-j}<\infty $, their iteration product converges. Negative powers give the same calculation for $u^{-1}$. We obtain 26.49  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-harnack-moments} \sup _{Q/2}u\leq C_2\left( int _ Q u^{p_0}ight)^{1/p_0}, \qquad \inf _{Q/2}u\geq C_2^{-1} \left( int _ Q u^{-p_0}ight)^{-1/p_0}. \end{equation} Here $C_2$ also depends on $p_0$ and the fixed cube size. Testing instead by $\eta ^2/u$ gives \[  \int \eta ^2|
abla \log u|^2 \leq C_3\int (|
abla \eta |^2+K^2\eta ^2).  \] For every subcube $S\subset Q$ of side length $\ell $, a cutoff supported in $2S\subset 3Q$, equal to one on $S$, has derivative bounded by $C/\ell $. Poincaré's inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give \[   int _ S|\log u-(\log u)_ S| \leq C_4(1+K\ell )\leq K_0,  \] where $K_0\geq 1$ is uniform and $(\log u)_ S$ denotes the mean. We spell out the exponential consequence of this mean oscillation bound. Write $f=\log u$ and fix $a>2$. Select the maximal dyadic subcubes $S$ of $Q$ on which $ int _ S|f-f_ Q|>aK_0$. Their total measure is at most $|Q|/a$. The parent of each selected cube has average at most $aK_0$, hence $|f_ S-f_ Q|\leq 2^ maK_0$. Outside their union, differentiation of dyadic averages gives $|f-f_ Q|\leq aK_0$ almost everywhere. Repeat this selection inside each chosen cube, subtracting its own mean. The union at generation $j$ has measure at most $a^{-j}|Q|$, and outside generation $j+1$ the accumulated mean changes and last oscillation give \[  |f-f_ Q|\leq (j2^ ma+a)K_0.  \] The intersection of all generations is null. Choosing $c>0$ so that $\exp (c2^ ma)<a$ and summing over the generations yields \[   int _ Q\exp \! \left( rac{c|f-f_ Q|}{K_0}ight)\leq C_5,  \] with dimensional constants. Now fix $k$ large enough that $p_0<c/K_0$. Multiplying the estimates for the positive and negative exponentials cancels $f_ Q$ and gives \[  \left( int _ Q u^{p_0}ight) \left( int _ Q u^{-p_0}ight)\leq C_5^2.  \] Combining this with ( 26.49 ) proves the result. Every constant comes from the stated coefficient bounds and the fixed cube. $\square$ Proposition 26.8.8 . Fix $0<\delta \leq \Lambda $. For every smooth real $v$ with \[  \delta \omega \leq \Omega _ v:=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\leq \Lambda \omega ,  \] let $ho _ v$ be its Gauduchon factor normalized by \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1})=0, \qquad \int _ Xho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V=1.  \] There is $C_ H\geq 1$, depending only on $X,\omega ,\mathrm{d}V,\delta ,\Lambda $, such that $C_ H^{-1}\leq ho _ v\leq C_ H$ on $X$ for every such $v$. Proof. Existence and uniqueness of $ho _ v$ follow from theorem 4.1.2 . Fix a real reference metric on $X$, and put $Q_ v=\Omega _ v^{n-1}$ and $J_ v=\Omega _ v^ n/\mathrm{d}V$. Since $d\Omega _ v=d\omega $, 26.50  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-hessian-cofactor-divergence} dQ_ v=(n-1)d\omega \wedge \Omega _ v^{n-2}. \end{equation} Both $Q_ v$ and $dQ_ v$ have uniformly bounded coefficients in fixed charts. Define a real tensor $A_ v$ and vector field $b_ v$ by \[  \langle A_ vd\phi ,d\psi angle \, \mathrm{d}V =n\, d\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge Q_ v, \qquad (b_ v\cdot d\phi )\, \mathrm{d}V =-n\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge dQ_ v.  \] Only the $(1,1)$ part of $d\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi $ contributes to the first identity; it is \[   rac{\mathrm i}{4\pi } (\partial \psi \wedge  ar\partial \phi +\partial \phi \wedge  ar\partial \psi ).  \] Thus $A_ v$ is symmetric and uniformly positive definite, with a uniform upper bound. The second identity and ( 26.50 ) give a uniform bound for $b_ v$. For $L_{\Omega _ v}\phi =n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi \wedge Q_ v/\Omega _ v^ n$, Stokes' theorem gives  egin{align*}  \int _ X\psi J_ vL_{\Omega _ v}\phi \, \mathrm{d}V & =-n\int _ Xd\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge Q_ v +n\int _ X\psi \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge dQ_ v\ & =-\int _ X\langle A_ vd\phi ,d\psi angle \, \mathrm{d}V -\int _ X\psi b_ v\cdot d\phi \, \mathrm{d}V. \end{align*} In particular, the adjoint equation for $ho _ v$ is \[  \operatorname {div}_{\mathrm{d}V}(A_ vdho _ v+b_ vho _ v)=0.  \] In each coordinate chart, multiplying the coefficients by the fixed smooth volume density converts this to Euclidean divergence form while preserving uniform ellipticity and a uniform bound for the vector coefficient. Lemma 26.8.7 applies. A fixed finite cover by inner cubes has a connected overlap graph, since $X$ is connected. Chaining its local estimates gives $\sup _ Xho _ v\leq C_ H\inf _ Xho _ v$. The normalization and $\mathrm{d}V(X)=1$ imply the claimed two-sided bound. $\square$ For a fixed $0<\varepsilon <1$, consider the full family 26.51  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-controlled-hessian-family} \mathcal V_\varepsilon = \{ v\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R):\sup _ Xv=0, -\varepsilon \omega \leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\leq \varepsilon \omega \} . \end{equation} Set $c_ v=\int _ X\Omega _ v^ n$ and $F_ v=\log (J_ v/c_ v)$, so that $\int _ X\mathrm e^{F_ v}\mathrm{d}V=1$. The density $F_ v$ is defined by an actual solution form, rather than prescribed before solving an equation. Theorem 26.8.9 . Let \[  j_-=(1-\varepsilon )^ n\min _ X rac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}, \qquad j_+=(1+\varepsilon )^ n\max _ X rac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V},  \] and take $C_ H$ from proposition 26.8.8 with $\delta =1-\varepsilon $ and $\Lambda =1+\varepsilon $. For every $v\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $, the exact maximizing current $T_ v\in \mathscr G_\omega $ for $F_ v$ is unique. Its determinant density $k_{T_ v}$ and the probability density $r_ v=\mathrm d
u _{T_ v,F_ v}/\mathrm{d}V$ satisfy 26.52  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-hessian-adjoint-bounds}  rac{j_-}{C_ Hj_+}\leq r_ v\leq  rac{C_ Hj_+}{j_-}, \qquad j_+^{-1/n} rac{j_-}{C_ Hj_+} \leq k_{T_ v}\leq j_-^{-1/n} rac{C_ Hj_+}{j_-}. \end{equation} In particular both densities are uniformly bounded at the critical exponent $n/(n-1)$, without an assumption on the lower mass. Moreover, \[  \| F_ v-F_0\| _\infty \leq n\log  rac{1+\varepsilon }{1-\varepsilon },  \] and this normalized family contains infinitely many distinct nonconstant densities on the fixed manifold $X$. Proof. Use the normalization of proposition 26.8.8 and put \[  N_ v=\int _ XJ_ vho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad T_ v= rac{ho _ v}{N_ v}\Omega _ v^{n-1}.  \] The factor equation and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-Stokes give \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge ho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1} =\int _ X\Omega _ v\wedge ho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1}=N_ v.  \] Hence $T_ v\in \mathscr G_\omega $. It is the $(n-1)$st power of the Gauduchon metric $\gamma _ v=(ho _ v/N_ v)^{1/(n-1)}\Omega _ v$. The equation $\Omega _ v^ n=c_ v\mathrm e^{F_ v}\mathrm{d}V$ gives $B_0(F_ v)=\log c_ v$. Thus theorem 26.6.2 identifies $T_ v$ as the unique exact maximizer, and $M(F_ v)=c_ v^{-1/n}$. The determinant and probability normalizations are therefore 26.53  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-hessian-adjoint-densities} k_{T_ v}= rac{ho _ v}{N_ v}J_ v^{(n-1)/n}, \qquad \Gamma _{F_ v}(T_ v)=c_ v^{-1/n} rac{J_ vho _ v}{N_ v}\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad r_ v= rac{J_ vho _ v}{N_ v}. \end{equation} Here $j_-\leq J_ v\leq j_+$ and, since $\int _ Xho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V=1$, also $j_-\leq N_ v\leq j_+$. The factor bound gives the first pair of inequalities in ( 26.52 ); the identity $k_{T_ v}=J_ v^{-1/n}r_ v$ gives the second. The critical norms are bounded by the respective upper constants because $\mathrm{d}V$ is a probability volume. The inequalities \[  (1-\varepsilon )^ n\leq  rac{J_ v}{J_0}\leq (1+\varepsilon )^ n, \qquad (1-\varepsilon )^ n\leq  rac{c_ v}{c_0}\leq (1+\varepsilon )^ n  \] give the bound for $F_ v-F_0$ by subtracting logarithms. To prove nontriviality, choose a nonconstant smooth real $\phi $. For small $t$, the potential $t\phi -\sup _ X(t\phi )$ belongs to $\mathcal V_\varepsilon $ and gives the same density as $t\phi $. Differentiation at zero gives \[  \left. rac{d}{dt}F_{t\phi }ight|_{t=0} =L_\omega \phi -  rac{\int _ XJ_0L_\omega \phi \, \mathrm{d}V}{\int _ XJ_0\, \mathrm{d}V}.  \] This function is nonconstant: otherwise $L_\omega \phi $ would be constant, its values at a maximum and a minimum would force that constant to be zero, and the strong maximum principle would make $\phi $ constant. Choose two points where the displayed derivative differs. The difference of the densities at these points is strictly monotone for $t$ in a small interval. These give infinitely many distinct densities, with at most one parameter having equal values at the chosen points. Discarding that parameter gives the nonconstant family. $\square$ Uniform bounds for the solution forms need not give derivative bounds, or even equicontinuity, for their normalized logarithmic densities. Example 26.8.10 . For every fixed $0<\varepsilon <1$, there are $v_ j\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $ with $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}	o 0$ such that their normalized densities $F_{v_ j}$ are pairwise distinct, bounded in $C^0$, and unbounded in $C^1$. This family is not equicontinuous. Nevertheless, both densities of its exact maximizers satisfy the uniform bounds of theorem 26.8.9 . Proof. Choose holomorphic coordinates centered at a point $p$, put $x=\operatorname {Re}z_1$, and take a smooth real cutoff $\zeta $ supported in the chart and equal to one near $p$. We may assume $0\leq \zeta \leq 1$. On the chart set \[   eta =dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(x^2/2) = rac{\mathrm i}{8\pi }dz_1\wedge d ar z_1.  \] This is a nonzero semipositive form of rank one. For a constant $a>0$ to be chosen, extend \[  w_ j= rac a{j^2}\zeta \sin (jx)  \] by zero outside the chart, and put $v_ j=w_ j-\sup _ Xw_ j$. The product rule gives  egin{align*}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j={}& -a\zeta \sin (jx) eta + rac aj\cos (jx) (d\zeta \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x+dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\zeta )\ & + rac a{j^2}\sin (jx)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta . \end{align*} All fixed forms in this expression have compact support after multiplication by the indicated cutoff or its derivatives. Thus a fixed $C>0$ bounds the operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j$ relative to $\omega $ by $aC$ for every $j\geq 1$. Choose $a$ so small that $aC\leq \varepsilon /2$. Then $v_ j\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $, and $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}\leq 2a/j^2$. Write $s=\operatorname {tr}_{\omega (p)} eta >0$. Since $x(p)=0$ and $\zeta =1$ near $p$, we have $\Omega _{v_ j}(p)=\omega (p)$ and \[  \partial _ x\Omega _{v_ j}(p)=\partial _ x\omega (p)-aj eta .  \] Differentiating the logarithmic determinant, and observing that its normalizing integral is constant in the spatial variable, gives the exact identity \[  \partial _ xF_{v_ j}(p) =\partial _ x\log  rac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}(p)-ajs.  \] These derivatives are pairwise different and their absolute values tend to infinity. Hence the densities are pairwise distinct and their $C^1$ norms are unbounded. Their uniform $C^0$ bound is part of theorem 26.8.9 . To check failure of equicontinuity, take points $p_ j^\pm $ with $x=\pm \pi /(2j)$ and all other real coordinates zero. For large $j$ they lie where $\zeta =1$, and $\Omega _{v_ j}(p_ j^\pm )=\omega (p_ j^\pm )\mp a eta $. The integral normalizing $F_{v_ j}$ cancels from the difference, so \[  F_{v_ j}(p_ j^-)-F_{v_ j}(p_ j^+) \longrightarrow \log  rac{1+as}{1-as}>0.  \] Indeed, $ eta ^2=0$ gives $(\omega (p)\pm a eta )^ n=(1\pm as)\omega (p)^ n$, and $as<1$ by the chosen form comparison. Both points tend to $p$, which proves the failure of equicontinuity. The exact-adjoint bounds still apply because the entire sequence lies in $\mathcal V_\varepsilon $. $\square$ The same estimate applies to the family with $\delta \omega \leq \Omega _ v\leq \Lambda \omega $ by replacing $j_-$ and $j_+$ with $\delta ^ n\min _ X(\omega ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)$ and $\Lambda ^ n\max _ X(\omega ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)$. Applying the estimate to a prescribed family of densities requires uniformly comparable solution forms. Thus this construction provides critical estimates when $v_-(\omega )=0$ for a larger smooth family, but leaves the question for arbitrary bounded families of continuous densities open.

Lemma 26.8.7 . Let $Q\subset \mathbb R^ m$, $m>2$, be a cube. Suppose that $u$ is a smooth strictly positive solution on a neighborhood of $3Q$ of \[  \operatorname {div}(A
abla u+Bu)=0, \qquad \lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I,\qquad |B|\leq K,  \] where $A$ is a smooth symmetric matrix field and $B$ is a smooth vector field. Then \[  \sup _{Q/2}u\leq C\inf _{Q/2}u,  \] where $C$ depends only on $m,\lambda ,\Lambda ,K$ and the side length of $Q$. Derivatives of $A$ and $B$ do not enter $C$. Proof. We first estimate positive and negative powers, then compare their small moments by an estimate for $\log u$. For $p
e 0,1$, test the weak equation by $\eta ^2u^{p-1}$, where $\eta $ is a smooth cutoff. The principal term is \[  (p-1)\int \eta ^2u^{p-2}\langle A
abla u,
abla uangle .  \] The other terms contain respectively $2\eta u^{p-1}A
abla u\cdot 
abla \eta $, $(p-1)\eta ^2u^{p-1}B\cdot 
abla u$, and $2\eta u^ pB\cdot 
abla \eta $. Taking absolute values after moving the principal term to one side and applying Young's inequality absorbs half of its energy. Thus, for either sign of $p$, 26.48  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-harnack-power} \int \eta ^2|
abla u^{p/2}|^2 \leq C_1p^2(1+|p-1|^{-2}) \int (|
abla \eta |^2+K^2\eta ^2)u^ p, \end{equation} with $C_1$ depending only on the ellipticity bounds. Each test is legitimate since this individual smooth positive solution is bounded above and away from zero on the cutoff support. Put $ eta =m/(m-2)>1$ and choose $p_0= eta ^{-k-1/2}$, with $k$ to be fixed later. Apply the Euclidean Sobolev inequality to $\eta u^{p/2}$ on nested cubes shrinking from $Q$ to $Q/2$. Choose the cutoff gaps proportional to $2^{-j}$ and the powers $p_ j=p_0 eta ^ j$. The positive powers never equal one: the closest two are $ eta ^{-1/2}$ and $ eta ^{1/2}$. Consequently the constants in ( 26.48 ), together with the cutoff terms from $
abla (\eta u^{p/2})$, grow at most polynomially in $p_ j$ and exponentially in $j$. Since $\sum _ j(j+1) eta ^{-j}<\infty $, their iteration product converges. Negative powers give the same calculation for $u^{-1}$. We obtain 26.49  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-harnack-moments} \sup _{Q/2}u\leq C_2\left( int _ Q u^{p_0}ight)^{1/p_0}, \qquad \inf _{Q/2}u\geq C_2^{-1} \left( int _ Q u^{-p_0}ight)^{-1/p_0}. \end{equation} Here $C_2$ also depends on $p_0$ and the fixed cube size. Testing instead by $\eta ^2/u$ gives \[  \int \eta ^2|
abla \log u|^2 \leq C_3\int (|
abla \eta |^2+K^2\eta ^2).  \] For every subcube $S\subset Q$ of side length $\ell $, a cutoff supported in $2S\subset 3Q$, equal to one on $S$, has derivative bounded by $C/\ell $. Poincaré's inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give \[   int _ S|\log u-(\log u)_ S| \leq C_4(1+K\ell )\leq K_0,  \] where $K_0\geq 1$ is uniform and $(\log u)_ S$ denotes the mean. We spell out the exponential consequence of this mean oscillation bound. Write $f=\log u$ and fix $a>2$. Select the maximal dyadic subcubes $S$ of $Q$ on which $ int _ S|f-f_ Q|>aK_0$. Their total measure is at most $|Q|/a$. The parent of each selected cube has average at most $aK_0$, hence $|f_ S-f_ Q|\leq 2^ maK_0$. Outside their union, differentiation of dyadic averages gives $|f-f_ Q|\leq aK_0$ almost everywhere. Repeat this selection inside each chosen cube, subtracting its own mean. title: Proposition 26.8.8
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.8.8 . Fix $0<\delta \leq \Lambda $. For every smooth real $v$ with \[  \delta \omega \leq \Omega _ v:=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\leq \Lambda \omega ,  \] let $\rho _ v$ be its Gauduchon factor normalized by \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1})=0, \qquad \int _ X\rho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V=1.  \] There is $C_ H\geq 1$, depending only on $X,\omega ,\mathrm{d}V,\delta ,\Lambda $, such that $C_ H^{-1}\leq \rho _ v\leq C_ H$ on $X$ for every such $v$. Proof. Existence and uniqueness of $\rho _ v$ follow from theorem 4.1.2 . Fix a real reference metric on $X$, and put $Q_ v=\Omega _ v^{n-1}$ and $J_ v=\Omega _ v^ n/\mathrm{d}V$. Since $d\Omega _ v=d\omega $, 26.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-hessian-cofactor-divergence} dQ_ v=(n-1)d\omega \wedge \Omega _ v^{n-2}. \end{equation} Both $Q_ v$ and $dQ_ v$ have uniformly bounded coefficients in fixed charts. Define a real tensor $A_ v$ and vector field $b_ v$ by \[  \langle A_ vd\phi ,d\psi \rangle \, \mathrm{d}V =n\, d\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge Q_ v, \qquad (b_ v\cdot d\phi )\, \mathrm{d}V =-n\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge dQ_ v.  \] Only the $(1,1)$ part of $d\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi $ contributes to the first identity; it is \[  \frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi } (\partial \psi \wedge \bar\partial \phi +\partial \phi \wedge \bar\partial \psi ).  \] Thus $A_ v$ is symmetric and uniformly positive definite, with a uniform upper bound. The second identity and ( 26.50 ) give a uniform bound for $b_ v$. For $L_{\Omega _ v}\phi =n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi \wedge Q_ v/\Omega _ v^ n$, Stokes' theorem gives \begin{align*}  \int _ X\psi J_ vL_{\Omega _ v}\phi \, \mathrm{d}V & =-n\int _ Xd\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge Q_ v +n\int _ X\psi \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge dQ_ v\\ & =-\int _ X\langle A_ vd\phi ,d\psi \rangle \, \mathrm{d}V -\int _ X\psi b_ v\cdot d\phi \, \mathrm{d}V. \end{align*} In particular, the adjoint equation for $\rho _ v$ is \[  \operatorname {div}_{\mathrm{d}V}(A_ vd\rho _ v+b_ v\rho _ v)=0.  \] In each coordinate chart, multiplying the coefficients by the fixed smooth volume density converts this to Euclidean divergence form while preserving uniform ellipticity and a uniform bound for the vector coefficient. Lemma 26.8.7 applies. A fixed finite cover by inner cubes has a connected overlap graph, since $X$ is connected. Chaining its local estimates gives $\sup _ X\rho _ v\leq C_ H\inf _ X\rho _ v$. The normalization and $\mathrm{d}V(X)=1$ imply the claimed two-sided bound. $\square$

title: Theorem 26.8.9
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 26.8.9 . Let \[  j_-=(1-\varepsilon )^ n\min _ X\frac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}, \qquad j_+=(1+\varepsilon )^ n\max _ X\frac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V},  \] and take $C_ H$ from proposition 26.8.8 with $\delta =1-\varepsilon $ and $\Lambda =1+\varepsilon $. For every $v\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $, the exact maximizing current $T_ v\in \mathscr G_\omega $ for $F_ v$ is unique. Its determinant density $k_{T_ v}$ and the probability density $r_ v=\mathrm d\nu _{T_ v,F_ v}/\mathrm{d}V$ satisfy 26.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-hessian-adjoint-bounds} \frac{j_-}{C_ Hj_+}\leq r_ v\leq \frac{C_ Hj_+}{j_-}, \qquad j_+^{-1/n}\frac{j_-}{C_ Hj_+} \leq k_{T_ v}\leq j_-^{-1/n}\frac{C_ Hj_+}{j_-}. \end{equation} In particular both densities are uniformly bounded at the critical exponent $n/(n-1)$, without an assumption on the lower mass. Moreover, \[  \| F_ v-F_0\| _\infty \leq n\log \frac{1+\varepsilon }{1-\varepsilon },  \] and this normalized family contains infinitely many distinct nonconstant densities on the fixed manifold $X$. Proof. Use the normalization of proposition 26.8.8 and put \[  N_ v=\int _ XJ_ v\rho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad T_ v=\frac{\rho _ v}{N_ v}\Omega _ v^{n-1}.  \] The factor equation and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-Stokes give \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge \rho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1} =\int _ X\Omega _ v\wedge \rho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1}=N_ v.  \] Hence $T_ v\in \mathscr G_\omega $. It is the $(n-1)$st power of the Gauduchon metric $\gamma _ v=(\rho _ v/N_ v)^{1/(n-1)}\Omega _ v$. The equation $\Omega _ v^ n=c_ v\mathrm e^{F_ v}\mathrm{d}V$ gives $B_0(F_ v)=\log c_ v$. Thus theorem 26.6.2 identifies $T_ v$ as the unique exact maximizer, and $M(F_ v)=c_ v^{-1/n}$. The determinant and probability normalizations are therefore 26.53 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-hessian-adjoint-densities} k_{T_ v}=\frac{\rho _ v}{N_ v}J_ v^{(n-1)/n}, \qquad \Gamma _{F_ v}(T_ v)=c_ v^{-1/n}\frac{J_ v\rho _ v}{N_ v}\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad r_ v=\frac{J_ v\rho _ v}{N_ v}. \end{equation} Here $j_-\leq J_ v\leq j_+$ and, since $\int _ X\rho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V=1$, also $j_-\leq N_ v\leq j_+$. The factor bound gives the first pair of inequalities in ( 26.52 ); the identity $k_{T_ v}=J_ v^{-1/n}r_ v$ gives the second. The critical norms are bounded by the respective upper constants because $\mathrm{d}V$ is a probability volume. The inequalities \[  (1-\varepsilon )^ n\leq \frac{J_ v}{J_0}\leq (1+\varepsilon )^ n, \qquad (1-\varepsilon )^ n\leq \frac{c_ v}{c_0}\leq (1+\varepsilon )^ n  \] give the bound for $F_ v-F_0$ by subtracting logarithms. To prove nontriviality, choose a nonconstant smooth real $\phi $. For small $t$, the potential $t\phi -\sup _ X(t\phi )$ belongs to $\mathcal V_\varepsilon $ and gives the same density as $t\phi $. Differentiation at zero gives \[  \left.\frac{d}{dt}F_{t\phi }\right|_{t=0} =L_\omega \phi - \frac{\int _ XJ_0L_\omega \phi \, \mathrm{d}V}{\int _ XJ_0\, \mathrm{d}V}.  \] This function is nonconstant: otherwise $L_\omega \phi $ would be constant, its values at a maximum and a minimum would force that constant to be zero, and the strong maximum principle would make $\phi $ constant. Choose two points where the displayed derivative differs. The difference of the densities at these points is strictly monotone for $t$ in a small interval. These give infinitely many distinct densities, with at most one parameter having equal values at the chosen points. Discarding that parameter gives the nonconstant family. $\square$

text: Example 26.8.10 . For every fixed $0<\varepsilon <1$, there are $v_ j\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $ with $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}\to 0$ such that their normalized densities $F_{v_ j}$ are pairwise distinct, bounded in $C^0$, and unbounded in $C^1$. This family is not equicontinuous. Nevertheless, both densities of its exact maximizers satisfy the uniform bounds of theorem 26.8.9 . Proof. Choose holomorphic coordinates centered at a point $p$, put $x=\operatorname {Re}z_1$, and take a smooth real cutoff $\zeta $ supported in the chart and equal to one near $p$. We may assume $0\leq \zeta \leq 1$. On the chart set \[  \beta =dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(x^2/2) =\frac{\mathrm i}{8\pi }dz_1\wedge d\bar z_1.  \] This is a nonzero semipositive form of rank one. For a constant $a>0$ to be chosen, extend \[  w_ j=\frac a{j^2}\zeta \sin (jx)  \] by zero outside the chart, and put $v_ j=w_ j-\sup _ Xw_ j$. The product rule gives \begin{align*}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j={}& -a\zeta \sin (jx)\beta +\frac aj\cos (jx) (d\zeta \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x+dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\zeta )\\ & +\frac a{j^2}\sin (jx)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta . \end{align*} All fixed forms in this expression have compact support after multiplication by the indicated cutoff or its derivatives. Thus a fixed $C>0$ bounds the operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j$ relative to $\omega $ by $aC$ for every $j\geq 1$. Choose $a$ so small that $aC\leq \varepsilon /2$. Then $v_ j\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $, and $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}\leq 2a/j^2$. Write $s=\operatorname {tr}_{\omega (p)}\beta >0$. Since $x(p)=0$ and $\zeta =1$ near $p$, we have $\Omega _{v_ j}(p)=\omega (p)$ and \[  \partial _ x\Omega _{v_ j}(p)=\partial _ x\omega (p)-aj\beta .  \] Differentiating the logarithmic determinant, and observing that its normalizing integral is constant in the spatial variable, gives the exact identity \[  \partial _ xF_{v_ j}(p) =\partial _ x\log \frac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}(p)-ajs.  \] These derivatives are pairwise different and their absolute values tend to infinity. Hence the densities are pairwise distinct and their $C^1$ norms are unbounded. Their uniform $C^0$ bound is part of theorem 26.8.9 . To check failure of equicontinuity, take points $p_ j^\pm $ with $x=\pm \pi /(2j)$ and all other real coordinates zero. For large $j$ they lie where $\zeta =1$, and $\Omega _{v_ j}(p_ j^\pm )=\omega (p_ j^\pm )\mp a\beta $. The integral normalizing $F_{v_ j}$ cancels from the difference, so \[  F_{v_ j}(p_ j^-)-F_{v_ j}(p_ j^+) \longrightarrow \log \frac{1+as}{1-as}>0.  \] Indeed, $\beta ^2=0$ gives $(\omega (p)\pm a\beta )^ n=(1\pm as)\omega (p)^ n$, and $as<1$ by the chosen form comparison. Both points tend to $p$, which proves the failure of equicontinuity. The exact-adjoint bounds still apply because the entire sequence lies in $\mathcal V_\varepsilon $. $\square$

title: 26.9 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem
search_title: Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.9 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem We keep the Hermitian background $\omega $ and replace the continuous logarithmic density by an integrable density. For an unbounded density, weak compactness of the test currents alone does not pass the determinant integral to the limit; uniform control of the weighted tails provides the missing upper semicontinuity. We use the following notation from section 14.27 , section 14.28 , with $\omega $ in place of $h$. For a nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, the subsolution threshold $b_\omega (f)\geq 0$ is, by theorem 14.27.2 , the largest $b\geq 0$ for which some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. For $p\in L^ n$, the root norm is $\rho _\omega (p)=b_\omega (|p|^ n)^{-1/n}$ if $p\ne 0$, and $\rho _\omega (0)=0$. The space $\mathcal D_\omega $ of proposition 14.31.3 consists of the $p\in L^ n$ with $\rho _\omega (p)<+\infty $, and $\mathcal D_\omega ^0$ is the closure of the bounded functions in $\mathcal D_\omega $, characterized by vanishing tails in proposition 14.31.5 . For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, $L_{\omega ,\gamma }(p)$ denotes the test quotient of section 14.28 , and theorem 14.28.1 gives $\rho _\omega (p)=\sup _\gamma L_{\omega ,\gamma }(|p|)$. Finally, $k_ T$ is the determinant density of $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ from theorem 26.8.1 . If $p\geq 0$ is measurable, define \[  D_ p(T)=\int _ Xp k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V\qquad (T\in \mathscr G_\omega ),  \] allowing the value $+\infty $. If $T=\gamma ^{n-1}/\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ for a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, then $D_ p(T)=L_{\omega ,\gamma }(p)$. Theorem 26.9.1 . For every nonnegative $p\in L^ n$, 26.54 \begin{equation} \label{eq:integrable-current-supremum} \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }D_ p(T)=\rho _\omega (p), \end{equation} with the value $+\infty $ allowed. If $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$, the functional $D_ p$ is finite, concave and weakly upper semicontinuous on $\mathscr G_\omega $, its maximum is attained, and the densities $p k_ T$, for $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, are uniformly integrable. Proof. For a smooth strictly positive $p$, we have $D_ p=\mathfrak D_{n\log p}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(n\log p)/n}=\rho _\omega (p)$, so theorem 26.6.2 , applied to $F=n\log p$, proves ( 26.54 ). By Hölder's inequality and theorem 26.8.1 , for every real $r>n$ there is a constant $C_ r$ such that, for every $q\in L^ r$, 26.55 \begin{equation} \label{eq:current-root-test-bound} \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }\int _ X|q| k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V \leq C_ r\| q\| _{L^ r}. \end{equation} Next, approximate a bounded nonnegative $p$ in $L^{2n}$ by smooth strictly positive functions. This estimate and ( 14.114 ) give uniform convergence on $\mathscr G_\omega $ of the corresponding functionals $D$ and convergence of the root norms, so the supremum formula holds for bounded $p$. For such $p$, the functional $D_ p$ is also upper semicontinuous and concave, by lemma 26.6.1 and uniform convergence. For general $p\in L^ n$, we use the truncations $\min (p,K)$ at positive integer levels $K$. Monotone convergence and the definition of $b_\omega $ through truncations give \[  \sup _ T D_ p(T)=\sup _ T\sup _ K D_{\min (p,K)}(T) =\sup _ K\rho _\omega (\min (p,K))=\rho _\omega (p).  \] This step only interchanges two suprema and gives no attainment. Now suppose $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$. The supremum formula applied to the tail gives \[  0\leq D_ p(T)-D_{\min (p,K)}(T) \leq \rho _\omega (p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} })\longrightarrow 0  \] uniformly in $T$, by proposition 14.31.5 . Hence $D_ p$ is finite and is a uniform limit of upper semicontinuous concave functionals, and compactness of $\mathscr G_\omega $ gives a maximizer. Finally, fix $1<q<n/(n-1)$. By Hölder's inequality and theorem 26.8.1 , for every measurable set $E$, \[  \sup _ T\int _ Ep k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \rho _\omega (p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }) +K C_ q\, \mathrm{d}V(E)^{1-1/q}.  \] Choosing first $K$ large and then the volume of $E$ small proves uniform absolute continuity. Since the total masses are bounded by $\rho _\omega (p)$, the densities are uniformly integrable. $\square$ For a nonzero density, a maximizing current gives a supporting probability for the threshold, as we show below. Whether the threshold is attained by an exact equation depends on the regularity of the maximizing current, which enters through the trace inequalities of 26.9.3 .

Monotone convergence and the definition of $b_\omega $ through truncations give \[  \sup _ T D_ p(T)=\sup _ T\sup _ K D_{\min (p,K)}(T) =\sup _ K\rho _\omega (\min (p,K))=\rho _\omega (p).  \] This step only interchanges two suprema and gives no attainment. Now suppose $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$. The supremum formula applied to the tail gives \[  0\leq D_ p(T)-D_{\min (p,K)}(T) \leq \rho _\omega (p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} })\longrightarrow 0  \] uniformly in $T$, by proposition 14.31.5 . Hence $D_ p$ is finite and is a uniform limit of upper semicontinuous concave functionals, and compactness of $\mathscr G_\omega $ gives a maximizer. Finally, fix $1<q<n/(n-1)$. By Hölder's inequality and theorem 26.8.1 , for every measurable set $E$, \[  \sup _ T\int _ Ep k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \rho _\omega (p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }) +K C_ q\, \mathrm{d}V(E)^{1-1/q}.  \] Choosing first $K$ large and then the volume of $E$ small proves uniform absolute continuity. Since the total masses are bounded by $\rho _\omega (p)$, the densities are uniformly integrable. $\square$

text: 26.9.1 The tail condition and perturbations of the density Vanishing tails are equivalent to continuity of the threshold under uniformly bounded multiplicative perturbations of the density that converge in measure. This explains the role of the tail condition: if it fails, a perturbation supported on sets of shrinking volume can lower the threshold by a fixed factor. Proposition 26.9.2 . Let $0\leq p\in \mathcal D_\omega $ be nonzero. The following are equivalent: $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$; the densities $p k_ T$, for $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, are uniformly integrable; whenever $F_ j$ are smooth real functions, uniformly bounded and tending to zero in measure, one has \[  b_\omega (\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}p^ n)\longrightarrow b_\omega (p^ n).  \] If the first condition holds, the convergence in the third also holds for bounded measurable $F_ j$ with the same uniform bound and convergence in measure. If it fails, there are smooth $F_ j\geq 0$, uniformly bounded and tending to zero in measure, such that \[  \mathrm{e}^{F_ j}p^ n\longrightarrow p^ n\quad \text{in }L^1, \qquad b_\omega (\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}p^ n)\leq 2^{-n}b_\omega (p^ n).  \] Proof. The first condition implies the second by theorem 26.9.1 . Conversely, $\mathrm{d}V(\{ p>K\} )\to 0$ as $K\to \infty $, so uniform integrability and ( 26.54 ) give \[  \rho _\omega (p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }) =\sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }\int _{\{ p>K\} }p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V \longrightarrow 0.  \] This is the first condition by proposition 14.31.5 . If $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$ and $|F_ j|\leq A$, then $p(\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n}-1)$ tends to zero in measure and its absolute value is at most $(\mathrm{e}^{A/n}+1)p$. The dominated-convergence criterion of proposition 14.31.5 makes its root norm tend to zero, and the triangle inequality gives $\rho _\omega (p\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n})\to \rho _\omega (p)>0$. Taking negative $n$th powers proves the third condition, also for bounded measurable $F_ j$. Suppose now that the tails do not tend to zero, and put $R=\rho _\omega (p)>0$. The formula of theorem 14.28.1 , which uses only smooth tests, yields $\delta >0$, numbers $K_ j\to \infty $ and smooth strictly positive $T_ j\in \mathscr G_\omega $ such that \[  \int _{\{ p>K_ j\} }p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V>\delta .  \] Since the finite measure $p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V$ is regular, we can choose a compact set $C_ j\subset \{ p>K_ j\} $ of mass greater than $\delta /2$ for this measure. By outer regularity of $\mathrm{d}V$, choose an open set $O_ j\supset \{ p>K_ j\} $ with $\mathrm{d}V(O_ j)\leq \mathrm{d}V(\{ p>K_ j\} )+1/j$, and a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi _ j\leq 1$ that equals one on $C_ j$ and has support in $O_ j$. Fix $A>0$ with $\mathrm{e}^{A/n}\delta /2>2R$, and set $F_ j=A\chi _ j$. Then $F_ j\to 0$ in measure, while \[  \rho _\omega (p\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n}) \geq \int _ Xp\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n}k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V >2R.  \] Since $b_\omega (\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}p^ n)=\rho _\omega (p\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n})^{-n}$, this gives the asserted uniform gap. Finally, $|\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}-1|p^ n\leq (\mathrm{e}^ A-1)p^ n\mathbf1_{O_ j}$, whose integral tends to zero by absolute continuity of the integral. This proves the last assertion and the converse to the third condition. $\square$ For $f=p^ n$, the perturbed densities satisfy $\mathrm{e}^{-A}f\leq \mathrm{e}^{F_ j}f\leq \mathrm{e}^ Af$ with a fixed $A$, so the continuity statement concerns only such order intervals. The instability under general $L^1$ approximation in section 14.31 involves approximations without these bounds. For attainment at one density, uniform integrability along a single maximizing sequence is enough, and this weaker condition also identifies the limit of its weighted measures. Proposition 26.9.3 . Let $0\leq p\in \mathcal D_\omega $ be nonzero and put $R=\rho _\omega (p)$. Suppose $T_ j\in \mathscr G_\omega $ converge weakly to $T$ and satisfy $D_ p(T_ j)\to R$. If the densities $p k_{T_ j}$ are uniformly integrable, then \[  D_ p(T)=R,\qquad p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V\rightharpoonup p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Consequently, a maximizing sequence for $D_ p$ with uniformly integrable densities $pk_{T_ j}$ has a maximizing current among its weak cluster limits. Proof. For positive integers $K$, put $p_ K=\min (p,K)$. Since $p$ is finite almost everywhere, uniform integrability gives \[  \varepsilon _ K:=\sup _ j\int _{\{ p>K\} }p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V \longrightarrow 0.  \] For every nonnegative continuous function $h$, the weight $hp_ K$ is bounded and measurable, so the upper semicontinuity of $D_{hp_ K}$ proved in theorem 26.9.1 gives \[  \limsup _ j\int _ Xhp k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \int _ Xhp_ K k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V +\| h\| _\infty \varepsilon _ K.  \] Now let $K\to \infty $. For $h=1$ this yields $R\leq D_ p(T)$, and the supremum formula ( 26.54 ) gives the reverse inequality. If $\Lambda $ is a weak cluster limit of the measures $p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V$, the same estimate for all nonnegative continuous $h$ gives $\Lambda \leq p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V$. Both measures have mass $R$, so they agree. Since these measures have bounded masses, they form a weakly relatively compact family, and every cluster limit has now been identified. The final assertion follows from the compactness of $\mathscr G_\omega $. $\square$

text: 26.9.3 Trace inequalities at the subsolution threshold Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero with $b=b_\omega (f)>0$. Recall from section 14.27 that a threshold subsolution is a function $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, and a threshold solution is one for which equality holds; threshold subsolutions exist by theorem 14.27.2 . A smooth Gauduchon test can be paired with the full current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ of a threshold subsolution, and by lemma 6.4.2 the resulting trace measure is bounded below by the determinant-weighted density. The nonnegative difference has a mass that depends only on the test. Along a maximizing sequence this mass tends to zero, uniformly over all threshold subsolutions. We write $\| \cdot \| _{\mathrm{TV}}$ for the total variation of a finite signed measure. Proposition 26.9.5 . Let $0\leq f\in L^1$ be nonzero and $b=b_\omega (f)>0$, and write $p=f^{1/n}$. Suppose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. For every smooth strictly positive $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, the measure \[  R_{u,T}=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge T-b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V  \] is positive and has mass \[  R_{u,T}(X)=1-b^{1/n}D_ p(T).  \] In particular, if $(T_ j)$ is a sequence of smooth strictly positive members of $\mathscr G_\omega $ with $D_ p(T_ j)\to \rho _\omega (p)$, then $\| R_{u,T_ j}\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\to 0$, uniformly over all threshold subsolutions $u$. If also $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$ and $T_ j\to T$ as currents, then $T$ maximizes $D_ p$ and \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge T_ j \rightharpoonup b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] In particular, for a fixed sequence $(T_ j)$ with limit $T$, this limiting probability is the same for all threshold subsolutions $u$. Proof. A smooth strictly positive $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ is $\gamma ^{n-1}$ for a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ normalized by $\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=1$. Lemma 6.4.2 proves positivity of $R_{u,T}$, and Stokes' theorem for currents gives $((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge T)(X)=\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$. This proves the mass formula. Since $\rho _\omega (p)=b^{-1/n}$, the nonnegative mass tends to zero along a maximizing sequence; it equals the total variation norm and does not depend on $u$. Under the tail hypothesis, theorem 26.9.1 gives uniform integrability of the densities $p k_{T_ j}$. Thus proposition 26.9.3 makes $T$ a maximizer and gives $p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V\rightharpoonup p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V$. Adding the error measures $R_{u,T_ j}$, which tend to zero in total variation, proves the limit formula. $\square$ The limit formula concerns smooth maximizing sequences. It does not define the product $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge T$ for a singular current $T$, nor does it show that the limit is the same for different maximizing currents. If a maximizing test is itself a smooth strictly positive form, the trace inequality becomes an equality of currents, and since $n\geq 2$ this forces an exact smooth equation. The local regularity needed for this comes from lemma 1.1.4 . Corollary 26.9.6 . Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero with $b=b_\omega (f)>0$. If $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, then $f^{1/n}$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth nonnegative function, and every threshold subsolution $u$ is smooth and satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=bf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] In particular a smooth threshold solution exists, and any two threshold subsolutions differ by a constant. Proof. Let $u$ be any threshold subsolution; one exists by theorem 14.27.2 . Write $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$, where $\gamma $ is the smooth Gauduchon metric given by the positive $(n-1)$st root of $T$, and set \[  a=\left(\frac{bf\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}.  \] Put $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Since $T$ maximizes, the positive measure $R_{u,T}$ of proposition 26.9.5 has mass zero, which gives the equality \[  A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=a\gamma ^ n.  \] The coefficient measures of the positive current $A$ are controlled by this trace measure, which is absolutely continuous. Thus $A$ has a matrix density that is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, with coefficients in $L^ n$ because $a\in L^ n$. For every smooth Hermitian form $\beta $, lemma 6.4.2 also gives \[  A\wedge \beta ^{n-1} \geq \left(\frac{bf\, \mathrm{d}V}{\beta ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\beta ^ n.  \] The resulting pointwise matrix inequalities hold almost everywhere, simultaneously for all positive definite matrices: on each coordinate chart, first use a countable dense family of constant positive matrices, realized on smaller charts by global smooth Hermitian forms, and then use continuity in the matrix. The variational formula for $(\det P)^{1/n}$ in the proof of lemma 26.6.1 therefore yields \[  \left(\frac{A^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\geq a \quad \text{almost everywhere}.  \] Here $A^ n$ denotes only the determinant of the measurable coefficient matrix of $A$; no nonlinear product of currents is used. The trace equality gives the reverse inequality, by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. Equality then forces all eigenvalues of $A$ relative to $\gamma $ to equal $a$, also where $a=0$. Consequently $A=a\gamma $ as currents. By lemma 1.1.4 , applied with $\theta =\omega $, both $a$ and $u$ are smooth, and $f^{1/n}=b^{-1/n}a(\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)^{1/n}$ has a smooth nonnegative representative. Since $u$ is smooth, we may now take the top power: $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=a^ n\gamma ^ n=bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Finally, the function $a$ was defined from $f$, $b$ and $\gamma $ alone, so two threshold subsolutions $u_1,u_2$ satisfy $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1=a\gamma =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2$. Their smooth difference is therefore pluriharmonic, hence constant on the connected compact manifold $X$. $\square$ If $f$ is smooth and strictly positive, theorem 26.1.3 provides a smooth strictly positive maximizing Gauduchon form, obtained from the smooth equation. The corollary therefore applies, and shows in particular that all threshold subsolutions, bounded or not, differ from the smooth solution by constants. Corollary 26.9.7 . Under the hypotheses of corollary 26.9.6 , let $u$ be the threshold solution with $\sup _ Xu=0$. If $u_\lambda $ is the unique bounded solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \lambda >0,  \] then $u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda \to u$ uniformly as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Proof. By corollary 26.9.6 , $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth function, so it belongs to $L^ p$ for every finite $p$. By proposition 14.27.4 , the constant $c$ for which $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a bounded solution is $b_\omega (f)$. Thus proposition 14.19.1 , with the trivial symmetry group, shows that the normalized family $u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $ is uniformly precompact as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ and that every cluster limit is a normalized solution with this constant. Each cluster limit is therefore a normalized threshold subsolution and equals $u$ by corollary 26.9.6 . If the whole family did not converge uniformly, a sequence staying at a fixed positive uniform distance from $u$ would have a uniformly convergent subsequence, a contradiction. $\square$ Corollary 26.9.8 . Suppose $\omega $ is Kähler. For a nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, the functional $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer in $\mathscr G_\omega $ if and only if $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth strictly positive function. Proof. The Kähler formula in proposition 14.27.4 gives $b_\omega (f)>0$. If a smooth strictly positive maximizer exists, the proof of corollary 26.9.6 gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=a\gamma , \qquad a\geq 0,  \] with $a,u$ smooth and $a\not\equiv 0$. Since $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$, the first-order equation in lemma 1.1.4 becomes $\mathrm{d}a=-aC$ for a smooth one-form $C$. Along any smooth path $\sigma $, this is the linear scalar equation \[  (a\circ \sigma )'=-(a\circ \sigma )C(\dot\sigma ).  \] whose solution is the initial value multiplied by a positive exponential. Since $X$ is connected and $a\not\equiv 0$, it follows that $a>0$ everywhere, and $f=b_\omega (f)^{-1}a^ n\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V$ is smooth and strictly positive. Conversely, if $f$ is smooth and strictly positive, the smooth equation and theorem 26.1.3 provide the maximizing Gauduchon form. $\square$ For a nonclosed background, the strict positivity of $f$ in corollary 26.9.8 fails, on every compact complex manifold of dimension at least two, including Kähler manifolds. Example 26.9.9 . On every connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n\geq 2$, with a fixed smooth strictly positive probability volume $\mathrm{d}V$, there is a nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ and a nonzero smooth nonnegative density $f$ vanishing on an open set such that $b_\omega (f)=1$ and $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer. Proof. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and a point $x$. Choose a smooth real function $\psi $ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \leq -\gamma $ on a coordinate neighborhood $U$ of $x$; in holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ centered at $x$, such a function is obtained by multiplying $-M|z|^2$, with $M$ large enough, by a cutoff that equals one near $x$, and then shrinking $U$. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ that vanishes on a smaller neighborhood of $x$ and equals one outside $U$. Put \[  a=L\chi ,\qquad \omega =a\gamma -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi .  \] Since $X$ is compact, $\omega $ is strictly positive for sufficiently large $L>0$: on $U$ the term $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ is at least $\gamma $, and outside $U$ the term $L\gamma $ dominates $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $. Set $f=a^ n\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V$. The smooth function $\psi $ satisfies $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =a\gamma \geq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (\psi )=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, so $b_\omega (f)\geq 1$. Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma ^{n-1}=0$ give \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ Xa\gamma ^ n =\int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Testing ( 14.104 ) with $\gamma $ therefore gives the opposite inequality $b_\omega (f)\leq 1$. Hence $b_\omega (f)=1$, the metric $\gamma $ attains the infimum, and the normalized current $\gamma ^{n-1}/\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is a smooth strictly positive maximizer of $D_{f^{1/n}}$. If $\omega $ were closed, corollary 26.9.8 would force $f$ to be strictly positive, contrary to its vanishing on an open set. Thus $\omega $ is nonclosed. $\square$ In example 26.9.9 , corollary 26.9.6 , corollary 26.9.7 show that every threshold subsolution is a constant translate of $\psi $ and that the normalized solutions of the exponential equations converge uniformly to $\psi -\sup _ X\psi $. Thus vanishing of the density on an open set does not by itself force nonuniqueness or the failure of this approximation. The restriction $n\geq 2$ in corollary 26.9.6 is necessary. On a compact connected Riemann surface $X$ with a Hermitian form $\omega $, a normalized Gauduchon current has bidegree $(0,0)$, and the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ makes it a harmonic function, hence the constant $(\int _ X\omega )^{-1}$. This single smooth strictly positive current maximizes for every nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ density, which need not have a smooth representative.

title: Corollary 26.9.6
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Corollary 26.9.6 . Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero with $b=b_\omega (f)>0$. If $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, then $f^{1/n}$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth nonnegative function, and every threshold subsolution $u$ is smooth and satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=bf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] In particular a smooth threshold solution exists, and any two threshold subsolutions differ by a constant. Proof. Let $u$ be any threshold subsolution; one exists by theorem 14.27.2 . Write $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$, where $\gamma $ is the smooth Gauduchon metric given by the positive $(n-1)$st root of $T$, and set \[  a=\left(\frac{bf\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}.  \] Put $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Since $T$ maximizes, the positive measure $R_{u,T}$ of proposition 26.9.5 has mass zero, which gives the equality \[  A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=a\gamma ^ n.  \] The coefficient measures of the positive current $A$ are controlled by this trace measure, which is absolutely continuous. Thus $A$ has a matrix density that is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, with coefficients in $L^ n$ because $a\in L^ n$. For every smooth Hermitian form $\beta $, lemma 6.4.2 also gives \[  A\wedge \beta ^{n-1} \geq \left(\frac{bf\, \mathrm{d}V}{\beta ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\beta ^ n.  \] The resulting pointwise matrix inequalities hold almost everywhere, simultaneously for all positive definite matrices: on each coordinate chart, first use a countable dense family of constant positive matrices, realized on smaller charts by global smooth Hermitian forms, and then use continuity in the matrix. The variational formula for $(\det P)^{1/n}$ in the proof of lemma 26.6.1 therefore yields \[  \left(\frac{A^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\geq a \quad \text{almost everywhere}.  \] Here $A^ n$ denotes only the determinant of the measurable coefficient matrix of $A$; no nonlinear product of currents is used. The trace equality gives the reverse inequality, by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. Equality then forces all eigenvalues of $A$ relative to $\gamma $ to equal $a$, also where $a=0$. Consequently $A=a\gamma $ as currents. By lemma 1.1.4 , applied with $\theta =\omega $, both $a$ and $u$ are smooth, and $f^{1/n}=b^{-1/n}a(\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)^{1/n}$ has a smooth nonnegative representative. Since $u$ is smooth, we may now take the top power: $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=a^ n\gamma ^ n=bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Finally, the function $a$ was defined from $f$, $b$ and $\gamma $ alone, so two threshold subsolutions $u_1,u_2$ satisfy $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1=a\gamma =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2$. Their smooth difference is therefore pluriharmonic, hence constant on the connected compact manifold $X$. $\square$

title: Corollary 26.9.7
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Corollary 26.9.7 . Under the hypotheses of corollary 26.9.6 , let $u$ be the threshold solution with $\sup _ Xu=0$. If $u_\lambda $ is the unique bounded solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \lambda >0,  \] then $u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda \to u$ uniformly as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Proof. By corollary 26.9.6 , $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth function, so it belongs to $L^ p$ for every finite $p$. By proposition 14.27.4 , the constant $c$ for which $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a bounded solution is $b_\omega (f)$. Thus proposition 14.19.1 , with the trivial symmetry group, shows that the normalized family $u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $ is uniformly precompact as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ and that every cluster limit is a normalized solution with this constant. Each cluster limit is therefore a normalized threshold subsolution and equals $u$ by corollary 26.9.6 . If the whole family did not converge uniformly, a sequence staying at a fixed positive uniform distance from $u$ would have a uniformly convergent subsequence, a contradiction. $\square$

title: Corollary 26.9.8
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Corollary 26.9.8 . Suppose $\omega $ is Kähler. For a nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, the functional $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer in $\mathscr G_\omega $ if and only if $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth strictly positive function. Proof. The Kähler formula in proposition 14.27.4 gives $b_\omega (f)>0$. If a smooth strictly positive maximizer exists, the proof of corollary 26.9.6 gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=a\gamma , \qquad a\geq 0,  \] with $a,u$ smooth and $a\not\equiv 0$. Since $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$, the first-order equation in lemma 1.1.4 becomes $\mathrm{d}a=-aC$ for a smooth one-form $C$. Along any smooth path $\sigma $, this is the linear scalar equation \[  (a\circ \sigma )'=-(a\circ \sigma )C(\dot\sigma ).  \] whose solution is the initial value multiplied by a positive exponential. Since $X$ is connected and $a\not\equiv 0$, it follows that $a>0$ everywhere, and $f=b_\omega (f)^{-1}a^ n\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V$ is smooth and strictly positive. Conversely, if $f$ is smooth and strictly positive, the smooth equation and theorem 26.1.3 provide the maximizing Gauduchon form. $\square$

title: Example 26.9.9
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Example 26.9.9 . On every connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n\geq 2$, with a fixed smooth strictly positive probability volume $\mathrm{d}V$, there is a nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ and a nonzero smooth nonnegative density $f$ vanishing on an open set such that $b_\omega (f)=1$ and $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer. Proof. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and a point $x$. Choose a smooth real function $\psi $ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \leq -\gamma $ on a coordinate neighborhood $U$ of $x$; in holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ centered at $x$, such a function is obtained by multiplying $-M|z|^2$, with $M$ large enough, by a cutoff that equals one near $x$, and then shrinking $U$. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ that vanishes on a smaller neighborhood of $x$ and equals one outside $U$. Put \[  a=L\chi ,\qquad \omega =a\gamma -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi .  \] Since $X$ is compact, $\omega $ is strictly positive for sufficiently large $L>0$: on $U$ the term $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ is at least $\gamma $, and outside $U$ the term $L\gamma $ dominates $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $. Set $f=a^ n\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V$. The smooth function $\psi $ satisfies $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =a\gamma \geq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (\psi )=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, so $b_\omega (f)\geq 1$. Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma ^{n-1}=0$ give \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ Xa\gamma ^ n =\int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Testing ( 14.104 ) with $\gamma $ therefore gives the opposite inequality $b_\omega (f)\leq 1$. Hence $b_\omega (f)=1$, the metric $\gamma $ attains the infimum, and the normalized current $\gamma ^{n-1}/\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is a smooth strictly positive maximizer of $D_{f^{1/n}}$. If $\omega $ were closed, corollary 26.9.8 would force $f$ to be strictly positive, contrary to its vanishing on an open set. Thus $\omega $ is nonclosed. $\square$

text: 26.9.4 A smooth maximizing form with an analytic degeneracy set We now allow the smooth maximizing form to degenerate. Where it is strictly positive, the argument of corollary 26.9.6 still determines the solution current and gives the equation. If the degeneracy set is a proper analytic subset, neither side of the equation charges it, so the equation holds on all of $X$. Uniqueness follows by passing to the maximum of two threshold subsolutions and applying lemma 1.17.2 . Theorem 26.9.10 . Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero, and assume $b=b_\omega (f)>0$. Suppose that $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth semipositive maximizer $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ that is strictly positive on $X\setminus Z$, where $Z$ is a proper analytic subset of $X$. Then every threshold subsolution $u$ is smooth on $X\setminus Z$ and satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=bf\, \mathrm{d}V  \] on $X$. In particular a threshold solution exists, and it has finite mass. The function $f^{1/n}$ has a smooth nonnegative representative on $X\setminus Z$. Any two threshold subsolutions differ by a constant. Proof. Put $p=f^{1/n}$ and $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, where $u$ is any threshold subsolution; one exists by theorem 14.27.2 . Fix a smooth strictly positive $T_0\in \mathscr G_\omega $, and for real $\varepsilon >0$ set $T_\varepsilon =(T+\varepsilon T_0)/(1+\varepsilon )$. Each $T_\varepsilon $ is a smooth strictly positive member of $\mathscr G_\omega $, so proposition 26.9.5 gives \[  A\wedge T_\varepsilon \geq b^{1/n}p k_{T_\varepsilon }\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] For a smooth semipositive form $T$ with coefficient matrix $P'$ relative to $\omega ^ n$, ( 26.39 ) gives $k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V=f_0(\det P')^{1/n}\omega ^ n$, so that $k_ T=f_0^{1-n}(\det P')^{1/n}$ is a continuous function of that matrix. Thus $k_{T_\varepsilon }\to k_ T$ uniformly on the compact manifold $X$. Since $p\in L^1$, passing to the limit gives \[  A\wedge T\geq b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The left side has mass one by Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$, and the right side has mass $b^{1/n}D_ p(T)=1$ because $T$ maximizes. Their difference is positive and has mass zero, hence 26.57 \begin{equation} \label{eq:semipositive-dual-trace-equality} A\wedge T=b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} On $U=X\setminus Z$ write $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$, where $\gamma $ is smooth and strictly positive, and set $a=(bf\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}$. The trace equality becomes $A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=a\gamma ^ n$ on $U$. On relatively compact subsets of $U$, it controls every coefficient measure of $A$ by an $L^ n$ density. The trace inequalities for all Hermitian forms and the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, used exactly as in the proof of corollary 26.9.6 , force $A=a\gamma $ on $U$. This step uses only the positivity of $\gamma $ on $U$, since the Hermitian test forms needed there can be taken to be global forms obtained by extension from smaller coordinate charts. The local regularity lemma lemma 1.1.4 makes $u$ and $a$ smooth on $U$. Taking the top power proves the equation on $U$, and $f^{1/n}=b^{-1/n}a(\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)^{1/n}$ is smooth and nonnegative there. Both $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)$ and $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ put no mass on the pluripolar set $Z$. Hence the equality holds on $X$, and its total mass is $b\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V<+\infty $. It remains to prove uniqueness. Let $v$ be another threshold subsolution and put $w=\max (u,v)$. By proposition 6.2.1 , \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (w)\geq \mathbf1_{\{ u\geq v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u) +\mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (v) \geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Here the pole sets carry no mass for any of the measures involved. Thus $w$ is also a threshold subsolution, and the preceding argument gives the same smooth current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=a\gamma $ on $U$. We apply lemma 1.17.2 to $u\leq w$ and to $v\leq w$: their complex Hessians agree on $X\setminus Z$, so $w-u$ and $w-v$ are constant. Hence $u-v$ is constant. $\square$

title: Corollary 26.9.12
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Corollary 26.9.12 . Under the hypotheses of proposition 26.9.11 , suppose in addition that the obstacle envelope $P_{\delta \omega }(u_0)$ of section 1.19 is not identically $-\infty $ for some real $0<\delta <1$. Then $v_\lambda \to u_0$ in capacity as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. In particular this holds if the threshold solution $u_0$ is bounded. Proof. Fix a sequence $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$. Proposition 26.9.11 gives $u_0-C\leq v_{\lambda _ j}\leq 0$ and $v_{\lambda _ j}\to u_0$ in $L^1$. For all $j$ with $\lambda _ j\leq 1$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (v_{\lambda _ j}) =c_{\lambda _ j}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_{\lambda _ j}}f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq b\mathrm{e}^{C}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The bounded functions $|\mathrm{e}^{v_{\lambda _ j}}-\mathrm{e}^{u_0}|$ tend to zero in $\mathrm{d}V$-measure. Since $f\in L^1$, their integrals against $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ tend to zero, so the error term in ( 14.10 ) tends to zero. We apply proposition 14.8.2 with $\theta =\omega $ and $\varphi =u_0$; its additional hypothesis that the $L^1$ limit $u$ satisfies $u\preceq \varphi $, in the notation of definition 1.12.1 , holds trivially, since $u=u_0$. This proves convergence in capacity along every sequence, and hence for the family. Finally, if $u_0$ is bounded, a constant below it is a competitor for $P_{\delta \omega }(u_0)$, so this envelope is not identically $-\infty $. $\square$

title: 26.9.6 Envelope criteria and extension across the degeneracy set

text:
26.9.6 Envelope criteria and extension across the degeneracy set The capacity criterion above requires the obstacle envelope of $u_0$ in a smaller background $\delta \omega $ not to be identically $-\infty $. We give two sufficient conditions of different origin: invariance of the Monge–Ampère mass controls the contact measures of envelopes of stretched truncations, while a sublinear bound on the singularity provides explicit competitors. Both conditions also give zero Lelong numbers. In the setting of theorem 26.9.10 , if the maximizing form has a globally smooth root of rank at least two, zero Lelong numbers then allow the threshold solution to be extended smoothly across the analytic degeneracy set. The setting is unchanged: $X$ has dimension $n\geq 2$, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form and $\mathrm{d}V$ a smooth positive probability volume form. Inequalities between quasi-plurisubharmonic functions refer to their canonical representatives, and $
u (u,x)$ denotes the Lelong number of $u$ at $x$. We will use the following consequence of lemma 1.17.7 , where $C_\omega $ is the bound for the Lelong numbers of $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions given there: if $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and, for every $0<\delta <1$, some $v_\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\delta \omega )$ satisfies $v_\delta \leq u$, then \[  0\leq 
u (u,x)\leq 
u (v_\delta ,x) =\delta 
u (v_\delta /\delta ,x)\leq \delta C_\omega .  \] Thus $u$ has zero Lelong numbers; the bound is uniform in $\delta $ because $v_\delta /\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Theorem 26.9.13 . Suppose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)=0$ for $1\leq j<n$. Put $V=\int _ X\omega ^ n$. For every nonzero $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, with $M=\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$, one has \[  b_\omega (f)= rac VM.  \] Every threshold subsolution $u$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=(V/M)f\, \mathrm{d}V$ and has mass $V$. Its obstacle envelope $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $ for any $0<\delta <1$, and $u$ has zero Lelong numbers. More generally, these last two conclusions hold for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=V$. Proof. By theorem 2.2.2 , every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function has mass $V$, and truncation therefore bounds every extended mass by $V$. For $f_ k=\min (f,k)$, integration of the bounded equation gives $c_\omega (f_ k)=V/\int _ Xf_ k\, \mathrm{d}V$, so the definition ( 14.101 ) gives $b_\omega (f)=V/M$. A threshold subsolution has mass at least $b_\omega (f)M=V$. Its mass is consequently $V$, and the nonnegative difference between its measure and $b_\omega (f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$ has mass zero. Now let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ have extended mass $V$. Normalize $u\leq 0$, put $\mu _ u=\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)$, and fix $a>1$. For $u_ j=\max (u,-j)$, let $w_ j=P_\omega (au_ j)$. Comparison with constants gives $-aj\leq w_ j\leq 0$. The bounded contact theorem theorem 13.1.3 shows that $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (w_ j)$ is concentrated on the contact set $C_ j=\{ w_ j=au_ j\} $. Since the two functions are canonical representatives and $w_ j\leq au_ j$ almost everywhere, this inequality holds everywhere. Both functions are $a\omega $-plurisubharmonic, so positivity and proposition 6.2.1 give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (w_ j) \leq \mathbf1_{C_ j}\mathrm{MA}_{a\omega }(w_ j) \leq a^ n\mathbf1_{C_ j}\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_ j).  \] For integers $j\geq N$, locality of the products on $\{ u>-N\} $ and the mass identity for bounded functions yield \[  \int _{\{ u_ j\leq -N\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_ j) =V-\mu _ u(\{ u>-N\} )=\mu _ u(\{ u\leq -N\} ).  \] Choose $N$ with $a^ n\mu _ u(\{ u\leq -N\} )<V$; this is possible because $\mu _ u$ is finite and puts no mass on the pole set of $u$. If $\sup _ Xw_ j<-aN$, the contact set $C_ j$ lies in $\{ u_ j<-N\} $, and the preceding inequalities contradict $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\omega (w_ j)=V$. Hence $\sup _ Xw_ j\geq -aN$ for $j\geq N$, and for smaller $j$ the bound $\sup _ Xw_ j\geq -aj$ suffices. The envelopes $w_ j$ decrease with $j$, and by compactness of normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions this uniform lower bound for their suprema prevents their limit from being identically $-\infty $. Their limit $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfies $w\leq au$, also at the poles of $u$. With $\delta =1/a$, the function $\delta w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\delta \omega )$ is therefore a competitor for $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$, so this envelope is not identically $-\infty $. Since $a>1$ was arbitrary, this holds for every $0<\delta <1$, and the Lelong estimate preceding the theorem completes the proof. The normalization $u\leq 0$ does not affect any conclusion. $\square$ Proposition 26.9.14 . Let $\psi \leq 0$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq -C\omega $ for some $C>0$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfy, everywhere on $X$, \[  u\geq -A(1-\psi )^\alpha -B, \qquad A>0,\quad B\in \mathbb R,\quad 0<\alpha <1.  \] Then $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $ for every $0<\delta <1$, and $u$ has zero Lelong numbers. Proof. Choose $\alpha < eta <1$ and $\varepsilon >0$ with $\varepsilon  eta C\leq \delta $. The number \[  K=B+\sup _{t\geq 1}(At^\alpha -\varepsilon t^ eta )  \] is finite, and $v_\delta =-\varepsilon (1-\psi )^ eta -K\leq u$. The function $t\mapsto -\varepsilon (1-t)^ eta $ is increasing and convex on $t\leq 0$, with derivative at most $\varepsilon  eta $. Applying the chain inequality for quasi-plurisubharmonic functions to $\max (\psi ,-j)$ and passing to the decreasing limit as $j	o \infty $, we obtain $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta \geq -\varepsilon  eta C\omega \geq -\delta \omega $. The limit is not identically $-\infty $ because $\psi $ is finite almost everywhere; at the poles of $\psi $ it takes the value $-\infty $, where the comparison with $u$ still holds. Thus $v_\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\delta \omega )$ is a competitor for $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ for each $\delta $, and the Lelong estimate preceding theorem 26.9.13 proves the last assertion. $\square$

The bounded contact theorem theorem 13.1.3 shows that $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (w_ j)$ is concentrated on the contact set $C_ j=\{ w_ j=au_ j\} $. Both functions are $a\omega $-plurisubharmonic, so positivity and proposition 6.2.1 give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (w_ j) \leq \mathbf1_{C_ j}\mathrm{MA}_{a\omega }(w_ j) \leq a^ n\mathbf1_{C_ j}\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_ j).  \] For integers $j\geq N$, locality of the products on $\{ u>-N\} $ and the mass identity for bounded functions yield \[  \int _{\{ u_ j\leq -N\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_ j) =V-\mu _ u(\{ u>-N\} )=\mu _ u(\{ u\leq -N\} ).  \] Choose $N$ with $a^ n\mu _ u(\{ u\leq -N\} )<V$; this is possible because $\mu _ u$ is finite and puts no mass on the pole set of $u$. If $\sup _ Xw_ j<-aN$, the contact set $C_ j$ lies in $\{ u_ j<-N\} $, and the preceding inequalities contradict $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\omega (w_ j)=V$. Hence $\sup _ Xw_ j\geq -aN$ for $j\geq N$, and for smaller $j$ the bound $\sup _ Xw_ j\geq -aj$ suffices. The envelopes $w_ j$ decrease with $j$, and by compactness of normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions this uniform lower bound for their suprema prevents their limit from being identically $-\infty $. Their limit $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfies $w\leq au$, also at the poles of $u$. With $\delta =1/a$, the function $\delta w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\delta \omega )$ is therefore a competitor for $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$, so this envelope is not identically $-\infty $. Since $a>1$ was arbitrary, this holds for every $0<\delta <1$, and the Lelong estimate preceding the theorem completes the proof. The normalization $u\leq 0$ does not affect any conclusion. $\square$

title: Proposition 26.9.14
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.9.14 . Let $\psi \leq 0$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq -C\omega $ for some $C>0$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfy, everywhere on $X$, \[  u\geq -A(1-\psi )^\alpha -B, \qquad A>0,\quad B\in \mathbb R,\quad 0<\alpha <1.  \] Then $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $ for every $0<\delta <1$, and $u$ has zero Lelong numbers. Proof. Choose $\alpha <\beta <1$ and $\varepsilon >0$ with $\varepsilon \beta C\leq \delta $. The number \[  K=B+\sup _{t\geq 1}(At^\alpha -\varepsilon t^\beta )  \] is finite, and $v_\delta =-\varepsilon (1-\psi )^\beta -K\leq u$. The function $t\mapsto -\varepsilon (1-t)^\beta $ is increasing and convex on $t\leq 0$, with derivative at most $\varepsilon \beta $. Applying the chain inequality for quasi-plurisubharmonic functions to $\max (\psi ,-j)$ and passing to the decreasing limit as $j\to \infty $, we obtain $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta \geq -\varepsilon \beta C\omega \geq -\delta \omega $. The limit is not identically $-\infty $ because $\psi $ is finite almost everywhere; at the poles of $\psi $ it takes the value $-\infty $, where the comparison with $u$ still holds. Thus $v_\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\delta \omega )$ is a competitor for $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ for each $\delta $, and the Lelong estimate preceding theorem 26.9.13 proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: A globally smooth root of rank at least two
search_title: A globally smooth root of rank at least two
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: A globally smooth root of rank at least two Theorem 26.9.15 . Assume the hypotheses of theorem 26.9.10 , with analytic degeneracy set $Z$, and let $\Phi _ f$ be the greatest threshold subsolution with supremum zero, from proposition 14.27.3 ; by that theorem it is the threshold solution with supremum zero. Suppose that the maximizing form is $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$ for a globally smooth semipositive $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ whose rank is at least two everywhere. If $\Phi _ f$ has zero Lelong numbers, then it is smooth on $X$; by theorem 26.9.13 , proposition 26.9.14 , this applies under either of the conditions above. Every threshold subsolution is then smooth, since these subsolutions differ by constants. Proof. Put $U=X\setminus Z$ and $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ f$. By theorem 26.9.10 , $A$ is smooth on $U$ and $\Phi _ f$ satisfies the equation on $X$; the root $\gamma $ is positive on $U$. Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ XA\wedge T=1$, while attainment gives \[  \int _ U(A^ n)^{1/n}(\gamma ^ n)^{(n-1)/n} =b_\omega (f)^{1/n}D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=1.  \] The difference $A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}-(A^ n/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$ is nonnegative and continuous on $U$ by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, and its integral vanishes. The equality case gives $A=r\gamma $ on $U$ with the smooth function $r=\operatorname {tr}_\gamma A/n\geq 0$; where $A^ n=0$, equality forces $A=0$ and $r=0$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ f$ is closed, \[  \mathrm dr\wedge \gamma +r\, \mathrm d\gamma =\mathrm d\omega \quad \hbox{on }U.  \] For a semipositive form $\gamma $ of rank at least two, the real-linear map $W_\gamma :\xi \mapsto \xi \wedge \gamma $ from real one-forms to three-forms is injective at every point. Indeed, write $\gamma =\sum _ k\lambda _ k\, \mathrm dx_ k\wedge \mathrm dy_ k$ at the point in suitable real coordinates $z_ k=x_ k+\mathrm iy_ k$, with $\lambda _ k\geq 0$ and at least two $\lambda _ k$ positive. For each index $j$ choose $k\neq j$ with $\lambda _ k>0$. The coefficient of $\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dx_ k\wedge \mathrm dy_ k$ in $\xi \wedge \gamma $ is $\lambda _ k$ times the coefficient of $\mathrm dx_ j$ in $\xi $, and similarly for $\mathrm dy_ j$. Hence $\xi \wedge \gamma =0$ forces $\xi =0$. Choose an auxiliary Riemannian metric. The left inverse $L_\gamma =(W_\gamma ^*W_\gamma )^{-1}W_\gamma ^*$ is smooth and uniformly bounded on compact $X$. Thus 26.58 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rank-two-extension-first-order} \mathrm dr=\alpha -r\beta ,\qquad \alpha =L_\gamma (\mathrm d\omega ),\quad \beta =L_\gamma (\mathrm d\gamma ), \end{equation} with smooth one-forms on $X$. In particular $|\mathrm d\log (1+r)|\leq C$ on $U$. Points of $U$ can be joined by short paths avoiding $Z$. In a coordinate ball, stratify $Z$ into countably many smooth strata of real dimension at most $2n-2$. For a fixed point outside $Z$, the endpoints of segments from it that meet one stratum lie in a cone of dimension at most $2n-1$, which is Lebesgue-null. Given two nearby points outside $Z$, choose a generic intermediate point in a ball of radius comparable to their distance; both connecting segments then avoid $Z$, and their combined length is bounded by a fixed multiple of that distance. Using a finite connected cover by coordinate balls, with intermediate points chosen in the overlaps, we also obtain a uniform bound for the lengths of connecting paths in $U$. The bound on $\mathrm d\log (1+r)$ now bounds $r$ on $U$, and ( 26.58 ) bounds its derivative. The short paths therefore give a unique locally Lipschitz extension of $r$ across $Z$. Since $Z$ is Lebesgue-null, the weak derivative of the extension satisfies ( 26.58 ) on $X$. The right side is continuous, so $r$ is $C^1$, and iterating makes it smooth. Set $S=r\gamma $. It is smooth and semipositive, and $\mathrm dS=\mathrm d\omega $ on $X$ by density of $U$. The current $R=A-S$ is therefore closed, and it is supported on $Z$. It is also positive: since $A=S$ off $Z$ and $S$ puts no mass on $Z$, the current $R$ is the restriction of the positive current $A$ to $Z$. The support theorem recalled in section 1.17 expresses $R$ as a nonnegative combination of currents of integration along the components of $Z$ of codimension one. Locally $S-\omega $ is smooth and closed, so it has a smooth local $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-potential, and the coefficients of $R$ are the generic Lelong numbers of $\Phi _ f$ along these components. All of them vanish, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ f=S-\omega $ is smooth. Taking a Euclidean trace and applying elliptic regularity gives a smooth function equal to $\Phi _ f$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere, since $\Phi _ f$ is its canonical representative. $\square$ The smooth root and its rank bound are hypotheses of the theorem: a smooth semipositive $(n-1,n-1)$-form need not have a smooth $(1,1)$-root across its degeneracy set. On a surface the rank condition already forces $\gamma >0$ everywhere.
