title: Two attained instances
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Two attained instances Example 26.9.16 . On the Hopf surface $X=(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto 2z\rangle $, the background $\omega =|z|^{-2}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$, so its Monge–Ampère mass is invariant. There are smooth densities whose threshold solutions are smooth and nonconstant and whose maximizing tests are smooth strictly positive forms. Proof. The form is invariant under $z\mapsto 2z$, so it descends to $X$, and it is positive. For $s=|z|^2$ and $F(s)=s^{-1}$, the identity $sF''+2F'=0$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(s^{-1})\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s=0$, while $\omega $ is not closed. Choose a nonconstant smooth real $q$ and small nonzero $\varepsilon $ such that $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varepsilon q)>0$. Put $V=\int _ X\omega ^2$, $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^2/V$, $f=A^2/\mathrm{d}V$ and $u=\varepsilon q-\sup _ X\varepsilon q$. Invariance of the mass gives $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V=\int _ XA^2=V$, hence $b_\omega (f)=1$ by theorem 26.9.13 . The form $T=A/V$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$, $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$ and $D_{\sqrt f}(T)=1$. For every smooth strictly positive $Q\in \mathscr G_\omega $, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and Stokes' theorem give $D_{\sqrt f}(Q)\leq \int _ XA\wedge Q=1$. Thus $T$ is a smooth strictly positive maximizer, and since $u$ is a threshold solution with supremum zero, corollary 26.9.6 gives $\Phi _ f=u$. This is a bounded nonconstant example. $\square$ Example 26.9.17 . Let $n\geq 3$, and view the smooth quadric of dimension $n$ as a double cover of $\mathbb P^ n$. For the restricted Fubini–Study form and a suitable smooth density, the maximizing test is a smooth semipositive form whose smooth root has rank at least two everywhere and degenerates along the ramification divisor. Proof. Let \[  X=\{ [w:z_0:\cdots :z_ n]:w^2=\textstyle \sum _{i=0}^ nz_ i^2\}  \subset \mathbb P^{n+1},\qquad F([w:z])=[z].  \] The quadratic form is nonsingular, and $F$ is finite of degree two, with smooth ramification divisor $Z=\{ w=0\} $. Local branch coordinates show that $\mathrm dF$ has rank $n-1$ on $Z$ and $n$ elsewhere. Let $\omega $ be the restriction to $X$ of the normalized Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^{n+1}$, and let $A=F^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, where $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the normalized Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^ n$. Then \[  u=\log \frac{\sum _ i|z_ i|^2}{|w|^2+\sum _ i|z_ i|^2}  \] is a smooth function on $X$ with $-\log 2\leq u\leq 0$, $\sup _ Xu=0$ and $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. The change of variables for the branched cover gives $\int _ XA^ n=2$, and Stokes' theorem gives $V=\int _ X\omega ^ n=2$. Set $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n/V$, $f=A^ n/\mathrm{d}V$, $T=A^{n-1}/V$ and $\gamma =A/V^{1/(n-1)}$. Since $\omega $ is closed, theorem 26.9.13 gives $b_\omega (f)=V/\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V=1$. Stokes' theorem gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ and $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$, and computing the determinant density gives $D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=1$. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, which remains valid for semipositive $A$, bounds $D_{f^{1/n}}(Q)$ by $\int _ XA\wedge Q=1$ for every smooth strictly positive $Q\in \mathscr G_\omega $. Thus $T$ is a maximizer, strictly positive off the proper analytic set $Z$, and theorem 26.9.10 gives $\Phi _ f=u$. Its root $\gamma $ has rank $n-1\geq 2$ on $Z$ and is positive elsewhere, as required. $\square$ The invariant-mass and sublinear conditions settle the envelope condition only in special situations. We do not know whether general moment or entropy bounds imply either of them, or the hypothesis on the smooth root. Corollary 26.9.18 . Under the hypotheses of theorem 26.9.10 , suppose in addition that $f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for some $p>1$. Then the normalized threshold solution $u_0$ is continuous, and the normalized greatest exponential solutions converge uniformly to $u_0$ as the exponent tends to zero. Proof. By proposition 14.27.4 , the constant $c$ for which $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a continuous solution is $b_\omega (f)$. The continuous normalized solution is therefore a threshold solution, and it equals $u_0$ by the uniqueness in theorem 26.9.10 . For $L^ p$ data the greatest exponential solution coincides with the bounded solution, as explained after theorem 14.34.1 . By proposition 14.19.1 , applied with the trivial group, the normalized family is uniformly precompact, and every cluster limit solves the threshold equation. Uniqueness identifies every cluster limit with $u_0$, which proves uniform convergence of the whole family. $\square$

title: 26.9.7 A full-mass point pole without a smooth maximizing test
search_title: A full-mass point pole without a smooth maximizing test
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.9.7 A full-mass point pole without a smooth maximizing test The envelope criteria above do not require $L^ p$ integrability of the density. In the following example on projective space, with a closed background, the threshold solution is unbounded, while its envelopes $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ in smaller backgrounds are not identically $-\infty $. The dual supremum is approached by smooth tests but attained by no smooth semipositive test. Proposition 26.9.19 . Let $X=\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 2$, and let $\omega $ be the normalized Fubini–Study form, with $\int _ X\omega ^ n=1$ and $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n$. For $0<\alpha <1$ put \[  \psi =\log \frac{\sum _{i=1}^ n|z_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ n|z_ i|^2}, \qquad u=1-(1-\psi )^\alpha , \qquad o=[1:0:\cdots :0].  \] The function $u$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, satisfies $\sup _ Xu=0$, has $o$ as its only pole, and has extended mass one. For every $0<\delta <1$, the envelope $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $. The measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)$ is $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and $f\notin L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for every $p>1$. Moreover, $b_\omega (f)=1$ and $\rho _\omega (f^{1/n})=1$, so $u$ is a threshold solution for $f$. No smooth semipositive $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ attains $D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=1$. Proof. The numerator in the definition of $\psi $ vanishes only at $o$, and locally $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _{i=1}^ n|z_ i|^2\geq 0$. The function $\chi (t)=1-(1-t)^\alpha $ is increasing and convex on $t\leq 0$, with $0\leq \chi '\leq \alpha $. Applying the chain inequality to bounded truncations of $\psi $ and taking the decreasing limit, we obtain $u=\chi \circ \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, with \[  A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq (1-\alpha )\omega .  \] The function $u$ is smooth off $o$, and it attains its supremum zero on $\{ z_0=0\} $. Since $u=-(1-\psi )^\alpha +1$, proposition 26.9.14 shows that all the envelopes $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ are not identically $-\infty $. To compute the mass, use the chart $z_0=1$ and write $s=\sum _{i=1}^ n|z_ i|^2$. A local potential $F$ for $A$, as a function of $s$, and the function $q=sF'$ are 26.59 \begin{equation} \label{eq:point-pole-radial-flux} \begin{aligned}  F(s)& =\log (1+s)+1-\left(1-\log \frac{s}{1+s}\right)^\alpha ,\\  q(s)& =sF'(s)=\frac{s+\alpha (1-\log (s/(1+s)))^{\alpha -1}}{1+s}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} The eigenvalues of $A$ are $q/s$ in the tangential directions and $q'$ in the radial direction. Polar integration gives the radial top-degree measure $nq^{n-1}q'\, \mathrm{d}s$, where the angular normalization follows from the Fubini–Study case $q=s/(1+s)$, whose radial density is $ns^{n-1}(1+s)^{-n-1}\, \mathrm{d}s$ and whose total mass is one. Consequently, for $0<s_1<s_2$, \[  \int _{\{ s_1<|z|^2<s_2\} }A^ n=q(s_2)^ n-q(s_1)^ n.  \] Here $q(s)\to 0$ as $s\downarrow 0$ and $q(s)\to 1$ as $s\to \infty $. On each compact annulus the extended measure equals the smooth top power, and it puts no mass on $o$ or on the hyperplane at infinity, since both are pluripolar. Exhausting the affine chart by annuli therefore gives extended mass exactly one. (This computation does not use the vanishing of the Lelong numbers.) Near $o$ write $L=1-\log s$. Differentiating ( 26.59 ) gives \[  \begin{gathered} \frac qs\sim \alpha s^{-1}L^{\alpha -1},\qquad q'\sim \alpha (1-\alpha )s^{-1}L^{\alpha -2},\\ f(s)\asymp s^{-n}L^{-1-n(1-\alpha )}. \end{gathered}  \] The smooth volume form, written in terms of $s$, is comparable to $s^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d}s$, so the contribution of a neighborhood of $o$ to $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$ is comparable to $\int ^\infty L^{-1-n(1-\alpha )}\, \mathrm{d}L$, which is finite. For every $p>1$, the corresponding integral of $f^ p$ contains an exponentially growing factor $\exp (n(p-1)L)$ and diverges. The measure is smooth off $o$ and puts no mass on $o$, so it is $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ on all of $X$. Since its total mass is one and $\omega $ is closed, theorem 26.9.13 gives $b_\omega (f)=1$, and hence $\rho _\omega (f^{1/n})=b_\omega (f)^{-1/n}=1$. Suppose that a smooth semipositive $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ attained this value. The positive current $A$ satisfies $\int _ XA\wedge T=1$ by Stokes' theorem for currents. On $X\setminus \{ o\} $, the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  A\wedge T\geq f^{1/n}k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The right side has total mass one by attainment, so the nonnegative difference of the two sides vanishes off $o$. Since $A$ is smooth and strictly positive there, the equality case gives $T=tA^{n-1}$ on $X\setminus \{ o\} $, also at points where $T=0$: applying the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality to the positive semidefinite coefficient matrix of $T$ conjugated by $A^{1/2}$ shows that all its eigenvalues agree, possibly at zero. The function $t=(T\wedge A)/A^ n$ is smooth and nonnegative on $X\setminus \{ o\} $. Since $A$ is closed, the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ becomes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t\wedge A^{n-1}=0$, a locally strictly elliptic scalar equation on $X\setminus \{ o\} $. All eigenvalues of $A$ tend to infinity at $o$, and since $n\geq 2$, so do all eigenvalues of $A^{n-1}$, which are products of $n-1$ eigenvalues of $A$. Since the coefficient matrix of the smooth form $T$ is bounded, it follows that $t\to 0$ at $o$. Set $t(o)=0$. The resulting continuous nonnegative function on compact $X$ is not identically zero, by the normalization of $T$, so it attains a positive maximum away from $o$. The strong maximum principle on the connected manifold $X\setminus \{ o\} $ forces it to be constant there, contrary to its zero limit at $o$. This excludes every smooth semipositive maximizing test; no assumption on the degeneracy set of $T$ was needed. $\square$ Corollary 26.9.20 . For the density and potential of proposition 26.9.19 , \[  \int _ X f\log f\, \mathrm{d}V<+\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \alpha <1-\frac1n.  \] For every real $r>0$, \[  \int _ X(-u)^ r f\, \mathrm{d}V<+\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \alpha r<n(1-\alpha ).  \] In particular, finite entropy of the density can coexist with an unbounded threshold solution of full mass and with the absence of a smooth semipositive maximizing test. Proof. Only a neighborhood of $o$ can contribute a divergence. There the preceding estimates give $f\, \mathrm{d}V\asymp L^{-1-n(1-\alpha )}\, \mathrm{d}L$, $\log f\sim nL$ and $-u\asymp L^\alpha $. Hence the entropy integral converges exactly when $n(1-\alpha )>1$, and the weighted integral exactly when $\alpha r<n(1-\alpha )$. In the equality cases both integrals are comparable to $\int ^\infty L^{-1}\, \mathrm{d}L$ and diverge. The negative part of $f\log f$ is bounded, hence integrable for the probability volume, so the entropy criterion is unambiguous. $\square$ These are integrals of the single density $f$. They should be distinguished from uniform moment or entropy bounds for the determinant-weighted probabilities of a maximizing sequence, as in theorem 26.9.24 ; since the present example has no smooth semipositive maximizer, it lies outside the setting of theorem 26.9.10 . The proposition concerns the explicit threshold solution $u$; identifying it with the greatest normalized threshold subsolution $\Phi _ f$ would require a separate uniqueness argument.

26.9.9 The classes of the divisorial components Uniqueness constrains the divisors along which the threshold solution can have positive Lelong numbers. A linear relation between their Bott–Chern classes would produce a global potential that changes the coefficients of these divisors while preserving the equation off the degeneracy set, contradicting uniqueness. We write $\{ D\} \in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$ for the Bott–Chern class of the current of integration $[D]$ along a prime divisor $D$, and $
u (u,D)$ for the generic Lelong number of $u$ along $D$. Corollary 26.9.22 . Under the hypotheses of theorem 26.9.10 , let $u$ be a threshold solution and let $D_1,\ldots ,D_ k$ be the prime divisors with $
u (u,D_ j)>0$. Then the classes $\{ D_ j\} $ are linearly independent in $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$. In particular their number is at most $\dim _{\mathbb R}H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$. Proof. Since $u$ is smooth off $Z$, these divisors are among the finitely many components of $Z$ of codimension one. Put $a_ j=
u (u,D_ j)>0$. By lemma 1.17.1 , \[  R=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\sum _ j a_ j[D_ j]\geq 0.  \] Suppose that real numbers $c_1,\ldots ,c_ k$ satisfy $\sum _ j c_ j\{ D_ j\} =0$. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\eta $ and apply lemma 23.7.1 to the currents of integration $[D_ j]$, with the integrable potentials $v_\eta ([D_ j])$ given there. Since the smooth representative in that lemma depends linearly on the Bott–Chern class, we obtain \[  h=\sum _ j c_ j v_\eta ([D_ j])\in L^1(X),\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\sum _ j c_ j[D_ j].  \] Choose $t
e 0$ sufficiently small that $a_ j+tc_ j\geq 0$ for every $j$. The distribution $u_ t=u+th$ satisfies \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t=R+\sum _ j(a_ j+tc_ j)[D_ j]\geq 0,  \] so it is represented by a function $u_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. On $X\setminus Z$, the function $h$ is smooth and pluriharmonic, so $u_ t$ has the same Monge–Ampère measure as $u$ there. Since neither extended measure charges the pluripolar set $Z$, $u_ t$ is another threshold solution. Uniqueness makes $th=u_ t-u$ constant. Hence $\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]=0$, and testing near a generic point of each of the distinct divisors $D_ j$ gives $c_ j=0$. $\square$ The conclusion concerns only the divisors along which the solution has positive generic Lelong number. It imposes no independence condition on the other components of codimension one of the degeneracy set.

title: 26.9.10 A branched projective example
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.9.10 A branched projective example The squaring map of projective space gives a smooth threshold solution whose maximizing form degenerates along the coordinate hyperplanes. The density is smooth, but its $n$th root is not differentiable along these hyperplanes. For this example take $X=\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 2$, with homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ n]$, and let $\omega $ be the Fubini–Study form normalized by $\int _ X\omega ^ n=1$. Set $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n$. Example 26.9.23 . For every $n\geq 2$, there is a smooth nonnegative density $f$ on $\mathbb P^ n$, vanishing precisely on the coordinate hyperplanes, such that $b_\omega (f)=1$ and $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth semipositive maximizer strictly positive off those hyperplanes. The threshold solution is smooth, but $f^{1/n}$ is not differentiable at a general point of any coordinate hyperplane. There is no smooth strictly positive maximizing form. The normalized greatest exponential solutions converge uniformly to the normalized threshold solution. Proof. Define the holomorphic map $F:\mathbb P^ n\to \mathbb P^ n$ and the semipositive form $A$ by \[  F[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ n]=[Z_0^2:\cdots :Z_ n^2],\qquad A=\tfrac 12F^*\omega .  \] The homogeneous formula \[  u=\tfrac 12\log \! \left(\sum _{i=0}^ n|Z_ i|^4\right) -\log \! \left(\sum _{i=0}^ n|Z_ i|^2\right)  \] defines a smooth function on projective space, and $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. The form $A$ is semipositive, and it is strictly positive exactly where every homogeneous coordinate is nonzero. Define \[  f=A^ n/\omega ^ n,\qquad T=A^{n-1}.  \] Since $\omega $ and $A$ are closed and cohomologous, Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ X f\omega ^ n=\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$; thus $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $. Every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ has extended mass at most one: each bounded truncation $\max (v,-k)$ has mass one, and restricting its Monge–Ampère measure to $\{ v>-k\} $ can only decrease that mass. Consequently an inequality $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (v)\geq c f\omega ^ n$ forces $c\leq 1$. The smooth solution $u$ gives the reverse bound, so $b_\omega (f)=1$. The determinant formula for smooth semipositive forms gives \[  k_ T=f^{(n-1)/n},\qquad D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=\int _{\mathbb P^ n}f\omega ^ n=1.  \] By ( 26.54 ) and $\rho _\omega (f^{1/n})=b_\omega (f)^{-1/n}=1$, the form $T$ is a maximizer. It is strictly positive away from the coordinate hyperplanes because $A$ is; on these hyperplanes $A$ has deficient rank, and hence so does the coefficient matrix of $T=A^{n-1}$. For the density root, use the chart $Z_0=1$ with coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ n$. Pulling back the Fubini–Study volume by $(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)\mapsto (z_1^2,\ldots ,z_ n^2)$ and including the factor $2^{-n}$ gives \[  f(z)=2^ n\left(\prod _{i=1}^ n|z_ i|^2\right) \frac{(1+\sum _ i|z_ i|^2)^{n+1}}{(1+\sum _ i|z_ i|^4)^{n+1}}.  \] Near a point of $\{ z_1=0\} $ at which all the other coordinates are nonzero, $f^{1/n}$ is $|z_1|^{2/n}$ times a smooth strictly positive function. Restricting to a real line transverse to that hyperplane proves nondifferentiability, also in the case $n=2$, where $|z_1|^{2/n}=|z_1|$. By symmetry of the coordinates, the same holds on every coordinate hyperplane. The absence of a smooth strictly positive maximizer follows from corollary 26.9.8 , since $f$ has zeros. Finally, $f$ is bounded, so corollary 26.9.18 gives the uniform convergence of the normalized exponential solutions. $\square$

title: 26.10 Nef limits and nonattainment
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.10 Nef limits and nonattainment We return to arbitrary dimension $n\geq 1$. If $\theta $ is nef and $h$ is a Hermitian form, then the backgrounds $\theta +\epsilon h$ lie in $\mathscr P$ for every $\epsilon >0$, directly from the definition of nefness; their volumes are therefore scalars of smooth equations. As $\epsilon $ decreases to zero, the infimum over Gauduchon metrics commutes with the decreasing limit of the background. Thus the boundary value is determined by smooth equations, even when no metric attains it. Theorem 26.10.1 . For every nef background $\theta $ and every Hermitian form $h$, \[  \lambda _\mu (\theta ) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h), \qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta ) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}c_{\theta +\epsilon h}(\mu ).  \] Both quantities on the right decrease as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, and their limits do not depend on $h$. Proof. For $0<\epsilon '<\epsilon $ the difference of the two backgrounds is the positive form $(\epsilon -\epsilon ')h$, so the monotonicity in proposition 26.1.2 shows that $\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)$ decreases as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Its limit is therefore the infimum over $\epsilon >0$. Infima over $\epsilon >0$ and over Gauduchon metrics commute, and for a fixed metric the quotient is affine in $\epsilon $. Hence \[  \begin{split}  \inf _{\epsilon >0}\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) & =\inf _\gamma \inf _{\epsilon >0} \frac{\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} +\epsilon \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma )}\\ & =\lambda _\mu (\theta ). \end{split}  \] Here the second equality holds because the coefficient of $\epsilon $ is positive, so the inner infimum is the value at $\epsilon =0$. This proves the first identity, and its right side is the definition of $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$, which does not involve $h$. The second identity follows by raising the first to the $n$th power, since $\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)^ n=c_{\theta +\epsilon h}(\mu )$ by theorem 26.1.3 . $\square$ If $X$ is Kähler and $\theta $ is closed and nef, choose $h$ Kähler. Each perturbed solution form is then closed and cohomologous to $\theta +\epsilon h$, so integrating its equation and applying Stokes' theorem gives \[  c_{\theta +\epsilon h}(\mu )=\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon h)^ n.  \] Letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=\int _ X\theta ^ n$ for every closed nef $\theta $ on a compact Kähler manifold and every $\mu $. We refer to this as the closed nef formula . Proposition 26.10.2 . Suppose $\theta $ is pseudoeffective and $\lambda _\mu (\theta )=0$. The infimum in definition 26.1.1 is attained if and only if $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$. Proof. Since $D_\mu (\gamma )>0$, a metric $\gamma $ attaining the value zero satisfies $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=0$. By lemma 4.3.3 , including its dimension-one case, $\theta $ is then smoothly $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. Conversely, if $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, Stokes' theorem makes every quotient zero, so every admissible metric attains the infimum. $\square$ For example, let $X$ be the ruled surface and $D$ the section of lemma 25.5.1 . The class $c_1(\mathcal O_ X(D))$ is nef, has zero square, and contains the nonzero positive current $[D]$. By the closed nef formula its volume is zero. A smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact representative would make $[D]$ itself $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact, which is impossible because $\int _ D\kappa >0$ for a Kähler form $\kappa $. By proposition 26.10.2 , no Gauduchon metric minimizes the defining quotient.

title: Theorem 26.10.1
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 26.10.1 . For every nef background $\theta $ and every Hermitian form $h$, \[  \lambda _\mu (\theta ) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h), \qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta ) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}c_{\theta +\epsilon h}(\mu ).  \] Both quantities on the right decrease as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, and their limits do not depend on $h$. Proof. For $0<\epsilon '<\epsilon $ the difference of the two backgrounds is the positive form $(\epsilon -\epsilon ')h$, so the monotonicity in proposition 26.1.2 shows that $\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)$ decreases as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Its limit is therefore the infimum over $\epsilon >0$. Infima over $\epsilon >0$ and over Gauduchon metrics commute, and for a fixed metric the quotient is affine in $\epsilon $. Hence \[  \begin{split}  \inf _{\epsilon >0}\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) & =\inf _\gamma \inf _{\epsilon >0} \frac{\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} +\epsilon \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma )}\\ & =\lambda _\mu (\theta ). \end{split}  \] Here the second equality holds because the coefficient of $\epsilon $ is positive, so the inner infimum is the value at $\epsilon =0$. This proves the first identity, and its right side is the definition of $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$, which does not involve $h$. The second identity follows by raising the first to the $n$th power, since $\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)^ n=c_{\theta +\epsilon h}(\mu )$ by theorem 26.1.3 . $\square$

26.11 Subtraction with a closed nef core Consider a path of backgrounds that starts in $\mathscr P$ and reaches its boundary at a nef point. If the path contains a closed nef class of positive top intersection, this closed core keeps the root volume positive up to and including the boundary, and adding a semipositive form, closed or not, preserves this lower bound. By proposition 26.2.2 , the total decrease of the root volume along the path is the integral of an explicit ratio formed with the minimizing Gauduchon metrics; we call it the subtraction cost. Two test metrics chosen at the initial point bound this cost from above, with explicit dependence on the density and on the derivatives of the added form. Throughout this section, $X$ is a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$ and $\Omega $ is a fixed Kähler form on $X$. Let $\alpha $ be a smooth closed nef real $(1,1)$-form, let $B\geq 0$ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, and let $t>0$. For real $s$, put \[  a_ s=\alpha +(t-s)\Omega ,\qquad 	heta _ s=a_ s+B,\qquad V_ s=\int _ Xa_ s^ n.  \] The class of $a_0$ is Kähler. Choose a Kähler representative $\kappa _0$ of $[a_0]$, and let $u_0$ be the smooth solution of the Calabi–Yau equation $\gamma _0=\kappa _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0>0$, $\gamma _0^ n=V_0\mu $. Define the fixed quantities 26.65  egin{equation} \label{eq:closed-core-fixed-tests}  egin{gathered} I_ B=\int _ XB\wedge \kappa _0^{n-1},\qquad U_\mu = rac{V_0+I_ B}{D_\mu (\kappa _0)},\ \Delta _\mu (B)=V_0^{-(n-1)/n}\int _ XB\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Theorem 26.11.1 . Suppose that $V:=V_ t>0$ and that there is a smooth compact complex curve $C\subset X$ with $\int _ C\alpha =\int _ CB=0$. Then $	heta _ s$ has a smooth positive representative for $s<t$, $	heta _ t$ is nef but has no smooth positive representative, and $	heta _ s$ is not nef for $s>t$. Moreover, \[  \lambda _\mu (a_ s)=V_ s^{1/n}\quad (0\leq s\leq t), \qquad \lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)\geq V^{1/n}>0.  \] For every choice of minimizing Gauduchon metrics $g_ s$ for $	heta _ s$, $0\leq s<t$, the ratio $\int _ X\Omega \wedge g_ s^{n-1}/D_\mu (g_ s)$ is a continuous function of $s$, and the subtraction cost satisfies 26.66  egin{equation} \label{eq:closed-core-cost}  egin{split}  0\leq \mathcal C & :=\int _0^ t rac{\int _ X\Omega \wedge g_ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (g_ s)}\, \mathrm{d}s =\lambda _\mu (	heta _0)-\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)\ & \leq \min \{ U_\mu ,V_0^{1/n}+\Delta _\mu (B)\} -V^{1/n}<\infty , \end{split} \end{equation} where the integral is improper at $t$. If $B\leq M\kappa _0$ for a constant $M\geq 0$, then \[  \Delta _\mu (B)\leq MV_0^{1/n},\qquad \mathcal C\leq (1+M)V_0^{1/n}-V^{1/n}.  \] Finally, there are a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $ho $ and a constant $\varepsilon >0$ with $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \varepsilon \Omega $ and $	heta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \varepsilon \Omega $. Proof. We first locate the boundary of $\mathscr P$ along the path. Let $s<t$. Since $\alpha $ is nef, for every $\delta >0$ there is a smooth function $v_\delta $ with $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta \geq -\delta \Omega $. Taking $\delta <t-s$ makes $a_ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta $ Kähler, and adding $B\geq 0$ gives a positive representative of $	heta _ s$. The same approximations show that $	heta _ t$ is nef. On the other hand, the hypotheses on $C$ and Stokes' theorem on the compact curve give \[  \int _ C(	heta _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)=(t-s)\int _ C\Omega  \] for every smooth $v$. At $s=t$ the right side vanishes, which excludes a positive representative of $	heta _ t$. For $s>t$, a representative with $	heta _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq -\delta \Omega $ and $\delta <s-t$ would contradict this identity, so $	heta _ s$ is not nef. Since every $a_ s$ with $s\leq t$ is closed and nef, the closed nef formula following theorem 26.10.1 gives $\lambda _\mu (a_ s)=V_ s^{1/n}$, including at $s=t$. The difference $	heta _ t-a_ t=B$ is semipositive, so monotonicity gives $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)\geq V^{1/n}$, while any fixed Gauduchon test bounds $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)$ from above. Since $	heta _ s=	heta _ t+(t-s)\Omega $, theorem 26.10.1 with the Hermitian form $\Omega $ identifies $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)$ with the limit of $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ s)$ as $s\uparrow t$. Write $f(s)=\lambda _\mu (	heta _ s)$ for $s<t$. The path has constant velocity $-\Omega $, so proposition 26.2.2 shows that $f$ is smooth and \[  H(s):= rac{\int _ X\Omega \wedge g_ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (g_ s)}=-f'(s).  \] In particular, the ratio $H$ is continuous and independent of the choice of minimizing metrics. For $r<t$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  \int _0^ rH(s)\, \mathrm{d}s=f(0)-f(r).  \] Since $H\geq 0$, letting $r\uparrow t$ and using the limit just established yields the identity in ( 26.66 ). It remains to bound $f(0)=\lambda _\mu (	heta _0)$ from above by two test metrics. The Kähler form $\kappa _0$ is Gauduchon, and since $\kappa _0$ is cohomologous to $a_0$, closed Stokes gives $\int _ X	heta _0\wedge \kappa _0^{n-1}=V_0+I_ B$; hence $\lambda _\mu (	heta _0)\leq U_\mu $. For the second test $\gamma _0$, the equation $\gamma _0^ n=V_0\mu $ and the cohomology class of $\gamma _0$ give \[  D_\mu (\gamma _0)=V_0^{(n-1)/n},\qquad \int _ Xa_0\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}=V_0,  \] so its quotient for $	heta _0$ is $V_0^{1/n}+\Delta _\mu (B)$. Combined with the lower bound $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)\geq V^{1/n}$, these two tests prove the upper bound in ( 26.66 ). If $B\leq M\kappa _0$, closed Stokes yields $\int _ XB\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}\leq M\int _ X\kappa _0\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}=MV_0$, which gives the remaining cost bounds. Finally, $V=\int _ X\alpha ^ n>0$, so the closed nef class of $\alpha $ is big by the nef-and-big criterion on compact Kähler manifolds recalled in [ SGPT ] . Hence it contains a Kähler current $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \varepsilon \Omega $. Adding $B\geq 0$ gives the last assertion. Unlike the first current, the second is not closed when $\mathrm dB
eq 0$, since its exterior derivative is $\mathrm{d}B$. $\square$ Such data arise from a bimeromorphic holomorphic map $p:X	o Y$ onto a compact Kähler manifold $Y$ that contracts a smooth curve $C$ to a point. Take $\alpha =p^*\omega _ Y$, with $\omega _ Y$ Kähler, and any smooth $B\geq 0$ vanishing on $TC$. Since $p$ has degree one, $\int _ X\alpha ^ n=\int _ Y\omega _ Y^ n>0$, while both curve integrals vanish. The second initial test separates the closed intersection number $I_ B$ from a correction that involves only $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B$. Proposition 26.11.2 . Set $S=\sum _{j=0}^{n-2}\gamma _0^ j\wedge \kappa _0^{n-2-j}$. Then 26.69  egin{equation} \label{eq:closed-core-differential-cost} \Delta _\mu (B)=V_0^{-(n-1)/n} \left(I_ B+\int _ Xu_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B\wedge Sight). \end{equation} If $-C_ B\kappa _0^2\leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B\leq C_ B\kappa _0^2$ in the sense of weak positivity of $(2,2)$-forms, then \[  \Delta _\mu (B)\leq V_0^{-(n-1)/n}I_ B +(n-1)C_ B\operatorname {osc}_ X(u_0)V_0^{1/n}.  \] Such a finite constant $C_ B$ exists for every fixed smooth $B$. Proof. The factors of $S$ are closed, and $\gamma _0^{n-1}-\kappa _0^{n-1}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0\wedge S$. Integration by parts therefore gives ( 26.69 ). Since $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B\wedge S=0$, the right side does not change when a constant is added to $u_0$, so we may assume $\sup _ Xu_0=0$. Then $-\operatorname {osc}_ X(u_0)\leq u_0\leq 0$, and the lower bound for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B$ together with the positivity of the summands of $S$ bounds the correction term above by \[  C_ B\operatorname {osc}_ X(u_0)\int _ X\kappa _0^2\wedge S =(n-1)C_ B\operatorname {osc}_ X(u_0)V_0.  \] The equality holds because the cohomologous Kähler forms $\gamma _0,\kappa _0$ have all mixed top intersections equal to $V_0$. Finally, restrict $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B$ to the complex two-planes of $TX$ and normalize by $\kappa _0$; compactness of the bundle of these planes bounds the restrictions and gives $C_ B$. $\square$ The potential $u_0$ solves a single complex Monge–Ampère equation, with density $V_0\mu /\kappa _0^ n$ relative to $\kappa _0^ n$. Its oscillation therefore carries the dependence on $\mu $, whereas the derivatives $\mathrm{d}	heta _ s=\mathrm{d}B$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	heta _ s=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B$ do not change along the path. For the closed core alone the cost is explicit. Put $P_ s=\int _ X\Omega \wedge a_ s^{n-1}$. Since $V_ s'=-nP_ s$, \[  - rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\lambda _\mu (a_ s) = rac{P_ s}{V_ s^{(n-1)/n}},\qquad \int _0^ t rac{P_ s}{V_ s^{(n-1)/n}}\, \mathrm{d}s=V_0^{1/n}-V^{1/n}.  \] Moreover $P_ s'=-(n-1)\int _ X\Omega ^2\wedge a_ s^{n-2}\leq 0$, since all classes on the segment are nef. Integrating $V_ s'=-nP_ s$ and using $P_ s\leq P_0$ gives 26.70  egin{equation} \label{eq:closed-core-nef-morse} V\geq V_0-nt\int _ X\Omega \wedge a_0^{n-1}. \end{equation} This argument does not use $V>0$, so a positive right side guarantees the hypothesis $V>0$ of theorem 26.11.1 . The following example shows that this sufficient condition is not necessary. Example 26.11.3 . On the blowup of $\mathbb P^2$ at a point there are data as above with $t=1$, $\mathrm{d}B
eq 0$, \[  \lambda _\mu (	heta _1)\geq  rac32,\qquad 0\leq \mathcal C\leq  rac{11}{\sqrt8}- rac32,  \] and an explicit current $	heta _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq  rac12\Omega $ at the nef endpoint. Proof. Realize the blowup as $X=\{ (x,[u:v])\in \mathbb P^2	imes \mathbb P^1:x_1v=x_2u\} $, with projections $p,q$ and exceptional curve $E=p^{-1}([1:0:0])$. Let $L=p^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS},\mathbb P^2}$, $Q=q^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS},\mathbb P^1}$ and $\Omega =L+Q$, with the Fubini–Study forms normalized to have integral one on projective lines. The incidence embedding makes $\Omega $ Kähler. The degree-one blowdown, a fiber of $q$, and the isomorphism $q|_ E:E	o \mathbb P^1$ give \[  \int _ XL^2=\int _ XL\wedge Q=1,\quad Q^2=0,\quad L|_{TE}=0,\quad \int _ EQ=1.  \] Take $t=1$, $\alpha =L$, $\kappa _0=2L+Q$ and $\mu =\kappa _0^2/8$. With $r=1-s$, the core volumes are $V_ s=1+4r+3r^2$; in particular $V_0=8$ and $V=V_1=1$. Choose a nonconstant smooth function $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ supported away from $E$, and put \[  b= rac13\int _ X\chi L\wedge \kappa _0,\qquad f=\chi -b,\qquad B=(1+f/2)L.  \] Since $\int _ XL\wedge \kappa _0=3$, we have $|f|\leq 1$ and $\int _ XfL\wedge \kappa _0=0$. Thus $B\geq L/2$ and $B|_{TE}=0$, so the curve $C=E$ satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 26.11.1 . Where $\mathrm{d}\chi 
e 0$, the form $L$ is symplectic, and wedging with $L$ is injective on real one-forms in real dimension four. Hence $\mathrm{d}B=	frac 12\mathrm{d}f\wedge L
e 0$. At the endpoint $	heta _1=(2+f/2)L\geq 3L/2$, and $\lambda _\mu (L)=1$ by the closed nef formula; this gives the lower bound for $\lambda _\mu (	heta _1)$. Since $\kappa _0^2=8\mu $, the initial solution is $\gamma _0=\kappa _0$ with $u_0=0$. Therefore $D_\mu (\kappa _0)=\sqrt8$, $I_ B=3$, $\Delta _\mu (B)=3/\sqrt8$ and $U_\mu =11/\sqrt8$, so $\lambda _\mu (	heta _0)\leq 11/\sqrt8$. The cost identity and the lower bound at the endpoint give the asserted estimate for $\mathcal C$. The pullback of $\{ x_1=0\} $ is $E$ plus a fiber of $q$, so $\mathcal O(E)=p^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)\otimes q^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$. Give this bundle its product metric $h_ E$, with curvature $L-Q$, and let $s_ E$ be its canonical section. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives, for $ho =	frac 12\log |s_ E|_{h_ E}^2$, \[  	heta _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho =B+	frac 12\Omega +	frac 12[E]\geq 	frac 12\Omega .  \] Finally, $\int _ X\Omega \wedge a_0=5$, so the right side of ( 26.70 ) is $8-10=-2$, although $V_1=1$. $\square$

Example 26.11.3 . On the blowup of $\mathbb P^2$ at a point there are data as above with $t=1$, $\mathrm{d}B
eq 0$, \[  \lambda _\mu (	heta _1)\geq  rac32,\qquad 0\leq \mathcal C\leq  rac{11}{\sqrt8}- rac32,  \] and an explicit current $	heta _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq  rac12\Omega $ at the nef endpoint. Proof. Realize the blowup as $X=\{ (x,[u:v])\in \mathbb P^2	imes \mathbb P^1:x_1v=x_2u\} $, with projections $p,q$ and exceptional curve $E=p^{-1}([1:0:0])$. Let $L=p^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS},\mathbb P^2}$, $Q=q^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS},\mathbb P^1}$ and $\Omega =L+Q$, with the Fubini–Study forms normalized to have integral one on projective lines. The incidence embedding makes $\Omega $ Kähler. The degree-one blowdown, a fiber of $q$, and the isomorphism $q|_ E:E	o \mathbb P^1$ give \[  \int _ XL^2=\int _ XL\wedge Q=1,\quad Q^2=0,\quad L|_{TE}=0,\quad \int _ EQ=1.  \] Take $t=1$, $\alpha =L$, $\kappa _0=2L+Q$ and $\mu =\kappa _0^2/8$. With $r=1-s$, the core volumes are $V_ s=1+4r+3r^2$; in particular $V_0=8$ and $V=V_1=1$. Choose a nonconstant smooth function $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ supported away from $E$, and put \[  b= rac13\int _ X\chi L\wedge \kappa _0,\qquad f=\chi -b,\qquad B=(1+f/2)L.  \] Since $\int _ XL\wedge \kappa _0=3$, we have $|f|\leq 1$ and $\int _ XfL\wedge \kappa _0=0$. Thus $B\geq L/2$ and $B|_{TE}=0$, so the curve $C=E$ satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 26.11.1 . Where $\mathrm{d}\chi 
e 0$, the form $L$ is symplectic, and wedging with $L$ is injective on real one-forms in real dimension four. Hence $\mathrm{d}B=	frac 12\mathrm{d}f\wedge L
e 0$. At the endpoint $	heta _1=(2+f/2)L\geq 3L/2$, and $\lambda _\mu (L)=1$ by the closed nef formula; this gives the lower bound for $\lambda _\mu (	heta _1)$. Since $\kappa _0^2=8\mu $, the initial solution is $\gamma _0=\kappa _0$ with $u_0=0$. Therefore $D_\mu (\kappa _0)=\sqrt8$, $I_ B=3$, $\Delta _\mu (B)=3/\sqrt8$ and $U_\mu =11/\sqrt8$, so $\lambda _\mu (	heta _0)\leq 11/\sqrt8$. The cost identity and the lower bound at the endpoint give the asserted estimate for $\mathcal C$. title: 26.12 Subtraction on warped products
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.12 Subtraction on warped products The closed core in section 26.11 keeps the endpoint big. On a warped product, the subtraction cost can instead be computed all the way to an endpoint that is not big. Its rate is determined by two inverse moments of the fiber coefficient, while its total integral remains finite even when the endpoint volume vanishes. Let $(B,\alpha )$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $m\geq 2$, put $W=\int _ B\alpha ^ m$, and let $C$ be a connected compact complex curve. Fix smooth strictly positive probability forms $\sigma $ on $B$ and $w$ on $C$. On $X=B\times C$, of dimension $n=m+1$, use $\mu =\sigma \wedge w$ and omit pullbacks. For a smooth function $a\geq 0$ on $B$ and a real number $t>0$, set \[  \theta _ s=\alpha +(a+t-s)w\quad (s<t),\qquad \theta _ t=\alpha +aw.  \] The endpoint is semipositive, hence nef. For $\epsilon >0$, write \[  H(\epsilon )=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{a+\epsilon },\qquad J(\epsilon )=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{(a+\epsilon )^2},\qquad H(0)=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{a},  \] allowing $H(0)=+\infty $, with $1/a=+\infty $ at a zero of $a$. Theorem 26.12.1 . For $s<t$, the full Gauduchon infimum is attained by a balanced metric and \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ s)=\frac{nW}{H(t-s)},\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ t)=\frac{nW}{H(0)},  \] where the last value is zero if $H(0)=+\infty $. Every minimizing Gauduchon metric $g_ s$ at $s$ has the same subtraction cost 26.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:warped-subtraction-cost} \frac{\int _ Xw\wedge g_ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (g_ s)} =\mathcal C(s) :=n^{-(n-1)/n}W^{1/n} H(t-s)^{-(n+1)/n}J(t-s). \end{equation} For every selection of these metrics, the improper integral satisfies 26.72 \begin{equation} \label{eq:warped-improper-subtraction} \int _0^ t\mathcal C(s)\, \mathrm{d}s =\lambda _\mu (\theta _0)-\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)<\infty . \end{equation} Proof. Put $\epsilon =t-s$ and $L=a+\epsilon $. Apply theorem 9.1.1 on the closed positive base to obtain \[  A_\epsilon =\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _\epsilon >0,\qquad A_\epsilon ^ m=\frac{W}{H(\epsilon )}\frac{\sigma }{L}.  \] The target has total mass $W$, so closed Stokes fixes its scalar. The construction of theorem 26.5.10 , now without a normalization of $W$ or a nonconstancy requirement on $a$, gives \[  \Omega _\epsilon =A_\epsilon +Lw,\qquad \Omega _\epsilon ^ n=\frac{nW}{H(\epsilon )}\mu , \qquad \gamma _ s=L^{-1/m}\Omega _\epsilon .  \] Indeed, \[  \gamma _ s^ m=L^{-1}A_\epsilon ^ m +mA_\epsilon ^{m-1}\wedge w  \] is closed: its first summand has top degree on the base, and its second has closed factors. Thus $\gamma _ s$ is balanced. Gauduchon Stokes and the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality give \[  \int _ X\theta _ s\wedge \xi ^ m \geq \left(\frac{nW}{H(\epsilon )}\right)^{1/n}D_\mu (\xi )  \] for every Gauduchon metric $\xi $. The metric $\gamma _ s$ attains equality, with numerator $nW$ and denominator $(nW/H)^{m/n}H$. This proves the full volume formula. For every fixed test, its quotient at $\theta _ t+\epsilon w$ decreases to its quotient at $\theta _ t$. The two infima, over $\epsilon >0$ and over the tests, commute, as in theorem 26.10.1 . Hence the endpoint value is the limit of the strict values. Monotone convergence of $H(\epsilon )$ gives the asserted value, including when the integral is infinite. The cost numerator for the displayed balanced metric is $WJ/H$. Dividing by its denominator gives ( 26.71 ). Also $\mathrm{d}H(t-s)/\mathrm{d}s=J(t-s)$, so differentiation of the volume formula gives $-\mathrm{d}\lambda _\mu (\theta _ s)/\mathrm{d}s=\mathcal C(s)$. By proposition 26.2.2 this is the cost of every minimizing metric, regardless of the regularity of the selection. On each interval $[0,r]$ with $r<t$, integrate this identity. Since $\mathcal C\geq 0$ and the root volume has the finite endpoint limit just proved, letting $r\uparrow t$ gives ( 26.72 ). $\square$ The identity applies to every smooth nonnegative coefficient, including coefficients with flat zeros. Finite-order zeros give more precise rates. Fix a Riemannian metric on $B$ for the following distance comparisons. Proposition 26.12.2 . Suppose that $Z=\{ a=0\} $ is a nonempty smooth compact real submanifold of positive codimension $d$, that $a\asymp \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,Z)^ k$ in a fixed tube for a real number $k>0$, and that $a$ is bounded below by a positive constant outside that tube. Put $r=d/k$. Then, as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, 26.73 \begin{equation} \label{eq:warped-subtraction-profiles} \mathcal C(t-\epsilon )\asymp \begin{cases}  \epsilon ^{(1-r)/n-1},& r<1,\\  \epsilon ^{-1}(\log (1/\epsilon ))^{-(n+1)/n},& r=1,\\  \epsilon ^{r-2},& 1<r<2,\\  \log (1/\epsilon ),& r=2,\\  1,& r>2. \end{cases} \end{equation} Each rate is integrable, and the endpoint volume is positive exactly when $d>k$. For $r>2$, the cost tends to \[  n^{-(n-1)/n}W^{1/n}H(0)^{-(n+1)/n}J(0)>0, \qquad J(0)=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{a^2}.  \] For finitely many disjoint zero components satisfying these hypotheses with codimensions $d_ i$ and orders $k_ i$, the same assertions hold with $r=\min _ i d_ i/k_ i$. Proof. The positive density and the tubular Jacobians are bounded above and below by positive constants. For $p=1,2$, radial integration therefore gives \[  \int _ B\frac{\sigma }{(a+\epsilon )^ p} \asymp 1+\int _0^ R\frac{u^{d-1}}{(u^ k+\epsilon )^ p}\, \mathrm{d}u =1+\frac{\epsilon ^{r-p}}k \int _0^{R^ k/\epsilon }\frac{v^{r-1}}{(1+v)^ p}\, \mathrm{d}v,  \] with the equality applying to the radial expression. For $r<p$ the last integral tends to a finite positive constant; for $r=p$ it grows logarithmically; for $r>p$ the unregularized moment is finite, and monotone convergence gives its positive limit. Applying this to $H$ and $J$ in ( 26.71 ) proves the five rates and the criterion $H(0)<\infty $ exactly when $r>1$. The power $(1-r)/n-1$ exceeds $-1$ for $r<1$, as does $r-2$ for $1<r<2$. At $r=1$, substitution of $\log (1/\epsilon )$ gives an integrable tail because $(n+1)/n>1$. The logarithmic and bounded rates are also integrable. When $r>2$, both inverse moments have finite positive limits, which gives the displayed limit. With finitely many disjoint components, the moments are finite sums of positive tube contributions and a bounded complement term; their smallest ratio determines the divergence, without cancellation. $\square$ Proposition 26.12.3 . The endpoint $\theta _ t$ is big exactly when $a$ is positive everywhere. If $a$ has a zero, there is no decomposition \[  \theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\chi +\beta  \] with $f$ smooth and real, $\chi $ smooth and closed with nef class and $\int _ X\chi ^ n>0$, and $\beta \geq 0$ smooth. Proof. Suppose that $\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta (\alpha +w)$ for a quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$ and $\delta >0$. Pull back an arbitrary smooth nonnegative top-degree form $\zeta $ on $B$. It is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed by dimension, so Stokes' theorem for distributions gives \[  0\leq \int _ X(\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\delta (\alpha +w))\wedge \zeta =\int _ B(a-\delta )\zeta .  \] A nonzero $\zeta $ supported where $a<\delta $ contradicts this inequality. Thus a zero excludes every strict current representative; no singular potential has been restricted to its zero fiber. Conversely, if $a>0$ everywhere, compactness makes $\theta _ t$ itself Hermitian, so it is big. For a proposed decomposition, the closed nef-and-big criterion used in theorem 26.11.1 supplies a global quasi-plurisubharmonic $v$ with $\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \delta (\alpha +w)$ for some $\delta >0$. Then \[  \theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f+v)=\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+\beta \geq \delta (\alpha +w),  \] contradicting the first part. This excludes any such closed core, including after a smooth change of gauge. $\square$ In the closed case $a\equiv a_0\geq 0$, put $P=\alpha +(a_0+t)w$ and $Q=tw$. These closed nef forms satisfy 26.79 \begin{equation} \label{eq:warped-closed-morse} \int _ XP^ n-n\int _ XP^{n-1}\wedge Q =nWa_0=\mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ t). \end{equation} This is the expression on the right of the closed Morse inequality discussed in section 34.20 ; the equality follows from $w^2=0$, $\alpha ^{m+1}=0$ and $\int _ Cw=1$. For nonconstant $a$, the exterior derivative $\mathrm{d}\theta _ s=\mathrm{d}a\wedge w$ is not identically zero, and the endpoint formula retains the specified probability $\sigma $ through $H(0)$. The comparison in ( 26.79 ) therefore concerns the constant closed case. For example, take $B=\mathbb P^ m$, normalized Fubini–Study $\alpha $, $\sigma =\alpha ^ m$, and $a([Z])=\sum _{j=1}^ m|Z_ j|^2/\sum _{j=0}^ m|Z_ j|^2$. Its law under $\sigma $ is $m x^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}x$ on $[0,1]$, by the radial integration used in theorem 26.13.2 . Hence $W=1$, $H(0)=m/(m-1)$ and $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ t)=(m+1)(m-1)/m>0$, while the endpoint is not big and admits no closed nef core of positive top intersection. Its sole zero has real codimension $2m$ and order two. The cost is therefore logarithmic when $m=2$ and tends to a positive finite value when $m>2$, by proposition 26.12.2 .

title: 26.13 Positive volume without bigness
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.13 Positive volume without bigness By corollary 26.1.4 , every big background has positive volume. For a closed nef class on a compact Kähler manifold the converse also holds: the volume is then $\int _ X\theta ^ n$, and a closed nef class with positive top self-intersection is big. We now show that the converse fails for nonclosed nef backgrounds, even on a projective manifold: such a background can have positive volume without containing a Kähler current. In the example, the coefficient of a fiber direction vanishes at one point of the base. A radial potential on the base compensates for this vanishing, and the determinant of the resulting current bounds every Gauduchon quotient from below. Bigness, on the other hand, is excluded by pairing with a closed semipositive form concentrated near the vanishing point. Throughout this section fix an integer $m\geq 2$, and put $n=m+1$, $t=(m-1)/m$ and $B=\mathbb P^ m$. Give $B$ and $\mathbb P^1$ their Fubini–Study forms $\omega $ and $w$, normalized by $\int _ B\omega ^ m=\int _{\mathbb P^1}w=1$. On $B$ define \[  x([Z_0:\cdots :Z_ m])= \frac{\sum _{j=1}^ m|Z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ m|Z_ j|^2}, \qquad a=x/t,\qquad p=[1:0:\cdots :0].  \] Thus $x$ is a smooth function on $B$ with values in $[0,1]$; it vanishes only at $p$ and equals one on the hyperplane $\{ Z_0=0\} $. On $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$, with pullbacks understood, set \[  h=\omega +w,\qquad \mu =\omega ^ m\wedge w, \qquad \theta =\omega +a w.  \] For $\epsilon >0$ put 26.80 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-volume-normalization} H_\epsilon =m\int _0^1\frac{y^{m-1}}{y/t+\epsilon }\, \mathrm{d}y. \end{equation} Lemma 26.13.1 . There are smooth real functions $\varphi _\epsilon $ on $B$ such that $A_\epsilon =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _\epsilon >0$ and 26.81 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-volume-smooth-density} A_\epsilon ^ m=\frac{\omega ^ m}{H_\epsilon (a+\epsilon )}. \end{equation} As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ they converge uniformly to a bounded continuous function $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\omega )$ that is smooth on $B\setminus \{ p\} $. On $B\setminus \{ p\} $ the current $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a smooth strictly positive form satisfying 26.82 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-volume-endpoint-density} A^ m=a^{-1}\omega ^ m. \end{equation} Moreover $H_\epsilon \to 1$ as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Proof. In the affine chart $Z_0=1$, write $s=|z|^2$. Then $x=s/(1+s)$ and $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+s)$. Polar integration gives 26.83 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-volume-integration} \int _ B b(x)\omega ^ m=m\int _0^1 b(y)y^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}y \end{equation} for every integrable function $b$ on $[0,1]$, since the normalized radial density of $\omega ^ m$ in the variable $s$ is $m s^{m-1}(1+s)^{-m-1}\, \mathrm{d}s$. In particular $\int _ B a^{-1}\omega ^ m=mt/(m-1)=1$, and monotone convergence in ( 26.80 ) gives $H_\epsilon \to 1$. Define $q_\epsilon \geq 0$ and $\varphi _\epsilon $ on $[0,1]$ by \[  q_\epsilon (x)^ m=\frac m{H_\epsilon } \int _0^ x\frac{y^{m-1}}{y/t+\epsilon }\, \mathrm{d}y, \qquad \varphi _\epsilon (x)=\int _0^ x \frac{q_\epsilon (y)-y}{y(1-y)}\, \mathrm{d}y.  \] Near zero, \[  q_\epsilon (x)=x\left(\frac m{H_\epsilon } \int _0^1\frac{u^{m-1}}{xu/t+\epsilon }\, \mathrm{d}u\right)^{1/m},  \] so $q_\epsilon $ is $x$ times a smooth positive function; moreover $q_\epsilon (1)=1$. Hence both apparent singularities of $\varphi _\epsilon '$, at $0$ and at $1$, are removable, and $\varphi _\epsilon $ is smooth on $[0,1]$. Composing with the smooth function $x$ gives a smooth function on $B$, again denoted $\varphi _\epsilon $. To compute $A_\epsilon $, recall that for a local potential of the form $F(s)$, with $q=sF'(s)$, the complex Hessian has the tangential eigenvalue $q/s$, of multiplicity $m-1$, and the radial eigenvalue $\mathrm{d}q/\mathrm{d}s$. For $F_\epsilon =\log (1+s)+\varphi _\epsilon (x)$ one finds $sF_\epsilon '=q_\epsilon (x)$. Differentiating the integral defining $q_\epsilon $ shows that both eigenvalues are positive, also at $s=0$ by the smooth factorization above. Their product relative to the Fubini–Study determinant is \[  \frac{A_\epsilon ^ m}{\omega ^ m} =\frac{q_\epsilon ^{m-1}q_\epsilon '}{x^{m-1}} =\frac1{H_\epsilon (a+\epsilon )}.  \] At a point of the hyperplane $\{ Z_0=0\} $, the smooth form $A_\epsilon $ is semipositive, as a limit of the positive matrices in the affine chart. Since the determinant just computed extends there with a strictly positive value, every eigenvalue is positive. This proves strict positivity on all of $B$ and ( 26.81 ). We now pass to the limit. For $x>0$, $q_\epsilon (x)$ tends to $x^ t$. To bound $q_\epsilon $ uniformly, note that $q_\epsilon ^ m$ is the distribution function of the probability density $\frac{m}{H_\epsilon }\frac{y^{m-1}}{y/t+\epsilon }$ on $[0,1]$. Relative to the probability density $my^{m-1}$, this density has a decreasing weight; relative to $(m-1)y^{m-2}$, its weight is proportional to $y/(y+t\epsilon )$ and hence increasing. If one probability density on $[0,1]$ has a decreasing weight relative to another, its average weight on $[0,x]$ is at least one and its distribution function is the larger of the two; an increasing weight reverses the inequality. Consequently \[  x^ m\leq q_\epsilon (x)^ m\leq x^{m-1}, \qquad \text{that is,}\qquad x\leq q_\epsilon (x)\leq x^ t.  \] The function \[  \varphi (x)=\int _0^ x\frac{y^ t-y}{y(1-y)}\, \mathrm{d}y  \] is bounded and continuous on $[0,1]$, since $t>0$, and smooth on $(0,1]$; its derivative extends smoothly at one. The integrable function $(y^ t-y)/[y(1-y)]$ dominates the derivatives of the functions $\varphi _\epsilon $, so dominated convergence gives uniform convergence $\varphi _\epsilon \to \varphi $ on $B$. Distributional convergence shows that $A$ is a closed positive current. On each coordinate chart, a smooth local potential of $\omega $ plus $\varphi $ is a uniform limit of the corresponding plurisubharmonic functions built with $\varphi _\epsilon $, including at $p$. Hence $\varphi $ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic. Off $p$, the limit $q=x^ t$ gives \[  \frac{A^ m}{\omega ^ m} =\frac{(x^ t)^{m-1}t x^{t-1}}{x^{m-1}}=\frac tx=\frac1a.  \] Smoothness of $\varphi $ off $p$ and the same determinant argument at the hyperplane $\{ Z_0=0\} $ prove ( 26.82 ). $\square$ Theorem 26.13.2 . The background $\theta $ on $X$ is smooth, semipositive, nef and nonclosed. It is not big, but 26.84 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-positive-volume-nonbig} \lambda _\mu (\theta )=n^{1/n},\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=n. \end{equation} For $\theta _\epsilon =\omega +(a+\epsilon )w$, one has \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _\epsilon )=\frac n{H_\epsilon },  \] and the smooth positive metrics 26.85 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-volume-minimizing-metrics} \gamma _\epsilon =(a+\epsilon )^{-1/m} \bigl (A_\epsilon +(a+\epsilon )w\bigr ) \end{equation} are balanced and minimize the defining quotient at $\theta _\epsilon $. Proof. The coefficient $a$ is nonnegative, and $\theta +\eta h>0$ for every $\eta >0$; this proves semipositivity and nefness. Since $a$ is nonconstant, $\mathrm{d}\theta =\mathrm{d}a\wedge w\ne 0$. Suppose that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \delta h$ for a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $v$ and some $\delta >0$. Choose a nonzero smooth function $f\geq 0$ on $B$ supported in $\{ a<\delta \} $. Its pullback $S=f\omega ^ m$ is a smooth semipositive $(m,m)$-form, closed because it has top degree on the base. Positivity and distributional Stokes would give \[  0\leq \int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v-\delta h)\wedge S =\int _ B f(a-\delta )\omega ^ m<0.  \] This contradiction shows that $\theta $ is not big, since every Hermitian form on $X$ dominates a positive multiple of $h$. For the lower bound on the volume, pull back the bounded potential $\varphi $ of lemma 26.13.1 . The positive current $\Omega =A+a w=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a smooth strictly positive form off $Z=\{ p\} \times \mathbb P^1$, where \[  \Omega ^ n=n a A^ m\wedge w=n\mu .  \] Let $\gamma $ be a Gauduchon metric. Since $\varphi $ is bounded, distributional Stokes lets us replace $\theta $ by $\Omega $ in the numerator of its quotient. The set $Z$ has zero smooth volume and $\Omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is a positive measure, so the pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality off $Z$ gives \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq n^{1/n}\int _ X (\mu /\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n =n^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma ).  \] This lower bound holds for every test in definition 26.1.1 ; no power of the current $\Omega $ along $Z$ is needed. For the upper bound, put $c_\epsilon =n/H_\epsilon $ and $\Omega _\epsilon =A_\epsilon +(a+\epsilon )w=\theta _\epsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _\epsilon $. Then $\Omega _\epsilon ^ n=c_\epsilon \mu $. The metrics in ( 26.85 ) satisfy \[  T_\epsilon =\gamma _\epsilon ^ m =(a+\epsilon )^{-1}A_\epsilon ^ m +m A_\epsilon ^{m-1}\wedge w.  \] The first term has top degree on the base and the second is a product of closed forms, so $T_\epsilon $ is closed; that is, $\gamma _\epsilon $ is balanced, and in particular Gauduchon. Smooth Stokes and ( 26.83 ) give \[  \int _ X\theta _\epsilon \wedge T_\epsilon =c_\epsilon \int _ X(a+\epsilon )^{-1}\mu =n, \qquad D_\mu (\gamma _\epsilon )=c_\epsilon ^{m/n}H_\epsilon ,  \] so the quotient of $\gamma _\epsilon $ at $\theta _\epsilon $ equals $c_\epsilon ^{1/n}$. The same arithmetic–geometric mean argument, applied to the smooth representative $\Omega _\epsilon $, bounds every Gauduchon quotient at $\theta _\epsilon $ below by $c_\epsilon ^{1/n}$. This proves that $\gamma _\epsilon $ minimizes, and gives the formula for $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta _\epsilon )$. Since $\theta \leq \theta _\epsilon $, the metrics $\gamma _\epsilon $, used as tests for $\theta $, also give $\lambda _\mu (\theta )\leq c_\epsilon ^{1/n}$. Letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ proves ( 26.84 ). By theorem 26.10.1 , this value is also the limit of the volumes of the Hermitian perturbations $\theta +\epsilon h$. $\square$ The value $n$ refers to the probability measure $\mu $ fixed above, but positivity holds for every smooth positive probability measure by proposition 26.14.1 . Thus positive volume does not characterize bigness for nonclosed nef backgrounds, even on a projective manifold. The construction needs $m\geq 2$, so that $t>0$ and the endpoint potential is bounded; it says nothing about surfaces, or about closed nef classes on general compact complex manifolds.

title: 26.13.1 Volume tests and threshold tests
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.13.1 Volume tests and threshold tests Two quotients are formed from the same pairing $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$. The volume quotient divides it by the determinant integral $D_\mu (\gamma )$, whereas the linear threshold $\kappa _ h(\theta )$ of corollary 4.3.2 divides it by the trace $\int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$. This threshold is positive exactly when $\theta $ is big, and we call it the bigness threshold; for the pseudoeffective but nonbig background $\theta $ of theorem 26.13.2 it vanishes. The same metrics can approach both infima, but need not do so. In the radial model, the volume-minimizing metrics approach the bigness threshold only in dimension three, while a second family of smooth balanced metrics approaches it in every dimension by concentrating on the fiber over $p$. Keep the data of theorem 26.13.2 , and put \[  T_\epsilon =\gamma _\epsilon ^ m,\qquad I_\epsilon =\int _ B(a+\epsilon )^{-2}\omega ^ m, \qquad M_\epsilon =m+I_\epsilon /H_\epsilon , \qquad g_\epsilon =M_\epsilon ^{-1/m}\gamma _\epsilon .  \] Write $Z=\{ p\} \times \mathbb P^1$. Its integration current $[Z]$ satisfies $\int _ Zh=1$ and annihilates $\theta $, since $\theta |_ Z=a(p)w=0$. Proposition 26.13.3 . The metrics $g_\epsilon $ are balanced, satisfy $\int _ Xh\wedge g_\epsilon ^ m=1$, and 26.86 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-test-pairings} \int _ X\theta \wedge g_\epsilon ^ m =\frac{n-\epsilon I_\epsilon /H_\epsilon }{M_\epsilon }, \qquad D_\mu (g_\epsilon ) =\frac{(n/H_\epsilon )^{m/n}H_\epsilon }{M_\epsilon }. \end{equation} Their volume quotients tend to $n^{1/n}$ as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. If $n=3$, then $g_\epsilon ^2$ converges weakly to $[Z]$, and 26.87 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-threefold-test-collapse} \int _ X\theta \wedge g_\epsilon ^2 \sim \frac6{\log (1/\epsilon )}, \qquad D_\mu (g_\epsilon ) \sim \frac{2\, 3^{2/3}}{\log (1/\epsilon )}. \end{equation} If $n\geq 4$, put $M_0=m+(m-1)^2/[m(m-2)]$. Then \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge g_\epsilon ^ m\longrightarrow \frac n{M_0}>0, \qquad D_\mu (g_\epsilon )\longrightarrow \frac{n^{m/n}}{M_0}>0.  \] Thus this family approaches the bigness threshold, which is zero, exactly when $n=3$. Proof. By the power formula in the proof of theorem 26.13.2 and ( 26.81 ), \[  T_\epsilon =\frac{\omega ^ m}{H_\epsilon (a+\epsilon )^2} +mA_\epsilon ^{m-1}\wedge w.  \] Since $A_\epsilon $ is cohomologous to $\omega $, closed Stokes gives $\int _ B\omega \wedge A_\epsilon ^{m-1}=1$. Consequently the two terms have $h$-traces $I_\epsilon /H_\epsilon $ and $m$, which proves the trace normalization of $g_\epsilon ^ m=T_\epsilon /M_\epsilon $. Subtracting $\epsilon w$ from $\theta _\epsilon $ subtracts $\epsilon I_\epsilon /H_\epsilon $ from the pairing $\int _ X\theta _\epsilon \wedge T_\epsilon =n$. Rescaling $\gamma _\epsilon $ by $M_\epsilon ^{-1/m}$ divides both the linear pairing and $D_\mu $ by $M_\epsilon $, proving ( 26.86 ). Polar integration gives \[  I_\epsilon =m t^2\int _0^1 \frac{x^{m-1}}{(x+t\epsilon )^2}\, \mathrm{d}x.  \] When $m=2$, put $q=\epsilon /2$. Direct integration yields \[  I_\epsilon =\tfrac 12\left(\log \frac{1+q}{q} +\frac q{1+q}-1\right), \qquad H_\epsilon =1-q\log \frac{1+q}{q}.  \] Hence $I_\epsilon \sim \tfrac 12\log (1/\epsilon )$ and $\epsilon I_\epsilon \to 0$. Since $H_\epsilon \to 1$, the asymptotics in ( 26.87 ) follow from ( 26.86 ). For the weak limit when $n=3$, note that the mixed positive term $2A_\epsilon \wedge w$ has $h$-trace two; divided by $M_\epsilon \to \infty $, it tends weakly to zero. The horizontal probability measure \[  I_\epsilon ^{-1}(a+\epsilon )^{-2}\omega ^2  \] on $B$ concentrates at $p$: outside any fixed neighborhood of $p$ its unnormalized density stays bounded, while $I_\epsilon \to \infty $. For a smooth $(1,1)$-test form on $X$, integration along the fibers $\{ b\} \times \mathbb P^1$ gives a smooth function on $B$. The convergence of these probability measures to the Dirac mass at $p$ therefore shows that the horizontal term of $g_\epsilon ^2$ converges to $[Z]$, because its coefficient $I_\epsilon /(H_\epsilon M_\epsilon )$ tends to one. For $m\geq 3$, monotone convergence instead gives \[  I_\epsilon \longrightarrow m t^2\int _0^1x^{m-3}\, \mathrm{d}x =\frac{(m-1)^2}{m(m-2)}.  \] In both cases $\epsilon I_\epsilon \to 0$. Using $H_\epsilon \to 1$ in ( 26.86 ) proves the remaining limits, including that of the volume quotients. $\square$ For $n\geq 4$ the metrics $g_\epsilon $ still minimize the perturbed volumes, and their quotients converge to $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$, but their normalized pairings with $\theta $ stay bounded away from zero. This does not contradict nonbigness: the bigness threshold is approached by a different family. Proposition 26.13.4 . For every $n\geq 3$ there are smooth balanced metrics $b_\rho $, $0<\rho <1$, with \[  \int _ Xh\wedge b_\rho ^ m=1,\qquad b_\rho ^ m\rightharpoonup [Z],\qquad \int _ X\theta \wedge b_\rho ^ m\longrightarrow 0, \qquad D_\mu (b_\rho )\longrightarrow 0  \] as $\rho \downarrow 0$. Proof. Choose a nonzero smooth function $f_\rho \geq 0$ on $B$, supported in $\{ x<\rho \} $ and normalized by $\int _ Bf_\rho \omega ^ m=1$. The form 26.88 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-localized-test-form} \Gamma _\rho =\frac{f_\rho \omega ^ m+\rho h^ m}{1+n\rho } \end{equation} is smooth, strictly positive and closed: the first summand has top degree on the base, and $h$ is Kähler. The positive-root construction in the proof of theorem 4.3.1 gives a unique smooth metric $b_\rho $ with $b_\rho ^ m=\Gamma _\rho $, and $b_\rho $ is balanced because $\Gamma _\rho $ is closed. Since $\int _ Xh^{m+1}=n$, its $h$-trace is one. Put $C_\theta =\int _ X\theta \wedge h^ m$. Since $a<\rho /t$ on the support of $f_\rho $, \[  0\leq \int _ X\theta \wedge \Gamma _\rho \leq \frac{\rho /t+\rho C_\theta }{1+n\rho }\longrightarrow 0.  \] The lower bound in the proof of theorem 26.13.2 gives $D_\mu (b_\rho )\leq n^{-1/n}\int _ X\theta \wedge \Gamma _\rho $, so the determinant integrals also tend to zero. The probability measures $f_\rho \omega ^ m$ converge to the Dirac mass at $p$ because their supports shrink to that point. Fiber integration, as in the preceding proof, gives the current limit $[Z]$, while the term $\rho h^ m$ tends to zero. $\square$ Thus the normalized current $[Z]$ is a weak limit of smooth balanced metrics normalized by their $h$-traces. It annihilates $\theta $, and its determinant-weighted measure vanishes by proposition 26.20.2 . The two families give explicit instances of the separation between the volume and threshold denominators described in proposition 33.2.1 , without any general smoothing result for Gauduchon currents.

The convergence of these probability measures to the Dirac mass at $p$ therefore shows that the horizontal term of $g_\epsilon ^2$ converges to $[Z]$, because its coefficient $I_\epsilon /(H_\epsilon M_\epsilon )$ tends to one. For $m\geq 3$, monotone convergence instead gives \[  I_\epsilon \longrightarrow m t^2\int _0^1x^{m-3}\, \mathrm{d}x =\frac{(m-1)^2}{m(m-2)}.  \] In both cases $\epsilon I_\epsilon \to 0$. Using $H_\epsilon \to 1$ in ( 26.86 ) proves the remaining limits, including that of the volume quotients. $\square$

title: Proposition 26.13.4
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.13.4 . For every $n\geq 3$ there are smooth balanced metrics $b_\rho $, $0<\rho <1$, with \[  \int _ Xh\wedge b_\rho ^ m=1,\qquad b_\rho ^ m\rightharpoonup [Z],\qquad \int _ X\theta \wedge b_\rho ^ m\longrightarrow 0, \qquad D_\mu (b_\rho )\longrightarrow 0  \] as $\rho \downarrow 0$. Proof. Choose a nonzero smooth function $f_\rho \geq 0$ on $B$, supported in $\{ x<\rho \} $ and normalized by $\int _ Bf_\rho \omega ^ m=1$. The form 26.88 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-localized-test-form} \Gamma _\rho =\frac{f_\rho \omega ^ m+\rho h^ m}{1+n\rho } \end{equation} is smooth, strictly positive and closed: the first summand has top degree on the base, and $h$ is Kähler. The positive-root construction in the proof of theorem 4.3.1 gives a unique smooth metric $b_\rho $ with $b_\rho ^ m=\Gamma _\rho $, and $b_\rho $ is balanced because $\Gamma _\rho $ is closed. Since $\int _ Xh^{m+1}=n$, its $h$-trace is one. Put $C_\theta =\int _ X\theta \wedge h^ m$. Since $a<\rho /t$ on the support of $f_\rho $, \[  0\leq \int _ X\theta \wedge \Gamma _\rho \leq \frac{\rho /t+\rho C_\theta }{1+n\rho }\longrightarrow 0.  \] The lower bound in the proof of theorem 26.13.2 gives $D_\mu (b_\rho )\leq n^{-1/n}\int _ X\theta \wedge \Gamma _\rho $, so the determinant integrals also tend to zero. The probability measures $f_\rho \omega ^ m$ converge to the Dirac mass at $p$ because their supports shrink to that point. Fiber integration, as in the preceding proof, gives the current limit $[Z]$, while the term $\rho h^ m$ tends to zero. $\square$

title: 26.14 Varying the probability measure
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
26.14 Varying the probability measure From now on $X$ is again an arbitrary connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$. Changing the smooth positive probability measure $\mu $ multiplies each denominator $D_\mu (\gamma )$ by a factor bounded above and below independently of $\gamma $. The value of the volume may therefore change, but its vanishing and positivity do not. Moreover, every smooth strictly positive potential solves the normalized equation for a suitable measure. Consequently, on $\mathscr P$ the volume is independent of the measure exactly when the total Monge–Ampère mass is independent of the potential. Proposition 26.14.1 . For smooth positive probability measures $\mu ,
u $, choose constants $m,M>0$ such that $m\mu \leq 
u \leq M\mu $. Then for every pseudoeffective $	heta $, \[  M^{-1/n}\lambda _\mu (	heta ) \leq \lambda _
u (	heta ) \leq m^{-1/n}\lambda _\mu (	heta ).  \] In particular, whether $\lambda _\mu (	heta )$ vanishes does not depend on the smooth positive probability measure $\mu $. Proof. Since $D_
u (\gamma )=\int _ X(
u /\mu )^{1/n}(\mu /\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$, the inequalities $m\mu \leq 
u \leq M\mu $ give \[  m^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma )\leq D_
u (\gamma )\leq M^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma )  \] for every admissible metric $\gamma $. The numerators of the quotients are nonnegative and do not involve the measure. Dividing and taking infima proves the assertion. $\square$ Proposition 26.14.2 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$. The value $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is the same for all smooth positive probability measures $\mu $ if and only if \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n  \] is independent of the smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. Proof. For a smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$, put \[  M_ v=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n, \qquad \mu _ v= rac{(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n}{M_ v}.  \] Then $\mu _ v$ is a smooth positive probability measure, and $v$ solves the normalized equation for $\mu _ v$ with scalar $M_ v$. Uniqueness of the scalar and theorem 26.1.3 give $\mathcal V_{\mu _ v}(\omega )=M_ v$. Hence, if the volume does not depend on the measure, neither does the mass. Conversely, suppose that all these masses equal one constant $M$. For an arbitrary smooth positive probability measure $\mu $, integrating the normalized equation gives $c_\omega (\mu )=M$, so $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=M$ for every $\mu $. $\square$ For instance, the nonclosed torus metric of example 2.3.1 has volumes that depend on the measure. If $n=2$ and $\omega $ is Gauduchon, Stokes' theorem shows that the smooth masses are all equal to $\int _ X\omega ^2$, so $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=\int _ X\omega ^2$ for every $\mu $. On the Hopf threefold of chapter 8 , each $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is finite and positive, although the upper mass $v_+(\omega )$ is infinite.

title: Proposition 26.14.2
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.14.2 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$. The value $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is the same for all smooth positive probability measures $\mu $ if and only if \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n  \] is independent of the smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. Proof. For a smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$, put \[  M_ v=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n, \qquad \mu _ v=\frac{(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n}{M_ v}.  \] Then $\mu _ v$ is a smooth positive probability measure, and $v$ solves the normalized equation for $\mu _ v$ with scalar $M_ v$. title: 26.14.1 Upper and lower masses
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.14.1 Upper and lower masses As the probability measure varies, the smooth equation realizes the mass of every smooth strictly positive potential, by the proof of proposition 26.14.2 . The extrema of the volume over all measures are therefore the extrema of these masses, and regularization of bounded potentials identifies them with the lower and upper masses $v_-(\omega )$ and $v_+(\omega )$ of definition 6.5.1 . The infimum simplifies further: at each Gauduchon metric an explicit measure maximizes the denominator, and this removes the density from the formula entirely. Throughout this subsection $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$, and $\mathscr M$ denotes the set of smooth strictly positive probability measures on $X$. Theorem 26.14.3 . One has \[  \inf _{\mu \in \mathscr M}\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=v_-(\omega ), \qquad \sup _{\mu \in \mathscr M}\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=v_+(\omega ),  \] where the supremum may be infinite. Moreover, 26.89 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-lower-mass-formula} v_-(\omega )^{1/n} =\inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\displaystyle \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\displaystyle \left(\int _ X\gamma ^ n\right)^{(n-1)/n}}. \end{equation} Proof. For each $\mu \in \mathscr M$, the smooth normalized equation realizes $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ as the mass $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ of a smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. Conversely, every such potential realizes its mass as $\mathcal V_{\mu _ v}(\omega )$ for the measure $\mu _ v$ in the proof of proposition 26.14.2 . Thus the set of volumes $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$, $\mu \in \mathscr M$, coincides with the set of these smooth masses. It remains to show that the smooth masses have the same extrema as the masses of bounded potentials, which define $v_\pm (\omega )$. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty $, theorem 1.11.1 gives uniformly bounded smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u_ j$ decreasing to $u$. Their Monge–Ampère measures converge by the monotone continuity of bounded products, and so do their total masses, since $X$ is compact. Every bounded mass is therefore a limit of smooth strictly positive masses. Conversely, smooth potentials are bounded. This proves the first two identities; no uniform bound on the masses is needed. For the last formula, take $n$th roots and interchange the infima over $\mu $ and over $\gamma $ in theorem 26.1.3 . For a fixed Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, Hölder's inequality and $\int _ X\mu =1$ give \[  D_\mu (\gamma ) \leq \left(\int _ X\gamma ^ n\right)^{(n-1)/n},  \] with equality for the smooth probability measure $\mu =\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$. The numerator is positive and does not depend on $\mu $, so the infimum of the quotient over $\mu $ is obtained by maximizing the denominator. This gives ( 26.89 ). For $n=1$ both denominators equal one, and the same argument applies. $\square$ Thus $v_-(\omega )>0$ if and only if $\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ has a positive lower bound over all Gauduchon metrics $\gamma $ with $\int _ X\gamma ^ n=1$. This lower bound fails on the threefold constructed in theorem 26.18.1 . By corollary 14.26.4 , positivity of $v_-(\omega )$ is also equivalent to solvability, in the background $\omega $, of the normalized equation for every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure. In the same way, each individual volume $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is finite, while their supremum $v_+(\omega )$ can be infinite. Proposition 26.14.4 . The infimum in ( 26.89 ) is attained if and only if the infimum of the masses $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ over smooth functions $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$ is attained. For every such minimizing potential $v$, the metric $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon. Proof. Suppose that a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ attains the infimum in ( 26.89 ), and put $m=v_-(\omega )^{1/n}$. The numerator of its quotient is strictly positive, so $m>0$. For the measure $\mu _\gamma =\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$, equality holds in the Hölder inequality above, so the test $\gamma $ gives $\lambda _{\mu _\gamma }(\omega )\leq m$. Theorem 26.14.3 gives the opposite inequality. Hence the solution of the smooth equation for $\mu _\gamma $ has mass $m^ n=v_-(\omega )$, which gives a minimizing smooth potential. For $n\geq 2$, $\gamma $ also minimizes the quotient for $\mu _\gamma $, so by theorem 26.1.3 the solution form is conformal to $\gamma $. Since both have volume forms proportional to $\mu _\gamma $, the conformal factor is constant, and the solution metric is Gauduchon. Conversely, let $v$ be a smooth potential minimizing the mass. For every smooth real $f$, the potentials $v\pm tf$ are admissible for sufficiently small $t>0$. The vanishing of the first variation of the mass therefore gives \[  \int _ X f\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}\bigr )=0 \quad \hbox{for every smooth real }f.  \] Thus $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon. Taking $\gamma =\Omega $ in the quotient and using Stokes' theorem for the Gauduchon metric $\Omega $ gives \[  \frac{\int _ X\omega \wedge \Omega ^{n-1}}{(\int _ X\Omega ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}} =(\int _ X\Omega ^ n)^{1/n}=v_-(\omega )^{1/n},  \] so the infimum in ( 26.89 ) is attained. In dimension one all metrics are Gauduchon and all masses equal $\int _ X\omega $. $\square$ The infimum over densities also makes sense beyond the positive cone. For a pseudoeffective smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$, put \[  \lambda _*(\theta )= \inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{(\int _ X\gamma ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}}.  \] The Hölder argument above proves \[  \lambda _*(\theta )=\inf _{\mu \in \mathscr M}\lambda _\mu (\theta ).  \] Like each $\lambda _\mu $, the function $\lambda _*$ is finite, nonnegative, concave, positively homogeneous, and invariant under smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ changes of $\theta $. Suppose $\theta $ is nef, fix a Hermitian form $h$, and for real $\epsilon >0$ choose a Hermitian representative $\omega _\epsilon $ of $\theta +\epsilon h$. Interchanging the infima over the test metric and over $\epsilon >0$, as in theorem 26.10.1 , gives \[  \lambda _*(\theta ) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}\lambda _*(\theta +\epsilon h) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}v_-(\omega _\epsilon )^{1/n}.  \] By gauge invariance, the last expression does not depend on the choice of representatives. This extends the lower-mass formula to the nef boundary. We do not compare $\lambda _*$ with other notions of lower volume for singular classes.

text: Proposition 26.14.4 . The infimum in ( 26.89 ) is attained if and only if the infimum of the masses $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ over smooth functions $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$ is attained. For every such minimizing potential $v$, the metric $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon. Proof. Suppose that a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ attains the infimum in ( 26.89 ), and put $m=v_-(\omega )^{1/n}$. The numerator of its quotient is strictly positive, so $m>0$. For the measure $\mu _\gamma =\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$, equality holds in the Hölder inequality above, so the test $\gamma $ gives $\lambda _{\mu _\gamma }(\omega )\leq m$. Theorem 26.14.3 gives the opposite inequality. Hence the solution of the smooth equation for $\mu _\gamma $ has mass $m^ n=v_-(\omega )$, which gives a minimizing smooth potential. For $n\geq 2$, $\gamma $ also minimizes the quotient for $\mu _\gamma $, so by theorem 26.1.3 the solution form is conformal to $\gamma $. Since both have volume forms proportional to $\mu _\gamma $, the conformal factor is constant, and the solution metric is Gauduchon. Conversely, let $v$ be a smooth potential minimizing the mass.
