In dimension one all metrics are Gauduchon and all masses equal $\int _ X\omega $. $\square$

title: 26.15 Curvature conditions for mass extrema
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.15 Curvature conditions for mass extrema We now ask when the lower and upper masses are attained by smooth potentials. At a smooth local extremum of the mass, the first variation forces the metric $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ to be Gauduchon, and the second variation gives a sign for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})$. On a threefold these necessary conditions are also sufficient, because the mass is then a polynomial of degree two in the variation. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $, and recall from chapter 2 the set $\mathcal H_\omega $ of smooth real functions $u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ and the mass functional $\mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$. For $n\geq 2$, theorem 2.2.2 , proposition 26.14.2 give the differential conditions under which $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is independent of the smooth positive probability measure $\mu $. By proposition 15.6.2 , the same conditions characterize when the difference $H_0-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}$ considered there is constant on probability measures of finite entropy, for a fixed smooth positive probability volume $\mathrm{d}V$; it suffices to test smooth positive probability measures. In dimension one the mass is always $\int _ X\omega $, so both conclusions hold automatically. Recall that a smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $T$ is nonnegative, written $T\geq 0$, if $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge \bar\alpha \wedge T\geq 0$ for every $(1,0)$-covector $\alpha $; in this bidegree this is the usual notion of positivity. The second variation of the mass produces integrals of the form $\int _ X\mathrm df\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge T$, and the following elementary lemma shows that their signs detect the sign of $T$. Lemma 26.15.1 . Suppose a smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $T$ satisfies \[  \int _ X \mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge T\geq 0 \quad \hbox{for every smooth real }f.  \] Then $T\geq 0$. Proof. Suppose instead that $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge \bar\alpha \wedge T<0$ at a point $x_0$ for some $(1,0)$-covector $\alpha $. Every $(1,0)$-covector is the $(1,0)$-part of a real covector, so we can choose a real linear function $\ell $ in local real coordinates around $x_0$ whose differential has $(1,0)$-part $\alpha $ at $x_0$. Then $\mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell $ is a positive multiple of $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge \bar\alpha $ at $x_0$, and after shrinking the coordinate ball, $\mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell \wedge T$ is strictly negative on it. Choose a nonzero smooth cutoff function $\chi $ supported in this ball and, for positive integers $k$, set \[  f_ k=k^{-1}\chi \sin (k\ell ),  \] extended by zero to $X$. Since $\mathrm{d}\ell $ is a constant nonzero covector in these coordinates, \[  \mathrm{d}f_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f_ k =\chi ^2\cos ^2(k\ell )\, \mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell +O(k^{-1}),  \] where $k$ times the remainder has uniformly bounded coefficients. In $\cos ^2(k\ell )=(1+\cos (2k\ell ))/2$, the oscillatory part contributes integrals tending to zero, as one sees by integrating by parts in a coordinate direction in which $\ell $ has nonzero derivative. Hence \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }\int _ X\mathrm{d}f_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f_ k\wedge T =\frac12\int _ X\chi ^2\mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell \wedge T<0,  \] which contradicts the hypothesis. $\square$ Proposition 26.15.2 . Let $n\geq 3$, and let $v\in \mathcal H_\omega $ be a local minimum of $\mathrm M_\omega $ for the $C^2$ topology. Then $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-1})=0, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})\leq 0.  \] At a local maximum the first condition still holds and the second inequality is reversed. Proof. For every smooth real $f$, the potentials $v+tf$ lie in $\mathcal H_\omega $ for all sufficiently small $|t|$. The vanishing of the first variation therefore gives the Gauduchon condition. The second variation is \[  \begin{aligned}  \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\right|_{t=0}\mathrm M_\omega (v+tf) & =n(n-1)\int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^2\wedge \Omega ^{n-2}\\ & =-n(n-1)\int _ X\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2}), \end{aligned}  \] where the last equality follows by integrating by parts twice, using that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})$ is both $\mathrm{d}$-closed and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. At a local minimum this second variation is nonnegative for every $f$, and lemma 26.15.1 , applied to $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})$, gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})\leq 0$. The case of a maximum is identical, with the opposite sign. $\square$ In dimension three these necessary conditions are also sufficient, and every local extremum is global. Theorem 26.15.3 . Assume $n=3$ and $v\in \mathcal H_\omega $. The following are equivalent: $v$ is a local minimum of $\mathrm M_\omega $; $v$ is a global minimum of $\mathrm M_\omega $ on $\mathcal H_\omega $; $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$. In this case $v_-(\omega )=\int _ X\Omega ^3$, and the infimum in ( 26.89 ) is attained. The corresponding statements for maxima hold with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \geq 0$, and then $v_+(\omega )=\int _ X\Omega ^3<+\infty $. Proof. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $, the preceding proposition shows that the first condition implies the third. Conversely, if $\Omega $ is Gauduchon, expanding the cube and integrating by parts gives, for every smooth real $f$, 26.92 \begin{equation} \label{eq:threefold-mass-dirichlet} \int _ X(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^3-\int _ X\Omega ^3 =-3\int _ X\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega . \end{equation} The form $\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f$ is nonnegative, so the right side is nonnegative if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$; then $v$ is a global minimum, and in particular a local one. By theorem 26.14.3 , regularization identifies the infimum of the masses of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials with $v_-(\omega )$, and proposition 26.14.4 proves attainment in ( 26.89 ). Reversing the sign in the same identity proves the statements for maxima, including the equality of $\int _ X\Omega ^3$ with the supremum over bounded potentials. $\square$ These conditions characterize smooth minimizers when they exist; neither argument produces a Gauduchon metric of the form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ in an arbitrary background. For the Hopf metric $\omega $ and the pulled-back Fubini–Study form $\alpha $ of chapter 8 , one has $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\alpha ^2\leq 0$, and $\omega $ is Gauduchon. Thus the minimum of the mass is attained by the constant potential and equals $6$, while the upper mass is infinite. On a surface, by contrast, the mass $\int _ X\omega ^2+2\int _ Xv\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ is affine in the potential, so a local extremum exists precisely when $\omega $ is Gauduchon, and then all masses are equal. In dimension $n\geq 4$ the sign condition of proposition 26.15.2 does not control the terms of order three and higher in the mass polynomial, and the argument above does not show that the conditions are sufficient.

title: Lemma 26.15.1
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Lemma 26.15.1 . Suppose a smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $T$ satisfies \[  \int _ X \mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge T\geq 0 \quad \hbox{for every smooth real }f.  \] Then $T\geq 0$. Proof. Suppose instead that $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge \bar\alpha \wedge T<0$ at a point $x_0$ for some $(1,0)$-covector $\alpha $. Every $(1,0)$-covector is the $(1,0)$-part of a real covector, so we can choose a real linear function $\ell $ in local real coordinates around $x_0$ whose differential has $(1,0)$-part $\alpha $ at $x_0$. Then $\mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell $ is a positive multiple of $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge \bar\alpha $ at $x_0$, and after shrinking the coordinate ball, $\mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell \wedge T$ is strictly negative on it. Choose a nonzero smooth cutoff function $\chi $ supported in this ball and, for positive integers $k$, set \[  f_ k=k^{-1}\chi \sin (k\ell ),  \] extended by zero to $X$. Since $\mathrm{d}\ell $ is a constant nonzero covector in these coordinates, \[  \mathrm{d}f_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f_ k =\chi ^2\cos ^2(k\ell )\, \mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell +O(k^{-1}),  \] where $k$ times the remainder has uniformly bounded coefficients. In $\cos ^2(k\ell )=(1+\cos (2k\ell ))/2$, the oscillatory part contributes integrals tending to zero, as one sees by integrating by parts in a coordinate direction in which $\ell $ has nonzero derivative. Hence \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }\int _ X\mathrm{d}f_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f_ k\wedge T =\frac12\int _ X\chi ^2\mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell \wedge T<0,  \] which contradicts the hypothesis. $\square$

title: Proposition 26.15.2
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.15.2 . Let $n\geq 3$, and let $v\in \mathcal H_\omega $ be a local minimum of $\mathrm M_\omega $ for the $C^2$ topology. Then $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-1})=0, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})\leq 0.  \] At a local maximum the first condition still holds and the second inequality is reversed. Proof. For every smooth real $f$, the potentials $v+tf$ lie in $\mathcal H_\omega $ for all sufficiently small $|t|$. The vanishing of the first variation therefore gives the Gauduchon condition. The second variation is \[  \begin{aligned}  \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\right|_{t=0}\mathrm M_\omega (v+tf) & =n(n-1)\int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^2\wedge \Omega ^{n-2}\\ & =-n(n-1)\int _ X\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2}), \end{aligned}  \] where the last equality follows by integrating by parts twice, using that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})$ is both $\mathrm{d}$-closed and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. At a local minimum this second variation is nonnegative for every $f$, and lemma 26.15.1 , applied to $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})$, gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})\leq 0$. The case of a maximum is identical, with the opposite sign. $\square$

title: Theorem 26.15.3
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 26.15.3 . Assume $n=3$ and $v\in \mathcal H_\omega $. The following are equivalent: $v$ is a local minimum of $\mathrm M_\omega $; $v$ is a global minimum of $\mathrm M_\omega $ on $\mathcal H_\omega $; $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$. In this case $v_-(\omega )=\int _ X\Omega ^3$, and the infimum in ( 26.89 ) is attained. The corresponding statements for maxima hold with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \geq 0$, and then $v_+(\omega )=\int _ X\Omega ^3<+\infty $. Proof. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $, the preceding proposition shows that the first condition implies the third. Conversely, if $\Omega $ is Gauduchon, expanding the cube and integrating by parts gives, for every smooth real $f$, 26.92 \begin{equation} \label{eq:threefold-mass-dirichlet} \int _ X(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^3-\int _ X\Omega ^3 =-3\int _ X\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega . \end{equation} The form $\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f$ is nonnegative, so the right side is nonnegative if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$; then $v$ is a global minimum, and in particular a local one. By theorem 26.14.3 , regularization identifies the infimum of the masses of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials with $v_-(\omega )$, and proposition 26.14.4 proves attainment in ( 26.89 ). Reversing the sign in the same identity proves the statements for maxima, including the equality of $\int _ X\Omega ^3$ with the supremum over bounded potentials. $\square$

title: 26.16 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
search_title: Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.16 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass On a threefold, the lower mass can be bounded below by a curvature condition. Consider a principal elliptic bundle over a Kähler surface, with a connection form $\eta $ whose curvature has real and imaginary parts $\alpha $ and $\beta $. If $\alpha ^2+\beta ^2$ is semipositive, the split metric $g$ built from the base metric and $\eta $ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\leq 0$. A cubic energy identity for bounded potentials then shows that no bounded potential has mass below $\int _ Xg^3$, and the determinant estimate of theorem 26.8.2 transfers this lower bound to every Hermitian form on the manifold. The same curvature sign excludes pluriclosed metrics on these manifolds. In this section $X$ is a connected compact complex threefold and $\mathrm dV$ is a smooth positive probability volume form. Products of bounded potentials are those of proposition 1.7.1 . For a Hermitian form $h$, $\mathscr G_ h$ denotes the compact convex set of normalized Gauduchon currents of section 4.4 , and $k_ T$ is the determinant density of $T\in \mathscr G_ h$ relative to $\mathrm dV$, as in theorem 26.8.1 .

title: 26.16.1 The bounded cubic identity
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.16.1 The bounded cubic identity When the square of a Hermitian metric $g$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, the mass of a bounded $g$-plurisubharmonic function differs from $\int _ Xg^3$ by a term that is linear in $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$. Its coefficient is a positive current playing the role of $\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u$. Lemma 26.16.1 . Let $g$ be a Hermitian form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,g)$ be bounded. The current \[  E_ u=\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)-u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u  \] is positive, and 26.93 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-cubic-energy} \int _ X(g+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =\int _ Xg^3-3\int _ XE_ u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g. \end{equation} If $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq 0$, then $v_-(g)=\int _ Xg^3$. Proof. Locally write $u=p-a$, with $p$ bounded plurisubharmonic and $a$ smooth. Expanding in $p$ and $a$ and using multilinearity, we obtain closed currents $C_ r=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ r$, not necessarily positive, with $C_0=1$. The recursive definition of bounded products, expanded in the same way, gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uC_ r)=C_{r+1},\qquad r=0,1,2.  \] By lemma 1.6.2 and invariance under smooth corrections, the weighted product $u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ does not depend on the local decomposition. On a smaller ball choose smooth bounded plurisubharmonic $p_ j$ decreasing to $p$, and put $u_ j=p_ j-a$. The same lemma gives $u_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, while boundedness gives $u_ j^2\to u^2$ in $L^1$. Hence \[  \mathrm du_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u_ j =\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^2)-u_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\longrightarrow E_ u.  \] The smooth currents on the left are positive, so their weak limit $E_ u$ is positive and has order zero. Now expand the cube. Repeated use of distributional Stokes gives \[  \int _ XC_3=0,\qquad \int _ Xg^2\wedge C_1=\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0, \qquad \int _ Xg\wedge C_2=\int _ XuC_1\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g.  \] Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ is closed, $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=0$, so the last integral equals $-\int _ XE_ u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$. This proves ( 26.93 ). If $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq 0$, the correction term is nonnegative, and $u=0$ attains the lower bound $\int _ Xg^3$. $\square$ Lemma 26.16.2 . Let $g,h$ be Hermitian forms with $v_-(g)=V>0$ and $h\geq c g$ for some $c>0$. Then 26.94 \begin{equation} \label{eq:determinant-background-transport} \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h}\| k_ T\| _{L^{3/2}(\mathrm dV)} \leq c^{-1}V^{-1/3},\qquad v_-(h)\geq c^3V. \end{equation} Proof. We first check that the determinant measure in ( 26.39 ) does not depend on the Hermitian form used to express it. Let $T$ be a positive $(2,2)$-current, and let $\sigma _ h=h\wedge T$ and $P=P_ h$ be its trace measure and coefficient matrix relative to $h$, as in section 26.6 . In an $h$-unitary frame let $G$ be the matrix of $g$, and set \[  a=\tfrac 13\operatorname {tr}(GP),\qquad \sigma _ g=a\sigma _ h,\qquad P_ g=a^{-1}G^{1/2}PG^{1/2}.  \] Comparing the defining trace pairings shows that $\sigma _ g=g\wedge T$ and $P_ g$ are the trace measure and coefficient matrix of $T$ relative to $g$, with $\operatorname {tr}P_ g=3$. Since $G>0$ and $\operatorname {tr}P=3$, one has $a>0$ even where $P$ is singular. Moreover $\det P_ g=a^{-3}\det G\det P$ and $g^3=\det G\, h^3$, so the factors $a$ and $\det G$ cancel in $\Gamma _0(T)$. The calculation applies to the matrix density on the whole trace measure, including its singular part. For $T\in \mathscr G_ h$ put $m=\int _ Xg\wedge T$. Then $0<m\leq c^{-1}$ and $U=T/m\in \mathscr G_ g$. By homogeneity, $k_ T=m k_ U$. Applying theorem 26.8.2 to $g$ gives the norm bound, and applying it again to $h$ gives the lower-mass bound. The supremum here is taken over all of $\mathscr G_ h$, including singular and degenerate currents. $\square$

title: 26.16.2 The curvature criterion
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.16.2 The curvature criterion We now describe threefolds on which the hypotheses of lemma 26.16.1 hold. Let $\pi :X\to B$ be a holomorphic principal elliptic bundle over a compact connected Kähler surface $(B,\omega )$, with fiber the elliptic curve $E=\mathbb C/\Lambda $ and fiber coordinate $z$. Assume that there is a smooth $(1,0)$-form $\eta $ on $X$, invariant under the action of $E$ and restricting to $\mathrm dz$ on every fiber, such that \[  \mathrm d\eta =\pi ^*F,\qquad F=\alpha +\mathrm i\beta ,  \] where $\alpha ,\beta $ are smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms on $B$. Put \[  Q=\alpha ^2+\beta ^2,\qquad e=\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta , \qquad g=\pi ^*\omega +s e,\quad s>0, \qquad A_ E=\int _ E\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\bar z.  \] We call $g$ the split metric. Theorem 26.16.3 . Suppose $Q\geq 0$ and $Q\not\equiv 0$. The split form $g$ is Hermitian, and its lower mass is 26.95 \begin{equation} \label{eq:elliptic-curvature-lower-mass} v_-(g)=V=3sA_ E\int _ B\omega ^2. \end{equation} Every bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,g)$ satisfies \[  \int _ X(g+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =V+\frac{3s}{2\pi }\int _ XE_ u\wedge \pi ^*Q\geq V.  \] Every Hermitian form $h\geq c g$, with $c>0$, satisfies ( 26.94 ). Thus the endpoint estimate of theorem 26.8.2 holds for every Hermitian form on $X$, with a constant depending on the form. The manifold $X$ admits no pluriclosed Hermitian metric. Proof. We suppress pullbacks in the curvature calculation. Comparing types in $\mathrm d\eta =F$ gives $\partial \eta =0$, $\bar\partial \eta =F$, $\partial \bar\eta =\bar F$ and $\bar\partial \bar\eta =0$. Hence \[  \partial e=-\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar F,\qquad \bar\partial e=\mathrm iF\wedge \bar\eta , \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}e=-\frac1{2\pi }F\wedge \bar F=-\frac1{2\pi }Q.  \] Since $e^2=0$ and the base has dimension two, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=-\frac{s}{2\pi }\pi ^*Q,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=-\frac{s}{\pi }\pi ^*(\omega \wedge Q)=0, \qquad g^3=3s\pi ^*(\omega ^2)\wedge e.  \] The form $g$ is positive, because $\pi ^*\omega $ is positive on directions transverse to the fibers and $e$ is positive on the vertical line. Fiber integration of $g^3$ gives $V$, and lemma 26.16.1 , lemma 26.16.2 give the mass identity and the endpoint bound. By compactness, every Hermitian form $h$ satisfies $h\geq cg$ for some $c>0$. Finally, $S=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ is smooth, semipositive and not identically zero. If a Hermitian form $b$ were pluriclosed, Stokes' theorem would give \[  0=\int _ Xg\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b =\int _ Xb\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=-\int _ Xb\wedge S<0,  \] where the last inequality holds because $b$ is strictly positive and $S$ is semipositive and nonzero on an open set. $\square$ Proposition 26.16.4 . The split metric $g$ is balanced if and only if $\omega \wedge \alpha =\omega \wedge \beta =0$. For such a primitive pair one has $Q\leq 0$, with strict inequality wherever the pair is nonzero. In particular, a balanced split metric never satisfies the hypothesis $Q\geq 0$, $Q\not\equiv 0$ of theorem 26.16.3 . Proof. One has $\mathrm d(g^2)=2s\pi ^*\omega \wedge \mathrm de$, and $\mathrm de$ has one component containing $\eta $ and one containing $\bar\eta $. These two vertical types are independent, so $\mathrm d(g^2)=0$ if and only if $\omega \wedge F=0$, which is equivalent to the two stated real identities. A primitive real $(1,1)$-form on a surface has eigenvalues $\lambda ,-\lambda $ in an $\omega $-unitary frame, so its square is $-\lambda ^2\omega ^2$. Applying this to $\alpha $ and to $\beta $ gives the sign of $Q$. In this case $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq 0$, so ( 26.93 ) bounds the masses of bounded potentials from above rather than from below, and gives no information on the lower mass. $\square$

title: 26.16.3 Negative-line-bundle quotients
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.16.3 Negative-line-bundle quotients The simplest examples of the curvature criterion come from negative line bundles. Dividing the complement of the zero section of a negative line bundle over $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$ by a dilation produces a principal elliptic bundle, and the logarithm of the fiber norm gives a connection form whose curvature is a multiple of a Kähler form on the base. Take $B=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, let $\omega _1,\omega _2$ be the pullbacks of the Fubini–Study forms of the two factors, normalized to have integral one, and put \[  \begin{gathered} \Omega =a\omega _1+b\omega _2,\quad a,b\in \mathbb N_{>0},\qquad L=\mathcal O(-a,-b),\\ X=L^\times /\langle v\mapsto \rho v\rangle ,\quad 0<\rho <1, \end{gathered}  \] where $L^\times $ is the total space of $L$ with the zero section removed. Equip $L$ with the Hermitian norm induced by the standard norms on the tautological bundles of the two factors. Let $r=\log \| v\| ^2$ and set $\eta =\partial r$. Proposition 26.16.5 . The quotient $X$ is a compact complex threefold, and the projection to $B$ is a principal elliptic fibration. For $g=\pi ^*\Omega +s\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta $, $s>0$, 26.96 \begin{equation} \label{eq:elliptic-line-lower-mass} v_-(g)=24\pi s ab\log (1/\rho ). \end{equation} Every Hermitian form on $X$ satisfies the endpoint bound of theorem 26.16.3 over its full set of normalized Gauduchon currents. The manifold has $H^2(X,\mathbb R)\ne 0$ and admits no balanced or pluriclosed metric. In particular, it is not diffeomorphic to a Hopf threefold $(\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \lambda z\rangle $, $0<|\lambda |<1$. Proof. In product coordinates, the squared norm of the standard local frame of $L$ is $(1+|z_1|^2)^ a(1+|z_2|^2)^ b$. Therefore \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=\pi ^*\Omega ,\qquad \mathrm d\eta =2\pi \mathrm i\pi ^*\Omega .  \] Dilation changes $r$ by a constant, so $\eta $ descends to $X$. The function $r$ changes by the nonzero constant $\log \rho ^2$ under the generator, so the action is free and properly discontinuous; the unit circle bundle, which is compact, times a fundamental interval for $r$ maps onto $X$, which is therefore compact. Each fiber is $\mathbb C^*/\rho ^{\mathbb Z}$. title: 26.16.4 A Calabi–Eckmann family without LCK metrics
search_title: A Calabi–Eckmann family without LCK metrics
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.16.4 A Calabi–Eckmann family without LCK metrics A Hermitian metric $\Omega $ is locally conformally Kähler , or LCK, if $\mathrm d\Omega =\vartheta \wedge \Omega $ for a closed real one-form $\vartheta $, its Lee form; such metrics are studied in chapter 29 . The quotients of the preceding subsection resemble Hopf manifolds. A second family shows that the curvature criterion also applies on manifolds that carry no LCK metric at all. Let $\tau =A+\mathrm iB_0$, where $A<0$ and $B_0>0$, and let $\mathbb C$ act holomorphically on $(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )^2$ by \[  t\cdot (z,w)=(\mathrm e^ t z,\mathrm e^{\tau t}w).  \] Write $X_\tau $ for the quotient and put $r_1=\log |z|^2$, $r_2=\log |w|^2$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto ([z],[w])$ descends to a projection $\pi :X_\tau \to \mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$; let $\omega _1,\omega _2$ be the pullbacks to the base of the Fubini–Study forms of the two factors, normalized to have integral one. Proposition 26.16.6 . The quotient $X_\tau $ is a compact complex threefold diffeomorphic to $S^3\times S^3$, and $\pi $ is a principal elliptic fibration over $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$. The form $\eta =\tau \partial r_1-\partial r_2$ descends to $X_\tau $, and for \[  g=\pi ^*(\omega _1+\omega _2)+s\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta , \qquad s>0,  \] one has 26.97 \begin{equation} \label{eq:calabi-eckmann-lower-mass} v_-(g)=48\pi ^2sB_0. \end{equation} Every Hermitian form $h\geq c g$, with $c>0$, satisfies \[  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h}\| k_ T\| _{L^{3/2}(\mathrm dV)} \leq c^{-1}(48\pi ^2sB_0)^{-1/3}.  \] There is no balanced, pluriclosed or LCK metric on $X_\tau $. Proof. Every orbit contains a unique point with $|z|=|w|=1$: the required parameter is determined by \[  \operatorname {Re}t=-r_1/2,\qquad \operatorname {Im}t=(r_2-Ar_1)/(2B_0).  \] These smooth formulas identify $(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )^2$ with $\mathbb C\times (S^3\times S^3)$, so the action is free and proper, and $X_\tau $ is diffeomorphic to $S^3\times S^3$. To obtain holomorphic charts, choose a nonzero coordinate $z_ k$ of $z$ and a branch of its logarithm, and use the action to normalize $z_ k=1$; the functions $z_ l/z_ k$, $l\ne k$, and $w_ jz_ k^{-\tau }$ are then local holomorphic coordinates on the quotient. Changing the branch of the logarithm accounts for the periods along the fibers. Thus $X_\tau $ is a compact complex threefold. The invariant form $\eta $ vanishes on the generator $z\partial _ z+\tau w\partial _ w$ of the action, so it descends. On an elliptic fiber it equals $\mathrm d\chi $, where $\chi =\tau \log v_1-\log v_2$ in terms of fiber coordinates $(v_1z,v_2w)$; its period lattice is generated by $2\pi \mathrm i\tau $ and $-2\pi \mathrm i$. Hence $A_ E=8\pi ^2B_0$. Direct differentiation gives \[  \begin{aligned}  F& =2\pi \mathrm i(\tau \omega _1-\omega _2),&  \alpha & =-2\pi B_0\omega _1,\\  \beta & =2\pi (A\omega _1-\omega _2),&  Q& =-8\pi ^2A\, \omega _1\wedge \omega _2>0. \end{aligned}  \] Since $\int _ B(\omega _1+\omega _2)^2=2$, theorem 26.16.3 gives the lower mass, the endpoint bound and the absence of pluriclosed metrics. Moreover $\mathrm d\operatorname {Re}\eta =-2\pi B_0\pi ^*\omega _1$. This nonzero semipositive exact form excludes every balanced metric by the Stokes argument at the end of the preceding proof, and hence also every Kähler metric. The quotient is simply connected, so the Lee form of a hypothetical LCK metric would be exact, equal to $\mathrm df$; multiplying the metric by $\mathrm e^{-f}$ would then give a Kähler metric, a contradiction. In particular $X_\tau $ carries no Vaisman metric, that is, no LCK metric with parallel Lee form. $\square$ The curvature criterion controls bounded potentials and the full set of normalized Gauduchon currents in these threefolds. Curvature pairs of changing sign, primitive curvature pairs and higher-dimensional analogues are not covered by this argument.

title: 26.17 Geometric bounds and determinant concentration
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.17 Geometric bounds and determinant concentration By theorem 26.8.2 , the determinant densities of all normalized Gauduchon currents are bounded in the critical space $L^{n/(n-1)}$ exactly when the lower mass is positive. Together with the mass-invariance criterion of theorem 2.2.2 , this gives geometric sufficient conditions for the critical bound. The critical exponent cannot be raised, even for currents that are powers of Kähler forms in one fixed class. The same concentrating family shows that currents approaching the maximum of the determinant functional for a fixed smooth density need not satisfy any uniform higher integrability, although the maximizer itself is smooth. Throughout this section $n\geq 2$ and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a smooth positive probability volume form. For a Hermitian form $h$, $k_ T$ denotes the determinant density relative to $\mathrm{d}V$ of a current $T\in \mathscr G_ h$, as in section 26.8 . Put $q=n/(n-1)$. Corollary 26.17.1 . Suppose $g$ is a Hermitian form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$, and put $V_ g=\int _ Xg^ n$. For every Hermitian form $h\geq cg$, $c>0$, \[  v_-(h)\geq c^ nV_ g,\qquad \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h}\| k_ T\| _{L^ q(\mathrm{d}V)} \leq c^{-1}V_ g^{-1/n}.  \] Equality holds in the determinant bound when $h=g$ and $c=1$. In particular, on a compact Kähler manifold or a compact complex surface, the critical norm is uniformly bounded over the normalized Gauduchon currents of each fixed Hermitian form. Proof. The identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=2g\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g+2\mathrm{d}g\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g$ shows that $\mathrm{d}g\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g=0$, so theorem 2.2.2 gives $v_-(g)=V_ g$. The quotient in ( 26.89 ) is monotone and homogeneous in its numerator, so $h\geq cg$ implies $v_-(h)^{1/n}\geq cV_ g^{1/n}$. Theorem 26.8.2 turns these lower-mass bounds into the asserted determinant bounds, with equality when $h=g$. A Kähler form satisfies both differential identities. On a surface, theorem 4.1.2 gives a metric $g$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=0$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$ for degree reasons. By compactness, each fixed $h$ satisfies $h\geq cg$ for some $c>0$. $\square$ For a fixed smooth $F$, theorem 26.6.2 gives a unique maximizing current for the determinant functional $\mathfrak D_ F$ of ( 26.39 ), and this current is smooth and strictly positive, so its determinant density is bounded. The following construction shows that currents approaching this maximum satisfy no uniform bound on higher moments of their determinant densities. Proposition 26.17.2 . Let $X=E^ n$, where $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$ carries its flat area form of total area one, and write $\omega _ i$ for the pullback of this form from the $i$th factor. Set \[  h=\sum _{i=1}^ n\omega _ i,\qquad \mathrm{d}V=\omega _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _ n,\qquad V=n!,\qquad \alpha =\frac{n-1}{n}.  \] For $F=0$, the unique maximizing current is $T_*=h^{n-1}/V$, with $k_{T_*}=V^{-1/n}$ and $\mathfrak D_0(T_*)=V^{-1/n}$. There are smooth strictly positive closed forms $S_\varepsilon \in \mathscr G_ h$, $0<\varepsilon <\min \{ 1/4,\mathrm e^{-1}\} $, such that \[  \| k_{S_\varepsilon }\| _{L^ q}=V^{-1/n},\qquad \mathfrak D_0(S_\varepsilon )\longrightarrow V^{-1/n},  \] while for every fixed finite $p>q$, 26.100 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-concentration-moments} \int _ X k_{S_\varepsilon }^{p}\, \mathrm{d}V \geq C_{n,p}[\log (1/\varepsilon )]^{-\alpha p} \varepsilon ^{2-2\alpha p}\longrightarrow +\infty . \end{equation} Their $L^\infty $ norms also diverge. Each $S_\varepsilon $ is the $(n-1)$st power of a Kähler form in the fixed class $V^{-1/(n-1)}[h]$, and has the same Bott–Chern, de Rham and Aeppli classes as $T_*$. No $S_\varepsilon $ attains the maximum of $\mathfrak D_0$. Proof. Put $H_ i=\bigwedge _{j\ne i}\omega _ j$. Expanding the wedge powers gives $h^{n-1}=(n-1)!\sum _ iH_ i$ and $h\wedge H_ i=\mathrm{d}V$. Thus $T_*=(1/n)\sum _ iH_ i$ is normalized, and the determinant formula gives $k_{T_*}=V^{-1/n}$. The smooth equation for $F=0$ is solved by the zero potential, since $h^ n=V\, \mathrm{d}V$; theorem 26.6.2 therefore gives the maximal value and the uniqueness of the maximizer. To construct $S_\varepsilon $, choose a nonnegative smooth function $\beta $ compactly supported in the unit disk in $\mathbb C$, of integral one, with $\beta \geq \beta _0>0$ on a disk of radius $r_0\in (0,1)$. On an embedded disk in the first elliptic factor put $b_\varepsilon (z)=\varepsilon ^{-2}\beta (z/\varepsilon )$, extended by zero; it has integral one. For $0<t<1$, set \[  \begin{gathered} f_{\varepsilon ,t}=1-t+tb_\varepsilon ,\qquad a=V^{-1/(n-1)},\\ \gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}=a(f_{\varepsilon ,t}\omega _1+\omega _2+\cdots +\omega _ n), \qquad T_{\varepsilon ,t}=\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}^{n-1}. \end{gathered}  \] The form $\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}$ is strictly positive, and it is closed because $f_{\varepsilon ,t}$ depends only on the first factor, which has real dimension two. Direct expansion gives 26.101 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-concentration-density} T_{\varepsilon ,t}=\frac1n\left(H_1+f_{\varepsilon ,t}\sum _{i=2}^ nH_ i\right), \qquad k_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}=V^{-1/n}f_{\varepsilon ,t}^{\alpha }. \end{equation} Since $\int _ Xf_{\varepsilon ,t}\, \mathrm{d}V=1$, the trace integral is one, so $T_{\varepsilon ,t}\in \mathscr G_ h$, and $\| k_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}\| _{L^ q}=V^{-1/n}$ because $\alpha q=1$. The mean-zero function $f_{\varepsilon ,t}-1$ has a smooth real potential $\psi $ on $E$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =(f_{\varepsilon ,t}-1)\omega _1$; for example, the mean-zero Fourier series solving $\Delta \psi =4\pi (f_{\varepsilon ,t}-1)$ in the area-one coordinates. Consequently $\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}-ah=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\psi )$. Since $T_*=(ah)^{n-1}$, the closed form $R=\sum _{j=0}^{n-2}\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}^{n-2-j}\wedge (ah)^ j$ satisfies \[  T_{\varepsilon ,t}-T_*=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\psi R).  \] This proves all the assertions about classes, including the case $n=2$, where $R=1$. Jensen's inequality and $f_{\varepsilon ,t}\geq 1-t$ give \[  V^{-1/n}(1-t)^\alpha \leq \mathfrak D_0(T_{\varepsilon ,t}) =V^{-1/n}\int _ Xf_{\varepsilon ,t}^{\alpha }\, \mathrm{d}V <V^{-1/n},  \] where the inequality is strict because $f_{\varepsilon ,t}$ is nonconstant and $0<\alpha <1$. On the product of the disk of radius $r_0\varepsilon $ with the other factors, we have $f_{\varepsilon ,t}\geq t\beta _0\varepsilon ^{-2}$, and this set has volume $\pi r_0^2\varepsilon ^2$. Hence \[  \begin{split}  \int _ Xk_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}^ p\, \mathrm{d}V & \geq V^{-p/n}\pi r_0^2\beta _0^{\alpha p}t^{\alpha p} \varepsilon ^{2-2\alpha p},\\  \| k_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}\| _\infty & \geq V^{-1/n}\beta _0^\alpha t^\alpha \varepsilon ^{-2\alpha }. \end{split}  \] Now take $t=1/\log (1/\varepsilon )$, which lies in $(0,1)$ by the restriction on $\varepsilon $, and $S_\varepsilon =T_{\varepsilon ,t}$. Then $\mathfrak D_0(S_\varepsilon )$ converges to its maximum, while both lower bounds diverge for $p>q$ because $\alpha p>1$. All constants are independent of $\varepsilon $. $\square$ If instead $t\in (0,1)$ is kept fixed in the same construction, then $\int _ Xk_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}^ p\, \mathrm{d}V\geq C_{n,p,t}\varepsilon ^{2-2\alpha p}$ and $\| k_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}\| _\infty \geq C_{n,t}\varepsilon ^{-2\alpha }$. Thus there are no uniform bounds on higher moments, either over the full normalized cone or along a maximizing sequence for one smooth density. Every member of these families attains the supremum $V^{-1/n}$ of the critical norm in corollary 26.17.1 , whereas the maximum of $\mathfrak D_0$ is attained only by $T_*$.

For a positive $(n-1,n-1)$-current $T$ of finite mass, let $\Gamma _{0,h}(T)$ denote the determinant measure of ( 26.39 ) computed with a positive auxiliary metric $h$. For a fixed positive current $T$ and fixed $\mathrm dV$, the measure $\Gamma _{0,h}(T)$ is independent of the positive auxiliary metric $h$. This statement includes singular and degenerate currents. Positive currents have measure coefficients. Choose a positive Radon measure $
u $ dominating them. For a smooth real form $\xi =i\sum \Xi _{ij}\, dz_ i\wedge d ar z_ j$, let $Q$ be the positive semidefinite Hermitian coefficient matrix characterized by $\xi \wedge T=\operatorname {tr}(\Xi Q)
u $. Then \[  \sigma _ h=\operatorname {tr}(HQ)
u ,\qquad P_ h= rac{nH^{1/2}QH^{1/2}}{\operatorname {tr}(HQ)}.  \] The formula holds on $Q

u . \end{equation} This expression has no $H$. Replacing $

The original geometric definition ensures compatibility under frame changes. Matrix AM–GM bounds it locally by a constant times a reference trace measure, proving local finiteness. Compactness gives a finite Radon measure. $\square$ Write $\Gamma _0(T)$ for this intrinsic measure. Theorem 26.17.4 . Let $ eta $ be smooth positive Hermitian with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}( eta ^ j)=0$ for $1\leq j\leq n-1$, $V=\int _ X eta ^ n$, and let $h= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ for a smooth global real function $u$. Then \[  \mathscr G_ h=\mathscr G_ eta ,\qquad \{ \Gamma _{0,h}(T):T\in \mathscr G_ h\}  =\{ \Gamma _{0, eta }(T):T\in \mathscr G_ eta \} .  \] Every measure in this common family has a density $k_ T$ satisfying \[  k_ T\geq 0,\qquad \| k_ T\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathrm dV)}\leq V^{-1/n}.  \] For every real or complex $p\in L^ n(\mathrm dV)$, 26.105  egin{equation} \label{eq:constant-mass-determinant-profile} \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h}\int _ X|p|\, \Gamma _0(T) =V^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n(\mathrm dV)}. \end{equation} All suprema retain singular and degenerate tests. Proof. Distributional integration by parts gives $\int h\wedge T=\int  eta \wedge T+\int u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T =\int  eta \wedge T$. This proves equality of the actual current sets; Lemma 26.17.3 proves equality of their measure sets. Take a smooth strictly positive real $r$ and put $M=\int r^ n \mathrm dV$. By theorem 9.1.1 there are a smooth potential $w$, a positive form $A= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ and a positive coefficient in its prescribed-volume equation. The mass-invariance hypothesis and theorem 2.2.2 determine that coefficient, giving 26.106  egin{equation} \label{eq:constant-mass-reference-equation} A^ n= rac{Vr^ n}{M}\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} In particular, the total mass of $A$ is $V$. title: 26.17.2 Fixed determinant data with degenerating ellipticity
search_title: Fixed determinant data with degenerating ellipticity

text: 26.17.2 Fixed determinant data with degenerating ellipticity Here $v_-(h)$ and $v_+(h)$ denote the infimum and supremum of $\int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ over bounded $h$-psh potentials $w$. Theorem 26.17.5 . On $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z))^ n$, $n\geq 2$, there are positive metrics $\omega _\varepsilon $ in a fixed Kähler class, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, with fixed complete current and determinant-measure families and fixed endpoint ( 26.105 ), while their least relative eigenvalue equals $\varepsilon $. They have uniformly bounded smooth coefficients and global potentials, and \[  v_-(\omega _\varepsilon )=v_+(\omega _\varepsilon )=n!>0.  \] The manifold has a global holomorphic volume form and $c_1=0$. Every displayed metric is already balanced and pluriclosed. Proof. Write $z_ j=x_ j+iy_ j$, $\beta _ j=(i/2)dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ j=dx_ j\wedge dy_ j$, $\beta =\sum _ j\beta _ j$, $V=n!$, and $\mathrm dV=\beta ^ n/V$. Set \[  u_\varepsilon =\frac{1-\varepsilon }{4\pi }\cos (4\pi x_1), \qquad a_\varepsilon =1-(1-\varepsilon )\cos (4\pi x_1).  \] For a function of $x_1$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(u''/(4\pi ))\beta _1$. Hence \[  \omega _\varepsilon =\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =a_\varepsilon \beta _1+\sum _{j=2}^ n\beta _ j.  \] These are globally periodic smooth positive closed forms with $\varepsilon \leq a_\varepsilon \leq 2-\varepsilon $ and $\omega _\varepsilon \leq 2\beta $. Their minimum relative eigenvalue is $\varepsilon $. They converge smoothly to a semipositive form losing rank on $\{ x_1\in \tfrac 12\mathbb Z\} $. All fixed-order smooth norms of the coefficients and potentials are uniformly bounded. Theorem 26.17.4 proves equality of the entire current data and the exact norm at every $\varepsilon $. Since $\omega _\varepsilon $ is closed, theorem 2.2.2 gives mass $V$ for every bounded $\omega _\varepsilon $-plurisubharmonic potential. The explicit formula also gives $\int _ X\omega _\varepsilon ^ n=V$, since $a_\varepsilon $ has mean one. Thus both extrema over bounded potentials equal $V$. The global form $dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dz_ n$ trivializes the canonical bundle; closed positive metrics are balanced and pluriclosed. $\square$

title: 26.17.3 The same obstruction for nonclosed pluriclosed metrics

text: 26.17.3 The same obstruction for nonclosed pluriclosed metrics Theorem 26.17.6 . On the fixed torus above, fix $0<\tau <1/2$. There is a positive nonclosed pluriclosed metric $h_\tau $ and a family $\Omega _\varepsilon =h_\tau +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon >0$, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/2$, with identical actual current sets and intrinsic determinant-measure families. For any fixed smooth positive probability volume their entire-family endpoint is \[  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_{\Omega _\varepsilon }} \int _ X|p|\, \Gamma _0(T) =V_\tau ^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n(\mathrm dV)},\qquad V_\tau =n!(1-\tau ^2/2).  \] Both bounded-potential masses equal $V_\tau $. All fixed-order smooth coefficient and potential norms are uniformly bounded, while \[  \min _ X\lambda _{\min }(\Omega _\varepsilon \mid \beta )=\varepsilon , \qquad d\Omega _\varepsilon =dh_\tau \ne 0.  \] The flat $\beta $ is a fixed balanced metric on this same manifold with $c_1=0$; each $\Omega _\varepsilon $ is pluriclosed. Proof. With the torus coordinates above set $s=\sin (2\pi x_1)$ and \[  \xi =\frac i2(dz_1\wedge d\bar z_2+dz_2\wedge d\bar z_1) =dx_1\wedge dy_2+dx_2\wedge dy_1, \qquad h_\tau =\beta +\tau s\xi .  \] The first relative Hermitian block is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1& \tau s\\ \tau s& 1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, so positivity follows from $|\tau s|<1$. Moreover \[  dh_\tau =2\pi \tau \cos (2\pi x_1) dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dy_1\ne 0.  \] Because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ is proportional to $dz_1\wedge d\bar z_1$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(s\xi )=0$. The first two-coordinate metric is thus pluriclosed, and its square is top degree on that complex surface. Expanding with the remaining closed curve factors proves \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_\tau ^ j)=0\quad (1\leq j\leq n-1),\qquad \int _ X h_\tau ^ n=n!\int _0^1(1-\tau ^2\sin ^2(2\pi x_1))dx_1 =V_\tau .  \] Use the same $u_\varepsilon $ and $a_\varepsilon $ as in Theorem 26.17.5 , now with $\varepsilon \leq 1/2$. Then \[  \Omega _\varepsilon =a_\varepsilon \beta _1+ \sum _{j\geq 2}\beta _ j+\tau s\xi , \qquad a_\varepsilon =\varepsilon +2(1-\varepsilon )s^2.  \] The first block of $\Omega _\varepsilon -\varepsilon \beta $ has diagonal entries $2(1-\varepsilon )s^2$ and $1-\varepsilon $, and determinant \[  \bigl [2(1-\varepsilon )^2-\tau ^2\bigr ]s^2\geq 0.  \] It is positive semidefinite; the remaining diagonal entries are $1-\varepsilon $. Hence $\Omega _\varepsilon \geq \varepsilon \beta $, with equality in the least eigenvalue at $s=0$. Also $\Omega _\varepsilon \leq 3\beta $, all fixed-order smooth norms are uniformly bounded, and the smooth semipositive limit loses rank at $s=0$. Since $d\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =0$, the exterior derivative is the displayed fixed nonzero $dh_\tau $. The lower-power expansion in the proof of theorem 26.17.4 applies to $\Omega _\varepsilon =h_\tau +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon $; it gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega _\varepsilon ^ j)=0$ for $j\leq n-1$, in particular pluriclosedness. Its volume is $V_\tau $, either by integrating the displayed determinant or by theorem 2.2.2 . That theorem also gives mass $V_\tau $ for every bounded $\Omega _\varepsilon $-plurisubharmonic potential, so both mass extrema equal $V_\tau $. Theorem 26.17.4 applied to $h_\tau $ gives equality of the entire current and measure sets and their exact endpoint for every $p\in L^ n$. The balanced trace is fixed as well: \[  \int _ X\Omega _\varepsilon \wedge \beta ^{n-1}=n!.  \] The off-diagonal term has zero trace and the mean of $a_\varepsilon $ equals one. The global holomorphic volume form gives $c_1=0$. The manifold itself is already Kähler, so these nonclosed metrics show that the complete determinant profile and positive bounded-potential mass extrema can stay fixed while the least relative eigenvalue tends to zero. The coexistence problem of 33.3.12 remains open. $\square$

The lower-power expansion in the proof of theorem 26.17.4 applies to $\Omega _\varepsilon =h_\tau +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon $; it gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega _\varepsilon ^ j)=0$ for $j\leq n-1$, in particular pluriclosedness. Its volume is $V_\tau $, either by integrating the displayed determinant or by theorem 2.2.2 . That theorem also gives mass $V_\tau $ for every bounded $\Omega _\varepsilon $-plurisubharmonic potential, so both mass extrema equal $V_\tau $. Theorem 26.17.4 applied to $h_\tau $ gives equality of the entire current and measure sets and their exact endpoint for every $p\in L^ n$. The balanced trace is fixed as well: \[  \int _ X\Omega _\varepsilon \wedge \beta ^{n-1}=n!.  \] The off-diagonal term has zero trace and the mean of $a_\varepsilon $ equals one. The global holomorphic volume form gives $c_1=0$. The manifold itself is already Kähler, so these nonclosed metrics show that the complete determinant profile and positive bounded-potential mass extrema can stay fixed while the least relative eigenvalue tends to zero. The coexistence problem of 33.3.12 remains open. $\square$

text: 26.17.4 Concentration at exact maximizers for varying roots Sharp determinant bounds also need not give uniform integrability of the determinant powers or preserve maximizers under weak current limits. Theorem 26.17.7 . On $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z))^ n$, let $\beta _ j=\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$, $\beta =\sum _ j\beta _ j$, $V=n!$ and $\mathrm dV=\beta ^ n/V$. There are smooth positive closed $A_\varepsilon =\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon $, $0<\varepsilon <1$, and $T_\varepsilon =A_\varepsilon ^{n-1}/V \in \mathscr G_\beta $ satisfying \[  \int _ X k_{T_\varepsilon }^{n/(n-1)}\mathrm dV=V^{-1/(n-1)}.  \] Each $T_\varepsilon $ is an actual dual maximizer for a specified unit $L^ n$ root. The potentials $w_\varepsilon $ have uniformly bounded oscillation and converge uniformly to a continuous canonical $\beta $-psh $w_0$. The currents converge weakly to $T_0=(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0)^{n-1}/V\in \mathscr G_\beta $, but $\Gamma _0(T_0)=0$. The power densities above are not uniformly integrable. Nevertheless every $w_\varepsilon $, including $w_0$, has bounded-potential Monge–Ampère mass $V$. Proof. Put $r=1-\varepsilon $ and \[  P_ r(x)=\frac{1-r^2}{1-2r\cos (2\pi x)+r^2},\qquad f_\varepsilon =\varepsilon +(1-\varepsilon )P_ r.  \] The positive periodic Poisson kernel has mean one and Fourier series \[  P_ r=1+2\sum _{m\geq 1}r^ m\cos (2\pi mx).  \] Define \[  w_\varepsilon =-\frac{2(1-\varepsilon )}{\pi } \sum _{m\geq 1}\frac{r^ m\cos (2\pi mx_1)}{m^2}.  \] For fixed $\varepsilon >0$ this is smooth. Differentiation gives $w_\varepsilon ''=4\pi (f_\varepsilon -1)$, and hence \[  A_\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon (x_1)\beta _1+ \sum _{j=2}^ n\beta _ j=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon >0.  \] It is closed, and $\int A_\varepsilon ^ n=V$. Theorem 26.17.4 and the smooth-root formula give \[  k_{T_\varepsilon }=V^{-1/n}f_\varepsilon ^{(n-1)/n}, \qquad k_{T_\varepsilon }^{n/(n-1)} =V^{-1/(n-1)}f_\varepsilon .  \] Thus the displayed power integral attains the upper bound over all currents, not a bound for a selected family. More precisely, $p_\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon ^{1/n}$ has $L^ n$ norm one, and $\int p_\varepsilon k_{T_\varepsilon }\mathrm dV=V^{-1/n}$, so $T_\varepsilon $ attains the original entire-family dual supremum for this varying root. No common fixed density is asserted. The Fourier series bounds $|w_\varepsilon |\leq \pi /3$ and implies uniform convergence to \[  w_0=-\frac2\pi \sum _{m\geq 1}\frac{\cos (2\pi mx_1)}{m^2}.  \] This limit is continuous and canonically $\beta $-psh by distributional positivity of $A_0=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0$. The probability measures $P_ r(x_1)dx_1$ converge weakly to the periodic Dirac mass at $x_1=0$, as follows from their Fourier coefficients $r^{|m|}$. Thus \[  A_0=\delta _{x_1=0}\beta _1+\sum _{j=2}^ n\beta _ j,  \] where the Dirac measure is tensored with Lebesgue measure in the remaining real coordinates. Its bounded local products are genuine Bedford–Taylor products. Locally the first-coordinate current $\beta _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0$ is pulled back from one complex coordinate, so its powers of degree at least two vanish in the bounded-product recursion. The remaining factors are smooth and closed. Multilinear expansion therefore contains at most one first-coordinate factor; the same expansion for $A_\varepsilon $ passes directly to the distributional limit. Consequently $T_\varepsilon \to T_0=A_0^{n-1}/V$ weakly. This current is positive, closed and normalized by $\int \beta \wedge T_0=1$. In its positive coefficient matrix the absolutely continuous part is proportional to the first diagonal matrix below; the singular part on $x_1=0$ is proportional to the second: \[  \operatorname {diag}(1,0,\ldots ,0),\qquad \operatorname {diag}(0,1,\ldots ,1).  \] Their ranks are respectively one and $n-1$, both less than $n$. With a measure dominating these mutually singular parts, formula ( 26.104 ) therefore gives $\Gamma _0(T_0)=0$. This is not the Monge–Ampère measure of $w_0$, which has total mass $V$ by theorem 2.2.2 . Away from $x_1=0$, $f_\varepsilon \to 0$ pointwise; its integral against $\mathrm dV$ remains one. Thus the positive power densities are not uniformly integrable: almost-everywhere convergence to zero and uniform integrability would force their fixed positive integrals to vanish. In particular $T\mapsto \int k_ T^{n/(n-1)}\mathrm dV$ is not continuous under these weak current limits, even with uniformly convergent continuous potentials. The intrinsic measures themselves satisfy $\Gamma _0(T_\varepsilon )\to 0$ in total mass; this follows from their uniform $L^{n/(n-1)}$ bound by splitting off arbitrarily small neighborhoods of $x_1=0$. The discontinuity concerns their power integrals , not that last measure limit. $\square$ The maximizing root varies with $\varepsilon $. This construction concerns the complete dual profile and the critical power integral; it does not give a sequence of exact maximizers for one fixed smooth density.

title: 26.18 Vanishing lower mass
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.18 Vanishing lower mass By ( 26.89 ), the lower mass $v_-(h)$ vanishes as soon as there are Gauduchon metrics $\eta $ whose degrees $\int _ Xh\wedge \eta ^{n-1}$ stay bounded while their volumes $\int _ X\eta ^ n$ tend to infinity. We construct such metrics on a compact threefold. Writing $\Gamma =\eta ^2$, the volume of $\eta $ is a determinant integral of the coefficient matrix of the positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed form $\Gamma $. The construction first concentrates the trace of a normalized form $\Gamma $ in one direction near a hypersurface, and then adds an average of compact rational curves that fills the two complementary directions. The degree stays bounded, while the determinant, and hence the volume of the positive root, becomes large. The smooth equation then converts these metrics into potentials whose masses tend to zero. Theorem 26.18.1 . There is a connected compact complex threefold $X$ such that, for every Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, there are smooth real functions $u_ j$ satisfying \[  h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0,\qquad \int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^3\longrightarrow 0.  \] In particular, $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian form $h$ on this manifold.

title: Theorem 26.18.1
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 26.18.1 . There is a connected compact complex threefold $X$ such that, for every Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, there are smooth real functions $u_ j$ satisfying \[  h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0,\qquad \int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^3\longrightarrow 0.  \] In particular, $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian form $h$ on this manifold. of theorem 26.18.1 . Fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, and choose $A>0$ with $h\leq A\omega $. Let $\eta _ j$ be the positive root of $\Gamma _ j$, so that $\eta _ j^2=\Gamma _ j$. These metrics are Gauduchon, and \[  P_ j=\int _ Xh\wedge \eta _ j^2\leq AC_2,\qquad R_ j=\int _ X\eta _ j^3\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Set $\mu _ j=\eta _ j^3/R_ j$ and solve the smooth equation in the background $h$: \[  h_ j=h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0,\qquad h_ j^3=c_ h(\mu _ j)\mu _ j, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0.  \] Since $D_{\mu _ j}(\eta _ j)=R_ j^{2/3}$, using $\eta _ j$ as a test in theorem 26.1.3 gives \[  0<\int _ Xh_ j^3=c_ h(\mu _ j)=\mathcal V_{\mu _ j}(h) \leq \frac{P_ j^3}{R_ j^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] The potentials $u_ j$ are smooth, hence bounded, so $v_-(h)=0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 26.18.2
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Lemma 26.18.2 . For $\delta >0$ put \[  C_\delta =\sup \left\{ \int _ XB_\delta \wedge \Theta : \Theta >0,\  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta =0,\  \int _ X\omega \wedge \Theta =1\right\} ,  \] the supremum being taken over smooth real $(2,2)$-forms $\Theta $. These numbers are finite and tend to infinity as $\delta \downarrow 0$. Proof. For fixed $\delta $, choose a constant $M_\delta >0$ with $B_\delta \leq M_\delta \omega $; this shows that $C_\delta \leq M_\delta $. Suppose instead that $C_{\delta _ l}\leq C$ along a sequence $\delta _ l\to 0$. Then $\int _ X(C\omega -B_{\delta _ l})\wedge \Theta \geq 0$ for every admissible $\Theta $, and in particular for the squares of Gauduchon metrics. By theorem 4.3.1 , there are quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ such that \[  C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l\geq B_{\delta _ l},\qquad \sup _ Xv_ l=0.  \] By theorem 1.4.2 , a subsequence converges in $L^1$ to a $C\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $v$, not identically $-\infty $. Since $\delta ^{-2}p(\zeta /\delta )\sigma _\zeta $ is an approximate identity in the variable $\zeta $, \[  B_{\delta _ l}\rightharpoonup \chi [\zeta =0],\qquad C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \chi [\zeta =0].  \] On a coordinate ball where $\chi =1$, add to $v$ a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function whose complex Hessian dominates $C\omega $. The resulting plurisubharmonic function has a current that dominates $[\zeta =0]$, so its Lelong number is at least one at every point of an open subset of this hypersurface. Smooth corrections do not change Lelong numbers, so the same holds for $v$. Siu's analyticity theorem, recalled in 1.13.1 , shows that $Z=\{ \nu (v,\cdot )\geq 1\} $ is an analytic subset of $X$. It is a proper subset because $v$ is not identically $-\infty $. Let $\widetilde Z$ be the inverse image of $Z$ in $\Omega $. It contains an open subset of $H_0\cap \Omega $, where $H_0=\{ w_0=z_0\} $. This surface is a projective plane with two points removed, so it is connected and irreducible, and the identity principle gives $H_0\cap \Omega \subset \widetilde Z$. Since $\widetilde Z$ is invariant under $g$, also \[  H_ k\cap \Omega \subset \widetilde Z,\qquad H_ k=\{ w_0=q^ kz_0\} , \qquad k\in \mathbb Z.  \] Now use the chart $z_1=1$ near the point $[0:1:1:0]\in \Omega $. There $H_ k$ is the graph $z_0=q^{-k}w_0$. For each fixed $(w_0,w_1)$ near $(1,0)$, every local holomorphic defining function of $\widetilde Z$ vanishes at the distinct values $z_0=q^{-k}w_0$, which tend to zero as $k\to +\infty $. The one-variable identity theorem makes each defining function vanish identically on a polydisk. Thus $\widetilde Z$ contains a nonempty open subset of the connected manifold $\Omega $, contradicting properness. Hence no subsequence of $C_\delta $ stays bounded as $\delta \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: 26.18.2 Averaging the trace and compact curves
search_title: Averaging the trace and compact curves
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.18.2 Averaging the trace and compact curves A large pairing with $B_{\delta _ j}$ means that $\Theta _ j$ has a large coefficient in one direction, but possibly only on a small set. Averaging by translations spreads this coefficient over a whole product region of size comparable to $\delta _ j$ in the vertical direction. A second average, this time of compact rational curves, fills the two complementary directions, which is needed for a lower bound on a determinant. Fix $j$ and write $\delta =\delta _ j$. For complex parameters $a,b,\tau $, the automorphisms \[  T_{a,b,\tau }[z_0:z_1:w_0:w_1] =[z_0:z_1+az_0:\mathrm{e}^{\tau }w_0: \mathrm{e}^{\tau }(w_1+bw_0)]  \] of $\Omega $ commute with $g$, and in the product chart they act by $(x,y,\zeta )\mapsto (x+a,y+b,\zeta +\tau )$.  Average $T_{a,b,\tau }^*\Theta _ j$ against the probability density \[  3^{-4}p(a/3)p(b/3)(3\delta )^{-2}p(\tau /(3\delta )) \sigma _ a\wedge \sigma _ b\wedge \sigma _\tau ,  \] and denote the result by $\widehat\Theta _ j$. It is smooth, strictly positive and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. The parameters range in a fixed compact set of automorphisms, so $(T_{a,b,\tau }^{-1})^*\omega \leq C\omega $ with one constant $C$, and a change of variables gives 26.110 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lower-mass-averaged-degree} \int _ X\omega \wedge \widehat\Theta _ j\leq C. \end{equation} Let $F_ j$ be the coefficient of $\sigma _ x\wedge \sigma _ y$ in the restriction of $\Theta _ j$ to the slices $\{ \zeta =\text{constant}\} $, and let $\widehat F_ j$ be the corresponding coefficient of $\widehat\Theta _ j$. Positivity gives $F_ j\geq 0$, and since the translations preserve $\sigma _ x\wedge \sigma _ y$, $\widehat F_ j$ is an average of translates of $F_ j$. At a point of \[  V_ j=\{ |x|,|y|<1/4,\  |\zeta |<\delta /4\} ,  \] every translation carrying it into $\operatorname {supp}B_\delta $ has $|a|,|b|\leq 5/4$ and $|\tau |\leq 5\delta /4$. On this range the first two averaging factors are bounded below by a positive constant, and the third by a positive constant times $\delta ^{-2}$. On the other hand, $\chi \leq 1$ and $p$ is bounded, so the number $J_ j$ of ( 26.109 ) is at most a constant times $\delta ^{-2}$ times the integral of $F_ j$ over $\operatorname {supp}B_\delta $. Comparing the two integrals gives 26.111 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lower-mass-spread-trace} \widehat F_ j\geq cJ_ j\quad \hbox{on }V_ j, \end{equation} with $c>0$ independent of $j$. The second average fills the two horizontal directions. Put \[  f(a,b)=p(4(a-1))p(b/2),\qquad \rho _ j(\tau )=4\delta ^{-2}p(2\tau /\delta ).  \] For parameters in the supports of these functions and $|u|\leq 1/16$, consider the holomorphic maps $\iota _{\tau ,u,a,b}:\mathbb P^1\to X$ defined by 26.112 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lower-mass-rational-curves} \iota _{\tau ,u,a,b}[z_0:z_1] =[z_0:z_1:\mathrm{e}^{\tau }(z_0+uz_1): \mathrm{e}^{\tau }(az_1+bz_0)]\in X. \end{equation} For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/16$, average their integration currents against \[  \rho _ j(\tau )f(a,b)\varepsilon ^{-2}p(u/\varepsilon ) \sigma _\tau \wedge \sigma _ a\wedge \sigma _ b\wedge \sigma _ u,  \] and call the result $T_{j,\varepsilon }$. Define $T_{j,0}$ in the same way, but with $u=0$ and without the integral over $u$. Lemma 26.18.3 . For $\varepsilon >0$, the form $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ is smooth on $X$, semipositive and closed, and \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge T_{j,\varepsilon }\leq C'  \] with $C'$ independent of $j$ and $\varepsilon $. For each fixed $j$, $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ converges smoothly to $T_{j,0}$ on compact subsets of the product chart as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. In this chart 26.113 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lower-mass-curve-local} T_{j,0}=\rho _ j(\zeta )\sigma _\zeta \wedge K_ f,\qquad K_ f=\int _\mathbb Cf(a,y-ax)\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi } (\mathrm{d}y-a\, \mathrm{d}x)\wedge (\mathrm{d}\bar y-\bar a\, \mathrm{d}\bar x)\, \sigma _ a, \end{equation} and on $\{ |x|,|y|\leq 1/4\} $ the form $K_ f$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of $\sigma _ x+\sigma _ y$. Proof. On the parameter supports, $|a-bu|\geq 3/4-2/16=5/8$. Hence the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1& u\\ b& a\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is uniformly invertible, and the projective line ( 26.112 ) lies in $\Omega $. Distinct deck translates of this line are disjoint: equality at a point fixes $[z_0:z_1]$, and invertibility of the matrix then forces the deck scalar to be one. Thus each map is an embedding onto a compact rational curve in $X$. The evaluation map from $\mathbb P^1$ times the open parameter domain to $X$ is a holomorphic submersion. Indeed, after fixing a projective gauge, variations of $u$ and $a$ span the two $w$-coordinates at points with $z_1\ne 0$, variations of $\tau $ and $b$ span them at points with $z_1=0$, and the coordinate on $\mathbb P^1$ supplies the remaining direction. For $\varepsilon >0$, the average is the integral along the fibers of this submersion of a smooth compactly supported parameter density, which proves smoothness. As an average of closed positive integration currents, $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ is closed and semipositive. All curve parameters lie in one compact subset of the domain where the matrix is invertible, so the $\omega $-areas of the curves are uniformly bounded. The weights in $\tau $ and $u$ have mass one, and the weight in $(a,b)$ has a fixed finite mass. This proves the degree bound. When $u=0$, the curve is given in the product chart by $\zeta =\tau $ and $y=ax+b$. Integrating in $b$ and $\tau $ yields ( 26.113 ); the $(1,1)$-factor there is the integration current of the graph of $y=ax+b$. On $\{ |x|,|y|\leq 1/4\} $, the density $f(a,y-ax)$ is bounded below by a positive constant for $a$ in a fixed small disk about $1$. The covectors $\mathrm{d}y-a\, \mathrm{d}x$, for $a$ in that disk, have no common nonzero annihilator, so integrating their squared absolute values and using compactness of the unit sphere in the $(x,y)$-directions gives the asserted lower bound. For general $u$, the curve is given by \[  \zeta =\tau +\log (1+ux),\qquad y=\frac{ax+b}{1+ux}.  \] On a fixed compact subset of the chart, $1+ux$ stays away from zero for all sufficiently small $u$. Solving for the parameters gives $\tau =\zeta -\log (1+ux)$ and $b=(1+ux)y-ax$. Regarding $\rho _ j$ as a smooth function on $E$, this change of variables also applies near the boundary of its support. The Jacobians, the density coefficients and any fixed number of their derivatives depend smoothly on $u$. Averaging against the approximate identity in $u$ therefore gives local $C^\infty $ convergence. This convergence is needed only for each fixed $j$; it is not uniform in $j$. $\square$

Thus each map is an embedding onto a compact rational curve in $X$. The evaluation map from $\mathbb P^1$ times the open parameter domain to $X$ is a holomorphic submersion. Indeed, after fixing a projective gauge, variations of $u$ and $a$ span the two $w$-coordinates at points with $z_1\ne 0$, variations of $\tau $ and $b$ span them at points with $z_1=0$, and the coordinate on $\mathbb P^1$ supplies the remaining direction. For $\varepsilon >0$, the average is the integral along the fibers of this submersion of a smooth compactly supported parameter density, which proves smoothness. As an average of closed positive integration currents, $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ is closed and semipositive. All curve parameters lie in one compact subset of the domain where the matrix is invertible, so the $\omega $-areas of the curves are uniformly bounded. The weights in $\tau $ and $u$ have mass one, and the weight in $(a,b)$ has a fixed finite mass. This proves the degree bound. When $u=0$, the curve is given in the product chart by $\zeta =\tau $ and $y=ax+b$. Integrating in $b$ and $\tau $ yields ( 26.113 ); the $(1,1)$-factor there is the integration current of the graph of $y=ax+b$. On $\{ |x|,|y|\leq 1/4\} $, the density $f(a,y-ax)$ is bounded below by a positive constant for $a$ in a fixed small disk about $1$. The covectors $\mathrm{d}y-a\, \mathrm{d}x$, for $a$ in that disk, have no common nonzero annihilator, so integrating their squared absolute values and using compactness of the unit sphere in the $(x,y)$-directions gives the asserted lower bound. For general $u$, the curve is given by \[  \zeta =\tau +\log (1+ux),\qquad y=\frac{ax+b}{1+ux}.  \] On a fixed compact subset of the chart, $1+ux$ stays away from zero for all sufficiently small $u$. Solving for the parameters gives $\tau =\zeta -\log (1+ux)$ and $b=(1+ux)y-ax$. Regarding $\rho _ j$ as a smooth function on $E$, this change of variables also applies near the boundary of its support. The Jacobians, the density coefficients and any fixed number of their derivatives depend smoothly on $u$. Averaging against the approximate identity in $u$ therefore gives local $C^\infty $ convergence. This convergence is needed only for each fixed $j$; it is not uniform in $j$. $\square$

26.18.3 The volume of the positive root The two averages contribute complementary blocks of the coefficient matrix of a $(2,2)$-form: the translated forms give a large vertical entry, and the curves give a positive horizontal block. A Schur-complement estimate combines them into a lower bound for the volume of the positive root. In the coframe $(x,y,\zeta )$ put $\mathrm{d}V_0=\sigma _ x\wedge \sigma _ y\wedge \sigma _\zeta $. For a real $(1,1)$-form $\xi $, let $H_\xi $ be its coefficient matrix in this normalization. A real $(2,2)$-form $\Theta $ corresponds to a Hermitian matrix $Q_\Theta $, which we call its cofactor matrix, by \[  \xi \wedge \Theta =\operatorname {tr}(H_\xi Q_\Theta )\, \mathrm{d}V_0.  \] Strict positivity of $\Theta $ is equivalent to $Q_\Theta >0$. If $\eta ^2=\Theta $ and $H=H_\eta $, expanding the wedge products gives \[  Q_\Theta =2(\det H)H^{-1},\qquad \eta ^3=\frac{3}{\sqrt2}(\det Q_\Theta )^{1/2}\, \mathrm{d}V_0.  \] Conversely, these formulas uniquely recover a smooth positive $H$ from $Q_\Theta >0$; this is the three-dimensional case of the root construction used in the proof of theorem 4.3.1 . We write $\Theta ^{3/2}=\eta ^3$. Lemma 26.18.4 . There are smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(2,2)$-forms $\Gamma _ j$ such that \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge \Gamma _ j\leq C_2,\qquad R_ j=\int _ X\Gamma _ j^{3/2}\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Proof. Write the cofactor matrix of $\widehat\Theta _ j$ in block form, with a $2\times 2$ Hermitian block $A_ j$ in the $(x,y)$-directions and a column $\kappa _ j\in \mathbb C^2$: \[  Q_ j=\begin{pmatrix} A_ j

& \kappa _ j

\\ \kappa _ j^*

& \widehat F_ j

\end{pmatrix}.  \] The cofactor matrix of $T_{j,0}$ has the form $\operatorname {diag}(B_ j,0)$. Let $I_2$ denote the $2\times 2$ identity matrix. The lower bound for $K_ f$ and the definition of $\rho _ j$ give a constant $c_0>0$ such that $B_ j\geq c_0\delta _ j^{-2}I_2$ on $V_ j$. Since $Q_ j>0$, the Schur complement $A_ j-\kappa _ j\kappa _ j^*/\widehat F_ j$ is positive definite, and \[  \det \bigl (Q_ j+\operatorname {diag}(B_ j,0)\bigr ) =\widehat F_ j\det \left(B_ j+A_ j- \frac{\kappa _ j\kappa _ j^*}{\widehat F_ j}\right) \geq \widehat F_ j\det B_ j,  \] by monotonicity of the determinant on positive Hermitian matrices. Combining the root formula with ( 26.111 ), we obtain \[  (\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,0})^{3/2} \geq c\delta _ j^{-2}\sqrt{J_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V_0 \quad \hbox{on }V_ j.  \] The smaller region $W_ j=\{ |x|,|y|<1/8,\  |\zeta |<\delta _ j/8\} $ has $\mathrm{d}V_0$-volume equal to a fixed positive constant times $\delta _ j^2$. Consequently \[  I_ j=\int _{W_ j}(\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,0})^{3/2} \geq c_1\sqrt{J_ j}>c_1j^2.  \] For this fixed $j$, lemma 26.18.3 gives smooth convergence of $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ to $T_{j,0}$ on the closure of $W_ j$. The cofactor matrix of $\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,0}$ is positive definite there, so the integrand of the root volume depends continuously on these smooth coefficients. We can therefore choose $0<\varepsilon _ j\leq 1/16$ so small that \[  \int _{W_ j}(\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,\varepsilon _ j})^{3/2} \geq I_ j/2.  \] Set $\Gamma _ j=\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,\varepsilon _ j}$. It is smooth, strictly positive and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. Its degree is bounded by ( 26.110 ) and lemma 26.18.3 , whereas its root volume is at least $c_1j^2/2$. $\square$ of theorem 26.18.1 . Fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, and choose $A>0$ with $h\leq A\omega $. Let $\eta _ j$ be the positive root of $\Gamma _ j$, so that $\eta _ j^2=\Gamma _ j$. These metrics are Gauduchon, and \[  P_ j=\int _ Xh\wedge \eta _ j^2\leq AC_2,\qquad R_ j=\int _ X\eta _ j^3\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Set $\mu _ j=\eta _ j^3/R_ j$ and solve the smooth equation in the background $h$: \[  h_ j=h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0,\qquad h_ j^3=c_ h(\mu _ j)\mu _ j, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0.  \] Since $D_{\mu _ j}(\eta _ j)=R_ j^{2/3}$, using $\eta _ j$ as a test in theorem 26.1.3 gives \[  0<\int _ Xh_ j^3=c_ h(\mu _ j)=\mathcal V_{\mu _ j}(h) \leq \frac{P_ j^3}{R_ j^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] The potentials $u_ j$ are smooth, hence bounded, so $v_-(h)=0$. $\square$

title: 26.18.4 Consequences for dimension and equations
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.18.4 Consequences for dimension and equations The example occurs in the smallest possible dimension: on a surface, comparison with a Gauduchon metric gives positive lower mass. Products with projective spaces carry the threefold degeneration to every higher dimension, and a product with the Hopf threefold produces, in addition, unbounded upper mass. Corollary 26.18.5 . Every Hermitian form on a compact complex manifold of dimension at most two has positive lower mass. In every dimension $n\geq 3$ there is a connected compact complex manifold on which every Hermitian form has zero lower mass. Proof. In dimension one the mass is $\int _ Xh>0$, and the surface case is corollary 26.17.1 . In higher dimensions we use the monotonicity and the homogeneity of degree $n$ of $v_-$, which follow directly from ( 26.89 ), to pass from a split metric to every Hermitian metric. For $n=3$ this is theorem 26.18.1 . For $n>3$, take the product of the threefold $X$ with $\mathbb P^{n-3}$, let $\kappa $ be a Fubini–Study form on the projective factor, and consider the split metric $h_0=\omega +\kappa $, with pullbacks understood. For the potentials $u_ j$ given by the theorem for the background $\omega $, \[  \int _{X\times \mathbb P^{n-3}}(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n =\binom n3\left(\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^3\right) \left(\int _{\mathbb P^{n-3}}\kappa ^{n-3}\right) \longrightarrow 0.  \] For another Hermitian form $h$, choose $A$ with $h\leq Ah_0$. Monotonicity and homogeneity give $v_-(h)\leq A^ n v_-(h_0)=0$. $\square$ Corollary 26.18.6 . In every dimension $n\geq 6$ there is a connected compact complex manifold with \[  v_-(h)=0,\qquad v_+(h)=+\infty  \] for every Hermitian form $h$. Proof. Take the product of the threefold above with the Hopf threefold of chapter 8 , with a split metric. Potentials pulled back from the first factor make the masses tend to zero, while the smooth potentials of theorem 8.0.1 , pulled back from the second factor, make them tend to infinity. In each case the product integral is $\binom 63$ times the product of the two factor masses. The metric comparison in the preceding proof handles the lower mass for every Hermitian form, and the metric independence in proposition 6.5.2 handles the upper mass. Products with projective spaces give every higher dimension by the same expansion of wedge powers. $\square$ Finally, fix a smooth positive probability measure $\mu $ on the threefold $X$. The smooth equation still gives $\mathcal V_\mu (h)>0$ for each Hermitian form $h$. With $\mathscr M$ and $\lambda _*$ as in section 26.14.1 , theorem 26.14.3 gives \[  \inf _{\nu \in \mathscr M}\mathcal V_\nu (h)=0, \qquad \lambda _*(h)=0.  \] Thus even a smooth strictly positive background can have vanishing infimum over densities. For the metrics $\eta _ j$ and numbers $R_ j,P_ j$ in the proof of theorem 26.18.1 , the measures $\mu _ j=\eta _ j^3/R_ j$ satisfy $\mathcal V_{\mu _ j}(h)\leq P_ j^3/R_ j^2\to 0$. Hence the densities $\mu _ j/\mu $ cannot be uniformly bounded above: a bound $\mu _ j\leq M\mu $ would give $\mathcal V_{\mu _ j}(h)\geq M^{-1}\mathcal V_\mu (h)>0$, by the comparison of denominators in the proof of proposition 26.14.1 . The example also shows that the endpoint estimate in theorem 26.8.2 fails for the full family of normalized Gauduchon currents: the supremum of the $L^{3/2}$ norms of their determinant densities is infinite, although every subcritical $L^ q$ norm, $1<q<3/2$, remains uniformly bounded by theorem 26.8.1 . For the same fixed background, theorem 26.8.5 , corollary 26.8.6 give uniform $L^\infty $ bounds for the exact maximizers and their adjoint probabilities in a small $C^{2,\alpha }$ family of smooth densities. A larger sufficient family is given by theorem 26.8.9 : uniformly comparable smooth solution forms yield uniform bounds for both densities, without derivative bounds on the varying Hessian. Endpoint estimates for arbitrary bounded families of continuous densities remain open.
