title: 26.18.5 A balanced metric and a finite upper mass
search_title: A balanced metric and a finite upper mass
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.18.5 A balanced metric and a finite upper mass Although every Hermitian form on the threefold of theorem 26.18.1 has zero lower mass, the metric $\omega $ of ( 26.108 ) is balanced and has finite upper mass. A direct calculation expresses the loss of mass under a potential as a vertical Dirichlet energy along the elliptic fibers. The same calculation shows that the degeneration cannot be realized by potentials that are the sum of a periodic function of $t$ and a function on the base: their masses stay above $8$. Put $D=\mathrm{d}t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$, so that $\omega =\alpha +\beta +D$. Proposition 26.18.7 . On the threefold $X$ of theorem 26.18.1 , the Hermitian form $\omega =\alpha +\beta +D$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2)=0,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =2\alpha \wedge \beta \geq 0, \qquad \int _ X\omega ^3=24\pi .  \] For every smooth real function $u$, 26.114 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lower-mass-vertical-energy} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =24\pi -6\int _ X\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta . \end{equation} Consequently $v_+(\omega )=24\pi $. In particular, $X$ has the bounded mass property, while $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian form $h$ on $X$. Proof. Although $t$ is defined only on the covering space $\Omega $, both $\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$ descend to $X$. The Fubini–Study potentials $\log \| z\| ^2$ and $\log \| w\| ^2$ give $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t=\beta -\alpha $. The forms $\alpha ,\beta $ are closed, and $\alpha ^2=\beta ^2=0$ since each is pulled back from a curve. As $D^2=0$, we obtain \[  \mathrm{d}D=-\mathrm{d}t\wedge (\beta -\alpha ),\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D=-(\beta -\alpha )^2=2\alpha \wedge \beta ,  \] \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2) =-2(\alpha +\beta +D)\wedge \mathrm{d}t\wedge (\beta -\alpha )=0.  \] In the last identity, the term involving $D$ contains $\mathrm{d}t$ twice, and $(\alpha +\beta )\wedge (\beta -\alpha )=0$. Thus $\omega $ is balanced, hence Gauduchon, and the formula for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ follows from that for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D$. On a fiber, write $\zeta =a+\mathrm{i}b$, where both real periods are $2\pi $. There $t=2a$ plus a constant, so \[  D|_ E=\frac1\pi \, \mathrm{d}a\wedge \mathrm{d}b, \qquad \int _ ED=4\pi .  \] Since $\omega ^3=6\alpha \wedge \beta \wedge D$, fiber integration and the normalization of the Fubini–Study forms give $\int _ X\omega ^3=24\pi $. The identity ( 26.92 ) for Gauduchon metrics on threefolds, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =2\alpha \wedge \beta $, gives ( 26.114 ). Its last integral is nonnegative. Thus every smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potential has mass at most $24\pi $, and the constant potential attains this value. Regularization of bounded potentials, as in the proof of theorem 26.14.3 , gives the same supremum over bounded potentials, so $v_+(\omega )=24\pi $. The metric independence in proposition 6.5.2 then gives the bounded mass property of $X$. The assertion about the lower mass is theorem 26.18.1 . $\square$ For an admissible smooth $u$, equality in the upper-mass bound holds precisely when $u$ is constant along every elliptic fiber. Indeed, $\alpha \wedge \beta $ is a positive volume form in the base directions, so the nonnegative integral in ( 26.114 ) vanishes exactly when the derivative of $u$ along the fibers vanishes. The fibers are connected, and smooth local sections then show that $u$ is the pullback of a smooth function on $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$. For the potentials with masses tending to zero in theorem 26.18.1 , the same integral instead tends to $4\pi $. A function $f(t)$ descends to $X$ when $f$ is $4\pi $-periodic, since $t\circ g=t+4\pi $. Even after adding an arbitrary potential pulled back from the base, such functions leave a positive mass gap. The sharp gap follows from the bounds on the first two derivatives of $f$ imposed by positivity. Proposition 26.18.8 . Let $\pi :X\to B=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$ be the elliptic fibration above, and put $L=4\pi $. Consider the smooth potentials \[  u=f(t)+\pi ^*v,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,  \] where $f:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ is smooth and $L$-periodic and $v\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$. The infimum of $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3$ over these potentials is $8$. Every such mass is strictly greater than $8$, and the infimum is approached already with $v=0$. Proof. Write $p=f'$, an $L$-periodic function with mean zero. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u =(1-p)\alpha +(1+p)\beta +\pi ^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+(1+p')D.  \] Positivity on the vertical line implies $p'>-1$. On the complex plane $\ker \partial t$, the form $D$ vanishes and the projection to the base is an isomorphism. For each value of $t$ modulo $L$, every base point has a point above it with that value. Hence, writing $\alpha _ B,\beta _ B$ for the two Fubini–Study forms on $B$, the form $(1-p(s))\alpha _ B+(1+p(s))\beta _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is positive on $B$ for every $s$. Integration over the two rulings gives $1-p>0$ and $1+p>0$. Thus $|p|<1$ and $p'>-1$; when $v=0$, these inequalities also suffice for strict positivity. In a logarithmic fiber coordinate $x+\mathrm{i}y$, both real periods are $2\pi $, $t=2x$ plus a constant, and $D|_ E=\pi ^{-1}\mathrm{d}x\wedge \mathrm{d}y$. Hence $\int _ E F(t)D=\int _0^ L F(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$ for every $L$-periodic function $F$. Only the derivative of $u$ along the fibers contributes to ( 26.114 ), and it equals $p(t)$ times the derivative of $t$. Fiber integration therefore gives 26.115 \begin{equation} \label{eq:elliptic-radial-mass} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =6\left(L-\int _0^ L p(s)^2\, \mathrm{d}s\right). \end{equation} We now bound $\int _0^ Lp^2$. Suppose first that $p\not\equiv 0$, and put $m_+=\max p>0$, $m_-=-\min p>0$ and $r=m_++m_-<2$. The function $G(s)=(m_+-s)(s+m_-)$ is nonnegative on $[-m_-,m_+]$. Choose an interval $I$ of length at most $L$ that runs from a maximum point of $p$ forward to the next minimum point. Since $p'\geq -1$, we have $G(p)\geq -G(p)p'$. Using that $p$ has mean zero, we obtain \[  \begin{split}  m_+m_-L-\int _0^ L p^2\, \mathrm{d}s & =\int _0^ L G(p)\, \mathrm{d}s \geq -\int _ I G(p)p'\, \mathrm{d}s\\ & =\int _{-m_-}^{m_+}G(s)\, \mathrm{d}s=\frac{r^3}{6}. \end{split}  \] As $m_+m_-\leq r^2/4$, it follows that \[  \int _0^ L p^2\, \mathrm{d}s \leq \frac{Lr^2}{4}-\frac{r^3}{6}<L-\frac43,  \] where the last inequality holds because the middle expression is strictly increasing in $r\in (0,2]$, as $L>2$. The inequality $\int _0^ Lp^2<L-4/3$ holds trivially when $p=0$. Equation ( 26.115 ) now gives the strict lower bound $8$. To prove sharpness, put $a=(L-2)/2$ and define an $L$-periodic function $p_0$ by \[  p_0(s)= \begin{cases}  1,& 0\leq s<a,\\  1-(s-a),& a\leq s<a+2,\\  -1,& a+2\leq s<L. \end{cases}  \] It has mean zero, $|p_0|\leq 1$ and $\int _0^ L p_0^2\, \mathrm{d}s=L-4/3$. Its distributional derivative is $-1$ on the descending interval and zero on the two constant intervals, and it has a positive atom where the period closes up. Thus $p_0'\geq -1$ as distributions on the circle. Let $\rho _\varepsilon $ be a nonnegative smooth periodic approximate identity of integral one, and set $p_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )(p_0*\rho _\varepsilon )$ for $0<\varepsilon <1$. Then $p_\varepsilon $ is smooth, has mean zero, and \[  |p_\varepsilon |\leq 1-\varepsilon , \qquad p_\varepsilon '\geq -1+\varepsilon , \qquad p_\varepsilon \longrightarrow p_0\quad \hbox{in }L^2.  \] Its primitive $f_\varepsilon $ is smooth and periodic, so $u_\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon (t)$ is admissible. By ( 26.115 ), its mass tends to $8$. $\square$ Proposition 26.18.9 . The threefold $X$ admits neither a pluriclosed Hermitian metric nor a closed Kähler current. Proof. By proposition 26.18.7 , the nonzero smooth semipositive $(2,2)$-form $\alpha \wedge \beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega /2)$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. If a Hermitian metric $\eta $ satisfied $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0$, Stokes' theorem would give \[  0<\int _ X\eta \wedge \alpha \wedge \beta =\frac12\int _ X\eta \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\frac12\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0,  \] a contradiction. The first inequality holds because $\eta $ is positive in the vertical direction at every point. Similarly, if a closed positive current $T$ satisfied $T\geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\varepsilon >0$, positivity and Stokes' theorem for currents would give \[  0<\varepsilon \int _ X\omega \wedge \alpha \wedge \beta \leq \int _ XT\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta =\frac12\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0.  \] Hence there is no closed Kähler current. $\square$ Since a compact complex manifold carries a closed Kähler current exactly when it belongs to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, as recalled in section 33.3 , the threefold $X$ lies outside this class. The example shows that a balanced metric does not guarantee positive lower mass, even together with bounded upper mass. The Hopf threefold, in contrast, has positive lower mass and infinite upper mass, so the two properties are logically independent, and the products in corollary 26.18.6 show that both can fail at once. In particular, in a theorem asserting solvability for every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure, bounded mass alone cannot replace the hypothesis of positive lower mass.

title: Proposition 26.18.7
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.18.7 . On the threefold $X$ of theorem 26.18.1 , the Hermitian form $\omega =\alpha +\beta +D$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2)=0,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =2\alpha \wedge \beta \geq 0, \qquad \int _ X\omega ^3=24\pi .  \] For every smooth real function $u$, 26.114 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lower-mass-vertical-energy} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =24\pi -6\int _ X\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta . \end{equation} Consequently $v_+(\omega )=24\pi $. In particular, $X$ has the bounded mass property, while $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian form $h$ on $X$. Proof. Although $t$ is defined only on the covering space $\Omega $, both $\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$ descend to $X$. The Fubini–Study potentials $\log \| z\| ^2$ and $\log \| w\| ^2$ give $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t=\beta -\alpha $. The forms $\alpha ,\beta $ are closed, and $\alpha ^2=\beta ^2=0$ since each is pulled back from a curve. As $D^2=0$, we obtain \[  \mathrm{d}D=-\mathrm{d}t\wedge (\beta -\alpha ),\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D=-(\beta -\alpha )^2=2\alpha \wedge \beta ,  \] \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2) =-2(\alpha +\beta +D)\wedge \mathrm{d}t\wedge (\beta -\alpha )=0.  \] In the last identity, the term involving $D$ contains $\mathrm{d}t$ twice, and $(\alpha +\beta )\wedge (\beta -\alpha )=0$. Thus $\omega $ is balanced, hence Gauduchon, and the formula for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ follows from that for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D$. On a fiber, write $\zeta =a+\mathrm{i}b$, where both real periods are $2\pi $. There $t=2a$ plus a constant, so \[  D|_ E=\frac1\pi \, \mathrm{d}a\wedge \mathrm{d}b, \qquad \int _ ED=4\pi .  \] Since $\omega ^3=6\alpha \wedge \beta \wedge D$, fiber integration and the normalization of the Fubini–Study forms give $\int _ X\omega ^3=24\pi $. The identity ( 26.92 ) for Gauduchon metrics on threefolds, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =2\alpha \wedge \beta $, gives ( 26.114 ). Its last integral is nonnegative. Thus every smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potential has mass at most $24\pi $, and the constant potential attains this value. Regularization of bounded potentials, as in the proof of theorem 26.14.3 , gives the same supremum over bounded potentials, so $v_+(\omega )=24\pi $. The metric independence in proposition 6.5.2 then gives the bounded mass property of $X$. The assertion about the lower mass is theorem 26.18.1 . $\square$

title: Proposition 26.18.8
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.18.8 . Let $\pi :X\to B=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$ be the elliptic fibration above, and put $L=4\pi $. Consider the smooth potentials \[  u=f(t)+\pi ^*v,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,  \] where $f:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ is smooth and $L$-periodic and $v\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$. The infimum of $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3$ over these potentials is $8$. Every such mass is strictly greater than $8$, and the infimum is approached already with $v=0$. Proof. Write $p=f'$, an $L$-periodic function with mean zero. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u =(1-p)\alpha +(1+p)\beta +\pi ^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+(1+p')D.  \] Positivity on the vertical line implies $p'>-1$. On the complex plane $\ker \partial t$, the form $D$ vanishes and the projection to the base is an isomorphism. For each value of $t$ modulo $L$, every base point has a point above it with that value. Hence, writing $\alpha _ B,\beta _ B$ for the two Fubini–Study forms on $B$, the form $(1-p(s))\alpha _ B+(1+p(s))\beta _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is positive on $B$ for every $s$. Integration over the two rulings gives $1-p>0$ and $1+p>0$. Thus $|p|<1$ and $p'>-1$; when $v=0$, these inequalities also suffice for strict positivity. In a logarithmic fiber coordinate $x+\mathrm{i}y$, both real periods are $2\pi $, $t=2x$ plus a constant, and $D|_ E=\pi ^{-1}\mathrm{d}x\wedge \mathrm{d}y$. Hence $\int _ E F(t)D=\int _0^ L F(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$ for every $L$-periodic function $F$. Only the derivative of $u$ along the fibers contributes to ( 26.114 ), and it equals $p(t)$ times the derivative of $t$. Fiber integration therefore gives 26.115 \begin{equation} \label{eq:elliptic-radial-mass} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =6\left(L-\int _0^ L p(s)^2\, \mathrm{d}s\right). \end{equation} We now bound $\int _0^ Lp^2$. Suppose first that $p\not\equiv 0$, and put $m_+=\max p>0$, $m_-=-\min p>0$ and $r=m_++m_-<2$. The function $G(s)=(m_+-s)(s+m_-)$ is nonnegative on $[-m_-,m_+]$. Choose an interval $I$ of length at most $L$ that runs from a maximum point of $p$ forward to the next minimum point. Since $p'\geq -1$, we have $G(p)\geq -G(p)p'$. Using that $p$ has mean zero, we obtain \[  \begin{split}  m_+m_-L-\int _0^ L p^2\, \mathrm{d}s & =\int _0^ L G(p)\, \mathrm{d}s \geq -\int _ I G(p)p'\, \mathrm{d}s\\ & =\int _{-m_-}^{m_+}G(s)\, \mathrm{d}s=\frac{r^3}{6}. \end{split}  \] As $m_+m_-\leq r^2/4$, it follows that \[  \int _0^ L p^2\, \mathrm{d}s \leq \frac{Lr^2}{4}-\frac{r^3}{6}<L-\frac43,  \] where the last inequality holds because the middle expression is strictly increasing in $r\in (0,2]$, as $L>2$. The inequality $\int _0^ Lp^2<L-4/3$ holds trivially when $p=0$. Equation ( 26.115 ) now gives the strict lower bound $8$. To prove sharpness, put $a=(L-2)/2$ and define an $L$-periodic function $p_0$ by \[  p_0(s)= \begin{cases}  1,& 0\leq s<a,\\  1-(s-a),& a\leq s<a+2,\\  -1,& a+2\leq s<L. \end{cases}  \] It has mean zero, $|p_0|\leq 1$ and $\int _0^ L p_0^2\, \mathrm{d}s=L-4/3$. Its distributional derivative is $-1$ on the descending interval and zero on the two constant intervals, and it has a positive atom where the period closes up. Thus $p_0'\geq -1$ as distributions on the circle. Let $\rho _\varepsilon $ be a nonnegative smooth periodic approximate identity of integral one, and set $p_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )(p_0*\rho _\varepsilon )$ for $0<\varepsilon <1$. Then $p_\varepsilon $ is smooth, has mean zero, and \[  |p_\varepsilon |\leq 1-\varepsilon , \qquad p_\varepsilon '\geq -1+\varepsilon , \qquad p_\varepsilon \longrightarrow p_0\quad \hbox{in }L^2.  \] Its primitive $f_\varepsilon $ is smooth and periodic, so $u_\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon (t)$ is admissible. By ( 26.115 ), its mass tends to $8$. $\square$

title: Proposition 26.18.9
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.18.9 . The threefold $X$ admits neither a pluriclosed Hermitian metric nor a closed Kähler current. Proof. By proposition 26.18.7 , the nonzero smooth semipositive $(2,2)$-form $\alpha \wedge \beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega /2)$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. If a Hermitian metric $\eta $ satisfied $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0$, Stokes' theorem would give \[  0<\int _ X\eta \wedge \alpha \wedge \beta =\frac12\int _ X\eta \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\frac12\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0,  \] a contradiction. The first inequality holds because $\eta $ is positive in the vertical direction at every point. Similarly, if a closed positive current $T$ satisfied $T\geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\varepsilon >0$, positivity and Stokes' theorem for currents would give \[  0<\varepsilon \int _ X\omega \wedge \alpha \wedge \beta \leq \int _ XT\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta =\frac12\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0.  \] Hence there is no closed Kähler current. $\square$

title: 26.19 Orders of degeneration at the nef boundary
search_title: Orders of degeneration at the nef boundary
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.19 Orders of degeneration at the nef boundary If $\theta $ is nef and $h$ is Hermitian, the volumes $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)$ are positive and, by theorem 26.10.1 , decrease to $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )$ as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. When this limit is zero, the rate of decay measures how degenerate $\theta $ is at the nef boundary. For a closed nef class on a compact Kähler manifold, choosing $h$ Kähler makes the volume of the perturbation the intersection polynomial $\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon h)^ n$, so it decays like an integral power of $\epsilon $ determined by the numerical dimension. For a nonclosed nef background the logarithmic rate of decay can be fractional, and it need not converge. We therefore define lower and upper orders of degeneration as lower and upper limits of this rate. Changing the probability measure or the perturbing metric only introduces bounded factors, so the orders are invariants of the background. Let $X$ again be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and $\mu $ a smooth strictly positive probability form on $X$. Let $\theta $ be nef and let $h$ be Hermitian. For $0<\epsilon <1$, put \[  a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon ) =\frac{\log \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)}{\log \epsilon }.  \] The logarithm is finite because $\theta +\epsilon h$ belongs to $\mathscr P$, so that its volume is positive. Proposition 26.19.1 . The limits \[  \underline a(\theta )=\liminf _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon ), \qquad \overline a(\theta )=\limsup _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon )  \] are independent of $\mu $ and $h$, and satisfy \[  0\leq \underline a(\theta )\leq \overline a(\theta )\leq n.  \] They are unchanged when $\theta $ is replaced by $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, with $f$ smooth, or by $r\theta $, with $r>0$. If $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )>0$, both limits are zero. Proof. Since $\theta $ is pseudoeffective, monotonicity and homogeneity give \[  \epsilon \lambda _\mu (h) \leq \lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) \leq \lambda _\mu (\theta +h), \qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1.  \] Thus there are constants $c,C>0$ such that \[  c\epsilon ^ n\leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)\leq C, \qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1.  \] Taking logarithms and dividing by the negative number $\log \epsilon $ shows that the quotients $a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon )$ stay bounded as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, and that their lower and upper limits lie in $[0,n]$. By proposition 26.14.1 , changing the smooth probability measure multiplies the volume by a factor between two fixed positive constants. The resulting error in the logarithm is bounded, and after division by $\log \epsilon $ it tends to zero. For another Hermitian metric $h'$, choose constants $c_2\geq c_1>0$ with $c_1h\leq h'\leq c_2h$. Then \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +c_1\epsilon h) \leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h') \leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +c_2\epsilon h).  \] For any fixed $t>0$ and small $\epsilon $, \[  \frac{\log \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +t\epsilon h)}{\log \epsilon } =a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;t\epsilon ) \frac{\log (t\epsilon )}{\log \epsilon }.  \] The last factor tends to one and the first is bounded, while the rescaling $\epsilon \mapsto t\epsilon $ does not change lower and upper limits as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Hence the left side has the same lower and upper limits as $a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon )$. Dividing the preceding inequalities by $\log \epsilon <0$ reverses them, and taking lower and upper limits proves independence of the metric. Invariance under smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ changes follows from that of $\mathcal V_\mu $. For scaling, homogeneity gives \[  \mathcal V_\mu (r\theta +\epsilon h) =r^ n\mathcal V_\mu (\theta +(\epsilon /r)h).  \] The bounded error $n\log r$ and the same rescaling argument prove scale invariance. Finally, if $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )>0$, then by theorem 26.10.1 the perturbed volumes lie between $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )$ and $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta +h)$ for $0<\epsilon \leq 1$, so both limits are zero. $\square$ We call $\underline a(\theta )$ and $\overline a(\theta )$ the lower and upper orders of degeneration of the nef background $\theta $. When they agree, their common value is the common order , and we then also say that $\theta $ has this order. The two orders can differ, and a common order can be irrational. Even when both are zero, the volume can tend to zero, at a logarithmic rate. The elliptic examples in section 26.19.1 exhibit each of these behaviors. Closed nef classes on Kähler manifolds, in contrast, degenerate polynomially. Proposition 26.19.2 . Suppose $X$ is Kähler, $\theta $ is closed and nef, and $h$ is Kähler. Set \[  r=\max \left\{ 0\leq k\leq n: \int _ X\theta ^ k\wedge h^{n-k}>0\right\} .  \] Then \[  \underline a(\theta )=\overline a(\theta )=n-r.  \] Thus $n$ minus the common order is the numerical dimension of the closed nef class of $\theta $. Proof. All the intersection numbers in the definition of $r$ are nonnegative. Indeed, the mixed integrals against $h$ of smooth positive representatives of $\theta +\delta h$ are positive, agree with the cohomological integrals by closed Stokes, and converge to the stated numbers as $\delta \downarrow 0$. The number for $k=0$ is $\int _ Xh^ n>0$, so $r$ is well defined. By the closed nef formula following theorem 26.10.1 , \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) =\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon h)^ n =\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk\epsilon ^{n-k} \int _ X\theta ^ k\wedge h^{n-k}.  \] As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, the leading nonzero term is a positive constant times $\epsilon ^{n-r}$, and taking the logarithmic quotient proves the assertion. By proposition 26.19.1 , the result holds for every Hermitian perturbation, not only for Kähler ones. $\square$ The orders can also be computed on the non-Kähler Hopf threefold $X$ of chapter 8 . Keep its forms $\omega =\alpha +\beta $, where $\alpha \geq 0$ is closed of rank two, $\beta \geq 0$ has rank one, $\alpha ^3=\beta ^2=0$, and $\int _ X\omega ^3=6$. Take $\theta =\alpha $, $h=\omega $, and $\mu _0=\omega ^3/6$. The metric \[  \Omega _\epsilon =\alpha +\epsilon \omega =(1+\epsilon )\alpha +\epsilon \beta  \] is strictly positive. Its volume is \[  \Omega _\epsilon ^3=\epsilon (1+\epsilon )^2\omega ^3 =6\epsilon (1+\epsilon )^2\mu _0.  \] Hence the zero potential solves the smooth normalized equation, and \[  \mathcal V_{\mu _0}(\alpha +\epsilon \omega ) =6\epsilon (1+\epsilon )^2, \qquad \underline a(\alpha )=\overline a(\alpha )=1.  \] By proposition 26.19.1 , the same orders are obtained for every smooth positive probability measure and every Hermitian perturbation. Each perturbed metric nevertheless has infinite upper mass. If $V_ j$ are the smooth potentials of theorem 8.0.1 , then \[  \Omega _\epsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\epsilon V_ j) =\alpha +\epsilon (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)>0,  \] and monotonicity of the determinant of positive matrices gives \[  \int _ X\bigl (\Omega _\epsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\epsilon V_ j)\bigr )^3 \geq \epsilon ^3\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^3\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Thus a finite order of degeneration at the boundary coexists with infinite upper mass at every positive perturbation.

title: 26.19.1 Elliptic surface volumes and order spectra
search_title: Elliptic surface volumes and order spectra
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.19.1 Elliptic surface volumes and order spectra On a product of two elliptic curves, a semipositive background whose coefficients depend on one factor only has an explicit volume. Solving the smooth equation reduces to a Poisson equation on that factor, and the volume of each Hermitian perturbation is governed by the harmonic mean of the perturbed vertical coefficient. The rate at which this coefficient vanishes therefore determines the order of degeneration. Zeros of finite order give fractional orders or logarithmic decay, while coefficients that vanish to infinite order can make the logarithmic rate oscillate. Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z)$, write $X=E_ z\times E_ w$, and fix \[  \omega _1=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\mathrm{d} z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z,\qquad \omega _2=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\mathrm{d} w\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w,\qquad \mu =\omega _1\wedge \omega _2,\qquad h=\omega _1+\omega _2.  \] Both area forms have integral one. Let $a,q,r$ be smooth functions of $z$ alone, with $a,q$ real and nonnegative, $r$ complex-valued, and $|r|^2\leq aq$. Set \[  \theta =\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\bigl (a\, \mathrm{d} z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z+ r\, \mathrm{d} z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w+\bar r\, \mathrm{d} w\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z+ q\, \mathrm{d} w\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w\bigr ).  \] This is a smooth semipositive form, and in particular it is nef. Proposition 26.19.3 . For $\epsilon >0$, put $g=q+\epsilon $ and $I=\int _ Eg^{-1}\omega _1$. Then 26.121 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-elliptic-volume} \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) =\frac{2}{I}\left(\int _ E(a+\epsilon )\omega _1- \int _ E\frac{|r|^2}{g}\omega _1\right), \end{equation} and the infimum defining this volume is attained by a smooth positive Gauduchon metric. In particular, if $a$ is a constant $b>0$ and $r=0$, then $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)=2(b+\epsilon )/I$. If $|r|^2=aq$, then 26.122 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-rank-one-elliptic-volume} \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)=\frac{2\epsilon (1+K)}{I}, \qquad K=\int _ E\frac{a}{q+\epsilon }\omega _1. \end{equation} Proof. Define \[  c=I^{-1}\left(\int _ E(a+\epsilon )\omega _1- \int _ E\frac{|r|^2}{g}\omega _1\right),\qquad A=\frac{c+|r|^2}{g}.  \] Since $(a+\epsilon )g-|r|^2>0$, we have $c>0$, and the definition of $c$ makes $A-a-\epsilon $ have zero mean with respect to $\omega _1$. Dividing its nonconstant Fourier coefficients by the corresponding nonzero eigenvalues of the flat Laplacian produces a smooth real function $u$ on $E$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(A-a-\epsilon )\omega _1$. Pull it back to $X$. The form $\Omega =\theta +\epsilon h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has coefficient matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A& r\\ \bar r& g\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, which has determinant $c$ and positive diagonal entries. Hence $\Omega >0$ and $\Omega ^2=2c\mu $, and theorem 26.1.3 gives ( 26.121 ). The metric $\gamma _*=\Omega /g$ has constant coefficient $1$ in the fiber direction, and its remaining coefficients depend only on $z$. Applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ to its base term or its mixed terms produces a repeated $\mathrm{d} z$ or $\mathrm{d}\bar z$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma _*=0$. Thus $\gamma _*$ is a smooth Gauduchon metric conformal to $\Omega $, and by theorem 26.1.3 it attains the infimum. The two special cases follow by direct substitution. $\square$ Proposition 26.19.4 . For each integer $m>1$ there is a smooth semipositive nonclosed form on $X$ with common order $1-1/m$. For each $b>0$ there is also one with \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)\sim \frac{2b}{\pi \log (1/\epsilon )} \quad (\epsilon \downarrow 0);  \] it has volume zero and both orders zero. Proof. In proposition 26.19.3 take $a=b>0$ and $r=0$. Fix a point $z_0\in E$ and a flat coordinate $\zeta =z-z_0$ on a small disk about $z_0$. Choose $q$ smooth, positive outside $z_0$, and equal to $|\zeta |^{2m}$ on that disk; a positive smooth extension exists away from the disk. For $m=1$, polar coordinates give \[  I=\int _ E\frac{\omega _1}{q+\epsilon } =\pi \log (1/\epsilon )+O(1),  \] and ( 26.121 ) gives the asymptotic formula of the statement. If $m>1$, the substitution $s=|\zeta |^2=\epsilon ^{1/m}t$ gives \[  I\sim C_ m\epsilon ^{1/m-1},\qquad C_ m=\pi \int _0^\infty \frac{\mathrm{d} t}{1+t^ m}>0,  \] so the common order is $1-1/m$. In the logarithmic case, $\lambda _\mu (\theta )\geq 0$ by semipositivity, while $\lambda _\mu (\theta )\leq \lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)\to 0$ by monotonicity; hence $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=0$. Moreover, the quotient of the volume by $\epsilon ^\delta $ diverges for every $\delta >0$, so both orders vanish. Finally, $\mathrm{d}\theta =\mathrm{d} q\wedge \omega _2\ne 0$, so these backgrounds are not closed. $\square$ Proposition 26.19.5 . For every $0<\alpha <\beta <1$ there is a smooth semipositive nonclosed background on $X$, with the same $\mu $ and $h$, such that \[  \bigl (\underline a(\theta ),\overline a(\theta )\bigr ) =(1+\alpha ,1+\beta ).  \] For every $0<\sigma <1$ there is such a background with common order $1+\sigma $. Proof. We use the rank-one formula ( 26.122 ), with coefficients that vanish to infinite order at one point at a prescribed oscillating rate. Step 1: the coefficients. For all sufficiently large $t$, define \[  p(t)=\frac{\alpha +\beta }{2} +\frac{\beta -\alpha }{2}\sin (\log \log t),\qquad P(t)=tp(t).  \] Choose $T$ so large that $0<c_0\leq P'(t)\leq d_0<1$ for $t\geq T$; this is possible because \[  P'(t)=p(t)+\frac{\beta -\alpha }{2\log t}\cos (\log \log t)  \] and $\alpha \leq p\leq \beta $. Fix $z_0\in E$ and a flat coordinate $\zeta $ centered at $z_0$. On $E\setminus \{ z_0\} $ choose a smooth function $t(z)\geq T$ that equals $|\zeta |^{-2}$ near $z_0$ and is bounded outside every neighborhood of $z_0$. Put \[  q=\mathrm{e}^{-t},\qquad a=\mathrm{e}^{-P(t)},\qquad r=\mathrm{e}^{-(P(t)+t)/2},  \] and set all three equal to zero at $z_0$. These functions are smooth and vanish to infinite order at $z_0$: we have $P(t)\geq \alpha t$, and every fixed derivative of $P$ grows at most polynomially in $t$, so by the chain rule each coordinate derivative is bounded by a polynomial in $|\zeta |^{-1}$ times $\mathrm{e}^{-c/|\zeta |^2}$ for some $c>0$. Since $|r|^2=aq$, the resulting $\theta $ is semipositive. It is not closed: the component $\mathrm{d} q\wedge \omega _2$ of $\mathrm{d}\theta $ contains both fiber differentials, and derivatives of the remaining terms cannot cancel it. Step 2: asymptotics of $I$ and $K$. Write $\epsilon =\mathrm{e}^{-L}$, and let $T_0\geq T$ be such that $t=|\zeta |^{-2}$ on the disk $\{ |\zeta |^2<1/T_0\} $. Outside this disk the integrands of $I$ and $K$ in ( 26.122 ) are bounded, so their contributions are $O(1)$, while polar coordinates on the disk give \[  I_{\mathrm{loc}}=\pi \int _{T_0}^\infty \frac{t^{-2}\, \mathrm{d} t}{\mathrm{e}^{-t}+\mathrm{e}^{-L}},\qquad K_{\mathrm{loc}}=\pi \int _{T_0}^\infty \frac{\mathrm{e}^{-P(t)}t^{-2}\, \mathrm{d} t}{\mathrm{e}^{-t}+\mathrm{e}^{-L}}.  \] The part of $I_{\mathrm{loc}}$ over $t\geq L$ is at least a fixed multiple of $\mathrm{e}^ L/L$. For an upper bound, use $(\mathrm{e}^{-t}+\mathrm{e}^{-L})^{-1}\leq \mathrm{e}^ t$ for $t\leq L$ and $(\mathrm{e}^{-t}+\mathrm{e}^{-L})^{-1}\leq \mathrm{e}^ L$ for $t\geq L$, and split $[T_0,L]$ at $L/2$. Thus 26.123 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-elliptic-I-asymptotic} \log I=L-\log L+O(1). \end{equation} The derivatives of $P$ and of $t-P(t)$ are positive and bounded away from zero. Splitting the integral for $K$ at $t=L$ therefore gives $K\leq C\mathrm{e}^{L-P(L)}$. On $[L,L+1]$ the denominator is at most $2\mathrm{e}^{-L}$ and $P(t)\leq P(L)+1$, so \[  c_1L^{-2}\mathrm{e}^{L-P(L)}\leq K\leq c_2\mathrm{e}^{L-P(L)};  \] the complementary $O(1)$ term is absorbed because $P(L)\leq \beta L$. Consequently $\log K=L-P(L)+O(\log L)$, and $K\to \infty $. Step 3: the orders. Combining these estimates with ( 26.122 ) and ( 26.123 ) yields 26.124 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-oscillatory-log-volume} \log \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\mathrm{e}^{-L}h)=-L-P(L)+O(\log L), \qquad \frac{\log \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)}{\log \epsilon } =1+p(L)+o(1). \end{equation} Since $\sin (\log \log L)$ oscillates between $-1$ and $1$, the lower and upper limits of $p(L)$ are $\alpha $ and $\beta $, which proves the first assertion. If instead $P(t)=\sigma t$, the same smoothness and integral estimates give the common order $1+\sigma $. In particular, $\sigma =\sqrt2-1$ gives an irrational common order. $\square$

title: Proposition 26.19.3
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 26.19.3 . For $\epsilon >0$, put $g=q+\epsilon $ and $I=\int _ Eg^{-1}\omega _1$. Then 26.121 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-elliptic-volume} \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) =\frac{2}{I}\left(\int _ E(a+\epsilon )\omega _1- \int _ E\frac{|r|^2}{g}\omega _1\right), \end{equation} and the infimum defining this volume is attained by a smooth positive Gauduchon metric. In particular, if $a$ is a constant $b>0$ and $r=0$, then $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)=2(b+\epsilon )/I$. If $|r|^2=aq$, then 26.122 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-rank-one-elliptic-volume} \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)=\frac{2\epsilon (1+K)}{I}, \qquad K=\int _ E\frac{a}{q+\epsilon }\omega _1. \end{equation} Proof. Define \[  c=I^{-1}\left(\int _ E(a+\epsilon )\omega _1- \int _ E\frac{|r|^2}{g}\omega _1\right),\qquad A=\frac{c+|r|^2}{g}.  \] Since $(a+\epsilon )g-|r|^2>0$, we have $c>0$, and the definition of $c$ makes $A-a-\epsilon $ have zero mean with respect to $\omega _1$. Dividing its nonconstant Fourier coefficients by the corresponding nonzero eigenvalues of the flat Laplacian produces a smooth real function $u$ on $E$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(A-a-\epsilon )\omega _1$. Pull it back to $X$. The form $\Omega =\theta +\epsilon h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has coefficient matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A& r\\ \bar r& g\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, which has determinant $c$ and positive diagonal entries. Hence $\Omega >0$ and $\Omega ^2=2c\mu $, and theorem 26.1.3 gives ( 26.121 ). The metric $\gamma _*=\Omega /g$ has constant coefficient $1$ in the fiber direction, and its remaining coefficients depend only on $z$. Applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ to its base term or its mixed terms produces a repeated $\mathrm{d} z$ or $\mathrm{d}\bar z$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma _*=0$. Thus $\gamma _*$ is a smooth Gauduchon metric conformal to $\Omega $, and by theorem 26.1.3 it attains the infimum. The two special cases follow by direct substitution. $\square$

title: Proposition 26.19.4

text: Proposition 26.19.4 . For each integer $m>1$ there is a smooth semipositive nonclosed form on $X$ with common order $1-1/m$. For each $b>0$ there is also one with \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)\sim \frac{2b}{\pi \log (1/\epsilon )} \quad (\epsilon \downarrow 0);  \] it has volume zero and both orders zero. Proof. In proposition 26.19.3 take $a=b>0$ and $r=0$. Fix a point $z_0\in E$ and a flat coordinate $\zeta =z-z_0$ on a small disk about $z_0$. Choose $q$ smooth, positive outside $z_0$, and equal to $|\zeta |^{2m}$ on that disk; a positive smooth extension exists away from the disk. For $m=1$, polar coordinates give \[  I=\int _ E\frac{\omega _1}{q+\epsilon } =\pi \log (1/\epsilon )+O(1),  \] and ( 26.121 ) gives the asymptotic formula of the statement. Finally, $\mathrm{d}\theta =\mathrm{d} q\wedge \omega _2\ne 0$, so these backgrounds are not closed. $\square$

title: 26.19.2 Comparison under an arbitrary modification
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.19.2 Comparison under an arbitrary modification The orders of degeneration are defined on a fixed manifold. We now show that pulling a nef background back by a modification can only increase them. Recall that a modification $\pi :Y\to X$ is a proper surjective holomorphic map that restricts to a biholomorphism between dense Zariski open subsets. The proof compares Gauduchon tests on $X$ with tests on $Y$. The pullback of a Gauduchon test is degenerate along the exceptional locus, and adding a small positive test on $Y$ repairs this. To control the effect of the added test uniformly, we first bound the pairing of pulled-back tests with a Hermitian form on $Y$ by their pairing with a Hermitian form on $X$, uniformly over the whole cone of tests. In this subsection $\pi :Y\to X$ is a modification of connected compact complex manifolds of dimension $n\geq 2$. We use Hironaka's analytic elimination of indeterminacies in the following form: there are a finite composition $p:Z\to X$ of blowups along smooth centers and a modification $F:Z\to Y$ with $p=\pi \circ F$. It is obtained by resolving the indeterminacies of the inverse meromorphic map $\pi ^{-1}\circ p$; the identity $p=\pi \circ F$ holds on the dense set where the maps are biholomorphic, hence everywhere. This classical input is discussed in section 34.15 . For an effective real divisor $D$, we write $\eta _ D$ for the curvature form of a smooth Hermitian metric on the corresponding real line bundle, as in section 26.21 . Lemma 26.19.6 . Let $p:Z\to X$ be a finite composition of blowups along smooth centers of codimension at least two, and let $h_ X$ be a Hermitian form on $X$. There are a constant $C_0>0$, an effective real divisor $D$ on $Z$ whose components are exceptional for $p$, and a smooth curvature form $\eta _ D$ such that 26.125 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-blowup-positive-metric} h_ Z=C_0p^*h_ X-\eta _ D>0. \end{equation} Every component of $D$ is mapped by $p$ into a set of complex codimension at least two in $X$. Proof. First let $q:M'\to M$ be one blowup along a smooth center, with exceptional divisor $E$, and let $h_ M$ be a Hermitian form on $M$. The restriction of $\mathcal O(-E)$ to each projective fiber of $E$ is $\mathcal O(1)$. A Hermitian metric on the normal bundle of the center therefore induces a metric on $\mathcal O(-E)|_ E$ whose curvature is positive on the tangent spaces of the fibers. Extend this metric to $\mathcal O(-E)$ on $M'$ by extending the smooth logarithm of its ratio to a fixed reference metric from the closed submanifold $E$, and let $\beta $ be its curvature. The semipositive form $q^*h_ M$ is positive off $E$, and at points of $E$ its kernel is exactly the tangent space of the fiber, on which $\beta $ is positive. Hence $Cq^*h_ M+\beta >0$ for every sufficiently large $C$: otherwise, unit tangent vectors violating the inequality for $C\to \infty $ would converge, by compactness, to a vector in the kernel of $q^*h_ M$ on which $\beta $ is nonpositive. With $\eta _ E=-\beta $, the curvature of the induced metric on $\mathcal O(E)$, this reads $Cq^*h_ M-\eta _ E>0$. For a composition of blowups, apply this step successively, with $h_ M$ the positive form already obtained on the previous blowup. Each step multiplies the previous divisor by a positive constant, pulls it back and adds the new exceptional divisor, so the divisor stays effective and exceptional. This proves ( 26.125 ). Each exceptional divisor maps into the image of its center, which has dimension at most $n-2$. $\square$ Lemma 26.19.7 . Fix Hermitian forms $h_ X,h_ Y$ for a modification $\pi :Y\to X$. There is a constant $K>0$ such that 26.126 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-uniform-pairing} \int _ Y h_ Y\wedge \pi ^*\Psi \leq K\int _ X h_ X\wedge \Psi \end{equation} for every smooth strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Psi $ on $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =0$. Proof. Use the factorization $p=\pi \circ F$ above and lemma 26.19.6 . By compactness there is $a>0$ with $h_ Z\geq aF^*h_ Y$. Pulling back the semipositive form $\Psi $ and integrating, we obtain \[  a\int _ Yh_ Y\wedge \pi ^*\Psi \leq \int _ Zh_ Z\wedge p^*\Psi =C_0\int _ Xh_ X\wedge \Psi -\int _ Dp^*\Psi .  \] Here the changes of variables use that $F$ and $p$ have degree one, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula, together with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p^*\Psi =0$, replaces the pairing with $\eta _ D$ by the integral over $D$. This last integral vanishes: on the regular locus of each component of $D$, the restriction of $p$ has rank at most $n-2$, so the restriction of the $(n-1,n-1)$-form $p^*\Psi $ is zero. Taking $K=C_0/a$ proves the assertion. $\square$ Proposition 26.19.8 . Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification of connected compact complex manifolds of dimension $n\geq 2$, and let $\theta $ be a smooth nef background on $X$. Then $\pi ^*\theta $ is nef. For fixed Hermitian forms $h_ X,h_ Y$ and smooth positive probability forms $\mu _ X,\mu _ Y$, there are constants $C,K>0$, independent of $\epsilon $, such that 26.127 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-main-modification-comparison} \mathcal V_{\mu _ Y}(\pi ^*\theta +\epsilon h_ Y) \leq C\mathcal V_{\mu _ X}(\theta +K\epsilon h_ X) \qquad (\epsilon >0). \end{equation} Consequently \[  \underline a(\pi ^*\theta )\geq \underline a(\theta ),\qquad \overline a(\pi ^*\theta )\geq \overline a(\theta ).  \] In dimension one a modification is an isomorphism and preserves both orders. Proof. Step 1: nefness. Choose $C'$ with $\pi ^*h_ X\leq C'h_ Y$. For $\epsilon >0$, pull back a smooth representative $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\tau \geq -\tau h_ X$ with $\tau <\epsilon /C'$; this gives a positive representative of $\pi ^*\theta +\epsilon h_ Y$. Thus $\pi ^*\theta $ is nef, and both volumes in ( 26.127 ) are positive. Step 2: regularized tests. The ratio $\pi ^*\mu _ X/\mu _ Y$ is smooth, nonnegative and bounded on the compact manifold $Y$, so there is $c>0$ with $\mu _ Y\geq c\pi ^*\mu _ X$. Fix a smooth Gauduchon metric $\gamma _0$ on $Y$, given by theorem 4.1.2 . For an arbitrary Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $X$, write $\Psi =\gamma ^{n-1}$, and for $\delta >0$ define $\Gamma _\delta $ by \[  \Gamma _\delta ^{n-1}=\pi ^*\Psi +\delta \gamma _0^{n-1}.  \] The right side is a strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form, and such a form has a unique smooth positive $(n-1)$st root, obtained by solving for the Hermitian matrix of the root from the positive cofactor matrix. Since the right side is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, $\Gamma _\delta $ is a smooth Gauduchon metric on $Y$. Step 3: the numerator. For $\epsilon >0$, lemma 26.19.7 gives 26.128 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-modification-numerator} \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\int _ Y(\pi ^*\theta +\epsilon h_ Y) \wedge \Gamma _\delta ^{n-1} =\int _ X\theta \wedge \Psi +\epsilon \int _ Yh_ Y\wedge \pi ^*\Psi \leq \int _ X(\theta +K\epsilon h_ X)\wedge \Psi . \end{equation} The first term in the middle is nonnegative because $\theta $ is nef, and the second is positive because $\pi ^*\Psi $ is positive on the set where $\pi $ is biholomorphic, so the limit is positive. Step 4: the denominator. We claim that 26.129 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-modification-denominator} \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}D_{\mu _ Y}(\Gamma _\delta ) =\int _ Y(\pi ^*\gamma ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}\mu _ Y^{1/n} \geq c^{1/n}D_{\mu _ X}(\gamma )>0. \end{equation} To justify the limit on the exceptional locus, represent $\Gamma _\delta ^{n-1}$ by its positive cofactor matrix. The density of $(\Gamma _\delta ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}$ is a fixed dimensional constant times the $1/n$th power of the determinant of that matrix, and this expression extends continuously to positive semidefinite matrices. Since $Y$ is compact, dominated convergence applies. The inequality follows from $\mu _ Y\geq c\pi ^*\mu _ X$ and the change of variables for the degree-one map $\pi $. Step 5: conclusion. Test the infimum defining $\lambda _{\mu _ Y}(\pi ^*\theta +\epsilon h_ Y)$ with $\Gamma _\delta $, use ( 26.128 ) and ( 26.129 ), and let $\delta \downarrow 0$. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $X$ this gives \[  \lambda _{\mu _ Y}(\pi ^*\theta +\epsilon h_ Y) \leq c^{-1/n} \frac{\int _ X(\theta +K\epsilon h_ X)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{D_{\mu _ X}(\gamma )}.  \] Taking the infimum over $\gamma $ and then the $n$th power proves ( 26.127 ) with $C=c^{-1}$. Dividing the logarithm of ( 26.127 ) by $\log \epsilon <0$ reverses the inequality. The bounded error $\log C$ and the rescaling $\epsilon \mapsto K\epsilon $ do not affect lower and upper limits, as in the proof of proposition 26.19.1 . This gives $\underline a(\pi ^*\theta )\geq \underline a(\theta )$ and $\overline a(\pi ^*\theta )\geq \overline a(\theta )$. Finally, a proper holomorphic map of degree one between compact Riemann surfaces is an isomorphism, which settles the case $n=1$. $\square$

The ratio $\pi ^*\mu _ X/\mu _ Y$ is smooth, nonnegative and bounded on the compact manifold $Y$, so there is $c>0$ with $\mu _ Y\geq c\pi ^*\mu _ X$. Fix a smooth Gauduchon metric $\gamma _0$ on $Y$, given by theorem 4.1.2 . For an arbitrary Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $X$, write $\Psi =\gamma ^{n-1}$, and for $\delta >0$ define $\Gamma _\delta $ by \[  \Gamma _\delta ^{n-1}=\pi ^*\Psi +\delta \gamma _0^{n-1}.  \] The right side is a strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form, and such a form has a unique smooth positive $(n-1)$st root, obtained by solving for the Hermitian matrix of the root from the positive cofactor matrix. Since the right side is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, $\Gamma _\delta $ is a smooth Gauduchon metric on $Y$. Step 3: the numerator. For $\epsilon >0$, lemma 26.19.7 gives 26.128 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-modification-numerator} \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\int _ Y(\pi ^*\theta +\epsilon h_ Y) \wedge \Gamma _\delta ^{n-1} =\int _ X\theta \wedge \Psi +\epsilon \int _ Yh_ Y\wedge \pi ^*\Psi \leq \int _ X(\theta +K\epsilon h_ X)\wedge \Psi . \end{equation} The first term in the middle is nonnegative because $\theta $ is nef, and the second is positive because $\pi ^*\Psi $ is positive on the set where $\pi $ is biholomorphic, so the limit is positive. Step 4: the denominator. We claim that 26.129 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-modification-denominator} \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}D_{\mu _ Y}(\Gamma _\delta ) =\int _ Y(\pi ^*\gamma ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}\mu _ Y^{1/n} \geq c^{1/n}D_{\mu _ X}(\gamma )>0. \end{equation} To justify the limit on the exceptional locus, represent $\Gamma _\delta ^{n-1}$ by its positive cofactor matrix. The density of $(\Gamma _\delta ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}$ is a fixed dimensional constant times the $1/n$th power of the determinant of that matrix, and this expression extends continuously to positive semidefinite matrices. Since $Y$ is compact, dominated convergence applies. The inequality follows from $\mu _ Y\geq c\pi ^*\mu _ X$ and the change of variables for the degree-one map $\pi $. Step 5: conclusion. Test the infimum defining $\lambda _{\mu _ Y}(\pi ^*\theta +\epsilon h_ Y)$ with $\Gamma _\delta $, use ( 26.128 ) and ( 26.129 ), and let $\delta \downarrow 0$. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $X$ this gives \[  \lambda _{\mu _ Y}(\pi ^*\theta +\epsilon h_ Y) \leq c^{-1/n} \frac{\int _ X(\theta +K\epsilon h_ X)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{D_{\mu _ X}(\gamma )}.  \] Taking the infimum over $\gamma $ and then the $n$th power proves ( 26.127 ) with $C=c^{-1}$. Dividing the logarithm of ( 26.127 ) by $\log \epsilon <0$ reverses the inequality. The bounded error $\log C$ and the rescaling $\epsilon \mapsto K\epsilon $ do not affect lower and upper limits, as in the proof of proposition 26.19.1 . This gives $\underline a(\pi ^*\theta )\geq \underline a(\theta )$ and $\overline a(\pi ^*\theta )\geq \overline a(\theta )$. Finally, a proper holomorphic map of degree one between compact Riemann surfaces is an isomorphism, which settles the case $n=1$. $\square$

title: 26.19.4 Positive-current subtraction and divisorial residuals
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.19.4 Positive-current subtraction and divisorial residuals Another way to change the order of degeneration is to subtract a positive current from the background. If $\theta -\beta $ differs from a positive current by a $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact term, then every Gauduchon pairing of $\theta $ dominates the corresponding pairing of $\beta $. When the residual $\beta $ is still nef, its perturbed volumes are therefore smaller, and its orders are at least those of $\theta $. The main example is the subtraction of the curvature form of an effective divisor. Such a subtraction can preserve the order, raise it by an integer or by a fraction, or produce unequal lower and upper orders; and the residual need not be nef. Proposition 26.19.10 . Let $\theta ,\beta $ be smooth nef real $(1,1)$-forms on a compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$, and suppose that \[  S=(\theta -\beta )+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0  \] is a positive $(1,1)$-current for some integrable function $\varphi $. For every Hermitian form $h$, every smooth strictly positive probability form $\mu $ and every $\epsilon >0$, 26.140 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-residual-volume-comparison} \mathcal V_\mu (\beta +\epsilon h)\leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h). \end{equation} Consequently $\underline a(\beta )\geq \underline a(\theta )$ and $\overline a(\beta )\geq \overline a(\theta )$. Proof. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, distributional integration by parts gives \[  \int _ X(\theta -\beta )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\langle S,\gamma ^{n-1}\rangle \geq 0.  \] Hence, for each test metric, the quotient for $\theta +\epsilon h$ is at least the quotient for $\beta +\epsilon h$, and taking infima gives $\lambda _\mu (\beta +\epsilon h)\leq \lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)$. Both sides are positive because $\beta $ and $\theta $ are nef, so raising to the $n$th power gives ( 26.140 ). Dividing the logarithms by the negative number $\log \epsilon $ reverses the inequality and proves both comparisons of orders. $\square$ For an effective real divisor $D$ with curvature form $\eta _ D$, the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $[D]=\eta _ D+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ for a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $. Thus proposition 26.19.10 applies to $\beta =\theta -\eta _ D$, with $S=[D]$, whenever $\beta $ is nef. For a convergent countable positive combination of divisors, the same argument applies only when its curvature representative is smooth and a global potential realizes the current difference. If $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is a positive current with $T-S\geq 0$, then $T-S=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-\varphi )$, so $\beta $ is the background of the positive current that remains after $S$ is removed from $T$. Proposition 26.19.11 . Subtracting the curvature form of an effective divisor from a smooth nef background, with a smooth nef residual, can preserve the common order, raise it by any integer between $1$ and the dimension or by a fraction, or produce a residual whose lower and upper orders differ. The residual can also fail to be nef. Proof. Integer jumps. On $E^ n$, where $E$ is an elliptic curve, let $\omega _ i$ be the pullback of a flat area form of integral one from the $i$th factor, and set $h=\sum _ i\omega _ i$ and $\mu =\omega _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _ n$. The divisor $F_ i$ obtained by fixing a point in the $i$th factor has $\omega _ i$ as a smooth curvature form: on that elliptic curve, any curvature form of the corresponding line bundle differs from $\omega _ i$ by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a solution of a zero-mean Poisson equation, so the metric can be adjusted, and then pulled back. For $\theta =h$ and $D=\sum _{i=1}^ kF_ i$, the residual $\beta =\sum _{i=k+1}^ n\omega _ i$ is smooth and nef. The perturbed forms are closed, positive and of constant density with respect to $\mu $, so the zero potential solves their equations, and theorem 26.1.3 gives 26.141 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-integer-residual-jump} \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)=n!(1+\epsilon )^ n,\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\beta +\epsilon h)=n!\epsilon ^ k(1+\epsilon )^{n-k}. \end{equation} For $n=1$ the same formula follows from $\lambda _\mu (\xi )=\int _ X\xi $. These examples realize each integer jump $1,\ldots ,n$. A nonzero divisor with jump zero is given by $\theta =2h$ and $D=F_1$, since then the residual is still strictly positive. A fractional jump. Use the background $\beta =b\omega _1+q\omega _2$ of proposition 26.19.4 , where $q=|\zeta |^{2m}$ near its unique zero and $m>1$. Choose $c>0$ and put $\theta =\beta +c\omega _2>0$ and $D=c(E\times \{ w_0\} )$, whose smooth curvature form is $c\omega _2$. The original background is strictly positive, so both its orders are zero, whereas the residual has common order $1-1/m$. Unequal orders. Let $\beta _{\rm res}$ be the oscillatory rank-one background of proposition 26.19.5 , and put \[  \theta =\beta _{\rm res}+ch>0,\qquad D=c(\{ z_0\} \times E)+c(E\times \{ w_0\} ),\qquad \eta _ D=ch.  \] The background $\theta $ has both orders zero: since $\theta \geq ch$, every test quotient is bounded below by a positive constant, while one fixed test gives a finite upper bound. Its smooth nef residual is exactly $\beta _{\rm res}$, whose lower and upper orders differ. In each of these examples, the residual plus $[D]$ is a positive current in the smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-class of $\theta $, and its divisorial part is exactly $[D]$ because the residual is smooth. We do not need this current to have minimal singularities; that case is treated in corollary 26.19.12 . A residual that is not nef. Blow up $\mathbb P^2$ at two distinct points. Let $H$ be the pullback of the class of the normalized Fubini–Study form, let $E_1,E_2$ be the exceptional curves, and let $L$ be the strict transform of the line through the two points. The pullback $\theta $ of the Fubini–Study form is smooth, semipositive and nef. Subtract curvature forms of $D=E_1+E_2$. The residual $\beta $ has class $H-E_1-E_2$, which is the class of $L$, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula for the total transform of the line shows that it contains the positive current $[L]$. The intersection numbers $H^2=1$, $H\cdot E_ i=0$, $E_ i^2=-1$ and $E_1\cdot E_2=0$ give \[  \int _ L\beta =(H-E_1-E_2)^2=-1.  \] If $\beta $ were nef, smooth representatives $\beta +\epsilon h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\epsilon >0$ would give $-1+\epsilon \int _ Lh\geq 0$ for all $\epsilon >0$, which is impossible. $\square$ For a prime divisor $D$ and $\delta >0$, consider the infimum of the generic Lelong numbers along $D$ of the positive currents $\theta +\delta h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$; its limit as $\delta \downarrow 0$ is the minimal multiplicity of $\theta $ along $D$. For a nef background all minimal multiplicities vanish, since every $\theta +\delta h$ has a smooth positive representative. Removing the divisor defined by these multiplicities therefore leaves a nef background unchanged. Removing the divisorial part of a particular positive current in the class of $\theta $ is a different operation, even when that current has minimal singularities. Corollary 26.19.12 . On the ruled surface $X$ of lemma 25.5.1 , keep its nef curvature form $\theta $, its section $D$ at infinity and its Kähler form $\kappa =\theta +\pi ^*\sigma _0$. For every smooth positive probability form $\mu $, \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon \kappa )=2\epsilon (1+\epsilon ), \qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\epsilon \kappa )=2\epsilon ^2.  \] The only positive current of the form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is $[D]$. It has minimal singularities, and removing its whole divisor leaves the zero background and changes the common order from one to two. Proof. Lemma 25.5.1 gives the uniqueness of $[D]$ and the nefness of $\theta $, and the calculation in the proof of proposition 25.5.3 gives $\int _ X\theta ^2=0$. Put $B=\pi ^*\sigma _0$. Then $B^2=0$, and \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge B=\int _ D B=1,  \] by the Poincaré–Lelong formula, Stokes' theorem and the fact that the section $D$ maps isomorphically onto the elliptic base. The closed nef formula following theorem 26.10.1 now computes both volumes by expanding the squares, for every $\mu $. Every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=[D]$, so any two such functions differ by a pluriharmonic function, hence by a constant; in particular each has minimal singularities. Since $\theta $ is itself a curvature form of $\mathcal O_ X(D)$, removing the whole divisor leaves the zero background. The two volume polynomials give the orders one and two. $\square$

title: 26.19.5 Integer orders in fixed projective cones
search_title: Integer orders in fixed projective cones
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: 26.19.5 Integer orders in fixed projective cones In the examples of section 26.19.1 the order is not an integer because a coefficient of the background vanishes at a point. We now consider backgrounds that are combinations, with strictly positive coefficient functions, of finitely many fixed closed semipositive generators on products of projective spaces and their linear blowups. Such backgrounds have integral orders even when they are not closed. The tool is a comparison with a closed semipositive form $B$ of constant rank. If $\theta $ is bounded above by a multiple of $B$ and, after the addition of a possibly singular potential, below by another multiple, then the Gauduchon quotients of $\theta +\epsilon h$ and of the closed form $B+\epsilon \Omega $ are comparable, and the latter have an explicit order. On a blown-up factor the pulled-back hyperplane form loses rank along the exceptional divisor, and the logarithmic potential of that divisor supplies the lower bound. Lemma 26.19.13 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$, let $\Omega $ be a Kähler form, and let $B$ be a smooth closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form. Suppose a smooth nef background $\theta $ satisfies \[  \theta \leq CB,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq cB  \] as currents, for constants $c,C>0$ and a real function $\varphi \in L^1(X)$. For every Hermitian form $h$ and smooth strictly positive probability form $\mu $, there are constants $k,K>0$ such that, for $0<\epsilon \leq 1$, 26.142 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-logarithmic-quotient-comparison} k\lambda _\mu (B+\epsilon \Omega ) \leq \lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) \leq K\lambda _\mu (B+\epsilon \Omega ). \end{equation} If $B$ has constant rank $R$, there are moreover constants $L,U>0$ with \[  L\epsilon ^{n-R}\leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) \leq U\epsilon ^{n-R},\qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1.  \] In particular, $\theta $ then has common order $n-R$. Proof. Choose $c_ h,C_ h>0$ with $c_ h\Omega \leq h\leq C_ h\Omega $. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, distributional Stokes gives \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\langle \varphi ,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma ^{n-1}\rangle =0.  \] The lower bound for $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ therefore gives $\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon h)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq k\int _ X(B+\epsilon \Omega )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ with $k=\min (c,c_ h)$, and the upper bound for $\theta $ gives the reverse inequality with $K=\max (C,C_ h)$. Dividing by $D_\mu (\gamma )>0$ and taking infima over all Gauduchon metrics proves ( 26.142 ); no rank hypothesis has been used. Now suppose that $B$ has constant rank $R$. Its $R$ positive eigenvalues relative to $\Omega $ are then bounded above and away from zero, uniformly on $X$. With $A_\epsilon =B+\epsilon \Omega $, compactness gives constants $m_0,M_0>0$ with 26.143 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-projective-pointwise-volume} m_0\epsilon ^{n-R}\mu \leq A_\epsilon ^ n \leq M_0\epsilon ^{n-R}\mu ,\qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1. \end{equation} For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, the pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  A_\epsilon \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq \left(\frac{A_\epsilon ^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n,  \] and hence $\lambda _\mu (A_\epsilon )\geq m_0^{1/n}\epsilon ^{(n-R)/n}$. In the other direction, the positive closed form $\gamma =A_\epsilon $ is itself an admissible test. Writing $A_\epsilon ^ n=f_\epsilon \mu $, we have \[  \begin{aligned}  D_\mu (A_\epsilon )& =\int _ X f_\epsilon ^{(n-1)/n}\mu \geq m_0^{(n-1)/n}\epsilon ^{(n-R)(n-1)/n},\\  \int _ X A_\epsilon ^ n& \leq M_0\epsilon ^{n-R}, \end{aligned}  \] so the quotient of this test is at most $M_0m_0^{-(n-1)/n}\epsilon ^{(n-R)/n}$. Raising both bounds to the $n$th power and using ( 26.142 ) gives the two-sided power bounds. The argument includes $R=0$; when $n=1$, $D_\mu =1$. Fixed positive factors do not affect the order, since their logarithms are divided by $\log \epsilon $. $\square$

title: Lemma 26.19.13

text: Lemma 26.19.13 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n$, let $\Omega $ be a Kähler form, and let $B$ be a smooth closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form. Suppose a smooth nef background $\theta $ satisfies \[  \theta \leq CB,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq cB  \] as currents, for constants $c,C>0$ and a real function $\varphi \in L^1(X)$. For every Hermitian form $h$ and smooth strictly positive probability form $\mu $, there are constants $k,K>0$ such that, for $0<\epsilon \leq 1$, 26.142 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-logarithmic-quotient-comparison} k\lambda _\mu (B+\epsilon \Omega ) \leq \lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) \leq K\lambda _\mu (B+\epsilon \Omega ). \end{equation} If $B$ has constant rank $R$, there are moreover constants $L,U>0$ with \[  L\epsilon ^{n-R}\leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) \leq U\epsilon ^{n-R},\qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1.  \] In particular, $\theta $ then has common order $n-R$. Proof. Choose $c_ h,C_ h>0$ with $c_ h\Omega \leq h\leq C_ h\Omega $. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, distributional Stokes gives \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\langle \varphi ,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma ^{n-1}\rangle =0.  \] The lower bound for $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ therefore gives $\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon h)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq k\int _ X(B+\epsilon \Omega )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ with $k=\min (c,c_ h)$, and the upper bound for $\theta $ gives the reverse inequality with $K=\max (C,C_ h)$. Dividing by $D_\mu (\gamma )>0$ and taking infima over all Gauduchon metrics proves ( 26.142 ); no rank hypothesis has been used. Now suppose that $B$ has constant rank $R$. Its $R$ positive eigenvalues relative to $\Omega $ are then bounded above and away from zero, uniformly on $X$. With $A_\epsilon =B+\epsilon \Omega $, compactness gives constants $m_0,M_0>0$ with 26.143 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-projective-pointwise-volume} m_0\epsilon ^{n-R}\mu \leq A_\epsilon ^ n \leq M_0\epsilon ^{n-R}\mu ,\qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1. \end{equation} For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, the pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  A_\epsilon \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq \left(\frac{A_\epsilon ^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n,  \] and hence $\lambda _\mu (A_\epsilon )\geq m_0^{1/n}\epsilon ^{(n-R)/n}$. In the other direction, the positive closed form $\gamma =A_\epsilon $ is itself an admissible test. Writing $A_\epsilon ^ n=f_\epsilon \mu $, we have \[  \begin{aligned}  D_\mu (A_\epsilon )& =\int _ X f_\epsilon ^{(n-1)/n}\mu \geq m_0^{(n-1)/n}\epsilon ^{(n-R)(n-1)/n},\\  \int _ X A_\epsilon ^ n& \leq M_0\epsilon ^{n-R}, \end{aligned}  \] so the quotient of this test is at most $M_0m_0^{-(n-1)/n}\epsilon ^{(n-R)/n}$. Raising both bounds to the $n$th power and using ( 26.142 ) gives the two-sided power bounds. The argument includes $R=0$; when $n=1$, $D_\mu =1$. Fixed positive factors do not affect the order, since their logarithms are divided by $\log \epsilon $. $\square$

title: Linear blowups and the fixed generators
search_title: Linear blowups and the fixed generators
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Linear blowups and the fixed generators The manifolds are products of factors of two kinds. A plain factor is $Z_ i=\mathbb P^{m_ i}$ with $m_ i\geq 1$; let $H_ i$ be its Fubini–Study form normalized to have integral one on lines, and set $\kappa _ i=H_ i$. A blown-up factor is \[  Z_ i=\operatorname {Bl}_{\mathbb P^{\ell _ i}}\mathbb P^{m_ i}, \qquad m_ i\geq 2,\quad 0\leq \ell _ i\leq m_ i-2, \qquad r_ i=m_ i-\ell _ i-1,  \] the blowup of $\mathbb P^{m_ i}$ along a linear subspace of dimension $\ell _ i$. We describe one such factor and suppress the index for the moment. In homogeneous coordinates $[z_0:\cdots :z_\ell :w_0:\cdots :w_ r]$ on $\mathbb P^ m$, with the center $\{ w=0\} $, the blowup has the incidence model \[  Z=\{ (x,[t])\in \mathbb P^ m\times \mathbb P^ r: w_ at_ b=w_ bt_ a\text{ for all }a,b\} .  \] Let $p:Z\to \mathbb P^ m$ and $q:Z\to \mathbb P^ r$ be the projections. In the chart $t_ j=1$, the equations $w_ a=t_ aw_ j$ are the usual charts of the blowup along $\{ w_0=\cdots =w_ r=0\} $. Writing $w=\lambda t$ shows that $q$ is locally a $\mathbb P^{\ell +1}$-bundle, with fiber coordinates $[z:\lambda ]$. Thus $Z$ is smooth, $q$ is a submersion, and the incidence inclusion is an embedding. With $\omega _ m$ and $\omega _ r$ the normalized Fubini–Study forms on $\mathbb P^ m$ and $\mathbb P^ r$, set \[  H=p^*\omega _ m,\qquad Q=q^*\omega _ r,\qquad \kappa =H+Q.  \] The form $\kappa $ is Kähler, as the restriction of a product Kähler form, whereas $Q$ is semipositive of constant rank $r$. Let $E=\{ w=0\} $ be the exceptional divisor. The coordinate section $w_ j$ of $p^*\mathcal O(1)$ vanishes exactly on $E+q^{-1}\{ t_ j=0\} $, so $\mathcal O(E)=p^*\mathcal O(1)\otimes q^*\mathcal O(-1)$. Give this line bundle the product metric, whose curvature is $H-Q$. For its canonical section $s_ E$, the function $\psi _ E=\log |s_ E|^2$ is locally integrable, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula, as in section 26.21 , gives 26.146 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-projective-exceptional-potential} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ E=[E]-H+Q,\qquad H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _ E/2)=\tfrac 12(\kappa +[E])\geq \kappa /2. \end{equation} On $X=\prod _ i Z_ i$, put $n=\sum _ i m_ i$, and pull back all forms from the factors. Fix smooth strictly positive functions $f_ i$ on $X$, and, for each blown-up factor, a smooth strictly positive function $g_ i$ on $X$; these functions may depend on all coordinates of the product. The fixed cone consists of the backgrounds 26.147 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-fixed-projective-cone} \theta =\sum _ i\bigl ((a_ i+b_ if_ i)H_ i+(c_ i+d_ ig_ i)Q_ i\bigr ), \qquad a_ i,b_ i,c_ i,d_ i\geq 0, \end{equation} where the terms involving $Q_ i$, and the parameters $c_ i,d_ i$, are omitted for plain factors. All coefficient functions and generators are fixed, and only the parameters vary. Every member of the cone is smooth and semipositive, hence nef. We say that $H_ i$ occurs in $\theta $ if $a_ i+b_ i>0$, and that $Q_ i$ occurs if $c_ i+d_ i>0$. Define 26.148 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-projective-effective-rank} R_ i(\theta )= \begin{cases}  m_ i,& \text{if }H_ i\text{ occurs},\\  r_ i,& \text{if }H_ i\text{ does not occur and }Q_ i\text{ occurs},\\  0,& \text{if neither occurs}, \end{cases} \qquad R(\theta )=\sum _ i R_ i(\theta ). \end{equation} The middle case can only occur on blown-up factors. Theorem 26.19.14 . Every background $\theta $ in the fixed cone ( 26.147 ) has common order $n-R(\theta )$. More precisely, for every smooth positive probability form $\mu $ and Hermitian form $h$ there are constants $L,U>0$, depending on $\theta ,\mu ,h$, such that 26.152 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-projective-power-bounds} L\epsilon ^{n-R(\theta )} \leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) \leq U\epsilon ^{n-R(\theta )},\qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1. \end{equation} Proof. Let $B_\theta $ be the sum of the forms $\kappa _ i$ over the factors in which $H_ i$ occurs and of the forms $Q_ i$ over the factors in which only $Q_ i$ occurs. It is closed and semipositive of constant rank $R(\theta )$. Since the coefficients are bounded and $H_ i,Q_ i\leq \kappa _ i$, we have $\theta \leq CB_\theta $ for some $C>0$. For the lower bound, let $s_ i=\min _ X(a_ i+b_ if_ i)>0$ for each blown-up factor in which $H_ i$ occurs, and put \[  \varphi =\sum _{\substack {i\text{ blown up}\\ H_ i\text{ occurs}}} (s_ i/2)\psi _{E_ i}.  \] By ( 26.146 ), $s_ iH_ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(s_ i\psi _{E_ i}/2)=(s_ i/2)(\kappa _ i+[E_ i])\geq (s_ i/2)\kappa _ i$. The remaining terms $(a_ i+b_ if_ i-s_ i)H_ i$ and all terms involving $Q_ i$ are semipositive. On plain factors in which $H_ i$ occurs and on factors in which only $Q_ i$ occurs, the relevant coefficient is bounded below by a positive constant. Taking the minimum of these constants gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq cB_\theta $ for some $c>0$. For $\theta =0$ take $\varphi =0$ and any $c>0$. Now apply lemma 26.19.13 with $\Omega =\sum _ i\kappa _ i$. $\square$ Members of the fixed cone need not be closed: by construction \[  \mathrm d\theta =\sum _ i b_ i\, \mathrm df_ i\wedge H_ i +\sum _{i\text{ blown up}}d_ i\, \mathrm dg_ i\wedge Q_ i.  \] If only one of these terms has a nonzero coefficient and the corresponding form, say $\mathrm df_ i\wedge H_ i$, is nonzero, then $\theta $ is not closed. On a blown-up factor, for instance, if $g$ is a small positive perturbation of a constant that varies along a fiber of $q$, then $\mathrm dg\wedge Q\ne 0$, since $r\geq 1$. On $\mathbb P^ p\times \mathbb P^ q$ with $p,q\geq 1$, a positive function $f$ that varies on the second factor gives the nonclosed background $fH_1$ of order $q$. Adding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a smooth function does not change the exterior derivative.

title: Equality of orders under modifications
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Equality of orders under modifications By proposition 26.19.8 , pulling back by a modification can only increase the orders. For the fixed cone, the orders are preserved. Proposition 26.19.15 . Replacing some plain factors by linear blowups as above preserves the order of every background in the fixed cone. More generally, for every modification $\pi :Y\to X$ with $Y$ a compact Kähler manifold, the pullback $\pi ^*\theta $ has common order $n-R(\theta )$, and satisfies two-sided power bounds with this exponent for every smooth positive probability form and every Hermitian perturbation on $Y$. Proof. For a product of linear blowups, pull back the coefficient functions and take the new coefficients of the forms $Q_ i$ to be zero. A form $H_ i$ that occurs on a plain factor becomes a form $H_ i$ that occurs on a blown-up factor, with the same rank $m_ i$, and factors in which nothing occurs remain so. Hence theorem 26.19.14 , applied on both products, gives the same order. For a general compact Kähler manifold $Y$, pull back the semipositive smooth remainders and the divisor identities used in the proof above. Each nonzero holomorphic section remains nonzero under the surjective map $\pi $, and the logarithm of the squared norm of its pullback is locally integrable, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ equal to the current of its effective zero divisor minus the pulled-back curvature. Hence \[  \pi ^*\theta \leq C\pi ^*B_\theta ,\qquad \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi \circ \pi )\geq c\pi ^*B_\theta .  \] Fix a Kähler form $\Omega _ Y$ on $Y$, and apply the first part of lemma 26.19.13 , which needs no rank hypothesis; the pulled-back background is semipositive and hence nef. Put $R=R(\theta )$. Pullback does not increase rank, so $(\pi ^*B_\theta )^{R+1}=0$, while \[  \int _ Y(\pi ^*B_\theta )^ R\wedge \Omega _ Y^{n-R}>0:  \] for $R>0$ the integrand is positive on the nonempty set where $\pi $ is biholomorphic, and for $R=0$ the integral is the Kähler volume. For any smooth positive probability form $\mu _ Y$, the closed nef formula following theorem 26.10.1 gives \[  \mathcal V_{\mu _ Y}(\pi ^*B_\theta +\epsilon \Omega _ Y) =\sum _{k=0}^{R}\binom nk\epsilon ^{n-k} \int _ Y(\pi ^*B_\theta )^ k\wedge \Omega _ Y^{n-k}.  \] All coefficients are nonnegative and the coefficient for $k=R$ is positive, so this polynomial is bounded above and below by positive multiples of $\epsilon ^{n-R}$ for $0<\epsilon \leq 1$. The comparison of quotients gives the same bounds for $\pi ^*\theta +\epsilon h_ Y$. In particular, the order upstairs equals the order downstairs. $\square$

text:
Subtracting effective divisors We now subtract effective divisors from members of the fixed cone. Let $\mathcal O(H_ i)$ and $\mathcal O(Q_ i)$ be the pullbacks of $\mathcal O(1)$ under the projections defining $H_ i$ and $Q_ i$, with their Fubini–Study metrics, whose curvature forms are $H_ i$ and $Q_ i$. Consider line bundles that are tensor products of integer powers of these bundles, negative powers included, and finite nonnegative real combinations of zero divisors of their nonzero holomorphic sections $s_
u $: \[   egin{gathered} D=\sum _

u \geq 0,\ \eta _ D=\sum _ i(\delta _ iH_ i+ho _ iQ_ i),\qquad \Phi _ D=\sum _

u |^2. \end{gathered}  \] Here $\eta _ D$ is the corresponding combination of the curvature forms of the fixed metrics, so that $[D]=\eta _ D+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ D$. The terms involving $Q_ i$ are omitted for plain factors. Lemma 26.19.16 . The coefficients $(\delta _ i,ho _ i)$ that occur for divisors $D$ of this form are exactly those satisfying \[  \delta _ i\geq 0	ext{ on plain factors};\qquad \delta _ i\geq 0,\quad \delta _ i+ho _ i\geq 0 	ext{ on blown-up factors}.  \] Proof. It suffices to treat one nonzero holomorphic section $s$, since nonnegative real combinations preserve the inequalities. Choose a point at which $s$ is nonzero and which lies outside all exceptional divisors, and fix the coordinates of the other factors. A projective line through that point inside a fiber of $q_ i$ has $H_ i$-degree one and $Q_ i$-degree zero. The restriction of $s$ to it is a nonzero section, so the exponent of $\mathcal O(H_ i)$ is nonnegative. On a plain factor, a line through the point gives the same inequality. On a blown-up factor, write the chosen point as $([z:w],[w])$ with $w
e 0$, and choose a linear map $A$ with $Aw=z$. The section of $q_ i$ given by $[t]\mapsto ([At:t],[t])$ passes through the point, and both $H_ i$ and $Q_ i$ have degree one on each projective line in its image. Such a line through the point exists because $r_ i\geq 1$, and $s$ restricts nontrivially to it. Its degree shows that the sum of the two exponents is nonnegative. Conversely, let $F_ i$ be the pullback under $q_ i$ of a hyperplane. An admissible pair $(\delta _ i,ho _ i)$ is realized by $\delta _ iE_ i+(\delta _ i+ho _ i)F_ i$, since $E_ i$ has curvature $H_ i-Q_ i$, and coefficients on plain factors are realized by hyperplanes. These are allowed nonnegative combinations and give every coefficient tuple in the stated range. $\square$ Theorem 26.19.17 . Let $	heta $ be in the fixed cone, with parameters $a_ i,b_ i,c_ i,d_ i$, and let $D$ be a divisor of the above form. Assume \[  a_ i\geq \delta _ i	ext{ for all }i,\qquad c_ i\geq ho _ i	ext{ for every blown-up factor}.  \] Then the residual $ eta =	heta -\eta _ D$ lies in the fixed cone, and the common orders $a( eta )$ and $a(	heta )$ satisfy \[  a( eta )-a(	heta )=\sum _ i igl (R_ i(	heta )-R_ i( eta ) igr )\geq 0.  \] Equality holds if and only if, for every factor,  egin{align*}  a_ i-\delta _ i+b_ i& >0& & 	ext{whenever }a_ i+b_ i>0,\  c_ i-ho _ i+d_ i& >0& & 	ext{whenever }a_ i=b_ i=0	ext{ and }c_ i+d_ i>0; \end{align*} the second condition concerns only blown-up factors. Proof. The residual parameters $(a_ i-\delta _ i,b_ i,c_ i-ho _ i,d_ i)$ are nonnegative, so $ eta $ lies in the fixed cone; in particular it is smooth, semipositive and nef. Also \[  (	heta - eta )+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ D=[D]\geq 0,  \] which is the positive-current comparison of proposition 26.19.10 . Apply theorem 26.19.14 to $	heta $ and to $ eta $. If $H_ i$ occurs in $	heta $ but not in $ eta $, the rank $R_ i$ drops from $m_ i$ to $r_ i<m_ i$ or to zero. If $H_ i$ does not occur in $	heta $, then $a_ i=b_ i=0$, and the range of lemma 26.19.16 together with $a_ i\geq \delta _ i$ forces $\delta _ i=0$ and hence $ho _ i\geq 0$; thus $Q_ i$ cannot appear in $ eta $ if it was absent from $	heta $. Therefore no rank $R_ i$ increases, each difference $R_ i(	heta )-R_ i( eta )$ is nonnegative, and the sum vanishes exactly when the generator that determines $R_ i(	heta )$ still occurs in $ eta $ for every $i$. This is the stated pair of conditions. $\square$ The parameter inequalities guarantee that the residual stays in the fixed cone; they do not describe all divisors whose residual is nef. Example 26.19.18 . On $Z=\operatorname {Bl}_{\mathbb P^\ell }\mathbb P^ m$, choose a smooth function $g>0$ with $\mathrm dg\wedge Q
e 0$. For $t>0$, the nonclosed positive background $	heta _ t=tH+gQ$ has order zero. Removing $sE$, with its fixed curvature form $s(H-Q)$ and $0\leq s\leq t$, gives \[   eta _ s=(t-s)H+(g+s)Q,\qquad 	heta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(s\psi _ E)=s[E]+ eta _ s.  \] Every residual $ eta _ s$ is nef and not closed. Its order equals that of $	heta _ t$ exactly for $s<t$, and at $s=t$ the order jumps by $\ell +1$. These examples realize each integer jump $1,\ldots ,m-1$. Proof. The lower bound $	heta _ t\geq \min (t,\min g)\kappa >0$ shows that $	heta _ t$ is positive. For $s<t$ the form $H$ occurs in $ eta _ s$ and the rank is $m$; at $s=t$ only $Q$ occurs, with rank $r=m-\ell -1$. The order formula gives zero and $m-r=\ell +1$, respectively. The exterior derivative of every residual is $\mathrm dg\wedge Q
e 0$. Finally, let $\ell $ range from zero to $m-2$. $\square$ At the endpoint $s=t$, the current $t[E]+ eta _ t$ in the class of $	heta _ t$ has a divisorial part, although the minimal multiplicities of $	heta _ t$ vanish because $	heta _ t$ is nef, as explained before corollary 26.19.12 . The construction uses three hypotheses in an essential way: the coefficient functions are strictly positive, the subtracted divisor keeps the residual in the fixed cone, and, for general modifications, the source manifold is Kähler. Without such hypotheses the question in 26.19.49 is open.
