title: 27.7.2 The Hopf equilibrium measure
text: 27.7.2 The Hopf equilibrium measure On the Hopf manifold, the quotient equilibrium measure is a Hermitian Monge–Ampère measure: the vertical part of the Hopf metric supplies the missing fiber direction. The constant relating the two measures combines the fiber probability with a coefficient of the top power. Use the Hopf manifold $X_ n$, $n\geq 2$, its projection $\pi :X_ n\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$, the Fubini–Study form $\sigma $ on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ with $\int \sigma ^{n-1}=1$, and the forms $\alpha =\pi ^*\sigma $, $\zeta $ and $\omega =\alpha +\zeta $ of chapter 22 ; recall that $\zeta ^2=0$ and that $\zeta $ has integral two on each fiber. Take $A=\mathcal O(1)$ with its Fubini–Study metric, so that $\theta =\sigma $, and keep the selecting potential $\psi $ and the weighted data $(K,w,\mu )$ above. On each elliptic fiber put $\nu _ y=\zeta |_{X_ y}/2$. The lift of a base measure $\tau $ is then \[  \mathcal L\tau =\tfrac 12\pi ^*\tau \wedge \zeta ,  \] in the fiber-integration notation of chapter 22 . Since $E\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$, theorem 22.2.1 gives $\mathcal L(\mathrm{MA}_\sigma (E))=(2n)^{-1}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (\pi ^*E)$, and theorem 27.7.2 becomes 27.24 \begin{equation} \label{eq:hopf-partial-equilibrium} \frac{(n-1)!}{m^{n-1}}B_{X_ n,m}\, \mu _ X \rightharpoonup \frac{1}{2n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (\pi ^*E). \end{equation} The factor $1/(2n)$ combines the fiber probability $1/2$ with the coefficient $n$ of $\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta $ in $\omega ^ n=(\alpha +\zeta )^ n$. The closed curvature form $\alpha $ alone gives nothing: by theorem 22.2.1 , descended potentials have zero Monge–Ampère measure with respect to $\alpha $, and the nonzero limit comes from the vertical form $\zeta $. For $n=3$ this gives a nonzero limit, with the normalization $2/m^2$, on a manifold without the bounded mass property (theorem 8.0.1 ). For a positive integer $k$, every $k\alpha $-plurisubharmonic function on $X_ n$ is pulled back from $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, by theorem 22.1.1 . An $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, by contrast, can have an isolated pole, and then it does not descend. Its selected sections still descend, so the pole is recorded by a vanishing condition on the base. The next two sections determine this condition and its effect on the kernels.

27.8 Isolated logarithmic poles on a fibration Return to a fibration with compact connected fibers, and let the selecting potential have isolated logarithmic poles on the total space. Every selected section descends to the base, and in large tensor powers it must vanish to a certain order at the images of the poles. This order is computed from integrability in all variables of the total space, so it differs from the order imposed by a pole of the same coefficient on the base by at most the fiber dimension. The jets in between span $O(m^{q-1})$ dimensions on a $q$-dimensional base. This is negligible after normalization by $m^ q$, so the kernel measures converge to the same quotient equilibrium measure as for the corresponding poles on the base. The comparison rests on the following elementary fact: for nested section spaces, the total variation of the difference of their kernel measures is the normalized codimension. Lemma 27.8.1 . Let $B$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $q\geq 1$, let $A	o B$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth Hermitian metric, let $v\in C(B)$, and let $
u $ be a smooth positive probability volume on $B$. For every integer $m\geq 1$ let $W_ m\subseteq V_ m\subseteq H^0(B,A^ m)$ be subspaces, both with the norm $\| \cdot \| _{m,v,
u }$, and put $d_ m=\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m$. Write $B_{V_ m,v}$, $B_{W_ m,v}$ for their kernels and $ eta _{V_ m,v}^{(q)}$, $ eta _{W_ m,v}^{(q)}$ for their kernel measures, defined as in section 27.1 with the space indicated by the subscript. Then \[   egin{gathered} B_{V_ m,v}-B_{W_ m,v}\geq 0,\ \|  eta _{V_ m,v}^{(q)}- eta _{W_ m,v}^{(q)}\| _{\mathrm{TV}} = rac{q!d_ m}{m^ q}. \end{gathered}  \] The determinant functionals of the two spaces, each normalized to vanish at the zero weight, satisfy \[  |\mathcal F_{V_ m}^{(q)}(v)-\mathcal F_{W_ m}^{(q)}(v)| \leq  rac{q!d_ m}{m^ q}\| v\| _\infty .  \] These statements include the case of zero-dimensional spaces. Proof. Extend an orthonormal basis of $W_ m$ to an orthonormal basis of $V_ m$ for the norm at the weight $v$. The difference of the kernels is the sum of the squared weighted evaluations of the $d_ m$ added basis vectors. It is nonnegative, and its integral against $
u $ is $d_ m$, which gives the total variation formula. For the determinant functionals, apply the first-variation formula of proposition 27.5.1 to each of the two fixed spaces, and integrate the difference along $t\mapsto tv$, $0\leq t\leq 1$. By what we have just proved, at each $t$ the difference of the kernel measures is positive with total mass $q!d_ m/m^ q$, so its integral against $v$ is at most $q!d_ m\| v\| _\infty /m^ q$ in absolute value. Since both functionals vanish at zero, this proves the last assertion. $\square$ Return to a submersion $\pi :X	o B$ and a pulled-back line bundle $L=\pi ^*A$ as in section 27.7 , and write $f=n-q$ for the fiber dimension. Proposition 27.8.2 . Pullback identifies the selected space $H^0(X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi ))$ with \[  V_ m=H^0\left(B,A^ m\otimes  igcap _{b\in Z}\mathfrak m_ b^{r_{m,b}}ight).  \] The space \[  W_ m=H^0\left(B,A^ m\otimes  igcap _{b\in Z}\mathfrak m_ b^{s_{m,b}}ight)  \] satisfies $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$ and \[  0\leq \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m \leq \sum _{b\in Z}\sum _{j=r_{m,b}}^{s_{m,b}-1}  inom {j+q-1}{q-1} =O(m^{q-1}),  \] where an empty inner sum is zero. The implied constant depends only on the points and their coefficients, not on $m$. Proof. Lemma 1.16.1 , applied with a point as center, gives \[  \mathcal I(m\varphi )_{p_ j}=\mathfrak m_{p_ j}^{\max \{ \lfloor ma_ jfloor -n+1,0\} };  \] away from the points $p_ j$ the ideal is the full structure sheaf. Every section of $L^ m$ descends to $B$, by the argument in proposition 27.7.1 . Near $p_ j$ choose submersion coordinates $(z,	au )$ with $\pi (z,	au )=z$. A pulled-back section has a local coefficient $g(z)$ that does not depend on $	au $, and its vanishing order at $(0,0)$ equals the vanishing order of $g$ at $z=0$. The conditions imposed by the points of one fiber are therefore vanishing conditions at the same base point, and the strongest of them is vanishing to order $r_{m,b}$. This proves the identification. For the dimension bound, map each section in $V_ m$ to its jets modulo $\mathfrak m_ b^{s_{m,b}}$ at the finitely many points $b\in Z$. The kernel of this map is $W_ m$, so local trivializations of $A^ m$ give an injection \[  V_ m/W_ m\hookrightarrow  igoplus _{b\in Z}\mathfrak m_ b^{r_{m,b}}/ \mathfrak m_ b^{s_{m,b}}.  \] Surjectivity of the jet map is not needed. In $q$ variables there are $ inom {j+q-1}{q-1}$ monomials of degree $j$, which gives the dimensions of these quotients. Finally $0\leq s_{m,b}-r_{m,b}\leq f$ and $s_{m,b}=O(m)$, which proves the bound, also when $q=1$ or $f=0$. $\square$ Equip $A$ with a smooth metric $h_ A$ and put $	heta =c_1(A,h_ A)$. u _ B$ on $B$, smooth fiber probabilities as in section 27.7 , and the smooth positive volume $
u _ X=\mathcal L
u _ B$ on $X$. Use the pullback metric on $L$, and for $v\in C(B)$ use the weight $v\circ \pi $ in the norm on $X$. We write $ eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)}$ and $\mathcal F_{X,m}^{(q)}$ for the kernel measure and the determinant functional on $X$ defined by these data and the selecting potential $\varphi $. Theorem 27.8.3 . Assume that $B$ is Kähler and that there is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,	heta )$ with positive non-pluripolar mass, locally bounded off $Z$, such that \[  \psi (z)=a_ b\log |z-b|^2+O(1)\quad \hbox{near each }b\in Z  \] in local coordinates $z$ on $B$. Let $E(v)=E_{	heta ,B}[\psi ]_{\mathcal I}(v)$. Then, for the selecting potential $\varphi $ of ( 27.25 ), \[   eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)} ightharpoonup \mathcal L igl (\mathrm{MA}_	heta (E(v)) igr ).  \] More precisely, the total variation distance between $ eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)}$ and the lift of the kernel measure on $B$ selected by $\psi $ is $O(m^{-1})$. The determinant functionals satisfy \[  \mathcal F_{X,m}^{(q)}(v\circ \pi )\longrightarrow \int _0^1\! \left(\int _ B v\, \mathrm{d}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (E(tv))ight)\mathrm{d}t.  \] The normalized dimensions $q!N_ m/m^ q$ converge to the total mass of the limit measure, which is finite and positive. If $n>q$, the kernel measures with the normalization $n!/m^ n$ tend to zero in total variation. Proof. By lemma 1.16.1 in dimension $q$, the space of sections of $A^ m$ selected by $\psi $ on $B$ is the space $W_ m$ of proposition 27.8.2 . Corresponding sections in $V_ m$ and on $X$ have equal norms, since their pointwise norms and the continuous weight are pulled back from $B$ and every fiber probability has mass one. As in proposition 27.7.1 , pulling back an orthonormal basis shows that the kernel measure on $X$ is the lift of the kernel measure of $V_ m$ on $B$. By lemma 27.8.1 , proposition 27.8.2 , the $q$-normalized kernel measures of $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ on $B$ differ by a positive measure of total mass $O(m^{-1})$, and so do their lifts. Apply theorem 27.6.3 on $B$, with the identity as Kähler modification; its hypotheses are among ours. It gives the convergence of the kernel measures of $W_ m$, and since the difference tends to zero, the asserted limit on $X$ follows. By the same lemma, the determinant functionals of $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ differ by at most $O(m^{-1})\| v\| _\infty $. The isometric identification of the norms and corollary 27.6.4 on $B$ give the limit of the functionals. Testing the constant function one proves the assertion about the dimensions. Since the $q$-normalized masses are bounded, multiplying them by $(n!/q!)m^{q-n}$ proves the last assertion. $\square$ If $	heta >0$, lemma 1.16.2 , applied on $B$ with the Hermitian form $	heta $, constructs the required $\psi $ whenever the coefficients $a_ b$ are sufficiently small. Off the poles, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ then dominates a positive multiple of $	heta $, so the non-pluripolar mass of $\psi $ is positive; it is finite because $	heta $ is closed and $B$ is Kähler. The same lemma, applied on $X$ with a Hermitian form, constructs $\varphi $. If the fibers have positive dimension, such a function $\varphi $ does not descend to $B$, since it is finite at the other points of a fiber containing a pole. The section formula of proposition 27.8.2 also shows that the kernels cannot recover the singularities of the selecting potential. Moving an isolated pole within its fiber does not change any selected space, and neither does adding further poles in that fiber whose coefficients do not exceed the largest one. For the fixed pullback metric $h=\pi ^*h_ A$, continuous weight $v\circ \pi $ and lifted volume $
u _ X$, all kernels and determinant functionals are therefore the same in every degree. The multiplier ideals on $X$ are nevertheless different: for large weights, the ideal of one potential is a proper ideal at a point where the ideal of the other is the full local ring. Under the hypotheses of theorem 27.8.3 , this loss of information occurs together with a positive limit at the growth rate $m^ q$. In the closed theory, by contrast, the limit envelope has the multiplier-ideal type of the selecting potential (theorem 27.3.1 ); this property is lost when the selecting potential is plurisubharmonic only with respect to a Hermitian form.

title: 27.9 A point pole on the Hopf manifold

text:
27.9 A point pole on the Hopf manifold On the Hopf manifold the comparison of section 27.8 can be made completely explicit. A single point pole selects the homogeneous polynomials whose degree in affine coordinates centered at the image point is bounded below, and summing the squared norms of the normalized monomials expresses the kernel as a binomial tail. The exponential rate of this tail determines the limit of the Fubini–Study potentials, and its concentration determines the limit of the measures. The limit potential has a pole along the entire fiber through the original pole, which makes the loss of the point singularity explicit. Since lemma 1.17.10 also applies on the base, the map $u=w\circ \pi \mapsto w$ identifies the competitors on $X_ n$ with the competitors for $E_ a$ considered above. Their largest members therefore correspond under pullback. Finally, theorem 22.2.1 and the measure formula on the base give the last identity. $\square$

title: 27.10 Singularities along a section over a divisor
search_title: Singularities along a section over a divisor

27.10 Singularities along a section over a divisor We now replace the isolated poles by a pole along the image of a holomorphic section of the fibration over a divisor of the base. The selected sections must then vanish to a certain order along that divisor. As for point poles, the normal variables in the fiber shift the integrability threshold only by a bounded amount, so this order differs from the order imposed by a divisorial pole on the base by a bounded number. Restriction sequences along the divisor show that each unit of vanishing order costs $O(m^{q-1})$ sections, and kernel convergence again reduces to the equilibrium theorem on the base. For the restriction sequences we need a bound for the dimensions of section spaces that is uniform over a range of twists growing linearly with $m$. Lemma 27.10.1 . Let $M$ be a compact complex manifold of dimension $d\geq 0$, and let $E,F$ be holomorphic line bundles on $M$. For each $C_0>0$ there is a constant $C_1$ such that \[  h^0(M,E^ m\otimes F^ j)\leq C_1m^ d \qquad (m\geq 1,\  j\in \mathbb Z,\  |j|\leq C_0m).  \] Proof. For $d=0$, the manifold $M$ is a finite set and the dimension is at most its number of points. Let $d\geq 1$. Fix smooth Hermitian metrics on $E$ and $F$, a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$, and finitely many coordinate charts with holomorphic frames, together with smaller subcharts that still cover $M$. For $|j|\leq C_0m$, the local weight of the metric on $E^ m\otimes F^ j$ has second derivatives bounded by $Cm$. At a point $p$ of a smaller subchart, multiply the frame by the exponential of a holomorphic affine function to remove the constant and real-linear terms of this weight at $p$. The new weight vanishes at $p$ and is bounded by $Cm|z-p|^2$ on a fixed neighborhood. A ball of radius $\varepsilon m^{-1/2}$ about $p$ lies in the chart, with $\varepsilon >0$ independent of $p$, $m$ and $j$, and on this ball the weight is bounded. The submean inequality for the holomorphic coefficient of a section $s$ on this ball gives \[  |s(p)|^2\leq Cm^ d\int _ M|s|^2\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where all constants depend only on the fixed charts, metrics, volume and $C_0$. Evaluation at $p$ has a one-dimensional target, so for an $L^2$-orthonormal basis $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ of $H^0(M,E^ m\otimes F^ j)$ its squared norm is $\sum _{\ell =1}^ N|s_\ell (p)|^2\leq Cm^ d$. Integrating over $M$ gives $N\leq C\operatorname {Vol}(M)m^ d$. $\square$ Let $\pi :X	o B$ be a surjective holomorphic submersion of connected compact complex manifolds, with connected fibers of dimension $r\geq 1$, and suppose that $B$ is Kähler of dimension $q\geq 1$. Fix a holomorphic line bundle $A$ on $B$ with a smooth Hermitian metric $h_ A$ whose curvature $	heta =c_1(A,h_ A)$ is positive. Let $Z\subset B$ be a nonempty smooth divisor, and suppose that $\pi $ has a holomorphic section $\sigma :Z	o X$ over $Z$; put $Y=\sigma (Z)$. Fix $c>0$ and a smooth metric $h_ Z$ on $\mathcal O_ B(Z)$, with curvature $\Theta _ Z$, such that $\alpha :=	heta -c\Theta _ Z>0$. Let $s_ Z$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O_ B(Z)$, and set $\psi =c\log |s_ Z|_{h_ Z}^2$. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$, chosen independently of $h_ A$. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus Y$ and that, in submersion coordinates $(x,z',w_1,\ldots ,w_ r)$ near each point of $Y$, 27.33  egin{equation} \label{eq:horizontal-center-singularity}  egin{gathered} \varphi =c\log \left(|x|^2+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^2ight)+O(1),\ Z=\{ x=0\} ,\qquad Y=\{ x=w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} , \end{gathered} \end{equation} with a locally bounded remainder. Here $x$ and $z'$ are coordinates on the base, and the vector $z'$ of the $q-1$ tangential coordinates is absent when $q=1$. Theorem 27.10.2 . The function $\psi $ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic, with positive non-pluripolar mass \[  \int _ B\mathrm{MA}_	heta (\psi )=\int _ B\alpha ^ q>0.  \] For every integer $m\geq 1$ put $\ell _ m=\lfloor mcfloor $ and $k_ m=\max \{ \ell _ m-r,0\} $. Under holomorphic descent, the spaces selected by $\varphi $ on $X$ and by $\psi $ on $B$ are \[   egin{split}  V_ m& :=H^0 igl (X,\pi ^*A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi ) igr ) =H^0 igl (B,A^ m(-k_ m Z) igr ),\  W_ m& :=H^0 igl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi ) igr ) =H^0 igl (B,A^ m(-\ell _ m Z) igr )\subseteq V_ m. \end{split}  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data, such that \[  0\leq \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m\leq Cm^{q-1}.  \] For $q=1$ the difference is at most $r\, \# Z$ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\alpha +c[Z]\geq 0$. The divisorial measure identity ( 15.31 ), applied with the residual form $\alpha >0$ and the bounded part zero, gives $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (\psi )=\alpha ^ q$, which proves the mass formula. Every section of $\pi ^*A^ m$ descends by proposition 27.7.1 . In the $r+1$ normal variables $(x,w)$, lemma 1.16.1 gives \[  \mathcal I(m\varphi )=(x,w_1,\ldots ,w_ r)^{k_ m}.  \] The local coefficient $g(x,z')$ of a pulled-back section does not depend on $w$. Expanding $g$ in powers of $x$, we see that $g$ lies in this ideal exactly when the coefficients of $x^ j$ vanish for $j<k_ m$, that is, when $x^{k_ m}$ divides $g$. This is an identity of germs in all tangential variables, so it holds at every point of $Z$. Outside $Y$ the function $\varphi $ is locally bounded. On the base, the same lemma in the single normal variable $x$ gives $\mathcal I(m\psi )=\mathcal O_ B(-\ell _ mZ)$. These facts prove the two identities and the inclusion. For $k_ m\leq j<\ell _ m$, the restriction sequence along $Z$, \[   egin{split}  0& \longrightarrow A^ m(-(j+1)Z)\longrightarrow A^ m(-jZ)\ & \longrightarrow  igl (A^ m(-jZ) igr )|_ Z\longrightarrow 0, \end{split}  \] shows that passing from vanishing order $j$ to order $j+1$ along $Z$ loses at most $h^0(Z,(A^ m(-jZ))|_ Z)$ dimensions. Apply lemma 27.10.1 on $Z$ with $E=A|_ Z$ and $F=\mathcal O_ B(-Z)|_ Z$; since $0\leq j\leq cm$, each loss is at most $Cm^{q-1}$, uniformly in $j$. There are at most $r$ steps, which proves the estimate. When $q=1$, the divisor $Z$ is a finite set and each restriction space has dimension $\# Z$, which gives the last assertion directly. $\square$ We call $\psi $ the reference potential , $W_ m$ the reference spaces , and $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m$ the defect ; the same terms are used for the analogous comparisons below. The following example shows that the order $m^{q-1}$ in theorem 27.10.2 is sharp. Example 27.10.3 . For all integers $q,r,k\geq 1$ and every real $0<c<k$, the hypotheses above are satisfied on $X=\mathbb P^ q	imes \mathbb P^ r$ with $B=\mathbb P^ q$ and $A=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ q}(k)$, for suitable choices made in the proof. For $q\geq 2$ the defect is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m = rac{r(k-c)^{q-1}}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1}+O(m^{q-2}),  \] and for $q=1$ it equals $\min \{ r,\lfloor mcfloor \} $ for every $m$. Proof. Use homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ q]$ on the base and $[W_0:\cdots :W_ r]$ on the fiber. Let $Z=\{ Z_0=0\} $ and $Y=Z	imes \{ [1:0:\cdots :0]\} $, and let $\omega _ B,\omega _ F$ be the Fubini–Study forms normalized to have top integrals one. Define \[  R_ B= rac{|Z_0|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ q|Z_ i|^2},\qquad R_ F= rac{\sum _{j=1}^ r|W_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ r|W_ j|^2},\qquad \varphi =c\log (R_ B+R_ F),\quad \psi =c\log R_ B.  \] The function $\varphi $ is smooth off $Y$ and satisfies ( 27.33 ). Over a common denominator, the numerator of $R_ B+R_ F$ is \[  \sum _{j=0}^ r|Z_0W_ j|^2+\sum _{i=0}^ q\sum _{j=1}^ r|Z_ iW_ j|^2,  \] whose logarithm is plurisubharmonic in each affine chart. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -c(\omega _ B+\omega _ F)$. Choose an integer $b\geq c$ and set $\omega =k\omega _ B+b\omega _ F$. This is a Hermitian form, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq (k-c)\omega _ B+(b-c)\omega _ F\geq 0$. On the base, $	heta =k\omega _ B$, $\Theta _ Z=\omega _ B$ and $\alpha =(k-c)\omega _ B>0$. Put $\ell _ m=\lfloor mcfloor $. Divisibility of homogeneous polynomials by powers of $Z_0$ gives the exact dimensions \[  \dim W_ m= inom {km-\ell _ m+q}{q},\qquad \dim V_ m= inom {km-\max \{ \ell _ m-r,0\} +q}{q}.  \] For large $m$, the two residual degrees differ by $r$ and equal $(k-c)m+O(1)$. Subtracting the two binomial coefficients, which are polynomials of degree $q$ in the residual degrees, gives the asserted leading coefficient and remainder. For $q=1$ the difference is $\ell _ m-\max \{ \ell _ m-r,0\} =\min \{ r,\ell _ m\} $ for every $m$. $\square$ The bounded shift of divisorial order thus has negligible normalized codimension. To compare the kernels under the hypotheses of theorem 27.10.2 , fix a smooth positive probability volume $
u _ B$ on $B$, smooth fiber probabilities, and the lifting map $\mathcal L$ of section 27.7 , and put $
u _ X=\mathcal L
u _ B$. Use the pullback metric on $\pi ^*A$ and, for a real function $v\in C(B)$, the weight $v\circ \pi $ in the norm on $X$. Write $ eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)}$ and $\mathcal F_{X,m}^{(q)}$ for the kernel measure and the determinant functional on $X$, as in section 27.8 , and \[  E(v)=E_{	heta ,B}[\psi ]_{\mathcal I}(v).  \] Corollary 27.10.4 . The total variation distance between the kernel measure $ eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)}$ selected by $\varphi $ on $X$ and the lift of the kernel measure selected by $\psi $ on $B$ is $O(m^{-1})$. In particular, \[   eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)} ightharpoonup \mathcal L igl (\mathrm{MA}_	heta (E(v)) igr ).  \] The determinant functionals, normalized to vanish at the zero weight, satisfy \[  \mathcal F_{X,m}^{(q)}(v\circ \pi )\longrightarrow \int _0^1\left(\int _ Bv\, \mathrm{d}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (E(tv))ight)\mathrm{d}t.  \] With the normalization $(q+r)!/m^{q+r}$ given by the dimension of $X$, the kernel measures tend to zero in total variation. Proof. As in proposition 27.7.1 , fiber integration identifies the norm on $X$ with the norm on $V_ m\subseteq H^0(B,A^ m)$, so the kernel measure on $X$ is the lift of the kernel measure of $V_ m$ on $B$. By lemma 27.8.1 , theorem 27.10.2 , the latter differs from the kernel measure of $W_ m$ by a positive measure of total mass $q!(\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m)/m^ q=O(m^{-1})$, and so do the lifts. Since $B$ is Kähler and $\psi $ has positive non-pluripolar mass, the equilibrium theorem used in the proof of theorem 27.7.2 applies to $W_ m$ and gives the weak limit. By lemma 27.8.1 , the determinant functionals of $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ differ by at most $O(m^{-1})\| v\| _\infty $, and corollary 27.6.4 , applied on $B$ with the identity modification, gives the limit of the functionals; its dominated convergence bound is $\| v\| _\infty $ times the bounded sequence of $q$-normalized dimensions. Finally, the $q$-normalized masses are bounded, so multiplying them by $(q+r)!m^{-r}/q!$ proves the last assertion. $\square$ Thus the selecting potentials of ( 27.33 ) admit the approximation asked for in 33.9.2 , whenever the curvature margin $	heta -c\Theta _ Z$ is positive.

title: 27.10.1 A bounded divisorial band from fiber integrability
search_title: A bounded divisorial band from fiber integrability
text: 27.10.1 A bounded divisorial band from fiber integrability The comparison of theorem 27.10.2 does not need the exact local form ( 27.33 ). It suffices to bound the selecting potential from below by a divisorial pole on all of $X$, and from above by an anisotropic model in a single chart over the divisor. The lower bound gives the inclusion of the reference spaces into the selected spaces. The upper bound forces vanishing along the divisor to an order that falls short of the reference order by a bounded amount: separate powers of the normal variables replace the shift by the fiber dimension with a weighted shift. The selecting potential may then be singular along a positive-dimensional subset of a fiber, and it need not descend to the base. Let $\pi :X\to B$ be a surjective holomorphic submersion of connected compact complex manifolds with connected fibers of dimension $f\geq 1$, and let $B$ be Kähler of dimension $q\geq 1$. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$, a holomorphic line bundle $A$ on $B$ with a smooth Hermitian metric $h$, and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Write $\theta =c_1(A,h)$, and use holomorphic descent to regard the selected spaces as subspaces of $H^0(B,A^ m)$: \[  V_ m=H^0\bigl (X,\pi ^*A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi )\bigr ) \subseteq H^0(B,A^ m),\qquad m\geq 1.  \] Let $D\subset B$ be a nonempty smooth connected reduced divisor. Fix a smooth metric $H_ D$ on $\mathcal O_ B(D)$, and write $s_ D$ for its canonical section and $\eta =c_1(\mathcal O_ B(D),H_ D)$ for its curvature. Lemma 27.10.5 . Let $r\geq 1$ and $\ell \geq 0$ be integers, let $p,b_1,\ldots ,b_ r$ be positive integers, and let $P>0$. The function \[  |z|^{2\ell }\left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)^{-P}  \] of $(z,w)\in \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^ r$ is locally integrable near the origin if and only if \[  \frac{\ell +1}{p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r\frac1{b_ j}>P.  \] In the case of equality, the integral diverges logarithmically. Proof. After integrating over the angles, substitute $x_0=|z|^{2p}$ and $x_ j=|w_ j|^{2b_ j}$. Up to a positive constant, the integral becomes \[  \int (x_0+\cdots +x_ r)^{-P}x_0^{(\ell +1)/p-1} \prod _{j=1}^ r x_ j^{1/b_ j-1}\, \mathrm dx_0\cdots \mathrm dx_ r  \] over a box near the origin. This box contains a small simplex $\{ \sum _ jx_ j<\delta \} $ and is contained in a larger one. On either simplex use the coordinates $\rho =\sum _ jx_ j$ and $x_ j=\rho y_ j$. The integral over $y$ is finite and positive, because all its exponents exceed $-1$, and the integral over $\rho $ is \[  \int _0^\delta \rho ^{(\ell +1)/p+\sum b_ j^{-1}-P-1}\, \mathrm d\rho .  \] This gives the threshold and the logarithmic divergence at equality. Bounded factors in the weight, holomorphic units and additional tangential variables do not affect this local test. $\square$ Theorem 27.10.6 . Suppose that $c>0$ and $u\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$ satisfy \[  \beta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-c\eta >0, \qquad \varphi \geq c\log \| \pi ^*s_ D\| _{H_ D}^2-C \quad \hbox{on }X  \] for a constant $C$. Suppose further that there is one submersion polydisk over an open subset of $D$, with coordinates \[  \pi (z,t,w,v)=(z,t),\quad D=\{ z=0\} ,\quad t\in \mathbb C^{q-1},\quad w\in \mathbb C^ r,\quad v\in \mathbb C^{f-r},  \] where $1\leq r\leq f$, on which \[  \varphi \leq \frac cp\log \left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)+C'  \] for positive integers $p,b_1,\ldots ,b_ r$ and a constant $C'$. Put \[  a=p\sum _{j=1}^ r b_ j^{-1},\quad L_ m=\lfloor mc\rfloor ,\quad K_ m=\max \{ \lfloor mc-a\rfloor ,0\} ,\quad \psi =u+c\log \| s_ D\| _{H_ D}^2.  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$, its non-pluripolar mass is $\int _ B\beta ^ q\in (0,\infty )$, and for every $m\geq 1$, \[  W_ m:=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )\bigr ) =H^0(B,A^ m(-L_ mD))\subseteq V_ m \subseteq H^0(B,A^ m(-K_ mD)).  \] Moreover $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=O(m^{q-1})=o(m^ q)$. For $q=1$ this difference is at most $\lceil a\rceil $ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta +c[D]$. Off $D$, locality identifies the non-pluripolar top power with $\beta ^ q$; the non-pluripolar product puts no mass on $D$, and neither does the smooth measure $\beta ^ q$. Hence $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\beta ^ q$, whose mass is finite and positive because $\beta >0$ and $B$ is compact. The one-variable integrability condition $\ell +1>mc$ gives $\mathcal I(m\psi )=\mathcal O_ B(-L_ mD)$, also when $mc$ is an integer. Since $u$ is bounded, the global lower bound implies $\varphi \geq \psi \circ \pi -C''$. Hence integrability on the base gives integrability of the pullback in every bounded submersion chart, which proves $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$. For the upper inclusion, take a nonzero section in $V_ m$ and let $\ell $ be its vanishing order along $D$; note that $D$ is irreducible, being smooth and connected. In the polydisk of the upper bound, the coefficient of the section is $z^\ell g(z,t)$, where $g(0,t)$ does not vanish identically on the open subset of $D$, since otherwise the identity theorem would increase the order along $D$. Shrink the polydisk about a point with $w=0$ at which $g(0,t)\ne 0$, so that $g$ becomes a holomorphic unit. The upper bound on $\varphi $ and lemma 27.10.5 then force $\ell +1>mc-a$. For an integer $\ell \geq 0$ this is equivalent to $\ell \geq K_ m$, which proves the upper inclusion. Since $\lfloor mc\rfloor -\lfloor mc-a\rfloor \leq \lceil a\rceil $, we have $0\leq L_ m-K_ m\leq \lceil a\rceil $. Use the restriction sequences along $D$ from the proof of theorem 27.10.2 for $K_ m\leq j<L_ m$. Each step loses at most $h^0(D,(A^ m(-jD))|_ D)$ dimensions, and by lemma 27.10.1 this is at most $Cm^{q-1}$, uniformly for $0\leq j\leq cm$. Since the number of steps is bounded, the estimate follows. For $q=1$ the connected divisor $D$ is a single point, and each restriction space has dimension one. $\square$ Corollary 27.10.7 . Keep the positivity condition $\beta >0$ of theorem 27.10.6 . Suppose that a nonempty compact smooth submanifold $Z\subset \pi ^{-1}(D)$ projects submersively onto $D$, and that near every point of $Z$ there are coordinates as in that theorem in which \[  Z=\{ z=w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} ,\qquad \varphi =\frac cp\log \left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)+O(1),  \] with fixed $c,p,b_ j$. Suppose also that $\varphi $ is locally bounded outside $Z$. Then $\varphi $ satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 27.10.6 , so its conclusions hold, and moreover \[  V_ m=H^0(B,A^ m(-K_ mD))\qquad (m\geq 1).  \] Proof. The local model is bounded below by $c\log |z|^2$ up to a constant. Near points of $\pi ^{-1}(D)$ outside $Z$, the function $\varphi $ is locally bounded, so the same lower bound holds there; away from $\pi ^{-1}(D)$ both functions are locally bounded. By compactness, finitely many charts give the global lower bound. The upper bound holds in any chart of the model. Conversely, if a section is divisible by $z^{K_ m}$, its residual coefficient is bounded and holomorphic in each chart of the model, and the strict inequality $K_ m+1>mc-a$ together with lemma 27.10.5 gives integrability there. Outside $Z$ the function $\varphi $ is locally bounded, which proves the reverse inclusion. $\square$ Such exact models exist with pole sets of positive dimension inside the fibers. Let $B$ be projective, let $A$ be ample, and let $X=B\times (\mathbb P^1)^ f$ with $\pi $ the first projection. Mark a point $o_ j$ in each of the first $r$ factors $\mathbb P^1$ of the fiber, and let $E_ j\subset X$ be the inverse image of $o_ j$. With smooth metrics on the corresponding line bundles, put \[  Q=\| \pi ^*s_ D\| ^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r\| s_{E_ j}\| ^{2b_ j}, \qquad \varphi =\lambda \log Q,\qquad c=p\lambda .  \] The common zero set of the terms of $Q$ is $D\times \{ o_1\} \times \cdots \times \{ o_ r\} \times (\mathbb P^1)^{f-r}$. Near it, the positive factors of the metrics give exactly the local model of corollary 27.10.7 , and $\varphi $ is smooth elsewhere. The inequality $Q\geq \| \pi ^*s_ D\| ^{2p}$ gives the global lower bound. Locally, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log Q$ is bounded below by a convex combination of the negatives of the smooth curvature forms of the terms; hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log Q\geq -C_0\omega $ for a constant $C_0$, first off the common zero set and then across it, after a quadratic correction, by the extension theorem for plurisubharmonic functions. Since $A$ is ample, there is $u$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. For sufficiently small $\lambda >0$ we then have $\lambda C_0\leq 1$, so that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-p\lambda \eta >0$. Thus the exact series of the corollary also occurs when $r<f$. Example 27.10.8 . Let $B=\mathbb P^ q$ with a hyperplane $D$, let $A=\mathcal O_ B(1)$, and let $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$. Let $\omega _ B,\omega _ F$ be the Fubini–Study forms normalized to have total mass one, and use the corresponding metrics on the divisor line bundles. For a point $o\in \mathbb P^1$ set \[  \varphi =\tfrac 14\log \bigl (\| s_ D\| ^4+\| s_ o\| ^6\bigr ),\qquad \omega =\omega _ B+\omega _ F.  \] Then $p=2$, $b_1=3$, $c=1/2$, $a=2/3$, and the reference potential $\psi =\tfrac 12\log \| s_ D\| ^2$ has mass $2^{-q}$. The spaces $V_1$ and $W_1$ agree, and for every $m\geq 2$ the defect is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m =\binom {\lceil m/2\rceil +q}{q-1} \sim \frac{2^{1-q}}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1}.  \] For $q=1$ the defect is exactly one for every $m\geq 2$. Proof. Locally, the complex Hessian of the logarithm of a sum of two squared norms of holomorphic sections is bounded below by a convex combination of the negatives of their curvature forms. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -\tfrac 12\omega _ B-\tfrac 34\omega _ F$ off the pole set, and across it by the extension theorem after a quadratic correction. Thus $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The pole set is $D\times \{ o\} $, along which $\varphi $ has the exact local model of corollary 27.10.7 . Here $u=0$, $\beta =\tfrac 12\omega _ B$, and $K_ m=L_ m-1$ for $m\geq 2$, while $K_1=L_1=0$. The spaces $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ therefore correspond to homogeneous polynomials of degrees $m-L_ m+1$ and $m-L_ m$, and since $m-L_ m=\lceil m/2\rceil $, the difference of their dimensions is the displayed binomial coefficient. $\square$ In this example $\varphi $ is finite on most of each fiber over $D$ and equals $-\infty $ on a proper subset of it, so $\varphi $ differs from every pullback of a function on $B$ by an unbounded amount. For $p=b_ j=1$ and $r=f$, the shift $a=f$ is the shift by the fiber dimension found in theorem 27.10.2 . Theorem 27.10.6 thus gives sufficient conditions for the approximation asked for in 33.9.2 ; we do not know which other fiber singularities admit such an approximation. The assumption $f\geq 1$ excludes only a trivial case. If the fibers have dimension zero, then $\pi $ is a covering, since $X$ is compact and $\pi $ is a submersion, and hence a biholomorphism, since the fibers are connected. If, in addition, the descended selecting potential is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic with finite positive mass, taking it as $\psi $ gives $V_ m=W_ m$.

title: Lemma 27.10.5
text: Lemma 27.10.5 . Let $r\geq 1$ and $\ell \geq 0$ be integers, let $p,b_1,\ldots ,b_ r$ be positive integers, and let $P>0$. The function \[  |z|^{2\ell }\left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)^{-P}  \] of $(z,w)\in \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^ r$ is locally integrable near the origin if and only if \[  \frac{\ell +1}{p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r\frac1{b_ j}>P.  \] In the case of equality, the integral diverges logarithmically. Proof. After integrating over the angles, substitute $x_0=|z|^{2p}$ and $x_ j=|w_ j|^{2b_ j}$. Up to a positive constant, the integral becomes \[  \int (x_0+\cdots +x_ r)^{-P}x_0^{(\ell +1)/p-1} \prod _{j=1}^ r x_ j^{1/b_ j-1}\, \mathrm dx_0\cdots \mathrm dx_ r  \] over a box near the origin. This box contains a small simplex $\{ \sum _ jx_ j<\delta \} $ and is contained in a larger one. On either simplex use the coordinates $\rho =\sum _ jx_ j$ and $x_ j=\rho y_ j$. The integral over $y$ is finite and positive, because all its exponents exceed $-1$, and the integral over $\rho $ is \[  \int _0^\delta \rho ^{(\ell +1)/p+\sum b_ j^{-1}-P-1}\, \mathrm d\rho .  \] This gives the threshold and the logarithmic divergence at equality. Bounded factors in the weight, holomorphic units and additional tangential variables do not affect this local test. $\square$

title: Theorem 27.10.6
text: Theorem 27.10.6 . Suppose that $c>0$ and $u\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$ satisfy \[  \beta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-c\eta >0, \qquad \varphi \geq c\log \| \pi ^*s_ D\| _{H_ D}^2-C \quad \hbox{on }X  \] for a constant $C$. Suppose further that there is one submersion polydisk over an open subset of $D$, with coordinates \[  \pi (z,t,w,v)=(z,t),\quad D=\{ z=0\} ,\quad t\in \mathbb C^{q-1},\quad w\in \mathbb C^ r,\quad v\in \mathbb C^{f-r},  \] where $1\leq r\leq f$, on which \[  \varphi \leq \frac cp\log \left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)+C'  \] for positive integers $p,b_1,\ldots ,b_ r$ and a constant $C'$. Put \[  a=p\sum _{j=1}^ r b_ j^{-1},\quad L_ m=\lfloor mc\rfloor ,\quad K_ m=\max \{ \lfloor mc-a\rfloor ,0\} ,\quad \psi =u+c\log \| s_ D\| _{H_ D}^2.  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$, its non-pluripolar mass is $\int _ B\beta ^ q\in (0,\infty )$, and for every $m\geq 1$, \[  W_ m:=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )\bigr ) =H^0(B,A^ m(-L_ mD))\subseteq V_ m \subseteq H^0(B,A^ m(-K_ mD)).  \] Moreover $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=O(m^{q-1})=o(m^ q)$. For $q=1$ this difference is at most $\lceil a\rceil $ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta +c[D]$. Off $D$, locality identifies the non-pluripolar top power with $\beta ^ q$; the non-pluripolar product puts no mass on $D$, and neither does the smooth measure $\beta ^ q$. Hence $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\beta ^ q$, whose mass is finite and positive because $\beta >0$ and $B$ is compact. The one-variable integrability condition $\ell +1>mc$ gives $\mathcal I(m\psi )=\mathcal O_ B(-L_ mD)$, also when $mc$ is an integer. Since $u$ is bounded, the global lower bound implies $\varphi \geq \psi \circ \pi -C''$. Hence integrability on the base gives integrability of the pullback in every bounded submersion chart, which proves $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$. For the upper inclusion, take a nonzero section in $V_ m$ and let $\ell $ be its vanishing order along $D$; note that $D$ is irreducible, being smooth and connected. In the polydisk of the upper bound, the coefficient of the section is $z^\ell g(z,t)$, where $g(0,t)$ does not vanish identically on the open subset of $D$, since otherwise the identity theorem would increase the order along $D$. Shrink the polydisk about a point with $w=0$ at which $g(0,t)\ne 0$, so that $g$ becomes a holomorphic unit. The upper bound on $\varphi $ and lemma 27.10.5 then force $\ell +1>mc-a$. For an integer $\ell \geq 0$ this is equivalent to $\ell \geq K_ m$, which proves the upper inclusion. Since $\lfloor mc\rfloor -\lfloor mc-a\rfloor \leq \lceil a\rceil $, we have $0\leq L_ m-K_ m\leq \lceil a\rceil $. Use the restriction sequences along $D$ from the proof of theorem 27.10.2 for $K_ m\leq j<L_ m$. Each step loses at most $h^0(D,(A^ m(-jD))|_ D)$ dimensions, and by lemma 27.10.1 this is at most $Cm^{q-1}$, uniformly for $0\leq j\leq cm$. Since the number of steps is bounded, the estimate follows. For $q=1$ the connected divisor $D$ is a single point, and each restriction space has dimension one. $\square$

title: Corollary 27.10.7
text: Corollary 27.10.7 . Keep the positivity condition $\beta >0$ of theorem 27.10.6 . Suppose that a nonempty compact smooth submanifold $Z\subset \pi ^{-1}(D)$ projects submersively onto $D$, and that near every point of $Z$ there are coordinates as in that theorem in which \[  Z=\{ z=w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} ,\qquad \varphi =\frac cp\log \left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)+O(1),  \] with fixed $c,p,b_ j$. Suppose also that $\varphi $ is locally bounded outside $Z$. Then $\varphi $ satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 27.10.6 , so its conclusions hold, and moreover \[  V_ m=H^0(B,A^ m(-K_ mD))\qquad (m\geq 1).  \] Proof. The local model is bounded below by $c\log |z|^2$ up to a constant. Near points of $\pi ^{-1}(D)$ outside $Z$, the function $\varphi $ is locally bounded, so the same lower bound holds there; away from $\pi ^{-1}(D)$ both functions are locally bounded. By compactness, finitely many charts give the global lower bound. The upper bound holds in any chart of the model. Conversely, if a section is divisible by $z^{K_ m}$, its residual coefficient is bounded and holomorphic in each chart of the model, and the strict inequality $K_ m+1>mc-a$ together with lemma 27.10.5 gives integrability there. Outside $Z$ the function $\varphi $ is locally bounded, which proves the reverse inclusion. $\square$

title: Example 27.10.8
text: Example 27.10.8 . Let $B=\mathbb P^ q$ with a hyperplane $D$, let $A=\mathcal O_ B(1)$, and let $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$. Let $\omega _ B,\omega _ F$ be the Fubini–Study forms normalized to have total mass one, and use the corresponding metrics on the divisor line bundles. For a point $o\in \mathbb P^1$ set \[  \varphi =\tfrac 14\log \bigl (\| s_ D\| ^4+\| s_ o\| ^6\bigr ),\qquad \omega =\omega _ B+\omega _ F.  \] Then $p=2$, $b_1=3$, $c=1/2$, $a=2/3$, and the reference potential $\psi =\tfrac 12\log \| s_ D\| ^2$ has mass $2^{-q}$. The spaces $V_1$ and $W_1$ agree, and for every $m\geq 2$ the defect is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m =\binom {\lceil m/2\rceil +q}{q-1} \sim \frac{2^{1-q}}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1}.  \] For $q=1$ the defect is exactly one for every $m\geq 2$. Proof. Locally, the complex Hessian of the logarithm of a sum of two squared norms of holomorphic sections is bounded below by a convex combination of the negatives of their curvature forms. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -\tfrac 12\omega _ B-\tfrac 34\omega _ F$ off the pole set, and across it by the extension theorem after a quadratic correction. Thus $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The pole set is $D\times \{ o\} $, along which $\varphi $ has the exact local model of corollary 27.10.7 . Here $u=0$, $\beta =\tfrac 12\omega _ B$, and $K_ m=L_ m-1$ for $m\geq 2$, while $K_1=L_1=0$. The spaces $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ therefore correspond to homogeneous polynomials of degrees $m-L_ m+1$ and $m-L_ m$, and since $m-L_ m=\lceil m/2\rceil $, the difference of their dimensions is the displayed binomial coefficient. $\square$

title: 27.10.2 Several crossing base divisors
text: 27.10.2 Several crossing base divisors Keep the submersion $\pi :X\to B$, the line bundle $(A,h)$, the selecting potential $\varphi $ and the descended spaces $V_ m$ of section 27.10.1 . Several divisorial singularities can be handled at once if the divisors cross normally. At their intersections the integrability test on the base separates in normal coordinates, and a bounded change of each divisorial order again costs only $O(m^{q-1})$ sections. For this we need the restriction estimate with all the divisorial twists at once. Lemma 27.10.9 . Let $M$ be a compact complex manifold of dimension $d\geq 0$, and let $E,F_1,\ldots ,F_ N$ be holomorphic line bundles on $M$. For each $C_0>0$ there is a constant $C_1$ such that \[  h^0\left(M,E^ m\otimes \bigotimes _{i=1}^ NF_ i^{j_ i}\right)\leq C_1m^ d \qquad (m\geq 1,\  j_ i\in \mathbb Z,\  |j_ i|\leq C_0m).  \] Proof. For $d=0$ the dimension is at most the number of points of $M$. For $d\geq 1$, use fixed smooth metrics, a smooth positive volume form and finitely many framed charts as in the proof of lemma 27.10.1 . The local weight of the metric is $m\phi _ E+\sum _ i j_ i\phi _{F_ i}$, whose second derivatives are bounded by $Cm$ uniformly over the stated range. After its constant and real-linear terms at a point have been removed by a holomorphic affine change of frame, it is bounded by a fixed constant on a ball of radius $\varepsilon m^{-1/2}$ about that point. The submean inequality then gives $|s(x)|^2\leq Cm^ d\| s\| _{L^2}^2$, uniformly in $x$, $m$ and the integers $j_ i$. Since evaluation has a one-dimensional target, an orthonormal basis satisfies $\sum _\ell |s_\ell (x)|^2\leq Cm^ d$, and integration gives the estimate. The constants depend only on the fixed bundles, metrics, charts, volume and $C_0$. $\square$ Let $D_1,\ldots ,D_ N$ be distinct nonempty smooth connected reduced divisors on $B$ whose union has simple normal crossings. For each $i$, choose a smooth metric $H_ i$ on $\mathcal O_ B(D_ i)$, and write $s_ i$ for the canonical section and $\eta _ i$ for the curvature. Theorem 27.10.10 . Suppose that $c_1,\ldots ,c_ N>0$ and $u\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$ satisfy \[  \beta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\eta _ i>0, \qquad \varphi \geq \sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\log \| \pi ^*s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2-C \quad \hbox{on }X.  \] Suppose that for each $i$ there is a submersion polydisk over an open subset of $D_ i\setminus \bigcup _{j\ne i}D_ j$, with coordinates $(z_ i,t_ i,w_ i,v_ i)$ as in theorem 27.10.6 , on which \[  \varphi \leq \frac{c_ i}{p_ i}\log \left(|z_ i|^{2p_ i} +\sum _{j=1}^{r_ i}|w_{ij}|^{2b_{ij}}\right)+C_ i, \qquad 1\leq r_ i\leq f,  \] where $p_ i$ and $b_{ij}$ are positive integers and $C_ i$ is a constant. Put \[  \begin{gathered} a_ i=p_ i\sum _{j=1}^{r_ i}b_{ij}^{-1},\quad L_{m,i}=\lfloor mc_ i\rfloor ,\quad K_{m,i}=\max \{ \lfloor mc_ i-a_ i\rfloor ,0\} ,\\ \psi =u+\sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\log \| s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ has non-pluripolar mass $\int _ B\beta ^ q\in (0,\infty )$, and for every $m\geq 1$, \[  \begin{split}  W_ m& :=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )\bigr ) =H^0\left(B,A^ m\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right)\subseteq V_ m,\\  V_ m& \subseteq H^0\left(B,A^ m\left(-\sum _ iK_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right). \end{split}  \] Moreover $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=O(m^{q-1})$. For $q=1$ this difference is at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta +\sum _ i c_ i[D_ i]$. Off the divisors the non-pluripolar measure equals $\beta ^ q$, and neither measure charges their union. Thus $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\beta ^ q$, with finite positive total mass. Near a point of an intersection, the divisors through that point are distinct coordinate hyperplanes $\{ z_ i=0\} $. If a holomorphic germ is divisible by each corresponding $z_ i^{L_{m,i}}$, then it is divisible by their product; its residual coefficient is bounded, and since $L_{m,i}+1>mc_ i$, Fubini's theorem gives integrability. Conversely, integrability at generic nearby points of each coordinate hyperplane forces divisibility by $z_ i^{L_{m,i}}$, by the one-variable threshold, and the divisor of the germ then gives divisibility throughout the chart. This proves \[  \mathcal I(m\psi )=\mathcal O_ B\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right).  \] Since $u$ is bounded, the global lower bound implies $\varphi \geq \psi \circ \pi -C'$, and integration in submersion coordinates gives $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$. For a nonzero section in $V_ m$, the polydisk over $D_ i$ on which the upper bound holds detects the generic vanishing order of the section along the irreducible divisor $D_ i$. The argument with a unit coefficient in the proof of theorem 27.10.6 , together with the strict integrability threshold of lemma 27.10.5 , shows that this order is at least $K_{m,i}$. Imposing all these orders proves the upper inclusion. To compare dimensions, raise the orders from $(K_{m,i})_ i$ to $(L_{m,i})_ i$, one divisor and one unit at a time. At each step, the restriction sequence loses at most \[  h^0\left(D_ i,\left.A^ m\left(-\sum _ j n_ jD_ j\right)\right|_{D_ i}\right), \qquad 0\leq n_ j\leq mc_ j,  \] dimensions. By lemma 27.10.9 with $E=A|_{D_ i}$ and $F_ j=\mathcal O_ B(-D_ j)|_{D_ i}$, this is $O(m^{q-1})$ uniformly over all steps, and there are at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ steps. When $q=1$, the distinct connected divisors are points, and each restriction space has dimension one. $\square$ The upper bounds are required only away from the crossings; integrability at the crossings is controlled by the global lower bound. Exact models can nevertheless have fiber poles over the crossings, as in the following example, where different divisors use separate fiber coordinates. Example 27.10.11 . Let $B=(\mathbb P^1)^ q$, $X=B\times (\mathbb P^1)^ q$ and $A=\mathcal O_ B(1,\ldots ,1)$. For each $i$, let $D_ i\subset B$ be the inverse image of a marked point in the $i$th factor of $B$, and let $E_ i\subset X$ be the inverse image of a marked point in the $i$th factor of the fiber. Use normalized Fubini–Study metrics on the corresponding line bundles, and write $\omega _{B,i},\omega _{F,i}$ for the pullbacks to $X$ of the normalized Fubini–Study forms on the $i$th factors of $B$ and of the fiber. Put \[  \begin{gathered} R_ i=\| \pi ^*s_ i\| ^2,\quad T_ i=\| s_{E_ i}\| ^2,\quad \varphi =\frac14\sum _{i=1}^ q\log (R_ i^2+T_ i^3),\\ \omega =\sum _ i(\omega _{B,i}+\omega _{F,i}),\qquad \psi =\frac12\sum _ i\log \| s_ i\| ^2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and theorem 27.10.10 applies with $u=0$, $c_ i=1/2$, $p_ i=2$, $b_{i1}=3$ and $a_ i=2/3$. The reference potential $\psi $ has mass $q!/2^ q$. With $L_ m=\lfloor m/2\rfloor $ and $K_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2-2/3\rfloor ,0\} $, the selected and reference spaces are exactly \[  \begin{split}  V_ m& =H^0\bigl (B,\mathcal O_ B(m-K_ m,\ldots ,m-K_ m)\bigr ),\\  W_ m& =H^0\bigl (B,\mathcal O_ B(m-L_ m,\ldots ,m-L_ m)\bigr ). \end{split}  \] They agree for $m=1$, and for $m\geq 2$ the defect is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m =(\lceil m/2\rceil +2)^ q-(\lceil m/2\rceil +1)^ q.  \] For $q\geq 2$ this is $q2^{1-q}m^{q-1}+O(m^{q-2})$, and for $q=1$ it is exactly one. Proof. By the calculation in example 27.10.8 , the complex Hessian of each summand of $\varphi $ is bounded below by $-\tfrac 12\omega _{B,i}-\tfrac 34\omega _{F,i}$, also across its pole set by the extension theorem after a quadratic correction. Summing proves $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The global lower bound follows from $R_ i^2+T_ i^3\geq R_ i^2$. For the upper bound over $D_ i$, away from the other divisors, place the $i$th fiber coordinate at its marked point; all the other summands are smooth there. The residual is $\beta =\tfrac 12\sum _ i\omega _{B,i}>0$, whose top integral is $q!/2^ q$. The theorem gives the required generic orders along every $D_ i$. Conversely, near a point where several of the pairs $(R_ i,T_ i)$ vanish, the density $\mathrm{e}^{-m\varphi }$ is comparable to the product of the factors $(|z_ i|^4+|w_ i|^6)^{-m/4}$ in disjoint pairs of variables. A descended coefficient divisible by every $z_ i^{K_ m}$ has a bounded holomorphic residual. Each factor is integrable because $K_ m+1>m/2-2/3$, and Fubini's theorem gives integrability at the intersections; elsewhere the same argument uses fewer factors. This proves the identity for $V_ m$, and the theorem gives $W_ m$. A line bundle $\mathcal O_ B(d,\ldots ,d)$ with $d\geq 0$ has $(d+1)^ q$ independent sections, the products of monomials in the separate factors. Since $K_ m=L_ m-1$ for $m\geq 2$ and $m-L_ m=\lceil m/2\rceil $, subtraction gives the displayed defect and its leading term. $\square$ As before, the selecting potential takes finite values and the value $-\infty $ in the fibers over the divisors, so it does not descend. Theorem 27.10.10 extends the sufficient conditions for 33.9.2 to normal crossing divisors; it does not cover base ideals of other forms, and it gives no necessary conditions.

title: Lemma 27.10.9
text: Lemma 27.10.9 . Let $M$ be a compact complex manifold of dimension $d\geq 0$, and let $E,F_1,\ldots ,F_ N$ be holomorphic line bundles on $M$. For each $C_0>0$ there is a constant $C_1$ such that \[  h^0\left(M,E^ m\otimes \bigotimes _{i=1}^ NF_ i^{j_ i}\right)\leq C_1m^ d \qquad (m\geq 1,\  j_ i\in \mathbb Z,\  |j_ i|\leq C_0m).  \] Proof. For $d=0$ the dimension is at most the number of points of $M$. For $d\geq 1$, use fixed smooth metrics, a smooth positive volume form and finitely many framed charts as in the proof of lemma 27.10.1 . The local weight of the metric is $m\phi _ E+\sum _ i j_ i\phi _{F_ i}$, whose second derivatives are bounded by $Cm$ uniformly over the stated range. After its constant and real-linear terms at a point have been removed by a holomorphic affine change of frame, it is bounded by a fixed constant on a ball of radius $\varepsilon m^{-1/2}$ about that point. The submean inequality then gives $|s(x)|^2\leq Cm^ d\| s\| _{L^2}^2$, uniformly in $x$, $m$ and the integers $j_ i$. Since evaluation has a one-dimensional target, an orthonormal basis satisfies $\sum _\ell |s_\ell (x)|^2\leq Cm^ d$, and integration gives the estimate. The constants depend only on the fixed bundles, metrics, charts, volume and $C_0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 27.10.10
text: Theorem 27.10.10 . Suppose that $c_1,\ldots ,c_ N>0$ and $u\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$ satisfy \[  \beta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\eta _ i>0, \qquad \varphi \geq \sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\log \| \pi ^*s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2-C \quad \hbox{on }X.  \] Suppose that for each $i$ there is a submersion polydisk over an open subset of $D_ i\setminus \bigcup _{j\ne i}D_ j$, with coordinates $(z_ i,t_ i,w_ i,v_ i)$ as in theorem 27.10.6 , on which \[  \varphi \leq \frac{c_ i}{p_ i}\log \left(|z_ i|^{2p_ i} +\sum _{j=1}^{r_ i}|w_{ij}|^{2b_{ij}}\right)+C_ i, \qquad 1\leq r_ i\leq f,  \] where $p_ i$ and $b_{ij}$ are positive integers and $C_ i$ is a constant. Put \[  \begin{gathered} a_ i=p_ i\sum _{j=1}^{r_ i}b_{ij}^{-1},\quad L_{m,i}=\lfloor mc_ i\rfloor ,\quad K_{m,i}=\max \{ \lfloor mc_ i-a_ i\rfloor ,0\} ,\\ \psi =u+\sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\log \| s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ has non-pluripolar mass $\int _ B\beta ^ q\in (0,\infty )$, and for every $m\geq 1$, \[  \begin{split}  W_ m& :=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )\bigr ) =H^0\left(B,A^ m\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right)\subseteq V_ m,\\  V_ m& \subseteq H^0\left(B,A^ m\left(-\sum _ iK_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right). \end{split}  \] Moreover $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=O(m^{q-1})$. For $q=1$ this difference is at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta +\sum _ i c_ i[D_ i]$. Off the divisors the non-pluripolar measure equals $\beta ^ q$, and neither measure charges their union. Thus $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\beta ^ q$, with finite positive total mass. Near a point of an intersection, the divisors through that point are distinct coordinate hyperplanes $\{ z_ i=0\} $. If a holomorphic germ is divisible by each corresponding $z_ i^{L_{m,i}}$, then it is divisible by their product; its residual coefficient is bounded, and since $L_{m,i}+1>mc_ i$, Fubini's theorem gives integrability. Conversely, integrability at generic nearby points of each coordinate hyperplane forces divisibility by $z_ i^{L_{m,i}}$, by the one-variable threshold, and the divisor of the germ then gives divisibility throughout the chart. This proves \[  \mathcal I(m\psi )=\mathcal O_ B\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right).  \] Since $u$ is bounded, the global lower bound implies $\varphi \geq \psi \circ \pi -C'$, and integration in submersion coordinates gives $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$. For a nonzero section in $V_ m$, the polydisk over $D_ i$ on which the upper bound holds detects the generic vanishing order of the section along the irreducible divisor $D_ i$. The argument with a unit coefficient in the proof of theorem 27.10.6 , together with the strict integrability threshold of lemma 27.10.5 , shows that this order is at least $K_{m,i}$. Imposing all these orders proves the upper inclusion. To compare dimensions, raise the orders from $(K_{m,i})_ i$ to $(L_{m,i})_ i$, one divisor and one unit at a time. At each step, the restriction sequence loses at most \[  h^0\left(D_ i,\left.A^ m\left(-\sum _ j n_ jD_ j\right)\right|_{D_ i}\right), \qquad 0\leq n_ j\leq mc_ j,  \] dimensions. By lemma 27.10.9 with $E=A|_{D_ i}$ and $F_ j=\mathcal O_ B(-D_ j)|_{D_ i}$, this is $O(m^{q-1})$ uniformly over all steps, and there are at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ steps. When $q=1$, the distinct connected divisors are points, and each restriction space has dimension one. $\square$

title: Example 27.10.11
text: Example 27.10.11 . Let $B=(\mathbb P^1)^ q$, $X=B\times (\mathbb P^1)^ q$ and $A=\mathcal O_ B(1,\ldots ,1)$. For each $i$, let $D_ i\subset B$ be the inverse image of a marked point in the $i$th factor of $B$, and let $E_ i\subset X$ be the inverse image of a marked point in the $i$th factor of the fiber. Use normalized Fubini–Study metrics on the corresponding line bundles, and write $\omega _{B,i},\omega _{F,i}$ for the pullbacks to $X$ of the normalized Fubini–Study forms on the $i$th factors of $B$ and of the fiber. Put \[  \begin{gathered} R_ i=\| \pi ^*s_ i\| ^2,\quad T_ i=\| s_{E_ i}\| ^2,\quad \varphi =\frac14\sum _{i=1}^ q\log (R_ i^2+T_ i^3),\\ \omega =\sum _ i(\omega _{B,i}+\omega _{F,i}),\qquad \psi =\frac12\sum _ i\log \| s_ i\| ^2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and theorem 27.10.10 applies with $u=0$, $c_ i=1/2$, $p_ i=2$, $b_{i1}=3$ and $a_ i=2/3$. The reference potential $\psi $ has mass $q!/2^ q$. With $L_ m=\lfloor m/2\rfloor $ and $K_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2-2/3\rfloor ,0\} $, the selected and reference spaces are exactly \[  \begin{split}  V_ m& =H^0\bigl (B,\mathcal O_ B(m-K_ m,\ldots ,m-K_ m)\bigr ),\\  W_ m& =H^0\bigl (B,\mathcal O_ B(m-L_ m,\ldots ,m-L_ m)\bigr ). \end{split}  \] They agree for $m=1$, and for $m\geq 2$ the defect is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m =(\lceil m/2\rceil +2)^ q-(\lceil m/2\rceil +1)^ q.  \] For $q\geq 2$ this is $q2^{1-q}m^{q-1}+O(m^{q-2})$, and for $q=1$ it is exactly one. Proof. By the calculation in example 27.10.8 , the complex Hessian of each summand of $\varphi $ is bounded below by $-\tfrac 12\omega _{B,i}-\tfrac 34\omega _{F,i}$, also across its pole set by the extension theorem after a quadratic correction. Summing proves $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The global lower bound follows from $R_ i^2+T_ i^3\geq R_ i^2$. For the upper bound over $D_ i$, away from the other divisors, place the $i$th fiber coordinate at its marked point; all the other summands are smooth there. The residual is $\beta =\tfrac 12\sum _ i\omega _{B,i}>0$, whose top integral is $q!/2^ q$. The theorem gives the required generic orders along every $D_ i$. Conversely, near a point where several of the pairs $(R_ i,T_ i)$ vanish, the density $\mathrm{e}^{-m\varphi }$ is comparable to the product of the factors $(|z_ i|^4+|w_ i|^6)^{-m/4}$ in disjoint pairs of variables. A descended coefficient divisible by every $z_ i^{K_ m}$ has a bounded holomorphic residual. Each factor is integrable because $K_ m+1>m/2-2/3$, and Fubini's theorem gives integrability at the intersections; elsewhere the same argument uses fewer factors. This proves the identity for $V_ m$, and the theorem gives $W_ m$. A line bundle $\mathcal O_ B(d,\ldots ,d)$ with $d\geq 0$ has $(d+1)^ q$ independent sections, the products of monomials in the separate factors. Since $K_ m=L_ m-1$ for $m\geq 2$ and $m-L_ m=\lceil m/2\rceil $, subtraction gives the displayed defect and its leading term. $\square$

title: 27.10.3 Fiber integrability on a modified base
search_title: Fiber integrability on a modified base
text: 27.10.3 Fiber integrability on a modified base Keep $\pi :X\to B$, $(A,h)$, $\theta $, $\varphi $ and $V_ m$ as in section 27.10.1 . A singularity of higher codimension on the base can become divisorial after a modification of the base. By lemma 1.22.15 , the integrability test upstairs then applies to the pulled-back section multiplied by the Jacobian. This fixed factor shifts the divisorial orders, while the restriction estimate still bounds the number of lost sections. Let $\rho :Y\to B$ be a modification of connected compact complex manifolds, and form the fiber product and its projections \[  X'=X\times _ B Y,\qquad \pi ':X'\to Y,\qquad \mu :X'\to X.  \] In local submersion coordinates one sees that $X'$ is smooth, that $\pi '$ is a submersion with the same compact connected fibers as $\pi $, and that $\mu $ is a modification. Let $R_\rho $ and $J_\rho $ be the relative canonical bundle and the Jacobian section of $\rho $, as in section 1.22.7 . The coordinate Jacobian matrix of $\mu $ is that of $\rho $, extended by the identity in the fiber variables, so \[  R_\mu =\pi '^*R_\rho ,\qquad J_\mu =\pi '^*J_\rho .  \] Put $\varphi '=\varphi \circ \mu $ and $\theta '=\rho ^*\theta $. Choose distinct nonempty smooth connected reduced divisors $D_1,\ldots ,D_ N$ on $Y$ whose union has simple normal crossings, together with smooth metrics $H_ i$ on $\mathcal O_ Y(D_ i)$, canonical sections $s_ i$ and curvatures $\eta _ i$. Theorem 27.10.12 . Suppose that $c_ i>0$ and $u\in C^\infty (Y,\mathbb R)$ satisfy \[  \beta =\theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\sum _ i c_ i\eta _ i>0, \qquad \varphi '\geq \sum _ i c_ i\log \| \pi '^*s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2-C.  \] Suppose that for each $i$ the function $\varphi '$ satisfies an anisotropic upper bound, with respect to $\pi '$, on a submersion polydisk over an open subset of $D_ i$ away from the other divisors, as in theorem 27.10.10 , with fixed $p_ i,b_{ij}$. Define $a_ i$, $L_{m,i}$ and $K_{m,i}$ by the formulas of that theorem, and put \[  \psi '=u+\sum _ i c_ i\log \| s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2, \qquad M_ m=\rho ^*A^ m\otimes R_\rho .  \] Then there is a unique $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ with $\psi \circ \rho =\psi '$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\rho _*(\beta ^ q),\qquad \int _ B\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\int _ Y\beta ^ q\in (0,\infty ).  \] The map $T_ m(s)=J_\rho \rho ^*s$ identifies $H^0(B,A^ m)$ with $H^0(Y,M_ m)$, and for $W_ m=H^0(B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi ))$, \[  \begin{split}  T_ m(W_ m)& =H^0\left(Y,M_ m\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right),\\  T_ m(W_ m)& \subseteq T_ m(V_ m) \subseteq H^0\left(Y,M_ m\left(-\sum _ iK_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right). \end{split}  \] Consequently $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$ and $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=O(m^{q-1})$. If $q=1$, the difference is at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi '=\beta +\sum _ i c_ i[D_ i]$. Thus $\psi '\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\rho ^*\theta )$, and proposition 1.22.12 gives the unique potential $\psi $ on $B$ with $\psi \circ \rho =\psi '$. On $Y$, locality off the union of the divisors and the fact that the non-pluripolar measure does not charge this union give $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta '}(\psi ')=\beta ^ q$. The measure identity in proposition 27.6.1 then gives the pushforward formula and the mass. Lemma 1.22.15 , applied first with weight zero and then with weight $m\psi $, gives the identification of the full section spaces and the formula for $T_ m(W_ m)$; here $\mathcal I(m\psi ')=\mathcal O_ Y(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i)$ by the integrability computation for simple normal crossings in the proof of theorem 27.10.10 . Since $u$ is bounded, the global lower bound gives $\varphi '\geq \psi '\circ \pi '-C'$. As $\rho \circ \pi '=\pi \circ \mu $ and $\mu $ is surjective, this descends to $\varphi \geq \psi \circ \pi -C'$, and integrability in bounded submersion charts proves $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$. For $s\in V_ m$, the transformation of multiplier ideals under $\mu $ gives \[  J_\mu \mu ^*s=\pi '^*T_ m(s) \in H^0\bigl (X',\pi '^*M_ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi ')\bigr ).  \] Hence, in each polydisk where the upper bound holds, the descended coefficient of $T_ m(s)$ vanishes to order at least $K_{m,i}$ along $D_ i$, by lemma 27.10.5 and the argument with a unit coefficient in the proof of theorem 27.10.6 . This is the vanishing order of $T_ m(s)$, including the Jacobian factor, and it proves the upper inclusion. The chain of restrictions along the divisors on $Y$ has at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ steps. On $D_ i$, each target is $(\rho ^*A|_{D_ i})^ m$ twisted by powers of the bundles $\mathcal O_ Y(-D_ j)|_{D_ i}$ in a linear range and by the fixed bundle $R_\rho |_{D_ i}$. Including the latter in lemma 27.10.9 with exponent one, we see that every target has dimension $O(m^{q-1})$, uniformly. Summing gives the estimate. For $q=1$ each divisor is a point and every target has dimension one. $\square$ The theorem requires the modification and the divisorial data to be given, with a positive residual; it does not say which selecting potentials admit such data. In the following model with a point pole on the base, both the residual and the Jacobian correction are explicit. Example 27.10.13 . Let $q\geq 2$, $B=\mathbb P^ q$, $A=\mathcal O_ B(1)$, $p=[1:0:\cdots :0]$ and $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$. Use the normalized Fubini–Study forms $\omega _ B,\omega _ F$ and the corresponding metrics, and for a point $o\in \mathbb P^1$ put \[  R=\frac{\sum _{j=1}^ q|Z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ q|Z_ j|^2},\quad T=\| s_ o\| ^2,\quad \varphi =\tfrac 14\log (R^2+T^3),\quad \psi =\tfrac 12\log R.  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega _ B+\omega _ F)$, and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\omega _ B)$ has mass $1-2^{-q}$. Let $\mathfrak m_ p$ be the ideal sheaf of $p$. The selected and reference spaces are exactly \[  \begin{gathered} V_ m=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ p^{k_ m}\bigr ),\qquad W_ m=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ p^{\ell _ m}\bigr ),\\ k_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2-2/3\rfloor -q+1,0\} ,\qquad \ell _ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2\rfloor -q+1,0\} . \end{gathered}  \] Their defect vanishes for $m<2q$, and for $m\geq 2q$ it is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=\binom {\lfloor m/2\rfloor -1}{q-1} \sim \frac{2^{1-q}}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1}.  \] Proof. Over a common denominator, $R^2+T^3$ is a sum of squared moduli of holomorphic coefficients of sections of $\mathcal O_ X(2,3)$, divided by the corresponding metric factor. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -\tfrac 12\omega _ B-\tfrac 34\omega _ F$, also across the common zero set by the extension theorem. Let $\rho :Y\to B$ be the blowup of $p$, with exceptional divisor $E$, and let $\tau :Y\to \mathbb P^{q-1}$ be the extension to $Y$ of the projection $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ q]\mapsto [Z_1:\cdots :Z_ q]$. Since $(\rho ,\tau )$ is an embedding, the forms \[  \alpha =\rho ^*\omega _ B,\quad \gamma =\tau ^*\omega _{\mathbb P^{q-1}},\qquad \beta =\tfrac 12(\alpha +\gamma )  \] satisfy $\beta >0$. The divisor bundle is $\mathcal O_ Y(E)=\rho ^*\mathcal O_ B(1)\otimes \tau ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{q-1}}(-1)$; its quotient metric has curvature $\alpha -\gamma $ and satisfies $R\circ \rho =\| s_ E\| ^2$. Thus the theorem applies with the single divisor $E$, $u=0$, $c=1/2$, $a=2/3$ and residual $\beta $. Along $E\times \{ o\} $ the pulled-back selecting potential has the exact local model $\tfrac 14\log (|z|^4+|w|^6)+O(1)$, and it is locally bounded elsewhere. If $T_ m(s)$ is divisible by $z^{K_ m}$, where $K_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2-2/3\rfloor ,0\} $, then lemma 27.10.5 gives integrability in every chart of this model; this gives the inclusion opposite to the upper inclusion of the theorem. In the blowup coordinates $Z_1/Z_0=z$ and $Z_ j/Z_0=zt_ j$ for $j\geq 2$, the Jacobian of $\rho $ is $z^{q-1}$. Hence, if a section $s$ of $A^ m$ vanishes to order $d$ at $p$, then $T_ m(s)$ vanishes to order $d+q-1$ generically along $E$. The two divisorial thresholds $\lfloor m/2\rfloor $ and $K_ m$ therefore give exactly the orders $\ell _ m$ and $k_ m$ above. Homogeneous polynomials of degree $m$ realize every jet of total degree at most $m$ at $p$. For $m\geq 2q$ we have $k_ m=\ell _ m-1$, and the additional jets of degree $\ell _ m-1$ are spanned by $\binom {\ell _ m+q-2}{q-1}$ monomials, which gives the defect. For $m<2q$ both orders vanish. Finally, in cohomology $[\beta ]=\rho ^*c_1(A)-\tfrac 12[E]$. The intersection numbers containing both $\rho ^*c_1(A)$ and $[E]$ vanish, because $\rho ^*c_1(A)$ restricts to zero on $E$. The normal bundle of $E\simeq \mathbb P^{q-1}$ is $\mathcal O_ E(-1)$, so $\int _ Y[E]^ q=(-1)^{q-1}$, while $\int _ Y(\rho ^*c_1(A))^ q=1$. Expanding gives $\int _ Y\beta ^ q=1-2^{-q}$, which is the mass of $\psi $ by the theorem. $\square$ The selecting potential is finite at most points of the fiber over $p$ and equals $-\infty $ at the point $(p,o)$, so again it does not descend, even up to a bounded function. The reference potential $\psi $ has a pole of codimension $q$ at $p$, and the Jacobian factor is what converts the divisorial orders along $E$ into vanishing orders at $p$.

Finally, in cohomology $[\beta ]=\rho ^*c_1(A)-\tfrac 12[E]$. The intersection numbers containing both $\rho ^*c_1(A)$ and $[E]$ vanish, because $\rho ^*c_1(A)$ restricts to zero on $E$. The normal bundle of $E\simeq \mathbb P^{q-1}$ is $\mathcal O_ E(-1)$, so $\int _ Y[E]^ q=(-1)^{q-1}$, while $\int _ Y(\rho ^*c_1(A))^ q=1$. Expanding gives $\int _ Y\beta ^ q=1-2^{-q}$, which is the mass of $\psi $ by the theorem. $\square$

title: 27.10.4 Semipositive residuals with positive volume
text: 27.10.4 Semipositive residuals with positive volume Strict positivity of the residual $\beta $ was used only to make the reference potential $\psi $ plurisubharmonic with positive non-pluripolar mass; the estimates for the divisorial orders do not use it. The section comparison therefore holds for semipositive residuals with positive top integral. In particular, it does not require the residual class to contain a positive form. Corollary 27.10.14 . In each of theorem 27.10.6 , theorem 27.10.10 , theorem 27.10.12 , replace the condition $\beta >0$ by \[  \beta \geq 0,\qquad \int _ M\beta ^ q>0,  \] where $M=B$ in the first two theorems and $M=Y$ in the third, and keep all the other hypotheses. Then all the conclusions remain valid. The same replacement is valid in corollary 27.10.7 . Proof. In each case the reference current is $\beta +\sum _ i c_ i[D_ i]$, which is positive. Locality off the union of the divisors, together with the fact that the non-pluripolar measure does not charge this union, gives the non-pluripolar measure $\beta ^ q$ on $M$. Its mass is finite because $\beta $ is smooth and $M$ is compact, and positive by assumption. In the case of a modified base, the potential descends and its measure is $\rho _*(\beta ^ q)$, by the same descent and measure identities as before. The multiplier ideal on the base depends only on the logarithmic divisorial orders and the bounded smooth term. The lower inclusion uses the global lower bound for the selecting potential, and the upper inclusion uses the anisotropic threshold in a polydisk where the upper bound holds; neither uses strict positivity of $\beta $. The restriction estimates concern fixed line bundles, whatever their curvature, and the Jacobian and the fixed canonical twist in the case of a modified base are unchanged. Hence the inclusions and dimension bounds in all three proofs remain valid. The reverse inclusion for the exact anisotropic model uses only its local integrability test and the local boundedness off the pole set, so it also remains valid. $\square$ The condition on the top integral concerns the chosen reference: a semipositive residual may have zero top integral. Conversely, a semipositive residual with positive top integral need not become strictly positive after any smooth change of gauge. The following example shows this, with an exact computation of the selected spaces. Example 27.10.15 . Let $q\geq 2$, let $\rho :B\to \mathbb P^ q$ be the blowup of $p=[1:0:\cdots :0]$, and let $E$ be its exceptional divisor. Let $\tau :B\to \mathbb P^{q-1}$ be the extension to $B$ of the projection from $p$, and put \[  \alpha =\rho ^*\omega _{\mathbb P^ q},\qquad \gamma =\tau ^*\omega _{\mathbb P^{q-1}},\qquad \kappa =\alpha +\gamma >0,  \] where $\omega _{\mathbb P^ q}$ and $\omega _{\mathbb P^{q-1}}$ are the normalized Fubini–Study forms. Equip $\mathcal O_ B(E)=\rho ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ q}(1)\otimes \tau ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{q-1}}(-1)$ with the quotient metric, whose curvature is $\eta =\alpha -\gamma $, and let $s_ E$ be its canonical section. For an integer $k\geq 1$, equip \[  A=\rho ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ q}(k)\otimes \mathcal O_ B(E) \quad \hbox{with curvature}\quad \theta =k\alpha +\eta .  \] Let $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$, with projection $\pi $ to $B$. For a point $o\in \mathbb P^1$, use the normalized Fubini–Study metric on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(o)$, and set \[  \begin{gathered} R=\| \pi ^*s_ E\| ^2,\quad T=\| s_ o\| ^2,\quad \varphi =\tfrac 12\log (R^2+T^3),\quad \omega =\pi ^*\kappa +2\omega _{\mathbb P^1},\\ \psi =\log \| s_ E\| ^2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=(k\alpha )^ q,\qquad \int _ B\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=k^ q.  \] The residual $k\alpha $ cannot be made strictly positive by a smooth change of gauge. Nevertheless, for every $m\geq 1$ the selected and reference spaces coincide as subspaces of $H^0(B,A^ m)$: \[  V_ m=W_ m=H^0(B,A^ m) =s_ E^ m\rho ^*H^0(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km)), \qquad \dim V_ m=\binom {km+q}{q}.  \] Proof. Since $(\rho ,\tau )$ is an embedding, $\kappa >0$. The quotient metric satisfies \[  \| s_ E\| ^2=\rho ^*\left(\frac{\sum _{j=1}^ q|Z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ q|Z_ j|^2}\right),  \] as in example 27.10.13 . The same calculation over a common denominator, now with coefficient $1/2$, gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -\pi ^*\alpha -\tfrac 32\omega _{\mathbb P^1}  \] off the pole set $E\times \{ o\} $, and across it by the extension theorem. Hence $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \pi ^*\gamma +\tfrac 12\omega _{\mathbb P^1}\geq 0$. Along the smooth pole set $E\times \{ o\} $, the function $\varphi $ has the exact local model $\tfrac 12\log (|z|^4+|w|^6)+O(1)$, and it is locally bounded elsewhere. It also satisfies the global lower bound $\varphi \geq \log R$. We may therefore take $c=1$, $u=0$, $p=2$, $b_1=3$ and $a=2/3$, with residual $\beta =\theta -\eta =k\alpha \geq 0$. Its top integral is $k^ q$, since the normalized Fubini–Study form has top integral one and $\rho $ is a modification. Corollary 27.10.14 , Corollary 27.10.7 therefore give \[  W_ m=H^0(B,A^ m(-mE)),\qquad V_ m=H^0(B,A^ m(-(m-1)E)).  \] Let $t\geq 0$ be an integer. A section of $\rho ^*\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathcal O_ B(tE)$, divided by $s_ E^ t$, gives a holomorphic section of $\mathcal O(km)$ on $\mathbb P^ q\setminus \{ p\} $, which extends across $p$ by Hartogs' theorem since $q\geq 2$. Pulling the extension back and multiplying by $s_ E^ t$ recovers the original section off $E$, hence everywhere by the identity theorem. Thus every section of $A^ m$ has the form $s_ E^ m\rho ^*s$, and the natural embeddings of $W_ m$ and $V_ m$ into $H^0(B,A^ m)$ both have this image. Its dimension is the number $\binom {km+q}{q}$ of monomials of degree $km$. Finally, let $C\subset E\simeq \mathbb P^{q-1}$ be a projective line; it is contracted by $\rho $. For every smooth real function $u$, Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ C(k\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)=0$, whereas a strictly positive form has positive integral over $C$. Changing the smooth metric on the divisor bundle changes the residual only by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a smooth function, so this proves the obstruction. Moreover, $\varphi $ is finite on most of each fiber over $E$ and equals $-\infty $ at the point $o$ of that fiber, so it does not descend, even up to a bounded function. $\square$ Thus the selected and reference spaces agree, although the selecting potential does not descend and the reference has positive mass. The reason is that $E$ is a fixed component of every section of $A^ m$: all global sections vanish along $E$ to order $m$, more than the local integrability threshold requires. As before, the criterion presupposes the global bounds for the selecting potential and a residual with positive top integral; it does not produce them for arbitrary fiber singularities.
