title: 27.10.5 Fixed exceptional orders and coefficient thresholds
search_title: Fixed exceptional orders and coefficient thresholds
text: 27.10.5 Fixed exceptional orders and coefficient thresholds In example 27.10.15 the fixed divisor $E$ absorbs the local integrability conditions. If the coefficient of the selecting potential increases, the selected sections must eventually also vanish at the point that was blown up. The following family shows when this happens, and when the mass of the reference potential vanishes. Keep the blowup $\rho :B\to \mathbb P^ q$ with $q\geq 2$, its exceptional divisor $E$, the extended projection $\tau $, the forms $\alpha ,\gamma ,\kappa $, and the quotient metric on $\mathcal O_ B(E)$ with curvature $\eta $ from that example, and write $x=\rho (E)$ for the point blown up. Let $k,e\geq 1$ be integers and equip \[  A_ e=\rho ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ q}(k)\otimes \mathcal O_ B(eE), \qquad \theta =k\alpha +e\eta  \] with the product metric. Let $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$ with its projection $\pi $, let $o\in \mathbb P^1$, and let $R=\| \pi ^*s_ E\| ^2$ and $T=\| s_ o\| ^2$ as before. For positive integers $p,b$ and a real number $c>0$, put \[  \varphi _ c=\frac cp\log (R^ p+T^ b),\quad \omega _ c=c\pi ^*\kappa +(cb/p+1)\omega _{\mathbb P^1},\quad a=\frac pb,  \] and let $V_ m(c)\subseteq H^0(B,A_ e^ m)$ be the space selected by $\mathcal I(m\varphi _ c)$, regarded on $B$ by descent. Proposition 27.10.16 . For every $c>0$ we have $\varphi _ c\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega _ c)$, and the selected space is \[  \begin{gathered} V_ m(c)=s_ E^{em}\rho ^*H^0\bigl (\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^{v_ m}\bigr ),\\ v_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m(c-e)-a\rfloor ,0\} ,\qquad m\geq 1, \end{gathered}  \] where $\mathfrak m_ x$ is the ideal sheaf of $x$. For $0<c\leq e+k$ put \[  d=\max \{ c,e\} ,\quad \delta =d-e,\quad \psi _ d=d\log \| s_ E\| ^2,\quad \ell _ m=\lfloor m\delta \rfloor .  \] Then $\psi _ d\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ and \[  \begin{gathered} \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi _ d)=\bigl ((k-\delta )\alpha +\delta \gamma \bigr )^ q, \qquad \int _ B\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi _ d)=k^ q-\delta ^ q. \end{gathered}  \] The reference spaces satisfy \[  \begin{split}  W_ m(c)& :=H^0\bigl (B,A_ e^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi _ d)\bigr )\\ & =s_ E^{em}\rho ^*H^0\bigl (\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^{\ell _ m}\bigr ) \subseteq V_ m(c). \end{split}  \] If $0<c\leq e$, both spaces equal $H^0(B,A_ e^ m)$ for every $m$. If $e<c<e+k$, the defect and the leading term of the dimension are \[  \begin{gathered} \dim V_ m(c)-\dim W_ m(c) =\binom {\ell _ m+q-1}{q}-\binom {v_ m+q-1}{q}=O(m^{q-1}),\\ \dim V_ m(c)=\frac{k^ q-(c-e)^ q}{q!}m^ q+O(m^{q-1}), \end{gathered}  \] where $\binom {q-1}{q}=0$. At $c=e+k$ the reference $\psi _ d$ has zero mass and \[  \dim V_ m(e+k) =\frac{(\lceil a\rceil +1)k^{q-1}}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1}+O(m^{q-2}).  \] If $c>e+k$, the selected space is zero exactly when \[  m(c-e-k)\geq a+1;  \] in particular, it is zero for every $m\geq \lceil (a+1)/(c-e-k)\rceil $. Proof. As in example 27.10.15 , the norm identity writes $R^ p+T^ b$ over the common denominator for $\mathcal O(p,b)$ on $\mathbb P^ q\times \mathbb P^1$, pulled back to $X$, and its numerator is a sum of squared moduli of holomorphic coefficients. The lower bound for the complex Hessian of the logarithm of such a sum, together with the extension theorem across the pole set, gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ c\geq -c\pi ^*\alpha -(cb/p)\omega _{\mathbb P^1}.  \] Thus $\omega _ c+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ c\geq c\pi ^*\gamma +\omega _{\mathbb P^1}\geq 0$. Hartogs' theorem, as in that example, shows that every global section of $A_ e^ m$ can be written uniquely as $s_ E^{em}\rho ^*s$ with $s\in H^0(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km))$. If $s$ vanishes to order $j$ at $x$, this section vanishes to order $em+j$ generically along $E$. In a chart of the pole set, $\varphi _ c=(c/p)\log (|z|^{2p}+|w|^{2b})+O(1)$. The argument with a unit coefficient in the proof of theorem 27.10.6 and lemma 27.10.5 require \[  em+j+1>mc-a, \quad \hbox{equivalently}\quad j\geq \max \{ \lfloor m(c-e)-a\rfloor ,0\} .  \] Conversely, this divisorial order gives integrability in every chart of the pole set, and $\varphi _ c$ is locally bounded elsewhere. The vanishing order of $s$ at $x$ equals the generic vanishing order of $\rho ^*s$ along $E$, as the blowup coordinates of example 27.10.13 show. This proves the formula for $V_ m(c)$. For $0\leq \delta \leq k$, the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ d=(k-\delta )\alpha +\delta \gamma +d[E]\geq 0.  \] The non-pluripolar measure does not charge $E$, and it equals the top power of the smooth residual $(k-\delta )\alpha +\delta \gamma $. The class of this residual is $k\rho ^*c_1(\mathcal O(1))-\delta [E]$. The mixed intersection numbers vanish and $\int _ B[E]^ q=(-1)^{q-1}$, as computed in example 27.10.13 , so its mass is $k^ q-\delta ^ q$. The divisorial ideal is $\mathcal I(m\psi _ d)=\mathcal O_ B(-\lfloor md\rfloor E)$. Since $em$ is an integer, $\lfloor md\rfloor =em+\ell _ m$, and the condition on $s$ is exactly $j\geq \ell _ m$. This gives the formula for $W_ m(c)$, and the inclusion follows from $\ell _ m\geq v_ m$. If $c\leq e$, both point orders are zero. For an integer $0\leq j\leq km+1$, homogeneous polynomials of degree $km$ realize every jet of total degree less than $j$ at $x$, and there are $\binom {j+q-1}{q}$ such jets. Hence \[  h^0\bigl (\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^ j\bigr ) =\binom {km+q}{q}-\binom {j+q-1}{q}.  \] For $e<c<e+k$ we have $0\leq v_ m\leq \ell _ m\leq km$ and $\ell _ m-v_ m\leq \lceil a\rceil $, and subtraction gives the exact defect. Each additional jet degree contributes $O(m^{q-1})$ monomials, which gives the bound, and $v_ m=m(c-e)+O(1)$ gives the leading term of $\dim V_ m(c)$. At $c=e+k$ we have $v_ m=\max \{ km-\lceil a\rceil ,0\} $. For large $m$, the allowed monomials have vanishing orders $km-\lceil a\rceil ,\ldots ,km$ at $x$, and each of these $\lceil a\rceil +1$ degrees has $k^{q-1}m^{q-1}/(q-1)!+O(m^{q-2})$ monomials, which proves the asymptotic formula. The residual is then $k\gamma $, whose top power vanishes. For $c>e+k$, a nonzero polynomial of degree $km$ vanishes at $x$ to order at most $km$. Hence $V_ m(c)=0$ exactly when $v_ m>km$, which is equivalent to $m(c-e-k)-a\geq 1$. $\square$ For $0<c<e+k$ the reference $\psi _ d$ has positive mass and the defect is $O(m^{q-1})$, so this family admits the approximation asked for in 33.9.2 . At $c=e+k$ the reference mass vanishes and the growth degree of the selected spaces drops to $q-1$; beyond this threshold the selected spaces eventually vanish.

The residual is then $k\gamma $, whose top power vanishes. For $c>e+k$, a nonzero polynomial of degree $km$ vanishes at $x$ to order at most $km$. Hence $V_ m(c)=0$ exactly when $v_ m>km$, which is equivalent to $m(c-e-k)-a\geq 1$. $\square$

title: 27.10.6 A semipositive residual with nonzero defect
search_title: A semipositive residual with nonzero defect
text: 27.10.6 A semipositive residual with nonzero defect Blowing up two points instead of one, we obtain a residual that is semipositive, cannot be made strictly positive, and still has positive top integral. Unlike the example with one blown-up point, the gap between the two divisorial thresholds now produces a nonzero defect of the largest possible order $m^{q-1}$. Counting the spaces requires the following elementary interpolation of jets at several points. Lemma 27.10.17 . Let $x_1,\ldots ,x_ N$ be distinct points of $\mathbb P^ q$, $q\geq 1$, and let $d,j_1,\ldots ,j_ N$ be nonnegative integers with $\sum _ i j_ i\leq d+1$. Then the map from $H^0(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(d))$ to the jets of order less than $j_ i$ at the points $x_ i$ is surjective. In particular, \[  h^0\left(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(d)\otimes \bigcap _ i\mathfrak m_{x_ i}^{j_ i}\right) =\binom {d+q}{q}-\sum _ i\binom {j_ i+q-1}{q},  \] where $\binom {q-1}{q}=0$. Proof. We may discard the points with $j_ i=0$; if no point remains, the target is zero. Choose an affine chart containing all the remaining points, and use the corresponding trivialization of $\mathcal O(d)$. For each pair $i\ne k$ choose an affine linear function $L_{ik}$ vanishing at $x_ k$ and nonzero at $x_ i$, and set \[  Q_ i=\prod _{k\ne i}L_{ik}^{j_ k}.  \] Given a jet $b_ i$ at $x_ i$, divide it by the invertible jet of $Q_ i$ at $x_ i$, and let $T_ i$ be the Taylor polynomial of degree at most $j_ i-1$ of the quotient. Then $Q_ iT_ i$ has the jet $b_ i$ at $x_ i$ and vanishes to order at least $j_ k$ at every other point $x_ k$, and its degree is at most $\sum _ kj_ k-1\leq d$. Hence $\sum _ iQ_ iT_ i$, homogenized to degree $d$, realizes all the prescribed jets. In $q$ variables there are $\binom {j_ i+q-1}{q}$ monomials of total degree less than $j_ i$, which gives the dimension formula. $\square$ Example 27.10.18 . Let $q\geq 2$ and let $\rho :B\to \mathbb P^ q$ be the blowup of the two points $x_1=[1:0:\cdots :0]$ and $x_2=[0:1:0:\cdots :0]$, with exceptional divisors $E_1,E_2$. Let $\tau _ i:B\to \mathbb P^{q-1}$ be the extension to $B$ of the projection from $x_ i$. With the normalized Fubini–Study forms, put \[  \alpha =\rho ^*\omega _{\mathbb P^ q},\qquad \gamma _ i=\tau _ i^*\omega _{\mathbb P^{q-1}},\qquad \kappa =\alpha +\gamma _1+\gamma _2>0.  \] Equip $\mathcal O_ B(E_ i)=\rho ^*\mathcal O(1)\otimes \tau _ i^*\mathcal O(-1)$ with the quotient metric, whose curvature is $\eta _ i=\alpha -\gamma _ i$, and let $s_ i$ be its canonical section. Equip \[  A=\rho ^*\mathcal O(2)\otimes \mathcal O_ B(E_1+E_2), \qquad \theta =2\alpha +\eta _1+\eta _2  \] with the product metric. On $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$, with projection $\pi $ and a point $o\in \mathbb P^1$, set \[  \begin{gathered} R_ i=\| \pi ^*s_ i\| ^2,\qquad T=\| s_ o\| ^2,\\ \varphi =\log (R_1^2+T^3)+\log (R_2^2+T^3),\\ \omega =4\pi ^*\kappa +7\omega _{\mathbb P^1},\\ \psi =2\log \| s_1\| ^2+2\log \| s_2\| ^2, \qquad \beta =\gamma _1+\gamma _2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\beta ^ q,\qquad \int _ B\beta ^ q=2^ q-2>0.  \] No smooth change of gauge makes $\beta $ strictly positive. Nevertheless, writing $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ for the selected and reference spaces as before, their images in $H^0(B,A^ m)$ are, for every $m\geq 1$, \[  \begin{aligned}  V_ m& =s_1^ ms_2^ m\rho ^*H^0\left(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(2m) \otimes \mathfrak m_{x_1}^{m-1}\mathfrak m_{x_2}^{m-1}\right),\\  W_ m& =s_1^ ms_2^ m\rho ^*H^0\left(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(2m) \otimes \mathfrak m_{x_1}^{m}\mathfrak m_{x_2}^{m}\right). \end{aligned}  \] The defect and the common leading term of the dimensions are \[  \begin{gathered} \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=2\binom {m+q-2}{q-1} \sim \frac{2}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1},\\ \dim V_ m=\frac{2^ q-2}{q!}m^ q+O(m^{q-1}),\qquad \dim W_ m=\frac{2^ q-2}{q!}m^ q+O(m^{q-1}). \end{gathered}  \] Proof. The map $(\rho ,\tau _1,\tau _2)$ is an embedding: away from the exceptional divisors $\rho $ is already an embedding, and along $E_ i$ the map $\tau _ i$ separates the tangent directions of $E_ i$ while $\rho $ detects the normal direction. Hence $\kappa >0$. The identity for the quotient metric is the one-point identity of example 27.10.15 , applied at each center. For each $i$, the calculation over a common denominator writes $R_ i^2+T^3$ as a sum of squared moduli of holomorphic coefficients over the metric denominator for $\mathcal O(2,3)$. Together with the extension theorem across the pole set, this gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -4\pi ^*\alpha -6\omega _{\mathbb P^1}.  \] It follows that $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 4\pi ^*\beta +\omega _{\mathbb P^1}\geq 0$. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta +2[E_1]+2[E_2]\geq 0.  \] The non-pluripolar product does not charge the divisors and equals $\beta ^ q$. The class of $\beta $ is $2H-[E_1]-[E_2]$, where $H=\rho ^*c_1(\mathcal O(1))$. As in example 27.10.13 , $H^ q=1$, the mixed intersection numbers involving $H$ and some $[E_ i]$ vanish, and $[E_ i]^ q=(-1)^{q-1}$; moreover, the two exceptional divisors are disjoint. Expanding gives $\int _ B\beta ^ q=2^ q-2$. Let $C$ be the strict transform of the line through $x_1$ and $x_2$. Both maps $\tau _ i$ are constant on $C$, so $\int _ C\beta =0$. By Stokes' theorem, $\int _ C(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)=0$ for every smooth real function $u$, whereas a strictly positive form has positive integral over $C$. This proves the obstruction, although the top integral is positive. The selecting potential satisfies $\varphi \geq \pi ^*\psi $. Its pole set is the disjoint union of the sets $E_ i\times \{ o\} $. Near either of them the other summand is smooth, and \[  \varphi =\log (|z|^4+|w|^6)+O(1),\qquad E_ i=\{ z=0\} ,\quad o=\{ w=0\} .  \] Thus $c_ i=p_ i=2$, $b_{i1}=3$ and $a_ i=2/3$. By theorem 27.10.10 , corollary 27.10.14 , $W_ m=H^0(B,A^ m(-2m(E_1+E_2)))$, and $V_ m$ is contained in $H^0(B,A^ m(-(2m-1)(E_1+E_2)))$; for an integer $\ell $, the strict local integrability condition $\ell +1>2m-2/3$ means $\ell \geq 2m-1$. Conversely, by lemma 27.10.5 , divisibility by these orders gives integrability in every chart of the pole set, and off the pole set the selecting potential is locally bounded. This proves equality for $V_ m$. Dividing a section of $A^ m$ by $s_1^ ms_2^ m$ gives a section of $\mathcal O(2m)$ away from the two centers, which extends across them by Hartogs' theorem since $q\geq 2$. The pullback of the extension, multiplied by $s_1^ ms_2^ m$, agrees with the original section everywhere, by the identity theorem. If the extended section vanishes to order $j_ i$ at $x_ i$, the corresponding section of $A^ m$ vanishes to order $m+j_ i$ generically along $E_ i$. The two divisorial conditions therefore give exactly the vanishing orders at $x_1$ and $x_2$ displayed in the statement. Since the two point ideals have disjoint supports, their product equals their intersection. Apply lemma 27.10.17 with $d=2m$ and orders $(m,m)$ or $(m-1,m-1)$; in both cases their sum is at most $d+1$. This gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \dim W_ m& =\binom {2m+q}{q}-2\binom {m+q-1}{q},\\  \dim V_ m& =\binom {2m+q}{q}-2\binom {m+q-2}{q}. \end{aligned}  \] Pascal's identity gives the exact defect, and the leading terms give both growth laws. For $m=1$ the vanishing orders for $V_1$ are zero, and the defect is already two. For $q=2$ the dimensions are $\dim W_ m=(m+1)^2$ and $\dim V_ m=m^2+4m+1$. $\square$ In this example the residual $\beta $ has zero integral over the curve $C$, so no smooth change of gauge makes it positive, and yet its top integral is positive. Thus the bound $O(m^{q-1})$ of corollary 27.10.14 cannot be improved to $o(m^{q-1})$ for semipositive residuals either. As in the previous examples, the selecting potential is finite on most of each fiber over $E_ i$ and equals $-\infty $ at the point $o$ of that fiber, so it does not descend, even up to a bounded function.

title: 27.11.1 The domination envelope
text:
27.11.1 The domination envelope We first compute the envelope on the base, using the affine chart $Z_0
e 0$. Set $z_ i=Z_ i/Z_0$, $s=|z|^2$, $l=k-c$, $s_0=l/c$ and $C=k\log k-c\log c-l\log l$. In this chart the reference weight of $A$ is $\phi _ A=k\log (1+s)$. Put \[  F_0(z)=  egin{cases}  k\log (1+s),& s\leq s_0,\  l\log s+C,& s\geq s_0. \end{cases}  \] As a function of $\log s$, $F_0$ is increasing and convex: its derivative increases to $l$ and then stays constant. Hence $F_0$ is plurisubharmonic. The two branches match to first order at $s=s_0$, and the tangent-line inequality gives $F_0\leq \phi _ A$. On a chart $Z_ j
e 0$ with $j\geq 1$, write $x=Z_0/Z_ j$ and denote the remaining ratios by $\zeta $. Near $Z$ the corresponding weight is \[  F_ j=c\log |x|^2+l\log (1+|\zeta |^2)+C.  \] Therefore $F_0$ and the $F_ j$ define a global plurisubharmonic metric weight $F$ on $A$, with a divisor pole of coefficient $c$ along $Z$ and a smooth remainder. Let $v\leq \phi _ A$ be a competing plurisubharmonic weight, that is, $v=\phi _ A+u$ with $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,	heta )$ and $u\leq 0$, and suppose that $v\leq c\log |x|^2+O(1)$ near $Z$. Write $v_0$ for its expression in the chart $Z_0
eq 0$. The obstacle gives $v_0\leq F_0$ on $\{ s\leq s_0\} $. On each complex line $z=t\xi $ with $|\xi |=1$, either $v_0(t\xi )\equiv -\infty $, or $v_0(t\xi )-l\log |t|^2$ is subharmonic on $|t|>\sqrt{s_0}$ and bounded above near infinity. In the coordinate $1/t$ the puncture at infinity is then removable, and the maximum principle bounds this difference by its boundary bound $C$. Varying $\xi $ proves $v\leq F$ on $B$. Consequently $F=\phi _ A+u_ c$ is the largest such weight, and its contact set $\{ F=\phi _ A\} $ is $D_ c$. We now return to $X$. By proposition 1.22.3 , every $\pi ^*	heta $-plurisubharmonic function has the form $u\circ \pi $ for a $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $B$. Restriction to the local section $w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0$ shows that $u\circ \pi \preceq \varphi $ implies $u\leq c\log |x|^2+O(1)$ near $Z$. Conversely, this divisorial bound and the inequality $|x|^2\leq |x|^2+\sum _ j|w_ j|^2$ give the domination $u\circ \pi \leq \varphi +O(1)$ near $Y$. A finite cover of $Y$ gives one constant there. On the compact complement of a smaller neighborhood of $Y$, the function $\varphi $ is bounded below and $u\leq 0$, so one constant works on all of $X$. The two competitor families therefore correspond to each other, which proves $\mathcal P(\varphi )=u_ c\circ \pi $. The pole of this envelope fills $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$, although $\varphi $ is finite on $\pi ^{-1}(Z)\setminus Y$.

title: 27.11.2 Binomial kernels
text:
27.11.2 Binomial kernels For a fixed integer $j\geq 0$, set $d=km$, $t_{m,j}=\max \{ \ell _ m-j,0\} $ and $\mathcal H_ m^{(j)}=H^0(B,\mathcal O(d)(-t_{m,j}Z))$. The choices $j=0$ and $j=r$ give $W_ m$ and $V_ m$. Give these spaces the reference norm defined by the Fubini–Study metric, zero continuous weight and the volume $
u _0=\omega _ B^ q$. For a binomial random variable $\operatorname {Bin}(d,R)$ with $d$ trials and success probability $R$, their kernels are 27.60  egin{equation} \label{eq:horizontal-binomial-kernel} B_{m,j}^0(R)=A_ dQ_{m,j}(R),\qquad A_ d= inom {d+q}{q},\qquad Q_{m,j}(R)=\mathbb P\{ \operatorname {Bin}(d,R)\geq t_{m,j}\} . \end{equation} To see this, apply the monomial norm formula ( 27.30 ) in degree $d$. Invariance under the coordinate circle actions makes the monomials orthogonal, and the selection keeps exactly those in which $Z_0$ has exponent at least $t_{m,j}$. Summing over the other exponents with the multinomial identity gives ( 27.60 ). Counting the selected monomials gives $\dim \mathcal H_ m^{(j)}= inom {d-t_{m,j}+q}{q}=C_ cm^ q+O(m^{q-1})$. We next bound the tails from below. Write $D(v\mid R)=v\log (v/R)+(1-v)\log ((1-v)/(1-R))$ for the relative entropy, and put $b=\lfloor dafloor =\ell _ m$. If $R\geq b/d$, the binomial mode $\min \{ d,\lfloor (d+1)Rfloor \} $ is at least $b$. Since $t_{m,j}\leq b$, the tail above $t_{m,j}$ contains this mode and is therefore at least $1/(d+1)$. If $0<R<b/d$, the mass at $b$ for the parameter $v=b/d$ is a largest mass, hence at least $1/(d+1)$. For the parameter $R$, the same mass is at least $(d+1)^{-1}\exp (-dD(v\mid R))$. Since \[   rac{\partial D(v\mid R)}{\partial v} =\log  rac{v(1-R)}{R(1-v)}\geq 0\quad (v\geq R)  \] and $v\leq a$, it is at least $(d+1)^{-1}\exp (-dD(a\mid R))$. Together with $u_ c\leq 0$, these cases give $Q_{m,j}\geq (d+1)^{-1}\exp (mu_ c)$, including the cases $b=0$ and $R=1$. Since $A_ d\geq d+1$, the reference kernels satisfy $m^{-1}\log B_{m,j}^0\geq u_ c$; at $R=0$ this holds in the extended sense. For the matching upper asymptotics, fix $0<R<a$. Stirling's formula at the first selected index $t_{m,j}$ gives the logarithmic rate $-kD(a\mid R)$. Since $t_{m,j}/d	o a>R$, the ratios of successive binomial masses above that index are eventually bounded by a number less than one, so the whole tail has the same logarithmic rate. For $R>a$, the binomial variance estimate gives $Q_{m,j}	o 1$. At $R=a$, the lower bound by the mode and $Q_{m,j}\leq 1$ give the logarithmic limit zero. The functions $m^{-1}\log Q_{m,j}(R)$ increase with $R$, and their limit $u_ c$ is continuous on each interval $[\delta ,1]$ with $\delta >0$. On a finite partition of such an interval on which the oscillation of $u_ c$ is small, monotonicity upgrades pointwise convergence to uniform convergence. The event that the first $t_{m,j}$ trials succeed gives \[  c\log R\leq  rac{t_{m,j}}m\log R \leq  rac1m\log Q_{m,j}(R)\leq 0.  \] Since $\log R$ is integrable against every smooth volume, dominated convergence proves global $L^1$ convergence of the functions $m^{-1}\log Q_{m,j}$, and the additional term $m^{-1}\log A_ d$ tends to zero. For the measures, the variance estimate gives $Q_{m,j}	o \mathbf1_{D_ c}$ away from $R=a$. The pushforward of $
u _0$ by $R$ is $q(1-R)^{q-1}\, \mathrm{d}R$, by the radial computation in the proof of theorem 27.9.2 applied to $1-R$. In particular the level set $\{ R=a\} $ has zero volume. Since $q!A_ d/m^ q	o k^ q$ and these constants are bounded, dominated convergence proves total-variation convergence of $q!m^{-q}B_{m,j}^0
u _0$ to $\mu _ c$, and \[  \mu _ c(B)=k^ q\int _ a^1q(1-R)^{q-1}\, \mathrm{d}R=(k-c)^ q.  \]

27.60 \begin{equation} \label{eq:horizontal-binomial-kernel} B_{m,j}^0(R)=A_ dQ_{m,j}(R),\qquad A_ d=\binom {d+q}{q},\qquad Q_{m,j}(R)=\mathbb P\{ \operatorname {Bin}(d,R)\geq t_{m,j}\} . \end{equation}

title: 27.12 Degenerate curvature and growing vanishing orders
search_title: Degenerate curvature and growing vanishing orders
text: 27.12 Degenerate curvature and growing vanishing orders In the compact models above, the vanishing orders are proportional to the tensor degree. To see the transition when the order grows more slowly, we pass to a model space of entire functions. There the local metric fixes the scale of the full kernel, while the selecting ideal creates a second, larger radius. Grouping the monomials according to the residues of their degrees expresses the transition at that radius through Poisson tails. In this section $r$ and $q$ denote new integers. Fix an integer $r\geq 1$. On $\mathbb C$, with coordinate $z=x+\mathrm{i}y$ and area measure $\mathrm{d}A=\mathrm{d}x\, \mathrm{d}y$, put $\phi (z)=|z|^{2r}$. For a real $m>0$, let $H_{m,r}$ be the Hilbert space of entire functions with norm \[  \| f\| _{m,r}^2=\int _{\mathbb C}|f|^2\mathrm{e}^{-m\phi }\, \mathrm{d}A.  \] For an integer $q\geq 0$, let $H_{m,r}^{(q)}$ consist of the functions vanishing to order at least $q$ at zero. Since the weight is bounded below on each fixed disk, the local submean and Cauchy inequalities bound point and jet evaluations, so this subspace is closed. Write $K_{m,r}^{(q)}(z,w)$ for its reproducing kernel, holomorphic in $z$ and antiholomorphic in $w$, and put \[  B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z)=\mathrm{e}^{-m\phi (z)}K_{m,r}^{(q)}(z,z).  \] Thus the ideal $(z^ q)$ selects the functions, while the smooth weight determines the norm. We use $\Gamma (a)=\int _0^\infty t^{a-1}\mathrm{e}^{-t}\, \mathrm{d}t$ for $a>0$. Proposition 27.12.1 . For every $m>0$ and integer $q\geq 0$, 27.61 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degenerate-fock-series} K_{m,r}^{(q)}(z,w)=\frac r\pi \sum _{k=q}^\infty \frac{m^{(k+1)/r}(z\bar w)^ k}{\Gamma ((k+1)/r)}. \end{equation} The series and all its derivatives converge uniformly on compact sets. For $\zeta \in \mathbb C$, 27.62 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degenerate-fock-scaling} m^{-1/r}B_{m,r}^{(q)}(m^{-1/(2r)}\zeta ) =\frac r\pi \mathrm{e}^{-|\zeta |^{2r}} \sum _{k=q}^\infty \frac{|\zeta |^{2k}}{\Gamma ((k+1)/r)}. \end{equation} Consequently, if $m$ tends to infinity through positive integers and $q=q_ m\to \infty $, the left side tends to zero uniformly on compact $\zeta $-sets. Proof. The monomials are orthogonal by rotational invariance. For every integer $k\geq 0$, polar integration with radial variable $\rho $ and the substitution $t=m\rho ^{2r}$ give \[  \| z^ k\| _{m,r}^2=2\pi \int _0^\infty \rho ^{2k+1}\mathrm{e}^{-m\rho ^{2r}}\, \mathrm{d}\rho =\frac\pi r m^{-(k+1)/r}\Gamma ((k+1)/r).  \] For an entire function $f(z)=\sum _{k\geq 0}a_ kz^ k$, Parseval's identity on circles and Tonelli's theorem yield $\| f\| _{m,r}^2=\sum _{k\geq 0}|a_ k|^2\| z^ k\| _{m,r}^2$. Thus the normalized monomials form an orthonormal basis, and those with $k\geq q$ form an orthonormal basis of the selected subspace. This proves ( 27.61 ). By Stirling's formula, the reciprocal Gamma coefficients decay faster than every fixed geometric progression, even after multiplication by any fixed power of $k$; this gives uniform convergence on compact sets together with all derivatives. Substituting $z=w=m^{-1/(2r)}\zeta $ gives ( 27.62 ). On a disk $|\zeta |\leq R$ of fixed radius, the series in ( 27.62 ) is bounded by the tail, from the index $q$ on, of the convergent series with $|\zeta |$ replaced by $R$. This tail tends to zero as $q\to \infty $, proving the last assertion. $\square$ For $r=1$ and $q=0$ the density is the constant $m/\pi $. For general $r$ and $q=0$ its value at zero is $rm^{1/r}/(\pi \Gamma (1/r))$, whereas it vanishes at zero when $q>0$. The scale $m^{-1/(2r)}$ therefore describes fixed vanishing orders, but a growing order requires a further rescaling.

title: 27.12.1 A uniform tail estimate
text: 27.12.1 A uniform tail estimate Grouping the monomial degrees by their residues modulo $r$ expresses the kernel through weighted Poisson tails. The estimate of Gamma ratios below removes those weights, with an error independent of the vanishing threshold. Write $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb E$ for probability and expectation. For $T>0$, let $N_ T$ be a Poisson random variable with parameter $T$, so that $\mathbb P(N_ T=\ell )=\mathrm{e}^{-T}T^\ell /\ell !$ for integers $\ell \geq 0$. For a real $0<\alpha \leq 1$, define \[  w_{\alpha ,T}(\ell )=T^{\alpha -1}\frac{\Gamma (\ell +1)}{\Gamma (\ell +\alpha )}.  \] All constants in the next lemma may depend on $\alpha $, but not on $T$. Lemma 27.12.2 . There is a constant $C_\alpha >0$ such that, for $T\geq 1$, \[  \mathbb E\bigl |w_{\alpha ,T}(N_ T)-1\bigr |\leq C_\alpha T^{-1/2}.  \] Proof. Recall that $\mathbb E N_ T=T$ and $\operatorname {Var}(N_ T)=T$. Stirling's formula, applied to the ratio of Gamma functions, gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \frac{\Gamma (\ell +1)}{\Gamma (\ell +\alpha )} & =\ell ^{1-\alpha }(1+O_\alpha (\ell ^{-1}))& & \quad (\ell \to \infty ),\\  \frac{\Gamma (\ell +1)}{\Gamma (\ell +\alpha )} & \leq C_\alpha (\ell +1)^{1-\alpha }& & \quad (\ell \geq 0). \end{aligned}  \] The second bound follows from the first after the constant is increased to account for finitely many small integers. Since $0\leq 1-\alpha <1$, it implies \[  w_{\alpha ,T}(\ell )\leq C_\alpha \left(1+\frac{\ell +1}{T}\right), \qquad \mathbb E(w_{\alpha ,T}(N_ T)+1)^2\leq C_\alpha \quad (T\geq 1).  \] For $T\geq 2$, consider the event $E_ T=\{ |N_ T-T|\leq T/2\} $. On this event, the expansion of the Gamma ratio and the bounded derivative of $s\mapsto s^{1-\alpha }$ on $[1/2,3/2]$ give \[  |w_{\alpha ,T}(N_ T)-1| \leq C_\alpha \left(\frac{|N_ T-T|}{T}+\frac1T\right).  \] By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, its expectation is at most $C_\alpha T^{-1/2}$. On the complement, Chebyshev's inequality gives $\mathbb P(E_ T^ c)\leq 4/T$, and the preceding second-moment bound together with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives the same estimate for the contribution of $E_ T^ c$. Enlarging the constant handles $1\leq T\leq 2$. $\square$ For integers $q\geq 0$ and $0\leq s<r$, put \[  L_ s(q)=\left\lceil \frac{q-s}{r}\right\rceil \geq 0.  \] If a monomial degree is written as $k=r\ell +s$, the condition $k\geq q$ becomes $\ell \geq L_ s(q)$. Proposition 27.12.3 . There is a constant $C_ r>0$, depending only on $r$, such that for $m>0$, $z\ne 0$ and $T=m|z|^{2r}\geq 1$, 27.65 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degenerate-poisson-comparison} \left|\frac{\pi B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z)}{mr^2|z|^{2r-2}} -\frac1r\sum _{s=0}^{r-1}\mathbb P\{ N_ T\geq L_ s(q)\} \right| \leq C_ r T^{-1/2} \quad (q\geq 0). \end{equation} In particular, the error is uniform in the vanishing order $q$. Proof. Let $\rho =|z|>0$ and put $\alpha _ s=(s+1)/r$ for integers $0\leq s<r$. Grouping the positive series ( 27.61 ) by the residues $s$ and using $T=m\rho ^{2r}$, we obtain the exact identity \[  \begin{split}  B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z) & =\frac r{\pi \rho ^2}\sum _{s=0}^{r-1} \mathrm{e}^{-T}\sum _{\ell \geq L_ s(q)} \frac{T^{\ell +\alpha _ s}}{\Gamma (\ell +\alpha _ s)}\\ & =\frac{rT}{\pi \rho ^2}\sum _{s=0}^{r-1} \mathbb E\bigl [w_{\alpha _ s,T}(N_ T) \mathbf1_{\{ N_ T\geq L_ s(q)\} }\bigr ]. \end{split}  \] Divide by $mr^2\rho ^{2r-2}/\pi =r^2T/(\pi \rho ^2)$ and apply lemma 27.12.2 to each of the finitely many residues. Since the indicators are bounded by one independently of their thresholds, the resulting error is uniform in $q$. $\square$

27.12.2 The limiting envelope and the transition scale A vanishing order proportional to $m$ removes the kernel density inside a fixed circle. Inside that circle the limit of the potentials is logarithmic, and outside it agrees with the smooth weight. Throughout this subsection, $m$ tends to infinity through positive integers. For $\lambda >0$, set $q_ m=\lfloor m\lambda floor $ and $R_\lambda =(\lambda /r)^{1/(2r)}$. Define \[  V_\lambda (z)=  egin{cases}  |z|^{2r},& |z|\geq R_\lambda ,\  \lambda \log (|z|^2/R_\lambda ^2)+\lambda /r,& 0<|z|<R_\lambda ,\  -\infty ,& z=0. \end{cases}  \] In the following theorem, $\delta _0$ denotes the unit point mass at zero. Recall that in dimension one the non-pluripolar measure of a subharmonic function discards the mass carried by its polar set. Theorem 27.12.4 . One has \[   rac1m\log K_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z,z)\longrightarrow V_\lambda (z)  \] pointwise with extended values and in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb C)$. Since $0\leq q_ m/m\leq \lambda $, the negative part on a fixed compact set is bounded by a constant plus $2\lambda |\log |z||$ near zero, which is locally integrable. Dominated convergence proves the $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ assertion. We turn to the envelope. The two radial expressions for $V_\lambda $ and their first radial derivatives agree at $R_\lambda $, because $rR_\lambda ^{2r}=\lambda $. Away from zero and that circle, direct differentiation proves ( 27.72 ). Since the first derivatives match, the circle carries no measure, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=\delta _0$ gives the atom at zero. The right side is positive, so $V_\lambda $ is subharmonic. For $t=|z|^{2r}/(\lambda /r)<1$, the inequality $\log t+1\leq t$ proves $V_\lambda \leq \phi $ inside the circle; outside it there is equality. Finally, let $v$ be subharmonic with $v\leq \phi $ and $v\leq \lambda \log |z|^2+C$ near zero. On the punctured disk $0<|z|<R_\lambda $, the function $v-\lambda \log |z|^2$ is subharmonic and bounded above near zero, so it extends subharmonically across zero. On the boundary circle it is at most $\lambda /r-\lambda \log R_\lambda ^2$, since $v\leq \phi =\lambda /r$ there. The maximum principle gives $v\leq V_\lambda $ inside the disk, and outside the disk this follows from $v\leq \phi $. Since $V_\lambda $ itself satisfies the conditions, it is the largest such function. Removing the atom at the pole gives the last assertion. $\square$ The measures in this theorem have infinite total mass on $\mathbb C$, so their convergence is asserted only on compact sets. The weighted potentials $m^{-1}\log B_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}$ converge to $V_\lambda -\phi $. The radius $R_\lambda $ is created by the selecting ideal even when $r=1$, whereas $r>1$ also reflects the curvature zero at the origin. For any integer sequence $q_ m	o \infty $, the transition at the boundary circle is governed by the central limit theorem for the same Poisson tails. Let $\Phi $ be the standard Gaussian distribution function, \[  \Phi (	au )= rac1{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _{-\infty }^{	au } \mathrm{e}^{-s^2/2}\, \mathrm{d}s \quad (	au \in \mathbb R).  \] Proposition 27.12.5 . Fix a real $	au $. Choose $z_ m
e 0$ with \[  m|z_ m|^{2r}= rac{q_ m}{r}+	au \sqrt{ rac{q_ m}{r}},  \] which is positive for all sufficiently large $m$. Then \[   rac{\pi B_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z_ m)}{mr^2|z_ m|^{2r-2}} \longrightarrow \Phi (	au ).  \] In particular, this applies both when $q_ m/m	o \lambda >0$ and when $q_ m/m	o 0$. Proof. We first recall the central limit theorem for Poisson variables in the form used here. For a fixed real $M>0$, Stirling's formula for $\ell !$ gives, uniformly over integers $\ell $ with $|\ell -T|\leq M\sqrt T$, \[  \mathbb P(N_ T=\ell )= rac1{\sqrt{2\pi T}} \exp \left(- rac{(\ell -T)^2}{2T}ight) (1+O_ M(T^{-1/2}))\quad (T	o \infty ).  \] Indeed, insert the expansion of the factorial in $\mathrm{e}^{-T}T^\ell /\ell !$ and expand the logarithm in powers of $(\ell -T)/T$; the cubic remainder is $O_ M(T^{-1/2})$. Riemann sums over bounded intervals therefore converge to Gaussian integrals, and Chebyshev's bound $\mathbb P(|N_ T-T|>M\sqrt T)\leq M^{-2}$ then allows $M	o \infty $. Consequently, if real thresholds $a_ T$ satisfy $(a_ T-T)/\sqrt T	o a\in \mathbb R$, then $\mathbb P(N_ T\geq a_ T)	o 1-\Phi (a)$; rounding changes the normalized threshold by at most $T^{-1/2}$, and $\Phi $ is continuous. Set $T_ m=m|z_ m|^{2r}$. Then $T_ m	o \infty $ and, for every integer $0\leq s<r$, \[   rac{L_ s(q_ m)-T_ m}{\sqrt{T_ m}}\longrightarrow -	au .  \] Apply the preceding Poisson limit in ( 27.65 ). The uniform error there tends to zero, and each of the finitely many probabilities tends to $1-\Phi (-	au )=\Phi (	au )$. $\square$ For a sequence $q_ m	o \infty $, put $R_ m=(q_ m/(rm))^{1/(2r)}$. At fixed $	au $, the radii in proposition 27.12.5 satisfy \[  |z_ m|=R_ m\left(1+ rac{	au }{2\sqrt{rq_ m}}+O_{r,	au }(q_ m^{-1})ight).  \] If $q_ m=o(m)$, these radii tend to zero, while their ratio to the scale $m^{-1/(2r)}$ of the full kernel tends to infinity; when $r>1$, they shrink to a curvature zero. To transfer this transition to a compact manifold, both the local comparison of norms and the error of the global extension must be uniform in the growing vanishing order. The next section establishes both estimates on a curve.

title: Theorem 27.12.4
text: Theorem 27.12.4 . One has \[  \frac1m\log K_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z,z)\longrightarrow V_\lambda (z)  \] pointwise with extended values and in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb C)$. The kernel measures converge locally in total variation: 27.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degenerate-kernel-measure-limit} \frac1m B_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}\, \mathrm{d}A \longrightarrow \mathbf1_{\{ |z|>R_\lambda \} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi . \end{equation} The function $V_\lambda $ is the largest subharmonic function $v$ on $\mathbb C$ such that $v\leq \phi $ and $v(z)\leq \lambda \log |z|^2+C$ near zero for some constant $C$. Its curvature current is 27.72 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degenerate-envelope-current} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\lambda =\lambda \delta _0+ \mathbf1_{\{ |z|>R_\lambda \} }\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi . \end{equation} Thus the limit in ( 27.71 ) is the non-pluripolar measure of this envelope, rather than its full distributional Laplacian. Proof. For fixed $z\ne 0$, put $\rho =|z|$ and $T=m\rho ^{2r}$. Then $L_ s(q_ m)/T\to \lambda /(r\rho ^{2r})$, and this limit differs from one when $\rho \neq R_\lambda $. Chebyshev's inequality and ( 27.65 ) therefore give 27.73 \begin{equation} \label{eq:degenerate-density-pointwise} \frac1m B_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z)\longrightarrow \begin{cases}  0,& 0<\rho <R_\lambda ,\\  r^2\rho ^{2r-2}/\pi ,& \rho >R_\lambda . \end{cases} \end{equation} The selected density is at most the full density, that is, the density with $q=0$. When $T\geq 1$, the same comparison with $q=0$ bounds it by $C_ r m\rho ^{2r-2}$; when $T\leq 1$, ( 27.62 ) with $q=0$ bounds it by $C_ r m^{1/r}\leq C_ r m$. Thus $m^{-1}B_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}$ is uniformly bounded on each compact set. Since the circle $\rho =R_\lambda $ and the origin have zero area, dominated convergence and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi =(r^2/\pi )|z|^{2r-2}\mathrm{d}A$ prove ( 27.71 ). To compute the limit of the potentials inside the circle, fix $0<\rho <R_\lambda $ and write \[  d_{m,k}=\frac{m^{(k+1)/r}\rho ^{2k}}{\Gamma ((k+1)/r)} \quad (k\geq q_ m).  \] The estimate of Gamma ratios from Stirling's formula gives \[  \frac{d_{m,k+1}}{d_{m,k}} \leq \left(\frac{rm\rho ^{2r}}{q_ m+1}\right)^{1/r} \left(1+\frac{C_ r}{q_ m+1}\right) \quad (k\geq q_ m)  \] for all sufficiently large $m$. The right side tends to $(r\rho ^{2r}/\lambda )^{1/r}<1$. Hence the sum of these terms lies between $d_{m,q_ m}$ and a fixed multiple of that term, and Stirling's formula yields \[  \frac1m\log K_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z,z) \longrightarrow \lambda \log \rho ^2+ \frac\lambda r\bigl (1-\log (\lambda /r)\bigr ) =V_\lambda (z).  \] For $\rho >R_\lambda $, the limit of the densities in ( 27.73 ) is positive. Hence $m^{-1}\log B_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z)\to 0$, and therefore $m^{-1}\log K_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z,z)$ tends to $\phi (z)$. At $\rho =R_\lambda $, put $k_ m=\max \{ q_ m,\lfloor rm\rho ^{2r}\rfloor \} $. Then $k_ m/m\to r\rho ^{2r}=\lambda $. The single monomial of degree $k_ m$ and Stirling's formula give $\liminf m^{-1}\log K_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z,z)\geq \phi (z)$, and the bound for the full kernel already proved gives the reverse inequality for the upper limit. At zero the selected kernel vanishes for all sufficiently large $m$. This proves pointwise convergence everywhere. For local $L^1$ convergence, the bounds for the full kernel give a uniform upper bound for $m^{-1}\log K_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z,z)$ on each compact set. The single selected monomial of degree $q_ m$ gives the lower bound \[  \frac1m\log K_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z,z) \geq c_ m+\frac{q_ m}{m}\log |z|^2,  \] where $c_ m$ is bounded as $m\to \infty $, again by Stirling's formula. Since $0\leq q_ m/m\leq \lambda $, the negative part on a fixed compact set is bounded by a constant plus $2\lambda |\log |z||$ near zero, which is locally integrable. Dominated convergence proves the $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ assertion. We turn to the envelope. The two radial expressions for $V_\lambda $ and their first radial derivatives agree at $R_\lambda $, because $rR_\lambda ^{2r}=\lambda $. Away from zero and that circle, direct differentiation proves ( 27.72 ). Since the first derivatives match, the circle carries no measure, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=\delta _0$ gives the atom at zero. The right side is positive, so $V_\lambda $ is subharmonic. For $t=|z|^{2r}/(\lambda /r)<1$, the inequality $\log t+1\leq t$ proves $V_\lambda \leq \phi $ inside the circle; outside it there is equality. Finally, let $v$ be subharmonic with $v\leq \phi $ and $v\leq \lambda \log |z|^2+C$ near zero. On the punctured disk $0<|z|<R_\lambda $, the function $v-\lambda \log |z|^2$ is subharmonic and bounded above near zero, so it extends subharmonically across zero. On the boundary circle it is at most $\lambda /r-\lambda \log R_\lambda ^2$, since $v\leq \phi =\lambda /r$ there. The maximum principle gives $v\leq V_\lambda $ inside the disk, and outside the disk this follows from $v\leq \phi $. Since $V_\lambda $ itself satisfies the conditions, it is the largest such function. Removing the atom at the pole gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 27.12.5
text: Proposition 27.12.5 . Fix a real $\tau $. Choose $z_ m\ne 0$ with \[  m|z_ m|^{2r}=\frac{q_ m}{r}+\tau \sqrt{\frac{q_ m}{r}},  \] which is positive for all sufficiently large $m$. Then \[  \frac{\pi B_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z_ m)}{mr^2|z_ m|^{2r-2}} \longrightarrow \Phi (\tau ).  \] In particular, this applies both when $q_ m/m\to \lambda >0$ and when $q_ m/m\to 0$. Proof. We first recall the central limit theorem for Poisson variables in the form used here. For a fixed real $M>0$, Stirling's formula for $\ell !$ gives, uniformly over integers $\ell $ with $|\ell -T|\leq M\sqrt T$, \[  \mathbb P(N_ T=\ell )=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi T}} \exp \left(-\frac{(\ell -T)^2}{2T}\right) (1+O_ M(T^{-1/2}))\quad (T\to \infty ).  \] Indeed, insert the expansion of the factorial in $\mathrm{e}^{-T}T^\ell /\ell !$ and expand the logarithm in powers of $(\ell -T)/T$; the cubic remainder is $O_ M(T^{-1/2})$. Riemann sums over bounded intervals therefore converge to Gaussian integrals, and Chebyshev's bound $\mathbb P(|N_ T-T|>M\sqrt T)\leq M^{-2}$ then allows $M\to \infty $. Consequently, if real thresholds $a_ T$ satisfy $(a_ T-T)/\sqrt T\to a\in \mathbb R$, then $\mathbb P(N_ T\geq a_ T)\to 1-\Phi (a)$; rounding changes the normalized threshold by at most $T^{-1/2}$, and $\Phi $ is continuous. Set $T_ m=m|z_ m|^{2r}$. Then $T_ m\to \infty $ and, for every integer $0\leq s<r$, \[  \frac{L_ s(q_ m)-T_ m}{\sqrt{T_ m}}\longrightarrow -\tau .  \] Apply the preceding Poisson limit in ( 27.65 ). The uniform error there tends to zero, and each of the finitely many probabilities tends to $1-\Phi (-\tau )=\Phi (\tau )$. $\square$

title: 27.13 Localization on curves
text:
27.13 Localization on curves We now transfer the transition of proposition 27.12.5 to a compact curve. The selected sections concentrate on a shrinking disk around the distinguished point. When the remainder of the metric weight is negligible on that disk, the norm there can be compared directly with the model norm, and restriction to the disk gives an upper bound for the kernel. For the lower bound, positivity of the curvature away from the distinguished point permits a global $L^2$ correction of localized model sections that preserves the growing vanishing order. Let $C$ be a connected compact Riemann surface, let $x\in C$, and let $(L,h)$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $C$ with a smooth Hermitian metric. Fix an integer $r\geq 1$. Suppose that in a holomorphic coordinate $z$ centered at $x$ and a holomorphic frame $e$, \[  |e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\phi },\qquad \phi (z)=|z|^{2r}+O(|z|^{2r+1}).  \] Let $
u $ be a smooth positive volume form on $C$, written as $a(z)\, \mathrm{d}A$ in this coordinate, where $\mathrm{d}A$ is Euclidean area and $a(0)=1$. For positive integers $m$, choose nonnegative integers $q_ m$ such that \[  q_ m\longrightarrow \infty ,\qquad q_ m=o(m^{1/(2r+1)}).  \] Write $\mathfrak m_ x$ for the ideal sheaf of $x$, and equip \[  V_ m=H^0(C,L^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^{q_ m})  \] with the norm $\| s\| _ m^2=\int _ C|s|_{h^ m}^2\, \mathrm{d}
u $. Its density is $B_ m=\sum _ j|s_{m,j}|_{h^ m}^2$ for any orthonormal basis $(s_{m,j})$, and $B_ m=0$ if $V_ m=0$. As in section 27.12 , $\Phi $ denotes the standard Gaussian distribution function. Theorem 27.13.1 . For a fixed real $	au $, let $x_ m$ lie in the coordinate neighborhood and satisfy \[  T_ m:=m|z(x_ m)|^{2r}=q_ m/r+	au \sqrt{q_ m/r}.  \] Then 27.76  egin{equation} \label{eq:compact-growing-jets-upper} \limsup _{m	o \infty }  rac{\pi B_ m(x_ m)}{mr^2|z(x_ m)|^{2r-2}}\leq \Phi (	au ). \end{equation} If the curvature of $(L,h)$ is semipositive on $C$ and strictly positive on $C\setminus \{ x\} $, this ratio converges to $\Phi (	au )$. Proof. We compare $B_ m$ with the model kernels of section 27.12 on a shrinking disk, which gives the upper bound. For the lower bound, we cut off model polynomials concentrated near $x$ and correct them to global sections by an $L^2$ estimate. Put $z_ m=z(x_ m)$, $ho _ m=|z_ m|$, $R_ m=(q_ m/(rm))^{1/(2r)}$ and \[  S_ m= rac{mr^2ho _ m^{2r-2}}\pi .  \] Then $R_ m	o 0$ and $ho _ m/R_ m	o 1$, and $T_ m>0$ for all sufficiently large $m$. Positive constants denoted by $M$, with subscripts when needed, may change between estimates. They are independent of $m$ and of the argument of $z_ m$; they may depend on the fixed geometric data, $r$, $	au $, and fixed auxiliary cutoffs or radii. We write $q=q_ m$ when no confusion is possible. The model densities $B_{m,r}^{(q)}$ are those of section 27.12 . Step 1: the kernel on a shrinking disk. Fix a real $A>1$ and set $D_ m=\{ |z|<A R_ m\} $. On $D_ m$, \[  m|\phi (z)-|z|^{2r}|\leq M_ A mR_ m^{2r+1} =M_ A rac{q_ mR_ m}{r}=o(1),\qquad \sup _{D_ m}|a-1|=o(1).  \] The first limit follows from $q_ mR_ m=r^{-1/(2r)}(q_ m^{2r+1}/m)^{1/(2r)}	o 0$. Hence, on $D_ m$, the norm defined by $h^ m$ and $
u $ and the radial norm with weight $\mathrm{e}^{-m|z|^{2r}}\, \mathrm{d}A$ differ by a factor $1+o(1)$, uniformly over all holomorphic functions on $D_ m$. The same comparison holds for the corresponding pointwise weights at $z_ m$. For integers $k\geq 0$, let $I_{m,k}$ and $J_{m,k}$ be the squared norms of $z^ k$ on $D_ m$ and on the whole plane, respectively, with this radial weight. Polar integration gives \[   egin{aligned}  I_{m,k}& = rac\pi r m^{-(k+1)/r}\gamma ((k+1)/r,U_ m), & U_ m& =m(A R_ m)^{2r},\  J_{m,k}& = rac\pi r m^{-(k+1)/r}\Gamma ((k+1)/r), & \gamma (b,U)& =\int _0^ U t^{b-1}\mathrm{e}^{-t}\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{aligned}  \] Here $b,U>0$. By Parseval's identity on circles and Tonelli's theorem, the normalized monomials form a complete orthonormal system in the space of holomorphic functions on $D_ m$ with finite radial norm: the squared norm of a Taylor series is the sum of the squared norms of its monomials, so its partial sums converge in that norm. Therefore the density of the subspace of functions vanishing to order at least $q$ is \[  B_ m^{D}(z_ m)=\mathrm{e}^{-T_ m}\sum _{k\geq q} rac{ho _ m^{2k}}{I_{m,k}}.  \] Point evaluation is continuous by the local submean inequality, so this sum is also the supremum of $\mathrm{e}^{-T_ m}|f(z_ m)|^2$ over the unit ball of that subspace. Choose fixed real numbers $1<c<d<A^{2r}$ and put $k_ m=\lfloor rcT_ mfloor $. For large $m$, $k_ m\geq q$ and $U_ m\geq dT_ m$. Uniformly for $0\leq k\leq k_ m+1$, 27.79  egin{equation} \label{eq:truncated-gamma-comparison}  rac{I_{m,k}}{J_{m,k}}=1+O(\mathrm{e}^{-\eta T_ m}) \end{equation} for some fixed $\eta >0$. Indeed, let $G_ b$ be a random variable with Gamma density $t^{b-1}\mathrm{e}^{-t}/\Gamma (b)$ on $(0,\infty )$. A change of variable gives $\mathbb E\mathrm{e}^{sG_ b}=(1-s)^{-b}$ for $0<s<1$. With $b=(k+1)/r\leq cT_ m+O_ r(1)$, Markov's inequality yields \[  1- rac{\gamma (b,U_ m)}{\Gamma (b)} \leq \mathrm{e}^{-sU_ m}(1-s)^{-b}.  \] Since $d>c$, choose $s>0$ small enough that $sd+c\log (1-s)>0$. The right side is at most $M\mathrm{e}^{-\eta T_ m}$, as required. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the positive radial measure gives $I_{m,k+1}^2\leq I_{m,k}I_{m,k+2}$, so $I_{m,k+1}/I_{m,k}$ increases with $k$. By ( 27.79 ) and the asymptotics of Gamma ratios, \[  ho _ m^2 rac{I_{m,k_ m}}{I_{m,k_ m+1}} =(1+o(1))T_ m^{1/r}  rac{\Gamma ((k_ m+1)/r)}{\Gamma ((k_ m+2)/r)} \longrightarrow c^{-1/r}<1.  \] Choose $\kappa \in (c^{-1/r},1)$. For all large $m$, the ratio of consecutive terms $ho _ m^{2k}/I_{m,k}$ is at most $\kappa $ for every $k\geq k_ m$. Consequently, \[  \mathrm{e}^{-T_ m}\sum _{k>k_ m} rac{ho _ m^{2k}}{I_{m,k}} \leq  rac{\kappa }{1-\kappa } \mathrm{e}^{-T_ m} rac{ho _ m^{2k_ m}}{I_{m,k_ m}} =o(S_ m).  \] For the last equality, replace $I_{m,k_ m}$ by $J_{m,k_ m}$ using ( 27.79 ). The resulting term is one of the terms of the series for $B_{m,r}^{(k_ m)}(z_ m)$. In ( 27.65 ) for this kernel, each residue threshold divided by $T_ m$ tends to $c>1$, so Chebyshev's inequality makes all the Poisson tails tend to zero, and the comparison error is $O(T_ m^{-1/2})$. Hence $B_{m,r}^{(k_ m)}(z_ m)=o(S_ m)$. For the terms with $q\leq k\leq k_ m$, we use ( 27.79 ). Since $I_{m,k}\leq J_{m,k}$ for every $k$, we obtain \[  B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z_ m)\leq B_ m^{D}(z_ m) \leq (1+o(1))B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z_ m)+o(S_ m).  \] By proposition 27.12.5 , 27.80  egin{equation} \label{eq:shrinking-disc-transition} B_ m^{D}(z_ m)/S_ m\longrightarrow \Phi (	au ). \end{equation} The global norm of a selected section dominates its norm on $D_ m$. Restriction to $D_ m$ and the preceding comparisons of norms therefore give $B_ m(x_ m)\leq (1+o(1))B_ m^ D(z_ m)$, also when $V_ m=0$. This proves ( 27.76 ). Step 2: polynomials with almost all their norm near the point. From now on we assume the curvature hypotheses of the last assertion. Fix a real $c>1$ and put $K_ m=\lfloor cq_ mfloor $. Define \[  C_ m=\sum _{k=q_ m}^{K_ m} rac{ho _ m^{2k}}{J_{m,k}},\qquad p_ m(z)=C_ m^{-1/2}\sum _{k=q_ m}^{K_ m}  rac{ ar z_ m^{\, k}z^ k}{J_{m,k}}.  \] For large $m$ these are well defined, $\| p_ m\| _{m,r}=1$, and 27.81  egin{equation} \label{eq:model-polynomial-value} \mathrm{e}^{-T_ m}|p_ m(z_ m)|^2 =B_{m,r}^{(q_ m)}(z_ m)-B_{m,r}^{(K_ m+1)}(z_ m) =(\Phi (	au )+o(1))S_ m. \end{equation} Here the first equality holds because $p_ m$ is the normalized evaluation vector at $z_ m$ of the span of $z^{q_ m},\ldots ,z^{K_ m}$. The omitted kernel $B_{m,r}^{(K_ m+1)}(z_ m)$ is $o(S_ m)$ by ( 27.65 ), since its Poisson thresholds divided by $T_ m$ tend to $c>1$; the second equality then follows from proposition 27.12.5 . Choose $\delta \in (0,1/2)$ so that the coordinate disk $|z|<\delta $ satisfies $\phi (z)\geq  eta |z|^{2r}$ for a fixed $ eta \in (1/2,1)$, and such that $a$ is bounded above there. For a sufficiently large fixed $A>1$, 27.82  egin{equation} \label{eq:model-polynomial-localization} \int _{A R_ m<|z|<\delta }|p_ m|^2\mathrm{e}^{-m\phi }a\, \mathrm{d}A=o(1). \end{equation} To see this, write $p_ m(z)=\sum _{k=q_ m}^{K_ m}b_{m,k}z^ k$, so that $\sum _ k|b_{m,k}|^2J_{m,k}=1$. The lower bound for $\phi $, the orthogonality of monomials on circles and polar integration bound the left side by a fixed constant times \[  \sum _{k=q_ m}^{K_ m}|b_{m,k}|^2J_{m,k}\,   eta ^{-(k+1)/r} \mathbb P\{ G_{(k+1)/r}\geq  eta A^{2r}q_ m/r\} .  \] The exponential moment of $G_ b$ at $s=1/2$ gives, for $b,U>0$, \[   eta ^{-b}\mathbb P\{ G_ b\geq U\}  \leq \exp  igl (-U/2+b\log (2/ eta ) igr ).  \] Choose $A$ so large that $ eta A^{2r}/2>c\log (2/ eta )+1$. Since $(k+1)/r\leq (cq_ m+1)/r$, the last factor in the sum is $O(\mathrm{e}^{-q_ m/r})$, uniformly in $k$. This proves ( 27.82 ). On $|z|<A R_ m$, the norm defined by $h^ m$ and $
u $ and the radial model norm differ by a factor $1+o(1)$, as shown in Step 1, and the model norm of $p_ m$ on this disk is at most $1$. Fix a smooth cutoff function $\chi $ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, compactly supported in $|z|<\delta $ and equal to one near zero, and extend $\chi p_ m e^{\otimes m}$ by zero to $C$. The preceding estimates give 27.83  egin{equation} \label{eq:cutoff-polynomial-norm} \| \chi p_ m e^{\otimes m}\| _ m^2\leq 1+o(1). \end{equation} The numbers $\delta , eta ,A$ and the cutoff $\chi $ are fixed before $m$ tends to infinity. Step 3: a global correction with the same vanishing condition. Let $f_ m= ar\partial (\chi p_ m e^{\otimes m})$. Its support is contained in a fixed annulus on which $\phi $ has a positive lower bound. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the identity $\sum _ k|b_{m,k}|^2J_{m,k}=1$ give, for $|z|<\delta <1$, \[  |p_ m(z)|^2\leq \sum _{k=q_ m}^{K_ m} rac{|z|^{2k}}{J_{m,k}} \leq M(K_ m+1)m^{(K_ m+1)/r}.  \] Here we used that $\Gamma (b)$ has a positive lower bound for $b\geq 1/r$. Since $q_ m\log m=o(m)$, the factor $\mathrm{e}^{-m\phi }$ on the annulus dominates this growth of the coefficients. Regard $
u $ as a Kähler form on the curve; it defines pointwise norms of forms and the induced metric $h_{K_ C^{-1}}$ on the anticanonical bundle $K_ C^{-1}$. Choose a smooth cutoff function $\eta $ with $0\leq \eta \leq 1$, supported in the coordinate chart and equal to one near $x$; shrink its support if necessary. For a sufficiently small fixed $t_0>0$, the global smooth functions \[  \ell _ t=\eta \log (|z|^2+t^2),\qquad 0<t\leq t_0,  \] extended by zero outside the chart, are nonpositive. Their complex Hessians are nonnegative where $\eta =1$, and elsewhere they are bounded below independently of $t$, because $\eta =1$ near $x$. Choose a fixed smooth real function $\psi $ that equals a sufficiently large positive multiple of $|z|^2$ near $x$ and is cut off inside the chart, so that \[  \mathrm{i}\Theta (K_ C^{-1})+\mathrm{i}\partial  ar\partial \psi \geq 2
u  \] on a neighborhood of $x$ where $\eta =1$. Here $\mathrm{i}\Theta $ denotes the Chern curvature form, without the factor $1/(2\pi )$, so that the weight $\mathrm{e}^{-\psi }$ contributes $\mathrm{i}\partial  ar\partial \psi $. u . \end{equation} Indeed, near $x$ the two terms involving $h$ and $\ell _ t$ are nonnegative, and the other two together are at least $2

title: 27.13.1 Curvature quadrature domains
text: 27.13.1 Curvature quadrature domains The disk comparison above requires the error of the metric weight to be small throughout the disk carrying the norm. A larger range of orders is obtained by absorbing the harmonic part of this error into the holomorphic sections. The transition then takes place on the boundary of the region where the remaining obstacle potential detaches from the weight with first-order contact, and a quadrature identity for the curvature determines that boundary. Keep $C,x,(L,h),r,z,e$ and $\nu =a(z)\, \mathrm{d}A$ from section 27.13 , and assume that the curvature of $(L,h)$ is semipositive on $C$ and strictly positive on $C\setminus \{ x\} $. We now allow integers $q=q_ m\to \infty $ with $q=o(m)$. Write $V_{m,q}=H^0(C,L^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^ q)$, and let $B_{m,q}$ be its density for the norm of section 27.13 . Put \[  \rho =\phi _{z\bar z},\qquad t=q/m,\qquad R=(t/r)^{1/(2r)}.  \] Write $\mathbb D$ for the unit disk. Lemma 27.13.2 . Let $b>1$, and let $Q(R,\zeta )$ be a real function, jointly smooth for small real $R$ and $|\zeta |<b$, with $Q(0,\zeta )=|\zeta |^{2r}$. Write $Q_ R=Q(R,\cdot )$, and suppose that every $Q_ R$ is subharmonic and that $Q_{R,\zeta \bar\zeta }>0$ on a fixed neighborhood of the unit circle. For small $R$, let $U_ R$ be the largest subharmonic function on $\{ |\zeta |<b\} $ such that $U_ R\leq Q_ R$ and $U_ R\leq 2r\log |\zeta |+O(1)$ near zero. Then the noncontact set $\Omega _ R=\{ U_ R<Q_ R\} $ is connected, and its boundary is a radial graph near the unit circle. Let $F_ R:\mathbb D\to \Omega _ R$ be the conformal map with $F_ R(0)=0$ and $F_ R'(0)>0$. For every fixed $k$ and all sufficiently small $R$, depending on $k$, the map $F_ R$ and the harmonic function $(U_ R-2r\log |\zeta |)\circ F_ R$ depend smoothly on $R$ in the Hölder spaces $C^{k,\alpha }(\overline{\mathbb D})$, and they differ from their values at $R=0$ by $O(R)$. The arguments below use only finitely many of these norms, so the dependence of the range of $R$ on $k$ is harmless. Proof. Fix $k\geq 3$ and $0<\alpha <1$. Let $A^{k,\alpha }$ be the real Banach space of functions that are holomorphic on $\mathbb D$, of class $C^{k,\alpha }$ on its closure, and real at zero. For $h\in A^{k,\alpha }$ near zero set $f(u)=u(1+h(u))$. For small $h$, the map $f$ is univalent, with $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)>0$. On $|u|=1$ define \[  K(R,h)=f(u)(Q_ R)_\zeta (f(u))-r, \qquad T(R,h)=(P_-K,\operatorname {Re}[K]_0),  \] where $P_-$ is the projection onto the strictly negative Fourier modes and $[\cdot ]_0$ is the constant Fourier coefficient. The Cauchy projections are bounded on these Hölder spaces. This follows from the Hilbert kernel on the circle: subtract the value at the evaluation point, split the integral at twice the length of the increment, and use the Hölder bound for differences on the inner part and the bound for the differentiated kernel on the outer part. This gives the $C^{0,\alpha }$ bound, and commuting angular derivatives with the projections gives the $C^{k,\alpha }$ bound. The superposition operator $h\mapsto (Q_ R)_\zeta \circ f$ involves no derivatives of $h$ and is smooth. Thus $T$ is a smooth map into the product of the space of negative-mode functions with $\mathbb R$. At $(R,h)=(0,0)$ we have $T=0$ and \[  D_ hK(0,0)v=r^2(v+\bar v),\qquad D_ hT(0,0)v=(r^2\overline{v-v(0)},\, 2r^2v(0)).  \] This is a bounded real-linear isomorphism, so the implicit function theorem in Banach spaces gives a unique normalized branch $f_ R$ of solutions of $T(R,h)=0$, depending smoothly on $R$ in the fixed space, with $\| f_ R-\mathrm{id}\| =O(R)$. The branches obtained for larger $k$ agree with this one by uniqueness in the smaller space. For each fixed order, this gives the spatial estimates and the expansions in $R$ needed below, on a parameter interval that depends on the order. The equation $T=0$ prescribes only the real part of $[K]_0$; we show that the imaginary part vanishes as well. Since $P_-K=0$, the function $K$ extends holomorphically to $\mathbb D$, and $K(0)=[K]_0$ is purely imaginary. On the other hand, Stokes' formula gives \[  \frac1{2\pi \mathrm{i}}\int _{|u|=1}(Q_ R)_\zeta (f_ R(u))f_ R'(u)\, \mathrm{d}u =\frac1\pi \int _{f_ R(\mathbb D)}(Q_ R)_{\zeta \bar\zeta }\, \mathrm{d}A\in \mathbb R.  \] On the circle the integrand equals $(r+K)f_ R'/f_ R$, whose residue at zero is $r+K(0)$. Hence $K(0)$ is real as well, and therefore zero. Consequently \[  S_ R(\zeta )=\frac{r+K(f_ R^{-1}(\zeta ))}{\zeta } =r/\zeta +H_ R(\zeta )  \] with $H_ R$ holomorphic on $\Omega _ R=f_ R(\mathbb D)$, and $S_ R=(Q_ R)_\zeta $ on the boundary of $\Omega _ R$. Let \[  U_ R=2r\log |\zeta |+2\operatorname {Re}\int _0^\zeta H_ R(w)\, \mathrm{d}w+C_ R.  \] Its complex gradient agrees with that of $Q_ R$ on the boundary, so the difference $Q_ R-U_ R$ is constant there; choose the constant $C_ R$ to make it zero. Then the difference and its gradient vanish on the boundary. Since the tangential second derivative of the difference also vanishes there, its inward normal second derivative equals $\Delta Q_ R>0$. Hence $Q_ R-U_ R>0$ in an inner collar of uniform width. At $R=0$, \[  U_0=1+2r\log |\zeta |,\qquad |\zeta |^{2r}-1-2r\log |\zeta |>0\quad (0<|\zeta |<1).  \] By uniform convergence, this gap keeps a positive minimum on the remaining compact subsets of the interior for small $R$, and the logarithmic term controls a neighborhood of zero. Set $U_ R=Q_ R$ outside $\Omega _ R$. Since values and gradients match across the boundary, the Laplacian of the patched function carries no measure on the boundary. Its curvature is $r\delta _0$ inside $\Omega _ R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_ R\geq 0$ outside, so it is an admissible minorant. If $v$ is any competitor, then $v-U_ R$ is subharmonic on $\Omega _ R\setminus \{ 0\} $, bounded above near zero and nonpositive on the boundary. Removability of the singularity at zero and the maximum principle give $v\leq U_ R$ in $\Omega _ R$, and outside $\Omega _ R$ this follows from $v\leq Q_ R$. This identifies the envelope and shows that there are no further noncontact components. The radial graph property and the estimates for the harmonic part follow from the normalized map and its dependence on the parameter. We henceforth write $F_ R=f_ R$. $\square$ We apply the lemma to the given weight. By Taylor's formula with integral remainder, for small real $R$, \[  Q_ R(\zeta )=R^{-2r}\phi (R\zeta ) =|\zeta |^{2r}+R E(R,\zeta )  \] with a jointly smooth function $E$. Choose the holomorphic primitive with $G_ R(0)$ real, and write the envelope in $\Omega _ R$ as \[  U_ R=2r\log |\zeta |+2\operatorname {Re} G_ R(\zeta ),\qquad G_ R=1/2+O(R).  \] Set $D_ t=R\Omega _ R$. In the original coordinate $z$, the obstacle potential is $\phi _ t(z)=R^{2r}U_ R(z/R)$ inside $D_ t$ and $\phi $ outside. Replacing $\phi $ by $\phi _ t$ in this chart and keeping $h$ elsewhere defines a global singular metric on $L$. Its local potential is $C^1$ across the boundary, bounded above by $\phi $, and has the pole $2t\log |z|+O(1)$. On the boundary, $\phi _ z=t/z+g_ t'$ for a holomorphic function $g_ t$. Green's formula therefore gives the quadrature identity 27.85 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curvature-quadrature-identity} \int _{D_ t}\rho (z)f(z)\, \mathrm dA=\pi t f(0) \end{equation} for every function $f$ holomorphic near $\overline{D_ t}$. The curvature of the singular metric is $t\delta _ x$ inside $D_ t$ and the original curvature outside. Finally, we write the boundary as $\Gamma _ t=\{ R c_ R(\theta )\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }\} $ with a positive periodic function $c_ R$, where $c_ R-1=O(R)$ in each fixed norm used below.

The branches obtained for larger $k$ agree with this one by uniqueness in the smaller space. For each fixed order, this gives the spatial estimates and the expansions in $R$ needed below, on a parameter interval that depends on the order. Since $P_-K=0$, the function $K$ extends holomorphically to $\mathbb D$, and $K(0)=[K]_0$ is purely imaginary. On the other hand, Stokes' formula gives \[  \frac1{2\pi \mathrm{i}}\int _{|u|=1}(Q_ R)_\zeta (f_ R(u))f_ R'(u)\, \mathrm{d}u =\frac1\pi \int _{f_ R(\mathbb D)}(Q_ R)_{\zeta \bar\zeta }\, \mathrm{d}A\in \mathbb R.  \] On the circle the integrand equals $(r+K)f_ R'/f_ R$, whose residue at zero is $r+K(0)$. Hence $K(0)$ is real as well, and therefore zero. Consequently \[  S_ R(\zeta )=\frac{r+K(f_ R^{-1}(\zeta ))}{\zeta } =r/\zeta +H_ R(\zeta )  \] with $H_ R$ holomorphic on $\Omega _ R=f_ R(\mathbb D)$, and $S_ R=(Q_ R)_\zeta $ on the boundary of $\Omega _ R$. Let \[  U_ R=2r\log |\zeta |+2\operatorname {Re}\int _0^\zeta H_ R(w)\, \mathrm{d}w+C_ R.  \] Its complex gradient agrees with that of $Q_ R$ on the boundary, so the difference $Q_ R-U_ R$ is constant there; choose the constant $C_ R$ to make it zero. Then the difference and its gradient vanish on the boundary. Since the tangential second derivative of the difference also vanishes there, its inward normal second derivative equals $\Delta Q_ R>0$. Hence $Q_ R-U_ R>0$ in an inner collar of uniform width. At $R=0$, \[  U_0=1+2r\log |\zeta |,\qquad |\zeta |^{2r}-1-2r\log |\zeta |>0\quad (0<|\zeta |<1).  \] By uniform convergence, this gap keeps a positive minimum on the remaining compact subsets of the interior for small $R$, and the logarithmic term controls a neighborhood of zero. Set $U_ R=Q_ R$ outside $\Omega _ R$. Since values and gradients match across the boundary, the Laplacian of the patched function carries no measure on the boundary. Its curvature is $r\delta _0$ inside $\Omega _ R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_ R\geq 0$ outside, so it is an admissible minorant. If $v$ is any competitor, then $v-U_ R$ is subharmonic on $\Omega _ R\setminus \{ 0\} $, bounded above near zero and nonpositive on the boundary.
