title: 27.13.2 Gaussian transitions at curvature boundaries
text:
27.13.2 Gaussian transitions at curvature boundaries To prove the transition at the boundary $\Gamma _ t$, we again correct localized sections by an $L^2$ estimate. The singular metric of section 27.13.1 , whose curvature at $x$ is the point mass $t\delta _ x$, enforces the growing vanishing order of the correction. Its curvature vanishes on the rest of $D_ t$, so a bounded function varying on the scale $R$ must first restore strict positivity there. Lemma 27.13.3 . There are constants $c,C>0$ with the following properties, for all sufficiently large $m$. There is a smooth function $b_ R$, bounded independently of $m$, such that the metric on $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$ induced by the singular local potential $\psi _ m=m\phi _ t+b_ R$ on $L^ m$ and by the anticanonical metric of $
u $ has curvature at least $(c/R^2)
u $ on $C$. On annuli outside $D_ t$ whose radii are comparable to $R$, the lower bound improves to $(cq/R^2)
u $. If an $L^ m$-valued $(0,1)$-form $\alpha $ is supported on such an annulus, the equation $ ar\partial v=\alpha $ has a solution $v$, depending linearly on $\alpha $, with 27.86  egin{equation} \label{eq:order-preserving-correction} \| v\| _{h^ m}^2\leq C rac{R^2}{q}\| \alpha \| _{h^ m,
u }^2, \end{equation} where both sides are the $L^2$ norms defined by $h^ m$ and $
u $. If $\alpha $ vanishes near $x$, then $v$ is holomorphic near $x$ and vanishes to order at least $q$ there. Proof. Take $b_ R=|z|^2/R^2$ on a disk containing $D_ t$, and cut it off before the radius $3R$, so that its negative curvature is supported outside $D_ t$. This function is uniformly bounded and its Hessian is $O(R^{-2})$. On the support of its negative curvature, the curvature $mho $ is comparable to $q/R^2$; since $q	o \infty $, it absorbs the negative part. Inside $D_ t$, the function $b_ R$ contributes the curvature $c/R^2$. Elsewhere in a fixed coordinate disk, the original curvature is bounded below by a fixed multiple of $m|z|^{2r-2}$, and off that disk it is at least $cm$. Since $mR^2	o \infty $, all these bounds dominate $c/R^2$ and the bounded Ricci term of $
u $. We use the $L^2$ estimate for $ ar\partial $ with a pointwise lower bound for the curvature of a singular metric, in the form described in section 34.14 . As in the proof of theorem 27.13.1 , we regard $L^ m$-valued $(0,1)$-forms as $(1,1)$-forms with values in $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$ and sections of $L^ m$ as $(1,0)$-forms with values in the same bundle; this identification preserves the pointwise norms and brings in the Ricci term of $
u $. The estimate then reads as follows: if $H$ is a singular metric on $L^ m$ and the curvature of $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$ is at least $\lambda 
u $ for a continuous function $\lambda >0$, then \[  \int _ C|v|_ H^2\, \mathrm{d}
u \leq \int _ C\lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |_{H,
u }^2\, \mathrm{d}
u .  \] On the support of $\alpha $ we have $\lambda ^{-1}=O(R^2/q)$, $\phi _ t=\phi $, and $b_ R$ is bounded. Elsewhere $\phi _ t\leq \phi $ gives $\mathrm{e}^{-m\phi }\leq C\mathrm{e}^{-\psi _ m}$. These comparisons yield ( 27.86 ). Choosing the solution of minimal norm in the singular weighted Hilbert space makes the correction linear in its source. The estimate requires a continuous lower bound $\lambda $. We take $\lambda $ equal to $c/R^2$ inside $D_ t$ and to $cq/R^2$ on the exterior annulus, interpolating across a thin exterior collar of $\Gamma _ t$. For the cutoff sources used below, whose supports are separated from $\Gamma _ t$, the collar can be chosen to miss the source. For an exterior source whose support accumulates on $\Gamma _ t$, we let the collar shrink to $\Gamma _ t$; since $\Gamma _ t$ has zero area, dominated convergence in the integrals of $\lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |^2$ and weak compactness in the fixed weighted Hilbert space give the same estimate. The singular metric is handled by approximation, which gives the same estimate for a weak solution. Where the source vanishes, the Cauchy–Riemann equation in the sense of distributions makes the solution holomorphic. Near $x$, the weight is $|z|^{-2q}$ times a smooth positive factor. A holomorphic term $z^ j$ is square integrable against it precisely when $j\geq q$, so the solution has the required vanishing order. $\square$ Theorem 27.13.4 . Let $D_ t$ and $\Gamma _ t$ be as in section 27.13.1 . Let $d_ t(z)$ be the signed Euclidean distance from $z$ to $\Gamma _ t$, positive outside $D_ t$, and let $p_ t(z)$ be the nearest point of $\Gamma _ t$. For every fixed $M>0$, uniformly over points $z$ with $|d_ t(z)|\leq MR/\sqrt q$, 27.87  egin{equation} \label{eq:curvature-boundary-transition}  rac{\pi a(z)B_{m,q}(z)}{mho (z)} -\Phi  igl (2\sqrt{mho (p_ t(z))}\, d_ t(z) igr )\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} If $d_ t(z)=o(R)$ and $\sqrt q\, d_ t(z)/R$ tends to $-\infty $ or $+\infty $, the same normalized kernel tends to $0$ or $1$, respectively. Thus, for every sublinear order, the transition is centered on $\Gamma _ t$ and has length $1/(2\sqrt{mho })$. Proof. We pass to logarithmic coordinates adapted to $\Gamma _ t$, in which the norm of a section of order $q$ becomes Gaussian in the distance to the boundary. Restriction to a thin ring gives the upper bound, and localized trial sections corrected by lemma 27.13.3 give the lower bound. Finally we compare with the full kernel to obtain saturation. Throughout the proof, $c$ and $C$ denote positive constants independent of $m$, which may change from line to line. Step 1: the effective potential. Define on the unit disk \[   egin{aligned}  A_ R(w)& =G_ R(F_ R(w))+r\log (F_ R(w)/w),\  \Psi _ R& =Q_ R(F_ R(w))-2\operatorname {Re} A_ R(w)-2r\log |w|, \end{aligned}  \] where the logarithm uses the branch near one. Then $A_ R=1/2+O(R)$ and $F_ R=w+O(R)$ in every fixed norm used below. The effective potential $\Psi _ R=(Q_ R-U_ R)\circ F_ R$ is positive inside the disk, and its value and gradient vanish on the boundary. For $w=\mathrm{e}^{v+\mathrm{i}	heta }$ it has the expansion 27.90  egin{equation} \label{eq:curvature-ring-expansion} \Psi _ R=(2r^2+O(R))v^2+O(v^3), \end{equation} and the exact quadratic coefficient is $2(Q_ R)_{\zeta  ar\zeta }(F_ R(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }))|F_ R'(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta })|^2$. The maps need not extend holomorphically across the circle. To obtain charts that also cover a neighborhood outside the circle, we truncate their Taylor series at the degree $K=\lfloor q^{1/16}floor $ and denote the truncations by $F_ K,A_ K$. The Taylor coefficients of a function bounded in a sufficiently high fixed Hölder norm decay faster than a large fixed power of their index, so the truncation error is $O(q^{-10})$, together with the fixed number of derivatives needed here. Fix a small $c_0>0$. On $|w|\leq 1+c_0/K$ the derivatives of the truncations remain bounded and $F_ K-w,A_ K-1/2=O(R)$, because the factor $(1+c_0/K)^ K\leq \mathrm{e}^{c_0}$ controls the sums. In particular, $F_ K$ is univalent there for small $R$. Put $\delta =c_0/K$ and \[  \Psi _ K=Q_ R(F_ K)-2\operatorname {Re} A_ K-2r\log |w|.  \] The errors in the value and the first derivative of $\Psi _ K$ on the circle are $O(q^{-10})$, and uniformly for $|v|\leq \delta $, 27.91  egin{equation} \label{eq:polynomial-ring-expansion} \Psi _ K=(2r^2+O(R)+O(|v|))v^2+O(q^{-10})(1+|v|). \end{equation} Inside the disk, the effective potential has uniform positive quadratic growth near the circle, a positive lower bound on compact annuli farther inside, and logarithmic growth at zero. In the coordinate $z=RF_ K(w)$, a local holomorphic section of order at least $q$ at $x$ is uniquely represented, in the original frame, as 27.92  egin{equation} \label{eq:quadrature-section-gauge} s=w^ q\exp ((q/r)A_ K(w))f(w),\qquad |s|_{h^ m}^2=|f(w)|^2\mathrm{e}^{-(q/r)\Psi _ K(w)}, \end{equation} with $f$ holomorphic near zero. The volume in this chart is $R^2(1+O(R))\, \mathrm{d}A_ w$. Put $\eta =\sqrt{rq}\, v$. On each band $|\eta |\leq N$ with $N$ fixed, \[  (q/r)\Psi _ K=2\eta ^2+o(1).  \] Step 2: the upper bound. Let the observation point have coordinate $\eta _0$ in a fixed bounded interval. Restricting the norm to the band $|\eta |\leq N$ bounds the kernel from above by the kernel of the restricted space. For $f(w)=\sum _{j\geq 0}b_ jw^ j$, the limiting diagonal norms of the monomials on this band are \[  n_{j,N}= rac{2\pi R^2}{\sqrt{rq}}I_ N(j/\sqrt{rq}),\qquad I_ N(s)=\int _{-N}^ N \mathrm{e}^{2s\eta -2\eta ^2}\, \mathrm{d}\eta .  \] After normalization by $rq/(\pi R^2)$, the limiting upper kernel is 27.93  egin{equation} \label{eq:positive-mode-ring-kernel}  rac12\mathrm{e}^{-2\eta _0^2}\int _0^\infty  rac{\mathrm{e}^{2s\eta _0}}{I_ N(s)}\, \mathrm{d}s. \end{equation} The passage from sums to integrals uses Riemann sums with mesh $1/\sqrt{rq}$. To control their tails, bound $I_ N(s)$ from below by its integral over a fixed subinterval of $[-N,N]$ lying beyond every observation point $\eta _0$; this gives an exponential bound uniform in the mesh. Thus we may first pass to the Riemann integral and then let $N	o \infty $. Since $I_\infty (s)=\sqrt{\pi /2}\, \mathrm{e}^{s^2/2}$, the expression ( 27.93 ) tends to 27.94  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaussian-ring-limit}  rac1{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _0^\infty \mathrm{e}^{-(s-2\eta _0)^2/2}\, \mathrm{d}s =\Phi (2\eta _0). \end{equation} Step 3: the lower bound. Fix $T>0$, and use ( 27.92 ) with $f$ in the span of the monomials $w^ j$, $0\leq j\leq T\sqrt{rq}$. For $f=\sum _ jb_ jw^ j$, put $\| s\| _{\mathrm{trial}}^2=\sum _ j|b_ j|^2n_ j$, with $n_ j$ given by ( 27.96 ) below. Let $\chi $ be a radial cutoff function in the $w$-plane, supported in $|w|\leq 1+\delta $ and equal to one on $|w|\leq 1+\delta /2$. The annulus on which $\chi $ is not constant lies outside $D_ t$. Equations ( 27.91 ) and ( 27.92 ) bound the squared norm of the source, as a quadratic form on the entire span, by \[  \|  ar\partial (\chi s)\| _{h^ m,
u }^2\leq C(R\delta )^{-2}\mathrm{e}^{-cq\delta ^2}\| s\| _{\mathrm{trial}}^2;  \] the linear term $2jv$ in the exponent is absorbed because $\sqrt q\, \delta 	o \infty $. Lemma 27.13.3 gives a correction $g_ s$, depending linearly on $s$, with $ ar\partial g_ s= ar\partial (\chi s)$ and 27.95  egin{equation} \label{eq:shrinking-cutoff-correction} \| g_ s\| _{h^ m}^2\leq C(q\delta ^2)^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-cq\delta ^2}\| s\| _{\mathrm{trial}}^2. \end{equation} The constants here depend on $m$ only through $R$ and $q$. The factor $R^2$ in ( 27.86 ) cancels the factor $R^{-2}$ coming from the derivative of the cutoff; this cancellation is needed even when $q$ grows more slowly than every power of $m$. On this span, the Gram form of the global norm of $\chi s$ converges, in the sense of relative operator norm, to the diagonal form 27.96  egin{equation} \label{eq:gaussian-ring-gram} n_ j= rac{2\pi R^2}{\sqrt{rq}}\sqrt{ rac\pi 2} \exp (j^2/(2rq)). \end{equation} Indeed, the ratio of the weights is uniformly close to one on each fixed band in $\eta $. Outside such a band, the radial bound for the weight and Parseval's identity on circles bound arbitrary combinations by diagonal tails $\mathrm{e}^{-c\eta ^2+2T|\eta |}$. We first pass to the limit on a fixed band and then enlarge it. The positive lower bound of the effective potential on compact annuli and its logarithmic singularity at zero control the remaining part of the disk. This argument controls the whole quadratic form, without a factor depending on the dimension of the span. To evaluate the corrections we need a pointwise bound. Let $u$ be a section holomorphic on a disk of radius $R/\sqrt q$ centered at a point $z$ with $|z|$ comparable to $R$. Then a local submean estimate gives 27.97  egin{equation} \label{eq:shrinking-point-evaluation} |u(z)|_{h^ m}^2\leq C(q/R^2)\| u\| _{h^ m}^2. \end{equation} To prove it, multiply $u$ by the exponential of a holomorphic polynomial that removes the harmonic part of the linear and quadratic Taylor terms of $m\phi $ at $z$. After rescaling the disk to unit size, the remaining quadratic coefficient is bounded and the third-order error is $O(q^{-1/2})$, which proves the estimate. It applies to the corrections, because their sources lie on the cutoff annulus, away from the observation points. Together with ( 27.95 ), it shows that the kernel of the corrected global trial sections differs by $o(q/R^2)$ from the local trial kernel. After normalization, the lower limit is the integral in ( 27.94 ) with upper limit $T$ instead of infinity, and letting $T	o \infty $ gives the matching lower bound. Step 4: return to the original coordinate. Let $p$ be the nearest boundary point and $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }$ its preimage under $F_ R$. Then \[   egin{aligned}  v& = rac{d_ t(z)}{R|F_ R'(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta })|} +O(d_ t(z)^2/R^2)+o(q^{-1/2}),\  mho (p)R^2|F_ R'(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta })|^2& =rq(1+O(R)). \end{aligned}  \] Moreover, $mho (z)/a(z)=(rq/R^2)(1+o(1))$ in the band $|d_ t(z)|\leq MR/\sqrt q$. These identities convert $2\eta _0$ into the argument in ( 27.87 ) and give the normalization of the density there. This proves ( 27.87 ). Step 5: the full density and saturation. Let $B_ m^{m full}$ be the density of the full space $H^0(C,L^ m)$. At points with $|z|\asymp R$, it satisfies 27.100  egin{equation} \label{eq:mesoscopic-full-density} B_ m^{m full}(z)= rac{mho (z)}{\pi a(z)}(1+o(1)), \end{equation} uniformly in an $o(R)$-neighborhood of $\Gamma _ t$. We give a direct localization argument, which also yields the saturation statements of the theorem. Remove the harmonic Taylor terms of $m\phi $ at the observation point and rescale by $(mho (z))^{-1/2}$. On every fixed rescaled disk, the remaining weight tends to $|u|^2$, where $u$ is the rescaled coordinate, and the volume density tends to the constant $a(z)$. The Taylor estimate is uniform, because the third derivatives of $\phi $ at radius $R$ are $O(R^{2r-3})$, so the normalized third-order error is $O(q^{-1/2})$. Restriction to such disks bounds the evaluation norm from above, and the Gaussian norm of the constant function on them tends to $\pi $ as their radius grows. This proves the upper bound in ( 27.100 ). For the lower bound, take the holomorphic exponential canceling the harmonic Taylor terms, and cut it off on a disk of radius $\varepsilon R$ centered at the observation point, where $\varepsilon 	o 0$ and $\sqrt q\, \varepsilon 	o \infty $. Its local squared norm is $(\pi a(z)/(mho (z)))(1+o(1))$ times its squared weighted value at the center, which is one. The quadratic lower bound for the weight bounds the source on the cutoff annulus by an exponential factor $\mathrm{e}^{-cq\varepsilon ^2}$. Add the same bounded function of scale $R$ to the original metric and use the pointwise $ ar\partial $ estimate. The relative squared norm of the correction is bounded by $C(q\varepsilon ^2)^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-cq\varepsilon ^2}=o(1)$, after decreasing $c$ if necessary, and its value at the center is $o(1)$ by ( 27.97 ). This proves the matching lower bound. For saturation inside $D_ t$, use the polynomial chart above and put $u=1-|w|>0$. Restrict the norm in ( 27.92 ) to the exterior half-band $0\leq v\leq c/\sqrt q$. On this half-band every monomial $w^ j$, $j\geq 0$, has norm at least $cR^2/\sqrt q$. Parseval's identity on circles and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give \[  B_{m,q}(z)\leq C rac{\sqrt q}{R^2} rac{\mathrm{e}^{-cqu^2}}{1-|w|^2}.  \] If $u\sqrt q	o \infty $, this bound divided by $q/R^2$ tends to zero. The error $O(q^{-10})$ of the chart changes neither the hypothesis nor the conclusion. For saturation outside $D_ t$, cut off the localized Gaussian section at $z$ on a disk of radius \[  \varepsilon R,\qquad \varepsilon =\min \{ d_ t(z)/(3R),q^{-1/4}\} .  \] This disk lies entirely outside $D_ t$, and again $\varepsilon 	o 0$ and $\sqrt q\, \varepsilon 	o \infty $. Apply lemma 27.13.3 with the singular obstacle metric, which equals the original metric on the support of the source. The correction has negligible norm and value, and it vanishes to order $q$ at $x$. Thus a member of $V_{m,q}$ asymptotically attains the full Gaussian density, and ( 27.100 ) gives the reverse inequality. This proves saturation to one. $\square$

title: Lemma 27.13.3
text:
Lemma 27.13.3 . There are constants $c,C>0$ with the following properties, for all sufficiently large $m$. There is a smooth function $b_ R$, bounded independently of $m$, such that the metric on $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$ induced by the singular local potential $\psi _ m=m\phi _ t+b_ R$ on $L^ m$ and by the anticanonical metric of $
u $ has curvature at least $(c/R^2)
u $ on $C$. On annuli outside $D_ t$ whose radii are comparable to $R$, the lower bound improves to $(cq/R^2)
u $. If an $L^ m$-valued $(0,1)$-form $\alpha $ is supported on such an annulus, the equation $ ar\partial v=\alpha $ has a solution $v$, depending linearly on $\alpha $, with 27.86  egin{equation} \label{eq:order-preserving-correction} \| v\| _{h^ m}^2\leq C rac{R^2}{q}\| \alpha \| _{h^ m,
u }^2, \end{equation} where both sides are the $L^2$ norms defined by $h^ m$ and $
u $. If $\alpha $ vanishes near $x$, then $v$ is holomorphic near $x$ and vanishes to order at least $q$ there. Proof. Take $b_ R=|z|^2/R^2$ on a disk containing $D_ t$, and cut it off before the radius $3R$, so that its negative curvature is supported outside $D_ t$. This function is uniformly bounded and its Hessian is $O(R^{-2})$. On the support of its negative curvature, the curvature $mho $ is comparable to $q/R^2$; since $q	o \infty $, it absorbs the negative part. Inside $D_ t$, the function $b_ R$ contributes the curvature $c/R^2$. Elsewhere in a fixed coordinate disk, the original curvature is bounded below by a fixed multiple of $m|z|^{2r-2}$, and off that disk it is at least $cm$. Since $mR^2	o \infty $, all these bounds dominate $c/R^2$ and the bounded Ricci term of $
u $. We use the $L^2$ estimate for $ ar\partial $ with a pointwise lower bound for the curvature of a singular metric, in the form described in section 34.14 . As in the proof of theorem 27.13.1 , we regard $L^ m$-valued $(0,1)$-forms as $(1,1)$-forms with values in $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$ and sections of $L^ m$ as $(1,0)$-forms with values in the same bundle; this identification preserves the pointwise norms and brings in the Ricci term of $
u $. The estimate then reads as follows: if $H$ is a singular metric on $L^ m$ and the curvature of $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$ is at least $\lambda 
u $ for a continuous function $\lambda >0$, then \[  \int _ C|v|_ H^2\, \mathrm{d}
u \leq \int _ C\lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |_{H,
u }^2\, \mathrm{d}
u .  \] On the support of $\alpha $ we have $\lambda ^{-1}=O(R^2/q)$, $\phi _ t=\phi $, and $b_ R$ is bounded. Elsewhere $\phi _ t\leq \phi $ gives $\mathrm{e}^{-m\phi }\leq C\mathrm{e}^{-\psi _ m}$. These comparisons yield ( 27.86 ). Choosing the solution of minimal norm in the singular weighted Hilbert space makes the correction linear in its source. The estimate requires a continuous lower bound $\lambda $. We take $\lambda $ equal to $c/R^2$ inside $D_ t$ and to $cq/R^2$ on the exterior annulus, interpolating across a thin exterior collar of $\Gamma _ t$. For the cutoff sources used below, whose supports are separated from $\Gamma _ t$, the collar can be chosen to miss the source. For an exterior source whose support accumulates on $\Gamma _ t$, we let the collar shrink to $\Gamma _ t$; since $\Gamma _ t$ has zero area, dominated convergence in the integrals of $\lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |^2$ and weak compactness in the fixed weighted Hilbert space give the same estimate. The singular metric is handled by approximation, which gives the same estimate for a weak solution. Where the source vanishes, the Cauchy–Riemann equation in the sense of distributions makes the solution holomorphic. Near $x$, the weight is $|z|^{-2q}$ times a smooth positive factor. A holomorphic term $z^ j$ is square integrable against it precisely when $j\geq q$, so the solution has the required vanishing order. $\square$

title: Theorem 27.13.4
text: Theorem 27.13.4 . Let $D_ t$ and $\Gamma _ t$ be as in section 27.13.1 . Let $d_ t(z)$ be the signed Euclidean distance from $z$ to $\Gamma _ t$, positive outside $D_ t$, and let $p_ t(z)$ be the nearest point of $\Gamma _ t$. For every fixed $M>0$, uniformly over points $z$ with $|d_ t(z)|\leq MR/\sqrt q$, 27.87 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curvature-boundary-transition} \frac{\pi a(z)B_{m,q}(z)}{m\rho (z)} -\Phi \bigl (2\sqrt{m\rho (p_ t(z))}\, d_ t(z)\bigr )\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} If $d_ t(z)=o(R)$ and $\sqrt q\, d_ t(z)/R$ tends to $-\infty $ or $+\infty $, the same normalized kernel tends to $0$ or $1$, respectively. Thus, for every sublinear order, the transition is centered on $\Gamma _ t$ and has length $1/(2\sqrt{m\rho })$. Proof. We pass to logarithmic coordinates adapted to $\Gamma _ t$, in which the norm of a section of order $q$ becomes Gaussian in the distance to the boundary. Restriction to a thin ring gives the upper bound, and localized trial sections corrected by lemma 27.13.3 give the lower bound. Finally we compare with the full kernel to obtain saturation. Throughout the proof, $c$ and $C$ denote positive constants independent of $m$, which may change from line to line. Step 1: the effective potential. Define on the unit disk \[  \begin{aligned}  A_ R(w)& =G_ R(F_ R(w))+r\log (F_ R(w)/w),\\  \Psi _ R& =Q_ R(F_ R(w))-2\operatorname {Re} A_ R(w)-2r\log |w|, \end{aligned}  \] where the logarithm uses the branch near one. Then $A_ R=1/2+O(R)$ and $F_ R=w+O(R)$ in every fixed norm used below. The effective potential $\Psi _ R=(Q_ R-U_ R)\circ F_ R$ is positive inside the disk, and its value and gradient vanish on the boundary. For $w=\mathrm{e}^{v+\mathrm{i}\theta }$ it has the expansion 27.90 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curvature-ring-expansion} \Psi _ R=(2r^2+O(R))v^2+O(v^3), \end{equation} and the exact quadratic coefficient is $2(Q_ R)_{\zeta \bar\zeta }(F_ R(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }))|F_ R'(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })|^2$. The maps need not extend holomorphically across the circle. To obtain charts that also cover a neighborhood outside the circle, we truncate their Taylor series at the degree $K=\lfloor q^{1/16}\rfloor $ and denote the truncations by $F_ K,A_ K$. The Taylor coefficients of a function bounded in a sufficiently high fixed Hölder norm decay faster than a large fixed power of their index, so the truncation error is $O(q^{-10})$, together with the fixed number of derivatives needed here. Fix a small $c_0>0$. On $|w|\leq 1+c_0/K$ the derivatives of the truncations remain bounded and $F_ K-w,A_ K-1/2=O(R)$, because the factor $(1+c_0/K)^ K\leq \mathrm{e}^{c_0}$ controls the sums. In particular, $F_ K$ is univalent there for small $R$. Put $\delta =c_0/K$ and \[  \Psi _ K=Q_ R(F_ K)-2\operatorname {Re} A_ K-2r\log |w|.  \] The errors in the value and the first derivative of $\Psi _ K$ on the circle are $O(q^{-10})$, and uniformly for $|v|\leq \delta $, 27.91 \begin{equation} \label{eq:polynomial-ring-expansion} \Psi _ K=(2r^2+O(R)+O(|v|))v^2+O(q^{-10})(1+|v|). \end{equation} Inside the disk, the effective potential has uniform positive quadratic growth near the circle, a positive lower bound on compact annuli farther inside, and logarithmic growth at zero. In the coordinate $z=RF_ K(w)$, a local holomorphic section of order at least $q$ at $x$ is uniquely represented, in the original frame, as 27.92 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadrature-section-gauge} s=w^ q\exp ((q/r)A_ K(w))f(w),\qquad |s|_{h^ m}^2=|f(w)|^2\mathrm{e}^{-(q/r)\Psi _ K(w)}, \end{equation} with $f$ holomorphic near zero. The volume in this chart is $R^2(1+O(R))\, \mathrm{d}A_ w$. Put $\eta =\sqrt{rq}\, v$. On each band $|\eta |\leq N$ with $N$ fixed, \[  (q/r)\Psi _ K=2\eta ^2+o(1).  \] Step 2: the upper bound. Let the observation point have coordinate $\eta _0$ in a fixed bounded interval. Restricting the norm to the band $|\eta |\leq N$ bounds the kernel from above by the kernel of the restricted space. For $f(w)=\sum _{j\geq 0}b_ jw^ j$, the limiting diagonal norms of the monomials on this band are \[  n_{j,N}=\frac{2\pi R^2}{\sqrt{rq}}I_ N(j/\sqrt{rq}),\qquad I_ N(s)=\int _{-N}^ N \mathrm{e}^{2s\eta -2\eta ^2}\, \mathrm{d}\eta .  \] After normalization by $rq/(\pi R^2)$, the limiting upper kernel is 27.93 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-mode-ring-kernel} \frac12\mathrm{e}^{-2\eta _0^2}\int _0^\infty \frac{\mathrm{e}^{2s\eta _0}}{I_ N(s)}\, \mathrm{d}s. \end{equation} The passage from sums to integrals uses Riemann sums with mesh $1/\sqrt{rq}$. To control their tails, bound $I_ N(s)$ from below by its integral over a fixed subinterval of $[-N,N]$ lying beyond every observation point $\eta _0$; this gives an exponential bound uniform in the mesh. Thus we may first pass to the Riemann integral and then let $N\to \infty $. Since $I_\infty (s)=\sqrt{\pi /2}\, \mathrm{e}^{s^2/2}$, the expression ( 27.93 ) tends to 27.94 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaussian-ring-limit} \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _0^\infty \mathrm{e}^{-(s-2\eta _0)^2/2}\, \mathrm{d}s =\Phi (2\eta _0). \end{equation} Step 3: the lower bound. Fix $T>0$, and use ( 27.92 ) with $f$ in the span of the monomials $w^ j$, $0\leq j\leq T\sqrt{rq}$. For $f=\sum _ jb_ jw^ j$, put $\| s\| _{\mathrm{trial}}^2=\sum _ j|b_ j|^2n_ j$, with $n_ j$ given by ( 27.96 ) below. Let $\chi $ be a radial cutoff function in the $w$-plane, supported in $|w|\leq 1+\delta $ and equal to one on $|w|\leq 1+\delta /2$. The annulus on which $\chi $ is not constant lies outside $D_ t$. Equations ( 27.91 ) and ( 27.92 ) bound the squared norm of the source, as a quadratic form on the entire span, by \[  \| \bar\partial (\chi s)\| _{h^ m,\nu }^2\leq C(R\delta )^{-2}\mathrm{e}^{-cq\delta ^2}\| s\| _{\mathrm{trial}}^2;  \] the linear term $2jv$ in the exponent is absorbed because $\sqrt q\, \delta \to \infty $. Lemma 27.13.3 gives a correction $g_ s$, depending linearly on $s$, with $\bar\partial g_ s=\bar\partial (\chi s)$ and 27.95 \begin{equation} \label{eq:shrinking-cutoff-correction} \| g_ s\| _{h^ m}^2\leq C(q\delta ^2)^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-cq\delta ^2}\| s\| _{\mathrm{trial}}^2. \end{equation} The constants here depend on $m$ only through $R$ and $q$. The factor $R^2$ in ( 27.86 ) cancels the factor $R^{-2}$ coming from the derivative of the cutoff; this cancellation is needed even when $q$ grows more slowly than every power of $m$. On this span, the Gram form of the global norm of $\chi s$ converges, in the sense of relative operator norm, to the diagonal form 27.96 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaussian-ring-gram} n_ j=\frac{2\pi R^2}{\sqrt{rq}}\sqrt{\frac\pi 2} \exp (j^2/(2rq)). \end{equation} Indeed, the ratio of the weights is uniformly close to one on each fixed band in $\eta $. Outside such a band, the radial bound for the weight and Parseval's identity on circles bound arbitrary combinations by diagonal tails $\mathrm{e}^{-c\eta ^2+2T|\eta |}$. We first pass to the limit on a fixed band and then enlarge it. The positive lower bound of the effective potential on compact annuli and its logarithmic singularity at zero control the remaining part of the disk. This argument controls the whole quadratic form, without a factor depending on the dimension of the span. To evaluate the corrections we need a pointwise bound. Let $u$ be a section holomorphic on a disk of radius $R/\sqrt q$ centered at a point $z$ with $|z|$ comparable to $R$. Then a local submean estimate gives 27.97 \begin{equation} \label{eq:shrinking-point-evaluation} |u(z)|_{h^ m}^2\leq C(q/R^2)\| u\| _{h^ m}^2. \end{equation} To prove it, multiply $u$ by the exponential of a holomorphic polynomial that removes the harmonic part of the linear and quadratic Taylor terms of $m\phi $ at $z$. After rescaling the disk to unit size, the remaining quadratic coefficient is bounded and the third-order error is $O(q^{-1/2})$, which proves the estimate. It applies to the corrections, because their sources lie on the cutoff annulus, away from the observation points. Together with ( 27.95 ), it shows that the kernel of the corrected global trial sections differs by $o(q/R^2)$ from the local trial kernel. After normalization, the lower limit is the integral in ( 27.94 ) with upper limit $T$ instead of infinity, and letting $T\to \infty $ gives the matching lower bound. Step 4: return to the original coordinate. Let $p$ be the nearest boundary point and $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }$ its preimage under $F_ R$. Then \[  \begin{aligned}  v& =\frac{d_ t(z)}{R|F_ R'(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })|} +O(d_ t(z)^2/R^2)+o(q^{-1/2}),\\  m\rho (p)R^2|F_ R'(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })|^2& =rq(1+O(R)). \end{aligned}  \] Moreover, $m\rho (z)/a(z)=(rq/R^2)(1+o(1))$ in the band $|d_ t(z)|\leq MR/\sqrt q$. These identities convert $2\eta _0$ into the argument in ( 27.87 ) and give the normalization of the density there. This proves ( 27.87 ). Step 5: the full density and saturation. Let $B_ m^{\rm full}$ be the density of the full space $H^0(C,L^ m)$. At points with $|z|\asymp R$, it satisfies 27.100 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mesoscopic-full-density} B_ m^{\rm full}(z)=\frac{m\rho (z)}{\pi a(z)}(1+o(1)), \end{equation} uniformly in an $o(R)$-neighborhood of $\Gamma _ t$. We give a direct localization argument, which also yields the saturation statements of the theorem. Remove the harmonic Taylor terms of $m\phi $ at the observation point and rescale by $(m\rho (z))^{-1/2}$. On every fixed rescaled disk, the remaining weight tends to $|u|^2$, where $u$ is the rescaled coordinate, and the volume density tends to the constant $a(z)$. The Taylor estimate is uniform, because the third derivatives of $\phi $ at radius $R$ are $O(R^{2r-3})$, so the normalized third-order error is $O(q^{-1/2})$. Restriction to such disks bounds the evaluation norm from above, and the Gaussian norm of the constant function on them tends to $\pi $ as their radius grows. This proves the upper bound in ( 27.100 ). For the lower bound, take the holomorphic exponential canceling the harmonic Taylor terms, and cut it off on a disk of radius $\varepsilon R$ centered at the observation point, where $\varepsilon \to 0$ and $\sqrt q\, \varepsilon \to \infty $. Its local squared norm is $(\pi a(z)/(m\rho (z)))(1+o(1))$ times its squared weighted value at the center, which is one. The quadratic lower bound for the weight bounds the source on the cutoff annulus by an exponential factor $\mathrm{e}^{-cq\varepsilon ^2}$. Add the same bounded function of scale $R$ to the original metric and use the pointwise $\bar\partial $ estimate. The relative squared norm of the correction is bounded by $C(q\varepsilon ^2)^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-cq\varepsilon ^2}=o(1)$, after decreasing $c$ if necessary, and its value at the center is $o(1)$ by ( 27.97 ). This proves the matching lower bound. For saturation inside $D_ t$, use the polynomial chart above and put $u=1-|w|>0$. Restrict the norm in ( 27.92 ) to the exterior half-band $0\leq v\leq c/\sqrt q$. On this half-band every monomial $w^ j$, $j\geq 0$, has norm at least $cR^2/\sqrt q$. Parseval's identity on circles and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give \[  B_{m,q}(z)\leq C\frac{\sqrt q}{R^2}\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-cqu^2}}{1-|w|^2}.  \] If $u\sqrt q\to \infty $, this bound divided by $q/R^2$ tends to zero. The error $O(q^{-10})$ of the chart changes neither the hypothesis nor the conclusion. For saturation outside $D_ t$, cut off the localized Gaussian section at $z$ on a disk of radius \[  \varepsilon R,\qquad \varepsilon =\min \{ d_ t(z)/(3R),q^{-1/4}\} .  \] This disk lies entirely outside $D_ t$, and again $\varepsilon \to 0$ and $\sqrt q\, \varepsilon \to \infty $. Apply lemma 27.13.3 with the singular obstacle metric, which equals the original metric on the support of the source. The correction has negligible norm and value, and it vanishes to order $q$ at $x$. Thus a member of $V_{m,q}$ asymptotically attains the full Gaussian density, and ( 27.100 ) gives the reverse inequality. This proves saturation to one. $\square$

title: 27.13.3 Growth ranges and compact examples
text: 27.13.3 Growth ranges and compact examples In the coordinate $z$, the quadrature boundary $\Gamma _ t$ differs from the model circle $|z|=R$ by $O(R^2)$. Comparing this displacement with the transition width $R/\sqrt q$ gives the range of orders in which the uncorrected law holds for every metric. A holomorphic change of coordinate produces a compact example in which the displacement has exactly this size. Theorem 27.13.5 . Keep the setting of section 27.13.1 , fix the integer $r\geq 1$ and a real $\tau $, and consider observation points with coordinates $z_ m$ and the law 27.101 \begin{equation} \label{eq:optimal-growing-jet-law} \frac{\pi B_{m,q}(z_ m)}{mr^2|z_ m|^{2r-2}} \longrightarrow \Phi (\tau ),\qquad m|z_ m|^{2r}=q/r+\tau \sqrt{q/r}, \end{equation} where the second relation prescribes the radii of the observation points. If $q=o(m^{1/(r+1)})$, this law holds for every choice of the geometric data and every sequence of arguments of $z_ m$. This range is optimal: for every sequence $q\to \infty $ with $q=o(m)$ that is not $o(m^{1/(r+1)})$, there is a compact example satisfying the same hypotheses in which the law fails along a subsequence. For fixed geometric data, write $\Gamma _ t$ as $\{ |z|=R c_ R(\theta )\} $. Then ( 27.101 ) holds for every fixed $\tau $ and every sequence of arguments if and only if 27.102 \begin{equation} \label{eq:fixed-weight-jet-criterion} \sqrt q\, \| c_ R-1\| _\infty \longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Proof. By lemma 27.13.2 , $c_ R-1=O(R)$ in every fixed norm required here. The observation points in ( 27.101 ) satisfy \[  |z_ m|/R=1+\tau /(2\sqrt{rq})+O(q^{-1}).  \] Since the slope of the boundary graph tends to zero, the argument of $\Phi $ in theorem 27.13.4 is $\tau +o(1)$ whenever $\sqrt q R\to 0$, and this condition is equivalent to $q=o(m^{1/(r+1)})$. Moreover, $a(z)=1+o(1)$ and $\rho (z)=r^2|z|^{2r-2}(1+o(1))$ at these points, so the two normalizations agree. Thus theorem 27.13.4 proves the law for all data in this range. The same reasoning shows that ( 27.102 ) is sufficient. For necessity, suppose that ( 27.102 ) fails. On a subsequence, choose an angle realizing the maximal boundary displacement and observe at $|z|=R$ with $\tau =0$. A nonzero finite subsequential limit of the scaled displacement gives a nonzero Gaussian argument, and an infinite one gives saturation to zero or one. Radial and normal distances have relative error tending to zero, because the graph has vanishing slope. In either case the limit differs from $1/2$. It remains to construct the compact examples. On $\mathbb P^1$ choose a radial metric on $\mathcal O(d)$ whose local potential $f(u)$, $u=|w|^2$, equals $u^ r$ near zero, such that $g(u)=uf'(u)$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty )$ and tends to $d$, and such that $g(u)=d-\epsilon /u$ for large $u$, with a constant $\epsilon >0$. Such a smooth interpolation exists for a sufficiently large integer $d$: prescribe a positive function $g'$, equal to $r^2u^{r-1}$ near zero and to $\epsilon /u^2$ near infinity, with total integral $d$. Then $f=d\log u+\mathrm{constant}+\epsilon /u$ near infinity, so the potential in the frame at infinity is smooth with strictly positive curvature. Choose a smooth radial volume form equal to $\mathrm{d}A_ w$ near zero. For sufficiently small $t$, the hole $D_ t$ lies in the region where $f(u)=u^ r$ and equals the disk $|w|<R$: rotational invariance and uniqueness make it a disk, and its curvature mass is $rR^{2r}=t$. Hence the transition and saturation statements of theorem 27.13.4 apply to this compact example. Now use instead the coordinate $z$ defined by $w=z+cz^2$, with a constant $c>0$. In this coordinate the same compact metric satisfies $\phi (z)=|z|^{2r}+O(|z|^{2r+1})$, the volume form still has $a(0)=1$, and vanishing orders are unchanged. At the uncorrected observation point $z=R$ with $\tau =0$, \[  2\sqrt{mr^2R^{2r-2}}\, (|w|-R) =2c\sqrt r\, \sqrt q R,  \] and the normalizing factors computed in the two coordinates have ratio tending to one. If $q$ is not $o(m^{1/(r+1)})$, there is a subsequence on which $\sqrt q R$ tends to a positive finite number or to infinity. Theorem 27.13.4 , together with its saturation statement when the argument diverges, then gives a limit strictly larger than $1/2$. This proves that the range is sharp. $\square$

Choose a smooth radial volume form equal to $\mathrm{d}A_ w$ near zero. For sufficiently small $t$, the hole $D_ t$ lies in the region where $f(u)=u^ r$ and equals the disk $|w|<R$: rotational invariance and uniqueness make it a disk, and its curvature mass is $rR^{2r}=t$. Hence the transition and saturation statements of theorem 27.13.4 apply to this compact example. Now use instead the coordinate $z$ defined by $w=z+cz^2$, with a constant $c>0$. In this coordinate the same compact metric satisfies $\phi (z)=|z|^{2r}+O(|z|^{2r+1})$, the volume form still has $a(0)=1$, and vanishing orders are unchanged. At the uncorrected observation point $z=R$ with $\tau =0$, \[  2\sqrt{mr^2R^{2r-2}}\, (|w|-R) =2c\sqrt r\, \sqrt q R,  \] and the normalizing factors computed in the two coordinates have ratio tending to one. If $q$ is not $o(m^{1/(r+1)})$, there is a subsequence on which $\sqrt q R$ tends to a positive finite number or to infinity. Theorem 27.13.4 , together with its saturation statement when the argument diverges, then gives a limit strictly larger than $1/2$. This proves that the range is sharp. $\square$

title: 27.13.4 Corrections from the smooth weight
text: 27.13.4 Corrections from the smooth weight The boundary $\Gamma _ t$ can be expanded in powers of $R$, and the leading terms of this expansion give explicit corrections to the uncorrected law. Write \[  \phi (z)=|z|^{2r}+P_{2r+1}(z,\bar z)+O(|z|^{2r+2}),\qquad P(\theta )=P_{2r+1}(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta },\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta }),  \] where $P_{2r+1}$ is a real homogeneous polynomial of degree $2r+1$ in $(z,\bar z)$. Let $\Lambda $ be the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator of the unit circle, $\Lambda \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} n\theta }=|n|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} n\theta }$. The first boundary coefficient is given by 27.103 \begin{equation} \label{eq:first-boundary-coefficient} c_ R=1+Rb_1+O(R^2),\qquad b_1=-\frac{((2r+1)-\Lambda )P}{4r^2}. \end{equation} To derive this, write the interior obstacle, to first order in $R$ and in polar coordinates $(s,\theta )$ for $\zeta $, as $1+2r\log s+R H$ with $H$ harmonic. Matching values on the boundary $s=1+Rb_1$ gives $H|_{s=1}=P$; the terms involving $b_1$ cancel there, since the radial model already matches first derivatives. Matching radial derivatives then gives $4r^2b_1+(2r+1)P-\Lambda P=0$. If $P_{2r+1}$ is harmonic, then $\Lambda P=(2r+1)P$ and $b_1=0$, as it must be, since such a term can be removed by a change of frame. For $q=O(m^{1/(r+1)})$, the argument of $\Phi $ at the uncorrected observation point of ( 27.101 ) is 27.104 \begin{equation} \label{eq:first-growing-jet-shift} \tau +\frac{\sqrt q R}{2r^{3/2}}((2r+1)-\Lambda )P(\theta )+o(1), \end{equation} uniformly in $\theta $, and the normalized kernel differs from $\Phi $ of this argument by $o(1)$. The remainder is small because $\sqrt q R^2\to 0$ in this range. For $w=z+cz^2$ we have $P=2r\operatorname {Re}(c\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$, and the shift is $2\sqrt{rq}R\operatorname {Re}(c\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$, in agreement with the compact example above. For every fixed integer $J\geq 1$, the parameter construction of lemma 27.13.2 gives \[  c_ R=1+\sum _{j=1}^ J R^ j b_ j+O(R^{J+1})  \] in every fixed norm needed. The coefficients satisfy an explicit recursion, obtained by expanding the interior harmonic obstacle in powers of $R$. At order $j$, matching values determines the boundary data of the new harmonic term from the Taylor term of degree $2r+j$ of $\phi $ and all preceding coefficients, and harmonic extension determines the term itself. Matching derivatives then gives an equation $4r^2b_ j+\text{(known terms)}=0$; the new coefficient $b_ j$ does not enter the value equation of order $j$. For $j\geq 2$, nonlinear contributions of lower-order terms also appear. Replacing $\Gamma _ t$ by the curve given by the truncated expansion moves the center of the transition by $O(R^{J+2})$. This curve can therefore be used in place of $\Gamma _ t$ whenever \[  \sqrt q R^{J+1}\to 0, \quad \hbox{equivalently}\quad q=o(m^{(J+1)/(r+J+1)}).  \] If $b_1=\cdots =b_{j-1}=0$ but $b_ j\not\equiv 0$, the criterion ( 27.102 ) shows that, for this fixed weight, the uncorrected law holds exactly in the range $q=o(m^{j/(r+j)})$, and this range is sharp when all directions of observation are allowed. Indeed, the higher terms are relatively $O(R)$ at an angle where $b_ j\ne 0$. In the radial case $\phi =f(u)$ with $u=|z|^2$, the hole is a disk by uniqueness and rotational invariance. By ( 27.85 ), its boundary circle $\{ u=u_*\} $ is determined by \[  m u_*f'(u_*)=q.  \] With $\rho (u)=f'(u)+uf''(u)$, the asymptotic variance of the dominant monomial degree is $m u\rho (u)$, and the corresponding Gaussian argument is 27.105 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-growing-jet-argument} \frac{m u f'(u)-q}{\sqrt{m u\rho (u)}}. \end{equation} For bounded arguments, Taylor expansion at $u_*$ identifies it with $2\sqrt{m\rho (u_*)}(\sqrt u-\sqrt{u_*})+o(1)$. Hence theorem 27.13.4 proves this radial formula for all sublinear orders. For $f=u^ r+c u^{r+1}+\cdots $, the first shift at the uncorrected observation point is $c(r+1)r^{-3/2}\sqrt q R^2$, so the critical growth is $m^{2/(r+2)}$. This larger radial threshold does not apply in arbitrary coordinates. No fixed finite Taylor jet of the weight determines the correction for every $q=o(m)$. For example, near zero take \[  f(u)=u^ r+c u^ r \mathrm{e}^{-1/\sqrt u},\qquad c>0,  \] with the second term extended by zero at $u=0$, and interpolated globally as above. It has the same Taylor jet as $u^ r$ at zero to every finite order, but at $u=R^2$ its relative contribution to $uf'(u)$ is $c \mathrm{e}^{-1/R}(1+1/(2rR))$. For $q=\lfloor m/\log m\rfloor $, we have $\sqrt q \mathrm{e}^{-1/R}/R\to \infty $. Hence the uncorrected observation point with $\tau =0$ lies outside the true boundary circle by many transition widths, and the normalized kernel tends to one. The quadrature-domain correction includes this flat contribution.

27.14 A logarithmic kernel scale in two dimensions In the curve models above, the metric weight has a single homogeneous leading term. In two dimensions, a mixed monomial in the weight can compete with the pure monomials and introduce a logarithm into the scale of the kernel. For an explicit metric on $\mathbb P^2$, the relevant global section norm can be computed directly. Write $\mathrm dA$ for Euclidean area on $\mathbb C$. We first isolate the integral responsible for the logarithm. Lemma 27.14.1 . Set $W(a,b)=ab+a^3+b^3$ on $[0,\infty )^2$. As $t	o \infty $, \[   egin{gathered} J(t):=\int _0^\infty \int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-tW(a,b)}\, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db = rac{\log t}{3t}+O(t^{-1}), \ \int _0^\infty \int _0^\infty (a+b)\mathrm e^{-tW(a,b)} \, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db=O(t^{-4/3}). \end{gathered}  \] Proof. Put $A=t^{-2/3}$ and $B=t^{-1/3}$; the logarithm comes from the interval $A\leq a\leq B$. For $a>0$, the substitution $u=tab$ gives \[  H_ t(a):=\int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-t(ab+b^3)}\, \mathrm db = rac1{ta}\int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-u-u^3/(t^2a^3)}\, \mathrm du.  \] Since $0\leq 1-\mathrm e^{-v}\leq v$ for $v\geq 0$, \[  0\leq  rac1{ta}-H_ t(a)\leq  rac6{t^3a^4}.  \] Over $A\leq a\leq B$, the integral of this error is $O(t^{-1})$. Replacing $\mathrm e^{-ta^3}$ by one in $\int _ A^ B\mathrm e^{-ta^3}/(ta)\, \mathrm da$ costs at most $\int _ A^ B a^2\, \mathrm da=O(t^{-1})$ as well. Thus the middle interval contributes \[  \int _ A^ B\mathrm e^{-ta^3}H_ t(a)\, \mathrm da = rac1t\log  rac BA+O(t^{-1}) = rac{\log t}{3t}+O(t^{-1}).  \] For $a<A$, the bound $H_ t(a)\leq \int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-tb^3}\, \mathrm db=O(t^{-1/3})$ gives a contribution $O(t^{-1})$. For $a>B$, use $H_ t(a)\leq 1/(ta)$ and substitute $v=ta^3$ to obtain the bound \[  \int _ B^\infty  rac{\mathrm e^{-ta^3}}{ta}\, \mathrm da = rac1{3t}\int _1^\infty  rac{\mathrm e^{-v}}v\, \mathrm dv =O(t^{-1}).  \] Finally, $aH_ t(a)\leq 1/t$ gives \[  \int _0^\infty \int _0^\infty a\mathrm e^{-tW(a,b)} \, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db \leq  rac1t\int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-ta^3}\, \mathrm da =O(t^{-4/3}).  \] Symmetry proves the same bound for $b$. $\square$ On $L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)$, define a Hermitian metric by \[  |S|_ h^2([Z])=  rac{|S(Z)|^2}{ igl (|Z_0|^6+3|Z_0Z_1Z_2|^2+3|Z_1|^6+3|Z_2|^6 igr )^{1/3}} \qquad (S	ext{ a linear form}).  \] The denominator is positive away from zero and homogeneous of degree two in $|Z|$, so the metric is well defined and smooth. Its local weight is one third of the logarithm of a sum of squared absolute values of holomorphic cubic functions, so its curvature is semipositive. In the chart $Z_0
e 0$, put $z_ j=Z_ j/Z_0$ and $p=[1:0:0]$. The frame $e=Z_0$ has 27.106  egin{equation} \label{eq:logarithmic-projective-weight} |e|_ h^2=\mathrm e^{-\phi },\qquad \phi (z)=	frac 13\log  igl (1+3W(|z_1|^2,|z_2|^2) igr ). \end{equation} In particular the curvature vanishes at $p$. Proposition 27.14.2 . Let $
u $ be a smooth positive probability volume form on $\mathbb P^2$, invariant under the rotations of $z_1$ and of $z_2$, and write \[  
u =ho (z)\, \mathrm dA(z_1)\, \mathrm dA(z_2),\qquad ho _0=ho (0)>0  \] in the chart above. Give $H^0(\mathbb P^2,L^ m)$ the norm $\int _{\mathbb P^2}|s|_{h^ m}^2\, \mathrm d
u $, and let $B_ m$ be its kernel density. Then \[  B_ m(p)= rac{3}{\pi ^2ho _0} rac m{\log m} \left(1+O((\log m)^{-1})ight).  \] For the Fubini–Study probability volume, the leading constant is $3/2$. Proof. The homogeneous monomials form an orthogonal basis, because the metric and the volume are invariant under the two independent rotations and distinct monomials transform by distinct characters. At $p$, only $Z_0^ m$ has a nonzero value, equal to one in the frame $e^{\otimes m}$. Consequently $B_ m(p)=I_ m^{-1}$, where \[  I_ m=\int _{\mathbb P^2}|Z_0^ m|_{h^ m}^2\, \mathrm d
u =\int _{\mathbb C^2}(1+3W(|z_1|^2,|z_2|^2))^{-m/3} ho (z)\, \mathrm dA(z_1)\, \mathrm dA(z_2).  \] Here the omitted projective line $\{ Z_0=0\} $ has zero volume. By rotational invariance, the first derivatives of $ho $ vanish at zero, so $ho (z)=ho _0+O(|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2)$ near zero. In the variables $a=|z_1|^2$ and $b=|z_2|^2$, polar integration has Jacobian $\pi ^2\, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db$. Choose a fixed small $\delta >0$. On $W\leq \delta $, set $\ell (W)=	frac 13\log (1+3W)$. For constants $c,C>0$ independent of $m$, \[  cW\leq \ell (W)\leq W,\qquad 0\leq \mathrm e^{-m\ell (W)}-\mathrm e^{-mW} \leq CmW^2\mathrm e^{-cmW} \leq  rac Cm\mathrm e^{-cmW/2}.  \] The first estimate of lemma 27.14.1 bounds the integral of this error in the weight by $O(m^{-2}\log m)$, and the second bounds the error from replacing $ho $ by $ho _0$ by $O(m^{-4/3})$. On the complement $W>\delta $, the contribution to $I_ m$ is at most $(1+3\delta )^{-m/3}$, because $
u $ has mass one, and the corresponding tail of the exponential model is at most $\mathrm e^{-m\delta /2}J(m/2)$. Therefore \[  I_ m=\pi ^2ho _0J(m)+O(m^{-4/3})+O(m^{-2}\log m) = rac{\pi ^2ho _0}{3m}\log m+O(m^{-1}).  \] Inverting proves the first assertion. The Fubini–Study probability volume has the local expression \[  
u = rac2{\pi ^2}(1+|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2)^{-3} \, \mathrm dA(z_1)\, \mathrm dA(z_2).  \] It has mass one, since $2\int _0^\infty \int _0^\infty (1+a+b)^{-3}\, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db=1$, and its density at zero is $2/\pi ^2$. The leading constant is therefore $3/2$. $\square$ Thus the full kernel, without any selection, already has a logarithmic factor at this fixed curvature zero, and its coefficient depends on the volume density at $p$. The calculation does not give a transition for growing vanishing ideals; that would require control of the norms of the selected monomials on the moving scale, as in the curve case.

title: 27.15 Anisotropic point jets and isolated poles on fibrations

text:
27.15 Anisotropic point jets and isolated poles on fibrations Vanishing to a given order at a point couples the variables through the total degree, even when the metric weight splits as a sum. On a compact product of curves, this coupling becomes a half-space condition on independent monomial indices, and the transition on each curve factor determines the local law in higher dimensions. An isolated pole on a submersion with connected fibers gives a further application: its multiplier ideal does not descend to the base, although the condition it imposes on pulled-back sections does. Let $q\geq 2$. For $1\leq j\leq q$, choose integers $r_ j\geq 2$, at least two of them unequal, and numbers $\varepsilon _ j>0$. Put \[  Y=(\mathbb P^1)^ q,\qquad x=(0,\ldots ,0),\qquad d_ j=r_ j+1,\qquad L= oxtimes _ j\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(d_ j).  \] In the affine coordinates $z_ j$ and the product frame $e$, put $t_ j=|z_ j|^2$ and define the smooth metric and volume by \[   egin{gathered} |e|_ h^2=\mathrm e^{-\phi },\qquad \phi =\sum _ j\psi _ j(t_ j),\qquad \psi _ j(t)=\log (1+t^{r_ j}+\varepsilon _ jt^{r_ j+1}),\ 
u _ Y=a(t)\prod _ j\mathrm dA_ j,\qquad a(t)=\prod _ j a_ j(t_ j),\qquad a_ j(t)=(1+t)^{-2}, \end{gathered}  \] where $\mathrm dA_ j$ is Euclidean area in $z_ j$. In particular $
u _ Y(Y)=\pi ^ q$ and $a(0)=1$. Define \[  H_ j(t)=t\psi _ j'(t),\qquad G_ j(t)=tH_ j'(t),\qquad g_ j(t)=G_ j(t)/t,\qquad 	heta =c_1(L,h).  \] The metric extends across infinity: there its weight, in terms of $u=|z_ j|^{-2}$, is $\log (\varepsilon _ j+u+u^{d_ j})$, which has positive curvature at infinity. For $t>0$, $H_ j(t)$ and $G_ j(t)$ are the mean and the variance of the exponents $0,r_ j,d_ j$ taken with probabilities proportional to $1,t^{r_ j},\varepsilon _ jt^{d_ j}$. Hence $G_ j>0$, and $H_ j$ increases from $0$ to $d_ j$. Near zero, 27.107  egin{equation} \label{eq:anisotropic-weight-expansion}  egin{aligned}  H_ j(t)& =r_ jt^{r_ j}+(r_ j+1)\varepsilon _ jt^{r_ j+1}+O(t^{2r_ j}),\  G_ j(t)& =r_ j^2t^{r_ j}+(r_ j+1)^2\varepsilon _ jt^{r_ j+1}+O(t^{2r_ j}). \end{aligned} \end{equation} Thus $	heta $ is semipositive, and its rank drops along the coordinate divisors $\{ z_ j=0\} $. For integers $k_ m	o \infty $ with $k_ m=o(m)$, let $B_ m$ be the density of \[  V_ m=H^0(Y,L^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^{k_ m}),\qquad \| s\| ^2=\int _ Y|s|_{h^ m}^2
u _ Y.  \] The ideal $\mathfrak m_ x^{k_ m}$ of the point $x$ imposes vanishing of total order $k_ m$, rather than separate orders in the individual variables. As before, $\Phi $ is the standard Gaussian distribution function. Theorem 27.15.1 . Let $z=z^{(m)}$ be points of the affine chart, with $t_ j=|z_ j|^2$, such that $t_ j	o 0$ and $\mu _ j:=mH_ j(t_ j)$ satisfies $\mu _ j/k_ m	o \alpha _ j>0$, where $\sum _ j\alpha _ j=1$. Set $V=\sum _ jmG_ j(t_ j)$. If $(\sum _ j\mu _ j-k_ m)/\sqrt V	o 	au \in \mathbb R$, then 27.110  egin{equation} \label{eq:anisotropic-growing-transition}  rac{\pi ^ q a(t)B_ m(z)}{m^ q\prod _ jg_ j(t_ j)}\longrightarrow \Phi (	au ). \end{equation} The arguments of the coordinates $z_ j$ are arbitrary. For all sufficiently large $m$, 27.111  egin{equation} \label{eq:anisotropic-jet-dimension} N_ m:=\dim V_ m=\prod _ j(d_ jm+1)- inom {k_ m+q-1}{q}, \qquad N_ m/m^ q\longrightarrow D:=\prod _ jd_ j. \end{equation} Moreover $m^{-q}B_ m
u _ Y	o 	heta ^ q/q!$ in total variation. Proof. The proof reduces the kernel to a probability for a sum of independent variables, one for each factor, and applies the one-variable transition of section 27.13 to each of them. In each variable, the affine coefficient of a global section of $L^ m$ is entire, and its expression in the frame at infinity must be holomorphic, so it is a polynomial of degree at most $d_ jm$. Hence the monomials $z^\ell e^ m$, $0\leq \ell _ j\leq d_ jm$, form a basis of the global sections. A polynomial vanishes to order at least $k_ m$ at $x$ exactly when all its monomials have total degree at least $k_ m$, so the monomials with $\sum _ j\ell _ j\geq k_ m$ form a basis of $V_ m$. Once $k_ m\leq \min _ j(d_ jm)+1$, which holds for large $m$, all monomials of total degree below $k_ m$ are global, and counting them gives ( 27.111 ). Invariance under the rotation of each coordinate makes these monomials orthogonal. Their squared norms are $\prod _ jJ_{j,m,\ell _ j}$, where \[  J_{j,m,\ell }=\pi \int _0^\infty t^\ell \mathrm e^{-m\psi _ j(t)}a_ j(t)\, \mathrm dt, \qquad w_{j,m,\ell }(t)= rac{t^\ell \mathrm e^{-m\psi _ j(t)}}{J_{j,m,\ell }}.  \] These integrals converge even for $\ell =d_ jm$. title: 27.15.1 Corrected and homogeneous centers
text: 27.15.1 Corrected and homogeneous centers The transition in theorem 27.15.1 is centered at the radii determined by the functions $H_ j$. Replacing them by the radii of the homogeneous leading terms of the weight introduces a shift, which is negligible exactly in a range of orders determined by the largest exponent $r_ j$. Fix positive numbers $\alpha _ j$ with sum one and a real $\tau $, and set 27.113 \begin{equation} \label{eq:anisotropic-corrected-radii} R=\sum _ j\alpha _ jr_ j,\qquad T_ m=k_ m+\tau \sqrt{Rk_ m},\qquad t_ j=H_ j^{-1}(\alpha _ jT_ m/m). \end{equation} Then $\sum _ j\mu _ j=T_ m$ and $V\sim Rk_ m$, so ( 27.110 ) holds for every sublinear growing order. The radii $|z_ j|=\sqrt{t_ j}$ are asymptotic to $(\alpha _ jk_ m/(r_ jm))^{1/(2r_ j)}$. Proposition 27.15.2 . Keep $\alpha _ j,\tau ,R,T_ m$ as above, but use instead the homogeneous radii given by $t_ j=(\alpha _ jT_ m/(r_ jm))^{1/r_ j}$, and put $r_*:=\max _ jr_ j$. For the metrics of this section, the law \[  \frac{\pi ^ qB_ m(z)}{m^ q\prod _ jr_ j^2|z_ j|^{2r_ j-2}}\longrightarrow \Phi (\tau )  \] holds for every fixed $\tau $ if and only if $k_ m=o(m^{2/(r_*+2)})$. If $k_ m/m^{2/(r_*+2)}\to c\in (0,\infty )$, the left side instead tends to \[  \Phi \bigl (\tau +C_\alpha c^{(r_*+2)/(2r_*)}\bigr ),\qquad C_\alpha =\frac1{\sqrt R}\sum _{j:r_ j=r_*} (r_*+1)\varepsilon _ j(\alpha _ j/r_*)^{1+1/r_*}.  \] If that ratio tends to infinity while $k_ m=o(m)$, the limit is $1$. Proof. By ( 27.107 ), $\sum _ j\mu _ j=T_ m+\Delta _ m$ with \[  \Delta _ m=\sum _ j(r_ j+1)\varepsilon _ jmt_ j^{r_ j+1} +O\left(\sum _ jmt_ j^{2r_ j}\right),\qquad V\sim Rk_ m.  \] Since $r_ j\geq 2$, each error term is negligible compared with the corresponding positive correction. Consequently \[  \frac{\Delta _ m}{\sqrt{Rk_ m}}=(1+o(1))\sum _ j \frac{(r_ j+1)\varepsilon _ j(\alpha _ j/r_ j)^{1+1/r_ j}}{\sqrt R} k_ m^{1/2+1/r_ j}m^{-1/r_ j}.  \] At the critical scale only the indices with $r_ j=r_*$ contribute in the limit. Below it every term tends to zero, and above it a positive term diverges. The Gaussian limit of the normalized sum proved above applies in all three cases; in the last case its tightness gives probability one. Moreover, $a(t)\to 1$ and $g_ j(t_ j)/(r_ j^2t_ j^{r_ j-1})\to 1$, so the two normalizations agree. If $k_ m/m^{2/(r_*+2)}$ does not tend to zero, a subsequence has a positive finite or infinite limit, and the law fails at $\tau =0$. This proves both directions of the equivalence for these metrics. $\square$

u _ X=\int _ Y|s|_{h^ m}^2
u _ Y.  \] Pulling back an orthonormal basis proves the identity of densities. If $b_ m$ and $b$ are the densities, with respect to $
u _ Y$, of the measures in the total-variation limit of theorem 27.15.1 , then the corresponding densities on $X$ are $b_ m\circ \pi $ and $b\circ \pi $, and their $L^1(
u _ X)$ distance equals $\int _ Y|b_ m-b|
u _ Y$. This proves ( 27.115 ). The dimension formula ( 27.111 ) gives $\log N_ m/\log m	o q$ and the final normalization. $\square$

title: 27.16 Newton selection and moment-shell limits
text:
27.16 Newton selection and moment-shell limits On a product of projective lines, selecting the monomials whose exponents lie in the dilates of a fixed polytope gives a graded family of section spaces for which the lower bound for the potentials can be proved directly, without a general approximation theorem. The limit of the kernel measures depends on the dimension of the polytope. When this dimension is smaller than that of the manifold, the limit is carried by a family of real tori and differs from the mixed curvature measures of the envelope. Let $X=(\mathbb P^1)^ n$ with $n\geq 1$, and let $L=\mathcal O(k_1,\ldots ,k_ n)$, where each $k_ j$ is a positive integer. Equip $L$ with its product Fubini–Study metric $h$. On the torus $T=(\mathbb C^*)^ n$, in the standard frame $e$, write \[  r_ j=\log |z_ j|^2,\qquad \varphi _0(r)=\sum _ jk_ j\log (1+\mathrm e^{r_ j}),\qquad 	heta =c_1(L,h)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _0.  \] Put $P=\prod _ j[0,k_ j]$. Fix a nonempty rational polytope $Q$ contained in the interior of $P$ whose affine span has the form \[  \operatorname {aff}Q=b+W,\qquad b\in \mathbb Z^ n,  \] with $W\subseteq \mathbb R^ n$ a rational linear subspace. Set $d=\dim Q$ and $\Lambda =W\cap \mathbb Z^ n$. Let $\mathrm dq_\Lambda $ be the Lebesgue measure on $b+W$ normalized so that a fundamental domain of the lattice $\Lambda $ has volume one; when $d=0$, it is the unit point mass at $b$. Write $\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda (Q)$ for the volume of $Q$ with respect to $\mathrm dq_\Lambda $. In this section the selected spaces are defined directly by monomials, without a selecting potential: we select exactly the monomials with exponents in $mQ$, 27.116  egin{equation} \label{eq:newton-selected-spaces} V_ m=\operatorname {span}\{ z^\alpha e^ m: \alpha \in mQ\cap \mathbb Z^ n\} . \end{equation} Each of these monomials is a global section of $L^ m$, since $0\leq \alpha _ j\leq mk_ j$. Since $Q$ is convex, products of selected sections are selected, so these spaces form a graded family. Choose a smooth real torus-invariant function $w$ on $X$ such that the function $F=\varphi _0+w$ of $r$ has positive definite Hessian $D^2F(r)$ for every $r\in \mathbb R^ n$. Choose a smooth strictly positive torus-invariant probability measure $
u $ on $X$. On $T$ we then have $\mathrm d
u =a(r)\, \mathrm dr\, \mathrm d	au $, where $a>0$, $\int a\, \mathrm dr=1$, and $\mathrm d	au $ is the Haar probability measure on $(S^1)^ n$ in the angular variables. Give $V_ m$ the Hilbert norm $\int _ X|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm e^{-mw}\, \mathrm d
u $, and for an orthonormal basis put \[  \mathcal B_ m=\sum _ j|s_{m,j}|_{h^ m}^2,\qquad B_ m=\mathrm e^{-mw}\mathcal B_ m,\qquad U_ m=m^{-1}\log \mathcal B_ m.  \] As in section 27.1 , the density $B_ m$ includes the continuous weight.

Lemma 27.16.1 . The gradient $
abla F:\mathbb R^ n	o \operatorname {int}P$ is a smooth diffeomorphism. With $r(q)=(
abla F)^{-1}(q)$ and $F^*(q)=q\cdot r(q)-F(r(q))$, set \[  G_ Q(r)=\max _{q\in Q}\{ q\cdot r-F^*(q)\} .  \] Then $E_ Q=G_ Q-\varphi _0$ on $T$, and $E_ Q=-\infty $ on $X\setminus T$. Moreover, a global section $s$ of $L^ m$ belongs to $V_ m$ exactly when 27.117  egin{equation} \label{eq:newton-entire-growth} |s/e^ m|^2\leq C_ s\mathrm e^{mH_ Q(r)}\quad 	ext{on }T \quad 	ext{for some finite }C_ s. \end{equation} Proof. In the charts at infinity one sees that every global section of $L^ m$ is a polynomial of degree at most $mk_ j$ in each variable $z_ j$. If $s\in V_ m$, the growth bound follows from the triangle inequality, since $|z^\alpha |^2=\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r}\leq \mathrm e^{mH_ Q(r)}$ for $\alpha \in mQ$. Conversely, averaging the growth bound over the angles gives $\sum _\alpha |c_\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r} \leq C_ s\mathrm e^{mH_ Q(r)}$ for the coefficients $c_\alpha $ of $s$. If some $c_\alpha 
eq 0$ had $\alpha 
otin mQ$, a vector $u$ with $\alpha \cdot u>mH_ Q(u)$, which exists by separation, would contradict this bound along the ray $r=tu$, $t	o \infty $. Thus the growth condition controls each monomial separately, even though the monomials of $s$ may cancel pointwise. For $p\in \operatorname {int}P$, put $\delta _ p=\min _ j(p_ j,k_ j-p_ j)>0$. Since $w$ is bounded, 27.118  egin{equation} \label{eq:newton-coercivity} F(r)-p\cdot r\geq \delta _ p\sum _ j|r_ j|-\| w\| _\infty . \end{equation} By strict convexity, $F-p\cdot r$ therefore has a unique minimizer, at which $
abla F=p$. Conversely, every gradient of $F$ lies in $P$: compare the supporting hyperplanes of the convex function $F$ with the asymptotic slopes of $\varphi _0$. By the inverse function theorem the image of $
abla F$ is open, so it is contained in the interior of $P$. This proves that $
abla F$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\operatorname {int}P$. On a compact neighborhood of $Q$ in $\operatorname {int}P$, the inverse gradient and the first and second derivatives of $F^*$ are bounded, and the Hessian of $F^*$ is positive definite. We next show that $G_ Q-\varphi _0$ is a competitor. In a product chart in which some of the coordinates are inverted, the local potential of $G_ Q-\varphi _0$ is \[  \max _{q\in Q}\left\{ \sum _ j c_ j(q)\log |\zeta _ j|^2-F^*(q)ight\} , \qquad c_ j(q)=q_ j	ext{ or }k_ j-q_ j.  \] All $c_ j$ are bounded below by a fixed positive number. The expression is locally bounded above, tends uniformly to $-\infty $ at the coordinate hyperplanes when the other coordinates stay bounded, and is locally integrable by comparison with one fixed summand. At points where it is finite, a maximizing summand gives the submean inequality for plurisubharmonic functions; at points where it equals $-\infty $, this inequality is automatic. These local expressions glue. Boundedness of $F^*$ on $Q$ gives $G_ Q-H_ Q=O(1)$, and Fenchel's inequality gives $G_ Q\leq F$, that is, $G_ Q-\varphi _0\leq w$. Thus $G_ Q-\varphi _0$, extended by $-\infty $ on $X\setminus T$, belongs to $\mathcal C_ Q$ and satisfies the obstacle condition. Now let $v$ be any competitor. The obstacle condition holds everywhere: the exceptional pluripolar set has Lebesgue measure zero, and submean values over shrinking balls carry the inequality with the continuous obstacle to every point. Consider the maximum over the angles, $M(r)=\max _	au \{ v(\mathrm e^{r/2}	au )+\varphi _0(r)\} $, where $\mathrm e^{r/2}	au $ denotes the point with coordinates $\mathrm e^{r_ j/2}	au _ j$. By compactness, $M$ is upper semicontinuous. Rotating a point at which the maximum is attained gives the submean inequality for the invariant function $z\mapsto M(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)$, which is therefore plurisubharmonic on $T$. It extends across the affine coordinate hyperplanes by the local upper bound. If $M(r)=-\infty $ for some $r$, successive one-variable maximum principles would force this function to be $-\infty $ on the corresponding polydisk, contradicting $v
ot\equiv -\infty $. Thus $M$ is finite. In logarithmic coordinates this invariant function depends only on the real parts, so its positive complex Hessian shows that $M$ is convex. We have $M\leq F$ and $M\leq H_ Q+C_ v$. Comparing along rays shows that every supporting slope of $M$ lies in $Q$. At any $r$, choose such a slope $p$. Since $M\leq F$ gives $M^*\geq F^*$, convex duality yields $M(r)=p\cdot r-M^*(p)\leq p\cdot r-F^*(p)\leq G_ Q(r)$. Hence $v\leq G_ Q-\varphi _0$ on $T$. Submean values over shrinking balls and the uniform decay of $G_ Q-\varphi _0$ near $X\setminus T$ show that $v=-\infty $ on $X\setminus T$. Since $G_ Q-\varphi _0$, extended by $-\infty $, is already upper semicontinuous, this proves the identity for the envelope after upper regularization. $\square$

title: 27.16.2 Norms, lattice growth and the lower bound

text: 27.16.2 Norms, lattice growth and the lower bound Theorem 27.16.2 . The norms are nondegenerate and satisfy the Bernstein–Markov inequality of section 27.2 for the weight $w$. Writing $N_ m=\dim V_ m$, we have \[  N_ m=m^ d\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda (Q)+O(m^{d-1})\quad (d\geq 1), \qquad N_ m=1\quad (d=0).  \] For all sufficiently large $m$, 27.119 \begin{equation} \label{eq:newton-potential-error} |U_ m-E_ Q|\leq \frac{C}{m} \left(1+\sum _ j|r_ j|+\log m\right)\quad \text{on }T. \end{equation} Consequently $U_ m\to E_ Q$ locally uniformly on $T$ and in $L^ p$ for every finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms on $X$, and the closed positive currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ m$ converge weakly to $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}E_ Q$. Both $U_ m$ and $E_ Q$ equal $-\infty $ on $X\setminus T$. Proof. Since the volume form is smooth and positive, the norm is positive on every nonzero section. Orthogonality of the angular Fourier modes diagonalizes it: \begin{align*}  A_ m(\alpha )& =\| z^\alpha e^ m\| _ m^2 =\int _{\mathbb R^ n}\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r-mF(r)}a(r)\, \mathrm dr,\\  \mathcal B_ m(r)& =\sum _{\alpha \in mQ\cap \mathbb Z^ n} \frac{\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r-m\varphi _0(r)}}{A_ m(\alpha )}. \end{align*} For $q=\alpha /m$, the function $F(r)-q\cdot r$ has the unique minimum value $-F^*(q)$, attained at $r(q)$. Taylor's formula on a ball of radius $m^{-1/2}$ about $r(q)$, with uniform bounds on a compact neighborhood of $r(Q)$, yields 27.120 \begin{equation} \label{eq:newton-laplace-bounds} c m^{-n/2}\mathrm e^{mF^*(q)}\leq A_ m(\alpha ) \leq \mathrm e^{mF^*(q)}. \end{equation} The upper bound uses only the minimum and $\int a\, \mathrm dr=1$. Since $b\in \mathbb Z^ n$, we have $(m\operatorname {aff}Q)\cap \mathbb Z^ n=mb+\Lambda $. Counting fundamental cells of $\Lambda $ in $m(Q-b)$ gives the dimension estimate: the cells meeting the relative boundary of $m(Q-b)$ lie in a boundary layer of fixed width, and there are $O(m^{d-1})$ of them. The same cells give convergence of the lattice Riemann sums on $Q$. Every $q\in Q$ lies within $O(m^{-1})$ of $Q_ m=Q\cap (b+m^{-1}\Lambda )$: move $q$ by $O(m^{-1})$ towards a fixed relative interior point so that a ball larger than the covering radius of the lattice fits inside $Q$, and then round to a lattice point inside that ball. This works for all sufficiently large $m$, and for a singleton it is exact. Put $G_{Q,m}=\max _{q\in Q_ m}(q\cdot r-F^*(q))$. The approximation by the grid gives $0\leq G_ Q-G_{Q,m}\leq C(1+\sum _ j|r_ j|)/m$. The formula for $\mathcal B_ m$ and ( 27.120 ) give \[  G_{Q,m}-\varphi _0\leq U_ m\leq G_{Q,m}-\varphi _0+ \frac{(n/2)\log m+\log N_ m-\log c}{m}.  \] This proves ( 27.119 ). The selected monomials vanish on every component of $X\setminus T$. The functions $\log |z_ j|^2$ have finite $L^ p$ norms for each finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms, so ( 27.119 ) gives the global convergence, and differentiation in the sense of distributions gives the convergence of the currents. Fenchel's inequality $\alpha \cdot r-mF(r)\leq mF^*(\alpha /m)$ and ( 27.120 ) also give $\sup _ X B_ m\leq C N_ m m^{n/2}$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in the orthonormal basis, $\sup _ X|s|_{h^ m}\mathrm e^{-mw/2} \leq C m^{d/2+n/4}\| s\| _ m$ for $s\in V_ m$. The finitely many initial degrees can be absorbed in $C$, and a polynomial bound implies the Bernstein–Markov inequality with any positive exponential loss. $\square$

title: 27.16.3 The limit measure and the ambient metric

text:
27.16.3 The limit measure and the ambient metric For $q\in \operatorname {int}P$ and $	au \in (S^1)^ n$, let $\Psi (q,	au )=\mathrm e^{r(q)/2}	au $ be the point of $T$ with coordinates $\mathrm e^{r_ j(q)/2}	au _ j$. Thus $\Psi (q,\cdot )$ parametrizes the real torus $\{ r=r(q)\} $, and we call the image of $Q	imes (S^1)^ n$ the moment shell of $Q$. Here and below, $\langle S^ kangle $ denotes the non-pluripolar product of a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $S$; in top degree it is the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 6.1.2 . Theorem 27.16.3 . Against every continuous test function on $X$, 27.121  egin{equation} \label{eq:newton-moment-shell}  rac{d!}{m^ d}B_ m
u ightharpoonup \mu _ Q=\Psi _*(d!\, \mathrm dq_\Lambda \, \mathrm d	au ), \qquad \Psi (q,	au )=\mathrm e^{r(q)/2}	au . \end{equation} The mass of $\mu _ Q$ is $d!\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda (Q)>0$. If $d=0$, then $\mu _ Q$ is the Haar probability measure on one real $n$-torus. If $d<n$, then $\mu _ Q$ is singular with respect to smooth volume forms on $X$, and \[  \left\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}E_ Q)^{d+1}ightangle =0.  \] If $d=n$, then $\mu _ Q=\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}E_ Q)^ nangle $. Proof. For $\alpha \in mQ\cap \mathbb Z^ n$ and $q=\alpha /m$, the normalized monomial $z^\alpha e^ m$ gives the probability measure $\mathrm dP_{m,q}=A_ m(\alpha )^{-1} \mathrm e^{m(q\cdot r-F(r))}a(r)\, \mathrm dr\, \mathrm d	au $ on $T$. For every $\eta >0$ there is $c_\eta >0$ such that $F(r)-q\cdot r+F^*(q)\geq c_\eta $ whenever $|r-r(q)|\geq \eta $, uniformly for $q\in Q$: on a large compact set this follows from the uniqueness of the minima, and outside it from ( 27.118 ), which is uniform on $Q$. Together with ( 27.120 ), this gives $P_{m,q}\{ |r-r(q)|\geq \eta \} \leq C m^{n/2}\mathrm e^{-mc_\eta }$. Hence, for every continuous function on $X$, its integral against $P_{m,q}$ differs from its average over the torus $\{ r=r(q)\} $ by $o(1)$, uniformly in $q\in Q$. The identity $d!m^{-d}B_ m
u =d!m^{-d}\sum _\alpha P_{m,\alpha /m}$ and the lattice Riemann sums prove ( 27.121 ). When $d<n$, the measure $\mu _ Q$ is carried by the moment shell, which has real dimension $n+d<2n$, so it is singular with respect to smooth volume forms. For the curvature, note that $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}E_ Q=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ Q$ on $T$. By uniform strong convexity of $F^*$ on $Q$, the slope $q(r)$ maximizing $q\cdot r-F^*(q)$ over $Q$ is unique. 27.17 Rounding in multiplier-ideal kernel families The growth degree $\lim _ m\log N_ m/\log m$ of the selected spaces does not by itself determine a limit of the kernel measures. At a critical logarithmic coefficient, the rounding in multiplier ideals can produce different leading section counts in even and odd degrees, while the potentials still converge to the ideal envelope. In the following product example the growth degree is positive. Fix $q\geq 1$ and put $X=\mathbb P^1	imes Y$, where $Y=(\mathbb P^1)^ q$. Write $p_0$ for the projection onto the first factor. For $0\leq j\leq q$, let $\sigma _ j$ be the Fubini–Study form on the $j$th factor, normalized to have integral one, where $j=0$ refers to the first factor. Use \[  L=\mathcal O(1,\ldots ,1),\qquad 	heta =c_1(L,h)=\sigma _0+	heta _ Y,\qquad 	heta _ Y=\sum _{j=1}^ q\sigma _ j,  \] where $h$ is the product Fubini–Study metric and the forms $\sigma _ j$ are pulled back to $X$. We use the smooth positive probability measure $
u =\sigma _0\otimes 
u _ Y$, where $
u _ Y=\sigma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \sigma _ q=	heta _ Y^ q/q!$, and the continuous weight zero. On the affine line of the first factor define \[  \psi _0(z)=	frac 12\log |z|^2-\log (1+|z|^2),\qquad \psi =\psi _0\circ p_0.  \] In the coordinate $1/z$ at infinity, $\psi _0$ has the same expression. It equals $-\infty $ at $0$ and $\infty $, and 27.122  egin{equation} \label{eq:critical-selector-curvature} 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =	frac 12[D_0]+	frac 12[D_\infty ]+	heta _ Y\geq 0, \qquad D_0=\{ 0\} 	imes Y,\quad D_\infty =\{ \infty \} 	imes Y. \end{equation} We use $\psi $ as selecting potential, so that the selected spaces are $V_ m=H^0(X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi ))$, with the norm $\int _ X|s|_{h^ m}^2\, \mathrm d
u $. For an orthonormal basis $(s_{m,j})$, write $\mathcal B_ m=\sum _ j|s_{m,j}|_{h^ m}^2$ and $U_ m=m^{-1}\log \mathcal B_ m$. Let $\varsigma $ be the Haar probability measure on the circle $\{ |z|=1\} \subset \mathbb P^1$. Theorem 27.17.1 . Put $a_ m=1$ for even $m$ and $a_ m=2$ for odd $m$. Then \[  N_ m=\dim V_ m=a_ m(m+1)^ q,\qquad \lim _{m	o \infty } rac{\log N_ m}{\log m}=q.  \] The partial envelope ( 27.4 ) with $K=X$ and obstacle zero is 27.123  egin{equation} \label{eq:critical-ideal-envelope} E_{	heta ,X}[\psi ]_{\mathcal I}(0)=E=\psi +\log 2. \end{equation} The norms satisfy the Bernstein–Markov inequality, and $U_ m	o E$ locally uniformly on $X\setminus (D_0\cup D_\infty )$ and in $L^ p$ for every finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms; moreover, the currents $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ m$ converge weakly to $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}E$. u ightharpoonup \varsigma \otimes 
u _ Y$. The envelope has zero non-pluripolar top mass: $\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}E)^{q+1}angle =0$. Proof. By lemma 1.16.1 , \[  \mathcal I(m\psi )= \mathcal O_ X(-r_ mD_0-r_ mD_\infty ),\qquad r_ m=\lfloor m/2floor .  \] In the product affine frame, global sections are polynomials of degree at most $m$ in each variable. A global section belongs to $V_ m$ exactly when each of its monomials vanishes to order at least $r_ m$ along $D_0$ and along $D_\infty $, that is, when the exponent $\alpha _0$ of the first variable satisfies $r_ m\leq \alpha _0\leq m-r_ m$; the other exponents range from $0$ to $m$. There is one admissible value of $\alpha _0$ when $m$ is even and two when $m$ is odd. This proves the dimension formula. To identify the envelope, let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be a competitor, that is, $v\preceq _{\mathcal I}\psi $ in the multiplier-ideal order of section 1.12 and $v\leq 0$ quasi-everywhere. By theorem 1.16.3 , the Lelong numbers of $v$ at the points of $D_0$ and $D_\infty $ are at least $1/2$. Fix $y\in Y$ and restrict $v$ to the line $\mathbb P^1	imes \{ y\} $. The restriction is either identically $-\infty $ or $\sigma _0$-plurisubharmonic. In the latter case, its Lelong numbers at the two points over $0$ and $\infty $ are at least those of $v$: the supremum over a ball in the line is at most the supremum over the corresponding ambient ball, and division by $\log r^2<0$ reverses the inequality. By the identification of Lelong numbers with atoms in lemma 1.16.11 , the curvature measure of the restriction has atoms of mass at least $1/2$ at these two points. By Stokes' theorem its total mass is one, so these atoms exhaust the measure. The difference between the restriction and $\psi _0$ is therefore harmonic on the compact projective line, hence constant. In the odd case the two monomials in the first factor have equal norms, and the sum of their squared moduli contributes the factor $1+|z|^2$, which gives the second identity. The full kernel on $X$ is $(m+1)^{q+1}$, so evaluation gives $\sup _ X|s|_{h^ m}\leq (m+1)^{(q+1)/2}\| s\| _ m$ for every selected section. This polynomial bound proves the Bernstein–Markov inequality. The central binomial coefficient is the largest in its row. Hence $4^ k\leq C_ k\leq (2k+1)4^ k$, and $\log C_ k=2k\log 2+O(\log (k+1))$. Taking logarithms in ( 27.125 ) gives \[  |U_ m-E|\leq  rac{C_ q}{m}  igl (1+|\log |z|^2|+\log m igr ) \quad 	ext{off }D_0\cup D_\infty ,  \] because $|\psi _0|=\log (2\cosh (	frac 12\log |z|^2))$ is bounded by $\log 2+	frac 12|\log |z|^2|$. The function $\log |z|^2$ belongs to $L^ p$ for every finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms. This proves the convergence of the potentials, and differentiating the $L^1$ limit proves the convergence of the currents. For every $m\geq 2$, both $U_ m$ and $E$ are $-\infty $ on $D_0\cup D_\infty $. Let $P_ k$ be the probability measure on the first factor with density $C_ k\mathrm e^{2k\psi _0}$ with respect to $\sigma _0$. Under $P_ k$ the angle of $z$ is uniformly distributed, and $x$ has the beta distribution with parameters $(k+1,k+1)$, whose mean is $1/2$ and whose variance is $1/[4(2k+3)]$. Chebyshev's inequality and continuity of the test functions in the angle therefore give $P_ kightharpoonup \varsigma $. The measure identities \[  \mathcal B_{2k}
u =(2k+1)^ q P_ k\otimes 
u _ Y, \qquad \mathcal B_{2k+1}
u =2(2k+2)^ q P_ k\otimes 
u _ Y  \] prove both limits along even and odd degrees and the limit after division by $N_ m$. Since the two limits have different total masses, the $q$-normalized family does not converge. 27.18 Three monomial bands from a multiplier-ideal selection For an isolated logarithmic pole of coefficient one on a complex surface, the multiplier ideal in degree $m$ requires vanishing of order $m-1$, whereas domination by the pole would require order $m$. At the two base points of the pencil below, the multiplier-ideal conditions select three neighboring bands of monomials. All three contribute to the limit of the kernel measures, even though the competitor classes defined by multiplier ideals and by domination coincide. Let $X=\mathbb P^1	imes \mathbb P^1$, and let $L=\mathcal O(1,1)$ carry its product Fubini–Study metric $h$, with $	heta =c_1(L,h)$. Let $[T_ j:Z_ j]$ be homogeneous coordinates on the $j$th factor, write $z_ j=Z_ j/T_ j$, and set \[  \psi =\max \{ \log |T_1T_2|_ h^2,\log |Z_1Z_2|_ h^2\} , \qquad p_+=(0,\infty ),\quad p_-=(\infty ,0).  \] The two sections $T_1T_2$ and $Z_1Z_2$ of $L$ vanish simultaneously only at $p_\pm $, so these are the only poles of $\psi $. In local frames the potentials of $\psi $ are maxima of logarithms of squared moduli of holomorphic functions, so $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. On the torus $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ put \[  x_ j=\log |z_ j|^2,\qquad s=x_1+x_2,\qquad \varphi _ X=\log (1+\mathrm e^{x_1})+\log (1+\mathrm e^{x_2}).  \] Then $\psi =\max (0,s)-\varphi _ X$. In this model the norm is computed on the compact set $K=\{ x\in [-1,2]^2\} \subset (\mathbb C^*)^2$, which has nonempty interior. On $K$ let \[  w= rac{x_1^2+x_2^2}{2}-\varphi _ X, \qquad \mathrm d
u = rac19\, \mathrm dx_1\, \mathrm dx_2\, \mathrm d	au _1\, \mathrm d	au _2,  \] where $\mathrm d	au _ j$ is the Haar probability measure in the angle of $z_ j$. Thus $
u $ is a probability measure supported on $K$, not a smooth positive volume form on $X$. With $\psi $ as selecting potential, set \[   egin{aligned}  V_ m& =H^0(X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )), & N_ m& =\dim V_ m,\  \| \sigma \| _ m^2& =\int _ K|\sigma |_{h^ m}^2\mathrm e^{-mw}\, \mathrm d
u , & \mathcal B_ m& =\sum _ j|\sigma _{m,j}|_{h^ m}^2, \end{aligned}  \] where $(\sigma _{m,j})$ is an orthonormal basis. The norm is positive definite by the identity theorem on the interior of $K$. As in section 27.1 , we use $U_ m=m^{-1}\log \mathcal B_ m$ on $X$ and $B_ m=\mathrm e^{-mw}\mathcal B_ m$ on $K$. Only the values of $w$ on $K$ enter the norm and the envelope. Lemma 27.18.1 . For every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, \[  v\preceq _{\mathcal I}\psi \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad v\leq \psi +C_ v \quad \hbox{for some finite }C_ v,  \] where $\preceq _{\mathcal I}$ is the multiplier-ideal order of section 1.12 . Consequently, for every obstacle, the envelopes defined with these two conditions agree. At either pole, for every real $t>0$, \[  \mathcal I(t\psi )=\mathfrak m_{p_\pm }^{\max \{ \lfloor tfloor -1,0\} }.  \] Away from the poles, $\mathcal I(t\psi )$ is the full structure sheaf. Proof. Near $p_+$ use the coordinates $\zeta _1=z_1$, $\zeta _2=1/z_2$ and the frame $T_1Z_2$. In this frame the two pencil sections $T_1T_2$ and $Z_1Z_2$ have coefficients $\zeta _2$ and $\zeta _1$, so \[  \psi =\log \max (|\zeta _1|^2,|\zeta _2|^2) -\log (1+|\zeta _1|^2)-\log (1+|\zeta _2|^2) =\log |\zeta |^2+O(1).  \] The same calculation applies at $p_-$.
