title: 28 Bott–Chern classes and singular loci
text: 28 Bott–Chern classes and singular loci This part of the book returns to closed backgrounds. A closed real $(1,1)$-form has a Bott–Chern class, and positivity can then be asked of the class rather than of a chosen representative. On a compact Kähler manifold, the positivity of a class is described by its non-nef and non-Kähler loci, by intersection numbers and by volumes. The present chapter asks which parts of this description survive on an arbitrary compact complex manifold, where no Kähler metric controls masses, and how closed classes interact with the Hermitian equations of the preceding parts. In chapter 29 , closed classes arise from the Lee form of a locally conformally Kähler metric. Throughout the chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ as in the Conventions, and $\omega $ is a fixed Hermitian form on $X$; sections that require a Kähler manifold or a special geometry say so at their beginning. Without a Kähler class, Gauduchon metrics provide the substitute mass control. Pairing a closed current with the $(n-1)$st power of a Gauduchon metric eliminates its potential, so the currents of a fixed class whose negative part is bounded by a multiple of $\omega $ have uniformly bounded mass. With this compactness, regularization defines the non-nef locus through Lelong numbers of minimal currents and the non-Kähler locus through polar sets of Kähler currents. These loci separate the singularities forced by the class from those of a particular current. Restricted volumes, which describe the same loci on Kähler manifolds, behave differently: computed with a Hermitian error, they can be infinite even for the zero class. When $X$ belongs to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, pulling a class back to a Kähler resolution of each subvariety gives instead a finite restricted mass; on a smooth subvariety, its positivity detects bigness of the restricted class. For a divisorial trace with bounded remainder, the non-pluripolar mass is the top intersection of a nef residual class; positive mass produces a Kähler current, but possibly with a larger singularity than the trace. Closed classes also constrain the Hermitian Monge–Ampère equations of earlier chapters. A divisorial component of a positive current in a Hermitian background consumes Gauduchon trace but contributes no density to its non-pluripolar measure, so it can lower the largest coefficient of a subsolution. At the maximal coefficient, weak limits of maximizing Gauduchon tests annihilate the class of the divisor. On the elliptic threefold of section 26.18 , closedness forces every positive current to descend to the base surface. No closed class is big there, although small Hermitian perturbations of the boundary classes have positive variational volume, whose degeneration can be computed explicitly. Smooth solutions raise a metric question. For a big class on a compact Kähler manifold, the solution of the Monge–Ampère equation with a smooth positive density defines a Kähler metric on the ample locus, but its smoothness there does not determine the distance to the complement. Zeros of the density can come from ramification, from collapsed exceptional fibers or from a singular Hessian, and they give different normal lengths even when the determinant vanishes to the same order. For radial equations, boundedness of the potential and finiteness of the distance are governed by two different integrals: a continuous minimal remainder can have a complete end, whereas a Hölder remainder forces finite distance. For exponential equations with a divisorial pole, dividing the determinant by its tangential part gives a lower bound for normal length and a sharp logarithmic threshold for completeness. Explicit surfaces give exponential equations with unique finite-energy solutions and incomplete metrics. One solution has minimal singularities in a big non-nef class; another has a nef and big class but an unbounded cusp. At the boundary of the nef cone, smooth semipositive representatives have a different metric behavior. On a complex torus, a constant semipositive form whose kernel leaves are dense is the only closed positive current in its class, and adding a small fixed Kähler form produces metrics whose diameters tend to zero. An explicit family of flat metrics collapses in the same way at a class with many semipositive representatives, so the collapse depends on how the class is approached. On the resolution of a Kummer quotient, an irrational nef boundary class has many smooth semipositive representatives. Finally, in a family of blown-up projective planes, degree-zero curves on the nearby fibers force a larger singularity along one component of the central curve, so a prescribed semipositive metric on the special fiber does not extend to the family.

title: 28.1 Closed classes with Hermitian lower bounds

text: 28.1 Closed classes with Hermitian lower bounds Testing a closed current against a Gauduchon form eliminates its potential. The resulting trace depends only on the class, and it bounds the mass of every almost positive representative. Recall from section 23.4 that $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$ is the space of smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms modulo $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of smooth real functions, and that a class is pseudoeffective if it contains a closed positive current. It is nef if, for every $\varepsilon >0$, it has a smooth representative bounded below by $-\varepsilon \omega $ (section 23.6 ). Fix a class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$ and a smooth closed representative $\theta $. By lemma 23.4.1 , the closed real $(1,1)$-currents in $\alpha $ are exactly the currents $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ a real distribution, and the potential of a positive one is quasi-plurisubharmonic. A closed current $T$ with $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$ is called a Kähler current ; we also say that such a current is strict . The class $\alpha $ is big if it contains a Kähler current, that is, if $\theta $ is big in the sense of section 1.19 . None of these properties depends on the choice of $\theta $, because replacing $\theta $ by $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth only changes the potentials by $-f$. For a pseudoeffective class $\alpha $ and $\varepsilon >0$, let \[  \alpha [-\varepsilon \omega ] =\{ T\in \alpha :T\geq -\varepsilon \omega \}   \] be the set of closed currents in $\alpha $ whose negative part is bounded by $\varepsilon \omega $. Proposition 28.1.1 . For each fixed $\varepsilon >0$, the currents in $\alpha [-\varepsilon \omega ]$ have uniformly bounded distributional mass. Proof. Choose a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. For $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ in $\alpha [-\varepsilon \omega ]$, the current $T+\varepsilon \omega $ is positive, and since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma ^{n-1}=0$, Stokes' theorem for currents gives \[  \int _ X(T+\varepsilon \omega )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X(\theta +\varepsilon \omega )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] The right-hand side does not depend on $T$. Since $\gamma $ is comparable to any fixed reference metric, this trace bounds all coefficient measures of the positive current $T+\varepsilon \omega $. Subtracting the fixed smooth form $\varepsilon \omega $ gives the asserted bound for $T$. In dimension one the same argument applies with $\gamma ^{n-1}=1$ and the ordinary Stokes theorem. $\square$ Proposition 28.1.2 . The pseudoeffective cone in $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$ is closed and convex and contains no nonzero line. For a fixed Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, the trace functional $\ell _\gamma $ of section 23.4 is strictly positive on its nonzero elements, and the slice of pseudoeffective classes with $\ell _\gamma =1$ is compact. This slice may be empty. Pullback and pushforward by a compact modification are continuous linear maps on Bott–Chern cohomology and preserve pseudoeffectivity. Proof. The finite-dimensional space of smooth representatives in lemma 23.7.1 identifies Bott–Chern cohomology with a finite-dimensional vector space and gives it its usual topology; the trace functional is continuous for this topology. Its positivity and the absence of lines in the cone were proved in section 23.4 , and convexity follows by adding positive currents. Let pseudoeffective classes $\alpha _ j$ converge to $\alpha $, and choose positive closed representatives $T_ j$. Their masses $\ell _\gamma (\alpha _ j)$ are bounded, so by weak compactness a subsequence converges to a positive closed current $T$. Let $B_\gamma $ be the continuous smooth representative map of lemma 23.7.1 . Along the subsequence, $B_\gamma (T_ j)$ converges both to $B_\gamma (T)$ and to the representative of $\alpha $, so $T$ represents $\alpha $. Thus the cone is closed. On its mass-one slice, ( 23.3 ) bounds $B_\gamma (T)$ in the finite-dimensional representative space. The slice is therefore closed and bounded there, hence compact. The class maps of a modification are linear, and they are well-defined because classes can be represented equally by smooth forms and by currents. As linear maps between finite-dimensional spaces, they are continuous. Pullback preserves positive closed currents, since it can be computed on local plurisubharmonic potentials as in proposition 23.7.2 , and proper pushforward preserves positivity and closedness. Applying these maps to positive representatives proves the assertions about the cones. $\square$ This compactness is linear. The functional $\ell _\gamma $ pairs a closed current with a fixed smooth form; it is not a top-degree volume of the class, and it gives no bound for the Monge–Ampère masses of potentials. The same compactness shows that a nef class $\alpha $ is pseudoeffective. Indeed, choose smooth representatives $\theta _ j\in \alpha $ with $\theta _ j\geq -\varepsilon _ j\omega $, where $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. They have the same Gauduchon trace and hence uniformly bounded mass. A weak cluster value is a closed current, positive because the negative parts tend to zero, and it belongs to $\alpha $ because the smooth representative map of lemma 23.7.1 is continuous.

28.2 Minimal multiplicities and the non-nef locus In this section $\alpha $ is pseudoeffective. A current in $\alpha [-\varepsilon \omega ]$ may have singularities that the class does not force. To isolate the forced ones, take in each family a current with the mildest singularities and let the allowed negative error tend to zero. The Lelong numbers that persist define the non-nef locus. For $\varepsilon >0$ put \[  V_\varepsilon =V_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega }, \qquad T_{\min ,\varepsilon }=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\varepsilon ,  \] where $V_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega }=P_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega }(0)$ is the normalized envelope of section 1.19 . Since $\alpha $ is pseudoeffective, $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +\varepsilon \omega )$ is nonempty, so $V_\varepsilon $ is $(	heta +\varepsilon \omega )$-plurisubharmonic and $T_{\min ,\varepsilon }\in \alpha [-\varepsilon \omega ]$. Moreover, $V_\varepsilon $ has minimal singularities in this family: $u-\sup _ Xu\leq V_\varepsilon $ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +\varepsilon \omega )$. Definition 28.2.1 . For $x\in X$, the minimal multiplicity of $\alpha $ at $x$ is \[  
u (\alpha ,x)=\sup _{\varepsilon >0}
u (T_{\min ,\varepsilon },x).  \] The non-nef locus is \[  E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )=\{ x\in X:
u (\alpha ,x)>0\} .  \] As $\varepsilon $ decreases, the family $\alpha [-\varepsilon \omega ]$ shrinks, so the Lelong numbers of its minimal current can only increase; the supremum is therefore a limit as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Two Hermitian forms are comparable up to a constant factor, so the families defined by them are nested after rescaling $\varepsilon $; hence $
u (\alpha ,x)$ does not depend on $\omega $. Replacing $	heta $ by $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ changes the minimal potentials by $-f$ up to a bounded normalization error, which does not affect Lelong numbers. The smooth regularization of 1.15.1 turns vanishing Lelong numbers into an arbitrarily small loss of positivity. This gives the converse direction in the following characterization. Proposition 28.2.2 . For a pseudoeffective class $\alpha $, the set $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )$ is a countable union of analytic subsets. Moreover, \[  \alpha 	ext{ is nef}\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )=\varnothing .  \] Proof. By the monotonicity just noted, \[  E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha ) = igcup _{k,\ell \geq 1} \{ x:
u (T_{\min ,1/\ell },x)\geq 1/k\} ,  \] and each set in this union is analytic by Siu's analyticity theorem ( 1.13.1 ). If $\alpha $ is nef, each family $\alpha [-\varepsilon \omega ]$ contains a smooth current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. By minimality, $V_\varepsilon \geq f-\sup _ Xf$, so $V_\varepsilon $ is bounded and all Lelong numbers of $T_{\min ,\varepsilon }$ vanish. Conversely, if the non-nef locus is empty, every $T_{\min ,\varepsilon }$ has zero Lelong numbers. The regularization just recalled then gives a smooth representative of $\alpha $ bounded below by $-2\varepsilon \omega $. Since $\varepsilon >0$ is arbitrary, $\alpha $ is nef. $\square$ The approximating families cannot be replaced by the single family of positive currents in $\alpha $: even for a nef class, a positive current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $ itself may have nonzero Lelong numbers; see the example discussed in section 34.16 .

title: 28.3 The non-Kähler locus
text:
28.3 The non-Kähler locus A big class contains Kähler currents, but in general none of them is smooth. The points at which every Kähler current in the class is singular form its non-Kähler locus. Analytic regularization, maxima of potentials and the descending chain condition for analytic sets produce a single Kähler current whose singular set is exactly this locus. For an almost positive closed $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, write \[  E_+(T)=\{ x\in X:
u (T,x)>0\}   \] for its positive Lelong set , where $
u (T,x)$ is the Lelong number of a local potential of $T$ at $x$. Definition 28.3.1 . The non-Kähler locus of a big class $\alpha $ is \[  E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )= igcap _{T}E_+(T),  \] where $T$ ranges over the Kähler currents in $\alpha $. For a pseudoeffective class that is not big, we set $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=X$. Theorem 28.3.2 . Let $\alpha $ be big. There is a Kähler current in $\alpha $ with analytic singularities, smooth off its polar set, whose positive Lelong set is exactly $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. In particular this locus is a proper analytic subset, and \[  E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha ), \qquad E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=\varnothing \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \alpha 	ext{ is Kähler}.  \] Proof. Step 1: reduction to analytic singularities. By the analytic regularization of 1.15.1 , a Kähler current $T\in \alpha $ can be approximated by currents in $\alpha $ with analytic singularities and smooth remainder away from their poles. After a sufficiently small loss of positivity these are still Kähler currents, and their positive Lelong sets are contained in $E_+(T)$. Hence the intersection defining $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$ may be taken over Kähler currents with analytic singularities and smooth remainder. Step 2: intersections. Let $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1$ and $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2$ be two such currents. By lemma 1.3.1 , $\max (u_1,u_2)$ is the potential of a current dominating $\delta \omega $ for a common $\delta >0$, and its Lelong number at each point is the minimum of those of $u_1$ and $u_2$. Regularizing this current as in Step 1 gives a Kähler current with analytic singularities whose positive Lelong set is contained in the intersection of the two previous sets. Step 3: realization. The positive Lelong sets of Step 1 are analytic subsets of $X$. By the descending chain condition for analytic subsets of a compact complex manifold, some finite intersection of them is minimal, and it then equals the full intersection $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. Repeated use of Step 2 gives a single Kähler current with analytic singularities whose polar set, which is also its positive Lelong set, is contained in this finite intersection. Since $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$ is contained in the positive Lelong set of every Kähler current in $\alpha $, equality holds. Step 4: the two consequences. For a positive current $T\in \alpha $ and $\varepsilon >0$, we have $T\in \alpha [-\varepsilon \omega ]$, so minimality gives $
u (T_{\min ,\varepsilon },x)\leq 
u (T,x)$. Taking the supremum over $\varepsilon $ and then the intersection over Kähler currents $T$ gives $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. If the non-Kähler locus is empty, the current of Step 3 has no poles and is therefore a Kähler form in $\alpha $. Conversely, if $\alpha $ contains a Kähler form, using it in the defining intersection gives $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=\varnothing $. $\square$ Proposition 28.3.3 . The non-Kähler locus of a big class has no isolated points. Proof. Let $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi \geq \delta \omega $ be a current as in theorem 28.3.2 , and suppose that $x$ is an isolated point of its polar set. Choose holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ on a ball centered at $x$ that contains no other pole. For a sufficiently large constant $A>0$ and any real constant $C$, the local function $q(z)=A|z|^2-C$ satisfies $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \delta '\omega $ on a smaller ball, for some $\delta '>0$. Since $\Phi $ is smooth on a closed annular collar near the boundary of this smaller ball, we can choose $C$ so that $q<\Phi $ on the collar. Since $\Phi 	o -\infty $ at $x$, the function $\max (\Phi ,q)$ agrees with $q$ near $x$ and with $\Phi $ on the collar. By lemma 1.3.2 , it glues with $\Phi $ outside the ball to the potential of a Kähler current in $\alpha $ that is smooth near $x$. Its Lelong number at $x$ is zero, contradicting $x\in E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. $\square$ Bigness of a closed class has a strong global consequence. A compact complex manifold carries a Kähler current if and only if it belongs to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$; this is the classical modification criterion discussed in section 34.16 . Hence a compact complex manifold outside class $\mathcal C$ has no big Bott–Chern class at all, whereas the strictly positive nonclosed backgrounds studied in this book exist on every compact complex manifold.

title: Theorem 28.3.2
text: Theorem 28.3.2 . Let $\alpha $ be big. There is a Kähler current in $\alpha $ with analytic singularities, smooth off its polar set, whose positive Lelong set is exactly $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. In particular this locus is a proper analytic subset, and \[  E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha ), \qquad E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=\varnothing \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \alpha \text{ is Kähler}.  \] Proof. Step 1: reduction to analytic singularities. By the analytic regularization of 1.15.1 , a Kähler current $T\in \alpha $ can be approximated by currents in $\alpha $ with analytic singularities and smooth remainder away from their poles. After a sufficiently small loss of positivity these are still Kähler currents, and their positive Lelong sets are contained in $E_+(T)$. Hence the intersection defining $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$ may be taken over Kähler currents with analytic singularities and smooth remainder. Step 2: intersections. Let $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2$ be two such currents. By lemma 1.3.1 , $\max (u_1,u_2)$ is the potential of a current dominating $\delta \omega $ for a common $\delta >0$, and its Lelong number at each point is the minimum of those of $u_1$ and $u_2$. Regularizing this current as in Step 1 gives a Kähler current with analytic singularities whose positive Lelong set is contained in the intersection of the two previous sets. Step 3: realization. The positive Lelong sets of Step 1 are analytic subsets of $X$. By the descending chain condition for analytic subsets of a compact complex manifold, some finite intersection of them is minimal, and it then equals the full intersection $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. Repeated use of Step 2 gives a single Kähler current with analytic singularities whose polar set, which is also its positive Lelong set, is contained in this finite intersection. Since $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$ is contained in the positive Lelong set of every Kähler current in $\alpha $, equality holds. Step 4: the two consequences. For a positive current $T\in \alpha $ and $\varepsilon >0$, we have $T\in \alpha [-\varepsilon \omega ]$, so minimality gives $\nu (T_{\min ,\varepsilon },x)\leq \nu (T,x)$. Taking the supremum over $\varepsilon $ and then the intersection over Kähler currents $T$ gives $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. If the non-Kähler locus is empty, the current of Step 3 has no poles and is therefore a Kähler form in $\alpha $. Conversely, if $\alpha $ contains a Kähler form, using it in the defining intersection gives $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=\varnothing $. $\square$

title: Proposition 28.3.3
text: Proposition 28.3.3 . The non-Kähler locus of a big class has no isolated points. Proof. Let $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi \geq \delta \omega $ be a current as in theorem 28.3.2 , and suppose that $x$ is an isolated point of its polar set. Choose holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ on a ball centered at $x$ that contains no other pole. For a sufficiently large constant $A>0$ and any real constant $C$, the local function $q(z)=A|z|^2-C$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \delta '\omega $ on a smaller ball, for some $\delta '>0$. Since $\Phi $ is smooth on a closed annular collar near the boundary of this smaller ball, we can choose $C$ so that $q<\Phi $ on the collar. Since $\Phi \to -\infty $ at $x$, the function $\max (\Phi ,q)$ agrees with $q$ near $x$ and with $\Phi $ on the collar. By lemma 1.3.2 , it glues with $\Phi $ outside the ball to the potential of a Kähler current in $\alpha $ that is smooth near $x$. Its Lelong number at $x$ is zero, contradicting $x\in E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. $\square$

title: 28.4 Null loci and numerical restricted volumes
search_title: Null loci and numerical restricted volumes
text: 28.4 Null loci and numerical restricted volumes In this section $X$ is Kähler and $\omega $ is a Kähler form. For a closed class $\alpha $ and an irreducible analytic subvariety $V\subset X$ of positive dimension, the intersection number $\int _ V\alpha ^{\dim V}$ is computed by pulling back a smooth closed representative to a resolution of $V$; by Stokes' theorem it does not depend on the representative. For a nef class $\alpha $, the subvarieties on which this number vanishes form the classical null locus \[  \operatorname {Null}(\alpha ) =\bigcup _{\substack {V\subset X\  \mathrm{irreducible},\  \dim V>0\\ \int _ V\alpha ^{\dim V}=0}}V.  \] For a nef and big class, the classical theorem discussed in section 34.16 gives \[  E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=\operatorname {Null}(\alpha ).  \] The same equality holds on compact manifolds in class $\mathcal C$. For a pseudoeffective class that is not nef, intersection numbers are replaced by numerical restricted volumes. Let $V\subset X$ be an irreducible compact analytic subvariety of dimension $k>0$, with regular locus $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$. If $V\subset E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )$, the numerical restricted volume of $\alpha $ along $V$ is defined to be zero. Otherwise, for real $\varepsilon >0$, let $T$ range over the closed currents in $\alpha $ with $T\geq -\varepsilon \omega $ that have analytic singularities with smooth remainder and whose polar set does not contain $V$, and set 28.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bc-numerical-restricted-volume} \langle \alpha ^ k\rangle _{X\mid V} =\lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\  \sup _ T \int _{V_{\mathrm{reg}}} \bigl ((T+\varepsilon \omega )|_{V_{\mathrm{reg}}}\bigr )_{\mathrm{ac}}^ k, \end{equation} where the subscript $\mathrm{ac}$ denotes the absolutely continuous part of a measure on $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Because $T$ has smooth remainder, the integrand is the extension by zero of a smooth measure defined away from an analytic subset of $V$. The numerical null locus of $\alpha $ is the union of the positive-dimensional irreducible subvarieties on which ( 28.1 ) vanishes. The trace theory of [ Chapter 8 , SGPT ] expresses these restricted volumes as masses of trace currents on $V$; this is why singularity types and restrictions of multiplier ideals enter into the identification of this locus. Such a trace need not equal the pointwise restriction of a singular potential; see chapter 19 .

28.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bc-numerical-restricted-volume} \langle \alpha ^ k\rangle _{X\mid V} =\lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\  \sup _ T \int _{V_{\mathrm{reg}}} \bigl ((T+\varepsilon \omega )|_{V_{\mathrm{reg}}}\bigr )_{\mathrm{ac}}^ k, \end{equation}

title: 28.5 Restricted volumes and Hermitian perturbations
text: 28.5 Restricted volumes and Hermitian perturbations We return to an arbitrary compact complex manifold $X$ with a Hermitian form $\omega $. In ( 28.1 ), the negative part of $T$ is measured by a closed Kähler form. If the closed perturbation is replaced by the Hermitian form $\omega $, the supremum can be infinite even for the zero Bott–Chern class $\{ 0\} $ and $V=X$. Unbounded Monge–Ampère masses of smooth potentials, such as those on the Hopf threefold, already produce this failure. Proposition 28.5.1 . Suppose there are smooth real functions $v_ j$ on $X$, for positive integers $j$, such that \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j>0, \qquad \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Then for every $\varepsilon >0$, 28.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bc-zero-class-infinite-error-volume} \sup _{\substack {T\in \{ 0\} \  \mathrm{smooth,\  closed}\\ T\geq -\varepsilon \omega }} \int _ X(T+\varepsilon \omega )^ n=+\infty . \end{equation} This occurs for the Gauduchon form on the Hopf threefold in theorem 8.0.1 . Proof. Fix $\varepsilon >0$ and take $T_ j=\varepsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j$. Each $T_ j$ is smooth and closed and represents the zero Bott–Chern class. Moreover, \[  T_ j+\varepsilon \omega =\varepsilon (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)>0,  \] and its top mass $\varepsilon ^ n\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n$ tends to $+\infty $. The functions $v_ j$ on the Hopf threefold are provided by theorem 8.0.1 . $\square$ The currents $T_ j$ are smooth, so requiring analytic singularities with smooth remainder does not exclude them. Moreover, the supremum is infinite for each fixed $\varepsilon $, so letting $\varepsilon $ tend to zero afterwards cannot produce a finite limit. By contrast, if $\omega $ is Kähler and $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is smooth, Stokes' theorem gives \[  \int _ X(T+\varepsilon \omega )^ n =\varepsilon ^ n\int _ X\omega ^ n\longrightarrow 0.  \] On the other hand, the zero class is nef, its non-nef locus is empty, and its only positive representative is the zero current. Indeed, a positive representative $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ would make $u$ a global plurisubharmonic function on a compact manifold, hence constant. Thus ( 28.2 ) measures the nonlinear mass of the Hermitian error family rather than positivity of the closed class. A numerical theory of restricted volumes in a Hermitian background must therefore either control the approximating family or use a different invariant. Two qualitative loci avoid this supremum. The non-Hermitian locus of a big background is defined through its strict currents, whose exterior derivative is prescribed by the background; Dang's null locus tests failure of bigness after restriction to subvarieties. The singularities allowed in the first definition, and the equality of the two loci for nef and big backgrounds, are recalled in section 33.3 .

title: 28.6 Finite restricted masses of closed classes
search_title: Finite restricted masses of closed classes
text: 28.6 Finite restricted masses of closed classes The nonclosed error in proposition 28.5.1 destroys the cohomological bound on masses. On a compact Kähler manifold, by contrast, the non-pluripolar mass of a positive current in a closed class is bounded by a top intersection number. Pulling a class back to a Kähler resolution of a subvariety therefore gives a finite invariant: the supremum of the non-pluripolar masses of positive currents in the pulled-back class. It measures positivity along every subvariety, including subvarieties along which a given modification of $X$ fails to be an isomorphism. In this section and the next, $X$ belongs to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$. Then every irreducible reduced subvariety $Y\subset X$ has a resolution $\pi :Z\to Y$ with $Z$ a compact Kähler manifold: closed subspaces of a space in class $\mathcal C$ are again in class $\mathcal C$, and the Kähler modification theorem applies to $Y$. These classical facts are discussed in section 34.16 . In particular, a Kähler model of $Y$ is obtained directly, not as a proper transform under one fixed modification of $X$. Two such resolutions $Z_1,Z_2$ of $Y$ admit a common Kähler refinement. Indeed, apply embedded resolution to the closure in $Z_1\times Z_2$ of the graph of the induced bimeromorphic map. The resulting strict transform is smooth, and it is Kähler because the ambient resolution is a sequence of blowups of the compact Kähler product along smooth centers. A blowup of a compact Kähler manifold along a smooth center is again Kähler: add to the pulled-back Kähler form a small positive multiple of a curvature form of $\mathcal O(-E)$, which is positive in the vertical directions along the exceptional divisor $E$. For a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $S$ on a compact Kähler manifold $Z$ of dimension $k>0$, write $\langle S^ k\rangle $ for its non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure, that is, $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\eta (u)$ for any decomposition $S=\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $\eta $ smooth and closed (theorem 6.1.2 ). For a class $b\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R)$, set 28.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:closed-class-mass} \mathcal R_ Z(b)=\sup _{\substack {S\in b\\ S\geq 0}} \int _ Z\langle S^ k\rangle , \qquad \sup \varnothing =0. \end{equation} For a class $a\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$ and an irreducible reduced subvariety $Y\subset X$ of dimension $k>0$, let $j:Y\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, write $f=j\circ \pi $, and define 28.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-restricted-invariant} \mathcal R(a;Y)=\mathcal R_ Z(f^*a). \end{equation} Proposition 28.6.1 . The quantities in ( 28.3 ) and ( 28.4 ) are finite, and the latter is independent of the Kähler resolution. If $\eta \in b$ is smooth, $\kappa $ is Kähler and $C>0$ satisfies $C\kappa -\eta >0$, then 28.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:closed-class-mass-bound} \mathcal R_ Z(b+t\{ \kappa \} ) \leq (C+t)^ k\int _ Z\kappa ^ k \qquad (t\geq 0). \end{equation} Let $\mu :X'\to X$ be a modification and $Y'$ the proper transform of a subvariety $Y$ that meets the locus where $\mu $ is an isomorphism. Then \[  \mathcal R(\mu ^*a;Y')=\mathcal R(a;Y).  \] Proof. Step 1: Kähler forms. Let $\lambda $ be a Kähler form on $Z$ and $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(Z,\lambda )$ with $q\leq 0$. The truncations $q_ j=\max (q,-j)$ have mass $\int _ Z\lambda ^ k$ by theorem 2.2.2 , or by Stokes' theorem when $k=1$. Restricting their Monge–Ampère measures to $\{ q>-j\} $ and passing to the increasing limit gives \[  \int _ Z\langle (\lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ k\rangle \leq \int _ Z\lambda ^ k.  \] The smooth current $\lambda $ attains equality. Step 2: the mass bound. Put $A=C\kappa -\eta $. For a positive current $S$ in $b+t\{ \kappa \} $, the current $S+A$ is positive and belongs to $(C+t)\{ \kappa \} $. Since local non-pluripolar products are positive and multilinear, $\langle S^ k\rangle \leq \langle (S+A)^ k\rangle $, and Step 1 applied to the Kähler form $(C+t)\kappa $ yields ( 28.5 ). In particular $\mathcal R_ Z(b)$ is finite. The definition involves only the class, so the choice of its smooth representative or of the comparison form does not change the supremum. Step 3: modifications. Let $\rho :W\to Z$ be a modification between compact Kähler manifolds. By proposition 1.22.12 , every positive current in $\rho ^*b$ is the pullback of a unique positive current in $b$. Their non-pluripolar measures correspond on the locus where $\rho $ is an isomorphism, and neither charges the exceptional analytic sets. Hence their total masses agree and \[  \mathcal R_ W(\rho ^*b)=\mathcal R_ Z(b).  \] Applying this identity on a common Kähler refinement shows that $\mathcal R(a;Y)$ is independent of the resolution. The same argument compares resolutions of $Y$ and $Y'$, since their maps to $X$ agree on a dense open set and therefore everywhere on a common refinement. $\square$ On a compact Kähler manifold, positivity of this mass has a classical interpretation. We use two facts from Kähler pluripotential theory, discussed in section 34.16 : a class containing a positive current with positive non-pluripolar top mass is big, and in a big class a current with minimal singularities attains the volume, the largest non-pluripolar top mass; for a nef class this volume is the top intersection number. For a nef class, the Kähler current used here can also be obtained from the following normalized diagonal construction. Proposition 28.6.2 . Let $Z$ be a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $k>0$ and $b\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R)$. Then \[  \mathcal R_ Z(b)>0\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad b\text{ is big}.  \] If $b$ is nef, then 28.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-restricted-mass} \mathcal R_ Z(b)=\int _ Zb^ k. \end{equation} Suppose that $b$ is nef with $I=\int _ Zb^ k>0$. Fix a Kähler form $\kappa $, let $p_1,p_2:Z\times Z\to Z$ be the projections and $\Delta \subset Z\times Z$ the diagonal, and put \[  M=k\int _ Zb^{k-1}\wedge \{ \kappa \} .  \] Then there are $d>0$ and a closed positive $(k,k)$-current $\Theta $ in $(p_1^*b+p_2^*b)^ k$ with $\Theta \geq d[\Delta ]$ such that 28.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normalized-diagonal-current} K_ b=M^{-1}(p_1)_*(\Theta \wedge p_2^*\kappa )\in b, \qquad K_ b\geq (d/M)\kappa . \end{equation} Proof. If $\mathcal R_ Z(b)>0$, some positive representative has positive non-pluripolar top mass, so $b$ is big by the first fact above. Conversely, if $S\in b$ satisfies $S\geq \delta \kappa $ with $\delta >0$, then $S-\delta \kappa $ is positive and closed, and expanding the non-pluripolar product gives $\langle S^ k\rangle \geq \delta ^ k\kappa ^ k$. Hence $\mathcal R_ Z(b)>0$. Suppose now that $b$ is nef. For $t>0$, the class $b+t\{ \kappa \} $ is Kähler. Adding $t\kappa $ to an arbitrary positive representative of $b$ and using the Kähler mass bound of Step 1 in the proof of proposition 28.6.1 yields \[  \mathcal R_ Z(b)\leq \int _ Z(b+t\{ \kappa \} )^ k.  \] Letting $t$ decrease to zero gives the upper bound in ( 28.6 ). In particular, equality holds if $I=0$. Let $I>0$, and choose $L>0$ such that $L\{ \kappa \} -b$ is Kähler. Since intersection numbers of nef classes are nonnegative, \[  0\leq \int _ Zb^{k-1}\wedge (L\{ \kappa \} -b) =LM/k-I,  \] so $M>0$. The class $B=p_1^*b+p_2^*b$ is nef and satisfies \[  \int _{Z\times Z}B^{2k}={2k\choose k}I^2>0.  \] The classical mass concentration theorem along the diagonal gives $\Theta \in B^ k$ with $\Theta \geq d[\Delta ]$ for some $d>0$. When $B^ k\wedge p_2^*\{ \kappa \} $ is pushed forward by $p_1$, only the term containing exactly one factor $p_1^*b$ survives. Thus \[  (p_1)_*(B^ k\wedge p_2^*\{ \kappa \} )=Mb, \qquad (p_1)_*([\Delta ]\wedge p_2^*\kappa )=\kappa .  \] Since $\Theta -d[\Delta ]$ is positive, these identities prove ( 28.7 ); the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma for currents on the compact Kähler manifold $Z$ identifies the cohomology class computed in this way with the Bott–Chern class $b$. Therefore $b$ is big, and by the second fact above a current with minimal singularities in $b$ has non-pluripolar mass $\int _ Zb^ k$. This gives the remaining lower bound. $\square$ When $Y$ is smooth, the criterion descends to $Y$. Write $a_ Y=j^*a$ for the restricted class, let $\pi :Z\to Y$ be a Kähler modification with Kähler form $\kappa $, and choose a Hermitian metric $h$ on $Y$ and $C>0$ with $\pi ^*h\leq C\kappa $. If $K\in \pi ^*a_ Y$ satisfies $K\geq \delta \kappa $ with $\delta >0$, then descent of potentials (proposition 1.22.12 ) makes $\pi _*K$ a positive representative of $a_ Y$, and 28.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:strict-current-pushforward} \pi _*K\geq (\delta /C)\pi _*\pi ^*h=(\delta /C)h. \end{equation} Conversely, let $S$ be a strict positive representative of $a_ Y$. On a coordinate ball in the locus where $\pi $ is an isomorphism, $\pi ^*S$ dominates a positive multiple of the closed form $\kappa $, so the local expansion of the non-pluripolar product shows that $\pi ^*S$ has positive non-pluripolar mass on that ball. Consequently, $\mathcal R(a;Y)>0$ if and only if the restricted class $a_ Y$ is big. The Hermitian metric $h$ enters only through inequalities between currents; the products are compared with the closed form $\kappa $. Proposition 28.6.3 . Let $W$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $k>0$, let $g:W\to X$ be holomorphic, and suppose $\dim g(W)<k$. Then for every class $a\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$, \[  \mathcal R_ W(g^*a)=0.  \] Proof. If the image is a point, then $g^*a=0$ and ( 28.6 ) gives the assertion. Otherwise, choose a Kähler resolution $r:Q\to g(W)$ and resolve the graph of the meromorphic lift of $g$ to $Q$. This gives a Kähler modification $\rho :\widehat W\to W$ and a holomorphic map $F:\widehat W\to Q$ with $g\circ \rho =r\circ F$, where $r$ is also viewed as a map into $X$. Choose a smooth representative $\eta \in a$, a Kähler form $\kappa _ Q$ on $Q$, and $C>0$ such that $C\kappa _ Q-r^*\eta \geq 0$. Since $\rho ^*g^*\eta =F^*r^*\eta $, the forms \[  P=CF^*\kappa _ Q, \qquad A=P-\rho ^*g^*\eta  \] are closed and semipositive. Since $\dim Q<k$, we have $P^ k=0$. For any positive current $S\in g^*a$, the current $\rho ^*S+A$ is positive and lies in the nef class $\{ P\} $. Hence \[  \int _{\widehat W}\langle (\rho ^*S)^ k\rangle \leq \int _{\widehat W}\langle (\rho ^*S+A)^ k\rangle \leq \mathcal R_{\widehat W}(\{ P\} ) =\int _{\widehat W}P^ k=0.  \] Modification invariance (Step 3 in the proof of proposition 28.6.1 ) now gives the result. If the class has no positive representative, its invariant is zero by definition. $\square$ Corollary 28.6.4 . Let $a$ be a nef class on $X$. For every positive-dimensional irreducible reduced subvariety $Y\subset X$, \[  \mathcal R(a;Y)=\int _ Ya^{\dim Y}.  \] If $\int _ Xa^ n>0$, then 28.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-restricted-null-union} \bigcup _{\substack {Y\subset X\  \mathrm{irreducible},\  \dim Y>0\\ \mathcal R(a;Y)=0}}Y =\operatorname {Null}(a)=E_{\mathrm{nK}}(a). \end{equation} Proof. The pullback of $a$ to a Kähler resolution of $Y$ is nef: pull back smooth representatives with arbitrarily small negative part, and bound the pullback of $\omega $ by a multiple of a Kähler form on the resolution. Since the intersection number $\int _ Ya^{\dim Y}$ is defined through the same pullback, ( 28.6 ) gives the first assertion. The first equality in ( 28.9 ) then follows from the definition of the null locus, and the second is the classical theorem on nef and big classes recalled earlier in this chapter. $\square$ When $X$ is Kähler and $a$ is nef, the numerical restricted volume ( 28.1 ) along $Y$ is also $\int _ Ya^{\dim Y}$, so the two restricted invariants agree. Outside the nef case this comparison does not identify them: ( 28.4 ) is a supremum over all positive currents on a resolution of $Y$, and these currents need not extend to $X$.

Hence $\mathcal R_ Z(b)>0$. Suppose now that $b$ is nef. For $t>0$, the class $b+t\{ \kappa \} $ is Kähler. Adding $t\kappa $ to an arbitrary positive representative of $b$ and using the Kähler mass bound of Step 1 in the proof of proposition 28.6.1 yields \[  \mathcal R_ Z(b)\leq \int _ Z(b+t\{ \kappa \} )^ k.  \] Letting $t$ decrease to zero gives the upper bound in ( 28.6 ). In particular, equality holds if $I=0$. Let $I>0$, and choose $L>0$ such that $L\{ \kappa \} -b$ is Kähler. Since intersection numbers of nef classes are nonnegative, \[  0\leq \int _ Zb^{k-1}\wedge (L\{ \kappa \} -b) =LM/k-I,  \] so $M>0$. The class $B=p_1^*b+p_2^*b$ is nef and satisfies \[  \int _{Z\times Z}B^{2k}={2k\choose k}I^2>0.  \] The classical mass concentration theorem along the diagonal gives $\Theta \in B^ k$ with $\Theta \geq d[\Delta ]$ for some $d>0$. When $B^ k\wedge p_2^*\{ \kappa \} $ is pushed forward by $p_1$, only the term containing exactly one factor $p_1^*b$ survives. Thus \[  (p_1)_*(B^ k\wedge p_2^*\{ \kappa \} )=Mb, \qquad (p_1)_*([\Delta ]\wedge p_2^*\kappa )=\kappa .  \] Since $\Theta -d[\Delta ]$ is positive, these identities prove ( 28.7 ); the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma for currents on the compact Kähler manifold $Z$ identifies the cohomology class computed in this way with the Bott–Chern class $b$. Therefore $b$ is big, and by the second fact above a current with minimal singularities in $b$ has non-pluripolar mass $\int _ Zb^ k$. This gives the remaining lower bound. $\square$
28.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-restricted-mass} \mathcal R_ Z(b)=\int _ Zb^ k. \end{equation}
28.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normalized-diagonal-current} K_ b=M^{-1}(p_1)_*(\Theta \wedge p_2^*\kappa )\in b, \qquad K_ b\geq (d/M)\kappa . \end{equation}
28.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:strict-current-pushforward} \pi _*K\geq (\delta /C)\pi _*\pi ^*h=(\delta /C)h. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 28.6.3
text: Proposition 28.6.3 . Let $W$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $k>0$, let $g:W\to X$ be holomorphic, and suppose $\dim g(W)<k$. Then for every class $a\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$, \[  \mathcal R_ W(g^*a)=0.  \] Proof. If the image is a point, then $g^*a=0$ and ( 28.6 ) gives the assertion. Otherwise, choose a Kähler resolution $r:Q\to g(W)$ and resolve the graph of the meromorphic lift of $g$ to $Q$. This gives a Kähler modification $\rho :\widehat W\to W$ and a holomorphic map $F:\widehat W\to Q$ with $g\circ \rho =r\circ F$, where $r$ is also viewed as a map into $X$. Choose a smooth representative $\eta \in a$, a Kähler form $\kappa _ Q$ on $Q$, and $C>0$ such that $C\kappa _ Q-r^*\eta \geq 0$. Since $\rho ^*g^*\eta =F^*r^*\eta $, the forms \[  P=CF^*\kappa _ Q, \qquad A=P-\rho ^*g^*\eta  \] are closed and semipositive. Since $\dim Q<k$, we have $P^ k=0$. For any positive current $S\in g^*a$, the current $\rho ^*S+A$ is positive and lies in the nef class $\{ P\} $. Hence \[  \int _{\widehat W}\langle (\rho ^*S)^ k\rangle \leq \int _{\widehat W}\langle (\rho ^*S+A)^ k\rangle \leq \mathcal R_{\widehat W}(\{ P\} ) =\int _{\widehat W}P^ k=0.  \] Modification invariance (Step 3 in the proof of proposition 28.6.1 ) now gives the result. If the class has no positive representative, its invariant is zero by definition. $\square$

title: Corollary 28.6.4
text: Corollary 28.6.4 . Let $a$ be a nef class on $X$. For every positive-dimensional irreducible reduced subvariety $Y\subset X$, \[  \mathcal R(a;Y)=\int _ Ya^{\dim Y}.  \] If $\int _ Xa^ n>0$, then 28.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-restricted-null-union} \bigcup _{\substack {Y\subset X\  \mathrm{irreducible},\  \dim Y>0\\ \mathcal R(a;Y)=0}}Y =\operatorname {Null}(a)=E_{\mathrm{nK}}(a). \end{equation} Proof. The pullback of $a$ to a Kähler resolution of $Y$ is nef: pull back smooth representatives with arbitrarily small negative part, and bound the pullback of $\omega $ by a multiple of a Kähler form on the resolution. Since the intersection number $\int _ Ya^{\dim Y}$ is defined through the same pullback, ( 28.6 ) gives the first assertion. The first equality in ( 28.9 ) then follows from the definition of the null locus, and the second is the classical theorem on nef and big classes recalled earlier in this chapter. $\square$

28.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-restricted-null-union} \bigcup _{\substack {Y\subset X\  \mathrm{irreducible},\  \dim Y>0\\ \mathcal R(a;Y)=0}}Y =\operatorname {Null}(a)=E_{\mathrm{nK}}(a). \end{equation}

title: 28.7 Divisorial traces with bounded remainder
text: 28.7 Divisorial traces with bounded remainder The invariant $\mathcal R(a;Y)$ is a supremum over all positive currents in a class. The trace of a given potential on $Y$, on the other hand, carries a specified singularity, and its non-pluripolar mass can be smaller. Suppose that on a resolution the trace becomes a divisorial logarithmic term plus a bounded remainder. The non-pluripolar product then ignores the divisor and sees only the residual current, which has bounded potentials. The class of this residual current is nef, and its top intersection number computes the mass. We keep the assumption that $X$ belongs to class $\mathcal C$. Let $Y\subset X$ be an irreducible reduced subvariety of dimension $k>0$, let $\alpha _0$ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\alpha _0)$ be such that its pointwise restriction $v=u|_ Y$ is not identically $-\infty $. On a Kähler resolution $\pi :Z\to Y$, with $f=j\circ \pi :Z\to X$ as in section 28.6 , put $\alpha _ Z=f^*\alpha _0$ and $v_\pi =u\circ f$. When $Y$ is smooth, one may instead start from a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\alpha _ Y$ on $Y$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\alpha _ Y)$, and put $\alpha _ Z=\pi ^*\alpha _ Y$ and $v_\pi =v\circ \pi $. In both cases $v_\pi $ is the composition of a given potential with a map; the intrinsic multiplier-ideal trace of chapter 19 is a different construction. Suppose that on one such resolution 28.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-trace-decomposition} v_\pi =\ell +w, \qquad \ell =\sum _{j=1}^ N c_ j\log |s_ j|_{h_ j}^2, \qquad w\text{ bounded}, \end{equation} where $c_ j>0$, the $D_ j$ are prime divisors on $Z$, $s_ j$ is the canonical section of $\mathcal O(D_ j)$, and $h_ j$ is a smooth Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O(D_ j)$; the empty sum $\ell =0$ is allowed. Write $\Gamma =\sum _ jc_ jD_ j$ and $\gamma _ j=c_1(\mathcal O(D_ j),h_ j)$ for the curvature forms, and define the residual form and the residual class 28.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-trace-residual-class} \eta _ v=\alpha _ Z-\sum _ jc_ j\gamma _ j, \qquad b_ v=\{ \eta _ v\} =\{ \alpha _ Z\} -\{ [\Gamma ]\} . \end{equation} For singular $Y$, all assertions below are made on its resolutions. Lemma 28.7.1 . The current $R_ v=\eta _ v+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is positive and has bounded local potentials, and its class $b_ v$ is nef. Moreover, 28.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-trace-mass} \int _ Z\langle (\alpha _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\pi )^ k\rangle =\int _ ZR_ v^ k =\int _ Zb_ v^ k =\mathcal R_ Z(b_ v). \end{equation} If $v_1,\ldots ,v_ k$ satisfy the same conditions on $Z$, possibly for different closed backgrounds, then 28.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-trace-mixed-mass} \int _ ZR_{v_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge R_{v_ k} =\int _ Zb_{v_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge b_{v_ k}. \end{equation} Proof. Off the support $|\Gamma |$, we have $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\ell =-\sum _ jc_ j\gamma _ j$, so the current $\alpha _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\pi $ equals $\eta _ v+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ there and is positive. After the addition of a smooth local potential for $\eta _ v$, the bounded function $w$ is plurisubharmonic off $|\Gamma |$. By lemma 1.3.7 , it extends across the divisor as a bounded plurisubharmonic function that agrees almost everywhere with the original one; we use this extension to represent $w$. Thus $R_ v\geq 0$ on $Z$, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \alpha _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\pi =[\Gamma ]+R_ v.  \] Since $w$ is bounded, $b_ v$ is nef by lemma 23.6.1 . The non-pluripolar measure on the left of ( 28.12 ) agrees with $R_ v^ k$ off the divisor, and neither measure charges the divisor. This gives the first equality. Fix a Kähler form $\kappa $ on $Z$. For all sufficiently large real $t$, the smooth closed form $\eta _ v+t\kappa $ is Kähler, and $w$ is a bounded potential for it. Therefore \[  \int _ Z(R_ v+t\kappa )^ k=\int _ Z(\eta _ v+t\kappa )^ k  \] by theorem 2.2.2 , or by Stokes' theorem when $k=1$. Both sides are polynomials in $t$, so their constant coefficients agree; this gives $\int _ ZR_ v^ k=\int _ Zb_ v^ k$. The last equality in ( 28.12 ) is ( 28.6 ). Applying the same polynomial argument to positive linear combinations of the $R_{v_ i}$ and comparing coefficients gives ( 28.13 ). $\square$ We denote the common value in ( 28.12 ) by $\mathfrak r(v;Y)$ and call it the trace mass of $v$ on $Y$. When $Y$ is smooth, it is also the non-pluripolar mass of the trace current on $Y$ itself: \[  \mathfrak r(v;Y)=\int _ Y\langle (\alpha _ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ k\rangle ,  \] where $\alpha _ Y=\alpha _0|_ Y$ when $v$ is a restriction. Indeed, the currents on $Z$ and on $Y$ correspond on the locus where $\pi $ is an isomorphism, and their non-pluripolar measures give no mass to its analytic complement. A change of variables therefore identifies the total masses. Theorem 28.7.2 . The number $\mathfrak r(v;Y)$ does not depend on the divisor metrics or on the Kähler resolution carrying ( 28.10 ). If two potentials in the same closed background have the same ordinary singularity type and each has a decomposition of the form ( 28.10 ), then their residual classes agree on a common refinement, and in particular their trace masses are equal. Residual classes add when the traces and their backgrounds are added, and their mixed masses are given by ( 28.13 ). Proof. Changing a divisor metric changes $\ell $ by a smooth function, $w$ by its negative, and $\eta _ v$ by the corresponding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-term. Thus $R_ v$ is unchanged. The same cancellation occurs when a smooth change of the background is accompanied by the opposite change of the potential. Let $\rho :W\to Z$ be a modification with $W$ Kähler. Pulling back the decomposition, with the total divisor $\rho ^*\Gamma $ including all exceptional coefficients, gives a decomposition on $W$ with bounded remainder $w\circ \rho $, residual current $\rho ^*R_ v$ and nef residual class $\rho ^*b_ v$. Its mass is \[  \int _ W(\rho ^*b_ v)^ k=\int _ Zb_ v^ k.  \] For two decompositions on different resolutions, pass to a common Kähler refinement and pull both back in this way. At a generic smooth point of a prime component of the union of the two divisors, the difference of the logarithmic terms is $(a_1-a_2)\log |t|^2+O(1)$, where $t$ is a local defining coordinate of the component and $a_1,a_2$ are its two coefficients. The two potentials have bounded difference, and the resulting pair of inequalities forces $a_1=a_2$. Hence the total divisors coincide, and so do the residual classes in the common background. Finally, adding two decompositions adds both the divisors and the bounded remainders. The residual class of the sum is therefore the sum of the nef residual classes, and ( 28.13 ) computes its mixed terms. $\square$ Proposition 28.7.3 . Suppose that $\mathfrak r(v;Y)>0$. Then the class $\{ \alpha _ Z\} $ contains a Kähler current $\alpha _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p$ whose potential satisfies $p\leq v_\pi +A$ for some constant $A$. If $b_ v$ has a smooth positive representative on a resolution carrying ( 28.10 ), then on that resolution $p$ can be chosen with $p\sim v_\pi $, that is, with $p-v_\pi $ bounded. When $Y$ is smooth, the Kähler current and the corresponding inequalities between potentials descend to $Y$. Proof. Positive trace mass means $\int _ Zb_ v^ k>0$. Since $b_ v$ is nef, ( 28.7 ) gives a current $K=\eta _ v+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\geq \delta \kappa $ in $b_ v$, where $\kappa $ is a Kähler form and $\delta >0$. The current \[  [\Gamma ]+K=\alpha _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\ell +a)  \] is then a Kähler current. Since $a$ is bounded above on $Z$ and $w$ is bounded below, its potential $p=\ell +a$ satisfies $p\leq \ell +w+A=v_\pi +A$ for a constant $A$. If $b_ v$ has a smooth positive representative, $a$ can be chosen smooth, and then $p-v_\pi =a-w$ is bounded. For smooth $Y$, take $\alpha _ Y=\alpha _0|_ Y$ when $v$ is a restriction. By proposition 1.22.12 , $p=q\circ \pi $ for some $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\alpha _ Y)$. The current $\alpha _ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$ is strict by ( 28.8 ), and since $\pi $ is surjective, each inequality between potentials descends. The hypothesis of a smooth positive representative refers to the specified resolution: the pullback of a Kähler class under a further blowup need not be Kähler. $\square$ The trace mass can vanish even when the restricted class is big, because the non-pluripolar product ignores the divisorial part of the trace. Example 28.7.4 . Let $k\geq 1$, let $Y\simeq \mathbb P^ k$ be a hyperplane in $X=\mathbb P^{k+1}$, and let another hyperplane $H_ X\subset X$ cut out $H=H_ X\cap Y$. Let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form, normalized by $\int _ Y\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^ k=1$, and let $s_{H_ X}$ be a section of $\mathcal O(1)$ defining $H_ X$, measured with the Fubini–Study metric. For $c>0$ and $d\geq 0$, take $\alpha _0=(c+d)\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ on $X$ and $u=c\log |s_{H_ X}|^2$. The restriction $v=u|_ Y$ is not identically $-\infty $, and \[  \alpha _0|_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=c[H]+d\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}|_ Y, \qquad \mathfrak r(v;Y)=d^ k, \qquad \mathcal R(\{ \alpha _0\} ;Y)=(c+d)^ k.  \] Thus for $d=0$ the trace mass is zero, although the restricted invariant is positive. The divisor $c[H]$ is a nonzero part of the trace current, but the non-pluripolar top product discards it. The next example shows that the inequality $p\leq v_\pi +A$ in proposition 28.7.3 cannot in general be improved to $p\sim v_\pi $, even for a bounded trace. Example 28.7.5 . Let $\mu :Y\to \mathbb P^2$ be the blowup of a point, with exceptional curve $E$, let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^2$ with total volume one, and put $\alpha _ Y=\mu ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ and $v=0$. The decomposition ( 28.10 ) holds on $Z=Y$ with no divisor, the residual class $\{ \alpha _ Y\} $ is nef and big, and \[  \mathfrak r(0;Y)=\mathcal R(\{ \alpha _ Y\} ;Y)=1.  \] Nevertheless, there is no bounded $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\alpha _ Y)$ for which $\alpha _ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \delta \kappa $ with $\delta >0$ and $\kappa $ Kähler. Indeed, since $q$ is bounded, its restriction to $E$ is defined, and the disk criterion of lemma 1.22.1 gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q|_ E)\geq \delta \kappa |_ E,  \] because $\alpha _ Y|_ E=0$. Integration over the compact curve $E$ contradicts Stokes' theorem. Thus positive trace mass gives the one-sided comparison of proposition 28.7.3 , but a Kähler current in the class may need additional singularities. A subvariety contained in the null locus can nevertheless have positive restricted invariant; the union in ( 28.9 ) is needed to recover the locus. Example 28.7.6 . Let $\mu :X\to \mathbb P^3$ be the blowup along a line $L$, and set $a=\mu ^*\{ \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}\} $, where $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ has total volume one; the class $a$ is nef and $\int _ Xa^3=1$. Since $N_{L/\mathbb P^3}\simeq \mathcal O(1)\oplus \mathcal O(1)$, the exceptional divisor is $E=\mathbb P(N_{L/\mathbb P^3})\simeq \mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, and on $E$ the map $\mu $ is the projection to $L$. Hence $\int _ Ea^2=0$, whereas a section $Y$ of $E\to L$ satisfies $\int _ Ya=1$. Every irreducible subvariety not contained in $E$ has positive intersection number, because $\mu ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is positive on its nonempty open part outside $E$. By corollary 28.6.4 , \[  E_{\mathrm{nK}}(a)=E, \qquad \mathcal R(a;E)=0, \qquad \mathcal R(a;Y)=1.  \] The union of the subvarieties with zero invariant is the whole null locus $E$, although the curve $Y\subset E$ has positive invariant. Positivity along one subvariety does not place it outside the null locus.
28.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-trace-decomposition} v_\pi =\ell +w, \qquad \ell =\sum _{j=1}^ N c_ j\log |s_ j|_{h_ j}^2, \qquad w\text{ bounded}, \end{equation}
28.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:resolved-trace-residual-class} \eta _ v=\alpha _ Z-\sum _ jc_ j\gamma _ j, \qquad b_ v=\{ \eta _ v\} =\{ \alpha _ Z\} -\{ [\Gamma ]\} . \end{equation}

title: Proposition 28.7.3
text: Proposition 28.7.3 . Suppose that $\mathfrak r(v;Y)>0$. Then the class $\{ \alpha _ Z\} $ contains a Kähler current $\alpha _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p$ whose potential satisfies $p\leq v_\pi +A$ for some constant $A$. If $b_ v$ has a smooth positive representative on a resolution carrying ( 28.10 ), then on that resolution $p$ can be chosen with $p\sim v_\pi $, that is, with $p-v_\pi $ bounded. When $Y$ is smooth, the Kähler current and the corresponding inequalities between potentials descend to $Y$. Proof. Positive trace mass means $\int _ Zb_ v^ k>0$. If $b_ v$ has a smooth positive representative, $a$ can be chosen smooth, and then $p-v_\pi =a-w$ is bounded. For smooth $Y$, take $\alpha _ Y=\alpha _0|_ Y$ when $v$ is a restriction. title: Example 28.7.4

Let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form, normalized by $\int _ Y\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^ k=1$, and let $s_{H_ X}$ be a section of $\mathcal O(1)$ defining $H_ X$, measured with the Fubini–Study metric. title: Example 28.7.5
text: Example 28.7.5 . Let $\mu :Y\to \mathbb P^2$ be the blowup of a point, with exceptional curve $E$, let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^2$ with total volume one, and put $\alpha _ Y=\mu ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ and $v=0$.
