title: 28.12 Radial densities and metric completeness
text: 28.12 Radial densities and metric completeness For a radially symmetric equation, the mass of the density inside a ball determines the radial derivative of the potential and hence both eigenvalues of its Hessian. Boundedness of the potential and finiteness of the distance to the center are then expressed by two different integrals of this derivative, and suitable singular densities separate the two properties. Throughout this section $n\geq 2$, the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ n$ is normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^ n}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^ n=1$, and on the standard affine chart with coordinates $y\in \mathbb C^ n$ we put $\omega _{\mathrm E}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|y|^2$, so that $\int _{\{ |y|^2<S\} }\omega _{\mathrm E}^ n=S^ n$ for $S>0$. We write $s=|y|^2$. Theorem 28.12.1 . Fix $\lambda >0$ and a smooth positive function $D:(0,\infty )\to (0,\infty )$ such that $D(s)=\lambda ^ n/(1+s)^{n+1}$ for all sufficiently large $s$, and 28.26 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-total-mass} n\int _0^\infty s^{n-1}D(s)\, \mathrm{d} s=\lambda ^ n. \end{equation} Let $\mu _ D$ be the measure on $\mathbb P^ n$ equal to $D(|y|^2)\omega _{\mathrm E}^ n$ on the affine chart and to zero on the hyperplane at infinity; near that hyperplane it agrees with $(\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}})^ n$. Then the equation $\langle (\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n\rangle =\mu _ D$ has a unique normalized full-mass solution $q$. It is smooth off $y=0$, and on the affine chart its total local potential $\lambda \log (1+|y|^2)+q(y)$ is a radial function $U(s)$ satisfying 28.27 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-mass-ode} \begin{aligned}  m(s)^ n& =n\int _0^ s t^{n-1}D(t)\, \mathrm{d} t,\qquad m(s)=sU'(s),\\  m'(s)& =\frac{s^{n-1}D(s)}{m(s)^{n-1}}>0. \end{aligned} \end{equation} The tangential and radial eigenvalues of its Hessian are $m/s$ and $m'$. For any sufficiently small $s_0>0$, the solution is bounded, equivalently has minimal singularities, precisely when 28.30 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-bounded-criterion} \int _0^{s_0}\frac{m(s)}s\, \mathrm{d} s<\infty . \end{equation} The distance from the origin for the metric $\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$ on $\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ is finite precisely when 28.31 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-distance-criterion} \int _0^{s_0}\frac{\sqrt{m'(s)}}{2\sqrt{s}}\, \mathrm{d} s<\infty . \end{equation} If this integral diverges, the metric on $\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ is complete. Let $\pi :X=\operatorname {Bl}_0\mathbb P^ n\to \mathbb P^ n$ be the blowup at the origin, with exceptional divisor $E$, and let $s_ E$ and $\Theta _ E$ be as in section 14.22 . For $\theta =\pi ^*(\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}})+c\Theta _ E$ with $c>0$, the full-mass solution on $X$ whose measure is the pullback of $\mu _ D$ has potential $c\log |s_ E|^2+q\circ \pi +C$, generic Lelong number exactly $c$ along $E$, and mass $\lambda ^ n$. In a blowup chart $\pi (z,w)=(z,zw)$, its density relative to the Euclidean volume form of the coordinates $(z,w)$, normalized as above, is 28.32 \begin{equation} \label{eq:blowup-radial-density} |z|^{2(n-1)}D\bigl (|z|^2(1+|w|^2)\bigr ). \end{equation} Its ordinary singularity type is minimal precisely under ( 28.30 ). In the unbounded cases, the residual $q\circ \pi $ grows sublogarithmically and has zero generic Lelong number, but the type is not minimal. The metric off $E$ satisfies the same completeness criterion ( 28.31 ). Proof. Define $m$ by the first equation in ( 28.27 ). It is positive for $s>0$ and tends to zero at the origin. By ( 28.26 ) and the prescribed outer density, $m(s)=\lambda s/(1+s)$ for large $s$: the two expressions for $m^ n$ have the same limit at infinity and the same derivative for large $s$. Integrate $U'=m/s$, choosing the additive constant so that $U(s)=\lambda \log (1+s)$ for large $s$. The Hessian of $U(|y|^2)$ has eigenvalues $m/s$ and $m'$, and its determinant is $(m/s)^{n-1}m'=D$. Thus $q=U(|y|^2)-\lambda \log (1+|y|^2)$ extends by zero outside the affine chart and defines a positive current that is smooth off the origin. Subtracting its supremum gives the normalization. Since $U$ is increasing, it is bounded above near zero, so lemma 1.3.7 gives a plurisubharmonic extension across the origin, possibly with the value $-\infty $ there. If $U$ is unbounded, then $m(s)\to 0$ implies $U(s)=o(|\log s|)$: for each $\epsilon >0$, bound $m$ by $\epsilon $ on a small interval and integrate $m/s$. The closed non-pluripolar product equals $\mu _ D$ off the origin and puts no mass at the origin; the measure $\mu _ D$ has no atom there and has mass $\lambda ^ n$ by ( 28.26 ). Hence $q$ is a full-mass solution, and it is unique by the uniqueness of full-mass solutions in the closed theory, discussed in section 34.19 . Integrating $U'=m/s$ shows that $U$ is bounded near the origin precisely under ( 28.30 ). Write $R=|y|$. For a path approaching the origin, the metric norm of its velocity is at least a fixed multiple of $\sqrt{m'(R^2)}|\dot R|$, and radial paths attain this bound up to a fixed constant. Since $\mathrm{d} R=\mathrm{d} s/(2\sqrt{s})$, this gives ( 28.31 ). The metric is smooth and positive on compact subsets away from the origin, so divergence of the integral is equivalent to completeness of the metric on $\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $. On the blowup, apply proposition 14.22.1 and use the squared Jacobian $|z|^{2(n-1)}$. The closed non-pluripolar product is the extension by zero of the pullback density, has mass $\lambda ^ n=\operatorname {vol}([\theta ])$, and is unique in its full-mass class. By theorem 6.1.2 , the extended operator agrees with it on potentials that are continuous off $E$, even when the residual tends to $-\infty $ along $E$. Sublogarithmic growth gives the residual zero Lelong number, so the coefficient along $E$ is exactly $c$, but it does not give a bounded difference from $c\log |s_ E|^2$. The metric off $E$ is isometric to the metric on $\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, which proves the same distance criterion. The inner asymptotics considered below can be glued to the prescribed outer density while keeping ( 28.26 ): take a small inner amplitude or radius, join through a smooth positive annulus, and add a nonnegative smooth annular bump to supply the remaining mass. Thus each of these asymptotic behaviors occurs for a density satisfying the hypotheses of the theorem. The assertions below concern the total local potential $U$; subtracting a smooth background potential can change a leading smooth term. $\square$ In the next theorem, $f\sim g$ means that $f/g\to 1$ as $s\downarrow 0$. Theorem 28.12.2 . For the normalized family in theorem 28.12.1 , put $L=\log (1/s)$ for $0<s<1$. If $D(s)\sim Cs^{\ell -n+1}L^{-b}$ with $C>0$, $\ell >-1$ and $b\in \mathbb R$, put $\gamma =(\ell +1)/n$ and $K=(C/\gamma )^{1/n}$. Then 28.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:power-log-asymptotics} m\sim Ks^\gamma L^{-b/n},\qquad U(s)-U(0)\sim \frac K\gamma s^\gamma L^{-b/n},\qquad m'\sim \gamma K s^{\gamma -1}L^{-b/n}. \end{equation} The residual is bounded and Hölder continuous. In bounded blowup charts, its metric is comparable to $L^{-b/n}(|z|^{2\gamma -2}|\mathrm{d} z|^2+|z|^{2\gamma }|\mathrm{d} w|^2)$, and its distance to $E$ is of order $|z|^\gamma (\log (1/|z|))^{-b/(2n)}$. In particular, the metric is incomplete near $E$. If $D(s)\sim Cs^{-n}L^{-b}$, the local mass is finite precisely for $b>1$. In that range put $a=(b-1)/n$ and $K=(nC/(b-1))^{1/n}$. Then 28.34 \begin{equation} \label{eq:single-log-asymptotics} m\sim KL^{-a},\qquad m'\sim Ka s^{-1}L^{-a-1}. \end{equation} The potential has a finite limit at the origin, the solution has minimal singularities, and the distance is finite, each precisely when $b>n+1$; in that case $U(s)-U(0)\sim K L^{1-a}/(a-1)$. At $b=n+1$, $U$ diverges as $-K\log L$, and for $1<b<n+1$ as $-K L^{1-a}/(1-a)$. In these unbounded cases the solutions have full mass but not minimal singularities, and their metrics are complete near $E$. Their densities on the blowup lie in no $L^ p$ with $p>1$. If $D(s)\sim Cs^{-n}L^{-(n+1)}(\log L)^{-d}$ with $d\in \mathbb R$, put $C_*=C^{1/n}$. Then 28.35 \begin{equation} \label{eq:iterated-log-asymptotics} m\sim C_*L^{-1}(\log L)^{-d/n},\qquad m'\sim C_*s^{-1}L^{-2}(\log L)^{-d/n}. \end{equation} The potential is bounded precisely when $d>n$, with $U(s)-U(0)$ of order $(\log L)^{1-d/n}$. At $d=n$ it diverges as $-C_*\log \log L$, and for $d<n$ as $-C_*(\log L)^{1-d/n}/(1-d/n)$. The distance is finite precisely when $d>2n$, with remaining length of order $(\log L)^{1-d/(2n)}$. Thus for $n<d\leq 2n$ the residual is bounded and continuous but not Hölder, the solution has minimal singularities, and the metric is complete near $E$. All these critical densities have finite mass and lie in no $L^ p$ with $p>1$. In all cases the logarithmic coefficient of the solution along $E$ is $c$, whereas by proposition 14.22.1 a strict barrier can be chosen with coefficient $c+\delta $, for some $\delta >0$ independent of $\ell ,b,d$. Proof. We use the exact expressions ( 28.27 ). Each asymptotic formula follows by bounding $D$ between $(1\pm \epsilon )$ times its model and integrating the model; no derivative of an unspecified error term is taken. In the first case $m^ n\sim nC s^{\ell +1}L^{-b}/(\ell +1)$, which yields ( 28.33 ). Both Hessian eigenvalues are then comparable to $s^{\gamma -1}L^{-b/n}$, and the substitution of blowup coordinates gives the assertions about the metric and the distance. The positive power of $s$ makes the potential Hölder continuous, after the logarithmic factor is absorbed by a slightly smaller exponent. In the second case, $n\int _0^ s t^{-1}C(\log (1/t))^{-b}\, \mathrm{d} t$ is finite precisely for $b>1$, and it is then asymptotic to $nC L^{1-b}/(b-1)$. This gives ( 28.34 ). Since $\mathrm{d} U=-m\, \mathrm{d} L$, boundedness of $U$ is equivalent to convergence of $\int ^\infty L^{-a}\, \mathrm{d} L$, that is, to $a>1$. The distance is a constant multiple of $\int ^\infty L^{-(a+1)/2}\, \mathrm{d} L$ and has the same strict threshold. Explicit primitives give the stated finite and divergent behavior, including the logarithm at $a=1$. On the blowup the density is comparable to $|z|^{-2}(\log (1/|z|))^{-b}$; for every $p>1$, its $p$th power acquires an exponentially growing factor in logarithmic coordinates, so the density is not in $L^ p$. In the third case, $m^ n\sim C L^{-n}(\log L)^{-d}$. The criteria for the potential and for the distance become convergence of \[  \int ^\infty L^{-1}(\log L)^{-d/n}\, \mathrm{d} L \quad \text{and}\quad \int ^\infty L^{-1}(\log L)^{-d/(2n)}\, \mathrm{d} L,  \] respectively. Their thresholds are $d>n$ and $d>2n$, and direct integration gives the stated tails and divergent behavior. A bounded tail of order a positive power of $\log L$ tends to zero more slowly than every positive power of $|z|$, so the potential is not Hölder continuous. The mass integral is finite for every real $d$ because the principal factor is $L^{-(n+1)}$ with $n\geq 2$, and the same exponential argument excludes $L^ p$ for $p>1$. In particular, all the endpoint cases occur within the prescribed family of theorem 28.12.1 . $\square$

text: Theorem 28.12.2 . For the normalized family in theorem 28.12.1 , put $L=\log (1/s)$ for $0<s<1$. title: 28.13 Equations on products with a curve

text: 28.13 Equations on products with a curve On the product of a curve with a Hermitian manifold, a density depending only on the curve variable reduces the Monge–Ampère equation to a Poisson equation on the curve, even when the second factor is not Kähler. Explicit primitives then allow a comparison with the radial families. For a single logarithmic factor, boundedness of the potential and finiteness of the distance have the same threshold, whereas the iterated logarithmic family of theorem 28.12.2 separates them. Theorem 28.13.1 . Let $C$ be a compact Riemann surface with a positive $(1,1)$-form $\omega _ C$, let $(N,\omega _ N)$ be a compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $n-1$, and put $h=\omega _ C+\omega _ N$ on $C\times N$, the two forms being pulled back by the projections. Let $p_0\in C$, and let $F\geq 0$ be an integrable function on $C$, smooth and positive away from $p_0$, with $\int _ CF\omega _ C=\int _ C\omega _ C$. Then there is a function $v$ on $C$ such that $v\circ \operatorname {pr}_ C$ solves the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v\circ \operatorname {pr}_ C)=(F\circ \operatorname {pr}_ C)h^ n$, and the current of this solution has no divisorial component along $\{ p_0\} \times N$. Let $z$ be a coordinate centered at $p_0$, write $r=|z|$ and $\omega _ C=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )g(z)\, \mathrm{d} z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z$, and call a local potential of $\omega _ C+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ near $p_0$ a total normal potential . If $Fg=C_0r^{2\tau }$ near $p_0$, with $C_0>0$ and $\tau >-1$, then up to a smooth harmonic term the total normal potential is $C_0r^{2(\tau +1)}/(\tau +1)^2$. The solution is bounded and Hölder continuous, hence has minimal singularities, and the normal distance to $\{ p_0\} \times N$ is of order $r^{\tau +1}$. If $\tau =-a$ with $0<a<1$, the density is locally $L^ p$ exactly when $pa<1$. If $\tau $ is a nonnegative integer, the potential is smooth. If $Fg=C_0r^{-2}t^{-b}$ near $p_0$, with $t=\log (1/r)$, the mass is finite exactly for $b>1$. The total normal potential, which has no atom at $p_0$, is 28.36 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-log-primitive} P_ b(t)=\begin{cases}  \displaystyle \frac{4C_0t^{2-b}}{(b-1)(b-2)},& b\ne 2,\\[4pt] -4C_0\log t,& b=2, \end{cases} \end{equation} up to constants and smooth harmonic terms. It is bounded and continuous, equivalently the solution has minimal singularities, precisely when $b>2$, and it is then not Hölder continuous. The normal end has finite distance precisely when $b>2$. For $1<b\leq 2$ the end is complete, and the potential is unbounded and does not have minimal singularities, but it has zero Lelong number and trivial multiplier ideals. No density in this logarithmic family belongs to $L^ p$ for $p>1$. If $\omega _ C$ and $\omega _ N$ are Kähler, the unbounded solutions have full mass, and uniqueness in the closed theory excludes a different bounded solution for the same measure. A small strict logarithmic barrier along $\{ p_0\} \times N$ exists also when the solutions are bounded and have minimal singularities. Proof. On the curve, the real current $F\omega _ C-\omega _ C$ has integral zero and is therefore $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ for a global distribution $v$, unique up to a constant. Its quasi-subharmonic representative is smooth off $p_0$ by the local Poisson equation. Since $F\omega _ C$ has no atom at $p_0$, neither does the current $\omega _ C+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. Pull $v$ back to $C\times N$. Since every wedge product containing two factors from the curve vanishes, on the regular locus 28.39 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-product-equation} (h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=n(F\omega _ C)\wedge \omega _ N^{n-1} =(F\circ \operatorname {pr}_ C)h^ n. \end{equation} By theorem 6.1.2 , the extended product agrees with this smooth product off $\{ p_0\} \times N$ and gives that analytic set zero mass. The right side has the same property and finite mass. This proves the global equation, including the case in which the curve potential has a finite value at $p_0$ but is discontinuous there. For the power density, put $P_\tau (r)=C_0r^{2(\tau +1)}/(\tau +1)^2$. Direct differentiation gives $\partial _ z\bar\partial _ zP_\tau =C_0r^{2\tau }$, and the radial flux of $P_\tau $ through small circles vanishes as $r\downarrow 0$ when $\tau >-1$, so no Dirac term appears. The difference between the total potential and $P_\tau $ is therefore harmonic on the whole disk and smooth. To realize the model globally, cut off the local potential and solve the remaining smooth mean-zero equation on the curve. The normal line element of the metric is comparable to $r^\tau |\mathrm{d} r|$, which gives a distance of order $r^{\tau +1}$: a lower bound for all paths and an upper bound along a radial path. The $L^ p$ assertion is the convergence of $\int _0^\epsilon r^{1-2pa}\, \mathrm{d} r$. For the logarithmic density, $P_ b''(t)=4C_0t^{-b}$ and $\partial _ z\bar\partial _ zP_ b=P_ b''/(4r^2)=C_0r^{-2}t^{-b}$. The flux tends to zero for $b>1$, which excludes a logarithmic Dirac mass, and the same cutoff and smooth correction give a compact model. The mass of the density near $p_0$ is a constant multiple of $\int ^\infty t^{-b}\, \mathrm{d} t$, finite exactly for $b>1$, while the integral of its $p$th power, for $p>1$, diverges after the logarithmic change of variables. The primitive has a finite limit exactly for $b>2$, with tail of order $t^{2-b}$, which tends to zero more slowly than every power $r^\alpha $. The normal length is a constant multiple of $\int ^\infty t^{-b/2}\, \mathrm{d} t$, which has the same threshold. The projection to the curve bounds the length of every path from below by this normal integral, and a radial path with fixed point of $N$ attains it. For $1<b\leq 2$, $|P_ b(t)|/t\to 0$, so the Lelong number is zero. For every weight $k>0$, the integrand $\mathrm{e}^{-kP_ b}$ in polar coordinates is bounded by $\exp (-2t+o(t))$ with respect to $\mathrm{d}t$, which is integrable; hence all multiplier ideals are trivial. These properties do not imply bounded ordinary type. In a Kähler product, the normalized curve integral gives full non-pluripolar mass, and uniqueness of full-mass solutions in the closed theory, discussed in section 34.19 , excludes another bounded solution. A bounded competitor for the extended operator coincides globally with its deep truncations, so the same exclusion applies there. Finally, for $D=\{ p_0\} \times N$, a smooth metric on $\mathcal O(D)$ with curvature form $\Theta _ D$ and canonical section $s_ D$, and sufficiently small $\delta >0$, we have $h-\delta \Theta _ D>0$, so $\delta \log |s_ D|^2-C$ is a strict barrier. $\square$

title: 28.14 An incomplete metric in a big class

text:
28.14 An incomplete metric in a big class We now consider exponential Monge–Ampère equations whose reference measure has a nonintegrable pole along a divisor, and ask whether the solution defines a complete metric on the locus where its current is smooth and positive. A divisorial part of a solution with minimal singularities can cancel the pole and leave the deleted divisor at finite distance. On the blowup of the projective plane at a point, the resulting metric away from the exceptional divisor is the pullback of the Fubini–Study metric. The class is big but not nef, and the equation has a unique solution of finite energy. Finite energy refers to the classical closed theory of [ SGPT ] . For a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ with big class on a compact Kähler surface $Y$, and for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$ with minimal singularities, the Monge–Ampère energy relative to the envelope $V_	heta $ is \[  E_	heta (u)= rac13\sum _{j=0}^2 \int _ Y(u-V_	heta ) \left\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ j\wedge (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_	heta )^{2-j}ightangle .  \] For general $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$, $E_	heta (u)$ is the decreasing limit of $E_	heta (\max (u,V_	heta -k))$ as $k	o \infty $, and $\mathcal E^1(Y,	heta )$ is the set of potentials with $E_	heta (u)>-\infty $; they have full mass. Theorem 28.14.1 . There exist a smooth projective surface $Y$, a smooth irreducible divisor $E$, a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ with big class $\alpha $, a Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O_ Y(E)$, a defining section $\sigma $ of $\mathcal O_ Y(E)$, and a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ with the following properties. The equation 28.40  egin{equation} \label{eq:incomplete-divisorial-equation} \left\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^2ightangle =\mathrm{e}^{ho }|\sigma |^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \end{equation} has a unique solution $ho \in \mathcal E^1(Y,	heta )$, and this solution has minimal singularities. Moreover, \[  \operatorname {Amp}(\alpha )=Y\setminus E  \] is precisely the open set on which $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho $ is smooth and strictly positive. The restriction of this metric to every nonempty connected open subset of $Y\setminus E$ is incomplete. In particular, no dense Zariski open subset carries a complete induced metric. Let $p=[1:0:0]\in \mathbb P^2$, and let $\omega _2$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^2$, normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^2}\omega _2^2=1$. Proof of theorem 28.14.1 . The surface and the divisor. Use the incidence model \[  Y=\{ ([Z_0:Z_1:Z_2],[W_1:W_2])\in \mathbb P^2	imes \mathbb P^1: Z_1W_2=Z_2W_1\} .  \] The projections $\pi :Y	o \mathbb P^2$ and $q:Y	o \mathbb P^1$ identify $Y$ with the blowup of $\mathbb P^2$ at $p$, with exceptional divisor $E=\pi ^{-1}(p)$. Let $\omega _1$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^1$ with the same normalization as $\omega _2$, and write \[   eta =\pi ^*\omega _2,\qquad \gamma =q^*\omega _1, \qquad \Omega = eta +\gamma .  \] The form $\Omega $ is Kähler, being the restriction of a product Kähler metric. The linear map $(Z_0,Z_1,Z_2)\mapsto (Z_1,Z_2)$ defines a section $\sigma $ of \[  \pi ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)\otimes q^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1),  \] because on $Y$ the vector $(Z_1,Z_2)$ lies in the tautological line $[W_1:W_2]$. The section vanishes simply along $E$, which identifies this line bundle with $\mathcal O_ Y(E)$. For the product of the Fubini–Study metric and the metric induced on the tautological bundle, its squared norm is \[  s=|\sigma |^2=  rac{|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2}.  \] In a blowup chart $\pi (t,w)=(t,tw)$, $q(t,w)=[1:w]$, one has 28.41  egin{equation} \label{eq:incomplete-divisor-norm} s= rac{|t|^2(1+|w|^2)}{1+|t|^2(1+|w|^2)}, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log s=[E]+\gamma - eta . \end{equation} The current identity follows either from this formula and the second blowup chart or from the Poincaré–Lelong formula. The big class and its equation. Set 28.42  egin{equation} \label{eq:incomplete-current} 	heta =3 eta -2\gamma ,\qquad ho =2\log s, \qquad T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho = eta +2[E]. \end{equation} Thus $ho \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$. The class $\alpha =\{ 	heta \} $ is big, because the potential $\psi =(5/2)\log s$ satisfies 28.43  egin{equation} \label{eq:incomplete-strict-current} 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =	frac 12( eta +\gamma )+	frac 52[E]\geq 	frac 12\Omega . \end{equation} It is not nef, since $\int _ E	heta =-2$: the restriction of $ eta $ to $E$ vanishes and $q|_ E$ is an isomorphism onto $\mathbb P^1$. A nef class has nonnegative degree on every curve, by its defining smooth approximations. On $Y\setminus E$ define $\mathrm{d}V_ Y= eta ^2/s$. To check that it extends across $E$, put \[  \mathrm{d}\lambda _{t,w} =	frac {\mathrm{i}}2\mathrm{d}t\wedge \mathrm{d} ar t \wedge 	frac {\mathrm{i}}2\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm{d} ar w,  \] and let $\mathrm{d}\lambda _{z_1,z_2}$ be the analogous Euclidean volume in affine coordinates of $\mathbb P^2$. The normalized Fubini–Study volume is \[  \omega _2^2= rac{2}{\pi ^2}  rac{\mathrm{d}\lambda _{z_1,z_2}}{(1+|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2)^3}.  \] Since the complex Jacobian determinant of $(t,w)\mapsto (t,tw)$ is $t$, we obtain  egin{align*}   eta ^2& = rac{2}{\pi ^2}  rac{|t|^2\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _{t,w}}{[1+|t|^2(1+|w|^2)]^3},\  \mathrm{d}V_ Y& = rac{2}{\pi ^2}  rac{\mathrm{d}\lambda _{t,w}}{(1+|w|^2)[1+|t|^2(1+|w|^2)]^2}. \end{align*} The second expression is smooth and strictly positive at $t=0$. Interchanging the two homogeneous coordinates gives the extension on the other chart. The two extensions agree off $E$, hence everywhere on their overlap. The non-pluripolar product of $T$ agrees with $ eta ^2$ off $E$ and gives no mass to $E$. The smooth measure $ eta ^2$ also gives no mass to $E$, so \[  \langle T^2angle = eta ^2, \qquad \mathrm{e}^{ho }|\sigma |^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y =s^2s^{-1} rac{ eta ^2}{s}= eta ^2.  \] The right side of ( 28.40 ) is defined on $Y\setminus E$ and extended by zero on $E$, so no product of zero and infinity occurs. This proves the equation and gives $\int _ Y\langle T^2angle =\int _{\mathbb P^2}\omega _2^2=1$. Minimal singularities and energy. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$. Since \[   eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-ho )=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0 \quad 	ext{on }Y\setminus E,  \] the function $u-ho $ on $Y\setminus E$ descends to an $\omega _2$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^2\setminus \{ p\} $. By lemma 1.3.8 , it is bounded above, so $u\leq ho +C_ u$ there. This inequality holds almost everywhere on $Y$, and lemma 1.3.3 makes it hold everywhere. In particular $u=-\infty $ on $E$, and $ho $ has minimal singularities. Let $V_	heta $ be the normalized envelope of section 1.19 . Since $s\leq 1$, we have $ho \leq 0$, and minimality gives \[  ho \leq V_	heta \leq ho +C.  \] Thus $ho -V_	heta $ is bounded off $E$, and the energy is \[  E_	heta (ho )= rac13\sum _{j=0}^2 \int _ Y(ho -V_	heta ) \left\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ j\wedge (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_	heta )^{2-j}ightangle .  \] The mixed measures have finite mass in the closed Kähler theory and do not charge $E$. Therefore $u=ho $ almost everywhere on $Y\setminus E$ with respect to a smooth volume form, hence almost everywhere on $Y$, since $E$ has zero volume. By lemma 1.3.3 , $u=ho $ everywhere. The ample locus and incompleteness. The Kähler current in ( 28.43 ) is smooth off $E$. On the other hand, every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$ satisfies $u\leq ho +C_ u$, so its Lelong numbers at points of $E$ are at least those of $ho =2\log s$, which are positive. Thus every Kähler current in $\alpha $ is singular at every point of $E$, and theorem 28.3.2 gives \[  \operatorname {Amp}(\alpha )=Y\setminus E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha ) =Y\setminus E.  \] The current $T$ equals $ eta $ there, and it is strictly positive because $\pi $ is a biholomorphism away from $E$. Its nonzero divisorial part $2[E]$ prevents smoothness at every point of $E$. Let $U\subset Y\setminus E$ be a nonempty connected open set, and set $W=\pi (U)$. The map $\pi :(U,T|_ U)	o (W,\omega _2|_ W)$ is an isometry. Choose $x\in W$ and a smooth path $c:[0,1]	o \mathbb P^2$ from $x$ to $p$. Its first exit time \[  t_0=\min \{ t\in [0,1]:c(t)
otin W\}   \] is positive, and $c([0,t_0))\subset W$. The path has finite Fubini–Study length. For $t_ k
earrow t_0$, the lengths of its tails show that $c(t_ k)$ is a Cauchy sequence for the intrinsic metric of $W$. It has no limit in $W$: intrinsic convergence implies ambient convergence, and the ambient limit is $c(t_0)
otin W$. Thus $U$ is incomplete. Applying this argument to each connected component proves the assertion for a dense Zariski open set, which may be disconnected. $\square$ The cancellation $\mathrm{e}^{ho }|\sigma |^{-2}=s$ removes the pole, and the divisor $E$, which the metric collapses to the point $p$, stays at finite distance. Thus an exponential equation in a big class can have an incomplete metric even when its finite-energy solution is unique and has minimal singularities. In this example the class is not nef. Theorem 28.14.1 . There exist a smooth projective surface $Y$, a smooth irreducible divisor $E$, a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ with big class $\alpha $, a Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O_ Y(E)$, a defining section $\sigma $ of $\mathcal O_ Y(E)$, and a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ with the following properties. This measure is smooth and positive off $E$, but has infinite total mass. The classical comparison principle for full-mass potentials in the closed theory gives \[  \int _{\{ u<ho \} }\mathrm{e}^{ho }\, \mathrm{d}\mu \leq \int _{\{ u<ho \} }\mathrm{e}^{u}\, \mathrm{d}\mu .  \] Both integrals are finite, since the two Monge–Ampère measures have mass $1$. The integrand on the left is strictly larger, which forces $\mu (\{ u<ho \} )=0$. Interchanging $u$ and $ho $ gives $\mu (\{ ho <u\} )=0$ as well. Therefore $u=ho $ almost everywhere on $Y\setminus E$ with respect to a smooth volume form, hence almost everywhere on $Y$, since $E$ has zero volume. By lemma 1.3.3 , $u=ho $ everywhere. On the other hand, every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$ satisfies $u\leq ho +C_ u$, so its Lelong numbers at points of $E$ are at least those of $ho =2\log s$, which are positive. Thus every Kähler current in $\alpha $ is singular at every point of $E$, and theorem 28.3.2 gives \[  \operatorname {Amp}(\alpha )=Y\setminus E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha ) =Y\setminus E.  \] The current $T$ equals $ eta $ there, and it is strictly positive because $\pi $ is a biholomorphism away from $E$. Its nonzero divisorial part $2[E]$ prevents smoothness at every point of $E$. Let $U\subset Y\setminus E$ be a nonempty connected open set, and set $W=\pi (U)$. otin W\}   \] is positive, and $c([0,t_0))\subset W$. The path has finite Fubini–Study length. For $t_ k

otin W$. Thus $U$ is incomplete. Applying this argument to each connected component proves the assertion for a dense Zariski open set, which may be disconnected. $\square$

title: 28.14.1 A nef class with an incomplete null end

text: 28.14.1 A nef class with an incomplete null end Nefness of the class does not prevent incompleteness. In the next construction, the pole of the measure along a divisor $D$ does produce a complete cusp, but a disjoint curve $E$, on which the class has degree zero, lies at finite distance. Theorem 28.14.2 . There are a smooth projective surface $Y$, disjoint smooth divisors $E,D$, a smooth closed semipositive form $\theta $ with nef and big class, a smooth Hermitian norm on $\mathcal O_ Y(D)$, its defining section $\sigma $, and a smooth strictly positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$, such that the equation 28.44 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-incomplete-cusp-equation} \left\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^2\right\rangle =\mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma |^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \end{equation} has a unique solution $\rho \in \mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$. The solution has zero Lelong numbers and is smooth on $Y\setminus (E\cup D)$, where its current $\Omega =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ is strictly positive. The curve $E$ lies in the null locus of $\{ \theta \} $. Every dense Zariski open set on which $\Omega $ is smooth and strictly positive is incomplete, although every path in $Y\setminus (E\cup D)$ approaching $D$ has infinite length. The measure $|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has a nonintegrable pole along $D$ with smooth strictly positive coefficient. The solution is unbounded near $D$ and therefore does not have minimal singularities: since $\theta $ is semipositive, the envelope $V_\theta $ is zero. The theorem concerns nefness and bigness only; the additional compatibility identities of the geometric smoothing problem in section 28.14.2 are a separate question. The solution will be a radial function on $\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $, identified with $Y\setminus (E\cup D)$. Its current is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(\log |z|^2)$ for a convex function $F$ whose derivative increases from $0$ at $E$ to $1$ at $D$, and the volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ is defined from $F$. The following lemma constructs the profile $F$; its two end identities make the volume form smooth and positive across $E$ and $D$. Lemma 28.14.3 . There is $F\in C^\infty (\mathbb R)$ with $0<p:=F'<1$ and $p'>0$ such that, for $c=1/100$, some $B\in \mathbb R$ and $K=(9c^2/8)\mathrm{e}^{-B}>0$, 28.45 \begin{align}  F(t)& =B-3\log (1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}),&  pp'& =K\mathrm{e}^{F+t} & & (t\leq -2),\label{eq:nef-cusp-left-profile}\\  F(t)& =t+\log H(p(t)),&  pp'& =\mathrm{e}^{F-t} & & (t\geq 2),\label{eq:nef-cusp-right-profile} \end{align} where $H(p)=(1-p)^2(1+2p)/6$. At the two ends, \begin{align*}  F(t)& =B+3c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}+O(\mathrm{e}^ t),&  p'(t)& \sim (3c/4)\mathrm{e}^{t/2} & & (t\to -\infty ),\\  1-p(t)& \sim 2/t,& p'(t)& \sim 2/t^2 & & (t\to +\infty ), \end{align*} and $F(t)-t=-2\log t+\log 2+o(1)$ as $t\to +\infty $. Proof. For $t\leq -2$ put $L(t)=-3\log (1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2})$. With $q=c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}$, \[  p_ L=L'=\frac{3q}{2(1-q)},\qquad p_ L'=\frac{3q}{4(1-q)^2},\qquad p_ Lp_ L'=\frac{9c^2}{8}\mathrm{e}^{t}(1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2})^{-3}.  \] This proves the left identity for every additive constant $B$. Since $H'(p)=(p-1)p$, the increasing function \[  \mathcal T(p)=2+\int _{3/4}^{p}\frac{q}{H(q)}\, \mathrm{d}q  \] tends to $+\infty $ as $p\to 1$, because its integrand is asymptotic to $2/(1-p)^2$ there. Hence it has an inverse $p_ R(t)$, defined for $t\geq 2$ and on a neighborhood of $2$, with $p_ R(2)=3/4$ and $p_ R'=H(p_ R)/p_ R$. The function $F_ R=t+\log H(p_ R)$ has derivative $p_ R$ and satisfies the right identity. For $q=1-p_ R$, \[  (1/q)'=\frac{3-2q}{6(1-q)}\longrightarrow \frac12.  \] Hence $q\sim 2/t$ and $H(p_ R)\sim 2/t^2$, and the asymptotics at the right end follow. It remains to interpolate the derivatives. Set $d=p_ R(2)-p_ L(-2)>0$. Choose disjoint short collars in $[-2,2]$ at the two endpoints, and cutoffs $\alpha _ L,\alpha _ R$ equal to one on smaller collars. For small $\varepsilon >0$, the function \[  Q_0=\alpha _ Lp_ L'+\alpha _ Rp_ R' +\varepsilon (1-\alpha _ L-\alpha _ R)  \] is positive and agrees with the derivative germs at the endpoints. The collars and $\varepsilon $ can be chosen so that $\int _{-2}^2Q_0<d$. Adding a nonnegative smooth bump in the interior, with integral $d-\int _{-2}^2Q_0$, gives a positive function $Q$, and we put \[  p(t)=p_ L(-2)+\int _{-2}^ tQ(x)\, \mathrm{d}x.  \] This function matches both endpoint germs, is increasing and takes values in $(0,1)$. Integrating $F'=p$ with $F(2)=F_ R(2)$ gives the required $F$ and fixes the constant $B$ at the left end. The left expansion follows directly. $\square$ Proof of theorem 28.14.2 . The background and the pole. Use the incidence surface of theorem 28.14.1 , with blowup map $\pi :Y\to \mathbb P^2$ and exceptional curve $E$ over $[1:0:0]$, and let $\beta ,\gamma $ be the pulled-back Fubini–Study forms as there. Put $D=\pi ^{-1}(Z_0=0)$ and $A=\pi ^*c_1(\mathcal O(1))$. Then $E\cap D=\varnothing $, $A^2=1$ and $A\cdot E=0$. The class $A$ is nef, since it has the smooth semipositive representative $\beta $. Moreover $\{ \gamma \} =A-[E]$, and $\beta +\varepsilon \gamma $ is Kähler for $\varepsilon >0$. Thus \[  \frac{\beta +\varepsilon \gamma }{1+\varepsilon } +\frac{\varepsilon }{1+\varepsilon }[E]  \] is a Kähler current in $A$, which proves bigness. Choose an even nonnegative smooth function $\zeta $, supported in $[-1,1]$, positive on its interior and of integral one. The smooth convex function \[  U(t)=\int _\mathbb R\max (0,t-x)\zeta (x)\, \mathrm{d}x  \] satisfies $U=0$ for $t\leq -1$, $U=t$ for $t\geq 1$, and $U',U''\geq 0$. On $Z_0\ne 0$, write $z=(Z_1/Z_0,Z_2/Z_0)$, $s=|z|^2$ and $t=\log s$, and give the section $Z_0$ of $\mathcal O(1)$ the squared norm $\mathrm{e}^{-U(t)}$; this norm is constant near the affine origin. Near the line at infinity, use \[  w=Z_0/Z_1,\qquad v=Z_2/Z_1,\qquad h=1+|v|^2, \qquad s=h/|w|^2.  \] The section $Z_1$ then has squared norm $\mathrm{e}^{-U}/|w|^2=1/h$ near $w=0$. These formulas define a smooth Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O(1)$. Pull it back to $\mathcal O_ Y(D)$ and let $\sigma =\pi ^*Z_0$. Its curvature form $\theta $ and the norm of $\sigma $ are \[  \theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U(t),\quad |\sigma |^2=\mathrm{e}^{-U(t)},\qquad \theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h,\quad |\sigma |^2=|w|^2/h\quad \hbox{near }D.  \] The radial Hessian shows that $\theta $ is semipositive. It vanishes near $E$ and has rank one near $D$. In particular $V_\theta =0$, and the nef class has volume $A^2=1$. Extension of the potential. On $Y\setminus (E\cup D)\simeq \mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $, set \[  \rho =F(t)-U(t),\qquad \Omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(t),  \] so that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho =\Omega $. The eigenvalues of the Hermitian matrix of $\Omega $ are $p/s$ and $p'/s$, which are positive. Extend $\rho $ to $E$ by $B$ and to $D$ by $-\infty $. Near the affine origin, the smooth functions $F(\log (|z|^2+\varepsilon ))$ are plurisubharmonic and decrease to the continuous extension of $F(\log |z|^2)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Indeed, their two Hessian eigenvalues are $p/(s+\varepsilon )$ and $(s p'+\varepsilon p)/(s+\varepsilon )^2$, with $p,p'$ evaluated at $\log (s+\varepsilon )$. Since $\theta =0$ there, pulling back to $Y$ proves positivity near $E$. Near $D$ put $t_\varepsilon =\log h-\log (|w|^2+\varepsilon )$ and $g(t)=F(t)-t$. The local potentials $g(t_\varepsilon )+\log h$ decrease to $\rho +\log h$, and their Hessians are \[  p(t_\varepsilon )\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h +(1-p(t_\varepsilon ))\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (|w|^2+\varepsilon ) +p'(t_\varepsilon )\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi } \partial t_\varepsilon \wedge \bar\partial t_\varepsilon \geq 0.  \] Thus $\rho $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic on $Y$. Since $\rho $ is bounded near $E$ and grows like a double logarithm near $D$, all its Lelong numbers vanish. The volume form and full mass. With Euclidean area $\mathrm{d}A$ in each complex variable, the radial determinant is 28.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-cusp-radial-determinant} \Omega ^2=\frac{2}{\pi ^2}\frac{pp'}{s^2} \mathrm{d}A_{z_1}\mathrm{d}A_{z_2}. \end{equation} Define $\mathrm{d}V_ Y=\mathrm{e}^{-F}\Omega ^2$ off the two divisors. In an exceptional chart $z=(u,uv)$, the real Jacobian is $|u|^2$ and $s=|u|^2h$, so the left profile identity gives \[  \mathrm{d}V_ Y=\frac{2K}{\pi ^2h}\, \mathrm{d}A_ u\mathrm{d}A_ v.  \] At infinity, the map $z=(1/w,v/w)$ has real Jacobian $|w|^{-6}$, and the right profile identity gives \[  \mathrm{d}V_ Y=\frac{2}{\pi ^2h^3}\, \mathrm{d}A_ w\mathrm{d}A_ v, \qquad |\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y =\frac{2}{\pi ^2|w|^2h^2}\, \mathrm{d}A_ w\mathrm{d}A_ v.  \] The analogous second charts cover each divisor. The extensions are smooth and strictly positive, and they agree on overlaps because they agree on the punctured overlaps. The last expression exhibits the nonintegrable pole with smooth positive coefficient. On the complement of the two divisors, $\mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y=\Omega ^2$; we extend this density by zero on $D$. Both measures give zero mass to the two divisors. In polar coordinates on $\mathbb C^2$, the Euclidean volume is $\pi ^2s\, \mathrm{d}s$ times the normalized angular measure, so \[  \int _ Y\langle \Omega ^2\rangle =\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }2pp'\, \mathrm{d}t =p(+\infty )^2-p(-\infty )^2=1.  \] This proves the global equation and shows that $\rho $ has full mass. Bounded truncations and energy. Near $D$ write $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h$ and $\beta _ t=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )\partial t\wedge \bar\partial t$. These forms have rank one, and \[  \theta =\alpha ,\quad \Omega =p\alpha +p'\beta _ t,\quad \Omega ^2=2pp'\alpha \wedge \beta _ t,\quad \Omega \wedge \theta =p'\alpha \wedge \beta _ t,\quad \theta ^2=0.  \] Integration of $\alpha \wedge \beta _ t$ over the angular and projective variables gives $\mathrm{d}t$. Since $|\rho |=O(\log t)$ and $p'=O(t^{-2})$, the integrals of $|\rho |$ against $\Omega ^2$ and $\Omega \wedge \theta $ near $D$ are finite. Near $E$ the potential is bounded and $\theta =0$, and the remaining region is compact with smooth data. Choose $M$ so that $\phi =\rho -M\leq 0$, and set $\phi _ k=\max (\phi ,-k)$. For large $k$ the truncation changes $\phi $ only in the cusp near $D$, where $\phi =\log H(p(t))-M$ is strictly decreasing. If $\phi (T_ k)=-k$, then $k=2\log T_ k+O(1)$. On $\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $, the radial local potential of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ k$ is \[  G_ k(t)=\max (F(t)-M,t-k).  \] Near $D$, in the frame used above, the local potential of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ k$ is $G_ k(t)+\log |w|^2$, which equals the smooth function $\log h-k$; the term $\log |w|^2$ cancels the divisorial part of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ k(t)$. At $t=T_ k$, the derivative of $G_ k$ jumps upward from $p(T_ k)$ to $1$. Convolving $G_ k$ in $t$ with an even nonnegative smooth kernel gives convex functions decreasing to $G_ k$ as the scale decreases. The corresponding bounded local potentials converge uniformly on compact sets, so their Bedford–Taylor products converge. Integrating the smooth radial measures through the transition shows that the transition carries mass $1-p(T_ k)^2$ for $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ k)^2$ and mass $1-p(T_ k)$ for $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ k)\wedge \theta $. Beyond the transition, $G_ k$ is linear and both top-degree measures vanish. Since $\phi _ k=-k$ on the transition, its energy contributions have absolute values $k(1-p(T_ k)^2)$ and $k(1-p(T_ k))$, and both tend to zero because $1-p(T_ k)\sim 2/T_ k$. The contributions of the remaining region converge absolutely by the bounds above. At $E$, bounded potentials give no mass to the curve, in accordance with the vanishing radial boundary mass $p(-\infty )^2=0$. Consequently \[  E_\theta (\phi _ k)=\frac13\sum _{j=0}^2 \int _ Y\phi _ k(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ k)^ j\wedge \theta ^{2-j}  \] has a finite limit, and in particular is bounded below. This proves $\rho \in \mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$. Uniqueness follows from the full-mass comparison argument in the proof of theorem 28.14.1 , now with $\mathrm{d}\mu =|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ off $D$, extended by zero on $D$. Its total mass is infinite, but each exponential density $\mathrm{e}^{\rho }\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ and $\mathrm{e}^{u}\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ is a finite measure of mass $1$. Comparison on the two strict sublevel sets forces equality almost everywhere, and lemma 1.3.3 gives equality of the potentials everywhere. The two metric ends. Fix $v=v_0$ in an exceptional chart and write $h_0=1+|v_0|^2$. The restriction of $\Omega $ to the normal line $\{ v=v_0\} $ is \[  \Omega |_{v=v_0}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi } \frac{p'(\log (|u|^2h_0))}{|u|^2} \, \mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar u.  \] Its coefficient is asymptotic to $(3c\sqrt{h_0}/4)|u|^{-1}$, so the current has no smooth extension at any point of $E$. The radial path $u=r>0$ has finite remaining length, bounded by $C\int _0^{r_0}r^{-1/2}\, \mathrm{d}r$. At $D$ the normal coefficient is asymptotic to $2/(|w|^2t^2)$ and also diverges. Thus every open set on which $\Omega $ is smooth and strictly positive misses both curves. Let $W$ be a dense Zariski open set on which $\Omega $ is smooth and strictly positive. Its complement $Y\setminus W$ is a proper analytic set containing $E$, and by local finiteness of irreducible components and compactness it has finitely many components, which are curves or points. Each curve other than $E$ meets $E$ in finitely many points. Choose a point of $E$ that avoids all these intersections and all point components. In a sufficiently small chart around it, the complement of $W$ is exactly $E$, so a tail of the radial path above lies in $W$. Its points approaching $E$ form a Cauchy sequence for the intrinsic metric with no limit in $W$: the smooth positive metric induces the manifold topology of $W$, and the only ambient limit is the removed point. Hence $W$ is incomplete. Finally, on the cusp $\Omega =p\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t+p'\, \mathrm{d}t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$, both terms are nonnegative, and $p'\geq c_0/t^2$ for large $t$ and some $c_0>0$. The length of any path with $t\to \infty $ is therefore bounded below by a positive multiple of $\int |\mathrm{d}t|/t$, which diverges. Thus the end at finite distance is the null curve $E$, disjoint from the pole. $\square$

title: Theorem 28.14.2
text: Theorem 28.14.2 . There are a smooth projective surface $Y$, disjoint smooth divisors $E,D$, a smooth closed semipositive form $\theta $ with nef and big class, a smooth Hermitian norm on $\mathcal O_ Y(D)$, its defining section $\sigma $, and a smooth strictly positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$, such that the equation 28.44 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nef-incomplete-cusp-equation} \left\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^2\right\rangle =\mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma |^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \end{equation} has a unique solution $\rho \in \mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$. The solution has zero Lelong numbers and is smooth on $Y\setminus (E\cup D)$, where its current $\Omega =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ is strictly positive. The curve $E$ lies in the null locus of $\{ \theta \} $. Put $D=\pi ^{-1}(Z_0=0)$ and $A=\pi ^*c_1(\mathcal O(1))$. Then $E\cap D=\varnothing $, $A^2=1$ and $A\cdot E=0$. The class $A$ is nef, since it has the smooth semipositive representative $\beta $. Moreover $\{ \gamma \} =A-[E]$, and $\beta +\varepsilon \gamma $ is Kähler for $\varepsilon >0$. Thus \[  \frac{\beta +\varepsilon \gamma }{1+\varepsilon } +\frac{\varepsilon }{1+\varepsilon }[E]  \] is a Kähler current in $A$, which proves bigness. Choose an even nonnegative smooth function $\zeta $, supported in $[-1,1]$, positive on its interior and of integral one. The smooth convex function \[  U(t)=\int _\mathbb R\max (0,t-x)\zeta (x)\, \mathrm{d}x  \] satisfies $U=0$ for $t\leq -1$, $U=t$ for $t\geq 1$, and $U',U''\geq 0$. On $Y\setminus (E\cup D)\simeq \mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $, set \[  \rho =F(t)-U(t),\qquad \Omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(t),  \] so that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho =\Omega $. The eigenvalues of the Hermitian matrix of $\Omega $ are $p/s$ and $p'/s$, which are positive. Extend $\rho $ to $E$ by $B$ and to $D$ by $-\infty $. Near the affine origin, the smooth functions $F(\log (|z|^2+\varepsilon ))$ are plurisubharmonic and decrease to the continuous extension of $F(\log |z|^2)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Since $\theta =0$ there, pulling back to $Y$ proves positivity near $E$. Near $D$ put $t_\varepsilon =\log h-\log (|w|^2+\varepsilon )$ and $g(t)=F(t)-t$. The extensions are smooth and strictly positive, and they agree on overlaps because they agree on the punctured overlaps. On the complement of the two divisors, $\mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y=\Omega ^2$; we extend this density by zero on $D$. Both measures give zero mass to the two divisors. In polar coordinates on $\mathbb C^2$, the Euclidean volume is $\pi ^2s\, \mathrm{d}s$ times the normalized angular measure, so \[  \int _ Y\langle \Omega ^2\rangle =\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }2pp'\, \mathrm{d}t =p(+\infty )^2-p(-\infty )^2=1.  \] This proves the global equation and shows that $\rho $ has full mass. Near $E$ the potential is bounded and $\theta =0$, and the remaining region is compact with smooth data. Choose $M$ so that $\phi =\rho -M\leq 0$, and set $\phi _ k=\max (\phi ,-k)$. At $E$, bounded potentials give no mass to the curve, in accordance with the vanishing radial boundary mass $p(-\infty )^2=0$. Consequently \[  E_\theta (\phi _ k)=\frac13\sum _{j=0}^2 \int _ Y\phi _ k(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ k)^ j\wedge \theta ^{2-j}  \] has a finite limit, and in particular is bounded below. This proves $\rho \in \mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$. Uniqueness follows from the full-mass comparison argument in the proof of theorem 28.14.1 , now with $\mathrm{d}\mu =|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ off $D$, extended by zero on $D$. Its total mass is infinite, but each exponential density $\mathrm{e}^{\rho }\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ and $\mathrm{e}^{u}\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ is a finite measure of mass $1$. Comparison on the two strict sublevel sets forces equality almost everywhere, and lemma 1.3.3 gives equality of the potentials everywhere. The two metric ends. Fix $v=v_0$ in an exceptional chart and write $h_0=1+|v_0|^2$. The restriction of $\Omega $ to the normal line $\{ v=v_0\} $ is \[  \Omega |_{v=v_0}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi } \frac{p'(\log (|u|^2h_0))}{|u|^2} \, \mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar u.  \] Its coefficient is asymptotic to $(3c\sqrt{h_0}/4)|u|^{-1}$, so the current has no smooth extension at any point of $E$. The radial path $u=r>0$ has finite remaining length, bounded by $C\int _0^{r_0}r^{-1/2}\, \mathrm{d}r$. At $D$ the normal coefficient is asymptotic to $2/(|w|^2t^2)$ and also diverges. Thus every open set on which $\Omega $ is smooth and strictly positive misses both curves. Let $W$ be a dense Zariski open set on which $\Omega $ is smooth and strictly positive. Its complement $Y\setminus W$ is a proper analytic set containing $E$, and by local finiteness of irreducible components and compactness it has finitely many components, which are curves or points. Each curve other than $E$ meets $E$ in finitely many points. Choose a point of $E$ that avoids all these intersections and all point components. In a sufficiently small chart around it, the complement of $W$ is exactly $E$, so a tail of the radial path above lies in $W$. Its points approaching $E$ form a Cauchy sequence for the intrinsic metric with no limit in $W$: the smooth positive metric induces the manifold topology of $W$, and the only ambient limit is the removed point. Finally, on the cusp $\Omega =p\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t+p'\, \mathrm{d}t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$, both terms are nonnegative, and $p'\geq c_0/t^2$ for large $t$ and some $c_0>0$. The length of any path with $t\to \infty $ is therefore bounded below by a positive multiple of $\int |\mathrm{d}t|/t$, which diverges. title: Lemma 28.14.3
text: Lemma 28.14.3 . There is $F\in C^\infty (\mathbb R)$ with $0<p:=F'<1$ and $p'>0$ such that, for $c=1/100$, some $B\in \mathbb R$ and $K=(9c^2/8)\mathrm{e}^{-B}>0$, 28.45 \begin{align}  F(t)& =B-3\log (1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}),&  pp'& =K\mathrm{e}^{F+t} & & (t\leq -2),\label{eq:nef-cusp-left-profile}\\  F(t)& =t+\log H(p(t)),&  pp'& =\mathrm{e}^{F-t} & & (t\geq 2),\label{eq:nef-cusp-right-profile} \end{align} where $H(p)=(1-p)^2(1+2p)/6$. At the two ends, \begin{align*}  F(t)& =B+3c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}+O(\mathrm{e}^ t),&  p'(t)& \sim (3c/4)\mathrm{e}^{t/2} & & (t\to -\infty ),\\  1-p(t)& \sim 2/t,& p'(t)& \sim 2/t^2 & & (t\to +\infty ), \end{align*} and $F(t)-t=-2\log t+\log 2+o(1)$ as $t\to +\infty $. Proof. For $t\leq -2$ put $L(t)=-3\log (1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2})$. With $q=c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}$, \[  p_ L=L'=\frac{3q}{2(1-q)},\qquad p_ L'=\frac{3q}{4(1-q)^2},\qquad p_ Lp_ L'=\frac{9c^2}{8}\mathrm{e}^{t}(1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2})^{-3}.  \] This proves the left identity for every additive constant $B$. Since $H'(p)=(p-1)p$, the increasing function \[  \mathcal T(p)=2+\int _{3/4}^{p}\frac{q}{H(q)}\, \mathrm{d}q  \] tends to $+\infty $ as $p\to 1$, because its integrand is asymptotic to $2/(1-p)^2$ there. Hence it has an inverse $p_ R(t)$, defined for $t\geq 2$ and on a neighborhood of $2$, with $p_ R(2)=3/4$ and $p_ R'=H(p_ R)/p_ R$. The function $F_ R=t+\log H(p_ R)$ has derivative $p_ R$ and satisfies the right identity. For $q=1-p_ R$, \[  (1/q)'=\frac{3-2q}{6(1-q)}\longrightarrow \frac12.  \] Hence $q\sim 2/t$ and $H(p_ R)\sim 2/t^2$, and the asymptotics at the right end follow. It remains to interpolate the derivatives. Set $d=p_ R(2)-p_ L(-2)>0$. Choose disjoint short collars in $[-2,2]$ at the two endpoints, and cutoffs $\alpha _ L,\alpha _ R$ equal to one on smaller collars. For small $\varepsilon >0$, the function \[  Q_0=\alpha _ Lp_ L'+\alpha _ Rp_ R' +\varepsilon (1-\alpha _ L-\alpha _ R)  \] is positive and agrees with the derivative germs at the endpoints. The collars and $\varepsilon $ can be chosen so that $\int _{-2}^2Q_0<d$. Adding a nonnegative smooth bump in the interior, with integral $d-\int _{-2}^2Q_0$, gives a positive function $Q$, and we put \[  p(t)=p_ L(-2)+\int _{-2}^ tQ(x)\, \mathrm{d}x.  \] This function matches both endpoint germs, is increasing and takes values in $(0,1)$. Integrating $F'=p$ with $F(2)=F_ R(2)$ gives the required $F$ and fixes the constant $B$ at the left end. The left expansion follows directly. $\square$

title: 28.14.2 An incomplete metric with compatible flow data
search_title: An incomplete metric with compatible flow data
text: 28.14.2 An incomplete metric with compatible flow data Exponential equations of this kind arise as auxiliary elliptic equations in the smoothing of singular initial data by geometric flows; the completeness question for them is discussed in section 34.17 . In that setting the class, the divisor and the volume form are not arbitrary: they are determined by the initial potential through a log resolution. The following example shows that incompleteness persists under these compatibility conditions. Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\phi _0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ an initial potential with analytic singularities. Compatible data on a log resolution $\pi :Y\to X$ satisfy 28.48 \begin{gather}  \pi ^*\phi _0=\sum _ jm_ j\log |\sigma _ j|^2+\ell _0,\qquad \pi ^*(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _0)=\sum _ jm_ j[D_ j]+R_0, \label{eq:compatible-initial-resolution}\\  K_ Y=\pi ^*K_ X+\sum _ jb_ jD_ j,\qquad \pi ^*\mathrm{d}V_ X=\prod _ j|\sigma _ j|^{2b_ j}\mathrm{d}V_ Y. \label{eq:compatible-volume-resolution} \end{gather} Here $D=\sum _ jD_ j$ is a divisor with simple normal crossings, $\sigma _ j$ is a defining section of $\mathcal O_ Y(D_ j)$ with a smooth Hermitian metric, the numbers $m_ j$ and $b_ j$ are the coefficients of the pulled-back singularity and of the relative canonical divisor, $\ell _0$ is smooth, $R_0$ is a smooth closed semipositive form, and $\mathrm{d}V_ X$, $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ are smooth positive volume forms. If $\Theta _ j$ denotes the curvature form of the metric on $\mathcal O_ Y(D_ j)$, put \[  \lambda =\max _ j\frac{m_ j}{1+b_ j},\qquad \Theta =\sum _ j(1+b_ j)\Theta _ j,\qquad \theta =\lambda \Theta +R_0,\qquad |\sigma |^2=\prod _ j|\sigma _ j|^2.  \] The number $\lambda $ is the inverse of the exponential integrability index of $\phi _0$: by ( 28.48 ) and ( 28.49 ), $\mathrm{e}^{-q\phi _0}$ is integrable exactly when $q\lambda <1$. The metric in the next theorem is the solution of the auxiliary elliptic equation ( 28.50 ) in this background. Theorem 28.14.4 . There are compatible data ( 28.48 )–( 28.49 ) on smooth projective surfaces, with $\mathrm{d}V_ X=\omega ^2$, $R_0$ Kähler and $D$ a disjoint union of two smooth curves, such that the equation 28.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compatible-incomplete-equation} \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^2\rangle =\mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma |^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \end{equation} has a unique solution in $\mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$. The solution has the Lelong numbers of a potential with minimal singularities, but every dense Zariski open set on which its current is smooth and strictly positive is incomplete. The measure $|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has a nonintegrable pole with smooth strictly positive coefficient along both components of $D$. The class $\{ \theta \} $ in this example is not nef. Thus this theorem and theorem 28.14.2 show separately that neither the compatibility identities nor nefness of the class implies completeness. We do not know whether completeness holds when the class is nef and the compatibility identities hold. In neither example is the auxiliary metric identified with the metric of the maximal flow. The cusp in the example comes from a rotation-invariant solution of an exponential equation on $\mathbb P^1$ whose measure has a simple pole. Lemma 28.14.5 . On $\mathbb P^1$, let $z=Z_1/Z_0$, $r=|z|^2$, $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+r)$ and $h=r/(1+r)$, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\alpha =1$. For every $c>2$ there is a $c\alpha $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, depending only on $|z|$ and smooth off $0$, such that 28.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:fixed-volume-curve-cusp} g_1:=c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{e}^{u}h^{-1}c\alpha . \end{equation} It has zero Lelong number at $0$, mass $\int g_1=c$, and \[  \int _{\mathbb P^1}|u|\alpha +\int _{\mathbb P^1}|u|g_1<\infty .  \] Moreover, with $t=\log r$ and $s=-\log r$, there is $A\in \mathbb R$ such that, as $s\to \infty $, \[  \begin{aligned}  u& =\log (2/c)-2\log (s+A)+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}),\\  u_ t& =\frac{2}{s+A}+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}),\qquad u_{tt}=\frac{2}{(s+A)^2}+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}). \end{aligned}  \] Proof. Barriers and the radial inverse. Set $L=1-\log h=1+\log (1+1/r)$ and $w=-2\log L$. Differentiation gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=\left(-\frac2L+\frac2{rL^2}\right)\alpha ,\qquad Q(r):=\frac{c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\mathrm{e}^{w}h^{-1}c\alpha } =\frac{crL^2-2rL+2}{c(1+r)}.  \] The function $Q$ is positive, since $L\geq 1$ and $c>2$. Its limits are $2/c$ at $0$ and $1-2/c$ at infinity, so $0<q_-\leq Q\leq q_+<\infty $ for some constants $q_\pm $. Choose $a_0\leq \min (0,\log q_-)$ and $b_0\geq \max (0,\log q_+)$. Then $l=w+a_0$ and $H=w+b_0$ satisfy \[  c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}l\geq \mathrm{e}^{l}h^{-1}c\alpha ,\qquad c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H\leq \mathrm{e}^{H}h^{-1}c\alpha ,\qquad l\leq w\leq H.  \] Exhaust $\mathbb P^1\setminus \{ 0\} $ by the disks $|\zeta |<R$ in the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$, and solve the equation on them with boundary value $w$. For $q=|\zeta |^2$, the equation becomes \[  \Delta u=f(q)\mathrm{e}^{u}-g(q),\qquad f(q)=\frac{4c}{1+q},\qquad g(q)=\frac{4c}{(1+q)^2},  \] where $\Delta $ is the Euclidean real Laplacian. For $k>0$, the regular radial solution $v=V(q)$ of $(-\Delta +k)v=F(q)$ satisfies 28.54 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-cusp-volterra} V(q)=A_0+\frac14\int _0^ q\log (q/t)\bigl (kV(t)-F(t)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{equation} The $j$-fold iterate of the integral kernel applied to the constant $1$ is $q^ j/(4^ j(j!)^2)$, so successive approximation converges uniformly on every finite interval. The coefficient of $A_0$ in the solution is $\sum _{j\geq 0}(kq/4)^ j/(j!)^2>0$, so exactly one value of $A_0$ gives any prescribed value at $q=R^2$. Moreover, \[  V'(q)=\frac14\int _0^1\bigl (kV(qt)-F(qt)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] and this formula gives smoothness at $q=0$ by induction. The maximum principle for $-\Delta +k$ shows that this radial inverse is unique and preserves order. Choose $k\geq \sup f\mathrm{e}^{H}$ on the fixed disk, and let $T(v)$ be the radial solution of $(-\Delta +k)T(v)=kv-f\mathrm{e}^{v}+g$ with boundary value $w$; the right side is nondecreasing in $v$ on $[l,H]$. The barrier inequalities give $l\leq T(l)$ and $T(H)\leq H$, so the iterates of $T$ starting from $l$ increase and stay below $H$. The derivative formula gives a uniform bound for their first derivatives on the fixed interval. Compactness and monotonicity give uniform convergence; passing to the limit in ( 28.54 ) proves the equation, and the averaged derivative formula bootstraps the limit to smoothness. The same barriers bound the solutions on every fixed disk in $\zeta $ as $R\to \infty $. For an exact solution $U(q)$ of the nonlinear equation, \[  U'(q)=\frac14\int _0^1\bigl (f(qt)\mathrm{e}^{U(qt)}-g(qt)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] and induction gives bounds for all derivatives on compact intervals. A diagonal limit is therefore smooth on the $\zeta $-plane, including the point $z=\infty $, and satisfies $u=-2\log (-\log r)+O(1)$ at $0$. The asymptotics, mass and energy. In the variable $t=\log r$, the equation reads \[  u_{tt}=\frac{c\mathrm{e}^{u}}{1+\mathrm{e}^ t} -\frac{c\mathrm{e}^ t}{(1+\mathrm{e}^ t)^2}.  \] Put $v(t)=u(t)+c\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ t)$ and $V(s)=v(-s)$. Then \[  V''=k_0(s)\mathrm{e}^{V},\qquad k_0(s)=c(1+\mathrm{e}^{-s})^{-(c+1)},\qquad V=-2\log s+O(1).  \] Convexity and this sublinear decay imply $V'<0$ and $V'\to 0$ at infinity. Since $k_0'=O(\mathrm{e}^{-s})$ and $\mathrm{e}^{V}\asymp s^{-2}$, \[  J(s)=2\int _ s^\infty k_0'(\tau )\mathrm{e}^{V(\tau )}\, \mathrm{d}\tau =O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}s^{-2}).  \] Thus $(\mathrm{e}^{-V/2})'=\sqrt{c/2}(1+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}))$, and integration gives $\mathrm{e}^{-V/2}=\sqrt{c/2}(s+A)+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s})$. This identity and the differential equation give all three asymptotic formulas. The local potential $u+c\log (1+r)$ extends subharmonically across $0$ by lemma 1.3.7 . Its radial slope tends to zero at the puncture, so the extension adds no point mass. The density of $g_1$ is asymptotic to \[  \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\frac{2}{r s^2} \, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z.  \] Stokes' theorem for currents gives mass $c$. The energy integral at the cusp is bounded by $C\int ^\infty (\log s)/s^2\, \mathrm{d}s$, and the integral against the smooth form $\alpha $ is finite as well. $\square$ Proof of theorem 28.14.4 . The initial data and the resolution. Take $X=\mathbb P^1_ Z\times \mathbb P^1_ W$, with the pulled-back normalized Fubini–Study forms $\alpha ,\beta $ of the two factors, and put \[  \omega =6(\alpha +\beta ),\qquad \mathrm{d}V_ X=\omega ^2=72\alpha \wedge \beta .  \] Let $H=(Z_1=0)$ and $p=([0:1],[1:0])=(\infty ,0)$. Define \[  \begin{gathered} h_ H=\frac{|Z_1|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2},\qquad \eta =\frac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2} +\frac{|W_1|^2}{|W_0|^2+|W_1|^2},\\ \phi _0=2\log h_ H+2\log \eta . \end{gathered}  \] The zero sets of $h_ H$ and $\eta $ are $H$ and $\{ p\} $, which are disjoint. Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be the blowup at $p$, write $E$ for the exceptional curve, and set $H_ Y=\pi ^{-1}H$ and $D=H_ Y+E$. The surface $Y$ is smooth, compact, connected and projective, and $\pi $ is an isomorphism off $p$. Use $|\sigma _ H|^2=\pi ^*h_ H$ and $|\sigma _ E|^2=\pi ^*\eta $. Near $p$, put $x=Z_0/Z_1$ and $y=W_1/W_0$. In the blowup chart $x=a$, $y=ab$, \[  \pi ^*\eta =|a|^2A(a,b),\qquad A(a,b)=\frac1{1+|a|^2}+\frac{|b|^2}{1+|ab|^2}>0.  \] Thus $\pi ^*\eta $ defines a smooth Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O_ Y(E)$ across $E$. The second chart is obtained by interchanging $x$ and $y$, and the metric factors satisfy the transition rule. The sections $Z_0W_0$, $\sqrt2Z_0W_1$, $Z_1W_1$ of $\mathcal O(1,1)$ have summed squared Fubini–Study norm $\eta $, and near $p$ they generate the ideal $(x,\sqrt2xy,y)=(x,y)$. In the first chart $F=[1:\sqrt2ab:b]$, so $F|_ E$ is an isomorphism onto a line. Near $p$, \[  \eta =\frac{|x|^2+|y|^2+2|xy|^2}{(1+|x|^2)(1+|y|^2)}.  \] Thus $\phi _0$ has analytic singularities. In the convention $\frac1{2m}\log \sum |f_ j|^2$, the coefficient $2$ is obtained by raising the numerator to the fourth power and expanding it as a sum of squared holomorphic monomials. The resolved identities are 28.56 \begin{align} \label{eq:compatible-kahler-residual} \pi ^*\phi _0& =2\log |\sigma _ H|^2+2\log |\sigma _ E|^2,\\  R_0& =\pi ^*\omega -2\Theta _ H-2\Theta _ E =2\pi ^*\alpha +4\pi ^*\beta +2F^*\gamma .\notag \end{align} The first two terms of $R_0$ are positive away from $E$, and along $E$ their kernel is $TE$, on which $F^*\gamma $ is positive. Hence $R_0$ is Kähler. The resolved current is $2[H_ Y]+2[E]+R_0$, which shows that $\phi _0$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic away from $p$; since it is bounded above, it extends across $p$. In the notation of ( 28.48 ), $m_ H=m_ E=2$ and $\ell _0=0$. The Jacobian determinant of the blowup in the chart is $a$, so $b_ E=1$ and $b_ H=0$. Directly, $\mathrm{e}^{-q\phi _0}$ is integrable near $H$ exactly when $q<1/2$ and near $p$ exactly when $q<1$. Consequently $\lambda =\max \{ 2,1\} =2$, and 28.57 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compatible-auxiliary-background} \Theta =\Theta _ H+2\Theta _ E,\qquad \theta =2\Theta +R_0=\pi ^*\omega +2\Theta _ E. \end{equation} Since $\Theta _ E|_ E=-\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, the class $\{ \theta \} $ has degree $-2$ on $E$, so it is not nef. It is big, since the potential $3\log |\sigma _ E|^2$ gives the current \[  (\pi ^*\omega -\Theta _ E)+3[E],\qquad \pi ^*\omega -\Theta _ E=5\pi ^*(\alpha +\beta )+F^*\gamma >0.  \] The prescribed volume. Define $\mathrm{d}V_ Y=\pi ^*\omega ^2/|\sigma _ E|^2$ off $E$. In the chart above, \[  \mathrm{d}V_ Y=\frac{72\, \mathrm{d}A_ a\mathrm{d}A_ b}{\pi ^2A(a,b)(1+|a|^2)^2(1+|ab|^2)^2},  \] since the factor $|a|^2$ from the Jacobian cancels exactly. The second chart gives the extension on the rest of $E$, and the extensions agree on overlaps. Thus $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ is a smooth strictly positive volume form with $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}V_ X=|\sigma _ E|^2\mathrm{d}V_ Y$, as required in ( 28.49 ). Since $H_ Y$ and $E$ are disjoint, the measure $|\sigma _ H\sigma _ E|^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has a nonintegrable pole with smooth positive coefficient along each component. The solution and the minimal reference. Take $u$ from lemma 28.14.5 with $c=6$, pulled back to $X$ from the first factor, and put $g_ X=(6\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+6\beta $. This form is smooth and strictly positive near $p$, and \[  g_ X^2=\mathrm{e}^{u}h_ H^{-1}\omega ^2.  \] Set $P=2\log |\sigma _ E|^2$ and $\rho =P+\pi ^*u$. All three relative energy integrals of the canonical approximants therefore have finite limits. This proves $\rho \in \mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$; replacing $P+M$ by the normalized envelope $V_\theta $ changes the reference by a bounded amount and does not affect this conclusion. Uniqueness follows from the full-mass comparison argument in the proof of theorem 28.14.1 . The measure $|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has infinite mass, but the two exponential densities being compared have mass $72$. Comparison on the strict sublevel sets forces equality almost everywhere, and hence equality of the quasi-plurisubharmonic potentials everywhere. The missing metric boundary. The set on which the current is smooth and strictly positive is $Y\setminus (H_ Y\cup E)$: the cusp coefficient diverges at $H_ Y$, and the nonzero current $2[E]$ excludes smoothness along $E$. The smooth part $\pi ^*g_ X$ also degenerates along $TE$. Let $U$ be a dense Zariski open set on which the current is smooth and strictly positive. As in the proof of theorem 28.14.2 , choose a point of $E$ avoiding every other component of the analytic set $Y\setminus U$; in a small chart around it the complement of $U$ is exactly $E$. A transverse path $a=\xi >0$, $b=b_0$ lies in $U$ for small $\xi $ and approaches that point. Since $g_ X$ is smooth near $p$ and $\pi $ is smooth, the coefficients of $\pi ^*g_ X$ are bounded in the chart, so the path has bounded speed and finite remaining length. Its tails give an intrinsic Cauchy sequence with no limit in $U$, since its only ambient limit is the removed point and a smooth positive Riemannian metric induces the manifold topology. Hence every such $U$ is incomplete. $\square$

title: Lemma 28.14.5
text: Lemma 28.14.5 . On $\mathbb P^1$, let $z=Z_1/Z_0$, $r=|z|^2$, $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+r)$ and $h=r/(1+r)$, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\alpha =1$. For every $c>2$ there is a $c\alpha $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, depending only on $|z|$ and smooth off $0$, such that 28.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:fixed-volume-curve-cusp} g_1:=c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{e}^{u}h^{-1}c\alpha . \end{equation} It has zero Lelong number at $0$, mass $\int g_1=c$, and \[  \int _{\mathbb P^1}|u|\alpha +\int _{\mathbb P^1}|u|g_1<\infty .  \] Moreover, with $t=\log r$ and $s=-\log r$, there is $A\in \mathbb R$ such that, as $s\to \infty $, \[  \begin{aligned}  u& =\log (2/c)-2\log (s+A)+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}),\\  u_ t& =\frac{2}{s+A}+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}),\qquad u_{tt}=\frac{2}{(s+A)^2}+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}). \end{aligned}  \] Proof. Barriers and the radial inverse. Set $L=1-\log h=1+\log (1+1/r)$ and $w=-2\log L$. Differentiation gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=\left(-\frac2L+\frac2{rL^2}\right)\alpha ,\qquad Q(r):=\frac{c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\mathrm{e}^{w}h^{-1}c\alpha } =\frac{crL^2-2rL+2}{c(1+r)}.  \] The function $Q$ is positive, since $L\geq 1$ and $c>2$. Its limits are $2/c$ at $0$ and $1-2/c$ at infinity, so $0<q_-\leq Q\leq q_+<\infty $ for some constants $q_\pm $. Choose $a_0\leq \min (0,\log q_-)$ and $b_0\geq \max (0,\log q_+)$. Then $l=w+a_0$ and $H=w+b_0$ satisfy \[  c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}l\geq \mathrm{e}^{l}h^{-1}c\alpha ,\qquad c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H\leq \mathrm{e}^{H}h^{-1}c\alpha ,\qquad l\leq w\leq H.  \] Exhaust $\mathbb P^1\setminus \{ 0\} $ by the disks $|\zeta |<R$ in the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$, and solve the equation on them with boundary value $w$. For $q=|\zeta |^2$, the equation becomes \[  \Delta u=f(q)\mathrm{e}^{u}-g(q),\qquad f(q)=\frac{4c}{1+q},\qquad g(q)=\frac{4c}{(1+q)^2},  \] where $\Delta $ is the Euclidean real Laplacian. For $k>0$, the regular radial solution $v=V(q)$ of $(-\Delta +k)v=F(q)$ satisfies 28.54 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-cusp-volterra} V(q)=A_0+\frac14\int _0^ q\log (q/t)\bigl (kV(t)-F(t)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{equation} The $j$-fold iterate of the integral kernel applied to the constant $1$ is $q^ j/(4^ j(j!)^2)$, so successive approximation converges uniformly on every finite interval. The coefficient of $A_0$ in the solution is $\sum _{j\geq 0}(kq/4)^ j/(j!)^2>0$, so exactly one value of $A_0$ gives any prescribed value at $q=R^2$. Moreover, \[  V'(q)=\frac14\int _0^1\bigl (kV(qt)-F(qt)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] and this formula gives smoothness at $q=0$ by induction. The maximum principle for $-\Delta +k$ shows that this radial inverse is unique and preserves order. Choose $k\geq \sup f\mathrm{e}^{H}$ on the fixed disk, and let $T(v)$ be the radial solution of $(-\Delta +k)T(v)=kv-f\mathrm{e}^{v}+g$ with boundary value $w$; the right side is nondecreasing in $v$ on $[l,H]$. The barrier inequalities give $l\leq T(l)$ and $T(H)\leq H$, so the iterates of $T$ starting from $l$ increase and stay below $H$. The derivative formula gives a uniform bound for their first derivatives on the fixed interval. Compactness and monotonicity give uniform convergence; passing to the limit in ( 28.54 ) proves the equation, and the averaged derivative formula bootstraps the limit to smoothness. The same barriers bound the solutions on every fixed disk in $\zeta $ as $R\to \infty $. For an exact solution $U(q)$ of the nonlinear equation, \[  U'(q)=\frac14\int _0^1\bigl (f(qt)\mathrm{e}^{U(qt)}-g(qt)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] and induction gives bounds for all derivatives on compact intervals. A diagonal limit is therefore smooth on the $\zeta $-plane, including the point $z=\infty $, and satisfies $u=-2\log (-\log r)+O(1)$ at $0$. The asymptotics, mass and energy. In the variable $t=\log r$, the equation reads \[  u_{tt}=\frac{c\mathrm{e}^{u}}{1+\mathrm{e}^ t} -\frac{c\mathrm{e}^ t}{(1+\mathrm{e}^ t)^2}.  \] Put $v(t)=u(t)+c\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ t)$ and $V(s)=v(-s)$. Then \[  V''=k_0(s)\mathrm{e}^{V},\qquad k_0(s)=c(1+\mathrm{e}^{-s})^{-(c+1)},\qquad V=-2\log s+O(1).  \] Convexity and this sublinear decay imply $V'<0$ and $V'\to 0$ at infinity. The function $J=(V')^2-2k_0\mathrm{e}^{V}$ satisfies $J'=-2k_0'\mathrm{e}^{V}$ and tends to zero. Since $k_0'=O(\mathrm{e}^{-s})$ and $\mathrm{e}^{V}\asymp s^{-2}$, \[  J(s)=2\int _ s^\infty k_0'(\tau )\mathrm{e}^{V(\tau )}\, \mathrm{d}\tau =O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}s^{-2}).  \] Thus $(\mathrm{e}^{-V/2})'=\sqrt{c/2}(1+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}))$, and integration gives $\mathrm{e}^{-V/2}=\sqrt{c/2}(s+A)+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s})$. This identity and the differential equation give all three asymptotic formulas. The local potential $u+c\log (1+r)$ extends subharmonically across $0$ by lemma 1.3.7 . Its radial slope tends to zero at the puncture, so the extension adds no point mass. The density of $g_1$ is asymptotic to \[  \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\frac{2}{r s^2} \, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z.  \] Stokes' theorem for currents gives mass $c$. The energy integral at the cusp is bounded by $C\int ^\infty (\log s)/s^2\, \mathrm{d}s$, and the integral against the smooth form $\alpha $ is finite as well. $\square$
28.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:fixed-volume-curve-cusp} g_1:=c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{e}^{u}h^{-1}c\alpha . \end{equation}
28.54 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-cusp-volterra} V(q)=A_0+\frac14\int _0^ q\log (q/t)\bigl (kV(t)-F(t)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{equation}
28.55 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compatible-curvature-map} F^*\gamma =\pi ^*(\alpha +\beta )-\Theta _ E,\qquad \Theta _ H=\pi ^*\alpha , \end{equation}

28.56 \begin{align} \label{eq:compatible-kahler-residual} \pi ^*\phi _0& =2\log |\sigma _ H|^2+2\log |\sigma _ E|^2,\\  R_0& =\pi ^*\omega -2\Theta _ H-2\Theta _ E =2\pi ^*\alpha +4\pi ^*\beta +2F^*\gamma .\notag \end{align}
28.57 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compatible-auxiliary-background} \Theta =\Theta _ H+2\Theta _ E,\qquad \theta =2\Theta +R_0=\pi ^*\omega +2\Theta _ E. \end{equation}

title: 28.15 Normal length near a divisor
text:
28.15 Normal length near a divisor To prove completeness near a divisor, one needs a lower bound for the metric in the normal direction. A lower bound for the determinant alone does not give it, because the tangential eigenvalues may absorb the volume. Dividing the determinant by the determinant of the tangential block gives the normal Schur complement. A lower bound for it by the inverse square of a defining function of the divisor, weakened by at most the square of the logarithm of that function, forces completeness. For solutions of exponential equations, this bound follows from bounds on the density, the potential and the tangential determinant, and an example on a torus shows that the logarithmic exponent $2$ is sharp. In this section $X$ is again a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Hermitian form $\omega $. Let $D\subset X$ be a nonempty smooth effective divisor, and put $M=X\setminus D$. Let $s_ D$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O_ X(D)$, equipped with a smooth Hermitian norm, and set \[  R=|s_ D|,\qquad \tau =-\log R^2.  \] Rescale the norm so that $\tau \geq 1$ on $M$. Write $J$ for the complex structure. For a smooth positive real $(1,1)$-form $T$ on $M$, we use the Riemannian metric $g_ T(v,v)=\pi T(v,Jv)$ on real tangent vectors $v$. Thus, if $T=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )\sum H_{j\bar k}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$, then $g_ T(v,v)=\sum H_{j\bar k}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j(v)\overline{\mathrm{d}z_ k(v)}$, and Hermitian norms below use this normalization of coefficients. Near $D$, the form $\partial \tau $ does not vanish (see ( 28.59 ) below), and we define the tangential hyperplane field, the tangential block and the determinant \[  E_\tau =\ker \partial \tau ,\qquad B_\tau =T|_{E_\tau },\qquad \det _\omega T=\frac{T^ n}{\omega ^ n}.  \] Similarly, $\det _\omega B_\tau $ denotes the determinant of $B_\tau $ relative to the restriction of $\omega $ to the complex hyperplane $E_\tau $; when $n=1$, it is $1$. Proposition 28.15.1 . Suppose that there are constants $c>0$, $\tau _0\geq 1$ and $p\leq 2$ such that, on $\{ \tau >\tau _0\} $, 28.58 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normal-determinant-ratio} \frac{\det _\omega T}{\det _\omega B_\tau } \geq cR^{-2}\tau ^{-p}. \end{equation} Then $(M,g_ T)$ is complete. Proof. In a coordinate neighborhood meeting $D$, write $s_ D=z_1 e$, where $e$ is a local holomorphic frame with $|e|^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\psi }$ and $\psi $ is smooth. Then \[  \tau =-\log |z_1|^2+\psi ,\qquad \partial \tau =-\frac{\mathrm{d}z_1}{z_1}+\partial \psi .  \] Covering the compact divisor by finitely many such neighborhoods and comparing with the smooth background, we obtain, after increasing $\tau _0$, 28.59 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normal-gradient-comparison} c_1R^{-2}\leq |\partial \tau |_\omega ^2\leq C_1R^{-2} \quad \hbox{on }\{ \tau >\tau _0\}  \end{equation} for positive constants $c_1,C_1$. In particular, $E_\tau $ is a hyperplane there. At a point of this set, choose an $\omega $-unitary frame whose last $n-1$ vectors span $E_\tau $. Let $H$ be the Hermitian matrix that represents $g_ T$ as the quadratic form $w^*Hw$ in the complex components $w$, and write \[  H=\begin{pmatrix} h

& a^*

\\ a

& B

\end{pmatrix},\qquad S=h-a^*B^{-1}a=\frac{\det H}{\det B},  \] where $a$ is a column vector and $a^*$ its conjugate transpose. Completing the square gives, for a vector with components $(\xi ,\eta )$, \[  \begin{pmatrix} \bar\xi 

& \eta ^*

\end{pmatrix} H\begin{pmatrix} \xi 

\\ \eta 

\end{pmatrix} =S|\xi |^2+(\eta +B^{-1}a\xi )^*B(\eta +B^{-1}a\xi ) \geq S|\xi |^2.  \] For $n=1$ the same identity holds without the second term. For the complex components of a real vector $v$ we have $|\xi |=|\partial \tau (v)|/|\partial \tau |_\omega $, so ( 28.58 ) and ( 28.59 ) imply 28.60 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normal-length-bound} g_ T(v,v)\geq c_2\tau ^{-p}|\partial \tau (v)|^2 \geq \frac{c_2}{4}\tau ^{-p}|\mathrm{d}\tau (v)|^2, \end{equation} where $c_2>0$ is uniform. The last inequality uses $\mathrm{d}\tau (v)=2\operatorname {Re}\partial \tau (v)$. Define a continuous function $\Phi _ p$ on $[1,\infty )$ by \[  \Phi _ p(t)= \begin{cases}  0,& t\leq \tau _0,\\  \displaystyle \int _{\tau _0}^ t x^{-p/2}\, \mathrm{d}x,& t>\tau _0. \end{cases}  \] Integrating ( 28.60 ) along piecewise smooth curves shows that $\Phi _ p\circ \tau $ is Lipschitz for the length distance of $g_ T$; this also holds for curves crossing $\{ \tau =\tau _0\} $, since $\Phi _ p$ is locally Lipschitz and constant below that level. Since $p\leq 2$, $\Phi _ p(t)$ tends to infinity with $t$, so $\Phi _ p\circ \tau $ is a proper function on $M$. A Cauchy sequence for the length distance has bounded values of this Lipschitz function and hence lies in a compact subset of $M$. It therefore has a subsequence converging in the manifold topology. On a coordinate ball about the limit, the smooth positive form $T$ is comparable to the Euclidean metric, so this subsequence also converges for the length distance. The Cauchy property then gives convergence of the whole sequence, which proves completeness. $\square$ Corollary 28.15.2 . In the preceding setting, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be smooth on $M$, with $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ there. Suppose that, for some $\lambda >0$ and some positive $f\in C^\infty (M)\cap L^1(X,\omega ^ n)$, \[  T^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\omega ^ n\quad \hbox{on }M.  \] Assume that, near $D$, there are constants $c,C>0$, $q>1$, $a\geq 0$ and $b\in \mathbb R$ such that 28.63 \begin{equation} \label{eq:divisorial-three-bounds} f\geq cR^{-2}\tau ^{-q},\qquad u\geq -\frac{a}{\lambda }\log \tau -C,\qquad \det _\omega B_\tau \leq C\tau ^ b. \end{equation} If $q+a+b\leq 2$, then $(M,g_ T)$ is complete. Proof. The equation and the first two inequalities give $\det _\omega T\geq c\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda C}R^{-2}\tau ^{-(q+a)}$. Dividing by the third bound gives ( 28.58 ) with $p=q+a+b$, and proposition 28.15.1 applies. $\square$ Since $u$ is bounded above on the compact manifold $X$, integrability of $f$ also makes the measure $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\omega ^ n$ finite. The relevant tangential determinant is that of the intrinsic hyperplane field $E_\tau $, not that of an arbitrary block of coordinate directions.
