title: 28.15.1 The critical exponent on a compact torus
search_title: The critical exponent on a compact torus
text: 28.15.1 The critical exponent on a compact torus The exponent $2$ in corollary 28.15.2 is sharp. On a product torus, two explicit logarithmic profiles give a complete metric with $q+a+b=2$ and incomplete metrics with $q+a+b=2+\beta $ for every $\beta >0$. Both profiles have full mass, and the second one is bounded. Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z)$, let $\omega _ E=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )\, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z$, and put $X=E^ n$, $D=\{ 0\} \times E^{n-1}$ and $M=X\setminus D$. Write $\pi _ j:X\to E$ for the coordinate projections and $\omega _0=\sum _{j=1}^ n\pi _ j^*\omega _ E$. Choose radii $0<r_1<r_2<\mathrm{e}^{-1}$ and a smooth radial cutoff $\chi $ on the coordinate disk $\{ |z|<r_2\} \subset E$, equal to $1$ on $\{ |z|\leq r_1\} $ and to $0$ near its outer boundary, with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. For fixed numbers $A,\eta ,\beta >0$, set $L=-\log |z|^2$ and define on $E$ 28.64 \begin{equation} \label{eq:torus-length-profiles} v_{\mathrm c}=-A\chi \log L,\qquad v_\beta =\eta \chi L^{-\beta }. \end{equation} Both functions are extended by zero outside the disk, and at its center we set $v_{\mathrm c}(0)=-\infty $ and $v_\beta (0)=0$. The bounded profile also occurs in example 14.20.2 . We write $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ for the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ of theorem 6.1.2 . Lemma 28.15.3 . For $C>0$ sufficiently large, put $\theta =C\omega _0$. For either profile $v$ in ( 28.64 ), the function $u=\pi _1^*v$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the form $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is smooth and positive on $X\setminus D$, and \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\int _ X\theta ^ n.  \] The same $C$ may be used for the two fixed profiles. The bounded profile has minimal ordinary singularities; the profile $v_{\mathrm c}$ does not. Proof. For a twice differentiable function $G$ of $L=-\log |z|^2$, differentiation away from zero gives \[  \frac{\partial ^2G(L)}{\partial z\partial \bar z} =\frac{G''(L)}{|z|^2}.  \] On the inner disk this yields 28.65 \begin{equation} \label{eq:torus-profile-hessians} (v_{\mathrm c})_{z\bar z}=\frac{A}{|z|^2L^2},\qquad (v_\beta )_{z\bar z}=\frac{\eta \beta (\beta +1)}{|z|^2L^{\beta +2}}. \end{equation} Both densities are integrable at zero. Both profiles are locally integrable, and their distributional Hessians have no additional atom at zero. To see this, integrate twice by parts outside $\{ |z|=\varepsilon \} $: the boundary terms against a smooth test function are bounded by constant multiples of $\varepsilon |G(-\log \varepsilon ^2)|$ and $|G'(-\log \varepsilon ^2)|$, and both tend to zero for the two profiles. Thus ( 28.65 ) holds in the sense of distributions across the center. On the cutoff annulus all derivatives are bounded. Hence, for a sufficiently large common $C$, \[  \alpha _ v=C\omega _ E+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v  \] is a positive measure, smooth and strictly positive away from zero, with no atom at zero. Pairing $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ with the constant test function gives $\int _ E\alpha _ v=C\int _ E\omega _ E$. Let $Y=E^{n-1}$, let $\pi _ Y:X\to Y$ be the projection onto the remaining factors, and let $\theta _ Y$ be $C$ times the sum of the $n-1$ flat forms of $Y$. On $X\setminus D$ the smooth wedge product is \[  T^ n=n\, \pi _1^*\alpha _ v\wedge \pi _ Y^*\theta _ Y^{n-1};  \] for $n=1$ this means just $\alpha _ v$, with $Y$ a point. The right side defines a finite product measure on $X$ that gives $D$ zero mass. By theorem 6.1.2 , the non-pluripolar measure agrees with this product off $D$ and gives the pluripolar set $D$ zero mass, so the two global measures are equal. Integrating the product proves the full-mass identity. Since $\theta >0$, its envelope is $V_\theta =0$ (section 1.19 ). The bounded profile therefore has minimal ordinary singularities, whereas $v_{\mathrm c}$ is not bounded below by $0$ minus a constant. $\square$ We apply the preceding results with $\omega =\theta $. Choose a smooth norm on $\mathcal O_ E(0)$, the line bundle of the point $0\in E$, for which its canonical section has squared norm $|z|^2$ near zero; such a norm is obtained from any smooth norm by multiplying by a smooth positive function prescribed on a smaller disk. Pull it back to $X$ and rescale it by a constant. For some fixed $K>0$ we may then arrange \[  R^2=\mathrm{e}^{-K}|z_1|^2,\qquad \tau =L+K  \] near $D$, and $\tau \geq 1$ on $M$. For both profiles, $E_\tau $ is exactly the tangent space of the remaining torus factors near $D$, so $\det _\theta B_\tau =1$. Example 28.15.4 . Fix $\lambda >0$ and $0<A<1/\lambda $, and take $u_{\mathrm c}=\pi _1^*v_{\mathrm c}$ with the background of lemma 28.15.3 . This gives a complete metric on $M$ solving \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_{\mathrm c}) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_{\mathrm c}}f_{\mathrm c}\theta ^ n, \qquad f_{\mathrm c}\in C^\infty (M)\cap L^1(X,\theta ^ n),\quad f_{\mathrm c}>0,  \] where the right side is extended by zero on $D$. The three exponents in ( 28.63 ) can be taken to be \[  q=2-\lambda A>1,\qquad a=\lambda A,\qquad b=0,  \] so their sum equals the critical exponent $2$. Indeed, define $f_{\mathrm c}=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u_{\mathrm c}}\det _\theta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{\mathrm c})$ on $M$. On the inner disk the product structure gives \[  f_{\mathrm c}=L^{\lambda A} +\frac{A}{C|z_1|^2L^{2-\lambda A}}.  \] The substitution $L=-\log r^2$ in the radial integral shows that the second term is integrable precisely when $\lambda A<1$. The first term is integrable as well, and the density is smooth elsewhere. The identity of measures across $D$ follows from the preceding lemma. Since $\tau =L+K$, all three bounds hold with the stated exponents, and completeness follows from corollary 28.15.2 . Along a radial normal segment the divergence of the length at the critical exponent is also visible directly: \[  \int _0^{r_1}\frac{\sqrt A}{r(-\log r^2)}\, \mathrm{d}r=\infty .  \] For arbitrary paths, however, completeness requires the corollary, not just this family of radial paths. Example 28.15.5 . Fix $\lambda ,\eta ,\beta >0$ and take $u_\beta =\pi _1^*v_\beta $ with the background of lemma 28.15.3 . This is a continuous bounded solution of full mass with minimal ordinary singularities, and its metric on $M$ is incomplete, although \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_\beta )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\beta }f_\beta \theta ^ n, \qquad f_\beta \in C^\infty (M)\cap L^1(X,\theta ^ n),\quad f_\beta >0.  \] To see this, put $K_\beta =\eta \beta (\beta +1)$ and define the density by the equation on $M$. Near $D$ it is \[  f_\beta =\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \eta L^{-\beta }} \left(1+\frac{K_\beta }{C|z_1|^2L^{\beta +2}}\right).  \] It is integrable, and the global identity follows as before. Fix the other coordinates and let $z_1=r\downarrow 0$ along a radial segment starting at $r_0$, with $0<r_0<r_1$. title: Lemma 28.15.3
text: Lemma 28.15.3 . For $C>0$ sufficiently large, put $\theta =C\omega _0$. The bounded profile has minimal ordinary singularities; the profile $v_{\mathrm c}$ does not. Proof. For a twice differentiable function $G$ of $L=-\log |z|^2$, differentiation away from zero gives \[  \frac{\partial ^2G(L)}{\partial z\partial \bar z} =\frac{G''(L)}{|z|^2}.  \] On the inner disk this yields 28.65 \begin{equation} \label{eq:torus-profile-hessians} (v_{\mathrm c})_{z\bar z}=\frac{A}{|z|^2L^2},\qquad (v_\beta )_{z\bar z}=\frac{\eta \beta (\beta +1)}{|z|^2L^{\beta +2}}. \end{equation} Both densities are integrable at zero. title: Example 28.15.4
text: Example 28.15.4 . Fix $\lambda >0$ and $0<A<1/\lambda $, and take $u_{\mathrm c}=\pi _1^*v_{\mathrm c}$ with the background of lemma 28.15.3 . title: 28.16 Rigid boundary classes on a torus

28.16 Rigid boundary classes on a torus We now turn to the boundary of the nef cone. A nef class with zero top intersection number may have a smooth semipositive representative and yet leave little freedom to vary it. On a complex torus, the kernel of a constant semipositive form controls this freedom: when the leaves of the kernel are dense, the form is the only closed positive current in its class. The same condition decides whether adding a small fixed Kähler form produces metrics whose diameters tend to zero. For Kähler forms converging to the boundary in other ways, the diameters can tend to zero even at a class with many semipositive representatives. Let $X=V/\Lambda $ be a complex torus, where $V\simeq \mathbb C^ n$ and $\Lambda $ is a full lattice. Let $	heta $ be a translation-invariant semipositive real $(1,1)$-form of rank $r$ with $1\leq r<n$, and fix a translation-invariant Kähler form $\kappa $. The class $\alpha =\{ 	heta \} _{\mathrm{BC}}$ is nef and has $\int _ X	heta ^ n=0$. It lies on the boundary of the nef cone: a Kähler form in $\alpha $ would have positive top intersection number, whereas Stokes' theorem gives every representative the top intersection number $\int _ X	heta ^ n=0$. We call $\alpha $ rigid if it contains exactly one closed positive current. Let $K=\ker 	heta \subset V$, a complex subspace of dimension $n-r$, and let $H\subset X$ be the closure of its image in $X$. This is a connected real subtorus, which need not be complex. Diameters are computed for the Riemannian metric $g_\eta (v,w)=\eta (v,Jw)$ associated with a positive form $\eta $, where $J$ is the complex structure. Theorem 28.16.1 . The following are equivalent: $\alpha $ is rigid; $H=X$; $\operatorname {diam}(X,	heta +t\kappa )	o 0$ as $t\downarrow 0$. In the first case the unique current is $	heta $. The third condition is independent of the chosen translation-invariant Kähler form $\kappa $. Proof. Rigidity when $H=X$. Suppose first that $H=X$. By lemma 23.4.1 , a positive current in $\alpha $ can be written $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ quasi-plurisubharmonic, in particular $u\in L^1(X)$. For a constant real vector $v\in K$, the coefficient $T(v,Jv)$ is a positive Radon measure. Its total integral against Haar measure is zero, because $	heta (v,Jv)=0$ and the remaining part of the coefficient is a combination of constant-coefficient derivatives of $u$. Hence this coefficient vanishes. Writing $D_ v$ for differentiation along $v$ and using that $K$ is complex, we obtain \[  (D_ v^2+D_{Jv}^2)u=0 \quad 	ext{as a distribution for every }v\in K.  \] For a real linear functional $\ell $ with $\ell (\Lambda )\subset \mathbb Z$, let $\widehat u(\ell )$ be the Fourier coefficient of $u$ at the character $\exp (2\pi \mathrm i\ell )$. The identity above gives \[   igl (\ell (v)^2+\ell (Jv)^2 igr )\widehat u(\ell )=0.  \] Since the image of $K$ is dense, a nonzero character cannot vanish identically on $K$. Thus every nonconstant Fourier coefficient of $u$ is zero, and convolution with a smooth approximate identity shows that $u$ is constant. Hence $T=	heta $. Nonrigidity when $H
e X$. If $H
e X$, a nontrivial character of the real torus $X/H$ gives a nonzero $\ell $ that vanishes on $K$. Put $\phi =\cos (2\pi \ell )$. Since $K$ is complex, the form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi $ vanishes whenever one of its arguments lies in $K$. On a fixed complement of $K$, $	heta $ is positive definite and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi $ is uniformly bounded. Consequently, the forms $	heta \pm \varepsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi $ are semipositive for sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. They represent the same class, and they are distinct because a nonconstant smooth function on a compact torus cannot have zero $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. Hence $\alpha $ is not rigid. Collapse when $H=X$. Suppose again that $H=X$, and fix $\delta >0$. By density and compactness, there are finitely many vectors $k_1,\ldots ,k_ N\in K$ whose images form a $\delta $-net in the flat metric of $\kappa $. Put $R=\max _ j|k_ j|_\kappa $. Since $	heta (k_ j,Jk_ j)=0$, the straight path from $0$ to the image of $k_ j$ has $(	heta +t\kappa )$-length $\sqrt t\, |k_ j|_\kappa $. For $0<t\leq 1$ these metrics are bounded above by a fixed multiple of $\kappa $. Joining this path to a point within $\delta $ therefore gives \[  \operatorname {diam}(X,	heta +t\kappa ) \leq \sqrt t\, R+C\delta ,  \] since by translation invariance the diameter equals the supremum of the distances from $0$. Letting first $t\downarrow 0$ for this fixed net and then $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the third condition. No collapse when $H
e X$. If $H
e X$, choose $\ell $ as above. Its differential vanishes on $K$, so $|\mathrm d\ell (v)|\leq L|v|_	heta $ for some $L>0$, where $|v|_	heta $ is the seminorm defined by $	heta $. Since $	heta +t\kappa \geq 	heta $, the surjective map $\ell  mod \mathbb Z$ onto the circle of length one is $L$-Lipschitz for every $t>0$. Two points mapping to opposite points of the circle therefore have distance at least $1/(2L)$, and the diameters cannot tend to zero. This completes the proof of the equivalences. Since the second condition does not involve $\kappa $, neither does the third. $\square$ On a two-dimensional square torus, the slope of the kernel line decides rigidity. Example 28.16.2 . On $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z))^2$, for $a\in \mathbb R$ set \[  	heta _ a= rac{\mathrm i}{2} (\mathrm dz_2-a\, \mathrm dz_1) \wedge (\mathrm d ar z_2-a\, \mathrm d ar z_1).  \] Its class is rigid exactly when $a$ is irrational. In that case its ray is irrational, that is, no nonzero real multiple of its de Rham class is rational, and every family $	heta _ a+t\kappa $ as above collapses to a point in diameter. For rational $a$ the class is not rigid, and these diameters have a positive lower bound. Proof. The kernel is the complex line $z_2=a z_1$. Write $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$. An integral character has the form \[  \ell =m_1x_1+m_2x_2+n_1y_1+n_2y_2, \qquad m_ j,n_ j\in \mathbb Z,  \] and it vanishes on the kernel exactly when $m_1+a m_2=n_1+a n_2=0$. For irrational $a$, only the zero character does so, hence the image of the kernel is dense. For rational $a$, a nonzero such character exists. Now apply theorem 28.16.1 . The periods of $	heta _ a$ on the coordinate two-tori in the $(x_2,y_2)$ and $(x_1,y_2)$ directions are $1$ and $-a$, respectively. If a nonzero multiple of its class were rational, the first period would make that multiple rational, and the second would then make $a$ rational. This proves the assertion about the ray. $\square$ The fixed positive direction $\kappa $ in the theorem cannot be replaced by an arbitrary convergent family of Kähler forms, even when all the metrics are flat and Ricci-flat. Example 28.16.3 . On the same square torus let $	heta _0= rac{\mathrm i}{2}\mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm d ar z_2$ and, for $t>0$, put \[   eta _ t= rac{\mathrm i}{2}\left[ (t\, \mathrm dz_1+\mathrm dz_2) \wedge (t\, \mathrm d ar z_1+\mathrm d ar z_2) +t^2\mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm d ar z_2ight].  \] These are flat Ricci-flat Kähler forms, $ eta _ t	o 	heta _0$ smoothly, and \[  \operatorname {diam}(X, eta _ t)\leq t.  \] The limiting class $\{ 	heta _0\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$ is not rigid. Proof. The coefficient matrix of $ eta _ t$ is $\left( egin{smallmatrix}t^2& t\ t& 1+t^2\end{smallmatrix}ight)$, with determinant $t^4>0$. Its coefficients are constant, which gives flatness and Ricci-flatness. Represent a point by $(z_1,z_2)$ with real and imaginary parts in $[-1/2,1/2]$, and choose a Gaussian integer $k$ nearest to $-z_1-z_2/t$. The displacement $(z_1+k,z_2)$ represents the same point of the torus and has squared metric norm \[  |t(z_1+k)+z_2|^2+t^2|z_2|^2 \leq t^2/2+t^2/2=t^2.  \] The straight path along this displacement proves the bound for the distance from zero, and translation invariance gives the diameter bound. For $0<|s|<1/\pi $, the form $	heta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(s\cos (2\pi x_2))=(1-\pi s\cos (2\pi x_2))	heta _0$ is another semipositive representative, so the limiting class is not rigid. Finally, the coefficient matrix of $ eta _ t-	heta _0$ has eigenvalues $t^2\pm t$, so this difference is indefinite for $0<t<1$: the forms $ eta _ t$ do not approach $	heta _0$ from above. $\square$

title: 28.17 Nonrigid classes on a quotient resolution

text:
28.17 Nonrigid classes on a quotient resolution In contrast with example 28.16.2 , an irrational nef boundary ray can admit many smooth semipositive representatives. On a suitable two-dimensional torus, such representatives come from semipositive forms depending on a single real coordinate, with an irrational lattice direction making the ray irrational. If these forms vanish near the fixed points of the involution $z\mapsto -z$, they pass smoothly to the resolution of the quotient, a Kummer surface. Let $A=\mathbb C^2/\Lambda $ be a complex two-torus, let $Y=A/\{ \pm 1\} $, and let $r:X	o Y$ be the minimal resolution. The fixed points of the involution are the sixteen points of $A[2]=( rac12\Lambda )/\Lambda $, and their images are the sixteen singular points of $Y$. Lemma 28.17.1 . The surface $X$ is compact Kähler. Its exceptional set consists of sixteen disjoint projective lines with self-intersection $-2$. Proof. Blow up the sixteen fixed points on $A$ and take the quotient by the lifted involution. Near one exceptional line, a blowup chart has coordinates $(u,v)$ with $z_1=u$ and $z_2=uv$, and the involution is $(u,v)\mapsto (-u,v)$. The quotient chart has smooth coordinates $(s,v)=(u^2,v)$. On the other chart, $v'=1/v$ and $s'=v^2s$. These charts describe the total space of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-2)$ near its zero section. The quotient is therefore smooth and resolves the double point, with the stated exceptional curve. Doing this at all fixed points gives the compact surface $X$. Choose a flat Kähler form on $A$ that equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho $, where $ho =|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2$, on disjoint balls centered at the fixed points. Away from those points it descends to $Y$. On the resolution chart, \[  ho =|s|(1+|v|^2),\qquad ho ^2=|s|^2(1+|v|^2)^2.  \] Choose a smooth function $F$ on $[0,+\infty )$ with $F(ho )=cho ^2$ near zero, where $c>0$, with $F'>0$ on $(0,+\infty )$ and $F''\geq 0$, and with $F(ho )=ho -C$ for $ho \geq \delta $, for a sufficiently small $\delta >0$. Such a function is obtained by choosing $F'$ nondecreasing, linear near zero and equal to one beyond $\delta $. Replace the flat form in each ball by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(ho )$. This agrees with the flat form near the boundary of the ball and extends smoothly across the exceptional line. The resulting closed form $\eta $ is positive off the exceptional set, while along it $\eta $ is positive in the normal direction and zero in the tangent direction. To restore positivity in the tangent direction, choose a smooth cutoff $\chi $ equal to one for $ho \leq \delta $ and zero for $ho \geq 2\delta $. For $s
e 0$, set \[  q_ v=\chi (ho )\log ho -\log |s|.  \] Near $s=0$ this equals $\log (1+|v|^2)$, so it extends smoothly. On the overlap of the two charts, $q_{v'}-q_ v=-2\log |v|$ is pluriharmonic, so their $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ forms agree. They define a smooth closed form $R$ supported in the resolved ball, positive in the tangent direction along the exceptional line and semipositive where $\chi =1$. Hence $\eta +\varepsilon R$ is positive where $\chi =1$, including along the line. On the compact transition annulus $\eta $ is already positive, so $\eta +\varepsilon R$ remains positive there for sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, and outside the ball $R=0$. Adding these corrections in all the disjoint balls produces a Kähler form on $X$. $\square$ Fix now $a\in \mathbb R\setminus \mathbb Q$ and take for $\Lambda $ the lattice generated by \[  \lambda _1=(1,0),\quad \lambda _2=(a,1),\quad \lambda _3=(\mathrm i,0),\quad \lambda _4=(0,\mathrm i).  \] Write $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$. Since $y_1$ takes integer values on $\Lambda $, the coordinate $y_1 mod \mathbb Z$ defines a map from $A$ to the circle $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$. title: Lemma 28.17.1
text: Lemma 28.17.1 . The surface $X$ is compact Kähler. Its exceptional set consists of sixteen disjoint projective lines with self-intersection $-2$. Proof. Blow up the sixteen fixed points on $A$ and take the quotient by the lifted involution. Near one exceptional line, a blowup chart has coordinates $(u,v)$ with $z_1=u$ and $z_2=uv$, and the involution is $(u,v)\mapsto (-u,v)$. The quotient chart has smooth coordinates $(s,v)=(u^2,v)$. On the other chart, $v'=1/v$ and $s'=v^2s$. These charts describe the total space of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-2)$ near its zero section. The quotient is therefore smooth and resolves the double point, with the stated exceptional curve. Doing this at all fixed points gives the compact surface $X$. Choose a flat Kähler form on $A$ that equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $, where $\rho =|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2$, on disjoint balls centered at the fixed points. Away from those points it descends to $Y$. On the resolution chart, \[  \rho =|s|(1+|v|^2),\qquad \rho ^2=|s|^2(1+|v|^2)^2.  \] Choose a smooth function $F$ on $[0,+\infty )$ with $F(\rho )=c\rho ^2$ near zero, where $c>0$, with $F'>0$ on $(0,+\infty )$ and $F''\geq 0$, and with $F(\rho )=\rho -C$ for $\rho \geq \delta $, for a sufficiently small $\delta >0$. Such a function is obtained by choosing $F'$ nondecreasing, linear near zero and equal to one beyond $\delta $. Replace the flat form in each ball by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(\rho )$. This agrees with the flat form near the boundary of the ball and extends smoothly across the exceptional line. The resulting closed form $\eta $ is positive off the exceptional set, while along it $\eta $ is positive in the normal direction and zero in the tangent direction. To restore positivity in the tangent direction, choose a smooth cutoff $\chi $ equal to one for $\rho \leq \delta $ and zero for $\rho \geq 2\delta $. For $s\ne 0$, set \[  q_ v=\chi (\rho )\log \rho -\log |s|.  \] Near $s=0$ this equals $\log (1+|v|^2)$, so it extends smoothly. On the overlap of the two charts, $q_{v'}-q_ v=-2\log |v|$ is pluriharmonic, so their $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ forms agree. They define a smooth closed form $R$ supported in the resolved ball, positive in the tangent direction along the exceptional line and semipositive where $\chi =1$. Hence $\eta +\varepsilon R$ is positive where $\chi =1$, including along the line. On the compact transition annulus $\eta $ is already positive, so $\eta +\varepsilon R$ remains positive there for sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, and outside the ball $R=0$. Adding these corrections in all the disjoint balls produces a Kähler form on $X$. $\square$

title: 28.18 Semipositive metrics in a four-point blowup family
search_title: Semipositive metrics in a four-point blowup family
text:
28.18 Semipositive metrics in a four-point blowup family The preceding constructions keep the manifold fixed. For a family of compact manifolds and a line bundle on the total space, one may ask whether a semipositive singular metric on the restriction of the bundle to a special fiber is the restriction of a semipositive metric over a neighborhood of that fiber. In a family of blowups of the projective plane at four points, the answer is negative. The obstruction comes from compact curves on the nearby fibers on which the bundle has degree zero: the curvature of a semipositive metric vanishes on such a curve, and this persists on a component of the limiting curve in the central fiber. It forces the restricted metric to have a logarithmic singularity of coefficient one at a point of that component, whereas the prescribed metric has coefficient one half there. Varying these curves also identifies exactly which central metrics extend. Let $\Delta $ be a disk with coordinate $t$, and let $[x:y:z]$ be homogeneous coordinates on $\mathbb P^2$. Blow up $\mathbb P^2	imes \Delta $ along the four disjoint sections \[   egin{aligned}  p_1(t)& =[1:0:0],& \qquad p_2(t)& =[0:1:0],\  p_3(t)& =[1:1:t],& \qquad p_4(t)& =[0:0:1], \end{aligned}  \] write $\pi :\mathcal X	o \Delta $ for the resulting family and $X_ t=\pi ^{-1}(t)$ for its fibers. Let $H$ be the pullback of the hyperplane line bundle, let $E_ i$ be the exceptional divisor over $p_ i$, and put \[  L=2H-E_1-E_2-E_3-E_4,\qquad L_ t=L|_{X_ t}.  \] We use additive notation for tensor products of line bundles and also for their divisor classes, and we write $K_{X_ t}$ for the canonical line bundle. A singular Hermitian metric $h$ has squared norm $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi }$ in a local holomorphic frame $e$; the function $\varphi $ is its local weight , and its curvature is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $. The metric is semipositive if its local weights are plurisubharmonic. For an effective divisor with local equation $w$, the divisor metric on the associated line bundle is the singular metric for which the canonical section has norm one; its weight is $\log |w|^2$ and its curvature is the integration current along the divisor. Lemma 28.18.1 . The family is smooth and projective with rational surface fibers, and $L$ is effective on $\mathcal X$. For every $t
e 0$, $L_ t$ is generated by global sections, has square zero and is nef. For every integer $m\geq 1$, \[  H^0(X_ t,K_{X_ t}+mL_ t)=0\qquad (t
e 0).  \] Proof. Near one of the sections, coordinates centered on it identify the blowup with $\operatorname {Bl}_0(\mathbb C^2)	imes \Delta $. Since the four centers are disjoint, these charts prove smoothness and the submersion property. The blowup of the projective morphism $\mathbb P^2	imes \Delta 	o \Delta $ is projective and proper, and each fiber $X_ t$ is the blowup of $\mathbb P^2$ at the four points $p_ i(t)$. The quadratic forms \[  F_1=x(z-ty),\qquad F_2=y(z-tx)  \] vanish along all four sections and therefore lift to sections of $L$. They are nonzero, which proves that $L$ is effective. For $t
e 0$, their common zeros in $\mathbb P^2$ are exactly the four points. In suitable affine coordinates $(u,v)$ centered at $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, their linear initial terms are \[  (v-tu,-tu),\quad (-tu,v-tu),\quad (v-tu,v),\quad (u,v).  \] Each pair is linearly independent. Hence, after the exceptional divisors are subtracted, the transformed sections have no common zero on an exceptional curve. The two transformed sections therefore generate $L_ t$, and $L_ t$ has nonnegative degree on every irreducible curve. On a fiber, $H^2=1$, $H\cdot E_ i=0$, and $E_ i\cdot E_ j=-\delta _{ij}$. Hence $L_ t^2=0$, and $K_{X_ t}=-3H+\sum _ iE_ i$ gives $K_{X_ t}\cdot L_ t=-2$. A nonzero section of $K_{X_ t}+mL_ t$ would have an effective zero divisor whose intersection with the nef line bundle $L_ t$ is $-2<0$, a contradiction. This argument also excludes a nowhere-vanishing section, whose zero divisor would have intersection zero. $\square$ On $X_0$, let $\ell $ be the strict transform of the line $\{ z=0\} $, which passes through $p_1(0)$, $p_2(0)$ and $p_3(0)$. In additive notation, \[  \ell =H-E_1-E_2-E_3,\qquad A=2L_0-\ell =3H-E_1-E_2-E_3-2E_4.  \] Lemma 28.18.2 . The line bundle $A$ is generated by global sections. There is a semipositive metric $h_0$ on $L_0$ whose weight along $\ell $ is \[  \varphi _0=	frac 12\log |w|^2+	ext{a smooth function},  \] where $w$ is a local equation of $\ell $. It is smooth off $\ell $ and has analytic singularities. Proof. Consider the cubic forms \[  x^2z,\qquad xyz,\qquad y^2z,\qquad xy(x-y).  \] Their common zero set in $\mathbb P^2$ consists of the four central points. In affine coordinates at $p_1$, $p_2$ and $p_3$, their linear initial terms include $(z,y)$, $(z,x)$ and $(z,x-y)$, respectively, while at $p_4$ their quadratic initial terms include $x^2,xy,y^2$. These have no common zero on the corresponding exceptional projective lines. After the simple exceptional factors at $p_1,p_2,p_3$ and the double factor at $p_4$ are removed, the transformed cubics therefore generate $A$. Their Fubini–Study metric $h_ A$ is smooth and semipositive. Let $h_\ell $ be the divisor metric on $\mathcal O(\ell )$. Since $2L_0=A+\ell $, the square root of $h_ A\otimes h_\ell $ defines a metric $h_0$ on $L_0$, with \[  \Theta _{h_0}=	frac 12\Theta _{h_ A}+	frac 12[\ell ]\geq 0.  \] The stated form of the weight and of its singularities follows directly. $\square$ Lemma 28.18.3 . The strict transforms of the conics \[  F_1-2F_2=z(x-2y)+txy=0  \] form a surface $\Gamma \subset \mathcal X$. For $t
e 0$, its fiber $C_ t$ is a smooth compact rational curve with $L_ t\cdot C_ t=0$. The central fiber of $\Gamma $ is $\ell +q$, where $q$ is the strict transform of the line $\{ x=2y\} $. The curves $\ell $ and $q$ meet transversely at one point $p$, and $L_0\cdot q=1$. Near every point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $, $\Gamma $ is smooth and $\pi |_\Gamma $ is a submersion. Proof. The symmetric matrix of the quadratic form has determinant $-t/2$, so the conic is smooth for $t
e 0$. It passes simply through all four centers, so its strict transform is a smooth rational curve of class $L_ t$, and its degree against $L_ t$ is $L_ t^2=0$. At $t=0$ the conic is the union of the lines $\{ z=0\} $ and $\{ x=2y\} $. The second line avoids $p_1,p_2,p_3$ and passes through $p_4$. Each component has multiplicity one at every center it contains, so the central fiber of $\Gamma $ contains no additional exceptional component. The two lines meet at $[2:1:0]$, transversely and away from every center. Since $q=H-E_4$, we have $L_0\cdot q=1$. Away from the centers, the defining equation at $t=0$ has nonzero derivative in the directions of $\mathbb P^2$ at every point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $, which proves the assertion there. Near $p_4$, use the blowup chart $z=1$, $x=r$, $y=rs$. After the exceptional factor is removed, the equation becomes \[  1-2s+trs=0.  \] At the central point of $q\cap E_4$ we have $r=0$ and $s=1/2$, and the derivative in $s$ is $-2$. Thus $(r,t)$ are local coordinates on $\Gamma $ there. These two cases cover $q\setminus \{ p\} $. $\square$ Theorem 28.18.4 . There is no semipositive metric on $L$ over an open neighborhood of $X_0$ whose local weights, restricted to $X_0$, satisfy \[  \psi \geq \varphi _0-C  \] in compatible local frames, for a constant $C$. In particular, $h_0$ is neither the restriction of a semipositive metric on such a neighborhood nor of the same singularity type as such a restriction. Proof. Suppose that such a metric exists. Since $\pi $ is proper, we may shrink $\Delta $ so that the whole family lies in its domain: otherwise points outside the neighborhood over $t_ j	o 0$ would have a limit point on $X_0$ outside it. The lower bound makes the restricted weight finite at every point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $, because $\varphi _0$ is smooth there. Hence the restrictions of the weight to $\Gamma $ and to $q$ are not identically $-\infty $. Near a point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $, choose a product chart $(\zeta ,t)$ on $\Gamma $, as given by lemma 28.18.3 , and a holomorphic frame of $L$. The restricted weight $u(\zeta ,t)$ is plurisubharmonic and locally integrable. By Fubini's theorem, for almost every small $t
e 0$ its restriction to $C_ t$ is not identically $-\infty $, so the metric restricts to $C_ t$. The curvature of this restriction is a positive measure on the compact curve $C_ t$ of total mass $L_ t\cdot C_ t=0$, so it vanishes. Thus $u(\cdot ,t)$ is harmonic for almost every $t$. By lemma 28.18.5 below, whose proof does not use this theorem, the central slice $u(\cdot ,0)$ is harmonic or identically $-\infty $, and it is finite. Hence the restricted weight is harmonic near every point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $. The restricted metric on $L_0|_ q$ therefore has curvature supported at $p$. This curvature is a positive measure of total mass $L_0\cdot q=1$, so it is the Dirac measure $[p]$. In a coordinate $w$ on $q$ centered at $p$, the restricted weight is therefore $\log |w|^2$ plus a harmonic function, because their difference has zero distributional Laplacian. Since $\ell $ and $q$ meet transversely, $\varphi _0|_ q=	frac 12\log |w|^2+O(1)$. The difference $\psi |_ q-\varphi _0|_ q$ thus tends to $-\infty $ at $p$, contradicting the assumed lower bound. $\square$ The obstruction concerns the prescribed singularity type. Since $L$ is effective on the total space, the divisor metric of the zero divisor of a nonzero section of $L$ is a semipositive metric on $\mathcal X$, with a different restriction to $X_0$.

title: 28.18.1 The image of metric restriction
text:
28.18.1 The image of metric restriction The degree-zero conics also determine exactly which central metrics extend. We say that a semipositive metric $h$ on $L_0$ extends if there is a semipositive metric on $L$ over a neighborhood of $X_0$ whose local weights restrict to local weights of $h$; in particular, these restrictions are not identically $-\infty $. The following lemma is the slice argument used in the proof of theorem 28.18.4 . Lemma 28.18.5 . Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a product of disks $D_\zeta 	imes D_ t$ with $0\in D_ t$, and suppose that $u$ is not identically $-\infty $. Suppose that $u(\cdot ,t)$ is harmonic for almost every $t$. Then $u(\cdot ,0)$ is harmonic or identically $-\infty $. Proof. Since $u$ is locally integrable, Fubini's theorem gives $\partial _\zeta \partial _{ ar\zeta }u=0$ in the sense of distributions. On every fiber $X_ t$ with $t
e 0$ the two sections have no common zero, so the weight is not identically $-\infty $ there. e 0$, if $\phi _ B$ is the weight of $h_ B$ in the frame given by the section $\xi _2$, set \[  V(\xi _1,\xi _2)=\phi _ B(\xi _1/\xi _2)+\log |\xi _2|^2.  \] The other chart gives the same function, by the transition law of the metric. e 0$. title: 28.19 Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds
text: 28.19 Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds The compact manifolds studied so far in this chapter carry many closed positive currents, coming from divisors, fibrations or blowups. Inoue surfaces and their higher-dimensional analogues, the Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds, behave very differently. They are built from number fields, contain few or no complex subvarieties, and carry a natural closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form whose kernel is a holomorphic foliation by complex affine spaces. These leaves are Liouville and fill out real tori. As a result, every potential in this class is, up to a fixed logarithmic term, a continuous convex function of the transverse coordinates, so the class has no singular potentials at all, even though it contains positive currents supported on real hypersurfaces. In dimension three, a natural Gauduchon metric has an exactly quadratic mass functional of indefinite sign. Its masses lie on both sides of the background mass. These threefolds carry no Hermitian metric whose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ has a sign, so the known curvature criteria for bounded masses do not apply, and whether the masses remain bounded is an open question ( 33.3.16 ).

title: 28.19.1 The construction
text: 28.19.1 The construction Let $K$ be a number field of degree $s+2t$, with $s\geq 1$ real embeddings $\sigma _1,\ldots ,\sigma _ s$ and $t\geq 1$ pairs of complex conjugate embeddings $\sigma _{s+k},\overline{\sigma }_{s+k}$, $1\leq k\leq t$. Write $\mathcal O_ K$ for its ring of integers and $\mathcal O_ K^{*,+}$ for the group of totally positive units, that is, of units $\varepsilon $ with $\sigma _ j(\varepsilon )>0$ for $1\leq j\leq s$. Let $\mathbb H\subset \mathbb C$ be the upper half-plane. Write points of $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$ as $(w,z)$, with $w_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$, and put \[  \sigma _{\mathbb R}(a)=(\sigma _1(a),\ldots ,\sigma _ s(a)),\qquad \sigma _{\mathbb C}(a)=(\sigma _{s+1}(a),\ldots ,\sigma _{s+t}(a)).  \] An element $a\in \mathcal O_ K$ acts by the translation $(w,z)\mapsto (w+\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a),z+\sigma _{\mathbb C}(a))$, and $\varepsilon \in \mathcal O_ K^{*,+}$ acts by \[  (w,z)\longmapsto \bigl (\sigma _1(\varepsilon )w_1,\ldots ,\sigma _ s(\varepsilon )w_ s,\,  \sigma _{s+1}(\varepsilon )z_1,\ldots ,\sigma _{s+t}(\varepsilon )z_ t\bigr ).  \] A subgroup $U\subset \mathcal O_ K^{*,+}$ is admissible if its image \[  \Lambda _ U=\{ (\log \sigma _1(\varepsilon ),\ldots ,\log \sigma _ s(\varepsilon )):\varepsilon \in U\}   \] is a lattice in $\mathbb R^ s$. By Dirichlet's unit theorem, when $t=1$ every subgroup of finite index in $\mathcal O_ K^{*,+}$ is admissible. For admissible $U$, Oeljeklaus and Toma showed that the semidirect product $\Gamma =\mathcal O_ K\rtimes U$ acts freely and properly discontinuously on $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$ with compact quotient. The compact complex manifold \[  X=X(K,U)=(\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t)/\Gamma , \qquad n=\dim X=s+t,  \] is the Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold of type $(s,t)$. The same construction works if $\mathcal O_ K$ is replaced by any lattice $L\subset K$ of rank $s+2t$ that is stable under multiplication by $U$; for $s=t=1$ this produces the Inoue surfaces $S_ M$. The action is still free and cocompact: a point fixed by $(a,\varepsilon )$ with $\varepsilon \neq 1$ would have real coordinates $w_ j$, since $\sigma _ j(\varepsilon )\neq 1$ by injectivity of $\sigma _ j$, and $(\sigma _{\mathbb R},\sigma _{\mathbb C})(L)$ is again a lattice in $\mathbb R^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$. All results of this section other than corollary 28.19.4 hold, with the same proofs, in this generality, with $L$ in place of $\mathcal O_ K$; the only property of $\mathcal O_ K$ they use is that it spans $K$ over $\mathbb Q$. Corollary 28.19.4 also holds for every Inoue surface $S_ M$, since these contain no curves. The sources are discussed in section 34.16 . The functions $y_ j=\operatorname {Im}w_ j$ are invariant under the translations and are multiplied by $\sigma _ j(\varepsilon )$ under the unit $\varepsilon $. Hence the closed real $(1,1)$-form \[  \theta =-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sum _{j=1}^ s\log y_ j =\sum _{j=1}^ s\frac{\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw_ j\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_ j}{8\pi y_ j^2}  \] on $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$ is $\Gamma $-invariant and descends to a closed semipositive form on $X$, still denoted $\theta $. It has rank $s$ everywhere, and its kernel is spanned by the vectors $\partial /\partial z_ k$. The potential $-\sum _ j\log y_ j$ itself is not invariant, since a unit adds $-\sum _ j\log \sigma _ j(\varepsilon )$ to it.

title: 28.19.2 Potentials of the transverse form
text:
28.19.2 Potentials of the transverse form Two properties of the action force rigidity: the leaves $\{ w\} 	imes \mathbb C^ t$ are Liouville, and the real parts of the translations are dense. Lemma 28.19.1 . Since $t\geq 1$, the subgroup $\sigma _{\mathbb R}(\mathcal O_ K)$ is dense in $\mathbb R^ s$. Proof. A subgroup $G$ of $\mathbb R^ s$ is dense unless there is a nonzero linear form $\xi $ on $\mathbb R^ s$ with $\xi (G)\subseteq \mathbb Z$: the closure of $G$ is the sum of a linear subspace $V$ and a discrete subgroup of a complement of $V$, and if $V
eq \mathbb R^ s$ one can take $\xi $ vanishing on $V$ and integral on that discrete subgroup. Suppose $\xi (\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a))=\sum _ j\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)\in \mathbb Z$ for every $a\in \mathcal O_ K$. Since $\mathcal O_ K$ spans $K$ over $\mathbb Q$, the map $a\mapsto \sum _ j\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)$ is a $\mathbb Q$-linear map $K	o \mathbb Q$. The trace form of $K$ is nondegenerate, so there is $b\in K$ with \[  \sum _{j=1}^ s\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)=\operatorname {Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(ba) =\sum _{\sigma }\sigma (b)\sigma (a) \qquad (a\in K),  \] where $\sigma $ runs over all $s+2t$ embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb C$. Distinct field embeddings are linearly independent over $\mathbb C$, by Dedekind's lemma on characters. Comparing the coefficients of a complex embedding $\sigma _{s+1}$, which occurs only on the right, gives $\sigma _{s+1}(b)=0$. Hence $b=0$, and then $\xi _ j=\sigma _ j(b)=0$ for every $j$. $\square$ For $\varepsilon \in U$ and $y\in (0,\infty )^ s$, write $\sigma (\varepsilon )y=(\sigma _1(\varepsilon )y_1,\ldots ,\sigma _ s(\varepsilon )y_ s)$. Theorem 28.19.2 . Let $\mathcal F_ U$ be the set of convex functions $f:(0,\infty )^ s	o \mathbb R$ such that 28.68  egin{equation} \label{eq:ot-automorphy} f(\sigma (\varepsilon )y)=f(y)-\sum _{j=1}^ s\log \sigma _ j(\varepsilon ) \qquad (\varepsilon \in U). \end{equation} For $f\in \mathcal F_ U$, the function $u_ f(w,z)=f(y)+\sum _ j\log y_ j$ is $\Gamma $-invariant, and $f\mapsto u_ f$ is a bijection from $\mathcal F_ U$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. In particular, every $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is continuous and depends only on $y=\operatorname {Im}w$. Proof. We first note that a function $g$ on $\mathbb H^ s$ that depends only on $y$ is plurisubharmonic if and only if, as a function on $(0,\infty )^ s$, it is convex (with values in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$ and not identically $-\infty $). For smooth $g$ this follows from $\partial ^2g/\partial w_ j\partial \overline w_ k= rac14\partial ^2g/\partial y_ j\partial y_ k$. In general, convolution with a smooth radial kernel in $w$ produces smooth functions of $y$ alone; they decrease to $g$ if $g$ is plurisubharmonic, and they converge locally uniformly to $g$ if $g$ is convex, because a convex function that is not identically $-\infty $ on the open convex set $(0,\infty )^ s$ is finite and continuous there. Since decreasing limits of convex functions are convex and locally uniform limits of plurisubharmonic functions are plurisubharmonic, the claim follows. The identity ( 28.68 ) says exactly that $u_ f$ is invariant under $U$, and $u_ f$ is clearly invariant under the translations. On the universal cover, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ f=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)\geq 0$. Hence $u_ f\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and $f$ is recovered from $u_ f$, so the map is injective. Conversely, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and let $	ilde u$ be its lift to $\mathbb H^ s	imes \mathbb C^ t$. Since $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	ilde u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(	ilde u-\sum _ j\log y_ j)$ there, the function $q=	ilde u-\sum _ j\log y_ j$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb H^ s	imes \mathbb C^ t$. Step 1: constancy on the leaves. Fix $w^0\in \mathbb H^ s$. The restriction of $q$ to the slice $\{ w^0\} 	imes \mathbb C^ t$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, and it is bounded above because $u$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$. A plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb C^ t$ that is bounded above is constant, since its restriction to every complex line through two given points is a subharmonic function on $\mathbb C$ bounded above. Hence $	ilde u(w,z)=	ilde u(w,0)$ for all $(w,z)$. In particular, the function $F(w)=q(w,0)$ is not identically $-\infty $, because $	ilde u$ is not, and it is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb H^ s$. Step 2: invariance under real translations. The translations by $\mathcal O_ K$ and Step 1 give $F(w+\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a))=F(w)$ for every $a\in \mathcal O_ K$, since $\log y_ j$ does not change under real translations. For $r>0$, the averages $F_ r$ of $F$ over the Euclidean balls of radius $r$ are defined on $\{ w:\min _ jy_ j>r\} $ and continuous there, because $F$ is locally integrable, and they are invariant under the same translations. By lemma 28.19.1 and continuity, each $F_ r$ is invariant under all translations by $\mathbb R^ s$. Since $F_ r$ decreases to $F$ as $r\downarrow 0$, the function $F$ is invariant under all real translations as well, so $F(w)=f(y)$ for a function $f$ on $(0,\infty )^ s$. Step 3: convexity and automorphy. Since $F=f(y)$ is plurisubharmonic, the first paragraph of the proof shows that $f$ is convex, finite and continuous. Finally, $u=u_ f$, and invariance of $u$ under $U$ is ( 28.68 ). $\square$ Corollary 28.19.3 . On every Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold, all functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ are continuous. Consequently, they all have the ordinary singularity type of $0$, all their Lelong numbers vanish, all their multiplier ideals are trivial, and $P_	heta [u]=V_	heta =0$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Moreover $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=0$ for every $u$, so $	heta $ is nef but not big. Proof. Continuous functions on a compact manifold are bounded, so any two of them are equivalent, and their Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals are those of a bounded function. Since $	heta \geq 0$, the constant $0$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, so $V_	heta =0$, and $P_	heta [u]=P_	heta [0]=V_	heta $. By theorem 28.19.2 , locally $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)$ with $f$ continuous and depending on the $s$ real variables $y_ j$; the Bedford–Taylor products of such a current vanish in degree $s+1\leq n$, because they are limits of the corresponding products for smooth convex approximants of $f$, whose complex Hessians have rank at most $s$. Thus $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$. The form $	heta $ is smooth and semipositive, hence nef. Suppose that $ho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfied $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$. The function $ho $ is continuous, and on a small coordinate ball with coordinates $\zeta $ we may write $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ with $a$ smooth and $\delta \omega \geq \delta '\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|\zeta |^2$ with $\delta '>0$. Then $a+ho -\delta '|\zeta |^2$ is plurisubharmonic, and expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a+ho ))^ n$ as a sum of positive mixed Bedford–Taylor products gives $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (ho )\geq \delta '^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|\zeta |^2)^ n
eq 0$ on the ball, a contradiction. Hence $	heta $ is not big. $\square$ Singular currents nevertheless occur in this class. Let $s=t=1$, so that $X$ is an Inoue surface and $U$ is generated by a unit $\varepsilon _0$ with $\lambda =\sigma _1(\varepsilon _0)>1$. Fix $y_0>0$, put $y_ k=\lambda ^ ky_0$ for $k\in \mathbb Z$, and let $f$ be the continuous function that is affine on each interval $[y_ k,y_{k+1}]$ with slope \[  a_ k=- rac{\log \lambda }{(\lambda -1)y_ k}, \qquad f(y_0)=0.  \] Then $a_ k(y_{k+1}-y_ k)=-\log \lambda $, so $f(\lambda y)=f(y)-\log \lambda $, and the slopes increase because $a_{k+1}=a_ k/\lambda $ and $a_ k<0$. Thus $f\in \mathcal F_ U$. On the universal cover, \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ f=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)= rac1{4\pi }\sum _{k\in \mathbb Z}(a_ k-a_{k-1})\,  \delta (y-y_ k)\, \mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm dy,  \] with $a_ k-a_{k-1}>0$. The closed positive current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ f$ therefore has a continuous potential but is supported on the compact real hypersurface of $X$ formed by the images of the hyperplanes $\{ y=y_ k\} $, a three-dimensional torus that is a union of leaves of the foliation $\{ w=	ext{const}\} $. On an Inoue surface, $	heta $ represents the canonical Bott–Chern class. Indeed, the Tricerri metric $\omega _ T=8\pi 	heta +y\, \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z$ has $\omega _ T^2=(2/y)\, \mathrm i\, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d\overline w\wedge \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z$, so its normalized Chern–Ricci form $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (\omega _ T^2/\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d\overline w\wedge \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z)$, which is $-\mathrm i\partial \overline\partial \log \det \omega _ T$ divided by $2\pi $ and represents $c_1^{BC}(X)$, equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log y=-	heta $. Hence theorem 28.19.2 describes all positive currents in $c_1^{BC}(K_ X)$, and none of them has a pole. Arbitrary backgrounds behave differently, since a Hermitian form has potentials with logarithmic poles. Nevertheless, when $t=1$ their singularities are confined to finite sets. By a theorem of Ornea and Verbitsky (section 34.16 ), an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold with $t=1$ contains no complex subvarieties of positive dimension. Corollary 28.19.4 . Let $X$ be an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold with $t=1$, let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$. For every $c>0$, the set $\{ x:
u (u,x)\geq c\} $ is finite. Consequently, for every $k>0$ the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(ku)$ is trivial outside a finite set, and $\mathcal I(ku)$ has finite colength. Proof. By Siu's theorem ( 1.13.1 ), the set $E_ c=\{ 
u (u,\cdot )\geq c\} $ is a compact analytic subset of $X$. It is a proper subset, because $
u (u,x)=0$ outside the pluripolar set $\{ u=-\infty \} $, which has Lebesgue measure zero. Hence $E_ c$ is finite by the theorem of Ornea and Verbitsky. By Skoda's integrability criterion, recalled in [ SGPT ] , $\mathcal I(ku)_ x=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ whenever $k
u (u,x)<1$, so $\mathcal I(ku)$ is trivial outside the finite set $E_{1/k}$. A coherent ideal sheaf that is trivial outside a finite set has finite colength. $\square$

title: Lemma 28.19.1
text: Lemma 28.19.1 . Since $t\geq 1$, the subgroup $\sigma _{\mathbb R}(\mathcal O_ K)$ is dense in $\mathbb R^ s$. Proof. A subgroup $G$ of $\mathbb R^ s$ is dense unless there is a nonzero linear form $\xi $ on $\mathbb R^ s$ with $\xi (G)\subseteq \mathbb Z$: the closure of $G$ is the sum of a linear subspace $V$ and a discrete subgroup of a complement of $V$, and if $V\neq \mathbb R^ s$ one can take $\xi $ vanishing on $V$ and integral on that discrete subgroup. Suppose $\xi (\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a))=\sum _ j\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)\in \mathbb Z$ for every $a\in \mathcal O_ K$. Since $\mathcal O_ K$ spans $K$ over $\mathbb Q$, the map $a\mapsto \sum _ j\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)$ is a $\mathbb Q$-linear map $K\to \mathbb Q$. The trace form of $K$ is nondegenerate, so there is $b\in K$ with \[  \sum _{j=1}^ s\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)=\operatorname {Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(ba) =\sum _{\sigma }\sigma (b)\sigma (a) \qquad (a\in K),  \] where $\sigma $ runs over all $s+2t$ embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb C$. Distinct field embeddings are linearly independent over $\mathbb C$, by Dedekind's lemma on characters. Comparing the coefficients of a complex embedding $\sigma _{s+1}$, which occurs only on the right, gives $\sigma _{s+1}(b)=0$. Hence $b=0$, and then $\xi _ j=\sigma _ j(b)=0$ for every $j$. $\square$

title: Theorem 28.19.2
text: Theorem 28.19.2 . Let $\mathcal F_ U$ be the set of convex functions $f:(0,\infty )^ s\to \mathbb R$ such that 28.68 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ot-automorphy} f(\sigma (\varepsilon )y)=f(y)-\sum _{j=1}^ s\log \sigma _ j(\varepsilon ) \qquad (\varepsilon \in U). \end{equation} For $f\in \mathcal F_ U$, the function $u_ f(w,z)=f(y)+\sum _ j\log y_ j$ is $\Gamma $-invariant, and $f\mapsto u_ f$ is a bijection from $\mathcal F_ U$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. In particular, every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is continuous and depends only on $y=\operatorname {Im}w$. Proof. We first note that a function $g$ on $\mathbb H^ s$ that depends only on $y$ is plurisubharmonic if and only if, as a function on $(0,\infty )^ s$, it is convex (with values in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$ and not identically $-\infty $). For smooth $g$ this follows from $\partial ^2g/\partial w_ j\partial \overline w_ k=\frac14\partial ^2g/\partial y_ j\partial y_ k$. In general, convolution with a smooth radial kernel in $w$ produces smooth functions of $y$ alone; they decrease to $g$ if $g$ is plurisubharmonic, and they converge locally uniformly to $g$ if $g$ is convex, because a convex function that is not identically $-\infty $ on the open convex set $(0,\infty )^ s$ is finite and continuous there. Since decreasing limits of convex functions are convex and locally uniform limits of plurisubharmonic functions are plurisubharmonic, the claim follows. The identity ( 28.68 ) says exactly that $u_ f$ is invariant under $U$, and $u_ f$ is clearly invariant under the translations. On the universal cover, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ f=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)\geq 0$. Hence $u_ f\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $f$ is recovered from $u_ f$, so the map is injective. Conversely, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $\tilde u$ be its lift to $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$. Since $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tilde u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\tilde u-\sum _ j\log y_ j)$ there, the function $q=\tilde u-\sum _ j\log y_ j$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$. Step 1: constancy on the leaves. Fix $w^0\in \mathbb H^ s$. The restriction of $q$ to the slice $\{ w^0\} \times \mathbb C^ t$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, and it is bounded above because $u$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$. A plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb C^ t$ that is bounded above is constant, since its restriction to every complex line through two given points is a subharmonic function on $\mathbb C$ bounded above. Hence $\tilde u(w,z)=\tilde u(w,0)$ for all $(w,z)$. In particular, the function $F(w)=q(w,0)$ is not identically $-\infty $, because $\tilde u$ is not, and it is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb H^ s$. Step 2: invariance under real translations. The translations by $\mathcal O_ K$ and Step 1 give $F(w+\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a))=F(w)$ for every $a\in \mathcal O_ K$, since $\log y_ j$ does not change under real translations. For $r>0$, the averages $F_ r$ of $F$ over the Euclidean balls of radius $r$ are defined on $\{ w:\min _ jy_ j>r\} $ and continuous there, because $F$ is locally integrable, and they are invariant under the same translations. By lemma 28.19.1 and continuity, each $F_ r$ is invariant under all translations by $\mathbb R^ s$. Since $F_ r$ decreases to $F$ as $r\downarrow 0$, the function $F$ is invariant under all real translations as well, so $F(w)=f(y)$ for a function $f$ on $(0,\infty )^ s$. Step 3: convexity and automorphy. Since $F=f(y)$ is plurisubharmonic, the first paragraph of the proof shows that $f$ is convex, finite and continuous. Finally, $u=u_ f$, and invariance of $u$ under $U$ is ( 28.68 ). $\square$

title: Corollary 28.19.3
text: Corollary 28.19.3 . On every Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold, all functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ are continuous. Consequently, they all have the ordinary singularity type of $0$, all their Lelong numbers vanish, all their multiplier ideals are trivial, and $P_\theta [u]=V_\theta =0$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Moreover $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=0$ for every $u$, so $\theta $ is nef but not big. Proof. Continuous functions on a compact manifold are bounded, so any two of them are equivalent, and their Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals are those of a bounded function. Since $\theta \geq 0$, the constant $0$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, so $V_\theta =0$, and $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [0]=V_\theta $. By theorem 28.19.2 , locally $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)$ with $f$ continuous and depending on the $s$ real variables $y_ j$; the Bedford–Taylor products of such a current vanish in degree $s+1\leq n$, because they are limits of the corresponding products for smooth convex approximants of $f$, whose complex Hessians have rank at most $s$. Thus $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$. The form $\theta $ is smooth and semipositive, hence nef. Suppose that $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfied $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$. The function $\rho $ is continuous, and on a small coordinate ball with coordinates $\zeta $ we may write $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ with $a$ smooth and $\delta \omega \geq \delta '\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|\zeta |^2$ with $\delta '>0$. Then $a+\rho -\delta '|\zeta |^2$ is plurisubharmonic, and expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a+\rho ))^ n$ as a sum of positive mixed Bedford–Taylor products gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\rho )\geq \delta '^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|\zeta |^2)^ n\neq 0$ on the ball, a contradiction. Hence $\theta $ is not big. $\square$

Corollary 28.19.4 . Let $X$ be an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold with $t=1$, let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$. For every $c>0$, the set $\{ x:
u (u,x)\geq c\} $ is finite. Consequently, for every $k>0$ the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(ku)$ is trivial outside a finite set, and $\mathcal I(ku)$ has finite colength. Proof. By Siu's theorem ( 1.13.1 ), the set $E_ c=\{ 
u (u,\cdot )\geq c\} $ is a compact analytic subset of $X$. It is a proper subset, because $
u (u,x)=0$ outside the pluripolar set $\{ u=-\infty \} $, which has Lebesgue measure zero. Hence $E_ c$ is finite by the theorem of Ornea and Verbitsky. By Skoda's integrability criterion, recalled in [ SGPT ] , $\mathcal I(ku)_ x=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ whenever $k

title: 28.19.3 Monge–Ampère masses on threefolds
text: 28.19.3 Monge–Ampère masses on threefolds Now let $s=2$ and $t=1$, so that $X$ is a threefold. A totally positive unit has norm $\sigma _1(\varepsilon )\sigma _2(\varepsilon )|\sigma _3(\varepsilon )|^2=1$, so the form $y_1y_2\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ is $\Gamma $-invariant. The Hermitian form \[  \omega =\theta +\beta ,\qquad \beta =y_1y_2\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2,  \] descends to $X$. Write $\mathrm dV_0=(\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw_1\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_1)\wedge (\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw_2\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_2)\wedge (\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z)$ on the universal cover, and $\mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3$. A unit that fixes $y_1$ satisfies $\sigma _1(\varepsilon )=1$, hence $\varepsilon =1$ because $\sigma _1$ is injective. Hence the map $X\to T_ U=\mathbb R^2/\Lambda _ U$, $[w,z]\mapsto (\log y_1,\log y_2)$, has as fibers the real tori $(\mathbb R^2\times \mathbb C)/(\sigma _{\mathbb R},\sigma _{\mathbb C})(\mathcal O_ K)$, and for every $\Lambda _ U$-periodic function $g$ of $\varsigma =(\log y_1,\log y_2)$ there is a constant $c_ X>0$, independent of $g$, with 28.69 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ot-fiber-integration} \int _ Xg(\varsigma )\, \frac{\mathrm dV_0}{y_1y_2} =c_ X\int _{T_ U}g\, \mathrm d\varsigma . \end{equation} We shall use an elementary property of lattices in the plane: every lattice $\Lambda \subset \mathbb R^2$ contains vectors in each of the four open quadrants. Indeed, let $\ell >0$ be the length of a shortest nonzero vector of $\Lambda $, and let $0<\delta <\ell $. By Minkowski's theorem, the symmetric convex set $\{ k:|k_1-k_2|<\delta ,\  |k_1+k_2|<N\} $ contains a nonzero lattice point once $N$ is large. Such a point satisfies $(k_1+k_2)^2=2|k|^2-(k_1-k_2)^2\geq 2\ell ^2-\delta ^2$, hence $4k_1k_2=(k_1+k_2)^2-(k_1-k_2)^2>0$; replacing $k$ by $-k$ if necessary gives a point in the open first quadrant, and the line $\mathbb R(1,-1)$ gives the other two quadrants in the same way. If $\lambda $ lies in the open first quadrant and $\mu \in \Lambda $ is independent of $\lambda $, then $N\lambda +\mu $ also lies there for large $N$, so the first quadrant contains two independent lattice vectors. Proposition 28.19.5 . Let $X$ be an Oeljeklaus–Toma threefold of type $(2,1)$ with the Hermitian form $\omega $ above. The form $\omega $ is Gauduchon, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(y_1y_2)\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ is neither semipositive nor seminegative. For every smooth real function $u$ on $X$, \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^3+\frac{3}{16\pi ^3}\int _ X \operatorname {Re}\Bigl (\frac{\partial u}{\partial w_1}\,  \overline{\frac{\partial u}{\partial w_2}}\Bigr )\mathrm dV_0.  \] Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be bounded and depend only on $y$, and write $u=g(\varsigma )$ with $g$ periodic under $\Lambda _ U$. Then $g$ is Lipschitz, $P=1-\partial _1g$ and $Q=1-\partial _2g$ are nonnegative almost everywhere, and \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\frac{\int _ X\omega ^3}{|T_ U|}\int _{T_ U}PQ\, \mathrm d\varsigma .  \] There is a constant $c_ U\geq 1$, depending only on $\Lambda _ U$, such that every such $u$ satisfies $c_ U^{-1}\int _ X\omega ^3\leq \mathrm M_\omega (u)\leq c_ U\int _ X\omega ^3$. There are smooth $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, depending only on $y$, with $\mathrm M_\omega (u)>\int _ X\omega ^3$, and others with $\mathrm M_\omega (u)<\int _ X\omega ^3$. Consequently $v_-(\omega )<\int _ X\omega ^3<v_+(\omega )$. Proof. (1) Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ has constant coefficients and $y_ j$ is pluriharmonic, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(y_1y_2)\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2,  \] where \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(y_1y_2)=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\bigl (\partial y_1\wedge \overline\partial y_2 +\partial y_2\wedge \overline\partial y_1\bigr ) =\frac{\mathrm i}{8\pi }\bigl (\mathrm dw_1\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_2 +\mathrm dw_2\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_1\bigr ).  \] The Hermitian matrix of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(y_1y_2)$ in the basis $\mathrm dw_1,\mathrm dw_2$ is a positive multiple of $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0& 1\\ 1& 0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, which is indefinite. Accordingly, for $\eta _\pm =\mathrm dw_1\pm \mathrm dw_2$ the $(3,3)$-forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm i\eta _\pm \wedge \overline\eta _\pm $ are respectively negative and positive multiples of $\mathrm dV_0$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta $ is neither semipositive nor seminegative. Since $\theta $ is closed and $\beta ^2=0$, we have $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=2\theta \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta $, and this vanishes because every term of $\theta \wedge (\mathrm dw_1\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_2+\mathrm dw_2\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_1)$ repeats a differential. (2) By theorem 2.2.1 with $n=3$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$, $\mathrm M_\omega (u)-\int _ X\omega ^3=3\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. The form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ is closed, so Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\int _ X\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. Now $\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u=(\mathrm i/2\pi )\, \partial u\wedge \overline\partial u$, and a direct computation in the coordinates $w_1,w_2,z$ gives \[  \mathrm i\, \partial u\wedge \overline\partial u\wedge \mathrm i\bigl (\mathrm dw_1\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_2+\mathrm dw_2\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_1\bigr ) \wedge \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z =-2\operatorname {Re}\Bigl (\frac{\partial u}{\partial w_1}\,  \overline{\frac{\partial u}{\partial w_2}}\Bigr )\mathrm dV_0.  \] Collecting the constants $(1/2\pi )(1/8\pi )(1/2\pi )$ gives the formula. (3) Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has no components in the $z$-direction, $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+\beta $ splits into blocks, and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ if and only if $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By theorem 28.19.2 , $u=f(y)+\log (y_1y_2)$ with $f$ convex, so $g$ is locally Lipschitz, hence Lipschitz by periodicity. In the variables $\varsigma _ j=\log y_ j$, convexity of $f$ is equivalent to positivity of the symmetric matrix \[  H=I+D^2g-\operatorname {diag}(\partial _1g,\partial _2g),  \] as one checks from $y_ iy_ j\, \partial ^2f/\partial y_ i\partial y_ j=\partial ^2\Phi /\partial \varsigma _ i\partial \varsigma _ j-\delta _{ij}\, \partial \Phi /\partial \varsigma _ i$ for $\Phi (\varsigma )=f(\mathrm e^{\varsigma })=g(\varsigma )-\varsigma _1-\varsigma _2$. This condition is linear in $g$ with constant coefficients, so it is preserved by convolution with a smooth kernel on $\mathbb R^2$; the regularized functions are periodic, and they converge uniformly to $g$ with gradients converging almost everywhere. By the continuity of bounded Monge–Ampère products under uniform convergence and dominated convergence, it suffices to prove all assertions for smooth $g$ with $H\geq 0$. For such $g$, the function $u$ depends only on $y$, so $\partial u/\partial w_ j=-\frac{\mathrm i}2\partial u/\partial y_ j$ and the integrand in (2) is $\frac14\partial _{y_1}u\, \partial _{y_2}u=\partial _1g\, \partial _2g/(4y_1y_2)$. A direct computation gives $\omega ^3=3\theta ^2\wedge \beta =\frac{3}{64\pi ^3}\, \mathrm dV_0/(y_1y_2)$. By ( 28.69 ) and (2), \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\frac{\int _ X\omega ^3}{|T_ U|}\int _{T_ U} \bigl (1+\partial _1g\, \partial _2g\bigr )\, \mathrm d\varsigma =\frac{\int _ X\omega ^3}{|T_ U|}\int _{T_ U}PQ\, \mathrm d\varsigma ,  \] where the second equality uses $\int _{T_ U}\partial _ jg\, \mathrm d\varsigma =0$. The diagonal entry $H_{11}=P-\partial _1P\geq 0$ says that $\mathrm e^{-\varsigma _1}P$ is nonincreasing in $\varsigma _1$, that is, 28.70 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ot-p-monotone} P(\varsigma +\tau e_1)\leq \mathrm e^{\tau }P(\varsigma )\qquad (\tau \geq 0). \end{equation} If $P(\varsigma )<0$, the right side tends to $-\infty $ as $\tau \to \infty $, which is impossible for the bounded function $P$; hence $P\geq 0$, and likewise $Q\geq 0$. Thus $\partial _ jg\leq 1$. The lattice $\Lambda _ U$ contains two independent vectors $\lambda ,\lambda '$ with positive coordinates, and every point of $T_ U$ has the form $\varsigma +\tau \lambda +\tau '\lambda '$ with $\tau ,\tau '\in [0,1)$. Along $\tau \mapsto \varsigma +\tau \lambda $, the derivative of $g$ is at most $|\lambda |_1=\lambda _1+\lambda _2$, and its integral over $[0,1]$ vanishes by periodicity, so $|g(\varsigma +\tau \lambda )-g(\varsigma )|\leq |\lambda |_1$. Hence $\operatorname {osc}g\leq L$, with $L=|\lambda |_1+|\lambda '|_1$ depending only on $\Lambda _ U$. (4) Let $k$ belong to the dual lattice $\Lambda _ U^*=\{ k\in \mathbb R^2:\langle k,\lambda \rangle \in \mathbb Z\text{ for all }\lambda \in \Lambda _ U\} $, and put $g_\epsilon (\varsigma )=\epsilon \cos (2\pi \langle k,\varsigma \rangle )$. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ let $Au$ be the average of $u$ over the fibers of $X\to T_ U$, that is, over the translations $(w,z)\mapsto (w+r,z+\zeta )$ with $(r,\zeta )\in (\mathbb R^2\times \mathbb C)/(\sigma _{\mathbb R},\sigma _{\mathbb C})(\mathcal O_ K)$. These translations preserve $\omega $ on the universal cover. They do not descend to $X$ individually, but conjugation by a unit $\varepsilon $ carries the translation by $(r,\zeta )$ to the translation by $(\sigma _1(\varepsilon )r_1,\sigma _2(\varepsilon )r_2,\sigma _3(\varepsilon )\zeta )$, and this automorphism of the translation torus preserves its Haar measure because $\varepsilon $ has norm one. Hence $Au$ is a well-defined $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function depending only on $y$, and $c_ U^{-1}\int _ X\omega ^3\leq \mathrm M_\omega (Au)\leq c_ U\int _ X\omega ^3$ by proposition 28.19.5 . For smooth $u$, the integral of a $y$-derivative of $u-Au$ over a fiber vanishes, and so does the integral of an $x$-derivative. The cross terms between $Au$ and $u-Au$ in proposition 28.19.5 (2) therefore integrate to zero, and 28.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ot-fluctuation} \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\mathrm M_\omega (Au)+\frac{3}{16\pi ^3}\int _ X \operatorname {Re}\Bigl (\frac{\partial v}{\partial w_1}\,  \overline{\frac{\partial v}{\partial w_2}}\Bigr )\mathrm dV_0, \qquad v=u-Au. \end{equation} Since the extrema of the masses of bounded potentials equal the extrema over smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials (proposition 6.5.2 , theorem 26.14.3 ), $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $ if and only if the fluctuation term in ( 28.71 ) is bounded above on smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions; likewise, $v_-(\omega )>0$ if and only if $\mathrm M_\omega (Au)$ plus the fluctuation term is bounded below by a positive constant on such functions.

text: 28.19.4 Hermitian metrics whose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ has a sign Finally, we show that no Hermitian metric on these manifolds has a $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of constant sign, so that curvature criteria based on such metrics cannot settle the boundedness of the masses. Proposition 28.19.6 . Let $X$ be an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold of type $(s,1)$ with $s\geq 2$. Then $X$ admits no Hermitian form $\widetilde\omega $ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde\omega $ is semipositive, or seminegative, on every complex $2$-plane. Proof. Suppose $\widetilde\omega $ is such a form, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde\omega \geq 0$ on every complex $2$-plane; the other case is analogous. Average the lift of $\widetilde\omega $ over the translations $(w,z)\mapsto (w+r,z+\zeta )$, $(r,\zeta )\in (\mathbb R^ s\times \mathbb C)/(\sigma _{\mathbb R},\sigma _{\mathbb C})(\mathcal O_ K)$, as in the definition of $Au$ above. The averaged form $\overline\omega $ is again $\Gamma $-invariant and Hermitian, its coefficients in the frame $\mathrm dw_1,\ldots ,\mathrm dw_ s,\mathrm dz$ depend only on $y$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\overline\omega \geq 0$ on complex $2$-planes, because translations are holomorphic and positivity on $2$-planes is preserved by averaging. Let $h(y)>0$ be the coefficient of $\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z$ in $\overline\omega $. Invariance under a unit $\varepsilon $ gives $h(\sigma (\varepsilon )y)|\sigma _{s+1}(\varepsilon )|^2=h(y)$, that is, $h(\sigma (\varepsilon )y)=\sigma _1(\varepsilon )\cdots \sigma _ s(\varepsilon )\, h(y)$, since $\varepsilon $ has norm one. Hence $h/(y_1\cdots y_ s)$ is invariant under $U$, and since $\Lambda _ U$ is a lattice it is bounded between two positive constants: 28.72 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ot-h-growth} c\, y_1\cdots y_ s\leq h(y)\leq C\, y_1\cdots y_ s. \end{equation} Let $v$ be a nonzero vector in the span of $\partial /\partial w_1,\ldots ,\partial /\partial w_ s$, and let $P$ be the complex $2$-plane spanned by $v$ and $\partial /\partial z$. Write $\overline\omega =\sum _{a,b}g_{ab}(y)\, \mathrm i\, \xi _ a\wedge \overline\xi _ b$ with $\xi =(\mathrm dw_1,\ldots ,\mathrm dw_ s,\mathrm dz)$. Since the forms $\xi _ a$ are closed, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\overline\omega =\sum _{a,b}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_{ab}\wedge \mathrm i\, \xi _ a\wedge \overline\xi _ b$, and each $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_{ab}$ has only $w$-components. A term restricted to $P$ is nonzero only if it contains both $\mathrm dz$ and $\mathrm d\overline z$, which happens only for $\xi _ a=\xi _ b=\mathrm dz$. Hence the restriction of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\overline\omega $ to $P$ equals the restriction of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z$, and its sign is that of the value of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $v$. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\geq 0$ in the $w$-variables, and $h$ is convex in $y$. Let $R>1$ and put $A=(R,R^{-1},1,\ldots ,1)$, $B=(R^{-1},R,1,\ldots ,1)$ and $M=(A+B)/2$. By ( 28.72 ), $h(A),h(B)\leq C$, whereas $h(M)\geq c(R+R^{-1})^2/4$, which contradicts convexity for large $R$. In the seminegative case, $h$ is concave, so $t\mapsto h(t,\ldots ,t)$ grows at most linearly as $t\to \infty $; this contradicts the lower bound $h(t,\ldots ,t)\geq ct^ s$ with $s\geq 2$. $\square$ For $s=t=1$ the same averaging produces a coefficient $h$ comparable to $y$, which may be affine; indeed the Tricerri metric is pluriclosed. In dimension three, the curvature criteria for finite upper and positive lower mass recalled in section 34.16 require a metric with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \geq 0$, respectively $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$, and proposition 28.19.6 excludes both on threefolds of type $(2,1)$.

title: 29 Locally conformally Kähler geometry
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 29 Locally conformally Kähler geometry Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$. A locally conformally Kähler (LCK) metric is a Hermitian metric that becomes Kähler after local conformal changes, and its Lee form measures the obstruction to making this change globally. On a covering on which the Lee form is exact, the Kähler metric and its admissible potentials change by the same character under deck transformations. Descending this potential calculus to $X$ gives a twisted complex Hessian with a zeroth-order term, so that even adding a constant to a potential changes the metric. The standard Vaisman metric on the Hopf manifold illustrates the difference between the two potential theories: although it is locally conformally Kähler, its ordinary potentials have unbounded Monge–Ampère masses. Prescribing the volume while keeping the Lee class and the Gauduchon gauge couples the determinant equation with an equation for the conformal factor. For a volume invariant under the Lee and anti-Lee flows of a Vaisman metric, uniqueness for the ordinary smooth equation gives a potential that is constant along these flows. Stokes' theorem in the transverse directions fixes the normalizing constant, and changing the Lee form reconstructs the required Vaisman metric. On scalar Hopf manifolds, radial symmetry reduces the coupled equations to a periodic ordinary differential equation. Its positive solutions are ordered by their Lee periods, so the metric is determined by its Lee period and its volume; for a nonconstant radial volume, this metric is not Vaisman. A different compatibility condition gives rigidity: when an LCK metric is both Gauduchon and Chern–Ricci flat, the Bianchi and Bochner identities force its harmonic Lee form to be parallel. The Lee form also produces a closed curvature class that can be nonzero in Bott–Chern cohomology while vanishing in de Rham cohomology. Pairing these classes with all Gauduchon metrics defines the Lee–Gauduchon cone, which detects their pseudoeffectivity and is invariant under bimeromorphic maps. Strongly Gauduchon metrics exclude all nonzero positive de Rham-exact currents and bound the linear mass of closed positive currents by their de Rham classes. The Calabi–Eckmann example separates this condition from the presence of zero in the Lee–Gauduchon cone, and a balanced elliptic fibration shows that it still allows zero lower Monge–Ampère mass.

29.1 The Lee form and the Kähler covering A Hermitian form is locally conformally Kähler when its exterior derivative is controlled by a closed one-form. Definition 29.1.1 . A Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$ is locally conformally Kähler , or LCK, if there is a smooth real one-form $\lambda $ on $X$ such that \[  \mathrm{d}\omega =\lambda \wedge \omega , \qquad \mathrm{d}\lambda =0.  \] The form $\lambda $ is called its Lee form . The metric is strictly LCK if $\lambda $ is not exact. A strictly LCK metric is Vaisman if its Lee form is parallel for the Levi–Civita connection of the associated Riemannian metric. Fix an LCK metric $\omega $ with Lee form $\lambda $. On a compact manifold a nonzero parallel one-form cannot be exact: the differential of a function vanishes at a maximum, whereas a parallel form has constant length. Thus a nonzero parallel Lee form is automatically nowhere zero and not exact. The Lee form is determined by $\omega $, because the map $a\mapsto a\wedge \omega $ is injective on one-forms: after wedging with $\omega ^{n-2}$, this follows from the bijectivity of the Lefschetz map $a\mapsto a\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ on one-forms. Locally write $\lambda =\mathrm{d}f$. Then \[  \Omega =\mathrm{e}^{-f}\omega >0,\qquad \mathrm{d}\Omega =0,  \] so $\Omega $ is a Kähler form. Choose a connected regular covering $\pi :\widetilde X	o X$ on which $\pi ^*\lambda =\mathrm{d}F$, for example the universal covering. The quotient of $\widetilde X$ by its deck group is $X$. The same construction gives a Kähler form 29.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:lck-cover} \widetilde\omega =\mathrm{e}^{-F}\pi ^*\omega . \end{equation} For a deck transformation $\sigma $, the difference $\sigma ^*F-F=c_\sigma $ is constant, and \[  \sigma ^*\widetilde\omega =\chi (\sigma )\widetilde\omega , \qquad \chi (\sigma )=\mathrm{e}^{-c_\sigma }.  \] Thus $\chi $ is a homomorphism from the deck group to the multiplicative group of positive real numbers, which records how the Kähler metric is rescaled. Forms on $\widetilde X$ transforming by $\chi $ may equivalently be viewed as forms on $X$ with values in the flat real line bundle defined by $\chi $, the weight bundle . In this sense an LCK form is closed as a form with values in the weight bundle [ Section 3.4 , OV24LCK ] . Let $g$ be the Riemannian metric of $\omega $, let $J$ be the complex structure, and let $\lambda ^\sharp $ be the vector field dual to $\lambda $ with respect to $g$. On a chart where $\lambda =\mathrm df$, the metric $\widetilde g=\mathrm{e}^{-f}g$ is Kähler. For real vector fields $U,V$, the Levi–Civita connections $
abla $ of $g$ and $\widetilde
abla $ of $\widetilde g$ are related by \[  \widetilde
abla _ UV=
abla _ UV-	frac 12 igl (\lambda (U)V+\lambda (V)U-g(U,V)\lambda ^\sharp  igr ).  \] Substituting $JV$ for $V$ and using $\widetilde
abla J=0$ gives 29.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:lck-complex-connection} (
abla _ UJ)V=	frac 12 igl (\lambda (JV)U-\lambda (V)JU+g(U,V)J\lambda ^\sharp +g(JU,V)\lambda ^\sharp  igr ). \end{equation} Both sides are global tensors, so this identity holds on all of $X$. For $a\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, the conformal change $\omega '=\mathrm{e}^ a\omega $ replaces the Lee form by $\lambda +\mathrm{d}a$. In particular, the de Rham class $[\lambda ]$ depends only on the conformal class of $\omega $. If $\lambda $ is exact, the construction above gives a Kähler form on $X$ itself.

title: Definition 29.1.1
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Definition 29.1.1 . A Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$ is locally conformally Kähler , or LCK, if there is a smooth real one-form $\lambda $ on $X$ such that \[  \mathrm{d}\omega =\lambda \wedge \omega , \qquad \mathrm{d}\lambda =0.  \] The form $\lambda $ is called its Lee form . The metric is strictly LCK if $\lambda $ is not exact. A strictly LCK metric is Vaisman if its Lee form is parallel for the Levi–Civita connection of the associated Riemannian metric.

title: 29.2 Gauduchon representatives and the Lee class
