text:
29.2 Gauduchon representatives and the Lee class In the conformal class of an LCK metric, the Gauduchon representative is the one whose Lee form is harmonic. A closed $(1,1)$-form built from the Lee form pairs positively with this Gauduchon metric when the structure is strictly LCK, even though the form is de Rham exact. It therefore defines a nonzero Bott–Chern class, which obstructs Kähler modifications. Set \[  \lambda ^{\mathrm c} = rac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }(\lambda ^{0,1}-\lambda ^{1,0}),  \] so that $\lambda ^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f$ wherever $\lambda =\mathrm{d}f$. The closed real $(1,1)$-form 29.3  egin{equation} \label{eq:lck-lee-curvature} \kappa _\lambda :=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\lambda =-\mathrm{d}\lambda ^{\mathrm c} \end{equation} connects the Lee class with Bott–Chern cohomology. It is de Rham exact, but it need not be $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. Proposition 29.2.1 . An LCK metric is Gauduchon if and only if its Lee form is co-closed for that metric. Consequently, the Gauduchon representative in its conformal class has harmonic Lee form. Moreover, for every LCK metric, 29.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:lck-lee-degree} \int _ X\kappa _\lambda \wedge \omega ^{n-1} =(n-1)\int _ X\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1}. \end{equation} If $\lambda 
ot\equiv 0$, the right side is strictly positive. Proof. On a chart where $\omega $ is conformally Kähler, \[  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\omega ^{n-1}) =(n-1)\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1}.  \] Let $*$ be the real Hodge star of the Riemannian metric associated with $\omega $, and let $\mathrm d^*$ be the formal adjoint of the exterior derivative. By the pointwise Hodge-star identities for Hermitian metrics, $\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ is a fixed nonzero constant multiple of $*\lambda $. Consequently, the Gauduchon condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-1})=0$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{d}*\lambda =0$, that is, to $\mathrm{d}^*\lambda =0$. Since $\mathrm{d}\lambda =0$, co-closedness is equivalent to harmonicity. The Gauduchon representative exists by theorem 4.1.2 , and conformal changes preserve the LCK condition. Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{d}(\omega ^{n-1})=(n-1)\lambda \wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ give \[   egin{split}  -\int _ X\mathrm{d}\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1} & =-\int _ X\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \mathrm{d}(\omega ^{n-1})\ & =(n-1)\int _ X\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1}. \end{split}  \] For a real one-form, $\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c} =\mathrm i\lambda ^{1,0}\wedge \lambda ^{0,1}/(2\pi )$ is semipositive, and its trace with respect to $\omega $ is positive wherever $\lambda 
e 0$. This proves the last assertion. $\square$ The same construction applies to every closed real one-form and defines a linear map 29.7  egin{equation} \label{eq:lck-lee-bc-map} j_ X:H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R), \qquad [\lambda ]\longmapsto \{ \kappa _\lambda \} , \end{equation} which we call the Lee map . It is well defined, since replacing $\lambda $ by $\lambda +\mathrm{d}a$ replaces $\kappa _\lambda $ by $\kappa _\lambda -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$. Consequently, the pairing of $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ with any Gauduchon form $\gamma ^{n-1}$ is well defined. For a strictly LCK structure, the Gauduchon representative in its conformal class gives a strictly positive pairing by ( 29.4 ). In particular $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} 
e 0$, although its image in de Rham cohomology is zero. Corollary 29.2.2 . If $X$ carries a strictly LCK metric, then no class in $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$ is big. In particular, $X$ does not belong to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$. Proof. If there were a big class, the modification criterion recalled in chapter 28 would give a modification $\pi :Y	o X$ with $Y$ compact Kähler. The form $\pi ^*\kappa _\lambda $ is closed and de Rham exact, so the $\partial  ar\partial $-lemma on $Y$ gives a smooth real function $h$ on $Y$ with $\pi ^*\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. Since $\pi $ has degree one, pushing forward gives the current identity $\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\pi _*h)$. By Stokes' theorem, the pairing of this current with a Gauduchon form is zero, which contradicts ( 29.4 ) for the Gauduchon representative of the LCK structure. $\square$ For the Hopf manifold considered below, $\kappa _\lambda =\alpha $ is a smooth semipositive form, so its class is nef. Its non-nef locus is empty, whereas its non-Kähler locus is all of $X$, by the convention for classes that are not big in chapter 28 . These statements concern the closed class $\{ \alpha \} $; the Monge–Ampère equations on the Hopf manifold use instead the strictly positive, nonclosed form $\omega $. Proposition 29.2.3 . Suppose that $X$ carries a strictly LCK metric with Lee form $\lambda $ and that $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ is pseudoeffective. Then $X$ admits no balanced metric. Proof. Let $T=\kappa _\lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ be a closed positive current representing the class. It is nonzero, since the class is nonzero, and it is de Rham exact. If a Hermitian metric $b$ were balanced, then $\mathrm{d}(b^{n-1})=0$, and Stokes' theorem for currents would give \[  \int _ XT\wedge b^{n-1}=0.  \] This is impossible, since the mass of a nonzero positive $(1,1)$-current against a smooth strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form is strictly positive. $\square$ The balanced obstruction motivates the following conjecture. Conjecture 29.2.4 . If $X$ carries a strictly LCK metric with Lee form $\lambda $, then the Bott–Chern class $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ is pseudoeffective. The positivity in ( 29.4 ) tests the class only against the Gauduchon representative of the LCK metric. By theorem 4.3.1 , pseudoeffectivity requires a nonnegative pairing with every Gauduchon metric.

title: 29.2.1 The least eigenvalue of Lee curvature
search_title: The least eigenvalue of Lee curvature
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 29.2.1 The least eigenvalue of Lee curvature Fix a strictly LCK metric $\omega $ with Lee form $\lambda $. The volume along $\omega +t\kappa _\lambda $ increases as long as this form is positive. If the least relative eigenvalue of $\kappa _\lambda $ is a negative constant, the first boundary form has a kernel everywhere and its total volume is zero. This contradiction gives a pointwise positivity criterion. Set $Q=\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}\geq 0$. The form $Q$ is nonzero on an open set, since $\lambda $ is not exact and hence is not identically zero. Proposition 29.2.5 . On the interval where $\eta _ t=\omega +t\kappa _\lambda >0$, the polynomial $V(t)=\int _ X\eta _ t^ n$ has degree at most $n-1$ and \[  V'(t)=n(n-1)\int _ XQ\wedge \omega \wedge \eta _ t^{n-2}>0.  \] Proof. Since $\mathrm d\eta _ t=\lambda \wedge \omega $ and $\mathrm d\lambda ^{\mathrm c}=-\kappa _\lambda $, Stokes' theorem gives \[  0=\int _ X\mathrm d(\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \eta _ t^{n-1}) =-\int _ X\kappa _\lambda \wedge \eta _ t^{n-1} +(n-1)\int _ XQ\wedge \omega \wedge \eta _ t^{n-2}.  \] Differentiating the wedge polynomial proves the formula. The integrand on the right is positive wherever $\lambda \ne 0$, including when $n=2$. Its integral is therefore strictly positive. Finally, $\kappa _\lambda $ is closed and de Rham exact, so \[  \int _ X\kappa _\lambda ^ n =-\int _ X\mathrm d(\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \kappa _\lambda ^{n-1})=0.  \] This removes the coefficient of degree $n$. $\square$ Theorem 29.2.6 . If the least eigenvalue of $\kappa _\lambda $ relative to $\omega $ is constant on $X$, then it is zero and $\kappa _\lambda $ is semipositive. Its ordinary Bott–Chern class is nonzero and pseudoeffective. If all relative eigenvalues are constant, the rank is constant and lies between $1$ and $n-1$. In particular, the conclusion holds on a compact quotient $\Gamma \backslash G$ with left-invariant complex structure and strictly LCK tensors. Proof. Let $r$ be the constant least relative eigenvalue. If $r<0$, put $t_0=-1/r$. Then $\eta _ t>0$ for $0\leq t<t_0$, whereas $\eta _{t_0}$ is semipositive with a kernel at every point. Thus $V(t_0)=0$. The preceding proposition and polynomial continuity instead give $V(t_0)\geq V(0)>0$. This proves $r\geq 0$ and semipositivity. The nonnegative smooth form $\kappa _\lambda ^ n$ has integral zero by the same proposition, hence vanishes everywhere. Thus the least eigenvalue is zero at every point. Applying the Lee degree ( 29.4 ) to a conformal Gauduchon representative, as above, proves that the class is nonzero. The form $\kappa _\lambda $ itself represents it positively. Constant spectrum gives constant rank. The positive pairing ( 29.4 ) excludes rank zero, and the vanishing top power excludes rank $n$. On the stated compact quotient, the relative matrix is constant in a left-invariant frame, which proves the last assertion. $\square$ The class is also nef: the same representative is bounded below by $-\epsilon h$ for every Hermitian form $h$ and every $\epsilon >0$. Thus proposition 29.2.3 excludes balanced metrics under the least-eigenvalue hypothesis. The hypothesis concerns the chosen LCK metric. The other eigenvalues may vary, as the following examples show. They also explain why first degeneration of a volume ray need not force its total volume to vanish without the constant-minimum condition. Example 29.2.7 . On the scalar Hopf manifold $H_ n=(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto z/2\rangle $, for every $n\geq 2$, there is a strictly LCK metric with indefinite Lee curvature and a smooth semipositive representative of its ordinary Bott–Chern class. The first boundary reached for increasing $t>0$ in $\omega +t\kappa _\lambda $ has positive total volume. Proof. Fix $0<\epsilon <1$ and put \[  \rho =\sum _ j|z_ j|^2,\qquad \Phi =\rho +\epsilon \operatorname {Re}(z_1^2),\qquad \omega =\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho }{\Phi },\qquad \lambda =-\mathrm d\log \Phi .  \] The bounds $(1-\epsilon )\rho \leq \Phi \leq (1+\epsilon )\rho $ give positivity. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ and both $\Phi $ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ scale by $1/4$ under $z\mapsto z/2$, the metric and Lee form descend and satisfy the LCK equation. Polar coordinates identify the quotient with $S^{2n-1}\times (\mathbb R/(\log 2)\mathbb Z)$, so it is compact and connected. The Lee period from $z$ to $z/2$ is $2\log 2$, which proves strictness. Here $\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \Phi $. With $F_ i=\bar z_ i+\epsilon z_1\delta _{i1}$, its complex Hessian is \[  (\log \Phi )_{i\bar j} =\frac{\delta _{ij}}{\Phi } -\frac{F_ i\overline{F_ j}}{\Phi ^2}.  \] Relative to $\omega $, the eigenvalues are $1$ with multiplicity $n-1$ and $h=1-|F|^2/\Phi $. Writing $z_1=x+\mathrm i y$ and $B=\sum _{j>1}|z_ j|^2$, one finds \[  h=\frac{\epsilon ((1-\epsilon )y^2-(1+\epsilon )x^2)}{(1+\epsilon )x^2+(1-\epsilon )y^2+B}, \qquad -\epsilon \leq h\leq \epsilon .  \] At $(1,0,\ldots ,0)$ the spectrum is $-\epsilon ,1,\ldots ,1$, hence is indefinite. The bounded smooth function $u=\log \rho -\log \Phi $ is deck invariant, and \[  \kappa _\lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \rho \geq 0,  \] by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the Hessian of $\log \rho $. The correction also gives the standard Hopf conformal representative: $\mathrm e^{-u}\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho /\rho $. The first boundary occurs at $t_0=1/\epsilon $. At that value, \[  1+h/\epsilon =\frac{2(1-\epsilon )y^2+B}{\Phi }.  \] It vanishes only on the real $z_1$ rays with the remaining coordinates zero. The other relative eigenvalues of $\omega +t_0\kappa _\lambda $ equal $1+1/\epsilon >0$. The boundary form is therefore semipositive and its top power is positive on a nonempty open set, proving positive total volume. $\square$ Example 29.2.8 . For every $n\geq 2$, the same $H_ n$ carries a family of strictly LCK metrics whose least Lee-curvature eigenvalue is identically zero and whose remaining relative spectrum is nonconstant. Thus constancy of the least eigenvalue is strictly weaker than constancy of the whole spectrum. Proof. Put $q=|z_1|^2$ and, for $0<\epsilon <1$, define \[  \Psi =\rho +\epsilon \frac{q^2}{\rho },\qquad \omega _\epsilon =\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi }{\rho },\qquad \lambda =-\mathrm d\log \rho .  \] For $a=q/\rho \in [0,1]$, direct differentiation gives \[  \left(\frac{q^2}{\rho }\right)_{i\bar j} =\frac{2}{\rho }(q_ i-a\rho _ i)(q_{\bar j}-a\rho _{\bar j}) +2a\delta _{i1}\delta _{j1}-a^2\delta _{ij}.  \] The first two terms are positive semidefinite and $a^2\leq 1$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi \geq (1-\epsilon )\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho >0$. The potential is smooth on the punctured space and scales by $1/4$ under the deck map. Hence $\omega _\epsilon $ descends, satisfies the LCK equation and has Lee period $2\log 2$. Its Lee curvature is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \rho $, which is semipositive of rank $n-1$. The least relative eigenvalue is consequently zero everywhere. At $(1,0,\ldots ,0)$, the Hessian of $q^2/\rho $ is $\operatorname {diag}(1,-1,\ldots ,-1)$, giving the spectrum \[  0,(1-\epsilon )^{-1},\ldots ,(1-\epsilon )^{-1}.  \] At $(0,1,0,\ldots ,0)$ the term $q^2/\rho $ vanishes to fourth order, so its Hessian is zero and the spectrum is $0,1,\ldots ,1$. These spectra differ for every $\epsilon >0$. $\square$

Thus constancy of the least eigenvalue is strictly weaker than constancy of the whole spectrum. Proof. Put $q=|z_1|^2$ and, for $0<\epsilon <1$, define \[  \Psi =\rho +\epsilon \frac{q^2}{\rho },\qquad \omega _\epsilon =\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi }{\rho },\qquad \lambda =-\mathrm d\log \rho .  \] For $a=q/\rho \in [0,1]$, direct differentiation gives \[  \left(\frac{q^2}{\rho }\right)_{i\bar j} =\frac{2}{\rho }(q_ i-a\rho _ i)(q_{\bar j}-a\rho _{\bar j}) +2a\delta _{i1}\delta _{j1}-a^2\delta _{ij}.  \] The first two terms are positive semidefinite and $a^2\leq 1$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi \geq (1-\epsilon )\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho >0$. The potential is smooth on the punctured space and scales by $1/4$ under the deck map. Hence $\omega _\epsilon $ descends, satisfies the LCK equation and has Lee period $2\log 2$. Its Lee curvature is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \rho $, which is semipositive of rank $n-1$. The least relative eigenvalue is consequently zero everywhere. At $(1,0,\ldots ,0)$, the Hessian of $q^2/\rho $ is $\operatorname {diag}(1,-1,\ldots ,-1)$, giving the spectrum \[  0,(1-\epsilon )^{-1},\ldots ,(1-\epsilon )^{-1}.  \] At $(0,1,0,\ldots ,0)$ the term $q^2/\rho $ vanishes to fourth order, so its Hessian is zero and the spectrum is $0,1,\ldots ,1$. These spectra differ for every $\epsilon >0$. $\square$

title: 29.3 Ordinary and twisted potentials
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 29.3 Ordinary and twisted potentials Let $\omega $ be an LCK metric with Lee form $\lambda $. The Kähler covering provides a potential calculus compatible with the Lee equation. Conjugating the ordinary differential operators by the local conformal factor produces a twisted complex Hessian on $X$. For the fixed closed one-form $\lambda $, define \[  \mathrm{d}_\lambda =\mathrm{d}-\lambda \wedge , \qquad \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}_\lambda =\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}-\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge , \qquad D_\lambda =\mathrm{d}_\lambda \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}_\lambda .  \] On a chart where $\lambda =\mathrm{d}f$, these operators satisfy 29.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lck-gauge-operators} \mathrm{d}_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm{d}\mathrm{e}^{-f}, \qquad \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{e}^{-f}, \qquad D_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\mathrm{e}^{-f}. \end{equation} These identities show that $D_\lambda u$ is a real $(1,1)$-form for every smooth real function $u$, and that $\mathrm{d}_\lambda D_\lambda u=0$. Proposition 29.3.1 . Let $u$ be a smooth real function. Then \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)-\lambda \wedge (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u) =-\lambda \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,  \] whereas \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega +D_\lambda u) =\lambda \wedge (\omega +D_\lambda u).  \] Consequently, an ordinary potential preserves the LCK equation with the same Lee form precisely when $\lambda \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=0$. A twisted potential always preserves that equation, and it gives an LCK metric whenever $\omega +D_\lambda u>0$. Proof. The first identity follows from $\mathrm{d}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega =\lambda \wedge \omega $. The second follows from $\mathrm{d}_\lambda \omega =0$ and ( 29.8 ). $\square$ On the Kähler covering, a twisted potential becomes the automorphic function $\widetilde u=\mathrm{e}^{-F}\pi ^*u$, and 29.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lck-lift-potential} \mathrm{e}^{-F}\pi ^*(\omega +D_\lambda u) =\widetilde\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u. \end{equation} The top power $(\widetilde\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u)^ n$ transforms by $\chi ^ n$ under deck transformations, so its ratio to $\widetilde\omega ^ n$ is invariant and descends to $X$. A measure on $X$ is obtained from this ratio only after a metric in the conformal class has been fixed; the automorphic top-degree form cannot simply be integrated over the noncompact cover. The two kinds of potentials also differ in their normalization. Expanding the twisted Hessian gives 29.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lck-twisted-expansion} D_\lambda u =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\mathrm{d}u\wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c} -\lambda \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u +u\bigl (\kappa _\lambda +\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}\bigr ). \end{equation} In particular, $D_\lambda 1=\kappa _\lambda +\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ need not vanish, so adding a constant to $u$ can change the metric $\omega +D_\lambda u$. The usual normalization $\sup _ Xu=0$ is therefore not harmless for twisted equations. For a chosen Lee form $\lambda $ in its de Rham class, the real twisted Bott–Chern group in bidegree $(1,1)$ is \[  H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC},\lambda }(X,\mathbb R) =\frac{\{ \eta \in C^\infty (X,\Lambda ^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}): \mathrm{d}_\lambda \eta =0\} }{D_\lambda C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)}.  \] This is Bott–Chern cohomology with values in the weight bundle [ Section 18.5 , OV24LCK ] . It differs both from ordinary Bott–Chern cohomology and from the quotient of all backgrounds by ordinary $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-terms considered in chapter 24 .

text: 29.3.1 The Vaisman metric on the Hopf manifold Return to the Hopf threefold and the forms $s$, $\alpha $, $\beta $ and $\omega =\alpha +\beta $ of chapter 8 ; recall that $s=\log |z|^2$ on the covering $\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} $. The radial description makes the Lee form explicit and shows that this Gauduchon metric is also Vaisman. Proposition 29.3.2 . The Gauduchon form $\omega =\alpha +\beta $ of chapter 8 is Vaisman, with Lee form $\lambda =-\mathrm{d}s$, and \[  \kappa _\lambda =\alpha , \qquad D_\lambda 1=\omega .  \] In particular, the bounded mass property of definition 6.5.1 fails for the ordinary potential theory of a background that is simultaneously Gauduchon and Vaisman. Proof. Using $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ and $\beta =\mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s$, direct differentiation gives \[  \mathrm{d}\omega =-\mathrm{d}s\wedge \alpha =-\mathrm{d}s\wedge \omega , \qquad \mathrm{e}^ s\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{e}^ s)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2.  \] Although $s$ is not a function on the quotient, $\mathrm{d}s$ descends to it. Its integral along the loop induced by $z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-1}z$ is $-2$, so the Lee form is not exact. Let $g_{S^5}$ be the round metric on the unit sphere. Up to a constant factor, the Riemannian metric associated with $\omega $ on the cover is \[  \frac{|\mathrm{d}z|^2}{|z|^2} =\mathrm{d}t^2+g_{S^5},\qquad t=\log |z|.  \] The one-form $\mathrm{d}t$ is parallel for this product metric, which proves the Vaisman condition. Finally, $\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s=\alpha $ and $\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}=\beta $, so $D_\lambda 1=\omega $ by ( 29.10 ). The unbounded masses are given by theorem 8.0.1 . $\square$ The unbounded masses arise in the ordinary family $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, whose members need not satisfy the Lee equation. The volume problem within the class of Vaisman metrics imposes this additional geometric constraint.

title: 29.4 Volume equations in Gauduchon gauge
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 29.4 Volume equations in Gauduchon gauge Let $X$ again be a compact LCK manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$. Prescribing the volume of an LCK metric in Gauduchon gauge couples two equations: one for the determinant and one for the conformal factor. To compare metrics with a fixed Lee class, we first identify the twisted groups for cohomologous Lee forms. For a closed real one-form $\lambda $, smooth real functions $a,u$ and a smooth differential form $\eta $, multiplication by $\mathrm{e}^{-a}$ gives \[  \mathrm{d}_\lambda (\mathrm{e}^{-a}\eta ) =\mathrm{e}^{-a}\mathrm{d}_{\lambda +\mathrm{d}a}\eta , \qquad D_\lambda (\mathrm{e}^{-a}u)=\mathrm{e}^{-a}D_{\lambda +\mathrm{d}a}u.  \] We use this identification when comparing classes; the additive constant in $a$ corresponds to a constant rescaling of the weight bundle. Let $\omega _1$ be an LCK Gauduchon metric with Lee form $\lambda $, and let $\omega _2$ be an LCK metric with Lee form $\lambda +\mathrm{d}a$. If their twisted classes agree under the chosen identification, then \[  \mathrm{e}^{-a}\omega _2=\omega _1+D_\lambda u=:A>0  \] for a smooth real function $u$. Substituting $\omega _2=\mathrm{e}^ aA$ shows that $\omega _2$ has the same volume form as $\omega _1$ and is Gauduchon exactly when 29.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lck-coupled-equation} \begin{cases}  A^ n=\mathrm{e}^{-na}\omega _1^ n,\\  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (\mathrm{e}^{(n-1)a}A^{n-1}\bigr )=0. \end{cases} \end{equation} The scalar Hermitian equation of chapter 9 does not impose the second equation, and it uses $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ in place of $D_\lambda u$. The prescribed-volume Gauduchon theorem, theorem 9.9.1 , does not assert that its solution is LCK or lies in the given twisted class. Problem 29.4.1 . Does a compact LCK manifold have at most one Gauduchon LCK metric with a given Lee class, a given twisted Bott–Chern class and a given smooth positive volume form? This is the uniqueness problem posed in [ Question 47.56(3) , OV24LCK ] , with the identification of classes made explicit. The question concerns metrics: uniqueness of a scalar potential $u$ would additionally require control of the kernel of $D_\lambda $. The counterexamples with degenerate densities in chapter 11 concern ordinary potentials and do not decide this question.

title: 29.4.1 Invariant volumes on Vaisman manifolds
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text:
29.4.1 Invariant volumes on Vaisman manifolds The flows of the Lee and anti-Lee vector fields preserve a Vaisman metric. For a prescribed volume invariant under these flows, uniqueness for the smooth Hermitian equation forces the potential to be constant along them. Stokes' theorem in the transverse directions then fixes the normalizing constant, and changing the Lee form by the differential of the potential produces a Vaisman metric with the prescribed volume. Theorem 29.4.2 . Let $\omega $ be a Vaisman metric on $X$ with Lee form $\lambda $, and let $\mu $ be a smooth positive volume form invariant under the flows of both the Lee field $\lambda ^\sharp $ and the anti-Lee field $J\lambda ^\sharp $. Assume \[  \int _ X\mu =\int _ X\omega ^ n.  \] Then there is a unique Vaisman metric $\omega '$ with Lee class $[\lambda ]$ and $(\omega ')^ n=\mu $. We first describe the transverse geometry and the integration of transverse forms. Let $g$ be the Riemannian metric of $\omega $. Since $\lambda $ is parallel and not identically zero, it has constant squared norm $s=|\lambda |_ g^2>0$. Write \[  A=s^{-1}\lambda ^\sharp ,\qquad B=JA,\qquad 	au = rac{s}{4\pi },\qquad \eta =\kappa _\lambda .  \] Thus $\lambda (A)=1$ and $\lambda (B)=0$. Since $
abla \lambda =0$, the identity ( 29.2 ) gives 29.14  egin{equation} \label{eq:vaisman-normalized-form}  egin{split}  	au \omega & =\eta +\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c},\  \eta (U,JV)& = rac1{4\pi } igl (sg(U,V)-\lambda (U)\lambda (V)-\lambda (JU)\lambda (JV) igr ). \end{split} \end{equation} To obtain these identities, use $\lambda ^{\mathrm c}=-\lambda \circ J/(4\pi )$ and antisymmetrize $
abla \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$; the terms containing $
abla \lambda $ vanish. In particular, $\eta $ is a closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form whose kernel is the span $\mathcal F$ of $A$ and $B$. The field $A$ is parallel, and the same connection formula yields \[  
abla _ U B=	frac 12 igl (-JU+\lambda (U)B+\lambda (JU)A igr ), \qquad 
abla _ AJ=0.  \] The first identity shows that $B$ is a Killing field and that $[A,B]=0$. The second shows that $A$ is holomorphic, and integrability of $J$ then shows that $B=JA$ is holomorphic. Their flows preserve $g$, $J$, $\lambda $ and $\eta $. Consequently $\mathcal F$ is a holomorphic foliation by complex curves, and $\eta $ induces a Kähler form on each local transverse space. A form is called horizontal if its contractions with $A$ and $B$ vanish. A smooth function $v$ is basic for $\mathcal F$ if $Av=Bv=0$. For such a function, $\mathrm{d}v$, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ are horizontal and invariant under both flows; for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ this follows from Cartan's formula. Put $m=n-1$ and $\eta _ v=\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. Then 29.17  egin{equation} \label{eq:vaisman-basic-mass} \int _ X\eta _ v^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c} =\int _ X\eta ^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}. \end{equation} Indeed, $\eta _ v^ m-\eta ^ m=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$, where $T=\sum _{j=0}^{m-1}\eta _ v^ j\wedge \eta ^{m-1-j}$ is closed and horizontal. Since $\mathrm{d}(\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c})=\lambda \wedge \eta $, the differential of $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge T\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ plus a term containing the horizontal form $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge T\wedge \eta $ of degree $2m+1$, which vanishes because the transverse real dimension is $2m$. Stokes' theorem therefore proves ( 29.17 ). The following transverse maximum principle identifies the metric once its scale has been fixed. Proposition 29.4.3 . Let $\mathcal F$ be a foliation of a connected compact manifold $M$ with a transverse holomorphic structure of complex dimension $m\geq 1$. Let $\eta _0,\eta _1$ be transverse Kähler forms, and let $v$ be a smooth real basic function, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ computed in transverse holomorphic coordinates. Suppose \[  \eta _1=\eta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v, \qquad \eta _1^ m=\eta _0^ m.  \] Then $v$ is constant and $\eta _1=\eta _0$. Proof. The function $v$ is constant on each local plaque. On every transverse coordinate chart it satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \sum _{j=0}^{m-1}\eta _1^ j\wedge \eta _0^{m-1-j}=0.  \] This is a linear elliptic equation without zeroth-order term. Let $c=\max _ Mv$. If $v=c$ at some point, the strong maximum principle on a connected transverse chart shows that $v=c$ throughout that chart, and since $v$ is basic, $v=c$ on the corresponding foliation chart. Hence $\{ v=c\} $ is nonempty, open and closed, and connectedness of $M$ proves the assertion. $\square$ of theorem 29.4.2 . Replacing $\omega $ by $	au \omega $ and $\mu $ by $	au ^ n\mu $ does not change the Lee form or the assertion, and it makes the new constant $	au $ equal to one. We may therefore assume $	au =1$, so that $\omega =\eta +\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$. Write $\mu =f\omega ^ n$; since $\mu $ and $\omega ^ n$ are invariant under both flows, the positive smooth function $f$ is basic. Existence. By theorem 9.1.1 , there are a unique smooth function $u$ and a unique constant $b$ such that \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mathrm{e}^ b f\omega ^ n, \qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu=0.  \] Pullback by the flow of $A$ or of $B$ preserves the equation and the normalization, so uniqueness shows that $u$ is basic. Hence $\eta _ u=\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is a transverse Kähler form, and \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=n\eta _ u^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}.  \] Integrating over $X$ and using ( 29.17 ) and $\int _ X\mu =\int _ X\omega ^ n$ gives $b=0$. Set $\lambda _ u=\lambda -\mathrm{d}u$ and 29.18  egin{equation} \label{eq:vaisman-reconstructed-metric} \omega _ u'=\eta _ u+\lambda _ u\wedge \lambda _ u^{\mathrm c}. \end{equation} Here $\eta _ u=\kappa _{\lambda _ u}$ has kernel $\mathcal F$, while $\lambda _ u(A)=1$ and $\lambda _ u(B)=0$; together these facts give $\omega _ u'>0$. Direct differentiation gives $\mathrm{d}\omega _ u'=\lambda _ u\wedge \omega _ u'$. Since $u$ is basic, $A$ is a holomorphic Killing field for the Riemannian metric $g_ u'$ of $\omega _ u'$, and ( 29.18 ) gives \[  g_ u'(A,\cdot )= rac1{4\pi }\lambda _ u.  \] Since $\lambda _ u$ is closed, $
abla ^{g_ u'}A$ is symmetric, whereas the Killing equation makes it skew-symmetric. Thus $A$ and $\lambda _ u$ are parallel, so $\omega _ u'$ is Vaisman with Lee class $[\lambda ]$. Finally, $\eta _ u^ m$ has top transverse degree, and every term of $\lambda _ u\wedge \lambda _ u^{\mathrm c}-\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ contains a horizontal one-form. Therefore \[  (\omega _ u')^ n =n\eta _ u^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c} =(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu .  \] Uniqueness. Let $\widehat\omega $ be another Vaisman solution, with Lee form $\widehat\lambda =\lambda +\mathrm{d}v$, and denote by $\widehat s,\widehat	au ,\widehat A,\widehat B,\widehat\eta $ the corresponding objects for $\widehat\omega $. The form $\eta +\widehat\eta $ is de Rham exact and semipositive. Its top power is nonnegative and has zero integral, so it vanishes everywhere, and $\eta +\widehat\eta $ has a nonzero kernel at every point. The kernel of a sum of two semipositive Hermitian forms is the intersection of their kernels. Since both kernels are complex lines, they coincide, and both metrics define the same foliation $\mathcal F$. The nowhere vanishing holomorphic vector field $A-\mathrm iB$ trivializes the holomorphic tangent bundle of $\mathcal F$. The analogous field $\widehat A-\mathrm i\widehat B$ is a holomorphic multiple of it, and the multiple is constant because $X$ is compact. Write $\widehat A=aA+bB$ with $a,b\in \mathbb R$. Since $\widehat\lambda (\widehat A)=1$ and $\widehat\lambda (\widehat B)=0$, \[  \widehat A v=1-a,\qquad \widehat B v=b.  \] Both fields are complete and $v$ is bounded, so $v$ cannot grow linearly along their flows; hence these constants vanish, and $a=1$, $b=0$. Thus $\widehat A=A$, $\widehat B=B$, and $v$ is basic. From ( 29.14 ) we obtain the contraction formulas 29.19  egin{equation} \label{eq:vaisman-volume-contraction} \iota _ B\iota _ A\widehat\omega ^ n = rac{n}{4\pi \widehat	au ^ n}\widehat\eta ^ m, \qquad \iota _ B\iota _ A(\omega _ u')^ n= rac{n}{4\pi }\eta _ u^ m. \end{equation} Since the two volume forms are equal, $\widehat\eta ^ m=\widehat	au ^ n\eta _ u^ m$. Since $\widehat\eta =\eta -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ and $v$ is basic, integrating against $\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ and applying ( 29.17 ) twice gives $\widehat	au ^ n=1$. Thus $\widehat	au =1$ and $\widehat\eta ^ m=\eta _ u^ m$. Since $\widehat\eta -\eta _ u=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+u)$, proposition 29.4.3 shows that $v+u$ is constant. It follows that $\widehat\lambda =\lambda _ u$, $\widehat\eta =\eta _ u$ and $\widehat\omega =\omega _ u'$. $\square$

title: Theorem 29.4.2
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Theorem 29.4.2 . Let $\omega $ be a Vaisman metric on $X$ with Lee form $\lambda $, and let $\mu $ be a smooth positive volume form invariant under the flows of both the Lee field $\lambda ^\sharp $ and the anti-Lee field $J\lambda ^\sharp $. Assume \[  \int _ X\mu =\int _ X\omega ^ n.  \] Then there is a unique Vaisman metric $\omega '$ with Lee class $[\lambda ]$ and $(\omega ')^ n=\mu $. of theorem 29.4.2 . Replacing $\omega $ by $\tau \omega $ and $\mu $ by $\tau ^ n\mu $ does not change the Lee form or the assertion, and it makes the new constant $\tau $ equal to one. We may therefore assume $\tau =1$, so that $\omega =\eta +\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$. Write $\mu =f\omega ^ n$; since $\mu $ and $\omega ^ n$ are invariant under both flows, the positive smooth function $f$ is basic. Existence. By theorem 9.1.1 , there are a unique smooth function $u$ and a unique constant $b$ such that \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mathrm{e}^ b f\omega ^ n, \qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu=0.  \] Pullback by the flow of $A$ or of $B$ preserves the equation and the normalization, so uniqueness shows that $u$ is basic. Hence $\eta _ u=\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is a transverse Kähler form, and \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=n\eta _ u^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}.  \] Integrating over $X$ and using ( 29.17 ) and $\int _ X\mu =\int _ X\omega ^ n$ gives $b=0$. Set $\lambda _ u=\lambda -\mathrm{d}u$ and 29.18 \begin{equation} \label{eq:vaisman-reconstructed-metric} \omega _ u'=\eta _ u+\lambda _ u\wedge \lambda _ u^{\mathrm c}. \end{equation} Here $\eta _ u=\kappa _{\lambda _ u}$ has kernel $\mathcal F$, while $\lambda _ u(A)=1$ and $\lambda _ u(B)=0$; together these facts give $\omega _ u'>0$. Direct differentiation gives $\mathrm{d}\omega _ u'=\lambda _ u\wedge \omega _ u'$. Since $u$ is basic, $A$ is a holomorphic Killing field for the Riemannian metric $g_ u'$ of $\omega _ u'$, and ( 29.18 ) gives \[  g_ u'(A,\cdot )=\frac1{4\pi }\lambda _ u.  \] Since $\lambda _ u$ is closed, $\nabla ^{g_ u'}A$ is symmetric, whereas the Killing equation makes it skew-symmetric. Thus $A$ and $\lambda _ u$ are parallel, so $\omega _ u'$ is Vaisman with Lee class $[\lambda ]$. Finally, $\eta _ u^ m$ has top transverse degree, and every term of $\lambda _ u\wedge \lambda _ u^{\mathrm c}-\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ contains a horizontal one-form. Therefore \[  (\omega _ u')^ n =n\eta _ u^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c} =(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu .  \] Uniqueness. Let $\widehat\omega $ be another Vaisman solution, with Lee form $\widehat\lambda =\lambda +\mathrm{d}v$, and denote by $\widehat s,\widehat\tau ,\widehat A,\widehat B,\widehat\eta $ the corresponding objects for $\widehat\omega $. The form $\eta +\widehat\eta $ is de Rham exact and semipositive. Its top power is nonnegative and has zero integral, so it vanishes everywhere, and $\eta +\widehat\eta $ has a nonzero kernel at every point. The kernel of a sum of two semipositive Hermitian forms is the intersection of their kernels. Since both kernels are complex lines, they coincide, and both metrics define the same foliation $\mathcal F$. The nowhere vanishing holomorphic vector field $A-\mathrm iB$ trivializes the holomorphic tangent bundle of $\mathcal F$. The analogous field $\widehat A-\mathrm i\widehat B$ is a holomorphic multiple of it, and the multiple is constant because $X$ is compact. Write $\widehat A=aA+bB$ with $a,b\in \mathbb R$. Since $\widehat\lambda (\widehat A)=1$ and $\widehat\lambda (\widehat B)=0$, \[  \widehat A v=1-a,\qquad \widehat B v=b.  \] Both fields are complete and $v$ is bounded, so $v$ cannot grow linearly along their flows; hence these constants vanish, and $a=1$, $b=0$. Thus $\widehat A=A$, $\widehat B=B$, and $v$ is basic. From ( 29.14 ) we obtain the contraction formulas 29.19 \begin{equation} \label{eq:vaisman-volume-contraction} \iota _ B\iota _ A\widehat\omega ^ n =\frac{n}{4\pi \widehat\tau ^ n}\widehat\eta ^ m, \qquad \iota _ B\iota _ A(\omega _ u')^ n=\frac{n}{4\pi }\eta _ u^ m. \end{equation} Since the two volume forms are equal, $\widehat\eta ^ m=\widehat\tau ^ n\eta _ u^ m$. Since $\widehat\eta =\eta -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ and $v$ is basic, integrating against $\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ and applying ( 29.17 ) twice gives $\widehat\tau ^ n=1$. Thus $\widehat\tau =1$ and $\widehat\eta ^ m=\eta _ u^ m$. Since $\widehat\eta -\eta _ u=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+u)$, proposition 29.4.3 shows that $v+u$ is constant. It follows that $\widehat\lambda =\lambda _ u$, $\widehat\eta =\eta _ u$ and $\widehat\omega =\omega _ u'$. $\square$

title: Proposition 29.4.3
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Proposition 29.4.3 . Let $\mathcal F$ be a foliation of a connected compact manifold $M$ with a transverse holomorphic structure of complex dimension $m\geq 1$. Let $\eta _0,\eta _1$ be transverse Kähler forms, and let $v$ be a smooth real basic function, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ computed in transverse holomorphic coordinates. Suppose \[  \eta _1=\eta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v, \qquad \eta _1^ m=\eta _0^ m.  \] Then $v$ is constant and $\eta _1=\eta _0$. Proof. The function $v$ is constant on each local plaque. On every transverse coordinate chart it satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \sum _{j=0}^{m-1}\eta _1^ j\wedge \eta _0^{m-1-j}=0.  \] This is a linear elliptic equation without zeroth-order term. Let $c=\max _ Mv$. If $v=c$ at some point, the strong maximum principle on a connected transverse chart shows that $v=c$ throughout that chart, and since $v$ is basic, $v=c$ on the corresponding foliation chart. Hence $\{ v=c\} $ is nonempty, open and closed, and connectedness of $M$ proves the assertion. $\square$

text: 29.4.2 Radial volumes on scalar Hopf manifolds Let $n\geq 2$, put $m=n-1$, and consider the scalar Hopf manifold and its projection to $\mathbb P^ m$, \[  H_ n=(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \mathrm e z\rangle , \qquad q:H_ n\longrightarrow \mathbb P^ m.  \] Let $\omega _{\rm FS}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ m$, normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^ m}\omega _{\rm FS}^ m=1$. The function $r=\log |z|^2$ is well defined modulo $2$ on $H_ n$, so its differential is a global one-form. Set \[  \alpha =q^*\omega _{\rm FS}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r,\qquad \beta =\mathrm dr\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r.  \] Both forms are defined on $H_ n$. The form $\alpha $ has rank $m$, and its kernel is the complex radial line; the form $\beta $ has rank one, and its kernel is the complementary horizontal subspace. Thus $\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta $ is a positive volume form. On each elliptic fiber of $q$, where $z$ moves along a complex line through the origin, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r=\mathrm d\arg z/(2\pi )$, so \[  \int _{q^{-1}(x)}\beta =2,\qquad \int _{H_ n}\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta =2.  \] We consider all metrics of the radial form 29.20 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-lck-family} \omega =C(r)\alpha +D(r)\beta ,\qquad C,D\in C^\infty (\mathbb R/2\mathbb Z),\quad C,D>0. \end{equation} The circle $\mathbb R/2\mathbb Z$ of values of $r$ is oriented by increasing $r$. The Lee period of such a metric is the integral of its Lee form over a radial loop along which $r$ increases from $0$ to $2$. Lemma 29.4.4 . Every metric of the form ( 29.20 ) is strictly LCK. Its Lee form and Lee period are \[  \lambda =l(r)\, \mathrm dr,\qquad l=\frac{C'-D}{C},\qquad L=-\int _0^2\frac{D}{C}\, \mathrm dr<0.  \] The metric is Gauduchon if and only if $C^{m-1}(C'-D)=k$ for a constant $k$. In terms of the positive smooth $2$-periodic function $F=C^ mD$, this condition is equivalent to 29.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-lck-periodic-ode} C^ mC'=kC+F,\qquad D=\frac{F}{C^ m}. \end{equation} Every positive periodic solution has $k<0$, and 29.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-lck-period-identities} \begin{gathered} k\int _0^2C\, \mathrm dr+\int _0^2F\, \mathrm dr=0, \\ l=kC^{-m},\qquad L(C)=-\int _0^2\frac{F}{C^{m+1}}\, \mathrm dr. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Proof. The differential identities are \[  \begin{gathered} \alpha ^{m+1}=\beta ^2=0,\qquad \mathrm d\beta =-\mathrm dr\wedge \alpha ,\\ \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\beta =-\alpha \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =-\alpha ^2. \end{gathered}  \] They give $\mathrm d\omega =(C'-D)\mathrm dr\wedge \alpha =\lambda \wedge \omega $. The closed form $\lambda $ is the Lee form, since wedging one-forms with $\omega $ is injective. The integral of $C'/C$ over a period is zero, which proves the formula for $L$; since $L\neq 0$, the Lee form is not exact. Two radial Lee forms have the same de Rham class exactly when their periods agree: a difference with zero period has a periodic primitive, and the radial loop detects the converse. For a smooth function $G$ of $r$, the chain rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=G'\alpha +G''\beta $. Also $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(G\beta )=-G\alpha \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$, so \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(G\beta )=-G'\alpha \wedge \beta -G\alpha ^2.  \] Expanding the powers of $\omega $ therefore gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \omega ^ m& =C^ m\alpha ^ m+mC^{m-1}D\alpha ^{m-1}\wedge \beta ,\\  \omega ^ n& =nC^ mD\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta , \end{aligned}  \] and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ m)= \bigl [(C^ m)''-m(C^{m-1}D)'\bigr ]\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta .  \] Since $(C^ m)''-m(C^{m-1}D)'=m\bigl (C^{m-1}(C'-D)\bigr )'$, this vanishes exactly when $C^{m-1}(C'-D)$ is constant. Multiplying the identity $C^{m-1}(C'-D)=k$ by $C$ gives ( 29.21 ). Since $C^ mC'$ has zero integral over a period, integrating ( 29.21 ) gives the first identity in ( 29.22 ), which forces $k<0$. The formulas for $l$ and $L$ follow from the formula for the Lee form. $\square$ Lemma 29.4.5 . For fixed $F>0$ and each $k<0$, there is at most one positive $2$-periodic solution of ( 29.21 ). If $k_2>k_1$, the corresponding solutions satisfy $C_2>C_1$ everywhere and $L(C_2)>L(C_1)$. Proof. Suppose $k_2>k_1$, and put $R=C_2-C_1$. At a zero of $R$, the equation gives $R'=(k_2-k_1)C_1^{1-m}>0$. Such zeros are isolated, so there are finitely many on the circle. A periodic differentiable function cannot cross zero only upwards, since returning around the circle would require a downward crossing. Hence $R$ has no zero and a constant strict sign. The identity $\int _0^2C_ i\, \mathrm dr=-\int _0^2F\, \mathrm dr/k_ i$ shows that this sign is positive, and the formula for $L(C)$ in ( 29.22 ) then gives $L(C_2)>L(C_1)$. For equal $k$, uniqueness for the smooth scalar equation $C'=kC^{1-m}+FC^{-m}$ on $C>0$ shows that two solutions which meet coincide. Two solutions which never meet are strictly ordered, which contradicts the equality of their integrals. This proves uniqueness for fixed $k$. $\square$ Theorem 29.4.6 . For every positive smooth $2$-periodic function $F$ and every $L_0<0$, there is exactly one metric of the form ( 29.20 ) which is Gauduchon, has Lee period $L_0$, and satisfies \[  \omega ^ n=nF(r)\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta .  \] Proof. Fix $k<0$, put $c=-k$, and let $f_0=\min F>0$ and $f_1=\max F$. The constant functions $f_0/c$ and $f_1/c$ are a subsolution and a supersolution, respectively, of $C'=C^{-m}(F-cC)$. By comparison, the forward flow of this equation preserves the compact interval $I_ k=[f_0/c,f_1/c]$ of positive numbers, and existence and uniqueness for smooth ordinary differential equations give a continuous time-two map $I_ k\to I_ k$. Its difference from the identity is nonnegative at the left endpoint and nonpositive at the right one, so the intermediate value theorem gives a fixed point; if $f_0=f_1$, the constant $C=f_0/c$ is the solution. Since the equation is periodic, the solution through a fixed point extends to a smooth positive periodic solution. It is unique by lemma 29.4.5 and satisfies 29.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:radial-lck-ode-barriers} \frac{f_0}{-k}\leq C_ k(r)\leq \frac{f_1}{-k}. \end{equation} By lemma 29.4.5 , the period $L(k)=-\int _0^2F/C_ k^{m+1}\, \mathrm dr$ is strictly increasing in $k$. It is also continuous. Indeed, for $k$ in a compact neighborhood of any $k_0<0$, ( 29.25 ) gives uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds for $C_ k$, and the equation then bounds all derivatives. Any sequence $k\to k_0$ therefore has smoothly convergent subsequences, and the equation and uniqueness identify every limit with $C_{k_0}$. Thus $C_ k\to C_{k_0}$ uniformly, which gives continuity of the integral. The same bounds imply $L(k)\to 0$ as $k\uparrow 0$ and $L(k)\to -\infty $ as $k\to -\infty $. Hence exactly one $k$ has period $L_0$. For this $k$, set $D=F/C_ k^ m$. The identities of lemma 29.4.4 show that $C_ k\alpha +D\beta $ has the required properties. Conversely, every metric of the form ( 29.20 ) with these properties gives a positive periodic solution of the same equation, so the ordering of the periods also proves uniqueness. $\square$ Proposition 29.4.7 . Let $\omega $ be a metric as in theorem 29.4.6 , with Lee form $\lambda $. There is a positive smooth function $U$ on $H_ n$ with $\omega =D_\lambda U$; in particular, the class of $\omega $ in $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC},\lambda }(H_ n,\mathbb R)$ is zero. If $\omega _1,\omega _2$ are two such metrics, with positive potentials $U_1,U_2$ and cohomologous Lee forms $\lambda _1$ and $\lambda _2=\lambda _1+\mathrm da$, then for every choice of the additive constant in $a$, \[  \mathrm e^{-a}\omega _2-\omega _1=D_{\lambda _1}(\mathrm e^{-a}U_2-U_1).  \] In particular, among metrics of the form ( 29.20 ), a solution of ( 29.11 ) is determined by its volume form and Lee class, even if the potential $u$ in ( 29.11 ) is not assumed radial. Proof. Write $l=kC^{-m}<0$ and $f(r)=\int _0^ rl(s)\, \mathrm ds$ for real $r$. Then $f(r+2)=f(r)+L_0$. The solution of $U'-lU=C$ given by \[  \begin{aligned}  U(0)& =\frac{\mathrm e^{L_0}}{1-\mathrm e^{L_0}} \int _0^2\mathrm e^{-f(s)}C(s)\, \mathrm ds,\\  U(r)& =\mathrm e^{f(r)} \left(U(0)+\int _0^ r\mathrm e^{-f(s)}C(s)\, \mathrm ds\right) \end{aligned}  \] is positive on $[0,2]$ and satisfies $U(2)=U(0)$. Since the equation is periodic, all derivatives also match at the endpoints, so $U$ defines a positive smooth function on $H_ n$. By ( 29.8 ), its twisted Hessian is \[  \begin{split}  D_\lambda U & =(U'-lU)\alpha + \bigl [U''-2lU'+(l^2-l')U\bigr ]\beta \\ & =C\alpha +(C'-lC)\beta =\omega . \end{split}  \] This proves that the twisted class is zero. The identity $\mathrm e^{-a}D_{\lambda _2}U_2=D_{\lambda _1}(\mathrm e^{-a}U_2)$ of section 29.4 gives the formula for the difference. For two metrics of the form ( 29.20 ), equal volume forms give the same function $F$, and equal Lee classes give the same period, so theorem 29.4.6 applies. This uniqueness concerns the metric, not the potentials representing it. $\square$ Proposition 29.4.8 . If $F$ is nonconstant, the metric of theorem 29.4.6 is not Vaisman. Proof. The radial complex line is orthogonal to $\ker \mathrm dr\cap \ker \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$. On a radial complex line, use a logarithmic coordinate $w=x+\mathrm i y$, so that $r=2x+\text{constant}$ and $\beta =\pi ^{-1}\mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm dy$. The Riemannian metric of $\omega $ restricts there to $D\pi ^{-1}(\mathrm dx^2+\mathrm dy^2)$, whence \[  |\mathrm dr|_\omega ^2=\frac{4\pi }{D},\qquad |\lambda |_\omega ^2=4\pi k^2\frac{C^{-2m}}{D}.  \] A parallel Lee form has constant norm. Since $k\ne 0$, the Vaisman condition would therefore imply $D=Q C^{-2m}$ for a constant $Q>0$. At a maximum and at a minimum of $C$, where $C'=0$, the Gauduchon identity would then give $kC^{m+1}+Q=0$. This equation has only one positive root, so the maximum and the minimum of $C$ coincide. Thus $C$, $D$ and $F=C^ mD$ would all be constant, a contradiction. $\square$ Example 29.4.9 . For \[  \begin{gathered} 0<\varepsilon <\min \left\{ \frac12, \frac{(3/2)^{1-m}}{4\pi }\right\} , \\ C=1+\varepsilon \cos (\pi r),\qquad D=C'+C^{1-m}, \end{gathered}  \] the metric ( 29.20 ) is Gauduchon and non-Vaisman, with Lee form $\lambda =-C^{-m}\mathrm dr$ and density $F=C^ mC'+C$. The probability volume $\mathrm dV=\frac12\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta $ gives $\omega ^ n=2nF\, \mathrm dV$ and $\int _{H_ n}F\, \mathrm dV=1$. Proof. Since $1/2<C<3/2$ and $m\geq 1$, we have $D\geq (3/2)^{1-m}-\pi \varepsilon >\frac34(3/2)^{1-m}>0$. The Gauduchon identity holds with $k=-1$, giving the Lee form and the positive density $F=C^ mD$. Its values $F(0)=1+\varepsilon $ and $F(1)=1-\varepsilon $ differ, so proposition 29.4.8 applies. The integral of $C^ mC'$ over a period is zero and the average of $C$ is one, so integration along the fibers of $q$ gives $\int _{H_ n}F\, \mathrm dV=1$. $\square$ The volume form in this example is not invariant under the flow of the Lee field of the Vaisman metric $\alpha +\beta $, which translates $r$, so theorem 29.4.2 does not apply to it. For the new metric, the Gauduchon condition states that $lF/D=lC^ m=k$ is constant; up to a constant factor, this quantity is the flux of its Lee field through the level sets of $r$, and here it equals $-1$. The radial classification answers 29.4.1 within the family ( 29.20 ); uniqueness among arbitrary LCK metrics remains open.

Since $k\ne 0$, the Vaisman condition would therefore imply $D=Q C^{-2m}$ for a constant $Q>0$. Thus $C$, $D$ and $F=C^ mD$ would all be constant, a contradiction. $\square$

title: Example 29.4.9

text: Example 29.4.9 . For \[  \begin{gathered} 0<\varepsilon <\min \left\{ \frac12, \frac{(3/2)^{1-m}}{4\pi }\right\} , \\ C=1+\varepsilon \cos (\pi r),\qquad D=C'+C^{1-m}, \end{gathered}  \] the metric ( 29.20 ) is Gauduchon and non-Vaisman, with Lee form $\lambda =-C^{-m}\mathrm dr$ and density $F=C^ mC'+C$. The probability volume $\mathrm dV=\frac12\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta $ gives $\omega ^ n=2nF\, \mathrm dV$ and $\int _{H_ n}F\, \mathrm dV=1$. Proof. Since $1/2<C<3/2$ and $m\geq 1$, we have $D\geq (3/2)^{1-m}-\pi \varepsilon >\frac34(3/2)^{1-m}>0$. The Gauduchon identity holds with $k=-1$, giving the Lee form and the positive density $F=C^ mD$. title: 29.5 Chern–Ricci flatness and Vaisman rigidity

29.5 Chern–Ricci flatness and Vaisman rigidity Return to an LCK metric $\omega $ on $X$ with Lee form $\lambda $. Chern–Ricci flatness expresses the Riemannian Ricci tensor through $\lambda $ and its covariant derivative. The Bianchi and Bochner identities then relate the part of this derivative that is not $J$-invariant to the divergence of the Lee field. When the metric is Gauduchon, this divergence vanishes by proposition 29.2.1 , and the identities force the Lee form to be parallel. We write $\operatorname {Ric}^{\mathrm{Ch}}=\operatorname {Ric}/(2\pi )$ for the normalized Chern–Ricci form, which represents the first Bott–Chern class $c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)$, with $\operatorname {Ric}$ as in 26.20.1 . Theorem 29.5.1 . Let $\omega $ be a compact strictly LCK metric that is Chern–Ricci flat, and let $g$ be its associated Riemannian metric. Put $A=\lambda ^\sharp $, $q=\mathrm d_ g^*\lambda $ and \[  S^-(U,V)=	frac 12 igl ((
abla \lambda )(U,V)-(
abla \lambda )(JU,JV) igr ).  \] Then \[  \int _ X|S^-|_ g^2\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g = rac12\int _ X|q|^2\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g.  \] For this metric the following conditions are equivalent: $\omega $ is Gauduchon; $q=0$; $A$ is real holomorphic; and $\omega $ is Vaisman. Proof. We keep the divergence terms in the Ricci tensor and compare the Bianchi and Bochner identities before imposing the Gauduchon condition. All norms, traces and contractions use $g$. Put \[  B=JA,\qquad S=
abla \lambda ,\qquad S^+(U,V)=	frac 12 igl (S(U,V)+S(JU,JV) igr ),\qquad u=|\lambda |_ g^2.  \] Closedness of $\lambda $ makes $S$ symmetric, and $\operatorname {tr}_ gS=-q$. The tensors $S^+$ and $S^-=S-S^+$ are orthogonal. Write $J\lambda =-\lambda \circ J$, so that $\lambda ^{\mathrm c}=J\lambda /(4\pi )$. Step 1: the Ricci tensor. We first show that 29.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:lck-ricci-real} \operatorname {Ric}_ g =nS^+-(n-1)S+	frac {q-u}{2}g +	frac 12\lambda \otimes \lambda +	frac n2 J\lambda \otimes J\lambda . \end{equation} Locally write $\lambda =\mathrm df$ and put $\widetilde g=\mathrm e^{-f}g$. The real conformal Ricci formula in dimension $2n$ is \[  \operatorname {Ric}_{\widetilde g} =\operatorname {Ric}_ g+(n-1)S +	frac {n-1}{2}\lambda \otimes \lambda +	frac 12\{ -q-(n-1)u\} g.  \] The local metric $\widetilde g$ is Kähler. Since the Chern–Ricci form of $g$ vanishes, the Ricci form of $\widetilde g$ is $n\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial f=(n/2)\mathrm d(J\lambda )$. Applying ( 29.2 ) to $(
abla _ UJ\lambda )(V)=-S(U,JV)-\lambda ((
abla _ UJ)V)$ and antisymmetrizing gives \[  \mathrm d(J\lambda )(U,JV) =2S^+(U,V)-u g(U,V) +\lambda (U)\lambda (V)+J\lambda (U)J\lambda (V).  \] Evaluating the Kähler Ricci form on $(U,JV)$ and comparing with the conformal formula proves ( 29.30 ). Taking its trace gives the scalar curvature \[  s=(n-1)q-	frac {n-1}{2}u.  \] Step 2: the integral identity. Write $\| \cdot \| $ for the $L^2(g)$ norm and set \[  E_ A=\int _ X S(A,A)\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g, \qquad E_ B=\int _ X S(B,B)\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g.  \] Since $S(A,A)=A(u)/2$ and $\operatorname {div}A=-q$, integration by parts gives 29.31  egin{equation} \label{eq:lck-aa-divergence} \int _ Xu q\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g=2E_ A. \end{equation} Pair the contracted Bianchi identity $\delta \operatorname {Ric}_ g+\mathrm ds/2=0$ with $\lambda $ and integrate. abla _ AJ=0$. If $T$ is the symmetric endomorphism defined by $g(TU,V)=S(U,V)$, then \[  (\mathcal L_ AJ)V=JTV-TJV.  \] Consequently $A$ is real holomorphic exactly when $S=S^+$. title: 29.5.1 A flat conformal gauge that is not Gauduchon
search_title: A flat conformal gauge that is not Gauduchon
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 29.5.1 A flat conformal gauge that is not Gauduchon The two preferred conformal representatives need not coincide. The following example keeps the complex surface and the conformal class fixed; the obstruction is to imposing both conditions in that class. Example 29.5.2 . There is a compact complex Kodaira surface with holomorphically trivial canonical bundle and a strictly LCK Chern–Ricci-flat metric $\omega $ that is not Gauduchon. No metric conformal to $\omega $ is both Gauduchon and Chern–Ricci flat, although the same conformal class contains a Vaisman metric. Proof. We construct the quotient and the two conformal metrics explicitly. On $G=\mathbb R^4$ use the multiplication \[  (x,y,z,t)(x',y',z',t') =(x+x',y+y',z+z'+xy',t+t').  \] The integer subgroup $\Gamma =\mathbb Z^4$ acts on the left by \[  (x,y,z,t)\longmapsto (x+a,y+b,z+c+ay,t+d).  \] Reducing $x,y,t$ and then $z$ to unit intervals gives a compact fundamental set, so $X=\Gamma \backslash G$ is connected and compact. The forms \[  e^1=\mathrm dx,\quad e^2=\mathrm dy,\quad e^3=\mathrm dz-x\, \mathrm dy,\quad e^4=\mathrm dt  \] descend to $X$, with $\mathrm de^3=-e^1\wedge e^2$ and the other derivatives zero. Declare $\phi ^1=e^1+\mathrm i e^2$ and $\phi ^2=e^3+\mathrm i e^4$ to be of type $(1,0)$. Since \[  \mathrm d\phi ^1=0,\qquad \mathrm d\phi ^2=-\tfrac {\mathrm i}{2}\phi ^1\wedge \overline{\phi ^1},  \] there is no $(0,2)$ component and the complex structure is integrable. The form $\Sigma =\phi ^1\wedge \phi ^2$ is closed and nowhere vanishing, hence is a holomorphic trivialization of the canonical bundle. In particular $c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)=0$. Projection to $x+\mathrm i y$ exhibits this quotient as the Kodaira elliptic bundle over $\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$. Choose a smooth unit-periodic function $f(x)$ with $C=1-f''>0$, and put \[  \lambda _1=-e^4+f'e^1,\qquad \eta _1=J\lambda _1=e^3+f'e^2,\qquad \omega _1=\lambda _1\wedge \eta _1+C e^1\wedge e^2.  \] This is positive and Hermitian, with Riemannian metric \[  g_1=\lambda _1\otimes \lambda _1+\eta _1\otimes \eta _1 +C(e^1\otimes e^1+e^2\otimes e^2).  \] The identities $\mathrm d\lambda _1=0$ and $\mathrm d\eta _1=-C e^1\wedge e^2$ give $\mathrm d\omega _1=\lambda _1\wedge \omega _1$. The Lee period along the $t$-circle is $-1$, so this metric is strictly LCK. Its Lee dual is $-\partial _ t$, which is Killing because all coefficients are independent of $t$. Closedness of the Lee form and the Killing equation make $\nabla ^{g_1}\lambda _1$ both symmetric and skew-symmetric; thus $\omega _1$ is Vaisman. Write $e^{1234}=e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3\wedge e^4$. The volume is $\omega _1^2/2=C e^{1234}$, whereas $\Sigma \wedge \overline\Sigma $ has constant density in this coframe. For $h=C^{-1/2}$, the conformal metric $\omega =h\omega _1$ has volume $e^{1234}$ and therefore is Chern–Ricci flat. Its Lee form is \[  \lambda =-e^4+\mathrm d(f+\log h).  \] Let $E_ i$ be dual to $e^ i$. Solving $g(A,\cdot )=\lambda $ gives \[  A=h'E_1+(f'h'-h^{-1})E_4.  \] The metric volume is $\mathrm dx\, \mathrm dy\, \mathrm dz\, \mathrm dt$, and the fields $E_ i$ have zero divergence for this volume. Hence $\operatorname {div}A=h''$ and $q=-h''$. For the choice \[  f(x)=\frac{\cos (2\pi x)}{16\pi ^2},\qquad C(x)=1+\tfrac 14\cos (2\pi x)\geq \tfrac 34,  \] one has \[  q(0)=-\frac{4\sqrt5\pi ^2}{25},\qquad q(1/2)=\frac{4\sqrt3\pi ^2}{9}.  \] Thus $\omega $ is not Gauduchon, and theorem 29.5.1 also excludes the Vaisman condition for this flat metric. Finally, if $\mathrm e^ v\omega $ is also Chern–Ricci flat, then the conformal Ricci formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=0$. The real pluriharmonic function $v$ is constant on the connected compact complex manifold by the maximum principle. A constant multiple of $\omega $ still has nonzero divergence of its Lee field, so no flat metric in this conformal class is Gauduchon. The metric $\omega _1$ already constructed is a Vaisman representative of the class. $\square$ Conjecture 29.5.3 . If $X$ satisfies $c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)=0$ and admits a strictly LCK metric, then $X$ admits a Vaisman metric. The analytic problem is to achieve Chern–Ricci flatness and the Gauduchon condition simultaneously within a family of LCK metrics. The conjecture asks for one Vaisman metric; it does not assert that the Lee form of every LCK metric on $X$ is parallel.

title: 29.6 The Lee–Gauduchon cone
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 29.6 The Lee–Gauduchon cone For the rest of the chapter, $X$ is an arbitrary connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$, not necessarily LCK. By theorem 4.3.1 , a class in the image of the Lee map $j_ X$ of ( 29.7 ) is pseudoeffective exactly when it pairs nonnegatively with every Gauduchon metric. For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, the form $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\gamma ^{n-1})$ is closed, and these pairings depend only on its de Rham class. The classes obtained in this way lie in the annihilator of $\ker j_ X$, where they form an open convex cone, and strict positivity against this cone detects every nonzero pseudoeffective class in the image of $j_ X$. Set $V_ X=H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$ and \[  K_ X=\ker j_ X,\qquad W_ X=K_ X^\perp \subset H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R),  \] where the annihilator is taken with respect to the Poincaré pairing \[  \langle [\lambda ],a\rangle =\int _ X\lambda \wedge a \qquad \bigl (a\in H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)\bigr ).  \] Let \[  \mathcal C_ X =\{ [\lambda ]\in V_ X:j_ X([\lambda ])\text{ is pseudoeffective}\} .  \] This is a convex cone, since pseudoeffective classes form a convex cone. The image of $j_ X$ lies in the kernel of the natural map from Bott–Chern to de Rham cohomology, and it can be strictly smaller than this kernel, as example 29.7.4 will show. Lemma 29.6.1 . The space $K_ X$ consists of the de Rham classes of real parts of closed holomorphic one-forms. Moreover, \[  \mathcal C_ X\cap (-\mathcal C_ X)=K_ X.  \] Proof. If $j_ X([\lambda ])=0$, write $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$. Since $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{d}=-\mathrm{d}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$, the form $\lambda +\mathrm{d}f$ is both $\mathrm{d}$-closed and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. Since the two equations separate the $\partial $- and $\bar\partial $-derivatives, its $(1,0)$-part is holomorphic and closed. Thus $\lambda +\mathrm{d}f$ is the real part of the closed holomorphic form $2(\lambda +\mathrm{d}f)^{1,0}$. Conversely, the real part of a closed holomorphic one-form is closed for both operators, so its image under $j_ X$ is zero. By proposition 28.1.2 , the pseudoeffective Bott–Chern cone contains no line. Thus $j_ X(\xi )$ and $-j_ X(\xi )$ are both pseudoeffective exactly when $j_ X(\xi )=0$, which is the identity $\mathcal C_ X\cap (-\mathcal C_ X)=K_ X$. $\square$ Definition 29.6.2 . The Lee–Gauduchon cone is \[  \operatorname {LG}(X) =\bigl \{ [\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\gamma ^{n-1})]: \gamma \text{ is a Gauduchon metric on }X\bigr \} .  \] For a closed real one-form $\lambda $ and any smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Gamma $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0$, integration by parts gives 29.34 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lck-lee-gauduchon-pairing} \int _ X\lambda \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma =\int _ X\kappa _\lambda \wedge \Gamma . \end{equation} The form $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma $ is closed, and both sides depend only on the cohomology classes involved. In particular, the class $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma ]$ annihilates $K_ X$, so $\operatorname {LG}(X)\subseteq W_ X$. Proposition 29.6.3 . The cone $\operatorname {LG}(X)$ is nonempty, convex and open in $W_ X$. Its linear span is $W_ X$. Proof. Let $\mathcal Z_ X$ be the real vector space of smooth $(n-1,n-1)$-forms $\Gamma $ satisfying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0$, and set \[  q_ X(\Gamma )=[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma ].  \] We first show that $q_ X(\mathcal Z_ X)=W_ X$. The inclusion into $W_ X$ follows from ( 29.34 ). If $[\lambda ]$ annihilates the image of $q_ X$, then by ( 29.34 ) the class $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ has zero pairing with every Gauduchon form. The generalized Lamari criterion, theorem 4.3.1 , implies that both $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ and $-\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ are pseudoeffective, so $[\lambda ]\in K_ X$ by lemma 29.6.1 . Thus the image of $q_ X$ and $W_ X$ have the same annihilator in $V_ X$, and since the Poincaré pairing between $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}$ and $H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}$ is nondegenerate, they are equal. Let $\mathcal Z_ X^+$ be the set of strictly positive forms in $\mathcal Z_ X$. By the linear-algebra construction used in the proof of theorem 4.3.1 , every such form is the $(n-1)$st power of a unique Hermitian form, which is then Gauduchon. Hence \[  \operatorname {LG}(X)=q_ X(\mathcal Z_ X^+).  \] By Gauduchon's theorem, $\mathcal Z_ X^+$ is nonempty, and it is a convex cone; hence so is $\operatorname {LG}(X)$. For openness, choose forms $\Gamma _1,\ldots ,\Gamma _ r\in \mathcal Z_ X$ whose images form a basis of $W_ X$. If $\Gamma \in \mathcal Z_ X^+$, then $\Gamma +\sum _ i t_ i\Gamma _ i$ remains strictly positive for all sufficiently small real $t_ i$, and the images of these forms cover a neighborhood of $q_ X(\Gamma )$ in $W_ X$. This includes the case $W_ X=\{ 0\} $, with the empty basis. Since a nonempty open subset spans the ambient vector space, the assertion about the span follows. $\square$ Theorem 29.6.4 . The cone $\mathcal C_ X$ is closed, and \[  \mathcal C_ X =\{ \xi \in V_ X:\langle \xi ,a\rangle \geq 0 \text{ for every }a\in \operatorname {LG}(X)\} .  \] Conversely, \[  \operatorname {LG}(X) =\{ a\in W_ X:\langle \xi ,a\rangle >0 \text{ for every }\xi \in \mathcal C_ X\setminus K_ X\} .  \] Proof. The first equality is theorem 4.3.1 applied to the smooth closed form $\kappa _\lambda $, together with ( 29.34 ). It expresses $\mathcal C_ X$ as an intersection of closed half-spaces, so this cone is closed. If $a=[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\gamma ^{n-1})]\in \operatorname {LG}(X)$ and $\xi =[\lambda ]\in \mathcal C_ X\setminus K_ X$, choose a closed positive current $T=\kappa _\lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. It is nonzero because it represents the nonzero class $j_ X(\xi )$. Therefore \[  \langle \xi ,a\rangle =\int _ XT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}>0.  \] Conversely, suppose that $a\in W_ X\setminus \operatorname {LG}(X)$. Separating the point $a$ from the nonempty open convex cone $\operatorname {LG}(X)$ in the finite-dimensional space $W_ X$ gives a nonzero linear functional $\ell $ on $W_ X$ such that \[  \ell (a)\leq 0,\qquad \ell (b)\geq 0 \quad (b\in \operatorname {LG}(X)).  \] Indeed, in the usual separating inequalities the constant can be taken to be zero, by scaling the elements of the cone. By Poincaré duality, $\ell =\langle \xi ,\cdot \rangle $ for a class $\xi \in V_ X$ that is unique modulo $K_ X$, and $\xi \notin K_ X$ because $\ell \neq 0$. The first equality of the theorem gives $\xi \in \mathcal C_ X$, and then $\langle \xi ,a\rangle \leq 0$ shows that $a$ does not belong to the right side of the second equality. This proves the second equality; if $\operatorname {LG}(X)=W_ X$, there is nothing to prove. $\square$

title: Lemma 29.6.1
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Lemma 29.6.1 . The space $K_ X$ consists of the de Rham classes of real parts of closed holomorphic one-forms. Moreover, \[  \mathcal C_ X\cap (-\mathcal C_ X)=K_ X.  \] Proof. If $j_ X([\lambda ])=0$, write $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$. Since $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{d}=-\mathrm{d}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$, the form $\lambda +\mathrm{d}f$ is both $\mathrm{d}$-closed and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. Since the two equations separate the $\partial $- and $\bar\partial $-derivatives, its $(1,0)$-part is holomorphic and closed. Thus $\lambda +\mathrm{d}f$ is the real part of the closed holomorphic form $2(\lambda +\mathrm{d}f)^{1,0}$. Conversely, the real part of a closed holomorphic one-form is closed for both operators, so its image under $j_ X$ is zero. title: 29.6.1 Bimeromorphic invariance
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 29.6.1 Bimeromorphic invariance A modification induces an isomorphism on degree-one cohomology, and a class on the base is pseudoeffective exactly when its pullback is. These two facts identify the cones $\mathcal C_ X$, and duality then identifies the Lee–Gauduchon cones. Lemma 29.6.5 . Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification between connected compact complex manifolds, and let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then \[  \{ \theta \} \text{ is pseudoeffective} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \{ \pi ^*\theta \} \text{ is pseudoeffective}.  \] The pullback on real Bott–Chern cohomology in bidegree $(1,1)$ is injective. Proof. By proposition 28.1.2 , both pullback and pushforward preserve pseudoeffectivity; the pullback of potentials is the one used in lemma 1.22.13 . Since $\pi $ has degree one, \[  \pi _*\pi ^*\{ \theta \} =\{ \theta \} .  \] Indeed, the identity of currents $\pi _*\pi ^*\theta =\theta $ follows by integration over the locus where $\pi $ is an isomorphism, whose complement has volume zero. This left inverse proves injectivity and the reverse implication for pseudoeffectivity. $\square$ Degree-one cohomology is compared by moving cycles away from the image of the exceptional set. Lemma 29.6.6 . If $\pi :Y\to X$ is a modification between connected compact complex manifolds, then \[  \pi ^*:H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(Y,\mathbb R)  \] is an isomorphism. Its Poincaré dual is the isomorphism $\pi _*:H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(Y,\mathbb R)\to H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$. Proof. For a proper analytic subset $A$ of a connected complex manifold $M$, the restriction map $H^1(M,\mathbb R)\to H^1(M\setminus A,\mathbb R)$ is injective, and it is an isomorphism if $A$ has complex codimension at least two. Indeed, choose a Whitney stratification of $A$. General position moves every one-cycle off the strata, which have real codimension at least two. If those codimensions are at least four, it also moves every two-chain with boundary in $M\setminus A$ off the strata, relative to its boundary. Thus the map $H_1(M\setminus A,\mathbb R)\to H_1(M,\mathbb R)$ is surjective in the first case and bijective in the second, and dualizing over $\mathbb R$ gives the assertions about restriction. Since $X$ is smooth, there is an analytic subset $A\subset X$ of complex codimension at least two such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $U=X\setminus A$. Restriction from $X$ to $U$ is therefore an isomorphism, whereas restriction from $Y$ to $\pi ^{-1}U$ is injective. Every class on $\pi ^{-1}U\simeq U$ extends to $X$ and hence pulls back to a class on $Y$. The commutative diagram of restriction maps now shows that $\pi ^*$ is an isomorphism, and Poincaré duality and the projection formula give the assertion for $\pi _*$. $\square$ Theorem 29.6.7 . Let $X$ and $Y$ be bimeromorphic connected compact complex manifolds. Under the natural identification of their first de Rham cohomology groups, and the Poincaré-dual identification of their de Rham cohomology groups of degree $2n-1$, the spaces $K_ X,W_ X$ and the cones $\mathcal C_ X,\operatorname {LG}(X)$ correspond to those of $Y$. Proof. First let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification. Holomorphic pullback commutes with $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$, so \[  j_ Y(\pi ^*\xi )=\pi ^*j_ X(\xi ).  \] By lemma 29.6.5 , a class $\xi $ lies in $\mathcal C_ X$ if and only if $\pi ^*\xi $ lies in $\mathcal C_ Y$, and likewise for $K_ X$ and $K_ Y$, since the pullback is injective on Bott–Chern classes. By lemma 29.6.6 , every degree-one class on $Y$ is of the form $\pi ^*\xi $. Thus the isomorphism $\pi ^*$ in degree one identifies the two cones and the two kernels. Its dual $\pi _*$ identifies $W_ Y$ with $W_ X$, and theorem 29.6.4 gives \[  \pi _*\operatorname {LG}(Y)=\operatorname {LG}(X).  \] For a bimeromorphic map between $X$ and $Y$, resolve its graph to obtain modifications $p:Z\to X$ and $q:Z\to Y$ from a compact complex manifold $Z$. The preceding argument applies to both maps and identifies the cones and kernels via $(q^*)^{-1}p^*$ and its Poincaré dual. These identifications do not depend on the resolution: they are compatible with restriction to a common open set on which the original map is an isomorphism, and by the injectivity of degree-one restriction proved above, this determines each class. The dual identifications are therefore canonical as well. $\square$

title: 29.6.2 Balanced metrics and the Hopf cone
search_title: Balanced metrics and the Hopf cone
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 29.6.2 Balanced metrics and the Hopf cone If zero belongs to the Lee–Gauduchon cone, then the image of $j_ X$ contains no nonzero pseudoeffective class; this is the case when $X$ carries a balanced metric. On the Hopf threefold, by contrast, the Lee form spans a ray of classes with pseudoeffective image under $j_ X$, and the Lee–Gauduchon cone is an open half-line. Corollary 29.6.8 . The following conditions are equivalent: \[  0\in \operatorname {LG}(X),\qquad \operatorname {LG}(X)=W_ X,\qquad \mathcal C_ X=K_ X.  \] A balanced metric implies these conditions. On a manifold in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, one has $W_ X=\{ 0\} $ and $\operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} $. Proof. An open cone in a finite-dimensional vector space that contains zero is the entire space, since scaling a neighborhood of zero reaches every point. The two dual descriptions in theorem 29.6.4 now prove the equivalences, including the case $W_ X=\{ 0\} $. If $b$ is a balanced metric, the form $b^{n-1}$ is closed and of pure type, hence also $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. Thus $b$ is Gauduchon and gives the element $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(b^{n-1})]=0$ of $\operatorname {LG}(X)$. On a compact Kähler manifold the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma gives $j_ X=0$, since every $\kappa _\lambda $ is closed and de Rham exact. Thus $K_ X=V_ X$ and $W_ X=\{ 0\} $, and since $\operatorname {LG}(X)$ is nonempty, $\operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} $. By theorem 29.6.7 , this conclusion extends to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$. $\square$ Consequently, a nonzero pseudoeffective class in the image of $j_ X$ obstructs balanced metrics on every compact complex manifold bimeromorphic to $X$. For LCK manifolds, 29.2.4 would provide such a class. For the Hopf threefold of chapter 8 , with the Lee form $\lambda $ of proposition 29.3.2 , the covering description identifies the underlying manifold with $S^1\times S^5$, so $V_ X=\mathbb R[\lambda ]$. The class $j_ X([\lambda ])=\{ \alpha \} $ is nonzero by ( 29.4 ), and it is pseudoeffective because $\alpha \geq 0$. Its negative multiples are not pseudoeffective, since their pairing with the Gauduchon metric $\omega $ is negative. Thus \[  K_ X=0,\qquad \mathcal C_ X=\mathbb R_{\geq 0}[\lambda ],\qquad \operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ a\in H^5_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R): \langle [\lambda ],a\rangle >0\} .  \] The same manifold has unbounded Monge–Ampère masses by theorem 8.0.1 . The positive ray detected here controls pairings with cohomology classes, which are linear and do not bound those nonlinear masses.
