title: 29.7 Strongly Gauduchon metrics
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: 29.7 Strongly Gauduchon metrics As in section 29.6 , $X$ is an arbitrary connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$. The closed form underlying a strongly Gauduchon metric pairs positively with every nonzero closed positive $(1,1)$-current, and this pairing depends only on the de Rham class of the current. It therefore bounds the mass of closed positive currents in terms of their de Rham classes and excludes nonzero positive de Rham-exact currents. The Lee–Gauduchon cone, by contrast, tests only the de Rham-exact Bott–Chern classes in the image of $j_ X$. On the Calabi–Eckmann threefold this image vanishes while a nonzero positive exact current exists, so the two conditions differ. Definition 29.7.1 . A Hermitian metric $\gamma $ is strongly Gauduchon if $\gamma ^{n-1}$ is the $(n-1,n-1)$-component of a smooth closed real $(2n-2)$-form. Write the closed real form in the definition as \[  \Theta =\gamma ^{n-1}+\beta +\overline\beta , \qquad \beta \text{ of type }(n,n-2).  \] Then $\partial (\gamma ^{n-1})=-\bar\partial \beta $. Conversely, this equation and its conjugate give $\mathrm{d}\Theta =0$, because all other components of $\mathrm d\Theta $ have a type with an entry exceeding $n$. Thus $\gamma $ is strongly Gauduchon if and only if $\partial (\gamma ^{n-1})$ is $\bar\partial $-exact. Applying $\bar\partial $ shows that a strongly Gauduchon metric is Gauduchon. Every balanced metric is strongly Gauduchon, with $\Theta =\gamma ^{n-1}$. Proposition 29.7.2 . If $\gamma $ is a strongly Gauduchon metric, then $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\gamma ^{n-1})]=0$; in particular $0\in \operatorname {LG}(X)$. Moreover, $X$ admits a strongly Gauduchon metric if and only if there is no nonzero positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$ that is de Rham exact. Proof. Put $\Gamma =\gamma ^{n-1}$ and use $\beta $ as above. Then \[  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma =\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi } (\bar\partial \beta -\partial \overline\beta ) =\mathrm{d}\! \left(\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi } (\beta -\overline\beta )\right).  \] Thus $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma ]=0$. Next, let $S$ be a real current of degree one such that $T=\mathrm{d}S$ is a nonzero positive $(1,1)$-current, and let $\Theta $ be a closed real form with strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-part $\Gamma $. By type considerations and Stokes' theorem for currents, \[  \int _ XT\wedge \Gamma =\int _ XT\wedge \Theta =0.  \] But the first integral is strictly positive because $T\ne 0$ and $\Gamma >0$, a contradiction. Thus a strongly Gauduchon metric excludes nonzero positive exact currents. Conversely, suppose that no strongly Gauduchon metric exists. In the real Fréchet space of smooth $(2n-2)$-forms, let $\mathcal Z$ be the closed subspace of closed forms, and let $\mathcal P$ be the open convex cone of forms with strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-part. This cone is nonempty, since it contains $h^{n-1}$ for any Hermitian metric $h$. The two sets are disjoint, because the positive $(n-1)$st root of the $(n-1,n-1)$-part of a form in their intersection would be a strongly Gauduchon metric. The Hahn–Banach separation theorem therefore gives a nonzero real current $T$ of degree two such that \[  T|_{\mathcal Z}=0,\qquad T(\Theta )\geq 0\quad (\Theta \in \mathcal P).  \] Fix $\Theta _0\in \mathcal P$. If a real form $\Psi $ has zero $(n-1,n-1)$-part, then $\Theta _0+t\Psi \in \mathcal P$ for every $t\in \mathbb R$, so $T(\Psi )=0$. Thus $T$ is of type $(1,1)$. For any semipositive $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Gamma $, we have $\Gamma +\varepsilon \Theta _0\in \mathcal P$ for $\varepsilon >0$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $T(\Gamma )\geq 0$; thus $T$ is positive. Since $T$ annihilates every exact test form, it is closed. By the de Rham theorem for currents and Poincaré duality, its cohomology class is determined by its pairings with closed forms of complementary degree. All these pairings vanish, so $T=\mathrm{d}S$ for a real current $S$. Thus $T$ is a nonzero positive exact current, which proves the converse. $\square$ Equivalently, $X$ admits a strongly Gauduchon metric if and only if every nonzero pseudoeffective Bott–Chern class has nonzero image in de Rham cohomology. Indeed, a closed positive current representing the zero Bott–Chern class has zero pairing with a Gauduchon metric and therefore vanishes, so the Bott–Chern classes of the nonzero positive de Rham-exact currents are exactly the nonzero pseudoeffective classes with zero de Rham image. The same criterion characterizes the manifolds on which de Rham classes control the masses of closed positive currents. Corollary 29.7.3 . Fix a Hermitian metric $h$ on $X$ and a norm on $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$. Then $X$ admits a strongly Gauduchon metric if and only if there is a constant $C>0$ such that every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ satisfies 29.35 \begin{equation} \label{eq:strong-gauduchon-class-mass} \int _ XT\wedge h^{n-1}\leq C\| [T]_{\mathrm{dR}}\| . \end{equation} Under this condition, the family of closed positive $(1,1)$-currents whose de Rham classes belong to a fixed compact set is weakly compact, and the image of the pseudoeffective Bott–Chern cone in $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$ is a closed convex cone containing no line. Proof. Suppose that $\gamma $ is strongly Gauduchon, and choose a smooth closed real form $\Theta $ whose $(n-1,n-1)$-part is $\gamma ^{n-1}$. By compactness, $h^{n-1}\leq A\gamma ^{n-1}$ for some $A>0$. Positivity and type considerations then give \[  \int _ XT\wedge h^{n-1} \leq A\int _ XT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =A\langle [T]_{\mathrm{dR}},[\Theta ]_{\mathrm{dR}}\rangle .  \] The last pairing is a fixed linear functional on the finite-dimensional de Rham group, which proves ( 29.35 ). Conversely, this bound forces every closed positive de Rham-exact current to vanish, and proposition 29.7.2 gives a strongly Gauduchon metric. For the compactness assertion, the bound gives uniformly bounded trace masses. A weak limit of such currents is positive and closed, and its de Rham class is the limit of their classes, as one sees by pairing with a finite basis of smooth closed forms of complementary degree and using Poincaré duality. Thus the family is weakly closed, and the usual weak compactness of positive currents with bounded mass proves the assertion. Let $c_ j$ be a convergent sequence in the image cone, and choose closed positive currents $T_ j$ with $[T_ j]_{\mathrm{dR}}=c_ j$. By the compactness assertion, a subsequence converges to a closed positive current representing the limit of the classes. Its Bott–Chern class is pseudoeffective, so the image cone is closed. Convexity follows from addition and nonnegative scaling. Finally, if both $c$ and $-c$ lie in the image, choose closed positive currents $T$ and $S$ representing them. Their sum is de Rham exact, so ( 29.35 ) gives $T+S=0$, and positivity gives $T=S=0$, hence $c=0$. $\square$ Example 29.7.4 . There is a connected compact complex threefold $X$ with \[  \operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} ,\qquad V_ X=K_ X=W_ X=0,  \] but with no strongly Gauduchon metric. Moreover, $X$ has a nonzero pseudoeffective Bott–Chern class whose de Rham image is zero; this class is not in the image of $j_ X$. Proof. Consider the holomorphic action of the additive group $\mathbb C$ on \[  \widetilde X=(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )\times (\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} ), \qquad t\cdot (z,w)=(\mathrm{e}^ t z,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t}w).  \] The action is free, since $\mathrm{e}^ t=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t}=1$ forces $t=0$. It is also proper. Indeed, if both $(z,w)$ and $t\cdot (z,w)$ range in compact subsets of $\widetilde X$, then the norms of the four vectors $z$, $w$, $\mathrm e^ tz$ and $\mathrm e^{\mathrm it}w$ in $\mathbb C^2$ are bounded above and away from zero. Writing $t=a+\mathrm i b$, the ratios of these norms bound $\mathrm{e}^ a$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-b}$ above and away from zero, so $a$ and $b$ stay bounded. A free proper holomorphic action has local holomorphic slices, and its quotient $X$ is a Hausdorff complex manifold of dimension three. Every orbit meets $S^3\times S^3$ exactly once, at the image of $(z,w)$ under the group element with \[  a=-\log |z|,\qquad b=\log |w|.  \] These expressions depend smoothly on $(z,w)$, so the slice $S^3\times S^3$ identifies the quotient with $S^3\times S^3$ as a smooth manifold. In particular, $X$ is compact and connected, and \[  H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)=H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R) =H^5_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)=0.  \] It follows that $V_ X=K_ X=W_ X=0$ and $\operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} $; the latter cone is nonempty by Gauduchon's theorem and lies in the zero group $H^5_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto ([z],[w])$ is invariant under the action and descends to a holomorphic map \[  p:X\longrightarrow \mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1.  \] It is a submersion, because the map on $\widetilde X$ is a submersion and the orbits of the action lie in its fibers. Let $\eta $ be the sum of the Fubini–Study forms on the two factors. The smooth form \[  \alpha =p^*\eta  \] is closed, semipositive and of rank two everywhere. It is nonzero and de Rham exact, since $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)=0$. By proposition 29.7.2 , $X$ admits no strongly Gauduchon metric. The Bott–Chern class of $\alpha $ is nonzero: otherwise $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$, and the integral of $\alpha $ against any Gauduchon form would vanish, contradicting $\alpha \geq 0$ and $\alpha \ne 0$. The class is pseudoeffective, since $\alpha $ is a positive representative. Finally, $j_ X$ has zero domain, so this class is not in its image. $\square$ Thus $0\in \operatorname {LG}(X)$ does not imply the existence of a strongly Gauduchon metric, and hence does not imply the existence of a balanced metric. On the threefold of proposition 26.18.7 , which carries a balanced and hence strongly Gauduchon metric, let $\alpha ,\beta $ be the two pulled-back Fubini–Study forms. The nonzero class $\{ \beta -\alpha \} $ has zero de Rham image, and neither it nor its negative is pseudoeffective, by proposition 28.9.2 . Every Hermitian form on this threefold has zero lower mass in the sense of definition 6.5.1 . Thus the existence of a strongly Gauduchon metric guarantees neither injectivity of the map from Bott–Chern to de Rham cohomology nor the positive lower mass needed for solvability with every finite non-pluripolar measure.

title: Definition 29.7.1
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Definition 29.7.1 . A Hermitian metric $\gamma $ is strongly Gauduchon if $\gamma ^{n-1}$ is the $(n-1,n-1)$-component of a smooth closed real $(2n-2)$-form.

title: Proposition 29.7.2
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Proposition 29.7.2 . If $\gamma $ is a strongly Gauduchon metric, then $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\gamma ^{n-1})]=0$; in particular $0\in \operatorname {LG}(X)$. Moreover, $X$ admits a strongly Gauduchon metric if and only if there is no nonzero positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$ that is de Rham exact. Proof. Put $\Gamma =\gamma ^{n-1}$ and use $\beta $ as above. Then \[  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma =\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi } (\bar\partial \beta -\partial \overline\beta ) =\mathrm{d}\! \left(\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi } (\beta -\overline\beta )\right).  \] Thus $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma ]=0$. Next, let $S$ be a real current of degree one such that $T=\mathrm{d}S$ is a nonzero positive $(1,1)$-current, and let $\Theta $ be a closed real form with strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-part $\Gamma $. By type considerations and Stokes' theorem for currents, \[  \int _ XT\wedge \Gamma =\int _ XT\wedge \Theta =0.  \] But the first integral is strictly positive because $T\ne 0$ and $\Gamma >0$, a contradiction. Thus a strongly Gauduchon metric excludes nonzero positive exact currents. Conversely, suppose that no strongly Gauduchon metric exists. In the real Fréchet space of smooth $(2n-2)$-forms, let $\mathcal Z$ be the closed subspace of closed forms, and let $\mathcal P$ be the open convex cone of forms with strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-part. This cone is nonempty, since it contains $h^{n-1}$ for any Hermitian metric $h$. The two sets are disjoint, because the positive $(n-1)$st root of the $(n-1,n-1)$-part of a form in their intersection would be a strongly Gauduchon metric. The Hahn–Banach separation theorem therefore gives a nonzero real current $T$ of degree two such that \[  T|_{\mathcal Z}=0,\qquad T(\Theta )\geq 0\quad (\Theta \in \mathcal P).  \] Fix $\Theta _0\in \mathcal P$. If a real form $\Psi $ has zero $(n-1,n-1)$-part, then $\Theta _0+t\Psi \in \mathcal P$ for every $t\in \mathbb R$, so $T(\Psi )=0$. Thus $T$ is of type $(1,1)$. For any semipositive $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Gamma $, we have $\Gamma +\varepsilon \Theta _0\in \mathcal P$ for $\varepsilon >0$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $T(\Gamma )\geq 0$; thus $T$ is positive. Since $T$ annihilates every exact test form, it is closed. By the de Rham theorem for currents and Poincaré duality, its cohomology class is determined by its pairings with closed forms of complementary degree. All these pairings vanish, so $T=\mathrm{d}S$ for a real current $S$. Thus $T$ is a nonzero positive exact current, which proves the converse. $\square$

title: 9 Theory under mass bounds
text: 9 Theory under mass bounds

title: 30 Volumes under bounded mass
text: 30 Volumes under bounded mass In a Hermitian background, Monge–Ampère masses need not be bounded above or away from zero. On the standard Hopf threefold the masses of smooth admissible potentials of a Gauduchon form are unbounded (theorem 8.0.1 ), while on the threefold of theorem 26.18.1 every Hermitian form $h$ admits smooth admissible potentials whose masses tend to zero. In this part such bounds are imposed explicitly. The upper bound is the bounded mass property of definition 6.5.1 : $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $ for one, and hence for every, Hermitian form $\omega $ (proposition 6.5.2 ), where $v_+(\omega )$ and $v_-(\omega )$ denote the supremum and the infimum of the masses of bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions. A lower bound takes one of two forms. In chapter 31 , which does not assume bounded mass, it is positive lower mass $v_-(\theta )>0$ of a semipositive background $\theta $. In this chapter and in chapter 32 , which assume bounded mass, it is usually a positive lower singularity volume of the particular potentials involved, rather than a bound for all bounded potentials. In a closed background, the non-pluripolar mass of a potential depends only on its ordinary singularity type. In a nonclosed background, potentials of the same type can have different masses, so a singularity type carries two numbers, the infimum and the supremum of the masses of its members. These lower and upper singularity volumes keep the order information needed for comparison. Bounded mass makes the upper volume finite, and a positive lower volume prevents the auxiliary envelopes used below from collapsing. Together these bounds turn a small upper-volume deficit into a large admissible stretch, and this relates equality of volumes to the relative full-mass class and to ordinary envelopes. The upper volume of the maximum of two potentials measures how far apart their ordinary envelopes are. On models with a uniform positive lower-volume bound, the stretching estimate controls three-point comparisons, monotone limits and convergence in capacity. The comparison itself need not satisfy the triangle inequality, even on the projective plane, and at zero volume it can identify distinct models (example 30.6.2 ). Finite chains nevertheless give a complete metric once the reciprocal of the lower volume is included to prevent escape to zero volume. Analytic regularization identifies the multiplier-ideal models among the resulting limits, and strict barriers allow these comparisons to persist under small changes of background. On a curve, the polar part of the curvature current determines the ordinary model, and the volume comparison is the total variation of polar measures. This description extends to the zero-volume boundary. Taking the atomic part gives the nearest ideal model, while diffuse polar curvature measures the failure of analytic approximation. Area rescaling and smooth gauges then describe changes of background, including the collapse of all normalized potentials when the backgrounds converge uniformly to a form of zero area. Throughout the chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with the bounded mass property, and $\theta $ is a big smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, not necessarily closed; bigness means that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, some $\varepsilon >0$ and a Hermitian form $\omega $ (section 1.19 ). From section 30.12 on, we work instead on a compact Riemann surface with the backgrounds specified there. We recall the notation used from earlier chapters. For quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, $u\preceq v$ means $u\leq v+C$ for a constant $C$, and $u\sim v$ means $u\preceq v\preceq u$; the classes of $\sim $ are the ordinary singularity types (definition 1.12.1 ). Similarly, $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$ means $\mathcal I(tu)\subseteq \mathcal I(tv)$ for every $t>0$, and $u\sim _{\mathcal I}v$ means that these multiplier ideals are equal (section 1.12 ). For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ is the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 6.1.2 , which is finite under bounded mass by proposition 6.5.3 . The lower and upper singularity volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ of definition 13.3.1 are the infimum and the supremum of $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$ over all $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\sim u$. A statement about $\operatorname {vol}_\theta $, without a bar, is asserted for both volumes. Given an obstacle $f$, we denote by $P_\theta (f)$ the regularized upper envelope of the $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions lying below $f$, and we write $P_\theta (u,v)=P_\theta (\min (u,v))$ for the rooftop envelope and $V_\theta =P_\theta (0)$ (section 1.19 ). The ordinary envelope $P_\theta [u]$ is the regularized supremum of all $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $h\preceq u$ and $h\leq 0$ (definition 1.19.4 ), and $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ is the multiplier-ideal envelope of definition 16.2.1 , defined in the same way with $h\sim _{\mathcal I}u$ in place of $h\preceq u$. We call $u$ an ordinary model if $P_\theta [u]=u$, and an ideal model if $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=u$. Both kinds have supremum zero, and every ideal model is an ordinary model by corollary 16.2.4 . Finally, $\nu (u,x)$ denotes the Lelong number at $x$, and a potential is called analytic if it has analytic singularities in the rational-coefficient convention of section 1.13 .

title: 30.1 Comparison of singularity volumes
text: 30.1 Comparison of singularity volumes Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta $. By proposition 6.5.3 , theorem 6.1.2 , the mass of every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic potential is at most $v_+(\Omega )$. Hence, for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  0\leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) \leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)<+\infty .  \] If $\theta $ is closed, both volumes equal $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, because in the closed theory the non-pluripolar mass depends only on the singularity type [ SGPT ] . For a nonclosed background the two volumes can differ even at $u=0$, as example 2.3.1 shows. Both volumes increase when the background increases or the singularities become milder. In the proof, a rooftop envelope for the lower volume and a maximum for the upper volume produce competitors of the required singularity types, and locality of non-pluripolar products confines the error to sets whose mass tends to zero. Theorem 30.1.1 . Let $\theta _1,\theta _2$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$. Suppose $\theta _1$ is big, $\theta _1\leq \theta _2$, and $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$ satisfy $u_1\preceq u_2$. Then \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1) \leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2),\qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2).  \] Proof. We first treat the lower volume. After adding a constant to $u_1$ we may assume $u_1\leq u_2$. Choose $v_2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$ with $v_2\sim u_2$ and, for real $t>0$, consider the rooftop envelope \[  p_ t=P_{\theta _1}(u_1+t,v_2).  \] Since $u_1\leq u_2\leq v_2+C$ for a constant $C$, the function $u_1-C$ is a competitor; moreover $p_ t\leq u_1+t$. Hence $p_ t\sim u_1$. By the contact theorem (theorem 14.7.4 ), the measure $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(p_ t)$ is carried by the union of $\{ p_ t=u_1+t\} \subset \{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} $ and $\{ p_ t=v_2\} $. On the first set, ordered contact in background $\theta _1$ (proposition 6.2.1 ) bounds it by $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1)$. On the second set, $p_ t$ is also $\theta _2$-plurisubharmonic and lies below $v_2$; positivity of the mixed products (lemma 6.1.1 ) and ordered contact in background $\theta _2$ bound it by $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2)$. Therefore \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(p_ t) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} }\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1) +\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2).  \] As $t\to +\infty $, the first measure on the right has total mass tending to zero: the sets $\{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} $ decrease to a subset of the pole set of $u_1$, and $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1)$ is a finite measure that puts no mass on pluripolar sets. Integrating and letting $t\to +\infty $ gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1)\leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2)$, and taking the infimum over $v_2$ proves the first inequality. For the upper volume, choose any $v_1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ with $v_1\sim u_1$, and put $w_ t=\max (v_1,u_2-t)$ for $t>0$. This function is $\theta _2$-plurisubharmonic and satisfies $w_ t\sim u_2$. On the set $D_ t=\{ v_1>u_2-t\} $, locality and positivity of the mixed products imply \[  \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(v_1) \leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(w_ t).  \] The sets $D_ t$ exhaust the complement of the pole set of $v_1$, which carries no mass. Integrating and letting $t\to +\infty $ therefore gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(v_1)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2)$, and taking the supremum over $v_1$ proves the second inequality. $\square$ Adding a positive current also increases both volumes. For the lower volume, the potential of the added current is subtracted inside an envelope, which produces a competitor in the original background. Proposition 30.1.2 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$ for a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ on $X$. Then, for either the lower or the upper volume, \[  \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_{\theta +\eta }(u+v).  \] Proof. The form $\theta +\eta $ is big: adding the positive current $\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ to a strictly positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ gives a strictly positive current $\theta +\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho +v)$. For the upper volume, add $v$ to each competitor $u'\sim u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then $u'+v\sim u+v$, and positivity of the mixed products shows that $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\eta }(u'+v)\geq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u')$. For the lower volume, choose $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\eta )$ with $w\sim u+v$, and let $p=P_\theta (w-v)$. Since $w-v=u+O(1)$ outside the pole sets, a translate of $u$ is a competitor and $p\leq u+C$ for a constant $C$. Thus $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $p\sim u$. By the contact theorem, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ is carried by $D=\{ p+v=w\} $. Furthermore $p+v\leq w$ everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . Positivity of the mixed products and ordered contact therefore give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\eta }(p+v) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\eta }(w).  \] Integrating and taking the infimum over $w$ proves the assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 30.1.1
text: Theorem 30.1.1 . Let $\theta _1,\theta _2$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$. Suppose $\theta _1$ is big, $\theta _1\leq \theta _2$, and $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$ satisfy $u_1\preceq u_2$. On the second set, $p_ t$ is also $\theta _2$-plurisubharmonic and lies below $v_2$; positivity of the mixed products (lemma 6.1.1 ) and ordered contact in background $\theta _2$ bound it by $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2)$. Therefore \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(p_ t) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} }\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1) +\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2).  \] As $t\to +\infty $, the first measure on the right has total mass tending to zero: the sets $\{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} $ decrease to a subset of the pole set of $u_1$, and $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1)$ is a finite measure that puts no mass on pluripolar sets. Integrating and letting $t\to +\infty $ gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1)\leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2)$, and taking the infimum over $v_2$ proves the first inequality. For the upper volume, choose any $v_1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ with $v_1\sim u_1$, and put $w_ t=\max (v_1,u_2-t)$ for $t>0$. This function is $\theta _2$-plurisubharmonic and satisfies $w_ t\sim u_2$. On the set $D_ t=\{ v_1>u_2-t\} $, locality and positivity of the mixed products imply \[  \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(v_1) \leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(w_ t).  \] The sets $D_ t$ exhaust the complement of the pole set of $v_1$, which carries no mass. Integrating and letting $t\to +\infty $ therefore gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(v_1)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2)$, and taking the supremum over $v_1$ proves the second inequality. $\square$

title: Proposition 30.1.2
text: Proposition 30.1.2 . Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$ for a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ on $X$. Then, for either the lower or the upper volume, \[  \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_{\theta +\eta }(u+v).  \] Proof. The form $\theta +\eta $ is big: adding the positive current $\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ to a strictly positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ gives a strictly positive current $\theta +\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho +v)$. For the upper volume, add $v$ to each competitor $u'\sim u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then $u'+v\sim u+v$, and positivity of the mixed products shows that $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\eta }(u'+v)\geq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u')$. For the lower volume, choose $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\eta )$ with $w\sim u+v$, and let $p=P_\theta (w-v)$. Since $w-v=u+O(1)$ outside the pole sets, a translate of $u$ is a competitor and $p\leq u+C$ for a constant $C$. Thus $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $p\sim u$. By the contact theorem, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ is carried by $D=\{ p+v=w\} $. Furthermore $p+v\leq w$ everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . Positivity of the mixed products and ordered contact therefore give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\eta }(p+v) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\eta }(w).  \] Integrating and taking the infimum over $w$ proves the assertion. $\square$

title: 30.2 Volume deficits and relative full mass

30.2 Volume deficits and relative full mass The upper-volume deficit measures how far one potential can be stretched away from another, and the positive lower volume of the less singular potential prevents the stretching envelopes from collapsing. We use the stretching envelopes of chapter 13 . For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $b\geq 1$, the competitor family $\mathcal A_ b(u,v)$ consists of all $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})v\leq u$. When it is nonempty, its upper envelope is the $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function $Q_ b(u,v)=P_	heta (bu-(b-1)v)$, which again belongs to $\mathcal A_ b(u,v)$. For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, the relative envelope class $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,\varphi )$ of definition 13.4.1 consists of all $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $u\preceq \varphi $ and $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )
eq \varnothing $ for every $b\geq 1$. Lemma 30.2.1 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $u\preceq v$, and put \[  \delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (v)>0, \qquad D=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (v) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u).  \] If $b>1$ and $b^ nD<\delta $, then $\mathcal A_ b(u,v)
eq \varnothing $; that is, the stretching envelope $Q_ b(u,v)$ is defined. Proof. Adding constants to $u$ and $v$ only translates the competitors, so we may assume $v\leq 0$. Write $V=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (v)$. Since $D<b^{-n}\delta $, the definition of the upper volume gives $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $w\sim u$ and 30.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:relative-volume-deficit} V-\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_	heta (w)<b^{-n}\delta . \end{equation} After a translation of $w$ we may also assume $w\leq v$. For positive integers $j$, put \[  w_ j=\max (w,v-j),\qquad h_ j=Q_ b(w_ j,v).  \] The function $v-bj$ is a competitor for $h_ j$, and the defining convex inequality together with $w_ j\leq v$ gives $h_ j\leq v$. Thus $v-bj\leq h_ j\leq v$, so $w_ j\sim v$ and $h_ j\sim v$, and $h_ j$ decreases as $j$ increases. We claim that the decreasing limit $h$ of the $h_ j$ is not identically $-\infty $. If it were, theorem 1.4.2 would give $\sup _ Xh_ j	o -\infty $. By theorem 14.7.4 , the measure of $h_ j$ is carried by the contact set $C_ j=\{ b^{-1}h_ j+(1-b^{-1})v=w_ j\} $. Positivity of the mixed products and ordered contact for $b^{-1}h_ j+(1-b^{-1})v\leq w_ j$ give \[  \mathrm{MA}_	heta (h_ j) \leq b^ n\mathbf1_{C_ j}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (w_ j).  \] Fix a positive integer $k$. If $h\equiv -\infty $, then $h_ j\leq -bk$ everywhere for all large $j>k$. Since $v\leq 0$, every point of $C_ j$ then satisfies $w_ j\leq -k$, hence $w\leq -k$. Moreover $w_ j=w$ on $\{ w>-k\} \subset \{ w>v-j\} $, so locality gives \[   egin{split}  \delta \leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_	heta (h_ j) & \leq b^ n\int _{\{ w\leq -k\} }\mathrm{MA}_	heta (w_ j)\ & \leq b^ n\left(V-\int _{\{ w>-k\} }\mathrm{MA}_	heta (w)ight). \end{split}  \] Here the first inequality uses $h_ j\sim v$, and the last uses $w_ j\sim v$. Letting $k	o \infty $ contradicts ( 30.1 ), since the finite non-pluripolar measure $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (w)$ gives no mass to the pole set of $w$. This proves the claim. Consequently $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and $b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})v\leq w$. If $w\leq u+C$, then $h-bC\in \mathcal A_ b(u,v)$, which proves the lemma. $\square$ Proposition 30.2.2 . Let $\pi :Z	o X$ be a smooth compact modification. There is a finite constant $C_\pi $, depending only on $\pi $ and $	heta $, such that, for $u,v,\delta ,D$ as in lemma 30.2.1 , \[  0\leq 
u (u\circ \pi ,z)-
u (v\circ \pi ,z) \leq C_\pi \min \left\{ 1,\left( rac D\delta ight)^{1/n}ight\}  \qquad (z\in Z).  \] The same estimate holds for generic Lelong numbers along every prime divisor on $Z$. Proof. Let $C_\pi $ be the uniform bound for Lelong numbers of $\pi ^*	heta $-plurisubharmonic functions on $Z$ given by lemma 1.17.7 . Since $u\preceq v$, the difference of Lelong numbers is nonnegative, and it is at most $
u (u\circ \pi ,z)\leq C_\pi $. This proves the assertion when $D\geq \delta $. If $D<\delta $, then by lemma 30.2.1 every $b>1$ with $b^ nD<\delta $ admits some $h\in \mathcal A_ b(u,v)$. Pulling back the defining convex inequality and taking Lelong numbers gives \[  
u (u\circ \pi ,z)-
u (v\circ \pi ,z) \leq b^{-1} igl (
u (h\circ \pi ,z)-
u (v\circ \pi ,z) igr ) \leq b^{-1}C_\pi .  \] For $D>0$, let $b\uparrow (\delta /D)^{1/n}$; for $D=0$, let $b	o \infty $. Taking generic values along a prime divisor proves the divisorial assertion. $\square$ At zero deficit every finite stretch is possible. This leads to a second description of the relative envelope class. Fix a reference potential $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Definition 30.2.3 . The relative full-mass class of $\varphi $ is \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,	heta ,\varphi ) =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\preceq \varphi , \  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\varphi )\} .  \] Conversely, convex combinations turn the envelope condition into equality of volumes. Theorem 30.2.4 . Suppose $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\varphi )>0$. Then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,\varphi ) =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,	heta ,\varphi ).  \] Every member $u$ of this class also satisfies $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\varphi )$. Proof. First let $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,\varphi )$. For each $a\in (0,1)$, a member of $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )$ with $b=(1-a)^{-1}$ gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ such that $a\varphi +(1-a)h\leq u$. By theorem 30.1.1 , proposition 30.1.2 and homogeneity, for either volume, \[  a^ n\operatorname {vol}_	heta (\varphi ) \leq \operatorname {vol}_	heta (a\varphi +(1-a)h) \leq \operatorname {vol}_	heta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_	heta (\varphi ).  \] Letting $a	o 1$ proves that both volumes of $u$ equal those of $\varphi $; this direction does not use positive lower volume. Conversely, let $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,	heta ,\varphi )$. Then $D=0$ in lemma 30.2.1 with $v=\varphi $, so $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )
eq \varnothing $ for every $b>1$. For $b=1$ the family contains $u$. This is the defining condition of $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,\varphi )$. $\square$

text: Lemma 30.2.1 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u\preceq v$, and put \[  \delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v)>0, \qquad D=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] If $b>1$ and $b^ nD<\delta $, then $\mathcal A_ b(u,v)\neq \varnothing $; that is, the stretching envelope $Q_ b(u,v)$ is defined. Proof. Adding constants to $u$ and $v$ only translates the competitors, so we may assume $v\leq 0$. Write $V=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v)$. Since $D<b^{-n}\delta $, the definition of the upper volume gives $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim u$ and 30.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-volume-deficit} V-\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)<b^{-n}\delta . \end{equation} After a translation of $w$ we may also assume $w\leq v$. For positive integers $j$, put \[  w_ j=\max (w,v-j),\qquad h_ j=Q_ b(w_ j,v).  \] The function $v-bj$ is a competitor for $h_ j$, and the defining convex inequality together with $w_ j\leq v$ gives $h_ j\leq v$. Thus $v-bj\leq h_ j\leq v$, so $w_ j\sim v$ and $h_ j\sim v$, and $h_ j$ decreases as $j$ increases. We claim that the decreasing limit $h$ of the $h_ j$ is not identically $-\infty $. If it were, theorem 1.4.2 would give $\sup _ Xh_ j\to -\infty $. By theorem 14.7.4 , the measure of $h_ j$ is carried by the contact set $C_ j=\{ b^{-1}h_ j+(1-b^{-1})v=w_ j\} $. Positivity of the mixed products and ordered contact for $b^{-1}h_ j+(1-b^{-1})v\leq w_ j$ give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (h_ j) \leq b^ n\mathbf1_{C_ j}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ j).  \] Fix a positive integer $k$. If $h\equiv -\infty $, then $h_ j\leq -bk$ everywhere for all large $j>k$. Since $v\leq 0$, every point of $C_ j$ then satisfies $w_ j\leq -k$, hence $w\leq -k$. Moreover $w_ j=w$ on $\{ w>-k\} \subset \{ w>v-j\} $, so locality gives \[  \begin{split}  \delta \leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (h_ j) & \leq b^ n\int _{\{ w\leq -k\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ j)\\ & \leq b^ n\left(V-\int _{\{ w>-k\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)\right). \end{split}  \] Here the first inequality uses $h_ j\sim v$, and the last uses $w_ j\sim v$. Letting $k\to \infty $ contradicts ( 30.1 ), since the finite non-pluripolar measure $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)$ gives no mass to the pole set of $w$. This proves the claim. Consequently $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})v\leq w$. If $w\leq u+C$, then $h-bC\in \mathcal A_ b(u,v)$, which proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Definition 30.2.3
text: Definition 30.2.3 . The relative full-mass class of $\varphi $ is \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\preceq \varphi , \  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )\} .  \]

title: Theorem 30.2.4
text: Theorem 30.2.4 . Suppose $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )>0$. Then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ).  \] Every member $u$ of this class also satisfies $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )$. Proof. First let $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. For each $a\in (0,1)$, a member of $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )$ with $b=(1-a)^{-1}$ gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $a\varphi +(1-a)h\leq u$. By theorem 30.1.1 , proposition 30.1.2 and homogeneity, for either volume, \[  a^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (\varphi ) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (a\varphi +(1-a)h) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (\varphi ).  \] Letting $a\to 1$ proves that both volumes of $u$ equal those of $\varphi $; this direction does not use positive lower volume. For $b=1$ the family contains $u$. This is the defining condition of $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. $\square$

title: 30.3 Domination and ordinary envelopes
text: 30.3 Domination and ordinary envelopes Since $u\preceq P_\theta [u]$, monotonicity gives one inequality between the volumes of a potential and those of its ordinary envelope. For the reverse inequality we identify a limit of obstacle envelopes by means of contact support and a domination principle. In the domination argument, positive lower volume guarantees that the stretching envelopes are defined. From now on we write $\mu _ w=\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)$ for $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Theorem 30.3.1 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have positive lower volume, let $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\preceq \varphi $, and let $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ u\leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ v,  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. Put $\ell =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )>0$ and $\mathcal E_\varphi =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. We may replace $v$ by $\max (u,v)$: by locality, the hypothesis is unchanged on $\{ u<v\} $, and by upward stability (proposition 13.4.2 ) the new $v$ lies in $\mathcal E_\varphi $. Thus we may assume $u\leq v$. Translate $u,v$ by the same constant so that $v\leq \varphi $, and then translate all three potentials so that $\varphi \leq 0$. The idea is to stretch $u$ away from $v$; the stretched potentials keep lower volume $\ell $, and this is incompatible with a strict inequality $u<v$ on a set of positive volume. Set \[  q_ b=Q_ b(u,v),\qquad D_ b=\{ b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})v=u\} .  \] Lemma 13.4.3 gives $q_ b\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $q_ b\leq u$. Since $b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})v\leq u$ with contact set $D_ b$, contact support and positivity of the mixed products give \[  b^{-n}\mu _{q_ b}+(1-b^{-1})^ n\mathbf1_{D_ b}\mu _ v \leq \mathbf1_{D_ b}\mu _ u.  \] Here $\mu _{q_ b}$ is carried by $D_ b$. Choose $b$ so large that $(1-b^{-1})^ n>c$. On $D_ b\cap \{ u<v\} $ the hypothesis bounds the right-hand side by $c\mu _ v$, and subtracting finite measures shows that $\mu _{q_ b}$ vanishes there. Thus $\mu _{q_ b}$ is carried by $D_ b\cap \{ u=v\} \subset \{ q_ b=u\} $. Since $q_ b\leq u$, ordered contact for this pair and theorem 30.2.4 , which gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ b)=\ell $, now yield 30.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-domination-fixed-tail} \ell \leq \mu _{q_ b}(X)\leq \mu _ u(\{ q_ b=u\} ). \end{equation} Suppose now that $u<v$ somewhere. Then there is $\delta >0$ such that $\{ u<v-\delta \} $ has positive Lebesgue measure; otherwise $u\geq v$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . On this set the convex inequality gives $q_ b\leq u-(b-1)\delta $. The family $q_ b$ decreases in $b$ and is bounded above by $u$. Its limit is $-\infty $ on a set of positive measure, so it cannot be $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and is therefore identically $-\infty $. Hence theorem 1.4.2 gives $\sup _ Xq_ b\to -\infty $. The sets $\{ q_ b=u\} \subset \{ u\leq \sup _ Xq_ b\} $ then have $\mu _ u$-mass tending to zero, because $\mu _ u$ is finite and puts no mass on the pole set of $u$. This contradicts ( 30.4 ). $\square$ Corollary 30.3.2 . For $u,v$ as in theorem 30.3.1 and $\lambda >0$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\mu _ u\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\mu _ v \quad \Longrightarrow \quad u\geq v.  \] If $\mu _ u\leq c\mu _ v$ on $X$ for a finite $c\geq 0$, then $c\geq 1$. Proof. Fix $\delta >0$. On $\{ u<v-\delta \} $ the weighted inequality gives $\mu _ u\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \delta }\mu _ v=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \delta }\mu _{v-\delta }$. Theorem 30.3.1 , applied to $v-\delta $ with $c=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \delta }<1$, gives $u\geq v-\delta $; now let $\delta \downarrow 0$. If the second assertion failed, the theorem would apply with the same $c<1$ to every translate $v+A$, $A\in \mathbb R$, and would give $u\geq v+A$ for all $A$. This is impossible at a point where $u$ and $v$ are both finite. $\square$ The next lemma concerns the envelope obtained by replacing the obstacle $0$ in definition 1.19.4 by a potential $w$. Lemma 30.3.3 . Let $u,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $P_\theta (u,w)\not\equiv -\infty $, and define the relative obstacle envelope \[  P_\theta [u](w)=\left(\lim _{C\to \infty }P_\theta (u+C,w)\right)^*.  \] Then \[  \mu _{P_\theta [u](w)} \leq \mathbf1_{\{ P_\theta [u](w)=w\} }\mu _ w.  \] Proof. Set $p_ C=P_\theta (u+C,w)$ for $C\geq 0$ and $p=P_\theta [u](w)$. The envelopes $p_ C$ increase with $C$, lie between $p_0$ and $w$, and converge to $p$ in capacity by lemma 1.8.12 . By the contact theorem, $\mu _{p_ C}$ is carried by $\{ p_ C=\min (u+C,w)\} $. Assigning the points where $u+C=w$ to the second term, ordered contact gives \[  \mu _{p_ C}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ p_ C=u+C<w\} }\mu _ u +\mathbf1_{\{ p_ C=w\} }\mu _ w.  \] The first measure has total mass at most \[  \varepsilon _ C=\mu _ u(\{ u\leq \sup _ Xw-C\} )\longrightarrow 0,  \] because $\mu _ u$ is finite and non-pluripolar. Testing against nonnegative continuous functions and applying the lower semicontinuity of lemma 6.3.1 gives $\mu _ p\leq \mu _ w$. The bounded quasi-continuous weight $\chi =\min (1,(w-p)_+)$, defined arbitrarily on the pluripolar set where $w-p$ is undefined, vanishes on $\{ p_ C=w\} $, since $p_ C\leq p\leq w$. Thus $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _{p_ C}\leq \varepsilon _ C$. Weighted lower semicontinuity gives $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _ p=0$, so $\mu _ p$ is carried by $\{ p=w\} $. Together with $\mu _ p\leq \mu _ w$, this proves the lemma. $\square$ Theorem 30.3.4 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $p=P_\theta [u]$, \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] If this volume is positive, then also \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p),\qquad u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,p),\qquad P_\theta [p]=p.  \] Proof. Since $u\preceq p$, monotonicity gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. In particular, the lower volumes agree if $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)=0$. Suppose henceforth that $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)>0$. Normalize $u\leq 0$, so that $u\leq p$, and choose any $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim p$. Fix $K\geq 0$ with $p-K\leq w\leq p+K$. The rooftop envelope $p_ C=P_\theta (u+C,w)$ satisfies $u-K\leq p_ C\leq u+C$ for each $C\geq 0$, so it is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and equivalent to $u$. Its regularized increasing limit $r=P_\theta [u](w)$ satisfies \[  P_\theta (u+C+K,0)-K\leq p_ C\leq w, \qquad p-K\leq r\leq w\leq p+K.  \] Indeed, the leftmost potential lies below $u+C$, and below $p-K\leq w$ because $P_\theta (u+C+K,0)\leq P_\theta [u]=p$; it is therefore a competitor for the rooftop. Letting $C\to \infty $ gives the lower bound for $r$. Thus $r\sim p$, and proposition 13.4.2 puts $r$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,p)$. By lemma 30.3.3 , $\mu _ r$ vanishes on $\{ r<w\} $. Theorem 30.3.1 , with coefficient $c=0$ and reference $p$, gives $r\geq w$; hence $r=w$. Since $p_ C\to r$ in capacity, lower semicontinuity of the total mass (lemma 6.3.1 ) and $p_ C\sim u$ yield \[  \int _ X\mu _ w\leq \liminf _{C\to \infty }\int _ X\mu _{p_ C} \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] Taking the supremum over $w\sim p$ gives $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$, and hence equality of the upper volumes. Theorem 30.2.4 then gives $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,p)$ and equality of the lower volumes. Finally, proposition 13.4.5 gives $P_\theta [p]=P_\theta [u]=p$. $\square$ The ordinary envelope $P_\theta [u]$ is in general less singular than $u$. When the pole set of $u$ is a compact set of Hausdorff dimension zero, however, the full local Monge–Ampère product of theorem 1.6.9 is defined, and the ordinary envelope preserves its restriction to the pole set. Bounded mass controls the local approximations in every degree, and the products of lower degree put no mass on the pole set. Theorem 30.3.5 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$, and let $S\subset X$ be a compact set of Hausdorff dimension zero. Suppose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus S$, has pole set $\{ u=-\infty \} =S$, and has positive lower singularity volume. Put $p=P_\omega [u]$ and $p_ m=P_\omega (u+m,0)$ for real $m>0$. For $v=u$, $v=p$ and $v=p_ m$, the weak limit \[  \Phi _ v=\lim _{k\to \infty } (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (v,-k))^ n  \] of the bounded truncations exists and is a finite positive measure, which we call the full Monge–Ampère measure of $v$. On each coordinate chart, its restriction $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ v$ equals $\mathbf1_ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+q))^ n_{\mathrm{full}}$ for every smooth function $q$ making $v+q$ plurisubharmonic there; in particular, it does not depend on $q$. Moreover, \[  \mathbf1_ S\Phi _ p=\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ u,  \] and $\Phi _{p_ m}\to \Phi _ p$ weakly as $m\to \infty $. Proof. Step 1: the rooftops. Adding a constant to $u$ changes neither $p$ nor the family $(p_ m)_{m>0}$, apart from a shift of the parameter $m$. We may therefore assume $u\leq 0$. Then \[  u\leq p_ m\leq \min (u+m,0),\qquad p_ m\uparrow p,  \] where the increasing limit is understood after upper semicontinuous regularization. Thus $p_ m\sim u$, and $p_ m$ and $p$ are locally bounded off $S$. By theorem 30.3.4 , $p$ is an ordinary model with the same volumes as $u$. By lemma 1.8.12 , $p_ m\to p$ in capacity. On compact subsets of $X\setminus S$ the potentials have a common bounded range, so all bounded local products converge there, by the bounded product theory of section 1.6 . Step 2: full measures. Let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be locally bounded off $S$, and put $v_ k=\max (v,-k)$. On each chart choose a smooth $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \omega $, so that the functions $v_ k+q$ are plurisubharmonic and decrease to $v+q$. Theorem 1.6.9 then gives full weak limits in every degree, \[  W_ j(v)=\lim _{k\to \infty }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ k)^ j, \qquad \Phi _ v=\lim _{k\to \infty }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ k)^ n.  \] Indeed, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ k+q)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$, and the powers can be expanded in the closed positive powers of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ k+q)$ and smooth forms. The local limits patch together because the approximating bounded currents are global. The limits are currents of order zero with finite mass on the compact manifold $X$, and $\Phi _ v$ is positive. Stokes' theorem for the bounded potentials $v_ k$ gives $\int _ XW_ n(v)=0$. Consequently 30.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:small-pole-full-total} J(v):=\Phi _ v(X) =\int _ X\omega ^ n+ \sum _{j=1}^{n-1}\binom nj \int _ XW_ j(v)\wedge \omega ^{n-j}. \end{equation} The measure $\Phi _ v$ equals $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)$ off $S$. Every closed positive power of degree less than $n$ in this expansion has coefficient measures vanishing on $S$, by corollary 1.13.2 . Thus only the top closed power contributes to $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ v$. This identifies $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ v$ with $\mathbf1_ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+q))^ n_{\mathrm{full}}$ and proves independence of $q$. These assertions are local on each chart and do not require a single chart containing $S$. Finally, $J(v)\leq v_+(\omega )$, since every truncation $v_ k$ has mass at most $v_+(\omega )$. Step 3: convergence of the lower-degree powers. We need local trace bounds for the closed powers of $p_ m$ that are uniform in $m$. Fix a relatively compact coordinate neighborhood and write $\kappa =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$. Choose $B>0$ with $B\kappa \geq \omega $ there, and $A>1$ with $A\omega -B\kappa \geq \kappa $. For $p_{m,k}=\max (p_ m,-k)$, the closed current $T_{m,k}=B\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_{m,k}$ is positive and \[  Q_{m,k}:=A\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_{m,k}\geq T_{m,k}+\kappa .  \] Expanding $Q_{m,k}^ n$ with the smooth positive difference $Q_{m,k}-T_{m,k}\geq \kappa $ gives, for $1\leq j\leq n$, \[  \binom nj T_{m,k}^ j\wedge \kappa ^{n-j} \leq Q_{m,k}^ n, \qquad \int _ XQ_{m,k}^ n\leq A^ n v_+(\omega ).  \] The last bound holds because $Q_{m,k}=A(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p_{m,k}/A))$ and $p_{m,k}/A$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. Letting $k\to \infty $ gives trace bounds, independent of $m$, for every full closed power of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p_ m+B|z|^2)$. For $j<n$, every subsequential weak limit of these closed positive $(j,j)$-currents puts no mass on $S$, again by corollary 1.13.2 . Off $S$ the bounded capacity convergence identifies the limit with the corresponding full power of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p+B|z|^2)$, which also puts no mass on $S$. Hence the limit is unique. Expanding back in the smooth correction and using a finite coordinate cover yields \[  W_ j(p_ m)\longrightarrow W_ j(p),\qquad 1\leq j<n.  \] Hence ( 30.5 ) gives $J(p_ m)\to J(p)$. Step 4: the residual measures. Let $R=\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ u$. Since $p_ m-u$ is bounded, the equality case of lemma 1.6.10 , applied on each chart after a common smooth correction, gives $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _{p_ m}=R$ for every $m$. The total masses $J(p_ m)$ are bounded by $v_+(\omega )$, so along any sequence $m_ i\to \infty $ a subsequence of $\Phi _{p_{m_ i}}$ converges weakly to a measure $\eta $. Since $\Phi _{p_ m}-R$ is positive, so is $\eta -R$. Off $S$, $\eta $ equals $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (p)$, by the bounded convergence of Step 1, and its total mass is $\lim _ mJ(p_ m)=J(p)$ by Step 3. The measure $\Phi _ p$ has the same total mass and the same restriction to $X\setminus S$, so \[  \Phi _ p(S)=\eta (S)\geq R(S).  \] On the other hand, $u\leq p$, so the inequality in lemma 1.6.10 gives $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ p\leq R$ on each chart. Together with the previous inequality, this forces $\Phi _ p(S)=R(S)$, hence $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ p=R$, which is the asserted equality of residual measures. It also gives $\mathbf1_ S\eta =R$, since $\eta -R\geq 0$ and $\eta (S)=R(S)$. As $\eta $ and $\Phi _ p$ also agree off $S$, we conclude that $\eta =\Phi _ p$. Every weak subsequential limit of $\Phi _{p_ m}$ is therefore $\Phi _ p$, which proves the convergence $\Phi _{p_ m}\to \Phi _ p$. $\square$ Corollary 30.3.6 . If $\varphi $ is an ordinary model of positive lower volume, then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):P_\theta [u]=\varphi \} .  \] Proof. The first equality is theorem 30.2.4 . Membership in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ implies $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $ by proposition 13.4.5 . Conversely, if $P_\theta [u]=\varphi $, then theorem 30.3.4 puts $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. $\square$

title: Theorem 30.3.1
text: Theorem 30.3.1 . Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have positive lower volume, let $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\preceq \varphi $, and let $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ u\leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ v,  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. Put $\ell =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )>0$ and $\mathcal E_\varphi =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. We may replace $v$ by $\max (u,v)$: by locality, the hypothesis is unchanged on $\{ u<v\} $, and by upward stability (proposition 13.4.2 ) the new $v$ lies in $\mathcal E_\varphi $. Thus we may assume $u\leq v$. Translate $u,v$ by the same constant so that $v\leq \varphi $, and then translate all three potentials so that $\varphi \leq 0$. The idea is to stretch $u$ away from $v$; the stretched potentials keep lower volume $\ell $, and this is incompatible with a strict inequality $u<v$ on a set of positive volume. Set \[  q_ b=Q_ b(u,v),\qquad D_ b=\{ b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})v=u\} .  \] Lemma 13.4.3 gives $q_ b\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $q_ b\leq u$. Since $b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})v\leq u$ with contact set $D_ b$, contact support and positivity of the mixed products give \[  b^{-n}\mu _{q_ b}+(1-b^{-1})^ n\mathbf1_{D_ b}\mu _ v \leq \mathbf1_{D_ b}\mu _ u.  \] Here $\mu _{q_ b}$ is carried by $D_ b$. Choose $b$ so large that $(1-b^{-1})^ n>c$. On $D_ b\cap \{ u<v\} $ the hypothesis bounds the right-hand side by $c\mu _ v$, and subtracting finite measures shows that $\mu _{q_ b}$ vanishes there. Thus $\mu _{q_ b}$ is carried by $D_ b\cap \{ u=v\} \subset \{ q_ b=u\} $. Since $q_ b\leq u$, ordered contact for this pair and theorem 30.2.4 , which gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ b)=\ell $, now yield 30.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-domination-fixed-tail} \ell \leq \mu _{q_ b}(X)\leq \mu _ u(\{ q_ b=u\} ). \end{equation} Suppose now that $u<v$ somewhere. Then there is $\delta >0$ such that $\{ u<v-\delta \} $ has positive Lebesgue measure; otherwise $u\geq v$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . On this set the convex inequality gives $q_ b\leq u-(b-1)\delta $. The family $q_ b$ decreases in $b$ and is bounded above by $u$. Its limit is $-\infty $ on a set of positive measure, so it cannot be $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and is therefore identically $-\infty $. Hence theorem 1.4.2 gives $\sup _ Xq_ b\to -\infty $. The sets $\{ q_ b=u\} \subset \{ u\leq \sup _ Xq_ b\} $ then have $\mu _ u$-mass tending to zero, because $\mu _ u$ is finite and puts no mass on the pole set of $u$. This contradicts ( 30.4 ). $\square$
30.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-domination-fixed-tail} \ell \leq \mu _{q_ b}(X)\leq \mu _ u(\{ q_ b=u\} ). \end{equation}

title: Corollary 30.3.2
text: Corollary 30.3.2 . For $u,v$ as in theorem 30.3.1 and $\lambda >0$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\mu _ u\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\mu _ v \quad \Longrightarrow \quad u\geq v.  \] If $\mu _ u\leq c\mu _ v$ on $X$ for a finite $c\geq 0$, then $c\geq 1$. Proof. Fix $\delta >0$. On $\{ u<v-\delta \} $ the weighted inequality gives $\mu _ u\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \delta }\mu _ v=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \delta }\mu _{v-\delta }$. Theorem 30.3.1 , applied to $v-\delta $ with $c=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \delta }<1$, gives $u\geq v-\delta $; now let $\delta \downarrow 0$. If the second assertion failed, the theorem would apply with the same $c<1$ to every translate $v+A$, $A\in \mathbb R$, and would give $u\geq v+A$ for all $A$. This is impossible at a point where $u$ and $v$ are both finite. $\square$

title: Lemma 30.3.3
text: Lemma 30.3.3 . Let $u,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $P_\theta (u,w)\not\equiv -\infty $, and define the relative obstacle envelope \[  P_\theta [u](w)=\left(\lim _{C\to \infty }P_\theta (u+C,w)\right)^*.  \] Then \[  \mu _{P_\theta [u](w)} \leq \mathbf1_{\{ P_\theta [u](w)=w\} }\mu _ w.  \] Proof. Set $p_ C=P_\theta (u+C,w)$ for $C\geq 0$ and $p=P_\theta [u](w)$. The envelopes $p_ C$ increase with $C$, lie between $p_0$ and $w$, and converge to $p$ in capacity by lemma 1.8.12 . By the contact theorem, $\mu _{p_ C}$ is carried by $\{ p_ C=\min (u+C,w)\} $. Assigning the points where $u+C=w$ to the second term, ordered contact gives \[  \mu _{p_ C}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ p_ C=u+C<w\} }\mu _ u +\mathbf1_{\{ p_ C=w\} }\mu _ w.  \] The first measure has total mass at most \[  \varepsilon _ C=\mu _ u(\{ u\leq \sup _ Xw-C\} )\longrightarrow 0,  \] because $\mu _ u$ is finite and non-pluripolar. Testing against nonnegative continuous functions and applying the lower semicontinuity of lemma 6.3.1 gives $\mu _ p\leq \mu _ w$. The bounded quasi-continuous weight $\chi =\min (1,(w-p)_+)$, defined arbitrarily on the pluripolar set where $w-p$ is undefined, vanishes on $\{ p_ C=w\} $, since $p_ C\leq p\leq w$. Thus $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _{p_ C}\leq \varepsilon _ C$. Weighted lower semicontinuity gives $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _ p=0$, so $\mu _ p$ is carried by $\{ p=w\} $. Together with $\mu _ p\leq \mu _ w$, this proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Theorem 30.3.4
text: Theorem 30.3.4 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $p=P_\theta [u]$, \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] If this volume is positive, then also \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p),\qquad u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,p),\qquad P_\theta [p]=p.  \] Proof. Since $u\preceq p$, monotonicity gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. In particular, the lower volumes agree if $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)=0$. Suppose henceforth that $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)>0$. Normalize $u\leq 0$, so that $u\leq p$, and choose any $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim p$. Fix $K\geq 0$ with $p-K\leq w\leq p+K$. The rooftop envelope $p_ C=P_\theta (u+C,w)$ satisfies $u-K\leq p_ C\leq u+C$ for each $C\geq 0$, so it is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and equivalent to $u$. Its regularized increasing limit $r=P_\theta [u](w)$ satisfies \[  P_\theta (u+C+K,0)-K\leq p_ C\leq w, \qquad p-K\leq r\leq w\leq p+K.  \] Indeed, the leftmost potential lies below $u+C$, and below $p-K\leq w$ because $P_\theta (u+C+K,0)\leq P_\theta [u]=p$; it is therefore a competitor for the rooftop. Letting $C\to \infty $ gives the lower bound for $r$. Thus $r\sim p$, and proposition 13.4.2 puts $r$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,p)$. By lemma 30.3.3 , $\mu _ r$ vanishes on $\{ r<w\} $. Theorem 30.3.1 , with coefficient $c=0$ and reference $p$, gives $r\geq w$; hence $r=w$. Since $p_ C\to r$ in capacity, lower semicontinuity of the total mass (lemma 6.3.1 ) and $p_ C\sim u$ yield \[  \int _ X\mu _ w\leq \liminf _{C\to \infty }\int _ X\mu _{p_ C} \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] Taking the supremum over $w\sim p$ gives $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$, and hence equality of the upper volumes. Theorem 30.2.4 then gives $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,p)$ and equality of the lower volumes. Finally, proposition 13.4.5 gives $P_\theta [p]=P_\theta [u]=p$. $\square$
