title: Corollary 30.3.6
text: Corollary 30.3.6 . If $\varphi $ is an ordinary model of positive lower volume, then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):P_\theta [u]=\varphi \} .  \] Proof. The first equality is theorem 30.2.4 . Membership in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ implies $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $ by proposition 13.4.5 . Conversely, if $P_\theta [u]=\varphi $, then theorem 30.3.4 puts $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. $\square$

title: 30.4 Strict barriers and background variation
text:
30.4 Strict barriers and background variation Positive lower volume permits a small stretch away from any less singular potential, and the admissible stretch depends only on the lower volume and a mass bound. Mixing the stretched potential with a strict potential produces a strict potential lying below the original one. The same bound for mixed masses controls the change of the lower volume under a small smooth perturbation of the background. Throughout this section, $\omega $ is a fixed Hermitian form on $X$. Lemma 30.4.1 . Let $u,r\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, with $u\leq r$, and assume $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)>0$. For a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq 	heta $, set \[  b_0=1+ rac{\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)}{2^{n+1}n\, v_+(\Omega )}.  \] Then $\mathcal A_ b(u,r)
eq \varnothing $, so that $Q_ b(u,r)$ is defined, for $1\leq b\leq b_0$, and \[  \lim _{b\downarrow 1}\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (Q_ b(u,r)) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u).  \] Proof. Put $K=v_+(\Omega )$. Since $0<\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)\leq K$, we have $1<b_0\leq 2$. After a common translation we may assume $u\leq r\leq 0$. Suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $\mathcal A_ b(u,r)=\varnothing $ for some $1<b\leq b_0$. Set \[  u_ j=\max (u,r-j),\qquad v_ j=u+(b-1)u_ j, \qquad q_ j=P_	heta (v_ j-(b-1)r).  \] Here, as for stretching envelopes, a competitor $g$ for $q_ j$ is required to satisfy $g+(b-1)r\leq v_ j$, which is meaningful also at common poles. Off the poles the obstacle $v_ j-(b-1)r=u+(b-1)(u_ j-r)$ lies between $u-(b-1)j$ and $u$. Hence $q_ j$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic and $q_ j\sim u$. As $j$ increases, $q_ j$ decreases. A $	heta $-plurisubharmonic decreasing limit would belong to $\mathcal A_ b(u,r)$, so the limit is identically $-\infty $, and $\sup _ Xq_ j	o -\infty $ by theorem 1.4.2 . Let $C_ j=\{ q_ j+(b-1)r=v_ j\} $. By the contact theorem, $\mu _{q_ j}$ is carried by $C_ j$. The current $b	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q_ j+(b-1)r)$ equals $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ j)+(b-1)(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r)\geq 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ j$. Positivity of the mixed products and ordered contact in background $b	heta $ therefore give \[  \mu _{q_ j}\leq \mathbf1_{C_ j} igl ((	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+(b-1)(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j) igr )^ n.  \] On $C_ j$ we have $q_ j=u+(b-1)(u_ j-r)\geq bu$, because $u_ j\geq u$ and $r\leq 0$. Fix $k>0$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $q_ j\leq -bk$ everywhere, so $C_ j\subset \{ u\leq -k\} $, and consequently 30.6  egin{equation} \label{eq:positive-volume-stretch-tail} \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u) \leq \mu _{q_ j}(X) \leq \int _{\{ u\leq -k\} } igl ((	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+(b-1)(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j) igr )^ n. \end{equation} To estimate the right-hand side, note that for any $s,t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $0\leq i\leq n$, positivity of the non-pluripolar mixed products and proposition 6.5.3 imply \[   egin{aligned} &  inom ni\int _ X(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s)^{n-i}\wedge (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t)^ i\ & \quad \leq  inom ni\int _ X(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s)^{n-i}\wedge (\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t)^ i\ & \quad \leq 2^ n\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\Omega ((s+t)/2)\leq 2^ nK. \end{aligned}  \] The second inequality follows by expanding $(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} rac{s+t}2)^ n$; for the possibly unbounded average, apply this expansion to its truncations at constant levels, which remain $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic. Expanding the integrand in ( 30.6 ), and using $(b-1)^ i\leq b-1$ for $i\geq 1$, gives \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u\leq -k\} )+n2^ nK(b-1).  \] The measure $\mu _ u$ is finite and puts no mass on the pole set of $u$, so the first term tends to zero as $k	o \infty $. By the choice of $b_0$, the remaining error is at most half of $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)>0$, a contradiction. Thus $\mathcal A_ b(u,r)
eq \varnothing $ for $1<b\leq b_0$; for $b=1$ the family contains $u$, and $Q_1(u,r)=u$. Put $h_0=Q_{b_0}(u,r)$ and, for $1<b\leq b_0$, $t=(b-1)/(b_0-1)\in (0,1]$. The inequality $h_0\leq b_0u-(b_0-1)r$ shows that $(1-t)u+th_0$ is a competitor for $Q_ b(u,r)$, and $Q_ b(u,r)\leq bu-(b-1)r\leq u$. Hence \[  (1-t)u+th_0\leq Q_ b(u,r)\leq u.  \] Addition, homogeneity and volume monotonicity give \[  (1-t)^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (Q_ b(u,r)) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u).  \] Letting $b\downarrow 1$ proves the limit. Undoing the common translation changes neither the volumes nor the nonemptiness of the competitor families. $\square$ Corollary 30.4.2 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ has positive lower volume, then there are $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $\varepsilon >0$ with \[  w\leq u,\qquad 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \varepsilon \omega .  \] Proof. Translate $u$ so that $u\leq V_	heta $. By bigness, there are $ho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $\delta >0$ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \delta \omega $; after a translation, $ho \leq V_	heta $. By lemma 30.4.1 with $r=V_	heta $, there is $b>1$ for which $h=Q_ b(u,V_	heta )$ is defined. Put \[  w=b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})ho .  \] Since $b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})V_	heta \leq u$ and $ho \leq V_	heta $, we have $w\leq u$; moreover $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq (1-b^{-1})\delta \omega $. Undoing the translation of $u$ by the same translation of $w$ gives the assertion with $\varepsilon =(1-b^{-1})\delta $. $\square$ Proposition 30.4.3 . Assume in addition that $	heta \geq 0$. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)>0$, then $P_{\varepsilon 	heta }(u)
ot\equiv -\infty $ for some $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. Proof. By corollary 30.4.2 , choose $w\leq u$ and $\delta >0$ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \delta \omega $. Choose $C>0$ with $	heta \leq C\omega $, and $0<t<\min (1,\delta /C)$. Then \[  (1-t)	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq (\delta -tC)\omega \geq 0.  \] Thus $w$ is a competitor for $P_{(1-t)	heta }(u)$, and $\varepsilon =1-t$ has the required property. $\square$ For a reference potential $\varphi $, the positive-volume model condition reads 30.10  egin{equation} \label{eq:li-model-condition} P_	heta [\varphi ]=\varphi ,\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\varphi )>0. \end{equation} When $	heta \geq 0$, proposition 30.4.3 shows that ( 30.10 ) implies the smaller-background model condition ( 13.26 ) of section 13.5 . If moreover $v_-(	heta )>0$, the converse holds. Indeed, if $P_{\varepsilon 	heta }(\varphi )
ot\equiv -\infty $, then a translate of the same competitor shows that $P_{\varepsilon 	heta }(\psi )
ot\equiv -\infty $ for every $\psi \sim \varphi $ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and lemma 13.5.2 gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_	heta (\psi )\geq (1-\varepsilon )^ nv_-(	heta )$. Hence \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\varphi ) \geq (1-\varepsilon )^ n v_-(	heta )>0.  \] Without the lower bound $v_-(	heta )>0$, the same lemma still shows that each potential equivalent to $\varphi $ has positive mass, but not that these masses are bounded away from zero. A small smooth increase of the background changes the lower volume by at most a linear error, and a strict potential lying below $u$ gives a multiplicative comparison for both volumes. Proposition 30.4.4 . There is $C>0$, depending only on $	heta $ and $\omega $, such that, for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, every $\varepsilon \in [0,1]$ and every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ with $	heta \leq \eta \leq 	heta +\varepsilon \omega $, \[  0\leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (u) -\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)\leq C\varepsilon .  \] If $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)>0$, there is also $\delta >0$, depending on $u$, such that, for every $\varepsilon \geq 0$ and every smooth $\eta $ with $	heta \leq \eta \leq 	heta +\varepsilon \omega $, both singularity volumes satisfy \[  \operatorname {vol}_	heta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\eta (u) \leq (1+\varepsilon /\delta )^ n\operatorname {vol}_	heta (u).  \] Proof. Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega $ with $\Omega \geq 	heta $ and $\Omega \geq \omega $, and set $C=n2^ n v_+(\Omega )$. For every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $1\leq k\leq n$, the mixed-mass estimate in the proof of lemma 30.4.1 , applied to $s=v$ and $t=0$, together with $\omega \leq \Omega $, gives \[   inom nk\int _ X(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}\wedge \omega ^ k \leq 2^ n v_+(\Omega ).  \] Expanding in the smooth positive perturbation and using $\varepsilon ^ k\leq \varepsilon $ yields \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\eta (v) \leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{	heta +\varepsilon \omega }(v) \leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_	heta (v)+C\varepsilon .  \] Each $v\sim u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is also a competitor for the lower volume in background $\eta $. Taking the infimum over these $v$ proves the upper bound for $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (u)-\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u)$. The lower bound is background monotonicity (theorem 30.1.1 ). Now assume that $u$ has positive lower volume, and choose $w\leq u$ and $\delta >0$ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \delta \omega $ by corollary 30.4.2 . The case $\varepsilon =0$ is immediate. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $t=\varepsilon /\delta $. The potential $tw$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,t(	heta -\delta \omega ))$, and the form $\eta +t(	heta -\delta \omega )$ is big, since adding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1+t)w)$ to it gives a form at least $(1+t)\delta \omega -t\delta \omega =\delta \omega $. Addition and monotonicity give \[   egin{split}  \operatorname {vol}_\eta (u) & \leq \operatorname {vol}_{\eta +t(	heta -\delta \omega )}(u+tw)\ & \leq \operatorname {vol}_{(1+t)	heta }((1+t)u) =(1+t)^ n\operatorname {vol}_	heta (u). \end{split}  \] Here we used $\eta +t(	heta -\delta \omega )\leq (1+t)	heta $, which holds because $\eta \leq 	heta +\varepsilon \omega $, and $u+tw\leq (1+t)u$. The lower bound is again background monotonicity. $\square$

title: Lemma 30.4.1
text: Lemma 30.4.1 . Let $u,r\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, with $u\leq r$, and assume $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)>0$. For a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta $, set \[  b_0=1+\frac{\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)}{2^{n+1}n\, v_+(\Omega )}.  \] Then $\mathcal A_ b(u,r)\neq \varnothing $, so that $Q_ b(u,r)$ is defined, for $1\leq b\leq b_0$, and \[  \lim _{b\downarrow 1}\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (Q_ b(u,r)) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] Proof. Put $K=v_+(\Omega )$. Since $0<\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\leq K$, we have $1<b_0\leq 2$. After a common translation we may assume $u\leq r\leq 0$. Suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $\mathcal A_ b(u,r)=\varnothing $ for some $1<b\leq b_0$. Set \[  u_ j=\max (u,r-j),\qquad v_ j=u+(b-1)u_ j, \qquad q_ j=P_\theta (v_ j-(b-1)r).  \] Here, as for stretching envelopes, a competitor $g$ for $q_ j$ is required to satisfy $g+(b-1)r\leq v_ j$, which is meaningful also at common poles. Off the poles the obstacle $v_ j-(b-1)r=u+(b-1)(u_ j-r)$ lies between $u-(b-1)j$ and $u$. Hence $q_ j$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and $q_ j\sim u$. As $j$ increases, $q_ j$ decreases. A $\theta $-plurisubharmonic decreasing limit would belong to $\mathcal A_ b(u,r)$, so the limit is identically $-\infty $, and $\sup _ Xq_ j\to -\infty $ by theorem 1.4.2 . Let $C_ j=\{ q_ j+(b-1)r=v_ j\} $. By the contact theorem, $\mu _{q_ j}$ is carried by $C_ j$. The current $b\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q_ j+(b-1)r)$ equals $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ j)+(b-1)(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r)\geq \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ j$. Positivity of the mixed products and ordered contact in background $b\theta $ therefore give \[  \mu _{q_ j}\leq \mathbf1_{C_ j}\bigl ((\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+(b-1)(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\bigr )^ n.  \] On $C_ j$ we have $q_ j=u+(b-1)(u_ j-r)\geq bu$, because $u_ j\geq u$ and $r\leq 0$. Fix $k>0$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $q_ j\leq -bk$ everywhere, so $C_ j\subset \{ u\leq -k\} $, and consequently 30.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-volume-stretch-tail} \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) \leq \mu _{q_ j}(X) \leq \int _{\{ u\leq -k\} }\bigl ((\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+(b-1)(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\bigr )^ n. \end{equation} To estimate the right-hand side, note that for any $s,t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $0\leq i\leq n$, positivity of the non-pluripolar mixed products and proposition 6.5.3 imply \[  \begin{aligned} & \binom ni\int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s)^{n-i}\wedge (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t)^ i\\ & \quad \leq \binom ni\int _ X(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s)^{n-i}\wedge (\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t)^ i\\ & \quad \leq 2^ n\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\Omega ((s+t)/2)\leq 2^ nK. \end{aligned}  \] The second inequality follows by expanding $(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\frac{s+t}2)^ n$; for the possibly unbounded average, apply this expansion to its truncations at constant levels, which remain $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic. Expanding the integrand in ( 30.6 ), and using $(b-1)^ i\leq b-1$ for $i\geq 1$, gives \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) \leq \mu _ u(\{ u\leq -k\} )+n2^ nK(b-1).  \] The measure $\mu _ u$ is finite and puts no mass on the pole set of $u$, so the first term tends to zero as $k\to \infty $. By the choice of $b_0$, the remaining error is at most half of $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)>0$, a contradiction. Thus $\mathcal A_ b(u,r)\neq \varnothing $ for $1<b\leq b_0$; for $b=1$ the family contains $u$, and $Q_1(u,r)=u$. Put $h_0=Q_{b_0}(u,r)$ and, for $1<b\leq b_0$, $t=(b-1)/(b_0-1)\in (0,1]$. The inequality $h_0\leq b_0u-(b_0-1)r$ shows that $(1-t)u+th_0$ is a competitor for $Q_ b(u,r)$, and $Q_ b(u,r)\leq bu-(b-1)r\leq u$. Hence \[  (1-t)u+th_0\leq Q_ b(u,r)\leq u.  \] Addition, homogeneity and volume monotonicity give \[  (1-t)^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (Q_ b(u,r)) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] Letting $b\downarrow 1$ proves the limit. Undoing the common translation changes neither the volumes nor the nonemptiness of the competitor families. $\square$

30.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-volume-stretch-tail} \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) \leq \mu _{q_ j}(X) \leq \int _{\{ u\leq -k\} }\bigl ((\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+(b-1)(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\bigr )^ n. \end{equation}

title: Corollary 30.4.2
text: Corollary 30.4.2 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has positive lower volume, then there are $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varepsilon >0$ with \[  w\leq u,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \varepsilon \omega .  \] Proof. Translate $u$ so that $u\leq V_\theta $. By bigness, there are $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\delta >0$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \omega $; after a translation, $\rho \leq V_\theta $. By lemma 30.4.1 with $r=V_\theta $, there is $b>1$ for which $h=Q_ b(u,V_\theta )$ is defined. Put \[  w=b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})\rho .  \] Since $b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})V_\theta \leq u$ and $\rho \leq V_\theta $, we have $w\leq u$; moreover $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq (1-b^{-1})\delta \omega $. Undoing the translation of $u$ by the same translation of $w$ gives the assertion with $\varepsilon =(1-b^{-1})\delta $. $\square$

title: Proposition 30.4.3
text: Proposition 30.4.3 . Assume in addition that $\theta \geq 0$. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)>0$, then $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(u)\not\equiv -\infty $ for some $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. Proof. By corollary 30.4.2 , choose $w\leq u$ and $\delta >0$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \delta \omega $. Choose $C>0$ with $\theta \leq C\omega $, and $0<t<\min (1,\delta /C)$. Then \[  (1-t)\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq (\delta -tC)\omega \geq 0.  \] Thus $w$ is a competitor for $P_{(1-t)\theta }(u)$, and $\varepsilon =1-t$ has the required property. $\square$
30.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:li-model-condition} P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi ,\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )>0. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 30.4.4
text: Proposition 30.4.4 . There is $C>0$, depending only on $\theta $ and $\omega $, such that, for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, every $\varepsilon \in [0,1]$ and every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ with $\theta \leq \eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon \omega $, \[  0\leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (u) -\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\leq C\varepsilon .  \] If $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)>0$, there is also $\delta >0$, depending on $u$, such that, for every $\varepsilon \geq 0$ and every smooth $\eta $ with $\theta \leq \eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon \omega $, both singularity volumes satisfy \[  \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\eta (u) \leq (1+\varepsilon /\delta )^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (u).  \] Proof. Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega $ with $\Omega \geq \theta $ and $\Omega \geq \omega $, and set $C=n2^ n v_+(\Omega )$. For every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $1\leq k\leq n$, the mixed-mass estimate in the proof of lemma 30.4.1 , applied to $s=v$ and $t=0$, together with $\omega \leq \Omega $, gives \[  \binom nk\int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}\wedge \omega ^ k \leq 2^ n v_+(\Omega ).  \] Expanding in the smooth positive perturbation and using $\varepsilon ^ k\leq \varepsilon $ yields \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\eta (v) \leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \omega }(v) \leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)+C\varepsilon .  \] Each $v\sim u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is also a competitor for the lower volume in background $\eta $. Taking the infimum over these $v$ proves the upper bound for $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (u)-\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$. The lower bound is background monotonicity (theorem 30.1.1 ). Now assume that $u$ has positive lower volume, and choose $w\leq u$ and $\delta >0$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \delta \omega $ by corollary 30.4.2 . The case $\varepsilon =0$ is immediate. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $t=\varepsilon /\delta $. The potential $tw$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,t(\theta -\delta \omega ))$, and the form $\eta +t(\theta -\delta \omega )$ is big, since adding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1+t)w)$ to it gives a form at least $(1+t)\delta \omega -t\delta \omega =\delta \omega $. Addition and monotonicity give \[  \begin{split}  \operatorname {vol}_\eta (u) & \leq \operatorname {vol}_{\eta +t(\theta -\delta \omega )}(u+tw)\\ & \leq \operatorname {vol}_{(1+t)\theta }((1+t)u) =(1+t)^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (u). \end{split}  \] Here we used $\eta +t(\theta -\delta \omega )\leq (1+t)\theta $, which holds because $\eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon \omega $, and $u+tw\leq (1+t)u$. The lower bound is again background monotonicity. $\square$

title: 30.5 Monotone limits
text:
30.5 Monotone limits We now show that ordinary envelopes and singularity volumes are continuous along monotone sequences whose limit has positive lower volume. For increasing sequences, contact support identifies the limit of the envelopes before its volume is known. For decreasing sequences of models, a uniform small stretch keeps a positive lower-volume bound. Normalized compactness then preserves the convex inequalities given by the deficit lemma, and strict barriers allow the background to decrease at the same time. Theorem 30.5.1 . Let $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be an increasing sequence such that $u=(\lim _ j u_ j)^*$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and has positive lower volume. Then \[  \left(\lim _ jP_	heta [u_ j]ight)^*=P_	heta [u], \qquad P_	heta [u_ j]\longrightarrow P_	heta [u] \quad 	ext{in capacity},  \] and \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u_ j)
earrow \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u),\qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u_ j)
earrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u).  \] For every fixed smooth compact modification $\pi :Z	o X$, \[  \sup _{z\in Z} igl |
u (u_ j\circ \pi ,z)-
u (u\circ \pi ,z) igr | \longrightarrow 0.  \] Proof. Step 1: the envelopes. Translate so that $u\leq 0$, and set $p_ j=P_	heta [u_ j]$, $p=P_	heta [u]$ and $s=(\lim _ jp_ j)^*$. The $p_ j$ increase, and $u\leq s\leq p\leq V_	heta $. By theorem 30.3.4 , the lower volume of $p$ is positive and $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,p)$. Upward stability (proposition 13.4.2 ) puts $s$ in the same class. The ordinary envelope can use $V_	heta $ in place of zero as obstacle (see the remark after definition 1.19.4 ); that is, $p_ j=P_	heta [u_ j](V_	heta )$. Hence lemma 30.3.3 gives \[  \mu _{p_ j}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ p_ j=V_	heta \} }\mu _{V_	heta }.  \] The fixed bounded quasi-continuous weight $\chi =\min (1,(p-s)_+)$, defined arbitrarily on the pluripolar set where $p-s$ is undefined, vanishes on $\{ p_ j=V_	heta \} $, because $p_ j\leq s\leq p\leq V_	heta $. Since $p_ j	o s$ in capacity by lemma 1.8.12 , lemma 6.3.1 gives $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _ s=0$. Thus $\mu _ s$ vanishes on $\{ s<p\} $, and theorem 30.3.1 , with reference $p$ and coefficient $c=0$, yields $s=p$. This proves the assertions about the envelopes. Step 2: the upper volumes of the envelopes. Choose any $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $w\sim p$, and $K\geq 0$ with $p-K\leq w\leq p+K$. Define $r_ j=P_	heta [u_ j](w)$; this is meaningful because $u_ j-K\leq p-K\leq w$, so that $P_	heta (u_ j,w)
ot\equiv -\infty $. For $C\geq 0$ the competitors compare as follows: \[  P_	heta (u_ j+C+K,0)-K \leq P_	heta (u_ j+C,w)\leq p_ j+K.  \] The leftmost potential lies below $u_ j+C$ and below $p_ j-K\leq p-K\leq w$. For the upper bound, note that the middle term minus $K$ lies below $w-K\leq p\leq 0$ and is more singular than $u_ j$, so it is at most $p_ j$. Taking the increasing limit in $C$ gives \[  p_ j-K\leq r_ j\leq p_ j+K,\qquad r_ j\leq w.  \] The $r_ j$ increase with $j$ and converge in capacity to $r=(\lim _ jr_ j)^*$, and $p-K\leq r\leq w\leq p+K$. Thus $r\sim p$, so $r\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,p)$. Lemma 30.3.3 gives $\mu _{r_ j}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ r_ j=w\} }\mu _ w$, and weighted lower semicontinuity with the weight $\min (1,(w-r)_+)$ shows that $\mu _ r$ vanishes on $\{ r<w\} $. Domination with reference $p$ gives $r=w$. Therefore \[  \int _ X\mu _ w\leq \liminf _ j\int _ X\mu _{r_ j} \leq \lim _ j\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (p_ j),  \] where $r_ j\sim p_ j$ justifies the last inequality. Taking the supremum over $w\sim p$ and using volume monotonicity proves \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (p_ j)
earrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (p).  \] Step 3: the volumes of $u_ j$. Put $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (p)>0$ and $D_ j=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (p)-\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (p_ j)$. Since $D_ j	o 0$, we can choose $b_ j>1$ with $b_ j	o \infty $ and $b_ j^ nD_ j<\delta $ for all large $j$. With $a_ j=1-b_ j^{-1}$, lemma 30.2.1 gives $h_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ such that \[  a_ jp+(1-a_ j)h_ j\leq p_ j  \] for all sufficiently large $j$. Addition, homogeneity and monotonicity of the lower volume, together with theorem 30.3.4 , give \[  a_ j^ n\delta \leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (p_ j) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u_ j)\leq \delta .  \] Since $a_ j	o 1$, this proves the convergence of the lower volumes, and shows that $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u_ j)>0$ for all large $j$. For such $j$, theorem 30.3.4 identifies the upper volumes of $u_ j$ and $p_ j$, and also those of $u$ and $p$; Step 2 therefore gives the asserted upper-volume limit. Finally, proposition 30.2.2 , applied to $u_ j\preceq u$, gives the uniform convergence of Lelong numbers on each fixed modification. $\square$ For the results on decreasing sequences, fix smooth real $(1,1)$-forms $	heta _ j$ with $	heta \leq 	heta _{j+1}\leq 	heta _ j$ that converge uniformly to $	heta $; the constant sequence $	heta _ j=	heta $ is allowed. The proofs first treat a fixed background, using normalized auxiliary potentials, and then handle the varying forms by means of corrected envelopes of tail suprema. Theorem 30.5.2 . Suppose that $q_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$ are ordinary models, $q_ j=P_{	heta _ j}[q_ j]$, decreasing to $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Then $P_	heta [q]=q$ and \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{	heta _ j}(q_ j)\searrow \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (q).  \] If $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (q)>0$, then also \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{	heta _ j}(q_ j)\searrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (q),  \] and, for every fixed smooth compact modification $\pi :Z	o X$, \[  \sup _{z\in Z} igl |
u (q_ j\circ \pi ,z)-
u (q\circ \pi ,z) igr | \longrightarrow 0.  \] In this case all generic divisorial Lelong numbers converge. Proof. Step 1: the fixed point and positivity of the limit volume. Since $q\leq q_ j\leq 0$, monotonicity of the envelope in the background and in the potential gives $q\leq P_	heta [q]\leq P_{	heta _ j}[q]\leq P_{	heta _ j}[q_ j]=q_ j$. Apply proposition 30.2.2 in each background $\theta _ j$. Since $\theta _ j\leq \theta _1$, its proof works with one Lelong bound $C_\pi $ for $\pi ^*\theta _1$, independent of $j$. This proves the uniform convergence on each fixed modification, and taking generic values gives the divisorial assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 30.5.3
text: Proposition 30.5.3 . Suppose that $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ decrease to $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and that $u$ has positive lower volume. Then \[  P_{\theta _ j}[u_ j]\searrow P_\theta [u] \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _ j}(u_ j)\searrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] When these conditions hold, the lower volumes converge to that of $u$ in background $\theta $, and the Lelong numbers converge uniformly on every fixed smooth compact modification. Proof. Normalize $u_ j\leq 0$ by a common translation. Set $p_ j=P_{\theta _ j}[u_ j]$, $p=P_\theta [u]$ and $q=\lim _ jp_ j$. Since $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _ j}(u_ j)\geq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)>0$, theorem 30.3.4 in background $\theta _ j$ shows that every $p_ j$ is an ordinary model with the same volumes as $u_ j$. The envelopes decrease, and the uniform convergence of the backgrounds gives $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Since $u\leq p\leq q$, the limit $q$ has positive lower volume, and theorem 30.5.2 gives, for either volume, \[  \operatorname {vol}_\theta (q) =\lim _ j\operatorname {vol}_{\theta _ j}(p_ j) =\lim _ j\operatorname {vol}_{\theta _ j}(u_ j), \qquad P_\theta [q]=q.  \] If $q=p$, these equalities and theorem 30.3.4 show that both volumes of $u_ j$ converge to those of $u$; in particular the upper volumes do. Conversely, if the upper volumes converge, then $u$ and $q$ have the same upper volume, so $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,q)$. By corollary 30.3.6 , $P_\theta [u]=q$, that is, $q=p$. For the Lelong assertion, proposition 30.4.4 shows that the upper-volume deficit between $u$ and $u_ j$ in background $\theta _ j$ tends to zero. Apply proposition 30.2.2 with the common lower bound $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)>0$ and the uniform Lelong bound for $\pi ^*\theta _1$. $\square$

title: Corollary 30.5.4
text: Corollary 30.5.4 . For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _ j}(u)\searrow \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] If this limiting volume is positive, then also \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _ j}(u)\searrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u),\qquad P_{\theta _ j}[u]\searrow P_\theta [u].  \] Proof. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $. Uniform convergence gives $\theta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ j\omega $ with $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$, so the volume limits follow from the two estimates in proposition 30.4.4 ; monotonicity makes them decreasing. In the positive-lower-volume case, apply proposition 30.5.3 to the constant sequence $u_ j=u$. $\square$

title: Corollary 30.5.5
text:
Corollary 30.5.5 . Suppose that $Y$ has the bounded mass property. Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega _0\geq 	heta |_ Y$ on $Y$ and a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq 2\Omega _0$ on $Y$ with $v_-(\Omega )>0$. Then \[

title: 30.5.1 Recovery of envelope systems
text:
30.5.1 Recovery of envelope systems We return to the big background $	heta $ on $X$ and apply the monotone limits above to the envelope systems of chapter 25 . Fix real numbers $a<c$. Recall that $\mathscr T_{a,c}(	heta )$ consists of the pointwise concave, decreasing families $\Gamma =(\Gamma _	au )_{	au <c}$ of ideal models in background $	heta $ that are constant for $	au \leq a$ (definition 25.1.1 ). An envelope system $ oldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(	heta )$ is a compatible family of such curves $\Gamma ^\eta =(\Gamma ^\eta _	au )_{	au <c}\in \mathscr T_{a,c}(	heta +\eta )$, indexed by the Hermitian forms $\eta $ (definition 25.2.2 ). The map $\mathsf E$ projects a curve in background $	heta $ to a system, and $\mathsf R$ takes a system to its limiting curve $(\mathsf R oldsymbol \Gamma )_	au =\lim _ j\Gamma ^{h/j}_	au $, for any Hermitian form $h$ (theorem 25.3.1 ). The system is recovered from its limit if $ oldsymbol \Gamma =\mathsf E\mathsf R oldsymbol \Gamma $. Compatibility fixes every local divisorial Lelong number of the slices before the perturbation tends to zero, and recovery means that these numbers do not increase in the limit. A positive limiting lower volume rules out such an increase. Concavity propagates positivity from the constant left part to every finite parameter, so a single condition on the initial slice suffices for the whole system. Theorem 30.5.6 . Let $ oldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(	heta )$, fix a Hermitian form $h$, and put $\Gamma =\mathsf R oldsymbol \Gamma $. Then \[  \lim _{j	o \infty }\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{	heta +h/j} (\Gamma ^{h/j}_ a) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\Gamma _ a).  \] In particular this limit is independent of $h$. If it is positive, then $ oldsymbol \Gamma =\mathsf E(\Gamma )$, and for every $	au <c$ both singularity volumes satisfy \[  \operatorname {vol}_{	heta +h/j}(\Gamma ^{h/j}_	au ) \searrow \operatorname {vol}_	heta (\Gamma _	au ), \qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\Gamma _	au )>0.  \] Proof. Every ideal model is an ordinary model by corollary 16.2.4 , and the retraction theorem gives $\Gamma ^{h/j}_	au \searrow \Gamma _	au $ in the decreasing backgrounds $	heta +h/j$. Thus theorem 30.5.2 proves the identity for the initial lower volumes, including the case where the limit is zero. Suppose that this limit $\ell $ is positive. For $	au \leq a$, the slice is $\Gamma _ a$. For $a<	au <c$, choose $r\in (	au ,c)$ and put $s=(	au -a)/(r-a)$, so that $	au =(1-s)a+sr$. Concavity gives \[  (1-s)\Gamma _ a+s\Gamma _ r\leq \Gamma _	au .  \] Homogeneity, proposition 30.1.2 and volume monotonicity imply \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\Gamma _	au ) \geq (1-s)^ n\ell >0.  \] Theorem 30.5.2 now gives both volume limits for every fixed $	au <c$. It remains to show that the slices keep their multiplier ideals in the limit. Fix $	au <c$ and write $q=\Gamma _	au $, $q_ j=\Gamma ^{h/j}_	au $ and $	heta _ j=	heta +h/j$. By proposition 30.4.4 , the upper volumes of the fixed potential $q$ in the backgrounds $	heta _ j$ converge to its upper volume in $	heta $, which is the limit of the upper volumes of the $q_ j$. Consequently \[  D_ j=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{	heta _ j}(q_ j) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{	heta _ j}(q)\longrightarrow 0, \qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{	heta _ j}(q_ j) \geq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (q)>0.  \] After discarding finitely many indices, choose $b_ j>1$ with $b_ j	o +\infty $ and $b_ j^ nD_ j<\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{	heta _ j}(q_ j)$. Since $q\leq q_ j$, the stretching lemma lemma 30.2.1 in background $	heta _ j$ gives $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$ such that \[  (1-b_ j^{-1})q_ j+b_ j^{-1}v_ j\leq q.  \] Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq 	heta +h$, so that all $v_ j$ are $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic. By lemma 1.5.1 , there is $\alpha >0$ such that $\mathcal I(\alpha v_ j)=\mathcal O_ X$ for all $j$; additive normalization does not change these ideals. Let $E$ be a local divisor over a coordinate neighborhood $U$, with generic Lelong number $
u _ E$ and log discrepancy $A_ U(E)$ as in section 1.17 . Lemma 1.17.8 , with $m=\alpha $, gives $
u _ E(v_ j)\leq A_ U(E)/\alpha $. Taking Lelong numbers in the convex inequality therefore yields \[  0\leq 
u _ E(q)-
u _ E(q_ j) \leq  rac{A_ U(E)}{\alpha b_ j}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Compatibility gives all components the same multiplier ideals, so $
u _ E(q_ j)$ is independent of $j$, and hence equal to $
u _ E(q)$. Blowing up a point on a local modification converts its pointwise Lelong number into such a divisorial number; on a curve the point itself is a divisor. Thus all Lelong numbers of $q$ and $q_ j$ on all local modifications agree, and theorem 1.16.3 gives $q\sim _{\mathcal I}q_ j$. This holds at every parameter $	au <c$, so proposition 25.3.2 proves recovery. $\square$ The lower bound $(1-s)^ n\ell $ may tend to zero as $	au \uparrow c$; the theorem gives no positive lower bound that is uniform up to the cutoff. The hypothesis is invariant under a smooth change of background $	heta '=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, through the gauge bijection of proposition 25.4.1 : the estimate there makes the transported initial slice ordinarily equivalent to $\Gamma _ a-f$, and the map $u\mapsto u-f$ preserves the curvature currents and hence both singularity volumes. The ruled-surface system of theorem 25.5.2 , which is not recovered from its limit, has zero initial limiting lower volume, so the theorem does not apply to it.

title: 30.6 Cauchy convergence of model potentials
text: 30.6 Cauchy convergence of model potentials The maximum of two potentials is a common upper bound for both, and the sum of the two upper-volume deficits from this maximum measures how far apart their ordinary envelopes are. A uniform positive lower-volume bound controls how this quantity changes when a third potential is introduced, and this replaces the triangle inequality in the Cauchy argument below. From now on we write $U(u)=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ and $M=U(V_\theta )$; by monotonicity, $U\leq M$ on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. We also fix a smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ for $L^1$ norms. Definition 30.6.1 . For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, define \[  d_\theta (u,v)=2U(\max (u,v))-U(u)-U(v).  \] For $\delta >0$, put \[  \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )= \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):P_\theta [u]=u, \  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\geq \delta \} .  \] We call $d_\theta $ the volume comparison . A sequence is $d_\theta $-Cauchy if $d_\theta (u_ j,u_ k)\to 0$ as $j,k\to \infty $, and it converges to $u$ for $d_\theta $ if $d_\theta (u_ j,u)\to 0$. The volume comparison is finite, nonnegative and symmetric. It need not satisfy the triangle inequality (example 30.11.1 ), which is why we do not call it a distance. It depends only on the ordinary singularity types, since replacing either input by an equivalent one changes the maximum by a bounded amount. Monotonicity also gives 30.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:volume-comparison-basic} |U(u)-U(v)|\leq d_\theta (u,v),\qquad u\leq v\  \Longrightarrow \  d_\theta (u,v)=U(v)-U(u). \end{equation} In the separation result below, the restriction to positive lower volume is necessary, even for a closed positive background. Example 30.6.2 . For every $n\geq 2$ there are a closed positive $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on the projective manifold $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1}$ and two ordinary models $a\not\sim b$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1},\theta )$ such that \[  P_\theta [a]_{\mathcal I}=b,\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (a) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (b)=0,\qquad d_\theta (a,b)=0.  \] For every $n\geq 3$, the same assertions hold for a suitable nonclosed positive form $\theta $ on a projective manifold of dimension $n$ with the bounded mass property. Proof. Take the closed positive product background of example 16.6.23 on $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1}$. Its models satisfy $a\leq b$ and $U(a)=U(b)=0$. Thus $\max (a,b)=b$, and the defining formula gives \[  d_\theta (a,b)=2U(b)-U(a)-U(b)=0.  \] The other assertions are part of that example. For the nonclosed case use example 16.6.24 ; its models are again ordered and have zero upper volumes, so the same calculation applies. $\square$ Proposition 30.6.3 . For potentials $u,v$ of positive lower volume, \[  d_\theta (u,v)=d_\theta (P_\theta [u],P_\theta [v]),\qquad d_\theta (u,v)=0\  \Longleftrightarrow \  P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [v].  \] There is $C_\theta >0$, depending on $\theta $ and $\mathrm{d}V$, such that, for $u,v\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, \[  \| u-v\| _{L^1}\leq 2C_\theta \min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (u,v)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} .  \] Proof. Translate the inputs below zero, and put $p=P_\theta [u]$, $q=P_\theta [v]$, $m=\max (u,v)$ and $r=P_\theta [m]$. Since $u\leq p$, $v\leq q$ and the envelope is monotone, \[  m\leq \max (p,q)\leq r.  \] All these potentials have positive lower volume. Theorem 30.3.4 and monotonicity therefore give $U(m)=U(\max (p,q))=U(r)$, while $U(u)=U(p)$ and $U(v)=U(q)$. This proves the first identity. If $d_\theta (u,v)=0$, then $U(u)=U(v)=U(m)$, since both are at most $U(m)$. Thus $u,v\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,m)$, and theorem 30.2.4 , proposition 13.4.5 give $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [m]=P_\theta [v]$. Conversely, if $p=q$, the first identity gives $d_\theta (u,v)=d_\theta (p,p)=0$. Now let $u,v\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and set $s=d_\theta (u,v)$. By theorem 1.4.2 , there is $C_\theta $ bounding the $L^1$ norm of every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic potential with supremum zero. Since ordinary models have supremum zero, the estimate holds if $s\geq \delta /2$. Suppose $0<s<\delta /2$ and put $t=(2s/\delta )^{1/n}$. The upper-volume deficit from $u$ to $m$ is at most $s$, and the lower volume of $m$ is at least $\delta $. Thus lemma 30.2.1 , with $b=t^{-1}$, gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that \[  (1-t)m+th\leq u.  \] For each competitor $g$ for $P_\theta [h]$ (so $g\leq 0$ and $g\preceq h$), the potential $(1-t)m+tg$ lies below zero and is more singular than $u$. Since $u=P_\theta [u]$, it lies below $u$, and taking the envelope gives \[  (1-t)m+tP_\theta [h]\leq u.  \] Hence $0\leq m-u\leq t(m-P_\theta [h])\leq -tP_\theta [h]$, and $\int _ X(m-u)\, \mathrm{d}V\leq tC_\theta $ because $P_\theta [h]$ has supremum zero. The same argument applies to $v$, and adding the two estimates gives the assertion, since $|u-v|\leq (m-u)+(m-v)$. If $s=0$, the argument works for every $t\in (0,1)$; let $t\downarrow 0$. $\square$ Although the triangle inequality fails, the volume comparison satisfies it up to an error that is controlled uniformly on $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$. Proposition 30.6.4 . For $u,v,w\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, 30.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-volume-comparison-modulus} d_\theta (u,w)\leq d_\theta (u,v)+d_\theta (v,w) +2nM\min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (v,w)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} . \end{equation} Consequently every $d_\theta $-convergent sequence in $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ is $d_\theta $-Cauchy, and its limit is unique. Proof. Put $s=d_\theta (v,w)$. If $s\geq \delta /2$, the inequality follows from $d_\theta (u,w)\leq 2M$. If $0<s<\delta /2$, set $t=(2s/\delta )^{1/n}$. Lemma 30.2.1 , applied to $v\preceq \max (v,w)$, gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  (1-t)\max (v,w)+th\leq v.  \] This inequality also gives $h\leq v$. Set $r=\max (u,v)$ and $z=\max (u,v,w)$. Where $z=\max (v,w)$, the inequality above bounds $(1-t)z+th$ by $v\leq r$; where $z=u$, both $u$ and $h$ lie below $r$. Thus \[  (1-t)z+th\leq r.  \] Addition, homogeneity and volume monotonicity give \[  U(z)-U(r)\leq \bigl (1-(1-t)^ n\bigr )U(z)\leq nMt.  \] Since $\max (u,w)\leq z$, it follows that \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (u,w) & \leq 2U(r)+2nMt-U(u)-U(w)\\ & =d_\theta (u,v)+U(v)-U(w)+2nMt\\ & \leq d_\theta (u,v)+s+2nMt. \end{split}  \] Here the last step uses ( 30.13 ). For $s=0$, the same proof works with every $t\in (0,1)$; let $t\downarrow 0$. This proves ( 30.14 ). Applying it with the limit as the middle point shows that a convergent sequence is Cauchy. If a sequence converges to two limits, applying it with a member of the sequence as the middle point shows that the two limits have volume comparison zero; by proposition 30.6.3 , they are equal. $\square$ Theorem 30.6.5 . Every $d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ converges for $d_\theta $ to a unique element of $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$. It also converges to that element in $L^1(X,\mathrm{d}V)$. Proof. The plan is to dominate a fast subsequence by the ordinary envelopes of its tail suprema; these decrease to the limit, and the stretching lemma controls the volume they add. Choose a subsequence $a_ j$ of the given sequence such that \[  d_\theta (a_ j,a_{j+1})<\delta \, 2^{-(j+1)n} \qquad (j\geq 1).  \] For $k\geq 0$, set \[  v_ j^ k=\max (a_ j,\ldots ,a_{j+k}),\qquad v_ j=\left(\sup _{l\geq j}a_ l\right)^*.  \] For every $l\geq j$, lemma 30.2.1 with $b=2^ l$, applied to $a_ l\preceq \max (a_ l,a_{l+1})$, gives $h_ l\leq a_ l$ satisfying \[  (1-2^{-l})\max (a_ l,a_{l+1})+2^{-l}h_ l\leq a_ l.  \] The argument by cases in the proof of proposition 30.6.4 gives \[  (1-2^{-l})v_ j^{l+1-j}+2^{-l}h_ l\leq v_ j^{l-j}.  \] Consequently \[  U(v_ j^{l+1-j})-U(v_ j^{l-j})\leq nM2^{-l}.  \] Summing from $l=j$ to $j+k-1$ and then letting $k\to \infty $, using theorem 30.5.1 , yields \[  0\leq U(v_ j)-U(a_ j)\leq nM2^{1-j}.  \] Here $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has lower volume at least $\delta $, because $a_ j\leq v_ j\leq 0$; this also justifies the use of that theorem. Put $q_ j=P_\theta [v_ j]$. By theorem 30.3.4 , $q_ j$ is an ordinary model with the same two volumes as $v_ j$. The sequence $q_ j$ decreases, and each $q_ j$ has supremum zero. By normalized compactness, its decreasing limit $q$ is not identically $-\infty $, so $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By theorem 30.5.2 , \[  q=P_\theta [q],\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\lim _ j\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ j)\geq \delta , \qquad U(q_ j)\longrightarrow U(q).  \] Both $a_ j$ and $q$ lie below $q_ j$. Hence \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (a_ j,q) & \leq \bigl (U(q_ j)-U(a_ j)\bigr )+\bigl (U(q_ j)-U(q)\bigr )\\ & \leq nM2^{1-j}+U(q_ j)-U(q)\longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] To treat the whole sequence, apply ( 30.14 ) with a late member $a_ j$ of the subsequence as the middle point. The Cauchy property makes the first term small for all sufficiently late members of the original sequence, while $d_\theta (a_ j,q)$ makes the other two terms small. Thus the original sequence converges to $q$. Uniqueness follows from proposition 30.6.4 , and the $L^1$ estimate in proposition 30.6.3 proves the last assertion. $\square$ The non-strict inequality $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta \geq \delta $ in the definition of $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ is essential for completeness. Example 30.6.6 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form of integral one on a compact Riemann surface, and let $0<\delta <1$. The ordinary models of mass strictly greater than $\delta $ do not form a complete space for $d_\theta $. Proof. Fix a point $x$, and let $g_ x\leq 0$ be the Green function used in theorem 19.3.1 , with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ x=\delta _ x-\theta $, where $\delta _ x$ is the Dirac measure at $x$. For $0\leq a<1$, put $q_ a=P_\theta [ag_ x]$. The current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ag_ x)$ equals $a\delta _ x+(1-a)\theta $, with non-pluripolar mass $1-a$. Since the background is closed, both singularity volumes of $ag_ x$ equal this mass, and theorem 30.3.4 gives \[  q_ a=P_\theta [q_ a],\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ a)=U(q_ a)=1-a.  \] Since $g_ x\leq 0$, the potentials $q_ a$ decrease as $a$ increases, and ( 30.13 ) gives $d_\theta (q_ a,q_ b)=|a-b|$. Choose $a_ j<1-\delta $ with $a_ j\uparrow 1-\delta $. The sequence $q_{a_ j}$ is $d_\theta $-Cauchy, and every term has mass $1-a_ j>\delta $. By ( 30.13 ), any $d_\theta $-limit has upper volume $\lim _ j(1-a_ j)=\delta $. In this closed background the two volumes coincide, so no such limit has mass strictly greater than $\delta $. $\square$

title: Definition 30.6.1
text: Definition 30.6.1 . For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, define \[  d_\theta (u,v)=2U(\max (u,v))-U(u)-U(v).  \] For $\delta >0$, put \[  \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )= \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):P_\theta [u]=u, \  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\geq \delta \} .  \] We call $d_\theta $ the volume comparison . A sequence is $d_\theta $-Cauchy if $d_\theta (u_ j,u_ k)\to 0$ as $j,k\to \infty $, and it converges to $u$ for $d_\theta $ if $d_\theta (u_ j,u)\to 0$.
30.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:volume-comparison-basic} |U(u)-U(v)|\leq d_\theta (u,v),\qquad u\leq v\  \Longrightarrow \  d_\theta (u,v)=U(v)-U(u). \end{equation}

title: Example 30.6.2
text: Example 30.6.2 . For every $n\geq 2$ there are a closed positive $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on the projective manifold $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1}$ and two ordinary models $a\not\sim b$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1},\theta )$ such that \[  P_\theta [a]_{\mathcal I}=b,\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (a) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (b)=0,\qquad d_\theta (a,b)=0.  \] For every $n\geq 3$, the same assertions hold for a suitable nonclosed positive form $\theta $ on a projective manifold of dimension $n$ with the bounded mass property. Proof. Take the closed positive product background of example 16.6.23 on $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1}$. Its models satisfy $a\leq b$ and $U(a)=U(b)=0$. Thus $\max (a,b)=b$, and the defining formula gives \[  d_\theta (a,b)=2U(b)-U(a)-U(b)=0.  \] The other assertions are part of that example. For the nonclosed case use example 16.6.24 ; its models are again ordered and have zero upper volumes, so the same calculation applies. $\square$

title: Proposition 30.6.3
text: Proposition 30.6.3 . For potentials $u,v$ of positive lower volume, \[  d_\theta (u,v)=d_\theta (P_\theta [u],P_\theta [v]),\qquad d_\theta (u,v)=0\  \Longleftrightarrow \  P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [v].  \] There is $C_\theta >0$, depending on $\theta $ and $\mathrm{d}V$, such that, for $u,v\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, \[  \| u-v\| _{L^1}\leq 2C_\theta \min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (u,v)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} .  \] Proof. Translate the inputs below zero, and put $p=P_\theta [u]$, $q=P_\theta [v]$, $m=\max (u,v)$ and $r=P_\theta [m]$. Since $u\leq p$, $v\leq q$ and the envelope is monotone, \[  m\leq \max (p,q)\leq r.  \] All these potentials have positive lower volume. Theorem 30.3.4 and monotonicity therefore give $U(m)=U(\max (p,q))=U(r)$, while $U(u)=U(p)$ and $U(v)=U(q)$. This proves the first identity. If $d_\theta (u,v)=0$, then $U(u)=U(v)=U(m)$, since both are at most $U(m)$. Thus $u,v\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,m)$, and theorem 30.2.4 , proposition 13.4.5 give $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [m]=P_\theta [v]$. Conversely, if $p=q$, the first identity gives $d_\theta (u,v)=d_\theta (p,p)=0$. Now let $u,v\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and set $s=d_\theta (u,v)$. By theorem 1.4.2 , there is $C_\theta $ bounding the $L^1$ norm of every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic potential with supremum zero. Since ordinary models have supremum zero, the estimate holds if $s\geq \delta /2$. Suppose $0<s<\delta /2$ and put $t=(2s/\delta )^{1/n}$. The upper-volume deficit from $u$ to $m$ is at most $s$, and the lower volume of $m$ is at least $\delta $. Thus lemma 30.2.1 , with $b=t^{-1}$, gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that \[  (1-t)m+th\leq u.  \] For each competitor $g$ for $P_\theta [h]$ (so $g\leq 0$ and $g\preceq h$), the potential $(1-t)m+tg$ lies below zero and is more singular than $u$. Since $u=P_\theta [u]$, it lies below $u$, and taking the envelope gives \[  (1-t)m+tP_\theta [h]\leq u.  \] Hence $0\leq m-u\leq t(m-P_\theta [h])\leq -tP_\theta [h]$, and $\int _ X(m-u)\, \mathrm{d}V\leq tC_\theta $ because $P_\theta [h]$ has supremum zero. The same argument applies to $v$, and adding the two estimates gives the assertion, since $|u-v|\leq (m-u)+(m-v)$. If $s=0$, the argument works for every $t\in (0,1)$; let $t\downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: Proposition 30.6.4
text: Proposition 30.6.4 . For $u,v,w\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, 30.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-volume-comparison-modulus} d_\theta (u,w)\leq d_\theta (u,v)+d_\theta (v,w) +2nM\min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (v,w)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} . \end{equation} Consequently every $d_\theta $-convergent sequence in $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ is $d_\theta $-Cauchy, and its limit is unique. Proof. Put $s=d_\theta (v,w)$. If $s\geq \delta /2$, the inequality follows from $d_\theta (u,w)\leq 2M$. If $0<s<\delta /2$, set $t=(2s/\delta )^{1/n}$. Lemma 30.2.1 , applied to $v\preceq \max (v,w)$, gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  (1-t)\max (v,w)+th\leq v.  \] This inequality also gives $h\leq v$. Set $r=\max (u,v)$ and $z=\max (u,v,w)$. Where $z=\max (v,w)$, the inequality above bounds $(1-t)z+th$ by $v\leq r$; where $z=u$, both $u$ and $h$ lie below $r$. Thus \[  (1-t)z+th\leq r.  \] Addition, homogeneity and volume monotonicity give \[  U(z)-U(r)\leq \bigl (1-(1-t)^ n\bigr )U(z)\leq nMt.  \] Since $\max (u,w)\leq z$, it follows that \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (u,w) & \leq 2U(r)+2nMt-U(u)-U(w)\\ & =d_\theta (u,v)+U(v)-U(w)+2nMt\\ & \leq d_\theta (u,v)+s+2nMt. \end{split}  \] Here the last step uses ( 30.13 ). For $s=0$, the same proof works with every $t\in (0,1)$; let $t\downarrow 0$. This proves ( 30.14 ). Applying it with the limit as the middle point shows that a convergent sequence is Cauchy. If a sequence converges to two limits, applying it with a member of the sequence as the middle point shows that the two limits have volume comparison zero; by proposition 30.6.3 , they are equal. $\square$

30.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-volume-comparison-modulus} d_\theta (u,w)\leq d_\theta (u,v)+d_\theta (v,w) +2nM\min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (v,w)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} . \end{equation}

title: Theorem 30.6.5
text: Theorem 30.6.5 . Every $d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ converges for $d_\theta $ to a unique element of $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$. It also converges to that element in $L^1(X,\mathrm{d}V)$. Proof. The plan is to dominate a fast subsequence by the ordinary envelopes of its tail suprema; these decrease to the limit, and the stretching lemma controls the volume they add. Choose a subsequence $a_ j$ of the given sequence such that \[  d_\theta (a_ j,a_{j+1})<\delta \, 2^{-(j+1)n} \qquad (j\geq 1).  \] For $k\geq 0$, set \[  v_ j^ k=\max (a_ j,\ldots ,a_{j+k}),\qquad v_ j=\left(\sup _{l\geq j}a_ l\right)^*.  \] For every $l\geq j$, lemma 30.2.1 with $b=2^ l$, applied to $a_ l\preceq \max (a_ l,a_{l+1})$, gives $h_ l\leq a_ l$ satisfying \[  (1-2^{-l})\max (a_ l,a_{l+1})+2^{-l}h_ l\leq a_ l.  \] The argument by cases in the proof of proposition 30.6.4 gives \[  (1-2^{-l})v_ j^{l+1-j}+2^{-l}h_ l\leq v_ j^{l-j}.  \] Consequently \[  U(v_ j^{l+1-j})-U(v_ j^{l-j})\leq nM2^{-l}.  \] Summing from $l=j$ to $j+k-1$ and then letting $k\to \infty $, using theorem 30.5.1 , yields \[  0\leq U(v_ j)-U(a_ j)\leq nM2^{1-j}.  \] Here $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has lower volume at least $\delta $, because $a_ j\leq v_ j\leq 0$; this also justifies the use of that theorem. Put $q_ j=P_\theta [v_ j]$. By theorem 30.3.4 , $q_ j$ is an ordinary model with the same two volumes as $v_ j$. The sequence $q_ j$ decreases, and each $q_ j$ has supremum zero. By normalized compactness, its decreasing limit $q$ is not identically $-\infty $, so $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By theorem 30.5.2 , \[  q=P_\theta [q],\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\lim _ j\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ j)\geq \delta , \qquad U(q_ j)\longrightarrow U(q).  \] Both $a_ j$ and $q$ lie below $q_ j$. Hence \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (a_ j,q) & \leq \bigl (U(q_ j)-U(a_ j)\bigr )+\bigl (U(q_ j)-U(q)\bigr )\\ & \leq nM2^{1-j}+U(q_ j)-U(q)\longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] To treat the whole sequence, apply ( 30.14 ) with a late member $a_ j$ of the subsequence as the middle point. The Cauchy property makes the first term small for all sufficiently late members of the original sequence, while $d_\theta (a_ j,q)$ makes the other two terms small. Thus the original sequence converges to $q$. Uniqueness follows from proposition 30.6.4 , and the $L^1$ estimate in proposition 30.6.3 proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Example 30.6.6
text: Example 30.6.6 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form of integral one on a compact Riemann surface, and let $0<\delta <1$. The ordinary models of mass strictly greater than $\delta $ do not form a complete space for $d_\theta $. Proof. Fix a point $x$, and let $g_ x\leq 0$ be the Green function used in theorem 19.3.1 , with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ x=\delta _ x-\theta $, where $\delta _ x$ is the Dirac measure at $x$. For $0\leq a<1$, put $q_ a=P_\theta [ag_ x]$. The current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ag_ x)$ equals $a\delta _ x+(1-a)\theta $, with non-pluripolar mass $1-a$. Since the background is closed, both singularity volumes of $ag_ x$ equal this mass, and theorem 30.3.4 gives \[  q_ a=P_\theta [q_ a],\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ a)=U(q_ a)=1-a.  \] Since $g_ x\leq 0$, the potentials $q_ a$ decrease as $a$ increases, and ( 30.13 ) gives $d_\theta (q_ a,q_ b)=|a-b|$. Choose $a_ j<1-\delta $ with $a_ j\uparrow 1-\delta $. The sequence $q_{a_ j}$ is $d_\theta $-Cauchy, and every term has mass $1-a_ j>\delta $. By ( 30.13 ), any $d_\theta $-limit has upper volume $\lim _ j(1-a_ j)=\delta $. In this closed background the two volumes coincide, so no such limit has mass strictly greater than $\delta $. $\square$

title: 30.7 Rooftops and capacity convergence
text: 30.7 Rooftops and capacity convergence A small upper-volume deficit also controls the rooftop envelope of two potentials. For a finite family it suffices that the sum of the deficits stays below the lower volume of a common upper bound. Applying this criterion to stretched potentials gives increasing lower bounds for a suitable subsequence of models. Together with the decreasing upper bounds of the preceding section, they turn convergence for the volume comparison into convergence in capacity. Lemma 30.7.1 . Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ N,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, with $N\geq 1$ and $u_ i\preceq w$. If \[  \sum _{i=1}^ N\bigl (U(w)-U(u_ i)\bigr ) <\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (w),  \] then the rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u_1,\ldots ,u_ N)=P_\theta (\min _ iu_ i)$ is not identically $-\infty $. Proof. Whether a finite rooftop envelope is identically $-\infty $ does not change under bounded changes of its obstacles. By the definition of $U(u_ i)$, we can choose $v_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v_ i\sim u_ i$ whose masses satisfy \[  \sum _{i=1}^ N\left(U(w)-\int _ X\mu _{v_ i}\right) <\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (w).  \] Translate so that $v_ i\leq w\leq 0$, and put \[  v_{i,k}=\max (v_ i,w-k),\qquad p_ k=P_\theta (v_{1,k},\ldots ,v_{N,k}).  \] The common competitor $w-k$ gives $w-k\leq p_ k\leq w$, so $p_ k\sim w$. The $p_ k$ decrease as $k$ increases, and a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic limit would be a competitor for $P_\theta (v_1,\ldots ,v_ N)$. Suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $P_\theta (u_1,\ldots ,u_ N)\equiv -\infty $, so that $P_\theta (v_1,\ldots ,v_ N)\equiv -\infty $ as well. Then the $p_ k$ decrease to $-\infty $, and normalized compactness gives $\sup _ Xp_ k\to -\infty $. Fix $s>0$ and choose $k>s$ so large that $p_ k\leq -s$. Iterating proposition 13.1.5 , which bounds the measure of a rooftop by the measures of its obstacles on the contact sets, and using locality on $\{ v_ i>-s\} $, we obtain \[  \begin{split}  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (w) & \leq \int _ X\mu _{p_ k} \leq \sum _{i=1}^ N\int _{\{ v_{i,k}\leq -s\} }\mu _{v_{i,k}}\\ & \leq \sum _{i=1}^ N\left(U(w)-\int _{\{ v_ i>-s\} }\mu _{v_ i}\right). \end{split}  \] Here we used $v_{i,k}\sim w$, and $w-k<-s$, which gives $v_{i,k}=v_ i$ on $\{ v_{i,k}>-s\} =\{ v_ i>-s\} $. Let $s\to \infty $. The measures $\mu _{v_ i}$ are finite and put no mass on pluripolar sets, so the resulting inequality contradicts the choice of the $v_ i$. $\square$ To control the volume of a rooftop envelope, we first stretch each obstacle away from the maximum of the two, and then move both stretched potentials a fixed fraction back toward this maximum. By the lemma, the resulting potentials have a rooftop envelope that is not identically $-\infty $. Proposition 30.7.2 . Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, with $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)>0$, and suppose that $d_\theta (u_ j,u)\to 0$. For all sufficiently large $j$, the rooftop envelope $p_ j=P_\theta (u_ j,u)$ is not identically $-\infty $, and \[  d_\theta (p_ j,u)\longrightarrow 0,\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p_ j) \longrightarrow \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] Proof. Put $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$, $m_ j=\max (u_ j,u)$ and $s_ j=d_\theta (u_ j,u)$. After discarding finitely many indices, choose $b_ j\to \infty $ with $b_ j>1$ and $b_ j^ ns_ j<\delta $. The upper-volume deficits of both $u_ j$ and $u$ from $m_ j$ are at most $s_ j$, while $m_ j$ has lower volume at least $\delta $. Thus lemma 30.2.1 shows that the stretching envelopes \[  G_ j=Q_{b_ j}(u_ j,m_ j),\qquad H_ j=Q_{b_ j}(u,m_ j)  \] are defined. Choose $a\in (0,1)$ with $2nMa<\delta $, and set \[  g_ j=(1-a)m_ j+aG_ j,\qquad h_ j=(1-a)m_ j+aH_ j.  \] These potentials lie below $m_ j$, because $G_ j\leq u_ j$ and $H_ j\leq u$. Addition and monotonicity give \[  2U(m_ j)-U(g_ j)-U(h_ j) \leq 2\bigl (1-(1-a)^ n\bigr )U(m_ j) \leq 2nMa<\delta .  \] Lemma 30.7.1 , with $w=m_ j$, therefore shows that $r_ j=P_\theta (g_ j,h_ j)$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. For large $j$, put $t_ j=(ab_ j)^{-1}<1$. Since $r_ j\leq g_ j$ and $r_ j\leq h_ j$, the defining inequalities for $G_ j$ and $H_ j$ show that \[  (1-t_ j)m_ j+t_ jr_ j\leq u_ j,u.  \] The left-hand side is therefore a competitor for $p_ j$, so $p_ j\not\equiv -\infty $. For either volume, addition and monotonicity give \[  (1-t_ j)^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq (1-t_ j)^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (m_ j) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (p_ j) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u).  \] Since $t_ j\to 0$, this proves $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p_ j)\to \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$; and since $p_ j\leq u$, ( 30.13 ) gives $d_\theta (p_ j,u)=U(u)-U(p_ j)\to 0$. $\square$ For ordinary models, finite rooftop envelopes are again ordinary models. Their normalization prevents collapse when the number of obstacles tends to infinity. Theorem 30.7.3 . Suppose $u_ j,u\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and $d_\theta (u_ j,u)\to 0$. After passing to a subsequence and relabeling it, there are ordinary model potentials $v_ j,w_ j\in \mathcal M_{\delta /2}(\theta )$ such that \[  w_ j\leq u_ j\leq v_ j,\qquad w_ j\leq u\leq v_ j,  \] $v_ j$ decreases to $u$, $w_ j$ increases with $(\lim _ jw_ j)^*=u$, and \[  d_\theta (v_ j,u)+d_\theta (w_ j,u)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The original sequence converges to $u$ in capacity. Proof. Step 1: upper bounds. For large $j$, the rooftop envelope $r_ j=P_\theta (u_ j,u)$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic by proposition 30.7.2 . It is an ordinary model: since $r_ j\leq 0$ and the envelope is monotone, $r_ j\leq P_\theta [r_ j]\leq P_\theta [u_ j]=u_ j$ and likewise $P_\theta [r_ j]\leq u$, so $P_\theta [r_ j]$ is a competitor for the rooftop and equals $r_ j$. The sequence $u_ j$ is $d_\theta $-Cauchy by proposition 30.6.4 , and $d_\theta (r_ j,u)=U(u)-U(r_ j)\to 0$ by proposition 30.7.2 . Choose a subsequence so that \[  d_\theta (u_ j,u_{j+1})<\delta \, 2^{-(j+1)n},\qquad U(u)-U(r_ j)<\delta \, 4^{-(j+1)n}.  \] The tail-maximum construction in the proof of theorem 30.6.5 gives \[  v_ j=P_\theta \left[\left(\sup _{l\geq j}u_ l\right)^*\right] \searrow u,\qquad d_\theta (v_ j,u)\longrightarrow 0.  \] Indeed, that construction produces the unique $d_\theta $-limit, which here is $u$. The models $v_ j$ satisfy $v_ j\geq u_ j$ and $v_ j\geq u$, and have lower volume at least $\delta $. Step 2: lower bounds. By lemma 30.2.1 and the choice of the subsequence, the stretching envelopes \[  H_ l=Q_{4^ l}(r_ l,u),\qquad K_ l=Q_{2^ l}(r_ l,u)  \] are defined. Their defining inequalities show that $(1-2^{-l})u+2^{-l}H_ l$ is a competitor for $K_ l$ and that $K_ l\leq u$. Together with addition and monotonicity, this gives \[  (1-2^{-l})u+2^{-l}H_ l\leq K_ l\leq u, \qquad U(u)-U(K_ l)\leq nM2^{-l}.  \] Choose $j$ so large that $nM2^{1-j}<\delta $. For every $k\geq 0$, the sum of the deficits of $K_ j,\ldots ,K_{j+k}$ from $u$ is less than $\delta $, so lemma 30.7.1 shows that their rooftop envelope is not identically $-\infty $. Since $r_ l\leq u$, the stretching envelope $Q_ b(r_ l,u)$ decreases as $b$ increases; hence, for $l\geq j$, \[  Q_{2^ j}(r_ l,u)\geq K_ l.  \] Thus $R_ j^ k=P_\theta (Q_{2^ j}(r_ j,u),\ldots ,Q_{2^ j}(r_{j+k},u))$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The convex inequality for each obstacle gives \[  (1-2^{-j})u+2^{-j}R_ j^ k \leq w_ j^ k:=P_\theta (r_ j,\ldots ,r_{j+k})\leq u.  \] For either volume, 30.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:tail-rooftop-volume-bound} (1-2^{-j})^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (w_ j^ k) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u). \end{equation} The argument used for $r_ j$ shows that $w_ j^ k$ is an ordinary model. For fixed $j$ it decreases in $k$ and has supremum zero, so normalized compactness shows that its limit $w_ j$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The lower-volume conclusion of theorem 30.5.2 passes the lower bound in ( 30.22 ) to $w_ j$. This bound is positive, so the upper-volume conclusion of the same theorem passes the bound for the upper volume as well. Step 3: convergence. The $w_ j$ increase, since each is defined by fewer obstacles than the previous one, and $w_ j\leq r_ j\leq u_ j$, $w_ j\leq u$. After discarding finitely many indices, they have lower volume at least $\delta /2$, and ( 30.22 ) gives $d_\theta (w_ j,u)\leq nM2^{-j}$. By proposition 30.6.3 , $w_ j\to u$ in $L^1$, so $(\lim _ jw_ j)^*=u$. The two monotone sequences $v_ j$ and $w_ j$ converge to $u$ in capacity by lemma 1.8.12 , and the bounds $w_ j\leq u_ j\leq v_ j$ give $u_ j\to u$ in capacity along the chosen subsequence. Since every subsequence of the original sequence has a further subsequence of this kind, the original sequence converges to $u$ in capacity. $\square$

title: Lemma 30.7.1
text: Lemma 30.7.1 . Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ N,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, with $N\geq 1$ and $u_ i\preceq w$. title: Proposition 30.7.2
text: Proposition 30.7.2 . Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, with $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)>0$, and suppose that $d_\theta (u_ j,u)\to 0$.
