title: 30.9 Model comparison under background changes
text: 30.9 Model comparison under background changes A smooth change of decomposition $(\theta ,u)\mapsto (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,u-f)$ preserves the curvature current but changes the zero obstacle used to normalize models. Taking the ordinary envelope again gives an exact correspondence that preserves the volume comparison. An increase of the background changes the volumes; a common positive lower-volume bound controls this change uniformly, and this allows analytic approximants whose curvature error tends to zero. Proposition 30.9.1 . Let $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. For every $\delta >0$, the map \[  G_ f:\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )\longrightarrow \mathcal M_\delta (\theta '), \qquad G_ f(p)=P_{\theta '}[p-f],  \] is a bijection with inverse $q\mapsto P_\theta [q+f]$. It preserves both singularity volumes, and \[  d_{\theta '}(G_ f(p),G_ f(q))=d_\theta (p,q).  \] It takes analytic models to analytic models and ideal models to ideal models. Proof. The map $u\mapsto u-f$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ that preserves curvature currents, singularity types and hence both singularity volumes. Also $\max (u-f,v-f)=\max (u,v)-f$, so \[  d_{\theta '}(u-f,v-f)=d_\theta (u,v).  \] By proposition 16.3.1 , $G_ f(p)+f\sim p$, that is, $G_ f(p)\sim p-f$. Thus $G_ f(p)$ has the same volumes as $p$, and it is an ordinary model by theorem 30.3.4 ; in particular $G_ f(p)\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta ')$. Since the volume comparison depends only on ordinary types, the displayed identity follows. Taking the ordinary envelope of $G_ f(p)+f\sim p$ gives $P_\theta [G_ f(p)+f]=P_\theta [p]=p$. The same argument with the two backgrounds interchanged proves that the map is bijective with the stated inverse. Subtraction of a smooth function and bounded changes preserve analytic singularities. If $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$, proposition 16.3.1 also gives \[  P_{\theta '}[p-f]_{\mathcal I}\sim p-f\sim G_ f(p).  \] The ideal envelope is an ordinary model by corollary 16.2.4 , and ordinary models of the same ordinary type coincide; hence $P_{\theta '}[G_ f(p)]_{\mathcal I}=P_{\theta '}[p-f]_{\mathcal I}=G_ f(p)$. The inverse map gives the converse. $\square$ For the rest of this section and the next, fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta +2h$, a rational number $\kappa >0$ and an analytic $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\rho \leq 0$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa h$; such $\kappa $ and $\rho $ exist by bigness and theorem 1.15.1 . Put $K=v_+(\Omega )$. For $\delta >0$, set \[  b_\delta =1+\frac{\delta }{2^{n+1}nK},\qquad \kappa _\delta =(1-b_\delta ^{-1})\kappa .  \] These constants stay fixed while the potentials and backgrounds vary. Proposition 30.9.2 . Let $\beta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\theta \leq \beta \leq \theta +h$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )$ satisfy $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta >0$. For every $\varepsilon \in [0,1]$ and every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ with $\beta \leq \gamma \leq \beta +\varepsilon h$, both singularity volumes satisfy \[  \operatorname {vol}_\beta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\gamma (u) \leq (1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n\operatorname {vol}_\beta (u).  \] Proof. Normalize $u\leq 0$, so that $u\leq V_\beta $, and note that $\rho \leq V_\beta $. Since $\Omega \geq \beta $ and $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta $, lemma 30.4.1 , applied in the big background $\beta $, shows that $H=Q_{b_\delta }(u,V_\beta )$ is defined. The potential \[  w=b_\delta ^{-1}H+(1-b_\delta ^{-1})\rho  \] satisfies $w\leq u$ and $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq (1-b_\delta ^{-1})(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )\geq \kappa _\delta h$. The addition argument in the proof of proposition 30.4.4 , with $h$, $\kappa _\delta $ and $t=\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta $ in place of $\omega $, $\delta $ and $t$, therefore gives the upper bound, with constants independent of $\beta $ and $u$. The lower bound is volume monotonicity. $\square$ Corollary 30.9.3 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have lower volume at least $\delta >0$, and let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\theta \leq \eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon h$, where $0\leq \varepsilon \leq 1$. Then 30.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:vanishing-background-comparison} \left|d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])-d_\theta (u,v)\right| \leq 2K\left((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{equation} Proof. The preceding proposition, with $\beta =\theta $ and $\gamma =\eta $, applies to $u$, $v$ and $m=\max (u,v)$, and their upper volumes in background $\theta $ are at most $v_+(\Omega )=K$. Thus, for $x=u,v,m$, the errors \[  e_ x=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (x) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (x)  \] lie between zero and $K((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1)$. The difference $d_\eta (u,v)-d_\theta (u,v)$ equals $2e_ m-e_ u-e_ v$, whose absolute value is at most twice this bound. Finally, the projection invariance in proposition 30.6.3 , applied in background $\eta $, gives $d_\eta (u,v)=d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])$, which is the comparison appearing in ( 30.25 ). $\square$ In particular, for $p_ j,p\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and $\theta \leq \eta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ jh$ with $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$, \[  d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad d_{\eta _ j}(P_{\eta _ j}[p_ j],P_{\eta _ j}[p])\longrightarrow 0.  \] Here the backgrounds $\eta _ j$ need not be monotone in $j$. The next result allows the analytic approximants themselves to belong only to the larger backgrounds $\eta _ j$. Theorem 30.9.4 . Let $p$ be an ordinary model of positive lower volume, and let $\eta _ j$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with $\theta \leq \eta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ jh$, where $\varepsilon _ j\geq 0$ tends to zero. Then $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if there are analytic $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta _ j)$ with \[  d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The $a_ j$ may be required to be ordinary models in their respective backgrounds. Given any such analytic approximants, convex combinations with the fixed potential $\rho $, with rational coefficients, produce analytic $b_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ whose ordinary envelopes satisfy \[  d_\theta (P_\theta [b_ j],p)\longrightarrow 0, \qquad P_\theta [b_ j]\longrightarrow p \quad \text{in }L^1\text{ and capacity}.  \] Proof. Suppose first that $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. By theorem 30.8.3 , there are analytic ordinary models $r_ j$ in background $\theta $ with $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$ and a common positive lower-volume bound. Corollary 30.9.3 and projection invariance in background $\eta _ j$ give $d_{\eta _ j}(r_ j,p)\to 0$, so $a_ j=r_ j$ works. One can also use the ordinary models $a_ j=P_{\eta _ j}[r_ j]$, since $P_{\eta _ j}[r_ j]\sim r_ j$ by proposition 16.2.7 . Conversely, suppose that such $a_ j$ exist. Normalize them below zero, and put $m_ j=\max (a_ j,p)$ and $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)>0$. Inequality ( 30.13 ) and proposition 30.9.2 give \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j),\quad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(m_ j) \longrightarrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] Indeed, the upper volume of $p$ in background $\eta _ j$ tends to its upper volume in background $\theta $, and the differences of $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(m_ j)$ from $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(p)$ are bounded in absolute value by $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p)$. Enlarge the errors $\varepsilon _ j$ to positive rational numbers tending to zero, and put \[  c_ j=\frac{\kappa }{\kappa +\varepsilon _ j},\qquad b_ j=c_ ja_ j+(1-c_ j)\rho ,\qquad r_ j=P_\theta [b_ j].  \] As in the proof of theorem 30.8.3 , $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ j\geq 0$ and $b_ j$ has analytic singularities. Choose $A>0$ with $\theta \leq Ah$, and set \[  \widehat\theta _ j=\theta +(1+A/\kappa )\varepsilon _ jh, \qquad \widehat m_ j=P_{\widehat\theta _ j}[m_ j].  \] Then $\widehat\theta _ j\geq \eta _ j$ and $c_ j\widehat\theta _ j\geq \theta $. Since $r_ j\sim b_ j$ and $\rho \leq 0$, the potential $r_ j/c_ j$ is a nonpositive $\widehat\theta _ j$-plurisubharmonic function more singular than $a_ j$, hence more singular than $m_ j$. Therefore $r_ j\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. Also $p\leq \widehat m_ j\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. The lower volume of $m_ j$ in background $\eta _ j$ is at least $\delta $. For large $j$, proposition 30.9.2 applies with $\beta =\eta _ j$, $\gamma =\widehat\theta _ j$ and $\varepsilon =(1+A/\kappa )\varepsilon _ j$. Consequently \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _ j}(m_ j) \longrightarrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] By theorem 30.3.4 , $\widehat m_ j$ has the same upper volume in background $\widehat\theta _ j$ as $m_ j$. On the other hand, \[  c_ j\eta _ j+(1-c_ j)(\theta -\kappa h)\leq \theta .  \] Addition, applied to $c_ ja_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_ j\eta _ j)$ and $(1-c_ j)\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,(1-c_ j)(\theta -\kappa h))$, and background monotonicity therefore bound the upper volume of $b_ j$ below by $c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)$. Since $r_ j\sim b_ j$, the two comparisons yield \[  \begin{split}  c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j) & \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (r_ j) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\max (r_ j,p))\\ & \leq c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _ j}(m_ j). \end{split}  \] Here the last inequality uses $\theta \leq c_ j\widehat\theta _ j$ and $\max (r_ j,p)\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. Both outer terms tend to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$, which proves $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$. By proposition 16.2.7 , $r_ j=P_\theta [b_ j]_{\mathcal I}$ is an ideal model, so theorem 30.8.4 gives $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. For large $j$, the upper-volume deficit from $r_ j$ to $\max (r_ j,p)$ is small, and lemma 30.2.1 with $b=2$ gives a convex lower bound for $r_ j$ whose first term is $\frac12\max (r_ j,p)$. Volume addition gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (r_ j)\geq 2^{-n}\delta $. Thus proposition 30.6.3 , theorem 30.7.3 give the asserted $L^1$ and capacity convergence of the models $r_ j$. $\square$ Since the volume comparison depends only on singularity types, the theorem asserts convergence of the ordinary models $P_\theta [b_ j]$, not of the analytic potentials $b_ j$ themselves. When the background errors may have either sign, $p$ need not be admissible in the perturbed backgrounds; the next section constructs reference models there.

title: Proposition 30.9.1
text: Proposition 30.9.1 . Let $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. For every $\delta >0$, the map \[  G_ f:\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )\longrightarrow \mathcal M_\delta (\theta '), \qquad G_ f(p)=P_{\theta '}[p-f],  \] is a bijection with inverse $q\mapsto P_\theta [q+f]$. It preserves both singularity volumes, and \[  d_{\theta '}(G_ f(p),G_ f(q))=d_\theta (p,q).  \] It takes analytic models to analytic models and ideal models to ideal models. Proof. The map $u\mapsto u-f$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ that preserves curvature currents, singularity types and hence both singularity volumes. Also $\max (u-f,v-f)=\max (u,v)-f$, so \[  d_{\theta '}(u-f,v-f)=d_\theta (u,v).  \] By proposition 16.3.1 , $G_ f(p)+f\sim p$, that is, $G_ f(p)\sim p-f$. Thus $G_ f(p)$ has the same volumes as $p$, and it is an ordinary model by theorem 30.3.4 ; in particular $G_ f(p)\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta ')$. Since the volume comparison depends only on ordinary types, the displayed identity follows. Taking the ordinary envelope of $G_ f(p)+f\sim p$ gives $P_\theta [G_ f(p)+f]=P_\theta [p]=p$. The same argument with the two backgrounds interchanged proves that the map is bijective with the stated inverse. Subtraction of a smooth function and bounded changes preserve analytic singularities. If $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$, proposition 16.3.1 also gives \[  P_{\theta '}[p-f]_{\mathcal I}\sim p-f\sim G_ f(p).  \] The ideal envelope is an ordinary model by corollary 16.2.4 , and ordinary models of the same ordinary type coincide; hence $P_{\theta '}[G_ f(p)]_{\mathcal I}=P_{\theta '}[p-f]_{\mathcal I}=G_ f(p)$. The inverse map gives the converse. $\square$

title: Proposition 30.9.2
text: Proposition 30.9.2 . Let $\beta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\theta \leq \beta \leq \theta +h$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )$ satisfy $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta >0$. For every $\varepsilon \in [0,1]$ and every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ with $\beta \leq \gamma \leq \beta +\varepsilon h$, both singularity volumes satisfy \[  \operatorname {vol}_\beta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\gamma (u) \leq (1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n\operatorname {vol}_\beta (u).  \] Proof. Normalize $u\leq 0$, so that $u\leq V_\beta $, and note that $\rho \leq V_\beta $. Since $\Omega \geq \beta $ and $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta $, lemma 30.4.1 , applied in the big background $\beta $, shows that $H=Q_{b_\delta }(u,V_\beta )$ is defined. The potential \[  w=b_\delta ^{-1}H+(1-b_\delta ^{-1})\rho  \] satisfies $w\leq u$ and $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq (1-b_\delta ^{-1})(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )\geq \kappa _\delta h$. The addition argument in the proof of proposition 30.4.4 , with $h$, $\kappa _\delta $ and $t=\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta $ in place of $\omega $, $\delta $ and $t$, therefore gives the upper bound, with constants independent of $\beta $ and $u$. The lower bound is volume monotonicity. $\square$

title: Corollary 30.9.3
text: Corollary 30.9.3 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have lower volume at least $\delta >0$, and let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\theta \leq \eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon h$, where $0\leq \varepsilon \leq 1$. Then 30.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:vanishing-background-comparison} \left|d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])-d_\theta (u,v)\right| \leq 2K\left((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{equation} Proof. The preceding proposition, with $\beta =\theta $ and $\gamma =\eta $, applies to $u$, $v$ and $m=\max (u,v)$, and their upper volumes in background $\theta $ are at most $v_+(\Omega )=K$. Thus, for $x=u,v,m$, the errors \[  e_ x=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (x) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (x)  \] lie between zero and $K((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1)$. The difference $d_\eta (u,v)-d_\theta (u,v)$ equals $2e_ m-e_ u-e_ v$, whose absolute value is at most twice this bound. Finally, the projection invariance in proposition 30.6.3 , applied in background $\eta $, gives $d_\eta (u,v)=d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])$, which is the comparison appearing in ( 30.25 ). $\square$
30.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:vanishing-background-comparison} \left|d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])-d_\theta (u,v)\right| \leq 2K\left((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{equation}

title: Theorem 30.9.4
text: Theorem 30.9.4 . Let $p$ be an ordinary model of positive lower volume, and let $\eta _ j$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with $\theta \leq \eta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ jh$, where $\varepsilon _ j\geq 0$ tends to zero. Then $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if there are analytic $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta _ j)$ with \[  d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The $a_ j$ may be required to be ordinary models in their respective backgrounds. Given any such analytic approximants, convex combinations with the fixed potential $\rho $, with rational coefficients, produce analytic $b_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ whose ordinary envelopes satisfy \[  d_\theta (P_\theta [b_ j],p)\longrightarrow 0, \qquad P_\theta [b_ j]\longrightarrow p \quad \text{in }L^1\text{ and capacity}.  \] Proof. Suppose first that $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. By theorem 30.8.3 , there are analytic ordinary models $r_ j$ in background $\theta $ with $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$ and a common positive lower-volume bound. Corollary 30.9.3 and projection invariance in background $\eta _ j$ give $d_{\eta _ j}(r_ j,p)\to 0$, so $a_ j=r_ j$ works. One can also use the ordinary models $a_ j=P_{\eta _ j}[r_ j]$, since $P_{\eta _ j}[r_ j]\sim r_ j$ by proposition 16.2.7 . Conversely, suppose that such $a_ j$ exist. Normalize them below zero, and put $m_ j=\max (a_ j,p)$ and $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)>0$. Inequality ( 30.13 ) and proposition 30.9.2 give \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j),\quad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(m_ j) \longrightarrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] Indeed, the upper volume of $p$ in background $\eta _ j$ tends to its upper volume in background $\theta $, and the differences of $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(m_ j)$ from $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(p)$ are bounded in absolute value by $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p)$. Enlarge the errors $\varepsilon _ j$ to positive rational numbers tending to zero, and put \[  c_ j=\frac{\kappa }{\kappa +\varepsilon _ j},\qquad b_ j=c_ ja_ j+(1-c_ j)\rho ,\qquad r_ j=P_\theta [b_ j].  \] As in the proof of theorem 30.8.3 , $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ j\geq 0$ and $b_ j$ has analytic singularities. Choose $A>0$ with $\theta \leq Ah$, and set \[  \widehat\theta _ j=\theta +(1+A/\kappa )\varepsilon _ jh, \qquad \widehat m_ j=P_{\widehat\theta _ j}[m_ j].  \] Then $\widehat\theta _ j\geq \eta _ j$ and $c_ j\widehat\theta _ j\geq \theta $. Since $r_ j\sim b_ j$ and $\rho \leq 0$, the potential $r_ j/c_ j$ is a nonpositive $\widehat\theta _ j$-plurisubharmonic function more singular than $a_ j$, hence more singular than $m_ j$. Therefore $r_ j\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. Also $p\leq \widehat m_ j\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. The lower volume of $m_ j$ in background $\eta _ j$ is at least $\delta $. For large $j$, proposition 30.9.2 applies with $\beta =\eta _ j$, $\gamma =\widehat\theta _ j$ and $\varepsilon =(1+A/\kappa )\varepsilon _ j$. Consequently \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _ j}(m_ j) \longrightarrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] By theorem 30.3.4 , $\widehat m_ j$ has the same upper volume in background $\widehat\theta _ j$ as $m_ j$. On the other hand, \[  c_ j\eta _ j+(1-c_ j)(\theta -\kappa h)\leq \theta .  \] Addition, applied to $c_ ja_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_ j\eta _ j)$ and $(1-c_ j)\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,(1-c_ j)(\theta -\kappa h))$, and background monotonicity therefore bound the upper volume of $b_ j$ below by $c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)$. Since $r_ j\sim b_ j$, the two comparisons yield \[  \begin{split}  c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j) & \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (r_ j) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\max (r_ j,p))\\ & \leq c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _ j}(m_ j). \end{split}  \] Here the last inequality uses $\theta \leq c_ j\widehat\theta _ j$ and $\max (r_ j,p)\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. Both outer terms tend to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$, which proves $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$. By proposition 16.2.7 , $r_ j=P_\theta [b_ j]_{\mathcal I}$ is an ideal model, so theorem 30.8.4 gives $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. For large $j$, the upper-volume deficit from $r_ j$ to $\max (r_ j,p)$ is small, and lemma 30.2.1 with $b=2$ gives a convex lower bound for $r_ j$ whose first term is $\frac12\max (r_ j,p)$. Volume addition gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (r_ j)\geq 2^{-n}\delta $. Thus proposition 30.6.3 , theorem 30.7.3 give the asserted $L^1$ and capacity convergence of the models $r_ j$. $\square$

title: 30.10 Two-sided background perturbations
text: 30.10 Two-sided background perturbations A potential in the original background may cease to be admissible when the background decreases. Mixing it with the strict potential $\rho $ restores positivity, and ordinary projection then gives a model in the new background. The volume comparison controls the error of this transport uniformly on models with a common positive lower-volume bound, and it shows that the resulting notion of analytic approximation does not depend on the strict potential used in the correction. We first make the estimate of the preceding section uniform for pairs of forms near $\theta $. Lemma 30.10.1 . For every $\delta >0$ there are $C_\delta >0$ and $\varepsilon _0>0$ with the following property. Let $\beta ,\gamma $ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with \[  \theta -\varepsilon h\leq \beta \leq \gamma \leq \theta +\varepsilon h, \qquad 0\leq \varepsilon \leq \varepsilon _0,  \] and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )$ satisfy $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta $. Then both singularity volumes satisfy \[  0\leq \operatorname {vol}_\gamma (u)-\operatorname {vol}_\beta (u) \leq C_\delta \varepsilon .  \] For two such potentials $u,v$, one also has \[  \left|d_\gamma (P_\gamma [u],P_\gamma [v])-d_\beta (u,v)\right| \leq 2C_\delta \varepsilon .  \] Proof. Put $\theta _0=\theta -\kappa h/2$ and $h_0=(1+\kappa /2)h$. Since $\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa h/2$, the form $\theta _0$ is big, and $\rho $ is a strict analytic potential for it with the rational margin $\kappa /(2+\kappa )$ relative to $h_0$. Let $\varepsilon \leq \min (\kappa /2,1/2)$. Then $\theta _0\leq \beta \leq \theta _0+h_0$ and $\beta \leq \gamma \leq \beta +2\varepsilon h_0$, so proposition 30.9.2 applies with $\theta _0$, $h_0$, $\rho $ and a fixed Hermitian form $\Omega _0\geq \theta _0+2h_0$ in place of $\theta $, $h$, $\rho $ and $\Omega $. These choices do not depend on $\beta $ and $\gamma $. Since the volumes in background $\beta $ are at most $v_+(\Omega _0)$, the multiplicative estimate of the proposition implies the additive estimate, with a constant $C_\delta $ independent of $\beta $, $\gamma $ and $u$. Applying it to $u$, $v$ and $\max (u,v)$, the three-error calculation in the proof of corollary 30.9.3 and projection invariance in background $\gamma $ give the second assertion. $\square$ We now define the transport. Choose $A>0$ with $\theta \leq Ah$ and put $B=2(1+A/\kappa )$. For $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $p\leq 0$, a number $\varepsilon $ with $0<\varepsilon <\min (\kappa /2,1/B)$, and a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ with $\theta -\varepsilon h\leq \eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon h$, set 30.28 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-model-transport} c_\varepsilon =1-\varepsilon /\kappa ,\qquad T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p) =P_\eta [c_\varepsilon p+(1-c_\varepsilon )\rho ],\qquad \widehat\theta _\varepsilon =\theta +B\varepsilon h. \end{equation} The mixed potential $c_\varepsilon p+(1-c_\varepsilon )\rho $ is $\eta $-plurisubharmonic, since $1-c_\varepsilon =\varepsilon /\kappa $ and therefore $\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(c_\varepsilon p+(1-c_\varepsilon )\rho )\geq \eta -\theta +\varepsilon h\geq 0$. Theorem 30.10.2 . Let $p\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, and let $\varepsilon $ and $\eta $ be as above. The transport $T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)$ of ( 30.28 ) is an ordinary model in background $\eta $, of lower volume at least $c_\varepsilon ^ n\delta $, and its volumes satisfy 30.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-transport-volume} c_\varepsilon ^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (p) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\eta (T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)) \leq c_\varepsilon ^ n\operatorname {vol}_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }(p). \end{equation} For $p,q\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, 30.30 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-comparison-error} \begin{split} & \left|d_\eta (T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p),T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(q)) -c_\varepsilon ^ n d_\theta (p,q)\right|\\ & \qquad \leq 2c_\varepsilon ^ nK \left((1+B\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{split} \end{equation} For fixed $p$, these models tend to $p$ in $L^1$ and in capacity as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Finally, suppose that two choices of the strict analytic potential $\rho $, of its rational margin $\kappa $ and of error bounds $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$ are admissible for the same backgrounds $\eta _ j$. Then the volume comparison in background $\eta _ j$ between the two transports of $p$ tends to zero. Proof. Write $c=c_\varepsilon $, $s=1-c$, $v=cp+s\rho $ and $T(p)=T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)$. Since $s\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,s(\theta -\kappa h))$, addition gives $\operatorname {vol}_{\theta -s\kappa h}(v)\geq c^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (p)$, and since $\theta -s\kappa h=\theta -\varepsilon h\leq \eta $, monotonicity gives the lower bound in ( 30.29 ) for $v$. In particular $v$ has positive lower volume in background $\eta $, so theorem 30.3.4 shows that $T(p)=P_\eta [v]$ is an ordinary model with the same two volumes as $v$. Since $\varepsilon <\kappa /2$, we have $c\geq 1/2$, and the choice of $B$ gives \[  c\widehat\theta _\varepsilon -(\theta +\varepsilon h) \geq \varepsilon (cB-1-A/\kappa )h\geq 0.  \] Since $\eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon h\leq c\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $, every competitor $w$ for $T(p)$, that is, every nonpositive $\eta $-plurisubharmonic $w\preceq v$, satisfies $w/c\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\widehat\theta _\varepsilon )$ and $w/c\preceq p$, because $\rho \leq 0$. Taking envelopes, and using that $v\leq 0$ is itself a competitor, yields 30.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-transport-bounds} cp+s\rho \leq T(p)\leq cP_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[p]. \end{equation} Volume monotonicity, together with theorem 30.3.4 in the larger background $\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $, proves the upper bound in ( 30.29 ). Now let $q\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and $m=\max (p,q)$. The same pointwise bounds give \[  cm+s\rho \leq \max (T(p),T(q)) \leq cP_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[m].  \] Consequently the upper volumes of $T(p)$, $T(q)$ and of their maximum lie between $c^ n$ times the respective upper volumes of $p$, $q$, $m$ in the backgrounds $\theta $ and $\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $. The lower volumes of $p$, $q$ and $m$ are at least $\delta $, and their upper volumes are at most $K$. By proposition 30.9.2 with $\beta =\theta $ and $\gamma =\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $, each of the three errors $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (T(x))-c^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (x)$, $x=p,q,m$ (with $T(m)$ read as $\max (T(p),T(q))$), is nonnegative and at most $c^ nK((1+B\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1)$. As in the proof of corollary 30.9.3 , this proves ( 30.30 ). For fixed $p$, corollary 30.5.4 , lemma 1.8.12 give $P_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[p]\to p$ in $L^1$ and in capacity along every decreasing sequence $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. An arbitrary sequence $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$ is handled by comparing with the decreasing sequence $\sup _{k\geq j}\varepsilon _ k$, since the envelopes increase with the background and lie above $p$. Quasi-continuity and integrability give $cp+s\rho \to p$ in both senses. The bounds ( 30.33 ) prove the asserted limits. To compare two choices along a sequence $\eta _ j$, denote their coefficients by $c_ j^{(i)}$ and their upper backgrounds by $\theta +B_ i\varepsilon _ j^{(i)}h$, $i=0,1$. Put $c_ j=\min _ i c_ j^{(i)}$ and $a_ j=\max _ i B_ i\varepsilon _ j^{(i)}$. Since the envelopes are nonpositive, both transported models lie below $c_ jP_{\theta +a_ jh}[p]$. Moreover $\eta _ j\leq c_ j(\theta +a_ jh)$, by the form inequality above for an index attaining the smaller coefficient. The upper volume of the maximum of the two transported models is therefore at most $c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta +a_ jh}(p)$, which tends to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. Each of their individual upper volumes is at least $(c_ j^{(i)})^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$ and at most the upper volume of the maximum, so it has the same limit. Hence their $d_{\eta _ j}$-comparison tends to zero. $\square$ For $p_ j,p\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, ( 30.30 ) shows that $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$ if and only if the comparisons of the transported models tend to zero along backgrounds whose errors tend to zero. The next criterion allows approximants chosen directly in those backgrounds. Theorem 30.10.3 . Let $p$ be an ordinary model of positive lower volume. Let $\varepsilon _ j$ be rational numbers with $0<\varepsilon _ j<\min (\kappa /2,1/B)$ tending to zero, let $\eta _ j$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with $\theta -\varepsilon _ jh\leq \eta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ jh$, and put $p_ j=T^\rho _{\eta _ j,\varepsilon _ j}(p)$. Then $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if there are analytic $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta _ j)$ with \[  d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The approximants may be required to be ordinary models. This condition does not depend on the choice of the strict analytic potential and of the admissible error bounds used to transport $p$. For every such analytic approximation, the convex combinations with $\rho $ of theorem 30.9.4 give analytic potentials in the original background whose ordinary envelopes converge to $p$ for $d_\theta $, in $L^1$ and in capacity. Proof. Suppose that $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. By theorem 30.8.3 , there are analytic ordinary models $r_ j$ in background $\theta $ with $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$ and a common positive lower-volume bound. The transports $a_ j=T^\rho _{\eta _ j,\varepsilon _ j}(r_ j)$ have analytic singularities: the convex coefficients are rational, and ordinary projection preserves the singularity type of an analytic potential by proposition 16.2.7 . The estimate ( 30.30 ) gives $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)\to 0$. Conversely, assume that such analytic approximants exist, and put $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. By theorem 30.10.2 , the lower volume of $p_ j$ is at least $c_{\varepsilon _ j}^ n\delta \geq 2^{-n}\delta $. The upper-volume deficit from $a_ j$ to $\max (a_ j,p_ j)$ is at most $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)$, which tends to zero. Applying lemma 30.2.1 with $b=2$ in background $\eta _ j$, and then addition, gives \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)\geq 2^{-2n}\delta  \] for all sufficiently large $j$. Put $\beta _ j=\theta +\varepsilon _ jh$. Lemma 30.10.1 , with $\beta =\eta _ j$ and $\gamma =\beta _ j$, and projection invariance in background $\beta _ j$ imply $d_{\beta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)\to 0$. Also $d_{\beta _ j}(p_ j,p)\to 0$. Indeed, ( 30.33 ) bounds $\max (p_ j,p)$ above by $c_{\varepsilon _ j}P_{\widehat\theta _{\varepsilon _ j}}[p]$, and $c_{\varepsilon _ j}\widehat\theta _{\varepsilon _ j}\geq \beta _ j$ by the form inequality in the proof of theorem 30.10.2 . Hence the upper volume of this maximum in background $\beta _ j$ is at most $c_{\varepsilon _ j}^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _{\varepsilon _ j}}(p)$, which tends to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. The upper volumes of $p_ j$ and $p$ in background $\beta _ j$ lie between $c_{\varepsilon _ j}^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$ and this bound, so they have the same limit. Project $a_ j$, $p_ j$ and $p$ to ordinary models in background $\beta _ j$. Their lower volumes have a common positive bound, and their upper volumes are bounded by $v_+(\Omega )$, since $\beta _ j\leq \Omega $. The three-point estimate ( 30.14 ) in background $\beta _ j$ therefore gives $d_{\beta _ j}(a_ j,p)\to 0$, with constants independent of $j$. Now theorem 30.9.4 , applied with the backgrounds $\beta _ j$, shows that $p$ is an ideal model and gives the stated approximation in the original background. For another choice of transport, theorem 30.10.2 shows that the two reference models in background $\eta _ j$ have volume comparison tending to zero. The lower-volume bound just proved and the same uniform three-point estimate transfer the convergence condition in both directions. This proves independence of the choice. $\square$

title: Lemma 30.10.1
text: Lemma 30.10.1 . For every $\delta >0$ there are $C_\delta >0$ and $\varepsilon _0>0$ with the following property. Let $\beta ,\gamma $ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with \[  \theta -\varepsilon h\leq \beta \leq \gamma \leq \theta +\varepsilon h, \qquad 0\leq \varepsilon \leq \varepsilon _0,  \] and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )$ satisfy $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta $. Then both singularity volumes satisfy \[  0\leq \operatorname {vol}_\gamma (u)-\operatorname {vol}_\beta (u) \leq C_\delta \varepsilon .  \] For two such potentials $u,v$, one also has \[  \left|d_\gamma (P_\gamma [u],P_\gamma [v])-d_\beta (u,v)\right| \leq 2C_\delta \varepsilon .  \] Proof. Put $\theta _0=\theta -\kappa h/2$ and $h_0=(1+\kappa /2)h$. Since $\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa h/2$, the form $\theta _0$ is big, and $\rho $ is a strict analytic potential for it with the rational margin $\kappa /(2+\kappa )$ relative to $h_0$. Let $\varepsilon \leq \min (\kappa /2,1/2)$. Then $\theta _0\leq \beta \leq \theta _0+h_0$ and $\beta \leq \gamma \leq \beta +2\varepsilon h_0$, so proposition 30.9.2 applies with $\theta _0$, $h_0$, $\rho $ and a fixed Hermitian form $\Omega _0\geq \theta _0+2h_0$ in place of $\theta $, $h$, $\rho $ and $\Omega $. These choices do not depend on $\beta $ and $\gamma $. Since the volumes in background $\beta $ are at most $v_+(\Omega _0)$, the multiplicative estimate of the proposition implies the additive estimate, with a constant $C_\delta $ independent of $\beta $, $\gamma $ and $u$. Applying it to $u$, $v$ and $\max (u,v)$, the three-error calculation in the proof of corollary 30.9.3 and projection invariance in background $\gamma $ give the second assertion. $\square$

30.28 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-model-transport} c_\varepsilon =1-\varepsilon /\kappa ,\qquad T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p) =P_\eta [c_\varepsilon p+(1-c_\varepsilon )\rho ],\qquad \widehat\theta _\varepsilon =\theta +B\varepsilon h. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 30.10.2
text: Theorem 30.10.2 . Let $p\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, and let $\varepsilon $ and $\eta $ be as above. The transport $T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)$ of ( 30.28 ) is an ordinary model in background $\eta $, of lower volume at least $c_\varepsilon ^ n\delta $, and its volumes satisfy 30.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-transport-volume} c_\varepsilon ^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (p) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\eta (T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)) \leq c_\varepsilon ^ n\operatorname {vol}_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }(p). \end{equation} For $p,q\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, 30.30 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-comparison-error} \begin{split} & \left|d_\eta (T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p),T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(q)) -c_\varepsilon ^ n d_\theta (p,q)\right|\\ & \qquad \leq 2c_\varepsilon ^ nK \left((1+B\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{split} \end{equation} For fixed $p$, these models tend to $p$ in $L^1$ and in capacity as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Finally, suppose that two choices of the strict analytic potential $\rho $, of its rational margin $\kappa $ and of error bounds $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$ are admissible for the same backgrounds $\eta _ j$. Then the volume comparison in background $\eta _ j$ between the two transports of $p$ tends to zero. Proof. Write $c=c_\varepsilon $, $s=1-c$, $v=cp+s\rho $ and $T(p)=T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)$. Since $s\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,s(\theta -\kappa h))$, addition gives $\operatorname {vol}_{\theta -s\kappa h}(v)\geq c^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (p)$, and since $\theta -s\kappa h=\theta -\varepsilon h\leq \eta $, monotonicity gives the lower bound in ( 30.29 ) for $v$. In particular $v$ has positive lower volume in background $\eta $, so theorem 30.3.4 shows that $T(p)=P_\eta [v]$ is an ordinary model with the same two volumes as $v$. Since $\varepsilon <\kappa /2$, we have $c\geq 1/2$, and the choice of $B$ gives \[  c\widehat\theta _\varepsilon -(\theta +\varepsilon h) \geq \varepsilon (cB-1-A/\kappa )h\geq 0.  \] Since $\eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon h\leq c\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $, every competitor $w$ for $T(p)$, that is, every nonpositive $\eta $-plurisubharmonic $w\preceq v$, satisfies $w/c\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\widehat\theta _\varepsilon )$ and $w/c\preceq p$, because $\rho \leq 0$. Taking envelopes, and using that $v\leq 0$ is itself a competitor, yields 30.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-transport-bounds} cp+s\rho \leq T(p)\leq cP_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[p]. \end{equation} Volume monotonicity, together with theorem 30.3.4 in the larger background $\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $, proves the upper bound in ( 30.29 ). Now let $q\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and $m=\max (p,q)$. The same pointwise bounds give \[  cm+s\rho \leq \max (T(p),T(q)) \leq cP_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[m].  \] Consequently the upper volumes of $T(p)$, $T(q)$ and of their maximum lie between $c^ n$ times the respective upper volumes of $p$, $q$, $m$ in the backgrounds $\theta $ and $\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $. The lower volumes of $p$, $q$ and $m$ are at least $\delta $, and their upper volumes are at most $K$. By proposition 30.9.2 with $\beta =\theta $ and $\gamma =\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $, each of the three errors $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (T(x))-c^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (x)$, $x=p,q,m$ (with $T(m)$ read as $\max (T(p),T(q))$), is nonnegative and at most $c^ nK((1+B\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1)$. As in the proof of corollary 30.9.3 , this proves ( 30.30 ). For fixed $p$, corollary 30.5.4 , lemma 1.8.12 give $P_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[p]\to p$ in $L^1$ and in capacity along every decreasing sequence $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. An arbitrary sequence $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$ is handled by comparing with the decreasing sequence $\sup _{k\geq j}\varepsilon _ k$, since the envelopes increase with the background and lie above $p$. Quasi-continuity and integrability give $cp+s\rho \to p$ in both senses. The bounds ( 30.33 ) prove the asserted limits. To compare two choices along a sequence $\eta _ j$, denote their coefficients by $c_ j^{(i)}$ and their upper backgrounds by $\theta +B_ i\varepsilon _ j^{(i)}h$, $i=0,1$. Put $c_ j=\min _ i c_ j^{(i)}$ and $a_ j=\max _ i B_ i\varepsilon _ j^{(i)}$. Since the envelopes are nonpositive, both transported models lie below $c_ jP_{\theta +a_ jh}[p]$. Moreover $\eta _ j\leq c_ j(\theta +a_ jh)$, by the form inequality above for an index attaining the smaller coefficient. The upper volume of the maximum of the two transported models is therefore at most $c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta +a_ jh}(p)$, which tends to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. Each of their individual upper volumes is at least $(c_ j^{(i)})^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$ and at most the upper volume of the maximum, so it has the same limit. Hence their $d_{\eta _ j}$-comparison tends to zero. $\square$

30.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-transport-volume} c_\varepsilon ^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (p) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\eta (T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)) \leq c_\varepsilon ^ n\operatorname {vol}_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }(p). \end{equation}

30.30 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-comparison-error} \begin{split} & \left|d_\eta (T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p),T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(q)) -c_\varepsilon ^ n d_\theta (p,q)\right|\\ & \qquad \leq 2c_\varepsilon ^ nK \left((1+B\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{split} \end{equation}
30.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:two-sided-transport-bounds} cp+s\rho \leq T(p)\leq cP_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[p]. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 30.10.3
text: Theorem 30.10.3 . Let $p$ be an ordinary model of positive lower volume. Let $\varepsilon _ j$ be rational numbers with $0<\varepsilon _ j<\min (\kappa /2,1/B)$ tending to zero, let $\eta _ j$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with $\theta -\varepsilon _ jh\leq \eta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ jh$, and put $p_ j=T^\rho _{\eta _ j,\varepsilon _ j}(p)$. Then $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if there are analytic $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta _ j)$ with \[  d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The approximants may be required to be ordinary models. This condition does not depend on the choice of the strict analytic potential and of the admissible error bounds used to transport $p$. For every such analytic approximation, the convex combinations with $\rho $ of theorem 30.9.4 give analytic potentials in the original background whose ordinary envelopes converge to $p$ for $d_\theta $, in $L^1$ and in capacity. Proof. Suppose that $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. By theorem 30.8.3 , there are analytic ordinary models $r_ j$ in background $\theta $ with $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$ and a common positive lower-volume bound. The transports $a_ j=T^\rho _{\eta _ j,\varepsilon _ j}(r_ j)$ have analytic singularities: the convex coefficients are rational, and ordinary projection preserves the singularity type of an analytic potential by proposition 16.2.7 . The estimate ( 30.30 ) gives $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)\to 0$. Conversely, assume that such analytic approximants exist, and put $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. By theorem 30.10.2 , the lower volume of $p_ j$ is at least $c_{\varepsilon _ j}^ n\delta \geq 2^{-n}\delta $. The upper-volume deficit from $a_ j$ to $\max (a_ j,p_ j)$ is at most $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)$, which tends to zero. Applying lemma 30.2.1 with $b=2$ in background $\eta _ j$, and then addition, gives \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)\geq 2^{-2n}\delta  \] for all sufficiently large $j$. Put $\beta _ j=\theta +\varepsilon _ jh$. Lemma 30.10.1 , with $\beta =\eta _ j$ and $\gamma =\beta _ j$, and projection invariance in background $\beta _ j$ imply $d_{\beta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)\to 0$. Also $d_{\beta _ j}(p_ j,p)\to 0$. Indeed, ( 30.33 ) bounds $\max (p_ j,p)$ above by $c_{\varepsilon _ j}P_{\widehat\theta _{\varepsilon _ j}}[p]$, and $c_{\varepsilon _ j}\widehat\theta _{\varepsilon _ j}\geq \beta _ j$ by the form inequality in the proof of theorem 30.10.2 . Hence the upper volume of this maximum in background $\beta _ j$ is at most $c_{\varepsilon _ j}^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _{\varepsilon _ j}}(p)$, which tends to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. The upper volumes of $p_ j$ and $p$ in background $\beta _ j$ lie between $c_{\varepsilon _ j}^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$ and this bound, so they have the same limit. Project $a_ j$, $p_ j$ and $p$ to ordinary models in background $\beta _ j$. Their lower volumes have a common positive bound, and their upper volumes are bounded by $v_+(\Omega )$, since $\beta _ j\leq \Omega $. The three-point estimate ( 30.14 ) in background $\beta _ j$ therefore gives $d_{\beta _ j}(a_ j,p)\to 0$, with constants independent of $j$. Now theorem 30.9.4 , applied with the backgrounds $\beta _ j$, shows that $p$ is an ideal model and gives the stated approximation in the original background. For another choice of transport, theorem 30.10.2 shows that the two reference models in background $\eta _ j$ have volume comparison tending to zero. The lower-volume bound just proved and the same uniform three-point estimate transfer the convergence condition in both directions. This proves independence of the choice. $\square$

title: 30.11 A complete metric on positive-volume models
search_title: A complete metric on positive-volume models
text: 30.11 A complete metric on positive-volume models The three-point modulus controls convergence even though $d_\theta $ need not satisfy the triangle inequality; two lines in the projective plane already show the failure. A complete metric can nevertheless be constructed from finite chains, as in the metrization of uniform structures. Continuity of the lower volume controls the chain estimates locally, and the reciprocal of the lower volume prevents Cauchy sequences from escaping to the zero-volume boundary. Example 30.11.1 . Let $\theta $ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^2$, normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^2}\theta ^2=1$. There are analytic ordinary models $p,q,r$ of positive lower volume such that \[  d_\theta (p,q)>d_\theta (p,r)+d_\theta (r,q).  \] Proof. Write $|Z|^2=|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2$ in homogeneous coordinates. Fix a rational $a\in (0,1/2)$ and put \[  u=a\log \frac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z|^2},\qquad v=a\log \frac{|Z_1|^2}{|Z|^2},\qquad w=u+v.  \] With $H_ i=\{ Z_ i=0\} $, the corresponding currents are $a[H_0]+(1-a)\theta $, $a[H_1]+(1-a)\theta $ and $a[H_0]+a[H_1]+(1-2a)\theta $. The background is closed, so each singularity volume equals the non-pluripolar mass, which is the mass of the smooth part: \[  U(u)=U(v)=(1-a)^2,\qquad U(w)=(1-2a)^2.  \] The maximum $\max (u,v)$ has the ordinary type of \[  z=a\log \frac{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2}{|Z|^2}.  \] To compute its volume, blow up the common point $[0:0:1]$ of $H_0$ and $H_1$. Denote the blowup by $\pi :Y\to \mathbb P^2$, its exceptional divisor by $E$, and the pencil map $[Z_0:Z_1]$ by $f:Y\to \mathbb P^1$. For the Fubini–Study form $\omega _1$ of mass one on $\mathbb P^1$, the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(z\circ \pi )=a[E]+\beta , \qquad \beta =(1-a)\pi ^*\theta +af^*\omega _1.  \] Here $\beta $ is smooth and semipositive. Also \[  \int _ Y(\pi ^*\theta )^2=1,\qquad \int _ Y\pi ^*\theta \wedge f^*\omega _1=1,\qquad (f^*\omega _1)^2=0.  \] The mixed integral is one because every fiber of the pencil maps onto a line. By lemma 28.7.1 and change of variables off $E$, \[  U(\max (u,v))=\int _ Y\beta ^2=1-a^2.  \] Since $w\leq u$ and $w\leq v$, ( 30.13 ) and the definition of $d_\theta $ give \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (u,v)& =4a-4a^2,\\  d_\theta (u,w)+d_\theta (w,v)& =4a-6a^2. \end{split}  \] Set $p=P_\theta [u]$, $q=P_\theta [v]$ and $r=P_\theta [w]$. By proposition 16.2.7 , these models have the same analytic singularity types as $u$, $v$ and $w$, and their lower volumes are at least $(1-2a)^2$. By projection invariance (proposition 30.6.3 ), they have the same comparisons, and the difference between the two sides is $2a^2>0$. $\square$ We return to the big background $\theta $ on the $n$-dimensional manifold $X$. Write $L(p)=\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$, and let \[  \mathcal M_+(\theta )=\bigcup _{\delta >0}\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )  \] be the space of ordinary models of positive lower volume. We keep the notation $U$ and $M$ of section 30.6 . Proposition 30.11.2 . For $p,q\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, 30.36 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-lower-volume-modulus} |L(p)-L(q)|\leq nM\min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (p,q)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} . \end{equation} If $p_ j,p\in \mathcal M_+(\theta )$ and $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$, then $L(p_ j)\to L(p)>0$. Proof. Put $s=d_\theta (p,q)$ and $m=\max (p,q)$. If $s\geq \delta /2$, the bound follows from $|L(p)-L(q)|\leq M$, and if $s=0$, then $p=q$ by proposition 30.6.3 . Suppose $0<s<\delta /2$ and take $t=(2s/\delta )^{1/n}$. The upper-volume deficit from either $p$ or $q$ to $m$ is at most $s$, while $L(m)\geq \delta $. Thus lemma 30.2.1 gives a potential $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  (1-t)m+th\leq p.  \] Volume addition and monotonicity imply $L(p)\geq (1-t)^ nL(m)\geq (1-t)^ nL(q)$, so $L(q)-L(p)\leq (1-(1-t)^ n)M\leq nMt$. Interchanging $p$ and $q$ proves the bound. For the last assertion, put $s_ j=d_\theta (p_ j,p)$. Whenever $0<s_ j<L(p)/2$, the same stretching argument applied to $\max (p_ j,p)$ gives \[  L(p_ j)\geq (1-t_ j)^ nL(p),\qquad t_ j=\left(\frac{2s_ j}{L(p)}\right)^{1/n}.  \] If $s_ j=0$, then $p_ j=p$. Hence $L(p_ j)\geq L(p)/2$ for all sufficiently large $j$, and ( 30.36 ) with $\delta =L(p)/2$ gives $L(p_ j)\to L(p)$. $\square$ Theorem 30.11.3 . There is a complete metric $\mathfrak d_\theta $ on $\mathcal M_+(\theta )$ such that 30.37 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-model-metric-convergence} \mathfrak d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} A sequence $p_ j$ is $\mathfrak d_\theta $-Cauchy if and only if it is $d_\theta $-Cauchy and the sequence $1/L(p_ j)$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb R$. On each $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, the metric $\mathfrak d_\theta $ and the comparison $d_\theta $ define the same uniform structure, and the restriction of $\mathfrak d_\theta $ is complete. Proof. Step 1: a decreasing family of symmetric relations. Set $C=1+M$ and $m(p)=L(p)/C$, so that $0<m(p)<1$. Put $a_1=1$, $a_{k+1}=na_ k+1$, and choose $0<\varepsilon _1<1$. Recursively choose $\varepsilon _{k+1}>0$ so small that, with $r_ k=4^{a_{k+1}}\varepsilon _{k+1}$, \[  3\varepsilon _{k+1}<\varepsilon _ k,\qquad 3r_ k+4nM\left(\frac{2r_ k}{C}\right)^{1/n}<\varepsilon _ k.  \] Let $\mathcal U_0=\mathcal M_+(\theta )^2$ and, for $k\geq 1$, set \[  \mathcal U_ k=\left\{ (p,q): \left|\frac1{m(p)}-\frac1{m(q)}\right|<\varepsilon _ k, \quad d_\theta (p,q)<\varepsilon _ k\min \{ m(p),m(q)\} ^{a_ k}\right\} .  \] These symmetric sets contain the diagonal and decrease with $k$, and their intersection is the diagonal by proposition 30.6.3 . We claim that 30.38 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-metric-triple-composition} \mathcal U_{k+1}\circ \mathcal U_{k+1}\circ \mathcal U_{k+1} \subset \mathcal U_ k\qquad (k\geq 0), \end{equation} where composition of relations means joining successive pairs. For $k=0$ this is immediate. For $k\geq 1$, suppose $(p_{i-1},p_ i)\in \mathcal U_{k+1}$ for $i=1,2,3$, and put $m_*=\min _{0\leq i\leq 3}m(p_ i)$. The reciprocal differences along this chain have total less than $3\varepsilon _{k+1}<1$, so $1/m(p_ i)>1/m_*-1$. Hence $m(p_ i)\leq 4m_*$ for every $i$: if $m_*\leq 3/4$, this follows from $1/m_*-1\geq 1/(4m_*)$, and otherwise from $m(p_ i)<1$. Each successive comparison is therefore less than \[  e=r_ k m_*^{a_{k+1}}.  \] All four models have lower volume at least $Cm_*$. Applying ( 30.14 ) with $\delta =Cm_*$ twice, first with middle point $p_2$ and then with middle point $p_1$, yields \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (p_0,p_3) & \leq 3e+4nM\left(\frac{2e}{Cm_*}\right)^{1/n}\\ & \leq \left(3r_ k+4nM\left(\frac{2r_ k}{C}\right)^{1/n}\right)m_*^{a_ k}\\ & <\varepsilon _ k\min \{ m(p_0),m(p_3)\} ^{a_ k}. \end{split}  \] Here $(a_{k+1}-1)/n=a_ k$, $a_{k+1}\geq a_ k$ and $m_*<1$. The endpoint reciprocal difference is less than $3\varepsilon _{k+1}<\varepsilon _ k$, proving ( 30.38 ). Step 2: the chain metric. Define 30.42 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-model-chain-metric} \mathfrak d_\theta (p,q)=\inf \sum _{i=1}^ N2^{-k_ i}, \end{equation} where the infimum runs over finite chains $p=p_0,p_1,\ldots ,p_ N=q$ and integers $k_ i\geq 0$ with $(p_{i-1},p_ i)\in \mathcal U_{k_ i}$; we call $\sum _ i2^{-k_ i}$ the cost of the chain. A single edge in $\mathcal U_0$ gives $\mathfrak d_\theta \leq 1$. Reversing and concatenating chains gives symmetry and the triangle inequality, while diagonal edges with arbitrarily large indices give $\mathfrak d_\theta (p,p)=0$. We next prove the inclusions 30.43 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-chain-entourage-bounds} \{ \mathfrak d_\theta <2^{-(k+1)}\}  \subset \mathcal U_ k\subset \{ \mathfrak d_\theta \leq 2^{-k}\}  \qquad (k\geq 1). \end{equation} The second inclusion follows by using a single edge. For the first, we prove by induction on the number of edges that every chain of cost less than $2^{-k}$ has its endpoints in $\mathcal U_{k-1}$, simultaneously for all $k\geq 1$. For one edge this follows because the $\mathcal U_ k$ decrease. For a chain of cost $A<2^{-k}$, choose $l\geq k$ with \[  2^{-(l+1)}\leq A<2^{-l}.  \] Split the chain at the first edge at which the cumulative cost reaches $2^{-(l+1)}$. The subchains before and after this edge both have cost less than $2^{-(l+1)}$, so by induction their endpoint pairs lie in $\mathcal U_ l$; an empty subchain is interpreted as a diagonal pair. Every edge cost is a power of two smaller than $2^{-l}$, so the middle edge lies in $\mathcal U_{l+1}\subset \mathcal U_ l$. By ( 30.38 ), the endpoints of the whole chain form a pair in $\mathcal U_{l-1}\subset \mathcal U_{k-1}$. This completes the induction and proves ( 30.43 ). Since the $\mathcal U_ k$ intersect in the diagonal, $\mathfrak d_\theta $ separates points, so it is a metric. Step 3: convergence and completeness. By ( 30.43 ), $\mathfrak d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$ if and only if $(p_ j,p)$ eventually lies in every $\mathcal U_ k$. This implies $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$. Conversely, if $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$, then proposition 30.11.2 gives $L(p_ j)\to L(p)>0$, so for each fixed $k$ both inequalities defining $\mathcal U_ k$ hold eventually. This proves ( 30.37 ). The same inclusions show that a $\mathfrak d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence is $d_\theta $-Cauchy and has Cauchy reciprocal lower volumes. These reciprocals are bounded, so a tail of the sequence lies in some $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$. By theorem 30.6.5 , the sequence converges there for $d_\theta $, and hence for $\mathfrak d_\theta $. This proves completeness. Conversely, a $d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence with Cauchy reciprocal lower volumes has a common positive lower-volume bound on a tail, and then both inequalities defining each $\mathcal U_ k$ hold for all pairs of sufficiently late terms. This proves the Cauchy criterion. On $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, ( 30.36 ) controls the reciprocal differences uniformly in terms of $d_\theta $, while $m(p)\geq \delta /C$ controls the second threshold in $\mathcal U_ k$. Thus $\mathfrak d_\theta $ and $d_\theta $ define the same uniform structure there. Continuity of the lower volume makes $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ closed for $\mathfrak d_\theta $, so the restriction of $\mathfrak d_\theta $ to it is complete. $\square$ Corollary 30.11.4 . The ideal models in $\mathcal M_+(\theta )$ form a closed, hence complete, subspace of $(\mathcal M_+(\theta ),\mathfrak d_\theta )$, and the analytic ordinary models of positive lower volume are dense in it. Equivalently, this subspace is the metric completion of the analytic ordinary models of positive lower volume with the restricted metric. Proof. By theorem 30.8.4 , an ordinary model of positive lower volume that is a $d_\theta $-limit of ideal models is again an ideal model. The same theorem, which relies on theorem 30.8.3 , gives the density of analytic models. Now apply ( 30.37 ) and the completeness of $\mathfrak d_\theta $. $\square$

By proposition 16.2.7 , these models have the same analytic singularity types as $u$, $v$ and $w$, and their lower volumes are at least $(1-2a)^2$.
