title: Proposition 30.11.2
text: Proposition 30.11.2 . For $p,q\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, 30.36 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-lower-volume-modulus} |L(p)-L(q)|\leq nM\min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (p,q)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} . \end{equation} If $p_ j,p\in \mathcal M_+(\theta )$ and $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$, then $L(p_ j)\to L(p)>0$. Proof. Put $s=d_\theta (p,q)$ and $m=\max (p,q)$. If $s\geq \delta /2$, the bound follows from $|L(p)-L(q)|\leq M$, and if $s=0$, then $p=q$ by proposition 30.6.3 . Suppose $0<s<\delta /2$ and take $t=(2s/\delta )^{1/n}$. The upper-volume deficit from either $p$ or $q$ to $m$ is at most $s$, while $L(m)\geq \delta $. Thus lemma 30.2.1 gives a potential $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  (1-t)m+th\leq p.  \] Volume addition and monotonicity imply $L(p)\geq (1-t)^ nL(m)\geq (1-t)^ nL(q)$, so $L(q)-L(p)\leq (1-(1-t)^ n)M\leq nMt$. Interchanging $p$ and $q$ proves the bound. For the last assertion, put $s_ j=d_\theta (p_ j,p)$. Whenever $0<s_ j<L(p)/2$, the same stretching argument applied to $\max (p_ j,p)$ gives \[  L(p_ j)\geq (1-t_ j)^ nL(p),\qquad t_ j=\left(\frac{2s_ j}{L(p)}\right)^{1/n}.  \] If $s_ j=0$, then $p_ j=p$. Hence $L(p_ j)\geq L(p)/2$ for all sufficiently large $j$, and ( 30.36 ) with $\delta =L(p)/2$ gives $L(p_ j)\to L(p)$. $\square$
30.36 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-lower-volume-modulus} |L(p)-L(q)|\leq nM\min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (p,q)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} . \end{equation}

title: Theorem 30.11.3
text: Theorem 30.11.3 . There is a complete metric $\mathfrak d_\theta $ on $\mathcal M_+(\theta )$ such that 30.37 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-model-metric-convergence} \mathfrak d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} A sequence $p_ j$ is $\mathfrak d_\theta $-Cauchy if and only if it is $d_\theta $-Cauchy and the sequence $1/L(p_ j)$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb R$. On each $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, the metric $\mathfrak d_\theta $ and the comparison $d_\theta $ define the same uniform structure, and the restriction of $\mathfrak d_\theta $ is complete. Proof. Step 1: a decreasing family of symmetric relations. Set $C=1+M$ and $m(p)=L(p)/C$, so that $0<m(p)<1$. Put $a_1=1$, $a_{k+1}=na_ k+1$, and choose $0<\varepsilon _1<1$. Recursively choose $\varepsilon _{k+1}>0$ so small that, with $r_ k=4^{a_{k+1}}\varepsilon _{k+1}$, \[  3\varepsilon _{k+1}<\varepsilon _ k,\qquad 3r_ k+4nM\left(\frac{2r_ k}{C}\right)^{1/n}<\varepsilon _ k.  \] Let $\mathcal U_0=\mathcal M_+(\theta )^2$ and, for $k\geq 1$, set \[  \mathcal U_ k=\left\{ (p,q): \left|\frac1{m(p)}-\frac1{m(q)}\right|<\varepsilon _ k, \quad d_\theta (p,q)<\varepsilon _ k\min \{ m(p),m(q)\} ^{a_ k}\right\} .  \] These symmetric sets contain the diagonal and decrease with $k$, and their intersection is the diagonal by proposition 30.6.3 . We claim that 30.38 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-metric-triple-composition} \mathcal U_{k+1}\circ \mathcal U_{k+1}\circ \mathcal U_{k+1} \subset \mathcal U_ k\qquad (k\geq 0), \end{equation} where composition of relations means joining successive pairs. For $k=0$ this is immediate. For $k\geq 1$, suppose $(p_{i-1},p_ i)\in \mathcal U_{k+1}$ for $i=1,2,3$, and put $m_*=\min _{0\leq i\leq 3}m(p_ i)$. The reciprocal differences along this chain have total less than $3\varepsilon _{k+1}<1$, so $1/m(p_ i)>1/m_*-1$. Hence $m(p_ i)\leq 4m_*$ for every $i$: if $m_*\leq 3/4$, this follows from $1/m_*-1\geq 1/(4m_*)$, and otherwise from $m(p_ i)<1$. Each successive comparison is therefore less than \[  e=r_ k m_*^{a_{k+1}}.  \] All four models have lower volume at least $Cm_*$. Applying ( 30.14 ) with $\delta =Cm_*$ twice, first with middle point $p_2$ and then with middle point $p_1$, yields \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (p_0,p_3) & \leq 3e+4nM\left(\frac{2e}{Cm_*}\right)^{1/n}\\ & \leq \left(3r_ k+4nM\left(\frac{2r_ k}{C}\right)^{1/n}\right)m_*^{a_ k}\\ & <\varepsilon _ k\min \{ m(p_0),m(p_3)\} ^{a_ k}. \end{split}  \] Here $(a_{k+1}-1)/n=a_ k$, $a_{k+1}\geq a_ k$ and $m_*<1$. The endpoint reciprocal difference is less than $3\varepsilon _{k+1}<\varepsilon _ k$, proving ( 30.38 ). Step 2: the chain metric. Define 30.42 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-model-chain-metric} \mathfrak d_\theta (p,q)=\inf \sum _{i=1}^ N2^{-k_ i}, \end{equation} where the infimum runs over finite chains $p=p_0,p_1,\ldots ,p_ N=q$ and integers $k_ i\geq 0$ with $(p_{i-1},p_ i)\in \mathcal U_{k_ i}$; we call $\sum _ i2^{-k_ i}$ the cost of the chain. A single edge in $\mathcal U_0$ gives $\mathfrak d_\theta \leq 1$. Reversing and concatenating chains gives symmetry and the triangle inequality, while diagonal edges with arbitrarily large indices give $\mathfrak d_\theta (p,p)=0$. We next prove the inclusions 30.43 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-chain-entourage-bounds} \{ \mathfrak d_\theta <2^{-(k+1)}\}  \subset \mathcal U_ k\subset \{ \mathfrak d_\theta \leq 2^{-k}\}  \qquad (k\geq 1). \end{equation} The second inclusion follows by using a single edge. For the first, we prove by induction on the number of edges that every chain of cost less than $2^{-k}$ has its endpoints in $\mathcal U_{k-1}$, simultaneously for all $k\geq 1$. For one edge this follows because the $\mathcal U_ k$ decrease. For a chain of cost $A<2^{-k}$, choose $l\geq k$ with \[  2^{-(l+1)}\leq A<2^{-l}.  \] Split the chain at the first edge at which the cumulative cost reaches $2^{-(l+1)}$. The subchains before and after this edge both have cost less than $2^{-(l+1)}$, so by induction their endpoint pairs lie in $\mathcal U_ l$; an empty subchain is interpreted as a diagonal pair. Every edge cost is a power of two smaller than $2^{-l}$, so the middle edge lies in $\mathcal U_{l+1}\subset \mathcal U_ l$. By ( 30.38 ), the endpoints of the whole chain form a pair in $\mathcal U_{l-1}\subset \mathcal U_{k-1}$. This completes the induction and proves ( 30.43 ). Since the $\mathcal U_ k$ intersect in the diagonal, $\mathfrak d_\theta $ separates points, so it is a metric. Step 3: convergence and completeness. By ( 30.43 ), $\mathfrak d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$ if and only if $(p_ j,p)$ eventually lies in every $\mathcal U_ k$. This implies $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$. Conversely, if $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$, then proposition 30.11.2 gives $L(p_ j)\to L(p)>0$, so for each fixed $k$ both inequalities defining $\mathcal U_ k$ hold eventually. This proves ( 30.37 ). The same inclusions show that a $\mathfrak d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence is $d_\theta $-Cauchy and has Cauchy reciprocal lower volumes. These reciprocals are bounded, so a tail of the sequence lies in some $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$. By theorem 30.6.5 , the sequence converges there for $d_\theta $, and hence for $\mathfrak d_\theta $. This proves completeness. Conversely, a $d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence with Cauchy reciprocal lower volumes has a common positive lower-volume bound on a tail, and then both inequalities defining each $\mathcal U_ k$ hold for all pairs of sufficiently late terms. This proves the Cauchy criterion. On $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, ( 30.36 ) controls the reciprocal differences uniformly in terms of $d_\theta $, while $m(p)\geq \delta /C$ controls the second threshold in $\mathcal U_ k$. Thus $\mathfrak d_\theta $ and $d_\theta $ define the same uniform structure there. Continuity of the lower volume makes $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ closed for $\mathfrak d_\theta $, so the restriction of $\mathfrak d_\theta $ to it is complete. $\square$
30.37 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-model-metric-convergence} \mathfrak d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation}
30.38 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-metric-triple-composition} \mathcal U_{k+1}\circ \mathcal U_{k+1}\circ \mathcal U_{k+1} \subset \mathcal U_ k\qquad (k\geq 0), \end{equation}
30.42 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-model-chain-metric} \mathfrak d_\theta (p,q)=\inf \sum _{i=1}^ N2^{-k_ i}, \end{equation}
30.43 \begin{equation} \label{eq:model-chain-entourage-bounds} \{ \mathfrak d_\theta <2^{-(k+1)}\}  \subset \mathcal U_ k\subset \{ \mathfrak d_\theta \leq 2^{-k}\}  \qquad (k\geq 1). \end{equation}

title: Corollary 30.11.4
text: Corollary 30.11.4 . The ideal models in $\mathcal M_+(\theta )$ form a closed, hence complete, subspace of $(\mathcal M_+(\theta ),\mathfrak d_\theta )$, and the analytic ordinary models of positive lower volume are dense in it. Equivalently, this subspace is the metric completion of the analytic ordinary models of positive lower volume with the restricted metric. Proof. By theorem 30.8.4 , an ordinary model of positive lower volume that is a $d_\theta $-limit of ideal models is again an ideal model. The same theorem, which relies on theorem 30.8.3 , gives the density of analytic models. Now apply ( 30.37 ) and the completeness of $\mathfrak d_\theta $. $\square$

title: 30.12 Model potentials on curves
text:
30.12 Model potentials on curves On a curve the preceding theory becomes explicit. The part of the curvature current carried by the pole set determines the ordinary envelope, and its atomic part determines the ideal envelope. Comparing these two measures describes both the zero-volume boundary and the failure of analytic approximation for diffuse polar singularities. Total variation of the polar measures keeps this singularity data and at the same time controls convergence of the model potentials in capacity. In this section, $Y$ is a compact connected Riemann surface, $	heta $ is a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form on $Y$, and $A=\int _ Y	heta $. By Stokes' theorem every bounded $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function has mass $A$; thus $Y$ has the bounded mass property, $	heta $ is big, and the preceding results apply with $Y$ in place of $X$. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$ write $T_ u=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and let $\mu _ u=\mathbf1_{\{ u=-\infty \} }T_ u=T_ u^{\mathrm{pol}}$ be the polar curvature of $u$ (section 1.6.1 ); in this and the following sections, $\mu _ u$ no longer denotes $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)$. A positive measure carried by a polar set will be called a polar measure. Since $	heta $ is closed, the two singularity volumes of $u$ coincide with \[  U(u)=\int _ Y\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=A-\mu _ u(Y).  \] Fix a nonpositive Green kernel $G$ for $\eta =	heta /A$, as in section 19.3 , so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ xG(x,y)=\delta _ y-\eta $, where $\delta _ y$ is the Dirac measure at $y$. We write $\| \cdot \| _{\mathrm{TV}}$ for the total variation norm of finite signed measures. Lemma 30.12.1 . For a polar measure $\mu $ on $Y$ with $\mu (Y)\leq A$, put \[  w_\mu (x)=\int _ YG(x,y)\, \mathrm{d}\mu (y),\qquad p_\mu =P_	heta [w_\mu ].  \] Then $p_\mu \sim w_\mu $, $\mu _{p_\mu }=\mu $ and $U(p_\mu )=A-\mu (Y)$. Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$ satisfies 30.44  egin{equation} \label{eq:curve-polar-envelope} P_	heta [u]=p_{\mu _ u}. \end{equation} Consequently $\mu \mapsto p_\mu $ is a bijection from the polar measures of mass at most $A$ onto the set of all ordinary models on $Y$. Proof. The bounds for the Green kernel give $w_\mu \in L^1(Y)$ and \[  T_{w_\mu }=\mu +(A-\mu (Y))\eta .  \] In particular $w_\mu $ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic, and its polar curvature is $\mu $. We claim that, for every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$, 30.45  egin{equation} \label{eq:curve-polar-domination} v\preceq w_\mu \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad T_ v\geq \mu . \end{equation} The forward implication follows from corollary 1.6.8 , which gives $T_ v\geq \mu _ v\geq \mu _{w_\mu }=\mu $. Conversely, if $T_ v\geq \mu $, the distribution $v-w_\mu $ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v-w_\mu )\geq -(A-\mu (Y))\eta $, so its quasi-subharmonic representative is bounded above on the compact curve $Y$. By lemma 1.3.3 , $v\preceq w_\mu $. Thus $p_\mu $ is the upper envelope of all $v\leq 0$ with $T_ v\geq \mu $. This family is closed under maxima by ( 1.14 ). By Choquet's lemma the envelope is the limit of an increasing sequence of such maxima, which converges in $L^1$; hence the current inequality $T_{p_\mu }\geq \mu $ passes to the limit. Also $p_\mu \geq w_\mu -\sup _ Yw_\mu $. Hence $b=p_\mu -w_\mu $ has a quasi-subharmonic representative that is bounded below, and compactness bounds it above. Therefore $p_\mu \sim w_\mu $. The positive measure \[  T_{p_\mu }-\mu =(A-\mu (Y))\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b  \] charges no polar set because $b$ is bounded. This proves $\mu _{p_\mu }=\mu $ and $U(p_\mu )=A-\mu (Y)$, and ordinary equivalence gives $P_	heta [p_\mu ]=P_	heta [w_\mu ]=p_\mu $. For arbitrary $u$, take $\mu =\mu _ u$. Then $T_ u\geq \mu $, so ( 30.45 ) gives $u\preceq p_\mu $, and $U(u)=A-\mu (Y)=U(p_\mu )$. If this mass is positive, corollary 30.3.6 gives ( 30.44 ). If it is zero, then $\mu (Y)=A$ and $T_ u=\mu =T_{w_\mu }$. The difference $u-w_\mu $ is then harmonic on $Y$ and hence constant, which gives the same conclusion. Finally, every ordinary model $p$ equals $P_	heta [p]=p_{\mu _ p}$, and distinct polar measures give distinct models because $\mu _{p_\mu }=\mu $. $\square$ Theorem 30.12.2 . For every $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$, 30.46  egin{equation} \label{eq:curve-model-volume-distance} d_	heta (u,v)=\| \mu _ u-\mu _ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} In particular, $d_	heta $ is a metric on the set of ordinary models on $Y$. For positive atomic measures $D,E$ of mass at most $A$, let $q_ D,q_ E$ be the ideal models of lemma 19.5.2 , with polar curvatures $D$ and $E$. Then 30.47  egin{equation} \label{eq:curve-ideal-volume-distance} d_	heta (q_ D,q_ E)=\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Proof. By ( 1.14 ), the polar curvature of $\max (u,v)$ is the minimum $\mu _ u\wedge \mu _ v$ of the two measures. The formula $U=A-\mu (Y)$ therefore gives \[   egin{split}  d_	heta (u,v)& =2U(\max (u,v))-U(u)-U(v)\ & =\mu _ u(Y)+\mu _ v(Y)-2(\mu _ u\wedge \mu _ v)(Y)\ & =\| \mu _ u-\mu _ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{split}  \] The classification in lemma 30.12.1 shows that $d_	heta $ separates ordinary models, and the triangle inequality follows from that of the total variation norm. By lemma 19.5.2 , the ideal models are exactly the models whose polar measures are atomic, which gives ( 30.47 ). $\square$ Corollary 30.12.3 . The ordinary models on $Y$ form a complete geodesic metric space for $d_	heta $. The ideal models form a closed geodesically convex subspace, which is the metric completion of the analytic ordinary models of positive mass. Proof. By lemma 30.12.1 , theorem 30.12.2 , the space of ordinary models is isometric to the set of polar measures of mass at most $A$ with the total variation norm. This set is closed in total variation: a limit is positive, satisfies the mass bound, and is carried by the countable union of polar carriers of the sequence. Completeness therefore follows from that of finite signed measures. For two such measures $\mu ,
u $, the measures $\mu _ t=(1-t)\mu +t
u $, $0\leq t\leq 1$, remain in this set and satisfy \[  \| \mu _ t-\mu _ s\| _{\mathrm{TV}}=|t-s|\, \| \mu -
u \| _{\mathrm{TV}}.  \] Their models give a constant-speed geodesic. The atomic measures form a closed convex subset, since a total-variation limit is carried by the countable union of the sets of atoms of the sequence. Restricting to finitely many atoms and approximating the coefficients from below by rational numbers, with an arbitrarily small further decrease if needed, approximates every such measure by finite atomic measures with rational coefficients and mass strictly less than $A$. Their models have analytic singularities by lemma 19.5.2 , and ( 30.47 ) gives the density. $\square$ The models of positive mass do not form a complete space for $d_	heta $: for a fixed $x\in Y$, the models of $tA\delta _ x$ form a Cauchy family as $t\uparrow 1$, with a limit of zero mass. For the complete metric of theorem 30.11.3 , this family is not Cauchy, because its reciprocal lower volumes diverge. The two metrics induce the same topology on models of positive mass but have different Cauchy sequences near the boundary. The metric $d_	heta $ also controls convergence of the potentials at the zero-mass boundary. There the polar part exhausts the limiting curvature current, so its total variation controls the whole current. Theorem 30.12.4 . Let $p_ j,p$ be ordinary models on $Y$. If $d_	heta (p_ j,p)	o 0$, then $p_ j	o p$ in $L^1$ and in capacity. If $U(p)=0$, then in addition 30.51  egin{equation} \label{eq:curve-zero-mass-current-variation} \| T_{p_ j}-T_ p\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2d_	heta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Proof. Write $\mu _ j=\mu _{p_ j}$ and $\mu =\mu _ p$. By ( 30.46 ), $\mu _ j	o \mu $ in total variation. Thus $U(p_ j)=A-\mu _ j(Y)	o U(p)$. If $U(p)>0$, the models lie in a common $\mathcal M_\delta (	heta )$ for all large $j$, and proposition 30.6.3 , theorem 30.7.3 apply. Suppose that $U(p)=0$. Then $T_ p=\mu $ and $\mu (Y)=A$, while $T_{p_ j}-\mu _ j$ is a positive measure of mass $A-\mu _ j(Y)=\mu (Y)-\mu _ j(Y)$. Consequently \[  \| T_{p_ j}-T_ p\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \| \mu _ j-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}+A-\mu _ j(Y) \leq 2\| \mu _ j-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}},  \] which proves ( 30.51 ). By normalized compactness, each subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $L^1$ to a function $q$ with supremum zero. Then $T_{p_ j}	o T_ q$ weakly, so $T_ q=T_ p$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q-p)=0$. Hence $q-p$ is constant, and the normalization gives $q=p$. This proves $L^1$ convergence of the whole sequence. Finally, apply lemma 1.6.6 on finitely many nested coordinate disks: both terms on its right-hand side tend to zero, and the comparison between local and global capacities in section 1.8 gives convergence in capacity. $\square$ For potentials with supremum zero, weak convergence $T_{p_ j}ightharpoonup T_ p$ is equivalent to $p_ j	o p$ in $L^1$, by theorem 5.1.1 and normalized compactness. It need not imply convergence in capacity, even when the sequence and the limit are ideal models. Indeed, scaling the area-one construction in theorem 16.4.2 gives zero-mass ideal models converging to zero in $L^1$. Convergence in capacity would contradict theorem 7.3.1 , since their damped measures vanish while the limiting measure is $	heta $. Conversely, convergence in capacity does not imply convergence of the polar parts in total variation. Moving a single pole gives an example, even within the zero-mass boundary. Example 30.12.5 . On $\mathbb P^1$ with the Fubini–Study form $	heta $ of area one, there are zero-mass ideal models $p_ j,p$ with $p_ j	o p$ in capacity but $d_	heta (p_ j,p)=2$ for every $j$. Proof. In the affine coordinate $z$, where $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$, put for $a\in \mathbb C$ \[  p_ a(z)=\log  rac{|z-a|^2}{(1+|z|^2)(1+|a|^2)}.  \] This function extends to $\mathbb P^1$, has supremum zero by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and satisfies $T_{p_ a}=\delta _ a$. Hence it is the ideal model with polar measure $\delta _ a$, by lemma 19.5.2 . Choose $a_ j
e 0$ tending to zero and set $p_ j=p_{a_ j}$, $p=p_0$. On the complement of any fixed disk about zero the convergence is uniform, including near infinity. Small disks about zero lie in sublevel sets $\{ p_0<-t\} $ with $t$ large, so their capacities tend to zero as the radius tends to zero, by ( 1.26 ). Therefore $p_ j	o p$ in capacity. Since $\| \delta _{a_ j}-\delta _0\| _{\mathrm{TV}}=2$, ( 30.46 ) gives the asserted distance. $\square$ Return to the general curve $Y$. Write $\mu _ u=D_ u+\sigma _ u$, where $D_ u=\sum _{x\in Y}
u (u,x)\delta _ x$ is the atomic part and $\sigma _ u$ has no atoms. Set $	au (u)=\sigma _ u(Y)=A-U(u)-D_ u(Y)$, the diffuse polar mass of $u$, and let $\mathcal A_+(Y,	heta )$ denote the set of analytic ordinary models of positive mass. Proposition 30.12.6 . For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$, 30.52  egin{equation} \label{eq:curve-analytic-distance-defect} \inf _{a\in \mathcal A_+(Y,	heta )}d_	heta (u,a) =d_	heta (u,P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I})=	au (u). \end{equation} On ordinary models, $p\mapsto P_	heta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ is a $1$-Lipschitz retraction onto the ideal models, and $P_	heta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ is the unique ideal model nearest to $p$. There are $a_ j\in \mathcal A_+(Y,	heta )$ with $d_	heta (u,a_ j)	o 0$ if and only if $P_	heta [u]=P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. Proof. The ideal envelope of $u$ is $q_{D_ u}$, by lemma 19.5.2 . For any positive atomic measure $E$ of mass at most $A$, the nonatomic measure $\sigma _ u$ and the signed atomic measure $D_ u-E$ are mutually singular. Thus ( 30.46 ) gives 30.53  egin{equation} \label{eq:curve-finite-analytic-comparison} d_	heta (u,q_ E)=	au (u)+\| D_ u-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Among ideal models, the minimum is attained exactly at $E=D_ u$. Since the analytic models of positive mass are dense among the ideal models (corollary 30.12.3 ), this gives ( 30.52 ). Taking the atomic part does not increase total variation, which proves the Lipschitz assertion. Finally, lemma 30.12.1 shows that $P_	heta [u]=p_{\mu _ u}$ equals $q_{D_ u}=p_{D_ u}$ if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$, that is, $	au (u)=0$. $\square$ Example 30.12.7 . There is an ordinary model $p$ on $Y$ with zero mass whose multiplier ideals $\mathcal I(tp)$ are trivial for every $t>0$. It satisfies \[  P_	heta [p]_{\mathcal I}=0,\qquad \inf _{a\in \mathcal A_+(Y,	heta )}d_	heta (p,a)=A.  \] Proof. Choose a compact real interval inside a coordinate disk. Construct a binary Cantor set $K$ in it: at level $k$ there are $2^ k$ pairwise disjoint intervals of length $r_ k=\exp (-4^{k+1})$, each containing its two children of level $k+1$, and $K$ is the intersection of the unions over all levels. Let $\sigma $ be the probability measure on $K$ assigning mass $2^{-k}$ to each interval of level $k$. It has no atoms. Put $u(x)=A\int _ YG(x,y)\, \mathrm{d}\sigma (y)$, so that $T_ u=A\sigma $. On the chosen compact coordinate disk, $G(x,y)\leq \log |x-y|^2+C$ for a fixed constant $C$. For $x\in K$, integrating over the interval of level $k$ containing $x$, and using $G\leq 0$ elsewhere, gives \[  u(x)\leq A2^{-k}(2\log r_ k+C)\longrightarrow -\infty .  \] Thus $u=-\infty $ on $K$, while $u$ is smooth off $K$, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=-	heta $ there. Hence $K$ is polar, $\mu _ u=A\sigma $ and $U(u)=0$. By lemma 30.12.1 , $p=P_	heta [u]$ has the same polar curvature. Since this measure already has mass $A$, we get $T_ p=T_ u$, and therefore $p=u-\sup _ Yu$. The Lelong numbers of $p$ vanish because $\sigma $ has no atoms, so all its multiplier ideals are trivial and its ideal envelope is zero. Finally $	au (p)=A$, which gives the distance by ( 30.52 ). $\square$

title: Lemma 30.12.1
text: Lemma 30.12.1 . For a polar measure $\mu $ on $Y$ with $\mu (Y)\leq A$, put \[  w_\mu (x)=\int _ YG(x,y)\, \mathrm{d}\mu (y),\qquad p_\mu =P_\theta [w_\mu ].  \] Then $p_\mu \sim w_\mu $, $\mu _{p_\mu }=\mu $ and $U(p_\mu )=A-\mu (Y)$. Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ satisfies 30.44 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-polar-envelope} P_\theta [u]=p_{\mu _ u}. \end{equation} Consequently $\mu \mapsto p_\mu $ is a bijection from the polar measures of mass at most $A$ onto the set of all ordinary models on $Y$. Proof. The bounds for the Green kernel give $w_\mu \in L^1(Y)$ and \[  T_{w_\mu }=\mu +(A-\mu (Y))\eta .  \] In particular $w_\mu $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and its polar curvature is $\mu $. We claim that, for every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$, 30.45 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-polar-domination} v\preceq w_\mu \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad T_ v\geq \mu . \end{equation} The forward implication follows from corollary 1.6.8 , which gives $T_ v\geq \mu _ v\geq \mu _{w_\mu }=\mu $. Conversely, if $T_ v\geq \mu $, the distribution $v-w_\mu $ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v-w_\mu )\geq -(A-\mu (Y))\eta $, so its quasi-subharmonic representative is bounded above on the compact curve $Y$. By lemma 1.3.3 , $v\preceq w_\mu $. Thus $p_\mu $ is the upper envelope of all $v\leq 0$ with $T_ v\geq \mu $. This family is closed under maxima by ( 1.14 ). By Choquet's lemma the envelope is the limit of an increasing sequence of such maxima, which converges in $L^1$; hence the current inequality $T_{p_\mu }\geq \mu $ passes to the limit. Also $p_\mu \geq w_\mu -\sup _ Yw_\mu $. Hence $b=p_\mu -w_\mu $ has a quasi-subharmonic representative that is bounded below, and compactness bounds it above. Therefore $p_\mu \sim w_\mu $. The positive measure \[  T_{p_\mu }-\mu =(A-\mu (Y))\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b  \] charges no polar set because $b$ is bounded. This proves $\mu _{p_\mu }=\mu $ and $U(p_\mu )=A-\mu (Y)$, and ordinary equivalence gives $P_\theta [p_\mu ]=P_\theta [w_\mu ]=p_\mu $. For arbitrary $u$, take $\mu =\mu _ u$. Then $T_ u\geq \mu $, so ( 30.45 ) gives $u\preceq p_\mu $, and $U(u)=A-\mu (Y)=U(p_\mu )$. If this mass is positive, corollary 30.3.6 gives ( 30.44 ). If it is zero, then $\mu (Y)=A$ and $T_ u=\mu =T_{w_\mu }$. The difference $u-w_\mu $ is then harmonic on $Y$ and hence constant, which gives the same conclusion. Finally, every ordinary model $p$ equals $P_\theta [p]=p_{\mu _ p}$, and distinct polar measures give distinct models because $\mu _{p_\mu }=\mu $. $\square$
30.44 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-polar-envelope} P_\theta [u]=p_{\mu _ u}. \end{equation}
30.45 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-polar-domination} v\preceq w_\mu \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad T_ v\geq \mu . \end{equation}

title: Theorem 30.12.2
text: Theorem 30.12.2 . For every $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$, 30.46 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-model-volume-distance} d_\theta (u,v)=\| \mu _ u-\mu _ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} In particular, $d_\theta $ is a metric on the set of ordinary models on $Y$. For positive atomic measures $D,E$ of mass at most $A$, let $q_ D,q_ E$ be the ideal models of lemma 19.5.2 , with polar curvatures $D$ and $E$. Then 30.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-ideal-volume-distance} d_\theta (q_ D,q_ E)=\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Proof. By ( 1.14 ), the polar curvature of $\max (u,v)$ is the minimum $\mu _ u\wedge \mu _ v$ of the two measures. The formula $U=A-\mu (Y)$ therefore gives \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (u,v)& =2U(\max (u,v))-U(u)-U(v)\\ & =\mu _ u(Y)+\mu _ v(Y)-2(\mu _ u\wedge \mu _ v)(Y)\\ & =\| \mu _ u-\mu _ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{split}  \] The classification in lemma 30.12.1 shows that $d_\theta $ separates ordinary models, and the triangle inequality follows from that of the total variation norm. By lemma 19.5.2 , the ideal models are exactly the models whose polar measures are atomic, which gives ( 30.47 ). $\square$
30.46 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-model-volume-distance} d_\theta (u,v)=\| \mu _ u-\mu _ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation}
30.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-ideal-volume-distance} d_\theta (q_ D,q_ E)=\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation}

title: Corollary 30.12.3
text:
Corollary 30.12.3 . The ordinary models on $Y$ form a complete geodesic metric space for $d_	heta $. The ideal models form a closed geodesically convex subspace, which is the metric completion of the analytic ordinary models of positive mass. Proof. By lemma 30.12.1 , theorem 30.12.2 , the space of ordinary models is isometric to the set of polar measures of mass at most $A$ with the total variation norm. This set is closed in total variation: a limit is positive, satisfies the mass bound, and is carried by the countable union of polar carriers of the sequence. Completeness therefore follows from that of finite signed measures. For two such measures $\mu ,
u $, the measures $\mu _ t=(1-t)\mu +t
u $, $0\leq t\leq 1$, remain in this set and satisfy \[  \| \mu _ t-\mu _ s\| _{\mathrm{TV}}=|t-s|\, \| \mu -
u \| _{\mathrm{TV}}.  \] Their models give a constant-speed geodesic. The atomic measures form a closed convex subset, since a total-variation limit is carried by the countable union of the sets of atoms of the sequence. Restricting to finitely many atoms and approximating the coefficients from below by rational numbers, with an arbitrarily small further decrease if needed, approximates every such measure by finite atomic measures with rational coefficients and mass strictly less than $A$. Their models have analytic singularities by lemma 19.5.2 , and ( 30.47 ) gives the density. $\square$

title: Theorem 30.12.4
text: Theorem 30.12.4 . Let $p_ j,p$ be ordinary models on $Y$. If $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$, then $p_ j\to p$ in $L^1$ and in capacity. If $U(p)=0$, then in addition 30.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-zero-mass-current-variation} \| T_{p_ j}-T_ p\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Proof. Write $\mu _ j=\mu _{p_ j}$ and $\mu =\mu _ p$. By ( 30.46 ), $\mu _ j\to \mu $ in total variation. Thus $U(p_ j)=A-\mu _ j(Y)\to U(p)$. If $U(p)>0$, the models lie in a common $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ for all large $j$, and proposition 30.6.3 , theorem 30.7.3 apply. Suppose that $U(p)=0$. Then $T_ p=\mu $ and $\mu (Y)=A$, while $T_{p_ j}-\mu _ j$ is a positive measure of mass $A-\mu _ j(Y)=\mu (Y)-\mu _ j(Y)$. Consequently \[  \| T_{p_ j}-T_ p\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \| \mu _ j-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}+A-\mu _ j(Y) \leq 2\| \mu _ j-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}},  \] which proves ( 30.51 ). By normalized compactness, each subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $L^1$ to a function $q$ with supremum zero. Then $T_{p_ j}\to T_ q$ weakly, so $T_ q=T_ p$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q-p)=0$. Hence $q-p$ is constant, and the normalization gives $q=p$. This proves $L^1$ convergence of the whole sequence. Finally, apply lemma 1.6.6 on finitely many nested coordinate disks: both terms on its right-hand side tend to zero, and the comparison between local and global capacities in section 1.8 gives convergence in capacity. $\square$
30.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-zero-mass-current-variation} \| T_{p_ j}-T_ p\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation}

title: Example 30.12.5
text: Example 30.12.5 . On $\mathbb P^1$ with the Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one, there are zero-mass ideal models $p_ j,p$ with $p_ j\to p$ in capacity but $d_\theta (p_ j,p)=2$ for every $j$. Proof. In the affine coordinate $z$, where $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$, put for $a\in \mathbb C$ \[  p_ a(z)=\log \frac{|z-a|^2}{(1+|z|^2)(1+|a|^2)}.  \] This function extends to $\mathbb P^1$, has supremum zero by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and satisfies $T_{p_ a}=\delta _ a$. Hence it is the ideal model with polar measure $\delta _ a$, by lemma 19.5.2 . Choose $a_ j\ne 0$ tending to zero and set $p_ j=p_{a_ j}$, $p=p_0$. On the complement of any fixed disk about zero the convergence is uniform, including near infinity. Small disks about zero lie in sublevel sets $\{ p_0<-t\} $ with $t$ large, so their capacities tend to zero as the radius tends to zero, by ( 1.26 ). Therefore $p_ j\to p$ in capacity. Since $\| \delta _{a_ j}-\delta _0\| _{\mathrm{TV}}=2$, ( 30.46 ) gives the asserted distance. $\square$

title: Proposition 30.12.6
text: Proposition 30.12.6 . For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$, 30.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-analytic-distance-defect} \inf _{a\in \mathcal A_+(Y,\theta )}d_\theta (u,a) =d_\theta (u,P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})=\tau (u). \end{equation} On ordinary models, $p\mapsto P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ is a $1$-Lipschitz retraction onto the ideal models, and $P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ is the unique ideal model nearest to $p$. There are $a_ j\in \mathcal A_+(Y,\theta )$ with $d_\theta (u,a_ j)\to 0$ if and only if $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. Proof. The ideal envelope of $u$ is $q_{D_ u}$, by lemma 19.5.2 . For any positive atomic measure $E$ of mass at most $A$, the nonatomic measure $\sigma _ u$ and the signed atomic measure $D_ u-E$ are mutually singular. Thus ( 30.46 ) gives 30.53 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-finite-analytic-comparison} d_\theta (u,q_ E)=\tau (u)+\| D_ u-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Among ideal models, the minimum is attained exactly at $E=D_ u$. Since the analytic models of positive mass are dense among the ideal models (corollary 30.12.3 ), this gives ( 30.52 ). Taking the atomic part does not increase total variation, which proves the Lipschitz assertion. Finally, lemma 30.12.1 shows that $P_\theta [u]=p_{\mu _ u}$ equals $q_{D_ u}=p_{D_ u}$ if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$, that is, $\tau (u)=0$. $\square$
30.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-analytic-distance-defect} \inf _{a\in \mathcal A_+(Y,\theta )}d_\theta (u,a) =d_\theta (u,P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})=\tau (u). \end{equation}
30.53 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-finite-analytic-comparison} d_\theta (u,q_ E)=\tau (u)+\| D_ u-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation}

title: Example 30.12.7
text: Example 30.12.7 . There is an ordinary model $p$ on $Y$ with zero mass whose multiplier ideals $\mathcal I(tp)$ are trivial for every $t>0$. It satisfies \[  P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}=0,\qquad \inf _{a\in \mathcal A_+(Y,\theta )}d_\theta (p,a)=A.  \] Proof. Choose a compact real interval inside a coordinate disk. Construct a binary Cantor set $K$ in it: at level $k$ there are $2^ k$ pairwise disjoint intervals of length $r_ k=\exp (-4^{k+1})$, each containing its two children of level $k+1$, and $K$ is the intersection of the unions over all levels. Let $\sigma $ be the probability measure on $K$ assigning mass $2^{-k}$ to each interval of level $k$. It has no atoms. Put $u(x)=A\int _ YG(x,y)\, \mathrm{d}\sigma (y)$, so that $T_ u=A\sigma $. On the chosen compact coordinate disk, $G(x,y)\leq \log |x-y|^2+C$ for a fixed constant $C$. For $x\in K$, integrating over the interval of level $k$ containing $x$, and using $G\leq 0$ elsewhere, gives \[  u(x)\leq A2^{-k}(2\log r_ k+C)\longrightarrow -\infty .  \] Thus $u=-\infty $ on $K$, while $u$ is smooth off $K$, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=-\theta $ there. Hence $K$ is polar, $\mu _ u=A\sigma $ and $U(u)=0$. By lemma 30.12.1 , $p=P_\theta [u]$ has the same polar curvature. Since this measure already has mass $A$, we get $T_ p=T_ u$, and therefore $p=u-\sup _ Yu$. The Lelong numbers of $p$ vanish because $\sigma $ has no atoms, so all its multiplier ideals are trivial and its ideal envelope is zero. Finally $\tau (p)=A$, which gives the distance by ( 30.52 ). $\square$

title: 30.12.1 The ordinary-type topology on a curve
search_title: The ordinary-type topology on a curve
text: 30.12.1 The ordinary-type topology on a curve We now compare the polar metric with the topology on ordinary singularity types introduced in section 16.6 . That topology also uses the ordinary envelope, but it measures the total variation only of the atomic part of the curvature. On ideal models the atomic part is the whole polar measure, so the two topologies agree there. On arbitrary ordinary models, diffuse polar mass can concentrate without being detected by the atomic total variation. We keep $Y$, $\theta $, $A$ and the decomposition $\mu _ u=D_ u+\sigma _ u$, and we use $\eta =\theta /A$ for $L^1$ norms. Let $\mathfrak S(Y,\theta )=\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )/{\sim }$ be the space of ordinary singularity types, and write $[u]$ for the class of $u$. Recall from proposition 16.6.2 that $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ is the uniform topology on $\mathfrak S(Y,\theta )$ generated by the $L^1$ distances between ordinary envelopes and between ideal envelopes, by the total variation of divisorial Lelong numbers on each fixed modification, and by the controlled ideal relations $\mathcal U(t,a)$ of ( 16.5 ). For ordinary classes put 30.54 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-ordinary-type-distance} d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([u],[v]) =\| P_\theta [u]-P_\theta [v]\| _{L^1(\eta )} +\| D_ u-D_ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Theorem 30.12.8 . The finite pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ induces $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ on $\mathfrak S(Y,\theta )$. For $0\leq s\leq A$, the classes of ideal models \[  \mathcal C_ s=\{ [q_ D]:D\text{ positive atomic},\  D(Y)\leq s\}   \] form a complete metric space both for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ and for the distance $\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}$ between $[q_ D]$ and $[q_ E]$, and these two metrics induce the same topology. The space $\mathcal C_ s$ is not totally bounded if $s>0$, and $\mathcal C_0=\{ [0]\} $. Proof. A smooth compact modification of a smooth curve is an isomorphism, and the divisor weight of a point is one. Hence the divisorial distance in proposition 16.6.2 is exactly the atomic total variation, and the two summands of ( 30.54 ) are among the coordinates defining $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. Conversely, suppose that a net $[u_ j]$ converges to $[u]$ for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $. The ideal envelope of $u$ is $q_{D_ u}$, by lemma 19.5.2 . Convergence of the atomic parts in total variation implies $L^1$ convergence of these envelopes, by theorem 30.12.2 , theorem 30.12.4 . These results also apply to nets: the map $D\mapsto q_ D$ goes between metric spaces, so sequential continuity is equivalent to continuity. It remains to check the controlled ideal relations. At a point $x$ with local coordinate $z$, the multiplier ideals on the curve are \[  \mathcal I(tu)_ x=(z^{\lfloor tD_ u(\{ x\} )\rfloor }).  \] This follows from theorem 1.16.3 , lemma 1.16.1 : on a smooth curve the Lelong number at $x$ determines the ideal, and the logarithmic germ with that Lelong number has the displayed ideal. Write $D_ j=D_{u_ j}$ and $D=D_ u$, and fix $t>0$ and $a>1$. The set $F=\{ x:D(\{ x\} )\geq 1/(2t)\} $ is finite. At its points, $aD_ j(\{ x\} )\geq D(\{ x\} )$ and $aD(\{ x\} )\geq D_ j(\{ x\} )$ eventually. Outside $F$, the bound \[  \sup _ x|D_ j(\{ x\} )-D(\{ x\} )|\leq \| D_ j-D\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow 0  \] makes both $\mathcal I(tu)_ x$ and $\mathcal I(tu_ j)_ x$ unit ideals for large $j$. Hence both inclusions in ( 16.5 ) hold eventually at every point. This proves that $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ induces $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. The map $D\mapsto q_ D$ is injective, so $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ is a metric on $\mathcal C_ s$. The positive atomic measures of mass at most $s$ are closed in total variation: a limit is positive, satisfies the mass bound, and is carried by the countable union of the sets of atoms of the sequence. Completeness of the space of finite signed measures therefore gives completeness for total variation. A $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal C_ s$ is Cauchy in total variation; its limit is again atomic, and theorem 30.12.4 gives convergence of the envelope coordinate. This proves completeness for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ as well as the equality of the two topologies. If $s>0$, fix $0<b\leq s$ and infinitely many distinct points $x_ j$. The measures $b\delta _{x_ j}$ have pairwise total-variation distance $2b$, so $\mathcal C_ s$ is not totally bounded for either metric. For $s=0$ only the zero measure remains. $\square$ By lemma 19.5.2 , for $0\leq \delta \leq A$ the set $\mathcal C_{A-\delta }$ consists exactly of the classes of ideal models of mass at least $\delta $. The whole set $\mathcal C_ A$, including the models of zero mass, is complete. Its subset of positive mass is incomplete: for a point $x$, the measures $D_ j=A(1-1/j)\delta _ x$ form a Cauchy sequence whose limit $A\delta _ x$ has zero mass. For general ordinary classes, the corresponding statement concerns a pseudometric. Put \[  \mathcal G_{\theta ,\delta } =\left\{ [u]:P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I},\quad \int _ Y\mathrm{MA}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})\geq \delta \right\} .  \] For $0\leq \delta \leq A$ this set is complete for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $, since every class $[u]$ in it is at distance zero from $[q_{D_ u}]\in \mathcal C_{A-\delta }$; limits need not be unique as ordinary classes. The set is not totally bounded when $\delta <A$. At $\delta =A$ the pseudometric vanishes identically on it, although it contains distinct classes by proposition 16.6.4 . The union of these sets over all $\delta >0$ is incomplete, by the same one-atom sequence.
30.54 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-ordinary-type-distance} d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([u],[v]) =\| P_\theta [u]-P_\theta [v]\| _{L^1(\eta )} +\| D_ u-D_ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation}

For $0\leq s\leq A$, the classes of ideal models \[  \mathcal C_ s=\{ [q_ D]:D\text{ positive atomic},\  D(Y)\leq s\}   \] form a complete metric space both for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ and for the distance $\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}$ between $[q_ D]$ and $[q_ E]$, and these two metrics induce the same topology. Write $D_ j=D_{u_ j}$ and $D=D_ u$, and fix $t>0$ and $a>1$. The set $F=\{ x:D(\{ x\} )\geq 1/(2t)\} $ is finite. At its points, $aD_ j(\{ x\} )\geq D(\{ x\} )$ and $aD(\{ x\} )\geq D_ j(\{ x\} )$ eventually. Outside $F$, the bound \[  \sup _ x|D_ j(\{ x\} )-D(\{ x\} )|\leq \| D_ j-D\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow 0  \] makes both $\mathcal I(tu)_ x$ and $\mathcal I(tu_ j)_ x$ unit ideals for large $j$. A $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal C_ s$ is Cauchy in total variation; its limit is again atomic, and theorem 30.12.4 gives convergence of the envelope coordinate. This proves completeness for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ as well as the equality of the two topologies. If $s>0$, fix $0<b\leq s$ and infinitely many distinct points $x_ j$. The measures $b\delta _{x_ j}$ have pairwise total-variation distance $2b$, so $\mathcal C_ s$ is not totally bounded for either metric. For $s=0$ only the zero measure remains. $\square$

title: 30.12.2 Concentration of diffuse polar curvature
text: 30.12.2 Concentration of diffuse polar curvature The atomic total variation cannot be omitted from theorem 30.12.8 . On $\mathbb P^1$ with its Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one, fix a rational $0<\tau <1$ and take the atomic probability measures $\nu _ j$ and the ideal models $r_ j=P_\theta [(1-\tau )q_ j]_{\mathcal I}$ of proposition 16.4.3 , choosing the rational approximations so that the largest atom of $\nu _ j$ tends to zero. The ordinary and ideal envelopes of $r_ j$ both tend to zero in $L^1$, and for each $t>0$ and $a>1$, the pair $([r_ j],[0])$ eventually lies in $\mathcal U(t,a)$. The currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r_ j$ converge weakly to $\theta $. Nevertheless, \[  d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([r_ j],[0]) \geq \| D_{r_ j}\| _{\mathrm{TV}}=1-\tau >0.  \] Thus these weaker conditions do not imply convergence for $\tau _{\theta ,0}$, even at a fixed positive mass. The opposite difficulty concerns diffuse polar mass: the pseudometric controls the ordinary envelope in $L^1$, but not the total variation of the diffuse measure itself. Proposition 30.12.9 . For the Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one on $\mathbb P^1$, the space $(\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta ),d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta )$ is incomplete. In fact, there is a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence without limit consisting of ordinary models of one fixed positive non-pluripolar mass, all with trivial multiplier ideals. Proof. Choose a nonatomic polar probability measure $\sigma $ with compact support in an affine chart, using the Cantor construction in example 30.12.7 . Fix $0<c<1$ and a point $x$ in that chart. Translating and shrinking the support towards $x$ gives nonatomic polar probability measures $\sigma _ j$ supported in disks about $x$ with radii tending to zero. Let $p_ j=p_{c\sigma _ j}$ be the ordinary models of lemma 30.12.1 . Their polar measures are $c\sigma _ j$, their masses are $1-c$, and $D_{p_ j}=0$. Hence their Lelong numbers vanish, their multiplier ideals are trivial, and their ideal envelopes are zero. We claim that $p_ j\to q_{c\delta _ x}$ in $L^1$. Write $q_ y=q_{c\delta _ y}$. Rotations of $\mathbb P^1$ preserving $\theta $ and sending $x$ to $y$ can be chosen to depend continuously on $y$ near $x$. They transport $q_ x$ to $q_ y$, so continuity of translations in $L^1$ gives $q_ y\to q_ x$ in $L^1$ as $y\to x$. Set \[  w_ j=\int _{\mathbb P^1}q_ y\, \mathrm d\sigma _ j(y).  \] The common $L^1$ bound for normalized potentials makes this integral well defined. The function $w_ j$ is nonpositive, its curvature current dominates $c\sigma _ j$, and $w_ j\to q_ x$ in $L^1$. By ( 30.45 ), $p_ j$ is the upper envelope of all $v\leq 0$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq c\sigma _ j$, so $w_ j\leq p_ j$. By normalized compactness, every subsequence of $p_ j$ has a further subsequence converging in $L^1$ to some $v\leq 0$. The inequalities $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_ j\geq c\sigma _ j$ pass to the limit and give $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq c\delta _ x$. Since $q_ x=p_{c\delta _ x}$, the same envelope description gives $v\leq q_ x$. The lower bound $w_ j\leq p_ j$ gives $v\geq q_ x$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. This identifies every cluster point and proves the claim. Since $P_\theta [p_ j]=p_ j$ and $D_{p_ j}=0$, the classes $[p_ j]$ form a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence. A limit $[v]$ would satisfy $D_ v=0$ and $P_\theta [v]=q_ x$. This is impossible: the ordinary envelope preserves all multiplier ideals and hence all atoms, whereas $q_ x$ has an atom of mass $c$ at $x$. The sequence therefore has no limit in $\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta )$. $\square$ On ordinary models, $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ and the topology of the polar metric $d_\theta $ are also different. Choose the Cantor support of $\sigma $ inside a positive real interval in the affine coordinate $z$, away from zero. The rotations $R_ j(z)=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\varepsilon _ j}z$, with $0<\varepsilon _ j\to 0$, move this support off itself. Put $p=p_{c\sigma }$ and $\widetilde p_ j=p\circ R_ j^{-1}$. By rotation invariance of the envelope, the $\widetilde p_ j$ are ordinary models with polar measures $c(R_ j)_*\sigma $, which have no atoms. Continuity of rotations in $L^1$ yields $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([\widetilde p_ j],[p])\to 0$, whereas the polar measures have disjoint supports, so $d_\theta (\widetilde p_ j,p)=2c$ by theorem 30.12.2 . Conversely, polar total variation controls both terms of ( 30.54 ), by theorem 30.12.4 . Thus $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ is strictly weaker than the polar metric topology on ordinary models, although the two agree on ideal models. The failure of continuity under smooth gauge changes with a fixed zero obstacle (proposition 16.6.6 ) gives a further difference: the polar metric is invariant under such changes, by section 30.13 .

title: Proposition 30.12.9
text: Proposition 30.12.9 . For the Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one on $\mathbb P^1$, the space $(\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta ),d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta )$ is incomplete. In fact, there is a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence without limit consisting of ordinary models of one fixed positive non-pluripolar mass, all with trivial multiplier ideals. Proof. Translating and shrinking the support towards $x$ gives nonatomic polar probability measures $\sigma _ j$ supported in disks about $x$ with radii tending to zero. Let $p_ j=p_{c\sigma _ j}$ be the ordinary models of lemma 30.12.1 . Their polar measures are $c\sigma _ j$, their masses are $1-c$, and $D_{p_ j}=0$. Hence their Lelong numbers vanish, their multiplier ideals are trivial, and their ideal envelopes are zero. We claim that $p_ j\to q_{c\delta _ x}$ in $L^1$. Write $q_ y=q_{c\delta _ y}$. Rotations of $\mathbb P^1$ preserving $\theta $ and sending $x$ to $y$ can be chosen to depend continuously on $y$ near $x$. They transport $q_ x$ to $q_ y$, so continuity of translations in $L^1$ gives $q_ y\to q_ x$ in $L^1$ as $y\to x$. Set \[  w_ j=\int _{\mathbb P^1}q_ y\, \mathrm d\sigma _ j(y).  \] The common $L^1$ bound for normalized potentials makes this integral well defined. The function $w_ j$ is nonpositive, its curvature current dominates $c\sigma _ j$, and $w_ j\to q_ x$ in $L^1$. By ( 30.45 ), $p_ j$ is the upper envelope of all $v\leq 0$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq c\sigma _ j$, so $w_ j\leq p_ j$. By normalized compactness, every subsequence of $p_ j$ has a further subsequence converging in $L^1$ to some $v\leq 0$. The inequalities $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_ j\geq c\sigma _ j$ pass to the limit and give $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq c\delta _ x$. Since $q_ x=p_{c\delta _ x}$, the same envelope description gives $v\leq q_ x$. The lower bound $w_ j\leq p_ j$ gives $v\geq q_ x$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. This identifies every cluster point and proves the claim. Since $P_\theta [p_ j]=p_ j$ and $D_{p_ j}=0$, the classes $[p_ j]$ form a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence. A limit $[v]$ would satisfy $D_ v=0$ and $P_\theta [v]=q_ x$. This is impossible: the ordinary envelope preserves all multiplier ideals and hence all atoms, whereas $q_ x$ has an atom of mass $c$ at $x$. The sequence therefore has no limit in $\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta )$. $\square$

title: 30.12.3 Convergence for all obstacles
text: 30.12.3 Convergence for all obstacles We keep the compact curve $Y$ and its positive form $\theta $ of area $A$. The topology $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ of 16.6.4 is generated by the topologies $\tau _{\theta ,F}$ for all smooth obstacles $F$, in which the ordinary and ideal envelopes below $F$ replace those below zero. On a curve the envelopes below $F$ are still determined by the polar measure, and their ideal counterparts by its atomic part. This gives a description of $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ by a single pseudometric and allows a comparison with polar total variation. Choose, as in proposition 16.6.7 , a countable family $\{ F_ k\} _{k\geq 1}\subset C^\infty (Y,\mathbb R)$ that is dense for the uniform norm, with $F_1=0$. Write $d_{O,F}$ and $d_{I,F}$ for the $L^1$ distances between the ordinary envelopes $P_{\theta ,F}[\cdot ]$ and between the ideal envelopes $P_{\theta ,F}[\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$, which define $\tau _{\theta ,F}$ (section 16.6 ), and put 30.55 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-all-obstacle-distance} \begin{split}  d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta ([u],[v]) & =\| D_ u-D_ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\\ & \quad +\sum _{k=1}^\infty 2^{-k}\bigl (\min \{ 1,d_{O,F_ k}([u],[v])\} \\ & \qquad \qquad +\min \{ 1,d_{I,F_ k}([u],[v])\} \bigr ). \end{split} \end{equation} Proposition 30.12.10 . The pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ induces the uniformity of $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $. Two classes have distance zero if and only if they have the same polar curvature. The closure of the analytic classes is $\{ [u]:\mu _ u=D_ u\} =\mathcal G_\theta $, where $\mathcal G_\theta =\{ [u]:P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\} $ as in ( 16.6 ). On each set $\mathcal C_ s$, $0\leq s\leq A$, the pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ is a complete metric inducing the topology of total variation of the atomic measures. On ordinary models, polar total variation implies convergence for $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $. Proof. Step 1: envelopes below an obstacle. For any smooth $F$, translating the competitors by $F$ gives \[  P_{\theta ,F}[u]-F=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F],  \] and likewise for the ideal envelope. The background $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F$ on the right is a smooth real form of area $A$, though it need not be positive. We claim that these two envelopes are the models of $\mu _ u$ and of $D_ u$, respectively, in that background, in the sense of proposition 30.13.1 . Set $\mu =\mu _ u$ and let $w_\mu $ be its Green potential, and put $r=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[w_\mu -F]$. By the gauge bounds of proposition 16.3.1 , $r+F$ differs from $P_\theta [w_\mu ]=p_\mu \sim w_\mu $ by a bounded function, so $r\sim w_\mu -F$. Hence $r=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[r]$ is an ordinary model, and its polar measure is $\mu $. Moreover $u-F\preceq r$, and both have mass $A-\mu (Y)$. If this mass is positive, corollary 30.3.6 , applied in the big background $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F$, shows that $P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F]=r$. If it is zero, the curvature measures of $u-F$ and $w_\mu -F$ both equal $\mu $, so these functions differ by a constant, and again $P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F]=r$. The assertion for the ideal envelope follows in the same way from ideal projection and the classification of atomic models. It also follows that the envelope $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ is the upper envelope of all $v\leq F$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \mu $. Step 2: the uniformity. By proposition 30.13.1 , polar total variation gives $L^1$ convergence of these models for every fixed $F$. The same assertion for atomic measures gives continuity of every ideal-envelope coordinate with respect to the total variation of the atomic parts. The controlled ideal relations are also implied, uniformly, by atomic total variation: for fixed $t>0$ and $a>1$, the bound $\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}<(a-1)/(at)$ guarantees both inclusions in ( 16.5 ), by the formula for multiplier ideals on a curve. Indeed, if $tE(\{ x\} )\geq 1$, the bound gives $aD(\{ x\} )>E(\{ x\} )$; otherwise the target ideal is the unit ideal. Interchange $D$ and $E$ for the other inclusion. Each divisorial coordinate is the atomic total variation. Therefore the envelope terms in the series, together with the atomic term, generate exactly the uniformity of $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $: finitely many coordinates control the sum up to its uniformly small tail, and the sum controls each fixed coordinate. Step 3: zero distance and analytic closure. By Step 1 with $F=0$, distance zero forces equal polar measures; the classification at every obstacle proves the converse. The same classification shows that the ordinary and ideal envelopes agree at every $F$ if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$. Hence theorem 16.6.9 identifies the closure of the analytic classes. Step 4: the sets $\mathcal C_ s$. For a $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal C_ s$, the atomic measures converge in total variation to a measure of mass at most $s$, which is again atomic. The convergence of models in Step 2 gives convergence of every obstacle coordinate, and the summable tail then gives convergence for $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $. Conversely, convergence for $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ implies convergence of the atomic parts, because of the first summand. This proves completeness and the equality of topologies on $\mathcal C_ s$. Finally, polar total variation controls the atomic part and all ordinary-envelope coordinates, which proves the last assertion. $\square$ On a curve, membership in the relative envelope class of the ideal envelope has the same polar criterion, including for ideal envelopes of zero mass. Corollary 30.12.11 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ put $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. The following are equivalent: \[  \begin{gathered} u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q),\qquad \mu _ u=D_ u,\\ P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I},\\ P_{\theta ,F}[u]=P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \quad \text{for every smooth real }F. \end{gathered}  \] This also holds when $D_ u(Y)=A$, that is, when $q$ has zero mass. Proof. The classifications of ordinary and ideal models in lemma 30.12.1 , lemma 19.5.2 show that $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$. Step 1 of the proof of proposition 30.12.10 shows that this is equivalent to equality of the envelopes at every smooth obstacle. Membership of $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q)$ implies the latter by proposition 16.6.8 . Conversely, assume that $\mu _ u=D_ u$. By lemma 19.5.2 , $\mu _ q=D_ u$. Ordinary equivalence preserves polar curvature by corollary 1.6.8 , so every potential equivalent to $q$ has non-pluripolar mass $A-D_ u(Y)$, by Stokes' theorem. Hence \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q)=A-D_ u(Y).  \] If $D_ u(Y)<A$, then $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, and proposition 30.8.2 puts $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q)$. If $D_ u(Y)=A$, the positive curvature measures $T_ u$ and $T_ q$ both dominate $D_ u$ and both have total mass $A$. Hence $T_ u=T_ q=D_ u$. The distribution $u-q$ is harmonic, and therefore constant on the compact connected curve. Thus $u=q+C$ for a constant $C$, and proposition 13.4.2 gives $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ,q)$ also in this case. $\square$ Proposition 30.12.12 . For the Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one on $\mathbb P^1$, the pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ is incomplete on $\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta )$: some Cauchy sequence of ordinary models of one fixed positive mass with trivial multiplier ideals has no limit. On ordinary models, its topology is strictly weaker than that of polar total variation and strictly stronger than $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. Proof. Use the diffuse polar probability measures $\sigma _ j$ concentrating at a point $x$ and the models $p_ j=p_{c\sigma _ j}$ from the proof of proposition 30.12.9 , with $0<c<1$. Fix a smooth obstacle $F$ and put $q_{y,F}=P_{\theta ,F}[q_{c\delta _ y}]$. Rotations preserving $\theta $ and sending $x$ to $y$ can be chosen to depend continuously on $y$ near $x$; they transport the obstacle $F$ to its composition with the rotation. Since envelopes below two obstacles differ by at most the uniform distance between the obstacles, continuity of rotations in $L^1$ gives $q_{y,F}\to q_{x,F}$ in $L^1$ as $y\to x$. The uniform $L^1$ bound near $x$ makes the average $w_{j,F}=\int q_{y,F}\, \mathrm d\sigma _ j(y)$ well defined. It lies below $F$, its curvature current dominates $c\sigma _ j$, and it converges to $q_{x,F}$ in $L^1$. The description of envelopes below obstacles in Step 1 of the proof of proposition 30.12.10 gives $w_{j,F}\leq P_{\theta ,F}[p_ j]\leq F$. These bounds and normalized compactness give $L^1$ precompactness. Every cluster point of the envelopes has curvature at least $c\delta _ x$, so it is at most $q_{x,F}$, and the lower bound gives the reverse inequality. Hence $P_{\theta ,F}[p_ j]\to q_{x,F}$ for every $F$. The ideal envelopes of the $p_ j$ below $F$ all equal $P_\theta (F)$, since their multiplier ideals are trivial, and their atomic parts vanish. Thus $[p_ j]$ is a $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence. Since $F_1=0$, a limit would also be a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-limit, which proposition 30.12.9 excludes. For the strict comparison with polar total variation, use the rotated diffuse models $\widetilde p_ j=p\circ R_ j^{-1}$ from the end of 30.12.1 . For every smooth $F$, \[  P_{\theta ,F}[\widetilde p_ j] =P_{\theta ,F\circ R_ j}[p]\circ R_ j^{-1}.  \] The same obstacle bound and the $L^1$ continuity of rotations give convergence to $P_{\theta ,F}[p]$. All atomic parts vanish, so $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta ([\widetilde p_ j],[p])\to 0$, whereas the polar total-variation distance remains $2c$. Proposition 30.12.10 gives the implication in the other direction. Finally, the sequence in proposition 16.6.6 converges for the zero obstacle but not for some smooth obstacle. By Step 1 of the proof of proposition 30.12.10 , replacing its members by their ordinary models does not change any obstacle envelope, so $d^{\mathrm{all}}_\theta $ is strictly stronger than $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ already on ordinary models. $\square$

title: 30.13 Background changes on curves
Proposition 30.13.1
text: Proposition 30.13.1 . Polar curvature identifies $\mathcal M(\sigma )$ with the set of polar measures of mass at most $A_\sigma $. Write $p_\sigma (\mu )$ for the model with polar measure $\mu $. Then \[  U_\sigma (p_\sigma (\mu ))=A_\sigma -\mu (Y),\qquad d_\sigma (p_\sigma (\mu ),p_\sigma (\nu ))=\| \mu -\nu \| _{\mathrm{TV}},  \] and ideal projection corresponds to taking the atomic part. The space $(\mathcal M(\sigma ),d_\sigma )$ is complete and geodesic, and convergence for $d_\sigma $ implies convergence in $L^1$ and in capacity. If $A_\sigma =0$, its only member is the smooth potential $u_\sigma $ of lemma 1.8.14 . Proof. Suppose first that $A=A_\sigma >0$, and write $\sigma =A\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,A\eta )$, the inequalities for ordinary envelopes in proposition 16.3.1 give \[  P_{A\eta }[v]+\min _ Yh \leq P_\sigma [v-h]+h \leq P_{A\eta }[v]+\max _ Yh.  \] For a model $p$ in background $A\eta $, the potential $q=P_\sigma [p-h]$ therefore satisfies $q+h\sim p$, and since the envelope depends only on the ordinary type, $P_\sigma [q]=P_\sigma [p-h]=q$. Conversely, for $q\in \mathcal M(\sigma )$, the same bounds with $v=q+h$ show that $P_{A\eta }[q+h]\sim q+h$, and taking the envelope back recovers $q$. Thus $p\mapsto P_\sigma [p-h]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal M(A\eta )$ onto $\mathcal M(\sigma )$. Smooth gauge changes preserve curvature currents, and ordinary equivalence preserves their polar parts by corollary 1.6.8 . Consequently the bijection preserves polar curvature. It also preserves singularity volumes, and subtracting the same smooth function commutes with maxima. The classification and the distance formula of lemma 30.12.1 , theorem 30.12.2 , applied to the positive form $A\eta $, now give the first assertions. The same gauge bounds for ideal envelopes show that the transported ideal projections are ordinarily equivalent. Both are ordinary models by corollary 16.2.4 , and ordinary models of the same type are equal. Thus the bijection commutes with ideal projection, which still takes the atomic part. Completeness and the geodesics follow from the identification with polar measures, as in corollary 30.12.3 . For convergence to a model of positive mass, note that $\sigma $ is big because $\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(-h)=A\eta >0$, and that the convergence of the polar masses gives a common positive lower-volume bound; then apply proposition 30.6.3 , theorem 30.7.3 . For a limit of zero mass, the current estimate ( 30.51 ) follows from the same polar decomposition as before. Normalized compactness and the uniqueness of harmonic functions give $L^1$ convergence, and lemma 1.6.6 on a finite cover gives convergence in capacity. If $A_\sigma =0$, lemma 1.8.14 leaves only $u_\sigma $ after normalization. Its curvature current vanishes, and both envelope operations fix it. All assertions reduce to statements about the zero measure and the one-point metric space. $\square$

title: Corollary 30.13.2
text: Corollary 30.13.2 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\sigma )$ put \[  q=P_\sigma [u]_{\mathcal I},\qquad \mu _ u=\mathbf1_{\{ u=-\infty \} }(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u),\qquad D_ u=\sum _{y\in Y}\nu (u,y)\delta _ y.  \] The following are equivalent: \[  \begin{gathered} u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\sigma ,q),\qquad \mu _ u=D_ u,\\ P_\sigma [u]=P_\sigma [u]_{\mathcal I},\\ P_{\sigma ,F}[u]=P_{\sigma ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \quad \text{for every smooth real }F. \end{gathered}  \] If $A_\sigma =0$, all four conditions hold for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\sigma )$. Proof. Suppose first that $A=A_\sigma >0$, and write $\sigma =A\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. Put $v=u+h$ and $q_+=P_{A\eta }[v]_{\mathcal I}$. The gauge change preserves the curvature current and its pole set, hence both $\mu _ u$ and $D_ u$. By proposition 16.3.1 , $q+h\sim q_+$. The gauge invariance of the relative envelope class and its invariance under equivalent references (proposition 13.4.2 ) give \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\sigma ,q) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad v\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,A\eta ,q_+).  \] By corollary 30.12.11 , this is equivalent to $\mu _ u=D_ u$. The gauge bounds for the ordinary and ideal envelopes, corollary 1.6.8 and the classifications in the positive background $A\eta $ identify the polar curvatures of $P_\sigma [u]$ and $P_\sigma [u]_{\mathcal I}$ with $\mu _ u$ and $D_ u$, respectively. Both envelopes are ordinary models, the ideal one by corollary 16.2.4 . The classification of models in proposition 30.13.1 therefore shows that they are equal if and only if $\mu _ u=D_ u$. For a smooth real $F$, the bijection $a\mapsto a+h$ between competitors gives \[  P_{\sigma ,F}[u]+h=P_{A\eta ,F+h}[v],  \] and the same identity for the ideal envelopes. Indeed, this bijection preserves the obstacle bound, the ordinary order and multiplier-ideal equivalence, and addition of $h$ commutes with upper regularization. Since $F\mapsto F+h$ is a bijection of the smooth obstacles, corollary 30.12.11 gives the remaining equivalence. If $A_\sigma =0$, lemma 1.8.14 gives $u=-h+c$ for a constant $c$, and the curvature current of $u$ vanishes. Thus $\mu _ u=D_ u=0$. All potentials in this background are smooth and ordinarily equivalent, so their ordinary and ideal competitor families below every obstacle coincide, and they are nonempty after a constant translation. The reference $q$ is ordinarily equivalent to $u$, and proposition 13.4.2 gives $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\sigma ,q)$. $\square$

title: Theorem 30.13.3
text: Theorem 30.13.3 . Let $\theta _0,\theta _1$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms on $Y$ with positive areas $A_ i=A_{\theta _ i}$, and put $\lambda =A_1/A_0$. The map \[  F_{10}:\mathcal M(\theta _0)\longrightarrow \mathcal M(\theta _1), \qquad F_{10}(p_{\theta _0}(\mu ))=p_{\theta _1}(\lambda \mu ),  \] is a bijection and satisfies 30.59 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-background-homothety} \begin{split}  d_{\theta _1}(F_{10}(p),F_{10}(q))& =\lambda d_{\theta _0}(p,q),\\  U_{\theta _1}(F_{10}(p))& =\lambda U_{\theta _0}(p),\\  P_{\theta _1}[F_{10}(p)]_{\mathcal I} & =F_{10}(P_{\theta _0}[p]_{\mathcal I}). \end{split} \end{equation} For a third smooth background $\theta _2$ of positive area, the same construction gives $F_{21}F_{10}=F_{20}$. Proof. Multiplication by $\lambda $ is a bijection from the polar measures of mass at most $A_0$ onto those of mass at most $A_1$. By proposition 30.13.1 , it gives the asserted bijection, and the distances satisfy \[  \| \lambda \mu -\lambda \nu \| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\lambda \| \mu -\nu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}.  \] The volume identity follows from $A_1-\lambda \mu (Y)=\lambda (A_0-\mu (Y))$. Taking the atomic part commutes with multiplication by $\lambda $, which gives the ideal-envelope identity. The area ratios multiply, proving the composition rule. $\square$

title: Proposition 30.13.4
text: Proposition 30.13.4 . Choose a smooth real $h$ with $\theta _1=\lambda \theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. For $p\in \mathcal M(\theta _0)$ and $q=F_{10}(p)$, 30.63 \begin{equation} \label{eq:curve-background-obstacle-bound} \begin{gathered} q=P_{\theta _1}[\lambda p-h],\\ \lambda p+\min _ Yh\leq q+h\leq \lambda p+\max _ Yh. \end{gathered} \end{equation} If $U_{\theta _0}(p)=0$, then \[  q=\lambda p-h-\sup _ Y(\lambda p-h).  \] Proof. The form $\theta _1-\lambda \theta _0$ has integral zero, so the scalar Poisson equation gives $h$, as in lemma 1.8.14 . Write $p=p_{\theta _0}(\mu )$. Scaling the competitors in the ordinary envelope shows that $\lambda p$ is an ordinary model for $\lambda \theta _0$. The gauge construction in the proof of proposition 30.13.1 therefore makes $P_{\theta _1}[\lambda p-h]$ an ordinary model in background $\theta _1$. The curvature current of $\lambda p-h$ in this background is $\lambda (\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)$, so its polar measure is $\lambda \mu $. The construction preserves this measure, which gives the first identity in ( 30.63 ). The function $\lambda p-h+\min _ Yh$ is a competitor for $q$, which gives the lower bound. If $v\leq 0$ is any competitor for $q$, then $v+h-\max _ Yh$ is $\lambda \theta _0$-plurisubharmonic, nonpositive and more singular than $\lambda p$, so it is at most $\lambda p$. Taking the upper envelope gives the upper bound. These inequalities hold also at the poles, and off the common pole set they imply $|q-\lambda p|\leq \operatorname {osc}_ Yh$. At zero mass, the polar measures exhaust the curvature currents of both $p$ and $q$. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q-\lambda p+h)=0$, and the uniqueness of harmonic functions together with the normalization $\sup _ Yq=0$ gives the last formula. $\square$

Using the background as an additional coordinate gives a complete space that includes the zero-area boundary. The singularity coordinate still records the diffuse polar curvature, and taking its atomic part still gives the nearest ideal model. Indeed, a $b$-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in every $C^ k$ norm; the limits agree and define a smooth form, whose area is nonnegative by $C^0$ convergence. Conversely, convergence in every $C^ k$ norm gives convergence for $b$: a finite part of the sum becomes small, and the tail is uniformly small. The metric space $(\mathscr M(Y),D)$ is complete. Its restriction to each fixed-background fiber is the polar metric $d_\sigma $. title: 31 Relative equations under positive lower mass

section: 12.5 Relative equations under positive lower mass
text: 31 Relative equations under positive lower mass Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, with a smooth semipositive big real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ and a model reference $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Given a nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $, we seek solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $, $\lambda >0$, and of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu $, $c>0$, relative to a prescribed model reference. The main difficulty is to keep the singularity condition when approximating $\mu $: a bounded difference from the reference may be lost in the limit. We assume that the reference $\varphi $ satisfies ( 13.26 ): $\varphi $ is an envelope fixed point, $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $ in the sense of definition 1.19.4 , and $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )\not\equiv -\infty $ for some $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. Throughout this chapter, unless explicitly stated otherwise, we assume that $\theta $ has positive lower mass: 31.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-positive-lower-volume} v_-(\theta )>0. \end{equation} Here $v_-(\theta )=\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (0)$ is the infimum of $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$ over all bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; see definition 6.5.1 and the discussion following definition 13.3.1 . The bounded mass property is not assumed. Approximating $\mu $ by measures with $L^ p$ densities gives solutions of the ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $ by theorem 14.11.1 , but the constants in their bounds $|u-\varphi |\leq C$ need not remain uniform, so a limit can leave this type. What survives the limit is membership in the relative envelope class of definition 13.4.1 : stretching the potential away from $\varphi $ by any finite factor still leaves an envelope that is not identically $-\infty $. Positive lower mass of $\theta $ prevents these stretched envelopes from collapsing. On disjoint contact sets, one finite measure controls the rooftop envelopes of arbitrarily many potentials. Consequently, a sequence of potentials whose measures are dominated by a fixed finite measure has, after extraction, a common lower envelope in the relative class. This envelope keeps limits in the class and controls the measures of deep sublevel sets, so convergence in capacity passes to the Monge–Ampère measures themselves. When the dominating measures are bounded Monge–Ampère measures that vary with the potentials, exponential comparison provides the common envelope instead. For a positive exponent the solution is unique. At exponent zero the scalar is unique, but the normalized potential need not be: on projective manifolds with nonclosed Hermitian backgrounds, the same smooth measure can have several smooth normalized solutions (corollary 31.7.2 ). Since bounded mass is not assumed, members of the relative class may have infinite extended mass; the envelope constructions of section 13.5 remain available for them. The solutions constructed below have finite mass because the right-hand sides of their equations are finite. Fix $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ with $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )\not\equiv -\infty $, and write \[  \mathcal E_\varphi =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ), \qquad \mathcal E_0=\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,0), \qquad \mu _ u=\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u).  \] Here $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\psi )$ denotes the relative envelope class of a reference $\psi $ (definition 13.4.1 ), and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta $ is the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 6.1.2 , a positive measure whose total mass may be infinite. As in definition 1.12.1 , $u\preceq v$ means $u\leq v+C$ for a constant $C$, and $u\sim v$ means $u\preceq v\preceq u$. For $u,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $b\geq 1$, we use the stretching envelopes $Q_ b(u,w)=P_\theta (bu-(b-1)w)$ introduced before definition 13.4.1 , and the rooftop envelopes $P_\theta (u_1,\ldots ,u_ N)=P_\theta (\min _ iu_ i)$. Fix also a Hermitian form $\omega \geq \theta $ for capacity and a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ for $L^1$ convergence. For $a\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, proposition 13.4.5 gives $P_\theta [a]=P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $. Since $a-\sup _ Xa$ is one of the competitors defining $P_\theta [a]$, it follows that 31.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-normalized-model-bound} a-\sup _ Xa\leq P_\theta [a]=\varphi . \end{equation}

title: 31.1 Equations for finite measures

text: 31.1 Equations for finite measures For a positive exponent, the right-hand side $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $ changes when $u$ is translated, and this fixes the additive constant. At exponent zero, translation leaves the equation unchanged; instead, a positive scalar in front of the prescribed measure is needed to match its mass. Theorem 31.1.1 . Let $\mu $ be a nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure on $X$. Then: For every $\lambda >0$ there is a unique $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ with $\mu _ u=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $. There are $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and a unique $c>0$ with $\mu _ u=c\mu $. The theorem is proved in section 31.6 . The case of the reference zero, which has minimal singularities because $\theta \geq 0$, is treated first in theorem 31.5.1 ; its solutions then serve as comparison potentials for the reference $\varphi $. For general measures the theorem asserts membership in $\mathcal E_\varphi $, not a bounded difference from $\varphi $.

title: 31.2 Domination
section: 12.5 Relative equations under positive lower mass
text: 31.2 Domination The domination principle compares a potential $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ with a potential $v$ whose measure is larger on $\{ u<v\} $. We first treat the case in which $\mu _ u$ is finite. Stretching $u$ away from $\max (u,v)$ produces envelopes whose measures are bounded, by contact support, by the fixed measure $\mu _ u$; the small tails of this finite measure then exclude collapse. By theorem 13.5.3 and ( 31.1 ), the uniform lower mass bound is \[  \mu _ a(X)\geq \kappa :=(1-\varepsilon )^ n v_-(\theta )>0 \qquad (a\in \mathcal E_\varphi ).  \] Theorem 31.2.1 . Let $u\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ have finite $\mu _ u$, and let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $v\preceq \varphi $. If, for some $0\leq c<1$, \[  \mu _ u\leq c\mu _ v\quad \hbox{on }\{ u<v\} ,  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. It suffices to prove $u\geq w$ for $w=\max (u,v)$. Upward stability (proposition 13.4.2 ) gives $w\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, and locality gives $\mu _ u\leq c\mu _ w$ on $\{ u<w\} $. For $b>1$ put $q_ b=Q_ b(u,w)$, which belongs to $\mathcal E_\varphi $ by lemma 13.4.3 . It satisfies $q_ b\leq u$, and by contact support its measure is carried by \[  D_ b=\{ b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})w=u\} .  \] On $D_ b$ the potential $b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})w$ touches $u$ from below, so positivity of mixed products and ordered contact give \[  b^{-n}\mu _{q_ b}+(1-b^{-1})^ n\mu _ w\leq \mu _ u.  \] Choose $b$ so large that $(1-b^{-1})^ n>c$. Comparing this inequality with $\mu _ u\leq c\mu _ w$ on $D_ b\cap \{ u<w\} $ forces both $\mu _ w$ and $\mu _{q_ b}$ to vanish there. Since $\mu _ w(X)$ may be infinite, this subtraction is first carried out on common finite truncation levels of the potentials, where all measures are finite; exhausting the complements of the pole sets then gives the assertion for the extended measures. It follows that $\mu _{q_ b}$ is carried by $D_ b\cap \{ u=w\} \subseteq \{ q_ b=u\} $. Since $q_ b\leq u$, ordered contact applied once more gives 31.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-contact-fixed-measure} \mu _{q_ b}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ q_ b=u\} }\mu _ u, \end{equation} with coefficient one, independent of $b$. As $b\to \infty $ through the integers, the potentials $q_ b$ decrease, because the obstacles $bu-(b-1)w=u-(b-1)(w-u)$ do. Suppose that they decreased to $-\infty $ identically. Then theorem 1.4.2 would give $M_ b:=\sup _ Xq_ b\to -\infty $, and ( 31.3 ) would imply \[  \kappa \leq \int _ X\mu _{q_ b} \leq \mu _ u(\{ u\leq M_ b\} )\longrightarrow 0,  \] because $\mu _ u$ is finite and does not charge the pole set of $u$. This is impossible, so the decreasing limit $q$ is not identically $-\infty $. Now fix $a>0$. On $\{ u<w-a\} $, the defining inequality of $q_ b$ gives $q_ b\leq u-(b-1)a$, so $q=-\infty $ at every point of this set where $u$ is finite. Since neither $q$ nor $u$ is identically $-\infty $, their pole sets have zero smooth volume, and hence so does $\{ u<w-a\} $. Thus $u\geq w$ almost everywhere, and then everywhere by lemma 1.3.3 . In particular $u\geq v$. $\square$

u $. To keep the limit in $\mathcal E_\varphi $, we construct, after passing to a subsequence, a common lower envelope in this class. Partitioning the contact set of a finite rooftop according to the obstacle it touches shows that the rooftop measure is again dominated by $
u $, with no factor depending on the number of obstacles. A summable integration error, combined with the lower mass bound $\kappa $, then prevents the stretched rooftops from collapsing, uniformly in the number of obstacles. Lemma 31.3.1 . Suppose $u_ j\in \mathcal E_\varphi $, $u_ j	o u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ in $L^1(X)$, and $\mu _{u_ j}\leq 
u $ for a fixed finite non-pluripolar measure $

u $, lemma 1.23.1 gives \[  I_ j=\int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{u_ j}-\mathrm{e}^ u|\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ j}\longrightarrow 0.  \] We extract, once and for all, a subsequence with $I_ j\leq 2^{-j}$ along which $u_ j	o u$ almost everywhere for smooth volume. Partition their contact sets according to the first index at which the minimum is attained. u , \qquad \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{p_{j,N}}-\mathrm{e}^ u|\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{p_{j,N}} \leq \sum _{\ell =j}^ N I_\ell \leq 2^{1-j}. \end{equation} The first bound has no factor $N$, because each piece is controlled by the restriction of the same measure $

u (X)\exp \! \left( rac{\sup _ X r_{j,N}}Bight). \end{equation} On the other hand, choose $K>0$ with $B^ n
u (\{ u\leq -K\} )<\kappa /2$; this is possible because $u
ot\equiv -\infty $ and $
u $ does not charge its pole set.
