title: 33 Problems in Hermitian pluripotential theory
text: 33 Problems in Hermitian pluripotential theory Throughout this chapter $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$. The Hermitian forms, volume forms and backgrounds needed for each problem are fixed in the section where the problem is stated. Many arguments in this book begin with linear control. A uniform bound on Gauduchon traces makes a family of positive currents relatively compact, and Gauduchon duality expresses scalar invariants through optimization over test currents. Most of the questions below arise because such linear control does not determine the nonlinear data of a limit, namely its Monge–Ampère mass and its singularities. Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$ that fails the bounded mass property of definition 6.5.1 . By proposition 6.7.1 , corollary 6.7.2 , currents $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with integrable coefficients can converge in the coefficient $L^1$ norm, with Gauduchon trace measures converging in total variation, while their determinant masses are infinite. By proposition 16.3.3 , even the relative envelope class $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,0)$ of definition 13.4.1 contains potentials of infinite mass. Passing from linear bounds to an exact equation therefore requires additional control of the nonlinear limit. Two further requirements recur. Positivity of a scalar invariant does not imply strict positivity: the smooth semipositive background on a projective manifold in theorem 26.13.2 has positive Gauduchon variational volume but is not big. Likewise, an envelope realizing prescribed divisorial lower bounds may acquire larger orders, and then it does not recover the prescribed singularity type. Thus the mass of a limiting solution, strict positivity of a current, and exactness of its divisorial orders have to be checked in their respective arguments.

title: 33.1 Threshold equations and singular limits
text: 33.1 Threshold equations and singular limits Solving a Monge–Ampère equation with singular data involves two separate steps: one constructs a subsolution at the optimal coefficient, and then passes to a limit of approximate solutions without losing Monge–Ampère mass. Throughout this section, $h$ is a Hermitian form on $X$ and $\mathrm{d}V$ a smooth positive probability volume form. We write $v_-(h)$ and $v_+(h)$ for the lower and upper masses of $h$ (definition 6.5.1 ), $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)$ for the extended Monge–Ampère measure of $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ (theorem 6.1.2 ), which may have infinite mass, and $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ for the relative envelope class with reference $0$. For a nonzero nonnegative density $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, the density threshold $b_ h(f)$ is the largest $a\geq 0$ for which some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ (theorem 14.27.2 ); such a $u$ with $a=b_ h(f)$ is called a threshold subsolution. Finally, $\mathcal D_ h$ is the space of density roots $p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$ whose root norm $\rho _ h(p)=b_ h(|p|^ n)^{-1/n}$ is finite (proposition 14.31.3 ). In two regimes the equations are solved for arbitrary finite non-pluripolar measures. For a semipositive big background $\theta $ with positive lower mass and a model reference satisfying ( 13.26 ), theorem 31.1.1 solves both the equation with a positive exponent and the normalized equation. For an arbitrary smooth big background $\theta $, theorem 32.7.1 , theorem 32.7.2 solve both equations under bounded mass and positive lower volume of the model reference. The existence theorem for $L^ p$ densities in the minimal ordinary singularity type, in section 14.15 , requires neither mass property; in the second regime, corollary 32.8.3 also places the solutions for $L^ p$ densities in the prescribed ordinary model type. Under bounded mass the reference may also vary. Suppose the ordinary model references converge for the volume comparison $d_\theta $ of section 30.6 and have a common positive lower bound for their lower volumes, and the densities converge in $L^1$ of a fixed finite non-pluripolar measure. Then, by theorem 32.5.4 , theorem 32.7.3 , for a fixed positive exponent the solutions converge in capacity and their Monge–Ampère measures converge in total variation. At exponent zero the scalars and the measures converge, and every $L^1$-convergent subsequence of normalized solutions converges to a solution of the limiting equation; singling out one limit potential requires a further uniqueness or selection argument. To remove these mass hypotheses, one must replace each place where they enter the compactness arguments. The proof in the semipositive regime uses finite auxiliary contact measures to construct a common lower envelope, and then obtains the limit for a moving measure from convergence in capacity and control of deep sublevel tails. The proof for an arbitrary big background uses finite upper relative volumes to construct a rooftop between classes and to maximize the weighted measure. In either case one must still prove that the measure of the solution is finite; the formal existence of the envelopes does not give this.

title: 33.1.1 Individual density thresholds
text:
33.1.1 Individual density thresholds One must distinguish solvability for all measures from solvability for one fixed density. By corollary 14.26.4 , the normalized equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=c\mu $ has a solution in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ for every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $ exactly when $v_-(h)>0$. When $v_-(h)=0$, theorem 14.26.3 produces a probability density in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, bounded below by a positive constant, that admits no positive scaled subsolution. Such obstructing densities are dense in $L^1$, although every smooth strictly positive density is solvable. The compact threefold of theorem 26.18.1 has $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian form $h$, so the obstruction does occur. For one nonnegative density $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, the threshold $b_ h(f)$ is the decreasing limit of the normalization constants of the bounded truncations $\min (f,k)$, see ( 14.101 ). An argument with upper envelopes and damped continuity shows that a subsolution attains this coefficient, but it proves neither an exact equation nor finiteness of the mass. Smooth comparison tests alone do not detect the threshold, by theorem 14.27.5 . On the other hand, the Gauduchon formula of theorem 14.28.1 expresses the root norm as a supremum of linear tests, which makes $b_ h$ upper semicontinuous in $L^1$. The densities with positive threshold are those whose roots $f^{1/n}$ lie in $\mathcal D_ h$, and this space does not depend on the Hermitian form (proposition 14.28.2 ). With the norm $\| p\| _{L^ n}+ho _ h(p)$ it is a Banach space; it equals $L^ n$ when $v_-(h)>0$, and it is complete for $ho _ h$ alone exactly when $v_+(h)<\infty $, by proposition 14.31.3 , proposition 14.31.4 . Problem 33.1.1 . Let $h$ be a Hermitian form on $X$ with zero lower mass, $v_-(h)=0$, and let $\mathrm{d}V$ be a smooth positive probability volume form. Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero, with positive density threshold $b_ h(f)>0$. Does there exist $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V?  \] Determine the singularity type or envelope class in which such an equation should be posed. The hypothesis $v_-(h)=0$ is what makes the problem open. For $\lambda >0$, write $u_\lambda $ for the greatest solution of the exponential equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, when it exists (theorem 14.34.1 ). When $v_-(h)>0$, corollary 31.7.1 solves the threshold equation in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ for every nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ density: comparison of finite measures identifies the scalar, and dominated continuity shows that every $L^1$-convergent subsequence of the normalized greatest exponential solutions $u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $ converges in capacity. This covers the Hopf example of chapter 8 , which has positive lower mass but not bounded mass. For $L^ p$ densities with $p>1$, the continuous solution of the normalized equation and proposition 14.27.4 answer the question without any lower mass assumption. At zero lower mass, theorem 14.29.3 solves the threshold equation with finite mass for explicit densities on a split product with projective space; these densities are integrable but belong to no $L^ p$ with $p>1$. There the background $h$ is a nonclosed Hermitian form, and the canonical solutions $u$ belong to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$; moreover, for every $0<\delta <1$, the envelope $P_{\delta h}(u)$ of section 1.19 , the largest $\delta h$-plurisubharmonic function below $u$, is not identically $-\infty $. More generally, theorem 14.29.5 solves the exact finite-mass equation for every nonzero integrable density from a closed Kähler factor, with the appropriate change of reference volume. The threshold is the split background's mass divided by the integral of the factor density. On the product of the elliptic threefold with $\mathbb P^2$, this gives threshold $240\pi $ for every probability density from that factor. An arbitrary density on the product need not have this form, and the general problem remains open. For product measures from a projective-line factor, proposition 14.30.4 gives an exact finite-mass equation for every non-polar factor probability. In the separated sector, boundedness and continuity are exactly those of its logarithmic potential. When that potential is finite and continuous, theorem 14.30.5 identifies the attained coefficient over all genuine subsolutions, constructs the greatest exponential solution for every positive exponent, and gives whole-family uniform selection with error $O(\lambda )$. The Sobolev measure trace supplies existence, and bounded comparison extends greatestness to singular competitors. Weighted circle probabilities in proposition 14.30.6 give measures singular with respect to smooth volume. The zero-lower-mass specialization retains the factor hypothesis. These product criteria do not classify arbitrary measures on a fixed Hermitian manifold. A different geometric condition applies directly to singular measures on a fixed Hermitian manifold. The probability $ho $ of ( 14.99 ) is chosen from a coordinate ball before the datum. If $
u $ is finite, nonzero and has bounded density with respect to $ho $, proposition 14.25.1 , theorem 14.25.3 give a strict Hölder scaled subsolution and a unique bounded exponential solution for every positive exponent. In addition, corollary 14.25.2 gives a normalized Hölder solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)=c
u $ with $c>0$ obtained as part of the solution. This includes bounded densities on one of the spheres and needs neither a product decomposition nor positive lower mass. It is a sufficient condition; it does not classify arbitrary individual measures or identify a homogeneous threshold coefficient. For the data of 33.1.1 , corollary 14.34.2 shows that the greatest exponential solutions $u_\lambda $ exist for every $\lambda >0$, that the scalars $c_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \sup _ Xu_\lambda }$ converge to $b_ h(f)$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, and that the measures $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V$ converge in total variation. What is missing in general is convergence in capacity of the normalized potentials. If $f^{1/n}$ lies in the subspace $\mathcal D_ h^0$ of density roots with uniformly vanishing tails (proposition 14.31.5 ), proposition 14.34.3 gives a modulus for the errors of the scalars and of the measures; a rate linear in the exponent would require further control. For $n\geq 3$, a power capacity bound ( 14.115 ) supplies both root tails and the compactness needed for an exact equation. By theorem 14.32.1 , the threshold is positive and finite, the root belongs to $\mathcal D_ h^0$, and a subsequence of the normalized clipped solutions converges uniformly to a continuous solution at $b_ h(f)$. The logarithmic density of theorem 14.32.2 satisfies this condition on every fixed Hermitian background, while belonging to no $L^ p$ with $p>1$. Its reference potential is continuous but not Hölder, and its root tails have the bound ( 14.118 ). These conclusions use the capacity assumption on the fixed datum. Whether all positive-threshold roots have vanishing tails, and whether tails alone imply an exact equation at zero lower mass, remain open. Positivity and integrability of $f$ do not make the threshold positive, and exponential equations can be solvable even when it vanishes. For zero threshold, theorem 14.34.5 gives a sufficient growth condition in the radial variable, and theorem 14.34.6 constructs a single strictly positive probability density with $b_ h(f)=0$ whose exponential equation has, for every positive exponent, a greatest solution of finite mass; all its solutions are unbounded. In that construction the projective factors are chosen after the collapsing sequence on the base. For this density, proposition 14.34.8 shows that any choice of exact exponential solutions has total mass tending to zero as the exponent decreases to zero; the argument says nothing about convergence of the normalized potentials. In general, the set $\Lambda _ h(f)$ of positive exponents for which the exponential equation is solvable is an upper interval, by proposition 14.34.7 . A necessary criterion on the density for solvability at zero threshold, solvability for an arbitrary prescribed concentration family, and an extension to arbitrary non-pluripolar measures are open. Suppose that $a=\inf \Lambda _ h(f)$ is positive. By proposition 14.34.10 , $a$ belongs to $\Lambda _ h(f)$ if and only if there are exact solutions at exponents decreasing to $a$ whose suprema are bounded below; if $a
otin \Lambda _ h(f)$, the total masses of every such sequence of solutions tend to zero. The common upper barrier of lemma 14.34.9 also shows that the greatest solutions become monotone in the exponent after a logarithmic correction. Consequently, by proposition 14.34.11 , they are continuous from the right in $L^1$ and in capacity at every exponent in $\Lambda _ h(f)$, and their Monge–Ampère measures converge in total variation. At every interior exponent, proposition 14.34.12 gives a left limit in $L^1$ and in capacity that solves the equation at that exponent and lies below the greatest solution; the equation measures converge in total variation. By proposition 14.34.13 , these potentials can differ at only countably many exponents. Whether a positive endpoint can fail to belong to $\Lambda _ h(f)$, or an actual jump from the left can occur, remains open.

title: Problem 33.1.1
text: Problem 33.1.1 . Let $h$ be a Hermitian form on $X$ with zero lower mass, $v_-(h)=0$, and let $\mathrm{d}V$ be a smooth positive probability volume form. Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero, with positive density threshold $b_ h(f)>0$. Does there exist $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V?  \] Determine the singularity type or envelope class in which such an equation should be posed.

title: 33.1.2 Dual attainment and exact equations
text: 33.1.2 Dual attainment and exact equations For the current formulation of the dual problem, suppose $n\geq 2$. By Gauduchon duality, the threshold is determined by a maximization problem over test currents. Let $\mathscr G_ h$ be the compact convex set of normalized Gauduchon currents, the positive $(n-1,n-1)$-currents $T$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ and $\int _ Xh\wedge T=1$ (section 4.4 ), and let $k_ T$ be the determinant density of $T$ (theorem 26.8.1 ). For $0\leq p\in \mathcal D_ h$, the root norm $\rho _ h(p)$ is the supremum of $D_ p(T)=\int _ Xp\, k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V$ over $T\in \mathscr G_ h$. A maximizing current can turn the threshold inequality into an equality, provided its regularity, or control of its weighted moments, prevents loss of mass in the limit. For roots in the closed order ideal $\mathcal D_ h^0$, theorem 26.9.1 , proposition 26.9.4 show that the supremum is attained and represent all supporting probabilities of the threshold functional by maximizing currents. These probabilities are absolutely continuous, and by proposition 26.9.5 the trace errors along smooth maximizing sequences tend to zero in total variation. Uniform integrability along a single maximizing sequence already gives attainment and convergence of the determinant-weighted measures of that sequence (proposition 26.9.3 ), but it does not give the representation of all supporting probabilities. Regularity of a maximizer has strong consequences. Let $n\geq 2$ and let $f$ be a nonzero density with $b_ h(f)>0$. If $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer, then $f^{1/n}$ is smooth and nonnegative, and every threshold subsolution is smooth and solves the equation exactly, uniquely up to constants (corollary 26.9.6 ). For a Kähler background, corollary 26.9.8 shows that such a maximizer exists exactly when $f$ is smooth and strictly positive. The strict positivity fails for nonclosed backgrounds: on every compact complex manifold of dimension at least two, example 26.9.9 gives a smooth strictly positive maximizer for a density vanishing on an open set. Theorem 26.9.10 weakens the hypothesis to a smooth semipositive maximizer that is strictly positive outside a proper analytic subset $Z\subset X$. It still gives an exact equation on all of $X$, smoothness of the solutions off $Z$, and uniqueness of threshold subsolutions up to constants. The proof takes the maximum of two subsolutions and uses a Gauduchon integral to eliminate the divisorial part of their difference; no singularity type is prescribed in advance. The prime divisors along which the threshold solution has positive Lelong number have linearly independent Bott–Chern classes, by corollary 26.9.22 . In this regime write $b=b_ h(f)$ and $c_\lambda =\exp (\lambda \sup _ Xu_\lambda )$ for the greatest exponential solutions $u_\lambda $, $\lambda >0$. By proposition 26.9.11 , the whole family of normalized solutions converges in $L^1$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, it has a fixed lower barrier, and $b\leq c_\lambda \leq b\mathrm{e}^{C\lambda }$ for a finite constant $C$ independent of $\lambda $. If the envelope $P_{\delta h}(u_0)$ of the normalized threshold solution $u_0$ is not identically $-\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$, the convergence also holds in capacity (corollary 26.9.12 ); for $L^ p$ data with $p>1$ the threshold solution is continuous and the convergence is uniform (corollary 26.9.18 ). In example 26.9.23 the solution is smooth, but the root $f^{1/n}$ is not differentiable on $Z$. For general $L^1$ data we do not know whether $P_{\delta h}(u_0)\not\equiv -\infty $ holds automatically, nor how regular the solution is across $Z$. The moment criterion of theorem 26.9.24 requires no regularity of a maximizing current. Suppose that the supremum-normalized $h$-plurisubharmonic functions have uniformly bounded first moments against the determinant-weighted probabilities of one smooth maximizing sequence. Then the exponential solutions have a fixed lower barrier, and their normalized cluster limits lie below the greatest normalized threshold subsolution $\Phi _ f$ of proposition 14.27.3 . If, in addition, $P_{\delta h}(\Phi _ f)\not\equiv -\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$, the lower-barrier criterion gives convergence in capacity along subsequences and an exact threshold equation, without either mass property. An entropy bound on these test probabilities implies both the bound on first moments and the uniform integrability along one sequence used above. By proposition 15.6.1 , such an entropy bound is equivalent to a uniform bound for $H_0$, the convex dual of the normalization functional with zero reference (chapter 15 ). An entropy bound does not, however, give the condition on $P_{\delta h}(\Phi _ f)$. Attainment by a singular current therefore does not settle the equation by itself. The roots from a closed factor form a closed subspace of $\mathcal D_ h^0$ isomorphic to $L^ n$ on that factor, by proposition 14.31.6 ; some of these roots belong to no higher $L^ r$ space, and their tails decay only as a power of $\log K$. At zero lower mass we do not know in general whether the root-tail condition $f^{1/n}\in \mathcal D_ h^0$ suffices for an exact threshold equation, or even whether $\mathcal D_ h^0=\mathcal D_ h$. By proposition 26.9.2 , the tail condition is equivalent to continuity of the threshold under logarithmic perturbations $\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}f$ with $F_ j$ uniformly bounded and tending to zero in measure. This is continuity on order intervals, not continuity of the threshold under arbitrary $L^1$ perturbations. Convergence in capacity cannot be replaced by $L^1$ convergence in these arguments. On a curve, the ideal envelopes with finitely many logarithmic poles in theorem 16.4.2 have zero non-pluripolar mass, yet they converge in $L^1$ to a smooth potential of positive mass. The existence theorems obtain the stronger convergence from their measure bounds; representing the measure by a carrier, even within a prescribed singularity type, does not provide it.

title: 33.1.3 Regularity of singular solutions
text: 33.1.3 Regularity of singular solutions Regularity estimates provide the compactness needed to single out a limit as the exponential parameter tends to zero. In this subsection $\theta $ is a smooth big real $(1,1)$-form, and $\rho $ is the strict barrier with analytic singularities fixed in section 14.12 , with pole set $Z$ and regular locus $\Omega =X\setminus Z$. For bounded solutions with $L^ p$ density, $p>1$, theorem 14.5.1 gives continuity wherever $\rho $ is locally bounded. A locally Hölder continuous solution with minimal singularities is smooth on $\Omega $ when the density is smooth and positive there (theorem 14.17.1 ), and global $L^ p$ control of the density gives the Hölder hypothesis (theorem 14.16.1 , corollary 14.17.11 ). For a fixed reference $\eta $ with $\rho \leq \eta \leq 0$, corollary 14.14.2 shows that the potentials $u$ with $\eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta $ and uniformly bounded $L^ p$ densities form a compact family for uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $. Since the reference need not have minimal singularities, this compactness does not by itself make the potentials regular. In the minimal type, the convergence of scalars and densities in proposition 14.16.2 identifies the equation satisfied by every cluster limit of the normalized exponential solutions. Smoothness of the density on an open set is not enough. On a compact Kähler manifold with a smooth positive volume form, theorem 28.10.1 proves that the full-mass solution is smooth on the ample locus of every big class, nef or not. Smoothness of the density only on the ample locus, however, does not imply global $L^ p$ integrability. On an arbitrary open set where the density is smooth, it does not even imply continuity of a bounded solution with minimal singularities: theorem 14.20.4 gives a compact Kähler counterexample with constant density on a ball. When the background has smooth local potentials, theorem 14.20.1 gives a sufficient condition in terms of smooth boundary traces on small balls. Among prescribed singularity types, the resolved logarithmic types of theorem 14.21.1 admit Hölder remainders when their residual form is positive, while for exceptional minimal poles theorem 14.22.2 , theorem 14.22.4 give a Hölder remainder on the target and quantify the loss of integrability caused by the Jacobian. Neither result covers arbitrary prescribed types, and neither derives a global Hölder bound from information on the density confined to the regular locus. At a zero of the density, even smooth data need not give a smooth residual: proposition 28.11.4 , example 28.11.6 give a necessary vanishing order and show that it is not sufficient. Beyond these resolved and explicit geometric cases, the regularity questions are open. For the nonlogarithmic projective types of section 15.14 , the central density criterion gives residual regularity across the pole and smoothly through density zeros. Perturbing the same singular reference as an everywhere radial obstacle instead gives a globally $C^{1,1}$ residual, zero near the pole, with open free regions of zero measure (theorem 15.15.2 , corollary 15.15.3 ). Fixed-support bounded $C^2$ obstacle families satisfy the derivative stability of theorem 15.15.4 , and proposition 15.15.5 transfers the full envelope to any fixed positive Hermitian product factor. These explicit ordinary-type regimes do not cover general singular references or ideal weighted envelopes.

title: 33.1.4 Uniqueness and selection
text: 33.1.4 Uniqueness and selection Where the density vanishes, the linearized equation degenerates, and the zero set can separate regions where it is elliptic. The question is whether the difference of two solutions can vary from one such region to another. Throughout this subsection $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$, $f$ is smooth and nonnegative, and potentials are normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. On $\mathbb P^3$, theorem 11.6.1 gives a nonclosed Hermitian form and a smooth nonnegative density with two distinct smooth normalized solutions; there the density vanishes on an open set. The construction of theorem 11.7.1 has uncountably many smooth normalized solutions for a density that is positive off two disjoint real hypersurfaces, and after a modification of the background, theorem 11.8.1 achieves exactly quadratic vanishing on those hypersurfaces. Thus neither a zero set of zero volume nor vanishing of finite order guarantees uniqueness. In all these examples the background is a Hermitian form with bounded mass; the degeneracy responsible for nonuniqueness lies in the density and in the solution forms. These examples restrict any geometric use of the equation. A construction assigning a canonical potential to arbitrary nonnegative data must specify a selection procedure and prove that it is well defined; existence in the minimal ordinary singularity type does not provide one. The scalar, which is unique, and for strictly positive data the corresponding variational volume, remain meaningful without uniqueness of the potential. In low dimension uniqueness holds under additional conditions. On a compact Hermitian surface, 11.3.2 proves uniqueness for $C^2$ potentials when the common density is continuous and positive on a dense set, with no differential condition on the metric; in dimension three, 11.3.1 uses instead a sign condition on $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. The two arguments rest on different integration identities: the cofactor identity ( 11.20 ) and a signed estimate for the quadratic difference. When $\{ f>0\} $ is connected and dense, theorem 11.4.1 shows that two bounded normalized solutions with the same positive scalar coincide; the theorem applies to the measure $cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ after the smooth positive ratio $\mathrm{d}V/\omega ^ n$ is absorbed into the density. In all the counterexamples above whose zero set consists of hypersurfaces, including the real-analytic example of 11.9.1 , the positivity set has three connected components. None of them contradicts 33.6.1 , which concerns strictly positive densities $\mathrm{e}^ F$ with $F$ continuous. For a fixed nonzero density $f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, the exponential equation does select a solution. By theorem 15.12.1 , a weakly compact set of norming probabilities determines the limit: as the exponent tends to zero, the suitably shifted exponential solutions converge to the greatest subsolution of the critical equation that satisfies the integral normalizations given by these probabilities. In a Hermitian background the convergence is uniform; in an arbitrary smooth big background it holds in $L^1(X)$ and locally uniformly off the pole set of the strict barrier. The selected limit inherits the symmetries of the data (proposition 14.19.1 ), and in the projective example theorem 14.19.3 identifies it with the explicit symmetric $C^{1,1}$ solution of proposition 11.6.2 . Selection thus coexists with nonuniqueness of the normalized critical equation. For the merely integrable radial densities on zero-lower-mass products, theorem 14.35.2 determines the whole supremum-normalized limit, even with joint variation of the density parameter and exponent. Scalar centering has a finite limit exactly below the moment boundary of proposition 14.35.3 ; at the boundary and above it diverges. For logarithmic product models with positive residual, theorem 15.13.3 also gives selection under independent variation of the reference coefficients, background, density and exponent; centering follows each varying critical scalar. Selection for arbitrary integrable data and general varying singular reference types remains open. Dual attainment gives a different criterion. In dimension at least two, suppose that $f\neq 0$, that $b_\omega (f)>0$, and that $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizing Gauduchon current. Then the normalized threshold solution is unique, and the whole family of normalized solutions with positive exponent converges uniformly to it (corollary 26.9.6 , corollary 26.9.7 ). The density of example 26.9.9 satisfies this condition although it vanishes on an open set. The size of the zero set alone therefore does not decide uniqueness; the dual condition also depends on the background. For prescribed radial nonlogarithmic types, theorem 15.14.2 gives a different kind of regularity: a relative density error $O(r^\delta )$ controls the residual after the singularity is subtracted. The critical $C^1$ and $C^2$ thresholds are attained and are sharp by proposition 15.14.4 . Positive cumulative central mass allows smooth crossing of density zeros, and proposition 15.14.5 gives an open zero annulus with a globally smooth residual. The product construction corollary 15.14.6 transfers this regularity under a zero-lower-mass factor hypothesis. These are radial criteria; they do not imply regularity or uniqueness for general nonsymmetric data.

title: 33.2 Positive Gauduchon volume and bigness
text: 33.2 Positive Gauduchon volume and bigness Fix a smooth strictly positive probability form $\mu $ on $X$. For a pseudoeffective smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, the Gauduchon variational volume $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=\lambda _\mu (\theta )^ n$ of definition 26.1.1 is an infimum over Gauduchon metrics, whereas bigness asks for one potential $u$ making $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ strictly positive. Bigness implies $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )>0$ (corollary 26.1.4 ). The converse fails for nef nonclosed backgrounds: for every $n\geq 3$, theorem 26.13.2 constructs a smooth semipositive background $\theta $ on $\mathbb P^{n-1}\times \mathbb P^1$ with $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=n$ that is not big: no current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of a Hermitian form. In this example a radial potential compensates the determinant, while a closed test current carried by a degenerate fiber detects the missing strict positivity. Positivity of $\mathcal V_\mu $ does not depend on the choice of $\mu $ (proposition 26.14.1 ), but the infimum over all such $\mu $ is a different invariant: by theorem 26.14.3 it is the lower mass, and it vanishes for every Hermitian form on the threefold of theorem 26.18.1 , although Hermitian forms are big. In dimension one, positive volume and bigness are equivalent, since the volume is $\int _ X\theta $. For a closed nef class on a compact Kähler manifold, $\mathcal V_\mu $ is the top self-intersection, and the equivalence is the nef-and-big criterion recalled in [ SGPT ] . On a compact Kähler manifold, theorem 26.11.1 also gives bigness when a closed nef core of positive volume is supplemented by a semipositive form. Whether positive volume implies bigness for general nef nonclosed backgrounds on surfaces is open. In higher dimension, any such criterion requires geometric hypotheses that exclude the radial obstruction.

title: 33.2.1 Collapse of normalized Gauduchon tests
text: 33.2.1 Collapse of normalized Gauduchon tests The root volume and the bigness threshold divide the same pairing by different quantities. Positive volume can fail to imply bigness only if these denominators separate along tests approaching the threshold, and the following calculation isolates this degeneration. For the radial background of theorem 26.13.2 , the normalized $(n-1)$-st powers of a family of balanced test metrics (definition 4.1.1 ) converge weakly to the integration current of the degenerate fiber (proposition 26.13.4 ). The volume-minimizing family approaches the bigness threshold only in dimension three, by proposition 26.13.3 . Fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, and let $\theta $ be a smooth pseudoeffective real $(1,1)$-form. For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, abbreviate the pairings by \[  A_\theta (\gamma )=\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}, \qquad A_ h(\gamma )=\int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] The threshold $\kappa _ h(\theta )$ of corollary 4.3.2 is the infimum of the quotient $A_\theta /A_ h$ over Gauduchon metrics, and it is positive exactly when $\theta $ is big. The root volume $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ is the infimum of $A_\theta /D_\mu $, with the determinant denominator $D_\mu (\gamma )$ of definition 26.1.1 . Proposition 33.2.1 . Let $h$, $\theta $ and $\mu $ be as above, and let $(\gamma _ j)$ be a sequence of Gauduchon metrics. Suppose $n\geq 2$, $\lambda _\mu (\theta )>0$, and $\theta $ is not big. If \[  A_ h(\gamma _ j)=1,\qquad A_\theta (\gamma _ j)\longrightarrow 0,  \] then $D_\mu (\gamma _ j)\to 0$. Such sequences exist. More generally, fix a real number $\delta >0$. If $A_ h(\gamma _ j)=1$ and \[  A_\theta (\gamma _ j)\longrightarrow \kappa _ h(\theta ), \qquad \liminf _ jD_\mu (\gamma _ j)\geq \delta >0,  \] then \[  \kappa _ h(\theta )\geq \delta \lambda _\mu (\theta ).  \] In particular, positive root volume then implies bigness. Proof. Suppose first that $\theta $ is not big. Since $\theta $ is pseudoeffective, the threshold criterion of corollary 4.3.2 gives $\kappa _ h(\theta )=0$, so there are Gauduchon metrics whose quotients $A_\theta /A_ h$ tend to zero. Multiplying a Gauduchon metric by a positive constant multiplies $A_\theta $, $A_ h$ and $D_\mu $ by the same factor; for $n\geq 2$ this factor can be chosen to make $A_ h=1$, without changing either quotient. This gives the sequences in the first assertion. By the definition of the root volume, every Gauduchon metric satisfies 33.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-collapse-basic} \lambda _\mu (\theta )D_\mu (\gamma )\leq A_\theta (\gamma ). \end{equation} Dividing by the positive root volume proves the first assertion. Applying the same inequality to the sequence in the second assertion and taking lower limits gives $\delta \lambda _\mu (\theta )\leq \kappa _ h(\theta )$. If the root volume is positive, then $\kappa _ h(\theta )>0$, and the threshold criterion gives bigness. $\square$ The quotient $D_\mu /A_ h$ is always bounded above. Indeed, the smooth equation for $h$, or ( 33.1 ) with $\theta =h$, gives \[  D_\mu (\gamma )\leq \lambda _\mu (h)^{-1}A_ h(\gamma ).  \] What is missing for the converse direction is a lower bound for $D_\mu $ along suitable sequences minimizing the threshold. Compactness of normalized potentials does not give compactness of these Gauduchon metrics. In dimension one this normalization issue does not arise: the root volume is $\int _ X\theta $, and $\kappa _ h(\theta )=\int _ X\theta /\int _ Xh$. Positive volume and bigness are therefore equivalent by the same threshold criterion. One way to rule out this collapse is to deform the test metrics. Solving a Gauduchon equation replaces the volume density of a test metric while keeping the Aeppli class of $\gamma ^{n-1}$. When $\theta $ is closed, this leaves the numerator $A_\theta $ unchanged. For nonclosed $\theta $, integration by parts leaves derivatives of the background, so such a deformation must also control the change of the pairing; this is the additional estimate needed to use the smooth equation against collapse.

title: 33.3 Closed positivity and geometric equations
text: 33.3 Closed positivity and geometric equations A closed Kähler current places the manifold in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, whereas a strictly positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ in a nonclosed background keeps the torsion $\mathrm{d}\theta $ of that background. This distinction links the passage from positive volume to bigness with the geometry of the manifold, and it limits what a scalar potential equation can prove. Throughout this section $\mu $ is a smooth strictly positive probability form on $X$, and we use balanced and pluriclosed metrics in the sense of definition 4.1.1 . The geometric results from the literature used below are stated, with their precise hypotheses and sources, in section 34.20 .

title: 33.3.1 Nef classes, bigness and the Fujiki class
search_title: Nef classes, bigness and the Fujiki class
text: 33.3.1 Nef classes, bigness and the Fujiki class A compact complex manifold belongs to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$ exactly when it carries a closed Kähler current, that is, a closed positive $(1,1)$-current bounded below by a positive multiple of a Hermitian form. The transcendental Grauert–Riemenschneider conjecture asks whether a closed nef real $(1,1)$-class $\alpha $ with \[  \int _ X\alpha ^ n>0  \] is big. For such a class, bigness is equivalent to $X\in \mathcal C$; the precise statements and sources are given in section 34.20 . The obstruction can be expressed through Monge–Ampère mass. Under the same hypotheses on $\alpha $, one has \[  \alpha \text{ is big}\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad v_+(h)<\infty  \] for a Hermitian metric $h$ on $X$, where $v_+(h)$ is the upper mass of definition 6.5.1 . There is also a characterization of $\mathcal C$ by bounded mass together with positivity of an upper volume of some closed Bott–Chern class; that volume is different from the Gauduchon variational volume $\mathcal V_\mu $. Both results are stated in section 34.20 . The Hopf threefold fails bounded mass, but it is not a counterexample to the conjecture, since a counterexample would also need a closed nef class with positive top self-intersection. A proof of the conjecture must explain why this closed positivity forces bounded mass. The elliptic threefold of theorem 26.18.1 is the complementary test case: it has bounded mass but no big closed class. By proposition 28.9.2 , its nef cone is the nonnegative span of the classes of two smooth semipositive forms of rank one, and every top self-intersection vanishes. This example of zero lower mass therefore does not bear on the conjecture either. The explicit boundary calculation of proposition 28.9.5 describes its degeneration without identifying a nonclosed metric with a closed class. The Gauduchon variational volume of definition 26.1.1 splits the conjecture into two possible steps: 33.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:dp-two-bridges} \int _ X\alpha ^ n>0 \quad \stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow }\quad \mathcal V_\mu (\alpha )>0 \quad \stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow }\quad \alpha \text{ is big}. \end{equation} Neither implication is known on arbitrary compact complex manifolds. The second concerns closed nef backgrounds; the projective counterexample of theorem 26.13.2 has a nonclosed background and does not decide it. On a compact Kähler manifold both implications follow from the usual volume formula for nef classes and the classical nef-and-big criterion. Without closedness, positivity of $\mathcal V_\mu $ cannot characterize $\mathcal C$, since every Hermitian metric $h$ on every compact complex manifold satisfies $\mathcal V_\mu (h)>0$. Problem 33.3.1 . Let $\alpha $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ whose class is nef with $\int _ X\alpha ^ n>0$, and let $h$ be a Hermitian form on $X$. Prove a positive lower bound for the root volume $\lambda _\mu (\alpha )$ of definition 26.1.1 , and rule out the collapse of proposition 33.2.1 along a sequence of Gauduchon metrics minimizing the bigness threshold $\kappa _ h(\alpha )$. The test metrics can be normalized by $\int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=1$. By proposition 33.2.1 , a positive lower bound for $D_\mu (\gamma )$ along one sequence minimizing the threshold would give the second implication. Solving a Gauduchon equation changes the volume density of a test metric while keeping the Aeppli class of $\gamma ^{n-1}$; since $\alpha $ is closed, it also keeps the pairing with $\alpha $. The missing estimate is control of the trace normalization and of the determinant denominator after this change. Prescribing a volume density alone does not give this estimate.

33.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:dp-two-bridges} \int _ X\alpha ^ n>0 \quad \stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow }\quad \mathcal V_\mu (\alpha )>0 \quad \stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow }\quad \alpha \text{ is big}. \end{equation}

title: 33.3.2 Positive lower mass and concentration
text: 33.3.2 Positive lower mass and concentration Positive lower mass is an integrability property of the Gauduchon tests at an endpoint exponent. It is independent of finite upper mass: the threefold of theorem 26.18.1 has $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian metric and carries a balanced metric of finite upper mass, while the normalized Hopf metric has $v_-=6$ and $v_+=\infty $. Let $n\geq 2$, let $h$ be a Hermitian form and $\mathrm{d}V$ a smooth positive volume form. Recall the set $\mathscr G_ h$ of normalized Gauduchon currents (section 4.4 ) and the determinant measure $\Gamma _0$ of ( 26.39 ), and write \[  \Gamma _0(T)=k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad T\in \mathscr G_ h.  \] By theorem 26.8.2 , 33.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:pvp-endpoint-geometric} v_-(h)>0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h} \| k_ T\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathrm{d}V)}<\infty , \end{equation} and the exact value of the supremum is $v_-(h)^{-1/n}$, including the value $+\infty $. Uniform estimates for every smaller exponent $1<q<n/(n-1)$ hold without either mass property. In the example of zero lower mass, the endpoint estimate fails already for smooth strictly positive tests. Positivity, the condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ and the trace normalization alone therefore do not control concentration at the endpoint exponent. Problem 33.3.2 . Let $n\geq 2$ and let $h$ be a Hermitian form on $X$. Find geometric conditions, beyond the metric identities in corollary 26.17.1 , that imply the endpoint estimate in ( 33.3 ), and explain how they exclude the degeneration of zero lower mass constructed in section 26.18 . Corollary 26.17.1 proves the endpoint bound when some Hermitian metric $g$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$, which includes all compact Kähler manifolds and all compact complex surfaces. For a fixed smooth strictly positive density, theorem 26.6.2 gives a smooth maximizing current with bounded determinant density. However, proposition 26.17.2 produces maximizing sequences in fixed Kähler classes whose moments diverge at every exponent above the endpoint. Exact maximizers and maximizing sequences therefore require different estimates. For principal elliptic threefolds over Kähler surfaces, theorem 26.16.3 gives a geometric sufficient condition: the sum of the squares of the two real curvature forms is nonnegative and not identically zero. A bounded cubic identity then gives positive lower mass, and the determinant bound transfers to every Hermitian background. These manifolds admit no pluriclosed metric; proposition 26.16.5 , proposition 26.16.6 give explicit families. A primitive pair of curvature forms has the opposite sign, by proposition 26.16.4 , so this criterion leaves the general problem open. The balanced condition and bounded upper mass do not suffice, even together, as the threefold of theorem 26.18.1 shows. On this elliptic fibration, the identity ( 26.114 ) relates the failure of the lower bound to a vertical Dirichlet integral, and the horizontal curvature forms $\alpha ,\beta $ of section 26.18 have a positive exact product $\alpha \wedge \beta $, which excludes pluriclosed metrics and closed Kähler currents. These calculations give geometric information about this example, but not a classification of all degenerations of the lower mass. For equations the consequence is exact: in a Hermitian background, corollary 14.26.4 characterizes positive lower mass by solvability of the normalized equation for all finite non-pluripolar measures. When the lower mass vanishes, even a positive density in $L^1$ bounded away from zero can admit no positive scaled subsolution. The remaining questions about equations concern specified measures or additional geometric hypotheses, and, separately, the effect of the exponential weight.
33.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:pvp-endpoint-geometric} v_-(h)>0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h} \| k_ T\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathrm{d}V)}<\infty , \end{equation}

title: 33.3.3 Primitive elliptic bundles
text:
33.3.3 Primitive elliptic bundles On a primitive elliptic bundle, the variation of the top-degree mass is a vertical Dirichlet integral. This gives the exact upper mass and a positive lower bound for separated potentials. The lower mass over all potentials remains a geometric question, since the collapse construction over a product of curves does not transfer directly to a base without curves. Let $(B,\eta )$ be a connected compact Kähler surface and let $L	o B$ be a holomorphic line bundle such that \[  \int _ Bc_1(L)\wedge \eta =0.  \] Choose a smooth Hermitian metric on $L$ whose curvature is primitive with respect to $\eta $. Such a metric exists: for an arbitrary metric, the trace of the curvature with respect to $\eta $ has mean zero by the condition above, and the scalar Poisson equation gives a smooth change of metric that cancels this trace. Let $c$ be the resulting smooth closed curvature representative of $-c_1(L)$, so that $\eta \wedge c=0$. Write $\pi :L	o B$ for the bundle projection and $w$ for a nonzero vector in a fiber, with norm taken in the chosen metric. On the complement $L^	imes $ of the zero section, put \[  t=\log |w|^2,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t=\pi ^*c.  \] For $q>1$, form the quotient \[  X=L^	imes /\langle w\mapsto qwangle , \qquad \pi :X\longrightarrow B, \qquad T=2\log q, \qquad A=\int _ B\eta ^2,  \] where we use the same symbol $\pi $ for the induced projection. The action increases $t$ by $T$. It is free and properly discontinuous, and the compact annulus $1\leq |w|\leq q$ meets every orbit. Hence $X$ is a connected compact complex threefold; in this subsection it replaces the general manifold of the chapter. Over a trivializing open set $U\subset B$, a local holomorphic frame of $L$ identifies the fibration with $U	imes (\mathbb C^*/q^{\mathbb Z})$.  Since $\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$ are invariant under the action, they descend to $X$, and we set \[  D=\mathrm{d}t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t,\qquad \omega =\pi ^*\eta +D.  \] The form $D$ has rank one; it is semipositive and positive on the vertical line, and its kernel projects isomorphically onto the tangent space of $B$. Hence $\omega $ is Hermitian. Proposition 33.3.3 . The metric $\omega $ is balanced and satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\pi ^*(c^2)\geq 0,\qquad \int _ X\omega ^3=3TA.  \] For every smooth real $u$, 33.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:primitive-elliptic-mass} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =3TA-3\int _ X\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge  igl (-\pi ^*(c^2) igr ). \end{equation} In particular $v_+(\omega )=3TA$, and the canonical bundles satisfy $K_ X\simeq \pi ^*K_ B$. If $c_1(L)
e 0$ in real cohomology, $X$ admits neither a pluriclosed metric nor a closed Kähler current. If $c_1(L)=0$ in real cohomology, the chosen $\omega $ is Kähler. Proof. Write $a=\mathrm{d}t$ and $b=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$. Then $\mathrm{d}a=0$, $\mathrm{d}b=\pi ^*c$, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}a=-\pi ^*c$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b=0$. Consequently \[  D^2=0,\qquad \mathrm{d}D=-a\wedge \pi ^*c, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D=-\pi ^*(c^2),  \] \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2)=-2\pi ^*(\eta \wedge c)\wedge a=0,  \] so $\omega $ is balanced. Since $c$ is primitive, its eigenvalues relative to $\eta $ are $\lambda $ and $-\lambda $ for a function $\lambda \geq 0$, so $c^2=-\lambda ^2\eta ^2$. This proves the asserted sign of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. To compute the volume, fix an elliptic fiber $E=\pi ^{-1}(b_0)$, where $b_0\in B$. In a logarithmic fiber coordinate $x+\mathrm{i}y$, the real periods are $\log q$ and $2\pi $, while $t$ equals $2x$ up to an additive constant and $D|_ E=\pi ^{-1}\mathrm{d}x\wedge \mathrm{d}y$. Thus $\int _ ED=T$. Since $\omega ^3=3\pi ^*(\eta ^2)\wedge D$, the volume formula follows. For the mass identity, expand the cube in ( 33.4 ). The terms with one and with three factors $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ integrate to zero, because $\omega ^2$ is closed and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is exact. For the remaining term, put $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. Integration by parts gives \[  \int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2\wedge \omega =\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge S =-\int _ X\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge S,  \] where the last equality uses $\mathrm{d}S=0$. This proves the identity. Its last integral is nonnegative, and $u=0$ attains the upper bound $3TA$. Since smooth and bounded potentials have the same mass extrema, by theorem 26.14.3 , this proves $v_+(\omega )=3TA$. If $c_1(L)=0$ in real cohomology, then $c$ is exact and Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ Bc^2=0$. The pointwise identity $c^2=-\lambda ^2\eta ^2$ then forces $c=0$, and $\omega $ is closed. Otherwise $S=-\pi ^*(c^2)$ is nonzero, smooth and semipositive. For a pluriclosed metric $\gamma $, Stokes' theorem would give \[  0<\int _ X\gamma \wedge S =\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma =0,  \] a contradiction. Likewise, a closed positive current $R\geq \varepsilon \omega $ with $\varepsilon >0$ would give $0<\int _ XR\wedge S=\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$. All these pairings are pairings of currents with smooth forms. Finally, let $w$ be a local holomorphic fiber coordinate given by a frame of $L$, and let $\sigma $ be a local holomorphic two-form on $B$. The form $\pi ^*\sigma \wedge \mathrm{d}w/w$ is invariant under the quotient action. Changing the frame of $L$ adds to $\mathrm{d}w/w$ a horizontal one-form, whose wedge product with $\pi ^*\sigma $ vanishes. These local sections of $K_ X$ therefore have the transition functions of $\pi ^*K_ B$, which proves $K_ X\simeq \pi ^*K_ B$. $\square$ For separated potentials, positivity bounds both the amplitude and the downward slope of the vertical derivative. The sharp variance bound under these two constraints determines how much mass such a potential can lose. For $M,T>0$, set \[  F(M,T)=  egin{cases}  T^2/12,& T\leq 2M,\  M^2-4M^3/(3T),& T\geq 2M. \end{cases}  \] Lemma 33.3.4 . If a smooth real $T$-periodic function $p$ has mean zero, $|p|<M$ and $p'>-1$, then \[   rac1T\int _0^ T p^2\, \mathrm{d}s<F(M,T).  \] The supremum of the left side over this class is $F(M,T)$. Proof. For $p=0$ the inequality holds because $F(M,T)>0$. Otherwise set $a=\max p>0$, $-b=\min p<0$ and $r=a+b$. Integrating $-p'<1$ over a forward interval $I$ from a maximum to the next minimum gives $r<|I|\leq T$; also $r<2M$, since $|p|<M$. The function $G(s)=(a-s)(s+b)$ is nonnegative on the range of $p$. Since $p$ has mean zero and $-p'<1$, integration over $I$ gives \[  abT-\int _0^ T p^2\, \mathrm{d}s =\int _0^ T G(p)\, \mathrm{d}s \geq -\int _ I G(p)p'\, \mathrm{d}s = rac{r^3}{6}.  \] As $ab\leq r^2/4$, the average of $p^2$ is at most $r^2/4-r^3/(6T)$. This expression increases strictly for $0<r<T$, and its value at $r=\min \{ 2M,T\} $ is $F(M,T)$. Since $r<\min \{ 2M,T\} $, the strict inequality follows. For sharpness, consider the following $T$-periodic profiles $p_0$. When $T\geq 2M$, let $p_0$ be constant equal to $M$ and to $-M$ on two intervals of length $(T-2M)/2$ each, joined by a descent of slope $-1$ and length $2M$, and close the period by an upward jump. When $T\leq 2M$, let $p_0(s)=T/2-s$ for $0\leq s<T$, with its upward jump at the end of the period. In both cases $p_0$ has mean zero, $|p_0|\leq M$, $p_0'\geq -1$ in the sense of distributions, and the average of $p_0^2$ is $F(M,T)$; both constructions apply when $T=2M$. Convolution with a nonnegative periodic approximate identity preserves the mean and the bound on the distributional derivative, and multiplication by $1-\varepsilon $ makes both inequalities strict. As the convolution scale and $\varepsilon $ tend to zero, the resulting smooth functions converge to $p_0$ in $L^2$, which proves that the supremum is $F(M,T)$. $\square$ Proposition 33.3.5 . Suppose $c_1(L)
e 0$ in real cohomology, and put \[  \kappa =- rac{\int _ Bc^2}{A}>0.  \] Every smooth potential $u=f(t)+\pi ^*v$ with $f$ of period $T$, $v\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$ and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ satisfies \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 >3TA igl (1-\kappa F(\kappa ^{-1/2},T) igr )>0.  \] Let $\lambda \geq 0$ be the nonnegative eigenvalue function of $c$ relative to $\eta $, so $c^2=-\lambda ^2\eta ^2$, and put $M_0=1/\max _ B\lambda $. For the subclass $v=0$, the exact mass infimum is \[  3TA igl (1-\kappa F(M_0,T) igr )>0.  \] It is approached by smooth potentials $f(t)$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(t)>0$, and it is not attained by such potentials. Proof. Put $p=f'$. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u =\pi ^*(\eta +pc+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(1+p')D.  \] Positivity on the vertical line implies $p'>-1$. Over every point of $B$, the function $t$ takes every value modulo $T$, so restriction to $\ker \partial t$ shows that $\eta +pc+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is a Kähler form on $B$ for every value of $p$. Its square has integral \[  \int _ B(\eta +pc+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^2=A(1-\kappa p^2)>0,  \] since primitivity removes the mixed term and Stokes' theorem removes the exact terms. Hence $|p|<\kappa ^{-1/2}$. Only the vertical derivative enters ( 33.4 ), because $-\pi ^*(c^2)$ has top degree in the base directions. For a $T$-periodic function $F_0$, integration over a fiber gives $\int _ E F_0(t)D=\int _0^ T F_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$, and therefore \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =3TA\left(1- rac\kappa T\int _0^ T p^2\, \mathrm{d}sight).  \] Now apply lemma 33.3.4 with $M=\kappa ^{-1/2}$. The formula for $F$ gives $F(M,T)<M^2$, which proves positivity of the bound. For $v=0$, diagonalizing $c$ with respect to $\eta $ shows that the horizontal positivity condition is exactly $|p|<M_0$; together with $p'>-1$ it also suffices for positivity of the full form. Moreover $\kappa $ is the $\eta ^2$-average of $\lambda ^2$, so $\kappa \leq M_0^{-2}$. Lemma 33.3.4 with $M=M_0$ therefore proves the claimed positive lower bound and its nonattainment. The smooth approximating functions in its proof have mean zero and hence periodic primitives $f_\varepsilon $, and the potentials $f_\varepsilon (t)$ prove that the bound is sharp. $\square$ The proof of the first bound does not show that it is sharp for separated potentials over an arbitrary base: positivity of the classes $[\eta ]+p[c]$ alone does not provide one function $v$ that makes all the representatives $\eta +pc+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ positive. For the threefold over $\mathbb P^1	imes \mathbb P^1$ of section 26.18 , where $A=2$, $\kappa =1$ and $T=4\pi $, the bound is $8$ and it is sharp. A base without curves rules out the averages of horizontal curves used in the known collapse example. The following construction uses the period theorem for K3 surfaces and the description of their Kähler cone [ Theorems 7.4.1 and 8.5.2 of the online version , HuyK3 ] . Example 33.3.6 . There is a K3 surface $B$ with $\operatorname {Pic}(B)=\mathbb Z[L]$, $c_1(L)^2=-4$, and a Kähler form $\eta $ orthogonal to $c_1(L)$. It has no compact curves. The associated $X$ has trivial canonical bundle, a balanced metric of finite upper mass, and no pluriclosed metric or closed Kähler current. It has no divisors, and every compact irreducible curve is an elliptic fiber. Proof. In a hyperbolic plane of the K3 lattice, choose a basis $e,f$ with $e^2=f^2=0$ and $e\cdot f=1$, and put $\ell =e-2f$. This vector is primitive and has square $-4$. Choose a period in $\ell ^\perp $ outside the hyperplanes perpendicular to integral vectors not in $\mathbb Z\ell $. Such a period exists by Baire's theorem: the period domain in $\ell ^\perp $, of signature $(3,18)$, is nonempty and each excluded hyperplane is proper. The period theorem and the description of integral $(1,1)$-classes give the asserted Picard group. An irreducible curve would have nonzero class, because its Kähler area is positive, and hence square $-4m^2<-2$ for some integer $m
eq 0$, contradicting adjunction. Thus there are no curves. The orthogonal complement of $\ell $ in $H^{1,1}(B,\mathbb R)$ has signature $(1,18)$. Choose a class of positive square there, with sign chosen so that it lies in the component of the positive cone containing the Kähler classes. Since there are no rational curves, the Kähler-cone theorem shows that this class is Kähler; choose $\eta $ in it. Proposition 33.3.3 then gives the assertions about the metric and the canonical bundle. If a divisor $Z\subset X$ dominated $B$, the push-forward of its integration current would be $\pi _*[Z]=m$ for a positive generic degree $m$. Stokes' theorem and the projection formula would then give \[  0=\int _ X[Z]\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =m\int _ B(-c^2)>0.  \] Thus no divisor dominates $B$. The image of any other irreducible divisor would be a curve or a point; the base has no curves, and a fiber has dimension one, so both alternatives are impossible. Likewise, the image of an irreducible compact curve is a point, and the curve is therefore an entire elliptic fiber. $\square$ Put $V=3TA$. The root volumes of complementary tests can be computed explicitly for one radial family. For smooth real $T$-periodic functions $a,g$, consider \[  \Gamma =a(t)\eta ^2+g(t)\eta \wedge D.  \] Proposition 33.3.7 . The form $\Gamma $ is strictly positive and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed exactly when $a$ is a positive constant and $g>0$. For such a form put $ ar g=T^{-1}\int _0^ Tg(s)\, \mathrm ds$ and $d_\Gamma =\int _ X\omega \wedge \Gamma $. Its positive square root and volume are \[  \gamma =\sqrt a\, \eta + rac{g(t)}{2\sqrt a}D, \qquad \int _ X\gamma ^3= rac32TA\sqrt a\,  ar g \leq  rac{d_\Gamma ^{3/2}}{\sqrt V}.  \] Equality holds exactly when $ ar g=2a$, without requiring $g$ to be constant. In particular every degree-one test in this family has root volume at most $V^{-1/2}$. Proof. Since $\eta \wedge c=0$, the form $g\eta \wedge D$ is closed. The chain rule gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\eta ^2)=a''D\wedge \eta ^2,  \] the $a'c\wedge \eta ^2$ term having excess base degree. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0$ forces $a''=0$, and periodicity makes $a$ constant. In a positive coframe with $\eta =\sigma _1+\sigma _2$, $D=\sigma _3$, the complementary coefficient matrix of $\Gamma $ is $\operatorname {diag}(g,g,2a)$. Hence positivity is exactly $a,g>0$. The displayed $\gamma $ is positive and squares to $\Gamma $. Multiplication and fiber integration give \[  d_\Gamma =TA(a+ ar g),\qquad \gamma ^3=	frac 32\sqrt a\, g\eta ^2\wedge D.  \] For fixed $d_\Gamma >0$ set $s=d_\Gamma /(TA)$. Then $0<a<s$, $ ar g=s-a$, and $\sqrt a(s-a)$ has its unique maximum at $a=s/3$. Substitution proves the bound and its equality condition. $\square$ For the divisor-free threefold of example 33.3.6 , theorem 4.5.1 gives divergent transverse pairings against normalized Gauduchon tests. The radial family above has bounded root volume at fixed degree, even when $g$ concentrates arbitrarily strongly. Large transverse pairings do not by themselves give unbounded root volumes or a sequence of potentials with masses tending to zero. Problem 33.3.8 . Determine the lower Monge–Ampère mass (definition 6.5.1 ) of the primitive elliptic bundles above, for instance of their balanced metrics $\omega $ from proposition 33.3.3 , in particular for the bundles of example 33.3.6 . Does it vanish whenever $c_1(L)
eq 0$ in real cohomology? The estimates for separated potentials do not answer this question; the known collapse over $\mathbb P^1	imes \mathbb P^1$ uses potentials outside that class. On the K3 example every compact curve is vertical, so averaging over such curves cannot produce the horizontal directions used in lemma 26.18.3 . A proof of collapse would therefore need a different construction, while positive lower mass would require a bound for all admissible potentials or for all normalized Gauduchon tests.

title: Proposition 33.3.3
text: Proposition 33.3.3 . The metric $\omega $ is balanced and satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\pi ^*(c^2)\geq 0,\qquad \int _ X\omega ^3=3TA.  \] For every smooth real $u$, 33.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:primitive-elliptic-mass} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =3TA-3\int _ X\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \bigl (-\pi ^*(c^2)\bigr ). \end{equation} In particular $v_+(\omega )=3TA$, and the canonical bundles satisfy $K_ X\simeq \pi ^*K_ B$. If $c_1(L)\ne 0$ in real cohomology, $X$ admits neither a pluriclosed metric nor a closed Kähler current. If $c_1(L)=0$ in real cohomology, the chosen $\omega $ is Kähler. Proof. Write $a=\mathrm{d}t$ and $b=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$. Then $\mathrm{d}a=0$, $\mathrm{d}b=\pi ^*c$, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}a=-\pi ^*c$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b=0$. Consequently \[  D^2=0,\qquad \mathrm{d}D=-a\wedge \pi ^*c, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D=-\pi ^*(c^2),  \] \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2)=-2\pi ^*(\eta \wedge c)\wedge a=0,  \] so $\omega $ is balanced. Since $c$ is primitive, its eigenvalues relative to $\eta $ are $\lambda $ and $-\lambda $ for a function $\lambda \geq 0$, so $c^2=-\lambda ^2\eta ^2$. This proves the asserted sign of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. To compute the volume, fix an elliptic fiber $E=\pi ^{-1}(b_0)$, where $b_0\in B$. In a logarithmic fiber coordinate $x+\mathrm{i}y$, the real periods are $\log q$ and $2\pi $, while $t$ equals $2x$ up to an additive constant and $D|_ E=\pi ^{-1}\mathrm{d}x\wedge \mathrm{d}y$. Thus $\int _ ED=T$. Since $\omega ^3=3\pi ^*(\eta ^2)\wedge D$, the volume formula follows. For the mass identity, expand the cube in ( 33.4 ). The terms with one and with three factors $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ integrate to zero, because $\omega ^2$ is closed and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is exact. For the remaining term, put $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. Integration by parts gives \[  \int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2\wedge \omega =\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge S =-\int _ X\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge S,  \] where the last equality uses $\mathrm{d}S=0$. This proves the identity. Its last integral is nonnegative, and $u=0$ attains the upper bound $3TA$. Since smooth and bounded potentials have the same mass extrema, by theorem 26.14.3 , this proves $v_+(\omega )=3TA$. If $c_1(L)=0$ in real cohomology, then $c$ is exact and Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ Bc^2=0$. The pointwise identity $c^2=-\lambda ^2\eta ^2$ then forces $c=0$, and $\omega $ is closed. Otherwise $S=-\pi ^*(c^2)$ is nonzero, smooth and semipositive. For a pluriclosed metric $\gamma $, Stokes' theorem would give \[  0<\int _ X\gamma \wedge S =\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma =0,  \] a contradiction. Likewise, a closed positive current $R\geq \varepsilon \omega $ with $\varepsilon >0$ would give $0<\int _ XR\wedge S=\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=0$. All these pairings are pairings of currents with smooth forms. Finally, let $w$ be a local holomorphic fiber coordinate given by a frame of $L$, and let $\sigma $ be a local holomorphic two-form on $B$. The form $\pi ^*\sigma \wedge \mathrm{d}w/w$ is invariant under the quotient action. Changing the frame of $L$ adds to $\mathrm{d}w/w$ a horizontal one-form, whose wedge product with $\pi ^*\sigma $ vanishes. These local sections of $K_ X$ therefore have the transition functions of $\pi ^*K_ B$, which proves $K_ X\simeq \pi ^*K_ B$. $\square$

33.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:primitive-elliptic-mass} \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =3TA-3\int _ X\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \bigl (-\pi ^*(c^2)\bigr ). \end{equation}

title: Lemma 33.3.4
text: Lemma 33.3.4 . If a smooth real $T$-periodic function $p$ has mean zero, $|p|<M$ and $p'>-1$, then \[  \frac1T\int _0^ T p^2\, \mathrm{d}s<F(M,T).  \] The supremum of the left side over this class is $F(M,T)$. Proof. For $p=0$ the inequality holds because $F(M,T)>0$. Otherwise set $a=\max p>0$, $-b=\min p<0$ and $r=a+b$. Integrating $-p'<1$ over a forward interval $I$ from a maximum to the next minimum gives $r<|I|\leq T$; also $r<2M$, since $|p|<M$. The function $G(s)=(a-s)(s+b)$ is nonnegative on the range of $p$. Since $p$ has mean zero and $-p'<1$, integration over $I$ gives \[  abT-\int _0^ T p^2\, \mathrm{d}s =\int _0^ T G(p)\, \mathrm{d}s \geq -\int _ I G(p)p'\, \mathrm{d}s =\frac{r^3}{6}.  \] As $ab\leq r^2/4$, the average of $p^2$ is at most $r^2/4-r^3/(6T)$. This expression increases strictly for $0<r<T$, and its value at $r=\min \{ 2M,T\} $ is $F(M,T)$. Since $r<\min \{ 2M,T\} $, the strict inequality follows. For sharpness, consider the following $T$-periodic profiles $p_0$. When $T\geq 2M$, let $p_0$ be constant equal to $M$ and to $-M$ on two intervals of length $(T-2M)/2$ each, joined by a descent of slope $-1$ and length $2M$, and close the period by an upward jump. When $T\leq 2M$, let $p_0(s)=T/2-s$ for $0\leq s<T$, with its upward jump at the end of the period. In both cases $p_0$ has mean zero, $|p_0|\leq M$, $p_0'\geq -1$ in the sense of distributions, and the average of $p_0^2$ is $F(M,T)$; both constructions apply when $T=2M$. Convolution with a nonnegative periodic approximate identity preserves the mean and the bound on the distributional derivative, and multiplication by $1-\varepsilon $ makes both inequalities strict. As the convolution scale and $\varepsilon $ tend to zero, the resulting smooth functions converge to $p_0$ in $L^2$, which proves that the supremum is $F(M,T)$. $\square$

title: Proposition 33.3.5
text: Proposition 33.3.5 . Suppose $c_1(L)\ne 0$ in real cohomology, and put \[  \kappa =-\frac{\int _ Bc^2}{A}>0.  \] Every smooth potential $u=f(t)+\pi ^*v$ with $f$ of period $T$, $v\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$ and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ satisfies \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 >3TA\bigl (1-\kappa F(\kappa ^{-1/2},T)\bigr )>0.  \] Let $\lambda \geq 0$ be the nonnegative eigenvalue function of $c$ relative to $\eta $, so $c^2=-\lambda ^2\eta ^2$, and put $M_0=1/\max _ B\lambda $. For the subclass $v=0$, the exact mass infimum is \[  3TA\bigl (1-\kappa F(M_0,T)\bigr )>0.  \] It is approached by smooth potentials $f(t)$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(t)>0$, and it is not attained by such potentials. Proof. Put $p=f'$. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u =\pi ^*(\eta +pc+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(1+p')D.  \] Positivity on the vertical line implies $p'>-1$. Over every point of $B$, the function $t$ takes every value modulo $T$, so restriction to $\ker \partial t$ shows that $\eta +pc+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is a Kähler form on $B$ for every value of $p$. Its square has integral \[  \int _ B(\eta +pc+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^2=A(1-\kappa p^2)>0,  \] since primitivity removes the mixed term and Stokes' theorem removes the exact terms. Hence $|p|<\kappa ^{-1/2}$. Only the vertical derivative enters ( 33.4 ), because $-\pi ^*(c^2)$ has top degree in the base directions. For a $T$-periodic function $F_0$, integration over a fiber gives $\int _ E F_0(t)D=\int _0^ T F_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$, and therefore \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =3TA\left(1-\frac\kappa T\int _0^ T p^2\, \mathrm{d}s\right).  \] Now apply lemma 33.3.4 with $M=\kappa ^{-1/2}$. The formula for $F$ gives $F(M,T)<M^2$, which proves positivity of the bound. For $v=0$, diagonalizing $c$ with respect to $\eta $ shows that the horizontal positivity condition is exactly $|p|<M_0$; together with $p'>-1$ it also suffices for positivity of the full form. Moreover $\kappa $ is the $\eta ^2$-average of $\lambda ^2$, so $\kappa \leq M_0^{-2}$. Lemma 33.3.4 with $M=M_0$ therefore proves the claimed positive lower bound and its nonattainment. The smooth approximating functions in its proof have mean zero and hence periodic primitives $f_\varepsilon $, and the potentials $f_\varepsilon (t)$ prove that the bound is sharp. $\square$

title: Example 33.3.6
text: Example 33.3.6 . There is a K3 surface $B$ with $\operatorname {Pic}(B)=\mathbb Z[L]$, $c_1(L)^2=-4$, and a Kähler form $\eta $ orthogonal to $c_1(L)$. It has no compact curves. The associated $X$ has trivial canonical bundle, a balanced metric of finite upper mass, and no pluriclosed metric or closed Kähler current. It has no divisors, and every compact irreducible curve is an elliptic fiber. Proof. In a hyperbolic plane of the K3 lattice, choose a basis $e,f$ with $e^2=f^2=0$ and $e\cdot f=1$, and put $\ell =e-2f$. This vector is primitive and has square $-4$. Choose a period in $\ell ^\perp $ outside the hyperplanes perpendicular to integral vectors not in $\mathbb Z\ell $. Such a period exists by Baire's theorem: the period domain in $\ell ^\perp $, of signature $(3,18)$, is nonempty and each excluded hyperplane is proper. The period theorem and the description of integral $(1,1)$-classes give the asserted Picard group. An irreducible curve would have nonzero class, because its Kähler area is positive, and hence square $-4m^2<-2$ for some integer $m\neq 0$, contradicting adjunction. Thus there are no curves. The orthogonal complement of $\ell $ in $H^{1,1}(B,\mathbb R)$ has signature $(1,18)$. Choose a class of positive square there, with sign chosen so that it lies in the component of the positive cone containing the Kähler classes. Since there are no rational curves, the Kähler-cone theorem shows that this class is Kähler; choose $\eta $ in it. Proposition 33.3.3 then gives the assertions about the metric and the canonical bundle. If a divisor $Z\subset X$ dominated $B$, the push-forward of its integration current would be $\pi _*[Z]=m$ for a positive generic degree $m$. Stokes' theorem and the projection formula would then give \[  0=\int _ X[Z]\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =m\int _ B(-c^2)>0.  \] Thus no divisor dominates $B$. The image of any other irreducible divisor would be a curve or a point; the base has no curves, and a fiber has dimension one, so both alternatives are impossible. Likewise, the image of an irreducible compact curve is a point, and the curve is therefore an entire elliptic fiber. $\square$

title: Proposition 33.3.7
text: Proposition 33.3.7 . The form $\Gamma $ is strictly positive and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed exactly when $a$ is a positive constant and $g>0$. For such a form put $\bar g=T^{-1}\int _0^ Tg(s)\, \mathrm ds$ and $d_\Gamma =\int _ X\omega \wedge \Gamma $. Its positive square root and volume are \[  \gamma =\sqrt a\, \eta +\frac{g(t)}{2\sqrt a}D, \qquad \int _ X\gamma ^3=\frac32TA\sqrt a\, \bar g \leq \frac{d_\Gamma ^{3/2}}{\sqrt V}.  \] Equality holds exactly when $\bar g=2a$, without requiring $g$ to be constant. In particular every degree-one test in this family has root volume at most $V^{-1/2}$. Proof. Since $\eta \wedge c=0$, the form $g\eta \wedge D$ is closed. The chain rule gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\eta ^2)=a''D\wedge \eta ^2,  \] the $a'c\wedge \eta ^2$ term having excess base degree. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0$ forces $a''=0$, and periodicity makes $a$ constant. In a positive coframe with $\eta =\sigma _1+\sigma _2$, $D=\sigma _3$, the complementary coefficient matrix of $\Gamma $ is $\operatorname {diag}(g,g,2a)$. Hence positivity is exactly $a,g>0$. The displayed $\gamma $ is positive and squares to $\Gamma $. Multiplication and fiber integration give \[  d_\Gamma =TA(a+\bar g),\qquad \gamma ^3=\tfrac 32\sqrt a\, g\eta ^2\wedge D.  \] For fixed $d_\Gamma >0$ set $s=d_\Gamma /(TA)$. Then $0<a<s$, $\bar g=s-a$, and $\sqrt a(s-a)$ has its unique maximum at $a=s/3$. Substitution proves the bound and its equality condition. $\square$
