title: 33.3.4 Null loci and the singularities of the Chern–Ricci flow
search_title: Null loci and the singularities of the Chern–Ricci flow
text: 33.3.4 Null loci and the singularities of the Chern–Ricci flow Return to the general manifold $X$ of dimension $n$. Let $\omega _0$ be a Hermitian metric, taken as the initial metric of the Chern–Ricci flow, and suppose that the flow has a finite maximal time $\tau $. With the Ricci convention of corollary 26.20.4 , the limiting background $\theta _\tau =\omega _0-\tau \operatorname {Ric}(\omega _0)$ is nef. To identify the region where the flow converges smoothly as the complement of a null locus, one first needs bigness of $\theta _\tau $. The dual currents detect the failure of strict positivity, but the degeneration of their determinants does not by itself locate an analytic exceptional set. For a big smooth background $\theta $, the non-Hermitian locus $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta )$ is the intersection of the singular sets of the strict currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, those bounded below by a positive multiple of a Hermitian form, whose potentials have almost analytic singularities ; one such current attains the intersection. Here a potential has almost analytic singularities if it is locally a positive multiple of the logarithm of the norm of an ideal up to a bounded remainder, and this remainder becomes smooth after subtracting the divisorial logarithms on a suitable log resolution. This is the class of singularities used in the theorem stated in section 34.20 . For nef and big $\theta $, define \[  \operatorname {Null}(\theta ) =\bigcup _{\substack {V\subset X\text{ irreducible analytic}\\ \dim V>0,\  \theta |_ V\text{ not big}}}V,  \] where bigness on a singular subvariety has its intrinsic analytic meaning. By the theorem recalled in section 34.20 , the equality $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta )=\operatorname {Null}(\theta )$ holds for nef and big smooth backgrounds on arbitrary compact complex manifolds. The numerical criterion recalled there has additional hypotheses: bounded mass on $X$ and positive lower volume on its positive-dimensional submanifolds. The flow theorem recalled in section 34.20 identifies the finite-time singularities of the Chern–Ricci flow with the null locus under positive limiting lower volume, for arbitrary initial metrics in dimension two and for Guan–Li initial metrics in higher dimensions, that is, those with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega _0=0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega _0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega _0=0$. Positivity of $\mathcal V_\mu $ cannot replace these hypotheses, as the example below shows. The calculation with currents in corollary 26.20.4 applies to arbitrary initial metrics. When $\tau <\infty $, there are normalized Gauduchon currents $T$ annihilating $\theta _\tau $: \[  \int _ X\theta _\tau \wedge T=0.  \] If $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta _\tau )>0$, the determinant-weighted measures of all such currents vanish, by proposition 26.20.2 . This is a precise statement of degeneracy, but it does not imply that their traces concentrate on analytic sets, since a smooth positive semidefinite matrix can have deficient rank on a whole open set. Theorem 26.20.5 shows that positivity of the variational volume does not imply bigness at the end of the flow: in every dimension at least three, there is a Chern–Ricci flow with finite maximal time whose limiting background is nef, not big, and has positive $\mathcal V_\mu $. Thus being the endpoint of a flow does not exclude the radial obstruction. In this model, proposition 26.20.6 shows that every normalized annihilating current has its trace supported on the degenerate fiber, with a vertical coefficient matrix of rank one. This support follows from the explicit semipositive representative, not from the vanishing of determinants alone. If $\theta _\tau $ is big, whether by assumption or under additional hypotheses, the parabolic theorem recalled in section 34.20 gives convergence as currents and smooth local convergence off $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta _\tau )$. Combined with nefness and the null-locus theorem, this identifies the analytic exceptional set. The example above does not contradict this conditional theorem, but any further numerical or geometric criterion must impose enough structure to exclude its nonbig endpoint. The local continuity of envelopes and the homogeneous replacement arguments of theorem 14.7.1 provide an elliptic foundation away from the poles of a strict barrier; the parabolic estimates are a separate input. Completeness of the limiting metric requires an additional estimate. In theorem 28.14.1 , the metric defined by the unique finite-energy solution of a divisorial exponential equation in a big closed class is incomplete on every nonempty connected open subset of its ample locus, because its minimal divisorial singularity cancels the prescribed pole. Nefness alone does not help: theorem 28.14.2 keeps a nonintegrable pole with smooth positive coefficient and a complete cusp, but has a disjoint null curve at finite distance; its solution has zero Lelong numbers and finite energy, but is not of minimal ordinary type. The construction of theorem 28.14.4 with compatible initial data also gives an incomplete auxiliary metric, with the exact identities for the resolution and the prescribed volume, but its class is not nef. Simultaneous nefness and compatibility remain a separate question, and none of these elliptic examples decides whether the limits of an evolving flow are complete; see section 34.17 . For integrable poles weakened by logarithmic factors, corollary 28.15.2 gives a sufficient condition for completeness in terms of the density, the potential and the tangential determinant; the proof controls normal lengths and applies in arbitrary Hermitian backgrounds. The torus models of example 28.15.4 , example 28.15.5 attain its critical exponent and show that it is sharp, even for a Kähler background and full mass. Their pole coefficients need not extend smoothly and positively across the divisor, so the geometric smoothing question remains separate. The regularity of the residual also matters. By theorem 1.18.1 , a Hölder residual on a compact manifold that defines a smooth positive metric off its analytic singular set puts that set at finite distance. Continuity alone does not suffice: the prescribed radial densities of theorem 28.12.2 have bounded continuous minimal remainders and complete regular ends for the range $n<d\leq 2n$ of the exponent $d$ in that theorem. These examples concern the specified densities; they say nothing about compatibility with an evolving Chern–Ricci flow.

title: 33.3.5 Balanced and pluriclosed metrics
text: 33.3.5 Balanced and pluriclosed metrics The balanced–pluriclosed conjecture asks whether a compact complex manifold carrying both a balanced metric $\beta $ and a pluriclosed metric $\omega $ must be Kähler. The two metrics may differ; a single metric satisfying both conditions is already Kähler by lemma 33.3.10 . The source of the conjecture and its formulation through a flow are given in section 34.20 . A manifold in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$ that carries a pluriclosed metric is Kähler, by the result recalled there. It would therefore suffice to construct a closed Kähler current from the two metrics. The scalar potential equation alone cannot produce the required closedness. Indeed, for every distributional potential $u$, \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)=\mathrm{d}\omega .  \] Thus if the pluriclosed metric is not closed, no potential in its background makes it Kähler; the finite-volume equation, including its smooth solution, does not change this differential datum. Similarly, the Gauduchon metric in a conformal class need not be balanced. Positivity and a scalar normalization cannot replace either missing closedness condition. The closed form $\beta ^{n-1}$ pairs trivially with exact real two-forms, so it can give a conserved trace along a flow. When $c_1(X)=0$ in real cohomology, the flow conjecture recalled in section 34.20 proposes that, in the presence of a balanced metric, the pluriclosed flow exists for all time and converges to a Kähler metric. The invariant examples cited there use the conserved trace. For general metrics, the analytic difficulty is to turn this integral into a pointwise bound. Parallel torsion gives a setting in which the integral constraint of a balanced trace becomes pointwise. Suppose $n\geq 2$, write $J$ for the complex structure of $X$, let $g$ be a Hermitian metric on $X$, and let $D$ be a real connection on $TX$ that preserves $g$ and $J$ and has parallel torsion $T^ D$: \[  Dg=0,\qquad DJ=0,\qquad DT^ D=0, \qquad T^ D(U,V)=D_ UV-D_ VU-[U,V].  \] The balanced and pluriclosed metrics considered below need not equal $g$. Write \[  E_ D^ k=\{ \alpha \in \Omega ^ k(X,\mathbb R):D\alpha =0\}   \] for the space of $D$-parallel real $k$-forms. Since $X$ is connected, evaluation at one point is injective on this space, so it is finite-dimensional. Its complexification inherits the decomposition by bidegree because $DJ=0$. Lemma 33.3.9 . There is a linear projection $S:\Omega ^\bullet (X,\mathbb R)\to E_ D^\bullet $ with $S\mathrm d=\mathrm dS$. Its complexification preserves bidegree and commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. It preserves strict positivity in bidegrees $(1,1)$ and $(n-1,n-1)$. Proof. Step 1: the projection. For a parallel form $\alpha $, the formula for exterior differentiation in terms of a connection expresses $\mathrm d\alpha $ as an algebraic contraction of $T^ D$ with $\alpha $. Since $DT^ D=0$, it follows that $\mathrm dE_ D^ k\subseteq E_ D^{k+1}$. The Hodge star of $g$ is also parallel and maps $E_ D^ k$ onto $E_ D^{2n-k}$. Consequently the pairing \[  E_ D^ k\times E_ D^{2n-k}\longrightarrow \mathbb R, \qquad (\alpha ,\beta )\longmapsto \int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta  \] is nondegenerate: pairing a nonzero $\alpha $ with $*_ g\alpha $ gives its squared $L^2$ norm, which is positive. Hence every smooth real $k$-form $\alpha $ determines a unique $S_ k\alpha \in E_ D^ k$ such that 33.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:parallel-projection-pairing} \int _ X S_ k\alpha \wedge \beta =\int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta \qquad (\beta \in E_ D^{2n-k}). \end{equation} This defines a projection onto $E_ D^ k$. For $\gamma \in E_ D^{2n-k-1}$ we have $\mathrm d\gamma \in E_ D^{2n-k}$, so Stokes' theorem gives \[  \int _ X\mathrm dS_ k\alpha \wedge \gamma =(-1)^{k+1}\int _ X\alpha \wedge \mathrm d\gamma =\int _ X S_{k+1}(\mathrm d\alpha )\wedge \gamma .  \] Both forms being compared are parallel, so nondegeneracy proves $\mathrm dS_ k\alpha =S_{k+1}\mathrm d\alpha $. Step 2: positivity. Fix $p\in X$. Let $H$ be the closure of the full $D$-holonomy group at $p$, a compact subgroup of the unitary group, with probability Haar measure $m_ H$. For a path from $p$ to $x$, write $P_ x:T_ pX\to T_ xX$ for parallel transport along it. The average \[  R_\alpha (x)=\int _ H h^*(P_ x^*\alpha _ x)\, \mathrm dm_ H(h)  \] is independent of the path, since a change of path acts by an element of $H$. It is an $H$-invariant tensor at $p$ depending smoothly on $x$, because paths can be chosen smoothly on each coordinate neighborhood. Average it over $X$: \[  a_ p=\frac1{\operatorname {Vol}_ g(X)} \int _ X R_\alpha (x)\, \mathrm dV_ g(x).  \] Being $H$-invariant, the tensor $a_ p$ extends uniquely to a global parallel form $\widetilde S_ k\alpha $. For parallel $\beta $, write $\alpha \wedge \beta =f\, \mathrm dV_ g$. Since parallel transport is unitary and $\beta $ is invariant under holonomy, averaging gives \[  R_\alpha (x)\wedge \beta _ p=f(x)\, \mathrm dV_{g,p}.  \] Integrating this equality shows that $\widetilde S_ k\alpha $ satisfies ( 33.7 ); hence $\widetilde S_ k=S_ k$. Every parallel transport and every holonomy element preserves reality, bidegree and the positive cones. A smooth strictly positive $(q,q)$-form, for $q=1$ or $n-1$, is bounded below by a positive multiple of the $q$th power of the fundamental form of $g$, uniformly on the compact manifold, and both probability averages preserve that lower bound. Therefore $S$ preserves strict positivity and bidegree. Comparing bidegrees in $S\mathrm d=\mathrm dS$ proves that $S$ commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. $\square$ The last step of the construction uses the fact, mentioned above, that a metric which is both balanced and pluriclosed is Kähler. Lemma 33.3.10 . If a Hermitian form $\zeta $ satisfies $\mathrm d\zeta ^{n-1}=0$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta =0$, then $\mathrm d\zeta =0$. Proof. For $n=2$, the balanced condition is the assertion $\mathrm d\zeta =0$. Suppose $n\geq 3$ and set $\alpha =\partial \zeta $. Since $\zeta $ is balanced, $\alpha \wedge \zeta ^{n-2}=0$, so $\alpha $ is a primitive $(2,1)$-form. Applying $\partial \bar\partial $ to the balanced power gives \[  0=\partial \bar\partial \zeta ^{n-1} =(n-1)\partial \bar\partial \zeta \wedge \zeta ^{n-2} +(n-1)(n-2)\alpha \wedge \bar\alpha \wedge \zeta ^{n-3}.  \] The first term vanishes because $\zeta $ is pluriclosed. For a primitive $(2,1)$-form, pointwise Hermitian linear algebra gives \[  -\mathrm i\, \alpha \wedge \bar\alpha \wedge \frac{\zeta ^{n-3}}{(n-3)!} =|\alpha |_\zeta ^2\frac{\zeta ^ n}{n!}.  \] Thus $\alpha =0$, and since $\zeta $ is real, also $\bar\partial \zeta =0$, so $\mathrm d\zeta =0$. $\square$ Theorem 33.3.11 . Let $D$ be a connection on $TX$ as above, preserving $g$ and $J$ and with parallel torsion. If $X$ admits a balanced metric and a pluriclosed metric, then it admits a $D$-parallel Kähler metric. Proof. Let $\beta $ be a balanced metric and $\omega $ a pluriclosed metric. By lemma 33.3.9 , $S(\beta ^{n-1})$ is strictly positive, parallel and closed. It has a unique smooth positive $(n-1)$-st root $B$. Indeed, after the fixed normalization of wedge powers, the corresponding map on matrices is $G\mapsto C=(\det G)G^{-1}$, whose inverse is \[  G=(\det C)^{1/(n-1)}C^{-1}.  \] By uniqueness the root is invariant under parallel transport. Thus $DB=0$ and $\mathrm dB^{n-1}=0$. Similarly, $P=S\omega $ is a parallel positive pluriclosed form. Consider the finite-dimensional space of real parallel directions of exact type \[  \mathcal A_ D=\{ (\mathrm d\xi )^{1,1}:\xi \in E_ D^1\} .  \] Every such direction is $\partial \bar\partial $-closed, since \[  (\mathrm d\xi )^{1,1}=\partial \xi ^{0,1}+\bar\partial \xi ^{1,0}.  \] For a parallel positive form $Q$, the volume functional has derivative 33.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:parallel-volume-variation} \left.\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\right|_{t=0} \frac1{n!}\int _ X(Q+t(\mathrm d\xi )^{1,1})^ n =\frac1{(n-1)!}\int _ X\xi \wedge \mathrm dQ^{n-1}, \end{equation} because the $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ parts of $\mathrm d\xi $ pair to zero with $Q^{n-1}$. Since $\mathrm dQ^{n-1}$ is parallel, nondegeneracy of the parallel pairing shows that all these derivatives vanish exactly when $Q$ is balanced. Apply this to the balanced form $B$. For $a\in \mathcal A_ D$, the function $\operatorname {tr}_ B a$ is parallel and hence constant. Its integral against $B^ n$ vanishes by ( 33.8 ), so it vanishes identically. Therefore every form in the positive affine slice \[  \mathcal P=\{ Q\in P+\mathcal A_ D:Q>0\}   \] has the same pointwise trace $\operatorname {tr}_ B Q=\operatorname {tr}_ B P=:C>0$. Evaluate the parallel forms at one point. The positive eigenvalues of $Q\in \mathcal P$ relative to $B$ sum to $C$, so they are bounded above by $C$. Thus $\mathcal P$ is bounded in its finite-dimensional affine space. Its closure is \[  \overline{\mathcal P}=\{ Q\in P+\mathcal A_ D:Q\geq 0\} ,  \] because $(1-t)Q+tP$ is positive for $0<t\leq 1$ whenever $Q$ is semipositive; in particular, this closure is compact. Since both forms are parallel, the relative eigenvalues and the relative determinant are constant on $X$. Hence \[  \frac1{n!}\int _ XQ^ n =\det (B^{-1}Q)\frac1{n!}\int _ XB^ n.  \] At a relative boundary point of $\overline{\mathcal P}$ the semipositive matrix is singular, so this volume is zero, whereas it is positive at $P$. A maximum of the volume on the compact set $\overline{\mathcal P}$ therefore lies in $\mathcal P$. At this interior maximum all the derivatives in ( 33.8 ) vanish, so the maximizing form is balanced; it is pluriclosed because it lies in $P+\mathcal A_ D$. By lemma 33.3.10 it is closed. Since it is positive and $D$-parallel, this proves the theorem. $\square$ The trace constraint in this argument is pointwise because the metrics and the directions of variation are parallel. This additional structure makes the positive slice compact and the volume vanish on its boundary; for a general family, the conserved balanced trace gives no such control. Problem 33.3.12 . Suppose that a compact complex manifold carries a balanced metric and a pluriclosed metric. Use the two metrics to construct closed positive data, such as a closed Kähler current, or to control a geometric flow that can change the torsion. Determine which estimate, beyond the finite balanced trace, prevents degeneration of the metrics. Can determinant estimates for Gauduchon currents contribute to that estimate? The complete determinant profile also need not control ellipticity. Under the lower-power $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed condition, theorem 26.17.4 computes its exact value on every $L^ n$ density root. The nonclosed pluriclosed family of theorem 26.17.6 keeps this entire profile, the bounded-potential mass extrema and a balanced trace fixed while its least relative eigenvalue tends to zero. Its torsion is fixed and nonzero. The underlying torus is already Kähler; the example shows which scalar data an additional estimate must go beyond, without constructing a pluriclosed-flow trajectory.

title: Lemma 33.3.9
text: Lemma 33.3.9 . There is a linear projection $S:\Omega ^\bullet (X,\mathbb R)\to E_ D^\bullet $ with $S\mathrm d=\mathrm dS$. Its complexification preserves bidegree and commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. It preserves strict positivity in bidegrees $(1,1)$ and $(n-1,n-1)$. Proof. Step 1: the projection. For a parallel form $\alpha $, the formula for exterior differentiation in terms of a connection expresses $\mathrm d\alpha $ as an algebraic contraction of $T^ D$ with $\alpha $. Since $DT^ D=0$, it follows that $\mathrm dE_ D^ k\subseteq E_ D^{k+1}$. The Hodge star of $g$ is also parallel and maps $E_ D^ k$ onto $E_ D^{2n-k}$. Consequently the pairing \[  E_ D^ k\times E_ D^{2n-k}\longrightarrow \mathbb R, \qquad (\alpha ,\beta )\longmapsto \int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta  \] is nondegenerate: pairing a nonzero $\alpha $ with $*_ g\alpha $ gives its squared $L^2$ norm, which is positive. Hence every smooth real $k$-form $\alpha $ determines a unique $S_ k\alpha \in E_ D^ k$ such that 33.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:parallel-projection-pairing} \int _ X S_ k\alpha \wedge \beta =\int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta \qquad (\beta \in E_ D^{2n-k}). \end{equation} This defines a projection onto $E_ D^ k$. For $\gamma \in E_ D^{2n-k-1}$ we have $\mathrm d\gamma \in E_ D^{2n-k}$, so Stokes' theorem gives \[  \int _ X\mathrm dS_ k\alpha \wedge \gamma =(-1)^{k+1}\int _ X\alpha \wedge \mathrm d\gamma =\int _ X S_{k+1}(\mathrm d\alpha )\wedge \gamma .  \] Both forms being compared are parallel, so nondegeneracy proves $\mathrm dS_ k\alpha =S_{k+1}\mathrm d\alpha $. Step 2: positivity. Fix $p\in X$. Let $H$ be the closure of the full $D$-holonomy group at $p$, a compact subgroup of the unitary group, with probability Haar measure $m_ H$. For a path from $p$ to $x$, write $P_ x:T_ pX\to T_ xX$ for parallel transport along it. The average \[  R_\alpha (x)=\int _ H h^*(P_ x^*\alpha _ x)\, \mathrm dm_ H(h)  \] is independent of the path, since a change of path acts by an element of $H$. It is an $H$-invariant tensor at $p$ depending smoothly on $x$, because paths can be chosen smoothly on each coordinate neighborhood. Average it over $X$: \[  a_ p=\frac1{\operatorname {Vol}_ g(X)} \int _ X R_\alpha (x)\, \mathrm dV_ g(x).  \] Being $H$-invariant, the tensor $a_ p$ extends uniquely to a global parallel form $\widetilde S_ k\alpha $. For parallel $\beta $, write $\alpha \wedge \beta =f\, \mathrm dV_ g$. Since parallel transport is unitary and $\beta $ is invariant under holonomy, averaging gives \[  R_\alpha (x)\wedge \beta _ p=f(x)\, \mathrm dV_{g,p}.  \] Integrating this equality shows that $\widetilde S_ k\alpha $ satisfies ( 33.7 ); hence $\widetilde S_ k=S_ k$. Every parallel transport and every holonomy element preserves reality, bidegree and the positive cones. A smooth strictly positive $(q,q)$-form, for $q=1$ or $n-1$, is bounded below by a positive multiple of the $q$th power of the fundamental form of $g$, uniformly on the compact manifold, and both probability averages preserve that lower bound. Therefore $S$ preserves strict positivity and bidegree. Comparing bidegrees in $S\mathrm d=\mathrm dS$ proves that $S$ commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. $\square$
33.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:parallel-projection-pairing} \int _ X S_ k\alpha \wedge \beta =\int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta \qquad (\beta \in E_ D^{2n-k}). \end{equation}

title: 33.3.6 Pluriclosed metrics under deformation
text: 33.3.6 Pluriclosed metrics under deformation Pluriclosed metrics persist under small deformations of the complex structure when the Aeppli number $h_ A^{1,1}$ stays constant. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold of real dimension $2n$, $n\geq 1$, and let $J_ t$, $t\in U\subset \mathbb R^\ell $, be a smooth family of integrable complex structures, where $U$ is an open neighborhood of $0$. Write $\Omega _ t^{p,q}$ for the smooth complex forms of type $(p,q)$ for $J_ t$. A pluriclosed form belongs to the kernel of $\partial _ t\bar\partial _ t$, and the corresponding Aeppli group is \[  H_ A^{1,1}(M,J_ t) =\frac{\ker (\partial _ t\bar\partial _ t:\Omega _ t^{1,1}\to \Omega _ t^{2,2})}{\partial _ t\Omega _ t^{0,1}+\bar\partial _ t\Omega _ t^{1,0}}, \qquad h_ A^{1,1}(M,J_ t)=\dim _{\mathbb C}H_ A^{1,1}(M,J_ t).  \] Constancy of this dimension gives a smooth family of projections onto the forms satisfying the closedness constraint, and positivity then persists near a given strictly positive form. Lemma 33.3.13 . The number $h_ A^{1,1}(M,J_ t)$ is finite. If it is constant near $0$, then, after shrinking $U$, the orthogonal projections \[  \mathcal P_ t:\Omega _ t^{1,1}\longrightarrow \ker (\partial _ t\bar\partial _ t)  \] for any smooth family of auxiliary Hermitian metrics vary smoothly with $t$ on smooth forms and preserve reality. Proof. Step 1: an elliptic operator. Fix $t$ and suppress it from the notation; the auxiliary metric defines the adjoints. Put $C=\partial \bar\partial $ and $E=\bar\partial \partial ^*$. The nonnegative self-adjoint operator 33.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:aeppli-elliptic-operator} \mathcal L=C^*C+CC^*+E^*E+EE^* +\partial \partial ^*+\bar\partial \bar\partial ^* \end{equation} is elliptic of order four. Indeed, at a nonzero real covector $\xi $, the principal symbols of $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $ are, up to the common factor $\mathrm i$, exterior multiplication by the $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ parts of $\xi $. These parts are orthogonal and have the same norm $r>0$. Split the exterior algebra according to which of these two directions are present. The four terms of order four act on the four resulting summands respectively, and the sum of their symbols is $r^4\operatorname {Id}$. The terms of lower order do not affect ellipticity. The quadratic form of $\mathcal L$ is a sum of squared norms, which gives the inclusion $\subseteq $ in \[  \ker \mathcal L=\ker C\cap \ker \partial ^*\cap \ker \bar\partial ^*.  \] For the reverse inclusion, note that $C^*=\bar\partial ^*\partial ^*$, $E=\bar\partial \partial ^*$ and $E^*=\partial \bar\partial ^*$ all vanish under these three conditions. Elliptic theory on the compact manifold gives a finite-dimensional space of smooth forms $\ker \mathcal L$, the orthogonal projection $\mathcal H$ onto it and the Green operator $\mathcal G$, with $\mathcal L\mathcal G=\operatorname {Id}-\mathcal H$. Step 2: the projection. Set $R=\mathcal L-C^*C$. Each term of $R$ has image in $\operatorname {im}\partial +\operatorname {im}\bar\partial $. Thus every smooth $(1,1)$-form $\alpha $ has the decomposition 33.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:aeppli-projection-decomposition} \alpha =\mathcal H\alpha +R\mathcal G\alpha +C^*C\mathcal G\alpha . \end{equation} The first two terms lie in $\ker C$, since $C\partial =C\bar\partial =0$, and the last is orthogonal to $\ker C$. Consequently 33.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:aeppli-closed-projection} \mathcal P=\operatorname {Id}-C^*C\mathcal G \end{equation} is the orthogonal projection onto $\ker C$. If $C\alpha =0$, the last term in ( 33.10 ) vanishes, so the Aeppli class of $\alpha $ is represented by $\mathcal H\alpha $. A harmonic form in $\operatorname {im}\partial +\operatorname {im}\bar\partial $ is zero, by orthogonality. This identifies $H_ A^{1,1}$ with $\ker \mathcal L$ and proves finiteness. Step 3: dependence on $t$. Now identify the varying type bundles and their $L^2$ spaces smoothly with those at $t=0$, using a unitary identification for the auxiliary metrics. The coefficients of $\mathcal L_ t$ then vary smoothly. Choose a circle $|z|=\varepsilon $ enclosing no nonzero eigenvalue of $\mathcal L_0$. The resolvents of $\mathcal L_0$ on this circle are bounded from $H^ s$ to $H^{s+4}$. The Neumann series for their perturbations gives smooth resolvents on the circle for small $t$, and the contour projections have constant rank. Constancy of $h_ A^{1,1}$ makes that rank equal to $\dim \ker \mathcal L_ t$. Hence the contour projections are exactly $\mathcal H_ t$, and $\mathcal L_ t$ has no additional small eigenvalues. The operators \[  \mathcal G_ t=(\mathcal L_ t+\mathcal H_ t)^{-1}-\mathcal H_ t  \] vary smoothly on every Sobolev scale, by the same inverse argument and elliptic regularity. Formula ( 33.11 ) therefore gives the asserted smooth family $\mathcal P_ t$. Complex conjugation sends $C_ t$ to $-C_ t$, exchanges $E_ t$ with $E_ t^*$, and exchanges the last two terms of ( 33.9 ). Thus $\mathcal L_ t$, $\mathcal H_ t$, $\mathcal G_ t$ and $\mathcal P_ t$ commute with conjugation. $\square$ Theorem 33.3.14 . Suppose that $(M,J_0)$ carries a pluriclosed Hermitian form $\omega _0$ and that $h_ A^{1,1}(M,J_ t)$ is constant near $0$. Then for small $t$ there is a smooth family of pluriclosed Hermitian forms $\omega _ t$ on $(M,J_ t)$ with the prescribed value $\omega _0$ at $t=0$. Proof. Let $\pi _ t^{1,1}$ denote the projection onto forms of type $(1,1)$ for $J_ t$, and use the operators of lemma 33.3.13 . Define \[  \omega _ t=\mathcal P_ t\bigl (\pi _ t^{1,1}\omega _0\bigr ).  \] These are smooth real $(1,1)$-forms satisfying $\partial _ t\bar\partial _ t\omega _ t=0$. At $t=0$ the projection fixes $\omega _0$, since $\omega _0$ already satisfies this equation. The tensors $\omega _ t(\cdot ,J_ t\cdot )$ converge uniformly to the positive definite tensor $\omega _0(\cdot ,J_0\cdot )$, which has a uniform positive lower bound by compactness. Hence they remain positive definite after shrinking $U$. $\square$ The construction projects onto $\partial _ t\bar\partial _ t$-closed forms and obtains positivity by continuity near $\omega _0$; closedness and conditions on the curvature would impose further equations. Thus the theorem provides pluriclosed metrics along a given deformation, while the balanced metric required in 33.3.12 remains a separate geometric condition.

title: 33.3.7 Morse inequalities and the choice of volume
search_title: Morse inequalities and the choice of volume
text: 33.3.7 Morse inequalities and the choice of volume In the closed Kähler theory, subtracting a nef class has a controlled cost in volume. For closed nef classes $\alpha ,\beta $ on a compact Kähler manifold, the transcendental Morse inequality states that \[  \operatorname {Vol}(\alpha -\beta ) \geq \int _ X\alpha ^ n-n\int _ X\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \beta ,  \] where $\operatorname {Vol}$ is the usual volume of a class. Its source, and the differentiability of the volume and the duality of cones that follow from it, are recalled in section 34.20 . To formulate an analogue on an arbitrary compact complex manifold, one must first choose the volume to be estimated. For nonclosed backgrounds, the intersection numbers on the right-hand side are in general not invariant under a change of representatives. Moreover, the upper volume of a class and $\mathcal V_\mu $ have different definitions and can behave differently with respect to finiteness. A Hermitian analogue must therefore specify which invariant it estimates. The first-variation formula gives a finite quantity to study. Fix smooth real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta ,\eta $ and $t>0$. Suppose that $\theta _ s=\theta -s\eta $ has a smooth positive representative for $0\leq s\leq t$, and let $\gamma _ s$ be a minimizing Gauduchon metric for its smooth equation. By proposition 26.2.2 and the fundamental theorem of calculus, 33.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:gaud-volume-subtraction-cost} \lambda _\mu (\theta -t\eta ) =\lambda _\mu (\theta ) -\int _0^ t \frac{\int _ X\eta \wedge \gamma _ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma _ s)}\, \mathrm{d}s. \end{equation} The quotient in the integrand does not change when the minimizer is rescaled. This identity holds on the positive segment $0\leq s\leq t$ and uses no bound on the upper Monge–Ampère mass. A uniform upper bound for its integrand gives a lower bound for the remaining root volume. On a compact Kähler manifold, theorem 26.11.1 extends the identity up to a nef endpoint that has no smooth positive representative, and bounds the resulting improper integral, when a closed nef core of positive volume is supplemented by a semipositive form $B$. Its test metrics keep the prescribed density, and ( 26.69 ) isolates the correction involving $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B$. There the endpoint is big because of the closed core; example 26.11.3 gives a nonclosed example with an explicit strict current at the endpoint. Positive volume at the endpoint alone cannot provide such a current, by theorem 26.13.2 , so a criterion going beyond the closed core must exclude that obstruction. For the warped products of section 26.12 , theorem 26.12.1 computes the finite improper cost for every choice of minimizing metric, and proposition 26.12.2 gives its rate from the codimension and vanishing order of the fiber coefficient. These paths can end with positive root volume but no big representative, and proposition 26.12.3 excludes every closed nef positive-volume core at a zero of that coefficient. Thus exact control of the subtraction cost in this product family does not supply a general bigness criterion. Problem 33.3.15 . In the setting of ( 33.12 ), find geometric hypotheses that control the integral on the right-hand side, the cost of the subtraction, up to a nef endpoint, beyond the regime of a closed nef core treated in theorem 26.11.1 . Determine when positive root volume forces bigness in the absence of such a core. For closed backgrounds, compare the resulting estimate with the classical Morse inequalities; for nonclosed backgrounds, the estimate should keep track of the differential data and of the dependence on $\mu $. The singularity and divisorial constructions of this book become relevant here: they measure how much positivity can be spent on imposed poles while the residual Gauduchon volume stays finite. They do not yet give the moving intersection product or the birational volume formula of the closed theory. For the nonanalytic ruled type of example 26.21.6 , the improper subtraction cost remains finite as the variational volume vanishes, while the upper ordinary-type volume has a positive limit. This family makes the choice of invariant explicit even for an imposed type with infinite first moment. Recovering a general moving product or birational formula remains a further goal.

title: 33.3.8 Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds
text: 33.3.8 Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds are not Kähler, yet they carry a closed semipositive form $\theta $ whose potentials are all continuous (theorem 28.19.2 ). On a threefold of type $(2,1)$, the natural Gauduchon metric $\omega =\theta +y_1y_2\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ has an exactly quadratic mass functional, indefinite in sign, and its masses on fiber-invariant potentials are bounded above and below by positive constants (proposition 28.19.5 ). The known curvature criteria for finite upper and positive lower mass in dimension three require a Hermitian metric whose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ has a sign, and these threefolds admit no such metric (proposition 28.19.6 ; see section 34.16 for the criteria). By ( 28.71 ), the remaining difficulty lies entirely in the fluctuation of a potential around its fiber average. Problem 33.3.16 . Let $X$ be an Oeljeklaus–Toma threefold of type $(2,1)$, with the Hermitian form $\omega $ of proposition 28.19.5 . Does $X$ have the bounded mass property, that is, is $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $? Is the lower mass $v_-(\omega )$ positive? Equivalently, writing $F(u)$ for the fluctuation term in ( 28.71 ), is $F$ bounded above on smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u$, and is $\inf _ u\bigl (\mathrm M_\omega (Au)+F(u)\bigr )>0$? The same questions can be asked for Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds of any type $(s,t)$ with $s\geq 2$. By proposition 6.5.2 , the answer to the first question does not depend on the choice of Hermitian form. A negative answer would require potentials whose fluctuations make $\operatorname {Re}(\partial _{w_1}v\, \overline{\partial _{w_2}v})$ large, while keeping $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. By lemma 28.19.1 , every nonzero Fourier mode on the fiber tori depends on $z$, so for a single mode $c(y)\cos (\cdots )$ the positivity of the $z$-coefficient of $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ bounds $|c|$ by a multiple of $y_1y_2$ divided by the square of the $z$-frequency; the frequencies in the $x$-directions are not controlled pointwise. Whether compactness and the automorphy under the units bound the fluctuation term is the content of the problem. Unlike the Hopf threefold of chapter 8 , the manifold contains no curves along which heat potentials could be concentrated, by the theorem of Ornea and Verbitsky recalled before corollary 28.19.4 . The rigidity in theorem 28.19.2 comes from two features of the null foliation of $\theta $: its leaves carry no nonconstant plurisubharmonic functions bounded above, and their closures are real tori on which translations act transitively. For the pullback of a Kähler form under a holomorphic fibration, the null leaves are the compact fibers, and $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions may have poles. Problem 33.3.17 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed semipositive real $(1,1)$-form on a compact complex manifold $X$ whose kernel has constant rank. Suppose that every leaf of the null foliation of $\theta $ is Liouville, in the sense that plurisubharmonic functions bounded above on it are constant, and that the closure of every leaf is a compact real submanifold whose real codimension equals the complex rank of $\theta $. Is every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function continuous? If not, describe the possible singularity types in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ in terms of the closures of the leaves.

The same questions can be asked for Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds of any type $(s,t)$ with $s\geq 2$.
