title: 33.4 Closed and twisted classes
text: 33.4 Closed and twisted classes A volume attached to a closed Bott–Chern class must not depend on the representative, while a volume equation for a locally conformally Kähler (LCK) form must preserve its Lee class and its twisted differential. The examples below show where ordinary Hermitian perturbations fail to respect these requirements. We use the LCK notions of definition 29.1.1 : for a closed one-form $\lambda $, $D_\lambda $ is the twisted Hessian of ( 29.8 ), and $j_ X\colon H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)\to H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$ is the Lee map ( 29.7 ); the associated Lee–Gauduchon cone is studied in section 29.6 . The non-nef and non-Kähler loci of chapter 28 separate closed currents with small negative errors from strictly positive closed currents. Any numerical restricted volume proposed for closed classes on general compact complex manifolds must be compatible with proposition 28.5.1 : if a Hermitian form $\omega $ fails the bounded mass property, as on the Hopf threefold, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ the supremum of $\int _ X(T+\varepsilon \omega )^ n$ over smooth closed representatives $T\geq -\varepsilon \omega $ of the zero class is already infinite. Since the failure occurs at each fixed error size, letting the error tend to zero afterwards cannot turn this expression into a class invariant. For $n\geq 2$, the subsolution threshold also constrains divisorial singularities. Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form, $\mathrm{d}V$ a smooth positive probability volume form and $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ a nonzero density with $b=b_\omega (f)>0$, and put $p=f^{1/n}$. If a subsolution at the threshold $b$ dominates the current of integration of an effective divisor $E$, then by proposition 28.8.1 the weak limits of every smooth maximizing Gauduchon sequence annihilate the class of every component of $E$. If one such sequence has uniformly integrable determinant-weighted densities, corollary 28.8.3 excludes divisors whose classes have suitable smooth semipositive representatives, for instance the hyperplane divisor on the Hopf threefold, and corollary 28.8.4 shows that a component with nef class has zero variational volume for every smooth density. Both conclusions hold under the root-tail condition $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$. Characterizing the components that can occur would require a realization theorem; note that the weak closure of smooth tests can be smaller than the set of all normalized Gauduchon currents (example 28.8.2 ). For a prescribed logarithmic divisor with a positive Hermitian residual, theorem 15.9.4 identifies the threshold on the entire one-sided class with that of the residual background. The ordinary class and relative envelope class have the same attained coefficient for smooth strictly positive data. A nonzero divisor then makes it strictly smaller than the global coefficient, and corollary 15.9.5 excludes divisorial components at the smooth global threshold. The projective product in example 15.9.6 computes this loss explicitly. These positive-residual results do not give a converse from an annihilating face for general integrable data. For closed classes on manifolds in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, section 28.6 defines a finite restricted invariant on each subvariety, independent of the Kähler resolution used to compute it. It is positive exactly when the class is big on the resolved subvariety, and for a nef class on $X$ the union of the subvarieties where it vanishes is the null locus. For a specified divisorial trace with bounded remainder, section 28.7 computes the mass of the trace itself and turns positive residual mass into a strict current, more singular than the trace. The nonclosed ruled family of section 19.10 goes beyond bounded residuals: theorem 19.10.2 computes both masses over the whole ordinary type, and proposition 19.10.3 identifies its ambient ideal orders, although the unbounded residual is invisible to those ideals. Positive lower volume gives a strict current in that ordinary type downstairs. It is preserved under pure pullback, while proposition 19.10.5 excludes a strict current in the pulled-back ordinary type and still allows a one-sided strict representative. The same obstruction holds after every nonempty finite composition of point blowups, including centers at poles. More generally, theorem 16.7.3 gives an exact ordinary-type strictness criterion for a finite logarithmic divisor plus a residual with arbitrarily small negative curvature. Its ambient ideals and, in the normal crossing case, all intrinsic traces are given by proposition 19.2.2 , even when the naive residual restriction is identically $-\infty $. Thus a general restricted invariant must specify which singularity relation its strictness criterion uses. Its construction for arbitrary nonclosed backgrounds, and its relation to intrinsic multiplier-ideal trace data outside these families, remain open. The LCK setting raises separate questions about equations. By corollary 29.2.2 , a compact strictly LCK manifold has no big ordinary Bott–Chern class. Its LCK form belongs instead to a twisted Bott–Chern class, whose representatives are described by the twisted Hessian $D_\lambda $. Prescribing the volume form of a Gauduchon LCK metric in such a class leads to the coupled system ( 29.11 ), whose second equation is the additional conformal condition imposed by the Gauduchon condition. 29.4.1 asks whether this system has at most one solution when the Lee class and the twisted class are fixed; the nonuniqueness examples for ordinary potentials do not decide it. On scalar Hopf manifolds the radial case is solved: for every smooth positive radial volume form and every negative Lee period, theorem 29.4.6 gives exactly one Gauduchon metric in the full positive radial family. By proposition 29.4.7 , this metric has a positive potential in its own Lee gauge, so its twisted class is zero, and the coupled system determines it among radial candidates. For nonconstant radial densities these metrics are not Vaisman (proposition 29.4.8 ). Uniqueness among arbitrary LCK candidates is open. Two geometric conjectures use the Lee form in different ways. 29.2.4 asserts that the class $j_ X([\lambda ])$, for the Lee form $\lambda $ of a strictly LCK metric, is pseudoeffective, that is, pairs nonnegatively with every Gauduchon metric; the LCK metric itself provides one positive pairing. 29.5.3 asks whether a compact complex manifold with vanishing first Bott–Chern class that admits a strictly LCK metric also admits a Vaisman metric. The rigidity theorem theorem 29.5.1 gives this when a single strictly LCK metric is both Chern–Ricci flat and Gauduchon; the remaining existence problem is to arrange these two conditions simultaneously. There is a pointwise sufficient condition for the first conjecture. If the least Lee-curvature eigenvalue relative to the chosen strictly LCK metric is constant, 29.2.6 makes it zero and gives a smooth semipositive representative of the nonzero ordinary Bott–Chern class. In particular this class is nef, and the balanced obstruction applies; compact invariant LCK quotients satisfy the criterion. The volume polynomial 29.2.5 supplies the argument. The two Hopf families show its scope: 29.2.8 has constant minimum but varying remaining spectrum, whereas 29.2.7 has indefinite Lee curvature and a smooth semipositive correction. In the latter family the first pointwise degeneracy retains positive total volume. A general LCK metric need not have constant minimum, so the unrestricted pseudoeffectivity conjecture stays open. The Lee–Gauduchon cone of section 29.6 makes part of this geometry invariant under bimeromorphic maps. Its dual is the cone of classes in $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$ whose image under $j_ X$ is pseudoeffective, and the strict inequalities defining it exclude $\ker j_ X$; the duality and its behavior under modifications are proved in that section. A nonzero pseudoeffective class in the image of $j_ X$ obstructs balanced metrics on every manifold bimeromorphic to $X$. On the Hopf threefold, the classes in $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$ whose image under $j_ X$ is pseudoeffective form a positive half-ray, although the Monge–Ampère masses there are unbounded. This cohomological invariant thus captures a geometric obstruction, while the nonlinear estimates for the scalar equation remain a separate task. The converse of its consequence for balanced metrics fails: the threefold of example 29.7.4 has zero Lee–Gauduchon cone but no strongly Gauduchon metric.

title: 33.5 Degeneration orders and finite-distance boundaries
text: 33.5 Degeneration orders and finite-distance boundaries Approximating a nef background by positive ones yields two kinds of boundary data: the rate at which the variational volume vanishes, and the distance traveled in the Hessian metric of section 26.5 . These need not detect the same boundary points. Throughout this section $\mu $ is a smooth strictly positive probability form on $X$. For a nef background $\theta $ and a Hermitian form $h$, the lower and upper degeneration orders $\underline a(\theta )\leq \overline a(\theta )$ of proposition 26.19.1 are the lower and upper limits of $\log \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)/\log \epsilon $ as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. They do not depend on $\mu $ or on the perturbation direction $h$, but they need not coincide. On a fixed product of two elliptic curves, proposition 26.19.5 realizes every pair $(1+\alpha ,1+\beta )$ with $0<\alpha <\beta <1$, as well as irrational common orders, and proposition 26.19.4 gives zero boundary volume with decay slower than every positive power of $\epsilon $. Equality of the two orders and their integrality therefore require additional geometry, as in the closed Kähler case, where the order is governed by the numerical dimension. Pulling back by a modification can only increase both orders (proposition 26.19.8 ), and a single blowup can increase them strictly, or remove positive limiting volume while both orders remain zero. Subtracting a positive current gives the same one-sided comparison when the residual stays nef. The perturbative minimal multiplicities of a nef background vanish, whereas in corollary 26.19.12 the boundary class contains a unique positive current, the current of integration along a divisor; it has minimal singularities, and removing it changes the order. The remaining questions, collected in 26.19.49 , concern equality of the orders and geometric restrictions on these behaviors. The Hessian metric gives boundary information of a different kind. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional space of smooth real $(1,1)$-forms containing no nonzero form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth, and let $\mathscr C$ be the open cone of elements of $V$ that admit a smooth positive representative. By proposition 26.5.1 , the metric $-D^2\log \lambda _\mu $ on $\mathscr C$ splits isometrically as the product of the logarithmic volume direction with the unit-volume hypersurface $\mathscr S=\{ \lambda _\mu =1\} $; consequently every path along which the volume tends to zero or to infinity has infinite length. Nevertheless, the blowup example of example 26.5.2 has boundary points at finite distance, represented by nef classes of positive volume. Completing the metric cone therefore cannot mean simply adjoining all nef classes, nor declaring every nef boundary point infinitely far away. Problem 33.5.1 . Let $\mu $ be a smooth strictly positive probability form on $X$, and let $\mathscr C$ be a cone of backgrounds in a specified finite-dimensional space $V$ as in section 26.5 , with the Hessian metric $-D^2\log \lambda _\mu $. Describe the metric completion of its unit-volume hypersurface $\mathscr S=\{ \theta \in \mathscr C:\lambda _\mu (\theta )=1\} $. Which boundary points admit a current representative, and which estimates for the minimizing Gauduchon metrics distinguish boundary points at finite distance from those at infinite distance? On a compact quotient of a complex Lie group, with $\mu $ the normalized invariant probability, theorem 26.5.5 answers the question for every fixed linear space of invariant backgrounds containing a positive form: the unit-volume hypersurface is complete, and its Cauchy sequences are exactly those whose coefficient matrices converge to a positive matrix. After normalization, nonzero singular limits of the coefficients lie at infinite distance. These assertions depend on the invariant probability and do not classify arbitrary cones of backgrounds or reference densities. On the Iwasawa manifold, theorem 26.5.9 extends the same coefficient metric and completion to every smooth reference density that is invariant along the central elliptic fibers; these are exactly the probabilities that maximize the variational volume of each invariant positive background. The minimizing forms need not be invariant, but their coefficient means still satisfy the spectral distance bounds. A reference density that varies along the fibers gives smaller volume, and the completion of its Hessian metric is a separate question. For the warped product cones of section 26.5.3 , on the product of a compact Kähler manifold with a curve, theorem 26.5.13 shows that the completion of the unit-volume hypersurface is a closed strip, a closed half-plane or the whole plane. Which ends lie at finite distance is decided by two ratios of real codimension to vanishing order, attached to the minimum set and the maximum set of the warping coefficient. Every end at finite distance is represented by a smooth semipositive, nef, nonbig form of volume one. The length estimates of lemma 26.5.12 are bounds for the variance of the traces of the balanced minimizers; they use the product probability and extreme sets consisting of finitely many disjoint strata with power-type vanishing. Other densities and other geometries of the extreme sets remain to be studied. The cone must be specified in 33.5.1 , since allowing additional directions can shorten distances along paths. The finite-dimensional calculations above do not define a distance on the whole infinite-dimensional quotient of backgrounds modulo $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of smooth functions.

title: Problem 33.5.1
text: Problem 33.5.1 . Let $\mu $ be a smooth strictly positive probability form on $X$, and let $\mathscr C$ be a cone of backgrounds in a specified finite-dimensional space $V$ as in section 26.5 , with the Hessian metric $-D^2\log \lambda _\mu $. Describe the metric completion of its unit-volume hypersurface $\mathscr S=\{ \theta \in \mathscr C:\lambda _\mu (\theta )=1\} $. Which boundary points admit a current representative, and which estimates for the minimizing Gauduchon metrics distinguish boundary points at finite distance from those at infinite distance?

title: 33.6 Weak Gauduchon adjoints
text: 33.6 Weak Gauduchon adjoints Let $\theta $ be a background with a model reference $\varphi $ and $\mathrm{d}V$ a smooth positive volume form, as in chapter 15 . For a bounded logarithmic density $F$, the normalized equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=c_\varphi (F)\mathrm{e}^ F\, \mathrm{d}V$ in the ordinary type of $\varphi $ determines a unique scalar, and $B_\varphi (F)=\log c_\varphi (F)$ is a concave functional of $F$ (section 15.1 ). For smooth data, differentiating the smooth equation produces a Gauduchon adjoint probability. At a continuous logarithmic density $F$, the supporting probabilities of $B_\varphi $, which form the set $\mathcal A_\varphi (F)$ of ( 15.5 ), provide a weak replacement. In the regimes of background and reference considered in chapter 15 , $\mathcal A_\varphi (F)$ is nonempty, convex and weakly compact, and its members are absolutely continuous (theorem 15.2.1 ). If this set consisted of a single probability, the scalar functional would be differentiable at $F$ even where no classical linearized equation is available. Conjecture 33.6.1 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$ and $\mathrm{d}V$ a smooth positive volume form, and take the nonsingular reference $\varphi =0$. For every real $F\in C(X)$, the set $\mathcal A_0(F)$ of supporting probabilities of the normalization functional $B_0$ at $F$ consists of a single probability measure. Equivalently, by proposition 15.2.3 , the concave functional $B_0$ is Gâteaux differentiable at every continuous logarithmic density. The conjecture holds at smooth $F$, by the linearized equation, and in the closed Kähler setting, where the normalization is explicit. By proposition 15.2.2 , it would imply that for any smooth approximations of $F$ the Gauduchon adjoint probabilities have a unique weak limit. A further sufficient condition is a bounded solution with continuous, everywhere positive complex Hessian. Then theorem 15.2.6 identifies a unique stationary supporting probability and the Gâteaux derivative. Proposition 15.2.7 gives its formula on $\mathbb P^1$ times any compact Hermitian factor for every positive continuous density of the stated product form; example 15.2.8 includes a non-Dini density on a non-Kähler threefold. The criterion does not prove that an arbitrary continuous density has a solution with such a Hessian. For bounded potentials there is a direct result. Suppose that $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon for every smooth $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$; this holds for every Gauduchon form on a compact surface. Then, by proposition 4.10.1 , the normalized Monge–Ampère measures of bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions extend the smooth adjoint probabilities and are continuous under convergence in capacity of uniformly bounded potentials. This defines no weak linearized operator, and it does not settle approximation by unbounded potentials in a general background. A Baire category argument gives a partial result. In every regime of background and reference considered in chapter 15 , theorem 15.2.4 shows that $\mathcal A_\varphi (F)$ is a single probability for $F$ in a dense $G_\delta $ subset of $C(X)$, and that at such $F$ all choices of supporting probabilities along uniform approximations of $F$ have the same weak limit. The assertion is generic for the uniform topology and does not exclude exceptional continuous densities. For $n\geq 2$, the compact formulation with currents gives a more precise target. By theorem 26.7.2 , the supporting probabilities at $F$ are exactly the normalized determinant-weighted measures of the currents $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ maximizing the functional $\mathfrak D_ F$ of ( 26.39 ). The conjecture thus asks whether all maximizers have the same weighted measure. Corollary 26.8.3 bounds the densities of these measures in $L^ q$, for every $1<q<n/(n-1)$, uniformly as $F$ ranges over a bounded subset of $C(X)$; the endpoint $q=n/(n-1)$ is included when $v_-(\omega )>0$. For $n\geq 3$, theorem 26.8.5 gives uniform $L^\infty $ bounds for both the adjoint density and the determinant density for smooth logarithmic densities in a small $C^{2,\alpha }$ ball around the logarithmic density of $\omega ^ n$ with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$, even when the lower mass vanishes, and by corollary 26.8.6 this ball contains distinct data with distinct exact maximizing currents. The controlled-Hessian family of theorem 26.8.9 gives a larger sufficient condition: if the smooth solution forms are uniformly comparable to the background, both densities have uniform two-sided bounds depending only on that comparison and fixed geometry. The divergence of the cofactor uses only the fixed torsion, so derivatives of the varying Hessian do not enter the constants. Example 26.8.10 gives such a smooth family whose densities have unbounded $C^1$ norms and no common modulus of continuity. Arbitrary bounded families of continuous data remain outside these hypotheses. These estimates alone give compactness but not uniqueness at continuous data. For a fixed smooth density the maximizing current is unique, smooth and strictly positive; nevertheless, proposition 26.17.2 shows that a sequence approaching the maximum can have unbounded determinant moments above the critical exponent. Another approach to the conjecture would be to show directly that the upper and lower directional derivatives of $B_0$ agree. More is known about the functional itself. Relative inequalities between positive residual forms give uniform convergence of the whole scalar functional, by the explicit bound ( 15.29 ) of theorem 15.8.1 . Under $L^1$ convergence of tests with a common $L^\infty $ bound, corollary 15.8.2 shows that the supporting probabilities have uniformly integrable densities whose weak $L^1$ cluster limits lie in the limiting supporting set. The adjoint probabilities at smooth tests, together with the value of the functional at zero, determine the whole functional by ( 15.30 ). None of these statements decides the conjectured uniqueness at continuous tests. For a singular reference or a degenerate background, the same uniqueness question makes sense under the hypotheses of chapter 15 . A geometric interpretation of the supporting probabilities, however, requires a well-defined weak linearization. For a smooth background $\theta $ and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, write $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and let $\rho $ be a measurable weight. The expression $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \theta _ u^{n-1})$ is not a definition until multiplication of the product $\theta _ u^{n-1}$ by $\rho $ has been justified. An explicit divisorial model shows what can go wrong. For the admissible reference of lemma 15.2.9 , the supporting set is a single probability and the residual linearization is well defined (proposition 15.2.10 ). Nevertheless, theorem 15.2.11 gives decreasing smooth approximations, with positive forms, whose classical adjoint probabilities have different weak limits, each carrying mass one half on the divisor. These potentials converge in capacity and their logarithmic densities converge in every finite $L^ p$, but their exponential densities concentrate and their smooth mass exceeds the relative mass. Within this fixed divisorial type, corollary 15.2.12 proves recovery, with an explicit estimate, under convergence in capacity and a uniform bound on the residual potentials. On the non-Gauduchon product surface of 15.13.4 , theorem 15.13.6 constructs a weak linearization for a logarithmic solution with continuous positive residual and identifies its full supporting set as a singleton. Uniform convergence of the positive residual forms, with the divisor fixed, gives convergence of both the weighted currents and their probabilities in proposition 15.13.7 ; pole-filling smoothings still retain unwanted divisor mass (example 15.13.8 ). For general singular references, adjoints that do not depend on the approximation still require control of the singularity type, of the mass and of the conformal multiplier.

title: Conjecture 33.6.1
text: Conjecture 33.6.1 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$ and $\mathrm{d}V$ a smooth positive volume form, and take the nonsingular reference $\varphi =0$. For every real $F\in C(X)$, the set $\mathcal A_0(F)$ of supporting probabilities of the normalization functional $B_0$ at $F$ consists of a single probability measure.

title: 33.7 Topologies on singularity types
text: 33.7 Topologies on singularity types A topology on singularity types must keep information that weak convergence of currents can lose. Deficits of upper volume achieve this when bounded mass and positive lower volume provide uniform control, and on curves polar curvature gives a complete description even at zero volume. The problem is to extend such control to degenerations in higher dimension and to backgrounds with unbounded mass. Throughout this section, for a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $P_\theta [u]$ is the ordinary envelope of definition 1.19.4 and $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ the multiplier-ideal envelope of definition 16.2.1 . An ordinary model is a potential $u$ with $P_\theta [u]=u$, an ideal model is one with $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=u$, and an analytic model is an ordinary model with analytic singularities. The lower and upper singularity volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ are the infimum and the supremum of the non-pluripolar masses over the ordinary singularity type of $u$ (definition 13.3.1 ).

title: 33.7.1 Weak convergence and singularity data
text: 33.7.1 Weak convergence and singularity data Weak convergence alone keeps little singularity information. The complete Gauduchon trace metric of corollary 5.2.1 induces the $L^1$ topology on normalized potentials, and the ideal metric of proposition 16.4.1 is the $L^1$ distance between the canonical ideal representatives $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. The completion of the ideal metric can acquire points that are not ideal envelopes of their own classes: on a curve, theorem 16.4.2 approximates every normalized potential by ideal envelopes with finitely many logarithmic poles and zero non-pluripolar mass. In particular, such envelopes can converge to a smooth potential with strictly positive curvature. This convergence does not hold in capacity, since damped continuity would then preserve their zero measures. A positive lower bound on the mass does not repair this. In proposition 16.4.3 , analytic ideal envelopes of one fixed positive mass converge in the ideal metric to the smooth model $0$, whose mass is larger. Nor can the normalization functional recover the lost data: on the closed model domain of theorem 15.10.1 , it records exactly the mass. The examples with positive residual in example 15.10.2 , example 15.10.3 have identical functionals and supporting sets but different poles, different multiplier ideals and different limits of normalized potentials, also for nonclosed backgrounds. An order bound gives more control than weak convergence. Let $h$ be a Hermitian form, let $\epsilon _ j\geq 0$ tend to zero, and let $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\epsilon _ jh)$ satisfy the one-sided bound $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}a_ j$ in the ideal order of section 1.12 , that is, $\mathcal I(ku)\subseteq \mathcal I(ka_ j)$ for all $k>0$. Then proposition 16.5.1 identifies the limit of the ideal envelopes from the convergence of divisorial Lelong numbers, and it shows that along such ordered analytic approximations, including dyadic regularization, the ordinary envelopes converge to $P_\theta [u]$ exactly when $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. Inclusions of multiplier ideals at fixed weights, as in corollary 16.5.2 , give the required convergence of divisorial numbers. Without the order bound, $L^1$ convergence together with convergence of every divisorial number is not enough, by example 16.5.3 . These tests make sense even when the upper volume is infinite. In contrast, in a Hermitian background analytic classes are dense for the ideal metric in the whole space (corollary 16.5.6 ), so density for that metric cannot characterize equality of the envelopes. The finite damped measures of chapter 7 control nonlinear limits throughout the space of potentials, including potentials of infinite mass. Since their weak continuity already follows from convergence in capacity, requiring it in addition imposes no further condition on multiplier ideals. For a Hermitian form $\omega $, the uniform topology $\tau _{\omega ,0}$ of section 16.6 on ordinary singularity types combines both envelopes with controlled inclusions of multiplier ideals and the total variation of divisorial orders on each fixed compact modification. By theorem 16.6.3 , the closure and the sequential closure of the analytic classes are both the set of ordinary classes with $P_\omega [u]=P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I}$. This characterizes the analytic closure in every Hermitian background, including classes represented by potentials of infinite mass. The topology is not $T_0$ on ordinary classes. Transport by a smooth gauge change of the background is exact when the obstacle changes with the background, but with the zero obstacle kept fixed it is discontinuous already on curves, even within a cutoff of positive mass (proposition 16.6.6 ). The uniformity of 16.6.4 , generated by the envelopes $P_{\omega ,F}[u]$ and $P_{\omega ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}$ below all smooth obstacles $F$ (definition 1.19.4 ), is invariant under smooth changes of background, and its analytic closure consists of the classes for which the two envelopes agree below every smooth obstacle (theorem 16.6.9 ). On curves this is the same analytic locus, but by proposition 30.12.12 the topology is incomplete and strictly weaker than polar total variation. In higher dimension, membership of $u$ in the relative envelope class $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I})$ suffices for equality below every obstacle (proposition 16.6.8 ), and under bounded mass and positive lower volume of the ideal envelope, equality at the zero obstacle is already sufficient (proposition 30.8.2 ). The fixed stronger potential in theorem 16.6.11 gives an explicit family in the sufficient relative envelope class on every positive Hermitian background. Its poles may contain a prescribed countable dense set, while its multiplier ideals are trivial at every positive weight. By proposition 16.6.12 , both envelopes equal the unrestricted envelope below every continuous obstacle. The stretching property is supplied by the construction rather than deduced from equality below zero. Several geometric cases are known without the volume condition. For every admissible smooth background on a curve, corollary 30.13.2 shows that equality at the zero obstacle, equality at all smooth obstacles and membership in the relative envelope class of the ideal envelope are equivalent. On products with separated backgrounds, proposition 16.6.30 computes both envelopes coordinatewise below separated smooth obstacles, also for curve backgrounds of zero area, and proposition 16.6.40 identifies equality at the zero obstacle with equality at every smooth obstacle, including obstacles that mix the coordinates and factors of zero area. This equivalence persists after adding a nonclosed auxiliary coefficient and a unit divisor (corollary 16.6.41 ), and for arbitrary compact complex auxiliary factors with a semipositive vertical term, without any mass bound on the ambient manifold (corollary 16.6.44 ). For divisorial fibrations over curves, corollary 16.6.20 gives the same equivalence at zero model volume, even with poles along whole fibers or with disconnected fibers, by reducing the obstacles to the cover formed by the fiber components. In example 16.6.18 the ambient background fails bounded mass, while the base potential belongs to the relative envelope class required for equality at all obstacles. Whether equality at the zero obstacle implies equality at all obstacles at zero lower volume in general, including backgrounds with unbounded mass, is unresolved.

title: 33.7.2 Volume comparison and analytic approximation
text: 33.7.2 Volume comparison and analytic approximation In this subsection $X$ has bounded mass and $\theta $ is a smooth big background. For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the comparison $d_\theta (u,v)$ of definition 30.6.1 is the sum of the deficits of the upper volumes of $u$ and $v$ relative to the upper volume of $\max (u,v)$, and $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ denotes the set of ordinary models with lower volume at least $\delta >0$. A common positive lower bound for the volumes converts a small deficit into a stretching estimate. The resulting quantitative $L^1$ bound, together with a modulus for three points that replaces the triangle inequality, gives separation and Cauchy completeness on $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ (theorem 30.6.5 ); the cutoff must be closed, as example 30.6.6 shows. The positive lower bound is also what prevents the comparison from identifying distinct ordinary models: example 30.6.2 gives two distinct models at zero lower volume with comparison zero, in positive closed backgrounds in every dimension at least two and in positive nonclosed backgrounds in every dimension at least three. Rooftop continuity gives monotone lower bounds, which yield convergence in capacity (proposition 30.7.2 , theorem 30.7.3 ). Analytic approximation detects exactly the ideal models. Theorem 30.8.3 corrects analytic regularizations so that they stay in the fixed background; their ordinary models converge for $d_\theta $ to the ideal envelope, and their comparison with the original potential tends to the excess of the upper volume of its ideal envelope over its own upper volume. Conversely, at positive lower volume, theorem 30.8.4 shows that ideal models are closed under this convergence. Although $d_\theta $ fails the triangle inequality even on analytic models on a projective manifold, theorem 30.11.3 constructs a complete metric on the ordinary models of positive lower volume with the same convergent sequences; its Cauchy criterion also controls the reciprocals of the lower volumes, which excludes approach to zero volume. By corollary 30.11.4 , the ideal models form a closed complete subspace, which is the completion of the analytic models of positive volume. Monotone limits show where positivity enters. For decreasing ordinary models in backgrounds that decrease uniformly to a smooth big form, theorem 30.5.2 gives continuity of the lower volume even when the limiting volume is zero; if the limiting lower volume is positive, the upper volumes and the Lelong numbers on every fixed modification are continuous as well. For increasing sequences in a fixed background, theorem 30.5.1 gives continuity of the ordinary envelopes and of both volumes under the same positivity condition. For arbitrary decreasing potentials whose limit has positive lower volume, proposition 30.5.3 shows that the ordinary envelopes converge exactly when the upper volumes do. Likewise, when the ideal envelope has positive lower volume, proposition 30.8.2 shows that the ordinary and ideal envelopes of a potential agree exactly when the potential and its ideal envelope have the same upper volume. There is an explicit divisorial positivity test on $\mathbb P^2$. Let $\kappa $ be the normalized Fubini–Study form, prescribe distinct hyperplanes $H_ j$ with summable coefficients $a_ j>0$, and put $A=\sum _ ja_ j$. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\theta =0$ and $\theta -A\kappa >0$, equality with the profile $\sum _ ja_ j\operatorname {ord}_ E(\pi ^*H_ j)$ on every smooth compact modification specifies one ideal type. By 30.8.6 , its ideal envelope is ordinarily equivalent to the logarithmic series, and every representative of this ordinary type has mass $\int _ X(\theta -A\kappa )^2$. The nonclosed example of 30.8.7 has infinitely many hyperplanes outside one pencil and positive lower volume. General positivity criteria from restricted ideals or divisorial orders, and the remaining zero-volume implications in 30.8.8 , remain open. The comparison is compatible with changes of background as long as these controls persist. A smooth gauge change, followed by ordinary projection, preserves it exactly (proposition 30.9.1 ). For a fixed potential and backgrounds decreasing to $\theta $, corollary 30.5.4 gives continuity of the lower volume and, at positive lower volume, of the ordinary envelope. The uniform estimate ( 30.25 ) allows the curvature errors of analytic regularization to tend to zero, as in theorem 30.9.4 . For perturbations of the background in both directions, a convex correction produces admissible transported models, with a uniform comparison whose limiting notion of convergence does not depend on the chosen strict reference; this gives the analytic criterion of theorem 30.10.2 , theorem 30.10.3 . None of these arguments covers loss of bigness or the boundary at zero volume in higher dimension.

title: 33.7.3 Polar curvature
text: 33.7.3 Polar curvature Let $Y$ be a compact connected Riemann surface with a smooth positive form $\theta $. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$, the polar curvature $\mu _ u=\mathbf1_{\{ u=-\infty \} }(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$ determines the ordinary model of $u$, and its atomic part determines the ideal model. By theorem 30.12.2 , $d_\theta (u,v)$ is the total variation of $\mu _ u-\mu _ v$, also at zero non-pluripolar mass. By corollary 30.12.3 , all normalized ordinary models form a complete geodesic space, and the ideal models form the closed subspace obtained by completing the analytic models of positive mass. On ideal models of positive mass this agrees with the topology of the source metric in theorem 19.5.3 , corollary 19.5.4 , for which this space is not totally bounded. Its completeness therefore has a different content from the compact completion obtained from weak convergence of traces. Keeping only the atomic part of the polar curvature is a $1$-Lipschitz retraction onto the ideal models and selects the unique nearest ideal model; by proposition 30.12.6 , the distance to the analytic closure is exactly the mass of the diffuse part of the polar curvature. The model of zero mass in example 30.12.7 has trivial multiplier ideals but positive distance from that closure. Convergence in total variation implies convergence in $L^1$ and in capacity, even at zero mass (theorem 30.12.4 ), whereas the moving pole of example 30.12.5 shows that convergence in capacity does not imply convergence in total variation. Degeneration of the background is also explicit on curves. Between smooth backgrounds of positive area, theorem 30.13.3 gives correspondences of the model spaces that rescale by the ratio of the areas and are compatible with ideal projection, also at models of zero mass. Under uniform convergence of the backgrounds, the corresponding normalized representatives vary uniformly in $L^1$ and in capacity (corollary 30.13.5 ). When the limiting area is zero, theorem 1.8.15 shows that all normalized potentials converge to the unique limiting potential, uniformly over the admissible families, and the unscaled diameters of the model spaces tend to zero. The joint space of theorem 30.14.1 treats the smooth background as a further coordinate. It is complete for the combination of smooth convergence of backgrounds and total variation of polar curvature, its analytic closure is exactly the ideal locus, even at zero area, and on each fixed background it restricts to the curve topology described above. In higher dimension, the realization of compatible singularity data and a replacement for the comparison of finite upper volumes are unresolved. Finite curve maps give another compatibility within the curve theory. For $r:C'\to C$ of degree $d$, a smooth base form $\beta $ of nonnegative area and $\sigma =r^*\beta $, 16.6.53 commutes both envelopes with pullback below every pulled-back smooth obstacle. The polar metric scales by $d$, and 16.6.54 gives a $1$-Lipschitz retraction with polar measure $d^{-1}r^*r_*\mu $, preserving polar mass and commuting with ideal projection. By 16.6.55 , this describes the closed complete subspace of models that descend to the original base of a compact curve map, with its original-base normalization. The cubic example shows that this averaging need not select a nearest model. These conclusions do not supply a complete topology for general higher-rank backgrounds. In dimension at least two the polar part of the first curvature current loses information. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, write $\operatorname {Pol}_1(u)=\mathbf1_{\{ u=-\infty \} }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$, and $\operatorname {Pol}_\pi (u)$ for the corresponding current of $u\circ \pi $ on a modification $\pi $ of $X$. By proposition 16.6.58 , distinct analytic ideal models with isolated logarithmic poles, whose multiplier ideals differ at suitable weights, all have $\operatorname {Pol}_1=0$. The blowup at the pole detects the coefficient on the exceptional divisor (corollary 16.6.59 ), but every fixed countable family of modifications misses some such models (corollary 16.6.60 ). Tracing polar curvature against Gauduchon forms gives a uniform normalization over modifications. Fix a family $\mathscr R$ of smooth modifications $\pi \colon Y_\pi \to X$ and Gauduchon forms $\eta _\pi $ on $Y_\pi $. The comparison $\delta ^{\mathrm{pol}}_\omega $ of ( 16.50 ) is the supremum over $\pi \in \mathscr R$ of the total variation of the polar curvature of $u\circ \pi $ traced against $\eta _\pi ^{n-1}$, normalized by the trace of $\pi ^*\omega $. By proposition 16.6.61 , it separates analytic models and, on curves, recovers the complete curve topology up to a constant factor. Bounded equivalence preserves polar currents (proposition 1.25.3 ), so transport by a smooth gauge change, followed by ordinary projection, preserves the comparison (corollary 16.6.63 ). Since polar curvature is closed for every pole set (proposition 1.25.6 ), equality of the scalar traces recovers the full polar currents on each modification (corollary 16.6.64 ). Arbitrary independent choices of the Gauduchon forms can nevertheless fail to induce the positive-volume topology, even for analytic ideal models on $\mathbb P^2$ (proposition 16.6.66 ). The space of polar trace coordinates is complete (proposition 16.6.62 ), and for sequences that are Cauchy for the comparison, proposition 16.6.65 gives compatible weak limits of the polar currents, all carried by the pole set of a single $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. Whether these limiting currents are realized by an ordinary model is a further problem. Even all modifications together do not make the first polar comparison separate models or give the right analytic closure. On every compact Kähler manifold of dimension at least two, proposition 16.6.69 constructs a nonzero ordinary model whose polar currents vanish on every modification, whose non-pluripolar volume is positive but strictly smaller than that of the zero model, and whose multiplier ideals are all trivial. More precisely, corollary 16.6.70 gives a complete ordered interval of such models with volumes $A-Mt^ n$ and mutual distances $M|s^ n-t^ n|$, where $A=\int _ X\omega ^ n$ and $M>0$ is a constant of the construction; for every $0<\delta <A$, the interval can be chosen inside $\mathcal M_\delta (\omega )$. Every first polar coordinate vanishes on this interval, and only its zero endpoint is ideal. Consequently every choice of Gauduchon forms identifies distinct models, and the closure of the analytic models for the polar comparison contains nonideal models. The same diffuse cutoff can be placed in a Hermitian background. Proposition 16.6.71 separates the loss $Mt^ n$ in the mass of the potential from lower-degree terms coming from the background. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ q)=0$ for $1\leq q<n$, the mass is the same for all bounded-equivalent representatives, and corollary 16.6.72 extends the whole interval of models to this Hermitian background; in particular the obstruction occurs on every compact complex surface with a Gauduchon form. For an arbitrary Hermitian background, proposition 16.6.73 computes the mass of each representative from finitely many torsion coefficients and the same loss $Mt^ n$. On a surface, corollary 16.6.74 shows that the mass is constant over the bounded-equivalence class exactly when $\omega $ is Gauduchon; otherwise even admissible smooth bounded perturbations change it, and the exact values would require optimizing these terms, which depend on the representative. Under bounded mass and positive lower mass, proposition 16.6.75 still gives positive lower volume and a strict gap in upper volume for the diffuse ordinary models, while their first polar currents vanish on every modification. By the same proposition, this obstruction holds for every Hermitian metric on every compact complex surface. The theorem on preservation of residuals, theorem 30.3.5 , distinguishes the diffuse parameters after ordinary projection. Consequently, in every background with both mass properties, corollary 16.6.76 gives a complete ordered interval of models throughout each range $0\leq t\leq t_0<1/C$, with $C$ the constant of proposition 16.6.71 . Its upper-volume coordinate is strictly decreasing and Lipschitz, although the torsion terms prevent the explicit power formula from being inferred, and every first polar coordinate still vanishes. The same theorem preserves the entire residual measure, so its location matters: in proposition 16.6.77 , two models carry residual mass $r$ in disjoint regions, have zero first polar data, and are at distance at least $2r$; when $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ q)=0$ for $1\leq q<n$, their two singularity volumes also coincide. A complete extension must therefore distinguish this spatial residual information. Even the full residual measure on the base is not enough. When $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ q)=0$ for $1\leq q<n$, proposition 16.6.78 uses anisotropic maxima on one diffuse pole set to build a compact metric family of ordinary models indexed by positive weight vectors. Fixing the product of the weights gives complete subfamilies of real dimension $n-1$ whose members have the same residual measure, the same two singularity volumes, trivial multiplier ideals and zero first polar currents on every modification. The comparison distance nevertheless separates them, through the symmetric difference of the associated coordinate rectangles. A complete extension must therefore also detect singularity information lost by the full base residual. The proposition does not assert that the full residual products agree on every modification. Return to a curve $Y$ with a smooth positive form $\theta $. On ideal models, the ordinary-type topology $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ is the topology of total variation of the atomic data, and its canonical metric includes the boundary of zero mass (theorem 30.12.8 ). On general ordinary models it is weaker than polar total variation: diffuse polar curvature can concentrate into an atom in the limit of the envelopes, which produces the Cauchy sequence without an ordinary-type limit in proposition 30.12.9 . Characterizing the analytic closure on the whole ordinary space and extending the model topology to a complete one are therefore separate requirements. Problem 33.7.1 . For a smooth big background $\theta $ on a manifold with bounded mass, theorem 30.11.3 gives a complete metrizable topology on the ordinary models of positive lower volume, in which the closure of the analytic models is exactly the set of ideal models. Extend this topology to ordinary models beyond bounded mass and positive lower volume, keeping the closure of the analytic models exactly the set of ideal models. The extension should keep the compatibility with smooth gauge changes and with two-sided perturbations of the background established in section 30.9 , section 30.10 , and it should treat limits of backgrounds that lose bigness or a uniform positive lower bound for the volume. On curves it should recover the complete topology of polar total variation of corollary 30.12.3 on all models. Determine whether the extension in higher dimension is completely metrizable. Any such extension must keep the singularity information that weak limits lose. Potentials of infinite mass are already covered by $\tau _{\omega ,0}$: for instance, the potential of proposition 16.3.3 has infinite mass, while its canonical envelopes, the ordinary and the ideal one, both equal zero. On curves, zero volume does not prevent completeness, but in higher dimension the stretching argument still needs a positive lower bound for the volume. There is nevertheless a restricted locus where a complete metric is known at zero volume. On the divisorial product locus of proposition 16.6.26 , polar curvature on the curve factor gives a complete metric whose analytic closure is exactly the set of ideal models; the top-degree volume comparison vanishes identically on this locus and therefore cannot produce this metric. The same restricted metric and analytic closure exist in a positive nonclosed background on a projective manifold (corollary 16.6.27 ), and the locus, the metric and the ideal projection persist when the second curve coefficient vanishes and the limiting background is not big (corollary 16.6.28 ). Proposition 16.6.31 gives a complete sum metric, with the same properties of ideal projection and analytic closure, on the locus induced by several independent curve models, and corollary 16.6.32 preserves this locus and metric through a nonclosed auxiliary coefficient and its nonbig limit at zero. When the curve coefficients vary, proposition 16.6.34 gives compatible weighted metrics, discarding vanishing coordinates, with uniform $L^1$ collapse when all curve areas vanish, and proposition 16.6.35 compares these metrics quantitatively across different sets of active coordinates, with the exact distance for ordered coefficients. Proposition 16.6.37 , Corollary 16.6.38 extend the construction to arbitrary smooth admissible curve backgrounds and identify the limiting singleton, and proposition 16.6.43 preserves the restricted complete metric through arbitrary compact complex auxiliary factors with semipositive vertical terms, independently of bounded mass on the ambient manifold.

title: Problem 33.7.1
text: Problem 33.7.1 . For a smooth big background $\theta $ on a manifold with bounded mass, theorem 30.11.3 gives a complete metrizable topology on the ordinary models of positive lower volume, in which the closure of the analytic models is exactly the set of ideal models. Extend this topology to ordinary models beyond bounded mass and positive lower volume, keeping the closure of the analytic models exactly the set of ideal models. The extension should keep the compatibility with smooth gauge changes and with two-sided perturbations of the background established in section 30.9 , section 30.10 , and it should treat limits of backgrounds that lose bigness or a uniform positive lower bound for the volume. On curves it should recover the complete topology of polar total variation of corollary 30.12.3 on all models. Determine whether the extension in higher dimension is completely metrizable.

title: 33.8 Trace realization and recovery
text:
33.8 Trace realization and recovery Prescribing divisorial lower bounds and taking an envelope may produce larger orders than those prescribed. Let $u$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ and $Y\subset X$ a connected compact submanifold of positive dimension along which $u$ has zero generic Lelong number, $
u (u,Y)=0$. As in chapter 19 , the trace data $	au _{Y,u}(E)$ of ( 19.1 ) are the asymptotic vanishing orders of the restrictions to $Y$ of the multiplier ideals $\mathcal I(tu)$, along prime divisors $E$ on smooth modifications $\pi \colon Z	o Y$. For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\Omega $ on $Y$, the trace envelope $\mathcal T_\Omega (u;Y)$ of ( 19.7 ) is the upper envelope of the nonpositive $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $a$ with $
u (a\circ \pi ,E)\geq 	au _{Y,u}(E)$ for all such $E$. The realization problem asks when these inequalities are equalities. Theorem 19.6.2 constructs the envelope in the restricted background itself and identifies it as the $L^1$ limit of the envelopes of the restricted analytic approximants, and theorem 19.6.3 shows that it pulls back exactly to every compact modification and is there the limit of the envelopes for vanishing Hermitian perturbations. When $Y$ has bounded mass and carries a Hermitian form of positive lower mass, corollary 30.5.5 proves equality in all divisorial inequalities for sufficiently large backgrounds $\Omega $; when $Y$ is Kähler, equality also follows directly from the closed theory (theorem 19.6.4 ). Ambient potentials with analytic singularities have exact ordinary restrictions. In higher dimension, theorem 19.7.1 realizes all orders when the data reduce to a problem on an ambient curve, with an ordinary type independent of a sufficiently large background. For general data, theorem 19.6.5 shows that in a larger Hermitian background the envelope has positive finite mass. Problem 33.8.1 . Let $u$ and $Y$ be as above, and suppose that $Y$ fails at least one of the two mass properties used in corollary 30.5.5 : bounded mass, and the existence of a Hermitian form of positive lower mass. Can the Hermitian background $\Omega $ on $Y$ in theorem 19.6.5 be chosen so that \[  
u  igl (\mathcal T_\Omega (u;Y)\circ \pi ,E igr ) =	au _{Y,u}(E)  \] for every prime divisor $E$ on every smooth modification $\pi $ of $Y$? If so, determine an ordinary or ideal singularity class of this realization that is compatible with changes of background, and prove its addition and approximation properties. The equality is required on all modifications, which is stronger than realizing the divisorial part of the data on one model. For that part, corollary 1.17.5 gives a canonical ordinary type by combining a Gauduchon bound for the mass of the divisorial current with a smooth decomposition of currents; it does not determine the trace data of higher codimension, which appear on further modifications. The exceptional divisor of theorem 23.8.1 describes the discrepancy between the canonical types on two models, together with a cocycle relation and approximation in linear mass. By example 23.8.3 , a nonzero exceptional term is compatible with an exact trace potential: the term records information absent from the divisorial part on the original model. Enlarging the background provides a competitor with controlled curvature, but it does not automatically exclude additional divisorial orders. In the proof for curve fibrations, every order on a further model reduces to a multiplicity in one variable. Under the two mass properties, theorem 30.5.2 controls Lelong numbers through the deficit of upper volume and a positive lower volume. The missing step is to extend such control beyond these mass conditions. Even exact realization does not control the mass of all representatives of the ideal class. In proposition 19.9.2 , on a product with the Hopf threefold, the realizing potential has finite extended mass, while another potential with the same multiplier ideals and the same trace numbers has infinite mass. A proposed characterization by volumes or by continuity must specify which representative, or which class of masses, it uses. Theorem 19.8.2 answers the realization question for the Hopf pair $(H_{n+1},H_ n)$, $n\geq 3$, when the ambient potential is pulled back from $\mathbb P^ n$ and has zero generic Lelong number along the projective hyperplane. Every Hermitian metric on $H_ n$ fails bounded mass, yet the same pulled-back potential realizes the trace data on all compact models. Within the invariant backgrounds $a\alpha +b eta $, corollary 19.8.5 , proposition 19.8.6 give an ideal class compatible with changes of background, addition, positive scaling and decreasing analytic approximation. Exactness persists in every larger Hermitian background. This settles the projective pullback case; general ambient data and background compatibility outside this family remain part of the problem.

title: Problem 33.8.1
text: Problem 33.8.1 . Let $u$ and $Y$ be as above, and suppose that $Y$ fails at least one of the two mass properties used in corollary 30.5.5 : bounded mass, and the existence of a Hermitian form of positive lower mass. Can the Hermitian background $\Omega $ on $Y$ in theorem 19.6.5 be chosen so that \[  \nu \bigl (\mathcal T_\Omega (u;Y)\circ \pi ,E\bigr ) =\tau _{Y,u}(E)  \] for every prime divisor $E$ on every smooth modification $\pi $ of $Y$? If so, determine an ordinary or ideal singularity class of this realization that is compatible with changes of background, and prove its addition and approximation properties.

title: 33.8.1 Recovery of compatible divisor systems
text: 33.8.1 Recovery of compatible divisor systems Prescribing finitely many divisorial poles leaves a smooth residual background. When the residual has a smooth positive representative, theorem 26.21.2 solves the residual equation for a smooth strictly positive probability measure, and every subsolution at the same scalar whose Lelong numbers along the prescribed divisors are at least the prescribed coefficients differs from this solution by a constant. Consequently a solution in the prescribed ordinary type has the same scalar and a smooth remainder. Passing to compatible data on all modifications requires keeping this positivity and this exact singularity information uniformly. Passing to all modifications raises two further issues. First, a smooth positive probability measure pulls back to a density that vanishes on the exceptional divisor, and the smooth dual formula cannot be applied to such a density until a degenerate extension has been proved. Second, the residual classes on two models are related explicitly: corollary 24.2.2 subtracts the Bott–Chern class of the effective exceptional divisor while keeping the prescribed exterior derivative. The approximating coefficients converge in linear trace mass, but this formula gives no transformation rule for the nonlinear volume. Exact pullback preserves singularity volumes by proposition 13.3.2 ; subtracting an exceptional divisorial class changes the background and is a different operation. Assigning an intersection number to a nonclosed form resolves neither the degenerate equation nor the question of volume. The envelope systems of chapter 25 are compatible families, over the positive Hermitian perturbations of a background, that record representatives of one multiplier-ideal class (definition 25.2.2 ). Their construction gives an order adjunction and an exact criterion for recovery: the limit as the perturbation vanishes must keep the prescribed ideal type. Under bounded mass, for a big background, theorem 30.5.6 gives a sufficient condition involving only the initial slices: their lower singularity volumes must have a positive limit as the perturbation vanishes. Concavity then gives positive lower volume at every finite parameter, and stretching preserves all local divisorial orders. The ruled-surface example of that chapter has zero residual volume and shows why recovery fails without such a condition. Problem 33.8.2 . Let $X$ fail the bounded mass property, and let $\theta $ be a smooth big background on $X$. Find a condition on a compatible Hermitian envelope system over $\theta $ (definition 25.2.2 ) that forces recovery of its ideal type at every finite parameter, and that reduces to the criterion of theorem 30.5.6 , a positive limiting lower volume of the initial slices, when bounded mass holds. Specify the invariant and the uniform estimates that replace the finite deficit of upper volume, and describe their behavior under modifications. On the scalar Hopf threefold, theorem 25.6.3 gives a sufficient condition despite unbounded ambient upper mass. If every positive scalar slice is invariant under the elliptic fiber action and the initial transverse limiting model has positive lower volume on $\mathbb P^2$, the system is recovered at every finite parameter and every positive Hermitian perturbation. The symmetry constructs the full transverse system rather than assuming survival of the limiting ideals. Example 25.6.4 supplies nonanalytic ideal data with exact positive transverse volumes. The recovery identity and transverse volumes survive modifications in the exact pulled backgrounds, and smooth gauge transport preserves recovery. A criterion for general nonsymmetric systems and arbitrary new Hermitian backgrounds on modifications remains unresolved. For a fixed finite divisorial support, proposition 26.21.3 settles the case where the residual stays in the positive cone: if the coefficients converge and the limiting residual background still has a smooth positive representative, the normalized smooth remainders converge smoothly, the singular solutions converge in capacity, their measures converge in total variation, and their logarithmic coefficients remain exact on every modification. Multiplier ideals can nevertheless jump at an integer coefficient. For divisors of sections moving in fixed finite-dimensional spaces, positive limiting weights and residuals give convergence of the full potentials (theorem 15.9.2 ), in each of the two regimes stated there. Recovery beyond the regime of bounded mass and positive volume, degeneration of residual positivity, and estimates uniform over infinitely many models all require further arguments.

title: Problem 33.8.2
text: Problem 33.8.2 . Let $X$ fail the bounded mass property, and let $\theta $ be a smooth big background on $X$. Find a condition on a compatible Hermitian envelope system over $\theta $ (definition 25.2.2 ) that forces recovery of its ideal type at every finite parameter, and that reduces to the criterion of theorem 30.5.6 , a positive limiting lower volume of the initial slices, when bounded mass holds. Specify the invariant and the uniform estimates that replace the finite deficit of upper volume, and describe their behavior under modifications.

title: 33.9 Sections, kernels and the dimension of growth
search_title: Sections, kernels and the dimension of growth
text: 33.9 Sections, kernels and the dimension of growth A Hermitian form is the curvature of a holomorphic line bundle only if it is closed, so the algebraic part of the theory must keep the closed curvature data separate from the Hermitian background. The weighted spaces of sections of chapter 20 , their multiplicative variant and their intrinsic flag bodies do this, and their dimension of growth can be strictly smaller than the complex dimension of the manifold. For the partial Bergman kernels of chapter 27 , the upper bound by the envelope is proved in general; a matching lower bound is known in the explicit regimes below, and the general problem is open. Let $L\to X$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth Hermitian metric of curvature $\theta $. If $X$ admits a modification from a compact Kähler manifold and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has positive non-pluripolar mass, theorem 27.6.3 proves convergence of the kernel measures normalized in full dimension. The proof keeps track of the relative canonical bundle, whose Jacobian factor corrects both the integrability condition of the ideals and the Hilbert norm. This geometric assumption implies the bounded mass property, although the birational transformation identities themselves do not require it. On a holomorphic submersion with descended data, the equilibrium theorem on the base gives a different exact limit on the total space. On the Hopf $n$-fold, the dimension of the selected space of sections of the $m$th tensor power grows like $m^{n-1}$, so normalizing by $m^ n$ would erase the limit; adding the vertical Hermitian form recovers a nonzero measure, with the factor computed in ( 27.24 ). Isolated point poles that do not descend are treated in theorem 27.8.3 : their projected jet conditions differ from the multiplier ideals on the base by only finitely many orders. For a single point pole on the Hopf manifold, theorem 27.9.2 proves the lower asymptotics of the potentials as well as convergence of the kernel measures in total variation. Moving the pole along its fiber leaves every selected space unchanged, so these limits recover the projected equilibrium, while the multiplier-ideal type of the original Hermitian weight can be different. Theorem 27.11.1 gives a further regime: a logarithmic pole along a section over a hyperplane, with arbitrary compact connected fibers of positive dimension. The growth degree is the dimension of the base. The partial potentials attain the domination envelope of the original singularity on the total space, and the kernel measures converge in total variation for every smooth positive volume used in the norm. The limit on the base is determined by the metric of the line bundle, and its lift keeps exactly the conditional probabilities on the fibers. For an interior rational Newton polytope with integral affine offset, theorem 27.16.2 , theorem 27.16.3 prove a lower bound by the envelope and a positive limit of the measures in the relative growth dimension. Here the smooth weight and the sampling probability are invariant under the torus, the logarithmic weight is strictly convex, and the target is the specified envelope of Newton growth. In lower dimension the limit lies on a real moment shell and differs from every mixed measure formed from the curvature of the envelope and a smooth Hermitian form on the ambient manifold. These results do not identify an arbitrary multiplier-ideal envelope. The multiplier-ideal family of theorem 27.17.1 has positive growth exponent and potentials converging to its ideal envelope, yet its kernel measures have two different limits: rounding at two critical divisors makes the leading term of the section count depend on the parity of the degree. Convergence of the normalized dimensions is therefore an additional necessary condition for a finite limit of the measures. This selecting weight has zero top non-pluripolar mass, so it lies outside the positive-mass regime above. For the two isolated base points of a pencil, theorem 27.18.3 , theorem 27.18.5 identify the full ideal envelope and prove a global lower bound for the potentials and a positive limit of the measures. The selected spaces consist of three neighboring bands of monomials and have dimension exactly $3m+1$, although their class of competitors at all weights equals the upper ordinary type class. The specified compact logarithmic box and Gaussian norm give intrinsic mass three. Locally uniform convergence away from the poles, convergence in every finite $L^ p$ and uniform convergence after exponentiation coexist with an unbounded additive error at each fixed degree. These spaces are not multiplicative, and this selecting weight also has zero top non-pluripolar mass. Problem 33.9.1 . Let $L\to X$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth Hermitian metric, and consider a series of selected spaces of sections of $L^ m$ with weighted $L^2$ norms, as in section 27.1 , together with its intrinsic growth dimension. Identify hypotheses on the series under which the partial Fubini–Study potentials attain the lower bound given by the envelope and the kernel measures, normalized in the growth dimension, converge. Relate the limiting measure to the Hermitian background while keeping track of the closed curvature and of the growth dimension of the series. Beyond the regimes treated above (isolated points, horizontal projective poles, descended data, interior Newton polytopes and the pencil example), the problem involves two tasks: producing enough sections with the required ideal constraints, and controlling the resulting measures. A Bergman upper bound gives neither. On a manifold that is not Moishezon, normalization by the ambient degree may already force every kernel measure to vanish, for reasons independent of singularity theory. Locality of Hölder regularity, and regularity of weighted extremal functions under a uniform density condition in capacity, give special cases of the regularity problem; see section 34.19 . These hypotheses do not cover every singular envelope, and they do not settle the problem of lower asymptotics above. On a fibration, the comparison of spaces of finite codimension in lemma 27.8.1 suggests a more specific question, which asks for an analytic description of the constraints on sections after descent. Problem 33.9.2 . Let $\pi :X\to B$ be a surjective holomorphic submersion of connected compact complex manifolds with connected fibers, where $B$ is Kähler of dimension $q\geq 1$. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and a holomorphic line bundle $A$ on $B$ with a smooth Hermitian metric $h$. Set $\theta =c_1(A,h)$. For positive integers $m$, identify \[  V_ m=H^0\bigl (X,\pi ^*A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi )\bigr ) \subseteq H^0(B,A^ m)  \] by holomorphic descent. Find geometric or analytic conditions that produce $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ of positive non-pluripolar mass such that, for all sufficiently large $m$, \[  \begin{gathered} W_ m=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )\bigr )\subseteq V_ m,\\ \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=o(m^ q). \end{gathered}  \] Determine which features of the singularities of $\varphi $ along the fibers suffice for this approximation. For descended continuous weights and probability norms, such an approximation, combined with lemma 27.8.1 and the equilibrium theorem on the base, would give the limits of the kernel measures and of the determinant functionals, although not by itself convergence of the potentials. For finitely many isolated poles, theorem 27.8.3 gives the stronger error $O(m^{q-1})$ under its hypothesis on the projected poles. Theorem 27.10.2 gives the same error for a logarithmic singularity along a section over a smooth divisor of the base, under the curvature margin stated there; its base reference is explicitly divisorial, and example 27.10.3 shows that the order of the error is sharp. The problem does not presuppose that every selecting weight in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ admits such a base reference. The band criterion of theorem 27.10.6 , which places $V_ m$ between two spaces of sections vanishing along a divisor, requires a global logarithmic lower bound for $\varphi $, a positive residual on the base after a smooth gauge change, and a single chart over a smooth connected divisor in which $\varphi $ has an anisotropic upper bound. It constructs a base reference of positive mass and gives the error $O(m^{q-1})$ for every tensor power. Corollary 27.10.7 computes the selected series exactly, including pole sets of positive dimension inside the fibers, and example 27.10.8 attains the order of the error. These are sufficient conditions; general selecting weights and necessary conditions remain to be understood. For finitely many divisors with simple normal crossings, theorem 27.10.10 gives the same error from a global lower bound by a sum of logarithms, one anisotropic witness for each divisor and a positive residual after subtracting all the divisorial terms. Example 27.10.11 computes the exact series for simultaneous poles in the fibers and attains the order of the error. The normal-crossing hypothesis provides a separated integrability test on the base; general ideal constraints on the base remain outside these results. Theorem 27.10.12 allows the divisorial data to live on a specified smooth modification of the base, provided the residual there is positive and the pulled-back selecting weight has the required lower bound and witnesses; the transformation rule for adjoint multiplier ideals keeps the Jacobian in the coefficient of the sections. Example 27.10.13 computes the resulting orders of point ideals on projective space and gives a sharp error for a base pole of positive mass in higher codimension. Which general selecting weights admit such modification data is open. In all three band criteria, corollary 27.10.14 allows a smooth semipositive residual with positive top integral. Example 27.10.15 lies outside the regime of strictly positive residuals: contracted exceptional lines obstruct every strictly positive smooth gauge, although the base reference has positive mass. There the exceptional fixed divisor makes the selected and reference spaces identical for every tensor power, which separates the local gap between orders from the global defect of sections; the positive volume of the reference remains part of the sufficient hypotheses. Proposition 27.10.16 computes this mechanism on the same family of blowups for every positive selecting coefficient, every integral fixed multiplicity of the exceptional divisor and any two anisotropic powers. A coefficient at most the fixed multiplicity leaves the whole space of sections. Above it, the selected spaces impose point jets of linearly growing order. As long as the coefficient stays below the fixed multiplicity plus the projective degree, the explicit reference has positive mass and the defect of sections is $O(m^{q-1})$. At that threshold the reference has zero mass and the sections grow with degree $q-1$; beyond it the series eventually vanishes. These exact model computations leave the general geometric criterion open. Example 27.10.18 shows that a nonzero sharp defect also occurs outside the regime of strictly positive residuals. On the blowup of projective space at two points, the residual is the sum of the pullbacks of the Fubini–Study forms under the two resolved linear projections; it has degree zero on the line through the two centers but positive top mass $2^ q-2$. Simultaneous interpolation of point jets gives the defect $2\binom {m+q-2}{q-1}$ for every tensor power. Thus a semipositive reference of positive volume does not force the local gap between orders to be absorbed by fixed divisors. Whether such conditions are necessary in general is open.

title: 33.9.1 Growing vanishing orders on curves
text: 33.9.1 Growing vanishing orders on curves Fix an integer $r\geq 1$ and, for each positive integer $m$, a nonnegative integer $q_ m$. The model of section 27.12 on $\mathbb C$ has the smooth weight $|z|^{2r}$ and the selecting ideals $(z^{q_ m})$. When $q_ m\to \infty $, the kernel vanishes in the natural rescaled limit, but it has a Gaussian transition at the larger radius $(q_ m/(rm))^{1/(2r)}$. For $q_ m=\lfloor m\lambda \rfloor $ with a real $\lambda >0$, the limiting kernel measure misses the atom at the pole of the limiting envelope current. On a compact curve with the curvature and local expansion of theorem 27.13.1 , that theorem transfers the Gaussian transition to global sections when $q_ m=o(m^{1/(2r+1)})$, and the construction with curvature boundaries in theorem 27.13.4 extends the corrected transition to every sublinear order. We record the original question; it is answered by theorem 27.13.5 together with the corrections from the weight in section 27.13.4 . Problem 33.9.3 . Let $C$ be a connected compact Riemann surface, let $x\in C$, and let $(L,h)$ be a smooth Hermitian holomorphic line bundle whose curvature is semipositive and strictly positive on $C\setminus \{ x\} $. Fix an integer $r\geq 1$. Suppose that in a local coordinate $z$ centered at $x$ and a holomorphic frame $e$ one has \[  |e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\phi },\qquad \phi (z)=|z|^{2r}+O(|z|^{2r+1}).  \] Let $\nu $ be a smooth positive volume form with local expression $a(z)\, \mathrm{d}A$ and $a(0)=1$, where $\mathrm{d}A$ is Euclidean area. For positive integers $m$, choose integers $q_ m\to \infty $ with $q_ m=o(m)$. Give \[  V_ m=H^0(C,L^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^{q_ m})  \] the norm $\| s\| ^2=\int _ C|s|_{h^ m}^2\, \mathrm{d}\nu $, where $\mathfrak m_ x$ is the ideal sheaf of $x$. Write $B_ m=\sum _ j|s_{m,j}|_{h^ m}^2$ for an orthonormal basis $(s_{m,j})$ of $V_ m$, with value zero when $V_ m=0$. Determine the growth ranges of $q_ m$ for which, for each fixed real $\tau $, every sequence of points $x_ m$ in the coordinate neighborhood satisfying \[  m|z(x_ m)|^{2r}=q_ m/r+\tau \sqrt{q_ m/r}  \] obeys \[  \frac{\pi B_ m(x_ m)}{mr^2|z(x_ m)|^{2r-2}} \longrightarrow \Phi (\tau ):=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _{-\infty }^{\tau } \mathrm{e}^{-s^2/2}\, \mathrm{d}s.  \] When this transition law fails, determine how further terms of the local weight change its center and scale. For the data of this problem, theorem 27.13.5 shows that the law holds in the optimal universal range $q_ m=o(m^{1/(r+1)})$, uniformly in the direction of observation; outside that range, a compact example obtained by a holomorphic change of coordinate violates the uncorrected law along a subsequence. For a fixed weight, the exact criterion is ( 27.102 ). In the whole range $q_ m\to \infty $, $q_ m=o(m)$, theorem 27.13.4 centers the transition on the boundary of the curvature quadrature domain and uses the normal length scale $1/(2\sqrt{m\rho })$, where $\rho $ is the density of the curvature. The first effective Taylor coefficient and the ranges of the corrections of finite order are computed in section 27.13.4 ; a flat perturbation there shows that no fixed finite Taylor jet of the weight determines the center to within the width of the transition for every sublinear sequence. This resolves the problem on compact curves as stated. In higher dimension, for ordinary point jets of growing total order on the explicit anisotropic product of section 27.15 , theorem 27.15.1 proves a Gaussian transition throughout the sublinear range of orders. The correct radial center includes the nonzero remainder terms of the weight, whereas proposition 27.15.2 gives the sharp, smaller range in which the homogeneous center can be used in this class. Theorem 27.15.3 transfers these laws through a submersion with compact connected fibers, with a pulled-back metric and a matched smooth volume; there the isolated selecting weight varies with the tensor power. Mixed or angular remainders, observation near the coordinate faces, other bases and general transfers through fiber selectors remain open directions.
