The character lattice is $\mathbb Z^3$, with semigroup generators \[  (1,0,0),\quad (0,1,0),\quad (0,0,1),\quad (-1,1,1).  \] The dual cone has primitive rays $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,1)$, $(1,1,0)$ and $(1,0,1)$. It is full-dimensional with four rays. The residue form $\Omega =\mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm dy\wedge \mathrm dz/x$ generates the canonical sheaf of this hypersurface; it equals $yz$ times the logarithmic torus form. Hence $w_0=(0,1,1)$, which pairs to one with each primitive ray. Write $d(m)=m_1+m_2+m_3$. Each semigroup generator has degree one. The logarithmic function $g$ differs by a bounded term from $\lambda $ times the maximum of the four linear forms given by those generators. Their convex hull is the section of $\sigma ^\vee $ by $d=1$, so \[  P(u_\lambda )=\{ \ell \in \sigma ^\vee :d(\ell )\geq \lambda \} .  \] Since $w_0\in \operatorname {int}\sigma ^\vee $ and $d(w_0)=2$, the character condition is $d(m)+2>\lambda $. The smallest allowed integer degree is $k=\max \{ 0,\lfloor \lambda \rfloor -1\} $. This also gives the ideal for whole holomorphic germs. Lift a germ to a convergent power series in $x,y,z,w$. On a smaller invariant neighborhood, angular Parseval and Tonelli force every nonzero character coefficient to satisfy the same test. All homogeneous terms of degree less than $k$ therefore vanish in the coordinate ring. They are multiples of the homogeneous relation $xw-yz$, and subtracting those finitely many terms leaves a lift of order at least $k$. Thus the germ belongs to $\mathfrak m_ o^ k$. Conversely, every degree-$k$ monomial is integrable by the character test, and bounded holomorphic coefficient germs preserve integrability. This proves the identity and its strict endpoint. $\square$

title: A.5 Extended measures and finite damping
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: A.5 Extended measures and finite damping Choose a resolution $\pi :Y\to X$. Two resolutions are isomorphic over the complement of a proper analytic subset of $X$, and their extended measures agree there. Since these measures do not charge pluripolar sets, the omitted analytic sets do not affect the comparison, even when the total mass is infinite. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ define A.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:space-extended-ma} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u) =\pi _*\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{Y,\pi ^*\theta }(u\circ \pi ), \end{equation} where $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{Y,\pi ^*\theta }$ is the extended measure of theorem 6.1.2 on $Y$. Theorem A.5.1 . The right-hand side of ( A.7 ) is the same for every resolution, including resolutions that modify regular points. It is a positive $\sigma $-finite Borel measure, gives zero mass to $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and to locally pluripolar sets, and may have infinite total mass; for bounded $u$ it is finite. Put $r_ n=\max (n-2,0)$. There are finite constants $C$ and, for each $q>r_ n$, $C_ q$, depending only on the fixed background data and, for $C_ q$, on $q$, such that for every nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and every $p>0$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{pu}\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u) \leq C(1+p^{-1})^{r_ n},\qquad \int _ X(1-u)^{-q}\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u) \leq C_ q.  \] The constants may be obtained on any one fixed resolution. Proof. Given two resolutions, choose a proper analytic subset $S\subset X$ containing $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and the images of both exceptional sets. Each map is an isomorphism over $X\setminus S$, and there the two measures are given by the same bounded local products, followed by truncation and exhaustion. On each resolution, the inverse image of $S$ is a proper analytic subset and has zero extended mass by theorem 6.1.2 . Hence both pushforwards give $S$ zero mass. This proves independence, including for resolutions whose exceptional sets lie over regular points. Positivity follows from positivity on $Y$. On $X\setminus S$ either resolution is a Borel isomorphism, so a countable exhaustion of $Y$ by sets of finite measure pushes forward to one on $X$; adjoining the null set $S$ proves $\sigma $-finiteness. A locally pluripolar subset of $X$ pulls back to a pluripolar set off the exceptional locus, and the exceptional locus itself has zero mass. This gives the asserted vanishing. If $u$ is bounded, its pullback is bounded on the compact manifold $Y$, and local bounded-product estimates give finite total mass. For general nonpositive $u$, apply theorem 7.6.1 on $Y$ to the smooth background $\pi ^*\theta $. Pushforward and the identity $u\circ \pi $ identify the weighted integrals exactly, and the constants come from $\pi ^*\theta $ and a Hermitian metric on $Y$. $\square$ We define convergence in capacity on $X$ as convergence in capacity of the pullbacks to a resolution, using a smooth Hermitian metric there. The local capacity comparison of section 1.8 makes the metric immaterial, and lemma 1.22.14 , applied on a common resolution, makes the choice of resolution immaterial. By theorem 7.6.1 and proper pushforward, both damped measures in the theorem depend weakly continuously on nonpositive potentials for this convergence in capacity. For nonpositive potentials $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ converging in capacity, the undamped measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u_ j)$ converge weakly if, in addition, their total masses are uniformly bounded and their masses on $\{ u_ j<-T\} $ tend to zero uniformly in $j$ as $T\to \infty $. Pullback preserves these mass and sublevel conditions. General equations on singular spaces require estimates for the degeneracy of the pulled-back background and of the density; see 33.10.1 . For the cone geometry below, a radial construction gives solutions in a prescribed logarithmic class and in the bounded class of a closed background.

title: A.6 Equations on projective cones
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
A.6 Equations on projective cones The residual construction of section 14.21 has a counterpart on a projective cone, which is a singular space. A logarithmic pole at the vertex becomes a divisor on the incidence resolution, and removing it leaves a positive residual background. The radial equation below determines both the solution and its normalization scalar. Uniqueness among bounded residuals holds because the lifted density is smooth and its positive locus is connected and dense, even though the density vanishes on the exceptional section. Let $B\subset \mathbb P^ N$ be a smooth connected, linearly nondegenerate, projectively normal variety of dimension $n-1$, where $N\geq n\geq 2$. Let $X\subset \mathbb P^{N+1}$ be its projective cone, with vertex $p=[0:\cdots :0:1]$, and let $	heta _0=\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}|_ X$ be the restriction of the Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^{N+1}$. Write the ambient homogeneous coordinates as $[Z:W]$, with $Z=(Z_0,\ldots ,Z_ N)$. The incidence resolution $\pi :Y	o X$ is a smooth $\mathbb P^1$-bundle $f:Y	o B$; its section $E=\pi ^{-1}(p)$ is contracted, and $\pi $ is an isomorphism off $E$. These cones are reduced, irreducible, compact and normal, hence unibranch, and their vertices are singular. Indeed, the homogeneous coordinate ring of $B$ is normal by projective normality. Adjoining $W$ preserves normality, and so do the degree-zero projective charts. Algebraic normality passes to the associated analytic space by the algebraic–analytic normality theorem. Smoothness and connectedness of $B$ give irreducibility. In the chart $W=1$, the ideal of the affine cone has no linear terms, by linear nondegeneracy. Its tangent space at the origin therefore has dimension $N+1>n$, so $p$ is singular. The incidence construction is the bundle of lines in $\mathcal O_ B\oplus \mathcal O_ B(-1)$ and has the stated contraction and isomorphism properties. Write \[   egin{gathered} \omega _ B=\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}|_ B,\qquad  eta =\pi ^*	heta _0,\qquad \sigma =f^*\omega _ B,\ d=\int _ B\omega _ B^{n-1},\qquad x= rac{\| Z\| ^2}{\| Z\| ^2+|W|^2}. \end{gathered}  \] The same symbol $x$ denotes its pullback to $Y$. Choose $\Psi \in C^\infty (\mathbb P^ N,\mathbb R)$ with $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi >0$ and $k\in C^\infty ([0,1])$ with $k>0$. Put $\psi =\Psi |_ B$ and define on $Y$ A.8  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-prescribed-data}  egin{gathered} s= rac{\mathrm{e}^\psi x}{1-x+\mathrm{e}^\psi x},\qquad \ell =\log (1-x+\mathrm{e}^\psi x),\qquad \sigma _\psi =f^*(\omega _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi ),\ B_\psi = eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\ell ,\qquad 
u =k(s)B_\psi ^ n,\qquad \mu =\pi _*
u ,\ I=\int _0^1 k(r)r^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d} r,\qquad M=ndI. \end{gathered} \end{equation} These data prescribe the measure $\mu $ before the equation is solved. The local form and the fiber integral below describe its degeneracy along $E$ and show that its total mass is $M$. Choose a local holomorphic lift $b(z)$ of the embedding of $B$, and write $S(z)=\sum |b_ j(z)|^2$ and $Z=t b(z)$. In these local coordinates $(z,t)$ on $Y$, \[   eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|t|^2S),\qquad \sigma =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log S.  \] On $0<x<1$ put $ho =\log (|t|^2S)$, $ho _\psi =ho +\psi $, $h(r)=\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ r)$ and $\zeta _\psi =\mathrm{d}ho _\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}ho _\psi $. Then $x=h'(ho )$, $s=h'(ho _\psi )$ and $\ell =h(ho _\psi )-h(ho )$. Differentiation gives A.9  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-radial-form} B_\psi =s\sigma _\psi +s(1-s)\zeta _\psi ,\qquad \sigma _\psi ^ n=0,\qquad \zeta _\psi ^2=0. \end{equation} Near $E$, a local potential of $B_\psi $ is $\log (1+\mathrm{e}^\psi |t|^2S)$; at $t=0$ its Hessian has rank one, in the transverse direction. At the infinity section, with $v=1/t$, a local potential is $\log (\mathrm{e}^\psi S+|v|^2)$; its tangential Hessian is $\sigma _\psi $ and its transverse coefficient is positive. These computations show that $B_\psi $ is smooth and semipositive, and positive off $E$. Since $n\geq 2$, its top power vanishes on $E$. Along a fiber, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}ho _\psi =\mathrm{d}(\arg t)/(2\pi )$ and $\mathrm{d}ho _\psi =\mathrm{d} s/[s(1-s)]$. Base components disappear after wedging with $\sigma _\psi ^{n-1}$, so ( A.9 ) gives \[  f_*
u =nI(\omega _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1}.  \] Since $\omega _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ is closed, Stokes' theorem on $B$ gives $\int _ B(\omega _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1}=d$, hence $
u (Y)=M$. Smooth measures give $E$ zero mass. Therefore $\mu (X)=M$ and $\mu (\{ p\} )=0$. Taking $\psi =0$ and $k=1$ gives $\int _ Y eta ^ n=d$.

title: A.6.1 Logarithmic poles at the vertex
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
A.6.1 Logarithmic poles at the vertex The logarithmic pole supplies the tangential positivity that $ eta $ lacks along $E$. Fix $0<a<1$ and put $\varphi =a\log x$, with value $-\infty $ at $p$. Set A.10  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-logarithmic-data}  egin{gathered}  eta _ a=(1-a) eta +a\sigma ,\qquad V=d(1-a^ n),\qquad c_ a=V/M,\ P_ a(s)=\left(a^ n+c_ an\int _0^ s k(r)r^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d} right)^{1/n},\ Q_ a'(s)= rac{P_ a(s)-a-(1-a)s}{s(1-s)},\qquad Q_ a(1)=0,\ q_ a=a\psi +(1-a)\ell +Q_ a(s),\qquad A_ a= eta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ a. \end{gathered} \end{equation} The singularities of $Q_ a'$ at $s=0$ and $s=1$ are removable. As the proof below shows, the form $ eta _ a$ is strictly positive everywhere, whereas $A_ a$ is semipositive and strictly positive off $E$. Off $E$, we may therefore view $A_ a$ as a positive form on $X\setminus \{ p\} $. Choose a relatively compact coordinate ball $O\subset X\setminus \{ p\} $ and a smooth compactly supported endomorphism $H$ of $T^{1,0}O$ that is self-adjoint and trace-free with respect to $A_ a$. For tangent vectors $v,w$ of type $(1,0)$ at the same point of $O$, define A.11  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-deformed-background} A_ H(v, ar w)=A_ a(\exp (H)v, ar w),\qquad \eta _ H=A_ H-A_ a,\qquad 	heta _ H=	heta _0+\eta _ H, \end{equation} where $\eta _ H$ is extended by zero. We call $H$ admissible if A.12  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-admissible-positivity} 	heta _ H>0,\qquad  eta _{a,H}:= eta _ a+\pi ^*\eta _ H>0. \end{equation} These are explicit open conditions on the prescribed data, and every sufficiently small $H$ satisfies them. Theorem A.6.1 . Let $H$ be admissible, and let \[  \mathcal C_{a,H}=\{ w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ H):\  \varphi -C\leq w\leq \varphi +C	ext{ for some }C<\infty \}   \] be the ordinary class of $\varphi $. There is a unique pair $(c,u)$, with $c>0$ and $u\in \mathcal C_{a,H}$ normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,	heta _ H}(u)=c\mu .  \] It is given by $c=c_ a$ and \[  u\circ \pi =\varphi \circ \pi +q_ a-K,\qquad K=\sup _ Y(\varphi \circ \pi +q_ a).  \] Every member of the class has finite extended mass. The solution has mass $V$ and is the same for every admissible $H$. For $H=0$, every member of the class has mass $V$. The solution is continuous with values in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$, is smooth off $p$, and tends uniformly to $-\infty $ at $p$. Its smooth residual $q_ a-K$ on $Y$ satisfies \[  (q_ a-K)|_ E=a\psi +Q_ a(0)-K.  \] If $\psi $ is nonconstant, this residual is not the pullback of any function on $X$. There are arbitrarily small admissible $H$ for which $	heta _ H$ is not closed. For every $w\in \mathcal C_{a,H}$ and every resolution $	au :Z	o X$, including resolutions that modify regular points, A.13  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-resolution-pushforward} 	au _*\left\langle  igl (	au ^*	heta _ H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w\circ 	au ) igr )^ nightangle =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,	heta _ H}(w), \end{equation} where $\langle \cdot angle $ denotes the non-pluripolar product on $Z$. The measure on $Z$ is finite. Thus the measure, the normalized descended solution and the scalar are independent of the resolution and of every common refinement. Proof. We first establish the divisor formula A.14  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-residual-divisor}  eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi \circ \pi )=a[E]+ eta _ a. \end{equation} Indeed, $\log x=\log |t|^2+\log S-\log (1+|t|^2S)$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |t|^2=[t=0]$. Along $E$ the kernels of $ eta $ and $\sigma $ are complementary, and $ eta >0$ off $E$. Thus $ eta _ a$ is a smooth Kähler form. Fiber integration also gives A.15  egin{equation} \label{eq:cone-logarithmic-mass} \int _ Y eta _ a^ n=nd\int _0^1[a+(1-a)x]^{n-1}(1-a)\, \mathrm{d} x=d(1-a^ n)=V. \end{equation} By ( A.10 ), $P_ a(0)=a$, $P_ a(1)=1$ and \[  P_ a'(s)= rac{c_ a k(s)s^{n-1}}{P_ a(s)^{n-1}}.  \] The numerator defining $Q_ a'$ vanishes at both ends, so $Q_ a$ is smooth. title: A.6.2 The bounded equation
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: A.6.2 The bounded equation Without a logarithmic pole, the residual background is $\beta $, which degenerates along $E$. The radial construction still gives a bounded solution, and closedness of $\beta $ gives an energy argument for its uniqueness. Put A.19 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cone-bounded-data} \begin{gathered} c_ b=\frac dM=\frac1{nI},\qquad R(s)=\left(c_ bn\int _0^1 k(sr)r^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d} r\right)^{1/n},\\ Q'(s)=\frac{R(s)-1}{1-s},\qquad Q(1)=0. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Here $R$ is smooth and positive, $R(1)=1$, and $Q$ is smooth at both endpoints. Theorem A.6.2 . For the same cone and prescribed measure, there is a unique pair $(c,u)$, with $c>0$ and $u$ a bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta _0}(u)=c\mu $. The scalar is $c_ b$. The smooth function $\ell +Q(s)$ on $Y$ is constant on $E$ and descends to a continuous function on $X$; its normalization with supremum zero is $u$. Every bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function has mass $d$. Formula ( A.13 ), with $\theta _0$ in place of $\theta _ H$, holds on every resolution and common refinement. If $\Psi =0$ and $k$ is nonconstant, or if $\psi $ is nonconstant, the solution is nonconstant. Proof. Set $P(s)=sR(s)$ with the data in ( A.19 ). Then A.20 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cone-bounded-radial-identity} P(s)^ n=c_ bn\int _0^ s k(r)r^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d} r,\qquad P(0)=0,\qquad P(1)=1. \end{equation} Smoothness and positivity of $R$ follow from its integral formula. Since $R(1)=1$, $Q$ is smooth at $s=1$, and its derivative is also smooth at zero. Put $U=\ell +Q(s)$. It is smooth on $Y$ and equals $Q(0)$ on $E$. On $0<x<1$, a local potential for $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ is $F(\rho _\psi )$, where $F(r)=h(r)+Q(h'(r))$. Differentiation gives $F'=P(s)$ and $F''=c_ bk(s)s^ n(1-s)/P(s)^{n-1}$. For $A=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$, it follows that A.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cone-solved-bounded-form} A=P(s)\sigma _\psi +\frac{c_ b k(s)}{R(s)^{n-1}}(B_\psi -s\sigma _\psi ),\qquad A^ n=c_ b\nu . \end{equation} This formula shows smoothness at zero directly. At infinity the horizontal coefficient is one and the transverse coefficient is positive. Thus $A$ is semipositive on $Y$ and strictly positive on $Y\setminus E$. By theorem A.2.1 , $U=u_0\circ \pi $ for some $u_0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _0)$. The proper surjection $\pi $ is a quotient map, so continuity of $U$ makes $u_0$ continuous. Subtracting $K_ b=\sup _ Xu_0$ gives the required solution. Let $w$ be a bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function. Its pullback $g=w\circ \pi $ is bounded and $\beta $-plurisubharmonic. Its bounded Monge–Ampère measure gives analytic sets zero mass and pushes forward to $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta _0}(w)$. Integrating the bounded expansion and using that $\beta $ is closed gives $\int _ Y(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)^ n=\int _ Y\beta ^ n=d$; this forces the scalar of any solution to be $c_ b=d/M$. The resolution identity follows from theorem A.5.1 . Now suppose that $w$ solves the equation, and put $q=U-K_ b$, $D=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ and $v=g-q$. The bounded integration-by-parts calculus of section 1.6 gives \[  0=\int _ Yv(D^ n-A^ n)=-\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}\int _ Y\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge D^ j\wedge A^{n-1-j}.  \] Each integral in the sum is nonnegative, so all of them vanish; in particular, so does the one with the smooth factor $A^{n-1}$. In the weak-gradient interpretation, strict positivity of $A$ on each relatively compact chart of $Y\setminus E$ forces $\mathrm{d} v=0$ there. Since $Y\setminus E$ is connected, $v$ is constant almost everywhere on it. The divisor $E$ has volume zero, so lemma 1.3.3 gives equality everywhere on $Y$. Surjectivity of $\pi $ and the normalization give $w=u$ on $X$. If $\Psi =0$ and the solution is constant, then $U=Q(x)$ is constant, so $Q'=0$ and $R=1$. Differentiating ( A.20 ) then gives $c_ bk=1$, so $k$ is constant. If $\psi $ is nonconstant, the restriction of $U$ to the infinity section is $\psi $, so the solution is nonconstant for every $k$. $\square$ Example A.6.3 . Without the assumption $\Psi =0$, a nonconstant $k$ does not force a nonconstant solution. Take $\Psi =\log 2$ and $k(s)=2/(2-s)^{n+1}$. Then $s=2x/(1+x)$, $\ell =\log (1+x)$ and \[  \frac{B_\psi ^ n}{\beta ^ n}=\frac{s^ n(1-s)}{x^ n(1-x)}=\frac{(2-s)^{n+1}}2.  \] Thus $\nu =\beta ^ n$. Since $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}(s/(2-s))^ n=nk(s)s^{n-1}$, one has $I=1/n$, $M=d$ and $c_ b=1$. The formulas ( A.19 ) give $R=1/(2-s)$ and $Q(s)=\log (2-s)$, hence $U=\log 2$. The normalized solution is zero, although $k$ is nonconstant.

On $0<x<1$, a local potential for $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ is $F(\rho _\psi )$, where $F(r)=h(r)+Q(h'(r))$. Differentiation gives $F'=P(s)$ and $F''=c_ bk(s)s^ n(1-s)/P(s)^{n-1}$. For $A=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$, it follows that A.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cone-solved-bounded-form} A=P(s)\sigma _\psi +\frac{c_ b k(s)}{R(s)^{n-1}}(B_\psi -s\sigma _\psi ),\qquad A^ n=c_ b\nu . \end{equation} This formula shows smoothness at zero directly. At infinity the horizontal coefficient is one and the transverse coefficient is positive. Thus $A$ is semipositive on $Y$ and strictly positive on $Y\setminus E$. By theorem A.2.1 , $U=u_0\circ \pi $ for some $u_0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _0)$. The proper surjection $\pi $ is a quotient map, so continuity of $U$ makes $u_0$ continuous. Subtracting $K_ b=\sup _ Xu_0$ gives the required solution. Let $w$ be a bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function. Its pullback $g=w\circ \pi $ is bounded and $\beta $-plurisubharmonic. Its bounded Monge–Ampère measure gives analytic sets zero mass and pushes forward to $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta _0}(w)$. Integrating the bounded expansion and using that $\beta $ is closed gives $\int _ Y(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)^ n=\int _ Y\beta ^ n=d$; this forces the scalar of any solution to be $c_ b=d/M$. The resolution identity follows from theorem A.5.1 . Now suppose that $w$ solves the equation, and put $q=U-K_ b$, $D=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ and $v=g-q$. The bounded integration-by-parts calculus of section 1.6 gives \[  0=\int _ Yv(D^ n-A^ n)=-\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}\int _ Y\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge D^ j\wedge A^{n-1-j}.  \] Each integral in the sum is nonnegative, so all of them vanish; in particular, so does the one with the smooth factor $A^{n-1}$. In the weak-gradient interpretation, strict positivity of $A$ on each relatively compact chart of $Y\setminus E$ forces $\mathrm{d} v=0$ there. Since $Y\setminus E$ is connected, $v$ is constant almost everywhere on it. The divisor $E$ has volume zero, so lemma 1.3.3 gives equality everywhere on $Y$. Surjectivity of $\pi $ and the normalization give $w=u$ on $X$. If $\Psi =0$ and the solution is constant, then $U=Q(x)$ is constant, so $Q'=0$ and $R=1$. Differentiating ( A.20 ) then gives $c_ bk=1$, so $k$ is constant. If $\psi $ is nonconstant, the restriction of $U$ to the infinity section is $\psi $, so the solution is nonconstant for every $k$. $\square$

title: Example A.6.3
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Example A.6.3 . Without the assumption $\Psi =0$, a nonconstant $k$ does not force a nonconstant solution. Take $\Psi =\log 2$ and $k(s)=2/(2-s)^{n+1}$. Then $s=2x/(1+x)$, $\ell =\log (1+x)$ and \[  \frac{B_\psi ^ n}{\beta ^ n}=\frac{s^ n(1-s)}{x^ n(1-x)}=\frac{(2-s)^{n+1}}2.  \] Thus $\nu =\beta ^ n$. Since $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}(s/(2-s))^ n=nk(s)s^{n-1}$, one has $I=1/n$, $M=d$ and $c_ b=1$. The formulas ( A.19 ) give $R=1/(2-s)$ and $Q(s)=\log (2-s)$, hence $U=\log 2$. The normalized solution is zero, although $k$ is nonconstant.

title: A.6.3 The quadric cone
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: A.6.3 The quadric cone Let $X=\{ Z_0Z_1=Z_2^2\} \subset \mathbb P^3$. Its base conic is the quadratic Veronese image of $\mathbb P^1$, so $n=d=2$. Its homogeneous coordinate ring $\mathbb C[\xi ^2,\xi \eta ,\eta ^2]$ is the invariant ring of the sign involution acting on the normal polynomial ring $\mathbb C[\xi ,\eta ]$, and is therefore normal; thus the base is projectively normal. In the chart \[  \pi (z,t)=(t,tz^2,tz),\qquad S=1+|z|^2+|z|^4,\qquad L=1+|t|^2S,  \] one has $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log L$. Differentiation gives \[  \det ((\log L)_{j\bar k})=\frac{|t|^2(SS_{z\bar z}-|S_ z|^2)}{L^3}=\frac{|t|^2(1+4|z|^2+|z|^4)}{L^3}.  \] Writing $\lambda _4$ for Euclidean volume, we obtain A.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cone-quadric-density} \frac{\beta ^2}{2}=\frac{|t|^2(1+4|z|^2+|z|^4)}{\pi ^2(1+|t|^2(1+|z|^2+|z|^4))^3}\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _4. \end{equation} The transverse vanishing order on $E=\{ t=0\} $ is exactly two. For $\Psi =0$ and $k=1/2$, one has $I=1/4$ and $M=1$, so $\mu _0=\theta _0^2/2$, extended by zero at $p$, is a probability measure. The logarithmic scalar and the solution mass are $c_ a=2(1-a^2)$ for every admissible deformation, including the nonclosed ones. This exact normalization follows from the preservation of the determinant. For $\Psi =0$ and $k(s)=1+s$, one has $I=5/6$, $M=10/3$ and $c_ b=3/5$. Put $R(x)=\sqrt{(3+2x)/5}$ and $r_0=\sqrt{3/5}$. The normalized bounded solution is A.23 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cone-quadric-bounded-solution} u(x)=-2(R(x)-r_0)+2\log \frac{1+R(x)}{1+r_0}. \end{equation} Indeed, $u'=-2/[5(1+R)]=(R-1)/(1-x)$, with a removable singularity at $x=1$. Thus $u=Q(x)-Q(0)$; it is strictly decreasing in $x$, and $u(p)=\sup _ Xu=0$. As a function of $x$ it is smooth on a neighborhood of $[0,1]$, and $x$ is the restriction of a smooth ambient function, so $u$ is the restriction of a smooth ambient function. Its prescribed measure is $\mu _1=(1+x)\theta _0^2$, of mass $10/3$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta _0}(u)=(3/5)\mu _1$, of mass two. Formula ( A.22 ) also shows how the lift of this measure vanishes along $E$. For a real parameter $\epsilon $, the function $\Psi =\epsilon |Z_0|^2/(|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2)$ is smooth on $\mathbb P^2$ and preserves $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi >0$ for sufficiently small $|\epsilon |$. Its restriction to the conic takes the values $\epsilon $ and zero at $[1:0:0]$ and $[0:1:0]$. For small nonzero $\epsilon $, the logarithmic residual is therefore nonconstant on $E$ and does not descend. Deformations supported away from $p$, including nonclosed ones, leave that residual and the full descended solution unchanged.

title: A.7 Logarithmic equations on normalized curves
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
A.7 Logarithmic equations on normalized curves On a curve the pulled-back background can be degenerate, but its total mass still determines the equation. A periodic Green function on the normalization compensates for the degeneracy. The normalization also gives direct control of descent, of the atoms at the poles and of continuity. Let $X$ be a connected compact reduced unibranch curve whose normalization is a torus: \[  \pi :E=\mathbb C/\Lambda \longrightarrow X,  \] a finite bijective holomorphic map, where $\Lambda \subset \mathbb C$ is a lattice. It is biholomorphic outside a finite set. Let $h$ be a Hermitian form on $X$ in the sense of the beginning of this appendix. In the flat coordinate $z=x+\mathrm iy$ on $E$, set \[  dA=dx\, dy,\qquad V=\int _ EdA,\qquad  eta _0=dA/V,\qquad  eta =\pi ^*h=b eta _0.  \] Here $b$ is smooth and nonnegative, positive over $X_{m reg}$, and may vanish at the other points. Put $H=\int _ E eta >0$. Every two-form on a curve is closed, and this is essential for the following construction. Lemma A.7.1 . There is a real periodic distribution $G$ with mean zero, smooth off zero, such that A.24  egin{equation} \label{eq:torus-logarithmic-green} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=\delta _0- eta _0,\qquad G(z)=\log |z|^2+	ext{a smooth function near }0. \end{equation} For $r\in L^ p(E, eta _0)$, $p>1$, its convolution satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} igl (G*(r eta _0) igr ) =\left(r-\int _ Er eta _0ight) eta _0.  \] The convolution is bounded and continuous, and it is smooth if $r$ is smooth. Proof. With the normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ fixed in the Conventions, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=(\Delta v)/(4\pi )\, dA$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=\delta _0$, as in lemma 1.16.11 . Cutting off this logarithm in a coordinate disk, with a cutoff equal to one near zero, gives a function $L$ on $E$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L=\delta _0+q eta _0$, where $q$ is smooth and $\int _ Eq eta _0=-1$ by Stokes' theorem. Let $e_\xi $ be the characters of the torus, with $-\Delta e_\xi =\lambda _\xi e_\xi $. The nonconstant characters have $\lambda _\xi >0$, growing quadratically on the dual lattice. Define the correction $S$, of mean zero, by its Fourier coefficients \[  S_\xi = rac{4\pi }{V} rac{(q+1)_\xi }{\lambda _\xi } \quad (\xi 
e 0),\qquad S_0=0,  \] where $(q+1)_\xi $ is the Fourier coefficient of $q+1$. Integration by parts shows that these coefficients decay faster than any power of $\lambda _\xi $. Hence the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=-(q+1) eta _0$. Conjugate symmetry of the coefficients makes $S$ real. Subtracting the mean of $L+S$ from $L+S$ proves ( A.24 ). In particular, $G$ belongs to $L^ r$ for every finite $r$. The convolution uses the group law and the Haar probability $ eta _0$. Write $K=G*(r eta _0)$. Testing against smooth functions and using Fubini's theorem proves its distributional equation. Smooth input gives smooth output by the same Fourier argument. For $p'=p/(p-1)$, Hölder's inequality gives \[   egin{aligned}  \| K\| _\infty & \leq \| G\| _{p'}\| r\| _ p,\  |K(z+s)-K(z)| & \leq \| r\| _ p\| G(\cdot +s)-G\| _{p'}. \end{aligned}  \] Approximating $G$ by smooth functions shows that translation is continuous in $L^{p'}$, and hence that $K$ is continuous. $\square$ Choose finitely many distinct points $q_1,\ldots ,q_ k\in E$ and weights $a_ j>0$, possibly none, with \[   egin{aligned}  A& =\sum _ j a_ j<H,&  M& =H-A,\  \Phi & =G*((H-b) eta _0),&  \Psi & =\Phi +\sum _ j a_ jG(\cdot -q_ j). \end{aligned}  \] The function $\Phi $ is smooth, and A.29  egin{equation} \label{eq:unibranch-curve-reference}  eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =M eta _0+\sum _ j a_ j\delta _{q_ j}. \end{equation} Thus $\Psi $ is a $ eta $-plurisubharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, whose logarithmic poles are exactly the points $q_ j$, with coefficients $a_ j$ measured on the normalization. The proper bijection $\pi $ is a homeomorphism, so we may define $\psi =\Psi \circ \pi ^{-1}$; its disk inequalities are proved below. The ordinary type of $\psi $ consists of the potentials $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with \[  w\leq \psi +C,\qquad \psi \leq w+C  \] for a finite constant $C$, the inequalities being understood for extended real values. Theorem A.7.2 . Let $0\leq f\in L^ p(E, eta _0)$ for some finite $p>1$, with $F=\int _ Ef eta _0>0$, and set $
u =\pi _*(f eta _0)$. Every potential in the ordinary type of $\psi $ has extended non-pluripolar mass $M$. In this type there is a unique normalized solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u , \qquad \sup _ Xu=0, \qquad c= rac{H-A}{F}>0.  \] Every member of the type that solves $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(w)=c'
u $ for some constant $c'>0$, with no regularity assumed, has $c'=c$ and differs from the normalized solution by a constant. The solution is continuous with real values off its finite pole set, and continuous at the poles as a map into $\mathbb R\cup \{ -\infty \} $ with the order topology. Its residual relative to $\psi $ extends to a continuous real function on $X$. If there are no poles, the solution itself is continuous with real values everywhere. The type and the equation do not depend on the choice of a resolution or of a common refinement. The measure $
u $ is non-pluripolar. Proof. Set $c=M/F$ and \[  v=G*((cf-M) eta _0),\qquad U=\Psi +v.  \] The lemma gives a bounded continuous $v$ and the positive current A.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:unibranch-curve-solution-current}  eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U=cf eta _0+\sum _ j a_ j\delta _{q_ j}. \end{equation} In each disk, adding a smooth local primitive of $ eta $ gives a function with positive distributional Laplacian, and hence a subharmonic representative. Continuity off the poles and the explicit logarithmic values identify this representative with $U$ as defined above. The same argument applies to $\Psi $. The supremum $S=\sup _ EU$ is finite, and we put $u=(U-S)\circ \pi ^{-1}$. Every holomorphic disk $g:\Delta 	o X$ lifts holomorphically to $\widetilde g=\pi ^{-1}\circ g$. Indeed, for a nonconstant disk the inverse image of the finite singular set is discrete, and off this set the lift is holomorphic. Since $\pi ^{-1}$ is a homeomorphism, $\widetilde g$ is continuous on the whole disk. Near an omitted point its image therefore stays in a bounded coordinate neighborhood in $E$, and the removable singularity theorem in one variable extends it holomorphically. A constant disk lifts to a constant map, and a nonconstant disk cannot have image in a finite set. Choose a smooth local primitive $\eta $ of $ eta $ near the lifted image, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta = eta $. Then $\eta \circ \widetilde g$ is a primitive of $g^*h$, and \[  u\circ g+\eta \circ \widetilde g=(U-S+\eta )\circ \widetilde g  \] is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. That the composition is subharmonic follows from decreasing smooth local regularizations and the holomorphic chain rule for the Laplacian. Any other primitive on the disk differs by a harmonic function. These are exactly the disk tests of definition A.1.1 , and the same argument shows that $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. A constant disk at a pole has the permitted restriction $\equiv -\infty $. A nonconstant lift meeting $q_ j$ with order $\ell $ gives the pole coefficient $\ell a_ j$. The homeomorphism $\pi $ gives continuity off the poles. Near a pole, the smooth logarithmic remainder of $\Psi $ and the bounded continuous function $v$ give continuity with extended values. The residual is the descent of $v-S$, including at the poles, so no difference of two infinite values is involved. The solution belongs to the stated ordinary type. For the mass and uniqueness assertions, let $w$ be any member of the type and put $W=w\circ \pi $. Pulling back along coordinate disks of the normalization shows that $W$ is $ eta $-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $. The two type inequalities make $W$ locally bounded away from $Q=\{ q_ j\} $, and at each pole they give \[  W=a_ j\log |z-q_ j|^2+O(1),  \] with value $-\infty $ at $q_ j$. The positive Radon measure $T_ W= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W$ has total mass $H$ by Stokes' theorem. Its atom at $q_ j$ has weight exactly $a_ j$. This follows from the planar atom identity of lemma 1.16.11 . Explicitly, choose a smooth local primitive $\eta $ of $ eta $ near $q_ j$, and let $m(r)$ be the circular mean of $W+\eta $ around $q_ j$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(W+\eta )=T_ W$, it satisfies \[  m'(r)= rac{2T_ W(B_ r)}r  \] for almost every $r$, by the divergence theorem and regularization. If $	au =T_ W(\{ q_ j\} )$, integration gives $m(r)/\log r^2	o 	au $, while the bounded logarithmic remainder gives the limit $a_ j$. Hence the non-pluripolar product of $W$, defined in dimension one by truncation, is \[  \langle  eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Wangle =\mathbf1_{E\setminus Q}T_ W.  \] Indeed, on each relatively compact set avoiding $Q$, a sufficiently low truncation equals $W$, and the indicator removes the poles. Its mass is $H-A=M$ for every member of the type. For ( A.30 ), removing the atoms leaves $cf eta _0$. The definition ( A.7 ) gives the asserted equation on $X$. A locally pluripolar set pulls back to a set on which some quasi-subharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, equals $-\infty $; such sets have zero flat area. Hence $
u $ is non-pluripolar. Suppose that $w$ solves the equation with a constant $c'>0$. Comparing total masses gives $c'F=M$, so $c'=c$. Since $\pi $ is a Borel homeomorphism and the atoms are fixed, $T_ W=T_ U$. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(W-U)=0$, where $W-U$ is an integrable function. Every nonconstant Fourier coefficient of $W-U$ vanishes, so the difference is constant almost everywhere. Subharmonic functions are determined by their averages over shrinking disks, so the values of $W$ and $U$ differ by the same constant everywhere, and the same holds on $X$. This includes members of the type with no regularity assumed. Finally, a resolution $ho :Y	o X$ factors through $E$ by the disk-lifting argument. The resulting proper holomorphic map $Y	o E$ has generic degree one. For smooth compact curves, the multiplicities in a fiber sum to the degree, so every fiber is a single point of multiplicity one, and the map is biholomorphic. The same holds for every common refinement, which proves the independence assertion directly. $\square$ The integrability hypothesis on $f$ refers to flat area on $E$. On $X_{m reg}$, the density of $
u $ with respect to $h$ is $(f/b)\circ \pi ^{-1}$; both measures give the finite singular set zero mass. No positive lower bound for $b$ and no bound for the density on $X$ is required.

A.7.2 A logarithmic endpoint for integrable data The hypothesis $p>1$ in theorem A.7.2 guarantees that the Green correction is bounded and continuous. For merely integrable densities, the solution can leave the ordinary type. The following family of densities locates the boundary exactly, and it also gives continuous residuals for some densities outside every $L^ p$, $p>1$. We keep the notation $X,E,h, eta , eta _0,H,\Psi ,\psi ,A,M$ of section A.7 , with $A<H$. Fix $q\in E$ and a flat coordinate $z$ centered at $q$, and put $r=|z|$ and $t=\log (1/r)$, so that $t>1$ on a small punctured disk around $q$. For $C_0>0$ and $\gamma >1$, choose a positive density $f_\gamma $, smooth away from $q$, which equals \[  f_\gamma =C_0r^{-2}t^{-\gamma }  \] on a sufficiently small punctured disk around $q$, and extend it smoothly and positively to the complement. Set \[  F_\gamma =\int _ Ef_\gamma  eta _0,\qquad c_\gamma =M/F_\gamma ,\qquad 
u _\gamma =\pi _*(f_\gamma  eta _0).  \] The local integral of $f_\gamma $ is finite exactly for $\gamma >1$. For every such $\gamma $, this density lies outside $L^ p(E, eta _0)$ for every $p>1$. Since $f_\gamma  eta _0$ is absolutely continuous on $E$, the measure $
u _\gamma $ is non-pluripolar by the pullback argument in the proof of theorem A.7.2 . Theorem A.7.4 . For this family, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u _\gamma $ with some constant $c>0$ has a solution in the ordinary type of $\psi $ if and only if $\gamma >2$. In that case $c=c_\gamma $, the normalized solution is unique in the whole type, and its residual is continuous but, on the normalization, not Hölder continuous for any positive exponent. For $1<\gamma \leq 2$, there is a solution $u_\gamma \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ of \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u_\gamma ) =c_\gamma 
u _\gamma  \] with non-pluripolar mass $M$, whose pullback to $E$ has the same multiplier ideals as $\Psi $ at every positive weight. It violates the lower inequality $\psi \leq u_\gamma +C$ of the ordinary type, and no solution with any positive constant exists in the ordinary type of $\psi $. Proof. The coefficient below differs from that in ( 28.36 ) because here $ eta _0=dA/V$. Define on the punctured coordinate disk A.34  egin{equation} \label{eq:unibranch-density-primitive} P_\gamma (t)=  egin{cases}  \displaystyle  rac{4\pi C_0}{V(\gamma -1)(\gamma -2)} t^{2-\gamma },& \gamma 
e 2,\[4pt] \displaystyle - rac{4\pi C_0}{V}\log t,& \gamma =2. \end{cases} \end{equation} Direct differentiation gives \[  P_\gamma ''(t)= rac{4\pi C_0}{V}t^{-\gamma },\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_\gamma =f_\gamma  eta _0  \] off $q$. The flux of $P_\gamma $ through the circle of radius $\mathrm{e}^{-t}$, which computes the mass of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_\gamma $ inside this circle, is \[  -	frac 12P_\gamma '(t) = rac{2\pi C_0}{V(\gamma -1)}t^{1-\gamma }\longrightarrow 0  \] as $t	o \infty $. These are the same flux and growth mechanisms as in theorem 28.13.1 , with the present normalization of area. title: A.8 Nonclosed equations on cuspidal products
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
A.8 Nonclosed equations on cuspidal products On a cuspidal curve, the pullback of a Hermitian form to the normalization degenerates at the preimage of the cusp, but adding a smooth potential turns it into a positive form. On the products below we perturb the background by a nonclosed form all of whose powers are $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. This fixes the mass of every bounded potential and gives an energy comparison, although the background is not closed. A perturbative solution near a constant-coefficient form then provides a positive solution against which every bounded solution can be compared. Fix $n\geq 2$. For $j=1,\ldots ,n$, let $E_ j=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$ with coordinate $z_ j$, and put $\kappa _ j= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$. Replace a neighborhood of a point $p\in E_1$ by the cusp with normalization $z\mapsto (z^2,z^3)$; equivalently, the holomorphic functions at the marked point are the functions on $E_1$ whose first derivative vanishes there. Denote the resulting compact curve by $C$ and its cusp by $q$. Put \[  X=C	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n,\qquad Y=E_1	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n.  \] The normalization $\pi :Y	o X$ is finite and bijective, hence a homeomorphism, and has generic degree one. The space $X$ is reduced, irreducible and unibranch, and its singular locus is $\{ q\} 	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n$. Choose a Hermitian form $h_ C$ on $C$ which near $q$ is the restriction of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(|x|^2+|y|^2)$, where $(x,y)=(z^2,z^3)$ are the coordinates of the cusp. Its pullback is $\eta =ho \kappa _1$, where $ho $ is smooth, positive off $p$, and A.38  egin{equation} \label{eq:cuspidal-reference-density} ho =4|z|^2+9|z|^4\quad \hbox{near }p. \end{equation} Write $\lambda >0$ for the average of $ho $ on $E_1$, and set \[  h_0=h_ C+\sum _{j=2}^ n\kappa _ j,\quad H_0=\pi ^*h_0=\eta +\sum _{j=2}^ n\kappa _ j,\quad K_0=\lambda \kappa _1+\sum _{j=2}^ n\kappa _ j,\quad \Omega =K_0^ n.  \] Forms on the factors are pulled back to the products without change of notation. Proposition A.8.1 . There are a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\alpha $ on $X$, mixing the factors $C$ and $E_2$, and a smooth real function $v_0$ on $Y$ such that, for every sufficiently small nonzero real $\varepsilon $, the Hermitian form $h=h_0+\varepsilon \alpha $ is not closed and \[   egin{gathered} H=\pi ^*h,\qquad k=H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0=K_0+\varepsilon \pi ^*\alpha \geq 	frac 12K_0,\ \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H^ r)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^ r)=0\quad (r\geq 0). \end{gathered}  \] Moreover $\int _ YH^ n=\int _ Yk^ n=:M>0$. Proof. Choose real smooth functions $A$ on $C$, supported away from $q$, and $B$ on $E_2$. Let \[  \alpha =\partial A\wedge  ar\partial B+ ar\partial A\wedge \partial B =\partial (A ar\partial B)+ ar\partial (A\partial B).  \] The form $\alpha $ is real and satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\alpha =0$. At a point where $\partial A=0$, $\partial  ar\partial A
e 0$ and $\partial B
e 0$, \[  \partial \alpha =-\partial A\wedge \partial  ar\partial B +\partial  ar\partial A\wedge \partial B
e 0.  \] Thus $\mathrm d\alpha 
e 0$. The form $\alpha $ vanishes near the singular locus. Its operator norm relative to $H_0$ is bounded on its support, and its norm relative to $K_0$ is bounded everywhere. Choose $|\varepsilon |$ so small that both norms, multiplied by $|\varepsilon |$, are less than $1/2$. This proves positivity of $h$ in the ambient sense, semipositivity of $H$, and the inequality $K_0+\varepsilon \pi ^*\alpha \geq 	frac 12K_0$. The equation $\partial _ z\partial _{ ar z}v=\lambda -ho $ on $E_1$, whose right-hand side has mean zero, has a smooth real periodic solution, obtained by dividing its nonzero Fourier coefficients. Its pullback $v_0$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0=(\lambda -ho )\kappa _1$, which proves the formula for $k$. The forms $H_0$ and $K_0$ are closed. Hence $\mathrm dk$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k$ come from the complex surface $E_1	imes E_2$, so that $\mathrm dk\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k=0$ for degree reasons, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}k=0$. The same identities hold for $H$. The Leibniz rule now gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^ r)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H^ r)=0$ for all $r$; this uses both torsion identities, not only pluriclosedness. Expanding $(H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0)^ n$ and integrating by parts shows that every term containing $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_0$ integrates to zero. Hence the masses agree, and positivity of $k$ makes them positive. $\square$ Fix an integer $s\geq n+3$ before making a further choice of $\varepsilon $. Use the Fourier Sobolev norm $\| w\| _{H^ t}^2=\sum _{m\in \mathbb Z^{2n}}(1+|m|^2)^ t|\widehat w(m)|^2$ on $Y$, and write $H^ t_0$ for the subspace of real functions in $H^ t$ with zero mean with respect to $\Omega $. In the remaining formulas, $\alpha $ denotes its pullback to $Y$. Theorem A.8.2 . For sufficiently small nonzero $\varepsilon $, depending on $n$, $s$ and the fixed forms, there are explicit constants $R,\delta >0$ such that every $g\in H^ s_0$ with $\| g\| _{H^ s}\leq \delta $ admits a unique $w\in H^{s+2}_0$ with $\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}\leq R$ satisfying \[  (k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n=(f_\varepsilon +g)\Omega , \qquad f_\varepsilon = rac{k^ n}{\Omega },\qquad k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 	frac 14K_0.  \] The constants may be chosen as in ( A.41 ). In particular, $w$ is of class $C^2$. Proof. Set $b_1=\lambda $ and $b_ j=1$ for $j\geq 2$. The operator \[  L_0w= rac{nK_0^{n-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\Omega } =\sum _ j b_ j^{-1}\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ j}w  \] has Fourier eigenvalues $\ell (m)=-\pi ^2\sum _ jb_ j^{-1}(m_{2j-1}^2+m_{2j}^2)$. It has an inverse $H^ s_0	o H^{s+2}_0$ of norm \[  A_0=\sup _{m
e 0} rac{1+|m|^2}{|\ell (m)|} \leq  rac{2\max _ jb_ j}{\pi ^2}.  \] Let $L_\varepsilon w=nk^{n-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w/\Omega $. It preserves zero mean because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-1})=0$. Fix $\varepsilon _0\leq 1$ within the positivity range. The finite expansion of $k^{n-1}$ gives \[  L_\varepsilon -L_0=\sum _{j=1}^{n-1}\varepsilon ^ jP_ j, \qquad P_ jw=n inom {n-1}{j}  rac{K_0^{n-1-j}\wedge \alpha ^ j\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\Omega }.  \] Choose bounds $e_ j$ for the norms $\| P_ j\| _{H^{s+2}	o H^ s}$, which are finite since multiplication by smooth coefficients is bounded on $H^ s$, and set $B=\sum _ j\varepsilon _0^{j-1}e_ j$. If $|\varepsilon |\leq \varepsilon _0$ and $|\varepsilon |A_0B\leq 1/2$, the Neumann series gives $\| L_\varepsilon ^{-1}\| \leq A:=2A_0$. The remainder is \[  Q(w)=\sum _{r=2}^ n inom nr rac{k^{n-r}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ r}{\Omega }.  \] For $s>n$, Fourier convolution and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, together with $\sum _ m(1+|m|^2)^{-s}<\infty $, make $H^ s$ an algebra. Multiplication by smooth coefficients and the finite expansion therefore give a constant $C_ Q$ such that, on the unit ball of $H^{s+2}$, \[   egin{aligned}  \| Q(w)\| _{H^ s}& \leq C_ Q\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}^2,\  \| Q(w)-Q(z)\| _{H^ s}& \leq C_ Q(\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}+\| z\| _{H^{s+2}})\| w-z\| _{H^{s+2}}. \end{aligned}  \] Each term of $Q(w)$ has zero integral against $\Omega $: for smooth $w$, its integral is $\int w\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-r})\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^{r-1}=0$, and Sobolev approximation gives the general case. The Sobolev embedding also gives a constant $D$ such that the pointwise operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ with respect to $K_0$ is at most $D\| w\| _{H^{s+2}}$. Choose A.41  egin{equation} \label{eq:cuspidal-contraction-radius} 0<R\leq \min \{ 1,(4AC_ Q)^{-1},(4D)^{-1}\} ,\qquad \delta =R/(2A). \end{equation} The equation is equivalent to $L_\varepsilon w+Q(w)=g$. The map $w\mapsto L_\varepsilon ^{-1}(g-Q(w))$ takes the closed ball of radius $R$ in $H^{s+2}_0$ into the ball of radius $3R/4$ and has Lipschitz constant at most $1/2$. Its fixed point gives existence and uniqueness in that ball. Since $k\geq K_0/2$ and the operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is at most $1/4$, the form $k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is at least $K_0/4$. The embedding $H^{s+2}\subset C^2$ follows from $s\geq n+3$. $\square$ The perturbation $g$ may depend on all torus variables. For example, writing $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$, every sufficiently small nonzero multiple of $\prod _ j\cos (2\pi x_ j)+\prod _ j\cos (2\pi y_ j)$ is an admissible perturbation with zero mean. Thus the construction does not force the solution to have separated variables. Lemma A.8.3 . Every bounded $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,k)$ satisfies $\int _ Y(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=M$. The same holds with $H$ in place of $k$. Proof. The products are the bounded products of proposition 1.7.1 . For $r\geq 1$, the bounded local recursion and Stokes' theorem on the compact manifold $Y$ give \[  \int _ Y k^{n-r}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ r =\int _ YU\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-r})\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^{r-1}=0.  \] Alternatively, one may convolve $U$ on the torus, add a fixed local positive quadratic function, and pass to the limit in the decreasing bounded expansion; every smooth integral vanishes by the same identity. Expanding the top power proves the assertion. The proof for $H$ is identical, since its powers are also $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed and its mass is $M$. $\square$ Proposition A.8.4 . Let $V$ be a solution $w$ given by theorem A.8.2 . If a bounded $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,k)$ satisfies $(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^ n$, then $U-V$ is constant. Proof. Convolve $U$, $V$ and $k$ with the same nonnegative radial kernel $\varrho _ j$ on the torus, of radius $r_ j\downarrow 0$, and write \[  U_ j=U*\varrho _ j,\quad V_ j=V*\varrho _ j,\quad k_ j=k*\varrho _ j, \quad A_ j=k_ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j,\quad B_ j=k_ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j.  \] Translations preserve positivity, so $A_ j\geq 0$ and $B_ j\geq  eta K_0$ with $ eta =1/4$. The forms $k_ j$ converge smoothly, and $V_ j$ converges in $C^2$. On lifted coordinate balls, choose a common positive quadratic function $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq k$. Convolution gives $q*\varrho _ j=q+b r_ j^2$ for a fixed $b>0$. The radial averages of the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $U+q$ and $V+q$ decrease as the radii decrease. Hence $U_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ and $V_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ decrease to $U+q$ and $V+q$; the identical constants cancel in the difference. Put $\phi _ j=U_ j-V_ j$ and $T_ j=\sum _{r=0}^{n-1}A_ j^ r\wedge B_ j^{n-1-r}$. The identities $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}k_ j=0$ and $\mathrm dk_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k_ j=0$ persist under convolution, since the torsion is still pulled back from $E_1	imes E_2$. Differentiating the monomials therefore gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ j=0$. Also $T_ j\geq B_ j^{n-1}\geq  eta ^{n-1}K_0^{n-1}$. Stokes' theorem applied to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi _ j^2)$ yields A.42  egin{equation} \label{eq:cuspidal-rough-energy} -\int _ Y\phi _ j(A_ j^ n-B_ j^ n) =\int _ Y\mathrm d\phi _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi _ j\wedge T_ j \geq  eta ^{n-1}\int _ Y\mathrm d\phi _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi _ j\wedge K_0^{n-1}. \end{equation} Only the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closedness of $T_ j$ is needed here. We treat the four terms on the left separately. Expand $A_ j^ n$ with respect to the local plurisubharmonic potential $U_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ and the smoothly converging coefficient $k_ j-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$. The weighted limit lemma 1.6.2 gives $\int U_ jA_ j^ n	o \int U(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n$. Decreasing convergence and the uniform convergence of $V_ j$ give the corresponding limit for $\int V_ jA_ j^ n$. Since $B_ j^ n$ has uniformly converging continuous densities, bounded pointwise convergence and dominated convergence give the limit of $\int U_ jB_ j^ n$. The term $\int V_ jB_ j^ n$ converges by $C^2$ convergence. A finite partition of unity gives the global statements. Since the two limiting measures are equal, the left-hand side of ( A.42 ) tends to zero. The flat Fourier Poincaré inequality now shows that the $L^2$ norm of $\phi _ j$ minus its average tends to zero. Bounded convergence gives $\phi _ j	o U-V$ in $L^2$, so $U-V$ is constant almost everywhere. Local smooth corrections and the canonical plurisubharmonic representatives extend this equality to every point. $\square$ Theorem A.8.5 . Let $f\in H^ s(Y)$ be strictly positive and set \[  
u =\pi _*(f\Omega ),\qquad c= rac{M}{\int _ Y f\Omega }.  \] If $\| cf-f_\varepsilon \| _{H^ s}\leq \delta $, there is a unique bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u .  \] The function $u$ is continuous and locally Hölder continuous of exponent $1/3$ in ambient coordinates. The measure $
u $ is non-pluripolar and gives the singular locus zero mass. On the regular locus its density with respect to $h^ n$ is $f/J$, where $J=H^ n/\Omega $; near the cusp this density is $\lambda f/ho $. The equation holds on every resolution and every common smooth refinement. Every bounded solution of an equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u')=c'
u $ with $c'>0$ has $c'=c$. Proof. The function $g=cf-f_\varepsilon $ has zero mean. Let $w$ be the solution given by theorem A.8.2 . The potential $v_0+w$ is bounded and $H$-plurisubharmonic. Descent through the resolution $\pi $ (theorem A.2.1 ) gives \[  u=(v_0+w)\circ \pi ^{-1}-\sup _ Y(v_0+w),  \] which satisfies the disk condition with the background $h$ itself. Since the normalization is a homeomorphism, $u$ is continuous. The definition of the extended measure and theorem A.5.1 give the equation. Any other bounded solution pulls back to a bounded $H$-plurisubharmonic potential. Since $\pi $ is a Borel homeomorphism, equality of the pushforward measures means equality on $Y$. Subtracting $v_0$ and applying proposition A.8.4 gives uniqueness. The mass identity of lemma A.8.3 forces the scalar of every bounded solution to be $M/
u (X)=c$. The singular locus pulls back to the divisor $\{ p\} 	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n$, which has zero smooth volume. If a set is locally pluripolar, a local plurisubharmonic function equal to $-\infty $ on it pulls back to a plurisubharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, away from that divisor; its pole set has zero smooth volume. Thus $
u $ is non-pluripolar. On the regular locus, the change of variables formula gives the density $f/J$. Near the cusp $\alpha =0$, so \[  H^ n=n!ho \, \kappa _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \kappa _ n, \qquad \Omega =n!\lambda \, \kappa _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \kappa _ n.  \] The ratio gives the density $\lambda f/ho $; the generic degree of $\pi $ and both factorials have been accounted for. For the Hölder assertion, put $d=z-z'$ and $a=z+z'$. Then \[  z^2-z'^2=da,\qquad z^3-z'^3=d(3a^2+d^2)/4.  \] If $|a|\geq |d|/4$, the first modulus is at least $|d|^2/4$, which controls $|d|^3$ on a bounded chart. Otherwise the second modulus is at least $13|d|^3/64$. Hence $|z-z'|\leq C(|z^2-z'^2|+|z^3-z'^3|)^{1/3}$. The $C^1$ regularity of $v_0+w$ in $z$ and in the other product coordinates gives the asserted ambient estimate. Every resolution $\sigma :Z	o X$ factors through $Y$: in the cusp chart, the quotient $y/x$ is bounded off the exceptional set and extends holomorphically to the smooth source, giving the normalization coordinate. Write $\sigma =\pi \circ \mu $. The map $\mu $ is a proper modification. The bounded pullback products agree off its exceptional locus, and they give this analytic set zero mass by proposition 1.7.1 . Hence their pushforwards agree on all of $Y$. This proves the equation on every resolution, and the same argument applies to further common refinements. The full potential is exactly $u\circ \sigma $, which is constant on every fiber, and surjectivity preserves all ordinary comparisons. $\square$ Existence alone holds for a larger class of data: on the normalization, the positive form $k$ places the equation in the bounded-mass regime of chapter 32 . The smallness condition above is needed for the quantitative regularity and for the positive solution used in the uniqueness comparison. Corollary A.8.6 . For the same $X$ and $h$, every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p(Y,\Omega )$, $p>1$, admits a bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)= rac{M}{\int _ Yf\Omega }\, \pi _*(f\Omega ).  \] Proof. The torus $Y$ is Kähler, so it has bounded mass by lemma 21.4.1 . Since $k>0$, zero is an ordinary model for $k$: $P_ k[0]=0$. Its lower volume is $M>0$ by lemma A.8.3 , because the potentials of the same ordinary type as zero are exactly the bounded ones. Hence theorem 32.1.1 , applied on $Y$ with background $k$ and reference zero, gives a bounded $k$-plurisubharmonic solution for the measure $f\Omega $, and its scalar is $M/\int f\Omega $. Adding $v_0$ and using theorem A.2.1 , theorem A.5.1 gives the normalized equation on $X$. The datum is non-pluripolar as in theorem A.8.5 . Neither smallness nor strict positivity of $f$ is needed for this existence statement. $\square$ The spaces $X$ contain no rational curves. Indeed, a holomorphic map $\mathbb P^1	o X$ lifts locally to $Y$ through the cusp normalization, and the local lifts glue by uniqueness. Every flat holomorphic one-form on $Y$ pulls back to zero on $\mathbb P^1$, so the lifted map has zero derivative and is constant. The results of this section depend on this explicit geometry, on the bounded ordinary type and on the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closedness of all powers of the background. Ambient Hölder regularity and uniqueness in the whole bounded class are proved only for data in the small Sobolev neighborhood above. The general problem 33.10.1 , including arbitrary pole types and backgrounds whose powers are not $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, remains open.

text: Theorem A.8.2 . The embedding $H^{s+2}\subset C^2$ follows from $s\geq n+3$. $\square$

title: Lemma A.8.3
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Lemma A.8.3 . Every bounded $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,k)$ satisfies $\int _ Y(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=M$. The same holds with $H$ in place of $k$. Proof. The products are the bounded products of proposition 1.7.1 . For $r\geq 1$, the bounded local recursion and Stokes' theorem on the compact manifold $Y$ give \[  \int _ Y k^{n-r}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ r =\int _ YU\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(k^{n-r})\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^{r-1}=0.  \] Alternatively, one may convolve $U$ on the torus, add a fixed local positive quadratic function, and pass to the limit in the decreasing bounded expansion; every smooth integral vanishes by the same identity. Expanding the top power proves the assertion. The proof for $H$ is identical, since its powers are also $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed and its mass is $M$. $\square$

title: Proposition A.8.4
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Proposition A.8.4 . Let $V$ be a solution $w$ given by theorem A.8.2 . If a bounded $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,k)$ satisfies $(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^ n$, then $U-V$ is constant. Proof. Convolve $U$, $V$ and $k$ with the same nonnegative radial kernel $\varrho _ j$ on the torus, of radius $r_ j\downarrow 0$, and write \[  U_ j=U*\varrho _ j,\quad V_ j=V*\varrho _ j,\quad k_ j=k*\varrho _ j, \quad A_ j=k_ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j,\quad B_ j=k_ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j.  \] Translations preserve positivity, so $A_ j\geq 0$ and $B_ j\geq \beta K_0$ with $\beta =1/4$. The forms $k_ j$ converge smoothly, and $V_ j$ converges in $C^2$. On lifted coordinate balls, choose a common positive quadratic function $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq k$. Convolution gives $q*\varrho _ j=q+b r_ j^2$ for a fixed $b>0$. The radial averages of the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $U+q$ and $V+q$ decrease as the radii decrease. Hence $U_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ and $V_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ decrease to $U+q$ and $V+q$; the identical constants cancel in the difference. Put $\phi _ j=U_ j-V_ j$ and $T_ j=\sum _{r=0}^{n-1}A_ j^ r\wedge B_ j^{n-1-r}$. The identities $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}k_ j=0$ and $\mathrm dk_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}k_ j=0$ persist under convolution, since the torsion is still pulled back from $E_1\times E_2$. Differentiating the monomials therefore gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ j=0$. Also $T_ j\geq B_ j^{n-1}\geq \beta ^{n-1}K_0^{n-1}$. Stokes' theorem applied to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi _ j^2)$ yields A.42 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cuspidal-rough-energy} -\int _ Y\phi _ j(A_ j^ n-B_ j^ n) =\int _ Y\mathrm d\phi _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi _ j\wedge T_ j \geq \beta ^{n-1}\int _ Y\mathrm d\phi _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi _ j\wedge K_0^{n-1}. \end{equation} Only the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closedness of $T_ j$ is needed here. We treat the four terms on the left separately. Expand $A_ j^ n$ with respect to the local plurisubharmonic potential $U_ j+b r_ j^2+q$ and the smoothly converging coefficient $k_ j-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$. The weighted limit lemma 1.6.2 gives $\int U_ jA_ j^ n\to \int U(k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n$. Decreasing convergence and the uniform convergence of $V_ j$ give the corresponding limit for $\int V_ jA_ j^ n$. Since $B_ j^ n$ has uniformly converging continuous densities, bounded pointwise convergence and dominated convergence give the limit of $\int U_ jB_ j^ n$. The term $\int V_ jB_ j^ n$ converges by $C^2$ convergence. A finite partition of unity gives the global statements. Since the two limiting measures are equal, the left-hand side of ( A.42 ) tends to zero. The flat Fourier Poincaré inequality now shows that the $L^2$ norm of $\phi _ j$ minus its average tends to zero. Bounded convergence gives $\phi _ j\to U-V$ in $L^2$, so $U-V$ is constant almost everywhere. Local smooth corrections and the canonical plurisubharmonic representatives extend this equality to every point. $\square$

title: A.42

title: Theorem A.8.5
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
Theorem A.8.5 . Let $f\in H^ s(Y)$ be strictly positive and set \[  
u =\pi _*(f\Omega ),\qquad c= rac{M}{\int _ Y f\Omega }.  \] If $\| cf-f_\varepsilon \| _{H^ s}\leq \delta $, there is a unique bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u .  \] The function $u$ is continuous and locally Hölder continuous of exponent $1/3$ in ambient coordinates. The measure $
u $ is non-pluripolar and gives the singular locus zero mass. On the regular locus its density with respect to $h^ n$ is $f/J$, where $J=H^ n/\Omega $; near the cusp this density is $\lambda f/ho $. The equation holds on every resolution and every common smooth refinement. Every bounded solution of an equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u')=c'
u $ with $c'>0$ has $c'=c$. Proof. The function $g=cf-f_\varepsilon $ has zero mean. Let $w$ be the solution given by theorem A.8.2 . The potential $v_0+w$ is bounded and $H$-plurisubharmonic. Descent through the resolution $\pi $ (theorem A.2.1 ) gives \[  u=(v_0+w)\circ \pi ^{-1}-\sup _ Y(v_0+w),  \] which satisfies the disk condition with the background $h$ itself. Since the normalization is a homeomorphism, $u$ is continuous. The definition of the extended measure and theorem A.5.1 give the equation. Any other bounded solution pulls back to a bounded $H$-plurisubharmonic potential. Since $\pi $ is a Borel homeomorphism, equality of the pushforward measures means equality on $Y$. Subtracting $v_0$ and applying proposition A.8.4 gives uniqueness. The mass identity of lemma A.8.3 forces the scalar of every bounded solution to be $M/
u (X)=c$. The singular locus pulls back to the divisor $\{ p\} 	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n$, which has zero smooth volume. If a set is locally pluripolar, a local plurisubharmonic function equal to $-\infty $ on it pulls back to a plurisubharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, away from that divisor; its pole set has zero smooth volume. Thus $
u $ is non-pluripolar. On the regular locus, the change of variables formula gives the density $f/J$. Near the cusp $\alpha =0$, so \[  H^ n=n!ho \, \kappa _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \kappa _ n, \qquad \Omega =n!\lambda \, \kappa _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \kappa _ n.  \] The ratio gives the density $\lambda f/ho $; the generic degree of $\pi $ and both factorials have been accounted for. For the Hölder assertion, put $d=z-z'$ and $a=z+z'$. Then \[  z^2-z'^2=da,\qquad z^3-z'^3=d(3a^2+d^2)/4.  \] If $|a|\geq |d|/4$, the first modulus is at least $|d|^2/4$, which controls $|d|^3$ on a bounded chart. Otherwise the second modulus is at least $13|d|^3/64$. Hence $|z-z'|\leq C(|z^2-z'^2|+|z^3-z'^3|)^{1/3}$. The $C^1$ regularity of $v_0+w$ in $z$ and in the other product coordinates gives the asserted ambient estimate. Every resolution $\sigma :Z	o X$ factors through $Y$: in the cusp chart, the quotient $y/x$ is bounded off the exceptional set and extends holomorphically to the smooth source, giving the normalization coordinate. Write $\sigma =\pi \circ \mu $. The map $\mu $ is a proper modification. The bounded pullback products agree off its exceptional locus, and they give this analytic set zero mass by proposition 1.7.1 . Hence their pushforwards agree on all of $Y$. This proves the equation on every resolution, and the same argument applies to further common refinements. The full potential is exactly $u\circ \sigma $, which is constant on every fiber, and surjectivity preserves all ordinary comparisons. $\square$

title: Corollary A.8.6
section: 8.3 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Corollary A.8.6 . For the same $X$ and $h$, every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p(Y,\Omega )$, $p>1$, admits a bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=\frac{M}{\int _ Yf\Omega }\, \pi _*(f\Omega ).  \] Proof. The torus $Y$ is Kähler, so it has bounded mass by lemma 21.4.1 . Since $k>0$, zero is an ordinary model for $k$: $P_ k[0]=0$. Its lower volume is $M>0$ by lemma A.8.3 , because the potentials of the same ordinary type as zero are exactly the bounded ones. Hence theorem 32.1.1 , applied on $Y$ with background $k$ and reference zero, gives a bounded $k$-plurisubharmonic solution for the measure $f\Omega $, and its scalar is $M/\int f\Omega $. Adding $v_0$ and using theorem A.2.1 , theorem A.5.1 gives the normalized equation on $X$. The datum is non-pluripolar as in theorem A.8.5 . Neither smallness nor strict positivity of $f$ is needed for this existence statement. $\square$
